Volume front matter

Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, carefully corrected by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscripts; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the most extensive editions completed in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following the individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and with headings at the upper margin of each page indicating the subject matter beneath; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what passages of their works, have commented upon the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of its correction, both the variety and number of reprinted works, the very convenient form of the volumes, constant and uniform throughout the course of the entire work, the modest price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been issued in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied therein in Latin translation alone.**

## In the Year of the Lord 1138: Rodulf, Abbot of Saint-Trond

[Col. 0009]

## Historical and Literary Notice

Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. VI, p. 115.

Rodulf, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Trond (Saint-Tron), in the diocese of Liège, provides an account of his own life from Book VIII of the *Chronicle of Saint-Trond* through Book XIII; from this account a few details must be extracted. He was born in the village called Monasterium, situated on the River Sambre, where there was an abbey of nuns wearing black garments. He pursued his studies at Liège until his eighteenth year; then, having become a monk at Porset near Aachen, he attained the offices of keeper, master of boys, cellarer, lesser and greater provost. Afterwards he went to the monastery of Saint-Trond, where again he taught boys; later he became dean or prior, and finally, in 1108, abbot. In 1121 he was also elected abbot of Saint Pantaleon in the diocese of Cologne, and he administered both offices, being most zealous for monastic discipline. See the *Royal Chronicle of Saint Pantaleon*, vol. I of Eccard, p. 927; Valerius Andreas, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 801; Swert, *Athenae Belgicae*, p. 665; Oudin, vol. II, p. 1010; *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, pp. 739, 958.

His works are as follows:

1. *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Trond*, of the Order of St Benedict, published by D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. VII; new edition, vol. II, p. 659.

2. A letter to Waleram, Duke of Limburg, advocate of the monastery of Saint-Trond, *On the State of That Monastery*: it appears in Aubert Miraeus’s *Codex of Pious Donations*, vol. I, p. 61 of the new edition; another appears at p. 520.

3. A letter to Stephen, Bishop of Metz, on the state of his monastery: this is Book IX of the *History of Saint-Trond*, p. 691.

4. A reply to the monastery of Saint Pantaleon, which had asked him whether it was lawful to accept anything for receiving boys. It appears in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, vol. II, p. 495, and p. 466 of the new edition.

5. *Life of Lietbert, Bishop of Cambrai.* It had been published anonymously by D’Achery, vol. IX (new edition, vol. II, p. 138); but Mabillon attributes it to our author on the authority of a manuscript codex of Anchin, where this subscription appeared: “Here ends the Life of Lord Lietbert, bishop, composed by a certain monk named Rodulf.”

6. Unpublished are various poems, which he himself mentions in Book VIII of the *History of Saint-Trond*, p. 690; and likewise Trithemius mentions, in the cited passage, a volume in seven books *Against the Simoniacs*. Mabillon found it at the monastery of Gembloux and describes its contents; but it later perished in a general conflagration of the monastery, as Martène and Durand testify in the preface to vol. IV of their *Amplissima Collectio*, p. 17. He also mentions, p. 687, *Compilations*, which were full of many divine sayings and decrees of councils, and likewise a Gradual composed by himself.

7. *Account of the Translation of St Gereon, One of the Soldiers of the Theban Legion.* It was published by Surius on 24 November, and also by Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, p. 1013.

8. *Life of Peter the Venerable*, ibid., p. 1187.

> [Note: [Col. 0009] This is by another Rodulf, a monk of Cluny. **Editor.**]

# Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Trond

Edited by D. R. Koepke, Ph.D.

(Georg Heinrich Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. X, p. 213.)

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0011A] Hardly any monastery among all those which found a celebrant of their foundation and affairs has provided more generous material for writing, or had more careful authors who, over a longer span of time, traced the vicissitudes of prosperity and adversity, than the monastery of Saint-Trond founded in Hesbaye. During seven hundred and thirty-eight years, four historians carried forward the deeds of the abbots of the monastery of Saint-Trond; and we may with good reason congratulate ourselves that in this volume of the *Monumenta Germaniae* we seem for the first time to be bringing them complete and entire into public light. For the years 628 to 1366—a great span of German history and one worthy of every remembrance—are comprehended in the twenty-one books of deeds which we here present.

[Col. 0011B] Certainly, the four writers of Saint-Trond who committed to posterity the memory both of earlier times and of their own could not all write with the same authority: they neither transmitted the more ancient material from their own recollection nor were all endowed with an equally fortunate talent for writing. Yet this is their merit: each brought to a satisfactory result, in his own place and according to his powers, what he was able to set forth. But greatest gratitude is due to the man who first set his hand to writing the affairs of Saint-Trond, and who by his example invited the others to attempt the same path which he had marked out. This man was Rodulf, Abbot of Saint-Trond, whose name was celebrated with distinguished honour among the people of his own day and who first laid the foundations of these deeds with most salutary purpose. Since, of all the writers of Saint-Trond, his name has been preserved, it is necessary to go somewhat further back in treating of him. Yet, because both he himself and the man who first took up the task of writing after him have written very fully about his youth and monastic life, his journeys, and the manner in which he administered the office of abbot, it will suffice here merely to sketch the matters which anyone can read more profitably in the author himself.

Rodulf

> [Note: [Col. 0011B] So far as I know, the first among more recent writers to mention Rodulf was Trithemius in his *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1120, where the following is read: “At about this time flourished Rodulf, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Trond on the borders of Brabant, of our order, in the diocese of Liège: a man most learned in the Scriptures in his own age, and no less venerable for the holiness of his regular life than for his literary learning. Among other works of his talent he wrote a notable volume *Against the Simoniacs*, divided into seven books; he also composed one book of a chronicle of past time, and certain other works unknown to us.” Almost the same things are read in Trithemius’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ed. Fabricius, p. 93: “Rodulf, abbot of Saint-Trond in the diocese of Liège, of the Order of the holy Father Benedict, German by nation, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through continual exercise and by no means poorly learned in secular letters, powerful in verse and prose and outstanding as a musician, no less distinguished in achievement than in learning. In both styles he wrote works not to be despised, among which are reported seven books *Against the Simoniacs*, one book of *Chronicles*, and many poems. He also composed several chants in praise of saints, with sweet and regular melody. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1125.” Thereafter historians of literature recorded Rodulf’s life, sometimes more carefully and sometimes more briefly: Possevinus, *Apparatus sacer*, II, 350; Valerius Andreas, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 707; Swert, *Athenae Belgicae*, p. 665; Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, p. 398; Gelenius, *On the Greatness of Cologne*, p. 365; Fisen, *Flowers of Liège*, p. 151; Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, V, 493; VI, 66, 124, 285; [Col. 0012C] Oudin, *Commentary on Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 1010; Dupin, *New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, IX, 183; Cave, *Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*, I, 571; Fabricius and Mansi, *Library of Writers of Medieval and Late Latin*, VI, 115; Foppens, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, II, 1082; Ceillier, *General History of Sacred Authors*, XXII, 68; *Literary History of France*, XI, 675; Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio*, IV, p. 17; *Gallia Christiana*, III, 958; Paquot, *Memoirs for the Literary History of the Low Countries*, II, 569; De Windt, *Library of Netherlandish Historians*, I, 26; *Supplement to the Art of Verifying Dates*, in the collection *New Memoirs of the Academy of Brussels*, VIII, 91.]

born of common parents at Monasterium on the Sambre, in the county of Namur, where Walloon was spoken, apparently before 1070,

> [Note: [Col. 0012C] This appears to be proved by what follows.]

was educated in every liberal art of that age at the celebrated school of Liège.

[Col. 0013A] Then, at Porset near the city of Aachen, in the time of Abbot Azelin, he professed his commitment to the monastic life in his eighteenth year, his mind having been raised to seek heavenly things by reading the lives of the saints.

> [Note: [Col. 0013D] VII, 2.]

When he had gradually advanced there to the office of provost, but had striven without success for a stricter observance of the Rule, he began to reside in other monasteries—for example, at Hersfeld after 1088,

> [Note: [Col. 0013D] In the time of Abbot Frederick, as he himself testifies in I, 5. Frederick is mentioned again in charters dated 1095 and 1099, in Wenk, *Hessian Regional History*, *Book of Charters*, vol. II, p. 51.]

and especially among the monks of Gladbach, who had adopted the stricter Cluniac norm as their guide of life. After Azelin’s death, which occurred in 1091,

> [Note: [Col. 0013D] Quix, a man most knowledgeable about the affairs of Porset, maintains in his notes, preserved in the Royal Library at Berlin, that Azelin died in this year. In the book which he wrote on the abbey of Porset, Azelin’s name does not occur even once; nor, so far as I know, has he been mentioned elsewhere.]

Rodulf decided, having left Porset, to take refuge in another harbour of religious life. He therefore went into Flanders and came as a guest to the monastery of Saint-Trond in the years

[Col. 0013B] 1099–1101.

> [Note: [Col. 0013D] The period in which Rodulf came to Saint-Trond cannot be defined more narrowly. He was received into the monastery during the rule of Abbot Theoderic, who died in April 1107, as V, 7 proves; and elsewhere, VI, 8, he testifies that, under that same Theoderic’s rule, he saw that within five or six years the monastery had been abandoned by seventeen monks. It follows that he was already living at Saint-Trond in 1101. VI, 2 proves that he attended the inauguration of the new crypt in 1102.]

Abbot Theoderic, who had perceived his happy disposition, retained him as companion and helper in order to restrain the fierceness of the monks of Saint-Trond that had arisen amid internal wars between abbots. For two years, as master of the schools, he instructed boys in the first elements of letters, and he most successfully corrected the rather barbarous chant of the monks according to Guido of Arezzo. Then, about 1103, having been elected prior, he began with the keenest zeal to reform monastic discipline into a better condition. Since Abbot Theoderic had given him free authority in this most salutary undertaking, he fought steadily against the unruly monks, corrected their habits, and repaired the half-ruined buildings of the monastery. In 1106, nearly despairing of the monks, he went into exile; but,

[Col. 0013C] recalled in that same year, he finally succeeded in 1107 in introducing Cluniac usages among the monks of Saint-Trond. How much hatred and envy he incurred through all this, he himself indicates sufficiently clearly, though suppressing his own name.

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] VI, 22.]

In other dangers also Rodulf was the most faithful helper of his abbot against Henry, Duke of Limburg, the chief advocate of the monastery, who was attempting to force upon the monks of Saint-Trond as abbot the monk Herimann. Yet far greater storms shook the monastery when, after Theoderic’s death in April 1107, a most difficult dispute arose concerning the election of a new abbot. For those who favoured Herimann obtained Henry V, king, as protector of their party, and through the king’s envoys and Count Gislebert of Duras, the advocate, Herimann was introduced into the monastery as abbot.

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] VII, 2.]

For this reason Rodulf was sent as envoy to Adalbero, Bishop of Metz, to whose lordship the abbey of Saint-Trond belonged; he joined Count Frederick’s army, together with Archbishop Frederick of Cologne and Duke Godfrey of Leuven, who were at the same time travelling to Verdun to see the king. During this expedition—which seemed to be undertaken by brigands rather than soldiers—

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] VII, 3, 4.]

he remained exposed for ten days to the utmost danger of his life and scarcely escaped the ambushes of his enemies. The hostility of his opponents then burst so violently against him that Rodulf withdrew to the safer place of the monastery of Saint Lawrence.

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] VII, 12.]

At last these disturbances returned to concord. At the council of King Henry, held at Liège in the same year, Herimann resigned the office he had usurped; Rodulf was elected abbot on 30 January 1108 and consecrated on 23 February.

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] VII, 15–16; VIII, 1.]

He was at last delivered from graver dangers by the death of Herimann, who in 1114 departed this life, not without great advantage to the monastery.

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] X, 12.]

But the abbot soon fell into new calamities. War broke out between Duke Godfrey of Leuven and Count Gislebert of Duras; in that same year, 1114, the monastery, scarcely yet restored, was also scorched in the fire which consumed the town of Saint-Trond.

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] X, 14–15.]

Having scarcely emerged from these waves of war, he was thrown back again into the deep sea. In the disturbances arising over the bishopric of Liège, Rodulf supported Bishop Frederick, who had been canonically elected, against Alexander, whom the emperor had confirmed. In 1121 he preferred to go into exile rather than communicate with that excommunicated man and his friends.

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] XI, 11, 13, 14.]

He first stayed at Saint Peter’s in Ghent; then he went to Cologne to attend the synod of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, at which Alexander promised that he wished to withdraw from the bishopric of Liège. A little later, on 6 September 1121, Rodulf was elected abbot by the monks of Saint Pantaleon and governed their monastery with great credit until 1123.

> [Note: [Col. 0014D] XI, 16–18. Cf. Letter 50, on the discovery of the Theban saints, and the *Chronicle of Saint Pantaleon* in Eccard, *Corpus of Medieval Writers*, I, p. 927.]

At that time he was present as a witness at the excavation of the relics of the Theban saints, some of which he sent to Saint-Trond.

[Col. 0015A] Finally, in June 1123, he returned to his monks at Saint-Trond, when, through the election of Bishop Adalbero, affairs at Liège had at last been pacified and restored to their former condition. But the state of domestic affairs offered a truly dreadful sight. During Rodulf’s exile, Gislebert, the advocate, had again plundered the monastery as if it were his own estate.

> [Note: [Col. 0015C] XII, 1.]

Beset by all these miseries, the abbot began to turn over in his mind another plan: to travel to Rome and seek consolation there. Thus, as companion of Alexander, formerly his enemy, who was going to seek absolution for his sins, Rodulf set out for Rome through Tuscany in 1126—not without fresh perils both of travel and of brigands. But when he found Roman affairs far otherwise than he had expected, he returned home in the following year, broken by bodily illness.

> [Note: [Col. 0015C] XII, 2–3.]

Nevertheless, in 1128 he again visited the thresholds of the apostles with the same Alexander, who had been summoned to Rome to expiate the simony by which he was accused of having obtained the bishopric in that very year after Adalbero’s death.

> [Note: [Col. 0015C] XII, 5–6.]

Yet in 1129 he seemed to have returned safely to his homeland only in order to be swept away by new storms. In that year the people of Saint-Trond were oppressed by a most cruel war, waged by Duke Godfrey of Leuven, whose duchy had been bestowed by the emperor on Waleram of Limburg, and by Count Gislebert, from whom the advocacy had been taken away on account of the countless injuries through which he did not cease to harass Saint-Trond.

> [Note: [Col. 0015C] XII, 7–8.]

When war broke out in 1135 between these very allies, Rodulf and his community suffered evils no less severe.

> [Note: [Col. 0015C] XII, 14.]

But after a long course of misfortunes he was delivered from all these miseries by death. In 1132 he had been so struck by paralysis that he could not walk without great effort.

> [Note: [Col. 0015C] XII, 9–10.]

After thirty years, during which in the office of abbot he had devoted all his zeal and all the powers of his soul to bringing the monastery of Saint-Trond into a better condition, he died on 6 March 1138.

> [Note: [Col. 0015D] Rodulf is also mentioned in several charters: in 1119, in a charter recording the division of rights between the monks of Saint-Trond living at Dunk and the parish priest, effected by Rodulf himself, in Miraeus, I, p. 520; then in 1131, in Bishop Andrew of Utrecht’s confirmation, granted to the monks of Saint-Trond, of the church of Aalburg, ibid., IV, p. 364; and finally in 1136, in Bishop Stephen of Metz’s confirmation of the monastery of Averbode, effected with Rodulf’s consent, ibid., I, p. 102.]

How successfully this was accomplished amid the gravest storms is proved by the catalogue of places and revenues which he partly recovered for Saint-Trond and partly acquired anew.

> [Note: [Col. 0015D] Cf. Rodulf’s letter to Stephen, Bishop of Metz, in Book IX, and X, 2.]

How much strength and time he spent in repairing and improving the buildings of the monastery, and how he brought that ruined, desolate monastery to completion, is attested for us by Rodulf’s continuator.

> [Note: [Col. 0015D] IX, 29–30; X, 13, 16–18; XII, 10.]

The great effort which he devoted to correcting monastic discipline also so elevated the monastery’s good repute among all people that the number of monks, scarcely seventeen or eighteen before Rodulf, exceeded twice that number in his time.

> [Note: [Col. 0015D] IX, 30.]

Through all this the monastery was raised to such a height of glory and prosperity that in later times it seemed capable only of declining. But as Rodulf served his own age by deeds, so he served posterity by writings.

Foremost among the books he composed are the *Deeds of His Predecessors, the Abbots of Saint-Trond*. He committed them to writing in order to preserve matters which had almost been obliterated by the negligence of his predecessors, and especially to admonish posterity that, avoiding their predecessors’ indolence, they should create written memorials of their own deeds. This admonition was all the more necessary because, apart from those who had undertaken to transmit the *Life of St Trond*,

> [Note: [Col. 0015D] The first man who resolved to transmit to posterity the life of St Trond, about a hundred years after the saint’s death, was the priest Donatus. His little work is read in Mabillon, *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century II, p. 1069, and in Ghesquier, *Acts of the Saints of Belgium*, V. [Col. 0016C] After him, a monk of Saint-Trond named Guicard undertook to write the life of the patron saint in the eleventh century. His book is obscured by I know not what darkness; but Theoderic, abbot, the third writer of the *Life of St Trond*, mentioned it in his book as follows: “Long before, Donatus [Col. 0016D] the deacon, and afterwards Guicard—both skilled in each language, even to the point of acting as interpreters—committed him [St Trond] to Latin.” Cf. Surius, *Acts of the Saints*, VI, p. 544. On Theoderic’s *Life of St Trond*, see Sigebert, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 171. The same Theoderic also wrote a sermon on the translation of Saints Trond and Eucherius, ibid., p. 566, which, however, is of no importance. Finally, there are Stepelin’s two books of *Miracles of St Trond*, composed before 1055; for they are dedicated to Abbot Guntram, in whose final years the tomb of St Trond began to be celebrated for miracles. They are read in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, century VI, part 2. In more recent times Gerard Moringus at Leuven in 1540, and Molanus in the *Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium*, devoted their efforts to the life of St Trond. Besides the foregoing works, they had at their disposal another little book, called the *Information of Lord Trond, Prior of the Place*. A book of this subject has not come to my knowledge.]

it had occurred to absolutely no one to set his hand to writing the history of Saint-Trond. The sources, therefore, from which the memory of earlier times could be drawn had almost all run dry. For virtually no memory had been preserved concerning what preceded the time of the first Adelard,

[Col. 0016C] that is, the year 999; nor did a fuller stream of history flow before the time of Adelard II, who governed the monastery from 1055.

If now you examine a little more carefully those thirteen books of the *Deeds* which the first editor, D’Achery, attributed to Rodulf alone, you will scarcely fail to notice that all of them could by no means have been written by one and the same author. Rather, another author followed closely in Rodulf’s footsteps. For

[Col. 0017A] Rodulf continued the affairs of Saint-Trond from Abbot Grimo through his own election in 1108, as is evident from the words which he added near the end of Book VII:

> “For there is not yet peace concerning Herimann; a grave disturbance concerning him remains still to be told. We reserve it for writing by him who, after Lord Theoderic, shall undertake to write the deeds of this abbot; and, if he proves a faithful and diligent reporter, he will insert into the deeds of this abbot what Herimann did to him and what end he finally met.”

Nor did he afterwards change his plan; rather, another received the pen laid down by Rodulf and, in the following six books—through the thirteenth—brought the history of Saint-Trond down to about 1136.

> [Note: [Col. 0017D] This was also perceived by the authors of *Histoire littéraire de la France*, XI, p. 675.]

For although Rodulf’s first continuator used almost the same method of writing

[Col. 0017B] and joined his narrative very closely to the earlier one, no one can doubt that Rodulf did not write these things, but rather the continuator did. To make this all the clearer, I shall add several passages which will confirm that conclusion beyond any doubt. In VIII, 17 the continuator has these words:

> “But what followed thereafter, until he [Rodulf] entered the abbacy, and how he entered it, I think has sufficiently been set forth by the writer of the preceding history; whoever desires to know these matters carefully should have recourse to him.”

In X, 10 he writes that he wishes to add certain supplements to Rodulf’s letter to Stephen, Bishop of Metz:

> “It is necessary,” he says, “that from this point we return to the earlier order of the narrative, so that, if Rodulf perhaps omitted anything or stated it too obscurely because too briefly, our narrative may restore and elucidate it.”

In XI, 2 Rodulf is “the lord abbot”; in XII, 9, in describing his illness, Rodulf is called “our head”; finally, in XII, 10 the author made him a witness of his narrative with the words, “as he himself

[Col. 0017C] used to recount.” To these arguments, which cannot be overthrown, there is scarcely any need to add that Rodulf himself speaks of his abbacy only with his name suppressed.

> [Note: [Col. 0017D] In Book VII.]

The continuator did not do this: he says that Rodulf was a handsome and well-educated young man and elsewhere that he was finely proportioned in person.

> [Note: [Col. 0017D] VIII, 4; IX, 17.]

No one, surely, will readily believe that such things could have been written by a man so modest. Finally, the second continuator indicated clearly enough in his preface that the earlier period had not been described by one author alone, in these words:

> “Since the tribulations of our church … deserved to be illumined by the pen of certain wise men,” etc.

Nor does it seem that these points can be shaken because in one or two places the continuator attempted in some fashion to write in Rodulf’s own person. He did so, for example, in VIII, 15, where these words are read:

> “Of these matters”—that is, the disturbances between Theoderic and Herimann—“we have touched on some part above.”

Yet Rodulf, not the continuator, described these disturbances. Elsewhere, concerning the same disputes between the abbots which he did not discuss, the continuator says: “which we have mentioned above.”

> [Note: [Col. 0017D] X, 5.]

For the composition of this work, which is contained in seven books, Abbot Rodulf set his hand to it after enduring many grave miseries. [Note: [Col. 0017D] I, 8. “But we who still survive, just as we have seen the scourges of God’s wrath and indignation begin upon our place, so we too groan daily in the most grievous anxiety that they have not yet ceased.” Compare with this III, 1, and the preface.] And, as far as I can see, he composed his book in a single continuous effort at the end of the year 1114 or in 1115. The arguments which seem to persuade me of this are confirmed by Rodulf in his last words cited above: he states that the usurper Herimann died most recently [Col. 0018B], an event which we read occurred in 1114. [Note: [Col. 0017D] X, 12.] Elsewhere, when about to relate the first burning of the monastery in 1086, he looked forward to another fire—and, unless I am mistaken, to that fire which consumed the town of Saint Trond on 19 July 1114—in these words: “Accordingly, we ourselves sometimes remember, and later have seen in our own time, not only that our town was utterly consumed by fire, but also,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0017D] This is related at greatest length in X, 14.] In one place he mentioned the monastery as restored anew in his own time, [Note: [Col. 0017D] III, 12; where it is apparent that by *ecclesia* he means not the building but the whole monastery.] yet, since he passed over in silence the church whose repair was begun with the utmost effort in 1115, [Note: [Col. 0018D] This is proved by X, 16, where *monasterium* is the same as our *Münster*. Add that Rodulf himself, in the letter to Stephen, bishop of Metz, which he wrote in 1136 as a kind of supplement to the *Gesta*, mentioned the church’s reconsecration in 1117 by Obbert, bishop of Liège, IX, 29.] we infer that the author did not continue writing beyond this year. Yet he did not publish the book at that same time; rather, he preferred to hand it down to posterity as a testament, as his words in the preface prove: [Note: [Col. 0018D] “While I was still placed in the flesh in which you now are agonizing.”]

[Col. 0018C] The sources from which the narrative could be drawn did not flow very generously. Rather, because of internal disturbances that were scarcely ever quieted, they were interrupted and extremely scanty; and Rodulf rightly laments vehemently now the negligence of former men, now conditions unfavourable to letters. [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, 2, 4; III, 10.] The books and documents which he could enlist for assistance were very few. He did indeed mention the monastery archive, but he declares that he was never able to find there what he sought; nor does the library seem to have provided better resources. [Note: [Col. 0018D] Preface; III, 11.] Among books he cited either Donatus’s or Theoderic’s *Life of Saint Trudo*, the *Life of Saint Remaclus*, and a certain codex in which, among other things, were read the names of ancient abbots down to Adelard II [Col. 0018D]; beside the later names there had been entered figures for the years of their reign and of Christ’s birth. These very slender notices, as he found them in the little book, he copied into the preface. [Col. 0019A] From another book he added a catalogue of Saint Trudo’s treasury, drawn up in 870 by envoys of Adventius, bishop of Metz. [Note: [Col. 0019C] I, 3.]

All the rest he derived from what he had learned through the truthful accounts of older brethren and eyewitnesses, or had himself seen with his own eyes over a long period, first as prior and then as abbot of the Trudonenses. In the preface he plainly indicated these authorities in the following words: “But I have learned the rest from the report of faithful men who saw these things, or of those who saw them; and those things which were done in my presence, or while I was already a young man, I shall commit, at least in part, to a memory indeed most faithful.” And a little later: “From the second Adelard down to myself, whatever I recount I either saw myself or could have seen; and what I did not see I learned from the account of those who saw it.”

[Col. 0019B] He followed the accounts of the ancients especially in the first book, which contains the history of the three abbots Adelard I, Guntram, and Adelard II, for the years 999–1082. [Note: [Col. 0019C] He himself gives examples in the preface of how he sought the monastery’s earlier history from senior brethren: “Nor was there anyone among the older brethren who said that he had ever found this anywhere by reading, or had ever learned it by hearing, as I was seeking to know.” This should be connected with what is related of Stepelin in VIII, 8, who was an authority for him on ancient matters.] But he could reap a much more abundant harvest for narration in describing the period between the death of Adelard II and that of Theoderic. In the remaining six books he handed down to posterity the history of those twenty-five years from matters which he had either heard from eyewitnesses [Note: [Col. 0019C] These are the passages in which he referred to the accounts of other witnesses: Preface: “What I learned by the account of faithful men I shall briefly relate.” I, 1, concerning Adelard I, who died in 1034: “Accordingly, even to the present [Col. 0019D] day such a memorial account about him is customarily related by many.” In the same place, concerning the same man: “they say,” and “I heard it related.” I, 3: “we learned that it happened”; in the same place, concerning Guntram: “we heard.” III, 3: “we heard,” concerning Abbot Lanzo, besieged in a tower in 1085 by the supporters of Liupo. III, 8: “it is said,” concerning Henry, bishop of Liège, when he saw Trudo’s town burned; he later heard of the city’s most unhappy disaster from certain monks who remained with us long afterwards—for example, the above-mentioned Stepelin, who lived in the monastery for a long time and had likewise been present as a witness of these events. IV, 4: “we heard,” concerning the fraud suffered by the monastery in 1088. IV, 11: concerning Liupo’s journey to the emperor in Lombardy in 1091, “as I learned from many.” V, 2: concerning the monastery’s poverty after Liupo’s death, “I heard several recount with their own mouths.” V, 6: “the brethren say.” VI, 5: he described the misery which oppressed the monastery in the early period of Theoderic, about 1101, “according to what we heard and for the greater part I myself saw.” VII, [Col. 0020C] 2: concerning the younger Herimann, he has one witness who was with him when he again broke into the monastery.] or had himself seen. [Note: [Col. 0020C] From the beginning of book VI onward Rodulf related what follows from his own knowledge, as the exact description of events proves and his own words attest. VI, 11: he himself saw with his eyes the great joy with which Abbot Theoderic was received in 1106 when he returned from exile. VI, 19: he worked with all his strength to establish peace between Henry, duke of Limburg, and Abbot Theoderic. He committed all the rest to writing as an eyewitness; compare VII, 3, 13.]

With such resources to aid him, he assuredly discharged the office of historian—writing what occurred truthfully and sincerely—in such a manner that one cannot deny him the praise of having performed his task well. For, so far as I know, he erred very rarely. [Note: [Col. 0020D] I, 6. He seems to have confused Empress Gisela with Saint Cunigunda, and in several other places, unless I am mistaken, he made mistakes in calculating years; for example II, 13; VI, 25.] Moreover, he aptly described in the following words the very clear ideal he formed for himself of the historian’s office: [Note: [Col. 0020D] IV, 11.] “Let no one attack me; let no one disparage me, if truth itself compels me to speak the truth; … it is the historian’s duty not to depart from the path of truth through flattery, affection [Col. 0020A], hatred, or fear. I shall therefore write, God being my witness, as I learned from many, and as I was able more truthfully to inquire from the brethren also who were among us at that time and who afterwards spoke these matters to me face to face.”

Nor did he neglect the critical discernment without which one who wishes to commit past events to memory can hardly do; rather, in examining individual witnesses’ accounts he shows himself a careful and prudent man, openly indicating in more than one place what seemed less worthy of belief. [Note: [Col. 0020D] Preface: “For concerning the other matters mentioned above I received nothing which I dare put forward with assured confidence.” I, 1: “But from what cause this happened especially, I did not learn through a fully reliable account.” I, 4: “We learned no more.” I, 5: “In what order, we did not learn.” In the same place: “But how he went from there to Hersfeld we do not know; yet we learned that he went from there.” I, 12: “Whether this was done by true or false suggestions of men, no one knows better than the Lord God,” etc. IV, 2: “Concerning the elder Herimann we learned nothing which seems worthy of memory.”] It is true, however, that he judged it preferable to pass certain things over in silence, declaring that he did so from regard for the dignity of his order. [Note: [Col. 0020D] Preface; IV, 11.]

Nor are deeper ideas absent from his narrative of events; he laid them, as it were, as a foundation beneath the entire narrative. Chief among these was a view which he repeatedly expressed in many passages: [Col. 0020B] [Note: [Col. 0020D] II, 1, 4, 8, 19; III, 2, 7, 9.] all the disasters inflicted upon the Trudonenses were punishments exacted by a just God because, in prosperity, they had allowed themselves to be swept away by the luxury and pride of seeking empty little glory. In judging political and ecclesiastical matters, it is scarcely surprising that the author took the side of the Roman pontiff, if one considers that he had been educated in the period when Gregory VII had begun to claim freedom for the papacy from imperial control. Thus he plainly declares that, in ecclesiastical affairs, greater obedience is owed to the Roman pontiff than to the emperor. [Note: [Col. 0020D] III, 2.]

If one now asks how he arranged so vast a mass both of events and of reflections, one can scarcely deny that he entered upon the one path by which one could proceed in writing matters so intricate and so disturbed. He himself described that path in these words at the beginning of book VI: “When we have related the various changes of abbots after the death of Abbot Adelard II, [Col. 0021A] we have by no means been able to preserve a fixed sequence of years because of their violence and the frequent expulsions and returns of the several persons. For, where no lawful order of succeeding abbots was maintained … an exact number of years for each could not easily be observed—especially since, even if it could have been, amid the habitual negligence always prevailing among us there was no one to devote effort to it.” Rightly and well: had the author enclosed all these matters in annals, he would have interrupted the abundant stream of the narrative at great cost to clarity.

Yet a man equipped with every resource of learning could scarcely satisfy himself merely by composing this single work of the *Gesta*. There survive many examples of his learning and diligence which must here be enumerated; some of them we shall append to this *Gesta*. In the first [Col. 0021B] place should be reckoned Rodulf’s letters, which contain, in part, supplements to the *Gesta* that are by no means negligible. Outstanding among these are the letter to Stephen, bishop of Metz, written in 1136; we owe its preservation to the first continuator, who prudently inserted it into the *Gesta* itself as, so to speak, its ninth book. Rodulf’s chief purpose was to enumerate the estates of the monastery which he had either newly acquired or wrested from unjust possessors. He had resolved to complete this inventory of property in due course, should new holdings be acquired; and for this reason he had commended to the bishop of Metz the task of preserving intact, by his authority, this condition of Trudo’s possessions. All this he drew from the Trudo archive. [Note: [Col. 0021C] IX, 22, 24.]

To the same [Col. 0021C] Stephen he wrote another letter, which may likewise be considered a supplement to the *Gesta*, concerning the injuries and vexations by which Count Otto of Duras, son of the advocate Giselbert, had long oppressed the monastery of Saint Trudo. Furthermore, in a letter to the Trudonenses written in 1122, he composed a very full narrative concerning the discovery of the relics of the holy Thebans and the period during which he lived among the monks of Saint Pantaleon. [Note: [Col. 0021C] Surius first published the *Acts of the Translation* in his *Lives of the Saints*; after him Martène and Durand published it from the Trudo codex in *Collectio amplissima*, VI, 1014.] A fourth and fuller letter is added: it contains a treatise addressed to these same monks of Saint Pantaleon, who had sought Rodulf’s advice concerning a certain rich man who had entrusted to them his son to be raised as a monk, while retaining his inheritance under the pretext of avoiding simony. The letter was written after 1123. [Note: [Col. 0021C] Mabillon published it together with Sibert’s letter to Rodulf in *Analecta vetera*, p. 465.]

A fifth letter, brief indeed, was sent between 1119 and 1138 to Duke Waleran concerning the rights of the advocate of Saint Trudo. Certain other works which he composed have either perished or perhaps await a fortunate discoverer. The first continuator attests that Rodulf himself compiled a catalogue of all his works; we regret that it was not copied by that continuator. [Note: [Col. 0021D] VIII, 15. There exists a volume of his shorter works, in the preface to which is found what he wrote, what he composed in song, and why and when.] The most important among them seems to have been a work in seven books against the Simoniacs, concerning which we read as follows: [Note: [Col. 0021D] At the time of Mabillon, a codex of this book was preserved in the monastery of Gembloux, but afterwards was apparently destroyed, an irreparable loss. Its subject may be inferred from Mabillon’s note in *Analecta vetera*, p. 465, for he had inspected the codex; it may properly be repeated here: “I found that volume, as also the two preceding letters, in the library of Gembloux, under this opening: ‘Rudolf, by the grace of God and of Saint Trudo what he is, sends greetings to his Liebert. I know that before the book I have been carried too fussily now here, now there,’ etc.” Then begins the preface: “Recently, brother Liebert, I wrote for you a little book which I had entitled *The Labyrinth of the First Simon*,” etc. In the first book he shows that simony is the first [Col. 0022C] and greatest heresy. In the second, he laments that at that time there was nothing, great or small, in the house of God which was not in some manner for sale. In the third, beginning from the rural districts—that is, from the priests of villages—he advances to the rulers and [Col. 0022D] authorities of churches, showing how clerics are customarily made and churches received. In the fourth, he passes from the countryside to the cities, treating the sale of prebends and every office in the Church. In the fifth, he raises against himself the objection that, while speaking of monks, he conceals their simonies. In the last two he clears himself of the objections themselves. Mabillon notes later that the same codex perished in a fire, *Annals*, VI, 125. Another codex was preserved in the monastery of Villers, according to Sander, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, I, 271.] “There exists also another volume of his, in seven books, which he wrote against the Simoniacs: four books arguing by reason, three by authorities.” [Col. 0022B]

He himself preserved a small fragment of it in the little work addressed to the monks of Saint Pantaleon, as is evident from the following words, which may properly be repeated here: “When, in order to prove these things”—that is, the arguments against the Simoniacs—“we once sported through the fields of the Holy Scriptures, we sprinkled our tracks with this ball, beset with many and varied flowers of authorities. There are volumes through which I am now too weary to run again in writing; yet, because of love for you, I should like to collect a few things.” No one will readily doubt that the author refers to the work praised above, which evidently had been published by him before 1123.

In the first year that he lived among the Trudonenses, at the command of Abbot Theoderic he composed a collection of canons, which the first continuator calls “most useful compilations, full of very many divine [Col. 0022C] sayings and of many decrees of councils.” [Note: [Col. 0022D] VII, 4. Compare Lebeuf, *Dissertations sur l’histoire de Paris*, II, 130.] To Alexander of Liège he sent, apparently in 1119, a letter concerning Alexander’s unjust seizure of the bishopric and canonical election; so far as I know, it has not survived. [Note: [Col. 0022D] XI, 6.] In addition, he composed two poems concerning the fire which consumed the town of Saint Trudo in 1114; by attacking Duke Godfrey of Leuven very sharply, he incurred his hatred. [Note: [Col. 0022D] X, 14.] He also wrote another poem on the Eucharist. [Note: [Col. 0022D] Only four verses of it survive, printed from Gropper, who first published them, in *Histoire littéraire de la France*, XI, 686. Bethmann observed in *Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, VII, 398, n. 47, that the *Life of Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai*, who died in 1076, is falsely attributed to Rodulf—a view first advanced by Mabillon in *Analecta vetera*, p. 465, and in the *Annals*, V, 102, and subsequently repeated by others. Nor can the *Life of Peter the Venerable*, abbot of Cluny, be assigned to our Rodulf, since this seems to be merely Fabricius’s conjecture in *Bibliotheca scriptorum medii Latinitatis*.]

Finally, he composed ecclesiastical chants and hymns, and wrote a gradual for regulating the rather unpolished chant of the monks. [Col. 0023A] [Note: [Col. 0023D] VIII, 5. See also the account of Rodulf’s death.] It is easy to infer that a man so devoted to writing books accumulated a great store of learning by reading other writers. Yet he adorned his books with sayings of the ancients less than others did; I have found only one passage from Horace. [Note: [Col. 0023D] IX, 30. I do not know who the natural philosopher is whose words he cites in the preface.] He more frequently cited the Fathers of the Church—Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and Benedict [Note: [Col. 0023D] All in the letter to the monks of Saint Pantaleon.]—as well as the canons, in writing and reading which he seems to have devoted the greatest effort, [Note: [Col. 0023D] II, 10, 11.] and the lives of Saints Maurus, Lucy, Lawrence, and Cecilia. [Note: [Col. 0023D] Letter to the monks of Saint Pantaleon.] So much concerning Rodulf.

Only a few things can be said concerning the first continuator of the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Trudo*. For not even the name of this monk of Saint Trudo [Note: [Col. 0023D] That he was such is evident in itself, and he himself indicated it, for example VIII, 5, 7, 11, and elsewhere.] has been handed down to posterity; but he left the best memorial of himself in the continuation, in which one finds him a historian scarcely inferior to Rodulf. He carried the [Col. 0023B] *Deeds of the Abbots* down to the year 1136, [Note: [Col. 0023D] XII, 15.] and he seems to have composed them not very long afterwards, between 1136 and 1138. Unless I am mistaken, this was done before Rodulf’s death on 6 March 1138. For the author would certainly not have passed in silence the final fate of a man whom he adorned with every praise, had it already happened at the time when he was to conclude his book. He expressly indicates that he had exhausted what he was to hand down, that no material for writing remained, and that he had reread what he had written earlier. [Note: [Col. 0023D] XIII, 2, 3.]

This agrees with the older codex of the *Gesta*, in which the brief narrative of Rodulf’s death is absent, though it is found in another Brussels codex. It therefore seems to have been added later, and, as far as I can see, by the second continuator, who appears to have referred to it in these opening [Col. 0023C] words: “Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138—after the death, as we have said before, on the day before the Nones of March, of Abbot Rodulf,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0023D] I, 1.] Thus the first continuation of the *Gesta* was written while Abbot Rodulf was still alive. [Note: [Col. 0024D] A single passage, VIII, 10, does not seem to stand in the way, from which one might perhaps infer that the continuation was written after Rodulf’s death; for it says that certain evil monastic practices had been restrained “throughout the whole period of his life.” Yet, in my view, those words need not be interpreted only in such a way that Rodulf’s life must be thought already past.]

Indeed, the author seems already to have been among the monks during Rodulf’s priorate, for the character of monastic life at that time could scarcely have been described so accurately by anyone other than an eyewitness. [Note: [Col. 0024D] VIII, 9, 10; X, 4. He was an eyewitness of the disturbances which arose after the death of Obbert of Liège in 1119: “Thus we saw, thus we heard, thus we write,” he says of them. XIII, 9: he says “we saw” concerning Rodulf’s time.] And, unless I am mistaken, he was one of Rodulf’s most faithful friends. He carefully recounts who in particular were the men who enjoyed the abbot’s intimacy, [Note: [Col. 0024D] VIII, 18. “And to such an extent—behold, I shall relate most faithfully a thing which I know with absolute certainty! before God, because I do not lie—that no brother could be so closely familiar with him, both carnally and spiritually,” etc.] and beyond doubt, in matters which [Col. 0024A] he had not himself seen, he had Rodulf as his witness. [Note: [Col. 0024D] VIII, 2 ff., in narrating Rodulf’s youth; for example XIII, 8, he has senior brethren as witnesses.] In one place he described at greater length what Rodulf felt and thought, and how great was the disturbance of his mind; all this could be handed down to posterity only on Rodulf’s own authority. [Note: [Col. 0024D] X, 12.] Thus he drew his history everywhere from the clearest sources, and composed it in the latter six books of the *Gesta*. We have already noted above that in his very manner of writing he looked to Rodulf as a most illustrious model, and that he especially sought to adapt his books to Rodulf’s as closely as possible and to make a single volume out of both portions; no one fails to see how successfully he accomplished this.

Forty-two years passed after this first continuator before one of the successors [Col. 0024B] whom Rodulf had urged to write history set himself to fulfil that exhortation; meanwhile, not a few events which could have been recorded more accurately earlier had become obscured by forgetfulness. The second continuator undertook in four books to write the history of Abbots Folcard, Gerard, and Wiric—that is, the years 1138–1183. He treated the first two in the two earlier books, and Wiric rather more fully in the two latter. For his chief purpose was to celebrate Abbot Wiric, in whose time he himself lived, as the abbot’s merits seemed to demand. He indicated this purpose in his final words: [Note: [Col. 0024D] IV, 32.] “It is therefore fitting that grateful remembrance of the works and manifold benefits of so great a father should be held in blessing among posterity, for whose uses [Col. 0024C] and advantages he is proved, clearer than daylight, to have laboured so outstandingly and so fatherly. Let us therefore offer him the common aid of prayers, praying that his spirit may rest in peace.”

These words also seem to make clear that the author undertook his work not very long after Wiric’s death in 1183. The time when he composed his book cannot apparently be fixed within narrower limits, since clearer indications are lacking; but it is evident that he was a contemporary of Wiric, who was elevated to the abbacy in 1155. For he indicates that he was contemporary with events in Italy in 1167: [Note: [Col. 0024D] III, 11. “Lest anyone doubt this and think that we, because we were not present at the event, being separated from them by a great distance of lands, report falsehoods,” etc.] in 1169 he was present as an eyewitness at the exhumation of the relics [Col. 0025A] of Saint Lietbert; [Note: [Col. 0025D] IV, 1. “And as we were praising God and His martyr Lietbert,” etc. In the same place: “We learned from the testimony of our elders that Duke Robert of Hesbaye … was buried there with his wife,” etc. IV, 2: “When the opening had been made … we found the sarcophagus,” etc.] likewise, he witnessed the miracle in which the arm of a certain soldier seemed to have been healed by the saints’ relics. [Note: [Col. 0025D] IV, 9. “And when we suddenly began the hymn,” etc.]

For the rest, he chiefly drew his literary resources from Saint Trudo’s archive. There are letters and public charters which he partly cited and partly inserted entire into the text itself. [Note: [Col. 0025D] I, 3: he cites charters granted to the Trudonenses by Stephen, bishop of Metz; I, 5: another concerning a dispute between Abbot Folcard and Arnold of Diest; I, 11: a charter recording the donation of a certain Tegnon; III, 10: instruments of confirmation by Alexander the archdeacon, Henry bishop of Liège, and Pope Victor; III, 7: in his narrative he followed letters sent in 1179 by Frederick I and Pope Adrian, one against the other; III, 11: he partly copied the letter of Rainald, archbishop of Cologne, concerning events in Italy in 1167.] Of books, so far as I know, he admitted only two among his sources: Sigebert of Gembloux’s continuation [Note: [Col. 0026D] I, 3.] and the *Triumph of Saint Lambert*, [Note: [Col. 0026D] I, 4.] which he generally excerpted rather than copied word for word.

Accordingly, as his resources were slighter, so in writing history he could not attain the same distinction as Rodulf and the first continuator. The supply of matters to be narrated seems to flow less generously; his narrative itself has less clarity and less of that unadorned charm. Everything is rather drier and more meagre, and less suited to move the mind. Nor are the events which he handed down to posterity of equal importance. The earlier historians had not restricted their attention to their own monastery alone, nor had they excluded the history of their province or empire from their task; the second continuator did this very often. Rather, he rested chiefly in more limited matters: enumerating the monastery’s rights and revenues, the donations of the faithful, describing newly constructed buildings, recounting discoveries of saints, and similar matters. Only in the second part of book IV did he finally turn his attention to other subjects. [Note: [Col. 0026D] But compare also III, 7; IV, 26.] Examples of learning are also extremely rare; in only one place, as far as I can see, did he cite a verse of Horace. [Note: [Col. 0026D] III, 6.]

At last, the third continuator who succeeded him determined to traverse a far wider field. He carried the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Trudo* from the year 1183 to the year 1366, and the plan he set himself was far more difficult to execute. For he tried to provide not only a continuation of the *Deeds* but supplements as well; and what Rodulf had been unable to accomplish two hundred and fifty years earlier—namely, to write about the beginnings of the monastery of Saint Trudo—the third continuator judged not too difficult for himself.

The earlier writers, being for the most part eyewitnesses of events, described chiefly their own times [Col. 0025D]; this man also undertook to investigate the very earliest times, in the manner, so to speak, of learned men [Col. 0026A]. Two parts of this continuation must therefore be distinguished: the first, in which, in three books, he recorded the origins of the monastery from the year 628 to 999; and the second later part, in which, in two books, he handed down to posterity the history of those abbots who governed the monastery from 1183 to 1366. The author composed this double continuation with the intention of joining his own books carefully to the older books of the *Deeds*: he prefixed the first part to Rodulf’s work, while attaching the other, as a third continuation, to the preceding material.

But he did not rest content with this alone. He attempted to arrange the entire history of the community of Saint Trudo and to reduce and combine into a single volume of the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Trudo* everything that he had either found written by others or written himself [Col. 0026B], so that the reader might descend from the most ancient times to events most recently accomplished. The author explained this design more fully in the preface to the first part; and the manner in which he carried it out is plainly shown by the Brussels manuscript in which these continuations have been preserved. For in a twelfth-century manuscript he found the *Deeds* of Rodulf and of the first continuator; to these he joined the second continuation, which was contained in a thirteenth-century manuscript.

> [Note: Col. 0026D] Preface to Part I. “Then, finding in an old little book the deeds, written down, of the three abbots who immediately succeeded Rodulf, I appended them in sequence.”

To this double volume he added, as its first part—

> [Note: Col. 0026D] Ibid. “The few things which I collected in order to continue the sequence of events, I took care to place before the books nobly arranged by the venerable lord Rodulf concerning the deeds of nine abbots.”

—and as its fourth part—

> [Note: Col. 0026D] Ibid. “Lastly, I placed the deeds of the twelve abbots who presided from the year of the Lord 1180” (an error for 1183) “until the death of Abbot Robert, who died in the year of the Lord 1366.” At the end of the same preface [Col. 0027C] one reads: “This compilation of the deeds of the abbots is divided into four parts: the first part contains three books, the second thirteen books, the third four books, while the fourth is completed in two books.”

—namely, the part which he himself had written in the fourteenth century. Yet even this did not suffice him. Wherever he thought that he could hand down more or better material to posterity than Rodulf [Col. 0026C], he erased no small amount from Rodulf’s book and inserted his own material into the text or wrote it in the margin, in part as though it had been written by Rodulf himself. He called these interpolations *Incidentia* (“Incidental Matters”). Finally, in order to reduce everything to a single arrangement, he also divided Rodulf’s book into chapters—a thing which had never occurred to Rodulf himself. In this way the fourth continuator created the corpus of Saint-Trudo writers.

Who this exact and diligent author was—whether a monk or perhaps an abbot of Saint Trudo—cannot be brought from darkness into light. One fact alone is clear: he was a man of Saint Trudo. He wisely refrained from treating events most recently accomplished, lest, as he himself declares in his preface, “if I pursued the truth of events [Col. 0026D], I might perhaps incur the offense of certain persons [Col. 0027A] who are still alive; or, if I departed from the truth, I might be stained with the mark of flattery or falsehood.” Doubtless for the same reason he brought his work to an end a considerable time after the year 1366. For in one place he mentions the year 1372,

> [Note: Col. 0027C] *Deeds of Robert*, ch. 11;

and elsewhere testifies that a certain plague lasted until the year 1383,

> [Note: Col. 0027C] *Deeds of Amelius*, ch. 5;

and Abbot Zacheus, Robert’s successor, whom he mentions near the end of the book, died in 1391.

> [Note: Col. 0027C] *Gallia Christiana*, III, 963.

This is the latest possible date for the writing, for I have found no indications of a later time.

The sources which he employed in composing the first part of the continuation are of diverse kinds. In the preface he described them thus: “Having finally examined the books of our library and the store of charters, the few things which, etc.” To these must be added the memory of ancient events transmitted orally among the monks [Col. 0027B]. It is true that, after removing all that the author copied, there remain certain items not unworthy of remembrance even after Rodulf.

He drew the chronological order and the foundations of the whole book from Sigebert, as is evident everywhere down to the end of the first part and in what he called the *Incidentia*; and in one place he copied the Affligem continuation of Sigebert.

> [Note: Col. 0027C] Year 1085.

Nor did he reap a smaller harvest from saints’ lives. The works which he called to his aid were these: Theoderic’s *Life of Saint Trudo*;

> [Note: Col. 0027C] Continuation, fourth part, first section, I, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10–13, 16, 18, 21–26; II, 8, 9.

the *Life of Saints Theodard*;

> [Note: Col. 0027C] I, 2, 3, 7, 12, 18.

Amand;

> [Note: Col. 0027C] I, 2, 5.

Chlodulf;

> [Note: Col. 0027C] I, 3.

King Sigebert;

> [Note: Col. 0027C] I, 5.

Remaclus;

> [Note: Col. 0027C] I, 5, 12.

Saint Beregis;

> [Note: Col. 0027C] I, 16.

Rener’s *Life of Saint Lambert*;

> [Note: Col. 0027C] I, 19, 20, 22.

the *Life of Hubert*;

> [Note: Col. 0027D] I, 28, 29.

the *Life of Eucherius*;

> [Note: Col. 0027D] I, 31; II, 3, 4, 6.

the *Vision of Saint Eucherius*;

> [Note: Col. 0027D] II, 5.

the *Life of Rigobert*;

> [Note: Col. 0027D] II, 3.

[Col. 0027C] Stepelin’s *Miracles of Saint Trudo*;

> [Note: Col. 0027D] III, 4, 7, year 1021.

the *Life of Bruno*;

> [Note: Col. 0027D] III, 13.

Sigebert’s *Life of Theoderic, Bishop of Metz*;

> [Note: Col. 0027D] III, 15.

and the *Life of Balderic*, [Col. 0027D] bishop of Liège.

> [Note: Col. 0027D] Year 1013.

[Col. 0028A] To these he added Martin of Poland,

> [Note: Col. 0027D] II, 10, 14, where he names Martin; 15, 20, 22; years 1003 and 1025.

and perhaps Martin the Minorite,

> [Note: Col. 0027D] II, 14.

though I would not confidently maintain that the latter was among the author’s sources. Certain other matters raise still greater doubt, which one might perhaps conjecture were among his resources. One or two passages recalled Fredegar to my mind,

> [Note: Col. 0027D] II, 4.

the *Deeds of Trier*,

> [Note: Col. 0027D] II, 15, 20.

and the *Chronicle of the Counts of Flanders*,

> [Note: Col. 0027D] II, 15.

but I can scarcely believe that he consulted the books themselves. He appears to have read Regino,

> [Note: Col. 0028C] II, 22. He cited all these written authorities collectively in one or two passages: I, 16, “as the history of the ancients relates”; II, 2, “the antiquity of the deeds is read”; III, 4, “the histories of celebrated men attest.”

but did not have him among his sources.

Finally come charters from the archives of Saint Trudo, which he either cited

> [Note: Col. 0028C] II, 2, 14, 15; III, 11, 14.

or copied for the reader’s benefit,

> [Note: Col. 0028C] II, 7; III, 5, 10, 11.

and epitaphs.

> [Note: Col. 0028C] III, 14, 16.

To these charters and to the reports of old men—

> [Note: Col. 0028C] II, 7, “as they say”; II, 23, “as they report”; III, 2, “according to the account of the ancients.”

—the author owed the things of greater importance [Col. 0028B] which he handed down to posterity.

He drew the second part of the continuation from almost the same sources. In composing it he used these chronicles: Vincent of Beauvais’s *Historical Mirror*;

> [Note: Col. 0028C] 1187, 1188, 1190, 1191, 1197, 1198, where Vincent is named; 1211–1214, 1226, 1245.

and a certain continuation of it;

> [Note: Col. 0028C] 1273, 1292, 1289, 1309; it is found in the oldest editions.

the *Life of Saint Lutgard of Aywières*;

> [Note: Col. 0028C] 1200.

Hocsem’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*;

> [Note: Col. 0028C] 1257, 1274, 1281, 1282, 1292, 1296–98, 1300, 1301, 1307, 1309, 1312, 1316, 1318, 1324, 1326–1328, 1331–1335, 1337, 1342, 1345, 1346.

and annals unknown to me.

> [Note: Col. 0028D] 1345.

Then come charters, partly cited—

> [Note: Col. 0028D] 1181, “as is contained in our charters”; 1227, where the charters themselves are the sources; 1258, “as is more fully contained in the letters drawn up concerning it.” Cf. also 1288, 1316, 1327, 1338.

—and partly incorporated into the text:

> [Note: Col. 0028D] 1250, letter of Abbot William; letter of Conrad, Cardinal of Santa Rufina; 1348, three letters of Pope Clement. 504.

epitaphs;

> [Note: Col. 0028D] 1221, of Abbot Christian; 1248, of Abbot Thomas.

and martyrologies.

> [Note: Col. 0028D] 1253.

He also derived many other things, by no means very few, from the memory of old men and popular report.

> [Note: Col. 0028D] 1189, “they report”; 1227; 1269; 1271, “it is believed”; 1248; 1300, “they say”; 1256, “according to reports,” “as was reported”; 1271, “as I heard reported”; 1308, “it was said.”

He himself gave this testimony concerning his sources in the preface: “I collected the deeds of these twelve abbots from various books here and there, and from the accounts of old men; and I inserted what I was able to see and hear in my own times.”

Yet when the continuator began to devote himself to writing, a considerable amount again seems to have been erased from human memory by forgetfulness [Col. 0028C–0029A]. For the material that he committed to writing in the first book concerning the first nine abbots—excepting only the first William—is of less importance; this covers the more than hundred-year period 1180–1297. Here he wrote rather about the internal affairs of the monastery than external matters: estates acquired or lost, stewardship, and debts with which the monastery was burdened beyond measure.

A fuller body of material was available to the author from 1297 to 1366, especially under Abbots Robert and Amelius—that is, from 1330 onward. What is read here concerns the whole province and the town of Saint Trudo more than the monastery. Along with the wars of dukes and counts, it deals especially with the municipalities of towns, which are mentioned very frequently, so that you may think yourself to be reading the history not of a monastery but rather of a certain city [Col. 0029B]. The matters supplied by the author in this second book are written sufficiently lucidly and clearly that you will undoubtedly prefer it to the former one.

Whether later writers of Saint Trudo found material after this fourth continuator is not entirely clear. There is one Brussels manuscript:

> [Note: Col. 0029D] MS 7647, seventeenth century; *Archiv*, VIII, 504.

in which a certain supplement is read, beginning with the words, “Zachaeus de Vrankhoven, etc.” This Zachaeus is Zazeus, successor of Abbot Robert. But whether this is a legitimate continuation of the *Deeds* or a catalogue of abbots, I do not know. Grammaye cites a *Chronicle of Saint Trudo*, 600–1560, by Abbot Robert (doubtless Rodulf) and four monks after him.

> [Note: Col. 0029D] *Catalogue des Historiens du Brabant*; cf. Le Long, *Biblioth.*, I, 790.

Nor can I offer anything more precise about the Chronicle of the town of Saint Trudo preserved in the Giessen library.

> [Note: Col. 0029D] *Archiv*, IX, 578.

Later writers have added very few notes to our Brussels manuscript concerning Arnold of Beringh and George Sarens, abbots in 1469 and 1493. In order that nothing may be omitted, we shall give these at the end, though in themselves they are of very slight importance.

Only in the sixteenth century were there, so far as I know, two men who wrote the history of Saint Trudo. The first was the already-mentioned Moringus, who produced a *Chronicle of Saint Trudo* beginning from the year 1410; it was later continued by another monk of Saint Trudo. John Latomus composed another work on the same subject; he died in 1578. The manuscript was formerly kept at Liège.

> [Note: Col. 0029D] Sanderus, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, II, 160.

Finally, few later writers, so far as I know, consulted the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Trudo* [Col. 0029D] as a source and drew material from it: Aegidius of Aulne;

> [Note: Col. 0029D] Ch. 11, 20, in Chapeaville, *Gesta episcoporum Leodiensium*, II.

the interpolator of the *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence of Liège*;

> [Note: Col. 0029D] *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, VIII, 262.

and Brusthemius, whose fragments Chapeaville published.

> [Note: Col. 0029D] II, 36, 37, 64, 65.

All these, if I see rightly, copied only the books of Rodulf and of the first continuator.

[Col. 0030A] Of the manuscripts which have come to our knowledge, we employed only two in preparing this edition. Yet these are, unless I am mistaken, the oldest manuscripts now extant, so that we may readily dispense with the rest. The two manuscripts are very closely related.

1) A parchment manuscript of the middle of the twelfth century, in octavo, which the Most Reverend de Ram, a man most deserving in Belgian affairs, caused to be sent to us from his library through the Most Reverend Cortens, Vicar General of Mechelen. It is our pious duty publicly to render the highest thanks to these two gentlemen. The manuscript is elegantly written in eleven and a half quires. Scribal abbreviations are neither many [Col. 0030B] nor unusual. The letter *e* frequently occurs in oblique cases of the first declension and in certain other words—for example, *in ecclesia*, *penitentia*, *accepit*, *fecit*, and so forth. But *e* is also written for *ae*; for instance, *pre* is written consistently. A stroke placed above the letter *i* is admitted only in a doubled letter. The chapters of the text are distinguished not by numbers but by colored initial letters; we have followed these in numbering the chapters of our text.

This is the manuscript upon which our edition rests, as it were, on its foundation. For it supplies the complete text of Rodulf and the first continuator without interpolations; and, except for one letter to the monks of Saint Pantaleon, all other letters and continuations are absent.

1*) MS 18181, parchment, late twelfth and fourteenth centuries, folio, [Col. 0030C] from the Burgundian Library in Brussels, formerly owned by Lammens.

> [Note: Col. 0030D] *Archiv*, VIII, 546.

It is very closely connected with manuscript 1, from which its earlier part was undoubtedly copied, as can be proved by quite a few examples. For certain errors recur:

> [Note: Col. 0030D] For example, I, 12: in both manuscripts *canis* is erroneously read for *canus*; V, 1: *abbatiam* erroneously for *abbatia*; VI, 5: *sibi* is wrongly repeated; VI, 19: *aeque* for *neque*; VI, 24: *lene* for *leve*; VII, 10: *in* is wrongly read in both manuscripts; X, 21: *propulsius* wrongly for *propensius*; XII, 4: *terra* wrongly for *terram*; XII, 9: *solum* wrongly for *totum*; and in the same place *paralicam* for *paraliticam*.

These are errors into which the scribe of manuscript 1 fell; and, apart from this, the two manuscripts very rarely differ from one another.

The manuscript consists of 203 folios. On fols. 31–118 are read the *Deeds* of Rodulf and the first continuator, which were written in eleven twelfth-century quires and undoubtedly at an earlier date formed a separate volume; they seem to have been written by three scribes. Likewise separate was the thirteenth-century manuscript that follows on fols. 123–144, in which, in three quires, is read the history of the abbots for the years 1138–1183 [Col. 0030D]. The abbreviations, which the scribes had used more moderately in the earlier part, now occur more frequently and more extensively: for example, *pr* for *pater* (“father”), *pria* for *patria* (“fatherland”), *mia* for *misericordia* (“mercy”), *ca* for *causa* (“cause”), and so forth.

On fols. 144–195 follow seven quires, written in the fourteenth century, containing the *Deeds* for the years 1183–1366. Here too the abbreviations are more extensive: *qis* for *communis* (“common”), [Col. 0031A] *m’ltine* for *multitudine* (“multitude”), and so forth. Finally, the same hand wrote on fols. 1–20 the first part of the *Deeds*, containing the years 628–999; on fols. 20–30 the same hand compiled the table of chapters for Rodulf’s *Deeds*. I have already pointed out that these chapters were established not by Rodulf but by the third continuator. They are therefore of no value, and this index is not to be reproduced in our edition.

The same man was also the interpolator who erased the authentic text in eleven places in Rodulf’s *Deeds* and inserted other matter in his own hand into the text or in the margin. Yet these interpolations are to be given little weight, for most often Rodulf’s statements are repeated in more expansive terms in order that he might more easily cite his chapters, by which he not infrequently divided the book contrary to its meaning. For this reason we have included among the variant readings the interpolations, which contain nothing authentic [Col. 0031B].

Finally, the author attempted to reduce this entire volume of the *Deeds* into a single body arranged chronologically, and at the top margin of the individual pages he placed in red letters this heading: “first—second—third—fourth part.” Since, however, we must restore the authentic form of the individual books, we have not followed the same order. Rather, we have assigned first place to Rodulf, the most ancient of these authors; then the first and second continuations will follow. So that we may not dismember what was written by the fourth author, we shall give the earlier part of the final continuation as the *Trudonian Supplement*, with the *Incidentia* arranged in chronological order; and in the last place we shall add the fourth continuation.

[Col. 0031C] Besides those just mentioned, the following manuscripts, all copied from manuscript 1*, are to be listed here:

1*a) Paris, Bibliothèque de l’Arsenal, historical Latin MS 35, written in 1479.

> [Note: Col. 0031C] *Archiv*, VIII, 357.

1*b) Brussels, Burgundian Library MS 16607, sixteenth century.

> [Note: Col. 0031C] Ibid., VIII, 544.

1*c) Brussels, Burgundian Library MS 14965, eighteenth century.

> [Note: Col. 0031C] Ibid., VIII, 541. For manuscripts of the monastery of Saint Trudo in general, see ibid., VIII, 48, 49; and for cartularies, VII, 844.

There is one edition of the *Deeds of Saint Trudo*, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium* [Col. 0032A],

> [Note: Col. 0031C] II, 659.

but it is extremely corrupt and prepared with the greatest carelessness. I do not know what manuscript the editor followed, since he did not mention it even in a word. The manuscript does not seem to have contained either interpolations or continuations; in variant readings it therefore agrees more with manuscript 1 than with 1*. Yet the variant readings are not infrequently so distorted that one may readily infer that the manuscript was a recent copy, whose carelessly written letters D’Achery could not read. He also omitted, with astonishing negligence, sometimes a smaller and sometimes a larger part of the narrative; these lacunae we shall note in their proper places under the siglum D.

Following D’Achery’s text, Bouquet published in his customary manner certain extracts from Rodulf’s chronicle.

> [Note: Col. 0031D] XI, 204; XIII, 591.

D’Achery was by no means the first [Col. 0032B] to become acquainted with the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Trudo*. Before him others had published individual fragments; their names seem worth setting down here. Molanus, so far as I know, was the first to cite the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Trudo* and to employ them as a resource in his book.

> [Note: Col. 0031D] *Natales Sanctorum Belgii*, where, by the words “as the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Trudo* attest,” he refers to the entry for 1227 in the third continuation.

In 1615 Saussaye—

> [Note: Col. 0031D] *Annales Ecclesiae Aurelianensis*, Paris, 1615, quarto, p. 271: “It seemed fitting at this point to insert word for word the chronology from the annals of Saint Trudo, which the aforesaid Abbot Remigius Watzonius sent us on 24 September, in the year of the Lord 1607, and which we ourselves carefully read in that monastery in the year 1600.” See also pp. 256, 258, 265.

—printed those portions of the *Deeds* that concern Saint Eucherius. He seems to have drawn these from Saint Trudo itself, from our manuscript 1*. In 1624 Miraeus mentioned the *Chronicle of Saint Trudo* here and there, and seems also to have possessed a manuscript containing the continuations.

> [Note: Col. 0032C] *Opera diplomatica*, ed. Foppens, I, 61, where he says: “Rodulf, abbot of Saint Trudo, wrote a chronicle of his monastery, which I possess in manuscript.” Cf. ibid., I, 493, 520.

In 1634 Medrisse followed. From extracts sent to him by du Chesne, he made public quite a few passages from the chronicles of Rodulf and the continuators.

> [Note: Col. 0032C] *Histoire des evesques de Metz*, p. 134; from it v. d. Hirsch collected the individual passages in *De vita et scriptis Sigeberti*, p. 231. He rightly conjectured that the first part of the *Deeds* was not composed by Rodulf.

Mantelius very often [Col. 0032C] consulted the *Deeds of Saint Trudo*,

> [Note: Col. 0032D] *Historia comitum Lossensium*, 1671, pp. 19, 38, 55, 57, 85, etc. Yet the narrative does not everywhere agree exactly with the wording of our text, so that I readily conjecture that he used not the authentic *Deeds* but a text expanded later.

and placed almost the whole of his *History of the Counts of Looz* upon this single foundation. Finally, in the *Acts of the Saints*, Henschenius published from a manuscript *Chronicle of Saint Trudo* fragments from the individual continuations concerning Saint Eucherius, Lietbert, and so forth.

> [Note: Col. 0032D] *Acta Sanctorum*, February III, 222, in the discussion of the translation of Saint Eucherius.

These were reprinted by Ghesquiere.

> [Note: Col. 0032D] *Acta Sanctorum Belgii*, V, 11 ff.

Written at Berlin in May 1848.

R. KOEPKE.

# RODULF’S DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF SAINT TRUDO

[Col. 0033]

[Col. 0033A] Rodulf to N., greetings.

It is known to all whom the generous hand of kindly fortune has given the opportunity to experience it that old wines, kept clarified in cool storehouses throughout the whole cycle of the year, are set aside for a time in autumn, while new must, still warm from its natural fermentation and not yet completely cleared, is more eagerly consumed. Why is this? Certainly not because new and cloudy wines are preferred to old and clarified wines as better; rather, because new things customarily affect the fastidious minds of human beings more pleasantly when the passion of desire rushes in, until, the passion of desire having been satisfied, they return with livelier appetite to the use of old things. Hence one who was not ignorant of natural philosophy says: “It is pleasant to use things alternately; alternation itself sometimes gives equal pleasure even to flavors that are unequal.”

Following the likeness of this observation [Col. 0033B], my beloved and ever-to-be-loved provost N. of Saint Dionysius [Col. 0034A], I send you a history newly fashioned on the anvil, concerning those things which have happened in ancient and recent times to our church. You delight in the use of old and new things; through it, then, taste our old and new affairs, through which you may affect your eager mind with a fitting passion. Although you may gain little instruction from it, you who seek to know new things together with old will nevertheless be able to learn what our church once was, from what height—

> [Note: Col. 0033] Thus MS 1; MS 1* has “from what eminence”; D reads “from what eminence.”
