—to what gulfs of the abyss it has frequently fallen, and how much labor I endure with the utmost difficulty upon the still-surviving ember of its former ruin, against the incessant assault of malignant blasts, lest it fly away altogether.

> [Note: Col. 0033] D reads “they endure.”

Your knowing this will benefit me in this respect: unhappy people are commonly able to bear their pains more evenly by recounting them [Col. 0034B] when they find persons who listen to them with familiarity and compassion.

> [Note: Col. 0033] D reads “have compassion.” MS 1* adds: “Farewell.”

# THE DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF SAINT TRUDO BEGIN

[Col. 0033]

[Col. 0033B] Rodulf, by the grace of God and of Saints Trudo and Eucherius abbot of their monastery, to all my successors, both abbots and monks, who are to serve God in this same monastery: may you be what you profess yourselves to be, and may you sometimes remember my sinful soul.

> [Note: Col. 0033] MS 1* reads *nobio* for *coenobio* (“monastery”).

Very often indeed, dearest brothers—

> [Note: Col. 0033] MS 1* adds “my”; it is absent in MS 1 and D.

—as I turned over the entire equipment of our library, while I was still placed in the flesh in which you now struggle, I burned with a strong desire to discover who and how many my predecessors had been, and of what profession: whether all had been monks or whether some had been canons; what the name of each was; and how many years each had presided. I confess that I was never able to discover what I desired. Nor was there any one among the older brothers who said that he had discovered this anywhere by reading, or had ever learned it by hearing, as I sought to know.

Whether this had happened through the habitual negligence of our scribes, or perhaps through the loss of books amid the very frequent desolations of the place, I likewise could in no way determine with certainty [Col. 0033C]. But the Life of our lord and saint of most blessed memory, Trudo, teaches that he was a cleric and priest, and the first builder of our monastery;

> [Note: Col. 0033] Whether this is the Life by Donatus, which may be seen in Ghesquiere, V, 23, or that by Theoderic, cannot be determined.

as does also the Life of blessed Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren [Col. 0034B], in which certain princes of kingdoms and rulers of churches are likewise mentioned, in whose times this lily of most holy purity of ours flowered. Yet neither there nor elsewhere is it made clearly known whether our monastery, first constructed by him, was initially governed by him himself or by someone else; whether those whom he established in it were clerics or monks; and when monks began to be in it.

As I often—indeed, as I have said, very often—burned with a strong desire to learn such matters, which were most worthy of faithful record, by reading or reliable report, I found a certain little book containing the Life of Saint Sylvester, the Translation of Saint Benedict, and also a sermon on the Assumption of Saint Mary ever Virgin. I have taken care to record here what I found in it. I therefore ask the readers of this little work of mine to excuse me [Col. 0034C] if I make you less certain than you might wish concerning matters of which I myself could not be more certain.

> [Note: Col. 0033] MS 1* reads *m. h. r.* [an abbreviated reading, uncertain].

This is my purpose in this little work: what I found almost obliterated through the negligence of others, I shall preserve by my own diligence, more purely sifted out, for future posterity. I wish to make the abbots and monks who will come after me in this monastery attentive to this matter,

> [Note: Col. 0033] Thus MS 1. MS 1* has an erased “Saint Trudo,” and adds the title “Preface of the First Book,” in which the interpolator wrote a prologue.

so that they may not fall further into the negligence of their predecessors, but may also leave their own successors a written memorial full of trustworthy testimony concerning their predecessors [Col. 0035A]. In it, when the uprightness or wickedness of each person may frequently be read, the upright, inspired by the example of their predecessors, may always advance more and more toward better things; and the wicked, ashamed as they imagine their own life, may at least thus repent of their evil deeds.

Receive then, my successors, certain names of abbots without the years during which they presided and without years of the Lord; certain others with only their own years; and others with both their own years and years of the Lord. All the rest I learned from the report of faithful men who saw these things or who knew those who had seen them; I myself also learned some matters.

> [Note: Col. 0035] Omitted by D.

Those things done in my presence, or when I too was already a young man, I shall commit in some measure to a most faithful memory; very many things I shall pass over, out of shame for our order and excessive weariness caused by a long account.

> [Note: Col. 0035] MS 1* adds a text as though it were the heading of what follows.

The names, therefore, of the abbots who formerly governed the monastery—

> [Note: Col. 0035] Omitted by MS 1*.

—of Saint Trudo are these:

> [Note: Col. 0035] The names in the catalogues of abbots in MS 1 are written in red.

Abbot Grimo;

> [Note: Col. 0035C] According to the charter of Count Robert, produced by the third continuator, II, 7, Abbot Grimo was governing the monastery during the interregnum into which affairs had fallen after the death of Theuderic IV, in the time of Charles Martel.

Abbot Reyramnus;

> [Note: Col. 0035] D reads Reimannus.

Abbot Hardebenus; Abbot Columbanus; Abbot Angelramnus; Abbot Ambrosius; Abbot Gislebertus; Abbot Adelboldus; Abbot Hildradus; Abbot Sabbatinus; Abbot Ermemmarus; Abbot Radulfus; Abbot Luodowicus; Abbot Ratbertus; Abbot Rodegangus. Thus far I have found their names without the number of years for which they presided.

Abbot Reynerus presided for 5 years.

> [Note: Col. 0035D] If you follow the charter of Ruechlinda, mother of Abbot Reynerus, in the third continuator, III, 5, he governed the monastery in the third year of Otto I. But it is quite evident that this year does not fit at all with the number of subsequent years. Therefore either the author erred in inserting the numbers, or, what comes closer to the truth, a name is missing from this catalogue of abbots. The continuator preserved two other charters, III, 10, 11, written in the twenty-first and twenty-third years of Otto I, that is, 957 and 959, in which mention is made of Adalbero, bishop of Metz, and abbot of Saint Trudo. He died in 964; according to the continuator, Abbot Theudefridus succeeded him and performed his office until 994. Adalbero, however, is said to have presided over the monastery for twenty years, that is, 944–964.

Abbot Theudefridus presided for 30 years.

> [Note: Col. 0036D] He died on 13 January.

Abbot Erenfridus presided for 4 years.

> [Note: Col. 0036D] He died on 5 November. On these days of death, see the third continuator, III, 16, 17.

Thus far I found the number of years during which they presided, but without years of the Lord. Abbot Adelard, most worthy of remembrance, presided for 35 years, that is, until the year 1034—

> [Note: Col. 0035] D reads 1039.

—of the Lord’s Incarnation. Abbot Guntramnus presided for 21 years—

> [Note: Col. 0035] D reads “twenty.”

—that is, from the year 1034—

> [Note: Col. 0035] D reads 1039.

—of the Lord’s Incarnation until 1055. Abbot Adelard presided for 27 years, that is, from 1055 until 1082—

> [Note: Col. 0035] D reads “the one hundred eighty-second.”

—of the Lord’s Incarnation. Thus far, and in this form, I found the material in the aforesaid little book.

After this Adelard, however, I shall set down only the names of those who either were abbots or wished to be regarded as abbots, down to our own entrance; for, contesting among themselves, they created such confusion of years that we could have no certain time for any one of them [Col. 0036B], except one, as we shall explain in the work that follows.

> [Note: Col. 0035] D reads “following.”

Their names were Lanzo, Luypo, Herimannus, another Herimannus, and our predecessor Lord Abbot Theodericus. Concerning the three abbots mentioned above—namely Adelard, Guntramnus, and the second Adelard—I shall briefly report what I learned from the narration of trustworthy persons.

> [Note: Col. 0035] Omitted by D.

For concerning the other abbots named above I have received nothing which I would dare put forward with assured confidence. But from the second Adelard down to myself, whatever I relate I either saw myself or could have seen; and what I did not see, I learned from the report of those who did see it.

**THE PREFACE ENDS. THE TEXT OF THE WORK BEGINS.**

[Col. 0035]

# BOOK ONE

> [Note: Col. 0035] These words are absent from MS 1*. “The preface ends” is absent from D.

[Col. 0035C] 1. Accordingly the first Adelard—

> [Note: Col. 0035] D adds: “was made abbot of this place in the year of the Lord 999.”

> [Note: Col. 0037A] “In the year [Col. 0037] ‘In the year … Theutonic’: interpolator 1* wrote this after erasing the preceding three lines. The bookbinder cut off Otto’s regnal number.] of the Lord 999, in the year . . . of the reign of Otto III, and in the twenty-seventh year of the episcopate of Notger, bishop of Liège, after the death of Erenfridus, abbot of this place, Adelard, the first of that name, succeeded. He did not have Theutonic as his native language, but, etc.”

—did not have Theutonic as his native language, but rather that which they incorrectly call Roman and which in Theutonic is called Walloon. He is said to have loved tenderly the household of our church. Hence, even to the present day, many people customarily recount the following memorial tale about him.

When, they say, a famine from the barrenness of the land occurred at some time in his day [Col. 0036C],

> [Note: Col. 0036D] The Annals of Liège testify that that land was afflicted by a great famine in the year 1006: *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, IV, 18. Cf. also Alpert, I, 6, ibid.

people of every sex and age came persistently and pitiably to the brothers’ almsgiving. Calling some of them to himself from time to time, he was said to ask jokingly: “Whose servant are you, man? And whose maidservant are you, woman?” When they replied, for example, that they belonged to Saint Lambert, Saint Peter, Saint Servatius, Saint Remaclus, or finally to any other saint [Col. 0037A], he would say: “What then have you to do with the household of Saint Trudo? Let your own lord feed you, whose servant you are.” But anyone who declared himself to belong to Saint Trudo heard him say paternally: “Then Saint Trudo, our lord, will feed you today; for you are our fellow servant.”

In his early years our church suffered most anxiously, as I have heard reported, from a lack of necessities. But I have not learned by a wholly trustworthy account what was chiefly the cause of this.

2. [Col. 0037B] Through the agitation of certain of his brothers, Theoderic, bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0037D] He is the second of that name, who held the see from 1006 to 1047.], became so incensed against him [Note: [Col. 0037C] The interpolator 1*, after erasing two lines, expanded these words thus: “In the second year of the prelacy of the first Adelard, after the death of Adalbero, third bishop of Metz of that name, Theoderic, the second of that name, his kinsman, usurped the bishopric. For Duke Theoderic of the Mosellans, who was also duke of Lotharingia, brother of the deceased Adalbero, having conferred the aforesaid bishopric upon his own son Adalbero, fourth of that name, still a boy, appointed Theoderic himself as the boy’s guardian. Theoderic, having excluded the boy from the city, usurped the bishopric for himself, captured the boy’s father in war, and remained in the bishopric. But after some time, at the instigation of certain monks, he became so hostile to Abbot Adelard,” etc.] that he carried him off and held him at Metz for some time, almost as an exile, while in the meantime administering our affairs through provosts. But when the bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0037D] It is not sufficiently clear who he was; for during the years 1006–1034 the Church of Liège was governed by five bishops: Notker, Balderic, Wolpodo, Durandus, and Reginhard.], in whose diocese he was, defended his right in the matter, Adelard was at last honourably recalled.

On his return he was attended by such favour that he caused his church not merely to abound in necessities, but also to shine gloriously, inwardly and outwardly, with varied ornament and diverse furnishings. We have seen only a very few of these things, and those the most precious; for the rest, along with very many other possessions, the fury of the raging simoniacs, contending among themselves over our abbey, had most ruinously dispersed in various ways and at different times, and buried in perpetual destruction.

[Col. 0037C] And lest anyone, seeing today the poverty of our church both in possessions and in treasure, suppose that it was always so meagre and stripped bare, I think it should neither be unwelcome to it nor shameful to us if I record here what I found noted in another book concerning our former treasury and the provision for the monks:

3. In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 870 [Note: [Col. 0037] 770 in D.], in the third indiction and the thirteenth year of the see of Lord Adventius, the glorious bishop, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, an inventory was made by his command from the abbey of Saint Trudo through his envoys, namely Fredelo and Herigaud.—From this too, as from many other things, the negligence of our people deserves rebuke: here they neglected to record the name of their abbot, who was then in charge, though not only the name of the bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0037] “name of the bishop of Metz,” 1*.] is found recorded here, but also the names of his envoys who made this inventory.—We found [Note: [Col. 0037] In manuscript 1 this catalogue is written so that one line is in ink and the next in red.] in the treasury of the church of Saint [Col. 0038B] Trudo:

A *reba* [Note: [Col. 0037D] Read *repa*: a cover for a bier or shrine.] for his body, made of gold and silver. Likewise, a *reba* of Saint Eucherius, embellished with silver. Likewise, one on the right-hand side of Saint Trudo. Likewise, an altar in honour of Saint Mary and [Note: [Col. 0037] “and Saint,” omitted in 1*; “and Saint Peter,” in D.] Saint Peter, adorned with gold and silver, with a *cyborium* [Note: [Col. 0037D] The same as the *reba* mentioned above.] above it; in the middle of the ciborium, a hanging gilded bronze crown. Likewise, an altar in honour of Saint Stephen, furnished with silver. One shrine adorned with gems and gold. Likewise, 21 shrines covered with silver. Ten crosses, both larger and smaller, furnished with silver. Three Gospel-book covers furnished with silver. Two silver pomegranates. Nineteen silver chalices with patens, both larger and smaller. Likewise, six patens. Likewise, one gold chalice with a silver paten [Note: [Col. 0037] “also” added in 1*.], for which eight and a half pounds of silver are owed. Likewise, three small gold crosses, [Col. 0038C] six silver ones, and two of copper. Five small altars furnished with silver. Three silver censers and one of copper. Seven silver candlesticks. Two silver boxes for carrying incense. Sixteen silver offertory vessels [Note: [Col. 0037D] A kind of chalice or paten.] [Note: [Col. 0037] 17 in D.]. Four silver cups, and two of copper. A silver *buxtile* [Note: [Col. 0037] This seems to be the correct reading; *suxtilem* in 1 and 1*.]. A silver Life of Saint Trudo, decorated with images. Five silver lamps, and seven of tin. Two silver crowns, and eight [Note: [Col. 0037] “and 8 … silver 2” omitted in D.] of copper, partly gilded. Two silver keys. Likewise, a small key of gold. Two *cambutae* [Note: [Col. 0038D] Bishops’ pastoral staffs.] covered with silver. Four banners. Thirty-three precious copes of *pallium* [Note: [Col. 0038D] That is, made from the material called *pallium*, here a kind of silk fabric.]. Twelve precious chasubles [Note: [Col. 0038D] The same as a *planeta*: a priestly garment which, according to Hrabanus, is the outermost of all vestments and protects and preserves all the others beneath it.] of *pallium*. Nine dalmatics with subdeacons’ tunics. Three silk cushions. Forty-four hangings, both larger and smaller. Likewise, one hanging with fringe [Note: [Col. 0038D] A border or fringe.] and pearls. Likewise, ten linen altar-cloths covered with silk [Note: [Col. 0038D] A curtain with which an altar is covered.]. Likewise, [Col. 0038D] 98 linen altar-cloths without silk. Four *facistergia* [Note: [Col. 0037] “facistergia … knife” omitted in D.]. Eight *fanones* [Col. 0039A] [Note: [Col. 0039D] A small cloth held in the hands during the office of Mass.] for offering. Six linen curtains and two woollen ones. Three ivory boxes. One *anappus* [Note: [Col. 0039D] Read *anaphus*, that is, a vessel.] with water. A copper hand-washing jug [Note: [Col. 0039D] A pitcher from which water is poured over the hands.]. Two *faldones* [Note: [Col. 0039D] A woollen garment.] with cushions. One knife mounted in gold. Small golden forks weighing five denarii of gold. One silver bowl [Note: [Col. 0039] “bowl … blade” omitted in D.]. Likewise, four and a half pounds of broken silver. One blade. Two copper *situlae* [Note: [Col. 0039D] A measure for liquids; thirty *situlae* made one *carrada*.]. Two silver rings, three copper ones [Note: [Col. 0039] “rings … 6 denarii” omitted in D.]. There still remain to be sought out 21 hanging gold earrings, very handsomely adorned with gems. Likewise, other hanging gold earrings weighing 13 denarii. Likewise, five *mancosi* [Note: [Col. 0040D] Women’s ornament: a bracelet.], weighing six denarii.

The monks themselves have 120 corbi of spelt assigned for their own use for making bread, amounting to 1,600 modii; 192 corbi of barley for making beer, amounting to [Col. 0039B] 1,920 modii. Together the spelt and barley make 312 corbi, amounting to 3,520 modii [Note: [Col. 0039] Correctly thus in D; 3,700 in 1 and 1*.]. Fifteen fattened pigs, 60 modii of legumes, and 24 modii of salt.

4. We have found, from the reliable record of the envoys of the bishop of Metz, that our treasury and the monks’ provision were once such as this—indeed, long before this Adelard—and that the greater part remained almost until his time; that he nevertheless restored certain things that had been lost; and that some things acquired through his zeal endured until our times, though not until our own prelacy. For, as we said above and shall set forth in their proper place in the third book and following books [Note: [Col. 0040D] In the third book and those following.], the most obstinate fury of the raging simoniacs, clashing among themselves over our abbey in various ways and at different times, most miserably [Col. 0039C] dispersed the exceedingly precious treasure of our church. Having irretrievably buried that inestimable splendour, it makes her sit mournful and pitiable even to this day, utterly full of the shame of her nakedness.

We have learned no more about Adelard except his death. Let us now turn to his successor.

5. After the first Adelard succeeded Guntram, born in the region of Hesbaye [Note: [Col. 0040D] A district on the left bank of the Meuse, between the rivers Mehaigne, which flows into the Meuse, the Demer, and the Dyle, into which the Demer here empties.], of free parentage, reared in our monastery from youth [Note: [Col. 0041C] After erasing seven lines, interpolator 1* inserted: “Thus, after describing and committing to writing the treasures of this monastery and the monks’ provision before the monastery itself was destroyed by the Normans, we must return to continue the history. In the time of this Lord Adelard, a praiseworthy young man named Guntram, [Col. 0041D] born in Hesbaye of free parentage and reared in this monastery from youth, flourished there,” etc.], and there most thoroughly trained in ecclesiastical offices and regular discipline.

At the time when his predecessor, namely Abbot Adelard, was held in exile by Theoderic, bishop of Metz, we have learned that—though we have not learned in what order—Poppo, abbot of Stavelot, first took charge of our monastery. [Col. 0039D] Meanwhile some of our monks lived as exiles away from our house in different [Col. 0040A] monasteries, tormented by the most grievous sorrow of having lost their shepherd. Among them were the outstanding and most devoutly noble men Gonzelin and Godezo, servants of God, brothers in the flesh indeed, but united in one spirit in God. When their shepherd at last returned to his flock, they too returned and were buried among us.

Meanwhile, when Poppo, first abbot of Stavelot [Note: [Col. 0040D] He died in 1048; see the Life of Poppo in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century VI, part 1, p. 569.]—acting, of course, in place of the exiled abbot—had come to our monastery to arrange a matter necessary to both parties, he entered the chapter of the monks, as we have heard, and began pastorally to deal with their faults. When he came to this Guntram, he perceived the remarkable quality of the young man’s elegant appearance and began, with discerning judgment, to foresee something devout and humble in him, wishing to bring it to light if experience should show it to be as it seemed to him. He therefore deliberately pressed upon him more severely an offered accusation of negligence, and with the goads of pious charity pierced his breast with humility. At last, as though he had received an affront, Poppo gave him the command under obedience to follow him on foot as far as the church of Stavelot, there to perform penance for his negligence.

Guntram was in the bloom of earliest youth, of most elegant appearance, taller than the men of our age, and of a build proportionate to his height. His voice was trumpet-like in its great volume, yet very sweet and not unworthy of his great body. We have said above that he was of illustrious birth and excellently trained in ecclesiastical offices and regular discipline. Things which commonly afford wandering young men abundant material for pride, this exceptionally handsome youth considered all the more beautiful in himself insofar as they were exercised under humbler obedience. Accordingly, he cheerfully set out on foot for Stavelot, keeping close to the foot of the commander in obedience, neither frightened by the shame of this unfamiliar pedestrian journey nor by the difficulty of the road.

When the delicate young man, weary and battered, arrived there, he was commanded, by order of the abbot—whom the porter had already informed of his arrival—to remain that night at the gate of the courtyard where guests were received, that is, outside the monks’ community. The pious father deliberately acted thus, so that Guntram’s tested humility might be exalted. The porter, therefore, discerning the pious humility and cheerful obedience of so splendid and noble a young man, made this famous among the monks, the prior of the church, and finally the abbot himself; and he readily obtained from them that so honourable and conspicuously obedient a youth should not be kept apart from the monks’ community. Thus he was admitted to the community, but assigned the last place. Yet he was judged taller, even than the elders, by the full height of his shoulders.

That night the annual Conversion of Saint Paul was solemnly celebrated according to custom (25 January). At the invitatory, he sang hymns, psalms, antiphons, and responsories sweetly and continuously, resounding like a very great trumpet; he delighted, without envy, the astonished ears and fixed attention of all the monks. When they came to that responsory [Note: [Col. 0041] “when they came to,” omitted in D.] which is brought by the *armarius* [Note: [Col. 0041D] The keeper of the monastery library, and likewise the precentor.] to the abbot for singing, the abbot signalled to the armarius to bring it to the aforementioned young man to sing in his place, where he stood at the end.

Guntram received with humility the obedience of singing the responsory; and by the marvellous novelty of his trumpet-like voice and the sweetness of his organ-like, flute-toned throat, he so delighted the entire choir and especially the abbot that, when the verse and the *Gloria Patri* had ended, the abbot immediately signalled him to come to him and ordered him to stand second from himself, instead of in the last place where he had stood. He remained there for some time, always held in greater admiration and reverence by everyone.

How he went thence to Hersfeld we do not know; but we have learned that he went there, because we know that he was made chamberlain to the abbot there [Note: [Col. 0042A] After erasing four lines, the interpolator inserted: “But after the tribulation which had befallen Lord Adelard the first, while the fellow-monks of this place, in exile, found lodging here and there in various monasteries, the aforementioned Guntram remained for a long time at the monastery of Hersfeld, situated in Thuringia, as a guest, and was made chamberlain to the abbot of that place. It is a place,” etc.]. It was a royal foundation, exceptionally renowned for the study of the liberal arts and of secular learning. We too stayed for some time with Frederick, abbot of that place [Note: [Col. 0041D] See the preface above concerning him.], and daily marvelled as if anew at the continual flood of his overflowing riches and the earnest effectiveness of the monks in the liberal arts.

The abbot’s chamberlain is not the same as the monks’ chamberlain. It is a high office, for he has abundant resources, commands the household servants, and receives, as it were, a third share of what is due to the abbot. While Guntram stayed there, the beauty of his person and the nobility of his character [Note: [Col. 0041] “and probity” added in D.] soon made him celebrated at the royal court, especially with the devout empress herself.

[Col. 0042A] 6. Meanwhile, the first Abbot Adelard, long since restored to our house and his office, died in 1034, having presided over the church for 35 years; and the news swiftly reached Hersfeld and the empress herself. Without delay, both parties deliberated how Guntram might be given the dignity of his native soil and the prelacy of his own house. Yet this was considered a small thing for so great a man [Note: [Col. 0041] “for so great a man” omitted in D.] [Note: [Col. 0041] “considered,” 1.], except that they maintained it would be much more pleasing and honourable to him to be exalted among his own [Col. 0042B] people than by an honour in a foreign land.

Hersfeld and the empress rejoiced in advancing him, but grieved that they should be deprived of such a great man. Therefore, honoured with great gifts by the abbot of Hersfeld [Note: [Col. 0041D] Bardo, abbot of Hersfeld from 1031 and made archbishop of Mainz in the same year. Meginher succeeded him at Hersfeld in 1035.], and especially by the empress herself [Note: [Col. 0041] Omitted in 1*.], he was sent to Metz with imperial and commendatory letters and an honourable escort, so that, with the bishop’s consent, he might be made abbot of our house—indeed, of his own house—without opposition.

Theoderic, then bishop of Metz, was considered the empress’s brother in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0042D] The author confuses Gisela, wife of Conrad II, with Saint Cunigunde. Cunigunde had already died on 3 March 1033; cf. *Annales Hildesheimenses*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS III. Her brother was Theoderic II, bishop of Metz. See also Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis S. Benedicti*, IV, 396.]. Thus, by God’s ordering, it happened that on one and the same day the empress’s envoys with Guntram and the delegation sent by the monks of our house appeared before the bishop. Having heard both embassies, the bishop postponed the matter until the next day. But after the two parties had withdrawn separately, when evening had become deeper, the bishop ordered two servants of his household to go ahead of Guntram to his lodging with the bishop’s gold candlesticks and lighted candles upon them. He also ordered those candlesticks to be left with Guntram as a gift for his service and honour; and from the episcopal court there were liberally sent whatever things he and his companions needed. Seeing this, the monks understood what was to happen; and in the morning they all cheerfully and unanimously agreed with the bishop that their fellow monk, the venerable Guntram, should be set over them.

7. Guntram was therefore made abbot at Metz and consecrated at Liège [Note: [Col. 0043A] “In the year of the Lord 1035, the ninth year of Conrad’s reign—second by name, but first by imperial anointing—and the eleventh year of Reginhard, bishop of Liège,” the interpolator 1* noted in the margin. [Col. 0043D] These particulars do not correspond accurately to Rudolf’s chronology.]. He found great poverty in our [Col. 0042D] house and little religious observance in our order. He promptly remedied both: the poverty from the gifts he had received from the empress and brought with him from the royal foundation, and the order through the strict discipline [Col. 0043A] he had learned at Hersfeld.

Soon the scattered monks returned, and some who had been in the secular world changed their habit and life among us. The place flourished most fragrantly with the venerable grey heads of religious elders and the diligent multitude of obedient young men. During the 21 years for which we know that he presided over it, our church grew greatly both in temporal goods and in spiritual renown.

8. In the final years of this man’s life, the tomb of our lord Saint Trudo began to shine with very frequent miracles, which he most diligently strove [Col. 0043B] to conceal. For, discerning shrewdly what was to come, he said that signs are given not to believers but to unbelievers (1 Cor. 14:22). Not long after him, certain of our people experienced this, for they were not afraid to offend God even amid the miracles themselves. But we who still survive, just as we did not see the scourges of God’s anger and indignation begin upon our house, so we still groan daily in deepest anxiety lest they have not yet ceased.

9. In the time of this Lord Abbot Guntram, the greater part of our tower was raised to the middle, together with both its vaults. Since, as we testified above concerning his youth, he was of elegant appearance, pleasing to men’s eyes in his tall stature and fitting bodily [Col. 0043C] bulk, and from this also [Note: [Col. 0043] “and from this also,” 1*.] very melodious in sweetly resonant song, the church of Liège [Note: [Col. 0043D] In Guntram’s time it was governed by the bishops Reginhard, Nithard, and Wazo.] granted him this honour: at its greatest solemnities he would be vested and would most honourably direct the choir from among [Note: [Col. 0043] “the middle,” 1*.] the singers, feeding the eyes of those present by the beauty of his great body and delighting the ears of his admirers by the sweetness of his trumpet-like voice.

What more need be said? No one like him arose in our house before him; whether anyone will arise after him, I do not know [Note: [Col. 0043] Omitted in 1*. “After he had presided for 21 years,” interpolator 1* inserted, after erasing the letter O.]. At last he died in the year 1055 of the Lord’s Incarnation, having confessed and been anointed. While the whole power of his mind still remained active, he wisely arranged his temporal estate upon the bed of his suffering and consoled his spiritual household in many ways. He left many gifts in silver, horses, [Col. 0044A] grain, and other provisions for his servants and household; and he left his monks food and clothing in the greatest abundance for more than the following year [Note: [Col. 0043] “he left” repeated in 1*.]. He lies buried in our church, now beside the outer part of the building toward the north, halfway along the wall joined to the monks’ enclosure.

10. Adelard the second succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0043] “In the same year,” interpolator 1* wrote above.], born of free parents in Brabant, from the village called Lovinium, near Louvain, and so named in diminutive form from it. From boyhood he was reared in our monastery under the abbots Adelard the first and Guntram. He was honourably educated, and not unskilled in carving and painting images. After holding several ecclesiastical offices, he was chosen abbot from the position of chief provost and consecrated.

He was held in great repute among secular people as abbot, abounding in wealth and incurring lavish expenses, since he had as lord the powerful and devout Albero [Note: [Col. 0043] Added in an erasure by a later second hand in 1.], bishop of Metz—namely Adalbero III, who held the see from 1046 to 1072, son of Duke Theoderic of Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0043D] See the genealogy of this family in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV, 348.]—brother of Duke Frederick [Note: [Col. 0043D] This is Frederick of Luxembourg, duke of Lower Lotharingia from 1048 to 1065. See Sigebert’s *Chronicle* and Stenzel, *Frankische Kaiser*, II, 119. Adalbero, bishop of Metz, and this Frederick were brothers, as Adalbero himself attests in a charter issued in 1065. Since this charter concerns the very *Deeds of the Trudonenses*, we shall give it in its proper place, though it has already been edited by others. The same charter shows that Frederick held the advocacy of the monastery of Saint Trudo through the benefice of his brother Adalbero, and that after Frederick’s death the bishop of Metz gave it to Udo, Frederick’s successor. This Udo, called in a charter of 1061 “the distinguished Count Udo of Limburg,” in Ernst’s *Histoire de Limbourg*, VI, 106, appears certainly to have been Frederick’s son-in-law and the father of Henry, count of Limburg, of whom more is said below; he was the same man who was also called Walmar, count of Arlon. Ernst, *loc. cit.*, seems to have demonstrated this beyond all doubt. See also below, V.3.].

No prince or advocate dared inflict any damage upon anything belonging to his bishopric. Rather, out of reverence and fear for his holiness—because the whole imperial court depended on him, and because his distinguished kinship extended throughout both kingdoms of Francia—our external goods were everywhere peacefully administered and increased. Moreover, the venerable Abbot Guntram had left him an abbey richly endowed [Col. 0044C] and filled with every good thing; secure in peace and abounding in possessions, he possessed it gloriously.

The tomb of blessed Trudo, too, contributed to increasing the magnitude of his wealth, daily shining with frequent and wonderful miracles. Their fame had spread throughout the whole world to such an extent that not only the circuit of the church but even the entire site of our town could scarcely contain the multitude of pilgrims. For almost half a mile from our town, along all the public roads leading to us in every direction, and across fields and meadows, so great a throng of pilgrims—nobles, free persons, and common people of both sexes—gathered almost daily, but especially on solemn days, that, dwelling in tents, leafy shelters, and curtained pavilions [Note: [Col. 0045D] Tents made from a certain kind of cloth called *cortina*.], they appeared to have besieged the whole town itself. The houses of the townspeople, already filled with others because of the multitude, could not hold them.

Then there was the abundance of merchants, who could scarcely bring on horses and carts, wagons and pack animals enough supplies to meet the needs of the pilgrim multitude. What shall I say of altar offerings? I shall pass over the animals—palfreys, oxen and cows, boars, rams, and sheep—which were offered in unbelievable numbers. But flax and wax, bread and cheeses, were reckoned by no weight, number, or price; silver thread and a heap of coins, scarcely exhausted when evening had already closed Olympus [Note: [Col. 0045D] Virgil, *Aeneid* I.374.], wearied very many guardians in receiving and storing them, and allowed them to do absolutely nothing else each day.

Thus the offering of pilgrims continually coming to the altar was not so much beyond counting as truly beyond estimation; and the name of blessed Trudo, with his most frequent and wonderful miracles, and our monastery, overflowing in riches, were more widely renowned than throughout the whole empire of the Roman world. For, if it is permitted to report truths even to those unwilling to believe them, the yearly revenue of the altar, rightly reckoned, was far greater than all the revenues of the abbey, whether then or now. This was true not for one or two years, but throughout the whole lifetime of this Abbot Adelard.

Secure in peace and abundance, therefore, he lived gloriously, with all in the kingdom showing reverence to us and ours: on the one hand because of the glorious miracles of the holy patron; on the other because of the power and nobility of our lord, the bishop of Metz, and of both those men. Whatever war [Note: [Col. 0045] “whatever war there was” omitted in D.] might be in the country [Note: [Col. 0046] “in an erasure,” 1; “in his own country,” D.], whatever discord in the kingdom, anyone who called himself the servant or handmaid of Saint Trudo travelled safely and dwelt safely upon his land.

The soldiers who, because of the attacks of their enemies, lived in our town after coming from the surrounding villages—though it was still without any wall or fortification—nevertheless remained in it with such security of peace that, if they had at some time advanced farther against their enemies and, as often happens, returned in flight, they received this favour of outstanding benefit through the merits and reverence of blessed Trudo: from the place at which the upper part of our monastery tower first became visible, their enemies ceased pursuing them.

11. Meanwhile, Abbot Adelard the second, carefully ensuring [Col. 0046A] that so great a yield of alms should not all go to idleness and luxury, did not allow the monastery—which seemed threatened with no collapse from either age or cracks—to be torn down through the rashness of presumptuous persons, monks as well as laymen. Instead, he had it rebuilt on a considerably greater scale in length and breadth, with a very strong wall and imposing columns, in an exceedingly beautiful work but at inestimable expense.

It was wonderful to see, and will be incredible to recount, from how far away and in how great a multitude, with what zeal and joy, people never ceased, night and day, to bring at their own expense and without payment, in wagons and carts, stones, lime, sand, timber, and everything necessary for the work. The very wall-stones and the great and exceedingly heavy stones set in the foundation [Col. 0046B] can faithfully testify to this: since such stones cannot be found in all Hesbaye, they are proved to have been brought from other regions.

Columns were brought by ship from Worms, down the Rhine to Cologne; other columns were brought from elsewhere in wagons. The people, village by village, eagerly hauled them onward, fastening ropes to the wagons, as though conveying them by land from Cologne to us. Without any aid from oxen or draft animals, they even carried them in groups across the bed of the Meuse itself, without a bridge, leading them to us with hymn-singing voices. What more? He saw the walls completed and almost the whole structure covered by a roof, except for some portion between the greater tower and the large arch placed before it.

[Col. 0046C] 12. At the same time he laboured no less faithfully to build churches throughout the abbey’s estates and to purchase noble villages and properties for our church from the altar offerings. He acquired for our church, buying it for 700 marks from Count Bruno of Hengebach, the half that we have in Villers [Note: [Col. 0045D] Perhaps Ville-en-Waret in the county of Namur, not far from Huy?] and all that we have in Moscha [Note: [Col. 0046D] Perhaps Moxhe or Moha, in the territory of Liège on the left bank of the Meuse?]. Likewise, he bought the whole village of Stades [Note: [Col. 0046D] Staye, not far from Saint Trond.] for 100 marks from Duke Frederick; and he acquired all that we have in Harches [Note: [Col. 0046D] Herk, on the river Herk, between Diest and Hasselt.] from Albert, count of Musal, together with a part of what we possess in Sarchinium.

For these things, however, he alienated much from the church treasury: among other things, a gold chalice of great weight and the gold frontal from the shrine of Saint Trudo. He also placed certain mills in pledge, and, overtaken by death, could not redeem them. The churches which he newly built throughout the abbey’s estates, or helped to rebuild in part, are these, by number and name: first, our greater church; second, Saint Mary Ever-Virgin’s in our town; third, Saint Gengulf the martyr’s in the same place; [Col. 0047A] fourth, at Alburg [Note: [Col. 0047C] According to Stepelinus, who wrote the miracles of Saint Trudo, in the district of Masau; see Ghesquier, I, 55.]; fifth, at Guimala; sixth, at Pire; seventh, at Scafe [Note: [Col. 0047C] Schaffen.]; eighth, at Guebechem [Note: [Col. 0047C] Webecom, not far from Diest.]; ninth, at Dunch [Note: [Col. 0047C] Donck.]; tenth, at Stades; eleventh, at Mere; twelfth, at Bevinges [Note: [Col. 0047C] Beringen in the province of Limburg, not far from Diest.]; thirteenth, at Horel; fourteenth, at Jemapia [Note: [Col. 0047C] Genappe in Brabant.]. He also had our house at Liège rebuilt from its foundations.

Although he willingly busied himself [Note: [Col. 0047] “although,” 1 and D; “while,” 1*.] with so many and such great works—works capable of draining even the imperial treasury—yet he was no less harassed by the lords of our church and by the tyrannical princes of the land, through frequent provisions demanded of him [Note: [Col. 0048C] A banquet which a vassal must provide for his lord at specified times.] and most burdensome exactions. Although the yield of altar offerings could sometimes be reckoned at one hundred pounds in a week, apart from what the audacious deceit of the custodians and the harmful rapacity of wicked hands had alienated here and there, still [Col. 0047B] amid these various cares and expenses he often appeared needy, and was needy in a more intolerable way because no one believed him on that account.

For Adalbero, bishop of Metz, of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0047] “the second” added in D and by a later hand in 1*.]—brother, as I said, of Duke Frederick; wall, arms, and peace after God and the saints; and the joyful abundance of our monastery—had now died. His successor Herimann [Note: [Col. 0048C] He held office from 1072 to 1090; see Lambert and Bernold.], because of the dissension he had stirred up against Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0047] “that is, Henry”; a later hand adds “IV” in 1*.]—the one who, much later, when almost all these men were already dead, died as a refugee at Liège during the persecution of his son—daily, as it were, stripped the abbot to the bone with most grievous demands. He forced churches and [Col. 0048A] revenues into the hands of his own beneficiaries, to their greater loss and ruin.

Once, when Adelard had been forcibly dragged to Metz at his command, Herimann dismissed him so heavily burdened with remembrance of it that Adelard there humbly prayed to the blessed protomartyr that he might first rest at home in the sleep of death rather than return again to Metz and fall once more into the violent hands of Herimann’s judgment.

Henry, bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0048C] 1075–1091; cf. *Annales Leodienses*.], Herimann’s contemporary, also very often summoned him to his court and grievously frightened him, ultimately allowing him no peace without very serious loss. For although his entire head shone white with grey hair and, as he declined into old age, seemed to remove from his enemies every suspicion concerning his private life, he was nevertheless not altogether regarded favourably by him. Whether this resulted from true or false accusations of men [Col. 0048B], no one knows better than the Lord God.

He gave much from the abbey as benefices to his own men, and, trusting in the altar offerings, he neither left nor established anything to serve the lights or other needs of the monastery. By then he was weary of living, since neither the altar offering nor the abundant yield of the then most richly endowed abbey could satisfy his oppressive anxiety. He would have resigned his office, intending to retire to Siegburg [Note: [Col. 0048C] A monastery of stricter discipline, founded by Anno on the river Sieg.], had not the care and devotion of his provost, named Gerard, held him back. At last he rested in peace in the year 1082 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0047] “8 December,” written above by interpolator 1*.], having presided over our church for 27 years.

**HERE ENDS THE FIRST BOOK** [Note: [Col. 0047] Omitted in D.]; **THE SECOND BEGINS.**

[Col. 0047]

[Col. 0047C] 1. After the death of Abbot Adelard II, most grievous evils and pains exceeding the pain of a woman in childbirth seized our church—such as have never been heard of in the whole world since the famous destruction of Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian. I judged it fitting to recount them in this second book from a loftier starting-point, so that the straight path of truth, set out in order, might relieve the traveller burdened by a long, level road.

For the Lord God, exceedingly merciful and of most patient forbearance, did not overthrow the condition of our church in hasty anger or in a sudden whirlwind of wrath; but [Note: [Col. 0047] “but … by terror” is lacking in D.] for a very long time he endured much, in mercy, and terrified it for many years by the continual and fearful dread of signs and miracles. But those who then lived abused God’s patience to their own reproach, stretching their lives ever further into luxury and idleness; and thus, through their blindness and contempt for God’s mercy, they at last did violence to his patience and forbearance. For—what is most dangerous and the greatest incitement to God’s wrath—they refused to understand that God’s scourge had come upon them because of their sins, and regarded only the contempt of those men through whom God was punishing them. Consequently, when at last they were driven by the intolerable whirlwind of God’s judgments, they were scattered to different regions of the earth and were exiled in body far more widely than they had previously been tossed about by an infamous name.

2. Therefore, as I said above, the miracles at the tomb of blessed Trudo were kept concealed, so far as this was possible and human effort could accomplish it, until a few years before the death of Lord Abbot Guntram. For, as a prudent man, he understood that they did not occur by his own merits or those of his brethren, but were a warning for the correction of his own life and character and those of his community [Note: [Col. 0049] *que* is lacking in 1*.], since he had read that signs are given to unbelievers, not believers. He therefore strove as much as possible to increase both the number and the merit of the brethren. Accordingly, from the most generous hand of the almighty Giver he obtained this blessing: that throughout all the days of his life peace and abundance accompanied his zealous religious observance.

But after his death (A.D. 1055), when Abbot Adelard II succeeded him, the miracles and powers of the tomb of blessed Trudo began to be treated less as an occasion for fear and reverence than for display and popular glory. An innumerable multitude of pilgrims frequented his tomb. They arrived not merely every day, but at every hour and instant of each day; and in the middle of the night there arose a loud disturbance of people coming and going. Whether the brethren wished it or not, they broke into every part of the cloister, especially because drinking the water of our well—which still survives—was said to bring healing when taken in the name of Saint Trudo, and did bring it to the sick who approached it. Lepers also are reported sometimes to have been cured there after washing in it.

Why say more? The oratory, choir, church, cloister, and meadow could not be found empty of the crowd by night or day. The continual disturbance of these noisy people caused great inconvenience and impeded the observance of the elders, who were accustomed and desirous to serve God in quiet and silence. But the younger men, to whom religious life was tedious and discipline hateful, first rejoiced secretly that this apparent necessity allowed them to disregard the commands of their mistress, the Rule. As time passed and familiarity with the throng of strangers became constant, they finally began openly and shamelessly to do everything as they pleased. They indiscriminately abused the various places and the alternation of both suitable and unsuitable hours; they rejected the rebukes of their elders with resentful hauteur; at times they behaved insolently and improperly even toward the abbot himself. Meanwhile, they zealously pursued illicit private possessions—what is the deeply rooted seed of all ruin in a monk’s soul, and the supreme destruction of an outward observance, scarcely ever to be escaped—and they did not refrain even moderately from access by secular persons, daring what was not expedient.

Thus some were unbridled by the swelling recollection of proud blood; others were inflamed by the prompting of the same arrogance, sometimes muttered seductively, sometimes voiced openly as a reproach. Their impunity made others, inferior in courage and birth, bolder to commit similar or even greater offenses, and made them more impatient if, perhaps deceived, they were deservedly punished by the sentence of regular discipline.

[Col. 0050A] 3. To this ruinous precipice of a church destined to perish there was added a great, as I might say, inducement to slipping: namely, that holy and religious men, who had been nurtured under Abbot Guntram’s discipline, were being taken from this life every day. The more their number diminished, the more presumption and indiscipline gained strength. Those of them who remained were very few; they lived in sorrow for themselves alone and did not dare to utter a word about the insolence of the young men. Why should I be restrained by shame and reverence for our order? The farther the glorious fame of Saint Trudo’s miracles was carried abroad in the reports of pilgrims, the more our secular-mindedness was reproached because of the frivolity of our conduct and the abuse of indiscipline. For every opportunity was available to those of our order who wished to perish, both from the coming and going of the foreign crowd, as I have said, and from the vast extent of the broken-down monastery requiring restoration.

4. And since blessed Benedict testifies that whatever is done wrongly by disciples concerns the abbot, the merciful and prudent guardian of our salvation stretched forth his hand to strike Abbot Adelard. For, acting far more leniently than was necessary for souls, he did not set himself against so great a danger to souls, to avert the destruction of God’s impending wrath. Therefore the Lord struck him and deprived him of reason, so that, amid the signs and miracles by which he daily warned through blessed Trudo that the lives of our brethren must be amended, he might also terrify the brethren thus warned, and make those whom he had terrified perceive that he had been deprived of reason because of their sins—the man by whose guidance they ought to have directed their wavering steps.

He was therefore taken to Liège, to the monastery of Saint Lawrence. After spending many days there in the crypt of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, behaving as madmen do, he at last deserved to be healed, through her intercession, at the tomb of Bishop Wulbodon. [Note: [Col. 0049D] He was bishop of Liège and died in 1021.] Yet not even so did the blindness of our people choose to perceive with what mercy and prudence divine compassion was extending to them the hand of mercy, warning the whole body of danger through the scourging of its head. Rather, they were borne onward with irresistible impulse toward everything that they desired and enjoyed, taking, as I said above, their opportunity from the clamorous crowd of pilgrims and from the vast scale of the broken monastery.

Then, if any person lacked anything for his own desire, the most lavish offerings at Saint Trudo’s tomb supplied each man, as he pleased, for the itch of his appetite. They took no care to keep their guilty hands from so great a sacrilege. These matters could not remain wholly hidden from our lords, the bishops of Metz and Liège; indeed, on the denunciation of enemies they began to believe things greatly exceeding the truth, and to burden the abbot beyond his capacity with most severe exactions and frequent hearings.

For the clerics whom the foolish indulgence of the abbot and elders had reared from childhood among our schoolboys for their own ruin spread abroad through many mouths a matter only too well known to them from their earliest intimacy, with worse embellishment. By letters sent at one time and personal representations at another, they most vehemently incited the bishops themselves to expel us all and introduce other monks. Their shameless tongues and still more shameless letters proved more ruinous, as I have said, to us who had educated them than all other informers and than rumor itself, which constantly enlarged the matter.

[Col. 0051B] Hence it came about that the two aforementioned bishops—Herimann of Metz and Heynricus of Liège—conspired in a common plan: if Abbot Adelard II, still living, should die, no abbot from among our own brethren should ever be given to us; rather, in order to eliminate their irreligiousness, some other religious man should be introduced. This was indeed a good and useful plan, if it had been carried out under the guidance of discretion rather than vindictive anger. Why say more?

5. On the eighth day before the Ides of December, Abbot Adelard II died. The election of the brethren was rejected at Metz. On the third [Note: [Col. 0051D] “Thirteenth,” D.] day before the Ides of August, a meeting was held in our chapter-house by both bishops, together with religious clerics and monks. Berengarius, abbot of Saint Lawrence, was present [Note: [Col. 0051D] He had governed his monastery since 1076; cf. Rupert, *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence of Liège*, ch. 44.], as was Franco, a man of great life and reputation, the devout master of the school of Saint Lambert. [Note: [Col. 0052D] On him see *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IX, 2.]

Before all who were assembled, letters of denunciation sent by those wicked clerics, our ill-chosen intimates, were read aloud. To these were added various additional and most shameful accusations against this man and that man among us. Then, because of this infamy, all the brethren together were ordered to be carried far and wide into exile among different monasteries. The whole weight of that day’s chapter was turned against us. For there was no one to pity those upon whom the long-suffering Lord, angered at last against men already hardened through their own blindness, was now bringing punishment.

Yet, after a hearing was sought and scarcely obtained, one man answered for all:

6. “Although our sins, O our lords and bishops, and you, holy assembly of clerics and religious abbots and monks, estrange your merciful hearts from compassion for us, nevertheless the rule of justice and of a merciful judgment ought never to be separated from the universal mother of virtues, holy discretion. If we have hitherto departed in any degree from the Rule of Saint Benedict which we profess, we believe that the Rule was given to monks so that violation of the Rule may be corrected by its own authority and sentence—yet according to that same Rule, so that, as rust is scraped from a vessel, the vessel of human frailty may not be utterly shattered.

“Although our sins have deserved it, we recognize—albeit late—that we have become a reproach to all around us. Yet not everything is true which hostile tongues, belonging to those who hate us, say against us. Therefore, if this is canonical, consonant with our Rule, owed to your religious calling, and most customary in ecclesiastical practice, give us, we pray and implore with minds and bodies bowed low—give, we beg, most merciful lords—an abbot, since ours has died.

“When he has been given us, we are prepared, under the guidance of the Rule and at his direction [Note: [Col. 0052D] That is, the abbot.], and with you present as well if you please, to make satisfaction and correction concerning all matters by which we have been defamed and of which we are accused today, whether the accusations be false or true. If we ought first to answer anyone concerning these things, let this holy assembly of yours decide it. Our own elected man, not only free from guilt but from every evil suspicion as well, cannot be rejected on any authority. But if he is rejected because of accusations against us alone, though they be false, let any other man whom you please be given to us. We do not object; indeed, we willingly consent, provided that, having a head, we may be cleansed and corrected under his eyes in the matters of which we are accused, whether in his presence or absence.”

[Col. 0052C] 7. That elected man was indeed an excellent person: a prudent and religious monk, highly learned in human and divine literature, long the provost of our house, named Gerard, one of the still surviving disciples of Abbot Guntram. But so great—shameful to say! [Note: [Col. 0051D] D reads “grief.”]—was the infamy of those electing him that prejudice prevailed over the merits of the man elected. And because, abusing God’s kindness and patience, they had for a long time turned the ear of their hearts away from his cry, they could not obtain the result of their petition—though just, though regular—by God’s just judgment. Why say more? The chapter was finally dissolved that day amid great anger and indignation on the part of the bishops.

8. Although they pretended not to feel themselves pressed by reason and regular authority, they nevertheless groaned inwardly. Yet, as ministers of wrath and the rod of the Lord’s anger against us, they could not consent even if willing. They therefore exerted themselves throughout that day to ensure that those who resisted being taken into exile should be driven by force and disgracefully from monastery and town on the next day, so that, once expelled, they might be received by no one in human compassion, not even as guests.

The bishop of Liège, Haynricus, went out in public clothed in episcopal vestments and, by proclamation, commanded all within his diocese neither to grant them lodging nor to refrain from plundering with impunity whatever they found them to possess when first encountering them. A thing pitiably miserable, and one which, unless it had occurred by God’s judgment, could be accepted under no judgment of God or men.

But lest we seem to condemn God’s hidden judgment in the judgment of these two bishops, let us reverently permit the just Judge, God, to punish our brethren’s sins through them. Let us only state truly, to their misery, that, although they did not understand [Note: [Col. 0053] D reads “being indulgent.”] that they were ministers of God’s wrath and the rod of the Lord’s anger, they nevertheless deserved to be so, and to punish the sins of others because of their own sins—and to do this not merely without respect for the monastic order, but even without compassion for sinful human beings in their most extreme human necessity. [Note: [Col. 0053] D reads “necessity.”]

For what Rule, what canon, what order, what laws authorize this: that monks, after their abbot’s death, who regularly ask for an abbot and wish, according to their Rule, either to clear themselves or to correct whatever rumor falsely alleges or truth testifies [Note: [Col. 0053] 1* reads “forbids.”] concerning them, should be compelled by a bishop to go into exile before an abbot has been given them; and that, unless they consent, all Christians in the diocese should be forbidden by episcopal vestment and proclamation to receive them as guests?

But let us, as we have said, reverently accept God’s just judgment within the unjust judgment of these men. And let us believe without doubt that God’s mercy is nearer to those whom he deigns to scourge in correcting them than to those whom he has chosen to be ministers of his wrath and rods of his anger—provided that the former know, in the humility of their conscience, how to accept God’s correction.

[Col. 0053C] 9. Therefore the bishops, neither yielding to the just petition of our brethren nor understanding that God was persecuting our brethren in them for both their sins and ours, despised our worthy election—an election which could not be rejected on any regular objection. As they had long resolved, on the following day they introduced into our monastery, before the astonished eyes of the monks, one Lanzo, abbot from the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz: a religious man indeed and most renowned among religious men. Yet nothing would have been detracted from his religious character if he had abstained from governing our monastery until canonical authority had drawn even an unwilling man to it.

10. For unless the authorities of the apostolic see deceive me—namely, Pope Celestine’s decree, and likewise Pope Nicholas’ repeated statement to Charles, king of the Franks, and Egilo, bishop of Sens [Note: [Col. 0053] Nicholas I, Epistle 20, Mansi XV, 391; Nicholas I, Epistle 21, Appendix in Mansi XV, 393. From “Only then” through “reward” are words of Celestine I.]—it is unlawful for anyone to intrude into another’s service and for one coming sideways into a camp in which he has not served to seize its command. Only then is one to be chosen from another church, if no worthy man can be found among the clerics or monks of that city to be ordained. For men of that church must first be sought [Note: [Col. 0053] Mansi reads “rejected.”] before [Note: [Col. 0053] Mansi reads “that.”] any are preferred from foreign churches.

“Let each person have the fruit of his own service in the church in which he has spent his life above all in its duties. Let no one intrude into another’s service, nor dare to claim for himself another’s reward due to another.” [Note: [Col. 0053] *alter* is lacking in 1*.] These are the authorities of the apostolic see.

11. But if anyone attempts to defend this lord and religious man, Abbot Lanzo, on the ground that the two bishops consented to his forcible elevation over us because of his renowned religious character, let him hear himself refuted by this authority of the same Pope Nicholas, addressed to the same Egilo: “What support,” he says, “does the consent of bishops provide where it is assembled not in accordance with the paternal rules but against the rules?” And shortly afterward: “Whatever gift of holiness anyone may possess, he ought not to seize the labors of others, since he is commanded in no way to covet any of his neighbor’s possessions. For by the very act by which someone takes away rights belonging to another, holiness loses its grace. For what holiness claims a reward owed to another? What holiness usurps for itself the fruits of another?”

Against these ecclesiastical authorities and prohibitions of the apostolic see, Lord Abbot Lanzo was introduced over us—though holy, though just, though religious, though supported by the consent of the two bishops—because our brethren’s sins had so deserved. Nevertheless, the grant of temporal possessions and the charge of souls entrusted to him were deferred by the bishops until the ninth day before the Kalends of September.

On the day of the chapter all our brethren assembled in the choir for Vespers, adorning it with handsome men of high rank and learning, thoroughly trained in every duty of ecclesiastical observance. A church was indeed blessed in possessing so many, such, and so great men, if they had not had God the Father angered against them because of their sins, or if they had known how to bear his anger in humility of heart and contrition of flesh. But why delay?

[Col. 0054C] 12. That same night, learning from friends that they would be forcibly and shamefully driven into exile on the next day if found in the cloister, they were overcome by fear—and, as human nature is, especially the fearful simplicity of monks—and sought safety in flight. Only one of them, named Luipo, choosing exile rather than flight, was sent to Liège under Abbot Berengarius at Saint Lawrence. Very few remained with Abbot Lanzo: namely Gerard, the provost whom our brethren had elected, also Bligerus, the elder Herimann together with another Herimann, his nephew, and Engo, who shortly afterward was sent into exile at Metz. Most of the others were scattered through Flanders and England, Denmark and Saxony, and the kingdom of the Germans.

A very small group, retaining their monastic habit, found lodging in various monasteries. The greater group, retaining nothing of the monk, wandered through different parishes in the manner of priests. And after God’s wrath had been appeased toward our house and he had restored to our brethren the grace of his mercy, we saw some of them grow old among clerics, dressed as clerics and in the order of canons: at Liège, in the monasteries of Holy Cross and Saint John; at Cologne, in the monastery of Saint George.

13. Meanwhile Abbot Lanzo, supported by the authority of the two bishops, began vigorously to administer our temporal and spiritual affairs, having summoned to himself a multitude of religious monks from the region of Metz. [Note: [Col. 0055] 1* reads “from the people of Metz.”] But, by what hidden judgment of God we do not know, he was divinely crushed by a most grievous adversity [Note: [Col. 0055] “In the year of the Lord 1085 Abbot Lanzo was grievously crushed,” wrote the interpolator in 1*, after two lines had been erased.], perhaps because he had been raised too high by human prosperity.

For in the third year of his authority over us [Note: [Col. 0055D] That is, A.D. 1086. If, as the following narrative indicates, the monastery really burned in 1085, the author erred in reckoning the abbot’s years: it was the second year. See also below IX.29; X.15.], on the seventh day before the Ides of March (A.D. 1085), that wonderful and most beautiful structure of our monastery fell in flames. The pious care of Abbot Adelard II had almost completed it, with columns unequalled in our land and roofing nearly impossible to reproduce. It was not, I say, misfortune, but—as I have said [Note: [Col. 0055] “as I have said” lacking in 1*.]—a hidden judgment of God: from one little house, though far distant, our monastery alone in the whole town was burned.

For a ball of burning straw, rising very high from the blaze-emitting fire of the little house, is said visibly to have fallen at last upon a stork’s nest on one of the two towers, the one beside the eastern apses on the south side.* Although the townspeople ran to the closed gate of the monastery, the brethren did not know the cause, and entrance was delayed for them so long that the unconquerable force of fire had occupied control of the entire building.

Thus that monastery fell—fell, that monastery the like of which our community will never again possess. Those marvelous columns, concerning which labor, expense, care, workmanship, beauty, and grandeur can scarcely be worthily described, were so utterly consumed and collapsed in the fire that of the twelve not one could be rebuilt resembling those that had gone before. But from so mournful a description we must now take a little breath; and, ending the second book, refresh the troubled mind in gentler leisure for beginning the third.

\* “Situated to the right of the chapel of Saint Trudo, at the upper edge,” added the interpolator in 1*.

**END OF BOOK TWO; BOOK THREE BEGINS.**

[Col. 0055]

[Col. 0055C] 1. While I am oppressed by the heavy pressure of my anxieties, I myself condemn as too thin and meanly torn whatever I seem to have woven into this ordered web. But what then? If the matter accomplished is not such as deserves to remain so, its very unworthiness will at least contribute this much: at some time it will compel an ashamed writer to change himself to a better style. Meanwhile, reader, observe what is written, not how well it is written.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1082, Abbot Adelard II died on the eighth day before the Ides of December. On the third day before the Ides of August, a chapter was held concerning our brethren by the two bishops, namely Herimann of Metz and Heinricus of Liège; on that night all our brethren were dispersed except the few whom I named above. [Note: [Col. 0055] D reads “whom we named.”] On the ninth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0055] The interpolator adds in an erasure: “in the following year.”], [Note: [Col. 0055D] It is clear from II.11 above that “September,” rather than “December,” which the manuscripts and d’Achéry give, is to be read.] Lanzo, abbot of Saint Vincent at Metz, undertook the governance of our abbey, in the manner [Note: [Col. 0055] D adds “mentioned.”] which I described in the second book. [Note: [Col. 0055] “which I described” is lacking in D.] In the third year after his entry our monastery was burned, namely on the seventh day before the Ides of March in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1085. [Note: [Col. 0055] Thus D.]

Hildebrand, who was also called Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0055] D and interpolator 1* add “VII.”], and Henry [Note: [Col. 0055] A later hand in 1* adds “IV.”], emperor of the Romans, who died at Liège while fleeing the persecution of his son, were miserably tearing kingdom and priesthood apart in every direction by most grievous dissensions. Therefore the emperor, having held at Mainz a council of bishops favoring him [Note: [Col. 0055] An erasure in 1*.], and strengthened, as he thought, by the authority of his pope called Clement—namely the archbishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0055] D reads “of the people of Ravenna.”]—caused Herimann, bishop of Metz, to be condemned in that same council as a public enemy of the empire, because he seemed to follow Gregory against the emperor. He caused him to be deprived of the whole dominion of Metz, [Note: [Col. 0056D] See Sigebert for this year and Mansi XX, 613. On Walo see Hugh of Flavigny, *Chronicle*.] and appointed in his place as bishop a certain Walo, abbot of Saint Arnulf at Metz. [Note: [Col. 0055] D has *abbatem*; interpolator 1* has “a certain abbot.”] [Note: [Col. 0055] The interpolator 1* reads “appointed Walo, called bishop.”] [Note: [Col. 0055] The interpolator 1* reads “appointed.”]

\* “But before these years,” the interpolator in 1*, after one erased line.

[Col. 0057A] 2. Meanwhile Luipo, one of our brethren—the man, I mean, who had received the sentence of exile at Liège in Saint Lawrence’s monastery—escaped exile by flight, compelled to do so because he learned that the bishop of Liège intended to send him farther away into exile. Through all whom he believed could be useful to him, and even through the emperor himself, he approached Abbot Lanzo with every humility, asking to be received in the cloister where he had been nurtured so that he might live in the same order as the others. But he could obtain this in no way.

He lived sadly and sorrowfully with his relatives at Louvain, sometimes at Salechem and at other places—he had, after all, been nobly born—upon his patrimony. [Note: [Col. 0057] The interpolator in 1* adds: “He lived thus until the following year, namely 1086.”] But when he heard of the enmities that had arisen between the emperor and Herimann of Metz, and that the emperor held in his own hand the bishopric adjudged away from Herimann, with all its appurtenances, and likewise our abbey under the same title, [Note: [Col. 0058] D reads “his.”] he spoke with our brethren who were exiled at Ghent in the monastery of Saint Bavo; also with certain men who, having spent some time with Abbot Lanzo, had eventually escaped; and likewise with some who were still with him. To pass over much that occurred here and there in the meantime, he finally obtained from the emperor the grant of our abbey from the emperor’s hand, and was introduced into it by two of the emperor’s counts: Gerard of the castle called Guassenberge [Note: [Col. 0058] 1* reads “Guastenberge.”], and his maternal uncle Gozwin, of the castle called Heinesberge.

These things seemed to be done for this reason: Lord Lanzo had entered without election and been imposed over the brethren’s election; and the bishopric of Metz, which appeared to have been taken from Herimann, was in the emperor’s hand, to whose head our abbey was attached. [Note: [Col. 0058D] 1* reads “was attached.”] Therefore the emperor seemed able to remove Lanzo as an intruder and give our brethren their chosen man.

Yet in our judgment this reasoning does not hold together. If anything had been done against the canons by the bishops against our brethren, Lanzo ought first to have been restrained by apostolic authority, rather than by the emperor’s unlawful power. But among mortals nothing is done justly and reasonably through mortals when God the just Judge, the rule of reason and justice, rises in anger after his patience has been overcome. Yet by this reasoning and in this manner Luipo first seemed to enter our abbey. Whether he then and later entered freely and through the door will be shown by the following events of his undertaking.

He entered on the seventh day before the Kalends of June (A.D. 1085), in a great display of soldiers, on the Monday of Rogation Days. Fearing Luipo’s tyranny, Lanzo kept himself within the walls and, occupying the tower with a few monks, made it his refuge for life. He was the first to make our tower a safeguard for his life. This later became a most destructive precedent for our people: trusting in so great a refuge, they rebelled to the destruction of our whole house. Yet the religious man did not understand it in this way [Note: [Col. 0057] Lacking in 1*.] when he climbed into it, for he had no thought except of preserving his life until he could escape safely with the bishop’s help.

But our people were seditious and most prone to every kind of disorder and division. They could readily remember this man’s necessity for evil purposes when an opportunity for rebellion and making accusations was offered them. Hence we ourselves at one time remembered, and afterward saw before our eyes, not only our entire town burned by fire, but also many most miserable events occurring there because of this tower, with a great shedding of human blood. [Note: [Col. 0057D] Cf. X.14–15.]

[Col. 0058B] 3. Therefore some of our brethren, who unwillingly endured Abbot Lanzo’s authority, immediately turned to Luipo. Almost all those endowed with church benefices, as well as the townsmen, swore allegiance to him. Meanwhile Lanzo celebrated the Rogation litanies [Note: [Col. 0057D] They are celebrated before Christ’s Ascension.] within the walls of the church with a few monks; Luipo celebrated them in the fields, as is customary, with many of our brethren and a crowd of laypeople.

We have found our people most ready for such seditions, easily swerving now this way, now that, even down to our own time; and we have sometimes experienced this most severely, for as long as even one of our monks remained who contrived to contend for our abbey. Why delay? At last Luipo’s men broke down the monastery doors leading toward the cloister and did not permit Abbot Lanzo, forced within the tower, to go out.

We have heard that he suffered such privation there that for several days poor little women fed him through the windows with coarse, dry bread and revived him with a very small vessel of water. [Note: [Col. 0057] 1* has “and revived.”] Thus and thus, these and other things were done between them for fifteen days. At last, on the fifteenth day, which was the Monday of Pentecost, namely the fifth day before the Ides of June, the bishop of Liège sent Abbot Berengarius from the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège. By a simple stratagem he rescued Abbot Lanzo from our tower and had him remain with that abbot at Liège in Saint Lawrence’s monastery.

He also made all that we appear to possess at Sesnin [Note: [Col. 0058] 1* reads “Seni”; D reads “Sesuin.”] [Note: [Col. 0058D] Seny, not far from Huy.], Jemeppe, Villers, and Oreye [Note: [Col. 0058D] Oreye, between Saint-Trond and Liège.] serve him there, while deciding what to do with Luipo.

After this Luipo immediately set out for Metz. There, in the presence of many of our brethren and of the leading townsmen, he restored the pastoral staff to Walo, who was said to be bishop there in place of Herimann, and received it back from him. The bishop of Liège complained to his abbots, archdeacons, and the entire church concerning this presumption of Luipo [Note: [Col. 0058] D reads “concerning this presumption.”] and his contempt for the church of Saint Lambert. By their judgment he excommunicated Luipo, together with all who adhered to him, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, namely the octave of Pentecost.

### 4

Alas, alas! Now, now the subject grows weightier: the most miserable account of our miseries. Beneath its burden, the mind, crushed by its own dullness, makes the pen dull as well, and, horrified by the shapeless monster and enormity of the subject, fears to come forth into the light. For here it must be told how, scarcely two years after that first and pitiable ruin of our temple, caused by a flame once thought wondrous, and while the temple’s ashes were still, as it were, warm, our entire town collapsed into something like a single spark, and how human blood not only defiled the temple’s half-burned and half-ruined walls, but also spattered higher and more abundantly over the very steps of the altars. [Col. 0059B]

What, then, was Luipo to do? He saw that Bishop Henry was altogether inexorable toward him; therefore he referred his case again and again to the emperor. The emperor, heavily occupied with his troubled kingdom and priesthood, deferred his case until the court at Aachen. A court was held at Christmas (A.D. 1087); the bishop and Luipo were present. There was a long conflict of words between them, both before and after the emperor. At last the bishop yielded, conquered more by fear of the emperor than by law. Luipo and all his associates were released from excommunication. Meanwhile, however, divine office was forbidden to all our brethren, until Luipo, having been granted safe-conduct and coming to a hearing, might be peaceably examined at Liège, if in some way the emperor’s petition concerning him could be carried out.
