Although, when the appointed day pressed, Luipo saw that he lacked the safe-conduct—namely, Conrad, bishop of Upper Utrecht, who had been promised to him before the emperor—he nevertheless proceeded on the appointed day. The servants of the bishop of Liège, lying in ambush for him near the village of Jupille, close to Liège [Note: Jupille on the Meuse, on its right bank.], severely beat and robbed him; yet they did not wholly deter him from his intended journey. The council sat; Luipo was ordered to enter. He did not refuse, provided that the possessions of which he had been robbed were restored to him and that the promised safe-conduct, who was to introduce him, should be present. Called again and again, and even a third time, he refused to come for the reason stated above; at last he was excommunicated. [Col. 0059D] Thus, sad, he returned to the cloister, arranged his domestic affairs, and immediately went back to the emperor. [Note: At this point, “Then Liupo, grieving, …”; interpolated in an erasure, 1*.]

Without delay, his supporters, having taken counsel together, resolved to fortify our tower and prepared whatever seemed necessary for fortification and siege. For such a task were chosen very daring young men, of great strength in body and kinship, but of very little judgment: so that, if the bishop of Liège wished to restore Abbot Lanzo, fear of the tower occupied by them might keep him from returning until their lord Luipo should return from the emperor after making peace. So great, by God’s judgment, was the blindness of those who seemed wiser and older in our town that they would not consider what a most evil end would result when the house of God, with their cooperation, consent, or failure to resist, was made a garrison of soldiers—indeed, a den of robbers and a refuge of sacrilegious men. [Col. 0060A]

Meanwhile these new castellans began to occupy the fortification they had built for themselves, with great contempt for God and abuse of ecclesiastical property. For with curtains and tapestries, of which our church then had many and precious ones, they covered on every side the exterior walkways of their new construction around the tower, sheltering themselves beneath and around them from the heat of the summer sun, and there drinking, eating, and sleeping luxuriously. [Col. 0060B]

They had joined to their fortification, as if it were an outer defensive work, the space of the monastery from the tower to the first arch before the tower itself; and through the windows of three towers set together, by means of huge beams stretched far outward, they had arranged a pleasant-looking walkway around the outside of the towers. There, as I have said, they most luxuriously abused curtains, tapestries, and other ecclesiastical utensils.

They also caused the rent and provisions belonging to the brethren’s prebend to serve their gluttony and lust with excessive prodigality. For scarcely eight brethren in all, great and small, then remained among us. Those who feared God were lodged, by arrangement of the bishop of Liège, in other monasteries; some, having cast aside their monastic clothing, lived in exile in clerical dress. But some of those who had remained with Luipo were not merely instigators but also accomplices in all these evils, and together with the fury of the seditious boiled up like oil in the fire of mad rebellion. [Col. 0060C]

### 5

When the leading townsmen wished—far too late—to restrain the insolence of those tower-men [Note: “of the tower-men” is absent in 1*.], they could no longer do so by any means; for, trusting in kinship, arms, and a strong and well-paid fortification, they were no longer willing, except unwillingly, to return from the excesses into which they had gone. Hence quarrels frequently arose among them, and bloody fighting took place in the middle of the market-place and within the very court. [Note: A passage is lacking in 1*.]

Then at last the multitude of pilgrims began to cease, who, as I said above [Note: “I said,” 1*.], had been accustomed to bring offerings daily to the tomb of blessed Trudo in a kind of rivalry. On the one hand, the horror of a warlike—indeed diabolical—appearance, which those robbers [Note: “robbers” is absent in 1*.] had imposed upon the house of God from their armed tower, discouraged them; on the other, the episcopal interdict frightened them, declaring that those sacrilegious men ought not to be supported from the offerings of the faithful. Why should I delay longer? [Col. 0060D]

### 6

Provoked by these and innumerable other acts of presumption by our people, the bishop of Liège at last moved an army to storm, no longer the church’s tower, but a den of robbers. Accordingly, on the Nones of July, Monday, he laid siege to our town and himself took his position before the gate which leads toward Sarchinium. [Col. 0061A] [Note: “In the same year of the Lord, namely 1086, which was Lanzo’s fourth year in this abbey,” added by the interpolator in the lower margin, 1*.]

At that time our whole town was fortified with a very strong rampart and crowned above with very stout posts and large planks [Note: “small beams,” D.]; over each gate wooden towers had been built, rising higher, floored through the middle, and clad all around with extremely strong wickerwork, impenetrable to the tips of arrows. Moreover, the monastery tower, very strong and rising like a high citadel in the middle of the town, stood like a mountain—the sort of structure that at that time would not have suited a monastery, but rather a most warlike city or a royal castle.

Then there was the monastery’s very strong wall, which, though its roofs had been burned in the preceding year, still stood wholly bare; by its long outer circuit and its wide inner space it provided most suitable and secure refuges for those living in the tower. [Col. 0061B]

Relying on these fortifications, as well as on the very great multitude of warlike and exceedingly bold men in which our town is known always to have abounded, on the first day of the siege they made frequent and exceedingly rash sorties against the army, so that they forced the bishop to change his position and summon a greater number of his men. They might not have feared that siege greatly, had they not, because of their unjust cause and the profanation of the house of God, possessed God as an avenging assailant. [Col. 0061C]

### 7

Accordingly, on the very next day [Note: 8 July, added by the interpolator in an erasure, 1*.], a dissension arose among them: some muttered about surrender, others cried out for resistance. Thus, against the will of those who had occupied the tower, others who now regretted their undertaking gave hostages to the bishop, on condition that, with their possessions and persons granted safety, the bishop should withdraw from the siege and the townsmen from rebellion.

But what prudence, what counsel, can finally escape the judgment of God’s wrathful judgment? For even repentance itself can sometimes be fruitless, when we regret an evil deed more because we may lose something of our temporal possessions than because we strive by satisfaction to appease the God whom we have offended.

At that time there was still a very grave and ancient feud, governed by the law of war, between the people of Brustem [Note: Brustem, a village near Saint-Trond.] and our people of Saint-Trond; now a lance, now an arrow, and most often a sword had consumed very many on either side, always including men among the better sort. [Col. 0061D] Therefore, when the people of Brustem learned that peace was being made between our people and the bishop, they took it very badly and dared to contrive, whatever it might be, for our destruction.

### 8

Setting aside the good faith under which the bishop had received our hostages, at the very hour when these had come before him, they leapt into our town by certain passages beyond the rampart. Our people suspected nothing less than this, because peace had been proclaimed and hostages already given, and therefore they were keeping themselves relaxed and had laid aside their arms.

First, then, fire was silently introduced; next, the foot-soldiers were stirred to the same purpose by shouts; finally the army invaded our entire town with fire and sword, in hope of plunder and desire to seize captives. They paid no heed to the bishop, protesting and almost left alone, who, unaware of the ambush planned by the people of Brustem, was deeply distressed on account of the hostages he had received. It is said that he shed tears and heaved a heavy sigh when he saw the victorious flame seize the church of blessed Mary ever Virgin. [Col. 0062A]

Although late in taking arms, our men nevertheless ran boldly to them. In streets, crossroads, and recesses of the roads better known to them than to their enemies, much enemy blood was shed. Yet, as the enemy continually hemmed them in here with fire and there with arms, a very severe battle was joined in the middle of the market-place. The clash of weapons and the groaning effusion of human blood made the face of that day grim and pitiable, and the whole expanse of the market-place horrible and bloody.

At last the multitude prevailed and forced our men back into the court. Alas, how much blood was shed there before our people could be driven within the gates of the monastery! For those upon the tower most wretchedly crushed the enemies near and far by every kind of defense; certain monks also, who lived with us long afterward [Note: “remained,” D.], armed themselves very vigorously for this necessary defense. [Col. 0062B–C]

### 9

It was pitiable to see, from the windows of the tower, the holy image of the Lord—that is, the holy Crucified One—hanging there, and the crowd in conflict shooting arrows at the exposed bier of Saint Eucherius. When those of our people who had survived flight or death had taken refuge within the church walls and closed the gates, the multitude of enemies, stirred by extreme grief for their slain and enticed by hope of greater plunder, began most carefully to search all around the monastery walls for some access to our people. At last, having broken through the wall on the south opposite the entrance to the crypt, and also through the windows, they began to burst into the monastery. [Col. 0062D]

Meanwhile our men, feigning fear and abandonment within by silence, allowed as many enemies as they wished to enter; then, making a sudden rush against them, they not only slaughtered them but, leaping upon the very altars, horribly sacrificed them there. Alas! There took place in the house of the Lord a most bloody slaughter, a most overflowing libation of human blood [Note: “human … overflowing” is absent in D.], so that, as great heaps of enemies cut to pieces limb by limb lay here and there and their entrails poured out, the insatiable rage of the furious sword’s point sprinkled not only walls and floors with human blood, but even polluted the altars and the tombs of Saints Trudo and Eucherius with the filth of torn-out intestines—alas, alas! [Col. 0063A]

Nor was this enough for this victory of ours, won so miserably. For here the still-living flame horribly licked round lifeless limbs cast into the surrounding fire [Note: “still living … licked round” is absent in D.]; there a heap of coals, made intensely hot by the conflagration, burned them miserably, with fetid stench and flowing gore.

Did your miracles portend this, blessed Trudo—those which had formerly occurred at your tomb for so many years, so numerous, so frequent, so stupendous, so glorious? They did indeed portend it. For when the negligence of our people’s life was not corrected by the gentle admonition of your miracles, but they rather, thoughtlessly puffed up, abused in luxury and sloth the inestimable fruit of offerings at the altar, they deserved at last to experience in themselves so terrifying and mournful a sentence of the judgments of God’s wrath. [Col. 0063B]

Long before, the sagacity of the prudent and religious Abbot Guntram had understood this. When these signs first began to occur in his time, he used to say on the authority of Holy Scripture that signs were first given to unbelievers, not to believers. Made humbler and more fearful by the divine admonition conveyed through those signs, he first took great pains to conceal the miracles occurring in his time, and then to correct his own life and that of his brethren—correction to which, he preached daily, those miracles exhorted them. Because our people refused to heed this, they were finally enveloped in the most wretched confusion of countenance which we have described. [Col. 0063C]

What more? Battle continued throughout the whole day. By the benefit of the intervening night, the enemies on both sides ceased. In our whole town not even the smallest house remained unconsumed by fire that day. That night all our survivors scattered in flight, since they had gathered nothing with which they could be supported in the monastery. The few who were in the tower, and who had been the greatest part of so many evils, although uncertain, did not yet withdraw that night; instead, having sent messengers to Count Arnulf of Looz, they handed the tower over to him. [Col. 0063D]

[Note: Arnulf IV, said to have been the son of Count Emmo of Looz, belonged to the family deriving its name from the castle of Looz, or Borgloon, near Saint-Trond, whose origins extend back to the tenth century. See Mantelius, *Historia Lossensis*, ed. Robyns, Liège, 1717, pp. 50, 84.]

### 10

Alas, alas! With what groans or what tears can I recount the still-glorious furnishings of our church’s treasure [Note: “on that day” is absent in D.], which had been carried into that tower, and how, by those surrendering and those receiving the tower, they were dispersed in what ways and in what quantities, and treated as objects of mockery—not only by men or matrons, but even by prostitutes and little women? On that day, on that very day, our church was stripped of all its inward and outward glory. [Col. 0063D–0064A]

The few monks who, because of extreme old age, could not leave the place during the siege, seeing the miserable appearance of the place within and without and nothing but ruin, except for a horrible solitude, tried somehow to leave. Taking the road toward Mergueles, they were seized, beaten, and robbed by our own most faithless people, never corrected by any judgment of God, and were sent to the bishop of Liège for punishment.

Among them were two men of great and handsome presence [Note: “men” is absent in 1*.], men thoroughly trained in letters and in the observance of our church. One was Prior Liebert, through whose diligence many excellent books are still kept in our library, and who had added many things to our church’s treasure; these, together with very many other goods in that devastation, were plundered by sacrilegious hands—not only by robbers, but also by our own people. [Col. 0064B]

The other was Stepelinus [Note: This is the man who, according to the third continuator, wrote in A.D. 1050 for Abbot Guntram a book *On the Miracles of Saint Trudo*, published by Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century VI, part 2; Ghesquier, V, 49, published several fragments from another manuscript.], whose burial we ourselves attended long afterward. The others somehow escaped, though most miserably. But the bishop, contrary to the expectation of our most faithless people, allowed them to depart unpunished; nevertheless, he forbade them his episcopal territory. [Col. 0064D]

### 11

These things happened on 8 July. Meanwhile Count Arnulf of Looz held the tower of our monastery as a garrison. When at last no boy, youth, old man, or monk remained in our monastery, and solitude, together with excessive horror, inhabited the naked and half-ruined walls of monastery and cloister day and night, it was exceedingly pitiable and mournful even for enemies to behold a spectacle so sad, mournful, and horrible in a house once so glorious. At evening, night, and morning hours, instead of the once-sweet choir of chanting monks, one heard there only the shrieks of bats and the ill-omened cries of owls.

Then the Lord’s threat through the prophet Isaiah concerning Babylon could most aptly have been spoken of it: “And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” (Isaiah 13:19).

And that of Jeremiah: “The Lord has cast down without sparing all the beauty of Jacob; in his fury he has destroyed its strongholds” (Lamentations 2:2). And below: “He has kindled in Jacob like a fire of devouring flame all around” (ibid., 2:3).

And a little later: “The Lord has become like an enemy; he has cast down Israel, he has cast down all its walls, he has destroyed its strongholds, and he has filled the daughter of Judah with the humbled man and the humbled woman. He has laid waste his tabernacle like a garden; he has destroyed his sanctuary. The Lord has caused feast and sabbath to be forgotten in Zion; in the indignation of his wrath he has despised king and priest. The Lord has rejected his altar; he has cursed his sanctuary; he has delivered into the hand of the enemy the walls of its towers” (ibid., 2:5–7). And a little above: “The enemy has stretched out his hand over all her desirable things” (Lamentations 1:10). [Col. 0064C–0065A]

### 12

I could proceed through almost the whole lamentation of Jeremiah over Jerusalem and find that it applies, even to the letter, most aptly to the lamentable misery of our church. For anyone who still now sees it inside and outside, though with much incredible labor and expense some part—indeed a great part—of the walls has been repaired, buildings rebuilt, property recovered, the number of brethren increased, and their order and life improved; and who had formerly been able to see it, while the church still flourished, in its beauty and the glory of its riches—has very little from which to console his sadness, since this is scarcely a shadow of its former glory.

But enough has been said here about these matters; let us return to the order of the narrative. [Col. 0065B] [Note: “But enough … let us return” is absent in D.]

### 13

Thus, while this misery, greater than we can describe, and this horror of solitude continued unceasingly in the monastery—apart from the soldiers of Count Arnulf, who, as a garrison in the tower, with profane presumption continually entered and left the monastery—the bishop of Liège at last took pity on the misery of the place, once so glorious and then so shameful. In the same year, shortly before August, he sent back to our place Provost Gerard, namely the man whom, as we said above, had been elected abbot. [Col. 0065C]

For when these evils had fallen upon our place, and Abbot Lanzo was living at Saint Lawrence’s in Liège—the bishop had placed him at Saint James’s in the same city, loving and honoring him as a prudent and religious man—he sent Gerard back, as I have said, before August, to build granaries, gather crops, and somehow repair a few small dwellings around the burned walls of the monastery. He was also to enclose the tomb of Saints Trudo and Eucherius within some sort of small chapel, and prepare a place in which brethren returning might begin to serve God and find some dwelling-place in which to remain.

When this had been done according to the time and resources of the place, the brethren began to return two by two—but only those who, execrating Luipo, had refused to abandon Lanzo. [Col. 0065D]

### 14

Abbot Lanzo, however [Note: “in the same year, namely 1086,” added by the interpolator in an erasure, 1*.], was the very last of all his people to return: namely, on 20 February, the feast-day of Saint Eucherius [Note: “namely,” 1*.]. As I have said, he began energetically to act according to the time and means of the place, yet never permitting any relaxation in matters belonging to our order. But he was hated beyond measure by almost all the townsmen, who said that he had caused the evils which had befallen them. [Col. 0066A]

At last the soldiers of Count Arnulf withdrew from the tower garrison, and our town began to be inhabited more freely. Meanwhile, while these and many other evils were occurring among us, and not so much the wheel of fickle fortune as the just wrath of the avenging God against our people allowed nothing firm, certain, or prosperous to remain to us, the church of Metz also, of which we are a member, was shaken by the most grievous collision of waves so much higher as the head is accustomed to surpass all its other members.

### 15

Thus Gualo, whom we said above had been placed over Herman, bishop of Metz [Note: “placed under,” 1*; III, 2.], seeing that he accomplished nothing—and indeed truly recognizing that he had gravely disgraced himself before men and condemned himself before God because, by an unlawful ascent, he had defiled the bed of his father while that father was still living—was led by repentance to make the humblest satisfaction. Before all the chief and more religious persons of the bishopric he came before Herman; and, for amendment of so unlawful a deed, he was placed under discipline in the monastery of Gorze and made guardian of boys, though formerly he had been called bishop of Metz. [Col. 0066B]

Later, however, we saw him recover his abbey, namely Saint Arnulf’s at Metz, because Bishop Herman had been moved to pity by the endurance of one most humbly doing penance [Note: D reads “penance” for “endurance”]. Yet the emperor did not even then allow Herman to be at peace; for immediately he fashioned another bishop of Metz against and over him, namely Bruno, son of the Count of Calw [Note: That is, Calw in Swabia. He was the son of Count Adalbert of Calw, often mentioned by Bernold. For this Bruno see also Waltram, II.30, who falsely says that he was a monk of Saint-Trond.]—a man noble indeed, but most frivolous, and most weighty only in falsehood. His brother Godfrey later became count palatine. [Col. 0066C–D]

### 16

Bruno, therefore, appropriating for himself through his agents those things which blessed Stephen the protomartyr appears to possess among us, repeatedly begged Abbot Lanzo by frequent and most humble letters to come to him; he wished to cloak his own intrusion by the authority of this man. But the constancy of the religious man did not consent in any way, recognizing as his own bishop and that of Metz only Herman [Note: Namely, Herman.], while Herman still lived and while he saw that see still vacant without canonical judgment.

What, however, could he do? So long as that intruder remained, he would either have to relinquish the abbey of Saint Vincent at Metz, which he held together with ours, or in some fashion look to him. Nor did he continue for long to hope much good for our community, since he feared that Bruno would fall upon him daily and saw himself intolerably hated by many of our townsmen because of the burning of the church and destruction of the place. For when he rose at night for the hymns of matins, he never dared go to choir unless escorted by a band of armed men, nor return otherwise. [Col. 0066D–0067A]

### 17

Wearied at last by so many evils and now almost despairing of peace, he began to arrange a pilgrimage toward Jerusalem, yet so secretly throughout that whole year and until he came to Liège that none of us was ever able to discover it. Thus, contrary to the profession of his life and the religious habit for which he was renowned [Note: D reads *invio latae*, an uncertain divergent reading], he began, both justly and unjustly, to turn into silver whatever he could scrape together throughout the entire abbey from his own prebend and that of the brethren [Note: 1* reads *suo* (“his own”) for *sua*; 1 and 1* read *corrodere* for *corradere*.].

Among other things, it is certain that, to the grave loss of our church, he then granted away whatever is now seen to be outside our demesne lands at Renhrode [Note: *Dominium*: property, demesne.]. He also caused the woods belonging to Mere and Burlo to be cleared, reserving for his pilgrimage the price received from them. [Col. 0067B]

He reduced the rent of the mill at Moyse near Villario to only five solidi. Long afterward, after many and prolonged complaints, the labor of our predecessor Lord Abbot Theoderic and of Ekard [Note: D reads “Gerard”], then provost, in our own time—especially through the active assistance of Provost Folkard—and our own care, at very great expense, recovered to our demesne lands from the hands of certain powerful men that arrangement, wholly annulled and destroyed. Rebuilt wholly anew, it could scarcely be retained against resistance, with great loss [Note: D reads “redeem” for “retain”]. [Col. 0068A]

Likewise, whatever we appear to possess in the village of Hallei [Note: Halle, westward from Saint-Trond.], he is accused of having granted as a benefice at that time to a certain powerful tyrant, Everard of Nodewet, receiving from him a mule on the very day of his departure.

Thus, after collecting much silver, both justly and, as I have said, unjustly [Note: “In the seventh year of his intrusion, which was the year of the Lord 1089, he secretly fled from our cloister, never to return”: interpolator’s annotation in the lower margin, 1*.], he left our town. No one knew where he was going except one of his own men [Note: “except one of his own men” is absent in D.]. Coming to Liège, into the crypt of Saint Lawrence, he surrendered to the bishop of Liège the care and staff of our abbey, to the astonishment of all our people who were present. [Col. 0068B]

Yet he sent back to us, through the hands of Provost Gerard [Note: D adds “his own.”], the copes, chasubles, and whatever remnants of our treasure he had taken; but he departed after confessing to the provost that he had left the brethren only provisions for one day’s living.

[Note: He does not appear to have gone to the Holy Land. In 1090 he subscribed a charter of Bishop Herman at Metz; in 1096 Urban II gave him a certain privilege; in 1099 he subscribed a charter of Bishop Richer of Verdun; and in 1098 he was expelled from his abbey. Calmet, *Histoire de Lorraine*, I, preliminary matter, pp. 395, 507, 512.]

**Here ends the Third Book. The Fourth begins.** [Note: “Book” is added by 1*.]

[Col. 0067]

### Book IV

Alas, alas, alas, Lord God! When Lanzo departed, we thought that, shipwrecked and stripped of our lost merchandise, we had at least reached harbor; behold, we see ourselves again rolled by a violent storm into the deepest abyss of the raging sea. [Col. 0067B]

Therefore the very few brethren of ours who had already returned—for Abbot Lanzo had sent ahead those who had come with him—sent to Metz a report concerning Abbot Lanzo, explaining how he had departed, and humbly asked that they might still be granted their first election, at least after so great a desolation of our place. Bruno consented—he who, after Gualo, had usurped the bishopric of Metz over Herman—but ordered that he himself would first come to us.

Meanwhile [Note: “In the same year,” added by the interpolator in the margin, 1*.], Provost Gerard consulted Bishop Henry concerning his second election and the unanimity of the brethren in choosing him. For each trusted the other most intimately, and it could not easily be understood which loved the other more. The bishop dissuaded him, pleading—as above—the unconquerable restlessness of the brethren, and also because he saw that Bruno, from whom Gerard would have to receive the staff, had invaded the bishopric over a canonical bishop still living. If Gerard entered through Bruno, the bishop could not give him canonical benediction. [Col. 0067C–0068B]

O Henry, Henry! It is indeed true and pious that a religious man ought not to enter through the hands of an intruder. But why did you not permit him to enter then, when he could have done so canonically—namely, while Herman still remained peaceably in his see? Oh, from how many evils would our church today be free, evils all imputed to you, since you prevented us from promoting the man through whom these and other future evils might somehow have been averted! [Col. 0068C]

Accordingly, after a few days had elapsed, Bruno came down to us, bringing with him none of the more honorable men of Metz. When he heard that Provost Gerard did not wish to receive the staff from his hand, he did not compel him in any way. Rather, rejoicing, he sold the abbey for a very great sum of money to one of our brethren, Herman, surnamed “the Bald” and “the Elder.” This Herman had a full brother, a man noble in birth and wealthy in ancestral estates, named Engeram; among other possessions, he is said to have owned—and did own—the village of Horfale. From his own property, Engeram gave in full everything that Bruno received from the sale of our abbey.

### 2

When Bishop Henry heard of this deed, indignant at the presumption, he wished immediately to excommunicate Herman. But the most urgent supplication of his intimate friend, Provost Gerard, opposed this. Gerard set before him and reminded him that, in a similar affair under Lanzo and Luipo, the first desolation of our church had occurred; he feared that something much worse could still arise from it, since the people no longer had anything, as they had the first time, to lose, and could very easily be stirred to revenge for past sufferings. [Col. 0068D–0069A]

The bishop, having heard the argument and considered the necessity of stormy times, consented; he neither cursed Herman nor blessed him. In truth, Herman was not sufficiently suited to this dignity, since we learned nothing about any virtues in him worthy of remembrance, whether secular qualities or literary learning.

### 3

Meanwhile Bruno, a most savage whirlwind over the remaining sparks of our ashes, carefully scattered to every wind whatever of ours and his was being stirred up among us. To pass over very many matters as comparatively small, among other things he sold our villages to a certain powerful and noble man, Otto of Diest, father of Arnulf: namely Guebechem, Palte, Haletre, and Guimale. Having received one hundred marks from him, he confirmed the transfer by whatever legal form he could. [Col. 0069B] [Note: Is Haletre Hallet in the territory of Liège?]

Then he went to Aachen for the court and never returned to us. For the people of Metz, unable to endure his insolence and provoked, God so willing, by the foolish pride of him and his followers, finally attacked him with arms and besieged him shut up within the monastery of the blessed protomartyr. At last, after the doors had been broken open above him, they pierced his soldiers here and there throughout the monastery with swords and lances: sacrificing some upon the very altars, pinning others to the altars themselves with twisted javelins. [Col. 0069C]

Bruno scarcely escaped, and on that very day the people of Metz entirely deprived him both of the honor and the title of bishop. [Note: According to Bernold, this had already occurred in 1088.]

What then could our miserable church do? After fire and sword, it bore this loss as even heavier, especially since there was no one who, even if able, was willing to take pity on us. Turmoil at Metz; at Liège, God’s and men’s indignation against us and our affairs; an abbot virtually nonexistent, since no proper answer could be given on his behalf in any need of ours.

4. It also happened at the same time, to add to our misfortunes, that, while our church of Alborg was neglected amid these and other disturbances of ours [Note: [Col. 0069] *Alburg* 1*. *Alboro* D.], having long remained shut, it finally fell, by judgment, into the hands of Conrad, bishop of Utrecht, a very formidable and powerful man [Note: [Col. 0070D] He supported the party of Henry IV.], and could not be recovered until it had cost us more than sixty [Note: [Col. 0069] Forty D.] pounds. Because of this need, the great golden chalice was then sold, worth far more than that sum of money, both for its weight of the finest gold and for the inestimable value of its marvelous gems [Col. 0070A] and workmanship. In this transaction we heard that the sellers of the object and the carriers of the silver dealt very fraudulently with us—as they often did—and above all our priests, who were always, and remain to this day, harmful plotters against the church and our brethren.

What more? God’s indignation had hemmed us in on every side, and no human compassion, especially not that of those close to us, came to our misery; indeed, our own household was ashamed to acknowledge itself as belonging to our church. While we were shaken by these great evils and many others that we omit—not merely shaken, but utterly uprooted—the Lord God touched the heart of Bishop Henry, not by our merits but by his own. Remembering how many evils had happened to us and ours in his short time, and that he himself had been the principal cause of them [Col. 0070B], he was inwardly touched by sorrow of heart—for he was a man of compassionate heart—and, crying out that he had sinned grievously against our church, he girded himself to help it in its troubles and, so far as humanly possible, to spare it from further injury.

First, therefore, he sent ten marks from his own resources to repair the church of Saint Mary ever Virgin, which had been burned during our siege. Then he sternly forbade Otto, that strong and noble man who had bought our villages from Bruno, to concern himself in any way with the property of our church, otherwise he would excommunicate him. For what had been done there could not be valid, having been done contrary to the laws of God and men. But Otto did not comply.

[Col. 0070C]

5. Therefore, at the bishop’s command, our brethren and a large body from the church, both mounted men and foot soldiers, came to him at Hales with the shrine and relics of Saint Trudo. But those belonging to Guebechem and to our other villages, which Otto had usurped for himself, met our saints from the other side of the river [Note: [Col. 0070D] The Meuse.], barefoot and clad in wool, in miserable dress and with the loudest lamentation, so that they moved even the bishop himself to tears. Accordingly, with a great procession of his own people and ours, the bishop brought our saints into Guebechem; and, after the divine sacrament had been celebrated there in the church [Note: [Col. 0069] “Saint [Trudo] in the church,” 1*.], he forbade Otto before the altar, by episcopal authority, to retain our villages. He gave satisfaction to all who stood by with the reasoning that the sale could not legally stand [Col. 0070D], since it had been made not by a bishop but by a thief and robber. He also addressed the people then and there, beginning: “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes” (Matthew 18:7). Thus, having dismissed our people in peace and great joy [Note: [Col. 0069] D adds “the bishop.”], he himself went on to lodge nearby among his own people.

[Col. 0071A]

6. Yet Otto did not rest even then; for, when the bishop had departed, he again subjected all those possessions to himself by oath, as before. It happened, by God’s ordering, that he dared this on a day of peace [Note: [Col. 0071D] Henry IV had publicly established the Peace of God at Mainz in 1085; cf. the table in *Monumenta Germaniae, Leges* II, 55.]. Hearing this, the bishop, being a very powerful man and no less noble, took it exceedingly ill. Coming to Liège, he vigorously complained before the equals and superiors of his bishopric about the contempt shown him and the violation of the peace. By their judgment he prosecuted Otto until he was adjudged guilty and compelled at last to make satisfaction: not only to relinquish our villages without any redemption on our part [Note: [Col. 0071] Omitted in 1*.], but also to pay the bishop one hundred marks for his favor. Thus, through God’s mercy, Saint Trudo’s intercession, and the bishop’s remarkable diligence, our church recovered [Col. 0071B] its possessions and retains them to this day.

7. Meanwhile, after Bruno, the author of this evil, had been irrevocably expelled from the city and bishopric of Metz, as I said above, Bishop Herimann returned to his see, though not yet wholly secure because of the emperor. He [Note: [Col. 0072D] That is, Herimann, bishop of Metz.] sent word that he would soon come to us, and ordered that not Herimann, whom Bruno had installed as abbot, but Provost Gerard should prepare his customary service, and that they should never bring Herimann before his sight.

When he came to Liège, Engeramnus, Herimann’s brother [Note: [Col. 0072D] Abbot of Saint Trudo.], wished to swear upon the holy things [Note: [Col. 0071] D reads “sacraments.”], accompanied by eleven free men, that absolutely nothing from the goods of the church had been given for his brother’s installation as abbot, but that everything had come from his own resources, and that he wished to demand nothing further from it. The bishop [Col. 0071C], kindly hearing him, deferred the matter until he should be at our place.

When he arrived there, he would receive us into no communion until he had absolved us from the ban by which, he said, we were bound on account of that excommunicated Bruno. On the following day, while sitting in the abbot’s chamber and conducting his affairs energetically, and meanwhile awaiting a huge meal prepared for him out of our impoverishment, one of several townsmen of ours who had been summoned before him for a hearing spoke thus with insolent mouth and indignant brow:

“Is this, excellent sirs, the bishop who, by stirring up such sedition in this church and our town over his abbots, caused all our possessions to be burned by fire and our parents—while we barely escaped—to be slaughtered by the bloody sword? And now [Col. 0071D], before the eyes of their children and amid the pitiable remnants of our ruin, he argues in court—the man to whom nothing should be repaid but death for such destruction of us and ours?”

8. Understanding these words, the bishop [Note: [Col. 0071] “Herimann,” inserted by the interpolator in 1*.] concealed the matter, though carefully investigated, under deep silence. Secretly he ordered his secretaries to prepare a horse for him [Note: [Col. 0071] 1. adds “his.”], saying that outside on the plain [Col. 0072A] he had to meet his nephew, namely [Note: [Col. 0071] The interpolator wrote “Henry” in an erasure in 1*.], the bishop of Liège. He immediately hastened with utmost speed to Huy [Note: [Col. 0072D] Huy on the Meuse.] and never afterward returned to us or to our affairs.

Apart from the loss which he had caused our afflicted community through the splendid service prepared for him, Herimann sent him two horses, for which the mill of Stades was pledged. Thus, in this way and that, our church daily fared worse between bishops and abbots; Herimann, however, remained in the abbacy. While these and other things went on for several years, Luipo had long since returned from the emperor without hope of assistance; still excommunicated, he stayed here and there at Leuven with his relatives. There he was seized by a most severe illness—or so it appeared. For there were some who said that it had been feigned, so that he might thus be absolved [Col. 0072B] by the bishop and return to his cloister, since he seemed almost to despair of life. Through his relatives—for he had been nobly born—he secured this: that, once absolved, he should be taken back to his cloister if he should happen to survive. But he quickly recovered, and began to remain as a private person among our brethren who had returned or were returning.

9. When the greater part of the brethren had returned, though they might have been frightened and corrected by God’s long and exceedingly prolonged punishment of them, they quickly forgot both their past faults and the punishments which had followed for them. In their life—and, I may say, still more in their religious observance—they became daily worse rather than better. Although they had experienced how much they had suffered through outsiders’ [Note: [Col. 0071] D reads “disputes.”] conflicts, and now had from among themselves a superior [Col. 0072C] by whom they would in no way have been burdened had they wished to live quietly, they refused to act so. Rather, by their words and deeds, miserably afflicting him every day, they trampled him as frogs trample a stick.

They had little or no concern for the almost annihilated resources of the church, the rebuilding of the burned monastery, or the repair from the foundations of the workshops and cloister. They wished only to serve the belly and things of the belly, demanding large portions of fish and measures of wine. Hence daily quarrels, at suitable and unsuitable times and places alike; hence curses; hence insults against miserable Herimann without any compassion [Note: [Col. 0071] All that follows, down to “for domestic necessities,” is absent from D.].

Thus it happened one day, when a measure of wine—or perhaps mead—was lacking to one of the brethren, that they rushed into his chamber [Col. 0072D]; and unless he had turned aside their aim with bold insults, they would have badly beaten him as well. The instigator and fuel of this evil was a certain brother of ours, Stepelinus. Every day he urged Luipo to recover the abbatial dignity taken from him; he reminded him that his nobility ought not to be despised; he mocked Herimann before his face and condemned him behind his back. With the excessive restlessness enabled by his tongue, he said that an ignorant man and a base person, unworthy of blessing, ought not to bear the name or honor of abbot.

But when Herimann—or rather God—could no longer endure these and many other things, the matter, worthy of grave attention, was reported through Herimann’s friends to the bishop of Liège. Up to fourteen marks of silver were promised to him and his men, that he might free the church from the intolerable malice of such men. This sum was paid in full, to the great loss of the church; and so it happened that, while they bit one another, they were consumed by one another. O hard hearts! O senseless animals! O blind breasts, rebelling against God amid the very scourges, while the hand of the Lord was still manifestly stretched out over them!

Luipo and Stepelinus were therefore summoned [Col. 0073B] to Liège for a hearing. Receiving them with a loud voice and grave indignation, the bishop said to Luipo: “Are you, Luipo, that man whose wickedness made me go to Saint Trudo and, for my sins, burn with fire that whole great town as well as the church of the most holy and ever-Virgin Mary?” Then, turning to Stepelinus, he said: “And you, gray dog, grown old in evil days, why do you rage against the remnants of a ruin still standing and of a pitiable desolation?”

Scorning to hear their answer, he said threateningly to Otto, our advocate standing beside him [Note: [Col. 0073C] This Otto is Count Otto of Duras, subadvocate of the monastery of Saint Trudo. The charters of Theoderic and Adalbero III, bishops of Metz, show that he had already held this office in 1060 and 1065; these charters, previously published elsewhere from our codex, will be given below. A charter from the cartulary of Saint Trudo, published by Mantelius, p. 55, proves that at the beginning of the eleventh century the counts of Duras possessed this advocacy. In it we find, in 1024, Gislebert, advocate of Saint Trudo, son of Count Godfrey; it does not seem excessively bold to conjecture that this Godfrey was Otto’s father. On this advocacy see also St. Genois, *Histoire des avoueries en Belgique*, p. 99.], father of Gislebert: “I command and command you to make peace for the church of Saint Trudo against these two enemies of God.”

Gislebert, son of Otto the advocate, then still a young man, immediately pursued them as they returned in great shame [Col. 0073C] to our house at Liège. Having severely beaten and shamefully torn them, he expelled them from the house, taking their riding horses and whatever they seemed to possess besides simple clothing. Stepelinus therefore withdrew to Muysen [Note: [Col. 0074C] Muysen, not far from Saint Trudo.], while Luipo remained at Leuven. Herimann was in the abbacy with little honor beyond the name alone; for, with the evils perpetrated by his superiors and new ones arising daily, he could scarcely scrape together enough for the few brethren who had returned to live on, sometimes even spending his own clothing on domestic necessities.

[Col. 0074A]

10. After a short interval had passed [Note: [Col. 0073] “With Emperor Henry’s permission, Bishop Herimann is received by the people of Metz into the city and is found dead in his bed that same day after dinner, A.D. 1090. After his death Henry I, bishop of Liège, his nephew, died in the following year; Obbert succeeded him in the bishopric in that same year.” Thus the interpolator from Sigebert, in 1*, after two erased lines in the text and in the lower margin.], both bishops died: Herimann of Metz and Henry of Liège. The emperor, meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0073] The interpolator of 1* added “then” in an erasure.], was staying in Lombardy [Note: [Col. 0074C] During the years 1090–1097.]. Thus it came about that every powerful man in our land usurped as much as he wished of what adjoined or lay between his territories.

Count Henry of Leuven, whose brother Godfrey held the county after his death—and this Godfrey later became the first duke of the people of Leuven [Note: [Col. 0074C] According to Sigebert, this occurred in 1106.]—was at that time regarded as the more powerful man in our region. Since, after Bishop Henry’s death and before any successor had been appointed, there was no one to resist him ecclesiastically, and even the duke himself [Note: [Col. 0074C] Godfrey of Bouillon, who had held the duchy since 1089.] did not dare to attack him with secular forces, he restored Luipo [Note: [Col. 0073] The interpolator of 1* wrote above: “while the see of Liège was vacant.”] to our abbacy [Col. 0074B], the brethren so wishing, while the laity partly assented and partly did not dare to object.

Thus Herimann, in the third year of his office [Note: [Col. 0073] The interpolator of 1* wrote above: “in his third year.”], was irrecoverably deprived of the honor and name of abbot, and remained in our cloister, quiet and never causing any disturbance therefrom. At last, consumed among us by a most severe and very prolonged sickness—and earlier tormented by great poverty because of the desolation of the place and by many hardships—he retained no strength beyond bones, sinews, and a pale skin stretched over them; while alive he was almost stripped of humanity. Finally, having confessed, been anointed, and received communion in our presence, he died and was buried in the brethren’s cemetery.

The day on which Luipo entered after Herimann’s expulsion was the Translation of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, namely the third Ides [Col. 0074C] of August, after Bishop Henry had died in that same year [Note: [Col. 0073] The interpolator of 1* added: “A.D. 1091.”] during the days of Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0074C] According to the Martyrology of Saint Lawrence at Liège, he died on 31 May; see *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence at Liège*, c. 44, no. 61, and Giles of Aurea Vallis. Pentecost fell on 1 June.]. On that same day, under Bishop Herimann and the aforesaid Henry, the earlier action took place by which, after our brethren had been expelled, Lanzo, abbot of Saint Vincent at Metz, was also established as abbot among us.

11. Then a certain canon of Saint Lambert, named Obbert, provost of the monastery of Holy Cross in that city, had already long before [Note: [Col. 0074C] This cannot have occurred before 1090. See also *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence at Liège*, c. 45.] gone to the emperor in Lombardy in hope of obtaining the bishopric of Liège, as indeed he did. Luipo, seeing an opportunity [Col. 0075A] to establish himself firmly in our abbacy, likewise went to the emperor in Lombardy around autumn.

Let no one attack or disparage me if truth itself compels me to speak truth: fear for my soul in the matter of lying, and God’s own threat through Holy Scripture. For every lie is from the devil (John II, 21), and “a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11). It is the historian’s duty not to deviate through flattery, affection, hatred, or fear. Therefore I shall write, with God as witness, as I learned from many persons and as I was able more truthfully to investigate from brethren who were with us at that time and afterward spoke these things with me face to face.

But what use is there in multiplying words about a profane matter? By a very great sum of money Luipo accomplished this [Col. 0075B] with the emperor: Obbert, having become bishop, returned to Liège and was consecrated; then, by the emperor’s command, he consecrated Luipo as abbot of Saint Trudo. In paying those to whom the emperor had assigned payments, and others to whom Luipo himself had made promises, many shameful and unlawful arrangements were seen, even on the very day on which he had been vested for consecration [Note: [Col. 0075D] This can only have occurred after 1 February 1092, when Obbert himself was consecrated bishop of Liège, according to the *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence at Liège*, c. 46; Luipo is also mentioned there in c. 47.]. It is more honorable to be silent about these than to speak. Let this alone suffice—and it is already too much to have said—that neither before nor then could we understand that he had entered according to God.

12. Shortly afterward, he groaned very heavily over the evils that had occurred among us through him, often revealing his weak conscience with sighs. He seemed to gird himself to wash away his sins by [Col. 0075C] many alms, by receiving the poor and pilgrims, and even sometimes by washing, drying, and anointing lepers with his own hands. He was indeed sharp, steadfast, and fearless in resisting the violence of advocates, as one nobly born into the freedom and lineage of the people of Leuven. But toward his relatives [Col. 0076A] and in domestic expenditure he was excessively lavish and ostentatious [Note: [Col. 0075] D reads “gluttonous.”], spending more on food and clothing than on the brethren, beyond what the abbey’s revenues could sometimes bear. Consequently he too often burdened peasants holding precarial lands [Note: [Col. 0075] Omitted in 1*.]. Nevertheless, he was regarded as an energetic cultivator of fields and rearer of livestock.

What then? Temporal affairs prospered in his hands; but among them there was neither fear nor any concern for maintaining or restoring religious observance and the former moral quality of the brethren. In his beginnings, little succeeded concerning the repair of the monastery and cloister; for he accomplished nothing in this respect worthy of remembrance. Yet he roofed and completed that fourth part of the cloister—that is, only the house on the west—which Abbot Lanzo had begun [Col. 0076B], and left it inside, above and below, wholly undecorated. In it we later saw such extensive alterations of rooms that we do not know by what name we should chiefly call it.

13. Once, during harvest-time, he returned from the field intensely hot and tired. In the evening, after he had drunk heavily with his household, he was very merry and was laid down in bed apparently well. At midnight he was found with almost all his limbs deadened, so that he could neither speak nor move; and he grew continually worse. Barely surviving somehow until [Note: [Col. 0075] Omitted in 1*.] first light, he finally expired, without confession, anointing, or communion. He died on the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 0075] The interpolator of 1* added: “A.D. 1093.”], having lived in the abbacy scarcely two years after his consecration [Col. 0076C], and was buried in our monastery.

In the same year Provost Gerard died, having first confessed, been anointed, and received communion; and so at last, in good remembrance, he was laid with his fathers in our monastery.

**END OF BOOK FOUR; BOOK FIVE BEGINS.**

[Col. 0075]

[Col. 0075C]

1. Considering the pressing weight of this mournful and miserable work, I who above—alas!—cried out three times would now, in taking up my subject, have need to cry out the same thing seven times and far more often. For the higher I advance, the more terrible waves I see rising before my face [Col. 0075D].

Therefore, after Luipo’s death—in and through whom the ship of our church, burdened by our sins, had sunk into the most grievous *Syrtes*, and insatiable Charybdis had swallowed whatever fruitfulness and splendor, inward and outward, had existed among us in the house of God—the duke [Note: [Col. 0075] The interpolator of 1* adds “of Lorraine and Bouillon.”], Godfrey [Col. 0076C], who afterward set out for Jerusalem and died there as king [Note: [Col. 0075] “Died there as king” is absent in D.], subjected our whole abbey to his own service. The buildings of our church and cloister had not yet been repaired; the brethren lived here and there almost in huts around the burned walls [Col. 0076D], with little religious observance among them and still less prudent counsel.

Among them was a certain Herimann, nephew of the Herimann mentioned above. He was nobly born and had been nurtured in our cloister from childhood; simple and without prudence, silent and patient in enduring injuries, but obstinate in taking secret revenge; extremely ready to presume anything [Col. 0077A], but most stubborn in refusing to abandon it; ignorant of liberal learning, trained only in the customs of his own church. Corrupted by the prompting of laymen and partly by those who had formerly occupied the tower because of Luipo, he seized, by a grant from the aforesaid Duke Godfrey, the administration of our entire abbey, hoping in this way eventually to obtain both the name and the revenues of abbot.

The brethren protested most vehemently against this grant [Note: [Col. 0077] D reads “loss.”], both because they knew him to be wholly unfit for such a charge and because they feared—as happened—that the entire abbey would be devastated to raise the money he had promised the duke for that grant. Yet the duke’s violence prevailed, and a very large sum of money was scraped together for him now from one place, now from another, to the greatest loss of the church. For our people of Testerbant alone [Col. 0077B] paid up to sixty marks and were finally compelled to beg, though they had previously been wealthy [Note: [Col. 0077C] A district between the rivers Lek, Waal, and Meuse. Ernst, *Histoire de Limbourg* II, 176, 232, conjectures that this place refers to those parts of the district of Texandria adjoining the district of Testerbant.]. Why enumerate individual cases? From whatever sources it was collected, the sum exceeded one hundred marks by I know not how much.

2. Thus and thus, again and again, even the few brethren then with us lived in the utmost poverty, shamefully naked and unbearably hungry. Some, as I heard them report with their own mouths, sometimes begged alms from those entering the monastery. Some who received something from parents, relatives, or friends lived for a while on it in the most meager fashion. Others, if they had books or clothes which they could more patiently do without, sold them and bought bread with the proceeds.

But Herimann [Col. 0077C], slavishly addicted to the counsels of laymen, including men considered among the more foolish, prevented the brethren’s voices, crying out over their needs, from attaining any result. He did so now before Bishop Obbert, Henry’s successor at Liège, now before archdeacons and other courtiers, by promising, giving, and lying. Hearing that, when the church had prevailed against the emperor [Note: [Col. 0077C] The emperor wished to install Adalbero as bishop at Metz in 1093; see Bernold under that year.], Poppo had succeeded Herimann [Note: [Col. 0077C] This occurred at Eastertide in 1093.], he set out for Metz, accompanied by a great crowd of laymen but by absolutely none of our brethren. There, by whatever corrupt means such things are usually done, he began to seek from Poppo the grant of the abbey.

Some of our brethren were present, sent by the others; they offered to Poppo, bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0077] Omitted in D. The interpolator of 1* wrote above “of Poppo.”], the canonical embassy of our church and likewise of the church of Liège [Col. 0078A], together with letters from the bishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0077C] Eigilbert.]. By these they steadfastly and reasonably rejected the proposal that Herimann should be given to them as abbot, even amid threats, beatings, and the plundering of their horses and clothes. But what followed? Money prevailed; the malice of laymen prevailed against the brethren. The abbey was granted to Herimann by this authority.

3. The brethren returned from there, torn, despoiled, and on foot through such a long and difficult journey. They tearfully laid the matter out in order before the church of Saint Lambert and its bishop: the losses which the church had suffered through Herimann [Note: [Col. 0077] “Which—greater” and what follows are absent in D.], the greater losses that they now feared it would suffer, and their own extreme lack of food [Col. 0078B] and clothing. At last, overcome by contempt for themselves and by our misery, even those whom Herimann’s money had at times led astray urged the bishop to summon the monks and Herimann for a hearing.

Herimann was summoned once, twice, and a third time. At last, when he refused to come, he was excommunicated and condemned by canonical procedure. Yet even so he did not yield [Note: [Col. 0077] “Nor did he yield” is absent in D.]. But fearing the bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0077] The interpolator of 1* added “of Liège.”], lest he expel him by military force as he intended, he left our town. After staying for some time at our village of Hales, to the church’s great loss, he went to Count Henry of Limburg [Note: [Col. 0077C] Henry of Limburg was son of Walram, count of Arlon, who first built Limburg castle, from which the entire province later took its name. Alberic discussed this family’s descent from Theoderic I, duke of the Mosellans, in his *Chronicle* under 1064. Henry’s mother was Judith, daughter of Frederick, duke of Lower Lorraine; Frederick died in 1065 and, according to Alberic, left dominion beyond the Meuse near Liège to his daughter and Walram’s wife. Ernst, in the opening of volume II of his *Histoire de Limbourg*, was the first after Duchesne, Bertholet, and others to set out this descent of the counts of Limburg in a clear scholarly discussion.], then the chief advocate of our church. He hoped through him either eventually to recover the abbey or to afflict it, as he did [Col. 0078C], by frequent injuries and many raids.

4. Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0077] “A.D. 1094,” interpolator 1*.], while the conflict between the bishop of Metz and Emperor Henry had not yet ceased, the emperor granted as a benefice to Count Arnulf of Loon that demesne portion which the bishop of Metz seemed to possess among us. Count Henry of Limburg took this indignantly, since he was our chief advocate. He entered our town with several horsemen, usurping for himself what Count Arnulf appeared to hold in it. He had also brought Herimann with him, intending to restore him to the abbey by force.

But the brethren despised him with such unanimity and constancy that they would neither ring the bell [Col. 0079A] [Note: [Col. 0079] D reads “have rung.”] nor perform the divine office while they knew him to be within the precincts of our monastery or its court. Though repeatedly assailed with terrors, threats, blandishments, and promises through Count Henry’s men, they were not moved in any way.

Herimann meanwhile hid in a corner of one of our granaries. His supporters came to him—men of the least weight and of no good reputation or counsel among us—and encouraged him to persist in his plan. They also inflamed Count Henry with insults to take terrible vengeance upon us for the contempt shown to him in the matter of his abbot.

Meanwhile Count Arnulf, having gathered a great multitude of his followers, would either have killed Count Henry in our town or shamefully driven him out, had not Count Godfrey of Leuven, who later became duke, rescued him by interceding at the humble request conveyed through Henry’s messengers [Col. 0079B]. Escaping safely under Godfrey’s escort, Count Henry took his abbot away with him. At once the bell for the third hour sounded among us, and the divine office, omitted because of him, began to be performed.

Enraged in the utmost degree by both rebuffs, Count Henry lodged Herimann with himself, seized, devastated, and afflicted everything of ours that he could, and commanded his followers to do the same [Note: [Col. 0079D] “He commanded. In A.D. 1095, the fortieth year of Henry IV’s reign and the third of his empire, and the fifth year of Obbert, bishop of Liège, after the simoniacal invader Herimann had rightly been rejected from this abbey in the preceding year, this formerly famous abbey lacked a pastor for about four years. Who could recount in full the violent assaults inflicted by tyrants?” These words were inserted by the interpolator after one erased line in 1*.].

Who could fully recount by what evils, and how great, the possessions of our church were then so dispersed that they were either wholly taken from us forever, or rendered almost useless to us through excessive and prolonged oppression? For Duke Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0079] The interpolator adds “of Lorraine and Bouillon.”], who afterward died there as king of Jerusalem, compelled whatever was ours [Col. 0079C] in Hesbaye and Testerbant [Note: [Col. 0079] *Testebrant* 1*.] to serve him at will. Count Henry seized what lay around and beyond the Meuse, in Ripuarian territory, and around the Rhine; Count Henry the Palatine [Note: [Col. 0079D] He died 12 April 1095. See Crollius, *Erläuterte Reihe der Pfalzgrafen*, p. 134, and Lavalley’s note in Ernst, *Hist. de Limb.* II, 175.] what we seemed to possess above the Moselle.

From that day we could never afterward recover the church of Fonce [Note: [Col. 0079D] Poncé, on the left bank of the Moselle, south of Metz.], not far from the city of Metz. It had still been held as ours in Abbot Lanzo’s time, and for a long time thereafter. Moreover, our bailiffs and certain men holding benefices from our church appropriated to their bailiwicks and fiefs whatever pleased them or seemed most advantageous at the time; and when we now wish to recover these things, they offer to swear that they had possessed them from ancient and lawful tenure of benefice or bailiwick.

[Col. 0080A]

5. Let no one, therefore, be surprised if today we live humbly, diminished in glory and wealth. Indeed, to those who consider carefully, it may seem more astonishing how, amid so many desolations of our place, enough still remained for a community to exist among us and for it to be called an abbey. At that time very few brethren remained with us; there was no order among them, no religious observance. Afflicted by want of food and clothing, they almost perished from hunger and cold; nor did they have cloistral workshops in which to conceal their necessities. So great were the misery, desolation, and dispersal of property that many, despairing that even the name of an abbey could remain in the place [Col. 0080B], seemed intent on turning it into a provostship of clerics, with six or eight clerics under it.

Amid these and countless other evils, when that once most noble and famous abbey of ours was already almost annihilated [Note: [Col. 0079] “Almost,” 1*.], divine mercy at last touched the hearts of the people of Liège. After holding a large assembly together, they began earnestly to consider how they might assist the desolated and almost annihilated abbey. But because our temporal property belonged to the men of Metz, while the care of souls belonged only to the people of Liège, some among them—as often happens—were not greatly attentive to assisting us. They said that this belonged only to him to whom the annual revenue of our church was owed, and that the people of Liège ought not to give us an abbot [Col. 0080C], but only to ordain one.

On the other hand, the wiser and more religious men maintained that the church of Liège could canonically do this: since the care of souls and the consecration of the abbot belonged to it, and since the church of Metz could not assist us because of its own troubles, the church of Liège should provide and ordain an abbot for a church under its pastoral care, without thereby taking anything away from what was owed to Metz. For it would not be lightly tolerable that so great a place, so great a name, and so great a former honor should be annihilated through the negligence of the church of Metz by the church of Liège.

6. A most diligent inquiry was therefore made whether any son of our church survived to whom the care of assisting his mother might suitably be entrusted. Our brethren, together with clerics and laymen who had known him, said that at Ghent, in the monastery of St Peter, there was living one of our brethren, named Theoderic, who had withdrawn from our house during the contention between the abbots Lanzo and Luipo.

> [Note: In this exile he composed, at the urging of Gerard, the book *On the Life of St Trudo*. In its preface he himself calls this little work a pledge sent from the straits of exile, and a booklet of exile. See it in Surius VI, 543, and what Ghesquier has given, V, 7.]

If he could be brought away from there, they thought him suitable to govern the abbey: for he was fluent in the Teutonic and Walloon languages, excellently educated in the liberal arts, second to none of his time in prose and verse, resonant with a sweet and lofty voice; of short but handsome stature and middle age. He would also know better how to sympathize with the infirmities of his brethren, since he had grown up among them from childhood and had seen and heard the evils they had endured in their tribulations. What more need be said? Bishop Obbert and the church of Liège rejoiced at this.

7. Thus, although elected by the brethren together with the clerics and laymen, he was at last, though only with difficulty, drawn from the monastery of St Peter at Ghent by their letters and messengers. Taken with them to Aachen, he was made to receive the grant of our abbey from the emperor’s hand, as was then customary. This was done through the emperor because the emperor had subjected to his own jurisdiction whatever the blessed protomartyr appeared to possess in our region, on account of Poppo, bishop of Metz, who held the bishopric without the emperor’s grant and consent. For the emperor still possessed, by ancient right throughout his whole realm, the prerogative that no one should be established as bishop therein without his grant.

Now, since, as I have said, Poppo had entered upon the bishopric of Metz without the emperor’s grant and will, and since for this reason the emperor had subjected to his own right the possessions among us of the blessed protomartyr, necessity required that he receive from the emperor’s hand the staff of our abbey, lest our house should perish miserably, laid waste during a prolonged contest between emperor and bishop. Therefore, while he was at Aachen, the bishop supplied him with provisions on his journeys there and during his stay; and, bringing him to Liège at his own expense, kept him with him until he could bring him to us after ordaining him abbot in person.

> [Note: D adds “there” after “kept him.”] Having installed him in the abbot’s place and commended him to the brethren and people, he promised, before all, that throughout his life his counsel and aid would be ready for him, provided that, acting vigorously for the recovery of the place, he did not despair because of its extreme desolation.

The staff was given him at Aachen on the third day before the Kalends of February [30 January]; he was consecrated abbot and priest at Liège on the Nones of March [7 March], in the year 1099 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

**Here ends Book Five; Book Six begins.**

[Col. 0081]

1. Since we have related the various changes of abbots after the death of Abbot Adelard the Second,

> [Note: Manuscript 1* reads “while”; D adds “after.”]
 we have been unable in any way to maintain an exact sequence of years, because of their violences and the frequent expulsions and returns of the several men. For where no lawful order of successive abbots was observed, but each expelled his rival as quickly as he could, while the latter prevented the former from ruling as far as he could, an exact number of years for each could not easily be preserved—especially since, even if it could have been, no one among our household, always negligent, devoted labour to it.

Accordingly, I shall now continue the years from the death of Abbot Adelard the Second to the entry of Abbot Theoderic into the abbey, and I shall endeavour to retie through these two what the schism of the intervening men tore apart, noting the years from the death of the one and the entry of the other according to the Incarnation of the Lord. Abbot Adelard the Second died in the year 1082 of the Lord’s Incarnation; Abbot Theoderic entered the abbey in the year 1099 of the same Incarnation.

> [Note: In the same year Godfrey of Bouillon, duke of Lorraine and prince of the Jerusalemites, died. After him, in the following year, Emperor Henry transferred the duchy of Lorraine to Count Henry of Limburg. These statements from Sigebert were added in the margin by another (third) hand.]

There were therefore seventeen years from the death of Abbot Adelard the Second to Abbot Theoderic’s entry into the abbey. Lanzo, Luipo, Herimannus, and another Herimannus, disputing among themselves for the abbey—one longer and another less long—filled them up, and permitted none of the others to possess any fixed period.

2. Therefore, in the year 1099 from the Incarnation of the everlasting Prince, after the long and protracted deaths through which all the neighbourhood had despaired of the church of St Trudo from the time of Lord Abbot Adelard the Second down to those days, a certain Theoderic, formerly reared in that same place, was at last recalled—whether more willingly or under compulsion I do not know—from Flanders, from the monastery of St Peter at Ghent, to govern that church. This occurred after letters had already been sent three times by Lord Bishop Obbert and the leading men of Liège; and on the Nones of March [7 March] he was consecrated priest and abbot of our house.

Believe me, you who read this: no power of intellect can express, nor any ability set forth, the desolation which he found within and without, as it truly was. Of the whole monastery, nothing but the tower was roofed. The inner walls had collapsed; the outer walls stood exposed in the widest ruin, enclosing in their midst a most miserable chapel above the tombs of Saints Trudo and Eucherius. After the burning of the church, our people could easily and cheaply have roofed the sanctuary, while the very strong wall still stood firm; but instead they had utterly demolished the whole of it.

> [Note: An interpolator has written above: “One of the intruded abbots.”]

Having rashly begun a larger work, they had already vaulted the crypt and carried it up to the windows of the screen. Lord Abbot Theoderic applied himself most ardently to this work; in a short time he completed in beautiful workmanship everything above the windows of the screen. Having built two piers and the walls rising above them beside the choir, he constructed in masonry the entire part of the monastery extending from the arch above the tomb of St Trudo eastward; he whitened it with lime, adorned it with glazed windows, furnished it with carved work, roofed it above, and paved it below. Likewise, he completed the crypt, which he found merely vaulted, with all the other things it lacked; and he caused its principal altar to be dedicated in honour of the blessed protomartyr Stephen.

> [Note: The interpolator noted: “In the same year, 1100, 3 Kalends of October [29 September].”]

In the year 1102 from the Incarnation of the Lord, he led us from the most wretched chapel over the tombs of the blessed Trudo and Eucherius into that crypt to sing.

> [Note: “Our crypt was dedicated by Lord Obbert, bishop of Liège, at the instance of Lord Theoderic.” These words are absent from both manuscripts 1 and 1*; but in the latter a fourteenth-century hand added them in the margin. They are also read in D.]

That day seemed to us, and indeed was, one of immeasurable joy, since there we began again to perform the offices and prayers according to rule, to stand in choir, and to approach the altar—things the brethren had been wholly unable to do for many years within the cramped chapel. For from the day on which the old monastery had been torn down and the new one burned and demolished, order and discipline had been utterly abolished, among the other desolations and calamities which, as we have related above, befell the brethren; above all because the physical setting in which they could be maintained was lacking.

3. One of the older brethren was therefore appointed guardian of the boys, though he could scarcely govern himself because of old age. While the old monastery still stood, he had seen their discipline and the order of the brethren. Thus the things belonging to religious life gradually began to revive, and through frequent discussion in chapter they advanced more abundantly.

After he led us out of the crypt into the most beautiful choir and into that part of the monastery which, from the tomb of the blessed Trudo and Eucherius eastward to the end of the work, he had partly built and partly restored, religious observance began to increase along with our joy, and the number of brethren grew somewhat. This was very seriously impeded, however, because the brethren had very few cloister workrooms, and those most wretched; the eastern and northern sides had nothing but a bare and very poor fence, through which not only people but also dogs and pigs could pass freely.

> [Note: *Officinae*: rooms in which were kept the things belonging to the food and other uses of the individual monks.]

That part of the cloister in which the brethren sit for reading and maintain their assembly in silence or speech had, in the middle, only a roofed space intersected by a wall, beneath which the brethren held their chapter. Half of the remaining half was still unroofed, and the varying harshness of the weather caused great discomfort, both in summer and winter, to brethren wishing to sit there. The brethren’s refectory and dormitory were one house—the house that ought to have been the western, fourth side of the cloister—also divided by a wall; below it were the boys’ school, the cellar, and the infirmary. But, as I have said above, all was without any fitting provision: there was no roofing before the doors of these rooms, perpetual mud in winter, and severe annoyance within from rain, snow, hail, and the north wind; nor was there any obstacle to prevent any animal from entering.

4. The infirmary had neither fire by day nor light by night, unless the brethren lying there procured these for themselves by whatever means they could, sometimes even out of their own food and clothing.

> [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 1* read: “procure them for themselves.”]

Nor was there light in the dormitory: the brethren lay in darkness throughout the night and went to Matins through darkness. This was especially grievous to them, because from the part of the house in which they slept, they had to cross in darkness to the other part in which they ate; then, on leaving it, beneath a roof partly wooden and partly thatched, both half-ruined, they had to make their way every night to Matins along the monastery wall, feeling their way and often falling or stumbling, and likewise to return from Matins through darkness.

If, during Matins, one of the brethren or boys wished at times to go out for the necessities of nature, he feared the terror of the darkness and the muddy difficulty of the long route.

> [Note: “and the difficulty of the long …” is absent in D.]

Meanwhile he suffered grievously from the demands of nature. In winter the brethren’s beds were sprinkled with thick snow; and when they rose for Matins, they found themselves white with snow upon their clothing, and when they returned, their entire bedding likewise. Because of the general intrusion of all who wished to enter, they could safely keep nothing of their bedding in the dormitory, nor anything of what was used at their table in the refectory. Therefore those who could afford them had locked wooden chests for beds, in which, when rising, they secured their bedding; those who could not suffered frequent injuries from thieves to their clothes. In the refectory they carefully kept small windows locked behind them in the wall, storing in them their napkins, knives, cups, and what remained from their table. For they had no means of providing for their needs except from whatever was left over or what they withheld from their own mouths; of this nothing, or very little, was given as alms.

5. The place which we then called, and now possess as, the *conventus* was a much-used passageway for both sexes, especially for morning Masses; there were frequent and gossiping conversations there with the brethren, by laymen and clerics, continuing until night. If some powerful person, as very often happened, wished to lodge with us, while the brethren miserably ate their bread here and there, that person reclined in the refectory at the brethren’s table—or, if the weather was milder and more pleasant, in the middle of the meadow. Knights rode up to the door of the refectory or into the middle of the *conventus*, dismounted there, and took care to show no reverence—not merely to the monks, but even to the holy places themselves—until the middle of the night.

I call God to witness that I cannot worthily apply my mouth or pen to this misery, so as faithfully to relate the great—and indeed greater—misery of the brethren, as we heard it and as I myself saw it for the most part.

6. The good man, Lord Abbot Theoderic, newly entering this Jerusalemite—indeed, I do not know whether rather Babylonian—desolation, found everything fallen at once and could not raise everything at once and suddenly. Yet, as I have related above, he directed both his mind and his untiring effort to repairing the monastery. When, through the grace of his eloquent speech, he preached to the people in the church of Blessed Mary on the days of Easter or Pentecost, he frequently drew from them ten, twelve, or more or fewer marks for the assistance of rebuilding the monastery.

Though occupied there and giving less attention to the cloister, he nevertheless established as soon as he could lights in the infirmary, dormitory, abbot’s cell, crypt, and before the altar of the blessed protomartyr, from the revenues of the church of Corbeek.

> [Note: Corbeek on the Dyle in Brabant.]
