These were to be administered by the hand of the church custodian from a rent of one mark and a half: he assigned one mark to the custodian for lighting, and a half-mark to the provost for the brethren’s prebend, which formerly paid only five shillings. Likewise, from the revenue of the church of Stades he assigned the custodian five shillings for lighting, which it pays no more than this. He re-established, after their complete abolition, alms for the poor: six rye loaves were to be given daily from the tithe of Brustem, which he redeemed after it had been pledged for ten marks.

Since he could not entirely take away the mill of Moys from a powerful man, who claimed to have acquired it for an annual rent of five shillings and, in addition, what was worth more, to have received it as a benefice from the hand of Abbot Lanzo, Theoderic expended much money and much labour until he brought matters to the point that the iron was removed and it gradually fell into ruin. No trace of the mill was left there save the water and the bank; this state endured down to our own time. He redeemed many other mills, which the malicious fraud of our usurers asserted had been heavily pledged for money or granted as benefices.

7. To store the ornaments of his Mass, he had two small chests made suitable for that purpose. By his own effort he acquired for them an amice adorned with a large and long gold embroidery, and an alb with a gold-embroidered neck-band, together with a clasp, beautifully fashioned of gold and pearls, by which it was fastened.

> [Note: French *orfroi*: embroidery; a border worked with the needle and distinguished by colours, gold, or silver.]

Likewise he acquired two girdles: one, broad and of fine black cloth, adorned at its end with gold embroidery three fingers broad; the other, of very fine cloth of varied colours, extending from the knot that girded him before the stomach all the way to its end, elaborately and very thickly woven throughout with golden threads. He also obtained a belt; a silver chalice with paten, gilded within and around the outer rims; a silver pyx; likewise a silver incense-boat and a silver vessel for wine, weighing three *firtons*.

> [Note: A *ferto*—formerly French *fertin*, German *Vierling*—is one quarter of a mark.]

He obtained also a gilded copper censer with silver chains; a small copper basin fashioned as a tailed animal, for receiving water for washing hands, with small silver images cast and chased within it; and three towels, one to spread over the altar, another beneath the book, and a third for drying hands. He also obtained a cross with a crucifix and a base elaborately worked with figures of the four Evangelists, both of copper but gilded; and a copper dove, ornamented above with gold and silver, containing water for washing hands.

He acquired a chasuble of black cloth, ornamented around the neck and from the neck to the feet in front of the stomach with broad gold embroidery; likewise a cope of nearly the same black cloth, ornamented around the neck and upon the crest of its hood with gold embroidery. Before the breast it had an embroidered panel more than a palm in length, equal in length and breadth, not merely gold embroidery but a solid fabric densely woven above with golden threads, having in the middle a little gem enclosed in a boss. All these things he newly acquired by his own effort for the service of his Mass and the adornment of the church.

He also redeemed one very fine cope of white cloth and a silver censer weighing seven marks. Later, after he had lent these to a certain archdeacon named Alexander, together with one excellent cloth which he himself had bought and a silver chalice, he was never able to recover them; our church has thus lost them to this day. He also bought entirely new one cloth sufficient to cover the high altar, of thick purple-coloured cloth, though pale, patterned in rather large roundels with images of beasts. This too is still kept among us today.

8. He cherished kindly the brethren whom he found, and added as many and such as he could. Yet he endured much from those whom the necessity of his too-small number compelled him to receive when they came out of other cloisters. Our townsmen, always maliciously talkative against us, frequently inveighed against him, saying that only eight or ten brethren consumed the revenues of so great an abbey. They paid no attention, nor were willing in the old malice of their blindness to consider, into what poverty their own fickleness and the contention of abbots through their faction had reduced the abbey, or how much had to be spent on rebuilding the monastery, cloister, and their appurtenances.

Compelled, I say, by this need arising from malicious tongues and slanderers, he had few brethren of his own and received unfamiliar monks coming from elsewhere. He often suffered both losses and injuries from such men: they wished to observe no rule; after being clothed anew from their nakedness and refreshed from their hunger, they either remained most burdensomely among us, or finally fled from us with loss, injury, and slander against us.

> [Note: In both instances, manuscript 1* reads “or” (*aut*).]

I myself saw seventeen such men leave us within five or six years, having been clothed among us in complete garments from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head. It would take very long to recount his effort and labour in improving our church within and without, and how greatly it prospered under him; yet tribulations and persecutions from certain persons never ceased in the meantime. I now wish to relate something concerning them.

9. In the first period of his entry into the abbey, his most grievous persecutor was Count Gislebert of Duras, our advocate.

> [Note: Duras, not far from Saint-Trond. For Count Gislebert see above, IV.9. His father Otto appears to have died between 1090 and 1099. If the *Life of Arnulf, Bishop of Soissons* is trustworthy, that Otto was the brother of Arnulf, count of Loon; cf. Mantelius, p. 50.]

The abbot could never placate him except by money damaging to the church being paid on his behalf. Moreover, Henry of Limburg, our greater advocate, frequently introduced into the town and even into the abbot’s cell, in opposition to Lord Abbot Theoderic, the aforesaid Herimannus, who, unable by force to retain the abbey that he had seized, had fled to Henry seeking protection. Henry was most eager to confirm him in the abbey, if only he could first have obtained the consent of the brethren and exacted allegiance to his Herimannus from the church’s faithful.

But the brethren stood most firmly against him face to face on behalf of Lord Abbot Theoderic. Moreover, by the authority of the bishop of Liège, it was decreed that, as long as Herimannus remained either in the abbot’s cell or anywhere in our whole town, the divine office should not be performed in our church and no bell should sound. Then Henry withdrew amid much confusion and indignation against us and our possessions; again receiving and protecting his Herimannus for our harm.

Good Jesus! When could I tell, or how could I tell, all the evil and damage which our church endured through these two?

> [Note: At this point manuscript 1 has a blank folio. Everything is therefore missing down to the words in chapter 13, “the people, recalling their evils,” etc. A later hand, which placed numbers at the upper margin of the folios, passed from XXV to XXVII, leaving the blank folio; hence these matters were not omitted by the scribe. Rather, the folio later fell out by chance—or, more probably, as it seems, was cut out. This may also be inferred because the blank folio is not attached to the quire but was inserted afterward.]

10. Meanwhile, when kingdom and priesthood were most violently disturbed, it happened that Henry III, august emperor of the Romans, having surrendered the imperial insignia to his son, likewise named Henry, and having been cast out of the kingdom, attempted to reign again.

> [Note: This occurred on 31 December 1105 at Ingelheim; cf. the *Annals of Hildesheim*.]

At that time this Henry, count of Limburg, seemed to be his greatest hope.

> [Note: The emperor had come to Liège to him at Eastertide in 1106.]

He had been made duke of Lorraine only a little earlier.

> [Note: The interpolator has written above “of Lorraine.” It occurred at Mainz, at Christmas 1101, according to the *Annals of Hildesheim*. It is certain that a little earlier in the same year the count was besieged by the emperor in Limburg castle.]

This affair ought nearly to have brought about the destruction of our church. For at that time he appeared to be not so much a duke as a king, since he had become the king’s protector; and there was no king, no bishop, no friend who dared to help us against so great a tyrant. This was especially so because certain utterly depraved men among our townsmen, and men most prone to faction from the party of Luipo and the Herimanni, daily incited him to it. Into the blazing furnace of their evil counsel they heaped oil, pitch, fat, resin, and every fuel of incitement: he should restore his Herimannus to our abbey, expel Theoderic, and make use of the most advantageous time now at hand, in which he could do this with the greatest freedom. He should have Herimannus blessed, since no bishop who had introduced him would ever dare oppose Henry.

Yet he could no more bend the brethren to his will than before. Leaving Herimannus, however, with guards familiar to him in the abbot’s cell, he departed after great devastation had been committed in our court and cloister among the things prepared for our food and clothing.

11. In the meantime Lord Abbot Theoderic had withdrawn to the castle of Count Gislebert of Duras, fearing for his life should he await that tyrant. As the latter left our town by one side, Theoderic entered by the other.

I call almighty God to witness that, unless I had myself seen it with my eyes and absorbed with my ears their groaning cries and sighs from the greatness of their joy, such affection and such devotion toward him among people of both sexes and every age could scarcely be believed—not by me, nor even by him to whom it was shown. Conversely, with what downcast face, with what modest speech, he humbled himself; with how abundant tears and wet cheeks was his entire face bathed! They wept because of the excessive love with which they burned for him; he wept because of the great humility by which he measured himself. Received with such triumphal applause and such favouring devotion of the people, he was conducted to the very door of his cell.

But those inside had barred it, and, struck by the tumult and indignation of the people, they expected nothing more certainly than to be pierced by their swords. As the barred door increasingly stirred the people to wrath and indignation, some nevertheless hesitated whether to rush in by force, while others were already preparing themselves with shouting for an assault. One of them, upon whose wisdom and counsel the entire town seemed to rely, burst forth in the midst with flaming countenance and a great-sounding voice:

> “Come then, men—come, men, if indeed you are men! Why do you stand guard here so feebly? Why do you watch at the doors of this dwelling? Why do you not at once break the barrier, or tear the very doors up by their roots, fling open the entrance, and rush in with flashing sword? As though these guilty men, held shut in here, were not by the will and judgment of God today to be beheaded by our swords! By their poisonous accusations and pestilential counsel your houses once blazed in ruinous fire; mothers were deprived of lawful marriage; your descendants were left without parents; you yourselves—alas, alas!—are without children and grandchildren. And behold, now again, to our insult and to the disgrace of your name and race, these importunate, obstinate, base parasites thrust themselves before our eyes, so that they may cast out the lord of those whose fathers, sons, brothers, descendants, kinsmen, friends, and servants they have slain; whose people they have driven by fire and plunder from wealth to want, from glory to disgrace. Let a few unarmed, cowardly criminals expel him, so that these lecherous men may swallow up what we wrested from their sword and flame at the peril of our lives; so that, like parricides deserving punishment, they may once more stir up sedition and civil war in our town, as they did once, as they did often, whereby the memorials of our stock and the last remnants of our remnant may utterly perish. If we were men, sons of men, would these things not now recoil upon their heads in the present moment?”  

Such were Guntramnus’s words.

12. This Guntramnus was a servant of our church, a man of most pleasing and great eloquence, tall in stature, with a bodily bulk very fittingly proportioned to his height; most valiant in war, bold in spirit, prudent in counsel, steadfast in affairs, handsome both in his graceful body and in his full countenance and most elegant face.

> [Note: “in affairs” is absent in D.]

Our townsmen, burning against such a man—one such that no one of our own will ever arise among us again—with malignant hatred and most wicked envy because of his excellence, killed him when a flying arrow struck his forehead; the author was unknown. One day, after his treachery had somehow at last been disclosed, they rose armed against him while he suspected nothing. Had chance not prevented him from defending himself at close quarters with the sword, what—and how great—a slaughter he would have made before he could fall!

> [Note: D reads: “what and how great.”]

He lies buried between the tower and the door which opens southward toward the brethren’s cemetery, by the wall, immediately upon leaving the door, at the right hand.

When such a man had thus, as I have said, addressed the people, the people at once turned to fury at the recollection of past evils. Like a bear made savage by tasting bloody flesh, it shouted against them with drawn sword, attempted to break down the doors and wrench away the posts, in order to kill by the sword’s edge all alike—monks and knights, lesser and greater. But the piety and kindness of Lord Abbot Theoderic at once interposed itself as a most secure shield against those wicked fires. Calling urgently to Count Gislebert, and summoning each of his men back by name, he scarcely at last obtained by many prayers that they should not rush upon those doomed men. When they had been calmed, he began to address his brethren before the people in this manner:

13. “Far be it from me, dearest brethren—far be it, I say, sweetest sons—that this sin against the Lord, this scandal among the people, should stain or darken my return to you and your devout affection for me and that of the people with anyone’s blood or with murder. We must not fight with these weapons; the wicked enemy is not to be cut down by this sword. He whose soldiers we are—Christ himself—is our armour. Blessed Paul, his standard-bearer, thus cries out to his fellow-soldiers: ‘Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and put on the breastplate of righteousness; and shod your feet in preparation for the gospel of peace; above all take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the burning darts of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God’ (Ephesians VI, 14).

“Armed with these weapons after the likeness of the good king David, we shall be able to attack this most arrogant, spurious, and uncircumcised man with confidence. When so great a blasphemer has been struck upon the forehead, and wounded in that part of the body in which Uzziah, presumptuous in the priesthood, blazed with leprosy, may he fall in leprosy; and when his head has been cut off by his own sword and he has been stripped of all his arms, may we ‘give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever, who alone does great wonders’ (Psalm XXXV, 1). And again, with our David let us say: ‘Blessed be the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war—my mercy and my refuge, my protector and my deliverer’ (Psalm XLIII, 1).”

14. When he had said these things, the people returned home, while he himself remained with us in the cloister. Those who had been shut up in the abbot’s cell, lest they should be killed by our men who had seized the tower from them, nearly all escaped that night. Apart from one monk who had come with Herimannus from Malmedy, scarcely anyone remained with him.

Yet certain utterly foul scoundrels and belly-gods from our town, among whom a given crust of coarse bread could readily purchase the name of a man of any dignity, and the withholding of the same could condemn an accused man to the gallows, frequently entered the cell where he was shut up. They fattened his lethargic brain with the stinking oil of their flattery, and in the meantime thus indulged their own gluttonous incontinence with him.

> [Note: *Leccatria* means incontinence; a *lecator* is a gluttonous, incontinent man; Flemish *lekker*, French *lichard*.]

The entire abbey, and especially the monks, looked to Lord Abbot Theoderic with the humble service of fidelity and the gaze of devout obedience, and mourned his distress with sufficiently bitter hearts. On the following day, when Lord Abbot Theoderic came to Liège at the summons of Bishop Obbert, he laid before the ears of the bishop and the church of St Lambert his injury, persecution, the arrogance of a revived Simon, and the invasion. He moved not only them to mournful compassion, but cast the entire city itself into deepest grief. For he was most beloved by clergy, people, and monks alike—most welcome for his great learning and the delight of his distinguished voice, and most serene in his gentle manners and cheerful countenance.

15. Nevertheless, such a grave crime by an impious usurper was not swiftly punished as befitted the dignity, discipline, and name of Liège. Yet this is no wonder. We readily grant them pardon when we consider the necessity of the time and their distress. For there was then no small disturbance, not only in that church but throughout the whole bishopric; and each person was pressed by anxious business concerning not merely the commonwealth but his own household affairs as well.

As we have mentioned above, the emperor Henry was anxiously labouring there to recover the state of the kingdom wrested from him. Because Bishop Obbert and Duke Henry were divided by cruel hatred and most grievous enmities, and likewise Count Godfrey of Namur and the same duke, the emperor worked most diligently first to restore them to peace and concord, so that the strength of their peace and concord might afterward be for him a hope and means of victory.

> [Note: On this matter see also the *Chronicle of St Pantaleon* in Eckhard I, 923.]

The walls of the whole city and church also trembled with fear of the waves of an impending war. For it was reported—and it was true—that the emperor’s son, Henry by name, was hastening with strong hand and the greatest indignation to seize the city.

> [Note: Henry V, having learned before Easter 1106 that Duke Henry of Lorraine and Bishop Obbert of Liège were supporting the emperor’s cause, was preparing to set out for Lorraine itself; cf. Ekkehard of Aura, under this year.]

16. While these troubles were in progress, and each man was attending more diligently to his own public and domestic affairs as necessity seemed to require, our own affairs were accordingly managed with less concern than was expedient for us. Yet after he had been summoned once and again [Note: lacking in 1*.], the bishop at last excommunicated him [Note: Herimann] and all his accomplices, ordering his archdeacon Alexander to expel him from the abbot’s cell and from his court. But Alexander wholly disregarded the order; for what reason and with what intention, let him himself consider.

The duke, however, not forgetful of the injury and insult done to him by Herimann [Note: “by Herimann” in 1*.], gathered his arms and forces against us in great fury and indignation, intending, on an appointed day, to make propitiatory victims in Herimann’s sacrifice of the flesh of any of our people whom he could not compel to attend the dedication of his Bel. But Count Gilbert, then the faithful helper of the lord Abbot Theoderic, now reconciled with him, engaged Count Godfrey of Louvain—who not long afterwards became duke [Note: In that same year, 1106, he received the duchy of Lower Lotharingia, taken from Henry of Limburg, according to Sigebert]—and manfully resisted him. Since Duke Henry did not dare to approach, Gilbert rendered all his effort fruitless, although Henry was his lord. Not long afterwards the lord Abbot Theoderic returned from Liège to our monastery, bearing with great patience his rival shut up in his cell.

17. And now the day was at hand on which the Count of Flanders [Note: Robert II, called “of Jerusalem,” reigned 1093–1112] was to meet the emperor at Antwerp. As the emperor set out thither, it happened that he passed through our place and lodged for one night in the abbot’s cell, in which that brother of unsound counsel was living. Since he did not dare openly to oppose the emperor’s occupation of the cell, while he feared that, if he left it, no return would thereafter be open to him, he went down into the cellar beneath the lodging and remained there throughout that night. Thus, when morning came and the emperor set out upon his way, he intended to come forth from those lower hiding-places and return to seize the cell.

But some of our boys, who had waited upon the emperor that night, acting on the counsel of our brethren, barred his entrance and did not permit him to return to the cell; nevertheless, they inflicted no insult or violence upon him or his retainers. When he realized that his opportunity of entering had been cut off, and feared that he was about to be suffocated by our boys as though in a tomb—that is, in that cellar—he at last burst forth from the pit into which he had wickedly condemned himself, like some new earth-born creature emerging by another little door into the light hateful to him. He became a great spectacle to the people and to the boys in the streets; a man without honour, a monk without shame, he rushed off to one of the houses in the market-place. After remaining there some days, he went again to the duke on Holy Saturday, the eve of the Lord’s resurrection.

When this plague had been removed and this bilge-water cast out of the ship of our church, the bell presently sounded, for it was the third hour; and after so many sorrowful days during which our choir had been silent, it was a great joy that we were now permitted to open our mouths in divine praises. For our monastery and the parish outside had for so long been under the bishop’s ban that no one might sing in them until Herimann had departed from the abbot’s cell and from the whole court and precinct.

18. When this was announced to Duke Henry—for perhaps at that very hour he was passing through our market-place—he blazed with incredible anger and roared with intolerable grief. Unless he avenged this injury done to him, so as to make an example for all, he vowed himself and all that was his, with an oath and a certain dreadful imprecation, to accursed death and cruel destruction. Inflamed, therefore, with violent anger, immense rage, and no slight indignation against us and ours, he took the abbot’s contempt for him more grievously to heart, and immediately armed himself with utterly unrestrained zeal for danger to the lives of us and our people, and for the ruin both of our property and of our limbs.

He ordered all his men, with fearful threats, to spare none of us, to distinguish neither monk from clerk nor clerk from layman [Note: *eque* in 1 and 1*.], to persecute cruelly, and with bestial fury to rage against us and ours. If they could seize any of our people, he decreed that some should be hanged without pity; that the eyes of others should be gouged out; the noses of some cut off; the hands of others amputated; the feet of others severed; and the legs of some broken. Those to whom he wished to seem more merciful and humane he ordered to be kept long imprisoned and finally redeemed for an extremely heavy weight of silver. And indeed those who feared losing nothing but money counted themselves far happier than the rest.

Thus all were seized by great fear, terror, and distress: the mind was stunned, the limbs failed, the knees knocked together, since none of us could go outside the town by any route without danger to life or loss of limb or property. He also hated Count Gilbert so much because he had opposed him on our behalf that he openly strove to accuse him of disloyalty and confidently sought on that account to deprive him of his hereditary fief. We still had several wagon-loads of wine at Cologne, which he immediately ordered to be reserved for his own use.

19. These and many other evils which he daily brought upon us—for he had also terribly threatened all our bailiffs [Note: “our” added by D], forbidding them to answer us in anything—grievously afflicted the mind of the lord Abbot Theoderic. Still more bitter was the news that he intended to grant as benefices to his retainers those possessions which owed obedience to us along the Moselle and also in Testrebant [Note: Testebrant in 1]. If this should happen even once in so stormy a tempest, our church would scarcely, or never, recover them; and our abbey would thereafter possess neither wine nor fish.

He was therefore afflicted with immense grief and fear, fearing also and being exceedingly anxious lest, in so great a commotion, someone should be killed, imprisoned, or despoiled because of him. But while he was oppressed beyond endurance by this burden of cares and anxieties, certain of his friends who were with the duke, seeing the distress, the danger to the townspeople, and the church’s intolerable and irreparable loss, still attempted through money to turn him away from the evils he planned against us. At last the hardness of black flint was softened, though scarcely, by a silver hammer; and, excepting Count Gilbert, he agreed that our abbot and his whole church should have peace.

But when the matter was finally reported to the lord Abbot Theoderic—for God knows that his friends had arranged this earlier without his knowledge—no argument, counsel, persuasion, or fear could induce him to consent unless the duke first removed every impediment he had placed upon the church’s affairs, and restored Count Gilbert and all the townspeople whom he had troubled on Theoderic’s account to firm peace and favour. This was at last granted, after remarkable and indescribable labour on both sides.

I was personally present at these events. On the Friday of the Lord’s Preparation, I rode to Liège in a single day to complete the arrangements; after staying there long on this business, I returned the same day, and immediately set out again with the lord abbot for Liège. There the money previously agreed upon was paid; Count Gilbert was restored to the duke’s favour; the townspeople were freed from fear; and, by the duke’s command, the church’s affairs were entirely settled.

Concerning Herimann, however, this was finally determined between the duke and the lord abbot: if, recognizing his guilt, he wished to come to satisfaction and penitence, he should be received mercifully; and, once his humility and obedience had been proved, the lord abbot should not disdain to make allowance for him according to the weakness of his disposition. But the inveterate malice of that pitiable man could in no way be humbled to satisfaction and penitence. He remained what he had been and assumed what he had not been.

20. Our church, grievously afflicted by this oppression of the duke and invasion by Herimann, languished for a long time. A gold chalice, of I know not what weight, together with its paten, which the lord Abbot Theoderic himself had acquired, was irretrievably sold in this necessity. The wood at Kircheym was cut down and sold; other resources were greatly diminished; and, what was more grievous and more to be lamented, all work on the monastery was abandoned and fell into ruin until his death.

But by God’s judgment, in that same year the duchy was taken from Henry [Note: “In the same year, in 1106, after the death of Emperor Henry III, the duchy of Lotharingia was adjudged to Henry of Limburg, our advocate”: interpolation in 1*, after erasure of two lines.] [Note: At the assembly held at Worms on Pentecost, according to the Annals of Hildesheim] and given to Count Godfrey of Louvain. The reason was that in the same week, namely on Thursday, the day of the Lord’s Supper, he had fought against the son of the deposed emperor Henry, the newly created king Henry, his lord, above the river Meuse before the bridge of the town of Guisez [Note: Visé, between Liège and Maastricht; Sigebert and Ekkehard agree concerning the date], and had put the king to flight after crushing his army.

To crown our evils, another calamity befell us—so much the more severe and intolerable because it came from a person formerly more familiar and friendly to us, and powerful. Count Gilbert, our advocate, and the lord Abbot Theoderic began to disagree with one another. The count demanded from him twenty-four marks of silver which he had given to Duke Godfrey of Louvain, because he had prevented Duke Henry from falling upon us on Herimann’s account after Herimann had been expelled from us; he also demanded whatever accumulated daily above that sum as interest. The abbot replied that he had promised him only five, and that he had already paid them.

Thus our evils were multiplied day after day. What was the count to do? Refusing altogether to yield to reason or truth, though the damage was double the amount of that silver, he plundered throughout the abbey whatever he demanded. Never would he be reconciled to the abbot at anyone’s request; instead, he turned to his lord Count Henry [Note: He had meanwhile escaped in that same year, 1106, from the prison to which King Henry had committed him, as Sigebert establishes] and to the abbot’s rival Herimann, and began to employ every device and power to have the abbot expelled and Herimann restored.

21. At that time [Note: A.D. 1107, interpolation] Adelbero was bishop at Metz [Note: V adds this; “the fourth”] after Poppo [Note: who had already died in 1103]. Although he frequently sent letters and envoys on behalf of the lord Abbot Theoderic to Counts Henry and Gilbert, he could do nothing, or little, to help him against them, except that by this he strengthened the spirits of our brethren and the wavering hearts of the fickle townspeople.

For a while both parties in the dispute were kept in suspense under this rope of contention. Since, therefore, he was deprived of human help from every direction and was most violently afflicted by those who ought most to have helped him, he decided to seek divine help in this manner: if he could reform the dissolution of our order—which through many diverse occurrences had long taken root among us, not without disgrace—by adopting the practices of religious monks.

A few brethren urgently pressed for this undertaking; but more regarded their long-established abuses as something very grievous to change, especially those who had fled from other cloisters and gathered among us. Yet, with God’s help prevailing through the better, though smaller, part of the brethren, the customs of Cluny were introduced into our monastery and cloister on the Kalends of March—1 March—which in that year was Friday, at the beginning of the fast [Note: A.D. 1107; interpolation in the lower margin]. To demonstrate these observances to us, the lord Stephen, abbot of St James at Liège, sent two of his brethren, and Berengar, abbot of St Lawrence in the same city, sent two.

The Cluniac order began to be taught among us with the most ardent zeal and practised with the greatest constancy—not in part, but entire. Our young men especially devoted themselves to it praiseworthily and, without any falsehood on our part, with great fervour; the elders acquiesced silently and with peaceful minds; and the schoolboys accepted discipline by daily exercise, without a heavy yoke. Those who had gathered among us from elsewhere and were unwilling to change their former frivolity departed; likewise some of our own brethren of the same frivolous disposition.

I wish here to record the names of those who were then alive when these observances were introduced among us, so that their glory may grow from this even in the present life, and so that posterity may understand how few brethren there were among us: Abbot Theoderic; I, Rodulf, prior; Sybert, secretary; Morung, provost; Folkard, cellarer and cantor; Engo, already old; and Gilbert, a mature young man.

On the first day when we began the order, five boys left the school: Thidelmus, Baldwin, Henry, Christian, and Franco, who afterwards cast off the habit and fled. All these had already become grown and could long before have left the school; but the prior’s diligence had kept them within the school until that day, fearing that if before the order began they had tasted, according to the old abuse, the pleasing and poisonous sweetness of frivolity and idleness outside the school, the necks of young men, unaccustomed to a strict and continual yoke, could no longer be bent to the order. [Note: “hatred,” *odii*, in 1*, for “idleness,” *otii*.]

The boys who remained in the school were Guazelin, Adulf, Guulbert, Frederic, and Humbert. Counting both seniors and juniors, we were seventeen. With this small number, assisted by those who had been lent to us from Liège, the order began, as I have said, to be observed with the greatest fervour, especially through the laudable zeal of the young men who devoted themselves to it.

22. If any one of us in particular, by his persistence and timely action, by his sagacity varied in a thousand ways, first persuaded the abbot’s mind to maintain these observances; if, amid much tribulation and distress of his own, amid hatred and envy, he at length gained from him the decision that they should be retained; and if through his zeal they flourished while he lived and grew cold when he died—whoever he may be, no one doubts, since great amendment in the brethren’s lives and progress in the church followed from these observances, that, while we are silent about him, he ought to be silent concerning the man for whose love he feared no adversity, hatred, envy, or danger, provided only that religion might be introduced and the place freed from the disgrace of former irreligion.

23. Thus the clouds of most grievous sorrow cast upon us by Henry had already been largely wiped away by the joys of the newly introduced order; and beneath the sweet yoke of the Lord the burden of our affliction was felt to be quite light. [Note: “light,” *lene*, in 1 and 1*.] The enemy saw and envied the prosperous success of our order, and was greatly troubled that, so to speak, we were advancing in it with giant strides. Therefore he filled with his most wicked spirit—behold, for I know not what number of times—the same Henry, long accustomed and most familiar as his instrument for afflicting our souls.

Henry, forgetting his earlier agreement with the lord Abbot Theoderic and the money, very harmful to us, which he had extorted from him in payment for his future favour, broke faith, did not reverence God’s judgment, and again without any delay undertook to force Herimann upon us. Kingship and priesthood, as I said above, were so disturbed and agitated against one another that ecclesiastical censure could then do nothing, or little, to help us against the violence of tyrants.

Herimann, through certain accomplices who were rather familiar at the royal court, also won the support of the king’s chancellor, named Adelbert, who afterwards became archbishop of Mainz. Through him, and with the king as a faithful helper, he pursued his restoration. But the matter concerning Herimann had not been made known to king and chancellor as the truth actually stood. Deceived therefore by the lies of Herimann’s supporters, they ordered, through letters and envoys to the bishops of Metz and Liège, that he be restored to our abbey; and news of his arrival was reported to us daily. Count Gilbert was ready to receive him and, because he had been our advocate, to introduce him into the abbey.

24. Amid these daily thunders of threatening rumour flying abroad, the high hand of the thundering God—long since stretched out most heavily against us from of old—suddenly pierced us with a most terrible lightning-flash. It removed from our midst the lord Abbot Theoderic, brought by an illness caused by bloodletting, scarcely five days old, into the way of all flesh.

Alas! With what mouth can I relate, with what pen write, the pressures, tribulations, and distresses which we then endured? Those who while Abbot Theoderic lived openly persecuted us because of Herimann could scarcely restrain their hands from tearing us alive or cutting us to pieces with swords. Those who had been accustomed secretly to lay snares for us then came forward openly, so much fiercer against us in public as they had previously been more secret. Very few shared our feelings and wished to do anything on our behalf that could produce the effect of any vigorous deed. Herimann was reported daily to be at the gates: by some invited, by others awaited. Yet the minds of all the brethren were firmly set against him, no less after the abbot’s death than before while he lived.

25. In this our oppression, tribulation, and distress, we found no persecutors more grievous than our three most powerful priests: namely Reyner of Hales, Hezelon of Mergueles, and a certain Lanzon from our town. While they were stirring up great dissensions and inciting the madness of laymen against us before and behind, we scarcely obtained permission to keep the dead abbot’s body unburied for a whole day, until his fellows, who had been summoned, could perform the funeral rites due to him.

Some of the priests and laymen acclaimed the approaching Herimann; others supported this man or that, according to the character of such factions; yet none of them followed our judgment. Hence, as I have said, they scarcely restrained themselves from burying him without the brethren’s funeral rites. As prior, I opposed their fury with steadfast authority, though at great danger to my life—first treated by them as nothing, assailed with many insults, and battered by still more injuries.

At length I prevailed. After waiting until the third day, we buried Abbot Theoderic. The lord Berengar, abbot of St Lawrence at Liège, performed his rites; a great multitude of counts, nobles, and people, including those faithful to him and his friends while he lived, followed his funeral; and the brethren made for him a great and pitiable lamentation, unrestricted weeping and wailing. For toward them he had shown the gentlest affection and great patience, a cheerful countenance and pleasant speech: he knew how to bear the wicked with equanimity, and to love and honour the good.

He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, 25 April, the day of the Greater Litany, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1107, having completed nine years [Note: thus in 1 and 1*.] in the abbacy, less three months and six days. [Note: Rather eight, from what he himself stated above in Book V, chapter 6.] During his time our church lost none of its possessions, except an allod lying toward Antwerp near Mechelen [Note: Mecheln], at a place called … [Note: In 1 and 1*, the place-name is left blank; “at a place called” is absent in D.]

This estate yielded each year twenty-five solidi of Antwerp coinage and weight on the feast of the Conversion of St Paul. He sold it under this necessity because our church could derive nothing from it owing to robbers and violent plunderers; his intention was to redeem, with its price, another allod nearer to us. He acted not on his own counsel alone, but on that of his superiors: the bishop of Metz, our advocates, and the peers of the church. But death overtook him, and Count Gilbert took from those men the money entrusted to them to redeem another allod for the church. Thus the church ultimately lost both the allod and its price.

He also lent to a certain archdeacon of Liège named Alexander a silver censer weighing seven marks, an entirely precious and new pallium, and a silver chalice weighing [Note: repeated in 1] a mark and a half; these we have not been able to recover to this day. After the abbot’s death, Count Gilbert also took from our church a most precious reliquary [Note: a chest in which saints’ relics are kept] which the abbot had lent him: namely, a panel one foot long and nearly as broad, engraved with silver on the outside, adorned and richly laden on the inside with purest gold and many choice gems in marvellous workmanship, and full of most precious relics [Note: “gems” in D].

**HERE ENDS BOOK SIX; BOOK SEVEN BEGINS.** [Note: “explicit” in 1*.]

1. Therefore, after the burial of the lord Abbot Theoderic, seeing that I could not endure the envy of my rivals, especially the now openly manifest hatred of those who, because of the introduction of the new order, were no longer permitted to misuse our cloister and to converse with the brethren at unsuitable hours and places, I asked on that same day, in the humblest submission, to be released from the priorate. I was released, though the brethren took it badly.

Moreover, all who eagerly awaited Herimann daily inflamed Count Gilbert, his wife, and every other person they could, with malicious slanders against me and accusations of my real or invented crimes. They were certain that so long as I remained with the brethren they could not prevail, by argument or counsel, in securing Herimann against us.

When the brethren had made their election and presented it to the bishop and church of Liège, and were about to proceed thence to Metz, they found there messengers of the emperor who had preceded them with imperial letters concerning Herimann. They also instructed the bishop orally that he should no longer trouble Herimann concerning our abbey. [Note: That is, the bishop of Liège.]

The bishop [Note: Obbertus, inserted above the line] had only recently been reconciled with the emperor. [Note: Already in 1106, after Henry IV’s death, he had come to the king at Aachen, as is recorded in the Annals of Hildesheim.] The emperor’s father had died at Liège, and the bishop had supported the father’s cause against the son; from fear of this, he did not sufficiently dare—though it did not befit him—to oppose the emperor’s violence. Nevertheless, he did not give his assent. So far as he could without forfeiting the emperor’s favour, he explained to the messengers why at St Trudo’s no one could any longer canonically become abbot, and added: “It is not mine to give the benefice of the abbey of St Trudo, but to bless its abbot. It belongs to the bishop of Metz; let him see whom he sends to me for blessing.”

There, as frequently elsewhere, the religious man Stephen, abbot of St James at Liège, showed the emperor’s messengers with great confidence and argument that the emperor laboured in vain for Herimann. It was established by Stephen’s ecclesiastical judgment and that of his fellow peers that Herimann had long since been condemned for invading this abbey, and that because of his obstinate incorrigibility he had also been excommunicated. Nor could he finally deserve absolution except after promising further amendment for his invasion and violence. This disturbance interrupted the brethren’s journey to Metz, and they returned to our cloister, intending to send their messenger to the bishop of Metz because of the urgent necessity.

2. Without delay Herimann arrived; brought by the emperor’s messengers, he was introduced into the abbey by Count Gilbert. Those who pleased him, and those who did not dare oppose him because of the count, made fealty and homage to him. Yet the leading and more honourable men of the abbey withheld their hands from his fealty and homage. All the brethren unanimously refused him not only the monastery and cloister, but even any conversation except through intermediaries—and that harshly. They would in no way assent to him unless he first came to a hearing and canonical examination, which he, as ever, so now also avoided, as though conscious of guilt.

His associates and advisers were utterly frivolous, lying men, unable to measure themselves, full of empty hope and every presumption, possessed of neither virtue nor judgment. The greater part belonged to that sworn faction of Luipo, still carrying their severed hands as a sign of their condemnation and outlawry. Surrounded by these wretched and most miserably wretched men, and, as we learned from one of them, bound to them by an oath upon the saints, he was carried madly, willingly and unwillingly, this way and that, according to their madness. Yet they plundered so freely even from him that he did not have bread and beer enough to sustain himself, nor anything besides a simple tunic with which to cover himself even in the harshest midwinter. What sort of man he was to himself—what do you suppose he would be to us?

3. Meanwhile a messenger was sought to carry to Metz an account of these evils. At the urgent entreaties of many brethren I was chosen and compelled for this task [Note: D reads *sumptibus*, “at expenses,” for *sum*, “I was”]. I feared—as later I grievously experienced—that whereas I had thought that by relinquishing the priorate the envy and hatred of the Herimann party toward me might be reduced, I should incur as much, if not more, by accepting this mission. Yet I obeyed, not counting my own life more precious than the church’s benefit.

But because of the Herimann party’s snares, I did not dare take the public road to Metz. I joined the army of Frederick, bishop of Cologne; Godfrey, duke of Louvain; Godfrey, count of Namur; and Arnold, count of Loon—two thousand knights, as I supposed, if not more—who were proceeding to the emperor at the city of Verdun. [Note: After celebrating Easter at Mainz on 14 April 1107, Henry wished to meet Pope Paschal II, who had come into France to hold a council, on the frontier of Lotharingia and France, according to the Annals of Hildesheim; he celebrated Pentecost at Metz on 2 June.]

We travelled from Liège to Huy, from Huy through Hesbaye and Villance [Note: Villance], then through the castle of Ivois [Note: Ivois near Mouzon], and so through another castle, Dun [Note: omitted in D; on the Meuse], finally reaching Verdun. Good Jesus! How can I recount what I suffered on that journey? When I thought we were to lodge in villages at night, suddenly, while it was scarcely the eighth hour of the day, the squires and some of the soldiers would loosen their horses, seize the whole fabric of two or three little villages, and tie great and small pieces of timber to their horses’ tails. By streams amid the green meadows they would build, in scarcely an hour, dwellings for themselves and their horses, carrying axes and other tools for such work, as well as sickles, while another group cut grass for the horses.

The lords, once their large and elaborate tents had been raised, lived in them as though in their own houses, passing the time leisurely until evening, either in meadows beside streams or beside woodland thickets pleasantly resounding with the varied songs of birds. But what was I, a monk with only one servant, to do? If I went to the villages, then either the army had already plundered them, and there were no villages left, all their inhabitants hiding in the woods; or, if any village nearby remained, I was certain I could keep nothing there throughout that night—on the one hand from peasants who had been despoiled and would come by night from woodland hiding-places to reconnoitre the army, and on the other from our own counts, plundering one another for themselves.

But if I remained among the army in the wide green meadows, to say nothing of lodgings and huts—which, even if I knew how to make them, I had no means to build—I did not know where to buy food, which I had not brought either for myself or for my horses, nor fodder for the horses. Nor did I dare separate my servant from me; if he remained alone, equally unknown to everyone, I did not know to whom in the army he could attach himself.

At last, entrusting myself and my belongings to God and blessed Trudo, I left the army and went on to a half-ruined little village nearby. I found no man there, only women, because they feared the army. Seeing that I was a monk, they rushed to meet me, competing over which of them could first have me as a guest that night, so that by my presence she might be defended from the rapacity of the most hostile squires.

When I turned aside to one woman whose house seemed to me better fortified by walls, at once all the women with their children and infants from the whole village left their homes and fled wailing to my lodging. They brought with them their piglets, hens, cocks, and other small animals, and shut them up inside the house and barn of my hostess. They offered me and my servant, free of charge, cheese, milk, and such oat bread as they had to eat, as well as hay and grain for the horses—all likewise free. But thanks be to God: I accepted nothing from them without payment. And by God’s protection, through the merits of St Trudo, I not only lost nothing that night, but, when the army departed in the morning, the frightened women recovered without any loss whatsoever all that they had brought into my lodging.

I remained awake through nearly the whole night, especially because the timid nature of the women made me tremble there where there was no cause for fear.

4. The following day, when the army moved at first light, I rose, bade farewell to my women, and joined our company. But because of the previous day’s exhaustion and the sleepless night, I spent the whole day sweating and gasping beneath the most oppressive heat of the sun, riding all that day with sleepy head and nodding as if my neck were broken.

That day, however, I bought for myself and my servant a little axe and a sickle. Thereafter, when the army halted, necessity being our teacher, we began, like the others, to make huts and shelters for ourselves, except that we abstained from plunder and breaking into houses. Cutting branches and larger pieces of wood, we made huts for ourselves, mangers for our horses, and some shade-shelters. For the stench of horse-dung and of men going aside not far from us to relieve themselves nearly killed me every day, often driving me to vomit. Then there was the thick infestation of large flies by day, and at night the troublesome swarming of bad gnats, humming faintly around one who wished to sleep and biting bitterly and often until blood flowed. [Note: 1* reads “stinging” for “driving”; D reads “infestation” for “swarming.”]

5. At length, after travelling almost ten days—a journey which we could comfortably have made in five—we came to Verdun and waited there because the emperor had not yet arrived. Hearing that the bishop of Metz was lodging at a village near Verdun called Dongei [Note: Dugny], I went to him there, gave him the brethren’s letter, and supplemented with an oral account their complaint and petition. He deferred answering me until Metz, intending there to act on this matter with the counsel of his leading men.

But while I stayed with him for some time, oh, how many disputes and contradictions I endured there from certain Herimann supporters! Count Henry of Limburg was there with the bishop, and the Herimann party had sent to him one of our priests, a most wordily contentious man named Hezelon from the village of Mergueles. His purpose was to report that the lord Abbot Theoderic was dead and urge Henry to assist Herimann with the bishop regarding the abbey. What conflicts we frequently had there, back and forth; and how narrowly I escaped the snares he laid for me between Dongei and Verdun, while for this necessity I rode almost daily to the bishop!

6. This estate, namely Dugny, which lies a short mile south of Verdun, was, as I then learned there from the people of Metz and from the inhabitants, one of those which our lord Saint Trudo, in his youth, conveyed at Metz, together with the rest of his freehold, to the blessed protomartyr Stephen. [Col. 0103B] It remained assigned to the table of the bishops of Metz until the time of Bishop Theoderic, who, when he was building at Metz a monastery of monks under the title of the blessed martyr Vincent, gave it in perpetuity as its own provision to the brothers serving God and blessed Vincent there. [Note: [Col. 0103] In the year 970; cf. *Life of Theoderic* by Sigebert, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV, 470 (*Patrologia* CLX).] But since, with God protecting me, they had been unable to do me any harm there, they were planning how they might catch me in an ambush on my return and either shamefully dishonour me or cruelly kill me.

But I was entrusted by the bishop to the prior of Saint Clement, named Azelin, who later became abbot of Gorze—for the bishop then had him with him as a wise and devout monk—and I went with him to Metz, waiting there for some time with him for the bishop. When the bishop came, after consultation he gave me two sealed letters to carry: one to the brothers, the other to Hermann. [Note: [Col. 0103] “one” 1*.] [Note: [Col. 0103] “the other” 1*.] He instructed the brothers that he wished soon to come to them, so that, being present among those present, he might by their counsel bring to an end the long rope of contention between them and Hermann. The letter to the brothers said that they were not to be broken by fear of anyone from justice and truth, since he did not wish Hermann to use any violence against them. The letter to Hermann, however, was so framed that it could be understood in two senses: by Hermann, as though the bishop assented to him; by the brothers, as though he opposed him. This ambiguity had been made so that, while Hermann was deceived by vain hope before the bishop’s arrival, which was expected daily, he might not, through his retainers, harass any of the brothers unwilling to agree with him; and so that the brothers might not be broken by fear because of the bishop’s uncertain attitude toward them.

7. Having received these letters and been dismissed by the bishop with the kiss of peace, I neither dared nor knew how to return by the road on which I had come; nevertheless, I feared the public road because of the ambushes of Hermann’s party, which they had laid for me in the greatest density. [Note: [Col. 0103] “because of” added by D.] Therefore, led by a messenger of the good man Azelin, I passed through [Col. 0104A] the castle of Briey—[Note: [Col. 0103] Briey, between Verdun and Metz.]—and that night lodged with very devout canons at the monastery of Saint Peter in the wood nearby, which they had newly begun to build. [Note: [Col. 0103] D omits the name of the place.] At daybreak, that is, on the feast of the Ascension of the Lord (23 May 1107), likewise receiving an escort from them, I came to the castle of Cuns, where there was a cell of the brothers of the monastery of Saint Hubert, and I stayed with them that night.

On the third day I reached Saint Hubert by a very long road through a dreadful, trackless wilderness: my brain almost scorched by the sun’s heat; the flesh of my horses grievously cut by certain flies in front, as though toothed, and by others behind, doubtless armed with extremely bitter stings; and their blood almost drained. Driven throughout that day by the movement caused by their most bitter punctures or their most savage [Col. 0104B] bites, they sprang this way and that beneath me in such distress that they could scarcely now carry me or proceed faster than a very slow step. Woe to that land, which God has cursed with the curse of such dreadful monsters!

On the fourth day, led by a certain cleric who feared captivity no less than I did, I know not by what byways, over the rocky ridges of very high mountains and through the marshy hollows of thick valleys, we and our horses were miserably exhausted throughout the day. Unable to leave the wood all that day, we finally spent the night in its midst in a most wretched little village. [Note: [Col. 0103] D lacks “nor—spent the night.”] Our ears were continually raised in alarm at every sound of anything whatever, lest perhaps we should be captured, or our horses should be stolen as we slept by the familiar raiding-place of those robbers. [Col. 0104C]

At dawn on the fifth day we fled the place, cursing it—the cleric taking his road, I another. The Cluniacs have a cell in the wood between Huy and Liège, called Saint Symphorian’s; when I came to it, they received me most kindly that night. On the sixth day we reached Liège, to the most pious and devout lord Stephen, abbot of Saint James. There, now in safety, I began at last to feel most acutely the pain I had contracted from the long hardship of the journey. Good Jesus! Repay to his soul the humane compassion which he showed my illness there—what a kindly countenance, what a generous hand, what consoling speech!

Some of our brothers had long been awaiting my [Col. 0104D] return there. Out of pious fear they wished [Note: [Col. 0103] “wishing to avert me” 1*.] to dissuade me from returning at that time to the cloister, since Hermann’s party had sworn themselves against me with utter obstinacy, and, at their lord’s command, the men of Count Giselbert were earnestly seeking to dishonour me. I confess: somewhat frightened, I hesitated in some doubt. But recovering my courage, and considering the most serious loss to the church if I did not go to the cloister, I contrived, by a remarkable but good stratagem, [Col. 0105A] to win over Count Giselbert’s wife, [Note: [Col. 0105D] Gertrude.] who was especially urging her lord and his men to support Hermann. From her I very easily obtained a peaceful escort from Liège to our cloister, and an order to Hermann and his men not to molest me in any respect.

For I had kept her mind in suspense by saying that perhaps I would come to terms with Hermann if he were willing to accept my counsel in accordance with the bishop’s merciful letters which I was carrying to him. She received this most willingly from my own mouth, and I then obtained from her whatever I wished concerning my peace. Indeed, I did not lie to her: for if Hermann were willing to accept my counsel in accordance with the bishop’s letters which I was bringing him—letters which, as I said, could be understood in two senses—I would agree with [Col. 0105B] him on this point: that he should withdraw from our church and allow us canonically to have an abbot. Once I could enter the cloister safely, I did not much fear Hermann afterward. Thus the cunning of a woman was deceived by monastic simplicity.

So, with bold face and bare head, I made for the cloister. I was an object of astonishment to all whom I met on the road, especially to those standing in the middle of our town as I passed. For there was scarcely an inhabitant of our district who did not know of their concerted obstinacy aimed at my life; but none of them dared oppose the countess.

8. When the brothers saw me unexpectedly in the middle of the cloister, they surrounded me with great astonishment and immense joy, as one restored to life from the tomb [Col. 0105C] or taken down from the gallows and returned alive to his community. As I recounted to them the hardships of my journey, they beat their breasts and gave thanks to God that they had at least received me alive.

Meanwhile the bishop of Liège had placed our monastery and its outlying churches under interdict for as long as Hermann remained in the abbey. Shortly afterward I handed the brothers the bishop of Metz’s letters to read, and explained to them, according to the bishop of Metz’s meaning, how they ought to understand the other letter sent to Hermann. Thereupon they were most strongly encouraged in their own position against him. But Hermann, receiving from my hand the letter which the bishop had sent him, and finding in it no meaning except the one pleasing to himself, showed it to his associates. He added that the bishop had instructed him, [Col. 0105D] when he came, to make peace with me if he could not reconcile us. This hope, though empty, nevertheless restrained them for the time being from carrying out, by an even more malicious deed, the fury which they had conceived against me [Note: [Col. 0105] D reads “us.”] in their malicious hearts. These events took place in May.

9. In the fourth week of July the bishop of Metz came to Liège, intending to proceed to our place. When our brothers met him, they first begged him, with all the humility of the most humble prayers, [Col. 0106A] not to listen to Hermann’s supporters against them. Then they firmly declared that, if he attempted to use force against them contrary to ecclesiastical rules, they would not fear to appeal against him even to Rome. The bishop promised them that he would do nothing concerning Hermann that was not canonical. But Hermann’s supporters, surrounding the bishop’s counsellors and attendants, won them over so completely by unbelievable promises—now pledging their word, now swearing oaths—that they made Hermann, who had come from Liège, return to our place in good hope.

The bishop went ahead; Hermann followed slowly. When we received the arriving bishop with a procession advancing to meet him, we sang to him with many tears and sobs [Col. 0106B] that responsory: “Look, O Lord, for the city once full of riches has been made desolate”; and another: “Remember, O Lord, your covenant, and say to the smiting angel: ‘Let your hand now cease’” (2 Kings 24:16). Then, after he had been brought into our chapter-house, there was read to him and his clerics that lamentable reading from Jeremiah: “Remember, O Lord, what has happened to us; behold and see our reproach” [Note: [Col. 0105] D omits the following words.] (Lamentations 5:1), and the rest.

When they came to the verse: “We have become orphans without a father; our mothers are like widows; we were driven by the neck; [Note: [Col. 0105] 1* reads “we threatened,” and the rest.] the weary were not given rest” (ibid., 3), the reader was first seized by such sobs and shed such abundant tears that his voice failed him when he wished to continue reading, and his sight was darkened by the overflowing tears as he looked before him. Then the whole [Col. 0106C] community, stirred in the same way to mournful weeping, inclined all the episcopal party at that hour toward pity and compassion for us; but that compassion and pity soon vanished from their hearts.

10. Nevertheless, rising from there, the bishop consoled us with humane words and commanded us to wait a little for the outcome in good hope. We kept silence; but Hermann’s supporters—or rather hunters—again and again, night and day, beset the bishop’s attendants and counsellors, indeed even every meanest person of his household, with the greatest promises and with things which scarcely anyone could have hoped for. They laboured most earnestly to bend the bishop’s mind to their cause, and this they accomplished.

Hermann had a nephew named Walter [Col. 0106D] of Harche, a free man who possessed very much in fiefs [Note: [Col. 0105] “feuds” 1*.] and estates. He cared nothing what he might promise, pay, swear, or swear falsely, pledging his many possessions as security in order to provide money, horses and palfreys, furs and grey and vair skins, [Note: [Col. 0106D] Squirrel skins; French *vair gris*.] and other garments, provided Hermann might be made abbot. His other accomplices likewise paid no attention at all to how greatly they lied against their pledged faith or perjured themselves, so long as they could force him upon us against our will. [Col. 0107A]

In the end, the total sum of money paid was reckoned by us to have amounted to seventy marks [Note: [Col. 0107] D reads sixty.] and something more, and to as many as forty-two horses and palfreys. So the report then ran—or rather, let the disgrace be attributed to them, not to me, if it is false. Yet we can truthfully report what we saw and heard while present: before the abbot’s lodging, where the bishop was staying, and throughout the whole court, there was every day a great traffic of incoming and outgoing horses and a clamour of men selling and buying them. These were given by Hermann’s supporters and friends to the bishop’s counsellors and attendants. Hermann himself stayed in our granary, at no great distance from [Note: [Col. 0107] 1* reads “in.”] the lodging where the bishop was staying, so that the messengers running to and fro [Col. 0107B] entered his quarters quite openly and discussed before him the quantity and quality of their most shameful commerce.

11. While these things were happening, we meanwhile suffered the most severe want of food and clothing, so much so that, while the bishop was present and Hermann was tyrannizing, on the feast-day of Saint Peter the Apostle, the Kalends of August, and on the feast of the Invention of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, our patron and lord, we found absolutely nothing to eat or drink for our table, and endured very many other necessities which it would take too long to enumerate here.

Why delay? All those members of the episcopal party then present, especially and most ardently the clerics, gravely corrupted and made shamefully abominable by their pursuit of this most wicked simony, [Col. 0107C] sought by the subtlest inquiry and most cunning contrivance how, after deceiving us, they might force Hermann upon us. Thus they hoped either to receive what had been promised them, to earn what they had received, or, if they could neither deceive us by trickery nor break us by force or argument, to retain from the deceived Hermann the great promises or gifts already made to them. They argued about this with us very often; and when they could neither overcome us by reasoning nor deceive us by craft, they assailed us with malicious words and many threats.

Yet, so that no one may remain unaware of what they proposed to us and what we answered them, we have taken care to note it here briefly. They said: “Since Poppo, who canonically succeeded Hermann in the bishopric of Metz, gave this Hermann an abbey at Metz, how dare you oppose the gift of one who was a canonical bishop?” The brothers replied: “We do not deny that Poppo of Metz was a canonical bishop after Hermann; but that Hermann did not receive a canonical gift from him we are prepared to prove by these arguments before a higher hearing.

“First, because through his knowledge both divine and human [Note: [Col. 0107] D omits “both divine and human.”] he is unworthy of the honour and title of abbot.

“Second, because, after the death of his abbot, while the brothers protested against him, he presumed to assume superiority over us by force, by money, and through the secular hand of Duke Godfrey, to whom nothing whatever belonged concerning either the spiritual or the temporal gift of our abbey; and he bound the men of our church to himself by oath and homage. [Col. 0108A]

“Third, because he alienated the goods of the church, oppressed the household, and tortured us with want of food and clothing.

“Fourth, because he went to Metz without the consent and election of all the brothers, and presumed to accept the gift which he received from Poppo, although our brothers were present there, openly opposed him, and requested a day and a hearing; moreover, the brothers had there in their possession letters from the bishop of Liège and others, namely from that same church, from the archbishop of Trier, and from the master of Metz, which opposed the gift to him along with our brothers.

“Fifth, because he also obtained that gift through money, and caused the brothers who opposed him to be grievously despoiled and flogged.

“Sixth, because, since he is not yet a monk—that is, since he has not yet made profession under the title of any church whatever, nor received the monk’s blessing—how does one who has not yet been blessed as a monk wish to be an abbot and blessed as abbot? And how will he give monastic blessing to monks when he has not yet received it himself? Or [Note: [Col. 0107] D lacks “Or—made profession.”] how will he cause others to profess when he has not yet professed?

“Seventh, because, although for these offences he was summoned once, twice, and a third time in canonical fashion to a hearing, he refused to come, and has therefore remained excommunicated down to this very day. If they were unwilling to believe that these things were so, a day and a hearing should be granted to us and to him; if he could clear himself of these charges, he would not be opposed.” [Col. 0108B]

When the men of Metz heard such things from us, they did not know what certain answer they could give us. Nevertheless, their burning greed for the very considerable money promised or already given them compelled them to take every twisting course. What happened at last? The bishop himself [Note: [Col. 0107] “Adelbero above—”] came into our chapter-house, in case the brothers’ constancy might perhaps be broken even by his presence. When it could not be broken, he urged us at least to endure Hermann among us in the abbot’s place until, in our presence at Metz, there could be an investigation of these charges against him.

The brothers cried out in every way for the day of that investigation; but they would not in any way allow that, before the investigation, he ought to remain among them in the place either of abbot or even of brother, especially since the church of Liège held him so fully to be excommunicated that it had forbidden the divine office in our church for as long as he was within our precinct and court. Nor did they dare communicate with one with whom the church of Liège did not communicate, because they were under its pastoral charge and communion. [Col. 0108C]

Under this disagreement our chapter was dissolved that day, to the great vexation of those who had been rewarded by Hermann and to the still greater vexation of those who were to be rewarded. Yet they left him and his followers as comforted as they had found them, and, taking with them the large sum of money they had received from him, a great number of horses, and skins and furs both vair and grey, they departed for Metz. [Col. 0109A]

After the bishop’s departure, our latter error proved worse than the former: all Hermann’s party were most savagely inflamed against our affliction—hunger, thirst, and nakedness. Yet, as regards the observance, they voluntarily omitted nothing, so far as human frailty could ever endure, in accordance with the evils that befell them.

12. The greater weight of these evils was turned upon me alone, and the hearts of all Hermann’s party burned most fiercely in rage against me. They thought that they could have prevailed if I alone had yielded, though, although much was done through me, [Note: [Col. 0109] “me” omitted by 1 and 1*.] not everything was done through me alone that prevented their success. At last Countess Gertrude, perceiving by what stratagem I had deceived her, [Col. 0109B] began to inflame her husband Count Giselbert, already angry with me, more vehemently with a woman’s indignation. Thus I did not dare entrust myself even within the walls of our ruined cloister, and often feared that I might be seized even inside the monastery itself.

Since I could not endure this danger to my life any longer, I secretly arranged through Count Arnulf of Loon that he should bring me safely out of our cloister under his escort and rescue my soul from the midst of lion-cubs. Accordingly, on 29 August he led me out, profoundly sorrowful that I was leaving a place familiar to me and had no hope of ever returning to the young men whom I had laboured much to train, or to the whole community for which I had worked so greatly.

[Col. 0109C] 13. For the desolation of the place and the brothers’ tribulation were far greater than anyone today could imagine. Hermann, having usurped the whole abbey for himself, a man without counsel and without prudence, conducted all things through utterly worthless, most lying, and most fickle men, while almost everyone who ought to have defended the justice of our church supported his violence. Hence I was then deeply grieved at my labour for that place and the many distresses which I had very often endured under Lord Abbot Theoderic: I was leaving to be trampled under the feet of the proud and impressed in the mud of their most miserable way of life what I had thought I could bring to the mature fruit of devout activity, while it was still in its most tender blossom. [Col. 0109D]

Thus I wept as I departed most bitterly, receiving no consolation for a long period afterward. Before long I went to Saint Lawrence at Liège, under the direction of the wise man Abbot Berengar. [Note: [Col. 0109D] He himself had been an exile a few years earlier; see the *Chronicle of Saint Lawrence of Liège*, near the end.] There, during the third week of September, I confirmed my stability. [Col. 0110A] Thanks be to those brothers, because with every kindness and with greater honour than I deserved, they earnestly sought to console the sickness of my recent grief.

Meanwhile neither Hermann could be moved from his obstinacy of mind, nor could the brothers be moved from their constancy by his harassment or by their own poverty. The miserable rope of this dispute was stretched out between the two sides until the emperor returned to Liège from his expedition into Flanders, in that same year, 1107, in the middle of December. [Note: [Col. 0109] 1* reads “brought to completion.”] [Note: [Col. 0109D] On Henry’s expedition against Count Robert of Flanders in October 1107, see Ekkehard of Aura and the *Annals of Hildesheim*, and the royal charter given at Liège on 23 December in Chapeaville II, 54, where, instead of “the Kalends of January,” one should read “the tenth day before the Kalends of January,” as Ernst corrected from the charter itself, *History of Limburg* II, 236.]

14. There, when the brothers cried out before the emperor, in the presence of the bishops and princes who were with him, that, contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers and the decrees of the canons, he wished violently to impose Hermann as their superior, though Hermann had formerly been expelled and excommunicated from their church and its prelacy, his fault so requiring, by the judgement of the leading men of the church of Liège, [Col. 0110B] the emperor ordered Hermann and the brothers to appear the next day. He wished to ascertain before the church of Liège whether Hermann’s case was as the brothers complained to him. For Hermann’s supporters had made known to the emperor that Hermann had suffered prejudice and that the brothers rejected him not canonically but obstinately.

On the appointed day for investigating this truth, the emperor sat in the chapter-house of Saint Lambert with his bishops and princes. Bishop Obbert of Liège sat with the archdeacons, provosts, deans, cantors, schoolmasters, and much other clergy. The abbots of the city also sat: Berengar, abbot of Saint Lawrence, and Stephen, abbot of Saint James. Hermann too entered [Col. 0110C] the chapter-house, compelled by much force and persuasion to come forward. The brothers were present as well.

Had you been there, you could have seen how little judgement the man had, how shameless his disposition, how dull his intellect. For among other things, his counsellors—who at that moment were very far away from him—had brought him to such a pass that in that winter he scarcely had anything with which to ward off the cold by some thick covering. In the midst of so great an assembly, driven by the necessity of biting cold, he wore over his little tunic the very cheap cloak in which he rode.

15. Then Bishop Obbert rose before all and recounted in order how the case against Hermann had formerly been handled by the judgement of his church; [Col. 0110D] why Hermann could no longer be abbot of Saint Trudo; and how, by obstinately persisting in and repeatedly committing the same offence, he remained under the bishop’s excommunication even to that very day. When he had finished speaking, he admonished under obedience the abbots, archdeacons, and all his clergy present there [Col. 0111A] whether the matter had formerly been conducted thus against Hermann. Repeating the case in the same course, they reached the same conclusion.

Then the emperor said to Hermann: “Brother, if you have anything to say against these charges, go out, take counsel, return, and answer.” Beside the emperor sat a supporter of Hermann, Adalbert, at that time exceedingly famous and famously powerful at the imperial court, later, as I said, made archbishop of Mainz. [Note: [Col. 0111D] In 1111; in 1112 he began, according to Ekkehard, to support the party hostile to Henry.] He was greatly confounded because, though willing, he could not help Hermann against the truth.

Hermann asked certain archdeacons and clergy to go out to give him counsel, but no one wished to go out with an excommunicated man. Then one [Note: [Col. 0111] 1* reads “the same one.”] of the princes, named Guibert, of [an unspecified place] near the river Albin [Note: [Col. 0111] D lacks “of …”] [Note: [Col. 0111D] Margrave Wicbert.] and the bishop of Ratisbon [Col. 0111B] [Note: [Col. 0112D] Bishop Hartwig of Regensburg.] said to the archdeacons and clergy of Saint Lambert: “It is fitting for you to go out with an excommunicated man to give him counsel, so that you may advise him to desist from the matter for which he is held excommunicated.”

Hearing this, some went out, and after contending for some time outside with the dull and obstinate man, at last brought him to the point that, when he re-entered, he confessed in the midst of all that he had sinned and erred. Prostrating his whole body, he begged absolution and promised that he would no longer commit such acts. There he was absolved and ordered to depart. Immediately all his retainers not only left him but, running ahead to his lodging, left him neither horse nor anything except what he had upon him as he stood and walked.

As evening was now falling, one of the canons [Col. 0111C] of Saint Peter at Liège found him standing alone before the chapel of Saint Trudo there in Liège, grieving and wholly unsure where to turn. Taking him that night to his own lodging, the canon helped him in the morning to cross the Meuse into the wood to Saint Symphorian, a dependency of the Cluniac cell. Our brothers, however, returned to their cloister with great joy. Such is the way laymen treat foolish monks who are excessively credulous toward them: they bring those eager for honour, but unworthy of it, to such honour!

The emperor then departed and held his court at Aachen on the Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0112D] Our author is correct against Ekkehard, who wishes Henry to have been at Mainz. See Böhmer, *Regesta*, no. 1983.] (25 December 1107).
