When our brothers heard that the bishop of Metz was there, they came to him [Col. 0111D] and charged him with all the evils they had endured, because he had allowed that tyrant’s violence to oppress them. Day after day he kept them in suspense concerning the giving of an abbot, and delayed so long—none of our brothers promising him anything for the abbey—that he returned with them to our cloister. [Col. 0112A]

At last, perceiving that an unfavourable report about him was flying everywhere because of what he had done to us concerning Hermann, and that the people of Liège and the better men of Metz were more openly charging him with the affliction of our church, not without the reproach of simony, he entered into secret counsel with his own men. In order to extinguish this infamy, he himself would go to Liège, take with him our better brothers, and there, by the counsel of the abbots and leading churchmen, decide about appointing an abbot over our brothers. And so he did.

16. In the fourth week of January 1108 he came to Liège and, at the election of our brothers who were there—namely Prior Guederic, Provost Morung, Sacristan Sibert, Cantor and Cellarer [Col. 0112B] Folkard—by the counsel of abbots and monks and also the leading clerics of Liège, with the leading men of Metz present, both clerics and laymen, acclaiming the same choice, and likewise the better members of the household of our church, he appointed as their abbot a man—whose name it is not mine to give here—. Our advocate, Count Giselbert, opposed this election with much protest.

But the brothers, and especially the men of our church, declared with the greatest constancy and freedom before the people of Metz and Liège that the advocate had absolutely nothing to do with such a matter. If the bishop wished to infringe this liberty of the church, none of them at all would participate in an innovation and violence hitherto unheard of among them. The most steadfast acclamation of the brothers and men of the church prevailed; and the advocate’s anger and indignation were kindled like a most vehement furnace against the new abbot and those most closely attached to him. [Col. 0112C]

These things were done at Liège in the house of Saint Trudo: that is, this abbot was installed on 30 January. On 2 February, the fourth day before the Nones of February, the feast of the Purification of Saint Mary, he entered the town and monastery of Saint Trudo. He was received with a procession of the brothers and a great multitude of townspeople of both sexes and every age; immediately, vested, he blessed the candles, conducted the procession with the others, and sang Mass.

On 23 February, the seventh day before the Kalends of March, he was consecrated abbot. That year this was the first day, namely the Sunday, of Lent, when is sung: [Col. 0112D] “He shall call upon me” (*Invocavit me*), in the year 1108 from the incarnation of the Lord, while Henry IV [Note: [Col. 0111] “fifth” in 1, corrected by a later hand in erasure, and in D.] was reigning as emperor at Rome—his father having died at Liège—while Paschal, after Urban, presided in the Roman papacy; Adalbero, fourth [Note: [Col. 0111] thus in 1, in an erasure, and in D; “fifth” in 1*.] after Poppo, at Metz; Frederick, after Hermann, at Cologne; and Obbert, after Henry, at Liège. [Col. 0113A]

The reason why the abbot’s consecration was delayed so long was our advocate at that time, Count Giselbert. By every means, both personally and through his friends, he opposed him: partly for Hermann’s sake, whom he had formerly supported and whom he then [Note: [Col. 0113] 1* reads “now.”] still wished to assist concerning the abbey; partly because he feared that the abbot would be most severe toward him if he ever attempted in any way to infringe the liberty of our church on account of his advocacy. [Col. 0114A] For peace had not yet been made concerning Hermann; there still remains a grave disturbance to be recounted, which we reserve for the man who undertakes to write the deeds of this abbot after Lord Theoderic. If he proves a faithful and diligent narrator, he will insert into this abbot’s deeds what Hermann did to him and what end Hermann finally met.

## First Continuation

[Col. 0113]

THE SEVENTH BOOK ENDS; [Note: [Col. 0113] “explicit” 1*.] THE EIGHTH BEGINS.

[Col. 0113B] 1. Lord Abbot Theoderic died on 25 April in the year 1107 from the incarnation of the Lord. The abbey was without an abbot until 30 January because of the disputes described above: Hermann’s party wished to impose their Hermann, while the brothers wished to have one canonically elected. At last, after their unspeakable labours and extraordinary hardships, the brothers’ canonical unanimity and united steadfastness prevailed. On 30 January, in the following year [Note: [Col. 0113] “in the following year” added by interpolator 1*.], Abbot Rodulf was appointed, in the manner described in the preceding book without his name being stated. On 2 February, the fourth day before the Nones of February, he entered, that is, on the feast of the Purification of Saint Mary; and on 23 February, the seventh day before the Kalends of March, he was consecrated.

2. This Rodulf was born in the village called Monasterium, situated above the River Sambre [Note: Sambre; Col. 0113D] [Col. 0113C] [Note: Moutiers, west of Namur; Col. 0113D], where there is an abbey of holy nuns wearing black garments. The place was founded in honour of Saint Peter the Apostle by Saint Amandus, bishop; there rests Saint Fredegaudus, a glorious confessor, most highly approved by miracles. His parents were commoners, but most Christian people, belonging to the household of that same church; they served with untiring devotion to the hospitality and feeding of the poor, and lived their married life without blame and without any stain upon their Christian conduct.

Placed at Liège under school discipline and literary study, he remained there until his eighteenth year; how greatly he advanced in verse and prose may clearly be understood from his writings and the little works which he later composed. Having then become a subdeacon and obtained freedom to go wherever he wished, he crossed with a clerical companion of his named Lambert to Porcetum [Note: Burtscheid; Col. 0114D], which lies beside the palace of Aachen. He did so both from affection for Lambert, who had confessed to him that he wished to become a monk there—as he had long vowed to God and to the saints of that place—and from a desire to see the region famous for hot waters issuing from the earth. Yet nothing was then further from Rodulf’s intention than becoming a monk.

[Col. 0114B] But when, at night, the Lives of the Fathers were customarily read at the monks’ conferences, he concealed himself in a suitably situated little place nearby, from which he could hear and understand all that was read. He did this not yet so much from a desire for edification [Note: “thus” in 1; absent in 1*; Col. 0113] as from a desire to hear the miracles in the lives of simple men which were read there, and for the novelty of an audience listening to a simpler style. As he listened more often and more eagerly—not so much to the rusticity of the style as to the wonderful sayings and deeds of the simple and most holy Fathers whose lives were read—he began to regard the wretchedness of the present life as utterly worthless, and nevertheless to be inflamed with contempt for the world; and he continually turned these thoughts over in his heart, meditating upon them by night upon his bed.

What more need be said? Within a few days the milky draught of those conferences had so grown together with his heart that he not only strengthened by his exhortation his companion, who was wavering somewhat about changing his habit, but himself changed his habit with him on one and the same day, in the eighteenth year of his age (1088?). Therefore, on the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul (25 January), both changed their habit and professed as monks at the place called Porcetum, beside the palace of Aachen, in the monastery of Saint John the Baptist, under Abbot Azelinus.

But when, after hearing the Rule, he saw that the brothers observed it in very few particulars, he began frequently to visit the religious monasteries of the diocese of Cologne, sometimes staying there for months or half a year, especially with the religious and devout Abbot Adalbero of Gladbach. This man was the first then to maintain there the order of Siegburg, whose monks were at that time especially renowned for discipline, religious life, and hospitality. The more eagerly Rodulf drank in their discipline, the more loathsome he found the laxity and excessive worldliness of his own place.

3. Meanwhile, when Abbot Azelinus died (1091), his excessive simplicity and burdensome old age having allowed both discipline [Col. 0115A] and temporal welfare to decline excessively without knowing how better to relinquish them, John, the custos and dean of the same monastery, succeeded him: a very old man, wholly incapable of such a ministry. For the brothers had chosen him as a person suitable to them, according to what they themselves were.

Then Rodulf, seeing that evils had multiplied and laxity had been strengthened, and most truly perceiving what would follow, despaired of reforming either the place or its order. Having obtained leave, he departed, setting out for Flanders, where he had heard that a religious monastic life was practised. He did not wish to go to Gladbach, where he had often stayed, because he sensed—as later happened—that if Adelbero, abbot of that place, died, the newly introduced order of Siegburg would collapse with him.

Previously at Porcetum he had frequently suffered many very grave injuries. First he had been appointed custos and schoolmaster of the boys, then cellarer, then lesser and greater provost. He and the companion with whom he had become a monk struggled almost daily for reform of religious observance, while the brothers resisted them with much abuse and injury, and they had little or no help in this from the abbot.

4. Therefore, greatly wearied [Note: thus in 1 and 1*; Col. 0115], as I have said, and despairing of reform in that place, he at last departed for Flanders. It happened, however, that his route lay through Saint-Trond, and that on that night our lord Abbot Theoderic received him as a guest. When Theoderic asked who he was, whence he came, where he was going, and with what purpose, he understood Rodulf’s good intention and observed that he was a handsome and well-educated young man. He began very shrewdly to contrive how he might retain him, believing him likely to be useful: first, to instruct his boys in discipline and learning; afterwards, to advance him, if it should happen—as it did happen—to some ecclesiastical office, within or outside the monastery.

Having persuaded him by the eloquence of his gracious speech to remain with him, he first entrusted to him the schoolboys for instruction in the disciplines of learning, and the writing of certain most useful compilations, full of very many divine maxims and decrees of many councils (1099–1101). In that first year Rodulf wrote for him that very useful volume containing much Scripture; and he taught boys who scarcely knew how to decline *musa* not merely to compose prose exercises but also verse.

He endured a most severe labour in introducing them to this, because he himself could not speak German, and some of the boys, on account of their youth, their still slight learning, and their native German language, could understand him neither in Latin nor, so to speak, in Gnalonic [uncertain reading; Col. 0116A]. Yet persistent labour, which conquers all things, prevailed; and in that same year he enabled them very readily to understand in a learned fashion whatever he wished to read to them.

He also instructed them in musical art according to Guido, and was the first to introduce it into our cloister. To the astonishment of the elders, he caused them, by sight alone and suddenly, to sing—with the silent art as teacher—what they had never learned by hearing.

At that time, as has been related in the preceding books, the condition of the place was still most wretched and lamentable. The brothers possessed neither cloister nor monastery, but only the bare, ruined, dreadful desolation of a church; and of the cloister they had merely one unfinished and uncultivated building, in one half of which they took their meals and in the other slept.

The brothers then present were these: first, our lord Abbot Theoderic; second, Boso the dean—for that was the title then used in that old order, whereas now he would be called prior [Note: “because” in 1; “who” in 1*; Col. 0115]; third, Stepelinus; fourth, Herimann, surnamed the Bald, of whom something has been said above; fifth, Sybertus; sixth, Engo; seventh, Morungus; eighth, Folkardus; ninth, Bovo; tenth, Ruzelinus. The boys from the school were Gislebertus, Gerardus, Thidelmus, and Baldwinus: these four alone. There were fourteen among brothers and boys, besides two guests, who departed shortly afterwards [Note: “between … guests” absent in D; Col. 0115. Cf. above VI, 17; Col. 0115D].

5. Thus, after nearly two years, Boso, then dean, died (1103), and Rodulf was chosen by all the brothers for that ministry and installed in his place [Col. 0116C]. At once he girded himself for reform of the order. Daily, in chapter and outside chapter, he conferred with the elders about the character and manner of the ancient observance formerly maintained while the prior monastery and cloister still stood.

When they showed him the customs of the old monastery, full of most honourable gravity and religious devotion, he gently persuaded them and instructed them by a soft and gradually advancing course to attempt to receive those customs, and so at some time, or at last, to scrape away the old rust of the disgrace stamped upon them. He himself was assiduous, night and day, at every hour in choir; and he was indefatigably attentive to singing the psalms in succession and modulating the chant sweetly and evenly.

But because he did not know how to sing according to the use of the cloister—for our manner of singing, we do not know how this came about, agrees with none of our neighbouring provinces [Col. 0116D]—he was deeply ashamed to stand in choir during the singing as though he were a useless block. With extraordinary [Note: “thus” in 1; “certain” in 1*; Col. 0115] and indescribable labour, despite a most severe illness of his head, he himself made, scraped clean [Note: He cleaned the parchment with pumice; Col. 0115D], pricked [Note: He placed awls in each leaf of the codex as guides for drawing lines; Col. 0116D], ruled [Note: He drew lines; Col. 0116D], wrote, illuminated, and set to musical notation a gradual [Note: “gradale” in 1*; Col. 0115], that is, a book in which the responsories were written [Note: Col. 0115D]. Syllable by syllable, so to speak, he examined the whole use, first learning it from the elders according to their ancient graduals.

Yet because in very many places he could not bring their use—owing to defective abuse and corruption of the chant—into conformity with the proper rule, and because he could not notate according to art anything not supported by regular and true-sounding reason, while he did not readily wish to depart from the use of the Church, he wore himself out, as I have said, in extraordinary and indescribable labour, but in vain as regards this one matter: he could not wholly retain the false use together with the true rule. He did, however, succeed in not omitting from the Church’s use anything that could be sung anywhere upon the monochord [Note: a musical instrument; Col. 0117D].

Still, because of the rather negligent haste with which he finished the work [Note: “proficiendi,” ‘advancing,’ in 1*; Col. 0117], he marked with high or super-high notes many things which should have been marked with low notes [Col. 0117B], and with low notes things which should have been marked with high or super-high notes. This he left uncorrected because other cares intervened.

In one year he completed that work with his own hand, as I have said: everything small and great pertaining to a gradual, together with the antiphons of the Rogation days and the blessing of the Paschal candle. Immediately the boys and young men, following his instruction and the model of the book, began not only to learn that art but also to notate their own books more accurately and carefully than he had done. When he saw this, he asked that his own book be removed from use, lest its lack of correction, the careless writing and notation of a hurried hand, should later bring him shame. But the boys and young men whom he had introduced would not allow their master’s memorial to perish lightly out of affection for him.

Therefore, in the latter part of the volume, between two *ascellae* [Note: apparently a sign resembling an arm; Col. 0117D], he wrote as follows:

> A gradual not so much regular as customary; finally, neither customary nor regular.

By this he indicated that, though he had notated it thus, he was not unaware of its errors, since he could not there maintain the rule because of the use, and the use because of the rule; and since, owing to haste, he had sometimes departed from the rule where careful attention might have enabled him to observe it.

6. Abbot Theoderic, seeing his zeal and ardour in religious observance, rejoiced exceedingly and gloried in him, willingly permitting everything belonging to the cloister to be arranged as Rodulf wished. But Rodulf [Col. 0117D] was afflicted greatly and almost continually by certain troublesome monks whom, because of the small number of our brothers, Abbot Theoderic allowed to lodge with us from other cloisters. Rodulf compelled them to live with us under rule and discipline, which they either had not learned in their own monasteries or had fled because they hated it. He used to say that he preferred to live religiously with few rather than irreligiously with many.

[Col. 0118A] 7. There was also at that time among us a certain abuse concerning clothing, based not upon ancient ordinance but recent presumption. The brothers’ tunics were not without hoods, as they are now, but had hoods attached to them, hanging down just as the hoods attached to cowls did. Thus, whenever they put on tunics, they went without cowls; and whenever they wore cowls, they never put on tunics, because the separate hoods hung fixedly from each separate garment.

Since this abuse was observed only by those who, notorious for irreligious conduct, were also called secular monks, Rodulf was deeply distressed that he and his brothers bore this mark, which could be corrected without any bodily hardship. The guest monks mentioned above [Col. 0118B] strongly resisted changing this abuse, and with artful flattery urged the others not to yield to Rodulf’s youthful presumption, especially because they should never have placed over themselves a man summoned from elsewhere.

8. But Rodulf frustrated their evil advice by prudent stratagem and good intelligence. Coming to one of the elder brothers, named Stepelinus [Note: See above III, 13; Col. 0118D], he asked how many years it had been since, as a boy, he had first entered our former cloister. When Stepelinus answered, “Nearly eighty,” Rodulf further elicited from him that, in his own childhood, he had seen elders in our cloister who had been no younger—indeed, older—than Stepelinus was himself.

When the elder asked why he inquired so carefully, Rodulf added: “Because, Father, I should like [Col. 0118C] to know whether, throughout so long a period—namely, one hundred and sixty years—of which you can remember either by the report of those whom you saw as eighty-year-olds, or by your own sight, since you yourself are today an eighty-year-old man in this cloister, you can remember in any way that this custom was anciently observed in this church: that brothers should not have hoods hanging from their tunics, as the other monasteries living religiously around us do not have them today.”

The elder replied: “I am entirely certain, both by the report of my elders and by my own sight, that their hoods hung only from cowls. But when, under Abbot Adelard II, the indiscipline and insolence of the young had grown strong, they presumed in recent times to introduce this abuse, so as to wear hoods fixed to both garments; yet the elders always maintained the first and ancient custom.”

Rodulf said to him: “Since this is so, Father, as you assert, why do we depart from that practice which was once common to all the holy and ancient Fathers in this our monastery also, and is still common to religious monks around us? It is shameful, abandoning the practice of religious men and the ancient custom of our monastery, to imitate the new presumption of foolish and undisciplined youths, and by so slight a change in bodily dress to be known everywhere among religious people as irreligious.”

Having by these and other persuasive words won and strengthened the minds of the elders, he finally proposed the same matter to the abbot, and easily obtained that every one of our brothers should remove the hood from his tunic, the abbot first removing his own.

9. But one man, expelled from the monastery of the Siegburg monks and received by our lord Abbot Theoderic, after his own stability had been secured, because of the small number of ours—as I said above—obstinately opposed this decree. The prior repeatedly warned him and finally commanded him under obedience to allow the hood to be removed from his tunic. For he had always worn it in this way from childhood among the Siegburg monks, while he saw that we were now doing the same according to the ancient custom [Col. 0119B]. But he accepted neither warning nor obedience [Note: “but … obeyed” absent in D; Col. 0119].

The prior, seeing the stubbornness of this hard-minded man, one day took the tunic hanging by his bed, sent it to the tailors, and had the hood properly removed and the tunic suitably altered after the fashion of the other brothers [Note: *alii* erased in 1; Col. 0119]. When, on a Sunday, he had taken out his cowl in the usual way and wished to go to Prime, he put on his tunic but did not find the hood. Mocking himself with a grim face as he looked around, he entered the choir without his cowl, wearing only the hoodless tunic, and throughout that Prime made himself a spectacle to the brothers with shameless brow [Note: “spectaculo” in 1*; Col. 0119].

But what followed? They came to chapter, and this display by an insolent man was punished according to the Rule. He was ordered at once to leave chapter and to put on beneath his tunic the cowl hanging beside his bed [Col. 0119C]. Whether willing or unwilling, our lord Abbot Theoderic made him proceed dressed like the others.

But he [Note: all that follows through “observed the sentence in no way” is absent in D; Col. 0119], nursing the deed done to him in the deep recess of his malicious mind [Note: Vergil, *Aeneid* I.209; Col. 0119D], though concealing it for a time, came secretly the next morning, while the prior slept after Matins, to the prior’s bed. He took away the hood from the cowl there, carried it off with him, laid the mutilated cowl back upon the bed, and returned to his own bed as though he had done no harm.

When day had already dawned and it was time for the prior to give the signal for the brothers to rise to prayer, he put on his cowl and saw it without a hood. At first he was greatly astonished; at last, from the cracking laughter of the secret author of the theft, he scarcely understood what had happened. What was he to do? His tunic had no hood, and that malicious craftsman [Col. 0119D] had removed the other one from his cowl. If he rose and went about in a hoodless garment, he would make himself a ridiculous spectacle to the brothers, especially to the author of this injury; if he waited longer and let the hour for rising pass, he would nevertheless have nothing more to wear.

At last, calling to himself one of the brothers already awake, he instructed him to bring the cowl [Col. 0120A] of one of the elders. That elder had not yet removed the hood from his tunic—perhaps reserved for this purpose by divine providence. Rising, therefore, Rodulf did what he had to do, and reported through the elders to the abbot the insult done to him.

The abbot and elders, enraged at that presumptuous man, resolved to have him publicly beaten with rods in the marketplace and then shamefully expelled from the cloister. But the prior entirely forbade this, saying that he ought to be spared, if not for the sake of so presumptuous a man, at least for the sake of our order among secular people. Therefore Abbot Theoderic came to chapter and, with a most severe beating, had him long and harshly chastised with two brooms; and only at the intercession of the brothers was he barely allowed to escape with a lighter penalty.

But the man observed the sentence in no way. Instead, daily piling fault upon fault, and being incorrigible, he was finally put in fetters. When he sought to stab the prior with a knife [Note: “and in fetters … stab” absent in D; Col. 0119], he was at last expelled from the cloister and allowed irrevocably to go wherever he wished.

The other brothers, however, advanced daily better and better in discipline, since the prior devoted all his effort to this, never ceasing despite this or any other insult or provocation [Note: “better and better” in 1*; Col. 0119].

10. He also caused another evil custom, long rooted among us through the insolence of equally lax youths, entirely to cease—not only among ourselves, but almost wholly among our lay people as well. On Rogation days, when according to ancient custom our procession arrived on the first day at Zepperen [Col. 0120C; Note: Zepperen, one league from the town of Saint-Trond; Col. 0119D], a very great part of the brothers, having hired horses by request or payment, immediately mounted there. Riding before the procession to Brustem, and then with the light young townsmen returning through the fields to the cloister before the eyes of all the people, they would now let their horses run at whatever speed they could, now sharply rein them in and wheel them this way and that, with poles poised, chasing or fleeing now these, now those.

They did not cease doing this throughout the three Rogation days: on the second day, when the procession went to Falmia [Note: the valley, one league south of Saint-Trond; Col. 0120D], and on the third to Mergueles. The result was that, on each of those days, whatever fish or cakes the brothers ought to have had for their table were given to those who had provided them horses, except for the very few who had not wished or had been unable to hire them by request or payment [Col. 0120D]. Even the schoolboys were attracted and bound by this most depraved custom.

Those brothers whom either choice or necessity made go and return on foot were severely exhausted when they followed home the people riding swiftly ahead of them, both by the long journey and by unaccustomed, rapid walking. Thus, among us, the Rogation days and the litanic supplications were like the sorties of soldiers and the wanton riding-about of soft young men.

[Col. 0121A] Rodulf the prior detested this abominable abuse. When, as others mounted, a horse was offered him to ride, he said that it became neither the rule of lay people, still less that of monks, nor any Christian at all, to perform penance on horseback, while treating the Rogation days as days of penance and supplication [Note: “days … penance” absent in D; Col. 0121]. In support of this he pleaded the nakedness of his stripped feet, fasting, and the fact that, with covered heads, they frequently performed the supplications of the saints by reciting their names.

By these and other reasons bearing upon the matter, he first persuaded Lord Abbot Theoderic [Note: “Theoderic” added in D; Col. 0121], and then the other brothers, that at last this riding should cease: both the indecent monastic laxity arising from it and the harmful diversion of their provisions and alms. Whoever among the brothers had strength should go; whoever did not should remain in the cloister. The route should be shortened so that those who went suffered no hardship from excessive fatigue.

Accordingly, under his priorate riding on the Rogation days began to cease, and it ceased throughout his lifetime. It so pleased the people that almost all were gradually led to speak and act likewise.

11. What shall I say of the solemn feast-days of Saints Trudo and Eucherius and Saint Remigius? (23 November, 13 January.) Certain of our clerics, because of the familiarity in which they themselves had been reared as boys in our cloister with our boys and other schoolboys; and certain others because of their religious devotion, had long ago obtained much favour with our predecessors. Consequently, at the above-mentioned solemnities they entered our choir each year for the principal Mass with reverence, clothed in albs like our brothers. If any of them had a voice, they sang the tropes [Note: verses sung before the entrance of Mass on principal feasts; Col. 0121D] then sung among us, or the gradual or Alleluia. They also dined with the brothers at their table in the refectory on those days with every propriety; then, rising and singing loudly what belonged to the feast, they preceded the brothers—who sang *Miserere mei, Deus*, “Have mercy on me, O God”—to the church.

But a custom which seems to have had a pious beginning in charity and religious devotion gradually began, as time passed, to be transformed into superstition and vice [Col. 0121D]. For although permission had formerly been granted only to those persons and under the conditions mentioned, it finally degenerated into a presumptuous abuse: any priests who came from the countryside on those days, more for the market than for the solemnity, entered our choir indiscriminately among the brothers and rushed to the principal Mass without any reverence. Some wore disgracefully torn secular clothing, front and back [Col. 0122A]; very few wore even black cloaks, and they lacked albs and surplices [Note: a distinctive garment of canons; Col. 0121D].

Then, contrary not only to our order but also to religious lay people themselves—indeed, to all rightly ordered Christians—during the performance of the sacred mysteries of Christ, two or three of those clerics sat about in the choir itself. They surrounded one or two of our brothers, or each one a single brother, and spent the remainder of the Mass together in idle talk, laughter, and jokes.

When, after very many intolerable acts of indiscipline, they came to the refectory, such a clamour and chatter of different and even unknown priests and clerics arose as they ate that the voice of the reader in the higher place could scarcely be heard, however loud. The longer the meal continued, the greater became the disturbance, stirred up by wine [Col. 0122B]. Their number was so great—for anyone who wished entered everywhere—that, after brothers had been assigned to serve them, scarcely five or six of us remained to eat at table. How much the provost spent that day—or rather, how much was scattered among them—could be understood neither by calculation nor by number.

How little order and discipline there was among us on those days, or rather how much disorder and danger to souls, I think it more honourable to pass over in silence than to describe. When the brothers rose from table, and some of the foolish and shameless clerics snatched away whatever came into their hands, another crowd at once sat down with the servants: namely, whoever in our court appeared to have any official concern throughout the year [Col. 0122C]. There was neither limit nor calculation to the noise or expense.

12. Seeing such things in the first and second year of his priorate, and groaning deeply over them, Rodulf strove by many carefully devised means and frequent censures against such great indiscipline; above all he pressed Abbot Theoderic that this evil and church-damaging custom should either be restored to the manner of earlier times or entirely destroyed.

Although the abbot saw that this could not be done without great commotion, he also saw that not to comply with the good intention of the prior would be harmful to the order and to his church. Therefore, when the annual recurrence of the feasts arrived, the clerics were told that none of them might enter our choir without religious dress [Col. 0122D]. Those who wished to attend the principal Mass were to stand, since it was spacious, within the chancel around the abbot, with reverence and silence, as befitted the feast and so great a mystery. If any of them wished to wear an alb or possessed a surplice, he was to stand last in our choir, after the brothers, likewise with reverence and silence.

After Mass, a house was to be prepared for them [Col. 0123A], but outside the refectory, where they would be served with no less abundance than the brothers. For the brothers could not bear, nor did their order permit, so great indiscipline and disturbance in both their choir and refectory.

But all of them were deeply offended and, full of indignation and anger, would not accept reason. They departed completely and would accept nothing unless the former abuse were allowed them. Thus, perhaps by God’s will, it came about that the disease long entrenched among us at last failed.

The lay people also, who on those days had been accustomed to eat with the servants in the refectory, were compelled, though very unwillingly, to dine in another house; the provost and cellarer provided there whatever they would have received in the refectory. This matter, however, stirred up much hatred and persecution against the prior for a long time, among lay people as well as clerics, since on those feast-days the priests gathering for the market always revived this grievance [Note: “those” in 1*; Col. 0123].

13. Nor should I omit this. If a general Mass were celebrated among us for someone deceased, the brother—namely, he who sang the Mass—received the entire offering. Claiming it as his own property, he contributed nothing from it to the common body of the others [Note: *redundabat*, “overflowed,” in D; Col. 0123].

Since, according to the Apostle, “avarice is the service of idols” (*Ephesians* 5:5), and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict (chapter 33), a monk ought to possess nothing as his own, Prior Rodulf opposed this vice and removed it from our midst with the greatest labour [Col. 0123C]. With the abbot presiding, he ordained that whatever was offered to any brother at any time or place should be common to all brothers, small and great. The proviso was added that, should the brother to whom an offering was made need some necessary small item, the prior should provide it for him out of that same offering—for example, a belt, knife, linen cloth beneath his head and shoulders, or something of similar modest value.

Whatever may be done otherwise in this matter, let our successors know that it was thus ordained: the brother who sang Mass that day might freely request for himself—yet entirely through the prior’s hand—whatever he lacked among smaller necessities. We were present at this decree and often saw such things requested and given, as we write here.

What was changed later—namely, that one part was set aside for covering with lead and another part for vessels to be kept around the altars—was not done in order that this should remain so permanently, but only for as long as it pleased the abbot and brothers.

14. And because two sides of the place which ought to have become our cloister were bounded by a very low, dry, half-ruined hedge and had no roof—namely, the east and north sides—while the west side, although it had a stone building, had nothing in front of its wall to protect brothers entering its workrooms from rain and mud [Col. 0124A], and because the entrances stood open on every side so that there was little or nothing to prevent lay people, and sometimes women also, from passing through the brothers’ place of assembly, Rodulf laboured with much anxiety, kindly and prudent skill, every effort, and great exertion among the officials, especially with our brother Folkardus. Folkardus was then regarded as second after the abbot in all our temporal affairs [Note: thus in 1; “and” absent in 1*; Col. 0123].

Rodulf urged that some buildings be erected to form a cloister and prohibit public passage through the midst of the brothers. His pious purpose did not fail him. Within a short time the eastern side was enclosed with a wooden structure. When this building was completed, with a covered walk first arranged in front of it [Col. 0124B], one part provided us with a sufficiently suitable chapter-house, the other with a dormitory.

Likewise, from approximately the middle of the convent as far as two-thirds of that western building, a covered walk was made, so that with the east, south, and west sides of the cloister roofed, one could go about properly through three sides. Only the north side still remained open and was closed by a door.

Because this enclosure kept the brothers from leaving the cloister, except those alone permitted to do so, and both sexes from entering it, and because Rodulf himself carried one key and the cellarer the other, he incurred the fierce anger and indignation of our advocate Countess Gertrude [Note: according to Mantelius, p. 65, she died in 1114; Col. 0123D], who rests among us in our cloister. She could no longer, according to her former custom, make her way through the middle of our cloister and the brothers’ assembly [Col. 0124C].

Many of our clerics and lay people sharply incited her against him, especially the servants of our court, who complained resentfully that they were excluded from their customary route through the cloister and from familiarity with the brothers. But though terrible threats thundered against him, and evident darts of words capable of penetrating even the hardest human hearts flew at him on every side, he remained undaunted and unbending, fearing only that he might receive less help than he wished in reforming the order and cloister.

Therefore, so that the brothers might have, according to the order, a means more readily to remain seated in the cloister for reading and singing and to maintain silence, he was the first to have, from his obedience, a book-cupboard made in the cloister [Col. 0124D], and books placed in it according to the number of the brothers.

15. Meanwhile he scarcely ever ceased from writing or notating; sometimes also he took delight in composed songs and in chants composed for the solemnities of saints. There survives a volume of his little works, in whose preface one finds what he wrote, what he set to melody, and why and when. There also survives another volume of his seven books against simoniacs: four arguing from reason [Col. 0125A], three from authorities.

I could not briefly relate how greatly he laboured for Abbot Theoderic’s cause; how faithfully and steadfastly, in how many places and which places, and before which persons, he stood on the abbot’s behalf, when great and foremost figures of kingdoms wished to expel Theoderic from the abbacy and intrude the aforesaid Herimann. Of these matters we have touched above upon some part.

16. After these and certain other good and bad events—few prosperous, many adverse—had occurred among us during several years of his priorate, Rodulf heard that the Cluniac customs had been introduced at Saint James’s in Liège by Abbot Stephen, also called Stepelinus, and that shortly afterward Abbot Berengar of Saint Lawrence had adopted them. Thus the lips of all religious people extolled them, and they were deemed worthy of more reverent treatment than in earlier years, whether through frequent hospitality or conversation. Moreover, many clerics and laymen alike were converted to them from the secular world; and as religious observance gained strength, both the number of brethren and the revenues of the church increased.

Rodulf, now seeing that the time had come when he might fulfill his desire to improve the customs and preserve religious observance among us, worked day and night with Abbot Theoderic by every means possible, so as to kindle him to introduce the same customs into our cloister as the third abbot after those two. For, he said, it was fitting that he, since he was not inferior to them in learning and worldly renown, and since our house bore an older and more celebrated name, should not be found less distinguished among men in religion and spiritual matters, nor less worthy before God. But when certain brethren obstructed this undertaking and he could not bring it to completion, he obtained leave from our house and departed to his own [Note: [Col. 0125D] Perhaps Porcetus?], without hope of returning, intending, after arranging his affairs there, to proceed to wherever he heard that the rule was observed more strictly.

Immediately some of the brethren and our servants, rejoicing both secretly and openly and glad that this had happened as they wished, because they could now act more freely according to their own will, learned not long afterward, when another prior had been set beside him for comparison, how greatly this man surpassed them in counsel, assistance, and honor. Therefore, deeply repentant after a few months, certain persons recalled him under another pretext, with the presence and assent of Abbot Theoderic. They assured him that, if he returned and resumed his priorate, the Cluniac customs would be introduced into our cloister within that year (1106). Only with difficulty did they finally prevail. Thus he who had departed shortly before the feast of the Nativity of Saint John returned in Advent, immediately after the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

17. Once his priorate had been restored to him, and an opportune place and time had been seized, together with the good will of the lord abbot and the brethren, he demanded fulfillment of the promise, now seriously and now jokingly; and he said that so good a matter ought not long to be delayed before being done. Through extraordinary exertions and frequent journeys to Liège—thereby stirring up against himself the intense hatred of many clerics and laymen there, and of some of our brethren—he finally brought it about that in the same year [Note: [Col. 0125] “of the Lord, 1107” inserted.] [Note: [Col. 0125D] That is, the year in which he made journeys to Liège, not that in which he returned to Saint Trond, as is sufficiently clear from what precedes.] on the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0125] “May” D.] (1107), which was Friday [Note: [Col. 0125D] Friday fell not on the first but on the second day of March; the fast began on 3 March. Thus the author seems to have erred in reckoning the day [Col. 0126D]; one should read: the sixth day before the Nones of March. But compare above, VI.21.], at the beginning of Lent, the Cluniac customs were introduced for observance in our cloister.

When they had been introduced, our brethren burned most fervently in their observance—beyond anyone’s hope. But shortly afterward, alas, alas! the lord Abbot Theoderic died, namely on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. What afterward occurred until he entered upon the abbacy, and how he entered it, I think the writer of the preceding history has sufficiently set forth in advance. Whoever wishes to know these matters more carefully should consult him.

18. After he was appointed abbot (30 January 1108), as a lover of the order and of those who loved it, he strove in every way to maintain the rule. And so greatly—I shall report what I know with complete certainty and fidelity; behold, before God, I do not lie—that no brother, however intimate with him in temporal or spiritual matters, could ever be loved by him with a perfect heart unless he knew him to love our order and had proved him faithful in the affairs of the church entrusted to him. Conversely, no brother was so rarely admitted to his presence that, even if he openly or secretly criticized his words, deeds, and life sharply, as he was often wont to do, provided only that he at some point ceased and showed himself a lover of the order and faithful in the church’s affairs entrusted to him, he would not most readily forgive him these and other, even grave, faults.

What more do you want me to say? I shall tell you, more briefly and more truly than I can, under Christ’s witness: nothing could commend a brother to him whom love of the beloved order and fidelity in the church’s affairs entrusted to him did not commend—not age, not familiarity, not fear, not kinship, not learning, not beauty, not noble birth, nor even any great usefulness. Because of these two [Note: [Col. 0126D] That is, those two virtues: love toward the order and fidelity.], those in whom they were found had influence with him [Note: [Col. 0126D] That is, those who excelled in these virtues prevailed in authority with him.] over anyone whatsoever; and those in whom they were absent had no influence, or very little, with him. In vain would anyone labor otherwise, whether to be pleasing to him by possessing these qualities or displeasing by lacking them.

[Col. 0127A] 19. He especially detested this vice and worked, by whatever power he could, personally and through those who reported to him, to eradicate it: no brother was to divert anywhere anything from the provisions assigned him in the refectory, but was to allow whatever exceeded his own need to be distributed to the poor through the hands of the almoner. Whenever he saw any of the lay brethren more readily seeking friendships, conversations, and various empty little glories, he never—or only unwillingly—wished to promote them to any obedience; nor those whom he understood in any way to be seeking this or that obedience [Note: [Col. 0127D] A dependent cell or provostship of a monastery, to whose administration individual monks were sent by the abbot’s command; subsequently, *obedientia* means every monastic office.], and whom he knew were eager for an opportunity secretly to give and receive something.

But to those for whom human favor was not dearer than an obedience, and who were content with an even and simple mind solely with the resources of the cloister, he said that the offices of the cloister ought to be given. Those whom worldly people praised to him for having gained their familiarity and frequent conversation, and for being able perhaps to obtain something from their kindly generosity [Note: [Col. 0128D] Generosity.], he judged unworthy to leave the cloister at all. But those whose roughness and silence were criticized, and who were reproached because they gave nothing to such people and accepted nothing from them, he safely allowed to go wherever they wished. He exalted silence among monks with such praise that he said monks could never be so perfect and chosen as to be able to maintain the order and discipline without the virtue of silence. He could never be broken by the proud obstinacy of subordinates; but by humility, although greatly injured, he was overcome more quickly than was sometimes expedient even for himself.

20. By these and other pursuits of good virtues—on the one hand through his own anxious and careful guidance, on the other through the devout obedience of his disciples—the sweet and fragrant ointment of our house’s good name began quickly to spread far and wide, while the foul scar upon our countenance, from the reproach of former lack of discipline, was gradually cleansed and healed by the hand of pious moderation. Hospitality was gladly offered to newcomers, especially to observers of our rule; and care was diligently taken after the brethren’s meal to feed the poor.

But because the outward goods of the world are very necessary for these and other matters of our order, and because to those who seek first the kingdom of God these things must then be added according to God’s promise, he began with complete vigilance and labor to apply himself, not only to preserving the church’s possessions which he had found intact, but also to gathering together those that had been scattered [Note: [Col. 0127] *ret* erased in 1.].

21. Therefore, on the first day when the men of the church were bound to render him fidelity and homage, he had the provost of the church, the cellarer, and certain elders sit beside him in his chamber, so that he might receive neither the hand nor the fidelity of anyone whom the brethren claimed was unjustly holding anything from their allowance. This matter produced many enmities against him, which nevertheless he escaped without serious loss, finally employing the counsel of that discretion necessary in every matter.

But so that his successors may know, and, knowing, may thereby become more diligent, with what care and fear, and with what zeal and labor, he preserved to the best of his ability and knowledge the profession which abbots and bishops alike customarily make before the altar, with the church as witness, before a vested bishop, themselves vested at their consecrations, I have determined to make this the end of the eighth book and to begin the ninth with the letter which he wrote to Stephen, bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0128D] He held the see from 1120 to 1163.], then lord of our house.

**THE EIGHTH BOOK ENDS; THE NINTH BEGINS** [Note: [Col. 0127] “Rodulf’s letter to Bishop Stephen” added by 1*.]

[Col. 0127]

[Col. 0127C] 1. To the venerable and reverend Stephen, bishop of the holy [Note: [Col. 0127] omitted in 1*.] church of Metz, Rodulf, by the grace of God and of Saint Trudo what he is, wishes salvation of soul and body.

During the years of my prelacy [Note: [Col. 0127] “in the twenty-eighth year” added by D.], that is, from the year 1108 [Note: [Col. 0127] omitted in 1*.] of the Lord to 1136, which was then in progress [Col. 0127D] when I was writing this, I have taken care faithfully to record here what has accrued to our church, namely the church of blessed Trudo in Hesbaye: whether recovered through my labor from property lost; acquired where it had not been possessed; restored through the effort of myself and our people from no or small revenues to some and greater returns; and what little property a few persons have bestowed for the souls of the faithful.

If anything in this record has escaped through failure of memory, or if hope still pregnant [Note: [Col. 0127] omitted in 1*.] has not yet brought something forth, when I remember the former and the latter occurs, I shall sometime append it to this work. Meanwhile, may I have God as witness to my conscience that I do not do this in order to appear vainly to glory according to man and not according to God in possessions whose smallness, even if I wished to boast, could bring me more shame than glory. Rather, I do it so that my successors, ashamed of my idleness and of the unprofitable duration of my prelacy, may gird themselves more vigorously and usefully not only to preserve these and other possessions of the church which they find, but to multiply them through their own labors and merits.

Yet anyone who has known the storms of the sea by which I have been tossed [Col. 0129A] and am still tossed may be more able to wonder that anything has meanwhile been preserved than acquired. Since I have described these storms more fully elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0129D] In the sixth and seventh books of the *Gesta*.], I have refrained from repeating them here. I do this also so that, while seeking pardon for my negligence, I may obtain this further favor from your clemency: that by your authority and seal it may be confirmed that no one after me may again involve in his predecessors’ errors what I have freed [Col. 0130A], but that these things may remain fixed as I have established them. If this is presumed, let it be void, and let the offender be subject to the ban of you and all your successors. For I obtained these things not without considerable loss of worldly goods, and sometimes scarcely escaped even with danger to my life; and to this day I am the object of perpetual hatred for those who grieve that they have lost them, although they held them unjustly.

[Col. 0129] **THE LETTER ENDS; THE TEXT BEGINS.**

[Col. 0129B] 2. Therefore, after the death of Abbot Adelard II, evils so great seized and held our church for many years as had not been heard of in any place since the most famous destruction of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0129D] The same words occur in II.1.]. They arose from disputes over our abbacy between the monks and the bishops—namely Herimann of Metz and Henry of Liège—while the monks strove violently to expel the abbot imposed by the bishops and to establish their own superior through simony. Thus the second expels the first, and the first the second; the third slips in between both; and the fourth presumes to seize the struggles of the three and occupy the place.

Their names are these: Lanzo, Luipo, Herimann, and again Herimann. Among them the contest was fought most miserably for seventeen years [Note: [Col. 0129D] Compare V.1.], so that within twelve years there were thirteen changes [Note: [Col. 0129D] In the years 1082–1094 the following changes occurred at the monastery of Saint Trudo: in 1082 Abbot Adelard II died; in 1083 Lanzo was introduced as abbot; in 1085 the monastery was burned, and in the same year Luipo was introduced as abbot by the emperor; in 1087 Lanzo returned; in 1089 Lanzo voluntarily resigned his office, and in the same year the elder Herimann bought the abbacy; in 1091 Luipo was again introduced as abbot; in 1093 Luipo died [Col. 0130D] and the younger Herimann was introduced as abbot; in 1094 he left the monastery, was brought back again, and again expelled.], one dying and another expelling another.

Under these men our whole town was reduced to ashes in one day, with the blood of many people shed there most cruelly [Note: [Col. 0130D] III.7 ff.]. Scarcely two years had passed since our own new monastery, a work of marvelous construction, and its cloister with all their appurtenances, had perished utterly consumed by fire [Note: [Col. 0130D] II.13.]. The tower, alone surviving the fire, became a stronghold for brigands; a treasure such as no church comparable to ours possessed perished, irretrievably dispersed; all the monks—absolutely all, I say—were scattered through various regions; at the place itself there remained only devastation and dreadful solitude [Note: [Col. 0130D] Compare III.11.].

3. During this tempestuous storm, our church at Alburch came into the power of Conrad, bishop of Utrecht, and the long misery of our house passed into the jurisdiction of that church by synodal law [Col. 0130B] and canonical judgment. To free it—though it was not thereby freed—the golden chalice of our church was sold off. Part of its price, namely sixty marks, was given to Bishop Conrad so that the church might be restored to our right; what remained of the price certain treacherous priests of ours treacherously squandered in this affair. Having received the money, the bishop ordered our people, by bare word only and not by canonical authority, to recover their own; not maliciously, indeed, but too carelessly. And so it happened.

Burchard, bishop [Note: [Col. 0130D] He died in 1112.], succeeded Bishop Conrad [Note: [Col. 0130D] He was killed in 1099; compare the *Annals of Hildesheim* for that year.]. Taking the opportunity that the church had not been freely restored to us under synodal laws, he assigned it to his own uses by synodal judgment. Thus he held it until my accession to the abbacy. To free it, in the same year (1108) in which I entered the abbacy, I went to Utrecht on the feast of Saint John; and, through the help of God and our advocate, Count Florent of Holland [Note: [Col. 0130D] Florent II, who ruled 1091–1122.], we brought the church home, restored free to us by ecclesiastical judgment, with a charter made on this matter and sealed with Bishop Burchard’s seal.

In that same year the church and the other goods we possess at Alburch yielded us at home a clear value of twenty-four [Note: [Col. 0129] Thus 1; D reads thirty-four; 1* lacks the figure.] marks of silver. It would take too long to tell with how much labor, care, and expense I brought this matter to conclusion during three full weeks, since I had to drag a very rich count, exceedingly burdensome with fat, by silver cords from Holland to Utrecht, and bend to myself with a hammer of the same metal the stiff neck of the bishop himself [Col. 0130D], and likewise that of the archdeacon of the church recovered.

4. In the administration of that same village there was a man named Gualdo who claimed to hold from the abbot as a benefice five solidi in pennies from [Col. 0131A] Tyele [Note: [Col. 0131D] Thielt near Aerschot.]. This was false; convicted, he acknowledged before the peers of the church that he owed these five solidi from his own land to the brethren’s allowance. For a similar lie, a certain Franco of Doureh, convicted by law and judgment, lost four solidi, less two pennies, in Antwerp pennies, and I restored them to the brethren’s allowance.

In the village of Hulsela [Note: [Col. 0131] Husela 1*; Hylsela D.] the reeve had secretly usurped so much of the rent for himself that, when recovered for our uses, it yields six solidi. In the same village the steward Hezelo claimed the flax tithe as belonging to his fief; deprived of it by law and judgment, he allowed the brethren to possess it for the making of the cloths belonging on the refectory table. A priest named Hezelo had, for many years under three abbots, so appropriated the whole church of Mergueles [Note: [Col. 0131] Everything that follows down to “can experience the fruits” is lacking in D.] to himself that, after defeating and confounding the abbots—now through Count Henry of Limburg, now through Gilbert of Duras, sometimes through the count of Leuven, sometimes through the bishop [Note: [Col. 0131D] Of Liège.] and archdeacon—by astonishing twists and indescribable contention, he expelled from the church one, another, a third, and I know not how many priests lawfully invested by the abbots.

Although excommunicated for this, he still sang Mass [Note: [Col. 0131D] The priest “sings” who has charge, as though of a chaplaincy, of a church dependent upon another, greater church.] and seized the tithe for himself, saying that he held it for five solidi, that those solidi were his benefice from the abbot, and that this was his perpetual and hereditary right. I restored this entire church, to which the brethren’s allowance was entitled, by law and judgment, after first suffering many losses and troubles from that priest. It now pays twenty solidi annually on the Nativity of Saint John [Col. 0131C].

5. Everything which we appear to hold at Sarchinio a powerful and prudent townsman of ours, named Cuntramnus, drew entirely into his fief, through the powerful aid of our advocate Gilbert. After Gilbert’s death his son Reyner succeeded him. Since it belonged to the brethren’s allowance, I brought him to the point of restoring everything to my authority, on condition that he should receive it again from my hand: that he should be our reeve there, paying annually into the provost’s hand fifteen solidi from the rent of the land and the mill-share for the brethren’s allowance; and that he should receive one third of the pleas, judicial dues, pastures, amercements, pledges, land claims, and everything belonging to such matters, while the provost should receive two thirds [Col. 0131D]. But if two or three pennies or a sextary of wine came to him, he should have that entire.

Whatever exceeded fifteen solidi he was to possess as a fief, and thereby be the abbot’s man; and the reeve was to receive the gift of the reeveship separately and the gift of the fief separately. I made this agreement unwillingly, but it could not be otherwise [Col. 0132A] because of the violence of Count Gilbert, who was strongly opposed to us in this matter.

6. At the time when the intruders and simoniacs contended for the abbacy, as I said above, whoever could seize anything of ours called it his own. It happened that for twenty-four years our village of Sesninc was occupied by a certain Count Bertholf of Vianne. He had granted it as a benefice to a free man named Gualter of Ambliz, and Gualter to Hubert of Asche. Yet they said that the church, which is also ours, was bound to pay only five solidi, and they never paid even these.

What need of many words? Through much labor, expense, and many journeys to our lord Alberon, bishop of Metz; to our chief advocate Henry of Limburg; and finally to Emperor Henry, who died at Utrecht, I brought it about—having rewarded both lords and intercessors with heavy payment—that we hold both the church and the village peacefully to this day, and that it serves the brethren’s vestry. I have elsewhere resolved to record worthily for memory when and how this village was granted to blessed Trudo.

7. In the village of Halmala [Note: [Col. 0132D] Halmael near Saint Trond.] a knight named Gontramnus said that he held in benefice hereditary land paying fifteen solidi. Since I could not wrest it from him, being opposed by our lords and advocates, through whom we ought especially to have been aided, I gave him an exchange—namely, a mill at Hales, which I had redeemed from another beneficiary of mine named Theymboldo—retained the rent, and assigned it to the brethren’s chamber.

One holding of land [Col. 0132C] lying between Halmala and Saint Trond pays twenty solidi on the feast of Saint John the Baptist. Two brothers, Everard of Overheym and Hezelo of Comite, said that they held it as a fief. By law, reason, and truth alone I compelled them to repent of the seizure and acknowledge to me the rent, which belongs to the abbot’s chamber. In our village named Vilario, a knight named Lambert held one holding. Since he could not establish that it was his fief, he said that he ought to pay from it annually only twelve pennies. Convicted by the judgment and testimony of the scabini and household, he was compelled to pay, and pays, six solidi annually.

In the same village there are two reeves, each of whom had usurped six *bonuaria* [Note: [Col. 0132D] The same as a *bonarium*: a definite measure of land bounded by limits; the boundaries themselves were called *bonaria*.] of land beyond his right [Col. 0132D]—six pay annually thirty sextaries of grain, one modius of oats, and forty pennies, and another six pay the same. By the judgment of the scabini and household we prevailed upon them to pay the aforesaid due.

8. The mill of Moyse, which pays twenty-five solidi, had been so completely lost through the opposition of powerful men [Col. 0133A] against us that not even the sign of a mill could be seen there on the river Mahange [Note: [Col. 0133D] The Mehaigne, which flows into the Meuse.], and no one dared put hand to its repair. At last, through much labor, money, and expense for rebuilding, we overcame the usurpers, so that without dispute it now pays the aforesaid due, and twelve pennies for the adjoining croft and four pennies for the neighboring marshland.

The mill of Mecerin [Note: [Col. 0133D] Perhaps Maiseret near Namur?] formerly belonged to the brethren’s table, but I found it occupied as a fief by a certain judge of ours named Udelric. When he died, he left two free sons, not by one mother, though nevertheless legitimate. One of them, named Alard, to whom the mill belonged, died childless, having earlier divided their portions between them. The other, Everard, survived. When he wished to succeed to the mill as a fief and could not do so by law—for I objected that it had belonged to the brethren’s allowance, and that his brother by another mother, lawfully separated from him, had left no heir after himself except the church—he was finally brought to the point of paying from it henceforth five solidi by hereditary right.

These five solidi I assigned, before the peers of the church in my chamber and before the brethren in chapter, to the prior and provost for the brethren’s meal, then and forever after [Note: [Col. 0133] omitted in 1*.]. Of them I appointed thirty pennies for the feast of Saint Quintin (31 October), which for a reason I shall explain elsewhere I established to be celebrated in albs and with twelve lessons; and thirty others for the day of my consecration, so that after my death these thirty pennies for my consecration may be transferred to the day of my anniversary. If anyone wishes hereafter to infringe this, let the brethren know that I both acquired and established it thus, and that it is to be administered through the hands of the prior.

To whichever reeve holds the mill, on the day when the brethren are given a meal from these pennies, there shall be sent to his house one portion of fish and as much wine and bread as belongs to one brother. I did not find the mill, brewery, and [Note: [Col. 0133D] Brewers’ workshop.] tavern which stand before the gate of our court; those who hold them can ascertain from their daily proceeds how much they pay annually, having been built in our time.

9. One of those four most pestilential winds which, as I said above, so shipwreckingly agitated our sea—namely Luipo—had granted as a benefice to a friend of his named [Col. 0133D] Lodeguicus three *bonuaria* of our cultivated land lying toward Mergueles, three at Kircheym, and three at Stades [Note: [Col. 0133] “and—Stades” lacking in D.], and had alienated them from the brethren’s table. When he died, he left a little son named Henry in the same injustice. When the latter demanded these same *bonuaria* from me as a fief, I refused to give them, because the brethren said that they had unjustly been taken from their table.

The dispute was long, and many men like him complained about me. Bishop Obbert of Liège also, since the boy was his kinsman [Col. 0134A], frequently assailed me on his behalf with blandishments, promises, threats, and terrors. Since he could not overcome me, he finally came in person to our monastery and lodging. Pressing me about the boy, I answered, thinking that I might escape better in this way: “It is the brethren’s allowance; without their consent I neither dare nor ought to act.” He immediately went to them in my absence and very easily persuaded their simplicity to grant it to him.

When I learned of this, I began to object altogether, declaring that I ought not follow their deceived simplicity but correct it. The bishop grew angry, threatened me, and produced witnesses from his own people and ours that I had agreed to this with him. At last, with remarkable effort, I prevailed. I retained the three *bonuaria* of the aforesaid cultivated land [Note: [Col. 0133] “aforesaid” added by D.; everything thereafter down to “Mergueles” is lacking.], lying beside our town on the road leading to Mergueles, and compelled him to relinquish them formally.

The remainder [Note: [Col. 0133] The following text down to “we restored to the brethren’s vestry” is wholly lacking in D.] [Col. 0134B] I surrendered unwillingly, but on this condition: for the three which his father had formerly held at Kircheym, the boy should receive three others at Stades and leave Kircheym free. The land left to us is twice as good as the other. Corrupted by the instigation of wicked men, the boy wished in the following year to take from me the harvest of this land and violently return to the relinquished fief. But although he met me in arms upon that very land and had with him Otto, son of Count Gilbert our advocate, God nevertheless gave us victory through the aid of our better advocate, blessed Stephen the protomartyr. The harvest was brought home before their eyes, and we have kept the land free to the present day.

[Col. 0134C] 10. In our town two men had usurped as a fief from rent-paying land belonging to the brethren’s table [Note: [Col. 0133] *feodum*, 1*.] as much as ought to pay forty-five pennies. One was called Ramundus the scabinus; the other was Henry, son of great Guntram. Pressed by us with law and truth, Ramundus acknowledged fifteen pennies and Henry thirty; and these sums were restored to the brethren’s allowance. There is a place before our court beside the spring where a brewery [Note: [Col. 0134D] A house in which beer is made.] formerly stood. Recovered through our labor from violence of fief, it pays six pennies.

In the ditch of our court, lying northward beside the almonry, are three crofts paying eighteen pennies, from which no revenue had formerly been received. I assigned these to the almoner [Col. 0134D] to feed thirteen poor persons on the day of my anniversary. I wrested from an usurper one holding which we possess in the village of Haverdorp, paying five solidi, and restored it to the brethren’s allowance. Likewise, in our village of Mere, I took another holding from another usurper; it pays the brethren’s allowance as much as the other holdings do.

Our reeve Henry of Guebecheym said that the flax tithe and fifteen modii of grain in that village, together with sixty capons and twenty cartloads of wood, belonged to his own uses [Col. 0135A]. We recovered them for our use, since he could not retain them by truth and justice. Likewise, in the same village, we recovered one mill which pays two solidi.

11. The mill of Mergueles, which now pays two and a half marks, Henry called Sualch, one of Luipo’s party, and his brother Godezo the cleric, had assigned to themselves as a benefice through the aid of our advocates [Note: [Col. 0135] omitted in 1*.], placing the miller under their fidelity and oath. After I had long contended against them and the advocates, I at last prevailed at great labor and loss, and restored the mill, with all that it pays, to the brethren’s uses.

What we appear to possess in the village of Alost [Note: [Col. 0135D] Aalst on the Dender in Flanders.], apart from the church, pays three pounds to the brethren’s vestry [Col. 0135B]. Wicked men, most cruel toward our church, falsely claimed that ten solidi of this were their fief. Since I never wished to invest them as usurpers and liars, for more than fifteen years they afflicted me with many troubles and insults. But, with God’s aid, in the presence of Duke Gualeramn, our chief advocate, and Stephen, lord bishop of Metz, we prevailed by judgment, justice, and truth, and restored it to the brethren’s vestry.

12. A townsman of ours, Arnulf by name [Note: [Col. 0135] “by name—violence” lacking in D.], imitating the violence of his father Baldric, wished to hold without service land which ought to serve the brethren for every bloodletting. This land comprises eighteen *bonuaria* and is called the holding of Nissen. It also owes other small services for the needs [Col. 0135C] of the abbot’s chamber: namely, whatever is fashioned in iron for his riding saddle, spurs, and pack-saddles, provided the abbot supplies the iron. Having received from the custodian glass, lead, tin, wax, and expenses, he repairs the broken glazed windows of the monastery, cloister, and abbot’s chamber. Supplied with iron [Note: [Col. 0135] “supplied—iron” lacking in D.], he makes and renews all keys of the monastery and chests, and likewise those of all workshops of cloister and court.

At the solemnities of Saint Trudo (23 November) and Saint Remigius (13 January), he assists the cellarer in serving distinguished guests according to ancient custom. When the brethren were bled [Note: [Col. 0135D] That is, blood was drawn by opening a vein.], the whole choir was bled together, sitting in order in one room with silence and psalmody. On that day the lord of this holding received as much as one brother at table. Although Arnulf had held these things so long that he said he held them as a free knightly fief, he was finally convicted and acknowledged this before Stephen, bishop of Metz, Duke Gualeramn our chief advocate, the peers of the church, and the servants of our court [Col. 0135D].

13. A certain Berenger, ministerial of the bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0135] Everything following down to “I restored to the brethren’s allowance” is lacking in D.], had seized our meadow in the village of Gemapia, likewise wishing to hold it as a fief [Col. 0136A]. It pays five solidi annually. I contended against him while he lived, until the end of his life; after his death I restored it to the brethren’s allowance, though his son still obstructs it.

My predecessor had granted four pounds in pennies as benefices to two powerful men: two to the reeve of the bishop of Metz in our town, and two to another man, whose name and identity it is not useful for us to remember. One of the two which the reeve held as a benefice I redeemed from him and restored to the abbot’s chamber. The other, though I could have redeemed it, I did not wish to do so, because I saw it was beneficial to the church for the bishop’s reeve to be the abbot’s beneficiary. The other two, which a person of suppressed name had held in the time of my predecessor and in mine, indeed more violently than justly, I nevertheless redeemed from him and caused him formally to relinquish; and I have restored them to the abbot’s chamber to this day [Col. 0136B].

14. The reeve of Stades claimed that twelve denarii and eight capons from the mill called Remigius’s Mill were his. Through my provost Folkard I pressed the case against him until he surrendered both the denarii and the capons to us. Before the gate of our court, in the hamlet called Scurehove [Note: [Col. 0136D] Perhaps Luttecoven, near Looz?], lie two small holdings which pay seven denarii, one four and the other three. I wrested these from two men who had possessed them unjustly and restored them to the brothers’ prebend. A wicked man and a most hostile enemy of our church, a ministerial of the bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0135] “of Metz” is absent in D.], had seized the wood called the wood of Godeledaleth, claiming that it was his fief. After I had extracted it from him despite much injury done to me, I leased it out at rent to others, who pay seven [Note: [Col. 0135] “ten” in D.] shillings from it every year for the brothers’ brewing-fund. [Note: [Col. 0135] All the remainder through the words “quiete hodie decimam” is lacking in D.] There is also a small holding in the marsh beside the road which leads from the eastern gate of our court toward the church of St Gengulf. A certain Frank, a chamberlain, claimed to hold this with a little house as a fief; being unable to retain it, he surrendered it. It pays the cellarer eight denarii.

15. A certain Conrad of Liège claimed to hold a brewery in our town as a fief. A long dispute between him and me came to this: he acknowledged it to belong to the brothers, since it pertained to their prebend, and agreed to pay from it eight shillings yearly. When he and his wife died, four shillings were to be paid on his anniversary and four on that of his wife. But if the brewery ceased to exist, whatever use the remaining site might be put to, it was to pay five shillings, thirty denarii on one anniversary and thirty on the other, for the brothers’ table.

When a nobleman named Engeram died, he left us, by a lawful conveyance made for him, so much allodial property in the village of Herebach as owes fifteen shillings yearly. The man who then seemed to be our abbot granted it as a fief to a certain serf of our church named Machelm. Later, with the holder’s consent, we recovered ten of these [shillings], five for the nobleman’s anniversary and five assigned to the infirmary.

16. A certain Adelbert had seized our village of Provin [Note: [Col. 0137D] Proven in Flanders.]. He had been one of the party of those four abbots whose ambitious contest had brought our abbey almost to utter destruction. With his accomplices, while abbot rebelled against abbot, he had occupied the tower of our church by force of arms. When he was captured, some others were hanged and others had their hands cut off; he too lost his right hand. Made an outlaw, he nevertheless did not cease from invading our village. There he claimed as belonging to his fief: all the straw of our grain, which in those regions is very expensive because of the scarcity of timber; sixty capons and sixty loaves at Christmas; thirty loaves and every demand upon the land at the feast of St John; and, moreover, whenever he went there or returned, he was to live on the brothers’ money and have no monk as master or companion.

Being an utterly vain and faithless man, he at one time reduced the village’s resources so far that in a year he paid me only five firkins and fifteen denarii; and even if he had paid everything due, it would have been little more than six marks of Cologne weight and purity. What labour, trouble, and loss I endured against this invader, who was scarcely ever to be apprehended; how he attacked me through our then chief advocate, Count Henry of Limburg, and his sub-advocate, Count Gilbert of Duras; and finally through Robert, Count of Flanders; and how I ultimately defeated him—I could recount only in a lengthy history. At last I defeated him and restored our village outright to the brothers’ clothing-fund, to be administered through the hands of the brother in charge of the vestment office without interference from any layman. In our later days it paid eight marks of silver of Cologne purity and weight yearly.

17. Among the tithes not formerly possessed and afterwards acquired is that of Barduwich in Testerbrant [Note: [Col. 0137] Thus in 1 and 1*.]. It now pays a mark and a half yearly. I assigned it to the annual service due to the bishop of Metz; and from its increase, the man who holds it is to be the abbot’s man. A nobleman, but a cruel tyrant, Arnulf of the castle of Rode [Note: [Col. 0137D] Near Aerschot.], had entered upon this tithe. My predecessor, Lord Abbot Theodoric, contended long against him but did not prevail. For Arnulf claimed to hold [Note: [Col. 0137] “have” in 1*.] it from the bishop of Utrecht.

I entered upon a most burdensome lawsuit over it. Wearied, but not exhausted, by many journeys to the court of Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0138D] Henry V.], I finally obtained the tithe at Aachen, in the emperor’s court, through a payment made between the tyrant and me. In the same district a marsh, formerly uncultivable, is now productive; the boundary of its tithe belongs to our church of Alburch. Gerard, called—and being by origin—a Fleming, had appropriated this tithe as though it were a new one, under the protection of the bishop of Utrecht. It would take very long to set forth what litigation I endured against lords so great and powerful, especially against the bishop of Utrecht, who supported him.

Compelled by extreme necessity, I turned to Count Florent of Holland, our advocate in that land. I divided the tithe with him, on condition that he should help us retain the whole; and so, under his protection, I prevailed, because neither the bishop nor Count Gerard [Note: [Col. 0137] “nor” in 1*.] dared offend him. Thus we possess the tithe peacefully today.

18. Of the few gifts which faithful persons, both living and dying, bestowed upon our church in our time for their souls, the following occurred.
