A knight named Adelger, from the village of Pumirs above the Moselle, came to us; having obtained fellowship with us, he conveyed to us a vineyard capable of producing three cartloads of wine. From the same village, a certain Gerard renounced secular life and turned to us, giving us four vineyards, three smaller and a fourth larger. These can produce two cartloads of wine. We celebrate their anniversaries, on which a distribution of wine is owed to the brothers from their gifts.

In the village of Runchirs [Note: [Col. 0138D] Runckelen, not far from Saint-Trond.] lived a nobleman named Hardechunut. For this deceased man, his wife Bertha, herself noble, gave us two holdings of land which pay twelve shillings yearly. Our advocate Count Gilbert gave us, for his own soul and that of his wife Gertrude, land paying twenty shillings and three denarii yearly. Between Saint-Trond and Sarchinium, a certain Libertus had a small allodial estate, which he left to the brothers at his death for his soul. It pays twelve denarii at the feast of St Remigius; these are added to another twelve which Hardechunut, while alive, had given to the brothers for his soul, and are distributed at the beginning of Lent for the brothers’ charitable meal in the refectory.

19. [Note: [Col. 0137] All the remainder through “Johannem Brunoni dedi” is lacking in D.] The tithe of Stades is divided into three parts: the priest has one, and two workers in wood and stone have the other two. I redeemed one of these two parts from one of the workers and his heirs, with the goodwill of all, because they were poor and could not redeem it from the pledge in which it lay. I added so much to them, without any violence or injustice, that they entirely surrendered it to me by the formal renunciation of *exfestucatio*. I granted it in perpetuity to the church custodian, so that from it a light might be maintained every night in the little tower toward the cloister. Its window is so arranged that the light from it is cast equally into the cloister and the monastery. From the same tithe the custodian must also provide, for every person before whom a night candle is placed, light while sleeping and a small service-candle.

20. From revenues that were nonexistent or small, these have been established for greater and better uses. The upper mill before the western gate of our court was built in our time; it can yield three denarii a day, and much more in expensive times. The upper mill of Gursemdrul [Note: [Col. 0139D] Gorssum, near Saint-Trond.] had never existed, but one built in our time now pays twenty-four measures of pure wheat yearly.

The wood of Meceres lay adjoining Duras castle and was also near our town and our little villages. Situated between the two, it had come to yield us nothing but scandals and bloodshed, since it was cut down daily by the neighbouring inhabitants, especially those of Duras. Forced by this necessity—though only after suffering many injuries from the castellans and the lord of the castle—lest the remaining timber should be reduced to no benefit whatever for the church, I handed it over for sale to faithful men. Whatever was received from it I assigned to repair the monastery, which, having been burned many years before, offered the gaping misery of ruin.

From the land made arable, thirty shillings and twenty denarii are paid yearly. Dividing these, I assigned ten shillings to the brothers’ brewing-fund, ten to roofing the cloister, and the remaining ten with the twenty denarii to the abbot’s chamber.

21. There was likewise a little wood near the village of Stades, which was being cleared daily by both our tenants and the reeve, as well as outsiders, without any benefit. Because of this necessity, I gave it over to bear crops, on the condition that five shillings should be paid yearly from the land; I assigned these to the brothers’ brewing-fund.

Another wood still remains near our town, called Bruderholt. A knight named Arnulf, our sub-advocate, claimed to hold it as a fief [Note: [Col. 0139] At this place, in the upper margin, manuscript 1 has added in a thirteenth-century hand: “He says that this is the land now held by Benbold of Thosen, Herman the knight of Brustem, and Godwin, son of the castellan of Brustem.”]. Although, by the judgment of the peers of the church, I extracted it from him with remarkable and great labour, I nevertheless could not retain it peacefully. I therefore granted it hereditarily to two men of Brustem, the brothers Lambert and Gerard, able to resist the invader by force and law. Each year they were to bring into our court as much wood as would suffice for brewing four batches of beer: one at the feast of St Remigius, another at the feast of St Trudo, a third at Christmas, and a fourth in March for the abbot’s chamber. They were never to clear the wood, but to guard and tend it diligently; they were to hold all its other profit from the abbot as a fief and to be his men on that account. Thus, had I not done this, I should have lost not only the wood but the very ground itself.

22. Reyner, the gruiter of our town, wished, after his mother’s death, to be heir in that office; and since this could not happen without much labour on our part, he acknowledged that five shillings and a pound of pepper were to be paid yearly to our church. I assigned these five shillings to the brothers’ meal on the anniversary of Adelbero, bishop of Metz, who came after Bishop Theodoric. For Theodoric, first, and Adelbero, second, had given the *gruit* to our brothers for their souls; and since on Theodoric’s anniversary the brothers received five shillings for a meal for his soul, they should also receive these five shillings for a meal on Adelbero’s anniversary. What the first gave, the second confirmed.

The five shillings and the pound of pepper are paid on the eve of Bishop Adelbero’s anniversary, just as five shillings and a pound of pepper are paid for Bishop Theodoric’s soul. All the dues from breweries which are paid on account of the *gruit* belong to the brothers’ beer, as the charter we possess concerning that jurisdiction testifies; it excepts no brewery whatsoever. [Note: [Col. 0139D] A tax paid by beer-brewers. [Col. 0140D] On this right, see the charters of the bishops of Metz appended to the *Gesta*.]

Several of our townsmen had so seized this right—some claiming it as their fief, others claiming to hold it in pledge—that only the smallest revenues reached the brothers. There was a long struggle between them and me; it continues in part even today. Yet I have defeated all but a few, without yet losing hope of victory over the rest. I cannot calculate the profit of recovering this right for the brothers, because whoever has a brewery among us destroys it whenever he wishes and turns it to other uses; hence what does not exist today may exist tomorrow. A brewery ought not be built without the abbot’s permission, but it may be destroyed.

I redeemed eight breweries which lay in pledge, from what God gave us and from a brother of ours named Gerard, who returned generously to us from a long pilgrimage. I assigned their revenues to buying lead for roofing the monastery; once it had been roofed, their revenues were to return, as before, to the brothers’ cellarer. They pay at least four marks yearly.

23. The church of Dunch paid only two pounds a year. The place in which it stands is secluded and pleasant: navigable water flows around it, and broad marshes cut off every approach except one, made by human effort rather than by nature. In this place, apart from the church and otherwise empty of every building, because I had no other place, I built a manor house and constructed a barn and a sufficiently suitable small cloister beside the church, together with workshops necessary for monks both inside and outside. Two brothers were appointed there to serve God and Blessed Mary; they live from the church with their servants, while still paying us, as before, two pounds yearly.

Let my successors know that the division between the brothers dwelling there and the parish priest was established as they will find it written here, so that, if they please and it is useful and they cannot do better, they may maintain it forever:

24. I, Rodulf, by God’s grace abbot of the monastery of St Trudo, give to Brother John the church of Dunch: in all matters a third part both of the great tithe and the small; the entire endowment; three *bonuaria* of land in Rotheem [Note: [Col. 0141D] Rothem on the Meuse.]; as many meadows near Dunch; the entire head-rent of the households, whatever it may be, in his parishioners both living and dead; and a third part, without exception, of the alms placed upon the altar on feast-days and ordinary days alike.

If from the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation onward any allodial property is given to the church by a noble or an outside parishioner, I reserve to my own power the right to assign it to whom I wish, unless the donor has specified the priest’s share. If a nobleman or an outside parishioner is buried there, the priest of the church shall sing the first Mass; whatever is offered to him, the abbot or monk holding the greater share shall have, and the priest shall claim nothing from the offering. In return for the above-described prebend, Brother John must provide for the council, synod, provisions, and the other obligations which his fellow beneficiaries provide.

Under this same division, after John I gave [it] to Bruno.

25. Concerning the bells which, either new or renewed, were made through my labour, I wished to write something here for the glory of God, by whose help I caused them to be made. Though they do not feed the belly, by the sweetness of their sound they summon and make attentive human ears and hearts to the praises of God. There are sixteen in all: namely, one small bell; two in the refectory; one for the parish of St Mary; one for St Gengulf; one which I sent to Metz to the blessed proto-martyr Stephen; one above our choir; and nine in our tower. How great is their sweetness, and how remarkable each is in its own tone and weight of size, is marvellous to see and delightful to hear. I affirm one thing: so many bells, and of such kind and size, could not today be made for one hundred marks.

26. [Note: [Col. 0141] All the remainder through “servitium preposito solveret” is lacking in D.] Blessed Trudo and his deputy, the abbot, possess three houses at Cologne. Two pay eighteen denarii in that currency; the third pays half a mark, although it is the abbot’s manorial house and owes him and all his household ready lodging. The two houses which owed eighteen denarii had, through the negligence always characteristic of our people, been brought under municipal law to such a point that they would irrecoverably have passed into the jurisdiction of the abbot of St Martin at Cologne, unless, when the final day of that lawsuit was unexpectedly reported to me, I had flown rather than ridden to it in scarcely half a winter day and night. Yet by judgment and justice I obtained the houses and received the rent. By what miracle, through the powers of St Trudo, I shall relate elsewhere.

The third house, since it is one of the principal towers of the city of Cologne, owes us this duty should the city be besieged: it must be fortified and defended with our guards and at our expense. We must take care, as we value it, that it suffer no ruin in wall or roof. All this was formerly the responsibility of the abbot and the provost of the Moselle; through the negligence, as I said, always characteristic of our people, the debt upon it had at one time reached seventeen marks. Later I brought our tenant there, Berner, to agree that he and all who might wish to live there after him should, if the city were besieged, or the house threatened any collapse or required repairs, pay the entire third part of the stipulated expenses, supply and maintain a third man there for the city’s defence, and nevertheless pay not less than half a mark.

27. St Trudo and his deputies also have a respectable manorial house at Liège. I expelled from it, after much litigation before the bishop, from the bishop to the advocate, and from the advocate to Emperor Henry, a most perverse invader who wished to hold it hereditarily, not without loss to myself and much labour. I therefore placed, and still place, in it yearly whom I wished and wish. The violent and unjust heir, once expelled, left me a house almost wholly unroofed, rotten, torn apart in its walls, and devastated. I spent nine marks on its repair in a single summer, apart from the provisions which I had while going there and remaining for some time.

I repaired it completely, with a new roof and new ceiling; I repaired the cracks in the walls with stone and mortar, plastered the walls with mortar, and whitewashed them with lime. I made in it a new chapel—previously there had been none—quite handsome and suitable for guests. I also made a new kitchen in the court and new stables, and closed all doors opening onto the street except a single gate through which one may conveniently enter and leave. I also recovered for myself the chamber by the gate, which some of our men claimed to hold as a fief, placing in it yearly whatever rent they pleased to give; the rent was two shillings. I therefore installed in it, without rent, a man to close and open the gate and guard the entire house within.

28. A certain palatine knight from the village of Cherpen had seized the property which we possess in the village of Beredorf, on the Cologne road. With the assistance of Frederick, bishop of Cologne, and with great labour on our part, I recovered it. It pays the provost of the Moselle at least half a mark yearly. I also recovered, with much care and labour, that which we possess near the village of Bruches, lying on the side of Aachen, and which serves the provost of the Moselle when he goes there—whether he wishes to stay in the holder’s house or in his own lodging at Aachen—from the man to whom it had been adjudged and who remained there violently without any regard [for right]. I settled it by hereditary right upon one whom the violent man would not dare oppose and who would render the due service to the provost.

29. Concerning the burned and ruined monastery, since I have written more fully elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0143D] II, 13.], I shall mention these things briefly: the grace of God and the patronage of the saints were with me in rebuilding it. All who saw the appalling chasm of such ruin despaired that it would ever be repaired. Therefore, from the piers and arch at the feet of our lord St Trudo, where my predecessor Abbot Theodoric ended his work, as far as the great tower, every part of the construction within the outer wall-faces rose in my time, except the piers and arch in the middle of the nave.

What had been done before me and under me I caused to be consecrated on the third day before the Kalends of October, by Obbert, bishop of Liège, in the year 1117 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the ninth of my ordination, and the thirty-second from the burning of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0143] “And the sixteenth from the consecration of the crypt.” Interpolation in the upper margin.]. [Note: [Col. 0143D] These numbers are each one too low. Rodulf was consecrated abbot on 23 February 1108, as he himself proves in VII, 15; therefore his tenth year was running, and the thirty-third year from the burning of the monastery, since it was consumed by fire on 9 March 1085.]

30. Of the cloister and all its appurtenances I found nothing that could remain as it was, nor could any guest spend the night there. There was only one utterly uncultivated building, inconvenient for the brothers’ use in both summer and winter because of its many defects. Yet it served them as refectory and dormitory, as cellar as well, and as a most miserable prison rather than an infirmary. The other parts were more often marked out by very ancient and half-ruined structures than enclosed by them.

Whatever monks need for their working buildings, I had first to construct hastily in wood as a temporary measure; then, little by little, to demolish these and build in stone from the foundations all around. Of this work I can still sing Horace’s words: “He who has begun has half the work.” [Note: [Col. 0144D] *Epistles* 1.2.40.] Because of many and scarcely describable tribulations, it rises slowly, though beautifully—especially as stone and lime are purchased and brought from two miles away, and a measure [of lime] is sometimes bought for seven or five denarii.

Before me, the number of brothers frequently fell, among smaller and greater numbers, to twenty-two or twenty-three. To this day it has not reached forty, though at one time only one was lacking; it has not yet fallen below thirty-five. Had untimely death or the flight of certain fickle men not taken them away, it would have far exceeded forty.

31. [Note: [Col. 0143] The end of this book is lacking in D.] Having set these matters down, I think it not useless, indeed very necessary, to inform my successors concerning the estates of the church which I found encumbered and have not yet been wholly able to free: how I proceeded against their invaders and before what judges; by what judgment; and to what point I brought the matter. Thus after me they may begin the rest where I have ended.

Let them know, then, that Count Otto and his son Gilbert of Duras—the former for the soul of his wife Oda, the latter for his mother’s soul—gave us so much allodial property in the village called Meldreges [Note: [Col. 0144D] Meldert, not far from Diest; cf. above IV, 9.], not far from the village of Lencholt, as can yield yearly, in rent, barley, flax, and chickens, if not more, twenty shillings. This was so that we might observe their memorial on the anniversary, and on that day a charitable distribution of wine and fish might be served to the brothers in the refectory. We observe the anniversary, but the charity owed us is not supplied.

For when the four men mentioned above contended over the abbey, the younger and last of them, Herman, expelled from the cloister and village, had attached himself to one of our reeves, John Hales [Note: [Col. 0144D] Cf. V, 3.], who was beyond words a devouring abyss and calamity to the revenues of that village. After the wood had been devastated there for more than a year and the whole substance of the village consumed by both parties, Herman rushed to Count Henry of Limburg, our chief advocate, hoping to be helped by him in recovering the abbey. Meanwhile the abbey was vacant and being variously plundered by many people. Then John seized for himself the property of Meldreges and until my time called it his fief.

On account of this and of his other innumerable crimes and disloyalties, after an extremely long and costly contest I brought him to the point that not only the reeveship and every fief were adjudged away from him, but even his inheritance and person were brought under our power. After a year and a half, his son Macharius sought our favour and came for the reeveship and paternal inheritance. But he refused to receive the fief, because I would not grant him the property of Meldreges, which his father had seized and which had returned to our hands by judgment. Soon he behaved in such a way that, more harmful and more faithless than his father, he was removed from the reeveship, and whatever he hoped to obtain from our hand, or seemed already to possess, was adjudged away from him. But the advocate, whose grant of this allod for his mother’s soul had been made for the brothers’ benefit, entered upon the property and restored possession [Note: [Col. 0145D] French *resaisir*: “to restore to possession.”]. Thus truth, judgment, and law were applied concerning this property. Only this still hindered us: a man among the powerful men of Leuven claimed to hold it in pledge. We have entered upon this lawsuit, which is not yet concluded.

32. Walter, a free man from Baccunguez castle, driven by wicked greed and enticed by the convenient pleasantness of our estate adjoining his castle, began to draw our adjacent property into his own uses as though it were his own, since, because of the aforesaid desolation of our church, there was no one to resist him. Our peasants say that between woodland and arable land there are about forty holdings belonging to us. They also say that, when the lords of Diest had once wished to seize them, Walter’s father had established by oath before our lawful advocate Count Otto that they were ours; and that, after he had appropriated them to his own property, our chief advocate Henry of Limburg, sent there by my predecessors, went there and restored them by law to the right of our church. Yet not even so did the greedy invader rest.

Our time came, and I found him in possession of our property. I appealed to our advocates and also to the duke, but no one listened, their ears stopped by money. What was I to do? I went to Emperor Henry, son of Henry who died at Liège. When he had heard my case, he caused me to be reinvested in the church’s estates through Godfrey, duke of Leuven, and our advocate Gilbert. The greedy invader cried out that violence was being done to him.

Again, in accordance with the emperor’s command, the duke of Leuven set a day on which, in the adversary’s presence, our men should go before and make a proper division between our estate and his. The day came. The duke was present, we were present, and Walter was present; with many free men there was a great crowd on both sides. Our men went over the estate, making its division. When they came to the water of the fishpond [Note: [Col. 0145D] French *vivier*, “fishpond”; Dutch *Weiher*.] lying below the castle, which Walter had dammed and by which he had concealed part of our allod, our men said that they could not make the proper survey until the water had first been let out, since the true boundary lay hidden beneath it. The adversary resisted by every means to prevent this.

Then one of our peasants, who knew the boundary better, stripped off all his clothes. Having tied on his back, between his shoulders, a golden cross which had previously been carried before the shrine of St Trudo there, he invoked the name of the Lord and the truth of the proper boundary, loudly called upon St Trudo, and leapt into the fishpond itself. Swimming through it lengthwise, he emerged unharmed; then, with our men, he completed the remaining boundary-marking both on land and in water. The adversary also made his own division, drawing part of ours into his and leaving part free to us. It could not be finished that day.

Another day was set, for the neighbouring free men to declare the truth. Corrupted by gifts, as rumour had it, they falsely claimed not to know the truth. Even so I did not, exhausted, rest; I again had the adversary summoned before the emperor at the court of Aachen. There, being greatly afraid for himself, he caused honourable men, both free and servile, to approach me, promising that he would acknowledge the whole allod as belonging to the church according to the survey we had made, if half were granted him as a fief, so that he and his heirs would become men of the abbot, while the church received the other half free and unencumbered. This pleased me—indeed, pleased me greatly. But our clergy and laity stubbornly protested, uttering certain disgraceful things against the adversary and against me also; sadly and sorrowfully, I was compelled by them not to do what, as I had predicted, I could no longer recover.

We therefore came before the emperor. My advocate appointed his spokesman, and the adversary his. The case was stated by both sides and put under judgment; the judgment was postponed until the next court session. Meanwhile the realm was disturbed and the emperor hindered, until he crossed into Italy [Note: [Col. 0145D] Since he calls Henry emperor, these events undoubtedly occurred before the second expedition into Italy, made in 1116; thus, as appears, in the course of 1115, as is also proved by the disturbance of the realm of which the author speaks.]. Our affair has remained unresolved in this manner to the present day.

33. I had almost passed over something which I ought to have mentioned earlier. The central one of our western towers has one [tower] on either side [Note: [Col. 0145] Manuscript 1 adds “tower.”], joined to it by the same wall. By the spiral staircases of each, one ascends to the first, second, and third storeys, as far as the bells; then, leaving the central tower lower, the two side towers rise higher in their pinnacles, and each has its own roof. Because of the various desolations of our church mentioned above, these had long stood unroofed and with roofs nearly rotten; the danger of decayed beams threatened a most ruinous collapse, especially of the bells. Some of the lead sheets had once been secretly removed by those who guarded the tower and used it as a stronghold; another part had been torn away to irretrievable loss by the force of the winds.

I therefore had them entirely reroofed anew. Beneath the beams supporting the bells I had another crossbeam set, with both ends fixed into the wall on either side; beneath that beam I set [Note: [Col. 0145] “set” in 1 and 1*.] a very strong wooden column to sustain it, resting on another beam below it, lying crosswise upon the lower beams from one side of the tower to the other. Thus the weight of the bells and the timbers supporting them, formerly borne by only six beams, is now equally borne by fifteen.

The tower beside the southern wing [Note: [Col. 0147D] That is, “part” or “side,” equivalent to what we call a *Flügel*, “wing.”], equal in height to the wall of the monastery, had been built long before my time. In my days it was completed and roofed with lead, and shines splendidly, distinguished above by a gilded cross. [Note: [Col. 0147A] Opposite this tower, toward the north, is another tower, likewise built before my time and equal to this in height and construction, situated between the apse facing the convent and the dormitory. These two towers had two storeys, of which the lower of either one was vaulted in stone; both upper storeys, however, were joined with thick wooden beams and boards laid above them, providing a firm floor for those ascending. Since the term *manica* is used here, it should be understood that it denotes the four extremities or wings: both those at the right and left of the great choir in the forward cross-shaped construction of the monastery, and also the lower chapel—now called that of St Eucherius—attached on the right, and that of St Lambert on the left. Interpolator, lower margin.]

*The Ninth Book ends; the Tenth begins.*

[Col. 0147]

1. The letter of Abbot Rodulf to Stephen, bishop of Metz, concerning the things which increased in the abbey during his time has now ended: things recovered from losses through his own labour and that of his associates; things acquired which had not been held; things advanced from no or small revenues to some and greater yields; [Note: [Col. 0147] From “sive” to “perduxerit” is lacking in D.] the few possessions given for the souls of the faithful; and the condition to which he brought matters that he found encumbered. It is now necessary for us to return to the earlier order of the narrative, so that, if he happened to omit anything or treated it too obscurely because too briefly, our narrative may restore and clarify it.

2. Therefore, while he, in accordance with the profession made by bishops and abbots at their consecration, was preserving what had been found, recovering what had been lost, gathering together what had been scattered, and correcting what had been neglected, a certain nobleman named Hardechenut of the village of Runchirs died near us. [Note: The name is absent in 1*.] [Note: See IX.18.] He left us from the allod of that same place only enough to owe us twelve solidi every year: six solidi on the first Sunday after Epiphany, and six solidi on the first Sunday after the feast of Saint John [Note: “five,” D.], and no further customary due whatsoever. There are two holdings from it, and, if you measure it, you will find more.

And because the predecessors of Abbot Rodulf had formerly granted to their servants in fief many things thus bestowed upon the church, so that from an entire alms-gift of this sort not even one anniversary meal remained for the brethren, he feared that the same might happen with this gift after his death. Therefore, in the presence of the leading men of the church and of those who gave and received this allod, he summoned all the brethren and decreed that these solidi should be received yearly by the prior of our church through the hands of the provost: six for the anniversary of the deceased, for the brethren’s meal, and six for what was necessary for the infirmary. For nothing at all had been assigned or established for it, except what the provost sometimes gave negligently and in very small amount.

Shortly afterward his wife Bertha, the wife of the same Hardechenut, died. For her as much was given to us as for her husband: namely, land beside that same land, paying twelve solidi—six on Saint John’s day and six on Epiphany. Abbot Rodulf solemnly established the same disposition for this: six solidi at her anniversary and six for the infirmary. Although our advocate Gislebert and his son Otto, heirs of the aforesaid free persons, had conveyed this land to our church by lawful donation, they nevertheless afterward allowed it to be invaded by their nephew Count Arnulf of Loon and never wished to resist him. [Note: This is Arnulf V, count of Loon, founder of the abbey of Averbode; Arnulf IV was a paternal cousin of Gislebert II, count of Duras. See above, IX.18. Mantelius, p. 92, wishes this Arnulf to be the same person mentioned in Henry IV’s charter of 1101, [Col. 0143D], and therefore conjectures that Arnulf IV had died before that time.]

3. For Countess Gertrude, who lies in our cloister, an allod was likewise given to us which pays every year twenty solidi and three denarii. Alost is situated on it, paying three solidi and three denarii [Note: “Alost … denarii” is absent in D.]; Assebruc [Note: Is this Assebruck in Flanders?], five solidi; and Steinvert, eight solidi. These together make sixteen solidi and three denarii; and three solidi are paid on the Kalends of May. There remains besides, near Steinvert, another portion of the same allod, paying four solidi on Saint Remigius’s day; and when this rent is brought, those bringing it owe absolutely nothing from it. [Note: “from it” is absent in 1*.]

A solemn arrangement concerning these revenues was made in the presence of her husband, our advocate Gislebert, and his sons Otto and Gislebert, Count Arnulf, and his brother Theoderic, [Note: The same Theoderic, brother of Arnulf V of Loon, occurs in the same charter of Henry IV concerning the restoration in 1101 of the village of Andenne to Count Godfrey of Namur: Miraeus I, 368. See also Wolters, *Codex diplomaticus Lossensis*, Ghent, 1849, pp. 33 ff.] at the request and through the efforts of Abbot Rodulf, because of the fear mentioned above. The whole rent was to be given yearly through the provost’s hands to the prior: six solidi from it for the brethren’s meal on her anniversary; when her husband Gislebert should die, six likewise on his anniversary; and the remaining eight solidi and three denarii for the infirmary.

4. Engeramnus, a nobleman of Horpale [Note: “Norpale” in 1.], had died long before these men. [Note: Mantelius, p. 72, led by reasons I do not know, conjectures that Gislebert V survived until 1138.] For his soul he had left us in the village called Herebac an allod which, besides other dues, ought to pay fifteen solidi; but the abbots had long ago given the whole of it in fief. Through the efforts of his provost Folcard, Abbot Rodulf recovered ten solidi of these [Note: “fifteen,” D.]; but, since they were acquired with difficulty and could scarcely be retained, he wished gladly to exchange them for another property if he could.

Concerning these ten solidi, Abbot Rodulf likewise decreed, by the counsel of his elders, that five should be used at Engeramnus’s anniversary for the brethren’s meal and five for the infirmary. If anyone should exchange them, those then in office were diligently to arrange that his anniversary should be provided for from the exchange-property and the remainder given to the infirmary.

Thus there are now twenty-five solidi and three denarii assigned to the infirmary. It must now be said what Abbot Rodulf decreed should be done with them. Eight solidi were for wood for the infirmary kitchen, when the sick had a kitchen of their own, and for making a fire before them in winter; six solidi for keeping a light continually burning there at night; three solidi and three denarii for the lesser light used while they ate and while Mass was sung there; and three solidi for buying utensils—namely vessels needed there, cloths, little tables, towels, and similar small articles.

The five solidi still remaining he left under this arrangement: if it should happen that the other twenty solidi and three denarii were not paid, what was lacking should be supplied from these; but if they were fully paid, whatever remained beyond those twenty solidi should be expended on the sick persons’ needs, on whatever the keeper of the infirmary, with the prior’s counsel, judged necessary—whether meat or other things—although meat ought to come from the provostship.

He decreed that this rent from every alms-gift should be collected by the provost from the debtors and, in their presence, handed over by the provost to the prior, so that, without greater trouble and without any expense, the provost might see that it was paid to him. But if any redemption arose from land upon the death of an heir, or if, when some fault had occurred, a living tenant paid a pledge or something similar beyond the rent, the provost was to have two parts of it—since he rode here and there at his own expense to obtain justice—and the prior the third part. The prior, however, was to answer to the keeper of the infirmary yearly for only these twenty-five solidi. [Note: “Of these twenty-five solidi [to] the keeper of the infirmary,” 1*.] If there were no keeper there, the prior himself was to administer the same funds, as also the anniversary endowments and other alms-gifts.

When one who held anything of this rent by hereditary right died, his successor was to come to the cloister and receive the hereditary gift from the hand of the provost and prior; otherwise it was not lawful. As for the light which the keeper had formerly supplied to the infirmary, Abbot Rodulf decreed that during winter it should be distributed through the four corners of the cloister from before the readings until after Compline. [Note: Among monks, the reading of sacred books, usually performed after supper.] [Note: Compline: the last church office, held at the beginning of the night.]

These few provisions from the alms-gifts received in his time he established for our infirmary, because he found nothing, small or great, assigned to it, except that the provost ought to supply meat to the sick and ailing, as he still ought to do; if meat were found in the abbot’s larder or in the court, he was to take from it what seemed suitable for the sick. For the Lord knows that through the disputes of abbots the church’s resources had fallen into such misery and poverty that the infirmary had neither a light at night nor a fire by day, nor did a sick man lying in bed have anything more than a healthy man in the refectory. If something did not suit his appetite, he made an exchange outside for what he desired within; sometimes he even deprived his mouth and appetite of something, from which he supplied his own need for light and fire.

This ordinance was not made by him so that matters should remain henceforth in so scanty a condition, but that he might somehow relieve the present need at that time. For it was his greatest wish and desire to add more if opportunities came to him, or to leave additions to be made by those who should come after him.

5. Very little fixed provision had been established for the brethren’s wardrobe; for the rest the abbots supplied as it came to them. Through their negligence the brethren very often endured great want of clothing, especially during the conflicts among abbots mentioned above. Yet I did not think it altogether idle here to state what then belonged to it, and what he afterward established and in what manner.

The entire estate of Provin belonged to it, as did the rent of Alost, three pounds; the church of Pirges, four pounds; the church of Dunc, two pounds; and the church of Guebechem, two pounds. But the estate of Provin had declined to such a small yield that it scarcely paid seven marks, though it had sometimes paid nineteen; thus from all these sources it finally scarcely reached seventeen pounds. [Note: “twenty-two” in D.] Wood for washing the brethren’s clothing came from the land called Manedac; [Note: Perhaps Montenaken, not far from Landen?] wood for the baths from Lare; [Note: Laer, near Landen.] and the allowances of washers and tailors from the mill of Grosmec.

6. Therefore Abbot Rodulf, considering that what abbots gave from their own resources for the brethren’s clothing was sometimes given only after labor, hardship, and prolonged previous deprivation, and fearing that the same could happen after him, thought it beneficial both for his soul and for the brethren to establish fully and designate the estates henceforth belonging to the brethren’s clothing. This was especially necessary because under him the number of brethren had increased and could not be clothed from the aforesaid provision.

He also wished to arrange matters so that this or that estate should not be divided from either its rent or its grain-revenue, but should serve whole and undivided in the capacity in which it ought to serve: so that, if a costly season came, the officeholder might receive fuller assistance from the grain, while, if grain sold cheaply, there might be rent to aid him. For he used to say that no officeholder could prosper from an estate if either its rent or its grain-revenue were lacking.

Accordingly he left Provin, as it was, to the brethren’s clothing, together with the rent of Alost, the church of Pirges, the wood, and the allowances of the servants, as he found them. But he retained in his own hand the rents from the church of Guebechem and the church of Dunc, because these villages belonged for the greater part to the abbot, for the reason stated above. He assigned to the brethren’s clothing the village of Sesninc with its church—since he had recovered it by his own exertion, labor, and great expense—and the village of Stades, excluding its church and Remigius’s mill, in both rent and grain-revenue. If, therefore, you calculate carefully, you will find that the wardrobe received something more than an income worth thirty pounds, ten pounds of which were added where formerly they had not existed.

7. In the village of Ham, [Note: The following, down to “curtilicius,” is absent in D.] [Note: Hamme, near Louvain.] which is in Texandria, the church possessed one holding paying thirty denarii. Since many sought it as a fief and we possessed nothing more there, Abbot Rodulf feared that someone might come after him and grant it to another in fief, as had nearly happened to him also. He therefore summoned the principal persons of the church—laymen, clerics, and monks alike—and assigned those thirty denarii, payable on Saint John’s feast, to the prior for the brethren’s use on the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, in order that they might celebrate that feast in white vestments, whereas previously they had scarcely celebrated it with three lessons.

He also added to the more solemn celebration of the same feast another thirty denarii, coming from Guebechem, from the place where there had once been a brewery and where now is the standing of a small court-building. When he had read in the book on the life of blessed Trudo [Note: Donatus, *Life of St Trudo*, ch. 15.] that, while still alive, he had first caused his monastery to be consecrated to God in honor of Saints Quintinus and Remigius, and had himself been buried before their altar; and when he saw that even to the present day the feast of Saint Remigius was celebrated both outwardly by the people and inwardly by the brethren, while for Saint Quintinus only a single collect was made, he wondered through what negligence this had happened concerning so great a martyr. He judged that it would be pleasing to blessed Trudo, who had dedicated himself and his possessions to God under Quintinus’s name, if Quintinus’s solemnity were celebrated in a place that, as I have said, had been dedicated to God in his name.

Accordingly, after composing from Quintinus’s Passion a most beautiful chant, with antiphons, responsories, and sweet-sounding hymns, he instituted the solemn celebration of his feast among us, assigning the brethren on that day an additional allowance in the refectory beyond the ordinary meal, as is written above in his letter. [Note: “as … is” is absent in D.]

8. The mill of Gursemdrul [Note: In an erasure, 1.] was made, reason so requiring, to pay two modii more than it had paid before: one of rye and one of wheat. On Saint Quintinus’s day he assigned half the rye to the poor at the alms-house, and the other half likewise to the poor at the same house on the day of his consecration, so that after his death it should be transferred to his anniversary.

From the other modius, of wheat, he decreed that on the feast-day of the same saint fine flour should be sifted and a loaf weighing two and a half marks should be given from it to every brother in addition to his daily bread. From the remaining flour common bread was to be made, and one loaf of the same weight was to be given to each of the chamberlains and servants in the court. The same was to be done from the other modius on the day of his consecration, and, when he died, on the day of his anniversary.

9. He restored to a certain Gueinric, our under-steward, one *bonarium* of land beside our cultivated field toward Mergueles, because he complained that it had been unjustly taken from him. [Note: The following, down to “cups for the brethren,” is absent in D.] This was on condition that he should pay twelve denarii from it yearly to the steward of our court for the use of the servants—namely cooks, bakers, washers, and the other members of our household—so that on Saint Quintinus’s feast they might have six denarii from it for drinking together, and six on the day of Rodulf’s ordination; these latter six, when he died, were to be transferred to his anniversary day.

Before the western gate of our court, between the mill mentioned above and the public road leading from the bridge to Saint Gengulf’s church, a little shop was constructed in his time over the stream beside the bridge, through the work of the cellarer and at the church’s expense, upon our lordship. From its rent or revenues—for they may at times be exchanged, so that it pays more or less—he assigned to the cellarer the duty of buying spoons, cups, [Note: A drinking vessel.] and goblets for the brethren in the refectory.

10. While he was laboring with remarkable zeal in recovering these things, acquiring those, and arranging each of them, great tribulations were not lacking. Our advocate, Count Gislebert, persecuted him inhumanly, and still more did the advocate’s wife, Countess Gertrude, his spouse. Thus she left him nothing, or very little, of all the revenues belonging to him, apart from the common food and clothing owed to the brethren.

This old hostility had begun in the time of Abbot Theoderic, because Rodulf had frequently and steadfastly resisted them during his priorate. Now that he had become abbot, he resisted more strongly and confidently, to the utmost of his power and beyond it, wherever he saw them infringing the church’s rights. For this reason the woman’s insolence went so far that, when our prior Guederic had on one occasion been sent to her, she threatened in burning anger and with an oath that, unless even the abbot’s common food and clothing were taken away, none of her own would be left to them.

11. Meanwhile the abbot was kept shut within the cloister, relieving his leisure and tedium by reading, prose, verse, and song, as one who neither had nor dared any place to which he could go. At last, despairing of human help, he turned to divine aid and arranged his journey to Metz during the Easter days (29 March 1114), not to any lord of his still living in the flesh, the bishop, but to blessed Stephen, the first martyr, the special lord and patron of our church after God.

There, after he had set forth before the peers of the church of Metz—monks, clerics, and laymen—the cause of his journey and his distress, and saw that no help could be given him by them, he turned tearfully, throughout the eight days he spent there, to the aid of the blessed first martyr. He reverently frequented a small oratory of blessed Mary ever-virgin in that monastery; and he entrusted his cause to their action with a heart all the more poured forth because he saw himself more completely deprived of human aid.

12. But as he travelled there, he lodged one night at the monastery of blessed Remaclus at Stavelot. [Note: “St Trudo” in D.] That night was the celebrated solemnity instituted because blessed Remaclus had recovered Malmedy for himself, [Note: Malmedy.] which Anno, archbishop of Cologne, had received from the hand of Emperor Henry, who died at Liège. Poppo the Second was then abbot there, and at the same time held the abbey of Prüm; how irretrievably he squandered both is not my purpose to say here.

On that night, at the first solemn Vespers, both abbots, dressed in white albs and precious copes, sat on festal seats placed on either side of the entrance to the chancel before the altar of blessed Remaclus. During the *Magnificat* and the following antiphon, Abbot Rodulf stood facing the altar, his head supported on the pastoral staff which he held in both joined hands. There he poured out a most bitter and abundant flood of tears over the necessity for which he travelled as a pilgrim. He often recalled to blessed Remaclus’s mind the friendship which Remaclus, then an old and holy man, and blessed Trudo, then a young man, had shared while both still lived in the flesh. [Note: “that” is absent in 1*.]

With pious reproach he also reminded him of the counsel for which Trudo had given to blessed Stephen the first martyr at Metz a great and illustrious memorial of his splendid inheritance and household—when there was now no bishop in the city to come to the aid of our distress and misery. What more need be said? The pious confessor heard the silent groans of that grieving heart and saw the streams of tears poured down the staff to the pavement.

He not only delivered the abbot on his journey from brigands placed in ambush against him, but truly went before him—truly went before him—with mighty power, and effectively pleaded his cause at Metz, not with Bishop Albero II, [Note: Rather, Albero IV.] but with blessed Stephen the first martyr and with the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, whose shrine in the church of that same first martyr is frequently made glorious by shining miracles.

For before the abbot returned from Metz to Stavelot to visit and pray again to blessed Remaclus, he was told on the way that the advocate’s wife mentioned above—the most grievous persecutor both of himself and of the church—had died (1114). And Advocate Gislebert, who had previously been his bitterest enemy, immediately went to meet him on his return from Metz with a friendly and supplicating expression, and promised that henceforth he wished most willingly to make amends for whatever wrong he had done him.

Nor did blessed Remaclus yet restrain himself. He powerfully crushed the many malicious and repeatedly renewed attempts of the followers of Herimann and of Herimann himself against the abbot, and caused them to fall from all hope. This Herimann withdrew, as before, to Saint Symphorian’s in the forest above Liège near Clermont. [Note: Clermont.] There he was seized by a severe illness from the groin downward and deprived of all power of walking. After long suffering he died and was buried there (1114), having first, so far as was possible, been reconciled through intermediaries to the abbot and the church. For he lived scarcely six years after Abbot Rodulf entered the abbacy; while Herimann lived, the latter was never without disturbance. Such was the end of Herimann, the one and last of those four winds, by whose storms we were often driven up to the heavens and cast down to descend into the abyss.

13. After the deaths of Herimann and the countess, a measure of peace was restored to the abbot and the church. Since he despaired of repairing the monastery because of its desolation and dared not undertake it because of poverty, he turned to building the northern fourth part of the cloister out of timber, like the eastern side, whereas before both were scarcely enclosed by a low hedge torn apart by age and decay.

He had the eastern side for the brethren’s dormitory and the northern side for the infirmary. Under its one roof were the wash-house, alms-house, and a small court in front with a postern. [Note: *curticula*: courtyard.] There was a handsome and spacious exit from and entrance into the cloister, in which the washing of the poor’s feet was performed and the small court before the gate was enclosed. Above was a granary; below, two chambers, one in which the chamberlain stored the brethren’s clothes, and another in which they were sewn.

Then came the infirmary, with a smoke-room or fire-room, a little chapel, a portico, [Note: *lobia*: portico.] a dispensing room, a private chamber, another more private chamber, and a garden before it, protected by gates, boards, and thorns, so that the air and greenery might refresh the sight of the sick. The building which had formerly been almost a prison for the sick he made into a cellar for beer and wine; and to the right of those entering he made a suitable lodging for the provost’s guests.

What had previously been the cellar he made into a handsome and spacious heated hall for himself and more important guests, with two other rooms on either side necessary for guests’ use. From these there was a convenient and private entrance into the monastery. The transept-wing (*manica*) was cut off from the monastery, and an oratory dedicated to Saint Lambert the martyr was made in it, suitable for guests who wished to hear or say Mass. In the wall of this wing, facing the monastery, there was a glazed window on each side, giving light both in the monastery and in this guests’ oratory. The keeper supplied this light from the five solidi which came to him from the church of Alost.

There was also from this oratory an entrance into another heated hall, which the abbot himself built broad and lofty for guests, likewise with its necessary appendages, so that the brethren should not be disturbed by guests in the cloister or need to leave their refectory because of them, as they had formerly been accustomed to do. Before these two halls were courts and porticoes, and a spacious and pleasant green enclosure for guests, with many trees bearing different fruits.

Of almost all these things he found nothing when he entered the abbey except a horrible ruin and shattered walls. And when, as I have said, he despaired of rebuilding the monastery because of its dreadful desolation, and feared to undertake so great a work because of the church’s slender resources, God inspired a certain matron of our town named Ruzela to begin building one pillar at her own expense. She began, raised, and completed it; may God reward her through the merits of Saint Trudo. [Note: “God … merits” is absent in D.] A certain Libertus, steward of this our greater court, imitated her and began and completed another beside it. After them, our townsmen began four pillars from the funds of their fraternities; two remained unfinished.

Perceiving, therefore, that this was the will of God and the saints, Abbot Rodulf took heart and, setting other things aside, energetically undertook that work alone. Thus, after the pillars had been raised with such labor and construction as no one can know unless he was present, he brought in a short time both walls of the church nave from the choir to the tower almost to completion.

14. But the devil, envying the growing work, saw in the princes of the realm, stirred up against Emperor Henry IV, an opportunity to impede our work; and he created factions. Because Count Gislebert, our advocate, was unwilling to abandon the emperor, while Duke Godfrey of Louvain opposed the emperor, [Note: He stood on the side of the conspiring princes with Archbishop Frederick of Cologne and Duke Henry of Limburg, according to Ekkehard of Aura under the year 1114.] the duke made an incursion into our town.

For the foolish people, apart from the common weapons of their bodies and the foolish boldness of their breasts, had prepared no means of resistance against him. The town ditch was worn away, ruined, and passable in more than a hundred places; there was no gate; the ground was continuous in place of bridges; and there were no timbers laid crosswise through the streets. Yet the people, foolishly bold and wrongly secure beforehand, rushed to meet him with hardened hearts. Contrary to everyone’s expectation, they held him off for a long time by manly force, and three times drove him out after he had violently entered, leaving a bloody trail and causing great slaughter among their own bodies.

But the enemies prevailed on the third occasion by their multitude and by being safer than ours beneath iron armor. They forced our people back within the court, which alone they had fortified against him. Immediately the entire town was burned by fire except for fifteen houses, which remained through the benefit of the marsh. [Note: “which … remained” is absent in D.] Meanwhile soldiers ranging everywhere plundered all our possessions, sparing churches no more than dwellings. When they departed in the morning, they gave whatever remained after the plundering to the flames; and the duke compelled all our villages which had survived the fire to submit to the service of himself and his men.

Since Abbot Rodulf twice described our calamity in sorrowful verse, we have thought it idle to repeat it here in prose. [Note: “This … expressed” is absent in D.] We mention only this concerning it: by expressing the truth in invectives against him, he produced great indignation and fuel for hatred against himself among the duke’s party.

15. The work on the monastery was then interrupted, since on that very day and at the same hour when the town was burning, the workmen still stood upon the rising wall and were just about to put the final hand to the uppermost work. [Note: “rising … upon” is absent in D.] But when they saw the great danger of the most severe fire over the choir, apses, and chancel-screen, they hastened there and, at grave danger to their lives and amid intolerable heat and burning, rescued those parts from the fire. In many places flame burst from the roofing beneath their feet and licked menacingly down from above upon their backs and heads. Thanks be to God, that part escaped the fire, though not without some damage from the breaking of the roofs.

The year in which these evils befell us was the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, the seventh of the abbot’s ordination, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, Monday, at the ripe harvest; the twenty-ninth year after the burning of the monastery and cloister during the contest for the abbacy between Lanzon and Luipo. [Note: Rather, the thirtieth.] It was thirty years and a little more after the burning of the town which occurred under Henry, bishop of Liège, and through him. [Note: Rather, twenty-nine. The author has confused the numbers; compare above II.13 and III.6.]

16. Although the duke of Louvain had inflicted all these evils upon us because of our advocate Gislebert, he nevertheless threatened still greater things. He would not release the church’s goods from invasion unless the ditch of the court, which they had raised against him, were first filled in. What more? What had been foolishly done through rashness was, so to speak, undone by grievous necessity: the court ditch was filled.

Then Abbot Rodulf, from the monastery tower around the northern side as far as the court gate facing east, spread the earth from the very great ditch inward rather than outward, because the court had on that inner side a great and unsightly precipice. He also moved the north-facing gate westward beside the mills. On the convenient level ground there—namely, between the eastern and western gates—the necessary workshops of the court were arranged in handsome order: two granaries; the lord’s house, broad and surrounded by stables necessary for the horses of arriving guests; two houses for the poor, one a summer dwelling and the other a winter warming-house for refreshment; around them a pleasant garden, useful for supplies of apples and herbs; then a bakehouse; behind it a brewhouse; and behind that a kitchen for wealthy guests, which, when necessary, served the brethren as a wash-house. In the middle and before these workshops was a well, useful to the court for every use of water.

Thus, when the court ditch had been filled and the duke’s anger appeased, our church recovered its vacant properties, which had been useless for many years. In the following year Abbot Rodulf began to prepare himself with such ardent zeal for repairing the monastery that, so to speak, he could scarcely rest at midnight without being continually present with the workmen before sunrise in the morning and until after sunset in the evening, urging the work forward as they busied themselves here with stone and there with timber. In that year he brought all the monastery walls up to a uniform height as far as the tower, and, after laying beams above, nearly roofed them over, with only a little remaining, though he did not cease daily and vigorously to complete even that.

Then at last he had demolished the little chapel which had been decaying for nearly thirty years above the tombs of Saints Trudo and Eucherius. Their tombs were enclosed below with a wall and above with forty squared boards, set in with elaborate timber-work in a double row, except for the entrance toward the altar. [Note: “except for the entrance” is absent in D.] A very beautiful smaller choir surrounded this work, reverent toward the bodies of the saints and suitable for the infirm brethren to sit in and for venerating and praying before the presence of the saints’ bodies. [Note: One side, on the left, is suitable for weak brethren to sit and hear Mass; the remaining side, on the right, is suited for hearing confessions and offering private prayers. This is an interpolation, with three lines erased.]

There was an entrance through the smaller choir to the altar and the saints’ tombs by two little doors on either side. Two iron doors before the altar separated the people from the brethren whenever they wished openly or secretly to proceed to the altar and the saints’ bodies to sing or pray. [Note: “and” in 1*.] The monastery wall and roof having thus been completed at very great expense, he caused it solemnly to be dedicated by Obbert, bishop of Liège, amid great joy and glory, in the ninth year of his ordination as abbot, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1117, on the third day before the Kalends of October, thirty-two years after it had been burned. [Note: These numbers too are each one too small.]

[Col. 0158C] 17. The relics which have been placed in the altars, and the altars in which they have been placed, are as follows. The principal altar, after the blessed and glorious and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, is consecrated in honour of Saints Quintin and Remigius, to whom Blessed Trudo dedicated the monastery first founded by him. It contains these relics: from the body of Saint Adrian, martyr; from the Lord’s tomb; from the Lord’s column; from the Lord’s crown of thorns; from the Lord’s olive tree; from Saint Theodore, martyr; from Saint Apollinaris, martyr and bishop; from Saint Nazarius; from Saint George; from Saint Maxelendis; from Saint [Col. 0158D] Christopher; from the garments of Saint Stephen, the first martyr; and of many others.

> [Note: [Col. 0157] “from … of many others” is absent in D.]

The altar behind the greater altar is consecrated in honour of Saint Martin, bishop, and Saint Christopher, martyr. It contains these relics: from the garments of Saints Trudo and Eucherius; from the bed of Saint Ulrich, bishop; from relics of Saints Christopher, Pancras, Victor, and Rumold, martyrs, and Bavo, confessor, [Col. 0159A] and of many others.

> [Note: [Col. 0157] “from … Christopher” is absent in D.]

The altar on the right side is consecrated in honour of Saint John the Baptist and Saint John the Evangelist. It contains these relics: from the bed of Saint John the Baptist, and from his cave, and of many others.

The altar on the left side is consecrated in honour of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul and of all the others. It contains these relics: from the body of Saint Amandus, confessor, Saint Valentine, martyr, and Saint Landoald, confessor; of Saint Firminus, martyr; and of many others.

> [Note: [Col. 0159] “and … of many others” is absent in D.]

The altar at the tomb of the blessed Trudo and Eucherius, in the lesser choir, is consecrated in their honour. It contains these relics: from the hair of Saint Mary; from the garments of Saint James, Apostle of the Lord; from relics of the [Col. 0159B] eleven thousand holy virgins; from the garments of Saint Rumold, martyr; from relics of the holy Apostles Peter, Paul, and Thomas; and of many others.

> [Note: [Col. 0159] “from … of many others” is absent in D.]

The altar on the right side, at the entrance to the monastery, is consecrated in honour of Saint Leonard and Saint Gertrude, virgin. It contains these relics: from the body of Saint Gertrude and of many others.

Another altar opposite this one, on the left side, is consecrated in honour of Saint Lambert, martyr. It contains these relics: from the hair of Saint Lambert, bishop and martyr; from Saint George, martyr; from the body of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor; from the body of Saint Gertrude, virgin; from Saint Vincent, bishop and martyr; from Saint Maurice, martyr; from the head of Saint Hippolytus, martyr; from Saint [Col. 0159C] Innocent, martyr; from Saints Marcellinus and Peter; and from the Holy Innocents.

> [Note: [Col. 0159] The remainder is absent in D.]

[Col. 0160A] 18. Mention has been made above

> [Note: [Col. 0159] IX, 25.]

of the number of the bells and the sweetness of their sound; but their names and weights, whether those which he had newly cast or old ones renewed, were omitted.

> [Note: [Col. 0159] “But let us speak of the names of the bells,” D. In D these words occur above, IX, 25, after “could not be made today.”]

The first was made of four hundredweights and somewhat more: a sweet-sounding *scilla*. The second, of twenty-one hundredweights, was made in honour of Saint Eucherius; he called it Aurelia and also blessed it. The third, of two hundredweights, he called Little Daughter (*Filiola*); this was given to the parish of Saint Mary. The fourth, of thirty-three hundredweights, was named Quintiana in honour of Saint Quintin, martyr. The fifth, Remigia, in honour of Saint Remigius, weighed seven hundredweights. The sixth, of six hundredweights, was called Benedicta in honour of Saint Benedict. The seventh, of more than eight hundredweights, he called Angustia, because it was made during that affliction [Col. 0160B] in which our whole town and abbey were burned or invaded by Godfrey, duke of Louvain. The eighth, made of more than six hundredweights, he called Druda in honour of Saint Trudo. Cast twice, it had a sweetness of sound equal to none of the others. The ninth was called Nicholaia; it had twenty hundredweights in the fire, but I do not know how much it exceeded that weight. The tenth, which because of its preciousness was sent to Metz, weighed four hundredweights; he called it Stephania and dedicated it to Blessed Stephen, the first martyr. The eleventh, which was transferred to the church of Saint Gengulf, likewise weighed four hundredweights, but was not of equal preciousness. The two *scillae* in the refectory, and the cymbal in the cloister—which was cast twice—may have had half a hundredweight in the fire. That which hangs above the choir [Col. 0160C] weighed more than a hundredweight. These weights together amount to 115½ hundredweights.

**THE TENTH BOOK ENDS; THE ELEVENTH BEGINS.**

[Col. 0159]

[Col. 0159C] 1. Eleven years before this consecration of the monastery, Emperor Henry died excommunicate at Liège. He was the son of Henry, son of Emperor Conrad, and had been deprived of kingdom and court because of the dispute between himself and the Roman apostolic pontiffs concerning the investiture of bishoprics by ring and staff from the emperor’s hand, and because of the simony which he practised in these matters. His son, also named Henry, reigned in his place; having persecuted his father together with the Roman Church, [Col. 0159D] he had deprived him of the kingdom.

When this man had begun to reign and had been confirmed in his kingdom with the greatest power and strength, he fell into the very offence by which his father had offended the Church and for which he had received sentence of deprivation; nor did he fear to commit deeds far greater and more wicked. For when he had come to Rome and was to be received in procession at the steps of Blessed Peter the Apostle by Lord Pope Paschal and the cardinals, [Col. 0160C] bishops and priests, deacons and all the clergy, the nobler Romans, and an innumerable populace, he suddenly broke faith, set aside his sworn oaths, scorned the hostages who had been given, and both he and his followers laid sacrilegious hands upon the lord pope, the anointed of the Lord, and upon all who appeared to be the heads of the ecclesiastical order and of the Roman people, and shut them up under guard (1111, 12 February). There each of his followers seized for himself whatever ecclesiastical ornaments he could: gold and silver, copes and chasubles, as each church had brought them for the adornment of the procession.

> [Note: [Col. 0159] Nothing concerning this matter is recorded in the Roman Annals or in Ekkehard of Aura.]

Why prolong the account? At last, compelled by grave necessity and a lamentable circumstance, the lord pope, not so much for his own sake as for that of the Roman nobles and his cardinals, bishops, priests, and deacons, who were held with him in cruel confinement, granted that he would give imperial consecration to the emperor, who was extorting it [Col. 0161A] rather than requesting it (11 April), and granted him a *pravilegium*—a wrongful privilege—rather than a *privilegium* concerning the investiture of abbots and bishops.

> [Note: [Col. 0161C] These are the words of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, at the Lateran council of 1112. Compare Ekkehard of Aura at this year.]

2. When this sad report and defiled renown spread through the Gallican Church, it immediately held an assembly

> [Note: [Col. 0161C] At Vienne, at the initiative of Guy, archbishop of Vienne. Compare Mansi, XXI, 73.]

(1112, 15 September), excommunicated the emperor, and condemned what had been done amid so great sacrilege and violence. The lord pope, however, did not violate what he had promised the emperor in their reconciliation; but he did not forbid the Gallican Church and all the sons of the Roman Church to use the keys of Blessed Peter the Apostle in response to the injury done to the supreme pontiff.

This sentence against the emperor was still suspended in the German Church, partly from fear [Col. 0161B] and partly, in certain persons, from favour. Not long afterwards Conon, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Roman Church, was summoned by it and sent to it.

> [Note: [Col. 0161C] He had already excommunicated the emperor at the Council of Beauvais in December 1114.]

A great council was assembled at the place called Friselart,

> [Note: [Col. 0161C] Compare Stenzel, II, 330; Mansi, XXI, 173.]

both of abbots and bishops and of a multitude of clergy and monks (1118, 26 July). In obedience to the summons, the lord abbot of our monastery, namely Rodulf of Saint Trudo, did not dare to be absent, lest he be suspended from the office and communion of the Church. At that council Emperor Henry was excommunicated, as he had been in the Gallican Church, both because of the aforesaid offence and because of the tyranny which he exercised against the Church.

> [Note: [Col. 0161] “then,” 1*.]

Because of the emperor’s adherents, the council was conducted and completed with much anxiety [Col. 0161C] and fear. Nor did Lord Abbot Rodulf return home with less anxiety and fear, since his journey went through, and into the midst of, the emperor’s adherents. Thus, in a kingdom already disturbed, a still greater disturbance arose.

3. Soon afterwards Obbert, bishop of Liège, died.

> [Note: [Col. 0161] The interpolator has written above: “in the year of the Lord 1119.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0161C] For the day, see the commemoration of the faithful in Chapeaville, II, 56. For the year—which the Annals of Rode prove to have been 1119, whereas others wrongly make it 1118—see Lavalley’s note in Ernst, *Histoire de Limbourg*, III, 4.]

(1119, 31 January). A great dispute arose concerning the bishopric; nevertheless, a day for election was jointly fixed. Before that day, Alexander, sacristan and archdeacon of the same church, seized staff and ring, presented himself to the emperor, and received them from him, thus being invested in the bishopric of Liège by an excommunicated hand. Because of this rash act and the false rope of contention, the appointed canonical election was long delayed, [Col. 0162A] until the assembly of Liège was drawn to Cologne

> [Note: [Col. 0161C] On the date, compare Aegidius of Aulne, ch. 21.]

(23 May), compelled by the authority of the metropolitan, namely Archbishop Frederick.

> [Note: [Col. 0162C] He held office from 1100 to 1131, according to Ekkehard and the Saxon annalist.]

Nor there did Lord Abbot Rodulf dare to be absent, always taking the greatest care lest he be struck for disobedience, just as he guarded against being defiled by communion with the excommunicated. There was elected there, therefore,

> [Note: [Col. 0161] “in the same year,” the interpolator.]

Lord Frederick,

> [Note: [Col. 0162C] Brother of Godfrey, count of Namur. Compare the *Life of Frederick* in Martène, *Collection amplissima*, IV, 1024, and in *Acta Sanctorum*, May VI, 725.]

chief provost and archdeacon of the greater church of Liège; and he was consecrated at Reims by Lord Pope Calixtus (26 October). Alexander and all his accomplices were excommunicated.

In the interest of brevity I have omitted here with what difficulty and danger the elect and his electors returned from Cologne to Liège. From Maastricht to the city, Alexander had laid for them the fiercest ambushes on both banks of the Meuse, setting troops at suitable places; he himself was also present among them. Yet, protected by God, they entered the city without injury; and, having excluded Alexander and driven him from the castle of Huy by siege, they endured him daily as a most grievous enemy. Only after many unsuccessful ambushes was Lord Abbot Rodulf at last received back unharmed into our monastery after this return.

> [Note: [Col. 0161] “is missing,” 1, 1*.]

This caused no small grief to our advocate Count Gyslebert and to all Alexander’s followers.

4. Therefore, after the emperor had been excommunicated

> [Note: [Col. 0161] Henry, D.]

at Friselart and Alexander at Reims, between these two events there arose great disorder and a cruel persecution of monks and clergy throughout the whole bishopric of Liège, such as had not been heard of since the time of the Arians. Alexander’s party was supported, with all his men, by Godfrey, then duke of Louvain; Count Gyslebert of Duras; Reyner, standard-bearer of the military force of Liège; Count Lambert of Montaigu;

> [Note: [Col. 0162C] Montaigu, between Aarschot and Diest.]

and almost the entire household of the church with its forces. Frederick’s party was defended by his brother Count Godfrey of Namur with his followers, though not all; Count Waleram of Limburg,

> [Note: [Col. 0162C] He was the son of Henry I, count of Limburg, whom Ernst, II, 250, seems rightly to conjecture died in this very year, 1119. He is the same man whose name elsewhere appears as Paganus or Paginus, occurring in the Annals of Erfurt under 1129 and in the Saxon annalist under 1036. See Ernst, III, 3, concerning this name.]

who later became duke; Gozguin of Valkenburg;

> [Note: [Col. 0162C] Fauquemont, Valkenburg, east of Maastricht.]

the whole city, apart from a few; all the abbots of the bishopric; the better and most numerous archdeacons and provosts; and a very great part of the clergy. That party was called Alexandrian, this one Frederican. The Alexandrians called the Fredericans guilty of treason against royal majesty and therefore persecuted them; [Col. 0163A] the Fredericans called the Alexandrians excommunicated along with the emperor and Alexander and therefore avoided them in ecclesiastical communion.

Accordingly, those who obeyed the Roman obedience under Bishop Frederick daily suffered plundering, robbery, captivity, fire, and sword at the hands of the Alexandrians. They spared no age, sex, or rank; they poured the whole heat of persecution upon the churches, monks and clergy alike. Many monks and clerics, wandering and homeless, ragged and half-naked, begged here and there. Thus we saw, thus we heard, thus we write.

5. Alexander, expelled from the city and castles, frequently withdrew under the aforesaid protectors to our town, and there vigorously promoted the conflagration of so many evils. All our townspeople favoured him, [Col. 0163B] being a people ever most fickle in such matters. In all Brabant and all Hasbaye there was no prince or lord who did not favour or protect Alexander. Count Arnulf of Loon alone remained neutral between the two parties, yet obeying Frederick more because of obedience to the lord pope than Alexander because of the emperor’s violence.

In the midst of a nation so wicked and perverse, amid the great distress of our spirits and bitter want of our bodies, though plundered and afflicted, our church nevertheless maintained obedience to the Roman Church with Lord Abbot Rodulf and kept itself undefiled by communion with the excommunicated. Therefore the severest anger, intolerable hatred, and rapine were directed against Lord Abbot Rodulf and against our brethren and all that was ours by almost all who [Col. 0163C] followed the emperor and their Alexander.

6. At that time and in those days Lord Abbot Rodulf wrote a letter to Alexander himself and another to one of his followers, rebuking them with great freedom of spirit, constancy, and authority for his unlawful usurpation and for the tyranny which they exercised daily against the Church. He also instructed them concerning what constituted canonical election, ecclesiastical promotion to a bishopric, and the emperor’s grant. These letters, if they are sought, will be found in the volume of his minor works.

> [Note: [Col. 0163] “These … will be found” is absent in D.]

But what followed? The Ethiopian did not change his skin, nor the leopard its spots.

> [Note: [Col. 0163] “nor … its spots” is absent in D.]

Meanwhile the lord of Louvain had distributed our villages, churches, and whatever of ours lay adjacent to his lordship among [Col. 0163D] his knights; and Count Gyslebert, our advocate, did likewise with those of our possessions subject to him. Henry, castellan of Kœn, an imperial ministerial, possessed what we seemed to have above the Moselle. Each of these lords—or rather, robbers—took whatever portion of our property came to him.

Only Lord Abbot Rodulf was lacking to the wishes of the Alexandrians and courtiers, who desired somehow to seize him and offer him to the emperor, to be dishonoured, as a great gift. [Col. 0164A] The old and newly intensified hatred of Advocate Gyslebert against him, together with continual slander before that tyrant, had contrived all this against him. But He who knows human hearts was witness that Rodulf had committed no offence against him except adherence to Roman obedience.

7. How often did the more faithful and better members of the Church approach the lord abbot with most humble prayers and pious entreaties, setting before him the storminess of the stormy time! They urged that, after security had first been promised him, he should allow himself to be presented to the emperor by faithful men, should hold fellowship with him only by a kiss and conversation, and should thereafter obtain the emperor’s peace and favour, both for himself and for our goods. When they could not prevail, because he steadfastly declared that he must preserve Roman obedience and catholic communion, [Col. 0164B] they assailed him with abuse, scorned him, and, cursing him with baleful omens, left him in anger alone.

For whenever the emperor came to Maastricht

> [Note: [Col. 0163D] Maastricht.]

or Liège, even his friends scarcely believed he could remain safe within the walls of our church itself; and the Alexandrians strongly stirred up this danger. Yet he continued, so far as he could, to keep them away from our church. If one of Alexander’s men celebrated Mass at one of our altars, he permitted none of ours thereafter to celebrate Mass there until it had been reconciled by a blessing bestowed by Bishop Frederick.

The days of holy Lent and likewise of the Lord’s Passion passed by (1129), and our whole church with the lord abbot struggled intensely in this affliction. Nothing [Col. 0164C] could help us: although, by the counsel and many entreaties of the faithful of the Church, we believed that we had bought peace and security, for ourselves and our goods, with twenty-four marks from the man of Louvain and twenty from the man of Duras, while we mortgaged under interest the possessions still remaining to us to meet this most burdensome exaction. The enemies of God and Holy Church lied concerning their promise and broke faith. They threatened that the end had now come: namely, that either the abbot should communicate with them, or should withdraw from the place and abbey, or should die there with all of us from hunger. And an occasion of this sort arose for the fulfilment of their long desire.

8. A matron, one of the leading women of the town, fell ill and drew near to death; there was no hope of life. Her sons and relatives came to the abbot and asked him, when [Col. 0164D] she died, to perform for her the Mass and funeral rites according to custom. What was he to do?
