It did not become him to consent to what he would not do; to refuse, and to state the reason to those asking, would cause a riot. What then? He answered that he did not dare. When they asked why, he said: “For the preservation of holy communion for myself. But if only the men would be absent, I should not fear to perform the Mass and funeral rites in the presence of the women.” They repeatedly pressed the same request, and repeatedly [Col. 0165A] received the same answer from him.

They did not regard Bishop Frederick

> [Note: [Col. 0165] Alexander, D.]

as a bishop, but as an invader and tyrant. “Then,” they finally said, “are the men excommunicated?” Angrily withdrawing, they roused a great popular disturbance; and the people, with the sons of the sick matron, brought a complaint against him before the advocate, with clamorous fury. “See, advocate,” they said, “it is clear that he regards both you and us as excommunicated, because under your leadership we went to Huy in the expedition of the duke.

> [Note: [Col. 0165D] Godfrey of Louvain.]

For this reason he will receive neither us into communion nor our dead because of us. It is certainly shameful enough for you and for the duke that you allow within our midst to remain safe an enemy of the emperor, who does not deny that he regards the emperor himself, you, and us as excommunicated.”

His friends and retainers secretly advised the abbot that, at least [Col. 0165B] while he remained sitting in his cell with two or three brethren,

> [Note: [Col. 0165] “with … sitting” is absent in D.]

he should send the community of brethren to the funeral. Seeking to turn him from his purpose, they said it was more useful to yield for the moment to the necessity of the times than to leave the church entrusted to him desolate. For he knew that one of two things threatened: either he must yield to their will or withdraw from the place. He could not be bent.

9. Since the discussion has now touched upon the duke’s expedition toward Huy, I shall briefly relate what it was. Alexander had occupied the castle of Huy. Bishop Frederick, together with his brother Count Godfrey of Namur, was holding him besieged within it; for the suburbs of Huy

> [Note: [Col. 0165] Huy, 1*.]

favoured Frederick more than Alexander.

> [Note: [Col. 0165D] Compare the Annals of Rode concerning these matters under 1121.]

To rescue Alexander, the duke brought his army [Col. 0165C] to Huy on one bank of the Meuse; our townsmen were in it—and this was what they reproached the advocate and duke with, so as to inflame them further against the abbot’s insult. On the other bank of the Meuse, Count Lambert descended from the mountain heights with an immense multitude upon those besieging the castle. Both sides fought fiercely: on the one side the duke, on the other Count Lambert, against both of whom fought those who were with Bishop Frederick and his brother the count of Namur.

The duke withdrew disappointed in his vain hope. Count Lambert was thrown from his horse and wounded in battle, and was led captive to Namur. Alexander, unable to endure the siege for long and greatly terrified by the words of Pope Calixtus, who had sent him word that he would shut against him the gate of eternal life unless he desisted, restored the castle to [Col. 0165D] Bishop Frederick. Having promised amendment and perpetual cessation, he was absolved by Bishop Frederick, with the few clerics adhering to him, in a public assembly at Liège; and, remaining at home, he kept unwilling silence for a time. Now let us return to the order of the narrative.

10. The advocate, who had long been bitterly hostile to the abbot, [Col. 0166A] was now inflamed still more to anger and fury by the above-mentioned reproach directed against him. He consulted the duke about what should be done with the abbot, and, having received his advice, came into the church courtyard on the second day of Easter (11 April), rang the bell, and summoned the people. There they all began together to make an uproar and complain about him, and in turn to favour his disparagement. When he was ordered to come out to them,

> [Note: [Col. 0165] “come,” 1*.]

he refused. The advocate deprived his retainers, who did not wish to deprive him, of their fiefs by his command.

> [Note: [Col. 0165] “command,” D.]

That whole day, considerable tumult was conducted amid the tumult. On the next day (12 April), Count Arnulf of Loon intervened and achieved nothing, since neither the abbot’s constancy could be changed nor the obstinacy of those dissenting from him. Thus, exhausted by the argument of the one side and the discordant clamour of the other, the matter was finally left thus: he must either withdraw from the place or communicate with the excommunicated.

He did not long hesitate about which course to choose. Being a prudent man, he quickly perceived that, although the need of the time wholly demanded his presence for the church entrusted to him, he should in no way bring upon his former honour and constancy the stain of mockery, nor corrupt noble beginnings with a shameful end. It distressed him to see the goods of the church plundered daily, while those who ought to have given aid gave none. Yet in his mind there struggled most painfully, on one side, affection for the brethren, whom he deeply loved and could not leave so desolate without grievous sorrow; on the other, the constancy with which he had most freely acted above to preserve catholic communion. But what followed? Zeal for the Church and the greatness of spirit belonging to an honourable and courageous resolve at last [Col. 0166C] won for him the victory in this conflict.

11. Therefore, assured of the brethren’s undefiled perseverance, he at last withdrew from the abbey, not without great lamentation from them and grief among the better people, despising present circumstances in contemplation of a better hope. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121, the thirteenth of his ordination,

> [Note: [Col. 0165D] “The fourteenth.” Compare below what Rodulf himself related of these events in the tract *On the Elevation of the Martyrs of the Theban Legion*.]

on the Wednesday of Easter (13 April), which that year was the Ides of April, he departed. He was honourably conducted by Count Arnulf of Loon, received by him with the greatest kindness as a guest, and liberally supplied. After spending a few days with him, though burdened by an illness of the head and eyes then widespread among many, he nevertheless set out for Flanders. Passing through Louvain, where the lord of Louvain gave him only leaves of words, he went thence by Affligem,

> [Note: [Col. 0166D] Affligem, between Ghent and Brussels.]

[Col. 0166D] and through the monastery of Saint Bavo, and finally came to Ghent, to the church of Saint Peter.

At that time Fulgentius was superior at Affligem, the first abbot of that place.

> [Note: [Col. 0165] “namely, in the thirty-fourth year of his ordination as abbot of that monastery,” interpolated in the margin.]

> [Note: [Col. 0166D] The Affligem continuation of Sigebert maintains that he had already died in 1120. He had governed the monastery from 1087; compare the Gembloux continuation of Sigebert.]

He was a man religious in life, together with his whole community, and devoted to hospitality. At Saint Bavo, Guulchricus was energetically [Col. 0167A] diligent in the administration of temporal affairs; at Saint Peter’s in Ghent was Arnulf, who later, while still alive, surrendered the abbey after being harassed by the brethren. In his time that place nevertheless abounded in an overflowing supply of food and clothing for sound brethren and sick alike, and the religious observances of the Cluniac order, introduced there through him, flourished under his rule.

> [Note: [Col. 0167D] This occurred in 1117; compare the Annals of Blandinium, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS V.]

Received by all the aforesaid men with pious humanity and compassion, he finally remained at Ghent under this same Abbot Arnulf

> [Note: [Col. 0167] “for four months,” the interpolator.]

until, from so firm a shore, he might watch for the time when God should command his winds and sea.

Meanwhile, while he stayed there, the paternal hand of the Lord added correction upon correction to him in its visitation, for his brother by the same mother—who had left with him in the role of servant but with a brother’s affection—died after a long illness. He lies [Col. 0167B] buried in the middle of the meadow before the western gate of the monastery, which a broad and well-ordered wall of paradise encloses on every side. His grave is marked by a polished, blackish stone. All who looked upon him marvelled at the firmness of spirit and serenity of countenance with which he received that visitation of the Lord, although inwardly he burned, as a man, with natural affection; above all marvelled Abbot Arnulf himself, who extended to him every kind of consolation with the greatest affection and practical care. Thus he remained there until after the death of Frederick, bishop of Liège, for whose obedience and for the communion of the Roman Church he endured the aforementioned hardship.

12. In the same year Bishop Frederick died, on 27 May.

> [Note: [Col. 0167D] The writer of his *Life* agrees, but Aegidius of Aulne gives 31 May. The epitaph which he preserves, as also the Annals of Rode under 1121, maintains that he was [Col. 0168D] killed by poison at Alexander’s instigation.]

Alexander was brought back into the city [Col. 0167C] by his supporters and with them. Apart from Alexander alone, whom Bishop Frederick had absolved on the condition that he should leave Huy and cease from the bishopric, none of his lay followers had been absolved; nor did he himself avoid their communion in any respect. It seemed both to him and to his followers that every opposition which had hitherto assailed them had been removed and taken away by Bishop Frederick’s death.

Summoned by Alexander, the duke of Louvain—though still excommunicated—came to Liège, strove to reconcile clergy and people to him, and in a full meeting of the chapter restored assent to his election. Those present from the Frederican party assented more by silence than with heart or mouth. It was then also jointly resolved to recall Abbot Rodulf, so that, with his co-operation—since he had possessed some [Col. 0167D] standing among the party of Lord Frederick and had become well known to the archbishop through the force of his constancy in persecution—they might more readily prevail in what remained to be done concerning Alexander. But knowing that he would be less inclined to return for their own sake, they sent word for him by letters and the seal of the church of Liège.

[Col. 0168A] He returned; but, on Alexander’s advice, though Alexander denied it, Advocate Gyslebert was not permitted to admit him into the abbey until he should understand and prove with what disposition and zeal Rodulf would defend his cause. While he remained at Liège, their mutual friends earnestly endeavoured to make peace between them. Abbot Rodulf did not refuse, but only in accordance with God and the salvation of his soul; Alexander wished to introduce neither this condition nor the other.

> [Note: [Col. 0167] “condition,” 1, 1*.]

Meanwhile he stayed at Liège, at Saint Lawrence’s. Heribrand was then superior there after Berengar.

> [Note: [Col. 0168D] From 1115 to 1130.]

But when Rodulf perceived, in what Alexander sought, that a snake lay hidden in the grass, and recognized that Alexander communicated with the excommunicated and that the assembled gathering was defiled by communion with them, [Col. 0168B] he bitterly regretted having come and most willingly wished to depart, lest he darken his other deeds, boldly accomplished, even by false suspicion. Yet he was not a little anxious and troubled, because he had no easy means of returning to Flanders: those through whose escort he would have to return saw him dissenting from them, and he feared that provisions for his sustenance would fail if necessity compelled him to remain at Liège longer.

The archbishop and duke were soon to meet at Maastricht, in order to establish everything in peace. In hope of this peace being confirmed,

> [Note: [Col. 0167] “of confirmation” is absent in 1*.]

he came peaceably to Maastricht. Nothing that had been promised was done there: the archbishop did not come and disappointed the duke who did come.

> [Note: [Col. 0167] “the duke who came” is absent in D.]

13. Seeing, therefore, that he had insufficient means to return to Flanders, he turned his mind toward Cologne, [Col. 0168C] to Archbishop Frederick. Descending from Maastricht, he came to the castle of Eysden.

> [Note: [Col. 0168D] Eysden, on the right bank of the Meuse, between Maastricht and Visé.]

There he found Andrew, chief provost of the church of Saint Lambert, who later became bishop of Maastricht,

> [Note: [Col. 0168D] He held office from 1127 to 1139; compare the Saxon annalist.]

and with him the leading men of the church who avoided communion with Alexander. Having mutually comforted one another there and strengthened one another in perseverance, he went to the nobleman Gozguin of the castle of Valkenburg, who also was a supporter and fellow-worker

> [Note: [Col. 0167] “co-optator,” 1*.]

of those favouring the Frederican party. After honourably keeping him for several days, Gozguin conducted him into the Ardennes to the archbishop, who happened then to be taking recreation amid the woods. The archbishop rejoiced at his arrival and comforted him with lodging and counsel.

In the morning, messengers from Alexander arrived: Henry, archdeacon [Col. 0168D] of the church of Saint Lambert and son of Count Conon, and Godescalc, canon of the church of Saint Servatius at Maastricht. They belonged to Alexander’s communion. The archbishop despised them and would not hear them because of the defilement of their communion. Nevertheless, he appointed for them, Alexander, [Col. 0169A] and all the clergy favouring him a day at Saint Cornelius’s,

> [Note: [Col. 0169C] Kornelimünster, or Inden.]

where he would hear them.

Meanwhile he brought Abbot Rodulf with him to Cologne and entrusted him to Robert, abbot of Saint Mary and Saint Heribert beyond the Rhine at Deutz.

> [Note: [Col. 0169C] Deutz.]

This Robert had been educated at Liège in the monastery of Saint Lawrence. Because of his distinguished reputation for learning in the sacred Scriptures, the archbishop had taken him into his own circle

> [Note: [Col. 0169C] On these matters, compare the passage from his book *On the Trinity*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS VIII, 261, where his Chronicle of Saint Lawrence at Liège is also found.]

and had made him abbot of the aforesaid place. Many great and splendid volumes of this man’s writings survive,

> [Note: [Col. 0169C] They were published at Mainz in 1631 folio, partly dogmatic and partly exegetical.]

which he left written from the divine page for the Church. While alive, his body could not rest even in sleep without his tongue throbbing and his lips moving in meditation upon the divine law.

> [Note: [Col. 0169C] He died 4 March 1135.]

[Col. 0169B] 14. Not long afterward, the day appointed for the Alexandrians arrived. [Note: [Col. 0169C] On this council see Kremer, *Academische Beiträge zur Gülich- und Bergischen Geschichte*, II, 215.] The archbishop attended, having summoned the leading men of the church of Cologne, and brought Abbot Rodulf from Deutz to Inden. For two days there was prolonged contention and prolonged debate concerning the canons. The archbishop avoided communion with Alexander and his party, and with all who had belonged to the obedience of Bishop Frederick. Alexander maintained that he and his clerics had been absolved by Bishop Frederick; the archbishop said that he regarded not only Alexander and his party, but all who were heads of the church of St Lambert, as excommunicated—except those who still, outside the city, remained under the obedience and communion of Bishop Frederick.

At last, when they asked why, the archbishop replied: “Because, after Bishop Frederick had died and been buried, you brought the duke of Louvain into your chapter [Note: [Col. 0169] ‘our’ 1*.] and into the church; and with him—indeed through him and on his account—you held an election, although he had been excommunicated by the apostolic lord, by myself, and by your own Bishop Frederick, and had not yet been absolved; likewise all those with him who had persecuted the church under Bishop Frederick.”

The archbishop did all this so that, once they had thereby been convicted and made satisfaction, their election of Alexander—made with, through, and because of excommunicated persons—might be null. Yet among those implicated in this contamination were honourable persons of the church: Archdeacon Almannus, Archdeacon Heynricus, Dean Seyfridus, Archdeacon Steppo, and many others, both greater and lesser. With the archbishop were, from the church of Liège, Andreas, provost of the major house; Emmo, archdeacon; Stephen, master of the schools, a man of venerable life; Reymbold, provost of St John’s; and several other men of good repute in the church, together with abbots.

Why say more? At last they all fell before the archbishop and obtained the absolution they had sought. Questioned by the archbishop, Alexander promised obedience, placing his consecrated hand in the archbishop’s hand. The archbishop commanded him, under holy obedience, not to concern himself further with the bishopric. He assented; and we who saw and heard this testify to it. Thus that assembly was dissolved on that day. The archbishop, having learned at that gathering how necessary Abbot Rodulf was to the church, gladly took him back with him to Cologne, while he considered what he should do with him, Rodulf having been entrusted to the aforementioned Abbot Robert.

[Col. 0170B] 15. Before long an occasion arose on which the leading men of the church of Cologne approached the archbishop: provosts, deans, cantors, and schoolmasters, as well as certain abbots, one of whom was Robert, abbot of Deutz, who brought Abbot Rodulf with him to that gathering. Present also was Cono, first abbot of Siegburg, who later became bishop of Regensburg. [Note: [Col. 0170C] He held the see in 1126–1132.]

Rodulf had intended to remain with him, because the place was renowned for religious observance and, owing to its high mountain, for the solitude beloved by monks. But divine providence had decreed otherwise concerning him. For behold, the brethren of St Pantaleon arrived; falling at the archbishop’s feet before the entire assembly, they complained that, after the death of their abbot Herimann, [Note: [Col. 0170C] Compare the *Chronicle of St Pantaleon* in Eccard, I, 927.] they had now lacked a shepherd for nine months, [Note: [Col. 0170C] The abbey had been vacant since 29 December 1120, as Rodulf himself demonstrates in his letter on the elevation of the Theban Legion.] that religious observance was perishing, and that the goods of the church were diminishing.

The archbishop immediately gave them the choice of electing. One party had chosen one man, another another; there was shameful dissension among them before the archbishop. For during the long period of nine months factions had increased rather than unanimity being achieved. Abbot Rodulf himself, out of reverence for our order, intervened in an effort either to unite them or at least to make them speak with discipline before so great an assembly; but he laboured in vain. Once and again the archbishop warned them concerning concord, gave them time for consultation, and withdrew with the others.

Accordingly, after taking counsel with the leading men of the church, it seemed good in everyone’s hearing to entrust that charge to Abbot Rodulf. Having never suspected anything of the sort, he first, prostrate upon the ground, gave thanks for his lords’ goodwill; then he resisted as far as reason and authorities [Col. 0171A] allowed and enabled him. But Egbert, dean and master of the schools of the major church—who later became a regular canon and bishop of Münster [Note: [Col. 0171C] He ruled in 1127–1131, according to the Saxon annalist.]—quickly met his objections with rulings from the canons: Rodulf had been driven from his seat because of Roman communion, while the abbey of St Pantaleon stood vacant.

At last he yielded, but only on the condition that nothing should be done otherwise than by the consent and election of the brethren of that place. This was done unanimously. Thus, in September, on the sixth day, a little before the Nativity of St Mary, he entered the abbey of St Pantaleon, [Note: [Col. 0171C] 8 September, in Rodulf’s above-mentioned letter.] introduced by the leading men of the church of Cologne and welcomed by a festive procession of the brethren and household.

16. The church of St Pantaleon was said from ancient times, by Roman privilege, to have possessed this right: that [Col. 0171B] its abbot should use sandals and a dalmatic, and should act in the archbishop’s stead at his processional stations throughout the city. But Archbishop Anno prohibited the sandals and dalmatic, while permitting him to act in his stead at the stations. This remained so until the time of Abbot Rodulf. Because he was a man of handsome, if one may say so, presence, and in divine service had a fittingly resonant voice, he attended the stations which he conducted, with the most numerous attendance of the people of Cologne and of women especially devoted to God.

The clergy, without any envy, rendered him solemn service and attendance as though the archbishop himself stood before their eyes. In a short time and without great labour, he finely restored the lapsed discipline and violated brotherly concord. Among those brethren he found the excellent virtue of pure confession and an untiring constancy in secret and public vigils and prayers. He opened to hospitality a door that had been shut—indeed barred—and repaired the ruined and unsightly houses, making them worthy of the archbishop’s own guests and of the abbot of the place. [Note: [Col. 0171] ‘for himself’ 1, 1*.] He never allowed anything prescribed for the brothers’ table to be diminished.

That year the church received 120 cartloads of wine, old and new together. He spent much on guests, especially monks and regular canons, for his door and table always stood open to them. Many, including leading men from the church of St Lambert who were still outside Liège because of Alexander, frequently found great refuge with him. Yet he was never in want; rather, he always had abundance. He was greatly loved by the household of the church because he treated it honourably [Col. 0172A] and in the disciplined German manner.

He often held gentle conversation with Jews, not disputing or reproaching them, but softening, by the handling and rubbing needed for the task, the hardness of their hearts. For this reason he was so loved by them that even their women went to see and speak with him.

17. The church of Liège still fluctuated grievously and had no certain hope of an appointed ruler. Adelbero, primicerius of Metz and brother of Duke Godfrey of Louvain, was already much spoken of; day by day report and expectation concerning him increased. During that period the emperor’s cause returned to peace and concord with the apostolic see, [Note: [Col. 0171C] Callistus II.] [Note: [Col. 0171] “In the year 1122,” interpolator in the margin.] [Note: [Col. 0172C] At Worms.] so that the emperor and his followers were absolved from the aforesaid excommunication.

Alexander, his ingrained itch not yet cured, [Col. 0172B] while the heads of the Lernaean hydra still panted about his breast, prepared golden and silver files with which to sharpen the hands and minds of the greedy to satisfy his own ambition. Bishop Frederick of Cologne, formerly harsh toward him, might have been softened by such instruments; but Rodulf, then abbot of St Pantaleon, with the help of Egbert, dean of the major house, and those who belonged to the party of the deceased bishop, utterly emptied the ambitious man’s vain hope. Therefore, when Alexander repeatedly found his efforts frustrated, he either concealed or abandoned his enterprise.

At last agreement was reached concerning Adelbero at Liège. [Note: [Col. 0171] “In the year 1123,” interpolator in the margin.] He was presented to the emperor, invested by his hand with the episcopal gift, and taken to Cologne for consecration. There our brethren—namely those of the monastery of St Trudo—appeared and demanded back their abbot for the aid of the church of Liège. Stephen, our lord bishop of Metz, also came to demand him back. There was great contention concerning him: some wished him to hold both abbeys; others that he retain that of St Pantaleon. Neither pleased him; his mind was set upon returning to his first bride.

The matter proceeded so far that, while still invested with the abbey of St Pantaleon, he honourably returned to ours; and, freely reinvested with that from which he had been unjustly driven, he possessed it securely while deliberating what course was best for him. And so it was done. After Adelbero’s consecration as bishop, in the year 1123, [Note: [Col. 0172C] Compare the *Annals of Liège* for this year, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV.] Rodulf returned with him to Liège; after being somewhat refreshed there, he was restored to our abbey and monastery by Archdeacon Heynricus in June.

*Here ends Book Eleven; Book Twelve begins.*

[Col. 0171]

[Col. 0171C] 1. The days during which Abbot Rodulf was away from the abbey amounted to two years and five months [Note: [Col. 0172C] Rather three, as is clear from what follows.] (April 1121–June 1123). During these, our advocate Gyslebert [Col. 0172C] and his son Otto squandered the revenues of the abbey at their own pleasure—not only those owing to themselves, but also those owed among us to the bishop of Metz. Nor did they show proper reverence even to sacred places. While residing in the abbot’s cell as though in his own house, the son did not refrain from intercourse with his new wife [Note: [Col. 0173D] Bertha, daughter of Godfrey of Buchain, lord of Rubemont; compare Mantelius, p. 78.] beside the walls of the consecrated tower.

But after the abbot’s return, some days after Pentecost—when he was met far from the town by many people and received in procession with greater glory than the disgrace in which he had departed—the advocate and his son withdrew from the abbot’s cell, plundered whatever they could at that time, and renounced future revenues. Their anger, indignation, and hatred against the abbot, however, were not diminished thereby but, as it were, increased in secret. For because Bishop Adalbero of Liège loved and respected him, had brought him back from Cologne with himself, and had restored him to our place, none of them dared [Col. 0173B] openly oppose him.

2. Thus, on his return, he found the resources of the church dissipated in many ways and grievously burdened by debts and interest. From what God had given him abroad, what he had brought with him and distributed day by day, he relieved the church’s common distress, especially that arising from debts and interest.

Before long, he demolished completely the cell situated beside the great tower. He regarded it as leprous and hated it because of the cohabitation just mentioned; moreover, since its beams had decayed and broken with age, it could not be repaired at modest expense. Beside another cell, which he himself had formerly built, he constructed a new one in place of the old, suitable for guests, with the necessary appurtenances, a chapel, and gardens. [Col. 0173C] He used its stones for the work on the dormitory building; after laying the foundations of a wall toward the east, he raised it somewhat above ground in that year.

He also hated it for another reason: it had once been suitable for the retreats of profane men, who had made for themselves a military stronghold from that adjoining sacred tower. He feared that this could still be done by them and their descendants. For Advocate Gyslebert had at one time so assailed him with grave injuries and hostilities that they might jointly station their soldiers there for the security of them both in the town, just as Abbot Theoderic had done with him, and before Theoderic the townsmen had done in their turns with that same advocate. Consequently many evils had arisen from that tower, and numerous crimes had been committed in the adjoining lodging. [Col. 0173D] He therefore demolished it, so that the tower might henceforth be less suitable as a fortification for rebels and the house of God might no longer be profaned by them.

Once, while sitting alone and reflecting on his miseries and former labours, he found himself unable, amid the unrest in which he lived, to see any way of bewailing his sins. He began to grow very sad and sorrowful, and to think of flight and of leaving his native land. Oh, how often, though perhaps he deserved it, did he turn over in his longing mind whether he might ever freely obey that voice of the Lord to Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12:1); and truly sing that saying of the psalmist: “I fled afar off and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. 54:8). He therefore intended to go to Rome and, on the journey, to determine with the counsel of religious men whether what he contemplated should be done; then to strengthen its accomplishment by apostolic blessing.

3. Meanwhile Alexander lived privately and quietly under Bishop Adalbero, content with the honours he had formerly possessed. It also came into his mind to go to Rome and, beyond the general absolution he had received, to obtain for himself personally from the favour of the supreme pontiff pardon for the disturbances he had caused in the church. Honorius [Note: [Col. 0173D] II, 1124–1130.] then presided at Rome after Callistus. [Col. 0174B]

Having first been reconciled, he and Abbot Rodulf undertook their pilgrimage together by way of St Giles, with complete affection and goodwill. When they had crossed the Alps and entered Italy, in 1126–1127, they reached Hose, another name for the town called Sena, [Note: [Col. 0174D] Siena.] one of the nobler cities of Tuscany. After spending the night there, they set out in the morning and encountered brigands about midday. Led away captive by out-of-the-way paths, they lost everything necessary for their pilgrimage. At last, after great labour and much fear, they scarcely recovered their horses, with the smallest possible expenses; nevertheless, they did not abandon the pilgrimage.

When they arrived at Rome, they found less consolation and compassion, both according to God and according to man, than they had hoped. [Col. 0174C] They therefore devoutly devoted themselves to the thresholds of the holy apostles and to the intercessions of many other saints, fulfilling their vows with tears and prayers, according to the measure of each man’s conscience.

4. After remaining there for several days, and seeing and learning concerning the apostolic lord and those around him things that they would not have believed if told them at home, their minds were drawn in different directions—especially Abbot Rodulf, who was well aware why he had left his country. As he lay awake by night and sat alone by day in Rome’s churches, he carefully and anxiously reconsidered what had been the purpose of his pilgrimage, and what he had learned on the road from religious men concerning the matter disclosed to them. He was also greatly troubled because everything necessary for carrying out what he had contemplated had already been stolen from him. Moreover, he heard that the land [Note: [Col. 0173] “land” 1, 1*.] to which he intended to make a further pilgrimage was polluted by an inveterate heresy concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

But concerning the direction of his own soul and of those entrusted to him, he had heard nothing different from religious men from what he had learned at home from ecclesiastical discipline and books held in common [Col. 0175A] by us and by them. In addition, a pain long afflicting him in the hip had worsened, a condition which physicians commonly call *chya* [Note: [Col. 0175] “sciatic [pain]” D.]; as it constricted his movement, it did not allow him even to ride without continual torment.

Recalled from his purpose by these necessities, after greeting the protections of the saints, kissing the thresholds of the apostles, and receiving the apostolic blessing, he intended to return home with the aforesaid companion. When they returned to the above-mentioned city of Hose, they found beyond expectation that all which the brigands had taken from them had been collected for them by their hosts and by all the citizens of the city. A great and hidden judgment of God: they reached Rome poor and returned home rich.

Why delay? Through many tribulations of mind, many sufferings of body, and the deadly dangers of Mount Jove, [Note: [Col. 0175D] St Bernard Pass.] they were at last received by the city of Basel. From there Alexander returned on horseback through Burgundy; Abbot Rodulf travelled by the shipwreck-prone Rhine as far as near Cologne, since, because of the above-mentioned affliction, he could not bear continuous riding.

5. Shortly afterward, [Note: [Col. 0175] “In the year of the Lord 1128,” interpolator in the margin.] Adelbero, bishop of Liège, rested in peace, on 1 January 1128. [Note: [Col. 0175D] Compare the *Annals of Liège* and Aegidius of Orval, ch. 23.] He was a simple and upright man, gentle, chaste, without avarice, of good character, nobler than noblemen.

Immediately the badly healed scar of Alexander’s old disease, twice previously broken open, burst forth for the third time. Panting after the bishopric like a wolf after prey that had slipped away from it, he began to cast aside every shame and fear of God. But why do we wish to utter in human ears what would be better kept silent than spoken in malediction? He attained what he wanted. How? As God [Col. 0175C] knows.

The monastery of St Vitus at Gladbach was the place of his consecration—[Note: [Col. 0175D] Aegidius, ch. 24, says that on 18 March Alexander obtained the bishopric by royal gift; Anselm of Gembloux confirms this, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS VI [*Patrologia*, vol. CLX]. The author appears to suggest that Alexander was consecrated on the feast of St Vitus, that is, 15 June; see Lavalley’s note in Ernst III, 18.]—a remarkable thing! He was consecrated by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, who had formerly acted so strongly against him. But Alexander, long steeped in the vices of avarice, could not withdraw himself from the slavery of idolatry, practiced through simony. Consequently, accused by his own clerics, he was summoned to Rome before Pope Honorius.

6. Alexander then thought it useful if he could take Abbot Rodulf with him. The abbot did not refuse, not so much for Alexander’s sake as because of the unfulfilled desire for his former pilgrimage still implanted in him. The whole journey was made in winter and was therefore scarcely endurable by a human body; nevertheless, they went.

When they had reached Rome, while the abbot slept at night, thieves—and, according to the neighbours, his own host—took from him [Col. 0175D] what he had prepared for the pilgrimage he had desired both formerly and anew. He therefore entirely abandoned this repeated purpose, since he judged, as far as he could conjecture, that it was not God’s will.

Alexander, after Pope Honorius had poured into him the wine of health-giving rebuke and the oil of fatherly admonition, returned home with Abbot Rodulf; thereafter he reverenced and honoured Rodulf in all things. On their return they celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Piacenza, and, as winter dangers increased, they passed through the city of Augusta [Note: [Col. 0176D] Aosta.] and with difficulty, near death, reached the little town at the foot of Mount Jove called Restopolis. [Note: [Col. 0176D] At the suggestion of C. L. Grotefend, this is Estrouble/Etrouble, at the foot of Mount Jove, below St Remy.]

Unable either to proceed or to turn back because of the very high drifts of snow, they spent the octave of the Lord there, beginning 1 January 1129. After several days, with a most difficult route shown them by guides called *marones*—for guides of roads are called *marones*—they covered two German miles and arrived at the little settlement of St Remy [Note: [Col. 0176D] Saint-Rémy.] on Mount Jove itself.

There, as though fixed in the jaws of death, they remained night and day in danger of death. The narrow little settlement was entirely filled with a multitude of pilgrims. From the highest and rockiest cliffs unbearable masses of snow frequently rushed down despite every obstacle, [Note: [Col. 0175] Omitted in 1*.] so that they utterly buried the houses beside them, some persons already seated at tables and others still lingering there; some whom they found inside were suffocated, while others were crushed and left helpless. They spent several days under this continual death in that ill-fated little settlement.

Then the *marones* of the mountain voluntarily offered themselves to the pilgrims and demanded heavy payment: they would open the tried route; the pilgrims on foot would follow them, then the horses behind the pilgrims; and in this way the trodden path would be levelled for the more delicate persons who were coming behind. Thus the *marones*, their heads covered with felt caps because of the extreme cold, their hands protected with shaggy gloves, their feet secured in boots and armed beneath the soles with iron spikes against slippery ice, carrying long spears to feel out the path beneath deep snow, boldly entered their customary route.

It was early morning. With the utmost fear and trembling, the pilgrims celebrated and received the holy mysteries, preparing themselves to enter upon imminent death. They competed to see who could first make confession to a priest; and because one priest was insufficient, throughout the church they confessed their sins to one another. While these things were being done in the church with the deepest devotion, the most sorrowful lament resounded through the street. For a dense ball of snow, like a mountain, suddenly slipped from the cliffs and overwhelmed ten *marones* who had left the settlement one after another, seeming to carry them down to the place of hell.

[Col. 0176D] Those who had at some time known the nature of this disastrous occurrence rushed with headlong speed to that murderous place. They brought back the dug-out *marones*: some lifeless upon poles, some half-alive, others with shattered bones dragged in their hands. One cried that she had lost her husband, another her brother; this man and that man cried that he had lost this one and that one. At so horrible a sight [Note: [Col. 0175] “course” 1*.] the pilgrims left the church, terrified; they hesitated briefly, fearing the same fate for themselves, then fled with all speed back to Restopolis. There was no further question, as before, of the route’s difficulty: it seemed easy to them when escape from danger of death was at stake.

There they celebrated the Epiphany of the Lord; after waiting for clear weather and hiring *marones*, they returned to the deadly settlement. Fear of death lending speed to their feet, they scarcely reached the middle of the mountain that day, sometimes crawling and sometimes falling. The following day, 7 January, after recovering their breath somewhat, they escaped the profane rites of Jupiter and, making for their native soil, arrived without grave difficulty.

But the abbot did not do so. Because of the harshness of the winter, the difficulty of the journey, and bodily weakness, he made shorter daily stages and followed [Col. 0177B] them slowly; but he did not catch up with them before they reached their homeland. Having therefore crossed Besançon, [Note: [Col. 0177D] Besançon.] the metropolitan city of Burgundy, with a small retinue, he was caught in an ambush by a wicked tyrant on the next day. He was painfully led and dragged by mountainous and wooded byways for three days; at last, stripped of necessities, he was allowed to depart on his journey.

7. Having now returned from Rome for the second time and recovered somewhat from the vexation of travel, he still did not rest from his earlier desire: perhaps he might find in his own country the repose that he had sought and not found outside it. But the hand of the Lord, long stretched out over us and not yet shortened, added another blow against our place through the accustomed angel, minister of His wrath, and admonished the transgressors [Col. 0177C] to return to their hearts.

For He allowed our advocate, Count Gyslebert, and his son Otto to be filled with an evil spirit, and stirred them irrevocably to every act contrary to law and right, for the oppression of the church’s household. Though humbly warned by Abbot Rodulf, frequently rebuked by his lord Duke Waleram of Limburg, and formally accused by our lord Stephen, bishop of Metz, Gyslebert was at last, because of his obstinacy and contumacy, deprived by lawful judgment of the advocacy. [Note: [Col. 0177] “In the same year of the Lord 1128,” interpolator in the margin.]

Because he was a man of stubborn character and little judgment, it happened in those same days, as his sins demanded, that the county and fief which he held from the bishopric of Liège were, at Bishop Alexander’s formal accusation, taken from him by his peers. What could he do? He had no forces with which to resist the aforesaid lords, while his high spirit would not allow him to remain quiet. He stirred up sedition in the kingdom and scandal among the people.

8. He therefore went to Godfrey, the former duke of Louvain, [Col. 0178A] enemy of the kingdom and emperor because of the duchy of Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0177] “of Lotharingia,” interpolator in the margin.]; this duchy had been taken from Godfrey and given to Count Waleram of Limburg, our chief advocate. [Note: [Col. 0177D] The *Annals of Rode* testify that this occurred in 1128; a document in Miraeus IV, 197, dated 13 June 1128, mentions Duke Paganus, that is Waleram. But he could hold only the land between the Rhine and Gete rivers, as the *Erfurt Annals* for 1129 demonstrate. See Ernst III, 18. Godfrey seems to have favoured the Staufen party.]

The calamity of this quarrel fell for the most part upon our church. Whatever of ours was subject to the advocate and former duke was either burned, laid waste, or made subject to him and his followers. The nearer they were to us, the more hostile they were. Only our town and monastery remained, where they did not yet dare to lay profane hands. The advocate’s chief aim was to introduce into our town, which had no fortification at all, his own forces and those of the men of Louvain; after burdening the townsmen by dispersal through lodging soldiers, he intended at last to carry them off captive.

But the abbot’s foresight turned aside his malice by prudent counsel. Through his lord Stephen, bishop of Metz, he secured the fact that Alexander, bishop of Liège, received our abbey and town under his protection. The bishop’s men and the townsmen swore one another faith, counsel, and assistance. Encouraged by this assurance, they began to renew the old ditch and established a fortification such as our land on the plain had never possessed.

For this reason the dissension grew with the utmost violence into ever greater evil: on one side the former duke of Louvain raged, on the other Count Gyslebert. They never spared the possessions of monks and clerics, whether in villages or churches. They captured every sex, every age, every rank, and tortured them with dreadful torments, even to death, in order to extort ransom. For these and other crimes the former duke of Louvain and Count Gyslebert, with all their followers, were excommunicated.

Afterward Durachium was besieged by Alexander, bishop of Liège, and Waleram, duke of Limburg, [Note: [Col. 0177] “In the year of the Lord 1129,” interpolator.] to relieve which Lord Godfrey of Louvain and Count Theoderic of Flanders assembled an army. A hard battle was fought before it, fiercely, on 7 August 1129. The counts of Louvain and Flanders were defeated and fled; more than four hundred men of the enemy fell in the battle. [Note: [Col. 0178D] Compare the accounts of this battle in Anselm of Gembloux for 1129 and in the *Annals of Rode*.]

The siege was resumed around the castle but could not be maintained long because the August harvest was pressing. It was therefore raised, though the destruction wrought by the tyrants continued through fire and sword. Under such [Col. 0178D] calamity and distress, although the resources of the brethren were much reduced in food and clothing, since for three years they endured this suffering, neither their discipline grew lukewarm nor their number diminished.

But when it pleased Him in whose hand are all powers and all rights of kingdoms, who troubles the depths of the sea and calms it when He wills, He said to the angel striking: “Stay your hand now, that the land may not be laid waste” (2 Sam. 24:16); and immediately there was a great calm. For the lords of Louvain and Durachium, and those who had been excommunicated with them, came to Liège; making ecclesiastical satisfaction in 1131, they received absolution and promised amendment. [Note: [Col. 0179D] Bishop Alexander agrees as to the date in a document in Miraeus I, 92; compare Ernst III, 32.] Thus the land ceased from wars.

Now, after the third [Note: [Col. 0179] “thus” 1*; “second” 1, D.] burning and devastation [Note: [Col. 0179] “and devastation” lacking in 1*.] of our abbey by the prince of Louvain—the first because of our advocate, Count Gyslebert, who was then opposing him on behalf of Emperor Henry IV; the second likewise because of that same man, who opposed us and was allied with him [Note: [Col. 0180D] See above, X.14. In fact this is the third devastation, as he demonstrates shortly below, XII.14.]—we were under the greatest anxiety [Col. 0179B] to repair our burned churches, mills, and demesne villages, just as men wounded in war are concerned to heal their wounds at home.

9. Amid these great and unceasing evils, Abbot Rodulf was intolerably afflicted, both by vexation of mind and by bodily pain from sciatica, which had so seized his entire [Note: [Col. 0179] “only” 1, 1*.] hip that he could do little on horseback or on foot. He therefore built for himself a little cell, suitable for his infirmity and for one wishing to live religiously, on the northern side beside the western [Note: [Col. 0179] “eastern” 1*.] apse of the monastery. Its door opened into the oratory, near the crypt and choir. He had also vowed to consecrate an altar in honour of St Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and St Basil the bishop, because the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin, our lady Mary, had no special oratory in our church.

But the healing hand of the Lord, which from ancient times had not been accustomed to leave the body of our church for long without purification, further deigned mercifully to touch our head; and it transformed the abbot’s sciatic suffering into paralysis. [Note: [Col. 0179] “paralica” 1, 1*.]

In March of the twenty-fifth year of his ordination, in 1132, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, Friday, in the days of holy [Note: [Col. 0179] Omitted in 1*.] Lent, Abbot Rodulf sat at table with the brethren in the refectory. On that very day he had given the brethren a general allowance of fish, relaxing abstinence out of human compassion. During the meal, roasted eels from the marsh were brought to him on a spit, and then other, smaller eels prepared with early herbs in broth. After he had eaten of them and, feeling nausea, had cast them aside, he put his hand to apples in a cup before him, steeped in wine. Having tasted a little of them, his left hand immediately began to grow heavy as lead, at intervals briefly becoming lighter; the corner of his lips on that side also seemed to be dying, and his tongue functioned with less than its accustomed ease.

Though very frightened, he did not interrupt the reading. After the meal, giving thanks with the brethren, [Col. 0180A] he withdrew to the western cell without pain but in great fear because of what had happened to him. There, discussing with his intimates what had happened in the refectory, he gave thanks to God because he thought he had escaped, though he had not escaped. Not long after the brethren’s conversations, he gradually felt his left leg becoming numb, so that he would not have dared go to bed without support. About midnight, when he awoke, he found himself deprived of all use of his left leg and arm. Deeply afraid for the use of his tongue and the soundness of his understanding, he most devoutly commended himself to the prayers of the brethren, that God might preserve for him both a tongue for confession and understanding for recognition. And the merciful kindness of God granted this to him.

[Col. 0180B] **10.** In the same year, around autumn, the fatherly hand of the Lord correcting him added such an illness to this affliction that the physicians despaired of him, and he scarcely seemed to retain the form of a human being. As he himself used to relate, on the night of the feast of Saint Michael he was so crushed by suffering that, as one who by sinning had offended the sight of the angels, he seemed to be punished by angelic blows. But after he scarcely escaped that illness and began to recover sufficiently from the paralysis to be able somehow to walk while supported by a staff, and sometimes to enter the brothers’ assembly, choir, and chapter-house, he most earnestly admonished the brothers to preserve religious observance and to avert from themselves the wrathful displeasure of God.

He also had a litter made for himself, in which he could conveniently be conveyed, even to distant places, wherever he wished, for the needs of the church. [Col. 0180C] He also applied both his attention and his effort to arranging the cloister’s masonry. In the following year (1133), opening the tower before the community, he enlarged what had formerly been a small arch into the great arch now visible, moving the entrance of the church to the right; and, in the blocked-up former entrance, he had an image of the holy Mother of God painted, so that it might receive fitting veneration from those entering and leaving.

He also carried the dormitory wall up to the beams on both sides, and the refectory wall on one side, together with the kitchen wall; and he marked out an exit from the cloister. He likewise laid out the chapter-house with three walls, the fourth being the church wall, with an arch for entry and two windows for light, with arched columns. [Col. 0180D] He raised the cloister wall, upon which the columns were to stand in a circuit from one end of the community building to the other, from a very deep foundation as high as was necessary for setting the columns; and, having erected piers around it, he marked the places for the intervening columns, as well as the place which was to serve the community of brothers for washing their hands. Already some of the beams, cut down, lay in the forest, with which the structure of the dormitory above and of the workrooms below was to be framed together. [Note: [Col. 0179] Missing in manuscript 1*.]

While the abbot urged the officials toward this work and was himself urged by the brothers, God raised up against us—behold, for I know not what time!—an angel of Satan, in order both to grieve us by hindering the work and to punish our sins by the loss of our resources. For his hand was still stretched out against us, and his anger had not turned away. This came about on the following occasion.

**11.** There is a class of hired workers whose occupation is to weave cloth from linen and wool; among ordinary people this class is regarded as insolent and proud above other hired workers. To humble their insolence and pride, and to avenge upon them an injury of his own, a certain poor peasant from the village called Inda [Note: [Col. 0181D] Corneli-Münster.] devised this devilish trick. [Note: [Col. 0181D] *Tegnam*: a deceit, trick.] Having obtained authorization from the judges and assistance from frivolous people [Col. 0181B] who delight in jokes and novelties, he constructed a ship in a nearby forest and, fastening wheels beneath it, made it movable over land.

He also secured permission from the authorities for it to be drawn from Inda to Aachen by ropes laid upon the weavers’ shoulders. Received at Aachen by a great procession of people of both sexes, it was then likewise conveyed by the weavers to Maastricht; there it was repaired and adorned with mast and sail, and brought to Tongeren, and from Tongeren to Los.

When Abbot Rodulf heard that this ship, assembled under an ill-omened auspice and launched under an evil bird, was approaching our town amid such zeal for paganism, he prophetically warned the people that they should refrain from receiving it, because evil spirits were being drawn along in it beneath this mockery, and because in the near future sedition would be stirred up through it, [Col. 0181C] resulting in slaughter, fires, and plundering, and the shedding of much human blood.

Throughout all the days in which that image of evil spirits remained at Los, our townspeople refused to listen to him crying out these warnings. Rather, they received it with the same zeal and delight with which the doomed Trojans dedicated the fateful horse in the middle of their public square. Immediately the weavers of the town who came too late to the profane watch beside this image were sentenced to banishment.

Good heavens! Who has ever seen such—if one may Latinize the expression—brutishness in rational animals? Who such paganism in those reborn in Christ? By sentence of banishment they compelled the weavers, night and day, to surround the ship with every kind of weaponry and to keep anxious watch over it continuously, night and day. [Col. 0181D] And it was remarkable that they did not compel them to sacrifice victims to Neptune before the ship, since ships are ordinarily his domain; but Neptune reserved them for Mars, who desired that offerings should be made to him from human flesh. This later occurred in many ways.

**12.** Meanwhile the weavers, with a hidden but heartfelt groaning, called upon God, the righteous judge, to avenge them upon those who subjected them to this disgrace. In accordance with the upright life of ancient Christians [Col. 0182A] and apostolic men, they lived by the labor of their hands, working night and day to feed and clothe themselves and to provide the same for their children.

They also sorrowfully asked and complained among themselves why this disgrace and violent insult had been imposed upon them more than upon other hired workers, when there were among Christians many other occupations far more contemptible than their own. Yet they considered no occupation contemptible by which a Christian could support himself without sin; they held that only that was avoidable and shameful which brought the defilement of sin upon the soul, and that a rustic weaver, though poor, is better than an urban and noble judge who exacts from orphans and despoils widows.

While, as I have said, they mournfully complained among themselves of these things and the like, before that abominable dwelling-place—I do not know whether I should call it that of Bacchus or Venus, Neptune or Mars, but, more truly, of all evil spirits—there resounded every kind of musician [Col. 0182B] singing shameful songs unworthy of the Christian religion.

The judges had also decreed that, apart from the weavers, whoever approached the ship so closely as to touch it must leave with the weavers a pledge snatched from his neck, unless he ransomed himself at whatever price they chose. But what am I to do? Shall I speak or be silent? Would that a spirit of falsehood were dripping from my lips! In the still fleeting daylight, with the moon now at hand, [Note: [Col. 0182D] Horace, *Odes* 1.4.5.] bands of married women, casting off feminine modesty, heard the noise of this folly and leapt from their beds with unbound hair: some [Col. 0182C] half-naked, others clothed only in a simple mantle. They brazenly mingled themselves with the dancers circling about the ship.

At times one might see a thousand souls of both sexes celebrating that monstrous and ill-omened sailors’ chant [Note: [Col. 0182D] A sailors’ song.] until midnight. When that execrable dance broke up, both sexes, sending forth a huge clamour of disorderly cries, rushed this way and that in Bacchic frenzy. What was then done there—[Note: [Col. 0181] “you might see [them] doing.” D.] let those tell it who chose to see and do it; it is ours to keep silence and to lament, since it has now fallen to us to pay the grievous penalty. [Note: [Col. 0181] “of those … to see” is missing in D.]

**13.** After these utterly wicked rites had been celebrated in the manner described for more than twelve days, [Col. 0182D] the townspeople discussed together what they should now do about taking the ship away from themselves. Those of sounder judgment, who regretted that it had been received, feared God because of what they had seen and heard, and feared for themselves because of what they conjectured would follow. They urged that it should be burned, or removed in one way or another. But the foolish blindness of some people insultingly resisted this salutary advice, for the evil spirits borne in it had spread among the people the notion that the place and inhabitants where it was found to remain would be marked with a more disgraceful name. [Col. 0183A] They therefore decided to take it to the village near us called Leugues. [Note: [Col. 0183D] Leeuw, between Tienen and Saint-Trond.]

**14.** Meanwhile, the lord of Louvain heard of the demonic jest involving that ship; and, having been instructed by religious men of his land that this monster should be avoided and kept out of his territory, he sent assurances of his favor and friendship to our townspeople. He humbly warned them not to violate the peace which had been renewed and confirmed by oaths between themselves and him—especially by bringing that devilish mockery into his neighborhood. If they called it a game, he said, they should find someone else with whom to play it there; for if, beyond this warning, they proceeded with it, they would break the aforesaid peace against him, and he would exact vengeance on them with sword and fire. [Col. 0183B]

He sent the same message to the lords of Durachium, who were also his men, bound to him by hand-pledges, intervening oaths, and hostages given. When he had already done this a third time, he was disregarded both by our townspeople and by the lords of Durachium. For, because of the sins of the inhabitants, the Lord wished to send upon our place the fire and arms of the men of Louvain.

Count Gyslebert, against the nobility of his lineage, joined himself to this plebeian folly and decreed that the land-ship should be drawn as far as Leugues, beyond the village of Durachium. This he did, to our ill fortune, with the whole multitude of our townspeople and with a great shouting of revelers. The townspeople of Leugues, wiser than ours and obedient to the commands of the lord of Louvain, [Col. 0183C] shut their gates and did not allow the monster of ill omen to enter their village.

The lord of Louvain, unwilling for the contempt of his requests and commands to go unavenged, appointed a day for the counts as for his own men; but they would not come either at the first, the second, or even the third summons. He therefore led out against them and against us an army of a great multitude of armed men, both foot-soldiers and knights. [Note: [Col. 0183] “In the year of the Lord 1135,” an interpolation.]

Setting our town aside, as being more strongly fortified and full of fighting men, he first attacked the men of Durachium. Although they resisted bravely, for some reason unknown to me he did not besiege the castle, though he could have done so; instead, he spent the night between Leugues and Durachium. [Col. 0183D] When on the following day he prepared to bring up his army and assault from four sides—for he had an enormous force—Adelbero, primicerius of Metz and maternal uncle of the sons of the lord of Louvain, arrived. Through his intervention, because the countess of Durachium was his sister [Col. 0184A] and Durachium was a castle of Saint Lambert, the lord of Louvain ceased from the attack and withdrew from the siege, after a promise had been given him that the men of Durachium would shortly be brought before his justice.

While these and other matters concerning the lords and among the lords were being discussed, the foot-soldiers and knights spread throughout all our surrounding region, giving our villages, churches, mills, and whatever they encountered over to fire and destruction. On their withdrawal, they divided among themselves, according to what lay nearest to each, the places that were farther from us. At that time the abbey was most grievously devastated, and everything necessary for the brothers was plundered.

This was the fourth devastation which the lord of Louvain inflicted upon our abbey within twenty-six years. [Note: [Col. 0183D] The author erred in the number: the first devastation occurred in 1114; this fourth one, as is clear from what follows, in 1136; thus the years stated do not add up.] The first was on account of Count Gyslebert’s disagreement with him [Col. 0184B] concerning Emperor Henry IV; [Note: [Col. 0184D] See above, X.14.] the second, with him, concerning Alexander, later bishop of Liège; [Note: [Col. 0184D] XI.6.] the third, when battle was fought before Durachium, [Note: [Col. 0184D] XII.9.] likewise on his account; the fourth, when the treaty between them was broken because of the evil arrival of the land-ship. All these great devastations took place because of Count Gyslebert—either through him or with him—apart from innumerable lesser devastations which he never ceased to inflict. [Note: [Col. 0183] “in … year” is missing in D.]

**15.** In about this year (1136), I took care to commit to writing, for the lasting memory of our descendants, what befell us through Abbot Rodulf. A certain man named Hezelo had died; he had been steward to the abbots under whom he had grown old. While [Col. 0184C] still living, knowing how to please his lords by familiar service, he used his intimacy and craftiness to obtain, as his fief, from the brothers’ table, a portion of cultivated land near our town, two portions of the cultivation at Stades, and the mill of Cotteym, which paid twenty-four *modii* annually.

At length he died without children, leaving the usufruct to his wife, as he had secured for her before the abbots and his peers. But after him rose his brother’s son, named Arnulf, desiring to possess by feudal and hereditary right, whether justly or unjustly, what his uncle had held. His patron in this matter was our advocate, Count Gyslebert, together with the more powerful men counted among the peers. There was a long dispute between this Arnulf and Abbot Rodulf. [Col. 0184D] Arnulf pressed the abbot with false but plausible claims and with the violence of the advocate, whose retainer he was. The abbot, being sufficiently learned in law, excluded him by legal arguments and true assertions, not only from the things which his uncle had appropriated from the brothers’ table, but even from the lawful fief [Col. 0185A] which he had possessed.

In short, the matter finally came to this: Arnulf relinquished the mill and cultivated land by the formal surrender of the festuca, and they were adjudged away from him before the peers; he retained what belonged to the office of steward. But the mill and land were adjudged to return to the brothers’ table after the death of the aforesaid wife, named Engelberga.

At that time the mill paid twenty-four *modii* of mixed grain by the Liège measure, one *modius* of wheat, two solidi, and four capons. [Note: [Col. 0185] “four capons … cultivated land” is missing in D.] Many persons were very frequently present at this dispute and settlement. We wished here to record the names of some necessary witnesses, so that after the death of the matron there might be no ambiguity concerning the mill and cultivated land restored to the brothers’ table.

These matters were transacted solemnly and publicly in the presence of Gyslebert, advocate and count, and Rodulf, abbot; with the following witnesses, peers of the church: Arnulf, former judge of the bishop of Metz; Everard, [Note: [Col. 0185] The remainder of this book is missing in D.] judge [Col. 0186A] of the abbot; Gontram of Alost; Walter of Kircheym; Guederic of Halmala; Ruthard surnamed Gimo; another Ruthard, reeve of our court; Arnulf, then alderman and the abbot’s cupbearer; Radulf the marshal; Ulric and Lietbert, chamberlains; another Ulric; Richolf; Adelard; Reyner of Miles; Reyner the grutarius; and more than a hundred townspeople, great and small.

This was in the year 1136 from the Incarnation of the Lord; the twenty-eighth year from Abbot Rodulf’s ordination; while Lothair, emperor from the land and race of the Saxons, reigned; while Peter Leo and Gregory the deacon, who after his consecration was called Innocent, [Note: [Col. 0185C] Innocent II.] contended for the papacy; while Stephen was bishop at Metz; Bruno II at Cologne; [Note: [Col. 0185C] He held office in 1132–1137.] Adalbero, formerly primicerius of Metz, at Trier; [Note: [Col. 0185C] 1131–1132.] and Adalbero II, of the same name, at Liège, [Note: [Col. 0185C] Adalbero II, 1136–1145.] elected and invested bishop after that primicerius, but not yet consecrated.

**HERE ENDS BOOK TWELVE; BOOK THIRTEEN BEGINS**

[Col. 0185]

[Col. 0185B] **1.** Since, in recounting the deeds of this Abbot Rodulf, occasion arose for us to mention how Alexander entered the episcopate of Liège, we consider that it will likewise not be unwelcome if we leave posterity a reliable account of his departure from the episcopate and the end of his life.

At Liège, the master of the schools at the church of Saint Martin had died. After his death, Bishop Alexander installed in the same office, for money, a certain young man named Theoderic—fairly well instructed in elementary scholarly learning, but not yet marked either by the dress or tonsure of clerical discipline. And although he had never previously held that or any other office in the city, the bishop placed him in that church without a canonry—that is, without a prebend.

When he was reproved for this and ought to have corrected it, he acted worse: for money, he likewise made him a canon. While he obstinately defended this case and gravely scandalized that church by it, he attacked more violently than the rest of his reprovers a canon of the same church, named Nicholas, so much so that he compelled him to appeal to the hearing of Lord Pope Innocent. [Col. 0185C]

There he was accused of simony by Nicholas himself. Summoned once and again at canonical intervals by the lord pope, he set out as though intending to go. But his consciousness of guilt delayed him in France; and when, despite sending to the lord pope distinguished envoys—the abbots, namely, of Stavelot and Lobbes [Note: [Col. 0186C] Leon of Lobbes; cf. Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, VI, 184. The *Annales Rodenses* confirm the same.] together with certain archdeacons—he could by no means obtain release from appearing for the hearing, he received a third canonical summons. Postponing it also, as he had the others, he incurred [Col. 0186B] the sentence of deposition at the Council of Pisa, with Lord Pope Innocent presiding, in the year 1135 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

When this dreadful news reached him, he fell into such bitterness of spirit that bodily illness immediately followed, so severe that, deprived of appetite for food and of the regimen prescribed for him, he was brought to his end. Yet, scarcely after making confession, receiving communion, and promising to adopt the life of regular canons at Mont Public near Liège, he finally breathed his last. [Note: [Col. 0186C] On the day before the Nones of July, according to Aegidius.] He received burial in the same place without episcopal obsequies (6 July). Such was the end of Alexander, formerly bishop of Liège.

**2.** Having set in order the matters which we had proposed to treat, no subject of that kind remains for writing; but the evils of our devastation, which we suffer daily, provide an abundant and exceedingly bitter cause for lamentation. [Col. 0186C] Lest their magnitude overwhelm a mind benumbed by idleness with its weight, and lest the stings of their bitterness drive it down even to the abyss of despair, the mind must be occupied with its customary exercise, so that bodily perceptions may have less room in sorrow. For fruitful occupations of the mind are accustomed even to lessen the bitter sufferings of the body. Therefore I am pleased to return to earlier matters and resume a subject for writing from those things which have been omitted.

**3.** When we were once rereading what was written there—that in the time of Lord Adventius, the glorious bishop of Metz, an inventory was made of the abbey of Saint Trudo [Note: [Col. 0186C] Above, I.3.]—and that it was stated how much spelt the brothers had for making bread, how much barley for beer, how many pigs for fat, how much salt, [Col. 0187A] and how much pulse, we were greatly surprised that they did not say whence these things came, and that they omitted what the brothers had for their *companium*, namely fish, eggs, and cheeses. No monastic communities live without these; nor did they state whether the brothers had any established provision for wine.

We were also greatly surprised, and still wonder, why they kept silent concerning the abbot’s table, since, according to the command of Saint Benedict, it is that table which must always be available for guests and pilgrims; and if, on some occasion—which is very rare—such persons are absent, however many brothers and whichever brothers the abbot wishes are to be called. Nor ought it to have been omitted how much belonged to the brothers’ clothing allowance, how much to the reception of guests, who are never absent from monasteries, how much to alms for the poor, [Col. 0187B] how much to maintaining the fabric of the church and supplying its lights, and from what source provision was to be made for sick brothers, whom the Rule commands to be treated more humanely and restored with meat.

Since monastic communities ought to have all these things and very many others, as we have said, we were greatly surprised that the describers of the abbey kept silent about them. For all these things cannot come from the grain alone which they listed. [Note: [Col. 0187] Everything up to this point is lacking in D.]

**4.** Therefore, wishing to set down more carefully the brothers’ prebend, established in antiquity, down to the desolation of the place caused by the quarrels of abbots and the many vicissitudes of wars, let us begin thus.

The daily bread of the brothers’ table weighed five Cologne marks: it was fine and white, made chiefly from spelt [Col. 0187C] and from sifted first flour. The boys’ bread weighed four marks but was of the same quality. Each brother’s portion of beer—beer, I say, such as no other monastic community possesses anywhere—was, between dinner and supper, one wine sextary. On Sunday, Tuesday, and Thursday, there was one sextary of wine among three brothers; on Saturday at the *mandatum*, among four.

But when the customs of Cluny came to us, whose observance of the *mandatum* is marked by much sobriety, we received one-sixth of a sextary of wine at dinner, and thereafter observed the *mandatum* according to Cluniac custom. Young brothers were never given wine unless the abbot or prior ordered it given to them, and even then more sparingly. On Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, if such a feast occurred, one sextary of wine was likewise given among three brothers.

The brothers also had pulse every day, prepared with fat on the days when it was eaten. [Note: [Col. 0187D] That is, with animal fat.] Likewise they had vegetables on three days in the week; but from the Assumption of Saint Mary every day until *Circumdederunt me*. When beef was eaten, the vegetables were abundantly seasoned with the fat of the meat. [Col. 0188A] The bowls both of pulse and of vegetables were large and well filled.

From the feast of Saint Remigius until the octave of Pentecost, the provost of Testebant gave fish every day between the two courses, namely pulse and vegetables: large pike, anchoraum [uncertain fish-name], salmon, or fresh herring. Of fresh herring, each brother received five; of *anchoraum*, a portion as broad as the palm of a man’s hand, with the thumb folded alongside it. The portions of pike and salmon were smaller, because the fish is more costly and more substantial. If other fish were supplied, suitable compensation was made for them.

But because there was always among us a constant and long-standing complaint concerning fish brought from Testebant—[Note: [Col. 0187] Testerbrant in 1*.] because it was either too salty or sometimes stinking [Col. 0188B] and rotten, and sometimes because, owing to winter, fish of any kind could not be obtained; and because the brothers were grievously afflicted with disgust by the daily use of one article—Abbot Theoderic and Rodulf, then prior, ordered substitutions. Fish was to be given whenever sound fish could be found and obtained; when this could not be done, it was to be exchanged for eggs fried in fat, for *artocreae*, or at times for cheese and eggs.

**5.** The provost of Hasbania, while the other provost was serving, gave supper every night: namely, four eggs for each brother, or half a cheese, or apples, or another fruit. Nor must it be forgotten that, if fasting days fell within this period or at any point in the year, the provost of Hasbania did not withhold the supper due; rather, he gave the dining brothers what could be eaten on that day. [Col. 0188C]

Moreover, from the feast of Saint Remigius to the octave of Pentecost, on every feast when the brothers were “in white,” the provost of Hasbania substituted for the pulse course a *jussellum*, [Note: [Col. 0187D] A little broth.] prepared with wine, eggs, and fat. He gave each brother a good portion of fresh fish and three *artocreae*, which by ancient right ought to contain five eggs and cheese, [Note: [Col. 0187D] Elsewhere, a food made of bread and meat.] without ever on this account reducing the portion from Testebant. [Note: [Col. 0187] Testerbrant in 1*.]

On the night of the feast of Saint Remigius and Saint Trudo, the same provost gave the brothers fresh [Note: [Col. 0187] “fresh … the same” is missing in D.] fish from the Meuse for supper. At that same supper, the brothers had one sextary of wine among four, even if on that very day they happened to have one among three at dinner. On the feast day of Saint Remigius and on the feast day of Saint Trudo, together with the brothers’ daily bread, there was given a *simila* weighing four marks between two persons.

The first dish on the table was what may be called *carpeia*: [Note: [Col. 0188D] Equivalent to *carpia*, French *charpie*; among Italians, *carpionare* means to season with pepper, vinegar, and other spices.] it was made from dried fish from Testebant, because it was shredded into small pieces and sprinkled with pepper together with finely chopped eggs. [Col. 0189A] The second dish, provided by the same provost of Hasbania, was fresh salmon boiled in water and peppered; the third was salmon of the same kind roasted and likewise peppered. Along with these came other roasted fish brought from the Meuse, which, by poetic license, we may call *roceae* [Note: [Col. 0189D] *Rutilus*, French *rose*.] and *bardi*. [Note: [Col. 0189D] Apparently the same as *barbus*, French *barbeau*.]

In addition, there were *pictantiae* [Note: [Col. 0189] *pietancias* in 1 and 1*.] between each two brothers: [Note: [Col. 0189D] A more sumptuous food portion, valued at one *picta*, i.e. a Poitevin coin.] some made from stuffed pike, others from salmon backs and their peppered eggs; finally came *artocreae*. In short, there was an abundance of many kinds of fish.

Although, in this fashion, the provost of Hasbania served together with the provost of Testebant at intervals of feasts, he nevertheless provided the bloodlet brothers with four eggs for breakfast [Note: [Col. 0189D] Equivalent to *jantaculum*, a meal by which the fast is broken before dinner.] and four for supper at all times, as well as meat in the infirmary, [Note: [Col. 0189D] The room of the sick.] provided it was available [Col. 0189B] in the court or larder; from there he took as much as was necessary. From the octave of Pentecost until the feast of Saint Remigius, the provost of Testebant ceased serving and the provost of Hasbania served every day.

**6.** On Sunday, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, each brother received bowls filled with good fish, in the quantity otherwise divided among three or two. Very frequently there were large portions of sturgeon; [Note: [Col. 0189D] *Siör*.] and, during the season when lampreys [Note: [Col. 0189D] Murena; French *lamproie*, *lamprete*.] were customary, one was shared among three. Moreover, the large fish called *balena* was frequently supplied in abundance.

On Tuesday, Thursday [Note: [Col. 0189] “Friday” in D.] and Saturday during the period described above, each brother received at dinner, between the pulse and vegetable courses, five eggs and half a cheese; for supper, four eggs or half a cheese. [Col. 0189C] Consequently, nothing was withheld from the bloodlet brothers on those three days from the eggs mentioned above. These same bloodlet brothers also received a quarter of a sextary of wine on three days for their bloodletting, although on some of those days they had one-third from the common entitlement at dinner.

On Rogation Days, each brother had at table a cake with his portion of fish. On Palm Sunday, pulse was replaced with ground beans; the same was done at the Lord’s Supper and on Holy Saturday. During the four days of Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost, they had at dinner two portions of fish, one from Testebant and another from Hasbania; and at supper on the first day, a cake with a little arm-shaped bread, [Note: [Col. 0190D] Equivalent to *bracellus*, German *Bretzel*.] though smaller than on Rogation Days.

From Easter until the octave of Pentecost, on every day when the brothers [Col. 0189D] were “in white,” the provost of Hasbania gave a *jussellum* and a portion of fish in addition to that from Testebant, and a *tanacetum* made with five eggs; or, in place of the *tanacetum*, a leek broth [Note: [Col. 0190D] *Poirata*, *porrecta*: a little broth made from leeks.] well prepared with eggs and fat. [Col. 0190A] From the octave of Pentecost onward, *artocreae* were given in its place. [Note: [Col. 0189] “in its place” missing in 1*.]
