The bread given to those serving in the abbot’s household, those serving in the court, and all arriving guests was taken from the common supply in the brothers’ cellar; [Note: [Col. 0189] “in” in 1*.] so also beer and wine, through the hands of the reeve responsible for the court. The marshal distributed fodder and feed for horses from the barn and granary, both to household members and to guests; for the brothers’ cellarer received and dispensed only those things that belonged to the brothers.

The abbot had no separate provision from the grain, beer, or wine, apart from the rents of certain villages, churches, and mills. From these he provided for his own table in his household, for those serving him, and for guests, both humble and great; for three annual services owed [Col. 0190B] to the bishop of Metz, whose redemption was six marks; and for the maintenance of the cloister buildings.

**7.** Each brother had annually for his clothing one new fur garment, two new woollen shirts, [Note: [Col. 0190D] A woollen undershirt or shirt.] new boots, four new leg-coverings [Note: [Col. 0190D] A covering for the legs.] for night and day, a large allowance for anointing themselves, and, between two occasions, eight foot-coverings, [Note: [Col. 0190D] Covering for the feet.] a cowl and tunic, breeches and hose, and the other things whenever and as often as they needed them.

The sources of these things and of the others mentioned above were the villages and churches which we shall name here. In Testrebant, in the village of Alburch, whatever we appear to hold, together with its church and all appurtenances of that estate. In the village [Note: [Col. 0189] The remainder, down to the words “of the same currency,” is lacking in D.] of Guimala, together with the church of Pirges, whatever we appear to possess there belongs to the rights of that estate. Likewise, in the village of [Col. 0190C] Pelte, the village of Guebechem, and the village of Hales, with their churches and the appurtenances of their respective estates.

The village of Mergueles, with its church and the church in the village of Saint Trudo, and with everything that we appear to possess there, within and without, together with its appurtenances. The village of Stades, with its church and what we appear to possess in Halmala. The church of Halles and the village of Meres, with the appurtenances of its estate. The church of Lare, with its village and many scattered parcels belonging to its estate.

At Masesele [Note: [Col. 0190D] Mazenzele, not far from Aalst.] a small village and church, from which we have scarcely ever received anything good. In the village of Provin, whatever we appear to possess there; likewise in the village of Hallei. At Kircheym, half the church and what we possess in the village. The church of Bovinges [Note: [Col. 0190D] Perhaps Bouvines?] and the village of Burlos, with the appurtenances [Col. 0190D] belonging to its estate. At Alost and Brustemia, whatever we appear to possess in them. At Orel and Gemmapia, what we possess there. At Sesninc, the church and what we possess in the village. The church of Corbeche and the church [Col. 0191A] of Engelmunthove. [Note: [Col. 0191D] Engelshoven in the vicinity of Saint-Trond.]

Beyond the Moselle, the church of Pumirs and the church of Bredal, together with the vineyards and allodial lands which we possess in those villages, and the properties which supplied the provost on his journey there, from which came the wine given to the brothers. In the territory of Antwerp, near the village of Mechele, an estate that paid [Note: [Col. 0191] “supplied” in 1*.] twenty-five solidi of Antwerp currency every year. In the district called Rin, not far from Antwerp, another estate paying fifteen solidi in the same currency.

8. We have also learned from our elders that, when our church flourished in peace, wealth, and religious observance, the large estate of Eltae [Note: [Col. 0191D] Elsen or Elsloo on the right bank of the Meuse.] and its church had belonged to us. It lies not far from Maastricht, above the Meuse. For many years the revenue of the altar at the tomb of blessed Trudo was so great and so regular [Col. 0191B] that, even if there had been nothing else, it alone could have sufficed for the needs of the whole church. Yet through the presumptuous audacity and rash presumption of abbots, much was taken from the brethren’s resources by grants of benefices, and from the treasury everything that pertained to the lighting and building of the monastery. Likewise, they granted as benefices at their pleasure the rents and estates which were given, or had been given, for the dead or for the brethren’s alms. At that time the alms for the poor were so utterly destroyed that what had belonged to them was not even left in memory.

Moreover, in the provostship of Testebrant our church lost through the negligence of abbots eight chapels, which supplied the brethren’s stipends. As evils increased through the quarrels of abbots and the disturbances of monks, [Col. 0191C] much of the brethren’s prebend perished through negligence, much was bestowed in benefices, and much was usurped by stewards through deceit. Two [Note: [Col. 0191] The following material, down to “frequent raids,” is absent in D.] miles not far from Metz lies an estate called Foncey, whose church was ours; that church, namely, was seized and retained by the lord whose estate it was at the time of the dissension concerning our abbey. Likewise, at the same time a very fruitful part of our estate of Sesninc was seized and is still held; Halley, once part of the brethren’s prebend, was given as a benefice.

In our town more houses and small enclosures, rents, and other servile dues are held in benefice than the provost now has in his own hand; all of these belonged to the brethren’s prebend. Moreover, in other manors, and in this one likewise, the brethren’s cultivated lands have nonetheless been curtailed [Note: [Col. 0191D] Diminished.] and granted as benefices, and mills have been granted either as benefices or as burdensome hereditary tenures. Of the allod which belonged to the manor of Guebecheym, one part has been granted as a benefice; another part, very extensive and long, has been seized by the surrounding freemen and is still held—thus through the negligence and treachery of the advocates. [Col. 0192A] But far more has been lost in the estate of Hales. For, among the lands belonging to Guebecheym and Hales, including fields, woods, and useful marshland, more than seventy holdings have been alienated from the church. At Brustemia, the entire rent that belonged to the brethren’s prebend. At Stades, a large part granted as a benefice; and at Kircheym, of the cultivated land.

9. What shall I say of the tithes, when almost all have either been granted under ruinous agreements or assigned as useless benefices to certain servants in return for work in the smithy? The very extensive possession of many meadows has been diminished, with little left to us. The estate near Machele, which paid twenty-five shillings in Antwerp currency, was sold without any recovery and without any exchange. That at Masesele is held [Col. 0192B] by a certain tyrant, though there is good hope of recovering it.

Our church will never overcome the lamentable losses caused by cleared forests. To say nothing of Peltae, Guimala, Guebecheym, and Halla, where they seem still to survive only very sparsely and as low growth, Meruguelges, Mecerin, and Stades possessed forests exceedingly dense and full of large trees. So also Mere and Lare, Kircheym, Burlo, Villeyr [Note: [Col. 0192D] Villers, of which name several villages exist near Liège.]; from the aforesaid forests came sufficient fencing [Note: [Col. 0192D] Hedges.] for their manors, timber for construction both in the monastery and in the cloister, and material for the lordly buildings in the estates and for their repair.

From them also came pork, which abundantly [Col. 0192C] sufficed throughout the year for the food and fat supplies of the abbot’s household, for guests, for the infirmary, and for the cellarer. All these things, once obtained freely, are now bought at a price—or we go without them. We once saw so great an annual surplus that Abbot Rodulf sent to Bishop Adalbero of Metz, at Aachen, to the emperor’s court, a covered wagon loaded with dried meats during Pentecost days. Firewood likewise came freely and in sufficient quantity for the abbot’s household, the brethren’s kitchen, guests, the bakehouse, the brewery, and the brethren’s washers—things which now must be bought at great cost from what we ought to eat or drink. Fodder for livestock was also available from the lordly lands in the estates; it brought great advantage in meat and cheese to the provosts and the abbot. Now it cannot be obtained because of the fraudulent dispersals by stewards, the violent nighttime exactions of advocates, and the frequent raids of robbers.

10. Besides this, great and irrecoverable [Note: [Col. 0191] “irreparable,” 1*.] loss has grown in these days for the church. For its household, greatly reduced today through the oppression [Col. 0193A] of advocates and the upheavals of wars, was once very extensive and spread far and wide. A very large part of it lived under this law: a man paid twelve pence yearly as the rent of his head; a woman, six; some of another legal condition, two pence; some, four.

Whenever a man of these conditions died, whether under our jurisdiction or another’s, if he had not yet married, he owed the church, as though to his heir, whatever remained to him of all his property. If he had married, but not to his proper mate—that is, to a woman who was not a handmaid of our church—he owed half his property. The same was true of a woman, except that, whatever husband she had borne children by, she gave the church only what appeared best among all her movable goods. If a man [Col. 0193B] was married to his proper mate, he gave the best of his clothing. If he possessed rent-paying and servile land, he gave the provosts at the manor an ox from the land, and from his person either another ox or the best thing he possessed. The same was done if riding-horses remained.

This revenue was once plentiful and very advantageous to the provosts and the abbot of our church, before our household was diminished by the floods of war, the attacks of advocates, the unfaithfulness of stewards, and our own exile, and before the property of those who remained was impoverished. But the masters of the head-rent, partly consenting and partly urging on account of wives whom they had married from the class subject to this law, [Col. 0194A] gradually carried some men to the point—and drew countless others after them—of wishing to reduce the rent of twelve pence to one, and all their other obligations after their death to twelve pence. Moreover, wherever they die under another jurisdiction, all that is owed to us apart from twelve pence is denied.

Those, however, who acknowledge the obligations and say that they wish to pay, having shared with the stewards a scheme of fraud and deceit, after someone’s death produce some utterly worthless, torn garment, or a lame sheep or a sickly sow; and, having received an oath that the deceased possessed nothing better, they swear—indeed, perjure themselves—without any fear of God, if allowed to do so; or the stewards [Col. 0194B] remit the matter to them, so that they depart without having sworn. Thus, in these and many other ways, the profit of the old advantage has been removed.

The revenue of the altar at blessed Trudo’s tomb, once beyond estimation, and from which the church formerly made good all its losses, now scarcely provides enough for the church to maintain its due lighting. Therefore, since so many hardships and deficiencies converge at once, let no one be surprised if the prebend within has been diminished, when the outward resources have been reduced in this way, and much more than I have said.

# FOUR LETTERS OF RODULF, ABBOT OF SAINT-TRUDO

[Col. 0193]

## I. LETTER [Note: [Col. 0193] This and all the following material are absent in D.] SENT FROM THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PANTALEON TO RODULF, ABBOT OF SAINT-TRUDO

[Col. 0193C]

To the most reverend father, lord RODULF [Note: [Col. 0193] R., 1 and 1*.], by God’s grace abbot: SIBERT [Note: [Col. 0193] S., 1 and 1*.], may you enjoy the peace above after the hardships of this life.

If it were within my power to come into the presence of your fatherhood, no roughness of the journey would stand in my way, no adversity in household affairs would call me back. For true love, which knows no measure, so penetrates my mind with longing for you that it compels me to remember how generous you once proved toward me [Note: [Col. 0193] When Rodulf was abbot of Saint Pantaleon; this letter therefore was plainly written after 1123. Cf. XII, 1.], and how, in return, I have not merely failed to respond in any way, but have until now been silent even in sending a greeting back. This is so far as human [Col. 0193D] service is concerned; otherwise, he who alone searches all things knows better with what devotion and how earnestly I include you in my private prayer.

There are certain accusations of detractors—or, more truly, slanderous speeches, dearest father—which trouble us most sharply. Against them the humility of the whole congregation urgently seeks the shield of your defense. They are as follows. A certain little boy was once offered to us by his parents; in their devotion, along with the boy they offered as much of their property as they wished. A man richer in possessions, but poorer and more avaricious in will, saw this and envied it; he immediately asked that his own son also be received.

Much time was spent in asking and resisting, because the parents wished to force the same boy upon us naked, by violence. At last, when his father was approached privately and asked to contribute something to the church from the goods God had granted him, he began to rage, saying that he did not wish to incur simony. Seized by this fury, he assailed us with many wrongs; he filled marketplaces and streets with agitation, stirred up citizens and ecclesiastical [Col. 0194D] persons, and declared that what we are commanded to give freely is, in our hands, available for a price.

“For,” he says, “if an ordinary man with money is readily admitted, while a nobler man who comes simply is repelled by many barriers of excuse, it is plain enough that not the person but the money is sought. [Col. 0195A] And when the man who was first rejected has brought a bag of money and obtained the entrance formerly refused, who does not see how much simony works and prevails here?”

Because he was a well-known townsman, this accusation disturbed us greatly. At last, when we were again approached by clergy and laity, we answered what we had said before: that it was fitting and just, and not contrary to canonical strictness, that one wishing to join himself, or one of his own, to a church should, if he had the means, contribute to the uses of that church.

But they say: “Monasteries were established for this purpose: that anyone wishing to renounce the world ought to be permitted to enter freely, and poverty or lack of any possession should not be an obstacle, because those whom God joins and associates he fills and satisfies with every good thing.”

These and many other objections are brought against us. We ask you to weigh them all in an even balance, and to write back plainly and clearly how we may rationally and canonically meet the slanderers of our order, and to explain how we ought to stand firm, without stumbling, amid this outcry. Whatever you decide in this matter shall remain among us inviolable, as though confirmed by the Apostolic See.

### Little Preface to the Reply

The chief purpose of the following little work is this: that this rich man, of whom there will be discussion, may abandon in the middle of the matter his parsimony and avarice, because these amount to idolatry. If he wishes his son to be received, let him allow to follow him to the church what is due to the son from his property. The church, however, must guard itself against every evil covetousness for his goods, because of simony, which expels sellers [Col. 0195C] and buyers from the church. Whether the rich man’s son comes empty or full-handed, if the church wishes to receive him, let it receive him; if it does not wish to do so, let it let him go: the decision lies within its discretion. By sound arguments and truthful authorities it will be proved to the rich man that a portion of his property, which ought to have come to his son in the world, ought justly and piously to follow him to the church to which he is offered. [Note: [Col. 0195] “Here ends,” added by 1*.]

## II. RODULF THE ABBOT’S REPLY TO THE LETTER SENT TO HIM FROM THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PANTALEON [Note: [Col. 0195] “from the monastery of Saint Pantaleon” absent in 1*.]

RODULF, by the grace of God and of Saint Trudo what he is, to Sibert, once my beloved son and now my dearest brother, prior in the monastery of Saint Pantaleon, and to all dwelling with him—both our lords and our brethren—salvation of soul and body in all devotion [Col. 0195D] and prayer.

We received your messenger as an angel of the Lord; we read your letter reverently as though it were sacred Scripture, grieving that we hear and see you so seldom through your letters and messengers. Concerning the matter on which your humility has deigned to consult our littleness, we had almost withdrawn our hand from writing, since there is no one who summons you to a hearing or draws you into judgment, and since sacred Scripture and apostolic commands on this matter are no less known to you [Col. 0196A] than to us.

Only the insolent talkativeness of meddlesome men disturbs your tender ears—men accustomed to see a speck in another’s eye while failing to notice the beam in their own, and to strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. Such persons should rather be passed over with silent derision than drawn out for long by the pleasing rope of contention. Yet, lest you should seem burdened by our total silence and to have run to us in vain, we shall perhaps discharge the matter in briefer speech than you would wish, for the sake of persons unworthy even of this reply, much less of the authority of a reply.

Come, then: a wealthy man, but miserly and avaricious, wishes to thrust his son upon you without any kind of offering, concealing the idol of his parsimony [Col. 0196B] and avarice beneath the false appearance of virtue—namely, lest he appear to commit simony through his offering. May God deliver you from the unjust and deceitful man! Wretched man, blinded by avarice, he does not see how gravely, while falsely claiming to avoid simony, he falls into idolatry through the worship of his parsimony and avarice; for avarice is the worship of idols. Nor does he wish to see how great an injury and false charge he wishes to bring against God and the church to which he wishes to entrust his son.

For that portion which ought to have fallen to the son in the world ought, by the law of God and of men, to follow him to the church to which he wishes to entrust him to God. To demand and wish to receive what is just is not simony at all; rather, it is robbery and avarice to retain what one ought justly to give.

[Col. 0196C] Blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Ten Strings of the Heart* [Note: [Col. 0195] Sermon 9, *On the Ten Strings*, ch. 20; Works, Venice edition, V, 62.]:

> “Do not increase your money under the appearance of piety.”

And not far afterward:

> “Men do indeed lie. Avarice is evil; they wish to cloak and whitewash it under the name of piety, so that they may seem to save what they save through avarice, as though they were saving it for their children. For, that you may know that this often happens, someone is said to ask: ‘Why does he not give alms?’ ‘Because he is saving for his children.’ It happens that he loses one child. If he was saving for his children, let him send that child’s share after him. Why does he hold it in his purse and leave that child out of his mind? Give him back what is his; give him what you were keeping for him. ‘He is dead,’ he says. But he has gone before you to God; let his share be given to the poor. [Note: [Col. 0195] Augustine reads: “is owed.”]
>
> It is owed to him to whom he has gone; it is owed to Christ, [Col. 0196D] for he has gone to Christ. And he himself said: “Whoever has done it to one of the least of these has done it to me; and whoever has not done it to one of the least of these has not done it to me” (Matt. 25:40).”

Let us consider whether this judgment of blessed Augustine can fittingly be applied to our wealthy miser. He wishes to cloak and whitewash himself under the name of piety, appearing to save what he saves through avarice on account of simony—or, as Augustine has it, on account of children. If he wishes to avoid simony and cast off avarice, let him do justice; for simony and avarice cannot coexist with justice. But what justice do we ask him to do, so that he may flee simony and avarice? Let him divide equally among his children what, allegedly for his children or in order to avoid simony, he retains and keeps. But he wishes to send one child away from himself and give him to God and holy Church. This is certainly good; but it is likewise good and just that he send that child’s portion after him or with him. Yet I believe that he wishes to send him out of the world for this very purpose: to retain the child’s portion in his purse. That, certainly, is neither good nor just, but wicked robbery, avarice, and sacrilege.

For, once he has offered the son to God, it is sacrilege to retain for himself the portion due to him. For he now belongs to the one to whom he has become given, and the portion due to him belongs to that one as well. [Col. 0197B] The sacrilegious man, therefore, despoils God and holy Church when he takes from one who belongs to God and holy Church those things which are owed by right. Let him therefore give him what is his; let him give back what he was keeping for him. “But he is dead,” he says. Certainly, he is dead to the world, but he lives to God. Let his portion be given to the poor of Christ and to the Church. It is owed to those to whom he has gone; it is owed to Christ, for he has gone to Christ.

Let our noisy, moneyed miser now fill marketplaces and streets and stir citizens and ecclesiastical persons. Wherever he turns, if after the offering of his son he retains what is owed to him, he will be an idolater and a sacrilegious man: an idolater because of avarice, sacrilegious because he robs God and holy Church.

Blessed Benedict agrees with blessed Augustine’s judgment in his teaching on the discipline of receiving brethren [Col. 0197C] and concerning the sons of nobles or poor persons [Note: [Col. 0197D] Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 59.]:

> “If the person received has any property, he should either first distribute it to the poor or, by making a solemn gift, bestow it on the monastery, reserving nothing at all for himself.”

A cruel father! He wishes neither himself to distribute to the poor in the street the goods which ought to fall to his son, nor to give them to Christ’s poor in the church, but to reserve all for himself. Indeed, when the brethren approached him privately and piously advised him to contribute something to the church from the goods God had granted him, he began to rage, saying that he did not wish to incur simony. Saint Benedict asks that a donation to the monastery be made, not secretly, but solemnly; this wretched man, seized by the Furies, calls it simony.

Again, in his teaching concerning the sons of nobles or poor persons [Note: [Col. 0197D] Ibid.]:

> “If they wish to offer anything to the monastery as alms for their own spiritual benefit, let them make a donation to the monastery from the goods that they wish to give.”

Perhaps he hears this and rejoices because Saint Benedict leaves it to his will. Yet certainly the holy man would have placed this in no one’s will unless he knew that it ought to be done, as something holy, just, and pious. Now, because what is holy, just, and pious cannot enter this man’s will, let him keep his possessions to his own destruction. Does he wish his son to be received empty-handed? Then let him arrange that he belongs to the number of those concerning whom blessed Benedict writes [Note: [Col. 0198D] Ibid.]:

> “But those who have absolutely nothing should simply make their request and, with the offering, offer their son before witnesses.” [Col. 0198A]

But now, since we have once begun to speak with our lords and dearest brethren, our heart, enlarged by great affection toward you, compels us to overstep the limits of our intended subject. We had proposed to make our discourse shorter, but the force of love draws it out. Let us then say something which our wealthy miser may be willing to hear, so that he may bear more calmly what he does not wish to hear.

Admissions from churches and into churches, of persons mature and immature alike, ought certainly all to be made freely, because of the command: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10:8), and because the Lord Jesus drives all sellers and buyers [Col. 0198B] from the temple. Since we know and gladly hear these things, we should not fail to know this also: such admissions ought especially to have two considerations—first, that the diminished number of those serving God in churches may be increased by those received; secondly, that the burden of God’s service may become more tolerable.

If the son of this wealthy miser is not needed for these purposes, because your number is sufficient and there is no deficiency in God’s service, we do not see why the church should be burdened with what is superfluous and unnecessary. What is superfluous should be cut off; what is unnecessary should not be taken on. Depart, therefore, brethren; depart from such a man, and do not touch his uncleanness, lest you seem to share in idolatry through his avarice and incur, through the same stigma, the charge of simony.

Just as it belongs to you to demand nothing from him or from any other person for such a matter, so it belonged to him—if he were a man of God and not of Mammon—to make, along with his son, an offering to the church from the portion of inheritance that ought to fall to the son, a church which ought thereafter to feed and clothe him. [Col. 0198C] But as he does not wish to do this, and you cannot and ought not compel him, but only advise him piously, so likewise, if you do not wish to receive his son, he cannot and ought not force you to do so.

Now I turn to you, wealthy miser; now I turn to you. I summon you: answer. Tell me: what spirit leads you, a good spirit or an evil one, when you wish to thrust your son into a monastery empty and naked though he is burdened with possessions at home? I ask this because the spirits of such men must be tested to see whether they are from God. Yet I do not doubt that you must answer, “A good spirit”; nor should you doubt that I shall affirm, “An evil one.” Hear how I prove it.

The good Spirit of the Lord never takes from anyone goods due to him, counsels avarice to no one, and never tears a father from affection for his son on account of property; rather, by generosity of hand and heart he binds and joins them together. But you, through the evil spirit of idolatry—which is avarice—take from your son the things due to him, things which he ought to offer with himself in the monastery to Christ’s poor who serve God there. Behold the evil spirit which leads you; and because you are proved to be led by an evil [Col. 0199A] spirit, you are rightly condemned.

I do not know whether you make a right offering; this I know, that you make an unjust division, because with an avaricious hand you withhold from your son, from the Church, and from God what belongs to your son and through him ought to belong to the Church and God. Thus, through this unjust division, you have also rendered your offering of your son unacceptable. Blessed Augustine says in the aforementioned book *On the Ten Strings of the Heart*: “Whatever you say, you owe to the dead what you were keeping for the living.” Therefore, according to the teaching of this blessed man, if you owe to one who is dead what you were keeping for him alive, much more justly do you owe to one dead to the world and living to God, with Christ’s poor in the monastery, those things which you were keeping for him while he lived mortally in this mortal world. But your avaricious hand will not allow it. This is what I say: the evil spirit of avarice leads you.

[Col. 0199B] Blessed Augustine again cries out against you in the same book; he cries out and says [Note: [Col. 0199D] Ibid., Works V, 63.]:

> “Surely, to whom do you entrust the things which you keep here and will not send after your son? You entrust to your agents the share of him who has gone before, and do not entrust it to Christ, to whom he has gone before?”

And a little earlier:

> “It will be kept here, where it can perish, and not sent there, where Christ is its guardian. Is your own steward more trustworthy to you, and Christ less trustworthy? See, brethren, that what men say is a lie: ‘I save for my children.’ It is a lie, my brethren, it is a lie; men are avaricious.”

What can you say against these things, wealthy miser? Though wealthy, you are a liar; though rich in money, you are avaricious. Why do you accuse God’s servants of simony because, in privately approaching you, they wished to strip you of avarice and, after avarice, of idolatry, requiring nothing from you but what justice dictates and mercy demands—as you refused to hear from blessed Augustine’s judgment and Saint Benedict’s Rule?

Whoever is of God hears God’s words; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God. Most justly, then, the gate of the monastery is shut against you by these two strongest barriers. Unjust censor, you dare also to pronounce unjust judgments concerning the institutions of monasteries. Profane pope, you promulgate indiscriminate decrees.

“You say, ‘Monasteries were established so that whoever wishes to renounce the world may freely enter.’” You are mistaken. Why, then, would blessed Benedict command those who seek admission to be received with such difficulty, tested with such delay, and instructed with such diligence, if all who come ought freely [Col. 0199D] to enter? Certainly, not so that all who seek admission may enter freely, but so that those whose spirits have been tested and found to be from God may be received according to the Rule. If your principle stood, your request would already have been granted, because it would not have been proved that the spirit of avarice was stirring you; rather, it would be thought that the Spirit of God was moving you.

And, to pass over other matters, the royal granaries themselves could not provide stipends for the intolerable multitude of people who would every day thrust themselves in for their varying needs and indiscriminate desires. But you say: [Col. 0200A] “Those whom God joins and associates he fills and satisfies with every good thing.” It is indeed true that those whom God joins and associates are so filled—not by empty confidence and foolish rashness. And in whose hands, do you say, does he fill and satisfy them? In the hands of idlers who expect food and clothing to fall to them from heaven? Certainly not; but in the hands of his stewards, who watch and work diligently night and day for the number entrusted to them.

Of idlers it is written: “Every idler is always in want” (Prov. 21:25). Therefore such people as yours are never satisfied with every good thing. Of those who preside: “He who presides, with diligence” (Rom. 12:8). Of those who do not work: “Whoever will not work shall not eat” (2 Thess. 3:10). And of such persons this too is written: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. 4:7).

[Col. 0200B] A person ought not, through foolish rashness and empty idleness, to tempt the Lord his God while he still has something to do diligently for his needs by rational counsel. Abraham is recorded to have done this when he said that his wife Sarah was his sister, lest he be killed by a king inflamed toward her by her excessive beauty. Likewise the holy patriarch Jacob, although through many divine benefits he had frequently experienced God’s love and protection toward him, saw that the land of Canaan was being pressed by famine and that it would reach even himself unless he [Note: [Col. 0199] “himself,” 1*.] made provision. So, lest he seem to tempt God, he did not languish in idle torpor, nor did he rashly expect God, his lover and protector, to rain grain from heaven for him—as he later did manna for the children of Israel in the wilderness. Rather, like a prudent man who knew well how to govern his household, [Col. 0200C] he sent his sons with money into Egypt, where he had heard grain was sold, and once and twice had brought from there as much as he knew his household needed.

When the apostle Philip saw the immense multitude of five thousand persons and had [Note: [Col. 0199] “having,” 1*.] only five barley loaves and two fish for refreshing them, he lacked reason and counsel in this matter, was astonished, and, as though despairing not of divine but of human power, said: “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not suffice for them, for each to receive a little” (John 6:7). Therefore the hand of the Lord’s blessing necessarily intervened, so that what a mere human being could not accomplish through reason or counsel, God omnipotent made possible by the powerful miracle of his strength, [Col. 0200D] for the increase of faith in that people.

Paul, the vessel of election, who knew that he had been chosen to bear the Lord’s name before Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel, and who knew that God cannot lie—who does not know by how many means, acts, and turnings he acted in order not to be handed over to the Jews for execution, and by what subtle counsel and reasoning he appealed to Caesar? A person ought rationally and without tempting God to flee faithfully to divine help only when the task immediately at hand exceeds human reason and counsel.

We have briefly run through these things so that, contrary to our censor’s opinion, all and sundry may not freely enter monasteries and, idling in sluggish leisure, expect God to feed them from heaven with every good thing. Rather, those who appear to govern monasteries should admit as many and such persons as they consider necessary, trusting themselves to God’s providence, but never being without diligence for themselves and their charges. [Col. 0201A]

Thus, those of old who founded monasteries observed by rational judgment that they should establish in them no greater number than they saw could be supplied with the allotted food and clothing. Of this we have many examples daily before our eyes, and we read that blessed Maurus, Saint Benedict’s disciple, did this [Note: [Col. 0201D] Cf. Faustus, *Life of Saint Maurus*, ch. 9, in *Acts of the Saints*, January I, 1049.]. If any necessities remained in surplus, they were for the poor, for guests—who are never absent from monasteries—and for various occurrences within and without. [Col. 0201B]

If we still need witnesses, we shall bring forward one who will suffice for thousands: our Lord Jesus Christ, the way of truth, the mirror and enigma of all goodness. Although no need can befall him and he is all-sufficient in omnipotence, he nevertheless chose to have a fixed number of disciples: seventy-two from the whole world on one side, and twelve apostles on the other; they were not thrust upon him by anyone, but chosen by himself. Though he could have ensured that they never hungered or thirsted, but always abounded in every good thing, he did not choose to do so. Instead, from what was sent to him by devout men and women, and from what those who followed him ministered to him, he arranged through his steward [Col. 0201C] to provide their stipends and to distribute what could remain to the poor and needy.

In this he left his disciples who came after him [Note: [Col. 0201] Omitted in 1*.] clear and reliable instruction: that receiving blessings and offerings from devout men and women in the world was not simony but justice, piety, and mercy; and that those who offered them committed not simony but justice, piety, and mercy.

Do you wish to be holier than the parents of the Lord Jesus? Although nothing holier could be offered to God in the Temple, neither in heaven nor on earth nor under the earth, than their own Son, the Son of God, they nevertheless did not wish to offer him without sacrifices and gifts. Anna, mother of Saint Samuel, did likewise: through the priest Eli she offered that same son to God with sacrifices and gifts. [Col. 0201D] Why, then, do you not do likewise, instructed by such examples? These are divine commands, including: “You shall not appear before me empty-handed” (Exod. 25:15).

But perhaps you say to me: “You ought to demand nothing.” And I say to you: You ought to withhold nothing. I do not sin if I ask from you what you justly owe me; rather, you sin if you deny me what [Col. 0202A] you justly owe. That you owe it justly has been sufficiently proved above.

The holy and glorious virgin Lucy, about to leave the world and go to God through martyrdom, left us a trustworthy memorial concerning the matter before us. She was very wealthy, and because of her tender age her property was being kept for her by her mother. Although she could, crowned with the glory and honor of martyrdom, be offered very acceptably to God, she nevertheless did not wish this to happen unless her property either went before her or accompanied her. She therefore said to her mother:

> “All that you were going to give me as I went to the author of my corruption, a mortal man, give to me as I go to the maker of my integrity, the Lord Jesus Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0201D] *Life of Saint Lucy*, in Surius, *Acts of the Saints*, VI, 892.]

The holy daughter would not have demanded this from her mother unless she knew it to be just and pious. For it is just and pious that the wealth of one who goes to God should precede or accompany that person in Christ’s poor. [Col. 0202B]

But why do we bring forward examples concerning women, as though we did not have similar examples concerning men, or as though parents alone ought to do this for their children and children not also for their parents? Certainly, what parents owe their children in this matter, children also owe their parents.

Blessed Lawrence had sent before him to God by martyrdom his pious father, Saint Sixtus; Lawrence himself was to follow after three days by martyrdom no less great. Although the sacrifice of their bodies, harshly slain, could have sufficed abundantly for the offering of both before God, he nevertheless wished the property which his pious father had left him, like a good son, to follow his father and go before himself, so that they might appear more glorious in the Lord’s sight. He therefore did not leave it [Col. 0202C] to his relatives or distribute it among his dependants, but scattered it and gave it to the poor; and therefore his righteousness remains for ever and ever. [Note: [Col. 0202D] *Acts of Saint Lawrence*, in *Acts of the Saints*, August II, 518.]

But if holy martyrs do this, though they have already washed away all their sins in their own blood, what do you, a sinful man, intend? You wish to offer your son to God in such a way that, sacrilegiously, you withhold from him what you owed to God in your son. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.

Even now let us take refuge in him whose words and deeds are the highest instruction for living perfectly. To one who asked, “What shall I do that I may obtain eternal life?” the Lord Jesus replied: “You know the commandments: Do not commit adultery; do not kill; do not steal; do not bear false witness; do not defraud; honor your father and your mother.” But he answered and said [Col. 0202D] to him: “Master, I have kept all these things from my youth.” And Jesus, looking upon him, loved him and said to him: “One thing is lacking to you: go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Mark 10:17–21).

In these words of the Lord we understand that whoever wishes to follow him perfectly must first distribute the possessions he has to the poor. But you say to me [Col. 0203A]: “I distribute the possessions I have to the poor and fulfill the commandment, so that at least in this way I may finally have an excuse for contributing nothing to the monastery.” And I say: You speak well when you say, “I give my possessions to the poor.” Therefore give the possessions you have to whatever poor persons you choose; but let the possessions that are your son’s go with him to the monastery, where you entrust him among Christ’s poor so that he may follow the Lord.

Again you say: “They are not poor, but abound in every necessity.” And I say: This is what the Lord says: “My servants shall eat, and you shall hunger” (Isaiah 65:13). Yet they truly are poor, and far poorer than those who wander through villages and run about the streets, to whom, in order to stir my indignation, you falsely say that you will distribute your goods. For how can any persons [Col. 0203B] be poorer than those dwelling in monasteries, who, for the Lord’s name, have deprived themselves both of power over their whole bodies, of the inclination of their whole minds, and of ownership of all their goods—such as you will find nowhere outside these communities? Those in the world are poor unwillingly; these in monasteries willingly. Indeed, the former are richer than these even in this respect: they feed their tongues, ears, and eyes, as often and as much as they please, upon various things according to their liking. The latter are poorer in this respect, because these things are not permitted them: they do not dare freely to drink in with their eyes even the heaven itself, common to every creature, nor the very air.

Therefore those rightly act, and fulfill the Lord’s commandment more abundantly, who give their goods to such poor persons, who are not only poorer than the poor but daily minister also to other [Col. 0203C] poor persons, pilgrims, and guests. There is great difference between poor persons and poor persons, as the examples of certain saints teach us, who, passing over some, devoted themselves with greater care to others. For, as we said a little above, there are unwilling poor and also willing poor. The unwilling poor rejoice in possessing as their own the few things that they have; and concerning the goods and riches which they do not possess, they enrich and burden themselves daily with unceasing desire. The willing poor, however, in imitation of Christ’s disciples, leave all their possessions, relinquishing even the desire to possess; and, following Christ’s footsteps, they betake themselves to monasteries of saints, in which, as though in prisons, they condemn themselves for the Lord’s name under strict custody.

They have nothing [Col. 0203D] of their own and do not wish to have anything, since they are pleased that it is not even permitted them to say of any thing, “It is mine,” but rather, because of common ownership, “It is ours.” Such men live from the offerings of the faithful, who at some time have given themselves, their goods, or their children to monasteries; and night and day, with watchful diligence, they serve God for the salvation of all the living and the dead. For the sake of such poor persons the Lord will say to their benefactors at the Last Judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me to drink; I was naked and you covered [Col. 0204A] me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matthew 25:34).

But to you and those like you—may God avert it through amendment of life—it will be said terribly: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me to eat; I was thirsty and you did not give me to drink; I was naked and you did not cover me; I was in prison, and you did not come to me” (ibid., vv. 41, 44). The holy women who went up from Galilee with the Lord Jesus understood well the difference between such poor persons and others. Leaving many thousands of poor people in their midst, they devoutly ministered to him and his disciples from their own resources. The apostle Paul, imitating the example of these holy women, passed by many thousands of poor people when he ministered with special care to the saints who were at Jerusalem.

[Col. 0204B] What? Do you suppose that Saint Cecilia could not find poor persons in the great city of Rome, she who, with all diligence, went three miles out from the city to those poor persons who were on the Appian Way, among whom Pope Saint Urban lay concealed? [Note: Cf. *Life of Saint Cecilia* in Surius, *Acts of the Saints*, VI, 525.] We surround you with so many and such great examples for this reason: that, having come to yourself, you may not say that you commit simony if, from the goods which God has bestowed upon you, you make an offering with your son to the Church, so that you may be able to provide the holy poor of Christ—who have, as it were, condemned themselves within it for the Lord’s name—with the necessary refreshment of the body; and may God free your soul and body from an evil hearing.

Now, having left these matters aside, let us return to refuting your indiscreet decrees. Monastic communities were not established in order that they should thoughtlessly receive, clothe, and feed the sons [Col. 0204C] of avaricious rich men at the Church’s expense, while their fathers, intent upon greater avarice and gain from the portion due to their sons, satisfy their own purses. Rather, they were established so that, living by their own labor and by the offerings of the faithful, they may receive according to the precept of the Rule those who are either altogether poor, or who, though formerly rich, have made themselves poor for God’s sake; or those who, making their possessions no longer their own, finally give themselves and their goods to Christ’s poor in monasteries.

The prudent foresight of the ancient fathers established that this should be observed with every diligence in such communities: no more persons should be received than the monasteries themselves could support, so that both those already present and those received might be free from the consuming leprosy [Col. 0204D] of murmuring, which is gravely wont to arise from want caused by an intolerable and freely admitted multitude. If certain modern men took this precaution, they would not today, with such shameless rapacity, invade the boundaries and tithes of ancient churches, nor go about cities and streets, nor, frequenting the houses of the rich, court the favor of matrons, so as to escape the poverty which they suffer because of their superabundant numbers by importunate and opportune begging. But reverence for the sacred order and religious habit prevents our speaking of these matters in detail.

But tell me: those who were assembled [Col. 0205A] and united at Jerusalem and in certain other places, for whom Paul earnestly urged that collections be made, and whom he diligently sent such collections—or carried them himself—were they saints and servants of God? Certainly they were, assembled and united through God and for God. Why, then, was Paul so greatly concerned for their number and sustenance, instead of waiting for them to be filled and satisfied from heaven by God through an angel with all your goods? Because he did not see that this pleased God. For, as was said above, so long as a person has the means, through rational judgment, to provide for his needs, he ought not to put the Lord his God to the test. Now that faith has long been established, the age of miracles has passed.

And, if we consider rightly, was not Paul an angel of the Lord [Col. 0205B] through whom he provided consolation and refreshment to the saints gathered in his name? You too can become an angel of the Lord, if you are willing to provide consolation and refreshment from your goods—which you withhold—to the saints kept enclosed in monasteries for the Lord’s name. What, moreover, shall we say of that holy and glorious multitude of believers whose heart and soul were one in the Church’s beginning? Did those who wished to enter it commit simony when they brought the goods they possessed before the apostles’ feet and made their private goods common? Certainly not; rather, they practiced piety, mercy, and justice. Upon two of their number the most severe sentence was executed, although they had withheld not all their possessions but only a part of them. What, then, will become of you, who wish to enter in through [Col. 0205C] your son in such a way that you wish to give neither the whole nor a part? They were punished through a man, by the irrevocable sentence of death, for withholding a part; and do you not fear God’s terrible judgment upon you for withholding the whole? May God grant you better counsel.

Thus far our discourse has addressed those who, burdened by the spirit of their avarice and stinginess, are borne downward over the empty plains of their talk; now it turns to those who, raised by the spirit of wisdom and understanding, hear lofty commands from the Lord Jesus upon the mountain above. Therefore, beloved brothers, flee every kind of simony, shaking your hands free of every gift. Simony is a most subtle art of the devil. It is threefold—or perhaps we ought better to call it triple—for the things by which it is bound together are three threads: service, hand, and tongue. By these three together, or sometimes by any one of them, the feet of some who seemed to walk simply are inundated; the eyes of others, who thought themselves lynx-eyed, are dazzled.

Let no one send you, by way of example, to the greater or more powerful persons, if any there are, in the Church who both practice and suffer simony. Examples must be taken from good things, not evil. Amen, I say to you: they shall receive their reward—eternal death—[Col. 0206A] unless they repent here and abandon what they hold through simony; and the greater and more powerful they are, the greater and more severe torments they shall suffer. But because you have deigned to ask advice from so far away, receive the counsel of our smallness—provided, however, that if you have something better, you do not abandon it for this.

If anyone offers either himself or his son to you to be received into the monastery, let him hear from you, with the simple eye of the mind and all purity of heart, without any evil covetousness, the counsel of Saint Augustine and the precept of Saint Benedict’s Rule, as has been related above concerning such matters. If he hears and obeys, well: you have saved his soul from death. If he does not obey, neither iniquity nor sin is yours if you do not receive him. For he was unwilling [Col. 0206B] to understand in order to act well, but stood in every evil way and did not hate avarice. [Note: MS. 1 lacks the text.] Dearest brothers, it is a great task in such a matter to have great purity of mind and no desire of avarice. For just as everyone who looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart, so everyone who, from ecclesiastical gifts, demands or covets anything through evil desire—or, I will say more, acts even in hope of recompense—becomes a simoniac, even if not here before the people, certainly before the divine eye.

When, at one time, we were ranging through the fields of Holy Scripture to prove these points, we sprinkled our tracks with this ball, strewn with many and varied flowers of authorities. The volumes remain; it now wearies us to run through them in writing, yet for love of you we gladly recall a few [Col. 0206C] things.

We know, therefore, and hold as certain, that all who sell and buy ecclesiastical things are simoniacs; that all simoniacs are heretics; and that no heretics are in the Church. Therefore all sellers and buyers are outside the Church. Saint Jerome affirms this with an entirely true proposition in his commentary on Matthew [Note: Works, ed. Vallarsi, vol. VIII]: “Every day,” he says, “Jesus enters the temple of the Father and casts out from his Church all alike—bishops and [Note: MS. 1* has *quam* (“as well as”).] priests and deacons, as well as laymen and the whole crowd—and he charges sellers and buyers alike with one crime. For it is written: ‘Freely you have received; freely give.’”

Behold: the Lord Jesus does not suffer sellers and buyers to remain in his Church even for one day. However [Col. 0206D] and however much those who ought to do this on his behalf may cease, he himself does not cease to do what is his own work. Therefore every day he casts out all persons, of whatever order, rank, or office; he spares none, neglects none, but casts out all every day. Where, then, are sellers and buyers? Outside the Church. What does Saint Gregory say of what is outside the Church? “Outside the Church,” he says, “there is no place of true sacrifice.” Sellers and buyers, therefore, are where there is no place of true [Col. 0207A] sacrifice.

Saint Augustine says of heretics that they are without doubt simoniacs: “They went out from us, but they were not of us”; and, concerning sellers and buyers, in his commentary on John: “They sell sheep, they sell oxen—that is, wretched peoples.” And to whom do they sell them, if not to the devil? O lamentable evil! Those whom the Son of God redeemed from the enemy’s hand with his precious blood, these sons of the devil sell to their father the devil. O how evil a seller, where the buyer is so utterly evil! May the goodness and mercy of Almighty God grant to us and to you that this heretical commerce, by which wretched peoples are sold to the devil and on account of which bishops, priests, deacons, laymen, and the whole crowd alike are cast out from the temple of God the Father, may always be far from us. Amen.

[Col. 0207B]

When anyone wishes to become a monk,  
let him divide into three equal parts everything he possesses.

[Col. 0208A]

Let him give one to the poor, and let one be kept at home;  
the third is owed to the saints to whom he will go.  
I declare this to be justice rather than simony.

If anyone wishes his child to become a monk,  
he ought to set aside from all that he possesses  
a share for the child, to carry with him into the Church which he is to enter.  
This is the Church’s best law, not simony’s.  
Imperial laws also decree this.

Simony, a heresy, drives out of the Church  
all who in it sell or buy anything;  
it drives them into hell, depriving them of the heavenly kingdom.

The Church’s benefices must be given freely and received freely,  
simony, the crossroad, having been driven away.

Whoever is found dying in this heresy  
shall never be delivered from the punishments of hell,

[Col. 0208B]

not even if he had suffered harsh martyrdom.

[Note: At this point manuscript 1 ends; what follows is read only in 1*.]

[Note: Formerly, in the Order of Saint Benedict, the offering of children was customary: parents consecrated their sons to God by a perpetual and irrevocable vow, as Saint Benedict prescribes in chapter 59 of the Rule. This was done by a threefold rite: namely, the offering of the children, whose hand the parents wrapped, together with their offering and petition, in the altar-cloth; a donation; and public documents confirming both. Examples of such documents may be read both in the *Chronicle of Novalesa* and in the notes on Guibert. Hence abundant revenues accrued to monasteries through the generosity of parents, who bestowed much wealth and extensive estates upon monasteries for the sake of their sons [Col. 0207C] whom they offered.

Certain persons, in the reign of Louis Augustus, surnamed the Pious, undertook to disapprove, indeed to abolish, this rite of offering children, long approved by the Church. Against those who wished to destroy the offering according to Saint Benedict’s Rule, Rabanus, then a monk of Fulda, wrote one book, as Rodulf the Monk attests in the *Life of Rabanus*. More than once I have requested this book, hitherto unpublished, from the monastery of Melk, where it is preserved in a manuscript codex of that library, as I read in an old catalogue of that same library which we now have on loan. This custom of offering children persisted until the twelfth century, when Rodulf flourished.

Having been asked by Sibert, prior of the monastery of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne, what answer he judged should be made to a certain wealthy miser who wished to give his son to this monastery without an endowment—the prior and monks opposing him, since they required from that rich man the portion of inheritance due to the son—Rodulf framed his answer so as sincerely to explain not only what he judged ought to be said to that miser, but also what counsel was expedient for the monks in this matter. In this he certainly performed the office of a good man and upright teacher.

Rodulf’s answer thus has two parts. In the first, he sharply censures such an avaricious man, who wished to defraud the son offered to the monastery of his due inheritance. His principal arguments are that it is a crime of avarice and sacrilege if he retains for himself the share of the son whom he has offered to God. “For,” he says, “the share due to him belongs to him whose possession he has now become.” Further, monasteries were not established to relieve the households of the rich of their burdens, but to support persons poor in property and income who wish to serve God, and rich persons devoted to poverty. Poor monks are to be preferred to needy laypeople, since they are not only poorer than the poor but daily minister also to other poor persons, pilgrims, and guests.

In the other part of the letter, Rodulf warns Sibert and his monks not to demand anything from that rich man, or from anyone else, for receiving children. They may admonish him to offer to the Church a portion of the inheritance which ought to fall to the son; but he ought not to be compelled to do this. It lies in the power of both parties: in that of the monks, to receive his son; in that of the father, to bestow a part of the inheritance upon the monastery. Neither party should be compelled in this matter.

In sum, the monks may demand nothing in receiving children or monks without falling into the crime of simony; for everyone who, from ecclesiastical gifts, demands or covets anything through evil desire—or, as he says, even acts in hope of recompense—is a simoniac, even if not here before the people, certainly before the divine eye.

Rodulf had been preceded, from the year 794, by the Council of Frankfurt, whose notable decree on this matter occurs in chapter 16: “We have heard,” say the Fathers, “that certain abbots, led by covetousness, demand payments from those entering a monastery. Therefore it has pleased us and the holy synod that no money whatsoever be demanded for receiving brothers into the holy order, but that they be received according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” Saint Benedict indeed established in chapter 58 of the Rule that a brother to be received should either first distribute whatever goods he has to the poor, or, having made a formal donation, convey them to the monastery—not as the price of a purchased reception, but as alms, as he explains in the following chapter. There he directs that the children of poor persons who have absolutely nothing be admitted freely.

Moreover, Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, religiously observed this law; his words in book IV, letter 49, are: “We ask nothing for making monks; but if anything is offered, because the Rule commands that it be received, we accept it. For our order requires that we be such persons as devote ourselves not to temporal profits but to gaining souls.” And certainly, since the monasteries of our order have been endowed for this purpose—that they may stand open, as asylums and refuges, to all who sincerely and wholeheartedly wish to turn from worldly corruption—it is intolerable inhumanity to exclude from them persons poor in earthly means but rich in grace and good will, and to reject as unworthy those whom God has called to the religious profession.

Let those who plead the poverty of monasteries in excuse of their action see to it. James of Vitry, cardinal, certainly did not accept that excuse when writing of the nuns of his time in chapter 15 of the *Western History*: they commonly and openly demanded money for their wretched admission into monasteries, alleging their poverty; and, caring nothing for the most evil crime of simony, they turned the house of prayer into a marketplace of trade. Yet it frequently happens by God’s just judgment that no monasteries suffer want more severely than those which demand such a dowry from women seeking religious life, contrary to the prescriptions of the sacred canons. —Mabillon.]

## III. LETTER OF ABBOT RODULF TO DUKE WALERAM

[Note: MS. 1* lacks this.]

[Col. 0209A]

To the glorious prince and his chief advocate WALERAM [Note: W. in MS. 1*], Abbot RODULF [Note: R. in MS. 1*] and the community of Saint Trudo offer faithful prayers and service.

[Note: An interpolator wrote in the upper margin: “On the law of the advocate.”]  
[Note: This letter was published under the year 1138 by Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, ed. Foppens, I, 61; it was written between 1119 and 1138.]

Because you have asked us, we briefly make known to you that our lord Saint Trudo sprang from the nobler stock of Frankish kings and dukes of Austrasia [Note: These and the following matters are read in Theoderic’s *Life of Saint Trudo*, in Surius]; that, for the love of God, he abandoned secular knighthood; that by angelic revelation and the admonition of Saint Remaclus he went to Metz; that he gave all his patrimony to Saint Stephen, the protomartyr; that he learned letters there, shone there through many miracles, and attained the virtue, learning, and rank of priesthood [Col. 0209B]; and that afterwards, returning to our land, he founded our monastery.

So great and so numerous were the estates which he gave to Saint Stephen the protomartyr that—apart from those which the lord bishop of Metz retains among his demesne lands and which many of his knights hold as benefices; apart from those which our church still possesses; and apart from many great properties which our church long ago lost—for among other things Bruges in Flanders was a freehold of Saint Trudo, where he also had a community of eighty monks—apart, I say, from these and many others, they were so many and so great that you hold from them in fief, for the advocacy, 1,100 *mansi*, of which Count Gislebert holds 300 from you, apart from the churches and their dependent serfs, and apart from the pleas and jurisdictions within the abbey.

Because Saint Trudo enriched the church of Metz with such great freeholds, holy and religious bishops and dukes endowed our church with greater freedom from advocates than any other. Therefore, since you requested it, we have sent you a copy of our charter concerning the liberty of our church and your right within it, since you are our chief advocate.

**(Year 1065.)** [Note: This charter is also printed in Duchesne, *Maison de Luxembourg*, proofs, p. 19; Miraeus, I, 62; Calmet, *Hist. de Lorraine*, I, proofs, p. 452; and Bertholet, *Hist. de Luxembourg*, III, proofs, p. 29.] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Adelbero [Note: the Third], by God’s grace bishop of Metz, wish it to be known to all that we came to the village of Saint Trudo called Sarchinia. Because of a dispute recently arisen concerning the advocacy of that place between my brother, Duke Frederick [Note: “of Lotharingia or of the Mosellans,” written by the interpolator in the margin], and the abbots of Saint Trudo [Note: Adelard II was then abbot], which advocacy I had granted to that same brother of mine as a benefice [Note: Cf. above, I.10 and V.3], I took counsel with our faithful men concerning what right belonged to us and to the advocate in that village itself and in the rest of the abbey subject to us. In the presence of that same advocate, I consulted the elders, that they should faithfully state concerning this business whatever they had learned from their elders or themselves had maintained down to that time, and should not, through fear or favor, incline toward either side by saying more or less than was true.

Bound by oath, they expressly declared that certain estates existed in that abbey—namely Burlou, Lare, Mere, Wilre [Note: near Maastricht], Kyrcheim, Staden, and Halmale—in which my predecessors had never granted the advocate any jurisdiction, because, being assigned to the maintenance of the brothers, they ought to obey no one but the provost and the cellarer [Col. 0210B] of that monastery.

But in the village of Saint Trudo and in the other villages of the abbey, they declared that to the duke—who, as said, held the advocacy as a benefice—or to an advocate appointed by him, one third denarius was to be assigned from the three general pleas and the high ban, if anyone should perhaps be killed or wounded within the village; the other two thirds were to belong either to me or to the abbot. Moreover, they testified that it was within the discretion of the abbot or my reeve lawfully and freely to hold pleas concerning whatever they wished without the advocate: namely lands, houses, marrying the wives of others, and dependent households; unless, perhaps, the seriousness of the affair required that the abbot or my official invite him to examine the matter.

When these things had thus been investigated in the aforesaid village and approved without anyone’s contradiction [Col. 0210C], some time having passed after the death of my brother of happy memory already mentioned, I ordered the same persons as before to come again into our presence in our castle of Saarbrücken [Note: *Salembrucca*], in the presence of Lord Udo, my brother’s successor, who held the same advocacy from us as a benefice, and Otto the sub-advocate. Having been admonished as before, they then expressly declared the same things which they had stated earlier. Therefore, on the advice of certain of our faithful men who were then with us [Note: MS. 1* reads “in the presence of”], whose names we have also ordered to be recorded below, and lest anyone afterwards be able or dare to infringe this, it pleased us to commit it to the written record for the memory of present and future persons alike. And so that it may be held firm and unshaken, we confirmed it with our own hand [Col. 0211A] and caused it to be confirmed by the testimony of our faithful men.

Done publicly in the aforesaid castle of Saarbrücken, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1065, in the third indiction, in the reign of Henry III.

Adelbero III, humble bishop of the holy church of Metz, subscribed. Lord Adelbero, primicerius; Lord Theoderic, his nephew; Lord Gervold, archdeacon; Lord Odelric, brother of Duke Gerard [Note: of Upper Lotharingia]; Frederick; Hermann; Riquin; Otto; Bernard; Stephen; Guntramn; Wigeric; Hermann; Hugh; Gervold; Leudold; Theoderic; Arnulf; Berengar; Lyedeco; Gislebert; Lyezeco; Adelstein; Wacelin; Guncelin; likewise Wacelin. I, Gislebert, acting in place of Lord Tyetfrid, chancellor of the church of Metz. Lambert the little man.

[Note: This is erroneous: [Gerard was] of Lower Lotharingia.]

**(Year 1060.)** [Note: Miraeus, I, 63; Meurisse, p. 364.] In the name of the holy and undivided [Col. 0211B] Trinity. Let it be known to all, present and future alike, how Lord Theoderic, bishop of the see of Metz, having stayed for some time in the monastery of Saint Trudo, fell ill there and came to his end [Note: Adelbero I, bishop of Metz, died at Saint Trudo; cf. continuation of the third part, book III, ch. 12]. With the counsel of his friends, he gave to that church and to the brothers serving God there the *scrutum* [Note: that is, *grutum*: dried barley from which beer is brewed; then the tax paid on beer; cf. IX.22] of that town: namely, authority to appoint and remove the person who prepared the material from which beer was made, and, from every beer brewed [Note: *brasciare*, “to make beer”; French *brasser*] in our town, to take six pitchers [Note: French *pichier*, a drinking measure] for the brothers’ use, which had belonged to his own service and that of his predecessors.

He did this for the remedy of his soul and of the souls of his other predecessors, so that their memory might endure not as before but more perfectly and firmly. I, Adelbero [Note: the Third], his successor both in kinship and office, though unworthy, having been appointed in the aforesaid place [Col. 0211C], and considering at once the reason and necessity for which the aforesaid brothers requested this from that same lord my [Note: A word seems to have fallen out before “predecessor”] bishop—namely, that their drink, which until then had been regarded as inferior, might afterwards be improved in some way—have decreed, by the authority of this written document, to record it and seal it with my seal. Since Lord Abbot Adelard II of that place and the other brothers also requested this, I decree that none of my successors may dare to infringe it; and that what he bestowed upon the aforesaid saint and those serving him for the remedy of his soul, I too have confirmed for the sake of my soul and those of my successors. Whoever he may be, let him do this to the detriment [Col. 0212A] of his soul.

This was done in the monastery of the aforesaid Saint Trudo, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1060, in the thirteenth indiction, in the reign of King Henry III, in the fourth year of his reign, in the forty-third year of the episcopate of the same Lord Adelbero, before suitable witnesses whose names are recorded below.

Names of nobles: Mark of Duke Frederick, advocate [Note: of Lower Lotharingia]. Mark of Count Otto, sub-advocate [Note: of Duras]. Mark of Count Folmar. Mark of Count Hermann. Mark of Richwin. Mark of Bardo. Mark of Hermann. Mark of Walbert. Mark of Ansfrid. Mark of Theoderic. Mark of Crath. Mark of Wazo. Mark of Otto. Mark of Guncelin.

Names of commoners of the household: Mark of Ramund. Mark of Lambert. Mark of Wichmann. Mark of Everard. Mark of Ascolf. Mark of Lyzecon. Mark of Stephen. Mark of [Col. 0212B] Lydecon. Mark of Ruthard. I, Ramund, acting in place of Lord Azo, chancellor, wrote and subscribed.

## IV. LETTER OF ABBOT RODULF TO STEPHEN, BISHOP OF METZ

[Note: In the upper margin are words apparently written in the hand of the interpolator: “Stephen, bishop of Metz,” the rest having been cut away by the binder. From these it is clear that this is the same letter of Abbot Rodulf which the interpolator identified in his index with these words: “Letter of Abbot Rodulf to Bishop Stephen concerning various injuries inflicted upon our church.”]

[Note: This letter supplements another addressed to the same man, printed above in book IX.]

Otto, son of our advocate Gislebert, invaded our village of Villers. Without any formal complaint, he seized my innocent reeve Anduard, though he was innocent; he carried him off to his own village of Worms, placed him in the stocks [Note: An instrument of torture by which captives’ feet are fastened; hence a prison generally], tortured him severely, and finally compelled him to ransom himself for two pounds. In the same village he seized our *scabinus* Francon; in one night he devastated for him six modii of grain and 200 sheaves [Note: French *gerbe*, our *garbe*] of grain; finally he compelled him, after capture and removal, to ransom himself for 48 shillings. On another occasion he took from the same man two oxen and made him ransom them. Likewise, on another occasion he took two oxen from the same man and made him ransom them.

In the same village he seized our *scabinus* Stephen and his brother Menard and compelled them to ransom themselves for 18 shillings. On another occasion, attacking the same men in the same village, he wounded and seized them, and compelled them to ransom themselves for 45 shillings. He took two oxen from our *scabinus* Walter. On one occasion, by threatening to plunder the livestock of the peasants of that same village, he compelled them to pay him more than 50 shillings. On another occasion, in the same way, he made them pay more than three pounds. On another occasion, in the same village, he made his retainers lodge for four days and nights, with a multitude of horses and palfreys, and by excessive devastation afflicted the whole village.

Because of a private war which he had, and for no cause of our church [Col. 0213A], his enemies rushed into the same village and, plundering it, carried off nearly 2,000 animals, both small and large, apart from the peasants’ household goods. Thus and thus a good village has been annihilated through him. We complained to his father; we gained nothing. These are a few of the many things which we lose because of our advocate.

Concerning certain brew-houses (*brascinae*) which we lost in our town through the violence of certain persons: after many complaints before the bishop of Metz, before the advocate, and judicial hearings, we obtained this result, that, when we had been summoned to Metz, the matter should be adjudicated anew before the leading men of Metz, our brethren. By the bishop’s messenger and seal our advocate was ordered, in accordance with the judges’ sentence, to assign the brew-houses to the brethren’s use [Col. 0213B] and to do us justice against the invaders. He refused; and so we lose them. Gerard of Durmale, his knight, takes from us every year one tenth and five solidi; and we can obtain from our advocate neither a day in court nor justice against him, though we have complained to him very often. Geldulf of Hacchedor [Note: [Col. 0213D] Perhaps Haccourt, near Liège?] takes from us land rendering thirty denarii. In the village of Lewes [Note: [Col. 0213D] Not far from Namur.] we lose one small holding through the advocate’s negligence. At Webecheym Otto of Bevere takes from us half a mill in the place called Langerodech, having diverted our water from its proper course. Godfrey of Diesteh built upon our freehold there, alienating it from us by drawing it into Diesteh. Walter of Bechenweiz burned one of our villages, Assent, [Col. 0213C] together with the whole church. On this matter, as on the others, we repeatedly summoned our advocate, whose man he is, to set a day and do us justice against him, but accomplished nothing. Thus that entire village remains desolate. At Seleche [Note: [Col. 0213D] Perhaps Seilles, near Huy?] we lose land rendering twelve denarii. Reyner, advocate of Saint Lambert, takes from our reeve Udelric of Burlo one *mansus* of freehold and adds it to his own freehold; nor, though repeatedly asked, does the advocate assist in recovering it. A certain Egebert takes from our man Gyslebert one *mansus* in the village of Hers [Note: [Col. 0213D] Herten, near Looz?] and draws it into the freehold of Count Arnulf. In the village of Hepene [Note: [Col. 0214D] Heppen, on the Meuse.] Count Arnulf’s servants take from that same man of ours, Gyslebert, one *mansus* of his fief; and through our advocate we can obtain no justice in any of these matters [Col. 0213D].

In our village of Burlo, from the feast of Saint John until Advent, now the father, now the sons, now their men, made thirty-two overnight stays in one year; on every such occasion they never had fewer than three hundred horses, and sometimes four hundred. Lord Otto entered the same village with his knights and assailed a certain Gozelin, our man, with demands for forced contributions; because he did not give as much as Otto demanded, he ordered his livestock [Col. 0214A] taken away to Worms, until he was compelled to redeem them for a mark of silver. Later he took three *firtones* from the same man. Likewise, he ordered the men of that village to appear before him, demanding from them whatever sum pleased him; because of this the reeve was compelled to give him two marks, lest he break the law of the estate court. In the same village he assailed our man Peter, and, when Peter refused to give what he demanded, ordered his squires with their horses to lodge with him for four nights, until necessity compelled him to pay half a mark. Likewise, there he became angry with a certain Baldric; because Baldric could not regain his favor upon his own terms, Otto violently carted away his entire harvest, which Baldric was forced to redeem for four pounds. Likewise, he took five *firtones* from a certain [Col. 0214B] Ramund. Likewise, in the same village he frequently lodged with Annelin the dean; but on one night, although Annelin had served the overnight guest excellently according to custom, Otto, departing in the morning, compelled him to give eight solidi. No one could count the overnight stays he made there, or the expenses he violently extorted from our men. The father likewise compelled thirty Liège measures of rye to be paid to him in that village.

In the village of Hales we are presently losing more than thirty *mansi* through a new practice, between Lord Reyner the advocate and those of Curtenaken [Note: [Col. 0214D] Cortenaeken, near Diest.]. There my reeve John—since the advocate does not do me justice against him, though he could do so with the greatest ease—takes so much from me, devastates so much in woods, meadows, cultivated fields, fisheries, [Col. 0214C] tenants, and everything belonging to the village, that it may exceed belief; and, holding by force a reeveship long ago adjudged against him, he tyrannizes there without the advocate’s restraining him. The damage he has done me in many ways during these ten years can certainly be reckoned at more than one hundred pounds. Moreover, his son Otto entered that village on the night of Saint Martin with nearly one hundred horses, and they remained there for eight days, now he himself, now his brother; of my rent of sixteen pounds they left me only twenty solidi and thirty denarii of debased coin, taking everything in our granary and everything the peasants owed us for the entire year. They have brought our village of Harches to ruin by their overnight lodgings and forced contributions. In our village of Orel, I cannot easily say how many evils [Col. 0214D] he and his sons did us. Among many things, these few are examples. Otto, his son, took from our reeve Robert one palfrey worth thirty solidi; his father took a cloak [Note: [Col. 0214D] A mantle.] worth four solidi, when he spent that night in Robert’s house with twelve men. The father imposed two forced contributions against the rights of our church, his son Otto two, and his brother Gyslebert one; together these were more burdensome than ten pounds.
