How often they entered our demesne house and [Col. 0215A] court there; how often, ravenously consuming what they found within, they devastated them; how often they burned the court’s hedges and the house’s walls and broke into our granary and storehouse—all this is manifest to every judge, since, whether we will or not, we must leave the place desolate, solitary, and without cultivation. Between forced contributions and overnight stays—now the father going out, now the son entering, then another arriving—our peasant cultivators flee as beggars.

On the night of Saint Lambert (17 September), he broke into our house, tearing off the bars, with twenty horsemen, and lived there at our expense overnight; on the night of Saint Trudo (23 November), with ninety horses; on the first Sunday of Advent, with thirty. His sub-advocate devastated our cultivation there for five days by turning eight horses loose in it [Col. 0215B] without a keeper; he took fifteen solidi as a forced contribution from the peasants. From August until Advent, whether personally or through his men, he made fifteen overnight stays there, and afterward countless ones each year. His son Otto sent his men into the granary of the priest in our village of Alesta [Note: [Col. 0215D] Alst, near Saint-Trond.] and had his wheat violently threshed out. When the priest sought the father’s help in this affair, he gave him five solidi; yet, since the son did not desist even then, he was compelled to give eight Liège measures of barley and half a mark. In the same village he took four marks from our man Franco, and half a mark from Franco’s brother. He established countless overnight stays there, both personally and through his men, living at our expense. At Kyrcheym Otto sent his men [Col. 0215C] to thresh the wheat in the granary of Dean Baldric, who held our church in that village; they did not leave until the dean paid him a mark. In the same village he imposed three forced contributions against the rights of our church. In our village of Mere he imposed one forced contribution, on account of which the men of that village, willing or unwilling, paid two pounds; in another year, likewise one. There he took twelve solidi from a certain man of ours, Godfrey, and fifteen solidi from the son of Godescalc of Halla. I could not easily describe how many overnight stays he made, or how inhumanely and mercilessly he treated its inhabitants.

In the village of Wimales he very often sent knights to lodge overnight, on one night with more than one hundred horses; sometimes they stayed from Thursday until Monday [Col. 0215D]. The father himself seized my reeve Theoderic in the same village, took him away captive with him, and held him until he extorted from him twenty solidi which he owed me from my rent. Humbert, our priest of Burlo, had lost our church by canonical judgment and, though excommunicated, refused to withdraw. The bishop, the archdeacon, and I went concerning this matter to Advocate Gyslebert [Note: [Col. 0215D] G. 1*.]. [Col. 0216A] He and I, having jointly sent messengers in August, stored the tithes of that church in the common granary; I had promised him half for his assistance. But after accepting a payment from the priest, he allowed him to break open our granary, take all the grain, and retain the church. For the souls of the father and mother of our advocate Gyslebert, we had an endowment worth fifteen solidi annually; a man of our church takes this from us and refuses to help us in the matter. His servant Adebert takes eight solidi from us every year. Likewise Heinrich, his servant, takes eight solidi from our property. For three years he despoiled us of a mill which our church had held peacefully for more than three hundred years and which rendered us grain annually; he also took our four ox-herds [Col. 0216B] and the servant of our marshal, and caused certain Flemings to hold it as a benefice—namely Godezo, a cleric, and his brother Heinrich. We offered a day in court, a hearing, and judgment concerning this; we achieved nothing until, after their deaths, we were forced to redeem it from the advocate for three marks.

He made Adelbert the one-handed [Note: [Col. 0215D] So called because he had lost a hand; cf. [Col. 0216D] IX, 16.] hold by force one entire village of ours, Provin, situated in Flanders and worth more than ten pounds annually, although we had never declined a day in court, a hearing, or judgment [Note: [Col. 0216D] “In accordance with.”]. When before Count Robert in Flanders, at Saint Othmar’s, we had recovered it by the judgment of the nobles present in his court, the advocate invaded our granary in the village of Mere and had all our grain [Col. 0216C] threshed and given to Adelbert, until he reconciled us and him upon a settlement harmful to the church. The reckoning of the damage we incurred from this was certainly greater than fifteen pounds.

Certain men of our town had received in trust from the hand of our predecessor Abbot Theoderic seven marks, which he had entrusted to their keeping from the sale of church freehold, with the church and its household as witnesses. When, after the abbot’s death, he extorted these from them wrongfully, they placed them upon the altar; but he took them with a presumptuous hand and thereby despoiled the church. The same abbot had lent him a phylactery from the church treasury, most richly adorned with gold, silver, and gems, worth more than ten marks, and filled with most precious relics. [Col. 0216D] He took this from our church. He restored to its invaders the village of Sarchin, which at great cost we had recovered from them by the judgment of princes before the emperor, until we entered into a damaging agreement with them.

In August, because we forbade his son Otto to give, contrary to law and justice, two *bonuaria* of our cultivated land, marked out for a certain man unjustly claiming them, on the next day he loosed his horsemen before [Col. 0217A] our town. Driving off my men, who suspected nothing of the sort, he carried away booty: four oxen and twenty-four unbroken mares. He broke one mill belonging to my reeve; when the reeve had repaired it, he took everything which he owed him. When setting out for Lombardy, he scraped together from every head of household belonging to the church, wherever he could hear one named, an extremely heavy payment and, from so many people, an unbelievable sum, against our charters, laws, and custom. Those who survived and still resisted the unjust exaction he left, with grave threats, to be seized and more heavily despoiled by his wife and son.

Thus our man Aleramnus was first seized and chained—a knight, indeed, and among the freer men of the church—and by his son Otto [Col. 0217B] imprisoned in his castle of Durach, until a heavy ransom was paid. Arnulf, his third-ranking sub-advocate and servant, likewise seized Gozuin, born among the freer men of the church, my man and knight; he took his palfrey, carried him off to his own house, kept him bound for a long time, tortured him in extraordinary ways, and finally compelled him to redeem himself. The same Arnulf violently broke into the house of my man Theoderic of Miles, severely wounded him and his wife, and took a horse worth one hundred solidi. Otto, his son, afterward seized the same Theoderic and, after despoiling him, forced him also to ransom himself. The father seized Robert, surnamed Lnthescal, a serf of the church, in response to our complaint; but he took him away otherwise than he ought, forced him to ransom himself, and retained him for himself. He finally seized Anelin of Niel, a serf of the church and [Col. 0217C] my man, after many afflictions and after he had fled into a church; he took from him an exceptionally fine palfrey and compelled him to take a maidservant as wife. This year, on Saint Trudo’s day, Otto seized a serf of the church who had brought the payment for his head to the altar; after long and severe torture, he compelled him to pay a heavy ransom. We complained to the father; we complained to you; you sent [representatives] once, twice, and three times, but achieved nothing. This same Otto seized another serf of the church, named Rodulf of Halmala, and compelled him to ransom himself for five marks. While his father was in Lombardy, he gathered the livestock of the peasants throughout all our villages into one place and made them ransom it for whatever amount pleased him. Whoever had given the departing father a single payment [Col. 0217D]—for example five or ten solidi—was compelled, while the son and mother remained, to give double, that is, ten or twenty. Furthermore, he compelled my provost to ransom our demesne estates from him: Burlo for thirty solidi, Orel for twenty, Vilarium for twenty-four, Mere for twenty, and others in the same fashion. When the father returned from Lombardy, he persecuted me and mine with harsher cruelty than before. At last he brought matters to such a pass that he would not allow me to leave the cloister; he deprived me so completely that he did not permit a brother to have more than the barest minimum [Col. 0218A].

I would be silent, but distress does not permit it. In the middle of holy Lent he broke into our cloister with his men; he took the brothers’ fish—the kitchen’s provision for five days. The Lord knows that he did not even leave for the brothers’ use those portions already cut up in the cooking-pot. In my presence he extorted from our reeve the keys of our granary. When our cellarer monk refused to give him the cellar keys, he had him stand before him while two knights stretched out both his arms in the form of a cross, so that he might thus extort the keys sought on every side. For the present I choose to keep silent about many other things, until God grants that you sit in judgment between him and me.

But this I report, this I complain of, this I proclaim: [Col. 0218B] in the presence of mine and his own men, he renounced his friendship toward me; he lays snares, practices enmities, and ordered his men to make peace for him with me by my death at last, or by whatever disgrace [they could inflict]. He ordered my men, as they love their safety and life, that, if summoned to a conference or chapter I should wish to go to Liège—to you—or to Cologne, to the archbishop, they should by no means follow me. By these and other evils which he inflicts upon me, I am held so captive that I dare not leave the cloister in any way. This I report to you; this I lament. Certainly, if you do not make amends, I shall appeal against you to almighty God the Judge. If you dare to do me justice, certainly I shall dare to proclaim with my own mouth against him in your presence and that of his peers these things written here, and many more [Col. 0218C] which I have still kept in reserve. But if I do not do so, refute me by the testimony of this writing; and, having become my enemy, you shall not live any longer. Farewell.

He seized Wederic of Burlo, our cleric, resident, and rent-payer, and forced him, after he had been afflicted with most shameful torture, to ransom himself in his castle for thirty-one marks. He fined Lantzo, our cleric and rent-payer, almost every year one pound, two, or more. He seized Heymezo of Wesheym [Note: [Col. 0217D] Wessem, on the left bank of the Meuse.], kept him captive in his castle, and, after holding and subjecting him to torture, compelled him to ransom himself for thirty-three marks; he compelled Rodulf of Hosduies to ransom himself after receiving five marks from him; Franco and Ramund, captured by him, paid four marks. At Alost he took two *bonuaria* of land [Col. 0218D] and gave them to Guntram and Rutard. He took four marks from Fulcric. From the church of Kyrcheym he took eight pounds in four years, everything paid to us from that church. He compelled Heinrich of Mosmale [Note: [Col. 0217D] Moumal, near Liège.] to ransom himself for I do not know how many marks; Everard of Gengleheym for seven marks; Benzo of Hesbines for five marks; Imezo of Assebruch [Note: [Col. 0218D] Assebrouck near Bruges.] for thirty solidi; and Theoderic for three marks.

## DEEDS OF THE TRANSLATION OF ONE KNIGHT OF THE THEBAN LEGION

(We publish these separately below.)

[Col. 0219]

[Col. 0219A] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, the first year of the reign of Conrad III [Note: [Col. 0219] Conrad III was elected on 22 February and crowned on 13 March 1138.], when it pleased Him who knows how to bring a human being forth from the womb of his natural mother and to call him back, once brought forth, into the bosom of his primal mother, that is, the earth, the venerable Father Abbot Rodulf, as the end of his life drew near, suffered from a grave illness in his left foot and leg, where a paralytic affliction had already settled upon him for seven years [Note: [Col. 0219] Six; cf. XII, 9.]. Hoping for recovery, he was carried to Liège in a litter commonly called a *rosbare*, and a certain skilled physician named Moses undertook his treatment. There, after two months, when the disease worsened and he had made no progress, he was brought back to his monastery scarcely breathing. Having summoned the brethren, after words of pious exhortation, after devoutly receiving the viaticum, and after [Col. 0219B] the sacrament of extreme unction had been completed, he gave up his spirit on the day before the Nones of March (6 March), after ruling for thirty years, one month, and seven days. He was [Col. 0220A] buried in the left aisle, before the entrance of the crypt and choir, on the north side.

After his death, before an election was held, the brethren had his cell broken up—the cell which he had prepared for himself when he began to be ill. It had been fitted within one of the four towers adjoining both aisles of the choir; that tower, after its stone screen had then been removed, was later made into the sacristy. The reason for destroying this cell was that the brethren’s repose might not thereafter be disturbed, as before, by his successor as abbot. This abbot was a man of great learning, not inferior to his predecessor Theoderic, as his various letters, prose compositions, prose sequences, and poems written among us testify. Among other things he composed antiphons, responsories, and chant for Saint Quintin and Saint Trudo at Lauds; and a hymn for the praise, *re. glo.*, with the antiphon for Saint Stephen, “O of charity” [Note: [Col. 0219] Here end the deeds of Abbot Rodulf, who wrote the second part of this compilation, with a few additions concerning the deeds of abbots. The same manuscript continues thus: “There follows first concerning the right of brewing, and concerning the right of evil *gruit* in faith.”].

## SECOND CONTINUATION OF THE DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-TROND

[Note: [Col. 0219] Here begin the chapters of the third part concerning the deeds of three abbots who formerly governed this abbey of the monastery of Saint Trudo from A.D. 1138 to A.D. 1180. Their names are Folcard, Gerard, and Wiric; their deeds are divided into four separate books. Chapters of the first book of this third part, concerning the deeds of Lord Folcard. This is written in an erasure of five lines; all is written in red, 1*.]

## CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK—ON THE DEEDS OF LORD ABBOT FOLCARD

1. On the election and consecration of Abbot Folcard.

2. On his lawsuit against the lord of Diest concerning the bannal obols.

3. On the right concerning brew-houses, *gruit*, the *gruiter*, and bad *gruit*. An incidental matter. Likewise, on freedom from toll. Likewise, on the quarrel between the duke of Brabant and the count of Limburg, and how the duke came to besiege the town of Saint-Trond.

4. On the castle of Bolioeyn, how it was recovered for the church of Liège through Albero II.

5. On the agreement concerning the annual revenue, made with the lord of Diest through the intervention on his behalf of many princes; concerning this we have letters.

6. On the monastery dormitory, begun earlier by another but completed by him; and on the many offices constructed and restored in his time.

7. On the renewal of the bond of peace and ancient agreement between the bishop of Liège and the men of Saint-Trond, from which the bishop was compelled to withdraw because of the rebellion of Advocate Count Otto and his men.

8. On the siege of the town of Saint-Trond by the duke of Louvain, the count of Namur, and the count of Durach; and on the lifting of the siege through the agreement of the townsmen with the count of Durach, brought about by the duke of Louvain.

9. On the resumption of construction of the cloistral and other buildings—work temporarily interrupted because of damage inflicted on the monastery during the aforesaid siege—and on the alms of Franco and his assistance to Lord Folcard for the Fabric.

10. On the light now hanging in the corner of the cloister walk by which one enters the church, established by the same Franco among the other great benefits he conferred upon us. Seek the letters concerning it in the cartulary, no. 88.

[Col. 0221]

11. On the alms of other townsmen, Tegno, Reyner, and Udelric, who established that a black Tournois [Note: [Col. 0221] “black Tournois,” 1*.] should be distributed to each poor person at the Lord’s Supper.

12. On the right concerning brew-houses, otherwise breweries: namely, the payment owed to our monastery from each brewery for the brewing of beer; certain leading townsmen of our church were attempting to take this away. First warned to desist, they refused to comply; but at length, excommunicated, though unwillingly, they restored what they had unjustly retained and thus obtained absolution.

13. On Folcard’s prediction against a certain townsman who stubbornly declared under oath that he would never pay the brew-house due.

14. On the three lamps endowed by him to be lit: one at the altar of Saint Trudo, another at the altar of Saint Peter, and a third at the altar of Saint Leonard. In the same chapter, under the concluding paragraph, on other townsmen who made satisfaction to our monastery concerning the retained right from their brew-houses and earned the benefit of absolution; and how certain men who disdained to repent died excommunicated.

15. On the alms of Reyner the *gruiter* and his wife. He was the hereditary *gruiter*, who retained one share of the *gruit* for himself and paid the remaining two to the monastery.

16. On the lawsuit of our house at Cologne, settled.

17. On the death of Lord Folcard and the alms acquired by him to be given to the brethren on the day of his anniversary.

18. On the feasts of Saints Lawrence, Lambert, Nicholas, and Mary Magdalene: he established a *pittance* for the brethren so that they might be solemnly observed.

## CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND BOOK—ON THE DEEDS OF LORD ABBOT GERARD

1. On the election of Lord Gerard as abbot.

2. On a certain house at Halen taken from us by our reeve and utterly destroyed by Gerard and his men.

3. On the synod held at Liège, which he disdained to attend.

4. On our village of Alym, which Otto, count of Durach and brother of Lord Abbot Gerard, granted to the brethren’s table; concerning this we have charters.

5. On the invasion by his nephew of the village and our goods of Alym; through his efforts what had been taken was restored, concerning which we have charters.

6. How Lord Gerard wished to resign the abbey, but the bishop of Liège did not agree.

7. How, at the urging of his relatives and friends, the bishop was prevailed upon to consent to his resignation of the abbey.

8. How, with the unanimous consent of the convent, he elected Abbot Wiric as his successor; then, in order to live as a private man, he obtained the places he desired, afterward returned to his own cloister, and died.

## CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD BOOK—ON THE DEEDS OF LORD ABBOT WIRIC

1. On the election of Lord Wiric, and how he obtained the grant confirming his election in the city of Metz.

2. On his consecration at Liège in the following year, and the claim brought against him by the canons of Saint John regarding the retention of a certain island occupied by his predecessor [Note: [Col. 0221] “occupied,” 1*.].

3. On his entry into the monastery and his provision of stones, columns, and other things necessary for repairing the buildings.

4. On the hearing of the aforesaid lawsuit at Liège by the judgment of nobles.

5. On the burning of the town of Saint-Trond and of a great part of the monastery, including two towers with mills and other offices.

6. On the repair of the monastery and rebuilding of our house at Cologne. Likewise, there, on the special use of cut stone for house roofs [Note: [Col. 0221] “Likewise—house roofs” added by another contemporary hand in 1*.].

7. On the disagreement between Pope Adrian and Emperor Frederick [Note: [Col. 0221] “Henry,” 1*.], and on the two men elected to the papacy who fought one another.

8. On Abbot Wiric’s journey to Italy with Henry, bishop of Liège; how he was kindly received by the apostolic lord, obtained renewed privileges for the monastery and the use of pontifical insignia; and how, returning thither on a second journey, he was received by him as a son.

9. On the injury inadvertently inflicted upon Lord Wiric by friends of the abbot of Floreffe.

10. On the incorporation of the church of Blessed Mary at Saint-Trond into the brethren’s provision.

11. On his being summoned by Alexander II to journey with him into Italy, to assist a troubled realm and priesthood, though he remained at home until he had prepared what was necessary for the journey.

12. On the interruption of Abbot Wiric’s journey to Italy with Alexander II, bishop of Liège, because of the danger of the mortality raging there.

## CHAPTERS OF THE FOURTH BOOK—STILL ON THE DEEDS OF LORD ABBOT WIRIC

1. On the discovery of the bodies and relics of Saint Libert the martyr and others.

2. On the discovery of the bodies of Saints Trudo and Eucherius.

3. On the translation of Saints Trudo and Eucherius.

4. On a miracle performed during the celebration of Mass on the day of this translation.

5. On the completion of the structure of Saint Trudo’s chapel.

6. On the splendid restoration of the shrine of Saints Trudo and Eucherius; on the careful and separate placing within it of the relics of holy pledges; on its being carried around the town in solemn procession; and on its being placed beneath the vault behind the altar.

7. On the repair of the great sanctuary screen, together with two smaller screens to right and left that threatened collapse, after its arching had first been removed at great expense.

8. On the screens, choir seats or stalls made; on the nave of the church from the upper screens to the lower arch, whose walls were plastered with cement and whose beams were adorned with a wooden panelled ceiling; and on the laid pavement.

[Col. 0223]

9. On the construction of a washing-house and bath-house, with rooms there necessary for them, and on various ornaments of this monastery’s treasury.

10. On the completed dormitory.

11. On the constructed refectory and the transfer of the kitchen to another location.

12. On the abbot’s heated chamber and other necessary offices.

13. On twelve specified feasts of saints; in order that they might be observed more solemnly, he assigned to them three pounds for the brethren’s refection.

14. On the part of the marketplace where fish are now sold, taken from us but restored to the monastery through the aid of Lord Theoderic, successor of the now deceased Lord Stephen, bishop of Metz; and on its conspicuous separation by a boundary marker between the limits of our monastery’s lordship and that of the bishop. Concerning these matters we have charters.

15. On how that same bishop, having been wronged by our people, seised into the emperor’s hands what he possessed among us.

16. On the war which Louis, count of Loon, began against Egidius, count of Durach, our advocate, and our people; and on the tower built and fortified with a ditch at Brustem.

17. On the war between Brustem and our town, and on the damage done by Count Louis to our men in our village of Borlo.

18. On the prohibition sent by Emperor Frederick to our people, forbidding them to involve themselves in the war between the two counts; how the count of Loon mocked our people as feeble-minded and afraid to go out and fight him; and on the booty daily carried off from the town by his men.

19. On the count’s war against our townsmen; how, after his villages had been devastated, he died at Brustem on 28 July, and his castle was besieged by our people; and how, after the count’s death, Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, having made a truce, caused the besiegers to return home.

20. On peace restored to our people and the harvesting of grain that had survived devastation; how, through Abbot Wiric’s skill, the emperor’s anger against our people, aroused by the complaint of the dead count’s son, was calmed; and how the damage inflicted upon the monastery by the father was restored by the son Gerard.

21. On the invasion of the castle of Berle; the devastation and burning of neighboring villages; and the damage then inflicted upon our monastery at Hoerle by the sons of the count of Musal.

22. How the count of Loon, with the aid of the count of Durach, defeated his adversaries; how they were united by marriage; and how firm peace was established between our people and the count of Loon.

23. On the embankment of the ditch raised around Brustem, which was the seedbed of every evil.

24. On the new cloister walk of polished stones completed by Abbot Wiric within one year.

25. On the village and castle of Brustem, surrendered by the count of Loon into the emperor’s hands because of fear of the count of Durach and our people; and on the interruption of work on the raised embankment.

26. On the reconciliation of Pope Alexander and Emperor Frederick I, ending the disturbance of Church and realm, which had been at odds for seventeen years.

27. On the hostile invasion of the county of Loon at Calmunt by Rodulf, bishop of Liège, and our people; how Count Gerard first prevailed, but on the following day, after his men had been slain, fled with a few of his followers and burned the town of Tongeren together with the monastery of Blessed Mary.

28. On the plundering and burning of the village of Loon, its monastery, and castle, by Rodulf, bishop of Liège, and our people of Saint-Trond.

29. On the burning of the monastery at Bilisia and the whole village; the destruction and burning of the castle of Mutenakem and other fortifications and villages, with their churches, numbering sixteen or more, carried out by the bishop’s soldiery; and on the peace finally made.

30. On the indignation of the duke of Louvain against our townsmen because they aided the bishop in such matters; and on the prohibition of imported merchandise from his lands to our people.

31. How the count of Loon’s complaint against our people, brought before the emperor, was defeated through the patronage of Rodulf, bishop of Liège; how the emperor commanded a peace agreement; and how the count was finally compelled permanently to discontinue the embankment raised before Brustem, so that it should not be completed.

32. On the death of Lord Wiric [Note: [Col. 0223] “Here end the chapters of the third part,” added by 1*.].

## PROEM

[Note: [Col. 0223] “Of the third part,” added by 1*.]

[Col. 0223A] Since the tribulations which have already befallen our church in past times, because of the fear and corruption of those who followed, deserved to be illuminated by the pen of certain wise men, it has seemed not inappropriate to us to commit in summary form to the memory of posterity the adversities that have befallen it in our own days and the benefits that have accrued to it. For just as younger men are formed toward better things by emulation of their elders, so surely the hearts of foolish sons, frightened by the calamities of their fathers who went before them, are recalled from the error of their own sloth. Lord Abbot Rodulf, a man most excellently learned in divine and human wisdom and second to none in his age, exhorts us by his example to begin this work. Having attained the summit of this office, he diligently discovered many things worthy of record and remembrance, almost obliterated by others’ negligence; arranged them in little books; and left them for future posterity to read. Whoever wishes may discover in the book he published on the deeds of the abbots his manner of life and restraint of character, and what and how great actions he endured amid the hatred of rivals for the improvement of the church and the order [Note: [Col. 0223] “Here begins the third part, concerning the deeds of the abbots of this place,” added by 1*.].

## HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK ON THE DEEDS OF LORD FOLCARD

[Col. 0225]

[Col. 0225A] **1.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, the first year of Conrad III’s empire by reckoning of his name, and the second year of Albero, bishop of Liège, after Abbot Rodulf had died—as we said above—on the day before the Nones of March (6 March), the brethren held an election and by common counsel chose Folcard, provost of the greater church, a man venerable in age and distinguished by worthy morals.

From the disposition of his earliest years he had been fittingly trained in the sacred observances of the monastery; through the administration of many offices he had proved himself wise in the judgment of all. Thus, like a veteran soldier deserving the reward of his labours, in which he had exerted himself outstandingly for the affairs of the church, he was deservedly raised to the summit of this dignity. What manner of man he was in it, and how great a diligence he showed in improving the affairs of the church and the brothers’ provision, [Col. 0225B] the following text of this work will make known.

Accordingly, having been regularly elected, as we have said, he set out with his companions for Stephen, bishop of Metz, to receive from him the grant confirming his election. But Count Otto of Duras, long hostile to him, wishing to invalidate his election, wrote to the bishop that he had not been canonically elected, but had usurped the name and dignity of abbot by unlawful presumption.

When the aforesaid Lord Folcard arrived at Metz, he did not find the bishop present. He waited there for several days, since rumour said that the bishop would return shortly. When he had returned, Folcard presented himself before him and, establishing the validity of his election by the testimony of his faithful men who were present, requested that the grant of election be conferred upon him. Yet he was greatly hindered there by having neglected to bring with him the commendatory letters of his church, as custom required. This, I think, he had omitted because he hoped that the bishop would readily trust the testimony of his grey hair; or, more probably, it had happened through the negligence of his own people.

But the bishop, influenced by the embassy of the aforesaid count—and in truth expecting to receive money from him—admitted the testimony of Folcard’s brethren and faithful men, but postponed investing him with the grant of election until the court of Conrad, third of that name but second by reckoning of consecration, which was soon to be held at Cologne.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] He celebrated Easter at Cologne on 3 April, and we know that until the 11th of the same month he ordered certain charters to be written. See Böhmer 2177–2181 and Jaffé, *Conrad III*, p. 8, no. 23.]

Meanwhile he sent one of his men, named Simon, who later became dean of the same church, to us, that he might investigate carefully the truth of the matter and the procedure of the election and faithfully report it to him.

The bishop, having been summoned to the court, came there; and the aforesaid elect of the brethren met him there, as he had been ordered. [Col. 0226A] Since the validity of his election had long before been fully established by the testimony of the brethren and faithful men of Saint Trudo, and by Simon’s aforesaid investigation, the bishop granted Folcard the confirmation of election that he requested. With letters given to him, he sent him to Albero II, bishop of Liège, uncle of Count Godfrey of Louvain, to be consecrated.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] See above, XII.14.]

Albero, a man of venerable memory, then presiding over the church of Liège, was to hold his court at Fosses during Pentecost. He ordered the aforesaid venerable man to come there; receiving him honourably when he arrived, he consecrated him abbot on the Wednesday of that feast, four days before the Kalends of June.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] This is erroneous: in the year 1138 Pentecost was celebrated on 22 May.]

Returning home from him, Folcard was received and enthroned by the brethren and people with great rejoicing and shouts of gladness. Then, as he had long conceived in his prudent mind, he took care, as the office of his assumed title required, to provide for what concerned the peace and advantage of the church, and he endeavoured to preserve and enlarge the possessions and rights of the church, honourably acquired by the labour of his predecessors.

**2.** Although he seemed to be of advanced age, he was resolute in spirit. He had girded himself with zeal, prudence, and courage; as no sluggish executor of his predecessors’ work, he offered an example to his followers, lest, given over to idleness, they permit the rights of churches to be diminished or lost in any way, but rather oppose themselves without hesitation as a strong wall against every assault of adversaries.

For in those things that he acquired for the church, almost lost before, by the great sweat of his labour, he left us a faithful memorial of his diligence and courage. On the very first day of his consecration, he requested from the bishop a day and hearing concerning the church at Diest. A complaint by his predecessor concerning the withholding of the *bannales* owed to our church had been brought under ban; but when that predecessor died, Bishop Albero II had not indeed released it canonically. He was, in fact, more hostile to our church than was fitting for so wise a man, because he had learned that Abbot Rodulf had not fully supported his election.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] On these matters see below, I.5.]

Having received a postponement of two weeks, Folcard returned and obtained that the matter be put under ban by canonical judgment. Arnold, the author of this injustice, having been convicted by synodal judgment, Folcard at last compelled him to make satisfaction to himself and the church. This Arnold had won the bishop’s friendship by frequent services and great military assistance rendered in an expedition, namely in the taking of Bouillon Castle.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] This castle, occupied by Count Reginald of Bar, was not taken until the year 1141; see the *Annals of Lobbes* and the *Triumph of Saint Lambert concerning Bouillon Castle*.]

And for a long time he had laboured greatly, but in vain, to prevent that church from rendering the respect due to our church.

[Note: [Col. 0227A] In his second year Abbot Folcard confirmed for Reiner the *grutarius* the right which he possesses in “bad gruit,” commonly called *kaedgruyt*. In the margin the same hand, apparently, adds this in different ink: “The charter which follows occurs at the end of the entire work.”]

**3.** In Folcard’s third year (1140), Lord Stephen, bishop of Metz, confirmed to our monastery the right of the *cambae*, that is, breweries, which he caused to be confirmed by the ban of the bishop of Liège. Seek copies concerning this, the *gruit*, and the right of the *grutarius* above.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] We shall append, after Rodulf’s book, copies of these charters together with the remaining documents to the *Deeds*.]

In the same year the aforesaid Stephen acknowledged that the burgesses of Saint Trudo were free from toll in the city of Metz. Seek a copy concerning this above.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] It is missing.]

In the same year, namely A.D. 1140, Godfrey [Col. 0227B] I “with the beard”—the first among the counts of Louvain, after the title of count had been changed, to be duke of Lotharingia and Brabant—was thereafter worthy, by his own merits and virtues, to be and to be called so by imperial authority.

[Note: [Col. 0227] Written above in different ink.]

[Note: [Col. 0227D] See above, XII.8. The author seems to maintain the view rejected by Ernst III.15: that Conrad had already restored the duchy of Lotharingia to Godfrey I. The witnesses differ as to the time of his death: 1138 is read in the continuation of Sigebert of Gembloux, 1139 in the *Annals of Bois* and the *Annals of Lobbes*; yet he occurs alive in a charter of 1140, concerning which see Ernst, I.1. See also Jaffé, *Conrad III*, p. 38.]

—[Continuation of Sigebert of Gembloux]—he died, a great glory of his native land, and was buried in the church at Affligem. His son Godfrey II succeeded him.

In the same year Henry, count of Limburg and advocate of the town of Saint Trudo, grieved that he had been deprived of the honour of the duchy of Lotharingia, which his father and grandfather had held, rebelled against Duke Godfrey II and invaded the revenues of his neighbouring possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] The second son of Waleran the Pagan, who appears to have died in 1139, on 16 July; see Ernst III.45, 49.]

Godfrey bore his insolence with difficulty and came to besiege the town of Saint Trudo, to Henry’s detriment, with a great army of horse and foot. But the townspeople forestalled the siege with submission, and, after appeasing him, were received into favour. This duke died in the fourth year of his duchy; he was succeeded by his son Godfrey III, then in the first year of his age.

**4.** Since we have mentioned this castle, it is fitting briefly to describe how it was seized and restored. In the following year, Hugh, son of the count of Bar, puffed up by the strength of his power, held the castle after seizing it by treachery. Having fortified it with a numerous garrison, he refused to restore it to the bishop.

[Triumph of Saint Lambert.]

But Bishop Albero, gathering aid from every side, led there a great multitude of troops together with the bones of Saint Lambert, and shut in by siege the aforesaid invader, who was boldly holding himself within the castle’s fortifications. Meanwhile, as the armies of both sides fought each other with all their strength, suddenly, by God’s hidden judgment, the aforesaid invader lost his mind. Drawn outside by his own men, who were offering the surrender of the castle, he was laid half-alive before the shrine of Saint Lambert. He immediately expired, stirring all present to veneration of the blessed martyr; and he might serve as an example to persons like himself, that they should not dare commit such a deed.

**5.** To return to the sequence of our narrative: in the fifth year of his prelacy (1142), the long-standing matter of contention between Abbot Folcard and Arnold of Diest was argued in a synod at Liège before the bishop. Justice favouring the abbot, Arnold was convicted and yielded. Through the efforts of Godfrey, duke of Louvain and nephew of the bishop, Henry of Limburg, and Count Otto of Duras, he barely obtained permission to pay ten shillings annually.

[Note: [Col. 0227] “of D[iest]” written above in different ink.]

He committed this payment to posterity in a testamentary document, to be made each year on the Wednesday of Pentecost. Yet if it were not paid on that day, the same church was again to cease from divine office, without reconsideration of the judgment, until the same debt of right had been restored in full to our church. A copy of this testament, confirmed with the seal of episcopal authority and deposited in the church so that no negligence of forgetfulness might obscure it, is readily available to those who wish to know. Thus the long-standing dispute which our church had against Arnold concerning its right was at last concluded and laid to rest through Abbot Folcard’s diligence.

For clarity concerning the foregoing, it should be known that the *oboli bannales* were dues paid to our monastery by various churches in redemption of the annual visitation by which they were legally bound every year to visit, with their relics, the thresholds of the monastery of Saint Trudo and there, at the saint’s altar, to offer one obol from each hearth through each inhabitant. It was over such a matter that this agreement was made with the lord of Diest.

**6.** While he laboured tirelessly for the church, spreading far and wide the sweet savour of his good reputation, and cherished the brethren entrusted to him with fatherly care under the discipline of monastic religion, he determined to rebuild from the foundations some of the cloister buildings and workshops, ruined by location, age, and extreme shabbiness, and to complete by enlargement others that his predecessor’s diligence had begun.

Thus, the work of good purpose which he had conceived in his prudent mind through God’s inspiration, he brought to completion with God’s assistance. The wall of the dormitory, which Abbot Rodulf had begun but not completed—death having prevented him from finishing it—Folcard raised from the lower beams and completed. Over the portion adjoining the tower, beneath which the chapter house lay, Abbot Rodulf had erected only a bare timber framework. Ill-fitted and not firmly joined, it moved in the wind and gave the brethren no little fear that it might suddenly fall.

But Folcard not only increased the wall’s height; he also caused the entire completed structure of the building, as far as he could, to be roofed with straw—that is, with a poor roof. Having demolished the old infirmary, exceedingly unsightly both in workmanship and age, he excavated the ground there and laid the foundations of a cellar. Upon it he also erected the building which is now the refectory; having roofed it with straw, he left it for the care of his successor to improve.

[Col. 0229B] **7.** It happened in these days that Lord Stephen, bishop of Metz, came here, and Albero, bishop of Liège, was also present with him. Stephen renewed, with the presence and consent of that same bishop, the covenant of peace and concord by which our people had been bound from ancient times, from the age of their predecessors, to those of Liège.

The same bishop confirmed, by an act of his authority, the grant of the *gruit* that had been made to us by his predecessors; and the aforesaid bishop of Liège, by the subscription of his own name and the threat of the ban, granted it to our church to remain free forever.

When these matters had been completed, Count Otto of Duras learned that our people had confirmed by oath a covenant of concord with the bishop. He was violently angered against them, declaring that an injury had been done to him because they had presumed, without him—although he was their advocate—to confirm any agreement of peace and concord with the bishop or with any men whatsoever. Having stirred up, as it seemed, Duke of Louvain and the count of Namur to avenge this injury done to him, he came to the bishop on an appointed day and repeatedly urged him, by himself and by others who supported him, to estrange himself from them and annul the covenant he had made with them.

The bishop, perceiving the hearts of the count and of his nephews—Duke Godfrey and the count of Namur—to be so stirred against them, was himself distressed with great grief of mind, because he was forced to deprive of the comfort of his aid those whom he had made his faithful friends.

[Note: [Col. 0229] Henry.]

[Col. 0229D] **8.** Count Otto, therefore, having obtained what he wished, and seeing them deprived of all aid, brought against them the aforesaid princes and as many powerful men as he could, as though he intended to destroy the town. He harshly afflicted them with a long siege while they were enclosed by the defence of their ditch. Yet the Lord had granted them a great abundance of bread, wine, and other goods, whereas those princes and the surrounding people suffered from almost every kind of severe scarcity and were compelled each day to obtain necessities of life from those whom they besieged.

Meanwhile our church was afflicted by grave loss of its possessions, and the villages surrounding us were freely plundered by raiders, with no one resisting. This greatly distressed Abbot Folcard, because he saw the church’s goods daily carried off and his brethren afflicted by scarcity of food and clothing, while there was no one to oppose the raiders.

Therefore, while the count’s army besieged them and they were maintaining themselves as best they could within the walls of the ditch, and while the few despaired of resisting the strength of the many, they at last took counsel and judged it advantageous to sound out Duke Godfrey’s disposition concerning terms of peace.

[Note: [Col. 0229] Godfrey, who died in that same year, 1142, according to the continuation of Sigebert of Gembloux and the *Annals of Rode*.]

They wished him to be mediator between themselves and the count: if the count advanced any just complaint against them, he should reconcile them to the count through mediation; but if they could by a just accusation charge the count with injustice and damage inflicted on them, he likewise should, judging both sides equally, reconcile each to the other. And this was done. The duke, moved by an agreement involving money and by the mediation of some of his own men, lifted the siege; and, after the townspeople had been reconciled to the count and peace sworn, he departed.

Thus our town, besieged from the fifth day before the Ides of August nearly until the feast of Saint Martin, was at last freed from the danger of siege after much affliction.

**9.** When the tumults of war had everywhere been quieted and peace restored to the church, Folcard diligently worked to complete the buildings of the cloister workshops which he had begun. Observing the zeal of his ardent purpose, Franco of Fuich, a citizen of our town, was moved to assist, from his own resources, in the expenses of the work which were troubling the abbot; he was well supplied with such resources. Admitted into the fellowship of the brotherhood, he became Folcard’s zealous fellow-worker in building, giving some things from his own goods and advancing many others on credit.

The abbot, seeing the man’s overflowing goodwill, extended to his wife as well the participation in the fellowship that he had granted him. He allowed them a separate allowance of the brethren for as long as they lived, and received their son into the cloister to be nurtured under the discipline of monastic life.

**10.** The same Franco had received in pledge from the abbot, for the redemption of ten marks, a certain allod of the church lying in our town at Burlo, called “the land of vineyards and breweries.” He restored it free to the church and established that a yearly commemoration of himself and his wife should be made from it.

Likewise, he gave six marks for stocking the cellar and the same sum for drawing the brethren’s wine, on this condition: once the brethren’s wine was stored in the cellar, the wine provost should again receive from it the same amount of money, so that in the following season, and each year thereafter, he should always have it ready as though Franco were still alive.

For construction of the chapel of the sick he also donated five marks. The abbot received these, but, because he needed much for his many building projects, spent them on his construction work. In a similar manner, wishing to establish a light in the chapel, Franco contributed five marks to the church for purchasing it; in return, he obtained for himself and his wife a place of burial in the same place.

The custodian of that time took charge of the aforesaid sum and spent it on the church’s uses; he promised that every night he would provide a light there and left to his successors, almost as a hereditary right, the duty of doing so. Some years later his wife died in the world and was buried before the chapter house, as may still be seen, in accordance with the grant made to them. After her death, he nevertheless took another wife; when she too died after some time, he sought marriage with a third wife.

[Note: [Col. 0231] MS. 1*: *connubiare quesivit*, “he sought to marry.”]

By her he had two daughters and a son. Leaving her and renouncing the world, he sought the monastery. Having lived honourably among us for several years according to the rule of life, he rests buried in the cemetery of the brethren.

**11.** Other laymen of honourable life then began to imitate this man, seeking the favour of the abbot and the fellowship of the brethren by frequent gifts of their generosity. Among them was one named Tegno, who contributed six marks to aid the buildings and obtained for himself and his wife a separate fellowship with the brethren. Among his other outstanding gifts of liberality, he gave the church the house of his residence, which pays us five shillings annually; he assigned these for the refreshment of the brethren on the anniversary of himself and his wife.

It seems not inappropriate to insert into this narrative the text of this donation, as it is contained in a document confirmed by writing and witnesses.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] It is missing.]

If the house of the aforesaid residence should collapse through age or be consumed by fire through any misfortune, the heirs shall rebuild it at their own expense, yet shall not refuse the annual rent. Because of the generosity of his devotion, it was granted to this man by the abbot and brethren that, if he should ever wish, through God’s inspiration, to be converted, he should be received and joined to the community.

Likewise Reiner, a man of honourable life, with his wife named Walswinde, had earned the spiritual fellowship of the brethren by frequent acts of liberality. In return for this favour, the abbot had granted them a separate allowance of the brethren until the end of their lives. They gave the church six shillings annually, which they assigned to the brethren’s charity on the day of their anniversary.

A certain Udelric held, by agreement, twelve measures of grain from the mill of Gorsine; from this he paid the provost every Saturday a sextary of salt to be spent for the brethren’s needs.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Horssum, in the vicinity of Saint Trudo.]

Wishing to leave these revenues free to the church for his soul, he ordained that the provost should receive the measure of this grain and provide the brethren with a supply of salt. He also gave us a dwelling lying before the gate of the courtyard, which paid him two shillings, and another situated in the marsh, paying six pence likewise. He requested that these same coins be distributed to the poor at the washing of feet on the Lord’s Supper.

Afterwards he became a convert among us and died; he assigned two measures of the aforesaid grain to be spent for the brethren’s refreshment on his anniversary.

**12.** Therefore, while Abbot Folcard, often supported by the assistance of honourable men, saw the work of building prosper in his hands and the church rejoicing on every side in firm peace, behold: a few years after Lord Stephen, bishop of Metz, had confirmed the right of the *pecarium*—that is, *bicarium*—of beer, which this monastery possesses from every *camba*, that is brewery, within the liberty of our town of Saint Trudo, men rose against him who drew him away from the harbour of tranquillity and drove him into the grievous affliction of stormy disturbances.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] That is, *bicarium*.]

Nearly all the more powerful leading men of our town attempted to deprive the church of the rights over breweries constructed in our town, asserting that they were subject to the right of no church. They believed that, if they prevailed in this violence against the abbot, they could retain those breweries free forever.

The abbot showed them the recently issued authorities of bishops and warned some of them who refused to pay the brewery due, declaring that those who attempted resistance had been excommunicated by sentence. But since he achieved nothing, he determined to complain to Stephen, bishop of Metz, concerning the violence inflicted on him by them—the same Stephen who had confirmed by written act of his authority the church’s right over breweries.

Stephen wrote back, warning them not to dare inflict any violence on the abbot, and instructing them to preserve the church’s rights by abiding by what he knew had been decided concerning their breweries at an earlier time. But since they did not even then cease, and persisted in the hardness of their former obstinacy, though often warned by the abbot to make satisfaction to the church, they were finally ordered to be excommunicated.

Greatly angered against the abbot over this, they approached their advocate, Count Otto, and asked his counsel about what they should do concerning the sentence of excommunication. With them he went to Liège to the bishop, intending to accuse the abbot of having pronounced against them an unjust sentence of excommunication.

The bishop, having heard the allegations of each side, asked whether those excommunicated had been excommunicated according to the procedure of ecclesiastical prosecution. The priest of the church affirmed that he had excommunicated them by ecclesiastical sanction and judicial procedure. The bishop likewise confirmed by his authority the sentence of excommunication pronounced against them, judging that they should not be absolved before they restored to the church its rights, which they had wickedly attempted to take away.

Thus compelled by necessity to make satisfaction to the abbot, they promised, though unwillingly, amendment and obedience of due submission, and were absolved from the bond of excommunication.

[Col. 0233A] **13.** Among the men of this conspiracy was a certain Ruthard, surnamed Gun, the abbot’s fiercest adversary in this conspiracy of the townspeople against the church. His proud contention against the abbot, which reason could not end, swift death ended.

For while both parties were fiercely stirred against one another over the aforesaid right, and while Ruthard, surrounded by many adherents, said that the abbot would never obtain that right, swearing that for this reason he would inflict very great losses upon the church, the abbot replied: “Why do you threaten that you will afflict me and my church, when you do not consider that you will be buried by me?”

Ruthard scorned this statement with derision and boasted in the vain confidence of youth that he would outlive Folcard, because he was younger. After a bitter altercation between them, they at last parted. Swollen with rage, he returned home; three days later he took to his bed and began to be tormented by a severe illness.

He summoned his friends and the chief men of the city and sent to the abbot, now humble and repentant, begging him to deign to visit him in his illness. The abbot consented to his request, came, anointed the sick man with oil, and graciously granted forgiveness for the wrongs he had committed against him.

Since Ruthard lacked offspring, he left the churches of God as heirs to his possessions, of which he had an abundance. He obtained from the abbot permission to give for his soul the goods that fell under the abbot’s jurisdiction. Accordingly, he gave our church fifteen shillings at the village of Engelmunshoven, assigning them for the purchase of lights: one at the altar of Saint Trudo, another before the altar of Saint Peter, and a third before the altar of Saint Leonard.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Engelshoven, near Saint Trudo.]

He contributed ten shillings to the hospital, payable from his property at Hesbin.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Hespen.]

He also donated five shillings to the church of Blessed Mary. Not long afterwards he died and was buried in the courtyard by the abbot, as Folcard had threatened him when he stood proudly against him.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] In the table of chapters these matters are rather inappropriately joined with the following chapter.]

**14.** There were besides many others guilty of the same conspiracy against the abbot. Having made satisfaction to the church, they deserved, as we have said, to be absolved from excommunication. Others, however, puffed up by fear of abandoning their obstinacy and unwilling to repent, died excommunicated.

One of these was Elias of Kyrkem. Though he possessed a brewery in the market, he could in no way be compelled, even while excommunicated, to pay any portion of the church’s due from it. Later he sold it to one of the city’s leading men, Arnulf by name, son of Otto the Rich; Arnulf’s heirs, paying us nothing from it, retain it free to the present day.

Thus Abbot Folcard, girded with zeal for justice and courage, fought alone against many and conquered. What scarcely any man younger than he could have achieved by labour, he, already worn out by age, courageously obtained through arduous toil against violent men; and he left it to his church for perpetual possession after him.

Adam, *scultetus* of the bishop of Metz—whose predecessor Arnulf, likewise *scultetus*, had also become a convert among us, a man eminent among his own people—came to the abbot under the guidance of reason, offered satisfaction for the hostility he had shown against the church, and, reconciled to the abbot, acknowledged in full the rights of that church. For his own brewery and that of his brother Guntram, he paid the abbot ten shillings.

The abbot, considering the necessary friendship of such a man, who was not his man, gave him ten shillings as a benefice, so that he might make him his man and render a faithful man more faithful and a friend more friendly. He gave him the holding of Herzo of Baltershoven, four shillings which a certain Arnulf of Halmale held, and likewise twelve pence paid by Lambert of the Marsh, surnamed Dume.

Since he had borrowed these from the brothers’ allowance, he compensated the provost with an equal number of shillings due to himself from the diminished city tithe.

In earlier times there was a brewery in the village of Meceres which served the office of the *scultetus*, and from which he paid the provost nine measures of beer annually. Since in Abbot Folcard’s days it had disappeared because of the inhabitants’ poverty, Folcard gave another brewery, built in the street called Stone Street beside the church of Saint Gengulf, to Everard, who at that time was *scultetus*. He prescribed how much beer Everard should pay from it: two measures on Maundy Thursday for the washing of the poor’s feet, part of seven measures to the provost’s workers when they cut the hay of the Meceres meadow, and another part to the reapers when the grain of our estate adjoining the city was cut.

Everard himself, honourable in knighthood and a man of great devotion toward God, had bought a dwelling between our courtyard and the church of Blessed Mary and built a hospital. To it he had given one meadow and an allod of land lying beside the spring called Saint Gengulf’s. These then brought only a small income to that house; now, however, since houses have been built on every side and many people live there, the same place pays the hospital thirty shillings every year.

**15.** Reiner the *grutarius*, a very worthy man and related by birth to the abbot, gave the church five shillings in the suburb of our town, in the place called New House, and established that an anniversary should be held therefrom in his name and in that of his wife Engheltrud.

There are also some other distinguished efforts of Abbot Folcard’s pious labour worthy of narration, which we judged it not unsuitable to insert in this work.

**16.** Therefore, while he rejoiced that he had defeated the violence of the townspeople and hoped for rest after the exhaustion of so great a labour, behold, an unexpected matter occurred to him, one he had not foreseen, which afflicted him with no less labour than that of the preceding time.

For when his dispute with the townspeople had been ended, he was sitting in the monastery of Saint Lambert and joyfully discussing with his companions his return home, a messenger of Cardinal Gerard suddenly arrived, ordering him to restore to the abbot of Saint Martin the rent from houses at Cologne, long withheld, or, if he refused, to come to Cologne to answer for it.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] He was cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Domnica.]

Returning home, he prepared the necessities for the journey as quickly as possible. Arriving in Cologne on the day after Epiphany, he received a postponement until the general hearing at Easter and returned. When the days of the sacred Resurrection had passed, he came to Cologne on the appointed day.

But the provost and dean of the greater church and the wisest of the clergy considered that the dignity of our order would be diminished if such eminent men came to contend against one another under the judgment of a lay person. They therefore decided to settle their dispute by the following arrangement.

They decreed that the house adjoining the wall should be ours, and that our church should possess it perpetually by right of freedom; but the other two houses, built on the opposite side of the street, since they were not ours, should pass into the right of the abbot of Saint Martin. Nor was this unjust. For Saint Evergisilus, founder of the church of Saint Martin, had freely granted to that place, where on the passage of that blessed bishop he had heard heavenly harmony, whatever was contained from the Grain Gate to the Rhine Gate, together with the market. Thus the two houses enclosed within the bounds of that same territory rightly passed into the jurisdiction of the aforesaid church.

The holdings of these three houses paid eighteen pence, of which one third accrued to our uses and the rest to those of the aforesaid abbot. Thus the reciprocal dispute of the abbots over their respective rights was settled through the skill of the clergy; what belonged to each was justly restored, and they avoided the judgment of lay persons, to which it did not befit them to submit.

**17.** These things, therefore, and many others which his predecessors in earlier times, though they had attempted them with great diligence, had been unable to acquire for the church, he—better, so to speak, reserved for those times and enjoying more favourable fortune—not only acquired, but also left to his sons for perpetual possession, free from every human claim or opposition.

As he was advanced in age and worn out by much labour from his youth itself, he drew near to his end. When the day of his calling was already approaching, he took to a sickbed; attended by the devout assembly of his brethren and sons, having confessed, received communion, and been anointed, he died on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the year 1145. He deserved a burial place in the middle of the monastery before the chapel of Saints Trudo and Eucherius.

He presided over the monastery for seven years, two months, and seven days.

This man of revered memory had also purchased from the heirs and given to the church a certain allod in the village of Hakendover, paying seven shillings. From it he had directed that six shillings be given for the brethren’s refreshment and twelve pence to the servants on the day of his death. Foreseeing the future and fearing that this allod might someday be taken from the church by the violence of the inhabitants, he ordained that the aforesaid amount should be supplied to the brethren and servants from the revenues of our neighbouring estates, which he himself had redeemed from pledge.

18. Moreover, he ordained that the day of the Lord’s Transfiguration, the commemoration of the blessed martyr Lawrence and of Saint Lambert, and likewise of Saint Nicholas and Mary Magdalene, should be celebrated solemnly; and in honor of these same saints he directed that two solidi be given to the brethren on each day of their respective solemnities. And, as reverence for his pious devotion increased, he established a light before the altar of Saint Nicholas, which, like the other provisions, he ordered to be paid for out of the aforesaid estates. Conrad, however, who at that time was provost-major of the church, being entangled in great anxieties over debts, with many prayers scarcely obtained permission from the abbot to mortgage them to him, though he faithfully promised that he would redeem them in the same year. But when, not many days later, that venerable father departed this world, the provost, forgetting his promise, neglected to redeem the mortgaged estates. Thus the brethren were deprived for a long time of the charity established for them by the abbot; nevertheless, they did not cease to celebrate solemnly the aforesaid commemorations of the saints.

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK  
### ON THE DEEDS OF LORD GERARD, ABBOT.

[Note: “[adds: of the third part,” 1*.]]

[Col. 0235]

[Col. 0235D] 1. In the year of the Lord 1145, in the eighth year of the reign of Conrad III, counted by his name, and the ninth year of the episcopate of Albero II, when Abbot Folcard died on the sixth day before the Ides of May [Note: “Above it is read: the fifth day before the Ides of May.”], Gerard, son of Count Gislebert, our advocate, was appointed abbot by the common election of the brethren. They seemed, indeed, to have chosen him chiefly by using the sounder judgment for this reason: because Count Otto, brother of this Gerard, was hostile to the church, and, with his brother presiding over them, he would inflict no further violence upon them, but would protect their possessions by his defense against the rapacity of other robbers. The senior members of the cloister having been sent after him, he was recalled from Cluny, whither he had gone a few days previously; and on the eighth day before the Kalends of August he was received by the brethren and people, with a great multitude of both sexes.

He governed the church in great peace and tranquillity, and suffered none of the troubles or hardships of affliction that his predecessors had endured. This memorial of his virtue and probity he left to posterity.

2. He took and utterly destroyed in the following manner the house of Macharius, his reeve at Hales, whose father John had repeatedly provoked Abbot Rodulf by the attacks of his arrogance. Macharius had fortified this house like a castle, on every side with ditches and watercourses. When Macharius, swollen with vain pride, opposed the abbot and carried out in deed, as though lawful to him, whatever pleased his mind, it happened that he grievously injured a servant of the abbot and, showing contempt for the abbot and for his messenger who had engaged the servant, even stripped him of his horse. Upon learning this, [Col. 0237B] the abbot blazed up in fierce anger against Macharius. Reporting the matter to his brother the count, he sought his aid against the robber and brought him with him as far as Hales in order to exact satisfaction from Macharius for the injury done to himself.

Admitted into the court, the count summoned Macharius, ordered the horse which he had taken to be brought before him, and, since Macharius could not excuse himself for the injury inflicted upon the abbot, expelled him from the house with his wife and children by the judgment of his men, delivering the house and all his possessions into the abbot’s hands. When the abbot had remained there for several days, and Macharius, being savage in spirit, did not deign to offer anything worthy of satisfaction, the abbot took counsel with his men. He levelled the earthen ditches, threw down the towers, and destroyed the whole house. Yet afterward, through the mediation of Count Louis of Loon [Note: “Son of Arnulf V, count of Looz.”], [Col. 0237C] he granted Macharius his favor and restored his dwelling, together with the other things which he had taken from him.

3. At that time Cardinal Gerard crossed from Rome into Gaul and, holding councils in many cities, came to Liège. Intending to hold his synod there, he ordered Abbot Gerard to be present. But the abbot placed the purpose he had formed above the cardinal’s command; setting out for Flanders, he scorned to come to Liège. The cardinal, indignant and declaring that an injury had been done to the pope in his own person, ordered our church to cease from the celebration of divine offices and prohibited the abbot, by the authority of blessed Peter and of the pope himself, from entering the house of God. Returning from Flanders, the abbot, compelled by necessity, followed the aforesaid Gerard, who was returning to Rome, as far as Trier; there he obtained his favor by means of money.

4. Not many days afterward, namely in the year of the Lord 1146, Lord Gerard obtained from Theoderic, count of Flanders [Note: “Theoderic of Alsace, 1128–1168.”], confirmation concerning our village and our possessions at Proviin. In the same year, when [Col. 0238A] Count Otto, brother of the same Lord Abbot Gerard, had come to his end under an increasing illness and was despaired of as to life, he gave to the church, for the redemption of his own soul and those of his heirs, a certain village called Aleym [Note: “On the lower Meuse.”]. Not long afterward he died and lies buried in the cloister, beside his mother, near the entrance of the monastery on the northern side.

When his funeral rites had been completed, in the presence of Henry II, bishop of Liège, and Count Arnulf of Loon, his brother Theoderic, canon of Saint Lambert’s, Bruno—who afterward obtained the archdeaconry of the same church—Arnulf of Curterse [Note: “Near Diest.”], and many other nephews of his, confirmed the count’s transfer by their authority and caused it to be established for the church in perpetuity by the bishop’s ban.

[Col. 0238B] 5. Nevertheless, the aforesaid Arnulf broke his promise and, five years after Otto’s death, in 1150, usurping the grant made to the monastery, committed violence; but the abbot, bringing suit against him, compelled him to make restitution. [Note: “A charter of Abbot Gerard concerning this matter, written in the year 1150, is printed in Mantelius, p. 75.”]

In the ninth year of the prelacy of Lord Renerus [Note: “Rather, Gerard. What follows is false: Albero II had already died in 1145; see Jaffé, p. 281. Henry II succeeded him and remained until 1164.”], which was the year of the Lord 1153, Albero II, bishop of Liège, died; Henry II succeeded him and governed for thirteen years. In the same year [Note: “1152.”], when Emperor Conrad III, counted by his name, died, Frederick I succeeded and ruled for thirty-seven years [Note: “Thirty-nine.”].

6. Thereafter Lord Gerard himself, weary of the evils and storms of secular affairs, wishing to live as a private person, desired to resign the gift of the abbacy into the hands of Henry II, bishop of Liège. But some took this ill, [Col. 0238C] and petition was made to the bishop of Liège that he should by no means consent. The bishop of Liège refused to grant the petitioner’s request; indeed, he expressly commanded him to preside with paternal solicitude over the house of God, whose governance he had undertaken.

7. But afterward, overcome by Gerard’s importunity, he yielded; and, at the urging of certain noble kinsmen and friends of Gerard, he consented to the deposition of one who wished it.

8. Therefore, being about to leave the abbacy in the year of the Lord 1155, he obtained from the brethren that he might be present at their election, so that by his authority he might approve the person and character of the man elected. And so it occurred, since the brethren willingly obeyed him in all things. On the day appointed for the election he was present with the brethren, and they elected Wiricus—[Col. 0238D] the church’s provost-major and librarian—as his successor and as a father to themselves, all acclaiming him with one voice.

After a few days had passed, now a private person, he went to Flanders, as he had long intended in his heart. He sought the monastery of Saint Peter, situated at Ghent, and, being honorably received by Abbot Sygerus, lived there with the brethren under the rule of common life for several years. Thence, summoned by the abbot of Cluny, he undertook the governance of one of their cells, three miles distant from us, named Bertreys [Note: “Near Montenaken, in the neighborhood of Waremme.”]. When he had presided over it for some time and through his diligence had made it better than he found it, he was persuaded by the counsel of those favorable to him to return to us. Abandoning the dwelling of that place, which had greatly pleased him before, [Col. 0240A] and the care of the house entrusted to him, he turned back to us. Having then lived honorably among us according to the rule for some time, he died in a good old age and obtained a place of burial in the monastery near the entrance to the choir, on the right-hand side toward the south. He governed the monastery for eleven years and lived nineteen years after relinquishing the abbacy; he died in that same year, 1174.

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK  
### A LITTLE BOOK OF THE DEEDS OF LORD WIRICUS, ABBOT OF THIS PLACE.

[Note: “[adds: of the third part,” 1*.]]

[Col. 0239]

[Col. 0239B] 1. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1155, Wiricus, provost-major and librarian of the church, having been elected by the brethren in the manner already described and appointed abbot in place of the departing father, set out for Worms, to the court of Emperor Frederick [Note: “Who had returned from Italy in September 1155.”], believing that he would find the bishop of Metz there. Not finding him, he hastened to Metz in search of him. By chance Hillinus, archbishop of Trier and legate of the Apostolic See, was then present. When Wiricus had been presented to him and explained the reason for his journey, supported by the approval of Hillinus’s authority and brought by him into the presence of Bishop Stephen, he obtained without any difficulty the grant of election which he sought. For since he had been known to and familiar with him before the election, it is no wonder that he could easily obtain whatever he requested, [Col. 0239C] even if the aforesaid archbishop had not been present as his supporter. Familiar acquaintance with the rich is very often of service to people in their necessities.

2. Having thus obtained the grant of election and preparing to return home, he was ordered by the aforesaid archbishop of Trier, who was bound to him by great affection, to join his retinue, and was brought as far as Trier. There the archbishop warmly commended him to Henry, bishop of Liège, who was returning from the emperor’s court, and earnestly requested him, out of affection for Wiricus, to assist him in his affairs. The bishop took him and all his companions with him to Liège; and on the day following his return, while celebrating Mass, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, 1156, he consecrated him abbot.

[Col. 0239D] When this became known, the canons of the church of Saint John the Evangelist came to the bishop. They said that they would not give their assent to his consecration until he had answered them, in the place of his predecessor, concerning an injustice which, as they asserted, had been done them by Gerard. For Abbot Gerard had drawn to his own side and taken from them a certain island called Edecus, situated within the boundary of our allod and that of those canons—justly, as he thought; unjustly, as they themselves maintained. Though he had been summoned four times to come before the bishop’s tribunal, he had neglected to appear. Therefore it was finally decreed by the judgment of noble persons [Col. 0240B] that the said island should pass freely into the right and possession of those canons.

When Abbot Wiricus was asked whether he would answer them concerning this complaint, he did not refuse. Having obtained a truce until the feast of Saint Lambert, 17 September, he returned home with his companions.

3. Received solemnly by the brethren and people, as was fitting, he immediately directed his mind to repairing the cloister. He hired workmen and purchased, at no small price, stones, columns, and the other things necessary for that work. Considering that the building of the intended work could not be completed without great expense, he set aside separately for the time being the portion of stones that had been brought to him. He waited until a more favorable season would allow other materials to be transported more conveniently, [Col. 0240C] and, with the help of God and the saints aiding him, he might transform the cloister into a form of beauty better than that which it then possessed.

For it was roofed with wooden shingles, which were nearly consumed with age; rain entered in various places through open cracks. Thus, in times of rain or snow, which often ran down to the wall, the entire community suffered serious inconvenience. The entire circuit of the cloister was also supported by wooden posts for the sake of the community; it was enclosed by an old wall, with columns, bases, and capitals, in rustic workmanship, as far as the wall of Saint Lambert’s chapel. We shall speak more fully of these matters later, when our narrative reaches that point.

4. Therefore, as we have mentioned above, when he had come to Liège on the Lord’s Day, namely the vigil of Saint Lambert, 16 September, [Col. 0240D] in order to answer the canons of Saint John as he had promised, and when neither party had been able in any way to bring their contentious dispute, prolonged from the first hour of the day until evening, to an end, finally, after Vespers had ended, it was decreed by the judgment of the nobles present that the sentence formerly pronounced concerning the same allod should remain valid, and that the church of Saint John should possess that island freely in perpetuity, without objection from any opponent. [Note: “1* reads: ‘they should possess.’”] Yet, through a remarkable turn of fortune and the intervention of impediments arising from various occasions, [Col. 0241A] it produced no fruits of benefit for them down to our own times.

5. While he was directing his mind to the repair of the cloister, wholly burning day and night with the anxiety of this undertaking, and while the church prospered under so suitable, though recently appointed, a ruler, behold: by the wondrous dispensation of almighty God, who never punishes the faults of sinners by an unjust judgment, we experienced both his great anger toward us and his grace. For in the first year of his consecration, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, when the city, kindled by suddenly rising masses of flame, was burning, and, with a great part of it already consumed, the conquering flame was licking what remained, while the brethren were offering to God the chants of the morning office, a slight spark, carried by the wind, fell beside the tower on the western side upon dry wood. [Col. 0241B] There, gradually increasing through fuel, the raging fire seized the dry material of the whole aisle; the heat of the flames, suddenly belching upward, also caught the roof rising above of the neighboring tower.
