Two men, promised a payment, swiftly climbed up. With great danger to their lives, they scarcely extinguished the fire and rescued the tower from impending conflagration. But the fire, spreading freely over the other nearby things [Note: “1* reads: ‘spreading abroad.’”], attacked the roof of the monastery on its eastern side, partly covered with wooden shingles and partly with lead. Though the brethren strove to remove what was within the monastery, and none could now resist it, the fierce flame consumed it all, our sins demanding it.

[Col. 0241C] The western tower on the northern side, together with the tower adjoining it in which the bells hung, remained unharmed, although the third tower was already ablaze, through the skill and labor of faithful laymen who drove the fire away from the bells. Nevertheless, the fourth tower, on the eastern side toward the south, burned when the devouring flame consumed everything nearby. Upon it stood a gilded cross with a large likewise gilded orb, which struck back the eyes of those looking from afar with the brilliance of its splendor.

The armarium, where chalices were customarily kept, also burned; likewise the forms [Note: “Folding seats for the chanters.”] in the choir, handsome for the beauty of their workmanship; seats too, quite convenient for the brethren either to stand or sit upon; and many other things, sufficiently precious because of their usefulness, perished, reduced to nothing by the raging fire.

[Col. 0241D] Likewise: when the monastery, with both apses, the two towers already mentioned, and the four aisles, had been burned, the chancel, together with two adjoining apses, remained unburned, protected by a stone vault [Note: “That is, *volta*, a vaulting or arch.”] arching over it. Moreover, the entire circuit of the cloister, the dormitory, the abbot’s lodging, and the refectory—partly roofed with tiles and partly with thatch—remained untouched by the fire in a wondrous manner.

Here anyone may observe that almighty God, in the marvellous mercy of his dispensation, wished us to experience both [Col. 0242A] his anger and his grace. For unless he himself, by the power of his mercy, had preserved the things that survived the fire, they could by no human power have been saved, since sparks from the completed conflagration were falling widely upon dry, as it were, straw.

The upper and lower mills, with everything adjoining them, were burned. A great pile of wood placed beside the wall of the refectory burned, while the thatched roof of that house remained unharmed. The fire also consumed the brewhouse, the bakehouse, the house in which the poor were fed, together with its orchard, and the small houses built here and there throughout the court. The granary alone, with the grain-store shining amid the fire all around, remained unburned. In the same year the monastery of Gembloux was burned.

[Col. 0242B] 6. Meanwhile the abbot had departed some days previously for Utrecht; and, with the business of his journey now completed, he was returning home, unaware of what had happened to his people. The news of this terrible devastation reached him while he was staying in our village of Alburch, and struck his mind and the minds of all present with the sorrow of grievous tidings. When, after the heavy sighs drawn from the depths of his breast by the sadness of this sudden news, he heard that the cloister and the other things mentioned had remained unburned, placing all his hope in God and his saint Trudo, and putting on the spirit of a strong man who can neither be cast down by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity, he urged his people to grieve more moderately over what they had heard and hastened home with all speed.

But when, approaching the monastery, he saw with his own eyes [Col. 0242C] the devastation of the recent fire, he groaned deeply under the sharp prompting of grief. Yet he did not despair of the help of God and of his holy patron, believing that he could build things better than those burned; immediately he manfully girded himself for the repair of the monastery. Within a few days, therefore, he erected over the bodies of the blessed Trudo and Eucherius a wooden structure, small indeed but suitable for the time, and caused the brethren there to chant day and night their customary praises to God.

Compelled, then, by the necessity of repairing the monastery, he interrupted the work on the cloister, to which he had already long directed himself with all the ardor of his mind. A few days later, one of the leading men of our village, named Rutard, drawing near to death as his illness grew worse, gave ten marks for conveying the brethren’s wine. He ordered these marks to be spent for the uses of the church in such a manner [Col. 0242D] that, when the brethren’s wine had been stored in the cellar, the same sum should be taken from there in the following year and thereafter should always be kept ready. [Note: “1* reads *expendendos*, ‘to be spent,’ in the masculine.”]

Moreover, he established that four anniversaries should be observed from it: his own, his wife’s, his father’s, and his mother’s. That is, if the aforesaid marks should perhaps be spent on other uses of the church, sixteen solidi paid from his property at Sarchinium to the provost should be given to the brethren for their refreshment on those same anniversaries.

While Abbot Wiricus [Col. 0243A] labored with every care to see whether he could in any way cover the bare face of the church, which by its vastness appeared dreadful and pitiable to the eyes of those who saw it, suddenly the occasion of another, similar anxiety arose. For our house at Cologne, one of the principal towers of the city, threatened collapse because its front wall hung precipitously; it lay close to the Rhine, and there was only a narrow public passage between it and the riverbank.

Therefore, during the days of the Nativity of the Lord, the people of Cologne sent a messenger to the abbot, commanding him to come to Cologne to repair his house, or, if he would not, that they themselves would complete at their own expense the repairs that had to be made. Thus Abbot Wiricus was surrounded by a wonderful [Note: “1* reads *mura*, ‘walls.’”] agitation of anxiety. Fearing that, if he neglected what the people of Cologne had ordered, [Col. 0243B] he might afterward somehow be hindered by them in repairing the same house, he entrusted the diligent completion of the buildings to his reeve Everard, a very worthy and energetic man, and to certain more diligent brethren. He then hastened to Cologne to repair the house, which was on the point of collapse.

Considering that it could not be repaired without great expense, he borrowed fifteen marks from a certain faithful person and, as though he already possessed all that was necessary for the repair, resolved, at the beginning of March 1157, to demolish it utterly, according to the saying of the comic poet:

> He who has well begun has half the work.

[Note: “Horace, *Epistles* I.2.40.”]

How much he spent in the very great labor of its destruction I pass over, wishing to preserve brevity. Once the foundation of the new work had been laid, since neither the stones themselves nor the mortar, because of their age, were suitable for the new construction, he completed the whole fabric of the house marvellously, between the feasts of Saint Gertrude and Saint Martin, with great labor and great expenditure, besides what he spent in going and returning.

Having installed a tenant in it, he caused five and a half marks to be paid to himself, whereas from the time of Abbot Theoderic, for almost forty-eight years [Note: “Rather, fifty; compare above, VI.26.”], [Col. 0243C] only half a mark, and scarcely even that, had been paid until then. For when the provost of Moselle came to Cologne to demand it, the tenant said that he had spent the rent on improving the furnishings of the house, and gave the provost nothing but smooth words of deceitful argument.

For the twenty-two years during which he held the church free, Abbot Wiricus annually received from its occupant the amount fixed as aforesaid. He had also previously redeemed it for eight marks when he was provost, against the will of his predecessor, who wished to sell it.

Thus [Note: “In the margin, a contemporary hand adds: ‘in the year 1157.’”], while, as has been said, he was occupied with repairing the house at Cologne, Everard the judge worked vigorously, [Col. 0244A] together with the other brethren to whom that care had been assigned; and the work at home zealously went forward. Through them he also repaired in the same year the aisle adjoining the chancel and the tower on the northern side, with large and strong materials; by swift work he restored it to a condition better than it had been before the fire. He roofed it by a new method of covering, until then unused in our parts and highly effective against fire: namely, with thinly cut stones.

As time went on, he completed the monastery itself, from the chancel as far as the tomb of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, in strong and admirable workmanship, and made it beautiful with the roof covering by which he had roofed the aisle. Thus, within sixteen years, through the diligence of the abbot and the brethren who were collaborators in the same work, a structure better and more handsome than the former was splendidly completed, from the chancel to the western towers, with the apses and aisles of the whole monastery.

[Col. 0244B] In the year of the Lord 1158, on the Nones of September, three suns were seen in the western part of the sky; but as two gradually disappeared, the sun of the day, which was the middle one, remained until sunset.

7. In the year of the Lord 1159, the fifth year of Abbot Wiricus [Note: “If one reckons 1155 as Wiricus’s first year, the fourth year was running from his consecration.”], when Pope Adrian died on the third day before the Kalends of September [Note: “Rather, 1 September.”], a grave contention concerning the papacy arose at Rome between Roland and Octavian. [Note: “I do not know whether the author had before his eyes those few words under 1160 in the Aquicinctine Continuation.”] For, with parties discordant among themselves, both had been elected to the honor of the papacy. One of them, namely Octavian, was favored by Emperor Frederick and his followers; the other, that is Roland, was supported against the imperial party by the power of many nobles, and especially by William the Sicilian.

[Col. 0244C] It seems not inappropriate to set forth briefly here the cause of this contention and discord between them. When certain hostile conflicts had arisen between Pope Adrian and Emperor Frederick [Note: “The arguments which follow are drawn from the letters of Adrian and Frederick found in the Aquicinctine Continuation of Sigebert.”], the emperor demanded homage and royal oaths from his bishops; in writing, he put his own name before the pope’s; and he forbade the pope’s cardinals access to the churches and cities of his realm, because he did not see in them the preachers of peace whom the church requires, but despoilers of churches. Provoked by these and other annoyances, the lord pope, seeing that Frederick, though often warned, would not amend his ways, threatened to excommunicate him.

Accordingly, as time went on, when report had already spread that he had entered Italy with an army [Note: “Frederick had already come into Italy in the middle of 1158.”] and, having subjected a great part of it to his power, had occupied without judgment or right certain possessions of Saint Peter, the apostolic lord at last, seizing this occasion, laid before the common assembly a matter of the greatest complaint: that Frederick had resolved to trample down [Col. 0245A] the Roman Church and violently take away for himself all its rights, both imperial and spiritual.

When all in the assembly were disturbed and considered what ought to be done, it was finally decreed that all who were present should swear, giving faith into the pope’s hands, that they must all stand unanimously, with unfailing resolve and even to the shedding of blood, for the honor and liberty of the Roman Church against the emperor and all princes. In order that this decree should not take effect, the supporters of the emperor’s party wisely and shrewdly opposed it, saying:

“Many kings indeed have injured the Roman Church, and at present the Sicilian—perhaps he himself was then present—who has grievously afflicted it [Note: “1* reads *ea*, ‘it.’”]; yet the Church has never armed itself against anyone by securities and oaths of this kind. But if this harmful remedy must be applied to a disease newly arising, let it be made more specifically against the Sicilian, who has injured it more than all others, and only afterward generally against all who have wished to oppress and humiliate this Church. Otherwise, if we arm ourselves in this way against this man, who is the advocate and defender of the Church, we may perhaps provoke him by every means to destroy our Church.”

[Col. 0245B] Convinced by their prudent reply, the supporters of the opposing party fell silent; the plan having thus been frustrated that day, they departed in shame. Nevertheless, afterward, having formed an open conspiracy against the emperor, they confirmed by oath to the lord pope that, should he excommunicate the emperor, they would adhere to his honor and will until death, and would aid him against the emperor in every way. Moreover, confirming these promises by oath, they added that, if it happened that the lord pope died, they ought to choose as future pontiff no one except one of those who had sworn.

They also bound the neighboring bishops by oath not to lay hands in consecration upon any man elected unless the faction of the Sicilian consented to him. In the year aforesaid, after Pope Adrian had died on the third day before the Kalends of September, all assembled according to custom to elect his successor. But because the election proceeded slowly on account of the conspiracy of the opposing party and of those not favoring the emperor, on about the third day [Col. 0245C] matters came to this: fourteen cardinals bound by the oath named Chancellor Roland, while the other nine, who were free of the oath, elected Octavian, cardinal priest, judging him worthy and useful for the government of the Church and for restoring the unity of peace and concord between the Church of God and the Empire.

But while the former hastened to clothe their elect in the mantle, before he had yet put it on, the others forestalled them. At the request of the whole Roman people, by the election of all the clergy, and with the assent of nearly the whole senate, they clothed their own elect in the mantle and, after enthroning him, placed him in the chair of blessed Peter. They then led him to the palace, with all the people acclaiming, the clergy singing a hymn to God, and all rites solemnly fulfilled in due order.

[Col. 0246A] The cardinals of the opposing party withdrew to a certain castle of Saint Peter and remained shut up there for eight days and more. Later, led out by the senators, they withdrew outside the City; and on the twelfth day, in a thing unheard of from the beginning of the world, they invested their elect with the mantle in a castle named Cesterna. At once they sent messengers throughout all Italy, dissuading bishops from coming to the consecration of their elect and threatening them with excommunication and perpetual deposition.

8. In the year of the Lord 1160, when all the magnates of the Empire had been summoned by the emperor to settle this discord [Col. 0246B] and appoint a suitable shepherd for the Church [Note: “At Pavia, where Pope Victor IV was confirmed in February 1160; see Boehmer, 2430–2431.”], Henry, bishop of Liège, was ordered to be present among the foremost, not as the least. He wished Abbot Wiricus to travel with him. Wiricus declined on account of the danger of the journey, but feared that, if he did not go with him, he would be charged by the bishop with the stigma of disobedience. When adequate money for his journey had been offered to him, he went to Italy, turning necessity into willingness.

Having completed a long and difficult journey, he came to Cremona, where Octavian—the pope Victor—was then staying. Relying on the friendship of certain clerics attached to the pope, and being presented by them to the pope for penance, he was held in a position of honor and favor greater than anyone could have expected. [Col. 0246C] These same clerics energetically and warmly managed his cause; and the apostolic lord, by his authority, confirmed as he wished the renewed privileges of our church and gave him great confidence of obtaining whatever his heart desired.

When he had been summoned to the pope on the vigil of Pentecost, after sweet words of friendly conversation, the pope voluntarily granted him, though he had not sought them, the use of ring and mitre as a memorial of himself, and ordered him to prepare himself for service at his Vespers. Seeing unexpected gifts freely offered to him, and that what others usually obtain either scarcely or only with labor was offered to himself, Abbot Wiricus accepted it, gave thanks, and, as commanded, presented himself vested for service at the apostolic lord’s Vespers.

On the following day, when the transalpine clerics—the Germans, Frenchmen, Englishmen, and those from the various provinces present—had obtained from the pope permission to celebrate Mass according to their own custom, he directed the choir by the apostolic lord’s command, because he delighted the ears of all with the gentle, melodious modulation of his exceedingly sweet voice.

[Col. 0246D] A few days later, about to return to his homeland, he took leave of the apostolic lord, who had treated him very paternally and kindly. On the feast of Saint James the Apostle, with a prosperous journey and all those whom he had taken with him in good health, he returned to his own country. Meanwhile Henry, bishop of Liège, who had compelled him to travel unwillingly with him, remained in Italy, hindered by the disturbances of various affairs.

Before the year of his return had ended, namely at Pentecost, 4 June 1161, Henry sent him a messenger from Italy, commanding him, putting aside every excuse, to hasten to meet him at the emperor’s court, which was to be held at Besançon. Abbot Wiricus perceived the intention of the bishop who had sent after him: that he ordered him to attend the court for no other reason than to burden him. Although he lacked the necessities for this journey, he nevertheless obeyed the command of the man who ordered him and came to the court.

Although it had been appointed for Besançon, it was held at Laon on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist [Note: “That is, Laon; see Boehmer, 2445 ff.; on this council see Otto Morena.”], and Pope Victor was there with Emperor Frederick. Therefore, treated very humanely and affectionately, as a son, by the goodwill of the apostolic lord and a certain spiritual privilege of intimacy with him, just as on his former journey, [Col. 0247B] Wiricus returned safely with all his companions, the pope also granting him favor and blessing and wishing him a prosperous journey.

9. In the same year, after the exhaustion of so great and arduous a journey, when rest had been granted him on every side and he was applying himself in every way to the restoration of the monastery, behold: not long afterward, that same year, by the gracious power of merciful God—who rebukes those whom he loves and chastises every son whom he receives—he was drawn back from the very gate of death which he had almost entered. Since I know that an account of what, when, and how this happened will benefit men [Note: [Col. 0247D] *men* 2.] wishing to imitate his virtue, I shall relate it briefly.

[Col. 0247C] Some days after his consecration had already passed [Note: [Col. 0247D] A.D. 1156.], while he was still newly presiding over the church, a certain Franco of Dumella, who held from him the tithe of Lesser Exele [Note: [Col. 0248D] Evel.], for which he owed him provisions after two years, came to him complaining that Abbot Gerard of Floreffe, contrary to the reverence due to his order, had violently and unjustly injured him in respect of his goods belonging to the church. For Abbot Gerard had granted him, despite the protest of this same Franco and without the knowledge of any of his brethren, the tithe of the aforesaid village [Note: [Col. 0248D] Of Saint Trudo.] for an annual payment of six solidi; and the aforesaid abbot of Floreffe, because through a certain spiritual intimacy he had influence with Bishop Henry, had procured confirmation of this arrangement by the bishop’s written authority.

[Col. 0247D] Therefore, when Abbot Wiricus had heard the complaint of his dependent against the violence of the aforesaid abbot, he asked him whether anything of those things of which he complained he had been deprived still remained anywhere within his legal possession and control. When he heard his testimony that three measures of rye still remained, he ordered him to take those measures and hold them under his authority until the matter between him and the abbot of Floreffe could be decided by judgment. For he considered that a man of [Col. 0248A] so great an order and standing would not have wished to inflict such violence upon him without some reason.

The man departed, took the grain as he had been ordered, and, when the messengers of the aforesaid abbot wished to take it away, forbade them by the authority of his lord. When he learned of this, the abbot of Floreffe angrily approached the bishop; complaining of the injury inflicted upon him, as he said, by Abbot Wiricus, he had him summoned to a hearing. Thus summoned, he came; and, questioned by the bishop concerning the abbot’s aforesaid complaint, he defended himself and replied:

“I do not recall having done this abbot any injury or injustice; but I wish to protect the goods of our church, wherever they may be, with the authority that I ought.”

When Abbot Gerard replied that he had received the tithe of the aforesaid village by agreement from Abbot Gerard, with the knowledge and testimony of sons of the church, and that he had the bishop’s written instrument concerning it, Abbot Wiricus, after many words of denial, added this:

“If no credit is given to my assertions, send any trustworthy messenger to the brethren of my church; let him carefully investigate how the matter was conducted. And if he finds any one of them aware of this testimony of his, then let him justly and freely possess forever that which he now unjustly seeks.”

On hearing this, the bishop was astonished: either because he had caused him to be summoned to a hearing over such a matter when the facts were quite otherwise, or because he had consented that untrue statements should be confirmed with his seal when they ought not to have been confirmed. But Abbot Wiricus, lest he put the aforesaid abbot to greater shame by covering him with a deep blush, redeemed the same tithe from the aforesaid Franco, who was his legal representative [Col. 0248C] in the matter, for eight marks; and, adding four solidi to the amount of the former agreement, granted it to the aforesaid abbot for an annual payment of ten solidi.

From this there arose grave and hostile conflicts between the same abbot of Floreffe and the aforesaid Franco. Since the latter, being fierce in spirit and full of deceit, was planning to plunder the abbot’s goods and, if he could, to kill him, the abbot, fearing for himself and his men, repeatedly and humbly begged Lord Abbot Wiricus, out of regard for his fear, somehow to make him his friend. Abbot Wiricus assented to his request, extracted from Franco a truce of almost five years, and appointed a day for the two men to be reconciled.

Since this was to take place, as was said above, in the very year of his return from the emperor’s court, on the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul (A.D. 1162, 24 January), and since he had gone there with a few of his men, he lodged that night in the house of the same Franco. Therefore, in the silence of the dead of night, while all were asleep, certain knights, called counts of the French, burst in with armed forces from every side, prepared to seize or kill Franco. Franco escaped swiftly with his men; some of the abbot’s retainers were captured; and the abbot himself, not knowing who he was, they severely wounded [Col. 0249A] in the right shoulder, along with a certain knight, his marshal, in the back.

Yet God in a wondrous manner, who permitted him to be wounded almost unto death, preserved his life amid the swords of the wicked, foreseeing that, as afterward became clear, his church would be nobly enlarged through him in buildings and possessions. For when some of his men had been captured and others had sought safety in flight, he alone remained. Nearly half alive, he had leaned his head against a nearby doorpost when one of the armed men, running through the darkened house, came upon him lying there. Seizing him by the neck, and thinking him one of his enemies, he brandished his sword as though about to cut off his head; but, his blow missing, he struck the doorpost, God thus protecting him.

Terrified by the fear of death, and drawing almost his last breath beneath the hand of the assailant, he was unable, because of the anguish of his spirit, to answer the question of who he was. The attacker, thinking that he had already died, withdrew. Recovering a little breath, while they were preparing to burn the house, he crawled away on hands and feet, aided by the cover of night, by what seemed to him the safer route, and escaped the imminent danger to his life. They, however, set the house on fire and departed victorious, laden with plunder.

When morning came, conscious of their guilt, they sent back to the abbot his horses and servants together with almost all the plunder, and, although late, deeply repented of having wronged him unknowingly. Carried thence by his faithful men to the town of Fuich, and soon afterward brought back from there to the monastery, he was at last wholly restored to health by the strenuous efforts of physicians, although very many who had tried medicine despaired of his recovery. [Col. 0249C]

But those who had committed this act against him afterward came to his knees for mercy, as commonly happens in satisfactions for offenses of this kind; and, making satisfaction through the penance of public confession that they had unknowingly sinned against him, they deserved the favor of his forgiveness.

In the same year Brustem was devastated and burned, along with other neighboring villages, by the count of Duras. [Note: [Col. 0249D] Aegidius; cf. Mantel, p. 80.]

10. Some days later Henry, the dean, who had held the church of Blessed Mary from almost the time of Abbot Rodulf, came to the end of his life as bodily illness grew worse. Anointed by Abbot Wiricus, and having restored to him the gift belonging to the church which he possessed, he died in the middle of June and was granted burial in the middle of the choir, [Col. 0249D] before the screen of the aforesaid church.

When his death became known, Archdeacon Alexander came to Abbot Wiricus to petition him for that same church; he also brought with him Henry, bishop of Liège, so that, with his support, he might more easily obtain what he had less power to obtain on his own. But Abbot Wiricus frustrated their petition by a prudent answer and, by a sufficiently cautious and shrewd pretext of excuse, prevented what they sought from being carried into effect. He maintained that he had long ago assigned it by oath to the brethren’s prebend, and that he was not permitted to revoke what he had established with the assent of many.

Although the refusal of their request had covered their faces with deep shame, he nevertheless purchased their favor by frequent services and a great gift; at last he obtained that they should release that same church by their own authority and assign it in perpetuity, free, to the brethren’s prebend, as had been determined. To prevent any of their successors from being allowed to infringe this, they confirmed it with the seal of their authority and with witnesses; and they prescribed how it was to discharge episcopal food-dues or archidiaconal rights.

In the following year, namely 1161, Abbot Wiricus obtained this confirmation of the church of Blessed Mary in the town and [Col. 0250B] of the church of Mylen from Alexander the archdeacon; and, two years later, from Henry, bishop of Liège, Rodulf’s successor; likewise, in the course of time, from Victor the supreme pontiff. Charters concerning these matters exist.

11. At the same time the Emperor Frederick, intending to lead an army into Italy [Note: [Col. 0249D] In November 1163 Frederick had departed for Italy for the third time.], gathered all the forces of the Roman Empire and ordered the aforesaid Henry, bishop of Liège, to follow him with the other magnates of the realm. Having followed him, he was soon afterward seized by illness and died in Lombardy. [Note: [Col. 0249D] He died at Pavia on 6 October 1161, according to Aegidius of Aurea Vallis [Col. 0250D].] His body, after the entrails had been removed and it had been boiled, was brought to Liège and honorably buried in the church of Saint Lambert.

He died in the year of the Lord 1164, in the ninth year [Col. 0250C] of Lord Wiricus’s prelacy. Alexander the Second, archdeacon and chief provost of that same church, succeeded him, elected with the consent of the clergy; but he presided over the same church scarcely three years.

For in those days, with empire and priesthood disturbed within Italy, the grave and almost daily tumults of public affairs compelled the Emperor Frederick to summon bishops and the magnates of the kingdom more frequently, in whose counsel he arranged what was to be done. [Note: [Col. 0250D] In November 1166 the emperor again set out for Italy.] The Milanese, having formed a conspiracy against him, were rebuilding their city, formerly destroyed by him; and almost all the cities of Italy, arming and provisioning themselves, were resisting his authority.

Therefore Rainald, archbishop of Cologne, and Alexander, the bishop of Liège mentioned above, having been summoned with the other magnates of the empire, set out for the emperor in [Col. 0250D] Italy (A.D. 1166, 27 November). Abbot Wiricus, ordered by Bishop Alexander to set out with him, remained at home for the time being in order to prepare himself, because necessities for the journey were lacking. He decided to follow him at Easter (A.D. 1167, 9 April)—for the bishop himself had gone ahead at Advent.

When winter had passed and he was about to depart, the mildness of the weather smiling upon him and the necessities of the journey prepared, he who had previously refused to remain despite the entreaties of friends dissuading him from this undertaking was drawn back from his plan by another circumstance. For common report had informed him that the emperor and his men were suffering adverse reverses and were living precariously, with their lives hanging in the balance amid the swords of enemies; moreover, that the road was dangerous for those wishing to travel there because of attacks by robbers; that Italy was laid waste by the army’s ravages; and that the land all around was grievously afflicted by war, fire, famine, and every other kind of misery.

Lest anyone doubt this and believe that, because we were not present at the event and were separated from them by a great distance of lands, we are reporting falsehoods, let him learn from the writings of those who were present that we speak the truth. Rainald, bishop of Cologne, eminent among his own people and, as it were, commander of the entire German army, reporting in writing to the people of Cologne and Liège this devastation of Italy and the battle and victory of the emperor’s soldiers against the Romans, says as follows:

“We have judged it worthy to communicate to you, as to our spiritual children, the inestimable victory of the most sacred empire. For the Romans, having marched far from the city of Rome in the greatest arrogance, pitched camp before Tusculum, where we had taken up position with all our own cavalry and that of the imperial chancellor, on the holy day of Pentecost itself (28 May). On the following day (29 May), that is, Monday, the lord of Mainz and the imperial chancellor [Note: [Col. 0251D] Christian.] were approaching with their cavalry and with the Brabanters. And when they were attempting to pitch their tents near the army of the Romans, the latter suddenly arranged their battle-lines and attacked them with fully forty thousand chosen fighters from the city.

“Meanwhile all our cavalry rushed in from every side, and by divine aid the Romans were broken and defeated in the field with such force, and driven from Tusculum as far as Rome, that the number of dead was reckoned at more than nine thousand, and that of captives at about five thousand. No one could sufficiently enumerate how many tents, coats of mail, other arms, horses, mules, asses, sums of money, and garments they lost there. Now, therefore, with the inestimable army of victory, we are encamped in God’s name before the gates of the City, laying waste all the land of the Romans with fire and sword.” [Note: [Col. 0251D] For the great differences among authors in their description of this victory, see Muratori, *Annals*, at the year 1167 [Col. 0252D].]

We have thought it worthy to insert into our narrative these passages from the writings of those who were present at these events, so that the reader’s mind might be more readily led to believe the things recounted above.

12. Therefore, in the year of the Lord 1167, Bishop Alexander of Liège having died, Rodulf succeeded him in the episcopate, in the twelfth year [Col. 0252B] of Lord Abbot Wiricus’s prelacy. When certain reports of these events had reached us from Italy, Abbot Wiricus, not disbelieving their assertion, was deterred from his intended journey both by the difficulty of travel and by fear of the epidemic raging throughout the army.

For not long after the victory had been won, Rainald, archbishop of Cologne, prince and standard-bearer of the army of all our party, was overtaken by that same epidemic and died in Lombardy. Alexander, bishop of Liège, who was with him, also ended his life there on the fourth day before the Ides of August. [Note: [Col. 0252D] According to Aegidius, the fifth day before the Ides of August.] Once the princes and leading men of the people had died, the impious pestilence, raging without number or distinction, destroyed the remaining common people.

## HERE BEGINS THE FOURTH BOOK

[Note: [Col. 0251] 1* adds: “of the third part.”]

[Col. 0251]

[Col. 0251C] 1. In the year of the Lord 1169, the fourteenth year of Wiricus’s prelacy, he intended to expend whatever money he had collected, by an honorable measure of thrift, for expenditure on the Italian journey, upon a memorial of better and nobler expenditure, God and Saint Trudo his patron thus consenting. Therefore, after demolishing [Note: [Col. 0251] Henschen’s codex reads *jacet* (“lies”) for *destructa* (“demolished”).] the chapel which he had built over the tombs of Saints Trudo and Eucherius when the monastery had been burned some years earlier, he ordered the ground to be dug more deeply in preparation for laying the foundations of a new work.

When, on the left side of the choir, that is, on the south side, the earth had been somewhat excavated with the joyful labor of all who were present, they suddenly found a sarcophagus beside the very entrance to the doorway, covered by a wall of the chapel that met it from the opposite side. An ancient tradition [Col. 0251D] among us held that Saint Libertus the martyr [Col. 0252C] lay buried there. When the sarcophagus was opened, the martyr’s bones were found.

That we might not doubt either his martyrdom or the place of his burial, the outcome confirmed our belief: his congealed blood was found there in the sarcophagus. All the flesh, together with almost all the bones except a few of the larger ones, had been consumed into ashes; and of the head nothing was found except the brain. Therefore, after the holy dust had been gathered and reverently placed with the bones in a clean cloth, while the bells rang and we praised God and his martyr with a voice of rejoicing, the people, stirred by sudden wonder, came running and themselves burst suddenly into devout praise of God and his saint. Taking from his bones and sacred ash the relics required, all the rest was reverently placed [Col. 0252D] in a shrine prepared for this purpose.

Digging on the right-hand side, as the plan of the future work required, they found in the corner of a small wall the bones of two persons: those of one larger and those of the other smaller. But lest we should perhaps be uncertain who these were, we learned by the testimony of our elders that Robert, duke of Hesbaye, who had received and most kindly and humanely protected Blessed Eucherius when he was exiled by Charles, was buried there with his wife. [Note: [Col. 0253D] Cf. continuation of the third part, 1, 2, 7.] They too were therefore moved and reverently placed in a certain shrine.

When they came, digging, before the entrance of the chapel, they found there the sarcophagus of a man unknown to us, but, in our judgment, one of great merit before God and glorious even in life, since he had been committed to burial in so solemn a place and with such reverence. Yet there were some who asserted that he was the companion of Blessed Libertus the martyr and had attained the palm of martyrdom with him. They inferred this from the sign of the large quantity of blood which they found congealed in the sarcophagus. His bones, like those of the others whom we mentioned, were reverently moved and transferred to another little chest.

2. Behind [Note: [Col. 0253] *Behind*—“translation” from the Henschen codex.] the altar of the chapel itself was a vault, very solidly built and compacted with firm cement, in which common opinion held that Saints Trudo and Eucherius were contained. The outcome disproved both this opinion and the assertion of our elders, who said—and had even left it in writing—that they lay in a crypt covered by a double vault. A vault was indeed found, and within it the bodies of the saints; but no traces whatever of a crypt could be found.

Therefore, after a small opening had been made in the rear part of the vault, we found a sarcophagus, and within it, in separate little shrines, the bodies of the two men. Lamps having been brought in and the little chests carefully inspected—for it was night—we all suddenly burst forth, at the abbot’s prompting, from the greatness of our joy into a voice of confession and praise, singing loudly, *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God.” Accordingly, Matins of that very saint were solemnly chanted in honor of our glorious patron.

When morning came and the bells resounded, all the people, learning what had happened, ran together; rejoicing in spirit, each offered whatever small gift he could, showing devoutly the affection he bore toward his patron. Thereupon, when talk began among the people concerning the translation of the saints’ [Col. 0253D] bodies, Abbot Wiricus hesitated for some time, uncertain what to do or where to turn. For it had not been his purpose to seek them beneath the earth or, should they perhaps be found, to translate them; rather, he intended to make the place of their burial, as befitted such great fathers, worthy of adornment by the novelty of beautiful workmanship.

Therefore, with the unanimous wish of all his men that they should be translated, he went to Bishop Rodulf, [Col. 0254A] who at that time presided over the people of Liège after Alexander the Second, and consulted him, together with the wiser and chief men of that church, about what ought to be done in this matter. Hearing the joyful report of this unexpected discovery, they all rejoiced with immense joy, praising God because the translation of fathers so great and such as these had been predestined by him to occur in their own times.

3. Accordingly, in the year of the Lord 1169 [Note: [Col. 0253] The corrector adds “same”; Henschen supplied this chapter.], the sixteenth year of the reign of Frederick the First [Note: [Col. 0254D] Rather, the tenth.], the fourteenth year of the ordination of Lord Abbot Wiricus, and the third year of the episcopate of Rodulf, bishop of Liège, the solemn elevation of the bodies of the same saints was performed on the very day of their translation, and they were translated for the second time.

Present that day with the bishop were Henry, chief provost of the church and likewise [Col. 0254B] archdeacon; Bruno and Rodulf, archdeacons; very many abbots, counts, and powerful men of secular rank; and, besides, an innumerable multitude of people of both sexes. The bishop himself, arrayed in priestly vestments, approached the place reverently with clerics singing the litany before him and with the order of sacred ministers. With great contrition of heart and spiritual exultation of soul, he raised their bodies; they were brought into the middle of the monastery for the people to see and placed in a shrine magnificently fashioned with gold and silver.

When this had been done, the abbot himself directing the choir, Mass in honor of the same saints was solemnly begun and fittingly sung by the bishop. After the canon, he decreed solemnly that the day of their translation [Col. 0254C] should henceforth be celebrated with festive rejoicing by all inhabitants of this place.

The procession which, on that day, could not be held because of the multitude of people who had flocked together, as is customary, was held on the Kalends of September, after a solemn preceding fast. The entire circuit of the city was enclosed by this procession of the saints’ bodies because of the imminent scourge of fire, which that year, after houses had been burned all around, had devastated cities and villages severely with a great conflagration.

Having therefore taken some relics from their sacred bodies for [Note: [Col. 0253] After *for*—“protection” is lacking in H.] health and for our perpetual protection, they were wrapped in a new pall and placed in separate shrines carefully secured with iron. Those shrines in which they had first lain, because they had wholly decayed through age [Col. 0254D] and dampness of the earth, were placed in the sarcophagus mentioned above and honored with the reverence due to their sacred ashes.

4. [Note: [Col. 0253] This chapter too is found in H.] While the work in which they were to be placed was not yet completed [Note: [Col. 0253] “were to be placed” is lacking in H.], and while, as has been stated, they stood in their shrine in the middle of the monastery, many came from far and wide to venerate them. A certain penitent knight from the regions of Normandy, his arm bound with iron, came to us after hearing of their fame; and with tearful sighs, as a diligent suppliant, he faithfully sought their intercession. [Note: [Col. 0255] *intercession* 1*.] Nor was he disappointed in the petition of his faith.

For the effective power of the saints before the Almighty, in response to the faithful petitioner, thus broke the iron bonds by which he was confined. The third day before the Kalends of October was a Sunday, which dawned festive according to custom, when, free from work, the people usually come to church. Because the anniversary of the dedication of our church was to occur on the following day, a larger crowd than usual had assembled.

Meanwhile, while the priest stood at the altar during the canon and the people stood around in silent reverence, the man lay prostrate before the saints’ bodies. Alone, with loud sobbing, as was soon apparent, he troubled the ears of Majesty, and with intent prayers besought it to have mercy on him through the merits of the saints. Suddenly, as if caught up in ecstasy, [Col. 0255B] he saw what appeared to be a cleric of comely form, shining white with age and radiant with great light, coming forth from the choir screen and proceeding toward the place where the shrine stood.

When he began to draw near him, he struck with the staff he carried in his hand the iron which encircled the man’s arm. Immediately it split into two parts and fell to the ground before his feet. The sound of the blow was so loud that it struck the ears of all sitting in the choir. The man was freed; and, believing that in this miracle he had also received forgiveness for his sin, he blessed God and his saints with joyful shouting, made the festal day notably more joyful for the assembled multitude by what had happened to him, and, as we suddenly began the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God”—the ringing of bells sounded together, and one voice of all resounded in praise of God and his saints.

5. Therefore, since Abbot Wiricus wished the work [Note: [Col. 0255] The corrector adds “of the chapel.”] he had begun to be completed quickly, and continually pressed the workmen to carry it out, after three years and more, with God’s aid he at last completed the whole according to his desire.

Although it is established that this was completed with great labor and great expenditure, nevertheless the testimony of inhabitants and even of persons coming from foreign lands affirms that no similar structure of stonework is found anywhere. The ingenuity of the industrious craftsman bestowed such beauty upon it that it surpasses all the palaces in our land, however splendid in elaborate variety. For he suitably arranged the rows of stones, inserting now white, now black stones alternately as the work required. He magnificently beautified the entire fabric of the chapel, divided by paneled work, with black columns and shafts, with highly polished bases and capitals carved in marvelous variety, inside and out; and by the beauty of the work he gave the builder’s name an enduring remembrance among mortals.

Moreover, he built in vaulted work the canopy which covered the altar, supported on four columns, and there Abbot Wiricus caused the life of his holy patron to be painted, insofar as this was possible. On the front of this canopy he placed an image of Majesty carved in white stone, with two images of angels, looking at one another face to face. [Col. 0256A]

Making the front portion of the chapel higher than the rest of the building, he adorned it inside in a straight line with polished panels and columns, shafts, and wonderfully carved capitals. Outside, he decorated it with eleven great images of white stone, disposed in remarkable order. In the middle [Note: [Col. 0255] Henschen has “looking back” after *middle*.] of the work he placed an image of Majesty. On its right he set an image of Saint Trudo, and on its left an image of Blessed Eucherius, as though bending their knees before it, worshipping it with hands humbly outstretched while it placed a crown upon each of their heads.

Above them—that is, on this side of the image of Majesty itself—he placed two angels lying obliquely, each holding a censer in his hands and gazing intently upon the same image. On the right he set images of Blessed Stephen the protomartyr, the special guardian of this house after God, and of Blessed Quintinus the martyr; on the left, images of Blessed Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, and of the abbot himself, holding in his hand a scroll: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house.”

He also inserted in the work four other images, carved from more elongated stone: David and Moses on the right, Solomon and Isaiah on the left. Each held in his hand a scroll bearing testimony to the merits of the saints, and each looked intently toward them with his index finger extended.

6. Once this work had been completed, he restored with distinguished workmanship the front of the splendid shrine of gold and silver in which, as has been said, the saints had been placed, carving upon it an image of Majesty with two images of saints wonderfully gilded. This shrine, nobly ornamented with gold by Abbot Guntran, had long before been sold by his successor, Abbot Adelard the Second, for the redemption of estates that he had acquired in great number for the church.

Therefore, after proclaiming a public fast for both brethren and people, [Note: [Col. 0255] Henschen has “placed back” after *therefore*.] he had them carried in solemn procession around the city. Then, after the solemn rites of Mass had duly been celebrated in their honor, he placed them, enclosed behind the altar beneath the canopy of the chapel, as our everlasting protection.

7. Some days before this work on the chapel was begun, the choir screen [Note: [Col. 0255] The corrector adds in the margin: “namely, the upper choir.”], which had survived the fire that had burned the monastery, had been damaged by age and the violence of the fire. Rain fell through the vault in every direction, and as the fissures increased there was no small fear among all that the same vault might suddenly collapse and kill those standing beneath it. But the ingenuity of the custos Arnulf, to whom the abbot had assigned this duty, and his manly application to the task, readily remedied the collapse threatening the vault by rapid work, though not without great expense.

For after obtaining large and sturdy timber, covering the roof partly with stone and partly with lead, he dismantled the vault; and he covered the choir screen suitably with woodwork rather than stonework, as before.

[Col. 0257A] 8. As time went on, the same custos nobly adorned the choir with suitable seats and stalls, plastered the monastery with cement, and paneled the entire nave from the choir screen to the lower arch. He also paved, with polished stone and fitting workmanship, the floor before the chapel of Saints Trudo and Eucherius almost as far as the tomb of Abbot Folcard.

Yet Abbot Wiricus did not then cease from labor. Rather, he either repaired the old things capable of repair, if one may put it thus, or built new things in place of old ones with work stronger and more noble.

9. Therefore, from the beams which had lain in the choir screen, and which could not be reused in the same work because of their age and smallness, he built beside our orchard a house in which the brethren might wash and bathe. He adorned it with an upper room and necessary chambers and covered it besides with a stone roof.

At this same time, through both his own zeal and the industry of Custos Arnulf, who labored diligently and faithfully for the beauty and adornment of the church, our church was enlarged in varied ornament: namely, with tapestries and hangings, silk copes and phylacteries, crosses, and other various kinds of ornament. Thus the saying of the psalmist may deservedly be applied to both: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of his house.”

10. Meanwhile, the brethren’s dormitory, the abbot’s heated chambers, and the building between the two which is now called the refectory—all roofed with thatch—troubled his mind greatly, and with pious concern day and night urged him to renew them into a more noble condition of beauty. He wished indeed to repair everything, but because the revenue was narrow and scanty he doubted whether he could sustain what he had undertaken, knowing beyond doubt that it would be reckoned folly if he appeared to attempt anything beyond his means.

Yet he was encouraged by the frequent exhortation of his followers not to lose heart, nor to omit through fear of some expense what necessity and paternal concern required. They also said that he ought not to despair of God’s and his patron’s aid; that whoever walked uprightly and faithfully trusted in the Lord with zeal for good works was never at any time deprived of the desire of his heart.

Thus, though willing, he was overcome; conscious of his own capacity to endure, he applied himself wholly to what they encouraged. Not long afterward he removed the reed roof of the dormitory [Col. 0257D] and set himself with ardent spirit to its restoration. Not doubting that his patron would grant him the benefit of cooperation, and fixing in him the whole anchor of his hope, he manfully undertook to complete the admirable structure of a vast building.

Saint Trudo, when asked, as always showed himself to his tireless laborer; and what the latter had begun through the zeal of pious affection, the saint brought with happy success to the completion of the finished work. The beams of the aforesaid building, though large, were short and scarcely reached halfway across the space between the two walls; they were supported by wooden columns placed in the middle of the dormitory. The ceiling, moreover, being of fragile wood, was very weak, already rotten with age, and altogether unfit to carry the weight of such a great building.

Since none of these things could be incorporated into the new work because of their inferiority, he removed them. He had the material of the new structure, raised by the swift industry of the craftsman, covered in haste, for the sake of the brethren who were sleeping scattered here and there in the corners of the cloister. Raising the outer wall of the dormitory in new stonework to match the height of the inner wall, he made three suitable windows in it.

Thus, God consenting, he completed the entire dormitory building with a marvelous speed of visible workmanship. Because of the natural harshness of the stones, however—for in winter it was inconvenient to the brethren because of the cold and in summer because of the heat—it was paneled the next year through his industry, so that a gentle moderation might protect those resting in [Col. 0258B] that house against cold in winter and heat in summer.

11. The dormitory having been completed in this way, he intended also to restore the adjacent building. For its roof was hanging down precipitously and, unless aid came more quickly, threatened a destructive collapse. He brought its walls to the height of the dormitory wall; he removed some beams and adapted others to the work in suitable fashion because they were far too short; he raised new timbering above it; and, like the dormitory, he nobly covered the entire house with an outstanding and elevated stone roof.

He also suitably laid a new clay floor, plastered the walls well with cement, and installed in it most beautiful glazed windows and seats suitable for diners. A fine paneled ceiling adorned the splendidly completed house, and he established it henceforth as the refectory, as had been planned when its foundations were laid. Since the kitchen was too far from that building, he arranged for a kitchen to stand where the cloister gate then stood, and correspondingly designated that the entrance to the cloister should be made where the kitchen had stood.

12. Thus, when the two buildings—the dormitory and the refectory—had been completed with marvellous workmanship and great expense, there nonetheless remained a third building, so much the more difficult to construct as it was to surpass the others in the distinction of its splendid beauty. For on the site where the refectory had formerly stood, and where guests had customarily been refreshed, he built a most beautiful chamber in which the provost of the church might hold court with his men and store what was to be expended for the brethren’s use. Above it he laid the foundations of a more elevated dwelling, in which he himself might live and rest; concentrating his whole attention upon this work, he distinguished that house by the beauty of its remarkable construction.

For, after installing large windows open to the air, through which someone standing in the house could direct his gaze far into the distance and see spread before his eyes almost the whole plain of the central part of the town, he completed the entire structure marvellously by the ingenious skill of a diligent craftsman. He further ennobled it notably with fireplaces and with a water-channel running through the middle of the chamber. Before its entrance, leaving a small space as though for a walk or passageway, he nevertheless built another chamber adjoining it, in which they might store the furnishings of his table and in which, after his meal, they might sit down to eat. Beside it he built another unoccupied house, and then, along the wall of the sleeve-like wing, another more private chamber, quite suitable for abbots and religious guests to reside in.

Below, after first raising the beams in the wall, he repaired his hall with workmanship more excellent than it had formerly possessed; and, richly carved, whitened also with plaster, and suitably furnished with glazed windows, seats appropriate to so great a house, and the necessary chambers, he adorned it becomingly. He also raised the wall of this same house on both sides by new work, bringing it level with the walls of the aforesaid buildings. In a marvellous arrangement of matching and well-suited equality, he covered the three houses, as though they were one, with one uniform and similar type of roof.

[Col. 0259B] Although he was undertaking works so great, so splendid, and deservedly worthy of everyone’s admiration, he did not do so out of any abundance flowing to him. Rather, as a prudent and provident man, he supplied his deficiencies by a measure of fitting economy, lest he lack necessary things. His greater assistance, however, consisted in the offerings of the faithful which came from the church of Blessed Mary, a source which he had long before acquired through the utmost effort, with certain of his household associates working toward the same end.

13. From these alms he assigned three pounds to the brethren, to be distributed for their refreshment on the feasts of twelve saints, which we have judged it not inappropriate to record below. From the ancient times of his predecessors these had formerly been celebrated with twelve lessons, in the manner of Sundays. But he, because of the reverent devotion which he had toward the saints and wishing their feasts to be celebrated more solemnly, assigned to the brethren one additional meal on each of those saints’ feasts, in honour of the saints themselves.

In January he ordered the feast of Saint Vincent the martyr and the Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle to be celebrated solemnly, in white vestments; in February, those of Saint Matthias and the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle; in March, Saint Benedict the abbot; on the Kalends of May, the Apostles Philip and James; in July, Saint James the Apostle; in August, Saint Peter in Chains; in the middle of the same month, Bartholomew the Apostle; in September, Matthew the Evangelist; in October, the Apostles Simon and Jude; and in December likewise Thomas the Apostle. He left these observances to his sons, to be maintained through all future generations as though by hereditary right, so that, while their memory is recalled among us with greater devotion, through their merits the grace of the Almighty may deign to protect all everywhere from adversities.

14. Therefore, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1169, and the ninth year of Abbot Wiric’s administration, Stephen, bishop of Metz, having died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, Theoderic, primicerius of that same church, succeeded as bishop in his see.

> [Note: [Col. 0259D] Stephen did not die either in the year 1169 or on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, but, according to the testimony of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January 1163—a year which the author also intended to identify as the ninth year of Wiric.]

> [Note: [Col. 0259] A corrector adds “third.” The same person wrote in the margin: “Note that this fourteenth chapter, according to its date, belongs in chapter 11 of the third book, but is placed here because of the continuity of the events narrated.”]

Coming to us on the Nones of the same month, in order that, as is customary with princes of the land, a newly elected lord might dispose at his pleasure of his goods which were among us and might learn what and how great were the possessions which the holy protomartyr had here, he found the minds of certain of our townspeople raised against him more violently than was right in defence of their claims. Accordingly, stirred by the complaint of Abbot Wiric, he restored to the church that part of the market-place adjoining the court of the church of Blessed Mary which the *scultetus* [sheriff] unjustly and violently possessed. And, lest any injustice thereafter be done to us, he separated his boundaries from ours by a straight line, placing a conspicuous marker in the middle of the market-place. When repeated messages sent to our people achieved nothing, he proceeded to the town, stayed with us for some days, and, upon learning that he possessed less among us than he had supposed, departed in anger.

15. Therefore, in the year of the Lord 1171, Lord Theoderic came to Metz and complained to his men that our people were each claiming his possessions for themselves as they pleased. Since, by frequently sending his stewards to them, he received less and less of his property and moreover suffered various injuries, he commanded them, by the authority of his lordship and in the manner of other princes, to come to Metz and answer for the injustice which they were doing him. When they often neglected to obey the summons, he was compelled by necessity to mortgage to Emperor Frederick, for two hundred marks, the possessions which he had among us, so that the emperor, by the lawful authority of his power, might compel them to obey him—men whose perverse violence he himself had been unable to bend to due reverence and submission either by laws or by justice.

> [Note: [Col. 0260D] That is, injustice or violence.]

Therefore, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, the emperor’s messenger came to us and, after carefully investigating the bishop’s possessions, seized them for the future service of his lordship. Not long afterward, when the emperor came to Cologne, Abbot Wiric, summoned by him, appeared there.

> [Note: [Col. 0260D] On 24 June 1171 the emperor was staying at Cologne. Böhmer, no. 2546.]

The emperor received him honourably and asked him, just as he had been faithful to the bishop in all the latter’s rights, likewise to show that same fidelity to himself and not to fail his messengers in their business among our townspeople.

16. In the same year, a few days later, Louis, count of Loon, imagining that whatever pleased his mind was lawful for him, disturbed the peace and, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, when harvest was already drawing near and the almost-ripe crop awaited the sickle, untimely summoned everyone to arms on the following pretext. He had built a strong tower in his estate of Brustem and surrounded it with a powerful garrison, fortifying the court of the church with a great rampart.

[Col. 0261A] Giles, count of Duras, a young man flourishing in age and most ready in spirit and hand for action, took this badly: namely, that the count had presumed to do this in his county without his consent, contrary to the enactments of princes and the rule of justice. For secular laws provide that no prince may erect a fortified post in another’s county without the consent of the one to whom that county belongs. For this reason a serious conflict of enmity and war arose between them. Each also complained against the other of many further matters quite deserving reciprocal redress. But the count of Loon, as though trusting in his rights and the display of his wealth, despised him as poor in resources and military equipment; while the young man’s bold spirit in turn impelled the other not to yield, but to resist.

This too increased their discord: the same count of Loon remembered an injury inflicted upon him by the young man’s father, who in earlier years, after laying waste the count’s villages everywhere with fire and sword, had also burned Brustem. Perhaps wishing to avenge this upon the son, although he knew that he was acting unjustly against him, he nevertheless refused to turn his mind from his obstinate purpose. Their hostile conflict was drawn out so far that they decided on both sides to avenge their injuries upon one another by the sword and slaughter.

17. One day, therefore, when the armies of both sides met between our town and Brustem, and battle-lines armed with iron joined combat in fierce spirit, victory fell to the fewer men, although the others were greatly superior in number of soldiers, because our side resisted bravely. At last the entire weight of the battle was directed against our people, because with loyal courage they defended the cause of their advocate, the count of Duras, and repeatedly crushed the more numerous army of the count of Loon by their bold valour. Since he could do nothing to them, he armed himself, as though to avenge his injury upon them, to plunder and devastate our property. First, he took thirty marks from the inhabitants of our village of Burlo as ransom for the village; had they not paid it, he would have consigned the village and all their possessions to cruel destruction.

18. Meanwhile, while the count of Duras had gone into Flanders to obtain the aid of soldiers, his army nevertheless continued daily engagements with the count’s knights. Abbot Wiric and our people, having taken common counsel, decided that it was useful, amid the pressing straits of their tribulation, to seek the emperor’s assistance. For in those same days he was holding his court at Nijmegen with a great gathering of the princes of the land. The forces of the count of Loon, however, increased daily, so that, confident of victory, he threatened to inflict upon them every great and terrible deed.

[Col. 0262A] Therefore, summoning certain of their more faithful men, who might energetically carry out so great a business, they informed the emperor—who, after God and Saint Trudo, was then their special lord by reason of the seizure made for him by the bishop of Metz—of what was being done against them. He sent them a faithful messenger, instructing them that, if they wished what they had lost to be restored to them, they should not go out through the gate of the town nor involve themselves in the disputes of the quarrelling counts. He also promised to repay whatever the count had received as ransom for our villages.

Thus, while our people refrained from war in accordance with the emperor’s command, the count’s knights did not cease to provoke them with frequent insults. They mocked them as though, stricken by fear, they did not dare go out from their town gates to meet them. The count himself, as though secure of victory, would at one time send his armed battle-line almost to the very gates of the town, as if it were going for a stroll, the more to inflame our men to fury; at another, he would seize violently, before they reached the town, goods for sale being brought in from outside; and at another, unexpectedly driving off their livestock as booty, he grievously wore them down with daily losses and mockery.

> [Note: [Col. 0261] “Estates” in 1*.]

When the emperor learned this through their messengers, he ordered them, defending themselves by his authority, to rise against the count with all the force of their power and take vengeance upon him for their losses.

19.  

> [Note: [Col. 0261] If one follows the table of chapters, chapter 19 begins with these words. The copyist wrongly carried chapter 18 down to the words “a venerable old man succeeded.”]

Meanwhile, while messengers were being sent from our people to the emperor and returned from him to them, Count Giles came back from Flanders, unsuccessful in his object, and was welcomed with the joyful favour of his men. A serious battle was joined on the next day; the army of the count of Loon was defeated and put to flight by our side. After the nearest villages had been laid waste and Brustem burned on the fifth day before the Kalends of August—namely, in the twelfth year after it had first been burned—the count’s castle was surrounded by our men under siege.

As they were planning to storm it, that same Count Louis, who had threatened to destroy our town and monastery, was suddenly seized by illness and unexpectedly died on the third day before the Ides of the same month. He was buried, as he had ordered while alive, before the hospital in his village of Los.

[Col. 0262D] After his death, Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, whose daughter the same count had betrothed to his son as wife, came to our men who were besieging the count’s castle and informed them that he had died. He arranged a truce and compelled the count’s men and our people to abandon the siege of the castle.

> [Note: [Col. 0261D] The third.]

In the same days Theoderic, bishop-elect of Metz, also died.

> [Note: [Col. 0261] The corrector wrote above: “in the same year.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0261D] 27 September 1172, as the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz* attest.]

In the eighth year of his episcopate, Frederick, a canon of the same church and a venerable old man, succeeded him.

20. Thus, with the war which the count had begun against our people ended, peace was restored to the land by God’s favour. The poor, who had been hiding miserably here and there, as though granted permission to live, were suddenly clothed in a new and changed joy; and each, competing with the others as best he could, safely stored in barns the remainder of the grain supply which had survived the impious devastation. For, by the will of the Almighty, the man who had cruelly oppressed them and subjected them without compassion to the yoke of tyrannical condemnation had fallen.

But while the emperor was holding his court at Aachen in those days, Gerard, son of the deceased count, came there with his mother.

> [Note: [Col. 0263D] Ermelinda; see Mantel, p. 112.]

He made many complaints to the emperor against the count of Duras and our people for the devastation of his land, and inflamed the emperor’s mind against them with grave indignation. The count of Duras had long before been summoned repeatedly by imperial messengers; not daring to appear, he had allowed the appointed deadline to pass. Consequently, by the judgment of the princes of the Empire, he and all his possessions had been adjudged to the emperor’s power as guilty of an offence against imperial majesty.

At length he came, and, questioned by the emperor why he had repeatedly neglected to come when summoned and why with unlawful recklessness he had ravaged the count’s land, he was guilty in both matters. Yet, through the intervention of friends, he escaped the severity of the sentence pronounced against him. Philip, count of Flanders, was there, together with many other princes closely related to him by blood; softened by their petition, the emperor mercifully pardoned what he had done. And because he too was related to the emperor, it seemed unbecoming for the emperor to exact anything from one who possessed nothing.

[Col. 0263C] Having taken counsel with his men regarding what he should do with our people, who were present there with their advocate, he began to direct the severe judgment of his punishment against them. When they were asked by him by what boldness or confidence they had ruined the count’s land by fire and sword, they asserted that they had acted under his own authorizing permission; he, however, denied it. By a fortunate turn of events, Abbot Wiric happened to have with him there the letters which the emperor had previously sent them, commanding them to defend themselves and rise against the count with all their strength. When he showed them to the archbishops of Mainz and Cologne and the other princes present, and produced as a witness the bearer who had received them from the emperor, they encouraged our people not to fear, in the hope of a favourable outcome, and reported to the emperor what they had heard.

> [Note: [Col. 0263D] Philip.]

But the emperor, like the man whose mind was daily drawn in different directions, recalled the past through their truthful report. In accordance with the saying of the comic poet, “The concerns of kings, as they are vehement, are likewise changeable,” he began to act against them somewhat more mildly and negligently. Examining with judicial severity other matters being argued there, he left the cause of our people and the count unresolved, as though overlooking it. The copy of the aforesaid letters was therefore of great benefit to them. Had he not possessed it there, they would certainly not have escaped the strict judgment of imperial punishment without grave loss of their property.

At Abbot Wiric’s insistence, the count of Loon was ordered to restore the money which his father had extorted from our people as Burlo’s ransom.

> [Note: [Col. 0263D] This appears to be the necessary supplementation; it is absent from the manuscript.]

He gave us as a pledge costly garments of his own apparel; a few days later, however, his mother redeemed them by paying the ransom-price.

21. In the following year, 1172, Hugh and Albert, sons of the count of Mousson, unable to endure being disinherited by that same Count Gerard, gathered an army and unexpectedly spread through his territory. They maintained that Bilzen and half of Calmunt, with their appurtenances, belonged to them by lawful right; yet they had never been able to obtain them from his father either by arms or by the laws of justice.

> [Note: [Col. 0263D] Bilzen.]

Secretly arming their strongest followers, they suddenly attacked Berlo Castle on Sunday and devastated and burned the villages of the entire surrounding district.

> [Note: [Col. 0264D] Berlo near Waremme.]

Nor even then could our church remain untouched by the devastation of its possessions: our village of Horle, half-burned, was utterly ravaged, and after its wheels had been smashed, our mill was set on fire by the raiders and consumed in fierce flames.

22. Count Gerard of Loon, seeing that he needed the military strength and courage of Giles, count of Duras, enlisted him as helper and ally against his enemies. After one of those enemies, namely Hugh, had died at Huy, he routed the other’s army and expelled him from the borders of his land. Thereafter, by the counsel of both households, he betrothed his sister to him as wife.

> [Note: [Col. 0264D] Adelaide.]

Reconciled with him, he established a firm pact of friendship and peace with our people.

23. Not long afterwards, that same Gerard was seized by illness and despaired of; at last, contrary to everyone’s expectation, he recovered and determined, as he had vowed during his sickness, to set out for Jerusalem. His brother Hugh, younger in age but more prone through rashness of spirit to every crime, thinking that all things which pleased him were permitted, acted on the advice of certain persons hostile to our town. He raised a huge rampart around Brustem and thereby created, as afterward became clear, great material for internal war and hatred between his people and ours.

[Col. 0264D] This undertaking could easily have been suppressed at the beginning of this growing evil; but the negligence and sloth of the leading men of our town—especially of the count of Duras, who acted badly in this matter—nourished the reckless boldness of a man digging on another’s allodial land. For the justice of secular laws could freely have forbidden what he had begun; and if the matter had had to be decided, as often happens among princes, by the sword, they would certainly have been easily superior to him in number and strength.

Before the rampart had yet been completed around the circuit of the village, Count Gerard returned from Jerusalem. He was received with the favourable joy of all his people and, by us also, with a solemn procession; he was honoured with great reverence, indeed with such honour as befitted one even more glorious than he. Considering the work on the aforesaid rampart and pondering many matters silently within himself, he did not rebuke his brother for the undertaking. That year, as though displeased by what had been done, he remained inactive.

Thereafter, prompted by the frequent counsel of his men, he zealously applied himself to completing it. For it seemed to him dishonourable if he should seek to leave unfinished what his brother had begun, as though in some respect inferior to him. Nor did he think anyone would oppose his undertaking, since no one had opposed his brother.

But Saint Trudo protected his town, which they were striving by every means through this act to oppress and humiliate; their plan was frustrated by the providence of the Almighty, who sees future things as present and knows the hidden things of the heart. For Hugh, the brother of Gerard and the seed-bed of all the evil which later arose between our people and the men of Loon on account of this rampart, died while still scarcely beyond the years of puberty. What kind of man he was, or would have been, may clearly be inferred and known even from this: he carried off, against law and right, the betrothed woman of his only brother. She nevertheless died within a short time of this union. Moreover, as many declared, had he survived with that wife, he would, with the aid of his father-in-law, have deprived his brother entirely of the right to the county and castles.

24. Meanwhile, Abbot Wiric, having built the offices of the cloister with marvellous workmanship, was repeatedly urged by the brethren that he should, as he had long ago vowed, renew and reform the cloister into a kind of new beauty. Judging it an excellent deed to leave his memory to posterity in blessing, he gladly resolved to comply with their request. For he had long since learned by many experiences not to despair of the help of God and of his most blessed patron, considering without doubt that, with that patron working alongside him, every work upon which he set his mind was directed into his hands.

He therefore built the wall of the cloister enclosure all around with polished slabs, and placed bases upon it in a fitting arrangement. Then he set up columns, now four *vivaria* columns [meaning uncertain], now paired black ones; joining them with suitable construction, he placed above them capitals splendidly carved. He divided above the space between the columns with stones cut in the form of arches and exceptionally polished, and completed the entire work successfully according to his wish within one year, to the wonder of all.

> [Note: [Col. 0265D] *vinarias* (“wine-cellar columns”) in 1*.]

25. In those same days Gerard, count of Loon, was striving with the greatest effort to finish the rampart of Brustem, begun by his brother Hugh as we have said above; but the work begun was entirely impeded by the opposition of Cuno, count of Duras. He had succeeded his brother Giles, still very much a boy, in the principality. The almighty Father, perhaps treating him as a beloved adopted son who was to be tested in His judgment, meanwhile chastised him with the scourge of His severity by afflicting him with leprosy.
