The count of Loon, having long experienced the spirited strength of our people and distrusting his ability to resist the men of Duras because of them, went to the emperor and surrendered to him his allodial property at Brustem together with the castle, so that by the protection of imperial authority he might bring to completion what he despaired of accomplishing by his own strength. On returning from the emperor’s court, elated by the confidence which he had conceived in the emperor, he invited all the surrounding people to aid him against the count of Duras and our residents. Now their open enemy, he announced his hostility and anger against them with indignation.

Meanwhile, the count of Duras, having no assistance apart from our people, set out to seek the aid of the count of Flanders, informing him of the injuries which he suffered from the count of Loon. The latter, moved by so sad an account from his nephew and compassionately yielding to his distress with kindly sympathy, sent letters warning the count not to harm him and ordering him not to disdain to meet him for a conference at Louvain. For he saw that his nephew, although a count, lacked almost everything, while the other abounded; accordingly, he laboured to arrange some compact of peace or friendship between them. Again, if he came with an armed force, he thought he could indeed defeat the count, but he grieved that for such a cause nearly the entire surrounding province might be reduced to nothing by the devastation of his army.

[Col. 0266C] The celebrated day of the appointed conference dawned, and the aforesaid princes met at Louvain as arranged, with a great gathering of their men. Asked by the count of Flanders, the count of Loon refused a truce, complained before everyone that grave injuries were being inflicted upon him by the count of Duras, and the consultation was thus dissolved that day. Each departed for his own lands, with the business for which they had come unfinished. Not long afterward, touched by late repentance, he voluntarily granted our people the truce which he had refused so great a prince, at the energetic urging of Godfrey, duke of Louvain, his brother-in-law.

> [Note: [Col. 0265D] He had as wife Imaina, daughter of Louis, count of Loon.]

He also temporarily suspended, though unwillingly, work on his rampart until another time.

26. In the year of the Lord 1177, the twenty-fifth year of Frederick’s empire, the tenth of Bishop Rudolf’s episcopate, and the twenty-second of Abbot Wiric’s prelacy, a few days before these events occurred, Pope Alexander, reconciled with Emperor Frederick, had absolved him and all the princes of his empire from excommunication. Each having adopted the other, one as father and the other as son, he returned with him into the unity of concord.

> [Note: [Col. 0266D] Twenty-third of the empire, twenty-sixth of the reign.]

For after Pope Adrian had died, Alexander had been elected to the height of the papacy together with Octavian, a cardinal-priest of venerable life. But, when the parties disagreed among themselves, he was rejected by the emperor; nevertheless, he outlived that same Octavian and his two successors.

> [Note: [Col. 0267D] Paschal III and Callixtus III.]

Thus, after the unity of the Church—disturbed for seventeen years by the dispute over the Apostolic See—had been restored, he sent letters ordering all bishops throughout the regions to come to Rome in mid-Lent. Rudolf, bishop of Liège, summoned, among others, all the abbots of his bishopric and ordered them to prepare to travel with him. Whoever preferred to remain behind out of fear of the journey was not to neglect to contribute something for the expenses of the one departing; otherwise, he himself would travel to Rome with him.

Abbot Wiric, already welcome to him because of the exceptional generosity of his liberality, obtained by yet more abundant gifts that, since bodily weakness prevented him from going to Rome in person, the bishop should carry with him the privileges of our church and have them confirmed with the present pope’s seal. This he did. When he came to Rome, although the unfavourable report of his actions had greatly offended the pope’s ears, nevertheless, because of his noble lineage, he was held before the pope in a distinction of honour greater than that of the rest.

This council was held in mid-Lent, on 5 March 1179; seven hundred bishops and a thousand abbots were said to have been present, together with innumerable companies of clerics of various orders.

> [Note: [Col. 0267D] Compare the acts of the council in Mansi, XXVI, 213: the bishops assembled, numbering 302, on the fifth, seventh, and nineteenth days of March.]

Among his other decrees, which he solemnly ordained as properly to be observed by all, the pope pronounced a sentence of excommunication against Octavian, a man of holy life, and his two successors, and judged by his authority null and void whatever they had decreed while alive.

27. In the following year, 1180, the bishop, having brought the business of his journey to the desired conclusion, at last returned to Liège by a successful route, all who had been in his company being safe and well. Both before this journey and after his return, he was repeatedly assailed by injuries from Gerard, count of Loon, who arrogantly and proudly imposed them upon him in the tithes and *precariae* of villages and churches belonging to him. Since he achieved nothing by threats and excommunication, he prepared to oppose the count’s pride and arrogance by force and arms.

Coming to us, and pressed by necessity, he renewed with our people the covenant of friendship and the constancy of fidelity, urging them together with him to avenge upon the count the injury done to himself and Saint Lambert. Learning this, the count too was not slower in resistance. Gathering a strong force of soldiers, on the second day before the Kalends of August he attacked the bishop’s knights and drove them in bloody flight from Chaumont to Tongeren.

> [Note: [Col. 0268D] Chaumont.]

Breaking by force into the town with his men, he captured many and carried away abundant booty in victory. On the following day, that is, the Kalends of August, the bishop, gathering a multitude of his men, overwhelmed him with his army before the same village and put him to flight. While all who could fled to the castle, he burned the entire village in a sudden attack. Meanwhile the count, escaping through a nearby wood with a few of his men, unexpectedly attacked Tongeren; having burned the town, he consumed the monastery of Blessed Mary in a severe fire.

On the following day, 2 August, while the bishop was besieging Chaumont, our people, asked by him, attacked Brustem. In the ninth year after they had burned it under Count Giles, they burned it again; after overcoming its first rampart, they forced the defenders into a narrower space and set about constructing siege-engines to take the castle.

28. Then, on the third day before the Nones of August, the bishop with his men and our people with the bishop attacked Los, the chief town of the county. As its inhabitants fled in fear of death and captivity, they burned the town and plundered immense spoils from the monastery and likewise from the castle.

29. On the next day, 4 August, the monastery of Saint Amor at Bilzen was burned together with the town by the bishop’s soldiery. Likewise the castle of Montenaken, deserted by its defenders, was destroyed by fire. After the surrounding villages had been ravaged and their inhabitants fled, all the count’s castles and fortifications were destroyed by enemies who spared nothing. When the bishop, having erected siege-engines, was striving to destroy Chaumont, Count Gerard was restored to his favour through the efforts of his maternal uncle, the count of Namur, and the count of Berg.

> [Note: [Col. 0268D] Engelbert.]

This was arranged on the condition that whatever the bishop had done to him should be void, and that he should thereafter inflict no injury upon him on that account. In this mutual conflict of the two against one another, more than sixteen churches, together with their villages, are reported to have been burned amid the grievous devastation of the whole surrounding province.

30. Therefore, once bishop and count had been restored to peaceful concord, Godfrey, duke of Louvain, was inflamed with furious indignation against our people, because, in aiding the bishop against the count, they had presumed to violate the peace sworn to him. He temporarily prohibited the market-goods brought from his land and swore that they had done this to their own ruin, hoping that, worn down by his threats, they would redeem his favour with money.

31. The count of Loon also turned against them all that he had suffered. He went to the emperor and recounted to him the sad history of his fortunes. Inclining the emperor to aid him in his calamities, he incited him against our people in revenge for himself. Frequently summoned by the emperor, they at last, compelled by necessity, consulted the bishop about this matter and required him by right to go to the emperor and excuse them concerning the count’s complaint. Promising in good faith to free them from every difficulty, he proceeded with them to the emperor’s court, which was to be held at Sinzig.

[Col. 0269A] While the count made many accusations against them to the emperor, the bishop energetically pleaded their case—indeed, his own—defending them from the charges by his patronage and openly declaring that what was alleged against them ought more rightly to be imputed to himself. The count, struck by his steadfastness and induced by the emperor, while the bishop likewise worked toward the same result, resolved to return with them to concord of peace. That peace was confirmed there upon the condition that the count should neither dig on the church’s allodial land, as he had begun to do, nor violently oppose the right of their advocate to dig. Thus the rampart which he had raised around Brustem—the seed-bed of all this discord from the beginning—remained unfinished when he was reconciled with our people.

32. In those days certain men rich in possessions, belonging to the household of our church, were residing at Cologne. Henry, duke of Limburg, wished violently to detach them against their will from the church’s jurisdiction, because he had long since sworn an oath concerning their property.

> [Note: [Col. 0269D] The third; Henry II had died in 1167.]

Driven by this necessity, Abbot Wiric went to Cologne. There the congenital weakness of his legs and feet became so much more severe than usual that, although all who had gone with him almost despaired of his recovery, he was scarcely able to return. Overcome by the affectionate concern of his household, who always wished him to remain with them, he applied medical aid to his sickness and to the bodily weakness growing heavier each day. Moderately helped by these remedies, although his limbs still ached and he hoped that he had now recovered, he suddenly, contrary to hope, fell into a fatal illness.

[Col. 0270A] Having been anointed and communicated, while the brethren offered devoted watches of vigil for him, after the matutinal synaxis he ended his final day in the year of the Lord 1183, on the Ides of December. He was buried beside Abbot Folcard, before the chapel of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, which he himself had long before built, as mentioned above, in notable workmanship with a laborious variety of stones. From the year of his election he presided over the church for twenty-five years less ten days, a prudent man, often favoured by good fortune in many matters, and

> [Note: [Col. 0269D] The copyist appears to be in error. Since above, II.3, he says that Wiric was elected in 1155, “twenty-eight” appears to be the reading required [Col. 0270D].]

[Col. 0270B] Ever taught, amid adversity, to hope for better things. Among the other benefits of his uprightness and generosity, which, as a pious father, he had permanently left for his excellent heirs to possess, he assigned two parts of the tithe of Aalst for their annual refreshment, and devoted whatever remained to the benefit of the sick. It is therefore fitting that the grateful memory of the works and manifold benefactions of so great a father be held in blessing among posterity, since it is proved more clearly than daylight that he laboured so outstandingly and so fatherly for their needs and advantages. Let us therefore offer him the common aid of our prayers, asking that his spirit may rest in peace. Amen.

[Col. 0269] Here end the Deeds of the Lord Abbot of this place, namely the monastery of Saint Trudo.

# THIRD CONTINUATION OF THE DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF TRUDO

[Col. 0269]

## FIRST PART

### HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Col. 0269C] Since knowledge of events which occurred in ancient times is highly beneficial, above all, to religious and ecclesiastical persons, it should be known that, after the many persecutions which Catholics suffered by divine permission from pagans and unbelievers—the Goths, Vandals, Huns, Lombards, and other barbarian peoples who had emerged from the seats and lands of their habitation—the hand of the Almighty, at last stretched out to punish the sins of the Christians inhabiting Gaul, sent upon them the wrath of His indignation through the pagan Normans, otherwise called Norwegians. Joined by the Danes, they ranged through Gaul and its adjoining provinces for about [Col. 0270C] sixty years [Note: Cf. below, II.21, under the year 896.], destroying numerous cities with towns and castles, brutally killing inhabitants of both sexes, and devastating holy places, churches, and monasteries with like ruin.

Among these, this monastery of Saint Trudo was so stripped of its treasures, precious ornaments, and abundance of books, and its splendid fabric was burned and overthrown, that concerning the abbey—formerly so famous—from the time of its foundation until the reign of Otto I, very little was found committed to memory. Therefore, in order that it might become known to the future sons and successors of the aforesaid monastery, at least in some measure, with what prosperity this place flourished before the persecution of those Normans and [Col. 0271A] what miseries it endured after its destruction, I finally examined the books of our library and the abundance of charters. I took care to place before the books nobly arranged by the venerable Lord Rodulf concerning the deeds of nine abbots a few matters which I had collected, so as to continue the sequence of events.

Then, finding in an old booklet the deeds of the three abbots who succeeded Rodulf immediately, I attached them. Finally, I set down the deeds of twelve abbots who presided from the year of the Lord 1180 until the death of Abbot Robert, who died in the year of the Lord 1366. I collected the acts of these twelve abbots from various books here and there [Note: *1 reads “children.”] and from the reports of the ancients, and inserted what I could see and hear in my own times. I also interspersed incidental matters, as they seemed appropriate, throughout several chapters of the books. [Col. 0271B]

[Col. 0272A] But when I reached present times, I ceased recording, leaving these matters to be investigated more fully by posterity [Note: *1 reads “to be carried out.”]; for, if I pursued the truth of events, I might perhaps incur the offence of certain persons who are still alive, while, if I departed from the truth, I should be stained with the charge of flattery or falsehood. Moreover, I humbly entreat and earnestly exhort my successors that, laying aside negligence, they may henceforth be diligent in committing notable events and deeds to written annals. By examining these, their successors may more cautiously avoid future dangers.

This compilation of the deeds of the abbots is divided into four parts: the first part contains three books; the second, thirteen books [Note: *1 reads “eleven,” incorrectly]; the third, four books; while the fourth is completed in two [Note: The author left this space blank, intending to add the number of books.] books.

### HERE BEGINS THE TABLE OF THE FIRST PART CONCERNING THE DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF THIS MONASTERY OF SAINT TRUDO, AND FIRST THE CHAPTERS OF ITS FIRST BOOK

[Col. 0271]

1. Chapter: On the birth of blessed Trudo.

2. On his vow to build a church.

3. On the death of his parents.

4. On the angelic admonition given to him and the instruction of Saint Remaclus.

5. On his journey to the city of Metz. Incidental matter [Note: *1 reads “incedentia.”]: on Saints Amandus and Remaclus. Incidental matter: on the death of King Dagobert and the succession of his sons. Incidental matter: on the six Pippins and Saint Gertrude.

6. On blessed Trudo’s progress in the studies of Holy Scripture.

7. On the appointment of blessed Theodard as abbot of the monastery of Stavelot.

8. On blessed Trudo’s ordination as priest and his return to Sarcinium.

9. On how our estate of Sene was bestowed upon blessed Trudo.

10. How Saint Trudo, returning home, visited blessed Remaclus.

11. How the people of Sarcinium came to meet him as he returned home.

12. On the first foundation of this monastery of Saint Trudo. Incidental matter: how Saint Remaclus resigned the bishopric of Maastricht. Incidental matter concerning Theodard’s succession.

13. On the first dedication of this monastery.

14. On the endowment of this monastery made by Saint Trudo, and the foundation of a monastery of eighty monks on the allod of that same saint, situated near the town of Bruges in Flanders. Incidental matter: on how the land of Flanders first became a county.

15. On the extensive possession which blessed Trudo had in Taxandria, now called Campine.

16. On the first establishment of monks in this place and the beginning there of divine worship.

17. On the office of preaching which blessed Trudo also received from Saint Remaclus.

18. On the churches at Zepperen and Falmia, which he visited on alternate nights. Incidental matter: on the martyrdom of Saint Theodard. Likewise: on the same subject.

19. On the election of Saint Lambert as bishop.

20. On blessed Lambert’s expulsion from the bishopric.

21. On blessed Trudo’s fasts and almsgiving.

22. On blessed Lambert’s restoration to his bishopric.

23. On the falling asleep of blessed Trudo.

24. On the miracles performed on the day of his funeral.

25. On Lothar, provost, who governed this monastery after blessed Trudo.

26. On the gift and alms bestowed upon our monastery by Pippin II and his wife Plectrude. Incidental matter: on Bede the priest.

27. On the martyrdom of Saint Lambert.

28. On the miracle at Saint Lambert’s funeral. On his successor Saint Hubert, publicly heard.

29. On the miraculous consecration of Saint Hubert at Rome.

30. On the transfer of the episcopal see and of blessed Lambert’s body from Maastricht to Liège, and the death of Saint Hubert. Incidental matter: on Pippin. Incidental matter: on the monastery of Monte Cassino.

31. On the creation of blessed Eucherius as bishop.

32. On the death of Lothar, provost of this place.

### HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND BOOK

1. On the first abbot of this monastery.

2. On the years of the Lord during which he presided, and on the six abbots and successors.

3. On blessed Eucherius’ expulsion from the bishopric.

4. On blessed Eucherius’ dispatch into exile in Hasbania. Incidental matter: on the death of Charles Martel.

5. On the revelation shown to Saint Eucherius: how Charles was tormented in hell, and on the serpent found in his tomb.

[Col. 0273] 6. On the death of Saint Eucherius. Incidental matter: on the foundation of the monastery of Fulda.

7. On the gift of our estates at Donch, and the villages there bestowed upon this monastery by Duke Robert, and on his tomb. Incidental matter: on the creation of Pippin III as king of France.

8. On the thief of this monastery who stole its treasure and was hanged by Pippin’s judgment.

9. On the miracle performed by blessed Trudo upon the boy of Saint Rodegand, bishop. Incidental matter: on the death of King Pippin. Incidental matter: on the Huns or Avars defeated by Charlemagne.

10. On Donatus the monk, who wrote the Life of blessed Trudo. Incidental matter: how Charles, having become emperor, put an end to the persecution of the Huns. Incidental matter: on the empire of Louis the Pious. Incidental matter: on the conversion of the king of the Danes to the faith.

11. On the beginning of the persecution by the Normans.

12. On Lord Drogo, bishop of Metz and abbot of this place.

13. On the gift made to this monastery in the time of Abbot Drogo by the nobleman Hotbert.

14. On the names of eight abbots succeeding Abbot Drogo. Incidental matter: on the hymn *Gloria, laus et honor* (“Glory, praise, and honour”), and how it finally [Note: *1 reads “p.”] came to be sung on Palm Sunday. Incidental matter: on the boundaries of the kingdom of Lotharingia, formerly called Austrasia. Incidental matter: on Emperor Lothar’s becoming a monk. Incidental matter: on the Danes, accomplices of the Normans. Incidental matter: on the bishops of Metz who succeeded him, and why some of them are styled archbishops.

15. On the customary provision formerly given to the monks of this place. Incidental matter: on how the land of Flanders became a county. Incidental matter: on the victory of the Franks over the Normans.

16. On the first translation of the bodies of Saints Trudo and Eucherius.

17. On the concealment of the bodies of blessed Trudo and Eucherius beneath an underground vault, made for fear of the Normans.

18. On the devastation of Lotharingia wrought by the Normans.

19. On the martyrdom of Saint Libert. On the devastation by the Normans of the monastery and town of Saint Trudo and of other monasteries and cities. Incidental matter: on the devastation of the cities of Trier and Metz. Incidental matter: on the pagan Hungarians.

20. On the return of the Normans from France to Lotharingia.

21. On the ruin and extermination of the Normans and their conversion to the faith. Incidental matter: on Adelbero I, bishop of Metz. Incidental matter: on the abbot of Prüm. Incidental matter: on the transfer of the empire from the Franks to the Germans. Incidental matter: on the assault of the Hungarians. Incidental matter: how the kingdom of Lotharingia devolved at the empire’s command.

22. On Ymo, abbot of this place.

### HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD BOOK

1. On Otto I beginning, during his empire, to restore this monastery destroyed by the Normans. Incidental matter: on the duke of Lotharingia. Incidental matter: in praise of Otto.

2. On King Otto’s arrival at our town and his compassion toward this monastery.

3. On the consecration of Abbot Reiner.

4. On the flogging inflicted by blessed Trudo upon Adelbero II, bishop of Metz.

5. On the alms of the mother [Note: *1 reads “merits.”] of Lord Abbot Reiner. Incidental matter: on the dispute between Otto and Louis, king of France. Incidental matter: on Otto’s victory over the duke of Lotharingia. Incidental matter: on Gerberga, Otto’s sister.

6. On the immersion of a falling spider in Abbot Reiner’s chalice at the hour of the consecration of the Eucharist.

7. How, after Abbot Reiner’s death, Lord Adelbero II, bishop of Metz, became abbot of this place.

8. On Lord Adelbero’s diligence in recovering revenues, on the endowment of the monastery with his paternal inheritance, and on the restoration of the buildings.

9. On the renewed consecration of the monastery after its first dedication. Incidental matter: on Lord Adelbero’s resistance to King Otto. Incidental matter: on the bishops of Liège. Incidental matter: on the granting of the duchy of Lotharingia.

10. On the servitude of the woman Guodrada, where it is shown that Lord Adelbero was abbot of this place.

11. On the alms of Zeizolf, where it is likewise clear that Lord Adelbero was abbot of this place.

12. On the death of Lord Adelbero, abbot of this place.

13. On our estates at Provin and the forest of Bruderholt, which the countess of Flanders bestowed upon the monastery. Incidental matter: on the succession of the bishop of Liège and the emperor.

14. On the foundation of the monastery of Saint Vincent and the town of Saint Trudo.

15. On the death of Lord Thietfrid, abbot of this place.

16. On the appointment of Lord Erenfrid as abbot of this place and his death.

Here ends the table of the first part of the deeds of the abbots of this monastery of Saint Trudo.

# HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK, CONTAINING THE ORIGIN, DEEDS, AND DEATH OF BLESSED TRUDO

[Col. 0273]

[Col. 0273A] 1. [SIGEBERT; THEODERIC, *Life of Saint Trudo*] In the year of the Lord 628, in the sixteenth year of the reign of Heraclius with his wife Martina, and in the fortieth year of Lothar II of that name [Col. 0274A], king of the Franks, son of Chilperic and his consort Fredegund—while John called Agnus presided over the church of Maastricht [Note: *1 reads “presiding.”]—Saint Trudo, chosen of the Lord, was born [Col. 0275A] that same year, more or less, at a place called Sarcinium in the territory of Hasbania, from noble parents worthy of God.

His father, named Wicbold, descended from the lineage of the kings of the Franks, a contemporary and kinsman in the direct line of the aforesaid King Chilperic. He governed by just laws the broad temporal lordship or county which he possessed by hereditary right in the regions of Hasbania, Campine [Note: Today Kempenland, on the left bank of the Dommel River and northward from the Nete River: the same region which the ancients called Texandria; see below, I.15.], and Flanders. His mother, named Adala, descended from the stock of the dukes of Austrasia and was a beloved kinswoman of Pippin I, duke of Austrasia; she reared this her only son for the salvation of many faithful people [Note: As far as I can see, our author was the first to supply this genealogy.].

2. [SIGEBERT, *Life of Saint Trudo*, ch. 3] In the year of the Lord 633, the twenty-first of Heraclius’ reign, and the second year of King Dagobert, monarch [Col. 0275B] of the three kingdoms—namely Francia, Neustria, now called Normandy, and Austrasia, now called Lotharingia—Saint Trudo, being in the sixth year of his life or thereabouts, gathered stones upon a level field in childlike fashion and built a little church. Prostrate in prayer there, he bound himself by a vow to build a church on his allod. A certain presumptuous woman looked upon it indignantly and scattered it with her foot; she was immediately struck blind by divine vengeance. But at the earnest request of the neighbours who gathered there, the boy invoked God’s mercy for her and restored her sight.

Incidental matter. [SIGEBERT] At about the same time Saint Arnulf was appointed bishop of Metz.

Incidental matter. [*Life of Saint Theodard*, ch. 4] At the same time a son was born to the aforesaid King [Col. 0275C] Dagobert. At the king’s humble request Saint Amandus baptized the child and gave him the name Sigebert. When, after the prayers had ended, the godparents did not at once answer the venerable priest who was baptizing him, the infant, forty days old, answered “Amen” in fully articulated speech, in the hearing of those standing around.

[Chapter 8] At about the same time, around the year 646, John called Agnus, bishop of Maastricht, died; and that same king appointed Saint Amandus, though unwilling, bishop of Maastricht. Incidental matter: after he had presided for three years, he entrusted the care of the episcopal see to Saint Landoald, the archpriest, and sought the solitary life [*Life of Saint Amandus*] and remained at the monastery of Elnone until the end of his life.

[Col. 0275D] 3. In the year of the Lord 644 or thereabouts, Saint Adala, mother of blessed Trudo, rested in peace. Her body, buried in the church at the village of Zelem [Note: A village near Diest.], an allod of Saint Trudo, was distinguished by miracles; placed in a fitting shrine, it was raised from the earth.

Incidental matter. [*Life of Saint Glodulf*] At about the same time Saint Glodulf, imitating the holiness of his father Saint Arnulf, became bishop of Metz after Georic, whom Arnulf had previously recognized in the spirit as appointed to succeed him in the episcopate [Col. 0276A].

Incidental matter. [SIGEBERT] In the year of the Lord 645, the third year of the reign of Constans or Constantine, the distinguished man Wicbold, father of blessed Trudo himself, fell asleep in the Lord in a good old age. Buried in the church of his allodial village named Wibekem after himself [Note: A village in the same region, not far from Diest.], he deserved to be raised up.

Incidental matter. In the same year Saint Remaclus was drawn from the solitary and monastic life by Dagobert, king of the Franks [Note: Rather by Sigebert II, according to the ancient *Life of Saint Remaclus*.; *Life of Saint Theodard*, ch. 5], and was ordained bishop of Maastricht around the year 650, against his will and overcome by entreaties.

4. In that same year the most blessed young man Trudo, bereft of both parents but needing no guardian, since he had already completed his seventeenth year, began to ponder how, with God’s grace, he might administer his paternal lordship and the most ample attached patrimonies of possessions so wisely [Col. 0276B] that an abundance of temporal things might in no way obstruct for him entrance into the everlasting inheritance.

[*Life of Saint Trudo*, I.7, 8, 12] While carefully reflecting upon these matters, he recalled the vow which, when a little boy, he had formerly made concerning the construction of a church on his own inheritance. As he wavered in this preoccupation of mind, sleep immediately stole over him. He saw an angel of the Lord standing beside him and urging him to go to Saint Remaclus, bishop, and to obey him in all that he commanded. Upon awakening, he hastened, according to the angel’s command, to the village of Septemburias. There he revealed the angel’s counsel to the bishop who was residing there. The latter said to him: “Go, my son, to the bishop of Metz, and hand over to blessed Stephen everything you possess in Hasbania. For I have learned by an angelic revelation that this will be acceptable to Christ.”

5. Therefore, on the next day, at early dawn, the venerable young man Trudo set out for the city of Metz. Presented there before the holy bishop Glodulf, and obedient to the counsel of his mentor, blessed Remaclus, he handed over to Saint Stephen all the patrimony which he possessed in Hasbania. Then Saint Glodulf adopted blessed Trudo as his son and, as he requested, entrusted him to a faithful man for diligent instruction in learning. By the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, within one year he knew how to chant the entire psalter; and in a short time he advanced so exceptionally in knowledge of the Scriptures [Col. 0276D] beyond human expectation that he marvelously surpassed his contemporaries.

Incidental matter. [*Life of Saint Amandus*; *Life of Saint Remaclus*] In the same year, King Dagobert granted, though unwillingly, Saint Amandus’ request to relinquish the burden of episcopal care, while he laboured in contemplation and preaching and had converted to the Catholic faith the inhabitants of Ghent, a famous town in Flanders. Yet, lest so famous a see lack the presidency of its own bishop, the king took counsel and [Col. 0277A] appointed Saint Remaclus, a monk from the monastery of Solignac [Note: Solignac in Aquitaine.], where he had lived under Father Eligius, as bishop of Maastricht, drawing him from the solitary life although he resisted.

At about the same time, in 638, the aforesaid king died of an intestinal flux, yielding up his spirit with great devotion. His first-born son Clovis succeeded him in the kingdom of Francia and Neustria. His other son was named Sigebert, whom his father had established some years before, while still a boy, in the kingdom of Austrasia, now called Lotharingia, appointing as his guardians Humbert, archbishop of Cologne, and Pippin, duke of Lower Austrasia. Following in the praiseworthy footsteps of his guardians, Sigebert grew in every moral quality and virtue, as became clear in the course of his reign [cf. FREDEGAR; *Life of Saint Sigebert*].

Incidental matter. In the following year, 639, the aforesaid Duke Pippin and mayor of the royal palace, whom King Dagobert had made archduke of all Austrasia, died in the Lord. His body was buried at Landen and, many years later, was transferred from there to the town of Nivelles, where it shines forth in miracles. His death struck the whole kingdom of Austrasia with grief [cf. *Life of Saint Sigebert*].

This Pippin, the first of that name, was the son of the magnificent prince Carloman. By his wife Saint Itta [Ytuberga], he begot a son named Grimoald, who succeeded his father in the duchy and, through the aid of Saint Cunibert, was made mayor of the palace in his father’s place; he died childless. The same Pippin also had a daughter named Begga, whom he gave in marriage to Duke Ansigise, son of Saint Arnulf, his companion [Col. 0277C]. She bore Pippin II, called the Fat, whose son was Charles Tudetes, or Martel. Charles, begotten by the concubine Alpaide, begot Pippin III, who, through the favour of Pope Zachary and on account of his prowess in victories, was made king of the Franks. King Charlemagne begot the fourth Pippin and made him king of Italy. The fifth Pippin, son of Louis the Pious, was made king of Aquitaine by his father. The sixth Pippin of that name succeeded his father in the kingdom of Aquitaine; when he died, the name Pippin was extinguished.

This first Pippin was one of the most powerful dukes in the kingdom of Austrasia, possessing by hereditary right the lordship of his duchies, whose territories were defined by distinct boundaries [Col. 0277D]. His duchy was called the duchy of Lower Austrasia; among its many other towns and castles, it included Brabant, which took its name from Brabo, a Trojan soldier and nephew of the great Hector. Moreover, a large part of Hasbania and Campine belonged to him. In our district he possessed two palaces: one smaller, in the place still called Landen, and the other larger, in the town called Nivelles.

[*Life of Saint Gertrude*] After the children already mentioned, Itta bore him a daughter named Gertrude, a virgin chosen by God, who in the fourteenth year of her age faithfully attached herself to her widowed mother.

Incidental matter. In approximately the same year [Col. 0278A] in which Pippin himself died, Saint Amandus, as was his custom, set out toward the town of Nivelles in order to sow the word of God. The widowed Itta invited him to dine. At the earnest prayers of the mother Itta and daughter Gertrude, he imposed the sacred veil upon both and consecrated their house as a church [*Life of Saint Amandus*; SIGEBERT]. A few days later he returned to the monastery of Elnone which he had chosen, and there, serving Christ with the greatest devotion, after these years he fell asleep in the Lord in the eighteenth year of the reign of this Constans or Constantine.

6. [*Life of Saint Trudo*, ch. 9] In the year of the Lord 650, the eighth year of Constans or Constantine, and the sixth year of Saint Remaclus’ episcopate, Saint Trudo, setting aside the liberal arts, turned his study to the investigation of understanding Holy Scripture [Col. 0278B]. How much he advanced in it was made apparent by those who had fallen and were restored through him.

7. In the same year King Sigebert of Austrasia, despairing of offspring [*Life of Saint Theodard*, chs. 4 and 7], with the cooperation of the mayor of the palace and Duke Grimoald, son of Pippin I, and of Saint Remaclus, built twelve monasteries. Of these, he consented that two should be built wherever Saint Remaclus wished. By virtue of this grant, the man of God founded one monastery in the diocese of Cologne, which he called Malmedy, and another in the diocese of Maastricht, which he named Stavelot. When their construction had been magnificently completed from the treasury of the pious king, the king, on Saint Remaclus’ advice, made Saint Theodard, a man adorned with learning and virtues, the first abbot of the monastery of Stavelot [Col. 0278C]. How diligently he imparted by word and example to those subject to him the discipline of holy religion in its full perfection was apparent from the disciples whom he trained. They lived so devoutly that many famous men—Saint Remaclus and Saint Lambert, bishops of Maastricht, among others—delighting in the purity of monastic life, lived there in later times to serve God.

Incidental matter. At about this time, after Grimoald, duke of Lower Austrasia and mayor of the royal palace of King Sigebert, had died, Pippin II, his nephew through his sister Begga, succeeded to the duchy and the mayoralty of the palace, around the year 656.

8. [SIGEBERT, *Life of Saint Trudo*, I.15–17] In the year of the Lord [Col. 0278D] 655, the twelfth year of Constans or Constantine, and the tenth year of Saint Remaclus’ episcopate, Saint Trudo, now sufficiently imbued with knowledge of Holy Scripture, was ordained priest by Saint Glodulf.

Likewise. In the same year, the venerable father Saint Glodulf, bishop of Metz, divinely inspired, kindly summoned Saint Trudo to himself and said: “Dearest son, you must visit your native borders for the advancement of the church of Saint Stephen—or rather, for the salvation of the inhabitants of Hasbania. For you will gain no small people for God and Saint Stephen, and you will prepare in your inheritance a perfect people to serve the Lord. I ask that you not be troubled because I command you to depart from here; for it is necessary that, as your merits require, many religious men should serve God in the inheritance which you handed over to Saint Stephen.”

Saint Trudo assented to the counsels of his pious father; and, both bathed in tears, after holy kisses from the bishop, he set out with his blessing. Likewise: as the venerable Trudo departed from the city of Metz, the city’s people accompanied him and said in tearful voices: “Why, holy father, do you thus leave us, who have always obeyed your commands? Happy Hasbania,” they said, “which will enjoy your presence, will be enriched by our loss, and will rejoice in our sorrow.” He answered: “Dear fellow citizens and members of God’s household, do not be distressed. Although I seem for a time to be removed bodily from your presence, I shall always be present in prayer.” And so, commending them to the divine majesty, he directed his journey [Col. 0279B] toward his native land.

9. The venerable Father Trudo, therefore, having made a successful journey, approached a certain village named Sene, which was the own allod of a noble knight. While this man was afflicted with a severe attack of leprosy and deprived of the sight of his eyes, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rise quickly: salvation and bodily health are near you. Send your servants to the meeting of the roads, and they will encounter a man of lowly appearance. If you wash yourself with the water from the washing of his hands, you will immediately be healed.”

Awakening, he joyfully revealed the vision to his household and sent messengers, as he had learned from the angel. When they had gone a little way into the open country outside the village, the man of God came to meet them and humbly asked the way that led to the church itself. [Col. 0279C] Recognizing him by his appearance, they were astonished for joy and said: “If you wish to go to the church, we shall accompany you; indeed, we shall gladly receive you for a meal.” Understanding that God’s grace had provided this for him, the holy man completed prayer in the church with an abundance of tears, then gratefully went with them to dine and entered the knight’s house with a blessing.

After pleasant conversation, when the table had been prepared for them to sit down, the nobleman ordered water to be brought for washing the hands of his sweet guest. When a towel [Note: *Touaille* in French, *dwele* in German in the *Saxon Mirror*, i.e. a cloth.] was offered for drying, the aforesaid nobleman, withdrawing his eyes aside, as he had learned from the angel, anointed his leprous limbs with this washing-water and immediately received health of his entire body [Col. 0279D]. Therefore he fell at the feet of his heavenly physician; and, with his whole household, bathed in a shower of tears, he proclaimed thanksgiving to God and Saint Trudo on high. But the man of God ascribed the gift of this cure not to himself, but rather to the power of his host’s grace of hospitality. Thus, with a contest of humility, the healed man and his healer approached the table.

When the meal was finished, this nobleman, who lacked offspring, effectively bestowed upon Saint Trudo his village with every right and inheritance, as it had descended to him allodially from his ancestors, and appointed the saint of the Lord as his heir. When the donor’s brother learned of this gift, he claimed the village for himself and did not fear to seize it violently. But the Almighty, avenging the injury inflicted upon His servant, immediately struck the invader of this village with a grave bodily sickness and left him contracted in his limbs as though a trunk. Then, coming to himself and moved by repentance, he sent messengers humbly to bring blessed Trudo to visit him and asked forgiveness. At the saint’s prayers, poured out to God in the sick man’s presence, all the knotting of his limbs was loosened and his former health restored. Immediately prostrate at Trudo’s feet, he restored what had been taken away, and offered his own village to the holy man, just as his brother had earlier offered his.

He answered him: “I accept what was taken from me and has now been restored; but I wish your village to be incorporated forever into the church of Metz.” This village is called [lacuna] [Note: Lacuna in *1*.] and lies near our aforesaid village of Sene. Its inhabitants, even to this day, are most faithful to blessed Trudo and regard themselves as belonging rather to the monastery itself, as to their own patrons.

10. Furthermore, the venerable Trudo [Note: Passage from “Trudo” to *invigilare* (“attend diligently”) in Henschen.] having been delayed somewhat from his journey by the foregoing affair, learned that Saint Remaclus, bishop, was staying near the town of Tongeren, and directed his route there. Brought into his presence and falling at his feet, both rose; and after mutual embraces, mingling holy conversation, Trudo recounted to his most beloved father the entire course of his journey and its events [Col. 0280C].

Then the bishop, reckoning as his own gains the advancement in learning and discipline in conduct of so great a priest, took him as his colleague in preaching Christ’s Gospel. Dividing the burden of pastoral care, he enjoined him by his authority to organize churches and administer the sacrament of penance. Thus the bishop began to devote himself more freely to contemplation with Mary, while Trudo, labouring diligently with Martha, attended to the care of the churches and preaching throughout the diocese.

11. [*Life of Saint Trudo*, II.1] After this, the man of God Trudo, seeking to fulfil the injunctions of blessed Glodulf, bishop of Metz, hastened to visit his native territory and directed his journey to Sarcinium, the place of his birth. When [Col. 0280D] the people of Sarcinium learned this from the report that had gone before, the whole district, in bands and in a procession gathered of men, women, and children, went out joyfully to meet their long-desired lord. When they saw him safe and sound, they embraced and kissed him, shedding tears for joy; delighting in his sweet speech, they asked for and received his blessing.

Accompanied into his Sarcinium by this tumultuous but friendly devotion of the people, he became all things to all: correcting some through consolation, reforming others through rebuke, and travelling through the district itself with the word of preaching. [Col. 0281A] He utterly cleansed away the dregs of paganism, which had not yet been completely emptied out there; and, as the religion of faith increased, he daily enlarged the church of the faithful with new peoples.

12. [Ibid., II.2] Therefore blessed Trudo, seeing that divine aid was present to him in the multitude of faithful people gathering around him, recalled the vow by which he had bound himself to God in childhood, concerning the construction of a church in his inheritance. He desired to establish a monastic rampart for the Christian host flowing to him [Note: *1 reads “to erect.”], where, intent with his fellow soldiers upon continual devotion and prayer against the darts of the most wicked enemy, he might triumph in Christ.

At last invoking the aid of the supreme Creator, he procured skilled craftsmen and assigned them a pleasant plain for founding the monastery in an elevated place toward the north, having on its left the river Cisindria [Note: The brook Cisinder flows into the river Gete.] flowing through the valley [Note: *1 reads “flowing.”] below. When the materials necessary for this work had been procured, the masons laid the foundations without delay; and in a short passage of time, the stone walls raised to a height gladdened the minds of onlookers.

Yet, while ardently occupied with the concern of so costly a work, God’s servant Trudo nonetheless faithfully fulfilled the office of preaching entrusted to him by Saint Remaclus.

Incidental matter. [*Life of Saint Theodard*, ch. 8; *Life of Saint Trudo*, II.17; *Life of Saint Theodard*, ch. 5; *Life of Saint Remaclus*; *Life of Saint Theodard*, chs. 5 and 7] At about the same time, in 661, Saint Remaclus, distressed that the goods of his church had for about thirty years been unjustly held and possessed by powerful and noble persons and that he could not stretch out his arms against the torrent [Col. 0281C], grew weary of secular disturbances and considered returning to the harbour of the solitary life. For this reason he approached King Sigebert [Note: Sigebert had already died in 656; the king of Austrasia was Childeric II. For Saint Remaclus see Heriger in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, VII, 185.], and at last, with great difficulty, was released by him from the burden of pastoral care.

Rejoicing that he had laid down the episcopal burden and escaped the shipwreck of the world, he sought the long-desired haven of repose in the monastery of Stavelot. There, devoted to the contemplative life, he dwelt there, made monastic profession, and, after many years, was called to the Lord and deserved to be buried in that same place, around the year 667.

Incidental matter. In the same year the nobles and courtiers, together with the urban populace, approached King Sigebert concerning the appointment of a bishop. After deliberating jointly with them, with everyone’s consent and also with the authority of the supreme pontiff, he appointed Theodard, abbot of Stavelot, bishop of Maastricht. A few days later he was consecrated by Saint Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne. He presided for twenty-eight years after Saint Maternus of Tongeren had been bishop. In the same year Saint Lambert, a youth of good disposition, was entrusted by his father, the distinguished man and count named Aper, to the instruction of Saint Theodard [Note: *1 has an omission; the *Life of Saint Theodard* reads: “he was imbued with liberal learning.”].

[Col. 0282A] **13.** [SIGEB. *Life of St Trudo* II, 2.] In the year of the Lord 657, the fifteenth year of the reign of Constans or Constantine, and the third year of the episcopate of Theodard, bishop of Tongeren, Saint Trudo had the monastery—which he had founded at his own expense on his hereditary estate and suitably raised up for habitation—dedicated by Saint Theodard, bishop of Tongeren, in honour of Saints Quintinus and Remigius, on 13 October.

**14.** Wishing fully to fulfil a vow divinely inspired in him long before, during his childhood, he richly endowed the aforesaid monastery from his productive and extensive patrimony. For, besides the lordship and possessions which he held in Hesbaye by succession from his parents—whence, as has been narrated above, he held very large estates in [Col. 0282B] Austrasia, afterwards called Lotharingia, which even now serve as incorporated endowments of the table of the bishops of Metz—among these was the estate of Dongei [Note: [Col. 0282D] Dugny; cf. Rudolf, *Deeds* VII, 6.], situated one mile from Verdun; after many years Theoderic, cousin of Otto I, appropriated it to himself—he also possessed, on his father’s side, the lordship of the town called Bruges with its appurtenances, which is now a celebrated town in the land now called Flanders. Near that town, at almost half a mile’s distance, is a monastery of black nuns, which has received its name from Blessed Trudo, namely Saint Trudo’s. This monastery [Note: [Col. 0282D] This is the Bruges-Elckhout monastery.] Blessed Trudo himself founded and endowed there on his own freehold estate, and established eighty monks in it; but for what reason the sex of those serving God there was later changed is unknown.

Incidentally. Since the narrative has touched upon the land of Flanders, it is fitting to note what its former condition was. It should therefore be known that a very fertile tract of land, now called Flanders, belonged to the kingdom of France. There kings customarily appointed from among the courtly magnates bailiffs and foresters to govern the people and collect annual revenues; nor was it called a county until the first year of the empire of Charles the Bald.

**15.** Moreover, the venerable Trudo held lordship and extensive hereditary possessions in Taxandria, the land now called Campine, which contains many liberties and villages. Among these, after the death [Col. 0282D] of the holy father, very many churches are known to have been dedicated in honour of Saint Trudo himself. Ancient possession makes clear that their right of patronage, together with that of the neighbouring churches, belongs in full right to the collation of the abbot and convent of this monastery of Saint Trudo.

**16.** [*Life of St Trudo* II, 2.] In the same year, or thereabouts, venerable Trudo, having endowed this monastery of his abundantly from his ample and productive patrimony—as Blessed Glodulf, bishop of Metz, had foretold him by revelation of the Spirit—gathered a multitude of the faithful and caused the office of divine worship to be solemnly begun there. As devotion grew, this place advanced daily in its reputation for praise. For the fame of so devout a monastic congregation having spread everywhere, very many sons of noblemen, both from the rank of palace officials and from the freedom of magnates, together with common people and converts from servitude, entered to bear Christ’s yoke, despising the burden of riches and cutting off the hair of their heads, in order to serve the heavenly king forever. Many nobles also devoted their own sons and grandsons, with extensive patrimonies, [Col. 0283B] to be enrolled in this holy community and placed under the instruction of so great a teacher.

[*Life of St Beregisus.*] About [Note: [Col. 0283] The words “About these times” are written in a contemporary hand on a slip inserted into the quire.] these times Saint Beregisus, born in the district of Condroz and recently committed by his parents to the monastery of Saint Trudo to be instructed in literary studies and the divine law under the religious habit, now, through the generosity of Prince Pippin, built the monastery of Andenne in honour of Saint Peter in the province granted to him [Note: [Col. 0283] “granted province” 1*.]. There he was associated, in the same habit, as father with clerics serving according to the canonical order. [Note: [Col. 0283] “This is now [the monastery] of Saint Hubert in the Ardennes, where Wazo, bishop of Liège, after the body of the said Saint Hubert had been brought there from Tongeren and . . . [word illegible], established monks in place of regular canons.” Added by another hand.]

Concerning the site of this monastery’s original foundation, lest the course of events become uncertain, it must be understood that Blessed Trudo did not begin to build this church from the screen of the sanctuary [Note: [Col. 0283D] The place of the altar enclosed by screens.], beneath which the crypt now lies, which Obbert, bishop of Liège, consecrated in the year [Col. 0283C] of the Lord 1101. Rather, beginning only at the spot where the arch now rises between the stalled choir [Note: [Col. 0283D] A *stallus* is the place in the choir where each monk had his seat; hence a stalled choir is a choir in which monks sit.] and the altar of Blessed Trudo, he erected the forward part of the monastery, as it were its head, which by ecclesiastical custom he called the screen and sanctuary. There he founded the first altar, consecrated in honour of Saints Quintinus and Remigius. Afterwards, in the course of time, when the choir of singers had been built, the remaining part of the structure was arranged, which could be called the nave of the church with its adjoining apses.

Behind the aforesaid screen, as the history of the ancients relates, within the place that is now the singers’ choir, a crypt was built which stood separately, as may still be seen in some ancient monasteries. [Col. 0283D] In the course of time an altar in honour of the holy apostles was also constructed between the altar of Blessed Trudo and the principal singers’ choir, within the sanctuary screen itself; it was called the high altar, and stood about nine feet from the altar of Blessed Trudo. For there is the site of the tomb of the aforesaid holy father. Thus it is recorded that this crypt and high altar existed from ancient times, but when and by whom they were built is unknown.

Concerning the site of the aforesaid old sanctuary, it should be known that it extends from the arch above and behind the chapel of Saint Trudo as far as the level space in front of that chapel, inclusive, for approximately the length of a human body. No body other than that, probably, of one worthy before God is to be buried there, because the relics of saints which are kept round about, to the right and left of Saint Trudo’s chapel, are contained there.

**17.** Moreover, the blessed man, notwithstanding his domestic care for the devout flock, at suitable times, accompanied by a company of attendants, travelled throughout the district of Hesbaye and strengthened countless people in the faith of Christ by the words and example of his teaching; while still living, he sent many of them on before himself to God.

[Col. 0284B] **18.** [*Life of St Trudo* II, 6.] On alternate nights, while the others rested, he was accustomed to visit alone and without witnesses, now the church of Martin situated in the village called Falmia, now the church of Saint Servatius and Blessed Genevieve situated in the village called Septemburias; after private prayers he would secretly return to the monastery before dawn. Each village was about three miles from Sarcinio because of the extensive wood that had lain between them from ancient times; now, however, a pleasant open plain leads there in only half a mile.

Incidentally. [*Life of St Theodard*, chs. 9, 10, 16 ff.] At the same time Blessed Theodard, grieving that the church of Tongeren had been greatly diminished in its possessions [Note: [Col. 0283] *mutulatam* 1*.], after the pious king of the Austrasians, Sigebert, had long since died, resolved to go to King Childeric and lay before him a complaint against the sacrilegious persons concerning the wrongs inflicted upon his church. As he set out on this journey, his opponents, fearing that the matter of their wicked usurpations would be brought before the magnates of the palace, adding evil to evil, set an ambush and attacked the saint of the Lord with weapons: they cut off his head and, having cast him to the ground, divided his limbs with swords.

Incidentally. In that same year, while the body of Blessed Theodard was honourably kept at the city of Gwangionum, now called Worms, Saint Lambert conveyed the body of his teacher with all diligence from Worms to the village called Liège, and buried it there with reverence.

[Col. 0284D] **19.** [RENERUS, *Life of St Lambert*, ch. 7.] A few days later, when the nobles, clergy, and people were consulting together about appointing a bishop, they assembled and approached the palace of King Childeric, who had received from his father Clovis the kingdom of Austrasia, formerly held by his now deceased uncle Sigebert. On an appointed day, with the agreement of the king, magnates, clergy, and whole people, Saint Lambert was elected bishop of Tongeren; although he refused, [Col. 0285A] he was enthroned and consecrated by Saint Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne, in the twenty-first year of his age.

Incidentally. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 663, the twenty-first year of the reign of Constans or Constantine, Saint Gertrude of Nivelles died.

**20.** In the year of the Lord 685 [673], the sixteenth year of Constantine the Younger, and the twenty-eighth year of the episcopate of Saint Lambert, King Childeric of the Franks was killed because of his severity. His brother Theoderic, rejected from the kingdom by the Franks some years earlier [670], was restored on the advice of the leading men of the realm. [SIGEB.; RENERUS, *Life of St Lambert*, chs. 10, 11.] At the counsel of Ebroin, mayor of the palace, he summoned the bishops to a synod and unjustly deposed several of them. Since Lambert had formerly been intimate with Childeric, King Theoderic attributed the whole blame for his expulsion to him through Ebroin and drove him from the episcopate. Lambert, however, bearing all things patiently, left the bishopric and chose the harbour of monastic quiet at the monastery of Stavelot. There, dwelling with his spiritual father Remaclus for seven years, he submitted himself to monastic disciplines.

**21.** [*Life of St Trudo* II, 6.] While the blessed man [Note: [Col. 0285D] Saint Trudo.] could scarcely support his frail limbs, both from his daily labour and from the maturity of age, he nevertheless often completed fasts of two and three days and rarely allowed himself sleep upon a softer bed. When those especially close to him reproved him for such conduct, he smiled or replied with the words of Job: “Man is born for labour, and the bird for flight.” He was merciful toward the poor dwelling round about him, [Col. 0285C] and so generous in almsgiving that they importunately sought and received from him the necessities of life as bodily children do from parents.

**22.** [SIGEB.; RENERUS, *Life of St Lambert*, chs. 12, 13.] In the year of the Lord 691, the seventh year of Justinian II, and the thirty-fifth year of Saint Lambert’s episcopate, after the tyrant Ebroin had been killed, Faramundus—whom Adewinus, archbishop of Cologne, had formerly, by means of money, ordained bishop of Tongeren from among his clerics—was deprived of office at the just insistence of clergy and people, expelled from the whole province, and Saint Lambert was restored to the episcopal chair of Tongeren by Pippin son of Ansegisel, prince of France and duke of Lower Austrasia.

[Col. 0285D] Incidentally. [*Life of St Trudo* II, 17.] In the same year Saint Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren, fell asleep at Stavelot and was buried.

**23.** [SIGEB.; *Life of St Trudo* II, 7, 8.] In the year of the Lord 693, the seventh year of Justinian II, and approximately the thirty-seventh year of Saint Lambert’s episcopate, the venerable servant of God Trudo came to his end at the Lord’s summons. Having gathered the brothers together, after sweet [Col. 0286A] words of holy exhortation, he most devoutly received the life-giving sacraments in the presence of all. Having made the sign of the cross, he immediately breathed out his spirit on 23 November, in the sixty-fifth year of his age. His body was buried before the altar which he himself had founded in his monastery, and shone forth through very many miracles, as the books of his deeds testify.

**24.** [*Life of St Trudo* II, 8.] A few days later, the pious flock, bereft of so great a pastor, prepared his funeral according to custom with groaning and an outpouring of tears. Surrounded by choirs of singers and with a crowd from the whole province gathered together, they bore it to the monastery while chanting in tearful voices. When it had been solemnly placed in the middle of the church before the altar, and after the completion of the Masses was being laid in the tomb, [Col. 0286B] before the earth thrown in had been levelled with the pavement, there suddenly spread such a wondrously fragrant scent that all present, as though in ecstasy, lost the use of their outward senses. So great a darkness also accompanied it for the space of one hour that no one recognized the neighbour standing beside him. Nor did a single day within the thirty days after this burial fail to shine with manifestations of miracles.

**25.** [Ibid. II, 13, 14.] After the death of so great a pastor, Provost Lothar governed the care of the pious flock vigorously; under him both the devotion of those dwelling there and the temporal possessions and revenues from the gifts of the faithful increased.

Again. At the time when Father Lothar himself presided over this monastery, a certain thief secretly stole an ox belonging to the brothers. The servant in whose custody the ox had been, because he pursued the thief who had taken it from him, was killed by the thief’s servant. Since the perpetrators of this crime had remained hidden, the aforesaid father, having ordered the brothers to fast with continual prayer, was granted knowledge of them by a clear sign from God. For the thief became mad and, shouting, was enveloped in mud and suffocated in a precipice. The other, guilty of the theft, was brought by his mother to the thresholds of the monastery of the holy father. Crying aloud that harsh flames were consuming him inwardly, he obtained healing through the merits of most blessed Trudo and was restored to health.

**26.** [Ibid. II, 10.] About the same time, when frequent miracles occurred at the tomb of Saint Trudo, Pippin II, prince of the Franks and duke of Lower Austrasia, made a pilgrimage there with the magnates and nobles of the realm. After completing his prayer, as a sign of devotion he granted to the monastery by solemn donation all the right which he held in the estate of Okinsala [Note: [Col. 0285D] Okinsala is Ekinsala in Theoderic. Ghesquier testifies that this estate cannot now be located, *Acta SS. Belgii* V, 48; we have followed him in determining the names of these places.] [Note: [Col. 0285D] Omitted in 1*.], which was then public fiscal land, to the altar of that saint; likewise another estate called Ham [Note: [Col. 0286D] Hamme, one league from the lordship of Meerhout.], located in Campine, for the use of the servants of God serving there. His venerable wife Plectrude also, in recompense for eternal reward, [Col. 0287A] offered a great sum of gold with precious stones to the altar of Blessed Trudo. Having engaged goldsmiths, she marvellously adorned it with costly workmanship.

Incidentally. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 697, the first year of the reign of Leo II, the venerable priest and monk Bede flourished in England at thirty years of age; he usefully spent the remainder of his life labouring diligently in the holy Scriptures.

**27.** In the following year, when Saint Lambert had charitably rebuked Prince Pippin concerning his adulterous liaison with Alpaida, he was martyred by Dodo, duke of the Ardennes and brother of that Alpaida, and buried at Tongeren, in the fortieth year of his episcopate and the sixty-first of his age [about 709]. His killers perished by a wretched death within the year. Seeing their destruction punished by the sword of divine judgment, Alpaida bestowed a generous hereditary alms upon the ministers of the church in order to appease God’s offence.

**28.** [*Life of St Hubert.*] While [Note: [Col. 0287D] These matters are not drawn from the *Life of St Hubert* published by Surius, vol. VI, but the author derived them from a later work which Aegidius of Orval had among his sources. He indicated it more accurately in these words in *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, in Chapeaville I, 130: “Let him reread that little book, which there is no doubt is both possessed and read by many among us, composed by trustworthy men concerning the life and conduct of the illustrious Count Hubert before his episcopate.” This seems to be the same *Life* which Surius also saw and mentioned in his note at the end of the *Life of St Hubert* VI, 56.] divine offices were being celebrated at the funeral around the body of the blessed martyr, a voice thundered from above, saying: “God sends you Hubert, a worthy successor to the new martyr Lambert, today ordained and consecrated as bishop through his Roman vicar, the pope.”

**29.** At the same hour, while Saint Hubert was staying in Rome in order to bring into effect the contempt for the world which he had conceived in his mind through the exhortation of Blessed Lambert, at the very hour of that saint’s passion an angel of God brought Pope Sergius from the place of Lambert’s martyrdom the pastoral staff of Saint Lambert together with his episcopal vestments. [Col. 0287C] Clothed in these by the angel, Hubert was consecrated bishop by the pope. While he was celebrating Mass there, Saint Peter appeared to him, giving him a key, as though of gold, as a sign of the power to bestow healing upon lunatics and the insane. Returning from Rome with the staff, episcopal vestments, and key divinely bestowed upon him, he was honourably received by [Col. 0288A] the people and clergy of Tongeren.

**30.** [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 711, the third year of Justinian III, Saint Hubert transferred the episcopal see from Tongeren to Liège. Divinely warned, he found the body of Saint Lambert still intact in its coffin, brought it to Liège, where he had suffered, and buried it. He was bishop for thirty-two years and died after those years in the year of the Lord 735, on 29 June, in the eighteenth year of Leo III; Floribert succeeded him and presided for eighteen years.

Incidentally. In the year of the Lord 713, the second year of Philippicus, Pippin the son died and made Charles Martel, son of Alpaida, heir of his principate.

Incidentally. In the same year Petronax, a devout citizen of Brescia, rebuilt the monastery of Monte Cassino [Note: [Col. 0287D] Omitted in 1*.], after 110 years had elapsed since it had formerly been devastated by [Col. 0288B] the Lombards.

**31.** [*Life of St Eucherius*, ch. 4.] In the year of the Lord 717 [Note: [Col. 0287D] “A.D. 717—he established” supplied by Sausseye.], the fifth year of Philippicus, Charles Martel, mayor of the palace and prince of France, at the insistence of the citizens of Orléans removed Blessed Eucherius, a monk of the monastery of Jumièges, against his will from the place of his profession, and appointed him bishop of Orléans in place of his uncle.

**32.** [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 727, the tenth year of Leo III, Provost Lothar, who after the death of Blessed Trudo had governed this monastery praiseworthily for about thirty-three years, as is thought, died. Note, reader, that although from the first year in which Saint Trudo founded this monastery until the present year no writing has been found to declare [Col. 0288C] what religious rule the monastic congregation of this place followed, it is nevertheless inferred from the fact that the man of God Trudo established a congregation of eighty monks near Bruges that, as there, so also in this place, monastic life existed from the beginning. [Note: [Col. 0288D] On this question, which has also greatly troubled more recent writers of history, see the study published by Ghesquier before Donatus’s *Life of St Trudo*, in *Acta SS. Belgii* V, 1.]

[Col. 0287] **The first book of the first part ends.**

**THE SECOND BOOK OF THE SAME WORK BEGINS.**

[Col. 0287C] **1.** In approximately the same year the venerable man [Col. 0287D] Grimo was the first to bear the title of abbot in this monastery. In the thirty-third year after the burial of Blessed Trudo, the first pastor of this congregation, he attained that office. Under him, as the number of professed members grew, regular discipline advanced so greatly that the approved reputation of the fervent religious life in this place attracted not only neighbours but also many distant faithful persons wishing to abandon the world.

**2.** This Abbot Grimo is the first of fifteen abbots of this place whose deeds have not been committed to posterity’s memory, as Lord Rudolf, abbot, states in the first book of the second part of these deeds of the abbots of this place, where he also gives each of their names. Yet, through the diligence of certain persons, sufficient information about the memory of this Abbot Grimo has been found, both in extracts from ancient deeds and in copies of old charters: namely, in what years of the Lord and under which emperor he presided over this monastery [Note: [Col. 0289] Omitted in 1*.], as will appear in the course of the narrative.

Grimo was succeeded by Reyramnus, the second abbot, and Hardebenus, the third; after him Columbanus was fourth abbot, then Ingelramnus fifth, and Ambrosius sixth. Only the names of these five abbots are found. After them came Ghiselbertus, the seventh abbot. Nothing else is found written concerning him except that a certain noble matron obtained from Abbot Reynerus the renewal of a charter [Col. 0289B] which many years earlier this same Ghiselbertus had once sealed for the ancestors of that matron concerning freedom from head-rent. This Ghiselbertus was, it is believed, predecessor of Lord Drogo, bishop of Metz and abbot of this place, concerning whom there will be an account below under the year of the Lord 838, the twenty-fourth year of Louis’s reign.

**3.** [SIGEB., *Life of St Eucherius* 7, 8.] In the year of the Lord 733 [Note: [Col. 0289] “A.D. 733—might sigh” supplied from the Sausseye manuscript.], the sixteenth year of Leo III, Charles Martel, prince of the Franks, at the urging of his followers, deprived Saint Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, of his office in the sixteenth year of his episcopate and sent him into exile, for two reasons. First, because he refused to agree when Charles appropriated the goods of churches and distributed their revenues as pay to soldiers; secondly, [Col. 0289C] because he refused to open the city of Orléans to Charles as he went to make war [Note: [Col. 0289] “war” S.] against Raginfrid, fearing danger to the citizens.

[*Life of St Rigobert.*] For the same reason Rigobert, archbishop of Reims, who had baptized Charles, was deprived of office by him because he refused to open his city.

**4.** [*Life of St Eucherius*, ch. 8.] At about the same time [Note: [Col. 0289] “year” Sausseye.] Charles, proceeding toward Paris, ordered Saint Eucherius to follow him on foot. After consultation, he sent him into exile at Cologne. When Eucherius was honourably treated there, Charles feared that he might perhaps seek the Alpine mountains and lodge a complaint before the apostolic see concerning the wrongs done to him. Charles therefore recalled him from Cologne and sent him to safer places, entrusting him to Robert, duke [Col. 0289D] of Hesbaye. Recognizing the blessed man’s kindness and holy manner of life, Robert gave him free authority to distribute alms to the poor from his own resources and abundant goods and to provide assistance for monasteries [Note: [Col. 0289] “monasteries” S.].

In gratitude, the bishop blessed the household and duke for such mercy and asked that he might be permitted to pray and celebrate Mass in the church of Blessed Trudo. When he freely obtained this, [Col. 0290A] he devoted himself with such fervour to continual service of God that not only did the monastic congregation of this monastery prosper through the diligence of its Abbot Grimo, but, advanced by the sweet teaching of so great a bishop and the perfection of his holy virtues, it continually longed for heavenly things, despising earthly ones. [Note: [Col. 0289] *adspiraret*, “might breathe/aspire toward,” S.]

Incidentally. [SIGEB.; cf. FREDEGAR.] In the year of the Lord 741, the twenty-third year of Leo III, the most victorious Prince Charles, after pacifying and enlarging the kingdom of the Franks, divided princely rule of the kingdom between his sons Carloman and Pippin, on the advice of his magnates. Seized by a severe fever, he died in peace at Paris on 22 October, in the twenty-fifth year of his principate. About the same time Theoderic II [Note: [Col. 0289D] Rather, IV.] king of the Franks died; Charles himself had formerly made him king after the death of Chilperic [Note: [Col. 0289D] II.] [Col. 0290B] [Note: [Col. 0289] A word is omitted in 1*.]. Childeric [Note: [Col. 0290D] III, the last of the Merovingians.] succeeded him.

**5.** [*Vision of St Eucherius.*] In the following year [Note: [Col. 0289] “In the year—he showed” from the Sausseye manuscript.] Blessed Eucherius began to fail in strength; but what he could render to God less fully through bodily exertion, he fulfilled through an ever-burning, more fervent ardour of spirit. One day, while he prayed more earnestly, he was caught up in the spirit and saw Prince Charles tortured with infernal punishments. When he asked his guiding angel why the gates of hell excluded so great a prince and defender of the kingdom, the angel replied: “Because he took tithes from churches and those who serve God, and distributed gifts from them to hired retainers, he will be punished by the judgment of the supreme King with eternal damnation.”

When the vision disappeared and the man of God returned to himself, he swiftly sent a messenger [Col. 0290C] to Boniface, his intimate friend, archbishop of Mainz, who was then residing at Paris, and reported what he had seen. Astonished at the vision, Boniface related the vision of Saint Eucherius to the abbot of Saint-Denis, in whose monastery the body of the aforesaid Prince Charles had been buried. A few days later, for some necessary reason, it happened that Charles’s tomb was opened. It was found wholly empty and entirely blackened, and a huge serpent was seen to emerge from it. When the outcome of this event was spread abroad everywhere, it checked the tyranny of many princes from seizing ecclesiastical possessions, lest they suffer a similar punishment. For Pippin III, son of the aforesaid Charles [Note: [Col. 0289] A word is omitted in 1*.], is recorded to have made many restitutions to churches and religious houses. [Col. 0290D] His brother Carloman also, setting aside his principate, put on the monastic habit in the monastery of Monte Cassino.

**6.** [*Life of St Eucherius*, ch. 9.] In the following year Blessed Eucherius, fortified by the saving sacraments, breathed out his last spirit. His body was honourably buried beside the tomb of Blessed Trudo on the . . . day of February [Note: [Col. 0289] Lacuna in 1*; Sausseye adds “twentieth.”], in the ninth year of his exile and the twenty-fourth [Col. 0291A] year of his ordination. The account of his life and deeds shows that his tomb was made illustrious by many miracles.

Incidentally. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 743, the second year of Constantine, son of Leo III, Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, an Englishman by nation, founded the monastery called Fulda in the forest of Buchonia, which is in Thuringia. It is said to be nobler than other monasteries in the regions of Germany; its chief abbot holds rank at the emperor’s court and serves the emperor with one thousand armed soldiers. Its first abbot was Saint Sturm, who died in the year of the Lord 780. About the same time Sigebald, bishop of Metz, flourished.

**7.** In the year of the Lord 745, the fourth year of Constantine, son of Leo III, the fourth year of Hilderic, successor of Theoderic, king [Col. 0291B] of the Franks, and approximately the fifteenth year of Grimo’s abbacy in this place, Robert, count or duke of Hesbaye, who at the command of the aforesaid Prince Charles Martel had charitably maintained the aforementioned Blessed Bishop Eucherius from his own resources until the latter’s death, desiring to promote divine worship, came to this monastery. He generously granted to Saint Trudo his freehold estate of Dung [Note: [Col. 0291D] Donck, not far from Diest.] with the adjacent villages Halen [Note: [Col. 0291D] Halen, not far from Diest, is a small Brabant town on the Gete.], Scaffen [Note: [Col. 0291D] Schaffen in the diocese of Mechelen.], Velpen [Note: [Col. 0291D] Velpen is now not far from the town of Saint Trudo. Miraeus, in whose *Opera diplomatica* I, 493 this very charter is printed, doubts whether it is Op-Velp or Neder-Velp.], and Merhout [Note: [Col. 0291D] So called today as well; at a certain lake named Meer in the territory of Sichen. According to Miraeus, Latomus says in his history of the monastery of Saint Trudo that he saw it among the Bruges archives.], with all their inheritances, fields, woods, meadows, fisheries, watercourses, and *wariscapia* [Note: [Col. 0292D] That is, *waterscapum*, watercourses.], together with the remaining rights, courts, and houses. There are several charters concerning these matters, one of which has the following text:

> He possesses worldly goods well who obtains for himself eternal rewards from things that perish. Considering this diligently in my mind, I, Robert, count, son of the late Lambert, have resolved to grant something from my hereditary possession to the bodies of the saints, that through their merits I may deserve forgiveness for my sins before the sight of God.
>
> Therefore, in God’s name, I make known to present and future persons that I, Robert, in the fifth year after the death of King Theoderic, on the seventh day after the Kalends of April [26 March] (742), by lawful transfer gave and assigned something of my freehold estate to the basilica of Saint Trudo, built in the village called Sarcinio, where that saint of God, according to the faith of all, rests in the body; the venerable abbot named Grimo is also seen to preside regularly over that church.
>
> I therefore transferred to the aforesaid place in the district of Hesbaye a certain locality called Dungo, with the basilica built there [Col. 0291D] which I constructed by my own labour in honour of Blessed Mary, Saint Peter, Saint John, Saint Servatius, and Saint Lambert; both that place itself and [Col. 0292A] the remaining villages or localities from my aforesaid property attached to it, namely Halon, Scaffnis, Felepa, and Marholt. These aforesaid places are in the districts of Hesbaye and Masuarensis [Note: [Col. 0292D] The district of the Mosarii—Masegau or Mosau—is the district situated on both banks of the river from Visé to ’s-Hertogenbosch. They maintain, however, that the county of Masuarensis differs from this and is situated, on account of the places named in this charter, in Taxandria. Cf. Ghesquier, *Acta SS.
