Belgii* V, 355; Wastelain, *Description de la Gaule Belgique*, pp. 202, 215.], all of which I transferred with the houses and courts lying there, with meadows, fields, woods, and so forth, as the copied record in the books of charters contains.

The body of this count or duke, and that of his wife, was buried in the sanctuary, not far from the tomb of Saint Trudo, on the left, before the site of the chapel of that saint. Many years later, namely in the time of Abbot Wiric [Note: [Col. 0292D] He held office 1155–1183.], when the foundations of the aforesaid chapel were being laid by him, it was, they say, found intact and placed in a stone sarcophagus.

Incidentally. In the year of the Lord 750, the ninth year of Constantine, son of Leo III, Pippin III, duke of Lower [Col. 0292B] Lotharingia, mayor of the palace and prince of France, was anointed king of France at the command of Pope Zachary by Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz. King Hilderic was deposed and tonsured as a monk. In the third year after this, the aforesaid Boniface was martyred in Frisia by enemies of the faith. His body was brought to the monastery of Fulda, which he had founded in Thuringia within the forest of Buchonia, and honourably buried.

**8.** [*Life of St Trudo* II, 8.] Some years later, in the time of the aforesaid King Pippin, the treasure of Saint Trudo’s monastery was secretly stolen by a certain man bearing the appearance of a pilgrim. Some time afterwards, the perpetrator of this sacrilege was exposed by another pilgrim who knew of the crime; by command of the aforesaid [Col. 0292C] king he was hanged, and the treasure, concealed in various places, was found and restored to the altar of Saint Trudo. A few days later [Note: [Col. 0291D] *vero* 1*.], a great part of this treasure, which the same thief had hidden underground, was unexpectedly found through the merits of Blessed Trudo by shepherds playfully digging in the earth, and restored to the abbot.

Incidentally. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 753, the twelfth year of Constantine, son of Leo III, Floribert, son of Saint Hubert and bishop of Liège, died; Fulcharius succeeded him and presided for fifteen years.

9. [Life of St Trudo II, 16.] In the year of the Lord 758, the seventeenth year of the reign of Constantine, son of Leo III, Saint Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, held the episcopate after Sigebald. He founded the monastery of Gorze within his diocese. He was a nephew, through his sister Landrada, of Pepin III, king of the Franks [Col. 0292D]. During his term of office he once came to the town of Sarcinium. One of his servants had incurred a penalty of correction for some offence [Col. 0293A]. Fearing that he would be disciplined with harsher blows, the boy fled to the monastery of our Saint Trudo. Members of the bishop’s household rashly pursued him and, wishing to drag him out by force, broke into the church doors. Immediately the right hand of the Most High opposed them: a fiery thunderbolt descended from heaven and lit the candles standing at the holy altars. Terrified by this, the perpetrators of such violence did not dare to lay hands upon the offender.

The holy bishop was summoned as witness to so great a miracle. He forgave the boy’s fault, punished his retainers with fitting satisfaction for their violation of so renowned a monastery, and, commending himself in his prayers to Saint Trudo, the patron under so powerful a protection, and imploring pardon, returned to the city of Metz [Col. 0293B].

[SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 763, he went to Italy, transferred the body of Saint Gorgonius to Gaul, and gave so great a treasure to the monastery of Gorze. In the following year he fell asleep in the Lord, and Angilram succeeded him in the episcopate.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 768, the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Constantine, son of Leo III, Pepin III, son of Charles Martel and king of the Franks, died. In that same year his son Charlemagne succeeded him in the kingdom. In the same year, after Fulcharius died, Agilfrid was taken from the palace of King Charles and made bishop of Liège; he presided for sixteen years.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 797, the sixth year of the empire of Constantine, son of Leo IV—his mother Irene having been rejected from the empire by Charles, king of the Franks [Note: this word is written in another ink over an erasure, Col. 0293], after the victory gained over the Huns—who were also called Avars—Henry, duke of Friuli [Col. 0293C], having despoiled the Avar prince Yrung in Pannonia, now called Hungary, sent an inestimable treasure to King Charles. In the same year Thadim, prince of the Avars, or of the Avar people, gave himself and his country to King Charles and received the grace of baptism.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 784, Agilfrid, bishop of Liège, died; Ogerbald succeeded him and presided for twenty-five years.

10. In the year of the Lord 802, when the empress Irene had been exiled by the Romans, Charlemagne—having already reigned thirty-three years over the Franks—was raised by the Romans to the imperial dignity. After the Roman empire had been separated from Constantinople and about 468 years had elapsed [Note: “and, after the empire …” is written by another hand in the margin, Col. 0293], he ruled for thirteen years. He obtained from the Romans the appointment as king of Italy of his son Pepin, the fourth of that name [Col. 0293D].

In the same year Angilram, who had then governed the church of Metz for forty-five years, was still alive. At his request Donatus, believed to have been a monk and exile of this place, wrote in a plain style the life and deeds of Blessed Trudo.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 803, the fourth year of Charlemagne’s empire, the pagan Huns—who, from the first year of Gratian’s reign, that is, from the year of the Lord 381, had emerged from the Scythian region lying on this side of the Maeotian marshes and driven the pagan Goths from their homes—after many years took the name of their king, who was called Avar, and were named Avars [Col. 0294A]. The Lombards, otherwise called Vinidi, received them into friendship; and, when setting out for Italy, they granted the aforesaid Huns or Avars Pannonia to inhabit—a province which they had occupied for many years after expelling its inhabitants. Having lived there for not a few years, they were conquered in war by the invading pagan Hungarians and lost Pannonia forever. Therefore, coming out against the Italians, they roamed through Italy and Gaul, devastating various places with slaughter, plunder, and fire, and exercised tyranny until the time of Charlemagne. Having gathered a multitude of nobles and common people and joined battle with them, he crushed those Huns so thoroughly that only the history of their deeds remained for posterity; then the persecution of the Huns ceased [Col. 0294B].

Incidental notice. In the ninth year of Charles, Gerbald, bishop of Liège, died; Waschand succeeded him. He built the women’s monastery of Andage in the Ardennes. At the same time [Note: “At the same time … monastery” is written in the margin by another hand, Col. 0293], at the monastery of Andain, later called the monastery of Saint Hubert, this same Waschand changed the institution of regular canons there and established a community of black monks. He transferred there from Liège the body of Blessed Hubert, finding it in a higher place beside the tomb of Saint Beregisus, founder of that monastery.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 814, Charlemagne died in the seventy-second year of his age. His son Louis the Pious obtained the empire and ruled for twenty-seven years. In the first year of his reign he had Bernard—the son of his brother Pepin, the fourth of that name—blinded, deprived him of the kingdom of Italy and of life, because he had conspired against him [Col. 0294C]. In the tenth year of his empire, Waschand, bishop of Liège, died; Pirard succeeded him and presided for nine years.

Incidental notice. In the same year Drogo, brother of this Louis, became bishop of Metz. In the following year [MART. POL.], Ariold, king of the Danes, together with his wife, son, and his own party of Danes, after many destructive incursions against the Franks, was finally overcome by the forces of Louis the Pious. He was baptized at Mainz and was honoured by Emperor Louis with gifts and with a part of Frisia granted to him as a benefice.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 836, Pirard, bishop of Liège, died; Hyrcanus succeeded him and presided for twenty-five years.

11. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 836, the twenty-third year of the empire of Louis the Pious [Col. 0294D], the pagan Northmen left their homes and peoples, attacked Gaul fiercely, and made the Frisians tributary. These Northmen were Danes by origin, but barbarian in language. They were called Northmen, as it were “northern people,” because they came from that quarter of the world. Owing to the sins of Christians, under various successive dukes and kings—namely Gundo, Grimundo, Alstagnus, Rollo, and many others—they roamed and repeatedly returned through Gaul, the kingdoms of the Franks and English, Lotharingia, and diverse provinces and principalities of the world for forty years, devastating them miserably [Col. 0295A; Note: “of diverse” 1*].

Although many thousands of them were repeatedly killed by Christians, and though they deserved to be baptized together with their leaders, those who remained escaped by flight. Having regained the number of their people, they did not cease despoiling towns, cities, and fortified places until the time of Arnulf’s empire, namely the year of the Lord 891.

12. In the year of the Lord 838, the twenty-third year of the empire of Louis the Pious, Drogo, bishop of Metz, was abbot over this monastery of Saint Trudo. He is believed to have succeeded Ghiselbert as the seventh in the number of abbots of this place; but I have not found recorded in memory in what year he began to be abbot or in what year he died.

[Col. 0295B] 13. In that same year a certain nobleman named Hotbert gave his goods, situated in a place called Hasnoth [Note: It is conjectured to be the same place as Halen, mentioned above at II, 7; cf. Ghesquier, *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* I, 308], in the district of Hasbania, to the church of Blessed Trudo, and ordered a charter to be drawn up from it. Its tenor is as follows [Note: The charter had already been published by Miraeus, p. 499]:

“Since this light swiftly runs its course and our days pass like a shadow, we ought, while we remain in the world, to give thought to the future judgment, so that, when the sudden day comes, it may find no one whatsoever unprepared. Therefore, in God’s name, I, Hotbert, reflecting upon God’s mercy for the remedy of my soul and the recompense of eternal goods, so that the most merciful God may deign to forgive me my sins and that I may possess eternal blessedness, as donor give by this deed of gift, and will to be given in perpetuity, to the basilica [Col. 0295C] of Saint Trudo, where he rests precious in body and where Lord Drogo, archbishop, appears to preside.

“This is what I give: my hereditary property in the place called Hasnoch, on the river Merbate, in the district of Hasbania or Diest: the estate with its demesne house [Note: reading: *in dominicato*, ‘on the demesne’] and the other buildings constructed upon that estate; and six occupied manses belonging or pertaining to that estate; together with lawful rights of way, *warescapiis* [uncertain: common rights or warrens], meadows, pastures, rights of exit and entry, movables and immovables; and woodland pannage for pigs, as much as may be found and as one’s own will may determine to send within; and whatever there appears to be there of my possession or lordship. All and entire, with the most devout affection of mind, I have conveyed to the aforesaid holy place, and in the presence of witnesses have confirmed it for perpetual possession, between the boundaries of Saint Trudo and Casalet, together with twenty-four dependants [*mancipia*].

“Done publicly in the monastery of Saint Trudo at Sarcinium, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July], in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of our lord Louis, most serene and orthodox emperor.”

Incidental notice. Observe, reader, that this Drogo was the thirty-ninth bishop of Metz. He was the fourth of five bishops of Metz to whom the Roman pontiffs, by a special privilege granted them, sent the pallium, commanding them to celebrate Mass vested in the pallium on specified days, as archbishops [Col. 0296A].

14. This Drogo, as is plausibly believed, was the eighth abbot of this monastery of Saint Trudo from the first abbot Grimo onward. By his diligence he adorned the monastery itself more devoutly with monastic discipline and enriched it with precious treasures and more generous revenues. During his time no prince dared disturb this monastery, both because of the authority of his virtues and because of the formidable majesty of Emperor Louis the Pious, his brother.

After this Abbot Drogo came Abbot Adelbold, believed to have been the ninth; then Abbot Hildrad, the tenth; afterward Abbot Sabbatinus, the eleventh; after him Abbot Ermenmar, the twelfth; Radulf, the thirteenth, succeeded him [Col. 0296B]; then Abbot Louis, the fourteenth; after him Robert, the fifteenth; then Chrodegang, the sixteenth; and Imizo, the seventeenth, succeeded him. A few events which occurred in Imizo’s time are recorded below in sequence.

Observe here, reader, that of the fifteen abbots of this place whom Abbot Rodulf lists continuously by name—seven of whose names are given above in chapter one of the second book, while the names of the other eight are here set down in order—these two abbots, namely Drogo and Imizo, do not belong to that list. Yet ancient notes and charters subsequently established that they too had been abbots of this place.

Incidental notice. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 841, the twenty-sixth year of Louis’s empire, this same Louis died and was buried at Metz. He left four sons [Col. 0296C]: Lothair, Charles called the Bald, Louis, and Pepin; this was the last Pepin, the fifth of that name. Lothair, his eldest son, seized the empire together with the kingdom of Francia and ruled for fifteen years.

In the second year of his reign Theodulf, abbot of Fleury, flourished [cf. MARTIN. MIN.], and was afterward made bishop of Orléans. Having been imprisoned, on Palm Sunday, while Louis was taking part in the solemn procession of that day, he went to the window of the lofty tower in which he was held and, raising his voice, devoutly sang in order the hymn *Glory, praise, and honour* (*Gloria, laus et honor*), together with the other verses composed by himself. Hearing this, the king took pity upon his exile and ordered him released; and from that time the aforesaid hymn has been sung on that day in the churches of Gaul [Col. 0296D].

Incidental notice. In the following year, after Louis the Pious died, Lothair I, his son, succeeded and ruled for fifteen years.

Incidental notice. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 844, the fourth year of Lothair’s empire, while his brothers were waging grievous war against Lothair over the division of the kingdom, the kingdom was divided into three parts and the brothers made peace with him. Charles received the western kingdoms from the British Ocean to the river Meuse; in that part the name Francia remained from then until now [Col. 0297A]. Louis received the eastern kingdoms: all Germany as far as the waters of the Rhine, and certain cities beyond the Rhine with their adjacent districts because of the abundance of wine. Martin’s chronicle adds a fourth brother, named Pepin, to these brothers, to whom Aquitaine fell as his share [Note: In fact Martinus Minorita here adds Pepin as a fourth to the three brothers].

[SIGEB.] Lothair, because he was older, was called emperor. He held all the kingdoms of Italy together with Rome itself, as well as the province and middle part of Francia between the Scheldt and the Rhine. This, having changed its name, since it had itself been called Austria, was named Lotharingia after this Lothair, the first of that name among emperors.

Lotharingia comprises these noble cities: Cologne, Trier, Metz, Verdun, Cambrai, and Liège [Col. 0297B], with all towns, castles, liberties, and villages situated under their dioceses. It also includes Ghent [Note: Gent], Louvain [Note: Lowen], Brussels, Mechelen [Note: Mecheln], Antwerp, Huy, Namur, Tongeren [Note: Tongern], Dinant [Note: Dinant], Saint-Trond, and moreover Aachen, which Charlemagne made the seat of this kingdom of Lotharingia, just as the city of Metz had been from ancient times. Under this kingdom there were also many duchies, counties, and lordships of princes, as is plainly evident to those who have surveyed the lands situated between the Scheldt and the Rhine.

Incidental notice. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 856, the sixteenth year of Lothair I’s empire, Lothair I divided the empire and kingdom among his sons: he gave the empire to his son Louis and the kingdom of Lotharingia to his younger son Lothair. Taking the monastic habit at the monastery of Prüm [Col. 0297C], he renounced the world and not long afterward died in Christ. A dispute was made concerning his soul: the angels claimed the soul of the monk, the demons the soul of the emperor; but through the prayers of the brothers the demons withdrew [cf. MART. POL.].

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 857, Adventius assumed the bishopric of Metz and presided for fifteen years. Who his immediate predecessor was is unknown.

Incidental notice. In the same year Hyrcanus, bishop of Liège, died; Franco succeeded him and presided for twenty-six years. About the same time the Danes, practising piracy, emerged through the port of the Flemings under their leader Alstagnus and invaded Francia with great force.

15. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 870, the fifteenth year of the empire of Louis II, Adventius, bishop of Metz, through his representatives sent from Metz to our monastery [Col. 0297D], caused an inventory to be made of all the furnishings and jewels [Note: *joyaux* in Ganorum; precious ornaments] of this place. Our people showed them a great abundance of precious treasures and utensils, both suitable for divine worship and seemly and honourable for human use. Moreover, the brothers’ very generous and regularly ordered allowance, with a written inventory and an explicit assignment of the revenues belonging to it, was recorded in writing by those same men [Col. 0298A], on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [15 August], in the thirteenth year of his episcopate.

Incidental notice. [*Gesta Trevirorum* 27.] In the year of the Lord 872, the seventeenth year of the empire of Louis II, Adventius, bishop of Metz, who had secured the promotion of his kinsman Bertulf to archbishop of Trier with Charles, king of Lotharingia and Provence, died after a few days. Walo succeeded him.

In the second year of Walo’s ordination, Pope John, the 105th of that name, out of reverence for the dignity of the kingdom of Lotharingia, whose capital was Metz, sent him the pallium and granted by open letters the feast days on which he might use it. Bertulf, archbishop of Trier, warned him concerning this use to put aside the pallium [Col. 0298B]. Walo replied that he was not the first but the fifth bishop whom the Apostolic See had deemed worthy to exalt with the honour of the pallium: first, Urbitus; second, Chrodegang, nephew through his sister of Pepin III, king of the Franks; third, Angilram; fourth, Drogo, son of Charlemagne and abbot of the monastery of Saint Trudo; “I became the fifth after them, with intervening successors.”

But Bertulf was not content with these assertions. Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, instructed Walo of Metz, in order to settle the dispute arising from such a controversy, to obey his metropolitan. Thus the pallium was set aside and the discord ceased.

From the account of this matter it is evident why the aforesaid bishops of Metz are styled archbishops, as is found recorded in charters or copies from the archives of our monastery of Saint Trudo [Col. 0298C]. In certain ancient charters of this monastery one reads “Theodoric” or “Stephen, bishop of the see of Mediomatrici,” which means the same as “bishop of Metz.” This arose because the city of Metz was the capital and seat of the kingdom of Austria, later called Lotharingia. In some chronicles one also finds *Mediomatricum* written in place of the name Metz.

Incidental notice. [SIGEB. MART. POL.] In the year of the Lord 877, after Louis II died, Charles the Bald ruled for two years. In the first year of his reign the county of Flanders began. For at that time it was not, as it now appears, of such great name and wealth [Col. 0298D], but was governed by bailiffs or foresters sent there by the kings of the Franks. Among these were the noble men Lideric under Pepin III, Ingerlaus under Charlemagne, and Andacer under Louis the Pious, governors of Flanders.

[Note: The following is by no means taken verbatim from that Chronicle of the Counts of Flanders called *Flanders the Generous*; nevertheless, nearly the same matters are read there, and without doubt our author drew his material from some similar chronicle of Flanders.]

In the course of time Baldwin, son of Andacer, a man of handsome appearance [Col. 0299A], succeeded in his father’s place and was admitted to the king’s court [cf. *Chronicle of the Counts of Flanders*]. When he was to be sent to Flanders, he abducted Judith, daughter of King Charles, who loved him, and carried her with him into Flanders. For this he was excommunicated by command of the king, with the consent of all the church through the bishops. Thereafter, through the intercession of bishops and nobles who advised this course, Baldwin and Judith, the king’s daughter, were admitted by Charles himself to pardon. The king graciously bestowed Flanders upon them as a county to possess in perpetuity.

Incidental notice. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 879, Charles the Bald died; his cousin Charles the Younger ruled for twelve years.

Incidental notice. In the third year of his reign, when many thousands of Northmen had been killed by the Franks and many more had been drowned with their ships at sea, greater security came to the inhabitants of Gaul, Francia, and Lotharingia [Col. 0299B]. Yet, lest that savage people return to the aforesaid provinces and kingdoms, they built crypts and underground hiding places in various cities and places to conceal ecclesiastical possessions and the relics of saints.

16. Therefore, in the following year or thereabouts (c. 880), the abbot then presiding over this monastery and its convent—renowned everywhere alike for observance of monastic discipline and for the enrichment of its temporal possessions—were made more hopeful by the slaughter in which the pagan Northmen had been humbled. Desiring to render their patron a greater honour of reverence than usual, after taking counsel [Note: “after taking counsel … placed” from the manuscript supplied by Henschen], they invited Franco, bishop of Liège, with one consent. He [Col. 0299C], first opening the burial-place [Note: Henschen: “the tomb-chest”], in the presence of many ecclesiastical and religious men and laymen, raised from below the holy relic of the precious bodies of Trudo and Eucherius and reverently placed it in an elevated place, amid the devout chant of psalm-singers.

17. In the following year (881), because a report was spreading that the Northmen would attack Lotharingia, the bodies of Saints Trudo and Eucherius were carefully lowered and hidden, through the diligence of the monks of this monastery, from the more elevated place in which they had formerly been deposited when their translation had been solemnly celebrated. They were placed within an underground crypt or vault [Note: “vault,” i.e. *volutio*; French *voûte*, a vaulted structure], recently constructed for this purpose beneath the chapel [Note: Henschen: “behind the altar”] of Blessed Trudo himself [Col. 0299D]. There they lay hidden for many years, until the time of Abbot Wiric, under whom they were solemnly translated again by Rodulf, bishop of Liège, as will appear below [Note: cf. above, *Continuation*, IV, 2].

18. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 883, the fourth year of the empire of Charles the Younger, the pagan Northmen, joined by Danes, turned aside from Francia and roamed through Lotharingia. They cruelly devastated with sword and fire Amiens, Arras, Corbie with the monastery of Saint Peter, Cambrai, Thérouanne, the territories of the Morini, Menapii, and Brabanters [Col. 0300A], and all the land on this side of the river Scheldt, together with the monasteries of Saints Walaric and Richarius. Then they advanced and entered the river Waal, which bursts from the side of the channel of the Rhine and flows between the Rhine itself and the Meuse. Landing at the embankment of the island of Batavia, situated between the Rhine and Waal—the centre of the duchy or county of Guelders—they entered it. After devastating it, they sailed across the aforesaid river Waal, destroyed the town of Nijmegen and the emperor’s palace there, and burned them.

19. In the same year the aforesaid Northmen, returning by way of the river Scheldt, devastated the celebrated town of Mechelen. Saint Libertus, son of the count of Mechelen, fled from their attack into Hasbania [Col. 0300B]. When those unbelievers pursued him, he entered this monastery of Saint Trudo for protection; the savage people cruelly slaughtered him before the altar of the aforesaid patron while he lay prostrate in prayer.

20. In the same year Godfrid and Sigefrid, kings of the Northmen, encamped with an innumerable multitude of their men beside the Meuse at a place called Haslon. They devastated and burned Liège, Maastricht, Tongeren, Cologne, Bonn, and the adjacent towns and castles. Stabling their horses in the palace at Aachen, they burned the town and palace itself. Moreover, they burned and destroyed the monasteries of Stavelot, Malmedy, Inda, and Prüm.

This monastery of Saint Trudo, no less splendid in religious devotion than the others and filled with temporal possessions [Col. 0300C], was under this catastrophe so utterly overthrown [Note: This undoubtedly occurred already in 881, when the *Annals of Fulda* attest that the district of Hasbania was devastated by the Northmen, Col. 0299D–0300D] that it was rarely inhabited until the time of Emperor Otto I. Therefore men and women of sacred order and profession fled and hid wherever they could most suitably do so, concealing the treasures of churches and the bodies of saints in safer places as far as they were able.

Incidental notice. In the same year Franco, bishop of Liège, died; Stephen, who composed the chant for the Finding of Saint Stephen, succeeded him.

Incidental notice. In the following year the Northmen attacked the diocese of Trier, overthrew all its castles, towns, and villages, and at last destroyed the city itself after taking it by assault, while the bishop was saved by flight [cf. *Gesta Trevirorum* 28]. After this they came as far as the city of Metz [Col. 0300D], defeated the Christians in pitched battle there, and destroyed and burned everything together with the city. In this battle, while the aforesaid Bertulf, archbishop of Trier, escaped by flight, Walo, bishop of Metz, fell slain; Robert succeeded him in the episcopate. This was the forty-seventh year during which the Northmen, roaming through Christian kingdoms and diverse provinces, devastated them with slaughter, plunder, and flames.

Incidental notice. [MARTIN. POL.] In the eleventh year of Charles the Younger’s empire, the barbarous people of the Hungarians [Col. 0301A] first attacked the province of Pannonia from Scythia. Having expelled the Avars, who were also Huns, they have remained there until the present day. Before baptism they used raw flesh for food and human blood for drink.

21. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 891, Charles the Younger died; his cousin Arnulf ruled for twelve years. In the first year of his empire, the Northmen, unable to take Paris, attacked various cities of Francia and devastated those they captured. In the fifth year of Arnulf’s empire, returning once more to Lotharingia, they despoiled Hasbania along the borders of the towns of Saint-Trond and Tongeren; having laid Brabant and Flanders waste, they fought near the city of Liège against the Christians and prevailed.

Against them King Arnulf, in that same year, engaged with a strong army on the river called the Dyle [Col. 0301B]. He struck down so great a multitude of warriors that scarcely one remained able to carry the grievous news back to the fleet. The remaining Northmen crossed the Meuse, roamed through and ravaged the land of Ripuarian territory and the Ardennes, and withdrew beyond the sea.

Ripuarian territory is a land abundant in provisions, containing the county of Jülich [Note: Iülich] and the strongholds of other princes. The Ardennes, or Ardenna, is a mountainous land abounding in wild animals, containing several famous monasteries; it stretches and extends from the city of Liège on one side to Metz, and on the other to the region before Cologne [Note: reading: *dilatur*, “it is extended,” 1*; Col. 0301D].

22. In the year of the Lord 896, the sixth year of the empire of King Arnulf [Col. 0301C], [MARTIN. POL.] the Northmen and Danes, who had reduced the kingdom of the Franks, Lotharingia, and other adjacent provinces almost to nothing over nearly sixty years, were so completely conquered in this year by the aforesaid Arnulf, Richard duke of Burgundy, and Robert count of Paris that they themselves implored God’s mercy and received baptism (A.D. 896). Then for the first time the wrath of God was turned into mercy, as is said in 2 Maccabees, chapter 7.

Incidental notice. [SIGEB.] In the year 903, Emperor Arnulf died; his son Louis III succeeded him and ruled for ten years.

Incidental notice. About the same time, Robert, bishop of Metz, died, and Adalbero I, brother of Frederick, duke of the Mosellans, a man of outstanding learning, succeeded him.

Incidental notice. In the eighth year of this Louis [Col. 0301D], Regino, abbot of Prüm, sent his chronicle—begun from the Nativity of the Lord and brought down to that year—to the aforesaid Adalbero for correction.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 912, Louis III died; Conrad, son of the count of Hesse, ruled for seven years. From this time the empire passed from the Franks and was permanently transferred to the Germans.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 920, Conrad died without the imperial blessing; Henry I, duke of Saxony, succeeded him [Col. 0302A] and ruled for eighteen years.

Incidental notice. In the third year of his reign, when the Hungarians were devastating Francia, Alsace, Germany, and Saxony, King Henry met them and destroyed them all to utter extinction.

Incidental notice. In the same year Stephen, bishop of Liège, died; Richarius, abbot of Prüm, succeeded him. He rebuilt the church of Saint Peter at Liège, destroyed by the Northmen.

Incidental notice. About the same time Henry, king of Germany, and Charles the Simple, king of Francia, made an alliance at Bonn. Charles restored the kingdom of Lotharingia to Henry, and the bishops and counts confirmed the matter by oath. In the sixteenth year of Henry, Adalbero I, bishop of Metz, was still flourishing.

23. In the times when our monastery was destroyed by the Northmen, there was, as they relate, a certain Imizo, abbot of this place [Col. 0302B]. He raised the bones of all his predecessor abbots from the various places in the monastery where they lay buried, placed them together in the sanctuary—that is, the small choir—beneath four marble slabs, and died within a year thereafter.

Incidental notice. After King Charles of Francia died, the Lotharingians, unwilling to be subject to Henry, king of Germany, withdrew from Henry’s allegiance at the instigation of Count Giselbert of Hainaut, to whom King Charles had formerly entrusted the duchy of Lotharingia. Henry prudently concealed his reaction; considering Giselbert’s power, he gave him his daughter Gerberga in marriage and entrusted the duchy of Lotharingia to him.

So that readers may not be unaware of the extent of the duchy of Lotharingia [Col. 0302C], it should be known that, as was touched upon above, it was formerly called Austria. It was a kingdom in its own right, at times joined to the kingdom of Francia, and then called the middle part of Francia. This Lotharingia extends in length from the borders of Burgundy to the sea of the Frisians, and in breadth from the Scheldt to the waters of the Rhine. It includes Hainaut with its adjacent lands, and all Brabant, which formerly extended from the city of Tournai [Note: Tournai, situated in Hainaut] to the bank of the river Velpe [Note: So also today; it flows into the Dyle from the left bank]. Of this, one part is now possessed by the counts of Hainaut, another by the counts of Flanders, and a third by the princes and dukes of Brabant.

Lotharingia also includes all Hasbania, Campine, Batavia with other principalities and counties, and the lands across the river Meuse [Col. 0302D] together with the Ardennes. These aforementioned territories belonged to Pepin, from whom the dukes of Brabant descended, and were called Austrasia or Lower Lotharingia. Moreover, the whole of this Austrasia or Lotharingia also contained the duchy of the Mosellans, now called the duchy of Lorraine, together with the three metropolitan sees—Cologne, Trier, and Mainz—the duchy of Limburg, and the intervening lands.

[Col. 0301] Here ends the second book of this first part.

THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SAME WORK BEGINS.

[Col. 0303]

[Col. 0303A] 1. [SIGEB.] In the year of the Lord 938, after Henry had died before receiving the imperial blessing, his son Otto, the first of that name, succeeded to the kingdom of Germany and prosperously ruled for twenty-four years before his consecration as emperor (A.D. 938). Otto, through his own industry improving the condition of kingdom and church, rebuilt two churches at Liège destroyed by the Northmen and restored monasteries.

2. In his second year or thereabouts (939), the forty-fifth year from the devastation of this monastery by the Northmen [Note: If Otto truly came to Saint-Trond in the second year of his reign, that is, in 937 or 938, not forty-five but fifty-six years had passed since the monastery’s destruction by the Northmen. Yet scarcely anything certain can be determined concerning the date when Otto stayed at Saint-Trond; his charters show that he came into Lotharingia neither in 937 nor in 938, Col. 0303D–0304D. The date 939, indicated by the author himself, is more possible. Yet by 938 Reyner already governed the monastery, as appears from what follows. See above, Rodulf’s chronology.], the aforesaid king, according to the account of the ancients, entered the town of Saint-Trond to dine while carrying out affairs of the kingdom.

After the meal, as he was about to depart and was standing with his chief men in an upper room of his lodging, he looked into the distance [Col. 0303B] and saw the walls of this ruined monastery rising up, piteously broken by the force of fire, with green branches lifting themselves high through the wide window-openings. He asked what this ruinous height of walls signified. He was told that the desolate spectacle had once been a renowned monastery, but that it had been reduced to nothing by Northmen’s fury, as he could see; that a few monks, serving God there on scant sustenance, remained desolate, their abbot having already been taken away.

Then the pious king groaned. Summoning the brothers, who agreed to this, he appointed as abbot a devout man among them named Reyner. With the king’s assistance, Reyner restored the necessary buildings and from that time supplied the brothers sufficiently with food and clothing.

[Col. 0303C] 3. Therefore, after the death of the aforesaid Abbot Imizo, Reyner, born in the district of Hasbania, was consecrated abbot of this place and presided for five years. Within a short time he gathered a multitude of monks and laudably instructed those subject to him in monastic discipline by word and example.

4. [STEPHEN, *Miracles of St Trudo*] This man, however, having been accused to Adalbero, the second bishop of Metz of that name—to whom belonged half of this town—by the denunciation of certain flatterers, was wholly unable, even through the intercession of distinguished men, to appease the bishop’s mind, though unjustly stirred up against him. For the bishop declared that the abbot would never have his favour. When the abbot was compelled by necessity to come to Metz and was brought before the bishop, he endured grave insults in return for his humble greeting; ashamed and abashed, he withdrew from the bishop’s presence. But the blessed man of God, St Trudo, not enduring the unjust insults inflicted on his servant, appeared to the bishop in a vision on a certain night; rebuking him with terrible words and scourging him with sharp blows, he immediately vanished. Upon waking, the bishop summoned his household and recounted what had happened to him in the vision; stripping his body bare, he showed them as witnesses to his story the bruised marks of the blows, with swelling of the flesh. A messenger was promptly sent, and the abbot, being asked, returned to the bishop and graciously forgave the injuries inflicted upon him. The bishop declared by firm promise that he would give him assistance in every matter for as long as he lived; and thus restored to the bishop’s favour, the abbot returned joyfully to his own place in the Lord.

5. In the following year (938), the venerable matron Ruechlinda, mother of Lord Abbot Reyner, granted to this monastery some part of her inheritance in the form of a written testament. Charters or copies of these are preserved in our archives, and their tenor is as follows:

“Let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church that, if we confer anything from our own possessions upon the places of the saints, we confidently trust that after the end of this life we shall without doubt receive from the Lord who repays an unfading prize. Therefore I, Ruechlinda, in the name of God, as donor, wish it to be granted in perpetuity to the monastery of St Trudo, built in the place called Sarcinio, upon the river Cysindria, in the district of Hasbania, where that precious confessor of Christ himself rests bodily, and where Lord Reyner, my son, is seen to preside as abbot over a multitude of monks living under the rule of the regular observance. And this is what I give for the remedy of my soul, so that after the course of this present life he may deign to bestow upon me the gifts of everlasting light: slaves bearing these names: Everard and his wife, with their children and many ..., etc.”

It follows at the end: “Done in the monastery of Sarchiensis, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the reign of Lord Otto the First in Germany (A.D. 938).”

Incident. [SIGEBERT] In the fourth year of Otto’s reign, Louis, king of France, invaded the kingdom of Lotharingia—which his father Charles had recently given to Henry, king of Germany—entering Lotharingia under the leadership of Gilbert, duke of Lotharingia, whose wife Gerberga was sister of King Otto; and he came as far as Alsace. When King Otto learned this, he entered Lotharingia and reached Caprimont; but afterwards, peace having been made, Louis returned to his own territory.

Incident. In the sixth year of his reign, Otto besieged the town of Breisach in Alsace [Col. 0304D], intending to take it from the knights Everard and Gilbert, his adversaries, who had occupied it. As the magnates of the realm abandoned him in spirit, Everard, count palatine, and Gilbert, count of Hainaut and duke of Lotharingia—who had formerly, by their treachery, turned Henry, duke of Bavaria and brother of King Otto, away from his brother—assembled a great army [Col. 0305A] and engaged Otto himself in war. But they were defeated by Otto’s army; many of their men were killed, Everard fell by the sword, and Gilbert [Note: Col. 0305D: “Ghiselberto,” 1*.] was drowned in the river Rhine.

Incident. About the same time, after Gilbert’s death, King Otto gave his sister Gerberga, Gilbert’s widow, in marriage to Louis, king of the Franks. A few days later Louis granted her that part of Lotharingia which he held.

6. About the same time, while Abbot Reyner was celebrating Mass one day, after the breaking of the sacramental host, he saw at the bottom of the chalice a spider of horrible size and colour. Horrified by the creature’s appearance, he was anxious what to do; but at length recalling to mind the power of divine might, trusting in the Lord, [Col. 0305B] he swallowed the sacrament in the chalice and afterwards suffered no inconvenience whatever. In the same year, after he had presided over this place for five years, he fell asleep in the Lord on the Kalends of March.

7. In the year of the Lord 944, the seventh year of the rule of Otto, king of Germany, the venerable father Adalbero II, bishop of the see of Metz, [STEPHEN, *Miracles of St Trudo*] who, because of the favour which he showed the monks, was called “father of monks,” compassionating the grave need of the desolate flock and desiring to be of greater benefit to it as it advanced in monastic observances, and to recover the temporal goods which during almost forty-five years had been unjustly possessed, through the tyranny of nobles and magnates, from this desolated place, divinely inspired, assumed the burden of the prelacy of this monastery [Col. 0305C] and became abbot.

8. Since he had formerly been estranged from his predecessor Reyner through malicious misinformation—and for this reason St Trudo himself had also rebuked him, as narrated above—he therefore devoted himself more ardently to every advancement of this monastery. He received back in part its lost inheritances, and enlarged its holdings through the benefactions of worthy persons whom he had persuaded. Moreover, from his own inheritance he endowed this church with six vineyards near the place called Manwen, together with their six small holdings and one dwelling, situated above the river Moselle in the village called Pomerium [Note: Col. 0305D: Pomerieux, three leagues distant from the city of Metz]; and he effectively induced other devout people, dwelling at the village of Bredal above the same river Moselle, to do likewise. He also raised the fabric of the monastery [Col. 0305D], employing increased numbers of workmen and incurring heavy expenses, and completed it with a firm roof nobly covered in cut stone.

9. When the work of the monastery had thus been completed for the most part, with the consent of Richarius, bishop of Liège, Adalbero himself, in person and with a multitude of people assembled, solemnly consecrated this monastery in the second year of his prelacy in this abbey (945), and in the 288th year from the first dedication of this monastery.

Incident. In the same year in which Lord Adalbero II, bishop of Metz [Col. 0306A] and abbot of this monastery of St Trudo, consecrated this monastery—that is, the eighth year of the rule of Otto I in the kingdom of Germany—the aforesaid Otto subdued all Lotharingia to himself, Adalbero alone, the aforesaid bishop and abbot, resisting him; Adalbero was brother of Frederick, duke of the Mosellans [SIGEBERT].

Incident. In the same year, upon the death of Richarius, bishop of Liège, Hugh I succeeded and presided for two years.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 947, the tenth year of Otto’s reign, upon the death of Hugh, bishop of Liège, Farabert, abbot of Prüm, succeeded; he presided for six years.

Incident. In the fifteenth year of Otto’s reign, Conrad, Otto’s son-in-law and duke of Lotharingia, because he had conspired against Otto, was captured by Bruno, archbishop of Cologne and guardian of the empire. When Otto returned, the duchy of Lotharingia [Col. 0306B] was given by Otto to his brother Bruno.

In the sixteenth year of Otto’s reign, upon the death of Farabert, bishop of Liège, Ratherius, a monk of Lobbes, succeeded.

10. In the year of the Lord 959, the twenty-first year of the reign of Otto I, a certain noble matron named Guodrada gave herself to the service of God and St Trudo, in the time of Lord Adalbero II, bishop of Metz and abbot of St Trudo, as is contained in an old charter, whose beginning and end are as follows:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church that a certain woman named Guodrada, coming to the monastery of St Trudo, where the saint himself rests in body and Lord Bishop Adalbero is seen to preside, there lost the freedom of her birth [Col. 0306C] and gave herself under the yoke of servitude to God and St Trudo, to serve them, etc.”

[Note: Col. 0306D: Nor did Miraeus, I, 503, print the remainder.]

It follows: “Done in the monastery of Sarchiensis on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the twenty-first year of the reign of the glorious [Note: Col. 0305D: “gloriose,” 1*.] Lord Otto, king of the Germans (A.D. 957). I, Eynard, chancellor, wrote [this].”

11. Likewise, in the twenty-third year of the same ruler’s reign (A.D. 959), a certain devout man granted abundant alms from his possessions at Bredal upon the river Moselle to the monks’ table. The charter concerning them begins thus:

“In the name of almighty God, I, Zeizolf, have delivered certain things of my property to the table of the brothers living in the monastery of St Trudo, etc.”

It follows: “With the consent of Adalbero, bishop of Metz, who appears to be abbot of that place itself, etc.”

It follows: “These things were done in the twenty-third year of the reign of Otto I.”

Note, reader, [Col. 0306D], that here I have recounted only a few things from two charters, whose copies are fully contained in the book of charters of our ancient monastery, so that no one may doubt that the aforesaid Lord Adalbero was abbot of this monastery.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 962, the twenty-fourth year of his reign in Germany or Alamannia, Otto I, summoned to Rome by the cardinals, was crowned emperor.

12. In the year of the Lord 964, the twenty-sixth year of Otto’s reign [Note: Col. 0306D: “Rather, the twenty-eighth.”], and the third year of his empire, Lord Adalbero II, bishop of Metz and abbot of this place, [Col. 0307A] after presiding over this abbey for twenty years, came one day to this monastery and fell upon a bed of sickness. Having summoned the brothers, after receiving the sacraments he fell asleep in the Lord on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. After solemn funeral rites, his body was buried beside the outer wall of the monastery itself, on the left towards the circuit of the cloister. Theodoric I, cousin of Emperor Otto, succeeded him in the bishopric of Metz, and Thietfrid in the abbacy of this place.

13. In the same year of grace, Lord Thietfrid was appointed abbot of this place. He presided for thirty years, under him religious life flourished and the total of possessions increased.

Incident. [SIGEBERT] In the following year or thereabouts, Conrad, son-in-law of Emperor Otto, formerly deprived of the duchy of Lotharingia, rebelled against Otto and defected to the Hungarians who were ravaging Germany, bringing them into Otto’s imperial realm. They were so crushed by the emperor in this war that thereafter they did not dare rise against the realm of the empire; in this conflict Conrad himself perished.

Incident. About the same time, as Emperor Otto travelled far away to defend the commonwealth, his brother Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, was appointed for a second time guardian and defender of Germany and Gaul.

Incident. [*Life of Bruno*] After this, the venerable Bruno was seized by fever and died. His body was brought to Cologne by Theodoric, bishop of Metz, his cousin, and honourably buried in the monastery of St Pantaleon, which he himself had founded. Folmar succeeded him in the archbishopric, and [Col. 0307C] his nephew Charles in the duchy of Lotharingia. In the seventh year of his empire, Otto I granted the duchy of Lotharingia to Charles, brother of Lothair, king of France, and son of Otto’s sister, on condition that Charles should reform his own excesses and oppose the assaults which his brother Lothair had conceived against Lotharingia.

14. At about this time, more or less, in the time of this Abbot Thietfrid, the illustrious lady Bertha, a widow consecrated to God and countess of Flanders, had made a pilgrimage to visit the thresholds of Blessed Mary at Aachen. On her return it happened that she visited the town of St Trudo out of devotion and poured forth humble prayers at the tomb of the aforesaid saint. As she stayed there for several days to rest, she fell upon a bed of sickness [Col. 0307D]. When this became known to her son Arnulf, an illustrious man and count of Flanders, he hastened as quickly as possible to the aforesaid place. There, in the presence of Theodoric I, bishop of Metz, and Abbot Thietfrid, at the request of his mother Lady Bertha, for the remedy of his own soul and those of his kin, he freely and hereditarily granted to God and Blessed Trudo, for the use of God’s servants serving God there, the village of Proviin, situated in the castellany of Ylensis beside the river Doula, with slaves, lands, tithes, woods, meadows, fisheries, and watercourses, together with [Col. 0308A] the parish church of that village and all its appurtenances. He further granted Blessed Trudo a wood situated not far from the village of Merwel, and a tithe at the village called Brustemium [Note: Col. 0307D: Brusthem, not far from St Trudo], so that through the merits of the aforesaid patron he might deserve to obtain pardon for their sins. This was done in the presence of several counts and other men, as is clearly recorded in the archives of our monastery’s privileges. When this was completed and her illness grew worse, the aforesaid countess, having received the ecclesiastical sacraments, breathed her last in the year of the Lord 967, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August. Her body was buried in the old crypt; later, in the time of Adalard II, it was translated and placed in the new sanctuary, beneath the vault in the wall of the left side of the upper choir, beside the high altar.

In her praise the following verses are found written:

> Bertha, consecrated to God, worthy of the heavenly trophy,  
> Lies here translated, and rightly merits remembrance.  
>   
> The lineage of royal descent shone brilliantly in her,  
> Yet she was not swollen with pride because she shone in splendour.  
>   
> Zealous in virtue, a countess prudent in all things,  
> Giving her possessions and herself to God, she attained him who is worthy.  
>   
> Herself an exemplar of goodness, devoted to St Trudo,  
> She granted by right the village of Proviin which she held,  
>   
> Giving a portion of the tithe from the village of Brustemium,  
> And adding also the wood which befits the church.  
>   
> Receive, Father Trudo, what the illustrious mother bestowed;  
> May she rejoice with you; render in return the gifts of prayer.  
>   
> Two days remained for the sun’s course through Cancer,  
> When she happily died. May God be life to her.

[Col. 0308C] Incident. In the tenth year of Otto’s empire, upon the death of Eraclus, Notger succeeded and occupied the bishopric of Liège for forty-two years.

Incident. [SIGEBERT] In the year of the Lord 973, Otto I—who was the first emperor of the race of the Alamanni or Germans, to whom the empire was transferred in perpetuity after being removed from the Franks—died with great devotion, after ruling for twenty-four years and holding the empire for twelve. At the beginning of his reign he had caused this ruined monastery to be rebuilt through his own diligence. His son Otto II, who had co-ruled with him for several years, succeeded and held the empire for ten years.

Incident. Since Germany has been mentioned, it should be known that there are two Germanies: Upper and Lower. Upper Germany is a very great region at the beginning of Europe. Under the name and designation of Germany, Scythia and Alania together with other lands commonly bear the title. Stretching together along the northern Ocean, it has the Maeotian marshes near its upper regions; it is also abundantly watered, as it passes through, by the very great river Danube, into which sixty navigable rivers successively flow and which, in its course, is called Hister because of changes of locality.

[Note: Cols. 0307D–0310C: Almost the same things are read in the seventh-century cosmography edited by Pertz in the *Commentaries of the Berlin Academy*, 1845, where among other things occur the following:]

> Scythia is called the first province of Europe;  
> It adjoins the Maeotian marshes and is adjacent to Alania.  
>   
> Then comes the place called Dacia.  
>   
> [lacuna]  
>   
> Germany is called the land adjoining the river Rhine,  
> Where are barbarous peoples, great in body,  
> Hardened in their hearts and ignorant of the regions of heaven.  
>   
> [lacuna]  
>   
> The Danube runs a long way among very great peoples,  
> Provides abundant rivers, and supplies the Slavs with sustenance, etc.

This land is exceedingly fertile in provisions and populous with barbarian peoples [Col. 0309A]; because of the fertility by which it produces peoples it was called Germania. From these regions once came forth Goths, Huns, Vandals, Lombards, and pagans of other nations, and finally the barbarian Northmen, eager to wage war against the Christians’ territories [Note: Col. 0310C: The word *causa*, “because,” seems to have fallen out; or *debellandi* here stands for *debellaturi*, “about to wage war.”].

The cause of their migration was as follows. The peoples settled within this region had multiplied into such a multitude that they could no longer live together. Thus, as those who have surveyed that land report, dividing their entire multitude into three parts, they cast lots to determine which part should leave its homeland and seek new settlements. The part to which the lot gave departure from its native soil and the pursuit of foreign fields bade farewell to its people and homeland, and set out with wives and children to seek [Col. 0309B] whatever lands they could inhabit. How inhumanly [Note: Col. 0309: “humaniter,” 1*.] they devastated Italy, Gaul, and many other Christian kingdoms in those times is attested by the histories of many eminent men.

Lower Germany, however, is the same as Alamannia: a land fruitful and abundant in provisions, filled with the habitation of wise and very strong people, with an innumerable multitude and professing the holy catholic faith. The sweet and pleasant river Rhine waters it on every side.

Incident. [SIGEBERT] In the fifth year of Otto II, Lothair, king of France, disturbed and devastated Lotharingia, and so returned home. The emperor pursued him with a multitude of armed men, and, ranging through France, devastated the territories of Reims, Laon, Soissons, and Paris with various destruction, sparing churches and monasteries nevertheless. At last, after they had taken counsel together in a place above the river Char, the king of France swore an oath concerning Lotharingia.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 984, upon Otto II’s death, his son Otto III, still a youth, succeeded; because of his diligence, Notger, bishop of Liège, was appointed his guardian by the leading men of the empire.

15. [SIGEBERT, *Life of Bishop Theodoric*] In the year of the Lord 984, Theodoric I, bishop of Metz and founder of the Benedictine monastery of St Vincent, situated on an island within the outer walls of the city of Metz, after he had recently campaigned in Italy for three years with Otto I, and in the eleventh year before this had placed in the aforesaid monastery many relics translated to Gaul, among which were pledges of St Vincent, levite and martyr, together with the blood of St Stephen [Col. 0310A], the protomartyr; and after among other endowments by which he had enriched that monastery he had bestowed the village of Dongei, neighbouring the city of Verdun, which had formerly been the marriage-property of St Trudo, died in the Lord. Adalbero III, son of Frederick, duke of the Mosellans, succeeded him.

Incident. [SIGEBERT] In the fourth year of Otto III, and the thirty-seventh year of Louis, king of the Franks—who, after his father Lothair, had reigned only one year—Louis died. The Franks wished to transfer the kingdom to Charles, duke of Lotharingia, uncle of this Louis; but because Charles deferred the matter for deliberation, Hugh Capet, son of the great Hugh, count of Paris, begotten by Hawide, sister of Otto I, usurped the kingdom and held it for nine years [Note: Col. 0309: a passage has fallen out in the manuscript]. The aforesaid Charles [Col. 0310B], his nephew, to whom the kingdom was due by paternal and ancestral succession, harassed him with many wars and victories for five years, but, his purpose frustrated, ended his final day. Thus the kings of the Franks from the stock of Charlemagne failed from that year onward. After the death of this Duke Charles, in the eighth year of Otto III’s empire, his son Otto succeeded him in the duchy of Lotharingia; in the course of time he grievously attacked this monastery of St Trudo contrary to right.

16. In the year of the Lord 994, the eleventh year of Otto III’s empire, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January [Note: Col. 0310C: The March manuscript gives a different reading; but correction as given here is clear from the following tomb inscription], Abbot Thietfrid of this place died. He was buried immediately beyond the burial-place of Abbot Gontram, beside the wall of the left side towards the cloister walk. Above his burial-place the following verses are written:

> Abbot Thietfrid, faithful through the divine gift,  
> Under the rule of faith guided God’s flock.  
>   
> Diligent in increasing brethren and possessions,  
> Serviceable to the church, he was dear to his homeland.  
>   
> For three tens of years the lordly shepherd of monks,  
> He departs to reign; he dies, not to die.  
>   
> His body is placed in this earth after the Ides of Janus;  
> May his spirit live rejoicing in the Lord in heaven.  
>   
> In the thousandth year, six years are subtracted from the age.

17. In the same year, after the death of Abbot Thietfrid, Herenfrid succeeded; he presided for four years. In the year of the Lord 999, after the death of Herenfrid, abbot of this place, on the Nones of November, Adalard I succeeded him.

[Col. 0309] Here ends the third book of the first part, *On the Deeds of the Abbots of This Monastery of St Trudo*.

## Supplement of the Third Continuator

[Col. 0309C] Incident. In the year of the Lord 1003 [Note: Col. 0309: We have taken these matters from the table of chapters and placed them here in their proper position. The interpolator, however, has headed the table of chapters thus: “Here begins the table concerning the thirteen books of the second part on the deeds of the abbots of this monastery of St Trudo. Within it are added certain chapters absent from the following books, and certain incidents, suitably to be inserted here and there among the chapters, are compiled; first is placed the prologue.”], after the death of Otto III [Col. 0310C], who had succeeded immediately to the empire by hereditary succession after his father and grandfather had previously died [Col. 0311A], a general council of the princes and leading men of the empire having been convened for this purpose, it was unanimously ordained that henceforth a son should by no right of inheritance succeed his father, nor a kinsman his kinsman, as emperor; rather, he who was elected by the officers of the empire should obtain the empire [cf. MARTIN OF POLAND]. This is still observed, as is found in the *Extra*, [Note: Col. 0311: “ex,” 1*.] *On Election*, *Venerabilem*, §1 [Note: Col. 0311D: c. 34, *X*, *de electione*, 1.6].

There are therefore seven electors: namely, three chancellors. The first, the archbishop of Mainz, is chancellor of Germany; the second, the archbishop of Trier, of Gaul; and the third, the archbishop of Cologne, of Italy. These three are ecclesiastical princes. The other four are secular: the first, the margrave of Brandenburg, is chamberlain; the second, namely the count palatine [Col. 0311B] of the Rhine, is seneschal; the third, the duke of Saxony, bears the sword; and the fourth, the king of Bohemia, is cupbearer. Hence the verses:

> The men of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne:  
> Each of these becomes a chancellor of the empire.  
>   
> The Palatine is seneschal; the duke bears the sword;  
> The margrave presides over the chamber; the Bohemian is cupbearer.  
> These appoint for all ages the supreme lord of all.

Note that, according to some, the king of Bohemia is not necessary unless the six aforesaid electors disagree; nor has he an ancient right, but he holds it today in fact, as Hostiensis notes on the canon *Venerabilem*.

Otto III and his father Otto II were so fierce and remarkable that [Col. 0311C] one was called the bloodthirsty pale death of the Saracens, the other the wonder of the world. But the grandfather of this third Otto, Otto I, was more Christian than all others. Through the general prayer of the churches throughout the entire empire, diligently completed through the efforts of his sister, an abbess—to whom he appeared after death—his soul was freed from purgatory and led by angels to heaven.

Incident. [SIGEBERT] Therefore, in the same year of the Lord 1003, when Otto III died childless, Henry, duke of Bavaria, nephew of Henry, brother of Otto I, became emperor and ruled for twenty-two years. Note here that there were more kings named Henry than emperors. [MARTIN OF POLAND] Thus, when Henry I is called emperor, he is called “first” in respect of the empire [Col. 0311D], but “second” in respect of the kingdom. For before him there was Henry I, king, who ruled only in Alamannia and not in Italy, and therefore did not receive the imperial coronation. The same is to be understood of the Conrads and the other successors.

In the year of the Lord 1005, in the third year of his reign, Emperor Henry, after many victories and wishing to devote himself solely to God, founded the bishopric of Bamberg. For the honour of that city, he transferred the episcopal see there from the city of Narni, with the pope’s consent [SIGEBERT]. Against this, Theodoric II, bishop of Metz, grieved that the emperor was assigning to the aforesaid church the dowry and inheritance of his sister Empress Cunegund, rebelled in the sixth year of his episcopate. Offended by this resistance, the emperor unlawfully gave to Duke Otto of Lotharingia, his kinsman, all the right which the aforesaid bishop held in this town, to that bishop’s prejudice. The aforesaid duke [Note: Col. 0311: “dux—tractare” supplied by Ghesquier], consulting his greed, not only presumed, in addition to his unlawful usurpation of the possessions of the church of Metz, to plunder the goods of this monastery most mercilessly against justice, but also to treat our household inhumanely [cf. STEPHEN, *Miracles of St Trudo*, Col. 0312B].

One night, when he had given himself to sleep, he saw in a dream that he was standing at the monastery gate, and that a certain old man in clerical dress came to meet him and asked where he was going. When he replied that he wished to enter the monastery, the old man declared him unworthy of entrance, since he had so often violated this divine sanctuary by so many sacrileges. But as he tried to resist the one opposing him and to enter the forbidden threshold, he immediately, as it seemed to him, felt a heavy blow [Note: Col. 0311: The upper part of the page, on which ten lines were written, is missing; it was consumed by fire in the burning of the library of Laam, as is noted in the manuscript itself. From the summary it is clear that St Trudo was the author of this miracle: “On the death of Otto, duke of Lotharingia, divinely inflicted by St Trudo because of his tyranny.”].

“... [lacuna; surviving fragments are materially uncertain: *ige ... atior ... risque ... sepe ... nstrata ... a ergo perseverans ... monasterium lucra sua c ... fratribus dolorem augme ... e ... cupiens accessit*; discernible sense: ‘... but persevering ... [he] approached the monastery, desiring to increase his gain and the brothers’ grief ...’]. Having completed, therefore, the matters for which he had come there, [Col. 0312C] as he was about to depart and was leaving the monastery gate [Note: Col. 0311: “monasterii—interiit” supplied by Ghesquier], he was suddenly struck in the shoulders by fevers as though by a deadly arrow. Crying aloud and shouting because of the excessive anguish of his mind, he addressed his own approaching death; and, with slow effort following his pack-animals as far as Maastricht, punished with a deadly death, he miserably perished, becoming an example of astonishment to all; the corrupted syntax does not preserve the connection with the following words: ‘who in the vision of his dream had driven him from the monastery, and whom, when rebuking him, he had despised.’”

[SIGEBERT] When he had thus died, Emperor Henry in the same year granted the duchy of Lotharingia to Godfrey, count of the Ardennes. Otto left behind no son, but a daughter, Ermegard, countess of Namur; from him also descended Godfrey, count of Bouillon and duke of Lotharingia, who later became [Col. 0312D] king of Jerusalem.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1007, Notger, bishop of Liège, died, having established very many churches and benefices at Liège; he was by nation a Swabian. Baldric II succeeded him and presided for eleven years. He was the son of Otto, count of Looz, born of Lutgard, daughter of Ermegard, countess of Namur, herself daughter of the aforesaid Duke Otto. Baldric’s brother [Col. 0313A] was Gilbert, who succeeded their father Otto in the countship some years later.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1010, the king of Hungary, formerly called Pannonia, with his people was converted to the catholic faith through the efforts of his wife, Queen Gille, sister of Emperor Henry. In the same year Henry himself was crowned emperor at Rome by Benedict VIII. Also in that year Emperor Henry besieged the city of Metz because Theodoric, bishop of Metz, was in rebellion against him; the city having been almost destroyed by the siege, peace was at last made.

Incident. [*Life of Baldric*] In the year of the Lord 1013, the tenth year of the empire of this Henry, Baldric II, bishop of Liège, began to build a fortress at the village of Hoegaarden, an allod of the church of St Lambert situated a little way inside the borders of Brabant, to ward off evildoers [Col. 0313B]. Lambert with the Beard, count of Leuven, opposed him. In the battle that ensued, the bishop was defeated, three hundred of his men having been slain. Returning to Liège after the slaughter of his followers and burdened by a wounded conscience, he vowed, on the advice of the discerning Bishop John, who was coming from Italy, that he would found a monastery to appease the Almighty for the redemption of the souls of those killed. Accordingly, in the next year, having fulfilled his vow, he built within the city walls, on an island, a monastery in honour of St James the Less. To it the same Count Lambert granted generous endowments from his own allod in satisfaction; Albert by name presided there as its first abbot.

Incident. [SIGEBERT] In the year of the Lord 1015, while Godfrey, duke of Lotharingia and count of the Ardennes, was ravaging the county of Mons [Col. 0313C], Lambert with the Beard, son of Reyner, count of Mons, came to the assistance of his uncle Count Reyner. A battle was joined at Florennes; four hundred of his men were killed, and Lambert himself fell with them. Lambert had married Gerberga, daughter of Charles, duke of Lotharingia, and with her received as dowry one part of the duchy of Lotharingia, namely the land now called Brabant, containing the towns of Leuven and Brussels with their appurtenances. On this account he was first, and the first count of Leuven [Note: Col. 0313: the reverse page has been eaten away by fire].

“... [lacuna; surviving fragments are materially uncertain: *post ... prim ... et post ... tuit ... tia primo ...*]. [Col. 0313D] Third chapter of the third part. ... A son likewise succeeded this Lambert.”

In the year of the Lord 1017, the fourteenth year of the empire of this Henry, Baldric II died and was buried in the crypt of the monastery of St James which he had founded. Wolbodo succeeded him and, in the same year, completed the aforesaid recently begun monastery by command of Emperor Henry; he presided in the bishopric for five years.

In the year of the Lord 1021, the twentieth year of the empire of Henry II and [Col. 0314A] the twenty-first year of the prelacy of Lord Adelard, Lady Herlendis, countess and mother of Count Godfrey of Duras, with her son’s consent granted to Saint Trudo one half of her village, commonly called the hamlet of Popliir, with all its jurisdiction, meadows, lands, waters, and everything else, for the anniversary observance of herself and of her firstborn son Adelbero, formerly primicerius of the church of Metz, now deceased. Both were buried in one tomb within the apse of the monastery beside the wall facing south, where there also stands an altar in honour of [Note: [Col. 0313] Seven lines are missing; the upper part of the leaf has been consumed by fire.] the Blessed Virgin. [Note: [Col. 0313D] The words “the Blessed Virgin” are taken from Mantelius, *History of Loss*, p. 55, who reproduced this entire passage up to these words from the *Chronicle of Saint Trudo* [Col. 0314D]. Another donation by Herlindis and her son Godfrey to Saint Trudo is recorded there as made on 4 November 1024.] [lacuna] [*The Miracles of Saint Trudo*, by Stepelinus.] It is read that Ghiselbert had conferred . . .; it is not known . . . . When a certain Omekinus learned this . . . he sought to extend the boundaries . . . and uproot the boundary-posts . . . at the outer limits of Saint Trudo’s woodland estate. [Col. 0314B] When defenders of both sides had assembled to settle the boundary dispute, he struck a certain tree with his heel and said: “By oath I assert that this place belongs to my lord, just as I can draw back this foot from here unharmed.” Immediately, therefore, as he had uttered false testimony, so God displayed true judgment: he caused not only his foot to rot away, but his whole body also to be consumed by a grievous wasting disease.

About this time, Abbot Adelard, continually and ardently considering how he might obtain some small portion of the relics of Stephen the Protomartyr, patron of the foundation of this monastery’s crypt, acted with the common counsel of the convent. [Note: [Col. 0313] The remainder of this same page is missing in the other column.] [lacuna] [Col. 0314C] . . . heard . . . that a small particle . . . of the saint’s relics was held there. Nothing of it could be imparted to anyone, nor did he dare presume to do so, for fear of offending the others. Then he said: “Will the divine mercy deign, through his merits, to grant me something from that bone?” “I hope in God,” he replied, “provided that you consent, that I shall by no means be disappointed of the pledges of my desire. I beg you, order the bone to be brought forward and entrust it to the venerable and holy martyr.” Why say more? At length, although with difficulty, the bishop was persuaded, and the bone was brought. When it was gently struck with a phlebotome, fresh blood immediately flowed forth, [Col. 0314D] which, received devoutly by the abbot’s hand in a vessel prepared for this purpose, Abbot Adelard, with the consent of the whole church of Metz, undertook joyfully to carry back to his own house.

Later certain persons reported that, when doubt arose concerning the aforesaid bone—whether it was truly from the body of Saint Stephen—the following was done, by the common counsel of the leading men of the church of Metz, to ascertain the truth of the matter; and when the uncertainty of all had been wiped away through the merits of the saint himself, [Col. 0315A] that blood flowed immediately after the stroke of the phlebotome, as has already been said. [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0313] The remainder of this same page is missing in the other column.] [lacuna] In the year of the Lord 1023 . . . Reginald succeeds and presides for thirteen years.

In the year of the Lord 1025, Henry II, second in the kingdom and first in the empire, in the seventh year of his reign and sixteenth of his empire, remaining in virginity with his consort Cunigunda, a virgin, at length fell into a sickbed. Having designated, on the advice of the leading men of the empire, Conrad—a man of royal lineage and distinguished freedom—he died [cf. Martin of Poland; Sigebert], and was buried in the church of Bamberg [Col. 0315B] which he himself had founded. After him, Empress Cunigunda—whose holiness Guntram, later abbot of this place, knew most intimately—died after ten years and was buried with the emperor. In the same year Conrad was elected and ruled for fifteen years.

In the year of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0315] “In the year of the Lord” omitted by Henschen.] 1045, approximately, the pious Father [Note: [Col. 0315] “abbot of Saint Trudo,” Henschen.] Cuntram, constantly anxious to raise the bodies of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, which [Note: [Col. 0315] “which . . . were” is absent in Henschen.] at the time of the persecution by the pagan Normans had both been transferred and again concealed beneath the earth, first caused to be made, at great expense in gold, silver, and precious stones, a shrine of goldsmiths’ work. In this he arranged that the pearls of these heavenly treasures should be honourably enshrined when exhumed, so that the brethren might obtain their patronage with all the greater [Col. 0315C] confidence because the gaze of those praying would continually have the sacred bodies of their patrons [Note: [Col. 0315D] That is, their bodies.] present before it. [Note: [Col. 0315] “would display,” Henschen.] Therefore, [Note: [Col. 0315] Henschen adds “in the year of the Lord 1045, approximately.”] when this work had been completed, diggers eagerly excavated the ground deep within the sanctuary behind the altar of Saint Trudo, where the bodies had been deposited. At length they reached the stone vault beneath which they were contained. Suddenly a cloud of immense darkness arose there, and the diggers were struck with such terror that, despairing of life, they fled in utmost haste into the upper air. Overwhelmed by great astonishment and beside themselves, after long sighs repeatedly broken off [Note: [Col. 0315] “bursting forth,” Henschen.] they could scarcely speak, their hearts beating and gasping. [Note: [Col. 0315] “beating and gasping,” Henschen.] When the abbot saw this, he was terrified by what [Col. 0315D] had occurred; he replaced the earth, filled in the trench, and abandoned the undertaking.

In the year of the Lord 1048, the ninth year of Henry III—third in the kingdom and second in the empire—and the eighth year of Wazo, bishop of Liège, Lord Theoderic II of that name, bishop of Metz, in the forty-ninth year of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0315D] Rather, the fortieth; he died in 1046.], having stayed for some time in our monastery, fell into a sickbed. [Col. 0316A] When he came to the end, at the request of the brethren of this place and after consulting his own men, he granted us the *scrutum* of this town: namely, the whole right in the gruit which belonged to him alone, together with the liberty of appointing gruiters, and the house with its appurtenances in which the gruit substance was prepared, situated opposite the hall of our abbot, with the public street in between. After his death Adelbero, his kinsman—the nephew of Adelbero III of that name through his brother Theoderic, duke of Lorraine or of the Moselle region—succeeded him. He was a most devout man and, after God and Saint Trudo, the most faithful defender of this monastery against all princes and tyrants to the end of his life. Incidentally, in the same year, on the death of Wazo, bishop of Liège, Theoduin succeeded him, [Col. 0316B] and presided for twenty-eight years.

In the year of the Lord 1050 [Note: [Col. 0315] “In the year of the Lord 1050 . . . reached” supplied by Ghesquier, V, 50.], in the sixteenth year of the prelacy of Lord Guntram, Stepelinus, a monk of this place, wrote for the prelate Lord Guntram a book concerning the miracles of Saint Trudo which became very frequent among us in the time of this Lord Guntram, numbering more than a hundred. He prefaced these with some miracles performed before that time. This Stepelinus was received into the order in this monastery while still a boy, about the twenty-first year of Lord Abbot Adelard I. In his boyhood he saw elders of praiseworthy life, who for eighty years and more served God and Saint Trudo devoutly in the monastic habit; he too reached the same number of years, as will be made clear in the eighth book of the second part. [Note: [Col. 0316D] That is, above, in Book VIII, chapter 8, of the first continuator of Rudolf.] After [Col. 0316C] these years, approximately, a certain noble castellan was walking incautiously and, falling from a height, suffered weakness in his legs. Stricken in heart, he turned toward conversion; having assumed the religious habit, he gave this monastery his allod, which we are said still to possess. In monastic life he exerted himself in good works all the more zealously because he knew that he had sinned more grievously in the world.

As was his custom, he came before the others prior to Matins in order to perform private prayers. He entered the sanctuary and, behind the high altar which then stood there, prostrated himself in prayer before the altar of Saint Trudo. Having dozed a little, he saw children of wonderful beauty running around the edge of the altar, weeping, groaning, pulling their hair, and, [Col. 0316D] clapping their hands, lamenting thus: “Alas, alas!” As they repeated this, the brother, pitying their innocent age, said: “Children, who are you, and what is the cause of such great sorrow?” The Innocents said: “We are children. Behold, the blood of our lord Saint Stephen will now be spilled.” After these words they disappeared. Awakening, he feared to neglect so precious a pledge through negligence. Having sought [Col. 0317A] permission to speak from the prior of our place, he reported the vision.

The brethren were therefore roused, and Matins was sung quickly. While Lord Abbot Guntram and the convent persisted in prayer, disciplines having been taken and confession made by all, the casket of the precious treasure was opened. That rosy, flowing blood was found to have risen to the upper rim of the tilted glass vessel.
