A skilled goldsmith was summoned, who made a spherical enclosure about the vessel of precious blood; thus it was stored in a reliquary secured on every side. This heavenly treasure—of whose genuine presence in this monastery no one should doubt—was protected, through the foresight of the praiseworthy elders of that time, in so secret a place that it can neither be damaged by fire nor carried off by the violence of robbers.

[Col. 0317B] In the year of the Lord 1132 after this event, the eighth year of the empire of Lothair, one of our servants, named Gozelin, on the night of the feast of Saint Martin (10 November), when evening had come, spread his bed to sleep above the place of the tomb of Lord Abbot Guntram. When the bells had been rung and Matins begun, he came down from the great tower to go to bed. Three men of striking appearance appeared to him, clothed in sacred vestments and surrounded by a bright cloud, standing in the middle of the monastery before the crucifix. One of them, seeming more eminent than the others, bore a pastoral staff marked with the sign of the Lord’s cross. While that matricularius [Note: [Col. 0317D] He is the sacristan’s assistant.] sat trembling and stupefied before the bed placed over the abbot’s tomb, those awe-inspiring figures seemed to approach him as though indignant and threatening. But when, terrified, [Col. 0317C] he fell sideways to the ground and resolved by a vow to move the bed, they disappeared. He at once showed reverence to the tomb and its occupant, removed the bed from there, and, made more devout, later set out for Jerusalem. We include this apparition here because it is suitable to the subject matter.

—Having described [Note: [Col. 0317D] This concerns Rudolf’s *Deeds*, I, 12, where the interpolator inserted these matters, which we have combined here with his other interpolations [Col. 0318D].] the enlargement and repair of the monastery, and in general the abundant provision of materials necessary for construction, it should be recorded in detail with what courageous devotion the pious care of this Lord Adelard [Note: [Col. 0318D] The Second.] began to enlarge the fabric of this monastery. First, on the site of the forecourt that lay beyond the then old crypt, he raised high a new chancel, also called the sanctuary, securely founded with two apses, and completed it beautifully vaulted with stone vaulting (in the year 1057). Within this work he completed a new and spacious crypt, vaulted throughout with stone ceiling-work. In this structure he erected seven altars. The first and greatest, in the centre of the sanctuary, he built in honour of Blessed Mary and Saints Quentin and Remigius. After it came another in honour of Saints Martin and Christopher; a third beneath the apse adjoining the sanctuary on the right, [Col. 0318A] in honour of Saint John the Baptist and Saint John the Evangelist; and a fourth beneath the apse on the left of the sanctuary, in honour of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul and all the others.

He arranged the altars in the crypt as follows: the principal one, standing in the centre, he founded in honour of the Holy Trinity, the Blessed Virgin, and Saint Stephen; the second, on the right there, in honour of Saint Benedict; and the third, situated on the left, in honour of Saint Gregory. When all these things had been duly completed, he raised the body of Lady Bertha, countess of Flanders, which had been buried in the old crypt in the time of Abbot Thietfrid. He transferred it to the left of the high altar in the sanctuary and honourably enclosed it beneath a vault in an elevated tomb, polished with Parian stone.

Since the aforesaid old crypt lay behind the old sanctuary discussed above in Book I, chapter 13, of the first part, [Col. 0318B] he filled it with earth and built there the choir of singers. Between it and the new sanctuary he made a pleasing ascent, extending it through seven steps. Later, seeing that certain monastery buildings erected by his predecessors remained insufficiently completed, he set his mind to finish them. Among these was our great tower. Devout Abbot Guntram had, in his time, raised it as far as the middle with two stone vaults; Adelard added a third level for ascent and, erecting two side structures somewhat lower, completed it at great cost. Moreover, although the nave of the monastery was by no means ruinous, he completed its restoration: the exceedingly strong piers were pulled down, handsome columns raised in their place, and the wall made level to the summit.

Thus in his time the fabric of this old church was enlarged anew to such an extent that, as is fittingly said by the doctors concerning well-completed churches, it could be said to have been formed according to the stature of a human body. For it had—and is still seen to have—the chancel, also called the sanctuary, as its head and neck; the stall-filled choir as its breast; the cross, extending on both sides of this choir with two arms or wings, as its arms and hands; the nave of the monastery as its belly; and the lower cross, likewise spreading two wings southward and northward, as its hips and legs. [Col. 0318D] Before Adelard’s time there had also long stood two beautiful apses, rising high with very strong walls and adjoining the nave of the church on the right and left. Where they joined the arms of the front cross, they had two prominent towers, one facing south and the other north, equal in height to the wall of the monastery. Where the said apses joined the wings or arms of the rear cross, they had two chapels: one on the right in honour of Saints [Col. 0319A] Eucherius, Leonard, and Gertrude; the other, toward the cloister, in honour of Saint Lambert.

And since the chancel or sanctuary and the apse are under discussion, it should be known that the chancel is the head and the lower part of the church facing east. It is also called the sanctuary because sacred things are stored or handled there, and it extends as far as the choir; hence, in Lent, a veil is customarily hung in church between the choir and the chancel or sanctuary. Apses, however, are exedrae or appendages attached to the sides of halls or churches to enlarge the space for walking.

Incidentally. [Sigebert.] In the year of the Lord 1057, when Henry II died in the empire, his son Henry III succeeded as emperor and ruled for fifty years. In his [Col. 0319B] third year, Stephen IX, brother of Godfrey, duke of Lorraine and count of Ardennes, became pope and died in the following year.

In the year of the Lord 1060, the fourth year of this Henry in the kingdom and the thirteenth year of Theoduin, bishop of Liège, and Adelbero, bishop of Metz, this same Adelbero, at the request of Abbot Adelard and the brethren of this place, confirmed the whole right of *scrutum* in gruit which his predecessor Theoderic II had recently granted to the church and brethren. Present there in the same monastery were Theoderic, duke of Lorraine or of the Moselle region, Adelbero’s brother and advocate of this town, and Otto, count of Duras, sub-advocate. Further notice will be made below of this gruit and its right. Before this year the aforesaid Theoderic, duke of Lorraine, was appointed advocate of this town, and he appointed in his place Otto, count of Duras, brother of Emmo, count of Loon.

In the year of the Lord 1063, approximately, a dispute arose between Lord Abbot Adelard and Duke Frederick, our advocate, regarding the advocate’s right. But by the declaration of the aldermen it was determined that from ancient usage the advocate has the third penny from the three general pleas and the great ban, and nothing from other matters, unless he is invited for that purpose by the bishop’s or abbot’s reeve in major cases.

Afterward, in the year 1065, upon the death of Duke Frederick, when his successor Lord Udo pressed the matter in the presence [Col. 0319D] of this Lord Adelbero, the same sworn aldermen declared and affirmed the same things as before.

In the year [Note: [Col. 0319] The interpolator appended these matters, marked as chapter 5, to Book II of Rudolf.] of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0319] “A.D. 1085 . . . space” in Henschen.], when the monastery was burned, the columns which had stood in place of piers gave way, and the two inner walls of the nave of the church collapsed. Their fall destroyed both altars of the old sanctuary: the lesser, namely that of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, and the greater, which stood before it, in honour of the twelve Apostles. The former, that of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, was later restored; of the latter even the traces have been obliterated.

After this [Col. 0320A] collapse, Abbot Lanzo wished to seek the bodies of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, which were concealed in that sanctuary; therefore he ordered digging to begin farther within, around their tomb. But the place was found to be so full of sarcophagi that scarcely at times was there a space of a single foot between one sarcophagus and another. Some reported concerning this that a certain Abbot Imizo of our place had caused the bones of all his predecessor abbots to be raised from the various places in the monastery where they lay buried, and had put them together in the aforesaid place in the sanctuary, enclosing them with four marble stones. He did not live beyond that year.

Moreover, when digging was carried out beneath the front part of the high altar there, a sarcophagus was found so placed that, when [Col. 0320B] the priest stood at this altar, the breast of the person resting there lay beneath his feet. When it was carefully opened, a certain person was found in it covered with a precious pall, but without the back of the head. Two bricks were likewise found there, one at the head and the other at the feet, but nothing was inscribed. Supposing that this concerned someone important, those present approached the body and, in blameworthy rashness, scattered the body limb by limb this way and that through the sarcophagus, seeking with lamps for any indications by which they might discover who he had been. But they found nothing.

Likewise, when a sarcophagus at the entrance to the little choir was opened, a certain person was found clad in a purple cope splendidly made with gold embroidery; but no indications of who he was were found. Nevertheless, very many thought that he was Saint Libertus. [Col. 0320C] At this spectacle all the assembled people marvelled that, as soon as the ornaments covering the bodies were touched, they dissolved into ashes.

At length digging reached the place where the saints had been deposited, and an opening was found in the wall of that vault or crypt, as thick as a human hand. One of the common people, moved by human curiosity and wishing to know what it contained, fastened a lighted candle to the end of a rod and put it through the opening into the crypt. A bystander rebuked him for this presumption and warned him with an agitated cry to abandon his undertaking. Hearing this, the people roared in tumultuous uproar: some who had learned about the matter forbade proceeding, while others who did not know the matter shouted that the investigation should continue. Frightened by their noise, he abandoned the undertaking. Abbot [Note: [Col. 0319] “Abbot . . . was done” in Henschen.] Lanzo also, afraid to proceed, sent the prior of the cloister to Henry, bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0319] “Herimann,” Henschen.], asking what should be done concerning either the bodies found or the future course of action. The bishop first reproved the act, then forbade proceeding, and finally commanded that, after the solemnities of Mass had been celebrated for the faithful departed and the commendation of souls performed, the sarcophagi should be closed, the bodies first sprinkled with holy water [Col. 0321A] and incensed, and then covered with earth. This was done.

[Sigebert, Continuator of Affligem.] In the aforesaid year 1085 [Note: [Col. 0321] The interpolator wrote these words in the lower margin at III, 2.], the Romans acknowledge Henry IV as emperor in name of his kingship; by their judgment the aforesaid Pope Gregory is deposed from the papacy, and that Clement is enthroned. In the preceding year the monastery of Affligem began.

[Sigebert.] In the year [Note: [Col. 0321] These words were added by the interpolator in the index which he compiled.] of the Lord, Pope Gregory VII died in exile, and Victor succeeded him. When he died, Urban II succeeded him in the third year thereafter, in opposition to the emperor and his antipope, and presided for eleven years.

In the same year, namely the year of the Lord 1086, according to reports of the elders of that time and accounts carefully written in the ancient books of our monastery, [Col. 0321B] a certain knight, to whom Count Arnulf of Loon, nephew of Count Ghiselbert of Duras, had entrusted the watch of our great tower, looked down in the untimely silence of the night upon the burned nave of the monastery while his fellow guards slept. He saw certain persons wearing garments resembling monastic dress proceed barefoot from the site of our cemetery to the tomb of Saints Trudo and Eucherius. The tomb, roofless and exposed to the open air after the recent fire, they reverently circled with acts of satisfaction and most humble supplications. Seeking to have a witness and confidant of this vision, he tried to wake the sleeping companion beside him; but he himself remained motionless and mute until the vision disappeared, [Col. 0321C] those whom he had seen having returned to their former place in the cemetery. Immediately, unable to bear the force of so great a vision, he was seized by such severe illness that on the third day, deprived of life, he was committed to burial.

In the year of the Lord 1096 [Note: [Col. 0321] These were added by the interpolator in the index.], Godfrey, duke of Lorraine and count of Bouillon, having first sold the castle of Bouillon with its villages to Otbert, bishop of Liège, for 1,300 marks of silver, set out for the Holy Land with Hugh, brother of the king of France, and the counts of Flanders, Provence, and Normandy, together with many princes and an innumerable multitude of people, estimated at 600,000. At the exhortation of Urban II all had first taken the sign of the cross; Jews unwilling to believe in Christ were killed.

In the year [Note: [Col. 0321] These were appended by the interpolator in the index.] of the Lord 1100, Godfrey of Bouillon and duke of Lorraine, through whose enterprise Jerusalem was captured by [Col. 0322A] Christians, having been made king of Jerusalem in the preceding year, died in this year. In the same year Emperor Henry compelled Henry of Limburg, who had rebelled against him, to surrender; after receiving him again into favour, with a large payment of money intervening, he granted him the vacant duchy of Lorraine.

Here it should be carefully understood that there are, and have been, two dukes of Lorraine. The duchy of one begins near the city of Metz and extends from there alongside the duchy of the duke of Austria; it is also called the duchy of the Moselle region. The other duchy of Lorraine lies on this side and has long been incorporated into the duchy of Brabant.

This [Note: [Col. 0321] Added by the interpolator in the index.] Lord Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0321D] Abbot of Saint Trudo.], distinguished above many gifts of divine and human grace by learning, was especially eminent in the composition of proses, rhythms, and metres. At Ghent, in the monastery of Saint Peter, where after the death of Adelard II, abbot of this place, he lived long in exile, he refined into more polished diction the life of our holy father and patron Trudo. Donatus the deacon, and, as is believed, a professed member of this house, had long before written it in a plain style at the command of the bishop of Metz. Theoderic did this at the urging of the often-mentioned Provost Gerard; its beginning is: “Therefore, in extolling . . .” He also composed the sermon read at the translation of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, beginning: “Glorious is the present day . . .” [Note: [Col. 0322D] See Surius, *Lives of the Saints*, VI.] together with certain responsories there: namely, these two, “O men of mercy,” and the antiphon “Of the eternal city,” and “Trudo of virtues,” with the antiphons, [Col. 0322C] responsories, and verses sung at the deposition of Saint Trudo. Prior Rudolf, a most learned man skilled in the music of Guido of Arezzo, at Theoderic’s command fitted these to melody in cento form.

In the year of the Lord 1126, Emperor Henry IV, who had imprisoned his father contrary to the law of nature, died without children. Lothair IV, elected king, succeeded him. In the third year of his reign he deprived Godfrey, count of Louvain, of the duchy of Lorraine and installed Waleran, count of Limburg. [Note: [Col. 0321] Interpolator, 1*, in the margin.]

In the year of the Lord 1127, Stephen, bishop of Metz, granted us for the use of the brethren one small court situated before the eastern gate of the court of our monastery. [Note: [Col. 0321] The first words are supplied from the manuscript by Henschen.]

## SECOND PART OF THE THIRD CONTINUATION

[Col. 0321]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0321D] Having long ago completed [Note: [Col. 0321] The first words are supplied from the manuscript by Henschen.] the three parts of the compilation concerning the deeds of the abbots of this monastery, it is fitting at least in this fourth part to collect the few things that remain, [Col. 0322D] because negligence omitted to record many matters worthy of remembrance concerning earlier fathers. Since, according to Gregory in his homilies, one who cannot bring a sheaf to the threshing-floor does well, lest he come empty-handed, to bring ears of grain: therefore, although the multitude of matters to be written, like the great sand, is overwhelmed by the waters of oblivion, nevertheless, so that the remnants of these annals may be preserved, and so that the few fragments may be gathered lest they perish, it has pleased us to divide this final part into two partial books.

The first contains the deeds of nine abbots, [Col. 0324A] whose names are these: Nicholas, Christian, John, Libertus, John, Thomas, William, Henry, William. The second book contains the deeds of three abbots: Ada, Amelius, and Robert. Among these deeds are inserted many events appropriate to annals.

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK OF THE FOURTH PART OF THE COMPILATION CONCERNING THE DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS, AND FIRST, THE DEEDS OF ABBOT NICHOLAS

[Col. 0323]

1. On the election of Abbot Nicholas.

2. On incorporation of the tithe of the church of Alburg. Various incidental events.

3. On the dispute concerning the office of our reeve or steward.

## ON THE DEEDS OF ABBOT CHRISTIAN

1. On the election of Abbot Christian.

2. On the office of reeve or stewardship and its redemption. Incidental matters concerning the empire of Frederick II and other events.

3. On the superstitious invention of an English monk.

4. On Saint Lutgard, prioress of Saint Catherine.

5. On the devastation of the city of Liège.

6. On the battle at Steps, and how the bishop invaded Brabant by fires.

7. On the battle near the bridge of Bouvines, where the princes conspiring against the bishopric were defeated.

8. On the death of Abbot Christian.

## ON THE DEEDS OF JOHN, FIRST ABBOT OF THIS NAME

1. On John’s nomination as abbot and his appointment.

2. How the visitation of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy was entrusted to him by Cardinal C., legate.

3. How, together with this abbey, I took charge of the abbey at Theux by command of Cardinal C.

4. How one half of the town of Saint Trudo was acquired for the church of Liège.

5. On the abbot of Saint Paul at Utrecht.

## ON THE DEEDS OF ABBOT LIBERTUS

1. On the election of Abbot Libertus.

2. On the office of our stewardship.

3. On the newly instituted feast of Saint Libertus.

4. On the transfer of the monastery of our nuns from the suburb of Saint Trudo.

5. On this abbot’s resignation from the abbacy.

## ON THE DEEDS OF JOHN, SECOND ABBOT OF THIS NAME

1. On the appointment of Abbot John to this abbey; on a loan at interest contracted in his time; and on the losses arising from this loan. Many incidental matters.

2. On this Abbot John’s resignation from this abbey.

3. On a loan at interest contracted by the prior and convent because of losses.

## DEEDS OF ABBOT THOMAS

1. On Thomas’s appointment as abbot, and on the burden of debts by which he found the monastery bound at interest.

2. On the office of our stewardship, and how he won the leading men of this town to his allegiance by gifts. Many incidental matters; on the death of the king of the Romans, the landgrave, and how William, count of Holland, was elected as his successor.

3. On the hospital of Saint Trudo and the recovery of pontifical ornaments.

4. On the number of nuns at Melin and the death of Abbot Thomas.

## ON THE DEEDS OF WILLIAM, FIRST ABBOT OF THIS NAME

1. On the nomination of Abbot William as abbot and his election.

2. On the suit which he pursued for six years against Lombard moneylenders in the Roman curia, and its settlement; likewise on other grave expenditures.

3. On acquisition of the advocacy at Alburg, and redemption of various monastery properties and of sixteen prebends which secular ministeriales and officeholders possessed hereditarily.

4. On the number of monks of this place, temporarily reduced by necessity.

5. On the purchase of fourteen dwellings and enlargement of our cloister court toward the sedge-marsh and the stone street.

6. On the mutual conflict of bishop and country, and the proscription at Vottem.

7. On the robbery of the innkeeper and the origin of the eight lords.

8. On the violence and injuries which the eight lords inflicted upon our monastery and upon the bishop-elect of Liège on account of the striking of coin, and on the siege of the town by Henry, duke of Brabant.

9. How the eight lords handed the lordship of the town over to the duke of Brabant, violated the monastery, drove out the abbot, violated the church of Blessed Mary, and took priests and aldermen captive.

10. On the proscription of the eight lords and on the bishop’s castle.

11. On the increase of the prebend, in monastic allowances of wine, refectory dishes, and clothing; and on the first foundation of the Beguines’ court at Saint Agnes, achieved through the work of Abbot William. Likewise, on the rent of the Friars Minor.

12. How our properties on the Moselle were sold; on the violence which the count of Loon and the duke of Brabant inflicted on us by usurping the jurisdictions of our monastery’s villages; and on the mill at Mechelen.

13. On the prebends of Blessed Mary and the lesser prebends; on alms at the gate; and on the pottage seasoned in a cauldron fixed above the furnace.

14. On not receiving into our congregation persons born of an illegitimate union. Likewise, on a wonderful apparition shown to Abbot William concerning the soul of a deceased fellow monk; and on his death.

## ON THE DEEDS OF ABBOT HENRY

1. On Henry’s appointment as abbot of this place. Many incidental matters.

2. On his resignation from the abbacy.

## ON THE DEEDS OF WILLIAM, SECOND ABBOT OF THIS NAME

1. On the appointment of William II to our abbacy and his praiseworthy life.

2. Incidental matters concerning the killing of the bishop of Liège and many other events; on the community established in the town with the consent of bishop and abbot for the duration of their agreed pleasure; and on the battle at Waremme.

3. On construction of our residence at Donk, on the channel of the river Herk, and on the death of this Abbot William.

## HERE BEGINS THE FOURTH PART, CONCERNING THE DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT TRUDO, DIVIDED INTO TWO PARTIAL BOOKS

Its first book contains the deeds of nine abbots; and first:

[Col. 0325]

## ON THE DEEDS OF ABBOT NICHOLAS

[Col. 0325A] 1. In the year of the Lord 1180, the twenty-eighth year of the empire of Frederick I and the thirteenth year of Rodolf, bishop of Liège, after the death on 11 December of Abbot Wiric of pious memory, Nicholas was elected on the same day and consecrated on 21 December.

2. In the second year of his prelacy (1181), the church of Alburg, together with all its tithe, revenues, and emoluments, was incorporated into the brethren’s maintenance, as is clearly set forth in our charters issued by Pope Lucius III and Baldwin, bishop of Utrecht.

Incident. In the third year of the same prelacy (1182), on 11 Kalends of April [22 March], lightning accompanied by dreadful thunder descended and entered the church of Saint Lawrence at Liège. It harmed no one; leaving the curtains untouched, it tore, but did not burn, the pallium of the high altar; and, while the altar-cloth remained unharmed, it shattered the seal of that altar into seven pieces. [Col. 0325B]

Incident. In the same year, on 3 Nones of November [3 November], the same church was reconsecrated by Rudolf, bishop of Liège.

Incident. In his fourth year of prelacy, that is, in the year of the Lord 1183, Godfrey III, duke of Brabant, set out for Jerusalem; and his son Henry, upon his departure, destroyed the castle of Jauche. [Note: [Col. 0325C] “Jauche?”] In that same year several heretics were burned in Flanders. In the following year, when Duke Godfrey of Brabant died, [Note: [Col. 0325C] “Godfrey III died in 1190.”] his son Henry [Note: [Col. 0325C] “The first among the dukes of Brabant.”] succeeded him and destroyed the castle of Duras.

Incident. In the following year of his reign, on 4 Kalends of May [28 April], the monastery of Saint Lambert at Liège and Saint Peter’s there, together with their cloisters and all their offices, as well as the bishop’s palace, were burned.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1186, our entire town of Saint Trond [Col. 0325C] was burned, along with the church of Blessed Mary; the monastery remained unharmed. In this fire many persons of both sexes, together with children, died by suffocation.

Incident. [VINC. BELLOV. [Col. 0326A] XXIX.] In the following year Saladin, the sultan, invaded the lands of the Christians. The Christians were defeated (1187), Jerusalem was besieged and captured, and the taking of the cross was preached. Philip, king of France, and Henry, king of England, together with the princes of the Catholic faith, took the cross for the liberation of the Holy Land.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1188, Henry, cardinal-bishop of Albano, celebrated Mass among us for two days, preached to the people, and confirmed many with chrism, on 4 Kalends of May [28 April].

Incident. In the same year at Paris, at a general council, many thousands of nobles and common people took the cross. That same night the moon was seen to descend to the earth and afterwards to return a little way to its place. At about the same time Emperor Frederick took the cross with the princes of the Empire, and Rudolf, bishop of Liège, departed with him. [Col. 0326B]

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1189, Henry, duke of Louvain, on the Nones of June [5 June], pursuant to the agreement of a peace concluded, rebuilt the castle of Duras, which he had destroyed some years earlier.

Incident. At about the same time the same duke, on the pretext of the advocacy, besieged and attacked the town of Saint Trond, [Note: [Col. 0326C] “On these matters see Gilbert’s *Chronicle of Hainaut*, ed. Chasteler, p. 201.”] but did not take it. They relate that during this or a similar siege by the duke there were in the town honorable and prudent aldermen and burgesses who, having taken counsel how they might incline the mind of so great a prince to goodwill, caused delicate *ignatiae* to be made, prepared in the town from ancient custom, which are called by another name *placentae*, “cakes.” Through distinguished men, with assurances of safe access given, they offered these to the duke while he was dining beneath his tents. They declared that the inhabitants of the town intended nothing hostile against his dignity [Col. 0326C] and begged that the mercy of his nobility might be poured out upon them. Then the duke, observing the humility of the prudent townsmen and gladly accepting the small gift, [Col. 0327A] after a few days raised the siege and graciously returned with his whole army to his own lands.

Incident. [VINC. BELL.] In the following year (1190), Emperor Frederick, arriving near Antioch with a very great army, fell from his horse and died in a small stream. And the prophecy spoken concerning him while he lay in the cradle was fulfilled: “He shall enter as a fox, reign as a lion, and die as a dog.” His son Henry V succeeded him by right of name and reigned seven years.

3. In the time of this abbot, although some of his predecessors had redeemed many benefices and goods of the monastery unjustly usurped by stewards, nevertheless more than twenty-seven offices or ministries were held by various persons, whether as fiefs or under another hereditary right, to the burden of the great expenses of our church. [Col. 0327B] Among these, the office of stewardship, or *scultetia*, was the cause of serious discord. For although this abbot had often litigated with Everard the steward, and the stewardship ought to have been adjudged away from him because of certain offenses, the abbot was at length persuaded by the entreaties of many to consent that Everard should hold the stewardship on this condition: that he might sell it to no one except the monastery, nor alienate it from the church, if the abbot or any successor of his should consent to buy it upon the excommunication of the aldermen and his own faithful men. Thus the dispute was settled.

Incident. [VINC. BELL.] In the year of the Lord 1191, after a long siege, the Christians captured the city of Acre, which they had taken by assault, on the condition that the pagans should depart with their lives safe, restore the Lord’s cross, and set the Christian captives free.

Incident. In the same year battle-lines of fighting men were seen descending from the air to the earth; after a wondrous battle had been fought among them, they suddenly vanished.

In that year Rudolf, bishop of Liège, returning from overseas parts after having presided for twenty-three years, is said to have perished by a cup of poison. After him, in the following year (1192), Albert, brother of Henry, duke of Lotharingia, was elected bishop.

## DEEDS OF ABBOT CHRISTIAN

1. In the year of the Lord 1193, the fourth year of Henry V’s imperial reign, [Note: [Col. 0327D] “Third.”] Nicholas, after governing vigorously for twelve years, weary of evils, withdrew from the abbacy on 5 Kalends of April [28 March]. Christian, elected on the same day, succeeded him and was consecrated on 9 Kalends of May [23 April]. [Note: [Col. 0327D] “This seems to be the correct reading; manuscript of Marchiennes.”] His paternal uncle was Abbot Werric; and a certain alderman called John Kint, chief of the Staplen kin-group, was his nephew. He was especially devout and zealous for religion.

2. In the time of this abbot, Everard, mentioned above, having become impoverished in temporal goods, wished, contrary to his promise, to alienate from the church the office of stewardship. [Col. 0327C] The abbot did not consent, but, considering the benefit of his church, redeemed it from him for a fixed sum of money. Later, being in need of money for necessary purposes, he arranged to pawn the said office to Otto the toll-collector, a powerful and very wealthy townsman, for an agreed sum. But the faithful men of the church, taking precautions lest both the abbot himself and the townsmen collectively might in future be excessively oppressed through the same Otto, procured that this agreement should have no effect. They decreed that the lord abbot must pay Otto ten Cologne marks as the penalty [Col. 0327D] imposed upon the party withdrawing from that contract; and so the abbot temporarily appointed a particular friend as steward.

Accordingly, meanwhile, on the advice of the faithful men of the church, a certain honorable townsman, Clement, and his wife Sigardis—being of the household of Saint Trond—paid eighty Cologne marks for the office itself, and, when the said Otto refused to remit the aforesaid ten marks, they paid him those marks as well. Clement, giving his lord a good destrier, [Note: [Col. 0328D] “A horse suited for war.”] [Col. 0328B] promised with his wife, before the peers of the church, that whenever the lord abbot or the convent should wish to redeem the stewardship, he would always be prepared to relinquish it upon repayment to him of eighty-eight marks of the aforesaid currency.

Incident. In the same year Albert the elect was consecrated bishop of Liège at Reims by sentence of Pope [Note: [Col. 0328D] “Celestine III.”] and was killed by order of the emperor in the third year after his appointment. In the same year Albert of Cuijk and Simon, son of the duke of the Ardennes, disputed over the bishopric. Simon became a cardinal, and Albert peacefully obtained the bishopric.

Incident. [VINC. BELL. XXIX, 59.] In the year of the Lord 1197 Emperor Henry died.

Incident. In the following year (1194), a great dispute arose over the election of an emperor, between Philip, duke of Swabia, and Otto, duke of Saxony. Otto was consecrated emperor and tyrannized against the Church, as appears in the *Historical Mirror*.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1199, our cloister at Dunc was burned together with its church, on the day before the Kalends of April [31 March].

Incident. In the same year Albert, bishop of Liège, died. Hugh of Petraponte succeeded him; he acquired for the church of Liège the castle of Moha with its county.

3. In the time of Abbot Christian a remarkable event occurred. A certain English monk came to us for the sake of hospitality. [Col. 0328D] Having learned from the brethren’s account how great an offering had formerly enriched this church through the merits of Saint Trond, and wishing to oblige the abbot, he devised a deception through which the cloister might be relieved of the debts by which it was bound. By means of certain underground channels, extended as far as the base of the great tower, [Note: [Col. 0327] *protractus*, “extended,” in manuscript 1*.] he caused water to bubble upward like a spring. [Note: [Col. 0327] This word is absent from manuscript 1*.] When the people saw this, they undoubtedly believed that Saint Trond had performed it miraculously; and it was publicized so widely that the faithful came together and loaded Saint Trond’s altar with great offerings. But because such hypocrisy could not remain hidden for long, after a few days the channel was uncovered, the spring dried up, and the trick by which it had been done became known. The matter was finally brought to the ears of the supreme pontiff, whose indignation against the abbot himself grew so hot that he deprived him of pontifical vestments and mitre.

4. [*Life of St. Lutgard*, 21, 17, 18, 22.] In or about the year of the Lord 1200, Lutgard, a most devout nun of the monastery of Saint Catherine, situated in the suburb of the town of Saint Trond, was there making solemn profession into the hands of Abbot Christian, as was customary. At the end, when according to the rule [Col. 0329B] she ought to offer the kiss of peace to the abbot as well as to her prioress and the other sisters, she recoiled from the touch of the holy man so greatly that she could scarcely be drawn to it by the sisters. In that encounter, as she later said, she felt no bodily contact.

Concerning the same woman. When this God-worthy Lutgard began to desire that, through the ministry of consecration by a bishop’s hands, she might be joined more perfectly to Christ, her sole husband, an opportunity arose for the bishop of Liège to consecrate several nuns there to God. Lutgard was therefore brought among the assembly of virgins to be consecrated. While the bishop, placing on each of their heads a garland interwoven from belts as the sign of a golden crown, [Note: [Col. 0329] *certum*, “certain,” manuscript 1*.] it was plainly seen by three devout persons standing by that the bishop honored Lutgard above the others [Col. 0329C] and placed a precious golden crown upon her head.

Concerning the same woman. After some time had passed, the prioress died, and Lutgard was elected by universal consent. From that time she planned to change both place and manner of life. When Master John of Lier, distinguished in every holiness, and Christina the Astonishing advised her [Note: [Col. 0329] “This or a similar word is wanting in the manuscript.”] to leave both position and prelacy and pass to the Cistercian monastery of Aywières, [Note: [Col. 0329D] “Aywières, not far from Liège.”] and she hesitated, Christ appeared to her and instructed her finally to make for the said place of Aywières. Obeying these warnings, she obtained permission and happily moved to that monastery in Brabant, after having been a nun for nearly twelve years in Saint Catherine’s monastery. When the nuns of Saint Catherine’s [Col. 0329D] saw this, they grieved inconsolably. Sympathizing with their grief, she received consolation from Blessed Mary, Christ’s mother: namely, that the cloister from which she was departing should be advanced both spiritually and temporally by her prayers. This transfer of Lutgard took place in or about the year of the Lord 1206.

Incident. [VINC. BELL. XXX, 1.] In the year of the Lord 1211 Frederick, king of Sicily, after Otto had recently been deprived of the Empire, was elected emperor; he was honorably received and consecrated at Rome, and ruled for thirty-four years. In the same year war began between Hugh, bishop of Liège, and Henry, duke of Brabant, over the county of Moha.

5. In the year of the Lord 1212, [Note: [Col. 0329D] “The author of the *Triumph of Saint Lambert at Steppes*, in Chapeaville II, 605 (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLIX, col. 287 ff.), discussed these matters and what follows at great length.”] and in the twentieth year of the same prelacy, on the Ascension of the Lord—which fell on the feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross—Henry, duke of Brabant, grieving that the county of Moha had devolved upon the bishopric of Liège, ravaged very many villages throughout the bishopric. With a great multitude of armed men he invaded and stormed the city of Liège, and carried off utterly an immense treasure of gold, silver, and other precious goods. Clerics and priests were despoiled; [Col. 0330B] all ecclesiastical furnishings and jewels were taken away; the altar of Saint Lambert was polluted with human blood; three men were killed in Saint Peter’s church; women and virgins consecrated to God were assaulted and violated; and, after many were killed in various places, many were drowned and very many others were taken captive. Having done these things, the duke returned with his men to his own territory.

After his departure, Hugh, bishop of Liège, immediately held a council at the town of Huy, excommunicated the duke, and proclaimed him excommunicate by a sentence pronounced. Having assembled a great army of three thousand horsemen and a very large multitude of foot soldiers, he hastened to destroy Brabant with the help and power of Count Ferrand of Flanders, Philip of Namur, Louis of Looz, and many other counts and nobles of France. [Col. 0330C] Hearing this, the duke was greatly troubled by fear. He approached the said count of Flanders and, through him, made peace with the bishop on stipulated terms, promising to compensate the people of Liège for all the damage inflicted upon them by his men and, moreover, to beg pardon on bended knees in Saint Lambert’s church for his offenses. Thus the said princes returned with their men to their own lands.

In the same year, the duke made an alliance with Philip, king of France, and married the king’s daughter [Note: [Col. 0330D] “Mary, the illegitimate daughter of King Philip.”] to himself. Raised up by this, he arrogantly refused to perform what he had promised the bishop.

Incident. [VINC. BELL.] At this time flourished Mary of Oignies, who knew in the spirit that, when the enemy’s incursion raged [Col. 0330D] through the bishopric of Liège, all the holy girls of her congregation would be preserved in the purity of their virginity.

6. In the year of the Lord 1213, [Note: [Col. 0330D] “A most exact narrative of these events was supplied by Reiner of Saint James, whom one might perhaps conjecture to have been among our author’s sources.”] and in the twenty-first year of the same prelacy, Ferrand, count of Flanders, ordered the bishop of Liège and the count of Looz to assemble armies and invade the duke’s lands from one side, [Col. 0331A] while he himself would invade them from the other. But as he was preparing to do this, Philip, king of France, the duke’s father-in-law, [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Father-in-law.”] invaded the count’s land with hostile intent. He forced certain towns in Flanders by force to surrender, captured some and overthrew others, and killed about two thousand Flemings in battle. Upon hearing this, the count abandoned the expedition he had planned against the duke and, pursuing the king, who had already returned home, captured the city of Tournai.

Meanwhile the duke gathered his entire army, entered the bishop’s lands again, devastated the town of Tongeren, burned Waremme, [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Waremme, near Saint Trond.”] Waleffe, [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Waleffe, near Huy.”] and other villages of the bishopric, and returned against the city of Liège. When he approached it and found it enclosed by very strong walls, he marvelled that such rapid fortification had been completed, withdrew, and directed his march toward Brabant.

Meanwhile Hugh the bishop and Louis, count of Looz, having assembled their armies, swiftly pursued the duke and found him with his entire army at the stronghold of Steppes, [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Steppes; this victory was won on 13 October 1213. Compare Reiner of Saint James in Chapeaville II, 227.”] situated near the village of Montenaken. Battle-lines were therefore arranged on both sides, a most severe battle was fought, and victory fell to the bishop of Liège. More than two thousand men of Brabant’s army were killed. The duke himself was compelled to seek safety in flight and came with a few men to the town of Louvain. The bishop then advanced into the duke’s lands and ravaged the towns of Leeuw, [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Leeuw, not far from Saint Trond.”] Landen, Hannut, [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Hannut, near Tienen.”] and many other villages of Brabant.

Incident. A few days later [Col. 0331C] Count Ferrand of Flanders, setting aside the expedition he had planned against the king of France, hurried to enter Brabant with a plentiful army. When the duke heard this, he was overcome with extreme fear, made peace with the count by paying a very great sum of money, and, through the count’s mediation, peace was made between the bishop and the duke. Thus the duke was compelled to fulfill what he had promised in the preceding year but had refused to perform. Coming to Liège, he humbly entered Saint Lambert’s church and, barefoot and on bended knees, begged the holy martyr’s pardon for his misdeeds in the presence of Bishop Hugh and of all the clergy and people. After these rites had been solemnly performed, he received absolution from the bishop and returned home. [Note: [Col. 0331D] “This took place on 28 February 1214.”]

7. [VINC. BELL. XXX, 1.] In the same year Frederick, who had been consecrated emperor in opposition to Emperor Otto, entered Germany, and the greater part of the princes of the realm adhered to him. Otto, now ex-emperor, came with a great army to Aachen, in order to proceed thence to the assistance [Col. 0332A] of his uncle, the king of England, [Note: [Col. 0332D] “John.”] against the king of France. Henry, duke of Brabant, joined him; after making an alliance with him, he promised to give Otto his daughter in marriage, [Note: [Col. 0332D] “Mary, whom Otto married in May 1214.”] in the hope that by Otto’s power he might still take revenge upon the bishopric of Liège.

After this alliance was made, [Note: [Col. 0332D] “12 July 1214, as the author of the *Triumph of Saint Lambert at Steppes* proves.”] Emperor Otto came with his entire army to Nivelles. When the dukes of Brabant and Limburg, the counts of Flanders and Boulogne [Note: [Col. 0332D] “Renaud.”] and other princes had arrived there in a great multitude, they secretly and unanimously formed a conspiracy against the bishopric of Liège: as soon as they obtained the victory they expected against Philip, king of France, they would immediately invade that bishopric and, after victory was gained, divide among themselves, as they had arranged, the city, towns, castles, fortresses, and villages [Col. 0332B] of Liège. But with God’s help and through the favor of Saint Lambert’s merits, their hope was frustrated, and, contrary to their wishes, what follows occurred.

Incident. In the following year, Otto the ex-emperor, Ferrand count of Flanders, and their associates—the dukes of Brabant and Limburg, the count of Boulogne, and many other counts, princes, and barons—advanced against Philip, king of France. The king met them with his own forces near the bridge of Bouvines [Note: [Col. 0332D] “Between Lille and Tournai, near Cysoing.”] (27 July 1214). Battle was joined; and although many nobles fell on both sides, victory finally fell to the king of the Franks. There the counts of Flanders, Boulogne, and Salisbury—namely, the brother of the king of England [Note: [Col. 0332D] “William, illegitimate son of King Richard I.”]—were captured with many others, and many were slain. Emperor Otto [Col. 0332C] and the dukes of Brabant and Limburg, after immense labors and dangers, escaped by flight with many other nobles.

Incident. In the same year the kings of France and England made peace.

Incident. In the same year, after Otto the ex-emperor’s flight in the battle of the bridge of Bouvines, all the princes of Germany who had still adhered to Emperor Otto, considering his cause hopeless, joined Frederick, who had been consecrated by the Roman Church. Frederick, with five thousand knights, proceeded toward Aachen, crossed the Rhine, and then intended to invade the duke of Brabant and his land because he was still a supporter of Otto. Hearing this, the duke was afraid and, through Hugh, bishop of Liège, obtained peace and Frederick’s favor.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1215, [Col. 0332D] and in the twenty-third year of the same prelacy, Pope Innocent III held the Lateran Council, at which Christian, abbot of this place, was summoned and attended among the other prelates of churches.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1216, and in the twenty-fourth year of the same prelacy, the Order of Preachers was confirmed by Pope Honorius III, [Col. 0333A] who in this year succeeded Innocent, who had intended to promote that order. Hence the verse:

> In twelve hundred and sixteen the Order that preaches began.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1219, and in the twenty-seventh year of the same prelacy, Pope Honorius confirmed the rule of the brethren of the Valley of Scholars. Likewise, he confirmed the rule of the brethren living on Mount Carmel, who were afterwards compelled by attacks of the pagans to scatter from that place into diverse parts of the world.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1221, and in the twenty-ninth year of the same prelacy, on the Kalends of September [1 September], nearly half the town [Col. 0334A] of Saint Trond and the church of the Holy Sepulchre were burned. In this fire only one man was burned to death.

8. This abbot, after he had presided for thirty years, at last fell into a sickbed; having devoutly received the sacraments of the Church, he fell asleep in the Lord and was buried in the choir of the chanters before the steps. His epitaph is inscribed in these verses:

> Here he had received his name from the name of Christ;  
> Therefore, by his life, he showed himself to be a Christian.  
> And because that father worshipped you, Mary, with a devout mind,  
> Stretch forth your hand, O Virgin, and save your Christian.

## DEEDS OF JOHN, THE FIRST ABBOT OF THIS NAME

[Col. 0333]

1. In the year of the Lord 1222, the twenty-second year of the empire of Frederick II, [Note: [Col. 0333D] “Second year of the Empire; twenty-fourth of Sicily.”] after the death of Abbot Christian on 15 Kalends of October [17 September], Master John of Saintes, dean of the church of Saint Mary at Aachen, was postulated as abbot of this place. The bishops of Liège and Metz [Note: [Col. 0333D] “John.”] rejoiced exceedingly at this and affectionately promised that they would support him in all matters. He humbly obeyed and was made abbot by a legate of the Roman Curia on 5 Nones of November [9 November].

2. In the same year the cardinal-bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, legate of the Apostolic See, on 11 Kalends of December [21 November], by the authority of his legation ordered and entrusted to him the visitation, in head and members, of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy.

3. [Col. 0333C] In the following year the said legate sent him an order in this form:

> C[onrad], [Note: [Col. 0333D] “Conrad.”] by divine mercy bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved in Christ John, abbot of Saint Trond: greeting in Christ Jesus. Although it has wisely been established in the sacred canons that individual offices should be entrusted to individual persons, nevertheless, after consideration of the qualities and circumstances of persons and places, several churches are often granted to one person by special favor. Therefore, since we have entrusted to you the abbey of Saint Heribert at Deutz, lest the monastery of Saint Trond suffer loss in temporal or spiritual matters through our commission, we grant you, by the authority of the legation with which we are entrusted, that, while you are abbot of Deutz, you shall remain abbot of Saint Trond; and that, by the authority of this present grant, you may rule both monasteries and their persons as their proper abbot, and may have full care for administering their temporal and spiritual affairs. Given at Siegburg, on 16 Kalends of March [14 February].

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1226, Blessed Francis began the Order of Friars Minor.

4. [Col. 0334B] In the year of the Lord 1227, by a solemn exchange, the chapter of Liège acquired for itself, in return for the court of Saint Lambert called Maidieres, situated in the diocese of Metz, the right which the church of Metz possessed in the diocese of Liège: namely, half of the town of Saint Trond with all lordship and jurisdiction, the other villages situated beyond the Meuse, people both noble, clerical, and lay, and whatever right it possessed in abbeys situated in the diocese of Liège. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “These details are partly taken from the very charter of the bishop of Metz, which, together with others of the bishops of Liège and Cologne, the chapter of Metz, and King Henry, is printed in Chapeaville II, 246. They were written in May [Col. 0334D] and June 1227.”] This exchange was confirmed by the archbishops of Trier [Note: [Col. 0334D] “Theoderic II.”] and Cologne, [Note: [Col. 0334D] “Henry I.”] Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0334D] “IX.”] and Henry, count of Holland and king of Germany, and by the bishops of Metz and Liège with their chapters.

Incident. In the same year Hugh, bishop of Liège, confirmed to the town of Saint Trond that all matters in the town should be conducted by the judgment [Col. 0334C] of fourteen aldermen, seven belonging to the bishop and seven to the abbot. [Note: [Col. 0334D] “By an ordinance issued 26 June 1227; Chapeaville, cited above.”] In this year, as is believed, the ancient fixed number of fourteen aldermen of Saint Trond was reduced to six. Therefore, so that thereafter the said number might continue in its full complement, the lord bishop of Liège, the abbot of this place, the aldermen, and the townsmen agreed as follows: each of these six aldermen then in office was to choose whichever townsman he wished for the office of alderman; and each of the said lords was to appoint one of the two remaining men. This was subject to the condition that henceforth, whenever an alderman’s office fell vacant, the surviving aldermen could choose a suitable alderman within forty days. [Note: [Col. 0333] *contingerit*, “should happen,” manuscript 1*.] If they failed to make the choice within the stated number of days, then the bishop or abbot to whom that alderman had belonged would appoint whichever suitable person he wished in his place. This practice is preserved to the present day. [Col. 0334D]

5. In the same year (1228), on 6 Nones of March [2 March], Walter, provost of this monastery, was appointed abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul at Maastricht, [Col. 0335A] which was nearly desolate and which he restored through his labors. On his anniversary we have one measure of rye for the brethren’s pittance.

Incident. In the same year Henry, duke [Col. 0336A] of Brabant, died, and his son Henry succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “This is erroneous: he died 5 September 1235. Compare Butkens, *Trophées des ducs de Brabant*, I, 198.”]

## DEEDS OF ABBOT LIBERT

[Col. 0335]

1. In the year of the Lord 1228, the seventeenth year of Frederick’s empire and the twenty-eighth of Hugh, bishop of Liège, after the death of Abbot John in the seventh year of his prelacy, on 10 Kalends of October [22 September], Libert succeeded him and, on 12 Kalends of February [21 January] 1229, was honorably consecrated in our church by Lord Hugh, bishop of Liège. In the same year certain chicks were seen in our town, some half-footed, others four-footed, and others three-footed.

In the year of the Lord 1230 Hugh, bishop of Liège, died on 6 Ides of April [8 April]. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “His commemoration is found on 3 Ides of April [11 April] in the Liège book; Chapeaville II, 251.”] He gave eighty pounds of white money to our church. John of Eppes, the second of that name, the chief provost, [Col. 0335B] succeeded him.

2. In the time of this abbot, Clement the steward, of whom an account has been given above, with the consent of the lord abbot and before the ministerials and aldermen, granted to the four sons of his brother Serisius the stewardship, or office of *scultetus*, which he had previously held in pledge, [Note: [Col. 0335] “*pro*, manuscript 1*.”] because Clement himself gave our church a certain tithe belonging to the office of *scultetus*. This was the small tithe from the whole town of Saint Trond.

3. This Lord Libert established the feast of Saint [Col. 0336A] Libert as a double feast, and acquired in perpetuity thirty Louvain shillings, which the abbot in office pays each year toward the brethren’s pittance.

4. In the year of the Lord 1231, the entire building of Saint Catherine’s monastery, situated in the suburb of the town of Saint Trond called “At Saint Catherine’s,” was transferred to a more suitable site irrigated by converging waters. The noble lady of Parwijs granted that site to the said monastery with all her temporal jurisdiction. During this transfer the holy body of Christina the Astonishing, [Col. 0336B] which had been buried seven years before [Note: [Col. 0335] “Omitted in manuscript 1*.”] at the site of the former monastery, was exhumed and transferred to the site of the new dwelling. In the same year, on the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene (22 July), Henry, duke of Brabant, besieged our town of Saint Trond.

5. In the year of the Lord 1232, on the day before the Nones of May [6 May], Abbot Libert resigned and withdrew from the abbacy at Huy in the presence of Lord John, bishop of Liège, after governing laudably and devoutly for four years, six months, and fifteen days.

## DEEDS OF JOHN, THE SECOND ABBOT OF THIS NAME

[Col. 0335]

1. In the year of the Lord 1232, in the … year of the empire, [Note: [Col. 0335] “A lacuna of approximately three letters in manuscript 1*.”] and the third year of the episcopate of John II, after Libert withdrew from the abbacy, John, abbot of Saint Lawrence at Liège, became abbot of this place on 8 Kalends of June [25 May], while retaining the governance of Saint Lawrence’s abbey. Within three years (1236) he borrowed from moneylenders at Troyes the sum of 2,005 Tournois pounds. In the fourth year, because payment of that loan was neglected, the abbot settled accounts with the Lombards; principal, interest, and expenses having been reckoned together, our abbey was bound to those moneylenders for 6,200 Tournois pounds, payable within four years. From this sum, in the meantime, the same abbot paid the same Lombard moneylenders 2,007 pounds in black Tournois currency. Thus after this abbot’s [Col. 0335D] death our monastery remained bound to those Lombards for 3,540 Tournois pounds, apart from interest.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1233, the church of Liège, [Col. 0336C] having written the numbering of the years of the Lord as beginning at Easter, now conformed itself to the churches of Rome and Cologne and began the years of the Lord from the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1238 (2 May), John II, bishop of Liège, died. [Note: [Col. 0336D] “On 6 Nones of May [2 May], according to Giles.”] William of Valence, elected and confirmed by Pope Gregory, succeeded him.

2. In the year of the Lord 1239, on the Kalends of February [1 February], John, abbot of this place, resigned the abbeys of this church and of Saint Lawrence at Liège, and took the Cistercian habit in the cloister of the Valley of Saint Lambert near Liège, where within a year he rested in peace. He had presided over this monastery for seven years and six months.

3. In the same year the prior and convent borrowed through Giles of Lavoir, [Col. 0336D] a citizen of Liège, eight hundred Paris pounds from the said Lombards; this amounted to 1,200 Tournois pounds.

## DEEDS OF ABBOT THOMAS

[Col. 0337]

1. In the year of the Lord 1239, the first year of William, bishop of Liège, after John II had withdrawn from this abbey, Thomas—before entering religion, parish priest of the church of Blessed Mary; born of middling townspeople; useful to the people; afterwards provost of this place; a prudent and diligent man—was made abbot. [Note: [Col. 0337] “Omitted in manuscript 1*.”] Through the negligence of his predecessor, he found the abbey bound to the Lombards at Troyes by a loan contracted at interest, as related above, in 3,540 Tournois pounds; likewise he found it encumbered, through the loan contracted by necessity by the prior and convent with the said Lombards, as stated already, in 1,200 Tournois pounds. Their total came to 4,740 [Col. 0337B] pounds in black Tournois currency.

In the second year of his prelacy (1240), Abbot Thomas paid the said Lombards 720 Paris pounds of debts incurred before his appointment; afterwards accounts were settled with the Lombards, and he paid 1,766 Paris pounds. Thus the entire amount which Abbots Thomas and his predecessor John paid at different times was 4,647 Paris pounds. This church consequently remained bound to the said Lombard moneylenders, on account of the loan mentioned above, for 2,747 Paris pounds.

2. Through his diligence this abbot acquired two parts of the office of *scultetus*. He placed in it a trustworthy man, who served as steward for eight months each year; for the other four months Walter of Stone House [Col. 0337C] served as steward by virtue of the third part of the stewardship belonging to him from his wife’s dowry.

3. In the year of the Lord 1240, through the diligent care of this abbot, the hospital which had stood in our cemetery was, with the consent of James, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, transferred to the place where it stands in Stapel Street, on the condition that the said hospital building situated in our precinct, together with whatever it is known to possess in Plankem Street in rents and revenues, should pass to our monastery in perpetuity; and, in compensation for this, we assigned to the aforesaid hospital six bonuaria of land from our cultivated estate at Schurovem and our mill at Stadem in perpetual right. We too shall be the hospital’s true patrons, as we have hitherto been. Around the same time the aforesaid abbot went to the Roman curia and obtained anew from Pope Innocent IV the use of pontifical vestments—which had been withdrawn by the pope because of Abbot Christian—so that he might use them solemnly. He also obtained from that pope several privileges for the benefit of our church. Incidental notice. In the same year (October), William, bishop of Liège, died in the transalpine regions and was buried at Florence; the see was vacant for two years. [Note: According to Aegidius, he died in October 1239; nor was the see vacant for two years, since already on 14 June 1240 Robert ordered the drawing up of the record concerning the dispute between the abbots of Saint-Trond and Gembloux: Chapeaville II, 266.] Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 1241, Robert I, bishop of Langres, became bishop of Liège by translation. Incidental notice. During this bishop’s time the Beguine movement began. Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 1245, upon the death of the landgrave of Thuringia, whom Pope Innocent IV had created king of Germany against Frederick, deprived of the Empire, [VINC. BELL. XXXI], the Empire was vacant for one year. In the following year, on 6 Kalends of November [27 October], Robert I, bishop of Liège, died. [Note: He died on XVI Kalends of November [17 October], according to the Necrology of Foullon, I, 340.] In the same year Henry, duke of Brabant, died, and his son Henry III succeeded him. Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 1247, William, count of Holland, nephew through the sister of Henry II, duke of Brabant, while Frederick II—though still alive—had been deposed from the Empire and was persecuting the Roman Church, was elected king of Germany through the efforts of Pope Innocent. In the same year Henry [Note: III.], cousin of William elected king of Germany and brother of Otto, count of Guelders, was placed over the church of Liège. [Note: On VI Kalends of October [26 September] 1247, according to Aegidius.] About the same time Pope Innocent IV instituted the feast of the sacrament of the Holy Eucharist to be celebrated by all churches of the faithful.

[Col. 0338C]

4. In the year of the Lord 1248, the first year of William, king of Germany, the blessed prioress and the whole convent of the monastery of Saint Catherine at Milen [Note: Melin, not far from Tongeren.] bound themselves by oath, under penalty of excommunication, into the hands of Abbot Thomas, that henceforth they should not increase the number of nuns and brothers and sisters beyond forty persons. Through the efforts of Abbot Thomas they obtained Pope Innocent IV’s confirmation of this agreement.

This abbot was an energetic and shrewd man. Since he had no kinsmen powerful enough to resist those wronging the monastery, he formed an alliance with John of Follonia, a powerful townsman; having bought five bonuaria of arable land and granted it to him in fief, he made him his vassal. He faithfully served him as a wall against adversaries.

In the same year Abbot Thomas died on 4 Kalends of November [29 October]. His body was buried before the altar of Saint Elizabeth, and bore this epitaph:

> Thomas the abbot performed deeds worthy to be read of, for by his teaching  
> he bound many who were sustained by his doctrine.  
> He had well proclaimed the divine word; and what the bitter  
> offender had done, he removed through confession.  
> The mitre restored to the Church’s adornment is present as the reward  
> of his labour, and by right he cannot die from remembrance,  
> for this carved epigram gives him living fame.  
> Readers of these lines, remember him.

## ON THE DEEDS OF WILLIAM, THE FIRST ABBOT OF THIS NAME

[Col. 0339]

[Col. 0339A]

1. In the year of the Lord 1248, the first year of William, king of the Romans, and the second year of Henry, bishop-elect of Liège, William, invested at Saint Mary’s in Aachen, was postulated as abbot of Saint-Trond, since he was a very devout and learned man. The king of Germany especially loved him and kept him as his secretary. An envoy was sent to the Roman curia for his confirmation, and it was obtained. Others say that on one day he put on the monastic habit, on the next he made profession, and on the third he became abbot, on 5 February.

Incidental notice. In the same year William, count of Holland and king-elect of Germany, besieged for six months the town of Aachen and the royal seat. By force of the waters flowing within the walls through high embankments raised for the purpose, he did not compel the citizens of Aachen to surrender; but at last he forced them, exhausted by hunger, to open the gates. Thus he was consecrated king of Germany by a legate of the Roman curia.

2. In the same year, when this abbot found this church pledged to the aforesaid Lombard merchants for 2,748 Paris pounds, the said Lombards demanded extremely heavy and intolerable interest, because for three years before his accession the instalments of the loan which should have been paid at various times had ceased. Therefore, although unwilling, the abbot was compelled by necessity to litigate with them for more than six years in the Roman court. At length, in the year of the Lord 1255, he made an accounting with them for 2,480 Paris pounds, to be paid in instalments within ten years. The abbot paid this entire sum within the appointed period. But because he sometimes did not pay an instalment at the stipulated time, he paid seventy-four Paris pounds in interest at different times.

Likewise, for negotiations which he had with these merchants at various places—Lyon, Laon, Cambrai, and elsewhere—and for witnesses and advocates, the abbot spent five Liège marks. The total of all the foregoing which Abbot William paid and expended for the debts of his predecessors within twenty-two years was 2,183 Liège marks. Likewise, the total of all that he spent by command of Pope Alexander [Note: IV.] for the twentieth, for cardinals, and for legates, within the sixty-first and seventy-first year, was 2,860 Liège marks; likewise, for damage from various wars and storms, 2,000 Liège marks.

Thus the sum of money which this church paid in various places on account of the usurious loan from the Lombards, over and above the principal, came to 4,000 Paris pounds, said then to have been worth 6,000 black Tours pounds. And thus everything was fully paid in the following year, 1265.

[Col. 0340A]

3. In the year of the Lord 1250, William, king of the Romans and count of Holland, out of the special favour which he bore toward Abbot William, granted to that abbot and his successors in perpetuity, to possess freely by feudal right, the advocacy which he possessed in full right by reason of the county of Holland over the goods of our church and the people dwelling in the villages adjoining our estates at Alburgh. Accordingly, the goods of our church there were worth twenty-five marks more annually than they had previously been.

The same abbot acquired, redeemed, and freed from encumbrance various goods of the church unjustly usurped by many persons, both in the dioceses of Utrecht and Liège. Likewise, this abbot—or perhaps one of his predecessors—acquired for the monastery by purchase one third of the profits which a certain townsman possessed hereditarily from the mill situated in the court of our monastery. Likewise, he redeemed our mill at Gorsembruel from the hereditary right which Christian, our advocate, held in it with his wife. Likewise, he recovered the office of villication in our village of Borlo.

Likewise, from the prebends of the servants and officers of this church, whose number was twenty-nine, he redeemed in his time as many as sixteen prebends: namely, the brewing-office, or chamberlainship—for these are the same—the *lotaria*, [Note: *Lota*, French *lot*, is a kind of fish; is this then a duty of supplying fish?] the gardenership, [Note: Care of the garden.] the cellarership, chamberlainship, kitchen-office, marshalship, and the rest.

Likewise, he redeemed from Walter of Domo lapidea one third of the office of scultetus in our town; his predecessor Thomas had earlier redeemed two thirds, and thus the office itself freely returned to the monastery.

Likewise, he enlarged our estate at Borlo—which before his time amounted to sixty bonuaria and thirteen virgae of arable land—by eighteen bonuaria, five large virgae, and fourteen small ones. The total arable land at Borlo in his time therefore amounted to one hundred bonuaria, twelve large virgae, and eight small virgae.

Likewise, whereas several persons held separate shares in our tithe at Borlo, he bought from them four shares for money: from the abbot of Heylesem [Note: Heylissen, near Tienen.] an eighth share; from the abbess of Boneef [Note: Bonesse, near Jodoigne.] another eighth; from the Teutonic brothers a twelfth; and likewise from Herman of Brustino a twelfth. These four shares yield fifty modii of rye, of which he assigned twenty-six modii of rye to the refectory’s pittance for Fridays.

[Col. 0341A]

4. During the time of this Abbot William, the number of monks, counting one lay brother, was thirty-five besides the abbot. Later, however, Lord Abbot William and the convent bound themselves by oath, as is contained in the following copy:

> To all who shall see the present letters, William, by the grace of God abbot, G., prior, and the whole convent of the monastery of Saint Trond, greetings and prayers in the Lord.
>
> We make known to all that, having weighed and diligently considered all our goods, revenues, and resources, as well as the pensions and various alienations [Note: “distractors,” 1*.] of our goods, and also the multitude of debts by which our church is at present, and has for many years been, heavily oppressed; having also considered the diversity and multitude of expenses which we must unavoidably bear in respect of ourselves and our officers, guests and poor persons, and various other matters which frequently arise unexpectedly and without provision, according to the demands of our profession and the changing circumstances of the times: by common consent we have judged it necessary to establish—and renew what had long since been established among us—that henceforth we shall receive no one as a monk, nor give anyone a monastic prebend, until the number of our monks has been reduced to thirty and our church has been freed from the burden of debts.
>
> But if anyone should raise a dispute against us on this matter, we shall stand for our right and defend ourselves, insofar as we can do so according to God and justice. We, Abbot William, and we, the convent, with the special will and permission of our said abbot, for the utility and necessity of our church—indeed, in order to avert its utter destruction—have promised and, having touched the Gospels, sworn to observe this firmly and inviolably. In testimony of this matter, we have caused the present letters to be confirmed with our seals. Given in the year of the Lord 1250.

This Prior Guntram was consecrated. On one occasion, when he reproved Abbot William for negligences, though not serious ones, he had the discipline of rods administered to him in chapter. This prior had a sister who was a nun at Herkenrode; she wrote for him a breviary which is still with us.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 1251 a great discord arose at Liège: first between clergy and laity, then between the great men and the common people, and finally between the people on one side and the clergy, canons, and leading men of the city on the other, to such an extent that the clergy departed from the city of Liège. But in the following year, when peace was restored, the people went barefoot and with lighted candles to meet the returning clergy. [Note: These events occurred in 1252 and 1253, as Hocsemius proves in Chapeaville II, 280; the author had him before his eyes at this point.]

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1253, Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See, conducted a visitation among us through commissioners. He also left in writing statutes imposing upon us several observances. A further visitation was afterwards made by his commissioners on the third day after Saint Lucy’s Day (15 December), as is found compiled at the end of the old martyrology.

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1252, Sir Reyner of Rolinghem gave his tithe of Berlinghem [Note: Berlingen, near Looz.] in perpetuity as alms to be distributed among the poor before the gate; it yielded five modii of rye and five modii of barley. From these he established that modii of rye and barley should be taken for our convent.

5. In the year of the Lord 1254, seeing that the workshops—namely the bakehouse, brewery, and other necessary buildings—situated in the court of our monastery toward the marsh were cramped, and being displeased by the noise and commotion of neighbouring townsmen dwelling there, who by means of fourteen dwellings—which they possessed hereditarily, extending from the place of the rear gate of the monastery court, facing east, to our mill, and likewise spread out from the mill to the cloister gate—caused many inconveniences and disturbances to us and our household, the abbot gathered a sum of money and bought the aforesaid dwellings in their entirety, together with the land, from the heirs. He immediately demolished all these dwellings, enlarged the court, and enclosed it with a wall.

6. In the same year the people of Liège established a commune, and a grave discord arose between Henry, bishop-elect, on one side, and the people of Liège and the country villages on the other. The elect, having summoned the Liège aldermen at Vothem [Note: Votem, near Liège.] and sitting in judgment, outlawed several men of Liège. For this reason the Liège people, being by no means lovers of peace, would hear nothing unless the aldermen’s judgment against the outlaws were revoked. At length, however, by the arbitration of four worthy men, and after the dissolution of the confederation which the Liège people had earlier formed with the country villages and the people of Saint-Trond, it was settled that the Liège aldermen might, when necessary, sit in judicial session at Vothem to proceed against transgressors.

Incidental notice. Soon afterwards the concord was dissolved. For the elect against the country and the country against the elect raged horribly against one another in repeated acts of arson, violence, and slaughter. During this conflict the castle of Waremme was burned by the men of Huy.

[Col. 0342D]

7. In the year of the Lord 1254, a wealthy foreigner came to live in our town. Having acquired a dwelling of notable hospitality, situated to the right of the church of Blessed Mary in the middle of that street, he married a kinswoman of Gottschalk of Repe, knight and alderman of our town of Saint-Trond.

After several years, a merchant from Huy, who was accustomed to lodge there, brought back money from the fair. The master of the lodging ordered him to enter first into the chamber assigned to him for rest. As he obeyed and advanced a little way, a balanced revolving trapdoor, maliciously prepared level with the floor, tilted downward under his weight and cast him into a prison.

Meanwhile, a maidservant, who had formerly been impregnated by the said merchant, happened to enter the horses’ stable. Looking at her lover’s horse, foaming and filthy [Note: That is, *bromosus*: foul-smelling, unclean.], standing at the manger, and not finding him although she sought him everywhere, she wailed and stirred up the entire neighbourhood, tearfully declaring that her impregnator had been suffocated.

At her cries the people ran together. The master of the lodging, conscious of this crime, secretly chose flight, never to return. Therefore the scultetus and aldermen, having taken counsel, went to the said lodging; but after making a search, they found no trace whatsoever of such a crime. Secretly encouraging the maid, they promised that she might depart freely if she identified for them the suspected places connected with the crime.

Then she said: “Let them search what may be concealed beneath the trapdoor of the storeroom [Note: Of the cellar.] situated at the entrance of that chamber.” They immediately went there; looking into the depth, they saw the merchant lying half alive. When some persons went down to draw him out, a certain pit opened inward, filled with bones and human bodies.

Therefore, after summonses extending over a fortnight [Note: A period of fifteen days.] had been made by the ban-bell, the master of the lodging, failing to appear, was outlawed. Since, according to the law of this town, the temporal goods of those committing robbery are confiscated, a question arose among the governors of this place—namely the aldermen and councillors—whether the wife of that robber, who knew nothing of her husband’s crime, ought to be deprived of her property. After admonition had been made by the scultetus, the aforesaid Gottschalk judicially pronounced, with the concurrence of the other aldermen, that the innocent wife’s property ought to be restored to her.

Because of this judgment of the aldermen, a very great tumult arose among the townsmen, so much so that Jordan of Pule, captain of the merchants, and his councillors rebelled against their lords, the bishop and the abbot, and violently despised and violated their jurisdictions.

Incidental notice. In the same year William, king of the Romans, subdued the Frisians. In the following year, on the Conversion of Saint Paul [Note: Rather, 28 January 1225, in the eighth year of his reign; cf. Boehmer, *Regesta Imperii*, 2nd ed., p. 36.], attacking the same people with a multitude of his followers upon the ice, he was killed when the Frisians prevailed, in the ninth year of his reign.

8. In the year of the Lord 1255, in the ninth year of the rule of King William, long since killed [Note: “killed,” 1*.], on the day before the Kalends of May [30 April], Jordan of Pule, captain of the merchants, with his accomplices and the commune, broke the lock of our watercourse above Willo’s meadow, otherwise called Wilbanid. Having released the water, he caused our fish to be taken by all who wished to fish, without fearing that in the preceding year seven persons had been publicly and expressly admonished under penalty of excommunication by Henry, bishop-elect of Liège, to make satisfaction to the monastery for such an offence.

In the following year, in July, the same Jordan, through the violence of the commune, caused our boat in the water of Willo’s meadow to be broken and smashed to pieces.

Incidental notice. In the same year Henry III, duke of Brabant, marching with a great army to invade the territory of Liège, pitched tents near the village of Straten, situated within the liberty of our town, and at the request of Henry, bishop-elect of Liège, besieged our town. But when the people of Saint-Trond surrendered to the elect under certain terms, [Note: Cf. Hocsemius I, 5.] he withdrew from the siege.
