Incidental notice. In the same year Henry the elect, not forgetting the earlier rebellion of the townsmen, attacked them with arms; but the townsmen referred the matter to the duke, and through the duke they were reconciled with the elect (cf. HOCSEM. I, 5).

9. In the year of the Lord 1256, Jordan of Puel and his associates, with the consent of the townsmen, according to the account of the old men, summoned the aforesaid Henry, duke of Brabant, to our town. They caused him to sit upon a great seat in the middle of the market-place and handed him the keys of the town gates. Grasping the keys in his hand [Note: “hand,” 1*.], he is said to have told his son, who accompanied him: “Behold, now I am lord of this town!” To which the son replied: “Indeed, dearest father—if only the grant had proceeded through the bishop and abbot, its true lords.”

On the same matter. In the same year, when the townsmen of Saint-Trond had procured the striking of coinage—which a certain townswoman had from ancient times held in fief from the bishop—to be transferred, to the detriment of their lord Henry, bishop-elect, to Henry, duke of Brabant, and had also bound themselves to render certain services of crossbowmen to that duke, the elect obtained from Pope Alexander IV a mandate compelling them to desist from their evil attempt. The execution of this mandate was entrusted to Abbot William. When, after being admonished in due legal form, they did not repent, they were at length excommunicated.

For this reason Jordan of Puel, with his accomplices Lambert of the Gate, Walter Rufi, John son of Tharisius, and other deans of the guilds, stirred up the armed commune. Taking with them the bailiff of Lewis and Dormale [Note: Dormael.], they marched out with unfurled banners and removed the ironwork of millstones from our mills at Gorsembruel and Merwile. Returning from there, with a multitude of foot-soldiers and twenty horsemen, they violently entered the monastery. Having broken down the doors and walls before the altar of Blessed Trudo, they rushed in and reached the step of the upper choir; terrified, Lord Abbot William and the brother-monks fled here and there into hiding.

These sacrilegious men were driven to such frenzy that some of them struck the shrine of Saint Trudo violently with their spears. It is said that among them were many of the great men and better townsmen, and many of the mansionarii. Advancing as far as the chapel of Saint Lambert, they beat upon the door with axes and clubs, endeavouring to break in and molest the lord abbot.

After this Jordan himself, a great part of his company [Note: “company,” 1*.], and the deans of the officers came to the cloister gate and struck at the barred doors [Note: “observed,” 1*.] with blows, but did not break them down.

Several days later, when these same sacrilegious persons were asked why they had presumed to inflict such abominations upon the monastery of Saint Trudo, they answered that these things had been done by command of the duke of Brabant, to whom they had shortly before handed the keys of the town gates as to their lord. The chief cause of their presumptuous violence, however, was that the lord abbot, executing the apostolic mandate, was pursuing the sentence of excommunication against them.

Therefore the lord abbot, still fearing their assault, fled to our estate at Donk on the day after the feast of Saint John the Baptist; several of the senior brethren, or—as was said—almost the whole convent, followed him there, until the townsmen’s savagery abated.

Likewise, on Friday, namely the sixth day after the feast of Saint John, the same persons who had earlier come with unfurled banners, horsemen, and a multitude of armed men, rushed upon the clergy, shouting from above the market-place. Pursuing them, they drove them into the church of Blessed Mary. They followed those who had committed themselves to the tower’s fortification, broke down two strong doors of the tower, and seized there Lord Clement, parish priest of Saint Mary, together with other priests or clerics, because they had wished to obey apostolic mandates. After bringing them down, they finally took counsel among themselves and allowed them to depart free.

One priest, named Adam, did not flee to the tower, but protected himself behind the high altar of the church of Blessed Mary in the chamber of confession. When they wished to rush upon him, he rose and took in his hands the pyx containing the most sacred body of Christ. Thus, although the church was full of armed men, they ceased to attack him.

On that same day Jordan and his men, with the whole tumult of the townsmen, came to the market-place and led away captive the aldermen of the town: Walter son of Ermegard, Walter of Domo lapidea, Robert Probus, Jordan Scofeel, Arkint, and Nicholas the knight, with many other townsmen who refused to consent to their wicked assaults. They put them in iron fetters like contemptible offenders, setting over them guards of the duke of Brabant at heavy expense.

[Col. 0346A]

10. In the same year Henry, bishop-elect of Liège, having feigned peace with the people of Saint-Trond, entered the town with a multitude of armed men following behind him [cf. HOCS. 5]. Therefore, when the aldermen had assembled in court, Jordan of Puel, otherwise called of the Lake, and his accomplices were judicially outlawed from their country, honour, and possessions as persons guilty of high treason.

Likewise. Afterwards, by order of the elect, the entrance of the Staplen Gate, by which one proceeds toward Brabant, was blocked with a strong earthwork. Angered at this, the duke gathered a force of knights against the elect’s multitude of armed men. But peace intervened, and the elect and duke were reconciled on this agreement: the judgment of forfeiture should remain in force; yet, by favour, if Jordan and his councillors chose to return to the town, they might reside there peacefully as outlaws.

Furthermore, it was stipulated that the elect might freely fortify the tower or castle, previously restored by him within the walls of our town and surrounded by ditches, facing toward Trajectum—which had been hindered by the aforesaid Jordan and his associates—in order to prevent the townsmen from daring henceforth to rebel. According to the report of the old men, a bridge built across the ditches above gave the bishop’s household free entrance to this castle.

11. In the year of the Lord 1257, a disagreement arose through Prior Guntram and the entire convent against Lord Abbot William, because they sought an increase in their monastic prebend of food and clothing. In the end both sides submitted the matter to Lord G., archdeacon of Liège, as arbitrator. Having carefully considered the causes of the complaints, he pronounced his award as follows.

First: in addition to the five Leuven denarii given every day to each brother for the kitchen, four vessels of rye from the monastery’s revenues should be assigned each Friday for purchasing a fish dish. Likewise, because on feast-days each brother received one sixth—that is, a sixth part of a sextary—for one day’s wine, the said arbitrator declared that a quarter of the measure of this town—that is, a fourth part of a sextary—should henceforth be given daily to each one. Likewise, concerning clothing: whereas scarcely a mark and a half had been given to each, he declared that henceforth three Liège marks, amounting to ten old grossi, should be issued.

Incidental notice. In the same year, after William, king of Germany, had been killed among the Frisians, the electors disagreed. Richard, count of Cornwall, obtained his election through money and was consecrated king of Germany at Aachen by Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, against the king of Castile [cf. HOCSEM. 5].

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1258, Abbot William gathered into one place the Beguines who served God under different parishes of our town, partly at Ghovelinghen, Rokendale, and the Holy Sepulchre, and partly at Saint Gengulf’s. In the suburb of Schurovem, on the allod and within the district of our monastery, he built a church in honour of Saint Agnes. To it he conveyed relics from the bodies of 132 saints. After houses had been built around it, he caused a strong wall to be placed around it for defence. For its perpetual commemoration, the mistress of the Beguines offers at the altar, on the day of Saint Trudo’s deposition, one gold denarius worth three old grossi. These Beguines are also bound to grind their grain at our mill at Mervile, as is more fully contained in the letters drawn up concerning this matter.

Likewise. In the same year, a discord between our monastery and the convent of Friars Minor living in our town was settled by arbitral composition as follows: the said convent shall pay us in perpetuity, for the place where they live and their church is situated, one gold denarius worth twelve Leuven denarii on the day of Saint Trudo’s deposition; and they shall have free burial, saving the right of the parish church.

Incidental notice. In the year of the Lord 1260, Abbot William brought from Cologne many relics, both of the holy eleven thousand virgins and of the Theban saints and Saint Gereon.

12. In the year of the Lord 1263, the estates of this monastery situated on the Moselle in the diocese of Trier, which Adalbero II, bishop of Metz and abbot of this place, had formerly bestowed upon us, were sold. The religious abbot and convent of Hemmenrode acquired them by purchase for 1,150 marks of good and lawful sterling, reckoning twelve sterling shillings for each mark. To this amount were added sixty cartloads of Moselle wine, to be delivered to the monastery within the three following years.

This sum of money was applied to the benefit of the monastery, both for paying the heavy debts at interest contracted by its predecessors and for redeeming and purchasing hereditary estates advantageously situated for the monastery itself.

Likewise. During this abbot’s time Count Arnold of Looz [Note: The eighth son of John, count of Looz. Arnold had sold part of the advocacy to Abbot William in 1282, as the records in Mantelius, p. 217, prove.] had no right in our village of Borlo, nor any revenues, according to the account of trustworthy old men, [Note: “juridical,” 1*.] except only at Sandicis mill there, which paid him one and a half old *mites*. [Note: A Flemish copper coin.] Likewise, in the other villages of this monastery—Engelmanshoven, Ham, Halen, Linkout [Note: Linchout, near Diest.] and the rest—he had no right except the advocacy granted to his predecessors for defending the monastery’s rights. But this count, forgetful of his own salvation, violently usurped our jurisdiction.

The duke of Brabant inflicted the same violence upon us in our villages situated under his lordship. Over this grave violence the devout Abbot William wept and groaned deeply; when his close friends reproved him for excessive impatience, he said that this alone remained to console him: that he had suffered such violence against his will.

Likewise. In the same year, on 6 Ides of July [10 July], [Note: So the text reads; it should not be read with the manuscript as VIII Ides of July, for Sunday fell on 8 July 1263.] on Sunday between None and Vespers, the middle and greater tower of our monastery fell, though the air was entirely calm. They said that the cause of this collapse was that the arch of the vault beneath it, under which stood the chapel of Saint Nicholas—where every day one of the brothers of our convent celebrates Mass—had first come apart.

Although at that very moment many honourable men had assembled before the altar of Saint Leonard to deliberate upon weighty matters, all escaped unharmed. But the two smaller bells of very fine harmony, together with the sixth-hour bell, fell and were shattered. The two larger bells, Aurelia and Catherine, though they fell, remained intact. Quintina, however, fell upon two beams without damage. They took it down together with the None bell and the ban-bell; our officers suspended the two other bells which had not fallen more securely, so that we might use them.

After the collapse of this tower, the fifteen lessons which used to be read below the bells before Matins began to be said in the choir.

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1269, our mill at Meetseren was transferred to our sisters’ monastery at Milen, by way of exchange for other hereditary estates.

13. In the time of this Lord William, whereas from ancient times, for the prebends of Saint Mary—which are bestowed on devout poor beguines and on a few men—one Liège denier was distributed each week to each recipient for two white loaves, this same abbot established and gave two Leuven deniers in place of that one Liège denier. The number of these prebends is twenty, and each has two white loaves, of the same wheat substance and weight as the loaves of the lords’ prebend, which are served to the aforesaid poor persons every Saturday. Moreover, for the aforesaid prebends there is given each week one half [Col. 0348D] of a quarter of one vessel of fine, sifted flour, which is divided equally among those holding the said prebends; besides this, the other half-quarter of flour is distributed every Saturday to the poor before the monastery gate. Likewise, in addition to these twenty prebends, the same Abbot William in his time established a similar prebend in honour of Saints Trudo, Eucherius, Quintinus, Remigius, and Libertus, [Col. 0349A] which is also called the prebend of Saint Trudo.

Concerning the same matter. In the same year, or thereabouts, James surnamed the Younger, provost of this place, a prudent and trustworthy man, having on various occasions been appointed executor of wills by several honourable and wealthy persons, acquired, for the remedy of their souls, certain hereditary revenues, purchased from the goods of the testators, sufficient in perpetuity for eighteen lesser prebends. From these each poor prebend-holder receives one loaf, commonly called *huesghenoetbroet*, of which fourteen somewhat whitish loaves are made from one vessel. For these prebends neither money nor flour is given. Likewise, it is believed that the same James, from the goods of testators, established or augmented [Col. 0349B] the prebends distributed to the poor within the cloister enclosure on Maundy Thursday: each receives one loaf, commonly called *huesgenotbroet*, as described above, and two herrings with one black Tours denier. The number of these prebends is 250. In revenues for alms of this kind, the same James formally caused this Abbot William, or another in the name of this monastery, to be enfeoffed with hereditary possession.

Concerning the same matter. There are also eleven loaves, made not from sifted flour but from flour as it is brought in bulk, which are made from half a vessel and given above the beguines’ court. From the Kalends of December, four vessels of peas were cooked each week for the poor persons’ *pottage*.

> [Note: [Col. 0349] Every kind of pulse or legume; in French, *herbes potagères* (“potherbs”).]

For seasoning this, three Leuven shillings were given. There was a large cauldron fixed over a furnace in the porter’s house, [Col. 0349C] like a brewer’s cauldron; from it the cooked pottage was ladled into vessels, carried to the gate, and distributed among the poor.

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1271, on the morrow of Epiphany, the aforesaid Lord James, provost, died. He left to the monastery 660 Leuven pounds and more. This money was applied to the final payment of all the debts of this church, so that in this year this abbey—which for the preceding forty years had been burdened with heavy debts—now owed nothing to anyone in any respect.

> [Note: Thereafter half a column was left blank; nevertheless, nothing appears to be missing.]

Likewise. In the time of this abbot, who is believed to have been abbot in the year of the Lord 1252, Christian, advocate of Saint Trudo, and Ida his wife granted to our monastery the upper mill and half the lower mill of Gorsembruel, so that from them there should be given [Col. 0349D] on the anniversary day of each of them, for the brothers’ *pitance*, one modius, and likewise one modius for alms to the poor in perpetuity. Likewise, the abbot and convent promised that for their souls Mass should be celebrated daily by one of our brothers at the altar of Saint Nicholas, situated beneath our great tower. Likewise, the same abbot and convent promised to give in perpetuity eight modii of rye to the brothers and lords reclining in the infirmary, and as many to the poor at [Col. 0350A] the gate, if anything should remain over from the services and rents with which the said mills had formerly been charged to our church of Saint Trudo.

Concerning the same matter. Regarding the daily Mass to be celebrated at the altar of Saint Nicholas, already mentioned, it should be known that after [Note: *hunc* in 1*.] the aforesaid tower collapsed in the year of the Lord 1263, as is apparent above, Mass could not be celebrated there. Therefore someone might perhaps doubt whether the daily Mass which ought to have been said at the aforesaid altar was wholly omitted. But it must plainly be believed that this abbot and his convent, men of great devotion and reverence, transferred that daily Mass to the altar of the most blessed Saint Trudo and upon it, where on each day the morning Mass is celebrated; on certain saints’ days, [Col. 0350B] however, this Mass is then celebrated at their altars.

14. In the time of this Lord William there were several monks of this house who were illegitimate sons of noble men. One of them was called Louis, son or grandson of Arnold, count of Looz, and he long survived the death of this Lord Abbot William. There was also one named Godfrey, son of Henry, bishop of Liège. The convent bore such admissions or intrusions with difficulty; and with the consent of Lord Abbot William, or of one of his successors, it was unanimously decreed that henceforth no one should be admitted as a monk of this place unless the person to be admitted, both parents, and the parents of both parents were born of a lawful marriage-bed.

At one time [Col. 0350C] a marvellous event occurred in the cemetery of this monastery of Saint Trudo, as I heard reported, which men supposed to have happened during the prelacy of this Abbot William.

> [Note: *accedisse* in 1*.]

There was a very rich man, accumulating wealth by every trifling means. As he belonged to the brotherhood of the guild of Saint Eucherius, after his death he was buried beside the brothers of that guild within the precinct of our cemetery. When his funeral rites had been performed according to custom and evening had come, certain young fellow-monks of this place, perhaps heated with drink, having dined in the infirmary, began to make merry and say: “If any one of us has courage enough to go to the grave of this dead rich man and bring back, before our eyes, some of the grave-earth, he shall pay nothing for the drink at this supper.”

Then one of them, handsome in body and mind, immediately [Col. 0350D] rose, went to the burial-place, and, as he stretched out his hand to take a little earth, someone came and gripped him fiercely by the arms. Feeling this, the young man resisted vigorously. After they had struggled for a long time, his assailant disappeared. The youth then bent down again, took earth in his hand, and carried it to his companions. Seeing that he had been delayed so long, and observing that he was without his habit, they asked where he had left his cowl. He then [Col. 0351A] related what had happened to him and added: “I shall return and bring back the cowl which he pulled from me.” As soon as he had come again to that place, he found the cowl upon the grave, but did not find the assailant. Having returned to his companions, he was so afflicted in mind that within a few days he was committed to burial.

MIRACLE. In the time of this abbot, a devout monk of this place departed this world. In that very night he appeared to the abbot and lamented that he had been assigned to the pains of purgatory. Sympathizing with him, the abbot asked by what means he could be more effectively delivered. “In the suburb called New Houses,” he said, “a poor little married woman dwells beneath a small house in that street; her penance will be of especial help to me.” And so that soul vanished.

Accordingly, when morning came, [Col. 0351B] a messenger was quickly sent. The woman was found in such a small house and called by the same name, exactly as the soul had foretold. When she was seated in the abbot’s presence and questioned concerning her condition and manner of life, she replied: “Dearest lord, I am a sinful married woman, conscious of no merit. I have a violent husband, given to frequent drunkenness. When, late in the evening, he comes from the [Col. 0352A] tavern into our little house, he finds me spinning; and when he sees me afraid, he continually afflicts me with curses and severe blows, and not without my deserts.”

> [Note: *absque* in 1*.]

Then the abbot said: “What do you do, daughter, after such grievous sufferings?” She answered: “I prostrate myself in prayer; then I recall Christ’s Passion, and at once I feel such sweet consolation in my mind that I count the burden of all miseries as nothing.” “O dearest woman,” said the abbot, “I ask you to make our brother, lately deceased, a participant in your penance and prayers.” She generously replied: “May it avail him wholly, if I have merited to offer Christ anything pleasing.” Thus he withdrew to his own place.

On the following night, as the abbot rested in his bed, that soul appeared to him in great brightness and gave him thanks; freed from its punishments [Col. 0352B] and ascending to eternal joys, it immediately vanished, resounding in a sweet voice.

> [Note: Some words appear to have dropped out: “rejoiced,” or something of the sort.]

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1272, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, Lord William of Rikle, after governing this monastery vigorously for twenty-three years, fell asleep in the Lord. His body was buried before the chapel of blessed Trudo, in the place of the old sanctuary.

# DEEDS OF HENRY OF WAELBEKE, ABBOT

[Col. 0351]

[Col. 0351C] 1. In the year of the Lord 1272, while the schism over the empire of the German kingdom continued between Richard, count of Cornwall, and the king of Castile, and while Henry, brother of the count of Guelders, presided at Liège, Lord Henry of Waelbeke was elected abbot, a man of high birth but simple.

Incident. In the same year, a man of Piacenza, of the family of the Visconti, archdeacon of Liège—whom Henry, son of the count of Guelders, his fellow canon, had formerly dishonoured by striking him on the cheek with his palm—was elected pope and called Gregory X. Having now been consecrated pope, he wrote a fatherly letter of exhortation to the aforesaid Henry, who had presided over the church of Liège some years earlier, urging him, by avoidance of vices and pursuit of virtues, to labour earnestly.

Incident. In the following year Rudolph I, count [Col. 0351D] of Habsburg, was elected king of the Romans by consent of the imperial electors [VINC. BELL. XXXI], and was crowned at Aachen. He vigorously restored to its former state the German kingdom, which had been completely neglected.

Incident. In the same year John, duke of Brabant, advanced with a multitude of armed men as far as the town of Lewis, intending to invade the bishopric of Liège, and pitched his tents above the ford commonly called Tvenne.

2. [HOCSEM. 8.] In the year of the Lord 1274, Gregory, in the third year of his pontificate, set out from the city of Rome and came to Lyons, where he convened a council for the passage to the Holy Land. Henry of Guelders, bishop of Liège, personally summoned, appeared there among the other bishops. When the people of Liège and the leading men of the other towns learned this, they sent envoys there [Col. 0352C] and accused the bishop of his excesses. At last summoned into the presence of Pope Gregory, and with the foremost theologians present there, Thomas Aquinas of the Order of Preachers and Bonaventure of the Order of Friars Minor, the bishop stood alone, his company of nobles excluded. A book was set before him for examination; when he was found illiterate, he was removed from the bishopric and ordered to depart after surrendering his ring. These things occurred in the twenty-seventh year of the episcopate of the deposed Henry.

> [Note: *destitui* in 1*.]

He returned shamefully to his own country and occupied episcopal castles throughout the bishopric. In the same year [HOCSEM. 10] John of Anghien, bishop of Tournai, was transferred to the bishopric of Liège at the same Council of Lyons by the aforesaid Gregory; the abbey [Col. 0352D] of the monastery of Stavelot, taken from the aforesaid Henry, was also conferred upon him.

Incident. In the following year, on the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene, a solemn procession was held. The entire people and many from the surrounding villages were gathered, and the shrine of Saints Trudo and Eucherius was carried with the greatest devotion and reverence.

Incident. In the same year, when a procession was being held at Maastricht with the shrine of Saint Servatius, and the multitude of people had reached the middle of the bridge, the bridge collapsed and 300 people were drowned in the river Meuse.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1276, Guy, count of Flanders, and John, duke of Brabant, with their followers burned several villages in the bishopric of Liège. In the same year the people of Huy and those of Dinant entered the territory of the count of Namur and burned many villages [cf. HOCS. 10].

[Col. 0353A] 3. In the year of the Lord 1277, the sixth of the prelacy of this Abbot Henry, when his brothers and kinsmen wished to dispose of the goods of this monastery as they pleased, and he, being faint-hearted, could not restrain them, [Col. 0354A] and was therefore daily and insistently harassed by the convent, he resigned the abbey into the hands of his ordinary, John, bishop of Liège.

# DEEDS OF WILLIAM THE SECOND, ABBOT

[Col. 0353]

[Col. 0353A] 1. After the aforesaid resignation, counsel having been taken, the whole convent unanimously transferred the votes of its election to the bishop himself, trusting in his fidelity to provide a suitable shepherd. At that time there was a monk at the monastery of Affligem, a man of great learning and venerable life, named William. The same bishop had known and loved him greatly while he was studying at Paris. He drew his origin illegitimately from the lineage of the lords of Mechelen. Desiring to promote him as suitable, the bishop immediately sent envoys to the Roman curia [Col. 0353B] for a dispensation and obtained it.

Accordingly, in the same year the bishop informed the convent through honourable men that he had provided them with a praiseworthy man to set over them, appointing a fixed day on which they should solemnly receive him as abbot, according to custom. Meanwhile, when the convent understood that he was born of an illegitimate marriage-bed, they resisted by every means. Wishing to restrain them, the bishop declared him legitimate, since the head of the Church, the supreme pontiff, had decreed that he should be preferred. On the appointed day, therefore, the bishop brought the abbot-elect to our town with an honourable retinue and urgently required the convent to go out in procession to meet him. But the convent, declaring that such a man ought not deservedly to be placed over such a monastery, still resisted.

[Col. 0353C] Seeing this, the bishop took a striking staff in his hand and compelled them all to put on white garments. Thus, a procession having been arranged, he was brought festively into the monastery and consecrated.

Concerning the same matter. This abbot was a man of exceptional devotion, zealous for religious observance, humble and prudent; acceptable to ecclesiastical and secular persons; moderately cheerful among his brethren and household; most diligent in Holy Scripture; learned in the sacred canons; and a good writer of verse.

Concerning the same matter. In the time of this abbot, the temporal lordship of the monastery suffered loss in no respect.

> [Note: *detrimento* in 1*.]

He kept with him an honourable master of the household or court, who at appropriate times walked in the market-place of the town. Whenever honourable men arriving from elsewhere lodged in the townsmen’s houses, [Col. 0353D] he went to them and brought them, once invited, to the table and presence of his lord the abbot. Graciously received by him, they often repaid greater expenses.

Incident. In the same year William, count of Jülich, seeking with a multitude of his men to bring the city of Aachen under his dominion, attacked it in war. But the people of Aachen resisted bravely, and the count, together with his sons William and Roland [Col. 0354A] and many noble and strong men, 350 in number, was killed.

Incident. In the following year (1277), after the death of Pope John, Nicholas III succeeded. He granted the brethren of the Cistercian Order a privilege that, during a general interdict, they might everywhere attend divine offices, except only in churches of the Friars Minor.

> [Note: *tercii* in 1*.]

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1281 Henry of Guelders, lately removed from the bishopric, urgently demanded from Bishop John a great sum of money which, as he asserted, he had spent for the benefit of the bishopric of Liège [cf. HOCSEM. 10]. At length it was agreed that they should meet on an appointed day at the village of Hoegaarden to negotiate.

> [Note: Hougarde on the Gete, near Jodoigne.]

When the bishop came there unarmed according to agreement, he was unexpectedly seized by the followers of the deposed Henry and forcibly carried away. Since he was corpulent and could not endure the impetuous course of the horse upon which he had been placed, his vital breath being cut off, he fell from the horse nearly suffocated in the hands of his captors. They left him in the fields near the cloister of Heylissem.

> [Note: Heylissem, near Tienen, a Premonstratensian monastery.]

The malefactors fled in confusion. At that very hour a little woman happened to come by; when she had placed the venerable bishop’s head, as he lay there, in her lap, he breathed his last after a few faint sighs.

Likewise. On the same day the townsmen of Saint [Col. 0354C] Trudo, intending to ransom their lord when they learned of the crime, pursued those guilty of it beyond the river Temera. The men of the count of Looz gathered against them, destroyed the bridges in every direction, and captured, stripped, and in some cases killed certain people of Saint Trudo whom they had separated from the men of Looz, whom they considered their friends. When this became known to the count, the captives were immediately set free.

Incident. In the same year very grievous wars were waged among Christian kingdoms. The Sicilian people, unable to endure French violence, killed in contempt of Charles, king of France, the French residing in their lands, of whatever sex or age; and, cutting open the sides of women made pregnant by Frenchmen, they drew out and killed the unborn children.

[Col. 0354D] In the same year wars were waged among the pagans, with countless people killed.

Incident. In the same year—

> [Note: This happened in 1282.]

—Florent, count of Holland, entered Frisia with a multitude of his men, in vengeance for his father William, king of the Romans, killed by the Frisians. He defeated the Frisians and subjected many of them to his lordship. Among them, in order to escape the danger of death, one Frisian dug up and delivered to the count his father’s body, which had been placed in a tree trunk [Col. 0355A] and buried behind the hearth of his house.

> [Note: Arcellæ.]

The count brought it with him to his own country with the greatest honour and buried it reverently.

Incident. In that year (1283), John I, duke of Brabant, crossed the Meuse with a very great army. Reinald, count of Guelders, with many nobles, met him near the village of Gulpen.

> [Note: Gulpen, between Maastricht and Aachen. In 1283 and 1284 the princes were to engage in battle at this place.]

Though the battle-lines on each side had been drawn up for combat, a truce was introduced and they departed from each other peacefully.

Incident. [HOCSEM. 14.] In the same year (1282), after the see of Liège had been vacant for a year following the death of John of Anghien, bishop, John, bishop of Metz, son of Guy, count of Flanders, was transferred by Pope Martin IV to the bishopric of Liège [Col. 0355B].

2. In the year of the Lord 1288, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Rudolph, king of the Romans, on 25 April, the townsmen of Saint Trudo repeatedly represented by complaints that grave and monstrous enormities were continually committed with impunity in that town. Lord John, bishop of Liège, and Abbot William, in order more effectively to restrain the malice of the wicked, having summoned a council of many wise and prudent men, decreed and granted that there should be a commune in the town itself, to endure only at the will of the said lords, as is contained in letters drawn up on this matter and preserved in our archives. This commune lasted a few years.

Likewise. In the same year [Col. 0355C] our great granary, situated beside the monastery orchard and full of crops of wheat, rye, and other produce, was burned by thieves.

Incident. In the same year, on 5 June, John I, duke of Brabant, wishing, by reason of the duchy of Lotharingia and as margrave of the Holy Empire, to preserve the public highway between the rivers Meuse and Rhine safe and free for travel, crossed beyond the Meuse with a great army and besieged the castle of Worringen.

> [Note: Worringen, between Cologne and Neuss. This most celebrated battle, and the other events connected with it, were described more fully than by others by Jan van Heelu in the Chronicle edited by Willems.]

He did so because the archbishop of Cologne, Siegfried—

> [Note: *Siverdus*; i.e. Sigfridus.]

—harboured there robbers who despoiled and captured merchants.

> [Note: *Raptores* in 1*.]

When the archbishop learned of this, he came with a multitude of his followers. With him he summoned the counts of Guelders—

> [Note: Reinald, son of Otto II.]

—and Luxembourg—

> [Note: Henry and Walram.]

—who charged Duke John with wrongdoing because he had acquired [Col. 0356A] the duchy of Limburg from the count [Col. 0355D] of Mont—

> [Note: Adolf. For when Ermengard, daughter of Walram IV, duke of Limburg, died in 1283, she having married Count Reinald of Guelders, Adolf, count of Berg, the counts of Luxembourg, and others claimed the duchy for themselves on account of their kinship with the Limburgers. Adolf afterwards ceded his hereditary right to John, duke of Brabant; against him the remaining princes entered into an alliance with the archbishop of Cologne.]

—in which they said that they had a right. Besides these, a multitude of princes came to the archbishop’s aid, gathering an innumerable army against the small force of the duke of Brabant.

The aforesaid duke, therefore, trusting in God’s aid, who favours just causes, drew up his battle-line. Refusing steadfastly to withdraw from the siege of the castle, he advanced onto the plain before the said castle and courageously awaited the advancing hostile forces. A most severe battle was then joined. After a great shedding of blood, victory fell to the Brabanters; but while the opposing side still charged bravely with its second battle-line, a third attacked in addition. The fighting continued so long that the battle, begun in the morning, lasted until evening. At last, however, after the count of Luxembourg [Col. 0356B]—

> [Note: Henry.]

—had been slain with his brother Walter of the Rock and two other natural brothers, together with many men-at-arms, nine hundred men in number, and after the rest had turned their backs, the duke held the field as victor. He captured the aforesaid archbishop, Reinald, count of Guelders, Adolf, count of Nassau, who not long afterwards became king of the Romans, and many other noble and renowned men. There Walram, lord of Valkenburg, with many other nobles, barely escaped by flight, while others were killed.

The duke, persisting in the siege, received the surrender of the aforesaid castle and destroyed it, thus making the passage there by the royal highway free and safe.

Incident. In the following year John I, the aforesaid duke, besieged the castle of Valkenburg; but through an amicable [Col. 0356C] settlement he withdrew from the siege, because the lord of Valkenburg, having done homage to the duke in order to obtain his favour, promised inviolably to maintain free passage for merchants.

Incident. In the same year Rudolph, king of the Romans, died. In that same year Tripoli, a city of Christians, was again taken by the Saracens. [Continuation of Vincent of Beauvais.]

3. In the year of the Lord 1291, the same Abbot William newly built on our allod of Dungen a beautiful hall with its appurtenances. He also caused the river Herk—

> [Note: *fluvium Herkam* in 1*.]

> [Note: The Herk, which flows into the Demer.]

—which flowed only beyond the residence, by the digging of a new channel wholly to enclose that court within the said Herk. It still does not cease to flow there by the dike along which one goes from the fields to the church.

In the time of this abbot there were among [Col. 0356D] the fellow-monks and lords of our monastery several [Col. 0357A] honourable persons and learned men, eloquent in the German, French, and Latin tongues.

Incident. [HOCSEM. 17.] In the following year, after the death of Rudolph, king of the Romans, Adolf, count of Nassau, was elected king.

Incident. In the same year John III, bishop of Liège, died. Guy, brother of the count of Hainaut—

> [Note: John.]

—was elected by one party of the chapter of Liège, against William, son of Bertold of Mechelen, a theologian elected by the other party.

Incident. Continuation of Vincent of Beauvais. In the same year Acre, a wealthy city long held by Christians, was captured after a long siege by the sultan of Babylon, as is narrated more fully near the end of the second part of Vincent’s *Mirror of History*.

Incident. On 5 July in the year of the Lord 1293, Celestine V was elected and consecrated pope. Previously he had lived the eremitical life for forty years, content with bread and water for sustenance. This man, craftily deceived, resigned the papacy. [HOCSEM. 20.] [Col. 0358A] Boniface VIII succeeded him, elected in the same year on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord; he made the Sixth Book of Decretals.

Incident. At about the same time John, duke of Brabant, was struck in the arm by the lance of a certain knight during a tournament at Bar. Gravely ill and confined to bed, he ordered the knight who had lanced him to be brought before him and completely forgave the cause of his injury. Having devoutly received the sacraments of the Church, he died. His son John II succeeded him.

Incident. [HOCSEM. 21.] In the year of the Lord 1296 Hugh of Chalon was made bishop of Liège by Pope Boniface VIII, and the elections formerly made of William and Guy, having been examined in the Roman curia, were annulled. In the year of the Lord 1297, the twentieth year of his prelacy, Abbot William, more devout among the devout, died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends [Col. 0358B] of May, and was buried in the middle of the nave of the church.

[Col. 0357] Here ends the first book of the fourth and final part of the *Deeds of the Abbots of this Monastery of Saint Trudo*.

# HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTER HEADINGS OF THE SECOND BOOK OF THE SAME PART—ON THE DEEDS OF ABBOT ADAM

1. How Adam was elected abbot.

2. On the overthrow of the money-changers’ tables and the rebuilding of our monastery tower; several incidental matters; and the war of Courtrai.

3. On the establishment of the commune by Woltermann and his accomplices, and the wounding of the schout.

4. On the nocturnal fires and violences committed in the New Court, and the interdict imposed upon the town.

5. On the outlawry of Woltermann and his accomplices; the amends made by the townsmen to the lords bishop and abbot; and the favour shown by the pope to the envoys of Abbot Adam.

6. On the prior of our monastery at Milen and the prebend that convent there shall administer to him; several incidental matters; the destruction of the Templars; the crusaders; and the death of Theobald, bishop of Liège, on Emperor Henry’s expedition against the Romans.

7. On those killed inside the church of blessed Mary, and the outlawry of their killers.

8. On the appointment of Henry of Rikle, prior of this place, as abbot of Saint Paul at Lower Maastricht, and the reconciliation of the church of blessed Mary; incidental matters concerning the civil war in the city of Liège and the war between the noble families of Hesbaye at Waremme.

9. On the commune of Ercam in our town, established with the consent of Bishop Adolf and the chapter of Liège, on account of which an interdict was imposed on the town.

10. On the appeal made by Abbot Adam and the convent to the Roman curia against the absolution by which Bishop Adolf absolved the townsmen; the burning of our boundary-post; the withholding of the rent of the brewing-vats, commonly called *panthsins*; and our hospital.

11. On the first and second visitation made in the head and members of this monastery by Bishop Adolf, who burdened this church unlawfully with excessive expenses; incidental matters concerning the dearth of grain and mortality among people, and the more generous alms then given to the poor before the gate.

12. On the annual aldermen; on our residence at Lewis.

13. How, during the interdict, the townsmen caused divine offices to be celebrated by an outside priest; how the convent stayed at Dungen and returned to the cloister; and the suspension for three years in the Roman curia of the suit against the bishop and the town. Incidental matters concerning the Liège opposition to Bishop Adolf; the battle at Dommartin; the battle on the hill near Huy; the defeat of the people of Saint Trudo at Waremme and their flight; the battle at Hasselt; and many other matters. Also concerning the peace settlement between the bishop and the country, and the antipope.

14. On the peace made at the New Court between the lords bishop and abbot and the town. Also on the alms of Lord John of Follonia; the incorporation into the abbacy of the goods of the cellarership; and twenty-six modii of rye belonging to the refectory.

15. On the death of Abbot Adam and his burial.

# DEEDS OF ABBOT AMELIUS

1. On the election of Abbot Amelius; several incidental matters concerning the wars between the bishop and the duke of Brabant.

2. On a captive carried away from the monastery court and brought back again; incidental matters concerning the first destruction of the cloister of Affligem, the peace made among the noble families of the Liège country by the judgment of twelve prudent men, and several other matters.

3. On our residence at the New Court, newly built by Abbot Amelius; also on the completion of the great court and the mill placed above the garden of our cemetery, commonly called *vrythof*.

4. On the relief of the town from the heavy burden of rents, in aid of which, among other measures and with consent of both lords, the common pastures were leased for a term of eighteen years.

5. How the old aldermen were seized, assessed, and removed; incidental matters concerning the epidemic and other things.

6. On the bishop’s expulsion from the country and the establishment of the commune of this town; incidental matters. Also concerning the battle at Vothem, the battle at Crisse, the battle at Tourinnes, the battle of Saint Trudo before the town of Lewis, and how the people of Saint Trudo submitted themselves to the will of the duke of Brabant.

[Col. 0359] 7. How John, duke of Brabant, usurped lordship over the town of Saint Trudo; annulled the privileges of the town, presented to him, by cutting off their seals in the sight of all; and caused the dwellings of many townsmen to be utterly demolished. Incidental matters concerning Emperor K.; the sect of the Flagellants; and the burning of the Jews.

8. On the death of Abbot Amelius and his burial.

# DEEDS OF ABBOT ROBERT

1. On the election of Abbot Robert.

2. On the manner of receiving an abbot or bishop.

3. On the manner of consecrating an abbot.

4. On the relief of the fief, the advocacy at Aelburgh, and the losses inflicted upon us by the count.

5. On the redemption of our town of Halchtre, the goods of Dola there, and the violent usurpation of Lord Reyner of Schoenvorst.

6. On the homicide—or rather robbery—committed at the beguines’ court, and the homicide committed in the cemetery of the church of blessed Mary; incidental matters concerning the discord and war between Wenceslaus, duke of Brabant, and Louis, count of Flanders; the second destruction of the cloister of Affligem; the conflict between the episcopal party and the Brabanters at the town of Landen; and the king of France carried captive into England.

7. On the modification of the obligation of the old aldermen; how some of the modern aldermen, defending themselves in the presence of both lords and the townsmen against many charges of wrongdoing, escaped; the judgment of appeal made to the aldermen of the see of Aachen; and the amicable settlement made by those aldermen of Saint Trudo with their lords.

8. On the special prerogative which from ancient times every abbot of Saint Trudo has in the abbey of Saint Bron, and which the abbot and convent there freely and effectively accorded to our Abbot Robert; incidental matters concerning the death of the count of Looz, to whose county’s lordship the inhabitants of the towns of Looz, Hasselt, and Herk were compelled to receive Bishop Engelbert, rendering him fealty.

9. On raising a commune in our town of Saint Trudo, which the bishop, despite Abbot Robert’s opposition and contrary to right, granted to the townsmen through money, while they were with him at the siege of Stockem Castle.

10. On the unjust declaration of hostility against us and the goods of our people made by Henry of Halbeke, esquire; the burning of our residence at Dola; and how the tenant of our town killed a man and burned the church itself.

11. On the violence of the masters of the commune, compelling the aldermen to choose the bishop’s schout as an alderman, against whom Abbot Robert appealed to the see of Aachen, where he obtained his claim; incidental matters concerning the county.

12. On the imprisonment of those said to have committed the robbery at the beguines’ court, and their various retaliatory executions; several incidental matters concerning the translation of the bishop of Liège and other things; Arnold of Rumiens acting as count of Looz; and how the people of Liège burned the town of Rumiens and the castle of Hamele.

13. On the expulsion of Abbot Robert from the city of Liège and the referral of the lawsuit to the Roman curia; incidental matters concerning the siege of Rumiens Castle.

14. On the first entry of John, bishop of Liège, without solemnity, and the ineffective negotiation of peace between the lords and the townsmen.

15. On the death of Abbot Robert, his burial, and how his adversaries were afflicted by many tribulations before his death.

# DEEDS OF ABBOT ADAM
[Col. 0359A] 1. In the same year of the Lord 1297, on 12 [Note: [Col. 0359] Something has dropped out in 1*, but it is evidently to be restored.] Kalends of May [20 April], namely the sixth day after the death of the aforesaid reverend Abbot William, in the seventh year of the reign of Adolf, king of the Romans, and the second year of Hugh, bishop of Liège, Adam, custodian of this monastery, was elected abbot. His election was tumultuous. For the prior—whom at least the elders and several worthy persons had then privately agreed among themselves should be chosen before the others—secretly yielding to their votes, declared, in the chapter-house at the appointed time, without consulting them, that this Adam, the custodian, should especially be elected. At this those who had not expected it were astonished; but while the others cried, “It pleases us! It pleases us!” all deliberation was set aside, they rose, and, with the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* begun, led the elect to the choir. At Liège, as is customary, he was presented; and, having been confirmed, was consecrated at Saint James’s.

He was a native of Ardinghen, of one of the more powerful families of [Col. 0360A] Hesbaye; of shrewd intelligence but scant learning, astute in temporal matters and most earnest in defending the rights of his church. For two years after his accession, sparing expenses, he made provision for himself and lived not outside the precincts but within his cloister, with a small household.

Incident. [HOCSEM, 23.] About this time a most savage war arose between Lord [Note: [Col. 0359A] Humbert.] of Awans—[Note: [Col. 0359A] Thus the manuscript consistently reads; these families are known to have been called Awans and Waroux. For this exceedingly bloody civil war, see the very full account by Jacques de Hemricourt, *Abrégé des guerres d’Awans et de Waroux*, in *Le miroir des nobles de Hasbaye*, ed. Salbray, Brussels, 1673, p. 336. Awans and Waroux are villages in the vicinity of Liège.]—with his kin, and the lineage of Waroux on the other side. In the same year the lord of Awans was killed by his adversaries of Waroux in a battle in the open country.

Incident. In the same year Saint Louis, king of France, was canonized by Pope Boniface VIII.

Incident. In the same year Philip, king of France, invaded Flanders with force, took Bruges, a wealthy town, together with other towns, and carried Guy, count of Flanders, and his eldest son Robert as captives into France, committing them to prison because he charged them with having conspired against him with Edward, [Note: [Col. 0360A] First.] king of England.

[Col. 0361A] Incident. [HOCSEM, 22.] In the year of the Lord 1298 Adolf, king of the Romans, was killed, together with a multitude of his men, by the army of Albert, duke of Austria, son of the late Rudolf, king of Germany. In the following year that duke was elected and crowned king of the Romans by the princes of the Empire.

2. In the year of the Lord 1299 certain money-changers [Note: [Col. 0361] *cambitores* (“money-changers”) in 1*.] set up their exchange tables within the jurisdiction of the lord of Liège, carrying on their trade outside the jurisdiction of our church, contrary to right. When the abbot learned this, he had their tables carried into the middle of the market-place; trampling them under his own feet, he ordered them cut to pieces. For, by the judgment of the exchange-court aldermen, the conduct of exchange belongs to the abbey, just as the striking of coin belongs to the bishop; this division had indeed from ancient times been made between the church of Metz and our own.

[Col. 0361B] Therefore, after the exchanges in the bishop’s jurisdiction had been destroyed, a respectable townsman named Peter, who later became an alderman, on behalf of the lord abbot, alone conducted the exchange business within the jurisdiction of our church, in a house next to the chapel of the clerics.

Incident. [HOCSEM, 24.] In the year of the Lord 1300 Hugh of Chalon is accused [Note: [Col. 0361] *criminatus* (“was accused”) in 1*.] before the Roman Curia by the chapter and citizens of Liège on account of several outrageous deeds which his brother, Lord John of Chalon, was said to have committed with the bishop’s consent. Accordingly, having been personally summoned and appearing before Pope Boniface, he was deprived of the bishopric, which was there bestowed upon Adolf of Waldeck, who was present. [Note: [Col. 0361] *presente* (“present”) in 1*.] Some say that the pope provided the same Hugh with another, lesser [Col. 0361C] bishopric.

Incident. In the same year the community of Bruges, contending with the magnates of their town over an imposed excise, killed many persons.

Likewise. About the same time, Abbot Adam, wishing to rebuild the great tower which had formerly fallen in the time of Abbot William I, engaged a celebrated mason. When the mason had designed the dimensions of the building as was fitting, but this did not please the abbot, who spared expense, he said: “If what I have well conceived does not please you, I prefer that you take another craftsman instead of me—one who will attend to your wishes rather than to the benefit of the building.” Thus he departed, and another came, who raised the tower to the height of the bells.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1301, Philip, king of France, having usurped the county of Flanders, [Col. 0361D] sent several nobles to Bruges to punish what the community of Bruges had done in the preceding year. Rising against the king’s messengers, they killed them all; and, electing as captain one Peter, a member of the clothmakers’ guild, all the common people conspired against the king under his leadership. Sending men from place to place, they killed all the king’s supporters, so that in the town of Erdenburgh [Note: [Col. 0361D] Erembodegem on the Dender.] they killed four thousand persons and seized their goods.

[Col. 0362A] Incident. [HOCSEM, 25.] In the same year Adolf of Waldeck was honorably received by the people of Liège as bishop of Liège, but died in that same year. Theobald, brother of the count of Bar, succeeded him.

Incident. In the following year the sons of Guy, count of Flanders, grievously resentful that their father and eldest brother were so held captive by the king of France, summoned their nephew the count of Namur [Note: [Col. 0361D] John.] and other relatives, as well as the aforesaid Peter with the Flemish communities, and besieged the castle of Courtrai, in which the king’s treasury was stored. When the king heard this, he sent Robert, his nephew, son of his brother Saint Louis, the late king, [Note: [Col. 0361D] No one fails to see that the author is greatly mistaken; [Col. 0362D] Robert was the brother of King Philip, and both were sons of Saint Louis.] with a multitude of princes from the kingdom of France and from provinces on every side, to drive the Flemings from the siege.

[Col. 0362B] But they would not yield; though few against innumerable foes, they all prepared for battle on foot, defending themselves with a small ditch and embankment, while the French boldly remained on horseback. Battle was therefore joined. The French, attacking their adversaries first, fell into the embankment of that ditch. For those in the front rank, successively pushed forward by those following, fell headlong; and those following were miserably hurled down by the troops coming behind them, so that they perished without swords being used by the opposing side. When the first and second lines had thus been destroyed, with few slain by the sword, the Flemings—who had prepared to turn their backs—became more courageous and killed without mercy every Frenchman who might have escaped the danger. Thus the third line arrived, won no glory, and took to flight.

[Col. 0362C] Many Flemings pursued them; and when, believing they would escape, they entered a certain ford, they were drowned with their horses, only a few escaping. Those who did escape were killed on the other side of the ford, except for one knight of Brabant, who was spared alive and, having been taken captive by men known to him, escaped.

There fell in that battle the count of Artois with many counts; likewise Lord Godfrey of Brabant, brother of Duke John, with three barons—namely John of Virson, his son, the lord of Wesemael, and the lord of Butersiim—together with many of the foremost men of Brabant; likewise the eldest son [Note: [Col. 0362D] John.] of the count of Hainaut, with many from Lorraine, Provence, and Gascony. Their number was estimated at eight thousand, both noble [Col. 0362D] and knightly men.

Incident. At the same time a serious war arose against the bishop of Liège, the canons, clergy, and aldermen, from the people of Liège and the inhabitants of the other towns.

3. In the year of the Lord 1302, Christian called Weilnere, having taken in marriage the lady of Busco, widow of a certain knight, was unable, because of obstruction by the friends of her first husband, freely to enjoy the goods and possessions belonging to the wife whom he had married. On this matter he repeatedly and urgently requested the aldermen [Col. 0363A] to provide him with full justice, because the possessions lay within the jurisdiction of our town; but he accomplished nothing, because, as was said, at the instance of the prayers of the opposing party, the said aldermen deferred consideration of the case from day to day.

Accordingly, on 12 Kalends of January [21 December], the same Christian, with his three brothers, privately assembled several town officials and laid before them the injuries done to him, requesting their assistance. On this occasion the townsmen, stirred up against the aldermen, elevated a certain townsman named Walter of Diest, called Wouterman, and made him captain.

In the following year, 1303, after the townsmen had assembled, the same Wouterman with his companions seized the aldermen on 7 July and committed them to custody as hostages in the Lombards’ house.

[Col. 0363B] When Arnold, count of Looz and advocate, had worked before dinner with the lord abbot for their release [Note: [Col. 0363] *laborassent* (“they had worked”) in 1*.], and they had sat down in the hall for their meal, the community, learning that Arnold Probus, an alderman, had fled out of the town, rushed furiously to arms and shouted that they must have the count with them. Therefore they entered the cloister gate by force and broke down the door of the hall. Meanwhile, however, the lord abbot sprang up from the table and hid himself in a secret place; the count was compelled to go with them to the house of the aforesaid Arnold Probus. At their demand, in his capacity as advocate, he struck the first blow with a rod; immediately many burst into the house, razed it to the ground, and plundered it.

Then, proceeding outside [Col. 0363C] the Stapel Gate, they destroyed the vineyard of the same Arnold Probus.

Likewise. Afterwards, as they proceeded to the market-place, they killed without cause Arnold, son of Lord Robert of Glinden.

Likewise. Returning thereafter to the cloister gate, some ran about with drawn swords. From this several of our fellow monks and lords became very afraid. Three of them climbed over the wall of our court and fled; one fell with his arm broken or twisted. But the townsmen brought them back to the monastery and did not allow them to depart.

Meanwhile, when the tumult had subsided, the aldermen were permitted to leave captivity on 12 July. About supper-time the lord abbot and the count, taking the aldermen with them, secretly withdrew [Col. 0363D] to safer places, followed by both reeves and the deputy advocate, out of fear of the community’s captains, who, having expelled them, usurped jurisdiction for themselves.

Concerning the same matter. In the same year, when our reeve John of Winde was one night [Note: [Col. 0363] *quedam* (“a certain [night]”) in 1*.] returning from the place where Abbot Adam was staying and secretly entered the town by the gate called Visseghat, he was savagely wounded by ambushers and hurried to the cloister. On learning this, the community, aroused under arms, assembled before our gate; striking it with dreadful blows, [Col. 0364A] they demanded that the reeve be handed over to them. Prior Henry of Rikle and other elders standing above the gate answered them earnestly, begging them to refrain from inflicting violence upon us at so unseasonable an hour of night. Softened by these humble pleas, they finally withdrew to their homes, Wouterman having urged this course.

4. In the same year, on the vigil of Saint Barbara [3 December], when the lord abbot had been at Alken, [Note: [Col. 0363D] Near Hasselt.] a village of the bishop, to negotiate with the bishop about weighty matters, a messenger came and secretly advised him not to return to the New Court for the night. On hearing this, he secretly prepared to travel toward Kerckem [Note: [Col. 0364D] Kerckem near Tienen.] to the house of his brother Godfrey, where he spent the night.

The captains of the community, however, having held secret counsel, hastened about [Col. 0364B] midnight to the New Court, intending to take him away captive. Coming armed to the hall and searching everywhere, they saw themselves frustrated in their criminal purpose when they discovered that the abbot was absent. Enraged at this, they set fire to the upper house, killed five horses, and tore and pierced many beds with swords; having taken the household goods, they departed.

At daybreak, our lay brother, the steward of our estate, had the slaughtered mares and the sword-torn beds placed on carts at that very New Court and thrown down into the middle of the market-place. [Note: [Col. 0363] *feci* (“I made”) in 1*; evidently *fecit* (“he made”) must be read.] At about the first hour, when townsmen had gathered to watch, and feathers streamed from the rents in the bedding and flew about everywhere, the same Brother Nicholas cried in a trumpet-like voice:

[Col. 0364C] “See, all you townsmen, these outrages which our townsmen have inflicted upon my lord abbot at the New Court, with burnings and plundering.”

The townsmen, astonished at the deed, greatly disliked it. Therefore the abbot, swiftly reaching Aachen with his aldermen, recounted to the aldermen of Aachen all the crimes committed against him and asked them, at a suitable time to be notified to them, to come to our court at Dung.

Concerning the same matter. Meanwhile, after the lord abbot’s return from the court of Aachen, an interdict was imposed upon the whole town, namely on the fifth day after the violence committed at the New Court [8 December]. A few days later, the parish priests and other priests, seeking safer places, withdrew for protection to [Col. 0364D] our court at Dung.

5. In the year of the Lord 1304, on the day before the Nones of February [4 February], Theobald, bishop of Liège, Adam, abbot of this place, and Arnold, count of Looz, with a great multitude of armed, selected men, in an open place situated between the town and Brustem, beside the road that runs toward Bautershoven on one side and, on the other, toward the place called Heirstake—bringing with them the aldermen of the court of Aachen, specially summoned for this purpose, and all the aldermen of the town of Saint [Col. 0365A] Trond—after mature deliberation brought a complaint against the townsmen for the above-mentioned acts of violence, and particularly against the individual persons who had usurped lordship over the town.

Having heard them, the aforesaid aldermen carefully ordered seats to be set up on the said road, so that they stood partly in the bishop’s jurisdiction and partly in the jurisdiction of the abbot, because there the boundaries of the two lords touched. When the aldermen had assembled, nothing was done because the ban-bell was not rung. But, after a certain fellow had been hired for one hundred Tournois pounds, he was secretly sent to the monastery; climbing the tower, he rang the bell for a long time.

Therefore, because the aldermen could not administer full justice within the town itself, and after warning had been issued by both reeves, when the bell’s sound had been heard, they judicially condemned as guilty of the crime of lèse-majesté, depriving them of honor, personal rights, possessions, and goods: Wouterman of Diest; the four brothers called Weilnere—Henry, Walter, Gunther, and Christian; John, son of John; and Herman Wisselere.

[Col. 0365B] While the bell continued to ring, the townsmen assembled under arms in the market-place. Hearing that armed men had gathered in the open country, they went out armed and drew up a battle line in the field behind the suburb’s gardens; but, on the count’s advice, returned to the town. When all this had been done, the lords and their followers departed for their own places.

After such outlawry had been pronounced, many townsmen began to avoid those captains, saying: “We do not wish, because of these men, to fall into the hands [Col. 0365C] of the lords.” Understanding this, and finding themselves treated day by day almost as strangers, despairing of others’ help, within a fortnight they left the town, abandoning wives and children with weeping and grief, about to fall from the greatest wealth into poverty.

Concerning the same matter. In the same year, after many negotiations, the townsmen came to their senses and were at last reconciled with their lords through an agreement of peace. They undertook to pay the aforesaid lords three thousand Tournois pounds as amends, with the additional condition that, according to the direction of worthy men, they should go out to meet their lords as far as the New Court, where they had formerly committed robberies and nocturnal burnings.

Accordingly, on Maundy Thursday, which that year fell on 7 Kalends of April [26 March], when the whole people had assembled, the individual persons who had rendered aid and support to the seven aforesaid captains in their excesses walked barefoot and bareheaded in linen garments. When they reached the place of the aforesaid court, kneeling and clapping their hands, they humbly begged forgiveness from the lord abbot and the convent and were received into favor. Then, in the manner of a procession, two by two, with the lord abbot and convent following, they proceeded into the middle of the monastery. There they remained standing until the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* had ended.

Concerning the same matter. After the Easter days had passed, several townsmen who had served the aforesaid Wouterman and his accomplices [Col. 0366A] and had not been received into favor by the lords were condemned and outlawed.

Incident. [HOCSEM, 29.] In the same year Pope Benedict XI, who succeeded Boniface after the latter had been killed by his enemies, belonged to the Order of Preachers. When he was either master of the order or provincial, he came to our town and was invited to the lord abbot’s dinner. As he entered the hall, a certain worthy man suggested that he converse with the abbot in French rather than Latin. Gladly accepting the suggestion and promising the sweet courtesies of friendship, they enjoyed themselves pleasantly, each explaining to the other the nature of his own station through mutual exchange of words; and thus that worthy man departed from the hall with thanks.

After some time, this same holy father, a cardinal, [Col. 0366B] was consecrated pope in this year. In the same year messengers from this monastery were sent to the Roman Curia concerning weighty matters. When these had been reported to the pope’s notice, he summoned those messengers and asked whether their case was that of the abbot who knew no Latin, who had recently given him such a pleasant dinner in the cloister of Saint Trond. When they affirmed this, the pope immediately ordered that their petition in every respect be brought to effect.

This pope, after presiding for nine months, died [Note: [Col. 0365D] 6 July 1304.]. Clement V succeeded him; he was the first to transfer the Roman Curia from Rome to Provence.

Incident. In the same year, at the request and expense of the smiths of the town of Saint Trond, with the consent of Abbot Adam and Henry, parish priest of Saint Mary’s, the chapel of Saint Eligius was built; an endowed altar was consecrated in it; and the guild fraternity of the said smiths arose.

[Col. 0366C] Incident. In the same year the common people rose savagely throughout almost all Lorraine and afterward everywhere through Brabant. But the leading men of Brussels resisted, whom the community had kept expelled; with the duke’s help, the community was put to flight in battle, many being killed, forty-five broken on the wheel, and others expelled from the country.

Incident. In the following year, 1305, peace was restored between Philip, king of France, and the Flemings; and Count Guy and his son Robert, after one part of Flanders had been assigned to the king, were released from imprisonment and restored to the county.

Incident. [HOCSEM, 29, 30.] In the year of the Lord 1307, the Templars were imprisoned throughout France, and in the following year, at the king’s instigation, their order was utterly abolished by Pope Clement at the Council of Lyon because of certain abominable deeds alleged against them. Hence, as was said, the pope’s greed and the king’s unrestrained will were the cause why many, at least, innocent persons perished; for all were burned by fire on the appointed day. Their possessions were immediately assigned to the brothers of the Order of Saint John, after an infinite sum of money had been given to the pope; and, their privileges having been annulled, the pope, after receiving a new sum of money, granted these same Hospitallers new privileges.

Incident. In the same year a great discord arose between the common people and the prominent men of Liège. Therefore, under Bishop Theobald, after the aldermen had left the city, an army of armed men was assembled so that many of the common people might be outlawed at Voethim. But, since the whole people stood in arms in opposition, peace was made.

6. In the year of the Lord 1308 it was determined by arbitral judgment between the monasteries of Saint Trond and Saint Catherine of Milen that the prioress and convent there should provide their prior, when continually or intermittently resident among them, with such a prebend in food and clothing as one of the fellow monks of the monastery of Saint Trond possesses, and should provide food for his servant.

Incident. [HOCSEM, 31.] In the year of the Lord 1309 [1308], on the first day of May, Albert, king of the Romans, slayer of his predecessor Adolf, [Col. 0367B] in the twelfth year of his reign was killed by his nephew, whose patrimony he had occupied. In the same year the noble Henry of Luxembourg was elected king of the Romans and was crowned at Aachen on the Epiphany of the Lord. In the same year his election was confirmed by Pope Clement.

Incident. In the same year, on 6 January 1309, a multitude of the common people, both men and women, came forth from the regions of Lorraine and beyond the Rhine, from cities, castles, and villages. With no one preaching, but of their own accord, they took the cross. On the pretext of a woman killed by Jews at Tienen [Note: [Col. 0367D] Tirlemont.], for whom no redress of justice had been obtained because the Jews had redeemed themselves by paying a great sum of money, and after the dead body of that woman—later regarded as martyred—had been found, [Col. 0367C] they pursued the Jews everywhere and indiscriminately killed those refusing to confess Christ. They destroyed the castles and strongholds of princes to which the aforesaid Jews fled for protection, and finally besieged Genappe, a castle of the duke of Brabant, with twelve thousand men.

But Duke John, with a multitude of his men, stood at their front with his battle line drawn up to resist them; immediately he killed many who were terrified and fled, and expelled them from his land. After some months, they came to the Roman Curia with forty thousand men and urgently asked Pope Clement to grant them a general crusading passage. [Note: [Col. 0367] *passigium* (“passage”) in 1*.] But the pope, observing that they had undertaken this enterprise presumptuously and without discernment, absolved them all from the vow they had made without authorization from the Apostolic See. Thus they returned home in great disgrace.

[Col. 0367D] Incident. [Continuation of Vincent of Beauvais.] In the same year an army of Christians with the Hospitallers took the island of Rhodes and five islands adjacent to it. The Hospitallers had first besieged it five years earlier; now, having captured it, they killed and expelled the Turks and other unbelievers dwelling there.

Incident. [HOCSEM, 32.] In the same year Henry, king of the Romans, sixth of that name by royal reckoning, with a multitude [Col. 0368A] of princes and nobles, and with Theobald, bishop of Liège, joined to him, went into Italy. There, after conquering many cities, he victoriously took Milan by war despite the resistance of the Guelphs, and there received the Iron Crown (1310). Then he besieged and captured the noble city of Brescia for a long time, so that he razed its walls to the ground (1311). In this siege his brother Waleran, lord of the Rock, died after being struck by an arrow. In the same year, having defeated the Guelphs and the king of Sicily, [Note: [Col. 0367D] Robert.] he subjected to himself almost all Lombardy and a great part of Tuscany.

In the same year many able men of his army, together with his royal consort [Note: [Col. 0367] *sorte* (“lot, fortune”) in 1*.] [Note: [Col. 0367] *regina* (“queen”) in 1*.] [Note: [Col. 0368D] Margaret.], Count William of Jülich, Gerard of Cassel, and John of Agemont, brother of the count of Looz, were carried off by an unfamiliar pestilential air.

[Col. 0368B] Incident. [HOCSEM, 32.] In the following year the same king entered the city of Rome with his army. As he advanced toward the church of Saint Peter, the king of Sicily, the Guelphs, and the Orsini resisted him, aided by a very great multitude of Romans. A severe battle was fought in the passage through the streets, in which many notable persons fell; among them, on the side of the king of Germany, was Theobald, bishop of Liège, who, although captured, was killed.

Thereafter the king, having gained the greater part of the city, was consecrated emperor at Saint John Lateran by two cardinals sent for this purpose by Pope Clement. Afterwards, having stationed faithful men there for the city’s defense, he left Rome and subjected to his power, by war or surrender, almost all the cities, towns, and castles of Tuscany, Campania, and Lombardy [Col. 0368C] (1312). Then, after punishing various resisters with penalties of death, he besieged the city of Florence and so withdrew to Pisa. [Note: [Col. 0367] *Pisanis* (“to the Pisans”) in 1*.]

7. In the year of the Lord 1311, on 4 May, while the truce between the lineage of Stapelen and Otto Militis with his lineage was still in force, this Otto, about the first hour, having summoned his kinsmen, entered with armed force a house on the south side of the market-place, commonly called *der Moer*. A certain man came and said to Otto’s sons and nephew: “Look, our enemies are now entering the church of Blessed Mary.”

They immediately, without consulting their father or friends—namely his sons, the brothers Damian and Nicholas, and his nephew Nicholas, together with seven others—rushed furiously into the church during the celebration [Col. 0368D] of Mass. They attacked Walter Burgelken, esquire, and his kinsmen, Arnold called Heere and another Arnold, his nephew, who suspected nothing of their ambush because a truce had been proclaimed. They compelled them to flee from the place of the altar, where Mass was already being celebrated, to the protection of the greater choir. Though they resisted bravely, they were at last killed. Going thence into the porch, they fell upon Lord Albertinus, knight and alderman, and wounded him mortally also; [Col. 0369A] he died a few days later.

When the prescribed time had elapsed, the crime of this abominable sacrilege was punished by the aldermen’s judgment as follows. The aforesaid Otto Militis, having been warned by the reeve, in the presence of his fellow aldermen disowned and declared outlawed his two aforesaid sons, Damian and Nicholas, and his nephew Nicholas, together with their seven accomplices. He further pronounced that the house from which those accused men had gone forth armed was to be destroyed and burned; and since that house stood within the jurisdiction of the lord bishop of Liège, it was likewise adjudged that the timber and stones of the destroyed house should be carried within the bounds of this monastery’s jurisdiction and burned by fire. [Note: [Col. 0369] *comburentur* (“they will be burned”) in 1*.] This was done [Col. 0369B] in the middle of the market-place.

8. In the year of the Lord 1312, the fourth year of Henry VI’s reign and the second of his empire, after the abbot of Saint Paul at Lower Utrecht had died, the convent, divided in the election, finally agreed that it would receive as abbot the man whom Guy, bishop of Utrecht, should provide for it. Therefore the bishop, diligently considering the matter, at length recalled that at the University of Paris he had had as a fellow student a monk from the monastery of Saint Trond who was skilled in various branches of learning and excelled others in eloquence and personal beauty. He immediately sent a messenger to him asking him to decide whether he would accept the abbacy.

After consulting his abbot, Lord Adam, and his friends, he consented, accepting the favor offered. Therefore [Col. 0369C] the aforesaid Abbot Adam sent for the suffragan of Liège, who solemnly consecrated Henry of Rikle, prior of this monastery, abbot of Saint Paul in this monastery of Saint Trond on Easter Day [26 March], with Lord Abbot Adam himself present and assisting on the right, and the investiture-holder of Brustem, formerly abbot of Averbode, on the left. On that same day he ordained several persons there as acolytes.

Thus consecrated, on the following Thursday, with a multitude of priests solemnly assembled among us, he celebrated High Mass. When all this had been honorably accomplished, the same Lord Abbot Adam had Lord Abbot Henry, honorably arrayed in garments and other necessary things [Note: [Col. 0369] *oportinis* (“necessary things”) in 1*; a word appears to have fallen out and must be supplied.] and accompanied by a suitable household, conducted to the aforesaid cloister of Saint Paul.

[Col. 0369D] There he was received with great reverence by Lord Guy, bishop of Utrecht, and enthroned in that abbey with the immense joy of that monastery’s convent. After obedience had been rendered to him in the chapter-house by each fellow monk, according to custom, he began diligently to correct the insolence of certain undisciplined men [Col. 0370A] and to instruct his subjects in the observance of the regular life by word and deed.

While he labored earnestly for almost [Note: [Col. 0369] A number appears to have fallen out.] years to bring their transgressions back to the strict rule of monastic discipline, and made scarcely any progress, in sorrow he began to long for the place from which he had come, desiring to return there and be content, if he could obtain it, with a simple monk’s prebend. Although he asked this earnestly, he did not obtain it. For almost half a year before the end of his life he spoke little or not at all; nevertheless he walked about, and, grieving thus over his sons’ indiscipline, fell asleep in the Lord.
