In the aforesaid year 1312, in the octave of Easter, namely on Saint George’s Day [Note: [Col. 0369D] In 1312 Easter was celebrated on 26 April; Saint George’s Day is 23 April.], the church of Blessed Mary, which had been violated in the preceding year, was reconciled by the aforesaid suffragan [Col. 0370B] of the vacant see of Liège. Hence the verses:

> With George’s sun, pleasing in its sweet doubled number—
With the church consecrated, the people of Saint-Trond rejoiced in jubilation. Occurrence. In the same year, on the vigil of Bartholomew (23 August), William, castellan of Warémme [Note: [Col. 0369D] Waremme.], attacking Lord Henry of Hermalle unexpectedly at Weer [Note: [Col. 0369D] Weer, not far from Saint-Trond.] with his men, wounded him seriously and killed his nephew John of Phason. Consequently, since this William was of the lineage of those of Awans, he offended many of his friends, so that they turned to his enemies, the Waroux. Occurrence. In the same year, while the see of Liège was still vacant, a dispute arose between the chapter of Liège and Arnold, count of Looz, over the guardianship of the country. [Note: [Col. 0369D] *Mamburnia*, “the mambournerie,” is the temporal administration of the bishopric of Liège during a vacancy of the see. On this celebrated battle, called *la Mal de Saint-Martin*, see Polain, *Esquisses historiques de l'ancien pays de Liége*, Brussels, 1837, p. 1 ff. BETHMANN.]

[Col. 0370C] For the count and the leading men of the city and of the country itself maintained that, during a vacancy of the see, the guardianship of the bishopric belonged to the said count. But the chapter of Liège opposed this claim; supported by all the people, it retained [the guardianship] and elected as provost of Liège Arnold of Blankenberg, a nobleman. Therefore, on the fourth Ides of August, the count entered the city after sunset with many armed men. When the silence of night had come, the aldermen and leading men of the city, wishing to put into effect the hatred which, it was said, they had long borne against the chapter of Liège and the common people, assembled together under arms and roused the common people with shouting and the burning of houses. Meeting them as they ran through the streets and gathered in the marketplace, they killed them. Among these they killed Walter of Bruenshorne, a canon of Liège [Col. 0370D], who did not know the cause of the outcry.

At last, when the commune flocked together under arms, a fierce battle was fought. On learning this, the aforesaid provost immediately came with his men to assist the common people; thus the leading men and aldermen were compelled to retreat as far as Saint Martin’s. [Col. 0371A] Renewed in spirit, however, they again put their opponents to flight and killed the provost himself before the church of Saint Hubert. When morning came, the aforesaid common people again attacked the aldermen and magnates near the cloister of Saint Martin. Although at first they resisted stoutly, they were finally unable to withstand such numbers and were forced to turn their backs. Their pursuers killed them without mercy outside the gate, in the streets, and within the houses of the cloister.

Some of them, seeking refuge within the church of Saint Martin, climbed the fortified tower. But when the opposing party set fire beneath it, some threw themselves down from above among the swords of their enemies; the rest were suffocated and burned to death with the tower itself as it caught fire. There fell there among the magnates, both by sword and by fire, John [Col. 0371B] and Louis Surlet, John de Rosa, James de Cornu, Baldwin and Henry of Saint-Servais, and all the aldermen except four—able and honourable men—as well as many of their kinsmen. Their number was 120 armed men. Their goods were plundered by the common people and their dwellings demolished. Of the commune, about sixty men fell there.

Occurrence. In the year of the Lord 1313, about the beginning of June, the castellan of Warémme entered the village of Berle by force of arms with his men and killed eight men of the lineage of the lord of Berle before the castle.

Occurrence. In the same month, on the sixth Ides of June [Note: [Col. 0371D] See Hocsem, I, 33, concerning these matters.], Lord Henry of Hermalle, with all those favouring the party [Note: [Col. 0371] *partem* 1*.] of the Waroux on one side, and William, castellan of Warémme, with all the supporters of those [Col. 0371C] of Awans on the other, met in open country between the villages of Fexhe and Warémme, otherwise called Warenne. There, all the men of noble birth from Hesbaye and the county of Looz, together with many from the land of Namur and Brabant, were drawn up courageously in two opposing battle-lines. At the sorrowful and most humble prayers and entreaties of the count of Looz, they refused to grant a truce.

The count therefore withdrew sorrowfully from both parties, and a most severe battle was joined. Victory finally fell to the party of Lord Henry of Hermalle and the Waroux. The castellan of Warémme escaped with some of his men by flight; the castellan of Montenaken was killed with several—or two—knights; and John of Lobosgh, natural brother and standard-bearer of the lord of Wesemael, was killed with several other armed men, whose number [Col. 0371D] was fifteen or more. The lord of Wesemael and the lord of Liedekerke withdrew with their men into the church of the aforesaid village. As many of the opposing party pursued them, Lord William of Berle and other equally prudent knights set themselves as a wall opposite the house of God; bravely presenting their backs before the church doors, they restrained their men from breaking in. Thus those who had obtained the protection [Col. 0372A] of the church all returned unharmed to Brabant. Many others escaped by hastening to the fortification of Warémme castle, while the rest scattered in flight in every direction [Note: [Col. 0371] *fugam* 1*.].

Occurrence. In the same year Emperor Henry VI, in the fifth year of his reign and the third of his empire, after receiving the sacrament of the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 0371] *eucharie* 1*.], on the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary [Note: [Col. 0372D] He died on 27 August at Buonconvento.], was poisoned in the city of Pisa. Immediately confined to a sickbed, after extreme unction he most devoutly gave up his spirit.

Occurrence. [HOCS. II, 4.] At about the same time Louis, duke of Bavaria, and Frederick, duke of Austria, were elected against one another because of disagreement among the electors.

Occurrence. In the same year, 1313, the fifth year of the reign and the third of the empire of Emperor Henry VI, after the death beyond the Alps of Theobald, bishop of Liège, Adolph of [Col. 0372B] Mark was appointed bishop of Liège by Clement V at Avignon. Received as bishop on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, he found the greatest discord in the country and many enormities perpetrated during the vacancy of the see. [HOCSEM. II, 2.] Nevertheless, to win the goodwill of all, he pardoned the people of Liège for all offences previously committed.

### 9.

In the year of the Lord 1314, the second year of the vacancy amid the discord of the empire, Bishop Adolph and the entire chapter of Liège, through the payment of a sum of money, setting aside the fear of God and despite the protest and opposition of our abbot, granted that a commune should be established in the town of Saint-Trond, to endure forever. Once it had thus been established, the rulers of the townsmen began everywhere to violate the rights of our monastery. Because of this rashness, having been convicted before the official of the court of Liège, individual persons were excommunicated, and an ecclesiastical interdict was imposed upon the whole town. But since they had by no means yet turned their hearts away from the injuries inflicted upon us, the lord abbot took the aldermen with him and departed from the town.

### 10.

In the year of the Lord 1316, the same Bishop Adolph, having once again received from our townsmen a large sum of money, legally absolved in fact those townsmen who had for nearly two years lain hardened beneath sentences of interdict and excommunication. His mind’s eye, dazzled by the cloud of payment, acted now as before: just as he had previously granted an unlawful concession contrary to right, so now he absolved them, though bound by sentences of interdict and excommunication. When an appeal against this absolution had been made on our behalf to the Roman [Col. 0372D] curia, the bishop himself, adding evil to evil and setting aside the fear of God, sent his marshal with two canons of the church of Liège to this town of Saint-Trond. At the prompting of perverse and utterly deceitful men, as was later discovered, they usurped all the jurisdiction of the church, declaring that we had no right whatsoever in the town. Thus, in indignation, they took the sword from our schultheiss and [Col. 0373A] the rod from our forester.

After this they went to the place of the pillory, which from ancient times had stood within the boundaries of the abbot’s jurisdiction, just as the gallows stands within the bishop’s jurisdiction. They placed combustible material there and burned it, then caused a new pillory to be made and set it above the marketplace, within the bounds of the bishop’s jurisdiction. For this reason we again appealed to the aforesaid Apostolic See.

On the same matter. Meanwhile, the town brewers were forbidden by the masters and rulers of the commune to pay our monastery the beer-rent, namely the *pecarium cervisiae*. Consequently, when our servants entered the breweries twice weekly as usual, the beer-rent was not paid at all. Seeing this, the convent appointed two of our fellow monks, who entered the breweries each week [Col. 0373B] and found many who refused to pay the rent. They found many others who, though they did not dare to hand it over directly, graciously consented to allow the monks to draw it from their vessels into jars [Note: [Col. 0373D] That is, a *hydria*, a measure for liquids.] brought for that purpose by boys [Note: [Col. 0373D] *Garçons*, “boys.”], and to carry it away with them. They also forbade the payment to us of the salt-measure, which likewise is our hereditary due.

Likewise. At this time Bishop Adolph of Liège, proceeding with bitter zeal against this monastery at the instigation of those who dealt perversely, was assisted by certain clerics and priests of the town who volunteered themselves for this purpose. By his command they went to the hospital of Saint-Trond, whose ordering and governance, in both temporal and spiritual matters, is known from ancient times to belong to our monastery of Saint-Trond through letters patent. [Col. 0373C] Casting aside the fear of God, they compelled—or caused—the master of the brothers of that hospital to bring before them the hospital’s privileges, which contained, among other things, the manner in which it had been transferred from our place to the neighbouring cemetery. Having inspected them in their cunning, they cut off the seals and annulled the documents to our prejudice, as those deposited in our archives attest.

### 11.

In almost the same year, notwithstanding that, because of gifts received from the people of Saint-Trond, the bishop had unlawfully made himself a party with the whole town of Saint-Trond in litigation against our monastery before the Roman curia, he came to our monastery [Col. 0373D] to conduct a visitation in head and members, setting aside the general rule of law. He came with 150 horsemen and remained there so long that the expenses rose to 1,500 pounds of black Tours currency. When Abbot Adam himself, at the convent’s request, had rendered an account of the revenues of the monastery’s possessions for fifteen years because of this visitation, the bishop, through one of his vicars, an archdeacon, appeared to seek to invalidate this account, asserting that an accounting could have no effect without his presence. But when the convent objected to him, asking why [Col. 0374A] he had not attended, he finally desisted.

Afterwards, instigated by Lord Engelbert, his maternal uncle, a canon of Liège, the bishop tried to sow schism among the fellow monks and lords of our convent against the abbot himself, but he did not prevail. Thus he entered a second time with sixty horses and made a visitation, troubling the worthy men of this monastery and consuming the monastery through heavy expenses. Compelled by the frequency of these visitations, the abbot himself repaired many things previously too greatly neglected, both in the adornment and furnishing of the choir and in the workshops.

On the same matter. Amid this disturbance this abbot was severely persecuted by the bishop and his secretary Engelbert, secular abbot and canon of Saint Lambert, the bishop’s uncle. But through Prior Geimar, son of Hugh [Col. 0374B], and other honourable elders—whom the abbot, at the beginning of his appointment, had avoided because of their steadfastness in righteous causes—he was effectively assisted, with the consent of the whole convent, and freed from the most serious charges brought against him.

Likewise. Whenever the wine, beer, or bread of the monastic allowance was insufficient, this Prior Geimar refused to strike the signal or hold the refectory until it had been made good.

Likewise. On one occasion, when this abbot served the convent wine that was inadequate, a devout monk of the convent absented himself from choir. When the abbot sought on that account to subject him to penance, the prior and elders did not permit it, since he had acted for the community as a whole.

Occurrence. [HOCS. II, 6.] In the same year there was throughout various kingdoms [Col. 0374C] of the earth a most severe general barrenness, mortality, and dearth of grain. In the parts of Hesbaye where we dwell, a modius of rye by the measure of Saint-Trond was bought for eleven florins. For from about the Nativity of Saint John until harvest the weather was continuously rainy, so that the grains inside were almost empty of flour. Therefore, when people rose from the table, since the bread was scarcely nourishing, they immediately became hungry and ate much more than they had formerly been accustomed to eat. Consequently, such famine oppressed the common and poor people that starving persons, walking through the streets, fell on their backs upon the ground and expired. Yet other edible provisions were at a reasonable price.

On the same matter. In the following year, however, a modius of rye by our measure of Saint-Trond was bought for nearly one florin.

Likewise. In the year of this dearth, abundant alms were distributed to the poor at the gate. For in the house of the almoner there had been constructed, either in the time of William the First, abbot [Note: [Col. 0374D] Compare above under the year 1270.], or in that of the present Abbot Adam, an oven with a large cauldron. On appointed days a pottage of peas and seasonings was cooked in it and distributed to beggars and poor people.

Occurrence. In the year immediately preceding this one, bitter discords greatly increased between the bishop and the country, and [Col. 0375A] mutual killings between the lineages of Awans and Waroux.

### 12.

In the year of the Lord 1317, with the consent of the chapter, the bishop granted the masters and sworn men in the town of Saint-Trond that, after the perpetual aldermen had been deposed, annual aldermen should be elected, seven of whom on their behalf should be appointed over one half of this town. When, by a malicious judgment, they had pronounced that the former aldermen should be deprived of their goods and honours, the latter nevertheless appealed against the judgment to the royal court. There, at the instance of Abbot Adam, the aldermen of Aachen adjudged that the annual aldermen should be removed; and this was done.

Occurrence. In the same year, after the death of Pope Clement V, who compiled the Clementine constitutions but, prevented by death, did not complete them, [Col. 0375B] John XXII succeeded. He completed the aforesaid Clementines and decreed that they should be read in the schools and generally observed.

Occurrence. [HOCS. II, 8.] In the year of the Lord 1318, the very strong castle of Haren [Note: [Col. 0375D] Not far from Tongeren.], which belonged to the lord of Valkenburg, was besieged and taken by the bishop of Liège and the duke of Brabant [Note: [Col. 0376D] John III.] because of the acts of violence which that lord had repeatedly inflicted upon the people of Maastricht from that castle. Its garrison was beheaded and the castle was destroyed to its foundations.

Occurrence. In the following year, many lepers were burned throughout France and Hainaut. They were said to have been bribed by Jews to contaminate springs and streams with poison.

In the year of the Lord 1322, Abbot Adam acquired by purchase a dwelling with its appurtenances, which we possess at Lewis, situated near the ditches, on the left [Col. 0375C] beside the gate. Some time afterwards he constructed there a broad hall with the necessary offices, and disposed of the old dwelling which we had there, commonly called Tenscheverstene, because it stood outside the fortifications of that town.

13. In the year of the Lord 1323 or thereabouts, after litigation had continued for about eight years between our monastery and our townsmen, so that an interdict had long remained in force over the whole town, the masters of the commune, with their accomplices, brought forward a certain insolent priest who set aside the fear of God, and caused the divine offices to be publicly celebrated by him in the church of Blessed Mary, alleging that they had appealed against the sentence of interdict and excommunication. [Col. 0375D] Because the parish priests of the churches of this town, when requested, refused to adhere to such a frivolous appeal, they suffered many injuries at the hands of the masters of the commune and the townsmen. Under the pressure of this and other disturbances, the entire convent left the cloister, abandoning the town, and came to our residence at Dungh, where Abbot Adam was then staying. While it remained there continuously for nearly fourteen months, several of our lords and brethren fell ill because of the unwholesome air. Among them Prior Geimarus, a praiseworthy man, died there. [Col. 0376A] In that same year, by command of the aforesaid Abbot Adam, after the poor stalls of the chanting choir had been broken up, he caused new and handsome ones to be made from the revenues of the custody of our monastery. In the following year, negotiations took place for suspending the lawsuit between our monastery and the town. Therefore the aforesaid abbot summoned the entire convent to come to our residence at Lewis, which he had newly built. When the convent had remained there for four months, the negotiation for suspension of the suit having been brought to completion, the convent returned to our cloister.

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1234, when litigation had by then continued, as usual, for six years, on account of the appeal made by our monastery against Lord Adulphus the bishop, Engelbert Fransoes, acting as archdeacon [Col. 0376B] in spiritual matters, Lord John of Balodio, commissioner in temporal matters, the aldermen on the bishop’s side, and the masters of the commune and the whole town on the other: at the urging of worthy men, with the consent of the adverse party and of our people, the suit was suspended for three years, by consent and favour of Pope John XXII, through removal of the sentence and suspension of the interdict. If meanwhile an agreement of peace should occur, well and good; otherwise, where the litigation had paused, there it was to resume, and the sentence of excommunication and the interdict were to revive as before.

Likewise. During this three-year suspension of litigation nothing was accomplished toward a peace agreement; but, after some time, the cause of litigation was again suspended for three years, and when an honourable peace intervened in the meantime, it was laid to rest, as appears subsequently. [Col. 0376C] Incid. In the same year of the Lord 1324, the people of Liège, daily raging against the bishop, appropriated to themselves goods belonging to the episcopal table; they captured, killed, and burned those well-disposed persons who supported the bishop, and violated the truces of reconciliation established between the bishop and the country. [HOCS. II, 11.] On account of this, on the vigil of Saint Thomas (20 December), the bishop transferred the court of officiality, together with the courts of the archdeacons [Note: [Col. 0375] “archbishops,” 1*.], to the town of Huy; and afterward, about the feast of Saint Matthias (24 February), the city and people were subjected to ecclesiastical interdict. Thereupon, falling into still worse conduct, they employed apostates and priests who did not fear God, hired for money, to celebrate Masses [Note: [Col. 0375] omitted in 1*.], to bury the dead in cemeteries and churches, [Col. 0376D] and compelled the people to receive ecclesiastical sacraments from those profane persons. They oppressed the canons of Liège with threats and brazenly intruded themselves upon them when they did not dare to resist. Consequently, compelled by necessity, the greater part transferred their chapter and dwellings to the town of Huy. But Pope John ordered the remaining third of the canons of Saint Lambert, still residing at Liège for their own convenience, to present themselves before the apostolic presence within two months; this was carried out in the third year thereafter. [Note: [Col. 0375] “pope,” 1*.]

Incid. [HOCS. II, 12.] In the year [Col. 0377A] of the Lord 1326 [Note: [Col. 0377D] “In 1325, if you follow Hocsem and Jacob of Hemricourt.”], on the morrow of Bartholomew (25 August), the lineage of the Waroux, together with the people of Werfengeis and a multitude from other groups on one side, and the lineage of the Awans, with the castellan of Warémme and the people of Hanef and their other supporters on the other, met at Dommartin. There, in a pitched battle fought on foot, a terrible conflict took place; but at last victory fell to the Awans and their supporters. On the opposing side fell Henry of Hermale, John of Landriis, John of Cervo, Lambert of Hardwemont, John Polens of Waroux, Helin of Latiens, knights, and many other worthy men of Werfengeis; among the other noble lineages, more than forty fell [Note: [Col. 0377D] “and,” 1*.], while the rest escaped by flight. On the side of the Awans, however, two brothers of the castellan of Warémme [Col. 0377B] fell by the sword: Arnold, newly made a knight, and Butorus, an esquire, with twelve esquires. And because, as was reported, this conflict had been undertaken while the truces were still in force, the bishop, through mediated agreements, pardoned the offence of the defeated party. But when the people of Liège sought to defend the offence of the prevailing party, the bishop assembled a great army and, aided by the king of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0377D] John.] with eleven counts, advanced against the people of Liège at Crestengueis [Note: [Col. 0377D] Crichegné, near Liège], where the castellan was reconciled to the bishop through negotiations [cf. HOCSEM. II, 14.].

Incid. In the year of the Lord 1327, the bishop, perceiving that he could not resist with his own armed men the violence of the city and country of Liège, sought the assistance of the Roman pontiff. When this became known, the people of Liège sent solemn envoys [Col. 0377C] to the aforesaid curia, bearing accusatory charges. As they proceeded, when they came near the wood of Vermand, certain friends of the bishop lay in ambush for them; they were seized and held captive for a long time, over which great unrest arose at Liège.

Incid. [HOCS. II, 13.] In the same year Charles [Note: [Col. 0378D] the Fourth.] king of France died, and the queen of Navarre [Note: [Col. 0378D] Joan.] was pregnant. [Note: [Col. 0378D] “He died 1 February 1328.”] After him Philip, son of Charles, count of Valois, brother of King Philip the Fair, was, as the nearest heir, taken up to govern the kingdom as future king, unless a son should be born to the aforesaid pregnant queen, Charles’s widow. But when, after a few months, the queen gave birth to a daughter, Philip was established in the kingdom.

Incid. In the following year (1328), John III, duke of Brabant, besieged the castle of Valkenburg; but an agreement intervening, [Col. 0377D] he withdrew from the siege. In the following year (1329), however, he besieged the castle again and, having captured it, destroyed it.

Incid. [HOCS. II, 14.] In the year of the Lord 1328, the people of Liège reproached the people of Huy through envoys because they had ill observed the letters of confederation made at Fehe between the city and the good towns, since they allowed those who had captured their ambassadors to walk freely within the town of Huy [Col. 0378A] and harboured the bishop there. Therefore, after breaking the aforesaid letters, the people of Liège renounced allegiance to the town of Huy.

Incid. In the same year, on the third day of Pentecost, namely 11 Kalends of June, the people of Liège, Tongeren, and Saint-Trond, with their other confederates, assembled together under arms and destroyed the castle of Gilles de Cervo, a townsman of Huy. Proceeding at dawn on the following morning, they attacked the suburbs of Huy; but while the inhabitants resisted for a long time, the people of Huy, flowing into the town in a multitude of armed men to aid them, occupied the hill of the old castle, in order more forcefully to crush their adversaries from above.

There Raso of Cantumerula, who had been present when the ambassadors of Liège sent to the Roman curia had recently been captured, passed beyond the defile with fifteen chosen esquires; seeing the people of Liège coming toward him on the ascent of the hill, he raised his lance and charged them, but was cut down and fell with his companions. [Col. 0378B] When the valiant bishop of Liège learned this, and understood that his adversaries were gathered on the hill’s slope, on the sixth feria within the octave of Pentecost, which was 6 Kalends of June, he left the town of Huy with a few knights and esquires—namely John of Hardwemont, John of Landriis, and others of the lineages of Waroux and Werfengeis, sixty men in all—and ascended Mount Arbone, commonly called *de kaie te Hoie*. There, seeing his adversaries, the people of Liège, Tongeren, and Saint-Trond, numbering three thousand, and with many of the lineages of Awans and Hosemont joining them, he advanced and courageously took his stand with his few men at the narrow approach to the ascent of that hill.

When the opposing party climbed up boldly toward him, a most severe battle began about the first hour. Although the bishop, greatly pressed by many with only a few men, struck down several with his own hand, his brother Conrad arrived, together with Razo of Printhaghem, the castellan of Musal, and nine others on one side; and from the other side of the hill came Reyner of Arkenteil with fifteen fresh men. Forcing themselves in at the bishop’s flanks and breaking through at the front of the conflict, they struck down many of the adversaries. Seeing this, very many of the people of Liège attempted to climb the slopes of the hill in order to crush the bishop’s men from behind, but were held back by volleys of stones from the people of Huy stationed on the hilltop, the stones being brought by women. Thus, as the battle continued from the first hour until [Col. 0378D] the ninth, victory went to the bishop. There fell from the lineages of Awans and Hosemont, together with other supporters, John lord of Hanef, Baldwin of Genef, and Amelius of Bovengistier, commander of the army of the town of Saint-Trond, whom the bishop struck down with the weapon he held in his hand while the man was reviling him.

Many famous esquires also fell there, among them Stephen of Zittert, master of the commune [Col. 0379A] of Saint-Trond. On his return he had intended to impose many burdens upon our monastery, but the unbridled horse on which he rode carried him into the midst of the enemy, and left him slain and thrown to the ground. Thus, after many of the Liège party had been captured and three hundred men killed, the rest, noblemen and commoners alike, turned their backs in flight. The people of Huy, standing above on the hill and awaiting the outcome of the battle, pursued and despoiled them; but at the bishop’s command they refrained from slaughter. On the bishop’s side only five men fell.

In the conflict of this battle, as some asserted, Saint George was seen armed and riding through the air above the bishop’s army. For this reason the bishop afterward ordered the feast of Saint George to be celebrated, although it had not previously been [Col. 0379B] observed as a feast.

Incid. In the same month, on 3 Kalends of June, the day after Trinity Sunday, the people of Liège, Tongeren, and Saint-Trond, with the lineages of Awans and Hosemont, again took the field under arms and destroyed the granges [Note: [Col. 0379D] *grange*: barn.] and dwellings of worthy men who had earlier assisted the bishop.

Incid. In the following month, on 3 Kalends of July, which was the day of the sacrament, the people of Liège again marched out with the people of Tongeren and assigned the bishop and his supporters a battlefield. But when they perceived that these were prepared to resist, they returned home. On that same day the whole commune of Saint-Trond, having marched in arms as far as beyond the River Jechora [Note: [Col. 0379D] The Jere, which flows into the Meuse.] near Warémme in support of the people of Liège and Tongeren against the bishop, rested about the dinner hour and attended to feasting. Having separated somewhat from one another, they chose pleasant green places to sit. When the cry arose, “To arms! To arms!”, all gathered into battle array and stood courageously. But when their army commander, the elder Eustace of Halmale, relying on the steadfastness of the people of Saint-Trond, went forward with a few of them to scout out the enemy’s ambushes, the townsmen of Saint-Trond suspected that out of fear he had turned to flight from them, and began to scatter.

Before they could return to battle array, Lord John of Hardwemont, with a few of his Waroux and Werfengeis men, charged them, and they immediately turned their backs. There, while few resisted, one hundred men fell and about thirty were captured. Many also escaped at the entrance to the castle; some escaped by fording [Col. 0379D] to the bank. Finally, very many of our townsmen, wounded and unable to flee because their breath was cut off with panting, were slaughtered alive and stripped naked by robbers who accompanied the townsmen from the town itself as though they were friends. Many who had not been mortally injured by enemies perished at the hands of the robbers. A few days later five of these robbers were seized in the town. Four were dragged by horses and placed alive upon wheels; the fifth, because he belonged to honourable [Col. 0380A] magnates of this town, was not dragged to the place of the condemned, but was led away bound. The wife of one of them, who was called Merquard, took part in such throat-cuttings.

In the same month, the people of Liège and Tongeren and their accomplices of the lineages of Awans and Hosemont again ranged through the country of Hesbaye and the county of Looz with a multitude of armed men, seeking to destroy and expel from the country all who adhered to the bishop, together with the bishop himself. Thus, after destroying castles here and there, on the feast of the Translation of Saint Benedict (11 July), they burned and destroyed the tower of Landriis with all the buildings there. Afterwards, on the feast of Saint Margaret (12 July), they destroyed the castle of Here [Note: [Col. 0379D] Héron, near Huy.] and burned the entire village.

Incid. In the same year, in August, these same people besieged the castle of Hardwemont [Col. 0380B] [Note: [Col. 0379D] Hargimont.]. When it was finally surrendered to them, they destroyed it about the feast of Saint Giles; likewise they overthrew the towers at Velrois [Note: [Col. 0380D] Velroux, near Liège.] and Oborn [Note: [Col. 0380D] “Perhaps Obourg?”] (1 September 1328). Indeed, they destroyed villages and strongholds everywhere to such an extent that scarcely any place of refuge remained for the bishop and his supporters, apart from the town of Huy alone, where he and the chapter of Liège, with the secondary churches and courts of Liège, and the lineages of Waroux and Werfengeis, held a secure refuge.

Incid. In the same year, on 7 Kalends of October, the feast of Saint Firmin, the count of Guelders [Note: [Col. 0380D] Reynald II.] came with a multitude of armed men to help the bishop of Liège at the village of Huselt, in order to avenge the injuries inflicted on the bishop by the people of Liège. While they were pitching their tents, at the hour of Vespers [Col. 0380C] the people of Liège and Tongeren unexpectedly came upon them while they were unaware, wishing to crush them by surprise. Before the bishop and his men had armed themselves, the men of Guelders resisted bravely; but as the others prevailed by force, some of the Guelders men fell. When they were almost compelled to turn their backs, the bishop charged the people of Liège with a strong force. The men of Guelders recovered their strength and gave him assistance as though about to engage anew. After a long and very fierce conflict, victory at last fell to the bishop and the count of Guelders. Twelve hundred men of Liège and Tongeren fell there; four hundred of them were captured by the men of Guelders, while the rest fled.

Incid. In the same month the bishop, with the people of Huy and the lineages of Waroux and Werfengeis, joined by a few other strong men and the count of Guelders, besieged the town of Tongeren [cf. HOCSEM. II, 15]. But the count was unwilling, at the bishop’s urging, to continue in the siege and instead returned home with eighty of the wealthier men as captives, contrary to the law of war, as was said. The bishop saw that the people of Tongeren were courageously fortifying their gates and defences from within against the erected engines, using earth and stones; and the people of Huy were unwilling to attack them. Therefore, at the urging [Col. 0381A] of princes, though unwillingly, he agreed with the people of Liège and Tongeren to negotiate peace.

At last the people of Liège and Tongeren were reconciled with their lord through payment of fifty thousand livres tournois. When he ceased attacking the town, they promised henceforth to inflict no troubles upon their lord the bishop; not to violate the praiseworthy and ancient customs of the country; and never from that hour rashly to presume to overturn judgments of the aldermen rendered in any place. Hostages from Liège and Tongeren were sent to the town of Huy to remain there until documents had been drawn up and seals attached.

About this time, a few townsmen of Saint-Trond who appeared favourable to their lord the bishop, fearing the attack of the masters [Col. 0381B] of the commune of Saint-Trond, moved for protection, many of them being sheriffs, aldermen, and officials, to the episcopal village of Alken. On this account the aforesaid masters of the commune sought some of these men at night with armed force while they rested in their own houses, but the latter escaped as best they could through back doors. They also violently seized the goods of others who had fled the town.

Therefore the bishop and his supporters, seeing that the people of Liège and Tongeren and their accomplices had humbly submitted to peace and reconciliation under agreed conditions, while the people of Saint-Trond alone, although they had recently been defeated at Warémme by the bishop’s supporters, did not seek reconciliation, devised with his confidential advisers a surprise attack upon the town itself. At dawn, armed men were to proceed through the ditches from the new houses, along the bottom of the ditch to the bridge at the Cloppem gate, and thus seize the town, because its defences were weaker there. [Col. 0381C] This, however, was not carried into effect, because negotiations for peace took place soon afterward, as will appear below. Because of this plan secretly to seize the town of Saint-Trond by surprise, a very strong tower was built some years later between the Cloppem gate and the Cattle Gate, so that hostile access from that side might be repelled.

Incid. Concerning the antipope. In that same or the preceding year [Note: [Col. 0381D] In this very year.], a certain Friar Minor [Note: [Col. 0381D] Peter of Corbara.] allowed himself, under the pretext of a fraudulent privilege of the Roman clergy, to be crowned pope and called Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0381D] V.]. Having made cardinals, he attached himself as pope to Louis, duke of Bavaria, who three years earlier had been crowned with the imperial diadem by the same fraudulent privilege [Note: [Col. 0381D] “On 17 January 1328 Louis was crowned emperor at Rome.”], as though he were emperor [cf. HOCSEM. II, 15]. Wherever Louis captured cities, there he resided as pope and conferred benefices. After he had persisted in this condition for nearly five years [Note: [Col. 0382D] Only until the following year, 1329.], he was brought by a certain prince [Note: [Col. 0382D] The count of Donoratico.], in whom he trusted, after the prince had received a large sum of money [Col. 0382A] from Pope John, to Avignon, before the presence of the true pontiff John himself. With a rope tied around his neck, he humbly confessed his guilt and publicly abjured his heretical presumption, and was absolved. Held in honourable custody, he died not long afterward.

Incid. In the same year (1328), on the vigil of Saint Bartholomew (23 August), when the count of Flanders [Note: [Col. 0382D] Louis I.] had been driven from the county of Flanders by the insolence of the commune, Philip [Note: [Col. 0382D] VI.] of Valois, king of France, entered Flanders and prevailed after fighting a most fierce battle against the Flemings. Fourteen thousand Flemish men died there, and thus he freely restored to the count his own land, subdued on every side. This happened in the second year of his reign.

[Col. 0382B]

14. In the year of the Lord 1329, Adulphus, bishop of Liège, coming to his senses, repented of the injuries which he had inflicted upon our monastery. He observed that the people of Saint-Trond, with whom he himself had fourteen years earlier continued in the Roman curia a lawsuit begun against this monastery, still persisted in hardness, although in the preceding year the people of Liège and the other towns had returned to an agreement of peace with him. Therefore, when the abbot of Saint-Trond came one day to his court at Alken on business, the bishop spoke of the injuries which [Note: [Col. 0381] “which,” 1*.] the people of Saint-Trond had inflicted upon him, and the abbot spoke of the three-year suspension of litigation that had not expired. Through God’s inspiration, both became friends and unanimously agreed to negotiate peace, not separately, but jointly with the people of Saint-Trond, [Col. 0382C] now humbled by war.

After some days the people of Saint-Trond, realizing that their lords had become close friends, sent honourable and prudent men to negotiate an agreement of peace. After long negotiations with the townsmen, the lord abbot refused a hearing so long as they did not lay down the commune. Then, having taken counsel, they sent two honourable townsmen to the New Court and presented to Abbot Adam letters of the commune sealed with the seals of the bishop and chapter of Liège. When he had annulled them, he added: “Look! Look! On account of these letters I have spent more than ten thousand florins.”

In the same year, on 29 December, when the bishop of Liège with his counsellors, and Abbot Adam with his friends, had assembled at the New Court, [Col. 0382D] a great negotiation was discussed at length [Note: [Col. 0381] “tractus,” 1*.], so much so that three honourable mediators rode five times from the New Court to the townsmen, and back again to the New Court, from nightfall until twilight of the following day. At last peace was confirmed in this manner: they promised never to raise up the commune, nor to accept one offered without the consent [Col. 0383A] of both lords, and the rest, as is set forth in detail in the letters preserved in our archives.

Furthermore, by consent of all, the following solemn procession was held. On the appointed day, while Lords Adulphus of Liège and Adam, abbot of this place, were at the New Court with many distinguished men, the whole people assembled in the marketplace and proceeded in the following order to meet their lords as far as the field opposite the mill of our monastery at Merwile. First went the captains of the dissolved commune, together with two hundred of the more honourable townsmen, stripped of their outer clothes and walking in shirts and breeches, bareheaded and barefoot, carrying unsheathed swords laid point-first upon their breasts. The remaining townsmen followed in their clothing. [Col. 0383B] When they reached the said field, they fell down upon bent knees and humbly begged forgiveness from their lords with one voice. Having been kindly received into favour by their lords, and freely pardoned all the enormities of their excesses, the bishop graciously took one of their swords by its hilt in his hand, brandished it, and said: “See: if it pleased me, I would now kill you.”

When these things had been done, the letter of the peace agreement was publicly read before all in the vernacular, according to its entire tenor. All approved it with one voice and, raising their right hands, bound themselves by oath, for themselves and their successors, not to contravene it in the future, under penalty of automatic excommunication. Then, following the bishop and abbot with [Col. 0383C] their company, they proceeded to the town. When they had entered within the town gate called the New Gate, the aforesaid lords, seeing the procession of priests and clerics coming to meet them, humbly dismounted from their horses. With the aforesaid townsmen proceeding before them in their nakedness, they entered the monastery; and, after the hymn *Te Deum* had been sung with antiphons, all returned joyfully to their own homes.

Likewise. In the same year, when Lord John of Follonia, priest [Note: [Col. 0383] “J. of F., priest,” in erasure.], whose father had received as a fief from Abbot Thomas five *bonuaria* of land bought with money of our monastery, on condition that—because he was among the greater and leading men of this town—he would faithfully provide the abbot with assistance and support at a suitable time, as he had in fact effectively done, was confined to a bed of sickness: he conveyed the aforesaid five *bonuaria* of feudal land into the hands of Lord John of Diest, conventual prior of this monastery of Saint-Trond, to this end: that from the revenues of the aforesaid land there should first be paid six perpetual measures of rye, as a refectory pittance, only for those eating there on Wednesdays. He further willed and ordained that the surplus revenues should be faithfully distributed by the almoner, at the feast of Saint Nicholas, in bread to the poor at the gate, on behalf of the pittance-master of our aforesaid monastery then in office. To these ordinances [Col. 0384A] Lord Abbot Adam, with many vassals present, consented in every respect on the vigil of All Saints.

Likewise. In his time, Abbot Adam granted our property at Kerkim to his brother, Godfrey of Kerkim, an esquire, for cultivation—not permanently, but temporarily. After the abbot’s death, the children of the aforesaid Godfrey claimed to hold that property for permanent cultivation, but this was untrue. Abbots should therefore beware of granting monastic property even temporarily to their relatives for cultivation.

Likewise. Before this abbot’s time, there had from ancient days been revenues belonging to the office of cellarer, distinct from the abbot’s revenues. From them the cellarer supplied the convent with food in the refectory and distributed to each person his portion of wine wherever it was due. [Col. 0384B] But after this man became abbot, those revenues were incorporated into the abbot’s revenues. He provides the convent with bread, wine, ale, fuel, salt, table provisions, towels, servants, and the other necessities customarily supplied.

During this abbot’s time, his cellar contained excellent red wines, which the elders preferred to all other wines. When the abbot learned this, he proposed that, if they preferred to drink such desirable wine, it would please him greatly. But when the convent asked from what land this wine had come, and learned that it was not from the Rhine, they would by no means drink it, for they asserted that only Rhine wine constituted their allowance.

Likewise. This abbot acquired for the convent, as a Friday refectory pittance, twenty-six hereditary measures of rye from and above our tithe at Borlo, just as his predecessor William I had earlier granted another twenty-six measures which he had acquired. Thus the convent has there from the said tithe fifty-two hereditary measures of rye. He also caused the hall of our residence at Dungh to be extended eastward by the width of one arch-bay. He likewise erected from the foundations both the house of the stronghold there and the stronghold’s house at the New Court; on account of the building of these he was accused at the aforesaid visitation.

Incid. In the year of the Lord 1330 Engelbert, canon of Liège and paternal uncle of Adulphus, bishop of Liège, who was said to have procured many injuries against our monastery, came to us and stayed overnight. [Col. 0384D] As he was approaching death from an abscess in his throat, he summoned the lord abbot to himself and humbly begged to be forgiven for the adversities which he had striven to inflict upon the monastery. He firmly promised that, if he could recover from that illness, he would henceforth desire with all his strength to be a faithful promoter of this church. A few days later, having devoutly received the sacraments of the Church, and with his illness worsening, scarcely able to speak [Note: [Col. 0383] “eliqui,” 1*.], he requested burial here and died. He was honourably buried before the altar of Blessed Mary, in the monastery apse, to the right of the chapel of Saint Trond.

Incid. In the same year, when peace between [Col. 0385A] the bishop, Adam, and the citizens of Liège had been negotiated, the canons of Liège and of the secondary churches each returned to reside in their colleges at Liège; and the peace agreement that had been reached was confirmed by charters.

15. In the year of the Lord 1330, Adam of Ardinghem, abbot of this place, after governing vigorously, died in the thirty-third year of his prelacy, on 8 Ides of August, about midnight, having devoutly received communion and extreme unction. On the third following day, his body was buried with solemn obsequies in the middle of the nave of this monastery, in one tomb with his predecessor. [Col. 0386A] This abbot left adequate provisions to his monastery. He owed nothing to any creditor for provisions or other necessities, and a great sum of money was thought to be kept in his archives. When these were opened by the prior and elders, with the straps of the money-bags hanging outside their fastenings, many empty bags were found; only fifty pounds of old gros were discovered there. On this account grave suspicion rested upon his household relatives.

## Concerning the Deeds of Abbot Amelius

[Col. 0385]

[Col. 0385B] **1.** In the same year of the Lord 1330, the eighteenth year of Adolph, bishop of Liège, while the Empire was vacant because of the excommunicated Louis of Bavaria [Note: Baurum, 1*.], Amelius of Sconouwen, otherwise called Masscereil, was elected abbot of this place on 13 November; and, after a few intervening days, he was consecrated in the presence there of the abbots of Saint James at Liège and Saint Giles. It happened. [HOCSEM. II, 16.] In the following year Peter Andricas, who had long governed the community of Liège as its captain, was outlawed at Vothem with thirty-nine of his supporters by judgment of the aldermen. It happened. In the same year the bailiff of Tienen [Note: that is, of Tirlemont] pursued, on the order of John, duke of Brabant, the cloths of merchants of the town of Saint Trond which had been conveyed to the fair. When the wagoners had deposited them for protection in a nearby church [Col. 0385C] situated within the borders of Brabant, they were violently seized and carried off by that same official. When certain merchants of the aforesaid town resisted the plunderers, they were grievously wounded. Therefore the duke was required by the church and city of Liège, through ambassadors [Note: See Hocsem II, 17, where [lacuna] was one of these envoys. Compare also the passage of John the priest in Chapeaville II, 411.], to restore what had been taken, lest they be compelled to commit like acts against Brabant [Note: conpallantur, 1*.]. The duke replied: “I am prepared to negotiate with the bishop; but I shall grant no truce to the men of Saint Trond, who have injured me.”

It happened. [HOCSEM. II, 17.] In the year of the Lord 1332, on 23 April, Bishop Adolph; John, king of Bohemia; the archbishop of Cologne [Note: Waleram]; the counts of Guelders, Jülich [Note: William], Bar [Note: Edward], Namur [Note: John], and Looz [Note: Louis]; and the lord of Valkenburg [Col. 0385D] [Note: Reynald], with their followers, renounced their fealty to the duke of Brabant. All of them, except the archbishop of Cologne and the count of Bar, having taken counsel with the leading men of the territory of Liège because of injuries inflicted on them by the duke, entered Brabant. They burned Hannut and the adjacent villages.

It happened. In the same month, on 26 April, Quasimodo Sunday, Bishop Adolph, after the recently concluded reconciliation with the territory, accompanied by the aforesaid princes, entered the city through the gate of Saint Walburga—clergy and people having gone out in procession to meet him. He had been absent from the city for seven years [Note: obsens, 1*.]. Dismounting from his horse and entering the chapel of the aforesaid virgin, he put on his pontifical vestments. Then, with a solemn procession preceding him, he was honorably received by the city and entered the monastery of Saint Lambert.

It happened. On the fourth day of the same month the aforesaid princes, together with the count of Bar, assembled at Liège; and on the sixth day following, with the bishop and the army of Liège, their banner going before them, they ranged through Brabant for eight days, ravaging it with fire and plunder [Col. 0386C] as far as Mont-Saint-Guibert [Note: Mont-Saint-Guibert] and Jodoigne, burning part of the suburbs of Jodoigne. Duke John, with a multitude of armed men, sheltered within the cloister of Heylissem; and, after being invested there with the belt of knighthood [Note: The author is mistaken; as appears from Hocsem, several men were invested with the belt.], no one defended his cause in any respect. There, through the efforts of the count of Hainaut [Note: John], although the duke himself resisted, a truce was established until after the feast of John the Baptist. Thus on the day of Servatius everyone returned home. [Note: The letters concerning this peace were drawn up on 11 May 1332; see Ernst V, 40.]

It happened. This dispute was settled by the arbitration of Philip, king of France, in regard to the grounds of complaint arising from the injuries which the same duke had inflicted upon the bishop and the town of Saint Trond, as follows: first, the duke was to make satisfaction to the bishop of Liège for the injuries inflicted, and then the interdict was to be revoked; second, the damage suffered by the townsmen of Saint Trond through the cloths taken from them was to be restored. Both matters were carried out as the king had adjudged. But because no fitting recompense [Note: *récompense*, “compensation”] was obtained for the injuries inflicted by the duke upon the aforesaid counts, the duke of Brabant was again renounced by them.

It happened. In the year of the Lord 1333 John, duke of Brabant, sent ambassadors, bearing supplicatory letters from the queen of France [Note: Joan] and supported by very large sums of money, to Pope John XXII, seeking the establishment of a new diocese and episcopal see at the Brabantine town of Leuven; but he obtained nothing.

It happened. [HOCS. II, 18.] In the same year Bishop Adolph and the chapter of Liège sold to the count of Flanders [Note: Louis] the town of Mechelen, with its dependent appurtenances, for the sum of 100,000 royal coins, to be perpetually redeemable by the church of Liège under feudal right.

**2.** In the same year, the quarrel between Bishop Adolph and John, duke of Brabant, having been renewed, the aforesaid bishop came to our town of Saint Trond with John, king of Bohemia, who was assisting him [Col. 0387B] with fourteen counts, and with a multitude of armed men. From there, in the morning, with the aforesaid princes, on the Monday after the Ascension of the Lord (14 May), he attacked Brabant, plundering and destroying many villages as far as the vicinity of Jodoigne. The duke himself was within the cloister of Heylissem, situated on the border of Brabant, with some [lacuna] of a ditch raised around it. Toward evening, as the bishop and the other princes returned to the town, one of the knights of the king of Bohemia, taking with him the bailiff of Jodoigne as a prisoner, placed him in fetters in the stable of this monastery beside his horses. At daybreak he led him outside the court of our cloister and handed him over to the bishop’s schout to be guarded. When this became known to the prior and convent, they immediately [Col. 0387C] approached the bishop and urgently demanded the return of the man carried away from the place of our immunity. The bishop at once summoned his schout, restored and delivered the aforesaid captive, freed, to the site of this cloister; and thus that man, giving thanks to our convent, returned free to his own home on the following day.

It happened. In the same year, near the end of January, the quarrel between the Brabanters and the men of Liège having been renewed, Conrad of the Mark, brother of Bishop Adolph, together with the men of Saint Trond—whose army commander was the knight Raso of Printaghe—attacked by force of arms the village at the fortress of Landen, which the duke had fortified. After a hard battle there, the men of Saint Trond climbed over the defences, put the rebels there to flight, killed before the barrier the valiant knight Sir Henry called “the Worthy” of Winde, together with others, took nearly twenty-five men prisoner, plundered the village, and burned it.

It happened. About the same time, after the count of Flanders had justly renounced his fealty to John, duke of Brabant, because the latter had allied himself against him with the men of Mechelen, the aforesaid duke fortified the famous cloister of Affligem as [Col. 0388A] a military stronghold. From the summit of its lofty tower, everything occurring in the market square of the town of Aalst could be clearly observed. Accordingly, after Duke John’s guards had departed from the cloister stronghold, the army of the count of Flanders, William [Note: Rather, Louis of Nevers, who was count of Flanders at that time], angered by this, burned and destroyed the cloister together with its church. Then the abbot and convent, after taking counsel, placed many of their fellow monks in their priories and lived in the town of Brussels.

It happened. [ID. II, 21.] In the same year the count of Jülich received the surrendered castle of Rode beyond the Meuse, on condition that the duke of Brabant did not dislodge the count from the siege within fifteen days. When this did not occur, the castle was handed over to the count.

It happened. On 5 May 1335 peace was confirmed between the lineages of the Awans [Awaus] and the Waroux [Warois], with all their kin and descendants on both sides. Since they had raged against one another in bloody killings for more than thirty-eight years, at last, through the efforts of the chapter of Liège and the entire territory, it was solemnly decreed, under the perpetual penalties of retaliation and banishment from the country, that henceforth none of the aforesaid descendants should rise against another under any pretext of waging war. Compelled by fear of this statute, they chose six honorable men from one side of the adversaries and the same number from the other, who made compensatory settlements for those slain on either side. By mutual obligation they decreed that the authority of these twelve chosen men to punish violators of the peace should remain in perpetuity; whenever one of them died, another from his lineage was immediately [Col. 0388C] to be substituted.

It happened. In the same year Pope John XXII died, and Benedict was elected in that year. He was consecrated in the following year.

It happened. In the year of the Lord 1336, Louis of Looz having died without offspring, the chapter of Liège showed from ancient charters that the county had devolved upon the church of Saint Lambert. [HOCS. II, 22.] Against them Thierry, lord of Heinsberg, nephew through the eldest sister of this Louis [Note: Matilda married Godfrey, lord of Heinsberg; see Mantel, p. 248. Compare also the passage of John the priest published by Chapeaville II, 437.], asserted that the county belonged to him, since he was the eldest nephew; and a long dispute arose over this.

It happened. In the same year Pope Benedict wrote most severe letters of rebuke to Adolph, bishop of Liège, because he was said to neglect the rights of his church on behalf of his nephew through his sister, this Thierry [Note: Thierry’s father, Thierry, had married Cunigunda, sister of the bishop of Liège. See Mantel, p. 265.]. The case over the county was litigated for a long time in the Roman curia, but finally Thierry was established in the county in the year of the Lord 1340 through a legate sent to the region. [Note: The text had read MCCCXLIII, but the final III has now been erased.]

It happened. [ID. II, 23.] In the following year John, duke of Brabant, was excommunicated and cursed at Liège because of the many offences he had committed against the church; and the *Media vita* [“In the midst of life”] was sung against him [Col. 0389A] in the church of Saint Lambert.

It happened. In the same year the king of England [Note: Edward III] came into Brabant. Afterwards he came to Louis, duke of Bavaria, who styled himself emperor and whom Pope John had earlier excommunicated. About the same time, the aforesaid king, as vicar of the emperor, sat in judgment at the village of Herk, within a grain-house. There the duke of Brabant, among the other princes, held a drawn sword above the king’s head as margrave [Note: that is, *marchio*, “margrave”] of the Empire.

**3.** In the year of the Lord 1340 Abbot Amelius demolished the old, ruinous hall with its appurtenances at the New Court, and rebuilt a loftier new one with its appurtenances, square in plan, upon a stone wall extending from the bottom of the fishpond. To it he added a stone chapel [Col. 0389B] with a stone vault, likewise an altar consecrated in honor of [lacuna of three or four letters], and a chimney in its uppermost gable. He later deeply regretted that, passing over a more necessary building within the cloister, he had built that residence so expensively outside it.

In the same year the same abbot began to complete up to its summit the great middle tower of the monastery, which his predecessor Abbot Adam had formerly raised, after its collapse, from the foundations to beyond half its height, by building up squared walls. By raising above it a lofty wooden roof, covered with cut stone, he made it conspicuous from afar; and he completed it in nearly two years.

In the following year, when grave disputes arose between the bishopric of Liège and John, duke of Brabant, our townsmen, anticipating that this town would be besieged by the aforesaid duke and wishing to avoid the danger of famine, considered how they might acquire a mill ordinarily turned by teams of horses, which could not be destroyed by the missiles of stone-throwing engines. Having taken counsel, they concluded that nowhere could such a structure be more suitably placed than in the court and place of our immunity, commonly called the Vrythof, since they imagined it to lie at the middle and centre within the circuit of the walls. Therefore, approaching the aforesaid abbot, they obtained what they desired, binding themselves as follows: after the war had ended, if, following a warning from the abbot himself or any successor of his, they did not remove the mill and its house at their own cost within two months, then thenceforth the whole [Col. 0389D] structure would freely devolve into the possession of the monastery. And so they built it with permission; concerning this we possess letters.

**4.** In the year of the Lord 1340, when our town of Saint Trond was burdened with heavy debts in the form of payments [Col. 0390A], so that the aldermen said that they could not sustain the town’s burdens, unless its temporal lords supplied appropriate counsel, Lords Bishop Adolph and Abbot Amelius, having taken counsel with the townsmen and with the consent of the entire town, chose—or consented to the choice of—twelve honorable townsmen. They were to collect the revenues and levies [Note: *la taille*, “the levy”] from the whole town and, for its benefit, dispose of them in this matter without the aldermen. Because the income derived from saleable goods [Note: A contemporary hand wrote another word after erasing the one originally present; shortly afterwards the same hand supplied in the margin the words “impositions of levies.”] [Note: Revenues from goods for sale.] did not suffice to pay such heavy liabilities, it was unanimously ordained that every year all the townsmen should pay levy-assessments according to the value of their property: the wealthier men seven florins, and then decreasing amounts, until the payments were reduced. In order that the foregoing might have greater [Col. 0390B] force, the aforesaid lords, at the townsmen’s request, consented that the common pastures be leased out for eighteen years. [Note: They were to be granted at rent.] In return for this favor the townsmen gave the bishop of Liège 1,600 florins in ready money, and promised the abbot in their open letters that, upon his demand, they would pay him 1,100 florins.

It happened. [HOCSEM. II, 27.] On 25 April 1342 Pope Benedict XII, of the Cistercian Order, died. He was succeeded by Clement VI [Note: quartus, “fourth,” 1*.], of the Order of Saint Benedict and a native of Limoges, who was consecrated on 7 May. In the same year, on 7 June, at the [lacuna of approximately seven letters] hour of the day, the famous town of Mechelen was almost wholly reduced to ashes.

It happened. In the same year Godfrey, the only son of Thierry, lord of Heinsberg, the future count [Col. 0390C] of Looz, fell in a military engagement against pagans. Through his mother he was the nephew of Adolph, bishop of Liège.

**5.** In the year of the Lord 1344, when this town had become so burdened with innumerable debts through the incompetent administration of its aldermen and councillors that, had the diligence of guarantors [Note: Sureties, guarantors.] not provided against it, it would have fallen altogether into desolation, the people were summoned by the ban-bell. The bishop, the abbot being absent because of illness, entered our court called the Vrythof and, with the townsmen’s consent, caused the aldermen then present to be taken away as prisoners: some to be committed to the residence of his schout, and others to the house of the abbot’s schout, so that after mature deliberation they might be corrected for their misconduct.

[Col. 0390D] But a few months later, in the same year, on 3 November [ID. II, 30], Bishop Adolph himself died at the castle of Clermont, which he had acquired, after having governed the church of Liège vigorously for thirty-four years. After his death Engelbert, provost of Liège and his nephew through a brother, was elected bishop.

Concerning the same matter. In the following year, 1345, the same bishop-elect and Abbot Amelius, wishing to bring to completion what had been begun in the preceding year by Bishop Adolph with the knowledge of his chapter, concerning the correction of aldermen and councillors, removed the aforesaid aldermen and councillors from the offices of alderman and councillor because of their misconduct in governing the town. With the consent of the whole community of this town, they disciplined them and punished them by a monetary penalty. The aldermen and councillors promised never again to involve themselves in the government of this town unless with the consent of both lords and the townsmen; and so they were released from captivity.

In the same year Engelbert, the bishop-elect, became bishop of Liège with the consent of Pope Clement VI [Col. 0391B] and was consecrated.

It happened. In the same year the plague epidemic, otherwise called the groin-pestilence, after it had ranged through various overseas kingdoms of the gentiles, at last passed through the kingdoms of Christians—through Gaul, Alemania, Germany, England, and various other provinces—and struck down an innumerable multitude of people. It came in this manner. Growths, especially in young people, arose in the glandular parts of the body, for the most part in the form of a nut or date; these were immediately followed by an unmeasurable burning of fevers, so that people frequently died within three days. If anyone survived three days, however, he had hope of life. [Note: The words from “Growths arose” through “hope of life” are read almost verbatim in Paul the Deacon II, 4.] This plague was contagious to such a degree that not only the touch or breath of the sick, but even their coverings [Col. 0391C] and clothing infected the healthy. From the present year onward it endured intermittently, now in this province and now in that, until the following year of the Lord 1383.

Concerning this plague it is read in the annals, under the year of the Lord 546, the eighteenth year of the reign of Justinian I, that it raged after the death of Saint Remigius of Reims from Alemania as far as Francia; likewise afterwards in the provinces of Romania in the year of the Lord 563, the thirty-sixth year of the reign of the aforesaid Justinian; likewise in the year of the Lord 592, the ninth year of the reign of Maurice, in the first year of the pontificate of Saint Gregory the pope. To him the mercy of God concerning the groin-pestilence was revealed, because he saw an angel standing upon the summit of a high castle, who lowered an upraised naked sword and enclosed it in its sheath.

It happened. In the same year William [Note: the Fourth], count of Holland [Col. 0391D] and Hainaut [ID. II, 31], under the pretext of invading the land of the Frisians, bought from the citizens of Utrecht a large quantity of provisions and arrows. Having obtained these, he assembled a strong force of armed men, unexpectedly declared war on those same citizens, and besieged their city. But, as they resisted stoutly and the count perceived that they still possessed provisions sufficient for two years, after a long siege he concluded a peace agreement with them.

It happened. [Col. 0392A] In the same year, against the counsel of his uncle Lord John of Beaumont, the aforesaid count entered Frisia on 26 September. Excessively hasty [Note: festivus, 1*.], with scarcely a third of his men—and with two divisions not yet advancing [Note: aggressuris, 1*.] to his aid—he engaged in a field battle in a place enclosed by embankments. There, as the Frisians gradually came upon them and dug through the embankments, the count with his company, caught fast in muddy mire as the floodwaters increased, was killed without any resistance at all. Those who, turning their backs, tried to escape the swords of the Frisians sank into the deep waters like stones. Hence these verses:

> A thousand, C three times, X four times, and five once—on Cosmas’ night—  
> Holland and Zeeland mourn, and Frisia also deprives them of their count.

[Col. 0392B] Likewise, a single verse:

> On Cosmas’ night mourned the Hollanders whom Frisia struck down.

It happened. [Hocsem II, 32.] In the same year [Note: According to Hocsem, in the year 1346], the abbot of Saint Nicaise of Ghent came to Liège by command of the supreme pontiff with apostolic letters. He absolved Thierry, lord of Heinsberg—who had litigated against the chapter of Liège for nearly ten years over the county of Looz—from excommunication, and lifted the interdict which had long been imposed throughout the whole territory of Looz.

6. In the same year the people of Liège, together with the good towns of the whole territory of Liège, had conspired against Bishop Engelbert; and they entered into reciprocal leagues and brotherly confederacies with the Flemings, promising to render each other timely aid. Therefore, [Col. 0392C] seeing himself driven out on every side, the bishop sent word to the people of Saint-Trond that he wished in every respect to deal graciously with them concerning their offences and excesses against himself, if they would consent to grant him peaceful entry into and departure from their town. But they were altogether unwilling to comply.

When Lord Abbot Amelius saw that the townsmen were hardened against the bishop, he made all arrangements and left the town. Going to our manor at Dola, he took with him several aldermen [Note: [Col. 0391] 1* reads adduxit, “brought.”], who remained there with him for a long time; and he maintained them honorably. After some days the bishop, having taken counsel, resolved to outlaw at Vothem the leaders of the people of Liège who opposed him; but the people of Liège by no means permitted this.

Concerning the same matter. In the year of the Lord 1346, in July, Charles, King of the Romans, with the [Col. 0392D] electors of the Holy Empire and a great multitude of princes and armed men, marched with a strong force toward the royal seat at Aachen, in order to be crowned there King of Germany. [Note: He was crowned at Bonn.] Bishop Engelbert of Liège went forth to meet him and, by humble prayers, obtained that the king, with the others accompanying him, should proceed to a place called Vothem. There the aldermen of Liège, sitting as judges, [Col. 0393A] were intending to outlaw the adversaries of, and those who had committed injuries against, the aforesaid bishop.

Near that place the whole city of Liège, together with the people of Huy, stood massed within a ditch raised for their defence, fully armed and ready vigorously to resist the aldermen’s sentence. The aforesaid King Charles, his father the King of Bohemia, and the multitude of their companions had no doubt of gaining victory. But behold: Lord of Valkenburg suddenly broke in and rushed upon the people of Liège with an assault. When the opponents standing in the front gave way before him, he was voluntarily enclosed among the enemy and fell.

After his fall, the people of Liège, who had previously been almost despairing, became more courageous. Attacking from the other side of the battle-line the valiant men of the armies of the Counts of Hainaut [Note: Adolf V.] and Guelders [Note: Reinald III.], they resisted; and there fell among the [Col. 0393B] men of Guelders and Hainaut forty renowned and noble men. This done, that whole gathering of most noble lords turned its back and withdrew without anyone pursuing them, leaving the people of Liège, now victorious, free possession of the field of battle. The people of Saint-Trond took no part in this battle. It happened. [Hocsem, II, 33–34.]

In the same year, on 26 August, Philip, King of France, fought unsuccessfully against Edward, King of England, at Crécy. For when the latter had advanced into territory not [Note: “this” 1*.] far from Amiens, having with him only 3,000 armed men, he found the aforesaid King of the French with 150,000 [Note: “with 150,000” 1*.] mounted men prepared for war. When battle was joined, the French were amazingly struck down, not by weapons at close range but pierced by arrows from afar; and victory fell to the King [Col. 0393C] of England. While the King of France was pulled back from behind by those guarding him, John, King of Bohemia, and the Counts of Alençon [Note: Charles, brother of King Philip.], Flanders, and Blois, together with a multitude of nobles and knights, perished. It happened.

In the same year the people of Liège, together with the other towns of the territory, pursued the noble lords of the land who had assembled at Vothem in aid of the Bishop of Liège, and destroyed their property. On 3 September they besieged the castle of Clermont [Note: On the right bank of the Meuse.]; and, aided by the people of Dinant, on the fifteenth day of the siege they destroyed the castle, surrendered to them with the lives of its defenders spared, down to the ground. It happened.

In that year, on 4 September, after an interdict in favor of the Bishop of Liège had been publicly proclaimed at Liège by apostolic authority, the major and minor churches, together with certain [Col. 0393D] religious houses, not without fear silenced their organs. Against this the people of Liège appealed; the restored abbot of Belli, the brothers of the Valley of Scholars, the Dominicans, Carmelites, and Cross-bearers, as well as many secular priests, adhered to them in one fashion or another. It happened.

In the same month the castle of Hamal was besieged. After it had for some time been attacked with mangonels [Note: A mangonel: a projectile-throwing engine.], it was finally destroyed, the lives of the defenders being spared.

About the same time [Col. 0394A] our townsmen, not fearing to violate the promise by which they had bound themselves to observe the peace made in the new court, established a commune in the town on their own authority, infringing many jurisdictions of their lords. Their adviser and supporter was a certain priest named John, called of Merwile, a learned man and capable in many things, but to his own harm, because he turned every grace bestowed upon him by God not toward God but toward habitual vices. Among other deeds which he committed, after stirring up the entire town to arms, he himself went armed to burn the dwellings of many men from the territory of Loon.

Likewise. About the same time Matthias of Bernym, master of the commune, when one day the sluice of Willo’s meadow, otherwise called Wilbant, which was customarily shut with the key of our monastery, was opened for a reason, [Col. 0394B] immediately drew out the bolt of our key and inserted another on behalf of the town.

About the same time Brustem was burned by our people, and the village of Bautershoven was set on fire by knights and men-at-arms from Hesbaye who favored the Bishop of Liège. Fifteen men from our town, having gone farther out in defence against the burning, were killed in the fields short of the aforesaid village. Several of them resisted courageously, though in vain.

In the aforementioned year, on 2 October, the people of Saint-Trond went to the village of Aelst and burned seven dwellings of honorable men, because those men had assembled at Vothem against the people of Liège and Huy in aid of the bishop. But on their return to the town, when they had turned aside on their way before the manor-house, [Col. 0394C] someone standing within the manor-house provoked them with insulting cries. Angered by this, they came up behind to the manor-house, killed one man of that village before the entrance to the manor-house, rushed into the church, and, with plunder, carried off to the town and imprisoned several honorable men who had fled there for protection. It happened.

In the same year, in October, about the feast of Simon and Jude [Hocsem, II, 34], truces were made between Bishop Engelbert and his party on the one hand, and the people of Liège and their party on the other. These were to last from All Saints’ Day of that year until the same feast of the following year, on the condition that the aldermen of Liège should wholly revoke the judicial sentence which they said they had pronounced against the leaders of the commune of Liège on the day [Col. 0394D] of the battle at Vothem.

Therefore, on the said day of Simon and Jude, 28 October, all the aldermen except one assembled and went out to an open place near the new booths. There, sitting judicially, they revoked the judgment of forfeiture and outlawry which they asserted they had pronounced, saying that certain things had there been omitted which concerned the substance of the case. It happened.

In the year [Col. 0395A] of the Lord 1346, after the death of Louis, Duke of Bavaria, who styled himself emperor and had been excommunicated by Pope John, Charles, the eldest son of John, King of Bohemia, was elected King of the Romans—the fourth of that name. Pope Clement IV [Note: Sixth.] approved that election. It happened.

In the year of the Lord 1347, about the middle of July, the people of Liège, enraged against Lord Rainer of Argenteal, charged him with this: in the preceding month certain men from the territories of Dalhem [Note: Dalhem near Visé.] and Valkenburg, after burning Miremort [Note: Mirmoit.], had unexpectedly killed there 120 men friendly to the people of Liège. Therefore they besieged the aforesaid castle of Argenteal [Note: Argenteau, not far from Liège, on the right bank of the Meuse.] with armed force.

Bishop Engelbert, seeing that the people of Liège had violated the truces proclaimed in the preceding year, now brought over to the military party on his side [Col. 0395B] John, Duke of Brabant, who promised him timely aid against the people of Liège. A great sum of money had first been promised to him, with this added condition: whatever strongholds or liberties his men might take by storm or receive in surrender within the bishopric of Liège, he was not to retain for himself but must freely hand over to the bishop. When this did not escape the notice of the people of Liège, they attacked more insistently the castle which had long been under assault, took it by storm, and demolished it. It happened.

In the same year 1347 [cf. Hocsem, II, 341], the second year of the reign of Charles IV, the people of Liège, Huy, and Dinant, together with the other towns of the territory, knowing that the bishop himself had stirred up many princes of the lands to aid him, set their army in motion. Having gathered together all the men of the territory, commoners as well as soldiers, they pitched camp between the villages of Tourins [Note: Tourines.] and Walevia [Col. 0395C] [Note: Waleffe near Huy.].

The Bishop of Liège, however, was not idle [Note: That is, he pitched camp.].
