He was attended by a multitude of noblemen: the Counts of Guelders, Jülich [Note: William VII.], Loon, the Mark [Note: Adolf II.], and Hainaut, with their brothers, nobles, and the best knights drawn from their counties; also present were Rudolf and Louis, brothers of the Count of Namur, many barons, their subjects, and knights expelled from their country for supporting the bishop. The number of all these was estimated at 100,000 horsemen and 600,000 [Note: Thus 1*.] foot soldiers, counting the army of the Duke of Brabant, which had not yet arrived.

Therefore, on the eve of the vigil of Mary Magdalene, 20 July, the people of Liège and the towns of the territory drew up a battle-line numbering about 250,000. They stood so courageously massed together that the bishop and those aiding him resolved not [Col. 0395D] to engage that day. Messengers were sent, and the next day was appointed to the people of Liège for battle. Thus, at sunset, the people of Liège and the other towns scattered among various neighboring villages for the night’s rest.

But the Bishop of Liège, sleeplessly following the counsel [Col. 0396A] of Thierry, Count of Loon, summoned his men to arms before the first light of dawn; gathering his host, he occupied the open place appointed for battle, 21 July. When this became known, the people of Liège, with the whole territory, came forward successively and hurried to the agreed battlefield, because they had spent the night dispersed among the villages.

When the bishop saw his adversaries arriving successively in separate companies, at the Count’s signal he and a few men of Hesbaye, together with the count and his entire retinue, rushed upon the enemy with trumpets sounding. A most severe battle began. The people of Liège and their allies resisted with the greatest courage, but because scarcely a fourth part of the Liège army was present in that first clash of battle, victory finally went to the bishop and the count, though not without the loss of many of their own men.

When the [Col. 0396B] people of Liège turned their backs in flight, about the first hour of the day the Counts of Guelders and Jülich, and the other aforesaid counts and barons, arrived. Coming after the battle had begun, they attacked the people of Liège and struck down, not without cost to themselves, twelve thousand—and, below and above that number, without measure—who resisted most stoutly.

At last the Duke of Brabant arrived with his son Henry, who had been made lord of the people of Mechelen, and with all the knights, townsmen, and villagers of the whole of Brabant. Arriving over the fields after the battle was ended, they were moved by compassion and gave aid to those mortally wounded.

Concerning the same matter. When the people of Liège, seeking escape, attempted to return home in companies scattered here and there, to win their way out by resistance, and had been struck down at various crossroads, at last three companies of officials, advancing with unfurled [Col. 0396C] banners, saw the episcopal forces pursuing them. They drew themselves into battle-array, close-packed together like a wall. The episcopal troops and the men of Guelders surrounded them in a circle; and as small pieces are cut from a sheer rock with chisels, so they plucked now these men, now those, from that line with lances and swords, until they had struck down all those who defended themselves to the last.

In that conflict many men of Guelders fell: namely, the lords of Culemborg and Batenburg, Ro. of Erkle, Bertold of Oyen, and many of their men.

Concerning the same matter. On that same day, when the people of Huy, after the rout of their men, were withdrawing from battle toward their homes and approached the castle of Musal, the bailiff of the castle, with men chosen for this purpose, attacked them while exhausted by flight, killing and capturing them. At last the bishop pursued from behind a certain company of the men of Huy, [Col. 0396D] among whom were the knights Walter and Arnold of Hautepen with eighty men-at-arms of their lineage. The same bailiff and his men confronted them in front. But after they had defended themselves and reached the entrance of the gates, with many of their own men struck down, the episcopal troops withdrew home.

[Col. 0397A] The number killed on the side of the people of Liège and the other good towns was 21,000 men. On the following day, 22 July, the bishop and all the princes who had come to his aid assembled by agreement in the open place. The Duke of Brabant and all the other aforesaid princes unanimously resolved that whatever liberties or towns they should compel to surrender within the bishopric, they must restore entirely to the bishop.

Concerning the same matter. On the same day, despite the bishop’s protest and his tearful resistance with all his strength, the Duke of Brabant caused the tower of Walevia and all the villages of Hesbaye on this side of Liège, from Huy to the county of Loon, to be burned, in revenge for himself and contrary to the law of war, because he had come to the bishop’s aid for payment.

[Col. 0397B] Concerning the same matter. When the people of Saint-Trond were ready to set out toward Tourins to assist the people of Liège on the appointed day of battle, the people of Liège instructed them not to come to the field of battle, for the preservation of their town. Being situated on the borders of Brabant, they would be more able effectively to repel the duke’s attacks.

Therefore, on that very eve of Saint Mary Magdalene, lest they perhaps be charged with inactivity while their fellow-members were fighting in battle that day against the lord of Liège, the masters and commune of the entire town, despite the dissuasion of the more prudent townsmen, hastened with armed force to attack the town of Leuven. Having advanced as far as the defences of that town, they caught the people of Leuven unprepared and overturned the barriers with their obstructions. Some of them, seeing scarcely any resistance [Col. 0397C] from the people of Leuven, entered as far as the outer gate. Others climbed to the high roof of an imposing house standing in the suburb before the gate, and harassed the people of Leuven with arrows so that they could not pass between that hospital and the aforesaid gate.

Had there not been in that suburb a great quantity of goods, brought there by the inhabitants of neighboring villages for protection, the people of Saint-Trond would have captured the town had they pressed on against the fleeing inhabitants. But enticed by the abundance of plunder, they partly burned the suburb and returned home. Some on both sides were wounded by arrows, while about eighteen men of Leuven were killed.

When the people of Saint-Trond had advanced as far as the village called Bodenhoven, a certain count from the [Col. 0397D] parts of Germany, named Thierry, Lord of Dune, who was on his way to Calais [Note: Calais, then under siege by Edward III, King of England.] to serve for pay, entered the town of Leuven. Seeing what had been done there, he urged the townsmen to pursue their enemies. Revived in courage, they went out beyond the ditches into the fields, with that count leading fifty of his men-at-arms.

When the people of Saint-Trond learned this, they drew their army back behind them and, compacted into one body, marched against their pursuers. When the count [Col. 0398A] saw their number and realized that the few could not resist the many, he made them all withdraw within the defences. As he himself followed last, with the enemy coming up, his horse, moving restively, fell with him into the ditch of the stronghold. Seeing this, some of the people of Saint-Trond tried to take him prisoner alive, but others who came up killed him in the ditch.

After this they advanced no farther, because the people of Leuven, seeking refuge in flight, threw down their bridges behind them. Thus the people of Saint-Trond returned home at the ninth hour, rejoicing beyond measure in their triumph. When they had entered the town, the bells in the church towers were rung festively, and very many of them entered our monastery. They offered great praises to Saint Trudo, whose shrine had stood for three days in the middle of the aforesaid monastery before [Col. 0398B] his chapel, though their hands were still stained with human blood.

There also a certain brazen woman brought a missile hurled by the people of Leuven against our townsmen and fastened it to the shrine of the saint of God, thinking to offer praise from the leavened thing.

Likewise. And because, according to Solomon, sorrow often overtakes the end of joy (Prov. 14:13), and the Psalmist says, “Weeping will lodge at evening, but joy comes in the morning” (Ps. 29:6), on that same day, at the hour of Vespers, honorable men came to Saint-Trond, declaring that the people of Liège had been defeated and that the Bishop of Liège had gained victory in the battle. Then great fear and grief arose throughout the town, and they could fittingly have cried out the words of Isaiah [Note: The words are mistakenly attributed; they are Jeremiah, Lamentations 5:15.]: “Our dancing has turned into mourning.”

Concerning the same matter. On the same [Col. 0398C] day, the Duke of Brabant, still remaining with his army in the fields, was informed of the violence of the people of Saint-Trond against the people of Leuven. In inflamed anger, recalling how many injuries had repeatedly been inflicted upon his men from that town, he decided with his secretaries to surround that town with his army on the next day and raze it to the ground.

When Lord Rainer of Schoonvorst, made a baron in that battle and brother of our Lord Abbot Amelius, learned this—he was then dwelling outside the monastery at our manor of Dola because of the townsmen’s insolence—he informed our fellow monks, that they should make provision for themselves. Hence the greatest fear struck the whole convent: many left the cloister, while others remained, tearfully imploring Saint [Col. 0398D] Trudo [Note: “implore” 1*.] to deign to preserve his church from ruin.

Likewise. On the following day, 22 July, the feast of Mary Magdalene, the bishop and the princes aiding him besieged the town of Tongeren, burning the whole suburb. Yet its townsmen resisted manfully and went out beyond their gates against those attacking them. During this siege, the people of Liège and the other towns of the territory were reconciled with their lord Bishop Engelbert, promising, within fixed terms and upon giving hostages, to pay him [Col. 0399A] 150,000 old écus. They also promised the Duke of Brabant that they would serve him for forty days at their own expense with 600 foot soldiers, when required [Note: “required” 1*.].

Concerning the same matter. While this was occurring, the people of Saint-Trond, distressed [Note: “distressed” 1*.], wholly deprived of and despairing of every assistance from the city and townsmen of Liège and from their own lords, feared the arrival of the Duke of Brabant with his very great army. They sent their secretaries to the duke, asking him to deal mercifully with them; they offered to receive him as their superior advocate and declared that, in the course of the war, whenever he should lead out all Brabant, they would render him service in the same manner as the town of Diest did when it was under arms. They also asserted that the townsmen of Saint-Trond would be ready to make those same promises.

[Col. 0399B] Therefore, when the duke had heard their declarations [Note: corrected in an erasure.] and taken counsel, he somewhat softened his fierce disposition. When the people of Tongeren ratified the peace made by the city and towns of Liège with the lord Bishop of Liège for the aforesaid sum, the bishop and those aiding him raised the siege after three days, on the eve of Saint James, 24 July. He rendered thanks to all who had given him timely assistance in so victorious a triumph; and so, the army having been disbanded, each returned home.

The Duke of Brabant, however, intending to preserve the people of Saint-Trond from harm on account of the aforesaid promises, commanded throughout the entire army of Brabant that no one should take the road through the town of Saint-Trond. Thus it happened that this plentiful army, [Col. 0399C] turning aside to the right and left from the entire district of that town, caused injury to no one, neither in the crops of the fields, then ripening for harvest, nor in anything else whatever.

Concerning the same matter. On the next day, 25 July, the feast of Saint James, the aforesaid duke approached the village called Heere [Note: Heers, near Saint-Trond.] and sent messengers to announce his arrival to the people of Saint-Trond. They immediately took counsel and, anxiously providing for the safety of their town, their persons, and their goods, went out in great numbers, humbly and unarmed, to meet the lord duke, fearing the consequences of their own offences.

When they had gathered in the open plain situated between the town itself and the dependency of the village of Brustem called Bruxkem, the aforesaid duke came up [Col. 0399D] with his multitude of armed men and encircled them like a crown. Thus distressed, they took off their hoods, fell upon their knees, and humbly offered themselves to the duke’s will and mercy. They acknowledged him as their superior advocate; moreover, to the ringing [Note: “and” 1*.] of the bell of the whole town, as stated above, they promised everything according to the entire manner of the town of Diest.

[Col. 0400A] The aforesaid duke graciously accepted their humility and promise. He allowed them, as though condemned to death, to return unharmed to the town. Then, turning aside with his entire retinue to the left from this town’s district toward Brabant, he sent only a few of his men into Saint-Trond itself to spend the night there at their own expense. They openly displayed the standards and banners of the Duke of Brabant, unfurled for all to see at the prominent lodging-houses around the market-place, until the morning of the next day.

O how much grief of heart must the good townsmen—so often sheltered beneath the wings of the flying eagle and delivered from the rushing teeth of wild beasts—have felt when, with faces turned away and eyes cast sideways, they beheld the clawed lion displayed openly!

Consider, reader, the aid of protection granted by blessed Trudo, [Col. 0400B] invoked through the tearful sighs of the monks of this place. In such peril he not only rescued from every loss the monastery of his servants, which he had built on his own allodial land, but also wonderfully and beyond measure saved these townsmen, set under the dominion of his paternal jurisdiction, from the wrathful indignation of the great prince, the Duke of Brabant, and of the people of his land, whom these townsmen had gravely offended many times.

Concerning the same matter. I judge it also probable that the aforesaid Duke of Brabant, because of the favor and assistance he had often shown toward this abbey, was beneficially preserved by Saint Trudo himself, the saint of the Lord, from despoiling this place. For in the time of Emperor Henry I, Otto, Duke of Lotharingia, from [Col. 0400C] whose stock this John, Duke of Brabant, descended, entered this town and, in his own presence, allowed his men sacrilegiously to plunder the goods of this monastery. As soon as he left the gate of the cloister, Saint Trudo—as that duke himself admitted from a convincing sign—struck him a heavy blow between the shoulders. In great pain, he barely made his way to Maastricht; on the third day he breathed his last and left an only daughter. [Note: Compare above, year 1005.]

Moreover, some time afterward a man of great devotion and learning came to this town. When he heard that the Duke of Brabant and his whole country, although they then and for a long time had greatly hated the people of Saint-Trond, had nevertheless received them into peace without devastation upon returning from the battle in which the people of Liège had been defeated, he immediately asked whether the body of any saint [Col. 0400D] of God was kept in this place. When he was told that the body of the founder of this monastery rested here whole, together with the bodies of two other saints, he said: “Without doubt, be assured that this place has been saved through their patronage.”

This man was Brother John of Liemcule of the Order of Saint Francis. Some time afterward, while publicly preaching steadfastly against the heretical perversity of the Flagellants, he came secretly, sick as an exile, to the convent of the brothers at Saint-Trond, and happily fell asleep in Christ.

7. In the same year, on 9 September, that is, on the day after the Nativity of the Blessed Mary, which fell on a Sunday, the Duke of Brabant came to the town of Saint Trudo—not, as the people of Saint Trudo feared, to demolish its walls, but to secure lordship over the town for himself as a stronghold against the territory of Liège. Therefore the duke, proceeding unjustly against the promise which he had made to the bishop, entered our monastery with a great company of knights and townsmen and rang the ban-bell as a sign of lordship. Then, proceeding to the middle of the marketplace, he compelled the townsmen to swear fealty to him [Col. 0401B]. Summoning the aldermen of the lords bishop and abbot who were then present on their behalf, he appointed, contrary to the fealty by which they were bound to the aforesaid lords, fourteen aldermen from his own hand, and twelve councillors from the other townsmen.

On the following day he presided publicly in the marketplace to administer justice, with the aldermen whom he had appointed and those placed under the advocate; and he ordered the privileges and charters of this town to be brought to him. When he understood that they were contrary to himself, he annulled them with scissors which he held in his hand. The seneschal of Brabant, the duke’s special secretary, who was at that time quite familiar with us, secretly proposed to us that, if we chose to sell or exchange for other possessions the jurisdictional lordship which we possess in that town [Col. 0401C], his lord the duke would in every respect satisfy our wishes. When he was answered that we in no way wished to alienate the patrimony of Saint Trudo, divinely bestowed upon our monastery, he ceased this solicitation.

Incident. In the same month the aforesaid duke sent to the town of Saint Trudo the reeve of Thenismont. At his command the townsmen razed to the ground the residence of Sir Franco called Probus, knight, because he refused, contrary to his fealty to his lords the bishop and abbot, to become an alderman on the duke’s side. Some months later, a very wealthy townsman named Herbord Scat, who had formerly been compelled to accept the office of alderman when the duke himself appointed aldermen, wishing to be reconciled with his true lords, whose vassal he was, left the town [Col. 0401D]. When, though often summoned, he would not return, his house in Brustem Street was razed to the ground in the presence of the aforesaid reeve.

About the same day, the house of the parish priest of New Houses (*de Novis Domibus*), from which our convent of Saint Trudo has annually six florins for the pittance, was, through the efforts of that reeve, to be adjudged to Thenismont for the duke’s fisc, because that priest had left the town and adhered to the bishop. But at the urgent prayers of the prior on behalf of the convent, the reeve, being informed by townsmen favourable to us in this matter, desisted from what he had begun [Col. 0402A].

Concerning the same matter. Meanwhile, in that same year, about the Nones of December, the bishop of Liège, seeing that the duke continued day by day to usurp jurisdictional lordship over the town of Saint Trudo, caused the greater and lesser reeves of Thenismont, together with thirty-five persons from among the townsmen of our town of Saint Trudo, to be summoned to judicial combat. When this became known, the aforesaid duke earnestly commanded them not to fear this summons, because he wished to preserve all of them unharmed from such proceedings. Encouraged by this exhortation, the aforesaid thirty-five, fearing nothing and neglecting the fortnightly terms and other customary procedures in such cases, were pronounced by sentence of the superiors to be punishable by outlawry.

Likewise. After some days the bishop, seeing that the people of Saint Trudo, recently subjected to the duke’s lordship [Col. 0402B], did not fear the curse of outlawry under the imperial peace and took no care to be reconciled with their lords, sat solemnly in the tribunal, as was customary, in the presence of seven archdeacons. Under the law of the peace of judicial combat granted to the bishops of Liège by the emperors, he outlawed and pronounced excommunicated four persons among the aforesaid thirty-five townsmen of Saint Trudo. When these four had been so severely punished, the rest—both aldermen and councillors, as well as townsmen of other rank—began to fear that they might suffer the same penalty. Accordingly, assembled in their *lobium* [Note: [Col. 0401] A portico before the court, where laws were pronounced, oaths were sworn, and similar acts took place.], in the presence of the reeve of Montisten and other townsmen favourable to the duke, they publicly declared that they did not wish to be deprived of their offices.

Concerning the same matter. The bishop, however, having deliberately outlawed the four townsmen of Saint Trudo [Col. 0402C], did not wish to proceed against the rest with the rigour of the law of judicial combat [Note: [Col. 0401] “but” added in 1*.]. He wrote many secret letters to individual persons, promising, if they wished to come to their senses, to guarantee them against enforcement of the outlawry. He also sent public letters to every administrative district, that they should withdraw from their evil undertakings, because he would receive all of them back into peace.

Therefore, on Laetare Jerusalem Sunday, 30 March [Note: [Col. 0401] The scribe left a space of three letters.] 1348, the entire populace having assembled within the convent of the Friars Minor, discord arose between the duke’s supporters on one side and others who wished to be reconciled with their true lords. When one of them said, “This refectory is too cramped for us!”, they immediately proceeded to the marketplace. There the captains, supporters of the duke, having first assembled in the marketplace with unfurled banners [Col. 0402D], stood ready to defend the duke’s party. But those of the opposing party came upon them, and their support increased so greatly that the duke’s supporters, compelled by fear of death, offered to be reconciled with their proper lords.

While this was taking place, certain townsmen, with the cloth-workers’ banner unfurled, approached the residence of the aforesaid priest, the leader of all these evils. Hearing their uproar and their violent assault upon the doors [Col. 0403A], he tried to escape their hands. Having climbed over the rear wall of his garden, he ran into the house of a certain dyer and concealed himself behind a large vat. Some of them, pursuing him and searching beneath beds and piercing the beds, finally found him; and they killed him by piercing him with swords and pointed knives. As was said, a certain matron gathered him, still breathing, into her lap and urged him to turn himself to Christ’s Passion and confidently trust in God’s mercy. He immediately showed signs of contrition by a gesture and died.

These things having thus been done, and all the inhabitants of this town wishing to be reconciled with their true lords, the bishop, desiring to provide for the salvation of their souls, sent to the parish clergy of the whole town, granting them authority to absolve the townsmen from the bond of excommunication [Col. 0403B] and from their offences; and he revoked the interdict which had long endured. Then the greatest thanksgiving was made in this town, as the people approached, in penitence, to receive the Eucharist at the following Easter season (20 April).

Concerning the same matter. Not many days afterwards, the aforesaid bishop of Liège, Engelbert, having recently sent ambassadors to the supreme pontiff Clement IV [Note: [Col. 0403D] Sixth.], lodging a complaint against John, duke of Brabant, that he had usurped half of the town of Saint Trudo belonging to the church of Saint Lambert, the aforesaid pontiff immediately wrote sealed letters to prelates, princes, and towns, as follows:

> Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Grand-Pré [Note: [Col. 0403D] Grandpré near Namur.], of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Liège, greeting.
>
> By other letters of ours, the form of which we send you enclosed with these present letters, we command you to urge our beloved son, the noble man John, duke of Brabant, to restore the town of Saint Trudo, which the same duke is said to have occupied in the diocese of Liège, to which it belongs. We also exhort, by various other letters of ours, our beloved son, the noble man Henry [Note: [Col. 0404D] Fifth.], duke of Limburg, son of the said duke of Brabant, and each and every noble and knight, as well as the councils of Brussels and Leuven, of the dioceses of Cambrai and Liège, and of the other good towns of Brabant, to exert effective efforts with that duke in this matter [Col. 0403D].
>
> Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, presenting these letters on our behalf to the said dukes, nobles, knights, and councils, you shall endeavour to procure from them a ready compliance with our prayers in this matter. Given at Avignon, 4 Nones of April, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

The tenor of the letter sent to John, duke of Brabant, is as follows.

Likewise. Clement, etc., to John, duke of Brabant, etc. [Col. 0404A]:

> A trustworthy report has recently reached the hearing of our apostolic office that, although the town of Saint Trudo, in the diocese of Liège, belongs by full right to the church of Liège—with only certain rights belonging to our beloved son the abbot of Saint Trudo, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the same diocese, and to the advocate of the aforesaid town, excepted—and although this is notorious in those regions and cannot in the least be unknown to you [Note: [Col. 0403] “letters” in 1*.], you nevertheless occupied and still hold that town in occupation, taking no care to restore it to the aforesaid church, although you have been requested to do so on its behalf.
>
> But since, son, your honour requires you prudently and carefully to endeavour to redress these matters, if they are true, lest you be marked, God forbid, as an assailant of the rights of that church which you ought to defend out of reverence for God, we earnestly request your nobility [Col. 0404B] that, considering what equity requires in this matter and what is due to justice, you restore the aforesaid town readily and generously to the said church, for reverence toward us and the Apostolic See and also for the sake of your own honour. In these and other matters aforesaid, conduct yourself in such a way that the church may deservedly be satisfied with you, and that we may pursue your devotion with fitting acts of favour. Given at Avignon, 4 Nones of April, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

Letter of Pope Clement VI sent to the townsmen of Saint Trudo:

> Clement, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the council and townsmen of the town of Saint Trudo, in the diocese of Liège, greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> We have heard with astonishment that you, though bound by devotion [Note: [Col. 0404D] That is, “by devotion.”] to the church of Liège as your lady and mistress [Note: [Col. 0403] “master” in 1*.] [Col. 0404C], have forgotten that devotion and departed from obedience and fealty to that church, voluntarily submitting yourselves to the lordship of our beloved son, the noble man John, duke of Brabant. Since these things, if true, accuse you of grave fault and stain you with the mark of a still graver blemish, we earnestly ask, require, and exhort your whole community, counselling you with paternal counsel, that, bringing the aforesaid matters under due consideration, you return to devotion and fealty to that church. Strive to be reconciled to it through the works of due satisfaction, so that it may abound toward you, as toward devoted sons and subjects, in its customary gracious favours, and that we may pursue your devotion with fitting acts of favour. Given at Avignon, 4 Nones of April, in the sixth year of our pontificate [Col. 0404D].

Likewise. Accordingly, in that same year, after the bulls had been sent to these parts by a swift messenger, the aforesaid abbot of Grand-Pré, intending to execute the apostolic mandate [Note: [Col. 0403] “executor” in 1*.], came to us in order to spend the night. On the following day he delivered to the rectors and aldermen of this town of Saint Trudo the letters addressed to them by Pope Clement, just as he had previously delivered letters to the duke himself and his son Henry, together with the towns of Brabant; and so [Col. 0405A] he returned home without hostility.

After the Easter days had passed, in that year [Note: [Col. 0405D] 1349, in which year Easter was celebrated on 12 April; in 1348, on 20 April.], on 16 April, new privileges were granted to the town. At the townsmen’s request, the twelve councillors, who according to the old privileges had held office for life, were henceforth to be appointed from year to year with the consent of the lords bishop and abbot [Note: [Col. 0405] “shall be appointed” in 1*.], so that the administration of the government of the whole town might thereafter become known to more persons.

Incident. In July of the year of the Lord 1349, Charles, elected king of the Romans for the second time, hastened with a strong multitude of princes and armed men to the royal seat at Aachen. When Engelbert, bishop of Liège, learned this, he accompanied him with a force of armed men. The people of Aachen, as is believed, opened their gates to him on the twenty-fourth day of that month by command of Pope Clement IV [Col. 0405B]. There, having received the crown [lacuna of eight letters], he peacefully returned home with his royal consort [Note: [Col. 0405D] Anne.].

Incident. In the same year, crossing the Alpine mountains, he received a crown [lacuna of eight letters] at Milan; proceeding farther, he received the imperial crown at Rome from the cardinal appointed for this purpose, without bloodshed [Note: [Col. 0406D] This was in fact done in the year 1355.].

Likewise, concerning the matter above. In the same year, on 24 July, Charles IV, in the fourth year of his Roman kingship and the third of his kingship of Bohemia, confirmed the privileges of the peace of the New Court and the privileges recently granted to our townsmen reconciled with their lords.

Incident. In the same year, about the Nativity of Saint John, men called Flagellants entered the territory of Hesbaye from the parts of Lower Germany. Their bodies were bare to the navel; their heads covered with hoods and caps; their feet bare. From the navel downward to the ankles they wore pleated linen garments, and they beat their own backs with knotted scourges having spiked knots at the ends, drawing blood. They asserted that by such bodily affliction they would escape the disease of the epidemic [Col. 0405C]. Advancing two by two in procession, they sang mournful songs. When these had partly ended, they bent their knees and, throwing their bodies violently to the ground, lay upon their backs with their arms stretched out in the form of a cross. Afterwards, raising themselves and kneeling, they recited a general confession, with priests accompanying them and proclaiming it [Col. 0405D]. Then they immediately rose, singing in a feigned ceremony of joy, put off the penitential sheet, so to speak, and resumed their ordinary clothing.

They performed this work of flagellation twice daily for thirty consecutive days [Col. 0406A], and often in churches, where, if divine offices of the canonical hours or preaching at stations were being performed, they declared their acts to take precedence. A multitude of noblemen, knights, and common people initially flocked in very great devotion to this heretical penance. Not only in the bishopric of our diocese of Liège but also in various dioceses, religious men—both monks and, for the most part, mendicants—as well as secular priests, went out from their residences along with laypeople and administered ecclesiastical sacraments to them.

But as time passed, their presumed religion, devised by certain apostates from religious life secretly lodged in the house of one woman beyond the Rhine, was carefully examined by learned men and found full of superstitions and heresies [Col. 0406B], tending—as later appeared—to the destruction of the holy Church and of the entire clergy. By ecclesiastical censure this superstition was brought to an end.

Incident. In the same year Jews were burned throughout all Germany, because a report circulated that they were poisoning wells and streams in order to destroy all Christendom, and that by gifts they were corrupting poor Christians to commit similar acts. Reeve-officials everywhere collected their property for the use of their lords. Among them the reeve of the city of Cologne was killed by Jews. At Cologne, where they possessed a street together with many houses hereditarily, and refused to resort to baptism, they set fire to their own houses and burned themselves within them with their wives and children [Col. 0406C]. Some are of the opinion that in this persecution of the Jews they were falsely accused.

8. In the year of the Lord 1350, Lord Amelius of Schoonouwen, abbot of this place, having lain paralysed in bed for nearly fifteen years but nevertheless vigorously preserving the rights of this monastery, purchased twelve hereditary *modii* of rye. Of these he assigned six *modii* to the table pittance for his anniversary, and the remaining six to the refectory pittance for those dining in the refectory on Mondays. He also acquired several books for this monastery and enlarged our possessions at the New Court. In the twenty-first year of his prelacy, on 20 February, he died. His body was honourably buried [Col. 0406D] in the middle of our stalls of the choir, behind the tomb of Abbot Christian, and covered with a great carved stone.

## HERE BEGIN THE DEEDS OF ROBERT, ABBOT OF THIS PLACE

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405D] 1. In the same year of the Lord 1350, in the tenth year of Pope Clement VI [Note: [Col. 0406D] Eighth.], in the sixth year of Charles IV’s kingship, and in the third year of his empire [Col. 0406D], on 24 February, which was Thursday and the feast of the blessed apostle Matthias, Robert of Craenewic was elected abbot of this place by the procedure of a mixed scrutiny, a man of praiseworthy life and a zealous champion of religious observance.

His consecration was delayed in the following manner. Pope Clement reserved to himself all prelacies and dignities, something unheard of in earlier times. Therefore, when messengers had been sent to the Roman Curia for confirmation of the election—or rather, for the obtaining of papal provision—the matter was brought before the consistory and long examined, because the ambassadors of William, archbishop of Cologne, were zealously endeavouring to obtain this abbey for the brother of the aforesaid archbishop, a monk of another monastery. At length, however, with the cardinals’ consent, the pope provided the elected man with the abbey, delivering bulls on 3 June 1351.

Our messengers [Col. 0407B], all matters having been successfully completed, returned prosperously. The aforesaid elect, who had resided at the New Court from the time of his election, was conducted to the monastery with an honourable retinue about the seventh hour of the day. Since not everyone knows the procedure for receiving an abbot, it is fitting now to describe it.

2. On the manner of receiving an abbot or bishop. First, when the approaching arrival of the elect is announced to the prior and convent, all immediately dress in white. With schoolboys, priests, and Friars Minor preceding them, they come out to meet him in procession. When they have proceeded as far as the space before the choir of the clerics’ chapel, where grain is customarily sold, they halt and await his arrival. On reaching the aforesaid chapel [Col. 0407C], and seeing the convent, he dismounts. The prior and one of the elders then approach him solemnly; one receives him reverently by the right hand and the other by the left. With the procession going before, he is conducted to the monastery, while the cantor begins the responsory *Honor virtus* with its verse [Note: [Col. 0407] “response” in 1*.].

Meanwhile, the prioress of Saint Catherine of Melin and her convent make a solemn station at the place of our immunity, situated between the monastery portico and the corner [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Coin*: a corner.] of the street. When the procession has reached the chapel of Saint Trudo, the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* having been begun, the elect—if the bishop is not present—prostrates himself alone in prayer upon a carpet-covered bench [Note: [Col. 0407] “spread over” in 1*.]. When the hymn is finished, he rises.

Then follows the responsory *Deum time*, with verse and repetition; then the versicle, “Save thy servant”; “Send him aid from above”; and the collect *Pretende, Domine*, *f. t.* When these have been completed, he is immediately led to the altar of Saint Trudo. Having prayed there, and the aldermen and townsmen having assembled for this purpose, he immediately swears the oath of fealty. Placing his right hand upon the cross carved on the altar-table, he repeats clause by clause the words spoken by one of the eloquent aldermen standing by, swearing as follows:

> From this day forward, and on this day altogether, I shall be faithful and loyal to Saint Mary, Saint Lambert, the bishop of Liège, the chapter of Saint Lambert, the good Saint Trudo, the convent of Saint Trudo, the count of Loon as advocate, and the town of Saint Trudo; I shall uphold for the town of Saint Trudo the letters, charters, and privileges which the lords have granted; I shall help preserve its liberties from diminution, and shall cause them to be preserved; and I shall act as an abbot of Saint Trudo ought to act, treating the poor equally with the rich and the rich equally with the poor. I shall not fail in this through friendship, kinship, or any kind of matter that may be done to me. So help me God and the saints.

He is then conducted in the same manner to the high altar; after prayer there, the aldermen lead him [Col. 0408B] to the ban-bell, which he rings as a sign of temporal lordship.

3. On the manner of consecrating an abbot. Having completed the solemn reception of the newly elected abbot of this monastery or of a new bishop of Liège, we must consider the rite for consecrating the new abbot. First, it should be known that if the elect, confirmed by the church of Liège, was consecrated outside before his entrance into the monastery, then, once the above-described reception has been completed, he may, if he wishes, celebrate Mass solemnly or proceed to dinner. If he has not yet been consecrated, then, when the bishop who is to perform the consecration has vested for the Mass office, the elect to be consecrated is placed in the middle of the upper choir, opposite the high altar, seated between two consecrated abbots [Col. 0408C]. After the offertory has been sung, the bishop completes the rite of consecration and gives him a ring. Leading him to the choir of chanters, he places him mitred and with staff in the abbot’s stall. After the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* has been sung, he again places him before the high altar between the aforesaid two abbots.

The abbot then makes without delay the oath customarily sworn by abbots of our order, in this manner: [lacuna; the column in the manuscript is left more than half blank after this point.]. After the oath has been made, the bishop, having received the sacrament of the chalice, administers the holy Eucharist to the consecrated man. When the Mass office is finished, the abbot enters the abbey house [Note: [Col. 0407] “enters” in 1*.] and invites diners as he wishes [Note: [Col. 0407] “last” in 1*.].

Accordingly, the aforesaid Robert was consecrated on the above-mentioned day by Theoderic, suffragan of Engelbert, bishop of Liège, with the abbots of Saint Lawrence and Saint James assisting [Col. 0408D].

Concerning the same matter. On the following Friday, at chapter hour, the same Abbot Robert came to chapter. In the presence of the prior and whole convent he promised, according to custom, that he would observe these three things: first, that he would recover what had been dissipated and alienated and preserve the rights of the monastery; secondly, that he would observe the good, ancient, reasonable, and approved customs of this monastery; thirdly, that he would not divert the goods of our pittance to other uses.

After this, the prior placed the Rule of Saint Benedict in his lap [Col. 0409A]. The prior and whole convent then approached Lord Abbot one by one, having first bent their knees, and, laying both hands upon the Rule which he held over his lap, each promised him obedience in this form: “Lord, I promise you obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” They immediately gave him the kiss of peace, mouth to mouth. When this was completed, the obedientiaries or officials, one by one, laid the keys of their offices upon the chapter mat, to be disposed of by the abbot; he immediately recommitted to each one the execution of his office.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1352 Pope Clement VI died. Innocent VI succeeded him.

4. In the year of the Lord 1353, Abbot Robert went to William [Note: [Col. 0409D] Fifth.], count of Holland, at the town and monastery of Middelburg. He was graciously received by him for dinner; having taken relief of the fief from him and paid one mark of silver for the relief—which our monastery owes for the advocacy over our goods and people in Alburgh and neighbouring villages—he returned to his monastery [Col. 0409B].

Concerning the same matter. In the same year, the aforesaid count, falsely informed by a certain Godfrey of Dumella—an usurper of possessions belonging to honourable men and entrusted to his fidelity by them, who enticed both princes and honourable men by predictions and superstitions—endeavoured effectively to hold as usurped all our goods situated both in Heusden and in Holland. This was because the tithe of Bardewyc, adjudged to that Godfrey by the judgment of our vassals at more than fifty [uncertain: perhaps an omitted monetary or land measure], and that adjudged to Lord John of Boechout in the abbot’s court, had been appealed by him to the count [Col. 0409C].

But since, according to the philosopher, injustice bearing arms is most savage, and since “it is hard to kick against the goad,” as Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles (9:5), the aforesaid abbot, having obtained the favour of the lord of IJsselstein, the count’s councillor and keeper of his seal, made peace with the count. He redeemed our goods, unjustly adjudged away, for 1,700 [Note: [Col. 0409] Seventeen in 1*.] Bruges écus, payable to the count within a month, and 300 payable to mediators on the day after the agreed period had elapsed. These matters having been completed, Abbot Robert obtained letters of quittance written and sealed in the count’s name, and thus was restored to possession of our goods adjudged to us by the count’s vassals [Col. 0409D].

When all expenses were reckoned—including the letters of restitution and many other incidental costs, with 500 florins given to Lord Florentius of Versele—the same abbot, on account of the said appeal, suffered losses amounting to 4,000 florins within four years.

Incident. About this time Lord Arnold of Rummen, nephew through a legitimate sister of Louis, count of Loon [Col. 0410A], having married the widow of a very wealthy knight, a great usurer, maternal aunt of Louis, count of Flanders, began to build a castle in his own village of Rummen [Note: [Col. 0410D] Rummen near Saint Trudo.]. Although he otherwise spared no expense, because he was then [lacuna of ten letters] Brabant, he most grievously oppressed rural people throughout Brabant, together with the common people subject to him. He compelled them for a long time to convey, without payment but at the cost of their own labour and expenses, stones, lime, and everything else necessary for building that castle.

Thus, after almost nine years, the castle having been elegantly completed, and afterwards all things suitable for rebellion having been placed in it, many reported that at night, while the guards slept, the windows of the castle could be heard shaken with a dreadful sound; and its towers [Col. 0410B], together with its great hall, seemed to be filled [Note: [Col. 0409] “filled” in 1*.] with gleaming flames streaming out through the windows. These might fittingly foretell the overthrow of the castle which, as will appear below, was to follow.

5. In the year of the Lord 1355, when Lord Reiner of Schoonvorst, baron, brother of Amelius of pious memory, predecessor of Robert as abbot of this place, had freely wished to restore our goods of Halchter and Dola, which he had unjustly held from the election of the aforesaid Robert as abbot, after many negotiations the same baron finally compelled the abbot, by allegations contrary to the truth [Note: [Col. 0409] *v. c.* erased afterwards.], to hold the lordship of the aforesaid village and its court with its revenues for only four years; once those years had elapsed, the abbot was to pay him 1,000 florins.

But in the following year, 1356, when war arose [Col. 0410C] between him and Lord Walram of Borne over the land of Valkenburg, the aforesaid Baron Reiner feared that the aforementioned goods of Halchter would be ravaged by his enemy. The former terms therefore having been annulled, and after exacting 1,000 florins and 120 écus from the abbot, he freely restored the village and court with their revenues to him.

Know here, reader, that the aforesaid Lord Reiner, while his brother Amelius, the aforesaid abbot, was alive, earnestly urged that the repeatedly mentioned village of Halchter, with its court and goods there, which he had occupied at the pleasure of his brother Abbot Amelius together with temporal lordship over that people, should be leased by our convent to him during his life at an annual rent. After deliberation on this question, the prior and elders [Col. 0410D], considering the fierceness and power of this man and his associates, laid the proposed matter before the whole convent. Finally, by the consent of all, he was answered that they wished to grant none of the monastery’s goods to anyone for life. So angered by this answer was he that he declared he would henceforth give the convent no assistance in anything.

But it is clear that they had taken the best counsel. Although he had no right in the aforesaid goods, our abbey nevertheless suffered losses of 2,150 florins and more, both in redeeming the aforementioned village and in the other expenses arising from this matter [Col. 0411A].

Moreover, it should be known that this same Lord of Schoonvorst—who, by permission of his brother Abbot Amelius, had previously received very great profits both from the monastery’s goods and [Note: [Col. 0411] *t. d. b. m. q.* erased.] from monetary penalties imposed upon the townsmen and aldermen, and who grievously oppressed and tortured our men at Halchter so that, sweating in the midst of the fields, they cried in weeping voices, “Avenge, Lord, the blood-price of our labour, which the violent exaction of Reiner of Schoonvorst has drunk!”—yet, forgetful of all this, when laid upon a sickbed and full of riches, made us no restitution.

Therefore let all who love the welfare of this monastery take care never to lease granges or other possessions for life to any powerful layman [Col. 0411B]. Yet greater precaution should be taken lest such things be granted to brothers or kinsmen of abbots, because they are recovered from such persons’ hands more ruinously than from strangers, as is shown above in the deeds of Abbot Ade.

Concerning the same matter. In the same year, 1355, Abbot Robert, because Gerard of Steinvorde defied him and later made suitable amends to Robert under compulsion, suffered losses amounting to 300 florins.

6. In the aforesaid year (1355), certain merchants caused one of their servants to be arrested and put in chains. He had brought to our town of Saint Trond merchandise entrusted to his care by them, [Col. 0411C] and asserted that it belonged to himself. But although they demonstrated the contrary by many arguments, he, fearing condemnation to the gallows, blinded with gifts the eyes of certain aldermen, as was said. By their contrivance it was judicially decided that it was not theft, even though he had brought his masters’ goods to places to which he had not been ordered; and thus he was freed from his chains. When, [Note: [Col. 0411] lacking in 1*.] after some time, he had fallen into poverty—as commonly happens to such persons—he lodged a complaint at Liège before Bishop Engelbert against the aldermen, alleging that they had accepted gifts from him unjustly. On learning this, those aldermen, as was said, caused the said servant to return to the aforesaid town under promise of peace. When several sworn associates of the aldermen learned of his arrival, as will later appear, [Col. 0411D] they murdered him by brigandage at the court of the Beguines, where he had secretly come at nightfall to dine beside the grandmother of his wife. At that time those responsible escaped punishment, because the bishop’s bailiff and certain aldermen, friends and kinsmen of those sworn associates, obstructed our sheriff, so that he could not produce witnesses against those notorious men.

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1356, a certain young man, passing one night before the bell’s appointed time through the cemetery of Saint Mary, was secretly murdered by certain men lying in wait for an adversary of their lord. He was innocent and reputed to be of good character, but was killed in place of the adversary for whom they were waiting. When that report [Note: [Col. 0411] “that,” 1*.] of so grave a crime grew among the people that evening, one of the culprits, standing at the entrance to the cemetery, struck in the face with an iron glove one of our servants, who was running with other townsmen to see the spectacle; the man struck knew him very well. Since the cemetery had thus been violated, for two years the bodies of the dead were buried, with the convent’s consent, in our garden called Vriithof.

Likewise. Such and many other murders, thefts, robberies, and acts of violence were long perpetrated in the town. From these arose a grave disturbance among the townsmen against [Col. 0412B] certain of the leading men and aforesaid aldermen. They charged that each of them, by mutual interchange, defended his own man and concealed his offence, lest criminals be punished.

Incident. In the aforesaid year 1355, on 5 December, John, Duke of Brabant, died and left the Duchy of Brabant to his daughter Joanna, whom he had previously joined in marriage to Wenceslaus, Duke of Luxembourg. [Note: [Col. 0411D] Son of John, King of Bohemia.]

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1356, Louis, Count of Flanders, who had legitimate offspring by the daughter [Note: [Col. 0411D] Margaret. See Radulfus de Rivo, *Gest. epp. Leodiens.*, ch. 3, in Chapeaville III.] of the aforesaid Duke of Brabant, the second-born, still living, seeing that no share in or of the aforesaid duchy had at that time been allotted to him, assembled a multitude of armed men, besieged the town of Antwerp, and received it into submission.

Incident. In the same year, after the feast of John, Bishop Engelbert, [Note: [Col. 0412D] He was an ally of the Count of Flanders.] through the marshal [Note: [Col. 0412D] Lambert of Elpey, according to Radulfus.] [Col. 0412C] and the bailiff [Note: [Col. 0412D] James of Chaboz, according to the same author.] of Hesbaye, stormed the town of Landen. On the following day a multitude of Brabanters arrived, overcame those few men of Liège, captured many of them, and compelled the rest to turn their backs. But when the aforesaid bailiff returned with a few men—he had been engaged in burning the neighbouring villages—the men of Liège, heartened by him, attacked the town again. The Brabanters’ army came out beyond the gates against them. But when battle was joined, victory fell to the men of Liège: many Brabanters were killed, and the men of Liège who had been prisoners were released from their bonds.

Incident. In the same year Wenceslaus, the new Duke of Brabant, in order more effectively to oppose the aforesaid count, entered the famous monastery of Saint Peter at Affligem. Having expelled the abbot and the whole convent and demolished the workshops, he surrounded the monastery—with its dormitory, refectory, and cloister—with a raised ditch; and, not fearing to commit sacrilege, he made it into a fortified castle for attacking Flanders, stationing armed guards there. [Col. 0412D] The count himself met him in open battle, won the victory, and compelled him to retreat. Therefore the guards of the castle fled lamentably; the Flemings immediately occupied it and [Col. 0413A] fortified it with armed guards.

After a few days the aforesaid count entered the Brabantine towns—Brussels, Louvain, and other liberties. Having there received their fealty, he appointed his own bailiffs there. After his departure, the Brabanters, setting aside the fealty they had shown to the count, sent for the duke and duchess and offered themselves to them. But after two months a peace settlement intervened, on condition that Wenceslaus should hold the duchy as long as the duchess lived, except only for the towns of Mechelen and Antwerp, assigned to the count, according to the arbitration of William, Count of Holland. [Note: [Col. 0413D] This peace was finally established in 1357; see Ernst V, 114.]

Some time after the peace settlement made according to the arbitration of Count William, the aforesaid Flemish knights occupying the stronghold—alas!—made out of Affligem monastery, [Col. 0413B] took precautions lest the Duke of Brabant should thereafter harass Flanders from that place by stationing soldiers there. They immediately propped up the lowest foundations with timbers, set fire to them, and departed. When the supports gave way under the force of the blaze, the entire structure collapsed, with the walls of the monastery, its very strong refectory tower, cloister, and most beautiful chapel of the Blessed Mary thrown down, except for the dormitory. When this became known to a prudent monk of that monastery, he ordered it quickly to be supported; afterwards, new foundations having been laid, this costly dormitory was preserved.

Incident. In the same year, John, King of France, with a very large army of his men, pursuing the son of the King of England, [Note: [Col. 0413D] Edward.] the Prince of Wales, who had recently entered France with a small body of chosen Englishmen, was defeated in battle in the midst of his kingdom near Poitiers [Col. 0413C] [Note: [Col. 0414D] Poitiers.]. Refusing to surrender, but resisting most stoutly, he was at last overpowered by the prince’s knights and thrown to the ground; he was raised up and taken by ship to England, together with his son Philip and many princes of France who surrendered. There, after several months, he died. [Note: [Col. 0414D] In fact he died at London in 1364, but not as a prisoner.]

## 7.

In the year of the Lord 1357, the former aldermen and councillors, recently deprived in the time of Abbot Amelius of the obligation by which they had bound themselves not henceforth to seek offices of trust in the government of this town except with the consent of the lords and townsmen, were now released from that obligation by means of an oath of fidelity to be rendered to our monastery, sworn upon the Gospels.

Likewise. In the following year (1358), Engelbert, Bishop [Col. 0413D] of Liège, intending to correct and remove the present aldermen of this town, who had been accused before him of many excesses and of the robbery committed at the court of Saint Agnes, as men implicated in it, came to our monastery seeking the consent of Abbot Robert. Perceiving how great a burden had fallen upon his monastery on the occasion of the removal of the former aldermen, Robert consented on this condition: that proceedings should be conducted not by violence but by the judgment and law of this town.

Accordingly, on the first day [Col. 0414A] of March, the Bishop of Liège summoned the people by the ringing of the proclamation-bell. After many discussions, the aldermen excused themselves there before all persons concerning the charges made against them; and the aforesaid bishop, who had come there to detain their persons, was put to shame and promised that they might depart free.

Likewise. After this, a certain man committed homicide near the mill of the monastery of Millen. Against this defendant the aldermen of Saint Trond, after depositions of witnesses, pronounced sentence according to due legal process. From that sentence the prioress, supported by the bishop’s counsel and aid, appealed to the aldermen of the Aachen tribunal. In the course of time, because that homicide had occurred within the liberty of our jurisdiction, the aforesaid aldermen were taken and brought back, at our monastery’s expense, once and twice, in order to receive [Col. 0414B] instruction and judgment from the aldermen of the Aachen tribunal. By their judgment, the principal sentence pronounced by the aldermen of Saint Trond remained in force and was not revoked; but the dispute was quieted when a settlement intervened. On account of this lawsuit our monastery suffered expenses exceeding 1,600 florins, and 400 florins in respect of a certain matter.

Likewise. In the same week in which the aldermen of Saint Trond were brought to the Aachen tribunal, the Bishop of Liège, after many discussions, seeing that he could not, as he had thought, correct and remove the aforesaid aldermen in the presence of the aldermen of Aachen, ceased from prosecuting them when a peaceful settlement intervened, through 600 florins to be paid by those aldermen and divided between the bishop, the abbot, and the advocate. [Col. 0414C]

## 8.

In the same year, in April, Abbot Robert, travelling through the County of Namur for certain reasons, turned aside to the monastery of Saint Gerard at Brogne. When the abbot of that place learned this, he swiftly sent honourable mounted messengers inviting him to his lord’s dinner and informing him that the entire convent was prepared to come out to meet him in procession, should this be pleasing to his fatherhood. Robert declined this and turned aside to lodging near the monastery itself. After resting briefly, the bells were rung for Mass.

When he entered the cloister to hear the Mass office, the abbot and convent of the aforesaid monastery, assembled together, greeted him with every mark of humanity and reverently led him to the choir of chanters, placing him in the abbot’s stall. When, after Mass, he set out for his lodging outside the monastery, he was by no means permitted to leave the cloister. Instead, he was taken to the abbot’s house; the convent was summoned there to dine, and the abbot of that place most honourably provided him and all his company with a cheerful and lavish feast. Among other pleasant conversations, the abbot stated [Col. 0415A] that the abbot of the aforesaid monastery was bound, whenever an abbot of Saint Trond newly arrived there, to proceed solemnly outside his monastery’s cloister to meet him with his whole convent, relics, and crosses; [Note: [Col. 0415] “him” added in 1*.] to conduct him honourably into the monastery; and, after prayer had been made there, devoutly to lead him to the abbot’s hall.

After dinner, all officials, both those of the abbot and those of the convent’s departments, were bound to lay down and hand over to him in his presence the keys of their offices. [Note: [Col. 0415] *officiarum*, “of the offices,” in 1*.] If perhaps any of the lord monks, fellow monks, was then committed to prison there or was detained or placed under any regular penance, that Abbot of Saint Trond could freely absolve him or them. When these matters had thus been recounted in order, they bade one another farewell, and Robert proceeded to complete his intended [Col. 0415B] journey.

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1359, on the Nones of May, at about the eleventh hour of the day, the third tower of this monastery, which faced south, fell. Barely half an hour earlier many aldermen and residents, who had long been discussing inheritances within the portico of that monastery, had departed unharmed. A certain boy of three years, sitting and playing beside the wall of this tower, was called away by his brother, scarcely six years old; immediately after his departure the tower collapsed.

Likewise. A year later, Abbot Robert, fearing the collapse of the larger tower, summoned a renowned master mason and had the wall of the larger tower which stood toward the monastery made thicker, and the arch beneath it rebuilt considerably narrower. When the workmen had carried the construction above half the wall’s height, on a certain day at the hour of Mass they piled in excessive quantity upon the supporting scaffolds the heavy stones which they had knocked from the tower wall for continuation of the new work on the old. Immediately the supports and scaffolds were shaken down, and two workmen standing at the top were thrown headlong below. One of them, internally ruptured, died on the fourth day; the other, though—Jesus!—recovered.

Incident. At the same time, a certain hired workman climbed onto the platform to work in the church of Blessed Mary. As he carelessly stepped upon the ceiling, which was made of very thin boards, he fell from above upon the pulpit in the lower choir. It broke apart; he fell to the pavement, burst, and died.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1360, [Col. 0415D] Theodoric, Count of Looz and Lord of Heinsberg, died on 21 January. [Note: [Col. 0415D] He died in 1361; see Mantelius, p. 279.] When his body was brought to the monastery of Herkenrode, it was not received for burial [Note: [Col. 0415D] Because he was excommunicated; see Radulfus de Rivo, 5.]; and so it was carried to the Augustinian convent at Hasselt and buried there.

Incident. After his death, the Bishop of Liège produced letters stating that a certain former count had voluntarily made that county a fief of Saint Lambert, and that it ought to devolve upon the church of that saint if any count should die without offspring. [Col. 0416A] Therefore the leading men of the church and city of Liège, except the nobles of the country’s knighthood, thought it right that the bishop should lay claim to the county, since it had devolved to the church. Thus, notwithstanding that the lord of Dalenbroeck, nephew through the brother [Note: [Col. 0416D] John, who had died earlier.] of the count—to whom the count himself had also bequeathed the county—and Lord Arnold of Rummen, the count’s cousin, sought to have the leading men of the country determine judicially which of the two should receive the county, the aforesaid bishop compelled the inhabitants of Looz, Herk, Hasselt, and other villages to receive him as count and render him fealty.

## 9.

In the year of the Lord 1361, the thirteenth year of Emperor Charles IV [Col. 0416B] and the eighteenth year of Engelbert’s episcopate at Liège, Godfrey of Dalenbroeck placed armed guards in the castle of Stockem [Note: [Col. 0416D] On the left bank of the Meuse near Maaseik.] to hold it for himself. In June the bishop and the whole country of Liège besieged the castle with a very large army.

Concerning the same matter. In the same month the townsmen of Saint Trond began working to obtain a commune for themselves, especially at the instigation of those who had formerly been removed from the aldermanship and council, together with their supporters. They considered that many serious excesses and acts of violence were committed by the sworn associates of the new aldermen. When Abbot Robert learned this, he assembled the entire town in our garden, Vrythof. He came to them with his whole convent, and, silence having been made and a notary summoned, caused the privileges concerning the prohibition against establishing a commune, and the emperor’s penalty imposed upon transgressors of those privileges, to be expounded publicly in the Teutonic language [Col. 0416C] in due order. He added that he was always prepared to correct whatever they could show to be uncorrected within his jurisdiction.

They replied that they charged nothing against their lord, but against the excesses of the aldermen. The aforesaid abbot then saw that every office of the ministerials agreed in raising a commune. Before the testimony of those present, he warned them all to desist from what they had begun, otherwise he would proceed against them under the specified penalties. On that same day, therefore, the chief promoters of the commune hurried to their fellow townsmen who had remained at the siege of the aforesaid castle. Taking with them [Col. 0416D] the masters of the communes of Liège, Huy, and other towns, they blinded the eyes of the lord of Liège with 4,000 florins and more, so that, contrary to his due promise, he granted them authorization, insofar as lay in his power, to establish a commune, on 27 June.

Having received sealed letters, they returned to the town, appointed two masters and twelve councillors, and after a few days usurped the government of the town at their pleasure, contrary to the jurisdiction of both lords [Col. 0417A] and to the town’s liberty. While the bishop and the whole country continued the siege, the guards were compelled, their lives being spared, to surrender the castle on the … day of the month of … . [Note: [Col. 0417] Thus 1*.] [Note: [Col. 0417D] At the beginning of June, as appears from Radulfus de Rivo, who shows in ch. 5 that the siege began on 7 May.]

When the aforesaid masters proposed to seek the lord abbot’s consent to the commune that had been established, he first summoned the entire convent to the chapter-house. Seeking the advice and final consent of all, he found them unanimous that they would by no means assent to the commune, but would support him with all their strength in resisting it. A few days later, when the lord abbot had gone to the New Court, the masters of the commune and their supporters came to him, insisting that he consent to the established commune. He replied: “I do not consent to the commune in any way; but I offer myself ready, insofar as I am bound, to correct such excesses as you may put forward.” [Col. 0417B]

Thereafter the abbot feared that they would try violently to compel him, while he remained there, to consent to the commune and their will, as had formerly been attempted, though in vain, in the time of Abbot Ada, as narrated above. By his friends’ advice he went to Liège. Arriving there around the following feast of Dionysius, he remained there for three years less three months. Though he repeatedly and diligently petitioned the bishop, the chapter of Liège, the city, and the towns of the country to procure that the people of Saint Trond—who, contrary to the oath they had sworn, had adopted a commune to the prejudice of his monastery—withdraw from their unlawful usurpations, he obtained no final answer. The chapter of Liège, however, always took his side. [Col. 0417C]

## 10.

In the same year (1361), after Pentecost (16 May), at the urging of honourable men, Abbot Robert ratified and confirmed the testament of Sir John of Halbeke, knight, concerning feudal goods—as the Count of Looz and the Lord of Lummen had previously done—according to the judgment of his vassals, for the benefit of the natural sons of the aforesaid Sir John. To these he assigned a fixed sum of money secured upon the aforesaid goods.

Henry of Halbeke, nephew through the brother of that Sir John, with armed retainers from Guelders and Jülich who adhered to him, unjustly renounced allegiance to Abbot Robert, his men, and the goods of the monastery on account of this legacy, by letters sent to our monastery before sunset. [Col. 0417D] On the next day, at twilight, he plundered and burned our village of Halchter and the court of Dola there, carrying off our men as prisoners. Since through his nocturnal incendiary agents he likewise inflicted damage upon the Lord of Heere, executor of the said Sir John, the latter’s efforts obtained his outlawry by the twelve guardians of the peace of Hesbaye; and three of his incendiary agents, captured at Heere, were broken on the wheel. [Col. 0418A]

Likewise. In the same year, since our upper residence at Dola, with its well-moated fortification, had still remained safe from fire, the abbot, on the counsel of his men, caused its straw roofs to be removed lest they could be burned by enemies. Behold another misfortune: when the abbot’s servants set fire to the roofing straw in order to deprive robbers of material for arson, a gust of wind immediately drove the flame back upon the buildings not yet unroofed and reduced everything, together with the fortification itself, to ashes.

Likewise. In the same year, on the feast of the Apostle Bartholomew (24 August), the same Henry, through his men, burned the Dola residence, then unroofed of straw, at twilight.

Likewise. Afterwards, in the middle of the night of the vigil of the Conception of Saint Mary [Col. 0418B] (7 December), the barn of our tenant who pays land-rent [Note: [Col. 0418D] One who pays a land-rent.] at Engelbamd, full of grain and hay, was burned by the same man. That same night our mill at Merwile was set on fire, but the fire was extinguished without great damage.

Likewise. In the fourth year after this (1362), in March, that same accursed man, with eighteen accomplices, killed the priest of Halchter before the cemetery, grievously wounded seven men, and carried off five prisoners.

Likewise. In the aforesaid year, on 8 April at twilight, one of the incendiaries of the wicked Henry was captured by the forester of the New Court near the bridge of Merwile while proceeding to burn the barn of one of our tenants. Handed over to the forester of our town, he voluntarily confessed that he had recently burned [Note: [Col. 0417] *incendiassie*, 1*.] the aforesaid barn [Col. 0418C] at Engelbamd, and that, had he not been captured, he would that very night have committed several more arsons. In his sack they found pieces of wood composed of sulphur and tow; when inserted into the roofs of houses or into the crops of barns, flames would break out either at that very hour, or on the next or following day, according to the invention of the wickedness of such men.

Having accused several accomplices in his crime, on the sixth following day (14 April), before the mill of Merwile—which he had set on fire on the preceding night—he was tied behind horses, dragged to the place of the condemned, and broken on the wheel.

Likewise. In the same year, on 3 June, Henry of Halbeke and his accomplices burned the church and eight dwellings in the village of Halchter. At the sound of the bell, men of Houthalen [Note: [Col. 0418D] Not far from Hasselt.] and other villages ran to Halchter. Having recovered the booty, they compelled the robbers to retreat. On Henry’s side three armed retainers and twenty horses were killed, and several others wounded; on the other side, one man of Halchter and two of Houthalen fell. Afterwards Abbot Robert appointed two guardians, through whom many accomplices of the aforesaid … [Note: [Col. 0417] Here the quire ends; the following one continues with the word “lord,” in the same hand; nothing has been cut away, but through the scribe’s negligence something appears to have been omitted.] [The surviving text resumes:] “to the lord of Rummen, for a specified sum of money, charters and letters concerning the county having been handed over to him, he himself makes mention …” [Col. 0419A] And when Emperor Charles arrived at Aachen shortly afterwards around the feast of All Saints, that Lord of Rummen, appearing before him, is said to have received investiture of the aforesaid county from him. In the following year a judgment is said to have been delivered at Prague for him and his heirs, before the bishop and that same Lord of Rummen, cited in due course to appear before the emperor, had appeared.

## 11.

In the year of the Lord 1363, two sworn associates, accused of the heinous robbery perpetrated at the court of Saint Agnes, were captured and long imprisoned. One of them was beheaded by judgment of the aldermen of Saint Trond; [Note: [Col. 0419] *decapitur*, 1*.] the other, detained by the sheriff of Montenaken and condemned by the aldermen of Veerte, was broken on the wheel at Brustem. [Col. 0419B]

Likewise. In the same year, three of four aldermen accused, as accomplices, of the aforesaid crime died at Liège, where they were residing for protection and had fallen ill. Although many said that they had been punished at the prompting of divine judgment by their sudden death, who knows? The fourth, after some time—namely, in the year of the Lord 1372 around the feast of All Saints—was accused of the same deed by suitable witnesses in the presence of the aldermen of Saint Trond at the place of judgment. Summoned by the proclamation-bell and cited through the customary fortnightly terms, he did not appear and was outlawed from his honour and his own right.

Likewise. In the aforesaid year (1363), the stone wall surrounding the court of the monastery was begun, and the part extending from [Col. 0419C] our gate to our mill was completed.

Incident. In that same year Bishop Engelbert received investiture from Wenceslaus, Duke of Brabant, as Count of Looz, of the fief of the advocacy of Saint Trond and of the fiefs of the castle of Duras and of Kaelmont.

Likewise. In the same year, two of the five sworn associates, defendants in the crime committed at the aforesaid court of Saint Agnes, were forestalled by the end of natural death and escaped retaliation for their misdeeds.

Likewise. In the following year (1364), the fifth accomplice in the aforesaid crime, asserting that he had been present at the crime and brought there but had not laid hands upon anyone, was buried alive on 21 May.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1364, in May, Engelbert, Bishop of Liège, was transferred by Pope Clement V [Note: [Col. 0419D] Urban V.] to the see of Cologne, [Note: [Col. 0419D] Successor of Archbishop Adolf of Mark.] [Col. 0419D] and John of Arkel, Bishop of Utrecht, to the see of Liège.

Incident. In the same year, Arnold of Rummen and Henry—by whom a great army had been assembled—were summoned to a judicial duel at Liège on 8 May and were declared contumacious. Of these, the knight John of Puteaux, together with his two brothers, made homage to the lord abbot in satisfaction; and at last that diabolical Henry bound himself to abide by the decision of two honourable knights.

Incident. In the year of the Lord 1362, Pope Innocent VI died. Since the cardinals disagreed about electing one from their own body, Urban [Note: [Col. 0419] corrected from *Clemens*.] V succeeded him; he had been abbot of Marseille, of the Benedictine Order. In the same year the masters of the commune erected a stone perron in the marketplace, surmounted by a cross and a gilded eagle.

Incident. In the same year, Lord Godfrey of Dalenbroeck, seeing that he could not resist the Bishop of Liège, who had been received as count throughout the whole county, sold to his kinsman [Note: [Col. 0420D] Arnold of Rummen.] all the right [Note: [Col. 0419D] Radulfus de Rivo, ch. 6, shows that this was done in 1363.] that he possessed in the County of Looz. … [Note: [Col. 0419] It appears that something is again missing; in the manuscript there is only the bare trace of a lacuna.] … With the aid of princes favourable to him, he attacked before the town of Herk with the unfurled banners of the arms of the County of [Col. 0421A] Looz. The inhabitants, prudently choosing flight through fear, shortly afterwards received him and rendered him fealty; but on the following day, after the army’s departure, those inhabitants again offered themselves to the men of Liège.

On the next day, which was the vigil of Pentecost (11 May), news of the matter spreading everywhere, the men of Liège and Huy, stirred by indignation with the whole country, advanced under arms as far as the Jeker River. Because of Bishop Engelbert’s absence, they chose John, Lord of Rochefort, as their guardian. On Pentecost, 12 May, the people of Saint Trond, at about Vespers, went out under arms to meet the country of Liège and entered the grange of the Teutonic lords at Obhere. There they spent the night, violently broke open various enclosures, [Col. 0421B] scattered their goods and sent the plunder to the town, and wilfully trampled down the unripe crops in the fields.

On the following fourth day (16 May), the mounted men of the whole country came to Rummen Castle and burned the village with its appurtenances. On the following day (17 May), turning aside to the village of Hamal, they burned the castle itself.

13. In the same year, on the octave of Pentecost, which fell on 19 May, our townsmen of Saint Trond, seeing that Abbot Robert had, since the preceding year, brought suit against them before the official of Liège on account of the commune which they had established against his will, and although they had recently lodged a complaint concerning this before the whole country, had made no progress, now, at the urging of the masters of the commune, took with them two townsmen from each craft and went to the city of Liège to incite the commune of Liège against the abbot himself. There, on the following Tuesday (22 May), when the aforesaid abbot appeared in the chapter at Liège with his friends, the men of Saint Trond, by giving gifts, won over to their side the greater part of the ministerial officers of Liège. They offered the lord abbot the choice either to seal the commune or to be expelled from the city or the country, granting him three days for deliberation. On the following day (23 May), the vigil of Corpus Christi, when the masters of Liège informed him that he must seal the commune or depart, at daybreak on Corpus Christi itself (24 May) he left the city with his belongings and household.

When this was announced to our convent before the procession, we were thrown into anxiety. During the departure and return of that solemn procession, we hurriedly had the valuables of the monastery and abbey conveyed by cart to our residence at Leeuw.
