Reserving the necessary clothing for our persons, we secretly sent our jewels and household goods, item by item, outside the convent, to be kept safely with trusted friends within and outside the town. After a few days had elapsed, that devout exile, Abbot Robert, having had his goods and possessions conveyed from Liège to the aforesaid town of Leeuw, came before supper to the New Court. On the following day, Sunday, receiving warning from secret friends to beware lest he be violently overpowered by the captains of the commune, he immediately moved to Leeuw and remained there.

After this, on 9 June, a certain babbler and leading adversary of the monastery, from the craft of the cerdones—i.e. shoemakers—stirred up, with his accomplices, a commune at the convent of the Friars Minor against our schout and one of the aldermen, charging them with having induced Abbot Robert to leave the New Court. Again, after dinner, this insolent man, with his followers and a small commune, procured—against the will of the masters—that the schout himself be banished for ten years. He was kept outside the town for a long time.

Likewise. In the same year, on the day after Saint James the Less (22 June), John of Arkel, previously the aforesaid bishop of Utrecht, having been appointed bishop of Liège by apostolic authority, received from Emperor Charles the regalia, expressly including the county of Loon, and came to the episcopal fortress of Franchimont. After a few days he entered the city of Liège, where he was peacefully received and was called John V of that name.

Likewise. About the same time the townsmen of Saint Trond repeatedly approached the newly created Bishop John with promises of money, asking that, like his predecessor Engelbert, he grant and seal the commune for them. He refused, but proposed to them that, if they would consent to him, he would exert all his strength to procure a complete peace between the abbot and themselves. Therefore, on the vigil of Saint Giles (31 August), the aforesaid townsmen lodged a grave complaint at Liège against the bishop in the presence of the masters of the whole country, all of whom supported the sealing of the commune. But when another day was again appointed—the day after the Nativity of the Blessed Mary (8 September)—the aforesaid bishop of Liège refused to consent.

Accordingly, when in the progress of the suit the town’s procurator had appealed from the interlocutory ruling to the delegate, namely the abbot of Saint James, and the townsmen of Saint Trond, while the appeal was pending, had caused Lord Abbot Robert to be summoned to proceed in the cause before that delegate, Abbot Robert asked that the case be referred to the Apostolic See, alleging that he could not litigate safely at Liège. Therefore the delegate, when the parties had appeared before him, referred the case to the Apostolic See, assigning them, after a period of two months, to present themselves before the Apostolic See. Within that time, by agreement of both parties, the date for appearing at the Roman Curia was extended until the first day of March, in hope of peace.

In the following year (1365), at the instance of the men of Saint Trond, the commune summoned the chapter of Liège and Abbot Robert to consent to the commune, but did not prevail.

Likewise. In the same year Abbot Robert, leaving the town of Leeuw, set out for the Roman Curia on 3 May. When the legal case against the establishment of the commune of our townsmen was reported in consistory, it was entrusted to the auditor of the Sacred Palace. Afterwards, about the feast of Dionysius, the abbot returned to these regions, leaving there one faithful agent. When, on his return, he arrived at Utrecht, the masters of Liège asked the new bishop John to cause the abbot to desist both from the appeal of judicial combat, by which he was prosecuting six townsmen of Saint Trond through a guardian, and from the suit against the town of Saint Trond. He consented to them in nothing; therefore the aforesaid abbot moved from Utrecht to the city of Cologne.

Likewise. About the same time, the townsmen of Saint Trond went out to attack the castle of Rummen. Advancing to the entrance of its outer ward, where costly structures of defenses and walls, fortified by encircling waters, presented a threatening appearance, they boldly forded their way up to the gate and walls, without fear of the missiles of crossbows and thunderous guns. Breaking violently into the whole structure, they burned it to the very foundations of the castle. And, as was reported, had they persisted in assaulting the castle, they would have taken it, because all but scarcely eight of its guards had gone to amuse themselves at certain wedding festivities in a neighboring village. Having burned all these things, the men of Saint Trond returned home. Shortly afterwards, as the guards were returning to the castle, they found five young men of Saint Trond picking cherries in the cherry trees; attacking them, they killed them.

Likewise. In the year of the Lord 1365, on 11 August, the castle of Rummen was besieged by Bishop John with the whole country and its knighthood. There, among the other mangonels or engines, the machine of the townsmen of Saint Trond threw stones of such weight that the besieged especially feared its discharge, since the fabric of the castle was shaken by it. Moreover, when on the vigil of Dionysius the bishop had caused a certain engine called a boar to be fitted against one of the castle towers, the wall was immediately broken by repeated terrible blows, and that tower fell. On the day after the aforesaid feast of Dionysius, a second boar was driven against another tower so forcefully that the castle’s masonry was breaking apart. Then the guards went up to the level platform prepared on the summit of the castle and resisted most fiercely, throwing sulphurous balls upon the boar-engine, along with burning firebrands and thunderous leaden balls, maiming and killing many of the attackers. At last, suffering force, they were compelled to surrender the castle, with only their persons spared: their number was 124, apart from six dead. [Note: Ralph of the Rivo, ch. 8, has only this, while agreeing in the rest.]

When they had been led to the prison of the castle of Musal, the towers and walls were thrown down and the remaining structures burned. That castle site was proscribed and forbidden to be rebuilt for one hundred years. Although during this siege many ecclesiastical men and women suffered grave losses of their possessions, especially the Teutonic lords and brothers, the goods of our monastery, both at the New Court and elsewhere, remained untouched, Lord Godfrey of Harduemont protecting us in person.

14. In the year of the Lord 1366 [Note: “1367” falsely in 1*.], on 22 February, John V, bishop of Liège, came with a few of his followers, without the knowledge of ourselves or the townsmen, about the hour of High Mass. He entered through the gate of our court into the monastery as a bishop making his joyful entry [Note: *Joyeuse entrée*.], but without any ceremony. Having assembled the aldermen together with the townsmen, he took the oath of fealty, as bishops of Liège are accustomed to do, upon the altar of Saint Trudo. He then went to ring the ban-bell; after it had been rung for a long time, he exhorted the assembled people to return to their senses concerning the government of the commune which they had attempted. On hearing this, the captains of the commune were utterly dumbfounded, as though half-dead.

Had he boldly said, “Let those who desire the safety of the town and my friendship come to me! I shall give you a government in which you ought deservedly to rejoice,” the greater part would have come over to him. But because he said, “Let each man come to his craft, to give me an answer,” they immediately [Note: *stanti* in 1*.] became more resolute and, encouraging one another, replied: “We do not wish to abandon the commune undertaken with the consent of Bishop Engelbert; rather, we wish to submit to the ordinance of the country of Liège.”

Therefore, on the following Tuesday, the feast of Saint Matthias (24 February), thirteen persons from among our townsmen were chosen, on the advice of the masters of Liège and Huy, who could establish peace with the lords. But in March, when peace was being negotiated at Liège, the masters of the country of Liège threatened to expel from the country and from the land of the count of Loon the envoys of the lord abbot who were giving him counsel, together with all who adhered to them, unless he himself consented to the commune. Yet on the following day, when those masters and the thirteen sworn representatives submitted in writing the articles of government devised for themselves, the answer was that the abbot was in no way willing to assent to these.

After this, about the beginning of May, when the dean of Saint Lambert, a theologian, and several experts in law had worked out a more moderate new constitution for the government of this town [Note: *concepte* (‘devised,’ feminine) in 1*, rather than the text’s *concepto*.], it was communicated to the aforesaid abbot, then residing at Cologne, because negotiations for a peace settlement were taking place. Since, through misleading information [Note: *ifotus* in 1*.], he believed this form of peace would be more favorable to himself than later proved to be the case, he immediately returned from Cologne to Saint Servatius at Utrecht. The men of Liège were striving to compel the bishop to be seized.

15. In that same year, 1366, while Abbot Robert was thus at Utrecht, he began to suffer fever on 11 May. As his illness was already worsening, on 18 May, about vespers, having received communion and been anointed, he gave up his spirit with great devotion and an outpouring of tears. After nightfall his body was placed in a covered cart and carried toward our monastery. Before midnight, when the driver lost his way, the cart overturned in an open field; the cart broke, and the bier sprang out and came apart. Blessed in all things is God, who had formerly scourged him while living with manifold afflictions, both in losses of temporal goods inflicted by tyrannical princes and other ensuing misfortunes, and with bodily illnesses; and who now, after his spirit had been saved unto eternity, permitted the lifeless trunk of his body to be dashed by such a crash.

Another cart having been obtained in the village called Herderen, the funeral was carried as far as the entrance of the town. There the convent, with priests and clerics, kept watch, while a multitude of people stood around. The body was taken from the cart and borne in procession to the monastery. It was honorably placed before the chapel of Saint Trudo; Mass having been sung, the body of the deceased was buried before the entrance of the crypt, as he had ordered while alive. Present there were the bishop of Liège, the dean of Saint Lambert, and other canons of his, who had assembled in order to attend the election to be celebrated.

Likewise. During the sixteen years in which he governed, this Abbot Robert suffered in various ways most grievous losses amounting to more than 20,000 florins. Yet he acquired for our monastery the residence of Borchgat with its stronghold and adjoining lands; likewise, the properties of Myrhope, insofar as they were rent-paying. Nevertheless, beyond payment of the debts with which the monastery was burdened, he left more than one thousand measures of rye, both as debts due and in ready store. On his anniversary, the convent has annually, for a pittance in the refectory from his paternal goods, four measures of spelt.

And know, reader, that two of the princes and two others of the common people, through whose tyranny and wrongful attacks the aforesaid Abbot Robert endured such great losses, were struck down long before his death both by the severe scourges of the highest Prince and of frenzy, and by burdens inflicted by earthly princes; and one of them, moreover, was openly smitten by the extremity of miseries. Thus the affliction in this life of those aforesaid wrongdoers—who in former times had so often invaded the possessions of this monastery—may deservedly be ascribed to Blessed Trudo, who mercifully punished them in body and goods that they might be saved in soul.

Likewise. Therefore, in the same year of the Lord 1366, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Charles IV, the eighteenth of his empire, the fifth year of Pope Urban V [Note: Another corrected this to “Urban”; the text has “Clement.”], and the third year of the episcopate of John V, bishop of Liège, after Robert, abbot of this place, had been buried, on the same day about the eleventh hour, a chapter having been called, the dean of Saint Lambert gave a short address concerning the proper manner of electing an abbot. When it was finished, the bishop and dean, with the others, left the chapter. There, in the secrecy of the chapter, after invocation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, Zazeus the sacristan was unanimously elected abbot by all.

Then the bishop was summoned and, with the elect placed between the prior and one of the elders, escorted him to the choir with the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*. He proclaimed his election, as ordinary, to the people assembled in the monastery, and on the following Thursday confirmed him when he was presented at Liège. These things having been done, the exequies of the deceased abbot were solemnly and honorably performed on 16 June, Abbot Helinand of Saint James celebrating Mass.

*Here ends the second book of the fourth and final part of the deeds of the abbots of this monastery of Saint Trudo.*

[Note: The following was written in a contemporary hand on the final pages after the fourth part of the *Deeds of Saint Trond*.]

Lest those things which happen in time slip away with time—for time is devouring—it is fitting to write down for future generations matters worthy of remembrance. In the year of the world 6668 according to the common reckoning of chronographers, and according to the Hebrews and the translation of Blessed Jerome in the year 5421; indeed, in the year from Christ’s birth 1469, on 7 March, the Tuesday after *Oculi*, at the ninth hour; while Pope Paul II held the pontificate; Frederick III, emperor of the Romans, was ruling; Louis XI, foremost among all kings, was king of the French; Edward IV was king of the English, together with Henry VI, now at this time imprisoned; Henry IV was king of Castile and León; Alfonso V king of Portugal; James III king of the Scots; John II king of Aragon and Navarre; Ferdinand I king of Sicily Proper; René of Anjou, duke of Sicily, also using the title of king of Aragon; Louis of Savoy, together with James, rightful holder of the kingdom of Cyprus; Christian I king of the Danes, Norwegians, and Swedes [Note: He had already been expelled by the Swedes in 1464.]; Casimir IV king of Poland; Matthias, a warlike soldier, holding the kingdoms of Hungary, Dalmatia, and Croatia; and George, a foreigner and not heir to the kingdom, occupying the kingdom of Bohemia; while Charles, by God’s grace duke of Burgundy, Lorraine, Brabant, Limburg, and Luxembourg, count and ruler of Flanders, etc., was reigning; in the presence of the illustrious-born, the reverend father in Christ Lord Louis of Bourbon, by God’s grace bishop of Liège, duke of Bouillon, count of Loon, and Guy de Brimeu, lord of Humbercourt, governor and guardian of the said duke of Burgundy by authority in the country of Liège and the county of Loon:

Arnold of Beringen, by the resignation of Lord Henry of Coninxhem, former abbot, and by apostolic confirmation, abbot by divine providence, solemnly entered the town of Saint Trond, Saint Trudo’s town. He was received with great rejoicing by all the clergy, senate, and people. He was consecrated by the venerable Lord John, bishop of Liberi, suffragan of the bishop of Liège, wearing priestly vestments, in the presence of the venerable Lords Gerard, abbot of Floreffe, and Siger, abbot of Heilissem, in the 780th year from the death of Saint Trudo, most glorious confessor. The reverend bishop of Liège and the aforesaid lord governor and guardian attended the consecration of this Lord Abbot Arnold, as did many other knights and nobles, likewise doctors, licentiates, masters, and other learned and experienced men. May God, who is blessed for ever, deign through the merits of Saint Trudo and of the saints, male and female, to preserve this new abbot long in tranquil peace and safety. Amen.

> So long as the boar [verb apparently omitted] the mountain ridges;  
> So long as fish [love] the rivers, and bees feed on thyme  
> And cicadas on dew; so long as rivers run into the sea,  
> So long as shadows roam the mountains and the sky pasture the stars,  
> His honor, name, and praises shall endure for ever.  
>
> [Note: Virgil, *Eclogues* V.76–78; *Aeneid* I.607–609. Grotefend.]

**ArnoLdVs de BerIngh Con VentVs pater abbas** — Arnold of Beringen, father and abbot of the convent.  
**II VIVs, nVnC sIt eI paX, leX, greX et deCVs oMne** — May he live; now may there be for him peace, law, flock, and every honor.

[Note: The italic letters are written in red.]

These verses give the years of Christ, 1469; moreover, [they give]

The origin of this monastery, when, after its name was changed,  
Sarchinium began to bear Trudo’s name:  
With M and L removed, the remaining numerals doubled  
[Note: i.e. 369; doubled, this number indicates 738, the year of the foundation of the monastery of Saint Trudo.],

While Bishop Lambert suffered martyrdom, and Saint Hubert,  
Last bishop of Maastricht and first bishop of Liège,  
Succeeded him; Floribert succeeded him  
After the translation of the see, which sacred Liège deserved,  
While Charles Martel ruled the sceptres of the Franks.

All vowels joined to D give the years  
Of the outstanding Bishop Louis.

The word *VoX* gives the years of Bishop Louis’s episcopate.

[Note: Fifteen occurrences of D followed by a vowel appear in verses 29–45; thus Bishop Louis’s years number fifteen. The same number is indicated by *vox* in verse 42. We owe this calculation to Grotefend.]

We mark the abbot’s years by hair and cowl;  
All categories are indicated in the words.

These things I, Hugh the chronographer, sang of the unconquered duke.

I lie among my own; Christ God is my heir.  
Why should anyone beware of violating my church?

My town is said to bear the name Trudonea,  
Joining together the lands of count and duke.

An alien sickle does not rightly rejoice in my harvest;  
Yet I was the first soil of the monastery.

The goods of holy Lambert or Hubert are not mine—  
Of Metz and of the empire—but goods won for God.

Not all can always be first;  
Nothing stable exists, nor anything violent for long.

My stiff-necked people, acknowledge me as your patron;  
Say with bent knees: “Trudo, patron, pray!”

Those joined to me know how to intercede  
Before God continually with sweet prayer and hymn.

If you strive to keep your patron’s commands,  
Your enemies will fail by air, water, fire, and land.

Therefore I shall be an enemy to your enemies; but to friends  
I shall give the fruits of joy with mercy.

Therefore, you covetous persons, refrain from touching the fruits of saints,  
So that they may stand for you before the Judge on the Day.

It is a great matter to offend the saints of the most high God,  
For wrath comes suddenly upon the wicked.

[Note: The following is found near the end of the codex, written in a later hand.]

George, surnamed Sarens, a native of Mechelen, a man above all pious and gentle, after being abbot of Boneffe was later declared abbot of this most celebrated monastery of Saint Trudo. On the Nativity of the Virgin Mother itself, in September of the year of salvation 1493, he assumed the monastic habit at Boneffe, in the sixteenth year of his age. He was born on the sacred feast of Saint Vitus itself, 15 June, Sunday, on the day after Corpus Christi, between the first and second afternoon hours, in 1477.

[Note: This record is found on the last folio of codex 1, in the same hand as the rest; it is absent from codex 1*.]

I, Adelard II (1055–1082), abbot of this place by the grace of God alone, grant to abbots and brothers who shall come after me a share and fellowship with all the saints. Hearing that in certain places more diligent care is taken of the poor than has hitherto been taken among us, we have resolved, for our common salvation, to improve that care according to their custom and to confirm it by letters under our own hand, so that it may be inviolably observed. Each day, at the Mandatum, three poor persons were given one loaf and bread portions from the brothers’ leftovers, with one *staupus*—a cup or measure of liquid, our *stof* or *stübchen*—of beer; and at the gate, three rye loaves, besides half a measure from the brewhouse for poor persons arriving from elsewhere. We afterwards added seven loaves: three for boys at the Mandatum and four rye loaves for other poor persons, together with half a measure of beer from the gruit.

It also seemed good to our lords and predecessor abbots, and to me, to provide some commemoration; and we have done this only for those whom we were able either to see or to know. On the anniversary of Lord Abbot Adelard I, four solidi shall be given to the brothers and twelve denarii for beer to the poor. Likewise, on the anniversary of Lord Abbot Guntram, the brothers shall have four solidi, while the poor shall have twelve denarii for beer and half a measure of bread. On my anniversary, however, eight solidi shall be given for the brothers’ service, and two for beer for the use of the poor, together with one measure of bread. We have established this so that, while I live, it shall be given on the anniversary of our consecration, but after our departure, on the anniversary of our death. This pound of denarii shall be paid from the allod of Herken, which we bought from Count G. of Musal; the bread, however, from Villarium.

Since we observe the anniversaries of our deceased brothers far too negligently, we judged it good to redeem once a year the omissions of the whole year: namely, on the first day after the Mass of All Saints, when a vigil, Mass, and commendation of the soul should be celebrated for them, with the bells ringing; on that day the brothers should also be given a charity of three solidi. [Note: The rest is lacking.]

[Note: These charters were written in 1* in the same hand which copied the final part of the *Deeds*.]

These are copies of charters concerning the right to the gruit or brewing-duty of the whole town belonging to our monastery. By reason of it, every week we receive from each brewery or brewhouse, whenever they brew, one *pecarium* of beer. The first of these is that narrated in the first part of this compilation on the deeds of the abbots, book I, chapter 22; its tenor is as follows: “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, let it be known to all, present and future, how Lord Theoderic, bishop of the see of Metz, etc.” [Note: The same charter is repeated which we gave above from the earlier, twelfth-century part of the codex.]

Likewise, concerning the same matter. The second follows, narrated in the third part of the compilation, book I, chapter 3; its tenor is as follows:

(1140) “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Stephen, by God’s grace bishop of the holy church of Metz, makes known to all, present and future, how Lord Theoderic, bishop of the see of Metz, having stayed for some time in the monastery of Saint Trudo, fell ill there and came to the point of death. With the counsel of his friends, he gave to that church and to the brothers serving God there the brewing-duty of the same town, which belonged to the service of himself and his predecessors. He did this for the remedy of his own soul and those of his other predecessors, so that their memory might remain there, not as before, but more perfectly and securely.

“Lord Adelbero, his successor both by kinship and in the office established in the aforesaid place, observing this and considering the reason and necessity for which the said brothers sought this from their lord bishop—namely, so that their drink, hitherto regarded as inferior, might thereafter be somewhat improved—decreed that it should be recorded by the authority of a written instrument and marked with his seal. Lord Abbot Adelard II of that place and the other brothers requested the same, so that none of his successors might dare to infringe it, and so that what he himself had bestowed upon the aforesaid saint and those serving him for the remedy of his soul, he might also confirm for the sake of his own soul and those of his successors.

“I too, Stephen, bishop of that same holy church of Metz, have renewed and confirmed this for the remedy of my soul and those of my predecessors, so that it may remain valid and unshaken, and that no one may henceforth be permitted to infringe it. Since this belonged to the service of our predecessors and ourselves, we establish and confirm under our own hand that no one may contest or withhold the rent which is lawfully due to the church of Saint Trudo from the aforesaid brewing-duty, from all taverns situated either within the town of Saint Trond or outside it but belonging to that town.

“This renewal and confirmation was made publicly, at the request of Lord Abbot Folcard and his brothers, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1140, indiction 3, while Innocent was pope at Rome, Conrad king, under the suitable witnesses subscribed below: Theoderic the primicerius; Albero and Walner, chaplains; Henry, count of Salm; Gerard of Rottei; Walter; Otto the marshal; Gerard; Richard.

“I, Albero II by name, by God’s grace bishop of Liège, at the request of Lord Stephen, bishop of Metz, have confirmed these things by the ban of our authority and strengthened them by subscription. Since it is the brothers’ prebend, no one may alienate or diminish it in any way. If anyone attempts to oppose this, or retains or claims anything of these things for himself, then, according to the decrees of the holy fathers, giver, receiver, and possessor alike shall be under anathema until he makes satisfaction and restores the church’s goods.”

Likewise, concerning the same. The third follows; its tenor is as follows:

“Stephen, by God’s grace bishop of Metz, to his faithful people dwelling in the town of Saint Trond: the grace of God and his own, if they obey. Church property is the vowed support of the faithful who live piously; whoever takes it away or diminishes it shall, according to the truthful sentence of the fathers, be subject with Judas the traitor to eternal damnation. We admonish you to beware of such conduct, lest you incur a like punishment of damnation.

“We make known to you that, when the cause of the brothers of the church of Saint Trudo had been laid before the counsel of our faithful men and carefully investigated, we gave our hand to truth and rendered satisfaction to justice. Therefore we judge firm and inviolable the alms which the generosity of our predecessors bestowed upon them—namely the rent of the gruit, according to the written authority [Note: “authority” appears to have dropped out.] which truth renewed for them concerning it and which the revered authority of our venerable brother Albero, bishop of Liège, confirmed at our request. We decree that those who act against this shall be subject to anathema and eternal damnation unless they repent. We command our men, by the fealty owed to us, to acknowledge the church’s right; if they neglect this, we shall not fail the church, but shall faithfully maintain its cause as the duty of our office requires.”

The fourth follows. It determines the right concerning the *mala gruta*, what belongs from it to the gruit-collector, and the six demesne breweries, which are free and pay no brewery-rent—that is, no *pecarium* of beer. It is also mentioned in the third part of the aforesaid compilation, book I, chapter 3. Its tenor is as follows:

(1139) “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be known to present and future alike how I, Folcard, by God’s grace abbot of Saint Trudo, in order to settle the lawsuit and contention which, in the time of my predecessor Lord Abbot Rodulf, was repeatedly and gravely raised concerning the gruit of this town, make, by the impression of my seal, a ban and confirmation concerning that same gruit in favor of Renerus, his wife Engeltrudis, and their heirs, according to their right and justice, which are known to all today.

“The same Renerus and his wife Engeltrudis had first taken this gruit in pledge for one hundred marks, in the presence of Lord Abbot Rodulf, from those who asserted that the gruit was their inheritance, namely Renerus, Robert, Hugh, and their sons. Later they added so much of their own that all of them surrendered by the rod that gruit and every hereditary right which they appeared to possess in it. Renerus and his wife Engeltrudis received it, by hereditary right, from the hand of Abbot Rodulf, before the brothers, aldermen, and peers of the church, for the use of themselves and their sons.

“That these things may remain valid and unshaken, they have been renewed in the same terms by us, as they had been done by our predecessor, lawfully and by hereditary right before the chapter, aldermen, and peers of the church, for the said Renerus, his wife Engeltrudis, and their heirs. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, indiction 2, epact 18, while Innocent was pope at Rome, Conrad king, Stephen presiding at Metz, Albero II at Liège, in the first year of our prelacy.”

The gruit-collector owes the church five pounds of pepper annually: at Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, the feast of Saint Remigius, and the feast of Saint Trudo. On those five solemnities, when he pays the pepper, he receives from the cellarer two loaves for elders, two for boys, two portions of fish such as the brothers have, and a sextary of wine. On the anniversary of Theoderic, bishop of Metz—namely, 30 April—who gave that gruit to the brothers, he also gives five solidi; and likewise, on the Ides of November, on the anniversary of Adelbero, bishop of Metz, who confirmed that gruit for the brothers, five solidi. On those days he has a prebend like any one of the brothers. He gives gruit free of charge to the demesne breweries; and of the gruit-rent from the breweries of this town, the church has two parts and the gruit-collector the third.

The following brothers were present at this confirmation: Prior Egebert, Baldwin, Henry, Fulbert, Eliold, Conrad.

## On the Right of Paying the Rent of the *Mala Gruta*

It should be known that the rent of the *mala gruta*, which Lord Theoderic II, bishop of Metz, of pious memory, together with the brewing-duty, had solemnly granted to our church in perpetual right—though it had previously belonged to his own church—was many years ago separated from the rent of the brewing-duty, commonly called *panthgiis*, and passed into the hereditary possession of certain townsmen. But by what means, or by what exchange for other inheritances, the grant of the aforesaid charter concerning the *mala gruta* was altered, so that these heirs pay only fifteen Leuven solidi to the provost of our church, cannot be determined from the charter archives of our monastery.

Moreover, it should be known that the hereditary right in the aforesaid “bad gruit,” having in the course of time devolved upon certain leading men of the town, has been divided into three parts. [Col. 0431D] One part of it, long ago devolved upon Lady Gertrude called Pondernuel, a female knight, was by her granted about the year of the Lord 1352 for the establishment of two benefices: one situated in our monastery at the altar of the Blessed Mary and Saint Anne, and the other at the altar of All Saints in the church of the Holy Sepulchre. The remaining two parts are divided thus: the heirs of the late Eustace called [Col. 0432C] Greve and the children of de Palude possess one part; the third part is held by the heirs of the late Sir Albertinus, knight, and of his cousin Ada of Saint Catherine, alderman of this town. The fixed revenues of this gruit are received upon and from the houses—namely, the brewery situated at the corner opposite the hall of our lord abbot, called the gruit-house, and the remaining adjoining dwellings as far as the corner upon the stream; and then from that corner to the other dwellings built on this side of the stream, as far as the public lane situated there. These dwellings pay no other ground-rent to our provost except the aforesaid rent.

Furthermore, by right of this gruit the aforesaid heirs receive, from every beer brewed within the jurisdiction of the town, one and a half Liège deniers—amounting to a fourth part of one old gros—whenever [Col. 0432D] they brew, except for five breweries, that is, brew-houses, called “lordly,” which are free from this payment for one brewing; but if they brew more than once in a week, they pay on the further brewing as do the others. There are three such breweries. One is situated in Plancstrate Street opposite our principal cemetery called Vriethof; the second lies between the church of the Blessed Mary and the residence of the Teutonic [Col. 0433A] lords, with several houses intervening on the other side; the third is in the new houses above the corner of the street toward the church. There are also two others, one called the Brewery of the Holy Spirit, and another situated in Salt Street beyond the stream, adjoining the dwelling standing above the corner; whenever brewing takes place in these, they pay no money. There is also a sixth, opposite the house of Everbodius, [Col. 0434A] in which, whenever brewing takes place, the brewer is given that sum gratis by the heirs of the gruit. At this brewery the aforesaid heirs are entitled, whenever brewing occurs, to eighteen quarts of beer, to be divided among themselves. Moreover, it should be known that these six lordly breweries, whenever they brew, are free from the beer-measurer’s rent which we receive from the remaining breweries within the liberty of the town.

[Col. 0433]

LETTERS OF RODULF.

(See above, col. 94.)

[Col. 0433]

LIFE OF LIETBER, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI.

(See volume CXLVI of the *Patrologia*, col. 1450.)

[Col. 0433]

ACCOUNT OF THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT GEREON, ONE OF THE SOLDIERS OF THE THEBAN LEGION.

(PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. X, p. 330.)

[Col. 0433B] Rodulf, by the grace of God what he is, to all who devoutly embrace the memory of the holy martyrs: fellowship with the martyrs.

In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1121, when Church and kingdom had already for some years been disturbed under Emperor Henry—whose father Henry died at Liège—many bishops, abbots, clerics, and monks of every order and rank had been expelled from their sees and were being driven about here and there because of communion with the emperor. They avoided that communion because Pope Callixtus II had excommunicated him, following against him the sentences of his predecessors Gelasius and Paschal.

In this crisis, for the same reason, and especially because I had supported the election and consecration of Frederick, bishop of Liège, I too was expelled from the monastery of Saint Trudo [Col. 0433C] on the Ides of April, Wednesday in Easter week, after I had presided there unworthily for already twelve years, two months, and, I think, fourteen days. In that same year I was mercifully received by Lord Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; through the effort of that church and the election of the brethren, I was made abbot of the monastery of Saint Pantaleon outside the city walls on the eighth day before the Ides of September, after it had been vacant since the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

Not many days afterward, at the request of a certain servant of God and great preacher, Norbert, the tomb of one of the Theban martyrs lying in the monastery of Saint Gereon was opened [Col. 0434B] in that monastery, beside the central pillar on the south side. Throughout the night religious clerics, monks, and abbots were present for the vigils and the digging, with every service, reverence, and devotion; and I too, a sinner, was present by command.

When the upper stone was lifted from the sarcophagus, after eight hundred and some further years since the martyrdom of the Thebans, there was found within it a large body, broad across the shoulders, muscular in chest and arms, clothed in a purple military cloak. This broad garment hung on either side to about three fingers’ breadth below his knees: it was a kind of fine mantle. Over it he wore another garment, no shorter, unknown to us by name but recognizable by its silk thread and [Col. 0434C] the colour of a nobler purple. Beneath it, next to the flesh, was likewise a silk garment, of a very white colour yet somewhat reddish. The whole body still appeared untouched from the chin—which alone remained of the head—to the feet; the outer surface of the garments, stockings, and shoes was still unbroken. For, as we could more truly conjecture, the persecutor’s sword had thus passed by chance between head and chin.

Only the part where the softness of the belly had been had sunk slightly, though modestly; the garment following it nevertheless remained unbroken. By this depression the chest and thigh-bones appeared to project more. Upon his breast [Col. 0435A] was found the sign of the Lord’s cross, made of gold embroidery, as could be discerned from the still-glittering sparks of gold metal in it. The embroidery was nearly one foot long and scarcely one finger broad. From his knees down to his feet, the shins lay straight and whole, decently arranged; they still wore intact stockings of cloth, everywhere patterned with round flowers like the eyes in a peacock’s tail. In these shoes his feet were still joined together as on the first day and raised upward from the heel; and, so far as the surface of the clothing was concerned, nothing at all could be seen in the whole body that had yet decayed or been disturbed.

Yet beneath the garments, as the outcome afterward proved, the flesh itself had already wholly dissolved into ashes together with the bones, except for a few [Col. 0435B] of the larger ones. But the unmoved integrity of the remaining ash presented to the eyes of those looking on the appearance also of intact flesh. O how glorious it was to behold the handsome form of Christ’s great-hearted soldier, magnificently clothed and seemingly still full of living strength! Had his head been present under a like incorruption of the body, one would have believed him asleep rather than dead.

At his head there was placed a turf of grass, extending from the head to the waist on both sides between his body and the sarcophagus. This turf—or rather these turfs, for they were several—were still wholly blood-red, as they had been soaked in the earth by the flowing blood of the martyr when, struck down, he fell to the ground.

And in the sarcophagi of three other martyrs, [Col. 0435C] opened on this occasion, we saw the same mighty works of God. The blades of grass in those very turfs still stood stiff, though dry; clotted blood kept them intact. The martyrs themselves are my witnesses that I held them with my own, though unworthy, hand; that I saw them with my own eyes; and that I offered them for others to see, even to the lord bishop sitting beside us and weeping much for joy and devotion. O what zeal, what love of Christ, what devotion of believers there was then among Christians, who in so great a persecution did not neglect even to take up the blood-soaked turfs! Why delay? These things were done in the hours of the night, amid the great weeping and singing of religious men.

When morning came, and the matter so glorious and desirable had been heard by the citizens and shown to many of them—for the open sarcophagus was covered only by a cloth—[Col. 0435D] the entire city immediately cried out that they would rather die than be deprived of so great a treasure and such a patron. Some among them also said that the body found was Saint Gereon himself, because of the beauty of its clothing and the body’s comeliness. Therefore the tumult among the people grew greater and greater, and all opposed Lord Norbert. At last the uproar was scarcely quieted when Theoderic, provost of Saint Mary ad Gradus, ascended the pulpit, calmed the people, and promised that deliberation concerning this matter should be deferred until the lord archbishop was present.

Nevertheless, to satisfy the people, the leading men decreed that the tomb should be closed by replacing the stone, after [Col. 0436A] the integrity of the body had first been carefully examined by the faithful, lest anything should be stolen from it. These things occurred on the third day before the Ides of October, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s incarnation. Meanwhile, night and day, down to the eighth day before the Kalends of December, the tomb was guarded with great devotion and many lights: by day certain clerics of that church chosen for the purpose sat around it with psalmody; by night others likewise kept vigil with psalmody, and at times were assisted by brethren of the church of the Holy Apostles.

After several days had thus passed, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, as stated, the lord archbishop came when summoned, together with abbots, provosts, and all the city’s communities; the people, however, were innumerable. With great reverence and great praises the tomb was opened for a second time, and the whole holy body was displayed. [Col. 0436B] Yet, from the shaking of the great stone, the flesh beneath the garments, which had turned to ash, had sunk in many places, as commonly occurs in such cases when new air, after so long a time, enters hidden bodies.

Two abbots were appointed, dressed in white vestments and stoles, one at the head and the other at the feet. I, a sinner, was one of them and sat at his head, although, as I said above, nothing of the head remained except the chin, since the murderer’s sword had removed it. Two other clerical priests also assisted in lifting the holy body, likewise dressed in white vestments and stoles. Reverently applying their sacred hands, they first gathered up the garments—not whole, because age did not permit it, but in large and small pieces, as carefully as they could.

[Col. 0436C] Around the shoulders, over the whole breast, and down to the waist, much blood was found clotted together, as it could have flowed in scattered streams from the severed head, out of the neck and the channels of the veins. All his garments were therefore carefully collected; but these, weighted by thick yet dry blood, were handled with special care and reverently placed separately in a chest suitably prepared for the purpose. With them was found and placed away his military belt of black leather, nearly one ell in length, still retaining its pieces whole.

At his left side, beside his body and belt, there was found an iron knob shaped like an egg, almost consumed by rust. We believed this to have been the pommel of his sword, but we found no piece of the sword itself. Later, however, certain persons who examined more carefully the [Col. 0436D] portions of relics that they had requested from it testified to me that they had found particles of iron. The shoes, largely intact, were put into the same chest; the stockings had entirely dissolved into ash. But when, after the garments had been removed, it came to gathering the flesh and bones, scarcely anything solid appeared even from the bones—and that only from the large ones—which age had not wholly reduced to ash or small particles.

A marvelous and most glorious thing! I call the holy martyrs themselves to witness, and also the whole multitude of religious persons who saw this for a long time: throughout the sarcophagus, all the ash of flesh and bones shone white like freshly poured lime. O how often there, with many tears, was sung, “and they washed [Col. 0437A] their robes in the blood of the Lamb”! O how often was repeated: “They washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb”!

At length the ash and the bloody turf together—the latter likewise dissolved into powder, but of an earthy and reddish colour because of the blood—were gathered up in a clean and precious cloth and placed in another, larger chest. Then, when both chests had been lifted up, many offerings were made for making a shrine for the holy martyr. The lord archbishop offered a silver dish; thereafter each person offered according to his devotion. On that day a great procession was also held around the cloister and the monastery, while bells rang and clerics, monks, and laypeople sang in German in their own acclamations.

When the procession was ended and the holy relics in their chests had been [Col. 0437B] placed upon the altar in the middle of the monastery, the Mass of the martyrs of that holy legion was begun and, by command of the lord archbishop, sung by me, a sinner. Before the canon, after the Gospel had ended, the lord archbishop addressed the people concerning the things then before their eyes and hands, and concerning what pertained to the salvation of souls, namely the holy Theban martyrs. When Mass was completed, the people departed in great joy.

Thereafter, through the care and devotion of our brother Echebert, some portions of this holy martyr’s relics were obtained through our mediation from Hermann, provost of that monastery, through whose effort and devotion the revealed body was translated. These relics are: from the finer garment that he wore next to his flesh; from [Col. 0437C] his military belt, of black leather, found about his loins; from the iron, apparently, of his sword, mingled with the blood and ashes of the garments and body, where the iron can still plainly be seen to glimmer as though in the middle of its sheath; and from his blood, together with the dust of his flesh, bones, and garments.

For while the pure ash of his flesh and bones lay separately, it was very like fresh lime or white flour. But after the pieces of clothing that could be collected whole, and the bones not entirely dissolved, had been gathered, everything else was collected into one powder: namely, the dust of the bloody turf, the dust of the bones, the dust of the flesh, and the dust of the garments. All these things mixed together also changed that former white colour. [Col. 0438A] We state this so carefully because we have said that the dust of flesh and bones had the colour of freshly poured lime: so that, when another colour is found in this powder, no one may nevertheless doubt that it comes from his true flesh and bones, indeed also from the bloody turfs and from his garments together.

When Brother Echebert presented these relics to me after bringing them, I recognized them as I had seen them in the tomb; and because of their presence I undertook faithfully to describe the order of the discovery, as it is read here, according to what I saw and handled with my own hands, though unworthy. Therefore I previously sent them to you through that same brother, to be transferred into the church of Blessed Mary at Dunc, so that from this written account of ours and from present contemplation of them there may now or hereafter be no doubt that they were taken from the body of a martyr of the holy legion of Theban martyrs. We therefore exhort, request, and command that our brethren dwelling at Dunc henceforth observe the feast-day of their martyrdom on the day of Saint Gereon with twelve lessons, and also observe the day of the arrival of these relics among them.

I, Rodulf, a sinner, wrote this to you, my dearest brethren and sons who are in the monastery of Saint Trudo in Hasbania, from the monastery of Saint Pantaleon [Col. 0438C] near Cologne. The aforesaid brother collected by his own efforts the other relics listed below; I have no other certainty concerning them than that he received them from a handmaid of God enclosed among us and from Christ’s faithful: relics of the holy virgins; of the holy Moors; from the cap of Saint Thomas the Apostle and his belt; from wax melted by the Lord’s fire; of Saint Pancras; and from the Lord’s tomb.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1138: LEO OF MARSICA, MONK OF CASSINO, LATER CARDINAL BISHOP OF OSTIA; AND PETER THE DEACON, MONK OF CASSINO.

[Col. 0439]

CHRONICLE OF THE MONASTERY OF CASSINO BY LEO OF MARSICA AND PETER THE DEACON

(Edited by W. Wattenbach in Pertz’s celebrated *Monumenta Germaniae*, *Scriptores*, vol. VII, p. 551.) (G)*

PROLEGOMENA.

I. LEO’S DEEDS, ORIGINS, AND WRITINGS.—AIDS FOR THE EDITION.

The records, committed to writing, of the monastery of Cassino—which our emperors have cultivated with devout veneration beyond others, and whose declining fortunes they have more than once vigorously aided—appeared, purged of numerous errors, in the third volume of this collection. [Note: [Col. 0439] See below the appendix to the *Chronicle of Cassino*.] After a long interval comes the *Chronicle* composed by Leo and Peter.

For the study of letters, prostrate after the Saracen invasion, was not revived to new strength in the plantation of Saint Benedict before the middle of the eleventh century. To avoid pursuing this at greater length, the distinguished Wilhelm Giesebrecht has dealt with it in his learned and ingenious dissertation, *On Literary Studies among the Italians in the First Centuries of the Middle Ages*. [Note: [Col. 0439] Berlin, 1845, quarto, p. 25 ff.] There one will find much concerning that outstanding company of men who, during the flourishing condition of the monastery under Abbot Desiderius, made Cassino renowned also for the study of letters and the liberal arts; and there, first among them, is a notice of our Leo, hitherto overlooked.

Cassino had always been closely connected with the counts of the Marsi, from whose stock there then lived among its monks [Col. 0441] Oderisius, Theodinus, and Transmundus. Giesebrecht’s conjecture is highly probable: that Leo, surnamed—as he himself says [Note: [Col. 0441] Prologue, book I.]—“the Marsican,” was connected with them either by blood or marriage. [Note: [Col. 0441] Loc. cit., p. 50.] Let us hear Alfanus, archbishop of Salerno. Having exhorted Theodinus [Note: [Col. 0441] Cardinal deacon; therefore the poem must have been written after 1061. See *Chronicle of Cassino* III.24.] to bring his companions into paradise after he himself had received the rewards of virtue, he finally adds:

> I pray that little Leo too may be in this garden.

And, addressing Pandulf, bishop of the Marsi and Theodinus’s paternal uncle, after recalling other relatives of his, he says:

> May the unblemished goodness of the boy Leo be pleasing to you,  
> Nor may he displease you: love him, that you may be loved;  
> Love him [Note: [Col. 0441] Thus Giesebrecht. Ughelli has: “that he may love you.”] so that he may always love you, and gladly  
> Be able often to render service to you.  
> With a sufficiently gentle mind he lives devotedly in the order  
> In which the work of the Almighty is perfected.

That our Leo is meant in these passages is not certain, but it is extremely likely. Certainly, when the foregoing poem was written to Theodinus, already a cardinal deacon, Theodinus is known to have been enrolled among the Cassinese brethren. How affectionately Leo himself speaks of Theodinus, and how gently of Transmundus, may be seen in *Chronicle of Cassino* III.17, 24, 25.

He had a brother John, a monk of Cassino, whom Peter the Deacon mentions in his sermon on the Octave of Saint Benedict, chapter 3. Leo himself commemorated his uncle John, bishop of Sora, [Note: [Col. 0441] II.16.] a monk of Cassino; [Note: [Col. 0441] III.34.] perhaps he was not different from that provost of Cassino whom Alfanus mentions in the cited passage among Theodinus’s friends. [Note: [Col. 0441] But he must be distinguished from another John, surnamed Marsican. While provost in the Capuan monastery, some wished, after the death of Abbot Richerius in 1055, to elect him abbot. This man, apparently formerly provost of Cassino, became abbot of Saint Vincent on the Volturno in 1058 and held office for twenty-two years, four months, and fifteen days; see *Chronicle of Cassino* II.89, 97; Desiderius, *Dialogues* I.6; *Chronicle of Volturno*, p. 514.] He was consecrated bishop by Gregory VII in the first year of that pontiff’s reign. [Note: [Col. 0441] Register of Gregory VII, in Mansi, *Councils*, XX, p. 125.]

Thus Leo of Marsica, scarcely past his fourteenth year, was received, educated, nourished, and advanced in the monastery of Cassino by Abbot Desiderius. [Note: [Col. 0441] 19 April 1058–1087.] [Note: [Col. 0441] Prologue, book III.] In his conversion he had as teacher Aldemarius, whom he says had once been [Note: [Col. 0441] III.24.] “a most prudent and noble cleric of the city of Capua and notary of Prince Richard.” While performing that office, Aldemarius subscribed a prince’s charter on 23 August 1059. [Note: [Col. 0442] Gattula, *Appendix to the History of Cassino*, p. 161.] In 1063 or 1064 he was sent as abbot to Sardinia; after returning, he was appointed cardinal abbot of Saint Lawrence by Alexander II. It follows that Leo was a novice between the years 1060 and 1064. [Note: [Col. 0442] Certainly the words in the cited passage scarcely permit another interpretation—namely, that Aldemarius, after his return from Sardinia, should be regarded as Leo’s teacher.]

If in II.16 we read that, when he was a little boy, Leo saw a certain priest more than a hundred years old who used to confess to John, bishop of Sora, the blinding of Abbot Manso, we cannot but conclude that John was not yet bishop at that time. [Note: [Col. 0442] In the same manner, what he adds—“of holy memory”—must be understood.] However this may have been, the boy of good natural endowment was soon received by Desiderius among his intimates and joined to him in close association. He was present at nearly all his affairs until Desiderius’s death; [Note: [Col. 0442] See Prologue, book III. He says that he himself witnessed the dedication of the church in 1071: III.25.] and, always gratefully remembering Desiderius’s benefits toward him, held his memory in the highest veneration.

Consequently Oderisius, Desiderius’s successor, entrusted Leo with the task of writing the *Life of Desiderius*—a task which he had formerly asked Alfanus [Note: [Col. 0442] Died in 1087.] to undertake, but unsuccessfully. [Note: [Col. 0442] Prologue, book I.] Yet Leo found no leisure at all for writing during that entire year, since he was constantly occupied with many affairs. For, in Peter’s testimony, [Note: [Col. 0442] *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 30.] “he was fully imbued with holiness and monastic discipline, and especially learned in the divine Scriptures.” He evidently turned early to the history of events and the examination of ancient records; and, having become librarian of the monastery, [Note: [Col. 0442] *Chronicle of Cassino* III.42. That he was also a priest is apparent from Peter the Deacon, *On the Birth and Death of the Cassinese Justorium*, chapter 51. J. B. Marus calls him dean in notes to Peter the Deacon, *On Illustrious Men*, 30, but I do not know on what grounds.] he was often employed not only in conducting the affairs of this place but also in the business of the Apostolic See.

From this *Chronicle* itself we learn that the Cassinese continually had lawsuits to pursue concerning the monastery’s possessions. How long each lasted and how much business they caused may be judged from one example. Leo himself wrote the account of the case of Saint Sophia at Benevento, [Note: [Col. 0442] “Brother Leo, librarian of the holy monastery of Cassino, who wrote this very memorandum”: these are his words.] which Gattula published from Peter’s register, *History of Cassino*, p. 54. While seeking to vindicate that place’s lordship for his monastery, [Col. 0443] he had “first at Rome, in the synod of the venerable Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0443] Apparently 1078; see below III.42 and Binius in Mansi, *Councils*, XX, p. 511.], and afterward at Melfi (18 September 1089) and Troy [Note: [Col. 0443] IV.7.] (11 March 1093), and again at Rome in the synod of the reverend Pope Urban, made formal complaint, both concerning many diverse other matters [Note: [Col. 0443] For example, concerning the church of Cingla; see below IV.18.] and concerning this chief business. Yet he had been unable to receive any justice from these proceedings down to that day. It happened that one day, by command of Lord Abbot Oderisius, he went to the court of that apostolic lord, who at that time was staying at Benevento.”

There, after a dispute had arisen with Madelmus, abbot of Saint Sophia, the pope ordered them to attend the next synod to be held at Bari “with their proofs,” intending there finally to bring the case to an end. “The time of the council came almost a month later” (1 October 1098); yet no judgment was pronounced even then. A few days later, after the pope had returned to Benevento, he heard the parties again but still did not pronounce judgment. “After several days,” Leo continues, “as we went with him in his service and repeatedly pressed for an apostolic sentence concerning this same matter, he wrote a letter from Ceprano to Anso, lord of the Beneventans,” commanding him to do justice to the Cassinese in his stead. It was issued on the third day before the Nones of November. “The following year the pope died; two years later Anso lost Benevento; and the matter therefore remained unfinished.” [Note: [Col. 0443] Compare *Chronicle of Cassino* IV.48, 60.]

We may suppose that Leo was occupied in conducting similar cases when he accompanied the abbot returning from Capua “on account of his office.” [Note: [Col. 0443] See Prologue, book I.] When Oderisius asked him about the task of writing the *Life* entrusted to him by Desiderius, Leo replied that he had not yet begun the work. “And when,” he said, “could I obey this command of yours? When, throughout almost this entire year, I have been occupied both in the service of the apostolic lord, by your order, throughout the Maritime region and Campania, and also in your own affairs, so that I have scarcely remained in the monastery for eight consecutive days?”

Accepting this excuse, Oderisius then entrusted to him the writing of the monastery’s entire history. Leo soon devoted himself with the utmost care to this great and much more burdensome work, apparently having been granted leisure; so that he seems to have begun writing after that year, 1098. But he did not complete the work he began, nor did he carry it beyond 1075. Yet he does not seem even then to have laid down his pen, until he was raised by Paschal II to the dignity of bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0443] And of Velletri. For that from the time of Mincius onward the two bishoprics were joined in such a way that a bishop was called from either diocese without distinction seems to me to have been demonstrated by Alessandro Borgia, *History of Velletri*, p. 214 ff., notwithstanding what F. A. Maroni, *On the Church and Bishops of Ostia and Velletri*, Rome, 1766, quarto, p. 71, may argue to the contrary.] and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 0443] Certainly, since in the catalogue of abbots manuscript 1 does not assign years of rule to Oderisius, to whom he dedicated his work (d. 1105), while manuscripts 3 and 4 do not assign years to Gerard (1111–1123), I do not deny that these abbots could have been added by the same person who added Oderisius II. In Peter’s testimony, Prologue, book IV, he was prevented by death from completing the work.]

We do not know when this occurred. On 31 March 1101, Odo, his predecessor, was still alive. [Note: [Col. 0444] Gattula, *History of Cassino*, p. 54.] Leo subscribed papal documents after Crescentius of Sabina and Peter, bishop of Porto, but before Cono of Palestrina; hence I do not know whether one may conclude that he was ordained after the former two but before Cono. Peter had succeeded Mauritius, who had set out for Jerusalem in 1100, by 1102; [Note: [Col. 0444] Falco of Benevento, at the beginning.] but Cono, having become a close associate of the pope at the Council of Troyes in May 1107, soon went to Rome, where he was ordained bishop and sent to Jerusalem. For in 1107 [Note: [Col. 0444] *Acts of the Saints*, January I, p. 833; Ekkehard of Aura, under the year 1116; Baronius, *Annals*, under 1107, chapter 18. Moreover, it is worth noting here that discussions among older writers concerning the cardinals of these times are wholly infected by two errors: first, that through the negligence of Martène, their first editor (*Thesaurus*, IV, p. 127), followed by the others, a portion of the acts of the Lateran Council of 1112 was joined to the acts of the Council of Guastalla; second, that the utterly false subscriptions to a document of Paschal II dated 27 December 1105 have been accepted as genuine. On the epitaph of Bernard, bishop of Palestrina, which Baronius incorrectly assigned to 1107, see Giesebrecht, *On Literary Studies*, p. 37.] a bishop of Palestrina is said to have been there; Cono was bishop in 1111.

On 12 February 1111 Leo was at Rome when King Henry V entered the City. When the pope was captured with the other cardinals, Leo escaped, dressed in lay clothing, with John, bishop of Tusculum. [Note: [Col. 0444] *Chronicle of Cassino* IV.38.] There is no reason to doubt that he assisted John in inciting the people to resistance. But although he had neither been captured nor subscribed to that agreement extorted from the pope, he could not absent himself from the king’s coronation, lest everything be thrown into disorder again. Acting in place of the bishop of Albano, he delivered the first address; then, exercising his own office, he anointed Henry—after he had been brought to the confession of the Apostles—between the shoulders and on the right arm. [Note: [Col. 0444] William of Malmesbury V.423; compare below IV.37, note.]

How reluctantly he did this may be inferred from the fact that, on the third day before the Nones of July, Paschal wrote from Terracina to “John, bishop and cardinal of Tusculum, and Leo, bishop and cardinal of Velletri, assembled together.” [Note: [Col. 0444] Thus the Vatican manuscript, according to Alessandro Borgia, p. 214, *History of Velletri*.] I think Leo is called bishop of Velletri in order that John of Tusculum might not seem to be placed after Leo, whether as a younger bishop after an older, or after the bishop of Ostia, whose church ranks first after the Roman Church. The pope writes:

> What you have done against my person—indeed, against your father—without the judgment and presence of the Church, although it seemed to you to arise from zeal for God, nevertheless, in my view, did not begin by a canonical path. For it is evident that not charity but rivalry dictated it.

He then exhorts them thus:

> Act for the Church within the Church, so that the Church itself may experience the zeal for God’s Church which you possess and display.

Through this admonition of the supreme pontiff, our Leo seems to have been recalled from association with his friends, [Note: [Col. 0445] Unless one prefers to assign that letter to another year, which seems less likely to me.] and to have judged that he ought rather to render service to the pope against comrades harsher than enemies. Receiving letters from Paschal, he came to Cassino and compelled Bruno, bishop of Segni, to resign the abbacy. [Note: [Col. 0445] *Chronicle of Cassino* IV.42.] After this business was completed in August or September of the same year, he returned to Rome, where he lodged in the monastery of Pallaria, subject to Cassino. [Note: [Col. 0445] IV.81.]

On 24 January 1112, in the altar of the church of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, he solemnly deposited the gridiron of that martyr; on the Kalends of February he dedicated the principal altar. [Note: [Col. 0445] Baronius, *Annals*, under that year.] Then, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, he played a leading role in the Lateran council and, now with the pope’s consent, did what the pope had not wished to be done violently and irregularly. For we read that the document condemning the privilege concerning the investiture of churches extorted from the pope was “drawn up by the common counsel” of Gerard of Angoulême, Leo of Ostia, Gregory of Terracina, Galon of León, bishops, and Robert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Eusebius, and Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of the Apostles. [Note: [Col. 0445] “Drawn up,” or perhaps “dictated”?] [Note: [Col. 0445] Martène, *Thesaurus*, IV, p. 128; Mansi, XX, 1212.] That is, I suppose, it was composed in words.

You see Leo as a companion of vigorous defenders of the Church, yet separated from John and Bruno, who were not even present at the council that day. [Note: [Col. 0445] For I am persuaded that the words in *Monumenta Legum*, II.B, p. 182, must be construed thus; compare William of Malmesbury V.426.]

After this, Leo was present at Benevento on 11 and 13 February 1113 when a dispute between the Cassinese and the abbot of Terra Maggiore was adjudicated, but, as a monk of Cassino, he abstained from pronouncing judgment. [Note: [Col. 0445] Gattula, *Appendix to the History of Cassino*, p. 714.] On 25 February 1114, at the Lateran, he subscribed the privilege of the church of Marsica; [Note: [Col. 0445] Ughelli, I, p. 892.] on 5 July, in the same place, another privilege received by the canons of Saint Mary in Porto at Ravenna. [Note: [Col. 0445] *Bullarium Lateranense*, p. 5.] He died before 1118, when Lambert is known to have been bishop of Ostia, [Note: [Col. 0446] On 21 March he was present at the election of Gelasius; Pandulf of Pisa, in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, III, p. 381.] on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. [Note: [Col. 0446] Necrology of manuscript 47, in Gattula, *Appendix to the History of Cassino*, p. 855.]

The works written by Leo are enumerated by Peter the Deacon in book *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, ch. 30, in these words:

> He composed sermons on Easter; on the Nativity; a History of the Pilgrims; a History of the Monastery of Monte Cassino, divided into four books; a Life of Saint Mennas; and very many other works which have not come to our knowledge.

Of these, some appear to have perished. The *Life of Saint Mennas* remains unpublished, although Gattula printed from codex 413 its prologue and epilogue together with the beginning of the translation, *History of Monte Cassino*, pp. 188, 911. He had written it at the command of Abbot Oderisius I and at the request of Count Robert, son of Rainulf, who had “recently” transferred the saint’s bones to Caiazzo in A.D. 1094. John Mabillon likewise extracted from a Cassinese codex, and ascribed to Leo, a sermon to be delivered on the feast of the translation, on 31 March; it was published in Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, 879–984. It contains a careful history of the translation, written in a plain but polished style, and one wholly suitable to our Leo.

He seems, moreover, to have prefaced the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* with the narrative which he wrote *On the Consecration of the Churches Built at Monte Cassino by Desiderius and Oderisius*. That it should be assigned to Leo has already been demonstrated by Camillo Peregrini.

> [Note: Col. 0446. *Series of the Abbots of Monte Cassino*, under Oderisius I.]

Nor, in my opinion, can anyone doubt it. For the author, who wrote after A.D. 1094 under Abbot Oderisius—

> [Note: Col. 0446. Apparently before A.D. 1103, since he does not yet mention the dedication of the church of St Stephen: *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV.23.]

—but had himself witnessed the consecration of the greater church in A.D. 1071—

> [Note: Col. 0446. For he himself says there: “Let none of those who read doubt that all these things happened thus; for we have described them not as transmitted by others, but as actually seen with our own eyes.” Compare *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, III.25.]

—openly declares that he had set before himself the writing of the *Deeds of Desiderius*. For, after a brief description of the church, he says:

> “Its dimensions, however, and character, and its ornaments—since it was not my purpose to describe them fully in this discourse—will, God willing and life accompanying me, be set forth more extensively elsewhere together with the remaining works of the aforesaid lord abbot. Here I shall relate, as far as I can, only with what glory and what concourse it was consecrated.”

And his final words are:

> “The names of all these persons, together with the relics of the other churches, we shall, with the Lord’s help, write in their proper places.”

These words, I say, lead me to believe that even then he had thought of writing the *Chronicle*. Having carried that work down to these times, he incorporated much from this little work, usually in the very same words—for the manner of writing is plainly identical in both. Peter the Deacon used the passages that followed. The work survives in Cassinese codex 47, whence Antonio Caracciolo published a transcript in *Four Ancient Chronicles*, Naples, 1626, quarto; together with that work it appeared again in L. A. Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, vol. V, p. 76. We have appended the latter part to Leo’s *Chronicle*.

[Col. 0447] **The Munich autograph codex.**

[Col. 0449] It remains to speak more exactly concerning the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*. In order that this may be done more successfully, a description of the manuscript codices should first be set forth. Besides the codices of the Ambrosian edition, which will shortly be discussed—

> [Note: Col. 0449. Beware of inferring from a passage of Ludovico Tosti, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, Naples, 1842, quarto, II, 317, that a codex of Leo exists at Velletri. You will find none there. — J. B. Marus, on Peter the Deacon, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 30, mentions a copy of Leo in which Lucas Holstenius noted variant readings from several manuscript copies.  
> [Col. 0450] But Bethmann sought this copy in vain in the Vatican Library.]

—we have the following.

1) The Royal Munich codex, among the Benedictbeuern manuscripts, no. 123, parchment, quarto. It contains the *Song of Songs*, the *Book of Wisdom*, *Ecclesiasticus*, various sermons, and finally, on folios 85–189 as now numbered, Leo’s *Chronicle*, which was bound together with those other works in more recent times by an ignorant man who cut away not a few matters written in the margins of the leaves. The earlier works were written in Germany, but the *Chronicle* is in a very beautiful and uniform Beneventan hand—

> [Note: Col. 0450. The doubled forms *i, b, d, c* are marked with strokes in only two places; elsewhere it lacks them.]

—examples of which we have supplied. Fourteen quires, of which the fifth and fourteenth are nevertheless binions, and the second has been enlarged by the insertion of a leaf, were numbered on their final leaves by a hand not very ancient. The parchment is strong and rather white. That of the first ten quires is palimpsest, so that its ruled lines do not coincide with Leo’s text and traces of the older writing appear between the lines. This older writing seems to be eleventh-century, in Roman script. The final four leaves are of the same parchment, already ruled, though no traces of letters are visible. On the remaining pages, where the parchment is somewhat thicker, twenty-two lines were drawn with a stylus, bounded in both margins by two vertical lines running from top to bottom.

At the foot of folio 1 a fifteenth-century hand wrote: “Benedictn peirn” [Benediktbeuern]; and at the end of the book: “This book belongs to this monastery, Benedictbeuern.” Yet it came to the monks of Benediktbeuern from another monastery. For it is Cassinese, and indeed Leo’s very autograph; this is evident from its entire appearance. It contains, so to speak, the first kernel of the work: a rather brief narrative written in various scribal hands, which Leo subsequently both corrected in his own hand and enlarged with innumerable additions, often by erasing a large part of the leaf and rewriting it in smaller letters.

At first he gave the first six quires, containing Book I, and the beginning of Book II in the three parts of the final leaf, to a scribe. Having already corrected and enlarged this in several places, Leo cancelled the whole of it. For a new version survives at the beginning of quire 7, in the hand of a second scribe; this was then taken up at folio 154 with the words “All these things” (II.43) by a third. The last four leaves, however, Leo wrote in his own hand, in very small letters and with almost no margin. He also rewrote folios 120 and 121 himself, after erasing everything formerly written there. Sometimes, moreover, when the margins of the leaves did not suffice for writing additions, he seems to have sewn on slips of parchment; these later perished, since marks placed in the text do not always have corresponding additions, as at I.45, II.7, and II.9, where no inserted matter is read in any codex.

We have marked what was written in this codex from the beginning with **I**; what the author’s hand added, though not all at the same time, with **1b**; and occasionally with **1c** what he wrote over it at another time. The narrative ends at II.92 with the election of Abbot Frederick, in the middle of a page, so that nothing appears to have been lost. But some material written in the margins of the leaves was taken from us by the folly of the bookbinder. Some of it has been preserved in a copy made already in the twelfth century at the monastery of Benediktbeuern, namely:

1*) The Royal Munich codex, among the Benedictbeuern manuscripts no. 146, small octavo. I believe that the autograph codex was brought to Benediktbeuern about A.D. 1137 by Abbot Engelscalc, who is said to have frequented Innocent II and followed Emperor Lothair.

> [Note: Col. 0450. *Monumenta Boica*, VII, pp. 36, 97.]

The monks of Benediktbeuern, since it was more difficult to read, copied it onto thick white parchment, defective through lacunae, in Roman script, of which we append a specimen. They copied it fairly accurately, but omitted some things written in the margin, especially those written in paler ink. Yet what they included shows that the codex was then still whole and undamaged.

This copy, however, suffered damage at an early date. The person who, about A.D. 1250, wrote a catalogue of the books of the church of Benediktbeuern designated our works as follows: “A book concerning the site of Monte Cassino. Likewise sixteen quires concerning Monte Cassino” (*Pez, Thesaurus*, III.3, pp. 622, 623). Sixteen, of course, is the last of the surviving quires, but it ends in the middle of II.4. Moreover, quires 1, 2, and 15 are missing. A fifteenth-century hand supplied all these most diligently, attaching and inserting paper leaves and little leaves, and everywhere mending damaged parchment leaves with pasted scraps. It derived these materials from codex 1, already mutilated at that time as it is now; consequently they are of no use whatever for our edition.

2) Cassinese parchment codex 851, now 450, thirteenth century, written in Lombardic characters, contains Leo’s *Chronicle* with Peter the Deacon’s continuation, and the anonymous Cassinese *Chronicle* for 1128–1212, all written in the same hand. The first page, elegantly illuminated, is reproduced in lithographic form in Ludovico Tosti’s *History of Monte Cassino*, I, 347.

> [Note: Col. 0453. That he everywhere printed *hc* for *k* is a remarkable error caused by the form of the letter *e*, as may be seen in the reproduced plate.]

Angelo de Nuce’s edition was most carefully transcribed from this codex, restoring only in their proper places diphthongs in place of simple *e*. He designated it A and added variant readings from codex B, that is:

[Col. 0451] **Royal Munich codex, formerly Benedictbeuern no. 146.**

3) Cassinese codex 202, parchment, twelfth century, in Latin script, contains Leo alone, ending at the end of Book III, ch. 34, after the words “Peter, prince of the apostles.” Since reliance was required upon Angelo’s fidelity in noting its variants, though he evidently omitted some, I have marked **ed.** those readings which, from his silence, are common to codices 2 and 3.

4) The Royal Stuttgart codex, paper, fifteenth century, carries Leo’s *Chronicle* to the same ending as no. 3. It adds the words “was founded” without making a rubric; it also includes part of Book I, ch. 45, after which it wrote: “Thanks be to God.” Then the rubricator adds:

> “This Chronicle was written by me, Brother Andrew Ysengrin of Landsberg near the river Lech, of the diocese of Augsburg, a professed monk and priest in the monastery of Blaubeuren in the diocese of Constance, not long after the year of my profession, namely about the year of the Lord one thousand four hundred and seventy-seven, more or less; I made that profession to the venerable father, Father Ulrich Kundig, abbot of this monastery of Blaubeuren.”

In both instances the corrupted name of the monastery has been corrected by erasure into *Blaubeuren*. But other errors of this kind remain, especially in the initial letters of the chapters; nor are errors lacking in Leo’s own words, so that Brother Andrew does not appear to have understood what he copied. He apparently used an exemplar written in Lombardic letters, since more than once he writes *at* or *it* for *t*, *que* or *qui* for *ejus*, and *lc* for *k*. Indeed, he omitted entire lines and joined together halves of different words, for example at I.35. Therefore he is not at all to be believed to have deliberately altered anything; and although he abounds in minor scribal faults, he appears otherwise to have copied his exemplar accurately.

> [Note: Col. 0453. On the blank first leaf of the codex there survive the following contemporary inscriptions: “A.D. 1503, Ulrich, duke of Württemberg and called count of Mömpelgard, assumed government on the Wednesday before the feast of Mary Magdalene, aged seventeen years, with the consent of all his subjects. A.D. 1503.” “Under Maximilian, king of the Romans, crosses of many forms and colours appeared in the garments of men and also upon their bodies throughout Germany, together with other signs of the Passion.” On a fragment of parchment leaf by which the book was formerly bound, a sixteenth-century hand wrote: “Two famous chronicles are contained in this book. The first concerns the holy Benedict, his life  
> [Col. 0454] and rule, and that of his successors at Monte Cassino and other monasteries. The second concerns the great Emperor Frederick and his successors.” And on a pasted paper fragment: “Ludwig Hasperger, schoolmaster.”]

These four codices differ from one another so greatly that they present to us the form of the work changed in very many places on three occasions, and wholly different each time.
