What ought to be thought concerning this would certainly remain uncertain, had not codex 1, the author’s autograph, supplied the desired critical standard and laid before our eyes Leo’s entire manner of writing. For there we have the first and still only begun form of the work. Even there it was carefully written and distinguished by larger letters and rubrics, yet not so that it can be regarded as complete. For it contains as yet only a few of the things which the author had promised in the prologue: privileges and other documents concerning the monastery’s individual possessions.

Accordingly, having obtained a fair copy of his work in progress, he first corrected what the negligence of scribes had corrupted—

> [Note: Col. 0454. For example, *lanbardiam* corrected to *lambardiam*; *inpostorem* to *impostorem*; *hujus cerei* to *hujusce rei*; *atto* to *Otto*; *sepulchro* to *sepulcro*; *mixtis* to *mistis*; *guiscardus* to *uiscardus*; *guacco* to *wacco*; *edificiis* to *aedificiis*; and very many others.]

—then altered very much in his own wording, so that the discourse might proceed more effectively; he then corrected matters that were less true and added new ones. Above all, having examined the documents of the Cassinese archive, he wrote summaries of them wherever space was available in the margins of the leaves, and then assigned each to its place by marks.

> [Note: Col. 0454. Yet more than once it happened that he inserted something in the wrong place or interrupted the thread of the discourse awkwardly; he later corrected this in several places. A manifest error occurs at I.16.]

While writing, he himself immediately corrected much, and added other things. Had I wished to record all of these, there would have been no end to the variant readings. To make his manner of writing known, it seemed sufficient to provide a specimen in the appended plate, in which I carefully indicated whatever appeared of any importance, omitting only the lighter corrections which he made immediately with the same pen as he wrote.

But after Leo had filled everything in this way through additions and corrections, a new copy became necessary. He therefore had the corrected and enlarged book transcribed. When this was done, he proceeded similarly to polish and expand it, added a continuation down to A.D. 1075, and declared himself “about to describe the remaining matters hereafter.”

> [Note: Col. 0454. III.17: “Hereafter we shall pursue the rest more fully,” III.18.]

Peter the Deacon, having obtained a codex of this kind and undertaken the task of continuing the work, added some things of his own: certain miracles taken from Desiderius’s *Dialogues*, and some matters concerning the deeds of his kinsmen, the counts of Tusculum, which we have relegated to the foot of the page. As for the other passages which Angelo de Nuce maintains that Peter altered in Leo’s words, we find them, with a few exceptions in the earlier part of the work, already in Leo’s autograph itself. Thus we may not impugn Angelo’s reliability in the passages that follow. Peter treated only Book III, ch. 34, more freely, because—

[Col. 0455]—the author had not yet sufficiently worked it out. Some errors, moreover, are to be attributed to the considerably later scribe of our codex, though he too performed his task fairly carefully.

> [Note: Col. 0455. He often erred by omitting words.]

Leo himself, however, had not yet laid down his pen. Continuing in the same manner, he prepared a new edition of the *Chronicle*, represented by codex 3: free of Peter’s additions, but often corrupted by scribal carelessness. In that edition the wording was changed in very many places and even the order of the chapters was more than once reversed, though few matters were altered or added. At II.56 he cut out an entire chapter. The author of the Cassinese *Chronicle* transmitted under the name of Anastasius, published in Muratori, *Writers*, II, 351, and the author of the *Chronicle of Volturno*, employed a codex of this sort for their own purposes. Peter the Deacon likewise borrowed Book I, ch. 20 of Leo’s *On the Octave of Saint Benedict* from codex 3.

Yet Leo was still not satisfied with what he had written. Having no new material to add—

> [Note: Col. 0455. At I.58 he speaks more accurately concerning St Sophia; in ch. 60 he adds “of Teano”; at II.1, “noble.”]

—he polished the wording anew in many places, and thus prepared his final edition, such as codex 4 presents. Where codices 2 and 3 differ, it almost always agrees with 3; but in other places, and these are very numerous, it presents the style once again corrected with great care. Since this codex is quite recent, it might be doubted whether someone other than Leo had performed this work for him. Yet the entire colouring of the style is Leo’s, and the changes have precisely the same character as the style which he had employed from the beginning: above all, he carefully avoided having the same word occur twice within a short space; moreover, he aimed at elegant and rhythmical prose, so much so that he dared even to alter Charles’s verses to Paul.

All doubt is removed by the fact that this same edition of the *Chronicle* was evidently already circulating a few years after Leo’s time. For Peter the Deacon, when writing many works, used it more frequently than his own edition. In his sermon *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*, in *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, II.69, 75, and in *On the Righteous Men of Cassino*, II.1, 2, 30, 57, 59, 63; III.8, he borrowed from a codex of this kind. Further, the forged bulls of Zacharias—

> [Note: Col. 0455. In Vicentino and du Breul, in the appendix to the *Chronicle*; Margarini, *Bullarium Cassinense*, I.3; Tosti, I.82.]

—and Benedict VIII—

> [Note: Col. 0455. There; Margarini, I.7; Tosti, I.251.]

—which already occur in Peter’s register and contain nearly whole chapters of Leo, present the same text as the Stuttgart codex.

> [Note: Col. 0455. See *Chronicle*, I.5; II.43.]

That these were taken from Leo, rather than copied by him from them, is evident from the fact that we see the words altered at different times in our codices, whereas Leo proceeds in exactly the opposite manner in using sources: at first he gives their very words, then makes them resemble his own style. It was possible, however, that Peter himself or some contemporary assumed the office of reviser; but then it could scarcely have failed to happen that in at least one of the many altered passages we should discover a style different from Leo’s manner of writing. Nor, indeed, does any reason appear why anyone other than the author should have undertaken such labour.

After Peter, Ambrogio Traversari, the celebrated General of the Camaldolese Order, who died at Florence on 21 October 1439, laid his hand upon the work. He undertook to correct and abridge the Cassinese *Chronicle*—

> [Note: Col. 0455. Apparently having obtained a copy of codex 2.]

—at the request of Ludovico Barbaro, Abbot of St Justina. Laurentius Vincentinus, a monk, published as Leo’s genuine work at Venice in 1513, quarto, the codex of this recension preserved in the monastery of St Michael of Murano, Venice.

> [Note: Col. 0455. No. 727; Mittarelli, *Codices of St Michael*, p. 42. Another is preserved in the Chigi Library, beautifully written, shelfmark J. VII.258, parchment, folio. — On the final leaf is written: “End of Book IV and of the final book of the history of the Cassinese monastery  
> [Col. 0456] published by Brother Leo of Marsi and Peter the Deacon, and polished by Brother Ambrosius, General of the Camaldolese; I, John, scribe of the most reverend father in Christ, Lord Mariotto of Arezzo, General of the Camaldolese, happily transcribed it at his command in the month of June, A.D. 1466. Thanks be to God.” That *Cassinese History of Leo of Ostia with Peter’s additions* which is found in Vatican Library codex 2961, paper, folio, sixteenth century, was abridged by Agostino Patrizi for the use of Cardinal Francesco Piccolomini. He did not say which codex he used, but it comes very close to Nuce’s edition.]

Jacques du Breul reprinted that edition at Paris in 1603, folio, together with Aimoin’s *Deeds of the Franks*.

Matthaeus Lauretus, a Spaniard and monk of Monte Cassino, who followed them, at Naples in 1616, quarto, did indeed use a Cassinese codex; but, acting as a reviser himself, he altered or cut away very much at will, and is worthy of no confidence. Since the distinguished Gattula has discussed these editions at length, *History of Monte Cassino*, p. 879 ff., what has been said here seems sufficient. A specimen of each edition may be found at III.49.

Angelo de Nuce, Abbot of Monte Cassino, was the first to publish the genuine work of Leo and Peter, Paris, 1668, folio, accurately and carefully. He added a very extensive commentary, but one which provides us with little that is useful, especially after the outstanding work of Erasmus Gattula—I mean the *History of Monte Cassino*, Venice, 1733, folio, to which he added a volume of *Additions* in 1734. Muratori ordered Angelo’s edition reprinted in *Writers of Italian Affairs*, IV, Milan, 1723, folio, together with additions to the notes that Angelo had published at Rome in 1670, folio.

Abbot Oderisius had instructed Leo to begin with Blessed Benedict, narrate the succession of abbots and the deeds and vicissitudes of the monastery, insert privileges and the other documents on which its rights and possessions rested, and add whatever “might meanwhile occur concerning the works or deeds of illustrious men of these regions only.” In order to accomplish this, Leo sought out books necessary for the undertaking. As a foundation he used the *Chronicles of Abbot John*, by which name he appears to mean the materials written in Cassinese codex 353 and published in Volume III of this collection: the *Life of Saint Benedict*, the Cassinese Chronicle, and the Chronicle of the Counts of Capua; together with Paul’s letter—

[Col. 0457]—to Charles—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.12.]

—the capitulary of Louis the Pious—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.16.]

—the pact of division—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.29.]

—and those matters which he transcribes at I.32 concerning the custom of the monastery. He further writes that he employed the *History of the Lombards*—

> [Note: Col. 0457. Paul, I.1, 2, 4, 5, 15; II.44.]

—and chronicles of Roman emperors and popes: namely, catalogues such as some of that period survive. He also appears to have known the *Deeds of the Popes*.

> [Note: Col. 0457. There is no reason to doubt that Leo used the *Deeds of the Popes*. For that little slip, inserted somewhat later by the scribe himself in Peter’s Register, contains nothing but: “Precept of King Charles [for] the Roman Church—Pope Adrian—the Lateran Library”; see Borgia, *On the Temporal Dominion*, etc., Appendix, p. 3. Besides this, nothing concerning these matters occurs in Peter’s Register. What the first hand wrote at I.12 was taken from elsewhere; what it added was from Adrian’s *Life*, compared with Erchempert, ch. 9. From the *Life of Stephen III* came I.8, adopting the boundary-description from ch. 12; I.18 from the *Life of Leo III*. But I do not know whence he received Louis’s pact, I.16.]

In the prologue, furthermore, he mentions only domestic documents: those, that is, of the monastery of Monte Cassino and of its dependent cells, St Angelo of Barreggia, St Liberator of Majella, and others. To these must be added the matters which he alone records concerning the monastery’s vicissitudes, buildings constructed under each abbot, and other things of this sort; he also used necrologies, inscriptions, and epitaphs. He inspected domestic records of the Volturnians—

> [Note: Col. 0457. The same records used by the author of the *Chronicle of Saint Vincent*, I.4, 12.]

—of Casa Aurea—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.37.]

—and of the Beneventans.

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.9, 20, 24; II.24.]

Besides these, he had at hand Gregory’s *Dialogues*—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.1, 2, 59.]

—the *Life of Saint Maurus* by Faustus, apparently interpolated by Odo—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.1, 3.]

—the *Salernitan Chronicle*—

> [Note: Col. 0457. He seems to attribute this at I.20 to Erchempert, with whose *History* it is joined in Vatican codex. But he borrowed only a few matters from it: see I.7, 8, 15; II.9, note.]

—the *Translation of the Twelve Brothers*—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.9.]

—attributed to Alfanus, or another older work of the same kind; writings of the same class concerning St Bartholomew—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.24.]

—and St Matthew—

> [Note: Col. 0457. II.5.]

—Charles’s verses to Paul—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.15.]

—Desiderius’s *Dialogues*—

> [Note: Col. 0457. I.19, 27; II.21, 22, 34 ff.]

—the Beneventan Annals—

> [Note: Col. 0457. Although this is doubtful; see I.49, note; II.11, 66.]

—and the Cassinese Annals.

> [Note: Col. 0457. II.9, 24, 25. Both were published in *Monumenta*, *Scriptores*, III.  
> [Col. 0458] But he also used other Cassinese annals, later copied by the Anonymous author excellently edited by Gattula, *Additions*, p. 827 ff. That this author did not use Leo’s work is evident because what both contain occurs only in Leo’s first codex, having later been altered or omitted by Leo himself; see II.37, 56, 59, 62.]

He also used the *Life of Saint Adalbert*—

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.17.]

—Peter Damian’s letter to Mainard—

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.16.]

—and a sermon on the vigil of Saint Benedict.

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.63, 64.]

From these writings and others now lost—though he drew from these latter not much, but some material, especially concerning the affairs of the Capuans—

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.2, 9, 10, 11.]

—also employing popular accounts—

> [Note: Col. 0458. I.37, note 61; II.24.]

—and adding what he had heard from contemporary witnesses—

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.16 (Andrew), 20, 34 (Peter), 72 (Mainard), 80.]

—he wove together a history which he thereafter corrected and enlarged with unceasing care. For he not only diligently added whatever he found in privileges and other documents of the archive, but also corrected and amplified very much both from books which he had used before and from others. Thus he had indeed already mentioned Erchempert—

> [Note: Col. 0458. I.9.]

—but only now called him into service.

> [Note: Col. 0458. I.12, 14, 20, 21, 22, 23, 25, 29, 30, 31, 35, 36, 40–42, 47.]

He further used the *Life of Romuald* written by Peter Damian—

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.17, 18, 19, 24.]

—and certain material, whose origin is unknown to us, concerning the Gaetans and Saracens—

> [Note: Col. 0458. I.43, 44, 50, 52.]

—the Hungarians—

> [Note: Col. 0458. I.55.]

—and Adhemar.

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.15, 24.]

He also used Roffridus’s narratives.

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.45, 48.]

When he was then about to prepare a new edition, he acquired an important aid: I mean Aimé’s *History of the Normans*, with whose help he revised what he had already written about them.

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.37, 41, 43, 56, 63, 66, 79, 82, 84.]

This work, of no slight usefulness, long remained hidden, but was recently brought to light by the distinguished Champollion-Figeac.

> [Note: Col. 0458. *The History of the Normans and the Chronicle of Robert Guiscard, by Aimé, monk of Monte Cassino; published for the first time by M. C. F. at Paris, 1835*, octavo. Original French title: *L’ystoire de li Normant et la chronique de Robert Viscart par Aimé, moine du Mont-Cassin; publiées pour la première fois par M. C. F. à Paris, 1835.*]

It was translated into French in the thirteenth century, since it appears to have reached us in no other form. The editor demonstrated in the prolegomena that its author, whom Leo does not name, was Aimé. Leo further added new extracts from donations and a few other matters concerning the times of the popes—

> [Note: Col. 0458. I.50, 52.]

—and concerning the exchange of Benevento for the bishopric of Bamberg.

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.46; compare also ch. 77.]

We do not know the sources of the continuation which he added, except for what he here too owed to Aimé—

> [Note: Col. 0458. III.15, 23.]

—and to Peter Damian’s letters.

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.98, 99; III [reference incomplete as printed].]

He names only Jaquintus as an eyewitness—

> [Note: Col. 0458. III.2.]

—but the prologue to Book III reveals that much rests on accounts by Desiderius and others; of the latest events he was himself a witness. Afterwards he used no new aids. He merely inserted a tale concerning Henry II—

> [Note: Col. 0458. II.47.]

—received, I know not from whose lips; Nicholas II’s constitution concerning the election of a pope, which then could have escaped no one’s notice; and a few matters concerning the counts of the Marsi, III.17, 23.

[Col. 0459] Using these sources, Leo composed his history. Sometimes he borrowed their very words, which he subsequently altered and polished through repeated care, so that the style might be uniform throughout. Nor was he devoid of critical skill. Rather, carefully comparing his authors with one another, he arranged them so that one might both correct and supplement another: for example, Desiderius’s *Dialogues* by the Cassinese *Chronicle*—

> [Note: Col. 0459. I.27.]

—the latter by Erchempert—

> [Note: Col. 0459. I.25, 35, 36.]

—and Peter Damian by what he had himself heard.

> [Note: Col. 0459. II.16.]

He reduced a great deal to a summary and took care that individual narratives should not exceed due limits. The style, as we now read it, polished with the greatest care, proceeds evenly throughout and is fairly pure.

> [Note: Col. 0459. The departures from the authority of good writers are approximately these: absolute nominatives, for example I.8, *ditatum* 27; II.74; III.23, *futurum*; I.32, *docendi*; II.92, *redeuntes*; III.7, *remorati*. Indeed, he often joins a nominative with ablatives absolute, as at III.19: “Hildebrand … after deliberation has been held, they elect.” He construes *venire* with the ablative, II.15, 30; *nocere* with the accusative, III.20; *dehortatus* is read as passive, II.17; *memoratus est*, II.90; *parvissimus*, III.10. I pass over other less correct usages or usages drawn from the language of the sacred books. In writing, he often joins prepositions to nouns, a practice we have not always retained.]

He quotes ancient authors only twice, once Sallust—

> [Note: Col. 0459. I.25.]

—and once Virgil—

> [Note: Col. 0460. III.13.]

—and Cicero’s judgement on Varro.

> [Note: Col. 0460. I.1.]

But once, when wishing to raise the tone of his discourse more highly, he interspersed verses of Paulinus of Nola without naming the author.

> [Note: Col. 0460. III.32.]

To men of that age this seemed superfluous. Leo likewise named his witnesses and authors only when he wished thereby to add greater authority to his words; and even names which he had placed at first he later removed.

> [Note: Col. 0460. Peter Damian, II.63; Roffridus, II.45, 48; compare ch. 72.]

Do not, therefore, impugn his reliability on this account: it is wholly sound and sincere. We may now judge it better from the entire character of the work; one who neglects the truth of events is not so painstaking in working out individual details. In very many passages where it is possible to compare his narrative with his sources, he sometimes erred, certainly; yet nowhere can he be accused of having altered anything at pleasure. On the contrary, he later carefully deleted tales which he had incautiously admitted at first, such as those concerning Barreggia and Empress Adelaide.

> [Note: Col. 0460. I.37, 61.]

The only place in which one might call his reliability into question is II.42, on the election of Abbot Theobald. There he had initially assigned a much greater role to the emperor than he later allowed—perhaps, I do not know, yielding to the abbot’s authority. Yet even there he erred by omission, not by adding or substituting falsehoods.

> [Note: Col. 0460. At II.91, 92 also, concerning Frederick’s election, he revised with the greatest care.]

Nor will you find in him any trace of those tales which others invented concerning the ancient greatness of the monastery, the prodigious donations of Desiderius, Tertullus, and others—men who even dared to forge false charter-documents to prove such claims. In writing, moreover, Leo set himself no task more than to explain the vicissitudes of the monastery, the titles to its possessions, and its other rights and privileges.

> [Note: Col. 0460. In these matters, which we can largely compare with the documents themselves, we never discover a trace of falsity and only rarely of error.]

He treated other events more briefly, but did not omit those of greater importance for the affairs of Italy or the Church as a whole. He presented the fortunes of southern Italy concisely, but in such a manner that their sequence is nowhere broken and that nothing necessary for understanding Cassinese affairs is lacking; throughout he maintained a measure than which one could scarcely find a more suitable.

He paid little attention to establishing the chronological order of particular events—

> [Note: Col. 0460. For example, I.1, 2.]

—although he proceeded knowingly and deliberately in the overall arrangement of events. But, seeing that exact chronological indication would create difficulty for him, he sometimes preferred to omit either it or the events themselves rather than investigate the truth with anxious care.

> [Note: Col. 0460. I.3; II.9, 15, 24.]

Nor did he sufficiently avoid errors in this respect, errors which abound, for example, at I.61 and II.9. On the other hand, his judgement cannot readily be blamed. He writes with a calm mind and, while generally favouring the popes, does not allow himself to be carried away by party zeal; he differs greatly from the declamations of his contemporaries and fellow-citizens, which rush on with blind violence.

In the following period, the Cassinese *Chronicle* was used by John, monk of St Vincent, who in composing the *Chronicle of Volturno* fell into almost every fault which Leo had cautiously avoided; then by Peter the Deacon; and by the author of that monstrous Cassinese *Chronicle* transmitted under the name of Anastasius, published by the distinguished Muratori, *Writers*, II, 351, from the papers of Constantine Cajetan.

> [Note: Col. 0460. Concerning the Chigi Library codex, see *Archivio*, IV, 529.]

Accordingly, the purpose of this new edition was to present the words which Leo appears to have written in his final revision, on the authority of manuscript 4. Its slighter and obvious errors we have silently removed; all its more serious ones we have conscientiously indicated. We have placed beneath the text the variant readings of the other manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0460] Wherever these contain anything new in subject-matter, we have indicated it by spacing between the type.]; and whenever it seemed worthwhile, we have had matter differing from manuscript 4 printed in two columns. Passages added in a single manuscript but later omitted by the author have sometimes been placed, together with material derived from Peter, between the text and the notes. Peter’s own hand can for the most part be readily recognized; elsewhere it can only be conjectured, especially when manuscript 1 is unavailable to assist us. There conjecture was necessary, since each reader may form his own judgment from the appended variety of readings [Col. 0461]. We reproduce the orthography employed by the author himself, as the autograph manuscript attests [Note: [Col. 0461] We have scrupulously retained it wherever the actual words of manuscript 1 are given, although it is likely that he later corrected, for example, a simple *e* used in place of a diphthong. Yet this very carelessness of one writing hastily seemed to show how, about this very period, the distinction between a vowel and a diphthong fell into disuse.]; and, where possible, we have retained his punctuation as well [Note: [Col. 0461] He used a simple comma and a raised point, a lower point and a final point, and a question-mark, which he placed above the word carrying the interrogative force and then repeated when the sentence ended. The very frequent corrections made to signs originally placed by the writer show the care he devoted to this matter also. We [Col. 0462] have not retained the signs themselves, but have always placed ours in the same position, except for question-marks, which we have omitted at the beginning of a sentence. Scribes close longer sentences with a comma marked by two points; Leo did not do this.]; elsewhere we have restored it according to the author’s practice. We give the order and numbering of the chapters from manuscript 4, adding the earlier numbers in the margin. In manuscript 1, the division of chapters is marked by an added letter *K*, and differs greatly from the later arrangement.

We have attempted briefly to explain matters that seemed to require elucidation. Besides Angelus’s commentaries, we have made extensive use of Gattula’s distinguished work and of the charter-documents printed there, as well as Tosti’s recently published *History of Monte Cassino*. Wherever possible we have added chronological indications, being much aided in this respect by Alessandro Di Meo’s *Annals of the Kingdom of Naples*, published at Naples in 1795 and 1810, quarto: a work of great learning and acute intellect, which has been of the greatest service to us, although marred by Pratilli’s inventions, to which its author gives too much credence.

## II. PETER’S BIRTH, LIFE, AND WRITINGS

[Col. 0461]

Peter, deacon and librarian of Monte Cassino, continued down to A.D. 1138 the chronicle which Leo had left unfinished. He was born, about the year 1107, from the most noble stock of the Counts of Tusculum [Note: [Col. 0462] See below, no. 50.], “of his father Aegidius, a Roman by nationality, son of Gregory, patrician and consul of the Romans” [Note: [Col. 0462] See Peter in Cas. manuscript 257, fols. 15–16, in Angelo de Nuce’s notes on the Prologue to Book IV. Angelus maintains that this was written by Peter himself, and Dr. Giesebrecht confirmed this to me when I asked him; after the words cited above he says that it scarcely differs from Book IV, chapter 66, except for the final words, which I have noted there. For a description of the manuscript see our *Annals*, [Col. 0463] V, 124. On Peter’s life compare IV, 40.].” This Gregory was the son of Gregory de Alberico, “duke and consul of the Romans” [Note: [Col. 0463] *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 113.]. We know that Alberic’s father was Gregory, whose mother seems to have been Marozia, who after the death of Alberic, prince and senator of all the Romans [Note: [Col. 0463] Marini, *Papal Diplomas*, C, p. 155.]—who died in A.D. 954—is called senatrix of all the Romans [Note: [Col. 0463] In the Subiaco Extracts, in Muratori, *Antiquities*, V, 769: “senatrix,” 8 Aug. 961; “of blessed memory,” 28 May 979; “Gregory, most illustrious man, son of Marozia the senatrix, by apostolic precept rector of the monastery of St Andrew the Apostle and of the monastery of St Lucy called Renatus,” 9 Feb. 981, ibid. — Benedict VII, son of Deusdedit, is called by Peter in the Catalogue of the Popes “of Tusculum,” *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, II, 4, and a relative of Alberic the Elder. The elder Alberic’s court was beside the basilica of the Holy Apostles, *Subiaco Extracts*, p. 773; the younger’s house was beside SS. Apostoli, Galetti, *On the Vestararius*, p. 14. I therefore think Marozia was related by blood to Alberic I, rather than his wife, for Benedict, monk of St Andrew, chapter 34, reports that he died during the very betrothal rites.], on 1 November 959. But because this is less certain, we append Peter’s genealogy from that first Gregory onward, with the aid of the manuscript history of the Counts of Tusculum compiled by the distinguished Galetti, extracts from which we received from Giesebrecht.

Boniface and Alexius*, p. 378; 2 December 999, “most excellent man called of Tusculum and naval prefect,” Galetti, *On the Primicerius*, p. 230. Peter the deacon calls him patrician in the catalogue of the popes. He is mentioned in the *Life of St Nilus* and in Thietmar IV, 30. The same man, as Provana conjectured (*Critical Studies*, p. 176), was sent as envoy to the emperor by Sylvester II, as his letter in the Bamberg manuscript attests, where he is called Gregory of Tusculum. He died, with his wife, before 11 June 1012, according to Galetti. Yet I do not maintain that the same man is meant in all these passages.]

He seems to have died in 1032, since Bonizo, p. 801, does not mention him; on 2 June 1045, “of blessed memory,” in Borgia, *Velletri*, p. 167. On him see Peter the Deacon, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, II, 60; III, 17; IV, 113; the Catalogue of the Popes; Register in Gattula, *History*, pp. 232, 233, 234, 236; Desiderius, *Dialogues*, III, prologue, Borgia, *Velletri*, p. 181; Galetti, *Primicerius*, pp. 83, 230; Ughelli, I, 98; Muratori, *Scriptores*, IIb, 525; Peter Damian, *Letter* 8, 4, who names Ermelina.]
