Compare *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, II, 60, 77; Desiderius, III, prologue; Gattula, *History*, p. 232; Nerini, p. 387; Peter Damian, *Opuscula*, 19, 3; Muratori, *Scriptores*, IIIb, 340–341; and Peter the Deacon’s catalogue of popes.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] In 1030 he elevated his son John; see the epitaph in Galetti, *Primicerius*, p. 83. In 1032 he claimed the title of patrician, Bonizo, p. 801; in June 1033, “Gregory of Tusculum” in a Farfa charter, according to Galetti; in 1058 he made Benedict X pope, Bonizo, p. 806; Leo of Ostia, II, 99. On 15 April 1059 he grants property for the soul of his son Peter, Borgia, *Velletri*, p. 181. He appears to have died on 30 January 1064, Gattula, *History*, I, 232; certainly before 18 February 1068, ibid., p. 233. On him see *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, II, 99; III, 17; IV, 133; Borgia, *Velletri*, p. 167; Nerini, p. 387.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] He is mentioned by Bonizo, p. 801, under 1032. I do not know whether he is distinct from the prefect of 1059 in the Roman Annals. Peter Damian, I think, addressed Letter 8, 5 to him; on 26 December 1065 he grants property to the monks of Monte Cassino together with his sons.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] 24 May 1064, in Gattula, *History*, p. 234.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] See no. 35.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] 30 January 1064, in Gattula, *History*, p. 232; 18 February 1068, ibid., p. 233; 24 September 1077, “of pious memory,” ibid., p. 236. On him see *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, III, 60; IV, 61, 113; and the letters printed below.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] About 1105, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 25; 1111, ibid., 39; 1116, in Falco of Benevento, under 1116. About 1128 he wrote the letter which we shall give shortly. He died in June 1130. He died on the Kalends of August: Monte Cassino necrology, manuscript 47.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] This Gregory is perhaps the man whom we find mentioned in 1098 with his son Theodulus in Sigebert under 1105. About 1128 he wrote letters.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] 24 September 1077, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, III, 60; Gattula, *History*, p. 236. Perhaps not distinct from the prefect who died on 2 April 1116, *Roman Annals* in *Monumenta*, *Scriptores*, V, 476, although Falco, under 1116, says that Ptolemy, son of this Peter, was his maternal uncle.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] See manuscript 257 and the letters.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] About 1128 she married.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] He married Bertha in 1117, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 61. In June 1130, indiction VIII, Ptolemy, by God’s grace consul of the Romans, son of the late Ptolemy of blessed memory, promises security by land and sea to the monks of Monte Cassino: Peter’s Register, fol. 252. In 1137 he received investiture from the emperor, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 125. On 14 March 1141, Ptolemy of Tusculum appears with his father-in-law Leo, son of Peter Leo, Nerini, p. 394. He died on 25 February 1153, *Chronicle of Fossanova*. On Ptolemy and his descendants, compare the note to IV, 25.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] See below, Landulf’s letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] In 1137 he was given as a hostage to Lothair, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 125; Maino, legate Raino, Martène, *Collection*, I, 757.]

[Note: [Col. 0464] 5 February 1163, Nerini, p. 404; 1168, Romuald of Salerno. Compare Borgia, *Velletri*, p. 247.]

[Col. 0463] Thus in A.D. 1115 Peter was offered by his parents to blessed Benedict under Abbot Girard [Note: [Col. 0464] Aged five, manuscript 257; *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 47: “in the first five-year period of his life”; *Chronicle*, IV, Prologue, chapter 66. But in 1128 he says that he was twenty-one years old, *On Illustrious Men*, 47, and manuscript 257. At twenty-three he wrote the *Life of St Placidus*, either while still in exile or immediately after his return; in 1133, other Lives, having been drawn away by friends from the continual examination of the monastic archive which Seniorectus had imposed upon him long before 1134. I therefore think that he was born about 1107.], and under the same abbot [Note: [Col. 0464] He died 17 January 1123.] he was educated for almost eight years [Note: [Col. 0464] *Chronicle*, IV, 66; manuscript 257; *On Illustrious Men*, 47.], receiving instruction from Guido, whom he says was outstanding in conduct and life and eminent in speech and intellect [Note: [Col. 0464] *On Illustrious Men*, Prologue.]. I consider this man identical with Guido, monk of Monte Cassino, who wrote the Vision of Alberic, “a man most distinguished in human learning, thoroughly approved in religion and life,” according to our Peter in *On Illustrious Men* (chapter 41; compare *Chronicle*, IV, 66), where he says that the same man wrote a *History of Emperor Henry*: “Moreover, he added what was lacking in the history of Monte Cassino, namely from the times of Oderisius I down to the present day.” But no trace of any of these works survives.

Besides Guido, Peter calls Peter the Deacon his teacher [Note: [Col. 0465] Ibid., chapter 39.], an eminent declaimer who “left the city of Teano, from which he came, came to Monte Cassino, and became a monk under Abbot Oderisius.” Under these masters Peter, from his fifth year as he says, devoted himself to interpretations of the sacred writings and ancient annals, but gave no attention at all to the liberal arts [Note: [Col. 0465] Prologue to Book IV: “most fully instructed in sacred letters,” chapter 108; compare chapter 113.]. Later, when Oderisius II “had relinquished the abbacy [Note: [Col. 0465] In 1126.], he was sent into exile through the envy of his rivals,” in A.D. 1128 [Note: [Col. 0465] *On Illustrious Men*, 47: aged twenty-one; ibid. and manuscript 257.], namely by Abbot Seniorectus [Note: [Col. 0465] 12 July 1127–4 February 1137.], because of his father’s intimacy with the Counts of Aquino, enemies of the Cassinese monks. He seems then to have withdrawn to Atina, since while in exile, in his twenty-first year, he wrote the Passion of St Mark, bishop of Atina, “at the request of Adenulf, count of that city” [Note: [Col. 0465] *On Illustrious Men*, 47. I think him identical with Adenulf, Count of Aquino, mentioned in *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 88, since Atina was subject to the Counts of Aquino. Peter added certain things about Atina to Leo, II, 79.].

At that time he received a letter from his uncle Ptolemy, in these words [Note: [Col. 0465] These letters, which Angelus published from manuscript 257 in the passage cited [Col. 0466], we present corrected by collation with that manuscript, through the kindness of Dr William Giesebrecht.]:

> “Ptolemy, descended from the Julian stock and most eminent consul of the Romans, greetings to Peter, his dearest nephew. It has been reported to our exalted station that Seniorectus has expelled you from Monte Cassino. Therefore, if you wish to return to us, I shall receive both you and your father honorably, and shall entrust to you all the basilicas of the Cassinese church. I send this letter to you through our nephew Landon, your cousin. Farewell. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, at the castle of Neptune.”

His uncle Gregory offered him another refuge, sending the following letter, copied by Jean Mabillon from a Cassinese manuscript and published by Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, col. 703:

> “Gregory, son of Gregory, consul of the Romans, greetings to his nephew Peter. We have received your letter, in which [M.: *quo*, ‘whereby’] you related that you had been expelled from Monte Cassino. I was filled with no small joy; for your father [M.: *meus*, ‘my’] abandoned me and my brother Ptolemy and attached himself to beggarly counts [Note: [Col. 0466] From Peter’s words cited above, I think that these were the Counts of Aquino.], with the result that he himself became nearly destitute and impoverished, and [M.: *ut*, ‘that’] you were expelled from Monte Cassino. Therefore I advise [Cassinese manuscript 257, fol. 30: *suade*, ‘advise’] your father to return to us. To you, moreover, I shall give my monastery situated at Villano.”

And he wrote the following to Peter’s father [Note: [Col. 0466] Manuscript 257.]:

> “Gregory, son of Gregory, consul of the Romans, greetings to his beloved brother Aegidius. It is found in Roman writings that no one ought to depart from the ancient path and the commands of his ancestors. But you, abandoning me and your brother Ptolemy and attaching yourself to beggarly counts, have not returned to us down to the present time; hence you have become poor, and your son has been expelled from Monte Cassino. Therefore strive to return to us together with him, so that we may take care of you as we do of ourselves. Know, moreover, that your sister Jadara has now been given in marriage.”

These admonitions seem to have recalled Aegidius from association with those counts. At any rate, our Peter was readmitted to the monastery not long afterward and was reconciled with Seniorectus. In the prologue to Book IV he says that he heard many of the things he wrote from Seniorectus’s own mouth; in the *Chronicle* he mentions him with much praise and dedicated several works to him, which he had undertaken to write at Seniorectus’s command.

His first work, as we have already said, was the *Passion of Blessed Mark and His Companions*, which, as he himself says, he wrote for Oderisius II. The people of Atina maintained that Mark, whom they held in great reverence there together with the martyrs Nicander and Marcian and St Daria, was their first bishop and a disciple of St Peter. Accounts of their deeds, together with the translation and miracles, written by others, survive and were published in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, VI, pp. 408 ff., 2nd ed.; Jean Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, II, p. 247; and *Acta Sanctorum*, April III, p. 558 and June III, p. 268. But that all these differ from Peter’s work is proved by the words from his *History of the Passion of the Holy Martyrs Mark, Nicander, and Marcian* cited by Ughelli in the passage named:

> “Among nearly all the cities enclosed within the boundary of the West, it is evident that Atina is most ancient. King Saturn, after he had been driven out by his son Jupiter, founded it as the second city in all the West after establishing the city of Siponto, and called it Atina. Whoever wishes to know to what height it rose, how powerful and learned it was, and what and how great artisans it possessed, should reread Livy’s *History* and Virgil’s *Aeneid*, and there he will find eloquently described the excellence which it once enjoyed.”

[Note: [Col. 0466] Indeed, he will seek it there in vain. The same author writes differently in the *History of the Trojan Race*, in Tosti, II, 118: “Capys the Trojan, building the city of Atina, gave it its name,” etc.]

Moreover, Peter appended to the history of St Mark the destruction and restoration of the city of Atina [Note: [Col. 0466] *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 47.] and described the discovery of the body of the holy martyr Mark [Note: [Col. 0466] *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 66; “the translation of blessed Mark in the city of Atina,” *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 47.], “as also the Life of St Daria, wife of St Nicander.” He added the *Miracles of the Holy Martyrs* [Col. 0467] *Mark, Nicander, and Marcian* [Note: [Col. 0467] All these are enumerated in the cited places.]. Since he was diligent in their cult, he wrote eight sermons on the feast of Blessed Mark, two on his vigils [Note: [Col. 0467] Or one; the other was on the vigil of Nicander and Marcian, according to chapter 47 of *On Illustrious Men*.], a sermon on St Nicander, and a sermon on the translation of St Nicander and Marcian. Further, he composed six hymns in their praise and dictated chants for Blessed Mark.

From this great abundance of writings Ughelli professed to have in his possession, in manuscript, the *Life of the Saints* with the history of the translation and miracles, as well as a song to be sung at the feast of Blessed Mark; but he published none of them and did not yield them even to Daniel Papebroch when requested. Papebroch doubted whether Ughelli had ever possessed them; but he is refuted by the words Ughelli cites from the Life written by Peter, which are not found in the others. Yet none of them, so far as we know, has reached us, except for several sermons preserved in Cassinese manuscript 361 [Note: [Col. 0467] See J. B. Marus on chapter 47 of *On Illustrious Men*.]. Peter, however, not content even with what he had himself produced, also obtained from Peter, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church and Cassinese monk, by entreaties, that the Passion of Blessed Mark should be adorned in verse [Note: [Col. 0467] *On Illustrious Men*, 43.].

I fear that he exercised, in the next little work which he seems to have undertaken, the same license for invention which we observed in the words quoted above. For, “being in the twenty-third year of his life” [Note: [Col. 0467] From the prologue of this Life, which Martène and Durand alone published from Mabillon’s papers, *Collection*, VI, col. 785.], he was urged by Bishop Gregory, whom I suspect to have been bishop of Terracina [Note: [Col. 0467] *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 42.], to translate from Greek into Latin the *Acts of St Placidus* attributed to Gordianus. For, as Peter himself states in another edition of the same Life [Note: [Col. 0467] In Constantino Cajetan, *Lives of Sicilian Saints*, I, 183; I know these only from Bueus’s dissertation.], a certain Symeon, priest of Constantinople, had brought them to Salerno in 1115, written in Greek by Gordianus, Placidus’s companion. John, a monk of Capua, had sent them to Monte Cassino to the monk Raynald, at whose exhortation Peter says that he translated them.

But in the earlier work, in which Symeon is not mentioned [Note: [Col. 0467] Indeed he writes: “For since from the very times of Blessed [Col. 0468] Benedict there had been very many learned men in the Cassinese school, no one had translated this Passion from Greek into Latin”; thus it appears by no means to have been recently brought there.], he says: “I was intending to send it to Ptolemy, consul of the Romans, but first judged that it should be polished by your [Note: [Col. 0468] Gregory’s.] resisting buskin.” You see that he had been reconciled with his uncle, but not yet—or only shortly before—with Seniorectus, since at first he had declined “to undertake it because of the disturbances of so great a monastery and the troubles of our exile.”

This Life, which begins “After the supreme King,” has not yet been published in full. Since it was inserted into the book *On the Righteous Men of Monte Cassino* [Note: [Col. 0468] A. Mai, *New Collection*, VI.B, p. 247.] with the prologue written to Gregory, it is plainly abbreviated, because readers are repeatedly referred to Gordianus’s work. Afterwards, not yet satisfied with the fables with which the Life falsely attributed to Gordianus abounds, he wrote it out anew and interpolated it with many fabricated tales. Some of these appear in the Life published by Surius [Note: [Col. 0468] VII, p. 746, 1st ed.; V, p. 637, 2nd ed.], Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0468] *Acts of the Saints of the Order of St Benedict*, I, p. 15.], and Bueus [Note: [Col. 0468] *Acta Sanctorum*, October III, p. 114.]; others lie hidden in the manuscript which the Cassinese call the *Register of St Placidus*. Although Peter attributed all these things to Gordianus, it is not entirely certain whether he himself inserted them. For after the end of the Life he proceeds as follows [Note: [Col. 0468] In Gattula, *History of Monte Cassino*, p. 916.]:

> “Thus far Gordianus, disciple of Father Benedict, who, etc. But Peter, Cassinese deacon, by command of the most reverend Raynald, archimandrite of Monte Cassino, extracted from the cosmography of Theophanes and from the chronography of the Roman pontiffs the things which occurred from the time of Pope Vitalian to the times of the emperors Henry and Alexius, and added them to the history already mentioned. It begins: ‘At that time when Emperor Constans …,’ etc.”

The exceedingly difficult questions whether the Greek Acts were ever written, whether Symeon the priest is fictitious, whether the paraphrase and letter of Stephen of Anici—otherwise unknown—were also invented by Peter, and whose offspring the utterly ridiculous letters and other documents contained in the *Register of St Placidus* are to be considered—which Gattula says was written in Lombardic letters in the age of our Peter and which was printed at the end of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Venice 1513 and Paris 1603—these questions, I say, do not need examination here, since they are irrelevant to our purpose. They were discussed with great learning and scholarship by James Bueus in *Acta Sanctorum*, October III, p. 65 ff.

It is sufficient for us to observe that Peter very readily lent his hand to every sort of little fable; and that if he did not himself invent them, he was most ready to adopt and turn them to his own uses. For these plainly false documents, not even mentioned in a word by Leo, were first brought to light by Peter. Thus the favour and gifts of Justin, Justinian, and Theoderic toward the monastery of Monte Cassino are mentioned in *Chronicle*, IV, 113; in his Register, moreover, he inserted both Tertullus’s monstrous donation [Note: [Col. 0468] Tosti, I, 77.] and Desiderius’s privilege of no better repute [Note: [Col. 0468] Ibid., I, 89.]. I mention these before the others because they evidently seemed either unknown to Leo or wholly unworthy of belief; but the bull of Benedict VIII [Note: [Col. 0468] Ibid., p. 251.] was copied word for word from Leo’s own text.

[Col. 0469] It can therefore scarcely be doubted that Peter himself recognized their falsity, particularly since after his return Seniorectus appointed him cartulary-keeper, archivist, and librarian of the monastery. We see him adorned with these titles scarcely after that man’s death, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV, 108. The year in which he returned to Monte Cassino is unclear [Note: [Col. 0469] See above, no. 50.]; but it seems to me to have been about 1130. For when in 1133 he wrote certain hagiographical works to Seniorectus, he speaks in the prologue to the *Life of St Severus* as follows: “For when he, namely Raynald, found our insignificance wavering in the lodging of the lawgiver, saw me entangled in monastic affairs, and recognized that the continual investigation of precepts and volumes prevented the soul of my heart from searching the God-speaking books,” etc. You see an outline of the occupation of a librarian; indeed, I think the very compilation of the Cassinese Register is indicated by these words.

For the *Register of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*, or, as he himself calls it, the *Book of Privileges*—a work of great size [Note: [Col. 0469] It contains 249 charters. Old catalogue of Cassinese manuscripts in Angelo Mai, *Spicilegium*, V, 221b.] and of the greatest usefulness, preserved entire at Monte Cassino and written in Lombardic letters—he arranged and ordered to be copied at the command of Abbot Seniorectus [Note: [Col. 0469] For manuscript 257, said to be autograph, is written in Latin letters.], and for it he “made a prologue at the request of Raynald, Cassinese subdeacon” [Note: [Col. 0469] *Chronicle*, IV, 66; *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 47.]. Its connection with our letters is such that we may properly append the preface entire from the distinguished Gattula’s book [Note: [Col. 0469] Appendix, p. 22.]:

> To the most reverend and most holy Father SENIORECTUS [G.: *Senioreto*], PETER, the least of his sons, offers the service of due obedience.
>
> Your venerable sagacity, Father, had long ago enjoined upon us [Note: [Col. 0469] Therefore he must have returned from exile long before.] that I should copy into one volume the privileges granted to our monastery by the Roman pontiffs. This was indeed a difficult undertaking, and unusual in our times, especially because the title-deeds rescued twice from [G.: *et*, “and”] fire have now been almost consumed by age and reduced to nothing. I did not know, therefore, what I should do or how I should accomplish it. When your prudence perceived this, it began to encourage our insignificance with such words:
>
> “You know more clearly how great is the transient love of country among those who love the world. No gifts, no threats, no disturbances caused the Romans to depart from love of their country; for they strove in every way both to defend it by arms and to adorn it with buildings. If they loved a perishable and earthly country with so great a love, consider what we ought to do for one eternal and unfailing. Indeed, when the most excellent Robert, prince of Capua [Note: [Col. 0470] He was expelled from Capua in 1134.], came to our court, and conversation occasionally arose concerning these matters, he began earnestly to urge us to bring to completion what you had once commanded concerning the writing of the privileges. Therefore, because the matter has been delayed until today, I both wish and command that the privileges of the pontiffs, the precepts of emperors, kings, dukes, and princes, and also the offerings of all the faithful, be copied in one volume.”
>
> When, therefore, I perceived your will in this matter, I obeyed, because I perceived that not to obey was impious and profane; for, as the divine utterance testifies, “to rebel is as the sin of divination, and to refuse compliance is as the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15:23). How much difficulty I experienced in this work will be shown most clearly by the offerings themselves. The history of the venerable Leo, bishop of Ostia, was a very great assistance to us in this matter. Beginning with the most blessed Father Benedict, he composed an exceedingly useful book concerning the affairs of the Cassinese monastery, in which he displayed such richness of understanding that he omitted scarcely anything that occurred in that monastery [Note: [Col. 0470] Yet he would have omitted matters of the greatest importance, if Peter’s own statements about Justinian, Justin, and the others were true.]. Following the diligence of so great a man in this work, although I was wholly unable to attain it with my unequal capacity of understanding, I nevertheless set down the order of the offerings as he had established it. I resolved, moreover, to divide this book into six divisions: privileges, precepts, offerings [Note: [Col. 0470] Giesebrecht told me that offerings are intermingled with renunciations.], libelli (documents), renunciations, and oaths. Therefore, with the dutiful service of humble devotion, I beseech the excellence of your fatherhood that your holiness may receive this little work with a most gracious mind; and, if you find anything perhaps deficient in it, kindly extend forgiveness.

He first composed the book at that time in such a way as to leave room for documents of a later period; for that much more recent material is contained in it is proved, for example, by Wibald’s letter printed from it [Note: [Col. 0470] Muratori, *Scriptores*, IV, 622.]. As regards the reliability of the work, we have already seen that he by no means abstained from accepting false documents; but he seems to have transcribed fairly accurately others of which copies survive. Erasmus Gattula drew much from it; Ludovico Tosti published some items. Moved, it appears, by the same pursuits, Peter “revised, at the command of Abbot Seniorectus, the History of the Destruction or Restoration of the Monastery of St Maurus, for which he also wrote a prologue”; for certain papal privileges concern the fortunes of that monastery.

But his friends’ admonitions prevented him from spending too much time on profane and secular studies. The first of these whom I mention is Alberic, trained in the same school of Guido as Peter. Alberic says of Guido’s little book on that remarkable vision [Note: [Col. 0471] F. Cancellieri, *Observations Concerning the Question Raised by Vanozzi … on the Originality of Dante’s Divine Comedy*, Rome, 1814, octavo; Alberic’s Vision is printed in that book, pp. 134 ff.]:

> “Someone, receiving it, added what he wished, removed what he wished, altered what he wished, and circulates it as though in our name, mocking and corrupting what he himself wrote … [lacuna] I found these and many other things fabricated in our Vision. For this reason Abbot Seniorectus summoned our insignificance and commanded that, revising it again, I should cut away the superfluous matter and restore what had been removed to its proper place. Therefore, having summoned Peter the Deacon, united with us in Christ’s love from, so to speak, our very cradles, I undertook three days’ labour and corrected it completely, cutting out the falsehoods and restoring the removed material to its proper place.”

Peter in turn gave proof of his friendship for Alberic in *Chronicle*, IV, 66, and among his works he lists his revision of Alberic’s corrupted Vision. No less intimate was his friendship with Raynald, subdeacon of Monte Cassino. I do not know whether this was that Tuscan who was later elevated to the abbacy and was subdeacon of Anacletus [Note: [Col. 0471] *Chronicle*, IV, 104. But from this one might conclude that he was subdeacon of the Roman Church, which perhaps he suppressed because Anacletus’s claim was doubtful.]. If so, the book *On the Illustrious Men of the Cassinese Monastery* would certainly have been written before 1137, when he became abbot; for in chapter 44 it says:

> “Raynald, Cassinese subdeacon, offered to Blessed Benedict as a little child, a man highly learned and in skill at verse-making in every respect comparable to the ancients, wrote verses in praise of the most holy Severus, bishop of Monte Cassino, addressed to Peter, deacon and librarian; also verses on the life of Blessed Benedict and Blessed Maurus; and hymns in praise of St [lacuna] Severus.”

But I would not press this point too strongly. Peter wrote this book—which Guido had undertaken seven years earlier but abandoned—to Pandulf, bishop of Teano [Note: [Col. 0471] *Chronicle*, IV, 66, 75, 108.]. It is rather meagre, but very useful to us for knowledge of many matters. It was first published by J. B. Marus [Note: [Col. 0471] With a supplement containing Peter’s Life, not very different from *Chronicle*, IV, 66, and manuscript 257.], with a commentary containing some material concerning Cassinese manuscripts, Rome, 1655, octavo; reprinted Paris, 1666; in the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyons, 1677, XXI, p. 347; in J. A. Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, Hamburg, 1718, folio, p. 165; in Muratori, *Scriptores*, VI, p. 9; and in Burman’s *Thesaurus*, IX, 329.

Besides this Raynald, Peter was joined in friendship with the deacon Raynald, whom he himself calls abbot in *Chronicle*, IV, 66—namely Raynald of Collemento. To him he says [Note: [Col. 0472] Prologue to the *Life of St Apollinaris*, in Angelo Mai, *New Collection*, VI.B, p. 257.]:

> “But you, brother most dear in Christ, and bound to me in an indissoluble love, so to speak, from our very rattles,” etc.

By this man’s influence, evidently, Peter was first induced after his return to write lives of saints. In the *Life of St Apollinaris*, which he inscribed to “the most reverend Raynald, adorned with the academic flowers, fellow-deacon of the Cassinese monastery,” he says: “After my permanent return to the citadel of Mount Cassino, from which I had been absent for a time, times, and half a time [Note: [Col. 0472] Daniel 7:25; 12:7.], you do not cease to awaken me, sunk in idle and slothful sleep …” Thus he seems to have composed this work even before the Register. It is, however, scarcely anything except a cento extracted from Leo’s chronicle, and so burdened with verbal prolixity that even the scribe of the Vatican manuscript added:

> I myself, the scribe, while avoiding superfluous labour …

I have omitted a great many things that are not to the point. That other Raynald, the subdeacon, drew Peter away from secular affairs and the handling of old charters, urging him to write the Life of Saint Severus, which, while not yet beyond the bounds of youth, he dedicated to Abbot Seniorectus. [Note: [Col. 0472] Angelo Mai, *Nova Collectio* VI, B, p. 250.] When he had completed it, he composed the Life of Guinizon, yielding to the requests of Richard, a monk of Monte Cassino, [Note: [Col. 0472] Apparently the same man who later became chaplain to Innocent II: *Chronicon Casinense* IV, 105.] in which he copied very much verbatim from Leo’s Chronicle, adding an account of several miracles. [Note: [Col. 0472] Published in *Acta Sanctorum*, May VI, p. 456, and corrected from the Vatican manuscript in Angelo Mai, *Nova Collectio* VI, B, p. 264.] He reports in *Chronicon Casinense* III, 48, that he wrote this Life “about seven years before this,” that is, around the year 1133. In the same words, ibid. IV, 7, he refers to a book *On Miracles*, namely those of the Cassinese monks, which seems to have been lost. There survive, however, the *Origins and Lives of the Righteous Men of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*, in which we find what he cites from that work, so that we should think it scarcely a different work, unless he himself distinguished the two. [Note: [Col. 0472] *Chronicon* IV, 66; *De viris illustribus*, ch. 47.]

But Peter’s character was such that he repeatedly reused what he had once written: he was his own plagiarist. For we encounter entire chapters of that book in the same words in the Chronicle. We have already observed a revised version of the Life of Saint Placid; we shall shortly see sections of the Chronicle listed by him as separate books concerning the righteous; and he inserted into the book *On the Righteous* the Lives mentioned above—of Saints Severus, Placid, Apollinaris, and Guinizon—together with their prologues, either entire or abridged. [Note: [Col. 0472] In this work only the Lives of Severus, Apollinaris, and Guinizon survive [Col. 0473], published by Angelo Mai in *Nova Collectio* VI, B, p. 245, from the Vatican manuscript; another, fuller and more prolix copy is preserved at Monte Cassino. From the latter the Life of Aldemarius was also published in *Acta Sanctorum*, March III, p. 489. These four Lives also survive in the Register of Saint Placid.] Most of the remainder he transcribed verbatim from the books of Gregory the Great, Desiderius, and Leo. We do not know the sources for others; much he received orally from people.

He also gathered together many miracles of Blessed Benedict, and tales of the discovery of his body that do not at all agree with Leo’s account, in his sermon for the octave of Blessed Benedict, written after 1134, of which he makes mention in §41, published in *Acta Sanctorum*, May III, pp. 288–297.

But we have now reached the period when the greatest dangers threatened the Cassinese community, while Peter had a most welcome opportunity to display his eloquence, subtlety of intellect, knowledge of law, [Note: [Col. 0473] The tale that, by Lothair’s command, he compiled a systematic collection of Lombard laws was long ago refuted by the distinguished Savigny, *Geschichte des römischen Rechts im Mittelalter* II, p. 200.] and acquaintance with past times. It would have sufficed merely to touch upon these matters, since his Chronicle is for us almost the sole and the richest witness concerning them, had this very fact not been the reason why Baronius and others judged that Peter must be denied all credibility. Angelo de Nuce answered them at length in his note to chapter 108. And first, I readily acknowledge Peter as author of the narrative, which throughout bears the flavor of his style.

There was at Monte Cassino his account of the dispute held before the emperor, which he had written in the imperial court itself, [Note: [Col. 0473] IV, 66. He also separately published the disputation with the Constantinopolitan.] beginning, according to J. B. Maro’s testimony in his note to chapter 47 of *De viris illustribus*: “Therefore, while in the presence of Emperor Lothair …” If it still survives, comparison with it would remove every doubt; but Angelo is wholly silent about it. Yet the entire character of the language is not unlike the passages that follow. These are partly confirmed by Lothair’s authentic privilege, [Note: [Col. 0473] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 250; Margarini, *Bullarium Cassinense* II, p. 153.] still reverently preserved by the Cassinese, and partly by letters written by Peter to Empress Richenza. Whether these are genuine or not is another—and a most difficult—question, one which I would not dare decide.

For those letters of Lothair themselves, and others which he mentions in the Chronicle, emerged only from the Cassinese archive—from manuscripts copied under Peter’s direction, namely his register and manuscript 257—and we do not know whether they are uncorrupted. [Note: [Col. 0473] The letter in *Chronicon* IV, 125, differs considerably [Col. 0474] from its other copy in manuscript 257.] Nevertheless, they agree with one another, and I cannot persuade myself that all are fabricated. Indeed, from Lothair’s own privilege we see that he was devoted in the highest degree to the Cassinese monastery; and his wording shows that the forged privileges of Justinian and Zacharias [Note: [Col. 0474] This privilege was also confirmed by the Roman pontiffs. See our *Annals* V, p. 319.] had been presented to him and accepted as genuine.

It therefore seems to me safest to conclude that the aged and devout emperor, caught by the cunning of a most crafty monk and charmed by his talkativeness, willingly listened to him narrating ancient events and gave him credence. Thus I believe that the entire disputation which he reports did take place; but I am far from attaching great weight to every individual word, and I do not allow myself to be deceived by the bombastic boasting of this glorious man. For much in it proves him false. He himself related in chapter 104 that Raynald had publicly been declared an enemy of the Empire by the emperor; he himself recounted the disputed election—yet in the disputation no trace of either appears. Next, he maintains that no papal envoys were present at the election of Abbot Seniorectus, though in chapter 94 he himself recounted their arrival and words. Finally, when Lothair came to Monte Cassino, matters are handled as though not a word on these issues had ever been said at Lago Pensile.

These points make it scarcely possible that the matter was conducted as narrated. Yet, if nothing of the sort had happened, I do not see how Peter could have persuaded himself that anyone would give credit to his inventions. The year alleged to have been falsely assigned to this affair moves me little. For a man of inaccurate memory, writing with an exceedingly hurried pen and assigning a date to an event, seems to have consulted the privilege granted by Lothair; since it was issued in September 1137, he mistakenly wrote the following summer as though it belonged to the same year. This could happen more readily because he first composed the disputation alone and later inserted it, as it stood, into the Chronicle. [Note: [Col. 0474] By a similar error, in chapter 112 he says that Lothair spent a year and a half under canvas; in chapter 115, a year and two months, although not a full year had elapsed after the court at Würzburg.]

Accordingly, when Raynald of Tusculum met the emperor at Lago Pensile, Peter came with him, having been specifically summoned: he was the monastery’s keeper of charters, librarian, and archivist. [Note: [Col. 0474] *Chronicon* IV, 108.] The emperor might have known him through the connections between the counts of Tusculum and the emperors. [Note: [Col. 0474] Cf. *Chronicon* IV, 125.] Moreover, since he had ordered the abbot to bring with him the emperors’ privileges, [Note: [Col. 0474] Lothair, Letter 3, in Muratori, *Scriptores* IV, p. 621; cf. *Chronicon* IV, 108.] it is easy to believe that the keeper of charters too was summoned.

When a day was set for the hearing, the monks appointed our Peter as their *apocrisiarius* and defender, to conduct their case against the cardinals. [Note: [Col. 0474] *Chronicon* IV, 66, 108, prologue.] He himself narrated how he did this, though with highly doubtful credibility. Still, it seems true that he ingratiated himself with both Lothair and Innocent. But of Innocent we know nothing further, except that Peter dedicated to him the Life of Saint Leo IX. [Note: [Col. 0474] *De viris illustribus*, ch. 47.] The letters already mentioned above attest Lothair’s affection.

[Col. 0475] If the letter in *Chronicon* chapter 125 and manuscript 257 is genuine—though it is not written in identical words—it appointed him Italian logothete, confidential secretary, clerk, auditor, keeper of charters, and chaplain of the Roman Empire. [Note: [Col. 0475] Cf. Letter 1 to Richenza, *Chronicon* IV, 66, 116.] He reports that this occurred in chapter 116, after the disputation with the Greek, through the intervention of Empress Richenza, Duke Henry of Bavaria, and Conrad of Swabia. Since he was lodging in the tent of Berthulf, [Note: [Col. 0475] B., notary, 22 September 1137, Martène, *Collectio* II, p. 102. Some privileges of Lothair were authenticated by Berthald, imperial scribe: Lami, *Deliciae eruditorum* IV, p. 162. Berthold, imperial chamberlain: Ughelli V, pp. 756, 777.] the chancellor, [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapters 108, 111.] he was ordered to remain with him in the imperial court “to perform the services of the Empire,” [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapter 114.] and he boasts of being his pupil. [Note: [Col. 0475] IV, 66; letter to Richenza; Prologue I, *On Notes*: “In part, [I rely] on our teacher, Chancellor Rudolf.”] But later he relates that Lothair said [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapter 125.] that he had made him a pupil of Henry, bishop of Regensburg and chancellor.

Indeed, Lothair entrusted to him the duty of preserving his predecessors’ enactments; and he was so delighted by Peter’s accounts of ancient deeds that he ordered him to write a history of the emperors. [Note: [Col. 0475] IV, 125; Wibald’s letter, Martène, *Collectio* II, p. 185.] While remaining with the emperor, Peter also then managed Cassinese business. [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapters 117, 118.] Then, after the abbot had been dismissed and Peter retained by Lothair, he returned to the monastery on account of illness; soon afterwards, by the emperor’s command, he came back to him and travelled with him to Monte Cassino. On departing thence, Lothair wished to take Peter with him, to perform imperial services continually. Only with difficulty did he allow Guibald to retain him, and, having highly praised him, commended him to Guibald’s affection. [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapter 125; Letter 1 to Richenza.]

Yet Lothair could not bear to be without him for long. When he came to Tivoli, he requested that Guibald send Peter to him. [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapter 125.] In replying, [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapter 125; Martène, *Collectio* II, p. 183.] after complaining at length of the oppression inflicted by neighbors, Guibald said:

> “You will learn the rest from the words of our son Peter, the drafter of this letter and in every respect a faithful servant of the Roman Empire. We have decided to send him into Germany, Saxony, Denmark, Swabia, and Lotharingia. Know, however, that he has not yet completed the history of the western emperors which you ordered him, Peter, to compose. For, crushed by diverse troubles and distresses, he has had more opportunity to weep than to write.”

Nevertheless, “because the length and conclusion of the journey prevented it,” Guibald changed his mind and kept him at home. [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapter 126. Peter lists both letters among his works.] There, astonishingly amid so great an affliction of the monastery, Peter dedicated to Guibald the little book *On the Holy Places*, or *Itinerary of the Holy Land*, collected, as he says, from all books, so to speak. [Note: [Col. 0475] According to the testimony of Jean Mabillon, he took much from Bede; see Martène, *Collectio* VI, p. 789, where the prologue is published.] Tostius published it from the now mutilated manuscript 361, *Historia Cassinensis* II, p. 121.

After Lothair’s death he addressed a letter to Empress Richenza, [Note: [Col. 0476] Cf. *Chronicon* IV, 124.] which Jean Mabillon extracted from a Cassinese manuscript and published in Martène, *Collectio* I, p. 756; *Annales Benedictini* VI, p. 623; and *Origines Guelficae* II, p. 540, together with another in which he consoled her after the death of Duke Henry. [Note: [Col. 0476] This and the following letter were also published by Angelo Mai, *Nova Collectio* I, p. 758.] He also congratulated “Conrad, most excellent emperor and most vigorous promoter of the Roman Empire,” in a very beautiful letter, according to the author’s testimony, [Note: [Col. 0476] IV, 66; *De viris illustribus*, ch. 47.] upon his recent election, and commended the Cassinese Church to his protection.

He also dedicated two small works to Conrad. These, with the rest, may be seen in *Chronicon* IV, 66; for there is too great a number of them to enumerate individually here, and of most of them we know nothing beyond their titles. [Note: [Col. 0476] In the catalogue of Cassinese manuscripts under Paul II, in Angelo Mai, *Spicilegium* V, p. 223, is mentioned Peter’s book *On the Dignity of the Roman Empire*. It begins: “These worthy …”] After Guibald’s departure, therefore, Peter enjoyed the favor and intimacy of Abbot Raynald, by whose command he added a continuation to the Cassinese Chronicle around 1140. Landulf, Peter’s kinsman, requested him from the abbot in the following letter: [Note: [Col. 0476] Angelo Mai, to *Chronicon* IV, prologue, from manuscript 257, collated again by V. D. Giesebrecht.]

> “Landulf, by the grace of God cardinal and abbot of Saint John, sends greeting and commendation to R., as to his lord. We request your fatherhood that, if you wish to retain my affection and service, you appoint Lord Peter, son of Egidius, who is the brother of my wife Guilla and my kinsman, to the church of Saint Benedict of Collis Insulae, because he is prudent and wise, and I wish to take counsel from him. Therefore I beseech you to send him there without delay, because he is exceedingly necessary to me both for my territory and for all that is mine.”

Whether he came, we do not know, nor do we discover anything further about him. For my part, he seems not to have lived much longer. [Note: [Col. 0476] It is certain that, after Egidius of Venosa was deposed as abbot by Alexander III, Peter the deacon was placed in charge of the monastery, with the title only of procurator, until provision should be made for a successor: Angelo de Nuce on *Chronicon* IV, prologue. But on whose testimony? That Peter, to whom the pope left the administration in 1168, was a dean and priest; he was elected abbot in 1174 and died on 8 July 1186: see the Anonymous Cassinese writer for that year. He is clearly distinct from our man from the persistent title “deacon” attached to the latter and from the silence of the author who, in chapter 47 of the book *On Illustrious Men*, added material after his death.]

For, since he wrote so much in a brief span of ten years, I think I may reasonably infer that so long as he lived he never ceased writing. Even if it were possible that some of the works enumerated in *Chronicon* IV, 66 were inserted later, still, had he survived long, we should surely find some indication of a later time either in his published works or in other writers’ inscriptions, [Col. 0477] whereas we find so many things that must be referred to earlier periods. [Note: [Col. 0477] The catalogue of emperors, etc., ends with Conrad, Innocent II, and Guibald: *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores* III, p. 219. If the Fulco whose Life he wrote was the abbot of Cava who died in 1146, Peter survived him; but this remains uncertain.] He died at Monte Cassino and was buried there. [Note: [Col. 0477] *De viris illustribus*, ch. 47.]

Peter added his continuation to the Cassinese Chronicle in the third year after the events conducted before Lothair, [Note: [Col. 0477] Prologue to Book IV. The words concerning Cardinals Gerard and Guido in chapters 109 and 121 seem to have been inserted after 1145, either by Peter himself or by another.] that is, in the year of the Lord 1140. But he did not leave untouched what Leo had written either. For Angelo de Nuce had already seen that the additions and alterations in manuscript 2 proceeded from Peter. This is inherently plausible, because they occur only in the manuscript which also contains the continuation; and it is confirmed because many concern the counts of Tusculum, Peter’s own kinsmen, concerning whom very similar material occurs in his catalogue of popes. [Note: [Col. 0477] Not yet published; see I, 61; II, 4, 27, 55, 60, 77, 99; III, 9, 17.]

There are also additions that betray the hand of an archivist: I, 59; II, 2, concerning the cell of Cinglensis, later taken away from the Cassinese; [Note: [Col. 0477] IV, 18, 70.] and concerning other possessions of the monastery, II, 26, 37, 52, 69. Nor are the additions concerning miracles at II, 59 and 80 foreign to Peter’s manner, so that we may attribute to his hand the other passages too in which manuscript 2 differs from the rest. We placed among the variant readings the minor matters and those which could with equal right be attributed either to Leo himself or to the scribe of the manuscript; to the rest we assigned their proper place between text and notes.

He wrote the continuation from the restoration of the church of Blessed Martin, [Note: [Col. 0477] Prologue to Book IV. He speaks in Leo’s person at III, 44 and IV, 70, although in Book IV he openly professes himself the author.] that is, from III, 34. In that chapter he altered and added so much that we judged it should be repeated at the beginning of his work. When, at Abbot Raynald’s command, he applied himself to writing, he says that he used the registers of the Roman pontiffs, Gregory VII and his successors, as well as the deeds of princes and dukes, which he sometimes excerpted and sometimes inserted as written; that he learned the rest from the accounts of Seniorectus and others; [Note: [Col. 0477] Albert, IV, 34; Carbo, IV, 55.] and that he saw much himself.

But I doubt whether he used Gregory VII’s register. He seems to have copied Victor’s register; of his use of Paschal II’s register there is certainty. [Note: [Col. 0477] IV, 35 ff.] After Urban II’s election, he has only a few items concerning him; of Innocent II and Anacletus, almost nothing except the case conducted before Lothair. He further copied the Cassinese annals, [Note: [Col. 0478] III, 36, 49, 50, 64; IV, 16, 18, 20, 79, 82, 97. Observe that Peter fell into the same error by which scribes, in copying the Anonymous Chronicle, were led to join the year-numbers of the following year with the events of the preceding year.] which were later transcribed into the Chronicle of the Anonymous writer; Amatus; [Note: [Col. 0478] III, 45.] Desiderius’s Dialogues; [Note: [Col. 0478] III, 38, 43, 51, 64. I think he took much from the lost Book IV.] Leo’s account of the dedication of the church; [Note: [Col. 0478] IV, 8–9.] the *History of the Holy War*; [Note: [Col. 0478] IV, 11.] Paul’s Life of Saint Gebizo; [Note: [Col. 0478] III, 48.] and the letters of Peter Damian. [Note: [Col. 0478] III, 38.]

What he took from these he generally copied word for word. Leo, on the other hand, created a new work from the accounts of various authors together with materials learned from elsewhere. Yet Peter differs from Leo much more in reliability, since he not only adduces donations and other privileges which we can scarcely accept as genuine, but is himself openly guilty of forgery. For at IV, 31, he inserts a letter of Bruno of Segni cobbled together from Peter Damian’s Opuscule 19; and, even if you insist this was done by Bruno himself, at IV, 42 he assigns to Bruno an oration composed out of Bruno’s own letters.

If you wish to excuse this as a practice formerly employed by many writers, in defending the monastery’s case before the emperor he invokes privileges never granted; from others which still survive he cites words which we seek in vain in them; and he either corrupts the very words of the canons or attributes them to false authors. Perhaps you might ascribe this to his carelessness, by which, for example, he repeatedly confuses Carloman with Charlemagne. But the other matter plainly proves him a forger. You see, therefore, how much caution is required in reading him.

For the rest, in the continuation which he carried down to the year 1138, he recounted the monastery’s fortunes fairly accurately, interspersing numerous miracle stories and some accounts of men distinguished for learning and intellect. Other events, however, he did not handle as Leo had, following the practice of briefly embracing the most important matters affecting Italy, especially southern Italy; rather, as though in blind impulse and entirely at random, he now narrates at excessive length and now suppresses in silence. Thus he did not touch even in a word events of the greatest importance that happened at Capua and Benevento. [Note: [Col. 0478] He describes at length the expedition of the crusaders until they reach Antioch, IV, 11; then, in three words, at chapter 16 he adds that Jerusalem was captured. See IV, 97 to observe how swiftly he passes from 1130 to 1136.]

A specimen of how little accuracy he showed in narrating individual matters is found at III, 70. He was quite unconcerned with chronological order, as the year-numbers enclosed in parentheses can tell at first glance. His style is careless and uneven, and not free from solecisms and other faults, although some should perhaps be charged to the copyist rather than Peter. When he comes to that disputation, he rises to a higher style, adorned with Virgilian flowers; but even these are so written as to reveal the traces of a hurried pen. It was his habit to begin little books, but only rarely to endure the labor of polishing them.

That he was nevertheless not wholly without literary skill is shown by the letters, [Col. 0479] composed with much greater care and not without grace. [Note: [Col. 0479] We must excuse the more inflated accumulation of clauses as the fashion of that age. In the letter to [Col. 0480] Conrad he takes much pleasure in mentioning the names and deeds of the ancient Romans.] Thus, although the Chronicle itself is of rather slight value, it should nonetheless be considered of no little usefulness, because it puts forward a number of facts about the popes, especially, and about Emperor Lothair, otherwise unknown and available for our use.

The sole manuscript of the Chronicle is preserved at Monte Cassino. We have already spoken of it above. After the unreliable earlier editions, it was published by Angelo de Nuce, whom we have followed, adding such notes as seemed necessary. We have not altered the manuscript’s spelling, except in a few instances that seemed alien to Peter’s practice. We have, however, restored in the appropriate places the diphthong which Peter is shown by manuscript 257 to have used, in place of simple *e*.

W. WATTENBACH.

**BEGINS** [Note: [Col. 0479] Thus manuscript 1, in red letters. In the edition: “Prologue to the Cassinese Chronicle.” It is lacking in manuscript 4.] **THE LETTER OF BROTHER LEO TO LORD ODERISIUS, VENERABLE AND MOST REVEREND FATHER OF THE MOST HOLY MONASTERY OF MONTE CASSINO.**

[Col. 0479]

To the lord and most holy father Oderisius, abbot of the venerable monastery of Monte Cassino, [Note: [Col. 0479] “O.” in manuscript 1.] Brother Leo, surnamed the Marsican, [Note: [Col. 0479] “Marsian” in manuscript 3.] the service of due obedience.

Long ago, most venerable Father, your blessedness had enjoined upon me that I should devote my labor to recording for the memory of posterity the splendid deeds of your glorious predecessor, Abbot Desiderius of holy memory, a man altogether singular and unique in his order in this age. [Note: [Col. 0479] “Your” in manuscript 4; “almost” in manuscript 1; “glorious and splendid” in manuscript 1; “in writing” added by manuscript 1, then deleted by the author; “to set down in writing” added by manuscript 1b.] You judged it wholly unworthy that you should imitate the indolence of the ancients of this place, who took almost no care to commit to writing the deeds or times of so many abbots; and if some happened to write anything about this, their works, composed in an altogether inept, rustic, [Note: [Col. 0479] “inept” in the edition; “and ragged” added in manuscript 1, but deleted by the author.] style, confer upon readers weariness rather than any knowledge.

Foreseeing most carefully that this should not happen to our Desiderius, your fatherhood resolved to appoint me to this work, [Note: [Col. 0479] “Your fatherhood” added by manuscript 1b; manuscript 1 first read: “it pleased the dignity of your command to assign me to this work”; “to this work” deleted, and “me” substituted by manuscript 1b.] imposing upon me a burden plainly beyond my strength. Overwhelmed by the mere thought of it, I feared to undertake it for almost a year. [Note: [Col. 0479] “Not without some disobedience” added in manuscript 1. Manuscript 4: *timuerint*, “they feared,” for *timuerim*, “I feared.” “And indeed, according to the Rule, I accepted the command of the one enjoining what had seemed impossible to me, without any contradiction, though not with any promise”; the words abbreviated “not … promise” are struck out. “But because (indeed, however, manuscript 1b) I did not humbly and patiently set forth to your fatherhood the reason for my inability, I confess that I acted negligently and foolishly” (“I confess” for “I acknowledge that I acted,” manuscript 1b). “Recently,” manuscript 1.]

Recently, therefore, as I was accompanying you on my official duty when you were returning from Capua, [Note: [Col. 0479] Omitted in manuscript 4.] you recalled, while walking, your own excellent command and asked whether I had fulfilled your wish concerning the writing of Desiderius’s deeds. [Note: [Col. 0479] “I was accompanying you” in manuscript 1; “your own command” in manuscript 1; manuscript 4 has *scribentis*, “of one writing,” for *scribendis*, “to be written”; errors of this kind are not always noted below.] Surprised by this sudden question, I was compelled to answer what was true: that I had done absolutely nothing about it. [Note: [Col. 0479] Manuscript 1: “Therefore I answered modestly and reverently: nothing.”] Then, recovering a little composure, I said: “And when could I have obeyed this command of yours, [Note: [Col. 0479] Omitted in manuscript 4; in manuscript 1b, “I said”; manuscript 1 has “when I could satisfy this command”; *parere*, ‘obey,’ written above by manuscript 1b.] when, throughout almost this entire year, occupied in the service of the apostolic lord by your command through the Maritime region and Campania, and also in the various affairs of your own self, I scarcely remained in the monastery for eight continuous days? For this work requires no small leisure, and so great a subject is not for someone occupied, but rather for one free from every care.” [Note: [Col. 0479] Manuscript 1: “by your command through the Maritime region and Campania; then …”; manuscript 4: “when”; manuscript 1: “rather for one at leisure and free from cares.”]

Having patiently accepted this reasonable explanation, and rebuking me for negligence with a very restrained reprimand, you said: “Now, then, seize the leisure you desire, and do not wish any longer to weave delays into writing about Desiderius. Indeed, I also wish and command that, since this matter has been postponed until this day, you begin your account with Father Benedict himself and, as a most diligent investigator, inquire into the succession, times, and deeds, from whatever sources, of all the abbots of our place down to Desiderius himself. [Note: [Col. 0479] “Reasonable” in manuscript 1, which he struck out; “to this day” in manuscript 1, “to the present day” in the edition; “B.” in manuscript 1; “that same” in manuscript 1; “the very same” in manuscript 1; added by manuscript 1b.] Scrupulously investigate what possessions or churches seem to have accrued to our monastery under each abbot, from whom, and in what manner; investigate as well the enactments of emperors, dukes, and princes, and the documents of all other faithful persons; and compose, in the manner of a chronicle, a history not a little useful to us and to those who succeed us. [Col. 0481] [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 4: *accesserunt*, “accrued”; “or churches” added by manuscript 1b; “and enactments of other faithful persons” added by manuscript 1b; manuscript 1 has *historiolam*, “a little history”; “compose” in manuscript 1.]

“Further, do not hesitate to append in their proper places, at least briefly, both the destruction and restoration of this monastery, accomplished on two different occasions, and whatever memorable matters may meanwhile occur concerning the works or deeds of illustrious men of these regions alone.” [Note: [Col. 0481] “Both—and also” added by manuscript 1b; omitted in manuscript 1; “of these regions” added by manuscript 1b; “connect” in manuscript 4.]

After I began to consider more carefully the weight of this command, [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1 originally: “Although before carefully considering this command I did not doubt that it was very burdensome for my smallness—even at the mere hearing of it—I nevertheless accepted it with assent; but after I began [to consider] the magnitude of the same command carefully …” This was altered by manuscript 1b. Manuscript 4: “The weight of this command …”; “in” added by manuscript 1b, 16.] thickets of many thoughts began to grow up around me on every side. Being unable easily, because of my poverty of understanding, to perceive from where or how I could accomplish it diligently, [Note: [Col. 0481] “cares” in manuscript 1; “irreproachably” in manuscript 1, changed by manuscript 1b to *naviter*, “diligently”; manuscripts 2 and 3: *gnaviter*, likewise “diligently”; manuscript 4: “through”; manuscript 1: “of my little talent,” corrected by manuscript 1b.] I did not know whether to choose to undertake or to refuse so great a work. [Note: [Col. 0481] The edition reads: “whether again, whether otherwise”; manuscript 1 first read: “then once more and again I began to ponder these same things with a mind in turmoil. Then for the first time I began more clearly to see the impossibility arising from my ignorance”; manuscript 1b altered this.] For rashness pricked me if I undertook it, disobedience if I refused.

Moreover, I remembered that my aforesaid lord Desiderius of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “I remembered the aforesaid lord of holy memory”; manuscript 1b: “I remembered my former lord”; manuscript 1c: “I remembered my lord.”] had formerly imposed this very task on Archbishop Alfanus of Salerno, a man most wise in our times; [Note: [Col. 0481] “Most wise and prudent” in manuscript 1, corrected by manuscript 1b.] but that he, perceiving the subject’s great laboriousness, had withdrawn himself from such a danger. [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “but he, on account of the magnitude of the matter, had withdrawn himself from the labor.”] If one who then possessed incomparable learning and eloquence guarded against subjecting himself to this burden, what was I to do, in whom there was neither any learning nor any eloquence whatsoever?

Again, my conscience troubled me as to why this work had not been entrusted by you to some other of our brethren, who were far more learned than I and more experienced in the practice of composition. [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “from the many brethren of our monastery, unquestionably much more learned than I and more expert in the practice of composition, whom …”] Your holy predecessor had either gathered them into this place from diverse regions of the world or most diligently caused them to be educated in this very monastery. [Note: [Col. 0481] “This place” in manuscript 1 and the edition; manuscript 1 continues: “and whom I could even name here individually, if I did not fear to offend the humility of those who despise human favor”; this clause was deleted by manuscript 1b.]

Tossed by these and such thoughts, I was in turmoil, [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “anxious and tossed about; I did not sufficiently see what I should do.”] because this matter was both too lofty to be reached by me and certainly too obscure to be investigated by me. [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1c: “because”; manuscript 1b: “because, beyond the fact that it exceeded my strength as a double burden, and moreover because of devotion …”] Yet because of the singular devotion which I had long borne toward your fatherhood, [Note: [Col. 0481] “toward” added by manuscript 1b.] I had long ago resolved never to refuse you anything. [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “never ever,” corrected by manuscript 1b; “not to obey,” corrected by manuscript 1b to “to refuse.”] At last, therefore, I made up my mind. [Note: [Col. 0481] “Therefore, [I made up] my mind,” manuscript 1, corrected by manuscript 1b.] Though previously faint-hearted I had feared to undertake the deeds of Desiderius alone, [Note: [Col. 0481] “I was exceedingly afraid,” manuscript 1, corrected by manuscript 1b.] I subsequently undertook to write, in whatever fashion possible, the deeds of all his predecessors, [Note: [Col. 0481] Omitted in manuscript 4.] trusting in God’s help and judging that this was altogether expedient for me. [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “ready for your obedience.”]

Accordingly, when I had found those little writings which seemed to have been written, although briefly, on this same subject in a ragged style, [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “I had found material scattered here and there, composed in a wholly unpolished and contemptible style; I added to this little work certain lines, though fragile.” Manuscript 1b: “I had found material scattered here and there; and especially …”] and especially the chronicle of Abbot John, who was the first to build our monastery at New Capua; and when I had also employed books necessary for this work—namely, the history of the Lombards and chronicles of the Roman emperors and pontiffs—and had diligently investigated privileges, enactments, and grants, and written documents of various names, namely those of Roman pontiffs, various emperors, kings, princes, dukes, counts, and other distinguished and faithful men, [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “and after examining donations, privileges, and grants”; manuscript 1b: “and after diligently examining donations, privileges, and grants, and writings of various—or rather, of various kinds—which seem to have come down …”; manuscript 1c: “after examining privileges and grants of various names, namely …”] insofar as these seem to remain to us after the two burnings of this monastery—[Note: [Col. 0481] See below I, 44, 48.] although I was unable to gain access even to all of those in their entirety—[Note: [Col. 0481] “in their entirety” added by manuscript 1c.] and finally, after carefully questioning those who had happened either to hear or to see closely the deeds of abbots of modern times: I undertake, according to the slender capacity of my little talent, to carry out what you commanded. [Note: [Col. 0481] “Having undertaken [it], with the Lord’s help,” manuscript 1 and the edition.] I do so relying more upon the obedience which I owe to you as father and lord than upon any learning—which I do not possess. [Note: [Col. 0481] “which I do not possess” added in manuscript 1, then deleted by manuscript 1b.]

May God and the grace of his Spirit be with me, [Note: [Col. 0481] “May [he] be with [me],” manuscript 4.] so that I may accomplish this as effectively as you have earnestly deigned to command me; [Note: [Col. 0481] Manuscript 1: “for I gladly desire to obey you in this matter”; manuscript 1b: “because you yourself have been zealous to command me.”] so that this little work may be most pleasing to you and useful to many. I have thought it necessary to set down these things briefly beforehand, as in a little preface, to protect myself, lest perhaps those who do not know the circumstances accuse me of rashness or presumption; [Note: [Col. 0481] “These things—excuse” added by manuscript 1b; manuscript 4: “necessities”; manuscript 4 adds “or presumption”; manuscript 1b: “be marked,” corrected to “be accused.”] so that, even if incompetence accuses me, the authority of the one who commanded may excuse me. [Note: [Col. 0481] Thus manuscript 1c; manuscript 1b: “even if my incompetence … [lacuna].”]

[Col. 0483]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “There will be,” added in 1c.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “as it were for readers’ relief,” written above the line in 1c.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “the abbots of this monastery,” written above the line in 1c.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “divinely,” written above the line in 1c.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] *bertario*, 1c.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] *perducata*, 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “moreover,” written above the line in 1c.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] 1c added “both at Teano and at Capua,” but immediately erased it.]

In three divisions, moreover, as it were for the relief of readers, I have resolved to divide this little book: because it has been granted chiefly to three abbots of this monastery, after blessed Benedict, to have laboured more than the others in restoring this place; and therefore perhaps it was granted them by divine providence to have lived longer than the rest in this office of governance. Having set blessed father Benedict, together with the four who followed him, as it were in a preface, I shall begin the first portion with Petronax, who, about one hundred and ten years after the Lombards’ destruction, began to restore this place. I shall carry it in due order down to the second destruction, which was wrought by the Saracens under Bertharius, and shall further append those events which were accomplished during the sixty-seven years when this place was deserted, by the seven abbots residing at Teano and Capua. The second part will begin for me with Aligernus, who devoted himself most zealously not only to the restoration of this monastery but also to the reconciliation of this whole land, which through the Saracens’ ravaging had been left without cultivators. When this section has thus been extended down to our Desiderius, and the deeds of those who presided over this monastery during that period have consequently been appended, Desiderius himself will be both the beginning and the end of the whole third part. He, inferior neither to Petronax nor to Aligernus—indeed, in my judgment, far superior—built anew for the Lord, as another Solomon in our times, a magnificent and most beautiful monastery, new and most precious, as it were a temple.

[Note: [Col. 0483] 1c reads, after Aligernus: “who, as though another Petronax appointed here from heaven, not only …”; *istius* (“of this”) is absent in 1c; in manuscript 1 the text from *in* to *studuit* is cut away.] 

[Note: [Col. 0483] 1c has “labour and effort” for “deeds”; it further reads: “especially those of Abbot Richerius, as though another David, with peace prepared, as though for every expenditure, for the construction of the new temple, himself …”] 

[Note: [Col. 0483] *despoerius*, 4; *terre*, 4; “new,” 1c; *spatiosissimum* (“most spacious”), 3.]

But if it pleases you to add a fourth portion to these three, with you helping and the Lord’s help, its beginning shall come from you.

[Note: [Col. 0483] “if it delights you,” 1c; the manuscript first had *si … iuvat* (“if it pleases you”) and corrected it in the same ink.]

Furthermore, I make this one request of both your fatherhood and the reader of this little work: that he deign to attend not to the writer’s lack of skill, but to its most useful subject matter.

[Note: [Col. 0483] “your,” 1; “your fatherhood,” 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “my reader,” 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “I should wish it to be requested,” 1; *expostulem*, “I entreat,” the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “in it,” 4.]

For just as, if an unskilled craftsman should fashion an imperial diadem from the purest gold and precious gems, although the work itself may seem improperly formed because of the craftsman’s lack of skill, it can nevertheless be valuable, both because of the precious material and because of the dignity of the very name; so too this little work, although because of the mediocrity of its style it may appear wholly contemptible, ought not to be considered unwelcome by anyone, because of the many useful matters which it contains.

[Note: [Col. 0483] *imperitiam*, “incompetence,” 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] *materiam*, 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “glorious,” 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “and precious gems,” 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “base,” 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “inactivity,” 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] 1c reads: “although it may appear altogether contemptible because of my ignorance, yet because of the most glorious deeds of glorious men …”; 1b originally read “despicable” and added “may appear,” but immediately deleted it.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “inactivity,” 1c and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] 1c: “not to be considered pleasing by someone”; 1 and 1b: “not to be considered unwelcome by someone.”]

For although I shall set forth, according to the measure of my knowledge, what must be said less elegantly but simply and faithfully, these things ought neither to be unwelcome to the learned, if envy is absent, nor to seem too profound for the less learned to understand.

[Note: [Col. 0483] “indeed,” added by 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “truly,” 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “yet those things,” 1, corrected in 1b.]

Yet I am confident that, even if not everyone, at least many will find this little history of ours pleasing; for in our own time, although one can scarcely find anyone willing to write something of this sort, many nevertheless may be found who delight either in hearing or in reading narratives of this kind.

[Note: [Col. 0483] “written above,” 1; “or,” 1b; “and if perhaps,” added by 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] In 1b, *gloriosa* (“glorious”) stands for *gloriosissima* (“most glorious”) in the phrase “the most glorious deeds of glorious men.”]

**The epistle ends.**

[Note: [Col. 0483] Thus manuscript 1; “Preface,” the edition; “Epistle containing the manner of a preface,” 4.]
