## HERE BEGINS THE CHRONICLE OF THE MONASTERY OF MONTE CASSINO

[Note: [Col. 0489] Thus manuscript 1. “Book one of the history of this monastery begins,” C and the edition.]

[Col. 0489]

[Col. 0489A] **I.** [GREGORY, *Dialogues* II, prologue and chapters 1, 3.]

Therefore the outstanding and most holy father Benedict, Benedict both by grace and by name, the first founder of this monastery of Monte Cassino, was, as blessed Pope Gregory writes fully in the second book of his *Dialogues*, a native of the province of Nursia.

[Note: [Col. 0489] “A native of Nursia,” absent in 4.]

At Rome his parents entrusted him to be educated in the liberal arts; but not long afterwards, to use the words of the aforesaid teacher, he departed knowingly unknowing and wisely unlearned.

Thus abandoning his literary studies and his nurse, he secretly fled to the place called Sublacus [Subiaco], almost forty miles distant from the City. There, in a certain cave, he remained for three years, known to no one except blessed Romanus, who had put on the habit of that holy way of life.

After this, discovered by shepherds and at last recognized by many, he was also visited frequently by nobles of the city of Rome. From Equitius he received twelve-year-old Maurus, and from the patrician Tertullus the still boyish Placidus, to be trained in monastic discipline. There too, with Christ’s help, he built twelve monasteries and assigned twelve monks to each, under appointed fathers.

[PAUL THE DEACON, *History of the Lombards* I.26.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] “Priest” is absent in manuscript 1.]

Then, yielding the place because of the persecution of the priest Florentius, he took a few brothers with him; and, accompanied by two angels and followed by three ravens that he used to feed, he arrived at this place at Christ’s command, after a journey of about fifty miles.

[Note: [Col. 0489] The words “whose … tradition” are absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0489B] Or from the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*, where the same words occur, in Tosti, *History of Monte Cassino* I, p. 129.]

Tradition relates that the celebrated Varro of so many centuries ago—the wisest of all Romans, in Cicero’s testimony—was founder of this seat.

[GREGORY, *Dialogues* II.8.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] “Anciently,” added in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] “In which,” 1.]

Here Benedict shattered the idol of Apollo, which had anciently been worshipped there by country people; he overthrew its altar, cut down its sacred grove, and built a monastery for himself. By continual preaching he converted the surrounding peoples to faith in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0489] “There also” is absent in 1; “shone forth” was added by 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0490B] Compare Cicero, *Philippics* 2.40; Varro, *On Agriculture* 3.5. Leo added these words on his own account.]

As for the many and various miracles with which he shone there, since these do not belong to the present work, anyone wishing to know of them will find them eloquently written in the aforementioned book of blessed Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 0489] “Which he had built,” 1 and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] “Added,” 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] “As many and of such kinds,” absent in 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] “Shone forth,” added in 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] “And there,” absent in 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] *construxerat*, “had built,” 1 and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0489] *esset*, “had been,” 1.]

[Life of Saint Maurus 4.]

Among these events, when one day it had been divinely revealed to him that the monastery which he had founded was to be destroyed by nations, and he therefore wept inconsolably, he was immediately comforted by a heavenly oracle. He heard that, through his merits nevertheless, the same place would attain a condition better and more extensive than it then possessed, and that from it the order of the Rule and discipline would spread into many regions of the Roman world.

[Note: [Col. 0489] 1b reads: “and that from there the order and norm of regular discipline would proceed and be spread through many different regions of the world.”]

[Note: [Col. 0489] *profecturum*, “would proceed,” 1 and the edition.]

[Life of Saint Maurus 26.]

In the very year in which he was about to depart from this life to Christ, he was asked to send his disciples into Gaul to establish a monastery. Although he was not unaware of the end of his days, he did not delay, but sent blessed Maurus there with the same envoys. With him he also took care to send blessed Faustus, who afterwards wrote his history in full, and three others.

[Note: [Col. 0489] Manuscript 1 omits the following passage. Manuscript 1b instead reads: “From this [the order] was disseminated, established, and observed throughout all Gaul, God permitting. About the same days …”]

Hence it came about that through this most holy man of God, Maurus, and his disciples, the whole order and norm of regular discipline which had been established in this place by the most blessed father Benedict was disseminated and spread throughout all Gaul.

It is believed that the man of God Benedict then also sent blessed Placidus to Sicily, where Placidus’s father, the patrician Tertullus, had granted eighteen estates of his patrimony to that man of God.

[Note: [Col. 0491] 1 reads “Placidus already [sent] to Sicily”; 1b, “Saint Benedict had already [sent] Placidus to Sicily”; 2, “the man of God Benedict then [sent] his disciple Placidus to Sicily.” Manuscript 1 breaks off after “he took care to send … blessed P[lacidus].”]

[Note: [Col. 0491] “On 3 October, in Sicily, the feast of Saint Placidus, most blessed martyr, with his companions Eutychius, Victorinus, and thirty others. For him his father, the patrician Tertullus, offered eighteen estates of his patrimony to the most blessed father Benedict.” *Martyrology* composed by command of Abbot Desiderius, in Gattola, *History*, p. 915.]

[Life of Saint Maurus 32; GREGORY, *Dialogues* II.37.]

Afterwards, when this holy man had commendably completed the course of his time, on the day when the Saturday of the most holy Easter was dawning—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—he ordered his disciples to carry him into the oratory of Saint John the Baptist. Praying in their hands, he departed to the Lord, in the year 542 of His incarnation, in the fifth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 2 has “in the year 543 of His incarnation, in the second indiction”; manuscript 3 has “in the year 542 of His incarnation, in the fifth indiction”; manuscript 1 omits the date.]

[Note: [Col. 0491B] “A.D. 542, indiction V,” was not taken from Gregory, but added by the author himself. Whether he calculated it or derived it from a source now unknown to us, I do not know. Certainly Justinian’s fourteenth year is A.D. 541; and the year 509 cannot in any way be accepted, whereas the former alone accords with the day recorded, perhaps from an interpolation by Odo in the *Life of Blessed Maurus*. If the account of Benedict’s meeting with Totila is to be trusted, Peter the Deacon may be correct, but the indiction must be corrected. I myself would suppose that Faustus assigned Benedict’s death to the vigil of the first Easter, which Odo misunderstood and thereby caused such great difficulties for later writers. For if Benedict had truly died on Holy Saturday, I do not think blessed Gregory would have passed this over in silence. Below, 3.73, Peter calculates seventy-three years from the death of blessed Benedict beginning with the year 509.]

He was buried in the same oratory, before the very altar which he had constructed after destroying the altar of Apollo, where he had already placed his blessed sister Scholastica.

[Note: [Col. 0491] At the erased place, several words had previously been written in 1b.]

He flourished in the times of the emperors Justin the Elder and Justinian, and of the Roman pontiffs John I and Felix IV, whom Saint Pope Gregory testifies was his great-grandfather; Theodoric the Arian was reigning in Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0491] 1 adds: “that is, in the fourteenth year of that emperor’s reign, and in the five hundred and ninth year from the Lord’s Passion, according to a most careful calculation he died.”]

[Note: [Col. 0492B] *Dialogues* 4.16, but “the third”; John the Deacon had already called him “the fourth” in *Life of Blessed Gregory* 1. ANG.]

[Note: [Col. 0492B] Compare the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*, *Scriptores* III, p. 200.]

**2.** [GREGORY, *Dialogues* II, prologue; PAUL THE DEACON, *History of the Lombards* IV.17; II.4, 7; IV.17; GREGORY, *Dialogues* II.17.]

This most holy father was succeeded in the government of the monastery by the most reverend man Constantine, a disciple of the same holy father. The third to preside over the same community was Simplicius; the fourth, Vitalis; and the fifth, Bonitus.

[Note: [Col. 0491] 1 and the edition read “after blessed Benedict presided”; the edition reads *ejusdem* (“of the same one”) for “the same.”]

While he presided, the Lombards, who had recently invaded Italy under Justin the Younger, entered the aforesaid monastery by night, when the brothers were asleep, as the cycle of 568 years from the Lord’s incarnation was turning. They plundered everything, but could not seize even one person there, so that the saying of the holy father Benedict might be fulfilled, which he had spoken to Theopropus:

[Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript 1 first added, then 1b deleted, “after Justinian, whom we mentioned above, was reigning”; the edition reads *deripientes* for *diripientes* (“plundering”).] “I could scarcely obtain that souls should be yielded to me from this place.”

[Note: [Col. 0491] “To me, that souls should be yielded from this place,” 1 and the edition.]

Thus the brothers fled from that monastery and went to Rome, carrying with them the codex of the holy Rule which the same father had written, certain other writings, a weight of bread, a measure of wine, and whatever household goods they could snatch away.

[Note: [Col. 0491] “With them,” added in 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0491] “Which the blessed Benedict had written,” 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0491] “Containing one pound by the loaf,” added in 1b and deleted in 1c.]

[Note: [Col. 0491] *suppellectilis*, corrected in 1b from *suppellex*.]

By permission of Pelagius, bishop of Rome, who then presided over the Apostolic See, they established a monastery beside the Lateran patriarchate.

[Note: [Col. 0492B] “Our author added this.”]

[Note: [Col. 0491] “And when they had been gratefully received by blessed Gregory, who at that time presided over the Apostolic See, by his permission they established nearby,” added in 1 and deleted in 1b.]

There they dwelt for approximately one hundred and ten years while the monastery of Monte Cassino remained destroyed.

[Note: [Col. 0491] *ferme* (“approximately”) is absent in manuscript 3; manuscript 4 reads *habitaculum* (“dwelling”) for *habitaverunt* (“they dwelt”).]

[Note: [Col. 0492B] “One hundred and thirty years,” manuscript 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0492B] Paul the Deacon, 6.40, has 110 years; Peter, in *Register* no. 86, 120; here and below, 4.89, he uses the more correct calculation of 130. ANG. Di Meo seeks to prove in the *Neapolitan Annals* that the destruction occurred in 577. In any case, one sees how little care Leo took in calculating dates, since, after correcting the pope’s name, he left the number of years unchanged. Yet at the beginning of the following chapter he removed the year of the Lord’s incarnation, evidently lest the conflicting figures confront the reader. For, by his own testimony, the restoration of the monastery of Monte Cassino took place in A.D. 720.]

**3.** [Life of Saint Maurus 5.]

Thirdly, meanwhile, while the aforesaid Boniface was governing the Apostolic See, the aforementioned Faustus, who had gone to Gaul with blessed Maurus, returned to the aforesaid Lateran monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0491] “Because the monastery of Monte Cassino had already been destroyed by the Lombards,” added in 1; 4 reads *Fausto* for *Mauro*; 1 and the edition read *praedictum* (“aforesaid”) for *praenominatum* (“previously named”).] There, compelled and requested by blessed Theodore—*Tehodoro* in 3—who was then the third to govern the same community after Valentinian of holy memory, the first abbot of that place, he composed a most truthful history of the life of blessed Maurus. The aforesaid Pope Boniface approved it, judged it worthy of praise, and confirmed it by his authority.

[Note: [Col. 0491] “Therefore, in the year 605 of the Lord’s incarnation, the second year of Phocas’s reign, when blessed Pope Gregory had died, Sabinian received the Roman pontificate. After he died a year and five months later, Boniface III acquired the Apostolic See, under whom the aforesaid …,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0492B] Leo added the number.]

4. [Paul the Deacon VI.40; Chronicle of Vulturno.] But when almighty God had determined, by His mercy, to restore the aforesaid monastery of blessed Benedict, and to spread throughout the world from the place of that same father the cenobitic institution which had taken its beginning there, it happened, by God’s ordering, that Petronax, a citizen of the city of Brescia and a man of great religious devotion, came to Rome, inspired by divine love. The most reverend Pope Gregory III, divinely inspired, urged him to seek this fortress of Cassino and to strive by his own efforts to restore the monastery of blessed Benedict, which had remained destroyed for so many years. When he consented, that venerable pontiff immediately sent with him several brethren from the Lateran community and also bestowed upon him various other aids.

Thus, arriving here at the sacred body of blessed Benedict, he began in the year of the Lord 720 to dwell both with those who had come with him and with several simple men whom he found had long been living there. Raised to the abbacy by those same brethren, he strove, with God’s help and through the interceding merits of blessed Benedict, to live under the teaching of the holy Rule, having suitably constructed dwellings and established there a community of many brethren.

Three noble men of Benevento—Paldo, Taso, and Tato, brothers—who about fifteen years earlier had begun, at their own expense, to build the monastery of Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ, near the source of the river Vulturnus, were powerful and wealthy; and both personally and through their dependents they gave very great assistance in this work until the restoration of this place.

In the church of blessed Martin, which he found small, he enlarged it by about sixteen cubits. There he made an apse and established an altar in honour of blessed Mary ever-Virgin and of the holy martyrs Faustinus and Jovita; in it he suitably deposited also the arm of one of those saints which he had brought with him from Brescia.

In the following period the most holy Pope Zacharias, who had succeeded Gregory, bestowed many aids upon him: several books of Holy Scripture; likewise a copy of the holy Rule which Father Benedict had written with his own hand; also the weight of a pound of bread and the measure of wine, which, as we said above, the monks fleeing during the Lombard invasion had once carried with them from there to Rome. With apostolic liberality he also granted him various ornaments for ecclesiastical service and several other things pertaining to the monastery’s various needs.

From this same most holy pope the aforesaid abbot was the first to receive a privilege that this monastery, together with all the cells belonging to it, wherever they might be built, should, in honour and reverence of the most holy Father Benedict, be wholly free from the jurisdiction of all bishops, and subject to the jurisdiction of no one except the Roman pontiff alone.

[Note: Col. 0493.] “Meanwhile, after some years had passed, namely in the time of Pope John VI, Gisulf the Elder, duke of Benevento, came into Campania with a strong force of his men and captured alike the fortress of Arpinum and Sora, a Roman city. Causing great burnings and devastations and carrying off certain captives, with no one able to resist him, he came as far as the place called Horrea and there pitched his camp. Pope John sent several priests to him with apostolic gifts, redeemed all the captives whom he had taken, and caused him with his whole army to return to his own country.” (From the Chronicle of Saint Benedict.)

“After some intervening years had passed, when, that is, the year 703 from the Lord’s Incarnation was already turning, Constantine, a most gentle and angelic pope, presiding over the Roman see, while Justinian the Younger ruled as emperor together with his son Tiberius, the monastery of Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ, began to be built near the source of the river Vulturnus by three noble brothers, citizens of Benevento—namely Paldo, Taso, and Tato, kinsmen of Gisulf, duke of Benevento. Of these Paldo himself became the first abbot there.” This 1b adds. The fact that many words were erased and deleted indicates that alterations were made after the foregoing material had been deleted; finally he deleted everything together.

[Note: Col. 0493C.] “Indeed, the fourth [Gregory]. Moreover, the autograph manuscript shows that Leo, having first drawn material from Paul the Deacon alone, subsequently worked it out more carefully after consulting the monuments of the people of Vulturno themselves. But he expressed the year in a rounded number, as they say; according to Leo’s own calculation it is 718. The year 720 is also found in the *Liber Pontificalis*, in Stephen Borgia, *Del dominio temporale*, p. 4. The monastery of Saint Vincent was founded in A.D. 702, when, according to the custom of that time, the year 703 was already being counted.”

[Note: Col. 0494C.] “He drew ‘Here … deposited’ from a source unknown to us, as he did many similar details reported under each abbot.”

[Note: Col. 0494C.] “Peter the priest mentions the privilege in the *Chronicle of Vulturno*. Tosti, *History of Cassino*, I, p. 82, reissued this spurious offspring of a later age, already rejected by Baronius. It is now found in the Register of Peter the Deacon.”

5. [Paul the Deacon VI.58; Chronicle of Saint Benedict.] Moreover Gisulf the Younger, nephew of Liutprand, king of the Lombards, who became duke of the Beneventans after Gotscalc, was travelling toward Rome in those days with a great army assembled. As he passed through this fortress of Cassino, then called Mello, he ascended with many others; and, finding the aforesaid brethren who then lived there to be living with considerable religious devotion in God’s service beside the body of the most holy Father Benedict, he was immediately touched by divine inspiration. He granted in writing to that same Father Benedict all the surrounding lands, both plains and mountains, and by secure deeds of gift bestowed them upon posterity to possess forever.

That is, within the following boundaries and limits:

As the boundary begins from the river called Carnellus, it ascends along the water called Bautra as far as Rivus Siccus; and as it ascends through that stream as far as the fork of Saint Martin; and there it rises through the mountain ridges and goes to the mountain called Cisinus; and thence proceeds to the rock called Corvarum; and goes through those ridges to the fork called Popplu; and thence proceeds to the lake called Vitecusus; and thence goes to Aqua Fundata; and rises to the mountain called de Sile; and thence goes to the headwaters of Rapido; and then rises to the mountain called Caballus; and proceeds to the mountain called Greater Rendenaria; and thence through the mountain ridges comes to Lesser Rendenaria; and thence goes directly along the feet of the mountains called Freselona; and proceeds to the waters of Mellarino; and descends along that water, with both banks, and goes to the Walls of Balnearia; and thence goes through the place called Anglone; and ascends to the fork of Valleluci; and goes through those mountain ridges and descends to the Written Rock; and thence ascends to the ridges of the mountain called Orticosa; and goes through the mountain ridges and arrives at the rocks called Falconari; and goes through two mountains, one called Spinacius and the other Porcacius; and thence goes to the crests of the mountain called Caria; and, descending, comes to the rocks above the water Vivola; and thence rises to the hill of Gimberutus; and descends into Quercetulum; and thence to the ditch beside Saint Damasus, whom the common people call Saint Amasus; thence it goes directly to Silix, at the place called the Arch of Aezzulus; and goes to the lake called Radeprand’s; and thence proceeds to the oak-grove (*Farnietum*); and thence to the stream called Marozza; and descends to the river Carnellus itself; and by that same river rises to the water called Cosa; thence through the ridges of Mount Saint Donatus; thence, descending over the little hills of Marri, it goes to the rocks at the foot of the mountain called Balva; thence through the Two Lions; and then, proceeding, rises through the ridges of the mountain above Casale; and descends along that mountain as far as the villages of Garigliano; thence to the rock called the Emperor’s Crypt; and thence proceeds to the already-mentioned river Garigliano; and ascends by that river as far as the earlier boundaries—together with all castles, villages, houses, churches, mills, waters, and all other things which at that time were held within the aforesaid boundaries. (Chronicle of Saint Benedict.)

[Note: Col. 0495C.] “I believe this is Leo’s conjecture. The *Chronicle of Saint Benedict* confuses this Gisulf with the elder one.”

[Note: Col. 0495C.] “Leo added this, apparently without using the charter itself, which is now missing from Peter’s Register; rather, he used confirmations by princes and kings that enumerate the same boundaries. The forger of Zacharias’s privilege, however, copied the words from this passage and used an edition of the *Chronicle* such as we give from manuscript 4.”

[Note: Col. 0495C.] “Compare the map of the Cassinese dominion in Gattula.”

[Note: Col. 0495C.] “The Liris, nearer its source, was called Carnellus; after being enlarged by the Rapido, it was called Garigliano. See Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 753 ff.”

[Note: Col. 0496C.] “Commonly Pecia. Gattula.”

[Note: Col. 0496C.] “The higher parts of mountains; hence Spanish *sierra*.”

[Note: Col. 0496C.] “A cliff, rock, or place situated on a rock; today *pesco*, according to Giustiniani in the *Dictionary of Neapolitan Geography*.”

[Note: Col. 0496C.] “This is now called Clarus, distinct from the other Rapido which rises above the Castle of Saint Elias. Gattula.”

[Note: Col. 0496C.] “Mount Cairo. Gattula.”

[Note: Col. 0496C.] “Later Famara. Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 121.”

[Note: Col. 0496C.] “See below, III.12.”

[Note: Col. 0495.] After “then held within the aforesaid boundaries,” 1b adds: “When these things had thus been granted and secured by the aforesaid duke to the blessed Father Benedict by lawful donation, he reserved for himself only the borderlands, for protection of the inhabitants against enemy raids; yet he ordered the inhabitants, both in seedtime and harvest-time, to obey the monks in supplying labour.” [From the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*.] “The same Gisulf also issued for this abbot a precept concerning the monastery of Saint Mary in Cingla, with all its appurtenances, and subjected it to this Cassinese monastery.” The second hand adds: “He also made a very liberal grant to blessed Benedict of the territory of Gentiana.” Afterwards he deleted the whole passage.

The wife of the same duke, named Scauniperga, converted a temple of idols that had anciently been built in the fortress of Cassino into a church in honour of the apostle blessed Peter, and with most devout remembrance for posterity bestowed there icons and the other furnishings appropriate to the services of a church.

[Note: Col. 0497C.] “From this Cassino itself the place was later called Saint Peter in the Monastery.”

6. [Note: Col. 0497C.] “From Gisulf’s charters in Gattula, *Historia*, p. 27, given at Alife in August, indiction II, and another at Benevento in October, indiction XIV.”

In the time of this duke, a Beneventan *sculdais*—that is, a local Lombard official—named Saracenus built from the ground up, in the place called Cingla in the territory of Alife, a church in honour of Saint Cassian. With the permission of the aforesaid duke, he granted it to the monastery of blessed Benedict, together with everything he was able to acquire there, and likewise his whole property and inheritance in its entirety, excepting all slaves, male and female, whom he had freed, because he had no son (A.D. 743, August).

When the place appeared very useful to the venerable Petronax, with the consent and very great assistance of the same glorious Duke Gisulf and his wife Scauniperga, he built there a monastery of maidservants of God in honour of blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin. The aforesaid duke further granted there the church of Holy Cross with all its territories and appurtenances (A.D. 745, October), which our provost Giselpert had bought from an abbot named Deusdedit, with the counsel and assistance of the same duke; and also several other churches and estates in the vicinity, as the records of that monastery show.

The aforesaid duke Gisulf, with the consent of the aforesaid abbot, then granted that monastery of the holy Mother of God to three maidservants of God (A.D. 747, May): namely, the abbess Gausana, Pancrituda, and Gariperga. Having left behind parents and all their possessions, they had chosen to live as pilgrims for God in these regions. This arrangement was confirmed on the condition that, as long as any one of them survived, each in turn after another should hold the governance of that place by undisputed and peaceful right; but after their deaths both authority and administration of the same place should return to the jurisdiction of our monastery.

At the same time the aforesaid duke made a very liberal grant from the territory of Gentiana to the Cassinese monastery.

[Erchempert 3.9.] Gisulf began to build the church of Saint Sophia at Benevento; but, prevented by death, he could not complete it. Arichis, who succeeded him, completed it magnificently; and, establishing there a community of nuns, he granted it to the monastery of blessed Benedict here at Cassino, as we shall show below.

[Note: Col. 0498C.] “These matters are not found thus in Erchempert’s manuscript; yet Leo himself testifies that he drew them from there. See Gattula, *Historia*, p. 54.”

7. [Chronicle of Salerno I.31, 32, 33, 5.] At the same time (747), Charles the Great, son of Charles king of the Franks, out of love for the heavenly kingdom abandoned his earthly kingdom and came devoutly to Rome, to the blessed apostle Peter. He bound himself to the service of that apostle.

Pope Zacharias ordained him a cleric; after a few days he sent him here to our monastery, to serve the Lord with the others under the discipline of the Rule, together with all his wealth. There, under the governance of the aforesaid abbot, he served the Lord with every humility and devotion for several years.

It does not seem pointless to commit briefly to writing, as an example for posterity, how great was this king’s humility in the monastery and how great his obedience. The aforesaid abbot, seeing Charles’s fervent purpose and wishing to test his steadfastness and endurance according to the tenor of the Rule—as it is written, “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God”—tried to impose upon him the care of the few sheep he had: namely, to lead them out daily to pasture, guard them as they grazed, and bring them back after grazing.

Charles embraced this duty as though it came from the Lord’s own mouth, with the greatest fervour, and strove carefully each day to fulfil what had been commanded him. One day, having taken the sheep somewhat farther away to graze, certain bandits suddenly rushed upon him and tried to seize by force some of the sheep entrusted to his care. Charles confronted them firmly and said: “Whatever the Lord has permitted you to do to me, I endure patiently; but I cannot, to the extent of my power, consent in any way to your taking away the sheep committed to my charge.” Yet those men of perverse mind stripped him completely and began to depart. Then Charles, unable to endure the shame of his private parts being exposed, forcibly snatched back only his breeches from them; the rest he allowed them to take patiently, unwilling to contend.

When he returned half-naked to the monastery and was questioned by the abbot and brethren, he related the occurrence in order. The abbot, however, wishing to discover whether he inwardly possessed the patience which he displayed outwardly, began to rebuke him severely and charge him with both negligence and pretence. Charles answered all this only by declaring that he had sinned. He was therefore ordered to clothe himself and to go out as customary to his assigned duty.

But on one day, as he was returning with the aforesaid little sheep, one of them began to limp badly. Seeing that on account of this he could not arrive at the appointed hour, Charles—formerly king, but then truly a monk—prompted by humility of heart, immediately placed the limping little sheep upon his shoulders and so returned to the monastery with them all. Yet, in order that such great humility might be shown to be inward and therefore genuine, and, once proven, be crowned, it happened while he was returning that the sheep which he carried on his shoulders urinated upon him. He who had once been supremely powerful, he who had formerly been distinguished by royal rank, endured this with such patience of heart and bore it with such strength of spirit that he neither put down the sheep on that account nor uttered to anyone even the slightest word of complaint.

When this was reported to the abbot by those who knew it, he marvelled greatly at the humility and endurance of so great a man; perceiving that the Spirit of God was truly in him, he ordered him thereafter to rest from that duty and instead to cultivate, as best he knew how, a small garden nearby.

Later, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, asked him to go to Francia to his brother King Pippin on certain matters useful to his realm. With difficulty, and only when the abbot reluctantly consented to the king’s request, he departed. There, delayed for some time by the affair for which he had gone, he died by God’s judgment (A.D. 754). Afterwards his brother King Pippin placed his body in a golden coffin, adorned with jewels, and sent it back here to his monastery together with many other gifts.

[Note: Col. 0500A.] “He strove to send it back. At that time in the same monastery Cyprian, priest and monk, composed the hymn of Saint Benedict: ‘Christ, glory and strength of the saints.’”

8. [Chronicle of Salerno I.] In those same days (749), Ratchis, king of the Lombards, marched with a strong army to capture the city of Perugia and vigorously assailed it on every side. Pope Zacharias went out to him and, through many prayers and admonitions and by granting him great gifts, compelled him to return to his own lands.

Mindful of those admonitions, the same king, not long afterward, inspired by a divine prompting, abandoned royal rank and glory. After reigning five years and six months, he came devoutly with his wife and daughter to Rome, to the thresholds of blessed Peter. There the aforesaid pope cut his hair, made him a cleric, and clothed him, together with his wife and daughter, in the monastic habit. Immediately thereafter, at the direction of that same apostolic pontiff, he came to this monastery and gave himself to be trained under the discipline of the Rule. After a life of considerable religious devotion pleasing to God, he died there.

To the present day there is a vineyard very near the monastery, commonly called Ratchis’s Vineyard; some of our people think that Ratchis himself both planted and cultivated it. His wife, named Tasia, and his daughter Rattruda, with the consent and assistance of the aforesaid abbot, built at their own expense a monastery of women not far from Cassino, in the place called Plumbariola. Enriched with many possessions, they lived there under great strictness and the discipline of the Rule and died there.

The aforesaid abbot was the sixth after blessed Benedict, in the times of the emperors Leo and Constantine; of the Roman pontiffs Gregory and Zacharias; and of Gregory, duke of Benevento, and the aforesaid Gisulf the Younger. Having governed this monastery for thirty-two years, he died on the day before the Nones of May (A.D. 750) and was buried in the portico beside the church of Saint Martin.

OPTATUS, the seventh abbot appointed after blessed Benedict, held office for ten years.

He lived in the time of the aforesaid Emperor Constantine and his son Leo, of the aforesaid Duke Gisulf, and of Pope Stephen II.

[Note: Col. 0501C.] “Rather Liutprand, whom the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict* omitted, and Arichis.”

At that time Aistulf, king of the Lombards, captured Ravenna and besieged Rome for three months (751). For this reason the aforesaid pontiff was compelled to go to Francia to the most excellent King Pippin (A.D. 753). Received by him with great glory and honour, he anointed Pippin and Pippin’s two sons, Charles and Carloman, as kings of the Franks (A.D. 754).

The same glorious king, together with his aforesaid sons, made a promise and grant to Saint Peter and his vicar concerning the cities and territories of Italy within the specified boundary: from Luni with the island of Corsica; thence to Surianum; thence to Mount Bardone; thence to Verceto; thence to Parma; thence to Reggio; thence to Mantua and Mount Silicis; together with the whole exarchate of Ravenna as it had been in ancient times, with the provinces of Venetia and Histria; and also the whole duchy of Spoleto and Benevento. He confirmed that donation with his own hand, those of his sons, and those of many of his judges and nobles.

Then the same king came to Italy with the aforesaid Roman pontiff, took Ravenna and twenty other cities from the aforesaid Aistulf, and brought them under the authority of the Apostolic See. On that account he was then also made patrician of the Romans.

The aforesaid abbot, having completed the course of his time, died on the day before the Nones of January (A.D. 760), and was buried beside his predecessor at the church of blessed Martin.

HERMERIS, the eighth abbot, held office for one year. He died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August (A.D. 760) and was buried beside the church of Saint Benedict.

GRATIANUS, ninth in the governance of this place, held office for four years and five months, in the times of the emperors mentioned above and of Arichis, duke and prince of Benevento.

[Note: Col. 0502C.] “The calculation is inconsistent with itself, since it reports Hermeris as dying in July and Gratianus in August; yet in the catalogue of abbots manuscript 4 has: ‘four years.’”

Concerning this Arichis, Lord Erchempert, in the history which he composed about the Lombard people after Paul the Deacon, reports as follows:

Arichis was the first at Benevento to order that he be called prince, whereas until his time those who governed Benevento had been called dukes. He also had himself anointed by bishops and placed a crown upon himself; and in his charters he ordered the following to be written at the end: “Written in our most sacred palace.”

[Note: Col. 0502C.] “Since he later added these words in the margin beside the words ‘prince of Benevento’ and subsequently transferred them here with critical signs, it is doubtful whether the author found them in his copy of Erchempert or inserted them here from another source; for they are absent from the Vatican manuscript.”

Textual and editorial apparatus omitted above

4. The heading is “[Paul the Deacon, VI.40; Chronicle of Vulturno].” The initial *Cum* (“when”) is reading 1. In the quoted Vulturno passage, *Cum … annis* (“after some intervening years”) is reading 1; it continues: “when, that is, the seven-hundred-and-third year from the Lord’s Incarnation was already passing, Constantine, a most gentle and angelic pope, presiding over the Roman see, while Justinian the Younger ruled with his son Tiberius, the monastery of Saint Vincent … began to be built.” Reading 1b adds that the many erased and deleted words show that alterations were made after the foregoing had been erased, and that finally everything was erased together. *Autem* (“but”) is absent in 4; *praefatum* (“the aforesaid [monastery]”) reads *praefati* (“of the aforesaid”) in 3; *miseratione illa sua omnipotentissima* (“by that most almighty mercy of his”) is abbreviated in 4; *ex ejusdem patris loco* (“from the place of that same father”) reads *loco et regula patris* (“from the father’s place and Rule”) in 1 and the edition. The clause *contigit, disponente Deo* (“it happened, by God’s ordering”) reads in 1: “the beginning of an occasion of this kind arose, so that.”

*Reverentissimus* (“most reverend”) reads *reverendissimus* in 2; “third pope Gregory” is corrected by the editor: “Indeed, fourth. Moreover, the autograph manuscript shows that Leo, who had drawn what he had from Paul the Deacon alone, later worked it out more accurately after consulting the Vulturnian monuments themselves. But he gave the year as a round number, as they say; by Leo’s own calculation it is 718. The year 720 is also found in the *Liber Pontificalis*, in Stephen Borgia, *Del dominio temporale*, p. 4. Saint Vincent’s monastery was founded in A.D. 702, when, by the usage of that age, 703 was already being counted.” *Coelitus* (“from heaven”) reads *divinitus* (“by divine agency”) in 1; *destructum manserat* (“had remained destroyed”) reads *erat destructum* (“was destroyed”) in manuscript a and 1. Reading 1b says that Gregory immediately made Petronax abbot and, with him, sent brethren; reading 1 says *dirigens* (“sending”) rather than *direxit* (“sent”), while manuscript a and 1b have the former construction. Reading 1 has “also some other aids for him” for “various other aids.”

For Petronax’s settlement, 1b adds “A.D. 720”; 1 reads “and not long afterwards,” and 1b adds “having been appointed abbot by them.” Reading 1 has: “having repaired dwellings everywhere and built [them] decently, [and] having established a congregation of many [brethren].” The editor notes that the following “Here … deposited” was drawn from an unknown source, like many such matters reported under the individual abbots. Reading 1c calls the three Beneventans kinsmen of the aforementioned duke; 1b instead has: “Since the said Beneventan brothers were powerful and wealthy, they helped greatly in the work, both personally and through their men, until its restoration”; it is absent from 1. *Germani fratres* means “full brothers”; the word *germani* is superscribed in 1, falsely. *Ceperant* (“had begun”) reads *ceperunt* (“began”) in 3. “In it” is absent in 1; 1 and 1b read “where also”; 1b has “the arm of the same saints,” whereas 1 has “the arm of one of them.”

For Zacharias’s gifts, “several” is absent in 1; *quam* (“which [Rule]”) reads *quem* (“which [masculine]”) in 1; *invasione* (“invasion”) reads *destructione* (“destruction”) in 1; *detulerant* (“had carried”) reads *detulerunt* (“carried”) in 4. *Cellis sibi pertinentibus* (“cells belonging to it”) reads *cellis suis pertinentibus* in 1 and the edition. The whole clause from “in honour” through “Benedict” is absent in 1; “wholly” is added by 4. The editorial note on the privilege reads: “Peter the priest mentions the privilege in the *Chronicle of Vulturno*. A spurious production of a later age, already rejected by Baronius, was reissued by Tosti, *Historia Casinensis*, I, p. 82. It is now found in Peter the Deacon’s Register.”

5. *Liutprand* reads *Luitprand* in 3; “nephew of Liutprand, king of the Lombards” is added in 1b; *Gotscalc* reads *Godescalc* in 1; 1 has “in the time of this man” for “in those days.” The words from “with a great army” through “as he passed” are absent in 1 and 2. The editor judges the identification of this Gisulf with the younger Gisulf to be Leo’s conjecture; the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict* confuses him with the elder. “With” is added in 4; “with great religious devotion” is added in 1 and the edition; *praedictos* (“aforesaid”) is absent in 1; 1 adds “who then lived there”; “in God’s service” is added in 4; *tactus* (“touched”) reads *compunctus* (“pierced with compunction”) in 1, and *divino* (“divine”) is added in 4.

The editor says that Leo added the boundary description, apparently not from the charter itself, now missing from Peter’s Register, but from confirmations by princes and kings which enumerate the same boundaries. The fabricator of Zacharias’s privilege copied its words from this passage, using an edition of the *Chronicle* such as that printed from manuscript 4. “Compare Gattula’s map of the Cassinese dominion.” The Liris, nearer its source, was called Carnellus; after enlargement by the Rapido it was called Garigliano (Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 753 ff.). Bautra is commonly Pecia. *Serrae* means the higher mountain ridges, whence Spanish *sierra*. *Pesclum* means a cliff, rock, or place on a rock, now *pesco*, according to Giustiniani’s *Dictionary of Neapolitan Geography*. The Rapido in the boundary is now called Clarus and differs from the other Rapido rising above the Castle of Saint Elias. *Capud* (“head”) is spelling 3. Mount Caria is Monte Cairo. *Orticosa* reads *Ortiasa* in 3 and 4; *Falconari* reads *Falconara* in 3, 4, and Zacharias’s privilege. *A voca.* means “at the water” in the manuscript. Gimberutus is given as “the hill called Gimberutus” in 1 and the edition. *Quercetulum* reads *Querquitulum* in 1 and *Quertitulum* in 2. Manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Saint Amasus, the common people”; 1 and the edition read “and then directly”; Zacharias’s privilege has “and then directly.” *Silicem* reads “Silix in the place” in 1 and the edition; *Aezzuli* reads *Jezzuli* in 3. *Marozzae* reads *Marocze* in 2. 1 and the edition read “the same river,” “Cosa, and as it rises through,” “Donatus, and how it descends over,” “Marri, and it goes,” and “to those rocks,” respectively. Balva was later Famara (Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 121); for the Two Lions, see below III.12. 1 and the edition add “those ridges” after “ascends through”; 2 omits “as far as … thence”; 1 reads “Garigliano, and then goes as far as”; 2 reads “to that very rock”; 1 and the edition read “and thence proceeds”; and 1 and the edition read “proceeds as far as.”

After “then held within the aforesaid boundaries,” 1b adds: “When these things had thus been granted and secured by the aforesaid duke to blessed Father Benedict by lawful donation, he retained only the borderlands, for the inhabitants’ protection against enemy incursions; yet he ordered them, both at sowing and harvest time, to obey the monks in the assistance of their labours.” [From the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*.] It continues: “The same Gisulf also made for this abbot a precept concerning the monastery of Saint Mary at Cingla, with all its appurtenances, and subjected it to this Cassinese monastery.” The second hand adds: “He also made a very liberal grant to blessed Benedict from the territory of Gentiana.” Afterwards the entire passage was struck out. The note on Scauniperga says: “From this, Cassino itself was later called Saint Peter in the Monastery.”

6. The editorial citation is: “From Gisulf’s charters in Gattula, *Historia*, p. 27, issued at Alife in August, indiction II, and another at Benevento in October, indiction XIV.” *A solo* means “from the ground up”; 1b and the edition read *fundamentis* (“from the foundations”). Reading 1b and the edition add “whom he had all given liberty to”; *concessit* (“granted”) reads *optulit* (“offered”) in 1b and 2. *Utilis* (“useful”) reads *delectabilis* (“pleasant”) in 1b; *apparuisset* (“had appeared”) reads *visus fuisset* (“had seemed”) in 1b and the edition. *Conjugis* (“wife”) reads *uxoris* in 1b and the edition; “God” is added in 4. The note identifies the church bought from Deusdedit as Saint John’s, near Alife. *Auxilio* (“assistance”) reads *adjutorio* in 1b and the edition; the words from “and also” through “show” are absent in 1b. The charter of the women’s monastery was issued at Benevento in May, indiction XV. *Concessit* reads *confirmavit* (“confirmed”) in 1b and 2; *Gausanae* reads *Gausani* in 1b and 2. *Eo utique* (“certainly on this condition”) is absent in 1b, as is *firmato* (“having been confirmed”); the edition reads *quaelibet* (“any one”) for *qualibet*. Manuscript 1b and 2 read “should hold [it] by peaceful right” for “should retain the government … by undisputed peaceful right.” The note on Gentiana states: “See below, chapter 14. Casa Gentiana lies within the boundaries of Liburia, in the territory now called Quarto, belonging to Marano.” The Erchempert note says that these words are not found thus in Erchempert’s manuscript, though Leo says he drew them from it; see Gattula, *Historia*, p. 54. *Non posset* (“could not”) is the reading of 1 and the edition; “a community of nuns” is the reading of 1b and the edition; “saint” reads for “blessed” in 1b and the edition. Reading 1b has a longer, subsequently struck-out continuation concerning Arichis’s grant of Gentiana to Abbot Theodemar and his devout offering to Saint Benedict.

7. *Hujus tempore* (“in his time”) is reading 1; *magnus* (“the Great”) reads *mannus* in 2. Reading 1 and the edition have “abandoning his earthly kingdom” for “having abandoned [it]”; 1 adds “with some of his faithful men”; 1 reads “gave himself to that apostle,” and 2 “gave himself to the apostolic [see].” *Ordinans* (“ordaining”) reads *faciens* (“making”) in 1 and 2; 1 and the edition add “of blessed Benedict”; *cum* (“with”) is absent in the edition; 1 has “with all his riches.” *Fuerit* (“was”) reads *fuit* in the edition; “briefly in writing” is reading 1. One expanded variant begins: “Finally, after a few days, seeing that Charles was fervent in purpose …”; another reads “wishing according to [the Rule].” Reading 1 repeats “seeing his fervent purpose.” “Which were at hand” describes the sheep in 1. The editorial note explains that *obedientiae* are monastic offices, especially the provostships of Cassino and its dependent cells. “Very greatly,” “daily,” “somewhat,” “upon him,” and “violently” are added by 4 or 1b as marked in the source. 1 has the longer speech: “Concerning the carrying off of the sheep which are entrusted to my care, I cannot consent, so far as I am able; but concerning myself I do not contend against whatever the Lord permits you to do.” The men’s further action is likewise included there. *Sibi* (“to him”) reads *illi* in 1 and the edition. 1 omits “from them”; 1b and the edition read “by them.” *Fuisset* reads *esset* in 1.

For the lame sheep, 1 and the edition begin “After a few days”; “therefore” reads for “then,” and 1 and 2 omit “at the appointed hour.” Reading 1 and the edition supply “he placed the same lame little sheep upon his shoulders.” 1b adds “the former king Charles, but then truly a monk.” Before the gate, 1 has: “Before he had entered the gate, as he was carrying it on his shoulders, he was soaked with urine.” The words “so that … be crowned” are added in 4; *perfundi* (“to be soaked”) reads *profundi* in the edition; *lutio* means “with urine.” “Formerly,” “royal,” and “rank” are added in 4; 1b adds “of heart”; the edition reads *ne* for *nec* (“nor”); 1 and the edition add *quidem* (“indeed, even”) after “slightest.” *Hoc* (“this”) reads *quod* (“which”) in 1, while 1b has *hoc*. *Sciret* (“knew how”) reads *posset* (“was able”) in 1. *Aistulfo* reads *Astulfo* in 3; 1 adds *publicae* (“public”) after “of his realm,” and 1b adds *suae* (“his own”); 1 ends at “asked [him].” The editor’s continuation reads: “He strove to send [the body] back. At that time, in the same monastery, Cyprian, priest and monk, composed the hymn of Saint Benedict: ‘Christ, glory and strength of the saints.’”

8. The heading is “[Chronicle of Salerno, I].” Reading 1 calls this “in his time”; 1b reads *veniens* (“coming”) for *pergens* (“marching”), and *pergens* for Zacharias’s “went out.” *Multisque* (“and many”) reads for *magnisque* (“and great”) in 1b and the edition. A second hand in 1 adds, after “to capture Perugia,” material that reverses the whole order of the narrative and attributes these events first to Abbot Optatus. The five years and six months are attributed by the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict* to Aistulf; the editor thinks that the source of the error. The *Chronicle of Salerno* and Zacharias’s Life have “sons,” not “wife and daughter”; this author follows the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict* and joins to it traditions received orally. 1 and the edition add “chief of the apostles”; 1 calls Zacharias “the prelate of the apostolic see,” and 1b and the edition name him. 1 and the edition add “of blessed Benedict”; 2 reads *transmittente* (“sending”) for *dictante* (“directing”), while 1 omits the latter phrase; 1 adds “living there” after “gave himself.” *In hodiernum* (“to the present”) is reading 1b, while 1 has the corrupt *inodiernum*. 1 has “some of ours think” for “some of our people”; 1 omits “and assisting.” Plumbariola is Piumarola; the site is by the stream now called Le Fontanelle. The erased addition in 1 names Liutprand, Lombard king; it is corrected in 2. The editor corrects the chronological list: “Rather Liutprand, whom the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict* omitted, and Arichis.” The abbot’s burial phrase is absent in 1 and the edition; 1b reads “the seventh day before the Kalends of September” for “the day before the Nones of January.”

For Optatus, 1 reads nine years. An erased passage in 1 had “his son Leo, and Pope Stephen II (corrected to III), and [Gregory] duke”; it was followed by the Ratchis narrative, which 1b transfers to Petronax’s time, beginning “When he had completed”; the earlier wording was “But the aforesaid abbot ….” The note on the following paragraph states that Leo did not take it from Anastasius, but from a schedule perhaps derived from Anastasius and later entered by Peter the Deacon into his Register as no. 86; whether the remaining material came from the *Gesta Pontificum* or was compiled from *Chronicle of Salerno* chapter 2 ff. is uncertain. The whole passage is absent in manuscript 1; compare chapters 12 and 16. *A. r. L.* is the edition’s abbreviation for “Aistulf, king of the Lombards.” The editor dates the stated event A.D. 756 and observes that Leo copied it from the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*, which gives no date. “With great glory” is absent in 4. *Vicario* (“vicar”) reads *vicariis* (“vicars”) in 3. The words “as it had been in ancient times” are absent in 1b, chapter 12. *Corroboravit* (“confirmed”) reads *corroboratam* (“confirmed [feminine participle]”) in the edition. *Demum* (“then, finally”) is absent in the edition. The note explains: Pippin first came with the pope in 754; he came alone a second time in 756 and then restored the cities to Saint Peter. The burial notice is absent in 1 and the edition.

For Hermeris, “held office for one year” is absent in 4; manuscript 2 adds: “in the times of the aforementioned Emperor Constantine and his son Leo, and Pope Stephen II.” For Gratianus, 1 and the edition read “ninth abbot after blessed Benedict”; 1b adds “and five months.” The calculation is inconsistent: Hermeris is said to die in July and Gratianus in August, whereas manuscript 4’s catalogue gives four years. The long historical dating in 1 names Aistulf, who took Ravenna and held Rome for three months under Pope Stephen, and Arichis, first called prince at Benevento; 1b corrects “duke” to “prince,” and 2 has a related abbreviated form. The editor says the material was first copied from the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*, p. 201, then enlarged and altered. “Concerning this Arichis” is reading 1; 1 adds “here he relates,” but below omits it. *Domnus* (“Lord”) is added in 1b. *Herchempertus* reads *Hercenbertus* in 3 and *Erchempertus* in 4; 1 calls him “a certain grammarian,” and 1b first “a monk and grammarian,” then deletes it. 1b adds “after Paul the Deacon”; “thus relates” is absent in 1. The Arichis extract is added in 1b. The final note explains that, since the author later added it in the margin beside “prince of Benevento” and then transferred it here by critical signs, it is uncertain whether he found it in his Erchempert manuscript or inserted it from another source; it is absent from the Vatican manuscript. The note on *scriptum in sacratissimo nostro palatio* reads: “Di Meo, *Annali napoletani*, III, p. 93, observed that this had already been customary under Arichis’s predecessors and is not found in Arichis’s charters.”

Source preparation: Canonical local restored source; two foreign-text recoveries preserved.

## 9. [ERCH. ch. 3]

Arichis founded within the walls of Benevento a most richly endowed and splendid temple for the Lord [Col. 0502C], which he named in Greek **ΑΓΗΑΝ ϹΩΦΗΑΝ**, that is, “Holy Wisdom” [*Hagia Sophia*]. He endowed it with very extensive estates , and with various resources ; and, establishing a convent of nuns, made his own sister abbess there, with absolutely all its appurtenances and possessions . [Col. 0503A] He transferred it under the jurisdiction of blessed Benedict at Monte Cassino, to remain there in perpetuity (November 774).





In this temple, therefore, he honourably brought together the bodies of the holy Twelve Brothers, which had been resting in various places throughout Apulia, including the places where they had been beheaded, and deposited them together beneath one altar, each in a separate reliquary, for the protection and honour of the homeland (15 May 760). Later, having obtained at different times from various parts of Italy the body of the precious martyr Mercurius, as well as the holy bodies of thirty-one other martyrs and confessors, he likewise brought them there and placed them with sufficient reverence at various altars around the high altar (26 August 768). 



While he was accustomed, with the utmost devotion, frequently to spend the night in prayer there—for his palace was near that place —it is reported that, one night as he prayed, the Twelve Brothers appeared to him and greeted him amicably, bowing their faces together. Supposing from their exceedingly grim appearance that they were strangers, he asked who they were who had presumed so boldly to enter the enclosure of the nuns at night. Smiling gently, they said:

“We are those, O prince, whom your devotion, having found us in various places, brought here with the greatest zeal and deposited with still greater care. How good and joyful this is for us, and how profitable for you through divine mercy, the last day will show.”



Having said this, the vision that appeared to the prince suddenly vanished. 

 In that same monastery he also caused the church of Saint Modestus, which a certain Leonianus had recently built within the same city and to which he had offered all his property by charter, leaving it at the disposal of the aforesaid prince, to be offered and confirmed by his own decree together with all its appurtenances.

The aforesaid abbot died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September (22 August 764) and was buried in the portico of the church of Saint Martin.

[Col. 0504A] **TOMICHIS, tenth abbot**, ruled for six years and five months. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of February (25 January 771).

## 10.





In his time a certain noble and very wealthy man of the city of Benevento, named Leo, gave himself and all his possessions, both movable and immovable, to this monastery. He placed the charter of this offering, written in his own hand, upon the body of Saint Benedict, in the presence of the aforesaid abbot Tomichis and of all the brethren as witnesses.

First, by charter, he granted freedom to all his male and female slaves. Afterwards, he placed them all, now free, together with their own estates and with everything that they appeared to possess, under the authority of the aforesaid monastery. The condition was that each of them should perform four days’ labour each month wherever it was necessary for the monastery; they were permitted to sell or give their goods or property to no one except among themselves. The goods of those who died without children were to pass into the jurisdiction of the monastery. Yet it was not lawful for the monks, as though they were free persons, to hand over their boys or girls to anyone for service. 

We have thought fit to record here, in summary apart from the rest, the names and numbers of his estates and dependants.

The estate of the priest Gaydepert: Adelpert, with four sons and their wives; Bonecausus, with four sons, their wives, and children; Grimoald, with four sons and their wives and children; Ciminulus, with his wife and children; Ursus, with his wife and children; Fuscari, with his wife and children. 

The estate of Grisi: Landulf, with his son Arnipert and two stepdaughters. Bonitus, with three sons and their wives.

The estate of the priest Cerbulus: Leoald, with four sons and their wives and children; Agenulfus, his nephew, with his sons; Desiderius, with three sons; Bassacius, with three sons and one son-in-law.

The estate of Lupus: Sadipertus, with his son and his son-in-law; Sico, with his son and his son’s wife; Stephanus, with two sons ; Formosus, with his three sons.

The estate of Lupus the painter : Maurus, with four sons; John, with his three sons.

The estate of Dulcipert: Bonerisius, with his son, his son’s wife, and their children; the three sons of Rajenolfus , with their wives and children.

The estate of Erfemarus: Bonus, Adelchis, Maio , Bonulus, John, and Ursus—all these with their wives and children; Rozzius, with his four sons, namely Leo, Stephen, Sellittulus , and Ciminulus, with their wives and children; Adelgarius, with one son and two sons-in-law.

Besides these, he granted to a certain aunt of his, for her own use during her lifetime, an estate called Pantanum near Benevento, with the slaves from Avellino and Transmonte belonging to that estate. This was on the condition that after her death everything should return to the jurisdiction of this monastery, just as the other matters mentioned above. 

**POTO, eleventh abbot**, ruled for seven years and five months.

He built below a small church in honour of Saint Benedict, on the site where the church of Saint Germanus now appears to stand. He also made another church in honour of Saint Michael the Archangel at the foot of the other mountain, in a very pleasant place where the olive grove of this monastery now stands. He adorned it with distinguished paintings and with worthy poems around it. Of these we shall copy here a few which, owing to their antiquity, we could scarcely read. Their opening, after some lines that could not be read at all , contained the following concerning the situation and character of the place :

> Fierce wolves used once to howl beneath the silent night,
>
> And foul-smelling foxes to yelp,
>
> And bears, their shaggy coats entangled, to growl with savage murmur,
>
> And bristly boars.

And a little later:

> The swift doe and fearful stags would run about together. 
>
> But when the excellent Father Poto undertook, with vigilant zeal,
>
> The governance of the sacred enclosure—

And again, a little later:

> Indeed, for the high-throned King who contains the vast world,
>
> To whom the dwellers in heaven, at his command, bring swift messages,
>
> He added this temple in the name of great Michael,
>
> Who drove from heaven the dragon reddened with blood.
>
> Yet this priest, overtaken by swift death,
>
> Left alike the altar and the sanctuary undedicated.

And so forth.

He died on the third day before the Kalends of July (29 June 778) and was buried beside the church of Saint Benedict.

**THEODEMAR, twelfth in succession to receive the abbacy from blessed Benedict**, ruled for nineteen years. He lived in the times of the emperors Leo, who was also called Zacharis , Constantine, and his mother Irene, and of Pope Hadrian; and during the rule of the Beneventans, the aforesaid Arichis and his son Grimoald.

## 11.

Beside the aforesaid church of Saint Benedict, which his predecessor had made, he constructed, in beautiful workmanship [Col. 0506B], a temple in honour of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, directly above the spring from which the River Lyris flows. 

The fourfold structure of this church rises upon twelve columns, so that four columns stand along each side. Upon these a tower higher than the porticoes beneath has been raised; four other towers have been erected at the several corners of the same portico around that tower.

He covered this temple with leaden tiles and adorned it with most beautiful figures , and with excellent verses. What was especially outstanding was that he furnished it with magnificent relics of almost all the apostles and of many martyrs and confessors. Of the aforesaid verses, we have thought fit to set down here only four, inscribed outside around the central tower:

> Because, when darkness was removed, the world deserved through you
>
> To possess light, O Virgin and most holy Mother,
>
> Lofty churches therefore rise for you throughout the world,
>
> And deservedly you are celebrated most gloriously in every land.



He also caused the church of Saint Michael the Archangel—which, as we said, had been left undedicated by his predecessor—to be dedicated with every honour. Beside it he constructed a cloister and several dwellings. 

[Col. 0507A]

## 12. [Life of Hadrian]

In his time (773), Karlomannus, son of Pippin , invited by Pope Hadrian , came with a powerful army of Franks, Alamanni , and Saxons against the city of Pavia, because of Desiderius, the most savage king of the Lombards, who had invaded the cities of Saint Peter. Besieging it for six continuous months, he captured it; and, having most victoriously subjected the whole Lombard kingdom to himself , he handed it over to his son Pippin. He carried the aforesaid Desiderius off with him into Francia in the year of the Lord 774. 

Meanwhile, while he was besieging Pavia, out of love for the Prince of the Apostles, on Holy Saturday of Easter (2 April) he came to Rome with many bishops, abbots, and dukes . Having celebrated the Easter feast there, he was reminded and asked by the aforesaid pope to fulfil in every respect that donation which his father Pippin had formerly made, together with himself, to blessed Peter and to his vicar, Pope Stephen.



The king assented to these requests with a ready and willing mind and ordered another promise of donation, patterned after the former, to be written by his notary Etherius . The king himself confirmed it with his own hand and caused all the bishops and abbots, as well as dukes and counts and many distinguished persons who had come with him, to subscribe there. He placed it with his own hand upon the altar of blessed Peter. Both the king himself and all his nobles bound themselves by a terrible oath to preserve it perpetually for blessed Peter and his vicars.



[Col. 0507C] [ERCH. ch. 2.]

After this, the same king, together with his son Pippin [Col. 0508A], and with a great army, went to Benevento against Arichis , who was the son-in-law of King Desiderius. Having fought him through diverse and varying engagements (787), Charles finally received from Arichis his crown and the greater part of his treasure, as well as his two children, Grimoald and Adelgisa, as hostages for peace, and withdrew. 

Terrified by fear of the Franks, Arichis added a new city to Benevento. He also wonderfully restored Salerno, anciently founded between Lucania and Nuceria .

The aforesaid king, returning prosperously from Benevento, came up here to blessed Father Benedict for prayer and commended himself both to him and to all the brethren serving God here. Then, at the request of the abbot or brethren, he—the first king to do so—ordered a charter of confirmation to be made for him concerning the whole of this land (25 March). 

By another charter (28 March) he confirmed to blessed Benedict the monastery of Saint Mary at Cingla, Saint Mary at Plumbariola, Saint Sophia at Benevento, and the other possessions that it then appeared to hold. He also confirmed all waters, with the banks on both sides, wherever they adjoined the lands of this monastery. He also granted authority that the monks should elect an abbot for themselves according to the tenor of the holy Rule, without prejudice or violence from anyone. 



After these events he returned to Francia and promptly sent letters to this abbot through Bishop Adelgarius. He asked him to send him several brethren from our monastery to demonstrate or establish in those regions the standard of regular discipline. 

This he did, sending him the Rule as well as the hymns that were then sung in this monastery according to the tradition of the Rule. He also sent the weight of a pound of bread, the measure of wine, and the measure of the cup which the servers ought to receive with the mixed wine. He sent him in writing all the customs that were then observed in this place. 

## 13.





In these times a certain man of the English people, mute and deaf, came with several companions of his own nation to the thresholds of the Apostles. Seeing his companions hastening to the shrine of Saint Michael the Archangel situated on Mount Gargano, he set out with them and came to this monastery. 

When they had entered the oratory and had together prostrated themselves in prayer before the body of the most holy Father Benedict, the others rose from prayer after a short while and began to pull him also so that he might rise and go away with them.

But he, pierced by a heavenly visitation, prolonged his prayer with the groans of his heart and the voices of his mind, as far as he could and knew how, imploring with a most faithful heart the help of blessed Father Benedict. And behold, after not quite an hour, raising himself from the place where he had been prostrate—blessed and wonderful is God in his saints!—he immediately recovered both hearing and speech , and began to speak most fluently not only in his native language, that is, English , but also in Roman [Latin].

Then, together with his companions, after offering many thanksgivings to God and the holy father, they departed, telling everyone everywhere how great a thing the Lord had done for him through the merits of blessed Benedict. 

## 14.



To this abbot the aforesaid Prince Arichis granted the greater part of the territory of Gentiana, in addition to what Duke Gisulf had long before granted to Abbot Petronax (ch. 6). 

[ERCH. ch. 4.]

At a later time his son Grimoald, whom we have said had been given to King Charles as a hostage , was, with that king’s permission, sent back to Benevento after his father’s death and made prince. By a charter of donation (September 788) he granted to blessed Benedict all his demesne lands, with male and female slaves, in the same territory of Gentiana; the cell of Saint Agapitus; the port of Trajectum ; the port of Vulturnum; and the whole fishery of the city of Lesina , together with its own inlet. 

At the same time (April 782), Hildeprand, Duke of Spoleto, likewise offered to this monastery the estate called Castrinianum, with all its appurtenances, in the county of Pinna ; and an olive grove at Tronto, in a place called Turri. In the county of the Marsi, at a place called Paternus, he gave an estate of five hundred modii [Col. 0510B], many households with all their property, and several fishermen on Lake Fucinus, together with the port of that lake called Adrestina. In addition he gave his wood named Cusanum. 

A certain wealthy Beneventan gastald, named Wacco , being on campaign, likewise offered to this holy monastery his son, named Wachipert , together with the properties specified below. 

An estate at Trane, where it is called Cimilianum; an estate at Trepurium; an estate at Ariano; an estate at Virgilie; an estate at Terranea; another at Vicario ; another at Crosta, with an olive grove; another at Culmo; another at Genne; another at Monte Nigro; at Massa; at Ripa; at Noceto ; at Corneto; at Tammaro ; at Latiniano; at Marsico; at Trelicio ; in the territory of Potentia; and an estate at Saint Agnes. 

He assigned his house within the city to his wife Tasia, but only for her lifetime. He granted freedom to all his male and female slaves, while retaining them under the jurisdiction and protection of this monastery, so that each man and woman should perform annual services wherever those appointed by us might direct.

## 15.

[Col. 0511A]

In the time of this abbot, Paul the Deacon, notary of the aforesaid King Desiderius, came to this monastery after the capture of Desiderius and the death of Arichis, prince of Benevento, and assumed the habit of holy religion. It is not irrelevant briefly to state who Paul was, what manner of man he was, and where he came from.

[P. D. IV, 37.]

He was by origin of the Lombard people. His great-grandfather, named Leupichis, came with the Lombards when they first entered Italy. Paul’s father was named Warnefrid , and his mother Theodelinda . [Chronicle of Salerno 9.] Educated from boyhood in the liberal arts, he acquired, through his ability, a very prominent place of intimacy at the court of King Desiderius and became a deacon of the patriarchate of Aquileia.

After Pavia had been captured, as we have said, he became very dear and intimate to King Charles because of his wisdom. Not long afterwards, however, he was accused before that king by certain envious persons of wishing to kill him out of loyalty to his lord Desiderius. The same king had him brought before him and asked whether the things being said about his intended murder of the king were true. 

He replied firmly that he had certainly always been most faithful to his lord and would persevere in that fidelity throughout his life. 

At this the king, suddenly inflamed by anger, ordered that his hands be cut off without delay. But immediately coming to himself and remembering his great learning and wisdom , he sighed and said:

“Even if we cut off his hands, where shall we now find so elegant a writer?”

And he said to the nobles standing by:

“Tell me, what do you think about this?”

They replied:

“O king, you rightly pity so great a man; but, lest he at some time send letters to anyone against you, order, if it please you, that his eyes be put out.” 

“And where,” said the king, “or when shall we be able to find so distinguished a historian or poet?” 

Seeing the good king’s kindly disposition toward him, they finally persuaded him to exile Paul to the island of Diomedes , which today is called Tremiti because of its three mountains. This was done. After he had remained there in exile for several years , a certain little man, who rendered him service for God’s sake , secretly removed him from that island and went with him to Benevento.

When Arichis saw him—Arichis, who had Adelberga, the daughter of the aforesaid King Desiderius, as his wife —both he and his wife rejoiced greatly and retained him honourably with them. During that time Paul adorned with very brilliant verses both palaces which the same prince had nobly built, one in Benevento and the other in Salerno. 

At the request of the same Adelberga, he added many things here and there from ecclesiastical histories to the Roman history which Eutropius had composed briefly. [Cf. *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*, p. 201.]

Finally, he appended to that history two little books extending from the time of Julian the Apostate, at which Eutropius had ended the history, down to the time of the first Emperor Justinian. He also composed in verse nearly all the short readings of the annalistic computation. [Chronicle of Salerno 36–37.] 

After Arichis died, Paul hastened to this monastery, as we have said. He became a monk and lived here for no short time. At the request of the aforesaid abbot or of the brethren, he produced a highly useful exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict , in which he attests many necessary matters concerning the ancient customs of this place. 



He also composed in elegant style the history of his people, that is, the Lombards, and several other writings. Among them he wrote reciprocal verses arranged in elegiac metre and a hymn concerning each of blessed Benedict’s miracles, in sufficiently eloquent language.

## Textual and editorial notes

Notes follow the supplied source order. Manuscript forms are retained alongside their English meanings.

1. **[Col. 0501]** Manuscript 1 adds *Arichis*; manuscript 1b deletes the name.

2. **[Col. 0501]** Manuscript 4 omits *A. S.*—the abbreviated Greek title *Agian Sophian*, “Holy Wisdom.”

3. **[Col. 0501]** In the endowment clause, manuscript 1 and the edition read *et*, “and.”

4. **[Col. 0501]** In “estates and various resources,” manuscript 1 and the edition read *ac*, “and.”

5. **Source:** `[Note: [Col. 0501] germanamque-ejus add. 1b.]` **English:** MS 1b adds the entire span *germanamque suam ibidem abbatissam efficiens, cum omnibus omnino pertinentiis et possessionibus ejus*: “making his own sister abbess there, with absolutely all its appurtenances and possessions.” The dash in *germanamque—ejus* marks this range, not two adjacent words.

6. **[Col. 0503C]** “He added these matters later, which we do not read in Erchempert.” Gattola, *Historia*, p. 50, prints Arichis’s diploma from the Register of Peter the Deacon: “Executed at Benevento, in the most fortunate palace, in the seventeenth year, in the month of November, in the thirteenth indiction, happily.”

7. **Source:** `[Note: [Col. 0503] In---obtulit et confirmavit add. 1c. sed ultimus versus a voce arbitrio abscisus est; quem servavit 1*. Prius haec scripserat: Pari etiam modo in territorio Aliphano idem Deo amabilis vir, ecclesiam in honore domini Salvatoris construxit (plurimisque praediis atque colonis ditavit add. 1b.) et puellare (nichilominus add. 1b. quod prius post Adelgisam scripserat) coenobium, instituit (instituens, filiam suam Adelgisam ibi in matrem prefecit 1b.); atque dicioni sancti Vincentii martyris subdidit. Quae ipse expunxit. Cf. Erch. c. 3.]` **English:** MS 1c adds the passage from *In* through *obtulit et confirmavit* (“offered and confirmed”), but the last line is cut off beginning at *arbitrio* (“disposal”); MS 1* preserves it. The author had previously written: “Likewise, in the territory of Alife, that same man beloved by God built a church in honour of the Lord Saviour, established a nunnery, and subjected it to the jurisdiction of Saint Vincent the martyr.” MS 1b adds “and endowed it with many estates and tenants”; it also adds *nichilominus*, “likewise,” which it had previously placed after *Adelgisam*. For “established,” 1b reads: “establishing [it], he appointed his daughter Adelgisa as mother there.” The author himself erased this earlier account. Compare Erchempert, chapter 3.

8. **[Col. 0503C]** “What follows he drew from the metrical *Translation of the Twelve Brothers*, which survives in Surius under 1 September and in our manuscript 280, ANG. But he added some material from the lessons of the Office of the Saints.”

9. **[Col. 0503]** At the deposit of the Twelve Brothers, manuscript 1 and the edition read *altare*, “altar.”

10. **Source:** `[Note: [Col. 0504C] Translationis historia exstat auctore ipso principe Arichis, impr. ap. Borgiam, Mem. di Benev. 1, p. 221. Quae de aliis sanctis addit, facile ipse Beneventi discere potuit. Corpora sanctorum 44 ibi requiescere, dicit etiam Robertus c. Bovian. a. 1119; Nov. apud Ughellum VIII, 243.]` **English:** The history of this translation of relics survives, written by Prince Arichis himself and printed in Borgia, *Memorie di Benevento* I, p. 221. What the author adds about the other saints he could easily have learned at Benevento itself. Robert, count of Bojano, also says that the bodies of forty-four saints rest there, in November 1119; see Ughelli VIII, 243.

11. **Source:** `[Note: [Col. 0503] v. ejus p. 1c.]` **English:** MS 1c has *v. ejus p.*, “his palace [was] nearby,” for the printed wording *vicinum loco illi palatium*, “the palace [was] near that place.” The initials are retained alongside their contextual expansion.

12. **Source:** `[Note: [Col. 0503] deest 4.]` **English:** MS 4 omits *erat*, “was,” in *palatium erat*, “the palace was.”

13. **[Col. 0503]** Manuscript 4 adds *a. s. d. r.*: “and, having brought them here, [he] deposited them more zealously.”

14. **[Col. 0503]** Manuscript 1c reads *duci*, “duke,” for *principi*, “prince.”
