223. **[Col. 0511]** `testatur` — “he attests” (the edition).

224. **[Col. 0511C]** “An exposition of this kind survives in Codex Casinensis 353; most recently, the distinguished scholar Tosti sought to claim it for our Paul, *Historia Casinensis* I, pp. 99 and following.”

225. **[Col. 0511]** `Historiam quoque gentis suae id est Langobardorum, et` — “also a history of his own people, that is, of the Lombards, and” is omitted in witnesses 1 and 2.

226. MS 1 and the edition add *etiam*, “also”. The source prints *1. ei.*; the last abbreviation is evidently a corruption of the usual *ed.*, “edition”, rather than a separate Latin reading.

227. **[Col. 0511]** `rec. et hymnum` — “also reciprocal verses and a hymn” (reading 1); `r. et hymnos` — “reciprocal verses and hymns” (the edition). The difference is singular `hymnum` (“a hymn”) versus plural `hymnos` (“hymns”).

To this man the aforesaid Charles [Note: [Col. 0511] *king* added in 1 and the edition.], who had ordered him into exile, upon hearing that he had assumed the monastic habit in this place, greatly rejoiced for him and sent him quite cordial and pleasant letters composed in verse [Note: [Col. 0511C] Our manuscript 257 contains them complete. ANG. From it Tosti published them, *Hist. Cas.* I, 105; and Giesebrecht, *De litterarum studiis apud Italos*, Berlin, 1845, 4to, p. 26. Yet Leo did not refrain from altering words even in these verses.]. From these it pleased him to insert several verses here. For, after some preliminary matter, addressing his little letter [Note: [Col. 0511] *cartom* in 1; *cartulam* in 1a.] thus [Note: [Col. 0511] *dest* in 1 and the edition.], he says:

> Hence, swiftly setting out, let my letter take easy flight,  
> [Note: [Col. 0511] “from Rome” written above the line in 1.]  
> Through woods and hills and valleys too, in headlong course,  
> [Note: [Col. 0513] *perpete* in 2.]  
> Seek the gracious dwelling of Benedict, dear to God.  
> For there is sure repose for those who arrive there weary.  
> Here vegetables abound for guests, here fish [Note: [Col. 0513] *fishes* in 1.], here bread;  
> Holy peace, a humble spirit, and the fair concord of the brethren,  
> Praise, honour [Note: [Col. 0513] *love* in 1, the edition, and manuscript 257.], and Christ’s worship together at every hour.  
> Say to the father and all the brethren: “Greeting and farewell.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0513] “Here, father, and” in 4.]  
> Joyfully embrace the neck of my sweet Paul,  
> [Note: [Col. 0513] “embrace kindly; say” in 1, 2, and manuscript 257, where “the neck—kindly” was added in a recent hand.]  
> Repeatedly saying: “Hail, excellent father, hail.” And so forth.  
> [Note: [Col. 0513] “And the rest” absent in 4.]

Paul likewise took pains to reply to him in verse and to return the greatest thanks for his visitation and greeting, and that of all the brethren [Note: [Col. 0513C] Paul’s metrical response is not preserved among us. ANG.]. [*Chronicle of Salerno* 37.] Now, mature in age, he completed the course of this life [Note: [Col. 0513C] The Cassinese necrology, manuscript 47, reads: “On the Ides of April, the lord Paul, deacon and monk, of venerable memory.” ANG.], and was honourably buried in the monastery cloister beside the chapter-house.

**16.** In the last [Note: [Col. 0513] “It is observed” added in 1b.] year of this abbot [Note: [Col. 0513C] Rather, of Gisulf; thus it is evident that these matters have been inserted out of their proper place. But, contrary to the agreement of the manuscripts, I did not wish to alter the order. Pseudo-Anastasius also places this here.] [Note: [Col. 0513] “sixteenth” added in 4.], the emperor Louis, surnamed the Kindly or [Note: [Col. 0513] *kindly or* above the line in 1c.] the Holy, son of this Charles, in the fourth year of his reign, convened at the palace of Aachen a gathering of very many abbots and religious monks from all Francia (10 July 817). He established seventy-two general chapters very useful for the observance of our order [Note: [Col. 0513C] There are seventy-one in Cassinese manuscript no. 252, three of which the copyist contracted into one.]; almost all reputable monasteries observe them as though they were the Rule of blessed Benedict. [Note: [Col. 0513] “In reputable monasteries and” in 1b and 2.]

This Louis [Note: [Col. 0513] “This sent to the pope” absent in 1. “Here Louis made a pact of constitution and confirmation with blessed Peter, after the example of his forebears Pepin and Charles, and with the lord Paschal, Peter’s vicar, and confirmed it by the sign of his own hand and those of his three sons” in the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0513C] This is the first mention of this pact.] [Note: [Col. 0513] *Lodeuucus* in 3.], after the example of his forebears Pepin and Charles, made with blessed Peter and his vicar, lord Paschal, a pact of constitution and confirmation. Confirming it by the sign of his own hand and those of his three sons, he caused ten bishops, eight abbots, fifteen counts, one librarian, one chamberlain, and one porter to subscribe it; and he sent it to lord Pope Paschal through Theodore the nomenclator, legate of the holy Roman Church.

At this time [Note: [Col. 0513] “At this time—place” added in 1b.] the church of Saint Vincent called Major, in the aforesaid place beside the Vulturnus, was built by Abbot Joshua of that place in a quite handsome work [Note: [Col. 0514C] It was dedicated in A.D. 808, according to the *Chronicle of Vulturnus*, book 2, but in the presence of Emperor Louis. Di Meo demonstrated in the *Annals of Naples*, under the year 818, that Joshua held office from 793 to 818.]. [Note: [Col. 0513] “Built in a handsome work” absent in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0513] “beside the Vulturnus” absent in 1b.] The aforesaid Abbot Theodemar died [Note: [Col. 0513] added in 4.] on the Nones of June [Note: [Col. 0513] thus in 1b; “the ninth day before the Kalends” in 1.], and was buried beside the church of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0513] *Here* in 1 and 2.].

**GISULF**, thirteenth abbot appointed from blessed Benedict, in the year of the Lord 797 [Note: [Col. 0514C] At its beginning, since in January he had already received Wacco’s donation. I think he was appointed while the aged Theodemar was still alive, something which we shall see happened more than once.], held office for twenty-one years.

**17.** Descended [Note: [Col. 0513] *Here* in 1 and 2.] from the noble stock of the Beneventan dukes, as soon as he became abbot he began to strive to find how he might enlarge the cramped spaces both of the church and of the other workshops, for the benefit of the brethren then dwelling below [Note: [Col. 0513] “of the brethren, the greater part of whom then lived below” in 1 and 2.]. [Note: [Col. 0513] *can* in 4.] For both the pleasantness of the site and a not inconsiderable abundance of resources urged him to this; at the same time, the narrow and steep habitation on the mountain was exceedingly laborious and was not sufficient for so numerous a multitude of brethren [Note: [Col. 0513] “and by then it was no longer sufficient” in 1 and 2.].

Accordingly, he instructed a certain brother Garioald [Note: [Col. 0513] absent in 1 and 2; *Carioald* in 2.], who after him discharged the office of overall care for that place [Note: [Col. 0513] added in 4.], to apply every effort to this undertaking and [Note: [Col. 0513] *that* added in the edition.] immediately make fit for the buildings of the new [Note: [Col. 0513] absent in 1 and 2.] monastery the place where Abbot Poto had formerly built a church of Saint Benedict [Note: [Col. 0513] “where Abbot Poto had earlier built a small church of Saint Benedict” in 1 and the edition.]. [Note: [Col. 0513] “concerning this matter—and” absent in 1.] He promptly undertook the command. Since all that place stood like a marsh, stagnant with reeds and water, he filled it throughout with much earth and heaps of stones; and on the site of the former little church he constructed a spacious basilica, in honour [Note: [Col. 0513] *honorem* in 1 and the edition.] of the Lord Saviour, in a quite beautiful work [Note: [Col. 0514C] It survived until 1694. Gattula, *History*, p. 71, where he supplied the architect’s testimony together with an illustration of the church.].

This basilica, supported here and there on twenty-four marble bases and columns [Note: [Col. 0513] “twenty-four” added in 1b.], and enclosed by broad porticoes, measures eighty-two cubits in length, forty-three in width, and twenty-eight in height. Above, it is wonderfully panelled with beams and cypress boards, and roofed with tiles [Note: [Col. 0513] “it has a cypress-panelled ceiling and is covered with tiles; he adorned the walls around it with beautiful figures” in 1.]; its surrounding walls are adorned with most beautiful figures [Note: [Col. 0513] *circuit* in 1 and the edition; absent in 4.]. Moreover, the flooring—how splendid and solid it is, how conspicuous for its variety of stones—and the enclosure of the choir, how it is bounded by beautiful great slabs of marble, are plainly visible to those who look upon them [Note: [Col. 0513] “conspicuous, and the enclosure of the choir” in the edition; “and—is enclosed” absent in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0515] *seeing* in 1 and the edition.].

In the central apse of the same basilica [Note: [Col. 0515] *its* in 1 and the edition.], which is reached by seven steps, he set up [Note: [Col. 0515] *established* in 1 and the edition.] an altar in honour, as stated, of the Lord Saviour. On the right he placed an altar of Saint Benedict; on the left he made an altar in honour of Saint Martin. He also made before that church [Note: [Col. 0515] “Before the same basilica he made an atrium” in 1 and the edition.] an atrium forty cubits long [Note: [Col. 0515] “forty-one” in 1.] and of equal width. He erected it all around on sixteen marble columns [Note: [Col. 0515] “number twelve” written above the line in 1b; “sixteen, eleven all around” in 4.], and placed stone channels around it near the pavement, so that water might always run off. On the eastern side of this atrium, facing the church, he made an apse and established there an altar of Saint Michael. In its middle [Note: [Col. 0515] “in—and erected” added in 1b.] he raised an exceedingly beautiful bell-tower upon eight great columns. On both sides of the same church he made many very large and beautiful buildings for various functions, for his own use as well as that of the brethren; he also paved the whole monastery precinct with large stone slabs because of overflowing water.

**18.** The aforesaid abbot likewise [Note: [Col. 0515] *again* in 3.] exerted himself no less diligently above, where he suitably built several dwellings. He also enlarged completely the church in which the body of blessed Benedict had been deposited, since it was small; roofing all its structure of cypress timbers with lead [Note: [Col. 0515] “and its roof” in 1 and the edition; *covered* in 1 and the edition.], he adorned it with various ornaments, both gold and silver. Above the altar of blessed [Note: [Col. 0515] *saint* in 1 and the edition.] Benedict he set up a silver ciborium; adorning it partly with gold and enamels [Note: [Col. 0515] *and* in 1 and the edition.], he sheathed the other altars of the same church with silver plates.

At the place called Valley of Light (*Vallis Luci*) [Note: [Col. 0515C] On the map in Gattula it lies a little above Saint Elia. We have “the Fork of V[allis Luci]” in 1, 5.], he built a church in honour of the Holy Angel [Note: [Col. 0515] “and established there various buildings for the monks’ use” added in 1, deleted in 1b.]. He also established [Note: [Col. 0515] *made* in 1.] a church for the holy martyr of Christ Apollinaris, in the place then called Albianus, but now called Saint Apollinaris after that martyr [Note: [Col. 0515C] South of Cassino, beyond the Liris.] [Note: [Col. 0515] absent in 1.].

He lived in the times of the aforesaid emperors Constantine and Irene, of the Beneventan princes Grimoald son of Arichis and another Grimoald surnamed the Treasurer, and of the Roman pontiffs Hadrian and Leo III [see Leo III]. Of the latter, after the Romans had deprived him of his eyes and tongue, almighty God wonderfully and powerfully restored both sight and speech. [Note: [Col. 0515] In 1, 2, and the edition: “He lived in the times of the aforesaid emperors Constantine and Irene, of the Beneventan princes [the aforesaid, added in 1b] Grimoald, etc.—namely the third, to whom—wonderfully restored sight and speech”; “namely—to speech” absent in 1. From there 1 and 2 continue: “but in the times of the emperors Constantine and Irene. Who, having been deprived—left,” as below.]

For this abbot [Note: [Col. 0515] “To this abbot the aforesaid prince Grimoald added on various occasions [property] in the place of Saint Martin” in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0515] added in 4.] the aforesaid Prince Grimoald, by his charter, confirmed (February 797) all free women who had been joined to the slaves of this monastery, from the time [Note: [Col. 0515] added in 4.] of the first Gisulf [Note: [Col. 0515C] “Both those from the time of lord Gisulf and those of lord Liutprand, or of our lord father of holy and sweet memory, and in our most fortunate time”: where it is apparent that the younger Gisulf is meant.] to that day, together with their sons and daughters and all that belonged to them. [Note: [Col. 0515C] From the register of Peter the Deacon, published by Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 18. Executed at Benevento in the most sacred palace, in the ninth year, second month, fifth indiction.]

By another charter [Note: [Col. 0516C] There, p. 19, from the same source. Executed in the tenth year, that is, 797 or 798.] he granted to this place the monastery of Saint Mary at Banza [Note: [Col. 0515] *Banze* in 1b and 2.], situated in the territory of Acerentia [Note: [Col. 0516C] Acerenza, formerly Acheruntia; cf. Horace, III.4.15.], with its male and female slaves and tenant farmers, and with all its possessions and appurtenances entire [Note: [Col. 0515] “of the same monastery” in 1b and the edition.].

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0516C] In Grimoald’s ninth year, in January, fifth indiction. Gattula, *Accessiones*, pp. 19–20, from the same Register, nos. 179–180.] the aforesaid Waco [Note: [Col. 0515] *Guacco* in 1b and 2; *Vaco* in 4.], a Beneventan, offered in the church of Saint Benedict (January 797), which he himself had built by the Gate of Rufinus within the city of Benevento on his own property [Note: [Col. 0515] “had built—Saint Januarius” is cut off in 1b; retained in 1*.], all his possessions: namely, his own house adjoining that church, with all its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0515] *its* in 1*.]; an estate at Septimum; an estate at Saint Angel at Pecte; an inheritance at Salerno; an estate at Caudis; an estate at Forcle; an estate at Saint Januarius, with male and female slaves; an olive-grove at Ariano; his mills on the river Sabbato [Note: [Col. 0515] “five clerical boys—should remain under the authority of the aforesaid monastery” added here in 1b and 2, omitted below.] [Note: [Col. 0516C] It flows near Benevento along with the river Calore; it joins the latter, and they finally flow into the Vulturnus. ANG.]; likewise [Note: [Col. 0515] *again* in 1b and the edition.] another house within Benevento, where he lived, together with its courtyard and kitchen; another new house beside the street where Saint Arthellais is [Note: [Col. 0515] *Archellais* in 2.], with its courtyard and appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0515] “its appurtenance” in 1b and the edition.]; likewise [Note: [Col. 0515] added in 4.] an estate below Apice and Toroniano, near the river Arvi [Note: [Col. 0515] *Arbi* in 1b and 2.]; an estate at Autiano and Ceppaluni; the Field of the Nepetas; another estate [Note: [Col. 0515] see note f.] at Crosta, with an olive-grove; and five clerical boys, with very many male slaves [Note: [Col. 0515] see note f.], besides many others whom he set free. This was on the condition that they should always remain under the authority of the aforesaid church [Note: [Col. 0517] “of the aforesaid monastery” in 1b and the edition.].

In the church of Saint Benedict situated at Casa Gentiana in the district of Liburia, which belonged to him, the same Wacco [Note: [Col. 0517] *Guacco* in 1b and the edition.] also offered the field of Porcari, the meadow called Porcile [Note: [Col. 0517] “the meadow also which is called P[orcile], and” in 1b and the edition.], and twelve families of slaves with all their appurtenances entire, dwelling in the place [Note: [Col. 0517] *village* in 1b and the edition.] called Balusanus [Note: [Col. 0517] *Balusanu* in 1b and 2.]; as well as his other male and female slaves dwelling in the aforesaid Casa Gentiana, together with all their property and possessions [Note: [Col. 0517] “all their goods” in 1b and the edition.].

When approaching death, Wacco offered and conveyed all these things entire, together with the aforesaid churches, to this monastery of blessed Benedict [Note: [Col. 0517] “offered in this [monastery]” in 1b and 2; “the same Wacco” absent in 3.], reserving only [Note: [Col. 0517] added in 4.] to his wife Tasia, for her life and under the protection of this monastery, the usufruct of half of all of them [Note: [Col. 0517] *these* in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0517] absent in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0517] “under the protection of this monastery” absent in 1b, 1*, and 2; *only* in 1b, 1*, and the edition; “for her life, with usufruct” in 1*.].

In these same days [Note: [Col. 0517C] In Grimoald’s third year, September. Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 21, from the register of Peter the Deacon. Caiatia, now Caiazzo, lies not far from Capua, to the west.] a man named Colo, from the territory of Caiatia [Note: [Col. 0517] *Cajazzano* in 1b and 2.], offered to the church of Saint Martin, a dependency of this monastery situated beside the Vulturnus, his entire estate at the place called Aditianus (September 808), with all property pertaining to it, on mountain and plain alike [Note: [Col. 0517] *above* in 1b and 2; “which is called Aditianus” in 1b and the edition; *itself* in 1b and the edition.]. Similarly, one Maximus [Note: [Col. 0517C] Register no. 85. AUG.], from the same territory [Note: [Col. 0517] *aforesaid* in 1b and the edition.], offered blessed Benedict all his property entire at the aforesaid place of Saint Martin.

This abbot issued a charter to certain people of Termoli [Note: [Col. 0517C] Termoli lies on the upper sea, near the mouths of the Biferno.], concerning all Saint Benedict’s property which we possessed there, for an annual rent of fourteen solidi and half of the entire pasturage. [Note: [Col. 0517] “This abbot made a charter—pasturage” absent in 1; “Here,” in the edition.] He died [Note: [Col. 0517] See above, p. 593, note e*.] on the ninth day before the Kalends of January (817) and was buried beside the church of blessed Benedict, before the chapter-house, on the left as one enters the church [Note: [Col. 0517C] “In his time the breviary concerning the dependencies of the March was made” added in 2.].

**APOLLINARIS**, fourteenth in rank, was raised to the abbacy [Note: [Col. 0517] “in the same year in which Sico was made prince at Benevento” added in 1.] and held office for eleven years. He lived in the times of the Roman pontiffs Paschal and Eugenius, and of Sico, prince of Benevento [Note: [Col. 0517] “Sico, who in the same year was made prince at Benevento” in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0517] “He lived—in the times of the Roman pontiffs Paschal and Eugenius, and of Sico, prince of Benevento” absent in 1; see below, p. 595, note f.].

**19.** [DESIDERIUS, *Dialogues* I.1.] Concerning this most holy man there is a celebrated report, confirmed by the testimony of our elders: once [Note: [Col. 0517] absent in 4.], when necessity compelled him to go out to inspect the monastery’s possessions, he needed to ford the river Liris. But since there was no boat by which he could cross, the man of God, filled with faith, fortified himself with the sign of the saving cross. Going to the riverbank, dressed and shod as he was, he entered it [Note: [Col. 0517] *it* in 1 and the edition.]; and thus, in a wondrous manner, after the example of the apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0517] “of the apostle Peter” added in 1b.], he was carried across to the farther bank with feet and garments alike dry [Note: [Col. 0517] “he was carried across with dry feet, so that” in 1 and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0517] “he was carried across to the bank with dry garments, so that” in 3.], so that he was thought to have walked not upon water but upon dry land [Note: [Col. 0517] *dry earth* in the edition.]. [Note: [Col. 0517] “He lived in the times of the Roman pontiffs Paschal and Eugenius” added in 1. The rest of this chapter is added in 1b, but in another order, thus: “In the days of this abbot, a certain nobleman named Arnipert—his immovable possessions. Rodegarius—the monastery. In the same time Trasemundus—established. Also a certain Capuan, Dachopert, offered—his.” Thus also in the edition.]

At the same time Trasemundus [Note: [Col. 0518C] The following donations from Peter’s Register were published by Gattula, *Accessiones*, pp. 27, 28, 30, 31. He omitted one Rodegarius, whose charter, ANG. noted, survives in Register no. 188.] a nobleman of Benevento offered to this monastery his houses within Benevento (5 May 820); also the estate he possessed at the place called *ad pantanum*, joined to the property of our monastery [Note: [Col. 0518C] See above, chapter 10.]; another estate [Note: [Col. 0517] *another estate* in 1b and the edition.] in the valley of Caudis, at the place called Laudecene; an estate at Forinum; an estate in the territory of Alife [Note: [Col. 0517] *Alifanis* in 1b; above, chapter 6, *Aliphano*.], at the place called Vulcanum; with all the appurtenances of those estates. He also declared all his slaves free, providing that they should perform three days’ labour per month for our officials in the place where they lived [Note: [Col. 0517] *live* in 2.].

Rodegarius, gastald of Benevento, made a hospice near Benevento from his own property [Note: [Col. 0517] “from his own goods, where he offered” in 1b and the edition.]. In it he offered his houses within the city, the church of Saint Saviour, which is situated outside Casa Maggiore, a mill at Tassile, and the tithes of all his property; and he placed it under this monastery.

A nobleman named Arnipert, a native of Compsa, offered blessed Benedict five estates in diverse places (March 823), with every one of their appurtenances, both movable and immovable [Note: [Col. 0517] “from his own goods, where he offered” in 1b and the edition.], and with very many male and female slaves. He also gave one tunic with a gold border [Note: [Col. 0519C] That is, an edge, hem, or band.], gold circlets, a gold band with pearls [Note: [Col. 0519] “one gold band” in 1b and the edition.], and likewise a gold clasp, together with half of all his movable property.

A cleric named Daniel, noble by birth and a native of Taranto [Note: [Col. 0519] “Daniel, a native of Taranto, noble by birth” in 1b and the edition.], when near his end (827) [Note: [Col. 0519C] In Sico’s time, fifth indiction.], conveyed himself and all his possessions to this monastery by a charter of offering, together with very many male and female slaves at Aquino and at the cell of Saint Gregory situated in its vicinity [Note: [Col. 0519] “Gregory, which is situated in its vicinity” in 1b and the edition.]. Hence some of ours not implausibly maintain [Note: [Col. 0519] *think* in 1b and the edition.] that the servants we still have today are descended from those slaves of the aforesaid Daniel [Note: [Col. 0519] “of the aforesaid men” in the edition; “of the aforesaid men” in 1b, in an erased place.] [Note: [Col. 0519] *begotten* in 1b.]. [Note: [Col. 0519] “Some, and not without reason, think” in 1b; “some now think throughout” in 2.]

Likewise a certain Dachenaldus, a Capuan [Note: [Col. 0519] “a Capuan by birth” in 1b and the edition.], offered to this monastery (827) [Note: [Col. 0519C] In Grimoald’s tenth year, where Gattula, book I, teaches that Sico must be read.] all his property entirely at the place called Cannetus [Note: [Col. 0519] *Cannetu* in 1b; *Cannetum* in 2.], and in various other places in [Note: [Col. 0519] added in 4.] the county of Caiazzo, with lands, tenant farmers, various animals, and all his movable and immovable goods. Dachopert, likewise a Capuan, similarly offered blessed Benedict (March 825) his estate at the place called Colimniana, with houses, courtyards, and all its appurtenances entire.

**20.** [ERCH. 9.] Moreover [Note: [Col. 0519] the entire chapter added in 1b.], Radechis [Note: [Col. 0519] *Radelchis* in 4.], count of Compsa, who after killing Grimoald [Note: [Col. 0519] *Grimoald* in 1b and the edition.] had established the aforesaid Sico as prince (817), not long afterwards, moved by repentance, abandoned the world, bound a chain around his neck, and came here to the monastery of blessed Benedict. The devil, grieving [Note: [Col. 0519] *grieving* in 4.] and also [Note: [Col. 0519] added in 4.] envying his exceedingly harsh and therefore fruitful penitence [Note: [Col. 0519] “and therefore fruitful” absent in 1b and 2.], often cried out around the monastery cloisters in the hearing of many, saying [Note: [Col. 0519] absent in 1b and 2.]:

> “Woe is me, woe is me, Benedict! Why do you wrong me so cruelly? Why do you pursue me so relentlessly? Was it not enough for you to drive me myself from here? In addition, you do not cease to claim for yourself my faithful followers from every quarter. Woe, woe is me!”  
> [Note: [Col. 0519] “Woe, woe is me” absent in 1b and 2.]

[*Chronicle of Radelchis* 57.] Furthermore, the aforesaid Prince Sico [Note: [Col. 0519] “This Sico” in 1b and the edition.], after he had long besieged and afflicted Naples, finally took away the body of the holy martyr Januarius from the place where it had been deposited [Note: [Col. 0519] “from the place where it had been deposited” absent in 1b and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0519] *deposited* in 3.], brought it to Benevento, and honourably laid it in the episcopal complex of that city with his former holy companions Festus and Desiderius [Note: [Col. 0519] “with Saints Festus and Desiderius, honourably laid in that episcopal complex” in 1b and the edition.], as is reported in the history of Lord Erchempert [Note: [Col. 0519] absent in 1b and 2; “as is reported in his history” subsequently added in another ink.]. [Note: [Col. 0519C] He added the final words later, after finding that an event heard from the Beneventans was confirmed by the *Chronicle of Salerno*, which he attributed to Erchempert; yet nothing there is said of Festus and Desiderius. The history of the translation survives in *Acta Sanctorum*, September, vol. VI, p. 888.]

**21.** [ERCH. 11.] In the third year of this abbot, Saracens coming from Babylonia and Africa [Note: [Col. 0519] “coming and Panormus” in 4.] occupied Sicily and captured Panormus, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 820 [Note: [Col. 0519] “entered Sicily” in 1b and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0519C] I do not know whence Leo derived the claim that Saracens, namely those of Spain, entered Sicily in that year. But his transferring the conquest of Panormus from Erchempert to this point is his own conjecture and has no foundation. It was captured in A.D. 832.]. [Note: [Col. 0519] “In his third year the Saracens entered Sicily, A.D. 820” in 1; “in this abbot’s third year the Saracens from Babylon, etc.” in 1b and the edition.] The same abbot died on 27 November 828 [Note: [Col. 0519] “the same abbot” added in 4.] and was buried near the church of Saint Benedict, beside the steps of the portico through which one then went to the church of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0519] “near the church of Saint Benedict” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0519] *then* added in 1b; *at that time* added in 4.].

**DEUSDEDIT**, fifteenth abbot, held office for six years, in the time of the princes Sico and Sichard [Note: [Col. 0519] “in the time of Prince Sico” absent in 1 and 2.].

**22.** To him the same Prince Sico [Note: [Col. 0519] *aforesaid* in 1 and the edition.] granted a charter [Note: [Col. 0520C] It is not extant. A donation made to Abbot Deusdedit by Duke Romuald, in the second indiction, at the place called the river Lauro, from Peter’s Register, was published by Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 32. It appears either forged or certainly corrupt. The river Lauro flows into Lake Lesina.] for the river called Lauro, with all its boundaries and fisheries, and all things which, on either side near that river, belonged by right to his palace.

[ERCH. 13.] [Note: [Col. 0519] “But he died on the seventh Ides of November (corrected to October) and was buried at the church of Saint Benedict” in 1; these words were deleted in 1b, which adds “When Sico died—restored.”] When Sico died (832), Sichard his son became prince, a man most wicked [Note: [Col. 0519] “a man, a man in every way” in 1b and 2.] and beset by every carnal vice, and above all most avaricious [Note: [Col. 0520C] He appears such from the *Chronicle of Salerno*.]. For money’s sake he seized the aforesaid venerable abbot, a man conspicuous for every holiness [Note: [Col. 0519] *spicuum* in 4; *conspicuum* in Erchempert.], and committed him to custody. [Note: [Col. 0519] *aforesaid* in 1b and the edition.] When this holy man [Note: [Col. 0519] added in 4.] died on 9 October 834 [Note: [Col. 0520C] Roman Martyrology, 9 October: “At Cassino, Saint Deusdedit, abbot, who, thrust into prison by the tyrant Sichard, there, exhausted by hunger and sufferings, gave up his spirit”; on this day his memorial is observed among us with a double rite. ANG.], at the place where he was buried [Note: [Col. 0519] thus in 1c; “and he was buried beside the church of blessed Benedict” in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0519] *where* in 1c and the edition.], he restored to their former health many afflicted with fever and oppressed with diverse ailments, as they sought with faith through prayers to his ashes and through his merits [Note: [Col. 0521] “through prayers and his merits” absent in 1b and 2.].

**HILDERIC**, sixteenth abbot [Note: [Col. 0521C] On him, Peter the Deacon, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9.], held office for seventeen days.

**AUTHPERT** [Note: [Col. 0521] *Authpert* in 1 and 2.], made seventeenth abbot in succession [Note: [Col. 0521] absent in 4.], held office for three years.

**23.** Lothair [Note: [Col. 0521] *Lutharius* in 3.], king of the Franks, son [Note: [Col. 0521] “son of Louis” added in 1b.] of the aforesaid Louis, issued a charter to him (21 February 835), confirming all that had hitherto been conferred upon this holy monastery by kings and princes [Note: [Col. 0521C] Published from Peter’s Register by Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 32.]. By another charter [Note: [Col. 0521C] There, p. 34, from the genuine original, dated in the thirteenth indiction, 21 February.] he confirmed to this monastery the large meadow called Cervarium [Note: [Col. 0521] “the large meadow which is called Cervarius” in 1 and the edition.], and slaves and many estates belonging to his fisc in the district of the Marsi.

[ERCH. 11.] Under this Lothair [Note: [Col. 0521] *Lothgarius* in 3.] the kingdom of the Franks was divided: he himself obtained the region of Aachen and Italy; his brother Louis [Note: [Col. 0521] *Lodevicus* in 3.] Bavaria; and Charles, born of another mother, Aquitaine. [Note: [Col. 0521] “From this Lothair—the kingdom was divided” added in 1b.]

Moreover Sichard, prince of the Beneventans [Note: [Col. 0521] *likewise* in 1.], granted to Saint Benedict by his charter (June 837) the woodland called Martoranus [Note: [Col. 0521] *then* added in 1 and deleted in 1b.], with its boundaries and limits, banks and waters, fishponds [Note: [Col. 0521] *fassariis* in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0521C] They seem to be fishponds.] and fisheries, and all contained within it, as it then appeared to belong by right to the palace. [Note: [Col. 0521C] There, p. 35, from the Register. Executed at Benevento in the sacred palace, in the fifth year, June, fifteenth indiction.]

At that time [Note: [Col. 0521] “In these times” in 1b and the edition.] a man named Rodegarius, from the territory of Compsa, offered this monastery four estates, with all their appurtenances, and several male and female slaves (June 835) [Note: [Col. 0521C] There, p. 35, from the Register: in the third year of the principate of our lord Sichard, June, twelfth indiction—read thirteenth indiction.].

Some little works and fine sermons by this abbot survive [Note: [Col. 0521] added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0521C] They survive at Cassino in manuscript 305. On him see Peter the Deacon, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 13, and I. B. Marus there. ANG.]. He died on 20 February 838 [Note: [Col. 0521] “He died—March” added in 1b.].

**BASSACIUS**, eighteenth abbot appointed from blessed Benedict, in the 363rd year of the Lord’s incarnation, 837 [Note: [Col. 0521C] Either the year must be erroneous if that privilege of Prince Sichard is genuine, or he was appointed while Authpert was still alive.], held office for nineteen years.

[Col. 0522A] **24.** In the third year of this appointment, while the aforesaid Prince Sicard was still alive, the body of the blessed Apostle Bartholomew was brought by divine ordinance from the island of Lipari to Benevento. [Note: [Col. 0521] The opening words of this chapter are absent in manuscript 1b; the edition of 1b adds “of this … and several other things.”] [Note: [Col. 0521] “Blessed Apostle” is “blessed” and “apostle” in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0521] “By divine ordinance” is absent in manuscripts 1b and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0521] “Into which … transported” is absent in manuscripts 1b and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0521C] A.D. 838, in August; but when the church had been completed, the altar was dedicated on 25 October 839, after Sicard’s death, in Bassacius’s third year according to Leo’s reckoning. Sermons delivered on the anniversary of the translation survive: one attributed to Bertharius, abbot of Cassino, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. V, August; another, more accurate, by Martin, a monk, addressed to Roffred, archbishop of Benevento, who held office from the year 1076, in Borgia, *Memorie Beneventane*, I, p. 333.] It had formerly been conveyed miraculously from Armenia to that island by sea, in a stone tomb and without any helmsman.

At about the same time Gontarius [Note: [Col. 0522C] Register no. 299. ANG.] abbot of the monastery of Saint Modestus, restored to blessed Benedict the properties which Abbot Authpert had formerly granted by a written deed of agreement to Prince Sicard: namely, the estate called Milazzano [Note: [Col. 0521] “Milactianum” in manuscripts 1b and 2.] with the church of Saint Mary, all its ornaments and appurtenances, in the district of Canosa; the estate called Plazano; the estate at Campi; the estate at Pastena; and one house [Col. 0522B] at Cannae [Note: [Col. 0521] “Canni” in manuscript 1b and the edition.] with all its substance [Note: [Col. 0521] Absent in manuscript 1b and the edition.]; together with fishing rights in the sea and all the appurtenances of the properties mentioned above. [Note: [Col. 0521] These notices concerning the traditions are written in the autograph manuscript individually in the margin wherever there was room, in an order different from the one given here from manuscript 4. The first was Agenardus, followed by Arnefrid, then Maio, fourth Gontarius, fifth Theodericus.]

In these same days [Note: [Col. 0521] Absent in manuscript 1b and the edition.]—in May 849—a certain Agenardus [Note: [Col. 0521] “Agenardus” corrected from “Ahgen” in manuscript 1b; “Hagenardus” in manuscript 4. “Aienardus,” “Agenardus,” and “Achenardus” occur in the diploma itself.] [Note: [Col. 0522C] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 36: in the tenth year of Sikenolf, indiction XII. He was a Capuan by origin; Lando, gastald of Capua, subscribed the charter.] Capuan gastald, made a charter of donation to this monastery of absolutely all the property he appeared to possess, both in the territory of Capua [Note: [Col. 0521] Absent in manuscript 1b and the edition.] and in that of Teano [Note: [Col. 0521] Absent in manuscript 1b and the edition.] and at Calinulo [Note: [Col. 0522C] Today Carinola, near Sessa.], together with male and female slaves and everything that belonged to him by hereditary right.

Likewise, a certain Arnefrid [Note: [Col. 0522C] Register no. 308. ANG.], an Alifan nobleman [Note: [Col. 0521] “Alifanus” in manuscript 1b and the edition.], offered to blessed Benedict his son Amelfrid, a cleric, together with his entire estate at the place called Patenaria and all the appurtenances of that estate; and also his entire share in the church of Saints Nazarius [Col. 0522C] and Vincent [Note: [Col. 0521] “Of” is added in manuscript 1b and the edition.] at the place called Anglena, with its ornaments and estates, and all [Note: [Col. 0521] “Absolutely all” is added in manuscript 1b and the edition.] its appurtenances and possessions.

A certain Maio [Note: [Col. 0521] “Likewise also a certain Maio” in manuscript 1 and the edition; “Likewise … their” is cut away in manuscript 1b but preserved in manuscript 1.] of Telese [Note: [Col. 0522C] Gattola, ibid., p. 36. The deed is dated in the third year of the prince, indiction IV. Telese lies in Terra di Lavoro, between the rivers Volturno and Calore.], when he was approaching death—in January 856—gave himself to this monastery together with all that was his: namely, one estate at Telesia [Col. 0523A] called Pulianellum [Note: [Col. 0523] “Pulianellu” in manuscripts 1 and 2.], and another [Note: [Col. 0523] “Another” in manuscript 1 and the edition.] at Alife [Note: [Col. 0523] “Alife” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], in which the church of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0523] “The church called Saint Peter” in manuscript 1 and the edition.] had been built, together with its woodland around that church and all the appurtenances of both estates, as well as the male and female slaves [Note: [Col. 0523] “All” is added in manuscript 1 and the edition.] living on those estates, and everything belonging to them.

Moreover, Theodericus [Note: [Col. 0523C] Register no. 398: in the fourth year of Prince Radelchis, in May, indiction VI. ANG. Squilla is still a village near Caiatia, not far from the Volturno.] count of Caiatia [Note: [Col. 0523] “Of Caiatia” is absent in manuscript 4; “of Calatia” in manuscript 4.] granted by his will, in May 843, to this place an estate called Squillae, with everything belonging to it [Note: [Col. 0523] “With … it” is absent in manuscript 1b and the edition.]; moreover, one silver bowl, three *scattones*, two *garales*, one golden *bandum*, three horses [Note: [Col. 0523] “Three horses” is absent in manuscripts 1b and 2.], and several other things.

[Note: [Col. 0523C] Among our people, *scattones* are the bowls by which sellers measure dry goods, such as lupins and similar things. ANG. A *garalis* is a kind of cup; a *bandus* is a banner or ribbon.]

This abbot lived during the pontificates of the Roman popes Sergius II, Leo IV, Benedict III, and Nicholas I, from whom he received a privilege of apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0523C] Register no. 4. ANG.] concerning the liberty and confirmation of this monastery. He lived also during the reigns of the princes Radelchis [Note: [Col. 0523] “Rathelchis” in manuscript 3.] and Siconolf, under whom the Beneventan principality was divided by a faction of the Capuans against one another [Note: [Col. 0523] “Thus, the Capuans” in manuscript 1; “Capuans” in manuscript 1b.]. Since we too were a very great part of their disaster, we have thought it necessary and appropriate to insert into this little history why and how it was divided, and on what occasion the Saracens were first invited here by them.

**25.** [Note: [Col. 0523C] These matters were taken from *Chronicon Casinese*, chapter 8, sections 4 and 17, and were later corrected and enlarged from Erchempert, chapters 14–17.] When the aforesaid Prince Sicard had been wickedly murdered by his own men in 839, the aforesaid Radelchis, his treasurer [Note: [Col. 0523] “Radelchis, treasurer of his palace” in manuscript 1.], succeeded him in the principality.

Meanwhile, the Capuans, over whom the gastald Landulf then presided [Note: [Col. 0523] “Castaldeus” in manuscripts 1b and 2.], and who, because of their many crimes, had Radelchis as a very bitter enemy [Note: [Col. 0523] “Who had the aforesaid Radelchis as a very bitter enemy because of their many crimes” in manuscript 1b.], fearing his rule excessively, took counsel and went to Siconolf, son of the aforesaid Prince Sico, who was then living in exile at Taranto [Note: [Col. 0523] “Was then living” is added in manuscript 1b.], and chose him as their prince. Siconolf, entering Salerno with those Capuans and with a very great force of Beneventans who hated the aforesaid Radelchis [Col. 0524A] rose against Radelchis in every possible way; and they began to contend against one another with all their strength.

But since, as Truth says, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Luke 11:17), and, as one of the authors says [Note: [Col. 0524C] He added this from his own source; “as Livy says,” in the pseudo-Anastasius.], “By concord small things grow; by discord the greatest fall apart” (Sallust, *Jugurtha* 10), each side summoned Saracen armies from different parts of the world against the other. Through their dissension, sword, and fire, these armies devastated for almost thirty years not only the whole principality but even the kingdom of Italy.

Radelchis was therefore the first to invite the Saracens to his aid, in 841, through a certain Pando, his faithful man [Note: [Col. 0523] “To his aid” is added in the edition.], who then governed Bari. [Note: [Col. 0523] “He invited them. They first crossed over near Bari; after besieging it for several days, they finally captured it by a nocturnal stratagem, and not long afterwards also obtained Taranto. Their …” in manuscript 1.] When the imprudent Pando had stationed them beside the walls of the city [Col. 0524B] [Note: [Col. 0523] “Wall” in manuscripts 1b and 2.] and along the seashore [Note: [Col. 0523] “The shore of the sea” in manuscript 1b and the edition.], they, cunning by nature, entered the city through hidden places in the dead of night. After killing many others, they gave Pando himself to the waves of the sea [Note: [Col. 0523] “Pando, the traitor to his country, to …” in manuscripts 1b and 2.].

Their king was named Calphon. Since the aforesaid Radelchis could not drive them from the city, he began to cultivate them as though they were allies and to call them to his aid [Note: [Col. 0523] “Thus, with whom Radelchis … the whole of Siconolf’s …” in manuscript 1b.]. Together with them he devastated the whole territory of Siconolf and reduced all Capua to ashes.

Siconolf, on the other hand, summoned Saracens from Spain and, in frequent battles, took almost every surrounding city from Radelchis by force, except Siponto; nevertheless, he also besieged Benevento in 843 [Note: [Col. 0524C] That is, he attacked it.].

**26.** [Note: [Col. 0524C] Leo took almost the entire chapter from *Chronicon Casinese*, chapter 10, but also used other ancient records now unknown to us. ANG.] The seventh annual cycle of the aforesaid abbot was now turning—that is, the year 843—when the aforesaid Siconolf came to the monastery of blessed Benedict. Under the pretext of a payment to be made to the Spanish Hagarenes, he carried off almost the entire treasury which the kings of glorious memory—Charles, and his brother Pippin, and Carloman, and Louis, sons of that same Pippin [Note: [Col. 0524C] It was the author, not the copyists, who fell asleep here, as the autograph manuscript shows here and elsewhere; yet Ang. de Nuce and others heap many reproaches upon undeserving copyists.]—and many other kings or devout princes had bestowed there [Note: [Col. 0523] “Brought away” in manuscript 1 and the edition.].

On the first occasion he took, in chalices and patens, crowns and crosses, *phialae*, *amuli*, *bokis* [Note: [Col. 0525C] Another reading is *bauca*, a kind of vessel; hence Italian *boccale* and our *Pokal*.], and brooches, one hundred and thirty pounds of the purest gold [Note: [Col. 0525] “Thirty” is added in manuscript 1b.]; moreover, a silk *sarica* [Note: [Col. 0525C] A purple mantle.] of *sylphori*, with gold and gems. In return for these things he promised to pay ten thousand Sicilian solidi. Therefore his kinsman Ursus [Note: [Col. 0525C] Count of Compsa; see Erchempert.], and Grimoald [Note: [Col. 0525] “Grimoaldus” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], made for this monastery a written undertaking of restitution [Note: [Col. 0525] “For this monastery” is added in manuscript 4.].

On a second occasion he took three hundred and sixty-five pounds of silver and thirteen thousand stamped gold solidi [Note: [Col. 0525] “Fourteen” in manuscript 2.]. He also took two silver *bazias* [Note: [Col. 0525C] They seem to be a kind of dish; English “basin.”], weighing thirty pounds [Note: [Col. 0525] “Weighing thirty pounds” in manuscript 1b and the edition.], and eight double *fundati* [Note: [Col. 0525C] Both cloths and vessels are designated in this way.]. He also took, in embossed work, one *bazia* and one Constantinopolitan *scatto* [Note: [Col. 0525] “Scatto” is absent in manuscript 4.], both of silver and gilded.

Again, after about eight months, he took five hundred pounds of silver in crowns, *bazias*, *amuli*, *garales*, and spoons [Note: [Col. 0525] “Of silver” is absent in manuscript 2; “silver” is added in manuscript 1b; “at the same time” in manuscript 1 and the edition.]. Ten months afterwards he came and broke open the monastery’s wardrobe or vestry, and took from it fourteen thousand *mazati* solidi. [Note: [Col. 0525C] I believe these were coined silver pieces; *mazza* means “hammer” in Italian. Above they are called *figurati*, and below *praedulati*.]

For these things Bishop Leo and his gastalds Peter and Landenulf swore upon the Gospels, the Cross, and the body of Saint Benedict that within four months they would restore that price to the monastery. Since they had no means of repaying it, they issued to this monastery a grant of Saint Nazarius in Canzia [Note: [Col. 0525] “Canziae” in manuscript 1; “Canzie” in manuscript 2.] [Note: [Col. 0526C] This was the name of that part of Campania lying north of the Volturno, on both sides of the Appian Way; in Peregrini’s time, Terra di Canzo. *Campania felice*, p. 467.] with all its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0525] “With all its appurtenances” is added in manuscript 4.].

Again, Lando [Note: [Col. 0526C] Perhaps Count of Capua?] and Aldemarius, his gastalds, came and carried away from here two thousand *praedulati* solidi. Likewise, when he went to Spoleto [Note: [Col. 0525] “Spoleto” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], his kinsman Maio took another two thousand [Note: [Col. 0525] “He took another two thousand *praedulati* solidi” in manuscript 1 and the edition.]. Finally, when he went to Rome in 844, the same Siconolf came and took a golden crown wonderfully adorned with emerald gems [Note: [Col. 0525] “Adorned with emeralds and sapphires” in the edition.], which had belonged to his father, Prince Sico [Note: [Col. 0525] “To that same man” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], for three thousand solidi.

The aforesaid sacrilegious man took all these things from Saint Benedict, but gained nothing from them either for himself or for his country; nor from that time onward could he win any victory [Note: [Col. 0525] “Was able thereafter to obtain any victory” in manuscript 1 and the edition.].

[Col. 0526A] **27.** [DESID. *Dialogues* 1; *Chronicon Casinese* 9.] Three years after these events [Note: [Col. 0525] “In these times, namely in the tenth year of this abbot, Pope S.” in manuscripts 1 and 2.], while Sergius II presided over the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0526C] The chronology was calculated with the aid of the *Chronicon S. Benedicti*.], from whom Emperor Louis was crowned, a huge multitude of Saracens was brought by fleet from Africa to Rome. In August they thoroughly plundered the churches of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, killing many people there. They then set out by the Appian Way and came to the city of Fundi [Note: [Col. 0526C] Fondi.].

After capturing and burning it, ravaging everything around it, and consigning all its citizens partly to captivity and partly to the sword [Note: [Col. 0525] “And all its citizens, partly to captivity and partly to the sword, and also all …” in the edition.], they encamped beside Gaeta. Against them an army of Franks sent from Spoleto [Note: [Col. 0525] “Siconolf” in manuscript 1.] was shamefully defeated and fled. The Saracens pursued them more vigorously and, on 10 November, finally reached the neighborhood of this monastery beyond the river called Carnello [Note: [Col. 0525] “The Liris” in manuscript 1b; “the river Liris” in manuscript 1.]. They burned the church of the Apostle Saint Andrew [Note: [Col. 0525] “And of Saint Apollinaris” in manuscript 1b; “burning Saint Apollinaris, immediately to …” in manuscript 1.] and then, arriving at the cell of Saint Apollinaris, martyr of Christ [Note: [Col. 0525] “Martyr of Christ” in manuscripts 1b and 2.], at the place called Albianus [Note: [Col. 0526C] See above, chapter 18.], hastened with every effort toward this monastery. Rumor had long before informed them of it, and from that place they could see it with their own eyes [Col. 0526B].

But because the lateness of the hour detained them that day, they pitched their tents there, intending certainly to hurry here the next day, destroy the entire monastery, plunder whatever might be found, and slaughter with the sword all who lived there [Note: [Col. 0525] “All …” in the edition; “all who lived here” in the edition.].

At that time the entire sky was completely clear [Note: [Col. 0525] “There” in manuscripts 1 and 2.], and the aforesaid river was so low that anyone could ford it on foot [Note: [Col. 0525] “If he wished” was added and then deleted in manuscript 1; deleted in manuscript 1b.]. When news of this reached the brothers, and they saw such a sudden and terrible death hanging over them [Note: [Col. 0525] “They saw such an immediate death hanging over them” in the edition.], they were struck with very great fear [Note: [Col. 0525] Added in manuscript 4.]. At once all, barefoot and with ashes scattered on their heads, came with litanies to blessed Benedict, praying for God’s mercy: that he might mercifully deign to receive their souls, whose bodies he had decreed in his judgment to give over to so sudden a death [Note: [Col. 0525] Absent in manuscript 3.].

While the brothers spent that whole night in vigils and prayers, Apollinaris, the abbot of holy memory of whom we spoke above [Col. 0527A] [Note: [Col. 0525] “Of whom we spoke above” is added in manuscript 4.], appeared in a vision [Note: [Col. 0527] “Meanwhile, appearing” in manuscript 1 and the edition.] to the most reverend Abbot Bassacius and said:

“Why, brother,” he said, “are you so troubled, or why do you carry such a sad and fearful heart?”

Bassacius replied: “Because, father, of the death of us all, which we see before our eyes, and because of the desolation of this holy place, which we immediately await.”

Apollinaris said: “Fear no longer, and drive all sadness and anxiety from your mind. For Father Benedict has obtained your deliverance from the Lord; know also that he himself has certainly come with us to your aid. Only complete your vows and supplications to the Lord, which we too are making with you before the Lord’s presence [Note: [Col. 0527] Absent in manuscript 4.], and be absolutely certain that the ferocity of the Saracens can now inflict no injury either upon you or upon this place [Col. 0527B].” [Note: [Col. 0527] Manuscript 1 adds: “But, restrained as speedily as possible by divine prohibition, they will hasten back to their own land.”]

When the abbot awoke and had told the brothers all these things, all fell upon their faces. With tears, sighs, and loud cries they began to render praise and thanks to God, blessing him with immense cries of joy [Note: [Col. 0527] “To glorify and bless him” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], because through the intercession of blessed Benedict he had been pleased thus to free them from the imminent danger. They devoted the rest of the night to hymns and praises of God.

“The Lord is faithful in his words and holy in all his works,” who deigned to promise the righteous man, saying: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation; I shall deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Psalm 49:15). [Note: [Col. 0527] The most holy Father Benedict also now most opportunely remembered and fulfilled what he had promised his disciples while living: “When I am more present with you after laying down the burden of the flesh, my sons, I shall by God’s grace be your constant helper and fellow-worker,” adds manuscript 1.]

And behold, around the morning watches [Note: [Col. 0527] “A little later” in manuscripts 1 and 2.], the sky—which, as we have said, had until then been completely clear in every direction [Col. 0527D]—was suddenly covered with dense, black clouds [Note: [Col. 0527] “Dense and dark clouds” in manuscript 4]. Lightning flashed, thunder roared, and such a violent downpour suddenly arose that the aforesaid river, rising beyond its banks, overflowed widely on every side.

When the Saracens rose in the morning [Note: [Col. 0527] “When morning came, therefore” in manuscript 1 and the edition.] and hurried to the riverbank, they saw from afar that the river which, as we have said, they could have crossed on foot the day before, could now scarcely be approached even at its banks. They began to search very carefully for some boat by which they might cross the river. But when they saw that every hope of crossing was denied them, and that they had been returned empty-handed from all the booty with which they had thought themselves heavily laden [Note: [Col. 0527] “Which they had thought themselves very heavily laden with” is added in manuscript 1b.], they raged—as is the way of a barbarous and savage nature—gnashing their teeth and, in fury, began to bite their fingers and hands [Col. 0528A].

They therefore set fire to the cells of this monastery named after the holy martyrs George and Stephen, and returned to their camp at Gaeta by way of the Two Lions (*duos leones*) [Note: [Col. 0527D] See below, III, 12.]. [Note: [Col. 0527] “By way of two stages” in the edition.]

After several days, when they had decided to return home [Note: [Col. 0527] Manuscript 1 adds, then deletes: “Seeing that they could not carry their horses.”], they abandoned all their weakened and hamstrung horses [Note: [Col. 0527] “Their horses” is added in manuscript 1b.], boarded their ships, and set out toward Africa [Note: [Col. 0527] “Sicily” in manuscript 1.]. When they were already so near their homeland that they could see the neighboring mountains, and were, in the sailors’ fashion, exchanging applause and congratulations among themselves [Note: [Col. 0527] “Exchanging applause and congratulations with one another” in the edition.], they suddenly saw one small craft darting back and forth among their ships. Only two men were visible in it: one, with beautiful white hair, bore the appearance of a cleric; the other was dressed in a monastic habit.

When these men carefully questioned them about where they were returning so joyfully from, and what they had done in those regions from which they were returning so heavily laden [Note: [Col. 0527] “In those regions from which they had set out” in manuscript 1; “in the regions from which they were returning” in the edition.], the Saracens confessed that they were returning from Italy and Rome itself, and that there they had perpetrated vast massacres, robberies, and burnings.

“And indeed,” they said, “we devastated the churches of Peter and Paul. Since we could not cross the river to plunder Benedict’s monastery, we set fire to its cells situated beyond the river [Note: [Col. 0527] “The Liris” in manuscript 1; “the river Liris” in manuscript 1b.].”

When they in turn asked the two men who they were, they received this answer: “We are those whose homes you boast so greatly of having plundered and burned. But you will very soon learn who we are.” At these words they suddenly disappeared together with the spoken word.

At once a violent storm arose, so great a tempest that it forced all their ships to founder: some collided with one another, and some were driven against mountains and rocks [Note: [Col. 0527] “Among” instead of “against” in manuscript 3.]. Only a few escaped [Note: [Col. 0527] “Who could escape” in the edition.], through whom these things became known to others.

In this way the Apostle Peter avenged his injuries. In this way Father Benedict delivered his monastery. [Note: [Col. 0527] Manuscript 1 has these sentences in reverse order.]

In the following period the most holy Leo was made pope. To prevent such a thing from ever happening again [Note: [Col. 0527] “Ever” is placed after “happen” in manuscript 1.], he built a castle of no small circuit around the church of blessed Peter the Apostle, with very strong walls [Note: [Col. 0527] “With excellent and firm walls” in the manuscript and edition.]. It is called to this day, from its founder’s name, the Leonine City.

**28.** [*Chronicon Casinese* 12, 14.] At that time also, Massar, commander of the Saracens, residing at Benevento in support of the aforesaid Radelchis, despised the Beneventans and oppressed them as severely as he could [Note: [Col. 0529] “And oppressed those same Beneventans” is added in manuscript 1b; “he oppressed them” in manuscript 1 and the edition.]. He devastated the monastery of Saint Mary at Cingla, captured the castle of Saint Vitus, forced the ancient city of Telesia to surrender through thirst [Note: [Col. 0529C] “Telesia” is absent in the edition and manuscripts 1 and 2.], and ravaged all the surrounding country.

Once, as he was travelling past this monastery of blessed Benedict [Note: [Col. 0529] Absent in manuscripts 1 and 2.], his barbarous mind was so transformed by heaven that, when one of his dogs caught a goose [Note: [Col. 0529] “His” in the edition.] in the monastery meadows, he himself ran with a whip and pulled it from the dog’s mouth. [Note: [Col. 0529C] *Auca* means “goose,” now Italian *oca*.]

Coming before the monastery gates [Note: [Col. 0529] “Coming before them” in the edition.], he immediately ordered them closed, lest any of his own men enter and inflict any violence there [Note: [Col. 0529] “Lest any of his men, entering there, inflict any violence” in manuscript 1 and the edition.]. Thus, after passing through Aquino and Arce [Note: [Col. 0529C] *Arce*.] and devastating the surrounding districts, he returned to Benevento.

At that time, when the year from the Lord’s incarnation 847 was passing [Note: [Col. 0529] “At that time … moved” is transferred here from the following chapter in manuscript 1b.], such a great earthquake occurred throughout the region of Benevento in June [Note: [Col. 0529C] The chronological notice, absent from *Chronicon Casinese*, was apparently taken from the *Life of Leo IV*, where an earthquake is assigned to indiction X.] that nearly all Isernia fell from its foundations, and a great multitude of people there perished, together with their bishop. The same earthquake also destroyed many houses at the monastery of Saint Vincent. Although this mountain too was shaken [Note: [Col. 0529] “Thus shaken” is absent in manuscript 192.], nevertheless, through the merits of most blessed Benedict [Note: [Col. 0529] “Blessed Benedict” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], not even one stone was moved from its place [Note: [Col. 0529] “It did not move even one stone from its place” in manuscript 1 and the edition.].

**29.** [ERCH. XIX, chapter 23.] [Note: [Col. 0529] Manuscript 1b adds: “About this time, Abbot Bassacius, asked by the leading men of the country, went to Francia and begged the glorious Emperor Louis to come to Italy and impose an end upon the devastation inflicted upon them by the wicked Saracens. He obtained this. The emperor therefore came to Bari and, after fighting the Saracens with all his strength for several days without result, went to Benevento. There, through God’s mercy, after not many days, on the vigil of Pentecost, the Saracens within Benevento were killed by our men; their leader Massar was captured, brought before the emperor, and beheaded by his command. Thus, after this, the same emperor returned home. ‘At that time … moved’—see chapter 28. ‘In these same times,’ etc.—chapter 31.”]

At the same time, after the aforesaid Lothar had died in 855, the kingdom of the Franks was divided fivefold. For, as we said above, Louis and Charles, his brothers, ruled Bavaria and Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0529] “Aquitaneam” in manuscript 3.]. His firstborn son, named Louis, received Italy by lot. His second son, Lothar, obtained Aix. The third, Carlittus [Note: [Col. 0529] “Carlettus” in manuscripts 3 and 4.], acquired Saxony [C. Cas. 18].

[Note: [Col. 0529C] Here again, after examining Erchempert, he changed and enlarged what he had initially copied solely from *Chronicon Casinese*, so that no authority should be attributed to him in preference to those sources. I believe that Bassacius’s embassy has been duplicated solely through his error.]

To this Louis, still quite young, the Lombards, afflicted by various calamities, humbly represented through the venerable Abbot Bassacius [Note: [Col. 0529] “Through the venerable Abbot Bassacius” was added later.], that he should come to these regions, rescue them from the devastation of the wicked Saracens [Note: [Col. 0529] Absent in the edition.], and deign to put an end to their immense sufferings [Note: [Col. 0529] Added in manuscript 4.]. This was obtained [Note: [Col. 0529] “And it was obtained” is absent in manuscript 4.].

Louis accordingly came to Benevento in 848 [Note: [Col. 0529] “Then” in the edition.], where he was received with the greatest honor by Radelchis and the Beneventans [Note: [Col. 0529] This phrase is absent in manuscripts 1b and 2.]. All the Saracens were handed over to him, and he ordered all of them to be led outside the city and immediately slaughtered on the very day of the vigil of holy Pentecost. Among them their leader Massar too was beheaded [Note: [Col. 0529] “Was beheaded” in manuscript 1 and the edition.].

The emperor then summoned all the Lombards and divided the whole Beneventan province equally between Radelchis and Siconolf, in the year of the Lord 851 [Note: [Col. 0529] Added later: “The year of the Lord … of the principality of Louis.”] [Note: [Col. 0530C] Di Meo, *Annali Napoletani*, under this year, proved that Siconolf died in 949.]. Thus, after not many days [Note: [Col. 0529] “After a few days” in the edition.], he returned home successfully.

Finally, the aforesaid princes Radelchis and Siconolf, unanimously confirming a compact for the division of the principality [Note: [Col. 0530C] This compact was edited from Codex Cassinensis 353 in Di Meo’s *Annali*, after Peregrini.], decreed that this monastery [Note: [Col. 0529] “The monastery of Saint Benedict” in manuscript 1 and the edition.] and the monastery of Saint Vincent should stand outside the allotment, saying:

“These monasteries do not belong to us at all, because they have been placed under the protection and immunity of the lords, the emperors Lothar and his son Louis [Note: [Col. 0529] “And Louis his son” in manuscripts 1 and 2.].”

**30.** [ERCH. 20.] Again, when the Saracens living at Bari [Note: [Col. 0529] “Holding Bari” in manuscript 1b; “living at Bari” in manuscript 2.] were trying to afflict and devastate Apulia [Note: [Col. 0529] “The whole of Calabria and all Apulia, and to afflict and devastate the whole Beneventan province” in manuscript 1b and the edition.], Calabria, and the whole Beneventan province, Abbot Bassacius, asked by the leading men of the country [Note: [Col. 0529] “Leading men” in manuscripts 1b and 2; “princes” in manuscript 4.], went to Francia together with Abbot James of Saint Vincent [Col. 0530C]. He compelled the aforesaid Louis to come again to these regions.

Louis came at once to Bari and fought the Saracens for several days with varying fortunes, in 852 [Note: [Col. 0529] The *Annals of St-Bertin* and Ademar calculate the years of the principality from December 853: after Sico, Peter, Ademar’s father, obtained the principality.]. But when he saw that he was accomplishing nothing because of the cunning and deceit of the Capuans, he sent Siconolf’s son into exile from Salerno and, granting the principality to Ademar [Note: [Col. 0531] “Immediately” is added in manuscript 1b and then deleted.], returned home.

**31.** [*Chronicon Casinese* 16.] In those same times, because Capua—also called Sicopolis—was often burned by fire on account of the crimes of its inhabitants, Count Lando and Bishop Landulf, with their other kinsmen, after taking counsel built it in a much more suitable and honourable manner by that bridge of Casilinum, as may still be seen today. This city had been built fifteen years earlier on the mountain called Trifliscus. [Note: [Col. 0531C] From Erchempert, chapter 24.] [Note: [Col. 0531C] *Chronicon Sancti Benedicti*, *Scriptores*, III, p. 205. That is, after old Capua was burned in 841, the counts withdrew to Sicopolis, which had been built under Prince Sico.] The construction took place in the year of the Lord 856. [Note: [Col. 0531C] He himself seems to have calculated the year.]

Not long afterwards the aforesaid Abbot Bassacius died [Note: [Col. 0531] “Bassacius died; after having presided for nineteen years” was deleted in manuscript 1b.], namely on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, and was buried with fitting honor beside the church of Saint Benedict, in the brothers’ chapter-house itself [Note: [Col. 0531] Absent in manuscript 4.].

[Col. 0531B] [*Chronicon Casinese* 19.] This abbot showed very great zeal, both above and below, in ecclesiastical affairs [Note: [Col. 0531] “Of this abbot” in the edition.]; he himself renewed all the altars [Note: [Col. 0531] “Below” is added in manuscript 1.] in the church of the Lord Saviour [Note: [Col. 0531C] Compare *Chronicon Sancti Benedicti*, p. 199.]. [Note: [Col. 0531] Manuscript 1 adds: “He was laid to rest on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April and was buried beside the church of Saint Benedict in the brothers’ chapter-house.”]

## Complete source-order textual apparatus

### Apparatus register, notes 1–60

1. **0521** 1b and the edition read the abbreviation *Hujus t. o.* (“of this whole [matter]”); 1b adds the passage from *Hujus* (“of this”) through *et alia nonnulla* (“and several other things”).
2. **0521** 1b has *b. B. a.* (“blessed Benedict, abbot”).
3. **0521** 1b and 2 omit *o. d.* (“of the aforesaid”).
4. **0521–0522C** The altar was dedicated in August 838, but the completed church’s altar on 25 October 839, after Sicard’s death and in Bassacius’s third year by Leo’s calculation. Two anniversary sermons survive: one attributed to Bertharius of Monte Cassino in *Acta SS.*, August V; the more exact one by the monk Martin for Roffred, archbishop of Benevento (from 1076), in Borgia, *Memorie Beneventane* I.333.
5. **0521** 1b and 2 omit *in … transvectum* (“into … conveyed across”).
6. **0521** In the autograph, these notices of transfers were marginal, each wherever there was room, in a different order from codex 4 used here: Agenardus first, then Arnefrid, Maio, Gontarius, and Theodericus fifth.
7. **0522C** Register no.299, Angelo.
8. **0521** 4 reads *r. huic dudum* (“to this long ago”), apparently omitting a whole verse.
9. **0521** 1b and the edition omit *res quas dudum Authpertus abbas per scriptum convenientie concesserat Sichardo principi* (“the properties which Abbot Authpert had long ago granted Prince Sicard by a deed of agreement”).
10. **0521** 1b and 2 read *Milactianum*.
11. **0521** 4 omits *c. in C.* (“estate at Campi”).
12. **0521** 1b and the edition read *Canni*.
13. **0521** 1b and the edition omit *substantia sua* (“its property”) after *Cannis* (“Cannae”).
14. **0521** 1b and the edition omit *His quoque diebus* (“In these same days”) before Agenardus’s gift.

32. But it does not seem superfluous to commit to writing here the custom observed at that time in this monastery during the Easter days. On the Tuesday after Easter, very early in the morning, all the brethren, both from the monastery below and from that above, clothed in sacred vestments and taking golden crosses for the procession, censers, and candle-stands, as well as Gospel-books, reliquary caskets, and various ecclesiastical ornaments and treasures, went forth. As these descended and those ascended, they joined one another at the city of Saint Peter, near the church itself.

Then those who had come from below began the responsory, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” and those from above followed with the same. When this was finished, the priest said the prayer. Thereupon, one by one and in order, all who had come from below approached and greeted and kissed both the lord abbot and the other elders from above. After this, beginning the litanies, all entered together the church of Saint Peter; and, after the prayer had again been said, they sang Terce, and then the Mass, “Come, blessed of my Father,” with mixed singing, that is, Greek and Latin, until the Gospel was completed.

The priest, then, with his ministers, being left to finish the Mass, all the others went out together, singing and chanting psalms, and made their way downwards. Near the monastery, beginning the litanies at the market-place of the merchants, they entered the church of the Lord Saviour. When these were finished, having washed their hands and put on solemn vestments, they all proceeded in order into the atrium to the altar of the blessed archangel Michael, and there stood waiting for the abbot. When he arrived, attended by the various and numerous offices of his ministers, immediately, while all the bells sounded, they proceeded solemnly with all the aforesaid ornaments; and, having entered the church, they began to sing the Mass of that day. When this was completed and Sext had been said, they went into the refectory singing *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God”—giving thanks to God, who had delivered them from all adversities and preserves the monastery and its inhabitants unharmed. And after the prayer had been said, they went out, took off their solemn garments, and so returned to eat.

On that day the chief provost, that is, of the lower monastery of Saint Saviour, provided a meal for all. When the meal was over, the brethren who had come from above, taking leave of the abbot and the other brethren, returned with a blessing.

In those times, moreover, it was customary that on the day before the Kalends of September [31 August] an assembly should be held at this place, together with the provosts of all the monks belonging to this monastery in the surrounding district, in order to be instructed by the abbot what they ought to do, what to avoid, what to correct, and how they ought to live in the presence and fear of God with regular observance. On the following day they were arranged, enrolled, and assigned to obediences in the several districts, according as was expedient.

**Bertharius, nineteenth abbot**, presided for twenty-seven years and seven months. He lived in the times of the Roman pontiffs Nicholas mentioned above, Adrian also, and John VIII, from whom he received a privilege concerning the complete liberty of this monastery (22 May 882).

[Note: Col. 0531: “sat,” manuscript 1, edition.]

[Note: Col. 0531: The words “He lived … received” are placed in the middle of the following chapter by manuscripts 1b and 2, and in chapter 38 by manuscript 1.]

[Note: Col. 0533: “also,” manuscript 4.]

[Note: Col. 0533C: This privilege, from the Register, was published by Gattola, *Historia*, p. 63.]

33. [*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book 1, chapter 19.] He was a disciple of his predecessor Abbot Bassacius, whose diligence he imitated in all things, and especially in ecclesiastical studies. He adorned a codex of the Gospels with gold and excellent gems, made a golden chalice of no small size, and provided many other ecclesiastical ornaments, both above and below. Being also highly learned, he composed several treatises and sermons, as well as verses in praise of the saints. His *Anticimenon*, concerning many questions of both the Old and New Testament, is preserved here; likewise some books on the art of grammar, and two medical codices, collected through his diligence from various sources on the innumerable benefits of remedies; and also very many verses, written with remarkable eloquence, to the Empress Angelberga and to other friends.

Remembering, therefore, the danger which had lately befallen the place from the Saracens under his predecessor—unless God in His mercy had averted it—he fortified all the upper monastery on every side with very strong walls and towers in the manner of a castle. He also began to build, at the foot of this mountain around the monastery of the Lord Saviour, a city, now San Germano.

[Note: Col. 0533: “abbot,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: Col. 0533: “provided”; the passage “He lived … received” is as above in manuscripts 1b and 2. Manuscript 1b adds: “He lived … This man, therefore.”]

[Note: Col. 0533: “This man,” in the edition; compare below, chapter 38, at the end.]

[Note: Col. 0533: omitted in manuscript 4.]

[Note: Col. 0533C: We preserve this work in our library in codex 187, together with other works of his in codices 169, 110, and 139. ANG. See Tosti, *History of Cassino*, I, 113; Peter, *On Illustrious Men*, 12.]

[Note: Col. 0533: “with walls and towers,” manuscript 1b, edition.]

[Note: Col. 0533: The words “He also began to build a city …” are added in manuscript 1b.]

At the time when the aforesaid walls of Eulogimenopolis—that is, the city of Benedict—were being built, a certain man, who for seven years had been suffering from a very severe illness and had entirely lost the use of his tongue, so that he could utter no word at all, served among the others in the work. One night, while the brethren were rendering their customary praises to the Lord in the church, this mute man, sitting near the base of a column in that church, fell asleep. Immediately Saint Benedict appeared to him in his sleep and gently struck him on the head with the staff which he carried.

“Have you come here to sleep?” he said. “Get up at once, and spit upon the ground three times.”

When the man awoke and did this, he immediately began in a clear voice to give thanks to God and to the most blessed Father Benedict, through whom he had deserved to recover his former use of speech. Seeing this, and learning how it had happened to him, all blessed the Lord and Benedict His servant.

[Note: Col. 0533: “who now for seven years …,” manuscript 1, edition.]

[*Ibid.*, chapter 20.] In these days, when Lupoald, bishop of the church of Teano, died, Hilary, deacon and monk of this monastery, was ordained bishop in that city.

34. At the same time, a certain Maurus, a wealthy man from the region of Liburia, offered himself to this monastery into the hands of the provost Angelarius, together with two shares of all his property, movable and immovable, at the place called *Ad filicem* (“At the Fern”); for he had given the third part to his only daughter.

Agelmundus, a citizen of Telesia, likewise offered himself to God in this place, with all the property of his substance entire, both in Telesia itself and in different places, except for two farmsteads which he gave to his daughter, a nun, and certain other things with some servants which he granted to the church of Saint Domninus at Telesia, which was a cell of this monastery.

A certain man named Maio, from the county of Teate, also offered to this monastery his estate called the *Fara* of Maio, with all its appurtenances, comprising in all 5,800 *modii* of land, and another estate called Mallie, with the church of Saint Peter and all its appurtenances. Likewise, a certain Stephen, a Capuan by birth, offered in this holy place, in various territories, eight estates, with male and female slaves and tenant-farmers belonging to those estates, and with all their appurtenances whatsoever.

The first of these is called Juncianum; the second, Clabazanum; the third, Decazanum; the fourth, Atdurum, on Mount Marsicus, with its whole territory near the estate called Campumutuli; the fifth is called Adcasale, likewise on Mount Marsicus; the sixth, Addiripatum, in the territory of Cantia; the seventh, Adpatricanum; and the eighth is called Adroselle, likewise in Cantia.

Theoderic, also a Capuan, made his offering to this monastery from the meadow of Patenaria, at the place called Spigianus. This abbot made a lease to Count Guy concerning Saint Angelo of Varriano and Saint Potitus, with all the appurtenances of those churches, together with 950 *modii* of land; for these he received 500 solidi immediately, while he received annually seven mancuses as rent.

He also granted to Suabilo, gastald of the Marsi, the usufruct, only for the days of his life, of the church of Saint Cosmas at Civitella, with its tenant-farmers, male and female slaves, and all its property and appurtenances whatsoever; and of two other churches belonging to that church, namely Saint Mary at Ellereto and Saint Leucius at Moscosi, likewise with servants, female slaves, and all their appurtenances; likewise also the church of Saint Benedict at Auritino, Saint Victorinus at Celano, and Saint Abundius at Arcu, near Lake Fucinus, with all their property and appurtenances in the same manner. For all these he received from him thirty pounds immediately, and annually, as rent, four pounds in the month of September.

Rodepertus, son of this Suabilo and a citizen of Benevento, offered to this monastery sixteen estates from his property, with all their appurtenances, and one new house within the city of Benevento, with a courtyard and its buildings. In these days a certain Leo and his wife Guilerona offered to blessed Benedict from their possessions one estate at Canosa and another at Saint Valentine, and a charter concerning Lake Romani, with its fishing rights and with all the appurtenances of the same estates.
