35. [*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book 1, chapter 28.] Meanwhile the most wicked king of the Saracens, named Seodan Barim, came out and came to Capua. Ravaging it entirely on every side, and traversing Cantia and Liburia while no one could resist him, he pitched his tents in the plain of Naples, killing very many daily and committing various atrocities.

[Note: Col. 0536C: Leo of Ostia, according to Di Meo, notes these events as though all had happened in the same year, although he says this nowhere.]

[Note: Col. 0535: “Barim and the whole,” manuscript 4.]

[*Erchempert*, chapter 29.] At that time Majelpotus, gastald of Telesia, and Wanpelpertus, gastald of Bovianum, having engaged Lambert, duke of Spoleto, and Gerard, count of the Marsi, went out against him as he returned from the ravaging of Capua. Falling upon him, they fought for some time in a contest of doubtful outcome. At last, however, the Saracens gained the victory: Gerard, Majelpotus, and Wandelpertus were killed in the battle itself, many others were captured, and others slain. Thereupon Seodan took great boldness, seized all the surrounding castles except the principal cities, and utterly destroyed them.

[Note: Col. 0535: “Guand.,” manuscripts 3 and 4.]

[*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book 1, chapter 30.] It was then the custom of the monks of the two monasteries, namely Saint Benedict’s and Saint Vincent’s, to visit one another during the days of holy Lent for the sake of charity. For they were then bound together by so close a bond of affection that, although the community of our monastery possessed certain servants of Saint Vincent, and they likewise possessed certain of ours, it pleased the fathers of both monasteries, Bertharius and Majo, that these should not be exchanged, but that their possession should remain forever unimpaired just as it then was.

[Note: Col. 0535: The words “for … remain” were added in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: Col. 0536C: He seems to have added this on the basis of an ancient record of the matter.]

[Note: Col. 0535: omitted in manuscript 4.]

One day, therefore, when certain brethren of this Cassinese monastery had gone, as was customary, to Saint Vincent’s, and were speaking with one another concerning their order, the exceedingly cruel Seodan suddenly came upon them there with his followers. When the monks learned the report of him, they immediately fled at full speed, though very frightened, yet unharmed, to a castle nearest their monastery. But the Saracens entered the monastery, devastated everything they found, smashed very much, and threw grain and legumes into the river which flows beside it. Digging here and there, they found the whole treasure of the church, which the monks had long before hidden in fear of them. And that most impious Seodan drank from sacred chalices and ordered incense to be offered to himself from golden censers.

[Note: Col. 0535: Manuscript 1 continues: “Yet Almighty God granted no less mercy then to blessed Vincent than He once granted to blessed Benedict: for although He surrendered possessions to the nations, He preserved souls. After …”; manuscript 1b continues: “when these had been destroyed …”]

Alas, thus the aforesaid monastery of Saint Vincent was burned by those thunderbolt-like men; some of the monks were killed, others scattered in different directions, and it remained thus desolate and abandoned for thirty-three years.

[Note: Col. 0535: Manuscript 4 reads: “After these things fire was sent in from every side. Thus …”; something appears to have been omitted.]

[Note: Col. 0536C–0537C: “Thus … it remained”: this was carelessly added later, for the monastery was in fact burned only in 881; the killing of the blessed monks is recorded in the Chronicle of Vulturnus on Tuesday, 10 October. I think that the precise dates of the other matters related here cannot be established; only that they happened before Louis’s arrival is certain.]

[Note: Col. 0537: added in manuscript 4.]

[Note: Col. 0537: Manuscript 1b, edition: “and it remained desolate and abandoned until thirty-three years …”]

[Note: Col. 0537C: So too the *Chronicle of Vulturnus*.]

But the wicked Seodan, on the third day afterward, approached the gates of the city of Capua, captured loaded wagons and various animals together with many people, and, coming near Teano, encamped there. When the venerable abbot Bertharius learned this, fearing greatly the coming of that wicked man both for the place and for the people, he sent him three thousand gold coins through his deacon Ragenald, and thus softened his ferocity.

[Note: Col. 0537: “his deacon,” edition.]

[Note: Col. 0537: Manuscript 1 has “sending him no small sum of money”; manuscript 1b, edition: “he sent him three thousand gold coins.”]

[*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book 1, chapter 33.] From there Seodan made for Venafro; having soon captured it and devastated the whole neighbouring region, he remained there for several days (A.D. 867). It was then the beginning of the days of Lent. Fearing the nearness of that faithless man, all the monks withdrew above to the protection of blessed Benedict.

[Note: Col. 0537: “Venaffrum,” manuscript 3.]

[Note: Col. 0537: “for some days there,” manuscript 1, edition.]

[Note: Col. 0537: “the monks of that most impious and wicked man,” manuscript 1, edition.]

After a few days that wicked man’s army came within about two stadia of the lower monastery, though this happened through an error of their guide. For, wishing to descend through the mountains to Atina, an old man who was their guide descended with them into the Round Valley, then into Rapido. When they reached the plain, they entered the church of Saint Elias and took what they found. Thence, by Circlariae, they came into the Lord’s garden, and by the grazing-land to the spring of Lucius. Coming to Peola, they killed that old man who had misled them on the way. Finally, carefully searching the hedge of Constantius, the olive-grove, and Matronula, and plundering all the cows and mares of the monastery that they found, they returned to their people at Venafro and, not long afterward, entered Bari.

36. The Lombards, therefore, seeing that they had been scourged from heaven for their sins, afflicted and at last pressed by great necessity, for the third time sent envoys into Francia to the aforesaid Louis, imploring and earnestly requesting that he would deign to come again into Italy and rescue them and their country from the most wicked race of Saracens.

Then King Louis, moved by these messengers, issued a general edict through all the regions of his kingdom, that no one at all should withdraw himself from this expedition. And so, having assembled a very great army and setting out together with his wife, the Empress Angelberga, in the year of the Lord 866, he entered the territory of Benevento by way of Sora, a city of Campania. In June he came to the monastery of this most holy father which is below, where he was received with the greatest honour by the venerable Abbot Bertharius, all the monks going out to meet him solemnly. On the following day he ascended the mountain to pray, and there too was received by the brethren with no less honour.

When he had gone round and inspected the whole monastery, praised it as excellently built, and made for blessed Benedict a charter confirming the whole abbey, according to what his imperial predecessors had already done, and had bestowed imperial gifts there, he commended himself very earnestly to the brethren and descended. After leaving there he went to Capua; having besieged it for three months, he captured it and destroyed the greater part of it. From there he went to Salerno and sailed to Amalfi. He also went to Puteoli and used its baths; returning through Naples and Sessula, he encamped in the Caudine Valley in December, and not long afterward entered Benevento.

Then, at Luceria, a city of Apulia, having assembled his whole army, he engaged the Saracens in battle (A.D. 867). Defeated in the first encounter, he afterward, with God’s aid, won a triumphant victory over them and captured all their camps. From there he advanced against Bari and besieged it for four years. Meanwhile he captured their very strongly fortified city of Matera and consumed it by fire and sword. After this he came to Venosa, and, posting a garrison of fighting men both there and at Canosa, ordered Bari to be vigorously attacked from every side; and so he returned to Benevento in August.

While Abbot Bertharius was staying there in his service, he completed with all diligence and care a small oratory within the monastery of Saint Sophia which his predecessor Abbot Bassacius had begun, and had it consecrated in honour of Saint Benedict, the holy father, by Stephen, bishop of the church of Teano. At that time the same emperor made for blessed Benedict a charter concerning one of his estates named Lajanum, at the place called Turturitus, and concerning Saint George, with all their property and appurtenances.

[*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book 1, chapter 22.] Meanwhile two counts attempted to rise against the emperor. When the emperor learned this, he pursued them as far as the Marsi. There, not daring to stand, they fled to Benevento. But while the emperor pursued them, he came to Isernia, which, attempting resistance, he assaulted and captured. Passing from there through Alife, he came by Telesia to the city called Saint Agatha. Since he could not capture it, he besieged it for many days. At last Abbot Bertharius, because the gastald Hisembardus, who held that city, was his kinsman, interceded for him with the emperor and obtained both favour for him and pardon for the city.

Adelchis, prince of Benevento, also, prostrate at the feet of the same emperor, obtained his favour both for the aforesaid men who had fled and for himself, who had dared to receive them.

[*Erchempert*, chapters 34–35.] While Louis, therefore, was staying at Benevento, the aforesaid Adelchis, spurred on by a diabolical suggestion, found an occasion in the insolent conduct of the Franks within the city and immediately rose against him while he was living in security. He seized him and committed him to custody; stripping all his soldiers, he expelled them from the city (13 August).

But God did not long allow an innocent man to be afflicted in vain. For within forty days, when an innumerable army of Saracens was coming from Africa, Louis was immediately released from prison; and, bound by oaths, he left Benevento on 17 September and reached Berola within three days. There he remained for about eleven months, during which time he killed, through some of his counts, first three thousand and then nearly nine thousand Saracens at Capua. After this, when he came to Capua in A.D. 872, the Saracens, learning of his coming, left the principality and went to Calabria. Ravaging it everywhere, they embarked on ships and, after suffering a very great storm, returned to their own country, all who could escape.

37. At the same time, when the aforesaid emperor had passed beside the island of Pescara, which lies on the border of the county of Penne, the place itself, once called Casa Aurea (“Golden House”), greatly pleased him. Judging it most suitable for the uses of the servants of God, the religious man ordered the bishops of Valva and Penne to build there a church in honour of the Holy Trinity and to gather religious men in that place for the service of God. When this was done, he endowed that church by imperial generosity with many and diverse benefactions in different places, as his charters record, and in his devotion commanded that his memory should always be kept there. Later, when the church had been enlarged by the abbots of that place, it was named, as they pleased, after Saint Clement.

This same most Christian emperor, about this time, built the monastery of Saint Michael, called Barregium, and strengthened it by his own charter in accordance with the tenor of the charters of his predecessors Charles and Lothair; confirming there all that it appeared to have possessed of old, both in its immediate district and in the territory of the Marsi, and in Balva, Teate, Penne, Aprutium, and Ascoli, namely: in Marsia, the cell of Saint Mary at Fondo Magno, with all churches and properties subject to it; Saint Eutychius at Arestina; Saint Paul above the Marsican city; Saint Mary at Oretino; Saint Gregory at Paterno; Saint Mary at Montorone; the church of Saint Saviour at Avezzano; Saint Antimus at Formae; Saint Michael at Alba; Saint Cosmas at Ellereto; and Saint Michael at Carseoli with its two cells. In Balva: the church of Saint Peter at Barbarano; Saint Saviour above the river; Saint Michael at Acqua Viva; Saint Michael at Floretum; the cell situated Between the Waters; and Saint Felicity at Furcona. In Penne: the church of Saint Mary at Cerqueto, and Petitianum. In Aprutium: the monastery of Saint Michael of Marano with all its cells and properties. In Ascoli: the church of the Lord Saviour called Caput Aquarum, with all its appurtenances; Saint Michael of Stabulo; Saint Michael of Feltriano; Saint Peter at Pectiniano; the estate of Casa Perende; also many male and female slaves in various places, and very many other things contained in its charters.

### 38. [Chronicle of Monte Cassino, ch. 26.]

At the same time Radoad, gastald in the estate of Aquino, built a castle beside Pons Curvus (“Crooked Bridge”); it retained that name from the situation and designation of the bridge.

The aforesaid emperor, after remaining at Capua for almost a year, took up the body of blessed Germanus, bishop of that city, and at last returned to Francia in the year 873, having stayed for about six years in various places in these regions.

[Note: Col. 0541: “Afterwards the same emperor, returning to Capua, when he had remained there for almost a year … hence 1c continues in the margin, with what had formerly been written erased: ‘at last he returned to Francia.’ But the aforesaid abbot lived in the times of the Roman pontiffs Nicholas, Adrian, and John VIII, from whom he also received a privilege for the complete liberty of this monastery. In his time Monecaus, a monk of this monastery, was provost in the church of Saint James of Tremiti, which was a cell of this abbey; under the name of this provost many charters of that place are preserved among us. This abbot was highly learned and wrote several treatises, etc.—‘than the old’ (ch. 33). The following two folios have been erased and, unless I am mistaken, written in a smaller hand by Leo himself.]

### 39.

While on his return he was staying at Saint Apollinaris in Ravenna in March 874, Angelarius, then provost of this monastery, came to him and lodged a claim concerning the cell of Saint Mary at Maurini in the county of Penne. About a hundred years earlier, in the reign of King Charles, Duke Hildebrand, through the agency of Benjamin, a monk of this abbey, had confirmed it by his charter. But certain persons were then asserting that they held those properties, as it were, from the emperor’s own side. Once the emperor had learned the truth of the matter and been moved by Angelarius’s prayers, he wrote and commanded by imperial authority that thereafter no one should presume either to retain or to remove anything from that cell, whether on his own behalf or on another’s; rather, it was to return peaceably and wholly free to the former lordship of our abbey, with its harbour, the mouth of the Gomano, and all its appurtenances and boundaries: namely, from Atri to the Gomano, to the river called Plomba, and to the sea, with the shore itself for fishing, and with the woodland of Boleiano—altogether about eleven thousand modii of land.

[Note: Col. 0542C: From Louis’s diploma, published by Gattola from Peter’s register, *Acc.*, p. 41. A confirmation of Charlemagne, though suspect, was published from the same register by Tosti, I, 93.]

[Note: Col. 0541: absent in 4.]

[Col. 0544A]

Concerning the lands of our aforesaid cell in the valley of Caudium, the same provost lodged a claim in the presence of Prince Adelchis against a certain Rodelgrim, who had fraudulently obtained them, and promptly recovered them. The prince issued a public command that henceforth no one should in any way acquire any lands of our monastery without permission from our abbot. This was because the aforesaid Rodelgrim, having deceived our monk Amelfrid, I do not know under which abbot, had acquired those lands as if by a written agreement.

[Note: Col. 0543: “of the remaining,” 3.]

[Note: Col. 0543: “of our aforesaid Saint Benedict at Benevento,” witnesses 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0543: added in 4.]

In the presence of Judge Louis he also brought a claim against a certain infant, Guandelmarius, concerning an estate of the monastery of Saint Sophia at Faffone near Benevento, which that infant held; and he recovered it by judicial decision.

[Note: Col. 0543: Ludoici, 1b and 2; Ludovici, 4.]

[Note: Col. 0543: Gualdemario, 3.]

[Col. 0544B]

In these same days Benedict and Sichard, brothers of Salerno, offered to this monastery their entire inheritance which they possessed near Teano, in the places called Scatunianus and Purpuranus, with all its appurtenances in their entirety.

### 40. [Erchempert, chs. 38–39.]

Not long afterwards the Saracens, having recovered their strength and occupied Taranto, began from there more vigorously to harass Bari and the surrounding regions. Meanwhile the people of Salerno, Amalfi, Naples, and Gaeta made an alliance with the Saracens and distressed Rome by naval raids. Therefore Charles, emperor at that time, son of Louis, was repeatedly appealed to by Pope John VIII in many letters; and he sent Duke Lambert and his brother Guy to his aid in 876. With them the same apostolic pope proceeded to Naples and Salerno. Guaifer, prince of Salerno, obeyed the pope in all matters, broke the alliance with the Saracens, and slaughtered many of them. But Sergius, duke of Naples, unwilling to separate himself from them, was immediately excommunicated by the pope; and not long afterwards, in 877, by God’s avenging judgment, he was captured and blinded by his own brother, Bishop Athanasius, and sent to Rome.

[Note: Col. 0543: Chapters 40, 41, 43, 44, and 45 are written on two folios, apparently in Leo’s own hand; but he himself later altered and expanded them in several places.]

[Col. 0544C]

[Erchempert, ch. 44.]

This same Athanasius, made duke in his place, made peace with the Saracens and settled them near Naples. Together with them he then began fiercely to ravage Benevento, Capua, Salerno, Rome, and Spoleto; and at that time many monasteries and churches, with villages and towns, were burned and laid waste by them.

[Note: Col. 0543: “Athanasius, his brother,” 1b and edition.]

[Col. 0545A]

[Note: Col. 0545: “and settled them,” 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0545: Spoletum, 4.]

[Note: Col. 0545: “by them,” added in 4.]

### 41. [Erchempert, chs. 46–47.]

In these days the people of Capua expelled Landulf, who had been canonically elected bishop, and chose as their bishop Landenulf, one of their nobles, a married man and a neophyte. By many prayers they began to press the aforesaid pope to consecrate him bishop for them. Therefore the venerable Abbot Bertharius and Leo, bishop of Teano, went to Rome and began to beseech the supreme pontiff not to yield in this matter in any way, for it would bring a grave calamity upon the people of Capua and much shedding of blood. The abbot said more plainly: “Apostolic man, know that if you consent to this, you will undoubtedly kindle a great fire, one which will reach even to you.” At first the apostolic pope was frightened by the steadfastness of so great a man; but in the end wickedness prevailed, and the aforesaid neophyte was consecrated bishop.

[Note: Col. 0545: “a certain Landulf,” 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0545: “they deceive the aforesaid pope, so that,” 1b and 2.]

[Note: Col. 0545: “that he might be consecrated bishop for them. Therefore,” 1b and edition.]

[Col. 0545B]

[Note: Col. 0545: profecto, “certainly,” 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0545: added in 4.]

[Note: Col. 0545: accendis, “you kindle,” 1b and edition.]

The Saracens, finding an opportune occasion in this civil discord, again plundered everything and once more devastated all things; therefore the aforesaid pope was compelled to come to Capua twice. Seeing that what our abbot had foretold had openly happened to him, he greatly repented. At length, after taking counsel, he consecrated as bishop, in 880, in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter at Old Capua, Landulf, whom we have said above was expelled; but he appointed Landenulf to preside over New Capua, and ordered the whole bishopric to be divided equitably between the two.

[Note: Col. 0545: oportunitatem, “opportunity,” 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0545C: It was also called Berelais, the amphitheatre, the arena, and the colossus; it lay where Santa Maria Maggiore now stands.]

[Note: Col. 0545: Landenulf, 3.]

### 42.

In these days the aforesaid Prince Guaifer was taken ill and became a monk in 880. He earnestly asked to be conveyed to this monastery; but because of the Saracen incursions he could not be brought here as he wished. When he had died, his body was carried and buried in our monastery near Teano.

[Note: Col. 0545: “this chapter written in the margin,” 1d.]

[Note: Col. 0545: “At about this time the emperor Basil of Constantinople died, and his sons Leo and Alexander succeeded to the empire. Their other brother, Stephen, obtained the patriarchate of that city after the expulsion of Photius, who had recently been anathematized by Pope Nicholas, because, while Ignatius, bishop of that city, was still living, he had ambitiously seized his see.” Added in 1b at the end of ch. 43; hence transferred here in 1, from Erchempert, ch. 52.]

### 43.

At that time a certain Pandenulf ruled Capua. While he remained faithful to the pope, he asked him to subject Gaeta to his dominion, for at that time the Gaetans served only the Roman pontiff. When the aforesaid pope had granted this, Pandenulf began to attack the Gaetans so fiercely in 881 that they were not permitted to go out even as far as Molae. A certain Docibilis then ruled them as duke. Considering that such disgrace inflicted upon himself and his people was intolerable, he sent to Agropolis and enlisted the Saracens living there. He brought them by sea to Lake Fundanus, to the place called Saint Anastasia; then, ascending from there by the river as far as Fundi, they disembarked from their boats like a sword drawn from its sheath, devastated everything around them, eventually reached Gaeta, and established their camp on the Formian hills.

[Note: Col. 0545: “After this Pandenulf, who was then ruling Capua while remaining faithful to the pope, asked him,” 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0545: Pandenolfus, 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0545: “the Gaetans, at that time,” 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0545: “he attacked the Gaetans fiercely,” 1b and edition.]

[Col. 0546B]

[Note: Col. 0545C: At the Paestan gulf.]

[Note: Col. 0545: “as though truly drawn from a sheath,” added above the line in 1c.]

[Note: Col. 0545C: Namely, on the hills between Formiae, Itri, and Gaeta. Numerous ruined huts or small cabins still stand there; constant tradition asserts that the Saracens built and inhabited them then, and they have no other reported origin. ANG.]

[Col. 0546C]

When the pope heard this, he was at once led to repentance, and by conciliatory speeches and letters, as well as many promises, began to urge the Gaetans to be reconciled to him and separate themselves from the Saracens. At last Docibilis complied with his admonitions, broke the alliance with the Saracens, and began war. In that war many Gaetans were killed and captured. Yet the Saracens, again requesting and receiving an alliance from Docibilis, returned the captives and were sent by Docibilis to live by the Garigliano, away from the Formian hills. There, with God’s permission because of our innumerable sins, they lived for nearly forty years, committed innumerable evils on every side, and shed much Christian blood. Frequently attacked and besieged in that place by various great men, they nevertheless remained unconquered and assaulted [the transmitted *expugnati* is materially uncertain] by them, through God’s judgment, until the appointed time.

### 44. (4 September 883.)

At the same time the monastery of the blessed father Benedict, where his most sacred body was buried, was invaded, destroyed, and burned by the aforesaid Saracens. Everything found there was plundered, on the day before the Nones of September, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 884, in the second indiction. Not long afterwards, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, 22 October, they likewise occupied, devastated, and burned the lower, larger monastery, killing many there; they also slaughtered with the sword the holy and venerable Abbot Bertharius himself beside the altar of blessed Martin. When they tried to burn the church of the Lord Saviour itself by setting fire to it in various places, they were unable to accomplish this through the mercy of almighty God. Thus that church alone, out of this whole monastery, was rescued from the Saracens’ flames. Laden with the monastery’s spoils, they returned rejoicing and triumphing to the Garigliano.

The monks, taking whatever furnishings, treasure, and charters of this monastery they had been able to snatch away, went with Lord Angelarius, then their provost, to live at Teano. Making Angelarius their abbot, they began to reside in the cell long before built there in honour of blessed Father Benedict, in the year and indiction written above. From Abbot Petronax to this man, one hundred and sixty-six years were completed.

### 45.

Nor should it be thought superfluous if here we append the memorandum which we have found to have been drawn up through the care of the aforesaid Abbot Bertharius, concerning the properties and cells of this monastery established in the March, specifically in Teate and Penne. These are known to have been granted hitherto to blessed Father Benedict by the kings Charles, Pippin, Lothair, and Louis, of saintly memory, or by various other faithful persons. Since most of their deeds of donation have been burned, we do not know what was contributed specifically by each individual.

[Note: Col. 0547: “this chapter was written in very small letters without margin” in 1b; omitted in 1e.]

[Note: Col. 0547: est, “is,” 1b and edition.]

[Note: Col. 0547C: Published by Gattola from this passage and Peter’s register, *History*, p. 78, where he adduces more material concerning the distinguished monastery of Saint Liberator.]

[Col. 0548A]

[Note: Col. 0547: Ludowico, 1b and 2.]

[Note: Col. 0547: “other religious men,” 1b.]

[Note: Col. 0547: “which … Orni” is written again at the end of the work in manuscript 4, with variant readings marked by 4.]

First, therefore, is the monastery of Saint Liberator, situated in the county of Teate above the River Laentus, at the foot of the mountain called Maiella, together with the church of Saint Michael on the side of Monte Piano, with the whole of that mountain, the castle of Saint Michael and all its appurtenances, the estate called Casale Prandi, the estate of Garifuli, the castle of Saint Peter, the estate of Saint Januarius, Valle Plana, and Luciano, with all their appurtenances and properties within the following boundaries.

On one side, the boundary is the torrent called Cripta Latronis (“Robber’s Grotto”), beneath the little mountain called Sarracenico, now called Praetorium. From there it rises to the boundary-marker of Maiella, which divides Saint Benedict’s holding from the royal lands. On another side, it descends thence to the water Frassiniga, and as this flows into the stream called Bacinnium; then from that ditch to the well of Capetano; then to the ditch of Saint Januarius and to Rosente. On the other side, the boundary is Bisara; then the road leading to the pool above Saint Donatus; thence to Ficarium; then to the ditch of Saint Lucy; and it rises by Cold Water to the boundary of Monte Piano, proceeds under those boundary-lines to the ditch of Garifuli, and so flows into the Alento. Within these boundaries the aforesaid kings reserved nothing at all for themselves, since this whole holding had been royal land, except for the church of Saint Vitalis with an appurtenance of only ten modii, which belongs to the bishopric.

Then the church of Saint Mary at Bacinnium with its appurtenance. Next, the church of Saint Felix at Pastoricium, with its boundaries and appurtenances. Its boundaries are these: on one side the River Pescara; on another, Lavinum; on another, the banks of Turri, with the estate itself where the church of Saint Benedict stands; and on another the spring of Troia, as it descends into Lavinum. The church of Saint Vitus above the River Lavinum. The church of Saint Elias at Sclangarium, with an appurtenance of twenty thousand modii. The estate of Caramanico. The monastery of Saint Comitius beside the stream Arullus, with many estates. The church of Saint Felix at Pulverium, with half of that estate within its boundaries: namely, at one end the monument; at another the aforesaid Pescara; at another the land of Saint Thomas; and at another Rosente, as it flows into the Pescara. Countess Hyselgarda offered all these things to blessed Benedict.

The church of Saint Callixtus; Saint Mammes, with the entire estate of Ilianum; Saint Mark; Saint Mary at Pontianum, with six hundred modii of land. The island between Pomarium and the castle called Calcaria, with approximately four hundred modii of land. The church of Saint Eleutherius and Saint Paul in the district of Boclanicum, at the place called Rupi, with seven hundred and eighty modii of land. The church of Saint Erasmus at Cerretum Planum, with its appurtenances and boundaries, and all mills built within these boundaries, together with the church of Saint Saviour and Saint Martin. The church of Saint Benedict, Saint Mary, Saint Comitius, and Saint Silvester at the place called Orni, with all their boundaries and appurtenances.

A certain Rainerius built this church of Saint Silvester and offered it to blessed Benedict with all its appurtenances, within these boundaries: on one side, the same *benna* (“pool”); on another, Seven Ways; on another, another *benna*; these join together. Fara Maionis and the *fara* called Biana, with their boundaries and appurtenances. This Maio was a kinsman of Potericus, provost of Saint Liberator under the aforesaid abbot, and he offered that same *fara* to this monastery; its total area is five thousand eight hundred modii of land. The estate of Saint Callixtus with all that belongs to it. The church of Saint Peter at the place called Mallianellum, with all its appurtenances and boundaries: at its head, the ditch of Lavite; at its foot, the road from that well; on one side, the *benna*; on the other, the river of Argelli. The same aforesaid Maio also offered this.

Within these boundaries are the church in honour of Saint Maurus and the monastery of Saint Renatus, situated between Antonianum and Pizzum Corvarium, with all their appurtenances. The church of Saint Callixtus above this Laentus, at the place called Vallis, with 6,060 modii of land. The church of Saint Mary above the *fara* of Laentus, with its appurtenance and boundaries: at its head, the road; at its foot, the Laentus; and on both sides, a ditch. The church of Saint Sabinus at Trevanicum; Saint Clement at Plombata; and the church of Saint Salvius in the same place. This Salvius, native of Campania, was a monk of this monastery; he held the aforesaid church of Saint Clement in obedience, and when he died God worked many miracles at his tomb.

The church of Saint Mary on the River Foro, at the place called Cannetum, with 4,060 modii of land. Four mills in the water of that same Foro. The church of Saint Peter at Jollianum, with 1,400 modii of land. The monastery of Saint Severinus. The church of Saint Mennas in the district of Ripe; Saint Andrew on the hill of Albe; Saint Peter at the place called Ari. The estate called Fenestre. The church of Saint Michael before the city of Ortona, with eight hundred modii of land. The castle of Ungo with its entire appurtenance; and within that appurtenance, Grosse and half the town of Tazze, with the entire appurtenance of Rapini and Comino. The church of the Holy Cross in the district of Roma, with 1,500 modii of land, and half of that castle of Casale with its appurtenances. The monastery of Saint Pancras with its entire appurtenance. The castle of Prata, Gessi, Civitella, and the valley of Saint Martin, with all their appurtenances. The church of Saint Peter in the old city of Teate, and beside it the church of Saint Paul. The church of Saint Thecla within the same new city, together with the gate facing east, which is still commonly called the Monks’ Gate. The church of Saint Theodore and the church of Saint Saviour within the city of Aternum, with half the harbour, which the aforesaid Countess Hyselgarda offered to blessed Benedict.

In the district of Penne there is [Note: [Col. 0551] added in 4.] the church of Saint Felix at Stabulo; the field of Gale; the monastery of Saint Benedict at Lauriano, and that of Saint Scholastica beside the river called Tabe [Note: [Col. 0551C] Tavo, which flows into the Salino.], with the entire estate of Moscufo [Note: [Col. 0551] Moscuffe 2.] and the estate of Gemberuti; and the church of Saint Angelus at Galbanico [Note: [Col. 0551] Galvanico 2.], with the entire estate itself and half of the castle of Laureto—namely, beginning at the pile situated in the middle of that castle, as it descends into the ditch [Note: [Col. 0551] ditch, in the edition.] of Rosiccle [Note: [Col. 0551] Rosiale 3; Rosicle 4.], with the church built there in honour of Saint Felix, and as far as the crossroads above Saint Felix; and as it proceeds through that valley into the ditch of Doreniano; and as that ditch descends into the river Tabe; and as the boundary ascends along that river as far as Paterno, where there is a church in honour of Saint Mary; and as it rises directly to the spring at Laureto, and thus returns to the aforementioned pile. Within these boundaries nothing whatsoever belongs to anyone except the monastery of Cassino.

At Colle Alto, six very large parcels of land [Note: [Col. 0551] land, in the edition.]. Half the village of Laverano. Half of Poggio Pollecante [Note: [Col. 0551C] *Podium* means “hill”: Italian *poggio*, French *puy*.]. The estate of Colle Alto [Note: [Col. 0551] estate, in the edition.]. A third part of the castle of Cese [Note: [Col. 0551] *cartello*; Cesa, in the edition.]. Half the castle of Colle Maio. The church of Saint Martin at Genestrula, with the whole estate. The church at Salaiano [Note: [Col. 0551] Saiano 3.] with 1,700 *modii* of land. [Col. 0551C] A fourth part of the city of Quana. Half the estate of Viculo. The estate of Carpeneto, with large uplands and plains. In the territory of Civitella [Note: [Col. 0551] Civitate 3.], 3,000 *modii* of land. The monastery of Saint Peter at Castroniano, with the church of Saint Cecilia and all its dependencies; and very many other things which we forbear to write here. All these, indeed, until that time the abbots of this place either retained as their own right or had granted to others at a rent, under the title of a *libellus* [lease].

[Col. 0552A] ANGELARIUS [Note: [Col. 0551] From here manuscript 1 continues.] was the twentieth abbot from blessed Benedict and held office for six years. He became abbot from the provostship of this monastery at Teano, as we have already said above (ch. 44) [Note: [Col. 0551] The words from “as” through “became” are absent in manuscript 1.]; after two years [Note: [Col. 0551] “after two years” is added in manuscript 1b.] (A.D. 886) [Note: [Col. 0551C] From Erchempert, ch. 61.] he began gradually to restore the monastery of the Lord Saviour, which, as we said above, had been burned by the Saracens. [Note: [Col. 0551] Manuscript 1 continued here: “But by God’s hidden judgment the monastery in which the brethren had begun to live at Teano was itself, not long afterwards, consumed by fire.” After deleting this, the editor transferred the following material to chapter 48 and added the remainder concerning this abbot in the margin, not all at one time.]

He lived [Note: [Col. 0551] “He lived, etc.” was added in manuscript 1b, but at the end of this abbot’s section.] in the time of Aio, prince of Benevento, Pope Stephen V, and his successor Formosus [Note: [Col. 0551] Manuscript 1b adds “of the aforesaid Pope Stephen, and.”]. The latter, Formosus [Note: [Col. 0551C] From the Chronicle of Saint Benedict, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS III, p. 204. But before Formosus’s pontificate, Ragemprand succeeded him.], Pope Stephen, who had succeeded him, ordered to be dragged from his tomb and cast away; and he declared all his ordinations invalid, on the ground that, although he had been bishop of Ostia, he had usurped the Apostolic See contrary to the decrees of the holy canons [Note: [Col. 0552C] Our author inserted this from his own resources, incorrectly, since Formosus had been bishop of Porto.] [Note: [Col. 0551] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “had invaded”; the manuscript adds in 1c: “and while his body was repeatedly tossed from place to place, blood even flowed from it … Ragemprand.”].

[Col. 0552B] 46. Under this abbot [Note: [Col. 0551] From “Under” through “monastery” is cut out in manuscript 1b; manuscript 1* omitted almost the whole chapter.] the land called Brezze [Note: [Col. 0551] Brizze in 1b; perhaps Preze in 4.] near Capua was offered to this monastery by a certain Castulus, an inhabitant of that place; it consists of a large meadow and woodland. Hermefrid [Note: [Col. 0551] Hermefrit 3.] too, a wealthy citizen of Ascoli and a subdeacon by office, offered himself by the hair of his head to our provost named Wamelfrid [Note: [Col. 0551] “his” in 4; Walmelfrid 2; Gualmelfrit 3; Guamelfrid 4.], together with absolutely all his movable and immovable property in those regions.

A certain Ingius of Benevento, about to undertake an expedition to Rome, likewise offered to this holy cenobium three estates from his property: one at the place called Turri, another at the place called Murece, and a third at the place called Mattici, with all their boundaries and dependencies [Note: [Col. 0551] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “his property, that is, an estate”; they read “at” instead of “in”; manuscript 4 reads “but another at” and adds “which.”].

Moreover, a certain Walamir, a native of the same city, giving himself to the monastic life in this place, offered at the church of Saint Benedict in Benevento called *Ad xenodochium* [“At the hospice”], a cell of this cenobium, one large estate in the territory of Ariano [Note: [Col. 0552C] It is not far from Benevento, toward the east.], at the place called Tricium, with all the dependencies of that estate in their entirety [Note: [Col. 0551] The edition reads “where”; this is omitted in manuscript 4, while the edition has “of that estate in its entirety.”]. [Note: [Col. 0551] The passage from “But also Walamir” through “Gaitruda” is absent in manuscript 1; see above, p. 612, note t.]

[Note: [Col. 0551] The edition prints, in reverse order, the passage from “To this abbot” through “dependencies” and the passage from “At the same time” through “should return.”]

At the same time Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0551] Anathasius 3.], bishop of Naples, declared that Casa Gentiana was under our obedience, so that neither he nor his successors should henceforth have any authority there or licence to ordain anyone in it or impose any condition there; but that, as it had belonged to us in ancient times, so thereafter it should return wholly to our authority and administration [Note: [Col. 0553] The edition reads “into our authority and administration”; manuscript 4 adds “and.”].

To this abbot a certain Adelmarius of Capua sold his entire estate at Anglena, near the church of Saint Vincent belonging to us, with fields, woods, meadows, and all the lands belonging to that estate. At the same time Lawrence, our deacon and monk, provost of the monastery of Saint Mary of Cingla [Note: [Col. 0553] Cingula 3.], made an exchange with a certain Landoarius of Capua involving certain lands at Calvo [Note: [Col. 0553C] Calvi.] and Calinulo, with the permission and consent, of course, of the aforementioned abbot Angelarius and Abbess Radelchisa [Note: [Col. 0553] Radelgisa 3.]. John also, priest and monk and provost of the aforementioned monastery of Cingla [Note: [Col. 0553] “the monastery of Cingla,” in the edition.], did the same concerning certain other lands for the same Landoarius, likewise by the permission and consent of that abbot and of Abbess Gaitruda [Note: [Col. 0553] The edition omits “and” and reads “the consent of the same Abbot Angelarius and Abbess Gaitruda.”].

Meanwhile, when the bishop of Teano had died, the aforementioned abbot was elected and ordained in that city by the clergy and people; there too he died and was buried, on the Nones of December [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscript 1b and the edition have: “The aforesaid abbot, however, not long afterwards, when the bishop of Teano had died, was made bishop there. Here …”; they read “buried on the Nones of December.” The Codex Cassinensis 47 reads: “On the Nones of December Angelarius, priest and abbot of this place, died.”].

RAGEMPRANDUS, elected twenty-first abbot in the aforesaid monastery at Teano (A.D. 889), held office for nine years and ten months [Note: [Col. 0553] “Ten months” is added in manuscript 1b.]. He sought and received from Pope John IX, according to the custom of his predecessors, a privilege for himself (A.D. 889, March) [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscript 1 reads “Qui tamen I.”; the edition reads “Qui videlicet abbas I.” [The abbreviated readings are uncertain.] [Col. 0553C] It survives in the Register of Peter the Deacon, no. 5: “Written by the hand of Leo, *scriniarius* of the holy Roman Church, in March, indiction II.” ANG.].

47. During his presidency [Note: [Col. 0553] “In these days A. … to the end of the chapter” was added in manuscript 1b and omitted by manuscript 1*.] [Note: [Col. 0553C–0554] Rather, under Bertharius. Our author first wrote this under Abbot Angelarius, to whom Herchempert appears to have been offered while Angelarius was provost. But, having also related the monastery’s fire under Angelarius, he corrected this and moved Herchempert at the same time to his proper place.] Adelgarius, a nobleman of Teano [Note: [Col. 0553] “of Teano” is omitted in manuscripts 1b and 2.], offered his son Herchempert to blessed Benedict together with offerings, a boy of exceptionally teachable intellect [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscript 4 adds “indeed.”] [Erchempert 61, 69, 65, 66.].

At the time when the Greeks and Neapolitans were besieging Capua (A.D. 886), that same Herchempert, travelling from Teano to Capua with seven other brethren, was, together with all of them, deprived of their horses and plundered by the Greeks near Anglena [Note: [Col. 0553] Omitted in manuscript 4.]; their servants too were captured. After the servants had been redeemed with silver, and only five horses recovered [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscripts 1b and 2 read “and five horses recovered.”], he alone, as he himself relates, remained on foot with his master and thus entered the city.

After this, when Atenulfus [Note: [Col. 0553] Atenolfus in manuscripts 1b and 2.] had obtained the gastaldship and had taken from the brethren everything belonging by right to our monastery in the territory of Capua (A.D. 887, January), the aforementioned Herchempert [Note: [Col. 0553] “By Abbot Angelarius” is added in manuscript 1b.] was sent to Rome concerning this matter to Pope Stephen. From him he brought the apostolic blessing to the brethren, obtained a privilege for the cenobium, and brought to the aforementioned Atenulfus letters of admonition requiring him immediately to restore everything he had taken, unless he wished to incur a sentence of excommunication [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscripts 1b and the edition read “to the venerable Pope Stephen and apostolic …” and “a privilege for the holy cenobium”; manuscripts 1b and 2 add “and to the aforesaid gastald.”]. Atenulfus received them and obeyed, ordering everything he had taken from us to be restored in full [Note: [Col. 0553] From “had taken” through “cut out” in manuscript 1b; from “obeyed” through “ordered” is also cut out there.].

This Atenulfus had also, long before, proposed to Pope Stephen that, if he would furnish him aid against the Saracens dwelling on the Garigliano, he would restore all the people of Gaeta whom he had recently captured and would render him the firmest fidelity [Note: [Col. 0554B] “Through Maion, abbot of Saint Vincent,” is added in manuscript 2. Manuscript 1b and the edition read “dwelling on the Garigliano” and “and fidelity to him”; the edition reads “the people of Gaeta.”]. But because the pope could not accomplish what he had requested, neither did he do what the pope had commanded [Note: [Col. 0553] From “but” through “had commanded” is cut out in manuscript 1b; the edition reads “had requested.”].

Theophylact too, the *strategos*, came in those days from Bari to Teano with an army and attempted to attack the same Saracens; but, daring nothing, he returned home [Note: [Col. 0553] “Too” in manuscript 1b and the edition; from “in those days” through “returned” is cut out in manuscript 1b.].

This abbot granted to the Empress Ageltruda, mother of King Lambert, under a *libellus* lease, for the days of her life alone, two cells of this monastery with all their property in Lombardy: one at the place called Laude [Note: [Col. 0554C] Lodi.], and the other at Persiceta [Note: [Col. 0554C] See ch. 54 and IV.18.]. In return, the empress sent him each year, as rent, three pounds of silver. [Note: [Col. 0553] Added by manuscript 1b in the margin and placed after “remained,” p. 615, line 8.]

He also made a *libellus* for a certain Gotfrid of the Marsi concerning the church of Saint Gregory at Serviliano [Note: [Col. 0553] “Of Saint Gregory” in manuscript 1b and the edition.], with male and female slaves and all its dependencies in the same county of the Marsi. [Note: [Col. 0553] The remainder is cut away in manuscript 1b, but so many words cannot have been written there.] In return he received every year a rent of fifteen *modii* of wheat, the same amount of wine, and one hundred fish in the month of October [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscript 2 reads “fifteen *modii* and fifteen *modii* of …”].

In those days a certain Sichelfrid of Capua [Note: [Col. 0555D] Compare ch. 24 above.] restored to this monastery the distinguished—that is, entire—estate of Patenaria [Note: [Col. 0555] “The estate at the place Patenara,” in manuscript 2.], which his grandfather had received from Abbot Bassacius under a written agreement and had retained [Note: [Col. 0555D] *l. e.* means “entire”; the edition reads “which his grandfather had received from Abbot Bassacius by written agreement and retained.”].

48. [Note: [Col. 0555] Thus I have corrected it. Manuscript 4 has: “In the seventh year of this abbot, indiction 14 …”; manuscript 1b and the edition have: “In the seventh year of this abbot, in which, while the brethren were dwelling at Teano, by God’s hidden judgment [the monastery was consumed] by fire.” From “The seventh … likewise” is added in manuscript 1b; compare p. 612, note m*.] The seventh yearly cycle of this abbot was now turning (A.D. 896), when, by the incomprehensible judgment of God, the monastery in which the brethren had begun to live at Teano was consumed by fire [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscripts 1b and 2 add “with all its wealth.”]. There too perished the Rule which blessed Benedict had written with his own hand [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “had composed.”], as well as the sacks in which food had been brought down from heaven, by God’s command, to that most holy father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “in which, by God’s command, food was brought down from heaven to the same holy Father Benedict.”]. Moreover, very many charters and precepts of the cenobium, granted to that monastery by individual emperors, dukes [Note: [Col. 0555] “Dukes” is added in manuscript 1b.] and princes, were burned together [Note: [Col. 0555] “Together” is added in manuscript 4.].

Among these, the documents concerning Casa Gentiana were likewise consumed by fire [Note: [Col. 0555] “The documents made concerning Casa Gentiana were likewise …” in manuscript 1 and the edition. [Col. 0555D] Yet at least a copy of Grimoald’s donation appears to have been preserved; compare ch. 14 above.].

For in the time of Abbot John, who was the third after this man [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1 reads “who was afterwards the fourth after this Angelarius”; manuscript 1b and the edition read “who was the third after this Ragemprand.”], when one day a discussion had arisen among the brethren before that venerable father as to which princes had granted the aforementioned Casa Gentiana to this monastery, a certain Maio, priest and grammarian, an old and truthful man [Note: [Col. 0555] “Most truthful” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], firmly asserted that he knew the matter with complete certainty. For he said [Note: [Col. 0555] The edition reads: “He said to the aforesaid Lord Abbot: ‘As I read,’ he said, ‘in the three aforesaid charters which were here …’]:

> “As I recall,” he said, “having read in three donation-charters that were in the archive of Lord Abbot Angelarius: first, Duke Gisulf granted the territory of Gentiana to the monastery of Saint Benedict [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “granted to Lord Abbot Petronax in the monastery of Saint Benedict.”]; later Prince Arichis granted greater portions there in Gentiana to this same monastery [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “likewise granted to Abbot Theodemar in this same monastery.”]. Again, his son Grimoald granted to Saint Benedict, by a charter of donation [Note: [Col. 0555] “By a charter of donation granted,” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], all his demesne property [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1b adds “his.”] with male and female slaves in the same place, Casa Gentiana; also the cell of Saint Agapitus, and many other things which I do not now remember [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1 and the edition read “very many other things which I do not now remember. Likewise …”].

> “The donation of those same princes concerning the ports of Trajectum and Vulturnum, and likewise concerning the fishery of Lesina, was also contained in those charters [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1 and the edition read “their donation concerning the port of Trajectum and the port of Vulturnum, but also the fishery of Lesina.”]. I read all these things, and renewed them in other charters [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “parchments”; the manuscript and edition read “and I myself renewed them from the commands of Lord Abbot Angelarius.”] at the command of that same Abbot Angelarius.”

[Note: [Col. 0555] The edition reads: “He said to the aforesaid Lord Abbot: ‘As I read,’ he said, ‘in the three aforesaid charters which were here …’”].

From the aforesaid fire at the monastery of Teano, whatever the brethren could in any way rescue from the church treasury was placed in the episcopal residence of that city. From this it is later reported that a not inconsiderable part of that treasury remained in the church [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1b and the edition read: “At that same time the aforesaid Abbot Angelarius was ordained bishop; not long afterwards he died and was buried in the same city on the Nones of December. On that occasion, a not inconsiderable part of the treasury remained in the church at Teano. This abbot …” From chapter 47: “The aforesaid abbot died on 8 Id. Nov.” Manuscript 1b and the edition read: “Thus a not inconsiderable part of the treasury remained in that church.”]. The aforesaid abbot died on November 6, the eighth day before the Ides of November [Note: [Col. 0555] The edition places “But the aforesaid abbot died on 8 Id. Nov.” after chapter 50.].

49. [Note: [Col. 0555] “In these times, S. …” in manuscript 1 and the edition.] At about this time (A.D. 899, November 6), Symbaticius [Note: [Col. 0555] Sabbaticius in manuscript 1, corrected in 1b; Ymbat. 3.], the patrician, coming from Constantinople, besieged Benevento for about three months and captured it on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November (October 18), in the year of the Lord 891 [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1 reads “captured Benevento in the year …”; corrected in manuscript 1b.].

Three hundred and thirty years had been completed since Zotto, the first duke of Benevento [Note: [Col. 0555] The edition reads “namely, 330 years from Zotto, first duke of Benevento.”]; throughout that period both the dukes and the princes of the Lombards had held that city.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] From the Chronicle of Saint Benedict, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS III, p. 201, to which the author added material drawn from Symbaticius’s charter, preserved in Register no. 136, from which Gattola published it, *H.*, p. 51. “Given in June, indiction 10.”]

This Symbaticius, being imperial *protospatharius* and *strategos* of Macedonia, Thrace, Cephallenia, and Lombardy [Note: [Col. 0555] From “This Symbaticius …” through “Lombardy” is cut out in manuscript 1b.], issued an *entilma* [imperial order] (A.D. 892, June) to the aforesaid abbot concerning the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento, Saint Mary of Cingla, and Saint Mary of Plumbariola [Note: [Col. 0555] Plombariola 3.]. He commanded sternly on behalf of the emperors that no one should presume to inflict in any manner any trouble or violence in the cases or possessions of the aforesaid cenobia belonging to the monastery of Cassino [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “subject to the monastery of Cassino, any injustice …”]. Whoever transgressed against them should know for certain that he would experience imperial wrath.

After Symbaticius [Note: [Col. 0555] “Thus,” in manuscript 1b; manuscript 1 reads “After him, Sabbaticius ruled there, George …”], George the patrician ruled at Benevento (A.D. 892) [Note: [Col. 0556D] In August, indiction X, he issued an *entilma* to Maio, abbot of Saint Vincent.]. When it had been held for three years and nine months [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “when he had held it, had sat in it …” [Col. 0556D] Not George but the Greeks, as the Chronicle of Saint Benedict correctly says.], Duke and Margrave Guy came and expelled the Greeks from there (A.D. 895, August), and ruled there for nearly two years [Note: [Col. 0555] Guidego 3; “duke and” is added in manuscript 1b.]; after him came Radelchis (A.D. 897, April) [Note: [Col. 0557] Adelchis in manuscript 1; Rachelchis 3. [Col. 0557A] “For two years” is added in manuscript 2.].

Thereafter the aforesaid Atenulfus, now count after holding the gastaldship of Capua, together with his son Landulf and thereafter their descendants, held the principality there for about 177 years (A.D. 899) [Note: [Col. 0557] The passage from “thereafter” through “177” is absent in manuscript 1.]. [Note: [Col. 0557] Manuscript 3 reads “six.” Manuscript 1b adds, from the Chronicle of Saint Benedict, p. 202: “At the same time Arnulf, king of the Franks, entered Italy and came as far as Pavia, wishing to reach Rome, but was compelled to return when famine and plague broke out together.” Manuscript 1 then continues: “At this time the Hungarians came into Italy in the year of the Lord 899,” from the Annals of Benevento.]

50. Meanwhile the aforesaid Atenulfus, having gathered a considerable army with the Neapolitans [Note: [Col. 0557] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “with Duke Gregory of Naples, and also with …”] and Amalfitans, came to the Garigliano against the Saracens. Having constructed a bridge of ships near Trajectum at the place called Setra, he crossed and attacked them.

While they were stationed there, one night, as they kept watch less cautiously, the Saracens with the people of Gaeta suddenly rushed upon them, struck down many of them, and fiercely pursued the rest as far as the aforementioned bridge [Note: [Col. 0557] “There,” in manuscript 1b and the edition; “Gaetans,” in the edition.]. But there, when our men at last resisted bravely, the Saracens turned their backs and were forced to shelter in their camp [Note: [Col. 0557] “Strongly,” in manuscript 1b and the edition. The edition adds: “But the aforesaid abbot died on 8 Id. Nov.”; see ch. 48.].

LEO, twenty-second abbot from blessed Benedict, likewise held office at Teano for fifteen years and seven months [Note: [Col. 0557] “Months” is added in manuscript 1b. From here manuscript 1 continues: “and he also received a privilege from Pope Sergius III, and likewise from Prince Atenulfus …” [Col. 0557C] Our author erred in seeking to date the period too precisely: in the fifteen years he found attributed to Leo, the final year was counted as whole. He held office fourteen years and seven months, as documentary evidence establishes.], in the time of Pope Christopher, who was expelled from the papacy and made a monk, and also of Pope Sergius III, from whom that abbot received the customary privilege [Note: [Col. 0557] “In the time of Emperor Leo and” is added in manuscript 2. [Col. 0557C] In the Register, no. 7, there survives Sergius’s privilege to Abbot Leo allowing him to have clerics ordained by whichever bishop he chose. ANG.].

51. He also acquired from the aforementioned Atenulfus, now prince [Note: [Col. 0557] “Prince Atenulfus,” in the edition.], a charter confirming all the offerings, grants, and possessions of this monastery (A.D. 902, May), chiefly because the records of this cenobium had first been consumed by fire here by the Saracens and then again at Teano (June) [Note: [Col. 0557] The passage from “chiefly because” through “had been” is added in manuscript 1b. [Col. 0557C] In Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 44, from the Register.].

[Note: [Col. 0557] The passage from “At this abbot’s intervention” through “might be necessary” is absent in manuscript 1; manuscript 1c inserts: “To him Waimarius … the estate with its dependencies.”]

At this abbot’s intervention [Note: [Col. 0557] “Moreover” is added in manuscript 4.], the same prince granted Mount Saint Eleutherius to the monastery of Saint Mary of Cingla [Note: [Col. 0557] Cingula 3.], for pasture for the animals of that place and for cutting wood for various uses. The river called Ete, from its source as far as the river Vulturnus, and thereafter the Vulturnus itself to the foot of the aforesaid Mount Saint Eleutherius, insofar as it belonged to the right of the palace, were granted so that the monastery might do in those waters whatever might be necessary for it.

This abbot, in the fifth year of his ordination (A.D. 904), began rebuilding this monastery, which had been wholly abandoned for twenty-seven years [Note: [Col. 0557] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “This”; the passage from “This abbot” through “abandoned” is added in manuscript 1b. [Col. 0558C] Leo himself wrote this in his autograph codex, so that the fault of the error cannot be shifted to copyists.].

Guaimarius [Note: [Col. 0557] Waimarius in manuscripts 1b and 2.], prince of Salerno, granted to him by charter (A.D. 900, August) one large estate at the place called Rota, with houses, woods, shrublands, vineyards and chestnut groves [Note: [Col. 0557] *castaneis*, in the edition.], male and female slaves, and everything belonging wholly to that estate [Note: [Col. 0557] “Belonging to that same estate,” in the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0558C] Gattola published the charter from the Register, *Acc.*, p. 45. Roderis, nephew of Rodelchisa, wife of Adelferius Rofrid, had lost the estate because of a conspiracy against the prince. Rota was situated near Saint Severinus. You will find the river and town of Sarno at the foot of Mount Vesuvius.].

The same Guaimarius [Note: [Col. 0557] Guamarius 3.], by another charter, granted to this monastery half an estate in the territory of Sarno, at the place called Lentiaria [Note: [Col. 0557] Jentiaria 3.], which had belonged to a certain Agenard [Note: [Col. 0557] Manuscript 4 adds “which.”]. Agenard himself had already offered this half to blessed Benedict, together with everything belonging to that estate.

He made a *libellus* for a certain Adelarius, a Roman citizen, concerning the church of Saint Benedict, which had belonged to us there from ancient times, on the condition that whenever our abbot or monks went to Rome to accomplish some business, he should receive them honourably in that church for as long as it was necessary for them to remain there, and should send sixty denarii each year to our monastery as rent [Note: [Col. 0557] The passage from “He made a *libellus*” through “should send” is absent in manuscript 1; “added in 4.”].

The aforesaid abbot died on August 17 (A.D. 914), the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0557] The words “the aforesaid abbot” are absent in manuscript 1.]. Both Ragemprandus and Leo held authority in that Teano cenobium itself, where they lived [Note: [Col. 0557] “Where they lived,” in manuscript 1 and the edition.], died, and were buried.

52. At the same time the aforesaid prince, seeing that the Saracens could not be driven from the Garigliano without a strong hand and an outstretched arm, sent his son Landulf to Emperor Leo at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0557] *Constantinopoli* in manuscript 1b and the edition.]. He reported all the evils which they had suffered for so many years at the hands of the Hagarenes, and begged and implored the emperor to deign to assist as quickly as possible the country afflicted and devastated by those same Saracens, and not to refuse to send him the aid of his army so that he might uproot them from the Garigliano [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 1b reads “and so that he might”; the edition reads “and that he might”; manuscripts 1b and 2 have the plural “might.”].

The emperor received him with sufficient honour and graciously promised that he would fulfil everything Landulf had proposed.

Meanwhile, after the aforesaid Atenulfus had died at Capua (A.D. 910), Landulf, having obtained permission from the emperor, returned and was received with great honour by his brother Atenulfus. The emperor, not forgetful of his promise, then sent into these regions the patrician Nicholas, surnamed Picingli [Note: [Col. 0559] The name is absent in manuscript 4; the following material reads: “having enlisted [him], with a strong …”; in manuscript 1, the Greek material after this has been cut away.], with a strong Greek force, and by imperial commands ordered him to destroy utterly the Saracens dwelling on the Garigliano [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 1* and the edition read “especially those dwelling on the Garigliano”; manuscript 1b and the edition read “should strive to destroy.”].

The aforesaid patrician came, endowed with great strength and very great prudence [Note: [Col. 0559] “And endowed with very great strength,” in manuscript 1b and the edition.]. He first endeavoured to detach from the Saracens those whom they had as their intimates and allies—namely, Gregory, duke of the Neapolitans [Note: [Col. 0559] “Duke of Naples,” in manuscripts 1b and 2.], and John, duke of Gaeta—by conferring upon them from the emperor the honour of the patriciate. Then, having joined the aforesaid brothers Landulf and Atenulfus, princes [Note: [Col. 0559] “Princes of Capua,” in manuscripts 1b and 2.], and having also summoned Guaimarius, prince of Salerno, and added all the Apulians and Calabrians to the overseas army, he pitched camp against the Saracens on this side of the Garigliano (A.D. 916).

When Pope John X learned this—he who three years earlier (A.D. 914, January) had seized the Roman See from the episcopal see of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0559] Thus corrected; manuscript 4 reads “and it itself”; the words are absent in manuscript 1b and the edition.]—he too arrived with Alberic [Note: [Col. 0559] Adelberic 3.], the margrave [Note: [Col. 0559C] Of Camerino and duke of Spoleto; see Di Meo, *Annals of Naples*, under A.D. 899.], and a strong force of fighting men, and took up position on the other side [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “came upon them.”]. Thus, besieging them from both sides for three continuous months [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 4 reads “besieging them and …”], they brought them to the utmost extremity.

When the Saracens were already suffering from extreme hunger, and no longer hoped by any means or contrivance whatever to escape our forces, and saw death before their eyes, they finally, on the advice of the aforementioned leaders Gregory and John [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 3 reads “of the emperors and leaders.”], burned all their houses. Then, fleeing in a united attack, they scattered through the nearby mountains and forests (August).

Our men pursued them relentlessly; scarcely a very few escaped from so great a multitude, while they killed all the rest. Thus, by the aid and mercy of God, they were completely driven from these regions in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 915, indiction three, in August [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 4 adds “in all things.” From “were driven out” through “August” is cut out in manuscript 1b but preserved in manuscript 1*. [Col. 0559C] It appears certain that this happened in A.D. 916, when Berengar was already emperor; that is the third year of John X.].

Blessed be God in all things.

JOHN, the twenty-third abbot from blessed Benedict, held office for nineteen years and seven months [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “nineteen years and months.”].

53. Born of a noble Capuan family, at the time when the aforesaid Abbot Leo died (A.D. 914, August), he was serving in the Capuan church in the office of archdeacon, endowed with genuinely religious and very honorable morals. But since for some time the community of brethren dwelling at Teano had been deprived of its own shepherd, and no one among them could be found who seemed suitable for so great a prelacy, then the princes Landulf and Atenulf, taking counsel with the monks, approached the aforesaid archdeacon and compelled him, by both admonitions and entreaties, to assume the government of the aforesaid community. When he at last consented, he became a monk; and not long afterward he was elected by all the brethren according to custom, and honorably consecrated by the aforesaid Pope John. Thus appointed abbot, he began to urge the brethren to leave Teano and go with him to dwell at Capua, a city which was both the chief of the surrounding cities and the residence of the princes, lords of that same land. Obeying his command, they all set out together to live at Capua.

Yet in that city no monastery had yet been built. In the place where it is now seen to stand, namely beside the gate of Saint Angelus, there was a very small and exceedingly poor church; beside it stood another similarly small and wretched little dwelling, woven from wattles, in which only three or four aged brethren lived. This place had formerly been acquired from the princes for building a monastery by Maio, abbot of Saint Vincent; and he had built there the little church and dwelling already mentioned. But after Godelpert had become abbot, he conferred with our aforesaid Abbot John and, with the permission or license of the aforesaid princes, exchanged this place with him (November), receiving in return another place of equal area, beside the church of Saint Mary called “of Landi Magister,” where the same Abbot John had previously intended to build our monastery. [Note: Col. 0561: “beside the church of Saint Mary called Landi Magister” added in 1b.]

Then Godelpert himself went to the aforesaid princes (November 16) and acquired another place on the river Vulturnus itself; there he began to build a monastery in honor of Saint Vincent, to gather there monks who had been scattered in various places, and to recover the goods and possessions of that monastery which had long been lost.

Our John, assisted by no small support from both relatives and friends, likewise began in the place already mentioned to construct from the foundations a monastery in honor of the blessed father Benedict. Within no long time he suitably completed a large and beautiful church, together with buildings appropriate for the various functions of the monastery; and there he gathered fifty and more monks to live according to the Rule. Through his zeal and care, with God’s grace going before, the monastery itself was quickly raised up and enriched with diverse resources both within and without. Among other things, this same abbot made there a missal codex with gilded silver covers and gems; likewise a Gospel-book of similar workmanship. He entirely covered the altar around its circumference with worked silver. He also made a most beautiful processional cross with gems and enamels. Two silver candlesticks; likewise a silver ewer with its aquamanile. Bronze vessels for various uses, weighing six hundred pounds. Many and various ecclesiastical books for the whole year. Chasubles, copes, albs, and dalmatics; and he supplied most adequately every kind of furnishing, both for ecclesiastical and domestic use.

At that time a quite remarkable sign occurred in the same monastery. For from the third hour of the day until nearly midnight, the high altar of that church emitted such an abundance of water, drop by drop like sweat, that all the vestments of the same altar were soaked.

[Note: Col. 0561: “This … were soaked” added in 1b.]

54. At Cassino, after the restoration of the whole greater church, when the same abbot had made certain ecclesiastical ornaments there, he also surrounded the high altar, in which the body of the holy father Benedict lay buried, with marble slabs of the purest white. From the aforesaid princes Landulf and Atenulf he received a charter confirming the whole abbey (A.D. 925, February 23). He also received another charter concerning the estate of Petra Mellaria, with its whole woodland and chestnut grove, all its appurtenances, and four *aldiones*—dependent persons—with their sons and daughters and all belonging to them (A.D. 928, April 25).

It should be known that the aforesaid princes gave us the estate of Petra Mellaria in exchange and received from us the estate of Saint Benedict at Pantano near Benevento; they offered it to Saint Sophia, a dependency of this monastery. This abbot made a *libellus* lease to Adelbert, son of Rainerius of Rastello, concerning certain estates of this monastery in the county of Modena, in the district called Persiceta, amounting to eight hundred *iugera*, at an annual rent of seven solidi. He also made another lease to the same Adelbert concerning certain possessions of this place in the district of Adili. Later Adelbert himself offered by his written deed to this monastery certain other estates of his own, which then appeared to belong to him in the same district of Adili.

The aforesaid abbot died on the day before the Kalends of April (A.D. 934), and was laid in honorable burial at the Capuan monastery. About these days the aforesaid John, usurper of the Apostolic See, was deposed by the Romans, and Leo VI was appointed in his place (A.D. 928, March).

ADELBERT, the twenty-fourth abbot, appointed by all the brethren on the sixth day after his predecessor’s death, ruled for nine years, and both lived and died at Capua. He lived in the time of Pope Stephen VII and Pope John XI, who was the son of Pope Sergius.

[Note: Col. 0563B: “in the year of the Lord 934” added in 2.]

[Note: Col. 0563: “Stephen VII and” absent in 1b.]  
[Note: Col. 0563C: Compare Liutprand II.48. Stephen VII, from A.D. 930, died.]

55. In the fourth year of this abbot (A.D. 937), innumerable Hungarians came against Capua, ravaged and plundered everything around it. They did likewise at Benevento; ranging through and devastating Sarno, Nola, and all Liburia, and since no one could be found able to resist so great a multitude, they returned to Capua and remained for twelve days in the field of Galliano. At that time, having captured many of our people, we expended no small amount in ransoming them. The total was as follows: a large silver crown with silver chains; a gilded silver censer; four silver cups; three silver spoons weighing one pound; twenty tareni; a rose-colored chasuble valued at fifteen Byzantine coins; another, with silver stripes, at sixteen Byzantine coins; and another with lions. Four cloth borders, four paces long and three palms broad; an altar cloth, rose-colored, at sixteen Byzantine coins; sixteen excellent carpets for sixty-seven Byzantine coins; *pannus admasurus* for eight Byzantine coins; three *hostiales* for thirteen Byzantine coins; two *castaneae* for eight Byzantine coins; and three silk cushions for ten Byzantine coins.

Then, elated by so great a victory and laden with such vast booty, they entered the country of the Marsi and began to do the same, burning and laying waste everything. But by the decree and help of the Almighty, the Marsi and Peligni assembled together, laid ambushes in very narrow places, and bravely fell upon them. Killing almost all of them, they tore from their hands an immense booty in gold, silver, textiles, carpets, and animals of every kind. Those among them who could escape the swords of the Marsi fled away and returned to their own land.

56. To this abbot John, consul and duke of the Neapolitans, by his charter confirmed and granted the church of Saint Cecilia, situated within Naples in the square called Palms, which had belonged from ancient times to our monastery, together with all its appurtenances. He likewise confirmed and granted the cell of Saint Severus at Sorrento, with all its substance and appurtenances; our cell at Casa Gentiana, with woodland, lands, woods, and everything belonging to us in that territory; and exemption for our monks from every market or port toll anywhere in the whole city of Naples.

At the same time a certain nobleman Agelmund of Vicalbo offered this monastery his estate called Pranduli, with all its appurtenances; another estate at Patenara, with vineyards, meadows, and all its appurtenances; and all that belonged to him by hereditary right, both in the city of Sora and in the castle called Sclavi. Under this abbot John, provost of Saint Liberator, made a lease of the goods of this monastery in the March, at Manoppello, Oliveto, Torre, and diverse other places; in return he received two hundred solidi and one hundred modii of land in the village of Gaulejani. Likewise Garipert, provost of various cells throughout the March and appointed by this abbot, made a lease of certain houses belonging to us at Larino. The same abbot made a lease to a certain Grimoald of Camerino of all the possessions of this monastery in the territory of Termoli, namely between the Biferno and Asinaricus rivers, the village of Guilliolisi, and the sea; receiving immediately one hundred solidi as the price and eight solidi as the annual rent.

[Note: Col. 0563: “And this chapter” added in 1c, which puts it first: “Under this abbot … Larino”; followed by “To this … grant.”]

BALDWIN, a Frankish by birth, the twenty-fifth abbot from Saint Benedict (A.D. 942). He lived in the time of the aforesaid princes Landulf and Atenulf and of Landulf, the latter’s brother. He received from Pope Marinus II a privilege concerning the customary rights of this monastery (A.D. 944, January 21).

[Note: Col. 0565: “continues from here” 1.]

[Note: Col. 0565: “twenty-fifth” 1, ed.]

57. In the time of this pope, Sico, bishop of Capua—a man certainly worldly and unlearned—was not afraid to act against divine and human ordinances. He violently took away the church of Saint Angelus in the place anciently called “at Diana’s arch,” now called “Ad Formas,” which his predecessor had long before granted to one of our monks for building a monastery there; and he gave it as a benefice to one of his deacons.

When this was reported to the ears of the aforesaid venerable Pope Marinus by the same monk, the pope immediately sent letters of apostolic authority to the aforesaid bishop. In them he attacked him sharply and sternly reproved him for ignorance of the canons, lack of literary knowledge, familiarity with secular persons, and even presumptuous violation of his predecessor’s enactments. He also ordered him without delay to restore the aforesaid church to that monk, so that a monastery might be established there, as his predecessor had ordained under obligation of anathema. He decreed that this monastery should remain forever free from disturbance and harassment by that bishop and by all his successors, under the protection and authority of the monastery of Saint Benedict, then at Capua. He further decreed that the deacon to whom the aforesaid bishop had granted the church should be excluded altogether from every association with that bishop except service at the altar. If the bishop should presume in any respect to disobey these commands, he was to know that from that time he would be deprived of priestly rank and bound by the bond of excommunication.

[Note: Col. 0565: “In the time of these popes” 1, 2.]  
[Note: Col. 0565: “a man, certainly, worldly and unlearned” absent in 1, 2.]  
[Note: Col. 0565: “Saint Angelus, which then belonged to …” 1, 2; “Saint Angelus, which formerly belonged to …” 3.]  
[Note: Col. 0565C: The temple of Diana Tifatina—so called from nearby Mount Tifata—was there. Even if every author were silent, this could be known from the inscribed stone monuments still extant there alone. Ang. Compare Velleius Paterculus II.25.]
