58. At the same time, when the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento had been taken away from this monastery by the violence of the princes, this same abbot, having produced the charters of Roman pontiffs and kings who had confirmed the aforesaid monastery to this house, immediately recovered it and brought it again under the jurisdiction of this monastery. But not long afterward, when he had been summoned to Rome by the aforesaid pope, and that pontiff had entrusted to him the abbey of Saint Paul because he was a man of great prudence, the monastery of Saint Sophia was again seized by the princes and withdrawn from our authority.

About these days, after Marinus had died and Agapetus succeeded to the Apostolic See (A.D. 946, March), this same abbot complained to him concerning the matter. The pope immediately wrote to the aforesaid princes, sharply rebuking them for daring to do such things, and at once admonishing and beseeching them to restore the monastery in its entirety to our abbot without delay. If they acted otherwise, they were to know that they would immediately be bound by the bond of anathema. Obeying his command, Prince Atenulf promptly returned the monastery itself to our abbot and, by his own charter, confirmed it forever to this monastery as it had originally been offered there by Lord Arichis (A.D. 943, January 30), together with everything later granted there by individual princes or any other faithful persons. At the same time, at the abbot’s request, he granted eight households of free persons to the cell of Saint Benedict at Caudi (A.D. 943, January 30). He also made for him another charter concerning the appurtenances of the whole abbey.

[Note: Col. 0565: In manuscript 1 this entire chapter was contained in three lines: “Atenulf likewise … confirmed his charter (?) to this monastery forever.” These were partly erased, and 1b wrote the present passage.]  
[Note: Col. 0566C: In this chapter the order of events and dates is greatly confused. Prince Atenulf is known to have died in A.D. 943, so that his name seems to have entered Agapetus’s letter through a scribe’s error. The beginning of the chapter derives from letters published from Peter’s *Register* by Gattola, *Historia*, p. 53. Compare Leo’s account of the cell of Saint Sophia in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 54. Di Meo considers both letters suspect. Stefano Borgia published the judgment delivered by Beneventan judges under Landulf II in A.D. 945, by which the monastery of Saint Sophia was exempted from the jurisdiction of Abbot Majelpot and the monastery of Cassino: *Memorie di Benevento* III, p. 23.]

59. About these days, when the princes, out of greed or desire for gain, had brought our monastery, then at Capua, under their own jurisdiction, and on that occasion the brethren dwelling there were in some fashion living a secular life, the aforesaid Pope Agapetus, having learned this through the representation of our abbot, immediately sent very severe letters of apostolic authority to the aforesaid princes. He strongly rebuked and reproached their wickedness for daring to commit so great a crime, and further commanded that they should no longer presume to exercise any lordship in that monastery. All the monks were immediately to return to their former monastery at Cassino with all the goods of the monastery, there to serve the Lord regularly under their own abbot; only two or three elderly brethren were to be left in the Capuan monastery. If either the princes or indeed the monks presumed to act otherwise, or if anyone attempted to seize anything from the goods of that monastery or make any arrangement concerning them without the abbot, they were to know that, unless they repented, they would be excommunicated by apostolic authority.

The aforesaid abbot also obtained from the same holy pontiff a privilege concerning the monastery of Saint Stephen near Terracina (A.D. 955, October 16), which, as is read in Saint Benedict’s *Life* (Gregory, *Dialogues* II.22), the blessed Benedict had shown by a marvelous appearance in a vision was to be built.

A charter of confirmation from Kings Hugh and Lothair concerning all the possessions of this place is also held by this abbot (A.D. 943, May 15). At that time those kings, wishing to restore to its former condition the monastery of Saint Angelus at Barregio, which had been destroyed by the Agareni [Saracens], confirmed by their own charter everything that earlier kings had granted there to it by royal donation.

[Note: Col. 0567: “About these days … excommunicated” added in 1b.]  
[Note: Col. 0567C: From an undated letter of Pope Agapetus to Prince Landulf, published from the Register by Gattola, *Historia*, p. 90.]  
[Note: Col. 0567: absent in ed.]  
[Note: Col. 0567: “entirely” 1b, 2.]  
[Note: Col. 0567: “the same most holy pontiff, through …” 1b.]  
[Note: Col. 0567: “our venerable Abbot Baldwin, reports” 1b.]

[Note: Col. 0567: “Cassino, leaving there only two or three elderly brethren, with all the goods … to serve. Which …” 1b, ed.]

[Note: Col. 0567C: Tosti published it from the Register, *History of Cassino*, p. 219. It seems remarkable that the Roman pontiffs regarded Baldwin as abbot of Cassino while Majelpot and Aligern exercised both the name and office at Cassino. Yet Hugh of Farfa calls him co-abbot, in a passage which we reproduce complete from Muratori, Dissertation 73: “The monastery of Cassino too was restored under the instruction of that Abbot Odo to the norm of regular order, having been destroyed in the devastation of the aforesaid Agareni, like very many monasteries of the Italian kingdom, as we have said. There he placed over it his disciple, the venerable abbot named Baldwin. His fellow-disciple and co-abbot, the bountiful father Aligern, succeeded him in government; Odo himself had trained Aligern from childhood in the path of the Rule at the aforesaid monastery on the Aventine, Saint Mary’s. Through him the aforementioned monastery was recovered to its present eminence, as many living persons remember.”]  
[Note: Col. 0567: “Of Hugh” 2 places in chapter 57: “of Hugh … confirmed.”]  
[Note: Col. 0567: “also” 1, ed.]  
[Note: Col. 0568C: Gattola published three documents given on the same day, *Accessiones*, p. 48 ff.]

[Note: Col. 0568B: In these times, when the church at Cingla had been devastated by Saracens, John, provost of that cell, took whatever furnishings or treasure he could in any manner remove, and with our abbot’s consent went to Capua, where he began to build a monastery. At the same time the venerable Pope Marinus confirmed in full, by privilege, that same church of Saint Mary at Capua, with all its possessions, to the Cassinese monastery.]  
[Note: Col. 0569C: In the same privilege mentioned above by Leo.]  
[Note: Col. 0568B: The same thing was likewise confirmed by John XV, Benedict VIII, Benedict IX, Leo, and Stephen IX, in the abbatiates of our abbots Baldwin, Aligern, Manso, Atenulf, Theobald, and Frederick.]  
[Note: Col. 0569C: Peter the Deacon collected the privileges of these and other pontiffs in his Register nos. 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, and 21; see also nos. 39 and 41. Ang.]

In those days, when Basil, imperial protospatharius, was at Salerno, our monks approached him at the abbot’s command. He made a charter of restitution and confirmation for all the appurtenances of this monastery throughout Apulia that at that time we had lost: namely, the church of Saint Benedict at Lesina with all its appurtenances; certain ruined houses within that city; the fishery of Lauri and another fishery in the same place; at Ascoli, a house with an upper room, estates, and wells; at Melessana, estates and wells; at Saint John in Ruliana, estates; at Saint Decorentius, lands; in old Canosa, the church of Saint Benedict, a mill, and estates; at Minervino, the cave in which is the church of Saint Saviour and lands; at Andria, vineyards and olive groves; and, at the stream called “of the Monk,” an estate. The aforesaid Basil caused all these things to be restored to our brethren, confirming them to us by a charter sealed with his own seal and forbidding anyone thereafter to presume to seize them.

[Note: Col. 0569: Here in manuscript 1 chapter 61 followed. When it was displaced by symbols, 1b wrote in the margin: “Abbot Majelpot is to be written here.” What follows is absent in 1; in manuscript 2 it is written in the middle of chapter 60; chapter 58 in 3 (?). “Basil also, imperial protospatharius, being at Salerno, when [our monks] approached him …” 2.]  
[Note: Col. 0569: *cartulam* (“little charter”) ed.]  
[Note: Col. 0569: “and” ed.]  
[Note: Col. 0569C: Register no. 112. Yet its dates cannot possibly be reconciled, whether through the Latin translator’s error or the copyist’s incompetence. It was given in October, indiction X, in the year 6520 from the beginning of the world, that is, 1011. No abbot is named there. Ang.]  
[Note: Col. 0569: absent in ed.]  
[Note: Col. 0569: “this” ed.]

MAJELPOT, the twenty-sixth abbot, ruled for six years.

[Note: Col. 0569: “He ruled … endowed” was added at different times at the end of chapter 60, after the six lines first written had been erased.]  
[Note: Col. 0569C: He was elected while Baldwin was alive, to whom he seems to have remained subject.]  
[Note: Col. 0569C: “He lived in the time of the emperors Romanus and Nicephorus” added in 2.]

60. Having been made abbot from the provostship of this monastery (A.D. 943), he received from the aforesaid prince Landulf a charter concerning generally all the goods and possessions of this monastery. [The source’s *rebus ac possessionibus* means “goods and possessions”; witness 1b and the edition add “and.”] Likewise, concerning the lands and estates in Liburia, at the place called *Ad Trefone* [“ad Treffone,” 3; “Atrefone,” 4], belonging both to our monastery and to his palace at that place [Register no. 210, ANG.]. The same prince also issued another charter [published by Gattola from the original, *Acc.*, p. 53] for this abbot (A.D. 944, August 30), specifically concerning the water of the river Saonis [“Saconis,” 4; it was formerly called the Savo; see Statius, *Silvae* IV.66; Pliny III.5, ANG.] and the other waters, with their banks and boundaries, and concerning free women who had been joined in marriage to the monastery’s servants; likewise concerning the appurtenance, or confirmation, of the entire abbey [“and” is added in 4; “same abbot,” instead of “the same prince,” in 4; “the aforesaid prince,” instead of “the same prince,” in 1b; “to the same abbot,” instead of “for this abbot,” in 1b; “prince Landulf,” instead of “the aforesaid prince,” in 1b; “his charter,” instead of “a charter,” in 1b].

Under this abbot, a certain Leo, priest of the city of Larino, who later became bishop of Termoli and Trivento [he is called a pseudo-bishop in the princes’ privileges. Gattola published Leo’s charter from the Register, *H.*, p. 130], offered this monastery the church of Saint Benedict (A.D. 945, August), situated within that same city, with all its goods and appurtenances [“and,” 1b]. Later, in the time of Abbot Aligern, the aforesaid prince [Prince Landulf, 1b] confirmed it to this monastery by his charter [“his own charter,” 1b] (A.D. 952, May 6; Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 55, from the original).

Likewise, a certain John, a monk by nationality a Capuan [Register no. 211. ANG.; “likewise, a certain J.,” 1b], offered in this place the church of Saint Vitus, built on Mount Saint Agatha above Capua [originally called Mount Tifata; it is now called Mount Saint Nicholas, from the chapel constructed on its summit, where once stood a most strongly fortified citadel. ANG.], near the place called Ferruzanum [it is still called Ferrazano, but it does not adjoin Mount Saint Agatha, from which it is separated by the intervening river Volturno. ANG.], together with the water [“that water itself,” 1b], mills, and absolutely all the appurtenances of that church [“of that place,” 3], as well as all its movable and immovable property [“of the same” is absent in 4].

This abbot granted a *libellus* to a certain Aregis of Teano concerning the church of Saint Adiutor at Alife [“of Alife,” 1b], with all its appurtenances, and concerning the wood called Catulisca, together with certain other possessions [“many possessions,” 1b] which we seemed to hold in the territory of that same city. In return he received from him, besides the annual rent, four bezants [“bisants,” 1b].

He also granted a *libellus* to a certain Judge Ursus [“Judge” is absent in 3] for fifteen years, concerning all the waters, fisheries, and lands of the entire district of Lesina, for three bezants and four hundred good eels each year in November [“each year,” edition]. [“November. Basil also, imperial protospatharius, etc.; see chapter 59.”]

After the death of that abbot [1b reads “of that abbot,” instead of “of the same abbot”], when Lord Adelbert [“Adelpertus,” 3], distinguished bishop of the church of Capua; Lord Arderic [“Harderic,” 4; “Bishop Arderic,” 1b], bishop of Teano; Leo, venerable abbot of Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ; and the most noble judges of the aforesaid city, Arechis and Sadelfrid; and Adenulf [“Atenulf,” 3 and 4], castald of the men of Aquino [see below, Book I], a most energetic man [“man” is added in 4], had assembled in the chapter-house of the Capuan monastery on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [“8 Kalends of November” is absent in 4], with everyone unanimously consenting and approving, Lord Aligern, then provost of this monastery—a plainly venerable and highly honourable man [“man” is added in 4], endowed with both divine learning [absent in 1b and 2] and secular prudence—was elected abbot by all the brethren with immense assent [“greatest,” 1b] and joy [“joy,” 1b and 2].

[The phrase “How the kingdom of Italy passed from the Franks to the Teutonics” is marked here as transferred from elsewhere; see below.]

61. It seems truly worthwhile at this point, since the history has advanced to that time, to touch briefly upon how the kingdom of Italy was transferred from the Franks to the Teutonics.

[At this point, an account of how the kingdom of Italy passed from the Franks to the Teutonics does not seem irrelevant. This chapter had been written by our author before the chapter on Majelpot; he therefore transferred it here after marking it with signs. 1, edition.]

[This chapter, evidently patched together from royal catalogues and popular narratives, teems with errors; we judged it superfluous to note them individually.]

Finally [the word “finally” is absent in witnesses 1 and 2], after the death of Louis, son of Lothair (A.D. 875, August 12), about whom we have already said more above—namely, he who, after dividing the Frankish kingdom with his brothers Lothair and Charles [1b reads “with his brother Lothair and Charles”], had retained Italy for some time [witnesses 1 and 2 add “by fortunate lot”]—Berengar of Friuli [1b adds “of Friuli”; the edition prints “Forojuliensis”], son of Everard [“Eberard,” 2; “Ev tard,” 3], margrave of Italy, seized the kingdom (A.D. 888) [“Berengar invaded the kingdom,” 1; “Berengar of Friuli, son of Everard, invaded the kingdom of Italy,” 1b; “King Berengar,” edition]. But soon, at the very beginning of his rule, having been defeated in two battles by Guy, son of Guy the count [“two battles,” 1b], he finally fled to Verona [“to Verona,” 1b].

[At that time, after the aforesaid Pope Agapetus II had died, John XI [rather John XII, although XIII in Peter’s catalogue, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *SS.* III, 219; here he confused one with the other], a Roman by birth and son of Alberic, consul of the Romans, succeeded him in the pontificate. Added in 2.]

After Guy had held the kingdom for approximately six years, he died from vomiting blood [“with a bloody flux,” added in 1b] (A.D. 894) [compare *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *SS.* III, p. 202] and handed it over [“transferred it,” 1 and 2] to his son Lambert [“Lampert,” 3].

When Lambert likewise died six years later [that is, after he had become emperor, A.D. 892], Louis, son of Boso, king of Provence, ruled for three years (A.D. 900). Against him Rudolph, son of the king of Burgundy, came into Italy once more [“while meanwhile Berengar was killed by his own men,” in 1 but deleted in 1b].

Meanwhile [“after these events,” 1], Pope John XI [“Pope John XIII,” 1; “rather, the tenth,” marginal note] joined with the magnates of Italy and drove Rudolph from it. He sent envoys and invited Hugh, duke of Aquitaine, who at that time excelled in the greatest prudence and abundant courage (A.D. 926). He was immediately made king and, together with his son Lothair, held the kingdom of Italy for several years with considerable strength and manliness (A.D. 926).

With this Hugh came Azzo, count of Burgundy [“Count Azzo,” 1b], uncle of that Berard who was surnamed Franciscus [“a kinsman of the same king,” 1 and 2; this begins quire XVI of manuscript 1*], from whom the counts of the Marsi were descended.

Not long afterward, the same Hugh crowned his son (A.D. 931) and joined him in marriage to the most noble Adelaide, who was connected with the leading men of Tuscany [“from the Tuscan nobility,” 1b]. But when, as an old man, he had begun to be despised by him and to suffer certain affronts and acts of ingratitude [“since he had already begun to suffer some troubles from him, as an old man,” 1 and edition], he left the kingdom to him and withdrew to Burgundy with all his treasure [“and all his wealth,” 1]. There he built at his own expense a monastery called Saint Peter of Arles, endowed it most richly [“building a very rich monastery,” edition], and became a monk there (A.D. 946).

Then, after nearly four years, Lothair suddenly fell into frenzy and ended his life (A.D. 950, November 22); and thus he brought the reign of the Frankish kings in Italy to an end.

[The following passage is the first recension’s wording, deleted in 1b: “After this, Albert, son of Berengar, a most energetic man, following his father’s example, seized the kingdom. Having captured Queen Adelaide, he brought her into his house, thinking that through her he would easily acquire and retain the whole kingdom more fully. For this reason all the princes of Italy, greatly disturbed, ordered Albert not to retain their lady the queen any longer on any terms, unless he wished to experience the hostility and anger of all; rather, he should release her honourably to go wherever she wished. After the queen had been released, she returned beyond the mountains to her relatives and immediately sent envoys to Otto, duke of Saxony, and obtained marriage with him. He promptly gathered a powerful army, came into Italy, expelled and put Albert to flight, and, seizing the kingdom by this opportunity, established it under the Teutonic kings.” The erased correction changes the reading “Berengar, with his son Albert” to “Albert, son of Berengar.”]

After his death, his wife Adelaide fled to her kinsman Atto [“Adelachis,” 3], into the exceedingly well-fortified fortress of Canossa [“a very strongly fortified fortress,” 1b and edition]. Meanwhile the aforesaid Berengar, desiring once more to seize the kingdom with his son Albert, a man of great energy [“a very energetic man,” 1b and edition], and therefore striving by every means to capture the aforesaid queen, besieged the fortress for nearly three years.

Atto, however, having taken counsel with the queen, sent a messenger to Otto, duke of Saxony, then glorious for his victory over the Hungarians (A.D. 955). They reported to him everything that was being done concerning them [the variant reads “concerning her,” with the queen alone as object] and begged him to cross into Italy without delay, free them from Berengar’s siege, and receive the queen herself in marriage together with the kingdom.

The fortress had now almost been forced to surrender to the enemy when, behold, by God’s providence, the messenger sent by the queen suddenly returned [the edition reads “sent by God to the queen”]. Since, because of the most careful siege, no entrance into the fortress was open to him [“given to him,” 1b and edition], the clever archer secretly fastened the letters and the ring that he had brought from the duke to an arrow and, taking up his bow, shot them into the fortress without anyone suspecting it [1b: “and, having seized his bow, shot them into it”].

The substance of the letters was as follows: the duke, having already crossed the Alps, had come to Verona, while his son Liudolf had preceded him to Milan [“was at Milan,” 4]; they should act manfully, since help would come to them shortly; and, with God’s help, he would act according to their wishes both in the matter of the marriage and in the other interests of the kingdom.

What more need be said? The duke arrived immediately, Berengar and Albert [“Alpert,” 3] were put to flight, and the siege was lifted. Two of Berengar’s daughters were captured and sent into exile in Teutonic territory [“his daughters,” 1b]. Otto soon obtained Adelaide in marriage, and from that time onward the Teutonic kings began to rule in Italy (A.D. 951). Not long afterward he entered Rome and received the imperial crown from the hand [“hands,” 1b] of Pope John XII, Roman pontiff [“of the Roman pontiff,” 1b; “of Pope John XII, Roman pontiff,” edition], in the nine hundred and sixty-second year of the Lord’s incarnation (February 2).

[Here manuscript 1 continued: “Moreover, since this abbot was of great prudence and power, the abbey of Saint Paul at Rome was granted to him; see chapter 58.” After this was erased in 1b: “In that same year, when the Roman emperor at Constantinople had died, Nicephorus was appointed. We therefore … may have.”]

We therefore, as we remember having said in the preface [“prefatory remarks,” 1b] to this work, think that it is time to bring this first little book to an end. We are not unaware that, just as the traveller’s labour is refreshed by lodging, so the reader’s attention is refreshed by the end of a book. At the same time, associating our new abbot with the new emperors of Greece and Italy, we shall pursue the subsequent times more freely in the narratives of the following book [the clause beginning “also with the new emperors…” is supplied by 1b and the edition]. We consider it especially fitting that the restoration—or rather, to put it so, the renewed beginning—of so great a monastery should have, together with its new abbot, the beginning of its own book, and that the subsequent times should, with the Lord’s favour, be pursued in the narratives of the following book [“should have its beginning, or opening, in its own book, with the Lord’s favour,” 1b; “and may the following times continue,” edition; the edition reads *prosequamur*, “let us pursue,” rather than *prosequantur*, “may they pursue”].

Here ends the first book.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND BOOK BEGIN

[I added the headings. The table of chapters is absent in manuscript 1, where there is no division of the books.]

1. On the appointment and zeal, or capture, of Abbot Aligern.  
2. On his vindication and the relinquishments of this territory, or the charters made for him by the princes. [“Relinquishment,” 2.]  
3. On the reconciliation of this territory, or restoration of the monastery.  
4. Likewise, on the charters of the emperors, both concerning this place and Saint Angelo at Barregio. [“Concerning this place and Saint Angelo at Barregio” is shortened in the edition.]  
5. At what time the body of the apostle Matthew came to Salerno. [The edition reads “came.”]  
6. On the offerings of certain persons in this place, and also on several exchanges made by the abbot.  
7. On the appurtenances of Saint Mary in the Grove.  
8. On the *libelli* made by the same abbot, the purpose for which he made them, and their rent.  
9. How the archbishopric of Capua was first established.  
10. How Prince Landenulf was killed, and how he was avenged.  
11. On a remarkable earthquake, and how the wood of the Holy Cross was brought to this monastery.  
12. On the accession of Abbot Manso.  
13. On certain persons’ offerings or *libelli*.  
14. How Prince Laidulf swore an oath to the same abbot, and what he granted him. [The edition reads “to him.”]  
15. How Landulf of Saint Agatha, having become prince, swore an oath to this abbot and what concessions he made to him. [The edition reads “of Saint Agatha.”]  
16. How he was deceived and blinded by the Capuans.  
17. On the arrival of Saint Adalbert at this monastery.  
18. Likewise, on the arrival of Saint Romuald and Saint Boniface at this place.  
19. How Count Oliban came here.  
20. How, or for what reason, Abbot John voluntarily resigned the abbey, and concerning his *libelli*.  
21. What vision was seen at his death.  
22. How Abbot John came here, why he went to Jerusalem, and how, warned in a vision to return, he received the abbey. [The edition reads “received it.”]  
23. On Saint Mary in the Cells.  
24. How Emperor Otto proceeded to Benevento, what he did in these regions, and how or where he died.  
25. On the works of that Abbot John.  
26. On exchanges and offerings, or *libelli*, made under him.  
27. On Saint Benedict at Sessa.  
28. On the departure of the aforesaid abbot for Capua, and on Abbot Docibilis.  
29. On the removal of Rotundulus and the substitution of Atenulf.  
30. How the monastery of Albaneta was founded.  
31. On the concessions of Emperor Henry and the works of Abbot Atenulf.  
32. On certain persons’ offerings in this place.  
33. How a portion of the Saviour’s linen cloth was brought to this monastery.  
34. On the restoration of the monastery of Barregio and the death of the man who restored it.  
35. The settlement, or relinquishment, of the dukes of Gaeta concerning the boundaries of this monastery. [“Cajeta,” edition.]  
36. On the offering of the island called Limata. [“Offerings,” 4.]  
37. How the Normans first came to these regions, and how they fought with the Greeks under the leadership of Melo.  
38. On the Normans established at Pignataro, and how Dattus was captured.  
39. How Emperor Henry came against Troia with an army, and how the abbot, fleeing him, died at sea. [The edition reads “Troia” as “Troila.”]  
40. How Prince Pandulf voluntarily surrendered himself to Belgrim, and how the same prince was rescued from death by him. [“Velgrim,” edition.]  
41. How the same emperor gave the principality of Capua to Count Pandulf of Teano.  
42. On the appointment of Abbot Theobald.  
43. How Saint Benedict healed the same emperor, and what gifts he bestowed on this place. [The words “and what [gifts]” are absent in the edition.]  
44. How, proving the writings concerning the translation of Saint Benedict to be utterly fraudulent, he burned them. [The editor corrects the heading to *fallacissima* (“utterly fraudulent”) and *exusserit* (“he burned [them]”); the apparatus records printed *fallacissime* (“most deceitfully”) and manuscript 4’s corrupt *exrisserit*.]  
45. How the same emperor had formerly been struck with illness through Saint Benedict.  
46. How the bishopric of Bamberg was exchanged for Benevento.  
47. A vision shown at the death of the aforesaid emperor to a certain servant of God.  
48. Reports concerning the body of Saint Benedict.  
49. On the appearance of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus.  
50. On Saint Benedict at Clia and Saint Nazarius.  
51. How Capitanata came into being.  
52. On the beginnings of Abbot Theobald and his works at Saint Saviour.  
53. Likewise, on his works in this place.  
54. How Lord Odilo, abbot of Cluny, came here and, on returning, sent the arm of Saint Maurus to this place.  
55. On certain persons’ offerings or *libelli*.  
56. On the return of Prince Pandulf.  
57. On the persecutions by the same prince and Todinus against this place.  
58. How the abbot returned to the Marches.  
59. How Pandulf ordered the treasure of this monastery and of the Capuan monastery to be carried off.  
60. What miracle took place in the construction of the church of Saint Scholastica at Gaeta.  
61. On the death of Abbot Theobald and the objectionable election of Basil.  
62. On the baseness of the same man and on certain persons’ offerings.  
63. How Emperor Conrad came here and how Abbot Richer was elected.  
64. How God rescued this place from fire.  
65. On the beginnings of Abbot Richer and on certain persons’ offerings in this place.

## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Thus in manuscript 3; manuscript 2 reads: “of the history of this Cassinese cenobium.”]

[Col. 0581A]

### ALIGERN

Abbot Aligern, happily appointed in this monastery as the twenty-seventh after blessed Benedict (A.D. 949, October 25), held office for thirty-seven years. He lived in the times of the first and great Emperor Otto, about whom we have spoken above, and of his son Otto II; of the princes Landulf and Pandulf, his son, who was surnamed Caput Ferreum, “Ironhead” [“who, when he was six years old, began to rule with his father’s will and consent,” added in 1], and of his brother Landulf, and likewise of Landulf’s son; and of the Roman pontiffs from John XII through John XV [one manuscript instead reads: “from John XV, and John XVI, and Benedict VII”]. From almost all of them, at different times, he received both privileges and charters, neglecting nothing.

Among these, Pope John XV, in honour and reverence for this place, added the following provision above the others in his privilege [“by apostolic authority,” 1b and 2]: namely, forbidding all bishops to take, on any pretext, from all the peoples subject to this monastery, or from all the churches belonging to it anywhere in the world, tithes of the living or offerings of the dead.

[The privilege was dated in the fifth year of his pontificate, on the third day before the Ides of November, third indiction (A.D. 989, November 11). Peter’s Register, no. 13. It contains these words and was given to Aligern, but its chronological indications must be false; they seem to have been repeated from privilege no. 15 of the Register, given to Manso, which Tosti published, *History of Monte Cassino* I, p. 233.]

### Consolidated apparatus retained from the supplied edition

The following source notes belong to the translated text and are retained here with their references. In section 60, the reading “goods and possessions” is *rebus ac possessionibus*; 1b and the edition add *et*, “and.” At *Ad Trefone*, witness 3 reads “ad Treffone” and witness 4 “Atrefone.” The reference is Register no. 210 (ANG.). The charter is identified as published by Gattola from the original, *Acc.*, p. 53; its source variants read “the same abbot” for “the same prince” in 4, “the aforesaid prince” for “the same prince” in 1b, “to the same abbot” for “for this abbot” in 1b, “prince Landulf” for “the aforesaid prince” in 1b, and “his charter” for “a charter” in 1b. “Saconis” is witness 4’s form of Saonis; the river was formerly called the Savo (Statius, *Silvae* IV.66; Pliny III.5, ANG.).

For Leo’s offering, 1b and the edition add “and” after “goods”; the later confirmation is “his charter” in 1b. John’s offering has “that water itself” in 1b, omits “absolutely all” in 4, reads “of that place” in 3 instead of “of that church,” and omits “of the same” in 4. John is recorded in Register no. 211 (ANG.); the notes identify Mount Saint Agatha’s earlier name as Mount Tifata and explain that Ferruzanum remains Ferrazano but is separated from the mountain by the Volturno. The Aregis libellus reads “of Alife” in 1b, “with” and “is called” in 1b where the base text has “of” and “which is called,” and “many possessions” in 1b; the four bezants are “bisants” in 1b. The Ursus libellus omits “Judge” in 3 and, in witness 1, omits the span “fifteen years” through “November”; the edition has “each year.” The concluding note reads: “Basil also, imperial protospatharius, etc.; see chapter 59.”

The election apparatus is: “Adelpertus” for Adelbert in 3; “Harderic” in 4 and “Bishop Arderic” in 1b; “Atenulfus” in 3 and 4; “man” is added after “most energetic” in 4; “8 Kalends of November” is absent in 4; “man” is added after “highly honourable” in 4; “divine learning” is absent in 1b and 2; “greatest” replaces “immense” in 1b; and “joy” replaces “assent” in 1b and 2. These variants concern the exact marked source words and are not general paraphrases.

In chapter 61, “finally” (*Denique*) is absent in witnesses 1 and 2. Witness 1b reads “with his brother Lothair and Charles,” and witnesses 1 and 2 add “by fortunate lot.” The form *Forojulensis* is added in 1b; the edition prints *Forojuliensis*; the patronymic is “Eberard” in 2 and “Evard” in 3. Witness 1 reads “Berengar invaded the kingdom,” 1b “Berengar of Friuli, son of Everard, invaded the kingdom of Italy,” and the edition “King Berengar.” Witness 1b adds “two” to the two battles and “to Verona.”

For Guy, 1b reads “not a long time” where the base says “approximately”; it adds “with a bloody flux.” *Tradidit* (“transferred”) is the reading of 1 and 2 against *reliquit* (“handed over”); 3 has “Lampert.” The note on Lambert explains that “six years later” means after he became emperor in A.D. 892. Witness 1 deletes the clause “while meanwhile Berengar was killed by his own men”; 1b deletes it. “After these events” replaces “Meanwhile” in 1. “Pope John XIII” is a witness 1 reading, with the marginal correction “rather, the tenth”; the fuller note says the author confused John XI with John XII, although Peter’s catalogue numbers him XIII. Witness 1 adds “with the magnates.”

Witness 1 corrects *Hugonem* to *Ugonem*; 1b adds “Count” before Azzo and “the aforesaid” before Hugh. “Of Burgundy” is absent in 1 and 2; “that Berard” is added in 1b; witnesses 1 and 2 read “a kinsman of the same king,” and the note states that quire XVI of manuscript 1* begins there. “Much” is added in 1b; the edition reads “the aforesaid Hugh.” The Adelaide note records *Adhel.* in 1b; 1b adds “from the Tuscan nobility.” Witnesses 1 and the edition read “since he had already begun to suffer some troubles from him, as an old man”; witness 1 adds “and all his wealth.” The edition reads “building a very rich monastery.”

The long deleted passage after Lothair’s death is expressly marked as the wording of 1b that was erased. Its correction is part of the source state: the initial clause was corrected from “Berengar, with his son Albert, a very energetic man” to “Albert, son of Berengar, a most energetic man.” The passage’s “Teutonic” is the beginning of the phrase “Teutonic kings,” not a completed independent sentence.

In the Canossa episode, witness 3 reads “Adelachis”; 1b omits “a certain” before Atto; 1b and the edition read “a very strongly fortified fortress.” The added 1b passage reports that the fortress was nearly forced to surrender, that the messenger had been sent by Atto and the queen to Otto, duke of Saxony, “then glorious for his victory over the Hungarians,” to ask him to come into Italy, free them from Berengar’s siege, and receive the queen in marriage. The source variant in the report to Otto reads “concerning her” and “he should report”; the access variant is “given to him” in 1b and the edition. The archer variant reads “having seized his bow, shot them into it” in 1b; the letter’s heading is “the tenor of the letters” in 1b and the edition. The letters say that the duke had crossed the Alps and come to Verona, while his son Liudolf had gone ahead to Milan [“was at Milan,” 4]; 1b and 2 add “with an army.” “Alpert” is witness 3’s spelling; 1b reads “his daughters.” The edition supplies “and received” in the sentence about entering Rome; 1b reads “hands,” “of the Roman pontiff,” and the edition “of Pope John XII, Roman pontiff.”

At the end of Book I, manuscript 1 continues with the note: “Moreover, since this abbot was of great prudence and power, the abbey of Saint Paul at Rome was granted to him; see chapter 58.” After that was erased in 1b: “In that same year, when the Roman emperor at Constantinople had died, Nicephorus was appointed. We therefore … may have.” The preface note reads “prefatory remarks” in 1b; 1b also changes “as” to “just as” and adds the clause associating the new abbot with the new emperors of Greece and Italy. The phrase “together with the new abbot” and the following clause are absent in the base witness but supplied by 1b and the edition. The edition reads *existimamus* (“we consider”) for *censemus* (“we think”), and “may the following times pursue” for the base’s *prosequantur*; its text prints *prosequamur*, “let us pursue.”

The chapter list preserves the source’s localized variants: chapter 2 has “relinquishment” in 2; chapter 4 omits “and” in the edition; chapter 5 has “came” in the edition; chapter 14 has “to him” in the edition; chapter 15 has “of Saint Agatha” in the edition; chapter 35 has “Cajeta” in the edition; chapter 36 has “offerings” in 4; chapter 39 has “Einricus” and the edition’s “Troila” against *Heinricus* and *Troja*; chapter 40 has “Velgrim” in the edition; chapter 43 omits “and what [gifts]” in the edition; chapter 44 is editorially corrected to *fallacissima* (“utterly fraudulent”) and *exusserit* (“he burned [them]”), against printed *fallacissime* (“most deceitfully”) and manuscript 4’s corrupt *exrisserit*; chapter 67 has “Vanaria” in manuscript C; chapters 68–69 have “Aquis” in manuscript C; and chapter 79 has “Saint Jerusalem” in the edition against the source’s “Holy Jerusalem.”

The source’s manuscript note states that manuscript 3 also numbers one hundred chapters, with this as the last; in manuscript 2 the ink changes after chapter 44, again at chapter 46, and again at chapter 66; chapters 48 to the end were written on a leaf sewn in later, no earlier than the end of the thirteenth century. The list from Angelo’s edition is therefore not silently merged with the first list: its distinct chapter numbers and readings are translated separately above, including the corrected “false writings” at 44 and the entries through 102.

At the opening of Book II, manuscript 3 reads “Thus”; manuscript 2 reads “of the history of this Cassinese cenobium.” The heading “Aligernus” is written twice in manuscript 1; the first recension survives for a page and a half, until “nevertheless,” where a new quire begins in another hand continuing through II.43. The date “A.D. 950” is added in 1b and deleted in 1c. The phrase “the Capuan princes” is added in witnesses 1 and 2; witness 3 reads “and of his son Landulf.” Witness 1b corrects “from John XII up to John XV” to “from John XV, John XVI, and Benedict VII.” In the phrase “from almost all of them,” witness 1b corrects *fere* (“almost”) to *videlicet* (“namely”). Witness 1 corrects “namely” to “that is.” The privilege clause “by apostolic authority” is added in 1b and 2, and “all” is added in 4. Its dating note is A.D. 989, November 11, fifth year of the pontificate, third day before the Ides, third indiction; Register of Peter, no. 13. The note says that the chronological signs must be false and seem repeated from Register privilege no. 15, granted to Manso and published by Tosti, *History of Monte Cassino* I, p. 233.

## I

This man, therefore, born by lineage among the nobles of Naples, was made a monk in the monastery of Saint Paul near Rome under the aforesaid Abbot Baldwin. Afterwards, having been transferred here by that same abbot and, after the death of Majelpotus, as has already been said, having been made abbot from being provost of this place, he began to restore this site, over and above what Leo and John, formerly abbots of this monastery, had begun.

This place, indeed, from the time of Abbot Bertharius, when it was burned by the Saracens (A.D. 883), had for approximately sixty-seven years, until his time, been neglected, abandoned, and almost completely desolate.

Earlier, however, under Abbot Baldwin, our monks—who until then had necessarily lived first at Teano and afterwards at Capua—had partly returned at the command of Pope Agapetus, as was related above (Book I, ch. 59).

Not only the monastery, but also the entire plain surrounding it, had then been so laid waste by Saracen incursions that scarcely anyone, indeed almost no one, could be found who ought to render any service to the servants of God dwelling there.

Moreover, the counts of Teano had advanced by invading the property of that monastery as far as the hill nearest the monastery, which they call Torocclus.

> Commonly called Trocchio. On its eastern slope there was a village inhabited down to our own time; it is now wholly abandoned, its few inhabitants having migrated to the nearby castle of Cervaro. — ANG.

The counts of Aquino likewise, under whom a certain Adenulf, surnamed Megalu, presided as gastald, held, from almost Cassino itself—which is not quite two miles distant from the city of San Germano—the entire district commonly called Flumetica, together with all its appurtenances.

> That is, the castles and villages around the river Liri, a part of the Cassinese territory still called *La Firmara*. [Possibly *Fiumara*?] — ANG.

The prudent abbot therefore began diligently to seek throughout the world the possessions which the monastery had formerly held, especially those which were contiguous and situated nearby. Having found and produced the grants and charters of those who had long ago bestowed them here, he made every effort to reclaim them from those who had plundered them in wartime.

But when he saw that by no arguments or entreaties could he bend the minds of those irrational robbers toward restoring them, he finally complained about the matter to Prince Landulf.

When the adversaries learned this, and were greatly offended by his zeal and diligence, seeing moreover that they could by no means remain quiet in the face of his vigilance and persistence, they daily considered how either to seize him or at least to inflict upon him whatever troubles they could.

All this, however, was brought about by the will and ordering of God, who providentially arranged that his capture and humiliation should result in the restoration of this place.

Accordingly, one day, while he was working on the construction of the fortress called Janula, which rises above and overlooks the church of Saint Germanus, the aforesaid Adenulf, also called Megalu, suddenly arrived with several soldiers and forcibly seized the abbot, carrying him off to Aquino as though he were some great spoil.

There, in the public spectacle of the citizens, he clothed him in a bearskin and set dogs upon him from every side to bark around him, as they truly would around a bear; and the most wicked man dishonoured the honourable man with many insults.

> The fortress is apparently so called because a temple of Janus had formerly been erected there, as Peter the Deacon relates in the *Register of Saint Placidus*, p. 121, in the *Acts of Saints Demetrius and his Companions*. — ANG.

When the aforesaid prince heard this, and was exceedingly indignant at so great an affront to so great a man, he immediately ordered Adenulf to go to Capua and render justice to the abbot before him in a lawful trial.

But Adenulf, foreseeing that he ought legally to suffer death for the crime committed, chose rather to rebel; relying on the considerable fortification of Aquino, he scorned to go to the prince’s court.

## 2

The prince, therefore, resolving to avenge both his own injury and that of the abbot, came to Aquino and surrounded with siege works and engines the residence in which the aforesaid rebel had fortified himself.

> Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, Paschal, a *strategos* sent by the emperor of Constantinople, came to this same Prince Landulf and, while the siege of Aquino was in progress, appointed him *anthypatos* and patrician, as he had been ordered by his lord. [This passage is found in manuscript 1 and was deleted in 1b.]

At last, seeing that he could not escape the prince’s hands, Adenulf put a rope around his neck and ordered himself to be dragged to the prince’s feet through the intervention of his wife.

When this had been done, the prince immediately handed him over to the abbot, bound as he was, together with all his possessions, so that the abbot might do whatever he wished both with him and with all that belonged to him.

Adenulf, seeing that by the just judgment of God he had come as a captive into the power of his own captive, immediately and most willingly drew up a deed of renunciation concerning all the monastery’s possessions which he had until then retained, and humbly handed it back into the abbot’s hands.

After this, with pardon for his crime, he was restored by the same abbot to his own liberty together with all his people.

By this opportunity Father Benedict gradually began to recover and receive back his possessions, which had long before been invaded.

Not long afterwards, the counts of Teano also, moved by God, made the same abbot similar documents of renunciation concerning the things which they themselves had retained.

The same abbot, therefore, delaying nothing and considering that the acceptable time must not be neglected, immediately requested and obtained from the aforesaid Prince Landulf and his son Pandulf a charter of liberty and confirmation of the whole abbey in its entirety, according to the boundaries written above: those which Duke Gisulf had first established in the time of Petronax and which Emperor Charles had afterwards confirmed, in the time of Theodemar, by an imperial charter.

> Peter the Deacon copied the charters granted by the princes to Aligern in his *Register*, no. 212 and following. Gattula published many from the originals, among which, however, I have not found these. For the one received on 6 May 952 (*Apc.*, p. 55) is different from it.

He also requested from those same princes a more specific charter concerning the castle of Saint Angel and the tower of Saint George, as well as all castles or fortresses which should thereafter be built within the monastery’s appurtenances, asking that each of them be individually granted to him.

> Later Pandulf, with his son Landulf, confirmed to him the castle of Janula, the castle of Saint Angel at Tudice, and the tower of Saint George, together with the other castles and towers: 7 June 967, Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 63.

Likewise, he obtained another charter (30 August 951) concerning the woodland of Casa Gentiana.

> Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 56.

He obtained another, moreover, concerning the whole fishery of Lesina with its own mouth, together with the church of Saint Focas situated there, and several houses within Lesina itself.

> These were also confirmed by Landulf IV, 27 January 980, *ibid.*, p. 66.

Afterwards, on 10 July 961, he received another charter from the aforesaid Pandulf and from his son Landulf concerning all the boundaries and appurtenances of this monastery.

> *Ibid.*, p. 58; p. 82. There is no mention of Adenulf in them.

Again, on 16 May 981, he received another charter concerning all the boundaries and appurtenances of this monastery.

Nevertheless, the adversaries of truth could not rest after all this whenever any opportunity arose. Now some men of Aquino, now some of Pontecorvo, and also some of Teano, endeavoured to dispute with us over the boundaries of this monastery.

But as often as they joined issue with our men in court, so often, defeated by the strongest arguments, they were compelled truthfully to renounce what they had falsely claimed.

> Examples are given by Gattula, vol. I, p. 67.

Hence it also happened that, on occasions of this sort, we possess many documents of such disputes or renunciations.

At that same time the abbot approached the princes already mentioned (10 July 961) and asked them to give our cell at Cingla a place outside the gates of Saint Angel for the construction of a monastery for the handmaids of God, because the monastery within the walls was considered too cramped and unsuitable for the women of God living there.

They, granting his request, designated a place outside the city wall where a castle and monastery might be built, and granted the area outside the wall as far as it extends to the river.

> A privilege of this kind survives in Gattula, vol. I, p. 59, although nothing is said there about the Cingla cell or the monastery to be constructed. Compare Otto II’s privilege of 13 October 981, *ibid.*, p. 99.

At the same time the aforesaid abbot received a seal from Marianus, imperial *anthypatos*, patrician, and *strategos* of Calabria and Langobardia (December 956), so that he might securely and without anyone’s opposition or impediment go wherever he wished to seek out all the inheritances or possessions of this monastery and recover them, provided that just and adequate proof was produced.

> In the *Register*, no. 153. The seal was made by Marianus the *anthypatos*. Its wording is as follows: “A seal made by Marianus the *anthypatos*, patrician and *strategos* of Calabria and Langobardia, and given to you, Aligern, venerable abbot of Saint Benedict. May you travel throughout the whole *thenia* of Langobardia and seek out every inheritance of the aforesaid monastery, and may you suffer no opposition from any judge of that *thenia,”* etc. At the end: “With our leaden bull we have sealed this present seal, and we granted our seal to the aforesaid abbot in the month of December, in the fifteenth indiction.” — ANG.

## 3

At last the prudent abbot, summoning farmers from every direction from neighbouring lands which had not been devastated by the Hagarenes, brought them, with all their households, to live upon those monastery possessions which required cultivators.

He made a *libellary* agreement both with those whom he found there and with those whom he himself brought in: from the three revenues of all that land—namely wheat, barley, and millet—they were to give the monastery a seventh part annually, and of wine a third.

They were to possess the remainder for their own use and that of their households; and this arrangement is still firmly observed today.

> The Cassinese monastery still possesses similar rights in the territory of Piedimonte, in the village of Saint Lucy, in the castle of Fella among the Calabrians, and elsewhere. — ANG.

When, therefore, the land had been largely filled and settled by inhabitants from various regions, he turned his attention to repairing or improving the monastery’s buildings, just as his predecessors Leo and John had long before begun.

He roofed the entire church which the aforesaid John had built, framing it with new cypress beams and covering it with tiles. He adorned its walls throughout with various colours and paved the floor with a variety of different stones.

He surrounded the altar of blessed Benedict itself on every side with silver panels, and also made the front of the altar of Saint John of silver.

He made a sizeable silver cross, with precious stones, and a Gospel book covered throughout with gilded silver, enamels, and gems; three silver crowns; chalices, censers, and various ecclesiastical ornaments; and very many books of different kinds.

Meanwhile, restoring several dwellings of this place, he began, as though he were another Petronax, to live with the brethren according to the tenor of the Rule and the ancient custom of the monastery.

At the Capuan monastery, after producing several ecclesiastical ornaments, bells, and some books, he added to the church on its western side a handsome sanctuary with its *confessio*, and painted it.

> The *titulus* here means the presbytery, the part of the church in which the altar stands. The *confessio* is the place beneath the high altar where relics are deposited. — DUC.

## 4

At the same time Otto I, in the third year of his empire, through the intervention of his aforesaid wife, the Empress Adelaide, made a general charter for this monastery (19 February 964), confirming everything that had hitherto been contributed to it by anyone in various places.

> Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 71, from the original.

Again, after approximately four years, Abbot Paul of Saint Vincent’s approached him and petitioned him on behalf of our aforesaid abbot. In the customary manner of the earlier emperors, he obtained from him another, fuller charter confirming the entire abbey (1 July 968).

> *Ibid.*, p. 72.

The same emperor granted to our abbot the monastery of Saint Angel of Barregio, with absolutely all its cells and appurtenances (25 May 970).

> *Ibid.*, p. 73.

At that time Alberic, bishop of the Marsi, held that monastery for the term of his life by a written grant from the same emperor. Five years earlier, the emperor had made for the monastery of Saint Angel a charter confirming all its property (12 February 964).

> P. 75.

Otto II likewise reconfirmed to the same abbot the aforesaid monastery of Saint Angel together with a charter confirming the entire abbey (6 August 981).

> P. 77.

Moreover, the aforesaid Alberic, bishop of the Marsi, in the presence of that emperor, who was then staying in the Marsian territory on a mountain called Cedici, made him a deed of renunciation concerning the monastery of Barregio and decreed that henceforth it should remain peacefully subject to this monastery.

For approximately six years earlier that same bishop had voluntarily bestowed the monastery of Saint Angel upon blessed Benedict by a deed of his offering.

Some years later Guinisius, bishop of the Marsi and son of the aforesaid Alberic, wished to raise a dispute concerning the same monastery, on the ground that he possessed an imperial charter concerning it as though it were his church.

Summoned and convicted by our monks in the court of the Marsian counts, he was compelled to remain silent.

On this account the three imperial charters which his father had acquired concerning the same monastery were returned to us.

> At that time (A.D. 974), when Pope Benedict VI died, Benedict VII, a kinsman of the aforesaid Alberic, consul of the Romans, was enthroned in the apostolic see. [This was after Boniface VII had been expelled.] — Tusculan Catalogue of Peter.

## 5

In the fifth year of this abbot, which is the year from the birth of the Lord 954, the body of blessed Matthew the apostle and evangelist—which had first rested in Ethiopia, where he had also suffered, afterwards in Britain, and finally in Lucania at different times—was at last found through a revelation of that same holy evangelist and translated to Salerno.

> In the story of this translation, which is full of fables, some material may be found in the *Acts of the Saints*, 21 September, and in Borgia, *Memorie Beneventane*, vol. I, p. 352.

Three years later, two suns were seen together in the sky, and for two days in July the sea became sweet from Naples as far as Cumae.

## 6

At that time Pope Benedict * granted the same abbot, by a privilege, certain estates of his in the county of Aprutium (10 January 977).

> Dated on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the third year of his pontificate. *Register*, no. 12. The other privileges, charters, and offerings recounted in this chapter are copied there. It would therefore be superfluous to compare each one separately. — ANG.

During these days the aforesaid Prince Pandulf, by his charter, granted to this monastery (7 October 968) the entire property of Arechis, son of Janipert, which he had possessed in Teano, both within and outside the city, together with the church of Saint Sylvester built within that city and all its appurtenances.

> Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 65, from the original.

He also made another charter for him (May 964) concerning the water of the river Saone, with the banks situated on both sides.

> *Ibid.*, p. 66; see below, ch. 83.

The aforesaid abbot brought a complaint before Pandulf against Count Bernard of Alife, because Bernard threatened to burn and destroy one of this monastery’s castles at the place called Curvara, and to plunder and beat the men of that castle.

Therefore the prince, moved by his complaints, decreed by a sealed charter that if the aforesaid Bernard, or any man subject to his authority, should presume to inflict any harassment or robbery upon that castle or its inhabitants, he should pay one thousand gold bezants, in addition to the penalty which the law prescribed.

Gisulf, prince of Salerno, son of Guaimar the Elder, together with his wife Gemma, made a charter for this monastery (September 972) concerning a fourth part of everything that Duke and Margrave Lambert was thought to have possessed in the county of the Marsi, in Balva, Forcone, and Amiterno, and in the March of Fermo and the duchy of Spoleto, excepting the slaves, all of whom he granted their liberty.

All these things had come to him by inheritance through Princess Itta, the grandmother of his wife Gemma.

> “The Younger.” The donation, made in the thirtieth year of Gisulf [the text is lacunose], in the fifteenth indiction, was published by Gattula from Peter’s *Register*, *Acc.*, p. 80. Leo interpreted it incorrectly: the whole inheritance is offered, one fourth part of which Gisulf declares that he had previously assigned by a written *morgincap* to Gemma, the wife of Itta’s grandson.

Count Borrellus of Petra Abundanti also made a deed of offering to this monastery concerning the monastery of Saint Eustasius, within the boundaries of that same castle, at the place called *Ad Arcum*, with all its property and appurtenances and with an appurtenant tract of land measuring 1,623 *modii*.

> In the territory of Trivento in Abruzzo. In the county of Molise, in the confirmation of the donation made by Princes Pandulf and Landulf, dated 12 March 977; this alone was published by Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 81. The number of *modii* is not given there.

Furthermore, a certain priest Joseph of the city of Larino offered to this monastery the church of Saint Lawrence, which he had built on his own inheritance near that city, with all its property and appurtenances.

Certain noblemen of Aquino, sons of the gastald Rodipert, likewise offered all their property to blessed Benedict in the territory of Aquino, at the place called Publica: extensive plains and many mountains.

Count Hildebrand of Sora, together with his brothers, made a charter for this place concerning half of the lakes of Taurinus and Julianus, which flow from Posta, with all the appurtenances of their half.

> These now form one lake, Lake Posta.

The princes Pandulf and Landulf afterwards confirmed to this monastery the whole of those lakes, together with the stream of Carpello and all their appurtenances.

Rachis, gastald of Vicalbo, also gave blessed Benedict his estate with the church of Saint Victorinus, near the aforesaid lakes, where Posta is now situated; and likewise two woodlands within the boundaries of Vicalbo, one at the place called Silva Plana and the other on Mount Albeto, with all their boundaries and appurtenances.

> Vicalvi, in the duchy of Alvito.

At the same time the men of Vicalbo acquired from the aforesaid abbot that height upon which the town of Saint Urban now stands, which had formerly belonged to us, in order to build a castle there; and in Vicalbo they gave him twice as much land as they had received.

The abbot, however, reserved for himself the church of Saint Urban, with the appurtenance of its property and with the whole estate within that town, extending in every direction for one hundred feet.

> Alvito, together with Comino, succeeded it in its place.

The same abbot gave in exchange to a certain Aimeradus of the Marsian territory certain churches and lands belonging there to this monastery: namely, the church of Saint Saviour in Avezzano, Saint Mary in Oretino, Saint Abundius in Arcu, Saint Mary in Montorone, and Saint Antimus in Vico.

From him he received, in the county of Teate, the church of Saint Elias and Saint Vitus, together with five thousand *modii* of land.

Likewise, he gave the church of Saint Comitius, Saint Elias, and Saint Vitus in the same Teate, and received there the church of Saint Tenestrus with three thousand *modii* of land.

In Comino he received five thousand *modii*, between Atina and Vicalbo, and the fork of Saint Leutherius.

> At that time this was the name both of the town and of the district.

Likewise, from the church of Saint Felix in Pulverio, which possessed 1,100 *modii* of land, he received one hundred solidi; as annual rent, five solidi.

During these days, when he brought a complaint in the court of the Marsian counts, the bank of Lake Fucino with its fishery was renounced, namely from the church of Saint Mary of Montorone as far as Saint Mary of the Marsh, a place then called Altoranum.

Two families of slaves, together with all that belonged to them, were also renounced.

He also brought a complaint in the court of Margrave Andrew, envoy of Emperor Otto (September 972), at Sulmona, against Count Oderisi of Balva, who retained two of our churches in the valley of Pectorano, namely Saint Stephen’s and Saint Eleutherius’s.

After the matter had been disclosed, he immediately recovered them.

> In the twenty-ninth year of Pandulf and the fourth of Landulf, in the fifteenth indiction. *Register*, no. 233.

Having summoned several men from the city of Termoli, he made an agreement with them that they should build a castle there, on our appurtenances at the place called Ripa Orsa beside the river Trigno, where they and all their people should live and cultivate the lands belonging to us there.

They were to give this monastery a third part both of the castle itself and of everything they produced there; they were to retain two parts for themselves.

> The river Trigno.

At the same time Sadelfrit, deacon of the city of Lesina, offered to this monastery one church belonging to him, called Saint Martin’s, built near that city at the place called Alchisi, with all its ornaments and appurtenances.

Guarnerius and Laidulfus a Basso of Larino likewise did the same concerning the church of Saint Germanus at the place called Aquarola near Larino.

John and Bonucius, citizens of Termoli, similarly did so concerning the church of the Holy Trinity, which they had built beside the sea on the shore called Petra Hermerissi.

In the same manner three churches at Lumisano were offered to this monastery: Saint Mary’s, Saint Peter’s, and Saint Benedict’s at the place called Maccla Bona, with all the property and appurtenances of those churches.

Guido of Ascoli likewise offered his estate at Casale, at the place called Forcae, comprising approximately 1,500 *modii* of land.

He offered it in the church of Saint Saviour at the aforesaid Ascoli, for the use of this monastery.

> Compare Book I, ch. 37.

A certain Emmo of the Marsi also offered to this monastery his inheritance at Comino, consisting of one hundred *modii* of land at the place called Ferrara, near Vicalbo.

### Textual apparatus and editorial notes

The supplied apparatus is translated here with its witness associations. The opening “I” is marked in the edition as chapter 5; witness 1 inserts “here” (*hic interponit*). “Neapolitan” is the reading of witnesses 1 and 2, while 4 adds “noble” and “by lineage.” Witness 1 and the edition read “aforesaid” for “predicted.” After *postmodum*, witness 1 has an expanded biographical passage: “After a short time, by God’s will and through the merits of blessed Benedict, he became abbot in this monastery; he had first been appointed provost here by that abbot, and then, after Majelpotus’s death as stated above, became abbot; afterward, as has been said above, he became abbot from the provostship of this place.”

Witness 1b corrects “which indeed” to “namely”; the edition reads “when” as “at the time when.” Witness 1’s earlier recension adds that only a very few brothers remained there; 1b reads “up to himself.” The return of the monks under Agapetus has variant wording: “by the pope’s order they had returned” in the first witness, while 1b and the edition read “they had partly returned, as has been related above.” “In the surrounding plain” is the reading of 1; 1b adds “then”; witness 1 reads “deserted,” and witness 3 omits “almost.” Witness 1 adds “in it.” Witness 1 and the edition read *ibi* (“there”) for printed *ibidem* (“in that same place”).

For the Teano and Aquino possessions, witness 1 reads “to” instead of “concerning”; witness 1 and the edition read “which is called Torocclus,” and the ANG. note identifies it as Trocchio, with the former village on its eastern slope and later migration to Cervaro. Witness 1 adds “the counts indeed”; witness 4 reads “a certain” for Adenulf. Witnesses 3 and the text read “Megalii/Megalu.” The ANG. note glosses Flumetica as the castles and villages around the Liri, still called La Firmara (possibly Fiumara). Witness 1b adds “whatever were contiguous and nearby.”

The source’s complaint to Landulf is qualified in witnesses 1–3 as “Prince Landulf of Capua.” Witness 1 and the edition expand “by no arguments” to “by no arguments or prayers,” and add “the irrational robbers.” Witness 4 adds “moreover”; manuscript 1 and the edition read “with his vigilance or persistence” rather than “with his vigilance.” Witness 1 corrects the phrase to “how they might capture him or inflict on him”; 1b preserves that correction. The transition “All this was brought about…” is an addition in witnesses 1 and 2, explicitly attributing the capture and humiliation to God’s providential restoration of the place.

At Janula, witness 1 reads “called” for “is called,” and witnesses 1 and 2 add that it “overhangs the church of blessed Germanus.” Witnesses 1 and 2 read “with robbers” for “with soldiers”; 4 adds “as a very great spoil.” Witness 1 omits the phrase “in the public spectacle of the citizens,” while the edition also omits it; 1 adds “publicly” to the dogs’ attack and has “he sent” rather than “he set.” The ANG. note explains the name Janula by a former temple of Janus, citing Peter the Deacon, *Register of Saint Placidus*, p. 121, in the *Acts of Saints Demetrius and his Companions*. Witness 1 and the edition read “the aforesaid prince”; the edition has “very greatly” for “exceedingly.” Witness 1b adds “so great” after “so great an affront.” Witness 1 and the edition read “he rebelled” for “he chose to rebel,” and “because of this crime” for “for the crime committed”; 1b adds “considerable” before “fortification.”

In section 2, the source cites *Chronicon Salernitanum*, pp. 162–164. The Paschal passage is present in manuscript 1 and erased in 1b: “Meanwhile, while these things were happening, Paschal, a *strategos* sent by the Constantinopolitan emperor, came to Prince Landulf and, during the siege of Aquino, appointed him *anthypatos* and patrician as his lord had commanded.” Witness 1 begins the submission sentence “At last, therefore, seeing…”; the edition has “At last then.” Witness 1 reads “immediately” for “at once.” The source’s fuller reading says the prince handed Adenulf over to the abbot “with all his possessions so that he might do whatever he wished both with him and with all his goods.” The source also says Adenulf “made a renunciation charter,” and witness 4 adds “all the possessions which he had retained.” Manuscripts 1 and 2 read *renuntiationis* (“renunciation”) for printed *refutationis* (“refutation”) in the Teano counts’ deeds.

The abbey charter was sought from Landulf and Pandulf, with 1 and the edition adding “and” before Pandulf. Peter the Deacon copied Aligern’s princely charters in his *Register*, nos. 212 onward; Gattula printed many from originals but not these, and the charter received 6 May 952 (*Apc.*, p. 55) is different. The special charter is for the newly built castle of Janula, Saint Angel’s castle, and Saint George’s tower, with each castle or fortress subsequently built in the monastery’s appurtenances to be granted individually; witness 4 reads “court” for “tower,” while 1b and the edition read “towers” for “fortresses.” Pandulf and Landulf later confirmed Janula, Saint Angel at Tudice, Saint George’s tower, and the other castles and towers on 7 June 967 (Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 63).

The Casa Gentiana woodland charter is dated 30 August 951 (Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 56). The Lesina charter concerns the entire fishery with its mouth, Saint Focas’s church, and several houses within Lesina; witness 4 reads “mouth” as “voice,” and Landulf IV confirmed it on 27 January 980 (*ibid.*, p. 66). The 10 July 961 charter is from Pandulf and Landulf; witness 1b adds that it was issued “with the intervention of Adenulf the gastald,” witness 2 reads “again,” and the references are *Acc.*, p. 58 and p. 82, with no mention of Adenulf in those documents. The 16 May 981 date belongs to this subsequent, separate *aliud rursus praeceptum* (“another charter again”), not to a duplicate repetition of the prior grant.

In the boundary disputes, witness 1b adds “over all these things they could not rest whenever an opportunity was given”; witness 4 adds “with us”; witness 4 omits “now some from Aquino.” Witness 1b omits the phrase “and also from Teano.” The source says “many records of such conflicts or renunciations”; 1b omits “or renunciations” and the edition reads “of this kind.” Gattula gives examples in volume I, p. 67. In the Cingla grant, manuscript 2 adds the land “outside the wall as far as it goes to the river”; Gattula, vol. I, p. 59, preserves a similar privilege but says nothing of the Cingla cell or the planned monastery; compare Otto II’s privilege of 13 October 981, *ibid.*, p. 99.

The seal note identifies Marianus as imperial *anthypatos*, patrician, and *strategos* of Calabria and Langobardia; witness 4 reads “the aforesaid” as masculine “the aforesaid [abbot].” Witness 1b and the edition read “anyone’s opposition,” and 1b adds “wherever he wished to go,” while 1b and the edition read “or” for “and,” and omit “everywhere.” The seal, Register no. 153, says: “A seal made by Marianus the *anthypatos*, patrician and *strategos* of Calabria and Langobardia, and given to you, Aligern, venerable abbot of Saint Benedict. May you travel throughout the whole *thenia* of Langobardia, seek every inheritance of the aforesaid monastery, and suffer no opposition from any judge of that *thenia*.” Its closing states: “With our leaden bull we have sealed this present seal, and we granted our seal to the aforesaid abbot in December, in the fifteenth indiction.” ANG.

In section 3, “Finally” is “then” in witness 1, and “thereafter” in 1b and the edition. Witnesses 1 and 2 omit “which had not been devastated by the Hagarenes.” The *libellary* agreement is explicitly a *libellari statuto*: from wheat, barley, and millet the seventh part annually, and from wine the third; witness 4 omits “with those whom he himself brought.” Witness 1 and the edition add “perpetually” to the statement that the arrangement remains observed. At *terra hac ex magna parte* (“this land, for the most part”), witness 1 and the edition have the abbreviated reading *p. hujus monasterii t. ex maxima p.*; the abbreviation concerns this monastery and its land, and is retained without conjectural expansion. The ANG. note records similar rights at Piedimonte, Saint Lucy, Fella among the Calabrians, and elsewhere.

For the building works, witness 1 and the edition expand “he roofed the church” to “he first roofed the whole church,” adding “wood” after cypress beams; the edition says he painted the walls “quite beautifully throughout.” Witnesses 1 and 2 add “before the altar of blessed Benedict”; the edition reads “with manifold” for “variety of different stones.” Witness 4 adds “of blessed Benedict”; 1 and the edition say he “decorated” the altar with silver panels. Witness 1 adds precious stones to the silver cross; 1 and the edition read “a gilded silver cross.” Witness 1 omits “three silver crowns,” and the edition reads “many and diverse books.” Witness 1 and the edition read “of the same place”; 1 reads “according to the tenor of the holy Rule.” At Capua, 1b and the edition read “enlarged” rather than “added.” The DUC note defines *titulus* as the presbytery, where the altar stands, and *confessio* as the place beneath the high altar where relics are stored.

Section 4 preserves a substantial alternative account in manuscript 1b: “From the first and great Otto, the monastery of Saint Angel of Barregio was granted to him, the monastery which we showed above had been built by Emperor Louis, with all its cells and possessions.” This begins with “At first, therefore, from Otto…” in 1b and is not a replacement for the principal account. Witness 4 adds “aforesaid” after “through the intervention of his wife”; the older hand of manuscript 1 ends after “empress.” The charter of 19 February 964 is from the original (Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 71); the fuller charter of 1 July 968 is *ibid.*, p. 72. Witness 3 omits the transition “not long afterward”; 1b and the edition supply the clause that by another charter Otto granted Saint Angel of Barregio with all cells and possessions, *ibid.*, p. 73.

The source calls Alberic’s deed a *cartula refutationis*; the edition reads “renunciation,” and manuscript 3 has “Barrigensi,” manuscript 4 “Barregenensi.” Witness 4 adds “approximately” before six years; 1b and the edition read “the aforesaid” before Saint Angel. The material deleted in 1b records that the episcopal renunciation was written in two prior lines. The note says Alberic had voluntarily offered Saint Angel to blessed Benedict six years earlier. Witness 1b changes “on this account” to “for this reason”; three imperial charters acquired by Alberic’s father were returned. Manuscript 2 adds the note that in A.D. 974, after Pope Benedict VI died, Benedict VII, Alberic’s kinsman, was enthroned, after Boniface VII was expelled (Tusculan Catalogue of Peter).

Section 5 begins as chapter 5 in manuscript 1. Witness 3 reads “nine hundred” for the base’s corrupted numeral; witness 1 and the edition expand “the body of blessed Matthew” to “the body of the most blessed apostle and evangelist Matthew.” Witness 1 corrects “Britain” to “Britanny.” The words “finally, at different times, in Lucania” are absent in 1b and 2 and in the earlier edition, while witnesses 3 and 4 also omit the “finally” phrase. The translation-history note cites *Acts of the Saints*, 21 September, and Borgia, *Memorie Beneventane* I, p. 352. The note about the two suns and sweetened sea is added in 1b; 1c adds “for two days of the month of July.”

At the opening of section 6, witness 1 adds “Pope Benedict also”; witness 1 omits “to the same abbot”; the date note gives “fourth day before the Ides of January, third year of his pontificate,” Register no. 12. The note states that all the other privileges, charters, and offerings in this chapter are copied there and need not be compared individually. Witness 1 reads “in the thirtieth year of his ordination” as an alternate date. Witness 1b omits “during these days.” Witness 4 omits “by his charter.” The Arechis reading is “Arechisi” in 1b, “Janniperti” in 1b, and “in the Teanense city” in 1b and the edition; Gattula printed this charter from the original, *Acc.*, p. 65. The Saone charter is dated May 964 and cited at *ibid.*, p. 66 and chapter 83.

Witness 1 omits the sentence introducing the complaint against Bernard. The source says “any harassment or robbery,” while the edition adds “even the least”; “its inhabitants” is “his inhabitants” in the edition. The Gisulf donation is with Gemma his wife in 1b and 2; 1b changes “made a charter” to “made a charter in this monastery.” The note corrects “Guaimar the Elder” to “the Younger,” dates the donation to Gisulf’s thirtieth year and fifteenth indiction, and says Leo misinterpreted it: the whole inheritance is offered, with one fourth previously assigned by written *morgincap* to Gemma, wife of Itta’s grandson. Witness 3 reads “Lampertus,” and the note says the document does not call him emperor. Witness 1b reads “Balva, Forcone, and Amiterno”; the edition follows it. Witness 1b reads “liberty” as “to liberty,” and 1b and 2 specify that the inheritance came through Gemma’s grandmother Itta.

Borrellus is “habundanti” in 1b; the charter is dated 12 March 977 in the confirmation by Pandulf and Landulf, and Gattula printed only that confirmation (*Acc.*, p. 81), where the number of *modii* is absent. The source’s 1,623 *modii* is followed by witness 4’s alternative “seven hundred and twenty-three *modii*.” Witness 1b adds “at that time” before Joseph and identifies him as a priest. Witness 4 adds *plana utique* (“plains indeed”) after “Publica is called”; the following “and very many mountains” belongs to the printed text rather than to that addition. Witness 1b reads “they made” for Hildebrand’s singular “he made”; 1b and the edition supply “in Saint Benedict.” Manuscript 2 reads “Carpello” as “Carnello.” The note identifies Vicalbo as Vicalvi in the duchy of Alvito and says that the two lakes now form Lake Posta.

Witness 4 adds the acquired height and “which formerly belonged to this monastery”; 1b reads “to this monastery,” and 4 adds “gave him.” The note says Alvito, together with Comino, succeeded Saint Urban. Witness 4 adds “certain” churches to Aimeradus’s exchange; 3 and 4 read “Aimirardus/Almeradus,” 3 and 4 “Oritino,” and 1b and 2 “Vico.” At the names of Saints Elias and Vitus, witness 1b and the edition have the abbreviated *Vit. et s. II.*; *Vit.* refers to Vitus, while the final OCR form *II.* is uncertain and is retained without conjectural expansion. The note says Comino was then both a city and a district. Witness 1 omits the entire sentence about Saint Felix through the five solidi annual rent; the edition reads “Polverio” and “1,100 *modii* of land.”

The Lake Fucino note has witness 1b and the edition reading “with him making the complaint”; witness 3 omits “which place was then called Altoranum.” Witness 1 omits the subsequent complaint before Margrave Andrew; the note dates it to the twenty-ninth year of Pandulf, fourth of Landulf, fifteenth indiction, Register no. 233. Witness 2 reads “in the valley of Balva.” Witness 4 adds “immediately recovered them.”

For Ripa Orsa, 1b and 2 read “in the appurtenances of this monastery”; witness 1 reads “Riga,” while the ANG. note identifies the Trigno. Witness 4 adds “with all their people” and “and cultivate the lands belonging to us”; 1b and the edition read “only a third part,” and 1b gives the precise scope as a third of the castle and of everything produced there. In the later offerings, 1b reads “constructed” (feminine) for the Saint Martin church and “all ornaments”; witness 2 reads “Larienenses”; the edition reads “called” for “named.” Witness 1b adds “John, son of Radefrit”; witness 2 omits the whole Termoli church sentence. Guido’s land measure is “approximately 1,500 *modii*”; 1b and the edition read “1,500” rather than “1,500 [plural form],” and the note cross-references Book I, chapter 37. Witness 1 omits Emmo’s final offering sentence. In that final phrase, the edition reads *loco* (“place”) for *monasterio* (“monastery”).

Around this time Gisepert, provost of Saint Sophia at Benevento, appointed to deal with this monastery’s affairs at Lesina and Termoli, recovered from Adelchis, bishop of Lucera, the lease-document which Abbot Angelarius had formerly made for him concerning everything that belonged to this monastery in the aforesaid Lesina. By that lease he again granted him half of the fishery itself and the river Laurus for fifteen years, at an annual rent of one pound of gold.
