[Note: [Col. 0591] The readings are *Thermole* (1b, 2), *illum* (“that one”; 4), and “Abbot A.” (1b). Manuscript 1b and the edition read *dimissa ei iterum* (“again granted to him”) and *a libra una* (“at one pound”); manuscript 1 lacks the text from “Hic” through the end of the chapter.]

This same Gisepert brought suit at the court of Termoli, before the many nobles and judges who were present there, against a certain Castelgard, who disputed with him concerning one of our estates in the same Termoli, at the place called Casale Mari, beside Saint George. This estate was called “of Theodosius.” Our Abbot Deusdedit had formerly bought it from Adelpert, the grandfather of that Castelgard, for five hundred gold solidi, together with houses, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, and waters, and likewise with the pasture which he held at Termoleto, within the following marked boundaries: at one end, the stream which runs from Saint George into the fishpond and as far as the Biferno; at the other end, the sea; on one side, the Biferno; and on the other, the living stream which runs into the sea.

[Note: The witnesses variously read *Castalgardo* and *Gastalgardus*; *Termoleto* is another form of *Termuleto*. The edition reads “fishpond” where another witness has “Vicar.”]

Having thus demonstrated his claim before those judges, he caused the aforesaid Castelgard to withdraw from it by a written instrument, with a stipulated composition of one thousand solidi should he ever wish to revoke this arrangement.

Constantius likewise, provost of Saint Benedict at Larino, brought suit at the court of Count Madelfrid against Azo, bishop of that city, concerning the church of Saint Benedict at Pettinari, which the same bishop had claimed for himself together with all its possessions. Having presented our claim and right, while the count judged and the bishop renounced his claim, he recovered it. Since it had been destroyed, he restored it from its foundations and established there the monastery which until then had been within the city; there he began to live religiously with the brethren.

*“Of whom we have mentioned above,” added in manuscript 2.*

### 7.

This abbot made a lease-document concerning the monastery of Saint Mary at Luco, at Lake Fucinus, for Raynald, count of the Marsi, according to those appurtenances and boundaries under which Walter, priest and monk, had delivered that church to this monastery nearly twenty years earlier, having received it from Countess Doda as a grant. It comprised approximately six hundred modii of land.

[Note: One witness reads “the church” instead of “the monastery”; another specifies “Luco and Saint Erasmus.” One manuscript adds “and boundaries.” The phrase “which is approximately six hundred modii of land” is absent from one witness.]

The monastery of Saint Mary, moreover, was later enriched far and wide with various and numerous churches and possessions by certain faithful persons. Of these, we have judged it fitting to record here those which we have been able to investigate:

The church of Saint Mary at Passarano, and Saint Sebastian there; the monastery of Saint Martin at Transaquas; the church of Saint Mary of Collelongo; Saint Restituta at Morrei; Saint Stephen, Saint Nicholas, and Saint Donatus in the valley of Sora; Holy Cross in the valley of Ortuccle; Saint Lawrence at Vico; Saint John at Besenge [possibly *Besenie*]; Saint Cyprian in the city of the Marsi; Saint Saviour in the territory of that same city; Saint Barbara there; Saint Ambrose at Secunzano; the monastery of Saint Mary at Cesis; Saint Leucius at Marano; Saint Blaise at Muscosi; Saint Erasmus at Pomperano; Saint Sylvester at Pireto; Saint Saviour at Camerata; and Saint Germanus at Petrella Romani.

[Note: The witnesses and editions vary in several names: *Ortuccle/Artuccle*, *Besenge/Besenle*, *Leucius/Fleuticius*, *Muscosi/Muscusi*, and *Camerata/Camarata*. One edition rearranges the order of some entries and reads “Saint Martin” where the principal text has “the monastery of Saint Martin.”]

All these churches, with all their movable and immovable possessions and appurtenances, had belonged from ancient times to the aforesaid monastery. In addition, there were the large and valuable inheritance of Peter Maimo at Auritino, the inheritance of Apicius at Paterno, and also the inheritance of Betto Rattrude at Avezzano.

[Note: One witness reads *Auretino* for *Auritino*.]

### 8.

Moreover, wherever the aforesaid abbot could ascertain more certainly anything concerning the possessions of this monastery which had been lost or alienated in earlier times, he devoted himself with the greatest zeal to recovering, reclaiming, or redeeming them, and also to making lease-documents.

[Note: One witness supplies “of the possessions”; another supplies “of our monastery.” Another reads “which he could recover” rather than “which he could ascertain.”]

He made lease-documents concerning the property of this monastery, or of Saint Angelus at Barrea, as is recorded in those same documents, with the utmost diligence, both in order to restore by such monies this monastery, formerly destroyed by the Saracens, and in order by this evidence to show for the future that all those things belonged to the jurisdiction of this monastery.

Thus, when he made a lease-document with the sons of a certain Giso of Abruzzo concerning the estate of Bigano, of approximately four hundred modii, he received six hundred solidi immediately; annually, however, as rent, twenty solidi.

[Note: One witness reads *Vigano* for *Bigano*. The text is incomplete after “received in the present …” in one witness.]

Likewise, in Abruzzo, for the estate of Tulliana, three hundred solidi; as rent, twenty-three. Likewise there, for the estate called Bassano, one hundred solidi; as rent, fifteen. Likewise there, at the place called Arole, for four hundred modii of land, six hundred solidi [manuscript 3: two hundred]; as rent, four. For the estate of Mariana, one hundred and sixty-eight solidi; as rent, seven. Likewise, for the estate of Tuliana and other property, sixteen pounds; as rent, twenty solidi. Likewise, from the same estate, three hundred solidi; as rent, sixteen.

[Note: The editions regularly supply “solidi” where the principal text omits it. One witness reads “two hundred” instead of “six hundred” at Arole. The rent for Mariana is absent from two witnesses. One witness adds “likewise there” before “from the estate.”]

In the county of Penne, for the estate of Saint Sylvester at Doliola, four hundred solidi; as rent, fifteen. For the estate of Saint George at Colline, two hundred solidi; as rent, ten. For lands at the place called Ciccle, five hundred solidi; as rent, ten. For lands at Paterno and Casa Punti, one hundred and sixty solidi; as rent, four.

In the Marsian territory, for Saint Victorinus at Celano and Saint Benedict at Tilia, six pounds; as rent, eight tremisses. At Balva, for Saint Mercurius and Saint Caesidius, four pounds; as rent, ten tremisses.

[Note: One witness expands the latter entry to “Saint Caesidius and other property at Flaterno.”]

Likewise there, for the church of Saint Benedict at Praetorium, two pounds; as rent, two solidi.

He also made a lease-document with a certain John, priest, and Marald, gastald of the city of Canne, concerning the fishery of that city at the place called Zappineta, for ten years; as rent, fourteen bundles of cuttlefish, each bundle containing forty good cuttlefish. Likewise, concerning the church of Saint Benedict situated in the same Canne, as rent, two solidi.

[Note: One edition reads “fourteen bundles each year.” Another witness reads “two prepared skins” instead of “two solidi.”]

He also made a lease-document concerning the fishery of Lesina and the river Laurus, at a rent of thirty bezants.

He made a lease-document with Landulf, count of Isernia, concerning the entire appurtenance of the lands called Capriata. Not long afterward that count restored them in their entirety to this monastery, giving his little son here for conversion together with other offerings.

He also made a lease-document concerning the church of Saint Andrew and all its appurtenances in the valley of Caudis, at the place called Paulisi, with a certain Leo, priest, and John Genco, solely in return for their many gifts and services.

[Note: The name after John is incomplete in one witness. A longer reading in another witness refers to the church of Saint Andrew in the valley of Caudis and to additional offerings.]

He did likewise with innumerable others in various places and provinces. We have judged it superfluous to enumerate or record them here.

[Manuscript 1 adds: “He died on the ninth day before the Kalends of December and was buried beside the church of Saint Benedict.”]

### 9.

[Editorial note: Much has been disputed concerning this passage. To state briefly what I think, I believe that Leo found in the documents of the Church of Capua a notice that John was consecrated in 966, when Aligern’s eighteenth year began, and that Otto II was made emperor at Christmas 968. Led by this, he believed that the father had died in 967. But when he later found in the *Annals of Cassino* that Otto had gone to Calabria in 969 and that his father was still alive—for he took that father to be Otto II—he thought that the year written above had to be changed and added the solar eclipse. Aligern’s eighteenth year is also given by the Chronicle of Atina in Muratori, *Scriptores*, VII, p. 909, which seems here to have used the same source as Leo.]

In the nineteenth year of this abbot [966; manuscript 1 originally read “eighteenth,” corrected in 1b], Pope John of Rome, exiled from Rome, came to Capua. At the request of the aforesaid Prince Pandulf, he then for the first time established an archbishopric in that city, consecrating there John, the prince’s brother.

[Note: One manuscript adds “the thirteenth”; another removes it. A fuller variant reads that John was consecrated there as archbishop, the prince’s brother.]

After him, Lord Leo, a monk of this monastery, exercised the archbishopric in that city for four and a half years and left the succession to that dignity to Gerbert, likewise a monk of this place.

[Note: One witness reads *Gilbert* for *Gerbert*; another specifies “the succession to the archbishopric.”]

[Manuscript 1c adds: “In that same year the sun was darkened at the third hour, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, so that many stars appeared.”]

[Editorial note: This occurred in A.D. 968, 22 December. Compare Liutprand, *Legatio*, 64.]

In the following year, after Otto I had died, his son Otto II, surnamed Rufus, came to Capua in 969. He went to Tarentum, then to Metapontum, and thereafter to Calabria.

[Manuscript 1c adds: “But two years after this, Prince Pandulf, fighting the Greeks at Bebinum, was captured by them and carried off to Constantinople; but after ten months he escaped and returned, installing his son Duke Landenulf in Gaeta, and died four years later.” Manuscript 1b adds: “a castle in Apulia,” and also “to Emperor Otto at that same Bebinum where he had been captured.”]

[Editorial note: Compare the *Chronicle of Salerno*, chapters 171 and following.]

Having thereafter prosperously returned to his own lands, in the year of the Lord 983 he again assembled a great army and descended into Calabria to fight the Saracens. But, by divine permission, he was defeated by them and could scarcely escape with only a few companions.

[Editorial note: One manuscript reads “thus”; another adds a long account of Prince Pandulf’s capture, imprisonment, escape, and death. One witness records that Emperor Otto returned to Capua and afterward went to Rome.]

Coming therefore to Capua, he confirmed the principality to Aloara, widow of Prince Pandulf, and to her son Landenulf. For Landulf and Atenulf, sons of that same Aloara, had perished in the aforesaid war.

[Editorial note: One manuscript adds: “In that battle Landulf, son of Prince Pandulf, died with his brother Atenulf and many others. The emperor, returning to Capua, …”]

The emperor himself, setting out for Rome to gather troops again and renew the conflict, died at that same time and was buried in the atrium of the church of the blessed Apostle Peter, in a porphyry basin.

[Manuscript 1 adds: “Rather, in a marble basin covered by a porphyry stone.”]

[Editorial note: He was buried, rather, in a marble basin covered by a porphyry stone—reportedly the same stone that had been placed upon Hadrian’s tomb, whose sarcophagus later received Innocent II. That stone, excavated under Fontana’s direction, contains baptismal water in Saint Peter’s church. For a fuller discussion of all these matters, see Bonanni, *De templo Vaticano*, chapter 22.]

[Manuscripts 1b and 2 add: “On the left as one enters the paradise of the same church.”]

His son Otto III received the kingdom.

### 10.

Aloara, therefore, having lived in her dignity for approximately eight years, left her son Landenulf in the principality. Four months later, when according to the princely custom of that city he had solemnly proceeded, on the Thursday of Holy Week, to the church of Saint Marcellus, he was cruelly killed by certain disloyal Capuans [20 April 993].

[Note: A fuller variant says that he was killed by certain men in the church of Saint Marcellus, to which he had proceeded from the palace on the fifth day of Holy Week.]

[Editorial note: Compare the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*, *Scriptores*, III, pp. 206–207; our author has nevertheless added certain details. Compare also Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 57.]

When this became known, Trasmund, count of Chieti and margrave, a kinsman of that prince, came to Capua nearly two months later to avenge his killing, with a considerable army gathered together and with Raynald and Oderisius, counts of the Marsi. He besieged and ravaged it for fifteen days.

[Note: One witness omits “a considerable army.” Another identifies Oderisius as count of the Marsi. An editorial note remarks that the addition “and margrave” appears incorrect.]

Subsequently, for this same vengeance upon the prince, Hugh the margrave, sent by the emperor, came to Capua with the aforesaid counts and besieged it on every side for many days, until those who had killed the aforesaid prince were handed over. Taking them, he hanged six of them on the gallows; the rest he punished with diverse and various penalties.

### 11.

About two years before this, a great earthquake occurred both at Capua and at Benevento, so that at Capua it overthrew very many houses and caused the bells of that city to ring by themselves [25 October 990].

At Benevento it cast down Vipera and destroyed fifteen towers; in these, one hundred and fifty men died.

[Editorial note: Compare the Beneventan Annals for 990. Vipera was a castle in the Beneventan district; nevertheless, our author seems to have been thinking of some statue. Benevento also had a quarter called Vipera, later Vico de Serpi, as De Vita reports in the *Beneventan Antiquities*.]

[Note: One witness reads “many” instead of “one hundred and fifty.”]

It destroyed a great part of Ariano and Frecento [Frigento]. It overthrew almost half the city of Compsa and killed its bishop together with many others. It submerged Ronsa, with nearly all who lived there.

[Editorial note: Ronsa was a settlement not far from Compsa. —ANG.]

About the same time, the brother of this Abbot Aligern, named Leo, a monk by profession, returning from Jerusalem, brought with him a substantial portion of the wood of the Lord’s Cross, encircled with gold, precious gems, and pearls, and most devoutly offered it to this holy monastery on the Nones of November [5 November].

[Note: One manuscript instead reads that it was “venerably placed in a silver reliquary”; that phrase was deleted in another witness. One witness adds “on the day of our Lord.”]

The aforesaid abbot died on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [23 November], in 985, and was honorably buried beside the church of Saint Benedict.

[Editorial note: In codex 47: “On the ninth day before the Kalends of December, Aligern, priest and abbot of this place.” Codex 353 contains an epitaph of Aligern, written in an eleventh-century hand, which Bethmann newly collated and which we append here.]

> Here lies buried that outstanding father Aligern,  
> who shall rise again through the life-giving pledge.  
> Renowned for native goodness and illustrious to the world,  
> he was born and reared in the city of Naples.  
>   
> Yet pondering the Lord’s commands, and leaving his homeland,  
> he joyfully hastened to where the head of the world is.  
> For he chose the refuge of the Church’s teacher,  
> to bow his neck to God under Father Baldwin.  
>   
> Having by regular teaching attained the heights of virtue,  
> he deserved to govern this sacred school,  
> from which all the bright breaths of light shine,  
> over sea, over lands, over mountain-ridges, and through chaos.  
>   
> Because it had at that time been brought to nothing,  
> he eagerly renewed it with every kind of effort.  
> Renewing timbers and laying tiles, he repaired the partitions,  
> and made the [lacuna] rough [lacuna] house possess painted decoration.  
>   
> What is effective and what is not, where virtue leads  
> and where error carries one—he himself knew, shrewd and steadfast in purpose.  
> No powerful person existed who could despise him,  
> or who could ask for what pleased him, since he could give everything.  
>   
> Grave in conduct, standing forth as a watchtower for monks,  
> he managed all things with a gentle and pious disposition.  
> Now that pious father, filled with merits such as these,  
> behold, is joyfully received from heaven by the choirs.  
>   
> He is laid within these precincts, duly, nine days before the Kalends  
> of the Roman month: December itself is at hand.  
> He ruled this pious monastery for thirty-seven years,  
> and thus passed upward.  
>   
> Now, when you read this inscription concerning monastic glory,  
> say: “May he now have eternal rest.” Amen.

[Editorial note: “Native goodness” is qualified in one manuscript by “supreme.” Another reads *tam* (“so”) instead of *tum* (“then”). The printed final reading is uncertain *plum*; codex 353 instead reads *adiique* (“and he went”). The Cassinese Annals report that he died in Indiction XIV, so that he did not complete his thirty-seventh year.]

MANSO, the twenty-eighth abbot, held office for eleven years.

### 12.

He was a cousin of Prince Pandulf.

[Editorial note: Prince Laidulf also calls him his blood-relative in his charter, in Peter’s Register, no. 235. —ANG.]

At the time when Abbot Aligern died, Manso was presiding over the monastery of Saint Magnus, situated near the city of Fondi. Trusting in the support of related princes, but not with the consent of all the monks of this place, he obtained the abbacy of this monastery.

[Note: One witness reads *Aliernus* for *Aligernus*. Another specifies that he obtained it “with the support of his relatives,” but not with the consent of all the monks.]

Consequently, some of the senior and better brethren of this monastery chose to leave rather than remain under him. Among them was Lord John of Benevento, who later became abbot; another was Lord Theobald, who likewise later became abbot; also Lord Liutius, one of the more devout and senior monks of this place; and five others whose names are not remembered.

The first three went to Jerusalem, while the other five went to Lombardy. Because of their great devotion to this place, Hugh the margrave received them most honourably. By his generosity they built five monasteries in those regions and established there the entire order according to the tradition of this monastery.

[Note: One witness instead says that Hugh founded five monasteries for them and granted them lands, where they established the monastic order according to the observance of this place.]

From the gift of this margrave, two silver crowns are kept here.

### 13.

At the same time, the aforesaid Otto III, through the intervention of his mother, the Empress Theophanu, issued a charter for this monastery [23 July 989], confirming, as was customary, all its appurtenances.

[Editorial note: Register no. 126. It was drawn up at Ingelheim.]

Moreover, Gisulf, count of Teano, made an offering to this monastery in August 996 of the place or castle called Casale Caspuli, with all its boundaries and appurtenances.

[Editorial note: “Son of the late Lord Paldulf, prince. Given in the fourth year of Landulf, or Laidulf, in August, Indiction IX.” Gattula published it in the *Accessiones*, p. 84, from Peter’s Register. Di Meo, in the *Neapolitan Annals* under 996, observed that not the castle itself but the land adjacent to it was given.]

Berteram, a nobleman of the county of Penne, also offered his property to blessed Benedict at the place called Fonte Tecta, together with the church of Saint Flavian, half the castle of Colle Carello, the castle of Monte Petitto, and his other estates. This comprised land of seven hundred modii [14 June 991].

[Editorial note: Fontecchia, in Abruzzo Ultra. —GATT.]

A certain Peter, priest of Campomaurano, offered to this place the church of Saint Mary, which he himself had built on his hereditary land beside the lakes of that city, together with many lands and all its appurtenances.

[Editorial note: Campomarano, now Civita Campomarano, lies in the county of Molise near Guardia Alfiera.]

Temmarius, also a distinguished man of Abruzzo, made a charter for Saint Benedict concerning all his appurtenance at Penne and in Abruzzo, together with the church of Saint Paul, the church of Saint John of Busseta, and estates in various places. This comprised land of one thousand one hundred modii.

[Note: One witness reads *Bosseta* for *Busseta*. Another says that after nearly three lines were erased—“Likewise Teuto also,” and so forth—manuscript 1b continues: “This abbot made …”]

Trasmund, a cleric, likewise made an offering of his estate in Abruzzo called Celli, with all its appurtenances and adjacent lands; this comprised three hundred modii of land. Grimoald, judge of Aquino, did the same concerning the church of Saint Angelus on the mountain called Aspranus, with considerable lands and its other appurtenances.

This abbot made a lease-document with certain of our own people, according to the tenor of Abbot Aligern’s arrangement, and stationed them around Saint Elias, so that they might restore that church, destroyed by barbarians, and cultivate the lands around it within the established boundaries.

He also made a lease-document with Landenulf, bishop of the see of Lucera, concerning the fishery of Lesina. For this the bishop annually paid, at Christmas, to the provost of Saint Sophia at Benevento, for the use of this monastery, twenty-six bezants as rent.

He also made a lease-document with Raynald, count of the Marsi, concerning the church of Saint Paul situated in the territory of Comino, in the appurtenance of the castle of the Seven Brothers, with its property and adjacent lands—namely, three hundred modii of land. He received from him fifty solidi immediately and, annually, five hundred tench.

[Note: One witness reads “its appurtenances” rather than “its adjacent lands.”]

Concerning the church of Saint Felix at Pulverio and Saint Maximus in the county of Teano, he made a lease-document and received three hundred solidi; as rent, eight solidi.

In the county of Penne: for Saint Angelus at Galiano, one hundred solidi; as rent, seven. Likewise there, for Saint Bonitus, fifty solidi; as rent, three solidi. Likewise there, for lands at Coronulas and at the spring of Ermo, one hundred solidi; as rent, one solidus. Likewise there, for lands at Pastina and in the valley of Albina, one hundred and sixty solidi; as rent, eight solidi.

Likewise, in Abruzzo, for a certain Odemund, from the estate of Mariano at the cistern and on the hill of Morta, one hundred modii of land, for one hundred solidi; as rent, five solidi.

[Note: One witness reads *Ademund* for *Odemund*. The text is incomplete in one witness after “for …” and resumes with “five.”]

At the same time, the citizens of Terracina, admonished by their bishop John because of a certain calamity which they were then suffering, unanimously vowed and promised on Easter Day [15 April 994] that every year they would give six thousand eels to this monastery. They ordered a written instrument to be made concerning this, with a terrible anathema imposed for the remembrance of posterity.

[Editorial note: “On the fifteenth day upon the beginning of April, which was the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, the second Sunday day—that is, the Sunday after Easter—as the reckoning of time establishes.” Tosti published this from Peter’s Register, *History of Cassino*, I, p. 243.]

### 14.

When this same abbot had received from Pope John XV the customary privilege [11 November 989], he also received from Prince Landenulf—who, as we have said, was cruelly killed by the Capuans at the church of Saint Marcellus—a charter confirming the whole abbey [991], in accordance with the tenor of his father’s charter.

[Note: One manuscript reads “John XX” instead of “John XV.” Another adds that the privilege was received in the third year of the abbot’s abbacy, by the prayers of Empress Theophanu, his mother.]

[Editorial note: Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 87, from the original. It was dated in Landenulf’s ninth year, Indiction IV.]

Laidulf, brother of this Landenulf, who succeeded him in the principality, granted fifteen leading households in the city of Aquino.

[Note: The text reads “fifteen families”; one edition interprets these as the leading families.]

In the ninth year of this abbot’s abbacy [993], he also swore complete security, and that during his life he would faithfully assist him concerning the entire abbey. He likewise issued a charter concerning Castro Coeli, with the whole mountain called Aspranus and its appurtenances [10 December 994].

[Editorial note: The ninth year belongs only to the charter, with which our author at first rightly connected it; for we hold that after Aligern’s death the see was vacant for several days. Laidulf made the oath at the very beginning of his principate, in Manso’s eighth year. Gattula published both, *Accessiones*, pp. 89–90.]

The same abbot ascended to the summit of that mountain. Finding there certain old buildings, he wished to build a fortress there; but, dissuaded because of the scarcity of water, he descended and built on the side of the same mountain the stronghold called Sicca, now called Roccasecca.

[Editorial note: Roccasecca; Thomas Aquinas was born there. —ANG.]

[Manuscript 1 adds: “That place was originally called Laurianum from the multitude of laurels which stood there, and he also built there a church in honour of Holy Cross.” Manuscript 1b deleted the first clause.]

### 15.

The aforesaid Emperor Otto, having deprived Laidulf of the principality and exiled him beyond the mountains in 999, because he was said to have consented to the murder of his brother, handed over the principality of Capua to a certain Adhemar of Capua, son of the cleric Balsam, whom he had brought up from childhood and dearly loved.

[Editorial note: One manuscript adds that he had shortly before made him margrave.]

Not long afterward—that is, after four months—this same Adhemar was expelled from the principality by the Capuans, and Landulf of Saint Agatha, son of Landulf, prince of Benevento, was appointed prince in his place.

[Editorial note: His own charters show him as prince from January 1000.]

He confirmed the whole abbey to the aforesaid abbot by oath, and caused twelve noble Capuans to confirm it by oath: the abbey in its entirety, with absolutely all its appurtenances within the principality of Capua, as it had been held under the aforesaid Princess Aloara and her son Landenulf, by whom it had formerly been confirmed to him.

He likewise confirmed in its entirety the county of Aquino, together with its bishopric, and the castle of Teramense, as well as the castle of Arce, with all their appurtenances, just as he then held and possessed them.

[Editorial note: Teramense was formerly called Interamna, where the Garigliano and the stream called delle Sogne meet.]

In addition, he confirmed the castle of Bantra, which had belonged to Count Lando, with all its appurtenances, in the same terms, together with various other conditions which the aforesaid abbot had thought fit to demand from that prince, as is contained in the text of the oath itself.

[Editorial note: Bantra later became Vandra, now deserted, situated where the Bantra—today called Peccia—joins the Garigliano. Across the Bantra stood Rocca di Vandro of Saint Evander.]

### Supplied textual apparatus

The opening Gisepert apparatus reads *Thermole* in 1b and 2 for printed *Thermule* (Termoli), *illum* ("that one") in 4 for *ei* ("to him"), and *abbas A.* ("Abbot A.") in 1b for *Angelarius abbas*. Manuscript 1b and the edition read *dimissa ei iterum* ("again granted to him") and *a libra una* ("at one pound"). Manuscript 1 omits everything from *Hic* through the chapter's end.

In the Castelgard action, witness 4 reads *Castalgardo* and witness 3 *Gastalgardus* for *Castelgardus*; witness 2 has *Termoleto* for *Termuleto*, and the edition has *Vicarium* for *vivarium* ("fishpond"). In the Constantius action, witness 2 reads *Lariano* for *Larino* and *Pettenari* for *Pettinari*; witness 3 reads *Madelfrit* for *Madelfrid*. At the restoration sentence the edition has the abbreviated reading *eam r. ibi m.* in place of the printed wording beginning *illam restaurans*; the source abbreviation is retained without conjectural expansion. The edition reads *infra* ("below/within") for *intra* ("within"), and witness 2 reads *monachis* ("monks") for *fratribus* ("brethren"). Witness 2 adds *Cujus supra meminimus* ("of whom we have spoken above").

At chapter 7, witness 1 originally read *ecclesia* ("church") for *monasterio* ("monastery"), corrected in 1b; witness 1 reads *Luco et Sancti Herasmi* ("Luco and Saint Erasmus"), and the editor locates Luco at Lake Fucino. Witness 1b adds the abbreviated *a. f.* at "appurtenances and boundaries" and *a. D. c. s. o.* at Doda's grant; the initials are retained because the apparatus does not securely expand them. Witness 1b and the edition read *oblatam* ("offered") for *concessam* ("granted"). Witness 1's *m. dudum t.* was corrected in 1b at the clause about the earlier transfer. The clause *quod est terra modiorum circiter sexcentorum* ("which is about six hundred modii of land") is in 1b and the edition but absent from 1. Manuscript 1 omits from the following *Quod* through *Avezano*, although a sign shows that something fell out.

In the church catalogue, witness 2 reads *et* ("and") for *a* ("by"). The edition has the abbreviated rearrangement *hic aliquanta scribamus quae investigare potuimus* ("let us write here some things which we could investigate") and puts the Saint Mary of Collelongo material and other entries in a different order; it reads *Sanctus Martinus* ("Saint Martin") for *Monasterium sancti Martini* ("the monastery of Saint Martin") and supplies its own Saint Restituta sequence. Witness 3 reads *Artuccle* for *Ortuccle*; witnesses 3 and 4 read *Besenle* for *Besenge*, with the editor asking whether *Besenie* is meant. The edition reads *giro* for *agro* and has an abbreviated Saint Mary sequence. Witness 3 reads *Fleuticius*, *Muscusi*, and *Camarata* for printed *Leucii*, *Muscosi*, and *Camerata*. Witness 2 reads *Auretino* for *Auritino*. Witness 4 adds printed *et* ("and") before Betto Rattrude's inheritance.

At chapter 8, the edition omits *aliquid* ("anything"). Manuscript 1 omits *hujus* ("of this"), while 1b and the edition read *nostri* ("our") there. Witness 4 adds *seu perditae* ("or lost"). Witness 1b adds the printed *praefatus abbas* ("the aforesaid abbot"). Witness 1 and the edition read *potuit* ("was able") for *poterat* ("could"), *maximum prae omnibus recolligendi* for the printed recovery phrase, and *habuit* ("had") for *habebat*. Witness 1b adds the clause from *seu* through *faciendi* ("or also of redeeming, and of making leases") and adds the lease catalogue through the chapter's end. At its opening, 1b and the edition have *autem quamplurimos sive* in place of printed *autem seu*, *ut* ("as") for *sicut*, and *ipsorum* ("their") for *hujusmodi* ("such").

The lease list reads *Vigano* in 1b and 2 for *Bigano*; witness 4 omits *in praesenti* ("immediately"). At the following Abruzzo entry witness 4 has the abbreviated *Prucio de curte q. d. Bass.*; the exact form is retained because its compression does not justify a fuller conjecture. Manuscript 1b and the edition add *solidos* throughout this portion, while 4 omits it; witness 3 reads 200 for 600 at Arole. Manuscript 1b and the edition insert *4. Item ibidem de* before the Mariana estate; manuscript 2 omits *solidos 168; pro censu*. Manuscript 1b and the edition read *item ibidem de* ("likewise there, from") at the next entry, and the edition reads *Tulliana* and *Doliosa* for *Tuliana* and *Doliola*. Witness 2 reads *Punzi* for *Punti*, and witness 3 *Celano* for *Celanu*.

Manuscript 1 omits the span from the Balva entry through the offering of the count's little son. In that span witness 2 reads *Caesidio et aliis rebus in Flaterno* ("Caesidius and other property in Flaterno"). The edition reads the annual cuttlefish rent with *censu super singulos annos quattuordecim*; witness 2 instead has *censu duarum pellium confectarum* ("a rent of two prepared skins") at the Saint Benedict entry. The edition transposes the material from *Fecit et libellum* through *parvulo* and from *De* through *bizanteorum*, and omits *cum aliis oblationibus* ("with other offerings"). Manuscript 1b and the edition supply an alternate Caudis/Saint Andrew opening, with *Paulisi* absent from 1b; Genco's following word is cut off in 1b. Manuscript 1b and the edition omit *multis dumtaxat* ("only many"); 1b and 2 read *aliquae* at the clause about other transactions, and 1b and the edition have the abbreviated conclusion *quae hic superfluum scribere duximus* ("which we judged superfluous to write here"). Witness 1 adds: "He died on the ninth day before the Kalends of December and was buried beside the church of Saint Benedict."

For the later chapters, the editorial note on John’s Capuan archbishopric says Leo likely used Capuan church documents, misdated Otto II’s accession and later added the eclipse; it cites the Chronicle of Atina in Muratori, *Scriptores* VII, p. 909. In chapter 9, witness 1 corrects “nineteenth” to “eighteenth,” adds “the thirteenth” after John (later erased in 1b), and witness 3 reads *archbishop* for *archbishopric*. The edition’s full reading says John was consecrated there as archbishop, the prince’s brother. Witness 1b adds Leo’s succession wording; the edition reads Gilbert for Gerbert and 1b/2 specify succession to the archbishopric. Manuscript 1c adds the eclipse at the third hour on 11 Kalends of January; the editorial note dates it to 22 December 968 and cites Liutprand, *Legatio* 64. Witness 1b adds “son” and “went to Metapontum”; witness 4 omits “then.”

The long manuscript addition after Otto’s Calabrian campaign says Pandulf fought the Greeks at Bebinum, was captured and taken to Constantinople, escaped after ten months, returned to Otto at Bebinum, installed Landenulf as duke at Gaeta, and died four years later; 1b adds “a castle in Apulia.” The source cites the *Chronicle of Salerno*, chapters 171 onward. Witness 1 corrects “Rome” to “Verona” in Otto’s departure; witness 1 and the edition say “returning.” Another addition records the death of Landulf, son of Pandulf, with Atenulf and others, and Otto’s return to Capua and Rome. The burial note says the emperor was rather in a marble basin covered by porphyry stone, with Bonanni, *De templo Vaticano*, chapter 22; 1b and 2 add “to the left as one enters the paradise.” Witness 1b corrects “received the kingdom” to “became emperor.”

In chapter 10, witness 1 and the edition begin *Praedicta vero Aloara cum* (“But the aforesaid Aloara, when”) rather than printed *Aloara igitur cum* (“Aloara, therefore, when”). The fuller witness 1b account specifies that Landenulf was killed by men in Saint Marcellus’s church after proceeding from the palace on the fifth day of Holy Week; the edition expands the same. The source cites the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*, *Scriptores* III, pp. 206–207, and Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 57. “Transmundus” is an alternate form of Trasmund; witness 1b adds “and margrave,” which the editor says is probably incorrect. Witness 4 omits “a considerable army”; the edition identifies Oderisius as count of the Marsi. The later sentence has “those who killed that prince” in 1 and 2, and the edition’s “the six” is the reading of the gallows clause.

For chapter 11, the edition omits “at Benevento”; witness 4 adds “indeed” before the death toll, witness 1 reads “many,” and 1b reads “150.” The place is “Fregento” in the apparatus, identified by the editor as Frigento; ANG. identifies Ronsa as a settlement near Compsa. Witness 1 reads “having returned from Jerusalem, he brought a portion”; the source’s phrase “placed reverently in a silver reliquary” is present in 1 and deleted in 1b; 1b adds “on the day of our Lord.” The burial sentence has “honorably” added in witness 4.

The Aligern epitaph’s apparatus must remain uncertain: one codex adds “supreme” to “native goodness,” another reads *tam* (“so”) for *tum* (“then”), and the final reading is uncertain—*plum* in the printed text, with codex 353 reading *adiique* (“and he went”). The editor cites the Cassinese Annals’ Indiction XIV dating, which implies that Aligern did not complete his thirty-seventh year.

Chapter 12’s heading note calls Manso the twenty-eighth abbot. Manuscript 1b adds the whole chapter (*totum caput*). The kinship reference is Laidulf’s charter in Peter’s Register no. 235. Witness 3 reads *Aliernus*; witness 1 and the edition add “support of the relatives”; witnesses 1 and 2 omit “Lord” before John and Theobald. Witness 1 says the first three went to Jerusalem and the other five to Lombardy; the edition expands Hugh’s benefaction to founding and granting lands for five monasteries and establishing the whole order according to this monastery’s observance. The note says the two silver crowns here came from Hugh’s gift.

Chapter 13’s apparatus retains Register no. 126 for Otto III’s 23 July 989 charter, drawn up at Ingelheim; 1b adds “through his mother,” and the edition reads “Theophanii.” The Gisulf note identifies him as son of the late Prince Paldulf, dated in Landulf’s fourth year, August, indiction IX; Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 84, from Peter’s Register, and Di Meo’s correction that adjacent land, rather than the castle itself, was given. Gattula’s note identifies Fontecchia in Abruzzo Ultra. Register nos. 237–238 cover Peter and Temmarius; Civita Campomarano lies in Molise near Guardia Alfiera. Witnesses 1b and 2 read *Bosseta* for Busseta; the erased three-line Teuto passage is followed in 1b by “This abbot made…”. “Transmundus” is the edition’s form for Trasmund. At *monte qui vocatur* (“the mountain which is called”), the edition reads *dicitur* (“is called”) for *vocatur*.

Witness 1b and the edition omit the entire sentence about the leaseholders around Saint Elias; it nevertheless belongs to the source. The Lucera lease has “at Christmas” in witness 4, “on the Nativity” in the edition, and “on the day of the Nativity” in 1b. The Marsi lease reads “its appurtenances” in 1b and the edition, and “in the present” in 1b for “immediately.” The Saint Felix/Saint Maximus entry is supplied by 1b and the edition. Witness 3 reads *Ademund* for Odemund; witness 2 omits the phrase “for one hundred solidi,” and an edition note says this lease follows Aligern’s arrangement and was already recorded in Book I, chapter 25. The Terracina vow has witness 1b and the edition “all unanimously”; witness 4 omits the calamity clause. Its date note is 15 April 994, the Resurrection, the second Sunday, as Tosti printed from Peter’s Register, *History of Cassino* I, p. 243.

In chapter 14, witness 1 corrects John XV to John XX and 1b preserves the correction; witness 1 adds a note that the privilege was received in the third year of the abbacy through Empress Theophanu’s prayers, later erased. The charter is dated 11 November 989; Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 87, gives Landenulf’s ninth year, indiction IV. The source reads “fifteen families” at Aquino; the edition interprets them as leading households. The ninth year belongs only to the Castro Coeli charter, while Laidulf’s oath was made at the beginning of his principate, in Manso’s eighth year; Gattula, *Acc.*, pp. 89–90. The source’s oath note says Laidulf swore complete security and faithful assistance for the whole abbey during his life; the alternative witness wording explicitly includes Castro Coeli with the mountain Aspranus. The Roccasecca note identifies the place and Thomas Aquinas; manuscript 1 adds that it was first called Laurianum and that a church of Holy Cross was built there, with that first clause erased in 1b.

Chapter 15 is absent from manuscript 1, although a sign marks its place; compare chapter 24. The source cites the *Chronicle of Saint Benedict*, *Scriptores* III, p. 207. One manuscript adds that Otto had recently made Adhemar margrave; two witnesses omit “after four months.” Charters show Landulf of Saint Agatha as prince from January 1000. For the appointment, the edition has the abbreviated *II. princeps supradicto a.* in place of the printed wording; its exact form is retained because the initial numeral or letters are uncertain. The edition also reads *Agathe filius Landulfi* (“[Saint] Agatha, son of Landulf”) at the same passage. The oath note is from Peter’s Register and Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 90; its dates are absent, and the editor warns that either the document is fictitious or Manso’s name was inserted by scribal error. Witness 1 reads “to him,” and the alternate wording states that Landulf obtained and swore the charter concerning Castro Coeli and Aspranus, confirming the whole abbey. Witness 2 omits the castle of Teramense; the editorial note identifies it with ancient Interamna at the confluence of the Garigliano and the stream delle Sogne. The Bantra note identifies it with later Vandra, now deserted, where the Bantra (Peccia) meets the Garigliano, opposite Rocca di Vandro of Saint Evander. At the final *tenore simili* (“in like terms”), the edition has the abbreviated *tenore quo supra dictum est c.* (“in the terms stated above …”); the final initial is retained without conjectural expansion.

16. Therefore, besides the many deeds which he performed vigorously—and, to speak somewhat more discreetly and in a somewhat worldly fashion of the father of so great a place—when he had equipped himself with very many knights and no small number of servants dressed in silk garments, and frequented the court of the emperor beyond the mountains with no less diligence, especially because of the construction of the aforesaid fortress, he kindled for himself throughout the whole principality the greatest fuel of envy and hatred. Thus he seemed to desire to claim for himself not only the abbey but also the principality. Hence it happened that, not long afterward, having been lured by treachery by the Capuans, he was captured and blinded.

[Editorial variants and notes: “and in a certain way, so that [s. d. t. l. p. l. s. g.]” (first edition; the abbreviated continuation is materially uncertain); “clothed” (first edition); the words “and—frequently” are added in manuscript 1b; “especially because of the construction of this fortification” (manuscript 1); “kindled” reads “inflamed” in the first edition, followed there by: “so that he was not merely striving to claim the abbey but also, as it were, the principality for himself.”]

To this envy was also added the wickedness of Alberic, bishop of the Marsi. For, after he had given the bishopric to his son, whom he had fathered by a prostitute, this wretched man had devoted his whole mind, if he could somehow obtain it, to acquiring the abbey of this place. Learning, therefore, that the aforesaid abbot was very hostile to the Capuans because of the matters mentioned above, he first spoke with certain utterly wicked monks and afterward with some exceedingly depraved Capuan citizens. He agreed that he would give them one hundred pounds of Pavia denarii if, after first blinding the abbot, they would hand over to him the monastery of Cassino, which thereafter, supported by their aid, he would possess without any obstacle of opposition.

[Editorial variants: “he had applied his mind” (first edition). Leo added the passage from “Learning” through “hostile”; the first edition reads “hostile.” The first edition has “ignorant of God”; Peter Damian has “laypeople who do not know God.” Another reading has “he finally made the agreement,” followed by an abbreviated statement that he would give one hundred pounds of Pavia coinage if they carried out the plan; manuscript 1 has “his own monastery,” and the first edition has “hand over.”]

That is to say, he would immediately send them half the price through his agents; he would send the other half when he received the abbot’s eyes into his own hands. When this had thus been firmly agreed between them, each side began to apply itself as best it could: the one to money, the others to wickedness. Accordingly, when that pseudo-bishop had collected money from every quarter, he sent it as he had promised.

[Peter Damian specifies that it was sent to the town of Saint Germanus. The words “so that they might arrange how they should proceed” are not found in Peter Damian. “He agreed at last” is another reading.]

Those wicked men, receiving it, concealed in certain hiding places the men who had brought it. Then, coming to the abbot, they deceitfully prostrated themselves at his feet and begged him to go to Capua; and, if he had any complaint against any one of them, to obtain lawful justice there.

[The first edition adds “prostrate themselves at his feet.”]

But the abbot, since he had long known their envy and suspected their malice, refused in any way to go there.

[The first edition reads “he said that he could not go there at all.”]

Then they, considering denial of God a trifling matter and believing that they could deceive him who is the inspector of all things, immediately brought out the Gospels and swore that they would lead him safe and unharmed to Capua and likewise bring him back safe and unharmed to Saint Benedict.

[The first edition reads “they regarded it as a small matter to deny God”; manuscript 4 adds “this.”]

While swearing this, however, they had fraudulently resolved in their minds that, after bringing him to Capua, they would also lead him to the church of Saint Benedict situated in that same city, so that, by this device of fraud, they might appear to avoid perjury.

[Manuscript 4 adds “also” and “which is situated in the same city”; the first edition reads “so that, by this device of fraud, they might avoid this perjury.”]

The abbot, deceived by frauds of this kind, believed them and went with them to Capua, suspecting no evil. But those who, long before, at the devil’s prompting, had conceived sorrow, at last gave birth to iniquity. As soon as they had brought him into the Capuan monastery—14 November 996—they seized him as they had planned, immediately tore out his eyes, carefully wrapped them in a little cloth, and secretly sent them by messengers to their lord, the bishop.

[The first edition reads “and”; manuscript 2 reads “they had conceived.”]

The messengers received them and, having become exceedingly joyful, began hastily to return to their lord.

[The first edition adds “that is, exceedingly joyful”; the first edition reads “eyes” rather than “eye.”]

But O eye of divine judgment, which never sleeps!

They had already reached the plain near Marsi called Mezius and, stopping there in security, were taking food, wearied by the journey. Then, behold, a certain traveler came from the Marsi. They questioned him, as is customary among travelers, about whether there was any news. He said: “The bishop of this land has died.”

[Peter Damian has “to the town of Saint Germanus”; manuscript 1 reads “Mezio”; the first edition reads “suddenly”; manuscripts 1 and 2 read “a traveler who had arrived.”]

At these words they were greatly astonished, and, saying with extreme scorn that he was a liar and an impostor, they hesitated entirely to believe him. But when he affirmed the matter with the utmost certainty and insistence, and carefully reported to them the day and hour of the bishop’s death, they immediately buried in that very place the eyes which they now carried in vain. Mounting their horses, they sped swiftly to the house of the unhappy bishop and found him deprived of life at the very hour at which the aforesaid abbot had been deprived of the light of his eyes.

[The first edition reads “he affirmed”; manuscript 4 has “he affirmed.” The first edition adds that the bishop’s house “was not far away.”]

That day was the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December—14 November. Up to this point the author had copied out Peter Damian.

Lest this perhaps seem doubtful or incredible to anyone: among those messengers whom the aforesaid pseudo-bishop had sent to undertake so great a crime was one named Andrew, a priest by office. I myself remember seeing him when I was still a very small boy, scarcely able to move himself in bed. Though he lived beyond his hundredth year, whenever he was questioned he used to confess all these matters in order, with tears, to my uncle John, bishop of Sora, of holy memory.

[The first edition adds “so that no one might perhaps think the story fictitious.”]

At that time Adenulf, surnamed Summucula, presided over the gastaldship of Aquino. He was the great-grandfather of those who are now called the counts of Aquino. As soon as he learned that the abbot had been blinded, he became joyful and overturned from its foundations the aforesaid Rocca Secca, which that same abbot had built shortly before.

[The first edition calls it “the fortress called Rocca Secca.” Manuscript 1b records in the margin: “In the thirteenth indiction, in the first year of the principate of Lord Landulf of Sant’Agata.” The date is approximately 1000.]

[Addition in manuscript 2: This abbot built in Capuan territory a church in honor of Saint Apollinaris; in Liburia, at Casa Gentiana, a church of Saint John; and at Casale a church of Saint Maurus, confessor of Christ.]

Moreover, his successor, Abbot John, wholly granted this abbot the church of Saint Martin beside the Volturno and the church of Saint Secundinus, together with absolutely all their appurtenances and possessions, so that he might live there honorably according to his own discretion for as long as he lived.

[The churches are situated in the territory of Caiazzo (manuscript 1b and manuscript 2). The first edition reads “he granted them entirely, with all their appurtenances and possessions, for the days of his life.”]

The aforesaid abbot died on the eighth day before the Ides of March, 8 March.

[The first edition adds that the abbot died not long afterward and was buried in the cloister of this monastery beside the church. Another version reads: “He was buried on the eighth day before the Ides of March and reverently laid to rest in the cloister of this monastery.” Manuscripts 2 and 3 omit parts of this addition. Compare chapter 19 below.]

17. At the same time (990), blessed Adelbert, bishop of the Slavs, left his bishopric with the permission of the Roman pontiff and came to this monastery, wishing to go to Jerusalem.

[An introductory form reads “In the days of this man”; another reads “During the same period.” The note refers to the Life of Saint Adalbert; concerning its Cassinese manuscript, see Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores IV, p. 577.]

But when the aforesaid abbot and several priors of this place had dissuaded him from going there, he accepted their counsel as though it had been given to him by God and resolved to spend his whole life here and never again go anywhere at all.

One day, however, certain priors of this monastery, speaking affectionately with him, said: “It is good, father, that you remain here with us, put on the monastic habit here, and lead here a life pleasing to God; for, since you are a bishop, you will be able both to dedicate our churches and to promote our clerics to ecclesiastical orders.”

[The words “and to promote our clerics” are not found in the Life. The first edition reads “you will be able to promote them most suitably.”]

Taking this statement very ill, he immediately went down and devoutly set out for the most holy man Nilus, whom he had learned was then living in the most religious manner at Valleluce with several Greek brothers.

[An addition reads “and returned to Rome”; another reads “At Valleluce.” The first edition reads “having gone there with sufficient devotion.”]

When he humbly sought suitable counsel from him and learned that he could not be received by him—for the aforesaid father declared that, because Adelbert had departed from our monastery in this way, he did not dare retain him, lest on that account he too should be expelled from there with his community—he finally returned to Rome on Nilus’s advice. He lived for some time in the monastery of Saint Boniface the martyr, and not long afterward was sent again by the Roman pontiff to his bishopric (994).

[Manuscript 1b specifies Pope John XX, though this conflicts with the usual numbering.]

Returning once more to Rome, he remained in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Boniface, seeing that he could accomplish nothing there; and once again his archbishop of Mainz sent him back to the Slavs. Afterward he was again sent to Slavonia (996). When he began to preach there, he was beheaded by barbarians for Christ and received martyrdom (23 April 997).

[This expanded account is found in manuscripts 1 and 2.]

In these same days Otto III received the imperial crown from the hand of the Roman pontiff (21 May 996).

[The first edition and manuscript 2 indicate that this is the end of the chapter; compare chapter 18 below.]

Not long afterward he captured the Roman senator Crescentius, who had fortified himself in the Castle of Saint Angelo in rebellion against him. Having deceived him by an oath, he seized him and immediately beheaded him as guilty of treason against imperial majesty (29 April 998).

[This episode is drawn from Peter Damian’s Life of Saint Romuald, chapter 25. One reading specifies “at the bridge of Saint Peter.”]

18. At that same time the man of God Romuald, together with blessed Boniface, a kinsman of the emperor who shortly afterward became a martyr of Christ in Russia, and with several other Germans from the army of the aforesaid emperor, came to this monastery of Saint Benedict for the sake of prayer.

[The entire chapter is added in manuscript 1b. Another manuscript has “At that time, the man of God.” The note refers to Peter Damian, Life of Saint Romuald, chapters 26–27.]

There he became seriously ill, but recovered very quickly through divine mercy and returned to his own country.

[An addition specifies “to his own monastery.” Another addition says that this occurred at the time when the same emperor captured and beheaded Crescentius, as stated above.]

19. About this time a certain Olibanus, a very wealthy count of Gaul, was admonished by the aforesaid man of God Romuald, to whom he had confessed his sins, that, leaving the world, he should come to the monastery of Saint Benedict under the pretext of prayer and there irrevocably devote himself to divine service, since otherwise he could in no way be saved.

[Another reading has *praetextu* (“pretext” or “guise”) rather than *obtentu* (“pretext” or “guise”) of prayer; manuscript 1b adds “by blessed Romuald.” The editorial note adds that these events occurred much earlier and had been written in the margin before the later inserted notices of Romuald and Crescentius.]

Without delay, leaving his possessions to his son, he came to this monastery with a great quantity of riches—namely, fifteen pack animals laden with treasure. Bidding farewell to those who had come with him, who until then had suspected nothing of what he intended, he himself, intending never afterward to depart, compelled them, weeping, to return to their own homes.

JOHN, the twenty-ninth abbot, sat for one year.

[The note observes that he was John, abbot of Capelle. See the Cassinese Annals and below, chapter 42. The editor does not think that John’s accession can be placed before 997, since twelve years and six months are assigned to John III; even with the seven months of Docibilis added, one scarcely reaches the year 1011.]

[Addition: At that time half the moon was turned into blood and half into blackness.]

20. This venerable man, now burdened alike by old age and sickness, perceived that he could not bear the weight of so great a government. Of his own accord, and with the consent and will of all the brothers, he appointed an abbot in his place.

[The first edition reads “he perceived that he could no longer bear the burden”; the phrase “of his own accord” is absent from manuscripts 1 and 2.]

Leaving the abbey, he withdrew with five brothers to the nearby hermitage, in the place now called Piretum. There, having built a small church in honor of Saints Cosmas and Damian, he lived in a somewhat solitary manner and spent the remainder of his life in spiritual works.

[The first edition reads “in honor”; manuscript 1b adds “somewhat solitary.”]

I heard from an old man that, when he had once gone out in a hostile manner against the settlement of this monastery called Piniatarium—whose inhabitants had formerly attempted rebellion—a certain church situated beside that settlement, together with several huts of the same peasants, was set on fire by those who had gone with him. Because of this, giving himself over to many and very great lamentations, he relinquished the abbey on the occasion thus provided.

[The first edition reads “when the inhabitants had attempted to rebel at the death of his predecessor.” Another reading has “sitting” rather than “giving himself over.” The first edition reads “he left the abbey because of this occasion.” Piniatarium is identified as a small village four or five miles south of Saint Germanus.]

This man made a lease-document (*libellus*) for a certain cleric named Trasmund, concerning certain estates belonging to this monastery in Abruzzo, spread over various places and amounting to nearly four hundred modii, for two hundred solidi and an annual rent of eight solidi.

[The readings include “Trasmund of Aprutium” and “concerning our estates”; another reads “in the same Abruzzo.”]

He likewise received the same price and rent for other lands at a place called Ciccle.

[Manuscript 1b and the first edition read “making a lease-document for other lands at Ciccle.”]

From a third part of the estate of Moscufe and from other lands granted under the title of a lease, he also received four hundred solidi; as annual rent, twenty-four solidi.

[The printed reading is “Moscuse.” Manuscripts 1b and 2 omit “granted.”]

21. [Desiderius, *Dialogues* II.11.]

When this man had died in the time of Abbot Theobald, that very night a religious brother named John was in the monastery of Saint Lawrence situated at Capua. He led a religious life far surpassing that of his companions.

[Manuscript 1b expands the passage: “He led a religious life far above his companions. On the night when the John whom we mentioned died …”; the first edition has a similar addition.]

On the night when the John of whom we have spoken died, this brother, anticipating the brethren’s customary vigils, suddenly, while he was praying, looked up and saw, as it were, a very great light in the air above this mountain. Within that light he saw the soul of John himself ascending to heaven.

When morning came, wishing to be assured of the vision, he went to Andrew, who then presided over the Capuan monastery, disclosed the vision which he had seen, and earnestly begged him to send one of his men immediately to this monastery, so that he might learn the whole truth of the matter carefully and report it to them on his return.

[The first edition reads “who then presided over our monastery situated within Capua.”]

The messenger set out. While some part of his journey still remained, he met a man coming from this monastery to Capua, who said that he was going to announce to the brothers living there the death of the aforesaid venerable man John.

When he carefully inquired about the hour of his death, he learned that John had departed from this world at the very hour when that John at Capua declared that he had seen his soul ascending to heaven.

[Manuscript 1b adds “ascending to heaven.”]

Then both returned to those who had sent them: one reported at Capua the death of John, while the other at Cassino reported the vision which had been seen concerning his death.

He died on the day before the Ides of March, 14 March.

[This agrees with the necrology cited by Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 853.]

JOHN, made the thirtieth abbot from Saint Benedict, sat for twelve years and six months.

[One correction reads “four months” rather than “six.”]

22. [Desiderius, *Dialogues* II.1.]

This man, descended from an illustrious family of Beneventan citizens but possessing from childhood still nobler character, held the dignity of archdeacon in the church of that city. Touched by divine love, in the time of Abbot Aligern he came to this holy monastery and, renouncing all the vanity of the world, put on the monastic habit.

After he had spent several years in the pursuit of holy religious life, and after Aligern’s death Manso had succeeded to the abbacy in the order already described, John departed from here and went to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. He remained for six continuous years on Mount Sinai.

[The first edition adds “at a later time”; another reading has “for six whole years.”]

Thereafter he lived for some time in Greece, on the mountain called Agion Oros—formerly Athos.

In that place, one night Saint Benedict appeared to him in a vision and handed him the pastoral staff which he seemed to be carrying in his hand. He ordered him to return as quickly as possible to the monastery of Cassino.

When morning came, he reported the vision to the father of the monastery. That abbot took care to advise and exhort him that, since this appeared to be the will of God, he should by no means neglect it, but should immediately hasten his return to the monastery of Saint Benedict, accompanied by heavenly grace.

Obeying the vision and the admonition, John returned to this place with Christ as his guide. His predecessor, Abbot John, received him with great joy, immediately appointed him prior, and not long afterward—since he himself, as stated above, was hindered alike by illness and old age—appointed him his successor. When the elder John withdrew to the hermitage, this John succeeded to the care of the monastery by the election of all the brothers.

[The first edition reads “he succeeds.”]

He lived in the times of Pope Sylvester II and John XVIII.

[The phrase identifying the abbots is added in manuscript 1b.]

In the first year of his administration, 25 May 998, he received from the aforesaid Emperor Otto a charter confirming the whole abbey, sealed with a golden seal.

[The first edition has an abbreviated expansion beginning: “In the first year of his ordination he received a charter confirming the whole abbey from Emperor Otto III …”; it does not say that Otto took a kingdom from Saint Benedict’s abbot. The note says that this charter is discussed in chapter 24. Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 91, describes the original as bearing a wax seal and having been issued at Rome in the palace.]

The emperor also remained for several days in this monastery and offered two silver crowns to Saint Benedict.

[Manuscript 1 omits the remainder of this sentence and chapter 23; manuscript 2 begins, “At the same time the same emperor …”; manuscript 3, “The same emperor …”.]

23. At the same time, Rainald, count of the Marsi, built the monastery of the church of Saint Mary called In Cellis, in the territory of Carsoli, on 1 February 1000.

[The note identifies Rainald as the son of the late Berard, a count of Frankish origin in the duchy of Spoleto and count of the province of the Marsi, as he describes himself in a charter published from the register by Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 101. The place was near Tagliacozzo.]

Enriching it with substantial possessions round about, he also confirmed in the same monastery the castle now called Celle, then called the castle of Saint Angelo, with all its appurtenances.

[Another reading says “then called the castle of Saint Angelo”; the first edition has “which is now called Celle.”]

Likewise, a certain priest Peter of the city of Tivoli, concerning the church of Saint Pastor situated near that city, made in the same monastery, together with all his relatives, a charter of offering with all its appurtenances.

[The first edition and manuscript 1b expand the passage: “Peter of Tivoli, making a charter of offering in the same monastery concerning the church of Saint Pastor, with all its appurtenances situated near that church.”]

24. In the third year of this abbot, which was the thousandth year from the Incarnation of the Lord, the aforesaid emperor came to Benevento and, on account of the penance which blessed Romuald had imposed upon him, went to Mount Gargano.

[The Cassinese Annals, followed here, anticipate Otto’s arrival and death by one year. In inserting, apparently from Peter Damian’s *Life of Saint Romuald* and from Beneventan accounts, material based partly on conjecture, the annalist fell into more serious errors: Otto visited Gargano in 999. See Wilmans, *Jahrbücher Ottos III*, p. 106.]

Returning afterward to Benevento, he asked the citizens for the body of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle. They dared at that time to refuse him nothing. After taking counsel with the archbishop who then presided over the city, they craftily offered him, in place of the apostle’s body, the body of blessed Paulinus, bishop of Nola, which had been decently preserved in the episcopal residence of that city.

[The first edition and manuscript 1b expand this: “They showed him the body and offered it to him”; another reading has “they craftily offered him the body.”]

He took it away and departed, deceived by this fraud. When he learned of it, he was exceedingly indignant. He honorably placed the body of the confessor which he had carried off at the Island in Rome.

[The editor cites a note of Robert of Torigni under the year 1156. Di Meo, *Annali del Regno di Napoli*, under 1001, argues that the body of the apostle was not taken from the Beneventans.]

Then he immediately returned to Benevento and besieged it on every side for some time. But, accomplishing nothing against it, he returned to Rome (1001).

[Another reading says “for many days”; manuscript 1b and the first edition add that he “again went against Benevento and besieged it.”]

As he was preparing to return to his own lands, he died at the town called Paternum (23 January 1002), not far from the city called Castellana.

[One manuscript reads “Castellina”; another says “Castellana, where he died.” The note identifies the place as Città di Castello.]

He was, it is said, poisoned by the wife of Senator Crescentius, whom we reported above (Book II, chapter 17) as having been beheaded by him and with whom he had been having illicit intercourse.

[The words “as is reported” are absent in manuscript 1b; manuscript 4 reads “whom.”]

But before his death could be recognized by those living around him, his body, embalmed with spices, was carried by his followers beyond the mountains and buried. His cousin Duke Henry was made king.

[The Cassinese Annals say that he died at Sutri; the editor is unsure whether Leo corrected this from the *Life of Saint Romuald*.]

[Cancelled insertion in manuscript 1b: The aforesaid Ademarius, elated by great power, came to arrange affairs at Aquino. Adenulf Summucula, whom we mentioned above, fortified himself in the praetorium at Aquino and resolved not to receive him. It happened one day that, while Ademarius had left his camp and was walking beside the city to inspect it, Adenulf secretly went out with several of his men to reconnoiter the plain, and suddenly, unexpectedly, the one encountered the other.

When Adenulf, terrified by so unforeseen an encounter, took flight alone, Ademarius and his men began to pursue him. But when those who had been with Adenulf saw this, they attacked them all together from behind. Some of Ademarius’s men were killed, others were put to flight, and Ademarius was captured and brought into the city.

Adenulf then, beyond all expectation, placed him on a curule chair, urged him to fear nothing, and afterward, when the Gospels had been brought out, became his faithful man according to custom.

Recognizing Adenulf’s great goodness toward him—goodness which a captive could never have hoped for—Ademarius immediately issued him a charter concerning the whole lordship of Aquino and ordered that thereafter everyone should call him not gastald but count. Thus he was the first count of Aquino, and this was the first charter of the counts of Aquino.

Not long afterward, that is, four months later, Ademarius was expelled from the principality by the Capuans, and Landulf of Saint . . . The remainder has been cut away.]

25. This abbot made a great silver-gilt shrine with enamels and gems of various colors. He also made two great candlesticks weighing fifteen pounds of silver, as well as two silver censers weighing six pounds. He also produced several large and beautiful ecclesiastical books.

[The first edition reads “he renewed” rather than “he produced”; another manuscript reads “he made.”]

He fortified the entire circuit of the monastery with walls and towers.

He also built a church in honor of Saint Nicholas, confessor of Christ, on the little hill beside the lord’s meadow, near the city of Saint Germanus.

[The first edition expands “Saint Nicholas, confessor of Christ.” Another reading says that the meadow was “where there had formerly been a cemetery of the dead.”]

Emulating him, Theobald, his prior, likewise fitted out a basilica for the same blessed confessor, Saint Nicholas, near the castle of Saint Peter, which is situated at the foot of this mountain, in an ancient crypt. This crypt, apparently situated beside the church of the same blessed Peter, had been constructed of enormous stones in the beautiful workmanship of the Gentiles, in honor of their demons.

[The printed text has “which is seen situated beside the church of the same blessed Peter”; other readings have “which is situated” and “which he enlarged beside the church.” Compare above, Book I, chapter 5.]

At that time, namely in the eighth year of this abbot, a great earthquake shook this mountain for fifteen days and more, so that in several places it split the church.

Beyond all expectation Adenulf seated him on a curule chair, told him to fear nothing, and, after the Gospels were produced, became his faithful man according to custom. Recognizing Adenulf’s goodness, beyond anything a captive could have hoped for, Ademarius immediately granted him a charter over the entire lordship of Aquino and ordered everyone thereafter to call him count rather than gastald. Thus he was the first count of Aquino, and this was the first charter of Aquino’s counts. Four months later the Capuans expelled Ademarius from the principality, and Landulf of Saint ….” The remainder was cut away.
173. **0609** The first edition adds *gemmis diversorum colorum* (“gems of various colours”).
174. **0609** MSS 1 and 2 have the abbreviated *duo librarum quindecim* (“two [candlesticks] of fifteen pounds”).
175. **0609** MSS 1 and 2 read, in abbreviated form, *ecclesiasticos renovavit magnos* (“he renewed large ecclesiastical [books]”); MS 3 has *ecclesiasticos fecit magnos* (“he made large ecclesiastical [books]”).
176. **0609** The first edition reads *sancti confessoris Christi Nicolai* (“Saint Nicholas, confessor of Christ”).
177. **0609** MS 1, corrected by MS 1b, adds *pratum est ubi cymiterium defunctorum antiquitus fuerat* (“the meadow is where a cemetery of the dead had formerly been”), followed by *Quem* (“which”).
178. **0609** MS 1b and the first edition read *domnicum* for *dominicum* (“the lord’s”).
179. **0609** The first edition specifies *Nicolao* (“Nicholas”).
180. **0609** MS 1b adds the abbreviated *quod est positum ad radicem hujus montis* (“which is situated at the foot of this mountain”).
181. **0609** MS 1 reads *quae juxta ejusdem [beati Petri ecclesiam sita videtur]* (“which seems situated beside the church of that same blessed Peter”); MS 1b reads *ampliavit* (“he enlarged [it]”).
182. **0609** MS 1b and the first edition have the abbreviated *gentilium opere pulchro* (“in the beautiful workmanship of the pagans”).
183. **0609** MSS 1 and 2 omit *in demonum suorum honore* (“in honour of their demons”).
184. **0609** The first edition has the abbreviated *ejusdem beati Petri ecclesiam* (“the church of that same blessed Peter”).
185. **0609** MSS 1 and 2 read *est* (“is”) for *sita videtur* (“seems situated”).
186. **0610B** Compare Book I, chapter 5 above.

[Col. 0611A] **26. Rainald.** [Note: [Col. 0611] This abbot made an exchange with the aforesaid Rainald, count of the Marsi, concerning Saint Mary at Luco, Saint Erasmus, Saint Sebastian, and Saint Angelus; in return for these he received, in the territory of Alife, an estate called Saint Stephen’s, with four hundred modii of land, and at Teano five hundred modii in the place called Campus. Manuscript 1 lacks this passage.] Moreover, the aforesaid count of the Marsi gave this abbot, by way of exchange, an estate at Alife called Saint Stephen’s, with four hundred modii of land, and another at Teano, of five hundred modii, in a place called Campus; and he received from him a document concerning Saint Mary at Luco, Saint Erasmus, Saint Sebastian, and Saint Angelus.

**Oderisius.** [Note: [Col. 0611] This abbot made an exchange with Oderisius, count of the Marsi, concerning the castle of Saint Urban and other churches and estates in Comino belonging to us—amounting to about nine hundred modii [added in manuscript 1b]—in return for the town called Casa Fortini [added in manuscript 1b], which the aforesaid count, then holding it on his wife Gervisa’s side [added in manuscript 1b], surrendered to the same abbot with nine hundred modii of land [one thousand in manuscript 1b]. This … manuscript 1.] This count, likewise the son of the same Rainald, surrendered to the same abbot the town which is called Casa Fortini [Note: [Col. 0611] The edition reads “qui” rather than “quod.”] [Note: [Col. 0611] The edition reads “Casofortini.”] [Note: [Col. 0611C] On the Garigliano, near Bantra.] with all its appurtenances—namely, a thousand modii of land—which the same count had received on the side of his wife Gervisa [Note: [Col. 0611] “Then held” in manuscript 2]; and in exchange he received from him the castle of Saint Urban and other churches or estates in Comino belonging to this place, [Col. 0611B] amounting to about nine hundred modii of land [Note: [Col. 0611] The amount is lacking in manuscript 4]. [Note: [Col. 0611] Manuscript 1b adds the text from “This same Oderisius” to the end of the chapter.]

In the last year of this abbot, this same Oderisius, together with his wife Gibborga, offered to this monastery the church of Saint Felix in Comino [Note: [Col. 0611] The phrase is lacking in manuscript 4.] [Note: [Col. 0614A] “Which formerly belonged to Saint Angelus of Barregio,” adds manuscript 2], an appurtenance of Saint Urban, with one hundred modii of land around it and another hundred at Atina [Note: [Col. 0611] Manuscripts 1b and 2 read “Atinum”], in the place called Vallis Bona, together with all the appurtenances of the same church [Note: [Col. 0611] “Appurtenances. Through these days also [came] Hubertus,” manuscript 1b] (May 1010).

[Note: [Col. 0611C] Daughter of Marquis Trasmund, as he himself says in a charter in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 327. A. de Nuce testifies that this offering was recorded in Peter’s Register, made at Comino in the year 1010 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the month of May, indiction VIII.]

At the same time three of our monks went to Walter, count of Lesina, and in his presence disputed with certain nobles of that territory [Note: [Col. 0611] “Of that territory” in the edition] concerning the fisheries of Lesina itself, the mills of Lauri, the church of Saint Peter there, and the other possessions of Saint Benedict, as was contained in their petition. When the aforesaid count had recognized the justice of our case, he ordered by his written instrument that all these things be restored in full to our monks [Note: [Col. 0611] “In full to our monks” in the edition], adding a penalty of two thousand bezants against anyone who should thereafter wish to contend with us further.

During these same days Hubert, bishop of the city of Fermo, offered to blessed Benedict, from the property lawfully his own, at the estate of Oppiano lands and vineyards, woods, meadows [Col. 0612A] and olive-groves—a considerable possession—and likewise at the estate of Paterno. Moreover, a certain Gaiderisius [Note: [Col. 0611] The edition reads “Gald”; in manuscript 1 the upper part of this line is cut away.] of that same city of Fermo made a charter in this monastery concerning one church belonging to him, called Saint Benedict, in the place called Sambucetum, with its property and appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0611C] Register, no. 248. ANG.].

Landulf, prince of Salerno, having become a monk under this abbot, offered to this monastery all the property belonging to him by hereditary right in the county of Saint Agatha (December 1004): namely, houses [Note: [Col. 0611] Manuscripts 1b and the edition read “houses” in the plural] and several estates, with olive-groves, vineyards, mills, and all their appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0611C] “In the sixth year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the reign of the glorious Prince Landulf, in the month of December, indiction III. Therefore I, Landulf, prince of the city of Salerno and now a monk in the monastery of Saint Benedict of the castle of Cassino, offer, etc.” He promised a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold bezants if he should act contrary to this. Register, no. 243.].

**Trasmund** [Note: [Col. 0611] “Moreover, Trasmund the count,” manuscript 1b and the edition. The edition and Peter’s Register read “Transmundus.”] also, a wealthy and noble cleric of Abruzzo [Note: [Col. 0612C] Son of Giso.
