Gattola published, from the Register, the charter which he ordered to be drawn up with his wife Armelda, daughter of Count Hugh: *Historia*, p. 196], whom we have already mentioned above (ch. 13), established as a monastery the church of Saint Nicholas, which is built beside the River Trutinus [Note: [Col. 0612C] Now the Tronto], in the place called Sumusianus, enriched with his possessions; and by a charter of his offering surrendered it under the jurisdiction of this cenobium (December 1004).

Likewise Teuto, son of Teuto, from the same Abruzzo, offered to this monastery (August 1005) the church of Saint John in the place called Scorzone [Note: [Col. 0612C] On a solitary mountain in the territory of Abruzzo. Gattola, *Historia*, p. 203, where he published the charter]; which he himself, enriched with his own possessions, had made into a monastery of nuns.

In the same manner Rainerius, son of Joseph, offered to blessed Benedict a church belonging to him, called Saint Nicholas, in the county of Penne, at the place called Sambuceta, with all its furnishings and appurtenances. This Rainerius, about six years earlier (July 1001), had made a charter [Note: [Col. 0611] Manuscripts 1b and 2 read “charter”] in this monastery concerning absolutely all the property and appurtenances of his estate which he appeared to possess in the counties of Penne, Chieti [Note: [Col. 0611] Manuscript 1b and the edition add “or Chieti”], Ascoli, and Abruzzo [Note: [Col. 0612C] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 102]: namely, the castles of Ambleto and Pharaone, and Murro [Note: [Col. 0611] Manuscripts 1b and the edition add “and Cantalupo, and Aterno, and Arche”], Cantalupo, Aterno, and Arche, and many of his estates—about eight thousand modii of land [Note: [Col. 0611] Added by manuscript 4].

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0611] “At the same time. In the time of Manson, abbot, etc., as above in ch. 13 … they ordered,” manuscript 1b. “Around these days Franco,” manuscript 1b.] the citizens of Terracina [Col. 0613A], instructed by John their bishop, offered in the monastery of Saint Stephen at Terracina (3 January 986) a fishery extending from the river of that city itself [Note: [Col. 0613] “Of the aforesaid city,” in the edition], at the place called Gambara, to the sea, imposing a penalty of three pounds of refined gold upon those who might in any way attempt to remove it [Note: [Col. 0613] The edition omits: “against those who should attempt to remove it in any way”]. Likewise Roffridus [Note: [Col. 0613] Manuscript 3 reads “Rofrithus”], the patrician, offered there a fishery of his own in the aforesaid river of Terracina, in the marsh called Trasectu [Note: [Col. 0613] “In the marsh of Trasectu, in the first part of the [river], from the [place] of Terracina,” in the edition].

[Note: [Col. 0612C] “In the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope in the most holy see of blessed Peter … indiction XIV, in the month of January, on the third day [a Sunday], in the first year of the reign, John, son of Crescentius the Roman patrician.” Gattola, *Historia*, p. 115, from Peter’s Register.]

Around these days a certain Franco, priest and monk, made a charter in this monastery concerning a church belonging to his own property, called Saint Benedict, in the territory of Monticelli, at the place Salabuca beside the Biferno, with all its property and appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0613] A small portion is cut away in manuscript 1b; it continues: “with Tresidius,” below].

To this abbot Lupus, son of Azzo of Abruzzo, made an offering [Col. 0613B] of all his property, with five churches: Saint Victoria at Murro, Saint Callistus at Colle, Saint Anthimus at Commejano [Note: [Col. 0613] “Comiano” in manuscripts 1b and 4; “Comelano” in the edition], Saint Archangel at Fauniano [Note: [Col. 0613] “Faumario” in manuscript 2], and Saint Andrew at Cesule; with about five hundred modii of land, and with absolutely all property belonging to him throughout Abruzzo.

Adam, also [Note: [Col. 0613] “Likewise” in manuscript 1b and the edition], surnamed Salichus [Note: [Col. 0613C] He was of Frankish stock, as his charter, no. 300, reports. ANG.], offered to this monastery the church of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0613] Manuscript 1b and the edition read: “one church belonging to him, called Saint Martin”] in the territory of Chieti, at the place called Cornecclanum, with one hundred modii of land around the same church and with its remaining appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0613] “Its appurtenances. Likewise he offered all his property,” manuscript 1b; the rest is cut away, but only a little. “This abbot … rent of eight solidi” seems to have been lost].

This abbot made a lease concerning Saint Bonitus [Note: [Col. 0613] “And its appurtenances,” added by the edition], Saint Angelus of Galiano, Saint Savior of Seriole, Saint Peter of Castriniano, Saint Felix of Montaniano, Saint Felix between the rivers, Saint Valentine, and Saint Mary at Aufiano [Note: [Col. 0613] “Ausano” in manuscript 2; “Caufiano” in manuscript 3], for four hundred *selidi* [solidi], and an annual rent of twenty solidi.

He did the same with Otteramus, gastald [Note: [Col. 0613] The edition reads “gastaldus”] of the Marsi, concerning Saint Clement at Avezzano, for one hundred solidi, and an annual rent of five *stamincae* [Note: [Col. 0614C] A woolen undergarment or shirt which certain monks used in place of a hair-shirt. Du Cange].

Likewise, concerning Saint Gregory of Serviliano, for thirty solidi and an annual rent of one hundred fish. Likewise, concerning the same place, an annual rent of four hundred fish.

He also made a lease to a certain monk named Trasari, concerning Saint Benedict at Canusio, Saint Savior at Monorbino [Note: [Col. 0613] “Menorbino, in the place Strajuniano,” manuscript 2], Saint Benedict at Juvenaze [Note: [Col. 0613] Manuscript 3 lacks “at”] [Note: [Col. 0613] “Juvenazze, in the place Orosano,” manuscript 2], and Saint Focas at Barano [Note: [Col. 0614A] The edition reads “Focatus.” [Note: [Col. 0614C] Perhaps Varano; compare above, book I, ch. 34]; together with the fishery of Lake Romani [Note: [Col. 0613] “The fishery at Lauromari,” manuscript 3], Saint Cassian at Filone, and all the appurtenances of this place in the city of Trani, together with all the appurtenances of those churches [Note: [Col. 0613] “Likewise” in the edition].

He did the same for the sons of Adelbert [Note: [Col. 0613] “Adelpertus” in manuscript 3] of Papiniano [Note: [Col. 0613] “Papinlano” in the edition], concerning four hundred modii [Note: [Col. 0613] “Four hundred modia” in the edition] of land in Abruzzo, for two hundred solidi and an annual rent of eight solidi.

He also made an exchange with a certain Tresidius of Chieti, receiving from him the church of Saint Lucy at Castellone, in the place called Insula, with all the property of that church [Note: [Col. 0613] “Of the same church,” manuscript 1b] and one hundred modii of land; and he gave him, in various places near Chieti, seventy modii of land [Note: [Col. 0613] “Seventy modia”; “to this Lupus, etc., see above,” manuscript 1b].

[Col. 0614B] **27.** [Note: [Col. 0614B] Moreover, at this time, after Pope Sergius IV had died (1012), Benedict VIII, a Tusculan by birth [Note: [Col. 0614C] This is also stated in Peter’s catalogue], son of Gregory, was ordained Roman pontiff. Added in manuscript 2.] During the same period [Note: [Col. 0613] “During the same period … one hundred” from John I, abbot, where these words are written in the margin and summoned here by signs; manuscript 1b] a monastery of Saint Benedict was built near Sessa, outside the gate called Ermemari [Note: [Col. 0613] “Hermerari” in manuscript 4], by Lord John, a monk of this place [Note: [Col. 0613] “John the priest and monk,” manuscripts 1b and 2]. There the aforesaid abbot granted all the estates and lands of this monastery that lie within the county of the aforesaid city, at the place Oronica, and the estates of Lota Alfani, as well as the estates on the Garigliano belonging to them, and the lands and estate of Lauriana [Note: [Col. 0613] The words from “the estates” through “estate” are lacking in manuscript 2; manuscript 1b corrects “estates” to “lands and estate”]. Only on this condition: that every year a rent of one hundred modii of beans should be paid to us from that same estate of Lauriana.

[Col. 0614C] **28.** [Note: [Col. 0613] “But that abbot himself,” manuscript 1. “The aforesaid abbot,” edition.] The abbot himself, while suffering many hardships from neighboring counts, withdrew for a time to Capua [Note: [Col. 0613] “The abbot, after enduring many hardships from various counts, when he was already advanced in years, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends, etc.,” manuscript 1; “changed and enlarged,” manuscript 1b]. Since he had been more than sufficiently severe toward the monks, and had sought, contrary to Benedict’s rule, to be feared by the brethren rather than loved, they thought—or rather hoped—that he would not return here again. They installed in his place as abbot a certain Docibilis, a Caetan by nationality and a man of simple life, from their own congregation [Note: [Col. 0613] Added by manuscript 4].

When he had gone into the March, as abbots customarily do, to inspect the monastery’s possessions, and was already returning with several horses and other considerable gifts given to him there [Note: [Col. 0615] The edition reads “having been given”], certain sons of Benzo, magnates of that region, suddenly attacked him near Penne and violently plundered everything he was carrying. When Count Bernard learned this, he immediately came to him and, showing himself greatly grieved by the matter [Note: [Col. 0615] Lacking in manuscript 4], generously restored to him as many horses as had been taken away.

When the same abbot came to the place called Furca Pennensis, he turned and cursed all the sons of Benzo; but blessing Bernard and all his people [Note: [Col. 0615] Manuscript 1b and the edition read “all his people”], he pronounced this terrible imprecation: that the house of Benzo should always be subject to Bernard’s house, and that divine vengeance [Note: [Col. 0615] “The sword of God’s wrath,” manuscripts 1b and the edition] should never depart from his house. We see this indeed happening even today.

But when, after seven incomplete months, Abbot John had returned here with matters settled and put in order [Note: [Col. 0615] “Returned,” manuscripts 1b and the edition], Docibilis went to Gaeta; and not long afterward, seized by illness, he asked to be brought back to this monastery [Note: [Col. 0615] “To be brought back to the monastery,” manuscripts 1b and the edition], where he died a peaceful death. Abbot John too, being now advanced in years, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March] [Note: [Col. 0615C] In 1011, as the charter of Oderisius cited in chapter 26 and the beginning of chapter 31 prove], and was buried beside the church of blessed Benedict [Note: [Col. 0615] Added by manuscript 4].

**29.** In the year in which he died, he had made a monk of a certain nephew of his, John surnamed Rotundulus [Note: [Col. 0615] “Rotundulus, made a monk not many days earlier”; “whom, when he was already near death, he made a monk,” manuscripts 1b and 2; “Rotundulus, whom he made a monk,” manuscript 3], and, as he came to his death, entrusted the abbacy to him [Note: [Col. 0615] “He appointed [him] in the abbacy,” manuscript 1 and the edition], with very few monks consenting to this, or rather with the monks enduring it under compulsion.

But the sounder and more substantial part of them [Note: [Col. 0615] “The wiser,” manuscript 2], taking this very ill and judging a novice entirely unfit to govern so great a community, after several months [Note: [Col. 0615] “Thus” in manuscript 1b; “not many days” in manuscript 1] sent word to Pandulf, prince of Benevento, to come and bring his son Atenulf to be appointed their abbot; for no one was more entitled than he to the honor of this place [Note: [Col. 0615] “Atenulf, abbot, to be appointed; no one,” manuscript 1].

When Emperor Otto had taken this Atenulf, still a boy, as a hostage from his father, he had ordered him to be brought up and kept in a monastery beyond the mountains. After some time, warned by his pope [Note: [Col. 0615] “So that he might flee without suspicion of any escape,” manuscript 1b and the edition], he put on monastic clothing and escaped. On the journey back he became gravely ill, and vowed thereafter of his own will to wear the cowl which, for the sake of escape, he had put on only as a pretense [Note: [Col. 0615] “On his return, Atenulf, having been a hostage beyond the mountains, became very ill and was made a monk. And this was done. Rotundulus …,” manuscript 1b]. Thus, returning to his father, he would not consent to be kept by him at court, and stayed until that time in the monastery of Saint Modestus, situated within the city of Benevento [Note: [Col. 0615] “In that same city of Benevento,” manuscript 1b; “near the episcopal residence,” manuscripts 1b and 2].

The prince, therefore, delighted by the news brought to him [Note: [Col. 0615] “By the news restored to him,” manuscript 4], came immediately to Cassino and, with the consent and assistance of the monks, expelled Rotundulus and entrusted his son to them to be installed in the abbacy, to the joy of all [Note: [Col. 0615] The text in manuscript 1b is cut off after “the consent and assistance of the monks … entrusted”].

Rotundulus, thus expelled [Note: [Col. 0615] “Therefore” in manuscript 1 and the edition], returned to Benevento; and through the support of his relatives and by the consent and grant of the aforesaid prince, received the abbacy of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Modestus [Col. 0616B] [Note: [Col. 0615] “Saint Modestus, which is situated within the same city of Benevento,” added by manuscript 1; deleted in manuscript 1b].

[Note: [Col. 0616B] In this year there was a severe famine, and salt failed. Thus the *Anonymous of Cassino* for 1011; the *Chronicle of Fossanova* for 1013; Atenulf’s charter, given in August 1011, is found in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 122.]

**30.** [Note: [Col. 0615] The chapter is added in manuscript 1b, after material previously written in seven lines was erased.] Around this time Lord Liutius returned. We have related above (ch. 12) that he had departed from here during the time of Abbot Manso and gone to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0615] “We showed,” manuscript 1b and the edition]. At first, near Salerno [Note: [Col. 0615] “In the principality of Salerno,” manuscripts 1b and 2], he remained for some time in a certain hermitage where the monastery of the Holy Trinity, called La Cava, is now known to have been built [Note: [Col. 0615] “Where the monastery of the Holy Trinity, called La Cava, is now known to have been built,” added by manuscript 1c and the edition]. There he was recognized by Prince Guaimar and held in the greatest reverence. Afterwards, on this mountain, at the place called Albaneta, he lived most devoutly until his death.

In this place, not long before, when a certain servant of God had chosen for himself a more secluded dwelling and had decided to build an oratory in an old cistern which he had found ruined there, he was considering in whose particular name he should build the church. It is said that a certain schoolboy happened then by chance to come there [Note: [Col. 0615] “To have come there unexpectedly,” manuscript 1b]. When the aforesaid man of God asked him whether he knew the art of singing, and he readily answered that he did, the man ordered him to sing whatever first came into his mind; for he had determined in his heart that, in honor of whatever saint the boy sang, he would immediately build the church in that saint’s name [Note: [Col. 0615] “Having determined in his heart,” manuscript 1b and the edition].

At once the boy began the responsory: “Come, my chosen one,” and sang the whole of it in a very sweet melody. The servant of God was greatly gladdened [Note: [Col. 0617] “The man of God,” manuscript 1b and the edition], and understood in some way that it pleased the most blessed Mother of God for her title to be honored in that place [Note: [Col. 0617] “To please,” manuscript 2]. He immediately built there, according to his modest means, a small church in honor of that same Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0617] “Built,” manuscript 1b and the edition], and remained there until his end, very devout in her service.

When, after some time, the aforesaid Liutius came there [Note: [Col. 0617] “Lord Liutius,” manuscript 1b], and the place pleased him greatly, he chose to remain there until death and persevere in the service of the holy Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0617] “In the service of God and his Mother,” manuscript 1b; “in the service of God, the Mother of God herself,” the edition].

He therefore returned to Prince Guaimar, to whom he had long been both spiritual father and intimate above all others [Note: [Col. 0617] “Guaimar, son of the aforesaid Guaimar,” manuscripts 1b and 2]. From him he obtained many and various ecclesiastical ornaments, a number of books [Note: [Col. 0617] “Very many,” manuscript 1b and the edition], and also a considerable amount of other equipment for the use of the brethren, Guaimar most willingly and generously allowing him to take whatever he wished.

He immediately made the aforesaid church of the Mother of God much larger than it had been [Note: [Col. 0617] “Larger in every respect than it was,” manuscript 1b], and decorated it with paintings; he also built around it dwellings of substantial size for the various uses of those living there [Note: [Col. 0617] “For their use,” manuscript 2]. There he began to live most religiously with about thirty brethren [Note: [Col. 0617] “To live religiously,” manuscript 1b and the edition].

He himself, more than the others content with every form of lowliness and hardship, had given himself to such humble work that, in the manner of servants, he sifted flour in the bakery for making bread [Note: [Col. 0617] “Shook out” or “sifted,” manuscript 1b], while Davidic songs never ceased from his lips [Note: [Col. 0617] “While the melody never ceased from his mouth,” manuscript 1b]. Persevering tirelessly to the end of his life in this humility of life and excessive austerity of abstinence, he died and was buried in this monastery during the time of Abbot Richerius.

**ATENULF, thirty-first abbot, ruled for eleven years: a man as humble and gracious as he was noble.**

**31.** [Note: [Col. 0617] “His,” etc., manuscript 1b and the edition. “In the second [corrected to ‘first’] year of his ordination there was a severe famine and salt failed; three years later Henry …,” manuscript 1, corrected in manuscript 1b.] In the third year of his ordination, namely in the year of the Lord 1014, when Easter fell, according to the reckoning, on the very day of Saint Mark, King Henry, of whom we have spoken above (ch. 24), came to Rome and received the imperial crown from the hands of Pope Benedict VIII. From that same pope the abbot also received a privilege [Note: [Col. 0617C] See Tosti, vol. I, p. 246].

At that time Emperor Henry himself, at the request of the same abbot and the entire community of this place [Note: [Col. 0617] “And with the intervention of Empress Cunigunda,” added by manuscript 1b], confirmed by a precept sealed with a golden bull all the possessions of this monastery [Note: [Col. 0617C] Tosti published the charter, given at Rome in 1014 without date, p. 249; but it was obtained neither through the intervention of the empress nor with a golden bull].

In particular and by name, he confirmed the property in the county of Termoli [Note: [Col. 0617C] In Register privilege 135, enacted at Chieti in 1022, indiction IV, on the Kalends of February. See also Register 131, in the appendix to Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 120. Here, however, privileges granted earlier seem to be intended], whose boundaries are: at the head, Rivus Planus; at the foot, the sea; on one side, the River Trigno, with its water and harbor; on the other, the stream called Ticcle [Note: [Col. 0617] “Tiale” in manuscript 3]; together with the castles of Petra Fracida and Ripa Mala, and the monastery of Saint Benedict built there. Likewise Fara, Ripa Ursa, Mons Bellus, Pescloli, with all their boundaries and appurtenances.

Likewise, elsewhere in the same county beside the Biferno, [the property] has these boundaries: at the head, the possessions of Saint Gregory; at the foot, the sea; on one side, the Biferno, with its water and half its harbor; on the other, the stream called Vivus [Note: [Col. 0617] “Which is called,” added by manuscript 4], with all its adjoining property; and also the church of the Holy Trinity and Saint George in the same city of Termoli, with all their possessions and appurtenances.

He also confirmed, by another precept [Note: [Col. 0617] “Moreover, at the request of his archbishop Pilgrim, two castles,” manuscript 1; “Moreover, also two castles,” the edition], the two castles in the territory of Comino, namely Vicalbum [Note: [Col. 0617] “Vicum Album,” manuscript 2] and Saint Urban [Note: [Col. 0618C] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 104. I sought in vain the precept concerning the monastery of Saint Valentine which *Historia*, p. 205, says he promised to issue.], after he had returned from beyond the mountains [Note: [Col. 0617] “After he had returned from beyond the mountains,” manuscript 1b], at the request of Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, in favor of this monastery (13 July 1018) [Note: [Col. 0617] The words “at the request of Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne” are lacking in manuscripts 1 and 2].

Some time previously, after his father’s death, Pandulf, prince of Capua, had issued a precept to the aforesaid abbot, his brother, concerning these places (5 May 1017, indiction IX) [Note: [Col. 0617] “Which, indeed, after his father’s death, Pandulf, prince, his brother, had made for the same abbot,” manuscript 1 and the edition], and likewise concerning the monastery of Saint Valentine in the same territory of Comino, with all its property and appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0617] “With all its property and appurtenances,” added by manuscript 1b]. That monastery, formerly destroyed by the Saracens [Note: [Col. 0617] “Destroyed long ago,” manuscript 1b and the edition], had not long before been restored by a certain Pontius [Note: [Col. 0617] “Ponzo,” manuscript 1b], son of Allo, from the county of the Marsi. When it had been represented to him that it had formerly belonged to this monastery, he restored it, as it had been rebuilt, wholly to the right and authority of this place for the love of God [Note: [Col. 0619] Manuscript 1b continues here: “At this time an offering was made,” ch. 32].

This Pontius, together with his son Berard [Note: [Col. 0619] “Bernard” in manuscript 2], also declared and renounced in our favor, in the court of the counts of the Marsi, the entire appurtenance of Opi and Peraccle in the territory of the Marsi, which had formerly belonged to the monastery of Barregio [Note: [Col. 0619] “Which formerly belonged to Saint Angelus of Barregio,” the edition].

**32.** [Note: [Col. 0619] Manuscript 1 places this sentence at the end of the chapter.] This abbot made for the church of Saint Benedict a silver crown weighing twenty-four pounds. He also built at the front of the same church a tall and excellent bell-tower [Note: [Col. 0619] “He also made a bell-tower,” manuscripts 1 and 2], in the middle of which he established an altar in honor of the Holy Cross [Note: [Col. 0619] “Built,” the edition].

Moreover, beside the door of the principal church, on the right and left, above marble columns, he erected two vaulted chambers. In one he established an altar in honor of the Holy Trinity; in the other he established an altar dedicated to Saint Bartholomew the Apostle. He caused the principal apse to be most beautifully painted with gold and various colors.

He restored and enlarged the church of Saint Stephen, which had stood outside beside the monastery gate and was already almost collapsing [Note: [Col. 0619] “The church of Saint Stephen, which was situated outside the monastery gate … an altar of Saint Adalbert,” manuscript 1], and added to it on the western side an altar of Saint Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0619] “An altar in it,” the edition], whom we said above (ch. 17) had become a martyr [Note: [Col. 0619] “He began also to paint the same church. He ordered the book of Saint Ambrose on Luke to be copied,” manuscript 1].

He built to a great extent the lower town around the church of the Lord Savior, which we mentioned above (book I, ch. 33) as having been begun by Abbot Bertharius [Note: [Col. 0619] “Which, as we said, was begun by the blessed martyr Abbot Bertharius, and is now called San Germano,” added by the edition; manuscript 1b reads: “He himself first began to make it, and built a large part of it,” with corrections and deletions].

[Note: [Col. 0619C] He also restored in the territory of the city of Atina the monastery of Saint Nazarius the martyr, which had formerly belonged to our cenobium. Prince Pandulf attests this in a charter in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 205; see below, ch. 51. Added by manuscript 2.]

The church of Saint Angelus, which Abbot Gisulf had formerly built in Valleluce [Note: [Col. 0619C] Compare book I, ch. 17], he restored when it was already old; enlarging it by adding a title [Note: [Col. 0619] Manuscript 1b reads “enlarged with many possessions into a monastery”], decorating it with paintings, and enriching it with substantial possessions [Note: [Col. 0619] The edition reads “endowed it”]. He also established there various workshops for the monks’ needs and made it a monastery of our own monks, although until then it had belonged to Greeks [Note: [Col. 0619] Namely, to Nilus and his companions, who had moved to Grottaferrata. ANG.].

[Col. 0620A] Under this abbot (18 April 1015), the church of Saint Peter called *Ad Iscleta*, in Campania, in the territory of Ceccano, was offered to this monastery, together with very extensive possessions around it, by Hubert and Amatus, counts of Ceccano and Segni.

[Note: [Col. 0619] “At this time” is in witness 1b; “second”; “here the chapter begins” in witness 1b. The following material was written in the margin at a different time.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “In this monastery” is in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0619C] Now Ceccano and Segni. “I, Hubert, count, son of Lord Leo, count, and of Lady Sergia, most illustrious woman, together with my wife Lady Constantia, jointly with Lord Count Amatus and Lady Maria, spouses,” in a charter in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 416, dated in the third year of Benedict VIII, indiction IX (13?).]

The church of Saint Angel in the territory of Ceprano, at the place called Cannuzzu, was likewise offered by Landuin and Raterius, consuls of Campania.

[Note: [Col. 0619] *Canuzzu* in witness 2; *Cannuzo* in witness 3; *Cannuzu, with all its appurtenances and boundaries* in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] *Racterio* in witness 2; *Ratherio* in witness 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0620C] “From the city of Berula,” says their charter, no. 273. ANG.]

A certain priest named Saphirus also offered this monastery the church of Saint Benedict at Capitignano, in the city of Murrone, together with all its possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0619] “A certain Saphirus,” added in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “The church of his own lawful property, called Saint Benedict,” in witness 1b; “that one,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “With all his things and appurtenances,” omitted in witness 1b and the edition.]

Peter and Martin, priests, likewise offered blessed Benedict the church of Saint Mary and Saint Apollinaris in the same Murrone,

[Col. 0620B] at the place called Casale Planum.

[Note: [Col. 0619] “Morrone” in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “Peter, priest and monk, and Martin, priest and monk,” in witnesses 1b and 2; “Peter, priest, and Martin, priest,” in witness 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “Saint Mary and Saint Apollinaris, likewise there at Murrone,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “With all the things belonging to it,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

Odemund, a certain man of Fermo, did the same with the church of Saint Michael of Torpelliano.

[Note: [Col. 0619] The material from “This same thing” through “Torpelliano” is absent from witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “This same thing was done”; the edition omits these words.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] *Odmundus* in witness 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] *Torpelleniano* in witness 3; “Torpelliano, with all its appurtenances,” in the edition. The grants of Faidolf, Temmo, and Oderisius follow: “Faidolf” in witness 1b; “Faidolf (Leo), Temmo, and Oderisius” in the edition.]

At the same time, in the same manner, the church of Saint Justa near Baranello, beside the Biferno, was offered to this monastery; likewise another church of Saint Justa near the castle of Eudolinus; the church of Saint Andrew of Cantalupo in the territory of Boiano; and also the monastery of Saint Benedict and the church of Saint Lucy near the castle of Baniolum, at the place called Old Mill; the church of Saint Mary of the Cross; and also the church of Saint Benedict in Abruzzo, with all their extensive properties and appurtenances.

[Note: [Col. 0619] “Baranello castle, that is, the river Baranello,” in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “Likewise” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “Eudolinus, from the rock of Saint Angel,” in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0620C] The monastery was later called “of the White Horse.” It exists in the territory of Civitanova, in the diocese of Trivento. Gattola, *Historia*, p. 207.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] The words from “near” through “blessed” are cut off in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “The church of the Cross, with very extensive ecclesiastical property and possessions. At the place called Tribio (Trivio in witness 3), there is likewise the church of Saint Benedict, with all its possessions,” in the edition. The grants of Rainerius, Albo (Adelpertus, Lupus), and Stephanus follow in witness 1b and the edition.]

(At the same time, January 1020) Stephen and Sylvester, priests of Larino, also offered in this place their church called Saint Mary, at the place called Monumentum.

[Note: [Col. 0619] *Bojanensi* in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “The church of Larino” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0619] “With all its appurtenances” is added in the edition.]

A certain nobleman from the province of the Marsi, namely Faidolf, son of Guelton, handed over to this place all the property belonging to him by right which he appeared to possess in that province, and two churches belonging to him: the church of Saint Thomas at Betuge and that of Saint Magnus at Castuli, with all their appurtenances and possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Faidolf,” added in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] *Betuie* in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0621C] “Leo, also, a priest and monk from the territory of Boiano, together with his other brothers, offered in this place the church of Saint Saviour and Saint Christopher of the castle of Petroso, with some of their possessions,” added in witness 2.]

Temmo, son of Teudelasius, likewise offered the church of Saint Felix at Carrufe to this monastery, with all its appurtenances.

[Note: [Col. 0621] The material from “Likewise” through “had received” is absent from witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Also” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] *Teudelasii* in witness 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “In this manuscript” is absent from the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “At the same time, the aforesaid,” in the edition.]

At that time (June 1012), the aforesaid Oderisius, count of the Marsi, together with his wife Gibborga, restored to blessed Benedict the church of Saint Paul situated in Comino, which his father had received from Abbot Manso by a *libellus*.

[Note: [Col. 0621C] Ch. 26. The charter appears in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 327, where Oderisius is said to be of Frankish origin and an inhabitant of the castle of Victualbus.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “They restored,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621C] Compare Book II, ch. 13.]

At the same time Rainerius, gastald of the city of Sora, offered blessed Benedict, from the goods of his inheritance in the territory of Arpino, the place called Collis de Insula, with all the adjacent lands and appurtenances of that place.

[Note: [Col. 0621] *Colles* in witnesses 1b and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Under this abbot, R.” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “At the same time Rainerius,” in the edition.]

A certain Albo of Abruzzo offered to this monastery (November 1020) the entire half of the castle of Saline belonging to him by hereditary right, together with the churches and all the appurtenances of those churches; this amounted to approximately seven hundred *modii* of land.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “By hereditary right,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “And all the churches and absolutely all the possessions and appurtenances,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Of the churches and of the aforesaid half,” in witnesses 1b and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Seven hundred *modia*,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621C] “Stephen also …” after three leaves in witness 1b. But I found nothing except what is read in ch. 26 concerning Lupus, son of Azzo. From there witness 1 continues: “This abbot …,” at the beginning of the chapter.]

Adelpert, son of a certain Azzo, did the same with his estates and portions in Abruzzo, namely, with two castles and several churches, together with four hundred *modii* of land.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “His, of the two castles in Abruzzo,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621C] In the same place, p. 109, dated November 1021, indiction III.]

Lupus, also of Abruzzo, did the same with the portions which he possessed in four churches: Saint Victoria, Saint Antimus, Saint Archangel, and Saint Andrew, together with a shore, his own fishing-ground in the sea, and five thousand *modii* of land.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “He did the same: Lupus (son of a certain Azzo, added in witness 2), of Abruzzo, likewise did this with his portions in the four churches, namely Saint Victoria, and so forth,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] The edition omits “and.”]

[Col. 0621C] 33. At the same time, certain monks coming from Jerusalem brought with them a piece of the linen cloth with which the Saviour wiped the disciples’ feet; and, out of reverence for this holy place, they most devoutly offered it here, on the sixth day before the Ides of December—that is, 8 December.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “At that time,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “The sixth day before the Ides of December,” added in witness 1b.]

But since many people placed no faith in this, they, trusting in faith, immediately placed the aforesaid piece upon the fire of a lighted incense-burner. It was at once transformed into the colour of fire, but shortly afterward, when the coals had been removed, it miraculously returned to its former appearance.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “No faith was placed in this,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “They,” added in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Which was lighted,” added in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “At once,” added in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “But after a little while,” added in witness 1b.]

When our brethren were considering how, or in what place, they should deposit so great a relic, it happened by divine providence that on that very day a wondrous casket was sent to this place by a certain noble Englishman. It is the casket in which the piece of the holy linen is now kept, delicately and most beautifully decorated in English workmanship with silver, gold, and jewels. Thus, with crystal placed over it, and the relic visibly enclosed, it was placed there with sufficient reverence.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “What they should do, or in what place they should put the relic,” in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] The words “from a certain noble Englishman” are absent from witnesses 1 and 2 and are added in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “To this place,” in witness 1, corrected in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Gold and jewels,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “And,” variant reading.]

It is the custom every year, on that very day of the Lord’s Supper, during the *mandatum* of the brethren—that is, the washing of the feet—

[Note: [Col. 0622C] Washing of the feet.]

for it to be brought by the mansionarii and placed in the midst, for two candelabra to be lit before it, and for it to be incensed without interruption by an acolyte throughout the entire duration of the *mandatum*. Finally, near the end of the *mandatum*, it is most devoutly adored by each brother in turn, with knees bent, and, after being adored, is reverently kissed.

[Note: [Col. 0621] The material from “and it is the custom” through “to kiss” is absent from witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “And, after being adored,” added in witness 4.]

34. Moreover, when the same abbot had received from his aforesaid brother, Prince Pandulf, a decree concerning the monastery of Barrea, together with all its boundaries, possessions, and appurtenances (10 May 1017), he promptly took care to send there a very religious brother of this congregation, named Azzo, so that he might devote himself to its restoration and reconciliation.

[Note: [Col. 0622C] Gattola, *Historia*, p. 125.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “With its boundaries, possessions, and appurtenances,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

For from the time when the Saracens, defeated and driven out by the Marsi and Peligni, withdrew there and protected themselves for some time because the place was strongly fortified with very lofty buildings, they themselves were burned together with the monastery by those who pursued them. The monks thereafter fled in different directions, and, as forests sprang up everywhere, the place became so entirely desolate and uninhabitable that scarcely a few brothers were willing to remain for any length of time beside the small old church which had escaped the fire, out of love for that venerable place.

[Note: [Col. 0622C] “Or rather Hungarians?” See above, Book I, ch. 55. Desiderius calls them Saracens in *Dialogue* II, 6, where he touched briefly upon this matter.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “And remained there,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Since the place itself,” added in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] *By them* in witness 1; *by those* in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Utterly desolate,” in witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Very few brothers,” in witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Very few indeed,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “Ancient,” added in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] “For any length of time,” added in witness 4.]

At that time the aforesaid Azzo was provost

[Col. 0623A]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Provost of the cell of that monastery of Barrea,” in witness 1, corrected in witness 1b.]

of the monastery of Saint Benedict in the district of the Marsi,

[Note: [Col. 0623C] Also called Saint Benedict in Venere, in the city of the Marsi and at Morro, near Lake Fucino. Gattola, *Historia*, p. 211.]

which at that time was richly endowed throughout the Marsi with cells, estates, lands, and various tenants in different places.

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Which was originally called Saint Mary Asprandana; now, from the name of the greater church constructed in the same place, it is called Saint Benedict of Marsia,” in witness 1.]

Since we have now come to this point, we shall briefly mention some of them. The cell of Saint Benedict at Auretino, with five hundred *modii* of land; Saint Gregory at Pentoma, with one thousand *modii*; Saint Mary at Illiara, with three hundred *modii*; Vicenda at Avezzano, one hundred *modii*; at the castle of Venere, at the place called Casale, from the mountain itself as far as the water, and on the other side of the water of Venere as far as the *casale* of Adelard, twenty *modii*; at the place called Calabrettum, one thousand *modii*; the inheritance of Guelto there, likewise one thousand *modii*; in the valley called Aquirana, likewise one thousand *modii*; and many other extensive possessions which we judged too lengthy to write down.

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Because we have come to that place, we touch briefly upon some of them,” added in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] *Oretino* in witnesses 1b and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] *Hyllara* in witnesses 1b and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “On the other side, from the water of Venere,” in witnesses 1b and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] *Adelrardi* in witness 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “From Saint Quintianus as far as Aquirana, one thousand *modii*,” in witnesses 1b and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Likewise one thousand *modii*, more or less, and so forth,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

The aforesaid Azzo divided the entire substance of this monastery equally, both its books and its animals and all its utensils, and took one part for the restoration of the aforesaid place. Having hired craftsmen, he immediately began by restoring the church, of which only the foundations remained, and then the other buildings.

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Of the cells,” in witness 1; absent from witness 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “The aforesaid Azzo,” absent from witnesses 1 and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Of the monastery,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Having summoned” in witness 1 and the edition.]

Afterward he returned to the abbot and obtained from him *libelli* for the men whom it was necessary to settle on the possessions of that monastery. Soon afterward he founded the castle nearest to that place, called Baiae.

[Note: [Col. 0623] “On the possessions,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] *Monastery* in witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] *Bale* in the edition.]

Finally, in the third year, when the church had been completed, the aforesaid abbot, at Azzo’s request, sent Angelus, bishop and at that time a monk of this monastery, with several brothers and twelve other clerics of Saint Germanus, to dedicate it solemnly.

[DESID. *Dial.* II, 6.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “To dedicate it solemnly,” in the edition.]

After this, not long afterward, the same Azzo appointed in his place a certain brother named Dominic, whom he himself had made a monk, and, now old and infirm,

[Col. 0624A]

returned to this monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Not long afterward, appointing in his place a certain brother named Dominic, whom he himself had made a monk, Azzo, already old and infirm,” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

While he lay for several days in the infirmary, drawing his final breath, a brother named Peter—at that time a young man, but in our own age, when we found him still living in this place, advanced alike in years and character—was sleeping that night in the brethren’s dormitory with the others. He thought he saw Michael the Archangel, in precisely the form in which painters customarily portray him, passing through the dormitory accompanied by another angel.

[Note: [Col. 0623C] “A brother who still survives and lives with us in the monastery; then a young man, but now advanced in years and character,” Desiderius.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] *Mainardus* in witness 1, corrected in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “As is customary to depict him in images,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

When that brother, with a certain special confidence, asked whether he was himself Michael the Archangel and where he was going, the blessed archangel answered that he was indeed the archangel Michael and that he was hastening to receive the soul of Brother Azzo.

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Whether,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “And that he was hastening to receive Azzo,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “And that he was plainly blessed,” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

Immediately that brother awoke and rose; rushing swiftly to the infirmary, he found that the same brother had already departed from this world.

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Immediately the brother,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0623C] Up to this point from Desiderius.]

The aforesaid Dominic, imitating the diligence of his own master, not long afterward constructed the fortress called Intermontes, not far from the monastery, and settled in that stronghold the colonists who had previously lived at the place called Civitella.

[Note: [Col. 0623] “Which is called,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “At the neighbouring place,” added in witness 1; “which was called Civitella,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0623C] It is still inhabited. ANG.]

35. At the same time a dispute arose between the dukes and counts of Gaeta and Traetto against this monastery, because we had begun to reclaim certain lands and woods in the confines of Aquino which had belonged to this monastery from ancient times. They had received these lands, not many years earlier, from Pope John VIII and Pope John X by privilege,

[Note: [Col. 0623C] The instrument concerning this matter, made at the command of Dauferius, count of Traetto, was published by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 109. Di Meo, *Annali di Napoli*, under the years 917 and 1014, considers it spurious.]

(12 June 873), on the ground that they had taken the most vigorous part in the destruction of the Saracens dwelling on the Garigliano.

[Note: [Col. 0624C] Docibilis and John, dukes and hypati of the Gaetans.]

[Note: [Col. 0624C] It is said that the bull of John VIII was issued in indiction V, that is, 872; this cannot be correct. The capitulary of John X contained the oath, imposed by the pope, which the Roman nobles swore to them; among these were Theophylact the senator and Adrian, father of Pope Stephen.]

But when the case had been brought before a judicial assembly at the castle of Argenteum (July 1014), at which Lord Abbot Atenulf had assembled with the prince of Capua and the archbishop of that city, and also with the duke of Naples and the bishop of Gaeta, together with many nobles and judges from different regions, their aforesaid privileges were first reread in the hearing of all. Then, on our side, the commands of the kings Charles, Hugh, and Lothair were reread: they had granted and confirmed these same lands to this monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0624C] Its ruins can be seen on a hillock near Minturnae, below Traetto. ANG.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] “This matter,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] “Pandulf.”]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] “Pandulf.”]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] “Sergius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] “Bernard.”]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “Lord Abbot Atenulf,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “In the presence,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] *Caroli* in witness 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] *Firmaverant*, “had made secure,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

When this had been done, the judges immediately demonstrated, both from Roman law and from Lombard law, that the Gaetans could in no way claim those lands, originally assigned to the monastery, for themselves, but that we ought to possess them wholly, lawfully, and securely.

[Note: [Col. 0625] “The judgments,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “When this was done, a decree by …,” in witnesses 1b and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “And,” in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] The relevant words are cited there: Liutprand, IV.1; Julian, *Novella* 110.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “That they could in no way belong to the Gaetans,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

When the judges’ sentence had been praised and confirmed alike by the prince and by all those sitting in judgment,

[Note: [Col. 0625] “When this judgment had been …” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] The material from “had been” through the end of the chapter is cut off in witness 1b.]

the aforesaid dukes and counts, seeing that they could not resist the authority of the laws, immediately drew up a charter of acknowledgment or renunciation concerning all those properties and handed it over to us. A penalty of one hundred pounds of gold was imposed if they themselves or their heirs should ever attempt in any way to break or revoke this settlement.

[Note: [Col. 0625] “And their heirs should ever attempt to break this,” in the edition.]

36. [Note: [Col. 0625] The entire chapter is absent from witness 1; compare below, ch. 65.]

At the same time Pandulf and Gisulf, counts of Teano, when the same abbot had brought the matter before the judgment of the judge and archbishop of Capua, acknowledged and renounced in our favour the entire appurtenance of Cesima, likewise imposing a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold should they attempt in any way to revoke that renunciation.

[Note: [Col. 0625] “A penalty of one hundred pounds,” in the edition.]

The sons of Unzo of the castle of Conca did the same concerning that castle and all its appurtenances, and concerning Pilano, Saint Felix, and Cesima. Our provost Andrew brought the matter before the assembly of Anthony the chaplain and Benzo, envoy of Emperor Henry; a penalty of five thousand bezants was imposed should they revoke it.

[Note: [Col. 0625] *Zunzo* in witness 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] In the territory of Teano.]

At that time a certain man of Aquino, named Magipert, offered himself to blessed Benedict, together with all the goods of his estate, both movable and immovable. In addition, he offered the island called Limata, surrounded by the rivers Carnello and Melfa, estimated at one hundred *modii*. He himself had bought this island not long before from the men of Pontecorvo. On one side it had 417 paces, on another 323, on another 200, and on the remaining side 300.

[Note: [Col. 0625] “The inheritance which …” in witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] Register no. 275. ANG.]

[Note: [Col. 0626C] The Melfa thereafter flows into the Carnello, not far from Ponte Curvo. ANG.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “The rivers,” added in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “Which island,” added in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “Before not much time had passed,” added in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] The words “200 on another side” are absent from the edition.]

37. In the seventh year of this abbot, that is, in 1017, the Normans, under the leadership of Melus, began to conquer Apulia.

[Note: [Col. 0629A] In the sixth year of this abbot the moon was wholly turned to blood; and in the following year … [the material is defective]. Thus the *Anonymous of Monte Cassino* under the years 1016 and 1017.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “In the sixth year of this abbot,” in the edition.]

But how and on what occasion the Normans first came to these regions, who this Melus was and whence he came, and for what reason he joined those same Normans, seems appropriately to be related in a concise narrative.

[Note: [Col. 0625] “Who or from where M. …” in witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “And for what reason he joined those same Normans,” absent from witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “It seems appropriate to relate this in a concise narrative.” The account of the people of Bari follows below.]

[Note: [Col. 0626C] From this point onward our author made extensive use of Amatus’s *History of the Normans*, both to supplement and to correct what he had previously written from other sources.]

About sixteen years before this,

[Note: [Col. 0626C] “A thousand years since Christ …” in Aimé.]

forty Normans, returning from Jerusalem in the garb of pilgrims, arrived at Salerno. They were men tall in stature, handsome in appearance, and highly skilled in the use of arms.

[Note: [Col. 0626C] I do not find the words from “men” through “highly skilled” in Amatus.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “Pilgrims, as they had gone to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer,” in the edition.]

Finding Salerno besieged by Saracens, and their spirits inflamed at God’s prompting, they requested horses and weapons from Guaimar the Elder, who then ruled at Salerno. They unexpectedly attacked the Saracens, killed many of them, put the rest to flight, and, with God granting it, gained a remarkable victory.

[Note: [Col. 0625] The words “they unexpectedly attacked” are absent from witness 4.]

[AMAT. I, 18, 19, 20.]

They were acclaimed by everyone in triumph, honoured by the prince with lavish gifts, and earnestly invited to remain with him. But they declared that they had done this solely out of love for God and the Christian faith; they refused the gifts and denied that they could remain there.

[Note: [Col. 0625] “They declared that they had done this out of love for God and the Christian faith,” in the edition.]

The prince therefore took counsel with his men and with the Normans themselves, sent his envoys to Normandy with those same Normans, and, like another Narses, sent there through them citron fruits, almonds, gilded nuts, imperial cloths, and horse-gear marked with the purest gold. By sending these things to a land that produced such goods, he not so much invited them to cross over as drew them across.

[Note: [Col. 0625] “Afterward, therefore, the aforesaid prince, having taken counsel with his men,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] “Thus I have corrected it; *suo*,” in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0625] *Amigdolas* in witness 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0626C] “Candied nuts,” in Aimé.]

In those days two magnates of that region, namely Giselbert, also called Buttericus, and William, surnamed Repostellus, were bitterly at odds with each other. At last they reached such a degree of criminal hostility that Giselbert killed William.

[Note: [Col. 0625] *Exitii*, “of destruction,” in witness 2.]

When Robert, count of that land, learned of this, he became extremely angry and threatened Giselbert with death.

[Note: [Col. 0625] *Rotpertus* or *Rotbertus* consistently in witness 3; *Robertus* in witness 4.]

Giselbert therefore, anticipating his lord’s anger, took his four brothers, Rainulf, Asclettin, Osmund, and Rodulf, together with several others; accompanied only by horses and arms, they joined our envoys in flight and eventually reached Capua, where the aforesaid Melus was then staying with Prince Pandulf.

[Note: [Col. 0627C] Amatus does not contain what follows.]

To return briefly to Melus: he was the foremost and most distinguished of the citizens of Bari—indeed, of all Apulia—and plainly a man of exceptional energy and prudence. But the Apulians could not endure the arrogance and insolence of the Greeks, who, not long before, from the time of the first Otto, had claimed Apulia and Calabria for themselves after enlisting Danes, Rus’, and Walloons as their allies. They therefore finally rebelled with Melus and with a certain Datto, likewise a most noble man and a kinsman of Melus.

[Note: [Col. 0627] “He was here the foremost and most distinguished,” in witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0627] “And the wickedness of the Greeks,” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0627C] The Annals of Bari give 1011 and 1013—that is, 1010 and 1012, since they appear to begin the year in the preceding March.]

But when the Bariots could not resist the army which the emperor had sent there,

[Note: [Col. 0627] “When the emperor, having heard this, sent an army to Bari,” in witness 1.]

after a short time they shamefully surrendered themselves and their property, and attempted wickedly to hand Melus over to the Greeks.

[Note: [Col. 0627C] The Annals of Bari give 1011 and 1013—that is, 1010 and 1012, since they appear to begin the year in the preceding March.]

When that most prudent man perceived this, he secretly fled with Datto and entered Ascoli. A few days later, fearing that the people there too might hand him over to the Greeks who were seeking him,

[Note: [Col. 0627] “Who were besieging him,” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

he left by night and went with Datto to Benevento; from there to Salerno, and then to Capua. Meanwhile he gave no time to idleness, but worked by every means to cast off Greek domination and free his homeland from their tyranny.

Meanwhile the Bariots sent his captured wife Maralda and his son Argyrus to the emperor at Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 0627] “Meanwhile … sent” is added in witness 1b.]

Datto, fleeing for refuge to our abbot, remained with him for several days.

[Note: [Col. 0627] “With his wife and sons,” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0627] “For some days,” in the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0627] “Had remained with him,” in witness 1; “had remained,” in the edition.]

At last, because of his loyalty to Emperor Henry, he was received by Pope Benedict, together with his household, to live in the tower of the Garigliano which that pope then held.

[Note: [Col. 0627] “Finally, because of his loyalty to Emperor Henry,” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0627] “Of the river Garigliano,” in witness 1b and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0627] “He was placed there,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

That tower had been built, as a defence against the Hagarenes, by John, the imperial patrician of Gaeta, son of the *hypatus* Docibilis, in the time of Pope John VIII.

[Note: [Col. 0627] “Which the same pope …” is absent from witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0627] “For their dispersal,” in witnesses 1b and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0627C] If he is speaking of the tower that still stands at the mouth of the Garigliano, it is asserted that it was built not by John, duke of Gaeta, in the time of John VIII, but by Pandulf—perhaps the first called Ironhead—after the expulsion of the Saracens, according to a stone inscription attached to the same tower:

> Once the Hagarene people ravaged this land,  
> ascending this river. Lest this happen again,  
> the heroic Prince Pandulf founded this tower,  
> that its builder might have glory and a memorable name. ANG.]

Meanwhile Melus was staying at Capua with the prince. When he learned of the arrival of the aforesaid Normans, he immediately summoned them, carefully investigated and learned their circumstances, and promptly entered into an alliance with them according to military custom (1017).

[Note: [Col. 0627] “Meanwhile, Melus was staying at Capua with the prince. In those days some Normans, nearly forty in number, came to Capua. Fleeing the anger of their lord, the count of Normandy, they and many of their companions, scattered in various directions, sought wherever they might find someone willing to receive them. They were men tall in stature, handsome in appearance, and extremely experienced in arms. Their principal men were named Giselbert Botericus, Rodulf of Todin, Gosmannus, Rufinus, and Stigandus. When Melus learned this, he immediately summoned them and …” in witness 1.]

Returning at once to Salerno and Benevento, he gathered many supporters, some drawn by hatred of the Greeks and others by affection for himself. With them, and together with the Normans, he immediately entered Greek territory and began courageously to attack those who resisted.

[Note: [Col. 0627] “And immediately, with the Greeks’ hatred,” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0628B] “With the Normans themselves,” in the edition; “with ornaments,” in witness 3.]

In three encounters with the Greeks—first at Arenola, second at Civitate, and third at Vaccaricia—he fought in open battle and defeated them three times.

[Note: [Col. 0628C] “Beside the river’s water called Fertor,” in William of Apulia.]

[Note: [Col. 0628C] In Capitanata, formerly the seat of bishops; it was later transferred to San Severo.]

[Note: [Col. 0628C] “Vaccarice: this is in Apulia, at Melfi, where there are now gentlemen who call themselves Vaccaire,” in the translator of Amatus I, 22. According to that translator, the Normans suffered their defeat there, after six victories. According to Lupus, the third battle was at Trani. The district of Corte Vaccarizza still exists in the land of Bari.]

He killed many of them, drove them as far as Trani, and recovered all the cities and towns of Apulia on this side which they had invaded.

[Note: [Col. 0627] “He conquered them,” in the edition.]

But in the fourth battle, at Cannae, famous for the ancient Roman disaster, he was defeated by the ambushes and stratagems of the catapan Boiano (October 1018), and lost more easily everything which he had easily recovered.

[Note: [Col. 0627] *Bobano* in witness 2; *Baiano* in witness 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0627] *Captapani* in witness 1, corrected in witness 1b, and in the edition.]

It is reported that in that battle only ten Normans remained out of two hundred and fifty, whereas an innumerable multitude of Greeks perished.

[Note: [Col. 0627] “But after the Normans, whose number had by then reached eighty, had been stationed with the prince of Benevento and Salerno, with the prince of Capua, and with Datto, he himself …,” in witness 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0628C] Amatus reports this concerning the sixth battle.]

[AMAT. I, 23.]

Melus, seeing himself deprived of military assistance, placed the surviving Normans partly with Guaimar and partly with Pandulf. He himself went beyond the mountains to the emperor, so that, if possible, he might persuade the emperor either to come personally to these regions to expel the Greeks from Apulia or, if he could not do that, to provide him with military aid.

[Note: [Col. 0628C] The words from “the Normans” through “establishing” appear to have been added by our author; Amatus reports what follows in only a few words.]

[Note: [Col. 0629] “He went to the aforesaid emperor,” in witness 1 and the edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0629] The words “from Apulia” are absent from witnesses 1 and 2.]

[Col. 0629A] At this time the counts of Venafro entered upon a possession of this monastery called Vitecuso,

[Note: [Col. 0629C] Vitecuso and Acquafondata are not far west of Venafro; see below, Book IV, ch. 6.]

and began to build a castle there, as well as at the place called Acquafondata. When this was reported to Abbot Atenulf, he sent soldiers, drove them from the boundaries of this monastery after inflicting injuries and blows upon them, and overturned from their foundations the structures they had built.

[Note: [Col. 0629A] Addition in witness 2.]

[Col. 0629B] **38. DESIDERIUS, Dialogues II, 22.]** Meanwhile, since the aforesaid abbot—or rather, this monastery—was being harassed by the great attacks of the counts of Aquino, and since neither reverence for the servants of God living here nor for Saint Benedict himself, the holy father, could in any way restrain their wickedness, the abbot, finally compelled by great necessity, enlisted for himself several very valiant men from among the aforesaid Normans, and stationed them in the town called Pignataro, to protect the monastery’s possessions. So long as the abbot himself survived, they carried this out vigorously enough and faithfully.

[Note: “rather, this” 1st edition.]

[Note: “aforesaid” 1st edition.]

[Note: “and beside himself” in manuscript 1; “and beside himself in the town of Pignataro, not far from the city of Saint Germanus” in manuscript 1b and the edition.]

In these days the aforesaid catepan Boiano [Baiano in manuscript 4 throughout] granted to this monastery, wholly and without reserve, the entire inheritance or property of a certain Maraldus of Trani, both within that city and outside it, wherever he appeared to have possessed anything.

[Note: From “During these days” through “appeared to have possessed” is absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: “appeared to possess,” edition.]

Accordingly, since the prince of Capua secretly favoured Basil, emperor of Constantinople, he had golden keys made and sent them to him, thereby surrendering both himself and the city of Capua—indeed, his entire principality—to imperial rule.

[Note: “handing over,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: At that time, in the month of May, the sea of Naples became fresh from midnight until midday. Added in manuscript 1b.]

Meanwhile Boiano, sending a substantial sum of money to that same prince, asked him, if he were truly loyal to Emperor Basil, to permit him to cross over in order to seize Dattus. Permission was granted; and immediately that same catepan came to the Garigliano with armed soldiers, in the year 1021, and, after besieging for two days the tower in which Dattus was residing, suspecting nothing of the kind, at last captured it by force, together with all who were staying there.

[Note: “besides,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “sending across,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “permit himself to cross to seize Dattus,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “immediately” is absent in manuscripts 1 and 2.]

[Note: “with no small army,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: Thus the Anonymous Cassinese; Lupus Protospatharius says that he entered Bari on 15 June.]

[Note: “added,” manuscript 4.]

[Note: “all who were with him,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

The abbot obtained from Boiano, by many entreaties, the Normans who had been there; but he was never able by any means to rescue Dattus from his hands.

[Note: “who” is absent in manuscript 2.]

[Note: “there,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: “the aforesaid Abbot Boiano,” manuscript 1 and edition.] Dattus was brought in chains to Bari and, a few days later, by order of the catepan himself, was sewn into a sack, after the manner of parricides, and cast into the sea.

[Note: Manuscript 1 and edition: “bringing him, bound, to Bari, after a few days he ordered him to be sewn into a leather sack and cast into the middle of the sea.”]

[Note: Compare Amatus I, 25, where Pandulf himself is said to have taken the tower by assault.]

**39.** When the emperor Henry of august memory heard all this—namely, the invasion of the Greeks, the prince’s double-dealing, and finally Dattus’s most cruel death—he reckoned that, if Apulia and the Principality were lost, Rome also, unless he hastened, and consequently all Italy, would soon be lost to him. Since Melus, who had twice crossed the mountains to him on this matter, had now died, he judged that there must be no further delay. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1022, having assembled a very great army from his whole kingdom, he came into Italy.

[Note: The text has been corrected thus: “the invasion”; manuscript 1 and the edition read “invasion, the prince’s double-dealing, Dattus’s most cruel death”; manuscript 4, “by Dattus’s most cruel death.”]

[Note: “Melus had crossed to him twice,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: Thus the Anonymous Cassinese. He entered Italy near the end of 1021.]

He himself passed through the Marches with the greater part of this army; but he sent Archbishop Poppo, patriarch of Aquileia, by way of the Marsian region, with eleven thousand armed men, as they report.

[Note: Patriarch of Aquileia.]

[Note: “that,” is absent in manuscript 1.] He sent Archbishop Pilgrim of Cologne ahead through Rome with twenty thousand men, to capture the prince and the abbot.

[Note: “Peregrinus,” manuscript 1; “Piligrimus,” manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “to capture,” is absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: “to capture,” singular, manuscript 1 and edition.]

For the abbot himself, together with his brother the prince, had been very seriously accused before the emperor concerning the capture and death of Dattus.

[Note: Edition: “Indeed the abbot himself.”]

[Note: “indeed,” manuscript 1; “truly” added in manuscript 1b.] When the abbot learned this from messages sent by friends, he judged that nowhere could he remain safe from the face of such power. The counts of the Marsi and the sons of Borrellus gladly promised that they would receive him; therefore, after taking counsel and sharing it with his brother, he finally resolved to give place to wrath. Desiring to flee to the emperor at Constantinople, he set out for Otranto, intending to embark upon the sea there.

[Note: “the abbot together with the prince his brother” added in manuscript 4.]

[Note: “and the sons of Borrellus” absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: “would receive him,” manuscript 1; “would be about to receive him,” manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “and having consulted with his brother” absent in manuscripts 1 and 2.]

[Note: Manuscript 1: “and, crossing by the Sangro to Termoli, desiring to go to Constantinople, entered the sea; but secretly …”]

[Note: “After these things were done”—that is, after Pandulf’s capture—Amatus I, 25.]

Meanwhile Saint Benedict appeared in a vision to the bishop of that city and said: “Go and tell the abbot that on no account should he attempt to enter the sea on this occasion; for if he does so, he will undoubtedly perish.”

[Col. 0631A] But he gave no credence whatever to such a vision and boldly entered the sea. Yet, so that the truth of the warning might be proved, by God’s hidden dispensation and judgment he suffered shipwreck with all his companions and was drowned in the sea, on 30 March.

[Note: “that on this occasion he should not attempt the sea,” edition.]

[Note: 30 March: III Kalends of April, Necrology of Monte Cassino, codex 47.]

When this was reported to the emperor, he is said to have declared: “He opened a pit and dug it out, and he fell into the hole that he made” [Psalm 7:16].

Among the other things which the aforesaid abbot carried away from here, whether books or ornaments, he also took with him nine charters of emperors and princes, and a charter concerning the place called Publica in the district of Pontecorvo; an exchange agreement concerning Calinulo; a charter concerning Mount Asprano, where the castle of Celi stands; and two charters of donation concerning Saint Erasmus of Capua.

[Note: From “Among the other things” through “Capua” is absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: “other things,” is absent in the edition.]

[Note: Manuscript 2: “When that same abbot departed from here, he carried off with him nine imperial charters sealed with golden bulls, as well as the charter concerning Casa Gentiana and the Lesina fishery; all these sank with him into the depths of the sea.”]

[Note: “Chelli,” manuscript 3.]

**40.** Therefore Pilgrim, since he did not find the abbot, fearing that perhaps the prince too might fall into a similar flight after his brother’s example, hurried to Capua and immediately surrounded it on every side with armed troops.

[Note: Compare Amatus I, 24.] But the prince, fearing the betrayal of the citizens—which he knew for certain they would commit—came out voluntarily to Pilgrim, as though despairing, yet hoping. He declared that he was not as guilty before the emperor as was alleged, and promised confidently that he would make his defence before him concerning the charges laid against him.

[Note: “Peregrinus,” manuscript 1; “Piligrimus,” manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “meanwhile,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “it,” manuscript 4.]

[Note: “but,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “as though despairing, yet hoping,” added in manuscript 4.]

[Note: “approached,” manuscript 1, corrected in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “concerning these matters,” added in manuscript 1b.]

Pilgrim, pleased at this, took the prince into custody and went to the emperor, who had already pitched camp before the Greek city of Troy, which the Greeks themselves had lately begun to build, in the year 1018.

[Note: “went,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “in that same year,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: See Di Meo under this year.]

The emperor, rejoicing at the prince’s capture, assembled his leading men, Italian and transalpine alike, and brought the prince before their judgment.

[Note: “at,” manuscript 1 and edition.] Countless accusers were present and cast his crimes in his very face. By the unanimous and equal judgment of all, it was decreed that he ought to undergo the sentence of death.

[Note: “the emperor,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “and all his great men assembled,” manuscripts 1 and 2.]

[Note: “ultramontane,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

But Pilgrim, to whose protection that prince had entrusted himself, took the sentence very grievously.

[Note: “himself” is absent in manuscript 2.] He approached the emperor as a suppliant and, relying on the support of many, secured the prince’s life both by arguments and by prayers. Nevertheless, the emperor ordered him to be bound with an iron bridle and taken with him into Germany.

[Note: Manuscript 1: “When this was reported to Pilgrim, he hastened to the emperor and, approaching him, obtained by his prayers that the emperor should spare him the sword.” Manuscript 4 lacks “But Pilgrim … sentence of death.”]

[Note: “weeping,” manuscript 2.]

[Note: “both by arguments and prayers,” edition.]

[Note: “bound with an iron bridle,” edition.]

[Col. 0632B] **41.** A few days later, when the people of Troy voluntarily surrendered themselves and all, from the least to the greatest, ran forth as suppliants and prostrated themselves at the emperor’s feet, he granted them pardon in his imperial clemency. Since, owing to the summer season, a people accustomed to continual cold could not remain long in these regions, he hastened his return day by day.

[Note: “into” is absent in the edition.]

[Note: “the emperor’s,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “all, from the least to the greatest, running forth as suppliants,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “for a long time in these regions,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

Coming to Capua, he entrusted the principality to Pandulf, count of Teano.

[Note: He confirmed it to Pandulf and his son John on 5 January 1023, as Pandulf’s grandfather Pandulf had held it, according to Peter the Deacon in the Register, published by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 122.]

But to Stephen, Melo, and Peter, nephews of the aforesaid Melus, since he could not at present restore their own lands to them, he granted the county of the territory of Comino. He also left them Normans as auxiliaries: Giselbert, Gosmann, Stigand, Thorstein the Bald, Walter of Canosa, and Hugh Fallucca, together with eighteen others.

[Note: Manuscript 1b adds: “He granted the county of Comino to Stephen and Peter, nephews of the aforesaid Melus. With them remained the Normans Giselbert and Gosmann, Stigand, Thorstein the Bald, Walter of Canosa, Hugh Fallucca, and several others.”]

[Note: “aforesaid,” edition.]

[Note: “to recover their own [lands],” edition.]

[Note: “the territory of Comino,” with “territory” absent in manuscript 2.]

[Note: “Normans” absent in manuscript 3.]

[Note: “and Gosmann,” edition.]

[Note: “Fallucca,” manuscript 2; “of Fallucca,” manuscript 3; “of Fallucca,” manuscript 4.]

[Note: “with Normans,” manuscript 3.]

[Note: He learned the number from Amatus, I, 29.]

[Col. 0631C] **42.** After this, when the emperor had arranged all his affairs, he came to this monastery with Benedict, bishop of Rome, on 28 June 1022. All the brothers having been assembled in chapter, the emperor exhorted them to deliberate on choosing an abbot for themselves.

[Note: Manuscript 1, corrected in manuscript 1b: “the principality, and after a few days, he arranged …”]

[Note: These matters are related very briefly in Amatus I, 17.]

[Note: “a few days afterward,” manuscript 1b and edition.]

[Note: “with the most reverend pope Benedict,” manuscript 1.]

[Col. 0632C] **42.** After this, when the emperor had arranged all his affairs, he came to this monastery with Benedict, bishop of Rome, on 28 June 1022. Meanwhile all the brothers gathered together and began, according to the rule, to deliberate among themselves concerning the election of an abbot, with the pope and emperor present.

[Note: “all together,” added in manuscript 4.]

[Note: “according to the tenor” absent in manuscript 4.]

[Note: “the apostolic lord and the emperor” added in manuscripts 3 and 4.]

John the abbot was still alive and present at that council: namely, he whom we showed above, in chapter 20, to have left the abbacy and withdrawn into the wilderness.

[Note: “was present,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

Several men therefore arose and urged that he should be restored to them as abbot. But the emperor, seeing him now in extreme old age, addressed him humbly, since he was highly learned: “Servant of God,” he said, “go and pray for yourself and for us, for such an obedience is not suited to your age.”

[Note: “They arose,” corrected to “There were,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: “and,” corrected to “who,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: “requested,” corrected to “urged,” manuscript 1.]

The lord Theobald was present at that time, a man distinguished alike by birth and character. At that time he was energetically administering the provostship of the March, from which he himself had sprung. A few days earlier, when the emperor was passing through the March, he had gone forth to meet him and had most vigorously rendered service for the honour and advantage of this place. The emperor therefore declared him worthy of so great an office, if indeed he pleased the brothers, recounting his virtues.

As some murmured about him for a while, as often happens in such matters, while others praised the emperor’s will, the emperor is reported to have said: “That we may distinguish those who wish this from those who do not, let all rise to whom my judgment is pleasing.” Almost all the senior men, both in rank and age, then rose, while the remaining younger men stayed seated. Then the emperor said: “It was more just, and it is more fitting, that we should follow the agreement and counsel of so many and such senior men in this matter; and in my judgment it is far more right that the younger yield to the will of the elders than that the elders yield to that of the young.”

[Note: “afterward” added in manuscript 1.]

[Col. 0634A] The lord Theobald also was present, a man distinguished alike by birth and character, who at that time was energetically administering the provostship of the March. Several men therefore proposed that the aforesaid Abbot John should be restored to the abbacy. But because he was now of decrepit age, he was judged unfit for so great a burden by the counsel both of the emperor present there and of the wiser brothers. After several and differing opinions, as is usual in such matters, had been expressed, Lord Theobald was finally declared worthy by the common will of all and elected abbot by the brothers. The emperor himself, together with the pope, warmly approved the election. Thus, on the following day, the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, he was solemnly consecrated by that same pope.

[Note: “the provostship from which he had sprung” absent in manuscripts 1b and 2.]

[Note: “and who rendered service to the aforesaid emperor … as far as ‘served’,” manuscript 1; compare below, chapter 52.]

[Note: “urged that he be restored,” manuscript 1b and edition.]

[Note: “and because,” added in manuscripts 3 and 4.]

[Note: “lord” absent in the edition.]

[Note: “adjudged,” corrected to “declared,” manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “the emperor, who happened then to be present,” manuscript 1b and edition.]

[Note: “the aforesaid Roman pontiff,” manuscript 1b; “the aforesaid pope,” edition.]

[Note: Amatus: “And by the prayer of the whole college of monks he confirmed Theobald, a man noble in lineage and more excellent in conduct, as abbot, and gave him the crosier.”]

[Note: “on the nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul,” superscribed in manuscript 1b; “on their feast of the Nativity,” edition.]

[Note: “by the most blessed pope, honourably consecrated,” manuscript 1b and edition.]
