[Col. 0634B] Therefore, being at last judged worthy by the common vote of all, he was elected abbot on 29 June 1022. The emperor rejoiced greatly that he had obtained this result, and on the following day Theobald was honourably consecrated by the aforesaid Pope Benedict.

[Col. 0633B] **43.** At that time the emperor was suffering a very severe pain. As he himself later related, although he had the greatest devotion toward this place and affirmed that he had nowhere seen an oratory more awesome or more venerable, he was nevertheless often troubled by the scruple of doubt whether Saint Benedict truly rested bodily in this place.

[Note: The same events, though not in the same manner, are related by Amatus I, 28, and Adalbert, *Life of Henry* V, 23–24. Our author copied the privilege of Benedict VIII, who was afflicted; after others Tosti published it from Peter’s Register, *History of Monte Cassino* I, p. 251, using a text unlike that supplied from codex 4.]

[Note: “excessive,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “whether,” manuscript 1; “whether … or not,” manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “father,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

Thus, already in the pain mentioned, neither fully asleep nor wholly awake, Saint Benedict himself appeared to him.

[Note: “to him” added in manuscript 4.] Approaching him as though to visit him, he asked where he was suffering. When the emperor immediately confessed his ailment, Father Benedict said: “I know that until now you have doubted that I rest here. But that you may doubt no longer, and may believe with complete certainty that my little body rests in this place, this shall be a sign for you: as soon as you rise today, you will urinate three stones, not small ones, and from that time forward you will suffer no more from this pain. And know that I am Brother Benedict.” Having said this, he immediately vanished.

[Note: “Saint Benedict appeared,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “more fully doubt,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “my … believe” absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: “believe that my little body rests,” edition.]

[Note: “as soon as you rise,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: “I myself am,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

The emperor awoke and immediately rose. In accordance with the vision, he was restored to his former health and gave the greatest thanks to God and Father Benedict. When morning came, he entered the assembly of brothers and, after the solemn words of chapter, said: “My lords, what do you advise me to give to the physician who cured me?” When they replied that he should freely take whatever pleased him from the monastery and give it to the physician, he said: “That will not do. Since Father Benedict visibly cured me this night, it is right, and indeed altogether just, that I should reward his healing from my own treasury.”

[Note: “Awakening,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “and,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “inexpressible,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “What,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “give,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “whatever, if it pleased him, from the monastery,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “giving,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: Manuscript 1: “It is as you suppose; but …”]

[Note: Manuscript 1 and edition: “Since Benedict, the father, took care of me this night, I ought to reward him from my own treasury.”]

Saying this, and with tears mingled with joy, he recounted to all what he had seen and heard. He added: “Now I have plainly and certainly learned that this place is truly holy, and that no mortal must any longer doubt that Father Benedict rests here together with his holy sister.” To confirm his words, he openly showed all of them the three stones which, according to the tenor of the vision, he had urinated a little earlier.

[Col. 0635A] All were astonished at so great a vision and at the emperor’s wondrous and speedy recovery, and gave praise and thanks to God. On that same day the emperor’s munificence offered these gifts to Father Benedict:

[Note: Manuscript 1: “to Benedict, in the presence of the Roman pontiff whom we have mentioned.”]

[Note: “Know that,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: “plainly” added in manuscript 1.]

[Note: “because this place is venerable and …,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: Manuscript 1 and edition: “that Benedict, with his holy sister, rests here.”]

[Note: “added,” manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “marvellous and swift,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

An Gospel-book, covered on the outside on one side with the purest gold and very precious gems; and within, wonderfully adorned with what are called uncial letters and golden figures. A golden chalice with its paten, worked with gems, pearls, and the finest enamels; a greenish-blue (*diapistinus*) chasuble adorned with golden bands; likewise a stole, maniple, and girdle, each woven with gold. Also a multicoloured (*diasprum*) cope with bands woven in gold, and a tunic of the same material adorned with gold work. Further, a greenish-blue cloth embroidered likewise with gold; and a silver bucket and cup of considerable size, from which the brothers were to drink on principal feasts.

[Note: In the enumeration of these objects, the privilege more closely agrees with the readings of codex 1, so that both seem to have used some older inventory of them; for the pope’s written grant seems to have perished early.]

[Note: “with very precious gems,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2: “adorned”; manuscript 1 adds, “and likewise a greenish-blue cloth interwoven with gold, with which the same chalice is offered.”]

[Note: The colour *diapisti* is greenish, according to Hugh Falcandus, preface to the *History of Sicily*.]

[Note: “stripes,” manuscript 4 consistently.]

[Note: “of the finest gold,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: “cloth,” manuscript 3.]

[Note: Manuscript 1: “each wholly woven with gold”; edition: “each woven with gold”; manuscript 4: “each woven with gold” in a grammatically altered form.]

[Note: “cope,” edition.]

[Note: Apparently variegated; see Du Cange, s.v.]

[Note: “stripes,” manuscript 4 consistently.]

[Note: The clause “together with a greenish-blue cloth likewise adorned with gold” is absent in manuscript 1.]

He also recovered from the Jews an altar-cloth of Saint Benedict which had belonged to King Charles. The Jews held it in pledge for five hundred gold coins. He also recovered a larger Saxon silver chalice with its paten, which Theoderic, king of the Saxons, had once sent to Saint Benedict.

[Note: “which had formerly been [King Charles’s],” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: That is, a drinking vessel.]

[Note: Since Theoderic, king of Bernicia, son of Ida, was a pagan, and I know of no king of the Saxons of that name other than he, I do not know whether this was that noble Saxon, lord of Hohseoburg castle, whom Carloman captured twice.]

Placing all these things together upon the altar of Saint Benedict in the brothers’ presence, he offered them. He asked the aforesaid pope to draw up at this place an instrument of his authority concerning them all, adding to that instrument the bond of an apostolic anathema, lest anyone should ever presume to take away either the things we have mentioned or any others which the emperor might thereafter grant to this monastery.

[Note: At this point the hand and ink change in quire 10, line 5.]

[Note: “and the most reverend Pope Benedict,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: “thereafter,” manuscript 1b and edition; “beforehand,” manuscript 1.]

The pope likewise, rejoicing greatly at the emperor’s recovery and emulating his generosity, offered Saint Benedict on that same day an excellent blue chasuble, suitably adorned with golden bands, and an excellent stole embroidered with gold, together with its maniple. Archbishop Pilgrim, too, for joy at the emperor’s recovery, likewise offered Saint Benedict an excellent purple chasuble, adorned around it with golden bands bearing the signs of the twelve months, together with a gold-wrought stole and one cope.

[Note: Manuscript 1 first placed “Pilgrim” before “pope,” but later altered it. “The aforesaid” was corrected in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: Manuscript 1: “the venerable apostolic lord, emulating their—corrected to ‘the emperor’s’—generosity, offered.”]

[Note: “on that same day” absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: “embroidered with the needle,” whence French *broder*; Du Cange.]

[Note: Manuscript 1: “Moreover Pilgrim”—corrected from “Peregrinus”—“the archbishop offered on that day to Saint Benedict …”]

[Note: “golden bands,” manuscript 1.]

After this, the most Christian emperor still considered that, because of his excessive love for this place, he had done too little. Admonished by Pilgrim and by Theoderic his chancellor, on the following day he issued a charter granting to this place the rock called Vantra. Its possessors had very frequently harassed this monastery like a band of robbers; therefore he wrested it from their hands and transferred it for the servants of God of this place to possess and retain forever.

[Note: “by the aforesaid Archbishop Pilgrim”—with “Peregrinus” corrected to “Piligrimus”—manuscript 1.]

[Note: “Piligrinus,” edition.]

[Note: “to this place” absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: The diploma calls it Bandra; it was issued in the original in 1022, and Gattola published it, *Accessiones*, p. 119. Compare above, chapter 15.]

He also issued another charter concerning all the possessions of this place throughout the world, according to the tenor of the charters of his imperial predecessors. By this charter he confirmed, by imperial authority, in this monastery the monastery of Saint Mary at Canneto, in the territory of Termoli. Thus, earnestly commending himself to Father Benedict and all the brothers, he returned home with their blessing.

[Note: “through which charter he also confirmed,” added in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: The privilege survives uninjured, but is dated 4 January 1023, at Paderborn. Gattola published it, *Accessiones*, p. 120.]

And, lest he appear in any way to forget the benefaction of so great a benefactor, as soon as he returned home he took pains to send here, to Saint Benedict, with the greatest expressions of thanks, an excellent rose-coloured (*diarodina*) chasuble adorned with golden bands, together with an alb and girdle, stole and maniple, such as befitted an emperor to send. Thereafter his devotion toward this holy place was so great that, if he had lived somewhat longer, he would have promised to serve God here, leaving the height of empire, under the habit of holy profession.

[Note: “most beautifully adorned,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “and so great … he promised” absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: From Amatus I, 28.]

**44.** Since he had been made entirely certain, both by the revelation which he had seen and by the recovery which he had experienced, that the body of Saint Benedict truly rested in this place, wherever thereafter he could find a written account of the translation of that holy father, he burned it in flames. He recounted to everyone what the Lord had shown and granted him in this place, and demonstrated reasonably from the course of that false translation narrative that these things were empty and fabricated. For, as the account relates, one and the same angel both urged them to steal [the body], incited the Roman pontiff to pursue them, and then again pressed them to flee.

[Note: The account of the translation was published in the *Acta Sanctorum* for 21 March, where it is attributed to a certain Adalbert.]

[Note: “and,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

But those who think themselves supported on this point by the testimony of Paul the Deacon, undoubtedly a truthful and distinguished historian, [Book VI, chapter 2], should know that it is customary for writers of events to follow popular opinion in their narratives. Thus, in Luke [2:48], blessed Mary calls Joseph the Lord’s father, saying: “Your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow”; and in Mark [6:26] Herod is said to have been grieved because the girl asked for the head of John the Baptist. No one can be unaware that neither of these statements was in fact true.

[Note: “As for those who …” manuscript 1b and edition; the rest of the sentence through “can be unaware” is added in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “of historical events” is absent in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “in their own narrative, they follow popular opinion,” manuscript 1b and edition.]

[Note: “John” added in manuscript 4.]

**45.** This same most religious emperor was also accustomed to relate the following to many people: that the very ailment from which he had now deserved to recover through Saint Benedict had likewise long before been inflicted upon him by that same saint, on the following occasion.

[Note: “to many people” is absent in manuscript 1.]

[Note: This also, “he himself,” manuscript 1.]

[Note: He was accustomed to relate it to Pandulf, prince of Benevento, who in his extreme old age was later made a monk by Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino. Lord Roffridus, still living, declares that he heard it from Pandulf’s own mouth; manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “then,” manuscript 3.]

While he was still duke, he was travelling and lodged in a certain monastery dedicated to the name of Father Benedict. Because the stables alone could not accommodate the multitude of his horses, his grooms, boldly and obstinately—as is the way of that sort of men—did not hesitate to place several horses in the chapter-house of the brothers, which stood beside the church.

[Note: Manuscript 1: “a certain monastery”; manuscript 1b: “a certain monastery beyond the mountains.”]

[Note: “dedicated,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “having lodged,” edition.]

[Note: “imperial,” manuscript 1, corrected in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: Manuscript 1: “the grooms [placed] horses”; manuscript 1b: “the grooms boldly and persistently [placed] horses”; manuscript 2: “the grooms boldly [placed] horses.”]

That same night Father Benedict appeared to the duke with a very grim and terrible countenance. He threatened him severely for treating his house in such a manner and struck his side with the rod which he carried in his hand. From that time he began to be tormented most severely by pain there.

[Note: “Father Benedict,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “to the emperor, then duke,” manuscript 1, corrected in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “grim and very terrible in appearance,” manuscript 1 and edition.]

[Note: “because he was treating his house thus,” added in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “also,” added in manuscript 4.]

**46.** This same emperor built, from the expenses of his own patrimony, a church in honour of Saint George at Bamberg in 1007.

[Note: From “This same emperor” through “retaining” is absent in manuscript 1.] Summoning Pope Benedict, he had it consecrated by him, established there an episcopal see, and granted it entirely to Saint Peter, fixing an annual payment of one excellent white horse with all its trappings and harness, and one hundred marks of silver.

[Note: “at Bamberg,” edition.]

Later Pope Leo IX, receiving Benevento from Henry, son of Conrad, by way of exchange, placed the aforesaid bishop of Bamberg under its jurisdiction in 1052, retaining only the horse mentioned above for himself.

[Note: That is, by way of exchange; see Di Meo, *Apparatus Chronologicus*, p. 280; *Annals* VII, p. 304; Borgia, *Memorie Beneventane* II, 16.]

[Note: “Corradi,” manuscript 2.]

[Note: Adalbert, *Life of Henry* V, 25, mentions only this.]

Beyond the other excellences or virtues which this emperor is said to have possessed, he is reported to have lived so chastely that, when he came to the point of death, in the presence of bishops and abbots, he summoned the relatives of his wife Cunigunde and, having entrusted her to them, is said to have declared: “Receive your virgin, whom you gave to me.”

[Note: “This most religious emperor,” manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “and abbots” absent in manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “summoned” absent in the edition.]

[Note: “Cunibunde,” manuscript 2.]

[Note: “returned,” manuscript 1b.]

[Note: “is reported: ‘Receive …,’” edition.]

[Note: Compare the same work, chapter 32.]

## 47. It pleases

[Note: [Col. 0637] Only witnesses 3 and 4 add this chapter; the Ang. edition of de Nuce displays it in the notes.]

[Note: [Col. 0638C] Adelbertus relates the same story, but more briefly, *l.* *l.* 33.]

At this point it is altogether fitting to insert a vision worthy of remembrance and destined to edify many, handed down to me by religious and wholly truthful informants, which the Lord wished to show to a certain servant of God at the death of that same emperor. On the night when the aforesaid emperor died (13 July 1024), this man, leaning out of the window of his little cell and praying to the Lord as usual, suddenly heard an immense uproar of certain persons hurrying past, laughing and rejoicing together.

[Col. 0639A] When, with ears alert, he wished inquisitively to learn what it was, and looked all around with his eyes, he immediately saw that what he had supposed to be a crowd of men was an innumerable throng of demons. Terrified at first, then recovering his courage and fortifying himself with the sign of the saving cross, he beckoned to one of them to come to him. The wicked spirit immediately obeyed and approached. The man of God said to him:

> “I adjure you by him who is to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire: do not hide the truth from me, but tell me: what is this, or where are you hurrying so swiftly, with such applause and rejoicing?”

“Heinrich,” he replied, “our dearest friend is dying, and we are hurrying to receive his soul; for, unless perhaps [Col. 0639B] God should wish to inflict injustice or violence upon us—which we certainly do not believe—he ought to be our inseparable companion.”

At this the man of God groaned deeply:

> “May the most merciful Lord not permit this,” he said, “that so great a man should come under the jurisdiction of your power. I have complete confidence, and am certain, in the greatness of his mercy, that he will grant you no power whatever over him; rather, he will send you back empty and deprived, with the confusion you deserve. Nevertheless, I command you by the same Redeemer of the world, our Lord, that you by no means fail, when you return here, to come back to me and report most truthfully whatever may happen in this matter.”

[Note: [Col. 0639] Witness 3 reads “he said” for *inquit*; witness 3 reads “God” for “Lord.”]

At these words the most wicked spirit vanished and departed; but the servant of the Lord applied himself to prayer more earnestly than usual. Then, after two days, [Col. 0639C] that malignant spirit returned to the man of God, his face cast down, mourning and sorrowful, just as he had been adjured. When the man of God asked him about the outcome of that great expedition of his and his companions, he replied:

> “Do not question me about this, since you can plainly perceive it from my appearance. Nor indeed would I have returned here today out of shame, had I not been bound by your adjuration, which I did not dare in the least to violate. For what we feared, and what you most grievously foretold, has happened to us in its entirety. When we stood ready to receive the aforesaid Heinrich, as belonged to our justice, and after many struggles with the angels who were striving to help him and take him from us, it was finally decided on both sides that, once his works, both good and [Col. 0639D] evil, had been placed in the balance, we should await which works would prove heavier. Our side gradually began to grow and, I confess to you, to tip down by no small amount. While we were applauding and already hastening to seize him, behold, unexpectedly that half-burned Laurence came running up, breathless, carrying a golden chalice [Col. 0640A] of no small size, which that same Heinrich had once offered in his basilica. Without delaying or asking anything, he hurled it upon the side of the balance opposed to us with such force and fury that he compelled it to weigh down to the very bottom. On this account the victorious angels joyfully received him, while we, deprived of every hope, withdrew, as you see, with great shame and confusion.

> “But lest you think that I have lied to you in any respect about these matters, send to the church of that burned man and have the chalice I mentioned sought out. If you do not find one of its handles broken—for it was placed in the balance so precipitately that, falling from it, it was shattered—do not believe anything I have related. But if you find it so, believe without doubt [Col. 0640B] that everything I have said is true—though I wish it had not been.”

[Note: [Col. 0639] Witness 3 reads “I said” for “I have related.”]

Having said this, he immediately disappeared like a shadow. When the servant of God heard these things, he fell on his face and gave thanks to God. Wishing to learn more certainly whether what the lying spirit had told him was true, he immediately sent to the aforesaid basilica of Christ’s precious martyr Laurence; and he found that the matter of the chalice had occurred exactly as the spirit had confessed. Greatly and exceedingly astonished at all this, he again and again offered many thanksgivings to the Lord: both because it had pleased him thus to free the aforesaid man from the hands of the demons, and because he had deigned, through a most deceitful spirit, to reveal the truth to him so effectively.

## 48. [Chapter 47.]

[Note: [Col. 0639] Witness 4 reads “when” for “since.”]

Since, in the course of this history, we necessarily mentioned a little earlier [Note: [Col. 0639] Witness 1 reads “it is fitting here.”] the body [Col. 0640C] of the blessed [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition reads “most holy.”] father Benedict (chapters 27, 44, and 45), it seems fitting here also to recall what that most blessed father deigned to show to Adam, a highly religious [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition reads “a very religious and most holy.”] man and custodian of his church. [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition adds: “the same blessed father.”] [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition reads “might be.”]

Accordingly, when Adam had gone to Rome on one occasion, as was customary, in order also to purchase the necessities [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition reads “for the useful needs.”] of this church, he lodged, as he had long been accustomed to do, at the monastery of the blessed Apostle Paul, over which Lord Leo, abbot [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition reads “Leo of holy memory.”], then presided. When one day those two most reverend men, namely Leo and Adam, were exchanging spiritual words with one another, the abbot began to inquire whether the reports then passing through the mouths of many were true [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition reads “whether the reports were false.”]: namely, that the body of blessed Benedict did not rest among us at all [Col. 0640D] [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition reads “that Benedict did not rest here at all.”], but had been secretly taken away beyond the mountains and transported elsewhere. He added:

> “To give this matter credibility, those who spread these reports say that no sign and no miracle occurs among you; whereas there, where they assert that he was transferred [Note: [Col. 0639] The first edition reads “carried,”] they affirm that innumerable signs are performed every day through his merits [Col. 0641A] [Note: [Col. 0641] The first edition reads “they say.”].”

At this Adam sighed deeply, took the abbot’s hand, and led him to the altar of the blessed Apostle Paul. There, with only those present, Adam placed his hand upon the altar and said [Note: [Col. 0641] The first edition reads “placed it and said”]:

> “By this body of the most blessed Paul, teacher of the nations, which the whole Christian community believes without any hesitation to rest here [Note: [Col. 0641] The first edition reads “to rest here again”]: what I am now about to tell you is utterly true and without any falsehood. Indeed, I too, having often heard such things about the body of blessed Benedict [Note: [Col. 0641] The first edition reads “having heard such things together with the others”], had at one time been led not merely into doubt, but even into despair and sorrow, so that I could scarcely show any devotion around his altar [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads “reverence”] or render him any reverence worthy of him [Note: [Col. 0641] Another witness reads “devotion”]. While I was thus tossed about for some time [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads “for several days”], proceeding with a sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads “lukewarm with sadness”] and fearful [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads “troubled”] mind, one day after Compline, having poured out a prayer at his tomb more devoutly than usual [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads: “one night, after a longer vigil than usual, having prayed with tears after Compline”], I lay down to sleep [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads “I lay down beside the church on my own bed”]. That most holy father then deigned to appear to me in a vision and say:

> “‘Why, Brother Adam, do you go about so dejected and sad? Why are you led astray into thinking so badly of me, as though I did not lie here bodily [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads: “as though I lay here together with my sister”?]? But because your service and devotion are very pleasing to me [Note: [Col. 0641] One edition reads “very pleasing before me”], henceforth be entirely certain that I rest here together with my sister Scholastica, and that I, together with her, must rise again in this place on the last day of judgment. Moreover, whenever you chant devoutly, pray attentively, and proceed fittingly, both by day and by night, I too am present with you. But that [Col. 0641C] I may render you free of doubt concerning all this: when, as usual, you have entered the church first at the morning hour, if you see something like a little rod of aromatic smoke issuing from my tomb and rising on high, believe that everything I have said is entirely true [Note: [Col. 0641] Three witnesses omit “everything I have said is.”’].”

Having said this, he disappeared. I immediately awoke, and, pondering within myself the mystery of so great a vision, overwhelmed at once with joy and tears, began to bless the Lord and the most holy father Benedict. Then, though trembling and afraid, I entered the church; I looked; I saw; and I believed, in accordance with what had been revealed to me, most unworthy though I was.

Moreover, know that what they say—that no miracle is shown by him among us—is wholly false. If I could recount to you everything which I received from our predecessors, or indeed the signs performed in our own times at his tomb, [Col. 0641D] [Col. 0642A] you would clearly see that this has been said from nothing but envy, or rather [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness adds “rather”], ignorance. Yet I shall tell you, out of many, one miracle not reported to me by someone else, but observed with these very eyes, in place of them all.

A certain demoniac named Andrew [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness adds “Andrew the demoniac”; another adds “from Bari”] from the city of Bari came one day to the monastery and, according to custom, was thrown down before the altar of that same father by the relatives who had brought him. While the brothers were chanting in the choir and the wicked spirit was uttering through the mouth of that wretched man certain foolish and dreadful cries, the most holy father Benedict suddenly appeared to me, as I stood nearby praying, standing before the altar itself [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness adds this phrase]. Striking the sufferer’s cheek with a considerable slap, he immediately expelled the evil spirit [Col. 0642B] from him. Thus healed, the man returned home with his relatives, giving thanks to God and Father Benedict.”

Adam confessed all these things to Abbot Leo before the very body of the blessed Apostle Paul, under what was in some sense a great necessity; but out of humility he concealed them from the others so thoroughly while he lived that none of the brothers of this place could know anything of them, until the venerable abbot Leo, after Adam’s death, told certain of our brethren [Col. 0642B] [Note: “Of these, the aforesaid Roffridus was one, from whom I learned this,” adds witnesses 1b and 2].

## 49. [Chapter 48.]

(*Desiderius, Dialogues II, at the end.*)

[Note: [Col. 0641] The first edition reads: “Here (thus in the edition) this same Leo, the most reverend abbot, also related another great matter.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] Desiderius received this from Leo and from Firmus, Adam’s nephew.]

This same Leo also related another wonderful matter, told to him by the truthful mouth of our Adam himself [Note: [Col. 0641] Witness 1b adds “our.”]. He said that on the feast day [Col. 0642C] of the holy martyrs Protus and Hyacinthus, Adam had gone outside the monastery gates on some business connected with the useful needs of his obedience [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads “I do not know what business”; another corrects it to “on some useful business of his obedience”]. Immediately, two most handsome young men in monastic dress met him. After greeting them humbly according to the monastery’s custom, and reverently asking who they were, he heard from them that they were called Protus and Hyacinthus [Note: [Col. 0641] The first edition reads “that they were Protus and Hyacinthus”], and that they had come to visit the brothers who had honorably celebrated their feast on that day [Note: [Col. 0641] The first edition reads “who had honored it sufficiently and devoutly in psalms and songs.”]

Having said this, they set out on their way and entered the monastery. Astonished by such answers, Adam paused briefly; then, recovering himself, he began to run quickly after them, asking everyone he met where the monks who had preceded him a little while before had gone. When they replied that they had seen no one enter the monastery gates before them that day [Note: [Col. 0641] One witness reads “no one seen entering the monastery gates that day”], he would not believe them [Col. 0642D]. He began to run hither and thither, again and again [Note: [Col. 0641] Omitted by one witness], asking each person he met [Note: [Col. 0641] Omitted by the first edition] most carefully about them [Col. 0643A] [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads “in no way”; another reads “not at all.”] But he was granted no further opportunity to see or speak with them [Note: [Col. 0643] The edition reads “to address them”; one witness reads “to address them further.”]

## 50. [Chapter 49.]

[Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads: “Here Adam built what Lord Leo, his teacher, had begun together with him, on…”]

This same [Note: [Col. 0643] The edition reads “the same”] Lord Adam built a cell, called Clia, on the nearby mountain adjoining Caira, in honour of Saint Benedict [Note: [Col. 0643] Added by witness 1b.] [Col. 0643C] [Note: The people still call the same mountain Chia, between Belmont and Saint Elias, to the north and east of Caira. — Ang.]. He also acquired, for the uses and needs of his obedience, the church of Saint Nazarius in Comino territory beside the river Melfa, which a certain priest, to whom it belonged by hereditary right, most willingly granted [Note: [Col. 0643] Witness 1b adds “the priest granting it”; the marginal reading is abbreviated and uncertain: “d. ciconia.” Witness 4 adds “most willingly.”]. He endowed it sufficiently with certain purchased landed possessions and with diverse ecclesiastical ornaments and books [Note: [Col. 0643] Witness 1 reads “he built [it],” corrected in 1b; witness 4 omits the words concerning the uses and needs of his obedience.].

## 51. [Chapter 50.]

[Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads “At that time”; witness 1b notes that the whole chapter was written in the margin.]

At this time the aforesaid catepan Boiano [Note: [Col. 0643] Witness 4 reads “Bajano.”] [Note: [Col. 0643] Witness 1b adds “of the Greek emperor”; witnesses 1b and 2 add “of whom we have already spoken above,” later deleted by witness 1c], having long before built Troia [Col. 0643B] at the head of Apulia, also built Draconaria [Note: [Col. 0643C] “Dragonara”], Florentinum [Note: [Col. 0643C] Also called Ferentino and Firenzuola; it stood eight miles from Luceria and now lies ruined], Civitas, and the remaining towns commonly called the Capitanata [Note: [Col. 0643C] That is, he enlarged and fortified them]; gathering inhabitants from the surrounding lands, he arranged for them to be settled thereafter. It should be known, however, that the name *Capitanata* is a corrupt popular form: properly it should be called *Catapanata*, from the office of the catepan who established it.

**Theobald II, the thirty-second abbot of this monastery, held office for thirteen years (1022–1035).**

## 52. [Chapter 51.]

Born of noble lineage in the March of Chieti, in the fourteenth year of his life [Note: [Col. 0643C] The following material is taken from a memorandum composed by Theobald himself in 1019 concerning his administration of Saint Liberator, published from the original by Gattula, *History*, p. 79. There it reads “fourteenth,” not “eleventh,” as in Gattula], he left home, parents, and all his property, and came to this monastery in the time of Abbot Aligernus. He was honourably received by him [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads “received kindly by him”; the text of Theobald himself] and clothed in the habit of holy religion. But after Aligernus’s death, when Manso had become abbot, as has already been said (chapter 12), he left here [Note: [Col. 0643] Added by witness 1b] and went to Jerusalem. On returning thence [Note: [Col. 0643] Added by witness 4], he received from Abbot John the obedience of the provostship of this monastery [Col. 0644A].

After administering it quite vigorously for some years, he was appointed by that abbot as provost in the monastery of Saint Liberator, situated in the county of Chieti beside the river Laento [Note: [Col. 0644C] Compare Book I, chapter 45]. When he found there a very small and exceedingly obscure church [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness corrects the reading], while the other buildings were wooden and old, within a short time [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads “a short”] he built the whole monastery from its very foundations with stone walls. [Note: [Col. 0644C] Theobald’s account reads: “When I had stayed there a few days, with God inspiring me…”] In the church, after adding about twelve cubits from its entrance [Note: [Col. 0644C] Theobald specifies “about three steps to the royal door and three cubits in height”], he constructed on the eastern side an apse of no small extent with its confession [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness adds “in length, and three in width”; three witnesses omit “and three in width”], and decorated the entire church with paintings and glazed windows [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness adds “excellent”; another deletes it. [Col. 0644C] Theobald reads “windows”].

Before the high altar he made an altar-front of silver received from relatives [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads “a very beautiful silver altar-front received from relatives”] [Col. 0644B], and gilded a considerable part of it [Note: [Col. 0644C] Theobald calls it “of marvelous beauty.”] He also made in that church two large silver censers weighing ten pounds, of handsome workmanship and partly gilded; and he presented there another silver censer [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads “another”; Theobald] which had belonged to his father [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads “a very beautiful one.”]. He made a silver chalice weighing six pounds [Note: [Col. 0643] One edition reads “with its paten” [Col. 0644C] Theobald adds “with two patens”], another weighing two and a half pounds [Note: [Col. 0643] Witness 4 reads “half a pound”; Theobald reads “two and a half pounds”], together with two smaller ones and one censer. He also made a cross of the purest gold, in which he reverently placed a fragment of the wood of the Holy Cross, together with other relics of saints [Note: [Col. 0643] One edition reads “in which he placed a particle of the wood of the Holy Cross, with other sacred relics.”]. He had five bells made there, not small ones [Col. 0644C] [Note: Theobald says “he bought three and ordered two to be cast”], and very many other ecclesiastical ornaments of various kinds, which I have refrained from inserting here. Among these he also ordered sixty different books to be copied [Note: [Col. 0644C] Theobald lists them individually; among the others, one Prosper, *History of the Angles*, a history of Paul Orosius, and the *Mediolanum*], four of which he adorned with coverings and silver work [Col. 0644C] [Note: [Col. 0643] One witness reads “with bosses and other ornaments”; another adds “with silver work.”]

At the time when Emperor Heinrich came down into Apulia (1022), as we have related above [Note: [Col. 0644C] He had related this in chapter 42 but later removed it], Theobald went out to meet him as he passed through the March [Col. 0645A], and served most energetically for the honour and benefit of this place. While the emperor was staying with all his magnates at the place called Saint Peter in Planaci [Note: [Col. 0645] One witness reads “in the palace.”] [Note: [Col. 0645C] The documents from which these facts became known to us seem to have perished. Yet a judicial notice survives in Peter’s Register, stating that Theobald, by the judgment of the emperor’s envoys, recovered the estate of Saint Mary in Morino from Ildeprand, son of the late Duke Transmund. Gattula published it in *History*, p. 77.], Theobald made a claim before them all against Counts Atto [Note: [Col. 0645] One witness reads “Otto”] and Pandulf concerning the property of Saint Benedict in the county of Termoli which they then held. These were, by name, five castles—Petra Fracida, Pescloli, Guardia [Note: [Col. 0645] A later hand adds “Ripa Mala, which is now called…”], Ripa Ursa, and Montebellu [Note: [Col. 0645] A later hand adds “and Ipsafae”]—together with the monastery of Saint Benedict and Saint Nicholas and the other churches situated within the appurtenances of those castles, within the following boundaries. At the head, Rivus Planus; at the foot [Note: [Col. 0645] Omitted by witness 4], the sea with its shore, ports, and fisheries; on one side, the river Trigno; and on the other [Col. 0645B] the stream called Teccle [Note: [Col. 0645] One witness adds “the stream called Teclum”; another writes “Teccle”].

In the presence of the aforesaid emperor and his magnates, the said counts surrendered all these things to the share of our monastery [Note: [Col. 0645] One witness reads “into the hands of the same emperor”], together with all their possessions and appurtenances within the boundaries we have mentioned [Note: [Col. 0645] Added by witness 1b and the edition]. The emperor himself invested the aforesaid Lord Theobald with all of them by his own hand, binding both the counts and all who might thereafter presume in any way to seize these things [Note: [Col. 0645] The following material is cut away in witness 1b] with a penalty of two thousand pounds of gold payable to this monastery [Note: [Col. 0645] The edition reads “to this monastery.”].

On a subsequent occasion, at the court of Count Trasmund [Note: [Col. 0645] One witness reads “Transmund”], he brought a claim against a certain Tresidius, who held many possessions belonging to the land of Saint Liberator. When Tresidius acknowledged and surrendered them, Theobald recovered everything.

[Col. 0645B] At the same time Prince Pandulf, coming to this monastery, issued a charter to Saint Benedict concerning the monastery of Saint Nazarius situated in the territory of the city of Atina (12 April 1032). He also made for that place a charter confirming all its appurtenances for the use of our monastery and granted a site for building a mill. [Note: [Col. 0645C] Gattula published this from the *Register*, *History*, p. 205; there too permission is granted to build a mill on the river Melfa. Another privilege survives in the *Register*, no. 279, as Ang. de Nuce testifies. This entire note is added by witness 2.]

## 53. [Chapter 52.]

After the same Lord Theobald had spent about fifteen years in the aforesaid provostship [Note: [Col. 0645] Witness 1 reads “more or less”; witness 4 omits “Lord” and adds “and” before the following clause.] and had been transferred, in the manner related above, to the abbacy [Col. 0646A] of this monastery [Note: [Col. 0645] Witness 1 reads “in the manner which we showed above, with God’s favor. Here then …”; the edition begins a new chapter at “Here then”], he received from the aforesaid Pope Benedict, who consecrated him, the customary privilege [Note: [Col. 0646C] *Register*, no. 18. — Ang.] [Note: [Col. 0645] Witness 1 reads “receiving.”]. During the two years that Emperor Heinrich survived, he lived in complete prosperity [Note: [Col. 0645] One edition reads “in the prosperity of his honor”] and made [Note: [Col. 0645] Witness 1 reads “acquired”; witness 1b adds “ecclesiastical ornaments.”] many ecclesiastical ornaments here. He ordered a silver cross to be made for processions on Sundays and two very large and handsome bells [Note: [Col. 0645] One witness reads “bells of marvelous size and beauty”; the edition reads “to be made”]. He adorned the altar of Saint Gregory with a silver frontal [Note: [Col. 0645] One edition reads “of very beautiful workmanship”]. He made a silver casket in which he reverently placed the portion of the wood of the Lord’s Cross which, as we showed above (chapter 11), had been brought here by the monk Leo. He covered a pastoral staff and its headpiece with silver [Note: [Col. 0645] One witness reads “the staff likewise with silver, of beautiful workmanship.”].

He added a small church in honour of Saint Nicholas beside the abbot’s chamber, on the north side of the church of blessed Benedict [Col. 0646B]; and he built another small chapel in honour of Saint Severus, bishop of Cassino [Note: [Col. 0645] The words “bishop of Cassino” are omitted by witness 2], in the place anciently and popularly called *Ad voltam sancti Severi* (“At the Bend of Saint Severus”) [Col. 0646C] [Note: This little church, often restored, still exists there. The place was called *Ad voltam* because the mountain path descends from there for travelers going toward Aquinum, leaving the broader road leading to San Germano. — Ang.]. He also constructed high walls and two towers, one on either side before the church courtyard, in the manner of a cloister.

He ordered a number of books copied, of which there had been great poverty here until that time. Their titles are as follows [Note: [Col. 0646C] Compare Tosti, *History of Cassino* I, 287]:

- The second part of Augustine’s *City of God*.
- The same author’s *On the Trinity*.
- The same author’s commentary on the Psalms, divided into two volumes.
- Gregory’s forty homilies.
- The first part of the *Morals*.
- Claudius on the Epistles of Paul.
- Rabanus’s *Etymologies*.
- A History of the Romans.
- [Col. 0646C] A History of the Lombards.
- An itinerary of the whole world with Jerome’s chronicle.
- Jerome’s complete martyrology.
- The Roman Pontifical.
- Isidore’s *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.
- The Edict of Lombard Law.
- A Harmony of Canons.
- Another book of canons.
- Decrees of the popes.
- Bede on Mark.
- Two hymnals for use in choir.

[Note: [Col. 0645] The abbreviated catalogue in witness 1/edition gives: Gregory’s forty homilies; the first part of the *Morals*; Augustine on the Psalms, divided into two volumes; Claudius on Paul’s Epistles; Rabanus’s *Etymologies*; the *History of the Romans*; the *History of the Lombards*; the Edict of Kings (witness 3: “Edict of Lombard Law”); Jerome’s complete martyrology (witness 1b adds this fuller form); the Roman Pontifical; Isidore—spelled *Ysidore* in witness 4—on Offices; the Harmony of Canons; a book of canons; Decrees (witness 1: “Decretal”); Bede on Mark; and two hymnals, etc.]

## 54. [Chapter 53.]

At the same time Lord Odilo, a man venerable in life and reputation, abbot [Col. 0647A] of the monastery of Cluny [Note: [Col. 0647] Witness 1b added the words from “abbot” through “arranged,” after erasing material written in seven lines; it also adds “At whose …”], came to this monastery with great devotion. Because of the profound reverence which he bore for the blessed father Benedict and, through him, for this place, he climbed the whole mountain on foot. When, according to the monastery’s custom, he had been honorably led into the chapter house [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness adds “by the abbot or the brothers”] after the solemn reading [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “the solemn words of welcome for so great a guest”] customarily given at the arrival of guests [Col. 0647C] [Note: These readings, customarily read before guests in the chapter house, survive in our manuscript 47 with this heading: “These chapters of divine authority, issued by blessed Gregory, pontiff of the city of Rome, are to be read before guests in the chapter house, according to the command of our most holy father Benedict, so that they may be edified.” — Ang.], that most reverend man said:

> “As we have heard, so have we seen: in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God, and on his holy mountain.”

Then, turning very humbly to the abbot, he said:

> “Beloved father, I ask of you a great gift, and I humbly pray that it may be granted to me without any opposition [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness adds “which I request with every desire”]. I wish and desire, most devoutly, to kiss the footprints of all the brethren.”

Theobald consented, though unwillingly, and could not in any way resist so great a devotion [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “it was in no way possible for him to resist it.”]

On the following day, the feast of blessed Benedict [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “the feast of that same most blessed father of ours”; another expands “after our abbot Theobald had invited him with many prayers, out of special religious devotion”], although repeatedly invited by our abbot to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, Odilo could by no means be compelled to celebrate public Mass in his presence.

Then, when the brothers were ready to go in procession, our abbot reverently offered the pastoral staff to Odilo’s hand. But Odilo very humbly refused it, saying that he was by no means worthy to carry such a staff in the presence of so great a man. He considered it utterly improper and against every rule that either he or any other abbot should carry a pastoral staff by hand wherever the vicar of Benedict—the abbot of all abbots—happened to be present [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “any abbot whatever.”].

As he was preparing to depart, Theobald, accompanying him with many brethren as far as the monastery gate [Note: [Col. 0647] One edition reads “the doors”], finally begged him earnestly, if it were possible [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “if ever he could”], to send some blessing from the relics of blessed Maurus [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “to this monastery”] to Benedict, Maurus’s teacher. The venerable man kindly received the request [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “receiving it very gladly”], replied confidently that it was possible, and willingly promised to do so if life permitted. Thus, after taking leave, he departed.

After the passage of seven years, he arranged for the complete bone of the arm of the most blessed Maurus to be sent here by six brothers of his monastery [Note: [Col. 0647] One edition reads “to delegate”], enclosed fittingly in a silver casket, beautifully fashioned [Col. 0648A] in the likeness of towers. At its arrival a very great multitude of all the people of this land came out to meet it, with profound devotion [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness omits “very”; another reads “most devoutly.”]. For the report had stirred them in such a way that, since blessed Maurus had long before been sent beyond the mountains into obedience and had now returned [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “they ought to hasten most eagerly to see him”], they ought to hasten most eagerly to meet him in a manner worthy of him.

Our aforesaid abbot had meanwhile withdrawn into the March [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “the Marches”] to escape the persecution of the Prince of Capua, as we shall set forth fully in due order below [Note: [Col. 0647] One edition reads “as we shall show fully below in its proper order”]. But the entire community of this holy place, filled with inexpressible joy, put on all their solemn vestments [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness expands: “with all the brothers clothed in solemn garments”] and, carrying many candles and censers [Note: [Col. 0647] Four witnesses omit the intervening words], went out with the greatest devotion to meet it as far as the old gate [Col. 0648B] [Note: [Col. 0648C] Understand the gate which opens into the area before the monastery, near the little church of Saint Agatha. See below, Book IV, chapter 73. — Ang.], some distance beyond the monastery enclosure.

Immediately, as though they had been granted to behold him alive in the flesh, they all fell together to the ground in adoration. Rising, they reverently kissed the holy casket, their tears mingled with joy [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “most devoutly and reverently, with tears mingled with joy”; another corrects “mixed” to “mingled”]; then, accompanying it most honorably with hymns and praises, they brought it into the monastery and placed it upon the venerable altar of his teacher Benedict [Note: [Col. 0647] Added by witness 1b].

How unlike, and how different, this procession receiving the most blessed Maurus was from that in which Father Benedict had once accompanied him with his whole congregation as far as the monastery gates [Note: [Col. 0647] Omitted by the edition] and sent him beyond the mountains [Note: [Col. 0647] The first edition reads “the gate”], although each was full of devout tears, we leave for the pious reader to consider.

In the meantime, some of the brethren, not wholly doubting, but wishing to be made absolutely certain of the matter, secretly opened the aforementioned casket from below, where it was unlocked and locked by a small silver key [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “which was opened and closed whenever necessary”]. Having seen the most sacred relics, they became, both for themselves who had seen them and for the others who had not, the cause of the surest faith.

When this was reported to the superiors [Note: [Col. 0647] One witness reads “to the abbot”; another, “they rebuked him, fearing…”], they strongly rebuked the brethren’s presumption. Fearing that, following their example, the holy relics might someday be mutilated if many people desired to see them [Col. 0649A], they carefully shut the aforesaid little casket [Note: [Col. 0649] One witness reads “shutting the little casket and immediately breaking the key into pieces with his own hand”] and immediately broke the key into pieces. Thus from that time onward, down to the present day, that sacred casket remained closed and unopened.

55. [Chapter 54.] About these days [Note: [Col. 0649] “About—of all his possessions” added by 1b.] Hugh [Note: [Col. 0649] Hugh, son of Docibilis, by birth; 1b, but he himself altered this.], a nobleman by birth from Gaeta, approaching the end of his life, made a charter (April 1040) in this monastery concerning half of the castle called Sujum [Note: [Col. 0649C] Suio, on the right bank of the Garigliano.], and also concerning absolutely all the property which appeared to belong to him by right of his parents, both in Gaeta and in the aforesaid Suio [Note: [Col. 0649] With *tam* written above the line in 1b: “both that which belonged to him in … and that which appeared …” in the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0649] “Appeared” is singular in 1b and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0649C] Rather later, in the time of Abbot Richerius; see the charter in Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 128.]

At the same time (January 1023), certain noblemen of the county of the Abruzzi, Lupus and Albertus, likewise offered [Note: [Col. 0649] “Likewise offered,” 1b and the edition.] to blessed Benedict a church belonging to them by right, called Saint Lawrence, in the place called Collenori [Note: [Col. 0649C] *Colle neri* in the document published from a transcript by Gattula, *Historia*, p. 316. They were brothers, sons of the late Tedaldus and Aczolinus, themselves sons of the late Samson.—This church, called Saint Lawrence of Salmo or Salinello, was situated in the territory of Teramo, today Podio Morelli. GATTULA.], near the river Salinum, with all the appurtenances and possessions of that church.

In the following year, a certain Benedict [Note: [Col. 0649] “A certain Benedict, with his wife Marenda,” 1b and 2.] from the castle of Monte Metulo made his offering in this monastery of the church of Saint John, situated within the boundaries of that same [Note: [Col. 0649] “Its own,” 1b and the edition.] castle, beside the river Trinium, with 270 modii of land on which the church itself was built, and with all its other possessions. [Note: [Col. 0649] From “beside the river” through “by birth” is cut away in 1b.]

Likewise, a certain priest from the territory of Bovianum, named Leo, offered in this place [Note: [Col. 0649] “Offered to blessed Benedict in this place,” the edition.] the church of Saint Christopher of the castle of Petroso, which [Note: [Col. 0649] “Which belonged to him, which,” the edition.] he himself had built from the foundations on [Note: [Col. 0649] “On his own property,” added by 4.] his own property, with all its possessions and appurtenances.

Another priest, named Franco, an Arpinate by birth, did the same concerning [Note: [Col. 0649] “An Arpinate made a charter of offering to this monastery of a church belonging to him in the territory of the aforesaid city, called Saint Lucy, with many lands around it and its other possessions and appurtenances,” 1b and the edition.] the church of Saint Lucy belonging to him in the territory of that same city, with very many lands around it and its other possessions in various places. The church also of Saint Angelus in the city of Morrone [Note: [Col. 0649] *Murrone*, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0649] “And also the church of Saint Angelus,” 1b and 2.] which is situated above the Hollow Stream, in the place called John Scutarius [Note: [Col. 0649] “Above the stream, in the place,” the edition.], was likewise [Note: [Col. 0649] “In the same manner,” 1b and the edition.] offered in this place with all that belonged to it.

Moreover, a certain nobleman of Termoli named Rappotus [Note: [Col. 0649] *Raptus*, 2.] offered in this monastery all his possessions and estates which he held at Larino, together with the church of Saint Mary of the Plain, the church of Saint Peter, and the church of Saint Terentian within that same [Note: [Col. 0649] “Aforesaid,” the edition.] Larino, with houses and lands, ornaments, and all the appurtenances of those churches. [Note: [Col. 0649] “And all the ornaments and appurtenances,” the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0649] “But also … of the churches” is absent from 1; “and also a certain nobleman of Termoli,” the edition.]

[Chapter 55.] At this very time [Note: [Col. 0649] “At this very time,” 1. The words “At this time … gilded its head” constitute a chapter in 1 and the edition.] a priest named Adelmodus, a Saxon by birth, came to this monastery [Note: [Col. 0649] “Out of love and devotion to blessed Benedict,” 1 and the edition.], and, most devoutly taking on the monastic habit [Note: [Col. 0649] “The habit of monastic profession,” 1.], had a silver cross made in this place [Note: [Col. 0649] “In this place,” added by 4.] from his own property, weighing nearly seventy pounds, and gilded a considerable part of it. [Note: [Col. 0649] “A larger silver [cross],” 1 and the edition.]

[Chapter 56.] In these same days [Note: [Col. 0649] *Hisdem*, 2.] [Note: [Col. 0650C] From Desiderius, *Dialogues*, book II.] a certain Paul, a man afterward renowned for holy conduct, came to this monastery. Having received the monastic habit from the hands of the aforesaid abbot, he was sent by him to reside at the monastery of blessed Benedict situated within the city of Capua. [Col. 0650B] There, under the discipline of his holy profession, he lived with such fervour that his life could serve as an example to earlier generations and to every religious man.

For the end of his life showed how pleasing to almighty God the life of that manner of living had been. When he had fallen ill and come to his last hours, on the very night on which he was to depart, a bishop of venerable life from the regions of Gaul, travelling to the shrine of the blessed archangel Michael situated on Mount Gargano, was lodging in the same city of Capua near the church of the holy martyr Lawrence. [Note: [Col. 0650C] Stephen of Desiderius.]

Rising in the dead of night and devoutly applying himself to prayer before that church, he suddenly turned his gaze toward the eastern quarter on his right and saw a most brilliant light, like the sun, issuing from our aforesaid monastery and penetrating the heavens. Astonished and at the same time exultant at this vision, [Col. 0650C] he immediately heard the sound of the monastery bell which, according to custom, signified a brother’s death. He understood with certainty that someone had died there whose soul was worthy to seek heaven in the light which he had seen.

The same holy bishop at once related what he had seen to his companions and promptly sent a messenger to the monastery, to learn who had died there that night and to report his name to him. When this had been done, the venerable bishop resolved to commemorate Paul’s name among the names of the blessed for as long as he lived. [Note: [Col. 0650C] Leo added this.] [Note: Added by 1 and 2.]

[Chapter 57.] At the same time [Note: [Col. 0649] “At this time,” 1b and the edition. “At this time, etc., to the end of the chapter,” added by 1b; a new chapter begins here in the edition.] the aforementioned [Note: [Col. 0649] “Aforesaid,” 1b and the edition.] prince Pandulf, who had been count of Teano, built [Col. 0651A] an oratory of Saint John the Baptist beside the church of the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0651] “Aforesaid,” 1b and the edition.] Capuan monastery [Note: [Col. 0651C] He had mentioned it in that account of the monk Paul, which he later deleted.], over the body, that is, of Lord Landenulf [Note: [Col. 0651] *Landenolfus*, 1b and 2; “the glorious prince L.,” 1b.], the prince whom, as we related above (chapter 10), the Capuans had killed. In that oratory, for the benefit of the same monastery, he offered an entire half of the estate called Anglum, with all its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0651] “With all its possessions without exception,” 1b and the edition.].

Much later, namely in the time of Abbot Desiderius, Benedict [Note: [Col. 0651] “Lord Benedict,” 1b and the edition.], the provost, bought the other half of that same estate from Count Pandulf of Presenzano [Note: [Col. 0651] “The count who is surnamed ‘of Presenzano,’” 2.], to whom it belonged by hereditary right [Note: [Col. 0651] “To whom it seemed to belong by hereditary right,” the edition.]. [Note: [Col. 0651] The following passage is cut away in 1b.]

At that time (October 1032), a certain abbess named Raimburga, of the city of Fermo, offered in this monastery her own monastery called [Col. 0651B] Saint Mary, in the place Leveriano [Note: [Col. 0651] *Levarino*, 2.] [Note: [Col. 0651C] Beside the river Aso, according to the document published from the register by Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 129.], and the church of Saint John of Garzania, and the castle of Barbulano with the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Blasius [Note: [Col. 0651] *Basilius*, 4.], together with absolutely all the possessions and appurtenances of those places.

[Note: [Col. 0649] The sentence beginning “At that time” and continuing through “with all its possessions” is added by 1b, but occurs in the middle of chapter 59.]

Peter also, son of Rainerius of the city of Sora, made an offering [Note: [Col. 0651] “Made a charter of offering,” 1b and 2.] to this monastery of the church of Saint Sylvester [Note: [Col. 0651] “Saint Sylvester, which was built,” 1b and the edition.] in the territory of Arpino, at the place called Valle de Frassu, with all its possessions and appurtenances.

Furthermore, during these days, the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0651] “The same,” 1b and the edition.] abbot granted by lease Saint Gregory of Paterno in the county of the Marsi to a certain Rocconius [Note: [Col. 0651] *Racconius*, 3; *Roccanus*, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0651] The name is absent in 4.], with all its appurtenances, for sixty solidi and an annual rent of eight hundred fish. He did the same with the mountain called Sabucus [Note: [Col. 0651] *Sabucu*, 1b and 2.] above [Col. 0651C] the Anio, for which he received forty solidi and an annual rent of two hundred fish. [Note: [Col. 0651] The ending is cut away in 1b. The words “the same … three hundred” are absent there.]

He did the same [Note: [Col. 0651] The edition reads: “The same [abbot] did.”] for the sons of Guanengus concerning lands in Calabretto [Note: [Col. 0651] *Calalielmi*, 4, with an entire line omitted.] [Note: [Col. 0651C] Calabrito, in the territory of Conza.], for sixty solidi and an annual rent of twelve denarii. Likewise, there, for the sons of William: forty solidi, an annual rent of two solidi, and three hundred fish. [Note: [Col. 0651] The edition reads “two hundred fish.”] Similarly, in the territory of Penne, he made a grant of the estate called Bocetula for 140 solidi and an annual rent [Col. 0652A] of six solidi. He also granted the church of Saint Benedict in Lombardy, on the estate of Pasturini, for an annual rent of ten solidi. [Note: [Col. 0651] From “Furthermore” through “ten solidi” is added by 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0652A] In these days Pope Benedict VIII died at Rome (1024), and John, his brother, a Tusculan by nation and son of Gregory, succeeded him in the pontificate. [Note: [Col. 0651C] The same appears in Peter’s catalogue.] Added by 2.]

56. [Chapter 58.] When the Emperor Henry of august memory died in the year of the Lord 1025 [1024, 13 July] [Note: [Col. 0651C] Thus the Anonymous of Monte Cassino.], and Duke Conrad, also called Cono, was raised to kingship through Henry’s election, Prince Pandulf was at last released, at Guaimarius’s entreaty, from the chains which he had deserved to wear perpetually [Note: [Col. 0651] From “Pandulf” through “again Teanensis” is absent from 4.] [Note: [Col. 0651] “Henry, by the judgment of the same Henry, was finally … in the year of the Lord 1025, by the judgment of his magnates,” 1 and 1b.]. [Note: [Col. 0651] *Cuonradus*, 4.]

Returning, he showed himself a man of complete gentleness and humility, came to this monastery, and, promising the abbot all friendship and fidelity upon oath, declared that henceforward he would regard him as father and lord. Immediately, gathering his former supporters from Apulia together with the Greeks and Boioannes [Note: [Col. 0651] “Boioannes the catepan,” 1b and 2; “together with Boioannes the catepan,” added by 1b, where it is better placed after “Greeks.”], while his kinsman Guaimarius [Note: [Col. 0651] “The Salernitan prince and the counts,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 0651] “His kinsman Count Rainulf and Arnulf, and the others from Comino,” added by 1b.] with the Normans [Note: [Col. 0651] Rainulf and Arnulf added by 2.] and the counts of the Marsi strove with all their power, he at last entered Capua, after it had been besieged and taken for a full year and a half. [Note: [Col. 0652C] He held it in May 1026; see Di Meo, *Annali Napoletani*, for that year.]

But Pandulf of Teano, whom we previously said had been made prince of Capua by the emperor [Note: [Col. 0651] “He fled to Naples together with his son John. But …,” 1, corrected by 1b.], was received into protection by the aforesaid Boioannes [Note: [Col. 0651] *Bajanus*, 3; 2 reads: “by the catepan Boioannes, together with his son John and all his people.”] and taken with all his people to Naples. But in the following year [1027], Naples too was taken by the prince of Capua and its military commander Sergius expelled [Note: [Col. 0651] From “and” through “expelled” is absent from 1.]; again Pandulf of Teano, fleeing from him to Rome, died there in exile. The prince of Capua held Naples for nearly three years. [Note: [Col. 0651] “For one year and five months. Therefore Sergius, duke of Naples, joining the aforesaid Rainulf to himself by kinship, made him count at Aversa and established him there with the Normans because of their hatred of the prince,” 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0652C] What he had previously written following the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, he later changed and expanded; compare Amatus I.40, where nothing certain is now read concerning the date.]

Thereafter Sergius, having recovered Naples, joined the valiant Rainulf to himself by marriage and, making him count at Aversa, established him there with his Norman companions because of their hatred and harassment [Note: [Col. 0651] “Persecution,” the edition.] of the prince. Then Aversa began to be inhabited for the first time (1030). [Note: [Col. 0651] “Then—and it began to be inhabited,” added by 1b. From this point 1 continues: “During this approximately [*itaque*; ‘therefore’ in 1b] three-year period, after Basil and then Constantine, emperors at Constantinople, had died, Romanus, his son-in-law [‘Romanus, his son-in-law,’ 1b], assumed the empire. Duke Conrad too, after Henry, received the kingdom of the Romans through Henry’s election. K. Meanwhile Pandulf, not departing from his former wickedness, not only did not diminish but rather increased day by day, and, concerning the devastation of this monastery …”]

Pandulf, moreover, not at all abandoning his former wickedness [Note: [Col. 0653] The edition reads: “and concerning the devastation of this monastery …”], and seeking, as it were out of hatred for the emperor, to satisfy his own malice by the destruction of this monastery [Note: [Col. 0653] “Striving,” 1.], invited—indeed [Note: [Col. 0653] “Rather compelled,” 1.] compelled—Abbot Theobald, under a pretence of goodwill, to remain with him at Capua, supposedly for the security of them both. He consequently would not permit him to return here; nevertheless, he issued for him the customary charter of the former princes confirming the whole abbey (12 April 1032). [Note: [Col. 0653] “He issued a charter,” added by 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0654C] Published by Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 131.]

At that time there was in [Note: [Col. 0653] “In the same Capuan [monastery],” 1.] the Capuan monastery a certain provost named Basilius, a Calabrian by birth, forceful in secular cunning. Formerly he had held a ministerial office at the episcopal house of Saint Stephen; because he was an intimate associate [Note: [Col. 0653] “A most intimate associate,” 1 and the edition.] of the prince, he had been frightened by Emperor Henry’s arrival and fled to this monastery. Later, made a monk by [Note: [Col. 0653] Added by 1b.] the aforesaid abbot, he had been held by him for some time in no small honour [Note: [Col. 0653] “For some time in very great esteem,” 1 and the edition.].

But when the same prince returned and, as we have said, recovered Capua, he summoned the aforesaid Basilius to himself [Note: [Col. 0653] “Summoning the aforesaid Basilius back to himself,” 1.] and caused him to be given the provostship of the Capuan monastery [Note: [Col. 0653] “He made him provost in the Capuan monastery,” 1.]. Forgetting utterly the benefits which the abbot had rendered him [Note: [Col. 0653] “The services,” 1 and the edition.], Basilius inflicted upon him every injury he could, and, puffed up by the prince’s friendship [Note: [Col. 0653] “Trusting in it, and with arrogant mind thus,” 1.], stood in choir at the office like a second abbot.

57. [Chapter 59.] Accordingly [Note: [Col. 0653] “Meanwhile Pandulf,” 1; “Pandulf, then,” the edition.] Pandulf made all the monastery’s men swear fidelity to himself, and, distributing all the castles and villages of the same monastery—except Saint Germanus, Saint Peter, Saint Angelus, and Saint George—to the Normans then attached to him and to his other retainers [Note: [Col. 0653] “Assigning the remaining castles or villages of the same monastery to the jurisdiction of Normans who then adhered to him and of other retainers,” 1.], set a certain Todinus, one of the monastery’s servants and a partner in his wickedness, over all the property which seemed to remain to the monastery [Note: [Col. 0653] “Over the possessions of the entire monastery which seemed to remain,” 1.]. He appointed him to stay at Saint Germanus, in the abbot’s own residence, and entrusted to him also the stronghold called Vantra, ordering all men, Normans as well as all others, to obey him in fidelity to himself [Note: [Col. 0653] “Appointing him and entrusting to him the above-mentioned stronghold called Vantra,” 1.].

Now, how utterly wicked and impious this Todinus [Note: [Col. 0653] 1 reads: “how unjust, how impious.”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “Striving thereby to please the prince,” added by 1 and 2.] proved toward God’s servants, and into what poverty and disgrace he reduced them and this holy place [Note: [Col. 0653] The edition reads “hunger, thirst, and disgrace.”], we cannot fully relate even if eloquence were at hand. I shall touch upon only a few examples: on the very feast of the Assumption of God’s holy Mother, they lacked wine even for the ministry of the altar.

Moreover, whenever he wished to expel a monk from the monastery [Note: [Col. 0653] “To drive him out,” 1.], disdaining, as it were, to tell him so, he ordered that the monk’s *justitia*—his portion or right—from its place at table be removed [Note: [Col. 0653] “He removed only from …,” 1 and the edition.] and put [Note: [Col. 0653] “He put,” 1 and the edition.] upon the floor. By this sign the monk could plainly recognize the reason for his expulsion, and from then on he did not dare remain any longer in the monastery.

He even brought [Note: [Col. 0653] 1 and the edition read: “Moreover, besides other things, he brought the most worthless …”] the most worthless lay members [Note: [Col. 0653] “Even” is absent from 1.] of the monastery’s household into the brothers’ refectory, which no layman had until then dared enter, to set bread and wine upon the tables. Thus at that time nothing remained for the monks but to break forth with Jeremiah into lamentation: “Servants have ruled over us, and there was no one to deliver us from their hands” (Lamentations 5:8).

There still remained Lord Leo, the chief guardian of the church. One day, entering the refectory and finding the servants whom we have mentioned performing that ministry, he was immediately inflamed with religious zeal [Note: [Col. 0653] Added by 4.]. He drove them out with great disgrace, then turned to his fellow brothers and said: “How long, then, shall we remain beneath such dishonour to our order, under the unjust and impious domination of our servants? Follow me: let us all leave this place together [Note: [Col. 0653] “Unanimously,” 1 and the edition.] and go beyond the mountains to the emperor, and let us lamentably recount to him the lamentable history of our calamity.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “Lamentably” added by 4.]

At this exhortation, all immediately roused their spirits [Note: [Col. 0653] “All together and with one accord,” 1; “unanimously,” the edition.] and began to follow him. [Note: [Col. 0653] 1b has *ita* (“thus”); 1 has *consecuti sunt* (“followed”).] [Note: [Col. 0653] “Outside the monastery,” added by 1.] When Todinus [Note: [Col. 0653] 1 reads: “When the same Todinus learned this through a messenger”; 3 has *Theodinus*; 1 has *Todinus*. “Very hastily,” the edition.] learned this through a messenger, he hurried up with the utmost speed; finding them already some distance from the monastery gate, he immediately dismounted from his horse and fell at their feet [Note: [Col. 0653] “Fell down,” 1 and the edition.], praying and urgently entreating with many [Note: [Col. 0653] “Many and great,” 1 and the edition.] expressions of satisfaction that they would deign to return, and promising to correct all things henceforth according to their wishes.

But seeing his great humility [Note: [Col. 0653] “Satisfaction,” 1 and the edition.] and promises, and believing that he sincerely pledged this [Note: [Col. 0653] “And seeing that he promised these things sincerely,” added by 4.], they, being of kindly and compassionate heart, returned without delay. Yet they gained little relief or consolation by this action. [Note: [Col. 0653] This sentence is absent from 4.] Since the aforesaid Todinus persisted in his wickedness [Note: [Col. 0653] This clause is absent from 3.], it happened, by God’s ordinance, that not long [Col. 0655A] afterward, namely under Abbot Richerius, this same Todinus was captured by some of our men, shorn, dressed in sackcloth, and set to sift flour in the millhouse, after the manner of servants. [Note: [Col. 0655C] Compare Amatus II.13.] [Note: [Col. 0653] “But since the aforesaid Todinus persisted in his wickedness, not long afterward, by the avenging God, he was captured, etc., and put …,” 1b and the edition; absent from 1.]

58. [Chapter 60.] Meanwhile our abbot [Note: [Col. 0655] “Our,” added by 4.] remained in the Capuan monastery indeed as abbot in name, but in truth like a captive [Note: [Col. 0655] “A certain captive,” 1.]: he did not dare go anywhere outside the city without an escort. Having endured this for nearly four years [Note: [Col. 0655] “Three,” 3; “very unwillingly,” corrected to “entirely unwillingly,” added by 1 but later deleted.], he secretly instructed Sergius [Note: [Col. 0655] The name was first written differently, then corrected to *Sergius* in 1.] duke of Naples, to come with soldiers on an appointed day to a designated place and take him away. This was done.

On the agreed day he left Capua, as if to take a walk, and went as far as the church of Saint Mark, at the foot of Mount Saint Agatha. From there, gradually and step by step, he joined the aforesaid soldiers [Col. 0655B] and went to Naples; after several days, he departed thence for the March. There, in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Liberator, in which he had formerly been provost, he lived most honourably for about five years until his death.

59. [Chapter 61.] After a few days [Note: [Col. 0655] “Moreover, the prince ordered his most faithful adherent Adelgisius,” 1 and the edition.] the most wicked prince ordered a certain faithful adherent of his, named Adelgisius, to come as quickly as possible to this monastery and swiftly carry off the emperor’s chasuble and chalice, together with several other principal ornaments of the church, to be pledged to the counts of Aquino and Sessa [Note: [Col. 0655] “To be put in pledge,” 1 and the edition.].

When he arrived and declared the purpose for which he had been sent, some of the brothers [Note: [Col. 0655] From “some of the brothers” through “should by no means be sent” is absent from 2.] judged that these objects [Note: [Col. 0655] *ea* (“these objects”) is absent from 1.] should by no means be sent, while others judged that they should by no means be retained, lest they experience worse things from the angry prince [Note: [Col. 0655] “Lest worse things should follow from the angry prince,” 1 and the edition.].

But when the messenger [Note: [Col. 0655] 1 and the edition read “that man.”] insisted absolutely, the aforesaid Adam [Note: [Col. 0655] Absent from 1 and 2.], who then had charge of the church, said: “Good sir [Note: [Col. 0655] “Good man,” added by 4.], I shall never give you, nor any other man [Note: [Col. 0655] “Any human being,” 1 and the edition.], these things which you demand. Rather, I shall put them [Note: [Col. 0655] *ea* (“them”) is absent from 1.] upon the altar of blessed Benedict himself, whose they are [Note: [Col. 0655] “Whose they are,” added by 4.]; let whoever dares remove them from there [Note: [Col. 0655] “Whoever wishes or dares,” 1 and the edition.].”

When he had done this, the other man immediately approached boldly [Note: [Col. 0655] 1 and the edition read: “He approached and …”] [Note: [Col. 0655] “As he was most ready to dare anything,” 1; “a bold and presumptuous man,” the edition.] and, just as he was stretching forth his impious hands toward the altar [Note: [Col. 0655] Several words concerning the altar are absent from 1 and 2.], while the monks stood by grieving: marvellous to tell! he immediately fell upon his face [Note: [Col. 0655] “He approached and fell,” 1 and the edition.] and was suddenly struck with an exceedingly violent paralysis [Note: [Col. 0655] “Epilepsy together with paralysis,” 1 and 2.], offering all present a spectacle concerning himself that was amazing, or rather pitiable. [Col. 0656A]

The next day [Note: [Col. 0655] “From that illness” is absent from 1.] he recovered from that illness in some measure [Note: [Col. 0655] “In some way,” the edition.] and returned without accomplishing his object to the prince. His mouth and one eye, however, remained distorted until his death [Note: [Col. 0655] “Remained so,” 1 and the edition.]. Whenever anyone asked how this had happened to him, he related it, to the great astonishment of those who heard.

The prince, to be sure, was somewhat awed by this event, but a good intention could not long endure in his evil mind. For not long afterward he again sent the aforesaid Basilius [Note: [Col. 0655] “Basilius, provost of the Capuan monastery,” 1; “Basilius the provost,” the edition.] and ordered him to carry off to himself all the treasure of this place [Note: [Col. 0655] “Taking it away, he carried it off,” 1.].

He also took from the Capuan monastery three silver crowns, a book adorned with gems, an excellent citron-coloured chasuble (*planeta diocetrina*) [Note: [Col. 0655] *Cetrina*, 1b and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0655C] Of a deeper citron-yellow colour.], and three altar-cloths: one with white pearls [Note: [Col. 0655C] That is, pearls.], another with a cross in Phrygian work [Note: [Col. 0655C] Embroidered with a needle in Phrygian work.] and white pearls, and a third with eagles. [Col. 0656B] He stored them all together [Note: [Col. 0655] Added by 1b.] in the fortress which he had shortly before built on the mountain of Saint Agatha overlooking Capua. [Note: [Col. 0655] 1b inserts here: “At that time … and its possessions,” a passage already read in chapter 51.] [cf. Desiderius, *Dialogues* I.9.] In that same fortress he had amassed countless spoils, taken by deceit and violence [Note: [Col. 0655] “Snatched away,” 1.], from various other churches, as well as from widows and orphans.

[Note: [Col. 0656B] But I shall recount how, after his death, that same prince was condemned by God, the just judge, for the chalice already mentioned. [Note: [Col. 0656C] The passage beginning “At a certain time” and ending “caused him to be healed” is taken word for word from Desiderius, *Dialogues* I.13; its conclusion has been altered slightly.]
