“the counts of Sesto”: compare Amatus II.40: Adenulf and Lando of Aquino had married daughters of Pandulf; Sesto lies on the right bank of the Volturno below Venafro. “captured him at Teano”: 1–2 identify Adenulf as brother of Count Lando of Aquino; 1 reads that Teano captured him, and 1b that Landulf captured him there. “considerable army”: 1–2 read “Normans as well as our own men.” “Cervaro”: 1 and the edition add “after taking counsel.” “the Wooden Bridge”: 1 and the edition call the adversaries “the aforesaid enemies.” “permission”: manuscript 1’s fuller phrase explicitly grants neither seeing nor speaking; manuscript 4 has *facultas*.

“with his wife and sons”: this is the 1b-and-edition addition after Adenulf’s restored oath. “to Salerno”: manuscript 1 specifies that destination and the edition continues the prior chapter. “Basil … confidence”: 1b and the edition read *adminiculo* (“support”); 1b reads “months,” “the aforesaid counts,” and “terrified by great fear.” For Basil’s last abbacy, manuscript 2 calls it “our cell,” and Gattola’s second witness calls the dead man the provost of the dependent Benedictine house.

**Corrections to the earlier running wording.** At “the commander himself fled,” the source note is specifically: *dux ipse* (“the commander himself”) is absent from the edition. At “Humphrey became count,” the manuscript-1 correction is *humfrida* → *Humfridus*. These replace the earlier malformed and tautological summaries.

### Source-critical apparatus and corrections

For Conrad’s charter, manuscript 4 has *Cuonradus*; manuscripts 1 and 2 add “that is, in the year of our Lord 1038, in which he was ordained.” The base’s “through prayer” is corrected to “through entreaties,” manuscript 1b adds “at Benevento,” and the edition’s reading is “his wife.” The charter is from the original, Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 137. Benedict IX’s privilege has “nevertheless, to him” in manuscript 1 and the edition; Register no. 20 addresses “our dearest son in the Lord Jesus Christ, Richerius, venerable and religious abbot consecrated by us,” and says that his consecration was received as a gift from the pious emperors Henry and Conrad. It is dated sixth indiction, Kalends of July, ANG.

Guaimar’s charter is Register no. 363, dated the second Ides of June in his twenty-second Salerno year, second Capua year, second Amalfi duchy year, and first Sorrento year; Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 140. The material concerning Magipertus’s offering of Limata is placed after chapter 67 in one manuscript, with material from the end of chapter 70 inserted; it says Magipertus offered the island, one hundred *modii*, and that the abbot built and had consecrated Saint Maurice there. The Saint Nicholas charter’s authenticity is doubted by Alessandro di Meo; Mabillon printed a specimen, *Diplomata*, Appendix, p. 116. The following-year eclipse notice is the Anonymous of Cassino under 1042.

Nantarus’s fuller wording in 1b and the edition says that, after gathering brethren for God’s service and acquiring books, ornaments, and land, he transferred Saint Nazarius with every dependency to the monastery with their consent. The Jeroinus sentence is absent in manuscript 1; the edition reads that Jeroinus, with C. D. and I. P., offered Saint Nicholas with all movable property. Register no. 379 identifies Geroinus as judge and John as priest and monk. John Scintus’s gift is “transferred by a charter of donation” in 1b and the edition; manuscripts 1 and 2 place it in Pontescurvo under Mount Saint Leucius, while 1b and the edition add “another church of Saint Mary.” Gattola’s references are *Hist.*, p. 213, p. 215, and *Acc.*, p. 169. The exchange note has “in the territory” in witness 2 and “to this monastery” in the edition.

Adelferius’s Saint Eustasius is “of Pantasia,” near Saint Julian; the note locates it in Capitanata, and 1b and the edition read “with the four churches subject to it.” Variant 4 reads “Marrone” for Morrone. Manuscript 1b omits the sentence about John and Ademarius from “they did the same” through “principal gate,” marked as a likely eye-skip. The Peter note reads “a certain Abbot Peter of Morrone made a charter in this monastery,” and 1b says the church was built in the territory of the city; 1b omits “all the possessions of both churches.” For Raienaldus and Leo, 1b reads “the property and dependencies,” the edition “the property belonging to it,” and 1b and the edition “near the aforesaid city”; the edition retains their names in the offering formula.

In Lando’s donation, manuscript 1 omits “Lando, priest of Aquino”; variant 4 adds “priest” and “gate,” while the edition reads “which he himself had built from the foundations.” The Vicalbo note is “which is called Vicalbo, with everything belonging to it,” in 1b and the edition; ANG. identifies no. 342 as Adam son of Peter and joint donors. From Saint Blaise onward manuscript 1b continues with “Meanwhile the Normans held all the castles around the monastery,” and refers to chapter 67 in manuscript 2; the following material is chapter 67 in this numbering and chapter 66 in another.

For chapter 73, “Picenum” identifies Ascoli; 1b reads “one” and “the other” for the two castles, adds their ornaments and property, and the edition adds “and.” The Cabine share appears to have been excepted in Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 145, where Richerius promised in July 1045 never to alienate it. The land measure is two thousand *modii* in 1b and the edition. The Dauferius lease, from “This abbot” through “bezants,” is absent in manuscript 1. The source’s placement note must remain: chapter 73 continues with “After this Guaimar”; that material is chapter 72 elsewhere. For Corbo, the edition reads “Trontu,” 1b and the edition “subject to this cenobium,” and both read “with all their goods and dependencies”; 1b reads “three thousand *modia*.” Gattola’s reference is *Acc.*, p. 146. The Tederic entry is part of the same chapter continuation.

Chapter 78’s note says manuscript 1b and the edition add “that he should not delay in sending them.” Stephen’s successor was Peter, son of his sister, not Solomon; the source explicitly marks this correction. The heading is placed in different positions in the manuscripts and must not be treated as an unmarked chapter break.

The Norman introductory note preserved in manuscript 1 describes William and Drogo, sons of Tancred, Walter and Petronius, sons of Amicus, leaving Aversa, setting up Atenulf the Elder, moving toward Apulia and Melfi, and fighting the Lombards in 1041; manuscript 1 breaks off after “when Drogo …”. Manuscripts 2 and 3 spell Maniakes *Maniacus* and *Maniachis*; William is *Guilielmus* (2), *Guillelmus* (3), and *Guiellelmus* (4), while the edition has *Umfridus* for Humphrey. The editorial note says Maniakes aspired to the empire only after becoming catapan again in 1042; the successor’s forms are “Duchane,” “Dulchiano,” and Greek *Dokeianos*. Aimé says Arduin was raised to high honor and placed over many cities without naming a locality.

The horse episode has the edition’s wording “when the horse was demanded from him” and “the horse was taken from him”; its revenge passage reads “with patient cunning, from that moment awaiting a suitable time for repayment.” Aimé’s speech says, “You live there like the mouse that is in the hole.” At Melfi, Aimé reads “now Lavello; fair Apulia.” The first battle was beside the Olivento; the Annals of Bari read “Dulibentis,” while Aimé omits the name. The printed note “the commander himself” is absent from the edition. The second battle’s Varangian note records Montepeloso in Basilicata; Exaugustus is “the vicar of Augustus” in Aimé, and the Annals of Bari call him Bugianus. The later Melfi distribution has Walter as Amicus’s son, “Frigento” in Meo against “Argyneze” in Aimé, Saint Archangel’s Rudolf as “Rudolf, son of Bebena” in Aimé, and Arduin’s share is denied in the edition. The source says Amatus has been copied up to this point; William’s death is “William is dead” in the edition, and Drogo’s is “was killed” in manuscripts 1 and 2. The source form *humfrida* is corrected to *Humfridus* in manuscript 1; Robert’s name is *Guiscardus*, corrected to “Visc.”, and manuscripts 1 and 2 preserve Amatus’s “After Count Robert died, Viscardus…”

The Aversa succession apparatus is retained: manuscript 1 reads “Aschettinus Rodelgeri”; the expanded note identifies Rudolf son of Oddo, Rudolf Trincanocte, William Bellabocca, and Richard son of Aschettinus, with Conrad’s name in manuscript 1. Aimé reads “Raidulf, count of Aversa.” The editor says Leo correctly inserted “William the count” in his earlier edition, citing a 1048 charter with William and Herimannus as counts, Richard’s 1050 co-rule, and Di Meo VII, p. 283.

In chapter 67, the fortress is Vantra (chapter 57). Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “they made an agreement with the abbot” for the protection offer; the edition reads “they would hand over the fortress in the same condition.” The Pignataro note has “the town called Pignataro.” The Assumption variant says both parties acted willingly and restored the fortress to the abbot. Manuscript 1 continues with the placement notice about Norman-held castles, excluding Saint Germanus, Saint Peter, Saint Michael, and Saint George; that passage is chapter 65 through “possessions.”

In chapter 68, the Sesto note identifies its territory on the right bank of the Volturno below Venafro; the edition adds “to the extent of their power.” Compare Amatus II.40: Adenulf and Lando of Aquino had married Pandulf’s daughters. Manuscripts 1 and 2 identify Adenulf as the brother of Count Lando of Aquino. The attack note reads “having assembled” in the edition, and the crossing note “they were unable to cross”; “remained assembled” is the edition’s reading at Saint Germanus. The Cervaro attack is “after taking counsel” in the edition. Manuscript 1 says the Normans bravely resisted; the edition says the Teano count was hastening to the abbot’s service. The source’s “the commander himself” is absent from the edition in the Olivento account. The brethren’s reply preserves the complete scope: they would surrender all monastery property and sooner lose their own lives than betray a man under protection. Manuscript 1 adds “thus”; variant 4 has “permission,” while manuscript 1 says permission was granted to see and speak with the abbot. Manuscript 1b and the edition add that Adenulf restored an oath of fidelity with his wife and sons.

In chapter 69, manuscript 1 reads “he immediately summoned him to Salerno,” and the edition continues the preceding chapter at that point. The journey note says “all the necessities” in the edition; manuscript 1 adds that a companion died during the Roman stay. The pestilence killed Siconulf and 2,500 people. The edition reads “for the injury” and “had regarded the place as insignificant.” The return variant is “with five hundred soldiers from Lombardy” in witness 4; manuscript 1b says he returned beyond the mountains on Guaimar’s advice for a stronger army. Basil’s support is “assistance” in 1b and the edition, “for several months” in 1b, and “having been greatly terrified” in 1b; variant 4 adds “in a dishonorable condition.” The closing note identifies Basil’s later abbey as the monastery of Saint Benedict subject to Cassino; Gattola’s witness reads “our cell.”

70. Nearly two years after Richer had gone beyond the mountains, he returned again with a fairly large force assembled. But Guaimar did not think it advisable to attack the Normans even with them. At last, after making all the Normans who held lands of the monastery swear fealty to the abbot, he dismissed the entire army to their homes; and the abbot returned to the monastery. Meanwhile, since the aforesaid townsmen of Saint Angelo still remained turbulent and were again urging the men of Aquino to receive them, the abbot, remembering how they had formerly deserted him at the time of his capture, assembled the Normans and attacked the same town. Having captured and plundered all its leading men, he demolished the encircling walls from their foundations. Thus at last he compelled those hitherto faithless and unruly people to remain quiet thereafter.

71. Moreover, when our Normans undertook to build and fortify as their stronghold the castle of Saint Andrew, the abbot ordered them to desist from what they had begun; but they were willing to show him absolutely no obedience and no respect in this matter. Therefore, seeing both that the strength of the Normans was increasing daily and that, since there was no one to help him, he was making no progress whatever, the abbot, grieving and sorrowing and not knowing where to turn, finally resolved to go beyond the mountains, never thereafter to return here. But when his own advisers had altogether dissuaded him from this course, and had urged rather that he take counsel how, with the help of Father Benedict, he might defend himself against such manifest perjurers, behold: by God’s will, not many days later their count, named Rodulf, came to the abbot’s court with not a few soldiers accompanying him (1045), intending, as was then thought, either to capture or to kill the abbot. But his grief—indeed, his deceit—was turned upon his own head.

For, when he had entered the church, after laying aside his weapons outside in accordance with custom, in order to pray there together with all the others (cf. Amatus II.41), suddenly all the monastery’s servants gathered together; they seized their horses and weapons, shut the doors of the church, and began all at once to ring the bells. Hearing this, the remaining inhabitants of the town, wholly ignorant of what was happening and greatly terrified, ran from every direction armed with various weapons. Disturbed, as the crowd commonly is, by the rumour that the abbot was being captured, they immediately burst in through the opened doors of the basilica and attacked the Normans, armed only with swords. Although the latter resisted and tried to defend themselves, at last vainly calling upon the faith of God which they themselves had long held cheap and violated, fifteen were cut down as the rest fled. The monks caught only the count, snatching him with difficulty from the mob’s hands and ordering that he be taken up to the monastery and held in custody.

After this they immediately went around the whole territory. Attacking the people, who were seized by sudden fear, they recovered almost the entire land that very day, with God’s help, except for the castle of Saint Victor and the aforesaid fortress of Saint Andrew. Then, without delay, they summoned the counts of the Marsi, the sons of Borrellus, and the other faithful supporters of the monastery to their aid. After recovering the town of Saint Victor a few days later, they marched to besiege and storm the fortress of Saint Andrew, into which the wife of the aforesaid count and the remaining Normans had withdrawn.

When they had remained there for almost thirteen days and could not prevail either against the fortification of the place or against the resistance of its occupants, the brethren who were present, angered at the besiegers, said at about the ninth hour of the day:

> “Why,” they said, “do you waste day after day in delays and consume time to no purpose, accomplishing nothing? Rise at last; attack the fortress all together and fear nothing. For your struggle is against God’s enemies, against our perjurers, against the vilest robbers. God will be present, and most holy Father Benedict, who will bring worthy confusion upon our adversaries, guilty of unbelief and perjury, and victory to us who rely upon justice.”

Inflamed by this exhortation, all immediately seized their weapons and, though the enemy resisted from within, attacked the fortress with every effort, using stones, missiles, and projectiles.

I am about to relate something wonderful, but entirely true, without any hesitation. While stones and darts were being hurled man against man from both sides, the Normans’ weapons and every missile coming from within, once mingled with ours, began—as though driven back inward by some powerful wind—to be turned against those who had thrown them and to wound many of them. Seeing this, the Normans were seized with the greatest astonishment; unable any longer to oppose God’s will, they immediately surrendered the fortress and delivered themselves into the hands of the monks. Protected by them only with difficulty, they returned to Aversa unarmed and half-naked. Their horses, arms, and money were all left to their enemies. Thus, by the aid and merits of blessed Benedict, this land was restored in its entirety to its rightful possession, and from that time onward, by God’s mercy, remained free from Norman assaults.

72. Finally, so that all these things may be believed to have been done by the will and help of Father Benedict: on the very night preceding that day, a certain peasant of the castle of Cervaro, named Jerome, was resting in his house. Awake in a dream, he saw himself returning by the road that leads from the castle of Mortula. Suddenly a monk of most venerable appearance, apparently weary from a long journey and carrying a staff in his hand, joined him on the road. As they walked together and reached the fork from which one turns toward the village of Saint Andrew, the monk asked his companion to rest a little from the labour of the journey. When the peasant agreed, he asked the monk where he had come from, so weary and exhausted.

The other replied: “It has now been a long time since I built a monastery on that mountain”—and at the same time he pointed with his finger to this mountain—“and lived there with the brethren. But after some time they began to be very ungrateful to me. Unable any longer to bear their troubles, I left them and went to Jerusalem; there I have stayed with blessed Stephen for forty years and more. Now, summoned by their frequent messages and prayers, I have returned. If henceforth they amend their conduct, I shall remain there with them; but if not, I shall immediately return by the road by which I came.”

Asked his name, he replied that he was called Benedict. They rose and resumed their journey. When the monk had entered the road leading to Saint Andrew and the peasant asked where he was going, he replied: “I am going this way, because I have something to do in this nearby fortress.” Waking up, the peasant told his lord, the archpriest Mainard, the dream that he had seen; and on that very day the fortress was taken in the manner described above.

Even today there are some inhabitants of that fortress who maintain that, in the very severe conflict between the two sides, they saw a certain monk fighting manfully against the Normans and most vigorously encouraging his own side, although none of the monks who were present then had taken part in that battle.

[Desiderius, *Dialogues* II.22.] Likewise, not many days earlier, another peasant had a very vivid vision that Father Benedict, pursuing all the Normans dwelling only in this territory, drove them before him with the staff he carried in his hand; beating them most severely, he banished them from this land far away with the greatest disgrace, no one resisting him even slightly.

These events concerning the expulsion of the Normans took place in the year of the Lord 1045, in the month of May, indiction 13. When afterward the men of Aversa resolved to avenge the injuries of their allies, Guaimar both dissuaded and prevented them. Then, when almost a year had passed, he came to this monastery with Drogo, count of the Normans, and many other leaders. At their most earnest request that the aforesaid Count Rodulf should be released and restored to his relatives, this was at last obtained with difficulty. First, however, an oath was exacted from Rodulf that he would never again concern himself with seeking any possession belonging to this monastery, and that he would never repay the abbot or any of ours with retaliation or requital for this deed or desert. Thus at last restored to his former liberty, and presented by the abbot with a thousand tareni offered that day by the aforesaid leaders, he returned to Aversa to his father-in-law.

73. [Chapter 74.] Since the abbot had long suspected Norman wickedness, he fortified each of the monastery’s castles with encircling walls and arranged for the peasants, who had until then lived in villages, to dwell there. At that time he also surrounded with larger walls the town of Saint Angelo, which he himself had formerly destroyed. Beside it he constructed an excellent bridge over the river Liri.

> [Note: Col. 0679: He had originally written this chapter together with the following one after chapter 75; he transferred it here by means of added signs.]  
> [Note: Col. 0679: “he himself,” 1, edition.]  
> [Note: Col. 0679C: Compare chapter 70.]  
> [Note: Col. 0680C: Compare below, III.25.]

74. [Chapter 75.] Furthermore, because of their hostility to Guaimar, the Gaetans summoned the aforesaid Adenulf, count of Aquino, and appointed him their leader. On hearing this, Guaimar immediately sent an army there. But Adenulf, vigorously confronting them, put some of them to flight in the first attack; he himself, however, was immediately captured and brought to Guaimar.

Meanwhile Pandulf, still persisting in his former wickedness and in his earlier hatred of this place, summoned the Normans who had been expelled from there. He promised them that he would easily restore to them the whole land of this monastery from which they had been driven, if they would give him assistance against Guaimar. They willingly promised this; and he immediately entered this land with a considerable army of both them and their allies, pitching camp at the first town, Saint Peter in Flea [now Saint Peter in Fine]. Unless God prevented him, he was about to overrun the whole land completely.

Therefore flight came again, tribulation and immense terror again invaded the entire land, so that the houses of some of the soldiers were then set in order up around the monastery for its defence. Since they no longer hoped for help from any human being, the abbot ordered the brethren to seek divine aid in this matter and, barefoot, to go with litanies through all the churches of the mountain.

When Adenulf learned this, he sent word to Guaimar that, if Guaimar would release him, he would immediately destroy Pandulf’s undertaking and would pledge by an inviolable oath perpetual fealty to Guaimar and every kind of protection to the monastery of blessed Benedict. For Pandulf, who held the sister of the counts of Teano captive, had refused to surrender her for Adenulf’s release. Accordingly Adenulf was very—and rightly—angered against Pandulf, complaining that he himself had not been redeemed for the sake of one woman.

This was done; and Adenulf, released on the terms he had fixed, came immediately to the abbot and disclosed the entire affair. The next morning he went up to the monastery amid the greatest joy of all. Devoutly, he placed upon the altar of blessed Benedict the emperor’s golden chalice and a diaper-patterned cope, which he had long before received from the aforesaid Pandulf as pledges. There the abbot presented him with an excellent horse, distinguished arms, and a most beautiful standard, and appointed him defender of the monastery.

Adenulf immediately sent word to Pandulf that he had returned and had been appointed defender of the monastery: Pandulf must depart from the monastery’s territory as quickly as possible, unless perhaps he wished Adenulf to expel him disgracefully. Pandulf did not believe this at all. Within two days Adenulf gathered a sizeable army from both relatives and friends; and, intending to engage Pandulf on the following day, he pitched camp in the field called *Ad perticellas* [“At the little poles”; the name is now obsolete]. At the sight of this Pandulf, at last believing the messages sent to him, immediately withdrew in confusion. Adenulf returned in peace to the duchy of Gaeta, which Guaimar had confirmed to him.

75. [Chapter 76.] After these events Count Rodulf, the aforesaid leader of the expelled men, forgetting—or rather holding of little account—the oath he had sworn, as is characteristic of a faithless and insatiably greedy race, resolved with certain companions in his wickedness to come again into this land for plunder. When this had been firmly determined among them, and a messenger had been sent to inform the abbot of the plan so that he might take precautions, Rodulf was found dead by sudden death one morning, on the very day he had intended to carry it out, through the terrible judgment of God.

This so terrified the other Normans that they no longer ventured to come into this land either to invade or to plunder it. Finally, as a manifest vengeance of this holy place, one hundred and fifty Norman soldiers of this same count perished within almost two years, in different places and by different deaths.

76. [Chapter 77.] The counts of Teano persistently promised a certain kinsman of the abbot, named Ardemannus, whom the abbot had stationed to guard the fortress called Vantra, both very great gifts and their sister in marriage if he would hand that fortress over to them. The shrewd man promised everything and agreed secretly to admit them at night, at a time appointed. But when they came to the place and hour arranged, he admitted Laidulf, one of the same counts, with several soldiers, suddenly shut the gates, and threw them all into chains. The rest, repulsed, returned home in deserved disgrace.

Afterward, at Guaimar’s request, the abbot was asked through Guaimar’s brother Guy, Count Rainulf, and Leo of Manso, an eminent man, to restore the count to his brothers. Considering that the prayers of such great men ought by no means to be rejected, he did what was requested: he accepted from the brothers of the aforesaid Count Laidulf an oath and renunciation, backed by an obligation of one hundred pounds of gold.

Ardemannus bore this affair most indignantly. He immediately rebelled in the same fortress and threatened to hand it over to the Normans. Greatly disturbed by this report, the abbot at once collected several soldiers and went to the fortress. By many entreaties and promises he could scarcely at last persuade Ardemannus to come down for a conference. But although he offered him satisfaction by weighty arguments and the greatest blandishments, he could not in any way placate him. The soldiers who were with the abbot then immediately seized Ardemannus and threatened him with instant death—even against the abbot’s will—unless he surrendered the fortress to them as quickly as possible.

Since the utterly wicked man did not yield even then and declared that he preferred to be killed rather than surrender the fortress, they immediately bound him upon wooden hurdles, armed themselves all together to storm the fortress, and approached carrying him before them. Meanwhile that evil man, filled with the devil, shouted to his men that they should crush him first rather than surrender the fortress to anyone. But those who were in the stronghold, seeing their lord the abbot, and at the same time both warned and frightened by him, immediately opened the gates, threw themselves at his feet, asked pardon, and restored the fortress to him without delay.

77. [Chapter 79.] (Desiderius, *Dialogues* III, Prologue.) Furthermore, at Rome Pope Benedict, having for twelve years besieged rather than sat in the apostolic see, was expelled by the Romans. John, bishop of Sabina, who was called Sylvester, was substituted into the Roman pontificate—not, however, without payment (1044). After he had held office there for three months, the expelled Benedict, aided by his relatives, the Tusculan magnates, drove out Sylvester and again occupied the Roman see.

Not long afterward, seeing that he was hated and detested by everyone, Benedict accepted a very large sum of money from a certain archpriest named John, who was regarded as somewhat more religious, and—alas!—sold him the papacy, in order thereafter freely to indulge his own desires in his ancestral household. The aforesaid archpriest, to whom the papal name Gregory had been given, had already presided over the apostolic see for two years and eight months when Emperor Henry, son of Conrad, on hearing of so many abominations concerning the Roman and apostolic see, inspired from heaven, entered Italy in the year of the Lord 1047 [i.e. 1046] and hastened to Rome.

Desiring to cleanse the apostolic see of so great a heresy, he halted at Sutri and decided to hold there a general council of bishops to deliberate upon so grave a matter (December). Accordingly he sent invitations and, after a great multitude of bishops, abbots, and religious men had assembled there, he suitably invited the Roman pontiff also, to preside over the council. In short, after the council had met and Gregory had been convicted of simony by synodal and canonical judgments, he voluntarily stepped down from the see, laid aside the episcopal insignia, fell prostrate on the ground, and humbly asked that pardon be granted him for the dignity he had invaded and purchased.

The emperor, greatly rejoicing at this, came to Rome with all the bishops of that council. In the church of blessed Peter the Apostle, with the Roman clergy and people assembled, after explaining what he had done at Sutri, he began at last to deliberate about the ordering of the Roman Church itself. An inquiry was therefore made as to who in that church might be considered worthy of so great a priesthood. Since, alas and sorrow, no one could be found—for all, following the example of their wretched head, were afflicted, besides other vices, especially with the plague of fornication and simony—a bishop of Bamberg was raised to be Roman pope by an election necessary rather than canonical, and was given the name Clement (25 December).

Because affairs of this kind had been conducted so usefully and so canonically, the Romans at that time bestowed upon Henry the dignity of patriciate and decreed that, in addition to the imperial crown, he should wear a golden circlet.

[Col. 0684B] 78. [Chapter 80.] After this the emperor raised an army (1047) and came to this monastery. Received with every honour by the brethren, he placed upon the altar of blessed Benedict an excellent purple chasuble adorned with gold and gems, together with another pallium of no small size. In the chapter house he offered the brethren several pounds of gold; then, commending himself to them most devoutly, he went to Capua.

There Guaimar surrendered Capua, which he had held for nine years, and restored it to the oft-mentioned Pandulf together with Pandulf’s son, after receiving much gold from them. Drogo, count of Apulia, and Rainulf, count of Aversa, came to him, offering many horses and very great sums of money; he confirmed by imperial investiture all the territory which they then held. There too, in accordance with imperial custom, he issued for our abbot a charter sealed with a golden bull (3 February).

Proceeding thence to Benevento, since the citizens would not receive him, he caused the Roman pontiff, who was then with him, to excommunicate that city. Confirming all the Beneventan territory to the Normans by his authority, he returned beyond the mountains, taking the former pope Gregory with him.

79. [Chapter 81.] (*Desiderius, Dialogues*, II.) After Clement had died beyond the mountains nine months later (9 October) [Note: [Col. 0685] “At Rome” is absent in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0685C] From Amatus III.14; but this is false.] the aforesaid Benedict, having returned once more to the pontificate, held him by force for about eight months [Note: [Col. 0685] “By force” is absent from 1b and 2.], until Damasus, bishop of Brixen [Note: [Col. 0685C] “Bishop of Brixen and pope at Palestrina,” from Amatus, same passage.], sent from Germany by the emperor, received the papacy. [Note: [Col. 0685] “Then Damasus succeeded him in the papacy from Germany,” 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0685] “The aforesaid,” “the aforementioned”; Damasus succeeded him in the papacy, from G., in 1; corrected in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0685C] “The aforesaid … retained”: Desiderius does not have this.] [Note: [Col. 0685] “Succeeded him in the papacy,” 1b and the edition.]

When he too died at Palestrina after twenty-three days (9 August) [Note: [Col. 0685] “At Palestrina” is absent from 1.] [Note: [Col. 0685C] 9 August, *Necrology of Monte Cassino*], the Romans, seeking Bruno, bishop of Toul, a German by nationality and descended from royal stock, from beyond the mountains, elected him as their pontiff and decreed that he should be called Pope Leo. [Note: [Col. 0685] “A German by nationality” and “adding this,” 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0685] “From beyond the mountains,” “from the ultramontane regions,” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0685C] Up to this point he has followed Desiderius.]

That holy pontiff, in the same year in which he was ordained, visited Mount Gargano for prayer. [Note: [Col. 0685] “Was”; [he] came to Capua. There, after the elder Pandulf had died, he consecrated as archbishop Hildebrand, the younger Pandulf’s brother, and then set out for Salerno, according to 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0685C] “In April,” according to the second manuscript of the *Annals of Benevento*, Vatican codex; therefore one or the other must have erred.] Returning from there, on Palm Sunday itself (1049, 19 March), he came to this monastery. [Note: [Col. 0685] “Very devoutly,” added in 1 and the edition.] Reverently received by the brethren, he solemnly celebrated Mass [Note: [Col. 0685] “Mass on that day,” 1.] and ate with them in the refectory. After the meal [Note: [Col. 0685] Added in 4.] he came into chapter and, thanking the brethren for his highly honourable reception, humbly commended himself to them and promised that, to the extent of his ability, he would honour and exalt the same monastery. [Note: [Col. 0685] “He gave very great thanks to the brethren for the honour shown him, and commended himself to them,” the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0685] “Everywhere exalt,” 1 and the edition.] He then went down; and on the following day [Note: [Col. 0685] “And on the next day”—the words “the hand of Frederick the deacon and chancellor” are deleted—he departed and went to Capua. There, after the elder Pandulf had died, he carefully examined Hildebrand, the younger Pandulf’s brother, elected by the people of Capua; he proceeded to Salerno, consecrated him there, and sent him back to Capua as archbishop. He then visited Mount Gargano for prayer and finally returned to Rome. [Corrected from “went back to Rome.”] On the day before the feast of St Michael, he dedicated the church of St Maurice at Limata, built by that same abbot, as stated above, and returned to Rome, 1b.]

On the following day he solemnly dedicated the church of St Maurice at the island called Limata, built by the aforesaid abbot [Note: [Col. 0685] “By the same abbot,” 1b and the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0686A] “And he solemnly dedicated the church of St Saviour in the territory of Atina,” added in 2.], and finally returned to Rome.

Richerius went to him and honourably obtained from him a privilege according to the custom of his predecessors. [Note: [Col. 0685] “The abbot, having gone to him, privately obtained, and so forth”; 1b and the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0685] “Having gone to him, he also honourably obtained from him the consecration and privilege. For until that time he had postponed his consecration. In the following year, etc. (chapter 82),” 1.] [Note: [Col. 0686C] Register, no. 21. ANG.] In it the same apostolic lord granted, by apostolic authority, the use of sandals and the dalmatic, as well as gloves, at the solemnities of Mass on principal feasts, both to him and to all who should thereafter be regularly promoted in this monastery, in honour of this holy place. [Note: [Col. 0685] The words “in which … granted” are absent from 1b; here they were inserted later: “In the same year Corbo … four thousand; see chapter 65.”]

Moreover [Note: [Col. 0685] “At that time the same apostolic lord” (or “holy pontiff,” 1b), occurs in 1b and the edition.], he granted to the same abbot, for the sake of hospitality, the monastery of Holy Jerusalem, called Suxorian, situated within the city of Rome, with all its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0686C] It is also called Holy Cross. Leo IX; the Sessorian palace. Victor II.] [Note: [Col. 0685] “To the aforesaid abbot, for the sake of hospitality, with all its appurtenances, granted” (“contradicted,” in the edition), 1b and the edition], and issued him a privilege concerning it (1049). [Note: [Col. 0686C] Gattola, *Historia*, p. 252.] He reserved to himself only the consecration of the abbot of that place, whom the abbot of Monte Cassino was nevertheless to elect.

80. [Chapter 82.] Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0685] “During these days, when the Capuans …”; 1. The chapter was originally written after chapter 82, but he later moved it.] [Note: [Col. 0686C] Compare *Desiderius, Dialogues*, I.10.] certain noblemen of Capua had carried on many disputes with the abbot concerning a certain castle of this monastery called Conca [Note: [Col. 0685] “Had caused” or “had brought about,” trying indeed to withdraw it from the monastery’s jurisdiction and reduce it to their own use. But since they could not prevail against the abbot in anything, 1 and the edition.], but, with the help of Father Benedict, had been unable to prevail against him. One day, after taking counsel, they decided to come raiding into this territory.

They therefore determined to begin their journey at evening, rest briefly at one of their estates near Teano [Note: [Col. 0685] “In the county of Teano,” 1 and 2], and then proceed at such an hour of the night that they might enter the boundaries of the monastery at dawn, rush in unexpectedly, and carry off as much booty as possible. They did as they had planned [Note: [Col. 0685] “Having come to the appointed place, when they had rested as long as seemed good to them,” 1.]. At about midnight [Note: [Col. 0685] Added in 1b.], mounting their horses, they set out for their intended destination.

A wonderful thing—but wholly certain, since it was related to me by one of those who took part in that mounted expedition. [Note: [Col. 0685] “Such a thing I am about to relate, yet without any hesitation it is wholly true, since I learned it from the mouth of one of them. From …,” 1.] From that hour until daybreak they travelled; and when they thought that they had reached the borders of this land and were urgently preparing to scatter abroad, as raiders customarily do, they suddenly looked around [Note: [Col. 0687] “Looked back,” 1 and the edition.] and found themselves in the place where they had mounted their horses.

Astonished and utterly bewildered, looking at one another, they finally understood that they had been blinded by the error of the night through the merits of Father Benedict. Although they thought they had travelled straight ahead for so long a time, they found themselves in the morning at the same estate from which they had risen, having gone round and round it. [Note: [Col. 0687] “And found themselves there from which they had risen, and thus …,” 1 and the edition.] Thus, filled alike with shame and amazement, they returned to Capua, themselves openly recounting to everyone whatever had happened to them. [Note: [Col. 0687] The words “themselves … had happened” are added in 1b.]

[Note: [Col. 0687A] [Chapter 83.] (Peter Damian, *Letter* I.9.) At that time a certain servant of God from the region of Naples lived as a solitary on a steep rock beside the public road. While he was chanting psalms at night and opened the window of his little cell—the observer of the hours—behold, he saw many black men like Ethiopians taking the road and driving pack-asses laden with hay in a long train. Curious, he asked who they were and for what purpose they were preparing this fodder for beasts of burden. The demons replied that it was not for feeding cattle, but rather fuel for fires in which human beings were to be burned. “For we are shortly expecting Pandulf, prince of Capua, since he is already lying sick.” Having heard this, the man of God immediately sent a messenger to the walls of Capua; arriving there, he found Pandulf already dead (981). After his death Mount Vesuvius burst into flames, and such a mass of sulphurous resin immediately flowed from Vesuvius itself that it formed a torrent and descended with rushing force into the sea. Added in 2.]

81. [Chapter 84.] In the following year, 1050, the aforesaid apostolic lord again came to this monastery [Note: [Col. 0687] “Pontiff,” 1 and the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0687] “This” is absent from the edition.] on the vigil of St Peter; and on the following day and the day after, he solemnly celebrated the Masses of the apostles Peter and Paul. Since that day was Saturday (30 June), he entered at the brethren’s invitation, washed the feet of twelve monks, and, having himself also been washed by them [Note: [Col. 0687] “And then went with them,” added in 1b.], went with them into the refectory to drink according to the custom of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0687] “Very devoutly,” 1 and 2; “went,” 3.].

He then went to Benevento and at last absolved it from the excommunication imposed by his predecessor Clement. [Note: [Col. 0687] Here, in manuscript 1, begins the final quaternion, which appears to have been written in Leo’s own hand.] In the next year (1051), coming to Capua [Note: [Col. 0687] “Came, and again proceeded to Benevento”; corrected from “coming,” and the word “again” deleted in 1.], he again went to Benevento, and thence proceeded to Salerno. [Note: [Col. 0687C] 5 July; from there he went to Salerno on 8 August, according to the *Annals of Benevento*.]

Afterwards, eagerly seeking to assemble soldiers from every quarter in order to expel the Normans [Note: [Col. 0687] The words “men from every quarter” are absent from 1 and 2.], he crossed the mountains to the emperor (1052). [Note: [Col. 0687] “He went away, intending to hire soldiers from there,” 1 and the edition.]

Gebeard, then bishop of Eichstätt, a Norican by nationality, a most prudent man and highly skilled in secular affairs, was the king’s counsellor. [Note: [Col. 0687] “Gebeard … accompanying him,” added in 1b.] But when, by imperial command, a very great army had been entrusted to the apostolic lord (1053), and they had already completed no small part of the journey, that bishop approached the emperor and strongly reproached him concerning this matter. By deceit he brought it about that the whole army should return [Note: [Col. 0687] “Is absent in 4.”], leaving only about five hundred of the apostolic lord’s relatives and friends [Note: [Col. 0687] “And” is absent from the edition.] to accompany him into these regions. [Note: [Col. 0688A] At that time the exchange was made between the same apostolic lord and the emperor concerning Benevento and the bishopric of Bamberg, as we have already related above (chapter 46). Added in 2.]

82. [Chapter 85.] In this year (1052) [Note: [Col. 0687C] June, according to the second recension of the *Annals of Benevento*], Guaimar, prince, was killed beside the coast of the Salernitan sea through a conspiracy of the Amalfitans, whom he had treated most indignantly [Note: [Col. 0687] “Whom they had treated,” 4.], together with certain of his kinsmen and men of Salerno [Note: [Col. 0687] The words “together with certain kinsmen” are absent from 1.], pierced with thirty-six wounds [Note: [Col. 0687] “Thirty-six wounds” is absent from 1.]. [Note: [Col. 0687C] From Amatus III.25.] He was dragged for some time along the seashore, most shamefully and amid great mockery [Note: [Col. 0687] “His body was dragged for a long time along the shore and treated with great mockery. But with the assistance of the Normans, …,” 1.], and the city together with the castle was seized by them. [Note: [Col. 0687C] III.26.]

But on the fifth day [Note: [Col. 0688C] 5 June, *Amatus* III.28; I fear that our author may have interpreted it incorrectly.] the city was recovered, with Norman assistance, by Guy, brother of the prince himself, and restored to his son Gisulf. [Note: [Col. 0687] “After the city had been recovered and restored to his son Gisulf,” 1. “During these days,” chapter 80.] The authors of so great a crime were slain: namely, four kinsmen of the same Guaimar and thirty-six others. [Note: [Col. 0688C] *Amatus* III.31.]

83. [Chapter 86.] At this same time Landenulf and Adenulf, noble brothers of the city of Capua, together with their nephew Peter, came together to this monastery for the sake of conversion, and offered in their entirety to blessed Benedict all their resources, inheritances, and possessions throughout the whole principality of Capua. [Note: [Col. 0688C] Register, no. 336. ANG.]

That is: the church of St Nicholas within Capua [Note: [Col. 0687] “Is absent in 4.”], with all its appurtenances; likewise their full shares in the churches of St Saviour and St Rufus, also within Capua; the orchard at the bridge of Casulino; the estate called Calabrina, with the church of St Nicander built there; lands and mills on the river Saone; an estate at Sala [Note: [Col. 0689] “Salam,” in the edition.], Adipsi Porcari; the estate called Rapedella, with its dependent woods and marshes; lands, woods, and meadows at Aucia itself [Note: [Col. 0689] “At the same Aucia,” 1b.]; the estate of Calinulo near the aforesaid Saone; an estate at the place called Cervianum; a share of the church of St James and of the estate at the place Bucinu, with the church of St Anastasia; lands, woods, and marshes at the place called Rustinitu [Note: [Col. 0689] “Marshes,” 1b.]; an estate in Cilicia with a share in the church of St John; estates and lands in the district of Liburia, at Porano [Note: [Col. 0689] “Paurano,” 1b.] near Lake Patria; a holding in the village of Cupuli; likewise holdings in the settlement of Pesenna; holdings at the place called Felice; lands in the wood of Mataloni, at Marcenisi, and at M[.....]drelle; an estate near Grecinianum, at the place called Senosa [Note: [Col. 0689] “Fenosa,” 2.]; an estate at Laneo [Note: [Col. 0689] “Laneto,” 3.], by the broken bridge. [Note: [Col. 0689C] The river Lanius, Latin *Clanius*, commonly Lagno. ANG.] Lands in the estate of Valentiana; and all the houses belonging to them within Capua [Note: [Col. 0689] “Is absent in 3.”].

84. [Chapter 87.] Having returned from beyond the mountains, the Roman pontiff again came to this monastery (1053) [Note: [Col. 0689] In this form it was first written immediately after chapter 79.], and commended himself very humbly to the brethren. [Note: [Col. 0689] “Thus,” 1b; “more than five hundred very warlike Lotharingian men did he bring with him; and, coming …,” 1.] Having been honourably lodged at San Germano, he was asked by the brethren to restore to them the monastery of St Stephen above Terracina. [Note: [Col. 0689C] From the pope’s privilege edited by Gattola, *Historia*, p. 117; issued before the journey undertaken to Germany.] He asked whether it had ever belonged to them. When they answered yes, he demanded that this be shown to him.

Accordingly, when the *Dialogues* of St Gregory had immediately been produced and it had been shown from the life of St Benedict how that same father had built it in a vision—either they did not know of, or did not have at hand, the privilege which Pope Agapetus had issued concerning it for Abbot Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0689] “Or had made” is absent from 1.] [Note: [Col. 0689C] Compare Book I, chapter 59]—the holy pontiff said: “Truly, what you ask is most just.” He at once ordered a privilege to be drawn up concerning it by Chancellor Frederick (20 May), and decreed that the monastery itself, with all its possessions, should be assigned to us.

At the same time (1053, 29 May), he also issued another charter for this monastery [Note: [Col. 0689] “He made … another precept … concerning freedom,” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 0689C] Ibid., p. 144.] concerning the freedom of this monastery’s ship in the Roman port: that it should always remain free, together with its master and all its sailors, from every condition and obligation of payment of dues.

After this, having joined to himself almost all the soldiers of these regions [Note: [Col. 0689] “Our countrymen,” 1; corrected in 1b.], he went into Apulia to fight the Normans, in the year of the Lord 1053. [Note: [Col. 0689] “In the year of the Lord 1053” is added in 1b; the words “and from there … Guiscard” are absent from 1.] On the apostolic side, Rudolf, already elected prince of Benevento, and Werner the Swabian raised their standards. [Note: [Col. 0689C] So the *Anonymous of Monte Cassino* and the *Annals of Benevento*.] The Normans, however, formed three divisions of their own: one was led by Count Humphrey, another by Count Richard, and the third by Robert Guiscard. [Note: [Col. 0689C] From Amatus III.37, where the commanders of the other side are called Rainulf and Rainier.]

When battle was joined (18 June) on the great plain near Civitate [Note: [Col. 0689] “Is absent in 1.”], our men gradually withdrew and fled, leaving only those who had come from beyond the mountains. Although these fought long and bravely, all were eventually slain in the battle; and, by God’s judgment, the Normans were victorious. [Note: [Col. 0689] “With Humphrey as leader, then their count,” added in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0689] “Victorious. The pope fled with a few men to Civitate. Thereafter, moved by repentance, Humphrey came to the pope,” 1.]

Thereafter Humphrey came to the pope and, taking him under his protection, brought him with all his people to Benevento, promising that whenever he intended to go to Rome, he himself would escort him as far as Capua. The pope entered Benevento on the vigil of St John the Baptist (1054) and remained there until the feast of Pope St Gregory. Falling ill there, he summoned the aforesaid count and was escorted by him to Capua. Having stayed there for twelve days, he at last summoned our abbot as companion for his journey [Note: [Col. 0689] “Having summoned him, our abbot, as companion for his journey,” added in 1b.] and returned to Rome. Not many days later, he rested in a holy death (19 April). [Note: [Col. 0689] “Is absent in 4.”] At his tomb Christ then worked many miracles. [Note: [Col. 0690C] Thus Desiderius, *Dialogues*, III.3.]

Among the innumerable marks of his goodness, this pontiff, as long as he resided in Rome, used three days each week to walk by night from the Lateran to St Peter’s in private clothing and barefoot, with two or three clerics, chanting psalms and praying. [Note: [Col. 0689] “This … went” is absent from 1.]

85. [Chapter 88.] In that same year, for the purpose of reconciling the Roman and Constantinopolitan churches, he had sent to Emperor Constantine, surnamed Monomachus, as legates men of very great prudence: namely, his chancellor Frederick, Humbert bishop of Silva Candida, and Peter archbishop of Amalfi. [Note: [Col. 0689] Thus corrected in 1b; 1 has “he sent.”] [Note: [Col. 0690C] In January, indiction VII, Leo’s letter to Michael the patriarch was issued. The report of the legates survives, and Leo may have seen it; nevertheless, he learned some things from elsewhere. Compare Peter the Deacon, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 17.]

They first came to this monastery, commended themselves most devoutly to the brethren, and then set out on their journey. [Note: [Col. 0691] “They came … and, receiving …”; 1b. “The emperor received them with honour and … sent considerable gifts through them to blessed Peter and also to the pope. When they had remained there several days and had discussed various matters …,” 1.] The emperor received them with the greatest honour and kept them in the palace for several days. During that time, striving to correct certain Greek heresies [Note: [Col. 0691] “But without prevailing”—corrected to “but not at all prevailing”—added in 1 and deleted in 1b.], they finally anathematized Patriarch Michael and Leo, bishop of Acrida, together with all their followers, by apostolic authority. [Note: [Col. 0691C] Acrida, or Achris, is a city of Macedonia, formerly metropolitan of Serbia and Bulgaria. ANG.]

But when the pope had died during those days (16 July), and they were preparing to return [Note: [Col. 0691] Thus 1b: “to return,” after the erased word “now”; “Theatine,” etc., in 1.], Monomachus honourably presented them with imperial gifts [Note: [Col. 0691] “Constantine Monomachus,” the edition.] and sent no small gifts through them to St Peter and to the pope. In addition, at their request, he granted that this monastery should receive every year two pounds of gold from his palace.

As they returned safely, Count Trasmund of Chieti seized them while they were passing through his territory [Note: [Col. 0691] “Them,” added in 1 and deleted in 1b.]; having taken almost everything they carried with great outrage, he finally released them. [Note: [Col. 0691] The continuation beginning “And thus …” and most of the upper part of the next column were supplied in 1b after the material written in four lines in 4 had been erased.] Thus Frederick returned to Rome.

86. [Chapter 89.] After the death of Pope Leo of holy memory, Hildebrand, then subdeacon of the Roman Church, was sent by the Romans to the emperor, so that—because no person fit for so great an office could be found in the Roman Church—he might bring from those regions whomever he himself, acting in the place of the clergy and people of Rome, had elected Roman pontiff.

When the emperor had agreed, and Hildebrand, by the initiative and counsel of the Romans, had requested Gebeard, bishop of Eichstätt, whom we mentioned above (chapter 81), the emperor became exceedingly distressed, for he held him very dear. Although the emperor declared him indispensable in every respect and judged one candidate after another more suitable for the office, Hildebrand could not in any way be persuaded to accept another.

For this bishop, besides possessing great practical wisdom, was, after the emperor, more powerful and wealthier than all others in the kingdom. Hildebrand therefore brought him to Rome, although the emperor was unwilling and the bishop himself also unwilling. For this reason, indeed, the bishop was afterwards said not to have loved monks. Giving him the name Victor, Hildebrand, with the assent of all, established him as Roman pope (1055), when almost a year had elapsed since Pope Leo’s death.

Since he had been a very great hindrance to his predecessor, as we have said above, whenever he suffered any annoyance from those around him, he used to say: “I deservedly suffer these things, because I sinned against my lord.” [Note: [Col. 0691] Added in 1b and 2: “And again he said: ‘It is fitting that Paul suffer what Saul did; that the lamb endure what the wolf committed.’”]

When the emperor learned that Frederick had returned from Constantinople bringing a very great sum of money [Note: [Col. 0691] “An enormous sum,” 1b.], he began to regard him with intense suspicion. For at that time he was bitterly hostile to Frederick’s brother, Duke Godfrey. He therefore wrote to the apostolic lord that he should arrest Frederick and endeavour to send him to him without delay. [Note: [Col. 0691] “And hasten to send him to him,” 1b.]

Frederick learned this through intermediaries [Note: [Col. 0691] The continuation after “learned” is cut away in 1b.] and secretly met our abbot near Rome, as the abbot was returning from Lucca, where he had gone to the emperor. Frederick urgently begged him to bring him to Monte Cassino and arrange for him to become a monk there. [Note: [Col. 0691] From this point 1 continues: “He confessed that he wished to come to Monte Cassino and become a monk there. Therefore, having been sent ahead …”; corrected in 1b.] The abbot most gladly consented, and Frederick was sent ahead with all his followers to the monastery. [Note: [Col. 0691] “Having been sent ahead, then, with …,” 1b.]

A few days later the abbot arrived with the emperor’s messengers, who were being sent to the princes. Immediately, in the presence of those messengers, Frederick cast aside the very precious garments which he then wore [Note: [Col. 0691] “Clerical,” corrected from “cleric” in 1.], put on the religious habit, and arranged that this action should be reported to the emperor through those same envoys [Note: [Col. 0691] “To the king through the same messengers,” corrected in 1.]. He thereafter joined himself to the brethren. [Note: [Col. 0691] “He announced himself to the brethren,” 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0691] “In these same days Victor, a German by birth and Roman pontiff, was ordained, and in this year the younger Pandulf issued a charter of concession to the abbot concerning the castle called Saraceniscum.” These words are deleted in 1. After their deletion, 1b continues: “Yet, still by no means secure from the emperor’s anger, he considered moving to a safer place. He therefore … remained.”]

Not long afterwards he asked the abbot to send him to the Tremiti Islands [Note: [Col. 0691] “To the Tremiti Islands,” 1b and the edition.], which he did. Then, because he began to make himself unwelcome to the abbot of that place on account of certain reprehensible things which he had found there [Note: [Col. 0691] “Reprehensible,” 2.], judging that he ought not to remain there, he left and went to the monastery of St John, called “of Venus” [Note: [Col. 0691C] It is situated in the territory of Lanciano. ANG.], where he stayed for several days.

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0691] “The whole of ‘At the same time …’ is absent from 1.”] the aforesaid abbot brought an action before the court of Cadolao, chancellor of Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0691C] Apparently bishop of Naumburg, who is called chancellor of the Roman palace in an imperial diploma received at Ingelheim on 20 November 1043. However, Cadolao, bishop of Naumburg, had already died in 1045. The man meant here is the bishop of Parma, who held several courts at that time but was never chancellor. Compare Schmitt, *Zeitschrift für Geschichte*, year 1847.], where he was with many bishops and counts of those regions, concerning a certain Dodo[.....], who held seven hundred *modii* of land belonging to this monastery in the county of Chieti, at the place called “At the House of Hildebrand”; and he recovered everything.

At the same time the aforesaid Counts Trasmund and Bernard bound themselves by oath to the same abbot concerning all the possessions of St Benedict in the counties of Chieti and Penne: that they themselves would not seize them and would defend them for our monastery against all men [Note: [Col. 0693] “For St Benedict,” 1b and the edition.], at the monastery of St Scholastica in Penne. [Note: [Col. 0693] “At Penne,” added in 1b.]

87. [Chapter 90.] In this same year (December 1054) [Note: [Col. 0693] This chapter is added in the margin in 1b; compare the note above.], Prince Pandulf the Younger issued a charter of concession to this monastery [Note: [Col. 0693C] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 151. It lies in a valley enclosed by high mountains; it is now also called the castle of St Blaise. Ibid., p. 752.] concerning the castle called Saraceniscum [Note: [Col. 0693] “Saracin.,” 1b; “Sarracen.,” 4], in the district of Comino, with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0693] “Its jurisdiction,” 1b.], although that castle appears to have been built within the ancient boundaries of our monastery. [Note: [Col. 0693] The words “although … built” are absent from 1b.]

Not long before, Counts Oderisius and Rainald of the Marsi, who then governed Comino, had confirmed that place to blessed Benedict by a charter of offering, together with its boundaries and limits. [Note: [Col. 0693] “Had conferred,” 1b.] Therefore, when certain men of Aquino complained against the abbot concerning this, because they had previously bought the same place from a certain Berard of the Marsi for one hundred bezants, they finally came to this agreement with him [Note: [Col. 0693] The following material is cut away in 1b.]: of their own free will, in the presence of certain judges, they would renounce to the lord abbot every complaint and legal claim concerning it and thereafter remain at peace, under a stipulated penalty of one hundred pounds of silver if ever they wished to contend further about it, except insofar as he might grant them something by written agreement.

The castle itself is said to be called Saraceniscum for this reason: when the Saracens had fled before our people at the time when they were expelled from the Garigliano, and the rest had been killed, some of them eventually reached that place. Hiding there for some time, they secretly carried off certain spoils from neighbouring inhabitants like brigands. When this became known to the people of Sora through one of their captive deserters, they reached the hiding place at first light, guided by the same deserter, and slaughtered with swords every one of them, although still drowsy and attempting to resist.

88. [Chapter 91.] At the same time [Note: [Col. 0693] “Not many days later, the aforesaid Trasmund …,” 1. “Meanwhile, as soon as he had obtained the papacy, the apostolic lord immediately returned beyond the mountains. Finding the emperor already ill, he remained with him until his death; and, making all the nobles of the kingdom swear allegiance to the little son whom his father had left in his hands, and confirming him in the kingdom, he returned to Tuscany. During these days the aforesaid Trasmund …,” 1b; these words were later deleted. The author notes that many additions and alterations were made to this chapter at different times, and that he has considered it unnecessary to record each one.] the aforesaid Count Trasmund fell gravely ill and, wishing to become a monk, asked Richerius to come to him. Submitting himself humbly to him and offering him a large sum of money, he granted to St Benedict three castles under his jurisdiction in the territory of Chieti (October 1055) [Note: [Col. 0693C] Executed at Chieti. Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 154. He calls himself the son of Count Atto (compare *Historia*, p. 84) and Gisla. The church of St Justa is not mentioned there.]: Monte Alberici, Frisca, and Muccla [Note: [Col. 0694C] Muccla of St Quiricus, with a harbour for ten ships; Victor II, in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 146], with its harbour and fishery, and the churches of St Mary, St Lucy, and St Blaise [Note: [Col. 0693] The words “of St Mary … of St Blaise” are absent from 1.], together with all the property and appurtenances whatsoever of those castles and churches [Note: [Col. 0693] “And of the churches” is absent from 1.], amounting to 5,500 *modii* of land. [Note: [Col. 0693] “*Modia*,” 1.]

He also granted the church of St Justa with all its appurtenances, amounting to 500 *modii* [Note: [Col. 0693] “*Modia*,” 1.]; likewise, in the territory of Penne, in the castle called Lastenianum [Note: [Col. 0693] “In the castle of Penne” (corrected to “the castle of Penne”), “which is called Lastenianum,” with …, 1.], he granted this monastery a church of St Nicholas with all its appurtenances, namely 3,000 *modii* of land. [Note: [Col. 0693] “*Modia*,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 0694C] Executed at Penne; ibid., p. 155.]

But when the aforesaid pope had passed through Ancona, the abbot went to him on Trasmund’s business. When Frederick learned that he had come to the monastery of St Liberator [Note: [Col. 0694C] To which the same Trasmund then made a donation, in December; executed at Chieti. Gattola, *Historia*, p. 84.], he went to him and, moved by the deepest repentance, begged that he might be allowed to return to Monte Cassino. This was immediately granted. Frederick at once returned here, while the abbot hastened to complete the journey he had begun.

Since the abbot had long been burning with severe fevers and, fearing death, was hastening his return day by day, he came to Aterno and, on the third Ides of December [Note: [Col. 0693] “Fourth” in 4; the words “third Ides of December” are absent in 3; “third,” *Necrology of Monte Cassino*.], was overcome by the violence of the fever and died. The brethren who were with him delayed no time: taking him up at that hour, when it was midnight, they set out and arrived at the monastery of St Liberator at first light. Having honourably performed his funeral rites [Note: [Col. 0693] “And buried him,” the edition.], they placed him in the tomb in which his predecessor Abbot Theobald had been buried, in the year of the Lord 1055. [Note: [Col. 0693] “In the year of the Lord 1055” is added in 1b.]

89. [Chapter 92.] Among other things, this abbot roofed the church of St Benedict with sheets of lead. He began a palace on the eastern side of the monastery, sixty-eight cubits in length, and brought it up to the upper floor. Before the church, around the court, he made covered walks of arches with little stone columns. [Note: [Col. 0695] “Marble,” 1.]

Although, because of the innumerable oppressions of those living around the monastery, as we have shown in part, he could not carry out work in the monastery, he was nevertheless the source of the beginning and all the material of the present works. By his effort and diligence, with God helping him through the merits of blessed Benedict, he rescued this land from the hands of the Normans.

When the brethren who had been with him returned to the monastery immediately after his burial, they all took counsel together and chose from the community Lord Peter, a man most religious and of most honourable bearing. [Note: [Col. 0695B] “A man …,” Col. 0695B.] Although he was unwilling and reluctant, objecting that his snowy old age was less suitable for so great an office and declaring that he would prefer to resume the deanery rather than undertake the abbacy [Note: [Col. 0695] “Preferring … and asserting,” added in 1b.], they established him as their abbot. Very few dissented [Note: [Col. 0695] “Very few,” 1; “few,” 1b.], judging Lord John, surnamed “the Marsican,” who was then provost at Capua [Note: [Col. 0695] “Was provost,” 1 and the edition], more worthy of this office [Note: [Col. 0695] “Of the monastery,” the edition.]. Yet John himself, guarding against and fearing that this burden might be imposed upon him, had obstinately sworn upon the altar [Note: [Col. 0695] “By the body of blessed Benedict,” corrected in 1b.] that he would never consent in any way to accept that abbacy. [Note: [Col. 0695D] He came from the same homeland as that John who became abbot of St Vincent in 1058; therefore I believe that they were not different men. See below, chapter 97.]

PETER, the thirty-fifth abbot of this monastery [Note: [Col. 0695] “Fifth and thirtieth of this monastery” is added in 1b.], held office for one year and five months.

[Col. 0695C] 90. [Chapter 93.] This man, a monk from childhood and not inadequately trained in ecclesiastical observances, grew to such religious and honourable habits, and proved to be of such angelic countenance and venerable bearing, that the Emperor Henry, when he came at that time to this monastery, rose quite humbly before him as he passed by; and testified that he had never seen throughout his whole kingdom a monk more honourable than he. [Note: [Col. 0695] “and—trained” is added in 1b; the phrase “than he” is absent in 1.] [The wording in 1b continues: “This emperor, however, having died in the following year, left his son Henry, still a little boy, as successor to the kingdom. After his death Pope Victor summoned the aforesaid Frederick from the monastery to himself; and, diligently learning all that Trasmund had done to him, the same, etc. (ch. 91).”] Our former abbot Basil, therefore, when he learned at Salerno of Peter’s ordination, immediately came to Capua and, offering the prince a very large sum of money, began urgently to entreat that this abbacy be restored to him. But because the prince had consented to Peter’s election, he declared that he could by no means do this, and directed Basil to remain at our monastery at Capua. Thus this prudent—indeed foolish—man both lost the Salernitan abbacy and did not at all deserve to acquire this one.

After some days, when the prince was asked by our brethren why he had established the abbot in our cell, he answered that he had done so unwillingly and, in a sense, under compulsion. Yet, if they wished to receive him in their own monastery, that would be most pleasing to him. [Note: [Col. 0695] 1b: “If he himself wished to come to Monte Cassino and receive him …”] Accordingly, the aforesaid Basil came to this monastery, humbly surrendered the staff of abbacy which he had until then retained, and after a few days was sent to Valleluce as provost.

In these days (21 September 1056), Henry and Roland, noble brothers of the city of Lucca, sons of Sisemund and Bertha, offered to this monastery the church of St George, situated within that city on their patrimony, near the postern called Guirigala, for a monastery to be established there, together with a garden, a well, houses, and all the considerable properties and appurtenances of that church, both within and without. [Note: [Col. 0696D] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 200.]

To build or organize this monastery, Lord John, Apulian by birth and surname, was sent. He had long exercised the office of dean in this our monastery (cf. *Desiderius, Dialogues*, I.3). Beyond the other distinctions of his goodness, he was endowed by divine gift with the grace of compunction and tears. Since it should not seem superfluous to show, even briefly, from matters certainly known to us what merit he possessed before God, we shall do so.

When the fame of his holiness spread far and wide, a certain woman grievously possessed by a demon was brought to him. Her escorts earnestly begged this man of God to pray to the Lord for her. Since he was kind and exceedingly compassionate, he immediately gathered the brethren and entered the oratory. After prayer had continued for some time, divine mercy, moved by his tears and groans, drove out the demon and permitted the woman to return in health to her own home.

Moreover, the wife of a distinguished man of Lucca, after being held for several days by a severe illness, had at last been brought by the violence of her sickness to such a state that, lying for three days without voice or sensation, she was considered no less than dead. Since every human hope had utterly failed, her relatives had recourse to divine assistance and humbly sent to the aforesaid man of God, asking that he would deign to supplicate the Lord for her. The gracious man delayed not at all, but immediately put on the sacred vestments and approached to offer the saving sacrifice to the Lord on her behalf.

When he had reached that place in the Canon where the names of the living are customarily recited, and with great devotion commended her individually and specifically to the Lord, she lay as if lifeless far from the monastery in her own house. She heard the voice of the priest remembering her and at once, as though he were standing beside her bed, awakened as if from a deep sleep and promptly answered him. Those present, astonished, began anxiously to ask her what she meant, or to whom she had so unusually replied. But she said: “Did you not see the venerable Lord John the provost standing here? Did you not also hear his voice calling me?”

Astonished and rejoicing together at the woman’s words, those present immediately sent to the monastery and ordered careful inquiry into what God’s servant was doing for her. On arriving, they found the aforesaid man of God standing at the holy altars and celebrating the solemnities of Mass to the Lord for her. It was established beyond doubt that she had recovered herself and spoken at the very hour when God’s servant had remembered her in the customary place of the Canon. Giving the greatest thanks to almighty God, they returned to those who had sent them and openly reported to all the matter exactly as it had occurred.

That woman, immediately restored to her former health, together with her husband always honoured the man of God with remarkable devotion. [Note: [Col. 0697C] “The woman … honoured” is absent in Desiderius.] It was also said that this same man of God possessed such grace that, if anyone suffering from fever faithfully drank water in which he had washed his hands after the solemnities of Mass, thereafter fever could exercise no power over that person.

Anselm, then bishop of the same city—a man of such authority and prudence that he later happily governed the Roman see—was once burning with a most violent fever. He suddenly remembered what he had long before heard, through the widely circulating report of many persons, concerning the aforesaid man of God. He immediately sent someone secretly to bring him some of that water. As soon as he drank it, with no delay at all, the whole force of the fever departed from him. That prelate was accustomed often to relate this to God’s glory and in praise of so great a man. Many other things too are reported concerning the miracles of the aforesaid servant of God, but they belong neither to the scope of this time nor to that of this book.

91. [Chapter 94.] Furthermore, when the pope heard of Richer’s unexpected death and Peter’s over-hasty election (1056), he took it very seriously. He immediately sent letters here, at first full of conciliatory expressions but afterwards of reproof, asserting that we ought by no means to have made this election without his counsel and the emperor’s will. Therefore two brethren were sent to him on behalf of the abbot and brethren, to set before him the whole truth and necessity of the matter. Envoys were also immediately sent to the emperor concerning the same affair.

Meanwhile the pope went beyond the mountains and found the emperor already ill. He remained with him until his death (5 October 1057); and, causing all the leading men of the whole realm to swear allegiance to the little son, about five years old, whom his father had left in his charge, he confirmed him in the kingdom and finally returned to Tuscany. Frederick then, having learned of the emperor’s death, confidently approached the pope. He fully related all that Trasmund had done to him and had Trasmund excommunicated.

At length Trasmund himself went to Rome to obtain absolution, restoring almost everything that he had taken from Frederick. After great satisfaction he obtained absolution; at Frederick’s and Humbert’s prompting, summoned and admonished by the pope, he voluntarily surrendered into the pope’s hand the castle called Frisa, which his wife had granted to St Benedict and which he, after her death, had seized by invasion. [Note: [Col. 0697C] See Victor II’s privilege; Gattola, *Historia*, p. 146.]

And because, as has already been said above, the same pope had taken it very ill that the election of the aforesaid abbot had been carried out without his knowledge—while certain hostile persons had also reported to him that not all the monks had agreed to it and that the abbot had been promoted to the office factiously and not canonically—he seized the occasion and ordered the abbot to come to Rome as quickly as possible with twelve monks, there to render him a full account of his appointment.

When the abbot had come to him as ordered, he was scarcely allowed, after two days, to enter the pope’s chamber with only two brethren. He was nevertheless honourably received; although the pope sometimes showed agitation of mind while they spoke, he was finally ordered to return to the monastery. There, in the presence of the whole community, either the pope himself or his delegates would fully investigate the case and determine what was canonical.

After the abbot’s return, not long afterwards Humbert the bishop was sent from the pope’s side to the monastery, with instructions that he should investigate the question of the appointment most diligently and, if he could find any ground there, immediately depose the abbot without any delay; but if the abbot should presume in any way to resist, he should strike both him and all his supporters with apostolic excommunication. Thus the pope had set his mind upon violently subjecting the abbey to himself, although no Roman pontiff before him had ventured this; for from the beginning, the election of the abbot had remained free to the monks, while consecration alone belonged to the pope.

Accordingly, on the very day of Holy Pentecost (18 May), the aforesaid Humbert entered the chapter of the brethren and declared to them the apostolic blessing, if they were willing to be sons of obedience. Nothing was asked of them that day; but, after Pentecost had been solemnly celebrated, on the Monday he explained why he had come. He set out in order what had formerly been reported to the pope concerning them and their abbot, seeking to know their will and receive their answer.

The elders answered that the election of the abbot of Monte Cassino belonged, by the authority of the Rule and apostolic grant, to no mortal whatever except its own monks; that this house, free by God’s authorizing, was in no way subject to any condition; that the election which they had made unanimously was wholly valid and canonical; and that they had acted as the monastic Rule commands and as the authority of almost all their predecessors among the popes had established. No place whatever had been given to ambition in that appointment. They could not have found among their own number anyone more honourable, more religious, or, finally, better to choose as abbot. The office had been imposed on him although he was unwilling and resisted it in every way; and all were unanimous in accepting his leadership. By God’s grace, they said, the practice of sedition had never existed in this monastery. Finally, they would never agree to accept one another over themselves by any person’s command.

When he had heard this reasoning, the bishop kept silence, seeing nothing at all that he could offer in reply; and so the chapter was dismissed that day.

92. [Chapter 95.] Meanwhile, just four brethren, deeply offended at these events and supposing that the apostolic envoy had come solely to depose the abbot, held a most foolish consultation among themselves without the knowledge either of the abbot or of the other brethren. They immediately sent word and summoned almost all the inhabitants of this territory, roused to arms, to come the next day as though in aid of the abbot.

Then, on the following day (20 May), when the brethren were rising from chapter in complete peace, an innumerable raging crowd suddenly arrived, armed with diverse weapons, asking who they were that wished to depose their abbot and desiring to destroy them. They might perhaps have done so, had not the abbot gone out to them and, only with difficulty, after setting forth many arguments, restrained their fury, adding: “Until now no one has been able to take the abbey from me; but today, through your foolishness, you have taken it away from me.” This was indeed entirely true.

For the aforesaid bishop was already preparing to depart, since he had found no objection to the abbot’s appointment. Once this sole occasion had been discovered, he summoned all the brethren together into the abbot’s chamber and protested at the great injury done to him—that is, to Roman envoys—before the very gates of Rome.
