The monks joined in his protest and likewise declared that they themselves had suffered the same injury; they asserted that they no longer wished to have an abbot who was maintained not by them but by the men of the territory.

Then they all returned together to chapter. Under the strictest pronouncement of anathema, Humbert began to inquire who had been the authors of so great a disturbance. Although both the abbot and the other brethren steadfastly professed themselves wholly ignorant of the matter, and he pressed them very hard on this affair, at last those four brethren rose. According to the monastery’s custom, they humbly prostrated themselves before the community and confessed that they alone, without the knowledge of the others, had been the authors of this crime.

The brethren, stirred to anger, immediately expelled them from the monastery’s cloister and ordered them to be placed under graver penalties in the guests’ house. Meanwhile the abbot spoke secretly with Humbert, promised willingly to resign the abbacy, and asked that a place be given him where he could live honourably.

On the third day thereafter (22 May), coming before all the brethren into the church and laying his staff upon the altar, he resigned the abbacy in the following manner. On the next day (23 May), that is, Friday after Pentecost, all the brethren assembled in chapter, with the aforesaid Humbert, legate of the apostolic see, presiding, and began to deliberate about choosing an abbot. Finally, with one consent and unanimous will, all were pleased to elect Frederick, who was distinguished by noble birth and great wisdom and, what was especially important to them, was a monk of the same community. Since this likewise seemed highly commendable to Bishop Humbert, he immediately handed him over to the brethren; amid the great joy and rejoicing of all, Frederick was elected abbot according to the monastery’s custom, in the year of the Lord 1057.

**FREDERICK**, a Lotharingian by birth, thirty-sixth abbot of this monastery, held office for ten months.

93. [Chapter 96.] Descended from royal stock, he was trained from boyhood in the liberal studies and lived as a canon at the church of St Lambert at Liège. Pope Leo then appointed him chancellor of the apostolic see. After Leo’s death he came to this monastery, and at last received the abbacy of this place in the manner related above.

Accordingly, after ten days, when all necessities for the journey had been prepared, he took eight brethren and, with Bishop Humbert, set out for the pope in Tuscany in order to obtain his consecration. The pope was greatly delighted by this. They related to him in order everything that had been done and how it had been done, while Humbert highly praised the religious life and conduct of our monks and the dignity of this place.

On the Saturday in the fast of June (14 June), he was ordained cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus; on the Nativity of St John he received consecration as abbot, and he remained with the pope until the feast of St Apollinaris (23 July). At this time he received from the pope, through the hands of the aforesaid Humbert, a privilege in which the pope, highly approving the transfer of the abbacy to him from Peter by the sounder counsel of the brethren, confirmed it for him by apostolic authority according to the custom of his predecessors.

[Note: [Col. 0701D] Victor II’s privilege, in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 145, reads: “Approving and confirming the election to the government of the aforesaid monastery, transferred to you by the sounder counsel of all the brethren in the presence of our representative from Peter the monk, who had been elected by the conspiracy of certain wicked men …”]

By the same authority he also granted him the use of sandals and of the other insignia, as the holy Pope Leo had earlier granted them to Abbot Richer. In every assembly of bishops and princes, he confirmed for him and his successors a seat above all abbots; and in their counsels and judgments, the first voice, nevertheless, before men of his own order. He himself later, similarly, during his own pontificate, confirmed these things for this monastery and, through it, for all abbots thereafter to be promoted in this monastery, granting them for ever in a solemn privilege. [Note: [Col. 0702D] Register no. 27; Angelo.] In that privilege he also, among other provisions, most sternly forbade the future occurrence of the disturbances called *levae* and the plunderings which he had learned were accustomed to happen here upon an abbot’s death.

94. [Chapter 97.] Having obtained leave to depart, he came to Rome. On the following Sunday (27 July), after solemnly celebrating Mass at St Peter’s, he was accompanied by a great crowd of Romans and ceremonially conducted with praise, in the manner of cardinals, to his titular church; afterwards he proceeded with no less attendance to the Pallaria, where he was lodging. [Note: [Col. 0702D] See below, III.36.]

There he remained until Thursday (31 July), in order to acquire vestments. When everything had been prepared for departure and he was about to leave the City immediately, Boniface, bishop of Albano, hurriedly returning from Tuscany, suddenly announced the death of the Roman pontiff in the City (28 July). Stunned by this news, he stayed. Then Romans, clergy and citizens alike, gradually and one by one began to gather around him.

The rest of that day, the whole night, and the following day were spent by them in deliberations on this matter. At last, when consulted what ought to be done and whom they should elect to so great a pontificate, he proposed to them five persons whom he considered the worthiest in those regions for election: Humbert, bishop of Santa Rufina; the bishop of Velletri, John; the bishop of Perugia; the bishop of Tusculum, Peter; and Hildebrand, subdeacon of the Roman church.

But when the Romans judged none of these suitable for the office and asserted that they wished to confer so great an honour only on him, he said: “You can do nothing concerning me except what God permits; and without his command you can neither confer nor take away this office from me.” There were, however, some who said that Hildebrand, still remaining in Tuscany where he had been with the pope, ought fittingly to be awaited. The others judged that no delay at all was appropriate. Therefore, early in the morning, all together in one counsel and harmonious will came to the abbot (2 August), forcibly drew Frederick from the Pallaria, and brought him to the basilica of St Peter called *ad Vincula* (“in Chains”) for the election.

There, following custom, they made his acclamation and decreed that he should be called Stephen, because the feast of Pope St Stephen was celebrated that day. Thus, with the whole City escorting him with acclamations, they led him to the Lateran patriarchal palace. At daybreak on the following day (3 August), all the cardinals, together with the clergy and Roman people, assembled before him, and amid the great joy of all he was consecrated supreme and universal pontiff in the basilica of St Peter.

After this, he sent the brethren back to the monastery, retaining only two to serve him. He ordered our provost to come to him immediately with twelve monks, whom he indicated by letter, so that he might take common counsel concerning both himself and them. They all went as he had commanded and returned after about ten days.

He remained at Rome for four continuous months, holding frequent synods with the clergy and people of the City. With special zeal he laboured to abolish the marriages of clerics and priests, and also unions of kindred persons. At last, on the feast of St Andrew (30 November), he returned to this monastery with a considerable Roman retinue and remained until the feast of St Scholastica (10 February 1058).

Because the vice of private ownership had gradually crept into this place in earlier years, he began in every way, opportunely and importunately, by reproving, entreating, rebuking, and also threatening most sternly, to insist that this vice be uprooted from the place in accordance with the command of the Rule. This he accomplished in very large measure. At that time he also completely forbade Ambrosian chant to be sung in this church.

[Col. 0704A] 95. [Chapter 98.] In these days (1057), Pandulf, bishop of the Marsi, a noble and ecclesiastical man, came to this monastery and was received by him with the greatest honour and affection (9 December). He also made him an episcopal privilege [Note: [Col. 0703D] Published by Ughelli among the bishops of the Marsi.] and granted him in this monastery the first place after himself in every assembly.

This bishop offered to the place a *planeta scaramangina*—a chasuble of scarlet *scaramanga* cloth; [Note: [Col. 0703D] *Scaramanga* was formerly a military garment; hence it denoted a kind of cloth.] a diapered cope with a gold band; a purple altar frontal with bands and gems; two silver censers; a gold chalice with its paten; two silver ewers; one silver incense-holder; a small silver cross containing wood of the Lord; one silver bucket; one great hanging with lions; and one excellent tapestry, besides several other things which we considered superfluous to record. He then received the brethren’s fellowship and blessing and returned, remaining from that time always most intimate and devoted toward this place.

In the same days (January 1058), Marinus, count of Traetto, offered to this monastery his whole and entire portion, namely the fourth part of the entire county of Traetto, half of the castle of Spigno, [Note: [Col. 0703D] Now Spigno and Le Fratte. Published by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 157. The donation is repeated in almost the same words under Abbot Desiderius; see below III.59.] and a fourth part of the castle of Fratte, together with the monastery of St Marinus, situated in the territory of the same town of Fratte, with all its possessions and appurtenances whatsoever. [Note: [Col. 0703D] The charter calls it St Martin’s, where the settlement of Castriforte now stands. Angelo; cf. below III.60.]

Gezzo and Peter, brothers of Pontecorvo, also gave to this place in these days the church of St Nicholas and St Blaise, which is in the castle of St John of Carica, with all the possessions belonging to that church. [Note: [Col. 0704D] No. 393. Angelo.]

96. But because the aforesaid pope had long been ill with the Roman fever, he became so seriously sick around the feast of the Nativity of the Lord (December 1057) that he believed himself certainly about to die. Desiderius was therefore chosen abbot by the counsel of the elders—as, God helping, we shall show in the appropriate place—and funds for an apostolic legation to the emperor at Constantinople were entrusted to him. The pope himself returned to Rome, took with him Alfanus, formerly Desiderius’s companion and then bishop-elect of the see of Salerno, ordained him first priest in the March fasts, then consecrated him archbishop on the following Sunday (8 March 1058), and sent him honourably back to Salerno.

97. [Chapter 99.] A few days later he ordered our provost John [Note: [Col. 0704D] See *Desiderius, Dialogues*, I.6.] to bring to him in person, quickly and as secretly as possible, the entire treasure of this church, in gold and silver only, promising that he would soon send back here things much more precious. He intended to meet his brother Duke Godfrey in Tuscany and, it was said, bestow the imperial crown upon him; then he intended to return with him to expel the Normans from Italy, whom he greatly hated.

Although the brethren were deeply saddened and grieved, they hastened at morning to carry out the pope’s order. A novice of good conduct named Leo, a citizen of Amalfi, remained in the church after the night office while the others departed, in order to pray. After his prayer he sat down for a little while and fell asleep.

In his sleep he saw a monk of venerable grey hair and a nun proceeding from the entrances of the apse to the middle of the church. The nun, bathed in tears, complained in a loud voice, and not without bitterness, as though because the church was being plundered. The monk walking beside her consoled her thus: “Do not weep, sister, do not weep; for all these things will without doubt shortly return to us.”

The brother awoke astonished at the vision. Going by chance to the sacristy and seeing what was being done, though he had been wholly ignorant of the order, he immediately obtained permission from the prior to speak and recounted in order the vision he had seen. All present began to weep. But because they did not dare omit what had been commanded, they took everything and conveyed it to the pope at Rome.

When he saw these things, he trembled all over. Then, when the aforesaid vision had been recounted to him and he had learned the immense grief of our brethren over the matter, he was moved to repentance and began to weep. Immediately taking from among these objects only one icon which he himself had brought from Constantinople, he ordered everything else swiftly to be brought back here.

When all had thus been received back, our aforesaid provost was hastening to return and had already completed a great part of his journey, when he suddenly received a message from the pope ordering him, after sending the treasure back to the monastery through companions, to return to him as quickly as possible. On his return, the pope invested him with the abbacy of St Vincent, as he had been asked by the sons of Borrellus, and immediately sent him to take possession of it.

[Note: [Col. 0705C] The *Chronicle of Vulturno*, p. 514, tells this somewhat differently: “The brethren began to seek an abbot for themselves, and in seeking found a suitable and prudent man, Lord John, Marsian by birth and brought up in this monastery. He held office for 22 years, 4 months, and 15 days.”]

98. [Chapter 100.] After this, having gathered bishops, clergy, and the Roman people within the church, he established under a most strict prohibition that, if he should die before Hildebrand, then subdeacon of the Roman church, returned from the empress to whom he was being sent by common counsel on certain affairs of state, no one whatsoever should presume to elect a pope. Rather, the apostolic see was to remain vacant and untouched until Hildebrand’s return, and then be arranged by his counsel.

Then he hastened into Tuscany and, not long afterwards, was suddenly overcome by illness and died, by God’s judgment, near the city of Florence, on 29 March. He was buried there with fitting honour. [Note: [Col. 0706B] Peter Damian relates in *On the Birth and Death of the Just*, ch. 58, and *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 17, that Christ showed many signs through the merits of his most sacred body.]

The brethren of this monastery who had travelled with him entrusted his chapel, which he had brought from here, to trustworthy men at Florence. Since they feared to return by way of Rome, the Florentine nobles assisted and escorted them; they took the route through the marches and returned to us with all the speed they could, the Lord granting success.

[Apparatus and editorial notes not otherwise represented above]

90. [Chapter 93.] [Col. 0695] In 1b, the words from “and” to “trained” are added; at the end of the line the text is absent in 1b. In 3, “church, garden, well, and houses” are absent. “And” is the reading of the edition. [Col. 0696D] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 200.

91. [Chapter 94.] [Col. 0697] In 1b the passage from “Hearing” through “had him excommunicated” is added; it reads *repentinam* (“sudden”) for “over-hasty,” while 2 lacks the latter word. “The election itself” is absent in 1b. 1b reads “After this”; its words “about five years old” are absent, and it reads *manus* (“hand”) for *manu*. “The same” is added in 1b. 1 originally read “and all [the things]” and was corrected in 1b.

A longer alternative continuation in 1 reads: “After this, when certain envious persons had reported to the pope that not all the brethren had consented to the abbot’s election, and that he had been promoted seditiously and by no means canonically, he was ordered to come to the next synod” (corrected to “to go to Rome”) “and duly answer, concerning his election, the accusations brought against him. Duke Adenulf having been asked, went to Rome with him and obtained from the pope that the abbot’s case should be examined not in the Roman synod but in the chapter at Monte Cassino, by prudent men sent from the pope’s side; a promise having been exacted from the abbot that, if the allegation against him could be proved true, he would voluntarily relinquish the abbacy. When the synod had been held and the abbot had returned, Humbert and Frederick were sent to the monastery on the pope’s behalf. On the day of Pentecost they entered the brethren’s chapter [lacuna], proclaimed [lacuna], and reported to them [lacuna].” 1 then has “he surrendered. And because, etc.”; 1b has the text of the edition. [Col. 0697C] See Victor II’s privilege; Gattola, *Historia*, p. 146. Another explanation is reported by the *Chronicle of Vulturno*, p. 154, “because he was exceedingly simple,” and by Amatus III.46, French: *non fu trop expert de chozes seculeres*, “he was not very expert in worldly matters.”

[Col. 0699] 1b reads *Honeste* (“honourably”). It originally named “Humbert and Frederick,” then corrected this and changed plural forms throughout to singular; nevertheless the scribe of manuscript 2 wrote the plurals “they might be able,” “they might depose,” and “they might strike with excommunication.” Manuscript 3 reads *reperiret* (“he might find”); 1b, *attemptare praesumpserit* (“had presumed to attempt”). “Holy” is absent in 4. 1 originally read “the aforesaid apostolic legates,” corrected in 1b to the singular. Manuscript 3 reads *pentecosten* (“Pentecost”) for *pasca*; the edition reads *quod* (“that”) for *propter quid* (“for what reason”). Several clauses, including “formerly,” “an answer,” and the request to learn their will, are additions in 1b. 1b explicitly reads “the election of the abbot of Monte Cassino … [they] had made”; it has “election by apostolic grant.” From “No place whatever” through “had existed” is absent in 1b, whose end is cut off. Manuscript 4 has *imperium* (“command”) for *imperio* (“by command”) and adds “over” before “themselves”; “and so” is absent in 4.

92. [Chapter 95.] [Col. 0699] Manuscript 1, after a gap, has “not trusting themselves well, and on account of …”; it reads “that the apostolic envoys might depose [him],” corrected in 1b. 1b has the wording “But when, on the following day, they were rising from chapter in all peace, behold an innumerable multitude of raging men [arrived]”; it also has, after “This was indeed true,” “Whereupon [lacuna] the apostolic envoys together with all (?) the brethren assemble in the abbot’s chamber.” “The aforesaid legates” was corrected in 1b to “the aforesaid bishop.” 1b adds that all the brethren assembled in the abbot’s chamber. The edition reads *vocat* (“summons”) for *convocat*; the same editorial reading is also recorded at the next occurrence. “Roman” is absent in 1. 1b adds “before the very gates of Rome,” and has “they complain with very loud outcries. When these [things had occurred] …” It further adds “an abbot any longer”; “all together” is its wording for the return to chapter. 1 reads “they returned and began”; 1b, “they went away to chapter.” “And Frederick” was added in 1b and then deleted by the editor. 1b reads “who they were” for “who had been.”

[Col. 0700–0701] Manuscript 1 first read “the envoys of the apostolic see … were pressing,” corrected in 1b to the singular. It continues: “they confessed that they alone, while the others were ignorant, had instigated this crime.” 1 reads *de monasterio* (“from the monastery”), corrected in 1b to *de claustro* (“from the cloister”); it has *piretum* for “guests’ house” and *allegant* (“they allege”), corrected in 1b to “they order [them] to be placed under graver penalties.” It originally had “Frederick and a companion,” corrected in 1b to Humbert alone. Manuscript 1 has “in the presence of the apostolic envoys,” corrected in 1b to the printed wording. It calls 23 May “Thursday in the Pentecost week,” corrected in 1b to Friday. It originally had “with Humbert and Frederick, apostolic legates, presiding,” corrected in 1b to the singular. 1 reads “wisdom, and likewise outstanding religious devotion”; 1b, “great wisdom.” “Which was especially important to them” is absent in 1. The year “of the Lord 1057” is added in 1b; manuscript 1 ends midway down that page.

93. [Chapter 96.] [Col. 0701] Manuscript 4 adds “of this place.” Manuscript 1 and the edition read *jejunii* (“fast”) in the plural. The privilege’s wording is: “We approve and confirm the election to the government of the aforesaid monastery, transferred to you by the sounder counsel of all the brethren, in the presence of our representative, from Peter the monk, elected through the conspiracy of certain wicked men.” Victor II’s privilege is printed in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 145. Manuscript 3 has the variant wording “he confirmed that custom for him by his apostolic authority.” [Col. 0702D] Register, no. 27; Angelo.

94. [Chapter 97.] [Col. 0701] Manuscript 4 has *cum* (“with”) before “no less attendance”; the edition reads *hujuscemodi* (“of this sort”). Manuscript 2 has *Perusinum* for *Perosinum*, *Hildeprandus* for Hildebrand, and *Fredericus* for Frederick. [Col. 0702D–0703D] The bishop of Velletri was John; the bishop of Tusculum, Peter. “Ambrosian chant” is also attributed to Ambrose in manuscript 4.

95. [Chapter 98.] [Col. 0703] Manuscript 2 reads “who” for “to whom,” and “into this monastery” for “in this monastery.” [Col. 0703D] *Scaramanga* was formerly a military garment and consequently denoted a kind of cloth. Manuscript 2 orders the hanging differently: “one [hanging] with lions; one great hanging for suspending.” The edition reads “to this monastery.” The charter calls the monastery St Martin’s; it stands where the settlement of Castriforte is now. Angelo; compare below III.60. Manuscript 4 reads “which” for “that,” *ezzo* for Gezzo, and has a damaged reading after “belonging to that church”: “of that church belonging …” [Col. 0704D] No. 393; Angelo.

96. Manuscript 4 lacks “by the counsel of the elders.”

97. [Chapter 99.] [Col. 0704D] The provost was John; see *Desiderius, Dialogues*, I.6. The *Chronicle of Vulturno*, p. 514, relates the matter somewhat differently, as quoted above.

98. [Chapter 100.] [Col. 0705C–0706B] The statement that, through the merits of his most sacred body, Christ displayed many signs is an addition in manuscript 2. Peter Damian reports it also in *On the Birth and Death of the Just*, 58, and *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 17.

99. [Chap. 101.] Meanwhile Gregory, son of Alberic [Note: [Col. 0705C] The Roman Annals themselves have *Alberic*, in *Monumenta SS.*, p. 470.], count of Tusculum [Note: [Col. 0707A] “Of the Lateran and of Tusculum,” 2.], having learned of the Roman pontiff’s death, joined Girard of Galera [Note: [Col. 0705] *Gaiera*, 4.] and several powerful Romans to himself. By night, with crowds of armed men everywhere rioting [Note: [Col. 0705] “everywhere with crowds of armed men,” added in 4.] and raging, they seized the rights of the Church, and set up as pope in the Roman see John, bishop of Velletri—afterwards surnamed Mincius [Note: [Col. 0706C] “Balordo, whence arose the word *minchione* [fool].” Di Meo, *Annals of Naples*, VII, 338. Peter Damian calls him *Mintio*, *Opusc.* XX, 3.]—although unwilling, as they report [Note: [Col. 0705] “it is reported,” 3.], giving him the name Benedict [Note: [Col. 0706C] Peter calls him “the Tusculan” in his catalogue of pontiffs.]. [Note: [Col. 0705] “Though unwilling, that he might be made pope in the Roman see,” is absent in 2.]

When Peter Damian, a man most devout and from childhood most studious in secular and sacred letters [Note: [Col. 0705] “and in secular and divine letters from childhood” is absent in 2.], whom Pope Stephen at that time had drawn away from the hermitage [Note: [Col. 0706C] At Fonte Avellana. A large part of this chapter is drawn from his Epistle III.4: namely, from “raging by night” through “was drawn.”] and made bishop of the Church of Ostia, heard of this [Note: [Col. 0705] *auditi*, 3; absent in 2.], he began, together with the other cardinals then present [Note: [Col. 0705] “who were present” added in 4; absent in the edition.], to resist as best he could [Note: [Col. 0705] “in whatever way,” 4.], protest, and pronounce fearful anathemas [Note: [Col. 0705] added in 4.]. But at last all these men, compelled by fear of his supporters, were forced to flee into various hiding places.

Thus the archpriest of the Church of Ostia, not ignorant either of the canons or of letters [Note: [Col. 0707B] “Priest Peter Damian.”], was seized and violently dragged by the satellites of Satan, so that he might raise the aforesaid Mincius to the height of the apostolate. [Note: [Col. 0707] “not … ignorant” is absent in 2.]

Meanwhile Bishop Humbert, returning from Florence with Peter, bishop of Tusculum, judged that Rome was not to be stayed in amid so great a storm [Note: [Col. 0707] “under so great a storm,” added in 4.]. A few days later he secretly set out [Note: [Col. 0707] “after a few days,” added in 4.] and hastened to celebrate Easter at Benevento. When on the Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper [15 April] he reached San Germano, he and his companion were invited and retained by the brethren for the sake of the feast.

100. [Chap. 102.] These, moreover, are the gifts of Frederick which this monastery received at different times:

A golden cross above [Note: [Col. 0707] “above the altar,” added in 4.] the altar, most beautifully adorned with gems and pearls [Note: [Col. 0707] “adorned with pearls,” read in the edition.], weighing a little less than two pounds; with its gilded silver tripod and an onyx shaft, suitably adorned with silver and gold [Col. 0708A] [Note: [Col. 0707] added in 4.], the two together weighing five pounds. Four gilded silver icons. One exceedingly beautiful golden icon with gems and enamels, containing a substantial portion of the Lord’s wood. One pair of crystal *ceraptata* [uncertain object-name]; another pair of silver. A Gospel-book decorated with gold and gems. Six copes. A large silver lantern, weighing five pounds, with niello [Note: [Col. 0708B] Italian, *niello*.]. A silver little pitcher for service at the altar. A gilded silver bucket with enamels. Also several hangings and door-curtains. Seven tapestries, and one larger than and more precious than any hanging. One antiphonary.

The second little book of this work, from Aligernus down to Desiderius, having at last been completed by the Lord’s favor [Note: [Col. 0707] added in 4.], we think it fitting and proper, if we are to describe as far as is permitted [Note: [Col. 0707] “as far as may be done,” added in 4.] the life, character, and deeds of that man in their entirety, and to begin from his very cradle, that we should dedicate the third beginning of this little history to his auspices, and thus weave together in order his remaining works, Christ’s grace accompanying us [Note: [Col. 0707] “and from his very beginnings,” “in order,” “accompanying,” “Christ,” and “grace,” added in 4.].

*Here ends the second book* [Note: [Col. 0707] Thus in 3; “History of the monastery of Cassino,” 2; absent in 4.]

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD BOOK BEGIN

[Note: [Col. 0707] Thus in 3. In 2: “The prologue concerning the life and acts of the most reverend Abbot Desiderius, who was also Pope Victor III, begins.” There the table of chapters is written after the prologue under the heading: “The prologue ends; the chapters of the third book begin.” In manuscript 3 the prologue is counted together with the chapters.]

1. On the birth [Note: [Col. 0707] In 2: “On the origin, childhood, and adolescence of D[esiderius]. On his reception of the monastic habit. On violence inflicted upon him because he received the habit. On Desiderius’s flight to the monastery of Cava. On his return to the monastery of St Sophia at Benevento. On Desiderius’s journey to the monastery of Tremiti and the monastery of Majella, and his return to St Sophia. On the arrival of Alphanus and Desiderius at this monastery. On D[esiderius]’s vision and his provostship, and Stephen’s archbishopric. On Desiderius’s election and confirmation by the pope. On Desiderius’s reception into the abbacy. How he began to renew the monastery and its buildings [“the buildings of the monastery,” 3]. Why Desiderius built Castel Nuovo. On … consecrated, and how … Calena was granted to St Benedict. On the restoration of St Benedict of S[alerno] and the exchange of St L[awrence], and how charters of St Benedict of Salerno belonging to us were found, hidden, and cut up out of envy for us. Chapter 15 = chapter 14 in manuscript 4, etc. and the edition; but manuscripts 2 and 3 frequently differ, and the division of chapters in 3 is the same as in 4.] or purpose of Desiderius.

2. How, after his father’s death, he secretly fled from his mother and put on the religious habit.

3. How he was found by his relatives and brought back to his mother.

4. How he fled again and stayed at Salerno in the monastery of Cava.

5. How he was again brought back to Benevento through Prince Landulf, was permitted to remain at St Sophia, and why he was called Desiderius.

6. How he first went to the monastery of Tremiti, then to Majella, and likewise returned to Benevento.

7. How he became intimate with Pope Leo; and how, joined to Alphanus of Salerno, he came first to the court of Pope Victor and then with him to this monastery.

8. On Desiderius’s vision, and how Alphanus was sent to the abbacy at Salerno, while he himself was sent to the provostship at Capua.

9. How Desiderius was elected and ordained.

10. On his zeal and the construction of the monastery’s workshops.

11. Why he built Castel Nuovo.

12. On the ordination of Pope Nicholas, and how he was consecrated cardinal and abbot by him.

13. How the same apostolic lord held a council at Melfi in Apulia; how St Mary of Calena was granted to St Benedict [Note: [Col. 0707] “the courts of the house of St Benedict,” 4.]; how St Benedict of Salerno was restored; and concerning the exchange of St Lawrence.

14. How the aforesaid pope ordained Lord Oderisius deacon, and appointed Lord Martin bishop at Aquino and Lord Peter bishop at Venafro [Note: [Col. 0709] “and at Venafro,” absent in the edition.].

15. How the same apostolic lord confirmed Richard in the principality and Robert Guiscard in the duchy [Note: [Col. 0709] “and Robert Guiscard,” absent in the edition.]; and how each acquired it. [Note: [Col. 0709] The edition instead has: “17. How the same prince issued a charter concerning the public square at Capua, where our monastery was situated. 18. How he partly granted and partly exchanged certain neighboring castles.”]

16. How the same prince partly granted us, partly exchanged, some neighboring castles; and concerning the exchange of Piedimonte.

17. On the offerings of certain persons in this place [Note: [Col. 0709] “certain churches offered and other offerings,” in the edition.].

18. How many and what ornaments Desiderius then either acquired or made [Note: [Col. 0709] “made, and concerning the bronze doors of the church,” in the edition.].

19. On the ordination of Pope Alexander and the dispute concerning Cadalous.

20. On the scourge of lightning bolts and the abbot’s vision concerning it.

21. How, at the request of Barisone [Note: [Col. 0709] “Baresone,” in the edition.], king of Sardinia, he sent twelve monks there, and how they were molested by the Pisans.

22. Likewise on the offerings of that king and another king in Sardinia, and on the Pisans’ satisfaction.

23. On the arrival of Duke Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0709] “Roffrid,” in the edition.] at Aquino and the Normans’ entry into the March [Note: [Col. 0709] *mar*, 4.].

24. How many brethren of this monastery were promoted to offices by the aforesaid father; and concerning the privilege made for us against Archbishop Hildebrand.

25. On the monastery of Tremiti, received and ordered by the aforesaid abbot.

26. How he demolished the old church and built a new one.

27. How, having summoned craftsmen from Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0709] *acersitis*, 4.], he decorated that basilica with mosaics and stones [Note: [Col. 0709] “with … glass and paintings. 30. How great the glory, etc.,” in the edition.].

28. On the various works in that church.

29. With how great glory he dedicated that church, and with what relics of saints he adorned it [Note: [Col. 0709] absent in the edition.].

30. On the crowds of people flocking here for absolution [Note: [Col. 0709] *conc.*, in the edition.].

31. On Queen Agnes [Note: [Col. 0709] “Agnete,” in the edition.] and her offerings.

32. On the various ornaments of that church. [Note: [Col. 0709] In the edition: “33. On its various ornaments, and how, for enlarging the cloister, he had the former workshops pulled down and rebuilt much more splendidly.”]

33. How, in order to enlarge the monastery’s cloister, he demolished the former workshops and rebuilt them far grander and better.

34. How charters of the monastery of St Benedict at Salerno belonging to us, long since found, were hidden and cut up out of envy for us. [Note: [Col. 0709] “They were. Desiderius begins,” 4; “The chapters end,” 3.]

34a. On the renewal of the church of St Martin; the construction of Desiderius’s small dwelling; and how he dedicated the churches of St Bartholomew and the towers of Paradise.

35. On Alberic [Note: [Col. 0709] “Aberic,” manuscript c.], and how, being summoned, he attended a synod. On Alphanus. On Amatus and Constantine the African.

36. On a demoniac and a certain lame woman healed by Pope Alexander; on the exchange of St Mary of Palladio; and on the grant of the city of Terracina [Note: [Col. 0709] “city,” manuscript c.].

37. On the restoration or offering and construction of the monastery of St Angelo in Formis.

38. On seven miracles performed through the merits of blessed Benedict [Note: [Col. 0709] *pats*, manuscript c.].

39. On certain renunciations and offerings.

40. On certain miracles performed through the merits of blessed Benedict in Gaul and here.

41. On certain offerings.

42. On a question raised before the apostolic lord concerning the church of St Sophia and the church of St Angelo in Formis.

43. On the miracles of certain monks of this monastery.

44. On certain offerings.

45. How Robert Guiscard took Sicily and Salerno, built the church of St Matthew the Apostle, reserving the arm for himself, and took very many places.

46. On money violently taken away and an interdict.

47. On certain offerings and confirmations.

48. On miracles of certain monks and the restoration of St Liberator.

49. [Col. 0711] On the cause of the disagreement between Emperor Henry and Pope Gregory, and how Robert Guiscard entered Romania.

50. On the archbishop of Ravenna, invader of the apostolic see, and how Desiderius went to the emperor, remained, and returned.

51. On the death of two monks of this monastery.

52. On the castle of Saracenisco and Suio.

53. How Robert Guiscard brought the apostolic lord to this place.

54. On the nocturnal vision of a certain John, and when the apostolic lord celebrated Mass.

55. On a portion of the life-giving Cross brought here, the restoration of St Benedict at Capua, and rain requested.

56. On certain offerings and Aldemarius, monk of this monastery.

57. On the death of Robert Guiscard and the arm of St Matthew the Apostle.

58. On the offerings of the same Robert in this monastery.

59. On certain offerings and exchanges.

60. On certain grants made by Desiderius and on certain offerings.

61. On certain offerings.

62. On Guaifer of Salerno.

63. On the books which Desiderius caused to be made.

64. On robbers.

65. On the death of Pope Gregory and deliberation concerning an election.

66. On the election made of Desiderius.

67. On the return of the elect to Cassino.

68. On the consecration of the elect as Pope Victor. On the body of St Nicholas.

69. On the church of St Peter and the vision of that Apostle.

70. On Guibert, heresiarch, and the persecution of the churches.

71. How Pope Victor sent an army into Africa against the Saracens, and on that army’s victory.

72. On the general council and its constitutions.

73. On the death of Pope Victor and the appointment of Abbot Oderisius.

74. How many and what ecclesiastical ornaments Pope Victor, formerly Abbot Desiderius, left in this monastery at his death.

## THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0711A] DESIDERIUS, the thirty-seventh abbot of this monastery and the fourth restorer and renewer of this place, ruled for twenty-nine years and five months.

For the first founder and builder of this monastery was the most holy father Benedict; Petronax was the second, Aligernus [Note: [Col. 0711] “third Aligernus,” in the edition.] the third; and this our Desiderius was the fourth. Almighty God [Note: [Col. 0711] Absent in 4.] held him so dear that what He had once promised to His faithful servant Benedict—namely, that indeed this place [Note: [Col. 0711] “place indeed,” added in 4.], which He had then judged fit to hand over to the nations for destruction and plunder [Note: [Col. 0711] “had been accustomed,” 4.], would attain a condition, fame [Note: [Col. 0711] “fame,” 4.], and glory far greater than it had then possessed—He deigned, as may be seen, to bring to fulfilment through him in our own time. [Note: [Col. 0711] “[lacuna] … had said in the account of the dedication of the church of Cassino.”] [Note: [Col. 0711] In 2: “In him, indeed, almighty God seems in our own time to have fulfilled even bodily that evangelical promise which says: ‘Amen I say to you, that everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life.’ Of this man, etc.”]

The subject-matter of the deeds of this truly admirable and singular man of his order is so rich, so manifold [Note: [Col. 0711] “than,” 4.], and finally so abundant that it could not seem unworthy of writing even [Note: [Col. 0711] Added in 4.] to Jerome himself, or certainly to Sulpicius, were they present. Yet I, although unskilled [Note: [Col. 0711] “the most unskilled of all, and …,” in the edition.] and inactive, and altogether unequal to so great a work, undertake nevertheless, relying on God’s help, to sketch his life and deeds as I can. I do so partly because the command of the most reverend Father Oderisius [Note: [Col. 0711] “most holy,” 2.] must not be scorned, and partly because of the great affection which Father Desiderius himself deigned to show me almost from my childhood, when, scarcely past my fourteenth year, he received me in this holy place [Note: [Col. 0711] “how gladly he received [me],” in the edition.], instructed, nourished, and advanced me.

Moreover, I have considered [Note: [Col. 0711] The edition reads: “seeing furthermore and grieving.”] that, along with the usefulness of so great a work, the memory of so great a man would gradually pass, through writers’ neglect, into oblivion and hence into contempt. Therefore, although I cannot do so fittingly, elegantly, or sufficiently [Note: [Col. 0713] “so as to embrace all his works completely; yet I shall undertake to touch upon those of Abbot Desiderius in some fashion,” in the edition.], I shall endeavor to commit to writing, for the glory of God, the sweet [Note: [Col. 0713] “holy,” in the edition.] memory of so great a man, and [Note: [Col. 0713] Added in 4.] the consolation of his sons, our brethren, whatever I can of his life and deeds.

I judge it more fitting to incur the reproach of ignorance with obedience and devotion than to be wholly silent about so excellent [Note: [Col. 0713] “precious,” in the edition.] a subject. I have determined it wholly unworthy that, though I cannot tell all, I should not endeavor to report at least something of his so many and so great works. I follow the prudent practice of hunters pursuing wild beasts: even though they cannot catch them all [Note: [Col. 0713] “take,” in the edition.], they nevertheless do not neglect to catch as many as they can.

And because the deeds [Note: [Col. 0713] “works,” in the edition.] of this great man [Note: [Col. 0713] “such a great,” in the edition.] are exceedingly many and almost innumerable, I acknowledge [Note: [Col. 0713] The edition reads: “I acknowledge that I shall omit many even among those things which I know.”] that I shall omit many things even among those I know. For if I had wished to write everything [Note: [Col. 0713] “if [I had wished] to write everything,” in the edition.], I should certainly have composed a long and unwieldy history, although I do not doubt that many of our brethren who remember these matters with me [Note: [Col. 0713] “the aforesaid things,” in the edition.] will reproach me for this. But, suitably consulting the weariness of readers, I judged it sufficient that only those matters most worthy of relation should be written down. For whatever is less fully found [Note: [Col. 0713] Absent in the edition.] in our writings is surely seen more clearly than daylight in his [Note: [Col. 0713] Added in 4.] works [Note: [Col. 0713] “is seen,” in the edition.].

The beginnings of this man’s life, since with Christ’s help I desire to begin my account from them, I learned from those who had been his [Note: [Col. 0713] “his,” in the edition.] companions from the cradle [Note: [Col. 0713] “learned,” in the edition.]. [Col. 0713C] I heard many of his praiseworthy acts from certain elders. [Note: [Col. 0713] In the edition: “Many things, moreover, I learned from the trustworthy report of his own old companions who had known him from infancy. Some things I also heard from elders.”] I learned other things from his own truthful mouth, when in his great kindness he frequently allowed me to remain close to him. Finally, I myself saw many of his other deeds with my own eyes, and was present at almost all of them until his death.

Therefore I wish to make my reader entirely certain that I shall make no additions from outside in this little work, and that I shall write nothing whatever about him except what I have learned to be true. For I remember reading in a straightforward sense: “Thou, O Lord, shalt destroy all those who speak a lie” [Psalm 5:7]; saving, of course, the other interpretation by which the saying is affirmed to concern heretics.

But if perhaps anyone, led by envy or malice, refuses to give credit to these things and supposes that I have devoted my labor to this work for the sake of favor, let him hasten here, if he pleases, open his eyes and see. Let him, setting envy aside, consider and admire, and believe from the things that are seen those deeds of his which cannot be seen. [Note: [Col. 0713] “of his deeds,” added in 4.] And believing, let him offer praise and thanks for this to the Giver of all good things. Thus at last let him recognize that out of his many deeds I have written but few, and of his greatest deeds the very least.

1. He [Note: [Col. 0713] “Desiderius,” 3; “Desiderius therefore,” 2; “he,” 4, which the rubricator painted in larger letters.] drew his lineage from the noblest stock of the princes of Benevento [Note: [Col. 0713] Born in 1027, since he died a sexagenarian in 1087; see his epitaph in Baronius under that year.], yet began from the first elements of childhood to be noble more in spirit than in flesh. From the very breasts of his mother, so to speak, he chose to devote himself rather to God’s service than to the vanities of the age.

While still a little boy, he took pains to frequent church, willingly to hear and read the divine readings, often to engage certain religious men in discussion of these things, and to express in himself whatever he could learn from them concerning good conduct. [Note: [Col. 0713] “he strove to express [them],” in the edition.] But his father [Note: [Col. 0713] Amatus III.49 calls him count of Benevento.], wishing to involve him in worldly affairs, and loving him uniquely as an only son, planned to perpetuate the name of his nobility through his descendants. Accordingly, when he had begun to reach adolescence, he sought to betroth to him a girl equally noble and by every means hasten the union, so that the two families might thereby be joined together.

But because God’s Spirit had kindled Desiderius’s heart with His fire for contempt of the world, the excellent boy intended to act in a manner wholly contrary to his father’s plan. By such secret gestures as he could, he indicated that he desired the desert rather than marriage. He would certainly have fulfilled his desire [Note: [Col. 0713] added in 4.], had not the watchful guardianship of his parents, their singular love, and their great concern prevented him.

2. Not many days later, by God’s judgment, his father was slain by the Normans. Desiderius, having somehow obtained the opportunity he had long desired, began by every means, although secretly, to strive to bring into action the desire he had conceived in thought.

He communicated his entire plan to a monk well known to him, a man quite prudent in worldly matters, named Jaquintus; it was from this man’s account that I learned these things. [Note: [Col. 0713] added in 4.] He disclosed his vow and declared his purpose, urgently begging him as a most faithful petitioner to help him in this matter. [Note: [Col. 0713] “confidently,” in the edition; “with a faithful petition,” in the edition.] He was then about twenty years old.

“You know, my father,” he said, “how my relatives have entangled me in this wretched world. But since, to tell you truly, I have long resolved to devote myself to God, I adjure and beseech you by God Himself: according to your knowledge and ability, free me from these bonds and secretly convey me, that I may serve God more freely, to some most remote solitude.”

Why say more? Jaquintus promised help in every respect, but warned [Note: [Col. 0713] “commanded,” in the edition.] him to beware lest this perhaps be a suggestion of demons. Yet when he recognized that Desiderius’s heart was steadfast in Christ in every way, and, testing him again and again [Note: [Col. 0173] “testing him,” 3; “testing him repeatedly,” 2.], found always what he had found before, one day, near evening, they mounted their horses together as though for a ride and left the city. Several servants followed them to [Note: [Col. 0715] absent in the edition.] the church of St Peter called Major, situated beside that city.

Entering it as if [Note: [Col. 0715] “as if for the purpose of prayer,” 4.] to pray, they left outside the doors, apparently for safekeeping, their horses and the sword which Desiderius then wore at his side [Note: [Col. 0715] “girded,” 3.]. Then, late in the day, they went out through a small rear door of the church, set out on foot [Note: [Col. 0715] absent in 2.], and began their journey. [Note: [Col. 0715] “began to proceed,” in the edition.] Though the place to which they had planned to go was no more than eight miles away, confused by darkness and fear, they scarcely arrived there on the following morning.

When the servant of God, a man named Santari, who led a solitary life there, saw them, he was greatly astonished and delighted. [Note: [Col. 0715] “the servant of God,” added in 4.] He immediately brought them into his cell, repeatedly kissed Desiderius, and began carefully to inquire why they had come in this way. When he learned Desiderius’s purpose, he was profoundly astonished that a boy so noble, so delicately reared, so wealthy, and especially so beloved by his parents [Note: [Col. 0715] “parents,” in the edition.], had come to serve the Lord under so strict a resolve, having so fervently despised all worldly pomp and vanity.

But knowing that nothing is difficult or impossible to God, he offered Him praise and abundant thanks. At Desiderius’s own especial insistence, he immediately stripped from him the old man with his deeds and then clothed him with the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God. Jaquintus soon returned to his own place, while Desiderius alone remained with Santari alone. [Note: [Col. 0715] “Desiderius” is his proper name, 4.]

3. As stated above, his servants waited in vain for him outside the church doors with his horses and arms. When at last they learned of his departure, they returned as quickly as possible to the city in the night now approaching [Note: [Col. 0715] “returned earlier,” in the edition.] and, with frightened hearts, reported to his mother and relatives what had happened. [Note: [Col. 0715] “they are reported,” 2.]

His mother spent that night in tears. At dawn his relatives and kinsmen mounted horses and scattered through the surrounding district [Note: [Col. 0715] “through various neighboring districts,” in the edition.] to look for him. At length, suspecting what had occurred and guided by the evidence of his virtue, they came to Santari’s cell. Immediately breaking into it violently, they found him clothed in the monastic habit. Furiously angry, they assailed the aforesaid servant of God with grave insults and much abuse; then, quite shamefully stripping Desiderius of the sacred garment, they tore it apart with their own hands. Against his will and resistance, they clothed him again in his former dress. [Note: [Col. 0715] “they clothed him in his former garment, against his will and resistance,” in the edition.]

Finally they put him upon a horse and, holding its reins themselves, returned to the city in triumphal fashion, driving before them what seemed a great prize. [Note: [Col. 0715] “finally,” 4.] Who could attempt to recount the tears, laments, and persuasions which his mother now cast away in vain upon Desiderius; or the rejoicing of his relatives—indeed, of the entire city?

For almost a whole year he lived under strict guard in his mother’s house, secular only in dress but celibate in mind. No one could induce him in any way to marry or undertake any worldly occupation. [Note: [Col. 0715] “or of any other worldly occupation,” in the edition.] Thus the Lord, who intended to appoint him a faithful and vigorous steward over His household, kept him pure and free from every stain of carnal contamination. Hence he was deservedly regarded by all the citizens as admirable [Note: [Col. 0715] “wonderful,” in the edition.] and desirable.

4. But when his mother had now almost ceased to suspect that he would flee, and since she could not keep him with her as a married man, she tried to retain him as a cleric. At first she allowed him to go to the bishop’s residence, which stood very near her house, only under guard; later, as her confidence increased, she frequently permitted him to go alone.

At that time a certain Siconulfus was provost in the monastery of St Sophia. Knowing Desiderius’s desire completely, he did not dare to act by day lest suspicion revive, but very frequently spoke with him at night at the bishop’s residence. Not many days later, coming to him by night with horses as was his custom, he secretly led him, clad in a cowl, to Salerno, and quickly returned to Benevento.

Desiderius immediately [Note: [Col. 0715] added in 4.] went to Prince Guaimar, his kinsman, explained the reason for his arrival, and asked that, since the obstinacy of his parents prevented him from daring to live as a monk in his homeland, he might be allowed to serve God peacefully there with him. If he could obtain this, he said, he would never depart. But if at some time Guaimar had to return him to his relatives, he should now rather grant him permission to hasten elsewhere. [Note: [Col. 0715] “should grant him permission to go elsewhere. Of this …,” in the edition.]

Guaimar was exceedingly delighted at his arrival [Note: [Col. 0715] “excessively,” in the edition.] and greatly marveled at such fervor in so young [Note: [Col. 0715] “so great,” 2.] an adolescent. He assented to his requests and kept him with him for several days, faithfully promising never to surrender him against his vow. At last, at Desiderius’s request, he sent him to the monastery of Holy Trinity called La Cava, not far from Salerno. [Note: [Col. 0715] Under Abbot Alferius, who died in 1050; see the Annals of Cava in *Monumenta SS.* III, p. 189, under 1050 and 1058, and the *Life of Alferius* in Muratori, *SS.* VI, p. 208.]

When his relatives learned this [Note: [Col. 0715] “pursuing,” 2.], they repeatedly and urgently appealed to Guaimar to return Desiderius to them. But the prince stood by the promise he had made to Desiderius. Therefore Landulf, prince of Benevento, weary of the entreaties of Desiderius’s mother and relatives, came to Salerno in person and demanded that Desiderius be returned to his kinsmen.

5. At length, therefore, it was obtained on this condition [Note: [Col. 0715] “that,” in the edition.]: that he should return to Benevento, but should be permitted, without hindrance or opposition from anyone, to remain under monastic profession at the monastery of St Sophia.

After they had arrived at Benevento, all his kinsmen, together with the city, rushed out to meet him. The prince, with the entire escort, accompanied him to the monastery. A very prudent and energetic man named Gregory was then abbot over that monastery. Receiving Desiderius with great joy, and because he was desired by everyone, he first ordered his name to be changed and that he should be called Desiderius. Until that time he had been called Dauferius.

6. After remaining there for some years in a most religious life, he repeatedly reflected [Note: [Col. 0717] “often reflected with himself,” in the edition.] that a monk could not become perfect in his own country. Meanwhile he heard of the monastery of Tremiti, situated in the Adriatic Sea upon an island called Diomedes [Note: [Col. 0717] “once called,” 2.] and about thirty miles from the land. Since he had long before acquired at Benevento the friendship of the abbot of that place, he obtained permission, though only with difficulty, and went there. Giving himself to a quite austere way of life, he remained there for a considerable time.

But the abbot loved him so deeply that, while still alive, he wished to hand over the abbey itself to him. Desiderius, however, inclined his mind toward subjection rather than preeminence, and therefore decided that he must leave that place. Once, when the abbot was going out to inspect the monastery’s affairs, he asked Desiderius to accompany him. Desiderius gladly embraced this opportunity to leave and thought it not to be postponed.

When they had gone together, as circumstances required, to the court of Count Trasmund [Note: [Col. 0717] “Transmund,” 3.] of Chieti, [Note: [Col. 0717D] “of Chieti.”] the count’s wife, greatly delighted at Desiderius’s arrival because he was her kinsman [Note: [Col. 0717] “his relatives,” 4.], obtained from her husband leave to keep him with her for a time, even against the abbot’s will. The author of this detention, it is said [Note: [Col. 0717] “says,” in the edition.], was Desiderius himself.

Hearing of the then-famous hermits dwelling on Majella, he desired to hasten there and serve God more secretly. He asked the aforesaid count to send him there, and this was done. After he had remained there for about three months, from the beginning of February until the third week after Easter [Note: [Col. 0717] “Sunday,” 2.], in severe abstinence, the above-named Jaquintus was sent there with letters from the apostolic lord to the prior of that hermitage. Their tenor commanded the prior, under threat, not to presume to retain Desiderius any longer, and likewise directed Desiderius himself not to linger there even for the slightest time. [Note: [Col. 0717] “not to attach even any small delays,” in the edition.] Thus he returned to the monastery of St Sophia.

[Col. 0718A] 7. Not many days later (1053), the most holy lord Pope Leo, having returned from beyond the mountains, entered Benevento. Since Desiderius had long been known and very [Note: [Col. 0717] exceedingly, ed.] dear to Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, he was made known and very familiar to that pope both through him and through Frederick, then chancellor; indeed [Note: [Col. 0717D] “Indeed—” may be read from Desiderius, *Dialogues*, III, Prologue.] he frequently assisted him in the service at the altar, and often read the Gospel at his Masses.

At the same time the aforesaid pontiff went down into Apulia to fight the Normans; but, defeated by them through God’s judgment, he returned to Benevento. Having ordained Huodelric [Note: [Col. 0717] Hodelric 3; Uodelric 2.] archbishop, [Note: [Col. 0718D] A bull dated 12 July 1053 survives.] whom he had brought with him, he returned to Rome after about nine months and died there (1054, 19 April).

Meanwhile Desiderius, [Col. 0718B] falling into no slight illness through excessive fasting and many vigils, went to Salerno for treatment. While he remained there for some time, Alfanus—who later obtained the archbishopric of that city, a most prudent and noble cleric—was joined to him in the closest friendship. By frequent exhortations urging him to despise the world, he finally obtained from him a promise that he would become a monk, provided he were first permitted to go to Jerusalem, as he had long conceived in his mind.

When this agreement between them had been confirmed, Desiderius returned to Benevento and, after not many days, summoned Alfanus to come to him. When the latter refused, or rather was afraid to leave Salerno, Desiderius went to him again; because of the fear of certain persons [Col. 0718C] hostile to him, he clothed him in his own cowl and led him out of the city by night, bringing him with him to Benevento.

But when noblemen and clerics began to visit Alfanus and duly cultivate his acquaintance because of his great prudence, while the intention of undertaking the journey to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0717] “of the journey to Jerusalem,” ed.] gradually began to grow cold in [Note: [Col. 0717] “and in,” ed.] his heart [Note: [Col. 0717] “mind,” ed.], and he declared that he wished in no way and at no time ever to be separated from Desiderius’ side, they spent some time [Note: [Col. 0717] “them,” ed.] at the monastery of Saint Sophia. Then suddenly the report spread abroad that Pope [Note: [Col. 0717] “Pope Victor,” ed.] Victor had come to Rome from beyond the mountains (1055), and would shortly be coming into these regions.

Alarmed by this news, because he supposed that his brothers [Col. 0718D] would be accused concerning the killing of Prince Guaimar [Note: [Col. 0717] “he no doubt knew they would be accused,” 2; “he supposed that they would be accused,” 3.], Alfanus resolved to go to and forestall the pope, and earnestly begged Desiderius to go with him. Because he possessed remarkable skill in singing and no small knowledge of the medical art, and had brought with him from home certain books of that art, he confidently expected to be held in high esteem at the court of the supreme pontiff.

Accordingly, having prepared [Col. 0719A] and made ready as many medicines as he could, they set out, together with the archbishop of that city, for the Roman pontiff in Tuscany, and found him staying at Florence. They quickly gained great familiarity with him and were treated with sufficient honour. But when they had stayed there for some time, and Desiderius had learned for certain that the pope would not be coming to these regions, but was moreover shortly to depart beyond the mountains, and when he judged residence at that pontiff’s court entirely useless [Note: [Col. 0719] “to be useless,” ed.] to his purpose, he began urgently in every way to press Alfanus to ask him at once for leave to return.

A few days earlier Peter had been elected abbot of this monastery by the brothers (December), and, in order to make his own ordination known, [Col. 0719B] had sent two brothers of this place to the pope. Thus Desiderius, having found the long-desired opportunity, approached the Roman pontiff together with Alfanus; prostrating themselves at his feet, they asked permission to depart. They added the request that, in order to live more religiously, he might send them to the monks who had come to him from the monastery of Cassino, and by his letters commend them to the abbot and brothers there.

The pope agreed, and they were accordingly sent with those brothers to this monastery, as they had requested. Received fittingly by the abbot and associated with the brothers, they lived among them for some time with considerable [Note: [Col. 0719] “exceeding,” ed.] honour and humility, and were held by all in the greatest affection. They also received monastic consecration from that [Col. 0719C] abbot, while Frederick rejoiced more than sufficiently at their arrival.

8. During these days Desiderius saw a vision not to be disregarded, which its outcome rather closely confirmed. He saw himself standing with Alfanus in a lofty and exceedingly beautiful tower situated beside the chapter-house of the brothers. In it Father Benedict appeared to be seated in a most fitting chair. Terrified [Note: [Col. 0719] “amazed and terrified,” ed.] and astonished at the sight of him, they did not dare to approach more closely. But blessed [Note: [Col. 0719] added in 4.] Father Benedict cheerfully beckoned to Desiderius and, extending his hand, commanded him to sit [Note: [Col. 0719] “seat,” 4.] beside him. Alfanus, however, since he had not been called by him, left [Col. 0719D] that house as if taking the matter as an affront.

This vision clearly seemed to foretell both that Alfanus would not remain long in this place and that Desiderius would assume Father Benedict’s role in this monastery. Not long afterwards Alfanus was claimed by Prince Gisulf: first he became abbot at Salerno in the monastery of Saint Benedict, and afterwards [Note: [Col. 0719] “thereafter,” ed.] obtained the archbishopric of that city. [Note: [Col. 0719D] Compare chapter 96 of Book II.] Desiderius, however, [Note: [Col. 0719] “indeed,” ed.] was sent as provost to the monastery at Capua. [Col. 0720A]

Richard, count of Aversa, was then besieging Capua. But when Pandulf, prince of that city, wished to impose upon Desiderius certain unworthy and superfluous demands in accordance with the custom of earlier times, Desiderius, steadfast as he was in spirit, did not think it proper in any way to agree with him in these matters. He left Capua and went to Richard. Having obtained from him protection for all the possessions of the monastery outside the city [Note: [Col. 0719] “received,” ed.], and thereafter having entered into very close friendship with him, he stayed for some time in the dependencies of that monastery, leaving very few brothers in the monastery and summoning the rest to himself.

9. Afterwards, when the aforesaid Frederick had been elected abbot of this place (1057), [Note: [Col. 0719] “of this place,” ed.] and then, as we have already mentioned above in its proper place, ordained [Col. 0720B] Roman pontiff, Desiderius went to Rome to him in August, having been expressly summoned by him [Note: [Col. 0719] “by Frederick himself,” ed.] with twelve other brothers of this place. There he was struck by Roman fever and returned here after a few days.

When the same pope came to this monastery about four months later (30 November), he was soon seized by a grave illness and nearly brought to his last extremity. He therefore summoned the priors of this monastery and gave them the choice of electing whom they wished as abbot. After taking counsel together, they considered first one man, then another, as is customary in such circumstances; but at last the common agreement of all turned toward seeking Desiderius. With united prayers they begged the pope that he might be granted to them as their father.

The pope declared that this election was very [Note: [Col. 0719] “sufficiently,” ed.] pleasing to him. For Desiderius had been very well known to him at Benevento from the time of Pope Leo; and, since Abbot Peter had received Desiderius less than two full years previously, Frederick had bound him to himself by close friendship. Thus, while still in his chamber, he confirmed the brothers’ election, saying that, although that [Note: [Col. 0719] “this monastery,” ed.] place then had many religious and spiritual men, endowed with much uprightness and prudence, they could not have selected anyone from their community more suitable for that office.

But [Note: [Col. 0719] “And,” ed.] because, while he himself lived, he had resolved to entrust that abbacy to no mortal [Note: [Col. 0719] “would entrust,” ed.], and had long intended to make Desiderius the Roman see’s apocrisiarius, or envoy, to the emperor at Constantinople, [Col. 0720D] he decreed that, if Desiderius returned while he himself was alive, he would honourably [Note: [Col. 0719] added in 4.] confer the abbacy upon him; but if it happened that he died before Desiderius’ return [Note: [Col. 0719] “conversion,” 4; “had died before his return,” ed.], the whole congregation was to receive Desiderius on his return as abbot without any opposition.

Accordingly, giving him Stephen the cardinal and Mainard—later bishop of Silva Candida—as travelling companions, [Col. 0721A] and describing him in the letters sent to the emperor as elected to the abbacy of Cassino, he dismissed him, commanding him to hasten back as soon as possible [Note: [Col. 0721] “as quickly as he could,” ed.] once his embassy was completed.

After this Frederick returned to Rome (1058, 29 March), then set out for Tuscany, and after a few days died at Florence, as we have already related above. [Note: [Col. 0721] “After—died” are absent in 2.] Desiderius, desiring to expedite the task imposed upon him, took everything necessary for so great a journey and, setting out with his companions [Note: [Col. 0721] “with those entrusted to him,” ed.], proceeded to the monastery of Saint John, called Saint John “in Venus,” [Note: [Col. 0721] “which is called in V[enus], as …,” ed.] intending to embark there.

But after remaining there vainly [Note: [Col. 0721] “remaining there vainly,” ed.] for several days, and not daring to put to sea because of the inclement weather, he made for Siponto. There [Note: [Col. 0721] “there,” ed.] he boarded a ship [Col. 0721B] bound for Bari. Through a certain bishop who had gone to Mount Gargano for prayer, he asked that the brothers be commended to him, and that they be informed that he had only then [Note: [Col. 0721] “only then,” added in 4.] embarked.

But since he was likewise delayed at Bari for some time because of a storm, [Note: [Col. 0721] added in 4.] he took care to send another messenger here, ordering him to report [Note: [Col. 0721] “to signify,” ed.] that, owing to the bad weather, he was remaining at Bari until that [Note: [Col. 0721] “that,” ed.] day. By divine providence—which had delayed him until then from receiving the honour of this place—it happened that on the day when that messenger [Note: [Col. 0721] added in 4.] arrived here, our brothers who had travelled with the pope also returned, after the pope had died and been buried at Florence. The brothers immediately took counsel and hastily sent two [Col. 0721C] brothers to recall Desiderius with news of the pope’s death. [Note: [Col. 0721] Manuscript 2 ends chapter 9 here.]

[Chapter 10.] At last Desiderius had adequately prepared all the necessities [Note: [Col. 0721] “all things sufficient and necessary for the journey undertaken,” ed.] for his intended journey, and was on the point of sailing with Argyrus, commander of the people of Bari, when, on Palm Sunday itself (12 April), toward evening, he received the aforesaid messengers [Note: [Col. 0721] “the same messengers sent to him by our brothers,” ed.]. They said that the pope had died and that all the brothers had urgently sent them to recall him [Note: [Col. 0721] “sent in haste by …,” ed.]; he should return as quickly as possible and assume the governance of the monastery, as the Lord had ordained, since all were eagerly awaiting him.

Desiderius was stunned by the blow of the pope’s sudden death. He immediately summoned his companions and disclosed what the messengers had brought. Together with Argyrus they began to consider anxiously [Col. 0721D] how they might return before the pope’s death became known. They did not doubt that, once his death was known, they would either be captured or molested by the Normans.

They at once bought or otherwise acquired several mounts for themselves and their companions, and on the following [Note: [Col. 0721] “the Monday after Palm Sunday,” 2.] day (13 April) began their journey. They came to Robert Guiscard, at that time count only of part [Note: [Col. 0721] “of only a part of Apulia,” 2.] of Apulia, but later duke of all Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, and asked to be permitted to pass safely through his territory. Since he was a man of great goodness, although he had already learned of the pope’s death, he granted them safe-conduct [Note: [Col. 0721] “to them,” ed.] and gave Desiderius three horses which he still needed.

Thus, with God granting success in all things, they returned without hindrance [Note: [Col. 0721] “came back,” ed.] and arrived rather late on the Easter vigil itself (18 April) at the town of Saint Germanus. On the Sunday of holy Easter (19 April), very [Note: [Col. 0721] “exceedingly,” ed.] early at dawn, as they went up to [Note: [Col. 0721] “as was customary at this monastery, they came here to …,” ed.] this monastery, they entered the brothers’ chapter-house in the customary manner. Humbert, bishop of Santa Rufina, Peter, [Col. 0722B] bishop of Tusculum, and Stephen the cardinal and Mainard, Desiderius’ companions, presided.

For, as we have related much earlier above (Book II, chapter 99), the aforesaid bishops Humbert and Peter, fleeing the simoniacal ordination at Mincio after the pope’s death, were travelling to Benevento to celebrate Easter. [Note: [Col. 0722C] “We related: then from Rome, Mincio,” 2.] But by God’s ordering they had been invited and detained [Note: [Col. 0721] “having been invited and retained,” ed.] by our priors for the grace of so great a festival.

After the solemn address for so great a solemnity [Note: [Col. 0721] “day,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0721] “so great,” 2; absent in 3.], Humbert, fully acquainted with the whole arrangement, immediately summoned Desiderius and ordered him, on behalf of all the brothers, to receive obedience as abbot, as had formerly been arranged by the pope. There was no delay after [Note: [Col. 0721] “No one intervened,” 2.] the command, no waiting for an answer. At once all rose and accepted Desiderius. [Col. 0722C] With the greatest praises they carried him to the church and honourably seated him in the abbot’s chair. All were filled with immeasurable gladness and joy, both for the solemnity of Easter and for his installation: in the year of the Lord 1058 [Note: [Col. 0721] “that is, in the year 1058 of the Lord’s incarnation,” 2; “in the thousand and fifty-eighth year of the Lord,” 3.], 19 April.

10. [Chapter 11.] Having assumed the abbacy, Desiderius began to strive and labour by every means so that what was said might truly be said. Seeing that all the workshops of the monastery were cramped in extent and misshapen in form, and ruinous both from age and neglect, so that all seemed covered by connected roofs and the exit of one was joined to the entrance of another, he was moved in spirit to undertake their renewal. Yet he was troubled because he had almost no resources with which to begin so arduous [Col. 0722D] a work.

At first, however, [Note: [Col. 0721] “therefore,” ed.] wishing as though to test what he could accomplish, he completed with quite suitable workmanship [Note: [Col. 0721] “suitable,” ed.] the palace which Abbot Richerius had long before begun on the eastern side of the monastery and carried as far as the upper storey. [Note: [Col. 0721D] Compare chapter 89 of Book II.] Beside it, toward the church, [Col. 0723A] he built a small but entirely adequate room in which books might be stored.

When he saw this had come about with a favourable result, he also resolved to rebuild from [Note: [Col. 0723] “from the foundations” absent in ed.] the foundations the house in which the abbots had customarily lived. It adjoined the church on its northern side; it was supported from below by the meanest forked timbers, [Note: [Col. 0723] “of wood,” ed.] [Note: [Col. 0723] “on its lower side,” ed.] and appeared for the greater part to be woven of wattles. [Note: [Col. 0723] “built of wattles; he resolved to build it from the foundations,” added in ed.] He added to it a palace with an apse, which the ancients used to call the *todericum*.

Thereafter, God inspiring and prospering him, he undertook with no less energy to renew the building which, because of its small size, held the resting brothers in separate upper rooms. [Note: [Col. 0723] “the brothers who were resting,” ed.] It stood on the southern side of the former building, which he intended [Note: [Col. 0723] “intended. For …,” ed.] to demolish completely in order to make room for a cloister. For, because of the summit of the mountain, which had scarcely any level ground, [Col. 0723B] the earlier abbots had with difficulty made even the semblance of a very small cloister in this place, beside the church apse. [Note: [Col. 0723] “indeed had scarcely any level ground,” ed.]

The new building was completed at a length of one hundred and sixty cubits and a width of twenty-four cubits; [Note: [Col. 0723] “and four,” ed.] its height varied because of the unevenness of the mountain, but was nevertheless very great. Having most beautifully roofed it with fir beams, [Note: [Col. 0723] “and roofing it very beautifully. He …,” ed.] he covered it with tiles and decorated it in various colours. Without delaying over this, [Note: [Col. 0723] “And delaying over nothing further,” ed.] he utterly demolished the old chapter-house and built a new one [Note: [Col. 0723] “and renewed it,” ed.]. He adorned it round about with a plaster cornice, glass windows, and a very fine [Note: [Col. 0723] added in 4.] pavement of variegated marbles; he likewise roofed it with tiles, [Col. 0723C] and painted it with an exceedingly lovely [Note: [Col. 0723] “ancient,” 4.] variety of diverse [Note: [Col. 0723] added in 4.] colours.

11. [Chapter 12.] Meanwhile the townspeople of Fratte, a race of restless and [Note: [Col. 0723] “namely, and,” ed.] treacherous men down [Note: [Col. 0723] “down to that time” absent in 2.] to that time, behaved like brigands. Allied with the people of Minturno and other neighbours, they never ceased, now secretly, now openly, to harass nearby towns belonging to us.

The boundary which had from ancient times divided us from them—namely, two stone lions [Note: [Col. 0723] “stone lions,” ed.]—stood not far from their fortress. Long before, they had maliciously broken the lions in secret and thrown them into a nearby well. Trusting in this deception, whenever we reckoned our boundary as lying between the two lions, as the imperial charters [Note: [Col. 0723] absent in 2.] prescribe, they mockingly [Note: [Col. 0723] “they said this” absent in 2.]—indeed obstinately—asserted that the statement referred to the lions placed beside the gates [Col. 0723D] of Saint George.

Desiderius bore their very frequent vexations with the greatest distress [Col. 0724A] and recalled the maxim: “The observance of our order requires the utmost peace and security.” Since he could not pacify them by either favours or arguments, he finally devoted himself entirely to forcibly checking their wickedness. Supported by the aid of Adenulf, duke of Gaeta, whose reconciliation with the prince he had secured, [Note: [Col. 0723D] See Amatus, IV.12–14.] he promptly built, with every effort against them, a fortress called properly New Castle, on the mountain named Perano. Thus he compelled them thereafter to protect what was their own, rather than invade what belonged to others.

12. [Chapter 13.] But, to return a little way, after the death of Pope Stephen of pious memory, the aforesaid Hildebrand returned from the empress. Finding that, contrary to the prohibition of that pope, the church had been usurped by [Col. 0724B] utterly wicked men, he stopped at Florence. By his letters he assembled the better men among the Romans on this matter, obtained their consent to all that [Note: [Col. 0723] “whatever,” added in 4.] he wished, and immediately, with Duke Godfrey’s support, elected Gerard, bishop of Florence, pope of Rome. He came with him and the duke to Rome in January (1059). There the aforesaid elect was enthroned in the apostolic see by the Roman clergy and people [Note: [Col. 0723] added in 4.] and took the name Nicholas.

Nicholas immediately excommunicated the aforesaid usurper together with all his supporters; later, through the intervention of some of his own party, he received him into communion and ordained that he should remain at the church of Saint Mary, called Major by the Romans, deprived of priestly office. [Note: [Col. 0723D] Compare *Annals of Rome*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, V, 471.]

He then ordered this monastery [Col. 0724C] that the lord abbot should meet him as soon as possible while he was proceeding to the March, in order that, in the approaching fast of March, he might receive both the rank of priest [Note: [Col. 0723] “priest,” ed.] and the dignity of the cardinalate [Note: [Col. 0723] “should receive the office,” 2.], together with consecration to the abbacy.

Accordingly, on the first Sunday of Lent (21 February), having prepared all necessities, Desiderius set out and joined the pope at the monastery of Farfa. Received there by him with the greatest friendliness and honour, he went with him to Auximum [Note: [Col. 0723D] Osimo.]. There, on the second Saturday in Lent, which that year fell on the day before the Nones of March, he was ordained cardinal-priest by the same pope; and on the following Sunday he received consecration to the abbacy. He received from him a highly honourable privilege, according to the custom of his predecessors (8 March). [Note: [Col. 0724D] In Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 159; Tosti, *History of Cassino*, I, p. 395.] By it the pope further granted him, for the dignity [Note: [Col. 0723] “namely, its dignity,” ed.] of the cardinalate and the honour of the most holy Father Benedict, his own authority throughout Campania and the Principality, Apulia [Col. 0725A] and Calabria as well, from the river Pescara as it flows [Note: [Col. 0725] “flows,” ed.] into the sea. [Note: [Col. 0725C] Namely, for the correction of all monasteries and monks.]

After receiving leave to return, [Note: [Col. 0725] “leave to return,” ed.] he came to Rome. On the following Sunday, in mid-Lent (14 March), he solemnly celebrated Mass at the church of blessed Peter and, accompanied by an innumerable multitude [Note: [Col. 0725] “a Roman multitude,” ed.] of Romans, was conducted with great acclaim to the titular church of Saint Cecilia across the Tiber.
