Thus he returned to this monastery for the feast [Note: [Col. 0725] “on the feast of blessed Benedict he returned,” ed.] of Saint Benedict.

But [Note: [Col. 0725] “And because he had been invited by that pontiff for the Easter feast, after the festival he returned, left the city, and went to Melfi, the city of Apulia, where the pope had then arranged to hold a council. At that synod Richard, prince of Capua, was present with many others and, admonished by the aforesaid Pope Nicholas, issued a charter to Saint Benedict concerning the monastery of Saint Mary at Calena with its dependencies. 14. At that time Gisulf …, 2.] because he had been invited to celebrate Easter with the pope, he immediately returned to Rome [Note: [Col. 0725] “returned” absent in 4.] and remained there until the synod was completed in the customary manner. At that synod (13 April), among the other measures solemnly established, the pope wrote with great discernment a decree concerning the ordination of the Roman [Col. 0725B] pontiff [Note: [Col. 0725C] Edited in *Monumenta Legum*, IIb, p. 177.]: namely, how and by what persons he ought to be ordained, whether in time of peace or war, following the ancient judgments of his predecessors. He confirmed it under a strict anathema by his own authority and that of all the priests present at that synod.

13. At the same time (24 June), the same pope came to this monastery on the feast itself of the Nativity of Saint John and, taking Desiderius with him, went down into Apulia. There, after holding a council at Melfi, Prince Richard, whom we have mentioned above, by the admonition or [Note: [Col. 0725] “and,” 3.] command of that pope, issued a charter to this place concerning the monastery of Saint Mary at Calena [Note: [Col. 0725] Cajena, 4.], situated in the borders of Apulia near [Col. 0725C] the town called Besti, [Note: [Col. 0725C] Now Vieste, on the borders of Apulia between Mount Gargano and the Adriatic Sea. Edited by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 161; judged suspect by Di Meo, III, but, in my view, without justification. It was issued some time after the synod had ended.] together with all its castles, villages, cells, and absolutely all its possessions in their entirety (23 August).

[Chapter 14.] Gisulf, prince of Salerno, also restored in full into the hands of the lord abbot the monastery of Saint Benedict at Salerno. [Note: [Col. 0725] “To Desiderius, complaining about this, he restored to this holy place the monastery [‘cell,’ 2] of Saint Benedict,” ed.] The violence of his ancestors had long before taken it away from us, [Note: [Col. 0725] “which the people of Salerno had until then violently withheld from the right of our monastery,” 2.] but, touched by the fear of God, he restored it and asked that it be ordered by him more religiously.

But when the abbot had been removed from there and a provost appointed, according to the custom of our cells, [Note: [Col. 0725] “established,” 2.] the people of Salerno took this very badly [Note: [Col. 0725] “The people of Salerno, taking this very badly, began to press the prince himself that he should allow that monastery to remain ordered as it had been before. The prince, compelled by their request, [the monastery of Saint Lawrence], ed.] and enviously. By prayers and excessive insistence they compelled the prince to undo this arrangement.

At last, after taking counsel, the prince granted in its entirety to our aforesaid abbot the monastery of Saint [Col. 0726A] Lawrence the martyr, built within Salerno [Note: [Col. 0725] “built within the city of Salerno,” 2.] on the side of the mountain. It belonged to him by hereditary right and was granted with all its dependencies, which were by no means small. [Note: [Col. 0725] “He offered this monastery in its entirety; yet he did not invalidate the restoration he had already made of the aforesaid cell,” ed. “But in manuscript 3 *violavit* [‘violated’] is written; and I am persuaded that several readings there should be read as in 4.”] He confirmed this by charter in this monastery, but did not violate the renunciation which he had made concerning the earlier monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0726A] Concerning [ [Col. 0725] these matters Leo had formerly placed, as the table of chapters at the end of the work attests, material which he later inserted in a suitable place. They are now preserved only in manuscript 2.] that same monastery of Saint Benedict at Salerno, lest perhaps its memory should escape us while we are occupied with many things, or lest a more suitable occasion for relating it should not occur, it seems necessary, though in an inverted order, to insert here the malice and envy of certain brothers of the aforesaid monastery. For, as we read that Aeneas said to his companions in Virgil [ [Col. 0726C] That is, Leo.], “Perhaps one day it will be pleasing to remember even these things.”

There was a legal advocate in the aforesaid city of Salerno, named Romuald. Because he was also advocate of that monastery, [Col. 0726B] he possessed great influence there; and so he had received from the abbot entirely trustworthy permission frequently to search through all the records and whatever charters of that place. At length, among the other documents, he found four large charters of donation. These clearly and fully established how, from the beginning, that monastery had been given to and made subject to our monastery by princes.

Moved by the greatest envy, he immediately stole and concealed them, brought them secretly to his own house without anyone at all knowing, and did not show them even to his sons until the day of his death. When he lay at the point of death, he summoned his elder son, named John. Revealing to him secretly the whole business, and holding the aforesaid charters in his hands, he said:

> “As you see, my son, I am without [Col. 0726C] doubt dying. I entrust these charters to your fidelity: if you wish to have my blessing, show them to no mortal whatever until your last day. Rather, as I myself have done, keep them secret with you and unknown to everyone. For if they come in any way to the knowledge of the lords of Cassino, they will not rest until they bring this monastery back under the jurisdiction of their monastery, from which it was long ago withdrawn through the zeal and skill of our forefathers.”

The son accepted with the charters the command of his father and, as though he were hiding something divine in the secret chamber of his breast, likewise kept them concealed until his own death. When he came to die, he summoned his brother, then abbot in his place, and handed them over to him under the same terms in which his father had left them to himself.

Not long afterward, that abbot was accused of certain crimes before Duke Roger, [Col. 0727A] arrested, and committed to custody in his own chamber. That abbot had long before disclosed the contents of the aforesaid charters to a certain pseudo-monk, his kinsman. This man too, no less wicked than those before him, recalled this wicked business and feared that the charters might be found with the abbot and might someday be turned to our advantage. He hurried to the abbot’s guards and, in a mournful voice, declared that he had entrusted four little charters constituting his own inheritance to the abbot, as his kinsman. He earnestly asked that they permit him to seek them out and remove them, lest they should perish when mixed with other effects.

The guards, suspecting no deceit in the monk’s words, immediately gave him permission to search for and take them away. When he found them, he brought them the next day, without the abbot’s knowledge, as they say, before the gathering of all the brothers. He showed and read them and disclosed the entire affair in sequence. All were astonished and indignant, and, as commonly happens in such cases, [Col. 0727B] different men gave different opinions.

At last the view of the majority prevailed: before the matter was made public, the charters should immediately be cut into tiny pieces. Thus it was done at once, envy and anger alike dictating the act. One of the brothers was commanded carefully to gather the fragments of the cuttings and throw them into the brothers’ privies. That all these things happened in this manner was later disclosed in sequence to his abbot, our fellow-brother Lord Jaquintus, by the very brother who had been commanded to dispose of the fragments, pricked by divine fear. I too received the whole account from the mouth of that abbot himself, lest anyone perhaps suppose it falsely or fabulously invented. [Note: [Col. 0727D] Between Capua and Nola. Added in 2.]

[Col. 0727B] 14. [Chapter 15.] At the following time the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0727] “above-mentioned,” ed.] pontiff came again into these regions. While at Acerrae, he ordained in the Lateran church as deacon the lord Oderisius, son of Oderisius, count of the Marsi, and a monk of this place from boyhood. [Col. 0727C] [Note: [Col. 0727D] *Aeneid*, I.203.] [Note: [Col. 0727] “appointed,” 4.]

He also deposed in the city of Aquino a bishop named Angelo, because he was a neophyte and an ill-advised squanderer of ecclesiastical goods, and because of certain [Note: [Col. 0727] absent in ed.] wicked deeds of his he had long before been excommunicated by Pope Leo of holy memory. In his place he consecrated bishop the lord Martin, a Florentine by birth, a truly religious and prudent monk among the priors of this place.

Peter also, bishop of the sees of Venafro [Note: [Col. 0727] Benefrane, 2.] and Isernia, a native of Ravenna and a monk of this monastery, [Note: [Col. 0727] “our monk; at that time he was consecrated,” ed.] was likewise consecrated at that same time.

Source preparation: Canonical local restored source checked directly; no foreign-text recoveries occurred in this chunk.

15. [Chapter 16.] In those same days he also confirmed to Richard the principality of Capua and to Robert [Col. 0727D] the duchy of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, after first receiving from them an oath and fealty to the Roman Church, as well as the investiture of the tribute from all their land—namely, twelve denarii each year for every yoke of oxen.

[Note: At the opening, the edition reads *Hisdem* (“those same”); manuscript 3 omits “the principality of Capua”; the forms *Rothberto* (manuscript 2) and *Rotperto* (manuscript 3) occur for Robert; the edition has “with an oath of fealty”; it omits “and likewise”; manuscript 2 omits “the tribute from all their land”; the edition reads “in each individual year.”]

[Col. 0727D–0728D. Both oaths that Robert, “by the grace of God and of Saint Peter duke of Apulia and Calabria, and, with the help of both, future duke of Sicily,” took are published by Baronius from the book of tributes under the year 1059, no. 70.]

But since the course of the history of these two great men—Robert, that is, and Richard—has brought them into mention, and since they, beyond the other mortals of their age, loved, enriched, and protected this place, and throughout their lives proved exceedingly devoted, faithful, and most friendly to our Desiderius, it seems fitting briefly to insert into this little work how each was advanced to the honor of his rank; for we remember that we promised this very thing above (Book II, ch. 66).

[AMAT III, 7, 10, 11; IV, 3, 4–7, 18, 23; V, 7, 18, 20, 23, 24–27; Col. 0728B VI, 13–22.]

[Note: The edition places “the course of the history of these men has brought mention” after *extiterunt*, and reads *hunc dilexerunt, ditaverunt ac protegerunt* (“they loved, enriched, and protected this place”); manuscript 4 reads *profectus* (“went forth”) for *provectus* (“advanced”).]

Robert’s brother Drogo, who was then count of Apulia, first granted him the castle of Saint Mark, which he himself had built not long before on the border of Calabria, and invested him likewise with all Calabria. But since Robert was exceedingly poor, and saw that he could not acquire it without a large sum of money for recruiting soldiers, he finally summoned to a conference Peter of Tyre, a very wealthy man, lord of the neighboring city called Bisignano [manuscript 4: Bestinianum]. From him he received twenty thousand gold pieces for his release.

As he was going to his brother, Gerard of Buonalbergo met him and was the first of all, as though in jest, to call him Guiscard (“the Wily”); Gerard then became his knight and gave him in marriage his aunt Alverada [manuscript 4: *amicam*, “female friend”; the edition reads “gave his aunt to him in marriage”]. Thus they entered Calabria together and in a short time captured almost all its cities.

After the death of his brother Humphrey (1057), having received his office, Robert besieged and captured the city of Reggio, and from that time began to be called duke. Thereafter (1059), having returned to Apulia, he also took Troia; and so, although at different times, he gradually subjected to his rule the whole land and all the Normans of those regions except Richard.

Moreover, when he learned that the aforesaid Alverada was related to him, he prepared a divorce and began to seek the sister of the prince of Salerno in marriage. This was done. Having bestowed many gifts upon Alverada, he went into Calabria with Sikelgaita [manuscript 4: Sikelgatta].

After this (1061), Robert’s great spirit turned to the defeat of the Saracens and the acquisition of Sicily. Crossing over with a strong army, he unexpectedly seized first Messina, which lay in the harbor; then Rimetum [editorial identification: Rametta?]. Next, at the city called Castro Giovanni, he fortified strongholds on all four sides, waged many highly successful wars there, received great gifts from the astonished lord of Palermo, built a castle named Saint Mark in the valley of Demena, and, after garrisoning Messina with soldiers, finally returned to Calabria laden with immense gold.

He then besieged and harassed Otranto [manuscript 2: Otrantum] until it surrendered to him. From there he enclosed Bari [manuscript 2: Varum] by land and sea, and after about four years entered it through the treachery of Argirizzo.

[Note: 15 April 1068.]

Accordingly, again setting out with a naval army for the conquest of Sicily and Palermo,

[Note: July 1071.]

within five months he took first Catania, then Palermo,

[Note: 10 January.]

and then Mazara (1072).

[Note: Manuscript 2 reads *Nazarim*, manuscript 3 *Mazarim*, and manuscript 4 *Masarim*; the editorial identification is Mazzara.]

Thus he invested his brother Roger with the whole island, while retaining for himself half of Palermo, Demena, and Messina; having received Saracen hostages and enriched with immense treasure, he returned to Calabria.

[Note: Manuscript 2 adds: “Let this brief notice of Robert suffice, because we shall write more fully in its proper place how he captured this island. Now let us write something concerning Richard.”]

Let this brief account of Robert suffice for the present, since we shall write more fully in its proper place how he captured this island. Let us now write something concerning Richard’s principality.

Richard, then, having obtained the county of Aversa, as we have already mentioned above (under the year 1050), began with all his might to seek the dignity of a principality and to direct his mind toward conquering the city of Capua.

[Note: From the middle of June 1058 he assumed the title of prince.]

[AMAT IV, 8.] After he had fortified three castles above it and was grievously harassing it by war, he finally accepted seven thousand gold pieces from the younger Pandulf and raised the siege—but only for a time. For when, after Pandulf’s death, his son Landulf succeeded him, Richard immediately came and renewed the siege. The Capuans offered much money; Richard desired nothing but the land. At last, pressed by severe famine, the citizens, after Landulf had withdrawn, admitted the man and consecrated him prince, retaining only the gates and the strength of the towers for themselves (21 May 1062).

For the moment the new prince dissembled, awaiting a more suitable occasion to demand this.

[AMAT IV, 13, 26, 28, 30, 31.]

Not long afterward he came to this monastery and was received with very great honor in a solemn procession; for he was exceedingly desirous of glory.

[Note: Leo added this sentence.]

Everything pleased him greatly. When the elders asked him for protection of the place, he most devoutly promised that henceforth he would be the most faithful defender of the whole monastery against all whom he could oppose. He then went into Campania and acquired almost the whole of it within three months.

Returning thence to Capua, he assembled the nobles and declared that it was now fitting for the towers and gates of the city to be handed over to him. The Capuans feared this and altogether refused to do so. Angered, the prince left the city and again surrounded it on every side with a most stringent siege.

Once more the citizens, hard pressed by severe famine, sent their archbishop Hilderic beyond the mountains to seek the emperor’s aid; but he who carried words received words in return and came back without any benefit.

[Note: Aimé’s French reads: “For at the court of the emperor of Germany it is customary that whoever gives a word receives a word.”]

Then the Capuans, abandoning all hope and unable any longer to resist, since no one at all brought them aid, finally surrendered the towers, the gates, themselves, and all that they possessed to the power of the prince, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1062, after they had for about ten years stoutly and vigorously resisted the Normans.

[Note: Amatus does not give the words “in the year … resisted.” The Anonymous of Monte Cassino supplies the year, but it is the year in which Capua was first conquered.]

After a short time, by divine judgment Teano was burned in the night; in the morning the prince arrived with an army, and, as the counts fled and the citizens willingly surrendered the city, he took it. Thus, since God prospered him in all things because of the wickedness of the inhabitants, he quickly subjected to himself all the dependencies of the principality of Capua, with their cities and castles.

[Note: The author supplied some material of his own in what follows.]

Yet amid all these successes he always gave thanks to God and Father Benedict, steadfastly professing that he was aided by Benedict’s merits and raised up by his prayers.

Moreover, although, as we said above, he had long ago made the lord abbot—then residing at Capua—his closest friend, thereafter he venerated him in every way as a father, entrusted himself entirely to his counsels, and willingly obeyed him as though he were his lord.

[Note: The edition reads *certissime* (“most certainly”) instead of “steadfastly,” and “to his counsels and commands.”]

[Chapter 17.] In the first year in which he was made prince together with his son Jordan (1058), he issued, according to the custom of earlier princes, a general charter for this monastery concerning all its dependencies and boundaries (12 November).

[Note: Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 161.]

In the following period (1063), he issued for our monastery at Capua a charter (22 April) concerning the public square between the city wall and the cloister of that monastery,

[Note: Ibid., p. 163.]

from which the brothers daily suffered great disturbance, both from all who passed by and from the chatter of neighboring women.

[Note: The edition reads *feminarum* (“women”) where the manuscript has *mulierum*.]

16. [Chapter 18.] Therefore Desiderius, supported by the friendship of so powerful a man through God’s dispensation, judging that so favorable a time was by no means to be neglected, began to press that prince, both with prayers and with substantial gifts, to grant peace and security to this monastery, which he confessed that he loved so greatly, and to confirm to the monastery in perpetual possession the neighboring castles by which we were continually harassed on every side, and which he had already brought under his own authority.

The prince most gladly assented to his wishes. First, he granted the castle called Mortula together with Casa Fortini.

[Note: Through the intervention of Pandulf son of Gualo. In the privilege printed in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 164, Richard speaks thus: “Let it be known to the understanding of all that Landulf, son of the late Pandulf, once prince, and Landulf, grandson of that Landulf, and the sons of the late Pandulf, John and Peter, brothers and sons of the late Gisulf, and Paldulf and Landenulf, brothers and sons of the late Laidulf, once count of Teano, plotted and took counsel against our life, and invited and introduced our enemies within our province. Therefore, according to Lombard law, all their property has devolved to our public authority, for us to do therewith whatever we may wish,” etc.]

Then he granted the town of Fratte (19 January 1065), of which we have already spoken above (ch. 11).

[Note: Of the same day; Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 165, from the original.]

In the following year he granted the castle likewise called Cucuruzzo [manuscript 2: Cucurrizzum].

[Note: Although the remaining chronological notices fit the year 1065 better, on 4 July 1066 Richard gave the Cassinese the monastery of Saint Savior on Mount Cucuruczu, in the county of Teano, confiscated because of the treason of the counts of Calatia and Peter, count of Vulturnum. Gattola, *Historia*, p. 312, from the original.]

He also granted the tower situated by the sea, at the very place where the river Liris flows into the sea,

[Note: Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 166. The edition reads “where the river Liris mingles with the sea.”]

and the castle of Teramo.

[Note: Taken from the counts for the same reason; ibid.]

All these, I say, with all their dependencies, he granted and confirmed in full to this place, separately by princely charters.

In exchange, the prince was given for the castle of Fratte the castle called Capriata with all its dependencies, together with three hundred additional Byzantine coins. For the castle of Teramo he was given the castle called Conca, which he had long before restored to us, together with the estate of Saint Felix of Miniano.

Furthermore, Desiderius exchanged at the same time with the counts of Aquino the town nearest the monastery, called Pesmontis, which was more hostile and burdensome to us than the rest. In exchange for it he granted them the castle called Cellarola [manuscript 2: Cellarellum] and Posta in their entirety, retaining for himself the lake of the same place with the small church beside it.

Of the portion of the estate of Saint Urban that then belonged to us—namely, 120 households—he granted Count Adenulf, individually, the right to hold them only during his lifetime, reserving to himself twelve households, with the church of Saint Urban and enough land for two yokes of oxen. The condition was that, if the aforesaid count wished during his lifetime to return to us those same households of men, we should give him fifty pounds of denarii; but otherwise, after his death, all those men should return under our authority.

17. [Chapter 19.] During the same period, churches and monasteries in various places were offered to this place. We append them below briefly and in their proper sequence, from the first year of Desiderius’s ordination until the dedication of the greater church [1058–1071], after which we shall describe the remainder.

[Note: The editor directs the reader: “The matters recorded here may, if useful, be sought in Peter’s Register.”]

The church of Saint Mary at Aurola, in the territory of Larino.

[Note: Gattola, *Historia*, p. 131.]

The church of Saint Benedict within the city of Alba.

The monastery of Saint Mary of Celle, in the territory of Carsoli.

[Note: See above, II, 23. It was given by Count Siginulf, son of Berard, an inhabitant of the castle of Saint Angelo. Gattola, ibid., p. 222.]

The monastery of Saint Benedict of Orbeto, in the place called Pascusano.

[Note: In the valley of Orbetu, in the province of the Marsi. Gattola, *Historia*, p. 226.]

The church of Saint Valentine within Ferentino in Campania.

[Note: Manuscript 2 reads: “Ferentino: monastery of Saint …”]

The church of Saint Mark of Carpenone, at Aquasonula.

[Note: Offered by Bernard, son of Laidulf, count of Isernia; ibid., p. 228.]

The church of Saint Demetrius within the city of Naples, in the district of Albina.

[Note: Manuscript 2 reads “monastery” instead of “church.”]

The church of Saint Peter at Orbeto, in the place called Morino.

The church of Saint Lucy near the castle of Rendenaria.

The monastery of Saint Euphemia in the March, in the territory of Teate.

[Note: The edition reads *Eufimie*. Manuscript 2 adds “with three hundred modii of land.” It was on the river Fauro; ibid., p. 230 (1063, indiction XV).]

The church of Saint Michael and Saint Mary at Comino, in the place called Pesclo Masculino [manuscript 2: Peschu Masculinu].

[Note: Manuscript 2 adds: “The church of the Holy Trinity and of Saint Felix at Saint Urban.”]

The church of Saint John of Conca, at Pilano [edition: Pisano].

The church of Saint Nicholas within Aquino, near the public square.

The church of Saint Blaise of Saint John at Baniarola.

[Note: In Limata itself, below the castle called Saint John, in the district of Pontecorvo; ibid., p. 266.]

The church of Saint Benedict in the territory of Arezzo, at Ficarola.

The church of Saint Michael of Algido.

[Note: Manuscript 2 calls it the monastery of Saint Michael of Algido.]

[Note: In the territory of Tusculum: the churches of Saint Peter at Plegi, Saint Felicity, Saint Lucy, and Saint Antoninus on Mount Porculo, in the territory of Tusculum. Added in manuscript 2.]

[Note: The Register calls these the churches of Saint Michael of Algido; but Saint Antoninus was given by Peter son of Gregory on 24 September 1077; see ibid., p. 236, and below, ch. 60.]

The monastery of Saint Agatha below the city of Tusculum.

[Note: Gregory son of the consul Gregory offered three parts of each property, and Octavian son of Alberic the fourth, on 24 May; ibid., pp. 232, 234, from Peter’s Register.]

The church of Saint Savior in that same city of Tusculum.

The church of Saint Mary surnamed *Ad vineas* (“At the Vineyards”), in the territory of Tusculum [edition: Tusculan territory].

[Note: Ibid., p. 233. Gregory, son of Gregory de Alberico, offered half of it on 18 February 1068.]

The monastery called Holy Jerusalem, in the territory of Tusculum.

[Note: The Register says that it was offered by the brothers Benedict VIII and Alberic, count palatine; ibid., p. 236.]

The monastery of Saint Michael at Pesclo, in the territory of Velletri.

[Note: Manuscript 2 adds that the Roman consul Gregory offered all these to blessed Benedict according to the tenor contained in the deed of offering.]

The church of Saint Mary of Uppa, in the territory of Carsoli.

The church of Saint Nicholas and Saint Moses near Campania, in the place called Turrici.

[Note: Manuscript 4 omits “Saint” before Moses.]

The church of Saint Michael at Bettorrito, in the district of the Marsi.

The churches of Saint Erasmus, Saint Michael, and Saint Donatus of Pomperano, likewise in Marsia.

[Note: Manuscript 2 adds “with three hundred modii of land” after the entry for Saint Donatus.]

The church of Saint Christopher and Saint Constantius, in the territory of Aquino.

The church of Saint Martin of Arpino.

The monastery of Saint Peter of Burgano, in the district of Lucera.

[Note: Manuscript 2 additionally lists the monastery of Saint Peter of the Lake, in the territory of Balvano, and the monasteries of Saint Peter of Burgano in the district of Lucera and Saint Peter of Avellana near the Sangro, with all their possessions and dependencies. Manuscript 4 reads *Purgano* for Burgano.]

All these churches, with all their possessions and dependencies, movable as well as immovable, were offered to this monastery and received by Desiderius within the period specified above.

[Col. 0733C] At that time Count Baldwin of the valley of Sora offered, or relinquished, to blessed Benedict three estates in Comino which he held from this monastery under a deed of exchange: namely, the church of Saint Urban with its entire dependency; the church of Saint Victorinus with the lake itself of Vicalbo; and the church of Saint Michael called that in Pratora, with all their dependencies and property, exactly as he had received them from us.

[Note: Manuscript 4 adds “by a deed” and the edition reads “with its whole dependency.” Manuscript 4 adds “and property” after “dependencies.”]

At the same time (March 1064), Count Paldus [edition: Pandulfus] of Venafro offered to blessed Benedict a fourth part of the castle called Sextum, half of his entire share in the valley of Venafro, in Teano, Calinulo, Calvo, and Caiazzo [manuscript 4: Cal.], and likewise in everything that he seemed to possess throughout the principality of Capua.

By another charter he offered to this place a fourth part of Cerreto Plain [manuscript 2: Cerretu] and Torcino, half of the castle of Saint George, of Vitecuso, and of Cerasolo,

[Note: “Of the castle of Cerasolu, an undivided half of three portions”; see Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 168, where both documents are found under the same day.]

and also the entire castle called Cerulano, with all its dependencies in full.

Count Landulf of Miniano also, coming to conversion, offered this monastery his estate not far from Miniano itself, with two churches, Saint Mary and Saint John.

[Note: Landulf Fusco, count of Miniano, is said by Richard to have been stripped of his goods because “he plotted and conspired against our life,” in September 1066; Gattola, *Historia*, p. 158.]

Furthermore Count John of Pontecorvo, surnamed Scintus, already named above (Book II, ch. 65), offered to this place the church of Saint Michael at the place called Merulano; the church of Saint Blaise beneath the castle called Pica; the entire estate of Baniolo and Sipizano; the castle called Pastina; and four holdings of land, not small, with all the possessions and dependencies of the aforesaid churches and estates (February 1066).

[Note: Manuscript 4 omits “to this place”; the edition reads *dicitur* (“is called”) for Pica and *appellatur* (“is called”) for Pastina; manuscript 2 reads “four holdings of land, not small.” Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 169.]

John, son of Landulf, count of Teano, by a charter confirmed and granted to this monastery his entire share in the castle of Mortula [manuscript 2: Murtula] and in everything that had belonged to him there on his father’s side in that castle (September 1070). His brother Landulf, a minor, likewise made the same grant concerning his whole other share.

[Note: Both documents are in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 170. The editorial apparatus expands the phrase as “on his father’s side in that castle.”]

Then a certain Pandulf, one of the nobles of Siponto, approaching death, made an offering to this monastery of fifty paces in the sea for fishing, at the place called Ad Rigora (May 1064).

[Note: The editor relocates this notice to the end of the chapter. Manuscript 2 calls Pandulf a Sipontine noble. Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 171, notes that Lombard law remained in force at Siponto under the Greek emperors.]

During those days Berard, count of the Marsi, made an offering to this place of the monastery of Saint Mary in the valley of Marculana; he sent it here with his son Todino, a youth of distinguished character who had long before entered religious life at the monastery of Rieti.

Later, when he himself came to this monastery, he restored to blessed Benedict the monastery of Saint Mary of Luco [edition: Lucu], together with the castle built above that church,

[Note: Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 171.]

with all the villagers living there and with all its dependencies throughout Marsia (November 1070).

Desiderius ordered that, under the title of a *libellus* grant, land measuring one thousand modii from the possessions of this monastery in various places subject only to his authority should be assigned to him, at an established annual rent of fifty solidi.

[Note: Manuscript 2 omits this entire sentence; manuscript 3 omits “subject only to his authority.”]

18. [Chapter 20.] Meanwhile Desiderius burned with a great desire to obtain ecclesiastical ornaments from every quarter, for in these we had until that time appeared exceedingly poor. But God, granting his aid, did not allow so good a desire in so great a man to remain ineffective, as will be seen in what follows.

Accordingly, partly by bringing funds from his own resources and partly by borrowing from his closest Roman friends, he raised the price of one hundred and eighty pounds and redeemed almost all the ornaments of Pope Victor which had been pawned here and there throughout the City. These were as follows.

A large *pluviale diarodanum*, a cope woven wholly throughout with gold, and likewise with golden fringes. A large citron-coloured *planeta*, a chasuble suitably decorated throughout with golden bands; another also, of *exametum* fabric, encircled with fringe. Likewise a dalmatic of *exametum*, distinguished with gold and white at the head, sleeves, and feet. A *tunica diapistin* with a very broad golden *urna* [term uncertain] at the hem, sleeves, and shoulders. Nine stoles woven with gold, with their maniples and semicinctures. A *pannus diarodanus* for a faldstool, with golden bands around it.

[Note: *Exametum* means woven with six threads or strands, whence our word “samite.” A faldstool is a folding chair or armchair. Manuscript 2 describes the cloth as *diarodanum cum listis aureis* (“diarodanum with golden bands”); manuscript 4 has *pro faldstorio* (“for the faldstool”).]

It is now fitting to add in detail what he made or acquired in church furnishings from the time of his ordination until the rebuilding of the greater basilica; the rest we shall relate more fully hereafter.

He covered a pastoral staff with silver and gilded it. Before the altar he made a gold panel set with gems, of about ten pounds’ weight; likewise a gold censer with gems and enamels, of two pounds’ weight. Having caused a book of Epistles for Mass to be copied, he decorated it with one golden cover and another of silver.

He also covered in silver on the outside a codex of the Rule of Saint Benedict, most beautifully adorned within. He did likewise with one and another altar sacramentary,

[Note: Sacramentaries are books containing the order of Mass.]

with two Gospel books, and with one Epistolary. For until that time both Gospels and Epistles were read from a complete missal; how unsuitable that was then is sufficiently evident now. He did the same to another small book containing processional prayers.

He also made a book for singing at the step or before the altar, and fitted it with wonderfully carved ivory boards ornamented with silver. He most diligently caused a codex to be copied containing the life of Saint Benedict, Saint Maurus, and Saint Scholastica. He made silver doors for the entrance of the choir, weighing about thirty pounds.

He made wooden seats around the choir, with their backrests adorned with handsome carving and painting. He also erected, outside the choir, a wooden step of the same workmanship, in the manner of an ambo, quite beautiful, from which both lessons at night and the Epistles and Gospels at the Masses of the principal feasts were to be read.

During those days also (1067), when a report became widespread that the king was coming into Italy, he went without delay to Amalfi. There he bought twenty silken cloths called *triblatti*,

[Note: That is, cloths of three colors, according to Peter Damian, Letter IV, 7.]

so that, if necessary, he might have something to give the king for the protection and honor of this monastery. He also acquired there a silver water-vessel weighing seven pounds, which he subsequently assigned to the ministry of holy water in the processions of Sundays, together with another vessel of the same metal and weight later given to him.

Since the king had turned back from his journey, he immediately ordered copes to be made from all the *triblatti*.

Then, seeing the bronze doors of the episcopal church of Amalfi, which greatly pleased his eyes, he at once sent the measurements of the doors of the old church to Constantinople and had doors made there accordingly. For he had not yet planned to rebuild the church, and for this reason the doors themselves were made so short, as they remain to this day.

[Note: He had them made by Maurus, son of Pantaleon, son of Count Maurus, of the Melfitan people; they were inscribed with the names of the church’s possessions. See Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 172.]

19. [Chapter 21.] But to return to what we were relating above: when the Apostolic died at Florence (19 July 1061),

[Note: Thus the Cassinese Necrology.]

after ruling the Church for two and a half years, a very great disturbance arose among the Romans concerning the appointment of a pontiff. The archdeacon Hildebrand, after taking counsel with the cardinals and Roman nobles, lest the dissension grow stronger, finally chose Anselm, bishop of Lucca, as Roman pontiff after about three months (1 October), and decreed that he should be called Alexander. Our Desiderius went to Rome together with the prince and supported him in all things.

When this came to the ears of the king and his mother [manuscript 2: “the empress and her son”], they were moved by the greatest indignation because these things had been done without their counsel and authority.

They likewise caused Cadalus, bishop of Parma, to be chosen pope beyond the mountains by the bishops of Piacenza and Vercelli alone, on the feast day of the Apostles Simon and Jude (28 October 1061). They immediately dispatched him to Rome, with a strong force of soldiers and much money, to attack and throw the Church into disorder.

[Note: Peter Damian mentions these bishops in Letter I, 21: the former was named Gregory and the latter Dionysius. Diematius took the closing words, “For he … was deposed,” from Peter Damian’s *Opusculum* 18.]

But by God’s favor, although very many Romans and likewise very many commanders adhered to that Cadalus through the king’s favor (1062), and even surrendered to him the Castle of Saint Angelo for the attack upon the city; although he came once and twice with great forces, squandered enormous sums of money, and inflicted much slaughter, no less upon his own men than upon others—at last he secretly left the aforesaid castle and fled shamefully with a few followers, nor did he thereafter attempt to come into these regions.

For in that same year, on 27 October—that is, on the vigil of the aforesaid Apostles Simon and Jude—he was condemned and deposed by the just judgment of God by all the German and Italian bishops who were then present with the king.

[Note: At Augsburg.]

### Restored source apparatus for sections 15–21

The following source-bound readings and editorial notices are restored with their Latin forms, meanings, and witness assignments.

**Section 15.** The edition reads *Hisdem* (“those same”); manuscript 3 omits “the principality of Capua”; manuscripts 2 and 3 have *Rothberto* and *Rotperto* for Robert. The edition has “with an oath of fealty,” omits “and likewise,” manuscript 2 omits “the tribute from all their land,” and the edition reads “in each individual year.” The edition places the history transition after *extiterunt* and reads *hunc dilexerunt, ditaverunt ac protegerunt* (“they loved, enriched, and protected this place”); manuscript 4 has *profectus* (“went forth”) for *provectus* (“advanced”). For Robert, manuscript 2 reads *cum pauper admodum esset, vicinae urbis dominum* (“since he was very poor, [he summoned] the lord of a neighbouring city”); manuscript 4 has *Bestinianum* for Bisignano; the edition expands “Guiscard” and reads “as if in play”; manuscript 4 has *amicam* (“female friend”) for “aunt,” while the edition says “gave his aunt to him in marriage.” Manuscript 4 omits “and,” adds “thereafter,” and spells Sikelgaita *Sikelgatta*. *Rametta?* is the editorial query for Rimetum. Manuscript 4 adds “at the city” and has *castra* (“strongholds”); manuscript 2 omits “and very many”; the edition has “immense” gold. Manuscript 2 has *Otrantum* (“Otranto”) and *Varum* (“Bari”). Bari is dated 15 April 1068; the Sicilian expedition July 1071 and Palermo 10 January. Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *Nazarim*, *Mazarim*, and *Masarim*; the editor identifies Mazzara. Manuscript 2 adds the transition to Richard.

For Richard, the edition expands his quest “to the dignity of the principality, and to direct his mind toward the conquest of Capua.” He assumed the title of prince from mid-June 1058. Manuscript 4 reads *artis*, an unclear or corrupt variant for *aptius* (“more suitably”); manuscript 2 omits his desire for glory, a sentence Leo added. Manuscript 3 omits “and gates.” The archbishop was Hilderic. Aimé’s French says: “For at the court of the emperor of Germany it is customary that whoever gives a word receives a word.” Manuscript 2 omits the clause that no one brought aid; the edition adds “and the towers” and has *virtuti* (“power”). Amatus lacks the year-and-resistance clause; the Anonymous supplies it, though it is the year of Capua’s first conquest. Manuscript 2 omits “and vigorously”; the edition has “fleeing.” The author supplied some following material; the edition has *certissime* (“most certainly”) and “to his counsels and commands.” Richard’s charters are Gattola, *Accessiones*, pp. 161 and 163; manuscript 4 omits “which,” and the edition has *feminarum* (“of women”).

**Section 16.** The edition reads *ducens* (“leading”) for “judging.” Mortula and Casa Fortini were granted through Pandulf son of Gualo; Richard’s privilege is Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 164. Fratte is dated 19 January 1065 (document, p. 165). On 4 July 1066 Richard gave the Cassinese Saint Saviour on Mount Cucuruczu in Teano county; manuscript 2 has *Cucurrizzum*, and the edition adds “with all its dependencies” (Gattola, *Historia*, p. 312). The edition reads “where the river Liris mingles with the sea” (Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 166). Teramo was taken for the same cause; the edition adds “with all their possessions,” manuscript 4 transposes “all their dependencies,” the edition calls Conca a *castellum* (“castle”), manuscript 2 has *Cellarellum* for Cellarola, and the edition has “and the Posta in their entirety.”

**Chapter 19 catalogue.** The editor directs readers to Peter’s Register. Manuscript 2 reads “churches and monasteries were offered in this place, in diverse places, which …”; the edition has *ipsius* (“of that same person/thing”) for Desiderius’s. The Saint Valentine note reads “Ferentino: monastery of Saint …” (manuscript 2). Manuscript 2 has “monastery” for Saint Demetrius; the edition has *Eufimie* for Saint Euphemia, manuscript 2 adds “with 300 modii of land,” and the site was on the Fauro in Teate territory (Gattola, *Historia*, p. 230; 1063, indiction XV). The edition has *Peschu*, manuscript 2 *Masculinu*. Manuscript 2 adds the churches of the Holy Trinity and Saint Felix at Saint Urban; the edition has *Pisano* for Pilano. Saint Blaise was in Limata below Saint John’s castle, in Pontecorvo (Gattola, p. 266). Manuscript 2 calls Saint Michael of Algido a monastery, and adds the churches of Saint Peter at Plegi, Saint Felicity, Saint Lucy, and Saint Antoninus on Mount Porculo in Tusculum territory. The Register calls them churches of Saint Michael of Algido; Saint Antoninus was given by Peter son of Gregory on 24 September 1077 (Gattola, p. 236, and below, ch. 60). For Saint Agatha, Gregory son of the consul Gregory offered three parts of each property and Octavian son of Alberic the fourth on 24 May (Gattola, pp. 232, 234). The edition has *Tusculanensi*. Gregory son of Gregory de Alberico offered half of Saint Mary *Ad vineas* on 18 February 1068 (Gattola, p. 233). Manuscript 2 adds Holy Jerusalem in Tusculan territory, offered by Benedict VIII and Alberic, count palatine, and Saint Michael at Pesclo in Velletri territory; it says the Roman consul Gregory offered all these to blessed Benedict by deed. Manuscript 4 omits “Saint” before Moses; manuscript 2 adds “with 300 modii of land” to Donatus of Pomperano. The Balvano entry remains only as manuscript 2’s addition: it adds Saint Peter of the Lake in Balvano territory, citing Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 179, for its offering by the counts of Balvano in April 1067, indiction VII. It also adds Saint Peter of Burgano in the Lucera district and Saint Peter of Avellana near the Sangro; manuscript 4 has *Purgano* for Burgano.

**Further donations.** Manuscript 4 adds “by a deed,” the edition “with its whole dependency,” and manuscript 4 adds “and property.” The edition has *Pandulfus* for Paldus and *Cal.* for Caiazzo; manuscript 2 has *Cerretu*. The Cerasolo note reads “of the castle of Cerasolu, an undivided half of three portions”; both documents are Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 168. The edition reads “with all the possessions and appurtenances wholly belonging to it.” Manuscript 2 reads “count of Miniano”; Landulf Fusco was stripped of his goods for plotting against Richard’s life (September 1066; Gattola, *Historia*, p. 158). Manuscript 4 omits “to this place”; the edition has *dicitur* (“is called”) for Pica and *appellatur* (“is named”) for Pastina; manuscript 2 reads “four holdings of land, not small”; the edition reads “with the possessions of the aforesaid churches and estates” (Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 169). Manuscript 2 has *Murtula*; the edition expands “on his father’s side in that castle.” Manuscript 2 adds that Landulf, his minor brother, made the same grant of his whole other share; both documents are Gattola, p. 170. The editor relocates the Pandulf notice; manuscript 2 calls him a Sipontine noble. The edition expands the fishing grant to “fifty paces in the sea … at Ad Rigora,” dated May 1064 (Gattola, p. 171). Manuscript 2 says Berard restored Saint Mary by charter; the edition has *Lucu*. Manuscript 2 omits the sentence beginning “Desiderius ordered”; manuscript 3 omits “subject only to his authority.”

**Chapter 20 inventory.** The edition reads “God granting, [the desire] could not remain ineffective in such a man.” The *pluviale diarodanum* (“rose-coloured cope”) is “large” in manuscript 2. The edition has *planetam diacitrinam* (accusative: “a citron-coloured chasuble”); manuscript 2 adds “large”; the edition has *quoque* (“also”). *Exametum* means woven with six threads or strands, hence “samite.” The edition reads “at head, feet, sleeves, and hands.” The tunic’s *urna* (“urn”) is retained because its referent is uncertain. Manuscript 2 has *diarodanum cum listis aureis* (“rose-coloured, with golden bands”) for the faldstool cloth; manuscript 4 has *pro faldstorio* (“for the faldstool”). The edition adds “it is fitting to indicate individually”; manuscript 2 adds “or acquired.” Manuscript 4 has corrupt *calicem* (“chalice”) for *codex*. Manuscript 2 has *ammonis* for *ambonis*; the edition has “also and” and “that they should be read.” The edition says the report spread that the king was entering Italy; the edition has *senix*. *Triblatti* are three-coloured cloths (Peter Damian, Letter IV.7). The edition reads “calls,” “certainly what,” and “which he might assign to the ministry.” Manuscript 2 says the Constantinopolitan bronze doors were made very beautiful; manuscript 3 says “ordered.” They were made by Maurus son of Pantaleon, son of Count Maurus, of the Melfitan people, and bore inscriptions of the church’s possessions (Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 172).

**Chapter 21.** The edition reads *redeam* (“I may return”); it expands “two years and a half during which he presided over the Church.” Manuscript 2 reads “among the Roman Church” and has *habitu* for *habito*. It reads “of the empress and her son” for “of the king and his mother”; the edition has *pervenisset* (“had arrived”) and *consensu* (“by agreement”). Peter Damian, Letter I.21, names Gregory and Dionysius; Diematius took the closing words from *Opusculum* 18. Manuscript 4 has *plurium* (“of several”); the edition reads “to that Cadalus”; manuscript 4 has *Symonis et Judae* (“of Simon and Judas”). The council was at Augsburg.

[Col. 0737C] 20. [CHAPTER 22.] Desiderius was now completing almost the fifth year of his ordination when this monastery was struck, more terribly than usual, by lightning through divine permission (A.D. 1063). For while the brethren were one day celebrating in church, as customary, the offices of the first hour, a lightning bolt suddenly darted down from heaven and struck dead in the choir the priest serving for the week, whose name was Manno, a man of honourable reputation; it threw the others standing about him to the ground as though lifeless. It also struck and killed a certain novice standing outside the choir before the great cross itself. In the chapter-house it knocked down the duty-table and left its keeper as if dead. [Note: It was an ancient custom to display in the exedra or chapter-house, for common information, a table recording the sequence of ministers and officials appointed to public duties during the week; this task was entrusted to one of the monks. These are the *tabulae officiales*, and this man is the *tabularius*, of whom this chapter speaks. Ang. appends an example from Cassinese records: “The order of the vicar requires that in the coming week Father Amicus shall sing Mass, Brother Desiderius shall read the Epistle, Brother Vincentius shall sing the Gospel, responsory, and verse, and Brother Andreas shall tend the lamp. Service in the kitchen, etc.”] It tore the face of an image of Abbot Richerius painted on a panel in the same chapter-house, cast it down, and struck in many places of the monastery. [Note: “of this [monastery]” 4.] This day was the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January].

Therefore, after taking counsel with the brethren, the venerable father decreed, in order to appease the wrath of God, that on the first Friday of every month all should keep a common fast; that, proceeding barefoot, they should celebrate a Mass specifically for this purpose; and that throughout the year, on every day, the prayer against lightning should be added to the public Mass and to special psalms. [Note: “be ordered” 2; “be added” 3.]

Moreover, Lord Peter Damian, of whom we have already spoken (Book II, ch. 99), came to this monastery. [Note: Cf. John, *Life of St Peter Damian*, 19, 20; Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 36, 16.] By word and example he zealously sought to kindle whomever he could for God’s service; and at last, with the consent and permission of the lord abbot, he obtained from the whole congregation, as a voluntary offering for the remission of all sins, that on every non-festal Friday of the entire year they should be content with bread and water, and that each should receive a discipline separately after making confession. [Note: Peter Damian himself attests this at the beginning of *Opusculum* 43.] In addition, they were to observe a three-day fast at the beginning of Lent every year.

As Desiderius often reflected upon this matter and prayed that it might be revealed to him what it meant that the aforesaid scourge should strike this place so frequently, one night Father Benedict appeared to him in a vision. When he anxiously questioned him among other matters about this, Benedict taught him that it was nothing other than the snares of the devil and his ancient envy against the place.

I myself, while I was still living in the monastery school, remember that on one night lightning struck the church and bell-tower six times during the second nocturn alone. On another occasion, it killed with one blow at the great gate two men standing far apart, together with a certain English goldsmith; and, more marvellous still, it did no harm to a little boy leaning upon the said Englishman. [Note: “hanging over” 4.] On another occasion it killed a certain old man passing near the tower of Paradise. [Note: “On another occasion—killed” is absent in 4.] On another, it slit the strap of one of the masons from the back of his head to his feet, yet did not deprive him of life.

21. [CHAPTER 23.] At the same time envoys came to this monastery on behalf of Bareso, king of Sardinia, [Note: “In the kingdom called Ore,” as he says in the privilege cited below.] through whom that king sent two large and excellent cloths to blessed Benedict and asked that some brethren from our congregation be sent to establish a monastery. [Note: “be sent” edition.] He promised and pledged that great honour and advantage would accrue in his kingdom to our interests, if, through our efforts, the practice of monastic religion—hitherto unknown in those regions—should henceforth become familiar among them in the form in which he had learned that it then flourished among us.

Accordingly, the venerable father, moved alike by such petitions and promises, after deliberate counsel chose twelve of the better brethren of this monastery. He lavishly supplied them with manuscripts of the divine Scriptures, various furnishings for ecclesiastical ministry, many relics of saints, and stores of various goods; he also appointed an abbot to preside over them [Note: Aldemarius; see ch. 24.], and sent them there with great honour in a ship belonging to the people of Gaeta.

Yet, Satan obstructing by God’s permission, the undertaking could not then come to fruition. The Pisans, driven by great envy of the Sardinians, came unexpectedly upon them in armed ships after our men had crossed safely to the island called Lilium [Note: In the Tyrrhenian Sea near Monte Argentario; in Latin, *Aegilium* or *Igilium*. Ang.], disembarked in boats, and were awaiting a favourable time for sailing. They treated both ours and all the others indiscriminately with extreme violence and plundered everything. Furthermore, those cruel men were already preparing to hang the leader of the said embassy on a gallows, had not one of our brethren given him a monastic habit, which he immediately put on.

Afterwards they burned the ship, restored only the clothing to our men, and, laden with everything else, returned joyfully to their own homes. The brethren of our monastery at Lucca, zealously searching in various places for our scattered brethren, found them and brought all except four, who had already passed to Christ, back to their monastery in hired vehicles. Later, although at different times, nearly all returned to us in that same year.

Moreover, one of our men saw a vision three days before these events occurred: namely, a little ship hurrying swiftly toward him, steered by a very handsome youth and by an old man shining more brightly than the sun, who held a sceptre in his hand. When it had come close to them, the sceptre-bearer rose at the prow and called the helmsman of our ship by name. When he answered, the old man, as if greatly moved, said: “Do you think that you will go safely to Sardinia in opposition to our cause? It certainly shall not be so.” Saying this, he struck the ship with a violent blow, turned it over, threw all its sails into the sea, and immediately vanished.

When the dream was recounted in the morning, different persons interpreted it differently. Some were greatly alarmed; others maintained that no attention should be paid to the deceptions of dreams. The pirates divided all the remaining things among themselves, but entrusted the chest of relics to one of their number, who had been the chief author of that crime, to keep in his own possession. They bound one another by oath that they would never, at any time or in any manner, restore it to anyone, unless perhaps they could not do otherwise.

But when that wretched man carried those relics of the saints to his house and, being a layman, kept them dishonourably and without reverence, God—terrible in his counsels toward the children of men!—struck him: one day, on entering that room for some purpose, he suddenly fell and expired. When this became known, great horror immediately seized everyone. On the following day they came barefoot, removed the aforesaid relics thence with immense reverence and honour, and, carrying them with great praises of God to the episcopal residence of the city, placed them there to be treated with the honour due to them.

22. [CHAPTER 24.] Meanwhile the king of the Sardinians, having received fitting satisfaction from the Pisans for such great injuries, again sent to this monastery, declaring that he remained much more ardent in his former devotion, and that we ought by no means to neglect the matter because of what had occurred. At last, after nearly two years, the same king eagerly received two brethren sent there and granted them, by royal command, the church of Blessed Mary at the place called Bubalis, and likewise Saint Elias on the Holy Mountain, together with the whole mountain, to establish a monastery; this grant included very many tenants and slaves, and great resources and possessions. [Note: In Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 174, from the original: “Nicita, levite and scribe, wrote in the palace of the king; in that hour there was darkness, and little light was in that hour, and great pressure weighed upon me,” etc. This was perhaps why he omitted to record the day.]

Emulating him in good, another king of the same Sardinia, named Torkytorius, also made a charter of his offering (A.D. 1066, 5 May) [Note: There, *Historia*, p. 154; concerning the place Call., dated in the village of Uta near Cagliari.] and sent it to this monastery. He granted Saint Vincent of Taberna, with many slaves and much property; Saint Mary at Tepid River; Saint Martha; Saint Pantaleon at Olivarum; [Note: So the edition and the doors of the Cassinese church; *Oliuanum* in Peter’s Register; *Oluianum* 4.] Saint George of Tulvi; and Saint Mary of Palma. That is, the aforesaid king conveyed by charter to blessed Benedict all these churches with all their appurtenances, to establish from them a monastery.

Moreover, an envoy of Pope Alexander was sent to the Pisans together with one of our monks, to command them that, unless they wished immediately to experience apostolic anathema, they must fully restore the cause of blessed Benedict which they had wickedly seized, purge themselves through due satisfaction, and never again presume in any way to trouble them. They promptly obeyed his commands, acknowledged that they had acted impiously against us, humbly sought pardon, and restored with very great devotion whatever of these things then remained or could be found—except only the relics of the saints, concerning which, as stated above, they had bound themselves by oath.

Not long afterwards, when Duke Godfrey came to Pisa and Desiderius went to him, for what reason I do not know, the duke intervened and exerted himself; after repeated satisfaction the Pisans were at last restored to his favour and promised that henceforth they would be most faithful both to the same father and to this place.

23. [CHAPTER 25.] Meanwhile the aforesaid Prince Richard, elated by many victories and successes, had subdued Campania and extended himself into the neighbourhood of Rome (A.D. 1066); he was seeking by every means the patriciate of the City itself. This reached the ears of the German king. Seeking both to rescue the possessions of Saint Peter from the hands of the Normans [cf. Amatus VI.9] and to receive the imperial crown from the hand of the apostolic pope, he came with a great expedition to Augsburg. [Note: He was there before the Purification, A.D. 1067, according to the Augsburg Annals.] There he awaited Godfrey, duke and margrave of Tuscany, who customarily preceded the king with his forces whenever the king was to enter Italy. But because Godfrey had gone far ahead, the king took this very ill, dismissed the expedition at once, and returned home.

The duke, however, surrounded by a very large army, approached Rome. [Note: This account is from Amatus.] When the Normans learned of his arrival, they were seized with the greatest terror and immediately fled, abandoning all Campania. Only Jordan and William, Richard’s son-in-law, called Mostarolus, prepared with their men to resist him at Aquino; the rest waited with the prince at Patenaria for the outcome. It was said that, if the duke crossed the Garigliano, all of them, armed as they were, would flee toward Apulia. During these same days our church lay in ruins.

Godfrey therefore, accompanied by the pope and the cardinals, came with his entire army to Aquino about the middle of May. There, for eighteen days, he fought the Normans, who resisted for their lives, with almost equal fortune. At last, through the efforts of the most energetic envoy William, surnamed Testardita, it was arranged that the duke and prince should meet for discussion, each on his own side of the bridge of Saint Angelo called Todici, since the bridge had been broken. Thus, after the duke had been given, as is said, no small sum of money by the Normans, he returned home.

During those days a star called a comet appeared for more than twenty days, bearing a huge tail behind it. [Note: The Anonymous of Monte Cassino assigns it to A.D. 1067; others to 1066.] It was thought to foretell the death of that duke, for he died not long afterwards. [Note: A.D. 1070.]

At the same time (A.D. 1067, according to the Anonymous of Monte Cassino; cf. Amatus VI.8), when the counts of the Marsi were divided from one another by deadly discord, the prince of whom we have spoken was summoned by one against the other. Rejoicing that this occasion offered him the long-conceived desire of acquiring Marsia, he set out thither, though not without some apprehension, even though surrounded by a great army and having Borrello’s sons as guides for the journey. After remaining there for several days, besieging the city of Alba on every side, and both making and receiving several attacks, he was ultimately unable to accomplish anything he had hoped. Leaving several Normans with the man who had hired him, he returned home.

24. [CHAPTER 26.] But since the aforesaid pope was exceedingly devoted to this monastery, and since Archdeacon Hildebrand both urged and encouraged him, he attached to his household for ecclesiastical service any brethren from this house whom he could obtain from the lord abbot, or else honourably promoted them as bishops or abbots.

Thus he summoned to Rome Todinus, son of Berard, count of the Marsi, [Note: Ch. 17; on him see Giesebrecht, *De studiis litterariis*, p. 44.] and made him a deacon in the Lateran patriarchate. He consecrated Aldemarius, of happy memory, an exceptionally prudent and noble cleric of the city of Capua and formerly notary of Prince Richard [Note: His privileges of 12 November 1058 and 23 August 1059 were issued through the hand of Aldemarius; Alerisius had succeeded him by 22 April 1063. Cf. Preface, p. 552.], who had been my master at my conversion and who had long before been ordained abbot over the brethren sent to Sardinia, as both cardinal and abbot of the church of Saint Lawrence called Outside the Walls, after he had returned to the monastery.

He also ordained Ambrose of Milan, a man no less prudent and learned, bishop of the church of Terracina. [Note: He occurs among the witnesses in October 1064 in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 228.] He appointed Gerald, a cleric most learned in every respect and German by birth, archbishop of the church of Siponto. [Note: He occurs in May 1064 there, *Accessiones*, p. 171.] At the same time Milo, provost of the monastery of Capua, was made bishop of the church of Sessa; and Peter, called by the surname of his father Atenulf, one of the Capuan nobles, who later became a cardinal at Rome, was sent, at the request of the prince of Salerno, to the abbacy of Saint Benedict at Salerno, of which we have already spoken.

At the same time (A.D. 1067, 10 May), the same pope granted Desiderius a solemn privilege, in addition to other provisions, concerning the complete liberty of this monastery: [Note: Edited from Peter’s Register by Tosti, *History of Monte Cassino*, I, p. 422.] by apostolic authority he forbade any bishop of any church, except the Roman pontiff, to presume in any manner to usurp any jurisdiction not merely in our principal church here, but also in all cells belonging to us anywhere in the world.

At this same time, when Hildebrand, archbishop of Capua, swollen with a certain arrogance, attempted to murmur against this authority, we made public complaint in the Roman synod. Convicted by the privileges of the Apostolic See, he confessed that he had sinned. Therefore, under a strict anathema, both he and all his successors were forbidden ever afterward to raise any question regarding it or ever to bring any suit whatsoever against this venerable place.

[Col. 0744A] 25. [CHAPTER 27.] Further, because at that time many shameful and abominable reports were circulated concerning the rulers of the monastery of Tremiti—which, as many privileges of the Roman pontiffs attest, had belonged to us from ancient times—authority was granted by the pope to Desiderius himself to investigate and regulate it as seemed best to him.

After removing from there Adam, abbot of that place, who had been convicted of many crimes, Desiderius entered the aforesaid island accompanied by Robert of Laurotello [Note: Son of Geoffrey, count of Capitanata, and nephew of Robert Guiscard; cf. below, IV.48.], and Petronus of Lesina, counts; by the bishops of Troia [Note: Stephen.], Dragonara [Note: Campone.], and Civitate [Note: Roger.]; and by the abbot of Terra Maggiore. [Note: Now Torremaggiore, west of San Severo.] There he most honourably appointed as abbot (A.D. 1071) Transmundus, son of Oderisius, count of the Marsi [Note: Brother of Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino; on him see Alfanus’s poems in Ughelli X, pp. 47, 76; cf. Giesebrecht, *De studiis litterariis*, pp. 32, 45.], a young man of notably excellent character, not without ability in prudence and letters, and trained from childhood in that place in honourable morals—if only he had not finally consented to the counsels of the worst brethren of that place, rather than listening to those whom our abbot himself had commanded him to heed.

For, a few days after our men had departed, he put out the eyes of three of the senior monks of that place and cut out the tongue of another; they had been accused before him by their companions of plotting rebellion on the island. When this was reported to our Desiderius, he received it most grievously and indignantly and was consumed with the deepest sorrow: for the misery of those who suffered, for the cruelty of him who gave the command, and finally—and this was the chief thing and wounded his heart most—for the disgrace of this place.

Since the solemnity of the dedication of our church was expected in that same year, Transmundus was awaited as one who would come to it and receive sentence according to the measure of his fault. When he came, Desiderius rebuked him in the assembly of the whole monastery with a very severe and fitting correction, subjected him to a graver penance, and did not allow him to remain there any longer.

But Archdeacon Hildebrand fully approved what Transmundus had done, affirming that he had acted not cruelly but vigorously and deservedly against wicked men. Before a full year had elapsed, he obtained him from the lord abbot, though with some difficulty; first entrusting to him the abbey of Saint Clement of the Island of Pescara, and shortly afterward also adding the dignity of the bishopric of Valva. [Note: A.D. 1073, according to the *Chronicle of Casauria* in Muratori, *SS.* II.2, p. 864; in the first year of Gregory VII. See this Register after Book I. For his conduct in the bishopric, see Di Meo, *Annali Napoletani*, VIII, p. 197.]

After this Desiderius ordered the monk Ferro, to whom the aforesaid Transmundus had entrusted the monastery, to come to him. Ferro refused to approach him; Desiderius, however, was in some manner ashamed to go into those regions because of what had happened. After a full year and about eight months, Desiderius complained of the matter to the duke returning from Sicily. The duke immediately sent there, compelled Ferro to leave, and delivered the monastery into Desiderius’s power (A.D. 1073).

Desiderius then entered the island in two armed galleys, accompanied by bishops, abbots, monks, and the already mentioned Petronus, count of Lesina, and was received by the monks of the place in a sufficiently honourable procession. On the next day he was solemnly invested by all the brethren of that monastery with the same abbey.

When asked to assure them that, during his lifetime, he would never subject that monastery to the monastery of Monte Cassino but would retain it under his own jurisdiction, he agreed. When also asked to decree that it should forever be free from every accusation or complaint of the Cassinese monks, he refused, replying that he would by no means do this, because it would not be just.

Having thus arranged matters as pleased everyone, and having left three of our brethren for the custody of the place, he returned. But later, after recalling the aforesaid brethren and committing the government of that place to another of our men, that man, following evil counsel and swollen with proud arrogance, assumed tyranny and resolved to rebel. He was summoned once and twice but scorned to come to Desiderius. After Desiderius excommunicated him, he was not many days later disgracefully captured with his supporters through the efforts of Desiderius’s faithful men and brought before him.

Desiderius soon absolved him from excommunication and again made him head of the cell at Ascoli. In the monastery of Tremiti, however, he entrusted his authority to the abbot of Terra Maggiore. When the latter died not long afterward, Desiderius, apparently now weary of the matter, restored responsibility for that place to the aforesaid Ferro, on the condition that Ferro should answer to him concerning it during Desiderius’s lifetime and, after Desiderius’s death, should surrender it into the hands of the Roman pontiff.

But enough of these matters. Let us now return to what went before and hasten to describe, as we ourselves witnessed them in person, how he built, dedicated, and adorned the new basilica of blessed Benedict.

[Apparatus and editorial notes]

[Col. 0737] At the chapter heading: “Q. i. f. o., edition.” The edition reads *quodam* (“a certain/on a certain”) for *quadam* (“on a certain [day]”); witness 4 reads *inortem* for *mortuum* (“dead”); the edition reads *pariter ac* (“and likewise”) for *ac porro* (“and further”); witness 4 reads *hujus* (“of this [monastery]”). In the decree, witness 2 reads *edici* (“to be prescribed”) and witness 3 *adjungi* (“to be added”). In the Peter Damian passage, witness 4 adds *consensu ac* (“with consent and”); witness 2 omits *quae tamen festivae non essent* (“which nevertheless were not feast-days”); the edition reads *contenti essent* (“they should be content”); witness 4 reads *imminentem* (“hanging over”) for *innitentem* (“leaning upon”); and witness 4 omits from the second *Altera* (“on another occasion”) through *extinxisse* (“had killed”).

[Col. 0738C] Compare John, *Life of St Peter Damian*, 19–20, and Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 36.16. Peter Damian himself is witness to the Friday discipline at the beginning of *Opusculum* 43. The ancient duty-table custom and its Cassinese example are as translated above.

[Col. 0738C] Bareso is said, in the privilege cited below, to reign “in the kingdom called Ore.”

[Col. 0739] The edition reads *venere* (“came”) for *venerunt*; *transmitti* (“to be sent”) for *mandari* (“to be commanded/sent”); *perventurum* (“would accrue”) for *proventurum*; and *deinceps* (“henceforth”) for *extunc* (“from then on”). Witness 4 adds *mox* (“immediately”), omits *tantis petitionibus simul ac pollicitationibus* (“by such petitions together with promises”), omits *simul* (“together/alike”), and omits *tam* (“both”). Witness 4 reads *misterii* for *ministerii* (“ministry”). The note identifies the appointed abbot as Aldemarius; see chapter 24. Witness 2 has the fuller phrase, “with God permitting and Satan obstructing, the undertaking …”; the edition reads *et hylares* (“and cheerfully”); witness 4 reads *ceperunt* (“took/captured”) for *reperiunt* (“found”); the edition reads *sibi* (“to himself”) for *illis* (“to them”); witness 4 reads *nauclericum* for *nauclerium* (“helmsman”); the edition reads *Qui* (“who”) for *Cui* (“to whom”); the edition reads *eorum* (“their”) for *suorum* (“of their number”); witness 2 reads *inde* (“thence”) for *ille* (“that man”); the edition reads *horror protinus* (“horror immediately”); witness 2 omits “of the city”; the edition reads *Dei laudibus* (“with praises of God”); and the edition reads *posuere* (“they placed”) for *posuerunt*.

[Col. 0739C] Lilium lay in the Tyrrhenian Sea near Monte Argentario; in Latin it was *Aegilium* or *Igilium* (Ang.).

[Col. 0740C] The grant is printed in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 174, from the original. Its difficult scribal dating clause reads: “Nicita, levite and scribe, wrote in the king’s palace; in that hour there was darkness, and little light was in that hour, and great pressure weighed upon me,” etc.; this may explain why he omitted the day. Torkytorius is spelled *Torchytorius* in witness 2 and *Torkcitorius* in witness 3. His charter is printed in the same author’s *Historia*, p. 154, concerning Call., dated at Uta near Carales. The editor prints *Olivarum*; the doors of the Cassinese church have *Oliuanum*, Peter’s Register *Oluianum*, and witness 4 *Oluianum*.

[Col. 0741] The edition reads *scilicet* (“namely”) for *videlicet*; in the papal warning it has a fuller reading, “unless they should wish at once to experience apostolic anathema”; witness 4 reads *inquiunt* (“they say”) for *nequiter* (“wickedly”), *arripuerant* for *abripuerant* (“had seized/carried off”), and *purgante* for *purgantes* (“purging themselves”); the edition reads *eos* (“them”) for *illos* (“them/those men”). Witness 4 adds *ipso* (“the duke himself”) and *tandem* (“at last”).

[Col. 0741C] Compare Amatus VI.9. The king was at Augsburg before the Purification in 1067, according to the Augsburg Annals. Witness 2 identifies Godfrey as duke and margrave of Tuscany; the edition reads *deberet intrare* (“was due to enter”) and *militia praecedere* (“precede with his forces”). Witness 2 reads: “ordered the expedition to remain; the duke …” instead of “dismissed the expedition”; the edition has *valde* (“very”) for *nimis* (“exceedingly”). This portion is from Amatus. Witness 2 reads *Mostarola* for *Mostarolus*; witness 2 adds “with all his men” at Patenaria; the edition reads *transiret* (“should cross”) for *transisset* (“had crossed”).

[Col. 0742C] The comet is assigned to 1067 by the Anonymous of Monte Cassino and to 1066 by others; witness 2 reads *fertur* (“is said”) for *putatur* (“is thought”); the edition has *mortis praenuntia* (“a foreteller of death”). Godfrey died in 1070. Witness 2 omits from *Eodem* (“at the same”) through *repedavit* (“returned”). The Marsian episode is dated 1067 by the Anonymous of Monte Cassino; compare Amatus VI.8. Witness 3 reads *adquirendi* (“of acquiring”) for *adquirendae* (“to be acquired”).

[Col. 0743] In chapter 26, compare chapter 17 on Todinus and Giesebrecht, *De studiis litterariis*, p. 44. Aldemarius’s privileges dated 12 November 1058 and 23 August 1059 were issued through his hand; by 22 April 1063 Alerisius had succeeded him; compare the Preface, p. 552. Ambrose occurs among witnesses in October 1064 in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 228; Gerald in May 1064 in the same author, *Accessiones*, p. 171. Witness 4 reads *Atenulfus* for *Atenulli*; the edition reads *agnomine* (“by-name”) for *cognomine* (“surname”), *nobilibus Capuanis* (“Capuan nobles”), and omits *factus est* (“was made”). The privilege was edited from Peter’s Register by Tosti, *Historia Cassinensis*, I, p. 422. The edition reads *locorum* (“places”) for *terrarum* (“lands/world”).

[Col. 0743] For Tremiti, the edition reads *divulgarentur* (“were spread abroad”) for *diffamarentur* (“were reported scandalously”), and has “authority was given by the apostolic [pope]” for *ab apostolico auctoritas data est*. It reads *subduxisset* (“had withdrawn”) for *removisset* (“had removed”), *Transmundum* for *Transmundus*, and has the fuller identification “son of Oderisius, count of the Marsi.” Witness 4 has *assensus fuisset* (“had assented”) for *consiliis fuisset assensus* (“had assented to the counsels”); the edition reads “with grief and indignation he received it” for the transmitted wording. The reading *Transmundus* is likewise attested by witness 2, whereas the edition has *gesserat* (“had done”) for *egerat* (“had carried out”).

[Col. 0744C–0745D] Robert of Laurotello was son of Geoffrey, count of Capitanata, and nephew of Robert Guiscard; compare IV.48. The bishops were Stephen of Troia, Campone of Dragonara, and Roger of Civitate; Terra Maggiore is modern Torremaggiore, west of San Severo. Transmundus was brother of Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino; see Alfanus’s poems in Ughelli X, pp. 47 and 76, and Giesebrecht, *De studiis litterariis*, pp. 32 and 45. The edition reads *aliquando* (“at some time”) for *aliquanto* (“somewhat”), witness 2 *Balvensis* for *Insula Pennensis*, and witness 2 *eidem* (“to that same man”) for *etiam* (“also”). His episcopal promotion is dated 1073 by the *Chronicle of Casauria* in Muratori, *Scriptores*, II.2, p. 864, in Gregory VII’s first year; see this Register after Book I and Di Meo, *Annali Napoletani*, VIII, p. 197, for his conduct as bishop.

[Col. 0745] Witness 2 adds “the duke was returning” from Sicily; witness 4 adds *jam* (“already”) before “the said count of Lesina,” omits “the island,” adds *die* (“day”), adds *est* (“was”), and omits from *Casinensi* (“Cassinese”) through *deinceps* (“henceforth”). Witness 2 reads *fratrum* (“brethren”) for *monachorum* (“monks”); the edition reads: “because he acknowledged that it would not be just for him to do so.” Witness 4 adds *loci* (“of the place”) before *custodiam* (“custody”); the edition reads *elegit* (“chose”) for *disposuit* (“resolved”). Witness 2 reads *praedicto* (“aforesaid”) for *Tremitensi* (“Tremitan”); the edition reads *manibus* (“hands”) for *in manus* (“into the hands”), and *nunc ad superiora* (“now to what went before”) for *ad superiora nunc*; witness 3 omits *vel dedicaverit* (“or dedicated”).

[Col. 0746A] **26.
