[Chapter 28.]** Thus the venerable abbot, established by divine providence in every prosperity and peace through the merits of our most blessed father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0745] “of our father B.,” ed.], and held in such honour by all around him that [Note: [Col. 0745D] “You will find the words ‘that—not merely … they strove’ likewise in the account of the consecration of the Cassinese church, published by Muratori, *SS.* V, p. 76, from Cassinese codex 47 after Antonio Caraccioli; it was apparently written by our Leo himself; see the preface, p. 555.”] not merely persons of middling rank but even their princes and dukes themselves gladly obeyed him and strove in all things to comply with his will as with that of their own father and lord [Note: [Col. 0745] *to obey*, ed. and codex 47.], turned his mind—certainly not without divine prompting—to demolishing the old church and building a new one more beautiful and more majestic. Although at that time very many of our elders considered this exceedingly burdensome and impracticable, and attempted by prayers, arguments, and every means to turn his mind from this purpose, since they believed that so great a work could not be completed during his lifetime [Col. 0746B], he, trusting in God, promised and awaited for himself the help of God alone in all things done for God.

Accordingly, in the ninth year of his appointment [Note: [Col. 0745] *year*, 4.] (March 1066), in the year 1066 of the divine Incarnation, in March, in the fourth indiction, he first built, beside the infirmary, a not very large basilica of Saint Peter, in which the brethren might meanwhile assemble for the divine offices [Note: [Col. 0745] *for the offices meanwhile*, ed.]. Then he undertook to raze to its foundations the aforesaid church of Saint Benedict, wholly unsuitable, both in its smallness and its ugliness, for so great a treasure and so great a community of brethren [Note: [Col. 0746D] “Indeed, it was too small for the brethren, whose number was increasing day by day, and unworthy of the most precious treasure of the body of the blessed father Benedict.”], [Note: [Col. 0745] omitted in 2.].

Because it had been built on the very summit of the mountain, lay exposed in every direction to violent blasts of wind, and had often been struck by fiery thunderbolts, he resolved [Note: [Col. 0745] “he resolved, trusting solely in God’s help,” 2.] to cut away the mountain’s rocky crest with fire [Note: [Col. 0745] *by fire*, ed.] and iron, and, by excavating below, to level a space [Note: [Col. 0745] *space*, ed.] sufficient for founding the basilica, in which he might lay its foundations. [Col. 0746C] Having appointed men to carry this out with all effort and the utmost diligence, he himself went to Rome. There, addressing all his closest friends [Note: [Col. 0745] “with appropriate access to all his friends,” ed.] and at the same time freely distributing money where needed, he bought in abundance columns, bases, and *lilia*—that is, entablatures [Note: [Col. 0746D] “That is, epistyles or entablatures.”]—as well as marbles of various colours. With great confidence he conveyed all these by hired ships from the City to the harbour, then from the Roman harbour by sea as far as the tower on the Garigliano [Note: [Col. 0745] “the tower of the Garigliano,” 2.], and from there to Suium. From there, however, he brought them with great labour to this place in carts.

And, that you may admire still more the ardour of the faithful who obeyed him: the first column was brought up here from the foot [Note: [Col. 0747] *beginning*, ed.] of the mountain solely by the multitude of citizens and the strength of their own necks and arms [Note: [Col. 0747] added in 4.]. For, adding to the labour, the ascent of this mountain was then extremely steep, narrow, and dreadful; for he had not yet cut into its heart in order to level and widen that road, as he did afterwards. At length, after the whole approach to the basilica had been levelled with no slight difficulty [Note: [Col. 0747D] That is, the sanctuary or inner approach.], and every necessity had been supplied in greatest abundance, he immediately hired highly skilled craftsmen [Note: [Col. 0747] “both Amalfitans and Lombards,” 2.]. Having laid the foundations in Christ’s name, he began the fabric of this basilica: 105 cubits in length, 43 cubits in width, and 28 cubits in height. Upon bases set beneath, he raised ten columns on one side and as many on the other, each nine cubits high.

[Col. 0747B] He also made ample upper windows: twenty-one in the nave; in the *titulus* [the transverse or entrance section], six long ones [Note: [Col. 0747] “and four round ones and two,” ed.] and four round ones; and two in the central apse. Raising the walls of each portico to a height of fifteen cubits, he divided them by ten windows on this side and as many on the other. Meanwhile, as he arranged to make the approach level with the basilica’s pavement—which was thought to stand about six cubits high—he dug less than three complete cubits and suddenly found the venerable tomb [Note: [Col. 0747] “the venerable tomb of the blessed father,” ed.] of father Benedict.

Having immediately consulted religious brethren and men of higher counsel [Note: [Col. 0747] omitted in 4.], he did not presume in any way to move it. At once, lest anyone should be able to steal anything from so great a treasure, he covered the same tomb, in the place in which it had lain, with precious stones; and over it [Note: [Col. 0747] “above it,” ed.] [Col. 0747C] he constructed a most beautiful chest of Parian marble, five cubits long, crosswise to the basilica—that is, from north to south. Thus the approach itself [Note: [Col. 0747] added in 4.] remained at its former elevation, so that one descends by eight steps from its pavement to the pavement of the basilica, beneath the very great vault which overhangs the same approach [Note: [Col. 0748C] “Apart, certainly, from that step by which one ascends to the altar from every side,” added in 2.].

Moreover, in the greater apse, on the eastern side, he set up an altar of Saint John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0747] “of blessed John the Baptist,” ed.], in the place where father Benedict had formerly built an oratory to him; on the southern side, an altar of blessed Mary, Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0747] added in 4.]; and on the northern side, an altar of blessed Pope Gregory. Beside the apse of the latter he constructed a two-roomed building for storing the treasury of the church’s ministry. This building [Col. 0747D] is customarily called the *secretarium* [sacristy or vestry] [Note: [Col. 0747] *was called*, 3.]. He joined to it another room of the same construction, in which the ministers of the altar ought to prepare themselves.

And since, for the sake of enlarging the church, he had taken away no small part of his own chamber [Col. 0748A] [Note: [Col. 0747] omitted in 4.], he accordingly made that chamber, joined to the aforesaid sacristy, larger and more beautiful than the former one [Note: [Col. 0747] “and more beautiful than the former,” 4.]. Beside it, namely beside the portico of the principal church, he founded a small but very beautiful chapel of Saint Nicholas, with a curved wall. From this chapel to the outermost front of the basilica, he extended, in matching workmanship, the quite venerable oratory of blessed Bartholomew the Apostle. On its façade, near the doors of the greater church, he raised from square and very large stones a remarkable tower, commonly called a bell-tower.

He also made [Note: [Col. 0747] “From ‘He also made’ to ‘is the ascent’ is omitted in 4.”] in front of the church the court which, according to Roman custom, we call the *paradisus*: seventy-seven and a half cubits long, fifty-seven and a half broad, and fifteen and a half high, with four columns and another four on its paired fronts, and eight and eight along each side, standing upon four-part bases [Note: [Col. 0747] “having, bearing,” codex 2.]. On its southern side he built beneath the pavement of that court, in vaulted work, a very large cistern of the same length [Note: [Col. 0747] thus in 2 and 3.]. Before the entrance to the basilica and also before the entry to the court, he formed above five arches which we call *spiculi* [Note: [Col. 0747D] That is, pointed arches.]. On the western side of the court, at each corner, he erected very beautiful chapel-towers: that of Saint Michael the Archangel on the right, and that of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, on the left. One ascends to these from inside the court by five steps.

Now outside the porch of the court and these chapels, because the ascent [Col. 0748C] to the church [Note: [Col. 0747] “to the church,” omitted in 4.] was very steep and exceedingly arduous [Note: [Col. 0747] “and too arduous an ascent,” omitted in 2.], he cut away the mountain itself for sixty-six cubits in length and the same in width, and seven cubits in height [Note: [Col. 0747] “in height,” ed.], so that from below to the very porch of the court one ascends by twenty-four marble steps, which he placed there, thirty-six cubits broad.

**27. [Chapter 29.]** Meanwhile he sent envoys to Constantinople to engage [Note: [Col. 0747D] That is, hire. “He sent to Constantinople and to Alexandria for Greek and Saracen craftsmen.” Aimé, III.49, from various parts of the world and also from the imperial city of Constantinople itself. Codex 47.] craftsmen skilled in mosaic work and in stone-setting. Some of these were to adorn the apse, arch, and porch of the greater basilica with mosaic; others were to pave the entire church with a variety of different stones.

[Col. 0748D] What degree of perfection the masters then sent to him attained in these arts may be judged from their works. In the mosaic each observer might almost suppose that he sees living figures and every kind of verdure; and in the marbles he might think that flowers of every colour bloom in beautiful diversity [Col. 0749A] [Note: [Col. 0749D] “So that you would think that they bloom not in stone but in flowers alone.” Codex 47.]. Since the teacher, Latin culture, had abandoned the practice of these arts for more than five hundred years, and since through his zeal, God inspiring and cooperating [Note: [Col. 0749] omitted in 4.], it deserved in our time to recover them, this man of consummate prudence took care that many boys of the monastery should be diligently instructed in the same arts, lest they should again disappear from Italy.

Nor did he provide for himself from his own people craftsmen eager only for these arts, but craftsmen supremely industrious in every craft that can be produced from gold, silver, bronze, iron, glass, ivory, wood, gypsum, or stone. But of these things elsewhere. Now let us set out how he decorated [Note: [Col. 0749] “partly decorated,” 2.] the basilica after its construction, and finally consecrated it [Note: [Col. 0749] “as far as we can,” 2.].

**28.** Covering the whole church, together with [Col. 0749B] the *titulus* and both [Note: [Col. 0749] *either*, 4.] porticoes, and likewise [Note: [Col. 0749] *and*, ed.] the porch, fittingly with lead roofs, he clad the apse and the great arch in mosaic. In the breadth of its circuit he ordered the following verses to be inscribed in large golden letters:

> So that, with you as guide, the righteous man may enjoy the homeland he has attained,  
> Father Desiderius has therefore founded this hall for you.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] In imitation of the verses which Constantine the Great ordered to be inscribed in mosaic on the great arch of the Vatican basilica:  
> “Because, with you as guide, the triumphant world rose to the stars,  
> victorious Constantine founded this hall for you.”  
> ANG.]

In the apse, on either side beneath the feet of the holy Baptist John and John the Evangelist, he had these verses written [Note: [Col. 0750D] I find these verses and the preceding ones among the poems of Alfanus in manuscript 280 of the Cassinese library. ANG.]:

> This house resembles Sinai, bearer of the sacred law [Note: [Col. 0749] *bearing*, ed.],  
> as the Law shows, which was once given here.  
> From here came forth the Law which leads minds up from the depths,  
> and, having been published, gave light throughout the regions [Note: [Col. 0749] *climates*, ed.] of the world.

He enclosed all the windows of both nave and *titulus* in panels joined together with lead and glass and fastened with iron [Col. 0749C] [Note: [Col. 0749] *arched*, 2.]. Those set in the sides of the two porticoes, however, he made of gypsum, though almost equally beautiful in decoration. Next, beneath beams, he installed a coffered ceiling remarkably adorned with different colours and figures, and painted all the walls with a very beautiful variety of every colour [Note: [Col. 0750D] Compare the narrative of codex 47, cited passage, p. 76.].

He also paved the entire floor of the church, together with the adjoining oratories of Saint Bartholomew and Saint Nicholas and his own chamber, with a marvellous profusion of cut stones, hitherto unknown in these regions [Note: [Col. 0750A] “Especially that part which is beside the altar and in the choir,” added in 2.]; and he marked out in a fitting variety of precious marble slabs the steps by which one ascends to the altar [Note: [Col. 0749] “ascends to the same altar,” ed.]. He enclosed the front of the choir, which he placed almost [Note: [Col. 0749] “almost in,” 2.] in the middle of the basilica, with four large marble slabs: one porphyry, another green; the remaining two [Col. 0749D], and all the rest around the choir, white [Note: [Col. 0749] *plain*, 2.].

He had the upper part of the church porch adorned [Note: [Col. 0749] “caused [it] to be made,” ed.] with most beautiful mosaic and arches over the lintels [Col. 0750A]; from there down to the very pavement, he covered the whole façade of the basilica with gypsum. Cladding the outside arches of this porch also with mosaic, he inscribed there in golden letters verses by the poet Mark [Note: [Col. 0749] “Mark the poet there,” ed.]. He ordered the other three sides of the court to be painted within and without with various histories from both the Old and the New Testament. He paved its entire circuit in marble [Note: [Col. 0749] “in a circuit,” omitted in 2.], covered it above with a coffered ceiling and tiles, and treated the porch of this same court and its twin towers in like fashion—painted, roofed, and marble-paved.

**29. [Chapter 30.]** When all these things [Note: [Col. 0749] “All these things,” ed.] had been completed within a period of five years [Note: [Col. 0749] *fifteen years*, 4.], God prospering and helping, [Col. 0750B] Desiderius resolved to dedicate the basilica with the greatest solemnity and immense rejoicing, for everlasting remembrance. Going to Alexander, pontiff of the supreme see, he most devoutly [Note: [Col. 0749] *most devoutly*, ed.] invited him to come to this dedication (1071) [Note: [Col. 0750D] “There, p. 77.”]. Alexander gladly assented; Desiderius also summoned with the greatest affection Hildebrand, the pope’s archdeacon, the other cardinals and Roman bishops, and many of the Urban clergy and nobility.

The day for this great solemnity was fixed, by the counsel of the pope and [Note: [Col. 0749] “and—of the pope” omitted in 4.] cardinals, on the Kalends of October, and letters of invitation from the same pope were sent to all the bishops of Campania, the Principality, Apulia, and Calabria. When news of this matter had spread far and wide, such a multitude of almost all Italy’s bishops, abbots, monks, [Col. 0750C] clerics, magnates, nobles, persons of middling rank, and men and women of every condition assembled on the appointed day that it would have been easier for anyone to estimate the number of stars in the sky than the number of them all. Thus all the workshops of the monastery, and even the roofs of all the workshops, every route of the mountain from bottom to top, and—what shall I say?—all the houses of the town, all the streets, and all the spaces of the surrounding fields far and wide were packed and crowded with masses of people gathered for so great a celebration.

During the three continuous days preceding and following that solemnity, provisions of bread and wine, and of an abundance of various meats and fish, were set forth so plentifully [Col. 0750D] that scarcely anyone [Note: [Col. 0749] “indeed anyone,” 2.] among so innumerable a multitude could be found who did not say that he had received enough [Note: [Col. 0749] “could be found. Thus those attending that great celebration …,” ed.]. Therefore, on the Kalends of October [Col. 0751A], when the year 1071 from the Lord’s Incarnation was running its course, the same basilica of blessed Benedict, with its five altars, was dedicated by the most reverend and angelic lord Pope Alexander, on a Saturday in the ninth indiction, with the utmost devotion of all who had assembled, immense gladness, the greatest rejoicing, honour, and glory [Note: [Col. 0751B] Thus also codex 47, so that Leo evidently began the indiction from the Kalends of January.].

Ten archbishops attended this great celebration: the Capuan [Note: [Col. 0751] that is, Capuan, 2.] [Note: [Col. 0751B] Ildebrandus. We append the names from the same codex 47.]; the Salernitan [Note: [Col. 0751] Manuscripts 3 and 4 arrange the names so as to show that they were written in two columns, which those manuscripts did not read correctly; codex 2 is better, since the cardinal bishops are joined together. “Capuan, Neapolitan, Amalfitan, Tranian,” etc., in 3 and 4. In codex 4, moreover, Salernitan, Surrentine, Sipontine, Acerentine, and Otranto bishops occur among the bishops, after the end, evidently, of the first column.] [Note: [Col. 0751B] Alphanus.]; the Neapolitan [Note: [Col. 0751B] John.]; the Surrentine [Note: [Col. 0751B] John.]; the Amalfitan [Note: [Col. 0751B] Omitted there.]; the Sipontine [Note: [Col. 0751B] Girardus.]; the Tranian [Note: [Col. 0751B] Bisantius.]; the Acerentine [Note: [Col. 0751B] Arnaldus, among the bishops.]; the Otranto bishop [Ydrontinus] [Note: [Col. 0751B] Bishop Hugh.]; and the Oria bishop [Oiretanus] [Note: [Col. 0751B] Oria, in Terra d’Otranto; omitted there.].

There were forty-four bishops [Note: [Col. 0751] *three*, 2.]: the bishop of Porto [Note: [Col. 0751] “Porto, Sabina, Anagni,” etc., 4, and apparently 3.] [Note: [Col. 0751B] John.]; of Tusculum [Note: [Col. 0751B] John.]; of Sabina [Note: [Col. 0751B] Ubaldus.]; of Segni [Note: [Col. 0751B] Erasmus.]; [Col. 0751B] of Anagni [Note: [Col. 0751B] Peter.]; of Berula [Note: [Col. 0751B] Honestus.]; of Terracina [Note: [Col. 0751B] Ambrose.]; of Gaeta [Note: [Col. 0751B] Leo.]; of Aquino [Note: [Col. 0751B] Martin.]; of Sora [Note: [Col. 0751B] Palumbus.]; of the Marsi [Note: [Col. 0751B] Pandulf.]; of Balva [Note: [Col. 0751B] Omitted.]; of Penne [Note: [Col. 0751B] Omitted.]; of Teano [Note: [Col. 0751B] William.]; of Cales [Note: [Col. 0751B] John.]; of Roselle [Note: [Col. 0751B] Later Grosseantus; omitted in codex 47. He, named Dodo, had already acted at Benevento in 1061 as vicar of Nicholas II; see Mansi XIX, 935.]; of Aversa [Note: [Col. 0752B] Geoffrey.]; of Nola [Note: [Col. 0752B] I do not know whether he is the same as John of Picenum, who remains in codex 47.]; of Avellino [Note: [Col. 0752B] Omitted.]; of Paestum [Note: [Col. 0752B] Maraldus.]; of Troia [Note: [Col. 0751] Manuscript 4 reads “Paestum, Melfi, Troia, Florentia, Lucera, Larino, Dragonara, Civitate, Guardialfiera, Termoli, Ariano,” if we restore the former order; and below, “Rubo, Monorbino, Venosa, Vieste, Molfetta.”] [Note: [Col. 0752B] Stephen.]; of Florentia [Note: [Col. 0752B] That is, Ferentino; Robert.]; of Melfi [Note: [Col. 0752B] Omitted.]; of Lucera [Note: [Col. 0752B] Omitted.]; of Dragonara [Note: [Col. 0752B] Campo.]; of Civitate [Note: [Col. 0752B] Roger.]; of Termoli [Note: [Col. 0752B] Nicholas.]; of Guardialfiera [Note: [Col. 0752B] “From Guarda Alfiera,” Peter.]; of Larino [Note: [Col. 0752B] William.]; of Ariano [Note: [Col. 0752B] Maynard.]; of Isernia [Note: [Col. 0751] *Serniensis*, ed.] [Note: [Col. 0752B] Peter of Venafro; see above, chapter 14.]; of Bovino [Note: [Col. 0752B] Albert.]; of Salpi [Note: [Col. 0752B] Omitted.]; [Col. 0752A] of Canne [Note: [Col. 0752B] John.]; of Rubo [Note: [Col. 0752B] “of Rubi,” William or Guibert.]; of Venosa [Note: [Col. 0752B] Constans.]; of Monorbino [Note: [Col. 0752B] Ignatius.]; of Vieste [Note: [Col. 0751] *Clig.*, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0752B] Bisceglie, John.]; of Molfetta [Note: [Col. 0751] *Melphiatensis*, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0752B] Molfetta, Baldwin.]; of Giovinazzo [Note: [Col. 0752B] John.]; of Monopoli [Note: [Col. 0752B] Peter.]; of Ostuni [Note: [Col. 0752B] Datto of Ostuni.]; of Taranto [Note: [Col. 0752B] Drogo, among the archbishops.]; of Perugia [Note: [Col. 0752B] Geoffrey.]; and the bishop-elect of Castellana [Note: [Col. 0752B] Theobald.], who was consecrated bishop on the second day after the dedication.

Among the magnates were Richard, prince of Capua, with his son Jordan and his brother Rainulf; Gisulf, prince of Salerno, with his brothers; Landulf [Note: [Col. 0752B] Pandulf, codex 47, namely the son of Landulf.], prince of Benevento; Sergius, duke of Naples; and Sergius, duke of Sorrento [Note: [Col. 0751] “Sergius, duke of … was present at that time, and therefore at so great a solemnity…” 2.]. There was also no small gathering of the counts of the Marsi and Balva, and of the sons of Borrell [Note: [Col. 0751] “But also a great crowd of the counts of the Marsi and the sons of the Balvenses,” ed.; *a great crowd*, 2.]. But it was wholly impossible, and beyond prudent counsel, to enumerate either the names or the countless number of the other powerful men and nobles, both native and Norman, from all the surrounding lands [Col. 0752B] [Note: [Col. 0751] “or the countless number,” 4.].

Duke Robert, however, was then besieging Palermo and therefore could not attend so great a celebration [Note: [Col. 0751] “Thus, then, with the fullest devotion and immense gladness of all these, with honour and especial glory [‘with the greatest honour and glory,’ as above, 3], the same basilica of blessed Benedict with its five altars was dedicated [‘was dedicated by Lord …,’ as above, 3] on the Kalends of October in the year 1071 from the divine Incarnation, in the ninth indiction, on Saturday,” ed.].

The aforesaid pope himself consecrated with his own hand the principal [Note: [Col. 0751] *central*, 2.] altars, bearing the names of blessed Benedict and [Note: [Col. 0751] “Benedict and Saint John,” ed.] blessed John [Note: [Col. 0751] *blessed*, ed.]. John, bishop of Tusculum, consecrated the altar situated on the southern side in honour of holy Mary, Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0751] “is situated in honour of the Mother of God,” ed.]. Hubald, bishop of Sabina, consecrated that on the [Col. 0753A] northern side in the name of blessed Gregory; and Herasmus, bishop of Segni, solemnly dedicated that of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0753] *dedicated*, ed.].

We have judged it appropriate here to state what patronages—that is, relics—of these saints were then deposited in the individual altars [Note: [Col. 0753] “the relics … deposited,” ed.]. In the altar of blessed Benedict are relics of the holy apostles Philip and James; of the martyrs Pope Alexander, Sebastian, Cyriacus, Chrysanthus and Daria [Note: [Col. 0753D] “That is, a bone of the leg, arm, head, and hip,” added in 2.], Abdon and Sennen [Note: [Col. 0753] *Sennes*, 4.]; and of the virgin Cecilia. Besides these, two silver reliquary chests containing very many pledges of various saints are honourably suspended within that altar in its upper marble [Note: [Col. 0753D] “The most reverend Pope Benedict, out of love and reverence for our most holy father Benedict, took these from the treasury of the Lateran palace and sent them to this Cassinese church in the first year of our abbot Theobald, in the year 1023 of the Lord’s Incarnation. This same most holy pope strictly forbade anyone to presume to remove anything from it. These relics are: of the wood of the Lord; of the blood of the Lord; of the Lord’s garments; of the crown of thorns; of the stone of the Holy Sepulchre; of the veil of holy Mary, Mother of God; of the apostles Peter and Paul, Andrew, John, James and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, Simon, Jude, and Matthias; a sponge with the blood of the holy protomartyr Stephen; relics of Lawrence, Pope Stephen, Pope Pelagius, Bishop Martin, Prudentius, Julian, Augustine, Christopher, Aemilianus, Nicander and Marcian, Alexis, Anastasia, Eugenia, John and Paul, the Forty Martyrs, and many others,” added in 2.].

In the altar of Saint John there is oil from [Col. 0753B] the lamp of the Holy Sepulchre [Note: [Col. 0754A] “From the sponge placed upon Christ with vinegar; from the stone of the Holy Sepulchre of holy Mary, Mother of God,” added in 2.]. Every year, by a most wonderful heavenly power, this lamp rises from the water of the Jordan, in the sight of all, on the Saturday of holy Easter [Note: [Col. 0753] *Saturday*, ed.], at the place where the Lord was baptized [Note: [Col. 0753] “from the manna of the sepulchre of Saint John: that is, ‘from the water … is’; and,” ed.]; manna from the sepulchre of Saint John the Evangelist; and relics [Note: [Col. 0754A] “of Saint Lawrence,” added in 2.] of Saint [Note: [Col. 0753] omitted in ed.] Sebastian and many others, which [Note: [Col. 0753] “which … had been,” omitted in 2.] had been deposited in his former altar.

In the altar of Saint Mary there is a relic of the stone of her sepulchre and relics of the martyrs Bishop Dionysius, Pope Stephen [Note: [Col. 0753] “of Bishop Dionysius and Pope Stephen,” ed.], the deacon Caesarius, Primus, and Felician. In the altar of Saint Gregory there are relics of the stone of the Holy Sepulchre, of Saint Mary’s garment, of the garments of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of the holy Forty Martyrs, as well as Pancratius, Valentine, and Hilary, Bishop Martin [Col. 0753C], and of the dalmatic of Saint Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0754A] “In the silver tower which is in the great arch these relics were placed: of the head of Saint John the Baptist; of the garments of Saint John the Evangelist, [Col. 0754B] Andrew the Apostle, Sebastian, and the Forty Martyrs; of the veil of Saint Agatha; and of the garments of Saint Susanna. In the apse of Saint John, in the crown of the Saviour: wood of the Lord and stone of the Holy Sepulchre,” added in 2.].

In the altar of Saint Nicholas are relics of the holy martyrs Cornelius [Note: [Col. 0753] “the holy martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian,” ed.] and Cyprian, Sebastian, Nicander and Marcian, Quirinus and Maximus, Bishop Phocas, Eutychius, and [Note: [Col. 0753] “Eutychius and the martyrs, and,” ed.] the Forty Martyrs; and hair of Bishop Saint Remigius. Above all these things, what we have not thought fit to leave unmentioned: at the time of construction, relics in bronze pyxides were reverently placed in the capitals of the individual columns of the basilica [Note: [Col. 0753] “during construction, reverently enough, in,” ed.]—relics of the holy martyrs John and Paul, Nicander and Marcian, and certain others [Note: [Col. 0754B] “Relics were placed of Saints Philip and James, John and Paul, Nicander and Marcian, Cornelius and Cyprian, Quirinus and Maximus, Sebastian, Phocas, Eutychius, the Forty Martyrs, hair of Bishop Saint Remigius, and many others,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0753] *martyrs*, omitted in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0753] omitted in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0753] *enough*, omitted in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0753] omitted in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0754B] “At the four corners of the bell-tower are these relics: wood of the Lord; stone of the Holy Sepulchre; garments of Saint Mary; stone from her sepulchre; [relics] of the holy apostles James, Philip, and Bartholomew; and Bishop Martin. In the cross of the bell-tower: wood of the Lord, relic of the head of Saint John the Baptist, Bartholomew the Apostle, and Cyriacus the deacon. In the façade of the church, in the [Col. 0754C] bronze cross: wood of the Lord, stone of the Holy Sepulchre, [relics] of Abbot Maurus, and of the holy martyrs John and Paul,” added in 2.].

[Col. 0754C] **30. [Chapter 31.]** After the celebration of the masses had thus been solemnly completed [Note: [Col. 0753] *therefore*, ed.], and the authority of apostolic power had granted remission of sins both to those who happened to be present at that time and to all who could come there during the eight following days out of devotion to so great a solemnity [Note: [Col. 0753] *to these*, ed.] [Note: [Col. 0753] *of all*, 2.], each returned home with the greatest and most abundant gladness.

Yet, through the favour of the aforesaid remission, such a crowd of people of diverse sex and age continued to gather from every direction throughout those same eight days that one might suppose scarcely any of those who had come together on the first day had returned home.

[Col. 0754D]

> Nor is there any end to the people gathering in a dense throng,  
> nor rest: they hasten from night toward the light,  
> and are impatient to await the day.

[Note: [Col. 0753] These verses were borrowed from Paulinus of Nola, *Natalis of Saint Felix* III, as Ang. de Nuce has already noted.]

> The peoples of Campania [Note: [Col. 0753] *Lucania*, 2; Paulinus.] gather; Apulian youth gathers;  
> [Col. 0755A] the Calabrians too, and all those whom each sea-current bathes,  
> the wave which resounds around [Note: [Col. 0755] *and*, ed.; *and*, Paulinus.]  
> all Latium on its left and right [Note: [Col. 0755] omitted in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0755] *surrounds with sound*, Paulinus.].  
> Rome herself, mighty through the sacred memorials of heavenly [Note: [Col. 0755] *celestial*, 3; Paulinus.] leaders,  
> Peter and Paul, gladly thins out,  
> pouring forth thousands toward the lofty walls  
> of friendly [Note: [Col. 0755] “the friendly walls of Nola,” Paulinus.] Cassino.  
> Devotion, love [Note: [Col. 0755] “and all things of Christ,” Paulinus.] of Benedict, overcome the hard journey,  
> and kindly faith overcomes it: God, present [Note: [Col. 0755D] I do not find “God present … Christ” in Paulinus.] to all there [Note: [Col. 0755] *of*, 2.] [Note: [Col. 0755] *there*, 3.],  
> is believed in; and Benedict is the glory of the supreme Christ.  
> A gracious [Note: [Col. 0755] “A gracious … tumults,” omitted in 2.] day is celebrated by great assemblies; let all utter fulfilled vows at the sacred doors;  
> all things of earth and heaven rejoice.  
> We too are blessed, to whom Christ grants to behold him [Note: [Col. 0755] “in his presence. And Christ grants us to see and behold the rewards of our patron, so great to those who give thanks to Christ.” Gratianus, Paulinus.]  
> [Col. 0755B] and celebrate the day, give thanks to so great a patron,  
> and rejoice amid the happy [Note: [Col. 0755] *happy*, 4.] tumult.

Moreover [Note: [Col. 0755] added in 4.], anyone would surely have considered himself faithless and altogether miserable if he had not made every effort to attend at least the end of so great a solemnity. From that time the fame of so great a celebration began to be spread almost throughout the entire Christian world. Henceforth this place, though from of old famous and noble through the merits of father Benedict, began to be held much nobler and more glorious; and the name of father Desiderius, already long great and celebrated among very many, began thenceforward to be spread more celebratedly and nobly throughout all the West [Note: [Col. 0755] “almost the whole,” 3.], his great prudence and piety being proclaimed by all. He was judged everywhere, by everyone, to deserve precedence over all the abbots of his time, in all places and lands [Col. 0755C] [Note: [Col. 0755] “not only in the western and eastern regions, but throughout the whole world,” ed.].

Accordingly, many began to come here from many distant regions: some from the desire of seeing Desiderius; others to behold this widely famed and celebrated [Note: [Col. 0755] “and so celebrated,” ed.] church [Note: [Col. 0755] *continuendi*, 4.]; and still others to enter religious life in this most holy monastery and serve God as long as they lived. Desiderius received them gladly, and so it came about that within scarcely two years the number of this community had increased to about two hundred. The degree [Note: [Col. 0755] *quantus* (“how great,” agreeing with *amor*); *quanta*, ed.] of love and devotion which kings and powerful persons of various lands—Italian, transalpine, and overseas alike [Note: [Col. 0755] “powerful persons of either sex,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 0755] added in 4.]—began to show toward the venerable father was attested by supplicatory letters [Col. 0755D] and fitting gifts. In these they earnestly commended themselves and all their people to his prayers and to those of the brethren living under him.

[Col. 0756A] **31. [Chapter 32.]** Nor does it seem fitting to pass over in silence the pious devotion of Empress Agnes. Like another queen of Sheba, led by a great desire to see another Solomon and another temple, she came here from the farthest bounds of Germany. Remaining there for almost half a year, she rejoiced and declared that she saw things far greater, both in relation to God and in worldly terms, than she had heard reported about this place [Note: [Col. 0755] “of herself, from,” ed.] [Note: [Col. 0755] omitted in ed.]. She rightly judged that the place, the father, and the brethren should be held more celebrated than the men of their order throughout the world.

She offered magnificent gifts to blessed Benedict, as befitted imperial dignity: a *planeta diaspera* [a figured or patterned chasuble] [Note: [Col. 0755] *diasperam*, 2.], woven wholly throughout with gold; an alb [Note: [Col. 0755] “an alb also,” ed.] adorned becomingly [Col. 0756B] [Note: [Col. 0755] “most becomingly adorned,” ed.] at shoulders, head, and hands with *frisum* [ornamental fringe or embroidery], and at the feet likewise surrounded with a fringed band nearly one cubit broad; together with an amice and breast-cloth; two purple copes adorned with precious golden bands [Note: [Col. 0756B] “A *pannus diarodanus* fringed with gold before the front of the greater altar,” added in 2.]; and also a great hanging with elephants, which they call a *dorsale* [Note: [Col. 0755] *dossale*, 2.].

She also gave a Gospel-book with a cast silver cover, most beautifully gilded in repoussé work [Note: [Col. 0755] “and most beautifully,” ed.], and two likewise cast silver candelabra, each weighing twelve pounds.

32. [Chapter 33.] It is now fitting, after the dedication of the church, to describe what remained of its adornment, so that thereafter we may more freely attend to the deeds of Desiderius, both in buildings and in all his other magnificences. [Note: “other” is an addition in manuscript 4.] [Col. 0756C]

Accordingly, he sent one of the brethren to the aforesaid imperial city with letters for the emperor and gold weighing thirty-six pounds, and ordered there to be made a golden panel for the front of the altar, with gems and very beautiful enamels. In these enamels he had represented certain stories from the Gospel, but almost all the miracles of Saint Benedict. This fellow-brother of ours was certainly [Note: “certainly” in the edition.] received most honourably by the Roman emperor [Note: manuscript 4: “emperor of the Romans”], and, for as long as he remained there, was treated honourably and reverently together with all his companions; and the emperor granted him imperial permission and resources to carry out whatever works [Note: manuscript 2: “ornaments”] he wished there.

He also made four cast bronze screens, to be placed before the altar, on either side between the choir and the entrance; likewise a cast bronze beam, with fifty candlesticks, in which an equal number of candles were to be placed on the principal feasts, while beneath it thirty-six lamps hung from bronze hooks attached to the same beam. [Col. 0756D; Col. 0757A]

This bronze beam, supported by bronze arms and hands, was joined to a wooden beam, which Desiderius had caused to be most beautifully carved and adorned with gold and coloured paint; and he set it above six silver columns [Note: omitted in manuscript 3.], four and a half cubits high and weighing eight pounds each, at the front of the choir. [Col. 0757]

Under this beam he hung five round icons, and set thirteen square ones above, of equal size and weight. Of the square icons, the aforesaid brother made ten at Constantinople in thick silver [Note: *grosso*, that is, “thick” or “coarse” silver], carved and gilded; some weighed fourteen pounds each, others twelve. He had all the round icons surrounded only by a silver frame [Note: manuscript 2 adds: “of four pounds”], while their remaining surfaces were painted with colours and figures by Greek skill. [Col. 0757B] Desiderius ordered three other square icons, of the same metal and dimensions, to be made by his own craftsmen in work by no means dissimilar.

A certain nobleman then sent Saint Benedict, from the imperial city, another round icon, covered on both sides with chased and gilded silver [Note: the edition reads “most wonderfully carved and gilded”], and encircled externally with silver bosses. Afterwards another like it was ordered to be made; both were hung, one on either side, in the altar canopy. [Note: manuscript 2 adds: “The aforesaid brother also brought with him from Constantinople two very beautiful large cast bronze lamps and seven small ones.”]

Desiderius further made another silver beam of about sixty pounds, likewise carved and gilded, which he placed in the great arch before the altar upon four partly gilded silver columns [Note: the edition reads: “he placed it upon columns having ten pounds of silver each and five cubits in height. He made …”]; each of these has ten pounds of silver and is five cubits high. [Col. 0757C] He also made two great silver crosses of thirty pounds each [Note: the edition reads “thirty pounds each”], whose images projected in wonderful carving [Note: the edition reads “quite wonderful”]; and he set them beneath the aforesaid beam, one on either side between the same columns, upon marble bases.

He covered the remaining three fronts of the high altar with eighty-six pounds of carved [Note: the edition reads “well carved”] and gilded silver. The fronts of the other three altars, however, are adorned on three sides with old panels.

He also made four beams for the altar canopy, covering them externally in the same manner with chased and gilded silver, and adorning their interiors with metal leaves [Note: *bracteae*, that is, thin plates] and colours. Two are six cubits long and weigh twenty pounds each; the other two are four and a half cubits long and weigh twelve pounds each, and were placed upon the old columns. [Note: manuscript 2 reads: “twenty and twenty. Six also …”]

He also made six large candlesticks, three cubits high, of stretched and carved sheets of silver, each [Note: *ana*, “each one,” from the Greek ἀνά] of five or six pounds; these are to be set in a straight line before the altar and lit with the largest candles on the principal feasts. [Col. 0758A]

He also made a wooden lectern for reading or chanting, far finer and loftier than the former one, reached by six steps; and by varied colours and leaves of gold he made it from beautiful into most beautiful. [Note: the edition reads “makes it.”] Before it he set upon a porphyry base a partly gilded silver column weighing twenty-five pounds, in the form of a great candlestick and six cubits high; upon it the great candle to be blessed on Holy Saturday is to be solemnly raised.

He also made a *pharus*, that is, a very great silver crown of about one hundred pounds, twenty cubits in circumference [Note: the edition reads “in circuit”], with twelve towers projecting externally and thirty-six lamps hanging from it. [Col. 0758B] He hung it outside the choir before the great cross by a sufficiently strong iron chain marked off with seven gilded apples.

33. Having written, however imperfectly, these matters concerning the construction, consecration, and partial adornment of the new basilica, let us return with our Desiderius to the completion of the remaining monastic buildings. [Note: manuscript 2 reads “however it may be” rather than “however imperfectly.”]

After the solemn dedication of the basilica had passed, the venerable abbot Desiderius saw, through God’s co-operating power and through the merits of Father Benedict, that everything which he had begun had reached completion as he desired. [Note: the edition reads “had reached completion.”] Thus made bolder—indeed, stronger—he resolved with great spirit to extend the whole enclosure of the monastery and, as he had already done with certain buildings, to renew the remaining workshops and offices together with those which he himself had constructed before the building of the church.

First, wishing to enlarge the cloister, which was clearly still too small for so great a community [Note: the edition reads “very small for so great a community”], he immediately demolished the old refectory. It had clung rather awkwardly to the side of the church and faced the chapter-house, and he himself had already enlarged it twice at different times. [Note: the edition reads “which he himself had already enlarged.”] In the farther part of the future cloister, beside the south side of the church court, he built a very handsome and sufficiently large refectory. He adorned the entire structure with various colours by the art of painters, roofed it with a ceiling of beams, and covered it above with tiles. [Note: the edition reads “roofed it.”] He established in it a very beautiful and elevated lectern, faced most fittingly with plaster and made visible to all.

The length of this building extends to ninety-five cubits, its width to twenty-three, and its height rises to fifteen. [Note: the edition reads “length” rather than “of the length.”] It has an entrance on the eastern side and an apse on the western; before the latter is set, crosswise, the quite spacious table of the abbot. [Note: the edition reads “very spacious.”] On its southern side it has fourteen windows [Note: the edition places “around the whole” here], but only two on its northern side; it also has two round windows in each end-wall and three around the pulpit, all elaborately fashioned in glass, plaster, and lead. [Note: the edition reads “in both plaster and glass.”]

Beside this building on the south he built the brethren’s kitchen [Note: manuscript 2 adds “quite spacious and beautiful”] in two connected vaults supported by only one column [Note: the edition reads “may support”]; and between it and the refectory he placed steps and a doorway, through which whatever is needed may be brought into or carried out of the refectory. [Col. 0759B] On the other side of the kitchen he established a storeroom, from which all necessities are to be supplied both to the refectory and to the kitchen.

After this, since the cloister still seemed insufficient for so great a multitude of brethren, this man of great spirit and very great confidence [Note: the edition reads “of great and very great confidence”] undertook completely to demolish the dormitory and chapter-house, which he himself had formerly constructed at very great expense and labour, as well as the old infirmary; and, under the pretext of enlarging the cloister, to make these buildings larger as well.

Since he intended to raise the outer wall of the dormitory far away from the other wall, above a great precipice of the mountain, he laid in the foundation a wall five cubits thick, for the sake of maximum strength [Note: manuscript 3 reads “for the sake of weakness”]; he extended it for two hundred cubits in length, raised it to thirty cubits in height, and placed it twenty-four cubits from the inner wall. [Col. 0759C]

This building, much larger, stronger, and more beautiful than the former, was most diligently roofed with tiles by the skill of craftsmen and adorned with the colours of painters. [Note: the edition reads “by the art of painters.”] On its southern side alone it has twenty large windows, three of which, the largest, are supported by three small marble columns. At its farther end he also constructed the brethren’s wardrobe, small indeed but sufficiently convenient and handsome. [Note: the edition inserts “he constructed” here.]

When all this had been completed in about three years, he immediately began to excavate the intervening mountain: one hundred and five cubits in length, forty-nine in width, and about ten in height. [Note: two manuscripts read “seven” instead of “ten.”]

He thus placed the chapter-house transversely on the eastern side, so that the inner corner of its façade is joined to the outer corner of the basilica’s façade [Note: two manuscripts read “the outer corner of the chapter-house”], while its apse appears to approach the dormitory. [Note: two manuscripts read “to approach.”] This building is fifty-three cubits long [Note: the edition reads “the length of the building”], twenty wide, and eighteen high. It has nine very beautiful glazed windows on one side and as many on the other; three round windows in the northern façade and two likewise round ones in the southern. It is amply adorned with a ceiling, pavement, and most beautiful paintings [Note: two manuscripts read “most precious paintings.”]

While these excavations were being made, we experienced so great a frequency of earthquakes that on one day we felt them seventeen times, while on several other days we felt them four times, twice [Note: manuscripts 3 and 4 read “two”], or even six or five times in a single day. Many of us thought that this did not occur without reason, because many burials in that place, perhaps of holy persons, had then necessarily been disturbed. At other times, earthquakes occur rather seldom in this place.

But because a great precipice remained on the inner side of the dormitory, he raised vaulted chambers alongside the building and filled the rest with earth and stones thrown in. Likewise, before the refectory, at the front of the cloister, he made a curved vaulted chamber into a very great cistern [Note: the edition reads “constructing”]; thus at last he levelled the entire surface of the cloister.

Then he built covered walking arches all around upon one hundred and ten small marble columns [Note: manuscripts 2 and 3 read “marble” in the masculine form and manuscript 3 adds “marble columns”], and extended the entire cloister to eighty-five cubits in length [Note: the edition reads “of eighty-five cubits”] and sixty-five in width. [Note: manuscript 2 reads “one hundred” for the length and “seventy” for the width; the edition reads “spread out” rather than “extended.”]

Since the part adjoining the great basilica [Note: two manuscripts read “the part of the greater basilica”], if levelled with the rest, would have made access to that basilica unsuitable, he made ambulatory arches beneath and above; and at each of its two corners [Note: manuscript 2 reads “at both angular corners”] he made marble steps by which one descends to the rest: fifteen from the chapter-house [Note: two manuscripts read “to the chapter-house”] and thirteen from the refectory. He paved all around with stone floors in Byzantine workmanship [Note: two manuscripts read “the workmanship of craftsmen”] and adorned it with most beautiful paintings.

When this work was completed, he lowered the upper floor of that palace, which Richerius had begun and he himself had finished, from its former elevation to the level of the cloister [Note: the edition reads “the cloister’s level”], and there established with a bath and other conveniences [Note: two manuscripts omit the words concerning the bath and other conveniences] a place of rest for the sick brethren.

On the western side of the cloister, beside the brethren’s refectory—namely, the cistern mentioned above—he suitably arranged a cell for novices [Note: the edition places “he arranged” here]. There, in accordance with the Rule [Note: Rule, chapter 58], the novices themselves were to meditate, rest, and eat [Note: the edition adds “and”]. Thus, finally, he taught the brethren, who had until then been more than sufficiently disturbed and troubled by so many works, that now, settled in a convenient and pleasant place of repose, they should henceforth devote themselves to the regular order the more strictly because the more orderly. [Note: manuscript 4 reads “henceforth” in a different position.]

When, with God’s favour, he had completed all this as he had vowed, and had most fittingly finished the internal offices of the brethren as he had desired [Note: two manuscripts read “as he had arranged them”], he girded himself, active and vigorous, likewise to repair the monastery’s external buildings. [Note: the edition places “himself” here.]

[Note: Up to this point is the hand of manuscript 1 of codex 3, in which the lower portion of the last leaf has been cut away; in place of that parchment another but contemporary hand has sewn in and written what follows down to “bakery.”]

First, on the western side, he raised a very strong wall and placed a gate about thirty cubits outside the old one, of squared and cut stones. [Note: two manuscripts read “a gate almost thirty cubits” rather than “about thirty cubits.”] Above it he fortified with a huge vault a very strong tower raised on four great columns. [Note: the edition reads “tower” in the accusative.]

But since outside there lay an immense precipice, while within was a great mound, he excavated the latter and filled the precipice with its stones and earth, making it passable despite the sloping approach. He then enclosed the entire monastery with a continuous wall on both sides, fortified with battlements in the manner of cities. [Note: two manuscripts omit “with battlements.”]

Beyond the aforesaid gate, beside the slope by which one ascends to it, he built a very large hospice for receiving pilgrims, with all its appurtenances. [Note: the edition reads “which leads to that gate.”] The building which had formerly been erected, in an unsuitable place near the basilica on the northern side, as a hospice, he rebuilt larger and more beautiful and adapted also for receiving guests; and in both of these reception-houses he supplied beds and every necessity in greatest abundance.

[Note: The edition adds: “Then, on the northern side, he built a palace of no small size for receiving all kinds of guests. He constructed the bakery with such splendour that …”]

On the same side, not far from the steps of the court, he built a bakery so spacious and beautiful that many arrivals, not knowing what it was, very often went there as if to some church in order to pray. [Note: manuscript 2 adds: “Desiderius did not cease, while these things were being done, to labour at seeking adornments for the church and, by whatever means he could and wherever he could, to procure things suitable to its beauty.”]

From this point [Note: the edition notes that the words of Peter, in which much has been changed and added, will be given below] Desiderius turned his whole heart to renewing the church of Saint Martin, which almost alone among the old buildings still remained within the monastic enclosure. [Col. 0762A]

When the former basilica of the same Saint Martin had been demolished, he began the fabric of the church: forty-three cubits in length, twenty-eight in width, and twenty-four in height [Note: manuscript 3 supplies these measurements; the corresponding numbers are missing in Migne]. It had windows on one side [Note: the number is missing in Migne] and as many on the other; sixteen columns; and wonderful stone screens made before the altar. He enclosed the windows with panels of lead and glass joined together and bound with iron. [Note: manuscripts 3 and 4 read “thus” rather than “in this way.”] Those situated in the porticoes he built in plaster, but with nearly equal beauty.

He fittingly covered the apse with mosaic and commanded the following verses to be inscribed there in golden letters:

> Once this place had been devoted to demonic rites,  
> and Apollo was worshipped in this temple.  
> But Father Benedict, hastening here, transformed it  
> to the honour of almighty God and in Saint Martin’s name.  
> After one hundred lustra, Desiderius demolished it,  
> old and small as it was; he renewed it, adorned it, and enlarged it.

[Note: *hausit* means “increased” or “enlarged”; manuscript 3 reads *auxit*, “increased.”]

How beautiful the pavement is can plainly be seen by those who look upon it. He made bronze doors at the entrance of the same church, and a silver altar-panel of about [Note: the number of pounds is missing in manuscript 3; after *juxta* the other contemporary hand continues, as noted above at Col. 0761.] pounds. Beside the same church he had small dwelling-rooms suitably built in which he might stay whenever he wished. Around the church he built a two-vaulted house for storing its ornaments [Note: manuscript 3 has “ornaments”; another manuscript has “ornament”].

After three years and as many months had passed from the dedication of the greater church, in the beginning of the year 1075 from the Saviour’s birth, on the third day before the Nones of January, the church of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, suitably situated on the western side of the greater church, was honourably dedicated by John, bishop of Sora, amid great joy and exultation of all the brethren. [Note: manuscript 3 adds: “Saint Bartholomew, page 3.”] There also a not inconsiderable portion of the holy arm of that blessed apostle was reverently deposited in a silver casket.

In the same year, about eight months later, the remaining two basilicas, most beautifully situated like towers at either extreme of the outer court, were consecrated with equal care and honour on the fourth day before the Ides of September. [Note: manuscript 4 reads “most beautiful basilicas.”] The one on the right, built in honour of Saint Michael the Archangel, was consecrated by the aforesaid John, bishop of Sora. [Note: manuscript 4 omits the words “was consecrated.”]

In it he also deposited these relics: of Saints Nicander and Marcian, Saint Vitus, Saints John and Paul, Saint Mercurius, and Saint Catherine [Note: manuscript 4 reads “of Saint Catherine”]; and the names of Saints Apollinaris the bishop, Protus, and Hyacinthus. The other, on the left, founded in honour of the blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, was consecrated by Leo, bishop of Aquino, to the divine majesty, in the presence of the lord abbot and the assembled community of all the brethren, with great joy and devotion. [Note: What follows has been supplied from the narrative of codex 47, following Muratori’s edition. Codex 3 ends here in larger letters, indicating that nothing further had been written, although the following leaf has been cut out.]

Moreover, when the sixteenth year—rather than the fourteenth—was then turning since this dedication, and the year 1090 since the Lord’s Incarnation, and when three years and sixty-three days had elapsed since the death of the reverend Abbot Desiderius, whose memory is always to be honourably revered, the church of Saint Martin, confessor of Christ, was dedicated at the command and under the presidency of his most reverend and worthy successor, Lord Oderisius. [Note: compare Book IV, chapter 8; one manuscript reads “the sixth year,” not “the sixteenth.”]

The venerable Abbot Desiderius had erected it most wonderfully and beautifully, on sixteen marble columns, at the very place near the monastery gate where it had once been built by the most blessed Abbot Benedict; and he had adorned it very well both with mosaic and with diverse colours of paintings.

It was dedicated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, the octave day of the same most blessed Martin, confessor of Christ, a Monday, together with its three altars, before a great gathering of men of various orders and with the greatest joy of all. The first and chief altar, in honour of Saint Martin himself, was dedicated by the venerable Lord John, bishop of Tusculum. The altar situated at the right of the basilica was consecrated in honour of Saint Erasmus the martyr by Lord Raynald, bishop of Gaeta, who had in that same year been appointed bishop of that church from this monastery of ours. The third, placed on the left, was blessed in honour of the glorious Ambrose, confessor of Christ, by Lord Honestus, the most reverend bishop of Veroli. Three other bishops were also present at this dedication: Lambert of Alatri, Roffridus of Sora, and Leo, bishop of Venafro.

The reason why the consecration of this basilica was delayed so long after Father Desiderius’s death was that the abbot, prevented by death, had left unfinished a certain part of the paintings and no small portion of the pavement. His successor took the greatest care to complete all these things and to add what was necessary; and thus he caused the church to be dedicated most honourably, as stated above.

Again, after three years and seventy-three additional days had elapsed, in the year 1094 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second indiction, on 30 January, a Monday, the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle was dedicated. [Note: compare Book IV, chapter 9.] It had been built from the foundations by the aforesaid Lord Abbot Oderisius [Note: compare Book IV, chapter 3] on the eastern side of the greater church, between its apse and the infirmary, with the brethren’s cemetery on the right and a small but very beautiful cloister on the left.

It was dedicated by the above-mentioned Lord Raynald, bishop of Gaeta, amid the great devotion and exultation of all the brethren; on that very day, by the merits of the most blessed Father Benedict and through divine mercy beyond all expectation, we recovered the castle called Fratta. It had been stolen from and seized from us three years earlier by neighbouring Normans, but on the thirteenth day [Note: the lacuna indicated here by Carraciolus is supplied in the Anonymous of Monte Cassino as follows: “and was recovered by our men on the twelfth day through the great power of God”], [lacuna] with the Lord’s help, it was recovered. In everlasting remembrance of that triumph, this solemn observance was established on the same day as the consecration.

The aforesaid basilica was established for the benefit of the sick brethren. It was most strongly roofed with timber and tiles, beautifully adorned with glazed windows, painted with varied stories of saints in beautiful diversity of colours, and furnished with a pavement artistically made from marble inlay of many kinds. But far more important than all this, it was most carefully consecrated with many distinguished relics of apostles, martyrs, and confessors of God. With God’s help, we shall write the names of them all, together with the sacred pledges of the other churches, in their proper places.

## THE CONTINUATION OF BOOK III, BY PETER THE DEACON, BEGINS

[Col. 0763]

34. Therefore, Christ being his guide, and knowing that everything had happened to him as he desired, Desiderius turned his whole heart to renewing the church of Saint Martin, which almost alone among the old buildings still remained within the monastic enclosure. [Col. 0764D–0765A]

Once the former basilica of the same Saint Martin had been demolished and foundations laid in Christ’s name, he began the church’s construction: forty-three cubits in length, twenty-eight in width, and twenty-four in height; it had nine windows on one side and as many on the other.

He raised the walls of both porticoes to sixteen cubits in height, marked each with four windows, and likewise distinguished them with four windows on the other side. The windows in the nave he enclosed with panels of lead and glass joined together and bound with iron. In the façade of the church he ordered three windows, and one in the apse, to be made with similar adornment. The windows in the porticoes, however, he built of plaster, though with equal beauty. He raised nine columns on one side and as many on the other.

Beside the church he also built, with a curved wall, a small but most beautiful structure for the service of that church. Before Saint Martin’s altar he had wonderful stone screens made. He fittingly covered the apse with mosaic and ordered these verses to be inscribed there in golden letters:

> Once this place had been devoted to demonic rites,  
> and Apollo was worshipped in this temple;  
> but Father Benedict, hastening here, transformed it  
> to the honour of almighty God and in Saint Martin’s name.  
> After one hundred lustra, Desiderius demolished it,  
> old and small as it was; he renewed it, adorned it, and enlarged it.

How conspicuous and beautiful the church’s pavement is, and how it is laid with a multitude of different marbles, is evident to every eye. He also ordered a most beautiful lectern, adorned with gold and colours by the ingenuity of painters, to be built there.

Before the altar of Saint Martin himself Desiderius ordered a silver, gilded, and most beautifully carved panel to be made, weighing forty-four pounds; upon it were carved almost all the narratives of the blessed Evangelist Matthew and of Saint Martin, confessor of Christ. He also made bronze doors at the entrance of the church.

Beside the basilica he built a small dwelling [Note: manuscript 3 reads “small dwellings”] in which he might stay, roofing it with laid beams and covering it above with tiles. When, with the Lord’s aid, he had completed these things as he wished, he caused the basilica of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle to be solemnly dedicated, on the third day before the Nones of January, by John—formerly a monk of this monastery and afterwards bishop of Sora—with the whole community of brethren. [Note: “Ruborum”; “Guilelmus” or “Guibertus.” The reading is uncertain.]

In its altar he deposited a considerable part of the apostle’s body in a silver casket; in it he also placed these relics: a piece of the stone of the Holy Sepulchre, and relics of Saints John and Paul, Vitus, Januarius, Hermes, and the Forty Martyrs.

Indeed, Desiderius enjoyed such authority and favour with the Roman pontiff that, in whatever churches or monasteries he wished that had been deprived of their own pastor, he had the right to appoint bishops or abbots from among his brethren.

Not long afterwards, he also caused the little chapels which, as we have said, had been set in the corners of the court in the manner of towers, to be dedicated with great joy on the fourth day before the Ides of September: one by the same John and the other by Leo, bishop of Aquino.

In the altar of Saint Michael the Archangel he deposited relics of Saints Nicander and Marcian, John and Paul, Vitus, Mercurius, and Catherine, and the names of Saints Apollinaris the bishop, Protus, and Hyacinthus.

Leo, bishop of Aquino, consecrated the altar of the chief of the apostles to the divine name [Note: the noted reading is “to the divine majesty”], in the presence of the lord abbot and the whole assembled community of brethren, with great joy and devotion. In that same altar these relics were deposited: of the five barley loaves; of the holy apostles Peter, Matthew, and James; of Nazarius and Celsus; of Januarius; of Felicissimus and Agapitus; of Sergius and Bacchus; of Nicander and Marcian; of Aurelius; of Protasius; of Fortunatus and his companions; and of the garments of the Three Children.

35. At about the same time Alberic, a deacon, a man most eloquent and learned, came to reside in this place. While established in this monastery, he composed a book on the virginity of Saint Mary; a book of compositions and salutations; a dialogue on Music; a work against Emperor Henry concerning the election of the Roman pontiff; the Life of Saint Scholastica, virgin of Christ; her homily; the Life of Saint Dominic; the Passions of Saint Modestus and Saint Caesarius; and a book on dialectic.

[Note: Cf. Peter Damian, *On Illustrious Men*, chapters 21 and 45, where he is called a philosopher and is said to have instructed Gelasius II. Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, V, p. 179.]

[Note: A. Mai published its prologue together with the homily in *Spicilegium Romanum*, V, p. 129.]

[Col. 0766C]

[Note: That is, Dominic of Sora; published in *Acts of the Saints*, January II, p. 442.]

[Note: “saints” in the manuscript.]

During his time a synod was held in the city of Rome (February 1079) against Berengar, deacon of the church of Angers. Among many things which he sought to maintain, he said that the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood was a figure. Since no one was able to withstand him, Alberic himself was summoned to the synod. When he had come there, after various kinds of disputation, and neither side yielded to the other, Alberic, having received leave for one week, produced a book against that deacon on the body of the Lord, strengthened by the testimonies of the holy Fathers. In it he demolished all Berengar’s assertions and consigned them to everlasting oblivion.

He also made verses on the Life of Saint Scholastica; rhythms for Easter, on the Day of Judgment, and on the punishments of hell; and very many letters to Peter, bishop of Ostia.

[Col. 0766D]

[Note: Two letters of Peter to Alberic survive in *Opuscula*, no. 37.]

He wrote rhythms on the joy of paradise, the day of death, and the penitent monk. He composed several other works as well, which have not come to our knowledge.

At that time also Alfanus, archbishop of Salerno and monk of this monastery, whom we mentioned above—a man most learned in the Holy Scriptures and thoroughly instructed in the knowledge of ecclesiastical doctrines—composed, in polished and most lucid language, the Passion of Saint Christina, and a book of hymns and verses.

[Col. 0767A]

[Note: 1058–1087. Cf. *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 19; Giesebrecht, *On Literary Studies among the Italians*, who published his unpublished poems, some more correctly than Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, X, p. 47 ff.]

Amatus also, bishop and monk of this monastery, wrote in these days verses on the deeds of the apostles Peter and Paul, and divided them into four books.

[Note: Bishop of Nusco; see Champollion-Figeac in the Prolegomena to the *History of the Normans*, whose ancient French version he published at Paris in 1835, octavo.]

[Note: He dedicated them to Gregory VII. A copy of the Bologna manuscript is preserved at Monte Cassino; see Tosti, *History of Cassino*, I, p. 417.]

Composing also a History of the Normans, he dedicated it to the name of that same abbot.

In the time of this abbot Constantine the African came to this place and, putting on the habit of holy religion, most devoutly offered to this holy place the church of Saint Agatha at Aversa, which Prince Richard had granted to him.

[Col. 0767B]

[Note: On him see Peter, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 23; Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, XIII, p. 123.]

It seems altogether necessary to commit to writing for the remembrance of posterity how great and what manner of man he was. Accordingly, leaving Carthage, from which he was native, he went to Babylon. There he was most thoroughly instructed in grammar, dialectic, geometry, arithmetic, mathematics, astronomy, and likewise physics, according to the learning of the Chaldeans, Arabs, Persians, Saracens, Egyptians, and Indians. Having spent thirty-nine years in mastering studies of this kind, he returned to Africa.

When the Africans saw that he was so completely learned in the disciplines of every nation, they planned to kill him. Constantine, recognizing this, secretly boarded a ship and arrived at Salerno, where he remained concealed for a time under the appearance of a poor man. Then he was recognized by the brother of the king of the Babylonians, who had come there at that time, and was held in great honor by Duke Robert. Thereafter Constantine departed and came to this place; and he became a monk in the manner related above.

[Col. 0767C]

While established in this monastery, he translated very many books from the languages of diverse nations, especially the following: the *Pantegni*, which he divided into twelve books, in which he explained what a physician ought to know; the *Practica*, in which he set forth how a physician should preserve health and treat illness; the *Book of Degrees*; *The Diet of Foods*; a *Book of Fevers*, translated from Arabic; a *Book on Urine*; *On the Internal Organs*; the *Viaticum*, which he divided into seven parts, namely, on diseases arising in the head; then on diseases of the face; on the organs; on diseases of the stomach and intestines; on the ailments of the liver, kidneys, bladder, spleen, and gall; and on conditions arising in the outer skin; an exposition of the *Aphorisms*; books called *Tegni*, *Megategni*, and *Microtegni*; an antidotary; the disputation of Plato and Hippocrates in opinions; *On Simple Medicines*; *On Women’s Diseases* (*De genecia*); *On Pulses*; *On Experiments*; glosses on herbs and species; and *On the Eyes*.

[Note: According to C. L. Grotefend, this book in a twelfth-century manuscript of the Hanover civic library bears this inscription: “To his lord Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, most reverend father of fathers—indeed, the shining jewel of the whole ecclesiastical order—Constantine the African, unworthy though his monk, [wishes] that their souls, endowed with inward and outward sight, may be enrolled in heaven.”]

[Col. 0768C]

[Note: He dedicated the book *On Affections of the Stomach* to Alfanus, most reverend archbishop of the church of Salerno, who suffered from a stomach complaint.]

[Col. 0768A]

36. In the following period the aforementioned Pope Alexander left the city and came to this monastery. Desiderius received him honorably. When he had entered the abbot’s chamber, built beside the church of Saint Nicholas, a demoniac who had come there at that time met him. When the holy pontiff saw him, he poured out prayer to the Lord and said to the demon: “I command you, unclean spirit, by the power of the Lord, to go out from this man and go to that place where no bird flies and no human voice resounds; and remain there until the Day of Judgment.”

[Col. 0768B]

Wonderful is God in his saints: he deigns swiftly to hear those who call upon him and trust in his mercy. For, at that pontiff’s command, the demon left the man, and all those present began to praise and bless God.

Nor does it seem right to pass over what almighty God deigned to work through this same servant of his. For, as he was passing through the city of Aquino, he found on the road a certain lame person lying there. Compassionating that person’s infirmity, the pontiff gave them to drink water in which he had washed his hands after the solemnities of Mass. As soon as the person drank it, they were restored to health and began to render the greatest thanks to God.

[Note: “a certain man” in the manuscript.]

[Col. 0768C]

The same most holy pontiff furthermore granted Father Desiderius a privilege concerning the monastery of Saint Mary in Palladio, with all its appurtenances, receiving from him the church of Holy Jerusalem, which the most reverend Pope Leo, as we have noted above (book II, chapter 79), had granted to our Abbot Richerius.

[Note: Above, II.94, and below, IV.81. A copy of this privilege is found in the Register, no. 31 (undated, according to Giesebrecht): “Alexander, etc. Therefore, dearest brother and fellow priest, because we especially desire your prudence to cleave to our side with a serene countenance, we give and grant both to you and to your successors, the abbots of Mount Cassino—upon receipt of the investiture of the monastery of Holy Jerusalem, which Deus, bishop of blessed memory, bestowed upon your predecessor Richerius for hospitality—the abbey of the holy martyrs Sebastian and Zosimus, which the common people customarily call by the usual name Palaria,” etc. ANG.]

The aforesaid Pope Alexander also personally granted our Desiderius the city of Terracina with its appurtenances.

[Col. 0769A]

When that pontiff had died (21 April 1073), the Roman clergy and people assembled together and elected Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Apostolic See, decreeing that he should be called Gregory. In the same year as his ordination, he came to this monastery and, taking Desiderius with him, proceeded to Benevento; returning from there, he went back to Rome.

At that time, while the aforesaid pope was celebrating the solemnities of Mass in the church of Saint Mary called Major on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, he was seized above the holy altar by certain faithless Romans. But through the strength and steadfastness of all the Romans he was recovered on the same day.

[Note: Two years later; the wording is taken from the Anonymous of Cassino under the year 1075.]

37. At the same time (February 1072), Prince Richard, by charter, offered to Saint Benedict the church of Saint Angel, called *ad Formas*. We wrote more fully above (book I, chapter 57), in the time of Abbot Baldwin, how it had been granted to us by Pope Marinus.

[Note: Published from the original by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 176. Di Meo, *Annals of Naples*, VIII, 116, considers it spurious; but, according to Bethmann, it is genuine.]

[Col. 0769B]

But because the archbishop of Capua held it at that time, the aforesaid prince, desiring to establish a monastery there, had exchanged it with him about seven years earlier (December 1065), giving in exchange another church called Saint John of Landepaldi, which then belonged to the palace, together with its ornaments, a considerable number of books, and all its property and appurtenances.

[Note: In the city of Capua. The instrument then drawn up was published from the Register of Saint Angel by Gattola, *History*, p. 253; Tosti, *History of Cassino*, I, p. 400, also gives a painted panel depicting that transfer.]

He received from that archbishop the aforesaid church of Saint Angel together with three other churches already worn away by age: Saint Saviour, Saint John, and Saint Hilary; and with everything belonging to those churches wherever situated. A penalty of sixty pounds of gold was imposed if ever either the archbishop himself or any of his successors should wish to remove this arrangement.

[Col. 0769C]

Having done this, in the same place he granted the church of Saint Angel of Olaldisi within Capua, with all its appurtenances (1065); likewise whatever belonged to the palace throughout all Sarzano, with all the peasants dwelling there; and everything which had belonged there to Count Gregory of the palace and to Peter, son of Doferius, at Saint Erasmus. With all these things, with all their appurtenances, and with the charter of exchange which he had received concerning them from the aforesaid archbishop, he offered the aforesaid church to this monastery of Cassino.

[Note: Near the street of Auloaldiski, in a charter published from the original by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 175.]

[Note: Near the Volturno, north of Mount Tifata; see Peregrini, *Campania Felix*, p. 373. ANG.]

Since the place was very pleasant and well suited for a monastery, he humbly asked Desiderius to devote particular care to it for his sake. Desiderius did so, taking one whole half of all movable goods from the monastery of Albaneta and sending them there, together with half the monks of that place.

[Col. 0769D]

[Col. 0770A]

Desiderius began to construct it afresh on the spacious scale visible today; and within a short time he gathered there forty and more monks to live according to the Rule.

38. At the same time, a certain peasant living in Apulia, burning with thirst, went to drink. Immediately the devil entered him and began to torment him most cruelly. His relatives brought him to this monastery and cast him before the body of Father Benedict; through the intervention of Benedict’s merits, he was immediately healed.

In those days, when in this monastery of Cassino there was in the vessel no more wine than a measure of one and a half palms for the provision of the whole monastery, the brother who guarded the wine-cellar went to report this to Father Desiderius.

[Col. 0770B]

The abbot replied: “Before I go to the court of Duke Robert, come to me, and I shall give you the means of buying it.” But on the following day the monk forgot Desiderius’s instructions and did not come to him. Desiderius set out upon his journey and went to Duke Robert’s court.

But he who fed the people with manna for forty years in the region of the desert caused the wine from which all drank to increase for three and a half months. A boy among the monastery servants, ignorant of heavenly mysteries, marvelled greatly that so much wine had lasted in the vessel. He went to the wine-cellar, measured the wine, and at that very hour it stopped, and increased no further. Then he came joyfully to the monk and said: “I have just measured the wine, and it is only as much as it was three months ago.”

[Note: That is, the wine-cellar.]

[Col. 0770C]

When the monk heard this, he beat him very severely. The boy fled before him, entered the cloister and the brethren, and related in order what the monk had done to him. Stephen of venerable memory, who at that time held the office of dean, summoned the monk and said: “Why have you beaten this boy so cruelly?”

Then the brother said: “God has already performed many times, through the merits of the most blessed Father Benedict, what he has now deigned to perform in the wine. But this boy went to the vessel and measured the wine; and thereafter it did not increase in the vessel.”

Hearing this, they blessed God, who had deigned in their time to renew in that place an ancient miracle.

[Col. 0770D]

One night, while Brother George, the sacristan, lay awake resting in his bed, he heard two boys in the church rendering praises to God with marvellous sweetness and delightful melody. Knowing certainly that there was no monk in the monastery with a boyish voice, he immediately arose and entered the church. Finding no one there, and recognizing the truth of the matter, he related in the morning, in order, to the brethren what he had heard. From this they said that a company of angels had been present at the relics of the blessed father.

[Note: “monastery” in the manuscript.]

[Col. 0771A]

[*Desiderius, Dialogues*, II.21.]

At another time, the aforesaid George had come to replenish the lamp hanging before the image of the Saviour painted above the church doors. Behold, he saw it suspended in the air by its stretched hooks, supported by no material whatever except air. George summoned the brethren who were at a distance and showed them what he marvelled at; afterward, they too, together with him, were witnesses of this miracle.

[Note: Read *aera* (“air”), as below, col. 775, line 20.]

On the night preceding the feast-day of the passing of our holy Father Benedict, while one of the custodians was replenishing at vigils the lamp hanging before the image of that blessed father, the lamp suddenly slipped and fell to the pavement, yet remained unharmed.
