Raised again, it fell again; set upright a third time, it slipped a third time; and in none of these falls did the lamp suffer breakage, the oil spillage, or the flame extinction.

When on one day one of the custodians had raised a lamp burning before the altar nearly to the very ceiling, the lamp suddenly slipped and fell to the pavement. Wonderful is God in his works! The lamp that fell was not merely unbroken, but neither was the oil spilled nor the flame extinguished.

[Col. 0771B]

[*Peter Damian, Letters*, VI.22.]

At that time a very notable miracle occurred in the monastery of the blessed Father Benedict built within the walls of the city of Salerno, which had been subject to this monastery of Cassino from the beginning of its construction. A ravenous wolf from the household of that monastery secretly attacked, seized, and carried off a little boy. His mother, pierced with grief, cried after it: “I adjure you, beast, by blessed Benedict, whose servant he is, do not carry my son any farther, but release him with all speed.”

[Col. 0771C]

When the wolf heard this, it immediately opened its mouth and put down the boy it was carrying. But it suddenly sprang upon another child, at once tore him to pieces, abandoned the mutilated body, and hurriedly carried off to its lair the severed head, fast held in its teeth.

39. About these days Michael, emperor of Constantinople, sent Father Desiderius very many gifts through messengers dispatched to him, asking that they continually entreat the mercy of almighty God for himself, his children, and the welfare of his empire. Moreover, out of reverence for Father Benedict and for the salvation of his own soul, he established by a decree sealed with a golden bull that every year this monastery should receive from the palace of the Constantinopolitan empire twenty-four pounds of gold and four cloaks (*pallia*), for the support of our community.

[Col. 0771D]

[Col. 0772A]

[Note: Register, no. 145, entitled: “Decree of Michael Constantine, emperor, that is, son of Constantine.” ANG. “I subscribed in red ink in April, indiction 4,” that is, 1081; but he was driven from the throne in 1078.]

Borrellus, son of the elder Count Borrellus, had deservedly gained Desiderius’s friendship because of certain services of his in this place. He most devoutly offered to Saint Benedict the monastery of Saint Peter called *de Avellana*, which his father had given to Saint Dominic for construction forty-four years earlier, and which Borrellus himself had enriched with a very extensive grant of lands. He offered it with churches, tenants, and all its appurtenances and possessions whatsoever—amounting to about five thousand modii of land (March 1069).

[Note: In the territory of Sangro; the diploma is in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 179, from the Register of Saint Peter, from which he also published what follows.]

[Col. 0772B]

Much later, when Walter, his nephew, wrongfully retained twelve farmsteads on the stream of Franculus belonging to that monastery, he came of his own accord to this monastery and renounced and restored them to us.

[Note: A memorandum concerning this matter survives in the Register of Saint Peter, published by Gattola in the same place.]

Not long after, Theodinus, Oderisius, and Bernard, counts of Balva, likewise offered to this monastery the monastery of Saint Peter in the valley of Lacu and another monastery of hermits at the place called Pratum Cardosum. These too had been founded by Saint Dominic not many years earlier. They offered them with five adjacent lakes, with churches and tenants, and with all their appurtenances and possessions whatsoever, both in the county of Balva itself and in the Marsican and Theatine territories.

[Note: 1067 [read 1069], indiction VII, April, in the same source. Di Meo considers both lordships suspect, since Leo omitted them.]

[Note: Alberic, *Life of Saint Dominic*, chapter 2. But he had already died in 1031; see above, II.59.]

[Col. 0772C]

In the same year certain Marsican nobles offered to Saint Benedict the castle called Meta in the valley of Orbeto, with all its boundaries and appurtenances; likewise the church of Saint Father at the place called Formae, and the church of Saint Donatus above those same Formae, with everything belonging to those churches; and, in addition, everything belonging to the aforesaid nobles by hereditary right, both at Formae itself and in Valle Frigida.

[Note: By Azzone, son of Azzone; but dated A.D. 1072, December, indiction X, in the same source, p. 180. Yet only one castle of Meta is named there.]

In the same year Leo and Gerard, consuls of Fondi, offered to blessed Father Benedict the monastery of Saint Magnus with all its dependencies; a fourth part of the fishery of Lake Fondi; the church of Saint Mary near the amphitheatre of the city of Fondi; Saint Maurus and Saint Martin at Tirille; Saint Andrew in Terracina; and Saint Nicholas in the city of Rome, at the place called *ad fossas*, with all their appurtenances and property.

[Note: 1072, September, indiction X, in Gattola, II, p. 259.]

[Col. 0772D]

Together with Richard called de Aquila, the same consuls likewise offered this place the church of Saint Onuphrius with its appurtenances. Since that place was suitable for constructing a monastery, Desiderius, desiring to establish one there, raised it through Gerard, provost of Saint Nicholas in Pica, who became the fifth abbot of this monastery after him, into the condition in which it is now seen.

[Col. 0773A]

In those days also Littefrid, consul of Fondi, made a charter to this monastery for everything belonging to him in the city of Fondi, the valley of Cursa, Aquaviva, Ambrife, Ynola, Campu de Mele, Vatera, one third of the fishery at Saint Anastasia, the monastery of Saint Archangel, and all that belonged to it by paternal or maternal right.

[Note: In the tenth year of Duke Littefrid, October, indiction XI, in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 180.]

[Col. 0773B]

At the same time John of Isernia, a nobleman, likewise offered this monastery of Cassino the monastery of Saint Benedict at Baniorala, with its two other cells, namely Saint Mary and Saint Lucy, together with all their appurtenances (September 1072).

[Note: “Banlarola” in the manuscript (?)] 

[Note: Not far from the castle of Ribomatrice, in the district of Pontecorvo. The charter, published from the Register by Gattola, *History*, p. 264, was written at Pontecorvo by order of Geoffrey Ridello, consul and duke of the city of Gaeta and lord of Pontecorvo. John of Isernia, his vassal (*fidelis*), had received from him the castle of Ribomatrice and the monastery as a fief. At the same time another Abbot John, with the monks’ consent, transferred that same monastery with those cells to the Cassinese by charter.]

Morinus, count of Benevento, did the same concerning four other churches: Saint Nazarius of Piperozza, Saint Peter of Sexto, Saint Barbatus of Ravenola, and Saint Martin of that same Furca.

40. I judge it worthwhile to append, for the memory and edification of posterity, what the Lord deigned to accomplish through blessed Benedict in Gaul in this year. A certain very powerful man, born of the people of the Gauls, had from infancy defiled himself with such abominable crimes that no part of his body was free from its own vice. As he approached death, he summoned the brethren of a certain monastery and requested that the monastic habit be bestowed upon him. But as soon as he was clothed in the sacred garments, he gave up his spirit.

[Col. 0773C]

The Lord deigned to show a servant of God living nearby what was being done concerning the dead man’s soul. For immediately after it departed from the body, a terrible multitude of demons bound it with fiery chains and tried to carry it to the infernal fires. The most blessed Father Benedict then stood in their midst, holding a pastoral staff in his hand.

The enemies, seeing that they were losing their prey, said: “Benedict, you know how many souls you have for a very long time taken from our hands. But this man, who has never done anything good: you act unjustly if you try to take him from our hands.”

The saint replied: “Lest I perhaps seem to act unjustly toward you, examine his deeds; and if, after he received my habit, he has in any degree been guilty of your works, let him remain yours.”

[Col. 0773D]

Then that company of the wicked, recognizing that it had been justly defeated, vanished through the thin air. Seeing this, the servant of God began to praise the mercy of Christ, who had deigned so wonderfully to deliver that soul from the demons’ hands.

In those same regions there is a monastery dedicated in honor of that same father. When the brethren there had solemnly celebrated his feast on the day on which the saint ascended to heaven, they came to supper and found that they had no fish. They began to complain about this to the abbot.

[Col. 0774A]

On the following night the most holy Father Benedict appeared to the abbot in a dream and said: “Why are the brethren sad?” He answered: “Because they had no fish the previous day.”

The saint said to him: “In my monastery at Cassino, I myself awaited the departure from the world of a cellarer who was burdened by the weight of sins. I helped him by my prayers, and almighty God established him in the rest of eternal life. Now send fishermen to the lake near the monastery, and there you will find abundantly what will enable you to quiet the brothers’ murmuring.”

When the abbot awoke, he sent fishermen with all speed to the lake. Seeing this, the brethren began to marvel, because the lake to which the fishermen were going produced only snakes and frogs. But the fishermen entered the lake, in which no fishing had ever occurred either before or afterward, and caught such a multitude of fish that they sufficed for the brethren’s food for eight continuous days.

[Col. 0774B]

A certain John, surnamed Benafranus, vice-count of Prince Jordan I, was a most wicked man, filled with every stain of vice. When he came near death, he asked to be brought to this place and to receive the habit of holy religion. His friends, favoring his request, led him to this monastery; and, receiving monastic garments before the body of the most holy Father Benedict, he immediately departed from the world.

After he had been buried, a certain peasant left the monastery and was making his way toward the open country. When he reached the church of Saint Severus, once bishop of Cassino, situated on this mountain, he found the devil standing in the road, of towering stature, with exceedingly long fingers and claws, holding a staff in his hand and glaring grimly at the peasant.

[Col. 0774C]

When the peasant came up to him, the devil said: “Where are you coming from?” Thinking that he was a man, the peasant answered: “From the monastery of Cassino.”

The devil said: “What has happened to John the vice-count?” The peasant replied: “After he became a monk, he immediately departed from the world.”

Hearing this, the devil began to complain, saying: “Alas, Benedict, for me! Alas, Benedict, for me! Why do you turn my servants to yourself every day? Why do you not cease to persecute me so savagely, so cruelly?”

[Note: Cf. above, I.20.]

[Col. 0774D]

[Col. 0775A]

After saying this, he glared at the peasant with a furious and flaming countenance and said: “Know with complete certainty that, if you had not today taken food and drink in Benedict’s monastery, and if you did not now have in your bosom bread brought from that same place, I would kill you at once without any delay.”

Immediately he hurled himself down the mountainside, dragging stones and trees along like a whirlwind. When the peasant saw this, trembling, he descended the mountain and related in order everything he had seen and heard.

When he came to the water called Casinus, the devil appeared to him again and said: “Are you still walking through this land?” Gnashing his teeth, he repeated what he had said before, struck the water of Casinus most violently with the staff he held, and disappeared. At the sound it seemed to the peasant that the whole earth had shaken; the water rose into the air like a river in a storm.

[Note: Or “the whole land”?]

[Col. 0775B]

Having returned to his home at Rivo Matricis, he was seized by sickness and ended his life after the third day.

41. At the same time Landenulf, who had been count of Calvi, disputed with us concerning the bed of the Garigliano River, maintaining that it ought by no means to belong to our castle of Mortula, and that the men of Criptis in that place owed us nothing. When the case had long been argued before the judges of Sessa, defeated by the arguments, he yielded and declared by charter that he had absolutely no right in any of these matters.

[Note: Ancient Cales, succeeded by Calvi.]

[Note: “owed” in the manuscript.]

[Col. 0775C]

Likewise Joffrid, surnamed Monius, came at the command of Prince Richard to this monastery and, in Desiderius’s presence, voluntarily declared in writing and renounced into his hands those fisheries in the Garigliano River beside the said currents: beginning at the stream called Vivus, which descends from Criptis, and extending as far as the stream which descends from Holy Cross and flows into the aforesaid Garigliano River. These fisheries had anciently belonged partly to this monastery and partly to Saint Saviour of Cucuruzzo; yet until that time the counts of Sessa had held them forcibly and unlawfully.

[Note: I have corrected the reading thus. The manuscript has “Loffridus” (?)] 

[Col. 0775D]

In the following period (February 1076), Joffrid surnamed Ridello, duke of the Gaetans, offered to this place the monastery of Saint Erasmus in the city territory of Formiae and the monastery of Saint Peter of Foresta in the district of Pontecorvo, with all their possessions.

[Note: In the territory of the city of Gaeta, at the place called *Ad Molas*. Gattola, *History*, p. 267.]

[Col. 0776A]

Then also Lando, lord of the city of Arpino, as he approached death (August), made a legal disposition to this monastery concerning everything that belonged to him by hereditary right: namely, half of Arpino, Monte Nero, Saint Urban, Vico Bianco, and Casa Silverii. A penalty of one hundred pounds of gold was imposed upon all who should seek to revoke this legal disposition.

[Note: He himself says: “I offered and transferred”; in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 181.]

42. At the same time, while the aforementioned Pope Gregory was holding a synod at Rome (1078), Leo, librarian of this place, who afterward became bishop of Ostia, by order of Father Desiderius made a claim concerning the cell of Saint Sophia at Benevento. The Beneventans had recently violently withdrawn it from the jurisdiction of this monastery.

[Note: Cf. his brief report on this affair in Gattola, *History*, p. 54, where he says that he had been able to recover no legal right. Cf. Preface, p. 552.]

[Col. 0776B]

When the matter had been brought to a hearing, our documents were read in everyone’s hearing: how Prince Arechis, founder of that church, had transferred it by charter to this monastery of Cassino; and then how all Roman pontiffs, emperors, kings, dukes, and princes had confirmed the aforesaid cell to this place.

Upon hearing this, Pope Gregory declared that the Beneventans could in no way withdraw from the authority of the monastery of Cassino a church originally assigned to it; rather, the church of Cassino ought wholly, canonically, and lawfully to possess that cell forever.

At the same synod he decreed that if anyone should receive investiture of a church from a layman, both giver and receiver should be punished by anathema.

[Note: 1075, if this refers to the first decree on the matter; but it was repeated in 1078.]

At the same time, while the aforesaid Pope Gregory was staying at Capua, the clergy of that city lodged envious complaints before him, saying that the church of Saint Angel, formerly belonging by right to the church of Capua, had passed into the jurisdiction of our monastery through an inequitable exchange.

[Note: From the pope’s decree issued at Rome, 7 December 1078, in Gattola, *History*, p. 254.]

[Col. 0776C]

[Note: Cf. chapter 37 above.]

The apostolic pontiff, unwilling at Desiderius’s request that this complaint should remain unexamined, diligently sought through competent and trustworthy men to investigate whether the exchange made for that church seemed equitable. Examining the matter most carefully, they found and proved that the church of Saint John of Landepaldi, given in exchange, had at the time of the exchange considerably greater possessions and ornaments.

[Col. 0776D]

Erveus, then archbishop of that city, likewise affirmed that he truly knew this. Once all uncertainty in the aforesaid dispute had been removed by this adequate testimony, the aforesaid apostolic pontiff ruled that both the archbishop and the clergy of Capua should forever refrain from this question and should raise no further suit concerning that exchange.

Immediately, by a privilege dated 7 December, he judged and decreed this to be firm and perpetually stable: that the same monastery should remain forever under the care and governance of the abbot of Cassino. By the same privilege he confirmed everything that had then been granted there or might be granted in the future; upon violators of this decree, unless perhaps they repented, he pronounced a sentence of excommunication, while for those who observed it he prayed that apostolic blessing and perpetual peace might ensue.

### 43. [DESID. *Dial.* I, 5, 8, 7.]

In those same days there was in this monastery a certain brother named Angelus, a venerable man endowed with every goodness. When he was closing his last day in this monastery, a demoniac arrived and began to cry out:

> “What have you done to me at this hour, Benedict? By taking the soul of the monk Angelus from my power on account of the carrying of a small cowl, you have joined him to your flock in heaven.”

As he said these things mournfully, suddenly the bell by which the death of the brethren is customarily announced sounded; and, going there, they found the aforesaid Angelus already deprived of life.

There was another monk in this monastery, named John [Note: [Col. 0777D] Venetian *Desiderius*.], who, when he had died and been buried in this place, was visited at his tomb by a brother suffering so severely from a hernia that, after the rupture of the intercutaneous membrane, his intestines were slipping between flesh and skin. There, prostrate with his whole body, he began to beseech the mercy of almighty God that, through the intercession of His servant John, He might deign to restore that rupture to its former soundness. But how much John’s prayer availed with God became clear: for the rupture was immediately healed.

At that time there was in this holy place a brother named Stephen [Note: [Col. 0777D] St. Venetian *Desiderius*.]. When he was entering in this monastery upon the way of all flesh, an old woman named Agundia, spending the night in prayer before the church of the holy Mother of God situated at the foot of this mountain, turned her eyes toward the mountain and saw a fiery column emerge from the infirmary and penetrate the heights of heaven. Having seen this, she immediately sent a messenger to the monastery; and he found Stephen to have breathed out his soul at the very hour when she had seen the fiery column ascend to heaven.

### 44.

Moreover, John, son of Count Hugh, following his father’s example [Note: [Col. 0777D] See above, II, 55. Gattola published this donation, *Hist.*, p. 267. But already on 23 September 1078 Prince Jordan had granted Suio to Desiderius, because Raynerius, with his other associates and kinsmen who lived in that castle, “committed such an offence that by law all their property was transferred to our fisc”; see Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 187.], offered and confirmed to Saint Benedict his entire share of the castle of Suio—namely, one half of it—with everything belonging to that half, both within and without; likewise his entire share in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Erasmus at Formiae (May 1079).

Likewise Sanso, son of Albert of the county of Penne, made a charter to this monastery of his whole hereditary portion: namely, one half of the castle called Planello [Note: [Col. 0778D] On the River Tavo. November 1080, indiction I; in Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 182.], with the church of Saint Stephen there, and one half of Pasiniano, with a tract of land measured at one thousand *modii*.

Duke Robert also, after taking Taranto, the most noble city of Apulia (June 1080), offered Saint Benedict the monastery of that city called Saint Peter Imperialis, with all its appurtenances; likewise 104 households of persons belonging to that place; and, in addition, his entire tithe of wheat, barley, wine, oil, and all the fish from his fisheries [Note: [Col. 0778D] “Which we now have there or shall have.” Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 183.]. A penalty of five hundred pounds of gold was imposed upon anyone who should seek to alienate it.

In those same times Palermo was taken by the same most vigorous duke (1072). Although I have touched above in part upon how, and on what occasion, that duke took Sicily [Note: [Col. 0778D] Leo, ch. 15.], it seems appropriate to insert the matter here for the memory of posterity.

### 45. [AMAT. V, 8, 10, 18, 20, 23, 25, 27.]

While Vulthuminus, the admiral, held the government of the city of Palermo, one of his servants, named Belchus, rose against him and deprived him of office and homeland. Driven out of Sicily, he fled for aid to the aforesaid Duke Robert.

Then the duke, having assembled a naval force, entered Sicily in 1061, intending under Christ’s leadership to conquer it [Note: [Col. 0778D] Not Robert himself, but Geoffrey Ridello.]. The Saracens engaged him with a strong army and, near the city of Messina, were promptly defeated with Christ’s help; the survivors sought safety in flight. Messina having been taken and its admiral killed, the duke came to the city of Rametta. Having made it tributary to himself, he came with one thousand horsemen and as many infantrymen to Castrum Johannis.

Against him Balcaoth, admiral of the Saracens, hastened with fifteen thousand horsemen and one hundred thousand infantrymen, and began a battle marvellous and unheard of in all former times: among the Christians not one horseman or infantryman was wounded or killed, while among the multitude of pagans slain their number could scarcely be reckoned.

The victorious duke then departed and came to the valley of Demena. There he built the fortress of Saint Mark, returned to Calabria, and, coming with an army against Bari, which holds primacy over all Apulia, laid siege to it. [Col. 0779A] Having received it in surrender after a long siege (1068–1071), he returned to Sicily with a military force. He took the city of Catania and ordered Palermo to be besieged.

[AMAT. VI, 14–19; VIII, 13, 12, 13, 14, 17, 23.] After besieging it for five months [Note: [Col. 0779D] “Five months” is not found in Amatus.], he finally obtained it as he wished. Seeing, therefore, that such things had turned out according to his desire, the duke assembled an exceedingly great army and prepared to encamp before Salerno (6 May 1076).

When Pope Gregory heard of this, he advised Father Desiderius to seek peace from the duke for Prince Gisulf; but Gisulf would not even deign to give an answer. The duke assembled his army and pitched his tents around Salerno. On the other side, Prince Richard, coming at the duke’s request, began with various engines of war to assault it most fiercely.

Hearing this, Desiderius went to Prince Richard [Note: [Col. 0779D] Amatus does not mention him.] and asked him to come with him to Gisulf. When they had come, after much fruitless discussion, Gisulf rejected their counsel and swore that under no terms would he make an alliance with the duke.

At last, when the city lacked necessities for food, its inhabitants began to eat the flesh of horses, dogs, asses, and cats [Note: [Col. 0779D] That is, felines.]. A dog’s liver was sold for ten *tareni*, a hen for nine, and one egg, as well as seven figs, for two denarii; a *modius* of wheat cost forty-four Byzantine coins. When the duke learned of their want, he came in the silence of the dead of night, surrounded by companies of soldiers, to the city walls. Breaking down the closed gate with stones, he captured Salerno (13 December).

Once the city had been taken, Robert ordered the church of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, to be built there [Note: [Col. 0779D] The passage from “Once the city” through “entered” is not taken from Amatus.]. In it he placed with the highest veneration the sacred body of that apostle; but he reserved, for the protection of himself and his sons, an entire arm-bone, enclosed in a silver reliquary.

[Note: [Col. 0779D] He placed upon it this inscription: “To Matthew, apostle and evangelist, patron of the city: Duke Robert, greatest triumpher of the Roman Empire, from his private treasury.” Di Meo, *Annals*, VIII, 191. It was dedicated in A.D. 1084; *Annals of Benevento*.]

Then the duke, joined by the prince and accompanied by an army, came to this monastery. Received honourably by Desiderius and the brethren, and commending himself to their prayers, he entered Campania with greater determination to conquer it.

When these events reached Pope Gregory’s ears [Note: [Col. 0779D] Amatus, VIII, 32, 31: for Peter appears to have reversed the order of events.], he separated the duke and prince from communion and, having gathered an army, prepared to march against them. When this was reported to the duke, he quickly returned with the prince to Capua on 19 December. The duke established a siege before Benevento, and the prince one before Naples [Note: [Col. 0780D] Thus far Amatus.].

The Neapolitans, terrified by the prince, earnestly prayed almighty God mercifully to deign to deliver them from the power of that prince (May 1077). While the city was being assaulted with the utmost violence, Saint Januarius, Christ’s martyr, was often seen armed, running through the camps with other white-robed figures, by the prince and his army. Thinking that he was the archbishop, the prince sent to ask why, contrary to his customary practice, he was going into battle armed with lance and shield. The archbishop replied:

> “As you, most illustrious man, see, I have lain sick in bed for many days. Let him himself see who that armed man is; for know certainly that Saint Januarius protects and defends this city.”

But the prince, refusing to believe his words, did not cease attacking the city. During this siege he died after being absolved from excommunication (5 April 1078) [Note: [Col. 0780D] Amatus, VIII, 34.], and was succeeded by his son Jordan.

Thereafter occasions of dissension and hatred arose between the duke and the prince. For the prince, favouring Pope Gregory, accepted 4,500 Byzantine coins from the Beneventans and destroyed the forts which the duke had established for the conquest of Benevento. He then conspired against the duke with all the counts of Apulia [Note: [Col. 0780D] Angered because of gifts demanded at the marriage of the duke’s daughter; see William of Apulia, III, 498.].

When this was reported to the duke, who was then staying in Calabria, he returned to Apulia with 460 knights. He attacked and took Ascoli, Monte di Vico [Note: [Col. 0780D] Vico della Baronia or Trivico.], and Ariano; then he prepared to march against the prince by the River Sarno.

Meanwhile Father Desiderius, hearing these things, went to the duke and urged him to return to peace. Robert obeyed his admonitions and made peace with the prince. The duke then set his army in motion and laid siege to the castle called Monticello [Note: [Col. 0780D] Monticchio is in the Capitanata; Carbonara and Monteverde in the further Principate; Genzano and Spinazzola in Basilicata. I have searched in vain for Petra Palumbi.]. Having taken it, he likewise acquired Carbonara, Petra Palumbi, Monteverde, Genzano, and Spinazzola.

Desiderius, moreover, distressed that the duke had long remained separated from the bosom of Mother Church, went to Rome and began to ask Pope Gregory to release the duke from the bond of anathema by which he had bound him. Having obtained this, Desiderius, a lover and preserver of peace, went with the cardinals to the duke and released him from the bond of excommunication [Note: [Col. 0780D] At Ceprano, 29 June 1080, Robert, peace having been made, received investiture from Gregory VII.].

### 46.

At that same time, the bishop of the church of Roselle [Note: [Col. 0781C] Dodo.] came to this monastery and deposited there a substantial sum of money. When this was reported to Prince Jordan, he sent soldiers and ordered the money to be taken from the church treasury and brought to him.

The brethren replied:

> “The money [Note: [Col. 0781] Thus the Register of Peter; the manuscript has *pecunia*, ‘money’.] entrusted to Father Benedict we shall by no means give to any living person. We place it in the treasury: from there, let whoever dares take it.”

But the soldiers, hearing this and intoxicated by the devil’s prompting, took the money from the church treasury and carried it to the prince.

When so great, monstrous, and unheard-of a crime reached the ears of Pope Gregory, he would not allow the offence of such audacity to go unavenged. Fearing that, by the example of this deed, our church might again be violated, he prohibited the divine office in the church of Father Benedict and ordered all the altars stripped. He declared that in such a crime he could accuse Desiderius and the brethren of excessive negligence and of timidity deserving severe punishment, and that he ought to be more gravely angered against our congregation, were he not restrained by the affection with which he had always loved this place.

Indeed, he considered it more tolerable that estates and castles belonging to us should be given up to plunder and devastation than that a holy place, famous and venerable throughout all Christendom, should be exposed to the danger of so great a disgrace.

But not long after the office had been prohibited in our church, the right hand of God did not delay vengeance. For the prince, author of so great a crime, lost his sight after receiving the money [Note: [Col. 0781C] I have found this confirmed by no other witness.].

Pope Gregory, likewise sitting in council, decreed that if any Norman, or any person whatsoever, should seize estates, monasteries, villages, or possessions of this monastery of Monte Cassino, and after being admonished twice or three times did not make amends, he should lie under excommunication until he repented and made satisfaction to the church [Note: [Col. 0781C] This is read in the Roman council of 29 November 1078; see, however, Di Meo, *Annals*, VIII, 172.].

### 47.

In the same year (19 September 1080), Prince Jordan, of whom we have spoken above, following the custom of earlier princes, made a general decree for this monastery concerning all its boundaries and appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0782C] Published from the original by Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 184.]. By this decree he also confirmed more specifically to the monastery all that both his father and he himself had granted, exchanged, or restored to it: namely the castle called Fracta, Terame, Piedimonte, Mortula, Cucuruzzo, and Torre a Mare, together with everything that from ancient times had belonged to this monastery throughout all Liburia, with the churches, boundaries, and appurtenances thereof.

All these things, I say, with all their aforesaid appurtenances, he specifically confirmed to this place, under a penalty of four thousand pounds of gold upon anyone who should presume in any way to use force against this grant.

Two years later (24 September 1082), the church of Saint Rufus within the city of Capua was offered to this monastery by the same prince [Note: [Col. 0782C] Ibid., p. 188, from the Register of Saint Angelo. It had been held by Herluin, the prince’s chaplain.]. It had formerly been granted and confirmed by oath to him by those to whom it belonged by hereditary right according to the custom of the country, together with male and female slaves, tenants, books, ornaments, and every appurtenance, both outside and within. A penalty of one thousand pounds of gold was imposed upon those attempting to violate this grant.

In those same days [Note: [Col. 0782C] A.D. 1082; but the twenty-fifth year of Jordan, indiction VI. Their property—the sons of John, Count Landulf of Aquino—had been confiscated because “they conceived and took counsel against our life.” Gattola published both charters from the originals, *Acc.*, pp. 187–188.] Count Adenulf and his brothers made their offering in this place of the Great Lake near the city of Aquino, with all the appurtenances of that place, in addition to the offering which Prince Jordan had made the year before (16 September 1081).

### 48.

At this time Guinizo, venerable confessor and monk of this monastery, departed this life. Since the narrative has reached the point at which his virtues occur, it seems altogether fitting to append some account of them to this little work.

During the time of the perverse Basilius, Guinizo had been sent on the business of this monastery to Theodinus, then residing as a servant in the fortress called Bantra. Asked to remain that night in the aforesaid fortress, he replied that he could not remain anywhere outside his cell. Then Theodinus, intoxicated with devilish poison, saw the servant of God enter the church for prayer and ordered the church to be locked with the greatest care. He handed to his wife the staff which the servant of God had carried in his hand [Note: [Col. 0782C] She is called Marotta in the *Life of Guinizo*.] and ordered it locked in a chest.

But the Creator and Redeemer of humankind, who does not abandon those who hope in Him, sent His angel. Preserving the seals upon the doors unbroken, the angel removed Guinizo from the church and set him down at the foot of the mountain.

As the sun was already declining toward sunset, peasants returning from the fields asked the inhabitants of the fortress whether anything new had recently happened in those parts. They answered that they had seen absolutely nothing except a solitary man, barefoot and carrying a crook in his hand.

Hearing this, the utterly wicked Theodinus immediately summoned the priest and began anxiously to inquire what had happened to the man of God. When they searched for him in the church and did not find him, they were filled alike with great astonishment and wonder. How almighty God removed His servant from that church while its doors were closed remains unknown to all mortals to this day.

Whoever wishes to know more fully the magnificent deeds of this man and the miracles of his disciple Januarius should reread the text of his life, written by us about seven years ago [Note: [Col. 0783C] G. Henschenius published it in *Acta Sanctorum*, May VI, 451, from a Monte Cassino manuscript. See below, IV, 66.].

At about this time Gebizo, of blessed memory, left Cologne, his native city [Note: [Col. 0783C] For he was a German, from the province called German Francia. Paul was sent to Monte Cassino by the Empress Agnes.], came to this place, and was made a monk by Desiderius. He was a man surpassing in humility and distinguished by the brightness of his integrity. Since it would not be irrelevant to show in part, from matters committed to writing, what merit he possessed before the Almighty, let us briefly touch upon some of them.

[PAUL, *Life of Gebiz.*] Before his conversion he had had an especially intimate friend, named Ado, an exceedingly wealthy merchant [Note: [Col. 0783C] A trader.]. On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, while Gebizo was praying, the devil appeared to him, accompanied by an innumerable host of demons. The man of God asked him:

> “Why are you rejoicing, most wretched one?”

And the devil said:

> “Because I have now triumphed over Ado’s soul; for I have just received it among our own.”

Having said this, he showed the aforesaid soul bound like a beast of burden and being dragged to punishments [Note: [Col. 0783C] He thought the man of God was rejoicing at the punishment, since Ado had at last inflicted certain injuries upon him.].

Then the man of God took upon himself the burden of penance for the wealthy man and began to pray almighty God to deign to rescue that soul from the power of the ancient enemy. When night came, the devil appeared and beat him with lashes so severely that he left him half dead, saying:

> “Why have you dared to pray to God for one who, because of his innumerable crimes, has come under our jurisdiction?”

Yet for this reason the man of God did not cease praying, until an angel of the Lord appeared and said:

> “Up to now I and my companions have laboured for Ado; but give thanks to God, because he has now been set free and joined to our fellow citizens.”

One night, while he was sitting on his bed, which was before the doors of the treasury at the very entrance of the basilica, he saw the brethren standing in choir. As though incense were being offered individually, smoke seemed to issue from each stall; its streams gathered above the altar of Saint Benedict. Seeing this, an angel of the Lord appeared and said:

> “What you see are the prayers of the brethren. They are gathered upon the altar so that Saint Benedict may present them before the throne of Majesty.”

There are, moreover, many miracles concerning this distinguished man [Note: [Col. 0783] Not many years ago—that is, after the Neapolitan edition—an entire folio was missing here from the parchment manuscript. It contained chapter 49, together with a few preceding lines and not many more following lines. It is best to veil in silence by whose fraud this happened. Therefore I warn my fellow Cassinese not to trust everyone. Some come to us in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. ANG. He himself had supplied this from the Neapolitan edition interpolated by Laureto. To this we added the text of the Venetian edition, which, though altered in wording more than that edition, is otherwise of better fidelity.].

[Col. 0783B] *(Venetian edition.)* [Note: [Col. 0783B] The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

…miracles. Whoever wishes to know them should read the history of his life, written by Paul the grammarian and monk of this monastery [Note: [Col. 0783C] On him see Peter, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 36.].

[Note: [Col. 0783C] Written at the order of Oderisius; published in Gattola, *Hist.*, p. 174, and copied by our Peter in his book *On the Origin and Death of the Just Men of Monte Cassino*, 51, where he is called Ebizo. In it I find these words, illustrating the habits of our countrymen: “He found a rather spacious house—being, that is, in a vision—in which he saw a pyre constructed of great logs, as is customary in cold and especially hyperborean regions. For there country people throw whole tree-trunks onto their masters’ hearths, so that they seem to build a pyre not from split wood but from huge beams. Yet they place them crosswise, one upon another, so that certain openings are made between the logs, through which tongues of fire emerge and all the spaces of the house are filled with heat.”]

At this same time, by Desiderius’s command, the church of Saint Liberator in the county of Chieti was rebuilt in a very handsome manner by Adenulf, provost of that place and monk of our monastery.

### 49.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1079 [Note: [Col. 0784C] Domnizo also assigns this to the year 1077.], Countess Matilda, fearing the army of Emperor Henry, devoutly offered the provinces of Liguria and Tuscany to Pope Gregory and the holy Roman Church. From this arose above all the cause and beginning of the hatred sown between the pontiff and emperor. Therefore, when the pontiff found an opportunity, he deprived the same emperor of communion because he was usurping for himself the rights of the Church.

But the emperor, having taken counsel with the magnates of the empire (23 February 1076), crossed the Alps and entered Italy to make peace with the pontiff. For three days he stood barefoot before the court of the pontiff, who had then withdrawn into one of Matilda’s strongly fortified castles. He sought peace both personally, through the princes of the empire, and through the intimates of the apostle (January 1077).

The terms of peace were that anything committed by either side should be absolved, and that the emperor should thereafter swear fealty to the Roman pontiff. When this affair had been brought to completion, the pontiff, assisted by Matilda’s counsels, sent one of his men beyond the mountains and dispatched the imperial crown to Duke Rudolf, urging him to rebel against the emperor.

When this was reported to the emperor in Italy, he immediately crossed into Gaul and, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1081 [1080], began war against that duke. In the first engagement he was defeated (27 January), but later emerged victorious (15 October) and slew the duke himself together with his army.

The emperor, therefore, not forgetful of avenging the injury, gathered an army and came to Rome (May 1081) [Note: [Col. 0785D] These matters occur in nearly the same words in the Anonymous of Monte Cassino under the year 1081.]; but, since the Romans resisted him together with the pontiff himself, he returned without effect in July.

**Anonymous of Monte Cassino.** In this same year Duke Robert crossed the sea with 15,000 armed men and entered Thrace to make war. Emperor Alexius advanced against him with 170,000 combatants and was defeated (19 October).

### 50.

[Note: [Col. 0785D] “Henry—established” is taken from the *Anonymous of Monte Cassino* under the year 1083. What follows, however, concerns earlier times. Henry was at Farfa in 1082.]

Meanwhile, in the following year Henry assembled an army and came to Rome (1083). He took Saint Peter’s portico by force and destroyed a great part of it; and, without the counsel and will of the Roman Church, he established the archbishop of Ravenna as an invader of the apostolic see.

When this was heard, nearly all the people of these regions conspired against the Normans with one mind and one will: when the emperor should pass through Rome, they would all rise unanimously against them. When the Normans discovered this, terrified, they took counsel together to conclude an alliance with the emperor by any means whatsoever, lest, if he took possession of Rome, he should join to himself the Romans and all the surrounding peoples and they themselves should be driven from their homes.

[Col. 0784B] *(Neapolitan edition.)*

…miracles. Whoever wishes to know them should reread the account of his life, written by Paul the grammarian and monk of this monastery [Note: [Col. 0783C] On him see Peter, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 36.].

[Note: [Col. 0783C] Written at the order of Oderisius; published in Gattola, *Hist.*, p. 174, and copied by our Peter in his book *On the Origin and Death of the Just Men of Monte Cassino*, 51, where he is called Ebizo. In it I find these words, illustrating the habits of our countrymen: “He found a rather spacious house—being, that is, in a vision—in which he saw a pyre constructed of great logs, as is customary in cold and especially hyperborean regions. For there country people throw whole tree-trunks onto their masters’ hearths, so that they seem to build a pyre not from split wood but from huge beams. Yet they place them crosswise, one upon another, so that certain openings are made between the logs, through which tongues of fire emerge and all the spaces of the house are filled with heat.”]

At this same time, by Desiderius’s command, the church of Saint Liberator in the county of Chieti was rebuilt in a very handsome manner by Adenulf, provost of the aforesaid place and monk of this monastery.

### 49.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1077, Countess Matilda of Liguria and Tuscany, fearing the anger of Emperor Henry, hostile to her, most devoutly offered the provinces of Liguria and Tuscany to Pope Gregory and the holy Roman Church. This affair, therefore, provided the fuel for discord and hatred between the pontiff and the Roman Empire. Accordingly, once the pontiff had found an opportunity, he separated the same emperor from communion with the Church because of the investiture of churches.

But the emperor, having taken counsel with the magnates of the empire (23 February 1076), crossed the Alps and entered Italy to make peace with the pontiff. For three days the emperor remained barefoot before the pontiff’s court; the pontiff had at that time withdrawn into one of Matilda’s most strongly fortified castles. The emperor sought peace personally, through the princes of the empire, and through the intimates of the apostolic see (January 1077).

The terms of the peace were that whatever had been committed by either side should be absolved, and that thereafter the emperor, according to the custom of his predecessors, should render fealty to the Roman pontiff.

Afterwards, when the emperor wished to seize the pope and Matilda by deceit [Note: [Col. 0785D] Laureto appears to have interpolated this from Domnizo, I, 2.], the fraud was discovered, and the pontiff, warned and aided by Matilda, returned to Rome. When Henry had relapsed into his former conduct, Gregory excommunicated him again and caused Duke Rudolf to be invested with the imperial crown.

When this was reported to the emperor in Italy, he immediately crossed into Gaul and, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1081 [1080], began war against the same duke. In the first open battle he was defeated (27 January), but later became victor (15 October) and killed the same duke with the sword.

The victorious emperor, mindful of avenging his injury, assembled an army and came to Rome (May 1081) [Note: [Col. 0785D] These matters occur in nearly the same words in the Anonymous of Monte Cassino under the year 1081.]; but because the Romans, together with the pope himself, resisted him, he returned without accomplishing anything in July.

**[Anonymous of Monte Cassino.]** In this same year Duke Robert crossed the sea with 15,000 armed men to make war upon Romania. Emperor Alexius came against him with 170,000 [Note: [Col. 0785D] Lupus has 70,000.] men to fight, began battle, and was defeated by him (19 October) [Note: [Col. 0785D] At Dyrrhachium.].

### 50.

[Note: [Col. 0785D] “Henry—established” is taken from the *Anonymous of Monte Cassino* under the year 1083. What follows, however, concerns earlier times. Henry was at Farfa in 1082.]

Meanwhile Emperor Henry, in another year, assembled an army and came to Rome (1083). He forcibly took Saint Peter’s portico [Note: [Col. 0786D] That is, the Leonine City; see Bonizo in Angelo Mai, *Spicilegium Romanum*, VI, 278; Stenzel, *Frankish Emperors*, I, 480.] and destroyed it in large part. Without the counsel and will of the whole Roman Church, he established the archbishop of Ravenna as an invader of the apostolic see.

When this was heard, nearly all the people of these regions conspired with one mind and one will against the Normans, so that, once the emperor had passed into Rome, all would rise unanimously against them. Learning this and fearing the danger, they took counsel among themselves to make an alliance, if possible, with Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0786D] Di Meo, in the *Annals* for 1081, shows that this is to be understood only of this Principality, where Jordan allied himself with Henry. Yet the sequel shows that Peter himself did not think solely of the rest.], saying:

> “Once the emperor has Rome, we shall thereafter have no end from him; joined with the Romans and the others dwelling around us, he will drive all of us out of these regions.”

[Note: [Col. 0785] From this point we again follow the Monte Cassino manuscript.]

[Col. 0787A] After this had been discussed and settled among them, and their envoys had gone to the emperor on this business and returned, they finally summoned Father Desiderius. Since they could find no one else in those regions in whom they might have confidence, and since they had sufficient trust in him, they entrusted to him all that they had planned and urged him to go with them to the emperor. Although, for their own security, they were making terms with the emperor, they nevertheless came with the intention of exerting every effort, for loyalty to the Roman Church, toward peace between the pope and the emperor. When this was reported to Pope Gregory, he separated the aforesaid emperor, together with all his followers, from the threshold of the Church. When the Normans learned of this, all who had previously loved the aforesaid pontiff sincerely [Col. 0787B] and faithfully withdrew from him, in body and soul, from that time onward.

Meanwhile the emperor sent a letter through the counts of the Marsi to Father Desiderius, directing him to come to him. Desiderius gave absolutely no reply to the letter, because he did not know what manner of greeting he should write to him. The emperor sent him another, sufficiently threatening letter, declaring that, because Desiderius had neither come to him nor answered his letters, he was to delay no longer in meeting him at Farfa—unless perhaps he wished to repent grievously.

To this Desiderius replied with “the service due from fidelity” as his greeting, because he believed that he owed the emperor no fidelity. Having set out many reasons for this in the letter itself, he wrote that because of the Normans he could not come to him; but that, if the emperor perhaps wished to make peace with the Roman pontiff, he would find [Col. 0787C] some opportunity to approach him. Finally, in order to encourage him toward peace, he wrote that neither royal power nor priesthood could remain unharmed amid so great a conflict.

Angered by this and stirred to great indignation against Desiderius, the emperor strictly forbade the envoys whom he was sending to the prince to say anything to Desiderius. He commanded the prince to harm Desiderius as much as he could, unless he came voluntarily to the emperor. When Father Desiderius learned this, he informed the Roman pontiff of all these matters by letter and asked what he ought to do; but he received no reply from him on the matter.

Again the emperor sent Desiderius letters, insisting that under no circumstances should he fail to come to him at Easter [Col. 0787D] and celebrate that feast with him. He sent another letter to the monks on the same subject. But Desiderius, still delaying, put off going to him. After the prince and all the Normans were setting out for the emperor, and the prince was urging Desiderius to go with him, the abbot summoned the brethren and said:

> “Distress surrounds me on every side. If I do not go to the emperor, danger and the overthrow of the monastery threaten; but if I go and fulfill his will, I incur [Col. 0788A] danger to my soul. If I go but do not do his will, danger to my body threatens; and I fear at the same time that the angered emperor may grant this monastery—which is under his protection and defense—to the Normans, as he may the whole Principality. Yet I shall go to him, surrendering myself to death and danger. For I shall not make my life more precious than the most holy father Benedict. Indeed, for the common salvation of your souls and bodies, and for the safety of this place, if it cannot be otherwise, I desire to be accursed by Christ. For though I were killed a thousand times, no one will separate me from love of this place. I do not refuse to meet not only an emperor, who is a Christian, but even any pagan or tyrant, provided that I may be able to free the affairs of the monastery from his barbarity [Col. 0788B] [*Historia miscella*; Gregory, *Dialogues* III.5; II.32]. For Pope Leo too, in order to free the city of Rome from devastation and fire, met King Genseric, an Arian; and Sabinus of Canosa invited Attila [Note: [Col. 0787D] Totila.]—likewise an Arian—to a banquet, received a cup from his hand, and drank; and Father Benedict similarly received Zalla, a man of Arian unbelief, even in prayer, in order to soften him concerning the affliction of a peasant.”

Having said this, he commended himself to Father Benedict and set out. Yet, under God’s protection, he took such care that throughout the entire journey and all the time he stayed there, although many bishops and distinguished men, very many of his own friends, and the emperor’s chancellor [Note: [Col. 0787D] Bishop Burchard of Lausanne authenticated diplomas during these years.] met him, he kissed no one, nor did he pray, eat, [Col. 0788C] or drink with any of them.

After he arrived at Albano, he neither went to the emperor himself nor sent anyone to him; throughout that whole week only threats from the emperor were sent to him. The emperor ordered him to swear fidelity and become his man by the placing of hands, and to receive the abbey from his hand. Desiderius, however, courageously despised all these demands, saying that he would do no such thing—not merely for the abbey, but not even for the honor of the whole world.

When the emperor saw him to be so rigid and unyielding, he became very angry and ordered the prince to take his envoys, come with them to the monastery, and deliver Desiderius into their hands. But after the prince had frequently spoken much good to him about Desiderius and had brought Desiderius before [Col. 0788D] the emperor, Desiderius yielded so far that, in the prince’s presence, he promised the emperor friendship and that he would assist him, so far as he could, in acquiring the imperial crown [Note: [Col. 0787D] Thus the Venetian edition; Ang. reads *ac requirenda*.], provided his own rank remained intact. [Note: [Col. 0788D] For this being turned into a reproach against him, see the letter of Hugh of Lyons in Mansi, *Concilia* XX, 632.]

Since these terms seemed light to Desiderius in comparison with the preceding demands, and since he could not do otherwise, he consented and promised this to him before the prince. When the emperor still demanded that he receive the staff of the abbey from him, Desiderius replied that, when he saw him possess the crown of the Roman [Col. 0789A] Empire, then, if it pleased him, he would receive the abbey from him; if not, he should let it go.

After this, the emperor, having received from the prince a payment of great [Note: [Col. 0789] Or “greatness”?] amount, confirmed by an order sealed with a golden bull the dependencies of the entire Principality of Capua, reserving to himself and to the Empire the monastery of Monte Cassino, with all its goods and appurtenances.

Meanwhile, for as long as Desiderius remained there, he daily and frequently disputed with the bishops who were with the emperor concerning the honor of the Apostolic See. He contended especially with the bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0789D] Odo.], who seemed also to favor Pope Gregory. The latter showed him a privilege of Pope Nicholas, issued with Hildebrand the archdeacon and one hundred and twenty-five bishops, declaring that a pope should never be made in the Roman [Col. 0789B] Church without the emperor’s consent; if this happened, he should know that he was not to be regarded as pope and was to be anathematized.

Desiderius openly refuted both him and all who supported him. He said that neither a pope, nor any bishop, archdeacon, cardinal, nor indeed any human being could rightly have done this. “For the Apostolic See is our mistress, not a servant nor subject to anyone, but set above all; and therefore there can be no reason why anyone should sell her as though she were a slave. If Pope Nicholas did this, it was undoubtedly done unjustly and most foolishly. The Church cannot and ought not to lose her dignity because of human folly; nor should this ever be accepted by us in any way. Nor, God willing, shall it henceforth happen [Col. 0789C] that the king of the Germans appoints the pope of the Romans.”

When the angry bishop replied, “If those beyond the mountains heard this, they would all unite and become one,” Desiderius answered: “Certainly, even if not only these men but the whole world gathered together as one against this, it could never exclude us from this judgment. The emperor may indeed prevail for a time, if God permits it, and inflict the force of ecclesiastical law; yet he will never be able to bend our consent to this.”

With these and many similar arguments he disputed with them daily and very frequently, refuting them with sound reasons. He also disputed vigorously with the archbishop of Ravenna on the same subject and defeated him with sound reasoning concerning the aforesaid privilege. He sharply rebuked him for having involved himself in the papacy [Col. 0789D]. When the archbishop attempted, but failed, to justify himself with many arguments, he replied that he had acted unwillingly: for had he not done so, the emperor would undoubtedly have deprived him of his office.

Desiderius, having received from the emperor an order concerning the possessions of this place, sealed with a golden bull [Col. 0790A], and having obtained the emperor’s permission to return, came back to this monastery.

### 51

At about this time the venerable Hugh, abbot of Cluny, a man of most celebrated life and reputation, came in great devotion to the threshold of Father Benedict. The venerable Desiderius received him honorably, as befitted so great a man. By joining the fellowship of the brethren of Cluny to our congregation, these same venerable men decreed that the memory of the Cluniac brethren among us, and of our congregation among them, should be kept forever in death and in life. [Note: [Col. 0789D] In Necrology manuscript 47, 3 Kalends of May: “Hugh, abbot of Cluny [Col. 0790D], and commemoration of the brethren of Cluny.”]

[*Desiderius, Dialogues* II.4.] At that time, in this monastery of Monte Cassino, after a certain brother named Gregory had departed from this world, so great a fragrance issued from the place where [Col. 0790B] he lay that the sweetness of the odor suddenly filled the whole monastery. While all wondered, a messenger came from the infirmary and announced that the monk Gregory had died.

There was in this monastery of Monte Cassino a brother named Randiscius [Note: [Col. 0789] He is called Randisius in the *Book of the Birth and Death of the Just of Cassino*, 60, and in an eleventh-century martyrology, at 2 Nones of September.], whose life and character the Lord deigned to reveal at the very point of death. When, his allotted time of life fulfilled, he paid the debt of death, the brethren began, as is customary, to commend his soul to almighty God. As he was already drawing his final breath, he began, with such strength as he could, to restrain the voices of those chanting, saying:

> “Be silent, be silent! Do you not hear what great praises resound [Note: [Col. 0789] Peter’s text reads *resonent*, ‘may resound.’] in heaven? Do you not see the boys singing praises? For their garments and faces are like [Col. 0790C] snow. Therefore, I earnestly beg you by God: be silent, and allow me to hear this most sweet song.”

As he said this, he breathed his last.

### 52

At a later time Jannellus and Scifridus, on behalf of themselves and their parents, surrendered to this monastery their rights in the castle of Saracenisco, with its appurtenances. They received forthwith from Desiderius two hundred Pavia silver coins, subject to a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold.

In those days Desiderius, before Prince Jordan, granted to Geoffrey, surnamed Monio, for the term of his life, the castle of Suio, on condition that he should acknowledge that castle from neither the prince nor any other man, but only from the aforesaid abbot and his successors; and that he should accordingly [Col. 0790D] serve this monastery and its abbots in rightful fashion. At his death the aforesaid castle was to return to the power of this place. [Note: [Col. 0790D] Compare below, IV.7.]

### 53

In another year (1084), Emperor Henry came to Rome with an army and began by every possible means to besiege the aforesaid Pope Gregory, who had fortified himself against him in the Castle of Sant’Angelo [Col. 0791A], employing various engines of war. When this was reported to Duke Robert, who at that time was attacking the emperor of Constantinople, he left his son Bohemond on that expedition [Note: [Col. 0791D] He had already done this in 1082.] and returned to Italy with the greatest speed. Gathering a very large army, he prepared to march against the emperor for the pope’s liberation.

When this was announced to Desiderius, he immediately sent a messenger to Rome to report both the pope’s liberation and the duke’s approach to the emperor. The emperor then left the City, namely because he lacked military protection, and entered Civita Castellana.

Duke Robert, however, arrived at Rome with his army near the church of the Holy Four Crowned Martyrs in the stillness of a stormy night. By the counsel [Note: [Col. 0791] Manuscript: *consilii*, “of counsel.”] [Col. 0791B] of Cencius, Roman consul, he set fire to the City. The Romans, struck by the unexpected event, were occupied in extinguishing the fire. The duke at once hastened with his army to the Castle of Sant’Angelo, drew the pontiff out from there, and without delay departed from Rome. He led Pope Gregory as far as this monastery; and our abbot supported that apostolic man, with the bishops and cardinals who had followed him, until his death.

### 54

It happened, while this same Pope Gregory was celebrating Mass, that a man named John stood apart near the step of the altar [Note: [Col. 0791] Manuscript: “at the foot”; this seems to be a gloss.]. When he turned his eyes toward the altar, he was suddenly rapt into ecstasy and saw a dove of snowy whiteness, whose throat appeared golden, standing upon the altar itself [Col. 0791C]. It immediately flew from there and rested upon Pope Gregory’s right shoulder; at once spreading its wings, it protected both of them. It remained so until the mingling of Christ’s body and blood in the chalice had taken place. Then, gathering itself upon the shoulder as before, it descended to the altar, gently bent its head over the Host, and—without that man understanding what this was—returned with swift flight to heaven, its beak full.

Afterward the man returned again to his senses and memory, so completely that no trace of this vision remained at all in his mind. But on the following night, when he had given himself to sleep, a man shining like the sun appeared to him in the doorway in the midst of his house, with a threatening expression. At the sight, he leaped from the bed where he lay [Col. 0791D] and, compelled by excessive terror, tried to flee. But the preeminent man restrained him with an outstretched hand, gently holding his arm. The fugitive, seeing that he could by no means escape that hand, stood unwillingly as though bound.

Then a certain man, sprinkled with snowy white hair and clothed in a white robe, suddenly came to his aid. Wiping away his distress with a consoling hand, he freed him from the captivity in which he was held. In a free voice he fearlessly asked who this being of such power or splendor [Col. 0792A] was. He was told, “This is the sun of righteousness.” The man then said, “I in like manner seek to learn your name.” The other replied: “You ought by no means to know my name; rather, answer me wisely concerning what I ask. Do you perhaps remember what you saw yesterday while standing in church?”

He, whose mind had been impeded by forgetfulness, began to turn over and consider within himself what the elder was asking. Suddenly he remembered and related to him in order the course of the event. “Go,” he said [Note: [Col. 0791] Manuscript: *inquam*, “I say.”], “and report this very thing as quickly as possible to the pope’s ears, so that he may steadfastly complete the work he has undertaken through the power of the Holy Spirit.” Immediately he vanished from his sight.

### 55

At this time a nobleman of the city of Amalfi, renouncing the world and all worldly things [Col. 0792B], came to this place. Received graciously by Desiderius and made a monk, he most devoutly offered to Saint Benedict a considerable portion of the life-giving and salvific wood of the Cross, adorned with gold and precious stones and set in a golden icon. He himself had carried it away from the imperial palace at Constantinople during the conspiracy made against Emperor Michael.

After this Desiderius went to Capua. Seeing the workshops of the monastery at Capua already in ruins, he directed his mind toward its restoration. The former church having been demolished, he ordered craftsmen to be brought in to produce column capitals of marvelous workmanship. Summoning Benedict, provost of that place, he commanded him to devote particular care to the restoration of the church, setting every other matter aside. Obeying his command, Benedict built the basilica of Father Benedict, exceedingly beautiful as it is now seen [Col. 0792C].

This church is 98 cubits in length, 52 in breadth, and 40 in height; it has nine columns on one side and the same number on the other. At that time, when the whole land was drying up, the brethren prayed for several days to almighty God and Father Benedict on this account, and the Lord granted rain in the greatest abundance. And, so that it might be believed to have happened through the merits of the most blessed Father Benedict, it was poured out only within the lands of the monastery; outside them, not even a single drop of rain fell.

### 56

At a subsequent time (April 1084), Theodinus, son of Maynerius of Trivento, offered this place [Col. 0792D] the monastery of Saint Saviour, situated near the river Trasta, together with the castle belonging to that monastery called Pesclatura, and two other churches—Saint Mary of Colle Rotondo and Saint Paul of Petra Corvina [Note: [Col. 0791D] Both are in the territory of Castellone. Edited by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 191.]—with all the movable and immovable property of the same churches.

Likewise Count Transmundus [Note: [Col. 0792D] Perhaps “son of Atto”; ibid., p. 192.] of Chieti offered (October) to this monastery three castles under his own jurisdiction in the county of Penne. One [Col. 0793A] is called Arseta, another Bacuccu, and the third Bisenti, together with land amounting to no less than ten thousand modii and more.

At approximately this time the man of God Aldemarius, a monk of this monastery and a distinguished worker of miracles, died at Bocclanicum. Since the subject requires it, some of his miracles should be briefly recorded in this little work for the remembrance of those to come. Once, as he was passing through Boiano, one of the inhabitants of the aforesaid place, wishing to kill him, hurled a weapon; his arm became so stiff that he could in no way bend it. When he saw himself seized by such punishment, he began to beg Aldemarius to deign to have mercy on him. The man of God offered prayer for him and immediately restored his persecutor [Col. 0793B] to health.

Nor does it seem right to pass over in silence that, if any sick person drank water blessed by the hands of the man of God, he was restored with the greatest speed to his former health.

During these days Prince Jordan offered to this monastery the church of Saint Agatha near Aversa (22 February 1086). Constantine the African, as we have already mentioned above (ch. 35), had formerly offered it to Saint Benedict together with its estates, tenants, and all its appurtenances, according to the endowment made by Prince Richard, Jordan’s father, and according to the terms under which Walter [Note: [Col. 0793D] William, manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0793D] Thus in the privilege edited from the original in the same place.] his chaplain, who had restored it, had held it until the day of his death. A penalty of one hundred pounds of gold was imposed upon violators of this offering.

### 57

In this same year Duke Robert, who had long waged many battles successfully against [Col. 0793C] the emperor of Constantinople and his armies and had captured many of his cities, died while on that expedition (17 July 1085). His body was brought back to Italy and buried in the Apulian city of Venosa.

Before his death he left instructions that the arm of the holy apostle and evangelist Matthew should be carried back and delivered to his son at Salerno by his chaplains [Note: [Col. 0793D] Roger was then besieging Cephalonia. Robert alone could have been in Italy at that time.]. [Note: [Col. 0793D] Compare ch. 45 above.] But they, poor in property and poorer in faith, divided among themselves the silver casket in which the holy arm was enclosed. Then they went to Jerusalem and kept the holy relics concealed with them until the day of their death. As death approached, without the knowledge of their companions, they handed the aforesaid relics over to their servants. How the servants brought the holy arm to this place in the days of Abbot Gerard will be recorded in its proper place (Book IV, [Col. 0794A] ch. 73).

It does not seem unworthy here to append, in some measure, for the knowledge of posterity, a summary of the offerings of this duke and his wife Sicelgaita. Above almost all mortals of their time, they endeavored to love, exalt, and honor this place, Father Desiderius, and our congregation.

### 58

The first time that the abbot went to Reggio to visit them, the duke gave him 600 Byzantine coins, five cloths, and one small golden ship [Note: [Col. 0793D] In which incense is placed in censers; see Du Cange, s.v.]. On another occasion, he gave one large cloth, and very many gems and pearls valued at 700 scyphati [Note: [Col. 0793D] That is, concave coins resembling bowls; many Byzantine coins of this type were then minted.].

Again, at Castrovillari [Note: [Col. 0793D] Castrovillari, in Calabria, district of Cassano.], he gave him 600 Byzantine coins, two thousand African tari, thirteen mules with thirteen Saracens, and one large carpet. Again [Col. 0794B], when he fell ill, he sent here one thousand scyphati. From Gallipoli he sent 300 Byzantine coins and two thousand tari.

When he first came here and went to Campania, he placed in the chapter house twelve pounds of gold and 100 Byzantine coins; upon the altar of Saint Benedict, 300 scyphati and three cloths; 100 scyphati for construction of the dormitory; 100 in the refectory; 40 in the guesthouse; twelve pounds of denarii in the infirmary; and 100 michaelati [Note: [Col. 0794D] Gold coins struck under Michael Ducas.] for painting the chapter house.

When he came to Aquino, he sent here 500 Byzantine coins. When he captured Bari, he gave Desiderius twelve pounds of gold. Again, the second time, when he marched against the city of Tivoli, he placed in the chapter house twelve pounds of gold, and on the altar 100 scyphati and one large cloth. The third time, when he returned from Rome with Pope Gregory [Col. 0794C], he placed in the chapter house one thousand Amalfitan solidi and 100 Byzantine coins upon the altar; and, departing from here, I sent 190 *farganas* [Note: [Col. 0794D] I cannot discover what *arganae* are. But *sarganae*—perhaps so written by the author and corrupted by the copyist—are, according to Suidas and Hesychius, wicker baskets or hurdles made of joined twigs, suitable for monks’ use. Ang. More plausibly, it is conjectured in the new edition of Du Cange that they are a species of fish.] to the brethren in the dormitory.

On another occasion he sent here one thousand tari for fish; again one thousand tari and one small ship worth one thousand solidi; again 400 Amalfitan solidi; again, from Romania, he sent here one thousand michaelati.

Moreover, when his wife fell ill, she sent Saint Benedict forty-five pounds of silver and one cloth. Again, when she came here after the duke’s death, she placed in the chapter house 300 scyphati and covered all the tables in the refectory with tablecloths. On another occasion they offered Saint Benedict a golden altar adorned with gems, pearls, and enamels; a silk altar-cover with a purple urn, adorned [Col. 0794D] with pearls and enamels; a small golden chalice; a purple chasuble with fringe and an eagle made of pearls; one tunic of gilded *pannus persus* [Note: [Col. 0794D] A color approaching blue or peach-blossom; French *pers*, Italian *perso*. Du Cange, s.v.]; [Col. 0795A] four copes; four silk albs; eight albs of cotton *matassa* [Note: [Col. 0795C] Also *metaxa*, a kind of cloth.]; one pair of candlesticks of crystal, onyx, and silver; another pair of silver candlesticks with crystal apples; one pair of silver basins [Note: [Col. 0795C] That is, bowls or dishes.] weighing seven pounds; a silver lantern weighing eight pounds; a silver casket on the altar with niello, weighing eight pounds; a large ivory casket; two gilded silver cups with niello, weighing fifteen pounds, from which the brethren drank on the principal feasts; a silver basin with its own *aquiminile* [water vessel], weighing twenty-four pounds; a larger crystal pitcher; a silver dish with niello, weighing fourteen pounds; another dish weighing sixteen pounds; two others weighing ten pounds; one large silk cloth with one *roto* [Note: [Col. 0795C] Perhaps *rocho*; Du Cange, s.v.], three others equally large, and four smaller; four altar hangings for the altar of Saint Benedict [Col. 0795B]; two Arabic curtains which hang above the choir; and two other curtains, hung around the choir during Lent.

Again, when she came here after the duke’s death, she placed in the chapter house five pounds of gold and gave two pounds in the infirmary—one for expenses, the other for building a bath. Beyond all these things, and many others that can neither be recalled nor counted, they offered Saint Benedict the monastery of Saint Peter Imperial at Taranto [Note: [Col. 0795C] Compare ch. 44 above.], with the tithe from the fishery and the tithe from their livestock [Note: [Col. 0795C] That is, animals.]; the monasteries of Saint Angel at Troia, Saint Nicander [Note: [Col. 0795C] Both in the territory of Troia, at the place called Pesmontis Majoris; he gave both in one privilege, edited from the original by Gattola, *Historia*, p. 275, dated October 1080. Compare below, IV.10.], Saint Anastasia in Calabria, and Saint Nicholas at Sellectano [Note: [Col. 0795C] In the territory of Bisignano; see Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 230]; and a warehouse [Note: [Col. 0795C] What Italians still call a *fondaco*, and we a bazaar.] at Amalfi, with their appurtenances.

In the following year (1086), the same Duchess Sicelgaita, with the consent [Col. 0795C] of her son Duke Roger, offered Saint Benedict, by a charter marked with a golden bull [Note: [Col. 0795C] Edited from the original by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 192. The town remained subject to the men of Cassino until 1805. It lies on the sea, westward from Bisignano.], the place called Cetraro in Calabria, with its entire harbor, all its appurtenances, and all the tenants dwelling there. She had formerly received it as dowry from her aforesaid husband, Duke Robert, on condition that so long as she lived the place should remain under her control; but after her death it should return to the right of this monastery, free from any claim by her heirs or successors. A penalty of one hundred pounds of gold was imposed upon anyone who attempted to violate this offering.

Moreover, through Desiderius she sent Saint Benedict a most precious altar, adorned with gold, enamels, pearls, and gems, and, far more precious than all these things [Col. 0796A], wonderfully decorated with the most sacred relics of the most blessed apostle and evangelist Matthew.

### 59

In that same year (July 1086), Count John, son of Landulf of Venafro, approaching death, ordered himself to be carried with his possessions to this monastery. He made for us an exchange of his castle, called Cardeto [Note: [Col. 0796C] Register no. 492. The castle is now ruined, but remains under the monastery’s jurisdiction, with a large forest. Ang. Edited by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 194.], which Desiderius had long desired because it lay adjacent and was very suitable for us.

In exchange for this castle, four churches which we possessed at Venafro were given, together with all their possessions and appurtenances: Saint Benedict called Pizzulo, Saint Mary in Sala, Saint Nazarius in Piperozzo, and Saint Benedict within the same city. A penalty of one thousand Byzantine coins was imposed upon all who might wish to undo this exchange [Col. 0796B].

During these days [Note: [Col. 0796C] That is, twenty-eight years earlier; but the year of the Lord’s Incarnation is not written in the charter, nor could Peter, it seems, calculate it. It was issued in 54, in the year of the countship of Lord Marinus and the seventeenth year of the countship of Lords Dauferius and Landon, uncle and nephews, and counts; October, indiction XIII, at Trajectum; in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 193. Compare above, II.95.] Count Marinus of Trajectum, together with his wife Oddulana, offered Saint Benedict his entire share in the county of Trajectum and in the castles of Spinium and Fracta, subject to a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold against those seeking to revoke it (October 1059).

During these same days Count Walter of Lesina [Note: [Col. 0796C] No. 503. Ang.] restored to Saint Benedict the river Lauri with its whole fishery; the very mouth of Saint Benedict with all its fishery and fishermen, both within and without, together with its entrance and exit; and also the church of Saint Focatus and the church of Saint Peter, with their appurtenances. These had been wrongfully held by the men of the city of Lesina. A penalty of two thousand Byzantine coins was imposed upon anyone who attempted to revoke this.

At that time Leo, son of Symeon, approaching death, offered through the hands of Desiderius to this place all his movable and immovable property, both within and outside [Col. 0796C] the city of Bari, subject to a penalty of one thousand solidi.

### 60

This abbot granted to Count Landon of Trajectum a fourth part of the same county of Trajectum, which, as we said above, Count Marinus had delivered to Saint Benedict with his wife Obdulana [Note: [Col. 0796C] The notary himself is inconsistent in writing her name.]; a fourth part of the castle of Fracta; half of the castle of Spinium; and a fourth part of the monastery of Saint Martin of Acquamundula, except for the monastery of Saint Marinus with its appurtenances. The condition was that, whenever called upon, he should faithfully serve the aforesaid abbot and his successors therefrom; after his death all these things were to return to the right of our monastery without any opposition.

He also made a grant to Count Transmundus of Chieti, extending to the third generation [Note: [Col. 0797D] The usufruct is retained for us until then. Ang.], of the castle of Monte, the castle of Muccla, and the castle of Frisa, with their appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0797D] Compare above, II.88.]. The condition was that in the third generation the aforesaid castles should return to the dominion of this monastery.
