At the same time (24 September 1077), Peter, son of Gregory, consul of the Romans, issued an order for this monastery concerning the church of Saint Antoninus on Monte Porculo, with all its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0797D] It survives in Peter’s Register, in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 236; but Gregory’s offering has perished, if indeed it was ever made. Compare above, ch. 17.]. Gregory, consul of the Romans, together with his son Ptolemy, had previously offered this church to Saint Benedict.

### 61

Likewise the illustrious Gregory, because of his very great devotion to Father Benedict and, through him, to this place, established with his aforesaid son Ptolemy [Col. 0797B] that our ship, together with its master and sailors, should always remain free from every condition and payment of rent; and that our monks should never pay any market toll or harbor toll anywhere within the whole law and jurisdiction of his authority, by sea or by land.

He also then offered Saint Benedict the church called Holy Jerusalem, with all its appurtenances, situated in the territory of Tusculum. He did so under the same terms by which he had earlier granted and confirmed to this monastery of Monte Cassino the monasteries of Saint Agatha, Saint Angel, Saint Lucy, Saint Felicity, Saint Peter at Plegi, Saint Saviour in the Tusculan territory, and Saint Mary in the Vines. [Note: [Col. 0797D] See above, ch. 17.]

At a later time (12 December), Prince Jordan [Note: [Col. 0797D] Acting alone, during his father’s lifetime; his father’s privilege has perished. Edited by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 186; compare p. 189.] issued an order for Desiderius concerning the lands which our men from [Col. 0797C] the castles of Teramo, Plumbariola, and Piedimonte had bought from men of Aquino. Concerning the castle of Saracenisco [Note: [Col. 0797D] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 189.], Suio [Note: [Col. 0797D] 23 September 1078, ibid., p. 187; compare above, ch. 44.], and Torre a Mare [Note: [Col. 0797D] 18 November 1085, ibid., p. 192.], with their appurtenances; likewise concerning Lake Aquino [Note: [Col. 0797D] 16 September 1081; above, ch. 47.], the church of Saint Rufus at Capua [Note: [Col. 0798D] 24 September 1082, ibid.], and the monastery of Saint Agatha at Aversa [Note: [Col. 0798D] 22 February 1086, ch. 56]: all these things, I say, with all their appurtenances, he confirmed to this monastery individually by princely charters.

Count Berard, son of Berard, count of the Marsi, at that time offered to blessed Benedict the monastery of Saint Mary in the valley of Porclaneco, and the castle of Roscolo, with its appurtenances. [Note: There survives in Peter’s Register a donation of the castle to the monastery of Saint Mary, made by Berard in the year 1048, in July, indiction XV. Gatt. *Acc.*, p. 195.] John the deacon likewise did so [Note: “deacon” in the corrected text.], together with his parents, in respect of the church of Saint Bartholomew at Arce, with [Col. 0798A] its appurtenances. [Col. 0797D] In those same days the priest Romuald made out a charter for this monastery concerning Saint John at Conca, with its dependencies. Moreover, Count Nubilo of the castle of Vipera offered to this place the monastery of Saint Eustasius within that same castle, and the churches of Saint Barbatus, Saint Eleutherius, and Saint Hilary, as well as the monastery of Saint Eustasius in the castle of Ribza, with all their appurtenances (October 1074). [Note: Gatt., *Hist.*, p. 282.]

Likewise Andrew, priest and monk, together with his parents, made an offering to this place of the church of Saint Blaise at Limata, below the castle called In Carica (April 1063). [Note: Ibid., p. 266.] At this time (13 February 1065) [Note: Year 1064, according to the Florentine reckoning, February, indiction XIII [read XVIII], in Gatt., *Acc.*, p. 195, from Peter’s Register. Compare above, II, 90.] Roland, a nobleman of the city of Lucca, offered to blessed Benedict his share in the monastery of [Col. 0798B] Saint George within that city; his share in the church of Saint Mary in the Palace; the castle of Alflexo; and the churches of Saint Matthew, Saint Mary at Curte Vecchia, Saint Nazarius in the borough of Saint Martin, and Saint Martin in that same borough; together with whatever appeared to belong to him in the counties of Lucca, Luni, Pisa, Pistoia, Florence, Volterra, Populonia, and Roselle.

Moreover, Countess Matilda, duchess of Liguria and Tuscany, whom I mentioned above, established an exemption for this place: our monks were never to pay market-toll or customs-duty in the cities of Pisa and Lucca, or anywhere throughout the lands of her jurisdiction. [Note: Under the same date, ibid., p. 201. Muratori, *Ant.*, I, 957.] Racterius, son of Peter, from the territory of the Marsi, also in those days made out a charter for this place concerning his entire share in the church of [Col. 0798C] Saint Benedict at Civitella, in the place called Pascusano. Rainald, son of Obbert, of the city of Atina, likewise did so together with his parents, concerning Saint Peter at Morini and Saint Lucy at Redenaria, with all their appurtenances.

Count Baldwin, son of Oderisius, count of the Marsi, made an offering to this place of the church of Saint Urban at Cominium, and of Saint Victorinus at Vicus Albus, together with the lake itself; and likewise of the church of Saint Michael at Pratora, with its appurtenances. Robert of Belloprato similarly made an offering of the church of Saint John at Poto, [Note: Within the boundaries of Pontecorvo, at the foot of the mountain of Ponte. Gatt., *Hist.*, p. 313, from the original.] with its appurtenances (April 1077). Peter and John, sons of Antenulf of Ceperano, at that time likewise made out a charter of offering concerning the church of [Col. 0798D] Saint Peter at Fabrateria, with its mountains, plains, [Col. 0799A] woods, and appurtenances.

In those same days Maio, judge of the city of Berula, together with his parents, through the hands of Desiderius offered this monastery the church of Saint Stephen within that city. Moreover Oderisius, son of Lando, of Baduco [Note: In the Roman Campagna.], came to this place and most devoutly offered to this monastery the church of Saint Mary situated beneath the castle itself; another church of Saint Mary in the aforesaid castle; those of Saint Paul and Saint Michael at Mozzani; and that of Saint Quinzianus (3 November 1080). [Note: Ibid., p. 816.] John, son of Liudinus, of the city of Aquino, also made an offering to this monastery of the church of Saint Martin within that city.

Raul Novellus likewise at that time made out a charter for this holy monastery concerning the churches of Saint John at Pantano, [Col. 0799B] Saint Lawrence at Casa Palumbi, Saint Marina on that hill itself, and Saint Blaise at Farneto, with all their possessions and appurtenances. Henry, son of Count Henry of the castle of Cremona, [Note: Crema; see the charter in Gatt., *Hist.*, p. 284.] also offered the monastery of Saint Benedict situated among the appurtenances of that castle, and the church of Saint Ambrose in the castle of Aire [Note: “Tire” in the corrected text.], with all their appurtenances (1 December 1097). Punzo, son of Benedict, did the same concerning two churches, namely Saint Felix [Note: “Saint” in the corrected text.] and the Holy Trinity, in the city of Saint Urban.

Count Pandulf of Aquino [Note: Rather of Cominium, as he himself says; see Gatt., *Hist.*, p. 289.] similarly at that time offered to this place the monastery of Saint Martin on the hill of Arcizzi, with its appurtenances. At that time a certain Bernard, a nobleman of the city of Aquino, made out a charter [Col. 0799C] for this monastery concerning the wood called Matrelle, in the place called “At the Twisted Stream,” in the territory of Aquino.

### 62.

In those days also Guaifer, [Note: Compare *De Justis Cas.*, ch. 49; *De viris ill.*, ch. 29; Amatus, pp. 155–138.] a man most wise and eloquent, left the city of Salerno, from which he sprang, came to this place, and, having been received by Desiderius, became a monk. Established in this monastery, he wrote the Life of Saint Secundinus. [Note: Published in the *Acta Sanctorum*, February II, p. 531. See the Life of Saint Lucius there, March I, p. 304.] He also wrote verses in praise of the Psalter; an account of the miracle of the man who killed himself and was restored to life through blessed James; [Note: A fragment of the poem was published by Cl. Tostius in *Hist. Cas.*, I, 414; there see concerning his other works preserved in Cassinese codex 280.] a homily on the Advent; one for the Nativity of the Lord; one on the Epiphany; and very many other works, which we have judged superfluous to record here.

### 63.

Desiderius devoted himself with the greatest zeal not only to buildings, but also to [Col. 0800A] copying books. [Note: Very many of these survive, though not all: our library has more than once been plundered. ANG. Compare Giesebrecht, cited work, p. 54; Federico, Duke of Gaeta, p. 124.] For he ordered a number of codices to be copied in this place, whose titles are as follows:

Augustine, *Against Faustus*; *On the Work of Monks*; *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*; fifty homilies; *On the Epistle to the Romans*; sermons; the Epistles of Paul; *On Genesis according to the Letter*; his epistles; his *Pastoral Rule*; *On the Baptism of Infants*. Ambrose, *On Events in the Church of Milan*; *On the Patriarchs*; *On the Faith, to Emperor Gratian*; his sermons. The Register of Pope Leo; the Register of Pope Felix; the Rule of Basil; Jerome on Ezekiel, on the Epistles of Paul, and on the Twelve Prophets; Eugippius; sermons of Severian; the history of Anastasius; the history of the Lombards, Goths, and Vandals; [Col. 0800B] the history by Bishop Jordanes concerning the Romans and Goths; the history of Gregory of Tours; Josephus, *The Jewish War*; the history of Cornelius together with Homer. [Note: The ancient catalogue of Corbie manuscripts agrees in a remarkable way, in Angelo Mai, *Spicilegium Romanum*, V, p. XIII: “Cornelius’ book On the Trojan War.”] The history of Erchempert; Bede on Tobit; *On the Holy Places*; a larger Gospel-book adorned with gold and precious stones, in which he placed these relics: of the wood of the Lord and of the garments of Saint John the Evangelist; sermons of Pope Leo; sermons of Gregory Nazianzen; *Teaching of the Fathers*; a sacramentary with martyrology; another sacramentary; an episcopal ordinal; Walafrid on the offices; on the Rule; four books of passionaries for the whole year; two daytime antiphonaries, always to be kept in the choir; a night antiphonary; *Lives of the Fathers*; *Institutes of the Fathers*; Acts of the Apostles with the [Col. 0800C] Catholic Epistles and the Apocalypse; the Epistles of Paul; Chronicles; Origen, Gregory, and Berengar on the Song of Songs; John Chrysostom, *On the Restoration of the Fallen*; the dialogue which he himself composed with Deacon Alberic [Note: He is called Theophilus in the edition prepared from the Vatican codex, formerly Cassinese, by J. B. Marus, Rome, 1651, quarto; reprinted by the Bollandists and by Mabillon.] on the miracles of the monks of this place; another dialogue; a dialogue on the life of Saint Benedict; Hilary’s works on mysteries and hymns; Sedulius on the Gospels; Juvencus on the Gospels; *Medicinalis*; a Psalter; Cresconius on the Libyan Wars; [Note: Edited from the fourteenth-century Trivulzian codex by P. Mazzucchelli, Milan, 1820, quarto; and, corrected through his own work and that of C. Lachmann, by I. Bekker in the *Collection of Byzantine Historical Writers*.] verses of Arichis, Paul, and Charles; verses of Paulinus; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*; Justinian’s *Institutes*; his *Novels*; Terence; Horace together with Geometry; Ovid’s *Fasti*; Seneca; Virgil together with the eclogue of Theodore [Note: “egogla” in the corrected text.]; [Note: Giesebrecht corrects this to “Theodulus.”] Donatus.

### 64.

[DESID. *Dial.* I, 13.] At this time, thieves entered by night the cellar of our monastery, [Col. 0801A] stole from it meat, cheese, and bacon, and filled their sacks with these wares. But when they went outside and tried to lift the sacks they had filled, they were wholly unable to do so. Then, abandoning their burden and attempting flight, they wandered about the monastery enclosure throughout the whole course of the night, yet could obtain no possibility whatever of getting out.

In those same days a very notable miracle occurred in the church built in honour of Father Benedict in the region of Liburia. A certain brother had been sent to receive the land-rent from the peasants. One rustic, from whom wheat was demanded, filled a sack with grain in the silence of the deep night, put it on his shoulders, and took flight. But there was brought against him, by the true King of heaven, the sentence: “He who walks in darkness does not know where he goes, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (John 12:35). For he who had exerted every effort and all diligence to fulfil the commands of the prince of darkness, thinking that he was proceeding along a straight road, walked throughout the whole night in a circuit around that farmyard. When daylight was restored to the earth, the rustic came to himself and perceived how matters stood. He wished to depart with the wheat, but could not; he wished to remove the wheat from his neck, but was utterly unable.

When the monk had completed the morning hymns and was leaving the church, he saw the man divinely bound. After learning from him the entire sequence of events, he offered prayer to God and to the most holy Father Benedict, and swiftly freed the rustic from the bond that held him.

At this time, moreover, a very great famine occurred through almost all Italy. [Note: 1085; Anonymous of Monte Cassino.] Then Desiderius, after taking counsel with the brethren, bestowed food abundantly upon the needy.

### 65.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1085, indiction 8, when Lord Pope Gregory VII, of venerable and ever-memorable memory, was detained at Salerno by severe illness, he was asked, on the third day before his death, by the bishops and cardinals then present with Desiderius what he commanded concerning the ordering of the Roman see after his death. He replied that, if they could by any means do so, they should promote that same Desiderius to this office. For, besides being at that time a cardinal-priest of the Roman Church, he was endowed with the greatest prudence, singular religious devotion, and abundant friendship with the neighbouring princes. But if they could not in any way bend him to this, they should hasten, after Gregory’s death, to elect as pope whichever of the following they could first secure: Hugh, archbishop of Lyons; Otto of Ostia; or the bishop of Lucca [Note: Anselm.].

Having established this, he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, a Sunday, and was honourably buried within the church of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, after sitting in the pontificate for twelve years, one month, and three days. [Col. 0802A] Since the Roman Church had been left without a shepherd, and heretics and schismatics were striving to attack her like wolves, Desiderius, together with the bishops, cardinals, and religious laymen who had hitherto faithfully remained in Catholic unity and in obedience to Pope Gregory, began unanimously to consider how they might order her in the most fitting manner.

They therefore sent out and summoned from every direction persons suitable to this office, so that by unanimous agreement, with God’s grace and help, they might elect from among them the person fit and suited for so great an office. After this the bishops and cardinals came to the aforesaid abbot and began to appeal to him on the ground of the judgement of the aforesaid pontiff, urgently beseeching him to assist the Church in its perilous necessity by accepting the papacy. He replied with the most resolute refusal that he would accept the papacy; yet he promised that in every other way which he knew and could employ, he would hold himself ready for the service of the Roman Church.

On the day of Pentecost (8 June), the bishop of Sabina [Note: Ubaldo.] and Gratian came from Rome to meet him. He told them what he had discussed with Pope Gregory concerning the ordering of the Church. Together with them he approached Prince Jordan and Count Raynulf [Note: Brother of Prince Richard I.], and, exhorting them to the service and assistance of the Roman Church, found them most willingly ready for everything. He then began earnestly to press the cardinals to deliberate without delay concerning the person to be chosen pope, and to send letters to Countess Matilda, that she should endeavour to have both the bishops mentioned above [Col. 0802C] and all persons judged fit for so great an office come to Rome without delay.

They neglected to do this, and secretly plotted with Prince Jordan to impose pastoral care upon the abbot himself. By many persuasions they strove somehow to bring him to Rome, thinking that they could impose it upon him by force. Perceiving this, he began utterly to refuse and oppose it. Thus, returning to this monastery, he again began to exhort the Normans, Lombards, and all whom he could to the service of the Roman Church, and found many of them ready and prepared for this undertaking. But because the heat of summer was excessive, they deferred going to Rome until the summer heat should lessen and the unhealthy season should pass.

When, however, the prince came into Campania with an army raised for the purpose of going to Rome, accompanied along with Desiderius by certain bishops of these regions, Desiderius, increasingly suspicious of the aforesaid designs, refused to go farther. He said that unless Prince Jordan, Count Raynulf, and the Roman bishops gave him their pledge while he was present that they would bring him no force in this matter, nor permit others to do so, he would not proceed with them in any way. They refused to give it, and for this reason the matter then remained unaccomplished.

### 66.

[Col. 0803A] Nearly a year had now passed in this uncertainty, during which there was no shepherd in the apostolic see and no one to care for the Lord’s flock, while Guibert, the heresiarch, together with his followers was tearing apart Christ’s sheep redeemed by blood. Around the Paschal feast, bishops and cardinals of the Roman Church assembled at Rome from various regions (April 1086). They summoned the aforesaid abbot to come to them as quickly as possible with the Roman bishops and cardinals then staying with him, and with Gisulf, prince of Salerno, who had then come from the cisalpine regions, [Note: Rather, from the transalpine regions, whither he had been sent by Gregory VII; see his epistle VIII, 23.] so that they might jointly deliberate on the ordering of the Roman Church.

Suspecting nothing that they were by then considering anything concerning himself, since no one any longer mentioned him, he took all the aforesaid persons with him and [Col. 0803B] came to the Roman city. On the day he arrived, the vigil of Pentecost (23 May), Desiderius urged that the summit of the pontificate be conferred upon one of those persons who appeared suitable either to the others or to himself; but the whole Roman clergy and people absolutely refused to consent. Throughout that day a great multitude of all who favoured the Catholic cause, clergy and laity alike, came to him. Toward evening, all the bishops and cardinals, together with the other Romans persevering in fidelity to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, assembled in the diaconal church of Saint Lucy near the Septizonium. All unanimously began to entreat Desiderius with many prayers not to refuse acceptance of the Roman pontificate, and to implore [Col. 0803C] him by all things divine and human to aid the imperilled Church, placed amid shipwreck. Again and again they all fell at his knees, some of them weeping.

But Desiderius, who had long since resolved to spend his life in quiet, and who preferred to finish his days in divine pilgrimage—that is, the monastic life—[Note: ANG.] began in every way to decline, firmly promising that he would never consent. They pressed him vehemently and persisted insistently; he resisted more vehemently and opposed them more persistently, saying:

> “Know certainly that if you use any force against me in this matter, I shall return to Cassino as soon as I can, and shall never again involve myself in it in any way. You, however, will thereby make a great mockery both of yourselves and of the Roman Church.” [Note: I have corrected “Rome” to “Roman.”]

Since the hour was now late and night was at hand, each returned home. At daybreak on Pentecost Sunday (24 May), they all again came to him unanimously and began to repeat the same arguments, while he nevertheless persisted in his once-fixed resolve. Seeing that they were achieving absolutely nothing, the priests and cardinal-bishops said to Desiderius that they were prepared to elect whomever he should advise. After taking counsel with Cencius, consul of the Romans, he finally determined that the bishop of Ostia should be elected pope.

After this they asked him to receive in the monastery of Monte Cassino the pontiff whom they would elect, and to maintain him with all his household until the Church should be restored to tranquillity, just as he had done for the aforesaid Pope Gregory. Desiderius most willingly promised to do so, and invested them with his pledge by means of the staff which he held in his hand.

But when they were on the very point of deciding upon the bishop of Ostia, one of the cardinals suddenly declared that this election was contrary to the canons [Note: Namely, that a bishop of another see should be transferred to the Roman see. ANG.] and cried out that he would never consent. The others maintained that the circumstances and necessity required them to tolerate this [Col. 0804B], but could not bend him to their view. Yet, as the wise Solomon testifies, “There is no wisdom, there is no counsel against God” (Proverbs 21:30).

Immediately the bishops and cardinals, together with clergy and people, grew angry at Desiderius’s obstinacy. Seeing that they could accomplish nothing with him by prayer, they resolved to finish the affair by force. Thus at last all together, with one agreement and purpose, seized him, dragged him against his will and resistance, and brought him to the aforesaid church of Lucy, martyr of Christ. There they elected him according to the custom of the Church and gave him the name Victor. But because, as we have said, they did all this against his mind and will, he put on the red cloak, while they could never induce him to put on the white one. [Col. 0804C]

### 67.

At that time the imperial prefect, sent by the duke [Note: Roger.] and his mother, because of the hostility arising from the refusal of the bishops and cardinals—at the prompting, however, of the prince of Salerno—to consecrate the archbishop of Salerno [Note: Alfanus II; Alfanus I died 9 October 1085. Compare the letter of Hugh of Lyons in Mansi, *Conc.*, XX, p. 633.], assembled day and night upon the Capitol with some men hired by ill-gotten money and inflicted the greatest persecutions upon the elected pope.

After four days the same elect left Rome, came to Ardea, remained there for three days, and then went to Terracina. There he laid aside the cross, mantle, and the other insignia of the pontificate in such a manner that he could never afterwards be persuaded under any circumstances to use them; for he resolved rather to end his entire life in divine pilgrimage than to submit his neck to the most grievous burdens [Col. 0804D] of so high an office. Every day he was pressed with prayers and most frequent tears; the great perils of the churches were put before him; the ruin of very many souls was urged upon him, and God’s anger was manifestly represented as threatening him for their sake. Thus he returned to Cassino.

Throughout the course of the entire year, however, his intention remained so steadfast [Col. 0805A] that he could not be turned by any arguments whatever toward their exhortations and prayers. Nevertheless, the cardinals and bishops who were with him did not on that account desist, but began to urge Prince Jordan to hasten and go with them to Rome for the consecration of the same elected pope. He came with a great army to this monastery, but partly at the urging of the elected pope and partly through fear of the summer heat, declined to proceed farther and returned.

### 68.

In the following year, in the middle of Lent (7 March 1087), a council of bishops assembled at Capua. [Note: Compare the letter of Hugh of Lyons to Matilda, cited above.] The aforesaid elected pope presided over this council with the Roman bishops and cardinals. Cencius, consul of the Romans, was also present with [Col. 0805B] other Roman nobles, as were Prince Jordan, Duke Roger, and nearly all their leading men. After the council had ended, the clergy and laity unexpectedly pressed him again with many prayers and tears, though he suspected nothing of it, and for two days he remained unmoved.

At last, when the duke and prince, together with the bishops and other Catholic men, lay weeping at his feet, compelled by many arguments and prayers he scarcely at length yielded. By resuming the cross and purple robe, he confirmed the former election on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, Palm Sunday. He then returned to Cassino and celebrated Easter there. When the feast was completed, he went to Rome with the prince of Capua and the prince of Salerno. Having crossed the Tiber with all his company near the city of Ostia, [Col. 0805C] he was seized by a severe illness and pitched tents outside the portico of Saint Peter’s.

Since the Ravennate heresiarch, who had seized the papacy during Pope Gregory’s lifetime, held the church of Saint Peter by armed force, the church was attacked and recovered by the prince’s soldiers, with God’s aid, in less than a full day. On the Sunday after Ascension Sunday, many Romans and nearly all the inhabitants of Trastevere met him with the greatest crowd and solemnity. The aforesaid elected pope was consecrated according to ecclesiastical custom by the Roman bishops—namely those of Ostia, Tusculum, [Note: John.] Porto, [Note: John.] and Albano [Note: Peter Igneus.]—with many cardinals, bishops, and abbots in attendance, and was installed in the apostolic see on the seventh day before the Ides of May. [Note: So also the Anonymous of Monte Cassino.]

On that same day the body of Saint Nicholas, confessor of Christ, was brought to Bari from the city of Myra, where it had rested for 775 years. [Note: The history of the translation was written by John, priest of Bari, and published in Mosander’s appendix to Surius, p. 397. Since he is there said to have died a few days after the Council of Nicaea, the total number of years is excessively large.] The aforesaid pontiff remained in Rome for about eight days and then returned with the aforesaid princes to this monastery.

### 69.

[Col. 0806A] After a short interval, Countess Matilda came to Rome and urgently petitioned the same pontiff through envoys that she might be worthy to enjoy his presence and have audience with him. She insisted that this was her principal reason for coming to Rome. Bodily weakness compelled him not to leave his place; but because he had resolved, for the benefit of the holy Church, to expose himself even to extreme dangers, he undertook a journey by sea.

When he reached Rome, the countess, her army, and the other faithful of blessed Peter received him with the utmost devotion and honour. He remained eight days at the church of blessed Peter. Then, on the feast of Saint Barnabas, after solemnly celebrating Mass at the altar of Saint Peter, he entered Rome through Trastevere on that same day, with the aid and assistance [Col. 0806B] of the aforesaid countess.

At that time he held under his jurisdiction the whole of Trastevere, the greater part of the Romans and of the nobles [Note: Perhaps “of the nobles also”?], almost the entire populace, the castle of Saint Angelo, the basilica of blessed Peter, and the cities of Ostia and Porto; he himself stayed near the island of Rome, [Note: Compare Bernold under this year.] which also lay within his jurisdiction. On the day preceding the feast of the apostles (28 June), a messenger arrived as if from the emperor’s party and removed all the consuls, senators, and Roman people from allegiance to the imperial crown. Then the Romans suddenly arrived and captured everything except the church of blessed Peter. They could not enter that church at all, because the men of the aforesaid pontiff guarded it from above.

But because the multitude of Guibert the heresiarch was very great, those on Pope Victor’s side, unable to resist so vast a host of enemies, withdrew into Trastevere or to the castle of Saint Angelo. At midday (29 June), the Ravennate heresiarch sang Mass in the church of Saint Mary between the towers, for he had captured both bell-towers [Note: That is, of the basilica of blessed Peter, between whose towers was the chapel of Saint Mary.] by setting fire and smoke beneath them. When the sun was already declining toward sunset, those who had remained in the church openly descended with their weapons and returned. Thus, alas for sorrow! the apostolic and universal church of blessed Peter lacked every office, both nocturnal and diurnal, on the day which was pre-eminently its feast. Thus the hope of Guibert the heresiarch was frustrated, for he had desired to celebrate Masses there on the feast of the apostles.

On the next day (30 June), the apostolic altar was washed by the heretics and Mass was celebrated there. On the following day (1 July), all returned to their own places, and that church returned to the jurisdiction of Pope Victor.

At the same time, while certain pilgrims were coming to blessed Benedict for prayer, a certain canon met them. When they asked who he was, he answered that he was Peter the apostle. They said to him, “Where are you going?” The holy apostle replied: “I am going to Brother Benedict, that I may celebrate the day of my passion with him; for I cannot remain in Rome, because my Church is oppressed by various storms.” When those men afterwards disclosed this to the brethren, they ordained for the memory of posterity that the feast of so great an apostle should be celebrated with the utmost devotion and solemnity, just like that of Father Benedict.

### 70.

Meanwhile Guibert the heresiarch, who, after taking an oath of fidelity to his lord Pope Gregory VII of blessed memory and rendering him obedience for nine years, had seized the apostolic throne, saw [Col. 0807B] Pope Victor held in the highest veneration by all. He released Emperor Henry from observance of the oath which he had formerly made to Pope Gregory at Canossa, a Tuscan stronghold, drew him to Rome, and began with him to assault the Catholic Church (1080).

Those who were on Pope Victor’s side in the regions beyond the mountains, learning that the emperor was staying at Rome, prepared to rebel against him. Emperor Henry came against them. In the various fortunes of war, as usual, the struggle lasted a very long time, with plundering, burnings, and killings on both sides. At last the aforesaid emperor left forces behind to resist in Germany, took an army partly his own and partly hired or common soldiery, and for four years devastated Rome and its suburbs, as far as he could, by plundering, fire, and slaughter. Finally, having enthroned his Simon more by payment than by force (1084), [Col. 0807C] he received the imperial crown from him. [Note: He was crowned on 31 March 1084. In these years he did not enter Italy.] He inflicted a most savage and long-lasting persecution, in Rome and throughout the Roman Empire, upon those who neither favoured him nor communicated with him and his accomplices.

As a result, the churches of nearly the whole Roman Empire were laid waste, the Christian religion was almost destroyed, and twenty thousand persons or more were slain in various regions, with the support of Guibert, the “counter-pope.” He also expelled Catholic bishops, abbots, and other rulers of churches, men eminent alike in learning and religious devotion. In individual cities, monasteries, or churches he installed in their place wicked and unlearned men—one each, or sometimes [Col. 0807D] two or even annual incumbents—by the detestable traffic of Simon Magus, his earlier master. Since there was no one to resist with arms, he raged far and wide in plundering holy places and Christians who did not favour him—indeed, even those who did favour him—with the will of Nero and Decius, though with less power.

That same Guibert, who far more rightly ought to have been called Pope Madman (*papa Demens*) than Pope Clement (*papa Clemens*), built a lofty tower in his little town called Argenteum [Note: See Bernold under the year 1098.] as if for his own defence, awaiting simoniacal angels with whom he might fly and plunge into the most foul Stygian marshes. That is, his legs, by God’s grace in every respect favourable to Pope Victor, had been broken and reduced to nothing. [Note: See Clementine Constitutions, Apostolic VI, 9; Arnobius II, 12; and others.]

No one rendered him apostolic reverence or obedience except the emperor and his accomplices, or those who had sold themselves to him by oath, either permanently or temporarily, for the sake of avarice, which is the service of idols. Many of these, to whom his treachery had become evident, were not present when he celebrated his execrable sacrifices, knowing that he had succeeded none of the Roman pontiffs, but had been imposed upon Pope Gregory as a perjurer, invader, and simoniac in the manner described above. For the Catholics, who defended faith and religion with zeal for God, adhered to Pope Victor, most eminent in learning [Col. 0808B] and religious devotion.

### 71.

Meanwhile, in the year 1087, Pope Victor burned with an intense desire to confound, trample down, and crush the unbelief of the Saracens dwelling in Africa. Having taken counsel with bishops and cardinals, he assembled a Christian army from nearly all the peoples of Italy, entrusted to them the banner of blessed Peter the apostle, and sent them against the Saracens dwelling in Africa under remission of all sins.

With Christ as their leader, when they had landed before the African city [Note: Mahdia; compare the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, 1087.], they attacked it with every effort and, with God’s help, captured it, after killing one hundred thousand fighting men of the Saracen army. And lest anyone doubt [Col. 0808C] that this occurred apart from the divine will—on the very day when the Christians obtained victory over the Saracens, it was also divinely made known in Italy
72. The aforesaid Pope Victor III left Rome and came to this monastery; having associated with himself bishops and cardinals, he solemnly dedicated the church of Saint Nicholas at Pica. Then, intending in August to hold a synod with the bishops of Apulia, Calabria, and the principalities, he went to Benevento. Presiding at this synod, the same apostolic lord said:

> “Your charity knows, dearest brethren and fellow bishops—and indeed it has not escaped the whole world—how many adversities the holy Roman and apostolic see, which by God’s authorship I serve, has endured; and how often it has been subjected to the blows and repeated batterings of the money-changers of the heresy of simony [Col. 0808D], so that the pillar of the living God seemed already almost shaken and tottering, and the net of the supreme Fisherman, swollen by rising storms, was compelled to sink into the depths of shipwreck.
>
> “For Guibert, the heresiarch, who during the lifetime of my predecessor Pope Gregory of holy memory invaded the Roman Church, has become the forerunner of Antichrist and the standard-bearer of Satan, and does not cease to trample down, kill, and tear apart Christ’s sheep. Having made himself the instigator, persecutor, augmenter, and kindler [Col. 0809A] of injuries against Pope Gregory, who could recount the tribulations and persecutions he inflicted upon him? He stirred up conspiracies and plots against him; drove him from the City; being perjured and simoniacal, deprived him, so far as lay in his power, of his priestly office; set the Roman Empire, peoples, and kingdoms in motion against him; and—what has not been heard of since the beginning of the world—though himself excommunicated and condemned, presumed to excommunicate that holy pontiff. Even now he does not cease to defile the city of Rome with sacrileges, murders, perjuries, conspiracies, shameful acts, and every mockery of vices and crimes.
>
> “Fortified by the perfidy of Simon Magus and made into his very workshop, summoning accomplices in his wickedness to this most impious and execrable crime [Col. 0809B], and gathering the emperor’s army, he has become an invader of the apostolic see. Contrary to the precepts of the Gospel; contrary to the decrees of prophets and apostles; contrary to the laws of the canons and Roman pontiffs; without any prior judgment of the cardinal bishops; without the approving vote of the Roman clergy; without the appeal to the fervour of the devoted people—he has made himself, in the holy Roman Church, the head of all malice, wickedness, and perdition.
>
> “But when the mercy of almighty God had called the aforesaid Pontiff Gregory, after his labours and struggles, to eternal rest, and when, with the unanimous agreement of the bishops and cardinals, the provincial bishops, and the Roman clergy and people, they had set our insignificance—resisting and refusing in every way—over the apostolic see [Col. 0809C], he, without fear of the judgment of the eternal Emperor, has not ceased until now to persecute Christ and the sheep for whom He shed His blood.
>
> “Therefore, by the authority of God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints, we deprive him of every priestly office and honour; separating him from the thresholds of the Church, we bind him with the bond of anathema.
>
> “Moreover, you know—and know well—what deceits and persecutions Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, and Richard, abbot of Marseilles, have inflicted upon me. Because of pride and ambition for the apostolic see, which they had hitherto secretly cherished, after they saw that they could not obtain it, they became schismatics in the holy Church. Richard had indeed taken part in making our election at Rome with the bishops and cardinals; but Hugh [Col. 0809D], coming to us shortly afterwards, threw himself at our feet and, although reluctantly and with resistance, rendered us the obedience due to the supreme pontiff; he sought and received from us a legation in the regions of Gaul.
>
> “So long as they saw that the weakness of our insignificance resisted the election made and approved by themselves, they urged us in every way not to cast off the burden laid upon us for the Church’s need [Col. 0810A]. But once they saw us bend to it, the heated furnace vomited forth the flame of ambition long conceived. Therefore, seeing the unanimity of all their brethren resist them more stubbornly in that criminal cause of scandal, they immediately separated themselves from their communion and ours.
>
> “Accordingly, by apostolic authority we command you to take care to abstain from them and not to communicate with them in any way, because they have voluntarily cut themselves off from communion with the Roman Church. For, as blessed Ambrose writes (Sermon 50), ‘he who separates himself from the Roman Church is truly to be judged a heretic.’  
>
> [Note: The wording ‘Roman Church’ is not found in Ambrose.]
>
> “We further decree that if anyone henceforth receives a bishopric or abbey from the hand of any lay person, he shall in no way be regarded among bishops or abbots, nor shall any hearing be granted to him as bishop or [Col. 0810B] abbot. Moreover, we forbid him the favour of blessed Peter and entry into the Church until, repenting, he abandons the position which he seized through the crimes both of ambition and of disobedience—which is the sin of idolatry. We establish the same concerning lower ecclesiastical dignities.
>
> “Likewise, if any emperor, king, duke, margrave, count, or any secular power or person presumes to confer investiture of bishoprics or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the bond of the same sentence. Nor is this surprising, since the three hundred and eighteen fathers assembled at the Council of Nicaea excommunicated all sellers and buyers, saying: ‘Let him who gives and him who receives be anathema.’
>
> [Note: This is not found among the canons of the Council of Nicaea. It is uncertain whether Canon 2 of the Council of Chalcedon was in the author’s mind.]
>
> “Therefore, whenever you do not avoid such bishops, abbots [Col. 0810C], or other clerics—if you hear their Masses or pray with them—you incur excommunication with them. To believe that such persons are even priests is utter error. Receive penance and communion from no one except a Catholic priest.
>
> [Note: Perhaps *suscipiatur*, ‘be received,’ rather than *suscipiatis*, ‘receive.’]
>
> “If no Catholic priest is present, it is better to remain without visible communion and to communicate invisibly with the Lord than to communicate with a heretic and be separated from God. For, as the Apostle says, ‘there is no agreement between Christ and Belial, nor any share for the faithful with the unbeliever’ (2 Cor. 6:15); for every heretic is an unbeliever. A simoniac, moreover, because he is a heretic, is therefore an unbeliever. Although Catholics cannot have Christ’s sacred communion visibly and bodily because of threatening heretics, yet, while they are joined to Christ in mind and body, they possess Christ’s sacred communion invisibly [Col. 0810D].”

When these things had been confirmed by the authority of all the bishops seated in the same council, copies were made and circulated throughout East and West.

73. At that same council the pontiff became seriously ill. After the council had been held for three days, he hurried back [Col. 0811A] to Monte Cassino. Ascending to this monastery with the bishops and cardinals, he ordered himself to be carried into the chapter-house of the brethren, and under the most stringent anathema forbade any of his successors to dare to sell or alienate landed dues, churches, villages, or any possessions belonging to this Cassinese monastery.

Likewise, he forbade any monk to dare to make a charter or deed without the knowledge of his abbot; should he do so, it was to be void. He also decreed at that time that all monasteries subject to the authority of this our Cassinese monastery should provide a meal each year for this congregation of ours.

[Note: In the Register of Abbot Bernard, fol. 130 verso, there is reported a statute of Abbot Desiderius made through the assembly of the monastery of Monte Cassino concerning the meal to be paid by the Cassinese provostships. —ANG.]

After this statute had been established by the unanimous consent of all the monks, the aforesaid bishops being seated and confirming it in the same chapter-house, he appointed [Col. 0811B] as abbot Lord Oderisius, a very religious man and Roman deacon, who was then serving in this monastery in the office of provost (14 September 1087).

Afterwards, having summoned the same bishops and cardinals, he admonished and commanded them to make every effort to elect Otto, bishop of Ostia, as pope as soon as possible, in accordance with what his predecessor Pope Gregory had long before decreed. Taking Otto by the hand, since he was present, he delivered him to the other bishops, saying:

> “Receive him, establish him in the Roman Church, and regard him as holding my place in all things until you are able to do this.”

When these arrangements and decrees had been made, he ordered a tomb to be constructed for himself in the apse of that chapter-house. On the third day thereafter he happily departed to [Col. 0811C] the Lord, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1087; in the 579th year after the passing of Father Benedict. He had presided in the governance of this monastery for twenty-nine years, four months, and sixteen days; and on the apostolic see, from the beginning of his election, for one year; from his consecration, for four months and seven days.

74. Moreover, Pope Victor left at his death in this monastery the following ornaments. Almost all of them, after the dedication of the church, he either acquired with the brethren of this monastery or recovered after they had been pledged by others.

Five gold-embroidered patterned chasubles, and three without gold. Three gold-embroidered *diarodanae* [uncertain vestments], two *diapisti* [uncertain patterned textiles], and another citron-coloured one. Seven gold-embroidered purple vestments, five other purple ones, and two *exametae* [uncertain vestments]. The chasuble of John the physician. Six ordinary chasubles and four Lenten chasubles. Eight ornamented dalmatics [Col. 0811D], and eleven others.

[Note: That is, decorated.]

Five ornamented tunics and nineteen others. Five [objects] for incense. Thirty-eight gold-ornamented copes and eighty-seven others. One hundred and ninety-three linen albs and ten silk ones. Nineteen gold-embroidered stoles with their maniples; three silver stoles with their maniples. Eighteen other stoles. Seven half-girdles. Three golden *fanones* for subdeacons, and fourteen others.

[Note: A type of garment.]

Two large gold-embroidered shirts with their amices [Col. 0812A], and seven others of silk.

Textiles for the altar of Saint Benedict: one frontal with pearls, another frontal embroidered with gold; three coverings with gold and two others without gold; eleven large and excellent surrounding hangings.

Textiles for the altar of Saint John: five surrounding hangings and five coverings.

Textiles for the altar of Saint Mary: one purple frontal with gold; a covering with enamels; four surrounding hangings; four coverings.

Textiles for the altar of Saint Gregory: one golden surrounding hanging and four others without gold; four coverings.

Nineteen large dossals. Thirty smaller dossals. Seven door-curtains.

[Note: Dossals are curtains hung on walls.]

Twelve gold chalices with their patens—seven larger and five smaller. A golden communion straw with a bend.

[Note: A straw for drawing wine during communion.]

Two Saxon silver chalices and seven other silver chalices. Two silver communion straws. Two gold censers; two gilded silver ones; two other very large silver ones; and eight other [Col. 0812B] silver ones. One pair of crystal candlesticks; another pair of silver with onyx; another pair of silver with crystal apples; and five other candlesticks. Two large silver lanterns and one ordinary lantern.

The Gospel-book of Victor himself. The Gospel-book of the emperor. The Gospel-book of Pope Stephen. The Gospel-book of the empress. Two Gospel-books of Brother Firmus.

[Note: See Giesebrecht, *De litterarum studiis*, p. 49.]

The Gospel-book of Abbot Aligernus. Two sacramentaries with silver. Two lectionaries: one with a golden cover, the other with silver covers. The Rule of Saint Benedict with silver covers. A large silver casket with gems and enamels. Two silver reliquary chests. Two large gold crosses with gems; two other smaller gold crosses; and three silver crosses for processions. A candlestick; a ewer with its aquamanile; a Greek censer [Col. 0812C], another with niello; a ewer with enamels—all of these silver. A gold pyx with enamels for the Lord’s Body, and another larger silver one with niello. Three small cups of *perna* [uncertain material]. Two onyx chalices. Two pairs of silver basins. One hundred pounds of unworked gold. Two gold stoles. An entirely golden imperial *fanon*. Twelve imperial *scaramangae*.

A silver crown above the altar of Saint John with five crosses, and another Greek cross. A gilded silver crown, adorned with precious stones and bearing six crosses. Another crown above the altar of Saint Benedict, bearing three crosses adorned with precious stones. At Saint Nicholas, a silver crown and a cast silver cross. Eleven silver crowns which he found in the old church.

[Col. 0812D] Let these brief remarks concerning the life and character of the most reverend Pope Victor III, and the restoration and adornment of this place, suffice. Certainly, as long as the course of this world continues to turn, his praiseworthy merit continually increases, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note: The remainder is lacking in manuscript c.]

## Here begins the Prologue of Peter the Deacon to Book Four of the *History of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*, addressed to the most reverend Rainald, cardinal of the apostolic see and venerable and pious abbot of the most sacred Cassinese monastery.

[Col. 0813]

[Col. 0813A] Peter the Deacon, servant in due obedience, to his venerable father in Christ, Rainald, of ever-memorable recollection, cardinal of the holy Roman Church and venerable abbot of the sacred Mount of Cassino.

The learned authorities of ancient times once continually strove to recount events, in order to display the power of their wisdom: what things, how great, or of what kind had happened favourably or unfavourably in the Roman Empire. They wished by every means to sharpen and polish the style of their intellect upon such matters, and through histories long desired displayed before emperors the shining flowers of their learning. Their highest concern and great keenness of mind were that what happened in one part should by no means remain hidden from the whole. Yet, eager for flattering and empty glory and blinded by vain arrogance [Col. 0813B], they laboured to spread far and wide throughout the circuit of the world the perishable glory of their self-exaltation.

But, most blessed father of fathers in Christ, your studious venerability, wishing to weave the remaining portion of the history of this sacred monastery, has deigned to enjoin this task upon our insignificance—indeed with a like zeal of ardour, but with a different love. For they wrote in order to obtain praise that was perishable, transient, momentary, and passing away; whereas your beatitude, protected by God, requires it so that we may be precious, illustrious, radiant, and praiseworthy before almighty God in the glory of future rest, often and repeatedly turning over in the secret place of our mind the words: “Our soul shall glory in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice” [Col. 0813C] (Ps. 33:3).

Accordingly, bowing my neck beneath the command of your instruction, I shall begin to write the fourth division of our chronicle, which the most eloquent Bishop Leo of Ostia, prevented by death, was unable to complete as he had intended.

[Note: Concerning the time when Leo became bishop, we have dealt above, p. 553. But, at the urging of my most friendly colleague Wilhelm Giesebrecht, certain additions are necessary. Leo, bishop of Velletri, was already a witness in 1109 in a charter preserved by Albinus in Vatican Codex Ottobonianus 3057, fol. 139. In 1113 Leo, “a man worthy of honour, whom Ostia proved a father by life and merits,” dedicated at Rome the altar of the church of Saint Saviour of the Primicerius, as an inscription in Galletti, *Del Primicerio*, p. 364 testifies. In another inscription in Martinelli, *Roma sacra*, p. 258, concerning the dedication of the church of Saint Matthew in Merulana on 8 April 1110, Raynerius of Ostia and the other bishops there named cannot in any way be reconciled with the remaining monuments of that period. According to the account in Borgia, *Velletri*, p. 215, concerning the body of Saint Mark, Leo seems already about the year 1100 to have been bishop of Velletri; therefore, as I agree with Borgia, also bishop of Ostia.]

But when I see so many and such great men in this most sacred monastery, filled with the liberal disciplines, I succumb, overcome by the burden’s weight. For they are the salt of the earth; by their words human minds are seasoned, lest they fail through the numbness of weariness. They are *Hisperulae* [perhaps “little globes”]—

[Note: I do not know whether Peter wrote thus; for the *sohaerulae* which he means, see Exodus 37:17.]

—and lilies set upon the sevenfold candlestick, who wash away the dense filth of sins and bring men back to the brightness of eternal light.

[Col. 0814A] Set among such men, when I had abandoned as idle, untaught, and unequal to it the work previously imposed upon us by you, your beatitude, following in every respect the path of the ancients, began to instruct us in words such as these:

> “Do not hesitate to gird yourself for the tasks entrusted to you. Lift up your eyes to the mountains [Ps. 120:1], that is, to the precepts of law and grace, and from there help will come to you. For it belongs to Him to accomplish what lies within us as willing; for planting belongs to human beings, but growth belongs to God. He separates those hastening to Him from friendship with flesh and blood, and draws them to His grace, raising them from the earth and from the pit of misery, and seating them with the princes of His people.
>
> “Therefore, trusting in His help, undertake that which is commanded you by us as a duty of obedience. At the same time, diligently investigate and carefully set down whatever has occurred in this monastery or elsewhere in the world from the happy passage of Father Desiderius to heaven [Col. 0814B]. Add also, in their proper places, those things which in our time Christ has accomplished in the eastern region through the pilgrim knights: include the times, places, persons, and only the principal deeds and wars, from the time when those pilgrims, with God’s help, began that journey until they recovered the holy city of Jerusalem and rescued from the hands of the profane the holy and venerable sepulchre of Christ, for which they had especially set out.”

[Note: Perhaps *evenerit*, “has occurred”; but compare p. 759, line 17.]

When I had ventured to take this to heart, I attempted, according to my powers, what you commanded, trusting in Him to whom all things are possible and who, in His lavish mercy, often reveals to little ones things hidden from philosophers and persons swollen with vain glory. He also gives even to the unlearned an explanation that will excuse the faults of our ignorance through the authority of so great a father commanding us.

Since the succession of abbots from the time of Father Benedict down to the restoration of the church of blessed Martin had been recorded by the aforesaid Leo, we, taking up the beginning of our writing from the restoration of that church, took care to add to that history those things from the life of the most holy Desiderius which had not been described, lest the third book should seem largely mutilated. Thereafter [Col. 0815A] we shall commit to writing, as best we can, the most reverend and religious Oderisius and the remaining abbots who succeeded him.

It should certainly be noted that what is to be written has been drawn from the registers of the Roman pontiffs, Gregory VII and his successors, and likewise from the deeds of princes and dukes; sometimes inserting merely their sense, but at other times their words and deeds as they were written. From the time of Abbot Girard, who received me into this learned Cassinese monastery in the fifth year of my life, down to the present day, I have learned some things from the mouth of the venerable Abbot Seniorrectus, a man singular in our order in his time; some I have seen with my own eyes; and some I have learned from the reports of our elders and other trustworthy persons.

Moreover, the things that happened to our monastery recently, about three years ago, under our Emperor Lothair [Col. 0815B], I myself saw while engaged in his expedition and serving as apocrisiarius, or envoy, at the imperial court on behalf of this sacred Cassinese monastery; I was present at almost all the events and words. If I perceive that these things do not displease your most holy fatherhood, I trust that they will please others also.

For, as you know, I have devoted no effort at all to the liberal disciplines. But from my fifth year, when, as I have related above, I came to this place through Christ’s generosity, I have attached myself, as the Lord granted according to our knowledge and ability, to expositions of sacred matters and ancient annals. If anyone speaks against us on this account, judges me uncultivated and unlearned, and declares that I ought not to have undertaken so great a work, let him clearly know that the mighty works of our Redeemer are almost reduced to nothing when they are investigated by the cleverness of human reasoning.

For He who once loosed a dumb animal into speaking words likewise gives speech in the hearts of His servants as He wills, in the measure He wills, and when He wills. Therefore He cries through the prophetic psalmist: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11; Ezek. 29:21); and elsewhere: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with Him, and is before all time” (Sirach 1:1). James likewise says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach them; and it will be given him” (Jas. 1:5); and again: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above [Col. 0815D], descending from the Father of lights” (ibid., v. 17).

And Paul, the most loving servant of the Lord, chamber of the Trinity, vessel of election, and singular teacher of the Church, cries:

> “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge; to another the grace of healings; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as He wills” (1 Cor. 12:8).

Therefore, if any knowledge, any ability, or any good is discerned in us, it must wholly be referred to the Author of all good things [Col. 0816A]. For He Himself said: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matt. 10:20). Through Him, in Him, and from Him stands every norm and origin of wisdom, knowledge, and goodness.

And if perhaps there are some things for which I may rightly be reproved by wise persons, let them attribute these to our ignorance; but if there are any things beyond reproach, let them ascribe them to God, not to me. For, kept away from the most learned men dwelling in this place by necessity and the disturbance of the times, I have composed this small work in a style not as I ought. For, as blessed Gregory testifies, when the mind is divided among many things, it becomes small in each one.

Just as painters portray the dark forms of human beings on panels with certain colours, when they apply tints that are neither proper nor fitting, so history falls from the height of lovely beauty if the mind is shadowed by thoughts and darkened by the gloom of worldly pressures [Col. 0816B]. Speech accomplishes one thing, hearing another, and understanding yet another—the understanding which God inwardly pours into the human mind.

Blessed Father Augustine, outstanding teacher, organ of the Church, friend of the true Bridegroom, and temple of the Holy Spirit, left in his writings this saying:

> “When we seem to learn something, we learn nothing; rather, we remember things which existed in our nature before sin.”

[Note: Augustine wrote similar things to Nebridius, *Epistle* 1.7, and *On the Greatness of the Soul* 20; compare *Retractations* 1.8. But I have found these exact words nowhere, and do not know whether what follows is Augustine’s or Peter’s.]

In some persons, indeed, natural knowledge has been destroyed through the defect of nature; in others it has remained, though somewhat obscured. But the mind of the historian [Col. 0816C] cannot shine forth while it labours under earthly cares and profits. For when a man is shaken by the whirlwinds of the world, his mind is shaken as well; and when he is at rest, it too rests—just as it naturally happens with fire when it is covered round about with straw and no breath of air is stirred: it neither consumes what covers it nor is utterly extinguished. But if it is moved ever so slightly, it immediately rises into flame.

Likewise, a mind covered by diverse cares can neither shine out in the adornment of speech nor produce anything splendid or finely adorned. For I, whom neither grammatical learning, nor the glory of eloquence, nor the expertise of the wise adorns, but only natural understanding—which Jesus Christ [Col. 0816D], my God and Lord, has poured into our soul and mind while restoring it by His customary mercy—shall endeavour, according to the command of your holiness and the example of the widow offering two small coins in the Temple, to offer your most holy religiousness what I can.

And although not purely, elegantly, ornamentally, or beautifully, I shall nevertheless endeavour to offer a small, turbid, and meagre libation. Therefore, Rainald, most blessed father in Christ and father of fathers, the sole glory in the world of Levitical wisdom and [Col. 0817A] monastic lineage,

[Note: I have corrected the reading thus; manuscript c has *levitici*.] you who have judged us worthy to choose for so great a work: if it please you, correct it with your polished and splendid speech. Attend not to the weakness of simple language, but to the history, most useful for our monastery.

For history is the witness of times, the register of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life, the messenger of ancient times, and the norm of all good things.

[Note: See Cicero, *On the Orator* 2.9.36.]

It is fitting for you to refine it, for the mercy of the heavenly King has made you the chariot and [Col. 0818A] charioteer of spiritual Jerusalem, Benedict’s vicar and abbot of abbots. Yet I earnestly beg that in this work you do not seek syllogisms of words or the trappings of rhetoricians, but rather, examining it carefully with the pious eye of the heart, strive to amend, correct, and cut away what is superfluous.

Now may Christ the Lord be the beginning and end of our discourse: He who is the Word, light, beauty, splendour, wisdom, and power of the Father.

*Here ends the Prologue.*

## Here begin the chapters of Book Four of the *History of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*.

On Pope Urban healed by Saint Benedict. 6. On the donation of Saint Mary in Luco, Saint Nicholas of the Soran Valley, the castle of Acquafondata, and Saint Stephen at Rivo Vivo. 7. On the castle of Suio. 8. On the dedication of the church of Saint Martin and the death of Duchess Sichelgaita. 9. How the men of San Germano were often rebellious, and on the building of the fortress of Janula. 57. Here end the chapter-headings of Book Four.

BOOK FOUR BEGINS.

[Col. 0823]

[Col. 0823A] ODERISIUS, the thirty-eighth abbot of this monastery, sat for eighteen years, two months, and eighteen days.

1. Descended by blood from the counts of the Marsi, he was received in his very childhood into this monastery of Cassino by Abbot Richerius, of revered memory [Note: [Col. 0823B] Cf. Book III, ch. 14.], and clothed with the habit of holy life. The aforesaid abbot, seeing that he despised worldly luxury, devoted himself to sacred reading, earnestly sought the contemplative life, and was an outstanding follower of the regular life, foretold that he would become abbot of Cassino. He had been appointed provost of this place by his predecessor Desiderius, of holy and ever-venerable memory, who was also Pope Victor. When this pontiff, as we have related above (Book III, ch. 73), had come to this place seriously ill [Col. 0823B], he ordered himself to be carried on a bed into the chapter-house of the brethren. There, in the presence of the bishops and cardinals accompanying him, he admonished the brethren to choose for themselves an abbot from that very community, as the Rule of Blessed Benedict prescribes [Note: [Col. 0824B] Ch. 64.]. Having taken counsel, the brethren unanimously declared Oderisius worthy to receive so great an office and chose him (1087, 14 September [Col. 0824A]). When they reported this to Pope Victor, he highly approved both their will and their election. He immediately had Oderisius summoned; though wholly unwilling and resisting, opposing it with all the strength he could, declaring as loudly as he could that he was weak and did not know how to govern so great an office, and beseeching him by God himself not to do this [Note: [Col. 0823] I have corrected *obstantem* to *obtestantem*, on the suggestion of V. D. C. L. Grotefend.], the pope invested him with the abbacy by staff and Rule.

2. After the death of the aforesaid pontiff, immense grief and despair seized everyone of our party; they scarcely knew what they ought to do or how they should take charge of the Church. Therefore, after the aforesaid bishops had scattered in every direction, numerous and frequent messengers and envoys of the Romans, of those beyond the mountains, and of Countess Matilda were sent to those same bishops. They urged and begged them alike [Col. 0824B] to attend to the ordering of the Roman Church and, assembling in one place, to strive to make a head for Christendom. With God’s help, the members would not fail the head; but unless it had a shepherd, the Church would easily and soon fall and be confounded.

At length, therefore, having again assembled from all quarters, together with our Abbot Oderisius they sent letters to the Roman clerics and laymen faithful to Saint Peter, asking that as many as could do so should come to Terracina in the first week of Lent (1088); and that those unable to come should represent their assent, by their own letters, in the person whom they themselves would elect by a united vote. Likewise they sent letters to all bishops and abbots dwelling throughout Campania, the Principality, and Apulia, asking that whoever could do so without canonical excuse should come in person to the stated place and time; and that those unable to do so should make every effort to transmit their agreement either through suitable persons or at least by letters.

This was done; and on the Wednesday of the first week of Lent, namely the eighth day before the Ides of March, they assembled at Terracina, a city of Campania: with the Roman bishops and cardinals named above [Col. 0825B], and with our Abbot Oderisius, there were forty archbishops, bishops, and abbots from various regions. From the city of Rome, John, bishop of Porto, brought in writing the embassy and unanimous consent of all cardinals and clerics favourable to the Catholic party alone; Benedict the prefect brought that of all faithful laymen. Some of the envoys from beyond the mountains and of Countess Matilda were also present, urgently beseeching them to devote themselves, with the aid and grace of the Holy Spirit, to the matter for which they had assembled, so that they might be able to bring joyful news to those by whom they had been sent.

On the following day (9 March), all met together in the episcopal residence of the said city, in the church of the blessed prince of the apostles and Saint Caesarius, the deacon of Christ [Col. 0825C]. When they had taken their seats, the bishop of Tusculum [Note: [Col. 0825D] John.] rose in their midst and set out in order everything which Pope Gregory had earlier decreed concerning the ordering of the Church, and which Pope Victor had decreed later; he also stated the reason why all had then assembled in the same place. Then the bishop of Porto and Benedict the prefect rose and likewise reported the embassy and agreement, both of the faithful clerics and of the faithful laymen from Rome, concerning this business: namely, that whomever they should then unanimously promote to this office, all would accept by equal and like consent as one to be established in the Apostolic See.

When the abbot of this monastery, the archbishop of Capua, and finally all those assembled had approved what had been done and said as good and right [Col. 0825D], and had earnestly implored almighty God with many prayers to deign at last to regard and relieve the misery and affliction of the Church, they finally resolved by common counsel that during the following three days—Thursday, Friday, and Saturday—they should specially observe a three-day fast in abstinence, and by continual prayers, almsgiving, and supplication seek that God would reveal to them a person worthy of so great a dignity.

Accordingly, on Sunday (1088, 12 March) [Col. 0826A], very early, they all assembled again in the same church. After discussing some matters among themselves concerning this affair, the three cardinal bishops who headed that council—the bishops of Porto, Tusculum, and Albano [Note: [Col. 0825D] Peter.]—rose and ascended the pulpit. Silence having been made, they declared with one voice that Otto, bishop, pleased them as the man to be elected Roman pontiff. When, as was customary, they asked whether this also pleased all the others, suddenly, in remarkable and complete unanimity, all cried aloud that it pleased them and unanimously proclaimed him worthy to be pope of the Apostolic See.

Then, when the bishop of Albano declared that it pleased them for him to be called Urban, all immediately rose, removed his woollen cloak, and clothed him in purple. With acclamation and invocation of the Holy Spirit, they led him to the altar of Saint Peter the Apostle and set him upon the pontifical throne [Col. 0826B], on the fourth day before the Ides of March. Mass having thus been solemnly celebrated by the same pontiff, all returned to their own homes rejoicing and giving thanks to God. But enough of these matters for now; let us describe how our abbot demolished the old workshops and built new ones.

3. Seeing, then, that Desiderius’s renewal of the monastery had prospered according to his wish, Oderisius zealously set about renewing the workshops that remained from the old buildings. He began by demolishing from the foundations the house for the sick which his predecessor Desiderius had long before constructed, at great expense and effort, together with a bathhouse [Col. 0826C]. Taking the opportunity to enlarge the monastery, he made the infirmary itself larger and better. Finally, building it on the slope of the mountain’s side, he extended it to a length of [Note: [Col. 0826C] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] cubits, a breadth of [Note: [Col. 0826C] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] cubits, and raised it to a height of [Note: [Col. 0826C] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] cubits.

This building, far more beautiful and stronger than the former one, was splendidly roofed with tiles and decorated by the work of painters; on its eastern side it had [Note: [Col. 0826C] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] windows. At its end he established a most beautiful chamber for the abbot. Beside it he also built the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0826D] Cf. above, col. 763.], of [Note: [Col. 0826C] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] cubits in length, [Note: [Col. 0826C] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] in breadth, and [Note: [Col. 0826C] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] in height. Above, it was marvellously ceiled with beams and boards and roofed with tiles; its surrounding walls were decorated with most beautiful figures [Col. 0826D]. The excellence, solidity, and manifold variety of marbles laid in its pavement are evident to every beholder. He enclosed the circuit of the choir with large slabs of two marbles [Note: [Col. 0825D] Or perhaps: of different marbles?]. Moreover, he installed two windows in the apse; in the façade, [Note: [Col. 0826D] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] on one side and [Note: [Col. 0826D] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] on the other. This church adjoins, at one end of its apse, the house of the most holy Father Benedict, and at the other end the infirmary.

Before the front of this same church [Col. 0827A], he made a cistern with arched masonry. On its northern side he built a cemetery, [Note: [Col. 0827A] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] cubits in length, [Note: [Col. 0827A] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] in breadth, and [Note: [Col. 0827A] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] in height, and roofed it with tiles. On the inner side beside the infirmary, he constructed a kitchen, a bathhouse, and a cistern of very beautiful workmanship. There too he raised the infirmary cloister upon [Note: [Col. 0827A] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] little marble columns, decorated it with paintings, and roofed it with tiles.

When this was completed, the exceedingly energetic man delayed in nothing. Near the atrium of the greater church, he built a palace in which distinguished persons might lodge, [Note: [Col. 0827A] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] cubits in length, [Note: [Col. 0827A] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] in breadth, and [Note: [Col. 0827A] The figures corresponding to these measurements are missing in Migne.] in height. He roofed it with beams and tiles and also ordered a cistern to be made beside it with arched masonry [Col. 0827B].

4. At this same time there was in this monastery a brother named Majo. The present narrative sets forth how he was killed by the devil and how he was rescued by the most holy Father Benedict. While he was living in the infirmary, worn out by old age, at the Nativity of the Lord he went out to the privies because of a bodily need. The devil appeared to him in human form and said:

> “I know where you are going; but, worn out as you are by enfeebling old age, you cannot make your way there through the darkness of night without assistance. Follow me; I shall be your guide on the journey.”

When the aforesaid brother heard this, thinking him a man rather than the devil, he began to follow him. When they reached the large window situated in the middle of the palace [Col. 0827C], the ancient enemy set the old man in that window, hurled him down from it, and killed him. The brothers searched for him throughout the night but did not find him. While they were looking everywhere and could not find him, a monk came to that same window, saw him dead, and showed the brothers where he lay.

On the following day, the same abbot exhorted the brethren with prayers to knock at the gate of eternal justice, that it might deign to reveal how or in what manner the aforesaid brother had departed from this world. Then the deceased man appeared in a vision to a certain brother and told him what had been done to him. He added that, after his death, the devil led him along a road full of coals and repeatedly rolled him in that fire; but Father Benedict at once came, took him from the power of the demons [Col. 0827D], and joined him to his own company.

Then the aforesaid abbot, together with the brothers, gave thanks to God for the deliverance of that soul. He decreed that whenever brethren died, an equal number of poor persons should be added to the washing of the guests’ feet until the thirtieth day; and that one further poor person should be added for the soul of his predecessor Desiderius. He also decreed that, whenever the brethren rise from chapter, they should always sing four psalms for the dead; and that, until the thirtieth day, as many psalms from the Songs of Ascents should be added to those four as there were deceased brethren [Col. 0828A]. Moreover, throughout the year, every Friday, as soon as the Mass for the dead has ended, they should proceed chanting psalms to the cemetery; having prayed there, they should afterwards dismiss chapter according to custom.

5. In these days [Note: [Col. 0827D] The year is 1091, if the bull of Urban II that reports these things and is dated at Capua, 1 April 1091, is genuine. It was most recently published by Tosti, *Hist. Cas.*, II, 83.], when the aforesaid Pope Urban came to this place, he was gravely afflicted by his habitual pain in the side. On the vigil of Father Benedict [Col. 0828B] (20 March), while he was tormented by the same illness and doubted whether Benedict’s body was present there, the saint visibly appeared to him and said:

> “Why do you doubt the presence of my body?”

The pontiff said to him, “Who are you?” And the saint replied:

> “I am Brother Benedict. Since you doubted that I rested in this place, let this be a sign to you, that you may doubt it no longer and may believe with complete certainty that I rest in this monastery of Cassino. As soon as the call for the nocturnal synaxis has sounded, you shall immediately be well.”

Having spoken thus, he disappeared. When the hour came, the pontiff was healed. He summoned Abbot Oderisius and said:

> “I confess that until now I doubted the presence of Blessed Benedict’s body. But because he visibly healed me this night and showed me that his body and that of his sister [Col. 0828C] most certainly rest here, let us rise and render the greatest praises to God.”

Having said this, he set out in order what Father Benedict had revealed to him. How great the joy and exultation of spirit felt by all at the recovery of so great a pontiff was, I omit to relate, because almost all who saw it are still alive.

6. At that time (1 May 1089), Gentilis [Note: [Col. 0827D] On the counts of the Marsi. Published by Gattola, *Hist.*, [Col. 0828D] p. 248. Cf. above, III, 17.], son of Count Baldwin, together with his nephew Transmund, offered Blessed Benedict the monastery of Saint Mary in Luco, with all its movable and immovable property; and the churches of Saint Nicholas in the Soran Valley, Saint Stephen at Rivo Vivo, Saint Restituta, Saint Mary at Morrei, and Saint Mary at Collelongo, with all their dependencies [Col. 0828D].

For that reason [Note: [Col. 0827D] “Moreover.”], Morinus [Note: [Col. 0828D] “I am Hugh, who am also called Count Morinus.” Gattola, *Acc.*, p. 201; see above, II, 37.], count of Venafro, offered Blessed Benedict the castle of Acquafondata. This castle, indeed—as the imperial charters declare—is known to have been situated from ancient times within the boundaries of this monastery. He gave it with all its dependencies [Col. 0829A], under a penalty of one thousand bezants. For this castle the same abbot paid him 115 pounds. (July.)

7. At the following time [Note: [Col. 0829D] Here the times must be especially confused. For all the letters and decrees of Urban II from the Ides of October 1088 onward were issued through the hand of John, deacon of the Holy Roman Church.
