On Raynald, see the following chapter.], the aforesaid Pope Urban again came into these regions and ordained John of Gaeta, a monk of this place from childhood, deacon in the Lateran patriarchate. At the same time (1093, 11 March), while he was holding a synod at the city of Troia in Apulia, our Abbot Oderisius lodged a complaint concerning the cell of Saint Sophia at Benevento [Note: [Col. 0829D] Through Leo; see his report in Gattola, *Hist.*, p. 54. He does not indicate the reason why he achieved nothing.], but because war broke out, he could obtain no justice in the matter.

In those days (1090), after Bishop Leo died in the church of Gaeta, Raynald, a monk of this monastery, was ordained bishop of that church. Likewise, on the island of Sardinia, Benedict, a monk of this monastery, was appointed bishop. Whoever wishes to know the miracles of this Benedict should read again the book entitled *On Miracles*, written by us nearly seven years ago [Note: [Col. 0829D] They are also narrated by Peter in the book *On the Birth and Death of the Just Men of Cassino*, ch. 45.].

At that time Richard, surnamed “of Aquila,” came to this monastery and confirmed to our abbot by oath that he would hold the castle of Suio from no person except this monastery of Cassino; that from the said castle he would render service to Saint Benedict according to the tenor of the agreement which Geoffrey Monius [Note: [Col. 0829D] The text has *Gaffridus*.] had made with Abbot Desiderius [Note: [Col. 0830D] See above, III, 52.]; and that at his death it should return to the authority of this monastery without anyone’s objection.

8. Moreover [Note: [Col. 0830D] These matters are taken from Leo’s report on the consecration of the church of Cassino, MS 47; see above, col. 763.], when the fourteenth year had already elapsed since the dedication of the greater church [Col. 0829C], and the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090 was running, three years, three months, and sixty-three days after the death of Pope Victor III, of revered and ever honourable memory, the church of Saint Martin, confessor of Christ, was dedicated (18 November), under the presidency and command of the aforesaid Father Oderisius.

The venerable Abbot Desiderius had, as we have related above (ch. 34), marvellously and beautifully raised this church on sixteen marble columns, in the very place near the monastery gate where it had once been built by the most blessed Father Benedict. He had also excellently adorned it with mosaic and various colours of painting. It was dedicated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, that is, on the octave-day of the same blessed confessor Martin [Col. 0829D], a Monday, with its three altars, amid a great concourse of men of different orders and the utmost joy of all.

The first and principal altar [Col. 0830A], in honour of Blessed Martin himself, was dedicated by the venerable Lord John, bishop of Tusculum. The altar situated at the right of the basilica was consecrated in honour of Saint Erasmus the martyr by Lord Raynald, bishop of Gaeta; in that same year, as we have stated above (ch. 7), he had been given to that church as bishop from this monastery of ours. The third altar, placed on the left side, was blessed in honour of Ambrose, glorious confessor of Christ, by Lord Honestus, most reverend bishop of Berula.

The following relics were deposited in Saint Martin’s altar: relics of Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist; Mark the Evangelist; Martin, bishop; Cornelius and Cyprian; Quirinus and Maximus; Stephen, pope and martyr; Sebastian [Col. 0830B]; Phocas, bishop and martyr; the Forty Martyrs; and an arm of Saints Faustinus and Jovita. In the altar of Saint Erasmus are relics of Erasmus himself, and of the martyrs Castus, Secundinus, and Hippolytus. In the altar of Saint Ambrose are relics of Ambrose himself, of Augustine the bishop, Pancratius the martyr, and a relic-name (*vocabulum*) of Saint Jerome the priest.

Three other bishops were also present at this dedication: Lambert of Alatri, Roffridus of Sora, and Leo, bishop of Venafro. The reason why the consecration of this basilica had been postponed so long after the death of Father Desiderius was that the same abbot, forestalled by death, had left some part of the paintings and no small part of the pavement unfinished. Indeed, he built it twice. The first time, after he had set the columns [Col. 0830C] and architraves in place, Desiderius went to Capua, and the church itself collapsed utterly. When he learned this, he broke out in these words:

> “Martin, priest of God and excellent shepherd, pray to God for us.”

At once this energetic man returned to this place and began to build the church anew from its foundations, as it is seen today. But death forestalled him, as we have said, and he could not complete it. His successor took the greatest care to finish it and add whatever seemed necessary, and thus caused it to be dedicated with the highest honour, as has been stated.

At that time Duchess Sichelgaita, wife of Duke Robert of blessed memory, whom we mentioned above, died [Note: [Col. 0830D] 16 April, *Necrologium Casinense*.]. Because of her supreme hope in Father Benedict, she caused herself to be brought to this monastery and asked to be buried in the paradise [forecourt] of this church [Col. 0830D], before the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter.

9. At the same time (1091), a certain knight named Richard, living in the castle called Spinium, when his granaries denied him provisions, hastened as quickly as possible to the same abbot and, offering prayers as the price, earnestly requested a little wheat with which to relieve his poverty. The abbot, moved with compassion for the petitioner’s need, readily promised that he would without doubt give him ten modii of wheat; and, in order to make good his word and assure him more fully, he foretold when and from where he would receive it.

But he, poor in possessions yet poorer in mind, resolved to repay the holy father Benedict with persecution for kindness and impiety for mercy, choosing rather to possess greater things with a curse than to remain content with little under a blessing. For, prompted by the devil, grievously envying one man’s consolation and another’s compassion, Richard hurried to report to his lord Raynald Ridello, then staying in the town called Trajectum, what he had found at the abbot’s disposal. He did so, however, not that his lord might be instructed by an example of charity, but so that, under the pretext of receiving wheat, a suitable opportunity might arise for handing over to him the castle called Fractae, where it was stored.

Then Raynald, lending an ear to the traitor’s counsel, secured Richard by oath that he would give him half of the aforesaid castle. Accordingly, on the feast of Saint Prisca, the leader of this wicked crime entered the said castle under the guise of a friend. A number of young men followed him, two by two, with downcast faces, and were received by the inhabitants of the castle into their common lodging. Once received, they suddenly passed from hospitality to lordship, not through merit of valour but through the mastery of fraud.

When this was reported to Abbot Oderisius, he sent to entreat Raynald to restore the castle to the monastery upon receipt of one hundred solidi. As Raynald disdained even to hear this, and, though admonished throughout a whole week by the abbot, refused to render justice to this place, he was excommunicated before the body of Father Benedict. On the fourth day Count Adenulf of Aquino, sent there by the same abbot with an army, was received by the townsmen into the castle and began by every means to besiege the citadel.

I shall relate things marvellous, yet wholly true. For although those who were in the citadel hurled stones and missiles singly upon the besiegers, no one was injured in any respect; and thus, through the intervening aid of God and the merits of the blessed father Benedict, they took the citadel by force (30 January), capturing all Raynald’s retainers who were found there, together with all their belongings.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] Tales which he repeated word for word from Leo, book II, chapters 71–72.]

And, that these things may be believed to have been done through the aid and will of Saint Benedict, a certain monk was seen walking about in the army, although none of the monks had then joined that battle.

On the seventh day, while the aforesaid abbot was at Capua with Pope Urban, in the presence of many clerics and nobles of Capua, the said Raynald came with all who were with him, barefoot, and made public satisfaction; thus he was released from excommunication.

On that same day on which we recovered the aforesaid castle, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094,

[Note: [Col. 0831D] “1093” in codex.]

in the second indiction, on the thirtieth day of January, the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle was dedicated. It had been built from its foundations, as we related above (ch. 3), by the same abbot, and was dedicated by Lord Raynald, bishop of Gaeta and monk of this monastery. In it were deposited the relics of the saints written below: of the chain of Saint Peter the Apostle; of Andrew the Apostle; James the Apostle; Philip the Apostle; Matthew the Apostle; Matthias the Apostle; the Holy Innocents; Stephen the Protomartyr; Pope Urban; Pope Felix; Pope Gregory; Marcellian and Mark; Cyriacus the deacon; Cosmas and Damian; Vitus the martyr; Sabinus, bishop of Canosa; Anthony of Constantinople; and Saint Lucina.

At that time Oderisius, son of Oderisius, count of the Sangri, approaching death, offered to Saint Benedict two castles belonging to him by right—namely Fractura and the Hill of the Angel—and whatever seemed to belong to him by paternal or maternal right throughout the whole county of Sangro.

10. About the same time (1090), Prince Jordan, of whom we have spoken above, having brought almost all Campania, withdrawn from the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, into submission, died at Pipernum on 20 November.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] Formerly Privernum.]

His body was brought to this monastery and buried beside the church of Saint Peter the Apostle. But when the Capuans learned of the prince’s death, they conspired against Richard, son of the aforesaid Prince Jordan, and against his mother; they seized the fortifications of the city of Capua and drove all the Normans from the city (May 1098). Richard withdrew with his mother to Aversa and summoned Duke Roger to his aid.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] See Anonymous of Monte Cassino, year 1098; Geoffrey Malaterra, IV.26–28.]

Roger arrived in the summer, devastated with fire and sword everything adjoining the city of Capua, and pressed the siege against them until the Capuans, compelled by necessity, restored the fortifications to the said Richard and, receiving him, inaugurated him as their prince (June).

Moreover, at that time (August 1090), Duke Roger issued a charter to Saint Benedict concerning everything which Duke Robert, his father, together with his wife, had granted to this place; and concerning the monastery of Saint Anastasia with its appurtenances in the territory of Follocastrum.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] Namely, in the diploma in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 205.]

He also granted, to this holy monastery, by a charter sealed with a golden bull, ten men in the same castle, with their families and possessions. Their names are these: Peter son of Mark with his family; Nicephorus with his family; Theodolus son of Dominus with his family; Andrew Sceloxellus with his family; Theodolus with his family; Marinus; Leo Dorcari;

[Note: [Col. 0833] Thus in the original and register; the codex has “Eodercari.”]

Condomitus Calazurus; Perechita; and Leo Fargadari. He also granted the monastery of Saint Nicholas in Bisiniano;

[Note: [Col. 0833D] In the territory of Bisignano; above, III.58, “in Selectano.”]

Saint Angel in Troia; Saint Nicander; Castellione;

[Note: [Col. 0833D] In the same territory of Troia.]

and a warehouse in Amalfi, imposing upon anyone seeking to remove these grants a penalty of five hundred pounds of the purest gold.

Likewise Bohemond,

[Note: [Col. 0833D] “Marcus, also called Abboamonte,” in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 205.]

his brother, in that year (19 August), confirmed by a charter sealed with a golden seal everything his father had bestowed upon this place, together with the monastery of Saint Peter Imperial at Taranto and all its appurtenances whatsoever, and his tithe of wheat, wine, barley, animals, and fish, which he then possessed or would thereafter possess.

11. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the third indiction, on the day before the Nones of April, Wednesday after the octave of Easter, from about the fourth watch of the night until dawn, innumerable stars were seen falling from heaven toward the west throughout all lands.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] This portent is mentioned by the *History of the Holy War*, p. 138, and by the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, whose words our author retained. But neither gives the day.]

At the same time there arose a movement of western peoples, innumerable and beyond estimation, unheard of and marvellous in all preceding ages. Surely no one who has read, heard, or seen anything anywhere can find that so many peoples, so many princes, throughout the whole world, ever conspired so suddenly, so unanimously, and so steadfastly, without the command of any man. Hence no one can doubt that this was undertaken, or even could have begun, only through heavenly prompting and divine ordinance.

Of all their great and manifold deeds, I have resolved to insert in this little work only a brief and concise account of the principal and most outstanding matters. For it is neither my intention to commit everything to writing in sequence, nor could such numerous and important things be treated without the considerable leisure of any prudent person and the labour of a lengthy and particular volume.

This movement is said to have begun in Gaul on the occasion of certain penitents. Because they could not worthily do penance among their own people for their innumerable crimes, and because, being laymen, they were deeply ashamed to live among those who knew them without arms, they pledged themselves with most ready faith to undertake, by the authority and counsel of Pope Urban of holy memory—a plainly wise and truly apostolic man, who had then gone into those regions on Church business (November)—the overseas journey to rescue the Lord’s Sepulchre from the Saracens, imposed upon them as penance and remission of their sins. They were made certain and assured that whatever adversity, danger, or hardship befell them would be accepted by the Lord in place of penance, provided that they abstained from their former wickedness.

Thus, as this report gradually flew from one person to another and from province to province, it is incredible to what a multitude the undertaking itself spread in a short time.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] Compare the cited work, p. 139.]

As a clear and special token of this expedition, they resolved by common counsel to sew upon their garments, at the right shoulder,

[Note: [Col. 0833] The codex has *scapulas*, “shoulders.”]

the sign of the holy cross, made from whatever material was available, and throughout the journey to cry out repeatedly in loud voices: “God wills it, God wills it, God wills it” (*Deus lo volt*).

[Note: [Col. 0834D] P. 140.]

And indeed it was now the will of God; in his most merciful and all-powerful compassion he had disposed this very thing: to deliver the Christians of those regions, who had for so long lived under the yoke and mockery of the Saracens, from their domination; to grant in his mercy that the holy places dedicated to his saving birth, passion, and burial—places which, because of our sins and those of our fathers, he had in his hidden judgment allowed the impious to invade and profane through so many years—together with the holy city of Jerusalem itself, might be recovered by our people; and mercifully to hear all the faithful throughout the world as they hastened without danger to visit and adore those places.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] From this point he follows his source more closely, although he also abridged it and did not preserve its words everywhere. The passages which he altered more freely have been distinguished by variation in type.]

Three companies were formed from all the multitude which had now assented to this undertaking. One part, with Duke Godfrey and his brother Baldwin, Count Baldwin of Mont, and a certain hermit Peter, followed by a vast crowd of Germans, entered Hungary and went to Constantinople by the route once established by King Charles (August 1096); there a very great multitude of Lombards and Langobards had already preceded them.

Another part, with Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles and the bishop of Le Puy,

[Note: [Col. 0834D] Adhemar.]

went through Slavonia. A third part came to Rome by the ancient road, namely Count Robert of Flanders, Count Robert of Normandy, Hugh called the Great, and William, son of Marchis;

[Note: [Col. 0835C] “Marchusi” in the cited work.]

with many others. All of these passed through our monastery of Monte Cassino, commended themselves most earnestly to Father Benedict and the brethren, and departed for Bari.

[Note: [Col. 0835C] “Who—are” was added by our author.]

Meanwhile Bohemond, son of Duke Robert surnamed Guiscard, of blessed memory—who first with his father and afterwards on his own account had long conducted many successful battles against the emperor of Constantinople and his armies—was on campaign with his uncle Count Roger in the region of Campania.

[Note: [Col. 0835C] At the siege of Amalfi in the cited work, p. 144, together with the Annals of Cava and Geoffrey, IV.24. He treated this entire passage more freely.]

When all these matters reached his ears in due order, he was immediately divinely inspired to undertake such service. He ordered silk cloth to be brought to him at once, divided it all into strips, and made crosses from it upon the garments both of himself and of all his own men, as well as of many others who gathered to him for this purpose, just as he had heard others had done. At the same time he ordered them all to shout in loud voices, “God wills it” (*Deus lo volt*).

All Roger’s soldiers, stirred by this report, flocked so suddenly and in such numbers to this association that the aforesaid count, leaving behind only a few men, returned sadly to Sicily. Bohemond at once returned to his own lands and prepared himself to set out on the aforesaid journey.

These captains went with him: Tancred, son of Marchis;

[Note: [Col. 0835C] “Marchusi” in the same source. Some hold that his mother Emma was Robert Guiscard’s sister, others his daughter.]

Robert son of Gerard; Richard of the Principate and his brother Rainulf; Robert of Ansa;

[Note: [Col. 0835C] They are absent there, but are mentioned later.]

Herman of Canne;

[Note: [Col. 0835C] They are absent there, but are mentioned later.]

Robert of Surda Valle; Robert son of Trostenius; Humphrey son of Rao; Richard son of Count Rainulf; Count Geoffrey of Ruscillon; a bishop and his brother Gerard, bishop of Ariano; Boellus of Chartres; Albered of Caniano; Geoffrey of Montescaglioso,

[Note: [Col. 0835C] That is, *caveoso*, Montescaglioso in Basilicata.]

and many others whose names we do not now recall.

After they had crossed the sea (1 November), they came to Valona,

[Note: [Col. 0835C] Aulon in Latin, La Vallona in Italian: a maritime city with a harbour on the western coast of Macedonia.]

where Count Robert of Flanders, Count Robert of Normandy, and many others who had crossed with them joined them. Proceeding thence, they came into part of Bulgaria, then into the valley of Adrianople,

[Note: [Col. 0836C] Adrianople, later Drinopolis.]

then to Castoria,

[Note: [Col. 0836C] A city of Macedonia, formerly episcopal.]

then Paphlagonia,

[Note: [Col. 0836C] “Palagonia” in the cited work, p. 145; formerly Pelagonia.]

and finally to the river Vardar (25 December).

[Note: [Col. 0836C] Formerly the Axius.]

When the emperor heard that Bohemond was coming, he sent a certain *choropalasium*—that is, a curopalates—

[Note: [Col. 0836C] That is, a curopalates.]

to conduct him and all his men safely and honourably as far as Constantinople. On arriving at the city of Rousion,

[Note: [Col. 0836C] Rhusion, on the river Nestus.]

Bohemond left the whole army there and went with a few men to Constantinople to speak with the emperor. There he found Duke Godfrey and his brother (February–March 1097).

Meanwhile the Count of Saint-Gilles, with the bishop of Le Puy, after many dangers, scarcely emerging from the land of the Slavs, came to Dyrrachium; proceeding thence, after several days he entered Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 0836C] *History*, p. 147.]

Yet all those whom we have mentioned, and especially the first arrivals, must be understood to have reached it not easily but with great difficulty, many distresses, and dangers. They suffered these in various places from Turks, Pechenegs, and other barbarians, as well as from the emperor’s own armies. Many perished—some by hunger, some by the sword, others from various illnesses and kinds of death. Nevertheless, Christ often granted victory to his pilgrims over the aforesaid barbarians.

The provident and cunning emperor then began to negotiate with the duke, the count, Bohemond, and their other companions. If they would give him security and fidelity under oath, he too would give them his pledge and protection, and would swear that he himself, with his army, would go with them by land and sea on the road to the Holy Sepulchre; that he would provide them with a market and generously restore whatever had been lost; and, moreover, that he would give Bohemond a territory fifteen days’ journey in length and eight in breadth on this side of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0836C] “Back from Antioch” in the cited work, p. 149.]

Although they long refused to do this after deliberation, at last, compelled by much unavoidable necessity, they consented to swear on the condition that, if the emperor faithfully observed the oath which he promised to make to them, they too would in no way violate theirs.

Once this was done, the whole aforesaid army crossed the strait and proceeded to the city of Nicomedia.

[Note: [Col. 0836C] That is, Nicomedia.]

Duke Godfrey, seeing that the road by which they had to pass to Nicaea was far too narrow for so great an army, since it ran through exceedingly steep and lofty mountains, sent ahead three thousand men with axes and other tools to cut and widen the road vigorously. He ordered iron and wooden crosses to be made and fixed above on tree-stumps as signs of the road.

[Note: [Col. 0835] “And—to be fixed” are absent from the cited work, but occur in the *Gesta Dei*; I suppose that they accidentally dropped out of Mabillon’s edition.]

At length they came to Nicaea, a very noble and strongly fortified city, known to be the capital of all Romania. There they pitched camp, and on the sixth day from the beginning of May

[Note: [Col. 0837D] The day of the Ascension in the cited work.]

they besieged it for seven continuous weeks.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] P. 153.]

During the first two days our men attacked the city so fiercely that they broke through part of the wall.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] P. 150.]

On the third day, when King Soliman of the Huns, whom we now call Turks,

[Note: [Col. 0837D] In the cited work, p. 156: son of the elder Soliman.]

with two hundred thousand horsemen,

[Note: [Col. 0838D] The *History of the Holy War* does not give the number.]

wished to enter by the southern gate, which was not yet guarded, to aid his allies, Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles suddenly fell upon them and crushed them with such force that, with scarcely a few escaping, he slaughtered the rest. Likewise, with God’s help, they defeated others who approached so proudly that they even brought ropes with them for binding our men; and they threw their heads within the city walls with slings and other devices to terrify those remaining inside.

Then, in order completely to obstruct every entrance to the city, each of the aforesaid great men built a wooden castle around it, and they began with various engines to break down the city’s towers.

After this, having taken counsel, they selected three of their wisest men and sent them to Babylon—that is, Cairo—

[Note: [Col. 0838D] Cairo.]

to the amir with a letter of this kind: he was to know that all the princes of the Franks were proceeding unanimously to Jerusalem, intending to open the road to the Lord’s Sepulchre, rescue the Christian land from the dominion of profane pagans, and, with Christ’s help, disgracefully expel them from it. He should now consider what he ought to do and choose whether he wished, on receiving the faith of Christ, henceforth to remain their friend, or, preferring friendship with pagans, to meet them in battle.

There was beside the city a lake of no small size, through which the Turks, going out in ships, brought some supplies to the citizens. Therefore, having taken counsel, they sent to the emperor asking him to send several ships to the city’s harbour and then have them transported by oxen across the mountains to the aforesaid lake. This was done. When the ships had arrived, they sent them by night onto the lake full of armed Turcopoles, whom the emperor had sent with the ships. At dawn they began to advance against the city.

When the Turks saw this, they were greatly astonished, not knowing whether these men belonged to their own party or to the emperor. But when they learned that the emperor had sent the ships, that he favoured our men, and that none of their own people could come to their aid, they were confounded, terrified, and wholly despairing. They sent to the emperor saying that, if they were permitted to depart unhurt with their wives, children, and arms, they would at once surrender the city voluntarily. The emperor then ordered them, once the city had been surrendered, to come confidently to him without fear.

Since the emperor had long promised to hand over to our men all the gold, silver, horses, and all the city’s equipment, and also to establish there a Latin monastery and hospice, they hoped that truth lay in his words; therefore they both approved and accepted the surrender (20 June).

[Note: [Col. 0838D] That is, “accepted.”]

But when the emperor had received the city, he was greatly rejoiced and did none of the things he had promised.

After this they struck camp. On the third day, when they had set out before dawn, confused by an error in the night, they were divided into two separate columns for almost two days. Meanwhile a vast force of Turks, Persians, and Arabs, gathered together, began at first light to advance against the column in which Bohemond was, shouting, shrieking, and grinding their teeth in their manner (1 July).

Bohemond, a man of great spirit, perceiving this, began to encourage his companions, saying: “O most valiant soldiers of Christ, do not be afraid, knowing that the Lord whose wars we wage is with us. Let the horsemen therefore go against them; let the foot-soldiers quickly spread the tents. What God wills concerning us, let him do.”

Count Robert of Normandy and Tancred were then with him. Meanwhile he sent messengers to the other princes, asking them to hurry as quickly as possible to their assistance. For the Turks and Arabs, beyond number, had surrounded them on every side, and they could not endure the weight of so great a battle alone.

When the others heard this, although they scarcely believed it and thought the message had been sent in jest, they nevertheless set out at once; and when they saw such a vast multitude of enemies, they were greatly amazed. Then, taking confidence from God, they formed their battle-lines. On the left wing stood Bohemond, Count Robert of Normandy, Tancred, and Richard of the Principate; Robert son of Gerard bore their standard. On the right wing stood Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Duke Godfrey, Hugh the Great, and the Count of Flanders. The bishop of Le Puy surrounded the enemy through the mountains.

As soon as all our men together cried out in their customary manner, “God wills it” (*Deus lo volt*), all the barbarians were immediately seized with such terror that they took flight as quickly as possible. Our men pursued them most vigorously and killed a very great multitude of them, while the rest scarcely escaped by the various byways.

It is reported on the testimony of trustworthy persons, and confirmed by the witness of the Turks themselves who escaped, that three noble knights seated on white horses, likewise bearing white banners marked with crosses, seemed to go before our army and pursue and kill every adversary. They conjectured that these were George, Demetrius, and Theodore, distinguished soldiers of Christ.

Nor should this appear either strange or incredible. For how could one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, unless the Lord had subdued them and God had delivered them up? For during a journey of three days thereafter our men found Turks slain and their horses, although none of our men had yet passed that way.

It is reported that four hundred and sixty thousand Turks and Persians gathered for that expedition, besides the Arabs, whose number is unknown.

[Note: [Col. 0839D] The cited work, p. 154, has three hundred and forty thousand.]

All the plunder—gold, silver, clothing, and animals—was considerable and was divided among all. This battle lasted from about the third hour until evening. It was fought on the day before the Kalends of July. On that field there fell, to the great grief of all, two noble and most blessed knights of our side, namely Geoffrey of Montescaglioso and William, Tancred’s brother; also five hundred and sixty-six horsemen and eleven thousand foot-soldiers. Of the Saracens, more than one hundred thousand fell.

[Note: [Col. 0839D] He added the numbers.]

After this it happened that Solima, commander of Nicaea, fleeing from there, encountered an army of about ten thousand Arabs coming to help their people. When they asked why he was fleeing in this manner, he replied:

“If you wish to believe me and take counsel for yourselves, turn back; otherwise, if you delay even a little, none of you will escape the hands of the Franks. For their God is certainly with them. Three days ago, when we had surrounded them on every side and defeated them, and already almost held them in our hands, we suddenly looked back and saw such an innumerable people as no man has ever seen. Mountains and plains alike were filled with armed men; and immediately, when all cried out, such fear and trembling suddenly seized us that we could think of nothing but flight. It would be most astonishing if any of that great multitude of ours escaped alive.”

When the Arabs heard these and such words, they immediately turned their backs. While fleeing before our men, wherever they came they boasted, saying, “We are those who defeated the Franks.” They devastated churches, houses, and villages; carried off the children of Christians captive; and burned everything which seemed likely to be necessary for our men.

As our army continually pursued them through waterless and desert places, it lost a very great number of horses; for several days the men themselves found nothing to eat except ears of grain in the fields. At last they came by Iconium to Heraclea.

[Note: [Col. 0839D] “Ercle.”]

There too, joining battle with no small force of Turks, they compelled the defeated enemy to flee.

From there Tancred and Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey, separated themselves from the army and entered the valley of Botentrot.

[Note: [Col. 0839D] Podandus, where the entrance into Cilicia lies.]

Tancred alone with his men advanced to Tarsus. There, fighting with Turks who met him not far from the city, he compelled them to take refuge within it and at once pitched his tents before the city gates. Baldwin also arrived and did the same. When the Turks saw this, they all fled that night in terror.

In the morning, the leading men of the city came out and voluntarily surrendered it to Tancred, whom they had seen fighting so bravely against the Turks the day before. Tancred left it to Baldwin, pushed forward, and similarly acquired Adana and Mamistra, and likewise all the castles as far as Antioch.

The rest, departing from Heraclea, entered Armenia, receiving its castles and cities partly by force and partly through surrender, and hastening as quickly as possible toward Antioch. When the vanguard of our army had come near, they encountered no small troop of Turks coming to bring aid to Antioch. Attacking them unanimously in Christ’s name, they killed many, put the rest to flight, seized a great quantity of horses, mules, and camels laden with various provisions, and that day pitched camp beside the bank of the river Farfar (20 October).

12. In these days (April 1091), Richard of Aquila, of whom we have spoken above (ch. 7), offered to Saint Benedict the church of Saint Elias at Ambrife; Saint Maurice’s on the mountain above the castle of Saint John of Carica; Saint Mary at the spring of Mount Cervario; and Saint John of Fabrateria in the place called Campusano, with lands, vineyards, houses, mills, and all their movable and immovable property.

[Note: [Col. 0839D–0840D] See I. B. Federici, *Degli antichi duchi di Gaeta*, Naples, 1791, quarto, p. 440.]

At that time the same abbot gave him twenty-five pounds.

Likewise Pandulf of Presenzano

[Note: [Col. 0839D] The codex has “Presensano.”]

[Note: [Col. 0840D] A count, son of Lord Pandulf, who was count of Teano; in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 206.]

offered to Saint Benedict his share of the castle of Mirtula,

[Note: [Col. 0840D] Elsewhere called Mortula. ANG.]

and the comital estate of Bantra, and Saint Saviour’s in Cucuruczo, with all their appurtenances, imposing a penalty of one thousand pounds of gold (September 1091). For this transaction Abbot Oderisius gave him ninety-six pounds.

Rudolf of Molise, count of Boiano,

[Note: [Col. 0840D] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 207.]

also made a charter to this place concerning the monastery of Holy Cross at Isernia and the castle called Balneus, with houses, lands, vineyards, waters, mills, woods, churches, and all their appurtenances, both within and without, imposing a penalty of one hundred and fifty pounds of gold (March 1092). He received one hundred pounds from the same abbot.

Peter son of Atenulf, together with his brother John surnamed Revere, did the same concerning Saint John in Campo Samni, with its appurtenances in the territory of Ceprano. Count Raynald of Pontecorvo

[Note: [Col. 0841D] Perhaps Geoffrey Ridello; Gattola, *Historia*, p. 294.]

did likewise concerning the monastery of Saint Paul in Furesta, with its appurtenances (March 1093).

Likewise Lando, formerly duke of the Gaetans, at that time (10 December),

[Note: [Col. 0841D] Gattola, *Accessiones*, 207 and the Register of Peter; compare Federici, *Duchi di Gaeta*, p. 442.]

made a charter to Saint Benedict concerning everything which belonged to him by paternal or maternal right throughout the duchy and principality of Gaeta: cities, castles, villages, churches, woods—everything and all things—imposing a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold.

13. In these same days Cidrus, vice-count of Prince Richard,

[Note: [Col. 0841D] Jordan calls him “his beloved vice-prince,” in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 187.]

came to this place, received the habit of holy religious life, and became a monk. It seems fitting to record, for the knowledge both of those now living and of posterity, what this man offered to this place at different times.

On his first occasion, he gave Lord Abbot Desiderius, when the latter began to renew the church of Saint Benedict, eight hundred Amalfitan solidi. On another occasion he gave him four hundred solidi. After this he gave him six pounds of denarii. Again he gave him three hundred solidi, with which an excellent *circitorium* was bought for the altar of Saint Benedict. On another occasion he gave one hundred pounds of silver. Again, for the altar-panel of Saint Martin, twenty-four pounds; and for renewing that saint’s books, forty-five solidi.

After Father Desiderius’s death he offered to Saint Benedict a precious golden cross with gems and pearls, a wonderful golden casket, and a golden inkstand richly adorned on every side with most precious pearls and gems. He also gave an imperial garment wholly gilded and fittingly ornamented with gems, enamels, and pearls; a purple pallium; and a gold band for a cope. For a silver crown he gave forty pounds; for the construction of the cemetery, twenty pounds; again fifty pounds of silver; and for the altar-panel of Saint Andrew, twenty pounds. He also gave many other things at various times for the brethren’s benefit.

Meanwhile Arnulf,

[Note: [Col. 0842D] Arnulf himself was already dead. His charter was published by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 208. It is dated in the thirty-eighth year of King Henry’s reign.]

a nobleman, together with all his relatives, in that time (May 1093), made a charter of donation to this holy place of the stronghold called Civitella in the duchy of Spoleto; of the monastery of Saint Saviour built there; of the church of Saint Peter of Montescopulo; of half the church of Saint Mary; of the church of Saint Agnellus at Cese; and of the estate at Petraccle, and at Alanu, Paganica, and Porcaria in the county of Narni, with all their movable and immovable appurtenances, imposing a penalty of five hundred pounds of silver.

14. At the same time, while the counts of Aquino raged in deadly hatred against the people of Sora, Jonathan, son of Prince Jordan, was summoned by those same Sorans against them. Rejoicing that by this means he had found an opportunity to acquire Campania, he summoned the Normans to himself and entered the city of Sora. There, after remaining for several years and both fighting and receiving some battles, Count Adenulf was captured by the same Jonathan and cast into the chains of prison. Then the brothers of the captured count—Landulf, Pandulf, and Lando—approached Abbot Oderisius and begged by every means that he should assist them in such grave need. Abbot Oderisius, taking several brethren with him, went to Jonathan, who was staying at Sora, and, speaking with him there, freed the aforesaid count from his bonds, on this condition: until he should pay Jonathan one thousand pounds, he was to hand over his sons to him as hostages. And this was done.

After this, the same count came to the monastery. The same abbot gave him one hundred pounds and lent him another hundred; and Count Adenulf gave, in his city of Sant’Urbano, all those persons whom the lord Abbot Desiderius of blessed memory had exchanged with him, with all their appurtenances in full, just as, eight days earlier, the lord Abbot Desiderius had held the exchange.

[Note: See above, III.16.]

This was on the condition that, from the approaching feast of Easter until the next Resurrection—or sooner, if it could be done—if Count Adenulf should repay one hundred pounds, whether in money or in other merchandise of such kind as might please the abbot or monks, the aforesaid persons should be restored to him in full. But if by the stated term he should not repay those pounds, then, by a charter lawfully written and confirmed by witnesses, he should forfeit all the persons already named, with all their appurtenances, which the aforesaid had held under Abbot Desiderius; provided, nevertheless, that until the stated term they should possess and hold those persons as they appeared to hold them at present.

Mount Alberto, with its vineyards and lands, is excepted, if he should build a castle there. Miluczu is also excepted, together with the property of his father-in-law and of his maternal uncle, the priest Lando. And he renounced in favor of this monastery the land belonging to it which is at Petra Scripta, which, after his father’s death, the same count had withdrawn from the jurisdiction of this place. When the term for repayment arrived, Count Adenulf, being summoned by Abbot Oderisius to repay the aforesaid pounds to the monastery of Monte Cassino, declared that he had nothing from which he could restore them to us.

15. In these same days Count Paldus, son of John, count of Venafro, restored to Saint Benedict the church of Saint Benedict at Venafro and that of Saint Benedict of Pizzuli, with all their appurtenances, under a penalty of one thousand bezants. Abbot Desiderius had given these in exchange to John, his father.

[Note: III.59.]

But Teudus, a nobleman—

[Note: Teudo, lord of the castles of Sculcula in Campania, Murolo, and also of the fortress of Vitolino; in Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 209, from the Register.]

—offered to this holy monastery the church of Saint Peter below the castle of Murolo; those of Saint Angel and Saint Martin above the same castle; and also eight households of persons, whose names are these: Aspranus with his household; Mampo with his household; John of Silva de Muli with his household; Benedict of Merco with his household; John of Adammo; and Leo of Raynerius—

[Note: He omitted Amatus of Datus and John Silbius, and did not give the remaining names accurately.]

—with all who belonged to them. Most devoutly he offered all these persons, together with all their property, to this place, under a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold (24 January 1094).

16. In the time of this abbot, Baldwin, lord of the castle called the Bridge of Saint Anastasia in the county of Telese, offered to Saint Benedict the church of Saint Dionysius of the aforesaid castle of Saint Anastasia.

[Note: Here another hand of the same period continues, the beginning of the chapter that had already been written having been erased.]

[Note: The same hand wrote what follows down to the end of chapter 25 on four leaves inserted later.]

He had found it very small and old, renewed and enlarged it from its foundations, endowed it with certain estates and tenant-farmers, and built dwellings around it. At the admonition of the aforesaid Pope Urban, he caused the lord Roffrid, archbishop of Benevento, solemnly to dedicate it. He gave it with its attached lands, vineyards, and woods; with trees, cultivated and uncultivated land; and with five ancient churches built within the same appurtenances, namely: the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, called Ad Arvente, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Angel, called Ad Gruttam, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Barbatus, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Julian, built in the territory of the castle of Limata and called Ad Pugnam, with all its appurtenances; and, moreover, the church of Saint Erasmus within the bounds of the same castle of the Bridge of Saint Anastasia, at the place called Ferrarisi, with six mills on the river Alento, which flows beside the aforesaid castle of the Bridge of Saint Anastasia; a fishery on the river Calore, at the place called Decembri; and a vineyard and wood situated at Cerra Domnica.

Robert, son of Count Rainulf—

[Note: Brother of Prince Richard I; 1094, indiction II; Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 713.]

—also restored to this holy place the church of Saint Mary of Cinglis, with its appurtenances (December 1094). Not long afterward Nicholas, priest of Venafro, adjudged and transferred to this monastery the church of Saint Nicholas in the city of Venafro, with all its appurtenances.

Countess Adelgrima—

[Note: Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 212.]

—daughter of Pandulf, prince of Capua, living in the Carsoli district at the castle called Auricula and widow of Count Raynald, son of Count Berard, adjudged and transferred four castles in the said Carsoli district in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in March: first, the castle named Auricula; second, that called Fossaceca; third, Camerata; and fourth, Piretus. She also gave three monasteries: the monastery of Saint John with its hospital; Saint John of the Valley of Calvula; and Saint Peter of Pireto—the aforesaid castles and monasteries with absolutely all their appurtenances.

In the same year (1097), a comet appeared, and the city of Antioch was captured by the Christians.

[Note: Anonymous of Monte Cassino, under the year 1097.]

In the following period, on the Ides of July, the worshippers of Christ took the city of Jerusalem (1099), and on the fifth day before the Kalends of October a fiery track was seen in the sky throughout the night.

[Note: The same source, under the year 1098.]

17. Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, sent Saint Benedict through his *choropalates*, John, a garment from his own back, brilliantly gilded (*oxychryseon*, ὀξυχρύσεον), in June 1098.

[Note: Ὀξνχρύσεον: gilded with shining gold. Ducange calls it *epiloricum* in the letter itself, in Gattula, *Historia*, p. 923; Muratori, *Antiquitates*, V, 387; Tosti, II, 93.]

The aforesaid abbot received this ambassador very honorably and decreed that the emperor should forever remain a participant in the good works performed at Monte Cassino. He sent his own envoy to him with letters, by which he took care to commend to him the Christians who had gone to Jerusalem to overthrow the perfidy of the pagans; and he charged him, for the remission of all his sins, with the direction and care of the pilgrims’ house at Monte Cassino. In the same way, he took care to send letters to Godfrey, king of Jerusalem, and to Bohemond, prince of Antioch, urging them not to wage war on the emperor.

On another occasion the same emperor sent eight pounds of Michaelite solidi, in remembrance, and a *triacontasimum* pallium for the altar of our church.

[Note: Τριακοντάσημον: adorned with thirty golden nails; Ducange.]

At that time, on 27 March 1097, our Abbot Oderisius received from Pope Urban a general privilege concerning the freedom of this monastery, both in its head and in the members constituted by its churches and castles; and concerning the dignity and use of pontifical shoes (*campagi*)—

[Note: Read *campagorum*, that is, pontifical footwear.]

—and gloves, dalmatic, mitre, and many other matters too lengthy to recount.

[Note: Gattula, *Historia*, p. 149.]

18. The same pontiff of the Apostolic See, Urban, having entered Gaul in 1096 on ecclesiastical business, as we have said above (ch. 11), at the full council of Tours, over which he presided in March, withdrew the monastery of Saint Maurus at Glanfeuil—

[Note: Glanfeuil in Anjou.]

—from the tyranny of the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés—

[Note: Saint-Maur-des-Fossés near Paris.]

—and restored it to its former liberty, to remain forever only under the direction and protection of the monastery of Monte Cassino.

[Note: He himself relates this more fully in the bull given at Terracina, 21 March 1097, in Gattula, *Historia*, p. 298.]

During these days Abbot Oderisius sent letters through George, a monk of his monastery, to Emperor Henry IV, by which he showed that he had succeeded Desiderius in the government of the monastery and in fidelity and service to the emperor. At the same time, the aforesaid Brother George, in the presence of the said Emperor Henry, his son Henry V, and Countess Matilda—

[Note: Certainly separately. Yet I have grave doubts about the emperor; concerning Matilda, see ch. 25. For these possessions see Tiraboschi, *Nonantula*, I, p. 445. I do not doubt that the privilege of King Desiderius in which they are first mentioned, in Tosti, I, p. 89, is spurious.]

—made a claim concerning possessions of the monastery of Monte Cassino situated in Liguria, which Aistulf and Desiderius, kings of the Lombards, as well as the emperors Charles, Pippin, and Lothair, and other God-fearing persons, had granted to Father Benedict.

He claimed the monastery of Saint Benedict in Persiceta, in the Modenese territory, within the boundaries of the river Fusculus and the boundary of Malmeniliacum; this monastery Duke Peter of the city of Ravenna had offered to Saint Benedict under Abbot Angelarius, together with the entire court of Persiceta, the court of Greniano, and the court of Monterione, with the mills of the two rivers, Fusculus and Gallicus. Then the monastery of Saint Mary at Laurentiacum beyond the river Gallicus. Not far from there is the monastery of Saint Domninus in the court of Argella, together with the High Wood, the Greater Wood, and the entire fishery called Caucenna, extending to the river Gambacane, to Rosalese, and to the court of Ragogusola. Then, below the public road, the monastery of Saint Vitalis with the entire court of Calderaria near the castle of Sala. The monastery of Saint John at Frassenetula, with the entire court itself as far as the Stone Road situated near the castle of Cedula.

[Note: Tiraboschi, in the cited place, directs that *Cellula* be read. It is now called Zola.]

The monastery of Saint Martin beside the Stone Road, in the hamlet of Marciano, with that entire court near the castle of Unciola—

[Note: Anzola.]

—and all demesne lands. The monastery of Saint Saviour at Pontelongo, with that entire court in the county of Modena: thirty *mansi* of land and sixty-one *iugera*. In the appurtenance of Monterione, on the upper and lower sides of the castle itself, very many parcels of land; a mill at the place called Campaldus on the river Fusculus; and the courts at Benselio, which Berta, daughter of the count palatine—

[Note: That is, daughter of the count of the palace; perhaps this ought to be restored to Peter.]

—of Pavia had offered to Saint Benedict within these boundaries: on the east, the boundary of Bisentula; on the south, the road called the Great Road and the boundaries of Maleandroni; on the west, the river Riolo below Castellione. At Postumiano, six [units]; at Laino, two *iugera*.

All these things, I say, with all their appurtenances and dependencies round about—hamlets, estates, demesne lands, villages, male and female rustics and colonists, cultivated and uncultivated land, divided and undivided, below and above—had belonged from ancient times by right to the monastery of Monte Cassino. Once the emperor had learned the truth concerning all these things, he commanded Countess Matilda, under a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold, to restore everything already named to the said brother on behalf and in the stead of the monastery of Monte Cassino.

At the same time, on 8 December 1098, the aforesaid pontiff restored to us the monastery of Saint Mary of Cinglis, concerning which a claim had long been made, both in the time of Abbot Desiderius and in that of this abbot, against the abbess of Saint Mary at Capua, who had forcibly entered there. Having examined the rights of both parties, he decreed by privilege that it should remain under the lordship and administration of this monastery.

[Note: From Urban’s privilege in Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 710; Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 629.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098 [1099], on the twelfth day of the moon, it suffered an eclipse at its rising and gradually returned to fullness on the Nones of June.

[Note: From the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, under the year 1099.]

In the same year Urban, pontiff of the Apostolic See, of blessed memory, died on 29 July. Raynerius, abbot of Saints Lawrence and Stephen—

[Note: Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls.]

—was substituted as pope in the Apostolic See on 13 August, and was given the name Paschal.

19. At the same time, in July 1098, Anso, rector of the principality of Benevento, in fidelity to the Roman Church, and his noble brothers Dauferius and Atenulf, John and Berard, Peter, Alfanus, and Liutprand, sons of Lord Dacomarus, governor of Benevento, offered to Saint Benedict the church of Saint Nicholas built above the New Tower of the city of Benevento, called Pagana. Their father himself had enlarged it. They gave it with houses, lands, mills on the river Sabato, and all its appurtenances.

[Note: In Gattula, *Historia*, p. 409.]

These brothers had previously issued a privilege for the said church concerning all their property. Count Berard of the Marsi also, in those days, offered to this monastery the church of Saint Martin in Marsican territory, near Lake Fucino, at the place called Filimini, with all its appurtenances, lands, vineyards, one service of fishermen, and their property (July 1097).

[Note: Di Meo, *Annali Napoletani*, IX, p. 25, says that the charter exists in Gattula. I sought it there in vain.]

20. Meanwhile, in February 1097, Rocca, daughter of Count Drogo, offered forty-six persons in the village of Sellectano and seven persons at Castellione, with all their immovable and movable property, their children, and others who, having left those lands, should return.

[Note: “In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1105, but among the Romans the ninety-eighth year of the reign of our lord Duke Roger, indiction V”; in Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 215.]

But Count Roger of Sicily and Calabria confirmed in 1098 all that his niece Rocca had given to this monastery, namely all that she had possessed in the village of Sellectano.

[Note: A.D. 1098, ibid., p. 216.]

In like manner Count Berard, son of Count Oderisius of Sangro, offered to Saint Benedict the entire appurtenance belonging to him within the bounds of Mount Aze for pasture, excepting the woods, cultivated lands, and enclosed meadows. He also offered the whole and entire place called Lacuvivo; the whole and entire place called Godi; whatever belonged to him at Pantana; the whole and entire Claranum and Muricentum; Altareofania; whatever belonged to him at the place called Saphinum; and the field of Armonia (February).

[Note: Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 218.]

Likewise, the nobleman Maxarus, inhabitant of the city of Alba in the Marsican territory, offered to this holy place his church of Saint Martin in the said territory, at the place called Sclavi, with thirty *modii* of land and all its appurtenances.

In these same days our Abbot Oderisius made an exchange with Benedict, bishop of Terracina, concerning the church of the blessed Apostle Andrew, situated in that city near the episcopal residence, with its cemetery, houses, and squares. In exchange for it he received the church of Saint Nicholas, situated outside the same city near the Albina Gate, with its cemetery, garden, and house; under a penalty of one hundred solidi should he seek to revoke this arrangement.

Then, when the sixteenth year from the death of Pope Gregory VII, the fourteenth from that of Victor III, and the second from the death of the second Urban and the succession of Paschal II had already elapsed, and the year 1100 from the Lord’s Incarnation was turning, Guibert, heresiarch and usurper of the Roman Church, died.

[Note: Anonymous of Monte Cassino, under the year 1100.]

Not long afterward, in August 1101, Count Landenulf—

[Note: The text has Landulf.]

—son of Count Laidulf, offered to Saint Benedict the whole and entire fortress of Camino, with its castle and appurtenances.

[Note: Bordering the town of Galluccio, in the diocese of Teano, according to Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 219, where he published the donation from the Register.]

In the following year Rocca, whom we named above, issued a privilege concerning the eleven persons whom she held in the village of Sellectano, with their households—

[Note: The text has *famulis*, “servants.”]

—lands, vineyards, and all that belonged to them.

[Note: A.D. 1102, indiction 2, while Count Roger was ruling; Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 217. See above, no. 98.]

She also offered by privilege the church of Saint Peter at Ferulitum, and half of the church of Saint Demetrius, which had been offered to the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, and half of all cultivated and uncultivated lands, mountains, plains, waters, mills, pastures and marshes, and of the port of the same sea, under a penalty of fifty pounds of gold.

[Note: A.D. 1104, the twentieth year of Duke Roger, indiction VII; this must contain an error. Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 217.]

[Note: There, she offers half of it to the church of Saint Benedict of Citraria, which seems to be near this church. She herself lived at Castro Ullano.]

21. Finally, our Abbot Oderisius received from the aforesaid Pope Paschal a privilege of grant concerning Saint Nicholas at Benevento and its freedom, with all that it then possessed: two mills under one roof, a *centimolum*—

[Note: A domestic mill driven by a beast of burden; Anglicus.]

—gardens with various trees, ten courts with their lands and woods and houses (17 November 1101). The same pontiff also added these churches: the church of Saint Nicholas at Urbiliano, near Petra Pedicina—

[Note: *Pelicina* in the privilege in Gattula, *Historia*, p. 411.]

—with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Nicholas called Rodenandi, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary called Rotunda, with its appurtenances; and a bath near the church of Saint Potitus.

22. At that time Laidulf, son of Peter Laidulf, a nobleman of the city of Capua, offered to Saint Benedict the entire tower called “Of the Sea,” situated within the boundaries of the city of Sessa, beside the mouths of the river Garigliano; also the water and channel of the said river, with its banks, and the land and wood called Pineta, together with other adjoining lands.

[Note: I. B. Federici, *Degli antichi duchi di Gaeta*, Naples, 1791, quarto, p. 162, warns that two towers must be distinguished. The one mentioned above at II.37–38 was built by John, patrician of Gaeta, but in the time of John X rather than John VIII; the other, on the left bank of the Garigliano and situated by the sea, was built by Pandulf.]

At the same time Count Walter gave houses and house-plots within the city of Teramo—

[Note: Terni.]

—a vineyard, land, mills, and mill-channels in the castaldy of Teramo, and a wood in the duchy of Spoleto, at the places called Cifalanum and Pracclepetanum; and a fourth share of the castle of John and Paul with its appurtenances.

[Note: A.D. 1102, the forty-sixth year of King Henry, indiction IX—read X; Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 219.]

The same Walter also gave all the property that had belonged to Ascarus in the valley called Praraccle and at Interamnes, except the church of Saint Paternianus with its appurtenance. He gave half of Cifelano, with its appurtenances; all that had belonged to Unald at Gruttule, Cinqualio, Sallano, Piano Episcopale, Ioniano, Producte, and Mandulano; land at Cinqualio; and land near the boundary of Gruttule.

[Note: A.D. 1103, the forty-seventh year of King Henry, indiction II (read I), ibid., p. 220.]

23. During this abbot’s presidency, in the year of the Lord 1103, the seventeenth year of his elevation, the church of Saint Stephen was dedicated by Benedict, bishop of Terracina, on the Nones of November. In it are deposited the relics of the saints set down below:

Of the cloth in which Christ was wrapped when he was born. Of the stone that stood at the entrance of the Lord’s tomb. Of the palm which the Lord held in his hand when the way was strewn before him. Of Saint Matthew the apostle; Bartholomew the apostle; Stephen the first martyr; Lawrence; Vincent; Sebastian; Cyriacus; the Twelve Brothers; Cosmas and Damian; Lucy and Geminianus; Marius and Martha; Tiburtius and Valerian; George; Hippolytus; Martin of Tours; Pope Stephen; Pope Callixtus; Pope Cornelius; Cyprian; Prisca; and Adelbert.

When the bodies of the holy monks Paulinus and Augustine, disciples of the most blessed Benedict, had been found buried in this church with two others, a demoniac came there and began to cry out: “Paulinus and Augustine, disciples of Benedict, together with their two companions, are driving me out.” While the devil repeatedly spoke these words through his mouth, the unclean spirit departed with blood. Abbot Oderisius then lifted up the bodies of the saints from there and reverently placed them in the wall of the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

[Note: The same account in *De Justis Casinensibus*, 20–21.]

24. Meanwhile Count William of the city of Mount Saint Michael the Archangel—

[Note: Or rather Henry, in the presence of his brother, according to John Mabillon, *Annales*, V, p. 399.]

—issued a privilege to Saint Benedict concerning the hospice outside the said city with its appurtenances, and granted to the same hospice lands and churches (April 1100). His brother Henry had earlier, in November 1099, granted land to a certain *zianus*—

[Note: That is, uncle: John, abbot of Curte, son of Guaimar, prince of Salerno. Henry was [the son] of Count Robert. Gattula, *Historia*, p. 412.]

—of his for the construction of that hospice. Finally, in April 1101, he granted to that hospice the church of Saint Nicholas at Tiliata with its appurtenances, under a penalty of one hundred ounces of gold.

[Note: Ibid., p. 413.]

John Comitellus also offered his share, namely the entire half of the church of Saint Benedict, to the aforesaid hospice. Ursus, surnamed Spina, likewise offered his share of the said church of Saint Benedict in that hospice. Furthermore, the priest Sico, Manus, Ursus, and Leo, noblemen of the said city, offered to that hospice the church of the Most High, built in the wood at Marruta, which they possessed from paternal or maternal property.

In the final year of this abbot, Duke Roger issued a privilege to this monastery concerning lands in the appurtenances of the city of Troia (December 1104).

[Note: Gattula, *Historia*, p. 158. Alessandro di Meo, *Annali Napoletani*, IX, p. 121, considers it suspect.]

25. Prince Richard II, moreover, through the intervention of Count Robert, gave this place the town of Pontecorvo with its appurtenances, except the outlying castles with their appurtenances, and except the fief of Richard of Aquila, which he held there for the life of Gualguanus (25 January 1105).

[Note: Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 223. The prince’s oath and the abbot’s account of money spent in this business are preserved there.]

Gualguanus had given that town to his wife as her dowry and left it to her when he died. But she scorned to give the said prince the security owed to him; against his will she allied herself with his enemies, made war against him, entered into dealings with them, and supplied them with grain. For this offense the aforesaid town came under the prince’s jurisdiction and power, and he gave it to the aforesaid Count Robert, brother of the said wife of Gualguanus; through this count, and from him, the aforesaid town was given to our monastery.

Robert, count of the people of Gaeta and of many others, son of the Count Rainulf named above—

[Note: Brother of Richard I. For the privilege see ibid., p. 222.]

—partly as a gift and partly for a price, granted and confirmed to this monastery, on 13 January, the town of Pontecorvo with its appurtenances, by concession of Prince Richard II, in the manner in which it had been granted to him by the aforesaid prince; namely, the town that Gualguanus appeared to possess three days before he died.

The noblewoman Berta, daughter of Unald, gave and offered to this monastery the church of Saint Martin built in the city of Spoleto, at the place called the Gate of Saint Lawrence, with all its appurtenances. Finally, the noblemen Tobald and Peter Caldina, together with four others, offered to this place gypsum (*gissum*?) on Mount Trequanzano at the castle of Argenti.

[Note: Perhaps gypsum mines?]

Robert of Buthone, a nobleman, and his wife Sica offered and transferred to Saint Benedict half of the church of Saint Peter built at Ferulitum, with all the endowments belonging to that church, and with the church of Saint Demetrius, lands, woods, plains, mountains, pastures, waters, mills, and marshes.

About these days, on 22 June, Countess Matilda granted to this place one third of the court of Saint Benedict called Pastorini.

[Note: Rather, she restored it, upon the claim in court of the aforesaid monk George (ch. 18), as also the church of Saint Benedict. It was published by Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 611.]

[Note: In the district of Persiceta.]

Hugh, count of Melisio, son of Count Raulis—

[Note: The same man who was called Rodulf in ch. 12; Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 224.]

—offered to Saint Benedict the entire castle named Vitecosum, with its appurtenances (September). Furthermore, the aforesaid abbot received from the aforesaid Pope Paschal a general privilege, dated 17 March, like that which he had received from Urban II, named above.

[Note: Gattula, *Historia*, p. 331.]

Ptolemy, consul and count of Tusculum, pledged to this abbot and his successors one vessel in whatever vessel monks of this monastery might be, so that they might be secure from him and his men at sea and on land, together with all their merchandise and all persons found in that vessel, when travelling to Sardinia and returning to Gaeta; with the penalty that anyone attempting to revoke this should forfeit all his property.

[Note: On the naval affairs of these counts, besides what we cited above, p. 563, see the war which Gregory and Ptolemy I waged with the people of Gaeta over a certain ship, ended by peace on 9 February 1105; I. B. Federici, *De duchi di Gaeta*, p. 463. On Ptolemy I see also the charter of Odo de Columna in Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, III, 777.]

The aforesaid Abbot Oderisius died on the fourth day before the Nones of December.

OTTO, the thirty-ninth abbot of this monastery, ruled for one year and ten months.

[Note: That this is the beginning of the chapter is apparent from its heading.]

26. He was born of the most noble lineage of the consuls of Fondi. In the very years of infancy he was offered to almighty God and clothed in the habit of holy life by Father Desiderius of venerable memory. After spending some years in the pursuit of holy religious observance, he was ordained provost in the monastery of Saint Nicholas at Pica. When Abbot Oderisius of pious memory died, and the brethren, as is customary in such matters, wished each to choose his own abbot for governing the abbey of this monastery, the elders, whose party was the sounder and more religious, greatly resenting this, made known to the brethren their wish concerning the same man and elected him abbot to govern this place.

[Note: From this point the primary hand continues.]

Prince Richard at that time was suffering from a very severe illness; and since he could not come to Monte Cassino for the installation of the same abbot, he sent vigorous men from his side to offer the abbot their faithful service. These matters having been thus accomplished, he died as his illness grew worse, and his brother Robert succeeded him in the principality.

[Note: Anonymous of Monte Cassino, under the year 1106.]

At the same time, after the death, on 7 August 1106, of Henry IV of august memory, who had disputed extensively with Pope Gregory VII concerning investiture of churches, his son Henry V took up the reins of government of the Roman Empire.

This abbot granted, by the form of a *libellus*, to Girard, son of Girard of Corvazzano, lands belonging to the church of Saint Benedict of Pastorino—

[Note: The text has *Pastorivo*.]

—down to the third generation, receiving at present 120 solidi in Lucchese money; and annually, as rent, three solidi from all crops annually produced there. He did likewise for Abbertus Raynaldus, Sicefrit of Falsabrina, and Albertinus, son of Boniface, concerning other lands there, receiving from him the same price. Prince Robert swore an oath to this abbot, confirming in customary fashion all the appurtenances of this monastery.

[Note: In Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 225.]

27. In this same year Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, sent through the *apocrisiarii* of his empire to Saint Benedict an excellent purple pallium, from which the aforesaid abbot adorned a cope with golden bands and ordered a tunic of the same lining to be made. Through these same envoys he also sent his own messenger with letters to the emperor, informing him that Abbot Oderisius had passed from this life and that he himself had succeeded to the government of the monastery and to the love and service of the same emperor.

In the same year, in March 1106, Carbonellus, a nobleman, offered to Saint Benedict the churches of Saint Gregory, Saint Nicholas, and Saint Agatha at Tarsia, at the place Pectianum, with all their property and appurtenances, under a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold.

[Note: In Calabria; cited in Gattula, *Historia*, p. 934.]

28. In the following period, as the same abbot was going to Capua, he had the chapel of Saint Angel ad Formas, newly built in honor of Saint Nicholas, dedicated by Bruno, bishop of Segni and monk of this monastery; Sennus, archbishop of Capua, was also summoned for this purpose. After the dedication had taken place, on the following day the same archbishop assembled a multitude of Capuans and other men and sent them armed to violate the same church, destroy its altar, and carry off its relics to himself. When this had been done, he complained against our abbot and the bishop just named that they had acted against the canons toward him in that dedication, not yielding to him as metropolitan in matters which it is fitting for an archbishop to perform. But our people and the said bishop asserted that they had done in agreement all that had occurred there.

When our people brought a complaint on this matter at Rome in synod, the same archbishop humbly promised that, together with the clergy and people of the city, he would make honorable reparation for the invasion of the church, destruction of the altar, and violence against the relics. And he did so.

At the request of our brethren, this abbot granted and confirmed to them the castle of Citraria with its appurtenances.

29. At that time, therefore, when the brethren were enduring many kinds of need, they complained of this to our abbot Otto [Note: “Octoni” in c.], and begged him, in accordance with the just command of the Rule [Note: Rule, ch. 64], to provide them with the necessities of the body [Note: “tribuant” in c.]; reminding him that, in the time of Father Oderisius, he himself had often made the same complaint to the said Oderisius. But the abbot, bearing this very indignantly and bitterly, confessed that he had sinned; he confessed that he had acted wrongly in having often opposed and contradicted Abbot Oderisius. He said that the brethren were offending both against God and against the Rule of Father Benedict, in preferring bodily necessities to the salvation of their souls; that they ought to remember that one must first seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to them (Matt. 6:33).

Why say more? Seeing that the same abbot was striving, contrary to the command of Father Benedict [Note: Rule, ch. 64], to be feared rather than loved, some of the brethren, without the knowledge of the rest, secretly sent letters to the aforesaid Pope Paschal, stating that he had not been elected by the unanimous consent of the brethren, but had been promoted to the office of the abbacy of Cassino tumultuously and by no means canonically. This charge, therefore, rendered the Roman pontiff wholly hostile to the same abbot. When the abbot learned with absolute certainty that this had been done by the brethren, he seized an occasion against them and expelled them from the monastery.

The brethren expelled from Cassino went to Rome and set forth before the pontiff, in order, the deeds and words involved. The pontiff sent the same brethren to remain at the monastery of the blessed Apostle Paul, and decided that some of them should stay with him in his own court. Leaving the City on ecclesiastical business and entering Gaul, he came to the monastery of Fleury, consecrated in the name of Father Benedict ([11 July] 1107) [Col. 0853B]. At that time the celebration of the utterly false translation of Saint Benedict was being held there. Declaring that translation false, the pontiff began, with the Italian cardinals, to celebrate not the office of the feast but that of the day.

But when the monks of the aforesaid place, together with certain Gallican bishops and cardinals, began to celebrate the translation, the pope poured out prayer to the Lord, earnestly entreating Him to deign to show him a sign of the truth in this matter. While they were celebrating the nocturnal synaxis, such stupefaction and dullness of mind seized them that they did not at all know what they were saying. Astonished by so great a miracle, they began without impediment to sing the regular office; for as soon as they intended to celebrate the chant of the translation, they were filled at once with horror and stupefaction [Col. 0853C]. When the most reverend pontiff observed this, he began to glorify and bless God and Benedict His servant.

When morning came, he summoned to himself the abbot and the priors of the monastery and ordered the altar to be removed from its place, so that all might openly learn whether that translation was true or not. He was unwilling that anyone should any longer be deceived by their evasions concerning the body of Saint Benedict, since he knew with complete certainty that the body had been found in the monastery of Cassino in the time of Pope Alexander. But they fell at his feet and began to beg him not to order the altar excavated, lest he destroy the monastery. They said that they possessed no certainty concerning the body of Saint Benedict, but only a report received from their elders; that, if the relics were not found [Col. 0853D], they knew with certainty that the monastery must be destroyed and its possessions plundered by anyone whatever.

Then the pope, moved by their prayers, kept silence, strictly forbidding and, on the authority of the Apostolic See, commanding that they should by no means thereafter presume to celebrate that utterly false translation. [Note: “There is neither force nor obligation to believe anything of all this. MEO. III, Ides of July: the pope was at Privas, on the Rhône. Mansi XX, 1025.”] The same apostolic lord, having arranged his affairs in Gaul, returned to Rome.

And because, as noted above, the aforesaid pontiff had been exceedingly stirred by what our men had done concerning the election of the abbot of Cassino [Col. 0854A], he admonished the brethren whom our abbot had sent to him to observe, in the election of an abbot, the ordinances of Father Benedict. When they maintained that the election of the abbot had been made by the unanimous consent of the brethren, and said that he had been promoted to that office not tumultuously but canonically, the pope replied:

> “How was your abbot canonically elected, when he granted obediences to those devoted and faithful to himself, and expelled his opponents from the monastery? But now return to the monastery. There, after his election has been fully examined by me or by my envoys, I shall determine what is canonical.”

After they had departed, those who hated the aforesaid abbot, recognizing that the apostolic lord had been moved against him, did not cease to inflict upon him whatever injuries they could [Col. 0854B]. Meanwhile, since the counts of Aquino did not at all cease their harassment of this place, the same abbot turned his mind to restraining their wickedness. He fortified each of the monastery’s castles with a surrounding rampart and caused the country people, who until then had lived in villages, to reside there. Thus he began in every way to prepare himself against the same counts.

It seems fitting, indeed, to append to the present history for the memory of posterity a miracle which Almighty God deigned to display in this monastery, to the praise and glory of His name.

30. At that very time, while John surnamed Affidatus had given his limbs to nocturnal sleep in a small dwelling adjoining the tower of Father Benedict [Note: See Gregory, *Dialogues* II.35, and Angelo de Nuce there; Gattola, *History*, p. 15.], he awoke and heard angels celebrating a sweet-sounding office before the nocturnal synaxis in the little chapel of the blessed Father [Col. 0854C]. Amazed by this, he asked Sebastian, who was resting beside him, whether the brethren had already risen for the night office. Sebastian replied that the first watch of the night still remained. Then the aforesaid John rose and approached the tower, which a fragrance of immense radiance and unheard-of scent filled.

Astonished, and perceiving what was in fact occurring, he went to Abbot Otto and related in order the things which had been seen and heard. Giving thanks to Almighty God, Otto determined that, in accordance with what had been revealed to Victor III, pope of venerable memory, and to Theodemar, servant of God [Note: “I have vainly tried to discover what this means.”], the aforesaid tower, with a spacious habitation, should be dedicated as an oratory of the Lord Saviour and of His mother, the Virgin Mary [Col. 0854D]. Having summoned workmen, he constructed a cellar between the dormitory and the church dedicated to Saint Stephen the protomartyr; but, overtaken by death, he was unable to complete it.

The sweetness of the aforesaid melody, the fragrance of the scent, and the immensity of the light are said by ancient men to have been seen and heard in the aforesaid tower on principal feasts; but especially, every year, when the day of the deposition of the blessed Father Benedict approaches, they are customarily heard and seen [Col. 0855A].

The aforesaid abbot died on the Kalends of October (1 October) 1107, and was buried beside the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle, in the cemetery of the brethren, on the left as one enters the aforesaid cemetery.

**The most blessed BRUNO, fortieth abbot of this monastery, held office for three years and ten months.**

31. Born in the province of Liguria from the distinguished stock of the citizens of Asti, but possessing from childhood still more distinguished qualities [Note: Read *illustriores*, “more distinguished.”], and adequately educated from boyhood in liberal studies, he became a canon of the bishopric of Asti [Note: “Rather, of Siena.”]. Desiring the kingdom of heaven, he left homeland and parents, and hastened to Rome, intending to come to this place so that he might serve God more freely under the monastic habit [Col. 0855B].

In those days (1079), Pope Urban II [Note: Gregory VII.] presided over the universal Church. It happened that, at the time when this man was making his way to this place, the bishop of Segni died. The same most reverend pontiff, seeing him fervent in divine service, said to him:

> “Just as the calm of the sea often brings danger to sailors, so for monks removed from the storm of the world, rest and security themselves are apt to bring a most ruinous shipwreck. Therefore it is fitting that you obey our admonitions and strive to govern the care of the church of Segni, which is imposed upon you by us, with so much the greater diligence and devotion as you possess learning and wisdom.”

When he would by no means assent to these words, the pope ordered him to proceed to the aforesaid city and, after ordaining a bishop there in the stead of the Roman pontiff, to go wherever he wished.
