The aforesaid man arrived there; and while he was attempting to carry out what had been imposed upon him, the same pope secretly sent letters to the people of Segni commanding that he be ordained bishop.

When these things came to his knowledge, he left the church of Blessed Mary in the silence of a stormy night and took flight. But as he endeavoured to carry out his plan, at a certain crossroads a virgin adorned in imperial dress, whose face shone like the sun, stood at a distance before him. When he asked her whence she came, who and what she was, and where she was going, she replied:

> “Know that I am the bride from whom you are not rightly fleeing. Therefore, on behalf of Almighty God, I command you to return to the church; and beware lest you should wish any longer to resist the will of God.”

Having said this, she vanished. Bruno, struck by so great an utterance of the Virgin and perceiving God’s will in his ordination, yielded, and, amid the rejoicing of all, accepted the episcopal throne [Col. 0855D].

Once ordained, however, he remained fixed in the intention he had previously held. Therefore, finding an opportunity, he came to this place under the aforesaid Abbot Oderisius. Those who had come with him wept, suspecting nothing of the kind concerning him, while he became a monk [Col. 0856A]. The people of Segni, grievously distressed at his absence, went to Pope Paschal II and begged him to compel Bruno to take up the care of his bishopric rather than, considering only himself, to wish to rest in quiet in the monastery of Cassino, remote from the storm of the world.

The pontiff, moved by their words, sent vigorous men from his side, through whom he ordered Bruno on behalf of the Apostolic See to devote himself to the care of his sheep and always to adhere to the Roman pontiff in ecclesiastical affairs. Moreover, he rebuked and reproved him for having dared, without the permission of the Apostolic See, to seek a monastery in which he himself would by no means permit him to remain [Col. 0856B].

To this the aforesaid Bruno wrote in reply [Note: “Either Bruno, or, as I think more likely, Peter here borrowed both sense and wording from Peter Damian, *Opusc.* 19, *On the Abdication of a Bishopric*.”]:

> “Undoubtedly all who are in the Roman Church know that, unless the madness of schism had raged against the Church, I should have fulfilled in deed, many years ago, what I have now done. But now, since Peter holds the helm in the Roman Church, the whole Church of Christ our God rejoices throughout the world; the whirlwinds of the winds are now silent, and the seas rest in calm. Therefore I am compelled to fulfil what I once vowed to God. For it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfil it (Eccl. 5:4).
>
> “But if anyone perhaps objects to me that I ought not to abandon a bishopric once received, I freely answer that there are many who do not abandon the rights of the pontificate and yet stand at the left hand, as the Lord says: ‘They became rulers, and I did not acknowledge them; they became judges, and not by my Spirit’ (Hos. 8:4) [Col. 0856C]. But those who, with a right intention, have relinquished a bishopric are certainly known to rejoice eternally with Christ in everlasting blessedness.
>
> “Nor do I lack examples of saints whose footsteps I have followed, who, leaving the tumult of the world, attained a quiet life. Therefore through you I earnestly entreat the supreme pontiff that he may not hereafter trouble me further; and I humbly beg that he not compel me to leave the peaceful harbour to which, under Christ’s guidance, I have come.”

Since by no argument he could bend either the same apostolic lord or the people of Segni, the aforesaid Abbot Oderisius asked the pontiff to permit the aforesaid man to serve God in this monastery under the monastic habit [Col. 0856D; Note: “the words *habitu in* are lacking in c.”], and that, in return for this concession, supported by the pontiff’s aid, he would spend forty days in the service of the Roman Church and [of] Segni [lacuna]. The same pope gave ear and acquiesced.

After this, sent into Gaul by the same pontiff and by our abbot [Note: “With the permission of his abbot V[.....]. Bruno.”], together with Bohemond, prince of Antioch [Note: As reported above; “We have found nothing about this legation.”], he held, in the stead of the Roman pontiff, a synod in those regions according to ecclesiastical tradition ([June] 1106) [Note: Poitiers; Mansi XX, 1205]. Returning thence also to Rome, on the forty-fourth day after the death of Abbot Otto he returned to this monastery, and the brethren placed him over the government and care of this coenobium ([13 November] 1107) [Col. 0857A].

The same apostolic lord later came to this place and declared before the assembly of brethren not only that Bruno was worthy to be abbot, but also testified that he would be a worthy successor to himself in the Apostolic See. Nor should it be thought that this man lived here idly, since he expounded for us such and so many books of Scripture. We shall disclose a summary of those which have come into our hands [Note: Compare *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 34, and Marum there]: on the Psalter; on Genesis; on Exodus; on Leviticus; on Numbers; on Deuteronomy; on Isaiah; on the Song of Songs; on Judges; and on the Apocalypse. He also composed sixty-nine sermons and 155 homilies for the feasts and Sundays of the whole year [Col. 0857B].

32. Moreover, at this time ([July] 1108), Adenulf, Lando, and Adenulf, counts of Aquino, drunk with diabolical madness, entered the castle of Terame through the treachery of its rustics, compelled the inhabitants of that castle to swear fealty to them, and began to plunder the towns belonging to the monastery. When this was reported to the aforesaid abbot, he sent to the same counts and began to admonish them to restore the castle to the monastery and desist from such great wickedness and plundering [Col. 0857C].

But they despised not only doing what he said, but even hearing it, and each day threatened worse things [Note: The text prints *mirabantur*; perhaps *minabantur*, “they threatened”?]. Then the abbot, having taken counsel with the brethren, separated these sacrilegious men from the thresholds of the church, and immediately summoned Prince Robert and invited him to recover the same castle. Robert gathered a very large army, came against the castle, and began to besiege it by every means. When he had remained there in hostile fashion for nearly fifteen days, the same counts sent to the abbot, offering that, if he would allow them to depart thence with their arms, they would immediately restore the castle to the monastery without any dispute.

When the abbot agreed, he recovered the aforesaid castle into the power of this monastery on the Ides of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1108 [Col. 0857D]. For that castle the same abbot paid the prince of Capua two hundred pounds.

33. When October arrived, the same apostolic lord came to this place and, having associated our abbot with himself [Col. 0858A], went to Benevento to celebrate a synod. There, following the footsteps of his predecessors, he decreed that whoever received the investiture of a church or an ecclesiastical dignity from the hand of a layman, and both giver and recipient, should be deprived of communion. He rebuked clerics for secular and costly clothing and forbade them to use such garments.

When he came to Capua, at the request of the same abbot he solemnly dedicated the church of Saint Benedict which Abbot Desiderius had restored within that city. There also he deposited garments of the most holy Father Benedict. Thus, having come to this monastery, he returned to Rome.

34. In these days ([November] 1110), Duke Roger made a decree for Saint Benedict concerning the sheep of this place [Note: In Tosti II, 97]: that neither he nor his successors should thereafter demand from them any payment or rent throughout all the territory of Mount Gargano; and that they should always have permission to lodge with the same sheep from the church called Passari as far as the bridge of Salpi, called the Lombards’ bridge, as far as the sea, and as far as the Ford of the Fig, under penalty of ten pounds of gold [Col. 0858B].

At that time ([September] 1108), Laidulf, son of Count Pandulf of Presenzano [Note: See ch. 12; Gattola, *Acc.*, 22], in the presence of the same abbot acknowledged and renounced his claim to his distinguished share in the castle of Mortula, Casa Fortini, Cucuruczu, and Rocca de Bantra, subject to a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold should he seek to revoke this.

John, bishop of the see of Trivento, together with Robert, son of Tristayn [Note: *Trostayni* in the charter in Gattola, *History*, p. 421; Limosano is situated in the county of Molise, on the Biferno.], lord of the castle of Limosano [Col. 0858C], likewise offered this place the church of Saint Illuminata, within the boundaries of the aforesaid castle of Limosano, at the place called Petra Maggiore, with all its churches and appurtenances, imposing a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold upon anyone seeking to revoke this ([June] 1109).

It seems altogether worthy to record here the wickedness and fraud of Alferius, bishop of Trivento [Note: He was already bishop in 1084; see Di Meo, *Annals*, at that year]. For, while he was provost in the same church of Blessed Illuminata, he knew that the aforesaid church had been subject, from the beginning of its foundation, to the monastery of Saint Eustasius and had been granted to that monastery in the same place by the princes of Benevento. Yet desiring at the same time to withdraw it from the jurisdiction of that monastery, he approached the provost who then presided over the monastery and humbly began to beg him to show him the charters of that place, saying that charters concerning his inheritance had been deposited there. He asked that he be allowed to remove them from there, lest perhaps they perish through age [Col. 0858D].

The provost, suspecting no fraud in his words, gave him permission both to search and to carry documents away [Col. 0859A]. At last, among the other documents, he found the decree made by the Beneventan princes concerning the church of Saint Illuminata for the monastery of Saint Eustasius. It clearly and openly stated how that church had been granted by the princes of Benevento to the monastery of Blessed Eustasius from the beginning of its foundation. Moved by envy of this and drunk with wicked madness, he stole it, concealed it, and, on returning to his own house, cut it into tiny pieces.

I heard that these things had happened from the mouth of Albert, a monk of this our coenobium, then living almost to extreme old age, lest anyone should suppose this account falsely written.

35. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, indiction 3, on the sixth day of June, a comet appeared. At the same time the aforesaid Pope Paschal II left the City and came into these regions. Summoning the duke and prince and all the counts of Apulia, Calabria, and the Principality, he received from them assurances that they would aid him against Emperor Henry, should necessity press upon him and they be called upon to do so [Col. 0859B]. When this had been done, he returned to Rome and bound all the Roman magnates by a similar oath.

Meanwhile Emperor Henry, gathering an exceedingly great army, entered Italy in December, wishing to receive from the same pontiff at Rome the dignities and rights of his predecessors, the ancient emperors, and the imperial crown. Thus he hurried his march daily. It was already winter (1111); and, when he had come into Tuscany, envoys were sent to Rome [Col. 0859C]. In the portico of Saint Peter, with Peter Leo and other envoys of the pontiff, the following agreement was deliberated between them (February):

That the emperor should, in writing, renounce in the pope’s hand, before clergy and people, on the day of his coronation, every investiture of all churches; and that, after the pope had acted concerning the regalia as written in another charter, he should confirm this by oath and leave the churches free, with offerings and possessions which did not manifestly belong to the kingdom, and should release peoples from oaths made against bishops.

He should restore and grant the patrimonies and possessions of Saint Peter, as had been done by Charles, Louis, Henry, and other emperors, and should help them to retain them [Note: “adjuvavit” in c.] according to his ability. He should not, either by his own act or counsel or through a subordinate person, cause the same pope to lose the Roman papacy, his life, or his limbs, or to be taken by an evil capture; nor should any of his faithful men who had provided him security do so—namely Peter Leo with his sons, whose possessions they should diligently prevent from suffering harm—or any others [Col. 0859D] whom the pope might name to the emperor. If anyone harmed them, the king should faithfully assist them [Col. 0860A].

For the observance of this security, he should give the same pontiff as guarantors Frederick [Note: Duke of Germany.], son of his sister; Margraves Engelbert [Note: of Istria.] and Theobald [Note: of Vohburg.]; Counts Herman and Godfrey; Count Palatine Frederick of Saxony; Berengar of Bavaria; Frederick the Saxon; Chancellor Albert; Cuno, Berengar’s brother; Sigeboth of Bavaria; Henry, duke of Carinthia; and Bertulf, son of Duke Bertulf. They were to swear to the pope security for his life, limbs, papacy, and freedom from capture. If the emperor did not observe all these foregoing conditions, they were to hold themselves, with their honours, bound to the Roman Church.

For the pope’s security, the king promised to give hostages on the following Thursday, and to send safely to the island under papal control his nephew Duke Frederick, Bruno bishop of Speyer, Conrad the nephew of Count Herman and Conrad’s son, and Henry, brother of Count Frederick [Col. 0860B]. If the pope received the hostages, he was to return them on the day of the coronation after the bridge had been crossed; and if perhaps the emperor were not crowned or did not cross, he was likewise to return them at the Castle of Saint Angelo.

The pope’s legates sent to the king were to be kept safe, both going and returning, by the king and his men; and if injury were ignorantly inflicted upon them, he was faithfully to assist in making amends. After the king had fulfilled these terms, the pope was to command the bishops present on the day of his coronation to surrender to the emperor and kingdom the regalia that had belonged to the kingdom in the time of Charles, Louis, Henry, and the emperor’s other predecessors. He was to confirm this in writing, under anathema and by his authority and justice, so that none of them, present or absent, nor their successors, should meddle with or seize the regalia—namely cities, duchies, marches, counties, coinage, tolls, markets, imperial advocacies, the rights of centurions, and estates manifestly belonging to the empire with their appurtenances, imperial military forces and castles [Col. 0860C].

Nor was the pope thereafter to trouble the emperor or the Roman Empire concerning these matters; and he was to confirm it by privilege under anathema [Note: “not” in l. l.], so that his successors should not presume to trouble it. He should receive the emperor graciously and honourably, crown him knowingly and without reservation according to the custom of his predecessors, the Catholic emperors, and aid him by the assistance of his office in holding the empire.

If the pope did not fulfil this, Peter Leo and all his men were to hold themselves bound to the emperor [Col. 0860D]. Unless the hostages escaped, he was to return them on the second day after the coronation; if the failure to crown him were due to the pope, he was likewise to return them.

When this had been agreed between them (9 February), the emperor, Chancellor Albert, Counts Herman, Frederick, and Godfrey, Frederick the Saxon, Cuno brother of Berengar, Sigeboth of Bavaria, Henry duke of Carinthia, Bertulf son of Duke Bertulf, and Chancellor Albert swore to it [Col. 0861A; Note: “Here one may reproach either Peter’s or the scribe’s negligence.”]. All these, after the emperor, swore in this order that, if the emperor should refuse to fulfil it, they with all their men would hold themselves bound to the Roman Church.

36. After these matters had thus been ratified, the same apostolic lord sent him letters [Note: “We do not possess them.”] in which he commanded him to give thanks to the Enlightener of all, who had deigned to enlighten the eyes of his heart so that he might recognize more inwardly and abhor more deeply his father’s wickedness, already notorious throughout the whole world. For the Apostolic See would receive him with fatherly kindness as one fleeing to the bosom of the eternal Father, and would wish to cherish him more familiarly among the children of Mother Church.

For if, as he promised by the declaration of his letters to the Apostolic See [Col. 0861B], he should take care to render, with full devotion of mind, obedience to the pope and his legitimate successors such as Catholic kings and emperors had rendered to the pope’s predecessors, then the pope would assuredly regard him as a Catholic emperor, preserve his honour by God’s grace, and endeavour to increase it. For if he wished to persist in the probity he had undertaken, great salvation would accrue to the Roman Empire through obedience to the Apostolic See [Note: Lauretius reads thus; R. has *magnam*, c. “salvation”]. For that reason he was prepared not merely to come to those regions but to expose his own person even to the utmost dangers.

But since the present condition of the times and affairs did not permit him to come to the emperor in person, he could make his will known through his own envoys, and the emperor could communicate his. Meanwhile the emperor requested that he permit his father’s corpse to be buried in a church [Col. 0861C]. The pope replied that the authority of Holy Scripture stood in his way and the reverence due to divine miracles forbade it. For he knew that God’s martyrs themselves, now set in heaven, had terribly demanded that the corpses of wicked men be driven from their basilicas, so that we who do not communicate with them while alive may not communicate with them when dead.

In February the emperor swiftly moved his camp toward the City. The pontiff, dispatching exhortatory letters everywhere, did not cease to invite the Normans and Lombards to the service of the Roman Church; but he who bore words received words. After this the emperor came to Rome on the third Ides of February, that is, the Saturday before Quinquagesima (11 February) [Col. 0861D]. When the Romans pressed him to confirm by oath the honour and liberty of the City, Caesar, wishing craftily to deceive them, swore in the Teutonic language that he desired what was just. Some Romans, however, recognizing this and crying out that there was deceit in the affair, withdrew into the City.

[Col. 0862A]

37. Therefore, when the pontiff learned that the emperor had arrived, he sent envoys to request security and hostages from him. Caesar gave him hostages and received hostages from him, and confirmed by oath security for the life, honour, limbs, and freedom from evil capture of the apostolic lord himself; also concerning the regalia and patrimonies of Saint Peter, specifically concerning Apulia, Calabria, Sicily, and the principality of Capua. Oaths were likewise made that he would leave entirely undisturbed all investitures of churches [Note: “investituram” in c.] and their property.

On the following day (12 February), the pontiff sent out to meet him at Mount of Joy, also called Marius’s Mount, banner-bearers of candles, cross-bearers, eagle-bearers, lion-bearers, wolf-bearers, dragon-bearers, men in white, defenders, grooms, and a very great multitude of people with flowers and palms [Note: c: “a very great multitude met him with branches”; Register of Paschal]. According to the custom of previous emperors, he swore two oaths: one at the bridge, the other before the gate of the portico, to the Roman people [Col. 0862B]. Before the gate he was received by Jews singing; at the gate, by Greeks singing.

There all the clergy of the city of Rome had assembled at the pope’s command, and they led him, after he dismounted from his horse, with acclamations as far as the steps of Saint Peter. When he had ascended the upper steps, Lord Pope Paschal was present there with many bishops, cardinal-priests and cardinal-deacons, subdeacons, and the other ministers of the choir school. On seeing him, the emperor dismounted and fell at his feet; then, rising, he gave him peace in the name of the Trinity upon mouth, forehead, and eyes, and performed the office of groom. Immediately, holding the pontiff’s right hand, he came amid great joy and shouting of the peoples to the silver gate [Col. 0862C].

There he made the imperial profession from the book and was designated emperor by the pontiff, and was again kissed by the pontiff. Then the bishop of Labicum pronounced over him the first prayer, as contained in the order [Note: David the Scot, appended to William of Malmesbury V, p. 423, *On the Deeds*, 13 April: “and when the prayer contained in the order had been begun by the bishop of Ostia, because the bishop of Albano was absent, by whom it should have been said had he been present.” The bishopric of Labicum seems by then to have been united with that of Albano. The Roman Order edited by Jean Mabillon has “the bishop of Albano” here. Richard, bishop of Albano, was then in Gaul.].

After entering the basilica, when he had come to the porphyry wheel, both men sat down after their seats had been placed. The pontiff demanded the restoration of investiture and the other provisions written in the charter of agreement, himself ready to fulfil the provisions contained in the other charter of agreement. The emperor withdrew with his bishops and princes into the part by the secretarium; there they deliberated at length as they pleased. Three Lombard bishops participated in this discussion: Bernard of Parma [Col. 0862D], Boso the Elder of Reggio, and Aldo of Piacenza.

As the hour was prolonged, the pontiff sent envoys and demanded that the tenor of the aforesaid agreement be fulfilled. Then the transalpine bishops fell at the pontiff’s feet and rose to kiss them. But shortly afterward the king’s intimates began little by little to disclose their deceits, saying that the written agreement could not be confirmed by authority and justice [Col. 0863A]. Although evangelical and apostolic authority was urged against them—that what is Caesar’s must be rendered to Caesar (Matt. 22:21), that no one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs (2 Tim. 2:4), and that, according to Saint Ambrose, one who acts thus is alien to the episcopal office—yet, although these and other apostolic and canonical authorities were brought against them, they persisted in their deceit and obstinacy.

38. Meanwhile, the emperor, wishing to deceive the pontiff by his assertions, said:

> “I wish the dispute which has hitherto existed between you and Stephen surnamed the Norman now to be brought to an end.”

For this Stephen had endured many dangers on account of his loyalty to the emperor. The pope replied:

> “The day has for the most part passed, and today’s office will be lengthy. Therefore, if it please you, let that which is yours first be fulfilled.”

But one of those who had come with the emperor immediately stood up in the midst and said:

> “Why are so many words needed? Know without doubt that our lord emperor wishes to receive the crown in the same manner as Charles, Pippin, and Louis received it.”

When the pope said that he could not fulfil this, Caesar, angered and led astray by the counsel of Albert, archbishop of Mainz [Note: Then chancellor.], and Burchard, bishop of the Saxons [Note: Of Münster.], did not fear to surround him with his armed soldiers. But as the day was already declining toward evening, the brethren advised that the emperor be crowned that same day and that discussion of the remaining matters be deferred until the following week. They rejected this also [Col. 0863C].

Meanwhile both the pontiff and all who were with him were held under guard by armed soldiers. At last they scarcely ascended to the altar of Saint Peter to hear the offices of the Mass; they could scarcely find bread, wine, and water for the performance of the divine sacraments. After Mass, the pontiff was compelled to descend from the chair and sat below, before the confession of Saint Peter, with the brethren. There, guarded by armed soldiers until the darkness of night, he was then led with the brethren to lodging outside the atrium of the church.

A considerable multitude of clergy and laity was captured with him. The emperor also mutilated, stripped, beat, or held captive boys, persons of various ages, and clerics who had gone out to meet him with flowers and palms [Col. 0863D]. Meanwhile John, bishop of Tusculum, and Leo of Ostia, seeing the pope held in chains, put on plebeian dress and withdrew into the City.

39. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0863D] The passage from “Therefore” to “they led away” is contained in book I in a few words. It seems to me that here it is set out more accurately from Leo’s account.], when the Romans heard that the pope had been captured, sudden uproar, grief, and lamentation seized them; immediately they put to death Germans who had entered the city for prayer, business, or sightseeing. But on the following day (13 February), going out from the City, [Col. 0864A] they joined battle; killing many of the emperor’s army and taking their spoils, they fought fiercely against the Teutons, so that they almost drove them from the portico, even throwing the emperor himself from his horse and wounding him in the face. When Count Otto of Milan saw this [Note: Cf. Landulf the Younger, 18.], he offered himself to death for the emperor and surrendered his horse; without delay, he was captured by the Romans and led into the City, cut to pieces limb by limb, and his flesh was left in the street to be devoured by dogs.

Then the emperor, seeing the Romans’ victory and the destruction of his own men, cried out and said: “Do you see, my soldiers, that I am being killed by the Romans, and yet you do not defend me?” At this cry one could see the swords of Germans and Romans flashing, some men being cut open from the head down to the breast; nor was there any respite for the dying. What a most destructive day that was for the Romans and their enemies, when so many thousands of men lay slain on either side! The River Tiber itself seemed reddened and stained with the blood of the slain. Day was now turning toward sunset when the Teutons, exhausted by battle, began to withdraw from the fight; for their courage, as Eutropius says [Note: I have not found this in Eutropius. Cf. Plutarch, *Marius*, ch. 26; Orosius V.15; *Historia Miscella*, book V.], just as it is greater than that of others in the first onset, is afterwards weaker than women’s. For they have something in common with their snows: as soon as they are touched by heat, they fail, turned into sweat, and melt away as though by the sun.

Therefore, when the Romans saw that the Cimbri had abandoned the battle, they turned to spoil and plunder; laden with the spoils of the slain, they began to return into the City. When Caesar noticed this, he ordered his men to attack together the Romans returning into the City burdened with spoils. When this was done, more died by crushing and suffocation than by the sword. Thus, amid so great a disturbance, fortune and the outcomes were various. But when the Teutons reached the Castle of Crescentius, the Romans, hurling spears from the castle, put them to flight. Moved by all these events, the Germans saw their camp being filled by the multitude of Romans and their army being hard pressed; they withdrew into their camp, and such terror seized them that throughout the following two days (14–15 February), by day and night, they remained under arms.

When night came, the bishop of Tusculum summoned all the Roman people and said to them:

> “Although words, dearest sons, do not add courage to us, nor make the vigorous out of the weak, nor restore the strong out of the timid: yet every cause is yours—for life, for glory, for liberty, for the defence of the Apostolic See. For you bear all these things in your right hands [Note: The wording from “Words” through “timid” was noted by the distinguished Stenzel as taken from Sallust, *Catiline* 58.].
>
> “For whoever desires peace, let him prepare for war” [Note: The editor observes that he feebly imitates Catiline.]. Your sons are held in chains against right and justice, and the basilica of the Apostle Peter, revered throughout the whole world, is filled with arms, corpses, and blood. What else can we say of this except evil? For the Church has been utterly crushed and laid waste. We therefore ask and beseech you to assist it and rise with all your strength to avenge so great an outrage; for where are the men to withstand them? They are swifter to flee than to resist. Trusting in the mercy of God and [Note: “and” also seems to be missing.] of ourselves, and of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, we absolve you from all sins.”

Thus encouraged by this exhortation, the Romans all bound themselves together by oath against the emperor and decreed that all who aided them should be regarded as brothers. When this was reported to the emperor, that same night he carried off the apostolic lord from there and fled from the portico with his army in such fear [Col. 0865B] that he left behind not only baggage but also many companions in their lodgings. Two days later, summoning his soldiers, he ordered the pontiff stripped of his garments. When this had been done, they bound him in chains and took him with them.

Then, proceeding as far as the foot of Mount Soracte, they crossed the channel of the Tiber beside the monastery of Saint Andrew and, travelling through Sabine territory to the bridge of Lucanus [Note: Where the Anio is crossed, below Tibur.], advanced into the more distant regions of the Roman city. Meanwhile some clergy and laypeople were dragged along bound with ropes. The pontiff, with two bishops—namely, the bishop of Sabina [Note: Crescentius.] and the bishop of Porto [Note: Peter.]—and four cardinals, was held at the castle of Trebicum; the other cardinals were held under guard at Corcodilum. No Latin dared speak with the pontiff. He was guarded by the emperor’s magnates and was even attended by them; but finally, both because of suspicion and for the sake of an agreement, he was brought back to the camp. This apostolic lord remained in that prison-cell for sixty-one days.

Meanwhile John, bishop of Tusculum, did not cease by letters to encourage, urge, and strengthen the spirits of the faithful to bring relief and assistance to the afflicted and abandoned Apostolic See. Then the prince, arriving at Paternaria with his followers, selected nearly three hundred knights and sent them to help the Romans. Arriving at Ferentino, they found Ptolemy and all the leading men of those regions favourable to the emperor. The emperor, however, had already crossed the Tiber with his whole army; consequently, since they could not enter the City, they returned to Capua.

40. While these disturbances were in progress, Duke Roger died, together with his brother Bohemond [Note: Anonymous of Cassino, under 1111; *Necrology of Cassino*, at 9 Kalends of March and the Nones of March.]. Their death brought great fear to the Normans, but the greatest boldness to the emperor, his army, and all the Lombards. [Col. 0866A] For they had indeed been greatly alarmed by the emperor’s arrival, fearing that they might be expelled from the principalities, Apulia, or Calabria; all chose strongly fortified places and built fortifications there against the emperor’s coming.

The prince, after taking counsel with his men, sent envoys to the emperor, seeking peace and security from him. Thus, although the emperor daily ravaged the Romans’ lands and tempted their minds by deceit and money, God granted the people such steadfastness that he could conclude no peace with them without the liberation of the pope and cardinals. Meanwhile he was distracted by various counsels; but, conscious of the crime he had committed, he thought that nothing further would be safe for him in the pope’s presence. Seeing, therefore, that what he had not expected had happened to him, he began to affirm on oath [Col. 0866B] that unless the pontiff complied with his will and carried it out, he would deal with the pontiff himself and all those whom he held in chains, killing some and mutilating others.

But when he could not bend the pontiff in this matter, he finally resolved, after full deliberation, to free all whom he had captured, provided that he secured from the pope a guarantee for the future. He busily pursued this, through his princes, through clergy, through laymen, and through Roman citizens. Yet the lord pope preferred to risk his life rather than consent to the investitures of bishoprics and abbeys, although the emperor claimed that by those investitures he conferred not churches or any offices, but royal rights alone. The gravest danger of schism was proposed, threatening [Col. 0866C] almost the whole Latin Church. Yet overcome by the sufferings of his sons, oppressed by heavy sighs and groans and wholly poured out in tears, he said: “I am compelled, for the liberation and peace of the Church, to endure and permit that to which I would by no means consent for the sake of my own life.”

For the bishops and cardinals who had been captured were demanded to confirm this guarantee; and otherwise neither the release of the captives nor, so far as it depended on them, the Church’s peace could be obtained. Since Count Albert of Blanderada and the other courtiers of the emperor would not permit the conditions to be set down in writing under oath, the pontiff said: “Since you do not permit the condition to be written down, I shall add it verbally.” Then, turning wholly to the emperor, he said: “We make these oaths to you in order that you may perform and observe the things which you have agreed.” The emperor and all his men assented most gladly and willingly.

Accordingly, on the pope’s word, they swore (11 April), in the field beside the bridge of Mammeus [Note: Ponte Mammolo, where the Tiburtine Way crosses the Anio.], which separated the Romans from the Teutons, [Col. 0867A] in the following manner: that the pope would no further trouble the emperor or his empire concerning the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys, or concerning injury done to him and his men in persons and property; that he would not repay any evil to the emperor [Note: Perhaps *imperatori*, “to the emperor”?] or to any person on account of this matter; and that he would never at all lay anathemas upon the person of the emperor. He would grant to that emperor and his empire, and confirm by his privilege under anathema [Note: The manuscript reads *confirmat*, “confirms.”], that bishops and abbots freely elected, with the emperor’s assent and without simony, should be invested by that emperor with ring and staff; and that a bishop so invested should freely receive consecration from the archbishop to whom it belonged.

If anyone should be elected by the people and clergy, he was not to be consecrated by anyone unless invested by the emperor; and archbishops and bishops should have liberty to consecrate those invested by the emperor. The pope would help him hold the kingdom, empire, and patriciate by the aid of his office. After confirming this by oath, the emperor at last swore that he would release that pontiff with the bishops and cardinals, and all captives taken with him or for his sake, and the hostages; that he would convey them safely within the gates of the Transtiberine city and would neither capture them further nor permit them to be captured.

He would preserve peace and security, both personally and through his men, for those remaining loyal to the Apostolic See and for the people of the Roman city, in their persons and property. If they kept peace with him, he would faithfully assist that pope, so that [Note: The manuscript has “and.”] he might hold the papacy securely and peacefully; he would restore the patrimonies and possessions of the Roman Church which he had taken; he would faithfully help him recover and hold, in the manner of his predecessors, all other goods which he ought by right to possess; [Col. 0867C] and he would faithfully obey that pontiff, saving the honour of kingdom and empire, as Catholic emperors obey Catholic Roman pontiffs.

After this, Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; Gebhard of Trent; Burchard of Münster; Burchard [Note: Read Bruno.] of Speyer; Albert the chancellor; Frederick [Note: the Palatine.]; Hermann; Albert [Note: of Blanderada.]; Frederick [Note: the Saxon.]; Berengar [Note: of Bavaria.]; Frederick [Note: of Freising.]; Godfrey [Note: of Swabia.]; and the counts Guarnerius and Boniface, margrave [Note: Of Savona and Saluzzo, according to Muletti, *Saluzzo* I, 412.], swore in this manner.

There remained the element of demand and coercion: a privilege permitting investiture was to be written personally for the emperor. Neither he nor his courtiers allowed the preparation of the document to be deferred until they were within the City, where the pontiff’s seal had been left. Therefore, on the following day (12 April), in the same field called the Field of the Seven Brothers, while they were moving camp, it had to be dictated; and, after crossing the Tiber near the Salarian Bridge, while the camp was set up at the Eighth Milestone, a secretary summoned from the City drafted that document in the darkness of night. The pontiff subscribed it there, though certainly unwillingly. [Col. 0868A]

When the emperor received the charter there, later, after they had reached the church of Saint Peter and after the reception of the crown, he presented it to the pope’s hand and received it from that hand not only against the pope’s will but also contrary to all custom (13 April). The emperor was crowned with all gates of the Roman City shut, so that none of the citizens might approach him. When he came to the breaking of the host, taking one part himself and giving the other to the emperor, the pope said: “As this portion of the life-giving body has been divided, so may whoever tries to break this pact be divided from the kingdom of Christ and God.”

After the coronation, once the solemnities of the Mass were completed, the emperor at once went out to the camp in the field; [Col. 0868B] the pontiff entered the City. From this time scandals of dissension and schism began to arise in the Roman Church.

41. In these same days, when our abbot Bruno had solemnly dedicated the church of Saint Thomas the Apostle, situated outside the castle of Vallefredda, a certain woman whom an unclean spirit grievously afflicted was brought to him. Moved by compassion for her misfortune, after prayer he gave the suffering woman to drink water in which he had washed his hands, and immediately drove the devil from her.

At the same time, in the regions of Germany, a certain priest was teaching a little boy Psalm 113. Leaving him, he went elsewhere, and the boy, overcome by sleep, fell asleep. The priest soon returned, woke him, and commanded him to read [Col. 0868C] the psalm. But the frightened boy began to recite other verses from his heart. Rebuked by his teacher to say the psalm rather than verses, he began to repeat them more and more. The priest, understanding that the boy was speaking through the Spirit, began to write them down from his mouth. The verses are these:

> “The king shall die, and the bear shall be slain, and there shall be terror in the lodging-place. Sun and moon shall send forth their poison, and the stars shall rain blood. The queen shall be destroyed, and her kingdom shall not stand; and there shall be a survivor. The king of the Christians came forth from his mother’s womb; she who bore him killed him. His eyes are like burning torches, and his nails like *gris* [Note: Perhaps *gruis*, “of a crane”?].”

On the following day, when the boy was questioned, he declared that he knew nothing of this.

42. The aforementioned abbot, having joined to himself Guala, bishop of Reggio [Note: The manuscript has “Legionensis”; *c* reads “Regionensis.”], Robert of Pavia [Note: The manuscript has “Parisiensis”; *e* reads “Pasiensis.”] [Note: Cf. Orderic Vitalis I.x, p. 762.], and other cardinals, began in every way to urge the pontiff to tear up the privilege which he had made for the emperor and bind him with the bond of anathema. Those [Note: The words “Those … attempted” are slightly modified from words which Bruno himself subscribed in the letter to Peter of Porto, in Baronius, 1111, no. 31.] who had been in chains with the pope said:

> “What we formerly preached, we preach [Col. 0869A] with one unanimous voice; and what we condemned, we condemn.”

Others, however, not only did not [Note: *non* is not lacking in the codex.] condemn the things done against the Apostolic and universal Church, but even attempted quite shamelessly to defend them. Therefore, while the Apostolic Church was shaken by dissensions of this kind, it was reported to the pontiff that the aforementioned man was the leader and standard-bearer of that discord and scandal.

When the said abbot heard this, finding an opportunity, he said to him [Note: He did not say this, but wrote it. The words “My enemies … is not” are taken from the letter to the pope; the rest from the letter to Peter, bishop of Porto. Both were published by Baronius under 1111, nos. 30–31; the latter, to Peter, by Martène from the Cassinese codex, *Collectio* I, 627.]:

> “My enemies tell you that I do not love you and that I speak ill of you; but they lie. For I love you as I ought to love a father and lord, and while you live I wish to have no other pontiff, as I promised you with many others. Yet I hear my Saviour saying to me: ‘He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’” (Matthew 10:37).
>
> “And the Apostle says: ‘If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema, maranatha [“Our Lord, come!”]’” (1 Corinthians 16:22). “Therefore I ought to love you; but I ought to love more him who made both you and me. Nothing must ever be preferred to so great a love. But that covenant, so foul, so violent, made with such great treachery, so contrary to every piety and religion, I do not approve. For who can approve that in which faith is violated, the Church loses liberty, the priesthood is abolished, the one and singular door of the Church is shut, and many doors are opened, through which whoever enters is a thief and a robber?
>
> “We have the canons; we have the constitutions of the holy Fathers from the times of the Apostles [Col. 0869C] down to you. We must walk on the royal road and turn aside from it neither to one side nor the other. All the Apostles condemn [Note: Apostolic Canon.] and exclude from the communion of the faithful all who obtain a church through secular power; for laymen, however religious they may be, have no authority to dispose of a church. This constitution of the Apostles is holy; whoever contradicts it is not Catholic. But everyone who defends heresy is a heretic; and no one can say that this is not heresy, which the holy and apostolic Church has called heresy in many councils, and has condemned and excommunicated together with its authors.”

Such an address furnished material for envy and hatred between the pontiff and the abbot. Among other things which he then said against the same abbot, he declared: “Unless I hasten to remove the abbey from him, it will happen that by his arguments he will take from me the Roman pontificate.”

Accordingly he sent a letter from the City to that abbot [Note: The *Life of St Bruno*, *Acta Sanctorum*, July IV, 483, says that all this happened through a conspiracy of monks; the following events are also narrated there differently.], in which he ordered [Col. 0870A] that a bishop ought not at the same time to be an abbot, and that the Apostolic See should no longer tolerate any bishop presiding over so famous an abbey. He also sent letters to the brethren through Leo, bishop of Ostia and monk of this monastery, commanding them no longer to render obedience to that man, but to elect for themselves, regularly and according to God, an abbot; if they acted otherwise, he would establish separate abbots in all the cells subject to this monastery.

When the abbot heard this, summoning the brethren he began to set before them the disagreement that existed between himself and the pontiff over ecclesiastical matters. At the same time he advised them that, if they wished an abbot whom he himself would choose, he himself would protect and defend both them and this place according to his power. There was then in this monastery a brother named Peregrinus, a Ligurian by nation, shrewd in secular cunning, to whom he had resolved to give the abbey. When the brethren learned this, they told the abbot that, as long as he wished to preside by the right of an abbot, they would all obey him as father and lord; but if he wished to leave the abbey, they would yield the election due to them by the precept of the Rule to no one whatsoever, but would themselves, according to ancient custom, elect an abbot.

When he heard this, thinking that he would accomplish it by force, he summoned armed soldiers to his aid to guard the monastery. On the next day, while the brethren peacefully entered the church to celebrate Mass, suddenly there arrived a furious crowd armed with various weapons, asking who they were that refused to carry out the abbot’s will. The brethren, taking this very indignantly, [Col. 0870C] rushed upon them together and expelled them from the monastery. When this was reported to the abbot, he came up to the monastery and summoned the brethren to himself:

> “I do not wish scandal to arise between you and the Roman Church because of me. Therefore receive the pastoral staff which you entrusted to me.”

Immediately placing it on the altar and giving the brethren absolution, he returned to his bishopric. There, living in holy conduct happily until the times of Abbot Oderisius II, he departed from the world on the day before the Kalends of September [Note: Rather, on 15 Kalends of August, when he is honoured as a saint, A.D. 1123.]. He was buried in the city of Segni, in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God and Virgin; and the Lord has not ceased to perform miracles at his memorial to the present day.

In these days, after the death of Benedict, bishop of the church of Terracina, Gregory, a monk of this monastery from childhood and most learned in the holy Scriptures, was appointed bishop of that church by the Roman pontiff [Note: Cf. *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 32.]. Likewise, in the monastery of Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ, Amicus, dean of this [Col. 0871A] monastery of Cassino, was appointed abbot [Note: Cf. Muratori, *Scriptores Italici*, I, p. 517.]; and in the Roman Church Oderisius [Note: Called sacristan of Saint Agatha by the Pisan Pandect.] and Roscemannus [Note: Of Saint George; later rector of Benevento: Falco, under 1120.] were ordained cardinal-deacons.

**GIRARD, forty-first abbot of this monastery, sat for eleven years and three months.**

43. Descended from the most noble lineage of the counts of the Marsi, he was offered to almighty God in this monastery during the first years of his childhood, received by Abbot Desiderius, and made provost in the monastery of Saint Nicholas at Pica. Later, by Oderisius, who succeeded Desiderius in the government of the monastery, he was appointed dean of this place. But after Otto’s death, when Bruno had become abbot in the manner related above (ch. 31), the Roman pontiff, greatly disturbed by his election, as we have already said, [Col. 0871B] wrote to him ordering him to relinquish the abbey and seek his bishopric. Fearing the danger of schism and discord, he left the abbey. Afterwards the brethren assembled in chapter and, with unanimous agreement, Girard was appointed abbot (October 1111).

In these same days Duke Roger of Apulia died, and his son William was substituted in his place (21 February).

44. At that time a transalpine knight, Hugh, surnamed of Albaspina [Note: *Ahbaspina* in manuscript *c*.], served with his arms among many counts in these regions and earned rich pay; in very prosperous circumstances he enjoyed the pleasures of delightful youth. For he was both quick with his hand and eloquent in speech. Coming to this monastery with no small devotion to celebrate holy Easter, the solemnity of the Lord’s Supper, with Rao, son of Rahel, [Col. 0871C] count of the city of Teano, his horse fell on the rough road of a descending hill. He suffered a most terrible fracture of his legs and could only be carried there as if on a bed.

Immediately he begged most earnestly to be placed before the body of blessed Benedict, and there, crying aloud with great shouts, he spent the entire day in tears. When the darkness of the following night was now putting an end to the day, the church custodian ordered some servants to carry him outside. But he began to protest by most solemn oaths that he would by no means leave unless he recovered, saying:

> “Here, here, before the body of him whose court I had come to visit with ardent desire—here, I say, having suffered so great a misfortune in the use of my body, lying here to his dishonour, I shall at once pay nature’s debt, unless he immediately grants me his customary assistance.”

After saying this, when all had withdrawn, he too fell partly asleep and was silent for a while. Then behold: he saw the most holy altar [Col. 0872A] in which the body of Father Benedict is enclosed, as though opened by divine power; and from it emerged a man of venerable grey hair, in the very vesture which abbots customarily wear in festal processions. Drawing nearer, he touched the place of the fracture with a kindly hand and said: “Behold, you have been made well; now cease your threats.”

The sick man at once rose healthy and unharmed, and spent that night in praises of the Almighty. When morning came, he made the event known and rendered magnificent thanksgivings to God and Father Benedict. After the feast had been celebrated with no less joy of mind than was fitting, Hugh returned to Teano. Growing warm with the ardour of heavenly fire, he bade farewell to the world and all worldly things; denying himself also, in accordance with the divine command [Col. 0872B], he followed Christ naked and unencumbered. Soon he built a hospice at the spring of Corrigia [Note: In the territory of Teano; the name survives. ANG.] and began to run toward the heavenly fatherland along so religious a course of life that he used no footwear and only woollen clothing.

After fifteen years he came here again and, as repayment for the health he had received, gave himself permanently as a servant to blessed Benedict. He often confessed with truthful lips the things related above. On the same day Rao, son of Rahel, surrendered on the altar of blessed Benedict all the appurtenances of our cell at Teano and swore [Note: His undated oath survives in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 229.] that he would leave it to us undisturbed, as it had been retained in the time of Prince Jordan, reserving to himself only this: that our men should be assigned to his service two days per week [Col. 0872C] for four years, and that in return he should remit from the customary annual rent which he receives from Casa Flamma or elsewhere one hundred tareni. When the term was complete, he was to leave all the rest undisturbed forever [Note: Manuscript *c* reads *dimittant*, “they shall leave.”].

45. Thereafter the pontiff sent word to our abbot that, having prepared everything, he should proceed to the City, namely, that in the following month of March he was to receive consecration of the abbacy. Having made the necessary preparations, he set out and arrived at Rome. There he received consecration and obtained from the pope a privilege concerning the complete liberty of this monastery (A.D. 1112, 4 February). When March arrived, a synod was held there (18 March 1112) [Note: Gattola, *Historia*, p. 333. “Given into our hands by the grace of God, to Girard consecrated as abbot of the monastery of Cassino, February, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, indiction IV, pontificate 13, at the Lateran.” If this was given in that year, he was consecrated before March.], at which the affair of the Apostolic See and the Roman Empire was discussed with all the bishops [Note: Perhaps “being present” has dropped out here, so that what follows may supply the main clause.].

The pope [Note: From the acts of the council; see *Monumenta Legum*, II B, p. 181.] professed that he had done what he did with the emperor not so much for his own liberation as for that of his fellow captives; he showed by firm and true reasoning that he was wholly Catholic. He confessed that the privilege which he had made, contrary to every right and justice, had been made under necessity. Whatever his predecessors [Col. 0873A] had decreed and condemned, he likewise confirmed and condemned in every respect. On hearing this, the bishops heard that written privilege—if it ought to be called a privilege—and utterly condemned it forever.

46. In the same year Emperor Alexius, whom we mentioned above, sent to Rome the bravest men of his empire with letters. By these he signified that he, the emperor, was deeply grieved, first, by the injury and captivity inflicted on the supreme pontiff by the emperor of the Romans [Note: A letter of this sort to the abbot of Cassino, from the Register of Peter, was published by Gattola, *Historia*, p. 929, and Muratori, *Antiquitates* V, 389; yet it makes no mention of a coronation.]; and then he gave thanks and praised the Romans because they had stood against him manfully and had not yielded to his will. Therefore, if he found their minds most ready and prepared, as had long ago been communicated to him from those regions, he himself, or his son John, wished [Col. 0873B] to receive the crown at Rome from the supreme pontiff, in accordance with the custom of the ancient faithful emperors.

The Romans sent back through the same messengers that they would be altogether ready, according to his wish. In May they selected nearly six hundred of their men and sent them to the emperor to conduct him. When they came to Cassino, our abbot received them honourably and sent envoys with them to the emperor, through whom [Note: *deest c*: “is lacking in manuscript c.”] he promised him service and prayer. When they had returned to Constantinople and, together with the Romans, had reported to the emperor what our abbot had done for them, the emperor judged that he should be counted among his friends. Through the brethren of this monastery he sent to blessed Benedict eight pounds of *michalati* solidi and a thirtieth-grade cloth [Col. 0873C] [Note: This perhaps relates to the letter published there, p. 924, sent in June, indiction V.]. Moreover, he instructed the same abbot that when he came to Rome to be crowned, the abbot should go out to meet him as far as Dyrrhachium and remain in his service with him until reaching the City.

47. In these days Hugh, son of Hugh the younger, of the castle of Fenuculi, together with Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, restored to blessed Benedict the church of Saint Peter at Russano; Saint John in the dependencies of the castle of Helicuso; Saint George in the castle of Feniculi; Saint Martin in the dependencies of the castle called Turrepalatium; and Saint Januarius in the dependencies of the city of Benevento, with the appurtenances of those churches—which, that is, his father had handed over to Saint Benedict until the day of his death.

[Col. 0873D] **48.** In the following year the aforesaid Pope Paschal again came into these regions (A.D. 1112) and, intending to hold a synod with our abbot, proceeded to Benevento. There, through Sennus, archbishop of Capua, he made a claim concerning the church of Saint Sophia in Benevento (February 1113), which had violently been withdrawn from the jurisdiction of this place; but he was unable to obtain any justice in the matter. [Note: From the pope’s privilege in Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 714. It was situated in the diocese of Larino, on the river Saccione. See above, II.32.]

He also made a claim against Benedict, abbot of Terra Maggiore, because he had seized the church of Saint Mary at Casale Piano, which belonged by right to this place. Although that abbot had formerly been expelled from the matter by Abbot Oderisius, the pope repeatedly sent letters and even imposed an interdict upon either the place or the order, compelling the same abbot to appear before him. Accordingly, for two days (11–12 February), the jurists were granted leave to argue. At last, the representatives of the monastery of Terra Maggiore alleged proof of forty years’ possession.

But their witnesses, professing testimony not from sight and hearing but from report, could be admitted neither by the laws nor by the canons. On the other hand, our men established interruption of the alleged forty- or thirty-year possession by arguments of this kind: they produced two monks of known religious standing, one a bishop and the other a deacon, who stated that they had been present when the aforesaid church of Saint Mary at Casale Piano was leased by Abbot Desiderius of blessed memory to the priest Rudolph, as was shown in the written instrument of lease, for an annual rent of six Byzantine coins. [Note: A.D. 1071.] Three lay witnesses were also produced by them, who professed that for forty years, before the monastery of Terra Maggiore had seized that church, they had seen monks of this monastery placed there as superiors. [Note: Thus corrected from the charter; c has *profitentur* (“they profess”).] [Note: “And Rudolph … paying the rent to the Cassinese monastery.” In the same place.]

Therefore, after considering the authority of the laws, the pope imposed perpetual silence upon the monastery of Terra Maggiore regarding this dispute; and finally, by privilege, decreed that the church at Casale Piano, with its possessions, should remain peacefully and perpetually with our monastery (13 February).

At that time (April), Count Robert of Laureto, coming to this monastery during Lent for the sake of prayer, together with his knight Oldibert, offered to Saint Benedict whatever belonged to him in the territory of Saint Martin at Pisile. [Note: From Robert’s privilege in Gattula, *Historia*, p. 344. Executed in the palace at Termoli. He is called “count of the counts of Laureto,” son of Robert.] [Note: That is, Oldibert, who had offered himself to the same monastery.]

In the following year (1114), Duke William, son of Duke Roger, came to this place (October) and by charter confirmed here everything which Dukes Robert and Roger had granted to Saint Benedict. Moreover, he confirmed the land which he had formerly granted to this place at Saint Justa in the territory of Troia; and he further ordained that our animals, which annually entered his land, should have pasture in the customary places, and should remain and return without opposition, molestation, or exaction by himself, his men, or any person whatsoever, under penalty of one thousand pounds of gold. [Note: Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 230. It does not say there that he came to Monte Cassino.]

He also issued another charter (August 1126) concerning Castelione di Baroncello, with its appurtenances, that the men dwelling there should be secure, undisturbed, and free from himself and his people, from every payment or rent. [Note: Territory of Troia. Gattula, ibid., p. 231.] [Note: “Solidi” in the original.]

But Constance, daughter of the king of the Franks, together with her son Bohemond, in the same year (April 1114), offered in the imperial church of Saint Peter in the city of Taranto eighty-six households of men with their property, and everything granted to that place by charters and offerings.

**49.** In the same year, while Pope Paschal was holding a synod at Ceprano (October), the archbishop of Cosenza brought a complaint against Count Roger of Sicily, who, having deposed him from his archbishopric, had ordered him to become a monk against his will and resistance. To this the pope replied:

> “This does not concern me. It belongs to the abbot of Monte Cassino to judge and decide such matters, since our predecessors bestowed this prerogative upon him. For the gifts and calling of God, as the Apostle says, are without repentance [Romans 11:29]. Therefore that gift which almighty God granted to blessed Benedict, and through him to the Cassinese monastery, cannot be overthrown by any reasoning. Let the abbot of Monte Cassino answer concerning such a matter.”

Then the abbot said:

> “God does not desire forced service. Therefore, if you have taken up the monastic profession against your will, it shall be yours either to abandon it or to retain it. Accordingly, we order you to lay down at the feet of our lord the Apostolic the habit of holy religion which you assumed unwillingly; thereafter, as I have already said, it shall be yours either to take it up again or to dismiss it.”

At once the man laid down his monastic garments at the feet of the supreme pontiff; but no one could by any means persuade him to resume them afterwards.

In the same council the same Apostolic invested Duke William with the duchy of Apulia and Calabria. There also, when Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, had been accused and could not clear himself of the charges laid against him, he fled to this place, declining to hear the pope’s sentence. But how, at the request of our congregation, he later recovered both his rank as pontiff and the pope’s favour, we shall write in its proper place. [Note: Chapter 61. See also Falco of Benevento for this year, and Romuald of Salerno.]

**50.** In this same year, when brethren of our monastery were returning from Sardinia, Saracen pirates attacked them and carried them bound into Africa. When our abbot learned this, he sought to send there the price for their ransom; but those who bore it were driven by the force of the winds to Sicily.

When this came to the notice of the illustrious Count Roger, moved by love for the most holy father Benedict, he sent his messengers to the king of the city of Calama, which the Saracens call Alchila, ordering him to permit the brethren to return to this monastery if he desired to enjoy his favour and live in his peace. [Note: It lies between Cirta and Hippo Regius and is now called Guelma; see Pagi, under A.D. 1114, no. 3.] The king of Calama immediately yielded to these weighty requests and handed the brethren over to the count’s envoys; for Azzo, dean of this holy place, had already died in that captivity. Coming through Africa to Sicily, they were honourably received by the same count and sent back to our monastery. [Note: Perhaps read *suscepti sunt*, “were received”?]

**51.** I think it worthwhile to append to the present little work those things which almighty God showed in order to make known the merits of the aforesaid dean.

[Note: These matters are found in nearly the same words in the book *On the Just Men of Monte Cassino*, ch. 62.]

When he had died in the same province, his body was buried in the church of Blessed Mary before the altar. Then, in the stillness of the dead of night, Saracens passing by, while the moon was casting out its rays, saw him sitting outside beside the doorway of the basilica, holding a book in his hand. Astonished, they began to call other Saracens, saying:

> “Run quickly, run; hasten here! For we see the priest of the Christians, who died this month, sitting before the doorway of the church.”

When the others heard this, they hurried out of the city gates toward the place. As they approached him, the man of God entered between the threshold and the doorway of the basilica and appeared nowhere again.

On a certain day the sacristan entered the church and found the lamp hanging over his tomb burning. Angrily he called the boy who regularly served him in the church and said to him, “Why did you leave the lamp lit?”

The boy answered, “When I closed the church, I extinguished all the lamps; but who lit this one I do not know.” [Note: The book has *qui*, “who,” while the printed text has *quis*.]

Recognizing what the matter was, the man extinguished the lamp and closed the church. Entering the church on the following day, he found it burning. When this happened repeatedly, it was reported to the king of the Saracens. Astonished at the unusual occurrence, and thinking that Christians had contrived it, he sent Saracens to extinguish the lamp and remove its oil. When this had been done, they entered the church the next day and found the lamp shining, and water burning in the manner of oil. They ran swiftly away and came to the king, recounting in order all that had happened.

Then the king ordered the lamp extinguished and Saracens to guard the church day and night, so that no Christian might enter it. Obeying his commands, they began to guard the church. But when night came, the Saracens watching the church lifted their eyes to heaven and saw a star from heaven shining above the lamp of the church. Astonished, they opened the church doors and saw the lamp shining; then they hastened to the king’s palace and began to recount in order what they had seen.

But when the king heard these things from his men’s own mouths, he disbelieved their words, ordering the lamp extinguished and the church guarded as before. Rising, he went to the house of the *callifa* which overlooked the church. [Note: Perhaps read *quae prospiciebat*, “which overlooked [it]”? Lauretus emended it to *quae liminabat*; the author of *On the Just Men*, in the cited place, says *quae ecclesiae imminebat*, “which stood over the church.” Pagi, under A.D. 1114, no. 4, takes the *callifa* to be a bishop or priest of the Christians.]

When night had come, lifting his eyes to heaven, he saw a star shining above the church lamp and kindling it with its ray. He immediately sent Saracens to the church, and on their return they reported that the lamp was burning. Then the king issued an edict that Christians should have free permission to enter the church.

**52.** At the same time Robert, bishop of Aversa, brought litigation before the Roman pontiff against this monastery concerning the church of Saint Agatha at Aversa. After this case had long and repeatedly been argued in the Roman curia between us and them, by command of the Roman pontiff and the cardinals, who found it burdensome to hear the same case so often in judgment, the bishop, together with the clergy of the church of Aversa, granted that same church to be held forever by our Cassinese monastery, under a penalty of fifty pounds of gold. [Note: A.D. 1113, indiction VII; Gattula, *Historia*, p. 281.]

This abbot granted by charter to the men dwelling in the castle of Saint Angelo lands and woods belonging to this monastery at the place called Tabulenla, according to the tenor of his predecessors’ grants; for this he received ten pounds of denarii.

Prince Robert confirmed to this abbot by oath the entire abbey without exception, together with every land, castle, and monastery, exactly as Abbot Otto had held them eight days before his death, and everything this monastery possessed within the principality of Capua. Andrew, consul and duke of the people of Gaeta, did the same concerning the land of Saint Benedict, and specifically concerning the castle of Pontecorvo with its appurtenances. [Note: Son of Richard of Aquila.]

**53.** At that time Benedict, bishop of the church of Fondi and monk of this monastery, began to contend against this monastery concerning money which his predecessor Contard had deposited in this place. He admitted that part of this money had been returned to the bishopric, but asserted that the other part was ours. [Note: Read *nostram*, “ours,” not “ANG.”]

Our abbot said that he knew nothing of the case. Since the dispute had long been extensively debated, because there was doubt both as to the amount of the money and whether less had been returned than had been received in deposit, [Note: Perhaps *dubitabatur*, “there was doubt,” rather than *dubitabat*, “he doubted”?] we finally reached this agreement: in consideration of this matter our abbot granted to the same bishop, for the term of his life, the monastery of Saint Nicholas at Pica, so that he should receive from it all the revenue which this monastery would have received, apart from the customary greetings in their seasons.

While still holding the office of provost in the church of Saint Nicholas at Pica, in the time of Father Desiderius, this abbot acquired from Gerard, Richard, and Leo, consuls of Fondi, the church of Saint Onuphrius with its appurtenances. Because the aforesaid place, built on a sloping mountain-side, was always exposed to the plundering of robbers, Gerard demolished it and built a monastery on a nearby hill in honour of Saint Onuphrius, confessor of Christ. Taking away half of all the movable property of the monastery of Saint Nicholas at Pica, and transferring there also some of the monks of the same place, he gathered sixteen brethren there to serve Christ.

Likewise, in the territory of Alife, he demolished to its foundations the church of Saint Mary at Cingla, and rebuilt it in the former place, magnificent and most beautiful, after the likeness of this church of Saint Martin. This abbot exchanged with Grimald, son of Maio of Aquino, land at Ulmito, receiving another parcel of land at Asprano with its appurtenances, under a penalty of fifty Byzantine coins.

[Col. 0878C] **54.** At about the same time, when the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115 was drawing to its close, on 19 February, the castle of our monastery called Suio, which had been taken from this monastery since the time of Father Desiderius, was restored into the hands of the aforesaid abbot. This occurred after the death of Richard of Aquila, who had held that castle, and after the capture of Alexander, who had married Richard’s widow; the people of Suio, unable to bear the insolence of Alexander’s tax-collectors, surrendered the castle to the abbot. [Note: Hugh of Gaeta had given one half of it to Abbot Theobald in January 1023, by a charter omitted by Gattula but mentioned by I. B. Federici, *De duchi di Gaeta*, p. 326. Afterwards, in 1040, he reserved a fourth part for his son, who in 1079 again gave the monastery an instrument concerning half the castle. See above, II.55; III.44.] [Note: 1115: “Abbot G. acquired the town of Suio,” *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*.]

When Rangarda, the wife of the aforesaid Richard, learned this, she secured through the treachery of its guards the tower called “By the Sea”; she withdrew from this place’s authority Lauriana, Casa Maggiore, Saint Benedict at Sessa, and everything in her jurisdiction that belonged to the Cassinese monastery. [Note: Now called [the place] of Saint Crestensis. Of the ancient estate of Lauriana scarcely any remains survive except the ruins of its church, near Saint Crestensis on the Gaetan road. ANG.] From then onwards she never ceased to inflict upon the Cassinese monastery whatever hostility and injury she could devise.

The abbot, however, did not delay. Raising an army, he began by every means to ravage the territory of Sessa with fire and sword. Richard, son of Bartholomew of Caleno, who was then at war with the same Rangarda over the duchy of Gaeta, confirmed to the abbot by oath the whole abbey in its entirety, and whatever it could thereafter recover in the territory of Fondi, the territory of Guy of Castro, the territory of the counts of Ciccano, and within the principality of Capua—in the counties of Aquino, Venafro, Alife, and Teano. He confirmed specifically the castle of Suio with its appurtenances, the right of going and returning with ships by the river Garigliano, the markets at the port of Suio, and particularly the lands which that Rangarda had taken away: namely, the court of Saint John at Currenti; the court of Lando by the sea; Casa Maggiore; Lauriana; Saint Benedict of Sessa; and the lands held by Gezzolinus.

Prince Robert did the same, confirming by oath to Saint Benedict the aforesaid castle of Suio with its appurtenances. [Note: By his charter he confirmed the Cassinese possession of Suio in February 1117; Gattula, *Accessiones*, p. 232.]

**55.** In the following year, in the month of May, the aforesaid Pope Paschal left Rome, came to this monastery, and, taking our abbot with him, went to Troia to hold a synod (August). On his return he solemnly dedicated the church of Saint Vincent, which Gerard, a monk of this monastery, had built from the foundations near the source of the river Volturno. [Note: The same year. We have already often seen Peter’s carelessness in reckoning dates. Yet that he should be thought to have reckoned the beginning of the year, in the Pisan manner, from March of the preceding year is excluded, for example, by chapters 32, 33, and 61.] [Note: Compare Falco of Benevento for this year.] In that church our abbot also offered two pallia.

In this abbot’s time Almannus, a monk of this holy monastery, died (September); how pleasing his life had been to God was made clear by his end. [Note: The passage from “Here” through “fast” is found in *On the Just Men of Monte Cassino*, ch. 53.]

Coming to this place from the city of Melfi, his native city, he lived with very strict discipline and great continence. Every night he remained naked beside the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle in the cemetery of the brethren, singing psalms and never ceasing to afflict his flesh with harsh strokes of a broom.

During the time of this abbot, when the same man died in the stillness of the night, Nicholas the cellarer, who was outside the monastery, raised his eyes and saw the roof open above, and from it a very great ball of fire emerge and be borne into the heights of heaven. Immediately sending a messenger to the monastery, he discovered that Almannus had died at the very hour when he saw the ball of fire depart from the monastery and seek the heights of heaven. This vision was seen not only by the cellarer outside, but also within the monastery by Carbo, one of the priors of this place, who is still alive.

As long as he lived, this man ate bread and water three days a week, and never broke his fast except on a specified feast-day.

**56.** Meanwhile, because the inhabitants of the city of Saint Germanus were frequently troublesome and rebellious toward our abbot, Gerard’s lofty spirit was stirred to repress their wickedness. Therefore, after taking counsel with Oderisius the provost and Seniorectus the dean, who later became abbots of this monastery, and with other prudent men, and calling to his aid the faithful men of this place, on the night of 16 January he seized the hill of Janula, which overlooks that city. Having taken hostages from the citizens, this energetic man began to rebuild the fortress of Janula, which had stood deserted and ruined since the time of Abbot Aligernus.

First, on the mountain summit, he built a very beautiful and very large tower; beside it he repaired two ruined ancient towers. Then, building most beautifully the abbot’s chamber, with its chapel and other offices, he enclosed the whole circuit of the fortress with a very strong wall. Thus at last he compelled the rebels and the faithless to remain peaceful. Likewise, he fortified the castles of Pontecorvo, Cardeto, Vitecuso, and Suio with walls and towers.

**57.** In these days, after the death of Albert, bishop of the church of Gaeta, Richard, a monk of this monastery from childhood, was made bishop of that church. [Note: Gattula has “Abbertus”; ANG has “Albertus.”]

Meanwhile, being concerned to subdue the savagery of the pagans, the Roman pontiff summoned Romans, Pisans, and others from various regions and sent them to the Balearic Islands, under remission of all sins (A.D. 1114). When they arrived, after long and strenuous warfare against the islands, they finally received them in surrender, having slain one hundred thousand Saracens by the sword. [Note: Fifty thousand according to the Pisan Chronicle, in Muratori, *Scriptores*, VI, p. 169.]

At this time also Hector, Pandulf, and Gisulf, sons of Pandulf of Presenzano, intoxicated by the malice of the ancient enemy, secretly seized the monastery’s castle called Camino and began in every way to harass the adjoining lands of this monastery. [Note: The printed text has *filius*, singular, “son.”] But the abbot, as he was high-spirited, raised an army and consumed their land with fire and sword.

In the same year the aforesaid pope left the City and came to this monastery. Having been received with the greatest honour, and having heard of the aforesaid sacrilegious men who had seized the already mentioned castle of Camino, during the very solemnities of Mass he separated the authors of so great an evil from the thresholds of the church unless they repented.

Why say more? Seeing God opposing them in all things, they restored that castle into the hands of our abbot. Coming to this monastery, with the whole congregation present, they renounced the aforesaid castle upon the altar of blessed Benedict.

Meanwhile Lando, son of Count Lando, following the custom of his ancestors and by no means ceasing from harassing this place, began to build a castle in the wood adjoining this monastery, called Tirille. There was then in this holy monastery John, chancellor of the Roman Church and monk of this monastery, whom I mentioned above. Judging such insolence intolerable, he took with him Seniorectus the dean and other brethren, approached the count, and began to adjure him in the name of the Roman pontiff not to build a castle on the possession of blessed Benedict unless he wished to experience apostolic anathema. Then, recognizing both the pontiff’s wrath and blessed Benedict’s justice, the count immediately withdrew from that place.

**58.** At that time a certain knight in Apulia was captured by a most wicked man in some conflict; bound with an iron shackle and chains, he was thrown into a pit. For many days he remained held fast in those bonds, anxiously imploring day and night the assistance of the most holy Father Benedict.

One night Benedict appeared to him and said, “Are you asleep or awake?”

The knight replied, “As you see, lord, in the secret chamber of my mind I ponder death more than the repose of sleep. But who are you, who have deigned to come to me? I humbly beg you to make yourself known.”

The saint said:

> “I am Brother Benedict, whose coming to your aid you requested. Now rise quickly. As for the chains with which you are bound, since because of the length of the journey you cannot carry them to my body at Monte Cassino, hang them at the tomb of Brother Otto the recluse, who kept my Rule most faithfully.
