And do not delay to go to Monte Cassino, there to render praise to God for your deliverance.”

When he had said this, the knight immediately rose; invoking the name of our Redeemer and of blessed Benedict, the chains upon his feet were at once loosed. Rising at once, he took every care to fulfill with all diligence what had been laid upon him. Finally, coming to Monte Cassino, he rendered the greatest praises to God and Father Benedict.

Arderadus, porter of this place, was travelling at midnight over the plains beneath the Cassinese mountain. Turning his eyes toward the monastery of the most holy Father Benedict, he saw a very great light, like the brightness of the sun, descend above that place. It first covered the church and afterwards the whole monastery, and remained for nearly half an hour; then at last the light which had appeared before his eyes was withdrawn. [Note: Perhaps read *sic*, “thus,” rather than *si*.]

At the same time Sergius, a monk of this monastery and by nationality an Amalfitan, as he was dying asked Gregory, priest of this place, not to leave him. Gregory complied with his request and remained with him. When the final hour of his life was now approaching, Sergius looked and saw the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, coming toward him. Immediately raising his hands upward, he began to cry, “My lady, my lady!”

When they asked him what he saw, he said, “Do you not see the most blessed Virgin Mary? Here indeed she is.” Having said this, he breathed out his soul.

**59.** In these days Peter, son of Peter Maio, of the city of Aquino, offered to blessed Benedict everything which seemed to belong to him within the boundaries of the aforesaid city, in the valleys of Opplosa, Surgili, and Cisternola, and everything which belonged to him at Suio, in the place called Casa Maggiore, under a fixed penalty of one hundred Byzantine coins.

Adenulf, son of Bernard of Aquino, likewise came to this monastery and offered to this holy place everything belonging to him by paternal or maternal right at Saint Urban.

At the same time (17 August 1115), Abbot Gerard granted to the vestry of this sacred monastery, for the benefit of the brethren, everything belonging to Saint Benedict in the county of Termoli, as well as the lands which had belonged to the knight Oldibert and which, as we have related above (ch. 48), Count Robert offered to this place. He attached the bond of anathema should any of his successors wish to remove this from the brethren’s vestry. [Note: In the printed text *inondatione*, “inundation,” for *innodatione*, “binding.”] [Note: In Gattula, *Historia*, p. 134, and *Accessiones*, p. 233.]

He also granted to the monastery of Saint John of Capua Petra Mellaria with its appurtenances.

It should indeed be known that, in the monastery of the girls of Saint John, an abbess ought, when necessary, to be elected by the nuns, as I myself remember reading in a privilege of Abbot Aligernus preserved at the monastery of blessed Benedict at Capua; but she must be approved and confirmed by the judgment of the abbot of Monte Cassino, by whose authority the abbess herself must also receive consecration. [Note: See Gattula, *Historia*, p. 126; compare below, ch. 76.]

**60.** The aforesaid pontiff, returning to Rome with our abbot in his company, planned to hold a synod in mid-Lent (March 1116). There our abbot also made a claim concerning the cell of Saint Sophia at Benevento, but was unable to obtain any justice in the matter.

At that time Pontius, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, came to the synod and boasted that he was “abbot of abbots.” When John the chancellor asked him whether the Cassinese had received the Rule from the Cluniacs or the Cluniacs from the Cassinese, Pontius answered that not only the Cluniacs but indeed all monks living throughout the Roman world had received the Rule of Father Benedict from the Cassinese monastery.

Then the chancellor said:

> “Therefore, if the standard of monastic religion flowed forth from the Cassinese monastery as from a living fountain, by right and merit the Roman pontiffs have granted this prerogative to the abbot of Monte Cassino: that he alone, as the vicar of Benedict the lawgiver, should be called ‘abbot of abbots.’”

At the same time the Romans were divided among themselves by deadly hostility against the aforesaid pontiff. For the greater part of those who had recently elected, against the pope’s will, the son of the deceased prefect [Peter, son of Peter] (April), laboured with all their strength against Peter Leo, even to the point of destroying some of his towers, because at that time, and with him, the pope had not consented to their will.

[Note: “Peter, son of Peter.”] [Note: “Of the pontiff” appears to have fallen out.]

When Emperor Henry heard these things—he was then in Liguria, after Matilda’s death, arranging her affairs—he was glad that matters did not agree well with the pope. He sent imperial gifts to the prefect of the City and to the Romans, announcing that he would soon be present. The pontiff meanwhile had withdrawn from the place and, as best he could, supplied assistance to Peter Leo, who was dwelling in fortified positions.

**61.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1117, the same emperor assembled an army and came to Rome. When Pope Paschal learned this, he left the City and came to this monastery. At the request of the entire congregation of this place, he restored to his rank Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, whom, as mentioned above (ch. 49), we reported deposed. [Note: 11 August 1116: Falco of Benevento, employing the Pisan computation.] Thus he entered Benevento by way of Capua.

Meanwhile, entering the city of Rome and knowing beforehand that the pontiff had departed, the emperor attracted consuls, senators, and nobles to himself, partly by gifts and partly by promises. To the most illustrious Ptolemy, descended from the stock of Octavius, son of the most magnificent Ptolemy, consul of the Romans, he gave his daughter Bertha in marriage. [Note: Illegitimate.] Bestowing very many gifts upon him, he confirmed by imperial authority forever to the aforesaid Ptolemy and his heirs everything which his grandfather Gregory and other ancestors had possessed or retained. [Note: Against this Ptolemy and Dulciaca, apparently his mother, the monks of Grottaferrata complained in 1140; see our *Annals*, VII.22. His sons were Raino, Jordan of Gavignano—Borgia, *Istoria di Velletri*, p. 247—and Jonathan, called “count of the Romans” in the Cassinese necrology on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, but “of Tusculum” in the plea of Otto, count palatine, of 1159, in Muratori, *Scriptores*, IIIb, p. 678. On 9 July 1155 he swore fealty to the pope—Mattei, *Memorie di Tusculo*, p. 162—but in 1170 surrendered Tusculum to Alexander III—Romuald of Salerno, p. 210—together with Raino; on him see our *Annals*, VII.23; IX.440; Muratori, *Scriptores*, IIIa, p. 462; *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, p. 141.]

Meanwhile the pope dealt with the prince and other Normans, seeking to have them unite against and resist the emperor, or at least furnish armed aid from the men of the aforesaid pontiff against the aforesaid Ptolemy, consul of the Romans and the emperor’s son-in-law.

Moreover, while Emperor Henry remained in Rome, he sought to celebrate the solemnity of Easter Day (25 March) with the great rejoicing of the Roman senate and people. Since he did not find the pontiff there and saw that, through the mediation of envoys, his positions could not at all be reconciled with those of the pope, he was compelled by the heat of summer to withdraw with his men into northern regions, promising that when the air had become temperate he would swiftly return to Rome.

When the Normans learned that the emperor had left the City, they selected about three hundred of their men and sent them against the Ptolemy mentioned above during the days of Pentecost. Entering Campania, they pitched camp near Pylus, a town of that province, and seized booty of men and beasts from there. When this was reported to Consul Ptolemy, he immediately summoned the knights whom the emperor had left to assist him and sought by night to send them against the Normans’ camp.

The Normans, however, learning of their arrival, fled at full speed and reached the castle of Acuto. The Germans pursued them, killing as many as they could find, and would have made a great slaughter of them had the castle not received the Normans. Having gained the victory, the Germans pursued the beaten and plundered Normans through villages and towns; and thus, after suffering these injuries, the Normans returned home one by one.

**62.** At this time, moreover, great earthquakes occurred throughout almost all Italy (January), so that the walls of many cities fell, churches were overthrown from their foundations, lofty towers collapsed, and many people were killed. Almost all springs also became muddy, and the lamps of churches moved through the air though no wind drove them. [Note: The *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*, under this year, and many others, mention these earthquakes.]

Then in the city of Verona the greater part of the buildings collapsed. Great *yatus* [reading uncertain; perhaps “gaps” or “chasms”] also occurred in those regions; countless trees, with green leaves, were uprooted and cast outside, and those places were covered with smoke. A child also spoke contrary to its age and foretold certain prodigies which afterwards came to pass.

While these disturbances continued, Simon, son of Hugh of Molise, died at Isernia; his body was brought to this monastery and buried in the atrium of the church of blessed Benedict.

**63.** In these days Robert, king of the English, sent envoys to this monastery, asking that they should implore the Lord’s mercy for him and for the welfare of his kingdom. Through them he also sought to send a golden chalice of no small size to blessed Benedict. [Note: But he was one whose brother had deprived him of the sceptre and held him captive. Nevertheless, it is not necessary that we change the name.]

At that same time Roger, called Scannacaballu, son of Lando, count of Calvi, came to this place and offered to blessed Benedict (January 1118), in Sicily at the place called Melazzeti, the settlement of Saint Andrew by the river Platiplatanion, within these boundaries: on the first side it adjoins the mountain called Marge, which lies to the east; on the second it adjoins the aforesaid river and the hill beside the river of Saint Venera; on the third, the settlement of Saint Nicholas of Melito, with the men belonging to him in that place—under a penalty of five hundred Byzantine coins. [Note: *Plotiplatamon* in the cited edition.] [Note: That is, a hill.]

64. In these same days Alexius, emperor of New Rome, Constantinople, who had conferred many benefits upon this holy monastery of Cassino and had loved it above all monasteries of the Latin name, completed the course of this life in the forty-fourth [Col. 0885B] year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0885D] Rather, the thirty-eighth.], and left the supreme rule of the eastern Romans to his son John Porphyrogenitus (15 August). Likewise, the aforesaid Pope Paschal, having returned from Benevento to Rome, died on 21 January; and John, chancellor, a monk of this monastery of Cassino from childhood, was elected Pope Gelasius by the clergy, senate, and people of Rome.

When these events came to the ears of Emperor Henry, he hastened to Rome and sent envoys to the same pope-elect. Through them he declared that, if the elect would observe the agreement which Pope Paschal had made with the emperor and confirm the conventions established between the Roman Empire and the Apostolic See, the emperor would immediately pledge fidelity to that elect and to the Roman Church [Col. 0885C]; otherwise, he would enthrone another pontiff in the Roman Church. Seeing, therefore, that his own grounds could not be reconciled with those of the Empire, the same elect entered the sea by way of the River Tiber and came to Gaeta with bishops, cardinals, and other clerics of the Roman Church, as well as the prefect of the city of Rome and many other Roman nobles.

When this was reported to the emperor, he immediately appointed Maurice, archbishop of Braga, whom Pope Paschal had deposed, as usurper of the Roman Church. The aforesaid elect, meanwhile, remaining at Gaeta, was ordained priest during Lent and was consecrated Pope Gelasius by the same bishops and cardinals. At that time Prince Robert of Capua and Duke William came to that pontiff in the same city [Col. 0885D] and rendered him their fealty. He then came to Capua and, together with the bishops and cardinals, excommunicated that emperor, the aforesaid usurper, and their accomplices. [Note: [Col. 0885D] On Palm Sunday, as he himself writes to Conon of Palestrina, Codex Udalrici 293. Pandulf of Pisa likewise reports that he then came to Cassino.]

At the feast of Easter (14 April), having placed upon himself [Col. 0886A] the diadem of the Roman world, he came with great praise and glory to the monastery of Father Benedict situated at Capua. After solemn celebration of Mass, he returned to the episcopal residence of the city, whose streets and arches had been adorned in the Roman manner. After this the same pontiff came to this monastery, where he was received with immense honour and joy by the whole community, and he remained in this region for many days.

Meanwhile Prince Robert, assembling an army, came to this monastery, intending to go with the pontiff to Rome, as he had promised. But, hearing that the emperor was besieging the town called Turricula, he stopped at Cassino; there he received the emperor’s envoys and returned to Capua. [Note: [Col. 0886D] Apparently Torricella, adjacent to Lake Trasimene.] The emperor, meanwhile, made a treaty with the townspeople, returned to Rome, and there, on the feast-day of Pentecost [Col. 0886B], was crowned by that same heresiarch; he then returned to Liguria.

When the aforesaid pontiff learned this, he returned to Rome; then, leaving that city, he went to Pisa and dedicated there the church of Saint Mary called *Ad domum* (“At the House”) (26 September), establishing for the first time an archbishopric in that city. [Note: [Col. 0886D] See the Pisan Chronicle in Muratori, *Scriptores*, VI, pp. 105, 169; Pagi, under the year 1118, nos. 10–11.] While the aforesaid pontiff was staying in that city, by his authority and that of Peter, archbishop of that city, Odemund and his sons offered to Saint Benedict the church of Saint Sylvester in Pisa, with its appurtenances (29 September). [Note: [Col. 0886D] See the charter in Gattola, *Historia*, p. 422.] Lambert, bishop of Ostia, later Pope Honorius, was present at this grant, together with other cardinals.

Thereupon the aforesaid pontiff departed with bishops and cardinals for the monastery of Cluny [Col. 0886C]. He was received there with very great honour by the abbot of the aforesaid place, remained there for some time, and after a few days died (29 January 1119); he was buried fittingly in that same monastery. The cardinals, therefore, seeing themselves deprived of so great a shepherd, took counsel, lest the Roman Church should longer lie exposed to the bites of schismatics. There they appointed as Pope Callixtus Guy, archbishop of Vienne, a man of royal lineage and highly learned in secular and ecclesiastical affairs.

The same pontiff, moreover, remaining there for some time, and Roscemannus, cardinal and monk of this monastery [Note: [Col. 0885] Something is plainly missing, perhaps: “sending him to Rome, and through him …”], … received by letter the unanimous consent to his election from that part of the Italians which favoured the Catholic cause alone. [Col. 0886D] Together with bishops and cardinals he came to the monastery of Blessed Maurus, situated at Glanfeuil and subject to this monastery of Cassino. At the request of the monks of Cassino who had accompanied him, and also of Gerard, abbot of the aforesaid place [Note: [Col. 0886D] Saint Maurus.], he solemnly dedicated the church of Maurus, that confessor [Col. 0887A] of Christ. In it he also placed, with the greatest reverence, the bodies of Saints Antony and Constantinian, who had gone from this monastery of Cassino into Gaul with Blessed Maurus. Thus coming to Rome, he was received with abundant honour by the clergy, senate, and people of Rome (3 June).

65. At that time, when the year one thousand one hundred and twenty from the Lord’s Incarnation was already passing [Note: [Col. 0887D] The Anonymous of Cassino agrees.], such great earthquakes occurred in this land that at Camino they destroyed a palace; at Cucuruzzu they overthrew a church together with its court; and at Bantra they cast to the ground a church, houses, and bell-towers. Many perished beneath the ruins; and we experienced this each day now nine, now seventeen, now twenty [Col. 0887B] or more [Note: [Col. 0887] Something appears to have fallen out: “times.”] times. [Note: [Col. 0887D] He appears to imitate Leo III, 33.]

At this time Father Benedict visibly appeared three times at a crossroads to a certain Spaniard near Termulae, and said:

> “Go and tell the abbot to cause all who dwell in the land under his jurisdiction to assemble barefoot at my monastery built at Cassino, to entreat almighty God; and let him himself, together with the brothers, perform litanies barefoot through all the churches of the monastery. For the sins of men have increased and their offences have multiplied exceedingly. Perhaps God will forgive their offences and fulfil the vows and supplications made to him.”

When asked who he was, he replied that he was Brother Benedict. The man rose, came to the abbot, and related in order what he had seen and heard. Therefore, when all were assembling above at the monastery to pray to God, in accordance with Father Benedict’s command, the devil, assuming the appearance of a lame man, met them on the steep side of the mountain. He told them that the church of the glorious Virgin Mary and the greater part of the city had been destroyed by an earthquake. Giving ear to his falsehood, they quickly abandoned what they had begun and returned to the city. When they arrived and saw that it was a diabolical illusion, on the following day they endeavoured, barefoot, to complete the litany which they had foolishly abandoned.

Then, during the first watch of the night, after an exceedingly great earthquake, the brothers rose from their beds and, barefoot, weeping and wailing, fled to Father Benedict. Pouring out prayers to him before his most sacred body, [Col. 0887D] they began to chant litanies at all the altars of the monastery. The Lord is faithful in his words: he promised to hear those who call upon him and trust in his mercy. For when the brothers had completed the supplication of the litany, not a single stone of [Col. 0888A] this place was moved thereafter.

When these things came to the knowledge of the neighbouring inhabitants, almost everyone living in the principality came here barefoot to Blessed Benedict, humbly begging the mercy of almighty God that, through the intercession of so great a father, he might deign to have mercy upon them. Nor were they disappointed in their expectation, for the trembling of the earth immediately ceased.

In that same year Prince Robert of Capua, of whom we have spoken above, died (3 June), and his son Richard was installed as prince by the Capuans. When he died shortly afterward, his uncle Robert succeeded him in the principality. [Note: [Col. 0887D] Rather, Jordan, his brother, succeeded after the death of Richard the son.]

66. In the time of this abbot, a remarkable miracle occurred in the province of Campania, altogether similar to one of ancient times. At Comino, in the fortress built [Col. 0888B] in honour of the Seven Holy Brothers, there was the son of a certain noble knight, named Alberic. When the boy entered his tenth year, he was seized by illness and brought to the point of death. For nine days and as many nights he lay motionless, without sensation, and as though dead.

During this period he was carried through places of punishment by the blessed apostle Peter and two angels, one called Emmanuel and the other Eloy. He was led to the mouth of the infernal abyss; then he was led into paradise, saw the dwellings of the saints, and was lifted into the aerial heaven. Having been sufficiently instructed by the blessed apostle Peter concerning the Old Testament, the punishments of sins, and the everlasting glory of the saints, he saw certain mysteries which he was forbidden to tell anyone. Thus he was carried by that apostle through seventy-two [Col. 0888C] provinces and was restored to life.

Whoever wishes to know this vision should read the connected account composed by Guido [Note: [Col. 0887] Thus Gattola; Guidono in Angelus.] a monk of this monastery of Cassino. [Note: [Col. 0887D] By command of Abbot Gerard; see the preface to the vision in Francesco Cancellieri’s observations, *Sopra l’originalità della Divina Commedia di Dante*, Rome, 1814, octavo, p. 134, and above, p. 568. It survives in Cassino manuscript 257, fol. 356.] Since it is on the lips of almost everyone, we have omitted to repeat it.

Thereafter Alberic, abandoning and despising worldly pomp, sought this monastery of Cassino. He was received very graciously by Father Gerard, clothed in the habit of holy religious life, and joined to the other brothers to serve Christ the King. Even to this day he possesses such abstinence and such gravity of conduct that no one can doubt that he saw and feared the punishments of sinners and saw the glory of the saints. From that time until now, by God’s grant, he has consumed neither meat nor [Col. 0888D] fat nor wine; he never uses footwear. To this day he perseveres in this monastery of Cassino in such contrition and humility of heart and body that, even if his tongue were silent, his life would declare that he had seen many things hidden from others, things either to be feared or to be desired. [Col. 0889A]

[Note: [Col. 0889C] What Peter here relates concerning his life and writings also occurs twice elsewhere, written in his own hand: (1) in Cassino manuscript 361, in the final chapter of the book *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*, in a different order. Since the ink is changed seven times there (namely at the words: “But while in exile”; “on Holy Saturday”; “the sermon on the translation of Saint Stephen”; “the book of shorthand signs”; “the translation”; “the chants”; and “of Saints N. and Marcian,” where it ends, leaving the page blank), and since the narrative is shorter, he seems to have written this version first. (2) Cassino manuscript 257, whose variant readings we append. It begins: “Peter the Deacon of Cassino, charter-keeper, archivist, and librarian, son of Egidius, a Roman by nationality, himself the son of Gregory, patrician and consul of the Romans, was offered to Blessed Benedict at five years of age under Abbot Gerard, A.D. 1115, and was educated under the same abbot for nearly eight years. But in the year 1128, at the age of twenty-one, when Abbot Oderisius II, successor of Abbot Gerard, had left the abbacy, the envy of his rivals caused him to be sent into exile. While he was in that exile, he wrote for the aforesaid Abbot Oderisius the Passion, etc.”]

At these times, moreover, Peter the Deacon, in the fifteenth year after the one thousandth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, was offered by his parents to Blessed Benedict in the first five-year period of his life. He was received by the aforesaid Abbot Gerard, clothed in the habit of holy religious life, and trained under the same abbot for twice four years. In the twenty-first year of his age he wrote, for Oderisius II, successor of the aforesaid Gerard, [Note: [Col. 0889C] But at that time he had resigned the abbacy and was a cardinal, as Angelus de Nuce rightly observes.] the Passion of the most blessed martyr Mark and [Note: [Col. 0889] “and” also in manuscript 2.] his companions; [Note: [Col. 0889C] See p. 565.] the Life of the distinguished confessor Fulco; [Note: [Col. 0889] Thus the manuscripts. Perhaps “the Life of Saint Placid,” manuscript 2.] the Passion of the most holy martyr Placid, disciple of Blessed Father Benedict; [Note: [Col. 0889C] P. 566.] and the Life of Saint Apollinaris, abbot, for [Note: [Col. 0889] “for the venerable R. A.” is absent from manuscript 2.] the most reverend Abbot Rainald. [Note: [Col. 0889C] It survives in the Register of Saint Placid, Cassino manuscript 515, fol. 126; see the Life of Saint Guinizon, fol. 141; the Life of Saint Severus, fol. 150. [Col. 0890C] He incorporated these same works into the book *On the Birth and Death of the Righteous Men of Cassino*. Compare p. 569.]

He wrote the Life of Saints Guinizon [Col. 0889B] and Januarius for Richard, monk of Cassino; [Note: [Col. 0889] “for R. M. C.” is absent from manuscript 2.] the Life of Saint Constantius, bishop and confessor, for Guarinus, bishop of Aquino; and the Life of Saint Severus, bishop of Cassino, [Note: [Col. 0889] “bishop and confessor,” manuscript 2.] for Abbot Seniorectus. He wrote a rhythmical poem on the last days, [Note: [Col. 0890C] It survives in the autograph manuscript, Cassino 361, from which L. Tosti, II, 120, published its beginning.] in which he seems to have followed the Apostle John closely, since Peter himself knew that, according to what is written there, the finite is used for the infinite. He also wrote an account of the destruction and restoration of the city of Atina, and of the discovery of the body of the blessed martyr Mark; and the Life of Saint Daria, wife of Saint Nicander.

He also wrote these sermons: eight sermons for the feast of Blessed Mark; two sermons for his vigils; and [Note: [Col. 0889] “a sermon on the octave of Saints Mark, Nicander, and Marcian, and two …,” manuscript 2.] two homilies on Saint Placid the martyr. [Note: [Col. 0890C] These, together with twelve sermons, survive in manuscript 515, fol. 64; the sermons also occur in autograph manuscript 361.] He wrote twelve sermons: two on the Lord’s Supper; one for Good Friday; one for Holy Saturday [Col. 0889C]; a homily for the feast of Saint Benedict; a sermon for Easter; one for the octave of Saint Benedict; one for the Ascension of the Lord; one for Pentecost; one for the feast [Col. 0890A] of Saint John the Baptist; one for Saints Peter and Paul; one for Saint Lawrence; and one for the vigil of Saint Mary. He wrote the book *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Cassino* for Pandulf, bishop of Teano. [Note: [Col. 0890C] See p. 568. The autograph survives in manuscript 361.]

He recorded miracles of monks of Cassino which had not yet been committed to writing. By order of Abbot Seniorectus, he revised the history of the destruction and restoration of the monastery of Blessed Maurus, for which he also wrote a prologue. He also made a prologue to the book of privileges; a sermon on the translation of the body of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, from Constantinople to the city of Rome; the *Births and Lives of the Righteous Men of the Monastery of Cassino*; [Note: [Col. 0890C] These survive in autograph manuscript 361.] a sermon for the feast of All Saints; two sermons on the Nativity of the Lord; [Note: [Col. 0890C] These three sermons survive in the same manuscript.] and one on Saint Stephen. He wrote a chronicle of the monastery of Cassino from the restoration of [Col. 0890B] the church of Saint Martin carried out by Desiderius down to this day. He collected an astronomy from ancient books.

Finally, sent as apocrisiarius, or representative, to Lothair III, emperor of the Romans, on behalf of the monastery of Cassino, after the emperor had granted him a seat at his feet, after he had placed him among the chaplains of the Roman Empire, after he had made him a disciple of Chancellor Bertulf, and after he had made him a confidential secretary, he appointed him logothete, recorder, and auditor of the Roman Empire. [Note: [Col. 0890C] Compare the letter to Richenza, Martène, *Collectio*, I, 757: “After he had made our littleness a disciple of Blessed …, after he had rewarded [me] with the office of logothete, recorder, and auditor, after he had granted [me] a seat at his feet, after he had made [me] a confidential secretary,” etc.; see below, chapter 125.] While this same Peter was at the court of the Roman Empire, he composed the disputation held before that emperor between himself and the adversary of the church of Cassino. [Note: [Col. 0890C] It does not survive at Cassino, but has been preserved, together with another disputation, in a copy made by the hand of Constantine Cajetan in 1602, in the Brancacciana Library, II, C. 22. Compare below, chapters 97 and 115.]

He abridged Solinus’s *On Miracles*. [Note: [Col. 0890C] A work of this kind is contained in Cassino manuscript 391, twelfth century.] He composed for Emperor Conrad a book *On the Kinds of Precious Stones*. [Col. 0890C] In composing an exposition on the Rule of Saint Benedict, he divided it into four books. [Note: [Col. 0890C] Manuscript 257, fol. 57: written by command of Seniorectus and Rainaldus Colementanus; Tosti, II, 118. Angelus de Nuce published part of it in the appendix to the *Chronicle*.] He wrote scholia on the Old Testament. [Note: [Col. 0890C] There, fol. 346. It begins: “It is the custom of Holy Scripture,” etc. I. B. MARUS.]

He wrote two letters to [Col. 0891A] Emperor Lothair by command of Abbot Guibald. [Note: [Col. 0891C] There, fol. 52. Letters to Richenza, fols. 37 and 368; to Conrad, fol. 37. Compare p. 571.] He wrote to Empress Richenza on the death of Emperor Lothair, and to the same woman on the death of Henry, duke of Bavaria. He composed a most beautiful letter on the election of Conrad II, emperor of the Romans. He enlarged a small book of shorthand signs and dedicated it to Emperor Conrad. [Note: [Col. 0891C] Published with Valerius Probus: Venice, 1525, quarto; Leiden, 1599, octavo; Geneva, 1602, quarto; and in collections of authors on the Latin language.] Correcting Vitruvius’s *On the Architecture of the World*, he abridged it. [Note: [Col. 0891C] See Poleni, *Exercitationes Vitruvianae*, II, 171.]

He translated from Greek into the Roman language the book of Heva, king of Arabia, on precious stones, addressed to Emperor Nero, which Emperor Constantine had carried from Rome to Constantinople nearly eight hundred years earlier. He composed two hymns in praise of Saint Justa, virgin and martyr. He corrected the corrupted *Vision of Alberic, Monk of Cassino*. [Note: [Col. 0891C] Manuscript 257, fol. 356.] [Col. 0891B] He composed a chronicle of the kings of the Trojan people, and of consuls, dictators, and emperors. [Note: [Col. 0891C] Manuscript 257. Fragments were published in *Monumenta Scriptores*, III, 219, and in L. Tosti, *History of Cassino*, II, 116.] He wrote the miracles of the holy martyrs Mark, Nicander, and Marcian; he composed six hymns [Note: [Col. 0891] In manuscript 2 the place after “number” is blank.] in their praise; and he composed chants for Blessed Mark the martyr. He wrote scholia on various sayings. [Note: [Col. 0891C] Manuscript 257, fol. 18.]

He wrote an exhortation to monks, [Note: [Col. 0891C] There, fol. 41.] in which he explains what they ought to keep and what to avoid: concerning the seven vices and virtues; the seven petitions; Rebecca and Isaac; King Uzziah and the priests; Moses, the three-day journey, and the three times; and the vision of Isaiah. He wrote a book of salutations, exhortations, [Note: [Col. 0891] “embellishments,” manuscript 2.] and reproaches. He collected from all ancient books an itinerary of the Land of Promise and dedicated it to Guibald, abbot of Cassino. [Note: [Col. 0891C] See the preface, p. 571.] He wrote the Life of Saint Pope Leo. [Note: [Col. 0891] “to Pope Innocent II,” manuscript 1 and 2.]

[Col. 0891C] He wrote a history [Note: [Col. 0891] These words are read in manuscript 257, written in the same hand but not at the same time: “A history of the Trojan people from Noah to his own times, which he described and dedicated to Ptolemy II, consul of the Romans. He wrote a homily in Lent, and also the disputation which he held with a certain Constantinopolitan for the Roman Church.” There the text ends.] of the Trojan people from the beginning of the world to his own times, and also a book describing prodigies and portents, dedicated to the most illustrious Ptolemy II, consul of the Romans. He wrote a most beautiful homily on Christ’s temptation in the wilderness, as well as the disputation which he held with a certain man of Constantinople on behalf of the Roman Church. He composed many other works which we refrain from recording here. [Note: [Col. 0891C] The catalogue of Cassino manuscripts in A. Mai, *Spicilegium*, V, 223, contains the book *On the Dignity of the Roman Empire*, beginning “Haec digni,” etc. Manuscript 257 also contains catalogues of Roman pontiffs and abbots of Cassino, a brief explanation of the Rule, and an epitome on the Rule of Saint Benedict for Emperor Lothair, beginning “Admirabili,” etc. You will find nothing there relevant to history. [Col. 0892C] Manuscript 515 contains the Life of Aldemarus (*Birth and Death*, ch. 69); at the end of manuscript 361, a work entitled *Synonyms of M. T. Cicero* has perished.]

[Col. 0892A] 67. Under the aforesaid Abbot Gerard, Gunnarius, a most noble Sardinian, [Note: [Col. 0892C] Of Laccon, in the kingdom of Ardar; Gattola, *Historia*, p. 424. Compare the confirmation of Gonnarius, king of Torres, *Accessiones*, p. 255.] following in the footsteps of his parents, Kings Bareso and Torkitorius, with the permission of his archbishop [Note: [Col. 0892C] Athu, or Azzu.] offered to Blessed Benedict the churches of Saint Peter at Nurki; Saint Nicholas; Saints John and Peter at Nugulbi; and Saint Elias and Saint John [Note: [Col. 0892C] These are not mentioned in the privilege.] at Setin, with all the appurtenances of those churches, for the provision of our clothing (24 May 1120).

Furatus of Gytil [Note: [Col. 0892C] Perhaps “of”; Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 237.] did the same, with the consent of the same archbishop and of Bishop Si Boni, in respect of the church of Saint Nicholas at Solio and of Saint Mary, [Note: [Col. 0892C] In another charter, a fragment of which Gattola published, *Historia*, p. 344.] with their appurtenances. Moreover, Comita, a most noble Sardinian, came at that time to this monastery and made a charter [Note: [Col. 0892C] Gattola published a fragment of it there; he did not publish the rest.] [Col. 0892B] for this place concerning the church of Saint Michael at Ferrucesi with its appurtenances. In like manner Marianus of Zori offered to this place the church of Saint George at Banarcatu with everything which it seemed to possess at that time.

Following his example, Muscunionia made a charter concerning her house at Solio, with slaves, slave women, and all her property. Susanna also, emulating that good example, offered to Blessed Benedict her house at Yscano, Mulana, Cortina, Myrra, Coquina, and Amendula, with slaves, slave women, and all her possessions. Vera, daughter of Gunnarius of Thori, likewise granted to this place her house at Coquina, with slaves and all that it seemed to possess. Constantine of Carvia did the same, making a charter of donation concerning the church of Saint [Col. 0892C] Peter at Symbrano, with all its appurtenances. [Note: [Col. 0892C] Tosti, *History of Cassino*, I, 421, published it.]

68. At that time (July 1120) the aforesaid Pope Callixtus left Rome and came to this monastery. Received by our aforesaid abbot with immense honour, he solemnly celebrated Mass that day and remained in this region for almost two months. [Note: [Col. 0892C] This conflicts with the letter of Eginus to Udalscalcus, in which the pope is still at Rome on the Kalends of July; Falco says that he entered Benevento on 8 August. Pandulf likewise testifies in his Life that he was at Cassino.] Our abbot maintained that pontiff with very great honour and took care to serve him most diligently in all his necessities. He then came to Benevento (8 August), went down as far as Apulia, received the oath of fidelity from Duke William according to the custom of his predecessors, [Col. 0893A] and returned to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0893D] In October at Benevento, according to the Roman-Salernitan chronicle.]

Afterward, gathering an army, he besieged and captured Maurice the heresiarch in the city of Sutri (April 1121), and banished him to the fortress of this monastery, [Note: [Col. 0893D] That is, Janula; see chapter 86. Yet it is certain that he was then relegated to the monastery of Cava.] which the same abbot had built from the foundations. While this most reverend pontiff was residing at Benevento, at the request of our abbot and the brothers he confirmed in perpetuity, by privilege of the Apostolic See, [Note: [Col. 0893D] In Gattola, *Historia*, p. 425, from the original.] to our community the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Nicholas at Nugulbi, Saint Elias at Setin, and Saint Peter at Nurci. Gunnarius, that distinguished man of whom we have spoken above, had offered them to Saint Peter, and afterward, by command of the same pontiff, had granted them [Col. 0893B] to Blessed Benedict (9 August 1120). [Note: [Col. 0893D] See the letter to the bishop of Volterra, Roger.] He decreed that clothing should always be provided for this community from the revenues of these churches, according to their means.

There was, however, a reservation of an annual census of four solidi in Pavia coinage to be paid to the sacred Lateran palace. He further added that all possessions and gifts which the aforesaid Gunnarius had given or should give to Blessed Benedict should likewise be preserved forever for the need of clothing; and that anyone who presumed to take away or diminish Gunnarius’s offerings, or to withdraw or alter them from the established provision of clothing for this holy community of Cassino, should be punished by anathema. [Col. 0893C]

He also sent a letter to the distinguished man Gunnarius and his wife Helena (10 August), [Note: [Col. 0893D] There, p. 426.] giving thanks, offering exhortation, and enjoining upon them, for the remission of their sins, that they should continue more steadfastly in what they had begun. The Roman See had confirmed by its authority both the churches and the gift which they had made to our monastery. It prohibited anyone from taking them away, diminishing them, or presuming in the future to exchange them without the consent of the brothers of Cassino; rather, they were always to remain peaceful and inviolate for the brothers’ clothing.

In the same manner he sent a letter to the bishop of Volterra, [Note: [Col. 0894D] In the same place; both letters are from Peter’s Register.] declaring how specially and pre-eminently this monastery of Cassino belonged to the protection [Col. 0893D] of the Roman Church. He further commanded him to ensure, out of reverence for Blessed Benedict, that the gift made to Blessed Benedict by the distinguished man Gunnarius and his wife should remain undisturbed and free from every molestation. For the Apostolic See had confirmed that gift by the authority of its written instrument, and, out of the liberality of the Apostolic See, had granted to our monastery certain churches which Gunnarius and his wife [Col. 0894A] Helena had offered to Saint Peter. He was not, therefore, to allow them to be taken away or harassed by anyone’s violence; rather, all were to be preserved peacefully and freely for the clothing of the brothers of Cassino.

69. It happened, while the same venerable pope was staying at Benevento (October), that Otto, archbishop of Capua, complained that the church of Capua had been despoiled of three churches which belonged to Saint Stephen and which this church of Cassino possessed: namely, Saint Benedict at Pyzzuli, Saint Angel at Odaldiscos, and Saint Rufus. He demanded that possession of them be restored to him through the Roman court. [Note: [Col. 0894D] Compare the notice written on this matter in Peter’s Register, in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 715.]

To this our abbot replied that neither the church of Cassino nor its officers had despoiled the church of Capua. He maintained that he was defended in manifold fashion regarding the aforesaid matters for which he was being sued, both by documents and by lawful, undisputed possession over time. He further showed that the appeal brought by the archbishop’s party was neither canonical nor lawful, and asserted this with many clear reasons.

After the two sides had contended for a long time concerning the matter, the pope ordered him to produce the grounds which our abbot possessed. A delay of three days having been granted, our party and that of the other man again appeared before the court, and the case concerning the same disputes was argued afresh. But when the archbishop’s party could show by no canonical or lawful reason that the monastery of Cassino ought to restore to it possession of the aforesaid [Col. 0894C] churches—since it was evident that the church of Capua had not been despoiled by that of Cassino—and when the discussion had lingered over this at length, the aforesaid pope at last ordered that the proofs of our monastery be shown to him.

When these had been presented and carefully read and examined with attention by the Roman cardinals and clerics—showing how Prince Richard and his son Jordan had granted those churches to this monastery and confirmed them by their command [Note: [Col. 0894D] Peter added “and had confirmed them” here; see above, III.37.]—the pontiff, after taking counsel, ordered that possession of the aforesaid churches should remain with this monastery as it then stood, both because of the many kinds of evidence, namely documents and length of possession, and because of the privileges granted to our monastery by the Roman pontiffs. [Col. 0894D]

70. Moreover, at this same time, in the presence of the same pope, our aforesaid abbot lodged a complaint concerning the church of St Mary at Cingla, which Count Rainulf—son of Count Robert of Caiazzo, mentioned above—had violently taken from the right of this monastery and subjected to the church of St Mary at Capua. Then the pontiff took care to send letters to the abbess of St Mary at Capua [Col. 0895A], ordering her to appear before the Apostolic See on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost and, in the presence of bishops and cardinals, to demonstrate to the Roman pontiff the right of her church.

[Note: Four of his letters to Abbess Alpherada and three to Count R. survive in Peter’s Register, fol. 31, according to Gattola, *Historia*, p. 49.]

But she, boiling with womanly fury, replied that she would by no means go to the pontiff’s court, nor would she obey his commands on any terms whatever. When this was reported to the aforesaid pope, he sent her letters stating that she now appeared to be seeking an evasion in the complaint of our abbot concerning the church of Cingla, since, after two deadlines had passed, she had not come to judgment nor sent suitable representatives to plead her case. Yet in all these matters the Roman Church had hitherto spared both her and her monastery; but it could not prolong further the examination of this case [Col. 0895B]. Therefore, setting aside every excuse, she was to present herself before the pontiff, or send representatives capable of conducting the business adequately in her stead. Otherwise, with the Lord’s help, the Roman Church would make restitution of the church of Cingla to the monastery of Monte Cassino.

Terrified by this ultimatum, the abbess went to Count Rainulf and begged and implored him to send letters to the Roman pontiff on her behalf. The count, bribed with money, assented to her wish; and, doing as the abbess had asked, sent letters to the aforesaid pope. After the pontiff had read the count’s letters, he granted his request and gave him a deadline, commanding the same count not to create any impediment in this affair, so that the matter might be decided [Col. 0895C] at the appointed time. For unless the abbess appeared before the Apostolic See by the fixed deadline, or sent suitable representatives on her behalf, he himself, with the Lord’s help, would make restitution of Cingla to the monastery of Monte Cassino, since he could no longer tolerate the complaint of the Cassinese abbot.

When the deadline arrived, our abbot went to Rome, wishing to obtain justice for our monastery and taking our title-deeds with him. But the abbess absolutely refused either to send a messenger or to go in person. Then the pope, after taking counsel with bishops and cardinals, sent letters to the abbess, expressing astonishment that, although he had frequently sent her apostolic letters concerning the dispute over the aforesaid church of Cingla, which had long been contested between the nuns and the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 0895D], and had already fixed three dates for her, she had neither come herself nor, in obedience to his just command, sent competent persons to decide the case on her behalf. In this, indeed, she was not seeking justice, but wished by evasions and pretexts to prolong the matter without limit.

It seemed reasonable, therefore, both to him and to the cardinals that the Cassinese church ought no longer to remain deprived of possession of the cell of Cingla because of delay or the pretext of her absence. For one who has been despoiled of a possession is not compelled, under the just provisions of the laws and the enactment of the holy canons, to resort to a legal action. Accordingly, by his own judgment and that of the cardinals, he ordered her, within twenty days after receiving the apostolic letters, to reinvest the Cassinese church fully in the cell of Cingla, without prejudice to the rights of her own monastery. The property of the church which it had possessed at the time of the spoliation was not to be removed by her or by her men.

But the abbess, unaware of what was about to come upon her, sent men who, contrary to the pope’s command, carried off books and whatever they found in the cell of Cingla. When the pope learned this, he sent her a letter saying that, although he had endured her with paternal kindness and gentleness, she, holding the pope’s patience in derision, took no care to fulfil any of his commands [Col. 0896B]; indeed, to the injury and contempt of the Apostolic See, she had despoiled the church of Cingla. Therefore, unless she wished to experience apostolic wrath, she was to take away nothing further from the property of the church of Cingla; rather, putting aside every pretext or evasion, she was to restore to that church what had been taken from it through her, and restore that church itself, with all its property, to the monastery of Monte Cassino.

But if she should persist further in contempt and fail to carry out the apostolic command within twenty days after receiving the letters, the Apostolic See would from that time forbid the celebration of divine offices in the church of Cingla; moreover, by the power of apostolic authority it would prohibit the abbess from every prerogative of governance in her monastery, until she had fully carried out the aforesaid restitution with its entirety [Col. 0896C] and had made full satisfaction to the Roman Church for her contempt.

When the abbess learned the pope’s will, she resorted to her customary weapons: she distributed money, opportunely and importunately, and declared that for no reason and on no terms would she fulfil the pope’s will. When this was reported to the pontiff, he again sent her a letter, declaring that the more patiently he endured her, the more she exalted herself in abundant pride and arrogance against the Roman Church. For four times and more he had written to her kindly and paternally in accordance with the just enactment of the sacred canons; yet she had utterly despised his commands and scorned the Roman Church, which is the mother and mistress of all churches, established not by another but by Christ the Lord, and which all the faithful therefore ought deservedly to honour. She, on the contrary, wished to deprive it of its power and dignity. Though so often admonished by the Roman Church, she had not merely been disobedient, but had added further disobedience.

For such insolence, the same pontiff forbade every divine office in that monastery of Blessed Mary, removed the abbess from the governance of that monastery, and bound both her and her supporters in this matter with the bond of excommunication [Col. 0897A].

Since not even thus could the Roman pontiff humble the abbess’s obstinacy, he ordered Count Rainulf, within twenty days after receiving the apostolic letters, to reinvest the monastery of Monte Cassino fully in the church of Cingla, and meanwhile to allow none whatever to plunder or carry away the goods of that church. But if he too should prove a contemner of the apostolic command—he who had been the cause and originator of this spoliation—the pope, unable to forgo the force of ecclesiastical justice in his regard, would, with the Lord’s help, pronounce a sentence of excommunication upon his person and his entire land.

Upon receiving the apostolic letters, the count summoned the abbess and set forth in order what the pope had commanded him. But she, inflamed with womanly passions [Col. 0897B], lavishly rewarded the prince, the count, and all their retainers, begging, demanding, and imploring that they press the count to undertake the abbess’s defence against the pope’s sentence and, in so critical a moment, give her aid; she entreated them with every means and effort in her power. The count, then bribed with the abbess’s money, promised to defend her against the pope’s sentence to the best of his ability.

When this was reported to the aforesaid pontiff, he commanded the count, saying that, since he was faithful to St Peter and the pope, the Roman Church truly loved him with affection and embraced his person, among other valiant and illustrious men, in the arms of especial love. Unless it were through him that this matter remained unsettled, it would prefer henceforth to treat him in the same manner; and for that reason the Church had until then done nothing by which he might seem to be burdened by the Apostolic See [Col. 0897C]. Therefore he commanded him, putting aside every delay and excuse altogether, to have the Cassinese abbot reinvested in the church of Cingla and its possessions. But if he presumed to act against this, the pope would forbid him divine offices and entry into all churches; and at the appointed term of twenty days he would excommunicate him personally, until he had fully reinvested the Cassinese abbot in the cell of Cingla, since he could in no way endure the outcry of the Cassinese brethren.

Likewise he sent letters to Otto, archbishop of Capua:

[Note: Gattola published them in the work cited, without date.]

He ordered him to regard Abbess Alpherada as deposed and excommunicated and not permit any divine office to be celebrated in that monastery of Blessed Mary; he was to have the sentence of interdict and excommunication pronounced by the Roman pontiff announced and observed throughout his diocese [Col. 0897D]. He also strictly forbade clergy and laity alike to presume in any way to enter that church contrary to his interdict or to associate with the excommunicated.

Meanwhile Count Rainulf, distressed that he had been excommunicated and separated from all divine mysteries because of a woman’s pride, promised that he would carry out the pope’s will if he could inspect the title-deeds of the Cassinese brethren. Accordingly, in the presence of the aforesaid Pope Calixtus and all the bishops and cardinals, the ancient and authentic charters of our monastery were read. They showed how Sarracenus, Beneventan *sculdahis*, to whom the place belonged by hereditary right, had built there from the foundations the church of Blessed Cassian—as we mentioned at the beginning of this book (ch. 6)—and, since he had no son, had granted to the same church, with the consent of Gisulf, duke of the Lombards, all his substance and possessions whatsoever; and how thereafter, by the authority of that duke, he had subjected the same church with all its possessions to this monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 0898B]; and how St Petronax, abbot, with the assistance of the same duke, built there a church in honour of St Mary, Mother of God, and made it a monastery of girls dedicated to God; and how Abbot Oderisius, in the time of Pope Urban, had recovered it after it had been taken from this monastery.

[Note: Compare book IV, ch. 18.]

The documents also showed how that same pope had summoned the abbess of the Capuan monastery concerning this matter by apostolic letters and an invitation from his own lips.

[Note: The manuscript reads *invitationem*, “the invitation.”]

They showed how the abbess, scorning to come to the pontiff, had neither accepted his admonitions nor submitted at all to judgment. Then, when the judgment of Pope Paschal concerning the matter had also been read in the presence of all:

[Note: Dated 31 March 1101; published by Gattola, *Historia*, p. 48.]

[Note: Rainulf’s charter reads *Ermannus*.]

the same count immediately, before John, cardinal of the title of St Eusebius, and Bermannus [Col. 0898C], subdeacon of the Roman Church, restored in its entirety to St Benedict the aforesaid monastery of St Mary, with all its appurtenances which it had held in his father’s time. Having caused a charter of renunciation and restitution to be drawn up, and confirming it with his own hand, he placed it upon the altar of St Benedict in September 1122, imposing upon violators of that decision a penalty of one thousand pounds of gold.

[Note: Gattola published it in the *Accessiones*, p. 716.]

71. In the same year Sparanus, abbot of the monastery of St Martin at Arce, came to this place in February and offered to St Benedict that church of St Martin with its appurtenances.

[Note: Gattola, *Historia*, p. 414.]

Rao of Banterone and his wife Auristella did the same with the church of St Peter, situated in the territory of Cosenza, at a place called Gaurano, and with the church of St Martin [Col. 0898D], at the place called Cupplatu, with all their appurtenances, imposing a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold.

Likewise Milo and Litulf, sons of Bernard of Aquino, and Milo, son of Milo, came to this monastery and offered to St Benedict nine households of persons belonging to them in the settlement called Pesmontis [Col. 0899A] and in the village of St Lucy. Their names are these: John, with his household; Conterius, with his household; Desiderius, with his household; Trostaynus, with his household; Peter, with his household; Bricius, with his household; Litulf, with his household; Hugh, with his household; John, with his household.

72. At that time, when the brothers of the Capuan monastery had given the monastic habit to a certain sick man already almost at the point of death:

[Note: From an undated letter of Calixtus in Peter’s Register, fol. 32.]

[Note: The manuscript reads *quemdam*, “a certain man.”]

the clergy of the church of Capua gathered there with an armed force. They found him already dead and, drunk with the spur of wickedness, stripped him of the monastic habit and threw those garments into the street to be trampled underfoot by passers-by. When Pope Calixtus learned this, he ordered the archbishop of Capua to correct, by God’s grace, the unheard-of and novel presumption of such great audacity [Col. 0899B], so that they should not presume in any way to do such things; nor should the archbishop himself offend God and the Roman Church in this matter. Since he knew that the monastery of Monte Cassino belonged to the jurisdiction of the Roman Church, he was not to trouble places belonging to it, either personally or through his agents.

From this venerable pope the aforesaid abbot also received a privilege confirming the complete liberty of this place, dated 16 September 1122.

[Note: Gattola, *Historia*, p. 335. Given at Berulis.]

It added that, should anyone violently take away possessions or property of our monastery or its cells, and should their bishops, after being admonished by our abbot, wholly refuse to do justice concerning them, the abbot might pronounce canonical excommunication against those same robbers after a second or third admonition [Col. 0899C].

In that same year, through sins demanding it, the city of Capua was given over to fire. When almost the entire city had been consumed, the fire threatened the monastery of St Benedict on every side. But the brothers, distrusting human resources and hoping in the aid of God alone, took the corporal of the chalice and placed it outside the monastery amid the fire. A wondrous marvel: the fire turned back and did not dare approach any nearer. All the citizens also saw a certain hand driving the fire away from the monastery. The corporal remained wholly unharmed by the fire’s injury, except that a small hole was made in its midst as testimony to the event.

73. Meanwhile, while this abbot remained at Benevento in the service of the pope:

[Note: Calixtus II was at Benevento from November 1121 to February 1122.]

he learned beyond all certainty that the arm of St Matthew, apostle and evangelist, was kept in that city.

[Note: See above, book III, ch. 57.]

Summoning the guardians of the said arm, he began most eagerly to ask how and by what course they had acquired the arm of that holy apostle. They reported that Duke Robert had brought it with him on the expedition which he had undertaken against Emperor Alexius, and had finally left it at his death to his chaplains [Col. 0900A], who afterward, on the day of their own death, had bequeathed it to them. The abbot then began earnestly to urge them to confer so great a pledge upon the monastery of Monte Cassino.

They promptly declared that they would do this if the abbot would receive them into this monastery, without any payment, whenever they wished to come to conversion. When the abbot gladly promised that he would do so, they immediately delivered the holy relics to him, to be carried to this place. Receiving the holy relics and kissing them for a long time, the abbot made haste to send them to this monastery through brothers of our congregation. At their arrival all the inhabitants of this land came out to meet them with great devotion and joy.

When the news reached our congregation [Col. 0900B], they were filled with inestimable rejoicing; clothed in solemn vestments and bearing lamps and incense, they went out as far as the Old Gate. Prostrating themselves on the ground, they venerated the holy evangelist; then, rising, they kissed it with the greatest reverence. With hymns and praises they brought it into the monastery, enclosed the holy arm in a silver casket fashioned in the likeness of towers, and suspended it in a silver beam before the altar of St Benedict, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1122.

74. In the same year, a certain cripple from the territory of Tours had resolved to visit Mount Gargano for prayer. When he reached the city of Aquino [Col. 0900C], as he rested in the silence of the deep night, the most blessed father Benedict appeared to him and said: “Rise quickly, make for the fortress of Cassino, and there, before the presence of my body, you shall give a garment, and without doubt you shall receive health.”

Then the cripple said: “Who are you, who promise us such great things?”

The lawgiver replied: “Setting aside every doubt, know that I am Brother Benedict, founder of the monastery of Monte Cassino.”

Having said this, he disappeared. The cripple immediately rose and related the event in detail to his companions. But they differed in their judgments, refusing faith to the vision. Some said that no one ought to believe deceptive dreams, for dreams had led many into error. Others, whose faith was sounder and more devout, judged [Col. 0900D] that this should by no means be done; rather, the benefit promised by the most holy father Benedict should be sought.

Then the cripple rose and climbed Mount Cassino with swift step and all the effort he could make. When he entered the church consecrated to Father Benedict in body and name, and came before the silver column in which a great candle is set, the cripple immediately began, through the interceding merits of Benedict, to be restored to his former gait [Col. 0901A].

Then Andreas, the custodian, who that day had charge of the church, heard the cripple shouting and ran quickly to him. Seeing that the calluses which had formed in the contraction of his limbs had burst and that blood was flowing from the joints, he hurried to the brethren in order to report the course of what had happened. But the cripple, leaving the church without the brethren’s knowledge, returned with swift step and great joy to his companions, who were waiting for him at the city of St Germanus.

When they beheld such great marvels, they approached Abbot Gerard and related the event in order. The venerable abbot, made most joyful by his recovery of health, gave thanks to almighty God and immediately sent him back to Cassino, to the body of Father Benedict. What joy of heart and what exultation there then was, I omit to tell, because all who saw it are still alive [Col. 0901B].

Afterward some senators, leaving the city of Rome, arrived at Mount Cassino. Seeing the same cripple, whom they had previously known to lie before the Lateran Palace, they asked how and in what manner he had been healed. When he recounted in sequence his restoration to uprightness, the senators did not at first assent to his words. But, stripping his limbs of his tunic and seeing the calluses broken into pieces, they rendered the greatest praises to almighty God and Father Benedict. As a perpetual memorial of the event, they hung the same cripple’s crutches before the doors of the church of the said Father Benedict.

I think it worthwhile to add the celebrated miracle, famous throughout the whole world [Col. 0901C], which the Lord then displayed at the remains of that same most holy father. On the very Sunday of the Resurrection, when a certain Etruscan, mute, blind, and deaf, arrived with his companions at the holy remains of Father Benedict, he received health in all his members.

75. In these days, Pandulf, surnamed “of Sesto,” intoxicated by the wickedness of the ancient serpent, and joined by a certain Odaldus as accomplice in his crime, did not cease to harass the lands adjoining those of our monastery. Our abbot gathered an army against him and laid waste all their land with fire and sword.

But Pandulf, moved by tardy repentance, came to this monastery and, by oath, renounced in favour of St Benedict and the same abbot, by charter, the castle of Vitecuso with its appurtenances, from which that conflict had arisen. Odaldus of Casale did the same concerning the castle called Aquafundata.

[Note: Casale is a fief distinct from the castle of Acquafondata, owing full legal obedience to the holy monastery of Monte Cassino. ANG.]

Together with Pandulf and their heirs, he bound himself to this monastery, so that if they or their heirs from then on, at any time, attempted by themselves or through any subordinate person to bring suit or a vexatious claim against St Benedict concerning this matter [Col. 0902A], they should pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold.

In these same days Rao, son of Raelis:

[Note: Lord of Teano.]

having assembled a band of robbers, plundered the castles of St Benedict, Suium and Mortula. When Pope Calixtus heard this, he ordered Pandulf, bishop of Teano—who under Pope Paschal had been given to that church as bishop from this our monastery—to summon the aforesaid Rao concerning it, so that he might restore the whole territory and presume no further to do such a thing in the land [Note: The manuscript lacks *terra*, “land.”] of St Benedict, which stood under the protection of the Roman Church. But if he did not wish to obey the bishop in this—or rather, the Roman Church—the bishop was to exercise canonical justice upon him; for whatever he did in the matter at justice’s prompting, the pope, with the Lord as author, would hold valid and confirm [Col. 0902B].

Then also, in 1122, Lord Pontius, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, because of the great devotion he bore to Father Benedict, came to this monastery of Monte Cassino with twelve brethren of his church.

[Note: Pontius came to Rome in April 1122 and took part in the battle near Ascalon in May 1123.]

After prostrating himself at the feet of our Abbot Gerard and inspecting the monastery’s workshops, he said: “I would rather be dean of Monte Cassino than abbot of Cluny.” Then, prostrating himself at the brethren’s feet and commending himself to their prayers, he set out for Jerusalem, promising St Benedict that after his return he would leave pastoral care and serve God more attentively in this holy monastery of Monte Cassino.

76. At the same time, when the possessions of the monastery of St Maurus, situated at Glanfeuil [Col. 0902C], were being plundered by certain persons, Gerard, abbot of that monastery, sent letters to our Abbot Gerard, asking him to urge Pope Calixtus in this matter; and he did so. Moved by his petitions, the pontiff sent the apostolic blessing to Glanfeuil and its brethren, and to the bishops of Germany:

[Note: Or perhaps Gaul?]

He ordered that the possessions of the monastery of St Maurus, which belonged by right to the monastery of Monte Cassino and had been seized by unjust robbery by the count of Anjou:

[Note: The younger Fulk.]

and by others, were to be restored in their entirety.

At the same time our Abbot Gerard granted to the brothers’ wardrobe the church of St Mary of Casale Piano, the monastery of St Benedict at Pectinari, and the church of St Nicholas in the castle of St Martin, with all the appurtenances of those churches.

[Note: All these have already been enumerated in the charter mentioned above in ch. 69.]

77. When the same abbot had now reached a very advanced age [Col. 0902D], on the anniversary day of Abbot Oderisius, 2 December, while he was chanting the office for the dead for him in the chapel of St Sebastian, after finishing the first vigil, as he intoned the antiphon, “My soul lives for God,” the aforesaid Abbot Oderisius visibly appeared to Abbot Gerard behind the altar of that church and beckoned him with his hand to come to him. When Abbot Gerard saw this, he fell upon his face and began to weep inconsolably. When the office was completed, he returned to his chamber weeping and lamenting.

Asked by the brethren why he wept, he revealed the reason and foretold that he himself would die shortly. Not long afterward, the same abbot, stricken by illness, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, in 1123, lost death and found life. He was buried in the chapter-house of the brethren at the head of Abbot Desiderius.

Abbot Oderisius, the forty-second after St Benedict, ruled for 3 years, 4 months, and 15 days.

78. This man, tracing the line of his origin from the family of the counts of Sangro [Col. 0903B], was received into this place under Oderisius of holy memory, clothed in the monastic habit, and excellently educated in the liberal disciplines. Appointed provost of this monastery by his predecessor Gerard, and possessed of much prudence and wisdom, he was made deacon in the Lateran church by the venerable Pope Paschal.

[Note: Compare above, ch. 42.]

When Abbot Gerard had entered upon the way of all flesh, the brethren assembled, as is customary in such cases. Since our congregation was then torn by very many dissensions and each proposed to choose an abbot according to his own will, at last they chose the same Oderisius as abbot by unanimous decision. They promptly sent letters to the aforesaid Pope Calixtus, reporting Gerard’s death [Col. 0903C] and Oderisius’s election. When the pontiff learned of his election, he sent apostolic letters to the brethren of this monastery, confirming the election and commanding:

[Note: The manuscript reads *mandans*, “commanding.”]

that they should endeavour to obey him in all things.

When March came, and the things necessary for the journey had been prepared, he came to Rome to be consecrated, as the pontiff had directed him. There he was honourably consecrated by the same pope, who happened then to be holding a synod, and was held in great honour by the cardinals and Roman nobles.

At this synod bishops and archbishops brought a complaint against monks, saying that nothing remained except that, once their rods and rings had been taken away, they should serve the monks: “For they hold churches, villages [Col. 0903D], castles, tithes, and the offerings of the living and the dead.” Repeatedly making these complaints before the pontiff, they said:

“The shame of canons has fallen; decency has been obliterated; the religious discipline of clerics has collapsed, while monks, despising heavenly desire, insatiably covet the rights of bishops and seek all things that are their own. Those who have left the world with its desires do not cease to long for the things that are in the world; and those to whom, through Blessed Benedict, a place is freely offered for resting from worldly cares [Col. 0904A] exhaust themselves opportunely and importunately in taking away the things that belong to bishops.”

[Note: Compare canons 17–19 of this council in Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, p. 285.]

While different persons held differing views about this matter, one of our men rose in their midst at our abbot’s prompting and said:

“Our enemies have gathered together and glory in their strength; but do you, our Lord, break their strength, that they may know that there is none other who fights for us except you, our Lord. For what are the brethren who dwell at Cassino to do, who day and night do not cease to beseech the mercy of almighty God for the salvation of the whole world? What are they to do if the grants of the Roman pontiffs are violated? The abbots of Monte Cassino have not served the Roman Church in such a way that, in the time of your apostolate, we should deserve to lose and be disinherited of those things which emperors, kings, dukes, princes, and Roman pontiffs have offered to St Benedict [Col. 0904B].”

While he advanced these and many other arguments, a bishop of Liguria said:

“Although the piety of my fellow bishops has brought a complaint against monks, our predecessors did not enrich monasteries without reason. From the beginning of the nascent Church, it is well known that there have been two orders: one to labour in word and doctrine, the other to devote itself to prayer; one to serve the active life, the other the contemplative. Therefore it is fitting that we should love monks rather than persecute them.”

Pope Calixtus then imposed silence and said:

“The church of Monte Cassino was founded not by men nor through a man, but by Jesus Christ. At his command Father Benedict came to that place, cleansed it from the filth of idols, and, by the composition of the holy Rule, the wonders of miracles, and the burial of his body, made it conspicuous to the whole world and the head of the entire monastic order. Furthermore, this venerable place has been restored by Roman pontiffs and continues as the unique consolation of the children of the Roman Church in adversity and their unfailing repose in prosperity. Therefore, following in the footsteps of our holy predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, we decree that the monastery of Monte Cassino, with all its appurtenances, shall remain forever free and exempt from the yoke of all mortals, and shall remain under the jurisdiction and perpetual protection of the holy Roman Church alone [Col. 0904D]. We order that all other matters remain to the monastery in the order in which they stood of old.”

At that same council, the venerable pope also took care to commend the soul of the aforesaid Abbot Gerard and all the possessions of our monastery to the bishops and archbishops. When the aforesaid abbot had finished all his business at Rome, he returned to this monastery and was received by all the brethren with an honourable and solemn procession.

79. Meanwhile the men of St Angelo in Todice [Col. 0905A], who had always been the leaders and authors of every tribulation and persecution arising in this place, joined themselves to the inhabitants of the castle of St Victor, conspired against the same abbot, and bound one another by oaths that they would render no fealty to this monastery of Monte Cassino or to its abbot unless he granted them remissions and settlements according to their will. When this was reported to the abbot, he immediately gathered an army and began by every means to devastate all their surrounding lands.

But when they saw that what they had not expected had happened, they were moved by tardy repentance, threw themselves at the abbot’s feet, and acknowledged that they had sinned and acted wickedly. They begged him most earnestly to grant them pardon for their crime. The abbot granted their request [Col. 0905B], forgave their offences, and, after extorting from them a considerable sum of money and receiving their fealty, compelled the hostile and perverse men to remain quiet and faithful.

Meanwhile, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1122:

[Note: Rather 1123, as the Anonymous of Monte Cassino has.]

on the day before the Nones of April, during the fourth watch of the night, while the brethren were chanting the nocturnal synaxis, countless stars were seen falling and, as it were, raining from heaven everywhere throughout the whole world.

At that time Count Pandulf of Sesto, mentioned above (ch. 75), came to this monastery and confirmed by oath to the same abbot the whole abbey in its entirety, and specifically the castle of Vitecuso with its appurtenances, concerning which, as we have related above, he had had a dispute with Abbot Gerard.

80. In these same days Savinus, a most noble man of Dalmatian birth [Col. 0905C], sent to this monastery two silver cups weighing about nine pounds, begging and earnestly requesting that the same abbot send some of our brethren to Dalmatia to demonstrate the monastic order, promising that no small benefit would come to this place through it. The abbot did not delay, but sent three brothers from this monastery there, supplying them most abundantly with codices of Holy Scripture and ecclesiastical equipment.

When Savinus had received the brethren, with the permission of the aforesaid Pope Calixtus and the consent of the archbishop of Ragusa, he offered to St Benedict the church of St Mary at the place called Rabiata, near the city of Ragusa, with its harbour and fishing rights [Col. 0905D], male and female slaves, and all its appurtenances and boundaries whatsoever.

At a later time Pope Calixtus came to this monastery. He excluded Count Godfrey of Ceccano, who had withdrawn the monastery of St Peter at Iscleta from this place’s jurisdiction, from the thresholds of the church until he should make worthy satisfaction.

[Note: Compare book II, ch. 32.]

Thus commending himself earnestly to Father Benedict and the brethren, he departed for Benevento [Col. 0906A]. In these days Homodeus and Albert were sent from this monastery as bishops in Sardinia, and Petronius and Adenulf as abbots in Dalmatia. At the same time the aforesaid Abbot Oderisius ordered most beautiful bronze doors to be made at the entrance of our church.

81. Lambert, bishop of Ostia, afterward Pope Honorius, came to this monastery at that time and began to ask the same abbot to grant lodging for himself and his household in the monastery of St Mary at Pallaria, just as his predecessor Leo had possessed on behalf of our monastery.

[Note: Compare book III, ch. 36.]

But the abbot, seeing that he sought this by right of his predecessor, and at the same time taking care that our church might not lose that place on this pretext, denied that he could do this [Col. 0906B]. The bishop, filled alike with indignation and anger, departed, awaiting an opportunity to injure and oppose the same abbot.

82. At the same time, Richard, surnamed Pignardus [Note: [Col. 0905D] He is called the son of Rao Pigardus in Jordan’s privilege.], lord of the castle of Pica, enticed by the promises of Richard of Caleno, summoned Leo, consul of Fondi, and his son Peter. After giving him a meal in his house, while Leo was with him under the security of an oath, and was also his co-godfather and friend, Richard—like the traitor Judas—hostilely seized him with all his men and handed him over to Richard of Caleno, as they had secretly conspired together. When this came to the knowledge of Pope Calixtus, he was deeply moved by so wicked and shameful a betrayal [Note: [Col. 0905] A word is either lacking, or *et* is superfluous.], and commanded the same abbot to strive to attack the aforesaid Richard by whatever means and efforts he could.

It happened, perhaps, that then [Note: [Col. 0905] Read *tunc*, “then.”] one of our men, because circumstances so required, set out for the city of Fondi. On the journey itself he was captured by the men of that same Richard, thrown from his horse, and subjected to very many indignities [Note: [Col. 0905] Perhaps *quam*, “than”?]; and, with the business for which he had gone left unfinished, he returned to the abbot. The abbot therefore, taking this opportunity, entered into an alliance with Octavian, brother of the aforesaid Leo, and, surrounded by troops of soldiers, began by every means to lay waste the dependencies of the castle of Pica.

But although for almost a whole year he had devastated and harassed that castle, Richard, recognizing with absolute certainty that Pope Calixtus would come against him with an army, secretly withdrew from the castle with his brothers, without anyone knowing. When this was reported to the abbot, he assembled a great army and came to the same castle. Received by its inhabitants, he long and vigorously besieged its citadel and took it by surrender, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123. [Note: [Col. 0906D] In 1124 the castle of Pica was acquired by Abbot O., and was confirmed to St Benedict by Pope Calixtus and Prince Jordan. *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*.]

Once Abbot Oderisius had obtained the town as he desired, he took care to notify Pope Calixtus by letter. Giving thanks to Almighty God for this, the pope invested blessed Benedict, by means of the ring he wore on his hand, with the castle, without any co-holder or participant whatsoever.

Richard, lord of Caleno, moreover, when he learned that our abbot held the aforesaid castle, was stricken with grief of heart. He hurried to Capua and, falling at the prince’s feet, begged, entreated, and implored him to come to his aid, so that he might be able to recover the castle. The prince assented to the requests of his kinsman, assembled an army, and set out to besiege and plunder this territory. But the abbot himself, surrounded by companies of soldiers, came to the castle of Bantra and did not allow him to enter the land of St Benedict.
