Accordingly, the prince, admonished by letters from Pope Calixtus and adjured by the oath he had sworn to the Roman Church not to ravage the land of St Benedict—or else [Note: [Col. 0907D] Read *aliter*, “otherwise.”] be subject to excommunication—summoned the abbot to himself. Receiving three hundred pounds from him, he issued to this monastery a princely charter concerning the aforesaid castle [Note: [Col. 0907D] Published from the original by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 240. The castle is there called Lupica.] (1125, February), and thus returned to the city of Capua.

At the same time Countess Adelasia, together with Count Ildebrand [Note: [Col. 0907D] Of Tuscany.], by command of the aforesaid Pope Calixtus [Note: [Col. 0907D] This is not read in the charter.], restored to blessed Benedict the church of St Martin at Armino [Note: [Col. 0907D] Beside the river Armino.], and that of St Columban, with their appurtenances, under a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold [Note: [Col. 0907D] Executed at Grosseto, without date. They were, however, situated in the diocese of Castro, later of Acquapendente; see Gattola, *Historia*, p. 416 ff.].

83. In these days the aforesaid Pope Calixtus died at Rome (1124, December) [Note: [Col. 0908D] 14 December, according to the *Necrology of Monte Cassino*.]. The cardinals divided: some set over themselves as pope, under the name Honorius, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, of whom we have spoken above (ch. 81); others set over themselves as Pope Celestine Theobald, cardinal of the title of St Anastasia. But because the stronger and more influential party was with Honorius, those who favored the aforesaid Theobald, seeing how matters were turning out, were led by belated repentance and returned to Honorius.

The same pope then informed our abbot that Peter’s ship was endangered amid the waves. He urged him to give assistance and to send monetary aid, declaring that he would regard as sons those who helped him in so grave a crisis, but those who did not as stepsons. Moved by such words, the abbot declared that he, who was then being called upon to render the help of assistance, ought to have taken part in the election, so that, as he was a participant in its troubles, he ought also to be a partner in its counsels.

When the brothers asked concerning the aforesaid pope whose son he was, who he was, and what sort and how great a man he was, the abbot replied that he did not know whose son he was; yet he knew one thing for certain: that he was full of letters from head to foot. [Note: [Col. 0908D] Pandulf of Pisa says similarly: “Born of the middling populace of the county of Bologna, yet well educated.”] This cause, therefore, stirred up between that pope and the abbot a perpetual evil of discord and enduring hatred.

84. At that time Leo, consul of Fondi, together with his son Peter, having been released from the captivity in which Richard, lord of Caleno, held them, came to this monastery. Honorably received by the same abbot, after the celebration of the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, he gave them fifty pounds at the request of the aforesaid Leo and his said son, and lent them fifty pounds, on the condition that they should restore those same fifty pounds to the monastery of Monte Cassino within one year, in gold and silver, or in silk cloths and other things suitable for the monks to receive (1125, 29 March).

In return for the aforementioned money which the abbot gave and lent them, the aforesaid Leo, with his son Peter, relinquished to blessed Benedict and the monastery of Monte Cassino all dependent possessions which had been offered to this monastery by any persons in his territory: namely, the church of St Magnus with its appurtenances; a share in the fishery of Lake Fondi; the monastery of St Onuphrius; St Elias at Ambrife; St Martin of Ynola [Note: [Col. 0908D] Now Lenola. ANG.]; St Martin at Tyrille; and whatever else had been offered to blessed Benedict by any persons in his land. The church of Monte Cassino and its abbots were to hold and possess these securely and peacefully, with free power to appoint provosts in the same churches and to do whatever should please our abbots, without any objection or disturbance from them. Moreover, he promised to provide a meal for the brothers every year.

85. Meanwhile, while the counts of Aquino were raging with deadly hatred against Landulf of St John, they began to complain against the abbot that he preferred Landulf to them, gave him money, lands, and houses, but treated them with contempt and regarded them as nothing. Since the abbot gave no hearing to this, they joined with certain of our own men and began to accuse him to Pope Honorius, alleging that the abbot of Monte Cassino was an enemy of the Apostolic See, extravagant, and a squanderer of the monastery’s resources.

Richard, lord of Caleno, meanwhile, never ceasing his attacks upon our monastery (1125), assembled an army and unexpectedly entered this territory. He destroyed by fire and sword the castles belonging to this monastery—St Apollinaris, St Ambrose, St Stephen, and part of the castle of St George [Note: [Col. 0908D] See *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*, under the year 1125.]—and, departing thence, plundered the monastery of St Nicholas at Pica completely. Thus he returned to his own lands.

86. In the same year (1125), Pope Honorius left the City and came up to this monastery. Received in a most honorable procession by the aforesaid abbot and the brothers, he solemnly celebrated Mass upon the altar of blessed Benedict and, already late in the day, returned to the city. Afterwards he removed the heresiarch Maurice from Janula, to which Pope Calixtus had exiled him, and relegated him to exile at Fumone. [Note: [Col. 0909D] The castle of Fumone in the territory of the Hernici, not far from Alatri, stands on a mountain summit. ANG. See *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*, under this year.]

There, in a full assembly of laymen, Pope Honorius summoned the same abbot and, raging against him with extraordinary hatred, rebuked him with vehement reproaches, shouting that he was a soldier and not an abbot, a scatterer and squanderer of the monastery’s substance. Then he immediately left the city and went to Benevento. [Note: [Col. 0910D] He was there in October, according to Falco.]

87. Furthermore, at this time, when Emperor Henry V had died (23 May), the consuls, prefects, dictators, dukes, and princes assembled and began deliberating concerning the election of an emperor. At last all decided to place the election in the discretion of the archbishop of Mainz and Lothair, duke of Saxony, so that all would without doubt elect whomever those two declared useful for the Roman Empire.

The archbishop, however, raging with deadly hostility against Emperor Henry’s family and wishing to exclude his nephews Frederick and Conrad from imperial eminence, judged, because of his hatred of them, that the aforesaid Lothair—highly experienced in arms, endowed with great piety and prudence, and having during many years subdued the Leutici and brought them under Roman rule—was useful and fit to receive the imperial dignity. Thus, by his cunning, the Roman Empire was transferred from the Teutons to the Saxons.

In these days also Rudolf, archbishop of Cosenza, offered to blessed Benedict the church of St Peter at Buda, with its appurtenances. Augustine, bishop of Narni, together with Count Oderisius, did the same with the church of St Nicholas at Guaytanello and the church of St Lucy [Note: [Col. 0910D] Together with the island of St Vitus. Privilege of Alexander III.], with its port and all its appurtenances in their entirety.

88. Meanwhile, after Pope Honorius had returned from Benevento to Rome, Count Adenulf, pursuing the same abbot with deadly hatred, sent letters to the pope, denouncing the abbot of Monte Cassino as a rival of the papacy and its honor. The pope, giving credence to his words, decreed that he should be removed from the abbacy of Monte Cassino. He immediately sent to him Gregory, bishop of Terracina and monk of this monastery, who under Pope Paschal had been made bishop of that city from our church, commanding the abbot to come to Rome and endeavor to answer, by the just sanction of the canons, the accusations brought against him.

When the abbot refused to go to the City unless the pope restored his favor to him, the pope summoned him three times, taking occasion from this. But because he knew that the pope was enraged against him, he delayed going. In the fifth week of the Lenten fast (1126), the same pope pronounced a sentence of deposition against him. He was found guilty of only one charge: that, having been summoned to the curia, he had delayed going. The pope said: “Even if he is blameworthy in nothing else, his pride is nevertheless a crime sufficient for condemnation; for all sins are forgiven to men, but God resists the proud.”

When the holy day of Palms arrived (4 April), the same Oderisius, deceived by the words of his advisers, again sat in the abbot’s chair, held the pastoral staff in his hand, and performed every duty of the abbot as he had before his deposition. This made the pope still more angry. At the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection (11 April), he separated Oderisius and all his supporters from the thresholds of the church, and ordered those obedient to him to be excluded from ecclesiastical communion.

From this there arose a most serious sedition and dissension between the monks and the people of the city. It happened then that the aforesaid Oderisius sent certain infantrymen with his arms to guard the castle of Janula. The townsmen, crying out over the ruin of St Germain, seized the infantrymen, took away their arms, and expelled them from the city. When Oderisius learned what had happened, he attacked the city and went to Pontecorvo to gather an army, threatening to destroy the city with its inhabitants.

They, after taking counsel, went up the mountain, met with the dean and the remaining brothers, and asked them to send letters to Oderisius, requiring him to return to the city and, if he had any complaint against them, to seek lawful justice concerning it. They said this, but intended otherwise, having resolved to kill him at the very crossroads of his journey.

After consultation, the dean decreed that they should return to the city, choose twelve of their wisest and best men, and come with them on the following day to this monastery, so that the brothers might take salutary counsel with them on the matter. After they departed, the dean, in the silence of night, sent a messenger to Oderisius, reported in order what had been done and said, and earnestly begged him to return to them. But Oderisius, knowing the treachery of the citizens, refused that he could then return to them.

At daybreak the citizens, as had been arranged, went up the mountain one by one, entered the monastery, and assembled in chapter. They began to repeat what had been determined the previous day between the monks and laymen concerning a peace settlement. [Note: [Col. 0909] Read *quae*, “which.”] As their discussion of the same matter continued at length, one of the citizens rose in their midst and said: “Why do you prolong the discussion in vain? Know with certainty that we shall not leave the monastery unless, after deposing Oderisius, you appoint another abbot according to our counsel.”

When the brothers said that under no reasoning and on no terms would they do this, the citizens immediately seized the monastery’s fortifications by treachery. Gathering together in the name of the supreme archimandrite, they pronounced through their archpriest a sentence of deposition and excommunication against Oderisius. Then they went at once to the fortress of Anagni; bribed with money those residing there; won them over to their purpose; took that fortification from its guards and demolished it. They struck with swords the opposing monks before the doors of the church of blessed Benedict, and began to swear by everything divine and human that, unless the monks immediately elected an abbot according to their will, they would slaughter some with the sword, drive others from the monastery, and send others bound to the pope.

Why say more? Seeing themselves placed in extremity of danger, the brothers sent messengers to Oderisius and instructed him to return to the monastery, either to satisfy the laymen or to relinquish the abbacy in accordance with their will. When Oderisius said that he would do neither, the brothers, compelled by necessity, promised to carry out the laymen’s will.

Thus Oderisius was cast out by his enemies and driven from his own seat: certainly a high-minded man, renowned for learning, adorned with eloquence. For, amid so many persecutions, he composed quite lucid and eloquent sermons for the principal feasts. From that time onward, however, various and great calamities did not fail to afflict this monastery of Monte Cassino.

We shall now describe how Nicholas’s election and expulsion took place.

## NICHOLAS, a Tusculan by birth, sat for 1 year, 1 month, and 16 days.

89. He had been received into this monastery of Monte Cassino and made a monk by Oderisius I of holy memory. Appointed rector at Suio by Abbot Gerard, he was afterwards made dean of this place by Oderisius II. Having administered that office for about one month, he was elected abbot by the brothers of this monastery (1126, June).

Certain of the priors, however, taking this very badly, secretly sent letters to Pope Honorius without the knowledge of the others, asserting that he had been elected factiously and by no means canonically. Since the pope did not yet know that Nicholas had been elected, he sent Gregory, cardinal of the title of the Apostles, to this monastery, commanding that, on Gregory’s advice, the brothers of Monte Cassino should unanimously elect Seniorectus, provost of the Capuan monastery, as their shepherd and abbot. By his diligence God would be honored; the condition of religious life in the renowned monastery of Monte Cassino would be strengthened; and the goods of the church, both spiritual and temporal, would be increased for the better. For he himself, if need arose, was prepared to uphold, defend, and assist the monastery.

When the aforesaid cardinal came to the monastery, he assembled the brothers and set forth in order what the pope had commanded. On hearing this, a great murmur suddenly arose among them. They said that the election of an abbot of Monte Cassino ought not to pass into another’s power, and that it was utterly unworthy and improper that the church of Monte Cassino, which under its predecessors had always been free, should be subjected to cardinals, to the disgrace of its own dishonor.

Then Gregory, imposing silence upon the brothers, said:

> “Know without doubt that I have not come here for Pope Honorius’s gain or for the honor of the Roman Church, but, if you permit it, to provide with Christ’s help for the salvation of your souls. The Roman Church has no need of your assistance or praise, for in Peter she merited from the Redeemer’s own mouth the proclamation of praise. What church or abbey, moreover, is found exempt from the yoke of the Roman See, by whose judgment heaven itself is bound and loosed? For all churches were founded by bishops, emperors, kings, or other faithful persons; but the Roman See was founded by the Son of God alone, and established upon the faith of the Apostle Peter. To Peter he also entrusted the rights of both earthly and heavenly dominion; and that Word which created heaven and earth founded the Roman Church.
>
> “And, omitting other matters, to come to those now under discussion: just as the chiefs of the apostles, Peter and Paul, consecrated the Roman Church with their blood, so the monastery of Monte Cassino had its foundation through blessed Benedict, who had been educated at Rome, and through the Roman citizens Maurus and Placidus. Nor do we doubt that you know very well how, after it had been destroyed by the Lombards, the brothers of the monastery of Monte Cassino lived beside the Lateran palace for one hundred and thirty years, and how at last the Roman pontiffs Gregory and Zacharias rebuilt the church of Monte Cassino. When it was again burned by the Saracens, it was restored once more to monastic order by holy Pope Agapetus.
>
> “Therefore, since the founders of this monastery came forth from the discipline of the Roman Church and its restorers were Roman pontiffs, it is fitting, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, that the Roman Church be called by right the mother and lady, and Monte Cassino her special and singular daughter. Turn over the charters of Monte Cassino; search its books; and you will be able to find what is now under discussion. But if you cannot, accuse me of falsehood; if, however, you can, do not resist the truth, do not oppose the Roman Church, and do not act contrary to its commands. Rather, from the breasts from which you have suckled the salvation of faith, strive in all things to obey its commands.”

Then the brothers, pointing to the necessity of the time, declared that they would fulfill the apostolic will if more prosperous times for obedience should arise. Thus the chapter was dismissed.

Oderisius, meanwhile, when he learned of Nicholas’s unexpected election, quickly came to the fortress called Bantra, distributed money at every opportunity and out of season, gathered soldiers from every quarter, and began utterly to destroy by fire and sword the castles that favored Nicholas.

90. In this same year, Geoffrey, son of Richard of Aquila, together with Richard, lord of Caleno, and Rao, son of Rahel, long and fiercely besieged the castle of Suio, and obtained it through the treachery and habitual betrayal of its inhabitants. Nicholas, upon learning this, summoned Robert, son of Prince Jordan, to his aid. He immediately sent to this monastery and ordered the following to be brought to him: silver ewers and basins weighing nine pounds and as many ounces, which Savimus, as we related above (ch. 80), had sent to blessed Benedict; the silver ewers and basins of Pope Stephen; the golden altar with precious gems; a golden chalice weighing four pounds; the large Saxon chalice which Theoderic, king of the Saxons, had once sent to blessed Benedict; Abbot Desiderius’s golden epistolary; Emperor Henry’s Gospel book with precious gems; another Gospel book; nine silver censers; the same number of silver crowns, some weighing nine pounds each and others twelve pounds, which Emperor Otto, Margrave Hugh, and other faithful persons had offered to St Benedict; a chalice of nine pounds; five other chalices; a basin of seven pounds; three pairs of candlesticks; four crowns weighing eighteen pounds each; two basins of eight pounds; a cauldron [Note: [Col. 0913D] A broad-bellied vessel in which water is heated. Du Cange.] of six pounds; a Gospel book; a large dish; the duke’s pitcher with its aquiminile; all these of silver; and a golden cross.

Having removed all these things from this church, he did not recover the castle, and stirred up an irreconcilable hatred of the monks against himself.

91. Meanwhile, when the citizens planned to seize the monastery again (1127), they approached one of the priors and promised him the deanship and a considerable sum of money if he would, to the best of his ability, cooperate with them in so wicked an undertaking. When he disclosed this to the brothers, they at once posted all their faithful supporters in the monastery’s fortifications. The citizens, unaware that the matter had been revealed, laid an ambush near the monastery when night came; but when they discovered that their plans had been exposed, they returned home filled with shame and grief.

At that time a certain Adenulf, lord of the castle of Spigno, anxiously and eagerly considering how he could by any means harass this monastery, first spoke with Richard, lord of Caleno, and Geoffrey of Sessa. He revealed the inmost purpose of his heart and earnestly asked that, by their support and help, he might bring the malice he had conceived to birth and effect. The traitors, delighted beyond measure, urged him to carry out his plan, saying that their help would not fail him. They declared that this would be wholesome, delightful, and pleasing to them.

Meanwhile, this same Adenulf summoned the men who guarded the fortress of Castrum Novum. He promised them money and undertook to make them distinguished and prosperous if they would hand over to him the fortress of the aforesaid Castrum Novum. But the traitors, enticed by bloody promises, summoned him in the silence of deepest night with certain bandits and, without the monk and the other townsmen knowing, surrendered the aforesaid fortress. [Note: [Col. 0913D] In 1127, according to the *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*.]

When this was reported to Nicholas, he did not know what to do or say. At length, after consulting with certain men who limped on the right knee [Note: [Col. 0913D] A proverbial expression indicating those whose fidelity was doubtful. ANG.], in order to recover the aforesaid castle he restored to Norman control the town of Pica, which his predecessor Oderisius had acquired [Note: [Col. 0913D] See ch. 82 above.], which Pope Calixtus had confirmed by a ring, and which Prince Jordan had granted by oath and charter. By this arrangement he recovered the aforesaid Castrum Novum. [Note: [Col. 0913D] *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*.]

At that time the aforesaid Geoffrey also restored the tower called *Ad mare* (“By the Sea”), the monastery of St Benedict at Sessa, the estate of Lauriana, Casa Maggiore, the estate of Lando by the Sea, and St John at the Currents, together with everything belonging to the aforesaid estates and dependencies.

92. In these days two brothers from Spain, Philip and Philibert, touched by heavenly desire, came in great devotion to the thresholds of Father Benedict. They offered to this holy place the church which they themselves had long before built in Spain on their own land beside the city of Logroño [Note: [Col. 0914D] Logroño.], in the place called Coadgranium.

Meanwhile, seeing that the Roman pontiff opposed him in all things, Oderisius, led by belated repentance, went to Rome. Falling at the pope’s feet, he resigned the abbacy of Monte Cassino into the hand of that apostolic lord [Note: [Col. 0914D] *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*, under the year 1127.], and restored the fortress of Bantra to the rights of this monastery.

At that time Rao, son of Rahel, came to this monastery and renounced in writing before blessed Benedict all the suits, complaints, and claims which he had had against this monastery concerning men who had belonged to the city of Teano and were then living in this territory, under a penalty of four hundred bezants.

At the same time Prince Jordan II came to this place and confirmed to the same abbot by oath the whole abbey in its entirety, according to the custom of his predecessors. [Note: [Col. 0914D] There survives only the oath he made to Oderisius, in June 1123, in Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 239.]

93. At the same time (1127), Pandulf, son of Landon, count of Aquino, began to build a castle in the forest of this monastery called Tyrilla. [Note: [Col. 0914D] It still exists, but is under the jurisdiction of the duke of Sora. ANG. “The castle of Terelle is built”: *Anonymous of Monte Cassino*, under the year 1127.] When this was reported to Pope Honorius, he sent him apostolic letters forbidding him to build a castle on the possession of blessed Benedict. But, despising God in the pope himself, he sacrilegiously constructed the same castle anew for the attack upon this place, as may be seen today.

Nicholas, wishing to obstruct his undertaking, built a castle against him on the mountain called Timmari. When the many disturbances and misfortunes of the monastery of Monte Cassino reached Pope Honorius’s ears, he removed Nicholas from the government of the abbey of Monte Cassino and separated from the thresholds of the church all who favored or adhered to him. He sent letters to this monastery, declaring that he would labor with eager purpose and diligent effort so that the ancient religious order might be restored in the noble and renowned monastery of blessed Benedict. Therefore, if they would place freely and without any opposition the disposition and ordering of the monastery of Monte Cassino in his hand and counsel, he would hasten as swiftly as possible to Monte Cassino and, by the Lord’s aid, endeavor to labor for the honor, welfare, and reform of the monastery in both spiritual and temporal matters.

The brothers, who greatly hated Nicholas because of his squandering of the church treasury and loss of territory, shut the gates against him when he came to the monastery. Immediately sending messengers to Pope Honorius, they reported in order what they had done and surrendered themselves and the monastery wholly into his power. Delighted by this affair, he sent Matthew, bishop of Albano, to this monastery, ordering the brothers to elect without any delay whomever Matthew, by the authority of the Roman See, should declare useful and fit for so great an office.

When the aforesaid Pandulf learned this, he unexpectedly came against the castle which Nicholas had built and razed it to the ground. Such was the outcome of Nicholas’s affairs.

## Seniorectus, forty-fourth abbot of this monastery from blessed Benedict, sat for 9 years, 6 months, and 19 days.

94. This man, offered to blessed Benedict from his earliest childhood, made a monk by Oderisius of holy memory, and most diligently educated and reared in every branch of regular discipline, was first sent to govern the monastery of Saint Mary at Luco, and afterwards the monastery of Saint Nicholas at Pica. He was elected to the abbacy of this monastery in the following manner. Thus, after he had administered the deanery of this holy house quite vigorously for three years, and afterwards had governed very prudently the provostship of the monastery of Capua, Nicholas having been expelled by order of Pope Honorius [Col. 0915D], he was elected from that same provostship of the Capuan monastery to the abbacy of this place. Indeed, when Conrad, cardinal of Saint Praxedis, had come to this place on behalf of the aforesaid pontiff for this matter, and had conferred now privately, now publicly, with them, he finally disclosed the apostolic will to the community. Then word was sent to him by common counsel that he should strive with all possible urgency to come to this monastery, so that the election of the abbot of Monte Cassino [Col. 0916A] might be discussed jointly by all. As he endeavoured to carry out the command, he was captured by Geoffrey of Aquila, who favoured Nicholas’s party, and committed to custody at Suio. When this was reported to the brethren, they began anxiously to consider what they should do; and, as is customary, different men held different views. Some proposed recalling Oderisius; others proposed electing an abbot according to their own preference.

Then the aforesaid Matthew, bishop of Albano, came into the chapter-house on 12 July and began to discuss the election of the abbot, asking whether they were willing to obey the apostolic commands. The brethren, however, having placed the matter in his decision, said that they wished in every respect to obey the Roman pontiff and promised that, whoever he should nominate with the counsel of the brethren, they would elect as abbot. Then, calling him by his own name [Col. 0916B], he asked the elders first and then the younger men whether such an election pleased them. Since all answered that they wished it, both by voice and by inclination of their heads—

> [Note: [Col. 0915D] Among us the custom is still observed that the elders approve aloud, but the younger men by bowing their heads, [Col. 0916D] what is proposed in the convent. ANG.]

—they immediately, by the unanimous consent of all, although he was absent, elected him abbot on the fourth day before the Ides of July [12 July], by command of the apostolic see, as we have already said. Nevertheless, some—indeed, for the most part through fear—took this ill, namely because during his time as dean he had proved excessively austere and strict in the discipline of this monastery, and because he had also been made abbot by the Roman Church.

Finally, from almost the time when he relinquished the deanery, and especially from the death of the venerable Abbot Gerard, when nearly all the senior brethren who had been made monks by Desiderius had departed this world, the religious discipline of the order began to weaken. This happened now through ambition for the abbacy itself [Col. 0916C], now through the brethren’s secret seditions, now through expulsions of abbots; and the brethren had fallen into such poverty that they suffered extreme want of every necessity. Nor was this without reason, since very many, compelled by necessity, could not maintain the path of the arduous life because of poverty. As these and other reports circulated widely, the apostolic lord, grieving that the church of Monte Cassino was dishonoured by such great reproaches and wishing to put an end to these evils, repeatedly pondered in his heart that sentence of the Rule:

> [Note: [Col. 0916D] Chapter 64.]

> “If, God forbid, the community has elected a corrupt person, and this becomes known to the bishop in whose diocese the place lies, or to abbots or neighbouring Christians, let them prevent the wicked consensus from prevailing,”

and so forth. Having deposed Oderisius, as was said above, and wishing to act similarly concerning his successor Nicholas, he completely separated the community from the thresholds of the church if they should presume thereafter to remain obedient to that same Nicholas.

Therefore the brethren, who already held the said Nicholas in great hatred because of his squandering of the church treasury, took counsel and barred him from entering the monastery. They quickly sent persons to report these matters to the Roman pontiff [Col. 0917A], asking him to send one of his own representatives through whom the pope might disclose his will to the community, so that, with his counsel and aid, they might elect an abbot for themselves. Then the apostolic lord sent the same bishop to this monastery, ordering him to place the same man over this community. Seniorrectus, therefore, having been released by Geoffrey, came to this monastery; and when his election had been confirmed by the brethren, they honourably placed him in the chair of Father Benedict.

Having received the abbacy, Seniorrectus began by every means alike to strive diligently to fulfil that for which he had been made abbot by the Roman pontiff. His mind was greatly, indeed exceedingly, troubled at times, both for the reform of our order and especially for the support of the brethren and the recovery of the land [Col. 0917B]. Meanwhile the townspeople, taking the opportunity, sought dispensations and concessions according to their own wishes, and even obtained them by force. Thus our former abbot Nicholas, supported and aided by Geoffrey of Aquila, retained a certain part of this territory—namely Myrtula, Saint Andrew, Cold Valley, and New Castle—and did not cease to harass the land which remained to this place.

For this reason Prince Jordan, summoned by the same abbot, came at once with a considerable force of soldiers. Marching against New Castle, where the nephew of the aforesaid Nicholas resided, he ordered all the neighbouring places to be devastated with fire and sword. But that man, seeing that the townspeople were deserting him and had secretly sent messengers to the abbot, immediately sought to send word to the abbot that, if he were allowed to depart safely with all his people [Col. 0917C], he would without delay immediately restore the castle to him. This being granted, he promptly surrendered that same castle into the abbot’s hands.

95. Meanwhile the apostolic lord, leaving Rome, came to this monastery, from whom this abbot first received consecration to the abbacy in this church. Afterwards, however, the pope began urgently to demand an oath from him and to insist absolutely that he swear fealty to the Roman Church. The brethren resisted and objected by every means, saying that the abbots of Monte Cassino had never done this. The pontiff, on the other hand, answered that what almost all bishops, archbishops, and abbots do, the abbot of Monte Cassino ought to do. [Col. 0917D] To whom—

> [Note: [Col. 0917D] That is, “to whom.” ANG.]

—our men replied that the Roman Church had exacted fealty from those others because they had often lapsed into heresy and held opinions contrary to the Roman Church [Col. 0918A]; but the church of Monte Cassino had never fallen into heresy and had never held views contrary to the apostolic see. When the pope heard this reasoning, he fell silent. Thereafter the pontiff departed from this place and entered Benevento. But enough of these matters.

96. Duke William, having already ruled the duchy for nearly sixteen years, died on 28 July 1127, and with him ended the whole family of Robert Guiscard which descended from him. After the duke’s death, Roger—

> [Note: [Col. 0917D] See the Anonymous of Monte Cassino under the year 1128.]

—heir and son of the late Roger, count of Sicily, brother of the aforesaid Duke Robert Guiscard, seized the duchy in 1128. The apostolic lord hastened against him with an expedition; but when peace had at last been made, he confirmed the duchy to him.

> [Note: [Col. 0917D] 22 August.]

In these same days, when Prince Jordan died [Col. 0918B] on 19 December 1127—

> [Note: [Col. 0917] Here begins the last quire, written by that other hand, though scarcely different; see above.]

—his son Robert succeeded him in the principality. He granted this monastery a privilege in March 1128—

> [Note: [Col. 0917D] Published by Angelo de Nuce in the notes to this passage, and by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 242, from the original.]

—concerning the remission of the *data* owed by the men of Casa Gentiana; concerning escheats—

> [Note: [Col. 0917D] That is, the three hundred tareni which we received every year from the men of Casa Genzana as the *data*. Likewise the lands left by men who die without heirs, called *scadiones*; those now existing or which shall exist hereafter.]

—concerning twenty modii of land in the territory of Saint Maurus at Casale; concerning fishing in sea and river throughout the whole territory from Castello to the sea; concerning the things granted by Jordan II, his father; Richard II and Robert, his uncles; Jordan, his grandfather; and Richard, his great-grandfather; and concerning persons who came to settle in the land of Saint Benedict or to make any grant to the monastery. A penalty of one hundred pounds of gold was imposed.

Robert, count of Molise, also granted this place a privilege concerning half of the castle of Serra—

> [Note: [Col. 0918D] Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 243, believes this to be the place now called Serra Capriola, where he published the charter of Hugh, count of Molise, confirming a donation made by his dying uncle Robert; it is dated June 1128.]

—which lies under the jurisdiction of the bishopric of Larino, with a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold [Col. 0918C]. Moreover Duke Roger—

> [Note: [Col. 0918D] “Helper and shield of Christians,” as he himself says in the privilege published by Gattola, in the place cited.]

—granted a privilege to Saint Benedict on 30 December 1129 concerning the things offered by Duke Robert and his wife Sichelgaita, and by their sons Roger and William, in Apulia, Calabria, the Principality, Salerno, and Amalfi; concerning the grants of princes, barons, and other faithful men; and imposed a penalty of three hundred pounds of gold. It was issued in the year of the Lord 1130 through the hand of Guarnerius, dean of Mazara.

> [Note: [Col. 0918D] Guarinus, master chamberlain of the said duke, also subscribed.]

97. Meanwhile Pope Honorius died on 14 February 1130. Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, was elected pope as Innocent II; and Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Callistus, was elected as Anacletus. Innocent remained for some time [Col. 0918D] in Rome, then went with the bishops and cardinals who favoured his party to the city of Pisa, leaving Conrad, bishop of Savona, as his vicar [Col. 0919A] in Rome. Peter the cardinal, moreover, bestowed a crown upon Duke Roger of Apulia and, by a privilege—

> [Note: [Col. 0919C] Published by Baronius in the *Annals* for the year 1130, no. 52.]

—confirmed to him the principality of Capua and the duchy of Naples together with Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily on 27 September, made him king, and drew him to his party. He ordered that bishops and abbots dwelling in the territory under his dominion should render him homage.

> [Note: [Col. 0919C] This is not found in that privilege. Baronius, in the place cited, no. 53, believes that it was written in another document of which only the opening words survive in the Register of Anacletus preserved at Monte Cassino.]

At the same time, in March 1132, Prince Robert, whom we mentioned above, granted this place a privilege as he had before, including a remission of fifty tareni from the *gualdo*.

> [Note: [Col. 0919C] That is, the five hundred tareni which we were accustomed to receive every third year from those holding lands of the *gualdo* for *calzati*, that is, for repairing roads; in the original diploma published by Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 245.]

It also concerned the mill-ford located on the River Volturno at the place called Cazoli, together with the crossing on both banks of the river. After this—

> [Note: [Col. 0920C] From the Anonymous of Monte Cassino under this year.]

—the aforesaid prince went to Pisa in 1134, and King Roger marched against the principality. For this reason [Col. 0919B] the prince came from Pisa to Naples, accompanied by a naval force. The people of Aversa submitted to his authority; but King Roger came against him, put him to flight, reduced Aversa to ashes in 1135, and gave the principality of Capua to his son Alfonso.

At that time, in 1136, Hubert, archbishop of Pisa and legate of the apostolic see, granted this monastery a privilege concerning Saint George of Baray and Saint Mary of Gennor. Innocent then entered the land of the Germans and Lotharingians in 1131 and was received near Liège by King Lothar in March. Innocent confirmed the staff and ring to Lothar in accordance with ancient custom—

> [Note: [Col. 0920C] Innocent did not grant this to the king when he requested it; whether he then promised him Matilda’s land I do not know. He opposed it at Rome on 8 June 1133, as Angelo de Nuce rightly observed.]

—and also assigned him the land of Countess Matilda. Then King Lothar—

> [Note: [Col. 0920C] From the Anonymous of Monte Cassino.]

—came to Rome, received the crown from Innocent, and returned on 4 June 1133. [Col. 0919C]

> [Note: [Col. 0919] Here begins: “Peter the Deacon’s Disputation for the Monastery of Monte Cassino.” Thus, while in the presence of Emperor Lothar the whole, etc.]

And while, so to speak, the whole Roman world lay peacefully at rest before him and those under his rule lay crushed—

> [Note: [Col. 0919] A word appears to be lacking.]

—he was repeatedly urged by letters from Pope Innocent, who was staying at Pisa in 1135, to defend the crown of the Roman Empire from the yoke of enemies, and, as a most vigorous and merciful Caesar, to free the divided Church for peace, concord, and unity. Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1135, gathering an immense and exceedingly great army from the whole Roman Empire, he entered Italy with his wife, the Empress Richenza, in 1136. Meanwhile great terror and mental stupefaction seized Ausonia—

> [Note: [Col. 0919] Lauretus emended *corrupit* to *corripuit*, “seized.”]

—and each asked another what they ought to say or do.

> [Note: [Col. 0919] The *Disputation* continues: “But the abbot…” and, after briefly narrating in nine verses what is treated here more fully in chapters 103–106, proceeds to chapter 107.]

[Col. 0920A] 98. Meanwhile Guarinus, the king’s chancellor, ordered Canzolinus, who was then in command at Capua, to send word to the abbot of Monte Cassino to come to him, and to seize him immediately when he came.

> [Note: [Col. 0920C] These matters and what follows should be compared with Wibald’s letter in Martène, *Collectio II*, p. 188.]

When the abbot learned this, he refused and replied that he was unable to go there at that time. But the chancellor, becoming more and more suspicious, ordered the abbot to meet him quickly when he came to Capua, so that they might jointly discuss the affairs of the kingdom with the barons of that land. It happened, however, that the abbot then fell seriously ill, and for this reason postponed going to him. When restored to health, he sent two brethren before Christmas to the chancellor, who was staying at Benevento, explaining the seriousness of his illness. The chancellor replied that after the feast he should proceed to him [Col. 0920B] at Capua; otherwise he himself would come to him.

On the feast of the Evangelist John, the aforesaid brethren returned and reported the rumour which they had gathered.

> [Note: [Col. 0920C] That is, “had absorbed” or “heard.” ANG.]

For while going and returning they had questioned the monastery’s friends and faithful adherents about the matter, and heard nothing except that he intended to seize the abbot. The abbot, not knowing what to do in such a matter, feigned illness. The chancellor, however, having joined to himself the elect of Capua—

> [Note: [Col. 0920C] William.]

—and Canzolinus, came to Monte Cassino as he had planned.

Meanwhile the elect of Aquino, stirred by the goads of envy and intoxicated by the poison of malice, sent word to the king’s chancellor through a squire that the abbot of Monte Cassino was preparing himself, not for them but against them, to receive Emperor Lothar and Pope Innocent. If they did not believe him to be speaking the truth [Col. 0920C], he said, they should demand the monastery of Monte Cassino from him: if he gave it, they would know he had lied; if he did not, they should most certainly believe him to be speaking the truth.

But the bearer of the letters, knowing what they contained, came to the monastery and disclosed to the abbot in order the actual situation. The abbot received and reread the letter from the squire and found everything as he had reported it. When the chancellor had arrived at San Germano with the elect of Capua and Canzolinus, Guarinus, elect of Aquino, came to them concerning the same affair. Though they deceitfully ordered the abbot to come down to them, setting aside every excuse, to arrange the affairs of the kingdom, he replied that because of illness he could not go to them; yet he sent [Col. 0921A] the priors of the monastery to the chancellor, so that in his presence they might refute the elect of Aquino concerning the aforesaid accusation and prove him wholly false.

When the elect denied having done this, they displayed the letter and laid out the whole matter in order. Then he was confounded and did not know what reply to make to the clear evidence. Those who were on the king’s side began to abandon their undertaking, and with feigned friendliness and anger spoke suavely to the people of Monte Cassino. Since they favoured the elect of Aquino, they swore that they had neither come for this reason nor believed it. But shortly afterwards, those who had conceived pain brought forth iniquity (Psalm 7:15): they immediately seized the bearer of those letters, tortured him with various punishments, and deprived him of his eyes.

The elect, moved by fear and terrified by the fury of the threatening citizens, was led out of the city by Canzolinus and returned to Aquino. The next day, on the vigil of Epiphany, 5 January 1137, they went up to the monastery. After the customary greeting and some conversation together, when the others had left, they began to demand of the abbot, in accordance with the king’s command, the surrender of the monastery, ordering absolutely that it be handed over to them at once in their presence—something unheard of from the beginning of time. The abbot, they said, should withdraw with twenty, or however many brethren he wished, together with the whole church treasury and all the monastery’s furnishings, to the fortress called Bantra. The remaining brethren should be distributed among the dependencies; four priests, with three or four brethren, should remain in the monastery to perform the divine office [Col. 0921C] at the body of Father Benedict. They asserted that they wished to do this for no other reason than that the church of Monte Cassino had great renown throughout the Roman world, was rich in every respect, and surpassed all the churches of Italy in gold, silver, and many other resources. If Emperor Lothar or other enemies of the king should obtain all these things, they said, great losses and injuries would result in his kingdom.

But they said this falsely. For, as afterwards became clear, they had planned to seize him while he was travelling and to steal all the aforesaid things; thus they would securely possess both the monastery and everything in it. After this unheard-of and utterly wicked command, the abbot denied that he could act without the common counsel [Col. 0921D] of the brethren of Monte Cassino. Having received permission to deliberate, those on the king’s side went outside.

Then the abbot summoned the priors of the monastery, explained why the chancellor had come, asked what each thought about it, and discussed with them in common counsel what was necessary in such a crisis. Yet all had one desire and one decision: that the monastery of Monte Cassino should under no condition and for no reason be handed over into lay power. They promised that they were wholly prepared to contend unto death for the defence of so great a place, and that before they would permit the monastery of Monte Cassino to pass into another’s power and lordship [Col. 0922A], they would eat the flesh of dogs, mice, and horses. For if the head remained unharmed, the remaining members might hope for safety, whatever loss or adversity might occur; but if the head perished, the other members, though they seemed sound, would perish together with the head.

When this had been decided by common counsel, the abbot addressed the chancellor, who came with Canzolinus, as follows:

> “Concerning the affairs of the monastery of Monte Cassino, about which you wished to question us, because both of the greatness of the matter and the shortness of the time, we have found ourselves unable either to deliberate or to discover what we might answer you. We therefore ask that you give us a period in which to summon all the brethren of our community who are stationed in the dependencies, so that, after taking counsel with them, we may discuss in common counsel what we ought to do.”

Then the chancellor, inflamed with the gall of bitterness, answered:

> “What counsel is there here? Or what counsel do you wish to have? There is no counsel here; there will be no delay, except that you fulfil the king’s command. For I do not grant you time for deliberation; rather, on his behalf I wholly command and order you to take care to answer at once what you have decided about this affair.”

The abbot replied:

> “We certainly cannot fulfil what you say, especially because we do not know whether the king commanded this, or for what reason he ordered it to be done.”

To him the chancellor at once gave this reply:

> “I am the king’s mouth and tongue; through me he speaks and disposes his rights. The reason why he ordered this is as follows: Lothar will come with his pope Innocent, and by this we wish to test you, to see whether you ought to remain with us in fidelity to the king and fight against Lothar to preserve his crown.”

The abbot answered:

> “We are ready to fulfil this when necessity requires it, and to confirm it for you now by oath through our faithful men. Moreover, we promise to prepare ourselves vigorously against the king’s enemies and, as far as we can, to defend and maintain the monastery of Monte Cassino against the emperor.”

When the chancellor asked with whom the monastery of Monte Cassino would defend itself against the emperor, the abbot replied:

> “When it is necessary, we shall endeavour to gather here from the city of San Germano and from all the land of Saint Benedict the strongest and most robust men. Thus, with your counsel, and with your soldiers coming to our aid if the situation requires it, we shall strive to defend and maintain the church of Monte Cassino against the emperor and his soldiers, so that the king suffers no loss or injury through the monastery of Monte Cassino.”

Immediately the chancellor cried out with great indignation:

> “Behold the king’s faithful men! Behold, see; behold, consider; behold, observe with whom the abbot of Monte Cassino thinks to resist the emperor: namely, with effeminate, faithless, and perjured men, who have never kept faith with blessed Benedict; who expelled Bruno, Oderisius, and Nicholas from the abbacy; who seized the monastery of Monte Cassino against right and justice [Col. 0923A]; who destroyed the castle of Janula—

> [Note: [Col. 0923] The text has *detruxerunt*, ‘they destroyed.’]

> —and struck with swords, before the altar of blessed Benedict, monks who resisted them.”

He and his companions began to say many things against the abbot, disgracefully abusing monks and laymen, dishonouring them with many and various insults, and denouncing them as deceitful and crafty. Since all mouths were silent in response, he finally departed in great indignation and anger, ordering and saying that they should make it their duty to give him an answer concerning the matter during that very day.

After he had departed, all the priors gathered together with the abbot, discussed the matter among themselves, drew deep sighs, and did not know what they ought to do. They were hemmed in on every side and did not know what choice to make, saying:

> “If we give the monastery into the hands of laymen [Col. 0923B], we incur the death of soul and body; but if we do not give it, we shall not escape their hands. Yet it is better for us to fall into the hands of men than to forsake the law of our God and see the evils of our people and of the saints.”

When these things became known to all, their hearts were immediately broken and their eyes darkened. Truly, their feast-days were then turned into mourning and their song into lamentation (Amos 8:10). This alone was said by all, from the least to the greatest; this was the settled judgment of all: that as long as they could, they would never surrender the monastery of Monte Cassino into lay power, even at the cost of their lives.

At last it seemed good to all to send messengers to the chancellor and his associates, to beg them humbly [Col. 0923C] to give them time in which they might deliberate fittingly about so great a matter and give an answer. But while the chancellor was walking around the monastery with his retainers, he came to the dormitory and ordered the height of the wall to be measured, so that ladders of the same length might be prepared to seize the monastery. When one of the brethren saw this, he reported it to the abbot.

99. At the same time, a certain brother named John, while paying nature’s debt and already lying without movement or voice, suddenly returned to himself and related that he had seen Father Benedict standing in the church with a multitude of dead monks. He saw King Roger entering that same church and carrying off the entire treasure [Col. 0923D] of the church of Monte Cassino. When Roger had reached the steps of the greater church, the dead men who were at a distance in the church rushed upon him and killed him. Having said these things, he added:

> “That you may know more certainly that I speak the truth, know that I shall immediately depart from the world. But if I live any longer after these things, know without doubt that what I have spoken was false.”

Having said this, he fell asleep. Such was the brother’s account. But we, considering and remembering the aforesaid vision, see that it has now been almost entirely fulfilled, since we see that nearly the whole treasure of this place has been taken away through the agency of King Roger. [Col. 0924A] All these events occurred on the day of the vigil of Epiphany, 5 January 1137.

100. After this the abbot and brethren decreed that twelve of the senior monks of the monastery should go barefoot to the city where the aforesaid chancellor and the elect of Capua were staying, humbly begging them to allow time for the brethren stationed in the dependencies to be assembled, so that, after consulting together with them, they might give a fitting answer concerning the aforesaid matter. When this had been done, the entire community followed them with lamentation and groaning as far as the gate of the monastery. When they had departed, the brethren returned to the church of blessed Benedict; who could recount how many tears were poured out there? For all [Col. 0924B] prostrated themselves on the ground, struck their heads against the pavement of the church, and with mourning and heartfelt cries implored the Lord’s mercy to look upon this place.

Finally, turning to blessed Benedict as though they saw him present, they said:

> “Most honourable and holy Father, after your departure from the flesh you promised that you would be more present to your disciples than if you were alive. Therefore, through the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we adjure you that, as you promised, you protect both us and this place and defend us from all evils.”

After this the brethren took up the wood of the life-giving cross, the arm of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, and of Saint Maurus, confessor of Christ, and resolved to proceed with litanies through the churches within the monastery. When they were rendering to the Lord prayers of supplication and praise in the church of Saint Martin [Col. 0924C], after completing the suffrages they departed thence for the church of Saint Stephen, the first martyr. One of the brethren had gone ahead to open the doors of the basilica, but found them locked. For the brother who held that church was one of the twelve who had gone to the chancellor, and he had inadvertently taken away with him the key which he had forgotten to leave behind.

When the brother who had gone ahead to open the church returned, he reported the situation and said that those walking first should return. Again, others and still others ran there, found the doors likewise shut, and took care to report it to the brethren. But the brother carrying the cross, not knowing what to do, encouraged those following him [Col. 0924D] and reached the doors of the church. As soon as he touched the bolts, they were divinely opened. Somewhat cheered by this, they gave thanks to God; and, after performing there with all devotion and contrition of heart the suffrages of the litanies, they returned to the church of Father Benedict and celebrated the masses of that day with mourning and sadness. Then was fulfilled in them what is spoken by the prophet: “Your feast-days shall be turned into mourning” (Amos 8:10).

But when the brethren who had been sent to the chancellor arrived at the place where Father Benedict once a year had spoken with his sister, the dean and the man who had earlier gone down with him for the same matter, learning of their arrival, sent them back to the monastery, saying that such an action would provoke the chancellor more to anger than bend him to mercy. When the chancellor heard that the brethren were making supplication to almighty God’s mercy through the churches of the saints, bearing the arm of Saint Maurus, he was lifted up in pride and began to threaten many things against the monks. He said that he would cut off their lips and noses and their garments down the middle to the buttocks; and, like another Nicanor, he uttered blasphemous words against God and His saints, declaring that the hope which the monks had in Benedict and Maurus was vain and would bring them destruction rather than safety.

Afterwards, stirred by violent indignation, he sent letters to the inhabitants of [Col. 0925B] Campania, Samnium, Apulia, Lucania, and Calabria, ordering them to come as quickly as possible, with various engines of war, to besiege and capture the monastery of Monte Cassino. When the abbot learned that the chancellor was planning his death and the seizure of the monastery, after consulting with a few men he sent envoys to Landulf of Saint John, who then favoured the emperor. He ordered him to come, take the monastery of Monte Cassino under his protection, and defend it against those seeking to capture it.

Since this could not be done by day, it was accomplished by night. Oaths having been sworn on both sides, on the third day after the feast of Epiphany, Friday, 8 January, the soldiers of the aforesaid Landulf were admitted into the monastery and the fortifications [Col. 0925C] were entrusted to them. Thereafter Landulf came to Monte Cassino and brought great reassurance to the abbot and brethren, and great dismay to their enemies.

When the chancellor learned that Landulf had come to Monte Cassino, he left the city of Aquino, where he was staying. Crossing the River Liri through Saint Angelo in Maiolisi—

> [Note: [Col. 0925D] It was also called Todici. ANG.]

—he went to Minianum. There he was struck by a most severe illness and ordered his notary to write letters commanding all who lived in the kingdom of King Roger to come and capture the monastery of Monte Cassino. As the notary strove to carry this out, he died suddenly.

> [Note: [Col. 0926D] The notary.]

After this, the abbot decreed with the brethren that they should implore the mercy of almighty God for three days [Col. 0925D], that in His abundant pity He might grant peace and tranquillity to the monastery of Monte Cassino. Because during those days they could not maintain silence amid the tumult and disturbance, they decreed that for three days, after Compline, one psalter should be sung each night in the church. But before they began this three-day observance, the abbot rose in chapter, asked pardon according to the monastery’s custom, and confessed his transgressions. Likewise all the brethren after him confessed that they had sinned against the Rule of Father Benedict. Then the abbot granted them forgiveness and absolved them from all excommunications pronounced in the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 0926A], by which they had ever been bound.

101. In these same days a certain brother named Bonus, exhausted, fell asleep in the church of Saint Stephen the first martyr after the morning synaxis. Blessed Benedict appeared to him in a vision and said:

> “You will suffer many misfortunes and disturbances, and a very great loss of possessions because of this affair. But trust in the Lord and in the power of His might, for my house shall yet be restored and returned to its former condition. I command you to entreat most blessed Maurus with every urgency of prayer, for by his intercession, without doubt, you shall be delivered from the imminent danger and disturbance.”

Having said these things, he disappeared. On waking, the brother disclosed in order to the abbot and brethren [Col. 0926B] what he had seen and heard. Therefore it was decreed in the common chapter of the brethren that every Sunday, at the entrance of the church, after the antiphon of blessed Benedict, the antiphon of blessed Maurus should also be added. Likewise, at all feasts on which a collect was to be said, as on ordinary days, his antiphon and prayer should be said.

Meanwhile the entire territory withdrew from fidelity to the abbot and brethren, except for the castle of Monte Cassino; the people of the castle of Saint Angelo were the cause and beginning of this act. For they were the first to receive the monastery’s enemies inside their castle and began to attack the monastery of Monte Cassino. Afterwards Bertulf the steward, by nation a Cymbrian, and Adenulf, surnamed the Marsican, were sent to Emperor Lothar because of this affair. Then all the dependencies throughout Campania, Picenum, Samnium, Lucania, and Calabria were seized and withdrawn from the right of the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 0926C].

The chancellor, who had been the head and author of so great an evil, reached his end at Salerno on the seventeenth day after he had arrived here on the vigil of Epiphany, 21 January. He cried out: “Benedict and Maurus, why are you killing me?” And while he repeated these words often, he died.

102. At that same time, a certain brother named Crescentius, a Roman by birth, saw in a vision a lake of immense size and fiery color, whose waves seemed to be borne up to heaven. In those waves he saw the soul of the same chancellor raised into the heights of the air and again plunged down into the depths. When he saw two monks standing beside this lake [Col. 0926D], they asked him whose soul it was that he saw afflicted by such great torments; the brother replied that he did not know. Then he who appeared to be an old man said to him: “This is the soul of Guarinus the chancellor, and it suffers these things because of the disturbance and tribulation which it stirred up against the monastery of Monte Cassino.” When the brother asked him who he was that uttered these things, he replied that he was Brother Benedict. On awaking from sleep, the brother affirmed, calling God and His saints to witness, that he had seen and heard these things.

Meanwhile, certain of our people began, against the abbot’s will, to negotiate concerning peace and concord with those who were on the king’s side, through the mediation of Richard, bishop of Gaeta. At last it came about (2 February) that, after the men of the obediences had sworn an oath on behalf of the brethren, the whole community had made a promise concerning the agreed settlement, and oaths had been sworn by the other party, peace was made. Thus that commotion and disturbance suddenly ceased—but only for a time.

103. On the third day after these events, the aforesaid abbot, overcome by illness, ended his life, on Thursday, the Ides of February.

> [Note: Col. 0927D] Rather, on the day before the Nones, to which date he is assigned in the Necrology of manuscript 47. That date then fell on a Thursday, and Peter himself reckons from it in the following chapter.

Throughout the night in which he died, the dean and the brethren began to consider how, before news of his death should be made public, they might expel the men of the above-mentioned Landulf, who held the monastery. Accordingly, having rewarded [Col. 0927B] those who were at their head, and having received from the king’s bailiffs an assurance that they might depart safely with all their possessions, all left the monastery under arms at midday and returned to their own homes. As a result, the abbot’s death remained publicly unknown until that hour. But, as the ninth hour approached, after his office had been celebrated, he was committed to burial on the right-hand side for those entering the cemetery, beside the steps where four disciples of Saint Benedict rest.

104. But, to return to the matter from which I digressed: while the abbot’s bier was still in the church, soldiers were sent by Canzolinus, chamberlain of the principality of Capua, to ensure that no one should dare, in his absence, to deliberate on the election of an abbot. The matter was therefore deferred and, despite the objections and grief of the monks, postponed until his arrival. When he came there, and the command of Father Benedict concerning the election of an abbot and the ordinance of the privileges were shown to him, he replied that the production of such documents was of no value for the present:

> “But defer it until my lord King Roger is informed. Otherwise, surrender the fortress of Bantra, and elect whom you please—provided, however, that he first swear fealty to the king.”

When the brethren said that they would not comply, he gathered an army and withdrew all the castles of the monastery of Monte Cassino from its authority.

Nearly six days had already passed amid this uncertainty, when, for the feast of the virgin of Christ Scholastica (10 February), brethren came from every quarter to the monastery and deliberated among themselves concerning the election [Col. 0927D] of an abbot. They divided into parties: one intended to elect Raynaldus of Collemente,

> [Note: Col. 0927D] Of Collemezzo, near Furcone, from the stock of the counts of the Marsi. *Peregrinus*, in Muratori, *SS.* VII, [Col. 0928D], p. 232.

who later became abbot; the other, Raynaldus of Etruria. But after much discussion, the former party finally thought it best to defer the election until they could send envoys to King Roger and to the Roman pontiff, then staying at Pisa, by whom they might make known the condition of the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 0928A] and await their counsel in so serious a matter. Yet, because they could in no way induce the other party to agree—those who had intended to elect the aforesaid Raynaldus of Collemente objecting and refusing—they seized that Raynaldus,

> [Note: Col. 0928D] That is, the Etrurian.

placed him in the chair of Father Benedict, and established him as their abbot. The rest, deeply offended by these proceedings, secretly sent a messenger with letters to Bertulfus the mansionary and Adenulfus, brethren of the monastery of Monte Cassino, whom Abbot Seniorectus had sent as envoys to Emperor Lothair. By these letters they reported that Seniorectus had departed from this world and that the same Raynaldus had been elected tumultuously and uncanonically, against their will. They asked them to beseech the emperor [Col. 0928B] and the pontiff on behalf of the entire community to appoint one of their own as abbot in the monastery of Monte Cassino and to give no assent whatever to Raynaldus’s election; declaring that they would sooner destroy the monastery, sooner depart from it, than accept him as their abbot.

When Raynaldus learned this with complete certainty, he secretly made an agreement with Canzolinus and other faithful men of the king. Having sworn fealty to him, he received their confirmation of the abbacy. Thus, after taking an oath from the monastery’s tenants, he was established in the abbacy of Monte Cassino by the son of Peter Leo, whose subdeacon he was.

When the messenger carrying the letters had arrived at Ravenna, where the emperor was then staying, the aforesaid brethren presented him to Emperor Lothair with the letters. They set forth what had happened to the church of Monte Cassino, that is, to the chamber of the Roman Empire [Col. 0928C]: how Seniorectus had died; how Raynaldus, who had sworn fealty to King Roger, had been elected abbot against the will of many; and how certain brethren, leaving the monastery, had escaped the hands of enemies and had suffered very many calamities. They then lamented that their dependents were in danger, that the monastery of Monte Cassino was being brought to ruin, and that they themselves had abandoned everything for loyalty to the Roman Empire—the sole power in which, after God and Father Benedict, the church of Monte Cassino had placed its hope.

Emperor Lothair, moved by compassion, and mindful also of how the church of Monte Cassino had been under the protection of his predecessors, was especially favorably disposed toward the said brethren because of his hatred for King Roger, whom he judged to be most hostile to the Roman Empire. In accordance with the tenor of the edict established by Pippin and Charlemagne,

> [Note: Col. 0928D] This kind of decree, attributed to Charles, is mentioned by this Pseudo-Anastasius, Muratori, *SS.* II, 363.

he enrolled them among the chaplains of the Roman Empire according to ancient custom. Having assembled the dukes, princes, and margraves of the Empire, he declared the benefactions granted by his predecessors to the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 0929A], and denounced the said Raynaldus, proclaiming him an open enemy of the Roman Empire,

> [Note: Col. 0929] Perhaps: “proclaimed.”

because he had accepted confirmation of the abbacy from an enemy of the Roman Empire, disregarding and despising the emperor, from whom the church of Monte Cassino had received its cities, castles, and all its possessions.

105. At that time Henry, duke of Bavaria and the emperor’s son-in-law, sent by the emperor himself together with Pope Innocent, entered Campania. Having pitched camp on the plain adjoining Monte Cassino, they sent Richard, chaplain of the aforesaid pontiff and monk of the monastery of Monte Cassino, to the monastery. They instructed him to say that, if the monks wished to receive them and render obedience to Pope Innocent, they would, to the utmost of their power, love them as sons, brothers, and companions [Col. 0929B], and would always keep the monastery of Monte Cassino under the emperor’s protection and defense.

But Raynaldus would not listen to this proposal, while the brethren were wholly willing, if an opportunity were afforded, to expel him from the monastery. Raynaldus therefore summoned the brethren to chapter and urged them to remain faithful to King Roger and preserve obedience to the son of Peter Leo, assuring them that help would not fail them. Finally, he admitted that he had received the abbacy from them, not from another: at their pleasure, if they wished, he would relinquish it; otherwise, he would retain it. But he spoke these things with his lips, not from his heart. For he had already secretly sent to Gregory, son of Adenulfus of San Giovanni, asking him to come with his army to Monte Cassino through the wood of Tyrillana, so that, supported by his assistance and aid, he might retain the monastery against [Col. 0929C] the pope, the duke, and the monks.

When Gregory arrived, he formed an alliance by oath with the same elect; receiving the monastery’s stronghold from him, he attacked the pontiff’s envoys with his soldiers.

> [Note: Col. 0929] The passage appears corrupt.

Having put them to flight, he gave his own men the greatest boldness. But when the pontiff’s apocrisiaries, or envoys, reached the city adjoining the mountain, they bound its citizens by oath to loyalty to the emperor, and so returned to the camp. Raynaldus, shut up within the monastery with Gregory, cut down the crops outside the monastery and destroyed everything, so that nothing might remain for the sustenance of men or beasts.

Nearly eleven days had passed when the duke, seeing both that the property of the monastery of Monte Cassino was being plundered [Col. 0929D] and that the time for battle was slipping away, took counsel and summoned Raynaldus. Receiving a golden chalice and hostages for four hundred pounds, he confirmed the abbacy to him on the emperor’s behalf, provided that he remained faithful to the emperor. Having guaranteed his safety from himself and his men, the duke ordered the imperial standard to be brought into the church of Saint Benedict and finally, amid great acclaim, raised upon the fortress overlooking the church.

The following day, breaking camp, he came with a great army before the city of Capua. There [Col. 0930A] Rao, son of Rahel, and Geoffrey of Aquila came and submitted themselves and their men to the authority of the pontiff, Prince Robert, and Duke Henry. When the Capuans saw the barons flocking in companies to the pope and duke, they prostrated themselves upon the ground and asked pardon. Having obtained it, they submitted themselves, their possessions, and their city to their lordship. Thus the entire principality of Capua, so to speak, abandoning Roger’s commands, threw itself at the pope’s feet and promised to perform all that might be commanded. Many indeed came to them because of the friendship they had had with Prince Robert; some because of their glory and their rewarding of services, which they hoped to receive from them; but most because of the hope they placed in them as in their own lords.

Meanwhile Henry, the emperor’s son-in-law, together with Pope Innocent restored the principality of Capua to Prince Robert. With a great army they pitched camp at the bridge of Saint Valentine, near Benevento (1137, 21 May). The duke and the apostolic sent envoys into the city, ordering that, unless the inhabitants wished to incur apostolic anathema and imperial wrath, they should surrender Benevento into their hands and establish the markets outside the city. But those in the city who supported the son of Peter Leo resisted them.

> [Note: Col. 0929] A word seems to have dropped out.

Since the envoys of Pope Innocent accomplished nothing, they were expelled from the city with their business unfinished; for Roger’s soldiers then in the city did not consent to the terms. Immediately assembling an army of five hundred cavalry and thirty thousand foot soldiers, they gathered outside the city to fight against them. [Col. 0930C] For this reason the pontiff, moved to anger, separated the Beneventans from the threshold of the church and ordered the duke to attack them with his army.

But when the duke’s shield-bearers in the first line turned their backs, the duke, observing the change in fortune, ordered his soldiers to ford the river, climb the mountain on which the city stood, and assault the city by the Golden Gate. Yet there was dissension within the city over the present circumstances: some said that the city ought to be surrendered to Pope Innocent and, according to ancestral custom, serve Saint Peter and his vicar; others urged by no means to do so, but to resist. Meanwhile the soldiers, fording the river, advanced toward the city. When the Beneventans perceived that the enemy was coming against them [Col. 0930D], they withdrew from battle and sought safety in flight. Those who were on the duke’s side pursued them more closely, entered the city with them, and in this manner received Benevento’s surrender (24 May).

> [Note: Col. 0929D] Falco reported these events more accurately and somewhat differently.

Having taken the city, they advanced to Troia, a city of Apulia. Receiving it from its citizens without a battle, they brought under their authority all the neighboring towns, together with Gargano and Siponto.

> [Note: Col. 0930D] The emperor himself had captured these on 8 May.

106. Meanwhile Emperor Lothair, leaving Ravenna at that time, brought the provinces of Umbria, Emilia, Flaminia, and Picenum [Col. 0931A] under his authority; he restored obedient cities to the jurisdiction of the Roman Empire and razed resisting ones to the ground. When he came to the monastery of Saint Martin at Salinis,

> [Note: Col. 0931D] This was a cell of Saint Liberator, in the district of Penne near the sea, in the territory of Saint Angelo; see Gattola, *Historia*, p. 314.

Transmundus, provost of Saint Liberator, approached him and, pleading with him on behalf of the Cassinese community, obtained an order that whatever had been taken from Saint Benedict in those regions should be restored.

Then, breaking camp, he pitched his tents before Bari, the capital of all Apulia. Received by the citizens of the city, he began by every means to attack the fortress magnificently built by King Roger. After besieging it for a long time with a rampart and various engines of war, and after many on both sides had been killed, he finally took it [Col. 0931B] with great labor and razed it to the ground. He brought all the cities of Apulia under the jurisdiction of the Roman Empire; and, after accomplishing these things, he went to Melfi, a city of Apulia, to appoint a duke (January). When he arrived there, he sent an army and ordered Salerno to be besieged.

During these days Bertulfus and John, brethren of the monastery of Monte Cassino, lodged a complaint before the same emperor against the people of Siponto, who had appropriated to their own dominion the monastery’s forest situated under the jurisdiction of the hospice. The emperor, yielding to their prayers, granted them his seal, ordering on his behalf that, unless they wished to incur imperial wrath, they should henceforth allow that forest to remain undisturbed under the monastery of Monte Cassino. He imposed a penalty of one thousand Byzantine coins [Col. 0931C] if they attempted to alter this arrangement.

107. But, to return to the matter from which I digressed: at the time when the same emperor, after crossing the Alps, entered Italy, he sent a letter to the abbot of Monte Cassino.

> [Note: Col. 0931D] Angelus published it at the end of the *Chronicle* from Peter’s Register; it was reprinted in the *Collection* of Muratori, *SS.* IV, [Col. 0932D], p. 621.

He declared

> [Note: Col. 0931] Namely, the account which follows, word for word, agrees with the *Altercatio*.

that from ancient times the church of Monte Cassino had possessed a reputation for religious observance and had always offered to others an example and model of holy life. Hence he trusted that, through the prayers of the brethren, this might be obtained from God: that He restore tranquillity to the universal Church and grant peace in their times. Since, therefore, by privilege of its ancient religious standing the church of Monte Cassino ought especially and uniquely to look to the Roman dignity, he ordered that they be admonished to return to him whom the whole Church had recognized as father, if fear of anyone had compelled them to depart from the unity of the Church [Col. 0931D].

For his part, desiring to offer the monastery of Monte Cassino every fitting protection, and knowing it to have been endowed with imperial benefactions, he ordered the abbot, when he had approached those regions, to come with the wiser members of the community to perform the office of chaplaincy,

> [Note: Col. 0932D] The words “to perform the office” are absent from the letter.

so that they might fully agree about measures necessary for safeguarding the monastery’s property [Col. 0932A].

He also sent another letter to the brethren,

> [Note: Col. 0932D] These letters, together with the preceding one, were published in the place cited; see note 36.

in which he declared that, if the matter did not rest with them, it was his purpose to consider the honor of the church of Monte Cassino in accordance with imperial generosity. Considering the dignity of so great a church and the religious observance which had flourished there above all others down to that time, he had resolved to look after and uphold that church as a special and singular house of his chamber. For he was greatly intent upon leaving, if God granted it, an enduring memorial of himself with Father Benedict as a mark of imperial honor.

Empress Richiza likewise sent letters to the brethren at that time,

> [Note: Col. 0932D] These letters, together with the preceding one, were published in the place cited; see note 36.

by which she signified that she had heard of the great religious observance anciently maintained by the church of Monte Cassino.
