She therefore asked that remembrance of her be kept [Col. 0932B] in the Cassinese church, so that through the intercession of the brethren God might grant peace to His Church in her times. She herself, insofar as she could with God’s help, would take thought for preserving the property of the church of Monte Cassino; provided only that the abbot should come to her promptly with the wiser brethren, so that they might fully agree concerning these and other matters.

108. After Seniorectus’s death, the emperor sent letters to Raynaldus, his successor,

> [Note: Col. 0932D] These letters, together with the preceding one, were published in the place cited; see note 36.

declaring that it had always been his custom to uphold and cherish those who belonged to the Roman Empire, and never to abandon those who had placed their confidence in him. Therefore Raynaldus should know without doubt that, for as long as he lived, the emperor would protect the rights of the church of Monte Cassino and would not subject to another power what belonged to its own jurisdiction [Col. 0932C] and to imperial dignity.

Since he had summoned a court at Melfi for the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul in order to appoint a duke, and had called there all the barons of the land, he ordered Raynaldus, setting aside all other concerns, to come to him with the wiser brethren and bring with him all the privileges, in order to show the rights of his church. He wished by his benefactions to secure this: that a memorial of himself should always remain at the church of Monte Cassino. If he could come for the aforesaid feast, he should do so; otherwise, he should come as soon as possible.

He also sent another imperial letter to Otto,

> [Note: Col. 0931] To Otto, etc.

the dean, and the brethren,

> [Note: Col. 0932D] He added the name; for the letter see the cited places.

notifying them that, insofar as God permitted, he did not wish in any respect to exceed the bounds set by his imperial predecessors, nor would he allow the rights of the church of Monte Cassino to be diminished in any way, following their example [Col. 0932D]. For the church of Monte Cassino had always remained vigorous in holy religious observance and had been a model of good life for all. He wished them to know that he had ordered their abbot to come to him and would, with the counsel of the princes, settle the cause of the church of Monte Cassino in such a way that it would lose none of its liberty during his reign.

But when the abbot still delayed going to him [Col. 0933A], he again sent another letter:

> [Note: Col. 0933D] We append here the letter, copied by Pertz from Peter’s Register: “Lothair, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, to Abbot R. of Monte Cassino, his favor and good will. We expected your presence with the duke. Since you did not come with him, we order you to come to us. We have heard, moreover, that certain [Col. 0934D] men of Saint Benedict, still remaining faithful to that Sicilian, are staying in your castles. We wish you to remove them cautiously, lest through them some impediment may arise for the church of Monte Cassino.”

By this letter he ordered that, since he had expected the abbot’s presence with the duke and the abbot had not come with him, he should come to the emperor. He had also heard that men of Saint Benedict remained faithful to “that Sicilian” and were still in the monastery’s castles; he wished them to be cautiously removed, lest an impediment be brought upon the church of Monte Cassino through them.

Compelled by the emperor’s command, the elect made ready everything necessary for the journey. Taking with him several brethren of the community, as well as Peter, Cassinese deacon, keeper of charters, librarian, and keeper of records—whom Emperor Lothair had summoned by name—he nevertheless set out not without hesitation. For friends and enemies alike believed that his friendships with the emperor’s enemies [Col. 0933B] would not pass without penalty.

> [Note: Col. 0933D] A word seems to have dropped out.

For this reason his friends despaired; his enemies, though outwardly appearing grieved, secretly rejoiced, hoping that a change in circumstances would bring them better prospects—a hope later proved true by events. But, suspecting certain brethren, he entrusted the monastery and its castles to his friends and kinsmen.

When the emperor’s envoys set forth the purpose of their mission before all, one party was alarmed. Because they were situated in the kingdom and under King Roger’s power, they judged that they ought neither to make peace with his enemy nor go to him. But the other party, which seemed the sounder, said that they should go to the emperor and obey all his commands. At last the abbot was compelled, on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, to set out. With him he took [Col. 0933C] from the Cassinese community the following persons, whose names and number we record lest they be consigned to oblivion: Pandulf, bishop of Teano and monk of the monastery of Monte Cassino; Maurus, *curopalates* of the palace of the emperor of Constantinople; John the chamberlain; the already mentioned Peter the librarian; Amfredus the vestararius, or keeper of vestments; Peter Maccabaeus; Peter and Hector, monks of the monastery of Monte Cassino; John, archpriest of the city of San Germano; and several other noble and prudent laymen from the land of Saint Benedict.

On the day he left the city of San Germano, they came to Teano and remained there four days awaiting some fresh news concerning the emperor. Proceeding thence, they reached Capua, expecting to receive kindly hospitality, as in their own home, in the monastery of Saint Benedict situated in that city [Col. 0933D]. Yet, as the event afterwards proved, their hope altogether deceived them. For Pope Innocent II had sent letters throughout all the monasteries adjacent to the church of Monte Cassino [Col. 0934A], ordering them not to obey the aforesaid elect or the brethren with him.

When they arrived, they knocked at the monastery gate. The brethren came out and gave them this reply:

> “Lords, we have by no means dared to oppose you, since it is clearer than daylight that this monastery has always been subject to the church of Monte Cassino and to you. But because we were compelled to promise the apostolic envoys under oath that we would not offer you hospitality, leave us outside and take whatever things you need from the monastery’s resources.”

On hearing this, the elect ordered his people to go to the church of Saint Vincent, built in the same city. When they arrived there, although those people too had been forbidden to receive them, yet, because shame prevented them from expelling persons already admitted [Col. 0934B], they generously served them with the things in which they abounded. The abbess of the monastery of Saint John also sent them all other necessities in abundance.

The next day they resumed their journey and came to Benevento by the Caudine Forks.

> [Note: Col. 0934D] Now *Lo stretto d’Arpaja*. ANG.

Departing thence, they passed through Frigento,

> [Note: Col. 0934D] Now Frigento.

and the fortress of Gisoald, and came to a castle called Guardia Lombardorum, where the most holy Pope Leo had once let blood before fighting the Normans and had rested for several days. Unwilling to enter the castle because of its smallness and ugliness, they lodged outside in the monastery of Saint Pope Leo, where they were received quite kindly and honorably, insofar as could be seen.

But because human frailty always inclines more toward evil [Col. 0934C] than toward good, the people of that place attempted to hand over the aforesaid elect and his brethren to Gilbert of Balbana and Robert of Murra, commanders of King Roger’s army. Yet the providence of almighty God, which had ordained that events should unfold very differently, confounded their plan. A certain religious woman living in the same church, aware of that scheme, caused Peter the Cassinese librarian to come to her and disclosed all that they had devised. When Peter heard it, he revealed to the elect and the others what had been disclosed to him and urged that they seek the very nearby castle. The elect and some of the brethren rejected this advice, declaring that they would not leave the monastery that day in any circumstances [Col. 0934D].

But the aforesaid Peter, judging that it was dangerous for him to remain there overnight, spoke with Amfredus the vestararius and hurried to the castle with his possessions. Several monks, observing what he had done, likewise departed, leaving the elect. When the elect saw that nearly all his followers had left [Col. 0935A], he too mounted his horse with the rest and went to the castle.

At dawn they left the castle and pursued their journey with the greatest haste. But scarcely three hours of the day had passed when they saw a multitude of soldiers descending the mountain slope against them. Suddenly overcome by fear, they turned to flight. When the soldiers lost all hope of taking them as they fled, they stopped pursuing and immediately returned to their own place. The monks, hastening their flight rather than a peaceful journey, passed through Cisterna and Monteverde, crossed the Aufidus, and came first to the city of Melfi, then to Lake Pensile,

> [Note: Col. 0935D] Lake Pesole, from which the Brandanus rises.

where the whole imperial army was encamped with Pope Innocent.

But when envoys of Pope Innocent met him outside the camp [Col. 0935B], they said that the pontiff had ordered him, before entering the camp, to satisfy the pope barefoot together with the brethren who were with him; to receive penance for the obedience they had rendered to the son of Peter Leo; and to confirm by oath

> [Note: Col. 0935] Something seems to have dropped out.

that he would dutifully carry out whatever the pontiff ordered and, renouncing and anathematizing the son of Peter Leo together with his followers, would obey. Raynaldus, moved by fear, replied that he appealed to Caesar and would take counsel with the emperor concerning the matter; and so he entered the camp.

After this (July), he began to display generosity toward everyone and bind all who came to him by gifts. Before the tents had even been pitched, he took care to send envoys to notify the emperor of his arrival. Then the emperor showed generosity to him and his brethren for love of Saint Benedict. Immediately he sent from his side Henry, duke of Bavaria and his son-in-law, together with Rudolf

> [Note: Col. 0935D] I do not know who this was. Otto, count palatine of the Rhine, and Otto, count palatine of Bavaria, accompanied the emperor into Italy.

and Otto, counts palatine, ordering them to remove the tent which had been pitched by the pontiff’s command beside the papal pavilion and to pitch it beside his own. He declared that, since the church of Monte Cassino had been made a special chamber of the Roman Empire by Carloman

> [Note: Col. 0936D] He means Charlemagne, or rather confuses the two, as will shortly become clearer.

and Pippin, it was in no way just that the emperor’s chaplains—that is, the monks of the church of Monte Cassino—should be separated from the emperor, but that their tent ought to be pitched beside his. This was done.

When the Roman pontiff learned that the Cassinese elect had been received by the emperor, he sent cardinals and began vehemently to press the emperor to compel the Cassinese monks to anathematize the son of Peter Leo by oath [Col. 0935D]. He complained that persons excommunicated and separated from the threshold of the Church had been received by the imperial majesty. But the monks refused, saying that the Lord in the Gospel (Matthew 5:34) and Father Benedict in the Rule

> [Note: Col. 0936D] Chapter 4.

had commanded them not to swear; that neither they nor their predecessors had ever had a custom of swearing; [Col. 0936A] and that they would swear fealty neither to the pope nor to anyone, since they could not remain faithful even to themselves if they did what God had forbidden through Saint Benedict and neglected what He had commanded them to observe. Thus they departed from the emperor that day.

The next day (7 July) the pontiff sent Aymericus the chancellor, and Gerard and Guido, cardinals, with the demand that the emperor either compel the Cassinese monks to anathematize the son of Peter Leo or refrain from association with them as with excommunicated persons. But the most clement and most devout emperor, wishing neither to anger the pontiff nor to cast down the church of Monte Cassino, gently addressed them and sent them back to the apostolic see. He said that the apostolic should send disputants before the imperial majesty to determine whether or not those whom he had received were excommunicated [Col. 0936B]; and that a day ought to be appointed on which both parties should meet in a hearing. The twelfth day

> [Note: Col. 0935] Or the third? See Jaffé, *Geschichte des Deutschen Reichs unter Lothar*, p. 221.

was appointed for these proceedings, and they returned to the pope with the business unfinished.

After they had left, the emperor ordered all the monks who had come with the elect to be brought before him. When they stood before the emperor after being presented by the palace eunuch, he ordered inquiry into their lineage, country, offices, and names. After they had declared their lineage, country, offices, and names, they were asked whether they had brought, as he had ordered, the commands of emperors and the privileges of Roman pontiffs. They answered that they had brought everything as he had directed and asked him to state what he had in mind. Caesar replied:

> “How beloved and desirable [Col. 0936C] the church of Monte Cassino was to our most invincible imperial predecessors is most clearly shown by the splendid gifts and commands given in gold and silver. It is also established that the relics of Carloman, the most holy and invincible emperor and Roman patrician, whose place, though unworthy, we have assumed, are buried in that church. In reverence for him, not only we who hold his office, but the entire Roman world—nobles and commoners, rich and poor—ought to honor, exalt, and cherish that place, and in every respect prefer it to all other places of this religious observance. Desiring ourselves, so far as possible, to follow these men, we had resolved to honor this place with magnificent gifts. But because the most blessed Pope Innocent forbids this, saying that you are separated from the Church [Col. 0936D], we order you to choose from among yourselves certain disputants against the advocates of the apostolic see. For we can in no way allow a place of such renown, religious observance, and dignity to be annihilated or perish in our time. We do not wish your elect to be present at this hearing, because the issue concerns him no less than it concerns the monastery.”

He had spoken. Then, by the emperor’s order, they returned [Col. 0937A] to their lodgings. When the monks reported to their elect what the emperor had said, they took counsel and chose Peter, the Cassinese deacon, librarian, keeper of charters, and keeper of records, as disputant and defender of their party.

When day had returned, the emperor’s envoys arrived (8 July) and told the aforesaid elect to send his monks to the emperor. The brethren came and, as custom required, stood outside the doors. They were immediately announced to the emperor and were at once ordered to enter (8 July). Having entered, the emperor ordered inquiry into the names, lineage, and country of those who were to dispute. Peter the deacon was presented: a Roman by birth, noble in lineage, and exceptionally learned in sacred letters. Next came Amfredus, English by lineage [Col. 0937B], a man of great eloquence.

After their lineage, names, and country had been presented, the office of each was asked. When this had been completed, inquiry was made as to whom they had chosen to speak for the church of Monte Cassino. The already mentioned Peter, Cassinese deacon, was presented. When all bore witness to him, Caesar, commanding silence, said:

> “Dismiss your brother to whom you bear witness, return to your lodgings, and, when the day has come, be ready to appear for disputation when our envoys have seen you.”

As they departed, he entrusted Peter the deacon to Bertulfus the chancellor, so that he might be presented when Caesar sat in judgment that night. The emperor passed almost the entire night without sleep and ordered all the acts of his imperial predecessors to be read aloud before him.

> [Note: Col. 0937] “All,” etc.

When morning came (9 July), and the morning synaxis had been completed and the life-giving mysteries celebrated, the emperor ordered a tribunal to be prepared for him in the tent. He sent envoys and summoned the Cassinese men; when they arrived, they were presented to the emperor. Cardinals sent by Pope Innocent were also present, together with very many advocates [Col. 0937C].

109. In the name of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, in the year of his Incarnation 1138 [Note: Col. 0937D: See Preface, p. 570], in the first indiction, on the seventh Ides of July [9 July], in the sixth year of the reign of the lord Lothair Caesar, most invincible emperor Augustus: while that same most invincible emperor was sitting at the Waters of Pensile, and Peregrinus, patriarch of Aquileia, was sitting with him, together with very many archbishops, bishops, and abbots, Gerard, cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross, was sent as advocate for the Roman Church [Col. 0937D], along with Guido, cardinal—both of whom afterwards governed the Roman Church [Note: Col. 0937D: The former was called Celestine II, the latter Lucius II. Col. 0938D: Cf. Preface, p. 572, n. 37]—Aymericus, chancellor and cardinal-deacon, Baldwin, cardinal-priest, who afterwards [Note: Col. 0938D: In 1138.] became archbishop of Pisa, Norbert [Note: Col. 0937: Read Bernard.] abbot of Clairvaux, and very many other nobles of the Roman city.

On behalf of the church of Monte Cassino, those present as hearers were Henry [Col. 0938A], duke of Bavaria and the emperor’s son-in-law; Conrad, duke of Swabia, who afterwards assumed the sceptre of the Roman Empire; Otto [Note: Col. 0937: Gebhard in Lothair’s privilege.] of Burchisin, the emperor’s cousin; Frederick, margrave of Ancona; Malaspina, margrave of Liguria; Henry, bishop of Regensburg; Anno [Note: Col. 0937: Adelbero there.], bishop of Basel; Anno, abbot of Lüneburg; and Gualfridus, palatine judge of the Roman Empire.

With these present, an assembly was held in the aforesaid place. When silence had been made, the emperor said:

> “This assembly will determine matters not only present and temporal, but also future and eternal. For it is established that the holy Fathers, who held different councils in different places [Note: Col. 0937: *Consilia*, ‘councils,’ in the corrected reading], when they had assembled to deliberate jointly upon one matter, clarified diverse matters arising from a single occasion [Note: Col. 0937: The passage is evidently corrupt and defective.]. So too, though the case of the Roman [Col. 0938B] and Cassinese Churches is to be treated here in particular, yet, with God’s help, diverse questions will be determined here; and thus the cause of one becomes the salvation of all churches established throughout the whole world.
>
> “We also, desiring to follow in the footsteps of our predecessors, have judged it fitting to attend this council and to have the scales of judgment weighed by our own judgment. We have assigned as defenders, at our side, eminent men for the two disputing parties, that they may prevent violence by either side. Therefore, invoking the power of the supreme Thunderer, let those to whom Roman laws are not displeasing take their seats and silently await the outcome of the proceedings, lest, while all speak or talk confusedly, truth be clouded.”

After the Augustus had said these things and much else, Conrad [Col. 0938C], duke of Swabia, appointed defender by the emperor, said:

> “The abundance of the imperial pronouncements has made me poor in speech; for the imperial Majesty has spoken so profoundly, so copiously, and so reasonably that its words seem to have proceeded not from a human but from a divine mouth. Yet it has seemed good to the dukes, margraves, and counts appointed defenders with me that, at the beginning of today’s session, the persons who are to dispute for each side should be declared, and whether anyone is permitted to take part in the disputation except those to whom authority has been granted. For the business of every assembly, and especially of a divine assembly, must be conducted in an orderly and rational manner, since nothing can be perfectly decided where the order of speaking is not observed.”

All approved what the duke had said. Inquiry was then made as to who would answer for each side [Col. 0938D], who the interpreters would be, and what place would be assigned to the disputants. Gerard, cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross, was chosen to answer for the Roman Church; Peter the deacon was likewise chosen, approved by the testimony of his brethren. The interpreters appointed were Bertulf, the emperor’s chancellor; Amfred, the vestararius; and Bertulf, the mansionarius. A place before the emperor’s face was assigned to Cardinal Gerard, while Peter the deacon was placed at the emperor’s feet [Col. 0939A].

Cardinal Gerard refused to allow the monk to sit at his feet, saying that it was improper and altogether unlawful for excommunicated persons to sit with the sons of the Church. But the emperor, wishing to put an end to the dispute, ordered Peter the deacon to sit at his feet from then on.

Then Cardinal Gerard began speaking as follows:

> “Holy and universal Church, most invincible emperor, which before you consecrated your predecessors, and after them consecrated you, as rulers of the whole Roman world, cannot cease to wonder why you have received persons excommunicated and separated from the thresholds of the Church.”

The emperor replied:

> “We rejoice that we have received the crown of our Empire from the Apostolic Church. We do not think that we have received excommunicated persons in any way [Col. 0939B]; nevertheless, if, as you say, they are excommunicated, this dispute has found [Note: Col. 0939D: Or perhaps, ‘will find’?] its occasion.”

Pandulf, bishop of Teano and a monk of Monte Cassino, said:

> “We cannot in any way understand how a cardinal of the Roman Church can assert that the Cassinese monks are excommunicated.”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “What have I to do with you, good man? You are alien to us. O strange, new, and unheard-of portent: that a trunk, its branches cut off and torn up from its roots, should raise new engines against the Church!”

The emperor replied:

> “Let every violence cease and be far away. For in councils each person, according to his ability, does not heap insults upon his neighbour, but rather endures all things patiently. We therefore decree that neither party inflict violence upon the opposing party, lest what is being done for the praise of God and the benefit of posterity [Col. 0939C] be turned into strife and quarrelling.”

Cardinal Gerard, resuming his speech, said:

> “Moreover, the holy and universal Church has decreed that the monks of the Cassinese monastery should confirm by oath that they will fulfil in all things the will of our lord Innocent, pious and universal pope.”

For Pope Innocent had already determined to scatter all the Cassinese monks among various places. But Lothair, the most merciful emperor, unwilling that the Cassinese Church should be destroyed, did not hesitate to oppose the pope’s will on behalf of that Church.

When Cardinal Gerard, defender of the Roman Church, had spoken concerning the monks’ oath, Peter the deacon replied:

> “We are not a little astonished that the lord cardinal has said that the monks ought to be bound by an oath [Col. 0939D], since the Lord in the Gospel taught that one should swear neither by heaven nor by earth nor by a hair of the head (Matt. 5:34).”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “We agree with what the monk has reported; but the Roman Church has decreed that the Cassinese monks are in no way to be received without an oath.”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “In the Rule of the most holy [Col. 0940A] Father Benedict, monks are forbidden to swear at all, lest perchance—God forbid!—they incur the crime of perjury [Note: Col. 0939D: Chapter 4.]. This too, namely the oath of monks, is prohibited not only by divine but also by human laws. For in the enactments of the great emperors Charles, Louis, Pippin, Carloman, Louis, Hugh, Lothair, Berengar, Albert, the three Ottos, the five Henrys, and Conrad, the following is found: ‘We decree that monks shall not be compelled to take an oath’ [Note: Col. 0939D: I have found this in no privilege before that of Lothair III.].”

As he said this, he showed to the emperor and to all the others the enactments of the aforesaid emperors, sealed with wax, lead, and golden seals, which they had issued to the monastery of Monte Cassino. On seeing them, the emperor took the aforesaid enactments in imperial purple, kissed them, and immediately burst forth in these words [Col. 0940B]:

> “We recognize from their seals that these are the enactments of great, holy, most invincible emperors, our predecessors. It therefore belongs to our Majesty to observe inviolate all the enactments of our predecessors. Therefore take care, on our behalf, humbly to ask the lord apostolic, you who have come in his stead, that he protect with us the enactments of our most holy imperial predecessors and deign, by his authority, to confirm them, as his predecessors did. For who hereafter will observe the enactments of Catholic emperors if these are despised by the Apostolic See? All members follow the head; nor can members be separated from the head without suffering great harm. Let the head therefore contend for the members [Col. 0940C], the father for his children, the shepherd for his sheep; for the wolf’s biting savagery will in no way prevail against the sheep if they are guarded by the shepherd’s vigilant care.
>
> “Let today’s session therefore end, and let each return to his own lodging. Let the cardinals lay our requests before the lord pope and be asked in our name to entreat him to foster with me the Cassinese Church. Let the monks report to their chosen abbot what has been said and consider what they ought tomorrow to answer to each objection. But when daylight has been restored to the earth, after three hours have passed, we decree that all return to the council. Whatever dispute has occurred today shall be written down by notaries appointed for the aforesaid persons, lest the matters which we are considering as especially beneficial to posterity be consigned to oblivion.”

When this had been said, the disputants [Col. 0940D] withdrew from the court, and the emperor returned to deal with the public business awaiting him.

110. On the following day (10 July), both parties to the disputation assembled. When they had entered and an opportunity to speak had been granted before [Note: Col. 0940D: Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.520], Cardinal Gerard said:

> “We conveyed the commands of your piety, most holy and invincible emperor, to the bishop of the supreme see [Col. 0941A]; but he replied that he could by no means do this, asserting that it would be easier for him personally to lay aside and trample underfoot his priestly vestments than to carry out what the emperor had asked.”

The emperor was silent for a little while. Then he ordered that the matters left over from the preceding day be debated. Cardinal Gerard said:

> “I remember that yesterday I dealt with the oath and fidelity of the Cassinese monks, and brought nothing to completion. Therefore, since we are to discuss the same matter before the emperor’s presence, I do not think it superfluous to set forth again for consideration the will of our lord Pope Innocent, after yesterday’s first report [Note: Col. 0941D: A word seems to have dropped out.]. Let the most invincible Majesty of your Empire know that the lord pope requires this of the Cassinese monks [Col. 0941B]: that by oath they confirm that they will fulfil his will in all things and will at all times be faithful and obedient to him and to his successors. Otherwise he will by no means permit them to exercise the divine ministries or to partake of the Lord’s body and blood.”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “It is clear that the lord cardinal has renewed yesterday’s contest and prepared our minds for revived struggles. Yet it seems to us more than sufficient that this proposition conflicts with the Lord’s command, since the Lord permitted no one to swear even by a hair of his head. As for the fidelity of which the lord cardinal speaks, it seems superfluous that we should be required by oath to promise what we have hitherto done willingly.”

Cardinal Gerard [Col. 0941C] said:

> “Standing before the presence of our lord Lothair Caesar, most invincible emperor, the monk has not feared to utter a falsehood, saying that the Cassinese monks have always maintained fidelity to the Roman Church, when it is plain to all who see rightly that they have remained schismatics until now, have torn Christ’s tunic, and have chosen for themselves an abbot ordained by schismatics.”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “It belongs to honourable men not to accuse someone of lying before he himself has made the lie evident to everyone; so that, when nothing can be alleged against it, not another person but his own conscience may rebuke him as a liar. Therefore, when the lord cardinal declared me a liar, he appears not to have acted rightly, since he has advanced no ground for my supposed falsehood. Let the charge be stated [Col. 0941D], let any objections that exist be raised; then let him accuse me of lying and declare me a speaker of empty words.”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “To put it briefly: when, abandoning Pope Innocent, you adhered to a schismatic, what else were you but unfaithful?”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “Tell me, I ask: did we abandon him, or did he abandon us?”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “When the Church had been seized by schismatics and was being torn by wolves, the most devout bishop was driven from his see; and so, leaving Italy, he hastened to Gaul.”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “Did not the good shepherd Jesus Christ, when describing the distinction—indeed, the unity—of the shepherd of shepherds united in himself, say: ‘The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep’ [Col. 0942A]?” (John 10:12.)

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “He showed this not only in words but also in deeds.”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “Again, the Lord himself, having described the actions of the best shepherd, wrote of the conduct of a hired hand: ‘The hired hand, who is not a shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming and abandons the sheep and flees.’ Do you believe these words are evangelical, or not?”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “Certainly, in the highest degree.”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “Should this be practised by the Roman pontiff?”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “They ought to be observed all the more by the prelate of the Apostolic See, inasmuch as he has received the special duty of preaching them to others.”

Peter the deacon replied [Col. 0942B]:

> “What then? Will the sheep be held accountable by the just Judge for anything the shepherd has done?”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “Not at all.”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “Then do not hold the monks accountable if, deprived of their shepherd, they were exposed to the enemy’s bites. For the apostolic lord ought, as the Lord says, not only not to abandon the sheep, but even willingly to embrace death for them.”

The emperor said in reply:

> “So far as appears, the monk has shown that, if they have committed any fault, it is the fault not of the sheep but of the shepherd. Therefore the mercy of the lord apostolic must again be asked to forgive with us what they have done against us. We therefore decree that today’s dispute now end. Being occupied with the affairs of the commonwealth, we cannot attend to these matters for long. Let each therefore return to his own place [Col. 0942C], to return tomorrow to the same contest.”

At this, with everyone’s approval, the assembly dispersed.

111. On the next day (11 July), when the most devout emperor sat down with his aforementioned magnates to hear what remained, he addressed the assembly in these words:

> “We do not doubt that it is known to all within the Roman world in what great and what kind of reverence our predecessors—the Roman emperors, that is—held the church of Monte Cassino, their singular and special chamber; how, exalting it above all the monasteries of the Roman Empire, they set it over them and honoured it from the beginning with their enactments and privileges. It would also be fitting for the lord apostolic to foster that same Church with me, [Col. 0942D] as, with God’s help, he will do after this dispute has ended.
>
> “But this must in no way be understood or called a dispute by anyone, since it is evident that members cannot contend with themselves; nor can the head say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you,’ nor the eye to the foot, nor any member to another member. For our more lowly members are often more useful. Let no one therefore think it improper what we decree to do, nor seek in any way to accuse us because we seem to defend the monastery of Monte Cassino [Note: Col. 0941D: ‘we seemed,’ corrected reading].
>
> “For when a mother, in anger, has struck her daughter, or a husband his wife, or a parent his child, it can happen that a person endowed with good character places himself between the angry father and the frightened child [Col. 0943A], and rescues the child from an excessive, though paternal, beating. When the father has come to himself and his fatherly anger has been turned into gentleness, will he complain that he has suffered any wrong from that man? Rather, he will give countless thanks because the man withdrew his son from his hands. Thus also the universal mother, the Roman Church, when she has laid aside her anger and come to rest, will thank our Empire because we rescued her daughter in anger.
>
> “Let the matters requiring debate therefore be debated, for I will by no means desist from these proceedings until my desire has been accomplished.”

After the emperor had said this and much else, Cardinal Gerard said:

> “As you ordered, most sacred emperor and ever Augustus, we conveyed the words and requests of your greatness to the lord Pope Innocent [Col. 0943B]; but he asserts that he can never endure receiving the monks without an oath and fidelity.”

Peter the deacon replied:

> “We think that we have done enough concerning these things before the lord emperor’s presence, both from the Lord’s command and from imperial edicts. But if you have anything further on these matters, state it.”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “Do you not know, most invincible emperor, that those whom your greatness defends conspired with Roger, count of the Sicilians, against the Roman Church and your most invincible Empire, and not only conspired, but also anathematized and deposed you? O unheard-of thing: that those who are bound should bind the free and loose those who are bound!”

The most devout emperor replied, after silence had been made:

> “What the Cassinese monks committed against me [Col. 0943C], I willingly endure and gladly forgive. But as for what they committed against the Roman Church and the lord pope, just as we forgive what they sinned against us, so let him forgive what they sinned against him.”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “Although we act in the place of our lord Innocent, pious and universal pope, we cannot decide such great and serious matters without him.”

With these words, and with the emperor’s approval, the assembly dispersed.

That night, while the emperor, as was his custom, kept vigil, Peter the deacon, kneeling before him, made the following plea on behalf of the Cassinese Church:

> “Since all mortals within the Roman world serve you, emperors, rulers, and princes, you yourselves serve the heavenly Emperor—mercy, peace, and justice. Otherwise the security of both lives [Col. 0943D] cannot be preserved unless it is governed by such administrators; for no one deceives the Emperor of all things, to whom the secrets of the heart are manifest.
>
> “Therefore, although it is fitting that your sublimity, invincible emperor, extend protection to all churches throughout the world, it is especially fitting that you extend and show it to the Cassinese monastery and fortify that Church against the snares of those who have denied us the use of speech and who regard as nothing the privileges granted by emperors to the Cassinese monastery. Indeed, I too counsel obedience and service to the Roman pontiff [Col. 0944A], but it is certain that almighty God must be preferred above all. For it is no wrong to anyone when churches are placed before mortal persons on account of devotion to divine worship.
>
> “The entire monastic order totters, heaves, is shaken, and suffers diverse injuries in the humiliation [Note: Col. 0943: *delectione*, ‘delight,’ in the corrupt reading.] of the Cassinese Church. Shall monks be removed from their offices while you are emperor? While you are emperor, is this requested and demanded: that monks take an oath? We therefore implore your clemency, most exalted conqueror, not to decree this, not to establish it, and not to subscribe to its decrees. Is it fitting in your time that the dignity of the Cassinese Church be abolished, so that the perverse will of cardinals may achieve its effect?
>
> “Nothing is greater than religion; nothing in the monastic order is holier or more exalted than Father Benedict [Col. 0944B]. What will the devout emperor Augustus Carloman answer? Will he not say to you: ‘I did not think that I had laid aside my Empire, because I had Lothair as a just and holy emperor. I did not grieve that I had relinquished my Empire, because I believed that my imperial enactments, especially those concerning monastic religion, would remain unshaken forever. At Monte Cassino I had erected memorials of piety, justice, and gentleness; I offered these spoils won from the pressures of the world. What more could my enemy take from me? Now, I say, now my decrees are abolished; now I receive a more grievous weapon in my body, when my institutions are condemned by the Roman pontiff. Now my Empire is taken from me, and, what is more grievous, by Roman pontiffs—and this in the presence of my brother, Emperor Lothair.’
>
> “For whom does the emperor of the Romans favour or benefit more than himself when he defends the institutions of his predecessors and the rights of the Cassinese monastery [Col. 0944C]? Let it therefore seem burdensome to no one if we defend the condition of monastic religion. Certainly, count one hundred and thirteen Roman pontiffs from Saint Benedict to Lord Pope Innocent: all cultivated, upheld, and loved the Cassinese religious order; none removed it.
>
> “Moreover, if we think reverend old age should be obeyed, let us introduce Father Benedict speaking: ‘Excellent emperor, father of your country, Caesar Augustus: reverence my grey hairs, to which long old age has brought me. Let my sons use the laws that I have bestowed upon them; for it is not improper that they should live according to my custom. Through them I brought the world beneath my laws; through them England and many nations were converted to Christ. Their salvation, protection, and help are mine.’”

After Peter the deacon had rehearsed these and many other matters, by the emperor’s command he went that same night to the tent of Chancellor Bertulf.

112. When the cardinals had therefore been summoned and assembled before the emperor (12 July), Cardinal Gerard said:

> “We conveyed to the lord pope what your sublimity deigned to command us yesterday. He received your requests graciously, but said [Col. 0945A] that you had imposed upon him an excessively burdensome case, which he could scarcely endure; for he could in no way, by no arrangement and on no grounds, relinquish the episcopal right which his predecessors had possessed in former times.”

Emperor Lothair said:

> “As we have often already shown, we ought to defend, exalt, and honour the Cassinese Church in proportion as we know it to have been more highly honoured and enriched by our predecessors. Let the lord apostolic therefore know that the castles, villages, estates, and all possessions of the monastery belong to our Empire; but we concede that the episcopal right, insofar as it is due to him, shall be his.”

Chancellor Bertulf said:

> “The apostolic lord ought to possess no right in the Cassinese Church, which is decreed to be the singular and special chamber of the Roman Empire [Col. 0945B], except the consecration of the abbot, which he is known to have possessed even by the concession of Emperor Henry.”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “Then let my counsel please your most invincible Empire, O Caesar. Let an oath establish security in temporal matters for you, and in divine matters for the apostolic lord.”

Emperor Lothair said:

> “It seems very dishonourable to our Empire not to observe the commands of our predecessors or obey their most holy enactments. For if we break our predecessors’ enactments, who will observe them? And how shall we compel others to observe them if we overthrow them ourselves? For law adjudicates the causes both of the giver and of that which is given. Whosever causes it adjudicates, it surely constrains under its own rule [Col. 0945C]. Therefore the law of emperors is established no less for emperors than for others; indeed, it is more fitting that those preserve it who possess the origin of their nobility.”

Cardinal Gerard said:

> “The lord pope also wonders not a little why, when the Church both chose and consecrated you as Caesar and ruler of the whole world, you seek to act against her on behalf of the Cassinese Church. He says that Church belongs not to you, as you assert, but to him, as do the other churches.”

Then the emperor said angrily:

> “Indeed, we greatly wonder why he was unwilling to do anything at our request, when, for love of him, we have spent a year and a half in tents with the Roman army, and have devoted to his service the money we received for carrying out public business [Col. 0945D]; when we have restored him to the Apostolic See and made all peoples beyond the mountains favour him. Why then should it be wondered at if we protect the Cassinese Church to the extent of our power, since this is known to have been done most gloriously by our predecessors?
>
> “They held it no differently from their own chamber, so much so that some, stripped of worldly troubles and fleshly hindrances, wished to be buried there rather than in their own homes. What need is there for me to recount the most holy, ever memorable, most invincible Emperor Augustus Charles [Col. 0946A], who, leaving imperial sceptres and the dignity of Augustus, lived there the monastic life? What should I relate also of Pippin, Charles’s own brother, who, being in Germany, when his brother Charles—who had gone to him as a monk—died, would not allow him to be buried elsewhere, but sent him back to the Cassinese monastery?
>
> “Ratchis also, king of the Lombards, abandoning his kingdom, came to that same venerable monastery and lived there the monastic life to the end. What also of the emperors Justinian, Justin, Theodoric, Pippin, Charles, Pippin, Charlemagne, the two Louis, Hugh, the two Lothairs, Albert, the three Ottos [Note: Col. 0945D: *Octonibus*, in the corrupt reading], and the five Henrys? What should I say of Michael the Roman and Alexius [Col. 0946B], who all loved the Cassinese Church and adorned it with great gifts?
>
> “The Cassinese Church was so truly an imperial chamber that emperors themselves came for its liberation with the entire might of the Roman army. For Henry, devout, most invincible, and most Christian emperor, entered Italy with one hundred and eighty thousand armed men to defend this Church; taking it from the hand of the prince of Capua, he restored it to its former freedom. Emperor Augustus Conrad also, and Henry his son, came with one hundred and sixty thousand warriors to defend the same Church when it was being subjected to the yoke of slavery under Pandulf—most wicked, I do not say prince, but tyrant.
>
> “Let us pass over recent things and deeds done in modern times. Let the deeds of the ancients [Col. 0946C] be brought forward, and let us see to whom the site itself properly belonged. For we read in the deeds of our predecessors that Varro, consul of the Romans, chose this place for himself from among all places of the Roman Empire, built it up, and rendered it illustrious with many monuments. After his death, Caesar granted the aforesaid fortress of Casinum with its appurtenances to Antony, as Marcus Tullius describes in his *Philippic*.
>
> “But perhaps it will be objected against us that Father Benedict, though the builder, was not the founder of this place, and that he was subject to the Roman Church. We reply that he built the place not alone, but with Roman nobles. For, on the report of the most blessed Pope Gregory, we have learned that Saint Benedict, together with Maurus, son of the senator Equitius [Col. 0946D; Note: Col. 0945D: Neither Gregory nor Leo calls him a senator.], and Placidus, son of the patrician Tertullus, was directed by God to build the Cassinese monastery.
>
> “Why say more? Either the Roman Church shall receive, as is just, the Cassinese Church—the chamber of the Roman Empire—or the Roman Empire will be separated irrevocably.”

Cardinal Gerard replied:

> “By no means, most invincible emperor, should your gentleness be angered by the commands of the lord apostolic, nor should the commands of Lord Innocent, pious and universal pope, seem unjust [Col. 0947A]. But if anything in these matters displeases you, let it be referred to him.”

With these words, the assembly of the fourth day was dissolved.

113. Accordingly, when morning came (13 July) and the great men of both parties had assembled before the emperor, Cardinal Gerard, acting in the place of the Roman Church, said: “Let Your Highness know, invincible emperor, that the apostolic lord has replied as follows to your message of yesterday: on your account he would not demand fealty from them, but he would not relinquish their oath or obedience. Meanwhile, he judged that we must debate the election of the abbot: on what grounds men under excommunication preferred to Christ’s Church an excommunicated man and, what is graver, a schismatic.”

Then Deacon Peter, beginning the discussion, said: “Let us hear what the lord cardinal wishes to say about the election of our abbot.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “The holy and universal Church is greatly astonished that you, excommunicated and cut off from the thresholds of the Church, dared, without the consent and will of our lord the pope, both to set over yourselves in the Church and to call ‘abbot’ an excommunicated man and a schismatic.”

Deacon Peter replied: “By putting forward various questions, eloquent teacher, you have produced scarcity for us out of great abundance, so much so that the diversity of your questions creates no small obstacle to our reply. Therefore, if it is not contrary to the holy empire and the other magnates, let one question out of these many be proposed and thoroughly examined. Once that has been done, if anything remains in the others that ought to be investigated, let it be sought.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “We consider that we have already done what the monk proposes, for I acknowledge that I have dealt with the election of the abbot.”

Deacon Peter replied: “If the question concerns the election of the abbot, let us hear what you wish to object on that matter.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “The first objection is this: why did you elect an abbot for yourselves without the consent and will of the Roman pontiff?”

Deacon Peter replied: “We remember that at the beginning of this council it was agreed that matters under inquiry should be proved not by persuasive words, but by the testimonies or examples of the ancients. Therefore, if you wish to bring forward any example or testimony, bring it forward.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “We have such an abundance of testimonies and examples that their very quantity produces want for us. Yet let it suffice to offer a few examples out of many. First among these comes to mind what is known to have happened concerning Frederick, first abbot of Monte Cassino, and later Stephen, pope. Therefore, before I recount the event as it happened, let the monk acknowledge: who elected Frederick after Peter had been elected, and who deposed that same Peter? Who elected Desiderius, Oderisius, Gerard, and finally Seniorectus? Since he cannot deny that the former was deposed and the latter ordained by apostolic authority, it will plainly appear that the election of the abbot of Monte Cassino belongs by apostolic right.”

Deacon Peter replied: “Concerning the first point you raised, let this answer suffice: although Roman cardinals were present both at Peter’s deposition and at Frederick’s election, nevertheless the former was deposed and the latter ordained not by cardinals but by the monks of Monte Cassino. [Note: Cf. book II, ch. 92.] Likewise, Oderisius I—whom, as you assert, the apostolic see ordained—must by no means be cast up against us, since the renewer of the monastery was permitted to make an ordination in the monastery, not by reason of apostolic right, but because he had renewed the monastery. [Note: Cf. book IV, ch. 1.] Yet, although the monks elected Oderisius while Pope Victor presided, the pontiff did not take away their power but supplied assistance to it. Besides, what precedent was there in the fact that the renewer of the monastery ordained an abbot not without the brethren’s consent? Abbot Gerard too was elected by the monks with the assent of Pope Paschal. [Note: Cf. ch. 43.] As for Seniorectus, whom you mentioned last, I do not know on what grounds you say he was elected by Pope Honorius, since I was present at his election and saw neither the pontiff nor even the pontiff’s messenger. [Note: Yet, according to his own testimony, two were present; ch. 94.] But, to speak of the ancient rulers and abbots of the monastery of Monte Cassino: tell me, who elected the most blessed Father Benedict in the Cassinese monastery?”

At this the cardinal fell silent.

Again Deacon Peter said: “It is established that the most holy Father Benedict was elected at Cassino by Him who made Moses king and god to Pharaoh. Therefore we must say that the monastery of Monte Cassino began neither from a human being nor through a human being, but received its origin from almighty God, who is beginning and end.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “The monk has invented a new manner of speaking, saying that the church of Monte Cassino began not through a human being but through God.”

Emperor Lothair said: “If my servant, at my command, does anything good or bad, why should it not be reckoned to me? Therefore, if something done by my servant at my command is attributed not to him but to me, much more must it be believed and said that the deed of blessed Benedict, which he performed at God’s command, is attributed not to him but to the Lord. Thus it is plain that the monk speaks truth, and that his critic is frivolous. But let the young man standing before our assembly explain how and in what manner blessed Benedict came to Cassino.”

Then Peter read aloud, in the hearing of the emperor and all present:

> “Warned by a divine revelation, blessed Benedict was commanded to leave the place and hasten to the fortress called Cassino. Immediately the holy man, accompanied by two angels and three ravens, came to Cassino after fifty thousand paces; in the temple of Apollo he established an oratory of blessed Martin, and where Apollo’s altar had been he built a church of John; and he converted the peoples dwelling round about to faith in Christ.”

[Note: “I find these words nowhere.”]

Emperor Lothair said: “We have now been sufficiently satisfied about these matters. Let your speech now return to the election of the abbot, so that through you the certainty of truth may become clear to us.”

Deacon Peter replied: “We have shown that the ordination of modern abbots was not in the least performed by the apostolic see; it remains now to set forth the ordination of the ancient abbots as well. We read in the Life of Saint Maurus, disciple of the holy Father Benedict (ch. 27), that the congregation of Monte Cassino, while blessed Benedict was still alive, had determined to elect Saint Maurus as their abbot after their master’s death. This surely would have been carried out had he not, by God’s favor, been sent to Gaul. But I ask you: tell me who elected, after blessed Benedict’s death, Constantine, Simplicius, Vitalis, Bonitus, Valentinian, Gregory, Theodore, John, Leo, Ursus, Agapitus, Leo, John, Theophilus, Adrian, Romanus, Petronax, Optatus, Hermerisius, Gratianus, Tomichis, Potho, Theodemar, Gisulf, Apollinaris, Deusdedit, Hilderic, Authpert, Bassacius, Bertharius, Angelarius, Ragemprand, Leo, John, Adelpert, Baldwin, Maielpoto, Aligern, Manso, John, Attenulf, Theobald, Richerius, Peter, Otto, Bruno, Oderisius, and Nicholas—whom you cannot possibly affirm were ordained by anyone other than the monks.”

[Note: Gregory through Romanus are abbots of the Lateran congregation. Apart from Peter, only pseudo-Anastasius includes them; Muratori, *Scriptores*, II, 354, where Romanus precedes Theophilus.]

[Note: Either Peter or the scribe omitted John III.]

Cardinal Gerard said: “We are not a little astonished that the monk, with irreverent boldness, has dared to discuss such matters concerning the election of the Cassinese brethren, when Benedict, most holy and distinguished author of the monastic Rule, commanded in his Rule (ch. 64) that if a congregation errs in choosing an abbot, or elects otherwise than it ought, the bishop in whose diocese the place lies must by no means permit it. The legislator granted this power not only to the bishop but also to the laypeople dwelling nearby. Why say more about the office of ordaining an abbot? Saint Benedict even commands that a priest within the monastery must in no way be expelled without the bishop’s consent and will (Rule, ch. 62).”

Deacon Peter replied: “I agree that the most holy Father Benedict said that a bad election by the congregation must be forbidden by the bishop. But what has such a command to do with those who conduct an election regularly and unanimously?”

Cardinal Gerard said: “To whom belongs the consecration of the abbot of Monte Cassino?”

Deacon Peter said: “To the Roman pontiff.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “Therefore, if consecration belongs to the Roman pontiff, election must likewise belong to him; for you have inflicted an injury upon the Roman see by electing an abbot without its knowledge.”

Deacon Peter replied: “We do not deny that an election was made, for neither ought we to do so; but we reject in every possible way the claim that the Roman see was injured.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “For the moment, you cannot deny that Seniorectus was elected abbot at the command of Pope Honorius.”

Deacon Peter replied: “I—I was present at the election, but I saw absolutely no bishop or cardinal.” [Note: See above, note 1622.]

Cardinal Gerard said: “Go where you will; argue whatever you please: you could never, under any circumstances, elect a subdeacon as abbot, and certainly not without the pope’s consent. For Pope Eugenius writes thus in his decrees: ‘Let such men be elected as abbots in monasteries as are endowed with Levitical or priestly rank.’”

[Note: Variant: *Sacerdotalem quoque honorem sint adepti*, “they have also attained priestly rank.” Mansi XIV, 1007.]

Deacon Peter replied: “Do you wonder that the laws of the Roman pontiffs are often changed, when He who created heaven and earth frequently alters what He promises according to merit? He assigned one hundred and twenty years for the repentance required of those living before the Flood; but because their minds had turned toward evil, subtracting twenty years, He brought the Flood upon the world. Did not God promise an eternal kingdom to the patriarch Judah and to King Solomon? God also foretold through the prophet Jonah that He would overthrow the Ninevites; yet, when they repented, He removed the destruction pronounced against them.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “What you have alleged on your own behalf does the lord pope no harm; for it is plainly evident that Father Benedict said the faults of the congregation must be corrected by the bishop of the place.”

Deacon Peter replied: “Canonical authority decrees that even the clergy of the humblest church may freely judge concerning the man to be set over them. Likewise, Pope Gregory the Teacher and one hundred and twelve other Roman pontiffs established for the monastery of Monte Cassino this decree: ‘When the abbot has died, the congregation itself shall elect an abbot for itself according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.’”

[Note: The alleged privilege is fictitious; see it in the appendix to the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* in Vincentius and Breul.]

[Note: In the privileges printed by Gattula, John VIII and Benedict II have nothing about election; Victor II and Nicholas II add, “and shall present him to the pontiff of the apostolic see to be confirmed and consecrated”; Urban II and Paschal II omitted this, while Leo IX and Calixtus II retain “to be consecrated.”]

Cardinal Gerard said: “What sort of abbot, then, must they elect: a Catholic, or one cut off from the members of the Church?”

Deacon Peter replied: “A Catholic.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “Must they elect a subdeacon, or a deacon or priest?”

Deacon Peter replied: “Canonical authority has decreed that they elect a deacon or priest.”

Cardinal Gerard said: “And if those to be elected do not exercise Levitical or priestly rank, how, according to the Rule’s command, will they read the Gospel lesson? How can they chant Mass? How can they loose or bind anyone? How will priests or deacons fall at a subdeacon’s feet? How will they place incense and bless priests or deacons? For readers, exorcists, doorkeepers, acolytes, and subdeacons are subject to the offices of Levites and priests; and if they are subject, how can they be placed over them? For, as Saint Sylvester says, a reader, exorcist, doorkeeper, acolyte, or subdeacon is not to be placed over a deacon or priest. Hence, when Father Benedict wished to send an abbot into Gaul, he sent there not a subdeacon or any other such person, but the most holy Maurus, a Levite. How, then, can the election of an excommunicated or schismatic subdeacon be considered valid?”

[Note: “I do not find these words in the decrees falsely attributed to him.”]

The emperor replied: “We have considered it proper to remit entirely to the monks of Monte Cassino whatever they have done up to now, whether justly or unjustly; and this is the sum of my petition, which I ask of the apostolic lord: that what they have done up to the present be forgiven them. Let today’s conflict therefore end. Let our request again be reported to the lord pope; on the fourth day we shall hear what he commands. We grant this matter also a delay for deliberation, so that we may hear decisively what he intends to do.”

When this had been said, each withdrew to his own quarters; but Deacon Peter remained in the emperor’s court. The cardinals then returned to the apostolic lord and reported all that had been said, declaring that there was a certain deacon on behalf of the church of Monte Cassino who alone debated against the Roman Church for his church.

There was then present one of the Cassinese monks who favored the apostolic lord against the welfare of himself and his church. Stepping forward, he said: “Let your apostolate know that this deacon, of whom your lordship has been informed, has been a monk almost from infancy. He has grown in that monastery to such intellectual power that he has perfectly understood most books of Holy Scripture—things which others can scarcely grasp even when teachers instruct them. If you bind this man with any bond, you will count all the others present as nothing.”

When Innocent the pope heard this, he asked what was the man’s lineage and country. The speaker replied: “His father was the son of Gregory, son of Gregory, of Alberic, duke and consul of the Romans.”

Then the pope said: “With God’s help, I will bind both him and the others with such a fetter that they will not dare utter a word against either me or my apostolic successors.” Stirred by vehement anger, he ordered the following words to be reported to the emperor after the fourth day: that lordship over the church of Monte Cassino belonged not to the emperor but to himself, as did that of the other churches. “For your love and at your request,” he said, “we had determined to remit fealty to the monks; but because they have not submitted themselves to our apostolate, we have judged it proper that these additional matters be required of them.”

The pontiff then sent his chaplain Benedict to Deacon Peter, commanding him to withdraw from the emperor’s service and cease fellowship with the Cassinese brethren. He said that he was more than sufficiently astonished that Peter, born of Roman stock, had preferred love for foreigners to his fellow-countrymen by abandoning the Roman Church. If, therefore, he would then leave the Cassinese and oppose them by whatever means he knew and could, the pope promised to have him among his own chaplains and to provide him with necessities.

Peter sent this answer: he thanked him for judging him so worthy and distinguished as to invite him into his service; nevertheless, he could not abandon companions placed in so critical a situation. But after the dispute had been concluded, he promised that he would remain, so long as he lived, in the service of the apostolic see and in fealty to the Roman pontiff.

After this the pope decreed that letters should be sent throughout all places adjacent to the monastery of Monte Cassino, ordering that they should not obey the Cassinese abbot and monks, and that all monasteries subject to provosts should elect abbots for themselves. But almighty God, who stretched out His hand to Peter when he was sinking, thwarted the pontiff’s plan and will.

To return to the narrative: when the cardinals had departed from the emperor’s presence, a certain monk of Cistello, standing at a distance, began to mock the Cassinese monks because they had adhered to the son of Peter Leo and had elected an abbot without the pope’s counsel. He said that such an election was invalid and that all acts of the man elected must be held as nothing, since he had invaded another’s see.

Turning to him, Deacon Peter said: “Tell me how he invaded another’s see.”

The Cistellese replied: “Because, being alien to the Church, he deprived the man who ought rightly to have been ordained according to Father Benedict’s command of the Cassinese chair.” [Note: Variant: *his* (C), “to these.”] Therefore both his acts and his election were invalid.

Deacon Peter said: “It is clearer than clear that his election was carried out according to the ancient custom of the monastery.”

The Cistellese replied: “Your Abbot Raynald was not an abbot; therefore his acts must be reckoned as nothing.”

Deacon Peter said: “Not only those living at Cassino, but also those dwelling round about, recognized him as abbot.”

The Cistellese replied: “I agree that they recognized him as abbot; but the election itself was fictitious and reprobate.”

[Note: In the *Altercatio*, Peter’s dispute with the Cistellese extends over four and a half pages.]

After these and many other arguments had been made, Emperor Lothair said: “Deacon Peter has answered clearly and sufficiently eloquently all the accusations brought by the Cistellese monk against our treasury—the church of Monte Cassino. But let this now be the end of this dispute. Let each return to his lodging; in the morning we shall return again to the contest.”

114. On the following day (14 July), when light had been restored to the earth, [Note: Cf. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.170.] the emperor summoned his magnates, sat in assembly, and commanded both parties to come before him for debate. When they had arrived, the Cistellese monk opened the dispute as follows:

“Benedict, shepherd and prince of the monastic order, in setting down the monastic Rule established how they ought to live. You, on the contrary, forgetful of his commands, have added many things and removed some; you do not fear to act otherwise than he commanded.”

Deacon Peter said: “State in the presence of our most invincible lord emperor what we do against the Rule.”

The Cistellese replied: “You act against the Rule in food, drink, clothing, and very many other matters.”

Deacon Peter said: “A false witness shall not go unpunished. The Cassinese monks act according to the Rule, not against it. We have garments that cover the body, prevent the shame of nakedness, and ward off the injury of cold (Rule, ch. 55).”

The Cistellese replied: “Why do you always wear black garments?”

Deacon Peter said: “Because Father Benedict used such clothing, so that even in dress he might seem to have renounced the world.”

As they said these and many other things, Emperor Lothair said to the Cistellese: “Although you have put forward varied and diverse arguments against the church of Monte Cassino, nevertheless, because Deacon Peter, faithful servant of the Roman empire, has answered your assertions quite lucidly and has removed every uncertainty from our minds, let each return to his lodging. In the morning we shall return to the contest. But let Peter remain in the imperial palace with our chancellor Bertulf, to perform services of the empire.”

[Note: These “other matters” occupy three pages in the *Altercatio*.]

When he had spoken these words, [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* II.790.] each returned to his tent. At nightfall the emperor sat in judgment and commanded that the deeds of Roman, Greek, Ishmaelite, and other emperors, kings, dukes, princes, and nations be recited from the imperial annals, and that their judgments be recorded one by one.

But when Titan’s radiance shone over the fields (15 July), the emperor, attending to morning business, [Note: Cf. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.465.] summoned the officials of the empire and commanded both parties to come before him. When they had arrived, the emperor, sitting in assembly, said: “We command that you support the opinions which are to be presented with testimonies from Scripture, so that, all twists of uncertainty being removed, we may hold firmly to justice, equity, and truth.”

[Note: Variant: *munitatir*, “may you fortify.”]

The Cistellese replied: “It would be right to debate with this young man speaking for the church of Monte Cassino, unless he and the Cassinese congregation had been branded with schism and heresy.”

Deacon Peter said, blushing: “Let the frenzied tongue be silent, which has broken forth into barking rather than fair speech.”

Emperor Lothair, interrupting his words, said: “Since you have begun to contend alone against all on behalf of the church of Monte Cassino, you must reply civilly, not furiously. For it is unbecoming that those who move in the imperial court and have become the emperor’s protodomestics should display anything dishonorable or foolish in speech, gait, or dress.”

Deacon Peter said: “If your servant has exceeded in speech at all, most merciful emperor and ever august one, the Cistellese compelled me; for from the beginning of the debate he began with insults and persists in insults.”

The Cistellese replied: “Tell us: where did I inflict insults?”

Deacon Peter said: “When you fastened upon us the label of excommunication and schism, then you inflicted insults upon the church of Monte Cassino.”

The Cistellese replied: “If you please, state what an insult is.”

Deacon Peter said: “An insult is one inflicted by deceitful words; but you did not fear to speak most falsely before the lord emperor when you defamed us for heresy.”

After they had debated at great length, Patriarch Peregrinus replied: “It is evident on just and fitting grounds that the Cistellese has been defeated by Deacon Peter; therefore this is the end of the dispute.”

[Note: *Piligrimus* in the *Altercatio*, where those “very many things” fill a page and a half.]

113. On another day (16 July), Cardinal Gerard came on behalf of the apostolic see. As the emperor sat in judgment, he said: “The Roman Church, most sacred emperor and ever august one, was founded not by human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ, who sent Peter, prince of the apostles, there and entrusted to him the keys of the kingdom of heaven; therefore the rights of the Roman Church ought not to be violated for love of anyone.”

When Deacon Peter replied that no Roman pope had ever received an oath from the Cassinese monks, Cardinal Gerard said that they had not demanded this because, until those times, the monks had remained in the unity of the Church; but after they had departed from the Church and become exiles, after they had committed schism in the Church, they ought not to be received without an oath. At Pope Innocent’s command he produced in their midst a chapter of the Council of Nicaea, stating that those returning from schism were not to be received without an oath.

[Note: This is not a decree of the Council of Nicaea, but a statute of other canons. ANG.]

Emperor Lothair said: “I did not assemble you for this purpose, to investigate the laws of the canons, but that you might deal kindly and civilly with the church of Monte Cassino.” They ought to remember the benefactions bestowed upon them in the Roman Church; remember what and how great dangers the emperor himself had endured for them with his army; how he had lived in tents for one year and two months; how many relatives and closest friends he had lost in the expedition. For, he said, the Cassinese brethren had not fled to just any enemy of the pontiff but to the Roman emperor and defender of the Church.

Finally, he declared that if they grieved him in this matter, they should know with certainty that from that day forward the Roman empire would be torn and separated from the pope, and that the pope would in every respect be regarded by the emperor not as a friend but as an enemy.

When the emperor’s whole army had acclaimed this at great length and rightly praised what he had said, the emperor petitioned the pontiff about the same matter: first through all the bishops, second through the archbishops, third through the patriarch of Aquileia, fourth through the abbots, sixth through the counts, seventh through the margraves and princes, eighth through Empress Richiza, and ninth through himself.

[Note: Either Peter or the scribe omitted the fifth rank.]

The pontiff then informed the emperor that he would accept his counsel concerning the church of Monte Cassino and fulfill his wish. Greatly delighted at this, the emperor again made haste to approach the pope in person. When he entreated him on behalf of the Cassinese church, the pope replied that he wondered why the emperor could not understand that he should not pray for men who had anathematized and deposed pope and emperor, had accepted the son of Peter Leo as pope, had accepted another crown above the crown of the Roman empire, and had persisted in their former wickedness to that very time.

Then the most merciful emperor, dissolved wholly into tears, ordered silence and said: “I do not deny that they did this so that the condition of the Cassinese monastery might come safely to us. For if they had not done so, that church would now lie overthrown by our enemies. Therefore I ask that you turn upon me the punishment with which they should be afflicted. If they must be beaten, I offer my back for them; if they must be deposed, I wish to be deposed.”

Then the pope said: “For love of you, we temper the rigor of the canonical sanction; for those who shared communion with excommunicated persons and anathematized their own pontiff would rightly deserve deposition. But we, using gentleness and mercy, forgive all that they have done wrongly for your sake—provided, however, that they anathematize the son of Peter Leo with his followers and promise obedience to me and to my successors.”

When this pleased the emperor, and the feast of the blessed martyr Symphorosa arrived (18 July), the emperor sent with the elect and the brethren Henry, duke of Bavaria and his son-in-law; Conrad, duke of Swabia, nephew of Emperor Henry V; Otto [Note: Variant: *Octonem* (C).] of Burchisin, his cousin; and likewise all the bishops, archbishops, counts, margraves, princes, and dukes of the Roman empire.

When they drew near the pope’s tent, the cardinals came out to meet them and asked whether he would renounce the son of Peter Leo and his followers. When he said that he would fulfill this requirement, they immediately made the elect swear these words. The text of the document was as follows:

> “I, Raynald, reject and anathematize every schism and every heresy that exalts itself against the holy catholic and apostolic Church. I also reject and renounce the son of Peter Leo, Roger of Sicily, and all their followers; and I shall obey Pope Innocent and his successors who enter canonically.”

When Raynald had sworn these words, they compelled the others likewise to swear. But they said that they had sworn to Father Benedict and his successors and therefore could not take an oath. Then Raynald, acting on behalf of Father Benedict and himself, commanded them to promise into the pope’s hand the obedience which they had until then rendered to blessed Benedict, his successors, and himself. Thus the brethren were compelled to swear in the hand of the bishop of Ostia, according to the wording of the charter, what the elect had sworn upon the Gospels.

[Note: Drogo.]

They further added: “If the church of Monte Cassino is separated from the Roman see, I shall not remain in the monastery of Monte Cassino and shall not obey the abbot, saving my fealty to the Roman empire.”

When these things had been completed to the pope’s satisfaction, they were released from the bond of excommunication and, barefoot, were received first at the pope’s feet and then to the kiss.

Pope Innocent summoned Deacon Peter and said to him: “I command and charge you by the power of the Holy Spirit, and I adjure you by the oath which today you have made to me and my successors: whenever you receive a letter or messenger from me or my successors, you shall no longer have power to delay or remain, but you must endeavor as quickly as possible to present yourself at the feet of the apostolic see and of the pontiff who shall be in office at the time. For I do not wish the Roman Church to be disturbed through you or to suffer any dispute.”

After this Raynald was brought before the emperor, received by him with immense honor, and established with the brethren among the chaplains of the empire. For until that day he had not been presented before the emperor’s eyes.

[Note: Here that *Altercatio* ends; but another *Altercatio* begins, on behalf of the Roman Church against a certain Greek: “Moreover, on the same day the messenger of John …,” etc. In the Caietan manuscript it fills fourteen pages; its ending had already then been lost. Apart from the words of Lothair found here, none of Lothair’s words occur there.]

In those days envoys of John, emperor of Constantinople, came to the august Lothair, offering congratulations and bringing great gifts because of the victory granted him by God against Roger.

[Note: Cf. *Annales Hildesheimenses*, 1137.]

Among them came a certain philosopher. Standing at a distance before the emperor, he began, with dog-like barking, to assail the holy Roman and apostolic see and the whole Western Church, saying that the Roman pontiff was an emperor, not a bishop, and calling the Roman clergy excommunicated and *azymites*—users of unleavened bread. Against him Deacon Peter turned and began in every way, opportunely and inopportunely, to dispute with him. But when night ended the above-mentioned debate, Emperor Lothair commanded them to meet at earliest morning before the imperial assembly, and that, if the Greek had anything against the Roman Church, he should obediently bring it forward.

116. When this had taken place, the Greek broke out in these words: “Men of understanding and vigorous intellect, consider and decide on the tribunal of your minds with impartial weighing whether an excommunicated person ought to hold discourse with a Catholic.”

But Deacon Peter, supposing that the Greek had hurled the weapon of excommunication against him, said to him: “If you please, state against whom you have directed the weapon of anathema: against me, or against the whole Western Church?”

The Greek replied: “Against both you and the whole Western Church.”

Deacon Peter said: “Why?”

The Greek replied: “Because you have transgressed the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.”

Deacon Peter said: “In what have we transgressed the ordinances of the Council of Nicaea?”

The Greek replied: “In that you added that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; for it is written in that council that the Spirit proceeds from the Father.”

Deacon Peter said: “If you call us excommunicated because we added that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, then you also are excommunicated, because you added that he proceeds from the Father alone.”

At this declaration the Greek fell silent. After a little while he addressed the same deacon thus: “We now see fulfilled in the Western region what the Lord says through the prophet: ‘As with the people, so with the priest’ (*Isaiah* 24:2), when pontiffs rush to war, as your Pope Innocent does; they distribute money, gather soldiers, and clothe themselves in purple garments.”

After these and many other arguments, as night brought the day to its end, the Greek translated his statements and Deacon Peter’s replies into Greek, to be conveyed to the patriarch of Constantinople and Emperor John. [Note: Peter published the same matters in Latin; see above, ch. 66.] He also then handed Deacon Peter in writing the authorities by which the Greeks defended their wives.

The emperor, moreover, exceedingly delighted by the dispute which Deacon Peter had held with the Greek, appointed that same deacon—through the intercession of the most pious Empress Richiza, Henry duke of the Bavarians, and Conrad duke of the Swabians—logothete, secretary, recorder, auditor, keeper of charters, and chaplain of the Roman empire.

117. The same Emperor Lothair, having assembled an army, directed a naval [Note: [Col. 0957D] Either *navalem* is to be read, or a word has fallen out.] expedition, over which Abbot Guibald of Stavelot had been appointed, against Salerno. A great battle therefore took place, and many fell on both sides.
