When the people of Salerno saw that the position of their city had changed, they held a council and submitted themselves and their city to the imperial clemency. This affair produced the greatest dissension between pope and emperor (Aug.): the pope maintaining that the city of Salerno belonged to the Roman Church, while the emperor, on the contrary, declared that it ought to belong not to the pope but to the emperor.

In these days Peter, deacon of Cassino, in the presence of the aforesaid emperor and the nobles, brought a complaint concerning the monastery of Saint Benedict at Bari, which the citizens of Bari had withdrawn from the jurisdiction of the monastery of Cassino, namely since the death of Father Desiderius, who was also Pope Victor III [Col. 0958B]. The emperor then summoned the people of Bari before him and ordered them to produce the title which they had concerning the aforesaid church. When they said that they had none, Peter the deacon, by the emperor’s order and in the hearing of all, read how Pippin and his son Charles the Great, and all succeeding emperors, had granted it to Saint Benedict and his monastery of Cassino. [Note: [Col. 0958D] I find its first mention in a privilege of Nicholas II, dated 1059.] The emperor, therefore, having recognized the right of the monastery of Cassino, ordered the people of Bari to restore the same church to Saint Benedict, imposing a penalty of one hundred marks of gold if they attempted to resist this.

Then the same Peter also complained against Count Robert of Laurotello, who had granted as a fief to one of his knights the church of Saint Scholastica, situated in the territory of Penne, together with many other possessions and churches [Col. 0958C]. By the judgment of the aforesaid emperor, through Gualfrid, judge of Bologna, and upon the said count’s renunciation, he immediately recovered them.

Moreover, because of the very great devotion and the singular help for which, after God, he trusted in Father Benedict, the same emperor bound under pledge all the magnates of Samnium, Liguria, Picenum, Pelignum, Apulia, Liburia, and the Principality: unless they wished to experience the wrath of the Roman Empire, they were, as soon as they returned to their own homes, to restore to the monastery of Cassino all Saint Benedict’s possessions which they had wickedly held, down to that day, from the time of Justinian the Great; a penalty of one thousand pounds of gold was imposed if they chose to prove contemptuous in this matter.

118. Raynald, having received leave to return from pope and emperor [Col. 0958D], went back to Cassino. Emperor Lothair, however, retained Peter the deacon and Bertulf the mansionarius with him on this same expedition. But because Peter was laid low by illness, having obtained leave from the emperor he withdrew to Cassino, intending to remain there for fifteen days.

The pope sent with the already mentioned Raynald Baldwin, cardinal-priest, who afterwards became archbishop of Pisa [Col. 0959A], ordering him to have the monks of Cassino reject and anathematize the son of Peter Leo and his followers, as Raynald himself had done, and to promise obedience to the pope and his successors. The brethren took care to carry out all these things as the pope had commanded.

At the same time the aforesaid Raynald was accused to the emperor by certain of his enemies, on the ground that he favoured King Roger and received his envoys. By chance Raynald had then fallen into a very serious illness. The emperor, disturbed by what was said about him, and considering him also an enemy of the Empire, sent him an imperial summons, commanding that he should not delay in coming to him without any postponement. He was also to send Peter the deacon, and the man who had been with Peter on the same expedition [Col. 0959B], together with the dean of Cassino, to him at once. Raynald, being held fast by grave illness, sent Peter the deacon to the emperor as he had received orders; he himself remained at Cassino.

In these same days the aforesaid elect sent messengers to Gregory, son of Adenulf of Saint John, whom we mentioned above, commanding him to come and fortify the monastery of Cassino against the emperor as before. When the brethren learned this beyond all doubt, they took care to notify the emperor. He immediately dispatched a troop of soldiers and ordered the monastery to be guarded in loyalty to himself. Raynald, foreseeing the schemes directed against him, withdrew to the chamber adjoining the infirmary. When Bruno, the emperor’s field commander, arrived [Col. 0959C], he entered the monastery with an army and at once ordered the same elect to be guarded by soldiers.

At the time when the emperor was staying at Capua, brethren from the monastery of Saint Vincent, Christ’s martyr, came to him and lodged a complaint against the church of Cassino: it had despoiled them, they said, of the castle of Cardeto, Vitecuso, Valle Rotonda, Saracenisco, and other possessions which were known to have belonged by right to Saint Vincent. Peter the deacon, whom I mentioned above and who wrote this history, was present at this affair. Considering such a complaint wholly intolerable, he began to ask them before the emperor under which emperor the aforesaid castles had been granted to the monastery of Saint Vincent. When they brought forward the time of Louis II [Col. 0959D], Peter the deacon replied that they had unjustly brought a suit against the monastery of Cassino, since it was established that the charter concerning Saint Benedict’s possessions had been drawn up in the time of Justin the Elder and Justinian, nearly three hundred years before Louis reigned.

Emperor Lothair, having perceived the claim of equity, gave judgment. It was neither just, he said, nor compatible with any reason, that the church of Cassino—which was the unique and special treasury of the Roman Empire [Col. 0960A]—should in his time lose any possession or castle which it was known to have held nearly six hundred years earlier. [Note: [Col. 0959D] Lothair therefore accepted those privileges as genuine, if what is narrated here is true; for you would search in vain for an instrument made concerning the matter. Peter also entered a certain privilege of Justinian in his Register. [Col. 0960D]] Therefore it ought perpetually and without any litigation to retain what had been granted to Saint Benedict. He imposed a penalty of one thousand pounds of gold on anyone who defied this decree. Having thus settled his affairs, he came with his whole army to the city of San Germano, Pope Innocent accompanying him (13 September). There he was received in honourable procession by the aforesaid Raynald, who was then under guard; and on that day the elect himself was guarded in the secretarium of the basilica of the Lord Saviour, but afterwards was sent back under no slight guard to the monastery, where he was to be examined.

[Col. 0960B] 119. On the following day (14 September 1137), the emperor sent Anno, abbot of the monastery of Lüneburg, and Peter, deacon of Cassino, to the monastery, commanding the brethren through them not to display anything disorderly or undisciplined in dress, speech, or gait. He himself, he said, would come to the monastery with cardinals, archbishops, abbots, princes, dukes, margraves, counts, and the more devout and prudent men of the Roman Empire; and if he found Raynald unworthy of so great an abbey, he would remove him at once and establish a suitable person in Saint Benedict’s chair.

He himself remained in the city to receive the circlet crown of the patriciate, for the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross was then being celebrated. At dawn [Col. 0960C], Empress Richiza climbed the entire mountain on foot, while the pope remained in the city. Emperor Lothair, attended by the countless multitude of his army, arrived at Cassino and was received by the brethren with the greatest honour, as befitted imperial dignity.

That day he offered Saint Benedict an excellent cope adorned with golden stripes; a chasuble with a lining of the same material; a pair of silver candlesticks weighing about fourteen pounds; one mark of gold; and nineteen marks of silver. The Empress Richiza placed upon the altar a Phrygian stole with its maniple, and a mitre suitably ornamented with gold.

That same day, while the most Christian emperor stood in the church, Raynald summoned the brethren to chapter [Col. 0960D] and began to declare that he had been elected by them. They need not trouble themselves over this matter: if they wished, he would immediately relinquish the abbey in accordance with their will. While he repeated these and many other statements, certain laymen came into the chapter-house and began to rebuke the brethren and dishonour them with very many reproaches because they wished to abandon their abbot at so critical a moment of danger. The brethren, stirred by indignation and anger alike, drove them from the chapter-house with blows, crying out that they no longer wished to have as abbot a man who wished to retain the abbey not through monks but through laymen [Col. 0961A].

Toward sunset Pope Innocent sent his messenger to the monastery, commanding the brethren, exhorting them by the faith and obedience they had promised to him and to Saint Peter, not to render further obedience to that elect and to endeavour as swiftly as they could to expel him from the abbey of Cassino. He promised his favour to those who obeyed such commands and decreed perpetual exile for those who despised them.

At dawn on 15 September, Aymeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Roman Church, Gerard, cardinal of Santa Croce, and the abbot of Clairvaux were sent by the same pope to examine the said Raynald and, according to the sanction of the canons, remove him from the government of the abbey [Col. 0961B]. The emperor sat in the chapter-house of Cassino with all the magnates of the Empire; Peregrine, patriarch of Aquileia, also sat there with archbishops, bishops, abbots, and cardinals. They ordered the elect to enter and brought many charges against him, declaring him a rebel and adversary of the Empire and saying that he had been ordained by schismatics.

Then one man rose before the emperor and began to say that, after Raynald had made peace with Henry, duke of Bavaria, he had shown himself an enemy of pope and emperor. Raynald and his companions contradicted this; whereupon the emperor ordered both parties to withdraw from the chapter-house, so that he might take counsel with the patriarch and cardinals on the matter [Col. 0961C].

While they sat in consultation, Patriarch Peregrine and Chancellor Aymeric said that he could by no means preside over so great a place, for many reasons: because he had been made subdeacon by the son of Peter Leo; because he had sworn an oath to King Roger; because excommunicated persons could not make an election contrary to the command of the canons; and finally because, contrary to ecclesiastical institutions, they had elected a man from the subdiaconate. They produced a chapter of Pope Eugenius [Note: [Col. 0961] See above, ch. 114.] writing thus: “In monasteries such men are to be elected and ordained abbots as are invested with Levitical or priestly rank,” and so forth. But as the sun was already declining toward sunset and threatening night, the assembly was dismissed at the emperor’s command [Col. 0961D].

120. On the following day, while the emperor sat in chapter with the prelates and magnates (16 September), the elect rose in the midst and wished to speak concerning the matters alleged against him. Before he could finish, some of the brethren rose in the midst and began, as before, to accuse him, saying that his election had been made factiously and not canonically. Those who supported the aforesaid elect began to reproach them with lying and falsehood [Col. 0962A]; thus they disputed before the emperor and assailed one another with various insults.

Moved by these speeches, the emperor rose, signalled silence with his hand, and said that he marvelled more than enough that so great and distinguished an assembly should speak so confusedly and disorderly and present its affairs with such disorder. He therefore commanded them, unless they wished to experience the anger of the Roman Empire, to state their business reasonably and without dissension. When he had finished speaking, he sat down; and, having ordered the rest to sit, he addressed the assembly as follows. He could not fully examine the disputed election of the abbot unless each party were heard separately.

Accordingly, all the archbishops, bishops, and abbots, by the emperor’s command, met behind locked doors with the party favouring the elected abbot [Note: [Col. 0961] Rather, the party which did not favour him, as is clear from what follows.] [Col. 0962B]. Once this had taken place and those assembled to investigate the election had taken their seats, Anno [Note: [Col. 0961] More correctly, Adelbero.] bishop of Basel said: “If you have anything against the elected abbot, put it forward reasonably and not tumultuously.”

Some of the brethren rose in the midst and began to accuse the elect, saying that for his election he had promised a gift of the tongue, a gift of the hand, and a gift of service, and that there were no suitable witnesses. While they disputed in this way, Pandulf the vestararius rose in the midst and said: “Although there are many matters which we might allege against the elect, there is one thing which seems intolerable in him: namely, that he was ordained by Peter, son of Peter Leo [Col. 0962C]. It is utterly unworthy that in so great a church, which is the head and mother of all monasteries, there should be a subdeacon as abbot—one who can neither celebrate the solemnities of Mass nor grant remission of sins.”

To this Bishop Anselm replied: [Note: [Col. 0961] Anselm of Havelberg is among the witnesses of the privilege of Lothair III.] “Though these brethren have said many things against their elect for which he ought to be deposed, this one point seems sufficient for his expulsion [Note: [Col. 0961] *Electionem*, ‘election,’ in C.]: as the Lord bears witness, a foundation which is upon sand cannot stand. Therefore, if it pleases those of you assembled to examine these matters, let us set aside the other allegations and hold to this one point alone.”

When the others approved this, they ordered the brethren to withdraw, and Raynald, with those who supported him [Col. 0962D], to enter and defend himself against the charges brought against him. When this had continued for a long time, the emperor, seeing that no end was being made, ordered those assembled to hear and investigate the matter to persuade the said elect to place himself in the power of Pope Innocent, of the emperor himself, and of all the magnates of the Roman Empire, so that whatever they should judge in the matter he would carry out without any objection. The elect resisted and opposed this in every way, but at length consented and placed himself, as they wished, under their judgment and power [Col. 0963A].

After this all returned to the emperor, and the bishop of Basel reported in order to the emperor and the others sitting there the deeds and words that had occurred. Finally, when the emperor asked whether those who opposed Raynald wished to submit themselves to the power of Empire and priesthood, he found them most readily prepared to do so. Thus the assembly of the second day was dismissed. These events took place on Wednesday and Thursday of the third week of September, the second day after the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

121. After this, men were sent on behalf of the emperor and the assembly to notify Pope Innocent, who was then staying at San Germano, of the course of events. On arriving, they found the pope very angry [Col. 0963B] and were forbidden to enter his presence, because the emperor with his magnates had presumed, while the Roman pontiff was present, to conduct an examination concerning the election of the abbot of Cassino. On this account he threatened to deprive of office the archbishops, bishops, and abbots who had been present at such an examination.

Those sent by the emperor returned without result and took care to report to the emperor what they had encountered with the pope. After consultation, the emperor sent this reply to the pontiff: what had been done had been done not deliberately but simply, not to dishonour him but to honour him; for the deeds and words concerned remained subject to his power, so that all would hold valid whatever he decreed upon the matter [Col. 0963C]. Therefore the pope should promptly send some men from his own side to reconsider the aforesaid election and determine what was just.

Appeased by such words, Innocent on the Ember Friday (17 September) sent Chancellor Aymeric, Gerard cardinal of the title of Santa Croce, who afterwards governed the Roman Church, and other cardinals to examine the election. When they arrived at the monastery and prolonged discussion of the matter, they assembled in the refectory, summoned all the senior members of the house, and said that the aforesaid Raynald could in no way remain in the abbey because he had been ordained by excommunicated persons. Then they began to question each man separately concerning the person to be elected abbot [Col. 0963D].

When some proposed various members of the community according to their preference, the cardinals left the place in which they were sitting, summoned the same elect within the monastery cloister, and commanded him on behalf of the Apostolic See to cease from the abbey itself, because he could no longer be abbot. They then returned to the pope and reported what had been done and said.

122. On the next day (18 September), they went up again to the monastery and sat in chapter. After the sermon delivered by the abbot of Clairvaux [Col. 0964A], the cardinals, by apostolic authority, forbade Raynald the abbey of Cassino. Then, rising with the emperor and the archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, princes, and margraves, they entered the church of Saint Benedict. Aymeric the chancellor, Peregrine patriarch of Aquileia, and Gerard the cardinal summoned Raynald and pronounced upon him the sentence of deposition. At their command, in the presence of the emperor and all the magnates of the Empire, he laid down upon the body of the most holy Benedict the staff, ring, and Rule. Such was the outcome of Raynald’s affairs.

123. Afterwards, when they came into the chapter-house, Gerard the cardinal rose in the midst and began to address the brethren in words of this kind: [Note: [Col. 0963] A word seems to have fallen out.] “You know, most beloved brethren, that according to the precept of the Rule an abbot is commanded to be elected by the brethren. But because you chose to place yourselves under the judgment and power of our lord Pope Innocent, you are now wholly deprived of the right to elect an abbot, except insofar as he permits you; and such an election belongs not to you but to the Roman Church [Col. 0964B].

“Yet, for preserving the unity of peace and concord, we do not wish to use this power in every respect. Rather, by command of the Apostolic See, we order you to choose twelve brethren from your community, who together with us may be able to elect an abbot worthy of so great a place.”

The brethren replied that according to ancient custom they wished to have a free election. The cardinals gave no assent to their words, and the greatest dissension arose between the two parties. The party which had been with the aforesaid Raynald declared that they would by no means consent to an abbot being chosen from the community of Cassino. The cardinals said they would agree on no account that an abbot should be elected from another monastery for the head and mother of all monasteries [Col. 0964C].

But as neither party yielded to the other, and they vainly beat the air with words in support of their own will, the chancellor finally became angry and, on behalf of the Roman Church, forbade them to presume to make any election at all. He then returned to the pope and set forth in order what had been done and said.

After this the emperor sent vigorous men from his own side to Pope Innocent and began to request that, out of love for him, the pope release the monks from the aforesaid obligation and grant them leave to elect an abbot. Moved by his requests, the pope granted, out of love for the emperor, what Caesar had asked. This was subject, however, to the condition that the monastery send him its imperial privileges and charters to be read. This was done.

Accordingly, before emperor and pontiff there was read the charter of King Charles concerning the election of an abbot [Note: [Col. 0963D] See I, 12.], and the privileges of Benedict VII and Leo IX. In them it was expressly contained how Henry the Pious had granted to Pope Benedict VII [Note: [Col. 0965] Rather, Benedict VIII.] the consecration of Theobald, abbot of Cassino, whom the emperor himself had appointed, and one meal [Note: [Col. 0965D] Not even the spurious privilege of Benedict VIII says anything about a meal.] on the journey to and from Benevento, while reserving all else to the Roman Empire [Col. 0965A]. The same was confirmed by Conrad and his son Henry [Note: [Col. 0965D] In their published privileges nothing is said concerning the election of an abbot.]. Likewise it was read from the charter of Charles [Note: [Col. 0965D] In Gattola, *Accessiones*, p. 14; cf. above I, 12.] that at the monastery of Cassino they should elect as abbot whomever they found better, worthier, and more faithful to the Roman Empire.

Overcome by such weighty considerations, the pontiff granted and confirmed the election of the abbot of Cassino to the brethren, and his ordination to Emperor Lothair and his successors. He reserved to himself and his successors the abbot’s consecration and the meal on the journey to and from Benevento [Col. 0965B]. [Note: [Col. 0965D] The same statements occur in the privilege of Lothair III.]

124. Now, with Christ’s favour, let us describe how Guibald was elected, and what manner and stature of man he was. He was a Lotharingian by birth and had become a monk in the monastery of Stavelot from boyhood. Fully educated in grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy, he received from Emperor Henry V the governance of the abbey of the same monastery of Stavelot.

At the time when Emperor Lothair entered Italy with Pope Innocent, this same Guibald was appointed by the emperor over the naval expedition and sent to Naples. On his way, when he came to Cassino, to the thresholds of Father Benedict, and learned that the church of Cassino had been thrown into confusion by the election of the aforesaid Raynald [Col. 0965C], he entered the chapter-house and began to exhort the brethren to live peacefully and concordantly according to Saint Benedict’s Rule. They ought, he said, to remember how the streams of holy preaching and the first principles of monastic life had flowed from that place through almost the whole world; what and how great things Father Benedict, trusting in divine power, had accomplished there; how by his bodily resting-place and the composition of his Rule he had made the monastery of Cassino the perpetual head of all monasteries; and, finally, that through the son of Peter Leo they had been severed and separated from the Church. They ought to labour that it might be reformed, that the streams of so great a place might return to their former state of brilliance, and that they might turn to Pope Innocent, whom the whole world followed.

Having spoken thus, he commended himself to Father Benedict and the brethren [Col. 0965D], and went to Naples. But after Raynald had relinquished the abbey in the manner recounted above, and the brethren had been divided because of what had happened to the monastery of Cassino on account of Raynald’s election, neither party yielding to the other, all finally agreed upon this decision: that an abbot for the monastery of Cassino should be elected from the emperor’s side [Col. 0966A].

When they reported this to Pope Innocent, he began wholly to resist and oppose it, asserting that he would by no means allow an outsider to be elected in the monastery of Cassino, or that that church should be subjected to any outsider—a church which had given to the Roman See Stephen VII [Note: [Col. 0965] Rather, Stephen IX.], Victor III, and Gelasius II as popes, and had provided many other churches with catholic and suitable pastors.

But because the pope could not by any means bring the affair to concord, and wished to restore Nicholas, whom Pope Honorius had expelled from the abbey, to the governance of the monastery, they laid the course of the matter before the emperor, then staying at Cassino. They begged, implored, asked, and urgently entreated him that, just as Henry the Great had appointed Theobald and Conrad with his son Henry had appointed Richer, so he too should appoint an abbot from his own side.

At their words the emperor dissolved into tears and said: [Note: [Col. 0966D] The words from “said” through “offered to the same men” occur, in nearly the same wording although in reverse order, in Peter’s letter to Richiza in Martène and Durand, *Collectio*, I, 759.] he would sooner allow all the privileges and grants of churches to be overthrown than permit anything to be diminished from the dignities of the church of Cassino; and he would sooner allow the elections of all bishops, archbishops, and abbots throughout the Roman world to be abolished than that of the abbot of Cassino alone. For if an abbot is not elected with the consent of the monks, he will not be an abbot; and whoever takes election from the monks overthrows all the rights of the monastery.

Who, indeed, would not marvel at the gravity of so great an emperor? When he had come to the chapter-house to settle the dissensions among the brethren arising from the abbot’s election, he did not leave it from the first hour of the day until evening, allowing himself neither food nor drink [Col. 0966C]; beneath the imperial cloak he displayed the novice-service of another warfare. For on every expedition in which I was with him, at the dawn of day he heard Mass for the dead, then Mass for the army, and finally the Mass of the day. Afterwards, with the most gracious Empress Richiza, he washed the feet of widows and orphans, dried them with his hair, and kissed them; he distributed food and drink liberally, relieved the grievances and oppressions of churches, and finally laboured at the business of the Empire. [Note: [Col. 0966D] The letter omits “together with Richiza.”]

For as long as he stayed at the monastery of Cassino, he went about the cloister and all the workshops of the monastery as though he were an abbot or some dean, desiring to know how each person lived under Saint Benedict’s instruction. [Note: [Col. 0966D] The letter adds “every night.”] At dawn he went barefoot through all the churches of the monastery [Col. 0966D]. Although he did these things, he was never separated from the company of bishops, archbishops, and abbots, so that there might be fulfilled in him what is written: “His discourse is with the wise” (Prov. 3:32). [Note: [Col. 0965] The reading should be *simplicibus*, “the simple.”] Yet while he did these things [Col. 0967A], he was a staff to the blind, food to the hungry, hope to the wretched, consolation to mourners; and he excelled in each virtue as though he possessed no others.

He honoured priests as fathers, clerics as lords, the poor as sons, and widows as mothers. Constant in prayers and ever-watchful in vigils, he offered tears to God, not to men. Let this brief account of so great an emperor suffice; now let us proceed to complete the account of Guibald’s election.

When the brethren’s wish concerning the election of an abbot came to the pope’s knowledge, he sent his chancellor Aymeric to Cassino, commanding the brethren to elect an abbot from their own community; otherwise they would not have leave to elect. When this was reported to the emperor, he took it heavily and most painfully, and through his envoys requested the pope to yield to the monks’ will; otherwise, he should know that from that day forward the Empire would in every way be divided from the pontificate [Col. 0967B].

When Innocent saw Emperor Lothair agreeing with the brethren in the election, he gave the monks authority to elect whom they wished. Guibald, as we have already said, was distinguished by great wisdom, honourable character, and probity; foreseeing what was to come, he had withdrawn from the place. The emperor then sent messengers to Guibald, ordering him to come to him at the monastery, for he had by chance remained on the same expedition. When he came and perceived the brethren’s wish, he began utterly to refuse and resist it.

The brethren then assembled in the chamber where the emperor was staying, with Empress Richiza, Peregrine patriarch of Aquileia [Col. 0967C], bishops, archbishops, abbots, and all the magnates of the Empire. They began earnestly and insistently to exhort him about this whole affair. But he steadfastly refused, declaring that he would never undertake so heavy and immense a burden.

The emperor, seeing Guibald resist by every means, handed him over to the brethren. They received him and appointed him abbot in the monastery of Cassino; and the emperor invested him, through the sceptre of the Roman Empire which he held in his hand, with the abbey of Cassino and all its possessions, as they had been granted to the monastery from the time of Justinian until that day. He said to him: “We do not receive from you an oath of fealty concerning the abbey of Cassino because you formerly gave us fealty concerning the monastery of Stavelot [Col. 0967D]. I do not wish your successors to cite you as a precedent and say that they owe no fealty concerning the monastery of Cassino to my successors because the majesty of our Empire did not require it from you. Rather, let them endeavour to render the customary fealty which abbots have rendered concerning the abbey of Cassino from the time of Charles onward.”

The emperor, having arranged the church of Cassino together with the monks, on the eighth day after he had arrived there (21 September) [Col. 0968A], commended himself to Saint Benedict and the brethren. Since he had reached an advanced age—namely, the hundredth year of his life—and did not ignore the end of his days, he descended with Guibald to the city of San Germano. Having commended the aforesaid abbot to the pope, he pitched tents beside the old city of Aquino.

Guibald came to the emperor, taking with him Otto [Note: [Col. 0967D] *Octone* in C.] dean of Cassino; Raynald, who became abbot after him; Peter the deacon; Bertulf the mansionarius; Amfred the vestararius; and very many others from the community. Then, at the emperor’s command, Duke Raginulf of Apulia [Note: [Col. 0967D] Perhaps Robert, count of Caiazzo.], who had been appointed by the same emperor, Robert prince of Capua, all the counts of the principality of Capua [Col. 0968B], the counts of Aquino, and the surrounding Normans rendered fealty to the said Abbot Guibald. They confirmed by oath upon the Gospels, the wood of the Lord, and the relics of the saints, the monastery of Cassino with all its possessions without exception.

On the day on which Guibald was appointed abbot, it was represented to the emperor through the same abbot how Pandulf, son of Landulf, count of Aquino, had wickedly and violently built a castle called Tirilla in the forest of the monastery of Cassino, and had plundered the monastery’s remaining neighbouring estates. Moved by this report, the emperor sent Bruno the field commander with a troop of soldiers and gave the said castle over to plunder and fire.

Raynald, seeing Guibald appointed contrary to his expectation [Col. 0968C], craftily endeavoured to ensnare and obstruct him. Fearing that he might be sent into exile in Germany, he displayed humility in body but not in heart, and promised Guibald obedience and fealty. Having thus received from him the provostship of Saint Magnus near the city of Fondi, he left the monastery and went to the fortress called Castrum Coeli. This fortress had once been built by Manso, abbot of Cassino, [Note: [Col. 0968D] Cf. book II, ch. 14.] and Raynald’s relatives had withdrawn it from the monastery’s authority. There he applied every effort and every exertion to recovering the abbey of Cassino after the emperor’s departure and taking vengeance on his enemies.

125. The emperor and the apostolic lord, celebrating the feast of Saint Maurice, martyr of Christ, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter [Col. 0968D], invited Abbot Guibald and the brethren of the monastery of Cassino to dine, saying: “I think—unless I am mistaken—that this will be my last day of eating and drinking with you.” The event afterwards proved this true.

When the meal was over, Emperor Lothair summoned Deacon Peter to his council and ordered him to proceed with him into Gaul, carrying the commands entrusted to him by his imperial majesty and continually performing imperial service. When Guibald heard this, he took it heavily and painfully [Col. 0969A], and began to beg that he might not be deprived of Deacon Peter’s service or consolation. Emperor Lothair, yielding to Guibald’s entreaties, in the presence of Peregrine, patriarch of Aquileia, together with archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other magnates of the Roman Empire, took Deacon Peter’s hand and entrusted him to Guibald, saying:

> “The majesty of our empire, preserved by God, has made this man whom you see a disciple of Henry, bishop and chancellor of Regensburg; it has rewarded him with the offices of logothete, secretary, and auditor, and granted him a seat at its right foot. He alone among the Roman people has been found to oppose the Constantinopolitans on behalf of the Empire and the Roman pontificate. Therefore, because you say that you do not wish to remain without him, I commend him [Col. 0969B] to your fidelity with the greatest zeal and deepest affection of heart, on this condition: that, if any traces of my regard or affection remain in your heart, you show them in him, and for our love hold him in the place of a most dear and only son.”

[Note: In his letter to Richiza, Peter continues after the words quoted from chapter 66: “After he had sufficiently instructed [him] concerning those things which pertain to eternal life, with you present and all the courtiers of the Empire standing by, he took my hand and, entrusting me to Abbot Guibald, said to him: ‘If any traces of my regard, if any of my affection remain in your heart, show them in this man, and … hold [him].’” The passage breaks off.]

On the same day, through the intercession of the Empress Richiza, that most devout and merciful emperor issued a charter to the aforesaid Abbot Guibald, confirming to the monastery of Cassino all its possessions.

[Note: This document survives intact, sealed with a golden bull. It was published by E. Gattula, *Acc.*, p. 250.]

The aforesaid emperor, taking leave of Abbot Guibald and commending himself to the brethren and to Father Benedict, accompanied by the aforementioned Pope Innocent, arrived near the Golden City. Having received an oath of fidelity from Ptolemy, duke and consul of the Romans and dictator of the Tusculans, and received his son Reginald as a hostage, he confirmed by the ring which he wore on his hand [Col. 0969C], to Ptolemy and his heirs in perpetuity, all the land which belonged to him by hereditary right through his parents.

[Note: Compare Peter’s letter to Richiza, in Martène, *Collectio* I, p. 757.]

At that time the same emperor sent from Cassino, on 30 September, a letter to Abbot Guibald, as follows:

> “Lothair, by God’s grace august emperor of the Romans, to his most beloved faithful servant Guibald, superior of Cassino, chancellor of the Roman Empire, arch-chaplain, and prince of peace: his favor and good will.
>
> “By imperial letters we command your fidelity to take care to send to our majesty, preserved by God, Peter, deacon of Cassino, who has been appointed by our imperial serenity Italian logothete, secretary, keeper of records, and chaplain of the Roman Empire. For the service of your fidelity you shall receive the reward of fitting recompense [Col. 0970A].
>
> “For you must know without doubt that our majesty and the colleagues of the Empire are unwilling to endure his absence, on account of his knowledge of antiquities and accounts of historical deeds. Send also through him all the charters of our predecessors which we remember having formerly entrusted to him for safekeeping at Acquapendente. Given near the suburb of Tivoli, on the day before the Kalends of October.”

[Note: The same letter is written in Cassino manuscript 257, fol. 38, in a contemporary hand. Compare Pseudo-Anastasius in Muratori, *SS.* II, 365.]

[Note: “To his most beloved faithful servant” is absent from manuscript 257.]

[Note: “Arch-chancellor” there.]

[Note: “From the emperor” there.]

[Note: There: “logothete; secretary; keeper of records; auditor and cartulary officer,” etc.]

[Note: “You must know without doubt … unwilling” is absent there.]

[Note: “Pensyles” there.]

[Note: “Aput” there.]

But those carrying the imperial letters, when they came to Cassino, found Guibald prepared for the war which everywhere threatened. For Raynald, who had been expelled from the abbacy by the emperor and pope, once he learned for certain that the emperor had departed, gathered a troop of soldiers from among those who favored King Roger. He also assembled the leading men of the surrounding territory, related to him by blood, and, being received by the settlers who inhabited the castle of Saint Angelo, he gave all the neighboring country over to fire and sword [Col. 0970B].

But when Guibald reread the emperor’s letters, encouraged and strengthened by the matters which the emperor had sent through his envoys, on the fourth day he sent through his own soldiers a letter to the emperor.

[Note: Written by Peter and published in Martène, *Collectio amplissima* II, p. 183.]

It contained the disturbances and hardships suffered by him, the monastery, and the entire province at the hands of Roger and his people, and requested from him aid and protection.

126. When King Roger learned that Emperor Lothair had withdrawn from Campania, he gathered an army and began more easily to recover all the land which he had easily lost, apart from Bari, Troia, and Naples [Col. 0970C]. On the other hand, Duke Reginald, acting for the emperor, stoutly resisted him with Germans and Apulians.

Guibald, foreknowing what was to come, again sent a letter to that same emperor, who was then staying in Tuscany. Among other things it contained:

[Note: The entire letter, copied by Jean Mabillon from a Cassino manuscript, was published by Martène and Durand, *Collectio* II, p. 186.]

> “Placed amid various tribulations, I hoped day by day for the arrival of your aid; but, as I see, my hope has deceived me. For from the reports of those coming to us at Cassino from your most devout serenity, we learned that you had already drawn near Aquileia. Even the hearing of this has excessively grieved our heart, and has struck it with so great a dart of sorrow that human tongues cannot tell it.
>
> “As for your venerable words [Col. 0971A], which you sent us through your messengers concerning the oath of the Normans and Lombards: would that it might not be reckoned against them. For it would have been better for them not to swear than to swear and commit perjury. All who dwell in these regions have apostatized and turned to Satan, and say and do nothing except what the devil writes in their hearts.
>
> “How many calamities, tribulations, and persecutions I suffer from them, I had intended to make known to you through my most beloved son Peter; but because the length and obstacles of the journey prevented this, I shall set it forth briefly. After your departure, Saracens, Normans, and Lombards, finding the land at peace, go wherever they please, devastating and laying waste, destroying everything [Col. 0971B] with fire and murder. They spare not even fruit-bearing trees, lest perhaps those whom mountain caves, precipitous ground, or secluded places conceal should be nourished by such food.
>
> “Thus, raging with the same cruelty, they have left no one untouched by their contagion and no place free from their attacks. They rage especially wickedly in the possessions of the monastery of Cassino, and likewise in other churches, basilicas of saints, and monasteries: houses of prayer are burned in greater conflagrations than cities and all towns. What the holy man cries out to the Lord has now been fulfilled in the churches: ‘Where our fathers praised you, there has been a burning of fire’ (Isa. 64:11).
>
> “The hour has now come when all who plunder [Col. 0971C], burn, and devastate our land; bind peasants and monks in chains; burden them with fetters and manacles; kill, sell, torture, and persecute them—believe that they are rendering service to God. Wherever they find the doors of a venerable sanctuary shut, they compete in opening the entrances by blows of their right hands, so that it may rightly be said: ‘As in a forest of trees they cut down its doors with axes; with axe and hatchet alike they cast them down; they burned your sanctuary with fire and defiled on the ground the tabernacle of your name’ (Ps. 75:6).
>
> “How many bishops, priests, deacons, monks, noble and ignoble persons of different sex and age are now killed by them! How many are tortured so that they may surrender whatever gold or silver, personal or ecclesiastical, they possess! And when, pressed by pains [Col. 0971D], they more readily give what they have, their cruel tormentors again press them, supposing that they have given only some part, not the whole; and the more they give, the more they believe each person possesses.
>
> “Neither the weaker sex, nor regard for nobility, nor reverence for the priesthood, nor the distinction of monastic dress softens their most cruel minds. Indeed [Col. 0972A], their rage is heightened where they see the honor of rank. Mature old age and venerable grayness, whitening the hair of the head like white wool, claim no mercy from enemies. Barbarian fury even tears little children from their mothers’ breasts and dashes innocent infancy to the ground. What the Jews once sang has now been fulfilled: ‘The enemy said, “I shall burn my borders and dash my little children upon the earth”’ (Judith 16:6).
>
> “In the buildings of great churches, houses, and cities, where they cannot accomplish destruction by fire, the walls are leveled to the ground, so that now not even a trace remains of the former beauty of the buildings. If anyone disbelieves our words, the cities of Pozzuoli, Alife, and Telese bear witness [Col. 0972B], showing nothing but that they once existed. Many other cities too are inhabited by few or by no residents; and even those which survive today are continually being laid waste, as they did to the city of Capua, which once, after the city of Rome, was both the head and glory of all Campania.
>
> “After they had emptied it of people and despoiled it of gold and silver, lest the place should yield even for an hour to impiety, they burned it with fire. They reduced its ancient free and noble liberty to slavery; they led the chief men into captivity; and they carried off gold, silver, gems, clothing, and whatever precious or valuable thing they found.
>
> “Who could recount how great and what injuries they and their duke have inflicted upon the monastery of Cassino [Col. 0972C], both after and before your arrival? For this reason, unconquered Emperor, we entreat you to come to the aid of your afflicted, destitute, and desolated treasury, lest at some time Saracens, Normans, and Lombards say: ‘Where is their emperor?’”

[Note: “Our heart has been struck” in Martène.]

[Note: Martène reads “they lay waste”; the manuscript, “they ravage.”]

[Note: Martène reads “they plunder”; the manuscript, “they despoil.”]

[Note: Martène reads “some”; the manuscript, “how much.”]

[Note: Manuscript M reads *dealbat*, “whitens.”]

The bearer of the letter, having reached Liguria, did indeed deliver the document to the most merciful Emperor Lothair, but could obtain no beneficial aid. For that emperor, worn out alike by illness and old age, seeing that the end of his life was now at hand, had withdrawn to Chiusa in Liguria. There he made Duke Henry of Bavaria, his son-in-law, his heir in the duchy of Saxony, and entered the jewel-like palaces of heaven to reign with Christ without end (4 December 1137) [Col. 0972D]. His body was brought to Mainz and honorably buried.

[Note: This account appears to be narrated less accurately than the testimony cited by Jaffé, *loc. cit.*, p. 223.]

[Note: This is indeed asserted to be true there, p. 230.]

127. After this, the dukes, princes, margraves, and all the nobles of the Empire assembled together (7 March 1138) and made Conrad, duke of Swabia and nephew of Emperor Henry V, sole ruler in elder Rome. At the same time Henry of Bavaria [Col. 0973A], son-in-law of the aforesaid Emperor Lothair, died (20 October 1139).

But, to return to the point from which I digressed: when Abbot Raynald learned for certain that King Roger had crossed the Faro, he gathered an army of relatives and friends (1137), entered the city of Saint Germanus after its citizens had received him, and planned to ascend the mountain the next day, seize the monastery, and recover the abbacy. Landulf of San Giovanni, sent by Abbot Guibald from the monastery, came against him, gained control of the city, put Raynald and his men to flight, and set fire to the city. Having captured many and defeated more, he returned up to Guibald at the monastery.

King Roger, surrounded by the phalanx of his army, came above [Col. 0973B] the city of Capua. Giving it to the flames, he compelled it to submit to his authority. Guibald, having consulted with the brethren, sent envoys to Roger, then staying at Capua, seeking peace from him and promising friendship. Roger treated their words as nothing and dismissed his envoys without effect, declaring that he could endure on no terms and by no agreement that an abbot appointed by the emperor should remain in the monastery of Cassino. Indeed, if Guibald should in any way fall into his hands, he would without doubt put him to death by hanging.

Terrified by threats so great and such as these, Guibald left the monastery of Cassino in Landulf of San Giovanni’s charge. On the fourth day before the Nones of November, without the brethren’s knowledge, with Landulf guiding him [Col. 0973C], he departed by night, giving the brethren authority to elect whom they wished.

[Note: By a letter published from Peter’s Register after the Chronicle by Angelo de Nuce, and reprinted in Muratori, *SS.* IV, p. 622.]

128. Twelve days had now passed since Guibald’s departure when the brethren assembled, invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, and elected Raynald [Col. 0974D], a monk of the same monastery, a man indeed most honorable in bearing, gait, and morals, and distinguished in divine and human learning.

[Note: “Colementanus,” according to the Anonymous of Cassino.]

He traced the line of his blood from the most noble family of the counts of the Marsi, in the province of Valeria. In the third five-year period of his life, under Oderisius II, he was offered to blessed Benedict. He shone above all his contemporaries of his age with such knowledge of conduct, such honorableness, and such steadfastness that the Lord’s saying might rightly be applied to him: “I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:16) [Col. 0973D].

For nations and kingdoms conspired against him; indeed, so to speak, the whole world rose against him. But, clothed with the helmet of salvation and breastplate of faith, and fortified by the protection of Father Benedict, he regarded as nothing the snares of his adversaries and rivals.

At that same time, when King Roger had recovered cities and castles as far as the borders of the monastery of Cassino, and kept them subject to his own strongest and harshest rule, because the abbot would in no manner or agreement consent to what Roger wished [Col. 0974A], he began to threaten that he would destroy the cities, castles, and everything belonging to the monastery. He sent messengers and ordered this to be announced to the abbot, the brethren, and all the people.

But, as commonly happens in such circumstances, the common people first became frantic; then, when their frenzy turned to fear, they fled with all their possessions, including wives and children, to the monastery of Cassino. Shortly afterwards, the aforesaid king made an agreement with the people of Cassino and granted a truce, so that all who had fled through fear of him might return with their belongings to their own homes.

129. In those days there was a brother in the monastery of Cassino named Albert, a Pelignian by nation, old in years, living a religious life, so that he often gave the other brethren cause for admiration and compunction [Col. 0974B]. Worn out by age, he was staying in the infirmary. Hearing the noise of the people who wished to carry their goods home, he asked some bystanders what this confused uproar of the people meant.

One of them said to him: “Can it be unknown to you who or what is the cause of this uproar among the people, when it is clearly very well known to all who inhabit these districts?”

When Albert answered that he knew none of these things, the man said: “King Roger recently threatened us that he would destroy both the monastery of Cassino and all the neighboring land. But, appeased by the mercy of almighty God, he has granted us a truce. Hence comes the uproar which you hear: the goods which the people had brought weeping to the monastery of Cassino through fear of him [Col. 0974C] are now being carried home rejoicing.”

Upon hearing this, the often-mentioned brother groaned and, drawing long sighs from his inmost heart, began tearfully to chant this psalm: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1). When he began to sing the verse, “Send forth your light” (ibid., 3), suddenly—wonderful to tell—an immense radiance descended upon him, so that he, who for some time had been deprived of sight, recovered the light of his eyes and was not deprived of the gift of that immeasurable light.

Without delay, he saw the doors of the church in which he was sitting opened, and two men, venerable in face and dress, entering toward him. Seeing them surrounded by divine light, he was terrified and sat back down, daring no longer to lift his eyes. Then they came nearer and said:

> “Rise, Brother Albert. Go and tell the abbot and brethren to strive to do penance for the sins they have committed. Let them go out barefoot, chanting the antiphon of blessed Mary, and perform litanies before the most holy body of blessed Father Benedict, if perhaps God, forgetful of your sins because of your lamentation and penitence, may drive such calamities from these places.”

Then the brother asked who they were and by what names they were called. To this one replied: “I [Col. 0975A] am Maurus, disciple of the most holy Father Benedict; this man too is Placidus, a disciple of the same father.” He added:

> “Take care not through sloth to omit telling those whom you have been ordered to tell the things now heard or seen by you; otherwise you will incur the punishment of contempt and sloth. Know also that by divine and just judgment you were deprived of bodily sight because you concealed in the secret place of your heart, revealing to no one what you had seen, those things which divine majesty had once deigned to show you in the chapter-house for the purpose of doing penance.”

For while that same brother had still been living in the cloister with the other brethren under the strict rule of the monastic observance, and was offering himself before the sight of the Divinity through vigils, fasts, prayers, and blows of brooms, one night, when he had entered the chapter-house [Col. 0975B], he was caught up in spirit. In the apse of that chapter-house he saw the judicial seats arranged, with the Lord sitting in judgment together with his mother, as is still seen there in the painting.

[Note: That is, “up to this point.”]

The more completely he made himself a stranger to human concerns, the more freely he began to attend to divine things. While he stood amazed at this vision, he suddenly saw the most holy Father Benedict arrive in the midst of the council, having Maurus at his right and Placidus at his left. With loud cries he addressed the majesty of the Almighty in these complaints:

> “King of kings, creator and redeemer of mortals, without whose will human frailty cannot exist at all, hear the voice of my complaint and look upon my monastery, which by your gift I undertook to build and govern forever [Col. 0975C]. For you, Lord, who behold thoughts from afar and call into being things that are not as though they were, showed me, while I was still clothed in mortal flesh, that this place would be destroyed; by a hidden judgment you said that you would hand over to barbarian nations the things I had prepared for the brethren; and you promised that after a little while it would be restored for the better.
>
> “This is seen to have happened today. For certain most wicked and God-hating men have risen against this place, trying to destroy the aforesaid place. The rulers of this place too, following not the footsteps of a good shepherd but of a ravening wolf, tyrannically tear with biting teeth the sheep entrusted to them. They convert to most shameful uses the goods and wealth collected for your service and honor [Col. 0975D]. They allow the people entrusted to them to wander like wanton cows; despising the causes of orphans and widows, they turn themselves to gifts alone. What end, great King of heaven, do you grant?”

When he had said these things, the saint fell silent and rested, having made an end there. Then behold: an innumerable multitude of demons, armed with forks and fiery hooks, arrived, having before them Crescentius, count of the Marsi. He had in his nostrils, as though they issued from a furnace, the great silver censers which a certain man had received as a pledge from the monastery of Cassino and had taken back contrary to the will of Abbot Seniorectus [Col. 0976A].

When the brother asked him why he was afflicted with such torments, he replied that he was being tortured for retaining the larger censers. He began to beg the monk to tell his son Berard what he had seen concerning him, and to ask him on his behalf that the aforesaid censers be returned to the monastery of Cassino. He added that this should be a sign to them: while he lived, he had set aside those censers and also a golden chalice apart from the other property, and no one knew this except Fusco and Transmund, his advisers.

When the brother returned to himself, he hesitated to tell these things. Thereupon it came about by the just judgment of God that he was deprived of sight. Since he would not distribute to his fellow servants the eternal light which he had seen and the talent which he had received to dispense, but buried it in the earth like a slothful servant, he justly lost his own light and talent.

But to return to what we left: when he had heard the warnings of the holy man Maurus, and they departed, the light which had illumined his eyes departed with them, so that he remained blind as before [Col. 0976B]. Yet, lest he be thought mad or a liar, he would not tell what he had seen or heard.

When the thirtieth day after he had seen these things dawned, that same brother was sitting in the place where he had seen the aforesaid vision—namely, in the church of Saint Andrew the apostle. The same most holy Maurus who had appeared above appeared again, rebuked him for refusing to tell what he had seen or heard [Col. 0976C], and spoke these words:

> “Brother, I commanded you to reveal to men the secrets of God which were disclosed to you through me; but you gave yourself over to contempt and sloth. Therefore you were liable, as one guilty of an offense against majesty, to be handed over to unquenchable punishments. But because the mercy of almighty God, which is better than life, pardons this offense entrusted to you, I command you not to be slothful in telling what has been revealed to you by me. If, God forbid, you do not do so, you will be handed over to eternal fires.”

Having spoken these words, the saint suddenly vanished into the thin air.

[Note: Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.278; IX.658.]

The brother immediately rose, summoned the abbot to himself, and recounted in order everything he had seen and heard. The abbot convened the brethren and set forth in order what the aforesaid brother had seen [Col. 0976D]. They left the chapter-house where they had been sitting barefoot and performed litanies before the body of Father Benedict with tears and weeping.

But because certain brethren considered these things delusions and would give them no assent, one day the aforesaid monk Albert had me summoned to him; after telling me the matter as he had seen it, he confirmed it by oath in my presence. Therefore I urge no one in any way to doubt this, lest they receive the punishment of their unbelief [Col. 0977A], so that, when they accuse me of false speech, they may be judged false witnesses and liars before the strict tribunal of Jesus Christ.

130. At that time Peter, son of Peter Leo, was removed from human affairs and died (25 January 1138). His supporters appointed Cardinal Gregory of the title of the Apostles in his place and decreed that he should be called Victor (March) [Col. 0978A].

Innocent, having lavishly expended immense money upon the sons of Peter Leo and those attached to them, drew them to his side. Thus the cardinals who had shared the communion of the aforesaid son of Peter Leo, deprived of all assistance, threw themselves at Innocent’s feet (May), after first receiving an oath from him that he would neither deprive them of office nor diminish their possessions—but only for a time.

[Note: Here the manuscript ends in the middle of a column. Yet, since while this was being printed I received through our Bethmann a more accurate description of the Cassino codices, it may be permitted to append it here.—Manuscript 450: parchment, folio, thirteenth century, elegantly written in two columns; the initial letters are very beautifully painted with a pen, but only through II.42. After the table of chapters follows the version published by L. Tosti. In the chapter lists certain items were supplied by a later hand; we have noted them there. Chapter IV.16 and what follows were written by another but contemporary hand, on four inserted leaves containing from “Saint Dionysius” through chapter 25, “4 December.” The same hand also wrote the final quire, chapters 96–130, and ends in the middle of the page. The principal hand wrote everything else, and also added the annals at the end. Nothing whatever was added or altered. Certain extraneous writings concerning revenues and monastic ritual were inscribed on blank leaves; on the last, in a thirteenth-century hand, is a letter of Abbot Roffrid, published by A. de Nuce in the *Life of Saint Benedict*, chapter 18.—The other manuscript, 202, folio, was written continuously in a twelfth-century hand; the lower portion of the last leaf was cut away, but parchment was sewn on. See p. 725, note n.]

## Appendix to the Chronicle of Leo and Peter: Chronicle of an Anonymous Author of Cassino

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. III, p. 222.)

[Col. 0977]

For the first time it is now published complete from manuscript no. 353 of the Cassino archive, on parchment, from the beginning of the tenth century, presented to the monastery’s founder, Abbot John I. It had previously been transcribed in mutilated form by Peregrini, p. 97, under the name “Short History of an Unknown Cassinese,” and included in Muratori’s *Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 264, and in Pratilli, vol. I, p. 179 ff.

The author, a monk of Cassino under Abbots Bassacius and Bertharius [Col. 0977B], committed to writing many things which he had experienced in person. His style was indeed unpolished and he was not very skilled in writing, but we owe him a considerable number of matters eminently worthy of knowledge. He seems to have begun his work while the city of Bari had not yet been recovered by Emperor Louis II, and, having begun with the division of the duchy of Benevento, he carried it down to the year 867. For this reason I consider him different from John of Cassino, abbot from 915 to 934, although Leo of Ostia in the preface to his *History*, and Peter the Deacon in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 15, when praising the chronicles of Abbot John—the first who built our monastery in new Capua—and the chronicle of Abbot John concerning the persecutions of this monastery and miracles done here, understood our manuscript.

[Note: Chapter 19, especially.]

[Note: Chapter 7.]

Peregrini had already observed that Leo used this book in composing his history. Yet it will become clear only when our edition is published that Leo followed the true reading of the manuscript extremely closely.

[Note: Namely, chapters 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 18, 19, 20, 22, 26, 27, 28, 30, and 33, for the most part verbatim, were inserted into Leo’s chapters I.25–29, 31, 33, 35, 36, and 38.]

We have judged it right to retain the division into chapters established by Peregrini, although chapters 3, 4, 11, 12, 15, 19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 32, and 33 are in no way marked off in the manuscript.

[Col. 0977B]

1. Certain of our brethren, wishing to know how many years had elapsed from the time of our most holy Father Benedict until now, moved by the same desire, have collected, as far as we could, an approximate calculation.

From the year 520 of the Lord’s incarnation, under Emperor Justinian, there are one hundred and eighty-one years from the days of that same most blessed Benedict to Abbot Petronax. And from Abbot Petronax to the present year (701) [Col. 0978B] of Lord Abbot Bertharius, who, God being his ruler, is the thirteenth shepherd in the monastery, about … years are counted; this is the year … of the Lord’s incarnation (867?).

[Note: Thus the manuscript; Peregrini read this as “the present year.”]

[Note: A blank space occurs.]

[Note: A blank space occurs.]

2. Something brief should also be remembered concerning the people of the Lombards and how they hastened into Italy. Narses the patrician, on account of the Gothic people which had invaded Italy, chose the Lombards as allies; together with his Greeks and Romans, he drove the Goths from those territories—that is, from Roman boundaries.

[Note: That is, “on account of the Gothic people.”]

Narses, residing at Naples, sent envoys to the Lombard people, instructing them to leave the poor fields of Pannonia and come to possess all Italy, overflowing with riches. At the same time he sent many kinds of fruits and other products in which Italy abounds, so that he might entice their minds to come.

The Lombards gladly accepted the joyful message, as being what they themselves especially desired, and raised their spirits in anticipation of future advantages. Then they entrusted their own homeland, namely Pannonia, to their friends the Huns, on the understanding that if the Lombards should ever need to return, they would reclaim their fields. Therefore the Lombards, leaving Pannonia with wives, all their children, and household goods, hastened to take possession of Italy.

They had lived in Pannonia for forty-two years [Col. 0979B]. They left it in April, in the first indiction (2 April 568), on the day after holy Easter, whose feast that year, according to the calculation, fell on the Kalends of April, when five hundred and sixty-eight years had elapsed from the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: “First indiction—calculation” is written in the margin in the same hand; it is by no means, as Peregrini supposes, a later addition attributed to John, abbot of Cassino and author of the chronicle of the counts of Capua.]

3. Afterwards, ruling Italy, they hastened to Benevento and entered it to dwell there.

[Note: Written in the margin.]

Their leader was Michael the archangel of the heavenly host. The Neapolitans were brought to faith in Christ. Alzeco the Bulgar was received with his people to settle there. Overcoming the peoples of the Greeks and Romans, the Lombards together occupied the whole territory of Benevento.

4. “Every kingdom,” as the Lord says, “divided against itself shall be desolated; and whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap.” Therefore the people of Israel, divided, were scattered throughout the world; and likewise this Lombard people, divided in mind [Col. 0979C], killed even their own princes.

Consequently the country was divided (839); the principality of Benevento was thus divided into two parts. The Franks and Saracens were respectively called in by one party against the other. Finally Saracen treachery captured Bari by night (842); afterwards they entered Taranto under siege, and subsequently devastated, destroyed, and reduced to the ground almost the whole kingdom with fire and sword, for nearly thirty years.

5. But when the Lombards suffered excessive dangers for their own deeds (866), greatly afflicted and compelled by necessity, they sent envoys to Francia and implored the merciful favor of the glorious Emperor Louis Augustus, that he might come with his people into their country and deliver them altogether and as swiftly as possible from the Saracens. When he came, he left this decree for his country:

6. “Ordinance concerning the raising of the army for the defence of the territories of Benevento, in the fifteenth indiction. Whoever has sufficient movable property to possess his full wergild shall proceed on campaign. But whoever has half a wergild shall join with another, the two equipping one contingent, so that they may be able to go properly equipped. Poor persons, however, shall proceed to guard the coast or the country; that is, those who possess more than ten solidi in movable property shall go to that guard-duty. But from him who possesses no more than ten solidi in movable property nothing shall be required.

“If a father has one son, and that son is more capable than his father, let him go equipped by his father. For if the father is more capable, let him go himself. If he has two sons, whichever of them is more capable shall go, while the other remains with his father. But if he has several sons, let all the more capable ones go; only one, the least capable, shall remain. Concerning undivided brothers, in accordance with the capitulary of our lord and father, we decree that, if there are two, both shall go. If there are three, the one who appears least capable shall remain, and the others shall go. If there are more, and all appear more capable, they shall go, while one less capable man remains.

“Under this condition we decree that neither by command, nor by advocacy, nor by any pretext whatsoever shall either a count or a gastald, or their officials, be excused or have anyone excused; except that in each county the count may leave one man to guard that place, and two men with his wife. Bishops, therefore, shall leave behind no layman. For whoever presumes to remain contrary to this ordinance, we have commanded that his property be immediately taken by the missi for our use, according to what we have ordered below, and that he be expelled abroad.

“[Note: Col. 0979: Read: “according to what we have ordered below.”]  

“We wish all to know that possessions have already been taken under this ordinance from our predecessors, but their holders deserved to recover them through mercy. Now, however, know most certainly that whoever has his property taken will scarcely obtain its restoration from us.

“From the river Po to the Trebbia, let Iotselmus be missus. Between the Po and the Ticino, Eriulfus; between the Ticino and the Adda, Erembertus; between the Adda and the Adige, Landebertus; from the Adige to Forum Julii, Teodoldus. Bishops Peter and Arthemius, joined by missi of bishops and counts: in Pisa, Lucca, Pistoia, and Luni, Teutmundus; in Florence, Volterra, and Arezzo, Rodselmus; in Chiusi and Siena, Andreas. In Wito’s district, Rimmo and John, bishop of Forcona. In Verengar’s district, Bishop Hiselmundus. Along the Italian coast, Ermefridus, Macedo, and Vulfericus.

“We decree that these men shall summon forth the people, provide for the guard, and cause the people to reside in fortified places, and indeed to do so peacefully. For if any missus dares to neglect ensuring that all the men remain—

[Note: Col. 0979: emended by the editor from *nominibus* to *omnibus*, ‘all’; Col. 0979D: i.e. *homines*, ‘men.’]

—let them immediately take his property and expel him abroad. And if the missus himself is found at fault, let him lose his own property. And if a count leaves exempted anyone, or his own vassal, beyond what we have stated above, let him lose his office. Likewise, if their officials leave anyone behind, let them lose both their property and their office. But if a count or one of our vassals remains because he is detained by some illness, or retains anyone as exempted, or if abbots or abbesses do not send forth all their men in full measure, let them themselves lose their offices, and let their vassals lose both property and benefice. As for bishops, any vassal of theirs who remains behind shall lose both property and benefice. Likewise, if a bishop remains behind without manifest illness, he shall make amends for such negligence by residing in that march until the army next proceeds there.

“And, that you may know most certainly that we wish to carry out this expedition fully, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it—

[Note: Col. 0979: The manuscript has the clauses in another order: ‘Insofar as He has deigned to grant it … and that you may know most certainly that we wish to carry out this expedition fully.’ The editor judged the sentences should be transposed.]

—we ordain that, should a bishop, a count, or one of our vassals be detained by an uncertain illness, the bishop through the best missus he has, but the count and our vassals in person, shall affirm on oath that they did not remain for any reason except that, because of a most certain illness, they were unable to do this.

“We wish all to bring with them every item of military equipment, so that, when we inspect and cause it to be enrolled—

[Note: Col. 0981: the manuscript reads *propspexerimus*, for *prospexerimus*, ‘we shall inspect.’]

—they may not appear negligent, but may deserve also to enjoy our favor. Let them have clothing for one year, and provisions until that country can have its new harvest. Whoever, in going or returning, causes a disturbance over feuds (*faidae*) shall incur danger of his life.

[Note: Col. 0981D: *fagidis*, i.e. *faidis*, ‘feuds.’]

“And because the fitting season of Lent is also at hand, in which the commandments of God must be observed, we decree that whoever violates the church of God, commits adultery, or commits arson, shall incur danger of his life. Whoever dares to take a horse, ox, *friskinga*, clothing, weapons, or other movable property shall make threefold compensation according to the law, and, as a free man, be sent before us by his lords with an *armiscara*, that is, a saddle upon his back, and shall endure this until our mercy is granted.

[Note: Col. 0981: the manuscript reads *lege liber cum a…*, apparently corrupt; the sense is ‘according to the law, [as] a free man, with an armiscara.’]

“Slaves, however, shall be flogged and beaten, and their masters shall restore what they have taken. But if a complaint comes to their lords and these do not correct such acts, then their lords shall make that compensation and be compelled to bear the same *armiscara* for as long as pleases us.

“And we decree this so that justice may be maintained on both sides: namely, our people, like their neighbors, shall buy what is necessary at a fair price; and neighbors shall in no way presume to sell more dearly than to their own neighbors. Whoever commits homicide indiscriminately and presumptuously shall incur danger of his life.

“For our route will be through Ravenna, thence in the middle of March to Pescara, with the entire Italian army accompanying us. But the Tuscans, together with the people who come from beyond, shall come through Rome to Ponte Curvo, then to Capua, and descend through Benevento to meet us at Lucera on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March].”

7. After these preliminary matters had thus been set forth and this law established, the aforesaid lord Emperor Louis Augustus, hastening with his equally glorious wife, the Empress Angelberga, to Benevento, came in the month of June to the monastery of the most holy father Benedict. There he was honorably received by the venerable Abbot Bertharius with the sacerdotal office, lamps and incense, and the praises of the brethren.

Ascending the mountain where the sacred body of the aforesaid blessed and pious father Benedict lies buried, he was received there with equal splendor; after making some offering there to Saint Benedict, and viewing the whole monastery, he descended in worthy admiration. There, frustrating the cunning of the Capuans, after a few days he besieged—

[Note: Col. 0981D: *possidens*, i.e. *obsidens*, ‘besieging.’]

—and gained Capua. He entered Salerno, sailed to Amalfi, used the baths at Puteoli, and by way of Naples reached the city of Sessula; then he encamped at Caudium. In December, aided by the grace of almighty God, he entered Benevento, in the seventeenth year of his imperial rule.

And behold, he engaged with the Saracens in battle (867), first gained from them the trophy of victory, and finally captured all their camps; only their cities remained, namely Bari and Taranto.

[Note: Col. 0981D: “These things, accordingly, were written before February 871.”]

For the glory of them all, the very strongly fortified city of Matera, was captured and reduced to nothing by fire and sword; but in August he returned to Benevento. While Abbot Bertharius was there in his service—for at the church of Holy Sophia an oratory had been begun by his predecessor, the most reverend Bassacius, and Bertharius completed it with every effort and built it in honor of Saint Benedict—it was dedicated by Stephen, bishop of the see of Teano, and the work was completed through the efforts of the deacon Angelarius.

8. If perhaps you wish to know, reader-to-be, why the Saracens came to dominate the region of the Beneventans, the occasion was as follows. Sichard, prince of the Beneventans, having been killed by his own men (839), Radelchis, *zetarius*—

[Note: Col. 0982D: keeper of the inner bedchamber of the palace, a chamberlain.]

—of the palace succeeded him in the principate. At that time Siconolf, a mighty warrior, son of Sico the great prince of blessed memory, was staying at Taranto.

Meanwhile, in those times the Capuans committed very many crimes: they even killed their own elders and parents, plundered all their possessions, and made themselves a lofty spectacle to the world. For this reason they feared to go to Benevento and obey the commands of their prince Radelchis. For they devised new engines of treachery—

[Note: Col. 0981: *chinis* appears to have been written in a later hand.]

—and went over to Siconolf at Taranto, the son of the aforesaid prince. Together with others who were their associates and equally like them in wickedness, they set up Siconolf as their prince. Not long afterwards he entered Salerno, and a great part of the Beneventan territory followed him.

Against him the anger of Prince Radelchis blazed, and he strove to drive him from the land. As they fought one another over a long period, no page can bear the record of how many evils they mutually inflicted, no teacher’s mind can expound them, nor has any writer the capacity fully to set them down. For at that time (841) the said Prince Radelchis, through Pando, gastald of Bari, invited transmarine Saracens to his aid—

[Note: Col. 0981: *invitabit*, i.e. *invitavit*, ‘invited.’]

—who, having long remained near Bari, seized the named city at the untimely hour of night, according to their custom. This city, in Greek usage called Βαρην (*Barēn*), receives the meaning “heavy” or “strong” in the sense of “arms”; and it long before acquired this name, so that, because of sinners’ crimes, the heavy or strong devastation of the Saracens might rage so excessively against us.

The first of these wicked arrivals was called King Kalfon. Their garments and footwear were scanty; they were not even properly girded with a belt—

[Note: Col. 0982D: Perhaps *fascia*, “a band” or “girdle”?]

—but carried only reeds in their hands. With them Radelchis devastated the whole territory of Siconolf and reduced all of old, principal Capua to ashes.

[Note: Col. 0982D: *primariam*, i.e. the old city.]

From then on everything alike collapsed from bad to worse. At this time a battle was fought between the two sides at Cannae.

9. [Note: Col. 0981, in the margin: “How the Saracens plundered the church of the blessed Apostle Peter and burned with fire the cells of Saint Benedict.”]

In these days the Saracens went out against Rome (August 846) and devastated the whole oratory of the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, and the church of blessed Paul. They killed many Saxons there, and very many others of both sexes and every age. Having captured the city of Fondi and plundered the neighboring places, they encamped near Gaeta in the month of September.

A Frankish army came against them, but, defeated by the Saracens on the fourth Ides of November [10 November], took flight. The Saracens pursued them, seized all that was theirs, and finally came to Saint Andrew, whose cell they burned with fire. When they reached the cell of the most blessed Bishop Apollinaris, called Albianum—

[Note: Col. 0982D: Bishop of Ravenna.]

—they saw nearby the mountain of the most blessed confessor of Christ; they hastened at once to proceed there, but the lateness of the hour prevented their crossing.

There was then such serenity of sky and dryness of ground that anyone who wished could cross the river on foot. But the monks of the most blessed Father Benedict, seeing death so near at hand, immediately exchanged the kiss of peace and begged the merciful Lord graciously to receive in peace the souls which they expected at once to pass swiftly into death. Straightway all, barefoot and with ashes sprinkled upon their heads, betook themselves with litanies to their patron, blessed Benedict.

While their fear was intense, their expectation dreadful, and their prayer to almighty God abundant, Bassacius saw in a vision his predecessor, Abbot Apollinaris, who said: “What is the matter with you? Why do you endure sorrow?” Bassacius replied: “Death hangs over us, father; should we not fear?” He said: “Do not fear. The pious father Benedict has obtained your safety.
