Therefore pray diligently to the Lord with litanies and the solemnities of Mass. May the Lord swiftly hear the voices of those crying to him. For we too, standing with you in the churches, do not cease together with the citizens of heaven to beseech the Lord Jesus Christ for you.”

When the shepherd Bassacius awoke from sleep and told this to the brethren, they all together blessed God in a loud voice, who mercifully saves those who hope in him. Then suddenly there came an immense rainfall, lightning flashes, and thunder so violent that the River Carnello—

[Note: Col. 0983C: The same river as the Liris and Garigliano. Pratilli.]

—overflowed its bounds; and the river which on the previous day the enemy could cross on foot, on the following day, repelled by divine restraint, they could not even reach at its bank.

They tried by every means to cross the river, but since they found no passage across to the monastery, they, in their dreadful barbarity, gnawed their fingers, ground or gnashed their teeth, and ran ragingly here and there. Nor did their customary crime fail them: they burned with fire the cells of the most blessed martyrs Stephen and George, and returned to their camps by way of the Two Leos.

[Note: Col. 0983C: A boundary of Cassinese territory, according to Leo of Ostia I.5.]

After a few days they invigorated their horses and began to sail. When they were near their own province—

[Note: Col. 0983: *proprius*, i.e. *propius*, “nearer.”]

—so that they could already see the neighboring mountains, they gave praise in their custom with sailors’ applause. Immediately there appeared among them a little boat carrying two men, one with the appearance of a cleric, the other dressed like a monk. These said to them: “Where do you come from, and where are you going?” They answered: “We return from Peter. We have devastated the whole oratory of Rome, plundered its people together with its territory, defeated the Franks, and burned Benedict’s cells with fire. And who are you?” The others said: “Who we are, you shall now see.”

Immediately a violent storm and a fierce tempest arose. All the ships were wrecked and all the enemy perished; not one at all remained to report such things to the others. Thereafter the venerable Pope Leo enclosed the oratory of blessed Peter with very strong and lofty walls, lest such an event should ever again occur at Rome.

10. At the same time (844), Prince Siconolf took a very great quantity of treasure from the monastery of the most blessed Benedict to pay tribute to the Spaniards—

[Note: Col. 0983C: “Spaniards,” i.e. Saracens; compare Prudentius, *Annals* for 844, *SS* I, 440. Col. 0983, in the margin: “The treasure of Saint Benedict which Siconolf took away.”]

—namely, on the first occasion, one silver basin—

[Note: Col. 0983C: apparently our “basin,” English *basin*.]

—one pair of *vaucae*—

[Note: Col. 0983C: i.e. *bauca*, a vessel.]

—one pair of gem-set and emerald *sporae*—

[Note: Col. 0983C: i.e. *sporones*, our “spurs.”]

—and a silk *surica* of *silfori*, with gold and gems.

[Note: Col. 0983C: A silk cloth. Adelung thinks the word is derived from Greek σιλφη, *silphē*, “cockroach.”]

On another occasion he took one hundred and thirty pounds of gold in vessels. On the third occasion, three hundred and sixty-five pounds of silver and thirteen thousand gold solidi bearing figures. On the fourth occasion, two *vatiae* weighing thirty pounds—

[Note: Col. 0984C: i.e. *batia*, *bazia*.]

—and seven double *fundati*.

[Note: Col. 0984C: A vessel of gold or silver.]

On the fifth occasion he likewise took fourteen thousand *matiati* and *praedolati* solidi.

[Note: Col. 0984C: Perhaps *purgatos*? Leo I.26 has *mazatos*.]

After these, he took one *batia* in *agrifis*—

[Note: Col. 0984C: Perhaps *anagrifis*, *anaglyphis*, as Leo reads.]

—and one *scapto*, a vessel fashioned in gilded Constantinopolitan workmanship.

[Note: Col. 0984C: It seems to be some sort of vessel.]

Then, on the ensuing sixth occasion, through Count Lando and the gastald Aldemarius, the same Siconolf violently took from the monastery two thousand *praedolati* solidi and the crown of the prince, his father Sico, adorned with gold and emeralds. Yet this did him no good, but destroyed his soul. Nor did it profit him, or indeed his country, that he strove to deceive the monks by promises; from that point he never again gained any triumph of victory.

11. In these days a most accursed battle was fought between the two princes at Cancellos.

[Note: Col. 0984C: Near the Caudine Forks.]

12. After some time had passed, Massar, a duke residing at Benevento in aid of Prince Radelchis, devastated the monastery of Mary, the most blessed Mother of God, at Cingla, and afterwards captured the castle of the saint called Vitus.

[Note: Col. 0984C: Near Isernia. Pratilli.]

Holding the castle of Telesia—

[Note: Col. 0983: the manuscript reads *telesimum*, perhaps for *Telesinum*.]

—he humbled Siti and devastated all Apulia, as well as the other places. At one point he came near the monastery of blessed Benedict; there his mind was so changed by divine action that, when one of his dogs wished to seize a goose in the meadows, he himself ran up with a whip and drove the bird from its captor’s mouth. As he stood before the monastery gates, he immediately ordered the gates shut, lest the following *magaritae* should dare to enter.

[Note: Col. 0984C: i.e. apostates, unbelievers, Saracens.]

After this he passed through Aquino and plundered Arce and the neighboring places. In November, after eight days, he returned to Benevento.

13. When Siconolf died at Salerno (849), his son Sico succeeded him in the principate only nominally. A little later, while still a boy, he was carried off into Francia.

14. In June 848 there was a great earthquake throughout the entire Beneventan region—

[Note: Col. 0985D: Compare the *Life of Leo IV*, ch. 12, where the earthquake is assigned to the tenth indiction. Leo of Ostia writes the year 847.]

—so that it utterly overwhelmed the city of Isernia and killed many people; finally it also killed the bishop of that city. There was a like collapse of buildings at Saint Vincent’s—

[Note: Col. 0985D: At the Volturno.]

—and the earthquake was equally violent at the monastery of blessed Benedict, yet not even one stone fell from its place. When this was reported to Massar, who had plundered ruined Isernia, he said: “The Lord of all is angry with that place; and shall I rage there any further? Certainly I shall not go!”

15. New Telesia is built near the old city, on the plain bearing its own name.

16. Meanwhile, as was briefly stated above, among the Capuans the sons of the gastald Landolf were prominent: Count Lando, Bishop Landolf, Pando the *marepahis*, and Pandinolf the gastald. But because of the crimes of its inhabitants, their city was frequently consumed by fire. Seeking neither the remedy of repentance, nor divine mercy, nor amendment of their crimes, they finally devised a certain plan and built a city at the bridge of Casolino, which in boastful sport they called “a second Rome.”

For as one who flees from the face of a lion falls upon a bear, so that city, moved away from the fire, collapsed in the same retribution into the abyss. The following poem tells the glory in which it was expected to rise:

> The city which first had long withered in the decay of age  
> Is seen—behold!—rising with ample walls.  
> Supported by throngs of senators, that city was powerful;  
> But this one too is called Capua, the second by name.  
> Count Lando, provident in all things for the aid  
> Of country and people, founded this city by diligent endeavor.  
>
> It is called the Golden Gate, because it bears the splendor of light.  
> May arms, salvation, enduring strength, and Christ remain  
> In this city for all time with its people;  
> May he drive hence the cruel enemy and malignant deceit,  
> And grant its citizens to enjoy the honor of peace!

17. At this time Taranto, besieged by famine, was captured by the Saracens (856).

18. At the same time Abbot Bassacius, at the request of the leading men of the country, went to Francia and besought the glorious Emperor Louis. He came to Bari and, insofar as was possible, fought against the Saracens with all his strength (848). After several days he came to Benevento. Therefore, on Saturday, the vigil of holy Pentecost, the Saracens were killed within the city of Benevento; while Radelchis held the principate, Massar was captured, brought before the emperor, and beheaded. Louis then returned to his homeland.

19. In these times Abbot Bassacius died (856), having completed nineteen years in rule. We who write saw the nature and extent of his zeal in churches above and below, and poems composed by him resound for us. Bertharius the priest, his disciple, succeeded him in office, energetic in conduct and life and conspicuous in every goodness. He enclosed and fortified the upper castle; he made a chalice for the service in honor of God; he wished that the lower city—

[Note: Col. 0986D: i.e. the city of Saint Germanus.]

—should be made, and began it. Our own age has fully learned how he fought with all his strength against the Saracens at Gaeta. The imperial charters made for the monastery show how he loved those entrusted to him and how greatly he strove on their behalf.

20. At that time Ademarius was prince at Salerno (854–860). Lupoald, bishop of the church of Teano, died. Hilary, a deacon and monk of Saint Benedict, was chosen to episcopal dignity.

21. Aloara of blessed memory, wife of Count Lando, was, through Suranus the physician and his intervention, so great a benefactress of the monks that throughout the whole month of May she provided stipends and fed the brethren.

22. Lambert, son of Wido, and Count Ildepert attempted to raise their hands against Emperor Louis. But when their treachery was reported, Louis pursued them as far as the Marsi. At last they fled before him to Benevento, to Prince Adelchis. Hildepert, however, passed on to Bari, where he was most willingly received by King Seodan and lived for as long as he wished.

Emperor Louis pursued them and came to Isernia; finding it disloyal to him, he took it by force of arms. Then he passed through Alife, and after many battles the city was captured. He came through Telesia to the city called Saint Agatha and began to assault it. Because it was very strongly fortified, he besieged it for many days; it was then the summer season. “No one ever,” as the apostle says, “hates his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Ephesians 5).

At last Abbot Bertharius took pity on Hisembard, his kinsman and gastald of the besieged city, and interceded for him with the Emperor Augustus. He obtained the emperor’s favor, and the emperor made an agreement with the city; immediately the city was subjected to the emperor’s jurisdiction. Prince Adelchis, prostrate at the feet of the most merciful emperor, obtained pardon both for himself and for the fugitive counts. Thereupon Louis returned to Francia. At this time the cleric Magenolf married Inga, niece of the empress.

23. Ademarius, allied with the Neapolitans, attempted some treacherous action against his own people. For this reason his eyes were torn out, he was deprived of the principate, and Waifer became prince of Salerno (860). The aforesaid Ademarius gave Sora, Arpino, Vico Albano, and Atina to the Franks, that is, to Count Wido. Landolf the gastald ruled in these places; when he lost them, he died of excessive grief.

24. Through the assistance of Count Lando and almost-priest [reading uncertain], a monastery is built at Teano for women servants of God.

25. When Count Lando died at Capua, his brother Pando succeeded him in the countship. Joined with Bishop Landolf, he drove the venerable Aloara, his kinswoman, from Capua. She went into exile with her children and her own possessions to live at Salerno.

At the same time the Neapolitans boldly attempted to come against the Capuans in war, on the day of the feast of blessed Michael. The Langobards, relying on his aid, marched out against the Quirites—

[Note: Col. 0986D: i.e. Romans.]

—and wreaked such slaughter among them that very many were killed by the sword, many were captured, and some threw themselves into the river; the few survivors returned wounded to their city. Caesarius, son of the *magister militum*, was captured, brought to Capua, and kept in iron fetters. This was the Neapolitans’ second disaster, like that which they had formerly attempted at Gargano against the blessed Archangel Michael. Hearing of what had happened to both sides, Seodan mocked it, saying: “Tow joined with felt have made war.”

26. At that time Rodoald, gastald of the village of Aquino, built a castle near Ponte Curvo.

[Note: Col. 0987D: Pontecorvo.]

When this had been done, he withdrew from the jurisdiction of the Capuans, and on account of this was violently harassed by them. In these days Magenolf, of whom we said a little above, was going to Francia in order to ask the glorious emperor for a place where he might live and dwell. Rodoald sent him a certain priest, Ursus, as envoy, asking him to return and dwell there with him, and to aid him with his protection against his persecutors.

Magenolf therefore turned back from his journey and entered Ponte Curvo. Not long afterwards he went to Salerno, took his wife, and returned with all his household goods and family to the castle. The mystery of iniquity did not remain hidden for long: one day, with his men, he seized Rodoald and confined him in custody; he also cast Rodoald’s two sons into a tower and took away all his possessions—treasure, livestock, dependants, slaves, people, castle, village—and subjected everything to himself.

He taught the rustic and undisciplined people whom he found to be very prudent in the manner of the palace; those who previously knew nothing except onions and garlic were now required to pay principal solidi in tribute, and they even marched armed in the army on campaign. When Rodoald had been offered to Saint Benedict, he was scarcely released through the venerable Abbot Bertharius and the monks, as Aesop, the teacher of fables, says: “Let him suffer this who has brought a stronger man into his own house!”

27. While the walls of the city of Eulogimenopolis were being built—

[Note: Col. 0987D: Eulogimenopolis, that is, “city of Benedict,” according to Leo I.33; see above, ch. 19.]

—a certain man was there with his companions to build the city. Because of a severe affliction, he had once lost the use of his tongue and for about seven years had been entirely unable to utter any speech. One night, exhausted by manual labor, while the brethren were performing God’s praises in the oratory of the most blessed Benedict, this mute man, sitting with others at the foot of a column, fell asleep. Blessed Benedict appeared to him in a vision, struck his head with a staff, rebuked him, and said: “Have you hurried here to sleep? Wake up, then, and spit upon the ground three times!” When he had done this, he rose from sleep and began to tell everyone of the benefit bestowed upon him; he spoke so perfectly that he did no less than he had been accustomed to do seven years earlier. And all together gave praise to God.

28. Meanwhile the sword of the Lord’s indignation ran here and there and raged upon the necks of sinners; having gone forth from its sheath, it devastated all the surrounding lands. That most impious and cruel robber—“may the Lord strike him with the sword of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming!” (2 Thessalonians 2)—that pestilent Seodan, once setting out from Bari, devastated all Capua, Cantiæ, and Lepore, and set up his most wicked throne in the plain near Naples. No day at all passed in which he did not kill five hundred persons or more; and he said that this was God’s part, so that the Gospel saying might be fulfilled: “Everyone who kills you thinks that he is offering service to God” (John 16).

For that slavish tyrant sat upon the corpses of the dead and ate like a foul dog. At last, as if waking from a heavy sleep, yet burdened and impeded by extreme miseries, Wandelpert, the gastald Maielpotus, and Count Garard—

[Note: Col. 0988D: Count of the Marsi; Leo I.35. Compare below, Erchempert, ch. 29.]

—with many other nobles hurried to Benevento to take common counsel for vengeance upon the Saracens. Their counsel was salutary, but its execution useless. They did not march in one column or with one and the same purpose through the cohorts; divided from one another, they advanced in disorder.

They approached the Saracens near Ariano. Seeing them, the Saracens immediately lay down on the ground, and the sun was already setting. But the men who had come from Benevento, weary as they were, exceedingly fatigued and very thirsty, entered battle at once. Immediately the Saracens sprang up suddenly; massed in a single column, they rushed upon them. The others turned their backs and began to flee. Very many were killed by swords; some fell, collided with each other, and were suffocated; others, unharmed by swords but dead from thirst, were found in ditches, hedges, and cavities of the ground. The Saracens, now victorious, completed the journey they had begun.

29. Between Capua, Teano, and Alife there is said to be a mountain in which an angelic power is present, after the likeness of the blessed Archangel Michael on Mount Gargano. Water is said to drip there, a crypt to be continually hollowed out, and a basilica to stand open; divine miracles are frequently performed there. At the exhortation of Bishop Landolf, Hilary, bishop of the church of Teano, dedicated altars there to the saints, and from that time signs and miracles of many healings have occurred in abundance, to the glory and praise of the name of Jesus Christ.

30. It is the custom among the monks of the two monasteries, namely of Saint Vincent the martyr and of blessed Benedict the confessor, during the days of holy Lent to offer one another a banquet for the sake of charity. One day, while the brethren at Saint Vincent were performing this spiritual observance and brethren from Saint Benedict were present for that purpose, on Friday Seodan, king of the Saracens, came suddenly upon them with his followers, as swiftly as a flying bird. The monks, though naked, nevertheless escaped unharmed to their castle.

Present was the mercy of him who says to his faithful: “My Father works until now, and I work; I say, I am with you all days; and [the text is corrupt:] no one can snatch from the hand of my Father out of my possessions—

[Note: Col. 0987: the manuscript reads *nepo*, apparently corrupt for *nemo*, ‘no one.’]

—for where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst.” Nor did the Lord grant less in this case than he had formerly granted to his faithful Benedict: though their goods were handed over to the nations, he nevertheless preserved their souls.

The Saracens demolished the whole monastery, breaking everything and throwing the grain and legumes into the river. As they dug here and there, they found a great quantity of hidden treasure: crowns, sacred vessels, and all the ecclesiastical splendor that could be found. The most wicked King Seodan drank from sacred chalices and ordered incense to be offered to him from golden censers.

On the third day he hastened with his servants at speed to the gates of Capua, taking laden wagons, animals, and very many people captive; and, returning that same day, he pitched camp near Teano. But the monks of the most blessed Benedict, fearing both his nearby arrival and danger to their own people, through the deacon Ragenald first offered him a payment under an agreement, so that they might be able to soften his ferocity.

31. Pando, gastald of the Capuans, went out to battle against Prince Waifer with his men; he himself fell first, and then those who were with him, and Prince Waifer gained the victory. At this time Seodan, with his entire army, attacked the city of Conza for forty days and besieged it fiercely for a long time; but the Lord delivered it by His protection, and Seodan withdrew from it with his men in disgrace. And the aforesaid Pando, holding Capua for two years and months [lacuna], died (A.D. 862) [Note: the editor supplied “atque de”; the passage is obscure], and left it to his son Pandinolf in the eleventh indiction. Pandinolf, son of the said Pando, was made gastald in the city of Capua and held it for nine months. Not long afterwards Bishop Landolf shut him out of the city; and, coming with his possessions, he settled at Sessa in the same indiction.

32. Landolf was to his fellow citizens not only bishop, but also count and judge; not only prelate, but likewise gastald; nor merely pontiff, but, like a soldier, he held authority over all.

[Note: What follows was added in the margin by a later hand. Peregrini had already noted that it derives from the *Chronicle of St Benedict*, likewise issued from the same manuscript, no. 353, and that this passage and the chronicles of the counts of Capua are attributed—on the testimony of Leo of Ostia, I.52—to Abbot John of Cassino, descended from a noble Capuan family. Peter the Deacon, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 15 (Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*, p. 173), states that this same John wrote a brief but most necessary chronicle concerning the persecutors of that monastery and the miracles performed there. It continues:]

879. For twelve years. When he died, his nephew Pandenolf was made gastald; 882. having resided there for three years and eight months, he was captured by his relatives; and Lando, brother of Bishop Landolf, was made gastald, residing for two years and ten months. 885. He was succeeded by his brother Landenolf, gastald of Capua, for one year and four months. 887. In the fifth indiction, in January, Count Atenolf took Capua, which he held for ten years; after these had elapsed he became [prince] of Benevento, ruling it for ten years and six months. 911.

33. (A.D. 867.) Again our benefactor—that is, the hostile enemy of all—Seodan came to Venafro; after he had begun [his attack upon] their city and devastated the whole countryside, he established himself round about it like a mighty king in the midst of the land. It was then the beginning of holy Lent.

[Note: This occurred in the third year of the principate of Lord Radelgar, in the fifteenth indiction; in the margin.]

On that day, as was customary, Abbot Berthar exhorted his most blessed flock on the holy Lord’s Day with divine precepts. When the brethren learned with certainty of his proximity, they hastened up to Saint Benedict. On the following day, Wednesday, the impious army of that king came near the monastery of Saint Benedict, at no great distance, about two stadia away. That is, when the Saracens wished to descend through the mountains to Atina, the man who guided them descended with them into the Round Valley, thence to the Rapido; and when they reached the plains, they began to plunder. Having entered the church of Saint Elijah and done some slight damage there, they went through Circlarius to the Lord’s Garden, and through Pascarium to the Fountain of Lucius, thence to Peolem; there they killed an old man before the railings, because he had misled them as to the road. Searching the places called Caesar’s of Constantius, the Olive-grove, and Matronola, and carrying off all the monastery’s beasts of burden and cattle, they returned late to their companions at Venafro. This was the end, through God’s driving them away, of the incursions into the lands of blessed Benedict by King Seodan and all his followers.

[Col. 0989]

# The Life of St Mennas by Leo of Marsi

(Extant in manuscript no. 413 of the Cassinese library. Gattula published the Prologue and Epilogue in *Historia Cassinensis*, vol. I, pp. 188 and 911.)

## Prologue to the Life of St Mennas

[Col. 0989C] I have undertaken to write, most reverend Father Oderisi, at your command, the life and manner of life of the distinguished confessor of Christ Mennas, together with the translation to Caiazzo, recently effected by divine disposition, of his holy relics from the place in which he had lived the solitary life.

[Note: Mennas, or Menna, led an eremitic life among the Samnites in the sixth century. His chief concern was always to possess nothing in this world, to seek nothing, and to kindle in all who came to him for charity’s sake a longing for eternal life. Illustrious through many virtues, he passed to heaven in A.D. 583 and was buried in the very place in which he had lived as a solitary. The Roman Martyrology remembers him on 11 November in these words: “In the province of Samnium, St Mennas, a solitary, whose virtues and miracles Saint Gregory the Pope records,” namely in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 26, where Gregory treats of him expressly. Leo of Marsi, monk of Cassino and cardinal of Ostia of the Holy Roman Church, a contemporary author, wrote the Life and the Acts of the Translation, which took place in 1094, chiefly at the urging of the illustrious Count Robert.]

For he himself had been earnestly entreated by the glorious Count Robert that you would deign to entrust the business of this matter to one of the brethren of the monastery of Cassino; not because he could not have found elsewhere, even in his own court, very many writers distinguished in learning and eloquent in speech, but because, as a man devoted to God and placing great confidence in the authority of the name of our place, he judged that ecclesiastical deeds ought more worthily to be written in plain words profitable for the edification of one’s neighbours than in high-flown, elaborately weighed words redolent rather of secular philosophy.

The said count pressed this request so strongly because, by God’s grant, he had himself lately merited to discover and translate the body of this most holy confessor, and because what blessed Pope Gregory had written concerning this holy man in the books of his *Dialogues* seemed too brief and, as it were, mentioned only in passing. So that all faithful peoples gathering for his festival might have material with which to occupy themselves that day in his festive praises, he asked not only that those matters which had been set forth in the most lucid style of so great a bishop should be enlarged and expanded with suitable passages gathered from every quarter, but also that several chants and melodies of sweet praises should be composed for the occasion, he being very devout in this regard.

Therefore, although unskilled and ineffectual, and having scarcely attained even the slightest knowledge of the liberal arts, yet presuming upon the authority of your command, I have applied my mind to carrying this out as best I could: so that glory may be given to God and to His most blessed confessor Mennas through the deeds of virtues and the glory of God’s saints; that due honour may be rendered to them; and that from examples of those deeds very great benefit may be brought to us. For, as the Apostle teaches, “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction.” Yet if my reader finds in this little work any fruit of edification, let him attribute it to the grace of God alone. If, however, he judges anything therein worthy of criticism, let him first carefully consider the authority of the one commanding me—which it was by no means permissible to despise—and deal mercifully with me. For I did not seize upon this task as an arrogant and shameless man, but, though in some manner compelled, I humbly obeyed your commands, most blessed Father. For I trust that I shall receive from this not only the reward of obedience which I owe you as father and lord, but also, through the merits of so eminent a confessor, I confidently hope to obtain in abundance the recompense of divine grace.

## Epilogue

[Col. 0991C] “Thus far we have written, in unskilled speech but with diligence, concerning the life and manner of life of the most blessed confessor of Christ Mennas, taking as our material the most lucid teacher and most holy Pope Gregory, its guide and collaborator; striving both to fulfil your command, as far as was possible” (he addresses Oderisi, the first abbot), “and to satisfy the will and devotion of the aforesaid magnificent Count Robert of Caiazzo. We do not insert in this writing his birth and death according to the practice found in most saints’ lives, because, not discovering anywhere who or what manner of man he was, or at what time he lived, and wholly guarding against falsehood—which God hates and which kills the soul—we do not wish to assert uncertain things as certain,” etc.

And at the beginning of this Translation of the saint he adds: “But now it pleases us to commit to writing for the knowledge of the faithful peoples the history of his translation according to the most certain trustworthiness of the events, so that henceforth no one may have any reason whatever to doubt the origin of this great solemnity,” etc.

# Acts of the Translation of St Mennas, Hermit and Confessor

By Leo of Marsi, monk of Cassino and cardinal of Ostia of the Holy Roman Church.

(Extracted by Mabillon from a Cassinese manuscript; published by Dom Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, p. 977.)

[Col. 0991D] That in these last and perilous times of ours (A.D. 1094)—in which, as the Apostle testifies, people are lovers of themselves (2 Tim. 3), seeking all things that are their own rather than those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2), and in which already, alas, “the godly person has failed, and truth has diminished among the children of men” (Ps. 11)—the heavenly mercy deigns to visit and gladden us by revelations of saints’ bodies: this benign and merciful God shows toward us solely through His ineffable grace and goodness, so that by one and the same work He may increasingly encourage the elect toward their reward and urge sinners to hope—indeed, to presume upon—the forgiveness of sins; and so that the ardour of divine love, which through the daily increase of iniquity is wont to grow cold, even in holy men, through a kind of adverse blast, may once more be rekindled in the breasts of the faithful as though by the most welcome breeze of the south wind.

Therefore let us all exult and rejoice in the Lord, as we gather solemnly to commemorate the sublime merits of our most holy patron, the glorious confessor of Christ Mennas. For it is fitting—and certainly altogether most fitting—that, since by the granting grace of God we have merited to possess his most sacred body, our minds should rejoice exultantly with every jubilation of spiritual gladness and should not cease to return proclamations of praise and thanksgiving especially to Him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect boon (Jas. 1). It is no less fitting that, while we commemorate the sacred annual observances of his translation, we too should transfer our minds from earthly actions and desires to heavenly and eternal things; so that, as we see people on earth venerate so greatly the clod of his body, we may consider what weight of glory he possesses among the angels in heaven, where indeed there is true and incomparable honour.

But now it pleases us to commit to writing for the knowledge of the faithful peoples the history of his translation, according to the most certain trustworthiness of the events, so that henceforth no one may have any reason whatever to doubt the origin of this great solemnity; but rather may strive, with every kind of devotion, to break forth both in heart and mouth into praise and glory of God, who makes His saints wonderful, saying: “Who is like You among the gods, O Lord? Who is like You, glorious among the saints, wonderful in majesty, working wonders?” (Pss. 86, 68, 72.)

When, therefore, the reckoning had reached about five hundred years since the passing of this holy man, and so precious and heavenly a treasure lay in a most worthless, very small, and very ancient place—not, I would say, an oratory, but a hut—quite unworthily in the very mountain and place in which he had lived a solitary life, indeed a most holy life, not far from the walls of Benevento but about eight miles away, and when almighty God had determined to reveal his most holy relics for the glory of His name and for the benefit of the faithful, the following occasion arose by His disposition.

One day, when the distinguished Count Robert, son of Count Rainulf—a man indeed energetic in secular affairs and, insofar as was permissible, exceedingly devout and zealous in divine matters—was sitting with the stonecutters and masons who were building with the greatest diligence, at his command, the church of the holy Mother of God at Caiazzo, and was anxiously considering where or how he might obtain saints’ relics with which, according to his devotion, he could honour that basilica of the Mother of God, it happened by divine ordinance that at that same hour Lord Madelinus, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento, together with Lord Guiso, abbot of the monastery of Saint Lupus, came to him concerning certain interests of their monastery.

As they sat together and discussed various matters among themselves for a while, the abbot eventually asked the count in conversation from where he hoped to obtain saints’ relics for the consecration of his church. Perceiving that the abbot had not asked him, without God’s prompting, the very question which he himself had shortly before been pondering in his heart, the prudent man answered: “God and His holy Mother will provide these things for the glory of Their name in whatever manner pleases Them.” The abbot replied joyfully: “What favour will you return to me if I show you not merely small, perhaps unknown or doubtful portions of saints’ bodies, but the entire body of a certain saint within the jurisdiction of your county, which you may immediately merit to obtain?”

Greatly exhilarated by this, and raised to hope by so great a promise, the count said: “There is certainly nothing in all my domain which it would be fitting for me blamelessly to give and for you to receive, that shall not be granted to you at once, if you carry out in deed what you promise in word.” The abbot immediately added: “I shall demand from you neither gold nor silver nor anything secular, which by no means suits my profession. Rather, I shall seek what is more fitting for your salvation, your honour, and indeed your office. I desire and request, therefore, that from this day you establish yourself as guardian, advocate, and defender of all things belonging to our monastery that are situated within your county alone, so that you may willingly restore to that holy monastery, insofar as it lies in your power, those things which have been taken away or diminished by certain wicked men. If you promise now that you will carry this out without fail, you shall immediately obtain what I too have promised.”

The count most readily assented at once to all his requests and, as the abbot required, appointed his own wife witness and intermediary to this transaction.

When these terms had thus been firmly agreed upon by both sides, the abbot told the count everything which he had read concerning this holy man in the *Dialogues* of blessed Gregory, everything he had seen, and everything he knew with the greatest certainty. “On the mountain,” he said, “which is today called Mount Saint Mennas by the inhabitants of the region, from the name of this man of God, this same man of God led the solitary life, as blessed Pope Gregory relates; and there, after the happy course of his departure, he was buried by the faithful. A very small church was built over his memorial, which survives to this day, though half ruined; and beyond doubt the saint’s body rests even now in that same church, as we have frequently heard affirmed both by our contemporaries and by our elders.

“For almighty and wonderful God performs in that place, even to the present day, a memorable miracle to commend the venerable memory of this saint. Near the church there rises a clear little spring, which is reasonably believed to have been used by the man of God while he lived. An ancient tradition of the inhabitants relates that it passes through the saint’s tomb itself. When women lacking the natural milk of childbirth drink this water devoutly, their breasts are immediately and marvellously filled by the abundance of heavenly grace and supply milk in plenty; and, what is more wondrous, the same is said to happen also to every kind of nursing animal.”

Having heard this, the count was filled with great joy and confidence and exerted himself with all his strength to seek—indeed, to search for—this incomparable pearl. The count immediately went with the aforesaid abbots to Alife, and two days later hastened on to Telese. While travelling, they encountered by divine prompting a certain peasant carrying two wooden chests; having immediately bought them for an agreed price, they carried them along to enclose the relics of the saint’s body. For, trusting with the greatest faith, he hoped without doubt that he would find what he desired.

When he arrived at Telese and ate [lacuna], with the burning flame of holy desire in his breast he would not allow the matter to be deferred or put off until the next day; he set out at once with the same abbot for the place, taking only a few companions so as to arouse no one’s suspicion. Yet, fearing that if the neighbouring inhabitants learned of this they would by no means allow it to be done, he commanded several armed men from the castle called Tocius to assemble there.

When they had been led to the oratory and, after praying, had gone outside, the aforesaid abbot called one of the brethren who lived there and, re-entering the oratory, began to ask him whether he knew with certainty the place in which the body of blessed Mennas rested. The man replied: “As we have received from the tradition of our elders, my Father, we hold it certain that this eminent confessor of God rests in this little church; but the precise place in which he lies hidden remains unknown to all.”

After they had gone out saying these things, the count, again greatly anxious and impatient of delay, entered the church with the abbot and several others. Carefully examining it all round, he hastened to do that for which he had come; yet he did not know where especially he ought to set his hands. But since the pavement of the oratory appeared, through age and damage, entirely rough and dug up, only a portion before the cross which stood there remained solid. Because of this, many suspected that the holy relics lay in that place. The count, however, did not consider this likely; and circling the church again and again, he sought some clearer indication.

At length, as the very devout man passed beside the altar, he suddenly looked behind it and saw an image of the holy man painted from the waist upward and marked with the letters of his own name. He immediately cried out for joy, as though he saw no longer an image but the reality itself, the very relics of the saint of God. All ran together; and, seeing the figure and letters of the holy man, they rejoiced, no longer doubting that they would immediately find what they sought.

The count himself, therefore, first invoking Christ, approached as a digger of the earth. The others followed. First they found the surface of the ground like a sandy mixture of lime. When this had at once been removed, they found earth; and after digging this up again, they struck a pavement of lime. Thinking themselves therefore to have attained their wish, they broke it up with great eagerness; but when it was removed, they again came upon plain earth. Accordingly they pressed on more earnestly and dug the earth itself somewhat deeper. Having removed it with no less energy, they found another pavement made of tiles; and after breaking this up too with every effort, they came for a third time upon earth similar to the first.

Wearied, they were almost preparing to lose confidence and abandon their undertaking, when the count’s fervour of faith and devotion, refusing in any way to rest, began to press forward more and more and ordered them to excavate the earth found there with still greater persistence. As this was done, they finally reached the stone by which the saint’s body was covered. Carefully and attentively lifting it, they found a treasure more precious than any price: namely, the entire body of the most blessed Mennas, sound and uninjured in its bones.

Who could proceed to recount the praises and thanksgivings offered to God, the joys and congratulations among men? But because half of the tomb lay under the altar in such a way that it could in no manner be moved or raised without violating the altar, the abbot advised that this should be reported to the archbishop of Benevento, so that by his permission they might break up the altar and raise the tomb together with the body just as it stood.

The count, however, taking what he judged the wiser counsel, said: “By no means, lest perhaps the archbishop not only refuse to permit the altar to be violated, but also refuse—indeed perhaps forbid—our taking away the body; and thereafter, if we do it, we incur no slight sin; while if we do not do it, we nevertheless incur the loss both of our vow and of this great distinction. If we cannot do what we wish,” he said, “let us wish what we can do.”

Therefore, with the greatest devotion and reverence, he ordered the holy relics to be lifted and very carefully placed in the two wooden chests. Having received them with praises and hymns, rejoicing and triumphing, they departed and on that same day—the day before the Kalends of April—arrived at the village called Squilla, where they spent the whole night keeping vigil beside the holy body.

On the next day, as Saturday, preceding the solemnity of Palm Sunday, was dawning, an innumerable multitude of clergy and people gathered. Taking up the holy relics of the confessor of Christ, the count himself, on foot, set out with all those assembled for about [Note: “Seven or three, I do not know how many,” inserted in the margin in an ancient hand] miles, and carried them to Caiazzo amid immense rejoicing and gladness, with hymns and confessions of praise. They placed them upon the altar of the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, with fitting honour and reverence, glorifying and blessing the Lord, who does not forsake those who trust in Him and rely upon His mercy.

These things were done in the year 1094 from the Incarnation of the Lord, to the honour and glory of the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be splendour and glory, praise and thanksgiving, now and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen. This, therefore, is the origin of this sacred solemnity; this is the venerable subject of today’s celebration. And therefore how good, how delightful, how fitting and how altogether just it is that, at the translation of the sacred body, the devout people of the faithful should rejoice with every expression of gladness, since it is beyond doubt that the army of angels also rejoices with them.

[Col. 0997]

# Account of the Consecration and Dedication of the Church of Cassino, by Leo of Marsi

(Muratori, *Scriptores Italici*, vol. V, p. 76.)

[Col. 0997B] It seems worthwhile to me, for the praise and glory of almighty God, to commit in some fashion to writing for the memory of posterity how the new church of this holy and venerable monastery was wholly renewed, built, and dedicated; at what time; and by what persons. For just as those who reveal things which they know ought to be concealed are to be condemned, so likewise those are ungrateful who conceal things which they foresee will benefit the edification of many. Although I do not trust that I can narrate this as fittingly as it deserves, nevertheless I judge it better that it should in some way be written in my own inadequacy than, to no small disgrace for us, be left untold through negligence in writing.

When, therefore, Lord Desiderius, of venerable memory, the thirty-seventh successor of our most holy and eminent Father Benedict, had by divine disposition been appointed in this venerable monastery of Cassino, which Benedict himself had once first built vigorously, with God as guide and supporter, he proved so dear and devoted to almighty God that it is evident that God wished to begin and accomplish through him what He had formerly promised His faithful servant Benedict: namely, that this place, which He had then resolved to give over to the Gentiles for devastation and plundering, would attain a condition, renown, and glory greater than it had possessed then.

Through the merits of Father Benedict God granted him so great a grace of His mercy that, among the fiercest peoples of the Normans, who not many years earlier had occupied every neighbouring and adjacent land, he lived so peacefully and quietly that not merely men of modest rank, but even their own princes and dukes, willingly obeyed him and strove in every matter to submit to his will no differently than to that of their own father and lord. Nor was there anyone dwelling round about who did not desire his favour and goodwill.

Established by God in such peace and tranquillity, after he had nobly built and constructed several buildings of this holy monastery, he finally applied his mind, not without divine inspiration, to renewing from the foundations the church which was indeed too small for the growing number of brethren and unworthy of the most precious treasure of the body of blessed Father Benedict. To speak briefly, its construction was begun with all effort and zeal in the year 1066 from the Incarnation of the Lord, together with its courtyard and porticoes, and within five years it was completed with every splendour and ornament.

He transported all its columns and every stone of its pavement from the city of Rome, with great labour and at no small cost; and he decorated the church itself most fittingly with marvellous works, nearly unknown in those times, employing at great expense craftsmen brought from diverse parts of the world and even from the imperial city of Constantinople.

Having painted the walls all around in a beautiful variety of colours, he adorned the apse, the great arch, and the courtyard with most precious mosaic. He distinguished the pavement of the entire church with so great, marvellous, and almost indescribable a variety of cut stones that one might think it blossomed not with stones but with flowers alone. All these things may indeed be seen and admired, but scarcely can anyone comprehend them as they deserve.

As for the size, character, and ornaments of the church itself, since it has not been my purpose to describe them completely in this account, and since they will, God willing and life accompanying, be set forth more fully elsewhere together with the other works of the aforesaid lord abbot, I shall relate only, to the best of my ability, with what glory and what great assembly it was consecrated.

At that time Pope Alexander II, of venerable memory, governed the holy Roman Church most wisely and religiously. The lord abbot, as was fitting, approached him with great devotion and requested that he would deign to attend the consecration of so great a church. Having quickly obtained this, as one more intimate with him than anyone else, he also most respectfully invited Archdeacon Hildebrand and the other Roman bishops and cardinals.

It seems good and not unworthy to me to record for memory the names and number of some bishops and magnates who were present—for it is not easy to remember everyone—so that from their multitude, together with the innumerable crowd of people then gathered from all regions, the glory of that dedication may be known. They were these:

John, bishop of Porto; John, bishop of Tusculum; Ubald, bishop of Sabina; Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno; Hildebrand, archbishop of Capua; John, archbishop of Naples; John, archbishop of Sorrento; Girard, archbishop of Siponto; Bisantius, archbishop of Trani; Drogo, archbishop of Taranto; Erasmus, bishop of Segni; Peter, bishop of Anagni; Honestus, bishop of Veroli; Ambrose, bishop of Terracina; Leo, bishop of Gaeta; Pandulf, bishop of the Marsi; Palumbus, bishop of Sora; Martin, bishop of Aquino; William, bishop of Teano; John, bishop of Cales, or Forcladio, as in the bull of Alexander II; Peter, bishop of Venafro; Geoffrey, bishop of Aversa; John, bishop of Picenum; Marald, bishop of Paestum; Albert, bishop of Boiano; Roger, bishop of Civitate; Campo, bishop of Dragonara; Stephen, bishop of Troia; Baldwin, bishop of Melfi; John, bishop of Canne; Robert, bishop of Florence; Nicholas, bishop of Termoli; William, bishop of Larino; Peter, bishop of Guardialfiera; John, bishop of Vigilio; Innacius, bishop of Montecorvino; William, or Guibert, bishop of Rubbo; Datto, bishop of Ostuni; Peter, bishop of Monopoli; John, bishop of Giovinazzo; Maynard, bishop of Ariano; Arnald, bishop of Acherontia; Constans, bishop of Venosa; Hugh, bishop of Otranto; Geoffrey, bishop of Perugia; and Theobald, bishop-elect of Castellaneta, who was consecrated bishop on the second day after the dedication.

Moreover, from the original charter of Alexander II, preserved in the archive of Cassino, the following additional ecclesiastical prelates are known to have attended this consecration of the church of Cassino:

Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church; Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia.

[Col. 1000A] After all the bishops, the cardinals subscribe to the said charter:

“I, Firminus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. Leo, cardinal. [lacuna] Stephen, cardinal-priest. Landulf, cardinal-priest. Leo, cardinal-priest, on behalf of all the cardinal-priests, deacons, and clerics of the Holy Roman Church.”

How many thousands of monks, with their abbots, gathered for the glory of so great a festival cannot be recalled, since indeed all of them could not even be seen.

The princes were Richard of Capua; his son Jordan; Jordan his uncle; Gisulf, prince of Salerno; Pandulf, prince of Benevento; Sergius, duke of Sorrento; and Count Raynulf.

Of the other powerful men, counts, and nobles from all the surrounding lands, so great a multitude was present that it would require much idle time even to recount their number, much less their names. And why should I mention the throng of people? It was undoubtedly so great that it filled not only the entire precinct of the monastery and the roofs of all its buildings, but even the roads from the summit of the mountain to its foot with such dense crowds that scarcely even the strongest man could make his way among them.

All these persons having gathered with the highest joy and special devotion for the observance of so great a festival, the aforesaid church was dedicated with the highest honour, as was fitting, on the first day of the Kalends of October, a Saturday, in the year 1071 of the divine Incarnation, ninth indiction, with its five altars. Of these, the aforesaid venerable Pope Alexander consecrated with his own hand two, namely those of Saint Benedict and Saint John; John, bishop of Tusculum, consecrated the altar of Saint Mary; Ubald, bishop of Sabina, that of Saint George; and Erasmus, bishop of Segni, that of Saint Nicholas.

When all this had been completed, the Mass solemnly celebrated by the Roman pontiff, many gifts offered by the people, and absolution granted by the same most blessed pontiff not only to those then present but also to all who would gather in devotion for the festival during the eight continuous days of the dedication, each person departed to his own home rejoicing and exulting.

The grace of this absolution drew such devotion and such a multitude from every side during those eight continuous days that one would almost not have considered oneself faithful if one had not shared in so great a solemnity. Let none of those who read doubt that these things occurred as stated; for we have written them not as handed down by others, but as truly seen with our own eyes.

When three years and the same number of months had passed after the dedication of this church, namely in the year 1075 from the Nativity of the Saviour, beginning on the third day before the Nones of January, the church of the blessed Apostle Bartholomew, fittingly situated on the western side of the greater church, was again dedicated with great joy and exultation among all the brethren, with honour, by John, bishop of Sora. A not insignificant portion of the arm of that blessed apostle was also reverently enclosed there in a silver chest.

In the same year, about eight months later, the remaining two very beautiful basilicas, placed on either side at the extremities of the towers of the outer courtyard, were consecrated with equal zeal and honour on the fourth day before the Ides of September. One of them, built on the right-hand side in honour of the blessed Archangel Michael, was consecrated to the divine majesty by the aforesaid John, bishop of Sora; the other, on the left-hand side, founded in honour of Peter, prince of the apostles, was consecrated by Leo, bishop of Aquino, in the presence of the lord abbot himself and the assembled body of all the brethren, with great joy and devotion.

Moreover, when the fourteenth year had already run its course from this dedication [Col. 1001B], and the year 1090 from the Incarnation of the Lord was passing, three years and sixty-three days having elapsed since the death of the reverend and ever honourably remembered Abbot Desiderius, under the presidency and command of Lord Oderisius, his most reverend and most worthy successor, the church of Saint Martin, confessor of Christ, was dedicated. The aforesaid venerable Abbot Desiderius had wonderfully and most beautifully raised it, on sixteen marble columns, in the very place where it had formerly been built by the most blessed Abbot Benedict, namely near the gate of the monastery; and he had excellently adorned it both with mosaic and with the varied colours of paintings. It was dedicated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, that is, on the octave-day of the same most blessed Martin, confessor [Col. 1001C] of Christ, a Monday, together with its three altars, in the presence of a vast concourse of men of different ranks and amid the greatest joy of all. The first and principal altar, in honour of Saint Martin himself, was dedicated by the venerable Lord John, bishop of Tusculum. The altar situated on the right side of the basilica was consecrated in honour of Saint Erasmus the martyr by Lord Raynald, bishop of Gaeta, who in that same year had been given from this monastery of ours to that church as bishop. The third, set on the left side, was blessed in honour of Ambrose, glorious confessor of Christ, by Lord Honestus, most reverend bishop of Veroli. There were also with them at this dedication three other bishops, namely [Col. 1002A] Lambert of Alatri, Roffridus of Sora, and Leo, bishop of Venafro. The reason why the consecration of this basilica was delayed so long after the death of Father Desiderius was that the same abbot, forestalled by death, had left unfinished some part of the painting and no small part of the pavement. His successor took the greatest care to complete all these things and to add what was necessary; and thus he caused it to be dedicated with the highest honour, as has been stated above.

Likewise, after three years and seventy-three additional days had elapsed, in the year 1094 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second indiction, on the thirtieth day of January, a Monday, the church of Blessed Andrew the Apostle was dedicated, under the presidency and command of the already-mentioned Lord Abbot Oderisius. He had built this basilica from its foundations on the eastern side of the greater church, between its apse and the infirmary, having the brothers’ cemetery on its right side and, on the left, a cloister—small indeed, but most beautiful. It was dedicated by Lord Raynald, bishop of Gaeta, mentioned above, with immense devotion and rejoicing of all the brethren, on the very day upon which we recovered, beyond all hope, by the merits of the most blessed Father Benedict and through divine mercy, the castle called Fratta. That castle had been stolen from us and seized by the neighbouring Normans three years earlier, but was recovered, with the Lord’s help, on the thirteenth day . . .; and, for the everlasting remembrance of that triumph, this solemn observance was established on the very day of the consecration. [Col. 1002C] The aforesaid basilica was established for the benefit of the infirm brethren. It is most firmly roofed with timber and tiles, excellently adorned with glazed windows, painted with various histories of saints in a beautiful diversity of colours, and furnished with a pavement artfully constructed with a varied inlay of marble. And, what is by far the chief distinction among all these things, it has been most carefully consecrated with many illustrious relics of apostles, martyrs, and confessors of God. With the pledges of the other churches, in their respective places, we shall write down the names of all these, with the Lord’s help.

[Col. 1003]

# A Short Work by Peter the Deacon and Librarian of the Sacred Abbey of Monte Cassino, On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino

Drawn from the most celebrated Barberini Library and elucidated with notes through the study and labour of Giovanni Battista Mari, a Roman, canon of Sant’Angelo in Foro Piscium.

(Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, V, 1.)

## Muratori’s Preface

The first person to bring this little book of Peter the Deacon, monk and librarian of Monte Cassino, from obscurity into public light was Giovanni Battista Marus, a Roman and canon of Sant’Angelo in Foro Piscium. Having transcribed it from a manuscript codex of the Barberini Library, he published it at Rome in 1655, together with the supplement of Placidus, a monk of Monte Cassino, and with his own notes. The book was then reprinted in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XXI, p. 345; likewise at Paris in 1666; and finally in the *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica* of the distinguished Johann Albert Fabricius, at Hamburg in 1718. There is no need for me to recount the author’s noble lineage, deeds, and writings, since, apart from others who treat of ecclesiastical writers, Marus himself has set down much concerning him in his notes; it would be labour wasted were I to relate more.

## To the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord J. Baptista Barsotto de Puccinis, Provost of Isny, Apostolic Protonotary, Counsellor of His Sacred Imperial Majesty, and Chamberlain to the Most Eminent Cardinal von Harrach

This little book comes to you, most illustrious Lord, for a double reason: of its own accord and by its own right. For all perceive in you such humanity, wisdom, and nobility that the whole world of letters is joined to you by goodwill no less than, of old, earth was joined to heaven by Homer’s chain. Nor is this surprising to me, who have discerned your singular character, by which that Pythagorean harmony is renewed among us—the harmony which the ancients say is heard among the heavenly beings. You abound, indeed, in virtues and nobility which are received among humankind so pleasantly, so amiably, and so harmoniously that they produce a harmony more than earthly.

Your lineage and ancestors are attested not only by your native Lucca, which recognizes its own blood in your veins, but also by Poland, mother and nurse of noble souls. Poland saw your grandfather, Giovanni Battista Puccini, as participant in and interpreter of Italian secrets with King Sigismund Augustus; and it dispatched him to Germany, to the Emperor Ferdinand II and to many other princes, as an acceptable administrator of the royal will—welcome to all, and dismissed by the Emperor and princes themselves not without honour and privilege. Your virtues, if modesty permits their mention, are praised and approved not by Rome alone, nor by Germany alone, but by almost all provinces to which the fame of your capability has reached. Bohemia certainly owes so much to your fidelity and prudence that the most eminent Archbishop of Prague has chosen, and wishes to have, no one but you at Rome as the manager of his affairs.

I should never finish speaking if I wished to describe your remaining honours, whether innate or conferred upon you by princes; moreover, I should wrong your modesty—and perhaps I have already done so. Yet these things had to be indicated, in order that it might be evident that this little book comes to you of its own accord. Virtue is a magnet: not only hearts, but little works also are drawn by this magnet.

Yet it hastens to you not only of its own accord but also by its own right, and is due to you. Who does not know how greatly you love the sacred family of Saint Benedict? How much you devise for the increase of its splendour? With what devotion you frequent, cultivate, and venerate the monastery of Subiaco? Nor is this without reason. For here that supreme athlete and teacher of Christian holiness escaped poisoned cups through a great miracle, eluded infernal snares, laid the foundations of an order so distinguished and so deserving of the Church; and—what is wonderful—he pours forth from heaven such streams of graces day after day that the place seems a workshop of heavenly generosity. I pass over the testimonies of the supreme pontiffs Paschal II, Urban V, Leo IX, Clement III and VI, Eugenius IV, John X, Benedict VI, and Saint Gregory the Great himself, by which Benedict’s shrine at Subiaco is commended as both a treasure of the Church and a nursery of the Benedictine family.

This book, moreover, was written by Peter the Deacon, monk and librarian of Monte Cassino. It contains nothing other than an account of the literary labours and the characters of the illustrious living men of Monte Cassino—that is, the proper and immortal ornaments of the very order to which you give so much. It therefore comes to you by its own right, to be supported also by your patronage and resources. Farewell.

Giovanni Battista Marus.

## Preface of J. Baptista Mari

[Col. 1005]

[Col. 1005A] When in past years we had brought forth into the light the *Dialogues* of Pope Victor III—formerly Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino—having rescued them from the Vatican Library, where they were contending with cockroaches and moths, a certain paltry pedant, after reading them, complained that we extolled the virtues of the Cassinese too highly. With a censorious brow he asserted that there were very few, or no, works to whose writing and publication the Cassinese had applied their talents; and that scarcely anyone among them had exercised himself in more serious literary labours or, stirred by the incentives of honourable glory, written anything down.

> O ludicrous and laughable thing, Cato,  
> Worthy of your ears and your loud laughter!

[Note: [Col. 1005] These *Dialogues* of Victor III, discussed below, were printed in vol. XVIII of the Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.]

Up to this point we have indeed listened with excessive patience to this rather silly detractor. Even if we wished to repeat all his utterances, it would plainly be an abuse of our leisure, especially since, with lofty brow, he has promised to produce marvels in writing.

[Col. 1005B] Although the monastic order has always had its detractors, as Saints Jerome in several places, Chrysostom in that celebrated *Shield of the Monastic Life*, and other ancients rightly report, never has this been done more boldly in our own age by shameless heretics. Among them the monastic order has become so detested that some refrain merely at first sight from reading books, however excellent, because they are marked only by the name of a monk. They even commonly give currency to the proverbial expression “more unlearned than a monk”—a saying capable of provoking laughter even in Heraclitus, obstinately mourning. Indeed, there was not lacking a certain hater of letters who was not ashamed, in detestation and disparagement of monks, to write—though the paper itself blushed and the ink turned vermilion at so great a storehouse of shamelessness—that certain holy Fathers designated by the monastic title had never been enrolled among monks, in order that he might cast their works into doubt. He most foolishly imagined this one weak, nerveless, fig-wood argument to be so solid and strong [Col. 1005C] that he was thereby released from the burden of proving the rest.

And although excessively false claims ought not to be refuted lest they seem capable of being believed—as Saint Athanasius rightly said in his letter to Epictetus, with the approval of Saint Epiphanius, *Heresy* 77—nevertheless, lest this peddler of trifles take our silence, though we know how scant our own resources are, for pride or ignorance; and knowing in addition that there are many persons of insufficiently firm judgment who believe whatever they hear or read unless they know it has been refuted, we have, without delay, remembering Ulpian’s statement, *On the Meaning of Words*, law 22, §1, “He pays less who pays later; for by time also less is paid,” and likewise the dictum of a celebrated great author, “Delay is servile for barbarians; immediate execution is kingly,” judged it right to publish for you, kindly reader, and for the public good, this little work, *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, written by the most distinguished Peter the Deacon, monk and librarian of the same monastery. Until now unpublished and long desired by many learned men, it was supplied to us from the celebrated Barberini Library through the singular kindness and generosity of the most distinguished Carlo Moroni, so that we might overthrow the calumnies of that detractor and convict him. To it, because of the similarity of subject, [Col. 1006A] we add a handwritten *Supplement* on likewise illustrious men of Monte Cassino, compiled by Placidus Romanus, monk and deacon of the same abbey.

We confess that it is small and slight—for things are to be appraised not so much by number and size as by value and weight—but it was written carefully and thoughtfully by our Peter. In the year 1115, when he was alive, he recorded much that illuminates the history of the Church, as may be read in Leo of Ostia’s *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, whose third book he completed and to which he added a fourth. It will also be most welcome and useful to those attracted to the study of learning and interested in knowledge of authors and books. Many things, certainly, are indicated in this little work, and especially in our notes, which deserve public light, since from concealment is brought forth knowledge of various ancient writers whose books were thought to have perished. If knowledge of these books and authors had been disregarded, they might perhaps have lain forever in darkness; and, as a tomb covers a body, so their names would have been buried for almost all ages, while their literary labours would have remained entombed in private libraries—to the great loss, certainly, of letters. For in this age a great part of learning consists in knowing which authors’ books ought to be read and which ought not.

For it is necessary to know who has written and on what they have written, and to know the springs from which may be drawn what will be of great use either in nourishing knowledge, producing virtues, or detesting vices; since without libraries religion is almost unarmed and wisdom empty. This consideration is in itself pleasant and worthy of a free-born person; it contributes greatly both to the selection of authors and to stirring the minds of students. As the trophies of Miltiades kept Themistocles awake, so the books of learned men mentioned in this little volume ought to inflame students’ minds to labour and praise. And as [Col. 1006C] learned men seem deprived of every consolation when reading is forbidden them—as this form of punishment was once inflicted by Tiberius on certain persons, according to Suetonius: “When some had been handed over to custody, he deprived them not only of the consolation of study, but even of the use of speech and conversation”—so they receive every consolation from reading.

The Angelic Doctor endured this; he valued the monuments of sacred letters so highly that he was accustomed to say that he would seriously prefer one homily of Blessed Chrysostom to the city of Paris, most abundantly rich in every kind of wealth, even in empires themselves. Books, indeed, as instruments of study, delight us from the marrow, converse with us, advise us, and unite themselves with us in a kind of living and witty intimacy. Finally, writings alone perpetuate mortals in a kind of immortal fame, and do not allow age to creep upon the deeds of the ancients which they hand down to posterity; so Peter of Blois teaches in Letter 77. Hence Martial rightly says:

> Neither theft nor ages harm written pages;  
> These monuments alone do not know how to die.

[Col. 1006D] At the end of his *Life of Saint Augustine*, Possidius, no false prophet, affirmed that Augustine’s memory would be perpetual because of the books he had written. He even cited this epitaph of a secular poet speaking of himself, which he wished inscribed on his tomb:

> Traveller, would you know whether a poet lives after death?  
> See: what you read, I speak; your voice, indeed, is mine.

[Col. 1007A] Moreover, it is worth knowing that from this most noble Cassinese academy there came forth not only almost innumerable monks filled with every kind of learning, but that there was also continual diligence, piety, and purpose in copying the volumes of the holy Fathers and other learned men. Thus, in doubtful matters, learned and scholarly men could safely have recourse, as to certain oracles, to manuscript codices and ancient printed editions from which true readings are restored. The most prudent emperors Theodosius and Valentinian so provided by law, *Theodosian Code*, book I, *On the Opinions of Jurists*; for not only are we lacking many authors, but even those we have at hand are not all equally corrected. Thus those must plainly be judged ridiculous who think it makes no difference to them whether they use a corrected or uncorrected book. For surely, if we use corrupted codices, nothing remains except that, like Ixion, we embrace a shadow in place of reality and error in place of knowledge.

Having made this observation, the following point must be added: the piety of the faithful in that earlier age joined such great diligence in accurate copying that not everyone was permitted indiscriminately to copy the Gospel, Psalter, or Missal. Men of mature age were selected for this task, so that errors might be more carefully avoided. This is noted in the capitulary of Aix-la-Chapelle, chapter 72: “If there is need to write a Gospel, a Psalter, or a Missal, men of mature age shall write with every diligence.” Indeed, no manual labour suits monks better than the office of writing, since in this task they preach to humankind with their hands, open tongues with their fingers, and silently give salvation to mortals. See what Gerson discussed at length in an entire book *On the Praise of Writers*, that is, copyists or scribes; and Trithemius, who likewise wrote a whole book *On Their Praises*. Consult Theophilus Raynaud of the Society of Jesus, another almost Didymus Chalcenterus, *On Good and Bad Books*, part III, erotema 4, fol. 309.

[Col. 1007C] They are moreover reported to have employed such industry and incredible zeal that, continually and as though at one task, some for a long time by day and night hammered upon the same anvil: they artfully bound written codices together; others corrected them with marvellous concentration of mind; others embellished them in red. In this they imitated the Emperor Theodosius, who, when free from public duties, wrote sacred books with such elegance that he acquired from this the name Calligrapher; Raderus is witness, *Aula sacra*, ch. 6. Indeed, they regarded it as a further sacrilege to touch sacred codices with unwashed hands.

We find something similar practised by the pagans as well, though they purified not only their hands but also their feet and ears. Plutarch, *On the Eating of Flesh*, Oration II, says: “Yet perhaps we err in touching these books without having purified hands, feet, and ears.” How pleasing this labour of copying was to divine goodness is recognized from a clear and manifest miracle. Trithemius relates, *On the Praise of Manual Writers*, ch. 6, that in a certain Benedictine monastery there was a monk who applied diligent and painstaking effort to writing volumes for the adornment of the library. Whenever he could be free from the divine office, he withdrew to the privacy of his cell and applied himself to this holy labour; hence he copied many works of saints with great devotion. When his bones were exhumed many years after his death, the three fingers of his right hand with which he had written so many volumes were found as whole and uncorrupted as if they had been placed in the grave at that same moment, whereas the rest of his body, as is customary, had been consumed to bones. A similar event concerning Richard, an English Premonstratensian, may be read in Caesarius, book XII, ch. 47.

[Col. 1008A] Hence men distinguished for piety and learning, observing that divine providence valued so highly this labour of copying—lest many monuments of the holy Fathers and ecclesiastical writers should perish, as would readily have happened unless they had been transmitted to posterity through the labour of monks—transferred to the flourishing Cassinese academy, then as it were a nursery of letters, an almost countless abundance of manuscripts and printed books. Thus today there is no library in all Italy even somewhat celebrated which is not enriched in some measure by their noble treasures. See what our Peter noted in the *Supplement to the History of Monte Cassino*, book III, ch. 62, in the Venetian edition, concerning the books which Abbot Desiderius alone, and afterwards Pope Victor III, caused to be copied. Then you will rightly give us credit; and to wish therefore to strip the sacred Cassinese asceterium of the praise deserved by its learning is to deny what is manifest—just as Zeno of old removed motion from the nature of things, Anaxagoras took whiteness from snow, and Epicurus took from the sun the magnitude granted it by all astronomers.

Let these trifles, then, be dismissed as deserving contempt by laughter rather than refutation by serious argument. After the fable spun by that talkative sycophant, let us produce [Col. 1008B] what the illustrious herald of ecclesiastical antiquity, Cardinal Baronius, inserted concerning the Cassinese in vol. IX of his *Annals*, under the year 716:

> “And this too may rightly be asserted without fear of falsehood: that never in the whole Christian world was there any monastery from which so many men distinguished for holiness and learning, and in such numbers, were chosen for the governance of the holy Apostolic See; so that it may plainly be said that it was once a nursery of sacred bishops, as what we shall say in its place will clearly show.”

Let this Proteus now turn himself into every form and attack the Cassinese academy as he pleases, together with those who, wallowing in the very dregs of ignorance and having burst all the barriers of shame, have called it idle and have even believed it destitute of all learning. We have wished to make this known to you, kindly reader: that shadowy assailants and Theonian teeth do not frighten the Cassinese abbey, so celebrated for the holiness and learning of its monks, when it sees open to itself the refuge of so many doctors, and when it has begotten from itself so many splendid sons who have enriched Christ’s Church with the monuments of their intellect and with every kind of humane letters. Remember Augustine’s saying that truth needs no defender, and that falsehood commonly falls without anyone impelling it and overthrows itself.

Finally, we earnestly ask that you not wonder if our Peter has not enumerated all Cassinese writers and all the literary labours of those whom he mentions. Especially since he had no intention of setting foot outside the ship—a fact easily discerned from his writings, as Hercules is known from his footprint. It must, however, be held for certain that, while Peter was still alive, many monuments of different writers remained hidden in various private libraries; and consequently he was unable to read everything or discover everything to his satisfaction—above all because he was a man occupied with public and private affairs—though he intended to record all at a more convenient time.

And if, perhaps, dear reader, this is not to [Col. 1008D] your taste, here is his defence: know that we can protect him from the charge of negligence, not only by the example that neither Trithemius nor Pantaleon, when writing of Germans; nor Sammarthanus, of Gauls; nor Ferdinand Matamoros, of Spaniards; nor Folieta, of Ligurians; nor Miraeus, of Flemings; nor Hebedjesu, of Chaldeans—brought out of darkness and obscure gloom last year through the service of the distinguished Abraham Ecchellensis and illuminated with most learned notes—nor others writing of their own fellow citizens or associates, at one time embraced all whom greater diligence or better fortune might perhaps have enabled them to include; but also by Varro’s maxim, confirmed by Columella in *On Agriculture*, that no one is reproached for leaving stubble for gleaning. “In a great forest,” he says, “it is the mark of a good hunter to track down wild beasts and capture very many; nor is anyone blamed for not catching [Col. 1009A] them all.” This is especially so when anyone performs his task well if he somehow satisfies a hungry reader, even though he does not wholly remove the hunger.

And, to speak plainly, if in old times a civic crown was given to one who saved a single citizen, what crown should all ivy-bearing musicians (*kissophoroi*, κισσοφόροι) weave for our Peter, since he has rescued from destruction the names not of one but of many illustrious men and has brought to light treasures previously unseen? The Wise One alone knows at what value each thing ought to be assessed.

Lastly, do not suppose that we also are doing a superfluous thing because Trithemius, Arnold Wion, and others have already treated Cassinese writers sufficiently. Know that in their catalogue they were not so careful as not to have failed to know many men, and that, of those whom they say they knew, they did not subsequently recount each individual work with precision. Therefore, studious reader, enjoy the labours of the Cassinese; and persuade yourself that, if love and zeal for letters inflame you—though we frankly admit that many have conceived weariness of letters because they see that things which were instruments of an honourable mind have become enemies’ nets—you should transcribe some writings of these literary heroes from the treasures of Cassinese polymathy, or compare printed editions with manuscripts.
