Know that in our times the price of books will not deter you, just as Plato is said to have bought three books of Philolaus the Pythagorean for ten thousand denarii, even when his finances were straitened, and later incorporated much from them into his own *Timaeus*, as the French jurist states in *Roman Antiquities*, book IV, part 2, ch. 16; and as Aristotle is believed to have purchased a few books of Speusippus for three Attic talents, whose value in Roman reckoning is seventy-two thousand sesterces, according to Aulus Gellius, book III, ch. 17.

[Col. 1010A] Nor should the example of Nicholas V, supreme pontiff, render your mind disturbed or faint-hearted: he promised five thousand ducats to anyone who brought him the Hebrew Gospel of Saint Matthew, as Eckius writes in his homily on Saint Matthew. The Cassinese, however, induced not by money but by zeal for divine glory, goodwill, and generosity, offer themselves ready to disclose these things to you; and, recognizing you as one who searches the chests of the ancients and seeks out manuscript exemplars, they will exhort, urge, and further press you with the spurs of grateful feeling to publish them. We also wish you to remember that this our most earnest desire to serve the commonwealth of letters is worthy of favour, not hatred, since we devote our whole effort to discovering these treasures for your benefit and that of the public. Farewell, my reader, and be favourable.

# On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Monte Cassino

[Col. 1009]

## Prologue

[Col. 1009B]

Compelled by your continual commands, venerable Bishop Pandulf, I have begun to set down in writing a difficult and most arduous undertaking: namely, a book concerning the illustrious men of the Cassinese abbey. It is a little work new at this time [Col. 1009C] and almost already consigned to oblivion. Would that those who examine it might perceive with how great sorrow of heart I have written it. For great amazement and dullness have filled the citadel of my mind: why, during the course of almost six hundred years, has there not been in the Cassinese school one person who would entrust this book even to cheap sheets? And this happened not from ignorance, but through fleeing labour and the tongues of detractors.

For now that oracle of the Divine Speaker has been fulfilled, in which we see persons loving themselves and seeking what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s, and devoting themselves most ardently to detraction. The work was first begun by Tranquillus and the Greek Apollonius [Col. 1010B], but was carried through to its end among the Romans by the most illustrious Jerome, Gennadius, and Isidore. And although nothing has been undertaken by others with such labour as does not yield to Jerome’s eloquence, after their departure from the world no one has been found to carry it to completion.

Moreover, our master Guido, outstanding in character and life, about seven years ago undertook to write that little work; but, seeing the materials for labour lying there in their heaviness, he abandoned it with the same ease with which he had begun it. If he, far superior to me in expression and thought, abandoned the undertaking, what am I to do—I, sluggish in keenness of mind, unpolished in speech, and entangled in various affairs? But let the following pen turn to what lies before it.

## Chapter One. On Saint Benedict

[Note: [Col. 1009C] Saint Benedict, Roman by nation, standard-bearer and prince of monks in the West, was born at Nursia in the year of the Lord 480, of his father Anicius Eupropius and his mother Abundantia, from the illustrious family of the Riguardati; he was born in the same childbirth as his sister Scholastica. His mother was the only daughter of the Count of Nursia and heiress of his property and surname. After giving birth to them, she died, as though she had already lived long enough in leaving behind descendants so great and such as these, and as though she had married for no other purpose than to become the mother of such saints.

His deeds were related at length not only by Saint Gregory the Great, pope and teacher of every virtue, in book II of the *Dialogues*—Gregory’s book which the scholars of Ingolstadt published in Greek and Latin in recent years—but also, as it were with ambitious praise, by the supreme pontiffs Alexander II and Victor II, by Johannes Trithemius, Cardinal Baronius, and Arnold Wion. Wion embraced the *Tree of Life* in two volumes, [Col. 1010C] in which the progeny of so great a Father is written with the greatest care and at length. Benedict Haeften, provost of the monastery of Affligem, should also be consulted: in the first prolegomenon to his book of monastic investigations, in the *Life of Saint Benedict*, he treats Benedict at length.

Besides the works mentioned by our Peter, the patriarch Benedict also wrote one book, *On the Order of the Monastery*, concerning how, as he says, the brethren ought to live religiously and diligently and to serve the Lord; it begins: “In the first nocturnal hours.” This book was printed together with the *Rule* by the Giunti at Venice in 1593, in sextodecimo, through the care of Arnold Wion. Yet certain words occur in this work which raise the suspicion that it should not be attributed to Saint Benedict; on this matter consult the said Haeften, fol. 1062.

He also committed to writing an address upon the departure of Saint Maurus, beginning, “If, beloved, there is cause for sorrow,” which is printed in full in Arnold Wion’s Benedictine Martyrology under 14 January. Likewise, he composed an address on the passion of Saint Placid and his companions, beginning, “As it belongs to a father to rejoice.” This was printed in the Sicilians’ letter to Saint Benedict, appended at the end of the Venetian edition of the Cassinese chronicle. You will find the aforesaid little works bound together in the newest *Library of the Holy Fathers*, and in the final place in the *Regular Theology* of the distinguished Father Caramuel of the Cistercian Order, also illustrated with most learned commentaries.

It should, however, be observed that although the letter to Saint Remigius, read at the end of the said Cassinese chronicle and elsewhere, is called into doubt by Cardinal Baronius in vol. VI of the *Annals*, under the year 707, together with the whole narrative—he thinks that an error has intruded through similarity of names—yet Peter Thyraeus recognizes it as genuine in his separate book *On the Possessed*. Further, after Baronius’s writings had appeared, neither Anthony de Yepes, defending it in the chronicle of the Order, nor Baldwin Moreau in the works of Saint Benedict, nor Georgius Colvenerius in his scholia on Flodoard’s history, offered any suggestion of doubt. We therefore leave it to the reader’s judgment, that by his own diligence he may determine what he judges should truly be attributed or assigned to Saint Benedict.

It must not here be enveloped in the darkness of silence that, most recently, in support of the authenticity of this letter, the said Haeften reports in his commentary on the *Life of Saint Benedict*, ch. 16, *Monastic Investigations*, that he found in an ancient manuscript codex in the library of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tournai another letter, written by the monks of Rheims to the Cassinese five hundred years after Saint Benedict’s death; there he prints it wholly and in full. Finally, whether all the aforesaid literary labours are genuinely the offspring of Saint Benedict is examined with customary diligence, learning, and scholarship by the aforementioned Caramuel in *Regular Theology*, part 2; we therefore refer the reader to him.

Saint Benedict lived sixty-three years: seven at Nursia, seven at Rome, thirty-five at Subiaco, and fourteen at Monte Cassino. Standing upright in the church, supported by the hands of his disciples—after first producing abundant deeds of perfect governance, leaving splendid monuments of piety, and gathering countless sheaves of merits—he breathed out his soul. It was seen to be led to heaven by an illustrious path, in the year of the Lord 543, on 21 March, at the third hour of the morning. The epitaph placed on his tomb, as Sylvester Maurolicus reports in book I of his *Sacred History of All Religious Orders*, in his treatment of Saint Benedict, was:

> Nursia bore me; the lofty cave of Cassino received me,
Me the summit carried off; the blessed court holds me. Moreover, a controversy exists concerning the day and year of Saint Benedict’s death, which Dionysius Petavius, a man most expert in chronology, sets forth and resolves in the *Rationarium temporum*, part two, book four, chapter 14. We refer the reader desirous of a fuller discussion of this point to that work.] Benedict, founder of monks, an outstanding man [Col. 1011A] and, after the Apostles, without equal, was a native of the province of Nursia. His father was named Eupropius, his mother Abundantia, his grandfather Justinian, and his nurse Cyrilla. After he had constructed twelve monasteries with Christ’s help, during the reign of the emperor Justinian, and had organized the aforesaid cells under provosts, he received a divine response addressed to him; accompanied by two angels, he came to Cassino to preach the Gospel and convert the pagans to Christ. There, destroying the temples of idols and building a monastery, he converted the neighboring pagans to Christ. In his old age, in that same monastery at Cassino, he wrote a Rule for monks, distinguished for discretion and eloquent in language; and two letters: the first to Remigius, archbishop of Rheims; the second to [Col. 1012A] his disciple Maurus, whom he had sent into Gaul to preach, composed in a most elegant style. He lived in the times of the emperors Anastasius, Zeno, Justin, and Justinian; he was buried at Cassino, in the church of Saint John the Baptist before the altar, where he is reverently honored by the whole world.

## CHAPTER II. ON FAUSTUS

[Note: [Col. 1012B] Saint Faustus, an Italian by nation, the chief follower and intimate companion of Saint Benedict, achieved such mortification of his senses and affections that he seemed beyond imitation. When he was seven years old, he was offered to Saint Benedict by his parents. After a complete formation in the regular vocation, he was at last sent with Blessed Maurus into Gaul in the year of salvation 542, according to Arnold Wion’s calculation of years; but according to the computation of the Church, in 535, to build a monastery. Having lived there for many years in great holiness, he finally returned to the Lateran monastery. The Gallican Martyrology of the illustrious André Saussay also testifies to this, in its supplement for 15 February, in these words: “The death of Saint Faustus, monk of Cassino and disciple of Saint Benedict, who for some time lived in the monastery of Glanfeuil, in the diocese of Angers on the Loire, under Saint Maurus’s instruction; afterward, returning to Italy, he finished his course at his Cassino,” etc.

[Col. 1012C] At this time Italy’s condition was most calamitous: as the Lombards raged cruelly everywhere, no city was so fortified and no place so remote that they did not break into it by their incursions. Nor could the monastery of Cassino escape the bitter calamity of destruction, which Saint Benedict too had foretold. Therefore the monks fled from that monastery to Rome and approached Pope Pelagius II. Kindly received by him, they built, beside the Lateran patriarchate, a monastery in honor of Saints John the Apostle and Evangelist and Pancras the martyr; and they lived there for one hundred and thirty years. While residing there, Saint Faustus most eloquently committed to writing the Life of Saint Maurus, abbot in Gaul and his fellow disciple. Maurus had passed into heaven at an age exceeding seventy, in the year of the Lord 584; but according to the chronology of the illustrious Guesnay, in his *Life of Saint John Cassian*, in 565. Faustus wrote it in the year of Christ 606, as is inferred [Col. 1012D] from the preface, in which Faustus himself speaks thus: “I showed this little work to the most blessed Pope Boniface; and that most holy pontiff, approving it, judged it worthy of praise and confirmed it by his holy authority.” This was Pope Boniface III, as Leo of Ostia testifies in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, book I, chapter 3: he began to hold the see in 606 and died in the same year, Pope Boniface IV succeeding him. Trithemius, therefore, must be corrected in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Faustus,” where he reports that he wrote to Boniface II.

That Life was published by Lippomano and Surius on 15 January, and by Mombritius, volume I. See the *Acts of the Saints* of the illustrious Bollandists for this day, in which the life, translation, and miracles of Saint Maurus are carefully described. See also the notes of the illustrious John Tamayo in the Hispanic Martyrology for 14 January. Hugh Menard, however, observed in his notes on the Benedictine Martyrology that the aforesaid acts were corrupt; nevertheless, consult him. The illustrious Philip Labbe of the Society of Jesus teaches, in his new *Library of Manuscript Books*, published at Paris in the preceding year, p. 206, that the library of the Discalced Carmelites [Col. 1013B] at Clermont in Auvergne possesses a manuscript Life of Saint Maurus, in verse and prose, written by Odo; a little book on his miracles; and a sermon on his translation to the monastery of Fossatus.

Sigebert treats Faustus’s deeds in chapter 32 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; likewise the Benedictine Martyrology under 15 February, Galesinus, Maurolycus, Trithemius, *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book II, chapter 2, and book III, chapter 3; Leo of Ostia, book II, chapter 3 of the *History of Cassino*; Vincent, *Mirror of History*, book XXI, chapters 68 and 69; and the illustrious Gerard John Vossius, *On Latin History*, book II, chapter 24. Saint Faustus was called to the rewards of eternal light about the year of the Lord 620.] Faustus, disciple of the same Father, was offered at Cassino when seven years old and sent into Gaul by the most holy Benedict with Maurus, provost of Cassino. After his return, by order of Abbot Theodore, he composed a very lucid Life of Blessed Maurus. He flourished in the time of the aforesaid emperors and was buried in the Lateran monastery.

## CHAPTER III. ON MARK

[Col. 1013A]

[Note: [Col. 1013B] Mark, most dearly loved by Saint Benedict, [Col. 1013C] was a man born by nature to exalt the poetic art, distinguished in conduct and way of life, and highly skilled also in secular literature. Lest Mark’s authority be lightly esteemed by some as that of an obscure writer, we have thought it not inappropriate to produce here certain testimonies of ancient writers concerning him. Paul the Deacon, book I, chapter 26 of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, says: “I have drawn all these things from the poem of the poet Mark, who, coming hither to that same Father, Benedict, composed several verses in his praise.” Aldrevald repeats the same in book II, chapter 4 of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*. Saint Peter Damian, sermon 8, on the vigil of Saint Benedict, says: “We have now plucked these things from the graceful poem of Mark, namely the disciple of that same Lord Benedict.” See also Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 33.

Besides the works listed by our Peter which remained unpublished, he also wrote in heroic verse certain miracles of the same Saint Benedict, his master, omitted by Pope Saint Gregory I. These poems, long hidden, are now found in print in the third volume of the poems of Dom Prosper Martinengius, Rome, 1590, quarto, through the study and labor of Arnold Wion, as Wion himself testifies in the *Lignum Vitae*; he also reports that they were found at Mantua in the monastery of Saint Benedict. Mark further wrote *Gnomas*, printed at Hagenau in 1531, and several other little works collected by Giovanni Pico, published at Paris in 1563, octavo. He flourished at almost the same time as Saint Faustus, that is, until the reign of the Emperor Heraclius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 610.] Mark, disciple of Father Benedict and monk of Cassino, was an outstanding man, exceptionally learned in the Scriptures. He composed, in most elegant verse, an account of the arrival of the most holy Benedict at Cassino, the site of the place, and the construction of the monastery.

## CHAPTER IV. ON SEBASTIAN

[Note: [Col. 1013D] The *Life of Saint Jerome*, the great Doctor of the Church, filled with many falsehoods and circulating without an author—as Cardinal Baronius testifies for the year 420, no. 49—does not seem to be attributable to our Sebastian, as some have erroneously done on their own judgment. For he committed to writing only the Life of Saint Benedict, disciple of Saint Jerome, his contemporary—not of the Doctor of the Church; and Arnold writes in the *Lignum Vitae* that he subsequently handed it down to be read in Benedictine monasteries. See Gerard John Vossius, a man of extensive and profound learning, *On Latin Historians*, under “Sebastian.” He flourished about the year of the Lord 560.] Sebastian, monk of Blessed Benedict, wrote the Life of Jerome, the eminent doctor, and handed it down to be read in churches. In it he shows very clearly what training Jerome received as a boy, what studies he pursued in youth, and what learning he possessed in old age.

## CHAPTER V. ON SAINT SIMPLICIUS

[Col. 1013B]

[Note: [Col. 1014B] Saint Simplicius, third abbot after the death of Saint Benedict, as Saint Gregory teaches at the beginning of book II of the *Dialogues*, was endowed with heavenly charisms and illustrious by every testimony of holiness. The verses which he wrote in praise of Saint Benedict’s Rule, together with various other Rules of holy monks, will shortly be brought to light by Lucas Holstenius, a man of outstanding learning and a foremost champion and defender of ecclesiastical antiquity. See what Haeftenius noted in tract 6, disquisition 1, *On the Promulgation of Saint Benedict’s Rule*, under “Simplicius”; Matthew Lauretus, *On the Presence of Saint Benedict’s Body in the Monastery of Cassino*, chapter 5; Hugh Menard, *On the Origin and Growth of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 870; and Antony de Yepes, *Benedictine Chronicle*, fol. 337, on the late promulgation of the said Rule. There the arguments of the most learned Antony Gallonius in the *Apology on Saint Gregory’s Monasticism against Abbot Constantine Cajetan* weaken and refute Cajetan’s objection.

Simplicius, resplendent with miracles, passed to the most auspicious place of unbounded blessedness about the year of the Lord 576. He was buried at Cassino with Constantine, his predecessor as abbot, beside his master’s body. Their bodies were first found by Abbot Desiderius and later by Pope Victor III, together with the sacred ashes of King and monk Carloman, in the year of the Lord 1071,* as is recorded from our Peter the Deacon’s manuscript sermon *On the Octave of Saint Benedict*. See the illustrious Marcus Scipio, *Eulogies of the Abbots of Cassino*, under “Simplicius”; he is also mentioned by Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, [Col. 1014D] book III, chapter 10; Leo of Ostia, book I, chapter 2 of the *History of Cassino*; Anastasius the Librarian, a monk, in the booklet *On the Translation of Saint Benedict*; and again our Peter, manuscript book *On the Origin and Life of the Just Men of Cassino*, chapter 10.] Simplicius, disciple of the most holy Benedict and [Col. 1014A] made abbot at Cassino after him, gave the Rule issued by his master to be publicly read to all monks. He also wrote several verses on the same subject. He lived in the time of Justin the Younger and was buried at Cassino beside the body of Blessed Benedict.

## CHAPTER VI. ON LAURENTIUS

[Note: [Col. 1014D] Arnold Wion, in the *Lignum Vitae*, testifies that the little works of Laurentius, monk of Cassino and later bishop, though of an uncertain see, survive in manuscript at Cassino, along with certain others, on the sixth shelf to the right of the library. Baronius, in the Martyrology for 28 September, mentions a history of Saint Wenceslaus, duke and martyr of Bohemia, who wore the Benedictine monastic habit but did not make profession, written by Laurentius. We also preserve it in manuscript in our modest repository of sacred manuscripts, under the heading: “Our Lord and Redeemer, to human sight,” etc. If God, best and greatest, grants success to our prayers and hopes, we shall publish it for the public good together with other hitherto unpublished Lives of saints.

Possevinus, in the *Apparatus*, under “Laurentius,” states that Laurentius also wrote the preface to the teachings of Dorotheus, found in volume II of the second edition [Col. 1015A] of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*. But Vossius, *On Latin History*, confesses that he does not sufficiently grasp Possevinus’s meaning, or else that Possevinus’s reasoning wholly escapes him. For our Peter the Deacon, whom Possevinus says wrote about this monk Laurentius, lived about the year of the Lord 1145; whereas the monk Laurentius who wrote Dorotheus’s preface was Hilarion, a monk of Cassino. That Hilarion flourished about the year of the Lord 1516, more than four hundred and fifty years after Peter of Cassino. For the Life of Saint Castrensis, bishop and martyr, consult [Col. 1015B] the illustrious Michael the monk in the *Sanctuary of Capua*. Laurentius flourished about the year of the Lord 750.] Laurentius, monk of the same monastery, inferior to none of his predecessors after the most holy Benedict in learning, became a bishop and adorned in verse the Life of Blessed Maurus and the Passion of Bishop Castrensis. He also composed a history of Saint Wenceslaus and an elegant sermon on the vigil of Blessed Benedict.

## CHAPTER VII. ON CYPRIAN

[Col. 1015A]

[Note: [Col. 1015B] The hymn which Cyprian composed on Blessed Benedict is preserved in the library of Cassino with this opening: “By the golden ray of the everlasting Sun,” etc., according to Arnold Wion in the *Lignum Vitae*. He wrote several other works as well. He was alive in the year of the Lord 760.] Cyprian, a priest who became a monk in the same monastery under Abbot Petronax, wrote a hymn on the miracles of Blessed Benedict to be sung on his feast [Col. 1016A]. He flourished in the time of the emperors Leo, Constantine, and Irene.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON PAUL

[Note: [Col. 1015B] Paul, surnamed Warnefrid, derived his origin from the Lombard people, the son of Warnefrid and Theodelinda. He was an apostolic man and a most learned prelate, deservedly called “Polyhistor” by Caspar Barthius; with extraordinary talent, acute judgment, and singular prudence he produced almost innumerable monuments of remarkable and refined learning. So that the curious reader may lack nothing concerning Paul, we give the words of Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Cassino*, book I, chapter 15:

“This man, indeed, derived his origin from the Lombard people. His great-grandfather, named Leupichis, came with them at the time when the Lombards first entered Italy. Paul’s father was named Warnefrid and his mother Theodelinda. In boyhood he was educated in the liberal arts and, because of his ability, attained a very important position of intimacy at the court of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards. He was chancellor of that king and deacon of the patriarchate of Aquileia. (Hence the byname Paul the Deacon, imposed from the dignity he obtained, clung to him permanently, although Raphael Volaterranus fails to notice this: he considers our Paul, the historian of Lombard history, and Paul the Deacon of Aquileia to be different persons.) After Pavia had been captured, he also became very dear and familiar to King Charles because of his prudence. Not long afterward, certain envious persons accused him before the same king of intending, out of loyalty to his lord Desiderius, to kill him. The king had him arrested and brought before him. When he asked whether what was said of him concerning the king’s death was true, Paul replied firmly that he had certainly been most faithful to his lord and would remain in that loyalty throughout his life. At this the king, suddenly inflamed with anger, ordered that his hands be cut off without delay. But immediately recovering himself and recalling Paul’s sagacity and prudence, he said with a sigh: ‘If we cut off his hands, where shall we find so elegant a writer?’ And he said to the nobles standing by: ‘Tell me what you think should be done in this matter.’ They replied: ‘Order that his eyes be torn out, lest at some time he send some letters to someone against you.’ ‘And where, or when,’ said the king, ‘shall we be able to find so outstanding a historian or poet?’ Seeing the king’s pity and goodwill toward Paul, they finally advised that he be exiled to the island of Diomedes, now called Tremiti from its three mountains.

“It was done. After he had remained there in exile for several years [ [Col. 1015D] Here is a variant reading from the manuscript of Leo used by Marus, differing from the edition in our collection. If it was as it had hitherto been read in his printed annotations, it was indeed monstrously corrupted and defective. We have restored the beginning of this passage to its correct reading. MUR.], at last he secretly made his way to the monastery of Cassino, renowned for its fame of holiness. There he became a monk, led a devout and religious life, and, surviving long into a good old age, rested in peace, having devoted himself beyond human measure to innocence, humility, and silence.” Thus Leo of Ostia.

Paul is said to have consecrated to immortality many other venerable and outstanding monuments of virtue which did not come to the knowledge of our Peter: namely, [Col. 1016B] a Life of Saint Benedict written in verse, which may be found in Paul himself, book I, chapter 26 of *The Deeds of the Lombards*. Arnold Wion mentions a poem on the Life of Saint Benedict written by Paul the Deacon, each of whose couplets ends with the same words with which it begins; Aymoinus gives it entire in his sermon on Saint Benedict, where he also gives a hymn by the same Paul containing the individual miracles of Saint Benedict. Paul further composed a Life of Saint Maurus the abbot, written with a certain remarkable artistry. It begins:

> Leader, way, life of your own; their honor and praise, glory, strength,  
> Jesus, light of light, leader, way, life of your own.  
>
> You, Almighty One, make dumb creatures speak.  
> Whatever pleases you, you, Almighty One, do.  
>
> Grant, I pray, that I may recount the great deeds of Saint Maurus,  
> Which he performed through you; grant, I pray, that I may recount them, etc.

He also wrote the Life of Saint Scholastica the virgin at the command of Emperor Charlemagne; it is found complete in the third book of the poems of Prosper Martinengius, to whom we therefore refer the curious reader. Likewise, at the command of the same Charles—who died at Aachen in 814, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, aged seventy-one—Paul arranged the histories and readings suitable to the feasts of the saints throughout the whole year. This arrangement was observed by the whole Church and has been kept inviolate down to our own times. We possess in manuscript this note of the arrangement as well. See Emperor Charles’s letter on this arrangement, prefixed to Alcuin’s homiliary.

Moreover, Paul composed several verses on the same Saint Scholastica, found in Arnold Wion’s Martyrology for 10 February. He also wrote the Life of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, formerly chief officer of the household of the king of the Franks and later bishop of Metz. It is found in Surius, volume IV, for 16 August, and in Bede, [Col. 1016D] volume III, although it is falsely attributed to Bede himself. Paul himself indicates in book VI, chapter XVI of *The Deeds of the Lombards* that he wrote a book on the deeds of the bishops of Metz, published by Marquard Freher in the *Corpus of Frankish Historians*. Galesinus testifies that he saw one book on the deeds of the bishops of Pavia. He wrote one letter to Emperor Charles, preserved in manuscript in the library of Cassino, on the right, bench III, no. 179. He wrote a Life of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr, found in Jacques Pamelius’s prolegomena to the works of Saint Cyprian. Verses addressed to Arichis, prince of Benevento and son-in-law of King Desiderius, have now been published by the illustrious Camillus Peregrinus, tireless investigator of antiquities and eminent historian, in his *History of the Lombard Princes*, [Col. 1017A] p. 235 in my copy.

He also celebrated in eloquent verses the deeds and praises of several saints. Outstanding in this genre is his poem on Saint John the Baptist, his patron and protector of the Lombard kingdom. Delighted by its piety and metre, the Roman Church appointed it to be recited; among sacred hymns it is easily foremost in elegance and grace. It begins:

[Col. 1017B] “That they may be able with loosened throats to resound,” etc.

He also composed a hymn on the passion of Saint Mercurius and another for the translation of the body to Benevento. Peter Pipernus of Benevento cites the first in book V, chapter 20 of *On the Effects of Magic*. There likewise survives an Alcaic-dactylic hymn from an old manuscript of the Lombard Church of Benevento, customarily sung in its rite on the feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mother of God, written, as is asserted, by our Paul. It begins:

> Who, mighty one, can with abundant utterance, etc.

We also preserve several manuscript fragments under Paul the Deacon’s name, though mutilated and full of gaps: namely, a Life of the most holy Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, written by Paul the Deacon the historian; an address at the passing of Peter Damian, on resigning the episcopate, in which Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, is mentioned; and Lives of Saint Peter of Damascus, bishop and martyr, and of another Peter, likewise a martyr, written by Paul the Deacon.

Other little works not yet submitted to the press adorn the library of Cassino: namely, manuscript codex no. 146, prefaced by Paul the Deacon’s sermon on the Gospel, “No one lights a lamp,” etc., beginning, “By these words of the holy Gospel,” etc. Likewise codex CXLV, p. 198: a Life of Saint Gregory I, Pope, written in three books by Paul the Deacon, beginning, “Gregory, from the city of Romulus, son of Gordian,” and ending, “On the Ides of March, in the reign,” etc. Likewise codex 305: a sermon by the same Paul the Deacon on the Blessed Virgin, beginning, “Although of all the Saints,” etc.; and his sermon on the Gospel passage, “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts,” etc., beginning, “The present reading of the holy Gospel,” etc. This homily is found among the little works of several holy Fathers published by Thomas Gallet at Lyons in 1615, p. 450. Henry Ernst, in the catalogue of the Medici Library, likewise reports that several homilies of Paul the Deacon are found in the celebrated Medici Library, Pluteus 17, among eight volumes [Col. 1017D] of homilies by different authors.

In the same archive at Cassino are manuscript folio commentaries by Paul the Deacon on the Rule of Saint Benedict. At their beginning is a most ancient picture of Saint Benedict and Abbot John, to whom he hands the Rule, although Hugh Menard has observed that the said commentary should be attributed to Ruthard, a monk and pupil of Rabanus and Strabo. See Haeftenius’s *Monastic Investigations*, book II, tract 5, disquisition 4. Likewise there is a letter of Paul the Deacon to Charlemagne, written in the name of Theodemar and the congregation of Cassino, mentioned by the Ostian in his *Chronicle*. In the same manuscript codex is appended a chronological collection by the same Paul, as some believe; the illustrious Camillus Peregrinus published it, together with a short history under the title *An Unknown Man of Cassino*, at the end of his *History of the Lombard Princes*. Paul is also said to have written one book of letters to various persons.

Finally, it should be observed that the author of the *Miscella* is falsely called Paul the Deacon, as Baronius, volume V of the *Annals*, and Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, prove. See the notes of the most learned Aubert Miraeus on Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 80, and especially Vossius, *On Latin History*, under “Paul,” and *Dissertation 7 on the Year of Christ’s Birth*, p. 5; and Camillus Peregrinus, *History of the Lombard Princes*, [Col. 1018B] who observed that Paul deliberately did not carry the history of the Lombards down to his own times and likewise veiled certain other matters in silence. Alphonsus Ciaconius, in the *Lives of the Popes*, under Leo, says: “The author of the *Miscella* is Paul—or rather John—the Deacon.” But whatever may be the writer’s name, it is certain that in almost all manuscript codices the name read is Paul, not John.

Paul flourished in the year of the Lord 704. Having devoted himself beyond human measure to innocence, humility, and silence, and having lived very austerely and strictly in the monastery of Cassino to the end of his life, he was buried at Cassino before the chapter house, resplendent with the glorious insignia of the greatest merits, as our Peter testifies in the manuscript book *On the Origin and Life of the Just Men of Cassino*, chapter XXV. There survive metrical letters of Charlemagne to our Paul, in which he greatly rejoices at the manner of life Paul had embraced and at the holiness of the sacred monastery of Cassino. We insert part of the letter here [Col. 1018C] so that the most illustrious emperor’s singular humanity toward learned men and his high esteem for the holiness of the sacred monastery of Cassino may be recognized:

> Hence, swiftly departing, may my letter on rapid wing,  
> Through woods and hills, and valleys too, in headlong course,  
> Seek the blessed dwelling of Benedict, dear to God;  
> For there is sure rest for those who arrive weary.  
>
> Here there are vegetables for guests, fish, and abundant bread;  
> Holy peace, a humble mind, and the beautiful concord of brothers;  
> Praise, love, and worship of Christ together at every hour.  
>
> Say to the Father and all his companions: “Greetings and farewell.”  
> Gladly and kindly embrace the neck of my Paul.  
> Say many times: “Hail, best Father, hail.”

Leo of Ostia mentions Paul in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, book I, chapter 17; Sigebert, chapter 80; Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book II, chapter 30; Arnold, [Col. 1018D] book V, chapter 91 of the *Lignum Vitae*; and Thomas Dempster in notes on Roman antiquities. Paul himself writes of himself in many places, as do innumerable others. In a very ancient manuscript codex we read that Paul was a cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, as also in the aforesaid manuscript book of our Peter, *On the Origin and Life of the Just Men of Cassino*, chapter 25, under the heading:

> On Paul, cardinal deacon, etc.

We think copyists or scribes intended to impose this deception on the reader, since in no ecclesiastical records do we find him admitted to the number of cardinals. Or rather, this doubt should be believed to have been introduced by Martin of Poland in the preface to his *Chronicle*, when in his work *On the Deeds of Emperors and Popes* he names a certain Paul, a Roman deacon and cardinal. Yet the difficulty is resolved: our Paul was a deacon of Aquileia and afterward a monk of Cassino; while the one from whom [Col. 1019A] Martin drew is called a Roman deacon and [Col. 1019B] cardinal. See Vossius, *On Latin History*.

There survives an epitaph of Paul the Deacon, composed in verse by Hilderic, monk and abbot of Cassino, a disciple of the aforesaid Paul. Through the singular kindness of the illustrious Carlo Borrelli, Regular Cleric Minor, it was supplied to us from ancient manuscript codex no. 256 of the library of Cassino; we now publish it for the first time.

## EPITAPH OF PAUL THE DEACON

> May fame, most clear, sing you illustrious through the ages,  
> Joined with the blessed companies of the stars.  
> What truthful Levite could set forth your triumphs,  
> Most eminent Paul, in words shining with light?  
>
> Yet, that the hurried reader and the traveler may know  
> That your limbs rest beneath this consecrated tomb,  
> It is fitting to unfold in worthy song, in brief,  
> The life-giving deeds of your beloved praise.  
>
> Long ago you drew your origin from the noble stock  
> Of the race of bards, [Col. 1019C] which then was distinguished  
> In strength, arms, and wealth throughout the world.  
> Worthy indeed was this, since you were born of such offspring  
> Where the river Timavus often has its bright courses.  
>
> By divine prompting, the royal court at once took you  
> To be nurtured, for the glory and light of your native land.  
> Then, beyond the Tiber, your gentle life and learning  
> Found favor with all peoples and lofty kings.  
>
> At the urging of the devout King Ratchis, you fittingly began  
> To penetrate all the heights of sacred wisdom.  
> When you had worthily mastered very many doctrines,  
> You adorned all the northern nations with glowing light,  
> Shining over them like Phoebus from the stars above.  
>
> But let these things now suffice. Though the glory of this fleeting age  
> Rejoicingly enriched you diligently with fitting treasures,  
> Devoted to the life of eternal light without end,  
> You boldly despised the honors of this world.  
>
> Trusting in the mercy of the immeasurable King of heaven,  
> With heart springing toward the Lord Christ you hastened here  
> To submit your neck beneath the enclosure of blessed Benedict.  
>
> [Col. 1019D] There, soon adorned by your examples, the sacred community  
> Began to shine forth like a flashing, glittering beam.  
> For in you continually dwelt piety, sweet love,  
> Nectar-like love of peace, conquering patience,  
> Wise simplicity, the highest concord,  
> And every good thing together, ever-venerable one.  
>
> Therefore now the jewelled kingdoms of heaven hold you,  
> While you retain through the ages likewise a starry crown.  
>
> May this sacred song of honor be pleasing and welcome to you.  
> I, your Hilderic, sang it weeping;  
> Grant, I pray, that I may attain everlasting rest  
> Through your holy prayers, Father ever to be loved.]

Paul, deacon of the patriarchate of Aquileia and notary of King Desiderius, came to Cassino under Abbot Theodemar and took on the monastic habit. Singular in holiness and dignity in his time, and trained in philosophy from childhood, he composed verses in praise of Blessed Benedict arranged in elegiac metre; hymns also to Saint John the Baptist and Saint Benedict; verses to Emperor Charles and to Arichis, prince of Benevento; [Col. 1018A] and he elegantly wrote the Life of Saint Fortunatus, bishop. He also produced fifty homilies, a Life of Saint Gregory the pontiff, an exposition of Saint Benedict’s Rule, and a very eloquent history of the Lombards’ entry into Italy, their origin, and their kingdom. He added a great many matters to Eutropius’s history. He also composed in rhythm all the short readings from the beginning of the world down to his own age, together with an annual computation [Col. 1019A]. He lived in the time of Emperor Charles and was buried in the same monastery, beside the church of Saint Benedict before the chapter house.

## CHAPTER IX. ON HILDERIC

[Note: [Col. 1019D] Hilderic subsequently became abbot of Cassino and died in the same month in which he was elected, namely in the year of the Lord 834, after holding office for seventeen days. We have given above the verses he composed on Paul.] Hilderic, pupil of the same Paul the Deacon, composed very lucid verses on his master’s origin, life, formation, learning, religious vocation, and habit.

## CHAPTER X. ON THEOPHANIUS

[Note: [Col. 1019D] He lived under Emperor Louis the Pious, in the year of the Lord 855. MUR.] Theophanius, a deacon, a most learned and eloquent man, published admirable verses on the construction of the monastery of the Lord Savior, on Saint Benedict’s arrival at Cassino, on the [Col. 1020A] miracles performed by him there, in praise of the holy Mother of God, and on the construction of the monastery of Saint Mary at Plumbariola.

## CHAPTER XI. ON BASSATIUS

[Note: [Col. 1019D] Peter does not explain what the little works are said to have contained which Bassatius, the eighteenth Benedictine abbot [Col. 1020A], wrote, [Col. 1020B] unless we are to understand that, since in his own time he saw the monastic order already in some measure corrupted in Liguria, Burgundy, and Germany, he corrected it by sermons and teachings. He died at Cassino, not without a reputation for holiness, in the year of the Lord 861, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [17 March], and was buried in the chapter house of the brothers beside the church of Saint Benedict, which he had adorned with magnificent decoration.] Bassatius, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, a man devoted to Holy Scripture and sufficiently instructed in the knowledge of ecclesiastical doctrine, composed certain treatises in a style quite polished and clear. He lived in the time of Emperor Louis.

## CHAPTER XII. ON SAINT BERTHARIUS

[Note: [Col. 1020B] Saint Bertharius, descending from the very kings of the Franks, a man conspicuous for such praise of holiness and blameless life, secretly departed from his own people, home, and country, ever revolving in his mind the saying of the ancient poet:

Whoever wishes to be devout, let him leave the royal courts.

Undertaking a religious pilgrimage, he accordingly came from Gaul as far as Monte Cassino; and as soon as he arrived there, he ordered the world to have his possessions. Reckoning all its ornaments, riches, and dignities—which, because of Bertharius’s surpassing nobility, modesty, and talent, were held out to him in no uncertain expectation [Col. 1020C]—as dung, he fled naked to the cross of the naked Christ, and attached himself to the Benedictines at Cassino. Then, after the death of Abbot Bassatius, he was chosen abbot by the common consent of the Fathers in the year of the Lord 856.

During these times Bertharius suffered many injuries from the Saracens who had invaded Italy, because he had summoned aid against them from Gaul and elsewhere and had frequently gone out against them, attacking them and driving them from those territories. Thus immense hatred was stirred up against him. Therefore, one day, the Saracens, having been conveyed by the river Liri, suddenly attacked Bertharius while he was celebrating in the chief church of the monastery of Saint Germanus, and slaughtered him with several monks, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November [22 October], in the year of the Lord 883, while Emperor Louis, son of Emperor Arnulf IV, was reigning. He had presided over the monastery of Cassino for not quite twenty-eight years, having filled up the full measure of his merits.

Consult Leo of Ostia, book I, chapter 46; the *Chronicle of Cassino*; Carlo Sigonio, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book VI; [Col. 1020D] and Camillo Pellegrino, *History of the Lombard Princes*, in the list of the abbots of Cassino, under Bertharius. The acts of his martyrdom, written by Ignatius of Prangia, prior of the monastery of Cassino, remain unpublished in our possession, with this opening: “At the time when the sacred Empire, for the protection of the affairs of the Roman Church,” etc. Labbe also mentions, in his *New Library of Manuscripts*, p. 365, the Life of the same Saint Bertharius composed by the said Ignatius and illustrated with notes by Constantine Cajetan. The Gallican Martyrology also mentions Saint Bertharius under 22 October. On the life and translation of the relics of Saint Bertharius to Monte Cassino, see Wion’s *Martyrology* under 22 October and 2 December.

Saint Bertharius, a distinguished philosopher and physician, wrote much in verse and prose before his conversion: namely, two volumes, gathered from various sources, on innumerable diseases, and several books on grammar. [Col. 1021B] But afterwards, changing his pursuit and becoming a physician of souls, he made one book of sermons and homilies, extant in manuscript in the Cassinese Library, codex shelf-mark no. 107; and one sermon on Saint Matthias the Apostle, beginning: “The illustrious and glorious feast.” See, however, the notes of the monk Michael on the fifth Calendar, under 24 February, in the Capuan *Sanctuary*. He wrote one sermon on Saint Romanus, abbot, beginning: “The day is present to us,” etc.; Arnold Wion likewise mentions it in the Benedictine *Martyrology* under 22 May. The aforesaid small works and treatises had not come to Peter’s knowledge.

[Col. 1021C] The sermon on Saint Luke the Evangelist, which our Peter indicated, is found in the Breviary of the Order of Saint Benedict and also in the Vallicellian Library, as Cardinal Baronius testifies in the *Martyrology* under 18 October. The verses to the Empress Engelberga, as likewise those on the life and death of the most holy Benedict, were printed at Rome in the year of the Lord 1590, and are found in the third volume of poems of Prospero Martinengo, together with two other poems not previously printed; they are also included in the notes to Arnold Wion’s Benedictine *Martyrology* under 21 March.

The book which he entitled *Antikeimenon*, that is, “of opposites” or “contrasts,” concerning the books of both Testaments, was printed at Cologne in the year of the Lord 1503, in octavo, under an uncertain author. For the name of our Saint Bertharius was then unknown to those who brought the book to light. It begins: “Since the first seven days are read in Genesis.” Leo of Ostia mentions this book in book I, chapter 32, in these words: “This man, namely Bertharius, highly learned, composed several treatises and [Col. 1021D] sermons, and also verses in praise of the saints. And his *Anticimenon*, on very many questions from both the Old and New Testaments, is kept here.” Fabianus Justinianus also mentions it in his universal index, under letter A, fol. 30, though unaware of the author’s name. This book is also preserved in a manuscript written in Lombard characters under the name of our Saint Bertharius in the Aniciana Library.

The most learned Leo Allatius, richly and skilfully furnished with every kind of learning and a devourer of books, writes in his work on illustrious men, entitled *Urban Bees*, under “Constantine,” that Bertharius’s works were in the possession of Abbot Constantine Cajetan. Saint Bertharius is discussed by Leo of Ostia in the passage cited; by Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men*; by Sigonio, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book VI; and by others.]

Bertharius, disciple of the aforesaid Bassatius and [Col. 1021A] afterwards made abbot of Cassino, was a man illustrious in birth and letters, conspicuous for uprightness, religion, and the crown of martyrdom. He wrote works not to be despised; but the principal ones are those which he issued after he had become abbot. He wrote a sermon on Saint Luke the Evangelist; composed a homily on blessed Scholastica; and produced an exceedingly difficult book of sayings from both the Old and New Testaments, calling it *Anticimenon* itself. On the life, death, and miracles of the most holy Benedict, and also to the Empress Engelberga and other friends, he composed admirable verses.

But when, because the sins of Christ’s worshippers demanded it, Italy was devastated by the Ishmaelites through God’s just judgment, and he alone for seventeen years and [lacuna] fought most fiercely against their savagery in defence of Christians, [Col. 1021B] the Saracens, having taken counsel, secretly boarded a ship and came to the monastery of the Lord Saviour, situated at the foot of Mount Cassino. [Col. 1022A] They entered the church and found Bertharius, Christ’s martyr, there. When they came to him, they said: “Are you Bertharius, who until now have defended the Christians and twice crossed the mountains to the emperor for their deliverance? It is therefore just that you should receive death for them and for the faith of your God.” Having said this, those same Saracens beheaded him beside the altar of Saint Martin for Christ’s faith.

He suffered in the time of Emperor Louis. His most sacred body was buried beside the church of Saint John the Baptist in the chapter-house at Cassino.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON AUTHPERT

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Authpert, the seventeenth abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, was elected on 16 October in the year 834 and presided for three years. He was taken from the company of mortals on the tenth day before the Kalends of March [20 February] in the year 837, and was buried at Cassino, during the reign of [Col. 1022B] Emperor Lothair. He was a man of composed character, outstanding in religion, not unsuccessful in talent, and of no mean literary culture, as Leo of Ostia testifies in *Chronicle*, book I, chapter 25, Venetian edition.

When he put off his mortal burden, he bequeathed to the Cassinese monks the library which he possessed, furnished with excellent books of every kind. Among other things, the following rare monuments of learning are said to have been given by Authpert: various manuscript homilies of Saint Epiphanius, bishop, extant in codex shelf-mark no. 305; likewise, codex 232 contains a book of Saint Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, *On the Formation of Man*, in the translation of Abbot Dionysius. The letter of Dionysius to Aegypius, priest, begins: “To the most holy lord [Col. 1022C] and greatly venerated by me.” Attached also to codex 232 is the book *On the Christian Life* by Fastidius, bishop of the Britons, who in Vatican codex 551 is called Fastidiosus. It begins: “That I, a sinner and the last, more foolish than the rest,” etc.; it occupies fourteen quarto folios. On this work see Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 56; and Vossius, *On Latin History*, book II, chapter 19, under Dionysius.

Likewise, on the fifth shelf to the left, codex shelf-mark no. 29 contains the *Etymological Dictionary* of Auxilius, priest, an excellent and very ancient book. On the same shelf, codex shelf-mark no. 30 contains various learned theological works by the same Auxilius, priest: first, 137 questions on the Hexaemeron; second, other questions, nearly all on Genesis; third, thirty-six chapters of distinctions; fourth, *On the Distinction of the Four Vices*; fifth, *On the Trinity*, in questions and answers, where he subsequently explains nearly all the names occurring in ecclesiastical matters—for example, what is a neophyte, a catechumen, or one seeking baptism; sixth, *On the Divine Offices*, by question and answer: for example, whence [Col. 1022D] the Mass takes its name, etc.; whence a station takes its name and what difference exists between a station and a fast; what abstinence is, etc.; what xerophagy is and what reconciliation is, etc.

Some assert that the aforementioned manuscript works, as well as almost innumerable others which now adorn the Cassinese Library, were given as a magnificent gift by our Authpert. For libraries in monasteries are, as it were, arsenals of spiritual warfare and treasuries of religious riches.

Besides the works set forth by our Peter, Authpert wrote various further homilies and sermons: on the Assumption of Blessed Mary, beginning, “The day is present to us, beloved”; on her Nativity, or a common sermon for her feasts, beginning, “Today’s celebration”; and a sermon on the feast of All Saints, beginning, “The day is present, beloved,” etc. These sermons are preserved in manuscript in the Cassinese Library, codex shelf-mark no. 305. A sermon in praise of Saint Matthias the Apostle is believed still to be unpublished.

[Col. 1023A] The following manuscript works circulate under the name of our Abbot Authpert, but incorrectly: a sermon *On Avarice*, very useful for secular men, containing eighty testimonies from Scripture, beginning, “The Church of the saints”; a sermon for the Purification [Col. 1023B] of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which is also printed in Alcuin’s Homiliary, beginning, “If the faithful carefully”; a sermon for the Dedication of a Church, beginning, “See the holy city Jerusalem”; a prayer against the seven-times-seven vices, beginning, “The highest and incomprehensible nature”; a homily on the Gospel passage of Saint Mark, “Jesus took Peter, James, and John,” beginning, “It can sometimes happen”; this appears in the Breviary of the Church of Atina, written in Lombard characters and divided into three lessons, under 6 August; and the Life of the holy Fathers Paldus, Tato, and Taso, abbots of the monastery of Saint Vincent at the Volturno, beginning, “The first parent of the human race.” On this see Ferrari’s *Catalogue of Saints* under 11 October, 11 January, and 11 December, and Bollandus under 11 January.

These aforesaid works are wrongly attributed to our Authpert, since they acknowledge as their author Ambrose Autbert, otherwise Ansbert, monk and abbot of Saint Vincent at the Volturno near Capua, who flourished in the year of the Lord 890 and was master in humane letters to Charlemagne. [Col. 1023C] On him see Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 91, and Aubertus Miraeus, supplement to *On Writers*, chapter 257. Some of his writings were printed at Cologne in the year of the Lord 1536, folio. Certainly, as regards the above-mentioned works, which we also preserve in manuscript, they bear the name of Ambrose Authpert, abbot of Saint Vincent, not of Cassino.

Moreover, this Authpert is called Rupert by some in the *Philosophical Library* and elsewhere, who say that he lived in 1040; but this is a double error, namely in the name and in the number of years. For no Rupert is found in the catalogue of Cassinese abbots, and in 1040 Richerius was abbot of the monastery of Cassino.]

Authpert, abbot of the same monastery, a man eloquent [Col. 1022B] and highly learned, composed, among many splendid monuments of his talent, very beautiful homilies in praise of Saint Matthias the Apostle, on the Purification of the holy Mother of God, and on other [Col. 1023A] saints. He lived in the time of Emperor Lothair.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON ERCHEMPERT

[Note: [Col. 1023C] Erchempert—called by others Herempert or Herembert—sprang from an illustrious Lombard stock, deriving his lineage from the dukes of Benevento. His father was named Radelgarius, his great-great-grandfather Rodoalt, and his paternal uncle Radolphus. [Col. 1023D] He was a man not undistinguished in nobility of blood and learning, and exceptionally knowledgeable in history; yet born only for the hardships of human life.

He wrote a chronicle, or history, of the Lombards, whose original is believed to have perished. Nevertheless, our Peter testifies in the supplement to the *Chronicle of Cassino*, book III, chapter 62, Venetian edition, that it was copied at the command of Abbot Desiderius of Cassino, who later became Pope Victor III. An epitome of this fuller history—or rather, a continuation of Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*—completed in the year 888, as is believed, by Erchempert himself, was first published from a Vatican manuscript by the distinguished Antonio Caracciolo of the Order of Clerks Regular, with notes, at Naples in 1626, quarto, together with the chronicles of Lupus Protospatharius, Falco of Benevento, and others.

Finally, the most learned Camillo Pellegrino appended the aforesaid chronicle or epitome, furnished with scholia, to his Lombard history with his customary diligence and learning. [Col. 1024A] Whoever wishes for more may consult his apparatus and notes. See also Philippe Labbe, *New Library of Manuscript Books*, part I, pp. 10 and 366.

Erchempert further wrote a poem on the life [Col. 1024B] of Landulf, bishop of Capua; see Michael the monk’s Capuan *Sanctuary*, and also the aforesaid Pellegrino’s preface to the said history, p. 15. The acts of the translation of Saint Matthew the Apostle are likewise thought to have been committed to writing by Erchempert, perhaps those published by Colonna, archbishop of Salerno. Yet the aforesaid acts, which we possess in manuscript, bear the name of Paulinus, bishop of Legio or London in Britain; their opening is: “Matthew, evangelist and apostle, when first into Judaea,” etc.

It should also be observed that the works to which our Peter gave the titles *On the Destruction and Renewal of the Monastery of Cassino* and *On the Incursion of the Ishmaelites* do not survive, unless we choose to say that both calamities were described in the aforesaid chronicle or history. Consult the distinguished Vossius, *On Latin History*, book III. Finally, Leo of Ostia often mentions Erchempert in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, from whom he seems to have drawn much, as in book I, chapters 9, 19, and 46. [Col. 1024C] It is likewise easy to see that Cardinal Baronius drew much from Erchempert’s history and inserted it in his annals. Read him under the years 871, 872, 874, and 912.

In what precise year Erchempert laid aside the burden of his mortal body is unknown. One may indeed suppose 889, since he had seen and described the year 888 as it ended, and had not carried his history further, although he had promised to do so. The aforesaid Pellegrino therefore conjectures that our Peter had not sampled Erchempert’s history when he reports that he flourished under Emperor Louis, whereas we know that he lived under Charles the Great. For Charles reigned from the year 881 to 898.]

Erchempert, deacon, likewise offered as a little child to Blessed Benedict, composed a sufficiently necessary history of the destruction and restoration of the monastery of Cassino and also of the Ishmaelite incursion. He lived in the time of Emperor Louis.

## CHAPTER XV. ON JOHN

[Col. 1024A]

[Note: [Col. 1024C] Abbot John, born in an illustrious family at Capua and kinsman of Princes Landulf I and Atenulf II, was a man unbroken in spirit, learned in letters, and as conspicuous in holiness as in learning. Formerly archdeacon of Capua, he became a monk of Cassino. At the time when, in the year of the Lord 915, the monastery of Cassino had been devastated by the Saracens and the monks were living at Capua, he was created abbot because of his exceptional maturity of character. Radiant with every virtue, he sought the thresholds of heaven in the year of the Lord 934. He was buried in the Capuan monastery and afterwards is recorded in the rolls of the saints of Cassino on the day before the Kalends of April [31 March]. Ferrari mentions him in the new catalogue of saints.

Leo of Ostia writes about him in *Chronicle*, book I, chapters 56, 57, and 58; our Peter in the manuscript work *On the Origin and Life of the Righteous Men of Cassino*, chapter 36; and Vossius in *On Latin History*. See Michael the monk’s Capuan *Sanctuary*, p. 157, where he treats John at length. The chronicle which he wrote concerning the persecutions of the monastery of Cassino and the miracles done there still remains unpublished. It is believed to be the work which Leo of Ostia says he used in the prologue of his *Chronicle*, in these words: “I have relied principally upon the chronicles of Abbot John, who first built [Col. 1025A] our monastery in New Capua.”

Camillo Pellegrino, *History of the Lombard Princes*, fol. 122, published another, hitherto unpublished chronicle of the later counts of Capua under the name of our Abbot John, though the autograph lacked John’s name. This was not uncommon among ancient writers, especially monks, who customarily concealed their names when publishing books out of modesty, as the most distinguished Sixtus of Siena noted [Col. 1025B] in his *Library*, book IV, under “Mammotreptus,” and Theophilus Raynaudus in connection with Raymond Jordan, who until then had borne the name “the Idiot.”]

John, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Cassino, a man noble in flesh and spirit, wrote a brief but highly necessary chronicle of the persecutions of that monastery and of the miracles performed there. He was buried in the monastery at Capua.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON THEODERIC

[Col. 1025A]

[Note: [Col. 1025B] Whoever wishes to know who Saint Firmanus was should consult Cardinal Baronius in his *Ecclesiastical Annals* under the year 993, where he also cites Saint Peter Damian, before whose time Firmanus lived. Hence Ferrari, in his catalogue of saints under 2 March, reads as follows: “Firmanus, born at Fermo in Picenum, flourished in admirable holiness. He was enrolled among the holy Confessors not by solemn rite, but by the mere erection of an altar or chapel.”

Arnold Wion, book II, chapter 78 of the *Tree of Life*, writes the following under Theodoric: “Theodoric, monk and priest of the monastery of Cassino, wrote one book on the life of Saint Firmanus, bishop, and one hymn on Saint Maurus, abbot.” Vossius, *On Latin History*, under Theodoric, calls him Firminus and says that he was the first bishop of Amiens in Gaul, who died as a martyr in the time of Diocletian, seven days before the Kalends of October [25 September]. But both, we believe, were deceived merely by the similarity of names, or perhaps by the reading of a corrupted manuscript. For our Theodoric wrote the life of Saint Firmanus, a confessor of the Order of Saint Benedict, not of Firmianus, bishop, nor likewise of Firminus, bishop.

Firmanus was indeed a monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabinus in the city of Fermo, but not a bishop; and he died before Pope Leo IX. Formerly an altar dedicated to this saint could be seen in Fermo Cathedral, and his feast was celebrated with a great concourse of people in the church of Saint James at the foot of Mount Gerio, where they had likewise consecrated an altar worthy of being seen. It is also recorded that Hubert, bishop of Fermo, granted not only the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, situated near the sea on the estate of Rejano, in the year of the Lord 1016 to Abbot Firmanus and the monks of Saint Benedict, but also many other goods and estates in the year 1010; Leo of Ostia recounts this in *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 26.

See the most learned Ughelli, eminent in every virtue, a constant cultivator and most diligent investigator in collecting ecclesiastical monuments, vol. II of *Sacred Italy*, in the catalogue of the bishops of Fermo under Hubert. [Col. 1025D] Theodoric flourished about the year of the Lord 1012.]

Theodoric, priest of the Cassinese school, a man deservedly to be praised among ecclesiastical writers, wrote in elegant style the history of Saint Firmanus, confessor of Christ, and a hymn in praise of the most blessed Maurus.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON STEPHEN

[Col. 1026A]

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Pope Stephen X, previously Frederick of the most noble family of Lorraine—some count him as the ninth, because they do not enter in the catalogue of pontiffs Stephen II of that name, successor of Pope Zachary, since he spent only three days in the pontificate; but this reason certainly ought not to erase him from the list of supreme pontiffs—was therefore brother of the great Godfrey, king of Jerusalem. He was indeed well known for nobility of blood, but far more illustrious in brilliance of mind and learning.

By Pope Leo IX, his kinsman, he was made cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Domnica in the year of the Lord 1050, and also chancellor and librarian of the Holy Roman Church. He was sent to Constantinople to reconcile [Col. 1026A] the Greek Church with the Latin. He deposed Michael Cerularius, patriarch of that city, and bound him with the bond of anathema. Returning from there, weary of the world and holding as certainly true the maxim of the philosopher celebrated by Plutarch in a special treatise, “Live in obscurity,” he sought Cassino. There, laying aside the insignia of honours, he wholly conformed himself to the exact rule of religious humility; and after two years, by the unanimous votes of the monks, he was created [Col. 1026B] abbot in place of Richerius in 1057, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June [29 May], the Friday after Pentecost, Peter having been deposed, because he had been rashly intruded.

In order to seek confirmation of the office conferred upon him—for it was not lawful to assume the Cassinese prefecture without the authorization of the Roman pontiff—he went to Florence, where Pope Victor II was then residing. From him he received not only the abbacy, which he had sought, but was also again made cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, having been archdeacon of Santa Maria in Domnica. By this second promotion he alone, contrary to expectation and desire, was appointed in 1057. On his return from Tuscany, while he was still staying at Rome, the death of Victor having been announced, he was chosen in the deceased pontiff’s place through Boniface, bishop of Albano, by a remarkable unanimity of the sacred senate. He was so unwilling and resistant that he had to be dragged by force from his lodging to the Basilica of Saint Peter in Chains. Mourning, he said to those arranging the pontificate for him: “You can do nothing concerning me except what God permits; and without His nod you can neither give me nor take this from me.”

On the following day, consecrated in the Vatican amid the great acclamation and rejoicing of every order, he was distinguished by the name Stephen X in the year of the Lord 1057, on Saturday, 2 August, because the feast of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, was celebrated that day. Thus Frederick, not yet four years a monk, was within almost one month in that year proclaimed abbot of Cassino, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and finally supreme pontiff.

He immediately governed the Christian commonwealth, though he had assumed it most unwillingly, with great prudence. Applying himself to restoring ancient discipline, he made many pious and prudent enactments, especially against concubinage and the many other vices of the clergy. Hence he ordered all clergy residing in Rome who had remained incontinent after Pope Leo’s prohibition to leave the assembly of clerics and the choir of the Church. God showed signs of vengeance against those disobedient persons who resisted his most holy ordinance, as [Col. 1026D] our Peter noted in the manuscript work *On the Origin and Life of the Righteous Men of Cassino*, chapter 58, concerning a certain priest who, living beside the canonry of Blessed Cecilia in Trastevere, refused to put away a woman, regarding these decrees as vain and frivolous. “While he was,” Peter says, “whole, vigorous, and healthy, he lay down in his bed to rest in the evening; but struck by the sudden punishment of divine vengeance, he died by a sudden death.”

The same pontiff also rebuked and corrected the lives of false monks and nuns; he condemned the Simoniacal heresy for ever. He made the Church of Milan, which for almost two hundred years had insolently withdrawn itself from subjection to the Roman Church, obedient to it. Finally, while wholly applying himself to the correction of depraved morals, yet always of weak health, he exchanged life for death—or rather for heaven—at Florence, amid the singular grief and mourning of all, on 28 April in the year 1058. He was buried there in the cathedral church [Col. 1027A] of Reparata, without any inscription, after sitting for ten months. During his whole life he had retained for himself the abbacy of Cassino; nevertheless, he appointed Desiderius, a monk of that monastery who afterwards was called Pope Victor III, as his deputy there, following the example [Col. 1027B] of Pope Leo IX, who had retained the bishopric of Toul during his life while appointing a suffragan.

He admitted Saint Peter Damian, though resisting, into the college of cardinals on the Ember Saturday of March, and also consecrated him bishop of Ostia. Accordingly Damian himself called Stephen “his persecutor” in a letter to Nicholas II. Likewise, Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, called him “holy Satan,” as an adversary with good intention, namely because he stubbornly opposed Hildebrand’s vows to return to the hermitage, in a letter addressed to Pope Alexander II.

The deeds of Stephen were written by Sigebert in his *Chronicle* under the year 1058; by Leo of Ostia in the *Chronicle*, book II, chapters 77, 96, 100, and 101, who writes that in his own time many miracles were performed at Stephen’s tomb; and by others. His holiness is mentioned in the martyrologies of Arnold Wion, Hugh Menard, and André Saussay. See also Lambert of Schafnaburg, *German History*, [Col. 1027C] under 1058; Frizon, *Purpled Gaul*; Sigonio, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book IX; and others.

Besides the works mentioned by Peter, he wrote a letter to Gervasius Barbet, forty-third archbishop of Rheims; it is found in volume II of the *Library of the Fathers*, volume VII of the *Councils* in Baronius under the year 1057, no. 33, and in Papirius Masson. Yet it is wrongly said to be addressed to William instead of Gervasius, since no archbishop of Rheims of that name is found in that whole century. He is said to have written various papal diplomas while discharging the office of librarian and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church. His decrees are said by Possevino, in the *Apparatus*, to have been printed at Cologne with others. If you wish to see more concerning Stephen’s writings, consult Rupipozeus, bishop of Poitiers, in his nomenclature; Cardinal Possevino in the said *Apparatus*; and Claude Robert under Gervasius Barbet.]

Stephen, pontiff of the Holy Roman Church, a most learned and exceptional man, formerly chancellor of the Holy Roman Church and abbot of the said monastery of Cassino, most noble alike in flesh and spirit after the death of Richerius, was travelling to the city of Rome [Col. 1027A] for the confirmation of his consecration when, after the death of Victor, ruler of the Church, he was elected Roman pontiff by the cardinals and bishops.

At Constantinople, together with Humbert, he wrote against Michael, the illegitimate patriarch of that city, a book *On the Body of the Lord*, in which he refuted everything that the Greeks brought forward against the Latin sacrifice. He also published another book on the same subject against a certain monk of Constantinople. He flourished in the time of Emperors Constantine and Henry, and was buried in the city [Col. 1028A] of Florence, where God does not cease, even to the present day, to work many signs through him.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON VICTOR

[Note: [Col. 1027C] Pope Victor III, Dauferius in the world and afterwards, as a monk, called Desiderius, was the only child of the Beneventan prince of Samnium. Born of the Epiphanius family in the year of the Lord 1027, he placed his loves and delights in heaven from his earliest years and secretly withdrew into the wilderness, for he was a stern despiser of the world. Then, through the intervention of the Roman pontiff, he was admitted among the Cassinese monks, desiring nothing but to remain hidden and unknown. Thus it could truly be said of him what is now read in the portrait of Thomas à Kempis: “In all things I sought rest, but found it only in hidden retreats and little books.”

Not long afterwards, namely in 1056, at the age of thirty, he was elected abbot of Cassino. Before the election he saw in a vision Saint Benedict, with a cheerful face, beckoning to him with outstretched hand and ordering him to sit beside him; this vision indicated that he was to become abbot of the monastery of Cassino. He was sent by the Roman pontiff as legate to Emperor Michael for the conduct of matters of great importance. Returning from that embassy, he again undertook the administration of the monastery of Cassino and was admitted by Pope Nicholas II, in the year of the Lord 1059, among the cardinals with the title of Saint Cecilia.

After Gregory VII had died at Salerno, Desiderius was, by universal consent, placed at the head of the Christian commonwealth. On receiving the news, as though struck by the unforeseen blow of a sudden calamity, [Col. 1028B] he could never be persuaded to consent to the election, expressly declaring that he did not wish to be pope. Laying aside the cross, scarlet mantle, and the other pontifical vestments—except the alb, which they could not put upon him while he resisted—he returned to his own people at Cassino in a noble flight from the world. But because it had been decided that no one else, while he survived and lived, should be raised to that summit of dignity, overcome by the importunate prayers of clergy and princes, he accepted the pontificate in the year of the Lord 1086, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June [24 May]. Yet he did not allow himself to be consecrated until the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April [20 March], Palm Sunday, in 1087, at the diaconia of Saint Lucy at the Septizonium.

At the time when Victor was celebrating the divine service in the monastery of Cassino, he ascended to the height of immortal glory in the sixtieth year of his age, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October [16 September]. Some suspect that poison had been poured into his cup through the plots of Emperor Henry IV and the antipope; see Genebrard, *Chronicle*, book IV. He was worthy to live an innumerable series [Col. 1028C] of years, having presided in the Apostolic See from the beginning of his election for one year and, from his consecration, four months and seven days. He is entered in the Benedictine Martyrology under 16 September with this encomium: “At the monastery of Cassino, the death of Blessed Victor III, Pope, most renowned for holiness of life and the glory of miracles.”

Emperor Michael of Constantinople, revering our Victor, who was widely famed, sent messengers and many gifts to him, asking him to pray to God for himself, his sons, and the condition of the empire. Leo of Ostia, in the prologue to book III of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, called Desiderius an admirable and exceptional man of his order; and Saint Peter Damian called him “the archangel of monks.” His tomb is seen in the chapel of Saint Bertharius, abbot and martyr, at the left side of the altar, adorned with this epitaph:

> Whoever I was, what I was, what kind and how great,  
> if anyone perchance wishes to learn, let the golden writings tell.
>
> [Col. 1028D] My stock was of magnates; Benevento my native land;  
> Desiderius my name; and you, Cassino, my glory.
>
> Despising an untouched bride, my mother, my homeland, and my kinsmen,  
> I hasten here and become a monk.
>
> Then made abbot, I strove in my time wholly  
> to renew this place—as it is now seen.
>
> Meanwhile I was renowned in the Roman City,  
> a priest of your Church, blessed Peter.
>
> Having discharged this office for five lustra less one year,  
> I then ascended as Victor to the Apostolic throne.
>
> And after scarcely four months and a half had passed,  
> having lived twice six lustra, I died and was buried here.
>
> The last light of the sun stood in the maidenly Sign,
When the true Sun, God himself, bore me hence.

He is said to have written much during his lifetime; among his works there survive only the *Dialogues*, published under this title: *Dialogues of Victor III, Roman Pontiff, formerly Desiderius, Abbot of Monte Cassino*. For in them are read various miracles performed by Saint Benedict and other monks in the Cassinese monastery [Col. 1029B] and elsewhere. A few years ago we published these at Rome in octavo, drawn from the Vatican Library, and elucidated them with notes. His chant composed concerning Saint Maurus—for he was most expert in music and the medical art—is read in the choir-school of the Cassinese monastery. Note, however, that the *magadium* named in that chant is the part of the lyre against which the plectrum strikes, that is, where the strings are struck with the right hand, as Budé observed. See Dom Jean Bona, of the Congregation of Saint Bernard, Cistercian Order, a most worthy abbot, a man furnished with every kind of literary learning and nobly equipped, in both verse and prose, with the powerful resources of all disciplines, *On the Harmony of the Church that Sings Psalms*, ch. 17, §3, no. 5, near the end.

[Col. 1029C] The deeds of Victor are treated by Leo of Ostia throughout book III; Binius in vol. VII of the *Councils*; Sigonius, book III of *On the Kingdom of Italy*; Arnold Wion, book V, p. 633 of the *Lignum vitae*; Albert Krantz; Baronius under the year 1087; Camillo Pellegrino, *History of the Lombard Princes*, in the series of Cassinese abbots under Desiderius; and others.]

Victor, likewise supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See and abbot of Monte Cassino, was filled with the compunction born of the fear of God, singular in chastity, and a monk by profession and practice. Leaving his bride at the wedding, he sought the wilderness and there assumed the habit of holy religion. His parents pursued his flight with raging fury; having found him [Col. 1029A], they stripped him of his monastic garb, clothed him in military garments, and led him as far as Samnium, to his mother’s house. Then, having found an opportunity, he escaped and sought the monastery of the Holy Trinity. From there he came to the hermitage of Majella, and then to Monte Cassino, where he received monastic consecration. Later, when made abbot, he renewed the entire Cassinese monastery. Moreover, together with Theophilus the deacon, he published four books concerning miracles performed by Blessed Benedict and the Cassinese monks. He also composed a chant for Blessed Maurus, in which anyone who follows the path of grammatical art will find the musical notes of the sounding monochord and the *magade* [*magadium*]. Later, made pontiff of the Apostolic See, he wrote many letters to Philip, king of the Franks, and to Hugh, abbot of Cluny [Col. 1029B]. He flourished in the times of the emperors Michael, Constantine, Alexius, and [Col. 1030A] Henry. He was buried in the apse of the chapter house at Monte Cassino.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON ALPHANUS

[Note: [Col. 1029C] Alphanus of Salerno, first a monk of Monte Cassino, then, at the request of Prince Gisulf, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Salerno, and finally appointed archbishop of that city, is recorded as having attended the Roman council under Pope Nicholas II in the year of the Lord 1057. He is said to have possessed so great a brilliance of learning joined to holiness of life that he was regarded as a miracle by the people of that age: a philosopher, theologian, and orator of the highest reputation, and exceptionally eloquent in poetic art. Nor should it be thought alien to episcopal dignity that he made especial use of poetry in the praises of God, since Paul, Doctor of the Gentiles, commands that God be celebrated in hymns and songs; [Col. 1029D] nor, from the very beginning of the nascent Church, have examples been lacking. In this company the leaders are Pope Damasus, Gregory of Nazianzus, John of Damascus, Paulinus, Fortunatus, Prosper, Sidonius, and the other bishops.

The writings which our Peter noted are published by the distinguished Ughelli at the end of vol.
