II of *Italia Sacra*, except for the verses which he wrote in praise of Romuald the legal advocate and Sigismund, monk of Monte Cassino, which we preserve in manuscript. Besides the works already listed, Alphanus composed certain notable treatises of profound meaning: one book *On the Union of the Word of God and Man*; one book *On the Union of Body and Soul*; and one book *On the Four Humours of the Body*. These monuments of most consummate learning existed as manuscripts in the Cassinese Library, on shelf 8 to the left. Whether they remain there today we have not yet discovered, although we have diligently sought them among the investigators of ecclesiastical antiquities.

The *Passion of the Holy Twelve Martyr Brothers of Benevento*—though they did not suffer on one day—which he wrote in heroic verse in honour of those saints for Brother Roffridus, a Cassinese monk, is read in Lippomano, vol. IV, and Surius, vol. VII, under 1 September; Galesinius also mentions it in the notes to his *Martyrology*. A manuscript is likewise preserved in our modest literary storehouse. It should nevertheless be noted that the published verses are corrected not only from this manuscript copy of ours, but that the heroic metre is also completed from another hundred verses hitherto unpublished. For it continues:

> Thus, in many seasons, the sacred bodies of the saints, etc.

[Col. 1030C] It ends thus:

> Now let the work, enclosed in its thousand verses, come to a halt.

God willing, we shall publish the aforesaid history corrected according to the authority of the said manuscript codex and complete in every respect. He also wrote commentaries on other saints, which Possevino lists though Trithemius passed them over. Books of other hymns and poems, together with epitaphs, have partly been printed in vol. III of Prospero Martinengo’s poems, quarto, Rome, 1589, and in vol. XII of the *Annals* of Cardinal Baronius; and partly at the end of vol. II of *Italia Sacra*. Among the minor works of Guaiferius of Salerno, Cassinese monk, codex no. 280 of the Cassinese Library, all Alphanus’s poems are now inserted.

Alphanus shone brightly upon all like the sun, showing his subjects examples of virtue and the path to happiness. He flourished in the last years of Henry III and the first of Henry IV, namely from the year of the Lord 1057 until [Col. 1030D] the year 1086, after the twenty-ninth year of his episcopate, in the month of May. He was also numbered among the saints, says Arnold Wion. Accordingly, Falcon’s *Chronicle*, published by the distinguished Antonio Caracciolo, must be corrected. Its index reads: “Alphanus, Archbishop of Salerno, died in the year 1121, succeeded by Romuald, writer of the *Chronicle*. Falco, p. 220.” He was the author of poems preserved by the Vatican Library, as Baronius attests, vol. XII, under the year 1111. He is distinct from that elder Alphanus who was consecrated archbishop in 1058, concerning whom Leo of Ostia speaks, book II, chs. 99 and 100. For our Alphanus, the author of the poems, was elected and consecrated Archbishop of Salerno by Pope Stephen X in 1057, not the elder Alphanus, as Leo of Ostia clearly teaches in the *Chronicle*, book II, ch. 97, and also book III, chs. 7, 8, and 35. See Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, under “Alphanus.”]

Alphanus, Archbishop of Salerno and monk of the Cassinese monastery, was a man learned in the Holy Scriptures and fully instructed in the knowledge of ecclesiastical doctrines. In bare and most lucid language he composed the *Passion of Saint Christina*; moreover, two hymns on the same virgin; verses on Saint Benedict addressed to Pandulf, bishop of the Marsi; a chant for Saint Sabina; verses on Saint Christina and Saint Peter the Apostle; and verses in praise of the Cassinese monks; on the site, construction, and restoration of the same monastery; a Sapphic hendecasyllabic poem on Saint Maurus; [Col. 1030B] likewise hymns upon him; three hymns on Saint Matthew; two on Saint Fortunatus; one on Saint Nicholas; [Col. 1031A] poems addressed to Atto, bishop of Theate; to Gisulf, prince of Salerno; to Sigismund, Cassinese monk; to William, grammarian of the same place; to Guy, brother of the prince of Salerno; to Geoffrey, bishop of Aversa; to Hildebrand, Roman archdeacon; to Romuald, legal advocate of Salerno; and to Roffridus, Cassinese monk; a heroic poem in honour of the twelve holy brothers; his metrical confession; verses on the Church of Saint John the Baptist at Monte Cassino; very many epitaphs of eminent men; and other works which have not come to our knowledge. He lived in the times of the aforesaid emperors and was buried at Salerno.

## CHAPTER XX. ON AMATUS

[Col. 1032A]

[Note: [Col. 1031B] Amatus was from the province of Campania, a writer of his age not to be despised, and afterwards a bishop, though of an uncertain see. He wrote for Pope Gregory VII *On the Deeds of the Apostles Peter and Paul*. He dedicated his *History of the Normans* to Abbot Desiderius, who became Pope Victor III. Our Peter is witness in the supplement to the Cassinese *Chronicle*, book III, ch. 35. Some affirm that it no longer exists except as a manuscript in the Cassinese Library—surely no small benefit to ecclesiastical and secular history, since many things worthy of knowledge are accurately described in it, and especially the customs and deeds of the Normans are faithfully set forth.

For careful observers have noticed that foreigners have generally observed and committed to writing the customs, rites, and antiquity of every people more accurately than the inhabitants themselves. We need not go far afield: the Greeks Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plutarch of Chaeronea, Dio Cassius, and Herodian treated Roman affairs more fully, each in his own genre, than the Latin writers Livy, [Col. 1031C] Velleius Paterculus, and the rest. Amatus was living in the year of the Lord 1070, when Alberic, Constantine, Guaiferius, and Alphanus likewise flourished among the Cassinese in holiness and learning.]

Amatus, bishop and Cassinese monk, most eloquent in the Scriptures and a remarkable versifier, wrote verses for Pope Gregory *On the Deeds of the Apostles Peter and Paul*, dividing them into four books. He also wrote *In Praise of the Same Pontiff*; *On the Twelve Stones*; and *On the Heavenly City Jerusalem*. He likewise produced a *History of the Normans*, divided into eight books. He lived in the times of the aforesaid emperors.

## CHAPTER XXI. ON ALBERIC

[Note: [Col. 1031C] Alberic, Cassinese monk and cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church of Saints Four Crowned Martyrs, was created by Pope Stephen X; others read, by Pope Alexander II. He was a most eloquent man, illustrious in his age for many virtues, and is again commemorated by our Peter the Deacon with a sufficiently honourable eulogy in the supplement to Leo of Ostia’s *Chronicle*, book III, ch. 35.

Within scarcely the interval of a whole week he produced, against the heresiarch Berengar, a book *On the Body of the Lord*, strengthened by the testimonies of the Fathers. By it he entirely overthrew all Berengar’s assertions, defeated and routed him for a second time under Gregory VII, in the Roman synod of 1079, and thus deserved to be called the defender of so great a sacrament. Subsequently Berengar, chiefly overcome [Col. 1031D] and defeated by Alberic’s arguments, moved to repentance, confessed his error, undertook a pilgrimage, and for the whole remainder of his life made satisfaction for his sin. He died in the year of the Lord 1088, on the day of Epiphany, at the age of ninety, and was buried in the church of Saint Cosmas near Tours. So writes Claude Robert in his *Gallia Christiana*, where he treats of the bishops of Angers. See the notes of the distinguished Aubertus Miraeus on Sigebert, ch. 154.

Berengar’s abjuration may be found in the chapter “*Ego Berengarius*,” *De consecratione*, distinction 2; another in the *Register of Gregory VII*, books III and VI, in the Synod. What gave occasion for this repetition is explained in the scholia on the councils, printed at Cologne in four volumes. See Bellarmine, book III *On the Eucharist*, ch. 8, col. 3; Blondus, decade 2, book III; Lanfranc; and Guitmund against Berengar.

Cardinal Baronius notes, vol. II, under the year 1059, that Leo of Ostia spoke very boastfully and most falsely concerning Alberic, in attributing to him more than is proper of the glorious victory won in the synod against Berengar. Matteo Laureto refutes this objection in *On the Existence of the Body of Saint Benedict*, ch. 42, p. 204. It is still more important to observe that the remarks which Baronius noted are not Leo’s, but those of our Peter the Deacon. Beginning after Leo with the restoration of the Church of Saint Martin—that is, at book III, ch. 34 of the Neapolitan edition—Peter continued the Cassinese *Chronicle*. In that section, namely ch. 35, the praises and eulogies of Alberic are written, or repeated anew, by Peter.

Our Peter mentions Alberic in his manuscript book *On the Life of the Just Men of Monte Cassino*, ch. 48, under Guaiferius, in these words:

> And when the eternal Judge had decreed to grant him [Guaiferius] the recompense of his labours and the everlasting crown, he was laid low by illness. Lying in bed, he was drawing out the last span of life and was now about to return to the Lord. Some of the brethren, keeping watch around his bed, began to fortify his death with the prayers of their devotions. When they had spent the greater part of the day in this service, [Col. 1032C] Alberic the deacon arose in their midst and began, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, to entreat Guaiferius that, after his departure from the world, he would take care to appear to him and reveal how he had been received and to what place he had been assigned. With these words, the aforesaid brother departed this world. Not many days afterward, the same Guaiferius appeared to Alberic in a vision and said to him: “Know in truth that I have passed into eternal life.”

These are Peter’s words. All Alberic’s writings are preserved in manuscript in the library of the monastery of Holy Cross of the Conventual Friars Minor of Saint Francis in Florence. The *Life of Saint Scholastica* is also preserved in manuscript in the Cassinese Library, codex no. 146, p. 253; after it follows a homily by the same Alberic, beginning: “You have heard, dearest brethren.”

In the *Life of Saint Dominic*, performer of innumerable miracles, a Cassinese monk and abbot near Sora in Italy—though he is painted in Cistercian dress, whereas it is certain that he lived long before the Cistercian reform, according to the Benedictine observances of Monte Cassino—written by our Alberic and published by the distinguished Bollandus, vol. II, under 22 January, some material is lacking which could be supplied from our manuscript copy. Baronius mentions Saint Dominic under the year 1031, and Ferrarius in the *Catalogue of Saints*.

Furthermore, it must be noted that he is distinct from another Alberic, likewise a Cassinese monk, who wrote a book concerning his vision and was born about the year 1101. For our Peter records in the supplement to Leo of Ostia’s *Chronicle*, book IV, ch. 66, that at the age of ten he sought the Cassinese monastery under Abbot Gerard, who ruled from 1111 to 1123. But Pope Stephen X, by whom our Alberic was admitted to the college of cardinals, died in 1058. He is therefore plainly shown to be a different person, and Bollandus must be corrected in the prolegomena to the aforesaid *Life of Saint Dominic*, where he supposes them to be one and the same.

Moreover, it should be observed that our Cardinal Alberic [Col. 1033C] did not write a book concerning his vision, as Arnold Wion, Possevino, Torrigius, and others carelessly noted. Our Peter would certainly have mentioned it in his catalogue of Alberic’s writings had he committed it to writing. The vision belonged to Alberic, a boy of Campanian origin from the town of Septemfratrum, who later sought the Cassinese monastery under Abbot Gerard, as we shall say below under Guy; our Peter recorded the foregoing matters in his supplement to the Cassinese *Chronicle*.

[Col. 1033D] Alphonsus Ciaconius and likewise the other writers who have recorded the deeds of the cardinals must similarly be corrected. They state that Cardinal Alberic was a Campanian from the town of Septemfratrum, because—deceived, we believe, by the similarity of the name—they suppose that Alberic the Deacon, Cassinese monk and later cardinal, and Alberic the boy were one and the same person. Letters of Saint Peter Damian to our Alberic survive in vol. I, book II, letters 20 and 21; in them he discusses certain questions proposed to him by Alberic. Platina also praises him in his account of Nicholas II, calling him a most learned man. Alberic flourished in the year of the Lord 1084; his age can sufficiently be inferred from his having taken up the pen for Pope Gregory VII against Henry IV.]

Alberic the deacon, a man exceptional in those times [Col. 1033A], wrote a book of compositions and salutations; hymns on Saint Nicholas; a *Dialogue on Music*; a book *On the Virginity of Saint Mary*; against Emperor Henry, *On the Election of the Roman Pontiff*; *On Astronomy*; hymns on the Holy Cross, the Ascension, Saint Paul, and Saint Apollinaris; the *Life of Saint Scholastica*, her homily, and hymns; three hymns on the Assumption of Saint Mary; hymns on Saint Peter; the *Life of Saint Dominic*; the *Passion of Saint Modestus and Saint Caesarius*; and a book *On Dialectic*.

In his time a synod was held in the city of Rome against Berengar, deacon of the Church of Angers. Among many things which he attempted to establish, he maintained that the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood was a figure. Since no one was able to withstand him, [Col. 1033B] Alberic himself was summoned to the synod. On his arrival, after various kinds of disputation, when neither side yielded to the other, Alberic obtained leave for one week and produced a book against the same deacon, *On the Body of the Lord*, strengthened by the testimonies of the holy Fathers. In it he destroyed all Berengar’s assertions and consigned them to everlasting oblivion. He also made verses on the life of Saint Scholastica; a rhythmical poem for Easter; *On the Day of Judgment*; and *On the Punishments of Hell*; a rhythmical poem *On the Joy of Paradise*; and very many letters to Peter, bishop of Ostia; *On the Day of Death*; and *On Monks*. He composed other works also which have not come to our knowledge. He lived in the times of the aforesaid emperors and was buried in the city of Rome near the Church of the Holy Four Crowned Martyrs [Col. 1033C].

## CHAPTER XXII. ON ARIALD

[Note: [Col. 1033D] He flourished in the year 1080. Muratori.]

Ariald, a Cassinese priest, wrote several treatises in elegant style. He lived at the same time as Alberic.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON CONSTANTINE

[Col. 1034A]

[Note: [Col. 1033D] Constantine determined, after the manner of those bitten by the *dipsas* serpent, to drink in greedily and without pause every branch of physical learning with a full throat, [Col. 1034C] so that all might afterwards confess that a new Hippocrates had shone forth upon the world. For this reason he took care to learn Hebrew, Syriac, Chaldean, Greek, Latin, Italian, Persian, Arabic, Egyptian, Ethiopian, and Indian.

He was a man by nature strongly inclined to investigate difficult and obscure matters in ancient books, so that no one surpassed him in his age and very few equalled him. Exact knowledge of every language, which has almost always been considered by itself sufficient to make men illustrious, occupied only a small part of the praises due to this truly polyglot man—yet, indeed, even this account is thin and meagre in proportion to his great merits. His collected works, printed with great care at Basel by Heinrich Petri in 1536, folio, are found. Labbe writes in the *New Library of Manuscripts*, book I, p. 50, that manuscripts also exist in the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, codex no. 439; the distinguished Bishop Tomasini of Cittanova likewise mentions some in various libraries of Padua in his *Paduan Library*. Constantine flourished about the year 1072, in the times of the emperors Michael, Constantine, Alexius, and Henry. See our Peter the Deacon in the supplement to the Cassinese *Chronicle*, book III, ch. 35; Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book II, ch. 70; and Arnold Wion, book V, ch. 98 of the *Lignum vitae*.]

Constantine the African, monk of the same monastery, was most fully educated in philosophical studies, master of East and West, and a newly shining Hippocrates. Leaving Carthage, from which he was himself native, he went to Babylon. There he was most thoroughly instructed in grammar, dialectic, physics, geometry, arithmetic, mathematics, astronomy, necromancy, music, and the medical science of the Chaldeans, Arabs, Persians, and Saracens. Departing from there, he went to India and gave himself to be trained in its learning. Having been fully instructed in the arts of the Indians, he sought Ethiopia, where he was again educated in Ethiopian disciplines. When [Col. 1034B] he had been abundantly filled with their learning, he proceeded to Egypt, where he was fully instructed in every Egyptian art.

Having thus spent thirty-nine years learning such disciplines, he returned to Africa. When people saw him so fully trained in the learning of every nation, they planned to kill him. Realizing this, Constantine secretly boarded a ship and arrived at Salerno, where he hid for some time under the appearance of a poor man. Then he was recognized by the brother of the king of the Babylonians, who had then arrived there, and was held in great honour by Duke Robert. Thereafter Constantine left and sought the Cassinese monastery. Received most willingly by Abbot Desiderius, he became a monk [Col. 1034C].

While living in that monastery, he translated very many books from the languages of different peoples, including especially the *Pantegnum*, which he divided into twelve books and in which he explained what a physician ought to know; the *Practica*, in which he set down how the physician should preserve health and treat illness, divided into twelve books; the *Book of Twelve Degrees*; the *Diet of Foods*; the *Book of Fevers*, translated from Arabic; *On Urine*; *On the Internal Organs*; *On Sexual Intercourse*; the *Viaticum*, which he divided into seven parts: first, *On Diseases Arising in the Head*; then *On Diseases of the Face*; *On the Organs*; *On the Afflictions of the Stomach and Intestines*; *On the Afflictions of the Liver, Kidneys, Bladder, Spleen, and Gall*; [Col. 1035A] *On Those Things Which Arise in the Generative Organs*; and *On All Those Things Which Arise on the Outer Skin*. He expounded the book of *Aphorisms*: the *Tegni*, *Megategni*, *Microtegni*, and *Antidotary*; the disputations of Plato and Hippocrates in aphoristic propositions; *On Simple Medicines*; *On Gynaecia*, that is, on the limbs and bodies of women; *On Pulses*; *Prognostics*; *On Experiments*; glosses on herbs and species; *Surgery*; and a book *On Medicines for the Eyes*.

This man spent forty years learning the studies of different nations; finally, old and full of days, he died at Monte Cassino. He lived in the times of the aforesaid emperors.

## CHAPTER XXIV. ON ATTO

[Note: [Col. 1035C] Atto, or Haito, or Hetto—for the name is written in various ways—flourished in the year 1070.]

Atto, pupil of Constantine the African and chaplain of the Empress Agnes, rendered into Latin, in elevated language, those works which the aforesaid Constantine had translated from different languages.

## CHAPTER XXV. ON PANDULF

[Note: [Col. 1035C] Pandulf, a Cassinese monk, was first made cardinal-priest by Pope Paschal II, then bishop of Ostia by Pope Innocent II in 1131. He died in 1134, as Arnold Wion writes, book II, ch. 9, p. 190 in my copy of the *Lignum vitae*, adding that this is the man to whom our Peter the Deacon dedicated this little work *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*. But his memory failed him: for that man was bishop of Theano, as is read from the catalogue of books prefixed by Peter himself to the supplement of the Cassinese history, book IV, ch. 66. From the aforesaid calculation of dates and other difficulties, the distinguished Ughelli observed in *Italia Sacra*, in the catalogue of bishops of Ostia, that perhaps our Peter erred regarding the title of the bishopric. See him, if you wish.]

Pandulf, bishop of Ostia, likewise offered as a little child to Blessed Benedict at Monte Cassino, wrote sermons on the feasts of the whole year [Col. 1035C]. He also composed a rhythmical poem in praise of Saint Mary and some other works which have not yet come into our hands. He lived in the times of the emperors Alexius, John, Henry, and Lothair.

## CHAPTER XXVI. ON PANDULF

[Note: [Col. 1035D] Camillo Pellegrino, distinguished for virtue and learning and most obligingly communicative with us, reports that some of the aforesaid splendid monuments of learning and scholarship are preserved in the Cassinese Library, codex no. 3, under the heading “Mathematical Catos.” Pandulf flourished in the year of the Lord [Col. 1036C] 1060.]

Pandulf of Capua, a priest who became a monk at Monte Cassino under Abbot Desiderius, learned in sacred and secular literature, wrote for Peter, abbot of Salerno [Col. 1036A], a book *On Calculation*; verses *On the Date of the Passover of the Hebrews*; *On the Solar Cycle for Finding Concurrentes*; *On the Lunar Cycle*; *On Finding the Weekday of the Passover of the Hebrews*; *On Finding the Years of the Lord*; *How Indictions Are to Be Found*; *On Finding the Moon of Each Day without the Discrepancy of Embolismic Months*; *How Those Who Think They Know Are Mistaken about How Many Hours or Points the Moon Shines during Each Night*; *By What Methods the Course of the Sun Is Divided*; *How Leap-Year Is Produced*; *On Finding the Weekdays of the Kalends*; *How and from What Source the Rules for Finding the Weekdays of the Months Proceed*; *How the Rule of Hebrew Dates Is Found from the Course of the Sun*; *On Finding the Weekday of Each Day*; *On the Four Seasons, in Which Dates the Solstices Ought Truly to Occur*; [Col. 1036B] *Where the Equinoxes Are Truly Believed to Occur*; *How the Advent of the Lord Is to Be Found*; *How the Letter of the Weeks May Be Found from Memory throughout the Whole Year*; *How Christ Suffered on the Third Day before the Kalends of April*; *How All Years Reckoned from the Origin of the World Are Mistaken*; *How the Fifteenth Moon Cannot Fall upon the Day on Which It Occurred*; *On the Assumption of Saint Mary*; and *On the Empress Agnes*. He lived in the times of the emperors Michael and Alexius.

## CHAPTER XXVII. ON LANDENULF

[Note: [Col. 1036C] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1150. Muratori.]

Landenulf of Capua became a monk under Abbot Desiderius. In simple style he wrote a book called [lacuna], in which he introduced the Lord, the Virgin Mary, and most holy Benedict speaking with righteous persons and sinners [Col. 1036C]. He lived at the same time as Alphanus.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. ON ODERISIUS

[Note: [Col. 1036C] Oderisius, son of Oderisius, count of the Marsi, a Campanian, formerly cardinal-deacon of Saint Agatha, a priest of Pope Nicholas II [as printed; the chronology is problematic], was made cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cyriacus in the Baths and abbot of Monte Cassino by Pope Urban II in 1087, on 16 September. Distinguished by the merits of holiness and learning, he went to his reward on 2 December 1105 and was buried at Monte Cassino in the Church of Saint Benedict. The Benedictine Martyrology mentions him on 2 December, and Ferrarius in the *Catalogue of Saints*. He is mentioned in an ancient stone in the Church of Saint John at Venere in the territory of Lanciano.

Alexius Comnenus, emperor of Constantinople, enjoyed a close friendship with Oderisius through letters. Though Henry IV, emperor, was an enemy of the Church, he was nevertheless a friend and patron of Oderisius’s monastery. For his deeds see Leo of Ostia, book III, ch. 15 of the Cassinese history, and Camillo Pellegrino in the series of Cassinese abbots under Oderisius. A letter of Oderisius to the monks of Fleury survives, quoted by Laureto, *On the Existence of the Body of Saint Benedict in the Monastery of Monte Cassino*, ch. 26, p. 122.]

Oderisius I, abbot of Monte Cassino, was supreme in humility, modest in chastity, endowed with spiritual illumination, and a remarkable versifier. He wrote several works which, because they are at hand, I omit to list. He lived in the times of the aforesaid emperors.

## CHAPTER XXIX. ON BENEDICT

[Col. 1037A]

[Note: [Col. 1037A] The manuscript minor works of Guaiferius or Gauferius, written in Lombardic script on ancient parchment, are preserved in the Cassinese Library under no. 280, marked with this title: “Homilies of Gauferius, monk of Monte Cassino.”

For the Advent of the Lord, it begins: “The words of the Holy Gospel.”
For the Nativity of the Lord: “From the Father of Majesty.”
For the Epiphany: “Of everlasting modesty.”
For Septuagesima: “Through the parable of the employer.”
For Palm Sunday: “The singular and most renowned.”
For the Lord’s Supper: “To the most glorious [—] of the Redeemer.”
*Passion of Saint Lucius, Pope*: “The most steadfast and illustrious pursuits of virtue.”
*History of Saint Secundinus, Bishop of Troia*: “On the good of love,” which you will also find briefly described in Ferrarius’s *Catalogue of Saints* under 2 February.

There follow in the same manuscript codex the poems of Gauferius, namely:

*In Praise of the Psalter*, beginning:

> I bring words of life, which Life, the Word, has marked.

*On the Miracle of Him Who Killed Himself*, beginning:

> Guilt plunged you into the dreadful ruin of death.

*On the Conversion of Certain Salernitans*, beginning:

> A very great new event is reported to have occurred at Salerno.

*In Praise of Saint Martin, Bishop*, beginning:

> Jewel of priests, stand by the prayers of your own.

[Col. 1037C] *In Praise of Saint Secundinus, Bishop of Troia*, beginning:

> Be present, wholly festive, on your own holy feast-days.

A hymn on the same Saint Secundinus:

> Christ, King of kings, price of the devout.

We too preserve in handwritten form all the aforesaid minor works and poems, to be brought forth for the public good. On the death of Gauferius, see what we noted above under Alberic; consult also our Peter in the supplement to the Cassinese *Chronicle*, book III, ch. 61, Venetian edition. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1060.]

Benedict, also called Guaiferius, a Salernitan, conspicuous for holiness and religious devotion, gracious in expression, great in intellect, and eloquent in speech, wrote for the bishop of Troia the *Life of Saint Secundinus* and his chant; verses in praise of the Psalter; *On the Miracle of the Man Who Killed Himself and Was Restored to Life through Blessed James*; *On the Conversion of Certain Salernitans*; *In Praise of Saint Martin*; *In Praise of Saint Secundinus*; hymns on the same saint; a homily [Col. 1038A] *On Advent*; sermons *On the Nativity of the Lord*, *On the Epiphany*, *On the Lord’s Supper*, *On Septuagesima*, and *On Palm Branches*; and the *Passion of Saint Lucius, Pope*. He flourished in the times of the emperors Alexius and Henry and of Abbot Desiderius.

## CHAPTER XXX. ON LEO
[Note: [Col. 1037C] Leo of Marsi, a Campanian, put on the monastic habit at Monte Cassino from boyhood. There he became renowned both for holiness of life and for his exceptional learning. While serving as librarian and dean of that monastery, he was appointed bishop and cardinal of Ostia by Pope Paschal II in the year of the Lord 1101. He was a man of great spirit; seeing that Emperor Henry IV was holding Paschal out of hatred, he stirred the people into revolt against him. He attended the Council of Vastello, and consecrated the high altar of St. Lawrence in Lucina, depositing the relics of many saints, especially material from St. Lawrence’s gridiron together with two ampoules of that martyr’s blood, on 15 October 1112, as may be gathered from a very ancient inscription of that church. Cardinal Baronius later entered it in his annals. Our Leo is also found subscribing the acts of the Lateran council under Paschal II, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. See what Lauretus has noted on our Leo in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, p. 79.

At the command of Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino, he wrote in three books a chronicle of his monastery, from the time of St. Benedict down to Abbot Desiderius, afterwards Pope Victor III. It was printed at Venice in 1513 and at Paris, and finally at Naples in 1616, through the work and with the notes of Matteo Laureti, a Spanish monk of Monte Cassino. A diligent reader, comparing those editions with the very ancient manuscript preserved in the Cassinese library [Col. 1038A], called the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, will readily recognize for himself that they have been seriously deprived of their integrity and are clogged with errors. For we often see—and experience to the great detriment of the commonwealth of letters—that in the course of printing certain things are omitted, added, or altered for the worse through the carelessness, audacity, malice, or perverse intention of copyists. The distinguished Luca Holstenius possesses a chronicle of Leo in which we have seen variant readings, drawn from the authority of several manuscript copies, noted in his own hand in the margins of the printed book.

But consult, if the matter concerns you, what Matteo Laureti noted in *On the Presence of the Body of St. Benedict in the Monastery of Monte Cassino*, ch. 41, p. 148; and Camillo Pellegrino, in the *History of the Lombard Princes*, in the series of Cassinese abbots, under Petronax. Then indeed you may maintain, in a symposium of learned men, that further polishing is not yet to be despaired of.

It should be observed that Baronius, vol. X of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 891, noted that Pope Formosus was incorrectly placed in the said *Chronicle* after Adrian and before Stephen, whereas it is entirely certain that he did not precede Stephen but succeeded him. Further, the sacrilege perpetrated by the schismatic Pope Sergius is attributed by Leo to the highly praiseworthy Pope Stephen, etc. [Col. 1038C] Yet we judge that this error easily crept in from a corrupt manuscript. See the said Laureti, in his notes to book I, ch. 45 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, and in *On the Presence of the Body of St. Benedict*, ch. 41, where he defends our Leo against the accusations of certain persons. Baronius certainly calls Leo, under the year 1059, “a most upright writer of his own time,” and, under 1077, “a writer of sincere faith.”

The *Life of St. Mennas, or Menna, Confessor*, which Peter testifies that Leo wrote at the command of Abbot Oderisius, is preserved by us in manuscript and has not yet been printed, together with the translation of his relics to the city of Caiatia and a detailed account of his miracles. God willing, we shall publish it for the public good along with other Acts of Saints. It begins: “The life and conduct of the outstanding confessor of Christ Mennas, etc.” His holiness is treated by St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book III, ch. 26; the Roman Martyrology, under 2 November; and Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 579.

Arnold Wion, *Lignum Vitae*, book II, ch. 9, fol. 188, further testifies that Leo wrote the *Life of St. Januarius, monk of Monte Cassino*. You will also find it described by our Peter the Deacon in the manuscript book *On the Origin and Life of the Righteous Men of Monte Cassino*, ch. 31, in the *Life of St. Guinizon*, whose disciple he was. See also the eulogies of Cassinese abbots by M. Antonio Scipione, p. 322. His remaining works, however, still remain unpublished.

Leo, an outstanding man, distinguished in his service to learning and an ornament of the sacred senate, died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April in 1115. This is plainly evident from the period during which he was alive, for he is found subscribing a bull of Paschal II granted to the Church of the Marsi in the year of the Lord 1115: “I, Brother Leo, bishop of Ostia.”]

Leo, bishop of Ostia and librarian, offered to Monte Cassino from childhood, was thoroughly imbued with holiness and monastic discipline, and exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures. He produced sermons on Easter and on the Nativity [Col. 1039A]; a history of the Pilgrims; a history of the chief monastery of Monte Cassino divided into four books; the *Life of St. Mennas*; and very many other works which have not come to our knowledge. He lived in the times of the above-mentioned emperors.

## CHAPTER XXXI. ON LEO

[Note: [Col. 1039B] Wion writes in book II, ch. 9 of the *Lignum Vitae* that he was created in the year of the Lord 1105 by Pope Paschal II; Ciacconius, however, says by Urban II. He wrote a great many letters, preserved in manuscript in the Vatican Library; twenty of these, written by our Leo, are found under the name of Urban II. Cardinal Baronius mentions them in vol. XI, under the year of the Lord 1088, though under the name of Leo of Ostia. The aforesaid letters now appear in vol. VII of Binius’s *Councils*. He also made Urban’s register [Col. 1039C], but we lack it.

Finally, it should incidentally be noted here that Cardinal Baronius in the place cited above, Possevino in his *Apparatus*, and others have been mistaken in thinking that Leo of Marsi, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, was the same man as our Leo, cardinal-deacon. They attribute Urban’s register and letters, which he committed to writing, to Leo of Ostia, thereby making one man out of two. In our judgment they were deceived by their sharing the same name and by the nearly contemporaneous promotion of two Cassinese monks into the body of cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. Hence the error arose.]

Leo, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church and monk of the Cassinese monastery, distinguished for learning and eloquence, wrote very many letters in the name of Pope Urban and also made his register.

## CHAPTER XXXII. ON GREGORY

[Note: [Col. 1039C] He was chosen provost of the Church of Terracina by Pope Paschal II. Afterwards our Gregory, richly endowed with extraordinary learning and adorned with every kind of knowledge, implanted seeds of virtue there and erased the rudiments of vice, especially forming his subjects by excellent precepts and morals. No second man upon whom the rays of the sun shone was better than he, as is evident from his works [Col. 1039D], which circulate in manuscript in many hands. He attended the Council of Vastello in 1106. He also subscribed a certain bull granted to the Church of Pisa in 1126. Our Peter again mentions him in the supplement to the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, ch. 42.

Cardinal Baronius testifies in the Roman Martyrology under 1 July that the Acts of Saints Castus and Cassius, bishops and venerated by the people of Sora, were written by our Gregory while he still wore the monastic habit. The Acts of St. Restituta, Roman virgin and martyr, whose feast is likewise celebrated at Sora on 27 May, are also said to have been written by Gregory, as is briefly recorded in Ferrari’s catalogue of saints.

There is in the Cassinese library manuscript no. 300, which contains a *History of the Journey to Jerusalem: how it was recovered, and how Antioch and Jerusalem itself were delivered from the invasion of the heathen by Christ’s faithful*. It begins: “At the time when Alexius held the reins of the Byzantine Empire, and Urban II, of blessed memory, governed the pontificate of the Roman see, there was in the region of Gaul a certain dweller in the wilderness named Peter, etc.” It carries the narrative down to the reign of Baldwin. Some think that this history is by the aforementioned Gregory, who at the request of Berard of Valva had also composed verses on the passage of the pilgrims to the Lord’s sepulchre [Col. 1040C] and the capture of the city of Jerusalem.

It should be noted that our Gregory is very different from the other Gregory, also a Cassinese and bishop of Sinuessa, discussed in the following chapter. Some, deceived by their common name, make one person out of two, attributing to the following Gregory the minor works which our Gregory committed to writing. Such an error is indeed first to be excused in Possevino’s *Apparatus*, under “Gregory,” and then in those who wrote on authors after Possevino.]

Gregory, bishop of Terracina, likewise offered to Monte Cassino as a child, was of retentive memory and lively intellect, and possessed such dignity, graciousness, and eloquence that some called him a Pillar of the Church. He wrote the passion of Saints Castus and Cassius; the passion of the holy virgin Restituta; the *Life of St. Gerard, Confessor of Christ*; a homily on the Assumption of the Most Holy Mary, Mother of God; chants for Saints Castus and Cassius; and hymns for them. At the request of Berard of Valva he composed most beautiful verses on the journey of the pilgrims [Col. 1040A] to the Lord’s sepulchre and the capture of the city of Jerusalem. He wrote a history of Jonah; verses on church dedications and the Easter festival; works on St. Andrew; and homilies on the festivals of the entire year. He lived in the times of the emperors Alexius, Henry, and John, and was buried at the church of Piperno.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. ON GREGORY

[Note: [Col. 1040C] He was bishop of Sinuessa; this, we think, is the proper reading, not “Limessa,” as we have observed wrongly written in some manuscript copies. He flourished about the year of the Lord 1120, a man learned in sacred literature and highly eloquent in the poetic art. His works are preserved in manuscript in the Cassinese library.]

Gregory, bishop of Sinuessa and monk of Monte Cassino, was great in talent and illustrious in eloquence. He wrote wonderful verses on the capture of the Cassinese monastery, in which he represented Blessed Benedict speaking to the Cassinese monks. He composed [Col. 1040B] many other works also, which have by no means come into our hands. He lived under the above-mentioned emperors and was buried in his own bishopric.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. ON BRUNO

[Note: [Col. 1040C] St. Bruno was born at Asti, from the most noble Soleri family [Col. 1040D]. Gregory VII made him bishop of Segni, as a reward for his virtues and learning, because in a public Roman council he had defeated Berengar, who held impious views concerning the sacrament of the altar, in disputation. Then, touched by a desire for the contemplative life, he laid down the burden of the episcopate and professed himself a monk of Monte Cassino in 1104. Subsequently, elected abbot of Monte Cassino by the unanimous vote of the monks on the Ides of November 1107, he presided there for three years and ten months. When these were completed, overcome by reverence for the pope, he returned to the Church of Segni, which he had accepted most unwillingly.

But lest we detract from the praises of so great a teacher through the inadequacy of our talent and pen, we leave his praise to others. Bruno’s works, divided into two volumes, were published at Venice in 1651 through the study and labor of Dom Mauro Marchesi, dean of Monte Cassino, and were also illustrated with scholia. Although not all the works described in our Peter’s catalogue are read there [Col. 1041C], many which Peter omitted are included. Some manuscripts are preserved at Turin in the most noble and celebrated library of the Serene Duke of Savoy, especially the commentary on all four Gospels; and some are in the library of the most illustrious Lord Carlo de Montchal, archbishop of Toulouse, as Philippe Labbe writes in the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, p. 199. Perhaps time, which conceals public things and reveals hidden things, will by God’s mercy soon enrich the world with such great treasures.

Consult Aubert Miraeus’s supplement to *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Bruno, and the distinguished Theophilus Raynaud of the Society of Jesus, *On Bad and Good Books*, part I, question 10, under Eusebius of Emesa and Bruno the Carthusian, fols. 131 and 138.

Bruno ascended from the valley of miseries to the mountains of eternity in 1125, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August. He had been distinguished by many miracles both in life and in death, and was later enrolled among the saints by Lucius III, as may be seen in the following marble inscription visible in Segni Cathedral:

> To the everlasting memory of Blessed Bruno, cardinal and bishop of the city of Segni, whom Lucius III, supreme pontiff, commanded to be enrolled among the saints in the Church of Blessed Mary, where his lifeless body rested [Col. 1042C], in the fifty-eighth year after his death. The Senate and People of Segni.

The Roman Martyrology mentions him under 18 July. Our Peter says more concerning him in the supplement to the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, ch. 33. See also the apparatus to the aforementioned published works of St. Bruno.]

Bruno, bishop of Segni and abbot of Monte Cassino, a most eminent and splendid defender and teacher of the Church, wrote, among the many excellent monuments of his genius, at the request of the canons of Segni, an exposition on the Psalter; on Genesis; on Exodus; on Leviticus; on Numbers; on Deuteronomy; on the Song of Songs; and on Judges. He also composed these sermons: on the praises of the Church at the dedication of a church; on Paradise; on Noah’s Ark; on the Tabernacle of the Covenant; on Solomon’s Temple; and on the woman through whom the Church is signified. On the holy city of Jerusalem; on basilicas dedicated by bishops. Likewise, on the Gospels: on the ornaments of the Church; on faith; hope; charity; the four virtues; humility; mercy; peace; patience; chastity; obedience; and abstinence. On the adornment of the Church; on the new world; [Col. 1041B] on new heavens; new clouds; new mountains; new trees; new powers; the new sea and fishermen; new birds; new rivers; new animals. Three sermons on the feast of feasts, that is, on the Holy Trinity; on the Nativity of the Lord; the Circumcision; the Epiphany; the octave of the Epiphany; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Easter; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the Nativity of St. Mary; the Annunciation; her Purification; and her Assumption. Three sermons on virgins; seven sermons on martyrs; a homily for the festivals of confessors; another for the feast of St. Benedict; with two sermons on bishops; four on the holy angel; five homilies on the apostles; three on several martyrs; two on one martyr; on the dedication of a church; on the Advent of the Lord; on the second Sunday of Advent; the third Sunday; two homilies on the Annunciation of Blessed Mary [Col. 1041C]; on the fourth Sunday of Advent; on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity; three homilies on the day itself; on St. Stephen; St. John the Evangelist; the feast of the Innocents; the first Sunday after the Lord’s Nativity; the octave of the Lord; and the Epiphany. On the first Sunday after the Epiphany; the third, fourth, and fifth Sundays. On the Purification of St. Mary; Septuagesima; Sexagesima [Col. 1042A]; Quinquagesima; Ash Wednesday and the wearing of sackcloth. Forty homilies from Friday and Saturday at the beginning of Lent through the Lord’s Supper. On the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; the Easter feast; Easter Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday; the first, second, third, and fourth Sundays after the octave of Easter, at the major procession; the feast of the apostles Philip and James; the Finding of the Holy Cross; the holy angel; the Ascension of the Lord; the first Sunday after the Ascension; Pentecost; the first Sunday after the octave of Pentecost; the second, third, and fourth Sundays. On St. John the Baptist; the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul and their feast-day; the first Sunday after the nativity of the apostles [Col. 1042B], with twenty-four homilies. On St. Lawrence; the Assumption of St. Mary; St. Matthew; the vigil of St. Andrew and his feast-day; a sermon on St. Scholastica; a sermon on the translation of St. Stephen from the city of Constantinople to the Roman citadel; verses in praise of St. Mary; a homily on the beheading of St. John the Baptist; and on the Nativity of St. Mary. He lived in the times of the above-mentioned emperors. He was buried in his bishopric near the city of Segni.

## CHAPTER XXXV. ON JOHN

[Note: [Col. 1042D] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1072. MUR.]

John the Physician, disciple of the aforementioned Constantine the African and monk of Monte Cassino, a most eloquent and learned man in the medical art, after the death of his master Constantine issued an aphorism quite necessary for physicians. He lived under the above-mentioned emperors. He died at Naples, where he left all the books of his master Constantine.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. ON PAUL

[Note: [Col. 1042D] Paul of Genoa flourished in the latter years of Henry III and the first years of Henry IV, namely in 1100. In the supplement to the *History of Monte Cassino*, book III, ch. 47, our Peter also calls him Paul the Grammarian. Though deprived of the light of his eyes, he possessed such keenness of intellect and such clarity in his other senses that he deserved to be revered by all. Of him one could truly say: “The Lord gives light to the blind.”

St. Ebizo, or Gebizo, whose life our Paul wrote, was born at Cologne and was a monk of Monte Cassino under Abbot Desiderius. Among his distinguished deeds it is related that he delivered by his prayers the soul of his friend Ado, whom demons were dragging to punishment. Our Peter also recorded this in the manuscript book *On the Origin and Life of the Righteous Men of Monte Cassino*, ch. 51, and in the supplement to the *History of Monte Cassino*, book III, ch. 47. See Hugh Menard in the Benedictine Martyrology under 20 October, and book I of the *Dialogues* of Pope Victor III, p. 20.

We believe that time has deprived us of his other works [Col. 1043C]. But what of it, when in these times there are men who, to excavate the trifles of profane antiquities, not only penetrate into the bowels of the earth but also pour out the bowels of their wealth, while they so disdain the unseen treasures of sacred monuments, which gladden souls, that they would rather spare a penny than seek out these literary riches?]

Paul, born in Liguria, a province of the Romans, deprived from earliest infancy by God’s hidden judgment of the power of sight, and therefore untrained in letters and philosophical studies, has down to the present day displayed such a miracle in himself [Col. 1043A] that everyone calls him another Didymus. After writing an account of the disputation between Romans and Greeks held in Constantinople under Abbot Oderisius, he came to the Cassinese monastery in the time of Pope Paschal II and Emperor Alexius. He wrote on Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the remaining prophets; on the Psalter; Matthew; Mark; Luke; John; the Epistles of Paul; and the Apocalypse. He learned not only grammar but all the other arts, solely by hearing, and retained them completely in his heart. He also wrote the *Life of St. Ebizo, monk of Monte Cassino*, who was like Hilarion. There are also other volumes of his works which have not yet come into our hands. He died at [Col. 1043B] the city of Tibur.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. ON BERNARD

[Note: [Col. 1043C] The *Life of St. Amicus, Confessor*, written by Bernard, is preserved in manuscript among our sacred records and remains unpublished. It begins: “Blessed Amicus, born of noble stock in the territory of the county of Camerino, etc.” The place where he was born is called Arabona in Picenum—the name of an abbey—near Monte Melone. St. Peter Damian mentions him, as Baronius noted under the year 993, where he writes that Amicus was canonized, though without the Church’s solemn rite. His feast is observed on 3 November, and he was renowned for many miracles. See what Laureti observed in the notes to the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, at the end of book III [Col. 1043D], and Arnold Wion in the notes to the Benedictine Martyrology. Bernard flourished in the year of the Lord 1120.]

Bernard, monk of Monte Cassino, thoroughly trained in the liberal arts, wrote an account of the miracles of St. Amicus, confessor of Christ and monk of Monte Cassino. He also wrote many other things which we have judged superfluous to enumerate. He died almost in our own time.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. ON JOHN

[Note: [Col. 1043D] Our John is different from the other John, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, whom Sigebert praises in the *Catalogue*, ch. 106. He was a friend of Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, and in 874 published four books on the *Life of Pope St. Gregory the Great* and wrote the deeds of Pope Clement, preserved in manuscript in the Cassinese library. See Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, under John the Deacon. Some therefore wrongly confuse their works with one another, making one man out of two.]

John the Deacon, most learned in sacred and secular literature [Col. 1044A], composed verses in praise of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, and very many other works which have not yet come to our attention.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. ON PETER

[Note: [Col. 1043D] He flourished around the year of the Lord 1080. MUR.]

Peter the Deacon, my teacher, an outstanding rhetorician, left the city of Teano, from which he came, and arrived at Monte Cassino, where Abbot Oderisius made him a monk. While residing in that monastery he further wrote a sermon on Septuagesima, on the Dedication of a Church, on the Nativity of the Lord, on the Epiphany, and many others.

## CHAPTER XL. ON LANDENULF

[Note: [Col. 1043D] He was alive in 1060. MUR.]

Landenulf, offered as a child to Blessed Benedict at Monte Cassino under Abbot Desiderius [Col. 1044B], thoroughly learned in the divine Scriptures and refined by most subtle exercise in their meanings, composed wonderful verses on the restoration of the Cassinese monastery, or chief monastery, and on Desiderius’s rule. Abbot Desiderius himself ordered these to be inscribed around the chapter house and cloister.

## CHAPTER XLI. ON GUIDO

[Note: [Col. 1043D] Guido lived in the time of Gerard, abbot of Monte Cassino, in the year of the Lord 1111, foremost among the most elegant writers of his age. The *Vision of Alberic*, mentioned above under Alberic, cardinal-deacon, is preserved by us in manuscript and bears this heading: “Because some are accustomed to obscure truth by falsehood.” A summary by our Peter appears in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* [Col. 1044C], book IV, ch. 68, Venice edition, in these words:

> In his time—that is, of Abbot Gerard, who ruled from 1111 until 1123—there occurred in the province of Campania a remarkable miracle, in every respect like those of ancient times. In the fortress of the Seven Holy Brothers, a noble boy named Alberic, when he was in his tenth year, was struck by illness and brought to the point of death. For nine days and as many nights he lay motionless and senseless, as though dead. During that interval he was led by the blessed apostle Peter and two angels through places of punishment, and came to the infernal abyss. At last, brought to the delights of Paradise, he saw the dwellings of the saints; then, lifted into the airy heaven and sufficiently instructed by the blessed apostle Peter concerning the Old Testament, the punishments of sinners, and the glory of the saints, he saw certain mysteries which he was forbidden to describe. Thus he was led by that apostle through seventy-two provinces and restored to life. Whoever wishes to know his vision should read the account written by Guido, monk of this monastery. We have omitted to write it here because it is on everyone’s lips. Thereafter Alberic himself, leaving behind the pomp of the world, sought the Cassinese monastery. He was received with most gracious affection by Father Gerard, received the habit of holy conduct, and professed military service to Christ the King. Even today he possesses such abstinence and such seriousness of conduct that no one doubts that he saw the punishments of sinners and the glory of the saints. From that time he has never tasted meat or drunk wine; he always goes barefoot; and he remains to this day—in the year 1115—in this Cassinese monastery in bodily affliction, contrition of heart, and humility. Though his tongue is silent, his life declares that he has seen many things, unknown to others, which are either to be feared or desired.

Thus far Peter. The *History of Henry*, by some misfortune, has not yet seen the light, while those who wrote about the affairs of Henry IV and Henry V have kept profound silence about Guido.]

Guido, priest of Monte Cassino, a man most eminent in secular learning and most approved in religion and life, [Col. 1045A] wrote a history of Emperor Henry, the vision of Alberic, monk of Monte Cassino, and verses on the fortune of the same. [Lacuna.] Moreover, he added the material lacking in the *History of Monte Cassino*, namely from the time of the first Oderisius down to this day.

## CHAPTER XLII. ON ROBOAS

[Note: [Col. 1045B] Roboas, or Noboas, flourished in 1120. MUR.]

Roboas, a deacon received as a child at Monte Cassino by Abbot Gerard, wrote at the request of some friends sermons for the festivals of the whole year, and the *Life of St. Leonard, Confessor of Christ*.

## CHAPTER XLIII. ON PETER

[Note: [Col. 1045B] Arnold Wion, *Lignum Vitae*, book II, ch. 9, calls Peter a subdeacon and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. By which pope he was promoted is unknown. Arnold, however, wrongly calls him a cardinal-subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, since ecclesiastical records of the Roman Church recognize cardinals only among bishops, priests, and deacons. He was alive in the year of the Lord 1120.]

Peter, subdeacon of the Roman Church and monk of Monte Cassino, likewise received as a child at Monte Cassino, at the request of Peter the Deacon and librarian adorned the passion of Blessed Mark in verse.

## CHAPTER XLIV. ON RAYNALD

[Note: [Col. 1045C] The hymns were printed in Cassinese breviaries in 1568 and 1572. See what Arnold noted of Raynald in book II, ch. 9 of the *Lignum Vitae*; Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, book III, ch. 7, p. 713; and Camillo Pellegrino, *History of the Lombard Princes*, in the series of Cassinese abbots, under Raynald.]

Raynald, subdeacon of Monte Cassino, offered as a child to Blessed Benedict, a very learned man whose skill in versification was in every respect comparable to that of the ancients, [Col. 1046A] wrote verses to Peter the Deacon and librarian in praise of St. Severus, bishop of Monte Cassino; verses also on the life of Blessed Benedict and Blessed Maurus; and hymns in praise of St. Severus, confessor of Christ and bishop.

*From Peter the Deacon’s Supplement to On Illustrious Men*

## CHAPTER XLV. ON GELASIUS

[Note: [Col. 1045C] Formerly John of Gaeta, a Campanian by birth, son of Crescentius, nobly born, he rose from being subdeacon and chief notary of the Holy Roman Church as chief signatory to Urban II to cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, and librarian. He was especially dear to Pope Paschal II, who called him the staff of his old age. Finally he was made pope under the name Gelasius II in 1118, on 22 January, and was acclaimed “Father of Justice.” After one year and a few days of pontificate, while at Mâcon he fell ill with pleurisy and ordered himself carried in a litter to the monastery of Cluny. There he died on the fourth day before the Kalends of February in 1119, illustrious in merits and outstanding in holiness. His body was laid upon the ground, covered with ashes and haircloth [Col. 1045D], and later buried in a marble tomb of Tuscan workmanship and white stone. Peter of Poitiers, surnamed the Venerable, abbot of Cluny and a contemporary of our Gelasius, set upon it the following epitaph:

> John, a man grave and wise in deed and word,  
> Having first, through much ability, become  
> From a monk an archdeacon and chancellor of the City,  
> When Bishop Paschal, through his merits, had been borne to the stars,  
> At last deserved to ascend the sacred see,  
> Worthy Gelasius to be second after the first.  
>   
> But because he was raised without the king’s command,  
> The prince raged terribly; and sweet daughter Gaul,  
> In her own manner, received the fugitive Father.  
> Had it been permitted him—believe this certainly—  
> Virtue, piety, and every uprightness  
> Would have increased under him,  
> And the peace of the Church flourished throughout the whole world.  
>   
> For black death snatched away the man when, as venerable shepherd,  
> He had scarcely completed his first year as pontiff [Col. 1046B];  
> With two days still remaining, he slept  
> In his own asylum of Roman right at Cluny.  
>   
> Thus placed among his beloved children,  
> He rests with the holy Fathers and longs that the Creator  
> And Judge of the world may someday come in power  
> And restore fallen ashes to their former limbs.  
>   
> Ever most blessed, therefore, shall Cluny remain,  
> Because the apostolic Father of the world and supreme priest  
> Of the Church—and one specially belonging to your mother—  
> Passed to heaven with you and rests buried in you.  
>   
> Nor do we think him less blessed here,  
> To whom Christ himself in his kindness gave this great gift:  
> That monks might continually behold their monk,  
> Their Father also, their dear pledge,  
> And, watering his tomb with tears,  
> Always hold him specially in their sacred prayers.

Concerning Gelasius’s praises Cardinal Baronius wrote under the year 1119: “After the martyrs who consummated martyrdom by the shedding of their blood, one would scarcely find among Roman pontiffs anyone who suffered greater things in a shorter span of life; for this reason he should be granted a more illustrious crown and celebrated with more famous praises.” Joannetti calls Gelasius a saint; Genebrard calls him a most holy man; the abbot of Ursberg calls him a prudent man, venerable, and one who always labored irreproachably for the Apostolic See.

See the *Life of Gelasius*, written by his contemporary Pandulf of Pisa and published through the work and care of Costantino Gaetani; Wion’s Martyrology under the said day; Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book X; and Hugh Menard’s notes to the Benedictine Martyrology under 27 January. Menard defends the most holy Gelasius against the slanders of Orderic Vitalis, monk of the monastery of Utica, or St. Evroul, in book XII near the beginning of his *Ecclesiastical History of the Normans*, written in the Theopompean manner. The *Passion of St. Erasmus, Bishop and Martyr* was printed at Rome in 1639 through the work and care of the aforementioned Gaetani. Baronius, in the Martyrology under 9 July, mentions the Acts of Saints Anatolia and Caesarius, composed in rhythmic verse by Gelasius; we believe these have perished through the ravages of time. Binius reports five of the letters Gelasius wrote, in vol. VII. See Baronius, vol. XII of the *Annals*, under 1118 and 1119. He compiled the register of his predecessor Pope Paschal II, which survives only in manuscript.]

Gelasius, pope of the Apostolic See, was offered as a child to Blessed Benedict at Monte Cassino under Abbot Desiderius and was taught by Alberic the philosopher. While residing in that monastery, he wrote the passion of St. Erasmus and St. Anatolia; he also adorned in verse the passion of St. Caesarius. Afterwards, having become chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1046B] he wrote the Register of Pope Paschal II. Finally, made pope in the Apostolic See, he excommunicated Emperor Henry on account of the investiture of churches; and, having entered Gaul to settle ecclesiastical affairs, he died at the monastery of Cluny.

## CHAPTER XLVI. ON JOHN

[Col. 1047A]

[Note: [Col. 1047A] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1120. MUR.]

John of Tibur, received at Monte Cassino by Abbot Gerard, wrote in a plain style sermons for the festivals of the whole year. He also produced several other works which have not come to our knowledge. He died in the time of Emperor Lothair.

## CHAPTER XLVII. ON PETER

[Col. 1048A]

[Note: [Col. 1047A] Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino, charter-keeper, archivist, and librarian of Monte Cassino, who committed this book *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino* to writing, was the son of Aegidius, a Roman by birth, himself the son of Gregory, patrician and consul of the Romans, of the counts of Tusculum. He was so learned in sacred and secular literature that he was considered foremost among the most elegant writers of his age. He died after 1140, leaving almost innumerable offspring of his talent for the benefit of the commonwealth of letters. Through the ravages of time and human negligence, some of these have perished or been scattered. Yet Peter himself set out their catalogue in book IV of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, ch. 68, Venice edition: “Alas, how many things cruel time reaps with its sickle!”

At present nothing else has been printed except the supplement to the third book of Leo of Ostia’s *Chronicle*, and the whole of book IV attached to that *Chronicle*. Our Peter began where Leo ended, namely in 1086, and continued through 1138. There is also the book *On the Notarial Signs in Roman Usage*, addressed to Emperor Conrad, published at Venice in 1525 through the efforts of Nicolaus Erythraeus, and most recently at Hanover together with ancient authors on Latin grammar, through the work of Elias Putschius. Some works not yet committed to print are preserved in manuscript in our storehouse of sacred writings. We do not refrain from mentioning them here, and they are: [Col. 1047C]]

Of the origin and life of the righteous men of Monte Cassino, beginning: “Benedict, the standard-bearer.” Scholia on various sayings, beginning: “Come, Word of God.” Scholia on questions of the Old Testament, beginning: “It is the custom of Holy Scripture to alter times.” An exhortation to monks, in which he shows what they ought to observe and what they ought to avoid, and treats of the seven vices and virtues. On the Patriarchs, King Uzziah, and Moses, beginning: “To all who [live] according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” A rhythmical poem on the last days, beginning: “When the thousandth year after Christ’s Passion has ended, Satan, prince of Avernus, shall be loosed from his chains.” A disputation on behalf of the monastery of Monte Cassino, beginning: “Therefore, while in the presence of Emperor Lothair.” A catalogue of the kings, consuls, dictators, tribunes, patricians, and emperors of the Trojan race, beginning: “[Col. 1047D] Saturn, son of Uranus.” A letter, sent in the name of Guibald, abbot of Monte Cassino, to Emperor Lothair, beginning: “After innumerable anxieties.” A second letter to the same emperor, beginning: “Placed amid various, manifold, and diverse tribulations.” A consolatory letter to Richiza, Roman empress, beginning: “Very often, unconquered Empress.” A consolatory letter to Empress Richiza on the death of Emperor Lothair III, beginning: “Although the severed sinew causes pain.” A consolatory letter to Emperor Conrad II on his election, beginning: “Blessing, and glory, and wisdom.” A sermon for Maundy Thursday, beginning: “Being about to write of the venerable Passion of the Lord.” A sermon for Good Friday, beginning: “Today the fourfold fabric of the world is renewed.” [Col. 1048A] A sermon for Holy Saturday, beginning: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale.” A sermon on the Resurrection of the Lord, beginning: “Let heaven resound today.” A sermon on the Ascension of the Lord, beginning: “Today heavenly things are joined to earthly.” A sermon for Pentecost, beginning: “The festal day of our Redeemer.” A sermon on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, beginning: “[Col. 1048B] Today the evangelical trumpet has shone forth in the world.” A sermon on the feast-day of the apostles Peter and Paul, beginning: “A most holy and blessed day.” A sermon on Saint Lawrence the martyr, beginning: “Today, the most sacred gift of God.” A sermon for the vigil of the Assumption of the most blessed Virgin, beginning: “Of the most holy and immaculate Mother.” A sermon for the feast of All Saints, beginning: “Today the glory of the eternal Emperor.” A sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, beginning: “Today salvation is restored to the world.” Another sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, beginning: “Today true peace has shone upon us.” A special sermon on the octave of Saint Father Benedict, treating of the abundance of his miracles, beginning: “Of the outstanding and most precious confessor Benedict.” The Life of Saint Placid, disciple of Saint Benedict, or his register compiled by our Peter around the year 1130, containing lengthy accounts of the [Col. 1048C] life and martyrdom of Saint Placid, and of the gifts of Tertullius, Emperor Justinian, and Pope Vitalian. The Life of Saint Severus, bishop of Monte Cassino, addressed to Abbot Seniorettus, beginning: “Since without your command.” The Life of Saint Apollinaris, abbot, addressed to Raynald, deacon of the monastery of Monte Cassino, beginning: “Exceedingly wonderful.” The Life of Saints Guinizon and Januarius, addressed to the monk Richard, beginning: “Being about to describe the origin, life, and death of Guinizon.” A sermon for the vigil of Saint Mark, bishop of Atina, beginning: “The vigils of the most precious martyr and pontiff Mark.” On the saints of Atina, namely Bishop Mark, Nicander, and Marcian, and their miracles, beginning: “While Emperor Domitian was persecuting the Church.” A sermon for the feast of these same martyrs, beginning: “Holy and venerable, dearest brethren.” [Col. 1048D] Sermons on Blessed Mark, bishop of Atina, separately from Nicander and Marcian. The first begins: “The same is the beginning, the celebration, and the joy of one”; the other: “The greatest of the prophets.” We hope that these above-mentioned little works, which we preserve in manuscript, will be brought to light for the common good of the world.

Moreover, our Peter wrote the Life of Saint Leo, pope, addressed to Pope Innocent II; likewise, a book *On Holy Places*, or an *Itinerary of the Holy Land*, comprising seven folios. He also wrote a book in which are set out the consular fasti and the succession of emperors, popes, and abbots of Monte Cassino. Further, he wrote an exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict, a work of considerable size; one fragment of it is cited by the distinguished Giovanni Bona in his book *On the Harmony of the Chanting Church*, chapter 12, §2, on the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary, p. 244. Likewise, there is a very ancient register, marked no. 86, written in Lombard characters [Col. 1049C] on parchment by order of Abbot Seniorettus, containing 259 folios, in which are included many charters granted to the monastery of Monte Cassino by Roman pontiffs, emperors, kings, and princes. The aforesaid manuscript works are kept in the library of Monte Cassino, in the first stall on the left upon entering.

Leo of Ostia, in his *History of Monte Cassino*; Trithemius; [Col. 1050C] Cardinal Baronius; Possevino in his *Apparatus*; Arnold Wion, in his *Tree of Life*; Camillo Pellegrino, in many places in his *History of the Lombard Princes*; and many others treat of the writings, praises, and life of our Peter the Deacon, who is distinct from another Peter the Deacon, likewise of Monte Cassino, who wrote the Life of Saint Athanasius of Naples. See also the aforementioned book *On the Harmony of the Chanting Church*, under “Peter,” prefixed to which is a rare and exquisite account of many authors with an assessment of their books.]

Peter the Deacon, archivist and librarian of Monte Cassino, was offered to Blessed Benedict at five years of age by his father Aegidius, a Roman by nationality, under Abbot Gerard; and under the same abbot he was educated for nearly eight years. But in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1049A] 1128, at the age of twenty-one, when Oderisius, successor to Abbot Gerard, had relinquished the abbacy, Peter was sent into exile through the envy of his rivals. While he was in that exile, at the request of Adenulf, count of the same city, he wrote for Abbot Oderisius the Passion of Blessed Mark and his companions; the Life of the distinguished confessor Falco; the Life of Saint Placid, disciple of Saint Benedict; the Life of Saint Apollinaris, abbot; the Life of Saints Guinizon and Januarius; and a rhythmical poem on the last days, in which he seems to have followed the Apostle John literally, although Peter himself knew that, as it is written there, the finite is used for the infinite. He added the destruction and restoration of the city of Atina to the history of Blessed Mark.

He also wrote the following sermons: eight sermons on the feast of Blessed Mark; a sermon for [Col. 1049B] his vigil; one on the vigil of Saints Nicander and Marcian; a sermon for Maundy Thursday; two for Good Friday; one for Holy Saturday; a homily on Saint Benedict; and sermons for Easter, the Ascension, the octave of Saint Benedict, Pentecost, the feast of Saint John the Baptist, Saints Peter and Paul, Saint Lawrence, and the vigil of Saint Mary. He wrote a book on the illustrious men of the monastery of Monte Cassino; he recorded the miracles of the monks of Monte Cassino which had not hitherto been written down. At the command of Abbot Seniorettus, he revised the history of the destruction and restoration of the monastery of Blessed Maurus, and wrote its prologue. At the request of Raynald, [Col. 1050A] subdeacon of Monte Cassino, he also wrote the prologue to the book of Privileges; a sermon on Saint Nicander; an account of the translation of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr from the city of Constantinople to Rome; *On the Origin and Life of the Righteous Men of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*; a sermon for the feast of All Saints; two sermons on the Nativity of the Lord; one on Saint Stephen; and a chronicle of the monastery of Monte Cassino from the rebuilding of the Church of Blessed Martin by Desiderius down to the present day. He compiled an astronomy from ancient books, abridged Solinus’s *On Miracles*, and wrote a book *On the Kinds of Precious Stones*. He divided his exposition of the Rule into four books. He wrote scholia on the Old Testament, two letters to Emperor Lothair, and one to Empress Richiza; he enlarged a small book of shorthand signs. He abridged Vitruvius’s work *On the Architecture of the World*. He translated the book of Heve [Evax], king of the Arabs, *On Stones*. [Col. 1050B] He corrected the hymn on Saint Christina, the Life of Saint Constantius, bishop, the letter to Emperor Conrad, and the corrupted vision of Alberic, monk of Monte Cassino. At the request of Raynald, subdeacon of Monte Cassino, he also wrote the Life of Saint Severus, bishop and confessor. He composed a sermon on Saints Nicander and Marcian, on their translation, and a chronicle of consuls, dictators, and emperors. He wrote an account of the translation of Blessed Mark in the city of Atina and of his miracles. He composed the chants of Blessed Mark and of Saints Nicander and Marcian. He died at Monte Cassino and was buried there.

Here ends the book *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*.

# SUPPLEMENT TO *ILLUSTRIOUS MEN OF THE MONASTERY OF MONTE CASSINO*, COMPILED BY DOM PLACIDUS THE ROMAN, MONK AND DEACON OF MONTE CASSINO

[Col. 1049]

## CHAPTER I. ON RICHARD

[Col. 1049C]

[Note: [Col. 1050C] The marble tomb of Richard Annibaldi of Molaria, lord of the castle of Molaria in Latium, within the Tusculan Mountains, a Roman nobleman and cardinal deacon of Sant’Angelo, may still be seen in the Lateran Basilica, [Col. 1051A] with this ancient inscription: “To the memory of Richard Annibaldi of Molaria, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and cardinal of Sant’Angelo, who was created by Pope Gregory IX at Rome in 1240 and died at Lyons during the general council in the year of the Lord 1274.” The aforementioned exposition on the Rule of Saint Benedict survives in the library of Monte Cassino.]

Richard, abbot and cardinal of Monte Cassino, [Col. 1050C] wrote an exposition of the Rule of our most holy Father Benedict. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1256 and was buried at Monte Cassino, after holding office for seven years.

## CHAPTER II. ON BERNARD

[Col. 1051A]

[Note: [Col. 1051A] Bernard Ayglerius, a Frenchman and monk of the monastery of Savigny in the diocese of Lyons, was chaplain to Pope Innocent [Col. 1051B] IV; in 1256 he became abbot of Saint-Honorat on the island of Lérins; then, by order of Urban IV, he was elected abbot of Monte Cassino in 1263. Later he was admitted to the college of cardinals by the same Urban, according to some; but, more probably, by Pope Clement IV, according to others. See Abbot Ughelli’s note to Ciaconius under Clement IV; Frizon, *Gallia Purpurata*; and Arnold Wion, book II, chapter 9, *Tree of Life*, p. 217. Certainly Charles I, king of France, esteemed him highly on account of his renowned prudence and virtue; when he undertook the journey into Italy, he wished Bernard both to accompany him on the journey and to share in and direct his counsels. How highly Pope Urban IV valued our Bernard may be learned from Urban’s letters to him; among many, the very learned Marco Antonio Scipio gives one in his *Elogia of the Abbots of Monte Cassino*, under Bernard. Among Bernard’s writings, only the *Mirror of Monks*, divided [Col. 1051C] into three parts, has appeared in print: Venice and Cologne, 1520, 16mo. A book on the Rule of Saint Benedict exists in manuscript at Monte Cassino and in the monastery of Saint Benedict at Mantua; his remaining studies are found in manuscript in the archive of Monte Cassino. Bernard died at Monte Cassino on the day before the Nones of April [4 April] in 1282, and was buried there.

One point, however, should be noted: our Bernard Ayglerius was omitted by Ciaconius and Panvinio from their list of cardinals, and was not named among the scarlet-clad, because they thought that Pope Clement IV had created no cardinal—as the very learned Pietro Coretino states in his *Chronology of the Bishops of Viterbo*. Consequently, for the vacancy following Clement IV, Ciaconius counted and named seventeen cardinals, omitting our Ayglerius, whereas there were in fact eighteen. Coretino infers this from a certain charter preserved in the archive of the city of Viterbo, which is given here in a transcription from the original, supplied through the singular kindness of the distinguished Domenico Magri of Malta, canon of Viterbo Cathedral. The charter grants Henry, cardinal bishop of Ostia—who published the *Summa* in canon law commonly called, from its excellence, the *Ostiense*—permission to leave the conclave, apart from his fellow colleagues, who besides Henry numbered seventeen. This is clearly shown by the seventeen seals in red wax hanging with images of saints, though worn away by time, on the charter printed below. From this Coretino concludes that there were eighteen persons in the conclave, among whom was our Bernard, created in Clement IV’s sole promotion; for Henry’s seal must be understood not to have been present, since he was seeking permission to leave the conclave and was not giving consent, for which consent a seal would have been appended to the charter. From this time the practice of the conclave came into force and has continued down to our own day. Previously, the cardinals assembled early in the morning in the cathedral church and cast their votes there [Col. 1052A] for choosing the supreme pontiff; when this had been done, they returned to their residences. But the people of Viterbo, at the urging of Saint Bonaventure, who was then living there, and under the leadership of Raynerius Gatto, closed the gates of the city and brought the cardinals into the episcopal palace near the cathedral; on the day of Pentecost they shut them all in there. Thus the conclave took its origin, as Panvinio also affirms with Ciaconius.

But because they nevertheless showed themselves stubborn and obstinate [Col. 1052B] concerning the election, Raynerius Gatto, then captain of the city of Viterbo and guardian of the conclave, who supplied the Fathers daily with necessary provisions, had the hall of the palace uncovered, as is read in the charter quoted above in these words: “Given at Viterbo, in the uncovered palace.” He compelled the cardinals to proceed to an election of the pope by the harshness of the weather and scarcity of resources. He had been instructed by Cardinal John the Englishman, surnamed of Toledo, a Cistercian monk and bishop of Porto, whom some mistakenly call “of France.” In reproach of his colleagues’ discord, John had urged, with certain witty barbs, that the aforementioned palace in which the election was to be held should be stripped of its roof and walls. Papirius Masson, Panvinio, Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, in the list of bishops of Porto under John, folio [unspecified]; and Odoricus Raynaldus, under the year of the Lord 1271, no. 162, §12, report this. Thus, once the hardness of their minds had been broken, after an agreement made among themselves, they created on 1 September 1271 as pope, under the name Gregory X, Theobald [Col. 1052C] Visconti, a native of Piacenza and archdeacon of Liège, who was outside the number of those Fathers and was then in Syria for Christ’s faith, after a vacancy of the see lasting two years, nine months, and one day.

A copy of the aforementioned charter is as follows:

> “We, by divine mercy bishops, priests, and deacons, cardinals of the most holy Roman Church, compassionating with brotherly affection the illness of our venerable brother H., bishop of Ostia and Velletri, strictly command and order you, Albert of Montebuono, podestà, and Raynerius Gatto, who act as captain for Viterbo, and the commune of Viterbo, by these presents and under the obligation of fidelity by which you are bound to us and to the Roman Church: since the same bishop has renounced before us, solely with respect to the present vacancy, the right and vote competent to him in the election of the Roman pontiff; since he desires that, notwithstanding his absence, we may freely proceed on this occasion without him to provide the Roman Church with a shepherd, intending to hold valid and acceptable the election or provision concerning the Roman pontiff which we shall judge fit to make without him and without his requisition; and since he has urgently requested that you be ordered to permit him to leave the palace in which we are confined, you are immediately to permit that bishop freely to depart from the said palace, and are not henceforth to detain him against his will in any manner. Given at Viterbo, in the uncovered palace of the bishopric of Viterbo, on the sixth day before the Ides of June [8 June], in the year of the Lord 1270, while the Apostolic See was vacant.”
