[In place of + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + seventeen hanging seals of red wax.]

Bernard, a Frenchman, abbot of Monte Cassino, also wrote on the Rule of Saint Benedict. He also published the *Mirror of Monks*. He compiled two registers: one of presentations to benefices and offices; the other of all investigations, rights, and properties [Col. 1052A] in the castles and villages of the monastery of Monte Cassino. He flourished in 1272. He was buried at Monte Cassino, after holding office for twenty-two years.

## CHAPTER III. ON IGNATIUS

[Note: [Col. 1052D] Michael [Col. 1053C] Poccianti writes the following concerning Ignatius, son of Manfred and descended from the most noble Squarcialupi family, a most learned man and most zealous in divine worship, in his *Catalogue of Florentine Writers*: “Ignatius Squarcialupi, Benedictine monk of the same general congregation and most distinguished abbot, a man renowned for holiness of life and knowledge of good letters, and an illustrious poet whose talent was continually admired by all, produced certain works both in verse and prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these are counted: a hymn on Virginity in hexameter verse; the letter of Saint Benedict to Scholastica, composed in Tuscan verses; orations delivered in many places of his congregation for the consolation of the Fathers; several other hymns, among which the foremost is that in honour of the most holy Trinity, which the Fathers [Col. 1053D] of Monte Cassino sing in their churches; and certain other works. Death took him from human affairs at Florence in 1520, and his bones rest in the Florentine abbey.” Thus Poccianti on Ignatius.

Besides the works mentioned, Ignatius also wrote, as Arnold Wion testifies in book I, chapter 16 of the *Tree of Life*, pp. 29–30, the following little works: *A Compendium on the Vision of the Illustrious Prince Ferrand Consalvi*, book I, beginning: “The divine [vision] of the illustrious Ferrand”; and a sermon *On the Aggregation of the Monasteries of Sicily to the Cassinese Congregation*, beginning: “The burden exceeds [our] strength.” In recent years Abbot Costantino Gaetani possessed a Sapphic poem in honour of the most holy Trinity; hymns on Saint Bertharius survive in manuscript in the library of Monte Cassino. Arnold, book I, chapters 15 and 16, book V, chapter 8; Covaccius, book VI; Peter Recordatus, dialogue 4, p. 457; the diplomas of Leo X, dated at Rome in 1314, the second year of his pontificate [an apparent date error in the source]; and Scipio, [Col. 1054C] *Elogia of the Abbots of Monte Cassino*, fol. 215, treat of him.]

Ignatius of Florence, monk of the Florentine monastery and abbot of Monte Cassino, distinguished by noble birth [Col. 1053A] and exceptionally learned in both sacred and secular disciplines, wrote a most beautiful sermon in honour of the most holy Benedict, which he delivered before a great gathering of monks and people when possession of the monastery of Monte Cassino was solemnly taken under Eusebius of Modena, abbot of the same monastery, in the year of the Lord 1505. He also wrote a Sapphic poem in honour and praise of the most holy Trinity, and published hymns in honour of Saint Bertharius, martyr and abbot of Monte Cassino. He flourished in the time of Leo X, to whom he was said to be related. He was buried in the abbey of the city of Florence, after holding office for nine years in this abbey of Monte Cassino.

## CHAPTER IV. ON BENEDICT

[Col. 1053B] [Note: [Col. 1054C] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1520. MUR.]

Benedict of San Severino, monk of Monte Cassino, was exceptionally learned in philosophy and the divine Scriptures. He lived in the time of Charles V and was buried at Monte Cassino.

## CHAPTER V. ON JUSTIN

[Note: [Col. 1054C] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1522. MUR.]

Justin, a Spaniard, professed monk of the monastery of Saint Justina and the ninety-seventh abbot of this monastery, was a man most learned in philosophy and sacred disciplines and a lover of history. He lived in the time of Emperor Charles V; he was buried in the monastery of Saint Justina, after holding office for one year in this monastery.

## CHAPTER VI. ON AUGUSTINE

[Col. 1053C] [Note: [Col. 1054C] The ninety-eighth abbot of Monte Cassino, descended from the Bonfili family, flourished in 1530. See Marco Antonio Scipio’s *Elogia*, p. 225.]

Augustine of Padua, professed monk of the monastery of Saint Justina and the ninety-ninth abbot of Monte Cassino, was a man most learned in philosophy and sacred disciplines. [Col. 1054A] He flourished in the time of the aforementioned emperor. He died at Brescia and was buried in the monastery of Saint Faustinus, after holding the abbacy of Monte Cassino for three years.

## CHAPTER VII. ON INNOCENT

[Note: [Col. 1054C] Innocent, son of Nicholas of Novara, was versed in Greek, Hebrew, Chaldean, and Latin languages and learned in every discipline. He died in 1557. Wion, book I, chapter 16, book V, chapter 8; Ulmus; and Marco Antonio Scipio in his *Elogia of the Abbots of Monte Cassino* treat of him.]

Innocent of Novara, professed monk of the Florentine monastery and the one hundred and fourth abbot of this monastery, was eloquent and highly learned in the divine Scriptures, and especially versed in philosophy and mathematics. He flourished in the time of Emperors Charles V and Maximilian. He died at Venice and was buried in the monastery of Saint George, after holding office in this monastery for three years.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON ANGELO

[Col. 1054B]

[Note: [Col. 1054C] Angelo was born at the town of Sangro, of the de Faggi family. If Plato’s saying is true that names generally correspond to things, he was like an angel: an example of ancient virtue and holiness, sparing and diligent with time, and a vigilant distributor of his hours. He possessed such poetic power that he could express almost anything he wished easily, copiously, and nearly extempore in verse. His published works are commonly handled by learned people, printed at Cologne. By a remarkable art of paraphrase he rendered the Psalms of David in imitation of the Hebrews, whom Jerome declares to employ metrical numbers in the Psalms, in much of Job, and in Jeremiah’s Lamentations. This paraphrase was printed at Venice in 1540, Basel in 1551, and Rome in 1587, in quarto. A Life of Saint Benedict in heroic verse was printed. The Treatise on the Forty Hours was printed at Florence in 1587, in duodecimo, and at Trent in sextodecimo. He died at Monte Cassino in 1593, aged ninety-three; some testified that, eight years after his body had been committed to the earth, they saw it entire and uncorrupted in the tomb.]

Angelo of Sangro, abbot and restorer of the monastery of Monte Cassino, became a monk at Monte Cassino in his youth under Vincent of Naples, abbot of this monastery. He was a reverend man, endowed with every goodness and holiness, tested in religious devotion and manner of life, deeply versed in the divine Scriptures, and an outstanding and admirable poet. He wrote almost innumerable works, of which, for brevity’s sake, I shall mention only these: a heroic poem on the ineffable name of Jesus; seven meditations on the seven last words of Jesus Christ, composed in the same poetic form; likewise works on God’s mercy, love, and goodness towards sinners; on the sinner’s hope in God; *The Mirror of the Sinner*; six exhortations for Holy Week; on the names [Col. 1054C] of Jesus; on contempt for riches and the vanity of human life; twelve elegies on Jesus’ compassion and love toward sinners; *The Triumph of Divine Love*; a Sapphic poem [Col. 1055A] on the Nativity of the Lord and on all the other feasts of the same; a funeral song on the Lord’s death; and on Jesus’ benefits to humankind.

He also wrote one book, in varied kinds of verse, on the praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary. There are also two books in which several very celebrated sacred observances of male and female saints are described in varied metres and their deeds are set forth in hymn-like measures. He composed in elegiac verse golden and divine sayings selected from David’s Psalms. Moreover, he wrote the Life of our most holy Father Benedict in heroic verse; twelve elegies on the Passion of the Lord; a paraphrase, ornamented in varied metrical forms, of the Psalter of King David; *On the Martyrdom of a Monk*; the Life of Blessed William the Anchorite in Sapphic verse; the Life of Saint Father [Col. 1055B] Benedict, of Saints Maurus and Placid, and of John the Baptist in heroic verse; another Life of Saint Benedict in Sapphic verse and in prose, containing a moral exposition; a treatise on the prayer of the Forty Hours; and a Psalter of the glorious Virgin Mary in Sapphic verse. He wrote many other poetic works, which it would take too long to enumerate individually. He also published dialogues, homilies, and many sermons in prose. He is living still today and has passed his seventy-eighth year.

## CHAPTER IX. ON HONORATUS

[Note: [Col. 1055C] Son of Marcus, born in 1502; praised by Bembo, Giovanni Cafa, Flaminio, and other most learned men. His very charming poems are also read in Giovio’s *Elogia*, and were printed in the *Delights of Italian Poets*. He published a notable work on the deeds of Alfonso d’Avalos, marquis of Vasto. On 30 January 1551 he was invested with the episcopal mitre by Pope Julius III and appointed tutor to Innocentio del Monte, the adoptive nephew of that pontiff and a cardinal. Ranutius Gerus [ [Col. 1055D] Banutius Gorus—that is, Janus Gruterus, who collected the *Delights of Poets*] mentions him in book I of *Illustrious Poets of Italy*, as does Caramella in his *Museum of More Illustrious Poets*, with this couplet:

[Col. 1055D]

> The poet is milky. Why “milky”? From where  
> does he have the name of milk? In verse he is bright and tender.

He attended the Council of Trent. He died at Rome in March 1564 and was buried there, after resigning his bishopric in 1562.]

Honoratus of Isernia, of the Fascitella family, was received as a monk at Monte Cassino under Vincent of Naples. Afterwards he was made bishop of [Col. 1055C] Insula in Calabria. He was a man highly accomplished in Greek, secular, and sacred letters, and an outstanding poet. He wrote very many works which, through the calamity of time, have not come into our hands. He flourished in the time of Emperors Charles V and Maximilian.

## CHAPTER X. ON GREGORY

[Col. 1056A]

[Note: [Col. 1055D] Arnold mentions him in book II of the *Tree of Life*, under Ecclesiastical Writers, letter G, with this heading: “Dom Gregory of Viterbo, doctor of both laws and monk of the congregation of Monte Cassino, otherwise Saint Justina of Padua, who flourished in the year of the Lord 1540. He wrote three homilies or sermons, as piously as learnedly, on the Gospel of John, ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ which begin thus: I. ‘A speakable discourse on the unspeakable Word in speakable words.’ II. ‘In the beginning was the Word.’ III. ‘It is not permitted to the children of truth.’ They are manuscripts in the possession of Dom Costantino of Syracuse, a monk of Catania.” Thus Arnold.]

Gregory of Viterbo, monk of Monte Cassino, was most learned in both laws. He flourished in the time of the said emperors and was buried at Monte Cassino.

## CHAPTER XI. ON BENEDICT

[Note: [Col. 1056C] Benedict Canophilus of Castel di Sangro wrote a *Compendium of Civil and Canon Law* and a *Summary of Things*. He also wrote a *Repetition on the First [Book] of the Decretals, On Constitutions, “Of the Forum of Forum and the Forum of Heaven”*; this treatise was printed at Venice in 1542, in octavo. Bernardino Bonfius, doctor of both laws, ordinary lecturer and dean at Padua, testifies that it was examined, approved, and deservedly commended in the Paduan academy by the most learned Marco Mantua and other distinguished men. He also wrote on the privileges of the Church and of ecclesiastical persons; on crimes against God and neighbour; and on their punishments. He flourished [Col. 1056D] in the year of the Lord 1550.]

Benedict Canophilus of Sangro became a monk at Monte Cassino under Ignatius of Florence, abbot of Monte Cassino. He was most learned in both laws. He wrote a great many books on canon law; he also published a certain *Repertory* in civil law and an extract on “the forum of forum and the forum of heaven,” which was printed. He flourished in the time of Charles V and was buried at Monte Cassino.

## CHAPTER XII. ON CHRYSOSTOM

[Col. 1056B]

[Note: [Col. 1056D] Chrysostom was elected archbishop on 21 October 1564, during the tenure of Ludovico Beccatelli of Bologna, as appears from the consistory acts.]

Chrysostom of San Gemiliano, a Calabrian, became a monk of Monte Cassino under Chrysostom of Naples, abbot; afterwards he was made archbishop of Ragusa. He was a man distinguished by holiness, reformer of the monasteries of the island of Malta near Ragusa, most learned in the sciences, and highly learned also in Greek. He translated various treatises from Greek into Latin. He flourished in the time of the aforementioned emperor. He died at Ragusa in our own time and was buried in his archbishopric.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON FLAVIUS

[Col. 1056C]

[Note: [Col. 1056D] Our Placidus, as also Arnold Wion in book II of the *Tree of Life*, calls this man Flavius incorrectly, since he is named Hercules Tombesius in the catalogue of the bishops of Ravello. He is recorded as having been invested with episcopal dignity on 18 September 1555. He died at Ferrara in 1570 and was buried there in the Church of Saint Francis. Marco Antonio Guarini, *Compendium of the History of the Churches of Ferrara*, book IV, p. 247, testifies; and the distinguished Ughelli states, under the bishops of Ravello, that he had read these words carved upon his tomb in the vernacular: “Hercole Tambusi, bishop, 1570.”]

Flavius of Ferrara, monk of Monte Cassino and later bishop of Ravello, was thoroughly instructed in the Greek and Latin languages. He was greatly beloved by Pope Julius III and was therefore made bishop by him. He flourished in the time of Emperor Maximilian.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON SEVERUS

[Col. 1057A]

[Note: [Col. 1057D] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1570. MUR.]

Severus of Aversa was received as a monk at Monte Cassino under Abbot Chrysostom. He was deeply versed in philosophy and most studious in the divine Scriptures. He flourished in the time of the aforementioned emperor and was buried at Monte Cassino in the cemetery of Saint Anne.

## CHAPTER XV. ON LUKE

[Note: [Col. 1057D] He flourished in the year 1570. MUR.]

Luke of Fratta became a monk at Monte Cassino under Abbot Chrysostom. He was keen of intellect and most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in philosophy. He flourished in the time of Emperor Maximilian and was buried in the monastery of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Mantua, where he publicly taught philosophy.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON JEROME

[Col. 1057B]

[Note: [Col. 1057D] He was flourishing in 1570. MUR.]

Jerome, a Neapolitan by birth and descended from the noble and distinguished Caracciolo family, became a monk in youth under Jerome of Monte Rubeo. He was eminent for humility, chaste in purity, and distinguished by prudence, greatness of spirit, gravity of character, and religious conduct: noble in flesh, but nobler in spirit, and sufficiently instructed in secular and sacred letters. He flourished in our own times, is still alive, and is titular abbot.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON PAUL

[Note: [Col. 1057D] He flourished in the year 1580. MUR.]

Paul of Alta Villa was received as a monk at Monte Cassino under Jerome of Piacenza, abbot. He was [Col. 1057C] most learned in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin letters, tenacious in memory, and quick in intellect. He lived in our own time and was buried at Monte Cassino, in the cemetery of Saint Anne.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON MATTHIAS

[Note: [Col. 1057D] He flourished in the year 1577. MUR.]

Matthias of Bergamo, monk of Monte Cassino, was versed in sacred letters and possessed such a powerful memory that he could recite from memory several books of the New and Old Testaments. He died in our own time and was buried at Monte Cassino, in the cemetery of Saint Anne.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON BENEDICT

[Note: [Col. 1057D] In the year of the Lord 1570. MUR.]

Benedict of San Germano became a monk at Monte Cassino [Col. 1057D] under Jerome of Piacenza, abbot. He was an outstanding man, of great intellect, very learned in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters, and most learned in philosophy and theology—so much so that in his time he had no equal in our congregation. He wrote commentaries on the Hebrew Psalter and on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, and a treatise *On Usury*. He also published expositions on the Psalms. In addition, he wrote on Aristotle’s books *On Interpretation*, [Col. 1058A] *Prior Analytics*, *Posterior Analytics*, and *On the Soul*. His treatise *On the Imitation of Cicero* was also published and committed to print. There survive disputations on Aristotle’s *Categories* and that most beautiful work entitled *Proverbs of Animals*. He also wrote an *Apology against Those Who Slander His Works*. He flourished in our own time and is still alive.

## CHAPTER XX. ON BERNARD

[Note: [Col. 1057D] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1570. MUR.]

Bernard of Genoa became a monk of Monte Cassino under Jerome of Piacenza, abbot of this monastery. He was eloquent and learned in philosophy and the divine Scriptures. He lived in the time of Emperor Maximilian and was buried at Monte Cassino.

## CHAPTER XXI. ON ANTHONY

[Col. 1058B]

[Note: [Col. 1058D] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1575. MUR.]

Anthony of Fratta was received as a monk at Monte Cassino under Laurus of Mantua, abbot of this monastery. He was a man of keen and great intellect, deeply versed in Greek and secular letters, and also highly trained in pontifical law. He wrote for the archive of Monte Cassino a repertory called *Polyanthea*, arranged alphabetically, in which one may readily find the jurisdictions, dignities, and every property which belonged or belongs to the monastery of Monte Cassino. He also published a book on the boundaries of the properties of the monastery of Monte Cassino; but death overtook him, and he left it unfinished. It was afterwards revised and [Col. 1058C] completed by me, Placidus the Roman, monk of Monte Cassino. He flourished in the time of Emperor Maximilian and was buried in the monastery of Saint Liberator of Majella.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON LUKE

[Note: [Col. 1058D] In the year 1570. MUR.]

Luke Anthony of Fermo became a monk at Monte Cassino under Jerome of Piacenza, abbot. He was most learned in philosophy and medicine. He flourished in the time of the aforementioned emperor. He died at Gaeta in our own time and was buried in the monastery of Saint Angel.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON PIUS
[Note: [Col. 1058D] Created bishop on 30 January 1576. A man distinguished for piety and goodness, a most zealous defender of ecclesiastical liberty. He died at Cassino in 1592 and rests buried there.] Pius, a Neapolitan by birth, deriving his origin from the noble and ancient Lottheri family of the city of Florence, [Col. 1058D] became a monk at Cassino under Innocent of Novara, abbot of this monastery. He was a man distinguished by piety and goodness, learned in the Holy Scriptures, and adequately instructed in civil law and ecclesiastical doctrine. Having lived religiously and commendably for twenty-five years in our Cassinese congregation, while prior of St Severinus in the city of Naples he was made Bishop of Fondi by Pope Gregory XIII. [Col. 1059A] Since he is still alive, I shall withhold my judgment concerning him, lest either flattery or truth be reproached in me on one side or the other.

## CHAPTER XXIV. ON THEOPHILUS

[Note: [Col. 1059D] Theophilus Martius, a nobleman of Siena, is mentioned by Peter Recordatus in his *Monastic History*. At Rome, in the basilica of St Paul, he is recorded as having been enrolled by Gregory XIII among the pontifical ministers of penance. Brother Isidore Ugurgierius Azolinus of the Order of Preachers wrote concerning his merits in a book entitled *Pomp of Siena*, title 21, p. 667. We possess a manuscript treatise, *On the Reform of the Calendar*, beginning: “It is indeed praiseworthy to undertake great things.” He died at Cassino in 1586.] Theophilus of Siena became a monk at Cassino under Abbot Angelo Sangrino. He was a man of penetrating intellect and highly learned in the sciences, but especially most learned in philosophy, mathematics, and theology, so that in his day he was held admirable in our Cassinese congregation. He flourished in our times and is still living. Twice he was summoned by the Roman pontiff, that his services might be used in certain ecclesiastical affairs. He published a treatise *On the New Restoration of the Calendar*.

## CHAPTER XXV. ON BENEDICT

[Col. 1059B]

[Note: [Col. 1059D] Benedict flourished in the year of the Lord 1570, deriving his origin from the noble de Uva family. The passions of Saints [Col. 1060D] Agnes, Agatha, Justina, and Catherine were printed at Florence in 1587, in quarto, as was the tragedy *Jephthah*.] Benedict of Capua was received as a monk at Cassino under Abbot Angelo Sangrino, a discerning man and highly learned in sacred and humane letters. In writing verse in his native tongue, however, he was an outstanding poet and admirable in our own times. He published one book of poems in the vernacular, in which he celebrates the martyrdoms of Saints Agnes, Agatha, Lucy, Justina, and Catherine. In the same language and metre he also wrote a treatise on the thought of death; a *Triumph of Martyrs, Confessors, and Virgins*; and one book of devout poems in diverse metres. There is also his tragedy of Jephthah, leader of the Israelite people. He wrote commentaries [Col. 1059C] on the poet Dante, and likewise published one book of letters in the vernacular. He flourished in our times and is still living.

## CHAPTER XXVI. ON JOHN

[Note: [Col. 1060D] He also wrote verses on Saint Febronia, virgin and martyr, printed at Rome in 1589 together with the works of Prosper Martinengo. Arnold Wion testifies, in Book II of the *Lignum Vitae*, p. 430, that he had read the aforementioned manuscript works, as also many others. Possevino too mentions him in his *Apparatus*. He was flourishing in 1590.] John the Evangelist, a Neapolitan by birth and descended from the noble Mormili family, was received as a monk at Cassino by Ignatius of Naples. He was a man of penetrating intellect and very well furnished with sacred and humane learning, but in the art of versification comparable in every respect to the ancients. He wrote very many treatises: namely, a book containing the principal feasts of the Lord, illustrated in various metres; a book *On the Praise of the Glorious Virgin Mary*, at the end of which his Psalter is sung in elegiac verse [Col. 1059D]; and a book containing the Lives of certain saints and hymns in various kinds of verse. There is another book of his poems, containing especially the following works: *On the Notable Victory of Christians over the Turks*, in the time of [Col. 1060A] Emperor Maximilian and Pope Pius V; *On the Praises of Cassinese Youth*; and appended to it a book of odes. At the end is contained a book of *Sorrows*, in which he sings elegiacally of his own troubles and those of his friends; there are also four eclogues by him. Moreover, he wrote innumerable epigrams; he also published several declamations and discourses, and two homilies in prose. Likewise, he wrote an exposition of Saint Paul’s Epistle to the Romans and of Aristotle’s *Perihermeneias* [*On Interpretation*]. In his native tongue he has written, and continues to write to the present day, very many devout poems in praise of the glorious Virgin Mary.

## CHAPTER XXVII. ON THOMAS

[Note: [Col. 1060D] He died after the year 1594 at Cassino. MUR.] Thomas of Eboli became a Cassinese monk under [Col. 1060B] Abbot Angelo Sangrino. He was a man distinguished by prudence and intellect, most learned in philosophy and the Holy Scriptures. He wrote a book of synodal regulations; a book, *Examination of Confessors and of Those to Be Promoted to Holy Orders and of Those to Be Sent to Parish Churches*; and he also published fifty sermons in the vernacular. He flourished in our times and is still living, and serves as vicar general throughout the whole diocese of Cassino.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. ON JEROME

Jerome, deriving his origin from the noble Sersali family of the city of Cosenza, became a monk at Cassino under Jerome of Piacenza, abbot of this sacred monastery. He was a man of shrewd and subtle intellect, [Col. 1060C] moderately learned in humane and sacred letters, but distinguished and admirable in experience of human affairs and in conducting business. He flourished in our times and was abbot of this Cassinese monastery. He was buried at Parma in the monastery of St John the Evangelist, where the general chapter of our congregation is held, in the year of the Lord 1577.

## CHAPTER XXIX. ON APOLLINARIS

Apollinaris of Bauco put on the monastic habit at Cassino in youth under Abbot Laurus of Mantua, where for almost thirty years he led a life more angelic than human. This man, of most upright life and adequately instructed in humane and sacred letters, [Col. 1060D] was so devoted to the Holy Scriptures that, for exercise and lest he become sluggish through idleness, he excerpted and wrote down countless golden sayings from the Old and New Testaments and from diverse Catholic and orthodox Fathers. Moreover, while dean [Col. 1061A] in this monastery of Cassino, he reluctantly and unwillingly assumed the care of novices. While carrying out this office, he enrolled me, though unworthy, in the community of Cassinese monks under Lord Matthias of Lignano, abbot of this monastery, when I was twenty years old, in the year of the Lord 1570. I judged that this about my master ought not to be passed over in silence, since it concerns the integrity and purity of his life. For such was his life that at the time of his death—namely, on the vigil of the Nativity of St John the Baptist—while at Mass the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* was being sung in church, his soul, leaving the prison-house of the body, was seen borne to heaven by angels. He was buried in the cemetery of St Anne in the year of the Lord 1581.

## CHAPTER XXX. ON ANDREW

[Col. 1061B]

[Note: [Col. 1061B] He flourished in the year of the Lord 1578. MUR.] Andrew of Sessa, a young man of excellent disposition and lively intelligence, left the city of Naples, where his parents had placed him to be educated in literary studies, came to Cassino, and became a monk under Isidore of Piacenza, abbot of this sacred monastery. Though small in body, he was great in intellect. Almost from the beginning of his monastic life, [Col. 1062A] because of his quick intelligence and experience of worldly affairs, joined with a singular prudence and skill, he devoted many years to the business of this our monastery. Among the many notable monuments of his intellect, while governing our territory of Citrarii, he wrote two registers of all the rights and properties presently possessed by our monastery in that territory. Moreover, being exceptionally learned in humane and sacred letters, he has, while still living, raised great expectation of himself among all persons. He is still alive and in our time serves as provost of this monastery of Cassino.

## CHAPTER XXXI. ON GREGORY

[Col. 1062B] [Note: [Col. 1061B] The most noble Cortesi family derived its origin from an imperial vicar named Louis Cortes, most noble among the French. As he was counsellor to Pepin, king of Italy and son of Charles, he had settled in the city of Modena. From this family [Col. 1061C] our Gregory was born, a man exceptionally learned in Greek and Latin letters. He had as his teacher Severus Varinus of Piacenza, a Cistercian monk, a man of rare and exquisite learning. From early youth he devoted himself to civil and canon law, and in the service of Cardinal Giovanni de’ Medici, later Pope Leo X, exercised the office of auditor of causes. At length, weary of the Roman court, he returned to his former studies and, by divine prompting, entered the community of Cassinese monks. Pope Paul III, induced by the fame of his virtue, probity, and learning, afterwards admitted him to the College of Cardinals, with the incredible unanimous consent of the entire senate, in the year of the Lord 1542, on 11 June, with the title of St Cyriacus in the Baths; he was also called bishop of Urbino. In addition, he was granted the privilege of wearing the purple, although he was a Benedictine monk; this had likewise been granted to Cardinal Philip de la Chambre, a Frenchman and likewise a Benedictine. Very many works of this most illustrious man [Col. 1061D] remain:

*That Saint Peter Was at Rome*, addressed to Adrian VI, Book 1. *Familiar Letters*, Book 1. These two were printed at Venice by Francesco Franceschi of Siena, in the year of the Lord 1573, quarto. *On Theological Instruction*, a book. *Hymns in Diverse Metres*, Book 1. A Sapphic poem on the *Life of St Honoratus, Archbishop of Arles*. A hymn to the Virgin Mother of God. A poem on Saint Honoratus. A poem on the island of Lérins. A treatise *On Ecclesiastical Power*. *On Original Sin*. [Col. 1062B] *On the Sack of the City of Genoa*. Many works on theology and philosophy. *Praises of the Island and Monastery of Lérins*. Certain poems in imitation of Catullus. They were issued from Aldus’s press together with Sannazaro’s book *On the Virgin’s Childbirth* [Col. 1062C]. A book of St Basil’s *On Virginity*, translated by his labour from Greek into Latin, is read. *On Illustrious Men of the Monastic Order*, Book 1, which, Arnold Wion reports in Book II of the *Lignum Vitae*, p. 216, was stolen and is therefore unavailable. He is said to have written many other works which have perished through the injury of time and human negligence. Four books on the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard are wrongly attributed to our Gregory by Cardinal Torrigio’s cataloguer in his book *On the Writers among the Cardinals of Holy Roman Church*, and by others, although they acknowledge Paul Cortesius, apostolic protonotary, as their author. Various letters of Dionysius Faucherius, monk of Lérins, in praise of our Gregory, survive in the *Chronicle of Lérins*. How highly the aforesaid Pope Paul valued his incomparable integrity, learning, and prudence may be known from the remarkable praises with which he honoured him when he enrolled him among the cardinals. Hear him speaking to him: [Col. 1062D] “Today, in these holy fasts and in our secret consistory, moved by your singular probity, piety, integrity, and learning, in the name of God and with the counsel of our venerable brothers, the cardinals of the same Holy Roman Church, we have created you cardinal of the Holy Roman Church,” etc. Sadoleto and Bembo mention Cortesius; one calls him most learned, the other a man of outstanding learning and an intellect almost divine. See also what the most learned d’Auberi noted in his *General History of Cardinals*, written in French, Part IV, published at Paris in 1647. He died at Rome in the year of the Lord 1548, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [21 September], and was buried at the church of the Holy Apostles, before the altar of St Eugenia.] Gregory Cortesius of Modena, first abbot of St Peter at Perugia, then of St Benedict at Mantua, and created cardinal of the Holy Roman Church by Pope Paul III in the year of the Lord 1542. He was doctor of both laws and highly instructed in the Holy Scriptures. He wrote very many poems in praise of St Peter, which are found in print. He died at Rome and was buried in the church of the Holy Apostles in the year of the Lord 1548.

Here ends the supplement of Lord Placidus the Roman, deacon, to *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Cassino*.

[Col. 1063]

# BOOK OF PETER THE DEACON ON THE BIRTH AND DEATH OF THE RIGHTEOUS OF THE MONASTERY OF CASSINO

(Edited from a Vatican manuscript by Angelo MAI, *Collectio nova*, vol. VI, pt. II, p. 245.)

In the Vatican manuscript Peter the Deacon’s little work *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*, formerly edited by J. B. Maro from a Barberini manuscript, precedes it. It is followed by Ludovicus Barbus’s *History of the Benedictine Congregation of St Justina*, edited by Pez. At last I publish Peter the Deacon’s hitherto unpublished middle book, *On the Righteous of Cassino*, in order to enlarge the biography of holy men and ecclesiastical history. Nor shall I inappropriately recall these narratives to the standard of secular criticism, for they commend themselves sufficiently by their simplicity, by the pious and candid spirit of their author, and by the receptive character of his age.

## I. BENEDICT

[Col. 1063A]

Standard-bearer, founder, lawgiver, and eminent teacher, illustrious in learning and illustrious in virtues: while still a child, he first joined together again a sieve split into pieces. He shattered a glass vessel containing a deadly drink by the sign of the cross alone. He brought forth water from the summit of a dry mountain. Like Elisha, he drew iron up from the depths of the waters. Through his disciple Maurus, he drew Placidus from the depths of a lake. A raven obeyed his commands. Florentius, who persecuted him, was slain by almighty God. Departing thence, the man of God built the monastery of Cassino, and there made a huge stone light by his prayer. By his prayer likewise he extinguished a false fire displayed to sight in the crops. He immediately restored to health a monk broken and disjointed in all his limbs. [Col. 1063B] He at once disclosed the deeds and thoughts of his monks. He foretold future events to the tyrant Totila. He foretold the instability of the city of Rome, the birth of Gregory, Roman pontiff, his name and office, and the destruction of the monastery of Cassino. He knew the hidden judgments of God. He exposed Exhilaratus’s theft. Recognizing through the Spirit the napkins received by a monk against his command, he immediately rebuked him. He knew the thoughts of one serving him. In a time of famine almighty God sent him two hundred measures of flour; by whom they were brought remains unknown to this day. Appearing in sleep to disciples far away, he showed them what they ought to do. Though still [Col. 1063C] in the body, he bound and loosed the souls of nuns already set in that invisible judgment. He cast out of the earth a monk who had left the monastery against his will and had been buried. He cured a leper by his prayer. The sky rained coins upon him. By his touch he immediately banished a disorder of the skin. A glass vessel thrown upon a stone remained unbroken. By his prayer he filled a dry barrel with oil. He struck a monk tormented by a demon with a slap and drove the unclean spirit from him. [Col. 1064A] By his glance alone he freed a bound rustic. He restored a dead man to life. He saw his sister’s soul penetrate heaven in the form of a dove. He saw the soul of Bishop Germanus carried to heaven by angels in a fiery sphere. The whole world, as if gathered beneath a single ray of the sun, was brought before his eyes. By his prayer he cured a woman and her son tormented by a demon. Moreover, he wrote the Rule of monks, outstanding in discernment and eloquent in style, in which all his deeds are found. Twice a week he merely tasted rather than took the least food, and wore only a hair-shirt. At his passing, his disciples saw a road paved with coverings and gleaming with innumerable lamps, stretching straight eastward from his cell to heaven; and an angel said to them: “This is the way by which Benedict, beloved of the Lord, ascended to heaven.” He was buried at Cassino, in the church before the altar of blessed John the Baptist. To this day he shines with such great virtues that neither tongue can explain them, nor ear hear them, nor hand suffice to write them.

## II. MAURUS

Provost of Cassino, a Roman by nation and son of Equitius, a man most celebrated and renowned, and, after Benedict the lawgiver, the first to walk upon the waters on his feet, after the example of the Apostle Peter. At the monastery of Cassino he cured a lame and dumb man. Arderardus, broken throughout his whole body, was immediately healed by him. He similarly healed his servant Sergius. He gave sight to one blind from his mother’s womb. [Col. 1064C] He restored to life Eligius, who had departed from the body and been assigned to places of punishment. By the Holy Spirit revealing it to him, he learned of the death of his master Benedict. He restored to health a cleric broken and disjointed in all his limbs. Those who slandered him were tormented by the devil and were healed by him. He restored life to the man from whom the devil had torn the soul. From a very poor vessel of wine he most abundantly satisfied sixty and more persons on three occasions, and left the vessel full. [Col. 1065A] By the sign of the cross he immediately healed the upper lip and nostrils of a man eaten away by cancer. He knew the secret judgments of God as angels disclosed them. In the seventy-second year of his age, afflicted by pain in his side, he gave up his spirit. He was buried at the right side of the altar of St Martin at Glanfeuil. No one ever subdued his body more by roughness, fasts, abstinence, vigils, and cold. During the days of holy Lent he wore neither tunic nor cowl, but only a sacred hair-shirt; and twice a week he merely tasted rather than took the smallest food. He wore a very rough *trogulus* from his shoulders to his loins. He rested on a bed over a heap [Col. 1065B] of lime and sand, except during Lent; for then, when excessive weariness compelled him, he took sleep standing or sitting. He never rose from his bed with the other brothers, but always anticipated the night hymns by remaining awake. Often he completed fifty or a hundred psalms, and sometimes the entire Psalter, before the nocturnal synaxis, except during the hours when he gave himself to prayer and tears. He devoted himself so fully to silence and reading that even St Benedict himself held him admirable for this.

## III. SCHOLASTICA

The sister of the most holy Father Benedict, united to him both by kinship of flesh and by holiness, followed him in conduct and in footsteps. By his will she established her dwelling on the boundary of Mount Cassino, [Col. 1065C] where she completed a happy life by a most happy end. Thus, as Joshua and Samuel once did, she changed the serenity of the sky into rain and thunder. The most holy Father Benedict saw her soul seek the heights of heaven in the form of a dove. She was buried at Cassino with her brother before the altar of St John the Baptist.

## IV. MARTIN

An outstanding man and magnificent worker of miracles, living first at Cassino and afterwards on Mount Marsicus, he lived for a long time with a serpent. Almighty God granted him water to drink from the stone of his cave. Almighty God terribly killed a woman who provoked him to obscene acts. By his prayer he kept unharmed a boy falling from the highest summit [Col. 1065D] of the mountain to its depths. He moved from place to place a great stone hanging over his cave. He was buried there on Mount Marsicus.

## V. FELICISSIMUS

A disciple of blessed Benedict, Roman by nation, most fortunate in name and most fortunate in deed, he was cousin of the most holy Maurus. Given to blessed Benedict as a boy, he followed his master’s way in all things until death.

## VI. FAUSTUS

At the age of seven he was offered to blessed Benedict at Cassino and sent by him with blessed Maurus into Gaul to build a monastery. He remained there forty years. Then, after the death of blessed Maurus, he returned to Rome and died full of days. He was buried in the Lateran monastery.

## VII. CONSTANTINIANUS

[Col. 1066A]

Likewise sent into Gaul with blessed Maurus, he died in the fortieth year after his arrival in Gaul. He was buried in the church of St Martin.

## VIII. ANTONIUS

Likewise sent with the same man, he died and was buried in the same year and at the same place as Constantinianus.

## IX. PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE AND DEATH OF SAINT PLACIDUS, MARTYR

They say that teachers among the gymnosophists have this custom: when they come to the river Ganges to drink of its water, they despise yellow metal and tread it beneath their feet. I, Peter, unworthy deacon of the chief monastery at Cassino, observing this, have written, Reverend Bishop Gregory, at your command, the deeds of most holy [Col. 1066B] Placidus in such a way that nothing is lacking from his life, although something is lacking from the power of his miracles. Indeed, when your fatherhood wished to impose this work upon me, and my inadequacy refused to undertake it because of the disturbance of so great a monastery and the miseries of our exile, and when I wished to lay this task upon you, who shine in the art of composition, your sagacity began to silence me with this answer: “Why are you afflicted by empty grief over the oppression of the monastery of Cassino? Do you not know that

> If Mount Sinai fell, which once gave the Law,  
> I would not therefore believe its offices had perished;  
> for the Rule remains, written by sacred fingers,  
> handed down to the blessed disciples Maurus and Placidus.

[Col. 1066C]

> If King Antiochus sold the altar for gold,  
> by Law and labour the Maccabee will rebuild a new altar.  
> ‘The bearer of the Law,’ he says, ‘is more present with you  
> after death than now; I shall be present to those who call.’

And if so great a Father promised that he would be more present after his departure from the world, why do you go about sorrowful over such disturbances? Have you now forgotten the hardships and the kinds of persecution suffered by all the heralds of truth? Has it slipped from your mind that [reading uncertain: the text has *levitas*] our Lord Jesus Christ set them apart to proclaim his Gospel to the whole world? For these are the seven stars in the right hand of God, holding seven trumpets, sent into all [Col. 1066D] the earth. Do you not know that the servant is ordered to be punished on account of the talent hidden away? Conquered, therefore, by such arguments, beloved bishop, I submitted to your command and began to raise my mind to write the Life of the most blessed man. Hence I think that this purpose took root in your mind not without the nod of the heavenly King: that the passion of so great a father, written by Gordianus, should be translated. For although from the very times of blessed Benedict there had been very many learned men in the school of Cassino, no one had translated this passion from Greek into Latin; almighty God deigned to accomplish this through us in your troubled time. I further intended to dedicate this little work to Ptolemy, consul of the Romans, but first I judged that it should be polished by your reluctant buskin. Yet it will be your task, Reverend Father, that, if I have put forth anything not weighed in the even balance of order, [Col. 1067A] it may be corrected by you. For, being in the twenty-third year of my age, it befitted me to be a disciple, not a master. Supported, then, by the protection of the heavenly King, I shall begin to write the life of so great a father.

# LIFE AND DEATH OF SAINT PLACIDUS, MARTYR

After the divinity of the supreme King had driven away and put to flight the darkness of idols by the ray of his light, he bestowed upon his Church many men throughout the world who, as stars adorn heaven, so adorned his Church by their life and miracles. From their radiant company, in the time of Justin the Elder, Benedict shone more brightly than the sun. The blessed Gregory, mirror and eminent teacher of the Church of God, set forth his Life in a most pleasing style. [Col. 1067B] But it must be plainly declared how this most holy Father embraced the rule of a more perfect life, founded the monastery of Subiaco, how most blessed Placidus came to him, and in what manner and place he departed and built a monastery in Varro’s most ancient school.

When he had resolved to abandon the entanglements of the world and seek the wilderness, the most holy Father Romanus found him and asked where he was going. When he learned his desire, he kept the secret and gave assistance; he bestowed upon him the habit of holy monastic life and ministered to him as far as he could. For three years, except to the monk Romanus, he remained unknown to men. But when God, the maker of all, chose to reveal Father Benedict to mortals, many in that region were gathered to him [Col. 1067C] for God’s service, so that he built twelve monasteries there. Having appointed provosts in them, he assigned twelve monks to each; but he retained with himself some whom he judged could more suitably be instructed while still in his presence. Then also noble and religious men of the city of Rome began to gather and to give him their sons to be nurtured for almighty God. Then Equitius gave Maurus, his offspring of good hope, and the patrician Tertullus gave the boy Placidus. From the time of his childhood Placidus followed abstinence, silence, vigils, chastity, and every holy virtue; and he made the path of obedience his own.

[Col. 1067D] One day, when water was lacking in the cellar, holy Placidus went out by his Father’s command to draw water from the lake. When he arrived there and carelessly put the vessel he held into the water, he himself fell in after it. The wave immediately carried him away and drew him inward from the shore for almost the distance of an arrow’s flight. But what can the cunning of the ancient enemy accomplish against the power of the Thunderer? For as soon as holy Placidus fell into the water, the Holy Spirit, who holds the chief throne in the hearts of the elect, revealed the event to the most holy Father Benedict. He at once called blessed Maurus with great haste, saying: “Brother Maurus, run quickly, for the boy Placidus, who went to draw water, has fallen into the lake, [Col. 1068A] and the wave is now carrying him farther away.” A wondrous thing, unheard of in all ages after the Apostle Peter! Having asked and received a blessing, Maurus went swiftly at his Father’s command. Believing that he was walking on land, he ran over the very rapid waters to the place where holy Placidus was being drawn by the wave, took blessed Placidus by the hair, and returned at a rapid run. When he returned to the Father, he recounted in order what had been done through him. But the most holy Father Benedict began to attribute this not to his own merits but to Maurus’s obedience. Maurus, on the contrary, said it was done solely through Benedict’s command and that he was not conscious of the power which he had exercised unwittingly. But in this friendly contest of mutual humility, the holy boy Placidus, who had been rescued, came forward as arbiter. [Col. 1068B] For he said: “As I was being drawn from the water, I saw the abbot’s sheepskin cloak over my head, and I perceived that he himself was drawing me out of the waters.”

Holy Placidus was also companion to Father Benedict when, one night, he climbed with him a dry rocky mountain. There, after prayer, Father Benedict placed three stones as a sign and returned with Placidus to his monastery, with all the others unaware. When, on the next day, the brothers who lived on that rock came to him because they needed water, the Father said: “Go and dig a little into the rock in which you find three stones one upon another.” They went and found the mountain rock already sweating; and when they made a hollow place in it, it was immediately filled with water, [Col. 1068C] which flows abundantly even now and descends from that mountain summit to the lower ground. Therefore no one should doubt that most blessed Placidus shared in so great a miracle, since his most blessed master wished him alone to be aware of this sign. Now it must be told how the most holy Father Benedict came to the monastery of Cassino.

A certain priest named Florentius, intoxicated with the poison of the ancient enemy, began to emulate the pursuits of the most holy Father; and so he sent bread infected with poison as a blessing. When the man of God avoided this through the Spirit, the wicked Florentius, unable to kill Benedict’s body with poison, [Col. 1068D] set himself to destroy his disciples’ souls. Thus he sent seven naked girls into the garden of the cell in which Benedict was staying, so that they might inflame their minds toward the perversion of lust. Seeing this and fearing a fall for his still tender disciples, Father Benedict ordered them to be guarded and resolved to yield place to envy.

While he pondered these matters anxiously in his mind, a heavenly revelation deigned to encourage him with this oracle: “Why are you sad, sweetest Benedict? Do you not remember what I declared when I said: ‘If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you’ (John 15:20)? For I have chosen you from all the inhabitants of the world; you shall be the heavenly trumpet of my Gospel, filled with my Spirit. Rise [Col. 1069A] now; go to the stronghold of Cassino and strive, by preaching the life-giving word, to convert to my worship the people of that province, who still serve the impious cults of idols, in whose hearts Satan’s cunning reigns, and who know and say nothing except what the cunning of the lethargic serpent has written in their hearts. For I shall be with you, and I shall not forsake you, and I shall confound all your adversaries, my most beloved servant. Go forth to battle against idols; be strengthened and be stout-hearted, for I shall give you the stronghold of Cassino, and there the seat of your name shall be forever.”

When the most holy Father heard this, he disclosed everything to his assembled disciples; and, after delivering to them a long discourse and exhortation toward progress, he finally said: “The command of our Lord Jesus Christ is at hand; we must obey; we must go. But you, stand firm and remain in the conduct and grace of holy religion.” Having said this, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 529, in the time of Emperor Justinian, he arranged all the oratories he had built, with the brethren attached to them under appointed provosts, and immediately began to make his way to the stronghold of Cassino with no companion’s assistance. But as he travelled alone through unknown places, two angels immediately appeared in the form of young men and showed so great a Father through the mountain wilderness where he ought to direct his steps. Three ravens also became inseparable companions to him throughout the way, constantly following his footsteps. When he reached the stronghold of Cassino, he shattered the idol, overthrew the altar, cut down [Col. 1069C] the groves that had grown up everywhere in the worship of demons, and founded the monastery of Cassino with the most devout Placidus and Maurus. By his bodily resting there and by the composition of his Rule, he made it the head of all monasteries. Where the temple of Apollo had stood, he built a church of St Martin; where Apollo’s altar had stood, he built a church of St John; and he converted the peoples dwelling around it to Christ’s faith.

At that same time the aforesaid Tertullus, patrician of the city of Rome, at the prompting of his son Placidus, made a grant to the monastery of Cassino of eighteen of his estates in Sicily, with seven thousand slaves and the ports of Palermo and Messina. [Col. 1069D] He imposed a penalty of fourteen thousand talents of gold upon anyone who should attempt to remove it. Meanwhile the most holy Father Benedict summoned his disciple Placidus, whom he had nurtured in the holiest and most religious manner, and sent him to Sicily for the protection of the estates which his father, the patrician Tertullus, had given to the monastery of Cassino. He said to him: “Gird your loins like a man to undertake the labour of warfare. Keep inviolate until the end of life the order of holy religion which Christ, King of all, Jesus, now gives you through me, just as you received it from me. Go now, sweetest son, to Sicily, imitating Jesus Christ, Son of God, our Lord, King of kings, who became obedient unto death (Philippians 2:8). Remember his saying: [Col. 1070A] ‘I have come not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me’ (John 6:38). Let not the hardship of a long journey disturb you. Recall the apostolic saying that ‘the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us’ (Romans 8:18). For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven. Those who contend in this life for Christ’s name shall receive eternal recompense in eternity: namely, that homeland ‘which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,’ which God has prepared for those who love him (1 Corinthians 2:9). Do not fear or be dismayed; be strengthened and be stout-hearted, for the lofty right hand of God the Thunderer shall be with you. Know this for certain: the harsher the things you endure in this world, the more abundant [Col. 1070B] the joys of heavenly rewards you shall receive from the supreme Maker. May Jesus Christ, Son of God, our Lord, always be with you and lead you to the fellowship of eternal life, which he will give to those who love him.” Having finished this speech and bestowed his blessing upon him, he sent him away.

But when Placidus had come to Sicily, he strove by every means to carry out what he had learned from his master; and in all the virtues in which his most perfect master Benedict had trained him from his very childhood, he advanced and grew day by day. This blessed man also founded churches and, after the custom of his most holy master, gathered brothers to serve there. It is superfluous, moreover, to inquire into his miracles: [Col. 1070C] for miracles do not make holy men, but rather a life pleasing and upright before God sanctifies a person. Yet because the cruelty of the Ishmaelites devastated the province of the Sicilians, Gordianus, a disciple of Father Benedict, residing at Constantinople, left written accounts of many deeds performed through him. For this Gordianus, sent by blessed Benedict to Sicily with blessed Placidus, described what he saw with his own eyes.

After it pleased the Lord, the King of kings, to free most blessed Placidus from the shipwreck of this present life, Mamucha, leader of the Saracens, arrived by ship with sixteen thousand seven hundred Saracens. He ordered blessed Placidus, with his brothers Eutychus and Victorinus, the virgin Flavia, and also Faustus, [Col. 1070D] Firmatus, and Donatus, together with thirty monks, to be seized and brought before him. After tormenting them with various kinds of torture, as Gordianus relates in the history of that martyrdom, he ordered blessed Placidus, after the cutting out of his tongue and the breaking of his arteries and teeth, to be beheaded with all his companions in the harbour of the city of Messana, in the province of Sicily. On the third day before the Nones of October [5 October], he ascended to the eternal kingdoms. Let us therefore, brothers, earnestly entreat him to pour forth prayers for the universal Church. He was buried in that same province, where blessings abound for those who seek them by devout prayer; through the help of him who lives and reigns with the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1071A] A fuller account of this life is read elsewhere. [Note: [Col. 1071] Understand this to mean the work of Gordianus, which is extant in the *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, I.]

## X. SIMPLICIUS

A disciple of Father Benedict, he was sent with blessed Maurus into Gaul. After Maurus’s death he returned to Rome with Faustus, died at the Lateran monastery, and was buried there.

## XI. CONSTANTINUS

Constantine in name and in deed: after the passing of Father Benedict he became abbot. A man greatly to be revered, he died at Cassino and was buried beside the body of blessed Benedict.

## XII. SIMPLICIUS

Simple in name and deed, he became abbot after Constantine. He died there at Cassino and was buried beside Father Benedict.

## XIII. VITALIS

After Simplicius he became abbot of Cassino; he died and was buried at Cassino.

## XIV. BONITIUS

The fifth abbot after Father Benedict, in the twenty-sixth year after Father Benedict’s passing, when the monastery of Cassino had been destroyed, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 568, he brought with him to Rome the brothers of the Cassinese monastery. Received by Pope Pelagius, [Col. 1071B] he built the Lateran monastery, leaving four or five brothers at Cassino to guard the body of blessed Benedict, the lawgiver. He died and was buried in the Lateran monastery. There he also left the Rule which Father Benedict had written in his own hand, and the sacks in which food had been brought to him from heaven.

## XV. PROLOGUE OF PETER THE DEACON TO THE LIFE OF SAINT SEVERUS, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR

To the most holy Seniorectus, outstanding abbot of abbots, residing in the monastic academy, [Col. 1071C] Peter, deacon of Cassino, wishes whatever is most fortunate in heaven and on earth.

As I have begun, at the command of your authority, to write the Life of the distinguished shepherd Severus, the diligent insistence of your beloved son Rainald, subdeacon of this chief monastery, has required it. Not content merely with the books of the ancients, he too, like the more eager Queen of Sheba, desires to receive from your eminence something new and divine. For when he found my lowliness wavering in the lodging of the lawgiver, saw me entangled in monastic business, and recognized that the continual investigation of precepts and volumes prevented the mind of my breast from searching the books that speak of God, he began with frequent prayers to urge me that, laying aside the tragic buskin, [Col. 1071D] calming the storms of my thoughts, and removing the clamours of the world, I should turn to theological inquiries and should not refuse to set forth Severus, hitherto untouched by ancient pens.

At last a useful labour and his affection moved me, so that devotion to so great a man compelled me to begin what ignorance of letters forbade. For “those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God,” as Paul, teacher of the nations, says; since they keep watch not so much for themselves as for others, through virtue and merit.

To hand down to later generations the deeds and character of men most excellent and illustrious has been customary from, so to speak, the very beginning of the world. For all those distinguished for brilliance of mind, pre-eminent in virtue, modest in chastity, formidable in arms, singular in skill, eminent in memory, and lofty in sophistic acuteness, recorded on pages the deeds of ancient men without envy, favour, ambition, or hatred. Very many also considered the narration of their own deeds an increase in moral improvement rather than arrogance. (Tacitus, *Agricola*.) Hence Paul too says: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4). The Lord likewise commanded Moses, patriarch of the Levitical order, saying: “Write this book, and place it beside the ark of the covenant, that it may be a sign and memorial for the children of Israel, lest they forget the Lord their God” (Deut. 31:26). And why was this? That he might show novices that the fathers of old had courageously completed their course [Col. 1072B] to the finish, so that, stirred by them, they might hasten more eagerly to approach the contest, follow their path, and obey the divine commands. For God anointed the children of the Church with the oil of the Holy Spirit, so that they might be made tested and fit for the struggle. For one who struggles has something to hope for: where there is contest, there is also a crown. One contends in this world and is crowned by Christ; the reward is gathered from the earth and rendered in heaven. Then prudence, chastity, justice, and wisdom flourished, when the virtues of the most famous men were described.

But, as I was about to write the life of so great and such a man, it was necessary to seek pardon for my youth. I would not have sought it, had I not known the savage, impious, bloody, and hostile madness of rivals toward historians; for it is established that they have often raged not only against the writers themselves but also [Col. 1072C] against their books. Yet our forebears displayed in this matter an outstanding proof of patience: they neither answered those men’s folly nor, on that account, ceased from writing annals. Indeed, they most elegantly recorded the golden age of Father Desiderius, virtues of character, and the most excellent and astounding miracles of the monks of Cassino. But enough of these matters. Let the following pen now return to recounting Severus’s praises.

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF SAINT SEVERUS BY THE SAME PETER

The height of the fortress of Cassino once flourished in such eminence that the loftiness of the Roman Empire dedicated it for all time to philosophical studies. Marcus Terentius [Col. 1072D] Varro, the most learned, judicious, acute, and eloquent of all Romans, lived there and possessed it by right of his own jurisdiction. This man, then, of such remarkable and outstanding learning, read so much that Roman nobility marvels that he had leisure to write anything; he wrote so much that scarcely anyone can read it all.

Moreover, he wrote forty-one books of *Antiquities*, dividing them into human and divine matters: he assigned twenty-five books to human matters and sixteen to divine. In that division he followed this arrangement: he gave six books each to four divisions of human matters, discussing who act, where they act, when they act, and what they do. Thus in the first six he wrote about human beings; in the second six, about places; in the third six, about times; and in the fourth and final six, about things. Four sets of six make twenty-four. But at the beginning he placed one separate book, treating beforehand of all matters in common. He preserved the same form of division in divine matters. So far as concerns what humans must offer to the gods—in persons, places, times, and sacred rites—he treated these four topics in three books each: for the first three he wrote about persons; the next, about places; the third, about times; and the fourth, about sacred rites, setting forth with most subtle distinction who offer, where they offer, when they offer, and what they offer. He wrote three further final books, etc.

At this point I have made an abridgment; for he speaks far too diffusely about the rest of Varro’s works. [Note: [Col. 1073D] Let no one think that knowledge of Varro’s works has been taken from us in this lacuna, which the copyist made. For Peter the Deacon was going to say nothing other than what is found in Augustine, *The City of God*, book VI, chapter 3.]

Concerning this Varro, indeed, Cicero says [Note: [Col. 1074D] In Augustine, cited work, VI.2.]: “As strangers wandering and erring in our own city, your books led us back home, as it were, so that at last we might recognize who and where we were. You have disclosed the age of our fatherland; you, the chronological ordering of times; you, the laws of sacred rites; you, those of the priests; you, domestic and public institutions; you, the sites, regions, and places; you, the names, kinds, functions, and causes of all things divine and human.”

Therefore the city of Cassino shone and flourished in highest distinction from the very beginning of its construction, through such an author and such studies. It was formerly called by three names: first Heraclea, then Old Forum, and finally Samnites. The Samnites, descended from the Sabines, called the same place Casinum from *casca*, for *casca* in ancient usage meant an older thing. But when Christ—the Word, power, and wisdom of the heavenly Emperor—determined to turn it into a school of true wisdom, he appointed for that city two leaders through whom it might become the mirror of the world, the dignity of heaven, the promulgation of law, and the norm, way, temple, and throne of justice and religion for the devout. Through them, indeed, the worship of perverse superstition was expelled from that place, and the spiritual wickednesses were driven from their lordly rule—not by material or glittering arms, not by diversity of legions, not by rhetorical ornaments of words, but eminent only through life, speech, signs, and miracles. [Col. 1073D] But since Gregory Chrysostom, the jewel of Jesus Christ, has written out the life of the lawgiver most fully, I shall begin to write the Life of the supreme and venerable bishop, the outstanding Severus.

The four hundred and first year from the Incarnation of the life-giving Word was passing [Note: [Col. 1074D] But in fact Valentinian III assumed imperial power in the year of Christ 424.], when Valentinian III, most fortunate and most excellent, assumed the throne of the Roman Empire to govern it. While he held the reins of the world, Severus, the man of the Lord, granted to Campania by the beneficence of the Almighty, [Col. 1074A] shone as bishop of the Church of Cassino at that time—like a topaz, radiant in the gravity of his character, the excellence of his life, and the brilliance of his virtues—when justice was shaken by injustice, piety by impiety, gentleness by severity, and the condition of the Catholic and Apostolic Church by the madness of the most impious Arians, Nestorians, Manichaeans, Circumcellions, Priscillianists, and Donatists.

Still in his tender years, he despised with all the effort of his mind the perishing joys of the world and strove by every means to build within himself a temple for the life-giving Spirit. For he was conspicuous in chastity, remarkable in holiness, and an exceptional protector of the poor, widows, and orphans. Hence, shining more brightly than light through these and other virtues, he was held so dear and admirable by all that they hoped to have him as father, lord, and, after the bishop’s death, pontiff. Among the other marks of goodness which divine grace had granted him, he was so fortified by the virtues of faith, hope, and charity that it was easy for all to perceive what honour Severus already foreshadowed in himself. Having thus passed through boyhood, when he reached the Pythagorean “fork in the road,” the following narrative will show what and how great a man, through the favouring mercy of God, he proved himself to be. I shall now briefly set forth how and in what order he attained the episcopal height.

It happened, then, that the bishop of the aforesaid city, paying the debt of nature, was called by the Lord to the homeland of heavenly blessedness, to receive his reward. [Col. 1074C] The holy Church of Cassino, deprived of the comfort of its shepherd, remained bereaved. But because Christ’s Church could not long remain without a ruler, all, after taking counsel together and grieving at the hardships of his servants, unanimously chose the most blessed servant of Christ, Severus, as bishop. When the man of God, out of humility, refused to accept this, he said: “Most beloved brothers, I do not perceive myself to be adorned with those virtues in which divine mercy exhorts a bishop to flourish.”

On the contrary, inflamed with godly ardour, they addressed him in these words: “Father, you are surely now despising Christ when you refuse to feed his sheep. For in that judgment you will be guilty when you are accused concerning the gift you have hidden. The manner of life of those who pass their lives in silence, although it helps by example, nevertheless does more harm through silence. Therefore the King of all gave you the seeds of the divine word, so that you might distribute them to those in need. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; rebuke, entreat, reprove, in all patience and teaching’” (2 Tim. 4:2).

Convinced by these words, Severus the shepherd no longer dared reject what he was commanded to undertake for the common salvation. Clothed in the virtues of love for God and neighbour, by the favouring grace of the eternal King [Col. 1075A] he was raised to the honour of the priesthood. Once ordained bishop, he cared for the flock entrusted to him all the more diligently because he knew himself to have been exalted above all. For he did not ignore that, in the future judgment of that terrible day, he would render an account to the Lord for the sheep committed to him. Thus he was sweet, kind, and gentle to all, though at times stern toward many and yet calm.

At that same time there arose at Constantinople Nestorius, a most pestilential and, beyond all heretics, most impious false patriarch: submerged in the sea of falsehood, minister of the devil, vessel of all perversity and wickedness, inventor of unheard-of rashness and superstition. Together with the most wicked Eutyches, he dared to burst into such folly as to affirm [Col. 1075B] that God the Word had not been incarnate, and that the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, had borne not God but merely a man. From this most pestilential root arose the impious heretics Acacius, Peter of Alexandria, and the perverse Dioscorus, whom the Roman pontiffs were never able to bring back to the bosom of Mother Church. Instead, doing worse day by day, they tore the Church of Christ throughout the whole East. For while all the priests of the world received the Council of Chalcedon, these men, infected by the hissing of the lethargic serpent, assailed it with insults.

Yet some Easterners, protected by divine defence, since they could not extinguish the stench of those foul serpents, adopted the final course of awaiting the assistance of defence from the pontiff of the Roman See. Those who lived in New Rome and throughout the East accordingly came to Old Rome and begged Felix, Roman pontiff, to deign to put an end to such great evils. Among them John, patriarch of Alexandria, came to Rome saying the same thing. Felix, the most holy pontiff, held a synod in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and sent two bishops and a defender of the Church to Constantinople, writing to Acacius that he should return to the bosom of Mother Church. When they reached Constantinople, they were detained at Acacius’s will, deprived of their letters, and thrown into prison. Threatening to kill them unless they communicated with him, he subjected them to various torments. On the appointed day, [Col. 1075D] the most wicked Acacius called together an assembly of heretics and, deceiving the envoys of the Apostolic See with gifts, compelled them to communicate with him, although the orthodox bishops then present protested and resisted to the contrary. Some of them suffered a most grievous persecution at Constantinople. After the papers had been removed, they attached the first written protest to a rope placed around a hook and hung it upon one of the legates; they put the second into a book; and they placed the third in a basket of vegetables. [Note: [Col. 1075] I draw these supplementary details from Theophanes, cited by Pagi in his *Critica on Baronius*, under the year of Christ 484.]

But Felix, the most holy pope, learning what had been done by the envoys, deposed them and resolved to convene a synodical council of bishops. [Col. 1076A] Therefore the priestly assembly flowed to Rome from almost all Italy; most holy Severus, bishop of Cassino, also came there. While that same most holy pope was presiding in the church of the apostle Peter, a synod was held in the city of Rome, at which sixty-seven bishops attended together with Saint Severus. There they pierced and condemned with the sword of the Holy Spirit Nestorius, Eutyches, Acacius, Dioscorus, Peter of Antioch, and John, the most wicked patriarch of Alexandria. Having made copies, they circulated them through East and West by the hands of orthodox believers. They also sent a letter concerning this matter to the clergy and people of Constantinople. Likewise, they transmitted to Acacius a letter of deposition and excommunication.

When those carrying the apostolic letters arrived at Constantinople, they reached the monastery of Dii. On Sunday, the monks of Dii presented the letter to Acacius in the sacristy. But those who belonged to Acacius’s party killed some of the monks who had delivered the letter and committed others to a prison cell. The most wicked Acacius, imitating his father the devil, acted worse day by day. But the watchful judgment of God came upon him before long: two months after his deposition, he lost both his present and future life.

Severus, the life-giving shepherd, increasing from virtue to virtue, urged the flock entrusted to him to strive for higher things. He strengthened some who laboured in good works, turned the negligent toward better deeds, cleansed what was unclean, watered what was dry, and uprooted every harmful thing. [Col. 1076C] Thus the lethargic serpent, seeing that those who were evidently returning daily to the Lord were being lost to him, did not cease daily to stir up new conflicts against the Church.

At that same time, the pestilential teaching of the Arians, Manichaeans, Circumcellions, Priscillianists, and Donatists defiled the African Church. Their madness so stained the hearts of the Africans that bishops, priests, deacons, and monks were rebaptized. For this reason Victor, archbishop of Carthage, came to Rome and took care to report to Pope Felix, with the bishops Donatus, Rusticus, and Pardulus, [Col. 1076D] what had happened in Africa. Then the most holy Felix assembled seventy-nine bishops in the city of Rome and held a synod in the Constantinian basilica. There he decreed that bishops, priests, and deacons who had been rebaptized should remain in penance until death and be reconciled at the point of death; but that monks, clerics, and laypeople of either sex should remain in penance for three years, then be admitted to sacramental communion, and never again be allowed to approach the church.

When the man of God Severus returned from that synod to the Church of Cassino, he began to devote himself to such works of mercy and became so lavish in almsgiving [Col. 1077A] that he could now freely say with blessed Job: “Compassion grew with me from infancy.” For which of Severus’s poor was not supported by his help? Or who, deprived of personal aid, did not experience Severus’s assistance? In accordance with the Lord’s command, he made friends for himself from the mammon of iniquity, that they might receive him into eternal dwellings. Wishing to walk toward them, he said: “How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and fails for thy courts” (Ps. 83:3).

When he had honourably completed the course of his time and knew that the end of his life was near, he summoned his clergy and said: “As you see, most beloved sons, I am walking the path of the fathers; and it now pleases me to sing that apostolic saying: ‘I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith’ (the citation printed as 1 Tim. 4:7); and now I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1:23). Therefore bring the words of my sermons back to mind. Love Christ; love peace and charity with your whole heart; trample underfoot the transient things of this world. All things that appear beautiful and delightful in this world are slippery and utterly vain, and by deceptive pleasure ensnare humankind. They are possessed with toil and viewed with envy; they make everyone suspicious, everyone fearful, and strive to plunge everyone into the abyss of eternal fire. In return for a happiness of brief duration, they bring everlasting misery.

“The things necessary for human beings, the things that can suffice for you, are few. Flee the wantonness of the flesh, through which God is excluded from the mind; abandon avarice; resist pride; defeat malice; hasten to conquer anger; reject empty talk; love mercy and judgment. Turn your heart away from the ways of the devil and the crafty devices of heretics, which lead not to life but to death, not to heavenly kingdoms but to cruel Tartarus. [Col. 1077C] Let no one deceive you: you will be judged according to your deeds. You will receive one of these two things, either punishment or everlasting glory. Look to Christ seated at the right hand of the Father; keep Christ’s commands; love Christ’s kingdom. Aim there; direct the eyes of your heart there; lift up your spirit and mind there. Do not look back. Preserve the dignity of your condition. In order that you may be able to know God, first look upon yourselves; consider what sort of persons you will be when you come into the presence of the eternal Emperor. Desire with heart and mind that glory which is eternal, where all things are tranquil, where all are at rest, where there is light, beauty, and splendour—where God himself is; where there is no night, no darkness, no misery, but joys full of blessedness.”

Thus Saint Severus the bishop addressed his clergy with these and similar words. After governing the holy Church of Cassino most holily and gloriously, he rendered earthly things to the earth and happily passed to the Lord on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July]. The people, seeing themselves deprived of so great a shepherd, raised his most sacred body with hymns and praises and honourably buried it in that same fortress of Cassino. There, [Col. 1078A] no one doubts that the Lord Jesus Christ, through the intercession of his merits, works many miracles to this very day. The most blessed bishop Severus flourished in the times of the emperors Valentinian III, Marcian, Leo, and Zeno, and of the Roman pontiffs Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, and Felix III.

At a certain time, a woman named Alserada in the city of Aquino suffered from a most grievous pain in her eyes. She began with every effort to seek the aid of physicians; but the more bodily remedies mortals applied to her eyes, the more her illness grew. When bodily light had now been entirely taken from her, pondering within herself the psalmist-prophet’s verse, “Call upon me in the day [Col. 1078B] of thy tribulation” (Ps. 49:15), “I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me” (Ps. 90:15), she began inwardly to magnify the mercy of almighty God, saying:

“Lord God almighty, who remainest in unapproachable light, who hast enlightened those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death by the precious blood of thy Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, I humbly entreat thy mercy, that thou wouldst deign to restore light to me, most miserable as I am—the light which, through my sins requiring it, I have lost—so that I may praise, glorify, and bless thy name now and for ever.”
