As she silently revolved these things in her heart, most holy Severus appeared to her and said: “What has brought you, woman, to such sorrow?” She replied: “Behold, lord, you see that, through my sins requiring it, I am wholly unable to behold the shining radiance of the sun, created by God [Col. 1078C] to illumine the world.” Saint Severus the bishop said to her: “Do you wish to be healed?” The woman replied: “I do, and I earnestly beg it.” Saint Severus said: “Go to my church, which is built on Mount Cassino, and there I shall restore you to health.”

Hearing this, the woman said: “By what name, most holy Father, are you called?” Saint Severus the bishop replied, putting aside all ambiguity: “Know that I am Severus, bishop of Cassino.” Having said this, he disappeared. The woman called her husband and said: “I can now cast off the blindness of my eyes, which until now has grievously covered our little body, if you favour our vows and do not oppose our purpose.” Her husband said: “Whatever you say, I shall do, and in all things I shall obey your will; only tell quickly, and with all speed, in what manner these things came to your knowledge.”

Then she said: “While I was imploring God’s mercy because of the pain in my eyes, behold, a certain man stood before me. Identifying himself as Severus, bishop of Cassino, he commanded me, if I wished to recover my sight, to go with all haste to his church, which is built on Mount Cassino.” When her husband heard such words from his wife’s mouth, he blessed the Lord; immediately rising with his wife, he began to travel toward Mount Cassino. Most holy Severus, observing the woman’s faith and devotion, did not allow her healing to be delayed long. Before she had approached [Col. 1079A] the church of that confessor, she received her sight.

Seeing this, her husband began to glorify and bless the Lord, who had deigned to work such a great miracle in his wife through most blessed Severus the bishop. When she reached the church of that bishop, she publicly related to all what the Lord had granted her through Saint Severus the bishop. The woman also paid vows of thanksgiving there to the Lord for the health of her body, and returned home praising and blessing Jesus, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong one Godhead, one majesty, equal glory, power, authority, and magnificence, now and always and through the eternal ages of ages. Amen.

## XVI. VALENTINIANUS

A disciple of Father Benedict, noble in birth but nobler in spirit, he was the fifth after most holy [Col. 1079B] Benedict in the Lateran monastery, which his predecessor Abbot Bonitius had built with the permission of Pope Pelagius. He was the first there to govern the Cassinese congregation. He rested there, buried.

## XVII. THEODORUS

After Valentinianus he became the third abbot there. Distinguished in life and holiness, he rested there.

## XVIII. GREGORIUS

Also a disciple of Father Benedict and conspicuous in holiness, he both lived and died in the monastery of Saint Stephen near Terracina.

## XIX. SPECIOSUS

The full brother of this Gregory, noble in birth and trained with his brother in secular studies, was made a monk by blessed Benedict together with his brother—as Saint Gregory relates in the fourth book of the *Dialogues*—[Col. 1079C] and was sent by Benedict to reside in the monastery of Saint Stephen near Terracina. He and his brother possessed much wealth in this world, but gave it all to the poor for the redemption of their souls and remained in that monastery.

When Speciosus had been sent to the city of Capua on business for the monastery, one day his brother Gregory was sitting and eating at table with the brothers. Raised in spirit, he looked and saw the soul of his brother Speciosus, though so far away, depart from the body. He immediately told the brothers, hurried off, and ran there, finding that same brother already buried. Yet he found that he had departed from the body at the very hour at which he had seen it. In this miracle Gregory was like his most blessed master Benedict, who saw the soul of his sister Scholastica seeking the heights of heaven.

## XX. PAULINUS

A disciple of Father Benedict, conspicuous in religious life and conduct, he lived at Cassino until his death. He was buried there in the very place where the church of Saint Stephen was later built. When his body was discovered in the time of Abbot Oderisius, a demoniac who came there was healed. Then the abbot, raising the body of Saint Paulinus with the brothers, reverently placed it in the wall of the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

## XXI. AUGUSTINUS

A disciple of blessed Benedict, approved in holiness, he lived there at Cassino and was buried beside the body of Saint Paulinus with two others. [Col. 1080A] But when the bodies of the saints had been found, a demoniac who came there began to cry out: “Paulinus and Augustinus, disciples of Benedict, together with their two companions, are casting me out.” As the devil repeatedly said these things through his mouth, the unclean spirit departed with blood. Abbot Oderisius then raised the saints’ bodies from there and buried them, with the body of blessed Paulinus, beside the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

## XXII. PETRONAX

Abbot of Cassino: when he wished to go to Jerusalem for the sake of salvation, he was instructed by Pope Zacharias and came to Cassino. Restoring that place, he lived there most holily and religiously until the end of his life.

## XXIII. CHARLES

King of the Franks and patrician [Col. 1080B] of the Romans: coming to Cassino, he laid aside his royal diadem and purple, became a monk, and there rendered diligent service to the brothers with all humility. He who formerly went about clad in purple and garments woven with gold and gems, afterwards, covered with a cheap garment, himself poor, ministered to the poor; for he was supreme in humility and great in innocence.

The abbot, in order to learn by experience the secrets of his heart, entrusted a few sheep to him to pasture. As he led them out to graze and brought them back for many days, he encountered a robber one day. When the robber rushed upon him, Saint Charles said: “Do what you wish; only do not seek to take away the sheep entrusted to me.” The robber immediately stripped Saint Charles completely. But Charles, unable to endure the nakedness of his body, rushed upon the robber, immediately threw him to the ground, and took away his breeches, leaving him all his other garments. When Charles came naked to Cassino with the sheep [Col. 1080C] and told the abbot what had happened, the abbot began to rebuke him most sharply; Charles answered nothing except that he had sinned. He was therefore ordered to be clothed and returned to his assigned obedience.

One day, as he was striving to return to the monastery with the sheep, one of them began to limp very badly. Seeing that he could not return to the monastery, Charles put the sheep on his shoulders and carried it back to the monastery of Cassino. But before he returned, it happened that the sheep soaked him with urine. Charles endured this so patiently that he neither took the little sheep from his neck on that account [Col. 1080D] nor said a word about it to anyone. When those who had seen it reported this to the abbot, the abbot recognized that the Spirit of God was truly in him and commanded him to rest from his obedience and cultivate, according to his knowledge, a garden.

At last he was sent to his brother Pippin in Francia and died there. His brother Pippin placed his body in a golden, gem-studded coffin and sent it back to the monastery of Cassino. There he was buried beside the body of blessed Benedict.

## XXIV. RADCHIS

King of the Lombards: coming to Cassino with his wife and daughter, he laid aside his diadem and purple and became a monk together with his children. A vineyard planted by that king, quite near the monastery, still exists to this day [Col. 1081A] and is still called by his name. His wife and daughter, building a monastery at Plumbarola from their own resources, ended their days there under a very strict rule of life.

## XXV. PAULUS

Deacon and monk of Cassino, he devoted himself beyond human measure to innocence, humility, and silence; there he lived very austerely and strictly until the end of his life. He was buried at Cassino before the chapter-house.

## XXVI. PROLOGUE OF PETER THE DEACON OF CASSINO TO THE LIFE OF SAINT APOLLINARIS, ABBOT

To the most reverend Rainald, fellow deacon of the monastery of Cassino and adorned with the flowers of learning, Peter, the least son of that same monastery, wishes the prize of everlasting [Col. 1081B] victory.

Most earnestly to be admired and exalted with every praise is the devoted zeal of holy men, who, while they see themselves harassed and shaken amid the rubbish of a perishing world, neither desire to be raised up by prosperity nor fear to be broken by adversity; but, panting after the sceptres of the unchangeable height and awaiting the laurel of eternal victory, are to be enrolled with equal weight not among those whose god is their belly, but among the soldiers of the supreme Emperor. Seeing you, venerable brother, placed in that purple-clad company of sages, striving, for the increase of faith and the praise of Jesus Christ, like another peaceable Solomon, to build by new expositions a new temple for the exalted Maker, you have deigned, for this very reason, to urge the scanty poverty of my understanding and, after my return for ever to the citadel of Mount Cassino, from which I had been absent “for a time, times, and half a time,” [Note: On the exile of Peter the Deacon, see the additions to his booklet *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*, ch. 47; likewise the letter of Ptolemy, consul of the Romans (on whom see our p. 247), in the notes to Book IV of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, in Muratori, *SS. RR. II*, vol. IV, p. 488.] to demand without ceasing, by repeated petitions and constant exhortations, that I awaken, drowsing in idle, inert, lethargic sleep, drive far away the harmful sleep of silence, and write the Life of the eminent Apollinaris. You repeatedly set and recall before my mind’s eye that God-speaking commandment which, bringing back to the grace of most splendid light the image of those who dwell not doxologically but simply in the gloomy horror and labyrinthine cavern, blessed them for eternity.

Therefore, dearest brother, neither wishing nor able to resist your requests, I proceeded slackly and hesitantly. Thus, while I was tossed upon the rocks of the sea and the lowest parts of our body were shaken with grim terror, the Rising One, who illuminates everyone in the world, no longer allowing me to lie hidden in harmful darkness, recalled to our heart that divine oracle: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, and He will give it to him” (James 1:5). And again: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (ibid., 17). Therefore, invoking Jesus Christ, Son of God, the beginning of light and the fountain and source of eternal wisdom—through whom we have access, in the one Holy Spirit, to the primal, life-giving, unfailing light—and looking to the unshaken author of doxological things, I shall endeavour to set down more fully the miracles of His servant, insofar as He Himself, the Fashioner, Sower, and Nourisher of the world, shall deign to grant them through His overflowing mercy.

But if even now my friends, who love me so greatly that they cannot be heretics without me, have ceased to gnaw and tear at me, and have judged me tasteless and foolish for writing, and, having become androgynous, have by their whispering made themselves brothels of demons and food for death, I have thought it more fitting to leave them to the examination of the great Judge than to answer them—especially since on the last day of judgment they will hear: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23). Yet I earnestly ask all who approach as polished readers of this work to pardon my natural disposition, and, while I am gathering material amid the ghostly chasms of the sea and the seaweed of the Atlantic, beneath which the cold serpent lies, to bring me back to the harbour of the heavenly city. May Jesus Christ, the almighty King, through whom, in whom, and from whom the beginning of wisdom subsists, be the author and standard-bearer of my discourse.

But you, dearest brother in Christ, bound to me by an indissoluble love from our very rattles, so to speak: according to the surpassing and pre-eminent trumpet of the excellent King, which commanded us to preach the Gospel to every creature and promised that eternal images would be given to us through the mystery of this matter, do not be reluctant to polish with your reluctant yet two-edged sword this little work, simply written by me. And according to the edge of learning entrusted to you, stop the unspeakable grunting of the swine—the ghostly leopard, which follows its sign and greedily embraces the muddy gains of the Cynics, grunting against the unconfused and most radiant pearl of the eternal Emperor, the school of the monastery of Cassino. But leaving these ghostly beings with their prince for condemnation in the pyres, and most often invoking the eternal Spirit who filled the lyre-player’s plectrum, I shall undertake to write, as the King of kings grants, the Life of the eminent hierarch Apollinaris, who broke the horns of the fierce rhinoceros.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

Accordingly, after that thousand-times happy one, adorned with the laurel and the fillets of the thumb, had reached the throne of the heavenly Emperor by a road strewn with cloaks and glittering with lamps, there arose in the chief monastery of Cassino—which that most holy Father had built, in accordance with the oracle of the Thunderer, upon the rock of faith, and which he had established by his bodily resting-place and the formulation of his Rule as the head and summit of all monasteries—very many most holy men after his blessed ascent into Christ’s kingdom. Relying upon heavenly aid, they fought against the prince of this world, trampled down his insolence with untiring courage of faith, stirred the hearts of their hearers by life and teaching to the service of the heavenly King, and shone with miracles in every respect comparable to apostolic and ancient ones.

From their most sacred and exceedingly radiant company, just as the morning star shines in the ethereal heaven, so the most holy and magnificent Abbot Apollinaris shone in that monastery in life and miracles in the times of the emperors Charles and Nicephorus. Chosen by almighty God before the foundation of the world, according to the apostolic saying, he possessed such holiness and religious devotion that the fame of his honourableness, his restrained life, and the gravity of his conduct, flying far and wide, drew many to the service of the heavenly Emperor. While still within the years of childhood, he was entrusted by those who loved him with unique affection to teachers for instruction in letters. As he moved among a band of boys his own age, he did not, as that age usually does, pursue childish trifles. For though he was a boy in years, he was an old man in gravity, modesty, and bearing.

But once he had been judged fit for the branding iron of the heavenly King, he was admitted to the rank of the ecclesiastical order and marked with clerical tonsure. While in that rank, he did not cease to seek difficult and higher things, such as seemed impossible to others. When his parents perceived his disposition, they came with him to Cassino and offered him to the supreme Maker and to Father Benedict. When the boy of the Lord reached youth, he began to devote himself to prayer and reading; and, so far as his father's permission allowed, he never ceased to undertake a demanding discipline. But Gisulf, abbot of that monastery, seeing that the young man’s mind was founded upon the rock of faith and panting after the heavenly prize, thereafter caused him to be ordained to the Levitical dignity of the priesthood. Once ordained, the most blessed man began with every effort to increase from virtue to virtue.

Now I shall briefly begin to relate how he undertook the governance of the throne of the chief monastery of Cassino. When Abbot Gisulf departed this life, all alike, with one wish, one mind, and deepest consent, were inspired to choose as father the most holy man Apollinaris, conspicuous in bearing and habit, whose life harmonized with governance, and to set him as vicar of Benedict the lawgiver. But the man of God Apollinaris, seeing that this rank of eminence was exceedingly grave and arduous beyond measure, and, as a disciple of humility, holding fast to the path in which the perfection of all virtues consists, declared himself unworthy of so great an honour. Yet the brothers judged him worthy to be placed over so great a school, to receive the throne of Benedict the lawgiver, to be a teacher and hierarch of heavenly contemplation, and, as a faithful servant, to return with gain the talents entrusted to him by the Son of the supreme King. On behalf of Father Benedict they commanded him. But the man of God, discerning in this the will of the Almighty, no longer refused to accept the office of governance.

But when Father Apollinaris, lawgiver, had received the throne in so great a school, what teacher could recount what manner of man and how great he was? Truly, to confess the truth, if Plato, prince of all sophists, were to rise from the deadly fires of the Acherusian jaws in which he is tormented, and if Marcus Terentius Varro, ally of the Romans, who surpassed all Latins with his plectrum, were restored from above, they would not think it unworthy to write the Life of so great and such a Father. In name and in deed he was the vicar of the most holy Father Benedict. Moreover, the report of his sanctity spread through nearly all Italy, and many were already wishing to leave the world and be trained under his teaching. On a second Mount Sinai—where Moses, standard-bearer of the New Testament, proclaimed heavenly laws to the peoples—one might have seen a heavenly choir dwelling under so great a Father: living indeed on earth, but standing in the presence of the Holy Spirit and of the supreme King. Then each person counted himself fortunate who was able either to live in so great a monastery or to give his possessions there.

One day, however, the holy man Apollinaris, because circumstances required it, went out to the estates of the monastery of Cassino. When he had reached the River Liris, he spoke to the man who had accompanied him: “Now, dearest son, walk along the riverbank, and if you find anywhere a boat by which we may cross the river, hasten back to me and make it known.” The man obediently carried out without delay what had been enjoined upon him. But after he had searched all the banks of the river, he at length returned to holy Apollinaris without success. When he came to him and was asked whether he had fulfilled his commands, he replied: “Most holy Father, I have already walked through and searched all the banks of the river, and I have not been able to find a boat.”

At this, Apollinaris, the eminent standard-bearer of the Thunderer, did not know what to do, where to turn, or what counsel to adopt. Finally, when he saw that earthly help had failed him, he turned to the aid of Him who said: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find” (Matt. 7:7), and so forth. Therefore, when holy Apollinaris, servant of the Lord, saw that he lacked a boat to cross the river, burning with the fire of the gracious Spirit, which does not burn but enlightens, he approached the riverbank full of faith. Fortifying himself with the saving sign of the cross, clothed and shod, he entered the river; and walking upon the waters, he was brought with dry feet to the nearer side of the stream, after the example of the prince of the apostles, so that he seemed to have walked not upon water but upon dry ground.

You are exalted, O Christ; great is your power, you who gave a new Peter to the monastery of Cassino and appointed him vicar to Benedict the lawgiver! Those who were present near that same river, seeing holy Apollinaris walking upon the water, were disturbed and terrified; believing themselves deceived by a ghostly illusion, they hastened to fortify themselves with the standard of the immeasurable King. Astonished at so great a miracle, they sent to the waters of the Liris, striving quickly to learn who he was, whence he came, who had walked on the water with his feet, and by what name he was called. When their messenger reached the riverbank and learned that he was holy Apollinaris, he hastened joyfully back to his companions. When they had learned everything from him in order, struck by so great a wonder, they raised their hands to the stars and began to praise the mercy of the exalted King, then came with all speed to the holy man.

When they came to him, they threw themselves upon the ground and began to entreat that the most holy Father would pour out prayers to God, ruler of all things, on their behalf. Raising them from the earth, the man of God urged them to meditate day and night upon the laws of the supreme Sower; rewarding them with his blessing, he sent them back to their own homes. Meanwhile this report spread through countryside and cities, and each person then thought himself most fortunate if only he could see him or receive his blessing. When the miracle of so great a Father had been reported to the brethren in the monastery of Cassino by those who had seen it, and they had carefully inquired in what manner and place it had occurred, they began to give thanks to the all-powerful Maker, saying: “We give you thanks, life and salvation of mortals, because you have exalted the monastery of Cassino with such glory that, in your special servant Apollinaris, the Church throughout the whole world magnifies you.”

But when the holy man of the Lord had completed the matters for which he had gone and returned to Cassino, he began from that time to be held in great veneration by the brothers. Yet the venerable Father Apollinaris, increasing from virtue to virtue, was not thereby lifted up into human glory.

While the fame of his virtues was spreading far and wide through the mouths of all, Radelchis, count of Compsa, who, after murdering Grimoald, had put Sico in his place as prince, heard of his virtues. Recognizing that he was guilty through the blood of the lord whom he had killed, he began silently to turn these thoughts over within himself: “Woe to me, unhappy man, who have committed so monstrous an offence! What shall I do? What counsel shall I take? I have sinned grievously, for I deprived my lord of life. Hurry, hasten, run for your life, wretch, while the Sun of justice gives you light.” As he silently turned over these and other thoughts, he resolved in his mind to go to the chief monastery of Cassino to see Father Apollinaris. When he came hastily to that place, he was presented, as he wished, before the eyes of most holy Apollinaris. Upon seeing him, he threw himself at his feet. When the man of God commanded him to rise, he asked why so great a man had wished to come to the school of Cassino.

Requesting a private place, the count disclosed the matter for which he had come. The man of God addressed him thus: “My son, do not let the enormity of your sins bring you to despair. For the same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, said to his disciples: ‘I came not to call the righteous, but sinners’ (Matt. 9:13). And again: ‘I tell you, there is great joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need penance’ (Matt. 15:8).” When Radelchis had received these and many further words of consolation and eternal life, he replied: “Father, the words uttered by you have pierced the depths of my heart. Therefore I earnestly beseech almighty God that He who granted me the will may also grant me the power.” Commending himself to the holy Father, he returned to the city of Compsa.

But those with whom the count had undertaken these counsels, seeing that he had returned, began anxiously to ask him what he had seen at Cassino. Then the count answered them: “I have clearly seen, to speak the truth, on the summit of Mount Cassino a heavenly choir dwelling upon earth, who, after the manner of heavenly spirits, at almost every hour and moment praise Sabaoth, reigning over the heavenly sceptres; for whom to live is Christ and to die is gain. And what can I tell you about their life? Our Lord Jesus Christ indeed chose them before the foundation of the world, that they might be holy and blameless in His sight. Even if the eloquence of the sophists were available to me, it would not altogether suffice to recount the praises of the brethren of Cassino. For on the summit of that mountain Jesus Christ, the eternal King of kings, has built a temple for Himself.”

After the count had said this, recalling what the most holy Abbot Apollinaris had said to him at Cassino, he despised the trifles and refuse of the world and trampled underfoot, trusting in the protection of the exalted King, the wiles of the lethargic serpent; scorning the fleeting abundance of possessions, with an iron chain fastened about his neck, he came weeping and wailing to the monastery of Cassino. Meeting holy Apollinaris, with knee and gaze bent down to the ground, he began to speak thus: “Have mercy on me, most holy Father; receive one who is penitent and sick, sunk beneath the Stygian flood; burn me with Benedict’s branding iron. For ‘those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill’ (Matt. 9:12). Receive the shedder of innocent blood; bring back to the folds a wandering sheep that follows the ghostly hydra, most worthy shepherd. For this reason the salvation, lofty glory, and honour of all gave you to mortals as a chief physician: that you might bring the wanton and dissolute back to the way of salvation. Free one who is lost; I beseech you by the immeasurable King of all.”

When Father Apollinaris saw the humility of so great a man, after praising God and speaking at length, he gave that count the rule of a holy profession. What manner of man and how great Racheldis afterwards became, and how resolutely he pleased the supreme Maker, may be understood from the words of the devil. For over a long space of time, with everyone hearing, that most wicked dragon did not cease day and night to cry throughout the cloister of the monastery of Cassino, weeping and wailing:

> Alas, Benedict, why do you wrongfully gnaw at me on every side?  
> Having first driven me out from here, now you seize my limbs.

The holy servant of the Lord, Apollinaris, having laudably completed the course of his time, summoned the brethren and foretold that the hour was at hand when he would be borne to the heavenly company. “Behold, as you see, dearest brothers,” Apollinaris said, “I am setting out upon the way of the fathers, and I desire to receive the hope which Jesus Christ deigned to promise to His faithful ones.” When he had finished speaking, he fortified himself by receiving the life-giving Body and Blood. After eleven years, during which he had governed the holy church of Cassino, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December [27 November], he happily departed to Christ. He was buried beside the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, in which holy Father Benedict also rests with his disciples.

Nineteen years after the passing of holy Apollinaris, in the time of the most holy Pope Leo, an innumerable multitude of Ishmaelites, Arabs, and Persians, carried from Babylon, Africa, and Sicily by their fleet into Italy, came to Rome. They plundered the churches of Saints Peter and Paul and killed innumerable Christians in those churches. Departing from there, they burned the city of Fondi after killing all its inhabitants. An army of Romans, Germans, and Lombards was sent against them, but was defeated by the Ishmaelites and sought refuge in flight. The Ishmaelites pursued them more fiercely, seized all their goods, gave the whole land to fire and sword, and at last came near Mount Cassino.

Meanwhile their most wicked leader summoned the most pestilent standard-bearers of the multitude. When they had come, he ordered the army to assemble as one; and when all stood before him, that assessor of wickedness said to them: “I congratulate your valour, excellent comrades, because I see that you have one mind and one will. For through the most excellent merits of our prophet Mohammed, we have plundered the churches of Peter and Paul, slain Christians, defeated the army of the Romans—unconquered throughout all former ages—and put the peoples of Italy to flight together with the German host by the sword. But while I seek to set forth the distinctions of your bravery, my mind grows dull and my plectrum is greatly impeded. Therefore, since it is so, and the Titanian radiance, turning toward its setting, is already trying to delay our march, let us halt in this place and await a more favourable turn of fortune. But when the sun gives its brightness to the fields, let us leave these lands with swift course, ascend to the summit of Mount Cassino, destroy, plunder, and burn Benedict’s monastery, and slaughter his disciples, delivering them to death.”

After that most pestilent man had deemed such orders to be observed, they pitched their tents at his command. The serenity of the sky was then so great that no covering of any cloud obscured it; for over a long period scarcely even a light drop of rain had moistened the fields. There was such drought in the Liris that anyone who wished could cross it on foot.

But when dark horror settled upon the earth, one Christian escaped from the camp of the Ishmaelites and came to the monastery of the Lord and Saviour. By every means he began to call for the most holy Abbot Bassatius. When brought before him, his clothing and his grief-stricken signs, mourning with every fountain of tears, showed what he was; and, when asked why he had wished to come at that hour, he began thus: “Would that the right hand of the Most High, who governs all things, had granted that I had never known you, most holy Father, never seen you!” When he had spoken thus, sprinkling his cheeks with streams of tears, he added: “Shall I speak or be silent? Shall I disclose the deadly destruction that will come from the Ishmaelites? Yet I shall reveal the vengeance of the disaster about to come upon the monastery of Cassino; for if I wish to be silent, the matter itself will cry out. Through their crimes, the Christian army, which had come to restrain the cruelty of the Ishmaelites, is fleeing through roads, fields, and valleys; the Ishmaelites have utterly devastated the Campanian plain, burned the city of Fondi, and declared that they are coming to burn and plunder the monastery of Cassino and kill the monks.”

When the brothers heard this and saw that so vast and dreadful a destruction threatened them, they became bloodless with fear. All human help deserted them. Giving one another the kiss of peace, they began earnestly to entreat the mercy of the Almighty, that He might graciously receive their souls, whose bodies He had delivered to the Saracens for slaughter in a horrible extermination. Rising very quickly, with ashes sprinkled on their heads and barefoot, they climbed to the summit of the mountain. When they reached the church of Saint John and announced the approach of the Ishmaelites to the brethren, they immediately fell before the body of most holy Benedict and began to cry out: “Help now, assist us, most holy Father, you who promised your disciples that after death you would be more present to them. Help and free us from the present danger. Entreat, most blessed Father of fathers, for our salvation and the stability of your monastery.”

As the brothers kept vigil throughout the whole night, striking the ear of the most high Maker with weeping and groaning and asking holy Father Benedict without interruption, the most holy Father Benedict, stirred—or, so to speak, spurred on—by the prayers of his congregation, spoke to the disciples: “Your brothers are placed in the last extremity, and you bear hearts of adamant against them. Follow me, and let us pour out prayers to the Lord Jesus Christ for them.” When he had said this, standing amid the saints, he said to them: “I do not doubt that you know what I have now risen to announce to your holiness. Therefore I invite you all together to their deliverance, and I ask you with one mind to approach the throne of the eternal King on their behalf.”

Immediately he approached the tribunal of the exalted empire. When he arrived, humbly entreating, he said: “Most gracious King of kings, I come as a suppliant to ask your mercy to grant me the life of my sons. For all things obey you; you said: ‘Ask and you shall receive’ (Matt. 7:7), and so forth. At your command I came to that place; by your command I established its laws; and I promised that after laying down the flesh I would be more present to them than if I lived. Certainly you see, ruler and nourisher of heavenly and earthly things, their affliction; you see their hearts crushed and humbled. They hold me bound by the written bond of my promise, and they do not cease to cry that, as a shepherd, I should guard, help, protect, and defend my flock. But what then shall I do, eternal Shepherd? What shall I say when I see my sons torn to pieces by the Saracens before the presence of my own body? Day and night, at every hour and moment, they do not cease to call upon me for their protection. They hope and trust that whatever I wish I can obtain from your mercy.”

As he prayed thus, he received this answer: “Why, sweetest Benedict, are you grieved? Why do you plead so earnestly for those whom you have freed through the intervention of your merits? Know beforehand that what you have asked has been granted you.”

Thus, while throughout the whole night the brethren had their heads sprinkled with ashes and were intent upon vigils and prayers, holy Apollinaris appeared in a vision to holy Abbot Bassatius and said to him: “Why are you so sorrowful, dearest son Bassatius?” He replied: “Because of death, most holy Father, and because of the desolation of this holy place, which we expect at any moment.” Holy Apollinaris answered: “Take courage in the Lord, sweetest son. Cast fear far away; drive sorrow far from your mind. Our Lord Jesus Christ has sent me, so that you may be without doubt and may make the minds of all the brothers certain by your report: you and holy Father Benedict have obtained deliverance for all of you from the Lord, and he has come with us likewise to help you. Therefore, with every uncertainty removed, be completely assured that for the present the ferocity of the Hagarenes will have no power to destroy you; rather, terrified by the force of divine power, they will hasten back to their own country.”

When the venerable abbot awoke, he called the brothers together and informed them in order of what had been revealed to him by holy Apollinaris. Strengthening them in the might of divine power, he urged them to pray urgently to almighty God. Strengthened by these divine consolations, they fell upon their faces, gave thanks to the Creator for so gracious a consolation, and spent what remained of the night in offering praises and prayers.

The serenity of the air was then so great that not even a thin little cloud could be seen in it. Suddenly the sky grew dense with clouds, thunder crashed, lightning and flashes gleamed, and such rain was poured upon the earth that the swollen River Liris seemed like a sea. At the dawn of day the barbarians rose from their camp and approached the riverbank, carefully searching whether they might perhaps find a boat or ford. But when every hope of crossing was removed, they began in fury to bite their fingers and hands. They burned with fire the cells of the monastery of Cassino situated beyond the river. Then they boarded their ships, spread their sails to the winds, and with a direct course reached Sicily.

Suddenly they saw a small boat swiftly moving here and there among their ships, in which there seemed to sit one cleric of venerable grey hair and another clothed in monastic dress. When the Ishmaelites carefully asked them whence they were returning so joyful and cheerful, they declared that they were coming from Italy, where they had delivered everything to fire and sword, and boasted that they had plundered the houses of Peter, Paul, and Benedict. “And you,” they said, “who are you, who have questioned us so anxiously and carefully?” “We,” they replied, “are called, one Peter and the other Benedict, whose houses you boast of having invaded. But you shall very swiftly learn what power and strength we possess.” When these words had been spoken, they were taken from the Ishmaelites’ sight.

At once, as the winds raged and the waves swelled, so great a storm suddenly arose that all the ships were either dashed together or driven against rocks and broken apart, so that from all that multitude of Ishmaelites scarcely a few survived to report these things to the citizens who had sent them. Two hundred and fifty-three years after the passing of holy Apollinaris, the most reverend Desiderius raised his body from the place of its first burial and placed it reverently in the wall of the church of Saint John the Baptist, beside the altar of blessed Pope Gregory.

> I, the scribe, while avoiding superfluous labour,  
> Omitted very many things irrelevant to the matter.  
>
> [Note: This is a copyist’s note. Unable to endure Peter the Deacon’s verbosity, he cut out a great many passages.]

## XXVII. DEUSDEDIT

Deusdedit, an abbot, was seized by a prince of Benevento on account of money, cast into prison, and killed there. When he had been buried in the monastery of Blessed Benedict, a certain distinguished man, shaken by the fierce heat of a severe fever, lay down in the very heat of the fever and fell asleep upon his tomb. Awakening, he began to give thanks with a loud voice, saying: “Blessed are you, O Lord God of our fathers, who have made me well through the merits of your servant Deusdedit.” When this reached the ears of the people, a great crowd of sick persons began to gather at his tomb and there to entreat the Redeemer of all for their health. God, heeding their vows, restored there to their former health many held by fever and oppressed by various illnesses who asked in faith.

## XXVIII. BERTHARIUS

Bertharius, abbot, [Note: I possess two homilies of this abbot and martyr Bertharius, on Saint Matthias the apostle and on Saint Scholastica, written in a very ancient codex. At a suitable time I shall publish them, together with other writings, as I think, of Cassinese authors.] noble in birth and noble in spirit, was beheaded by the Saracens for the faith of Christ in the monastery of the Lord and Saviour beside the altar of Saint Martin. He was buried above in the monastery of Cassino. Many others also suffered with him on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November [22 October].

## XXIX. ALIGERIUS

[Note: In Book II of the *Chronicle of Cassino*: Aligernus.] Aligerius, abbot and, so to speak, the third builder of the monastery of Cassino, populated the entire territory with people. Born among the Parthenopeans [Note: “Neapolitans,” as in the *Chronicle* and the cited book, ch. 1.], he became a monk at the monastery of Saint Paul at Rome under Alduin, abbot of Cassino, and not long afterwards was made provost of Cassino. Subsequently, after becoming abbot of Cassino, Aligerius began diligently to recover the possessions of the monastery.

One day a certain Adenulf, because Aligerius was recovering the possessions of the monastery of Cassino, arrived with soldiers, seized the abbot by force, and carried him off to Aquino as though he were the greatest spoil. There, as a public spectacle for the citizens, the wicked man clothed him in a bearskin, set dogs upon him from every side to bark around him as though he were truly a bear, and dishonoured the most holy man with many insults. When Prince Landulf heard these things, he ordered Adenulf to come to Capua and give justice to the abbot before him in legal judgment. But Adenulf, seeing that for the crime he had committed he ought lawfully to suffer death, chose instead to rebel. Trusting in the strong fortification of Aquino, he refused to go to the prince’s court.

When this was reported to the prince, he immediately came with an army to Aquino and surrounded by siege and engines the palace in which the aforesaid rebel had fortified himself. Therefore, seeing that he could not escape the prince’s hands, Adenulf put a rope around his neck and ordered that his wife drag him by her hands to the prince’s feet. When this had been done, the prince immediately delivered him, bound as he was, into the abbot’s own hands, so that the abbot might do whatever he wished with him and all that belonged to him. [Note: The *Chronicle of Cassino*, II.2, adds that the captive Adenulf restored to the abbot everything he had seized and was then dismissed by the abbot freely and unharmed.] The aforesaid abbot was buried at Cassino beside the church of Saint Benedict. Desiderius the abbot later raised his body from there and reverently placed it in the monastery church of Saint Benedict, beside the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God.

## XXX. PROLOGUE OF PETER THE DEACON OF CASSINO TO THE LIFE OF SAINT GUINIZO

[Note: The Bollandists obtained this Life of Saint Guinizon from the Cassino library and published it in vol. VI for May, p. 450 ff., with its prologue. The scribe of the Vatican codex omitted it; I have restored it to the sequence from the Bollandists’ edition. That Peter the Deacon’s Cassinese codex was fuller than the Vatican codex is shown not only by this example but also by the copyist’s admission on pp. 251 and 263 that, in the interests of honourable brevity, he removed parts of the work. The Bollandists report on p. 250 that the archetype of this commentary on the righteous men of Cassino, written in ancient Lombardic letters, is preserved under the strictest guard in the monastery of Cassino. Otherwise, the copy supplied to the Bollandists by an unskilled copyist was both unreliable and very corrupt, as the Vatican codex I use demonstrates.]

As I am about to describe the birth and death of the eminent Guinizon, whom the Redeemer of all caused to shine like a most brilliant star in these times, I invoke as fellow-worker and helper the Holy Spirit, who reveals mysteries and unlocks secrets beyond telling; who made that life-giving confessor shine in the monastery of Cassino especially at the very time when “truths have been diminished from the children of men” and “the holy man has failed.” I judge it altogether unworthy and most impious that the deeds of so eminent a senator of the heavenly court should remain hidden only in the chief monastery of Cassino, rather than that they should be sent forth to the churches of Christ constructed throughout the whole world of the Roman Empire, for the praise of Jesus Christ the eternal Emperor and the edification of all monks: how he fought with tireless strength against the most savage tyrant and, trampling down his insolence, overcame him.

For this task, indeed, I have been stirred and urged by the command of Richard, a venerable monk of that same abbey of Monte Cassino—not by any industry of my own. For one day, when he was speaking in that monastery about the miracles of the saints [Col. 1092A] and the punishments of the reprobate, among the many things which he then expounded he confessed that he was grieved because the miracles of so great a confessor were being consigned to oblivion, and because both his name and his wondrous deeds—by which he shone more brightly than all men of his age—were being hidden from the sight of mortals by the passage of time; and this especially at a time when the sciences of grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric flourished there in the highest degree. Having said these things, he began to urge my insignificance not to refuse to do for Guinizo what I had done for the most blessed Placid and Apollinaris.

Then I said: “Since the miracles of so great a confessor are related to the brethren by everyone, and have very often been reported and are well known, what need is there to write out his life?”

Richard replied: “Nor is it unknown to me [Col. 1092B] that his miracles are sufficiently evident; but do not be reluctant to commit to writing his most distinguished history, which will benefit both us and generations to come. For we must give attention and take more careful precautions lest the cunning of the ancient enemy tempt us in this matter, when we neglect to describe the lives of those who pleased our Redeemer in this monastery. Thus Scripture says: ‘The sons of my mother fought against me’ (Song 1:5). For then the sons of holy Church fight against the sons of their mother, the Church, when they cover their lives with the pestilential whirlwind of silence. What then will you do, who have written very many miracles of strangers, yet have disdained to hear those of our own brethren? Hence the Lord also says: ‘No prophet is accepted in his own country’ [Col. 1092C] (Luke 4:24). The foolishness of our silence produces grief for the wise and joy for the foolish. But I fear lest this be said to us on the supreme day of judgment: ‘I have begotten and nourished sons, but they, despising, have rejected me’ (Isa. 1:2). For he despises his father who scorns to commit the wondrous deeds of his brethren to writing. I ask this because his most sacred body rests in our church, and because what Victor, bishop of the Apostolic See, related concerning this holy man in the books of his *Dialogues* seems to have been written too briefly and very cursorily.”

When the venerable man had said these things, setting aside the inadequacy of my ignorance, I applied my mind to this undertaking; and, intending to write the life of this most holy confessor for the glory of our Redeemer, [Col. 1092D] I directed my thought to it. I knew beyond doubt that, in the narration of virtues, due honor is offered to him and very great benefit is bestowed upon those who hear. For, as God is my witness, whatever things have been written have been written for our instruction. But if a discerning [Col. 1093A] reader perhaps finds any good thing in this little work, let him ascribe it to the favor of the merciful Creator, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James 1:17). Meanwhile I humbly beg those who will read it to pray to Jesus Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, the universal Pontiff, for our sins: that, rescuing me from the tribunals of those who bark against me, and granting remission of my offences on the future day of righteous judgment, he may grant me the reward of having escaped punishment.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

At the time when the most serene Henry happily governed the Roman Empire, and Basil the Empire of Constantinople, while Benedict—preeminent in conduct and learning, and of most holy life—presided over the apostolic and universal Church, the gracious confessor Guinizo [Col. 1093B] shone more brightly than the sun at the monastery of Monte Cassino: a man truly wonderful, conspicuous for holiness, outstanding in humility, renowned for abstinence, radiant with the spirit of prophecy, gleaming with the splendor of virtues, and endowed with every goodness.

Born in farther Spain, he cultivated such abstinence in himself and pursued such patience that it could already be recognized more clearly by his parents that he had been chosen by heavenly mercy not for succession to his inheritance but rather for divine service. For in his little breast there already shone a spark of that divine light which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9). When, however, he had passed beyond childhood and reached that age at which the ancient enemy especially endeavors to ensnare the human race, he began to arm himself all the more eminently with the armor of faith, the sword of the word of God, and the breastplate of good works, [Col. 1093C] as he saw the fiery darts rising against him more fiercely. Thus he began, with all the desire of his mind, to ascend to higher things, to seek spiritual things, and to abandon things transient and perishable.

But the more he tried to cast off worldly cares, the more he was entangled in their snares. Seeing therefore that in his homeland he could not bring to completion what he had already conceived in his mind, he raised himself above himself; and, leaving his country as Abraham once did, he sought Monte Cassino, the head of the monastic order, and there began to live with the servants of God.

At that time, however, a most grievous storm of persecutions began to shake that same Church. For Pandulf, [Col. 1093D] prince of Capua, given beyond measure to wicked and unheard-of deeds, did not cease to inflict persecutions upon the monastery of Monte Cassino. First, adding sin to sin, he seized the most reverend abbot from the monastery of Monte Cassino and committed him to custody in the city of Capua. He made almost all the monks exiles from the Cassinese cloister, leaving only a few—who could scarcely make up twelve for the readings—beside the body of Saint Benedict. In that same monastery he installed Basil, a most wicked and utterly perverse accomplice in his own malice, as his own abbot rather than the monks’ abbot. Basil had first shamefully given the prince an oath with his own hands that, after all the monastery’s possessions had been handed over to him, he would retain nothing beyond twenty solidi a year.

Finally, after compelling all the men of the monastery to swear allegiance to him, and distributing all its castles and villages among the Normans who then adhered to him, he set over them a certain Theodinus, one of the monastery’s servants and like himself in wickedness. He appointed him to reside at Saint Germanus, in the very court of the abbot, and, moreover, gave him the fortress called Bantra; he ordered all there, Normans and others alike, to obey his allegiance. [Col. 1094A] Now how utterly evil and impious this same Theodinus proved toward God’s servants, and into what want and disgrace he reduced them and this holy place, I could not recount even if I possessed the eloquence of Varro or Cicero. So great was the misery that—to touch upon only a few instances—at the very feast of the Assumption of the holy Mother of God, they lacked wine for the service of the altar. Nothing then remained for the monks except, with Jeremiah, to break forth in lamentation: “Servants have ruled over us, and there was none to rescue us from their hands” (Lam. 5:9).

And since even these things did not satisfy that most rabid dog, after a few days the most wicked prince ordered one of his retainers, named Aldegisius, to come as quickly as possible to this monastery and swiftly carry away the chasuble and chalice of Emperor Henry, together with other chief ornaments of the church, to be pledged to the counts of Aquino and Sessa. When he came and announced the business for which he had been sent, Adam, the most reverend *paramonarius*—that is, church-warden—of that church, said: “These things which, [Col. 1094C] good man, you demand, I shall never give to you or to anyone else. Rather, I shall place them upon the altar of Saint Benedict himself, to whom they belong; let him who presumes to take them remove them from there.”

When he had done this, the man immediately approached boldly; but as he was just about to stretch out his sacrilegious hands over the body of Saint Benedict, he at once fell upon his face. Suddenly seized with most violent paralysis, he remained until death with mouth and eye distorted. When the most wicked Pandulf heard this, he sent the aforesaid Basil and ordered that through him all the treasure of this place be carried away to himself—the treasure which the emperors Charles of glorious memory, Pippin and Charles his brother, Louis, Lothair, Carlittus [uncertain reading], Otto, and Henry had offered to Saint Benedict. He stored it all together in the fortress of Saint Agatha.

Thus, when the possessions of the monastery had been utterly stripped away by that abominable prince, the man of God, Guinizo, asked leave of the brethren to lead an eremitic life. He made himself a cell on the same mountain, not far from the monastery; and there, persisting in prayers, fasts, and vigils, he began earnestly to entreat almighty God that he would, in his accustomed mercy, aid the monastery of Monte Cassino and bring its sons, scattered by the most wicked Pandulf, back again to that same church.

At that time, when the brethren of the aforesaid Cassinese monastery were oppressed by the utmost lack of provisions, recognizing the exceptional holiness, life, and character of the gracious Father Guinizo, they summoned him [Col. 1095A] into their midst and all addressed him thus:

“Dearest brother, it is not unknown to your love by what miseries we have long been oppressed and by what tribulations we are hemmed in. For now the sword has reached the soul; now the prince has brought desolation in this place to its completion. They have already plundered the whole monastery and diverted the possessions of Saint Benedict to their own uses. Most cruel hunger torments us, and we are wholly ignorant what means of life we may adopt. Yet, trusting in the mercy of almighty God, we humbly beg your brotherhood to hasten as quickly as possible to the court of the most pestilential Theodinus. For we trust in the Lord and in the power of his strength that he will grant relief to us, placed in so great a danger.”

Hearing this, the man of God said: “My brothers and lords, our one and singular remedy, why do you bear so sorrowful a mind? Trust in him who conquered the world, who strikes and heals, wounds and cures; who inflicts scourges here lest he punish eternally. Remember that our most holy Father Benedict promised that he would be more present than if he were alive. Therefore, giving thanks in tribulation, let us sing with Job that hymn: ‘If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not receive evil things?’ Yet I ask one thing of your love: pour out prayers for me to the Lord Jesus Christ and to the most holy Father Benedict, that he may make the face of wretched Theodinus favorable toward me and incline his mind to my entreaties, so that I may [Col. 1095C] obtain from him what I am about to request.”

Having said this, without any delay he prostrated himself at the feet of all the brethren and, taking up his staff, set out on his journey. As soon as he was presented to the cruel servant at the fortress, he was asked why so great a man had unusually wished to come there. The man of God answered him: “You should know that our coming to this place has undoubtedly been for this purpose: that you might provide our brethren, who are suffering want of food, with assistance in grain.”

Amid many verbal insults, as was his servile habit, Theodinus replied: “Why do you not work with your hands, as the Rule commands you?”

Then the man of God said: “Because some are sick, while others are now in feeble old age.”

But when the man of God persisted with many entreaties, Theodinus answered: “Lest I seem, after all, to make light of your words, if you are willing to remain with me this night, at dawn I will give you, for your sake, one hundred modii of millet.”

The man of God, perceiving that he was deceitfully contriving all this, answered that he would in no way violate the commandments of the Rule. But Theodinus, anxiously seeking in his mind where he might pour out the poisons of treachery, at last goaded by diabolical incentives, saw the servant of God enter the church to pray and silently turned over these thoughts within himself: “Since this man has not willingly wished to remain with us today, let him remain unwillingly.” Thus he had the church locked with the utmost care. He gave the staff which the servant of God had brought in his hand to his wife and ordered it shut up in a chest.

But the Creator of the human race, who does not abandon those who hope in him, sent his angel, who, leaving the seals of the doors unbroken, brought him out of the church and set the servant of God down at the foot of the mountain. Meanwhile peasants returning late from the fields according to custom, when questioned by the inhabitants of the fortress whether anything new had lately taken place in those parts, answered that they had seen absolutely nothing except a certain solitary man, barefoot, carrying a crook-staff in his hand. [Col. 1096A]

When the most wicked servant Theodinus heard this, he immediately summoned the priest and his wife Marotta, and began carefully to inquire what had happened to the man of God. When they said that he remained in the church, they hastened at once to bring him to Theodinus. Unable to find him, they took care to report this to him. His wife likewise searched for the staff which she had put in the chest, but could not find it. How almighty God brought his servant from the church while the doors were closed remains unknown to this day.

But when that same almighty God had determined to put an end to such great ravages, the brethren of the monastery of Monte Cassino went beyond the mountains to the emperor and reported the evils that they had suffered from Pandulf. They prayed him to deem it worthy to come to Italy and powerfully rescue the monastery of Monte Cassino from the hands of the most savage tyrant. This monastery had been established by the Lord Jesus Christ through Father Benedict as the head of all monasteries, and all emperors had held it in most reverent protection.

When Emperor Conrad [Col. 1096C] heard these things, inflamed with anger, he crossed the Alps with a very powerful army drawn from all the West and arrived at Rome. There, having taken counsel with the Romans, he sent valiant men from his side to the prince, commanding that, unless he wished immediately to experience the indignation of the Roman Empire, he should promptly restore to the monastery of Monte Cassino everything he had taken away. But when those sent by the emperor achieved nothing, Augustus, seeing himself despised by Pandulf, took up his army and came to Monte Cassino.

When this was reported to the brethren, they said: “The time for silence has passed, and the time for speaking has come. Behold, the day of our redemption has dawned. Let us go down and prepare all things necessary for the emperor’s servants.”

On the following day the emperor ascended the summit of the mountain to commend himself to Father Benedict. When he had entered the chapter-house with his son King Henry, the monks rose and all prostrated themselves on the ground before the emperor’s face. Rising again, they said: “Thus have we awaited you; thus have we desired to behold your face, just as the souls of the righteous are known to have awaited the Redeemer’s coming in hell.” Then again falling upon their faces, they told what evils, and how great, they had suffered from Pandulf for twelve years. The emperor then burst into tears and affirmed by oath that he had crossed into those regions for this one reason: that he might rescue the monastery of the most holy Father Benedict from the yoke of servitude and restore it to its former freedom.

Having stayed there for a time, [Col. 1097A] the emperor appointed Richerius abbot in the same monastery of Monte Cassino. Departing from there, he went without delay against the prince at Capua; and, appointing Guaimar prince there, he restored all the land to Saint Benedict.

The most wicked Pandulf, together with his Basil, went to the emperor at Constantinople; by God’s just judgment he was sent into exile by him. Theodinus, by God’s ordering, was captured by Abbot Richerius, beaten with rods, shorn, clothed in sackcloth, and put in a mill to sift flour like a servant. Of the Normans who had been assailants of so great a place, one hundred and fifty were consumed by diverse deaths within two years. Their count, who had planned to ravage the monastery’s land, died suddenly on the very day when he hoped to carry this out. Siconulf, count of Aquino and himself one of the persecutors, was struck by God’s judgment and died in the same year, together with two thousand five hundred inhabitants of his city.

Pandulf, although he endured punishment in this world for what he did in the church of Monte Cassino, did not lack punishment in the world to come. This will be proved more certainly if the things seen concerning him are brought forward.

For Sergius, master of the soldiers, who governed the city of Naples, entered a forest on the holy Saturday of Easter to hunt with his attendants. When nets had been spread, all scattered here and there through the forest with the dogs in pursuit of boars. A boar came in the hunters’ way and, before it could flee and become entangled in the noose of a net, was pierced with hunting-spears and yielded to their capture. As the sun declined toward sunset and gave clear signs of the late hour and approaching night, Sergius took the game they had caught and hastily set off home with all the others, leaving behind only one boy, named Pythagoras. He ordered him to follow with the gathered nets as quickly as possible.

As the boy obeyed his master’s commands and was following his lord at a swift run, two monks of exceedingly venerable appearance suddenly presented themselves before him on the road. Terrified with fear, the boy asked who they were. They said: “Drive every fear far from your mind, and follow us without fear.” As they proceeded together some distance through the same forest, [Col. 1097D] they came to a certain lake, very muddy and dreadful in appearance. There the seeming monks showed Pythagoras the aforesaid Prince Pandulf, bound in iron chains and submerged in the mud of the lake up to his throat.

Meanwhile two Ethiopians were seen twisting wild vines into the form of ropes. Binding the prince’s neck with them, they drew him, after he had been cast down into the depths of the lake, upward; and, after dragging him upward, they drew him down again into its depths. Seeing the Ethiopians alternate these turns, the boy, though seized by immense terror, nevertheless addressed Pandulf and asked him the cause of so great a punishment.

[Col. 1098A] Then Pandulf, weeping and wailing, broke forth in these words of answer:

“Although, O Pythagoras, many and infinite punishments have been prepared for me because of my many and infinite crimes, know that there is no other cause for this punishment, of which you yourself are an observer, except that, led by sacrilegious greed, I took a golden chalice from the monastery of the holy Father Benedict and took no care to restore it when dying. Therefore I earnestly entreat you, and I implore you through the Lord Jesus Christ, whose commands I, unhappy man, despised and so was cast into this pit: do not be reluctant to undertake the labor of a journey as far as Capua. Go to her who was joined to me as my wife and make known to her my punishment, which God has willed that you should learn by seeing it yourself. Tell her that you have learned from my words that the cause of my punishment is the removal [Col. 1098B] of the aforesaid chalice. Ask and implore her earnestly that she recall the love of our former affection and take care, swiftly and with every speed, that the stolen chalice be restored to the holy place.”

Pythagoras answered: “Your wife, I think, will not put faith in my words; nor will she believe either that I have seen you or that you yourself suffer such things.”

Then the prince said: “That my wife may place unambiguous faith in your words, give her this sign of certain proof: say that Pandulf, son of Guala, holds the aforesaid chalice in pledge. Ask in my name that, if any traces of conjugal love remain in her mind, she not delay to repay Guala the solidi for which the chalice was given in pledge, and to restore the chalice to the holy monastery; so that, as I deserve to suffer punishment for taking the chalice, I may deserve to be released from it when the chalice has been restored.”

When these things had been said, the whole vision was taken from the boy’s eyes. He returned home and was immediately seized by a grave illness which, increasing daily, ended his life within a short time. Before he departed this life, however, Guala, to whom the aforesaid chalice had been entrusted as a pledge, happened to come to Naples and hear in due order this vision from Pythagoras’s own mouth. Returning to Capua, he reported everything to the prince’s wife. But the woman made light of his words and took no care either to repay the money which her husband had borrowed or to receive the chalice for restoration to the church.

Having thus set forth these matters in advance, let us come to recount the miracles of Saint Januarius, disciple of Guinizo.

## XXXI. CONCERNING JANUARIUS, DISCIPLE OF GUINIZO

While he was being instructed in the teaching of Guinizo, he began to excel in great virtues of abstinence and obedience. Once, when he had been sent by his master to Aquino to repair the tools with which they customarily worked, he went to the house of a blacksmith and, offering payment, asked him to repair the tools. By nature Saint Januarius had a certain stoutness of body and such redness of cheeks that even remarkable abstinence could not diminish these two features in him.

The blacksmith therefore fixed his gaze upon Januarius and began to mock him with those standing by, attributing his stoutness and redness to richer foods and continual drinking of wine. To this false suspicion rashly made concerning him, Saint Januarius replied: “God is able to make you repent of your false opinion concerning my stoutness and redness.”

Meanwhile, while the blacksmith did not cease to perform the tasks of his craft, he drew from the fire a piece of iron glowing with excessive heat, placed it on the anvil, and it was accidentally struck from the tongs; leaping from the anvil, it fell to the ground. Saint Januarius immediately took it in his hand and restored it to the anvil, filling the bodies of all who stood present with trembling and their minds with astonishment. By this deed he made most plainly evident to all that he was neither stout through excessive gluttony nor red from habitual drinking of wine. For none of those present could any longer, even slightly, suppose Saint Januarius to be a glutton or a drunkard—the men in whose sight the almighty Creator had chosen to display a sign of so great a virtue.

When, after the tools had been repaired, Saint Januarius returned to his cell, his master rebuked him with vehement words because, yielding to mockery, he had presumed to perform a sign of virtue before their eyes. In amazement Saint Januarius asked him by whose revelation these things had been made known to him. Guinizo, the man of God, replied: “He through whose power it was granted to you outwardly to perform so great a sign has also granted me inwardly, by revealing it, to know it.” In this deed Guinizo, beholding the deed of his absent disciple, was like Elisha; while Januarius, in extinguishing the fiery power, was made like the three youths.

Not many days later, when he had been sent to the estate of Saint Germanus on monastery business, and Guinizo had already completed all his tasks, behold, he saw a man carrying on his shoulders a basket full of grapes which he had acquired by theft. When the venerable Father Guinizo, filled with the Holy Spirit, recognized this, he immediately shouted and commanded the man to come to him. Since the man knew himself guilty of his crime, he came swiftly to the servant of God. Guinizo at once reproved him for the crime he had committed, saying: “Where did you get these grapes, gallows-bird? Where have you brought them from?”

The crafty thief feigned innocence and asserted on oath that he had gathered them from his own vineyard. Then the man of God replied: [Col. 1099D] “It is not so; rather, you gathered them from such-and-such a vineyard.” At last, recognizing himself defeated, the man marveled at the kindness of so great a man and asked forgiveness for his offences. After the most holy Father Guinizo had long admonished him toward the path of upright life, he said: “Run, brother, run more quickly, and make every effort to carry these grapes back to the vineyard from which you stole them. For behold, I see the devil sitting upon them.”

Fulfilling the command at a very swift run, he took care to carry the same grapes back to the vineyard from which he had taken them.

The gracious Father Guinizo, having laudably completed the course of his allotted time, went to the Lord on the seventh day before the Kalends of June [26 May]. On the day when he departed this world, a certain brother at Benevento learned of his death through the Spirit and said to the brethren standing there: “With every doubt of hesitation removed, be entirely certain that on this day a man of great merit has departed to the Lord in the monastery of Monte Cassino.”

At these words the minds of all who heard were turned to astonishment, because the death of a man separated from them by nearly eighty thousand paces was announced to them with such certainty. Yet, examining the truth of the matter by more careful inquiry, they learned that Father Guinizo had indeed departed on the very day on which the aforesaid brother knew that a certain great man had died in the monastery of Monte Cassino and revealed his death to the others.

He was buried in the church of Saint Nicholas, confessor of Christ, in a leaden coffin at the right side of the altar, in the place called Ciconia. Saint Januarius his disciple, when dead, was laid there too with his master. To make their merits known, Christ does not cease to work miracles daily down to the present day.

## XXXII. LYUTIUS

A monk of Monte Cassino, Lyutius left that monastery and sought Jerusalem. On his return, he first remained for some time near Salerno in a certain wilderness, at the place called ad Cavam. Later he built a monastery on this mountain, in a place called Albaneta, and there began to live most religiously with about thirty brethren. He himself, more than the others, content with every lowliness and hardship, devoted himself to so humble an office that he sifted flour in the mill for making bread, in the manner of servants, [Col. 1100C] while songs of the Lord never ceased from his mouth. He persisted in this humility of life and excessive austerity of abstinence until the end of his life. He was buried in the monastery of Monte Cassino.

## XXXIII. JOHN

Born in the province of Apulia, John was for some time dean at Monte Cassino. Later, sent to the city of Lucca to build a monastery, he applied himself there unceasingly to fasts, vigils, prayers, and especially almsgiving. By the bounty of heavenly generosity he obtained such an abundance of tears and such a grace of compunction that no one was permitted to doubt that that fountain of his eyes and that great contrition of humble spirit could obtain many and very great things from the divine ears.

As the fame of his holiness filled every mouth, a certain woman cruelly and pitiably tormented by a demon was brought to him. Urged by great entreaties from those who had brought her, that he should pray to the Lord for her, he gathered the brethren together and entered the oratory. After he had prayed to the Lord for her for some time, he immediately expelled the unclean spirit from her.

In the same city a certain woman suffered from a severe sickness. As it worsened, she came to the point of death; for three days she lay without sense or speech, showing signs of life only by her pulse. When all despaired of her life, they began to ask the man of God to pray to the Lord for her. Then Saint John, clothed in priestly vestments, began to offer sacrifice to the Lord for her. When, during the solemnities of Mass, the woman’s name was mentioned by the man of God, she lay nearly lifeless in her own house far from the monastery, heard the voice of the priest naming her, and answered him as though he were present.

Those around her, astounded at the voice of one who had lain for three days as though dead, asked the woman whom she had answered. She said to them: “Is not Lord John, the superior, standing present at this bed? Did you not hear his voice calling me and awakening me from heavy sleep?” When she had said this, she was quickly restored to her former health.

They immediately sent messengers to the monastery to learn what the man of God was doing for her. When they entered the church, [Col. 1101B] they found the man of God standing at the holy altars and offering the sacrifice to the Lord for her health. On careful inquiry, they found that the beginning of her recovery had occurred at the hour when the man of God named her during the sacred solemnities of Mass and she answered him from her bed.

When Pope Alexander was ill with a severe fever and the sickness grew worse daily, he remembered that whoever, afflicted by fever, drank water flowing from the hands of Saint John after the solemnities of Mass would no longer be under the fever’s power. He therefore immediately sent persons to bring him some of that water secretly. Once the water was brought, as soon as he drank it, every infirmity of fever departed from him.

## XXXIV. CONSTANTIUS

[Col. 1101C]

Constantius was a priest at Monte Cassino, a distinguished man adorned with every excellence of character. In the time of Abbot Aligerius, he was sent to build a monastery of Saint Benedict in a place called Pectinarius. Since there was no water in that place, he went barefoot three times to the threshold of the prince of the apostles. There he began earnestly to ask the mercy of the eternal King that he who had brought water from a rock in the desert might, through the intercession of the prince of the apostles and the most holy Father Benedict, deign to grant water in that arid place.

After he had done this a third time, the blessed apostle Peter appeared and said to him: “The Lord has heard your petitions; the desires of your heart have been admitted before the sanctuary of his divinity. Rise now and begin to dig the earth in such-and-such a place; there you will find unfailing water.”

The man of God Constantius rose and went to the place which the apostle had shown him. When he had dug there, he found unfailing water, which supplies drink to the inhabitants down to the present day.

After Saint Constantius departed from the world, a very wealthy man from Dalmatia suffered shipwreck in the midst of the Adriatic Sea. He continually invoked the aid of the servant of God Constantius, saying: “Holy Constantius, if the things we have heard concerning you are true, we ask you now to help us, so that, rescued from this present danger, I may rejoice to have you as my father, my protector, and my lord.”

As he said these things continually, there was a great calm. Reaching port, he went with gifts to the tomb of the man of God, praising and blessing God.

## XXXV. JOHN

John, abbot of Monte Cassino, had been archdeacon of the city of Benevento. Despising worldly riches, he came to Monte Cassino and became a monk there, spending no small period of time in that place. He then went to Jerusalem and for six continuous years led an eremitic life on Mount Sinai. Afterwards he lived for some time in Greece on the mountain called ἅγιον ὄρος, “the Holy Mountain.” After many days Saint Father Benedict appeared to this same John in a vision, gave him the pastoral staff which he seemed to carry in his hand, and commanded him to return to the Cassinese monastery with all haste. John therefore rose, [Col. 1102B] returned to Monte Cassino, was appointed provost by Abbot John, and was later made abbot of Monte Cassino.

## XXXVI. JOHN

John, abbot of Monte Cassino, was a most holy and religious man. Leaving his abbacy, he led an eremitic life in the place called Piretus almost until his death. On the night when he departed the world, a monk named John, in the monastery of Saint Lawrence the Martyr built within the city of Capua, rose before the nocturnal synaxis in order to keep vigil. Looking up suddenly, he saw a great brightness of light in the air, and within it he saw the soul of this same John penetrate heaven.

When morning came, he immediately sent a messenger to the monastery of Monte Cassino and ordered him carefully to inquire what had happened there. As the messenger was making his way toward Monte Cassino, another messenger met him, saying that he was traveling to Capua to announce the death of Abbot John. When the first messenger asked him the time of the death, he discovered that John had been taken from this life at the very hour when the monk John saw his soul penetrate the heights of heaven.

## XXXVII. FELIX

Felix, a monk, was sent by the abbot of Monte Cassino to preside over shepherds and a flock. After he died and many signs occurred at his tomb, the bishop of Chieti raised his body from there and placed it reverently in a church, consecrating an altar over it. When a certain blind man came to that place, he received sight.

## XXXVIII. SALVIUS

[Col. 1102D]

Salvius, born in Campania, was sent by the abbot of Monte Cassino to the church of Saint Clement at Plumbata. After he died there, the divine Majesty worked many miracles at his tomb.

## XXXIX. ANGELUS
He was a monk at Cassino, a reverend man endowed with every goodness. When he had closed his last day, a certain demoniac who came there began to cry out, saying: «What have you done to me at this hour, Benedict? By carrying a small cowl, the angel has taken my soul away from me and joined it to your flock in heaven.» As he lamented these things, the signal customarily used to announce a brother’s death suddenly sounded; and when they went, they found the aforesaid angel already deprived of life.

## XL. AZO

[Col. 1103A]

At Cassino he was a monk of most devout life. He restored the church of the Blessed Archangel Michael in the royal valley, which had been destroyed by the Saracens. While he was drawing his last breath at Cassino, a monk named Rainald saw the blessed Archangel Michael, in the form in which he is customarily depicted, proceeding through the dormitory with another angel toward the infirmary. The brother said to him: «Are you Michael, the angel, prince of the heavenly host?» And he replied: «I am indeed.» And the brother said: «Where are you going, lord?» «I am going,» he said, «to the infirmary, to carry Azo with me to the heavenly court; for the time of his earthly life has been fulfilled.» Having said this, he disappeared. The brother immediately rose, went to the infirmary, and found the aforesaid Azo already dead [Col. 1103B].

## XLI. JOHN

A Venetian, he was a monk at Cassino, distinguished by patience, obedience, and humility. After he had died and been buried there, a brother suffering so severely from a hernia that the peritoneal membrane had ruptured and his entrails protruded into the flesh and skin, came to his tomb.
