There, prostrating his whole body, he began to beseech the mercy of the Almighty that, through the intercession of His servant John, He would deign to restore that rupture to soundness and its former condition. How powerful before God was the prayer of His servant John became clear: for the rupture was immediately healed.

## XLII. STEPHEN

A Venetian, he was a monk at Cassino. As he was closing his final day in that monastery [Col. 1103C], an old woman named Agundia, spending the night in prayer before the church of the holy Mother of God, turned her eyes toward the summit of the mountain and saw a fiery column emerge from the infirmary and pierce the heights of heaven. Having seen this, she immediately sent a messenger to the monastery and found that Stephen had breathed out his soul at the very hour when she had seen that fiery column penetrate the heights of heaven.

## XLIII. PAUL

A monk of Cassino, when he had died in the monastery at Capua, a certain bishop was travelling to Gargano that night for prayer. Having lodged in the city of Capua near the church of Saint Lawrence, he rose in the middle of the night and saw, on his right side, a splendid light like a ray of the sun [Col. 1103D] emerge from the monastery and penetrate the heights of heaven. While he wondered attentively at the light he saw, he heard from the monastery the sound of a bell signifying a brother’s departure. Immediately sending a messenger to the monastery, he found that Paul had departed from the world at the very hour when he had seen the brightness of the light seek the heights of heaven.

## XLIV. GREGORY

A monk of Cassino, when he had departed from this world, such a fragrance of perfume issued from the place where he lay that suddenly the sweetness of its scent filled the entire monastery. While all wondered at this, a messenger came from the infirmary and reported that the monk Gregory had died.

## XLV. RAYNERIUS

A monk of Cassino, young in years but aged in character, of exceptional humility [Col. 1104A] and singular obedience. When he had been sent into the territory of Theate for the benefit of the monastery, he was killed by the bandits of Count Oderisius, after everything he was carrying had been taken from him. Many miracles were divinely performed at his tomb.

## XLVI. ADAM

A *paramonarius*—that is, a church attendant—of Cassino, while travelling on business of the Church, met two young men dressed in monastic garments. When he asked who they were, one answered that he was Protus and the other Hyacinthus. They added: «We have come to give thanks to the brethren, because they celebrated the day of our feast with the highest reverence and devotion.» For it was the day on which they were crowned by martyrdom.

## XLVII. BENEDICT

[Col. 1104B]

Constantine, king of the Sardinians, sent to Cassino under Abbot Oderisius, asking them to send him one of the brethren who would receive the episcopate there. They therefore sent him a monk named Benedict, a man venerable in every respect. While he administered the office of bishop there very vigorously, a great multitude of sparrows, coming according to their usual custom, fouled the entire church with their droppings, together with all the vessels of the altar and even the altar itself. Since the man of God suffered this great annoyance daily, he made the sign of the cross and said: «I command you, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, neither to enter the church again nor to cause annoyance.» This has been observed down to the present day, so that no sparrow dares enter there.

Moreover, at one time the Saracens entered Sardinia; and when they came into Benedict’s bishopric, they began to seek the bishop. The man of God stood before the altar and began to pour forth prayers to almighty God. The Saracens entered the church and struck against the bishop, yet were unable to see him. All whom they found they carried off into captivity; but the bishop alone they could neither see nor seize.

## XLVIII. BENEDICT

A priest of Cassino, when he had been sent as superior to the monastery of Lucca, a certain nobleman of that city began grievously to harass that monastery. Seizing a field belonging to the aforesaid place, he claimed it as his own right. When the venerable Benedict repeatedly admonished him to restore the field to the holy place, the violent man said angrily: «If the field is yours by right and not mine, as you say, may God now, before I leave this field, show vengeance upon me and upon my beasts.» Immediately his eye burst, and his ox fell to the ground and died.

At another time, a nobleman had entrusted a considerable sum of money to the venerable Benedict. A cleric stole it, and the man of God had nothing with which to repay it. He therefore clothed himself in his priestly vestments and began to offer sacrifice to almighty God, praying that the Lord would deign to reveal who had taken the money. During the very solemnities of the Mass, an angel of the Lord came and informed him that the cleric [Col. 1105A] standing with him at the altar possessed the aforesaid money.

## XLIX. GUAYFERIUS

He was said to be a monk of admirable life at Cassino. Out of love for the heavenly kingdom he left the city of Salerno, from which he came, arrived at Cassino, and zealously endeavoured to serve almighty God under the rule of holy religious life. When the eternal Judge had decreed to grant him the recompense of his labours and the everlasting crown, he was laid low by illness. Lying in bed, he was drawing the last breath of life and was about to depart to the Lord.

Some of the brethren keeping watch around his bed began to strengthen his passing with the prayers of their intercessions. Having spent most of the day in this solemn rite, the deacon Alberic rose among them [Col. 1105B] and, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, adjured Guayferius to appear to him after his departure from the world and reveal how he had been received and to what place he had been assigned. When this was said, the aforesaid brother departed from this world. Not many days later, the same Guayferius appeared to Alberic in a vision and said: «Know in truth that I have passed into eternal life.»

## L. THEODEMARIUS

Born in the province of Le Mans, he was chaplain to the Empress Agnes. Having abandoned and despised the pomps of the world, he was making his way to Cassino. He came to the River Verde, which flows near Ceprano; after crossing it, the current seized his servant and began to drag him under. When he perceived this, he immediately gave himself to prayer there [Col. 1105C]. As soon as he rose from prayer, the current cast his servant out upon the bank.

When he came to Cassino, he received, as he desired, the habit of holy life. How great was the religious devotion and perfection of his life, and how pleasing he was to God, will be shown in what follows. One day, while he was offering sacrifice to almighty God, a lame man came begging alms. The man of God took his hand, and he was immediately healed. Nor does it seem proper to omit that, after the celebration of Mass, water flowing from his hands, when given to demoniacs to drink, healed them.

At the same time the bishop of Trani endeavoured to send to him his nephew named Phocas, whom an unclean spirit fiercely tormented [Col. 1105D], begging him to deign to pour forth prayers to almighty God for his deliverance. When he had prayed over him, he drove the devil away.

In those days Berengar, deacon of Angers, devised the heresy bearing his name, asserting that the sacrifice offered to almighty God was a figure, not the reality, of Christ’s body. When this was reported to the Roman pontiff, he urged men to entreat the Lord Jesus Christ in prayer, that He might deign to lead back to the way of truth the people redeemed by His blood. While all were imploring the Lord’s mercy for this, the aforesaid Theodemarius approached to offer the victim to God. When the moment of consecration arrived, he saw the aforesaid offering suddenly changed into flesh. When this was reported to the Roman pontiff [Col. 1106A], he gave thanks to the Dispenser of all good things and compelled Berengar and his followers to renounce that heresy.

When Stephen of Capua came from the city of Saint Germanus to Cassino, he went to pray to God at the altar of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin. The man of God Theodemarius had approached that same altar to celebrate the divine mysteries. When Stephen had risen from prayer, he happened to turn his eyes toward Theodemarius and saw upon his head a golden crown adorned with gems and pearls. Stunned by this vision, he went to Abbot Oderisius and set forth before him in order all that he had seen.

At another time, when this same man of God stood at the holy altars, the most holy man Ebizo was accustomed to stand with him. But, as human nature is sluggish [Col. 1106B] in God’s service, although often summoned he would refuse. On the day when Theodemarius was offering the sacred victim to God at the altar of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, the aforesaid Ebizo fell asleep and saw an angel of the Lord standing beside him and saying: «Ebizo, take heed and see whom you disdain to serve, and how angels serve him. Since you denied him service, the Lord has sent angels to serve him.» Two angels stood beside Theodemarius, one at his right and the other at his left.

At another time, while Theodemarius stood at the holy altars and offered himself to the Lord Jesus Christ in contrition of heart, those standing there saw a dove of snow-white colour resting on his right shoulder.

At that time, when the whole land was parched, Abbot Oderisius summoned the brethren [Col. 1106C] and urged them to entreat God and the Virgin Mary in prayer, that He who brought water from the rock in the wilderness might give rain to the dry world. The brethren approved this, and decided to go barefoot to the church of the Blessed Mary built on that same mountain and there supplicate the mercy of almighty God. When the appointed day came, the abbot commanded Theodemarius to go with the brethren and offer sacrifice to God for the dryness of the land.

As he endeavoured to carry out what had been imposed upon him, he began to think within himself that at Cassino no one was his equal or better; and that this task had therefore been assigned to him as being the better and holier man. When the litanies had been performed, the brethren returned to Cassino, but the sky remained as clear as it had been [Col. 1106D]. Seeing this, the man of God devoted himself to prayer and for three days without interruption diligently began to beseech God. At daybreak he rose and, spreading out his hands before the altar, said: «I shall not lower my hands until the Lord deigns to give us rain.» That very day such a flood of rain burst forth that the whole land was abundantly filled with water.

At another time, when he had come to Naples, a man afflicted with severe fevers was immediately healed through his prayer. In the city of Salerno, a peasant had a lame son. Bringing him from the farm to the abbot, he begged that some remedy might be granted to the lame boy. The abbot, seeing the man of God Theodemarius approaching him, threw the boy down before him and began to beg him to raise the boy from the ground. The man of God, ignorant of what was the matter, stretched out his hand, took hold of the boy, and said: «Rise.» Immediately he rose [Col. 1107A].

## LI. EBIZO

A monk of Cassino, while he was ringing the bell on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity to begin Mass, saw the soul of a certain count from beyond the mountains bound like a beast of burden and being dragged away to punishments. Astonished at the vision, the devil dragging that soul said: «Know that this soul, which you see has come into our jurisdiction, belongs to your lord, who died today.» When the man of God heard this, he groaned. At daybreak he came into chapter and said: «Know that my lord departed this world yesterday; therefore I earnestly beseech your holiness [Col. 1107B] to pour forth prayers to almighty God for him. For yesterday I saw his soul bound and dragged by demons to punishments.»

After relating this, he began with the brethren to pour forth prayers for that soul’s deliverance. When night came, the devil appeared and beat him with such lashes that he left him half-dead, saying: «Why did you dare pray to God for him, who, because of his sins, has come into our jurisdiction?» The attendants ran up, lifted him from the ground, and put him in bed. When another night came, as he prayed to God for that soul’s deliverance, the ancient enemy again beat him most severely. On the third night the devil scourged him with such blows that he fell from the bed onto the ground, and the attendants found him [Col. 1107C] half-dead.

As the man of God continually prayed for that soul’s release, Leo the Librarian, who afterwards became bishop of Ostia, came at the request of the man of God to celebrate the divine mysteries. When he came to the breaking of the victim, Ebizo fell asleep, and the devil appeared to him, saying: «By your psalms and prayers you have drawn the soul from my power.

[Note: [Col. 1107D] No one is obliged to accept the devil’s testimony. For what the biographer himself subsequently affirms also depends upon this saying of the devil. Yet it is the teaching of the Catholic Church that a sentence of damnation after death is irrevocable. [Col. 1108D] I have deliberately spared myself a theological discussion of this question here, since in my edition of the oration of Nicephorus Blemmydes I discussed at sufficient length the opinion of those who believed that the soul of the Emperor Trajan was liberated from hell by the prayers of St Gregory the Pope.]»

Then the man of God awoke, gave thanks to God, and set forth in order to the brethren what he had seen and heard. Meanwhile Germans arrived from Gaul, and the man of God inquired about the count’s death. He found that he had departed this world at the very hour when Ebizo had seen his soul dragged to punishments.

At another time, when the abbot had sent him to Venafrum, the devil appeared to him while he was stationed in the church [Col. 1107D] and began to address him thus: «Your abbot is more concerned about transitory and perishable things than about monks, and you have already suffered many evils. Now take this cloak and buy yourself bread with it.» The man of God answered: «May your cloak be with you unto perdition.» The devil immediately departed and cast down from the roof two stones with which he might have struck him.

At the time when he was about to depart this life, the blessed Mother of God appeared [Col. 1108A] to him and asked whether he wished to live longer in this life. «No,» he replied. And the Mother of God said: «Come to me.» Hearing this, he breathed his last.

### From the Life of the same Ebizo, composed by Paul, monk of Cassino

Ebizo was German by birth, from the province called German Francia. Since parents, relatives, and the leading men of his city hindered him from travelling far away and changing his habit, he seized an opportunity, went at once to the Empress Agnes, and, supported by her counsel and assistance, changed not only his city but also his people. Thus, becoming an imitator of Abraham’s pilgrimage, he was kindly received by Saint Desiderius, abbot of the monastery of Cassino. Under that lover of religion and helper of such men [Col. 1108B], he presented his body as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.

He wore against his flesh the harshest hair-shirt he could find. He was so devoted to fasting that he continually abstained even from fish, which are customarily called the food of cenobites. He never used eggs or fat; from his birth he never ate meat; nor did he use oil at all, except in common with the others. Finally, when there was a shortage of that liquid, an edict went forth from the father of the monastery that oil should be given to no one except at the solemn common meal. Thus he ate only boiled vegetables; and, more pitiably, when others dined better, he himself took poorer nourishment.

Except on Sundays and the chief feasts [Col. 1108C], he never took food before the ninth hour; three days each week he was content with bread and water alone. He maintained this rule throughout the entire year. He slept very rarely, lest he seem to transgress the saying, «Pray without ceasing» (1 Thess. 5:17). He was so devoted to silence that scarcely during a whole year would he speak, except for confession.

He made the chapel of Blessed Bartholomew—the lateral chapel adjoining the basilica of Saint Benedict—his tribunal, in order that the enclosed body might be denied all movement abroad by hours and moments. Dwelling continually there as in a desert, he could say without falsehood: «Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude» (Ps. 54:8). At no time did he leave the aforesaid building except through the demands of obedience or the compulsion of human necessity, so that he seemed able to say with blessed Job: «In my little nest I shall die» (Job 29:18) [Col. 1108D]. Hence, because human company was forbidden him, he conversed more often with angels or demons than with human beings.

Before his conversion he had had a most intimate acquaintance named Ado, a very wealthy man who conferred many benefits upon him, but in the end inflicted certain injuries upon him. The satellites of Satan, supposing that the man of God would rejoice at vengeance, appeared to him on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, as he prayed and was already nodding from excessive weariness, rejoicing in a kind of dance [Col. 1109A]. He asked them: «And why are you rejoicing?» They replied: «Because we have just triumphed over his soul.»

### Concerning the same Ebizo, according to Paul, monk of Cassino

He was also led in the spirit through pleasant places, and the owners of the dwellings were named to him. Among other things, a certain delightful place was shown to him, and he heard that it had belonged to the prophet Elijah.

Finally, he had asked God that before the setting of his life he might depart, purified by whatever sickness of suffering, into rest. At length his prayer was heard: he developed a fistula in the left side of his breast. Since it could scarcely be endured either by the brethren or by himself because of the increasing discharge and stench, his brethren persuaded him, for treatment [Col. 1109B], to go to the bishop of Venafrum, Peter by name, who had provided remedies for many suffering from such an illness. But he did not wish to cast aside what he had requested from God, and was scarcely compelled to go by the order of the venerable priest Gregory.

While he stayed at Venafrum for some days because of this, he did not interrupt the work of prayer, but sat secretly behind the altar of the basilica. Therefore the devil, the common enemy of the devout, no longer able to endure his envy, cast down a stone, intending, I think, to crush the Lord’s servant; but it shattered the wooden seat before which he sat. Since Ebizo in no way desisted from his customary prayers, when the people were gathering for worship and crowding the walls of the church, the malicious enemy—unable earlier to move him by terror—then approached Ebizo humbly in the guise of a monk, with a feignedly kind consolation [Col. 1109C], and began thus:

«Your abbot is more concerned about transitory and perishable things than about monks, and you have suffered many evils already. Therefore take off the cheap garment in which you are dressed, and put on the more becoming one which I bring, amid so great a crowd of people.»

For the apparent monk himself wore cheap clothing, yet Ebizo saw him carrying a finer cloak. As he carefully observed him, he who had come as though a young servant appeared now of mature age, now old—so that, I suppose, his words might have greater authority. When Ebizo saw his appearance change, he immediately recognized what he was and armed himself with the sign of the cross. At once that image disappeared; and as it vanished the whole structure of the church was shaken with such a tremor [Col. 1109D] that the people and clergy present fled outside. The bishop also, living nearby in the episcopal residence, was astonished by the earthquake. Seeing others wandering about, he began anxiously to ask what had happened to the servant of God and ordered that he be brought to him. Questioning him whether he had felt the earthquake, he learned fully what the man of God had seen and what had happened.

This bishop, through the merit of Ebizo’s worthy religious life and by God’s revelation, learned that he could not be cured and that he would soon put off the human body. He therefore sent him back to the monastery of Cassino, so that he might bid farewell to the world in his own monastery. While there he continued to implore divine help, and saw in a vision a long and joyful procession of persons clothed in white. Coming to its end [Col. 1110A], he asked who they were and why they were celebrating. The person whom he questioned replied: «It is not expedient for you to be taught this now, because you will shortly know.»

Meanwhile Desiderius, abbot of that place, came to visit him and said: «How are you, brother?» Ebizo answered: «Well, Father, through the assistance of your prayers.» Then Desiderius urged him to eat at least some fish to relieve his illness. Ebizo replied: «No, Father, no. Far be it from me now, placed at the point of death, to lose the abstinence which I have observed throughout my life. For I shall now be presented before the face of my Lord; now I desire to be dissolved and to be with him.»

Then Desiderius turned to the brethren and said: «This man is of stone, not flesh; he surpasses the measure of men. For throughout his entire life, as has already been said, the blessed man ate neither fish, nor meat, nor cheese, nor eggs, nor any allurement of fat [Col. 1110B]. O man rightly to be numbered among the highest Fathers of old, who even on the day of death would not relax the rigor of his abstinence!»

While the man of God lay weakened by that illness, a matron of remarkable stature, incomparable beauty, and imperial bearing appeared before him and addressed him, distressed by the sickness, in these words: «See that you do not fail, but be strong, and wait for me until I return»; for she seemed to be on a journey. He replied: «How, lady, can I wait for you, when I can scarcely remain in myself because of the heat of this ulcer?» Then she, whom he thought to be the Blessed Mary, gave this answer to the fevered man [Col. 1110C]: «Bear it bravely, for through this momentary burning you shall escape that intolerable and everlasting one.»

Receiving this consolation, he became more cheerful. A few days later, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October], the thirteenth day after he had returned from Venafrum, he closed his last day. He was buried beside the church of Saint Benedict. Later Desiderius removed his body from that place and placed it, with many others, at the head of the steps leading to the refectory.

The same Paul says: «Ebizo is comparable to blessed Gregory, who rescued Trajan from punishments. Certainly it is no more difficult to aid a pagan than a tax collector. For Ado had been a trader, and could not frequent markets without grave fault; and we have sufficiently authoritative Scriptures which assert that tax collectors are worse than pagans. Therefore it is no more marvellous to have liberated Trajan than Ado, although they differ in this: the latter, regenerated by water and the Spirit, is believed to have entered the kingdom of God, while the former was rescued only from punishments.»

## LII. RAIDERISUS

A monk of Cassino, when on one occasion he came to the castle of Saint Apollinaris during a great drought, the inhabitants, learning that he had arrived, begged him to deign to pour forth prayers to the Lord because of the drought. The man of God humbly obeyed their requests and approached the life-giving altar to offer sacrifice to almighty God. God’s mercy immediately came: at once a flood of rain burst forth.

## LIII. ALMANNUS

[Col. 1111A]

He was a monk at Cassino, and how pleasing his life had been to God was surely revealed by his death. Coming to this monastery from Melfi, his birthplace, he lived with the strictest discipline and continence. Every night he remained naked beside the church of the Apostle Saint Andrew, and did not cease to afflict himself with harsh blows from brooms while singing psalms.

In the time of Abbot Gerard, when this man died at night, Nicholas the cellarer, who was outside the monastery, lifted his eyes and saw the roof of the monastery open above, and a great globe of fire come forth from it and be carried to the heights of heaven. Immediately sending a messenger to the monastery, he found that Almannus had died at the very hour when he saw the globe of fire leave the monastery and seek the heights of heaven [Col. 1111B]. This vision was seen by Carbo within the monastery just as the cellarer saw it outside.

While he lived, he ate bread and drank water three days a week, and never broke his fast except on an appointed feast.

## LIV. FORTUNATUS

A native of the province of Spain, he came to Cassino to the body of blessed Benedict for the sake of pursuing a more devout religious life. With the permission of Abbot Richerius, he built himself a dwelling beside the church of the Apostle Saint Matthew and began there to serve almighty God with greater zeal.

One day, coming to the monastery of Cassino, he entered the church and encountered before the great cross a man grievously tormented by an unclean spirit. When the man came before him, with foaming mouth and flashing eyes he rushed at him [Col. 1111C]. The man of God stretched out his hands and said: «Most cruel robber, if you delight in human flesh, devour these fingers»—for he tore apart the people whom he held, while he devoured others with his teeth. When the priest Fortunatus had said this, the unclean spirit came out of him and filled the church with smoke and stench. Beside the church of Saint Matthew, he healed by prayer a demoniac woman who came to him.

## LV. ALPHANUS

Before he departed this life, the monk of Cassino saw in a vision a ladder erected from the place of his bed up to heaven. Stunned and amazed by this vision, he heard certain men clothed in white standing beside him say: «Climb upward by the ladder.» When he had reached the summit of the ladder, he saw that two rungs were missing [Col. 1111D]. Immediately he was snatched upward by the white-clad figures and led into a house shining with immense light.

When he awoke and recounted these things to the brethren, he disclosed his coming death; a few days later he closed his final day. His life was such: during Lent he never rested in a bed; he ate twice a week; psalms never departed from his mouth.

## LVI. JOHN

A disciple of Saint Romuald, he was sent by him with Olibanus to inhabit a certain place and remained there for several years. Leaving it, he set out for Jerusalem. When, descending from the mountain of Cassino, he had already reached the plains, his companion’s horse suddenly spun about in a frantic rush and struck John’s shin with its iron-shod hoof, breaking it [Col. 1112A]. Overwhelmed by intense pain and thrown to the ground, he had himself brought back to Cassino. Building a cell near the monastery, he remained in it for thirty years in holy conduct.

For he was eminent and exceptional in charity, abstinence, and humility, so that no one even within the cloister knew how he fasted. Among his other gifts of virtue, he so detested the vice of detraction that as soon as anyone opened his mouth to speak ill of another, the reproach immediately rebounded upon its utterer, as an arrow rebounds from the hardness of stone. After his death, several miracles were divinely performed through him there.

## LVII. PETER

Abbot of Cassino, he was of the greatest religious devotion. Perceiving that the burden of rule was too arduous for him, he abandoned the abbacy and withdrew to the Valley of Light [Col. 1112B], where he began to live religiously with the brethren.

One day, while the venerable Father and the brethren had gone out to cut crops and the weather was very clear, the sky suddenly grew dense with clouds; thunder crashed and great flashes of lightning began to gleam. Seeing this, the man of God commanded the brethren: «Let none of you leave the field; persist in the work begun, so that you may be able to complete it today.» Having said this, he gave himself there to prayer with tears.

Wonderful is God in His saints (Ps. 67:6), who deigns so swiftly to hear those who glorify Him and keep His commandments. For when heavy rain came down, not even a single drop fell in the field where the man of God stood with the brethren.

A wolf often came from the neighbouring mountain [Col. 1112C] overlooking the monastery and carried away its sheep. One day the wolf came as usual, took a sheep, and went off. When this was reported to the man of God, he entered the church and gave himself to prayer with tears. When he had completed it and gone out to the gate, he found the wolf holding the sheep in its mouth and bringing it to him. When the wolf came to him, it placed the sheep at his feet and immediately departed.

At another time, thieves entered the garden of the same monastery and tried to steal vegetables. Already laden with vegetables, they attempted to flee, but walked in circles throughout the whole night, unable to get out. When they were carefully questioned as to where they came from, who they were, and why they had come, they immediately confessed the theft of their crime and were released. The person who found them was a brother who kept the garden; at daybreak he found them walking about and unable in any way to find an exit [Col. 1112D].

## LVIII. STEPHEN

Abbot of Cassino and pontiff of the Apostolic See, born of royal lineage, educated from childhood in liberal letters, and exceedingly eloquent, he was chancellor to Pope Leo. Sent by him to Constantinople, he deposed the patriarch of that city and bound him with the bond of anathema. Returning, he became a monk at Cassino, and shortly afterward was elected abbot. Going to Rome for his consecration, he was consecrated by Pope Victor; but before he returned, the Roman pontiff died. Immediately he was seized by the senate, clergy, and people of Rome and consecrated to the Apostolic See [Col. 1113A].

There he fought unflinchingly against the marriages of clerics, priests, and also persons related by blood.

[Note: [Col. 1113] Here *pro* means «against,» as shortly below at the end of Victor’s life. Elsewhere among writers of the low Middle Ages it means «on account of.»]

He commanded all clerics at Rome who had remained incontinent after Pope Leo’s prohibition to leave the clerical assembly and the choir of the church. A certain priest lived beside the canonical house of Blessed Cecilia across the Tiber. He neither consented to put away a woman nor could ever judge these ordinances as anything other than vain and frivolous. One day, while he was safe, vigorous, and healthy, he lay down in his bed to rest in the evening; but struck by a sudden visitation of divine vengeance, he died an immediate death.

The same pontiff rebuked and corrected the lives of false monks and nuns; he condemned the Simoniac heresy forever [Col. 1113B]; and after this he died in the city of Florence. At his tomb Christ showed many signs according to his merits.

## LIX. VICTOR

Leaving his bride at their very wedding, he sought the wilderness. Afterwards, coming to Cassino, he received there the consecration of the monastic order. Once, while he slept, a vision worthy of notice appeared to him. He saw himself standing in the tower beside the chapter-house, where Father Benedict seemed to sit in a most fitting seat. Frightened and astonished by this vision, he did not at all presume to approach more closely; but Blessed Father Benedict cheerfully beckoned to him and, extending his hand, ordered him to sit beside him.

The event proved the vision true: afterwards made abbot, he renewed the entire monastery as it is now seen [Col. 1113C]. Moreover, when the monastery of Cassino was repeatedly struck by lightning, Saint Father Benedict appeared to him one night and taught him that it was nothing other than devilish snares and the ancient envy directed against that place itself.

Meanwhile, after the pontiff of the Apostolic See had died, he was ordained pontiff by all the clergy and people. He was buried at Cassino in the apse of the chapter-house.

## LX. RANDISIUS
At Monte Cassino he was a monk under Abbot Desiderius. What and how great his life had been, the Lord deigned to show at the very moment of his death. For when, his allotted span of life completed, he was paying the debt of death, the brethren began, as is customary, to commend his soul to almighty God. When he was [Col. 1113D] already drawing his final breath, he turned to the brethren and said: “Be silent, be silent. Do you not hear how great the praises resound in heaven? Do you not see the boys who sing praises to me? For their garments and faces are like snow. Therefore, I earnestly beseech you by God: be silent, and allow me to hear that most sweet sound.” As he said this, he gave up his spirit. He was buried beside the church of Blessed Stephen and Saint Martin, confessor of Christ. So long as he lived, he was held by all to be admirable and most holy.

LXI. SERGIUS,

a monk of Monte Cassino, an Amalfitan by birth, when he was dying in the lifetime of Abbot Gerard, [Col. 1114A] asked Gregory, priest of the same monastery, not to leave him. Gregory complied with his request and remained with him. When the final hour of his life was now approaching, he looked up and saw the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, coming toward him; and at once, raising his hands on high, he began to cry: “My Lady!” When they asked him what he saw, he said: “Do you not see the most blessed Virgin Mary? She is indeed here.” Having said this, he breathed out his soul.

LXII. AZO,

dean of Monte Cassino, was a native of the province of Campania. When he had been sent to Sardinia by Abbot Gerard and was returning to the monastery, he was captured by Saracens in the province of Africa and carried into captivity. When he died in that [Col. 1114B] province, his body was buried before the altar in the church of Blessed Mary. It happened, in the silence of the dead of night, that Saracens passing by, while the moon was casting its rays, saw him sitting outside beside the door, holding a book in his hand. Astonished, they began to call other Saracens, saying: “Run quickly, run! Make haste to come here: for we see the priest of the Christians who died this month sitting before the church door.” Hearing this, the others hurried out through the city gates and hastened there. When they approached him, the man of God entered within the threshold and doorway of the basilica and appeared nowhere. One day the custodian entered the church and found the lamp hanging over [Col. 1114C] his tomb burning. Angrily, he summoned the boy who continually served him in the church and said to him: “Why did you leave the lamp lit?” The boy replied: “When I shut the church, I extinguished all the lamps; but I do not know who lit this one.” Perceiving how matters stood, the man extinguished the lamp and shut the church. On another day he entered the church and again found the lamp burning. Since this repeatedly occurred, it was reported to the king of the Saracens. Amazed by the unusual occurrence and thinking that the Christians were fabricating it, he sent Saracens to extinguish the lamp and remove its oil. When this had been done, they entered the church the next day and found the lamp shining, with water burning after the manner of oil [Col. 1114D]. They fled from there at headlong speed, came to the king, and set out in order all that they had seen. Then the king ordered the lamp extinguished and Saracens to guard the church day and night, lest any Christian enter it. When night came, the Saracens watching the church lifted their eyes to heaven and saw a star from heaven shining over the lamp of the church. Astonished, they opened the church doors and saw the lamp burning. Running swiftly to the king’s palace, they began to report in sequence what they had seen. But when the king heard such things from his own men’s lips, he disbelieved their report and ordered the lamp extinguished and the church guarded [Col. 1115A] as before. Rising, he went to the house of the caliph, which overlooked the church. When night had come, he lifted his eyes to heaven and saw a star shining over the church lamp and kindling it with its ray. He immediately sent Saracens to the church, and they returned to report that the lamp was burning. Then the king issued an edict that Christians should have free permission to enter the church.

LXIII. LEO,

an Amalfitan, was a monk at Monte Cassino. Seriously ill near the end of his life, he asked the brethren attending him for water. When one of them delayed a little in drawing it and offered him water to drink, Leo refused, saying: “I do not want this water, because Odilo, abbot of Cluny, has just come here, brought me water, and refreshed me in my thirst.” Hearing this, they were astonished; and immediately the aforesaid brother departed from the world.

LXIV. JOHN

was a Caietan monk of Monte Cassino. As he lay in the infirmary at the point of death, George the custodian, sleeping in the vestry, saw a great multitude of brethren, as though going in procession, entering this monastery from its eastern side. While he marvelled at the vision, one said: “We have come to receive John.” At these words, the signal customarily sounded to announce a brother’s death immediately rang; George hurried there, found him dead, and understood that John had been a man of great merit, since that assembly of saints had come to receive his soul.

LXV. PETER,

[Col. 1115C]

whose surname was Cuculites, when he came to Monte Cassino through the grace of conversion, the devil met him at the church of Saint Severus, situated on the side of this mountain, and said: “You, abandoning my claims, are taking refuge with Benedict; [Col. 1116A] but I have obtained from God that your body be scourged, as Job’s once was, although I shall by no means be able to harm your soul, placed under so great a protector.” This afterwards became clearly evident. For when he came there, he lived most devoutly to the end of his life; yet his body was always oppressed by frequent and severe torments.

LXVI. RANDISIUS,

a monk of Monte Cassino and son of Count Burrellus, who for thirty years retained his former state [the wording is uncertain], when he became dropsical and approached death, saw Saint Stephen the protomartyr coming toward him with an innumerable crowd. Having related this, he immediately gave up his spirit.

LXVII. JOHN,

a priest of Monte Cassino, a native of Ravenna. The Lord deigned to show what and how great a man he was, and how powerful in life his prayer was with almighty God. For in the time of Abbot Gerard, when Sennes, archbishop of the church of Capua, had died, that archbishop appeared in a vision to the aforesaid abbot. The abbot said to him: “How are you?” And he replied: “For a long time I have been tormented in fire; but if you order John of Ravenna and John of Saint Angelo to offer the sacrifice to the Redeemer of all for me, I shall be freed from these torments.”

LXVIII. BENEDICT

was a monk of Monte Cassino under Abbot Desiderius, and came as provost of the monastery at Capua. How constant he was in psalmody, how zealous in almsgiving, how diligent in prayer, and how wakeful in vigils is clearer than daylight. [Col. 1116C] Stricken by illness at the Capuan monastery, he died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June]. He was buried before the door of that monastery, on the right hand of those entering the church, where to this day divine power does not cease to work marvellous miracles.

[Col. 1115]

PETER THE DEACON’S BOOK ON THE HOLY PLACES.

(Dom Tosti, *Storia della badia di Monte-Cassino*, Naples, 1842, quarto, vol. II, p. 121, from Monte Cassino MS no. 361.)

PROLOGUE. TO GUIBALD, ABBOT OF MONTE CASSINO AND STAVELOT.

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, 790.)

[Col. 1115D] To his lord and father in Christ, the venerable GUIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of the sacred Mount of Monte Cassino: the service of due obedience from PETER, deacon of Monte Cassino.

[Col. 1116D] With what fire of longing I have burned, venerable Father in Christ, and with what great and intense desire I have wished that almighty God might deliver you from adversities, I call God himself as witness—the God whom neither the hidden places of the mind nor the secret things of conscience deceive, and who is believed to be the judge of the very movements of the human soul. But since, in the prophet’s saying, a man’s way is not in his own hand, and a man’s steps are directed not by man but by the Lord, through the demands of our sins there has not come about what human desire longed for, but what God the Judge determined to be fitting for human merits. For since, as the impiety of all wicked men runs rampant, the condition of God’s Church is seen daily to be shaken, and since almost, so to speak, no one rises against them for the house of Israel—partly through love, partly through fear of secular powers—therefore our lord the emperor Lothair, of august memory, established Your Blessedness as abbot in the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 1117B], so that you might carefully and diligently deal with matters pertaining to the correction of the wicked and the salvation of the good, restrain the unbridled, and humble the proud; so that, justice recovered and religion restored, the body of the Church might serve God justly and mercifully, and might implore the mercy of almighty God for the preservation of the Roman Empire. Hence you are deservedly loved and revered by all good and wise persons. For who would reject the friendship of so great a man, despise his graciousness, or avoid his diligence? To pass over the other great and distinguished endowments of your intellect, you surpass all the wise men of the pre-eminent Roman Empire in Tullian eloquence, and at every hour and moment you excel the abundant generosity [Col. 1117C] of your predecessors. Seeing you, I say, crowned with such and so great garlands and adorned with laurels, I have taken care to send to your fatherhood an *Itinerary of the Holy Places*, however imperfectly composed by me and collected, as it were, from every book. I ask that it be confirmed by your eminence; and I beg you to attend in it not to the indolence of its compiler, but to the great usefulness of its subject matter. I do not suppose that you, as one new to these matters and hitherto unacquainted with them, will learn anything from this itinerary; rather, I ask that you recognize that we have here collected those things which you have already learned by the living testimony of those who went to the Lord’s tomb, or read in the various volumes of books. What inflexible and enormous obstacles have been placed in our way by the faithless and wicked, who limp upon both knees, I shall call not God now, but you yourselves who know, you yourselves who are faithful in heart, [Col. 1118B] as witnesses. Yet, in the small span left us through the bounty of divine mercy, I have produced this little work by heavenly generosity, nevertheless trusting in God that he will someday grant us victory over our enemies. For just as no work is ever sound or beautiful if its craftsman does not fit everything together as reason requires, so no writer overflowing with manifold verbosity will possess the power to produce writing wreathed in sweetness, as the most vigorous orator Horace left it in his writings, saying:

> He wins every vote who mingles the useful with the sweet, if, after he sets about writing, he does not examine his subject.

Now, with Christ’s favour, let this be the end [Col. 1118C] of this prologue.

END OF THE PROLOGUE.

HERE BEGINS THE BOOK ON THE HOLY PLACES.

[Col. 1117]

[Col. 1117C] The site of the city of Jerusalem rises in a circuit of no small circumference of walls, enclosing also within itself the neighbouring Mount Sion, which lies to the south and towers over the city like a citadel. The greater part of the city lies below the mountain, situated on the plain of a lower hill. Within the great circuit of its walls it has eighty-four towers and six gates. The first is David’s Gate, on the western side of Mount Sion. The second is the Gate of the Fuller's Village. The third is Saint Stephen’s Gate. The fourth is Benjamin’s Gate. The fifth is a small gate, from which one descends by steps into the Valley of Jehoshaphat. The sixth is the Gate of Tekoa. Yet the more notable among these are three gate-exits: one toward the west, another toward the north, and a third toward the east. On the south, however, the northern brow of Mount Sion rises above the city; and that stretch of wall, with its intervening towers, is shown to have no gates, namely, from the aforementioned David’s Gate as far as that front of Mount Sion which faces the eastern region in a sheer cliff. Indeed, beginning from the northern brow of Mount Sion, the site of the city slopes so gently toward the lower levels of the northern and eastern walls that rain falling there does not form pools, but flows like rivers through the eastern gates, carrying away with it all the filth of the streets and swelling [Col. 1118D] the torrent Kidron in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.

Those entering the city from the north must first, according to the arrangement of the streets, turn aside to the Constantinian church, where the Lord’s cross was discovered. Then, toward the west, the church of Golgotha is visible; in it appears also that rock which once bore the cross upon which the Lord’s body was fastened, and which now supports a great silver cross, while above it hangs a bronze wheel with lamps. Beneath the actual place of the Lord’s cross is a crypt hewn in the rock, where sacrifice for honoured dead is customarily offered upon an altar, while the bodies are meanwhile laid in the open court. To its west is the church of the Anastasis—that is, the Lord’s Resurrection—a round church encircled by three walls and supported by twelve columns [Col. 1119A]. Between each wall is a broad passageway; in three places of the middle wall—on the south, north, and west—it contains three altars. It has eight gates twice over, set through three corresponding walls; of these, four face the north-east wind and four the east wind. In its middle is the Lord’s monument, round and hewn from rock. A man standing inside can touch its roof with his hand. It has an entrance on the east, where that great stone had been placed; traces of its socket-holes remain visible within to the present day. On the outside it is wholly covered in marble up to the summit of its roof; the summit itself, ornamented with gold, bears a large golden cross.

On the northern side of this monument is [Col. 1119B] the Lord’s tomb, hewn in the same rock. It is seven feet long and three palms in measure, and rises above the pavement. Its entrance is on the south side, where twelve lamps burn day and night: four inside the tomb and eight along the right-hand edge. The stone which had been placed at the monument’s door is now fixed in place. Its smaller part forms a square altar before the entrance to the same monument; its larger part is in the eastern part of the church, where another four-sided altar stands beneath coverings. The colour of the monument and tomb appears to be a mixture of white and red. On the right side, adjoining this church, is the square church of the Mother of God. In the street joining the Martyrium and Golgotha is a recess in which the Lord’s cup, kept in a reliquary [Col. 1119C], is customarily touched and kissed through an opening in the cover. This silver cup, with two little handles on either side, holds the measure of a Gallic sextarius; and in it is also the sponge that served for the Lord’s drink. There too, at Golgotha, Abraham offered his son Isaac. Moreover, the soldier’s spear is preserved set into a wooden cross in the portico of the Martyrium; its shaft has been cut into two pieces.

These holy places lie outside Mount Sion, where the swelling of the ground slopes northward. In the lower part of the city is the Temple, situated near the eastern wall; there are few cisterns there. But the Lord’s tomb, of which we have spoken above, is built in the middle of the Temple; while the Temple is in the middle of the city, facing north, [Col. 1119D] not far from David’s Gate. Beyond the Resurrection is the garden in which Holy Mary spoke with the Lord. Behind the church, outside, is the midpoint of the world, where David says: “He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 73 [LXXIII]). Another prophet likewise says: “Thus says the Lord: This is Jerusalem; I have placed it in the midst of the nations” (Ezekiel 5 [V]). At Golgotha there is a portion of the life-giving wood of the cross upon which the Lord was fastened, and the inscription, kept in a silver casket. There also are the horn from which kings were anointed and Solomon’s ring. Not far from the world’s midpoint is the prison; there too is the binding; nearby are the scourging, the crowning with thorns, the stripping, and the division of the garments.

At Calvary, where the Lord was crucified, is [Col. 1120A] the split mountain; and one ascends Mount Calvary itself by seventeen steps. There hang nine lamps, each with a silver bowl (*nappa*, sic). Beneath is Golgotha, where Christ’s blood fell upon the split rock. Beneath Mount Calvary, toward the east, is the Lord’s Temple on the other side of the city, which Solomon built. It has four gates: the first on the east, the second on the west, the third on the south, and the fourth on the north, signifying the four parts of the world. On the outside it has eight angles; around each angle it extends for twelve paces. In the middle of the Temple is a great mountain enclosed by walls, on which was the sanctuary; there too was the Ark of the Covenant, which Emperor Vespasian carried to Rome after destroying the Temple. [Col. 1120B] On the left side of the sanctuary, on a rock, the Lord Jesus Christ placed his foot when Simeon received him in his arms; and the footprint has remained there, as though impressed in wax. On the other side of the rock is an open sanctuary, reached by ascending twenty-two steps. There the Lord prayed, and there Zacharias offered sacrifice. Outside the Temple is the place where Zacharias son of Barachias was slain. Over the rock in the middle of the Temple hangs a golden lamp containing Christ’s blood, which descended through the split rock. Toward the south, not far away, is Solomon’s Temple, in which he dwelt, which was constructed; it has twenty-five gates, and inside it has three hundred and sixty-two columns. Beneath it, not far away, are Christ’s cradle, his bath, and the bed of the holy [Col. 1120C] Mother of God. Beneath the Lord’s Temple, to the east, is the Beautiful Gate, through which the Lord entered sitting upon an ass’s colt; there too Peter healed the lame man. Toward the north is the church of Saint Anne, where Blessed Mary was nourished for three years. Nearby is the Pool of Bethesda, which has five porticoes. Near the Temple is the pool of Bethsaida; it is conspicuous for two basins, one of which is generally more abundantly filled by rain, while the other is discoloured by red water. From the spring of Mount Sion, which faces the east in a sheer cliff, the spring of Siloam bursts forth within the walls at the foot of the hill. It flows southward with an alternating access of waters: that is, not with continuous waters, but it bubbles up at fixed [Col. 1120D] hours and days, and is accustomed to come through subterranean hollows and caverns of very hard rock. On the highest plain of Mount Sion is a large church founded by the apostles, because there they received the Holy Spirit, and there Holy Mary died; in it the place of the Lord’s Supper is also shown. A marble column stands in the middle, against which the Lord was bound and scourged. Here is shown the rock on which Stephen, most blessed martyr, was stoned, situated outside the city.

In the middle of Jerusalem, where the Lord died and rose again with his cross set above him, stands a high column that casts no shadow at the summer solstice: there is the midpoint of the world. In the church called Holy Sion is the throne of James, the Lord’s brother, who was buried near the [Col. 1121A] Temple. It was founded at the place where the Lord appeared to the apostles after the Passion while they were dining and the doors were shut. Nearby is the gate through which the angel led Peter out. Of the Temple which Solomon built, only two pinnacles remain; one, which is very high, is that upon which the Lord was tempted by the devil; the rest has been destroyed. Near the gate was shed the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias. On leaving David’s Gate, one comes upon a bridge leading southward through the valley. At its midpoint, on the west, stands a great fig tree on which Judas hanged himself with a noose. Moreover, Aceldama lies on the southern side of Mount Sion: it covers some foreign and obscure dead with earth, and allows others to decay unburied. [Col. 1121B] A most Christian man stole the cloth from the Lord’s head immediately after his Resurrection and possessed it until his death, becoming wealthy. Dying, he asked his sons which of them wished to receive the Lord’s cloth and which his father’s other riches. The elder chose the treasures of material possessions; the younger chose the cloth. Immediately the former’s wealth dwindled until he was poor, while that of the younger brother increased along with faith; his possessions remained until the fifth generation. Thereafter it came into the possession of impious persons and increased their wealth so greatly that, even in our time, it remained among the Jews, until, after long disputes in which the Christians claimed to be Christ’s heirs and the faithless Jews asserted themselves to be heirs of their fathers, the Moorish king of the Saracens, who was judge in our age, was appealed to. He kindled a great pyre and prayed to Christ the Judge that the one who ought to wear this upon his head for the salvation of his own [Col. 1121C] people should be indicated. When the cloth was thrown into the fire, it fled swiftly away, flew out, and hovered for a long time in the highest air as though in play. At last, while everyone on both sides looked on, it gently deposited itself in the lap of one of the Christians. The next morning all the people greeted and kissed it with the highest veneration. It was eight feet long. The cloth with which Christ wiped his face, called by some the Veronica, was taken to Rome in the time of Emperor Tiberius. The reed with which his head was struck, his sandals, the cords with which he was bound, his circumcision, and his blood are reverently honoured in the Constantinian basilica at Rome. [Col. 1121D] Another, somewhat larger, cloth is likewise venerated in the church. It is said to have been woven by Holy Mary and to contain images of the twelve apostles and of the Lord himself, red on one side and green on the other.

Around Jerusalem the terrain appears rough and mountainous. Thence northward as far as the land of Arimathea, rocky and rugged regions appear at intervals; likewise thorny valleys spread as far as the region of Thamnyca. Toward Caesarea of Palestine from Jerusalem, although some narrow and short rugged places occur, there is chiefly a plain of fields interspersed with olive groves; the distance is seventy Roman miles. The length of the Promised Land from Dan to Beersheba extends for one hundred and sixty-five miles; [Col. 1122A] from Joppa to Bethlehem, forty-six miles. Near the wall of the Temple, or Jerusalem, on the east, one comes to Gehenna, which is the Valley of Jehoshaphat, stretching from the northern region southward; through it the torrent Kidron runs whenever it receives rainwater.

This valley, together with a small flat expanse of plain, is well-watered, wooded, and full of delights. In it is the tower of King Jehoshaphat, containing his tomb. To its right, cut and separated from the cliff of the Mount of Olives, is a house with two hollowed tombs: those of old Simeon and Joseph, husband of Holy Mary. In the same valley is a round church of Holy Mary, divided by a stone floor; in its upper part are four altars, and in its lower part one, [Col. 1122B] in the eastern section. To its right is an empty monument in which Holy Mary is said to have rested for a time. On entering, they see on the right a rock inserted in the wall, on which the Lord prayed on the night when he was betrayed, with marks of his knees impressed as though in soft wax. The Mount of Olives, one thousand paces from Jerusalem, equals Mount Sion in height but surpasses it in length and breadth. Apart from vines and olives, it produces few trees, but is fertile in wheat and barley. Its soil is not blighted, but grassy and flowering. On its highest summit, where the Lord ascended to heaven, stands a great round church with three roofed, vaulted porticoes surrounding it. The inner building could not be vaulted or roofed because of the passage of the Lord’s body; it has an altar toward the east protected by a narrow roof. In its middle, beneath the open sky, are visible the Lord’s final footprints where he ascended. Although earth is carried away from them daily by believers, they nevertheless remain, still preserving the appearance of footprints stamped into the ground. Around it stands a bronze wheel, rising as high as the summit and having an entrance on the west; above hangs upon pulleys a great lamp, burning all day and night. In the western part of the same church are eight windows, and the same number of lamps shine on that side. Each year on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, after Mass has been celebrated, a powerful blast of wind is accustomed to come down from above and cast to the ground all who are in the church. [Col. 1122D] A church built there displays Lazarus’s tomb, and a great monastery in the field of Bethany is surrounded by a large olive grove. Bethany is fifteen stadia from Jerusalem. On the southern side of the same mountain, a third church stands at Bethany, where before his Passion the Lord spoke with the disciples concerning the day of judgment. Across the torrent Kidron is a cave, and over it a church, at the place where, on Thursday after supper, the Jews seized the Saviour; this place is at the head of the Valley of Jehoshaphat. In the same valley stood the palm tree from which the children took branches when they cried “Hosanna.” Likewise, on the Mount of Olives is a cave containing a brightly shining altar, in which the Lord used to teach his disciples; above that cave [Col. 1123A] is a great holy church, and not far away is the martyr shrine of Saint Stephen. Not far from there is the place where the Lord prayed when his sweat became like drops of blood. On the road to Bethany is the village from which the she-ass was brought.

Bethlehem, six miles south of Jerusalem, is situated on a narrow ridge surrounded on every side by valleys. It is one thousand paces long from west to east, built at the edges of its level summit with a low wall lacking towers. In its eastern corner is a sort of natural half-cave: its outer part is the place of the Lord’s Nativity, and its inner part is called the Lord’s manger. This cave is entirely lined within with precious marble. Above the very place where the Lord was born stands a great [Col. 1123B] church of Holy Mary. A rock hollowed beside the wall receives the first washing of the Lord’s body, poured from the wall, and preserves it to this day; if by chance or human effort it is emptied, it nevertheless immediately, as one looks, overflows again as full as before. To the north of Bethlehem, in the adjoining valley, is a church. To the south, in the adjoining valley, is the tomb of Saint Jerome in a church.

Further east, at the Tower of Ader—that is, “of the flock”—one thousand paces from the city, is a church containing the tombs of the three shepherds who knew of the Lord’s birth. David’s tomb, however, is situated in Jerusalem. The royal road which leads from Helia Ceron has Bethlehem on the east and [Col. 1123C] Rachel’s tomb on the west. The pool where Rabshakeh uttered reproaches is near Bethlehem. Beside the cave’s entrance is the well whose water David desired. In the valley of Bethlehem also are memorials of the kings of Judah. Not far away is the church called *Ad Pastores* (“At the Shepherds”), where there is now a large garden carefully enclosed all around by walls. There is a very bright cave, containing an altar at the place where, as the shepherds kept watch, the angel appeared and announced Christ’s birth to them. At Anathoth is a tower in which the prophet Jeremiah lamented; it is four miles from Jerusalem. Twelve miles from Jerusalem is the tomb of the holy prophet Amos; the place is called Tekoa. On this route, opposite it, is the mountain which Herod excavated and on which he made himself a palace over the wilderness facing the Dead Sea. [Col. 1123D] At Thamnadsere is the tomb of the holy Joshua son of Nun; there too are the stone knives with which the children of Israel were circumcised a second time. A church has been built there; it is twenty miles from Jerusalem. On another mountain, at the second mile, is a church where the bodies of Saints Eleazar and Phinehas rest. One mile from Jerusalem, in the place called Cariathaim, where the Ark of the Lord was, a church has been built. Hebron lies in an open plain, twenty-two miles from Jerusalem. One stadium to the east it has the double cave, where the tombs of the patriarchs are enclosed by a square wall, their heads turned northward. [Col. 1124A] The tomb of Adam, the first-formed man, of darker and poorer workmanship, lies not far from them at the northernmost end of that wall. Memorials of the three women, poorer and smaller, are also seen. The hill of Mamre, one thousand paces north of these monuments, is very grassy and flowering, with a level plain on its summit. On its northern side is the trunk of Abraham’s oak, two men’s heights tall, enclosed by a church. On leaving Hebron northward, on the left side of the road, one comes upon a small pine-covered mountain, three miles from Hebron, from which pine timber is carried to Jerusalem on camels; for throughout Judea wagons and carts are rarely used. At the twenty-fourth mile from Jerusalem, near Hebron, is the spring in which Philip [Col. 1124B] the apostle and evangelist baptized the eunuch of Queen Candace. In the place called Terebinthus, where three angels appeared to Abraham, is Abraham’s excellent well and two very bright caves in which he lived; an altar has also been placed there, and before it stands a church. Not far away is the mountain as far as which Abraham led the angels as they went to Sodom. Within Hebron stands David’s house, of which some part still remains; for people still run to pray in the chamber where he stayed. Three hundred paces from Hebron, in the place called Abramiri, is Jacob’s house, where a roofless church has been built. Fifty paces from there is the tomb of holy [Col. 1124C] Caleb. Abramiri likewise has a vineyard containing a cave where the bodies of eleven sons of Jacob rest; Joseph’s bones, however, are buried separately in their own church. Not far from Hebron is the tomb of Abner son of Ner.

Jericho lies eighteen thousand feet eastward from Jerusalem. When it was destroyed for the third time from its foundations, Rahab’s house alone remained because of the sign of faith; for its walls still endure without a roof. The site of the city produces grain and vineyards. Between it and the Jordan, five or six miles away from it, [lacuna] the twelve stones which Joshua commanded to be taken from the Jordan lie in the church built at Gilgal, set along either side beside the walls of that same church; each can scarcely be lifted by two men.

Near Jericho is a copious spring, good for drinking and rich for irrigation. Formerly barren for producing life and somewhat unhealthy for drinking, it was healed by the prophet Elisha. Finally, a plain surrounds it, extending seventy stadia in length and twenty in breadth; in it are a marvellous abundance of gardens, various kinds of palms, excellent swarms of bees, and the finest balsam is produced there. We mention this with an added explanation because the cultivators cut the slender branches in their bark with sharp stones—the branches on which the balsam grows—so that, gradually distilling through these cavities, the liquid may gather itself in beautiful, dew-like drops. There grow henna (*cyprum*) and myrobalanum.

The water, like other spring-water, is cold in summer, warm in winter, and gentler in spring. The city itself was founded in a plain, over which rises a broad, bare mountain, unproductive; for its soil is sickly and barren, and therefore it is deserted by inhabitants. From the territory of the city of Scythopolis this region extends as far as the Sodomite country and the borders of Alphaltius [the Dead Sea], [lacuna] reaching for a hundred boundaries as far as Zoara of Petraean Arabia. There is also a mountain there called Iron Mountain.

Between these two mountains lies a great plain called Aulon, one hundred and twenty [stadia] in length; it begins at the village of Gennano and ends at the grove of Alfatium. The Jordan cuts through its middle, with its banks made green by the river’s flooding; for above the bank of the river the fruit of the trees is more abundant, but elsewhere it is far more scanty. Everything is dry except the riverbank.

The source of the Jordan itself is in the province of Phoenicia, at the foot of Mount Lebanon, where Paneas—that is, Caesarea Philippi—is situated. [lacuna] In the land of Trachonitis there is a spring whose form resembles a wheel, from which it has received the name Syla; it is fifteen Roman miles from Caesarea. It is continually so full of abundant water that it neither overflows nor ever diminishes. Into it Philip the tetrarch threw chaff. [lacuna] Hence it is clear that the Jordan has its source in Phiala, but, after underground channels, begins to flow at Paneas; it soon enters a lake and cuts through its marshes. Thence it directs its course and proceeds for fifteen Roman miles without any interruption as far as the city of Julia.

Afterwards it traverses Lake Gennesar in mid-current; then, after winding extensively, it enters Alfaltium—that is, the Dead Sea—and loses its excellent waters. For it is white in colour like milk, and for this reason it can be distinguished in the Dead Sea. Gennesar, that is, the Sea of Galilee, is surrounded by great woods; it is one hundred and sixty stadia long and forty broad. Its water is sweet and pleasant to drink, since it receives nothing thickened or muddy by marshy slime; for it is enclosed on every side by a sandy shore. It is surrounded by delightful towns: Julias and Hippos on the east, Tiberias on the west. [lacuna] The kinds of fish also surpass those in any other lake in taste and appearance.

The Dead Sea extends in length for eighty-five stadia as far as Zoara of Arabia, and in breadth for one hundred and fifty as far as the vicinity of Sodom. For that there were once wells of salt after Sodom and Gomorrah [lacuna] is wholly certain. It is visible at a distance to observers looking out from the watchtower of the Mount of Olives. Stirred by the collision of its waves, it casts up exceedingly salty salt; dried by the sun, this is collected and benefits many peoples. The Dead Sea receives no living creatures of any kind—neither fish nor creatures accustomed to waters [lacuna]. Indeed, if the Jordan, swollen by rains, carries fish flowing into it, they immediately die and float upon the dense water.

A lighted lamp floats there without turning over; extinguished, it sinks. All living things that are submerged, even when violently thrown in, immediately rebound. Persons unskilled in swimming, if they are thrown into it with their hands tied behind their backs, undoubtedly float. The water itself is barren and bitter, darker than other waters, [lacuna] presenting a resemblance [to something uncertain]. It is certain that bitumen wanders over the waters in a black liquid; those who approach in boats collect it. You would be amazed: there, bitumen is said not to yield to cutting by iron, but only to women’s blood, menstrual fluid, and urine. It is useful for caulking ships and for healing human bodies.

The region still preserves the appearance of punishment. There grow there fruits most beautiful, which arouse in those who see them a desire to eat; if you pluck them, they wither, dissolve into ashes, and raise smoke as though they were still burning. Indeed, in the days of summer a moderate vapour seethes across the expanse of the plain; thus, through the combined defect of excessive dryness and more corrupt moisture, the air inflicts pitiable diseases upon the inhabitants.

Therefore, at the place where the Lord was baptized, there stands a wooden cross as high as the neck, which is sometimes hidden when the water rises over it. From that place the farther, that is eastern, bank is a sling-cast away. The nearer bank is on the brow of a little hill, where the monastery of Saint John the Baptist was built. From it people customarily descend by a bridge supported on arches to that cross and pray.

At the far end of the river a square church is set upon four stone [lacuna], built of baked brick and roofed with plaster, where the Lord’s garments, preserved when he was baptized, [lacuna]. From the place where the Jordan leaves the outlet of the Sea of Galilee to where it enters the Dead Sea is an eight-day journey.

The locusts which blessed John ate are there even today: their little bodies are slender and short, in the shape of a finger of the hand; caught easily in the grass and cooked in oil, they provide food for the poor. In the same desert are trees bearing broad, round leaves, milky in colour and honey-sweet in taste. Their fragile substance is rubbed in the hands and eaten; this is said to be wild honey. There too is shown the spring of Saint John the Baptist, with clear water, protected by a stone roof and covered with plaster.

Whoever wishes to go from Jerusalem to the Jordan descends by the Mount of Olives. From the Mount of Olives Christ ascended into heaven, and there he made the *Our Father*. Mount Zion is to the south; there holy Mary died, there the Lord supped with his disciples, and there he sent the Holy Spirit upon the disciples.

In the church at Bethlehem is the table at which holy Mary ate with the three kings who were seeking Christ, the Son of God. There are sixty-four columns within that church. There rest the children killed by Herod for Christ. The foundations of the walls of the city of Jericho, which Jesus son of Nave overthrew, are still partly visible. The sycamore tree in which Zacchaeus climbed stands beside Rahab’s house. Not far from Jericho is the place from which Elijah was taken up into heaven.

Across the Jordan are very high mountains. Among them is one higher mountain called Naban, upon which Moses ascended when he saw the promised land and died. Gibeon is not far from Jerusalem; Joshua captured it. Emmaus, where after the resurrection the Lord ate with his disciples, is sixty stadia from Jerusalem. In the tower of Cades was Jacob’s house, whose foundations are visible even today.

In Galilee is the village of Some, from which came Abishag the Shunammite and the woman in whose house Elisha stayed; that house remains to this day. From Mount Hermon, which is exceedingly high, all Galilee is visible, and nothing is more beautiful. For though there is a vast plain, it contains nothing but vineyards and olive groves. There is a field in which the Lord ate with his disciples; there is a stone upon which the Lord placed his elbow, which may still be seen. Not far from that same mountain is a spring blessed by the Saviour, a spring effective against every infirmity.

In the village of Nain, in the house of the widow whose son was raised to life, there is now a church; the burial-place in which they wished to lay him remains to this day. In Nazara is a garden where the Lord was after he returned from Egypt. Near the city now called Neapolis is a fourfold church—that is, built in the form of a cross—in whose middle is Jacob’s spring, forty cubits deep, [lacuna] from which the Lord deigned to ask water of the Samaritan woman. This church is two Roman miles from the village which was formerly called Shechem. Five hundred paces from that church is a church in which holy Joseph rests.

The place where the Lord blessed and broke the loaves is on this side of the Sea of Galilee, north of the city of Tiberias: a grassy, level field, never ploughed since that time and containing no buildings, but showing only the spring from which they drank then.

Those who travel from Jerusalem to Capernaum go by way of Tiberias, then along the Sea of Galilee and the place of the blessing of the loaves. Not far from it is the city of Capernaum, without a wall, extending for a long distance along the seashore eastward, in a narrow site between mountain and lake, with the mountain on the north and the locality on the south.

Nazareth has no wall, but large buildings and two great churches. One is in the middle of the city, built above two mounds, where once stood the house in which the Lord was nourished as a child. This church, as stated, is supported by the two mounds and arches placed between them; below, between the same mounds, it has a most clear spring, from which water is drawn into vessels in the church by pulleys. The other church stands where the house was in which the angel spoke to Saint Mary. The cave in which she lived is large and very bright; an altar is placed there, and within the cave itself is the place from which she drew water. In the same city, where the synagogue had been, there is now a church in which the Lord read the book of Isaiah. Outside the town is the spring from which holy Mary drew water.

Mount Tabor, in the middle of the plain of Galilee, is three miles from Manasseh and north of the Sea of Cenereth. It is round on every side, very grassy and flowering, thirty stadia high. Its summit is level and very pleasant, extending over twenty-three stadia. There is a great monastery there, surrounded by a great forest, with three churches: one in honour of the Lord and Saviour, the other two in honour of Moses and Elijah. The place itself is surrounded by a wall and contains large buildings. It is much loftier and higher than Hermon; for all Galilee and the Sea of Tiberias are visible from it. The two mountains stand opposite one another.

At Endor is the house of the necromancer, to whom Saul went by night; the foundations of that house are still visible. In Tiberias there is now a church on the site of the house of the apostles James and John. There also is the sea of Tiberias, upon which the Lord walked on foot. At Capernaum, a church has been made from the house of the chief of the apostles; its walls still stand as they formerly did. There the Lord cured the paralytic. There too is the synagogue in which the Lord healed the demoniac, approached by climbing many steps; the synagogue is made of squared stones. Not far from it can be seen stone steps upon which the Lord stood.

There, beside the sea, is a grassy field with abundant hay and many palm trees. Near them are seven springs, each of which gives forth an inexhaustible quantity of water. In that field the Lord satisfied the people with five loaves and two fish. The stone upon which the Lord placed the bread has now been made into an altar. Those who come take pieces from that stone for their health, not without effect; it benefits everyone. Along the walls of this church runs the public road where the apostle Matthew had his tax-office. From there one goes up the nearby mountain, where there is a cave in which the Saviour, ascending, pronounced the Beatitudes.

Not far from there is the synagogue which the Saviour cursed. For when the Saviour was passing by and the Jews were building it, he asked them, saying, “What are you doing?” And they said, “Nothing.” And the Lord said, “If what you are doing is nothing, nothing shall ever be.” This remains so even today. For afterwards, whenever the Jews wished to build it, whatever they made by day was torn down by night; and in the morning its construction was always found at the same measure in which it had been when it was cursed.

Not far from there are the mountains of Gilboa, and the village of Gebus, where Saul and Jonathan died. At Jezreel, Naboth’s vineyard is now only a well. There too the foundations of the tower remain visible to this day; Jezebel’s tomb is still stoned by everyone. Not far from the city is the mountain on which the prophet Elijah sat when Jezebel persecuted him. At a distance is part of Mount Carmel; there is the place where Elijah consecrated an altar to the Lord.

Sebastia, formerly called Samaria, contains a church in which rest the bodies of Saint John the Baptist, Elisha, and Obadiah. At the second mile is a very high mountain, in which are two most bright caves: in one the prophets were hidden under Jezebel; in the other Saint Elijah sat.

At the twentieth mile from Shechem is the ruined temple at Shiloh, where also is the tomb of Eli the priest. At Bethel a church was built on the spot where Jacob, as he was going into Mesopotamia, saw a ladder stretching to heaven. There is also the tomb of the prophet who prophesied against Jeroboam. At the twenty-second mile from Jerusalem, between Sochehet of Judah and Zechara Muel, David killed Goliath the Philistine.

At Eleutheropolis is the place called Bycocyca, where is the tomb of the prophet Habakkuk. Fifteen miles from Eleutheropolis is the tomb of the holy prophet Ezra, in the place called Asoa. At the third mile, in the place called Chariassati—which was formerly called Morastites—is the tomb of the holy prophet Micah.

Taphnis is situated on the bank of the river Nile. There is Pharaoh’s palace, where holy Moses performed wonders before Pharaoh. Alexandria stretches from west to east; on the south it is bounded by the mouths of the Nile, and on the north by a lake [lacuna], whose harbour is more difficult than others. It is more capacious, as it were in the head and station of a human body, but narrower in its throat, where it receives the passages of sea and ships, by which a certain means of breathing is supplied to the harbour. Once anyone has escaped the narrowness and mouth of the harbour, the expanse of the sea extends far and wide, like the rest of the body’s form.
