On the right side of this harbour lies a small island, upon which stands the lighthouse—that is, a very great tower—burning at night with the mouths of flames, lest sailors deceived by darkness strike upon rocks and cannot make out the boundary of the entrance, which itself is continually troubled by waves colliding from either side. The harbour itself is always calm, with an extent of thirty stadia.

For those entering the city from the Egyptian side, on the right is the church dedicated in the name of blessed Mark the Evangelist, in which that most blessed man himself rested. Around the Nile they customarily make frequent embankments against the incursion of the water. If these happen to be breached through the negligence of their guards, they do not irrigate but overwhelm the lands lying below. Those who inhabit the plains of Egypt make houses for themselves over watercourses, with bridges of crosswise beams.

Memphis still contains the palace into which holy Joseph frequently went. Six miles from there, opposite the bank of the Nile, is the throne of Moses and Aaron. These aforementioned thrones are on a high mountain, where are two small towers reached by many steps. One had a roof; the other is without a roof. Moses ascended there when he spoke to the children of Israel while they were oppressed, and in the other he prayed. Below, all around, is a plain; there the children of Israel made bricks.

A thousand paces from there is a village on the riverbank, where holy Mary was with the Lord when she went into Egypt. Between Memphis and Babylon are twelve miles, where are very many pyramids, which Joseph made for storing grain. Heliopolis is twelve miles from Babylon. In the middle of this city is a huge plain, in which is the temple of the sun, and there is the house of Potiphar. Between Potiphar’s house and the temple is the house of Aseneth. There too is the garden of the sun, where is a great column called Bomon, upon which the phoenix is accustomed to alight after five hundred years. Although Egypt has extremely fertile places, nevertheless those occupied by the children of Israel are better.

The part of Arabia adjoining Palestine has an impassable route; for although there are fifteen stopping-places, [lacuna] those very places are without water. From Jerusalem to holy Mount Sinai are twenty-two stopping-places. Pelusium is the metropolis of the province of Augusta Nicaea; the province of Augusta Nicaea is in Egypt. From Pelusium to Mount Sinai are twelve stopping-places.

Before reaching Mount Sinai one encounters the fort of Clesma on the Red Sea, where the children of Israel crossed the sea dry-shod. The tracks of Pharaoh’s chariots are visible in the midst of the sands forever. The distance between the wheels appears far greater than that of the chariots of our own time, which are now made in the Roman Empire. For between one wheel and another there were twenty-four feet and more; the tracks themselves are two feet wide. Pharaoh’s chariot tracks come right up to the sea, where he entered it while wishing to overtake the children of Israel. At the place where the children of Israel entered the sea—that is, as far as Pharaoh’s tracks are still visible today—two markers have been placed, one at the right and the other at the left, made like little columns. This place is not far from the fort, that is, from Clesma.

Clesma itself is on the shore, that is, above the sea. There is a closed harbour there, which sends ships to India or receives ships arriving from India; for nowhere else in Roman territory do ships from India have access except there. The ships there are numerous and huge, and thus the harbour is famous for merchants arriving there from India. The official whom they call the *logotetema*, who goes as ambassador to India every year by order of the Roman emperor, has his residence there, and his ships are stationed there.

This is the place to which the children of Israel came while fleeing Pharaoh when they departed from Egypt. This fort was later placed there for defence and military discipline against Saracen incursions. The place itself consists of [lacuna], that is, sandy plains, except for that one mountain which projects into the sea. On the opposite side of this mountain porphyry marble is collected. For this is said to be why the sea is called the Red Sea: that mountain, which lies over a great extent above the Rose-Coloured Sea, possesses red, rose-coloured, or porphyry stone; indeed, the mountain itself is as though of a rose colour.

Yet this mountain was on the right of the children of Israel fleeing Egypt, when they began to approach the sea. For to those coming from Egypt the mountain rises on the right, very steep and very high, like a wall which one might think cut by human hands. This mountain is wholly barren, so that it has no fruit upon it. The children of Israel, departing from Rameses, first wandered through the midst of the sands; but when they approached the Red Sea, the mountain which had appeared on their right was near at hand. Joining themselves to that mountain, they came to the sea. The side of that high mountain lay on their right, and the sea on their left. Then, as they went on, the place suddenly appeared before them where the mountain joined—or rather entered—the sea, forming promontories.

The plain itself, where the children of Israel stayed with Moses on that night, is boundless and its level expanse immense. The place where the mountain projects into the sea is five hundred paces from the fort of Clesma. Between the fort and this mountain is the place at the mountain’s promontory where the children of Israel entered the sea and Pharaoh followed them. The crossing where they traversed the Red Sea dry-shod is eight thousand paces wide.

The Red Sea does not have this name because its water is red or muddy. It is so clear, transparent, and cold as though it were the Ocean Sea; there are there *cessae* [uncertain sea-creatures] of remarkable taste and sweetness. Every kind of fish in that sea is so flavourful as the fish of the Italian sea. Moreover, all things customarily desired from the sea are abundant there for food. There are conchs and various kinds of shellfish, and diverse and enormous *fondili* and *concleae* [shellfish; terms uncertain]. Along its shore lie various objects, larger and more beautiful than in any other sea. Coral is very abundant on that shore. The Red Sea itself is equal to the Ocean.

The desert of Shur is a wilderness of boundless and immeasurable desolation, where they travelled for three days without water. From the desert of Shur to Marah is one stopping-place along the shores of the sea. At Marah there are very few palm trees. There are also two springs there, which holy Moses sweetened. From there, for three days, on the left lies a boundless wilderness as far as the place called Arandara. Arandara is a place [lacuna]. At Elim a river flows, though it dries up at some season; but water is found in its channel or beside its bank. Grass is abundant there, and there are very many palm trees. From the crossing of the Red Sea, that is, Shur, no place so pleasant, with water so copious and so excellent, is found except this one. From there the half-stage is along the sea.

At last two exceedingly high mountains appear. On the left, before reaching the mountains, is the place where the Lord rained manna upon the children of Israel. The mountains themselves are extremely high and steep. On the other side of the mountains is a very level valley. On both sides of the valley these mountains are high and steep. Where the mountains open up, the valley is six thousand paces wide, and is considerably greater in length.

The mountains are hollowed out all around. These caves are so made that, if you wished to hang curtains, they would become most beautiful chambers. Each chamber is marked with Hebrew letters. At the far end of the valley there is also good and very abundant water, though not like that at Elim. The place itself is called the desert of Pharan, whence Moses sent spies to inspect the land. On either side this place supports neither fields nor vineyards—nothing is there except water and palm trees.

Near the village of Pharan, at fifteen hundred paces, those mountains narrow so that the valley is scarcely thirty paces wide. There the place is called Rephidim, where Amalek encountered the children of Israel, where the people murmured because of water, and where Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, met him. The place where Moses prayed when Joshua defeated Amalek is a very high, steep mountain overhanging Pharan. A church has now been built where Moses prayed. The place itself, how he sat and how he had stones beneath his elbow, is visible today. There also Moses, after defeating Amalek, built an altar to the Lord. The place rises for as much as five hundred paces, as though one were ascending a wall.

From Pharan to holy Mount Sinai are thirty-five miles. At Hazeroth there can still be seen how the enclosure of stone was made in which the children of Israel lived when they returned from the mount of God. There too are three thrones made of stone on a somewhat higher spot: one for Moses, the others for Aaron and Jethro. The cell where Mary, Moses’ sister, was separated for seven days still rises two feet above the ground.

From Hazeroth to holy Mount Sinai, amid mountains to right and left, the whole valley is full of tombs. Near the holy mountain, in the place called the Graves of Craving, everything is full of graves. Before reaching Mount Sinai there are six mountains which form a boundless, very level, and very beautiful valley. Across this valley holy Mount Sinai appears. The spot where the mountains open is joined to the place where are the Graves of Craving. From the place where it becomes visible as far as the mountain [lacuna] there are four thousand paces through this valley. The valley itself is very immense [lacuna] of the mountain of God; it is sixteen thousand paces long and four thousand broad. Whoever wishes [lacuna] to go to the holy mountain walks crosswise through that valley. This is the vast and very level valley in which the children of Israel stayed while Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights. The place where the calf was made is still shown today, for a great stone stands fixed there.

This, then, is the valley at whose head is the place where God spoke to holy Moses from the fiery bush. On one side there is an excellent ascent of the mountain, and on the other a descent; one crosses through the middle of the valley, and thus reaches the mountain of God. The mountain itself appears to be one all around; within, however, there are many, though all are called the one mountain Sinai.

There is a particular mountain whose summit contains the place where the majesty of God descended. This mountain stands in the midst of all the mountains; and although all those around it are exceedingly high, this central one, upon which the majesty of God descended, is so much higher than all of them that, when someone has ascended it, all those mountains which he had seen to be exceedingly high appear beneath Mount Sinai like little hills.

Although this central mountain, specially called Sinai, is higher than all the rest, it cannot be seen unless you have come to its own foot, before climbing it. But after you have descended from it, [lacuna] before one ascends it, he will not be able [to see it]. The mountains surrounding it are climbed with the greatest labour, since they are not ascended by winding paths; rather, they are climbed directly, as though up a wall, and descended directly.

On the summit of Mount Sinai, where the Law of Moses was given, a small church has been built. On the peak of that mountain no one lives; there is nothing there except the church alone and the cave in which holy Moses lived. The whole mountain is rocky, so that it has not even a shrub. From the summit of the central mountain, those exceedingly high mountains beneath appear like little hills.

From the summit of Mount Sinai may be seen Egypt, Palestine, the Red Sea, the Parthenian Sea which sends toward Alexandria, and also the lands of the Saracens. On Mount Horeb, which is joined to that mountain, is a church; before the church is the place where holy Elijah hid from Ahab. There is also shown the stone altar which Saint Elijah himself set up to offer to God.

Not far from there is the place where holy Aaron stood with the seventy elders. There is no roof in that place; nevertheless, there is a great rock, with a level surface above it all around, where they stood. In the middle is a stone altar. At the head of the valley beneath the mountain is a church on the spot where the Lord spoke in the bush; that bush is alive to this day and puts forth shoots. There is excellent water there.

In that valley it is also shown how each person had his dwellings. Of those dwellings, foundations still appear to this day, surrounded by stones as they were. There too is the place where the tabernacle of the covenant was first set up. On the other side one goes out between the mountains and begins to walk near the sea, so that suddenly one walks through sea water, and then suddenly for five hundred paces through the sand of the desert. For there is no road there at all; those who walk there set up markers at various places, and follow those markers by day, while at night the camels point out the markers.

From the Red Sea to the city of Arabia are four stopping-places. When the children of Israel departed from Egypt, as far as they went to the right, so far did they return to the left; and as far as they then went to the left, so far again did they turn back; and thus they did [lacuna].

> **Note [Col. 1133B]:** “This manuscript, badly damaged by time, lacks its ending.”

[Col. 1133]

## Prologue of Peter the Deacon to the Cassinese Register, addressed to Abbot Seniorectus

(Printed among the Prolegomena to the *Chronicon Casinense*, above, col. 470.)

[Col. 1133]

## The Cassinese Discipline of Peter the Deacon

(*Ancient Monastic Discipline, or a Collection of Authors of the Order of Saint Benedict, for the most part unpublished; the work and study of *** , priest and Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Blasius in the Black Forest.* Paris, 1726, quarto.)

## Notice

Saint Benedict committed to the abbot’s judgment such matters as he had left undefined in his holy Rule: for example, the measure of penances, the form and colour of clothing, and other things of that kind. He also gave his disciples authority, according to diversity of places or times, to introduce certain particular rites, usages, and customs, as is clear from the final chapter of the Rule.

Nevertheless, the holy man wished that usages and observances once introduced should remain firm and stable in monasteries. Accordingly, in chapter 63 he provided that: “The abbot must not disturb the flock entrusted to him, nor, as though using unrestricted power, make any unjust disposition . . . but according to the ranks which he has established, or which the brethren themselves have held, so let them approach the Peace, Communion, the intoning of the Psalm, standing in choir; and in all places whatsoever, let age not distinguish rank nor prejudice it,” etc.

There is therefore no doubt that, from the very first times after Saint Benedict, certain particular and native Cassinese rites or usages were established in addition to the precepts of the Rule; in these the Cassinese discipline was committed to writing for transmission to posterity. I think I see an example of this in Peter the Deacon’s unpublished Commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict. Some years ago Archangelus Brancaccius, abbot of Monte Cassino, a man of pious memory, sent me a copy accurately transcribed from the autograph.

For Peter, in the “brief clause,” as he calls it, of the said Commentary, described the customs and judgments which Saint Benedict established on the Cassinese mountain: “Keep,” he says, “the customs and judgments which blessed Benedict established in this place.” Whether they were truly established by Saint Benedict is not sufficiently clear. This I have established: the customs and judgments reported by Peter are older than all others on this matter which have survived to our time. For the usages and customs which were established at a later age by Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, even in the sacred Cassinese monastery, appear altogether more recent than these, as a comparison of the two proves.

Moreover, besides other things, the penitential canons appended at the end and the small number of principal feasts noted at the beginning attest the antiquity of these customs. Therefore, although Peter first wrote them down in the twelfth century, they nevertheless claim the first place among Cassinese customs because of their sacred antiquity.

## The Cassinese Discipline of Peter the Deacon

(Transcribed in the *Brief Clause* of his Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, from a manuscript of the Cassinese Library, never previously published.)

[Col. 1135]

[Col. 1135A] On chapter 27 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.

By these words the elder ought to console the erring brother:

“Love the Lord your God, brother, with all your heart and with all your soul; and keep the customs and judgments which blessed Benedict established in this place. Know that he commanded these things by God’s command: love your neighbour as yourself, and henceforth amend yourself from evils.”

The things which ought to be kept are these.

Especially, that he may be a monk in mind and body, purged and clean from every defilement. [Note: [Col. 1135C] All taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict.] Let him maintain humility and charity, love the fellowship of the saints, renounce his own will, embrace continence; obey his brethren, and serve God with all fervour. But let the abbot prescribe, say, or command nothing apart from the will of [Col. 1135B] God; let him cut away the faults of the brethren with charity, while the monk receives correction with the same disposition with which a sick man receives medicine. Let him possess nothing as his own. Let him serve the sick as though serving Christ [read: “let him serve”]. Let him not utter idle words. Let him not seek the honour of this world. As he has been converted, so let him sit, walk, sing the psalm, and communicate in church.

On Monday [Note: [Col. 1135C] The Cluniacs subsequently decreed, at the end of the tenth century, that every day after chapter the abbot or prior should assign to the individual monks their duties and manual labour.] let the craftsmen assemble before the dean, to receive from him the manual work which they must perform. Let no one begin any work unless prayer has first been said. When the work is completed, let prayer again be celebrated. On the principal feast-days—namely those of Saint Benedict, Saint Maurus, Saint Scholastica, the Dedication of the Church [Note: [Col. 1135C] That is, Rocentius; it nevertheless exceeds the time of Peter the Deacon.], the Ides of September, and the beginning of Lent—excepting those detained by illness [Col. 1135C], all monks holding obediences of the monastery of Cassino [Note: [Col. 1135C] *Obedientiales* or *obedientiarii*: monks sent to cells and priories, or obediences, and administering them. Peter [Col. 1136C] the Deacon uses the same word in Book IV of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, chapter 102.] shall return to the monastery of Cassino, so that they may celebrate the aforesaid days together.

Let no one look at another while eating; rather, each person shall look before himself. After they have risen from chapter, all shall repeat from memory what the abbot or dean has commanded. When the signal has sounded for any purpose, calling them together, no one shall remain behind without the abbot’s [Col. 1136A] command. When they enter church or leave church, or come to eat or drink, let them sing psalms. No one shall be admitted into the cloister unless he has first learned fully every custom of the monastery. In the refectory no one shall dare ask for anything except by a sign. [Note: [Col. 1136C] Hence the Cluniacs devised so many signs, as is clear from Bernard’s *Customs* and William’s Hirsau Constitutions.] The servers shall eat nothing except what has been prepared in common for the brethren, nor shall they dare prepare anything for themselves. When the dean strikes the cymbal for the meal, let him sing psalms. No one shall give another more than the other receives. As soon as the abbot leaves chapter, he shall go to visit the sick. The brethren shall have permission to visit the sick three days each week. Those who prepare the food shall themselves serve the brethren. No one shall be sent out alone on any [Col. 1136B] business without another brother. If the signal is given for them to go outside [Note: [Col. 1136C] It must be understood: for manual work; for no other reason was it permitted for all the monks to leave the cloister together.], no one shall remain in the cloister unless he has received permission from the dean. Those who go shall sing psalms. No one shall send his brother anywhere for any necessity without the dean’s order. No one shall take anything from the garden unless he has received it from the gardener. No one shall presume to eat anything in the refectory apart from the other brethren, before all eat together. No one shall set upon the table anything to eat except what he has received from the weekly server. Outside the monastery kitchen, no one shall have permission to cook food. No one shall possess anything beyond what is prescribed in the rule of the monastery; if he does possess it, it shall be taken away from him. No one shall leave the cloister or monastery [Col. 1136C] without the dean’s command. At night, when they awaken after sleep, let them pray. No one shall drink or eat before the hour or after the hour. No one shall wash or anoint another without the dean’s command. No one shall speak to another in the darkness. No one shall sleep with another in one bed. [Note: [Col. 1136C] Saint Benedict employed a similar precaution in chapter 22 of the Rule, “How Monks Should Sleep.”] No one shall hold another’s hand. Whether they walk, sit, or stand, let them remain [Col. 1137A] one cubit apart from one another. No one shall have his tonsure or beard shaved without the dean’s command. In monastic dress let no one devise any new adornment beyond that of the others. Let no one going anywhere leave a book carelessly behind. No one shall receive anything as a gift without permission. When they mix flour with water or make bread, let them sing psalms. No one shall presume to speak during the divine office. When a brother approaches death, the whole congregation shall sing psalms before him; and after he has been buried, after Vespers they shall sing seven psalms with litanies, all prostrate with their whole bodies upon the ground. No one shall sing psalms unless commanded. If anyone loses something, after asking pardon he shall receive from the clothing-store what he lost. Whoever finds something shall hang it before the dormitory for three days. [Col. 1138A] Let no one make mud in the house. All monks living in the monastery shall learn letters.

## Penitential Canons

Let a slanderer be separated from the assembly of the brethren and do penance for seven days on bread and water. Let an angry and violent man, unless he reforms, be placed last. Let a false witness, after receiving thirty-nine lashes, be placed last, and thus be deposed from every rank. If anyone, in pronouncing a false judgment, has shown partiality, let him be degraded from his seat. Let one who judges unjustly be justly condemned. Ministers of the altar, after Mass has been completed and before they leave the sacristy, shall wash their hands. Let a thief, after receiving thirty-nine lashes, be covered in ashes and haircloth, and eat bread and water.

[Col. 1137]

# THREE LETTERS OF PETER THE DEACON

(MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 760, from a Cassinese manuscript.)

## I. To Richiza, Empress of the Romans  
### A Letter of Consolation on the Death of Emperor Lothair and of Henry, Duke of Bavaria, Her Son-in-Law. (1139.)

[Col. 1137B]

To LADY RICHIZA, Empress of the Romans, protected by God, PETER THE DEACON sends, after the limits of this present life, the allotted portion of the eternal kingdom.

Most invincible Empress, many times I have begun to console Your Highness, and many times I have refrained. Very many things urged me to do so immediately—above all, loyalty to our deceased lord Emperor Lothair, and then the love of your imperial clemency toward us unworthy persons—so that, if I could not wholly quiet your tears, I might at least have wiped them away. Yet I knew that I should delay, because grief, while it rages fresh, ought not to be encountered too hastily, [Col. 1137C] lest those very consolations irritate, intensify, and inflame it still more. For we often see that even in illnesses an untimely remedy is most harmful.

Therefore I waited until grief itself should lay aside its strength, so that, softened by delay, it might in some measure permit itself to be touched and handled for the sake of accepting remedies. Yet before I engage with it, I shall stand beside it, recall certain things by which it may be stirred to remembrance, and uncover and bring forward what now seems, as it were, overlaid: namely, the best and customary kind of consolation.

Let those, then, weep and lament for a long time whose exceedingly delicate minds long prosperity has weakened and luxury has made effeminate; who have fixed all their hope in this world; [Col. 1137D] who either wholly fail to know what those eternal goods are, or, if they know them, neglect them because they are lulled by worldly pleasures. But those whose almost entire lifetime has passed amid various trials, whose citizenship, according to the Apostle, is in heaven, and who weigh with wise and discriminating hearts both the vanities of the world and the joys of heaven, endure even the gravest adversities with unshaken constancy.

Why should I continue to recount them? Count how many calamities, [Col. 1138B] how many misfortunes, have tossed you from your very infancy, since you were almost, so to speak, born amid them. Our lord Emperor Lothair of happy memory, who chose you as his wife, raised you to the imperial height, and entrusted to you alone all the business of the Roman Empire—after the many distresses which you endured with him, after you had, so to speak, travelled through the Roman world with him—when day by day you were hastening with him to return to the imperial residence, alas, grief of overwhelming weight over the loss of many companions bore you down.

I pass over all the dangers and fears which, pressing in upon you without interval, you endured with that great Caesar. And now, now, when you have not yet wholly composed your earlier griefs, while you were still mourning, grief has been added to grief. And when you thought that you possessed, as it were, the sole remaining consolation for so many afflictions in your living son-in-law HENRY, Duke of Bavaria, his untimely death was suddenly reported to you, though you expected nothing of the kind. [Note: [Col. 1137] In 1139, seized by a sudden illness at Quedlinburg, he died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, poison having been administered, as most writers state.] This was indeed the gravest fresh wound among all that befell you after the death of our lord Emperor Lothair. It did not merely break the surface; it divided your breast, I confess, and your very vitals. This blood did not flow from your uninjured body after a blow upon old scars; rather, as inexperienced soldiers cry out though only slightly wounded, while veterans, though pierced through, patiently and without groaning allow themselves to be treated.

For, most clement lady, the Apostle says that faithful persons are not to mourn as do others who have no hope: “For if [Col. 1138D] we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.” Therefore, most clement lady, we urge you to receive consolation. For what else is this death than the leaving of the body, the laying down of a heavy burden? You were born, Empress; you will die. Where will you go so that you may not die? What can you do so that you may not die? That the Lord your God might console you, he deigned by his own will to die. When you see Christ dead for you, do you disdain to die? Thus you will die, whether you wish it or not. Where will you escape? Where will you flee in order not to die? Whether today or tomorrow, it will happen; there is no doubt of it; it must be believed.

What, then, are you doing? Why do you fear and flee? It will happen. Therefore, my most devout lady, courageously put away from yourself lamentations, howlings, and, as it were, womanish commotions. For the more severe this grief of yours is, the greater the strength which you must summon, and the more fiercely you must engage, as with a familiar enemy already often defeated. Prosperity does not exalt a brave and wise person, nor adversity cast him down. He readily bears what he always expects. Sudden things are grievous to those alone; one who has neither swelled with fortunate circumstances nor shrunk when they changed possesses an unconquered soul, of firmness already proved, against either condition. [Col. 1139B] For even in prosperity he has learned what he could do against adversity.

To be affected with boundless pain when one loses someone most dear is foolish indulgence; to be affected by none is inhuman hardness. For not to feel pain is not human, and not to bear it is not virtue. The best moderation lies between the two: to feel longing and to restrain it—especially since it does not suit Your Excellency to grieve without measure. It is the greatest consolation to reflect that what has happened to you has happened to all before you and will happen to all.

Rejoice, then, that you had a husband who was Emperor of the Romans. Consider as most pleasant what you possessed, as human what you lost. Count it among the highest blessings that you had such a man. You ought not to consider how much longer [Col. 1139C] you might have had him, but how long you did have him. In this matter death chose to follow not your desire for fullness, but its own law. Only let your spirit stand ready for battle. Death will seize one person at one time, another at another; it will pass over no one and certainly exempt no one. Whoever is brought forth into life is appointed for death. But the mind of a wise person should never fear what is necessary and should always expect what is uncertain.

## II. To the Same Person  
### On the Same Subject. (The Same Year.)

To his most excellent and most devout lady Richiza, God-protected, great and peaceable Empress Augusta of the Romans, PETER, servant of your empire, sends, after the power of the present realm, eternal happiness.

Although a severed sinew hurts and a sorrowful spirit crushes the bones, yet our lord Emperor Lothair is not to be mourned as those are mourned who, as the Apostle says, have no hope. He has gone to his own place, where the highest good is, where all goodness, all justice, all piety, and all holiness are. He has gone to him who never ceases to call to those who keep his commandments: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest.” Elijah, hastening onward, asked that his soul might be taken from him.

And after much else:

Is death, then, to be grieved over? By no means. For what could be more absurd than to lament as though it were a special case something that you know has been prescribed for all? That is to raise one’s mind above its condition, not to accept the common law, to refuse fellowship, to be puffed up with a fleshly mind, [Col. 1140A] and not to know the measure of flesh itself. What could be more absurd than not to know who you are, and to desire to be what you are not? Or what could be more imprudent than to be unable to bear, when it occurs, that which you know will occur?

Nature itself calls us back and in a certain comparison with itself draws us away from such griefs. For what grief is so heavy, or what pain so sharp, in which the mind is not sometimes relaxed? Nature has this quality: however much people may be in sad circumstances, yet, if only they are human, they draw their minds away from sorrow for a little while. It is even said that there were certain peoples who mourned human births and celebrated deaths—and not unwisely. For they thought that those who had entered this age of life were to be mourned, whereas those who had emerged from the storms and waves of this world were to be attended with no unjust joy.

Death is equal for all human beings, without distinction even among the rich. This great Caesar kept it daily before his eyes. For, as we saw and experienced while we moved in his service, beneath the imperial cloak he displayed the apprenticeship of another soldiery. At the first dim light of dawn he first heard a Mass for the dead, then one for the army, and lastly the Mass of the day. Afterwards he distributed food and drink generously to widows, orphans, and other poor people; he relieved the disputes and oppressions of churches; and finally he laboured diligently over the care of the empire.

For as long as he stayed at Cassino, every night he went around the cloister and every workshop of the monastery like an abbot or any dean, wishing to know how each person lived under the instruction of Blessed Benedict. And when morning came, he went barefoot through all the churches of the monastery for prayer. [Col. 1140C] Yet although he did this, he was never separated from the company of archbishops, bishops, abbots, clerics, or monks, so that what is written might be fulfilled in him: “His conversation was with the wise and the devout.”

Who would not marvel at his gravity, when, in order to quiet the dissensions of the brethren which had arisen over the election of an abbot, he came to chapter and remained there from the first hour of the day until evening, indulging neither in food nor drink and not leaving it? The affection and love with which he loved the church of Cassino he showed when he said that he would sooner allow all the privileges and grants of churches to be overthrown [Col. 1140D] than anything be diminished from the dignities and privileges of the Church of Cassino; and that he would sooner allow the election of all bishops, archbishops, and abbots throughout the entire Roman world to be abolished than that of the abbot of Cassino alone. For he said: “If an abbot has not been elected with the consent of the monks, he is not an abbot; and whoever takes election from the monks overthrows all the rights of the monastery.”

And while doing all these things, he was nevertheless a staff to the blind, food to the hungry, hope to the wretched, and comfort to mourners. He so excelled in each virtue as though he possessed none of the others. He honoured priests as lords, clerics as fathers, the poor as sons, widows as mothers; he was frequent in admonitions, wakeful in vigils, and offered tears to God, not to men.

Tears flow over my cheeks, and though my mind is resolute I cannot conceal the pain I suffer. For after he had made my lowliness a disciple of Chancellor Bertulf, after he had rewarded me with the office of logothete, recorder, and auditor, after he had granted me a place at his feet, after he had made me one of his confidential servants, after he had sufficiently instructed me in matters pertaining to eternal life—while you were present and all the courtiers of the empire stood by—he took my hand and commended me to Abbot Guibald, saying to him: “If any traces of my affection or love for me remain in your heart, show them in this man; and for our love’s sake regard him as a most dear and only son.”

After the Emperor Augustus, the Roman Caesar, and one called father of his country had said these things, while he was striving together with Your Excellency to reconcile discordant clerics in peace, [Col. 1141B] he rendered body and soul to heaven. Take courage, therefore, most valiant lady, and, according to that precept of Solomon, “Receive consolation in return for sorrow.”

But perhaps you say: “How can I receive consolation, when I have lost him whom I loved?” Are not these things common to us with the world itself and the elements, since things created for a time cannot be possessed forever? She who preserves chastity has not lost her husband; she is not widowed in marriage who has not changed her husband’s name. Recall what David did. When he had lost his son, he rose, ate, drank, and said: “I shall go to him, but he will no longer return to me.”

Considering these things, therefore, most excellent lady, moderate yourselves in the face of impending sadness, and strive so that you may be able, as is fitting, to behold God with a blessed gaze. The congregation of Cassino also sends you its service of salvation, consolation, and prayer; and, commending to you the boy Mino, son of Lord Ptolemy, who is with you, they ask that you receive him as a son.

## III. To Emperor Conrad II  
### He Congratulates Him upon His Election as Emperor and Exhorts Him to Govern the Roman Empire Vigorously and Christianly, and to Protect the Monastery of Cassino. (The Same Year.)

To CONRAD, most excellent emperor and most vigorous extender of the Roman Empire, PETER THE DEACON wishes continual protection by the Lord’s shield and perpetual triumph over spiritual and bodily enemies by his victorious right hand.

Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving [Col. 1141D] be for ever to our almighty God, who through you and in you has raised up ancient miracles for us, and through your recent election renews for the Roman Empire the joys of old. For neither the destruction of Hannibal, nor the extermination of the Goths, nor the slaughter of Lucius Catiline, nor the downfall of Attila and Totila delights us as much as hearing of your magnificent election and continually proclaiming divine power in your successes.

Through you the glory and honour of the eternal city are extended and enlarged even to the rising of the sun, and, when unfaithfulness has been driven away, it receives dominion over rebellious nations. Through you the dignity of the Roman Empire is restored, exalted, and scarcely raised again to the ancient condition of rule enjoyed by the consuls Pompey, Scipio, Julius, Octavian, and [Col. 1142A] Trajan.

Therefore let all Christendom rejoice utterly in your election; let East and West be glad; let South resound with North; let the eternal city, mistress after God of all earthly things, celebrate feast-days and solemn days, offer vows and utter songs in praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, and renew its ancient harmony with voices harmonized in joy, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified.”

For God is indeed honoured in you, who chose such a man, one who may pursue a thousand and put ten thousand to flight. Behold: through the four quarters of the Roman world your deeds, labours, and notable struggles will be reported; almost every language speaks of the glory of your empire. For you have become, as the Apostle says, “a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.” You have become champions of the Lord: the glory, increase, honour, and wondrous diadem of the Roman Empire; the defence of the apostolic see; the consolation of the sorrowful; and the refreshment of the poor.

At last, through God’s mercy, the Roman city has received back its own son, and rejoices that from the ancient lineage of the Caesars it retains an emperor. Yet you, whom the divine majesty has chosen for so great an empire, ought and are bound to be the more humbly subject to him in all things the more you have been raised by him above other mortals. For if you ascribe all your deeds to his mercy and power, he who has granted you temporal rule will grant you perpetual triumph.

Therefore, invincible Emperor, guard the good of peace before all things and above all things. Let no rancour and no envy steal into your breast. Govern the Roman Empire subjected to you justly and mercifully, so that above all the Roman Church, through which you received the throne of the Roman Empire, may perceive—and joyfully perceive—that it has deserved such a great Augustus and has come under the rule of one who fears God.

Let no person's wealth ever so please you that justice does not always outweigh it in your breast, so that justice may lose the place of equity. For what profit is there in having received the helm of the Roman Empire if you do not strive to excel all mortals in mercy, justice, and indeed every goodness? Uprightness of soul ought to be a model and example of virtue not only for you but also for your successors.

Acting thus, [Col. 1142D] you will always have the cooperating grace of almighty God; by its aid you will subjugate all enemies and rejoice in peace both present and future. Know that the Church of Cassino daily entreats almighty God for the condition of your empire: that he may bring the works of his mercy begun through you to their worthy end; that he may protect and defend you from every evil; and that, after so great labour, he may grant you in the future citizenship in eternal life.

We ask Your Highness’s noble eminence, most exalted conqueror, to protect the Church of Cassino, mother of all monasteries; for it is known that it was once defended by the protection and enriched by the resources of your predecessors. You, [Col. 1143A] therefore, who are shown to equal them in the nobility of your wisdom, power, prudence, in all secular qualities, and—what is more excellent—in honourable morals, strive also to equal them in exalting the monastery of Cassino. Make Blessed Benedict your debtor on earth, so that you may deserve to receive in heaven a hundredfold whatever you have bestowed upon him.

For this purpose heavenly Providence, which governs all things and orders the whole universe from the beginning, at this very time—when, because our sins demand it, health has failed [Col. 1144A] and truth has been diminished among the children of men—has chosen for the Roman commonwealth a man of such vigour and prudence, that you may exalt the churches. May God, our Lord, who freely bestows the gifts of his goodness upon those who ask, protect and bless you with the right hand of his strength; and, your enemies of either substance having been separated, may he open to you, as you return to him with the palm of victory, the gates of heavenly life and grant you perpetual delight with him in heavenly goods.

[Col. 1143]

# RHYTHM OF PETER THE DEACON ON THE LAST DAYS

[Note: [Col. 1143A] With these verses the monk acutely depicts the sorrows of his own time; and, as it appears, one might conjecture that these verses were written while [Col. 1144A] the Church was afflicted by the schism of Anacletus, and perhaps after the reconciliation with Pope Innocent of the schismatic monks, among whom was Peter.]

(Dom Luigi TOSTI, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, vol. II, p. 119, from manuscript codex 361.)

[Col. 1143A]

When a thousand years  
From Christ’s Passion  
Have been completed,  

Satan, prince of Hell,  
Will be loosed from his chains,  
Whom Jesus Christ bound  
When he rose from the dead.

Then faith will be no more among brothers,  
Nor among married couples;  
Nor will servants keep faith,  
Nor children toward their fathers.  
For all things earthly and divine  
Will be mixed together.

Disciples will be set against teachers,  
Monks against abbots;  
And the three-headed dog Cerberus  
Will possess all things.

Former abbots, not abbots,  
Will exist in those times.  
They will make light of every good thing,  
And always do evil.  
They will abandon God’s discipline  
And have a reprobate mind,  
Slothful and proud,  
Dreadful and terrible.

They speak good things, but do evil;  
They devour all the sheep.  
They will devour and tear apart  
The sheep entrusted to them.  
They will be ravenous and gluttonous  
Like Antony.

They are exceedingly idle and sluggish  
In the work of God.  
But they will seek out  
Men’s hidden treasure.

Prelates will possess kingdoms;  
They will give sacred things to Simon.  
The sword, wrath, deceit,  
Thefts, and sacrileges rage.  
The laws of clerics  
Will be Epicurean;  
They will abandon divine laws  
And hold to Cynic ones.

All love women;  
They wrong women.  
Everywhere they run, everywhere they seek  
Women here and there.

“I did not know, and did not recognize,  
Your body, woman.”

They abandon God, they drive God away,  
So that they may have you alone.  
They will love great banquets  
And covet unmixed wines.

They order the doors to be watched,  
Lest a poor man come.  
But they salute Caesars  
And despise the poor.  
For they foresee and procure  
Gold and money.  
They will accuse traitors  
And love traitors.

They will rebuke, rebuke  
In all others what they themselves do.  
They sell God, they betray God,  
That they may possess honour.  
Gold binds, gold looses,  
And gives sacred orders.

They know how to practise wickedness;  
They never do good.

The origin of all these evils  
Is an errant pope,  
Very cunning and perverse  
Beyond all human beings.

Stripped and alienated  
From heavenly goods,  
He seeks his own profit  
Among God’s sheep,  
He who from the beginning  
Was the precursor of Antichrist.

The laws of all  
Will be those of adulterers and robbers,  
Deceivers and impostors,  
Most wicked evil men.  
They seek laws, they administer laws,  
In order to confound men.

Then despised and held cheap  
Will be he who serves God.  
For these people will prepare  
The way for Antichrist;  
Then will appear the accursed  
Son of the devil,

Shouting and crying aloud  
To his hearers:

“Princes and kings of the earth,  
Consuls and rich men,  
Counts and dictators,  
Governors and judges;  
[Col. 1144A] magistrates and tribunes,  
Caesars and wealthy men,  
Knights, strong men, and slaves,  
Prelates and clerics;

Cinnamon and amomum,  
Wine and oil;  
Purple, silk, scarlet cloth,  
And every ivory vessel—

If you want all these things,  
You shall deny Christ.  
I am he who made heaven,  
Who established the earth;  
Who created all things by a word,  
Who fashioned man.

Adore me, if you desire  
And love the world.  
I am God, I am great,  
I am your Lord.  
I am the Lamb, I am the Lion,  
Life, splendour, grace.  
I am the Word, I am salvation,  
The brightness of wisdom.  
I am God, I am the Son  
Of the great Almighty.

Let the temple of the great Lord  
Be repaired and renewed.  
Observe the most ancient laws  
Of the Hebrews,  
The laws of God, the laws of the great one  
Which he commanded Moses.”

[lacuna]

Christ God, you who restored  
The ruined world,  
Who descended from on high  
Into the Virgin’s womb,

Deliver Peter, O God,  
Most merciful Father.  
Protect and free Peter  
From the prince of Hell,

Whom John taught would be  
Released and loosed.

But he was released—  
[Uncertain, corrupt text:] “*Pem quem homo eccidit. ec.*”

[lacuna]

[Col. 1143]

# LETTERS OF PTOLEMY AND GREGORY, PETER’S UNCLES, TO HIM

(They are extant among the Prolegomena to the *Chronicle of Cassino*, above, col. 466.)

[Col. 1145]

# DESCRIPTION OF THE SACRED MOUNT OF CASSINO

(MABILLON, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II.)

[Col. 1145A]

Mount Cassino is divided into two peaks, like twin mountains: one higher, to the north, called Cairo, where there are no buildings; the other, somewhat lower, called Cassino, on which the text reads uncertainly, “it has been seen” (*in quo visum est*). The ascent to this mountain extends for nearly three miles by winding paths. When you arrive at the first gate, you encounter a somewhat dark vaulted passage, from which one ascends forty steps to the first court, paved with squared stones and adorned with porticoes. From there one goes up by almost as many steps into the atrium of the basilica, distinguished by columns and statues, and at last into the basilica itself.

In this four-sided portico stand statues of the supreme pontiffs and bishops who came forth from the monastery of Cassino; also, on one side ecclesiastical benefactors, on the other secular benefactors. At the church door both parents of Saint Benedict are displayed, together with a column of serpentine stone, on which, tradition says, stood an image of Apollo that the most blessed father shattered.

The church, though in a narrow place, is spacious and outstanding. Its double doors [Col. 1145B] are of bronze; upon the great door Abbot Desiderius, afterwards called Victor III, caused all the possessions of Cassino to be inscribed in silver letters. On either side of the nave there are in all eight chapels, each with its own hemispherical vault. Above the nave rises the choir behind the high altar, consecrated by Alexander II. On this side is situated “Vidi Feramoscae”; on that, “Petri Memonasterium monasterium” [as printed; the names and repetition are uncertain].

But because the summit of this mountain was too narrow to contain all the regular buildings, they say that the entire monastery was laid out upon three terraces and in three vaulted levels. Beneath the principal altar and choir lies a crypt with the altar of Saint Benedict and two others, named for Saint Placid and Saint Maurus. There also may be seen a perforated seat of porphyry, perhaps a bath-seat; the ancients called a seat of this kind a *solium*.

To the right of the church, facing south, stand the regular buildings: the chapter-house with its adjoining library; the court or cloister; the refectory joined to it; the dormitories; and the lodgings of the abbot and noble guests, ending in the tower believed to be the very one inhabited by Saint Benedict, adorned with a notable oratory and most exquisite paintings. Opposite the church stands the dormitory of the novices; adjoining it is the chapel of Saint Anne, in which is the monks’ burial place. On the left side of the church is the old chapel of Saint Martin, where poor [Col. 1146B] pilgrims are buried; their hospice and infirmary are visible on the same side beside the first court. This is the description of the monastery in its more recent condition. At the foot of the mountain lies the town of Saint Germanus, with another monastery and the abbatial palace; not far away lies the ancient city of Cassino, with remains of its old amphitheatre.

# THE CHRONICLE OF FALCO OF BENEVENTO, A.D. 1139–1142

(MURATORI, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, vol. V, p. 79. Milan, 1723.)

[Col. 1145]

# PREFACE OF ANTONIO CARACCIOLO

[Col. 1145C]

Falco was a notary and scribe of the Sacred Palace; and Innocent II, supreme pontiff, appointed him judge of his native city because of the steadfastness of faith with which he had upheld the papal cause amid those great disturbances. In this *Chronicle*, which he carries from the year 1102 to 1140, he describes the events of his own time—and especially those that occurred at Benevento—with such fullness and accuracy that, reader, you seem not to be reading but to be present.

And unless his style, harsh with barbarism, repels you, I do not doubt that in other respects you will praise Falco. He appears indeed to have pleased Baronius and Gordon, since both excerpted him with the pen, and the former cited him more than once in the *Annals*, the latter in the later volume of his chronological work. Enjoy, therefore, through my agency, this work now for the first time seeing the light, diligent reader, and farewell.

[Col. 1145]

# NOTICE OF CAMILLO PELLEGRINI
[Col. 1145D] Though unpolished and, indeed, half barbarous, the ancient chronicler Falco, whom I must now discuss, is nevertheless easily foremost among our medieval historians for faithful and by no means inept diligence. By office—as he himself relates of himself under the years 1133 and 1137—he was notary and scribe of the sacred Beneventan palace, and finally judge in that same city of his native land. He began a Chronicle, now extant mutilated at both beginning and end, from the year which at one time seemed to me to be 1077: the year in which, upon the failure of the succession of the Lombard princes of Benevento in Landulf VI, [Col. 1146D] that city began to be governed by the Roman pontiff through prefects, then commonly called Rectors. After that prince’s death, says the anonymous writer of St. Sophia, part III, no. 15, “the city was governed by the Roman Church”; for it had at last come into its power, for the reason set forth by the Ostian in book II, chapter 83, and briefly noted by me in connection with the Anonymous of Monte Cassino under the year 1051.

My reason for thinking so was Falco’s headless text itself. Before all else, in an abruptly broken narrative, it reports that nearly a hundred men of Benevento, both nobles and persons of honorable rank, whom the author himself calls “good men,” went to Rome and begged the pope—though in vain—to deign to confirm the elected pastor: that is, to give him strength and authority through his assent. These words seemed to concern some archbishop elected by the Beneventan people and requiring confirmation by the supreme pontiff according to the sacred canons. I conjectured that this had occurred in the aforesaid year 1077, because in the same Chronicle, immediately after these matters, under the year 1107, the death is recorded of Roffrid, archbishop of Benevento, to whom thirty-one years, two months, and twenty days are assigned. From this it could be established that an election disapproved by the Roman pontiff must have preceded Roffrid’s elevation. Accordingly Falco might most suitably have undertaken to describe his history from the beginning of a new archbishop and at the same time of a new pontifical government—a history which we now possess, gaping with a vast hiatus down to the year 1103.

Later, however, I judged that the matter stood otherwise. For I observed that Peter, [Col. 1147B] bishop of Porto, who was then present at Benevento, as the same author testifies, and scarcely escaped the arms of the Beneventans when they turned to sedition after their rejection by the pope, could not possibly be assigned to those more remote times. He did not then hold the bishopric of Porto, to which he was raised much later by Paschal II, but John did. I therefore abandoned that opinion and was convinced by sounder judgment that the Beneventans had asked the pope to confirm a pastor endowed with secular, not ecclesiastical, authority, whom they customarily called a rector. I did not doubt that Falco himself simultaneously explains this. For, a few days later, that bishop of Porto, restored to favor with the Beneventans, at their request—these are Falco’s words—“asked the lord pope to send a rector,” and he again appointed the monk Rosseman as rector: that is, as I think, restored the man whom the Beneventans had refused to accept, whence the sedition had arisen. Thus the entire dispute and quarrel was quieted.

Yet, although I maintain these points, I would not deny that the rector elected by the Beneventans held episcopal rank. Falco indicates his supporters, saying that civil war began because “the party of the bishop, ascending the bell-tower” of the cathedral church, “vigorously attacked Dacomarius’s palace,” situated in the lower part of the city to the northwest, now commonly called *la Commare*, “where that bishop,” namely the bishop of Porto, “was staying.” Therefore the rector sought by the Beneventans was a bishop, and the author explains that he was called Riso: “Those,” he says, “who seemed to be on Riso’s side placed arms and implements of war upon the bell-tower.”

Since the rector repeatedly appointed by the pope was a monk, moreover, and since we may observe in Falco that the care of that city was often entrusted to cardinals, and that in the year 1120 Rosseman the deacon, son of the aforesaid Rosseman, was ordained [Col. 1147D] rector by Callixtus II, no doubt can remain for us concerning Bishop Riso, then elected by the Beneventan people.

Falco, then, did not, as I once thought, begin the history of Benevento—embracing also the course of connected events—from the death of Landulf VI, prince of Benevento, and from the year 1077; rather, he began it from more recent origins. These, unless my conjecture again fails me, I judge to have been the very beginnings of the pontificate of Paschal II, and to precede the present text of Falco by scarcely one or two years. Paschal, successor of Urban II, was elected in August 1099; and in 1102, in the tenth indiction, as Romuald of Salerno reports in his Chronicle, he besieged Benevento with a very great army together with Roger, duke of Apulia, and did not desist until, having expelled the man who ruled in that city, he captured the city itself.

Could Falco have omitted these events among his own Beneventans, so memorable in appearance, [Col. 1148A] when he had undertaken to write their history through the immediately succeeding years—and when he could not even have selected a more fitting opportunity for writing? Since we cannot deny this on any plausible grounds, it follows that we should believe that he also set forth who that prince, unnamed by Romuald, was, and in what manner and year he gained the principality of Benevento. Yet Falco’s frustrated hopes will not remain wholly fruitless: his deficiency may in some measure be supplied from the narrative of the aforesaid author and from the statements of Peter the Deacon. In the continuation to the Ostian, book IV, chapter 19, Peter mentions an offering made about the year 1098 to Blessed Benedict and the monastery of Monte Cassino by Anso, rector of the Beneventan principality, in fidelity to the Roman Church, and by his noble brothers Dauferius and Atenulf, John and Berard, Peter and Alfan, and Luitprand, sons of Lord Dacomarius, governor of Benevento.

But in the diploma of that donation, or precept, itself—whose copy is found in the Register of the same Peter, p. 283—this rector Anso is called not Rector but Prince. By that title he is also designated by the same author in the same place, p. 32 verso, where, after reciting a letter which Urban II, returning from Benevento to Rome, issued at Ceprano on 3 November to his dearest son A., “lord of the Beneventans,” as it is there styled, ordering him to recognize the repeatedly examined rights of the monks of Monte Cassino over the possession of the church of St. Sophia in that city, he adds this note:

“The following year,” he says, “the pope died,” namely in 1099; “Anzo lost the principality after two years,” in 1101—an event which Romuald says occurred in the following year—“and therefore this business remained unfinished.”

Falco therefore undoubtedly set these events out more fully at the beginning of his Chronicle. Their order may now be conjectured by each person according to his own judgment, as seems more probable. Yet I shall offer this one point as my own view: Anso, or Anzo, seems to have appropriated the title of prince and dominion of Benevento from his position as rector—so Peter the Deacon calls him in the cited continuation—whether Pope Urban II connived at this or consented to it. Urban called him not prince but “lord of the Beneventans” in the aforesaid letter; and this was in no way tolerated by his successor Paschal. For from the more prolonged office of such a rectorship, which Anso’s father Dacomarius, a man indeed of great name, had long held, it was easy for him to desire and finally obtain a dignity received over a very long course of years in that city and increasingly acceptable to its citizens.

I was likewise at one time led by almost the same error to suppose that Falco’s history, which I thought carried from 1077 and from the beginning of Roffrid’s archbishopric to the beginnings of Guarmund, likewise archbishop of Benevento, had been composed by its author in Guarmund’s favor as late as 1142. In fact it now stops in 1140 without any suitable conclusion. [Col. 1148D] My conjecture pleased me because, from Baronius’s observation under the year 1113, I believed Falco to have held clerical office in that same church of Benevento. For in the work itself, under the year 1124, he seems to address an ecclesiastical man holding dignity, calling him by the honorable title of fatherhood. He says:

“Concerning the miracles which Jesus Christ, lover of humankind, has deigned to show before us all for the merits and honor of our aforesaid father Barbatus, I shall explain them, though in unpolished speech, to your fatherhood.”

And under 1118:

“Concerning the war of the aforesaid Count Jordan, if it please your charity, and of Count Rainulf, I shall relate something briefly.”

And similarly under 1137:

“I shall also explain to your brotherhood another matter which must not be concealed in silence.”

Yet he should be judged to have addressed by these titles and this manner of speech not some definite dignitary, but any reader whatsoever, modestly and courteously. [Col. 1149A] Under the year 1114 he makes this very clear when he says: “But if it does not seem burdensome to the reader’s charity, I shall not omit to write what was done at Benevento after the excommunication was imposed.” I therefore discarded this unsound opinion as well as the preceding one; and what I should now conclude on this matter, I have absolutely nothing to say.

I do not understand why Baronius regarded Falco as devoted to the clerical profession. It is established that Falco was taken from the lay office of notary and scribe of the sacred Beneventan palace, as I said at the outset, into the rank of a Beneventan judge. For although the princes had ceased, the Beneventan court continued to be called the sacred palace, as Prince Arichis had established it three hundred years earlier; and most palace offices remained, in fact or at least in name, such as the count of the palace. Falco himself is an explicit witness to this under 1114 and 1137.

When he reports that in the year 1133 he was made and elected judge of the city by the counsel of the rector, Cardinal Gerard, the constable Rolpoton, and other wise citizens, and subsequently confirmed by apostolic privilege of Innocent II, you should not suppose that he was appointed a praetor to decide lawsuits. Rather, believe that he was enrolled among the decurions, or, if you prefer, senators, who in most places at that period were called judges. Hence the noble court of Capua still preserves the ancient name received from judges of this kind.

There is frequent mention in Falco of many Beneventan judges, whom he often joins with wise men and often simply calls wise men. Their office, although perhaps concerned also with judicial matters, as is known to have been observed formerly at Gaeta, nevertheless embraced other public functions. When the Beneventans solemnly received Pope Callixtus II into their city in 1120, four citizens led his feet and the reins of his horse from the Leper Bridge to the gate of St. Lawrence, by which the city is entered from that side; then another four to the episcopal residence; and from the episcopal residence [Col. 1149C] four judges—John, Persicus . . . [the name of the judge described in third place is lacking], and Landulf—conducted him to the sacred Beneventan palace.

Likewise, in 1137: “The judges of the city of Benevento, together with the other citizens, approached King Roger and submitted the city of Benevento to the fidelity of Anacletus and to the love of the king himself.” To such an order of judges, then, Falco must be said to have been elevated from the notarial office, much as a man named Salernus is recorded by Hugh Falcandus as having been made judge of the city of Salerno from being a physician, though he did not abandon his medical practice.

Indeed, those who then exercised their votes in governing cities and formed the leading order—like the decurions formerly in colonies, and the senators at Rome—were everywhere called judges. Thus King William II, together with his mother Margaret, in a letter to Andrew the Stratigotus, the judges, and the whole people of Messana, quoted by Falcandus, seems to have addressed the whole city of Messana, just as if he had said in an older form, “To the order and people of Messana.” Pope John VIII long before used the same formula, writing: “To all the distinguished judges and the whole people of Naples,” a letter recorded among his Decretals, no. 67. In the same letter 205 he asserted that Landulf had been elected bishop of that city by the wish and equal consent of all the priests of God and judges, or of the entire people of Capua—the word *seu* here perhaps standing conjunctively for “and,” in a not uncommon usage, as I shall explain on a more suitable occasion.

That the order of those judges consisted solely of patrician men is indicated by the same pontiff in letter 206, writing to Guaifer, prince of Salerno, concerning the same elected bishop; he calls them a company of nobles whom in the preceding letter he had called judges. Yet by a special custom at Naples, Gaeta, and Pisa, with somewhat differing practice not suitably explained here, they were called consuls. Hence in our Falco under 1134 occur Alzopard and Canis, consuls of the Pisans. Examples are readily available, but not relevant to this purpose or place, and it is unnecessary now to repeat them.

I shall not, however, omit that Anastasius the Librarian, in his Life of Hadrian, twice speaks of “judges of the clergy” and “judges of the military estate,” whom he there calls primates of the Church; and in his Life of Stephen II, “nobles of the military estate.” He thereby denotes the two orders of the entire Roman people, ecclesiastical and lay, by the terms clergy and military estate. I believe that these nobles were sent out by the aforesaid Hadrian to meet Charlemagne as he approached Rome, when, as Anastasius says, he sent “all the judges” to meet him at nearly thirty miles from the city of Rome. Platina, insufficiently attentive to the text, seems to have referred the distance of the journey to the number of judges and judged that “three thousand” should be read. Even so he did not avoid an excessive assembly of judges, and supposed that those were called judges who were not occupied with base crafts—a meaning never at all observed.

I understand Peter the Deacon in the continuation to the Ostian, book IV, chapter 37, to mean these same judges, or nobles of the military estate—that is, the lay people of Rome—when he calls them, according to their dignities and offices, bailiffs, candle-bearers (*cereostatarii*—this is the correct reading there, not *cereostarii*), cross-bearers, eagle-bearers, lion-bearers, wolf-bearers, candidates, defenders, and grooms. From this it may be understood that judges must not always be referred to courts of law, and likewise that our Falco was not enrolled among ecclesiastical judges, since he states that he was appointed judge not of the clergy but of the city. But I have lingered too long upon these matters.

[Col. 1149]

# Chronicle of Falco of Benevento

## Julius de Syndicis of Benevento, to the Reader

A certain little book has come into our hands, most sweet reader, whose author was called Falco the notary, scribe of the sacred palace. In it are written many histories of the whole Neapolitan kingdom, but especially the deeds of the Beneventans among themselves, such as their civil wars, and also their conflicts against foreign Normans, as may there be seen. But because through the succession of long time it seemed close to decay and to the obscuring of its letters—as is apparent from the loss of its beginning and end, for two pages have been torn out and lost at each extremity—I undertook the burden of copying it, changing, however, Lombard characters into our Latin ones. Do not therefore be surprised if it has a beginning without a beginning and an end without an end. Farewell.

## Chronicle

[Col. 1151A] [lacuna] “... deprived him of his office at the city of Rome, and repeatedly stirred the minds of the Beneventans, that they should not consent to the archbishopric without the permission of the lord pope. At length, when his fellow citizens saw such madness, without delay they sent to Rome nearly a hundred noble and good men, begging the lord pope to deign to confirm the elected pastor. Having gone there, they petitioned him incessantly before all, namely in the most sacred synod which he had convened; but they were quite unable to obtain this.

“But those who had been sent, seeing this and returning thence, stirred the hearts of the others, saying: ‘Our fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers never suffered so great [Col. 1151B] an injustice.’ But why say more? Those who seemed to be on Riso’s side placed arms and implements of war upon the bell-tower. For they had heard that Peter himself, bishop of Porto, had formed a conspiracy, intending by force to plunder the treasures of the church and its goods.

“Then that bishop, seeing arms being placed in the bell-tower, became sorrowful and ordered his faithful men to be summoned, that they might deliberate what should be done concerning so great and such a matter. Meanwhile war began, because the party of the bishop, ascending the bell-tower, vigorously attacked the palace of Dacomarius, where that bishop was staying; and the bishop’s auxiliaries, fighting from Dacomarius’s tower, battled one another cruelly. Indeed, two young men gave up their lives in the conflict itself.

“At last, as night came on, the bishop, seeing himself surrounded, went up in the silence of midnight to the monastery of St. Sophia with certain men, and remained there for no long time. [Col. 1152A] Moreover, the citizens, compelled by fear and fearing that the bishop would harass them before the lord pope, constrained him until he should pledge his faith to them by oath, which he promised to do; and he asked the lord pope to send a rector, who again appointed the monk Rosseman rector.

### Year 1103, twelfth indiction

### Year 1104, thirteenth indiction

### Year 1105, fourteenth indiction

In January and February there was great snow, flooding of rivers, and a comet appeared in the west; for three days later the pope came to Benevento.

The following year Henry, king of the Germans, died.

### Year 1107, September, first indiction

The aforesaid Roffrid, archbishop of Benevento, died; he [Col. 1152B] sat for thirty-one years, two months, and twenty days.

In this year, in that same month of September, Abbot Madelmus died; and in this month of September Bernard was elected abbot on the feast of St. Michael.

### Year 1108, second indiction

There was a failure of wine and a mortality among animals; and Pope Paschal came to Benevento, who in November ordained Landulf archbishop.

### Year 1109, third indiction

Formatus died. Easter fell on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April].

> [Note: Col. 1151C] These numbers of years and indictions do not agree; and the present Chronicle suffers from the same discrepancy from the very first year under which anything is recorded down to 1112. It is plainly established, both from what I shall say below and from the date of Easter recorded here, that the indictions exceeding the correct reckoning by one must be corrected. For in the year 1109 Easter did in fact fall on VII Kalends of May, as will be clear to anyone who calculates the dates. —Peregrini.

On the second day after the beginning of November, the treasury of St. Mary was burned.

### Year 1110, fourth indiction

King Henry came to Rome and by fraud and deceit seized Pope Paschal and [Col. 1152C] the cardinals in February. In the same month Duke Roger died, and Bohemond his brother.

> [Note: Col. 1151C] From the correct sequence of preceding and following years recorded in the present Chronicle, this is plainly the year 1110. But it was not the fourth indiction but the third; nor do the events which Falco attaches to it belong there, [Col. 1151D] but to 1111. In the ancient Vatican manuscript used by Baronius, Paschal is recorded as captured by Henry in February, on the day before the Ides, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, in the fourth indiction, on a Sunday. All ancient monuments and authors agree completely with this, and these chronological markers accord well with one another.

> Peter the Deacon, in the continuation to the Ostian, book IV, chapter 40; Romuald of Salerno; the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, edited by me; and an anonymous ancient citizen of Bari, recently made known to me, who is almost a paraphrast of the Chronicle of Lupus Protospatarius and who will first see the light through me after these corrections, likewise assign the deaths of Duke Roger and Bohemond not to the preceding year. He further records that Roger died in February, as is said here, but Bohemond in March; and the obituary records of the monastery of Monte Cassino published by Caraccioli agree with him. [Col. 1152C]

> Falco, therefore, must be judged not to have followed the reckoning of years adopted by others. He is clearly found to begin years not in January but in March. For after heading almost every year, he immediately places the month of March; and events which happened in January and February, and even at the beginning of March, he consistently assigns to the same year to which he had assigned events occurring in the preceding months. Thus under the year 1112 he records Paschal’s arrival at Benevento in December and his holding a synod there in February; likewise under 1117 he records the same pontiff holding another synod there in April [Col. 1152D] but dying on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February; and under 1129 he records Pope Honorius consecrating Franco abbot of St. Sophia in the same city in August and dying in February.

> Moreover, at pp. 221, 245, 252, 254, 278, 296, 319, and 338 of Caraccioli’s edition, he carries years beyond December and, as I said, extends the year already begun even to March. Yet at pp. 190 and 320 he assigns the fourteenth and fifteenth days of that month, and at p. 201 the second day, to the new year. Thus he does not show himself to reckon years from the day on which the Word became flesh, namely 25 March, nor from the day of the Nativity or Circumcision. Nevertheless, he reckons them from the common epoch of the Nativity and assigns to them indictions consonant with the common calculation. [Col. 1153C] Accordingly, for the year 1110 he properly wrote the third, not the fourth, indiction, as the printed manuscript corruptly represents it; and he carried it in parallel course to March of the following year. No more authentic reading is to be sought there. —Peregrini.

### Year 1111, fifth indiction

### Year 1112, sixth indiction, March

> [Note: Col. 1153C] Write “fifth indiction,” as required by the chronological reasoning set out above. Cardinal Baronius further testifies under 1140 that this reading occurs in an old copy of this Chronicle: “Falco of Benevento,” he says, “carried his Chronicle as far as this year, having begun it in the year of the Redeemer 1112, fifth indiction.” Yet under 1113 he states of its beginning that it was begun from this very year and carried only twenty-seven years, through 1140; so that Falco seems to have made nothing of the earlier material, which he recognized to be both mutilated in itself and too meager for his work.

> Furthermore, in Falco’s words, “This year the building was begun,” or “was being built,” etc., the *to aedificium* (the word *building*) must be deleted, because it does not suit the sentence and is redundant; it is a gloss upon the abbreviated word *aedific.* The Apostolic, that is, the Roman pontiff, then Paschal II, when he came to Benevento, as Falco reports, at the beginning of December in this year 1112, subsequently held a synod there in February, namely February of the following common year, 1113. Peter the Deacon agrees with this in the continuation to the Ostian, book IV, chapter 48. He counts this arrival of Paschal in these parts as his second, placing the first in 1108, in October, as he relates in the same book, chapter 33; and he has Falco as his authority, who says that Paschal then ordained Landulf archbishop of Benevento in November.

> Therefore, when that same pontiff went to Benevento in this year, I believe that the church of St. Menna in the city called Sant’Agata dei Goti was consecrated; it had been built by Count R., that is, Robert son of Rainulf, mentioned by Peter the Deacon in the aforesaid book IV, chapter 25. Yet in an inscription set up there, certainly ancient in workmanship and bearing no sign of forgery, I read that it was done in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1109, on the second day before the Nones of September, in the fourth indiction, by the hands of Lord Paschal II, pope. This chronological dating, however, does not agree with itself; nor does anyone report that Paschal came to our region in that year and month. —Peregrini.

Pope Paschal, holding a synod at Rome, broke the agreement which he had made with King Henry. This year the construction—or building—of the oratory of St. Bartholomew the Apostle was begun. [lacuna]

After these and other events had taken their course, the Beneventans, seeing themselves afflicted by various sufferings from plunder, took counsel and sent Archbishop Landulf and Judge John to the aforesaid Apostolic, that he might deign to raise those citizens, oppressed by so great a calamity, to the harbor of safety. This was especially necessary because many Beneventans had often disturbed the city by internal conspiracies: some striving to establish Landulf Burrellus, others Anso, as rector of the city without the will of the lord pope.

[Col. 1153B] When the Apostolic heard this, he came to Benevento without delay on the second day after the beginning of December, and in February he convened a synod. After the synod had been held, while he was present in the sacred Beneventan palace and discovered the aforesaid conspiracy made on behalf of that Landulf Burrellus, he ordered the citizens to be summoned. He carefully asked them what ought to be done concerning so great and such a matter, since, as we have said, that conspiracy seemed likely to result in the betrayal and ruin of the city; and because certain citizens, in aid of Landulf himself, had seized by night the towers of the Upper Gate, expelled the guard of those fortifications, and held them by force for only one night.

At last, with God’s help and the support of many faithful Beneventans [Col. 1153C] whose judgment was sounder, the towers were recovered and restored to St. Peter. The citizens themselves then gave this response [Col. 1154A] to the lord pope: that he should summon those whom he regarded as suspect and obtain full justice from them. Why say more? The court having been convened, the supporters of evil were summoned, and the suspects were summoned. At last, lawful sentence having been pronounced, we saw some arrested, some expelled, the houses of some assigned to the fisc, and those of others destroyed. These matters having thus been done:
