Namely, in the year 1113, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of the aforesaid lord pope, in March, in the sixth indiction, that Apostolic lord himself, observing that the city of Benevento was oppressed on every side by various depredations, and learning that the goods of its citizens were daily carried off and ravaged by the surrounding Normans, took counsel and appointed Landulf of Graecia, an eminent and energetic knight, [Col. 1154B] constable of the Beneventans.

> [Note: Col. 1154C] Baronius, here and under 1114, calls him on the authority of this author Landulf of Graecia. I suspect that this family name arose from the lordship of a town formerly called Graecia, in the territory of Benevento, as is read in the royal Sicilian archive. I think that the name was variously pronounced, since Falco records below under 1121 Gerardus de Graecis, and under 1137 Thaddeus de la Graeca—certainly noble Beneventan men.

> Landulf seems to have received the office of constable from Pope Paschal in March, perhaps while Paschal was still staying at Benevento in this year 1113; in the following year, as Falco himself says, he relinquished the constableship and retired home in the same month in which he had been appointed, having remained in office only one year. Paschal did not, however, issue at Benevento in this year the letter dated XV Kalends of April to the patriarch of Antioch, quoted by William of Tyre, book II, chapter 27, but in 1117, as I shall say below. William also quotes another letter of the same pontiff, dated on the same day, to the king of Jerusalem, issued not while he was staying at Benevento but at the Lateran—an evident contradiction unnoticed by others. —Peregrini.

This was done so that, with God’s assistance and by Landulf’s prudence, the city and its descendants might remain secure from the habitual devastation of plunder, which very often threatened, and from the seditious conspiracies frequently raised against the lord pope. For he had learned that Landulf was prudent and spirited, a man of shrewd intelligence, by whose aid and skill he trusted that not only the Beneventan people entrusted to his governance, but also much of the Lombard population, might be rescued and freed from the servitude of the oppressive Normans. Landulf himself was of a warlike spirit and could not endure injuries done to the lowly; daily he threatened all enemies. If any enemy inflicted injury or plunder upon him, he desired rather to die first [Col. 1154C] than in any way allow the enemy to depart unpunished.

Why say more? This Landulf, the constable, [Col. 1155A] endowed on every side with valor and knowledge, did not deign to bend his neck to the threats of anyone. When, as has been said, he received the office of constable from the aforesaid lord Pope Paschal, he saw a castle which a certain Robert, surnamed the Slav, had built on Mount Sableta. This man was filled with every wickedness and devoted to depravity. Landulf anxiously negotiated with him that the castle should be destroyed.

Robert himself had built this remarkable and very laborious castle because of the war against the Beneventans and his enmity toward the city. Those dwelling in this castle had caused the citizens many indignities and much damage; indeed, some fellow citizens lost estates and possessions which they had held around that mountain for the construction of the castle itself. After the castle had been wonderfully constructed, its inhabitants, together with Robert’s retainers, sometimes captured Beneventans; sometimes, more cruelly, they deprived travelers of life together with their goods.

When the aforesaid Apostolic heard this at Rome, he excommunicated Robert until he should destroy that castle hostile to the city; Robert despised doing so. Why say more? When Landulf of Graecia himself had been appointed constable, he made an agreement with the aforesaid Robert, and Robert did what he had refused to do for the aforesaid pope: he destroyed and razed that castle to its foundations, after being given two excellent horses and two hundred solidi.

Then Constable Landulf himself confirmed an agreement with Count Jordan by oath, and daily rose in achievements [Col. 1155C] and in the acclaim of praise.

Prince Robert, and Counts Robert and Jordan, seeing that castle thus destroyed and that Constable Landulf was day by day increasing in power and wealth, were struck by envious zeal because of their hatred of the Lombards. Thinking that they were being dispossessed by his prudence, they conspired with all the neighboring Normans on every side, declaring that they would wage war upon Benevento and plunder it as long as Landulf himself appeared to be constable of the Beneventans.

When this oath had thus been confirmed, they came against Benevento with countless knights and foot soldiers on the twelfth day after the beginning of August. They encamped for only one day and night on the mountain called Guardia, believing that they would expel him and utterly lay waste the city. But on the very day they arrived, they began battle, were defeated, and some of them were captured. On the following night, terribly shaken by heavenly fear and by the Beneventans, they fled like brigands by byways, believing that they would be captured and shamefully held by the Beneventans that very night.

Indeed, as was heard from the mouths of many among them who told the story, if the constable himself, with a company of Beneventans and knights, had crossed as far as the church of St. Angelo at the Cross, or if any sound of a voice had been heard, both the enemy and the enemy’s military equipment and provisions would without doubt have been delivered [Col. 1156A] into the hands of the Beneventans.

When those Normans had thus departed, Landulf of Graecia himself, the constable, unable to endure the enemies’ attacks and repaying what he had received, promptly gathered about one hundred and eighty armed knights and an assembled multitude of about four thousand citizens. He went to the castle called Terrarubea and leveled it to the ground with fire and sword. A certain Robert called “of Sicily” died, burned in the fire of that castle. Thus they brought back to Benevento, with great rejoicing, an innumerable quantity of livestock and other property.

Not long afterward, Landulf again gathered a troop of horsemen and fellow citizens and stormed the castle of Apice. He destroyed [a feature omitted or corrupt in the text] of that castle and its mills, [Col. 1156B] and joyfully carried off plunder of livestock.

With all these things thus accomplished, the war of the Normans, of which we have spoken, began more fiercely; in it Landulf distributed an immense quantity of gold, silver, and horses. Meanwhile, while the constable himself, with a troop of soldiers, was keeping watch near the bridge of Serretella against enemy ambushes, behold, some fifty horsemen of Count Robert arrived, who were also lurking among the thickets with treacherous intent against the city. What shall I say? The ambushes having been revealed on both sides, a battle took place between them. At last, by the mercy of God intervening, the enemy party turned its back and took to flight, so that the constable himself led away twelve of their horsemen as prisoners, with all their arms [Col. 1156C]. Moreover, as we have said, the war having been vigorously undertaken on both sides, raids were very frequently made here and there.

It happened one day that Rao, lord of the castle of Ceppaloni, went with Landulf Burrellus, some one hundred and fifty other knights, and a multitude of infantry, to break up, so to speak, an *arcaturia*.

> [Note: [Col. 1155D] Falco calls an *arcaturia*—by a popular term then current and still used in many places—a fence of stakes constructed for public or private use, to restrain or confine the water of a perennial stream. PEREGR.]

When the constable saw them thus breaking it up on the river Sabato, unable to bear such audacity, he marched out into the open field by the church of the Seven Holy Brothers, accompanied by a company of soldiers. There they fought one another; but, sins intervening, the constable’s party, deceived by enemy ambushes and pursued across that plain, was defeated, so that twelve noble knights of the city, with their entire equipment of arms, were captured [Col. 1156D].

After all these things and others had thus taken place, all the enemies who had conspired for the war, seeing that the constable did not bend the knee to them but rather threatened them, and that the Beneventans continually followed him and his commands, began to harass the city more than usual, ordering that every vineyard standing about which they could reach should be cut down. This was done. Moreover, they ordered poor men and other men whom they found to be seized; when this decree was published, many people were taken prisoner.

[Col. 1157A] In the year 1114, in March, in the seventh indiction, while the vineyards were thus being cut down and men seized, certain Beneventans, driven by the sword of envy, sent the archbishop Landulf to the aforesaid pope, together with Rachisius, abbot of Saint Modestus, to report to him the hardship they suffered on every side. Going away, they disclosed to Pope Paschal the affliction they had seen, tearfully begging him to deign to come to the aid of his entrusted flock as a good shepherd. When their need had been laid before the lord pope, he commanded them:

> [Note: [Col. 1157D] Baronius reads: “The need . . . the lord pope commanded them,” etc., following the author’s unmistakably unlearned idiom and the excellent manuscript which he used. Yet he seems in some places to have departed from its authority and to have fashioned the wording somewhat more elegantly and in closer conformity with Latin usage [Col. 1158D]. I shall not now pursue each such instance, but only those requiring particular observation; it will suffice to have indicated the matter. PEREGR.]

that they should make peace for the city as best they could and assist the poor, lest the Apostle Peter lose the city he had acquired through some occasion; and that whatever plan for peace they discovered, they should report it back to him.

But the archbishop, on returning from Rome, acted otherwise than he had been instructed. He sent word to Constable Landulf that, in compassion for the necessity of the poor, he should lay down the constableship until the lord pope came to Benevento. Afterwards, whether by payment, services, or the prayers of the citizens, they should entreat the pope himself and restore him to his former honour—provided that the Normans should refuse to make peace, their oath, as stated, intervening.

When Constable Landulf heard this, answering in the sacred Beneventan palace before the faithful of Saint Peter, he said that he would never relinquish the constableship unless he were seized hand to hand and held by force. Moreover, he wished to see what peace the Normans wished to make with the Beneventans, and that the peace itself, set down in writing, should be sent to the lord pope [Col. 1157C]. Whatever the lord pope should command concerning peace, or concerning the laying down of the constableship, he would, he said, carry out before all.

How the constable himself came to be in the sacred Beneventan palace I shall relate. When, as was said above, the archbishop had returned from Rome, and with him had come Peter, bishop of Porto, and Romuald the deacon, cardinals of the holy Roman see, sent by the pope himself to find a peace, without delay, at their very arrival and before they had even been lodged, the people, stirred with a bestial mind, ascended the palace of Dacomarius, in which the constable lived, shouting:

> “Unless you quickly make the peace we desire, we shall all take up swords and die in the streets.”

They also uttered threats and insults against the constable [Col. 1157D], saying that they would not endure war for the constableship of one man and thus end their lives shamefully.

On the following day, the archbishop’s party placed arms and instruments of war upon the bell-tower, intending to drive Landulf out by arms and stones. When the bishop of Porto perceived the people’s sedition, he came with the constable and the faithful of Saint Peter to the prince’s court, and there addressed all present as follows:

> “Our lord pope has heard from some persons, and has learned from your archbishop, of the affliction and scarcity of food which you have long suffered and still suffer for loyalty to Saint Peter. Know therefore that he is grieved with all the affection of his heart and greatly distressed by what he has heard. For this reason he has sent us and your archbishop, so that, with God’s help, you may obtain peace. We therefore beseech and exhort your fidelity not to be moved by pride or fury while we, together with other wise men, may devise for you the counsel and aid necessary for peace. For no one can conduct so grave and laborious a matter with a hasty mind. Therefore let no one resort to arms, so that, if it please God, laying aside every fury, we may deserve to find peace.” [Col. 1158A]

While he said these and similar things, the voice of the people rose to the heavens, saying:

> “We cannot in any way listen to these prayers which you offer unless you give us peace with the greatest speed.” [Col. 1158B]

Then, when another day came, the people, unable to endure the delays and truces which were proposed, attacked the house of the judge Persicus. They would have destroyed it entirely, but he escaped through the aid of certain friends. Therefore the bishop of Porto, unable to quiet the popular disturbance, departed at the dawn of the next day, commanding the constable to go up into the prince’s palace and thus escape the tumult of the raging people. Complying with his command, he took up residence in the sacred palace. But let us return to the matter.

When the archbishop heard the constable’s words, he drew up in due form the confirmation of peace and sent it to him as he had requested [Col. 1158C]. Having heard the text of the document containing the peace, the constable said: “Behold, the settlement of peace is excellent. Now let it be sent to our lord, and let us follow whatever he commands.”

Meanwhile the archbishop himself, together with a certain man named Fulco, frequently summoned many citizens to the episcopal residence and said:

> “We have informed the lord pope of your need, and we have received from him authority to make an end with the Normans. It therefore seems superfluous to send the written peace back to him.”

But certain citizens, filled with hatred arising from other enmities and inciting the minds of others, openly cried out that they would not endure war for that man’s constableship. After taking counsel, they swore an oath within the episcopal residence that they would not permit that Landulf of the Graeca should be constable [Col. 1158D], until the lord pope, with the counsel of the Normans, had restored him to his office.

After this oath had been devised, the archbishop sent the bishop of Avellino and certain priests to the aforesaid constable, ordering him to relinquish the office as stated; he gave the same answer as before. Then, on another Saturday, the fourteenth day of March, the constable, armed with a band of his followers, went out into the middle of the street, saying:

> “I should like to see those who threaten to drive me from the palace and office. It is more honourable to surrender one’s life thus than to relinquish the office entrusted to me so shamefully, or bound by the promised weight of gold.” [Col. 1159A]

When the archbishop heard of the preparations for war and the mournful ringing of the palace bell, he ordered his supporters to be summoned, so that they might confirm with the Normans the peace they had proposed; but if the constable should wish to resist, he would have them ready. Meanwhile the archbishop’s party attacked the house of a certain faithful adherent of the constable because he did not agree with them. Hearing this, the constable hurried to defend the attacked house; and when he was seen, civil war began, so that some fought from bell-towers, others from the roofs of houses, and others in the streets. At last the archbishop’s party, with fortune turned in its favour, gained the victory and pursued the constable and his men as far as the prince’s palace. We saw some men wounded on both sides [Col. 1159B].

The constable, taking refuge in the palace, remained there for a little while, until the archbishop should give him a pledge of safety for his own person and for those who followed him. Meanwhile the citizens, unable to bear this delay and thirsting in their hearts for the peace they desired, threatened him with stones: unless he quickly came down from the palace, they would seize him by force and tear him limb from limb.

Landulf, seeing himself surrounded, surrendered himself to the archbishop and the citizens. He further confirmed by oath that he would not accept the constableship, the rectorate, or any public authority without the good will of the archbishop, Roffred the archpriest, Arechis the archdeacon, Roffrid son of Gaiderisius, Roffrid “of the Golden Gate,” Gervasius, and Vitalis son of John Gallus; and that he would not repay the archbishop and all the Beneventans with evil for evil, and, if anyone wished to do so, he would obstruct him without deceit or evil contrivance.

> [Note: [Col. 1159D] I write: “Roffrid son of Gaiderisius,” who in the year 1130 is called simply “Roffrid of Gaiderisius.” For that is how the passage should be read, not “of Garderisius,” since among the Lombards *Gaideris* was a personal male name, pronounced in a more Latin manner as *Gaiderisus* or *Gaiderisius*. From this passage of Falco one may understand how the names of parents very frequently once passed into surnames of sons and finally of the whole stock: namely, because children were customarily named in one way or another from the names of their parents, so that they might more easily be distinguished from others bearing a similar name in their family or neighbourhood. These names, once given, adhered more firmly to them and at last became family names; yet the little word *fili* (“son”) was not abbreviated, but was always written out—examples are sufficiently common [Col. 1160D].
>
> Very many such surnames derived from parents’ names are now readily recognized by everyone; nevertheless, some are not clear except to persons more skilled in antiquity—and even to them not all are clear. Since those personal names have now fallen out of ordinary use, the populace imagines that the family names arose not from them but from some other or unknown source. But I return to Falco, in whom this Roffrid appears here and in the year 1119. Alferius was surnamed “Of the Golden Gate,” which surname I conjecture was given to his family on precisely the same basis as a noble Salernitan line was named “De Porta” from its guard-duty at the Porta Rotensis. For in earlier times city gates commonly took names from their guards, as I have explained elsewhere, and sometimes bestowed their own names upon them. PEREGR.]

When this had been done, a similar pledge was received from the soldiers who had followed him. Thus each returned to his own home, and that Landulf of the Graeca, having laid down the constableship, withdrew to his house. That is, in the same month of March in which he had been appointed, he stepped down, having remained in office for only one year.

On the following Sunday, after these things had taken place, Count Robert arrived with a multitude of cavalry and infantry at the head of the Greater Bridge. There he himself, Rao lord of Ceppaloni, and Hugh of Castelpoto confirmed by oath the peace promised for all the days of their lives [Col. 1159D–1160A]. Count Jordan, Robert the Slav, and Girard de la Marra likewise swore to it.

Since, as related above, the archbishop had given assurances for the person of the constable and the other soldiers and footmen, as the constable had requested, he went home after laying down his office. For it seemed to the archbishop and the Beneventans that they were obtaining the peace they had long desired. Thereafter the constable, having received the assurance of safety and remaining at home, thought that he should undoubtedly do nothing else than devote himself securely to the care of his soul; for, as we have said, he was severely wounded.

His friends, therefore, and the faithful of Saint Peter, whose minds were faithfully grieved by his insults and injuries [Col. 1160B], consoled him day and night, though not openly. They urged him not to let his spirit be saddened over what he had suffered, since he had endured what they had seen and what had been done against him for loyalty to Blessed Peter.

But the archbishop and his supporters, hearing these things and filled with suspicion, hoped that Landulf was taking counsel to restore the constableship. They repeatedly sent to him ordering him to leave the city and abandon the company of his friends until the lord pope had restored him to his accustomed office, as stated above. Then the constable openly exclaimed to those who brought the words and to other fellow-citizens:

> “We are utterly astonished at such words, since I was compelled by the whole body of Beneventans to relinquish the constableship [Col. 1160C], and I have in no way seen the safety promised us by the archbishop put into effect.”

At last, seeing the obstinacy of the raging people grow ever more inflamed, the constable took counsel and, at dawn on Palm Sunday, set out for Montefusco with a few knights. Then the archbishop’s conspiracy, still not trusting the treachery it had begun, bound the judges John and Persicus, other nobles, and worthy men by the oath which the constable himself had sworn; and, putting aside all fear, it brought in other citizens, alleging that they thought those men would repay them for their hostile acts.

When news of this deed—more wicked than can be believed—reached the ears of the aforesaid apostolic lord, he was inwardly touched with grief at the expulsion of his beloved son the constable. With tears, as we heard, streaming down [Col. 1160D–1161A], he groaned in spirit and immediately, before all, deposed Archbishop Landulf from every office which he had received from the Roman see. Likewise, he bound all the archbishop’s followers with the bond of anathema until they should make satisfaction.

But, if it does not seem burdensome to the reader’s charity, I shall not omit to write what was done at Benevento after this excommunication had been imposed. For I call God to witness that I have set down nothing other than what I saw and heard written.

When this sentence of anathema against the adversaries of Saint Peter had been spread far and wide, the aforesaid apostolic lord sent to Benevento Anastasius . . . . . and the bishop of Albano, worthy cardinals of the Roman see, wishing to learn what the Beneventan people had in mind.

> [Note: [Col. 1161C] The printed manuscript of Falco presents two cardinals sent by the pope to Benevento in these words; yet below, on this same page, it makes only one cardinal, Anastasius, speak among the Beneventans and return from Benevento to Rome. In fact, one and the same Anastasius was then both cardinal and bishop of Albano. Baronius presents this reading, and the other passages consistently written to the same effect, from his manuscript. Moreover, he quotes the words “wishing to know what the Beneventan people had in mind” in this form: “wishing that the Beneventan people should acknowledge themselves”; and below: “know us for certain,” not “by command.” PEREGR.]

Once the cardinals had been lodged [Col. 1161B], three days later the whole assembly of the Beneventans met in the sacred Beneventan palace. There, before those cardinals, all the events that had occurred at Benevento and the origin of the war were recounted from the beginning. When they had heard these things, Anastasius broke into speech:

> “Lords and brothers, know that we have been sent to examine at Rome the affairs of which our lord pope had heard, and to investigate them. Therefore, as best we can, with God’s assent, we shall day and night offer counsel and aid for the advancement of your peace and welfare.”

When these and similar words had thus been spoken, everyone returned home.

Not many days later, the man named Fulco, of whom we have spoken, departed from this world’s prison, alas, wretch that he was, entangled in the bond of anathema [Col. 1162A]. After these things had taken place, the cardinal set out for Rome.

As Cardinal Anastasius was making for Rome, Pope Paschal assembled archbishops, bishops, and abbots, and, when October came after his first return, convened a council at Ceprano. To the crowded gathering of that sacred assembly Duke William and Prince Robert came, having assembled about a thousand horsemen. Landulf of the Graeca, the constable, summoned by special letters of the lord pope to the same sacred council, travelled there honourably. He was received most courteously by the lord pope; avoiding the Normans’ treachery, he crossed safely in a vessel.

But Count Jordan, fearing to go to so great a council, burdened with the weight of his many offences [Col. 1162B], sent his envoys. Archbishop Landulf, having summoned his suffragans and collected an immense quantity of gold and silver, proceeded with Count Robert to that assembly.

When such and so great fathers and nobles had assembled, in the midst of that very gathering, on Saturday, the apostolic lord granted Duke William the duchy of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily.

> [Note: [Col. 1161C] Baronius’s best manuscript read not “the duchy of Apulia” but “the duchy of Italy.” “Then,” you will say, “did the pontiff grant all Italy to Duke William at the Council of Ceprano?” Since this plainly seemed false, it persuaded the copyist to erase the name *Italia* and introduce instead *Apulia*, especially perhaps because he had observed that Peter the Deacon, in his continuation of the history of the bishop of Ostia, book IV, chapter 49, seemed to support his reading: “At the same council,” says Peter, “the same apostolic lord invested Duke William with the duchy of Apulia and Calabria.”
>
> But he was unaware that, according to a Greek idiom then used also by our Italians through their mutual intercourse with the Greeks, Falco used the common name *Italia* to denote Apulia alone, which the Greeks had taken from the Lombards and likewise from the Italian dynasts. Nor did he know that the later Calabria, situated by the Lower Sea, was not then included under that name, because it had never been lost to the Greeks and had never been held by the Italians after the time of Justin II. If he had not learned this from the authors cited above concerning Lupus and from Lupus himself, he could readily have understood it from more than one passage of Falco, in whom *Italia* frequently means not the whole land enclosed by the two seas and the Alps, but Apulia alone.
>
> I shall give unambiguous words of his to this effect [Col. 1162C], concerning Emperor Lothair’s destruction of a castle built near Bari by King Roger and his killing, by more than one kind of death, of its defenders after taking them by force: “At such and so great a victory all Italy, Calabria, and Sicily resounded.” This use of the term became so prevalent that the entire Italian region on this side of the Tiber was sometimes called simply *Italia*, as in an ancient charter of 1091 in the archive of the monastery of Cava. It concerns a donation to that monastery by Guaimar of Jefuno, descendant of the Lombard princes of Salerno, when he and his son made holy vows of religion to God there. “If,” says that distinguished man, “before our consecration death should come upon me and my son, in whatever place from the city of Rome in these regions throughout the whole territory of Italy, immediately,” etc.
>
> Hence it is that the Greek author Nicephorus Gregoras, with consistent usage, calls Charles of Anjou “king of Italy,” though, in the common speech of old, he was king of Apulia. But since I have now established this twice and it has been approved without difficult or doubtful assent by learned friends to whom I long ago communicated it, it is certainly superfluous to reinforce the point at greater length. Still, in passing, I shall add that almost the same thing happened to this *Italia* of ours when it was called simply *Italia* as, learned men know, happened formerly to the seven provinces of all Italy. They claimed the unqualified name *Italia* for themselves because they alone obeyed the magistrate called the vicar of Italy, while the others were subject to the vicar of the City.
>
> Nor should I omit that Falco did not falsely report that Pope Paschal at Ceprano confirmed Sicily also to Duke William, besides Apulia and Calabria—though Peter the Deacon omitted it—since Count Roger, William’s uncle, then held Sicily. For William, as our author reports under the year 1122, had not yet granted to that count his share of the city of Palermo, Messina, and all Calabria. PEREGR.]

When the council had been splendidly arranged, the apostolic lord complained tearfully before all concerning Archbishop Landulf: that he had expelled his constable Landulf, and had scorned to come to him when summoned by his letters [Col. 1163A].

But the archbishop, unwilling—or rather afraid—to enter that assembly without restoration of his see and office, lodged on an island near Ceprano. When he learned that the apostolic lord was making this complaint, he ordered certain Romans and also the prefect to be summoned, so that they might obtain from the lord pope mercy for him by whatever means they could. Indeed, the archbishop said that he would satisfy the lord pope concerning every grievance made against him, provided that the pope restored to him his place in the council and his office.

When the apostolic lord heard this, after taking counsel he restored both his place and office. Restored in this manner, the archbishop came without delay to the assembly on Monday with Count Robert. What more need be said? The apostolic lord ordered him, now restored, to be summoned by a certain deacon to render justice at once [Col. 1163B]. Rising immediately, he answered with a tearful voice before all:

> “First I give thanks to God, to Blessed Peter, and to you, our lord Pope Paschal, for the restoration of my place and office. But now, lord Father, I implore your fatherhood to have mercy upon me, whom Your Holiness planted in the Beneventan see.”

Hearing this, the apostolic lord said:

> “For what reason do you wish us to have mercy upon you?”

And the archbishop replied:

> “Lord, because I have heard that you are angry with me because, when you ordered me to be summoned by your letters, I did not come to your court.”

The apostolic lord said:

> “Why, as you assert, did you not come to the court when summoned?”

To this the archbishop answered:

> “Lord Father, compelled by fear of your anger and of certain persons making threats, I did not come when summoned; and you did not receive my envoys, who were bishops, while our adversaries afflicted with beatings another man whom I had sent previously.” [Col. 1163C]

The apostolic lord replied:

> “I did not hear your envoys, whom you call bishops, because they had not spoken words concerning the administration of justice; rather, they had come for your advantage. The other envoy whom you claim was beaten I neither saw nor did any report of him reach us.”

When the archbishop saw that he was hemmed in on every side by truthful answers, he devised another excuse:

> “Lord Father, you did not grant me a suitable period in which to come; therefore I could not come, nor, as I said, did I dare because I was compelled by fear.”

And the apostolic lord said:

> “But because you disregarded our letters, you now assert that you did not come to us out of contempt but out of fear. Yet I certainly granted you a suitable time for coming: from the Ides of April, with an intervening period of six months.” [Col. 1163D]

He therefore ordered the letter of summons to be read publicly:

> “Nevertheless, let these men deliberate and determine whether the excuse which you assert is canonical.” [Col. 1164A]

He ordered certain cardinals and archbishops, judges of the Roman see, to withdraw apart and pronounce judgment upon this excuse of the archbishop. They withdrew, debated that judgment for a long time, and then returned before all and rendered this decision:

> “Lord Archbishop of Benevento, since you assert that you did not come to the court when summoned not from contempt but from fear, we declare and judge that this is not a canonical excuse.”

When the judgment of such and so great fathers had been rendered, the apostolic lord ordered the chapters of the holy fathers, his predecessors, confirmed in councils and enacted concerning those who disdain authority, to be produced and read before all.

> [Note: [Col. 1163D] Baronius’s manuscript reads more aptly: “the chapters of the holy fathers, predecessors.” In Baronius, too, the remaining narrative concerning the deposition of Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, at that council is, in some places, closer to Falco’s sense and, in many minor places, revised into more decorous language. PEREGR.]

When these things had been accomplished [Col. 1164B], the cardinals and bishops discussed this great and weighty matter for a long time. But what more need be said? The deacon again summoned him to render justice. Rising immediately, he said:

> “For what, and concerning what, am I accused?”

The apostolic lord replied:

> “Because you accepted the regalian rights of Blessed Peter without our will, held the keys of the gates, seized the palace, expelled Landulf, took up helmet and shield, and compelled that Fulco to take an oath.”

When the archbishop heard this, he replied:

> “Truly, I accepted the regalian rights of Blessed Peter for no reason other than loyalty to you. For when you were at Benevento, you entrusted the city to me. I did not receive the keys of the gates; indeed, we fully acknowledge that this man who holds them is your faithful servant. I certainly did not take up a shield; I took a helmet to protect my head, lest I be crushed by some stone. I did not introduce the Normans, as you said; but I caused sixteen Lombards to enter the city to aid the people. I deny that Fulco’s oath was made by my command, and I deny the oath of the people.” [Col. 1164C]

After hearing all this, the apostolic lord again ordered the cardinals and the aforesaid judges to pronounce judgment on all these matters and on the contempt. When the archbishop heard this command, terrible as it were, he entreated Duke William, Prince Robert, Peter son of Leo, and the bishops, saying:

> “Lords, nobles, and brother bishops, I beg you: pray our lord Pope Paschal not to disgrace me thus before all and leave me dishonoured. But if it please his clemency, I shall seek exile, or cross the sea.”

> [Note: [Col. 1163D] Baronius reads the clause conjunctively: “and I shall cross the sea” [Col. 1164D], a sense appropriate to the matter. Yet the particle *vel* (“or”) was not disjunctive here, just as it was not disjunctive in Erchempert, *Description of the Kings of Italy*, no. 5, or in his *History of the Lombards*, no. 1. Nor is it disjunctive in the lives of holy men copied in ancient manuscripts which commonly bear the heading *Vita, vel obitus*—which in Italian is *Vita, et morte* (“Life and death”). Nor, finally, is it disjunctive in Canon 5 of the Council of Turin: “If anyone wishes to separate himself from his communion—that of Felix—let him be received into the fellowship of our holy peace, according to the letters of Ambrose, or of the priest of the Roman Church formerly issued.”
>
> Jerome Alexander the Younger laboured uselessly over this passage in *Dissertation II*, chapter 3, *On the Suburbicarian Regions*, asserting that *vel* there has an explanatory force, as though it meant: “according to the letters of Ambrose, or, to speak more truly, of the priest of the Roman Church.” For the sense is plain if the word is understood in its other customary meaning and used as a conjunction. Similarly, the allegedly disjunctive particle *seu* is conjunctive, both elsewhere and in the *Epitome of the Constitutions of Charlemagne*, title “On Metropolitans,” chapter 4: “Let bishops have authority to correct incestuous persons; and likewise let them have authority within their parishes to correct widows.” Vitus Amerbachius also laboured in vain over this passage, imagining that *seu* could have been omitted or that it was placed for *immo* (“rather”); it stands there for *item* (“likewise”). But this is by the way.
>
> Moreover, not far after the passage of Falco quoted above, his text is defective and must be restored from Baronius’s manuscript as follows: “But the judges, going forth at the command, returned, though with sorrow and delay, lest they pronounce such a judgment upon Archbishop Landulf. Yet when the judges themselves, as I said,” etc. PEREGR.]

Then those nobles went and threw themselves at the feet of the lord pope; as the archbishop had asked, they made supplication, but were wholly unable to obtain their request. The judges, acting upon the command, went away and returned, though sorrowfully and with delay, and rendered the following judgment upon Landulf.

While the judges, as I have said, delayed over the judgment [Col. 1165A], the apostolic lord ordered them under oath to state what was canonical, by the faith which they owed to Blessed Peter and to him. Then the bishop of Porto, first of all, although reluctantly and disturbed by grief at so great a judgment, said:

> “Because you accepted the regalian rights of Blessed Peter, held the keys of the gates, seized the palace, expelled Landulf, and scorned to come to the court when summoned, we pronounce upon you the sentence of deposition, because you acted against Blessed Peter and our lord pope.”

The archbishop of Capua and Cardinal Gregory affirmed the same. As the other judges wished to confirm the same judgment, Landulf himself, compelled by fear and struck by the sword of such a sentence, rose from the midst of that assembly. O reader, had you been present, what weeping you would have seen [Col. 1165B], and how pale the face of that Landulf, once adorned by the Beneventan see and everywhere more glorious than others, when he was deposed by the mouths of so great judges! What shall I say? When his seat had been raised, he left that dreadful council as one bereft of his senses [Col. 1166A].

In this year the church of Blessed Mary at the episcopal residence was enlarged through the counsel of Landulf of the Graeca. In this year Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, was captured; and Landulf of the Graeca, who had been expelled from the city of Benevento, returned after receiving the constableship.

With all these and other matters thus accomplished [Note: [Col. 1165C] In the old copy it may perhaps have been written, “the church of Blessed M. from the episcopal precinct,” which the copyist thought should be interpreted “of Blessed Mary,” whereas it ought to have been explained as “of Blessed Maximus”; as Falco himself provides evidence at the year 1123, saying that the aforesaid Landulf of Greca died on 12 Kalends of December and was buried at his own church of St. Maximus. Unless, rather, the name of Blessed Mary should there be restored. For a long time I hesitated whether the present entire annotation ought to be attributed to Falco, or whether it had been written in the margin of his manuscript by some outside annotator and finally incorporated into the text by an unskilled, inexperienced copyist. For it does not fit very well with either the preceding or the following narrative. Nor does Falco state that Archbishop Landulf was captured and cast into chains before or after his deposition, as is asserted here. Peter the Deacon, in the frequently cited *Continuation*, book IV, chapter 49, plainly declares that, refusing to hear the pope’s sentence, he fled from the Council of Ceprano to the monastery of Monte Cassino; and he further indicates, not obscurely, that he remained there until his restoration, since he affirms that, at the request of that congregation, he soon again received pontifical rank and papal favour—namely, when Paschal, travelling from Rome to Benevento in 1117, turned aside on the way to the aforesaid monastery.

Yet I finally judged that Peter the Deacon had discreetly passed over and concealed the imprisonment, or free custody, of so eminent a prelate. Elsewhere in this very narrative he also indulged his fellow monks by asserting that Landulf was restored to his rank at the request of the Cassinese congregation; whereas Falco relates that Landulf was reinstated in the archbishopric on the eleventh day of August 1116, before Paschal began his journey to Benevento and consequently before he went to Cassino. Baronius conjectures that this took place at the Lateran Council, already mentioned, held in March of that year, although under 1117 he agrees with Peter’s statement.

Falco’s preceding annotation, then, is not altogether spurious—altogether, I say. For, to speak frankly, I detect in it something of a self-conscious style, as though it had been reduced from some longer account into a briefer compass of words, contrary to the author’s manner. Had Falco not composed it in a freer form, he would not immediately have adopted that manner of expression and added: “With all these and other matters thus accomplished.” Who could fail to see that this presupposes a very full preceding narrative? PEREGR.], the apostolic himself set out for Troia on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, and there convened and confirmed a council [Note: [Col. 1166C] “With all these and other matters,” he says, “thus accomplished”—that is, as I have explained, both at the Council of Ceprano, held, as Falco himself noted, in October 1114, and during the months immediately following that council—the apostolic himself set out for Troia on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, namely in 1115, a year which he had not yet mentioned in the narrative, etc. Therefore the already mentioned year 1115 must be prefixed here; Baronius likewise assigns this Council of Troia to that year on the authority of this author.

But Paschal, as Peter the Deacon testifies in the repeatedly cited *Continuation*, book IV, chapter 55, “leaving Rome in May, came to the monastery of Monte Cassino; and, taking with him its abbot, Gerard at that time, he departed for Troia to hold a synod, and on his return solemnly dedicated the church of St. Vincent near the source of the river Volturnus.” Thus he writes. Falco moreover adds after the foregoing: “When the council had been confirmed and piously concluded, the pope returned to Benevento on the third day of September. Then, having settled the business pressing upon the city, the apostolic returned to Rome on the seventh day before the Kalends of October. At that time he dedicated the monastery of St. Vincent.” We had already learned this latter point from Peter.

Therefore Paschal, absent from Rome from March 1115, spent nearly four months in these places, during which he held the Council of Troia. Peter’s quoted words about another synod gathered in that city must not be understood as referring to one other than that described by Falco; the two authors’ agreement concerning Paschal’s dedication then performed at St. Vincent plainly proves this. Moreover, as I observed in my corrections to the Anonymous Cassinese under 1114, Peter says that Pope Paschal left Rome in the year after the Cassinese monks recovered Castellum Suium. He relates in chapter 54 that this happened in 1115—so his manuscript and the Neapolitan edition read—and says, therefore, that in the following year, that is, A.D. 1116, the pope left Rome to hold the Council of Troia. He uses the common era from the birth of Christ, which is certainly one year ahead of Falco’s reckoning; thus he does not conflict with Falco concerning the date of the said council.

Peter further reveals, by an involuntary admission, that the council was held in 1115. In chapters 60 and 61 he says that Paschal, accompanied by the abbot of Cassino, returned to Rome from the aforementioned synod and resolved to hold another council there in mid-Lent; he then withdrew because of disturbances raised by the Romans over the prefect, appointed against his will; and finally, in 1117, left the city—he had indeed previously returned there, as must be admitted, and Falco does not conceal this—and withdrew to Benevento in order to avoid King Henry, who was coming to Rome. If Paschal avoided the king’s approach in 1117, as all the other writers, and especially Falco, assign it to that year—Falco says that Paschal was at Benevento in April—then this was certainly after he had held a council at Rome in Lent of the preceding year, 1116, left and returned to the city, and had previously been at Troia in 1115, as stated. What Paschal did at Benevento on the two occasions when he passed through it then is absent from Falco. PEREGR.]. Almost all the nobles of Apulia, archbishops, and bishops assembled for the presence of that sacred gathering.

[Col. 1166B] When the assembly had been duly organized, among the other matters settled there, the Truce of God was established, so that [Col. 1167A] Count Jordan, the Count of Loritello, and the other barons of Apulia confirmed by oath in their presence the Truce of God [Note: [Col. 1167D] So also below under 1123: “They instituted the observance of the Truce of God”; that is, they entered into a truce or peace agreement. William of Newburgh, book V, chapter 3: “The truces which they call *treugae*.” William of Tyre, book I, chapter 13: “The peace which in the vernacular is called *treuga*.” It is certainly so called and so written by other authors as well; moreover our author has *treuva* twice under 1120, where the printer’s error perhaps gives *Treuna* in one place. I have said regarding Lupus that *g* and *v* were used interchangeably, as in *Ugo* and *Uvo*, etc. Thus *tregua* and *treuva* are the same. But *u* before *u* sometimes changed into *q*, whence *tregua* is now pronounced in Italian.

In Ivo of Chartres, letter 90, and in Lupus Protospatharius under 1089 and 1091, the more Latin form is called *trevia*. When I corrected that author, I doubted what sort of *trevia* he meant, as the unpublished Anonymous testifies, part II, no. 3. For when I had in mind the wars of the Norman nobles that were to be recorded, I did not observe that the passage concerned those rulers being reconciled after private hatreds or other causes, while citizens were mutually fighting one another with arms. All who held office and rank over others suffered immensely from this disease in the Lombard period, as the unpublished Anonymous of Salerno testifies in speaking of Sico, prince of Benevento; and likewise in the Norman age, as is clear from the aforesaid Lupus and Falco. Nor did persons of lower condition conduct themselves with any greater moderation; see, to omit others, Alexander of Telese, book I, chapter 21. PEREGR.] henceforth and for a period of three years. Thus the council having been confirmed and piously concluded, the pope returned to Benevento on the third day of September. Then the apostolic himself, settling the affairs of the city which pressed for decision, returned to Rome on the seventh day before the Kalends of October. At that time he dedicated the monastery of St. Vincent.

In the year 1116 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in March, in the ninth indiction, our aforesaid lord the apostolic convened a synod at Rome. In this year the prefect of the city of Rome died in March [Col. 1167B] [Note: [Col. 1168D] Shall I believe Falco a liar, or his text corrupted, or rather that these events, which he properly reports under 1116, have been assigned by others to the preceding year? They occurred in the fifth year of the peace made between Pope Paschal and King Henry in April 1111, as Peter the Librarian reports in Baronius, and in the sixteenth year of that pope’s pontificate—which, in Falco’s reckoning, is the already mentioned year of Christ 1115. PEREGR.]. After his death a terrible civil war arose, because the Romans had heard that Peter, son of Leo, with the apostolic’s advice, wished to appoint his own son as prefect. Therefore the people of Rome raised the dead prefect’s son to the office of prefect. Once he had been appointed, they sent to the aforesaid Pope Paschal, humbly requesting that he give his assent to their appointment and confirm it. But the apostolic gave them no assent whatever.

When the Romans learned this, they made a conspiracy and utterly overthrew splendid houses and many towers belonging to those who had conspired with Peter son of Leo to accomplish this. Consequently Ptolemy, the prefect’s maternal uncle, [Col. 1168A] and the apostolic’s other barons seized and held castles. It happened one day that the prefect himself, attended by a company of nearly fifty soldiers, went outside the city to reconnoitre the soldiers whom the apostolic had sent. The apostolic’s *comestabulus*—constable—having discovered this, attacked them unexpectedly, struck them down, and captured the prefect. When Ptolemy heard of the capture of his aforesaid nephew, he immediately took soldiers, attacked the pope’s aforesaid constable, freed his nephew, who was being held captive, and joyfully brought him back with him to his own possessions.

While these and other things were taking place at Rome, the aforesaid apostolic left the City and remained at a certain castle called Setia. For he saw that the sedition was becoming more and more inflamed and that Peter son of Leo was being fiercely attacked day by day. But after not many days had passed, seeing that the sedition was being pacified and diminishing, the apostolic, having taken counsel and assembled troops, entered Rome; then he entered the Lateran palace and there sang the solemn rites of Mass. When he had entered the city, the body of Romans that had rebelled against him was converted almost entirely to obedience to his command and will. Thus, having found tranquillity, the apostolic lived securely at Rome.

After these things had been done, the aforesaid apostolic restored Landulf, whom he had deposed, to the archbishopric on the eleventh day of August.

In the year 1117 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighteenth of the pontificate [Col. 1169A] of Lord Paschal, in April the pope himself held a synod at Benevento [Note: [Col. 1169B] Paschal was certainly residing not at Troia but at Benevento when he issued letters in this year: first, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, to the bishops and to Henry, king of England, letters which Baronius cites from William of Malmesbury; then, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of the same month, to the patriarch of Antioch. These were written, as the matter dealt with in them shows, after other letters long before addressed to the king of Jerusalem on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, and after others issued by the same pope to the aforesaid patriarch on the seventh day before the Ides of August. William of Tyre, book XI, chapter 27, records them all and assigns them to 1115; but those later letters to the patriarch—and why not the earlier ones also, given the distance of the places and the difficulty of the business transacted?—were sent after the aforesaid year had passed. As I said, they are recorded as given at Benevento on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, and therefore in 1117. For Paschal did not return to that city after 1115 until then.

William of Tyre contradicts himself, not me, when he prefaces associated papal letters as given on the same day to the aforesaid patriarch not at Benevento but at the Lateran. As for the Beneventan synod described above, which is also mentioned in the letters of Gelasius II to the archbishops and bishops of Gaul and others, quoted by Baronius from the aforesaid Malmesbury: Peter the Librarian is to be understood as speaking of it, not of the preceding Council of Troia, when he says in his *Life of Paschal*: “The lord pope, after holding the council which he had assembled in the regions of Apulia, returned with a Norman army into Campania”—that is, the region once called Latium—“and brought Pillo and Pullanum,” a town on the coast of St. Silvester, “into submission.” Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 61, calls it Pylium and says these events occurred at Pentecost. But the Librarian says: “Autumn was approaching, and heat and burning wearied the pontiff”; I should prefer “Summer was approaching.” And *Pullanum* is certainly Paliano.

Nor should the phrase “in the regions of Apulia” trouble you, since Benevento is not reckoned among them. At that time, and for some time afterwards, western foreigners commonly called the whole of Italy on this side of the Tiber “Apulia,” using the name of Apulia alone; and the inhabitants adopted this usage as well, because the Normans, through their initially glorious and successful achievements in Apulia, had drawn the attention of distant shores to themselves alone and to Apulia alone. Furthermore, the murder of Riso, archbishop of Bari, only briefly touched upon here by Falco, is described more fully by an Unknown citizen of the same city in his Chronicle, already mentioned above, as committed in the present year. Our author also refers Pope Paschal’s death to this year, in accordance with his own system of reckoning years. Paschal died, according to the aforesaid Librarian, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February and was buried on the eleventh day before them—our author has changed the day of burial into the day of death—that is, at the end of Falco’s year 1117 and the beginning of the common year 1118.

From the very brief narrative which Falco’s present text gives under the year described have fallen the matters which he says below under 1119 that he had previously noted concerning the destruction of Montemilitis and Monte Aperto. Indeed, they seem to have fallen from this passage and from no other. PEREGR.].

In this year Riso, archbishop of Bari, was murdered by Argyrus, a citizen of Bari, on the road to Canosa.

In this year Pope Paschal died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, and Pope Gelasius was elected.

In the year 1118 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Gelasius II, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in March, in the eleventh indiction: when the aforesaid pontiff Gelasius was elected to the papal throne by the unanimous vote and agreement of almost all the Roman people, he sent delegates into the regions of Apulia also, summoning them to attend the day of his consecration. [Col. 1169B] For, as we have related, when he was elected he was a deacon and chancellor, and could be consecrated only in the canonical season of fasting. When they received the summons, the bishop of Troia, [Col. 1170A] the archbishop of the city of Siponto, and many others hurried to the solemnity of his consecration.

But before the aforesaid elect Gelasius received the dignity of consecration, the aforesaid King Henry, having prepared ambushes, entered Rome in the silence of night, on the second day of March. The apostolic, secretly learning of the king’s entry, remembered how the king had captured his predecessor Pope Paschal and the cardinals by fraud and deceit. Without delay he summoned the cardinals, entered the river Tiber, and then, ploughing the sea with favourable winds, they reached Calenum [Note: [Col. 1170B] Did Gelasius, then, reach Calenum from Rome by sea? Pliny, indeed, in book III, chapter 5, places that city inland; but what of Pliny? Absolutely all writers place it farther from the sea. They call it not by this form, but by its original name—for *Calenum* is derivative—namely Cales. Thus although ancient writers frequently mention the Calenian municipality, citizen, territory, wine, battle, water, and so forth, you will scarcely find anyone besides Pliny who uses the simple name *Calenum*.

Almost all modern writers have fallen disgracefully into error here: either by wrongly distinguishing Cales from Calenum, or by correctly making the two cities one but perversely deciding that Calenum is now Carinola—which is itself inland—whereas it is in fact Calvi. They seem to have drawn the error from writers who lived after the Norman period and who were the first to begin calling Carinola *Calenum* in Latin. The Lombards, nearly eight hundred years ago, withdrew about two miles northward from the old city, called Forum Claudii, destroyed I know not by what accident—formerly Forum Poplium, according to Ptolemy, *Geography*, book III, table 6 of Europe; or Forum Popilium, according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I; but according to Pliny, book XIV, chapter 6, the Sullan colony, now an empty place called Civita rotta—and in a more defensible retreat built and named a new city, Calinium. But I have discussed these matters more fully elsewhere.

Meanwhile, since Calenum was never on the sea and it is not doubtful that Pope Gelasius then withdrew to his native city of Gaeta, it appears from an easy conjecture that the name *Cajeta* should be restored in Falco. He remained there for some time, was first consecrated priest and then pope before the Kalends of March, as Pandulf of Pisa reports in his Life; or, according to Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 64, in Lent. Our author speaks more precisely: “in the canonical season of fasting,” that is, in the spring Ember Days. For he was still a deacon when elected pope; in 1118 Ash Wednesday fell on the ninth, not before the octave of March. PEREGR.].

When the king learned of the apostolic’s departure, he sent to him at Calenum, asking him to return to the city, because he very gladly wished to be present at and confirm his consecration. But Pontiff Gelasius, thoroughly aware of his wickedness and the weapon of his treachery, said: “We are surprised at the messages of such a great man, since he recently informed us that he would come to us on the day of the Resurrection. Yet now we have learned that he has arrived by night and before the appointed time. I, with God’s assent, shall receive the confirmation of consecration; thereafter, wherever he wishes, he will find me ready for the business proposed.”

On hearing this, those who had been sent returned hastily to the king and reported to him everything they had heard from the aforesaid pontiff. Then the elect Gelasius, on the appointed day, was canonically and duly consecrated at Calenum by the cardinals who had left with him, in the March mentioned above.

When the king heard the pontiff’s reply, he devised a destructive plan: he appointed and consecrated as pontiff a certain Spanish archbishop—an invader of the Church, so to speak. [Col. 1171B] O crime and terrible danger! That king, who ought to have been defender and helper of the Roman See and of the whole Catholic Church, introduced a new heresy and dreadful kinds of death throughout the world. Therefore many Romans, whose minds remained steadfast in loyalty to the Roman Church, seeing and recognizing this heresy, said: “Alas, wretched men that we are! Formerly, by the ancient custom of our fathers, without the coming or permission of any king, we elected and consecrated whichever pastor we wished. But now, without the king’s permission, we shall no longer dare either elect or consecrate another.”

Then the aforesaid man and other Roman nobles [Note: [Col. 1171C] The passage is plainly mutilated, and also corrupt in the word *Calenum*, as I have said. What is missing here I cannot easily guess. Still, I would not deny that the authors of the letter were the same Roman nobles [Col. 1171D] who, as the aforesaid Pandulf of Pisa reports, rescued Gelasius from the hands of Cencius Frangipane. The pope received their letter through a messenger while staying at Capua, where he celebrated the following Easter with solemn ceremonial, according to both Pandulf and Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 64. Peter also says that he held a synod there and condemned King Henry and his idol, namely the antipope Burdinus, as Abbot Ekkehard of Aura says.

Perhaps at the same time Landulf of Greca, formerly constable of Benevento, as our author adds to the foregoing, sent his letter to the aforesaid Gelasius, reporting that Stephen, governor of Benevento, from the time Landulf had been deposed, had failed to administer justice to those in need and that, moreover, his houses and possessions had been destroyed by the Beneventans. But how Landulf came to be expelled again after he had received the aforesaid constableship once more in 1114 is not recorded in Falco. It is only possible to understand that this happened in 1117; for in August 1120 he was recalled to Benevento by Pope Callixtus, after living at Montefusco for three years. PEREGR.], after Gelasius had been canonically ordained at Calenum, sent envoys saying: “May it be known to Your Fatherhood, father and lord, that neither we [Col. 1171C] nor our friends have in any way lent counsel or aid to the consecration of that excommunicated man, wickedly made pontiff. And know that, with God’s help, the schemes and counsels of that most wicked man, the king, will shortly be destroyed; and you, by God’s favour, destroyer of error and malignity, will return with joy and honour to your proper see and place.”

After these things had been done, the aforesaid Landulf of Greca, formerly constable of Benevento, made his letters known to the aforesaid Gelasius and reported that Stephen, governor of Benevento, from the time Landulf himself had been deposed, had failed to do justice to those in need, and that, moreover, his houses and possessions had been destroyed by the Beneventans.

In this year the aforesaid Pope Gelasius went to Gaul on the second day of September and arrived at Pisa. When, as has been related, Pontiff Gelasius had come to the city of Pisa and consecrated the city’s archbishop, he took counsel and embarked on a ship; then, guided by divine mercy and favoured by favourable winds, he crossed the sea to the regions beyond the mountains. Immediately all the archbishops and bishops, and other nobles, received him with ineffable joy and immense honour. Thus received, Gelasius conferred with the aforesaid king of the English [Note: [Col. 1172C] The king of the English then was Henry I, [Col. 1172D] whom Falco had not previously mentioned. Gelasius, travelling into Gaul, could by no means have spoken with him. After the synod assembled at Vienne among the Allobroges at the beginning of 1119, Gelasius could not even address the king of the Franks except through messengers and letters; he personally addressed only lesser princes. Certainly the writers who describe the affairs of the aforesaid Henry do not record that he had a conference with any Roman pontiff except Callixtus II at Gisors and Innocent II at Chartres and Rouen.

Thus Falco is defective and, moreover, corrupt in this passage. If one understands him as speaking of a conference between the king and pope conducted by intermediaries, one makes him guilty of a most foolish expression; for by the same reasoning he ought not to have omitted that Gelasius also met the king of the Franks then. PEREGR.].

Thereafter the apostolic established that in the following March [Col. 1172B] he would hold a synod with the fathers of France and Germany, and there, through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, they would discuss at length the dispute between priesthood and kingship. But if I wished to describe in detail how much wealth and how many gifts of silver and gold that apostolic obtained in those regions, time would fail me before the abundance of material could be recounted. Yet before the appointed time for holding the synod arrived, he was overtaken by the burden of illness at the monastery of St. Peter called Cluny, where he was diligently residing. Immediately perceiving that he was being overcome by the severe collapse of his illness [Note: [Col. 1172D] This whole narrative, to the end of the present year, varies somewhat in Baronius. Compare the passages and follow whichever reading you judge the more genuine. PEREGR.], he ordered the bishop of Palestrina to be summoned and sought to lay upon him the summit of so great an honour, the Roman See. For he foresaw that, as human frailty requires, his body was about to dissolve.

Hearing the pontiff utter such words, the bishop replied: “Far be it, utterly far be it, that I, unworthy and unhappy, should undertake the summit of so great an honour and burden—especially when in our times the Roman See, subjected to the scourge of persecution, must be defended and fortified by God’s aid and by the power of temporal resources. But if you will accept my advice, let us elect the archbishop of Vienne, a man certainly religious, prudent in mind, and endowed with worldly capabilities, for so great a protection. For by God’s counsel, the merits of blessed Peter, and this man’s assistance, we believe that the Roman See, long oppressed amid the peril of such persecution, will be raised to serenity and triumph.”

Why say more? The bishop’s words pleased the sick Pope Gelasius, the other cardinals, and everyone else. Without delay they ordered that archbishop summoned, that they might fulfil and carry through their words in deed. Although the man called was wholly unwilling and declared himself unworthy of the summit of so great an office, nevertheless, by the ordering of heavenly mercy, while Gelasius was ill and consenting, he was advanced to the papal mitre. On the following day, Pope Gelasius, namely on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, happily departed from this prison of the world to the Lord at the aforesaid monastery.

Immediately, after taking counsel, the cardinals present there sent a careful delegation to Peter, bishop of Porto, whom Pope Gelasius had left at Rome as his vicar, informing him both of Gelasius’s death and of how they had elected that archbishop as Pope Callixtus. [Col. 1173B] On receiving the letter, the bishop of Porto was deeply grieved and shed tears over the death of the apostolic. At once he summoned the cardinals remaining with him and many faithful Romans, went up to the Capitol, displayed the letters that had been sent, and ordered them read. When they had been read, they praised the Lord Almighty with one voice and in agreement, because He had granted them as pontiff a prudent man endowed with good character. Yet they were deeply troubled by the death of Pope Gelasius.

When these things had been done, the aforesaid bishop, after taking counsel, arranged for an orderly message to be sent to Landulf, bishop of Benevento, to Hugh [Col. 1173C] the cardinal governing Benevento, and to the clergy and people of Benevento, announcing Gelasius’s death and Callixtus’s election. Landulf the bishop immediately had the citizens, all the priests, and the clergy of the episcopal church summoned to the sacred palace, in order to announce to them the course of events. When they had assembled, he ordered the letters read and explained. Without delay they unanimously approved and commended the election of the aforesaid Callixtus. Then they burst out singing *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God.” Thus the archbishop himself, Cardinal Hugh, a large throng of clergy, and a multitude of citizens descended singing from the aforesaid sacred palace to the episcopal church.

Afterwards, mounting a more elevated place, that bishop exhorted the citizens to maintain forever the hand of fidelity toward the Roman See. This done, they returned to their homes.

In the year 1119, and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Callixtus II, supreme pontiff and universal pope, [Col. 1174A] in March, in the twelfth indiction, in that same month of March the aforesaid archbishop of Benevento, seeing the city on every side thrown into confusion and devastation by various afflictions of plundering, and the churches of his diocese daily harassed by robbers, held a synod on the tenth day of that same March [Note: [Col. 1173D] At this Beneventan provincial synod, attended among others by Cardinal Hugh, whom Gelasius, when departing for Gaul, had appointed governor of Benevento, Archbishop Landulf pronounced a sentence of excommunication against those disturbing the property and affairs of the Beneventans. But Landulf of Pisa indicates that Hugh then performed outstanding service for the city’s defence: “The guardianship of the apostolic city of Benevento was entrusted to Cardinal Hugh by Gelasius, as we afterwards saw, not without an oracle of the Holy Spirit; for shortly afterward, when the pope died, unless Hugh had resisted and shrewdly opposed them in a thousand ways, the Normans, not the pope, would hold it today.”

Since it is clear that Falco says not a word concerning these successes, one must judge him deficient through injury done by another, his own negligence, or deliberate ill-will. He notes quite briefly, under this and the following year, that the aforesaid Hugh and Landulf maintained friendship with Jordan, count of Ariano and other places, a Norman by birth, against Rainulf, count of Avellino, Calatia, and many other towns, likewise a Norman, and his followers. Hugh’s energy, therefore, should be credited with preventing all those nobles from conspiring together at that time to the detriment of Benevento. PEREGR.].

The bishop of Tusculum was present at this sacred gathering, along with the aforesaid Cardinal Hugh and another cardinal; about twenty suffragan bishops of the Beneventan see and six abbots of monasteries were also present. Among the other measures established in this assembly, he bound under the bond of anathema all wrongdoers in Benevento and those who molested merchants coming to and returning from the city. When the assembly had been piously and duly concluded, each person returned home.

[Col. 1174B] Concerning the war of the aforesaid Count Jordan and Count Rainulf, if it please your charity, I shall relate something briefly. And since, as has been said, the castles of Montemiletto and Monteaperto had already been destroyed, the aforesaid Robert of Montefusco very frequently attacked another castle called Tufo. In order to alarm its lord and inhabitants by various terrors, he fiercely assailed it with continual engines of war. Then, upon an unheard-of report of death, having devised a plan, he ravaged with fire and sword the peasants’ crops, vineyards, and woods. He ordered the newly sown crops of the peasants—something never heard of since the beginning of time—to be turned over again and laid waste with rakes and ploughs.

But the lord of the castle, named Rao, disturbed neither by the storms of war nor by such deadly devastation, held that castle manfully and courageously in fidelity to Count Jordan. Moreover, Robert, Count Jordan’s already-mentioned uncle, daily plotted gatherings for sedition and hurled threats against him, being of a viperous heart. For he very often conferred with Count Rainulf and Robert of Montefusco concerning attacks upon Count Jordan himself and the dangers of losses to him. At last, disclosing the secret purposes of his heart which he was continually meditating, he asked Count Jordan for the castle called Templanum, so that he might remain his faithful man and friend all his days. His purpose was that the count should secure that castle by oath to a certain natural son of his [Col. 1174D] whom he loved.

When the count heard this, he was struck with distress of mind beyond belief and marvelled greatly at it. At once he summoned all his [Col. 1175A] barons and diligently sought their counsel on so great and such a matter. Recognizing both the count’s pressing circumstances and Robert’s treachery of heart, and seeing that he could not otherwise be brought back to fidelity toward the count, they advised him to grant his requests in every respect. Thus, after counsel had been discussed and confirmed in the presence of Archbishop Landulf, Cardinal Hugh, and other Beneventan magnates who had assembled for so great a spectacle, he fulfilled all Robert’s demands. Then, through the mediation of an oath, Robert became a faithful man and *canonicus* of Count Jordan.

> **Note: [Col. 1175D]** Clearly, when he received the castle of Templanum as a fief from Jordan, he became his *canonicus*, that is, his tributary; for a payment was commonly once called a *canon*, because it was paid according to a fixed rule or canon. Thus in Cassiodorus, book II, letter 25, occur “canonical solidi,” and in book XII, letter 13, and elsewhere, *canonicarii* are officials who exacted such payments. On these see also Cujas, in his exposition of Justinian’s Novel 128.  
> 
> Moreover, a little later in Falco I read: “he captured twelve of their knights, taking all their arms; among them the knight named Eternus and Brianus were brought captive to Ariano”: not “Eternus and Arianus.” PEREGR.

After these things had been done, he obtained one hundred knights for his service. Immediately, returning the favour for what he had received, he ravaged all the crops of the knights of Montefusco.

[Col. 1175B] It happened that one day, when Landulf of Greca, constable of Montefusco, was proceeding toward the already-mentioned castle called Tufo, surrounded by a troop of knights, Count Jordan, lying in ambush, attacked them, overthrew them, and captured twelve of their knights, taking all their weapons. Among these, the knight named Eternus and Brianus were led away captive. When Count Rainulf heard of the immense slaughter of his faithful men and could not bear to be so overcome by Count Jordan, he assembled a force of nearly four hundred knights and a multitude of foot-soldiers. Once they had been assembled, he repeatedly threatened to enter Count Jordan’s land and consume one of his castles with fire and sword. At last, taking that force of knights and foot-soldiers, he entered Count Jordan’s [Col. 1175C] territory. Yet, as he himself had often said, he did not dare attack one of Jordan’s castles or make preparation for the sound of war; rather, in order to enhance the glory of his own name and frighten Count Jordan, he entered the borders of the castle called Pesclum, and then returned home without any engagement having been prepared by his men.

But Count Jordan, being of prudent and wise disposition, recognized Count Rainulf’s insolence and understood that such boldness did not proceed from the treasuries of the wise. Accompanied by a troop of three hundred knights, he remained strictly about Rainulf’s borders. His purpose was not foolishly to pursue that count, but, should necessity arise, manfully to defend his own fortifications.

In this fifteenth year, on the day beginning the month of May, Archbishop Landulf of Benevento, mentioned above, having formed a salutary plan, publicly displayed before all the bodies of Saints Martian, Dorus, Potitus, Prosper, Felix, Cervelus, and Stephen, which from ancient times had lain in an unworthy [Col. 1176A] tomb.

> **Note: [Col. 1175D]** I restore “on the thirteenth day beginning,” for Landulf, after taking the holy relics from their ancient tomb in order to place them in a more fitting sepulchre, displayed them openly to all the Beneventan people, after two days had elapsed—namely, from 14 May through the next eight days, that is, until the twenty-first. Finally, on the following morning, “on the next day,” Falco says, namely, on “the tenth day remaining” of the month of May—that is, when ten days of that month remained, on the twenty-second—he placed them in the prepared coffin. Elsewhere I have noted that the Beneventans assembled by districts to celebrate vigils in honour of these saints throughout each of the said eight days, and that Falco omits the names of two districts. PEREGR.

After the bodies had thus been brought out, the aforesaid bishop ordered two of their bones to be placed before the eyes of all the citizens with great reverence, so that they might believe. Therefore, when the report spread through the city, a great concourse of men and women gathered; rushing forward, they wept, kissed those bones, and offered gifts. I myself, unworthy as I am, kissed those bones of the saints.

Two days after the bodies of those saints had been brought forth, the aforesaid bishop ordered all the priests of the city to be summoned to the episcopal residence, that they might discuss the praises to be rendered to such great saints. At once, after taking counsel, he commanded that first the priests of Porta Summa should come down to the episcopal residence rejoicing, [Col. 1176B] with candles and lamps, and chant praises to God and to the saints before their bones; second, the priests of Porta Aurea; third, those of Porta Ruffina; fourth, those of the outer district; fifth, those of the new city; and lastly the priests and men of the whole city. Thus, gathered as one in honour of God and of those saints, they might invoke the mercy of almighty God, that through the saints’ intercessions they might obtain forgiveness of sins.

The priests, hearing their shepherd’s commands, carried them out as he had ordered and came down in due order to the saints’ bodies with innumerable praises. If you, reader, had seen the crowd of men, women, and poor people singing before and behind, with candles raised high and lit, you would have rejoiced beyond human measure at [Col. 1176C] so great a joy and poured forth from the depths of your heart a stream of tears. You would have seen an unprecedented procession, and what the city of Benevento had not done in many years: it was now doing it for the honour and love of the saints.

Indeed, I call the King of heaven to witness that, even if my tongue uttered triple sounds and my voice were driven by an unceasing plectrum, I could in no way set down the weight of such joy and the abundance of such praises. Who among citizens living in this time could remember the city ever rejoicing in this way? I believe that when Blessed Bartholomew the Apostle, patron of the city, came, the city was likewise wholly filled with great joy.

For, so that the memory of the Beneventans might be exalted for two generations, all the abbots [Col. 1176D] of the churches, with great zeal, constructed wooden contrivances fashioned with marvellous workmanship. The priests of the new city, in order to appear more zealous [Col. 1177A] than all the rest, brought to the saints’ bodies a certain wooden machine entirely covered with innumerable candles and lamps. Beneath it we saw young men leaping about with drums and ringing citharas. We saw many bells and little bells within that structure. Finally, priests clothed in white, with banners and a great accompaniment of candles, chanted before the saints’ bones.

At last, Archdeacon Archisius, seeing such extraordinary and great rejoicing take place in every quarter and corner of the city, took counsel and ordered a marvellous wooden structure to be made in honour of the church of Saint Lawrence, which he governed, and of the whole city.
