There, reader, if you had been present, [Col. 1177B] you would have seen many craftsmen; there you would have seen hands at work in zealous labour. By their skill it was made in the likeness of a little ship. When it had been completed, he ordered a bell of great weight, many other sounding metal instruments, and many lighted candles to be placed upon it. He also placed there a man playing the lyre and trumpets shrieking toward the stars; around it horns clattered, drums were struck wonderfully, citharas and melodies of diverse kinds danced forth.

O reader, what exultation and what joy throughout every part of the city you would have seen had you been there! Truly, you would have thought and believed that another life and another condition of heart, eye, and body were being imitated. When such and so great music had been performed, to raise the archdeacon’s glory he yoked oxen to that structure, [Col. 1177C] and with the oxen yoked they drew it as far as the church of Saint Andrew. Then, because of the density of the buildings standing over the streets, the oxen could not draw it as far as the episcopal residence. At once, the machine, so heavy, was brought by the hands of many men to the saints’ bodies. When it had been brought there, the archdeacon himself and a company of clergy dressed in white sang vigils before the saints’ bones. When these were finished, each of us returned home.

On the next day, the aforesaid bishop—namely, on the tenth day remaining in the month of May—together with the bishops of Frigento, Monte Marano, and Ariano, placed the saints’ bodies in their resting place. Among them he included the body of Blessed John XXI, Archbishop of Benevento, who, as his inscription testified, had lived thirty-three years in the episcopate; likewise the body of Stephen the Levite, and the body of another saint whose name was unknown. The body of Bishop John himself, of Stephen the Levite, and of the other saint had been found beside the altar in which they rested, before the discovery of the aforesaid Saints Martian [Col. 1178A] and his companions.

For their venerable dedication, the archbishop remitted a fourth part of sins to all who had assembled to visit the saints. He granted the same also to all others who should come to this dedication up to the coming octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul. He also placed under the bond of excommunication all who should commit wrongdoing against those assembled for the dedication of such great saints.

In this year Landulf, Archbishop of Benevento, died on the fourth day beginning the month of August; and Roffrid, then archpriest, was elected.

[Col. 1178B] In this year, on the seventh day remaining in February, Judge Alferius of Porta Aurea died.

In the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Callistus II, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the month of March, the thirteenth indiction: in this year, in May, three days before the feast of Saint Eustace, there came a great flooding of the river Calore, such as no living person at that time could remember.

At the same time Count Rainulf, whom we have mentioned, having assembled an innumerable troop of knights and foot-soldiers together with Robert of Montefusco, advanced upon the aforesaid castle called Tufo. At once they climbed a certain heavily fortified hill. There, wonderfully constructing fortifications against the castle, [Col. 1178C] they surrounded it with ditch and rampart and set up wooden engines on every side. Having thus fortified the place, they very frequently and fiercely attacked Tufo. But Rao, lord of the castle, resisted manfully.

When Count Jordan heard that Count Rainulf had constructed fortifications against the castle of Tufo and had made every preparation for war, without delay he gathered an abundant force of horsemen and foot-soldiers and made for the castle called Montefalcone, not far from Count Rainulf’s tents. He then ordered Cardinal Hugh, governor of Benevento, Stephen the rector, and Roffrid the elect to be summoned.

> **Note: [Col. 1177D]** At this point, Falco, I would have wished you to be somewhat more careful. When you call Cardinal Hugh the governor and Stephen the rector, you imply that these were distinct offices, one superior to the other, and held by men of unequal rank. You do the same in the year 1127, where you speak of Walter, Archbishop of Taranto, governing Benevento, and William then rector with him. Yet you have yourself invented the distinction between these titles and do not openly explain the difference between their offices. More than once you call “rectors” indiscriminately both those who probably possessed the supreme power and those who had lesser authority. Indeed, in the year 1129 you say that Gerard the cardinal, appointed in place of the aforesaid Rector William, held not exactly the same, as I suppose, but a higher dignity [Col. 1178D] already mentioned. A holder of that rank customarily had under him an official, a lesser rector, as may be learned from Falco himself for the year 1137:
>
> “Before Pope Innocent left the city, he appointed Octavius the subdeacon, a prudent man of wise mind, rector of Benevento; together with Lord Cardinal Gerard, he diligently governed the condition of the city and the maintenance of peace.”
>
> Or the constable himself was lower in rank. The same author says in the year 1132 that supporters of Pope Innocent appointed Gerard, cardinal priest, rector of the Beneventans, and on another day conferred the office and authority of the constableship upon Rolpoto of Saint Eustasius. Thus appointed, he began with that cardinal to govern the state of the curia and distribute to each person the force of justice. The constableship, like that lesser rectorship, was regarded as the authority next below the supreme rector, [Col. 1179C] and every other office was inferior to them.
>
> Hence Landulf of Greca was compelled by the seditious Beneventans to confirm on oath—Falco’s words for the year 1114—that he would not accept the constableship, the rectorship, or any public *balia* (office of authority). Although one was endowed with a military and the other with a civil function, yet in Falco we do not find fixed laws at Benevento by which both were observed together; now one, now the other was employed. If, according to the demands of the time, arms had to be borne, a man suited to conducting war was placed in charge. Under the title of military magistrate he held both powers. Hence the aforesaid Constable Rolpoto is said to have governed the state of the curia and distributed the force of justice to each person; and in the year 1133, to have vigorously governed the curia with the faithful of Blessed Peter. But if no occasion for arms was present, not a constable but a rector was appointed; even he, as opportunity required, led knights forth to war, as is said of Rector William in the year 1127.
>
> Since these offices were interchangeable, as has been said, we now understand why Landulf of Greca, formerly Beneventan constable, sent letters to Pope Gelasius reporting that the Beneventan rector Stephen [Col. 1180D] had failed, since Landulf himself had been deposed, to administer justice to those in need. Therefore the constables and those lesser rectors, whether designated by one title or the other, presided equally over judicial and military contests; and, by the same reasoning, both cares were customarily entrusted to the supreme rectors themselves. “Pope Honorius,” says Falco for the year 1127, “commanded Walter, Archbishop of Taranto, to come to Benevento, diligently care for the affairs of the city, and defend the city by his counsel.” And for the year 1137 he says that Pope Innocent addressed the Beneventan people as follows:
>
> “We permit Cardinal Gerard to remain with you; he will watch continually over your interests and preserve peace among you.”
>
> Yet the rectors managed this peace only after taking counsel regarding the public order of the city—or, as they then said, after consultation with the judges. “The friends,” says Falco for the year 1131, “of Cardinal Crescentius himself and the aforesaid judges came courageously to him and urged him to maintain the state of the curia together with them.” PEREGR.

Having summoned them, Jordan sent them to Count Rainulf, instructing them to say that he would willingly receive justice from Count Rainulf and would himself render him justice. Hearing this, the count promised both to receive justice and willingly to pursue it. Why say more? They abandoned Tufo and gathered at the bridge of Saint Valentine, where a great throng of magnates assembled. Immediately, before all, faith having been given and received, they firmly confirmed a truce from the seventh day remaining in May until the Kalends of September; and in that truce they also established peace for the city of Benevento.

In this year, on the fifth day remaining in May, the Capuans appointed as their lord Prince Richard, son of Prince Robert, because his father the prince was ill. Once he had been appointed, the Archbishop of Capua, having summoned bishops and other prudent men, together with Roffrid, elect of Benevento, consecrated that prince on the Day of the Lord’s Ascension, the fifth day remaining in that May. On the eighth day after the consecration of this son, his father [Col. 1179B] the prince departed from this world. The son of that prince, after being consecrated, lived ten days. When he died, they appointed Jordan, brother of the aforesaid Prince Robert, to the dignity of the principality.

In this year the aforesaid Pope Callistus returned from the regions beyond the mountains and entered Rome on the ninth day beginning June. Therefore Peter, Bishop of Porto, then vicar with the other cardinals remaining at Rome, together with other companies of clergy and men and women alike, hurried out to meet that pontiff. Reader, had you seen the joy and delight of the Roman people, you would have said in wonder at their rejoicing that no pontiff had entered the City under such honour and triumph [Col. 1179C].

When Cardinal Hugh, then governing the city of Benevento, heard of the apostolic lord’s arrival, he hurried to Rome, and many citizens went with him. In the same year, on the ninth day beginning July, Rao, lord of Ceppaloni, died.

In this year Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia, passed to the Lord on the third day before the Kalends of August. After the death of that abbot, a certain party of monks, on the last day remaining in July, elected as abbot a monk named Ademarius, nephew of Abbot Madelmus. The venerable dean John, John the grammarian—a man in every respect worthy of praise—Rao the priest and monk, and other wise monks did not consent to his election. Consequently, an unspeakable discord arose among them.

In this year our lord Pope Callistus, having taken counsel, came to Benevento and entered the city on the eighth day beginning August. When the Beneventan people heard of his long and widely desired arrival, filled with great joy, they came out two miles beyond the city. At last the apostolic lord was received by clergy, a multitude of monks, priests, and all the citizens with great glory and joy. Furthermore, all the Amalfitans adorned all the streets [Col. 1180B] for his arrival with silken garments, mantles, and precious ornaments. Beneath the decorations they placed golden and silver censers with perfumes and cinnamon. Four citizens led the feet of the apostolic lord and the reins of his horse from the Leper’s Bridge to the Gate of Saint Lawrence; then four others led him to the episcopal residence; and from the episcopal residence four judges—John, Persicus, [lacuna], and Landulf—escorted him to the sacred Beneventan Palace.

Reader, had you been present in the apostolic lord’s company and seen drums struck, cymbals ringing, and lyres sounding, you would truly have declared that no other apostolic lord had entered a city amid such triumph and joy. Not many days later, several citizens who had been friends of Landulf, the former [Col. 1180C] constable, petitioned the apostolic lord to grant him leave to live in the city. The constable had lived at Montefusco for three years. Pope Callistus, therefore, favouring the prayers of his faithful men, granted permission as they requested. They immediately went out to meet Landulf with Count Jordan, who had come on his behalf, and brought him into the city.

When Pope Callistus heard of the discord prevailing among the brothers of the monastery of Saint Sophia over the election of the aforesaid Ademarius, [Col. 1181A] he came to the monastery. Having assembled the brothers, he spoke fully and sufficiently about this election. At last, once the truth of the matter was known and it had been established that the election was neither canonical nor regular, it was judged null and void by Peter, Bishop of Porto, and the other cardinals who had gathered there. This was immediately confirmed by Pope Callistus. Why say more? He granted the brothers permission to elect whomever they wished as abbot. When this was done, the apostolic lord returned to the palace.

On the next day, the fourteenth day beginning August, the entire body of brothers entered their usual chapter-house. There, by the mediation of the Holy Spirit, they deliberated fully concerning the election to be made. Meanwhile the aforesaid venerable Dean John selected a brother suitable to bear so great a burden [Col. 1181B] and disclosed the person to the assembled brothers. He then asked each one whether the person was pleasing to him. With one voice and one accord they cried that he was worthy—worthy indeed. About fifty brothers had assembled; and while they were crying out, they seized that person, John the grammarian, a prudent man adorned with good character, and, though unwilling and resisting, with rejoicing caused him to sit in the abbatial chair. Before us all he cried aloud that he was unworthy and unfortunate.

Then the venerable sacred rite was performed, and a monk placed the pastoral staff in his hand; they established him in the chapter-house in the place of abbot. Immediately the dean first, then all the brothers, prostrated themselves at his feet according to custom, and he gave each the kiss of peace. After he had been elected, the community sent a messenger to Pope Callistus, reporting that John the grammarian had been elected. When the apostolic lord heard that the election had been conducted according to rule, it pleased him and he confirmed it.

Not many days later, the aforesaid Pope Callistus came to the monastery of Saint Sophia and, during the solemnities of Mass, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, consecrated as abbot the aforesaid John the grammarian, whom the monastic community had elected. On the day of his consecration, the dedication of the altar of Blessed Mercurius was celebrated at Saint Sophia.

Not many days later, Pope Callistus first set a delay concerning the election of the aforesaid Roffrid, so that he might be consecrated at the appointed time of the September fast. [Col. 1181D] When that time came, he ordained him priest in the sacred Beneventan Palace with great honour and care. On the following Sunday, before ten bishops, suffragans of the see of Benevento, he raised him to the episcopal mitre. Among them was the venerable John, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia. On the day of his consecration, the feast of Saint Januarius was celebrated.

In this year, two days after the consecration of the aforesaid Archbishop Roffrid, Pope Callistus, having taken counsel, deposed Stephen, who had then been rector, [Col. 1182A] and appointed as rector the deacon Rossemannus, son of the monk Rossemannus.

In the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Callistus II, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in March, the fourth indiction.

> **Note: [Col. 1181D]** The printer omitted the numeral denoting ten; for this year was reckoned as the fourteenth indiction. PEREGR.

In this year Lady Labinia, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary at Porta Summa, was seized by a severe illness. Seeing that she was approaching the passage of death, she took counsel and ordered all the handmaids of God, her sisters, to be summoned. When they had been called, she addressed them thus:

> “I believe, dearest sisters, that your prudence is not unaware how many labours I have endured for this monastery and for your beloved community. Hence, with God’s favour and the aid of your prayers, the condition of this monastery has flourished [Col. 1182B] and attained the summit of perfection. But now, as you see, I am held in the danger of a severe illness, and I am certain that I shall soon be released from this body. I therefore humbly ask your fellowship to favour my requests, especially since, God being witness, I shall ask nothing of you except what benefits the monastery. For I have foreseen in my heart that after my departure discord over the election will arise and the monastery’s affairs will suffer harm. Therefore, if it please your charity, let this dissension be removed while I yet live, and let us appoint as abbess the person whom I shall name.”

Why say more? She named Bethlehem, daughter of Count Gerard of the Greeks. When they heard the name of the person, she pleased them, and they approved the effort toward the election. After these things, the aforesaid Lady Abbess Labinia passed [Col. 1182C] to the Lord. Immediately they ordered Roffrid, Archbishop of Benevento, and Rachisius, Abbot of Saint Modestus, to be summoned, that they might confirm and establish the action. Favouring their petition, they confirmed it. Not many days later the archbishop himself came to the monastery and consecrated that abbess according to the order of the Rule, while we and many other men looked on. John, the venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia, and the aforesaid Rachisius, Abbot of Saint Modestus, attended her consecration on the fourth day beginning April.

In this year, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June, Robert of Montefusco was torn to pieces with swords at Benevento by Roger, son of Trogisius, and his brothers. Alas for the wretch! Reader, had you seen him with his head horribly cut, his limbs divided and scattered in pieces, you would have been moved to pour out a fountain of tears over him and marvel at so great and terrible a murder. The aforesaid John, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia, hurried with certain brothers to the corpse; and, seeing it, he was marvellously horrified and wept still more marvellously. Without delay he ordered the man, bloodied in this fashion, to be carried to the monastery, where they buried him according to the rite for Christians who had been slain.

> **Note: [Col. 1181D]** Aymoin of Fleury described this rite somewhat more clearly in his *Life of Saint Abbo*, chapter 20, when treating of Abbo’s death: “For some time there was doubt as to where he ought to be laid. Then it was agreed by all that, since he had been killed innocently and for the truth, which is Christ, he should be laid in the church”; and below: “On the morning of Wednesday, he was buried in a stone sarcophagus, unwashed, in the very garments in which he was clothed, as is the custom for those who have been slain.”
>
> He says “unwashed,” because in earlier times the bodies of deceased persons were commonly washed before burial and dressed, so far as possible, in more becoming clothing. But this was not done for those killed without cause, because it was believed that, if their blood had not been washed away, it would cry unceasingly to divine vengeance against their assailants, according to what is read in Genesis 4: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.” But King Chilperic, another Nero of his time, as Gregory of Tours states in *History*, book VI, final chapter, when he had been killed, was washed, clothed in finer garments, and buried in the Basilica of Saint Vincent at Paris. PEREGR.

Immediately Count Jordan hurried to Montefusco and, after agreements had intervened, brought that castle under his own authority.

[Col. 1183A] In the same year, the aforesaid Pope Callistus, having assembled an army, advanced upon the city called Sutri. That Gregory whom the aforesaid king had made pope held that city. Why delay longer? Having gathered their forces, they captured the city and bound Gregory, shamefully afflicted with injuries beyond belief. Then they placed him upon a camel and brought him captive to Rome, stripped of his own clothes, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May. Pope Callistus, giving thanks to God and to the Apostle Peter and filled with great joy, entered the City in triumph. Then, having taken counsel, he sent Gregory to the monastery of the Holy [Col. 1183B] Trinity called Cava.

After these things had been done, the aforesaid Pope Callistus, having taken counsel, went to Salerno on the fifth day beginning September, in order to confirm the security of peace with Duke William and Count Roger.

> **Note: [Col. 1183D]** Falco says that these events occurred after Callistus had forcibly dragged the antipope Maurice from the city of Sutri and sent him to the monastery of the Holy Trinity called Cava—the first time he was sent there, as has been noted on the Cassinese Anonymous. Indeed, Baronius also agrees that Maurice came into Callistus’s power in this year, 1121, which, as we have explained concerning the aforesaid Anonymous, had not happened earlier.
>
> Yet the same Duke William, as Romuald of Salerno reports—and Baronius follows him—had in the preceding year, before the antipope’s capture, become the liege man of Pope Callistus in the Beneventan palace, receiving the duchy from him by a banner; and in the same month he received the pope most dutifully when he came to Troia. Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 68, gives an account not inconsistent with this: Callistus went down from Benevento to Troia and, after receiving fealty from Duke [Col. 1184C] William according to the custom of his predecessors, returned to Rome and afterwards captured Maurice.
>
> I would not rashly deny faith to these authors. Yet I consider that this was not done at Benevento, for Falco—who describes at greater length the many things Callistus did there—would not have passed it over in silence; rather, it was first done at Troia, which seems to have been the reason why the pope proceeded there, and finally was done again at Salerno in 1121, with the intervention also of Count Roger of Sicily. PEREGR.

In this year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, Alfanus, Archbishop of Salerno, died. After his death, the aforesaid Pope Callistus consecrated Romuald, cardinal deacon, Archbishop of Salerno in the middle of September.

In this year Robert the Slav died on the tenth day remaining in December, as did Rachisius, Abbot of Saint Modestus. At his death John the Venerable, Abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia, hurried there with certain brothers. He immediately conveyed the body, prepared according to custom, [Col. 1184A] to the monastery for burial; then, after the funeral rites had been completed, it was placed in a marble tomb.

I shall also explain another matter, if it please you. On the seventh day before the Kalends of March, Agnes, abbess of the monastery of St Peter the Apostle, situated within the city of Benevento, went up to the sacred palace at Benevento and lodged a complaint against Bethlehem, abbess of the monastery of St Mary, built at the Upper Gate. She maintained that Bethlehem had been made abbess of the aforesaid monastery of St Mary against Agnes’s will, affirming that this monastery lay under her jurisdiction and was subject to the monastery of Blessed Peter. When the Apostolic Lord heard this:

> [Note: On the seventh day before the Kalends of March, at the end of Falconian year 1121 and the beginning of the common year 1122, before Callixtus, then staying at Benevento, Falco reports that Agnes, abbess of the monastery of St Peter the Apostle, brought a complaint against Bethlehem, abbess of St Mary. By this statement, though not in any clearer wording, he disclosed that the pope, having left Salerno, had gone to Benevento. At that time, I think, Abbot Suger of St Denis encountered him at the city of Benevento in Apulia—by which he means all this Italy on this side of the Tiber, as he himself says in the *Life of Louis the Fat*—having been sent there by King Louis on certain affairs of the realm. [Col. 1184D] The corrupted manuscript reads “Botontum,” not Beneventum; nor is it Bitonto, as Baronius reads it, who assigns this to Callixtus’s preceding arrival among us, when in fact Callixtus went on into Apulia and to Troia. That this happened in 1122, when Callixtus was again at Benevento, must be admitted on Suger’s own testimony: he says that the antipope Maurice had already been defeated and that in the following year the same pope held the Lateran council, which is known to have occurred in 1123, as I shall say shortly. But I do not know whom the author there means by the robbers of Italy and Apulia then subdued by Callixtus. In any case, Baronius overlooked this second arrival of Callixtus at Benevento, though Falco did not. PEREGR.]

he ordered the aforesaid Bethlehem to be summoned [Col. 1184B], so that justice might be done in the matter. She came at once, heard the complaint, and through her advocates replied that she ought not to give credence to Agnes’s assertions unless they were proved by written evidence.

Then, because the Apostolic Lord was very ill and could not hold court in his presence, he instructed Dionysius, bishop of Tusculum, Chrysogonus the chancellor, Robert of Bari, and other cardinals to act as judges in this affair and, after examining the evidence, settle the dispute between the two monasteries. This was done.

When these proceedings had taken place, the aforesaid Abbess Agnes, through her advocate, produced a privilege by which Leoprand, formerly duke of the city of Benevento, had granted and conveyed the aforesaid church of St Mary with all its appurtenances under the right and lordship [Col. 1185A] of the aforesaid monastery of St Peter the Apostle. She also produced privileges by which Prince Pandulf and his successors had confirmed that same church of St Mary under the authority of the aforementioned monastery of Blessed Peter. Again she presented other privileges and documentary evidences belonging to that monastery.

In response, Bethlehem, abbess of the monastery of St Mary, through her advocate produced documents and instruments belonging to the same monastery. They contained proof that, during the preceding fifty years down to the present, an abbess had continuously presided over the monastery of St Mary. The first of these had been named Labinia, the second Sicelgarda, and others whose names were read in their documents. We ourselves remember from recent times that Abbess [Col. 1185B] Labinia was the second to preside over that monastery. Likewise, the same evidences stated that the women placed over the monastery had independently presided over and conducted its causes and affairs.

When the privileges and documents of both sides had been produced and read, the aforesaid cardinal-judges withdrew and delivered their judgment upon the complaints they had heard. After deliberating on the judgment, they communicated it, by common counsel, to Lord Pope Callixtus, that he might confirm the decision which they had reached. Pope Callixtus immediately confirmed and ratified their determination. The judgment was as follows: that henceforth and forever the aforesaid monastery of St Mary should have its own abbess, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff; and that [Col. 1185C] the community of sisters living in that monastery of St Mary should have power to elect whichever abbess it wished, provided always that the portion of that monastery should annually pay to the aforesaid monastery of St Peter the customary due: namely, four offerings and two candles at the Nativity of the Lord; the same at the Resurrection; and the same at the Assumption of Blessed Mary.

The Apostolic Lord ordered the judgment itself to be put in writing and directed that it be attested by all the aforesaid cardinals appointed as judges in the matter. In this written judgment the pontiff himself subscribed with his own hand. Once the judgment had thus been confirmed and ratified, he entrusted it to the venerable Abbess Bethlehem, adorned with the testimony of so many and such distinguished cardinals, so that henceforth and for perpetual [Col. 1185D] ages the portion of her monastery might remain undisturbed and free from any harassment or molestation on the part of St Peter. Furthermore, by a sealed privilege he confirmed the same monastery of St Mary with all the possessions belonging to it, so that it might remain inviolate at all times and retain its force without opposition from anyone.

[Col. 1186A] In the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the fourth year of the pontificate of the aforesaid Lord Callixtus II, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in March, the fifteenth indiction:

In this year Duke William, son of Duke Roger, went down to Count Roger, son of Roger, count of the Sicilians, complaining of Count Jordan of Ariano and asking him to grant an aiding hand, the strength of his knights, and financial resources, so that through his aid he might take vengeance upon Count Jordan. When the duke arrived before that count, he began his appeal with many prayers and tears:

“Most excellent count, I have come down to your power, both because of the bond of kinship and because of the greatness of your wealth, to complain of Count Jordan and humbly request that, protected by your aid [Col. 1186B], I may take vengeance on him. For when one day I was entering the city of Nusco, behold, Count Jordan came before the gate of that city, surrounded by a troop of his knights, and, heaping many insults and reproaches upon me, threatened: ‘I shall cut short your cloak.’

> [Note: In Holy Scripture, 2 Samuel 10, Hanun, also as an insult, cut the garments of David’s servants in half, up to the buttocks. The Septuagint reads “mantles,” a reading our author seems to have followed. Likewise Guarinus, Chancellor of King Roger, in Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 100, loudly declared that he would inflict similar insults by similar threats upon the monks of Monte Cassino: he said that he would cut off their lips and noses, and cut their garments in half up to the buttocks. Because those subjected to this insult, once so commonly inflicted, attempted to cover both private parts with their hands as they departed, it gave occasion for the customary jibe applied to people whom we note to have returned, or to be returning, to their homes in disgrace. PEREGR.]

“Then, ranging all around the city of Nusco, he thoroughly plundered it. Since I could not prevail against him, I endured it unwillingly and asked for a day of vengeance.” After this, that count dishonoured us at all times with many and various injuries. Why say more? The duke granted the same count one half of his shares in the city of Palermo, Messina, and all Calabria, that he might give him aid in all these matters. Immediately the count gave him six hundred knights and five hundred ounces of gold [Col. 1186C].

Without delay the duke advanced against the land of Count Jordan. On the feast-day of St John the Baptist he took the castle of Roseto and many other places from him. Then, on the feast of Saints John and Paul, he attacked the castle of Montegiove, destroyed it with fire and sword, captured fifty knights there, and joyfully carried away their arms and spoils. Proceeding thence, he besieged the castle of Apice, where the count was staying. Crescentius the cardinal, then rector of Benevento, hastened to the duke’s aid with a company of Beneventans. In short, he brought both that count and the castle of Apice under his control.

Count Jordan therefore threw himself at the duke’s feet—as we ourselves who were present saw—and begged mercy [Col. 1186D]. The duke, compelled by many entreaties, especially those of Count Rainulf, who was present, released him and allowed him to go wherever he wished. The count hurried to Montefusco; and after these events he submitted the city of Ariano and the borders of his entire county to the duke’s authority.

When Count Jordan had gone up to Montefusco, he remained there fifteen days. Immediately Landulf of Greca, his adversary, after securing a conspiracy, expelled him from Montefusco. Thus expelled, Jordan went to the castle of Morcone and lived there for a year. When these things had been done, the duke besieged Montecorvino, near Salerno. Lord Fulco, the lord of that castle, being unable to resist, submitted the castle to the duke’s authority.

At the same time Richard, son of Guarinus of Formari, was murdered by his peasants. When the aforesaid duke heard that Richard had been murdered in this manner, he gathered an army and hurried to Montevico. He took unheard-of vengeance upon the murderers, destroyed that castle with fire and sword, and hanged by the noose two priests who had consented to Richard’s death.

After these and other affairs had been concluded, the duke sent back to Count Roger the knights whom he had received from him [Col. 1187B]. When Count Jordan, as we have said, had been disinherited, he took the Castle of the Marsh by a plan devised with the counsel of Hugh the Infant, Raoul of Bosco, and Raoul of Fraineta. When the aforesaid duke heard that the castle had been taken, he gathered an army and besieged it for three months. At length, seeing that it could not be captured so quickly, he asked Prince Jordan of Capua to bring him assistance; and in return for that assistance he granted him the castle of Apice and Acerra.

Immediately the prince gathered an army, came before the castle of Apice, and encamped on this side in the plain. Moreover, the duke instructed the Beneventans to give assistance neither to himself nor to Count Jordan; and he gave and [Col. 1187C] granted them all the *fidantiae* and payments issuing from the lands of the Beneventans, from the castle of Fenuculo to the castle of Montefuscolo. This pleased the Beneventans, and, once the agreement had been confirmed, both sides swore to it.

When Count Jordan saw himself thus compelled, he submitted himself and the Castle of the Marsh into the hands of the aforesaid prince. He and his aforesaid associates departed thence and returned home; Count Jordan entered the castle of Morcone. Peace having thus been confirmed, the prince returned to Capua and retained the castle of Apice and Acerra for many years. Then the duke stationed troops of horse and foot against the castle of Morcone, intending to bring both the count and the castle under his power, but he was wholly unable to do so.

Afterward the aforesaid duke went to Salerno and obtained rest from the many and varied exertions which he had endured. Thus, until the day of his death, the land of his duchy was silent and at peace, free from the storms of war. In the same year, on the twelfth day of August, such an abundance of fish appeared in the river Calore that women and men caught them with their hands alone, without nets.

In the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Callixtus II, supreme [Col. 1188A] pontiff and universal pope, in March, the first indiction, the aforesaid Pope Callixtus, having adopted a plan for salvation, ordered that almost all bishops, archbishops, and abbots beyond the mountains, and the pastors of the churches of all Italy, so to speak, should be summoned, in order that, once a holy synodal conference had been established, the agreement made with Emperor Henry might be confirmed forever.

> [Note: Robert of Monte and the Ciccan Chronicle also assign this Lateran synod to the present year; Rigord likewise adheres to that opinion in his account of Louis, as has been explained above. [Col. 1188D] Baronius, however, assigns it to the preceding year. PEREGR.]

Roffridus, bishop of Benevento, honourably hastened to attend this sacred assembly. When so great and distinguished a council had been organized, the Apostolic Lord ordered the privilege of the oath establishing peace, which the aforesaid emperor had issued, to be brought forward and read before all who had assembled. It was immediately confirmed and approved by all.

Among the other decrees made there, [Col. 1188B] they established the observance of the Truce of God. The Apostolic Lord also bound with the bonds of anathema anyone who should attempt to remove the city of Benevento from the authority of St Peter. There were many other decrees which we have thought it too long to attach to this little work, judging that I should add tedium if I included everything in such a book. You will find all the rest written and recorded elsewhere.

We heard, moreover, and indeed learned as fact, that in the time of the aforesaid Apostolic Lord so great and firm a peace came within the city of Rome that no citizen or foreigner dared to carry arms, as had been customary. When the council had been held, the aforesaid Apostolic Lord Callixtus came to Benevento and dealt with certain Beneventan affairs.

In the same year the aforementioned Landulf of Greca died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [Col. 1188C] and was buried at his church of St Maximus. When the aforesaid Pope Callixtus came to Benevento, he had the aforesaid Archbishop Roffridus summoned to hear accusations brought against him by certain citizens. He had been accused of having acquired the dignity of archbishop simoniacally.

Then the prelate summoned some of his suffragan bishops and priests of the city, went up to the sacred palace, and, having heard the accusers, requested a delay. When the delay had been granted, he replied: “Most holy Father, I am ready, in accordance with canonical institutions, to clear myself of these accusations and to follow your command.”

At last he first swore [Note: This was the canonical purgation observed by Juret in connection with Ivo and by others; I shall not repeat it. PEREGR.] with two bishops and three priests that he had not entered the archbishopric simoniacally.

[Col. 1188D] In the year 1124 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Callixtus:

In this year the aforesaid Roffridus, bishop of Benevento, after taking counsel, removed the body of our most holy father Barbatus, bishop of Benevento, from the altar-tomb in which it had rested through the course of many years. That altar was not kept in the fittingly honourable state which it deserved, especially because the structure of the new episcopal palace extended to the site of that altar. It was therefore necessary to remove it in accordance with the requirements of the building [Col. 1189A].

The aforementioned archbishop ordered his two suffragan bishops to be summoned, so that, with their counsel and assistance, such a great and abundant treasure might be found. At once, after calling certain citizens and clergy, Archbishop Roffridus entered the church in the silence of midnight, approached the altar named above, and, before them all, with the aid of the bishops, broke it open. When the altar had been broken, relics of saints whose names are unknown were found. After these had been removed, he ordered digging deeper, so that the long-desired pledge of the aforesaid body might be seen.

Without delay a precious stone was discovered, enclosed on every side by a severe and wondrous work of labour and supported by iron bars. When it had been found, immense joy seized those who were trying with all their strength to lift the stone. But because the stone was firmly held by the hardness of the construction, it was broken into pieces by the agreement of all. When it had been raised, by the favour of divine grace the body of most blessed Barbatus was found.

The aforesaid archbishop was the first of all to enter the place; rolling amid the bones and ashes, with great joy and resounding praises, he displayed them publicly in the midst of the assembly. O reader, what joy and exultation you would have seen when, in our times, we found pearls so long desired! The bones having been gathered were borne to the altar of St Sebastian while the clergy sang hymns.

When morning came, the whole city poured forth in companies and praised God, creator of all, who had deigned to grant them so great a body of Blessed Barbatus. We ourselves saw some of [Col. 1189C] his bones and kissed them. When these things had been done, the archbishop ordered first the priests of the Upper Gate, together with the clergy and laity, to go down to the episcopal church and keep vigils before the most sacred body of Barbatus.

At once, by command of the archbishop, the priests assembled; and, with candles and lamps lighted, accompanied by a great company of laypersons of every sex and age, we went down rejoicing. Thus each gate of the city performed its vigil on successive days until the eighth day. When the eighth day arrived, the day before the Kalends of June, the aforesaid archbishop, assisted by two bishops, placed the body of Blessed Barbatus beneath a stone altar. Having placed it there, he dedicated the altar in honour of Blessed [Col. 1189D] Barbatus. A great multitude from the city gathered for the solemnity of this dedication, that Almighty God might forgive their sins.

The archbishop, as already mentioned, ascended to a raised place so that he could be seen and heard by all, and, with divine clemency favouring him, remitted a portion of sins. He granted the same remission to all others who should devoutly attend that dedication until the octave of the feast of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

I shall now describe to Your Paternity, though in unpolished speech, the miracles which Jesus Christ, lover of humankind, deigned to show before the eyes of us all, through the merits and in honour of our aforesaid father Barbatus. While, as written above, the venerable body of the Blessed One was kept before all at the altar of St Sebastian for eight days [Col. 1190A], a man named John the Shoemaker entered the episcopal church and threw himself upon the ground before the body of most holy Barbatus, watering it with tears. The clergy and people standing by immediately asked why he wept, and he disclosed from the beginning everything that had happened.

“While I was resting in bed in the silence of night, asleep with the sleep due to my body, behold, there appeared before my eyes a man venerable for his grey hair, clothed in shining white garments. Gradually coming closer, he approached my bed and said: ‘Why did you not come yesterday with the others to sing the vigils before my bones?’

“And I replied: ‘Father, because, as is known, severe pain held my arm and my right hand. For six months, miserable as I am, I have been afflicted with this infirmity.’ I added: ‘Tell me, Father, by what name are you called?’

“And he said: ‘Barbatus, formerly bishop of the city of Benevento.’ He added: ‘Show me at once that arm and hand.’ At last, because I was tormented by pain, I did not extend my hand very quickly; nevertheless, he touched it when extended, and the pain fled with such rapidity as though it had never held my hand and arm. Immediately, when morning came, I rose and wondered at the health that had so swiftly arisen. Therefore I have come to give thanks and praise to God, creator of all, and to Barbatus, the most holy bishop, through whose merits I have escaped.”

When these things had been done and narrated, all the bells of the episcopal church were ordered rung, so that the people of the city might assemble to hear and see such a great miracle. [Col. 1190C] Almost the whole city immediately poured forth, and we praised, blessing the most glorious physician of all physicians. I, the writer, felt with my own hands his arm and hand, which had been healed; his neighbours testified that they had known him to be ill for a long time. Having seen this, we returned home filled with joy.

I shall also relate another miracle which Christ Jesus, redeemer of humankind, performed in those days to the glory of our aforesaid father Barbatus. A peasant living in the castle of Montefusco, hearing the report of the great man’s sanctity, came to Benevento. For many years he had limped because the sinews of his leg and foot had withered. He was continually gripped by dreadful pain and, as if his foot were bound [Col. 1190D] to his buttocks, the miserable man was tortured at every hour.

At once he prostrated himself before the Basilica of St Barbatus, imploring God, redeemer of all, to restore him to his former health. As he prayed in this manner, he was seized by heavy sleep and remained there for the space of one night, as though half-dead. In the silence of that night, behold, a man of advanced age, adorned with venerable grey hair, appeared; as we heard from the man’s own mouth, he awakened him thus:

“Rise quickly, hasten to seek the altar consecrated in my name, and there, through the favour of the Saviour’s mercy, you shall obtain the long and widely desired joy of health.”

He replied: “Who are you who promise me the weight of so great a treasure?”

“Barbatus,” he said, “bishop of the city of Benevento.”

Immediately the lame man took courage to speak: “I cannot, unhappy as I am, go on in this way. Do you see how I remain tortured with this withered foot? Having heard the fame of your holiness, I came swiftly, riding on a little ass, that through your intercessions I might gain the joy of desired health.”

Without delay Father Barbatus stretched out his hand and touched the withered foot and shin, saying: “Hasten swiftly; having received health, prostrate yourself before the altar.”

On hearing this, he who had been lame rose up healthy and praised God with a loud voice, through whom such gifts of health were bestowed upon him, through whom joys were granted him. In the morning he entered the church to render thanks to God and Father Barbatus. The man who had been lame immediately related to the arriving people everything that had happened to him, and how he had limped for a long [Col. 1191B] time because of contracted sinews. He also declared that the aforesaid Bishop Barbatus had appeared to him and that through his intervention he had received the health he desired.

Meanwhile the report of so great a miracle spread through the districts and every corner of the city, and the citizens hastened in companies to see the man. Having seen him, we praised the maker of all and returned home.

Not many days later, a certain woman with withered hands and contracted sinews ran to seek the benefits of Bishop Barbatus. She lay before the altar and, with streaming tears, invoked the mercy of the Saviour. Almighty God looked down upon her tears from on high and, wishing to reveal the glory of his confessor Barbatus and the nature and greatness of his triumph before Him, before [Col. 1191C] all who had assembled that woman began to raise her hands, so withered, toward heaven. Then she broke out in a clear voice, declaring that she had felt the aid of health in her hands and contracted sinews. She opened her fingers, truly bent before, and, through the favour of divine grace, all the joints of her fingers were released. At this nearly the whole people hurried together, and we magnified in blessing the King of Heaven and our father Barbatus.

In this year there was such an abundance of wine that, as we and many others saw, one hundred *saumae* were sold for thirty denarii. In the same year the aforementioned Pope Callixtus departed to the Lord on the twelfth day of December. After his death, all the cardinals chose Lambert, bishop of Ostia, as pope, Honorius. Callixtus himself [Col. 1191D] had governed the pontifical see for five years and nine months. Immediately upon his ordination, Pope Honorius appointed Peter, cardinal-priest, as rector at Benevento.

In the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the first year of Lord Honorius, in March, the third indiction:

In this year, when the eleventh night of October came, a new and terrible portent occurred at Benevento; and, as we heard, also in other cities and towns adjoining the city of Benevento. That night, while we were all given over to our proper sleep, an unprecedented earthquake suddenly occurred, so that, terrified, we all expected death. Immediately the people of the city awoke, boiling over with tears and sobs, and hastened to the episcopal church; while some citizens hurried to the monastery of St Sophia, and we hurried to pray to God, redeemer of all.

The earthquake occurred with such terror that towers, palaces, and every building in the city shook and trembled. The ground and rocks, through fear of so great a convulsion, were split in two; the city walls too collapsed and levelled certain houses to the ground. We testify before the eternal King that you could see the earth quaking beneath your feet. What shall I say? Stunned by so great an earthquake and dried up by unwonted fear, we thought of descending to the depths. Thus [Col. 1192B], until sunrise, clinging to the holy places amid groans and tears, we prayed with many weepings to the Lord, the saving physician of bodies and souls, that he might grant the bowels of his mercy to us unworthy people.

They asserted that the earthquake occurred a third and, as was reported, a fourth time that night. On the following day, about noon, behold, another earthquake came shaking everything; reader, had you been present, you would have seen with your own eyes every building in the city tremble and quiver.

The aforesaid Pope Honorius, who was then staying in the sacred palace at Benevento, felt that night the shock of so great an earthquake, left the chamber, and hurried to the basilica of St John. He immediately prostrated himself upon the ground and invoked with streaming tears the mercy of God the Saviour before the altar. [Col. 1192C] A marvellous and unheard-of thing for all living people, which nowhere in these times, nor in the memory of anyone able to recall it, had happened so plainly! We remember and affirm that an earthquake’s shock had come once at night; but now the storm of earthquakes continued very frequently by day and night for as many as fifteen days.

Terrified by the earthquake, the citizens hurried with litanies and great sobbing tears, men and women, and little children crying to the Lord, to the episcopal church and to the church of Pope St Leo. Indeed, the aforesaid Pope Honorius summoned the cardinals and, barefoot, poured forth to God great prayers and tears about this matter.

In the year 1126 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in March, the [Col. 1192D] fourth indiction, Emperor Henry died.

### Year 1127 of the Incarnation of the Lord

In this year Duke William, previously mentioned, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of August [26 July]. Immediately his wife cut off before all who were present the hair which she had nurtured as beautiful and luxuriant; with tears streaming and her cries raised to the stars, she threw herself upon the breast of the dead duke. Without delay the report of the duke’s death struck every quarter of the city of Salerno; and so, in crowds and at headlong speed, all the people hurried to the palace, wishing to see the corpse of that dead duke.

> **Note:** [Col. 1191D] Our author likewise relates, under the year 1138 [Col. 1192D], that Duke Rainulf was committed to burial with the whole clergy and people of the city of Troia divided, that is, into companies. Nor, in almost any different manner, does Hugh Falcandus say that the death of King William I was mourned:
>
> “Throughout the whole three days women and noble matrons, [Col. 1193B] especially Saracen women, whose grief at the king’s death was not feigned, clothed in sackcloth, with hair unbound, proceeding day and night in companies, preceded by a multitude of maidservants, filled the entire city with lamentation, answering [Col. 1193C] with mournful song to the beaten drums.”
>
> Thus too, at the death of Bono, Duke of Naples, as is read on his tomb, the Neapolitans mourned in companies. Nor was this custom observed only in mourning of this sort, but also in public rejoicing. Falco himself, under the year 1139, says: “When the Roman people heard of the arrival of Lord Pope Innocent, they went out to meet him in crowds and received him with great joy and honour.” Indeed, they proceeded to, assembled for, and celebrated the principal sacred solemnities in no other order at that time.
>
> I understand Anastasius the Librarian in this sense when, speaking of Leo III, he says that at Rome, on the day when that pontiff was deprived of tongue and eyes by Roman clerics, after the greater Litanies had been proclaimed, all alike—men and women—came in devout disposition in companies to the church of the blessed martyr of Christ Laurence, called Lucina, where the aforesaid station was held. Nor did they depart except in companies. This is what St Paulinus of Nola means in *Natalis* 7 by “to release the gatherings from the church.”
>
> That such companies were assembled by districts [Col. 1193D] I learn from Gislebert, *Life of St Romanus*, book II, chapter 15, in the Bibliotheca Floriacensis. There he speaks of the mother of a certain boy, deaf and lame, who had seen in a dream that she had carried her son to churches of the saints and had sought healing for him:
>
> “After seeing these things, when daylight came, she heard the inhabitants saying that they ought to go to St Romanus and celebrate a special sacrifice of prayers. Undertaking this labour with all diligence together with them, and joining their company, she brought her only pledge [her child] to the thresholds of the aforesaid protector.”
>
> But observe that this was a special and laborious sacrifice. For the inhabitants of the individual districts, gathered into separate companies together with the ecclesiastical men of their district—whose chief concern it was to lead the procession and to make it as splendid as possible for the honour both of their own name and of their churches—used, on appointed days, if the feast extended over several days, to proceed to celebrate the sacred vigils. They sang sacred songs and carried candles, [Col. 1194B] lighted lamps, and banners together with platforms of greater or lesser size, fashioned with varied craftsmanship, to be kept for a time in the church of that saint whose feast was being celebrated, as a token of devout worship. [Col. 1194C]
>
> Our Falco offers a notable example of this sacred rite under the year 1119. A small trace of it is still kept by the Campanians on the feast of the Finding of St Stephen the Protomartyr. They call *fajos* the little constructions carried by the priests of designated churches to the cathedral church: the word is a corruption of the ancient Lombardic *fara*, which in the Lombard Laws, book III, title 12, and in Paul the Deacon, book II, chapter 7 or 9, means “generations” or “lineages.” For the individual *faji* clearly seemed to be certain emblems of the individual districts, encompassing the stocks or kindreds of the urban people assembled for that synaxis.
>
> This derivation of the name fully pleases me. Yet they might also seem to have been called *phaji*, as though *phalae*: towers so called by the ancients, according to Servius on *Aeneid* IX and Isidore, *Etymologies* XVIII.7, which they most closely resemble in form. But I do not believe that our constructed *faji* were so called from *faji*, that is, from the green branches of trees of that name, or of other trees, which the people of Salerno, district by district, and the diocesan people, town by town, assembling at the cathedral church, formerly brought as signs of joy and honour even at the solemn feast of the Translation of St Matthew the Apostle. I learned this from an old Ritual book of that church, beautifully illustrated with such little pictures. [Col. 1194D]
>
> Still less do I believe they were called so because, like *phari*—lighthouses—they shone by attached burning reeds or lamps at night while the procession moved. Torches indeed were carried in such processions, as has been said, and proceeding to hold and celebrate vigils was then described by an ancient expression; but it is by no means certain that this particular service was nocturnal. Gislebert says in the words quoted above: “When daylight came, the woman heard the inhabitants saying that they ought to go to St Romanus,” etc.  
> **PEREGR.**

[Col. 1193A] And after seeing him, remembering his humility and piety, they tore out their hair and cheeks, and wonderfully invoked their father and lord. At once the archbishop of the city, having summoned the clergy to carry the body, came; and, when it had been honourably laid upon a bier, four horses which the duke had loved were led before the bier as far as the episcopal church of St Matthew, and likewise four golden banners were placed before him.

Reader, if you had been present, you would have seen the people of both sexes mourning; and you would have declared in amazement that no duke or emperor had ever been buried amid such grief. Therefore, when the funeral rites had been celebrated according to custom, they buried that duke in a costly prepared tomb.

And when the report of that duke’s death was spread through all parts of Apulia, the previously mentioned Count Jordan, [Col. 1193B] because he had been disinherited by that duke, took military assistance and ascended Montefusco on the very day of the said duke’s burial. Since he had many friends there, that count gained possession of Montefusco. Then he seized the cities and towns of his entire county and thus recovered in full what he had lost.

Furthermore, when fifteen days had passed, Robert son of Richard asked the said count to come to his assistance, so that he might be able to take the city of Fiorentino. Count Jordan, therefore, being of an ardent spirit, took soldiers and hurried there without delay. [Col. 1194A] At once, with trumpets sounding, the city was attacked on every side. The count sprang toward a certain gate and strove to enter; but the guards of the tower, seeing such audacity, began to resist with stones and swords. At length, by a judgement of God, the count was crushed beneath a hail of stones and, through an unhappy death, lost both his life and the whole extent of the county which he had acquired.

When Roger, Count of the Sicilians, learned of Duke William’s death, he prepared seven ships and arrived at Salerno with arms and all necessities. He remained there ten days, unwilling indeed to disembark, but staying on board night and day. He summoned the citizens of Salerno and their archbishop Romuald; and when all had assembled near the shore, Count Roger began thus:

> “Lords and brothers, as your wisdom knows, my uncle Robert Guiscard, duke of good memory, conquered and acquired this city, which your prudence now holds, by strength of spirit and great prudence. After his departure, Duke Roger, his son and our cousin, held it peacefully with your prosperity. Then Duke William, his heir and son, ruled manfully until the present time. But now, by the judgement of God, Duke William himself has died without a son. Therefore I, [Col. 1195A] who have sprung from his lineage, appeal to your civic community, if it pleases your nobility, that you may take counsel and, loving me above any other, accept our lordship and the bond of affection. For, with the Lord’s help and while life endures, you shall attain the strength of a better condition and the riches which you possessed in former times.”

Why say more? After taking counsel, those citizens entrusted the city of Salerno to his fidelity, all the citizens carefully confirming this by oaths and promising never to abandon their loyalty. Count Roger immediately swore that he would neither seize them nor permit them to be seized without judgement and without fault; that he would not lead them on campaign for more than two days; that he would not take the castle of Torre Maggiore from their [Col. 1195B] control; and that, if anyone took it, he would restore it by his assistance to their control. When these things had been done, he entered the city and stayed there honourably.

But when the people of Benevento heard that the count had acquired the city of Salerno, they sent him certain wise men of the city, promising a bond of affection and services. The count, however, graciously sent gifts and presents in return to the Beneventans, promising, while life endured, to repay them.

When these and other matters had thus occurred, the count subjected to his authority the entire duchy of Amalfi on every side. Proceeding thence, he gained possession of the city of Troia, Melfi, and almost all parts of Apulia. He also reduced to his dominion Landulf of Montemarano, Landulf of San Barbato, Rao of Fraineta, and the young Hugh, [Col. 1195C] with all their dependencies. Having accomplished these things, victorious and exultant, he returned to Sicily.

Immediately, having taken counsel, he raised his proud mind to assume the dignity of the duchy, and ordered all who dwelt in his lands to call him Duke Roger; and this was done. Moreover, he sent Lord Pope Honorius many gifts of gold and silver, further promising the city of Troia and Montefusco if the pope would grant him the banner and title of the duchy. Yet Pope Honorius did not deign to grant this to him at that time. Hence much discord and bloodshed arose. How and when the aforesaid Pope Honorius granted him the duchy I shall describe in what follows, if life remains to me. [Col. 1195D]

When the aforesaid Roger, Count [Col. 1196A] of the Sicilians, heard that Pope Honorius could not be bent by his petitions, he ordered the aforesaid Rao of Fraineta, the young Hugh, and all his supporters around the city of Benevento to take as many Beneventan prisoners as they could and to harass the city with many afflictions. They truly carried this out more severely than had been commanded, especially Rao of Fraineta, who had long hated the city.

William, then rector of the Beneventans, perceiving the ferocity and attacks of the said Rao of Fraineta, took counsel. On the feast day of St Martin he summoned all quarters of the city to take up arms and hasten against Rao. They went most willingly, in order to exact vengeance for the injuries they had received. But [Col. 1196B] Rao had concealed with him about fifty knights and many foot-soldiers. He therefore sprang upon them unexpectedly, captured many Beneventans who had turned to flight, and found them disgracefully in and outside the River Sabato. Thus he led them away captive with him to the castle of Ceppaloni; and, after binding them, he took their goods of silver and gold as ransom.

After all the things related above had occurred, Pope Honorius, finding that he could accomplish nothing useful or effective for the city of Benevento, took salutary counsel and went to Capua on the third day before the Kalends of January [30 December]. At once the said Prince Robert received him with the greatest attentiveness and ordered him to lodge with great rejoicing in the palace of the bishopric of Capua.

> **Note:** [Col. 1195D] Nothing has previously been said in Falco either about the plight in which the city of Benevento then stood, or about the arrival of Pope Honorius there and his other actions in this year 1127; yet the speech delivered by that pontiff at the assembly of Capua and described below gives some explanation of these matters. Nor has anything been said previously about Prince Robert. No one, therefore, will deny that these matters are now lacking in Falco.
>
> But perhaps deliberately, though certainly in a crude manner, he has Honorius recount in a public speech the things which he had suffered. For the remaining matters concerning Prince Robert we must consult Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 96, and the Cassinese Anonymous corrected by me. That is: in the same year 1127 in which Duke William of Apulia departed this life, Jordan II, Prince of Capua, also died (his death is marked in the ancient obituary books on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December]); and he was succeeded in the principality by the aforesaid Robert, [Col. 1196D] his son, the second of that name.
>
> Falco had certainly explained this more fully, just as he also described Robert’s inauguration. He recounts how the Archbishop of Capua—then Otto—by the privilege of his predecessors and according to the ancient rite of the Lombard princes, in the presence of the great and eminent pontiff Honorius, with the assembled throng of religious men and gathering of bishops (in Falco one should read “bishops,” not “archbishops with abbots,” as summoned by the pope to that solemnity, unless one prefers both; for Roffridus, elected archbishop of Benevento, was also present at the elevation of Prince Richard III in 1120, described by the same author), anointed the said Robert with the dignity of the principality—that is, poured holy oil upon him—and confirmed him.
>
> This occurred in January, at the beginning of the common year 1128, which for Falco remains 1127 until the following March. Moreover, because the Archbishop of Capua cannot be judged to have been endowed with the said privilege before the dignity of the Principality of Capua had been confirmed by imperial authority under Otto I, while Pandulf surnamed Ironhead governed that city—of whom I have touched briefly in book I and shall speak more fully in book II of the *History of the Lombards*—it seems that he received this prerogative from no one but John XIII, who raised the Church of Capua to an archbishopric at about the same time, in 968.
>
> It is strange how those who resent the precedence of our church over their own, which was granted comparable splendour somewhat later, daily turn to new arguments and even produce, as though from their sleeves, ancient documents and authors that have been abridged—I do not believe by fraud. I shall not now expose their falsity, for they are themselves, one to another, judges of their own error. But why do they begrudge us this privilege of seniority, recent though it is in comparison with the exceedingly ancient dignity of the see of Capua, arising from the very beginnings of the Christian Church?
>
> Certainly those who at the beginning of the present century argued most acutely and learnedly about the suburban regions voluntarily agreed that the Church of Capua, and no other, was adorned with archiepiscopal office throughout all Campania at that time; although otherwise in disagreement, they did not hesitate to assert this constantly as an established fact. The speech delivered by Pope Honorius at the Campanian assembly and described by Falco may be read in many respects in a better form in Baronius.  
> **PEREGR.**

Without delay Pope Honorius [Col. 1196C] ordered archbishops and abbots to be summoned, so that they might assemble for the prince’s anointing. They came on the appointed day with immense rejoicing to the church of Capua.

The Archbishop of Capua, according to the privilege of his predecessors, in the presence of that great and eminent pontiff Honorius, with the assembled throng of religious men and gathering of bishops, anointed and confirmed the aforesaid Robert in the dignity of the principality. What great feeling of exultation and joy was present! We call the living King of Heaven to witness that no prince of old had been honoured with such jubilation and delight. We learned, indeed, from the testimony of those who were present that five thousand men assembled for [Col. 1196D] the anointing of so great a prince.

When Pope [Col. 1197A] Honorius saw so great a multitude of bishops and worthy men, after the prince had been consecrated he ascended to a higher place and began as follows:

> “Lords and dearest brothers, as your charity has known, it is long since I left the Roman See and came peacefully to the city of Benevento, which belongs in a special way to the Roman See; putting aside every storm, I sojourned among our neighbours.
>
> “But two days after our arrival, Count Roger, the adversary of blessed Peter, brought nearly four hundred knights around the city of Benevento to bring about the city’s ruin and our unheard-of disgrace. They truly plundered the citizens’ goods at every hour and continually subjected their possessions to devastation. We endured all [Col. 1197B] their attacks and considered how they might be made to desist from their obstinacy.
>
> “Moreover, the said Count Roger formed a most grievous alliance with the young Hugh and Rao of Ceppaloni for the destruction of the city, thinking that we would yield to fear of him and comply with his wicked demands. Hugh and Rao, bound by such a conspiracy, began daily to consume the territory of the city with fire and sword. As we saw all that was being brought upon us, awaiting only the mercy of Almighty God, we invoked the aid of the heavenly King and of blessed Peter.
>
> “Then, lest the city of Benevento be utterly thrown into disorder by such afflictions, we sought the aid of friendly soldiers; and thus, as best we could, we began to resist their obstinacy. When [Col. 1197C] we had gone to the city of Troia on certain pressing affairs, the said Rao of Ceppaloni seized about two hundred Beneventan citizens who, to avenge the insults they had suffered, had gone out on the feast day of blessed Martin into the territory of that Rao. By divine wrath and a fury sent from heaven, he held them captive and bound them naked in the depths of a prison.
>
> “Then he gave certain of the captive citizens to the young Hugh, a man of wicked memory and a dreadful tyrant, to be subjected to tortures and punishments. Hugh tore out their teeth by the roots and mutilated them limb by limb; after receiving their ransom, he sold them off. Rao himself does not cease continually to afflict those whom he retains with the danger of hunger and cold. Why say more? Every [Col. 1197D] outrage that can be imagined is inflicted upon the captured Beneventans.
>
> “Moreover, day and night they threaten to bring against the city of Benevento that Count Roger, given over to anathema, [Col. 1198A] and to subject to their dominion and power the city drawn forth by the power of blessed Peter. Further, he threatens all of you who hold the lordships of cities and the strength of castles with many terrors and various assaults: that he may take from each of you your fortifications and strongholds in which you trust; that he may dispose of your life according to his own will; that, as and when he wishes, he may make foreigners out of citizens and make poor and needy men out of wealthy men.
>
> “Knowing the wickedness of his mind and his schemes from certain indications of the signs, through those who have suffered them until now, we have avoided them far and wide. Fleeing his promises as a deadly poison, we did not obey in any way, nor, so to speak, did we deem them worthy [Col. 1198B] of being received by our ears. For what vast heaps of gold and riches he promised, if only we would be willing to grant him the dignity of the duchy! Rejecting those many kinds of promises of wealth, both for the honour of the Roman See, which I have striven to preserve, and because I feared at every hour your exile through terror, I cast them away and despised them before God, maker of all ages, who searches hearts and minds.
>
> “Believe me: he had promised such riches for your disgrace and expulsion, thinking to force me entirely to his will and to obtain my consent to your banishment. But I, embracing the bond of your affection, would choose rather to die with you than to adhere to his wicked promises.
>
> “Therefore, dearest [Col. 1198C] brothers and sons, life and the hardship of death lie within your choice and will, provided that you are willing to fight and are eager mutually to defend the strength of honour. I have found your prudence most certain. Nothing remains except that, casting aside all sloth and putting away the torpor of your hearts, you defend the dignity of the Roman See, which constantly intercedes for all of you, and endeavour to preserve for yourselves and your sons the strength which you possess.
>
> “Come therefore to the rescue, most valiant men and distinguished warriors; and while a time of prosperity is at hand, let us raise with all our strength to lofty things the rigour of that justice which we embrace. For God, who is the way of justice and the light of truth, and the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, will daily deliver us and, from [Col. 1198D] his holy throne, will grant us aid with accustomed mercy.”

While Pope Honorius, with tears streaming, proclaimed these and many similar things, all the soldiers and people [Col. 1199A] assembled raised their voices and cried with one accord that, for fidelity to blessed Peter and to him, they would hand over themselves and all that was theirs.

Finally Robert, newly established as prince, promised publicly as follows:

> “Behold, venerable Father, I commit to your authority both the person whom you see and the strength of my whole principality which you have entrusted to me; and all things shall be subject to your command.”

Count Rainulf, and many other nobles and bishops who had assembled, made the same promise. What promises, reader, would you have seen had you been present, and what tears sprang from their promises! If I had wished to relate them all, the hearers would have been wearied.

When Pope Honorius heard that this multitude had granted a concord agreeing with his exhortations, he gave thanks to God the Saviour of all and [Col. 1199B] to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, who aids those who hope in him and supplies daily help. Then, by the authority of God, of the blessed Virgin Mary, and of the merits of the holy Apostles, he granted them this reward: to those who had undertaken penance for their sins, should they die in that expedition, he remitted all their sins; but to those who did not die there and had confessed, he granted remission of half.

When the said prince and Count Rainulf heard that Pope Honorius had bestowed the grace of so great a benefit, enriched with immense joy, they departed with all who had assembled, each to his own place. Without delay, with heralds sounding forth, they summoned the whole territory of their principality and county, so that every man might prepare himself for the pope’s [Col. 1199C] assistance. All the people consented to their command.

Meanwhile the said prince and Count Rainulf came before the pope and informed him of the plan for safety which they had devised: first, they said, the young Hugh ought to be summoned by that count, since they seemed bound to one another by securities given and received. The pope agreed to their words and commended their faith.

Immediately the count sent certain of his nobles to summon Hugh, that he might submit to justice. He added instructions that Hugh should accept hostages and sureties so that, after every security had been provided, he might come to the count’s court for justice to be done. Why say more? He would neither provide hostages nor come to the count’s court.

The count therefore immediately laid everything before Pope Honorius. Then the said prince and count, as they had promised, gathered a great force of knights and an innumerable multitude of foot-soldiers and marched against the castle of the young Hugh, called Lapillosa. When William, then rector of the Beneventans, heard that this castle had been besieged, he proclaimed throughout every quarter of the city by the voice of a herald that they should take up arms and hurry to that expedition. The people, prepared with the necessary equipment for the campaign, hastened there most swiftly.

Three days later the said rector, taking with him about two thousand men, advanced against that castle. And when it had been so fiercely besieged, the wood which had long grown up for the castle’s [Col. 1200A] protection was quickly cut down and burned. Then the Beneventan people, united as one, attacked the castle’s fortification; having attacked it, they vigorously stormed it. It could indeed have been taken and burned, if Count Rainulf’s assistance had come; but because that count was unwilling to give assistance to the extent he could, the weary Beneventan people returned to their camp.

On the following day, seeing that the help of the count and prince was not present as vigorously as they had promised the pope, the Beneventan people, seized by fear and weariness, marvelled at such delays. When morning came, the said prince ordered his tent and its equipment removed. Then Count Rainulf excused himself from remaining in so great an expedition because of the snowy and dangerous season at hand, and thus departed together with the prince.

Their rector, perceiving these excuses, ordered all the people to return to the city. Without delay, obeying the command, they returned at rapid pace. That siege took place on the fourth day before the Kalends of February [29 January].

The said pope, who was staying at Montesarchio, learned that the castle had been thus abandoned and, disturbed by unheard-of grief because the promises of the prince and count had not been fulfilled in his regard, groaned in sorrow beyond belief. Immediately he set out and went to Roman territory. The prince and count excused to Pope Honorius their deceitful intrigues. But the pope kept in the secret of his heart all that [Col. 1200C] had been done and heard; looking at them with a grim expression, so to speak, he hastened on as he had conceived in his mind.

When these matters had been accomplished, he ordered Walter, Archbishop of Taranto, to come to Benevento, diligently attend to the city’s affairs, and protect the city by his counsel. He further directed the said rector to entrust to that archbishop the solidi received from the royal revenues, so that the city’s soldiers might be armed from them and assistance furnished according to their strength. The rector delayed distributing those solidi to the soldiers until he had received the command in the pope’s own letters; and, once the command had been received, he distributed those solidi to the cavalrymen.

### Year 1128 of the Incarnation of the Lord, in the Fourth Year of the Pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius, in March, Sixth Indiction

In this year Pope Honorius came to Benevento with two hundred Roman knights. He found Prince Robert of Capua, Count Rainulf with a great army, and a multitude of Beneventan citizens attacking and besieging fiercely the castle of the tower of the palace. This castle belonged to the young Hugh. Hugh himself was pressing opposition against the said prince and Count Rainulf; and when the castle had been besieged and vigorously assaulted, its lord, unable to defend it, surrendered it into the power of the prince and count.

When this had been done, the said Pope Honorius heard that Roger, Count of the Sicilians, persisted daily against his will [Col. 1201A] and held the regions of Apulia. He summoned Prince Robert and the count, ordering them to gather an army and hasten against Count Roger. Why say more? The pope himself descended into Apulia with the prince and count.
