He ordered Grimoald of Bari and Tancred to be summoned, so that all might unite in opposition to the Count of the Sicilians; and this was done.

Count Roger, perceiving that the pope was coming against him with a strong army of knights and foot-soldiers and with those barons, withdrew into the mountains, avoiding the pope’s strength lest any evil should somehow befall him. Thus, in the burning sun of July, the pope besieged the count for forty days.

Meanwhile the said prince, because he was physically delicate and unable to endure hardship, [Col. 1201B] began to withdraw from fidelity to the pope. He planned how to abandon the pope’s camp and return home; he had his tents removed and attempted to set out. When the pope perceived the prince’s treachery and that of the other barons, terms were arranged. He promised through the chancellor Americus and Cencius Frangipane that he would give the duchy to Count Roger, and that the count should come to Benevento, where he would confirm to him the dignity of the duchy.

When this had been done, the pope returned to Benevento. The count, having gathered his army, came to Benevento and made camp on Mount St Felix. Then, after the terms had been agreed between them and the promises were to be fulfilled, on the eighth day of the Assumption of St Mary [22 August], [Col. 1201C] the pope granted the dignity of the duchy to that count in the sight of nearly twenty thousand men, namely at the Ponte Maggiore beside the riverbank after sunset. For, because many matters intervened, the whole day had been spent disputing with one another.

Because the count was afraid to enter the city of Benevento, the pope therefore went out beyond the city, as has been said, to the said bridge and conferred on him the dignity of the duchy. When he had received the duchy, that duke swore upon oath that he would neither act nor consent to any action by which blessed Peter, Lord Pope Honorius, or his Catholic successors should lose the city of Benevento, and that he would neither take nor permit the taking of the Principality of Capua. When all this had been done, he returned to Salerno and then went back to Sicily. [Col. 1201D]

Not many days later Pope Honorius, having taken counsel, returned to Rome. But before he entered the city of Rome, a party among the Beneventans, on the second day of September, killed William, then [Col. 1202A] rector of Benevento, in the sacred palace of Benevento, with drawn swords.

That wretched rector, trying to escape the rage of that faction, fled behind the altar of St John in the chapel of the palace. There he hid himself beneath the feet of the priest John, who was then celebrating Mass; but he could not escape. He was struck there with daggers, dragged out of the palace, and thrown outside. They tied a rope to his feet and thus, alas for the wretch, dragged him through the city street as far as the charnel-place of St Laurence, covered with stones.

> **Note:** [Col. 1201D] “Through the street of Benevento,” he says, not “through the streets”: the street which then also led from the sacred palace of Benevento—situated in reality and in name in the upper district of the city—in a straight course, and over no shorter a route than the whole length of the city then extended, and now extends, to the Gate of St Laurence in the lower district.
>
> Outside this gate there was customarily a *carnaria*, as there also was at the Porta Nuova of Salerno and at the likewise New Gate of Capua, formerly the Castle Gate and now called the Naples Gate. That is, it was an open-air place enclosed by walls, to which persons executed by hanging—perhaps the source of its name, since in Latin a *carnarium* is a chamber in which salted meat is hung—or killed by another form of punishment, as well as the bodies of the very lowest persons for partial burial, were carried. In Italian it was then called *carnaro* or *carnajo*, a word which the Florentine Academy, in its Dictionary under *carname*, says means “the common burial-place of hospitals or similar places.”
>
> Therefore, if one says that this type of burial and the *carnaria* belonged to the church of St Laurence, still situated outside the aforesaid Beneventan gate of the same name, where ruins of very ancient works are visible, and to its hospital, which existed there, I shall not object.  
> **PEREGR.**

After his death, the people of the city, seized by fury, destroyed the houses of Poto Spitameta, John and Guislitius the judges, Transo, Laurence, and Louis the physician. They themselves, together with Dauferius the judge, fearing the people’s violence, fled to Montefusco. [Col. 1202B] Immediately the people, having established a commune among themselves, almost all swore that henceforth, for seven complete years and forty days, the said Poto Spitameta and the other above-mentioned men who had left the city should not be inhabitants of the city.

In the same year John, abbot of St Sophia, died on the eighth day of November, and Franco, then *mansionarius* [church official], was elected. When the said pope heard that the rector’s death had occurred in this manner, he was greatly troubled with grief and threatened the city of Benevento that he would pursue vengeance for such a crime.

Immediately, after taking counsel, they sent envoys to the said pope, to say that the rector’s death had been brought about by foolish and wicked men, asking him to send a suitable rector and to grant peace to the Beneventans. [Col. 1202C] The pope, having taken counsel, sent us Lord Gerard the cardinal as rector.

### A.D. 1129 from the Incarnation of the Lord

In this year the aforesaid Pope Honorius came to Benevento, and in the month of August consecrated the aforesaid Franco as abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia. He urged the Beneventans, who had formed a commune, to recall to the city of Benevento the aforesaid Poto Spitameta together with the citizens already mentioned, whom they had expelled from the city; but he was unable to obtain this. Therefore the apostolic, greatly angered, left Benevento and withdrew to a certain village called Leocabante. There he asked the aforesaid Duke Roger, who was staying there, to come in the following month of May with an army [Col. 1202D] and take vengeance upon the citizens of Benevento; and that duke swore an oath that he would do so. Then that apostolic went to the castle of Ceppaluni and caused the city to be plundered; thus, greatly enraged, he returned to Rome.

And in this year Roffridus, then archbishop, brought out from the altar the bodies of Saints Januarius, Festus, and Desiderius, [Col. 1203A] where they had lain from ancient times, and where indeed they had not been kept with the honour befitting that place. Therefore the bones of the aforesaid saints were placed, with great honour and rejoicing, in the basilica which Walter, archbishop of Telese, had caused to be built out of devotion to those saints—while we watched and kissed their bones.

In the same year Pope Honorius, in the middle of the month of February, entered upon the way of all flesh unto the Lord. Lord Innocent was elected; but after Innocent, on that same day at the third hour, Peter, bishop of Porto, elected Peter, son of Peter Leo, as Anacletus. Thereupon, condemning the election of Innocent, they confirmed the election of Pope Anacletus. [Col. 1203B] When Leo Frangipane, who followed Innocent’s party, heard of Anacletus’s election, he began to exhort the Roman citizens who were his faithful adherents and friends to support him with their assistance. Then Leo, brother of the aforesaid Anacletus, opened the treasury and appealed to nearly all the Roman people to defend his brother’s election according to their means; and this was done. Thus a most savage civil war began fiercely on both sides.

### A.D. 1130 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in March, eighth indiction

When the aforesaid Anacletus had been elected, he informed the Beneventans how he had been elected and ordered them to render him fealty. [Col. 1204A] The aforesaid Innocent, now consecrated pope, seeing the divisions among the Roman people and the civil wars daily arising, took counsel and crossed the mountains to the king of the Franks and to the other faithful supporters of the Roman See. They received him honourably and with diligent care. Immediately he held a synod at Rheims, at whose assembly nearly one hundred and fifty archbishops and bishops, as we have heard, convened. There he bound that Anacletus and his supporters with the bonds of excommunication.

In the same year the aforesaid Roffridus, archbishop of Benevento, died, and Landulf, son of Roffridus of Garderisio, was elected archbishop.

In the same year the aforesaid Anacletus came to Benevento; [Col. 1204B] then he went to the city of Avellino and agreed with the aforesaid Duke Roger that he would crown him king of Sicily. Having settled these matters, Anacletus returned to Benevento, while the duke went back to Salerno and then to Sicily. In that same year Anacletus sent his cardinal, named Count, to that duke; on the day of the Nativity of the Lord he crowned him king in the city of Palermo. Prince Robert of Capua placed the crown upon his head,

> **[Note: Col. 1203B]** The agreement concerning Roger’s coronation as king was first made between him and Anacletus at Avellino in this year, somewhat before the fifth day before the Kalends of October [27 September]. Then, on the aforesaid day, Anacletus—having already returned from Avellino to Benevento—drew up a diploma concerning the royal title and the granting of the kingdom to him; it is preserved in Baronius. Finally, at the festival of the Lord’s Nativity immediately following, the coronation was performed at Palermo, in the manner set out above by Falco, but more fully by Alexander of Telese, book II, chapter 1 and following.
>
> Yet I am aware that some assert that Roger was crowned not once but twice, and that he was crowned for the first time not then but in the preceding year, on the Ides of May [15 May]. They say that, persuaded by his own decision, he was adorned with the royal crown at Palermo by the hands of four archbishops: namely those of Benevento, Capua, Salerno, and Palermo; many other bishops, abbots, and religious men were present, besides an exceedingly numerous company of dynasts and noble knights. They claim as the author of this account an unpublished *Chronicle of Maraldus*, a Carthusian monk, though they do not say how ancient it is.
>
> I cannot readily agree with them. All ancient writers are silent, especially Alexander of Telese, Roger’s well-disposed friend and intimate, who records that Roger’s coronation, carried out with the utmost expenditure and a great gathering of persons of every rank at Christmas, hence at the end of the year 1130, was effected by the authority of the antipope Anacletus, and describes it in the same manner as Falco. He would not have passed over an earlier coronation, even out of favour toward Roger: one celebrated with no lesser pageantry or gathering of bishops and nobles, indeed at a time when there was no schism in the Roman Church, when Honorius—then Roger’s closest friend—was pope. It was described only by Fazellus in the preceding century, *Decade* II, book VII; but alas, how incongruous are the things he combines.
>
> Whoever Maraldus may have been, he mentions only one coronation, as Fazellus does. Moreover, he plausibly imagined a crown placed upon Roger by the aforesaid archbishops. For it was fitting that a king who held Sicily, whose metropolis was Palermo, and all Italy on this side of the Tiber—almost comprehended within the former principalities of Benevento, Salerno, and Capua—should be crowned by the archbishops of those same cities. By ancient custom and privilege, it belonged to them to anoint their princes; accordingly, he might be adorned in one act with, as it were, a fourfold crown, in likeness of the four dynasties which the same king held under one kingdom. For, as they maintained, this was a practice drawn from ancient example in Holy Scripture.
>
> Thus Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, in the coronation of Charles the Bald for the kingdom of Lothair at Metz in 869—published together with the capitularies of that king—addressed the people: “When kings have acquired kingdoms, they have placed upon themselves the diadems of each.” Furthermore, that the crown was customarily placed upon a king not by one bishop but by several together is clearly evident from another description of that same coronation of Charles the Bald, appended at the end of the aforesaid capitularies. Maraldus states that this was observed in Roger’s alleged earlier coronation.
>
> But, to return to the true coronation of King Roger described by our Falco: “Prince Robert of Capua,” he says, “placed the crown upon his head.” This was fitting both to Robert’s rank—by which he surpassed all the other barons and even Sergius, the Neapolitan commander-in-chief, then subject to Roger, as Telese has it, book II, chapter 1—and to the subjection by which he was bound to him. For Prince Richard II, Robert’s uncle and predecessor, had once become the man of Roger, duke of Apulia, as Geoffrey Malaterra reports, book IV, chapter 26; the rights of that duchy had now passed to the present Roger.
>
> A very similar example is read in Rigord: Philip, king of France, was crowned at Rheims by the archbishop of Rheims, legate of the Roman See, with Henry, king of England, standing by and, on one side, holding the crown over his head in accordance with his due subjection. —Peregrinus.

to whom he did not render a worthy recompense. In the same year Anacletus consecrated the aforesaid Landulf archbishop at Rome. After all these things had been done, King Roger assembled an army and seized Amalfi. When the aforesaid Anacletus, as stated above, had spoken with Duke Roger at Avellino, he returned to Benevento. Having taken counsel, he summoned the aforesaid judges John, Dauferius, and Benedict, together with Louis the physician and Poto Spitameta; receiving two hundred solidi from them, he restored them to the city and granted them all their possessions. Then, with them and his other supporters, he considered how to break up the commune which had been sworn within the city since the death of the previously named rector William.

For it had very often been reported that, because of his hostility and the injury done to the city, that commune had been established especially from the time of Pope Honorius, so that the pope might not be able to harm those who had killed that rector. It had likewise been reported to him how Pope Honorius had come to Benevento after the death of the aforesaid rector and had spoken repeatedly with the citizens, asking them to allow those judges who had been exiled after the rector’s death to enter the city and return to their homes, though they had been destroyed; but he could not obtain this. Therefore, as we have said, Pope Honorius left the city of Benevento in great anger and discussed with Duke Roger the devastation of the city.

When these and many other things concerning that established commune had been reported to Anacletus, he immediately consulted with the aforesaid judges and his other supporters. Anacletus ordered Prince Robert of Capua, who then supported him, to be summoned [Col. 1205C] and to hurry to him, accompanied by a large force of soldiers. Having received the message, Robert hastened as instructed. Anacletus immediately planned with him the destruction of the commune and begged him to lend vigorous aid in this matter.

Why say more? On the appointed day, in the octave of Epiphany, while the aforesaid prince stood by with his men, Rolpoto of Saint Eustace was summoned, since he appeared to be the foremost and most ardent partisan of that commune; likewise Beneventus of John of Rocca,

> **[Note: Col. 1205D]** Correctly, not *Benevenutus*. Just as Salernus is called so in Falcandus from the name of the city Salerno, so here Beneventus is named from Benevento. If the sons of such men happened to acquire family surnames from their fathers’ names, some person might now readily suppose that families so named derived their origin from the princes of those cities. For it is well established that many families were, in like manner, named after places and towns they possessed; but the name of one’s native place also often passed into the name of a lineage. —Peregrinus.

and Roffridus of Anselm, Dauferius Barbae Maioris, and other followers of Rolpoto. Summoned to the palace of Dacomarius, where Anacletus was then holding council, they assembled to hear what Anacletus wished. On the other side Crescentius, then rector, had summoned nearly four hundred of his armed supporters [Col. 1205D] in order to seize those who had been summoned without a hearing.

At once Anacletus’s supporters, thus armed and possessing the prince’s support, rose up. Drawing their weapons, they disgracefully seized Rolpoto and all who had come with him, and held them bound in Dacomarius’s palace. Then they seized their friends whom they found in the streets. A certain John, a jester, so to speak, was butchered beyond belief with stones and various swords. [Col. 1206A] Thus butchered and afflicted with many wounds, he escaped half alive from their hands and lived many years thereafter.

After Rolpoto and his followers had been captured in this manner, Anacletus ordered the arrest of the judges Persicus and Roffridus, who had supported their actions and by whose counsel the commune had held sway for so long. But Persicus and Roffridus, learning of these plans through friends, silently left the city and escaped the hands of Anacletus and their enemies; thus they lived in exile for almost half a year. When Anacletus heard that Persicus and Roffridus had fled, he was extraordinarily distressed and wondered how his plan had been disclosed. For he had intended, if those judges were captured, to send them as prisoners to Sicily, never to return to Benevento. After these events, many of Rolpoto’s friends asked Anacletus to release Rolpoto from his bonds. Yielding to their prayers, he freed him; Rolpoto swore that he would never again uphold that commune, or any other. Anacletus expelled the other followers from the city, binding them by oaths not to enter it without the will of Anacletus himself or his rector.

When all this had been done, Anacletus went to Salerno on the Kalends of March [1 March] and then, having taken counsel, planned to return to Rome. When Rolpoto escaped from this captivity of Anacletus, he began, more and more extraordinarily, to devise many varied schemes in his heart [Col. 1206C] against Anacletus and his supporters, who had shamefully seized him and through whose contrivance he had sold his garden for sixty Romanati, which he had given to Anacletus. Rolpoto said that he would rather submit to death than leave unpunished his own captivity and that of his friends. He therefore began daily to try new plans and constantly to devise, with grim countenance and purpose, measures against his adversaries.

### A.D. 1131 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in March

Not many days having passed, the aforesaid Beneventus and his followers, on the eighth day of May, took up arms, entered Benevento, and occupied the house of Dauferius Basaforte. There [Col. 1206D] they held their position boldly. They sent word to their friends to appear in the square and come unanimously to their aid, taking vengeance upon the adversaries by whose counsel they had been expelled from the city. Without delay Beneventus and his followers began to fight vigorously with swords and stones.

When Crescentius the rector heard that they had entered the city so boldly, he was troubled and greatly astonished. He ordered the bell of the Palace to be rung, [Col. 1207A] so that all his supporters might hurry swiftly to expel them. Why say more? Drawing their weapons, they went down to the house of Dauferius Basaforte and endeavoured bravely to defend it, lest the city be disturbed by their invasion. But Beneventus and his companions, seeing that their friends’ help was not forthcoming, climbed up into Dauferius’s house and fled through other houses and streets. They left the city and escaped unharmed from the hands of their pursuers. As they fled, the pursuers demolished the house of Dauferius and those of others who had supported them. From that day much unheard-of discord arose among fellow citizens.

Meanwhile the judges Persicus and Roffridus, compelled by fear of their enemies, did not dare enter Benevento. At last, learning that Anacletus had arrived at Capua [Col. 1207B] on his way back to Rome, they took counsel and boldly entered Capua. There they humbly begged Prince Robert, then faithful to Anacletus, that through his intercession they might obtain Anacletus’s favour and permission to return to their possessions. Prince Robert immediately went to Anacletus and pressed him to grant this favour out of affection for them. Why say more? Granting the prince’s requests, Anacletus issued letters and gave them leave to return and to dwell safely in the city.

They returned and came to the Gate of Saint Lawrence, intending, with heads held high, to return to their homes as Anacletus had permitted. But a great crowd of enemies, rising up together with Crescentius, cruelly threatened [Col. 1207C] that they should not enter. Perceiving their insolence and the abundance of threats, they adopted the counsel of safety and returned to Anacletus, who was still staying at Capua. Immediately they threw themselves at his feet and reported everything said and done against them without delay. Angered at this, Anacletus began to threaten the Beneventans vehemently. At length, on the prince’s advice, he sent them back to the city, giving them his cardinal, so that, on seeing and hearing him, the citizens should give assurance and permit them peacefully to return to their homes. They came with the aforesaid cardinal; when he had been heard, all anger was set aside, and citizens remained at peace with citizens.

Meanwhile Rolpoto, relying on the help of his friends, was constantly devising by day and night new plans and gatherings [Col. 1207D] against Crescentius and his fellow conspirators, sometimes openly and sometimes in private. Rolpoto was planning to exact the penalty of vengeance from Crescentius and those agreeing with him, remembering his suffering and captivity, as well as the sale of his garden and how he had lost sixty Romanati through them. Crescentius, however, perceiving the murmuring of Rolpoto and his friends and the terror of their threats, left the palace of the court and remained at the monastery of Saint Sophia. For it had been reported to him [Col. 1208A] that, just as Rector William had been murdered in the palace, so he too was intended to be butchered there. Avoiding such ferocity and the harshness of death, he stayed, as though secure, within the monastery’s enclosure.

Crescentius’s friends and the aforesaid judges came boldly to him and urged him to maintain the position of the court together with them. But Crescentius would by no means comply with their exhortations and warnings. For his friends often truly reported to him that, if he returned to the palace, they would unexpectedly cut him limb from limb. Therefore, as we have said, avoiding their threats and terrors, Crescentius remained within that monastery until the feast of Saint Angel, celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September].

Moreover, seeing Rolpoto and his helpers day and night heap threats and insults upon him and plainly intend to rise against him, [Col. 1208B] Crescentius the rector began diligently to consider with his supporters how he might extinguish the flames of so deadly a poison. Meanwhile Rolpoto threatened at every hour that unless Crescentius restored the sixty Romanati which Anacletus had taken from him, he would, once all obscurity had been removed, take unheard-of vengeance upon Crescentius’s body. Crescentius therefore summoned all his supporters and began to discuss with them what should be done.

A certain part of his friends carefully urged and advised Crescentius, without deceit, to restore to Rolpoto those sixty Romanati from the revenues of the court, [Col. 1208C] so that they might at least thereby remain safe from so great a disaster and storm of fear. Crescentius said before them that he hesitated to repay the Romanati, especially because Anacletus had carried off that money in his coffers. He declared that he feared that, if he repaid the money without Anacletus’s counsel, he would undoubtedly incur Anacletus’s wrath.

While these and other events were taking place at Benevento, Crescentius sent his messenger to Anacletus, informing him of everything that had happened to him and how, because of the money taken from Rolpoto, he and his friends expected death every day. He further reported that, through fear of Rolpoto, he had left the palace and stayed in the monastery of Saint Sophia; “but now, concerning repayment of that money and the other matters which we have sent to you, send us word what must be done.”

> **[Note: Col. 1207D]** If you observe discordant forms of expression used in the same context, do not suspect that anything is missing here; likewise not under the year 1137, where a not altogether dissimilar expression is read. Such variation was not uncommon among medieval authors. See *Historia Miscella*, book XV, concerning Emperor Justin and Anastasius the Librarian, twice in the life of Silverius and in that of Vigilius. I omit the unpublished Anonymous of Salerno. —Peregrinus.

When Anacletus received this unfavourable message, he was troubled at heart. He summoned certain friends and discussed with them what ought to be done. Some of his friends maintained that the money should be returned, since his rector and the city were trembling in turmoil over it. But Anacletus, being of a viperous heart, rejected this counsel and directed Crescentius not to repay the money. If life remained to him, he himself would come to Benevento [Col. 1209A] and bring the whirlwind of this storm into the harbour of safety.

The messenger returned from Anacletus and gave Crescentius letters containing all these matters. Crescentius, relying more and more on the contents of the letters, carried them out. When Rolpoto heard that Anacletus had given this order and that Crescentius hesitated to repay the money, he began to burn with greater fury. With Prince Robert of Capua and Count Rainulf, he plotted how he might avenge himself upon Rector Crescentius and his friends, who had caused his ruin; later events proved this.

Because of these and other conflicts between them, and because of many old kinds of enmity recalled to mind, that concord could not be brought to the fruit of peace. Prince Robert and Count Rainulf, hearing Rolpoto’s sweet words and his promises of gold and silver, swore common oaths to assist one another whenever circumstances and time required it. But lest delay overtake me in writing, let us hasten briefly to those matters that are pressing and appear necessary.

In the following account, if life remains to us, we shall describe how the aforesaid Crescentius, with the aforesaid judges and their other friends, and nearly four hundred others, were exiled from the city on the occasion thus contrived. For if I wished to describe individually many things established by truth and seen by myself beyond all doubt, both time would fail and I, though uncultivated, would collapse exhausted beneath the sweat of so great a labour. [Col. 1209C] It profits readers and hearers nothing to advance lies full of vanity, when, as I have said, so many true things exist which, God favouring us, we endeavour to preserve for the memory of posterity.

### A.D. 1132 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in March, ninth indiction

> **[Note: Col. 1209D]** Write: “tenth indiction,” and under A.D. 1135, “thirteenth indiction,” not twelfth. Do not doubt the correct dating of the years, to which all the other indictions assigned by Falco agree well. Moreover, the chronological indicators described in several places in this chronicle agree especially well with them: namely under 1109, 1114, 1120 twice, 1122, and 1137. —Peregrinus.

The moon, abandoning the brightness of its rising, was changed into the colour of blood; beholding it, we believed it to be a portent. In this year Anacletus came to Salerno. In the same year King Roger, seeing that Tancred of Conversano, a man indeed prudent and courageous, was rebelling and resisting him, took counsel, assembled an army, and hastened against Tancred’s castle of Brindisi. He besieged it by land and sea [Col. 1209D] and, having marvellously conquered it, brought it under his authority. After this he assembled his army and hastened against the city of Bari. Without delay he began to attack that city with various engines. For fifteen days the city was besieged and attacked. At last, when the surrender of the citizens of Bari had been openly declared, [Col. 1210A] the city itself was delivered into the king’s power.

> **[Note: Col. 1209D]** Bari, therefore, was not taken by force by Roger; rather, its citizens surrendered, after a siege of nearly three weeks, as Alexander of Telese says, book II, chapter 21. He must not be understood otherwise. This is also plainly indicated by Falco’s language, customarily used of those who, defeated in judicial contests, yielded and publicly declared in writing that they relinquished a thing unjustly possessed to its lawful owners. So also Aymoin, book V, chapter 5, concerning Barcelona, received by Emperor Louis the Pious: “When the city had been handed over and opened”—which has the same meaning as “declared”—“the king first sent guards there on that day.” —Peregrinus.

Once the city had thus been seized, Prince Grimoald, a most remarkable man of martial spirit, was captured by certain fellow citizens and brought into the king’s power. The king immediately sent him captive to Sicily with his wife and sons, and thus subjected all Apulia to his authority. After this, the king threatened to disinherit Prince Robert and Count Rainulf.

In the same year, King Roger learned that Count Rainulf was inflicting many insults and hardships upon his wife Matilda, the king’s sister, whom he loved beyond belief. Having taken counsel, he ordered his sister to be summoned. Receiving her honourably, he comforted her with gentle conversation [Col. 1210B] and sent her to Sicily. In this year the king sent the aforesaid prince and Count Rainulf, with two hundred knights, to Rome to aid Anacletus. While they were absent, as I have said, he took from the count his wife, son, and the city of Avellino. When the prince and count returned from Rome, disturbed in mind and struck by immense grief, they wondered how the king had taken his wife; Count Rainulf in particular, whose beloved wife and son had thus been taken, complained, sometimes publicly and sometimes privately, with flowing tears that he had unjustly lost his wife and son.

Then they themselves and their friends asked Anacletus to obtain from King Roger the restoration of [Col. 1210C] the son and wife. Anacletus accordingly entreated the king through messengers to restore the wife and son to the count, but he could not obtain it. Therefore the count, inflamed with grief, sought an opportunity for vengeance. Why say more? Allied with the aforesaid prince, the commander-in-chief of the Neapolitans, and other friends, he came forth openly with two thousand horsemen and a multitude of infantry. He set out joyful and fearless, desiring rather to submit first to death than, disinherited by that man, to seek another’s possessions and go to unknown regions.

Holding before his eyes the fate of the city of Bari, of Prince Grimoald, and of Tancred, whom he had formerly loved, and how the king had afflicted them with evils, he prayed to die by the sword and perish by the blade rather than bow his neck [Col. 1210D] beneath so great and such a kingly power. Without delay the prince and count, as we have said, with two thousand horsemen and an innumerable multitude of armed infantry, intending to fight and defend themselves against the king’s design, made camp on the plain of Mount Sardo. They humbly prayed the King of Heaven [Col. 1211A] that, girded with heavenly help, they might escape the king’s threats and terror.

Every day the count tearfully entreated and admonished his men to put their trust in God alone, cast away fear, and lay aside terror. “It will be more gloriously told throughout the whole world,” he said, “that we, trusting in justice, defended what was our own and first died at the sword’s edge, than that, while we live, we suffered foreign hands to invade what is ours and turn us from prosperous citizens into strangers. Thus all speak with one voice and respond to their requests; and, keeping watch day and night, they invoked heavenly victory.

When, as we said above, King Roger had subjected the city of Bari to his authority and expelled Tancred of Conversano from all the bounds of Apulia, he assembled his army boldly and eagerly and came near the territories of Benevento. [Col. 1211B] On the thirteenth day after the beginning of July, the king made camp on the plain near the bridge of Saint Valentine, close to the city. Then, having taken counsel, he sent envoys to Prince Robert of Capua and Count Rainulf, demanding justice from them concerning many various complaints.

When the prince heard the envoys, he answered thus before all his followers:

> “Let your king, whom you name, know truly that we shall in no way render him justice until he restores to Count Rainulf his wife and son, and also grants to his authority the city of Avellino and the castle which he took from him.”

> **[Note: Col. 1211]** The castle, whose name the author or copyist omitted, is called Merculianum by Alexander of Telese, book II, chapter 22. —Peregrinus.

When the envoys had returned, the prince ordered all his soldiers—nearly three thousand in number [Col. 1211C]—and forty thousand armed infantry, whom he had ordered assembled, to keep vigilant with all their strength, prepared for an affair so great. Then he addressed them in a measured speech, begun in this manner, with discerning and diligent care:

> “Lords and brothers, we know with complete certainty that, to enlarge your liberty, you have left behind your homes, wives, sons, and all your goods; taking up only your weapons, you have assembled here, calling upon the mercy of God the Saviour alone. You have heard, and we too have learned in full truth, how he acted toward the city of Bari, and how he basely afflicted and exiled in chains such a great man as Prince Grimoald from the glory of his honour. What need is there for me to mention Tancred and his excellence? You yourselves have heard how, by contrived deceit, he took from him all his cities [Col. 1211D] and towns and sent him overseas.
>
> “I believe your valour is not unaware to what suffering he has reduced Count Giffredus through the loss of his cities. For he desires all powerful men and their riches with open throat; lest they resist him, he levels them to the ground and reduces their glory to dust without any hand of mercy. Alas for this wickedness, most deserving of death: that he should thirstily desire to consume the glory of us all and, with drawn sword and without a spring of mercy, consign us all to the peril of death!
>
> “Therefore, bravest men, come to the rescue—and, I say, help yourselves—so that, while time for help and counsel remains to us, we may be able to free ourselves from the jaws and unbridled power of so great a man. For the saving trust of God alone remains in all our resolve; let your consolation be enkindled by the arms you have taken up and by the loss of all your goods. For we ought to take comfort, so that hope in victory may be held. We are willing to shed blood for the enlargement of liberty and will by no means fall into foreign hands. Let us cast away this fear of death and die unanimously defending justice, that the fame of our courage may be found throughout the whole world.
>
> “The Lord, King of Heaven, brothers, may look upon our justice; and he who heard the prayers of the Maccabees when they cried out, may deign to receive our afflictions. [Col. 1212B] For what profit is there, beloved men, in remaining shamefully in this world and lying under afflictions, when, after the many miseries and perils which befall us, horrible death suddenly arrives and sets a limit and boundary upon our calamities and wealth? It will therefore be more glorious to perish for the justice in which we hope than to see the misfortunes of our people and, perilously exiled, close our final day.
>
> “Furthermore, we make known to your brotherhood that, for the security which we have given one another, let us provide hostages from among our sons and blood-relations. This ought to be done, and done with rejoicing, so that each of us, secure and having set fear aside, may pledge faith to the other [Col. 1212C] and the eagerness of strength.”

As the prince made this and similar exhortations, every knight and foot-soldier, prompted by divine mercy, gave assent and concord in response to the prince’s appeals. Thus each of the barons individually gave his own sons into the prince’s power as hostages.

The king’s envoys returned from the prince and immediately reported everything that had been enjoined upon them. When the king heard it, he again took counsel and sent other messengers to the same prince, bearing this message:

> “We are greatly astonished at what the prince has sent us, especially since at his persuasion and through his envoys I have now come into these regions, he having promised that he would do us justice concerning our complaints. We therefore await fulfilment of his promises and, on the appointed day tomorrow, summon [Col. 1212D] him to render us justice. Thereafter, if life remains to us, we shall consider what must be done in this matter.”

But the prince sent the king the very same answer that he had first given. King Roger, hearing the words of the prince and the count, was inflamed with great grief; and, learning that what he had conceived in his mind would turn out otherwise, he was deeply and repeatedly disturbed.

But the prince immediately ordered Crescentius the cardinal, rector of Benevento, and Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, to be summoned, so that they might hasten to the king himself with certain prudent citizens of Benevento. Having received the message, they took with them the Beneventan judges [Col. 1213A] and thirty other worthy men, and hurried to the king.

The king received them carefully and honourably, then spoke at length with them all, so that, bound to him by affection for himself and fidelity to Anacletus, and united by oaths, they might wage war against the prince of Capua and Count Rainulf.

> [Note: At Capua, then, Prince Robert persuaded the Beneventans to go to King Roger in order to enter into an alliance with him against himself? What could be more absurd? But take care lest a deceptive reading lead you into inventions equally remote from the truth. For Falco says: “The prince ordered [them] to be summoned,” etc.—that is, to himself—and adds besides that Cardinal Crescentius and Archbishop Landulf, having taken with them Beneventan judges and thirty other worthy men, hastened to the king, evidently intending to make an alliance with him. Therefore it was not the prince but the king who ordered them to be summoned. He had encamped on the plain of the bridge of St Valentine, near the city of Benevento, on the thirteenth day of July [Col. 1214D], and through envoys had once and again pressed Prince Robert to obtain justice from him regarding many and diverse complaints. But when he could not induce him to render the obedience due to him, he was greatly angered; and, realizing that what he had conceived in his mind would turn out otherwise, he was exceedingly disturbed. He immediately ordered Crescentius the cardinal, rector of Benevento—this is plainly what must be read, not “But the prince immediately”—and Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, to be summoned, etc. PEREGR.]

He therefore promised that he would grant peace to the city of Benevento and free the inheritances of the Beneventans from Norman servitude and tribute. In short, the cardinal, having heard him, returned to Benevento with the archbishop and the citizens. Without delay he ordered no small part of the Beneventans to assemble, in order to deliberate upon what they had received from the king.

But that part of the people which favoured the cardinal’s command went up to the court of the Sacred Palace [Col. 1213B]. There, setting out the matter and at once revealing what the aforesaid king promised the city, he sought their counsel. He also explained that the king was unwilling to transact this business without the confirmation of oaths. Why delay? When the king’s request had been heard, some of the Beneventans readily approved it.

Immediately in that Sacred Palace the citizens who had assembled—first the judges John, Persicus, Dauferius, Benedict, and Roffrid—swore that they would not, by deed, counsel, or consent, cause that king to lose his life or bodily members, or be captured; that they would wage open and continual war against the aforesaid prince and count; and [swore] the other matters read in the written capitulary, while preserving fidelity to Peter the Apostle.

When these things had been done [Col. 1213C], the cardinal came down from the palace and bound by the same oath as many persons throughout the city as he sought out. But when the Beneventans had thus sworn, a dreadful rumour shook the city of Benevento. Those to whom that oath was displeasing cried out openly that Cardinal Crescentius, together with Archbishop Landulf, the named judges, and certain Beneventans, had wished to hand over the city of Benevento to King Roger and surrender it to his power. They further asserted that they had received innumerable ounces of gold from the king.

And while this report was being circulated through the city, behold: suddenly a very great crowd of the city, having taken up arms, came out into the streets; seized with fury, it rose against Cardinal Crescentius and drove him into flight. [Col. 1213D] Compelled by fear, the cardinal fled the city and hurried to the king. He reported everything that had happened at Benevento, and how the crowd of the city had risen against him with stones and weapons in hand. [Col. 1214A]

Archbishop Landulf, seeing the cardinal flee in this manner, went up to the episcopal palace and remained there, compelled by fear. When these things had occurred, the people gathered in one body, drew their weapons, and openly cried that the oaths newly made to King Roger must not be observed:

> “We do not wish to be bound to the king in this manner, nor, constrained by oaths, to pant in his expeditions with Sicilians, Calabrians, and Apulians, exhausted beneath the blazing sun and by sweat. Accustomed to comfort, and never habituated to the perils of campaigning, we have no part in association with such a great and powerful king.”

After these events, the aforesaid prince and Count Rainulf, having received the news, sent the Beneventans words of peace and an assurance of safety:

> “Let it be known to you [Col. 1214B] that the prince, the count, Rao of Fraineta, and the young Ugo, upon the giving of oaths, will forever remit to the Beneventans all the pledges of fidelity and tributes which you used to pay us, provided only that you give aid neither to King Roger nor to us. Indeed, at this time we do not wish to receive your assistance, having regard for your city, lest on such an occasion the city of Benevento incur hostility. Yet we wish to pass through safely and to remain in still greater security, all fear set aside.”

In short, although this agreement displeased Cardinal Crescentius, rector of Benevento, it greatly and gladly pleased the Beneventans. The prince and Count Rainulf, having summoned their knights, came to the Great Bridge. Before Landulf, bishop of Benevento [Col. 1214C], and a great multitude of Beneventans, as we have discussed above, they, together with Rao of Fraineta and the young Ugo, swore. They also swore fidelity to St Peter, and ordered the terms of the agreement and the binding force of the oaths to be recorded in a sealed document. A written and sealed copy of that agreement was carefully displayed at every gate of the city, for the remembrance of posterity.

When the report of such oaths and of the agreement firmly made with the prince reached King Roger’s ears, he was struck with astonishment beyond belief. Wounded by grief of heart, he said that the city of Benevento, whose help he had expected, had attached itself to the affection of the prince and Count Rainulf. For, as we have learned from many persons, the king had come into the Beneventan territory for no other reason than to attack the prince with Beneventan assistance and force, and to drive him abandoned into flight. Thus, falling away from his purpose, he was continually tormented by varied thoughts [Col. 1215A], seeing plainly that he could not bring to effect what he had conceived in his mind.

“What then,” he said, “have I come here for from foreign and Sicilian regions, when, in the matters I devised, my courage has failed amid fickle fortune?”

Crushed by such distress, he divided his army into sections and arranged various battle-lines and companies of armed men, as though intending to lead them to battle. But the king himself, being of cautious disposition and fearful heart, and wishing that the pressure of his enemies should not become known, devised a pretence of preparing to fight and resist. On the following night he disclosed to his chamberlains and the wiser members of his council his departure, and made known his desire to withdraw from there. He immediately ordered it proclaimed by the herald that, when his banner was seen, the whole army should follow in whatever direction it was led.

When the herald’s announcement was heard, the men, sensing the king’s fear, prepared to depart as best they could. [Col. 1215B] Without delay, the companies of knights and bands of infantry divided, moving their camp from there in flight rather than resistance. I call the eternal God to witness, who knows the secrets of hearts: that withdrawal of the king may rightly be described and remembered as a nocturnal flight prompted by fear. That king, whose power had hitherto beaten against heaven itself, leapt under the shadows of night along byways and hurried onward at swift pace.

When morning came, he arrived near the territory of Salerno. There, exhausted and having for a little while laid aside the fear in his heart, he rested beside the streams of Mount Atrupaldi.

> [Note: There will elsewhere be a special discussion of the territory of Salerno. For the present I observe that Mount Atrupaldi is the hills past which the River Sabato flows, overlooking the town of Atrupalda; it is also sometimes called Atropalda, or, if one prefers to retain its original name, Tripalda, which still survives, for people say *L’Atripalda* for *La Tripalda*. Hence the townspeople persuade themselves, by a truly poetic fiction, that “Atrium of Pallas” or “Black Pool” gave occasion for the name.  
>
> But in truth, while during Lombard times the city of Abellinum still stood on the opposite bank of the Sabato—where there are now the monastery and church of St John the Baptist and conspicuous ruins of the ancient city—it appears that a watchtower was built on that high hill by a certain Paldus, and was accordingly called the Tower of Paldus, then by syncope *Tripaldi*, and finally Tripalda. [Col. 1216D] Most of the people of Abellinum seem to have taken refuge there when their native city was destroyed and compelled to move to a somewhat safer place. In the end they gradually descended again to the lower ground, attracted both by water suitable for various crafts and by devout reverence for the anciently excavated cemetery of St Hippolytus the Martyr. Thus the cemeteries of St Felix at Nola and of St Priscus, disciple of Christ, at Capua are known likewise to have been frequented by inhabitants from ancient times.  
>
> Yet in the records of the monastery of Cava, for the year 1174, I have read this town written *Truppoaldum*, in the opinion, I think, of the archivist, who had heard that it was named from a man and found no personal name nearer to *Tripaldi* than *Truppoaldus*, a name formerly customarily given to men. PEREGR.]

That king remained eight days on the plain of the bridge of St Valentine. While he remained there, his men wrought much destruction of grain [Col. 1215C] and ruin of movable property. When the king had thus left that place in flight, word reached the prince’s army. Immediately Rao of Fraineta, having summoned a troop of knights, vigorously and boldly pursued him. He pursued him gnashing his teeth and panting, with a breast thirsty for vengeance. At last Rao himself attacked certain of the king’s Saracens who were following him, captured them, and carried them away with him. He ordered one of them beheaded, and sent the head to the prince as a trophy of glory. The prince in turn sent that head to Capua, so that the renown of his praise might be heightened.

When the king heard of the slaughter and capture of his Saracens, he grieved greatly and abundantly. Moreover, moved by anger, he threatened that, when the time for vengeance came [Col. 1215D], he would repay in kind what he had received.

Then he moved his camp and, gathering his army, hastened to the very strongly fortified castle of Nocera, which belonged to the aforesaid Prince Robert. [Col. 1216A] Immediately, with trumpets sounding and tents prepared, he besieged that castle of Nocera near its walls and towers. Having fiercely surrounded it on every side, King Roger ordered the wooden bridge, long placed over the River Sarno where it is called Scafati, to be broken down and entirely removed from that place. He feared that Prince Robert and Count Rainulf, attacking him with a numerous host of enemies after hearing news of the siege, might assail him.

Thus, deeming himself secure, the king besieged that castle of Nocera and believed that, attacked on every side, it would submit to his will. Prince Robert and the count, learning that Nocera was so besieged [Col. 1216B], were utterly distraught and deeply grieved. Calling together all their men, they rushed swiftly to its relief. They hastened to Nocera castle, which they had heard was under siege, invoking the victorious Lord with the greatest urgency; they desired to die by the sword rather than be taken by so great an invader. As they raced there in this longing, they encamped on the bank of the aforesaid River Sarno.

They immediately dispatched scouts to ascertain whether the siege of the castle was true as they had heard. Once the truth was discovered, they began to consider together how they might courageously relieve the siege of that castle. Finally, having found a plan, they caused a bridge to be constructed and secured across the aforesaid River Sarno, so that, gaining strength, they might hasten in battle order against the king’s lines to lift the siege.

Then, after the bridge had been laid, the prince and the count ordered all their armed knights and a great multitude of their infantry to cross on the Sunday then at hand—namely the fifth day after the castle had been besieged. As they crossed the river without delay, the prince, using sound counsel, divided his thousand chosen knights into two companies. [Col. 1216C] Count Rainulf, however, being of prudent mind and concerned by the magnitude of his grief and the loss of his beloved wife, likewise divided his 1,500 horsemen into five troops. They had sent 250 knights to defend Nocera, and these fought bravely against the king.

While, as stated, the prince and count were thus ready and pressing for battle, news of them suddenly reached the king’s ears. [Col. 1217A] In short, the herald’s call sounded, ordering the entire army to arm for battle. At once, having taken up their arms, they appeared armed before the king. The king himself, as we have heard, divided his knights and infantry into eight battle-lines for the fight. When these had been so divided, they came together against one another.

Reader, if you had been present, how many tears you would have seen among the armed men on both sides, as they invoked the victorious God to look down from on high upon justice and to deliver innocent blood! Suddenly the king’s first line rushed against the prince’s company. They fought defensively according to their strength, and for a while there was battle between them.

As they fought, a dreadful fear suddenly seized the infantry of the prince and count. They turned their backs and fled as far as the named river. Many escaped by crossing the bridge. But another thousand, as has been reported to us, attempting to reach that bridge, entered the water of the river; thinking to save themselves, they lost their lives in that whirlpool, their weapons submerged in the thirsty waters. [Col. 1217B] What crashing noise and lamentation of the dying then arose! If I wished to write it all out, time would fail me before material for narration did.

But let us return to the subject. The prince’s second division, perceiving so great a slaughter of knights and infantry, gained strength and courage and came to the prince’s aid. The king’s lines, positioned opposite, likewise rushed to assist their king. Thus, with space between them, they fought fiercely and harshly.

Indeed, as we heard from the mouths of those who were present, the king’s party fought with such pressing spirit [Col. 1217C] that the prince’s battle-line, flight already begun, was failing in arms. But divine providence, whose ordering does not fail, looked down from on high upon the side of justice, as it appeared to our frailty.

For Count Rainulf, who stood opposite, saw the outcome of the battle already turning against them. With horses spurred on, surrounded by a troop of five hundred knights, he boldly attacked the king. He immediately gave strength and steadfastness to the prince in battle, and they assaulted the enemy with cries raised to the stars. Then the count’s second line ran up and, fighting fiercely, drove back the king for a time. Why delay? The third division of that same count, stirred by ardent spirit and recognizing that its own men were weary, advanced from the opposite side; like the three-day hunger of a lion sharpened by its teeth, it flew forward and entered the midst of the combatants. Thus, with the Lord’s help, that king was put to flight and slaughter. [Col. 1217D]

Behold, the cry of the fighting people rose to the stars, proclaiming the king’s flight and urging their own men to pursue, so that they might take vengeance, by the victory granted from heaven, upon such a great and powerful man. The king, wishing to restore courage and constancy to his knights so that they would not abandon the field in such disaster, began to stand firm with spear in hand and to reveal his name to his fleeing men. Yet the disclosure of his name brought no benefit, [Col. 1218A] nor did it afford aid to those in flight, since so great a victory had now arisen from the lofty throne of the Saviour for the prince and count.

The king, seeing his men flee beyond belief, threw down his spear. He thought only of escape and the preservation of his life. Spurring the remarkable horse on which he rode, he escaped in flight and extraordinary lamentation, as we have heard, accompanied by four knights. Thus, tightly pressed by such anguish and overwhelmed on every side by mental calamity, he entered the city of Salerno at sunset. When the citizens of Salerno learned of his flight, they received that king.

But Count Rainulf, taking armed knights, pursued the fleeing king close to the city itself. The count returned undaunted, for he had heard that the king had entered Salerno. On his return, together with the prince, he captured nearly twenty of the king’s barons and seven hundred knights, besides many others whose names we have passed over in silence. We heard that others who had been routed in flight were cruelly exposed to slaughter. [Col. 1218B]

In short, the entire army of the king, knights and infantry alike, was brought to flight, slaughter, and captivity. As for the abundance of gold, the unspeakable quantity of silver, the wealth of golden vessels, the infinite varieties of garments, the assemblages of horses, the mass of coats of mail, and all the movable goods taken in that victory—I call the eternal King of kings to witness: if I wished to describe everything individually, I should fail in writing before recording them all. In short, all that glorious abundance of movable wealth [Col. 1218C] came into the power of the prince and count.

The prince and count therefore rejoiced in so great a triumph granted from heaven. When all these things had happened, the thunderous report of victory and the disaster of the fleeing king resounded through Apulia, Sicily, and all Italy. Men marvelled greatly at the unheard-of slaughter and the terror of the king. No living person at that time remembered that so great a slaughter in battle had occurred among Christians.

When news of the victory reached the city of Benevento, behold, the people of the city, filled with great joy, assembled in jubilation at the episcopal palace and the monastery of St Sophia. There, with tears flowing, they gave thanks to God and Peter the Apostle. Then, taking a great multitude of large candles [Col. 1218D] and wooden lamps, they rejoiced in companies with clergy and priests, performing vigils and praises at the basilica of the blessed Apostle Bartholomew and at the monastery of St Sophia.

The whole population of the city rejoiced with ineffable joy, as though the entire victory had been won by the Beneventans. The day on which that battle was fought was the vigil of the blessed Apostle James, namely the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

> [Note: Why he says that the vigils of St James were celebrated on VIII Kalends, although in this year 1171 they truly fell on a Sunday, and though below, under the year 1139, he places the feast itself on VII Kalends, I shall explain there. But when news had reached Benevento that Prince Robert had won a great victory over King Roger on the aforesaid day: “Behold,” says this same author of ours, “the people of the city, filled with great joy, assembled in jubilation at the episcopal palace and monastery of St Sophia [Col. 1219D]; then, taking a great multitude of large candles and wooden lamps, they rejoiced in companies with clergy and priests, performing vigils and praises at the basilica of the blessed Apostle Bartholomew and at the monastery of St Sophia.”  
>
> I did not wish to pass over this unnoticed, so that you might see that sacred vigils were customarily celebrated in broad daylight, as I noted above, rather than at night, with the people and clergy carrying candles and wooden lamps in groups. Those lamps, indeed, do not correspond to the Campanian *fais*: the latter are affixed above the church choir as offerings presented to a saint; the former were carried away from the church and brought back for use whenever occasion required. PEREGR.]

In this year, on the twelfth day of August, Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, died.

After these events [Col. 1219A], the aforesaid King Roger, having consulted his council, went down into Apulia and stayed for a few days at the city of Melfi. He immediately ordered certain of his barons to be summoned and urgently commanded them to remain in his fidelity and affection. He also ordered them, according to their abilities, to beware of association with Tancred of Conversano. For King Roger himself hated him with deadly hatred and, as we have said above, attempted to drive him from all the territory of Apulia.

When this had been done, he returned to Salerno. There, surrounded by a great number of his nobles, he deliberated at length about his hostility toward the prince of Capua and Count Rainulf. He considered daily how he might defeat them, since, as we have said, we had heard far and wide that he had been defeated and put to flight by their strength. [Col. 1219B]

Not many days later, the aforesaid King Roger, by the counsel of Cardinal Crescentius, then rector of Benevento, and other Beneventans, as we have heard, plundered the city of Benevento. He carried men, women, and a multitude of animals captive to Montefusco. O reader, had you been present, what lamentation of the Beneventans you would have heard and wondered at in grieving! For the city, having received security from the king, continually went out to its possessions and vineyards without any doubt of danger, since it was the season of vintage.

On the very day when the cruelty of this plundering was carried out, almost the entire population of the city, having taken up arms, hurried in fury to the monastery of St Sophia, where the aforesaid cardinal [Col. 1219C] was staying. They immediately sent him, though unwilling, to the aforesaid king, so that he might release the citizens from the king’s chains and restore the innumerable plunder of the Beneventans. They said, indeed, that so great a plundering had been carried out by his counsel and that of his supporters.

Without delay the cardinal hurried to the king. Before everyone he swore in the words of the oaths that the plunder had not been carried out by his counsel. But, having come to the king, the cardinal could in no way obtain the return of that multitude of plunder and captive citizens.

After these events, the aforesaid king ordered his knights at all hours to rush upon the territory around the city of Benevento and bind as captives whatever citizens they could find. [Col. 1219D] The king himself, having prepared a ship, embarked upon the sea on the eighth day of December and crossed over to Sicily. But before preparing to sail, he had, through exchanged messengers, persuaded Bernard of Fraineta, lord of the castle of Balba, to surrender that castle to his power; and this was done.

He received from him, as we have heard, one hundred ounces of gold. Bernard himself withdrew to the city of Salerno. The king immediately ordered about one hundred armed men to be sent to fortify that castle. [Col. 1220A]

Rao of Fraineta, who was lord of the aforesaid Bernard, from whom he had held that castle, was wounded by grief of heart when he learned of the loss of that castle. He came to Benevento and urgently begged the people to help him and hasten swiftly. Then he approached Prince Robert of Capua and Count Rainulf and exhorted them to come to his aid.

The prince and the aforesaid count immediately, together with the Beneventans, hastened with all their strength to besiege that castle. There they promptly used wooden siege-engines to destroy the tower. But the guards who watched the tower feared nothing at all of the attacks brought against them. The king’s knights and infantry entered the castle in full sight of [Col. 1220B] the prince and Beneventans without concern, carrying weapons and all things necessary before everyone.

The prince, seeing such great steadfastness and eagerness of spirit among them, moved his camp away and entered the city of Capua. Count Rainulf and Rao of Fraineta, likewise troubled in heart, returned to their own places together with the Beneventan force that was present. Because fear intervened, they abandoned the wooden engines which Rao of Fraineta had caused to be brought for the siege. Immediately the men in that tower came out, seized those engines before everyone, and joyfully brought them inside. Thus the castle was abandoned and became more and more firmly bound under the king’s authority.

[Col. 1220C] At the same time, a certain party of the city of Benevento, having held a council, brought into the city of Benevento Lord Girard, cardinal-priest, who was with Pope Innocent. That party of the city maintained that Pope Innocent’s cause ought to be supported, while the election of Anacletus was contrary to the canons and unjust. In the middle of November, that party appointed the aforesaid cardinal rector of the Beneventans, in allegiance to the Roman Church and to the same lord pope.

On the day after his arrival, in the Sacred Palace of Benevento and before the assembled body of Beneventans, he granted the office and authority of constable to Rolpoto of St Eustasius. Rolpoto, thus appointed, began together with [Col. 1220D] that cardinal to govern the administration of the court and distribute the force of justice to each person. Finally, he urged the knights and retainers to help the city and rise against the king’s soldiers, enemies of the city; and thus he showed himself zealous for the city’s war.

But the constable of Montefusco, installed there by the king in order to inspire fear in the city of Benevento, ordered all the Beneventans’ vineyards and possessions to be devastated by fire and sword; and this was done. Therefore Rolpoto [Col. 1221A], Beneventan constable, seeing such great adversity continually rise against the city, immediately called the city’s districts to arms by a herald’s proclamation, repaying what had been inflicted. He ordered every man, armed, to assemble at the church of St Martian.

Those who favoured his commands, together with Count Rainulf, who had arrived with three hundred knights, attacked on the last day of January the castle of Farnitum, which belonged to Rao Pinella. In short, the entire settlement of peasants was consumed by fire and sword. Then the entire body of inhabitants, of both sexes and every age, fled in fear, abandoning their possessions. Thus many men, women, and little children were stripped and plundered by the citizens; and innumerable movable goods and animals were found in that town. [Col. 1221B]

The lord of that castle was taken captive. When this had been done, the Beneventans returned home on that same day. On the following day, a multitude of citizens hurried with the aforesaid count to the castle called Plescum. Robert of La Marra, to whom that castle belonged, admitted about one hundred armed men. The aforesaid constable Rolpoto, seeing their steadfastness, returned to the city of Benevento. Thus the Beneventans abandoned that castle, which thereafter remained safe and unharmed.

After these events, Roger, son of Count Jordan, who was held captive by Count Rainulf from the time when the aforesaid King Roger, as has been related above, had been put to flight, took the counsel of his friends and confirmed by oath [Col. 1221C] that he would maintain fidelity toward the prince of Capua, Count Rainulf himself, and the city of Benevento, and would continually oppose the said king. Robert of La Marra, Bartholomew of Petrapolicina, and other knights swore the same.

In the year 1133 of the Lord’s Incarnation, after these events, Tancred of Conversano, a very warlike man of prudent mind, together with Count Rainulf and other barons of Apulia, having adopted a salutary plan, summoned about one thousand knights and a large multitude of infantry, and invested the city of Venosa. The people of the city, expecting the freedom they desired, willingly submitted their necks to the fidelity of Tancred of Conversano. [Col. 1221D] He then brought other cities of Apulia under his power.

While these and other events were taking place in Apulia, Pope Innocent and Emperor Lothar arrived at Rome. We have heard that they brought with them two thousand knights. The pope was honourably received and entered the Lateran Palace, where he remained with great joy and abundance of honour. The emperor [Col. 1222A] encamped bravely with his army near the monastery of St Paul.

He sent, as we have heard, to Anacletus, asking him, after consulting religious men, to come and, through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, put an end to the magnitude of so great an error and bloodshed. But that Anacletus, as we have learned, scorned to do so.

When Prince Robert of Capua and Count Rainulf heard of the long-desired arrival of Pope Innocent and Emperor Lothar, they hastened to Rome, accompanied by a troop of about three hundred knights, together with Lord Gerard the cardinal, then rector of Benevento, and certain prudent Beneventan citizens. Going there, they immediately reported the whole course of the affliction which the city of Benevento had long suffered, [Col. 1222B] praying with tears that they might free the city of Benevento, continually oppressed by Count Roger of Sicily, and restore it to the liberty it had long and widely desired.

While the aforesaid Cardinal Girard was rector over the city, after taking counsel with the aforesaid Constable Rolpoto and other prudent citizens, he appointed Falco the notary, scribe of the Sacred Palace and author of this little work, as judge of the city.

> [Note: This author was certainly called Falco, not Fulco, as is read in some places in Baronius, perhaps through a printer’s error. Because the name gains a syllable in oblique cases, in Italian it is called *Falcone*; but the citizens of Benevento pronounce it *Falco*, and I do not blame them, since formerly both *Falco* and *Falcone* were commonly used indiscriminately; likewise *Leo* and *Leone*, *Pando* and *Pandone*, *Scipio* and *Scipione*, *Ugo* and *Ugone*, and so on. From these arose varied families and surnames at Capua and elsewhere: namely, *de Falco* and *de Falcone*; *de Leo* and *de Leone*; *de Pando* and *de Pandone*; *de Scipio* and *de Scipione*; *de Ugo*, or *de Uvo*, and *de Ugone*—which is one family. In it, nearly sixty years ago, Benedict de Uva, a close friend of my uncle Camillus, shone in poetic studies. PEREGR.]

Having made this appointment, as we have said, he returned to Rome. The cardinal immediately, together with the Beneventan citizens who were with him, reported to the aforesaid lord pope the city’s affairs and the many dangers which we suffered. Among other things, they informed him how, by the counsel of the constable and citizens, that cardinal had appointed Falco, scribe of the Sacred Palace [Col. 1222C], as judge.

In short, the pope, favouring their requests, confirmed the appointment. Through Gregory, the Beneventan elect, who had gone to Rome, he sent to the city of Benevento a signed privilege confirming the aforesaid Falco as Beneventan judge.

In the same year, thirty-two citizens of Benevento, who were held captive at the city of Salerno, were, with the Lord’s help, freed from their chains; the day of their liberation was the feast of Saint Eustace the Martyr. The prince and the count, therefore, going to Rome, did not obtain from the emperor what they wished. While they remained there, behold, unexpectedly the aforesaid Roger, king of the Sicilians, having assembled an army of Saracens, crossed the Strait; then he hastened at full speed into [Col. 1222D] Apulia, and immediately, having taken by force the city of Venosa, which Tancred had seized, and other cities, he destroyed them with fire and sword. He also killed their men, women, and little children by various kinds of death, and had some of them burned. We call the eternal King to witness: he raged with such cruelty against those Christians [Col. 1223A] as has scarcely, or never, been heard of in any age.

News was immediately brought to the prince and count while they remained in Rome: they must return with all speed and, resisting so great a tyrant, defend all Apulia and their possessions from the jaws of so great a plunderer. Accordingly, upon receiving the message, they returned quickly; and, with the herald’s voice sounding forth, they stirred up the entire principality of Capua and the city of Benevento, so that, taking up arms, they might manfully resist his treachery and tyranny. This was done and prepared.

Count Rainulf, therefore, taking about a thousand knights, hastened toward the territory of Troia. He immediately sent his envoys to the city of Troia, demanding that the citizens of Troia fulfil the oaths which they had promised to the count and prince. But the people of Troia, compelled by fear of the aforesaid king and placing faith in the king’s deceptively [Col. 1223B] peaceful words, utterly refused to favor the count’s will. Moreover, the bishop of the city had persuaded all the people not to abandon their loyalty to the king. Hearing this, the count remained there forty days and returned to Benevento.

While these and other things were happening, the aforesaid king besieged the city called Matera. Assaulting it fiercely, he took it through the people’s betrayal; and there he put in bonds Geoffrey, son of Count Geoffrey, lord of the city. When this had been done, he brought another city, called Ansa, under his power. Indeed, he found the treasure of Count Alexander in gold and silver. In short, he subjected to his dominion all the cities and strongholds of that same Count Alexander. Count Alexander, therefore, like a shipwrecked man, died—alas, unhappy man!—in the presence of the aforesaid Count [Col. 1223C] Rainulf.

Then the king himself devastated the city of Trani and all Apulia with fire and sword. What shall I say? The king himself did against Christians what has never been heard of in any age. Then, withdrawing his army, Roger himself, still not satiated with human blood, besieged Montepeloso, where Tancred of Conversano and Roger of Pleuto, brave and vigorous fighting men, were present; he remained there fifteen days. Tancred and the aforesaid Roger resisted King Roger and his army manfully and courageously. But King Roger, observing their steadfastness, ordered wooden siege engines and implements of war to be made against Montepeloso. The body of peasants of Montepeloso, sensing the king’s ferocity and the terrors of battle, [Col. 1223D] did not wish to fight against him; they cried out that they could not possibly defend themselves.

Why say more? With trumpets sounding and battle preparations begun around the walls, he assaulted Montepeloso on every side, amid cries raised to heaven. Tancred of Conversano and the aforesaid Roger, seeing the attack, mounted their horses and, with their knights, resisted as best they could. At last, divine judgment overtaking them, [Col. 1224A] and through their dreadful misfortune, the city of Montepeloso itself was taken. Tancred and that unhappy Roger, throwing down their arms, hid through secret and concealed places in the city. Yet they were found by their pursuers and brought before King Roger.

O what grief and unheard-of horror of tears! Had you, reader, been present, you would have been shaken and terrified by sorrow. He immediately ordered Roger himself to be hanged by a noose. He also ordered Tancred himself to pull with his own hand the rope of the noose.

> [Note: Col. 1223D] Observe the manner in which those formerly condemned to death by hanging were led to punishment. For the executioner held in his hand and went before them with the rope of the noose hanging from their neck. Peter the Deacon, Book III, chapter 47, has this sense in saying that the soul of a certain Ado, condemned to eternal torments, was seen by Gebizo, a monk of Cassino, bound like beasts of burden [Col. 1224D] and dragged to punishment. Nor should the passage in the Bishop of Ostia, Book II, chapter 2, be understood otherwise: “Seeing,” he says, “that he could not escape the prince’s hands, Adenulf put a rope around his own neck and ordered himself to be dragged by his wife’s hands to the prince’s feet”—that is, as one guilty of death. PEREGR.]

Alas, wickedness unspeakable and terrible to tell! Tancred himself, unwillingly, obeyed the king’s will. The entire army wondered and shuddered at the king’s actions, imploring the King of Heaven to deign to resist so great a tyrant and cruel man. After this was done, he ordered Tancred of Conversano, [Col. 1224B] a remarkable man, to be guarded. As we have heard, he was led captive into Sicily. Without delay, he destroyed the city of Montepeloso itself, its monasteries, its men and women, and all its inhabitants with their little children in the jaws of fire and sword.

Then, withdrawing his army, he came at full speed against the city of Troia. The citizens, because they had believed his deceitfully peaceful words, awaited him in confidence. Bishop William by name, summoning all the clergy of the city, the monks, and the citizens, met him before the king, clothed in white, with praises and processions. Thinking to soften the fierceness of his spirit, he brought before him, as we have heard, the bodies of saints for his honor. But the king himself, entering the city in fury and forgetting the security he had given, seeing [Col. 1224C] that procession and display, unmindful of the Catholic faith and an assailant of the Christian religion, destroyed that procession with blazing eyes.

“I do not want,” he said, “I do not want glory of this sort; rather, while life remains, I shall destroy them all and drive them all into exile.”

The clergy and people who had gone out to meet him turned to flight, and each concealed himself as best he could. Immediately he seized many citizens of Troia, together with women and their infants, and consigned them to chains. He ordered Judge Robert by name, and four other wise men, to be hanged by the noose. Many men of Troia, leaving all their possessions with their wives and children, fled to Benevento. Moreover, he ordered the houses of the Trojans and their goods to be consumed by fire and sword. O what lamentation of women and [Col. 1224D] children arose throughout the city of Troia! If my tongue uttered a hundred voices, I should fail in writing before I could recount every matter individually.

Not many days later, the aforesaid king assembled an army and hastened to the city of Melfi, which, as we have heard, he took forcefully and subjected to his power. In this year the aforesaid Prince Robert, seeing King Roger’s ferocity [Col. 1225A] and all Apulia brought to confusion and peril of death, and fearing also that the king himself would invade his principality, took counsel and hastened, with ships prepared, to the city of Pisa. There he was honorably received and asked for what reason he was undergoing the hardship of so great an undertaking. The prince, setting forth at once King Roger’s ferocity, threats, and the terrors he had inflicted, humbly begged that the city of Pisa would grant him aid and counsel, upon the terms of their agreement, as will be contained in the account below. On the eighth day before the Kalends of July, the prince embarked and crossed to Pisa; but how he dealt with the Pisans has not yet fully come to our knowledge. But let us return to the matter.

[Col. 1225B] When the aforesaid King Roger had laid waste the cities of Troia and Melfi, as we have learned, he divided the mass of his army into detachments and returned to the city of Bari. Meanwhile, the aforesaid Count Rainulf stirred up the whole principality of Capua, and the aid of all his land, and Rolpoto, constable of Benevento, and the districts of the city of Benevento and the corners of its districts, so that all, taking up arms, might resist the tyrant king.
