All with one mind and devout purpose served Count Rainulf’s will. They cried out that they preferred first to yield to death than submit their necks to the rule of the accursed king.

Why delay further? The count assembled one thousand selected and stoutly armed horsemen and nearly [Col. 1225C] twenty thousand foot soldiers. Constable Rolpoto, stirring up the city of Benevento with a herald’s voice, gladly led out with him an innumerable multitude of citizens. When they had gathered together, while the king was thus devastating Apulia, they adopted a vigorous plan and hastened against the castle called La Pelosa. This castle had belonged to Hugh the Younger, who, having broken his oath, had abandoned Count Rainulf and adhered to King Roger.

That castle was besieged and fiercely assaulted for four days. The count immediately ordered wooden engines to be set in place for demolishing the walls; the aforesaid count and constable manfully ordered that the water of the nearby river and the springs adjoining it be guarded day and night, lest the peasants draw from them. [Col. 1225D] Therefore, the knights holding that castle, seeing the terror of the engines and the peasants’ houses demolished by stones, and sensing the danger of approaching thirst, terrified lest they be taken by fire and sword, surrendered the castle to the power of the aforesaid count. Then, upon the exchange of oaths, they were bound in loyalty to the count.

Thereupon, after taking counsel, the aforesaid constable entered the city of Benevento joyfully with the Beneventans. The count, having assembled all his men, granted them leave to return to their own places, after they had confirmed by oath that, whenever necessity pressed, they would all gather, taking up arms; and thus each returned home.

In the same year Cardinal Crescentius, of whom we have made mention above, took counsel with the aforesaid King Roger [Col. 1226A] that all the vineyards and possessions of the Beneventans should be burned, intending to inflict terror upon the city of Benevento and thus subjugate it to the rule of the accursed king. The king, therefore, sharing in this wicked counsel, ordered that all the vineyards and inheritances of the Beneventans be consumed with fire and sword. Without delay, some of the vineyards and possessions were cut down, and some were burned.

Reader, had you been present, you would have been shaken and terrified by so great a cutting-down of vineyards and burning of possessions. We abandoned the vintage; enduring want of food, thirst, and kinds of death, we cried aloud with open voice that we would first submit our necks to the sea and terrible death rather than serve his rule. Who among mortals, hearing of the rage of so accursed a king, would not fear to come under [Col. 1226B] his dominion? We call the eternal King and the common Judge to witness: we do not read that Nero, the most cruel emperor of the pagans, exercised such slaughter against Christians.

When, as we have said, the aforesaid King Roger had cruelly devastated the cities and strongholds of Apulia and their men and women, he took counsel and came to Salerno. There he ordered certain nobles living near Salerno to gather; when they had been summoned, he discussed with them how he might destroy the citizens of Salerno and Amalfi, as he had those of Apulia, by a fierce hand. But because the time did not appear suitable to him, he left uncompleted what he had conceived in his heart, intending to accomplish it at an opportune time. Then, with a ship prepared, he embarked and crossed to Sicily on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

[Col. 1226C] We have further heard that twenty-three ships laden with gold, silver, and movable goods which he had plundered from the cities of Apulia sank in the depths of the sea. In those ships many men and women from all the cities of Apulia, and little children bound as exiles, were being carried away, never to see their homeland or parents again; they were drowned in that same shipwreck. O what great mourning and dreadful sorrow seized the whole territory of Apulia! Yet they praised the King of Heaven, because he had freed them from various kinds of death and from the danger of exile, and in a single moment had drawn them out of the abyss of this world.

While these and the other matters written above were occurring in Apulia, the aforementioned Pope Innocent and [Col. 1226D] Robert, prince of Capua, having adopted a plan for deliverance, embarked in mid-September and, with favorable winds, crossed to Pisa. For, as we have learned, seeking an army of ships, armed men, and the power of Emperor Lothair, they had resolved in their hearts, with the Lord’s favor, to rescue the city of Benevento, oppressed by many and various calamities, from the jaws of the accursed King Roger. Indeed, the aforesaid Prince Robert had gone to Pisa and had discussed the matter fully and abundantly with the consuls and wise men of the city, asking them to grant him the aid of a naval army. Yet they were unwilling to promise this without the people of Genoa.

At length, when their counsel had been concluded and oaths exchanged, they established an agreement: about the coming month of March they would hasten with [Col. 1227A] one hundred prepared ships carrying armed men against the accursed King Roger. We also heard that the Doge of Venice had lent his assistance. Therefore the prince returned to Rome and immediately disclosed to Lord Pope Innocent all that he had discussed with the Pisan and Genoese people; then, with that pontiff, they hastened to Pisa to confirm the agreement.

When, as has been stated, King Roger was making for Sicily, the aforesaid Crescentius, a cardinal in name only, seeing that he could not subject the city of Benevento by the power of the king himself as he had planned, began to grieve greatly along with the other Beneventans who had been expelled from the city. Then, by many various snares and conspiracies, he began to bind some by gifts and some by promises, oaths being exchanged. Indeed, he bound them to kill Constable Rolpoto and as many of his followers as they could find, and then, taking up arms, to seize the streets of the city while deceitfully crying “peace.” Once they had been bound by oath in this manner, the aforesaid Crescentius, deceiving other Beneventans of sounder judgment and greater prudence, ordered them to lend the aforementioned supporters of his a hand of counsel and aid. He sent money to some and promised rank and honor to others.

For, as we have learned, they planned to kill the aforesaid constable on the feast day of All Saints. But the Savior of humankind, who frustrates the counsels of the nations and whose counsel remains forever, overthrew their designs. Then [Col. 1227C] the aforesaid Crescentius, throughout the whole month of November, did not cease to discuss most subtly and earnestly with his aforesaid supporters the invasion and destruction of the city. In short, having devised a deadly plan, they decided that on the feast day of Saint Andrew the Apostle Crescentius himself, having assembled about two hundred knights and a plentiful multitude of foot soldiers, should come to cut down the Beneventans’ vineyards at the place called Rosetum.

When the Beneventan citizens saw that cutting, they would have to come out to defend their vineyards and fight. As they came out, the conspirators intended to attack Constable Rolpoto and put him to flight; indeed, by feigned loyalty and deadly fraud, they themselves would first turn their backs and surrender some of their own knights and foot soldiers as captives into Beneventan hands. Thereupon the aforesaid constable, together with the citizens, would immediately have to pursue and attack them; and while they pursued, some Beneventans who supported Crescentius and had bound themselves to the murder of the city would shut the gate of Saint Lawrence. Once that gate had been stoutly closed, the named constable and the Beneventans who had gone out with him could not re-enter the city. Thus Crescentius and the king’s knights would pursue the Beneventans as far as the aforesaid gate of Saint Lawrence, where they intended to capture him and whatever citizens they could find, and then slaughter them all piecemeal.

They also planned that one hundred knights should hide near the church of Saint [Col. 1228A] Angel at the Cross, which lies within the bounds of the Porta Summa. On learning of that slaughter and capture, they would force their way through the Porta Summa; then they would overwhelm men, women, little children, and all the city’s goods in the jaws of fire and sword, and so subject the city to the king’s power and rule. But the almighty Savior, who chastens and saves, who leads down to hell and brings back, and who after weeping and lamentation brings exultation, rejected their deadly counsels and accursed designs. He, I say, who frustrates the counsels of the nations and whose counsel remains forever, truly rejected and overthrew the schemes of the wicked; and events turned out very differently from what Crescentius had planned with his enemies.

O grief, terrible to tell! Under the specious [Col. 1228B] name of the Roman See, they intended to subject to the cruelty of the aforesaid King Roger, of execrable memory, the city of Benevento, which had long and widely persevered in the strength of liberty and loyalty to Saint Peter. We call the eternal King to witness: because the liberty of Benevento had been stoutly preserved, and through the merits of the Apostles Peter, Paul, and Bartholomew and of the other saints, we hoped without doubt that unhappy Apulia, held captive by that accursed king, and the provinces even to the Roman frontiers, would be rescued from that king’s hand and desire and restored to glory.

For it was right to hope and to hold continually before our eyes that Pope Innocent and Robert, prince of Capua, were laboring, with great exertion and undertaken danger, to redeem us all, as we stated in the preceding account; but now among the city’s enemies there was a plan to subject us all to death, plunder, and dispersion. But let us return to the matter.

The supporters of the aforesaid Crescentius, therefore, moved by haste and thirsting for Beneventan blood, did not await the arrival of the city’s enemies who had conspired with them, as stated above. Immediately, on the aforesaid feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle, they took up arms and came out into the streets. What shall I say? In their madness, striking the faithful of Saint Peter, they cried that they wanted peace. They wounded Judge Roffrid and Abbot Paroald with swords. A remarkable thing! [Col. 1228D] What good could such peace do to one already dead or struck unto death? We have seen and heard peace made firm and secure only after arms were laid down; yet, as they came out into the streets, they thought that nearly the whole city would obey their words and deeds.

Constable Rolpoto was not then in the city, for he had gone to speak with Count Rainulf. At once, seized by the spirit of loyalty, all the people of Benevento rose up. Taking up arms quickly, we held the city of Benevento courageously and zealously. Why say more? We seized those accursed men, Crescentius’s supporters. But when the constable came near the city of Benevento and heard that it was disturbed and reduced to such ruin, trusting in loyalty to Saint Peter, he entered the city, desiring to die first [Col. 1229A] rather than see the city so unexpectedly destroyed.

Taking up arms, he courageously and resolutely went up through the city street with certain Beneventan knights accompanying him and hastened to the Porta Summa. He found that gate firmly shut and honorably guarded by the faithful. Meanwhile the knights of Montefusco, together with the Beneventans who had been expelled from the city, came outside the Porta Summa in order to enter the city and fulfil the desires of their hearts, as they had planned among themselves. But when they saw the gate closed, they remained there for a little while. The faithful of Saint Peter mounted the tower of the Porta Summa, drove those knights away by throwing stones, and faithfully defended it. Without delay, those knights turned their backs and returned at headlong speed to their own men.

The constable immediately ordered the Porta Summa opened and pursued them remarkably with armed knights. Compelled by fear, they returned to Montefusco. During that pursuit, a certain man named John Benedicti, a Beneventan who had gone out with the aforesaid Crescentius, was captured. The aforesaid constable, returning to the city, governed the court resolutely with the faithful of Saint Peter. In short, he ordered the aforesaid John Benedicti to be hanged by the noose; then he ordered the other traitors whom we had seized to be hanged. He ordered John de Lepore, a man of accursed memory and a supporter of Crescentius, to be plunged headfirst into a pit, his feet raised on high. Alas, [Col. 1229C] unhappy man! He ended his life by an unheard-of death.

When these and other matters had thus run their course, the city of Benevento rested from so great a whirlwind and storm. Moreover, the aforesaid constable seized certain Beneventans held under that suspicion and ordered them to be bound in chains through Count Rainulf’s municipalities.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1134, in March, in the twelfth indiction. In this year the aforesaid Prince Robert returned to his principality of Capua on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, accompanied by two Pisan consuls, namely Alzopardo and Cane, wise men, and by nearly one thousand other Pisans.

> [Note: Col. 1229C] If, at the beginning of this Falconian year, which begins in March, Robert returned to his principality, this certainly did not happen on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, since it would thus have occurred at the end of that year, but on the fourth day before the Nones or the Ides. The prince himself, as this author records, embarked in the year 1133 on the eighth day before the Kalends of July and crossed to Pisa; and he made an agreement with the Pisans that around the coming month of March they would hasten, with one hundred prepared ships carrying armed men, against the accursed King Roger. PEREGR.]

He was diligently received by [Col. 1230A] the master of the soldiers of Naples and Count Rainulf. He disclosed before the aforesaid Pope Innocent all that he had arranged with the Pisans and Genoese, and how, by an oath, he ought to give three thousand pounds of silver to the Pisans coming to his aid. When the aforesaid master of the soldiers and Count Rainulf heard this, they rejoiced greatly; and, once all the prince’s acts had been recounted, they put faith in them. Without delay, collections were made through the churches of the city of Naples and the principality of Capua, and they rapidly gathered that money in silver. In short, they sent the treasure of silver itself to the Pisans, asking them to come speedily to their aid.

In their company they sent Gregory, the elect of Benevento, together with certain of his priests, [Col. 1230B] in order that he might make known to the lord pope, who was there, and to the Pisans, the distress of the city of Benevento. When these things had been done, the aforesaid King Roger came to Salerno with about sixty prepared galley-ships. He immediately sent those galleys to attack the city of Naples. When they came up to the harbor of Naples, battle was joined. The citizens of Naples, taking up arms, stoutly drove off those galleys. Afterwards, the galleys plundered the nearby Neapolitan forts and thus returned to the king.

When these and other matters had thus run their course, the aforesaid King Roger, having assembled an army of Sicilians and Apulians, came to the city of Avellino. Then, withdrawing his army, at dawn he rushed upon a certain castle called Prata, which belonged to William of Abinalia. [Col. 1230C] That castle had thought itself secure and unprepared for so great an army. What shall I say? In a single moment it was taken and consumed in the jaws of fire and sword; there, we heard, knights were killed, wounded, and captured. On the same day he took the castle of Altacauda, Gructa, and the places belonging to Rao of Fraineta beneath the mountain.

> [Note: Col. 1229D] I write *Raonem* [Rao], as Falco calls him several times; do not confuse him with another Rao, likewise lord of Ceppaloni, who had already died in the year 1120. Nor should you distinguish him from Radulf, as Alexander of Telese calls him in Book II, chapter 54; for the Normans seem also customarily to have pronounced this name, *Rao*, as *Rayno*, *Radulfus* or *Raydolfus*, and *Ranulfus* or *Raynulfus*. I shall not now offer examples of this. Rather, by comparison with our Falco I shall indicate in passing that Telese, in the passage mentioned, should be corrected: he has “Radulf of Frameto” instead of “Rao of Fraineta”; “Grintla Simonto,” [Col. 1230C] and “Altacunda” instead of “Gracta,” “Submontum,” and “Alta” or “Alzacauda.” Further, in the following chapter 55, [Col. 1230D] as also in the preceding chapter 25, he is corrupted in the name of the town Tressancti, for which in both places is now read *Cressanta*. The error plainly arose because the Normans, drawing a transverse line over a capital C, easily deceived a reader who could not distinguish it from T because of their very similar shape; hence Alexander himself, though abbot of the monastery of Telese, was considered and called abbot of Celese. Nor should I omit that in the same chapter 55 one should read *suis proceribus baronibusque instanter omnibus mittens*—“sending urgently to all his own nobles and barons”—not *principibus* (“princes”). I likewise read *procerum* in the same author, Book II, chapter 37, not *principum*. Certainly there were none who were princes under the otherwise great Count Rainulf. Falco, on this page 119, says that all the knights, nobles, and ecclesiastical men then assembled. But our author himself also needs help on that same page, where, a word having been lost, the text should read: “he sent forty horsemen and nearly a thousand Beneventan foot soldiers.” The word *pedites* (“foot soldiers”) is now absent. PEREGR.]

While these and other deeds were carried out by a cruel hand, fear invaded the city of Benevento and the whole principality of Capua. We therefore begged the Savior of all to assist us all with his customary mercy. Reader, had you been present, you would have marveled at the many tears and cries raised aloft [Col. 1231A] by the Beneventans, Neapolitans, Capuans, and all those dwelling round about. With hair unbound, we invoked the merciful Lord. Having seized those castles, King Roger returned and took Prince Robert’s castles—Palma and Sarno.

Hearing of such and so great a slaughter and invasion, the aforesaid Count Rainulf, Prince Robert, and the master of the soldiers sprang into action in a most remarkable manner. With heralds’ voices and sounding trumpets, they stirred up their cities, strongholds, and villages, so that every man able to bear arms might rise with all his weapons and confront so great a tyrant. Why delay further? We call the King of Heaven to witness: all the knights, nobles, priests, clerics, young men [Col. 1231B] and old men assembled; and, having gathered a remarkable and most powerful army, they hastened with great joy, saying openly: “It is better to die in battle than to see the misfortunes of our people and of the saints.” When they had assembled at the castle of Marigliano, the army encamped.

Rolpoto, constable of the Beneventans, sent to their aid forty horsemen and nearly one thousand Beneventans. When the aforesaid king perceived that Count Rainulf and the prince were thus prepared, he hastened against the castle of Nocera, thinking to take it in a moment, as he had the others. He stationed knights and archers around the river called the Sarno, lest the count cross over to him with his men. Meanwhile, the castle of Nocera was fiercely assaulted by the king’s army. [Col. 1231C] Roger of Sorrento, appointed there by the prince, with one hundred and fifty knights, many archers, and loyal armed men, did not fear any of the attacks made upon them and defended that castle courageously every day.

In short, through the betrayal of certain friends of the king, the castle of Nocera was given into the king’s power. Then the king brought under his power the castle of Sarno, Lauro, and all the strongholds. When the castle of Lauro had thus been taken, the aforesaid prince, Count Rainulf, and the master of the soldiers were greatly disturbed. They assembled about a thousand horsemen and a great multitude of foot soldiers, in order to wrench that castle of Lauro from the king’s power. But the nobles [Col. 1231D] of the prince and of Count Rainulf, having received the king’s money, delayed in giving them the assistance which they had sworn to give. Therefore the prince, moved by grief, hastened to Naples and crossed to Pisa.

The aforesaid Count Rainulf, recognizing the wickedness of his barons and that he could not resist so great a king, submitted his neck to the king’s power upon the exchange of an oath. When Rolpoto, constable of Benevento, heard that Count Rainulf had come under the king’s rule, he was dismayed in spirit. On the day of the Kalends of July he left the city of Benevento and entered Naples; more than one thousand Beneventans followed the constable. Three days later, the same Constable Rolpoto, struck by fear lest he be handed over into the king’s hands, prepared a ship and hastened to Pisa with some of his faithful men and his two sons. As they sailed, divine judgment overtook them: [Col. 1232A] the ship was wrecked, and he himself, with one of his sons and two of his faithful men, died amid the storms of the sea. His other son escaped.

Having received that count, the king seized Capua, Aversa, and the entire principality, went to Salerno, remained there not many days, and, having won his victory, returned to Sicily. The pontiff styled under the name of Anacletus came at full speed to Benevento and, by the power of that king, brought the city into obedience to his will; he ordered the houses of certain Beneventans destroyed. Prince Robert of Capua was honorably received by Pope Innocent, who was at Pisa, and remained there until the month of March.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1135, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent, in March, in the twelfth indiction. In this year, on the seventh day of April, the prince came to Naples with twenty ships and took Aversa and Cucculum. Having taken them, the prince returned to Naples and remained there with the Pisans. In the same year the aforesaid Count Rainulf came to Naples with four hundred knights and abandoned his cities and strongholds.

When this had been done, the aforesaid king came to Salerno in the middle of June, assembled an army, and marched against Aversa. He devastated it with fire and sword and plundered their possessions. Having inflicted that destruction, [Col. 1232C] the king came against Naples and besieged it for nine days, but the people of the city and the prince were not at all alarmed. Seeing that he could not take the city, the king left it, went to Aversa, and ordered it rebuilt.

When these things had run their course, the aforesaid Pisan people, together with another twenty ships which had arrived, went to the city of Amalfi, took it, and plundered all its goods. Enriched with great wealth, they returned to Pisa together with the prince. The king, learning that the Pisan army had returned, again besieged Naples. One day, on the feast of the Nativity of Saint Mary, when the king wished to begin a naval battle with the Neapolitans, suddenly a storm arose [Col. 1232D] and scattered all those ships, so that they were thought likely to sink in the deep. Thus they returned to the harbor of Pozzuoli. Then the king, seeing that he could act against the city neither by sea nor by land, ordered those ships to return, himself went back to Salerno, and then entered Sicily.

As Prince Robert returned to Pisa, he hastened, on Pope Innocent’s advice, together with Lord Gerard the cardinal and Richard, Count Rainulf’s brother, to the glorious Emperor Lothair. They were honorably received by the emperor, and the prince tearfully told him how he had lost his principality. He also begged him, for love of Pope Innocent, to assist him and restore what he had unjustly lost. The emperor, having bestowed many gifts upon him, promised [Col. 1233A] that he himself would come in that very year for the liberty of the Roman See and the restoration of the same prince. The prince then returned and recounted everything to Lord Pope Innocent.

In that same year the master of the soldiers went to Pisa to seek assistance from Pope Innocent and the Pisans. He was carefully received by the Pisans, and they most willingly promised to bring him aid; but by the counsel of certain enemies that promised aid was frustrated. Therefore the master of the soldiers, greatly troubled, returned to Naples and held his city manfully.

In the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the seventh year of Pope Innocent, while these and many other things were taking place, the aforesaid emperor sent word to Pope Innocent that he should await him, since, with the Lord’s favor, he promised that he would come at the feast of St. James, as he had pledged. [Col. 1233B] Rejoicing with spiritual joy, the pontiff sent to the master of the soldiers everything that the emperor had instructed him. Then the prince himself, hearing that the city of Naples was pressed by the peril of famine, came to that city with five ships, publicly announced the emperor’s imminent arrival, and returned in haste to Pisa.

Hurrying at once to the emperor, he found that he had descended from the Mountains [Note: [Col. 1233D] By the capitalized word *Montes* (“Mountains”), once the noun stands independently, we Italians mean the Alps; by the same usage as all mountain heights are so called, as Servius testifies on *Aeneid*, Book X: “By the Gauls they are called Alps”; properly speaking, however, they are the Gallic mountains, namely those by which [Col. 1234D] Gaul is separated from Italy. PEREGR.], and had pitched his camp above the city of Cremona. Immediately he threw himself at the emperor’s feet, tearfully begging him to help one who had been disinherited.

Meanwhile, the city of Naples was reduced to such harsh famine that many infants, boys, adolescents, young men, and old persons of both sexes breathed their last in the streets and houses [Col. 1233C] of the city. But the master of the soldiers and his faithful supporters, who watched over the city’s liberty and followed the honorable example of their forefathers, preferred to die first of hunger rather than bow their necks beneath the power of the accursed king.

Amid these events the aforesaid emperor sent his sealed letters through his own envoys to the master of the soldiers and his citizens. In them he wrote words of consolation, urging them to maintain their purpose of loyalty, for, with the Lord’s favor, he would soon hasten to their deliverance. Those envoys swore before everyone that they had left the emperor at the city of Spoleto. Not many days afterward, behold, another envoy of the emperor arrived, bearing letters likewise containing words of consolation, [Col. 1233D] and declaring that he had left him at the river Pescara. Again, in the following days, the emperor sent other letters, saying that he would soon come into Apulia and redeem Italy from such ruin.

Moreover, Archbishop Marinus of Naples, Philip of Acerra, a Neapolitan citizen of prudent intelligence, and Count Rainulf, who had long ago gone out to meet the emperor, likewise sent their letters of consolation to the master of the soldiers. Having received such letters and being thus sustained by such a promise, the Neapolitans, though forced by hunger, nevertheless awaited that emperor’s arrival. [Col. 1234A]

In the year 1137, and the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent [Note: [Col. 1234D] Baronius recounts, for this year, what Falco has described, often in the same words but slightly altered; likewise some other matters under the years 1138 and 1139. PEREGR.], in March, in the fifteenth indiction, the aforesaid Pope Innocent, who was then staying at Pisa, took counsel and departed from the city of Pisa, arriving at the city of Viterbo in order to confer with the aforesaid emperor.

The emperor therefore sent his son-in-law Henry, with three thousand horsemen, to Pope Innocent, adding that he would secure the Roman territories and restore his principality to Prince Robert. He himself planned to proceed to the Marches. The pope at once entered the Roman territories and brought the city of Albano and the entire province [Col. 1234B] of Campania under his allegiance. He did not wish to enter Rome, lest he be hindered by Roman affairs.

The aforesaid emperor, reaching the river Pescara, celebrated the Lord’s Easter there. Crossing that river, he secured the city of Termoli and the counts of that province; then, moving his army, he entered Apulia and took the city of Siponto and Monte Sant’Angelo on the eighth day of May. Such fear seized all Apulia that the entire people, as far as the city of Bari, were bound to his authority.

After these events the pope came to the city of San Germano and subjected it to his rule. Coming thence to Capua, he restored it to Prince Robert. Having done this, the aforesaid pope came to Benevento on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, and pitched camp beyond Mount San Felice, near Benevento, with Duke Henry, the emperor’s son-in-law.

At once he sent Lord Gerard, cardinal—a prudent and discreet man—near the city of Benevento, to speak with the Beneventans and ask whether they wished to establish a firm peace with him. Certain Beneventine citizens came to him, and they discussed the city’s reconciliation fully and at length. When this had been done, Cardinal Gerard reported to the pope all that had been said.

On the following day the pope, after taking counsel, moved his camp on Saturday. He crossed to this side of the aforesaid Mount San Felice with the army of Duke Henry [Col. 1234D] and ordered camp to be pitched boldly and courageously on the plain of St. Peter the Apostle, beside the river Sabato. The people of Benevento, however, could understand nothing of what was happening.

While the camps of the pope and duke were being pitched on the aforesaid plain of St. Peter, news of this great event struck the city of Benevento. Rossemannus, who then presided as the rival of the Roman See, stirred up nearly all the citizens to rise against the approaching pope [Col. 1235A] and resist them as best they could.

Without delay, the aforesaid Cardinal Gerard summoned Landulf, judge of Benevento, Louis the physician, and Malfrid of Grimaldo, the abbot, to discuss a peace settlement and surrender the city to Pope Innocent. The men who had been summoned went out and, favoring the pope’s requests, returned to the city.

At about the ninth hour, certain Beneventans went out and began fighting the Germans, thinking to frighten them and pursue them in flight. But their duke, named Henry, hearing that the Beneventans were thus attacking him, secretly ordered all his men to arm. Arranging that they should leave the camp in companies, he ordered them to ambush and forestall the Beneventans, who had so foolishly and furiously come out. [Col. 1235B]

Why say more? Suddenly the Germans sprang upon them, roaring like lions, and drove into flight as far as the Great Bridge those Beneventans who were fighting against them. In their flight about forty were captured, and some were slain. Among them, Peter called “of the People,” his head cut off—alas, miserable man!—breathed his last. Another, Priscian by name, the city notary, died there after suffering many wounds. Ten wounded men who escaped capture died within the city after forty days.

When the Beneventine citizens had thus been captured, slaughtered, and delivered over to death, fear immediately seized Benevento, and there was such mourning that, had you been present, reader, you would have thought yourself dying with them and perishing in great affliction.

When night came, [Col. 1235C] the citizens who had been captured were tightly bound in chains. But at daybreak, on Sunday, certain wise and discreet Beneventine citizens came to the pope. Having obtained everything that the pope had demanded, he immediately ordered the captive Beneventine citizens whom the Germans had seized to be released and allowed to return home. Thus, after oaths had been confirmed, many citizens who had gone out to the pontiff swore allegiance to Pope Innocent.

While these oaths were being completed, a Beneventine citizen named Jaquintus, who had been in exile for three years and was planning vengeance for injuries received, stirred up all the Germans to enter the city, seize as many people as they could, [Col. 1235D] and carry off their goods. They rushed forward in arms and hastened as far as the Gate of Ruffinus. But because those inside firmly shut that gate, they were unable to enter the city.

When news of this great incursion reached the ears of Pope Innocent, he ordered Duke Henry to be summoned, that he might restrain the army and prevent it from making such a deadly attack. The duke immediately hurried over and commanded the whole army to return to camp; thus the city escaped their invasion.

But Jaquintus entered through the postern called St. Renatus’s and, hurrying with several companions to the sacred palace of the curia, seized Crescentius, a cardinal opposed to Pope Innocent, [Col. 1236A] who was then hiding there. Without delay they led him through the street and delivered him as a captive to the pope.

Then, in that same street, Jaquintus found Bernard, called Count of the Palace, another opponent of that pope. Boldly, he attempted to seize him in order to hand him over as a prisoner to the aforesaid pope. Bernard, seeing that he was about to be so shamefully captured, shouted to certain companions riding with him that they should come to his aid as quickly as possible and rescue him from such captivity. They immediately drew their swords, struck Jaquintus, cruelly dealt him wounds, and threw him from his horse to the ground. Thus Bernard was freed from that captivity.

Extraordinary fear then seized the city. Forgetting their possessions, the stunned citizens [Col. 1236B] feared unprecedented destruction and plundering. Jaquintus, so cruelly wounded, was carried in the hands of some men to his sister’s house. Having lived nine days without consciousness or memory, he died.

The pope, hearing that he had been wounded and killed in this manner and had brought it upon himself by his own initiative, being a man of wise spirit and peaceful heart, raised no complaint against the Beneventans who had killed him. Bossemannus, who had then been bishop against the pope’s will and had held the city under a usurped title, fled in the silence of night, compelled by fear.

When all this had taken place, we—the aforesaid Judge Falco, Falco the son of Abbot Falco, Saductus, Pando, Potofridus, and Adonibezet—who had been exiles for three years, [Col. 1236C] returned to our homes with other Beneventans likewise in exile, by permission of the aforesaid pope. We praised the mighty deeds of the heavenly King, who brings exultation after tribulation and weeping. The aforesaid pope sent the above-named Cardinal Gerard into the city to receive allegiance from all the citizens; and this was done.

When all this had unfolded, Pope Innocent, having received oaths of allegiance, took counsel and set out on the eighth day before the Kalends of June to hasten to the aforementioned emperor. Arriving before the Upper Gate, the pope addressed the people of the city, who were waiting for him there, as follows:

> “We give thanks to you, brothers and lords, because with cheerful hearts and sincere intention you have rendered us allegiance. Therefore I ask your brotherhood and integrity to preserve peace and steadfast justice among yourselves. At present we cannot enter the city because of the many and diverse matters which I have resolved must be settled with the lord emperor. But when these have been settled by divine mercy, we shall return to you and deliberate concerning the city’s welfare. For now, we permit our aforesaid brother, Cardinal Gerard, to remain with you; he will diligently watch over your interests and preserve peace among you.” [Col. 1236D]

Having spoken these and similar words, the pope resumed his journey and made his way toward the aforesaid Emperor Lothair. He found him fiercely besieging the city of Bari. [Col. 1237A]

The aforementioned Cardinal Gerard remained in Benevento by order of the aforesaid pope. Immediately ascending the sacred Beneventine palace, he worked for the city’s welfare, having established peace on every side. Among his other arrangements, he especially preached with all his strength, in word and heart, that peace must be maintained.

Before leaving the city, the pope appointed the subdeacon Octavian, a prudent man of wise spirit, as rector of Benevento. Together with Lord Gerard, he diligently governed the condition of the city and the stability of peace. When the pope reached the emperor, he and the aforesaid Duke Henry were received by the emperor with extraordinary honor and joy.

Then the people of Bari attacked the castle of their city, exceedingly formidable and well fortified, which King Roger had ordered built for their oppression. Besieging it for forty days with German aid and great valor, they took the castle and razed it to the ground. [Col. 1237B] The castle’s defenders, because they could no longer defend it, were captured, slain, and cast into the sea.

Thus all Italy, Calabria, and Sicily resounded with so great a victory, and, giving thanks to the heavenly King for having been rescued from the jaws of so great a tyrant, rejoiced. Thereupon the whole coast as far as Taranto and Calabria strove to bind itself to the emperor’s allegiance.

When that castle of Bari had been taken, the pope and emperor came against the city of Melfi. They besieged it courageously and, after not many days, took it [Col. 1237C] and secured its allegiance.

Meanwhile the Pisan army, as it had sworn, arrived at Naples with one hundred armed ships. Without delay, by the aforesaid emperor’s order, it hastened against Amalfi, intending to ravage it with fire and sword. But the Amalfitan citizens, having devised a means of safety, gave a great sum of money and remained loyal to the emperor and the Pisans.

Then, hurrying against Ravello and Scala, they attacked them, seized all their goods, and consumed them in the mouth of fire and sword. They led men and women captive with their little children, and, rejoicing in this vengeance, exulted beyond belief.

Meanwhile, the aforesaid emperor and pope left Melfi [Col. 1237D] and descended into the territory of Potenza. There they stayed for about thirty days near the streams flowing from Lake Pesole. From there they bound all the towns and cities of Apulia to their authority.

Having done this, the emperor ordered the Pisan army to besiege Salerno. He also commanded Prince Robert and the master of the Neapolitan soldiers to besiege that same city of Salerno with all their strength and arms together with the Pisans. This was done on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

Moreover, he sent Count Rainulf, whom he held in great affection, with one thousand German soldiers against the city of Salerno. When they assembled near its walls, they laid siege to it. There were in fact four hundred knights in that city who, guarding the city, fought daily against the Pisans, [Col. 1238A] the prince, and all his men.

One day, as we have learned, they fought each other most fiercely. Some of King Roger’s Sicilian soldiers were taken captive and bound. The Pisan consuls, observing the city’s steadfastness and the presence of such a great force of knights, took counsel and ordered a wooden siege-engine, astonishingly lofty and more terrible than could be believed, to be built and raised with the utmost speed. Consequently, the city’s people, oppressed by the peril of death, waited for death.

When the emperor heard of Salerno’s steadfastness and that the Pisans were besieging it with fire and sword, he took counsel and hastened swiftly with the pope to the same city. [Col. 1238B] On the following day, the wise men of the city came to the emperor, and, agreements having been made, subjected the city to his authority. Some of those knights, having received assurances of safety, obtained leave to depart. Others, together with the aforesaid magnates of Roger, fled to the great tower above the city.

Thus the city was turned to joy and rejoiced beneath so great an authority. But when the Pisan people heard that the city of Salerno had been taken by the emperor without their counsel and consent, they were exceedingly distressed. In anger, they burned the wooden siege-engine they had made and prepared ships to return to Pisa. But compelled by the prayers and promises of Pope Innocent, they returned to obedience to the emperor’s will. Thus [Col. 1238C] that fortress of the Great Tower was abandoned because of their disagreement.

When these things had been accomplished, the aforesaid emperor and pope moved their camp and came to Avellino; then to Benevento. On this side of Urbiano, near the river Calore, they pitched camp at the church of St. Stephen on the second day of August.

When Pope Innocent had come to Avellino, he sought to appoint, in his own name, a duke for the defense of Apulia. But the emperor wished to appoint one in his own name, against the pope’s will. Therefore they disagreed with each other for about thirty days; but, after the counsel of wise men had been sought, this disagreement was ended.

Why say more? With divine mercy favoring them, the emperor himself [Col. 1238D] and all his men consenting, the pope chose in his own name, to the allegiance of St. Peter, Count Rainulf—a truly prudent and discreet man—as duke. Once he had been elected, the pope and emperor handed over and confirmed before everyone the banner in honor of the duchy. No one then alive could remember any duke having been elected with such joy and honor.

While they were camped in the aforesaid place, three days later, namely on the Kalends of September, the empress named Floridas, taking with her about one hundred soldiers, came to the church of the blessed apostle Bartholomew through the Golden Gate. Hearing the solemnities of Mass there, she offered a pallium upon the altar of Blessed Bartholomew and one pound of silver.

Out of joy, the Beneventine people of both sexes [Col. 1239A] hurried from every part of the city to behold the empress. For throughout innumerable courses of years we had not seen an empress or emperor. Giving thanks to God, we rejoiced because in our time we saw what our fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers could not see. Leaving the basilica of Blessed Bartholomew, she proceeded through the middle street of the city and, departing through the Upper Gate, returned to her army.

Three days after the empress’s arrival, the aforesaid pope entered Benevento and was honorably received by all the clergy and people. On the following day, sitting in the sacred Beneventine palace before the Beneventine clergy and people, he proclaimed that if anyone wished canonically and reasonably to object to the person or election of Gregory, bishop-elect of Benevento, he should openly state his objection. [Col. 1239B] But, with divine mercy assisting—and because the bishop-elect had kept his life religiously—none of the citizens objected to his election.

Seeing this, the pope gave thanks to God. He himself bore witness that the bishop-elect’s person and life were honorable and religious, and commanded him to confess his sins and, on the coming Sunday, receive consecration with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.

Why say more? When Sunday came, the pope entered the episcopal church and, on the fifth day of September, consecrated the bishop-elect. The patriarch of Aquileia attended his consecration, together with many other archbishops, bishops, and abbots—religious German men. Reader, [Col. 1239C] had you been present, you would truly have marveled and said that no archbishop of Benevento had ever been consecrated with such honor and reverence. After his consecration, the pope returned to the palace.

When these things had taken place, the judges and wise men of the city begged the pope to intercede with the emperor, that he might free the Beneventans from the ancient oppression which the city had suffered far and wide: namely, from the payments called *fidantiae* and from forced labor-services (*angariae*), the land-tax (*terraticum*), and all the dues which they had customarily paid to the Normans. “For we, and our fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, prayed to God that He would deign to grant the emperor’s coming to these regions, through whose arrival we might gain the strength [Col. 1239D] of liberty and security. Now therefore, most holy Father, since both will and power have been granted to do us good, we beseech you with the tears of all that you may rescue the city of St. Peter from so great a burden of tribute.”

The pope, moved by divine compassion and grieving over the city’s long oppression, sent the patriarch of Aquileia and other cardinals—and especially Cardinal Gerard, his cardinal-priest, a most venerable and discreet man—to the emperor, who was camped outside in the place mentioned above. They asked him to command Count Roger of Ariano and his barons to relinquish peacefully the *fidantiae* and all revenues which he had customarily received from the inheritances of the Beneventans. [Col. 1240A]

The emperor, accepting the pope’s petition, immediately summoned the aforesaid count, ordering him to come with his barons and, with an oath intervening, comply with the pope’s requests. The count came before the emperor and confessed that he had sworn and confirmed this in the time of the constable Rolpoto, who had requested it on behalf of the city. Finally, he compelled the barons whom he had brought with him to swear as the pope required: first Alferius Draco, Robert de la Marra, Bartholomew de Petrapulcina, Tadeus de la Graeca, Gerard de Lanzulinu, and Sarolus de lo Tufo. They swore as follows:

> “I swear and promise that from this hour henceforth I shall neither demand nor permit to be demanded, from all the inheritances of the Beneventans, *fidantiae*, forced labor-services, land-tax, olives, wine, *salutes*, or any payment whatsoever—namely from vineyards, rough lands, woods, chestnut groves, and churches. I grant free power in the inheritances of the Beneventans to hunt, fowl, and do whatever they wish in them and from them; and by this agreement I shall not disturb the city’s market, nor consent that it be disturbed. I shall observe all these things faithfully and without fraud.” [Col. 1240B]

After they had sworn in this manner, the emperor ordered him to summon his other barons of Montefusco to take the same oath. When this had been done, the aforesaid Cardinal Gerard, together with the wise men of the city, reported all these matters to the pope. This oath was made on the sixth day of September.

On the following day, Cardinal Gerard himself went with the judges to the emperor [Col. 1240C] in order to receive this oath from the count and his barons. Count Roger, however, refused to take the oath, confessing that he had taken it in former times; but he ordered his barons of Montefusco to swear: namely Raone de lo Tufo, Accardus, Gemundus, Eternus, Onfridus, and the others who received *fidantiae* around Benevento. When this was done, we gave thanks to God the Savior and to Pope Innocent, through whose power and grace we attained so great a liberty.

After these things had been accomplished, the aforesaid emperor moved camp from the aforesaid place and set out to return to Rome. He passed before the Upper Gate with all his army, and the aforesaid pope hastened with him on the ninth day of September [Col. 1240D; Note: [Col. 1239D] These matters entirely agree with what I observed in the series of the abbots of Cassino concerning the time when Innocent [Col. 1240D] and Lothair were together at Cassino. PEREGR.].

The emperor then pitched camp at the place called Tres-Sancti. Then, proceeding toward Capua, they passed on to Rome. Why say more? The emperor returned to the height and palaces of his empire; Pope Innocent went to the Lateran palace.

When the aforementioned King Roger heard that the emperor had begun his return journey, he assembled an army and came to Salerno. At once he advanced against Nocera and brought it under his power. Then, moving camp, he occupied all the land of Count Rainulf. Proceeding from there, he seized Capua in great fury and stormed it, ravaging it with fire and sword. He ordered all the spoils and riches of that city [Col. 1241A] to be destroyed, partly by fire and partly by force. He plundered the churches and their ornaments; women and nuns were subjected to disgrace. Having thus carried out these acts, he took Avellino and territory as far as the borders of Benevento.

Immediately Sergius, master of the soldiers of Naples, turned to Roger’s allegiance. Then the judges of Benevento, with other citizens, approached the king and subjected the city of Benevento to the allegiance of Anacletus and to the king’s favor, treating Pope Innocent’s allegiance lightly. After this, he assembled an army, arrived at Benevento, passed before the Upper Gate in the middle of October, and hastened to Mount Sarcus, which he brought under his power.

Proceeding from there, [Col. 1241B] he hurried swiftly against the city of Count Richard. The count abandoned it and fled to Duke Rainulf; thus Roger bound that city to his will. Capturing Mount Corvino, he ordered it consumed by fire and sword and plundered its spoils.

When the aforementioned Duke Rainulf heard that the king had entered Apulia to bring him disgrace and was daily planning its devastation, he assembled the people of Bari, Trani, Troia, and Melfi, together with fifteen hundred knights. He declared that he preferred to yield to death rather than live an unhappy life. Thus prepared, the duke came near the king’s army.

Meanwhile, the abbot of Clairvaux, a most remarkable and discreet man, who had come to that king to calm the disturbance of so great a conflict, [Col. 1241C] tried to bind the king and duke in a pact of peace. But because of the many and various claims at issue between them, it had not yet pleased God the Savior’s power that reconciliation should be established.

Why say more? The king divided his army and resolutely set it in battle array; the duke likewise arranged all his men wisely. The king’s first line advanced and entered among the duke’s armed troops. Immediately that line of the king was overthrown. The king himself, who was present with his other armed battle-lines, when God’s judgment came upon him, was struck by fear and was the first to turn his back in flight. Thus the entire king’s host fled headlong, abandoning all its equipment and tents, with an infinite quantity of gold and silver, [Col. 1241D] whose abundance human knowledge cannot number.

Why say more? The duke became victorious, captured and killed men from the king’s army, and he himself, the people of Bari and Trani, and the others whom he had summoned carried off that great wealth and the riches, enriched to their homes. As we heard, three thousand men died in the battle. There Sergius, master of the Neapolitan soldiers, died; there also Eternus of Montefusco, Gerard of Luzulino, Sarolus de lo Tufo, and many others, whose names we pass over in silence because they are difficult to enumerate. This battle was fought on the second day of October.

The aforesaid king, fleeing in this manner with his followers by night, reached [Col. 1242A] the castle of the Marsh on the following day and then hastened to Salerno. Not many days later, Rossemannus, bishop of Benevento, having consulted with the city’s judges and certain wise men, hurried to the king in order to console him and offer the city’s services. He further asked that the king grant to the Beneventine people the freedom of their possessions which the aforesaid emperor had conceded.

The king, accepting their petitions and seeking the favor of the whole city, made and sealed a privilege remitting all the *fidantiae* and exactions which we had customarily paid. Having received the charter, they returned to Benevento with ineffable joy. The text of the privilege is as follows:

> “In the name of the Lord God, the eternal Savior Jesus [Col. 1242B] Christ. In the year 1137 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the month of November, the first indiction. I, Roger, by the grace of God king of Sicily and Italy, helper and shield of Christians, son of Roger the first count: We are moved by the liberality of our royal excellence to bestow benefits with a more generous hand upon our faithful subjects, as persons who have deserved well of us, so that not only may they be found more faithful, but others also, encouraged by hope of reward, may be made readier in our service.
>
> “Therefore, venerable Rossemannus, archbishop of Benevento, who have always proved faithful in all things, we graciously assent to your petitions, and those of Bernard, constable of Benevento, the Beneventine judges, and very many other citizens. Because we have always found you to be our faithful subjects, for the love [Col. 1242C] of the Highest King, through whom we exist and reign, and for your love and loyalty which you bear toward us and will bear hereafter, we release and remit to you all that we and our Norman predecessors had concerning the city of Benevento: the following *fidantiae*, namely revenues in money, *salutes*, forced labor-services, land-tax, pasture-tax, meat-tax, Kalends-tax, wine, olives, relief-payment, and finally all other exactions, whether from churches or citizens.
>
> “We make all the aforesaid payments and possessions free and quit, from whatever source we had customarily received anything, so that, as long as you remain in loyalty to us and our heirs, you and your heirs shall remain free and quit from all the aforesaid burdens. [Col. 1242D] You shall have free power to hunt, fish, and fowl on your estates. And so that you may be able firmly to maintain this, we have caused this privilege to be sealed with our golden seal.
>
> “If any person—God forbid—whether great or lowly, should presume in any respect to violate the text of this our concession, let that person pay twenty pounds of the purest gold to our palace as a fine, and let this present privilege retain its former force. We have ordered the instrument of this concession to be written by the hand of Henry our notary and adorned with a golden bull. In the seventh year of our reign.”

When this privilege had been read before the Beneventine assembly, we gave thanks to God, the Savior of all, to the aforesaid king, and to the already mentioned bishop, because Jesus Christ in His mercy had deigned to grant us—and to offer us, not for our merits—the gift of liberty [Col. 1243A] and security which our grandfathers and fathers could not see.

Why say more? Because of this great benefit granted and confirmed to us, all the citizens promised services and honors to the aforesaid king and promised to serve at his command without offense [Note: [Col. 1243D] Perhaps: “without offense to the Roman pontiff.” The Beneventans, freed from all exactions by Roger’s privilege, promised him their services; but Anacletus had previously granted this. “We grant and confirm,” he says in the diploma cited above, “the aid of the men of Benevento against your enemies.” Falco reports that in the following year, 1138, they gave the same king proof of their obedience, when he says: “The aforesaid king accepted Lord Pope Innocent as father and lord, and commanded the city of Benevento and every part of his kingdom to accept him as father and lord. We, having received his letters, called that man lord and father.” Roger thus appears to have renounced the schism; yet peace between him and Innocent did not follow. In 1139, as our author likewise records, the aforesaid pope bound him with the bonds of excommunication in the Roman synod. PERGER.].

Moreover, Duke Rainulf, mentioned above, hearing that the king had thus been defeated and, dismayed in spirit, had entered Salerno with only a few men, took counsel and assembled about one thousand horsemen and a multitude of Apulian infantry. Without delay, leaving Troia captured, he bound it wholly to his authority. Proceeding from there, he came against the county of Count Roger of Ariano and immediately subjected to his rule Alferius Draco, Robert de la Marra, Robert de Petramajori, Robert [Col. 1243B] de Potofranco, and the other barons of that count. Finally, he compelled Count Roger himself to submit to his will.

When this had been done, the duke, surrounded by the valor of his followers, pitched camp near the castle of the Marsh on the Kalends of December. Meanwhile, the Beneventine people wondered at Duke Rainulf’s self-restraint, while they themselves, together with Lord Archbishop Rossemannus, watched day and night over loyalty and devotion to the aforesaid king and service to Anacletus.

I shall also explain to your brotherhood another matter that must not be passed over in silence. When the aforesaid abbot of Clairvaux, a man most remarkable and discerning, was discussing with the named king a treaty of peace and the unity of the Church, [Col. 1243C] the king repeatedly agreed with that abbot that three cardinals on the part of Pope Innocent, who had been present at his election, should come to the king himself, and three on the part of Anacletus; and that they should set before the king the procedure of each election. Then the king himself, having heard the procedure, would choose the holier and more just election of the two parties; and thus, with the favour of the Holy Spirit, would attain, with all the greatness of his realm, a firm peace, so far as this lay within his judgment and knowledge. For he knew and firmly believed that the Christians of the whole world favoured Innocent’s party and venerated his pontificate, while he alone, with the extent of his kingdom, stood in discord.

Accordingly, envoys were sent at once to Pope Innocent and Anacletus, and the king’s proposal was dispatched with all speed. It therefore pleased [Col. 1243D] them; and, their decision having been confirmed, on Innocent’s side Chancellor Aimeric and Cardinal Gerard, a man most venerable, came together with the aforesaid abbot of Clairvaux to Salerno, in order to examine this election. On Anacletus’s side Chancellor Matthew, Cardinal Peter of Pisa, and another cardinal named Gregory likewise hastened there.

[Col. 1244A] When these had thus assembled, that king, being of keen mind and prudent counsel, first examined Innocent’s party for four days, wonderfully and beyond what can be believed, until sunset; then he likewise investigated Anacletus’s party for four days. Having therefore carefully and diligently heard the arguments concerning the election of each party, the king ordered all the clergy and people of the city of Salerno, and the bishops and abbots of monasteries who had assembled, to be gathered together; and before them he began as follows:

“Lords and brethren, we believe that your wisdom is not unaware for what purpose I caused these cardinals of both parties to be summoned. For I thought, so far as our ability extends, to put an end to so great and weighty a matter and plainly to follow the path of justice. But because our mind is hampered by many [Col. 1244B] questions and various answers, I cannot by myself bring this great matter to a conclusion. Therefore, if it seems good to these lord cardinals, let them write down the order of each election, and let one cardinal from each party go down with me into Sicily. There, with the Lord’s favour, we shall celebrate the feast of the Nativity of Jesus Christ the Saviour; and there we shall find wise archbishops, bishops, and other men of prudent mind, by whose counsel I have hitherto followed Anacletus’s party. Then, by the counsel of these and other wise men, divine mercy inspiring us, we shall give this matter the most certain conclusion, so far as lies within my power.”

To this Cardinal Gerard replied:

“You should truly know that on our side all of us shall set down in writing the procedure of our party. For you have heard from our own mouths the course of the election; you have heard everything whatsoever was done concerning us. We shall indeed send Cardinal Guido of Castello, certainly a wise and discerning man, to come with you into Sicily, as you request. Thereafter, let matters be accomplished as may please your wisdom; may the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, enlighten your heart and lead you with an upright heart to the Church and to the light of truth.”

And, these things having been done, each returned to his own place. On the following day the aforesaid Cardinal Gerard returned with his companions; but the aforesaid Cardinal Guido alone remained, to depart with the king as had been arranged. Likewise, another cardinal was appointed on Anacletus’s side. When [Col. 1244D] this had been accomplished and a ship made ready, the king himself crossed over to Sicily.

Moreover Duke Rainulf, already named, vigorously besieged the aforesaid castle of Paludis, which he attacked daily with many battles and siege-engines. But, seeing that he could not take that castle, the duke took counsel, abandoned it, and withdrew into the district of Alife. There he immediately seized that [Col. 1245A] city and the fortification of its castle and brought them under his power.

In this year Anacletus, who had lived under the title of pontiff, died on the seventh day of January. He had sat for seven years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. Pope Innocent therefore immediately gathered strength and, supported by the power of his friends, vigorously fell upon his enemies. Bishop Rossemannus accordingly ordered all the bells of the city of Benevento to be rung, signifying Anacletus’s death.

In this year the aforesaid emperor, while returning to his empire, died in Tuscany; and after his death Conrad was raised to the empire by unanimous vote.

[Col. 1245B] In the year 1138, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Innocent II, supreme pontiff, in March, in the first indiction: when the aforesaid Anacletus had died, his cardinals, having taken counsel from Anacletus’s brothers, sent to King Roger, informing him of Anacletus’s death and asking whether, if it pleased him, they should establish a pope. The king therefore, in order to obstruct the cause of Pope Innocent, assented to their will and gave them authority to elect a pope. Having returned to Rome and assembled their supporters, in the middle of March they made Cardinal Gregory their pope and usurper, calling him Victor. But, aided by God’s mercy, that heresy and usurpation held sway only a short time.

After not many days had elapsed, Anacletus’s aforesaid brothers, recognizing so great a [Col. 1245C] disturbance, came to their senses and, with the Lord’s favour, concluded a firm peace with the aforesaid lord Pope Innocent. They themselves and all his adversaries turned to his allegiance; and that wicked man who had appeared under the name of Victor laid aside his vestment and mitre and submitted to Pope Innocent’s will. Thus, with great joy and exultant glory, the whole city of Rome rejoiced; and Pope Innocent himself was brought, with the Lord’s help, to the unity and concord of the Church.

After not many days had elapsed, the aforesaid apostolic, having taken counsel, came to Albano, intending, after assembling an army, to go to Duke Rainulf; but, struck by illness, he was unable to come. Meanwhile King Roger, having assembled an army, came into Apulia, [Col. 1245D] intending to subject to his authority the cities which the emperor had taken from him. Duke Rainulf, therefore, perceiving that king’s arrival, stirred up all the districts of Apulia so that they might stand unanimously against his fury. Without delay they hastened with all speed to the named duke, and so for nearly two months they resisted the ferocity of that king.

Meanwhile, as has been reported to us, the aforesaid king accepted Pope Innocent as father [Col. 1246A] and lord, and ordered the city of Benevento and every part of his kingdom to acknowledge that he had accepted him as father and lord. We, having received his letters, called him lord and father.

After these events Rao of Fraineta showed himself rebellious toward the city of Benevento and King Roger, and ordered the vineyards of the Beneventans to be cut down. The citizens therefore, having taken counsel, reported Rao’s depredations to the named king, asking him to rescue them as swiftly as possible from his hostilities. The king immediately, having assembled an army, set out; and by the force of his arrival he seized Montemaranum and other castles and burned them with fire. Then, arriving before Ceppalunum together with the Beneventans, he besieged it. On that very day he seized the peasants’ settlement; their goods were plundered, and all their houses [Col. 1246B] destroyed.

On the following day the towers and fortifications of the castle were surrendered into the king’s power. For Rao of Fraineta, compelled by fear of the king, had left that castle three days earlier with his wife and hastened to Duke Rainulf, together with Rao of lo Tufo and Orrico of Sarno, who likewise abandoned their castles while fleeing the king’s presence. The Beneventan citizens immediately and humbly begged the king to grant them leave to destroy that hostile castle of Ceppalunum. Why say more? The king, favouring the people’s petitions, permitted its demolition. Without delay the Beneventan people hurried in bands to destroy it; thus every building of the castle was torn out by the roots, and the whole city rejoiced at its destruction. For if I wished to describe all the cruelties and perils which we suffered at the hands of the lords of [Col. 1246C] that castle, neither tongue could speak them nor pen set them forth. Therefore, praising God, we gave thanks to the king, who granted it to us to destroy.

After these things, the aforesaid king entered the territory of Capua and seized the castle called Calvum.

> **[Note: [Col. 1245D]** This was truly Calvum—where ancient Cales had once stood, a place which had long remained deserted—and from the beginning of its construction it lay upon the very boundary of the Campanian territory. For it is to be understood from Erchempert, nos. 40 and 45, that in the year 879 it began to be built by Atenulf, who later became count of Capua and finally prince of Benevento, on the boundary of Calinium extending into Campanian territory; and because of it Pandonulf, then gastald of Capua, took offence. This description was not altered later, when its own district had been assigned to Calvum, as is made clear from an ordinance of Prince Pandulf in *Historia Principum Langobardorum*, book I, and from a privilege of Queen Joanna II in the archive of the city of Capua; it indeed remains so even now, as elsewhere discussed. PEREGR.]**

Moreover Duke Rainulf, having assembled an army, kept watch at all hours in order to fall upon that king by force and take vengeance. But the king, being of prudent counsel, encamped through mountainous and difficult places, and thus avoided the duke’s prudence and strength. The duke therefore, grievously distressed in mind, raged also in body because he could not express his heart’s pain. At last he stayed near Alife, believing that the king would come to Alife.

But the king, as we have said, fleeing the duke’s [Col. 1246D] steadfastness, returned from Castle Calvum and ordered his tents to be pitched in the territory of St Agatha, intending to go to Benevento. Thence, after moving his army, he encamped near Benevento at the place called Plancella and stayed there for two days. Then, having taken counsel, he withdrew thence, crossed the River Calore with his army in close order, and pitched camp by the Bridge of Valentine, remaining there two days.

The named Duke Rainulf, [Col. 1247A] being of prudent mind, stayed in the territory of Petraemajoris, considering how he might bravely and vigorously deliver the castle of Apice, which the king was threatening to besiege. The named king begged the Beneventans to hasten unanimously to his aid. Rossemannus, who was then bishop, compelled by his affection for the king, asked all the citizens and ordered them to assist him.

But when the king heard that the castle of Apice was to be manned by soldiers and prudent men, he took counsel, moved his camp, and ordered the castle of Petrapolicina to be attacked. He devastated it with fire and sword; then, proceeding onward, he seized other castles and ordered them burned. He seized and burned the bridge of Landulf, Farnitum, Campugattari, Guardia, and the city of [Col. 1247B] Alife. The king’s galleys and the countless mob of plunderers following him seized, carried off, and stripped all the property of the citizens and the ornaments of the churches; each took his share as he could.

Reader, had you been present, you would have been overwhelmed and distressed at so great a slaughter and devastation of a city, and you would have affirmed that since the time of the Greeks and pagans no such ruin and burning had befallen Christians. When he had thus destroyed the city of Alife, he moved his army from there and hastened into the territory of Venafrum, intending to subject those cities to his power. Immediately, by the command of cruelty imposed by that king, he ordered the city of Venafrum to be attacked and stormed. The citizens defended both themselves and their city as best they could. But the king, seeing [Col. 1247C] their steadfastness, threatened with a cruel command that they should fall upon that city. Immediately, through sins pressing upon them, that city, very strongly fortified and full of riches, was taken; all the goods and great wealth of the citizens were seized by the enemy, divided into portions, and reduced to nothing.

The men, women, and their little children fled through the mountains, leaving all their possessions in the hands of robbers and plunderers. Thus that city and its fortified towers were subjected to the king’s power. On hearing of such cruelty, the castle of Presenzano and Roccaromana submitted to the king’s will, as did other neighbouring castles round about. After these events, the king returned from there to Benevento [Col. 1247D] and encamped at the castle of Paludis on the twelfth day of September.

Meanwhile Duke Rainulf, unable to withstand so great a king, remained about the territory of Alife, shaken by grief of heart. Departing thence, the king went to the city [Col. 1248A] of Melfi, thinking to subject it to his authority; but he could not accomplish this. Returning from there, he went against the castle of Tocco. He immediately ordered wooden siege-engines to be made, by whose force the towers and fortifications of that castle might be destroyed; and thus a certain part of the towers was demolished. Meanwhile Duke Rainulf kept watch around him every day, lest that king should invade the lands of Count Roger of Ariano.

But the people of the castle, seeing the king’s power and fury, bowed their necks beneath his authority and dominion; and that castle was subjected to his lordship on the third day before the Kalends of October. He besieged the castle of Tocco for eight days. When this had been accomplished, the king moved his camp from there and, in very rainy weather, came to Benevento. He himself encamped within the church of St Peter the Apostle [Col. 1248B] situated near the city.

> **[Note: [Col. 1247D]** The ruins of this church still remain on the plain, to use the words of our Falco under the year 1137, beside the River Sabato. Theoderada, wife of Duke Romuald, who ruled from 961 to 977, built it; and she established there a convent of many handmaids of God, as Paul the Deacon reports, book VI, chapter 1. Yet in Roger’s time, I think, there were no nuns there; rather, they inhabited the monastery likewise called St Peter the Apostle, mentioned by Falco under the year 1121 and situated within the city. Theoderada appears to have built this church outside Benevento’s walls in pious imitation of the Basilica of St Peter, founded in the Vatican field outside Rome. I judge that this was likewise the sole occasion for the building, outside Capua, Tarentum, and Vienne—leaving aside Nola and other cities—of churches formerly dedicated to that saint with the highest veneration. The first is described by our monk Michael in his *Sanctuary*, part III; the second by Peter the Deacon, book III, chapters 43 and 57; and the third is mentioned in a diploma of Callixtus II in the Bibliothèque de Fleury. In later declining years, when the matter had become unknown, the common people—and afterwards the learned who followed them—devised very different, though pious, reasons for their construction. PEREGR.]**

His whole army was quartered within the city of Benevento and remained there three days. For a terrible and very dangerous period of rains had set in, and they were in no way able to go out to procure necessities for the army. Therefore, as we have said, they remained within Benevento to refresh the army.

Meanwhile the named king entered the city of Benevento on the fourth day of October. He carefully searched the churches, the city palaces, and the apostolic court; and, when his army had been refreshed, he moved camp from the city and encamped near the castle of San Severo. Proceeding from there, he brought the castle of Morcone under his power; and after this he seized the castles of San Giorgio and Petra Maggiore. [Col. 1248C] Count Roger of Ariano, hearing this, abandoned the castle of Apice and gave all the villagers leave to obey the king; he himself entered the city of Ariano. There, trusting in the aid of Duke Rainulf, he by no means wished to submit to the king’s will.

The king immediately bound the castle of Apice to his allegiance and himself stayed four days at the castle of Tamaro. The aforesaid duke, having assembled an army, came near the city of Ariano to guard it, lest the king should in any way invade it. Thus the king and duke laboured against one another. After this, the aforesaid king, leaving that castle of Tamaro, hastened into the territory of Melfi; proceeding from there, he brought the very strongly fortified castle [Col. 1248D] of St Agatha under his power, along with other adjacent castles. Meanwhile the named duke held the city of Melfi, lest the king should by any stratagem invade it.

The aforesaid king, recognizing that Duke Rainulf continually [Col. 1249A] resisted him and his men and defended the cities of Apulia, took counsel and ordered the castles which he had seized to be fortified and guarded by soldiers and armed men. The king himself went to Salerno, intending to return to Sicily, which he had left for a long time. But the named duke went down to Bari and visited the coastal districts, exhorting all the people that, at an opportune time, having gathered strength and arms, they should resist the king. With one accord and devoted heart they declared that they would be ready.

In the year 1139 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of the lord Innocent II, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in March, in the second indiction: in this year the aforesaid apostolic Innocent celebrated a synod at Rome on the eighth day of April. [Col. 1249B] Countless archbishops, bishops, and abbots assembled for the presence of that sacred gathering. There, among other measures established through the agency of the Holy Spirit, the aforesaid apostolic Innocent bound King Roger and all his followers with the bonds of excommunication, in the presence of all the Catholic men who had assembled.

In this year Duke Rainulf, mentioned in the preceding account, was seized by the burning heat of a most violent synochal fever and departed this world at the end of April in the city of Troia. William, the venerable bishop of that city, with the whole clergy and people, carefully and honourably committed the duke to burial within the bishop’s residence, while tears flowed. O what [Col. 1249C] grief invaded that city among all—virgins and widows, boys and old men, men and women, and soldiers! If I attempted to describe it thoroughly, neither days nor an abundance of words would suffice.

The people of Bari, Trani, Melfi, and Canosa, and all those who trusted in his rule and protection, forgetting consolation, tearing out their hair, lacerating their breasts and cheeks, mourned beyond human measure. For they mourned a most pious duke, devoted to the welfare of all, who governed the reins of his whole duchy with sweetness and gracious humanity, setting aside all fury. Why say more? Even the bitterness of his enemies, sharing in the sorrow of his death and grieving at his prudence, wept and [Col. 1249D] sympathized. Thus nearly all Italy spoke continually of his worth and battles.

But when the aforesaid King Roger heard that Duke Rainulf, a warlike and magnanimous man, had departed this world, he rejoiced beyond human measure, inflamed by a spirit of vanity and exaltation. Rejoicing indeed, and forgetful of the common lot of death, he was excited and conceived the plan of gathering an army, falling upon the territory of Apulia, and subjecting it to his dominion and allegiance. Why say more? Having prepared seven ships laden with armed men and great quantities of gold and silver, he crossed to Salerno on the seventh day of May. Immediately all the clergy and people of Salerno received that king with many praises and resounding hymns. Without delay the king sent letters [Col. 1250A] to all his people dwelling round about, ordering them to come to him with arms drawn. On receiving his letters, they obeyed his command. Then the king, having assembled an army, came to Benevento and hastened to attack his enemies.

In this year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, that mountain which seemed to be near the city of Naples cast forth powerful fire and visible flames for eight days, so that the neighbouring cities and fortresses expected death. From its eruption issued black and dreadful ash, and that ash was carried by the wind as far as Salerno, Benevento, Capua, and Naples. That fire was visible for eight days. Many citizens of Benevento and I, the writer of this [Col. 1250B] work, collected some of this ash; for thirty days, moreover, the ash was visible upon the ground.

When, as stated above, King Roger had assembled an army, he hurried against the count’s city and, attacking it most fiercely, bound it to his dominion. The count, seeking flight, entered Troia. Then that king brought the cities and castles of the Capitanata under his authority.
