Moreover, the duke, son of the aforesaid king, brought all the cities of Apulia and the maritime cities under his command, guaranteeing peace and security to all. Yet he could not take the very strongly fortified city of Bari, for the prince of the city kept four hundred soldiers with him, apart from fifty thousand resident citizens.

The named duke, recognizing that he could not [Col. 1250C] take Bari, assembled his army and came to his father, King Roger, who was staying in the territory of Troia. When they had gathered together, they began carefully to deliberate how they might subject the city of Troia to their power. Count Roger of Ariano, with seven hundred soldiers despairing of their lives, was staying four miles from the city of Troia. The citizens of Troia, along with outsiders who had fled to them from fear of the named king, were defending that city.

When the king realized that the city was defended by the strength of so many men, he left two hundred soldiers at the nearby castle of Bacharezza to harass that city. He himself, with the named duke his son and their assembled [Col. 1250D] army, came against the city of Ariano belonging to Count Roger. The king immediately besieged that city and ordered wooden siege-engines to be made for its assault. But the citizens and the soldiers who were with them feared none of the attacks brought against them, for they had introduced two hundred soldiers and nearly twenty thousand armed men into the city.

The king, seeing it so prepared and fortified, ordered the camp moved. Angered, he commanded that their vineyards, olive groves, trees, and crops—whatever could be found—be cut down and laid waste. Leaving the city, he remained for two days through its surrounding territory.

At the same time, the aforesaid pope Innocent, hearing that the above-mentioned Duke Rainulf had died, grieved exceedingly; and, after taking counsel, [Col. 1251A] he left the city of Rome, attended by a troop of a thousand horsemen and a great multitude of foot-soldiers, and then arrived at the city of San Germano. When the aforesaid king learned that the pope had departed from the city, he sent his envoys to the said pope concerning peace, and promised to carry out both the pope’s wish and his request. The pope, receiving the king’s envoys honorably, sent two cardinals to the king himself, setting forth the basis of peace and friendship and asking that the king himself hasten to the city of San Germano.

Why say more? The king received those cardinals attentively and honorably, abandoned the city of Troia, which he was besieging, and hastened at rapid speed to the aforesaid pope with his son the duke and his forces. Immediately negotiations concerning a treaty of peace were conducted through their envoys on both sides [Col. 1251B]. The pope therefore demanded from the king the principality of Capua, which he had unjustly taken away from Prince Robert. But the king in no way wished to restore that principality; and thus this dispute continued between them for eight days. When this had taken place, the aforesaid king, having assembled his whole army, hastened to the lands called those of Burello’s sons, and brought a certain part of the castles of those lands under his power.

But the pope and those with him, learning that the king had withdrawn into those regions, ordered a certain castle named Galluzzo to be attacked and devastated. Without delay the aforesaid king was informed that the said pope had already attacked that castle. Why say more? The king hurried at the greatest speed to the territory of San Germano, where the pope himself was staying [Col. 1251C]. Behold: suddenly a terrible report of the king’s arrival flew abroad, and immediately the king’s camp was pitched. The pope, Prince Robert of Capua, and the Roman soldiery, perceiving the king’s arrival, ordered all their camp to be moved [Col. 1252A], so that they might remain in a safer place.

But the duke, the king’s son, taking about a thousand horsemen, caught the pope as he was thus departing; having laid ambushes, he fell upon the pope’s soldiers. Sensing the force and the ambushes, they turned their backs and sought flight, escaping as best they could through various places in that region. The aforesaid prince, Richard of Sapacanina [Note: [Col. 1251C] Not thus, but “of Rupecanina,” which is the name of a town in the diocese of Alife. This Richard was Rainulf’s brother. Rainulf, having been count of Avellino and of many other cities and towns, was appointed duke of Apulia by Innocent and Lothair; and he was born of Count Robert, son of the elder Count Rainulf, the full brother of Richard I, prince of Capua, as has been stated elsewhere. PEREGR.], and a multitude of Romans escaped; but many horsemen and foot-soldiers died in the river, and we heard that many would be in the king’s captivity.

Pope Innocent, however, was proceeding after all his men, as though secure. Behold: unexpectedly a troop of soldiers attacked, alas for the sorrow! and seized him; dividing all his treasure and adornment among themselves, they brought him before the king’s presence, and, having thus loaded him with insults [Col. 1252B], they placed him captive in the tent which the king had sent to him. Subsequently they brought the pope’s chancellor Aimeric and the cardinals as captives.

On the tenth day remaining of the month of July, Pope Innocent himself was captured [Note: [Col. 1251C] Baronius does not have the word *stante* (“remaining”), and reads the phrase absolutely: “on the tenth day of July”; accordingly, he judged that this occurred on the sixth day before the Ides of July. But certainly Innocent was captured by Roger on the second day before the Kalends of August, when only ten days of July remained; for, on the fourth day, says the Anonymous of Cassino, he confirmed to him the whole land after peace had been made—namely, on the aforesaid day of the month—from which our author differs by only one day.

That day, he says, on which the aforesaid pope confirmed peace with the king, is the feast of Blessed James. Therefore, in the same Falco, before these words I would read: “The king himself, his son the duke, and the prince came before the pope’s presence on the seventh day remaining of July,” not “the seventeenth.” But in the preceding passages, as I have said, nothing should be changed. Nor should anything be changed where Falco speaks of the same Roger on p. 128, who crossed to Salerno “on the seventh day remaining of May,” from which same passage Baronius likewise expunged *stante*.

Certainly, when Falco says that Richard III was established prince by the Campanians on the fifth day remaining of May (perhaps the sixth, not the fifth) in 1120, and adds that he was consecrated by the archbishop of Capua on the feast of the Ascension of the Lord, the fifth day remaining of that same May, he plainly shows that the consecration occurred on 27 May [Col. 1252C], on which date in that year the feast of the Lord’s Ascension fell.

I once explained this passage of Falco in familiar conversation, according to my custom, to a friend and learned man—as I often also explained to him many other ancient matters less commonly known. At that time he embraced my interpretation with his approval; but I do not know why, when he later committed it to writing, he concealed the fact that he had profited by me in this matter—as he has done on more than this one occasion—and preferred to praise Baronius as altogether weighty and beyond dispute, though, as has been said, this point had escaped Baronius more than once.

When the ancients divided the complete days of each month into three sections—that is, the days of the month’s beginning, middle, and end—which they called “remaining days” (*dies stantes*) (Synesius, Epistle 4, divides months only into beginning and ending days), examples of which are exceedingly common, they seem in some fashion to have wished to imitate the Nones, Ides, and Kalends of the ancient Romans. But they introduced, among other differences, this exception: they indicated a remaining day by its distance from the last day of the month, not from the Kalends and beginning of the following month, as my same friend stated the matter, not as I had taught him. Falco, either ignorant of or unconcerned with this distinction, did not calculate days before the Kalends by a different reckoning from that by which he calculated remaining days. Thus he said that the feast of St James the Apostle was celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, whereas it is venerated on the eighth day before the Kalends and on the seventh day remaining of July. Yet he places the feast of St Angel in the year 1131 on the third day before the Kalends of October without error, for it is there enumerated. PEREGR.].

O how great the grief and abundance of sorrow that seized the minds of the faithful and the cities belonging to the pope! If I wished to describe it fully from its roots, neither days nor time would suffice. Why say more? Immediately the king, through his envoys, humbly and beyond what can be believed earnestly requested Pope Innocent, whom he held captive, to join hands in peace and concord. The pope, seeing himself bereft of strength and arms and desolate, assented to the king’s prayers and petitions. With capitularies and privileges confirmed on both sides, [Col. 1252C] the king himself, his son the duke, and the prince came before the pope’s presence on the seventeenth day remaining of July, and, throwing themselves at his feet, sought mercy and bent themselves wholly to the pope’s command.

Immediately they confirmed upon the Gospels [Col. 1253A] that they would render loyalty to Blessed Peter, Pope Innocent, and his successors canonically entering office, together with the other matters set down in writing. The pope at once granted King Roger the kingdom of Sicily by the banner; to the king’s son, the duke, he granted the duchy of Apulia; and to his other son, the prince, he bestowed the principality of Capua. On the day on which the aforesaid pope confirmed peace with the king, the feast of Blessed James the Apostle was celebrated: the seventh day before the Kalends of August. When these matters had been completed, the pope celebrated the solemnities of Mass, where he spoke fully and abundantly concerning the terms of peace. Thus joy and an abundance of gladness filled all men; and, magnifying the King of Heaven, they rejoiced over the peace confirmed and the hand of concord.

The people of Benevento, hearing that peace had been confirmed and that the king was bound to the pope’s will, triumphed in such joy and exultation [Col. 1253B] that, if I described it all, I should fail for want of time and words. Therefore, when peace had been confirmed with the named king, the pope entered Benevento on the day of the Kalends of August. The people of Benevento received him with great honor and heartfelt devotion, rejoicing exceedingly, as though they beheld Blessed Peter in the flesh.

But the king encamped outside the city of Benevento, because he accompanied the pope as far as the Gate of St Lawrence. On that same day, at Vespers, the king entered the city and, going up to the court of the lord pope, remained with him for some time. He then went to the episcopal palace and, entering the basilica of Blessed Mary and that of the Apostle Bartholomew, prayed for his salvation. He also entered the monastery of St Sophia and prostrated himself before [Col. 1253C] the altar of St Mercurius. Departing from there, he walked through the monastery’s cloisters, dormitory, and refectory; commending himself to the monks’ prayers, he left the city through the Upper Gate and returned joyfully to his camp.

Rossemannus, however, who daily fought against the pope’s will and had been consecrated archbishop by Peter Leonis, was expelled from Benevento; and the unhappy man hurried away with the lord king. When these things had been done, the lord pope destroyed the castle which that Rossemannus had ordered to be built at the Upper Gate. In these days the citizens of Naples came to Benevento and, surrendering the city of Naples to the loyalty of the lord king, received his son the duke; they submitted their necks to his allegiance.

Furthermore, the aforesaid king, having moved his army, went to Troia [Col. 1253D] and brought that city under his power. William, bishop of the city of Troia, and the people of the city sent envoys to the aforesaid king, asking him to enter the city and remain honorably and securely among his faithful men and friends. But the king, receiving the envoys, said: “I shall not enter the city so long as that traitor—Rainulf, that is—remains among you.”

Immediately those who had been sent returned to the city [Col. 1254A] and made the king’s intention known to all. Although the citizens were moved with grief by so great a response from the king, they nevertheless ordered four soldiers to break open the tomb, remove the corpse of Duke Rainulf, and carry it outside the city, so that, his anger appeased, the king might enter among them peacefully. The enemies of the aforesaid duke also ordered a certain knight named Gallicanus, who had been the duke’s most faithful man, to break open the tomb himself, and, as an insult to the deceased duke and despite Gallicanus’s own grief, to pull out with his hand the duke’s bones, still wrapped in flesh and stench. Gallicanus, compelled by fear and lest he incur the rage of so great a king, alas for the sorrow!, with seeming cheerfulness brought out with the others the duke’s bones, still covered, as we have said.

Immediately those who had been the duke’s enemies caused a rope to be tied around the dead duke’s neck [Col. 1254B] and dragged him through the streets as far as the city castle. Then, returning as far as the Carbonaria outside the city, where there was a muddy and foul-smelling pool, they drowned the duke’s corpse [Note: [Col. 1253D] Outside cities, beneath their very walls, such muddy and fetid pools were then customarily allotted to receive all filth. Giovanni Boccaccio described something of the sort in his tale of Master Simone in these words: “There were then in that district pits into which the workers of those fields made the Countess of Civillari empty [the contents], in order to enrich their fields.” [Col. 1254D] Perhaps the place long ago beneath the wall of Naples which is still called by its ancient name, Carbonaria, served the same purpose; but this was long before the age of Francesco Petrarch, who says that, while he was watching, a gladiatorial spectacle was exhibited there: *Familiares*, Book V, Epistle 6. PEREGR.].

Alas, wickedness beyond telling and a deed astonishing to recount! At once fear and mourning seized the whole city, so that every person desired death—both friends and enemies of that duke. I call the eternal King and Judge of the ages to witness: never have we read that such a horrible and enormous deed occurred in former generations, even among the sect of pagans. What advantage, indeed, did this display of cruelty bring that king? What victory or glory of majesty followed it? Rather, desiring to appease the fury of his mind, he did to the dead what he had been unable to do to the living.

[Col. 1254C] Truly, while the aforesaid duke lived, even though he had only a few men with him, the king himself did not dare in any way to approach the duke’s battle line, even if he pressed him with ten thousand armed men. Hence the king thought that the madness of his mind would be somewhat mitigated. But let us return to the matter. The duke, that king’s son, hearing of this deed, boldly approached his father, rebuked the course of the act, and begged his father that the dishonored duke might be given burial. The king therefore, favoring the petition of his son the duke, ordered him to be given burial. When this had been done, the people of the city waited for him to enter among them, as he had promised.

Yet he still did not wish to enter the city of Troia; but, moving his camp from there, he went to Bari, which he besieged by land and sea. When [Col. 1254D] the aforesaid pope entered the city of Benevento, he deposed every arrangement made by Peter Leonis and by Rossemannus. On the feast of the Assumption of St Mary and on the passion-day of Blessed Bartholomew, he went down to the episcopal palace and honorably celebrated the solemnities of Mass. Having done this, the aforesaid pope, repeatedly summoned by the Romans, set out on the second day remaining of September and, with the Lord’s favor, returned to Rome.

[Col. 1255A] In this year Gregory, bishop of Benevento, consecrated by Pope Innocent, entered Benevento on the second day at the beginning of September; and the lord pope appointed Guy, cardinal-deacon, rector of Benevento. But the Roman people, hearing of the arrival of Pope Innocent, went out in crowds to meet him and received him with great joy and honor. They then urged him, on their counsel, to break the peace which he had made with King Roger. But the pope in no way wished to consent to their petitions; indeed, he said that it had pleased the Lord that such a peace should have been made through his capture.

When, as stated above, the aforesaid king had besieged the city of Bari, Pope Innocent, while he was within the city of Benevento, [Col. 1255B] sent the bishop of Ostia, a most venerable man, to the city of Bari, admonishing the people of the city to submit their necks to the king’s allegiance and comply with his will. But the people of Bari, being proud in spirit and given over to arrogance, did not at all permit that bishop to enter the city and made no attempt whatever to believe his words. Why say more? On returning, the bishop reported the fierceness and arrogance of the people of Bari to the lord pope. Then, as has been said, the lord pope returned to Rome.

King Roger, therefore, observing the pride of that people of Bari, took counsel and ordered wooden engines and about thirty towers to be constructed, in order to overthrow the city’s walls and fortifications. When these had been completed, [Col. 1255C] he ordered the engines to be brought near the city wall with great force; and immediately the city’s towers and walls were broken down and overthrown. The city palaces lying within, near the wall, likewise collapsed in ruins. Thus for a space of two months, namely August and September, they endured that destruction and terror, as well as the severity of hunger and thirst. They bought one loaf of bread for six *romesenes*; and, as we heard, they ate horseflesh.

Finally, because both of hunger and of a popular uprising which had arisen among them, the prince of the city, one Jaquintus, sent certain citizens, together with Roger of Sorrento, to the aforesaid king, adding to their instructions that he would willingly surrender the city to him, provided that they might stand safely before him after peace had been received [Col. 1255D], that the king would restore to them the city’s captives whom he held, and that likewise the city would release the king’s men whom it held. Without delay this agreement and arrangement pleased both king and city; and so the people of the city, peace having been received, consented, and, oaths having been given, peace was established.

When these things had been completed, behold, a certain knight came whose eye the aforesaid prince of the city had ordered to be torn out. Throwing himself at the king’s feet, he begged him to do justice for him against the prince of Bari, who had plucked out the light of his eyes. The king, immediately inflamed with rage and astonished beyond belief, rapidly summoned the judges of Troia, Trani, and Bari to judge the agreement which the king had made with the city of Bari—namely, [Col. 1256A] that captives on both sides should be restored sound and unharmed.

Why say more? The judges of Bari ruled that that prince of the city, Jaquintus, who had ordered the man’s eye to be torn out, and his advisers should be in the king’s power. Immediately that prince and his advisers, a certain Guaiferius and Abiut, with their other associates, confessed before the king that by their command and counsel they had caused the light of the aforesaid knight’s eyes to be torn out. Without delay, the aforesaid king caused that prince and the said men, together with ten others, to be hanged by the noose; he caused ten others to be mutilated in eyes and limbs; ordered other prominent citizens to be bound and held in chains; and seized their goods. Thus he inflicted unheard-of vengeance upon that city of Bari.

Such fear and trembling seized the city that no man or woman dared to go openly through its streets and [Col. 1256B] lanes. With tears and sighs they invoked the Savior’s mercy, that he might deign to aid their affliction. These matters having been carried out, the king, after taking counsel, divided his army and went to Salerno on the fifth day remaining of October; there he dealt with his affairs and undertakings. Eight days before the beginning of October, the city of Bari had been thus afflicted and harassed. When the king himself arrived at Salerno, he took from his enemies all their lands and bound them by oath to hasten beyond the mountains; and this was done. But he sent his adversary Count Roger of Ariano, together with his wife, as a captive by a prepared ship to Sicily. Thus, having completed vengeance upon his enemies, on the fifth day at the beginning of November he crossed by armed ship to Palermo.

In this year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, at the first cockcrow, a great earthquake occurred, so that we thought houses would collapse. When, as we have said, Pope Innocent recovered the city of Benevento, he appointed as rector of the city of Benevento Guy, deacon of the Roman see, a man of great discernment and adorned with good character. This rector remained in the city until the Kalends of March. Then the pope sent another rector, a subdeacon named John, his kinsman, and that Guy returned to Rome.

In the year 1140, and the eleventh year of the pontificate of the aforesaid lord Innocent, in March, the third indiction. [Col. 1256D] In this year the aforesaid King Roger sent his son Anfusus, prince of Capua, with a great army of horsemen and foot-soldiers beyond the city of Pescara, in order to subject that province to his power. The prince, having received that army, accomplished with much labor what his father the king had ordered. Crossing Pescara, he seized many neighboring castles and villages, plundered their spoils, and consumed some of them with fire.

A few days later, the aforesaid King Roger sent his son Duke Roger with a thousand horsemen and a great force of foot-soldiers to assist the aforesaid prince. Thus the duke, joined with his brother the prince, subjected to their dominion, with great terror, that province bordering near the Roman territories [Col. 1257A]. Therefore the aforesaid Pope Innocent, troubled, took counsel with the Romans and sent cardinals to them, ordering them not to invade another’s lands or usurp the Roman boundaries. They replied in writing to the pope that they sought not another’s possessions, but wished only to recover the lands belonging to the principality [Note: [Col. 1257D] Did the province beyond the city of Pescara belong to the principality of Capua? We shall examine this elsewhere. PEREGR.].

While these and other events were taking place, the named king came to Salerno in the middle of July, with ships prepared, in order to learn what had been done by his sons, the duke and the prince, whom, as I said above, he had sent with armies; moreover, he planned to confer and meet with Lord Pope Innocent. Immediately that king, after taking counsel, left Salerno and, having assembled two hundred knights, came near the city of Benevento. With John, subdeacon of the Roman See and then rector of Benevento, and with other Beneventans, he spoke at great length and fully concerning peace, the welfare of the city, and the duty of maintaining fidelity to the apostolic lord. Proceeding thence, he entered Capua; after remaining there a few days and dealing with certain of his affairs, he hastened to San Germano.

Having immediately taken counsel, he sent messengers to the duke and prince, his sons, ordering them to return to him; for the king had heard that Pope Innocent was greatly disturbed and grieved by the invasion of that province. The duke and prince, having received the messengers, returned to their father; but they fortified with every necessity all the towns which they had taken. After this, the king himself dispatched messengers to the aforesaid pope, humbly requesting, if it could be done, that he might confer with him and wished to settle many and diverse matters. The pope, after taking counsel, replied that, both because of the severity of the weather and because other urgent affairs pressed upon him, he could not meet with him.

The king therefore, having assembled an army, returned to Capua; having encamped there for a while, he dismissed the entire army, giving everyone leave to return home. The king himself, taking five hundred knights, proceeded to Pescara, which, as we said above, his sons had taken. Proceeding from there, he traversed the entire region occupied by his aforesaid sons; and, after carefully examining all matters, he arrived at the city of Ariano. There he held a court of nobles and bishops and deliberated concerning countless affairs.

Among other measures of his administration, he imposed a dreadful edict, abhorrent to every region of Italy and tending toward death and poverty: namely, that no person living in his whole kingdom should accept *Romesinae* or distribute them in markets. With a deadly design he introduced his own coinage: one coin, to which he gave the name *ducatus*, valued at eight *Romesinae*, but found to be more copper than silver. He also introduced three copper *follares*, appraised at one *Romesina*. Because of these terrible coins the whole Italian people were reduced and oppressed by poverty and misery; and, because of that king’s deadly acts, they longed for his death and deposition from the kingdom.

Having thus introduced these deadly edicts and coins, the king assembled his knights and proceeded to Naples. The archbishop of Naples, named Marinus, ordered all the clergy of the city to assemble; he also summoned the citizens and, announcing the king’s arrival, urged them to receive him honourably and with great rejoicing. The citizens, together with the city’s knights, went out through the Capuan Gate into the plain which they call “Naples.”

> [Note: Col. 1257D] This plain was also identified by the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, no. 28, and by John the Deacon, *On the Bishops of Naples*, under St Athanasius. But why it was itself especially called after Naples or Neapolis is a question that learned Neapolitan men, skilled in every kind of antiquity, ought not to have passed over untouched. PEREGR.

They embraced the king himself with honour and attentiveness beyond belief, and thus he was escorted as far as the aforesaid Capuan Gate. Immediately the priests and clergy of the city came out to meet him at that same gate and brought him into the city with hymns and praises raised to the stars. At once four noblemen, holding the reins of his horse and the king’s feet, and four others, led the king as far as the city’s bishop.

If, reader, you had seen the multitude of people proceeding through the streets, and widows, married women, and virgins standing at the windows, you would have declared in astonishment that no emperor, king, or prince had ever entered Naples with such honour and rejoicing. Why say more? Enriched with such great honour, the king went down to the episcopal residence and lodged in the archbishop’s chamber. On the following day he rode through the whole city, within and without, and inspected its palaces and buildings. Then, with a ship prepared, he embarked for the castle of Saint Saviour, near the city. Having summoned the Neapolitan citizens there, he discussed with them certain matters concerning the city’s liberty and welfare.

> [Note: Col. 1257D] The king discussed with the citizens the immunity of the city of Naples, which Falco, in the terminology then customary, calls “liberty.” Thus under the year 1137: “He further requests,” he says, “that King Roger himself grant the Beneventan people the liberty of their possessions which Emperor Lothair had granted them.” The Sicilians feared that this immunity would be taken from them, according to Falcandus: “They had not found it difficult,” he says, “to persuade the chancellor that, if he remained long at that height of power, he would take away from all the peoples of Sicily the liberty which they had hitherto possessed.” And below: “That all the peoples of Sicily might be compelled to pay annual revenues and exactions, according to the custom of Gaul, which had no free citizens.”
>
> The Neapolitans, endowed with liberty and immunity of no different kind, made the merchants of the duchy of Amalfi who resided at Naples participants in it. The following is read in a privilege in the *Latin History of Naples*, book I, chapter 12: “As this city of Naples enjoys the pre-eminence of the privilege of liberty, so may you merchants, money-changers, and shopkeepers enjoy it for ever.” But what liberty? The privilege continues: “That no condition [I write *condictio*] concerning your persons or property, or those of your heirs and successors who are merchants dwelling at Naples, may be demanded; just as it is not demanded of Neapolitan citizens.”
>
> Therefore, in that privilege Neapolitan liberty is not being given precedence, as the author of that same *History* supposed—a liberty which had existed with the city from its foundation. He seems rather to have meant that liberty enjoyed of old by municipalities generally and by allied cities, and likewise by the Neapolitans themselves, from whom the Romans, as Livy says in book XXXV, required tribute and ships by treaty, while they appointed their own magistrates. Nor is it sufficiently established whether they surrendered it when, in the 663rd year from the foundation of the City, about 90 BC, during the Social War, when nearly all Italy conspired against Rome, Roman citizenship was granted to the allies and Latins by the Julian law. In this matter there was a great dispute among the Heracleans and Neapolitans, Cicero testifying in *For Balbus* that a large part of those communities preferred the liberty of their own law to Roman citizenship.
>
> Yet they finally renounced it, as the same Cicero indicates in *Against Rullus*, II. Having enumerated the colonies and municipalities of Campania which Rullus intended to occupy with his colonists, he states that not Naples but Puteoli was then under its own control: “They will fill the municipality of Cales. They will crush Teanum. They will bind Atella, Cumae, Naples, Pompeii, and Nuceria with their garrisons. But Puteoli, which is now under its own control and enjoys its own law and liberty, they will entirely occupy with a new population and immigrant forces.”
>
> Thereafter the old town itself of Puteoli, as Tacitus says in *Annals*, book XIV, received colonial status and a surname from Nero, since the rights of the original colony sent there—of which Livy, book XXXIV, and our Velleius, book I, speak—had already fallen into disuse, and those of the later colony, mentioned by Frontinus in the *Catalogue of Colonies*, had been abolished. Yet in Tacitus, *Histories*, book III, I judge Puteoli still to be classed among the municipalities. He says that the municipalities and colonies were stirred up by Claudius Faventinus and Apollinaris, and by Apinius Tiro; because of the Puteolans’ particular devotion to Vespasian, whereas Capua remained faithful to Vitellius—Capua was certainly a colony—municipal rivalry was mixed with the civil wars. Tacitus had said that they had obtained colonial status, not that a colony had been dispatched there.
>
> So too Pompey, as Asconius Pedianus relates in his commentary on the speech *Against Piso*, when establishing colonies in Transpadane Gaul, did not found them with new colonists; rather, leaving the old inhabitants in place, he gave them Latin rights, so that they could possess the rights held by the other Latin colonies—that is, so that by holding office they might obtain Roman citizenship. I strongly suspect that Naples was such a colony also, since it never abandoned its ancestral Greek customs.
>
> This city, which—remarkable to relate—after the Roman Empire, to use the words of Alexander of Telese, book II, chapters 12 and 66, whose opinion I do not now examine strictly, “was scarcely ever subject to anyone,” now submits to Roger at a mere spoken word. For it had obeyed the Greek emperors, not as conquered by arms but by an immemorial subjection, as did the rest of Italy even for a long time afterwards, through a long course of years. I shall discuss this in book II of the *History of the Lombards*. PEREGR.

Moreover, he gave each knight five *modii* of land and five villeins.

> [Note: Col. 1260C] “To each knight,” he says—not to each count or magnate—he gave in fief a small *modius* of land together with peasants bound to the soil, so that, after they had in like manner sworn an oath of fidelity to him, he might hold the city in stricter obedience, as though bound by a tie. I invoke Alexander of Telese, book II, chapter 37, concerning this same king: “Because,” he says, “he had discovered that the conspiracy of the aforesaid princes against him had been made with perjury, he was carried away by such indignation against them and burst forth in such fury of mind that he spared absolutely neither count, nor magnate, nor any knight who, being thus perjured, had raised their necks against him.” I read *procerum* (“nobles”) for *principum*, as I noted above.
>
> But observe the changes of time. Rullus once, as Cicero reports in *On the Agrarian Law*, II, decreed that five thousand colonists should be enrolled at Capua, selected by lot from the rural tribes, and ordered that ten and then twelve *iugera* should be allotted to each—roughly eight of our *modii* of land. Fazellus, *Posterior Decade*, book VII, not content with having confused several events, times, and persons quite wrongly, adds this also: that, after an agreement had been reached between Innocent and Roger, the king himself entered Naples amid the great applause both of his own men and of the citizens, and on that day created one hundred and fifty knights and spent two festive months there. Our author certainly has nothing of the sort, though I see that men of little discernment—for such men, in a very recent experiment, have shown themselves contrary to my expectation—cite him for this assertion. Furthermore, Falco himself expressly states that in this year Roger came from Sicily to Salerno in mid-July and, on the fourth day after the beginning of October, embarked and hastened to Palermo, being occupied in the meantime with various affairs and journeys. PEREGR.

He promised them, so long as life should accompany him, that he would bestow many gifts and possessions upon them. Meanwhile, in the silence of the night, the aforesaid king had the entire city of Naples measured externally, wishing to learn its total circumference. Careful measurement found it to be 2,363 paces around. When these paces had thus been determined and the people of the city had assembled, he began, as if from affectionate concern, to ask them in their presence whether they knew how many paces their city had in circumference. They professed that they did not know, marvelling beyond belief. The king then revealed the measurement of the paces encompassed by their city, as he had carefully discovered it. Therefore all the people proclaimed the king wiser and more diligent than his predecessors, and marvelled—for this had never been done—how that king had contrived to determine the city’s measure.

When all these things had been accomplished, he hastened to Salerno. After remaining there a few days, on the fourth day after the beginning of October, with a ship prepared, he put to sea and then hastened to Palermo. His son the duke remained in Apulia, while his other son, the prince, stayed at Capua.

When, as we have said, King Roger introduced the coins mentioned above, he directed Lord John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman See and rector of Benevento, together with the Beneventan citizens, to receive those coins within the city. On hearing this, the aforesaid rector was extraordinarily distressed. He said that he could not accept the coins without the lord pope’s permission, especially since their introduction tended to the ruin of all Italy. At last, after consulting with others, the rector reported the king’s edicts to the aforesaid pontiff and asked him to send instructions concerning what ought to be done in these matters.

Pope Innocent, having heard this, grieved beyond belief and was astonished at King Roger’s execrable deeds. At once he sent his letter to the Beneventans as follows:

> [Col. 1260B] “We have learned both from you and from others reporting truthfully to us of the king’s actions and the inventions of his coinage. Therefore we command you not to be frightened or to let your minds be disturbed any longer, for these things will pass away and can quickly be corrected. We, however, keep daily watch over your interests.”

When such a letter had been received and read, we gave thanks and, somewhat strengthened, drew breath again. After these things, Pope Innocent sent word to King Roger, indicating how the whole people of Italy and beyond had grieved over the introduction of these coins, and how they had come to the affliction of famine. [lacuna]

Thus far the Beneventan papyrus codex.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1139: MATTHEW, CARDINAL BISHOP OF ALBANO

[Col. 1261]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, p. 254, under the bishops of Albano.)

Matthew, a Frenchman born of noble and wealthy parents, was a monk in the province of Reims and prior of Cluny; he was elected cardinal bishop of Albano by Honorius II in 1125. From his earliest years he successfully united piety with mastery of learning. Formerly a canon of Reims, he professed the monastic life in the celebrated Parisian monastery of Saint Martin of the Fields, of which he was afterwards elected abbot. When later raised to the episcopate, he was so far from forgetting, amid the duties of the higher life, the discipline of his earlier profession that he added still harsher practices to the austerity of his life, and adorned the Church with very rare examples of holiness.

He was a close friend of St Bernard and his inseparable colleague in bringing those who had strayed into the service of the true pontiff. Under Honorius II he served as legate in Gaul, where, at the Council of Troyes, he confirmed the military institute of the Templars by granting favourable diplomas. Sent by the same pope as legate to Monte Cassino, he deprived Oderisius and Nicholas of office and arranged for Signoretto to be elected abbot of that place.

Meanwhile, when a schism had arisen between Innocent II and the antipope Anacletus, Matthew, with remarkable purity of heart, took Innocent’s side and denounced the antipope’s wicked attempts. When Peter Leo had expelled him from Rome, throughout a life full of hardship, whether in flight or pilgrimage, he kept excellent remembrance of his office and eventually brought the French and Germans whom he reached into service and obedience to the true pontiff. At the end of his life, together with St Bernard as his colleague, he also served as legate in Liguria; there he persuaded the Milanese to venerate Innocent as the true pontiff.

Finally, having returned to Pisa, where the pontiff was then staying, he contracted an illness through his labours and died on the holy feast-day of the Lord’s Nativity, while the sacred rite was still being celebrated at dawn, in the year 1139. He was buried at Saint Frigidianus and became famous for the glory of miracles. He also presided over the councils of Mainz and Paris. His life was written by the venerable Peter, abbot of Cluny, although his deeds and life are also narrated again in the Cluniac Chronicle. Baronius mentions him in volume XII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*. St Bernard sincerely expressed his praises there in certain letters, in which he either conducted most weighty affairs with a serious and judicious man, or nurtured mutual affection for the sake of holy friendship.

[Col. 1261]

## LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF MATTHEW, CARDINAL BISHOP OF ALBANO

### I. Diploma of Matthew, bishop of Albano, cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, concerning the agreement between Henry, archbishop of Sens, and the canons of Étampes. (Year 1127.)

[FLEUREAU, *Antiquités d’Estampes*, p. 40.]

[Col. 1261B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity: I, MATTHEW, by God’s grace bishop of Albano and cardinal legate of the Holy Roman Church; GEOFFREY, bishop of Chartres; and BURCHARD, bishop of Meaux:

We wish all the faithful, both future and present, to know that at Saint-Denis we brought about, with God as author, the following agreement between Henry, archbishop of Sens, and the canons of Étampes. By our counsel and that of the religious persons present, the same archbishop graciously granted them that they should forever provide, without simony, a priest for the church of Saint Basil which belongs to them. He himself shall impose neither any claim nor any due of office upon that priest; and, if the man is legally qualified and acceptable, the archbishop shall grant him the care of souls.

He also granted that, after the care of souls has been given to him, that priest shall pay the aforesaid canons the rent and shall provide them full security concerning it; and the archbishop shall in no way, either personally or through a subordinate, hinder that rent from reaching those canons. He himself, as priest and bishop, granted and promised that he would preserve and uphold this agreement whole and unshaken.

### II. Instrument of the cardinals concerning the settlement made between Stephen, bishop of Paris, and Theobald, archdeacon. (Year 1127.)

[*Cartulaire de Notre-Dame de Paris*, vol. I, p. 28.]

[Col. 1263B]

This is the agreement which we—Matthew, bishop of Albano; John, cardinal of the title of Saint Chrysogonus; and Peter, cardinal of the title of Calixtus—made, by command of Lord Pope [Honorius], between Lord Stephen, bishop of Paris, and Theobald, notary and archdeacon of the same Church.

The archdeacon may not appoint a priest in churches. The bishop shall assign churches only through the archdeacon, as through his minister: that is, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to the priest, while through the archdeacon he shall assign the church and its property to the church. The archdeacon may by no means suspend a priest from office if the bishop is in the diocese, and he may not depose him at all. Nor may he impose penances or grant reconciliation except by the bishop’s permission. The archdeacon may not excommunicate or absolve any cleric unless by the bishop’s mandate.

Whenever necessary, the bishop shall summon his parishioners through the archdeacon and call them to justice. If they despise this and he pronounces judgments, the bishop may excommunicate them; the archdeacon shall observe an excommunication so pronounced. The archdeacon shall not cause clerics to be promoted to orders except by the mandate and seal of the bishop, provided the bishop is in the province. But if the bishop has been absent for three months and the archdeacon has the bishop’s mandate, then, necessity urging, he shall cause clerics to be promoted and may canonically assign churches.

The bishop shall not levy collections in the archdeacon’s parish without the archdeacon, except when he goes to Rome, a council is held in the province, or he happens to receive the lord pope in his church; nevertheless, he shall do this after consulting the archdeacon. Since in these collections all expenses shall be the bishop’s, the archdeacon shall have no share. But in other joint collections the archdeacon shall receive one third, as is customary. The archdeacon, however, may not make collections throughout the whole parish without the bishop.

If anyone wishes, either voluntarily or at the archdeacon’s request, to give the archdeacon something of his own, the bishop must not oppose it in any way. The due which the French call *catate*, which the archdeacon owed the bishop up to this day, the bishop entirely remitted to the archdeacon at our request and for love of peace. Henceforth the archdeacon shall pay every due to the bishop, only so long as he remains in this peace and agreement.

Concerning the schools, over which discord arose between the bishop and the Parisian canons, Lord Theobald shall by no means act against the bishop’s will. If the archdeacon does not observe this peace, and, when once, twice, or three times admonished, does not correct his fault or refuses to do justice, then the bishop may, as before, demand every due owed to him.

If any cleric or layperson in the parish does an injustice to the archdeacon or another person and refuses to make amends through that same archdeacon, then, if the bishop is present and wishes to hear the case before himself, the archdeacon shall proceed no further until judgment, but shall refer his case to the bishop, who shall observe canonical justice toward him in all things. If the bishop is absent or refuses to hear it, the archdeacon shall administer justice, yet by mandate of the bishop—and this applies to laypeople.

We have made this agreement, saving in all things the authority and due reverence of the Apostolic See and of the lord pope. Present at and party to this peace, made by their counsel, were our venerable brethren Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Burchard, bishop of Meaux.

Done at Rome, at the Palladium, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1127, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

> [Note: Col. 1263D] What follows has been taken from the small cartulary, folio 46 verso. In another copy of the same agreement, there, folio 47, one reads: “The following witnesses were also present: Lord T., prior of Saint Victor; R., archdeacon of Cambrai; A., chancellor; T., archdeacon of Meaux; T., monk; Hugh, monk of Rebecq; Albert of Étampes.”

### III. Matthew of Albano confirms the election of Odo, abbot of Saint Peter of Chartres. (Year 1128.)

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, VI, 164.]

As it is pious to provide for the peace of God’s servants in the present, so it is fitting to provide for it in the future. Therefore I, MATTHEW, humble by God’s grace bishop of the Church of Albano, cardinal of the holy Roman and Apostolic See, and legate in Gaul, wish all the faithful whom it concerns to know that I have, in the chapter of that monastery and in the presence of the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, at his suggestion and request, by the authority of the Roman Church orally confirmed to the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, with Odo newly elected abbot presiding, the liberty of electing its abbot which it is known to have possessed hitherto. I have also promised that I would do this in writing and under my seal.

Therefore, repeating that same confirmation, by the authority of Lord Pope Honorius, whose office we exercise in the regions of Gaul, and by the power of the Roman See over which he presides, we decree and establish by this writing and seal that the election of its abbot by the chapter of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres shall be entirely free and secure from every ecclesiastical and secular power. As has hitherto been permitted, so let it be permitted to the monks forever, provided they act canonically, to elect as their abbot whichever person they wish; and let the person elected firmly obtain the office without anyone’s objection, prejudice, or deceit.

If anyone at any time should knowingly dare, by any device, to violate this our decree in any respect, we anathematize him, whoever he may be, by the authority of the lord pope himself and by the majesty of the holy and Apostolic See; and we exclude him from the kingdom of Christ and God unless he corrects this with worthy satisfaction.

### IV. Letter of Matthew, bishop of Albano, by which the monastery of Argenteuil is restored to the abbey of Saint-Denis, pursuant to the judgment of the Parisian council held at Saint-Germain-des-Prés. (Year 1129.)

[LABBE, *Concilia*, vol. X, col. 936.]

In the name of the highest God and our Saviour Jesus Christ: MATTHEW, by the disposition of divine grace bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See.

Since it is manifest that it belongs to the authority of our rank to labour faithfully and with the utmost solicitude for the worship of ecclesiastical religion, to remove everything unclean, and zealously to foster what is useful, we must most diligently attend to the office entrusted to us.

Accordingly, when recently at Paris, in the presence of the most serene lord Louis, king of the Franks, together with our brother bishops—the archbishop of Reims R. [Rainald], Stephen bishop of Paris, G. [Geoffrey] bishop of Chartres, G. [Goslen] bishop of Soissons—and many others, we were dealing with the reform of the sacred order in various monasteries of Gaul in which religious fervour had grown cold, there suddenly arose in the common hearing an outcry concerning the enormity and ill repute of a certain monastery of nuns called Argenteuil. In it a few nuns, living in manifold disgrace to the dishonour of their order, had for a long time polluted the entire vicinity of that place by their foul and infamous way of life. Since all who were present urged their expulsion, the venerable Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, produced in the assembly his exemptions, most securely confirmed by apostolic authority, and showed clearly enough that the aforesaid monastery belonged to the right of his church.

Therefore, after taking counsel with the brothers named above, and because by God’s mercy and the intercession of the holy martyrs we had seen that venerable monastery, especially in his time, shining with every religious virtue among the other monasteries of all Gaul, we provided not only for its rights but also for the misery of those women. We imposed upon it the obligation that, after placing the nuns in religious monasteries, it should establish there its own monks to serve God religiously.

And so that this grant of our restoration may henceforth be held most secure both by it and by posterity, we confirmed it forever by apostolic authority and the authentication of our seal—the bishop of Paris, Stephen, in whose parish it lies, having first acted and confirmed the same.

### V. Letter of Matthew, bishop of Albano, to the enrolled brethren, etc., abbots, etc.

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 419.]

To the enrolled brethren, senators of the heavenly court; to those abbots who have agreed to meet each year at Reims for the correction of the monastic order: Matthew, by God’s grace bishop of Albano, their brother and devoted friend—grace and peace from God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Paraclete Spirit who proceeds from both.

The fragrance of your strenuous virtue and most ardent religious devotion has reached even us, and the most sweet odour proceeding from your holy endeavours has filled our inmost being. Blessed be God, who, although the time of Antichrist presses close—whose coming, as it is written, will be preceded by want—has preserved such persons for these miserable times. To dispel the darkness which, almost palpable in its foul gloom, had obscured the monastic order in those regions, he has established you as bright lights and gleaming stars. He has illuminated not only your own places but also certain others with the rays of your holiness; and, in the ruined fabric of the monastic order in those cold regions, has founded and established you as firm and immovable pillars upon the good foundation, which is Christ.

And as that devout woman of the Gospel poured precious ointment upon the Lord’s feet, and the whole house was filled with its fragrance, so you too, after opening your fragrant caskets, have diffused a most pleasing and sweet fragrance in every direction. You may deservedly sing: “My nard has given forth a sweet fragrance.” For the more good spices are handled and ground, the more sweetly they breathe and the more delightfully they smell.

For in your cloisters, which formerly had been like shrines of pleasures—where the hedgehog dwelt, owls lodged, sirens sang, and hairy demons danced—you have now expelled and courageously condemned those things, and restored the glorious sheepfolds of Christ and delightful mangers: places in which Christ now feeds and is fed, refreshes and is refreshed, nourishes and is nourished, cherishes and is cherished, rejoices and takes delight. For the religion flourishing there, the humility vigorous there, the obedience reigning there, and the charity there which draws all people, embraces them, and makes them full, are like the good and holy mother Rebecca, who taught her beloved son Jacob to prepare foods upon which his father Isaac, whose name means “laughter,” gladly feeds; so too mother grace has taught you to prepare foods upon which our Lord Jesus Christ, the true laughter and our true joy, feeds gladly, delightfully, and with great eagerness, etc.

(In what follows, however, he censures perpetual silence instituted in cloisters, abbreviated psalmody, rural and manual work pursued to the neglect of the discipline of solitude, and a diminution of humility in the observance of religion; and finally concludes thus: “Beloved, I beg you, return to your heart, and do not walk in things great or in wonders above you.”)

### VI. Charter of Matthew, bishop of Albano, for the church of Saint Martin of the Fields

[DUCHENE, *History of the French Cardinals*, vol. II, p. 80.]

I, MATTHEW, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, make known to present and future alike that, in the presence at Hyenville of ourselves and of our brethren Reginald, archbishop of Reims; Goslen, bishop of Soissons; Bartholomew, bishop of Laon; Simon, bishop of Noyon; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; John, bishop of Orléans; Stephen, bishop of Paris; Burchard, bishop of Meaux; Geoffrey, abbot of Saint-Médard of Soissons; and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, our dearest son King Louis, at our request and that of all the aforesaid persons, and also at the prayers of Queen Adelaide, Count Ralph of Vermandois, and Philip, son of the king and designated king, made free from every customary due relating to property the land which the church of Saint Martin of the Fields possessed at Pontoise—except only for military service, summoned through the king himself or through his steward.

### II. Decree of Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the Holy Apostolic See, concerning the expulsion of nuns from the church of Saints Mary and John at Laon. [Year 4137.]

[Dom MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 301.]

MATTHEW, by God’s grace bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting to all the faithful.

What at the Council of Arras, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, was decided by our venerable brethren Rainald, archbishop of Reims; Bartholomew, bishop of Laon; Gislen, bishop of Soissons; the other bishops and abbots of that diocese; and other religious persons—namely, the expulsion of the nuns who were living less honourably in the church of Saint Mary and Saint John at Laon, and the installation there of an abbot and monks serving God religiously—King Louis of the Franks being present, consenting, and confirming it by his command: this we have approved in the assembly at Reims by the counsel and request of our venerable brethren, the archbishops of Reims and Sens, many abbots, and other religious persons; and we confirm it forever by the authority and protection of the Apostolic See.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1134: SAINT OTTO, BISHOP OF BAMBERG

[Col. 1267]

## LIFE OF SAINT OTTO

(*The Bishopric of Bamberg Chronologically and Diplomatically Illustrated*, by the work and study of P. Aemilianus Ussermann, librarian of Saint Blasien.—Printed at Saint Blasien, 1802.)

## SUMMARY HEADINGS.

[Col. 1267] I. Writers of his Life. II. Birthplace, studies, youth. III. He becomes known at the court of Emperor Henry IV. IV. Otto at the imperial court. V. His business there. VI. The bishopric of Bamberg offered by the king. VII. Otto refuses it, and finally accepts it. VIII. He comes to Bamberg. IX. His letter to the pope on this matter. X. By whom he is confirmed. XI. King Henry’s letters to Otto. XII. Otto is captured and freed on the journey to Rome. XIII. He asks to be consecrated by the pope. XIV. He is ordained by him at Anagni. XV. What he writes to his Church about this. XVI. The pope’s letters on the matter. XVII. Otto returns to his Church. XVIII. His care for the Church. XIX. He builds several monasteries. XX. And religious cells. XXI. Which he asks the pope to confirm. XXII. Certain other deeds. XXIII. The monasteries of Prüfening and Osterhofen. XXIV. The cathedral church. The pallium. XXV. He acquires estates for his Church. XXVI. Bruno’s letter to Otto. XXVII. The monastery of Banz. XXVIII. Otto becomes suspect to Emperor Henry. XXIX. Rebuked on account of the emperor. XXX. His abstention from assemblies of bishops. XXXI. What was the reason for this? XXXII. Generous toward the monastery of St Michael. XXXIII. The burial and lineage of Otto’s parents. XXXIV. The monastery of Michelfeld and Reinstorf. XXXV. Otto is again reproached for his absence. XXXVI. Peace restored. XXXVII. Otto’s Pomeranian achievements. XXXVIII. The condition of Pomerania at that time. XXXIX. Otto is invited there. XL. He prepares for the journey. XLI. He undertakes it. XLII. He comes to Pomerania through Poland. XLIII. Otto at Cammin. XLIV. At Wolin, or Julin. XLV. At Szczecin. XLVI. The Polish duke’s letter to the people of Szczecin. XLVII. Those who embrace the faith, with others. XLVIII. The duke of Julin establishes a bishopric. XLIX. Otto at Kołobrzeg and elsewhere. L. Rules of discipline delivered to the Pomeranians. [Col. 1269] LI. Teaching on the sacraments. LII. Otto returns to his homeland. LIII. His deeds after his return. LIV. Otto’s second holy expedition into Pomerania. LV. His sacred labours there. LVI. He obtains peace for the Pomeranians from the duke of Poland. LVII. Recalled home, he returns. LVIII. Events at home during his absence. LIX. Otto is summoned to a synod. LX. Certain deeds. LXI. Another journey of Otto into Bohemia. LXII. He endows various monasteries. LXIII. Concerning the monastery of Mallersdorf. LXIV. The Synod of Bamberg. LXV. Otto’s encyclical letter to the abbots of monasteries. LXVI. Otto’s final acts. LXVII. His last year. LXVIII. And his death.

[VITA.]

[Col. 1269]

[Col. 1269A] I. The Church of Bamberg, long tossed amid storms of so many years and evils, was, by God’s providence, delivered through the very man who had been their chief cause—I mean Emperor Henry IV. He had successively bestowed it upon two men, Hermann and Rupert, notorious for simoniacal practices; yet he was more fortunate in choosing the latter’s successor, Otto, who afterwards became the restorer and greatest ornament of his Church. Otto is therefore worthy that we should investigate somewhat more carefully both his earlier fortunes and his later deeds. For the moment, however, let us set aside the dispute concerning his descent from Andechs, lest we burden readers to no purpose with these non-genealogical trifles; though something will be said of them below. Let us proceed, then, to matters more certain, through which Otto earned praise and glory greater than any illustrious lineage could confer.

[Col. 1269B] But, in order that we may proceed safely amid so great a diversity of writers, it is useful first to indicate the principal sources from which we have drawn. We reckon various writers of his Life, mostly interpolated or of a later age, to whom the principles of our undertaking do not permit us to give credit, at least not in every respect. We shall therefore consider briefly those who seem nearer in time, and whom Fr. B. Sollerius also included among his documents in the preliminary commentary [Note: [Col. 1269D] Vol. I of July, Bollandists, p. 349.]. He calls these Sefrid, Ebbo, and Tiemmo, but so confuses them together that one cannot at all know what should be assigned to each.

This alone is certain: one of them, namely Sefrid, was either secretary or notary to St Otto and his companion in the Pomeranian mission. He himself reveals this more than once in the second book, when, speaking of that mission, he uses the first person plural. Since this is not observed in the other two books of Otto’s Life, it is an indication that they were written by other authors. Yet the prologue to the Life indicates that these authors were not much later [Note: [Col. 1269D] In the cited work, p. 378.]: “The matters written in this book are those which devout and most trustworthy men saw him perform with their own eyes and faithfully related to us, so that nothing of private affection or favour might be introduced into the testimony of truth, but that his works, which were done in God, might be set forth with the utmost sincerity and truth, for the honour of God and the benefit of the Church.”

It should also be noted that they never call Otto “saint,” but “blessed” or “venerable”; consequently, the work must have been committed to writing before the year 1189, that is, before his canonization.

II. Otto, then, derived his origin from Swabia or Alemannia, and was born about the year 1062. His parents, Otto and Adelheid, distinguished indeed by nobility but moderate in wealth, placed their son in his earliest years under instruction in letters; where this was done is not recorded. Thus carefully trained in letters, and having reached the years of discretion, he lost his parents. His brother Frederick, who was to become a knight, obtained the paternal estate. Certainly, the necrology of St Michael’s at Bamberg bears witness concerning this Frederick under 25 October: “Frederick, brother of Bishop Otto.”

Since Frederick did not furnish his brother Otto with means to continue his studies, Otto migrated to Poland, partly from necessity and partly from love of learning. There, opening a school for boys, he enriched and educated himself by teaching others, and within a short time became prosperous and honoured. He also learned the language of the people there. By this ability and by the elegance of his person, he first gained the familiarity of the great men and shortly afterwards the favour even of the duke of Poland himself, who kept him with him for several years as a cleric.

This duke is called Boleslaus by some, but was in fact Władysław, son of King Boleslaus II; out of reverence for the pope, however, he used only the title of duke. When his wife Judith, daughter of the duke of Bohemia, had died, Otto advised the duke to seek in marriage Sophia—whom others call Judith—sister of Emperor Henry IV and widow of Solomon, king of Hungary. Otto himself was therefore sent with others to Henry to request that bride from him. He obtained her in the year 1088 and accompanied her to Poland. He subsequently became her chaplain and bearer of letters to her brother Henry.

On this occasion he became known to King Henry and ingratiated himself ever more deeply into his favour, so that Henry at last requested him from his sister and her husband the duke as a man necessary for his service. He obtained him from them, though with difficulty, dismissing him with great gifts.

[Col. 1270C] III. Here the aforementioned biographers begin to differ from one another. They maintain that Otto, as Judith’s chaplain, came with her to Poland only at this time; and that, on the same occasion, because he frequently passed through Würzburg, he founded a hospice there, concerning which we have spoken elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1270D] Bishopric of Würzburg, p. 194.].

They also write that after Judith’s death Otto came to Regensburg and lived among the canons, until he was appointed steward of the household of the abbess of the Lower Monastery there; and that King Henry, while visiting his niece there, requested Otto and summoned him to his court. They further relate various proofs of friendship between the two, which there is no time to examine more fully.

But since nothing is otherwise established either concerning the year of death of Judith or Sophia, queen of Poland, or concerning any niece of King Henry who was abbess at Regensburg, the exact time when Otto came to the imperial court cannot be determined, although I think that it occurred only about the year 1096. At least this is beyond doubt: Otto had been in Poland before he came, by whatever means, to King Henry’s court.

This is plainly evident from the writer of the Life whom we follow, who testifies [Note: [Col. 1270D] Book II, ch. I, no. 53.] that the fame of Otto, bishop of Bamberg, flourished widely in the realms of Poland in the time of King Boleslaus III, “because his father”—namely Władysław—“had known and loved him in his youth as one obedient in the manner of his chaplain.” Indeed Boleslaus himself, in a letter sent to Otto [Note: [Col. 1271D] Documentary appendix, no. LXXVIII.], declares that he remembers Otto’s “most honourable conduct at the court of his father in the days of his youth.” This Boleslaus was born in 1086; therefore Otto must have remained in Poland at least until about Boleslaus’s tenth year, in order that Boleslaus could have known him.

IV. “The emperor,” our writer continues, “first exercising Otto in small matters, made good use of his familiar service in many things, and, whenever he had leisure, was accustomed to meditate with him upon psalms and private prayers.” Both this writer and the other writers of the Life recount at greater length many exercises of this kind in piety, especially in psalmody.

Our author also recalls that at this time Otto was made the king’s chancellor, after another had been raised to a bishopric. This was perhaps Humbert, who is found in Henry’s charters as chancellor from 1086 to 1102, and who in that same latter year became archbishop of Bremen. It may have happened there what Ebbo relates in the Life: that, when the pastoral staff and ring of the bishop of Bremen had been brought, the emperor entrusted these insignia for safekeeping to Otto, whom alone he specially loved. Perhaps he had intended that see for him, had not, a few days later, the episcopal insignia of Rupert of Bamberg, likewise deceased, also been brought to the king, and been intended by him for Otto.

This is plausible, but the dates do not agree. For Liemar of Bremen died on 17 May 1101 and had Humbert as his successor in that same year; Rupert, however, died only in the following year, on 11 June. Therefore envoys from both Churches could not have been present together to request a bishop from the king; nor was the king thereafter free to deliberate between the two elections, since the see of Bremen had already been granted in the earlier year to Humbert, whose office of chancellor the king then gave to Otto, his chaplain. At least the Saxon Annalist and others write that Otto was made bishop from chancellor, although no diploma acknowledged by him occurs [Note: [Col. 1271D] See Göttweig Chronicle, p. 302.].

[Col. 1271D] V. The biographers attribute another undertaking to Otto while he lived at court: namely, that King Henry entrusted to him the care of completing the construction of the church at Speyer. Conrad II had begun it, Henry III had enlarged it, but Henry III’s son finally completed it by the effort and diligence of our Otto.

This is the church of St Mary, or St John, now the collegiate church of St Guido, concerning which Hermann the Lame writes under the year 1047: Henry III “returned from Italy bringing with him, in great honour, the body of Blessed Guido, abbot of the monastery of Pomposa, and caused it to be buried in the basilica, then under construction, outside the city” [Note: [Col. 1272D] See vol. III of March, Bollandists, under the 31st day of the month.]. Hermann’s continuator states under the year 1056 that Emperor Henry, having died, “was conveyed to Speyer and buried beside his father and mother in the still unfinished church of St Mary which he himself had built.”

It remained unfinished for a long time, until, as stated, it was finally completed by Henry IV toward the end of this century. Into it he subsequently transferred, about the year 1097, his wife Bertha, who had been buried at Mainz since 1088 [Note: [Col. 1272D] Hildesheim Annals, under that year.]. After his own death, five years later, in 1111, he too was buried beside his forebears in the same church. So much for Otto’s beginnings; let us now consider his episcopate.

VI. When Bishop Rupert of Bamberg died on 11 June 1102, envoys of that Church attended the court, bringing his staff and ring and requesting a new shepherd from the king. But he appointed a period of six months in which to deliberate maturely on the matter, while the clergy and people of Bamberg prayed to God for a favourable outcome. When the truce had elapsed, the emperor informed the people of Bamberg that a bishop worthy of their Church had been found.

“Therefore, while the envoys, the chief and foremost men of that Church, clerical and lay alike, went to the court, all the rest, from the least to the greatest, on the Sunday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord, 21 December, bearing crosses and proceeding in procession, ascended the hill of Blessed Michael, that they might deserve to receive over themselves a vigorous, good, and capable guardian.”

When Henry graciously received the envoys and they asked about the shepherd, “he took his chaplain Otto by the hand and said: ‘Behold, this is your lord; this is the bishop of the Church of Bamberg.’” On hearing this, the noblemen standing around halted as if stunned, since they had hoped that someone from among themselves would be named. But the envoys of Bamberg, whose head, as may be inferred from another writer, was Count Berengar of Sulzbach, said: “We had hoped, though sadly, that we should receive as our ruler some man of lineage from among the lords and princes of our court, known to us; for who this man is or whence he comes, we do not know.”

Who, I ask, could from this imagine—even in a dream—that Otto was then descended from the noble and very famous family of the counts of Andechs? But the emperor, unable to endure this rejection of the person, said: “Do you wish to know who he is?” “We do,” they replied. “Truly,” he said, “I am his father, and Bamberg ought to be his mother. We cannot alter this word. But if anyone attempts to oppose this our appointment, which is from God, he will without doubt incur the displeasure of our indignation. For we are not led by fickleness or private advantage; rather, with single-minded purpose we have pursued in this matter what we have perceived to be most honourable and most necessary for that Church. Judgment concerning matters tested is not uncertain: through long experience and trial we have learned this man’s patience, discernment, and diligence in carrying out small affairs; we know his vigour in great business. Finally, his absence will be a great hindrance to our household, whose affairs he has been accustomed to dispatch in every respect energetically and faithfully.”

[Col. 1273A] VII. But what did Otto do in the meantime? He threw himself at the emperor’s feet and with many tears begged to be excused from the office laid upon him. He professed himself poor and unworthy, and asked that the dignity be transferred to others among his distinguished, noble, powerful, and wealthy fellow chaplains.

“Do you see,” said the emperor, “how this man is driven by ambition? He has now refused for the third time; he has already asked that two bishoprics offered to him be transferred to his companions. We wished to place him in the bishopric of Augsburg, when Sigefrid died in 1096; but he said that it was just that those who had preceded him in the labours and duties of our court should come first to repose. Afterwards he acted in like manner concerning the bishopric of Halberstadt offered to him by us” [Note: [Col. 1273D] In 1101.].

Without delay, having delivered the ring and staff, the emperor invested him and committed him to the envoys. “In that very moment, while still at court, he made a vow to the Lord that he would never remain in the bishopric unless he should deserve to receive both consecration and investiture canonically, by the consent and petition of his Church, from the hand of the apostolic lord. He celebrated Christmas at Mainz with the emperor; then, retaining some and dismissing others of the envoys who had come for him, he remained at court for almost forty days with great dignity and honour, the emperor himself and the whole court showing him the highest respect.”

Such was Otto’s singular nomination to the episcopate, glorious and honourable alike to him and to King Henry.

VIII. “After this,” our writer continues, “the prince ordered the bishops of Augsburg and Würzburg and other honoured men of his court to conduct Otto, with most honourable companionship and an immense retinue, to his see at Bamberg on the vigil of the Purification of the Blessed Ever-Virgin Mary—which in the year 1103 was the Sunday of Sexagesima—while all the clergy and people waited in great longing and expectation.”

Ebbo adds that, when he had completed the journey and reached the village of Ampferbach, all the leading men of Bamberg came out to meet him and received their most eagerly awaited father with great rejoicing. “Accordingly, as he approached the place where he could first behold the cathedral monastery, he dismounted from his horse, removed his shoes, and displayed the humility of his heart by the condition of his body. Barefoot, he trod through February’s cold, snow, and ice as far as the church of Blessed George. Clerics and monks met him in a long procession, together with noble laymen in a vast multitude and all the people of the Church of Bamberg, in splendid procession and ceremonial, with the ornaments and relics of the saints, with hymns and confessions suited to the person and the occasion. So great was the rejoicing and the splendour of his reception that it cannot be explained in words.”

IX. At this point the writers of the Life seem to disagree more sharply. The writer whom we have followed thus far states that Otto, “a few days after his reception, before arranging his other affairs,” sent his envoys to Paschal II at Rome with a letter, which he quotes together with the pope’s reply. The other writer, Ebbo, asserts that Otto deferred “the grace of his consecration for a long time, that is, for three years,” in order to prepare himself the better for it.

He traces the true cause of this delay to the conflict of that time: Archbishop Ruthard of Mainz, by whom Otto ought to have been consecrated, “as though a rebel against the emperor, and for that reason expelled from his see, had been living in Thuringia for eight years; and very many bishops in the German lands had been punished by suspension from priestly office.” Otto therefore asked to be consecrated by the pope himself, sending him another letter.

These letters differ from the former ones, yet neither bears a certain date. Of the two, however, the earlier letter seems more consonant with the object Otto had proposed to himself at his nomination. He says:

“To you, therefore, most holy Father, and to our holy mother the Roman Church, I devoutly submit my neck and ask aid and counsel concerning my affairs. For while I had lived for several years in the service of my lord the emperor, and had found favour in his eyes, suspecting investiture from the hand of a prince, I once and again refused the bishopric when he wished to give it to me. But now, for the third time, he has appointed me to the bishopric of Bamberg; yet I shall by no means remain in it unless it please your Holiness to invest and consecrate me through yourself. Whatever, therefore, your judgment may decide concerning me, signify it through envoys to me, your servant, lest perhaps I run in vain if I begin to run to you.”

X. The pope, having read this letter, rejoiced, especially because few bishops in the German kingdom showed reverence to their mother Church. He replied:

“Paschal, to Otto, beloved brother, bishop-elect of the Church of Bamberg. A wise son makes his mother glad. Your deeds and your counsel show you to be a prudent man. We have therefore judged it fitting to honour you and assist your advancement. Doubting nothing of our goodwill, present yourself to us as soon as you are able; for we are certain that divine Wisdom knows how to make good use even of evil men” [Note: [Col. 1273D] Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, p. 688.].

These letters seem to have been issued in 1103 and concern Otto’s confirmation in the bishopric, from which he sometimes reckons the years of his episcopate. But this confirmation must be distinguished from the ordination or consecration of which Ebbo speaks, which was performed only in 1106, as we shall shortly say. With this distinction, the two writers are easily reconciled.

XI. Otto, therefore, now a bishop confirmed by Henry IV, received on 15 July 1103 a most extensive privilege for his Church [Note: [Col. 1274D] Documentary appendix, no. LV.], in which Henry again counts him as the seventh bishop of the Church of Bamberg, not including Hermann, who had been deposed.

To the same year, although not dated, belong other letters of the same emperor to Otto, congratulating him upon the beginning of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 1275D] Ludwig, *Writers on Bamberg*, p. 814.] and offering most excellent admonitions. After expressing his joy that Otto had been honourably received by his Church, he says:

“We advise, exhort, and request that what you do, you should do in such a way that you do not lose the first fruits of your good reputation by relaxing your hand; for a good beginning without an end is like a beautiful body without a head. Let no one turn you from ecclesiastical choice according to justice and utility by fear, bend you by price, or seduce you by the deceptive honey of persuasion; for if, having been tested by all these things, you are found approved, you will easily repel them all. But if you judge anything too burdensome for your own powers, make it known to us through the authority of our command; we shall without doubt come to your assistance.”

Other letters of Emperor Henry IV to the bishop of Bamberg, however, create no small difficulty; they bear neither his name nor a year [Note: [Col. 1275D] In the cited work, p. 815.]. In them he summons the bishop to join an expedition against Count Robert of Flanders, to be undertaken around the Kalends of November. All historians agree that this expedition was undertaken by the emperor in late autumn 1102, at which time Otto was not yet bishop and the see of Bamberg was still vacant. This letter, therefore, could have been sent neither to Otto nor to Rupert, who had already died.
