Either the name of the Church is erroneous, or the letter was merely drawn up during the vacancy in case a bishop should meanwhile be appointed—hence the absence of a name. We think it more likely, however, that the title “Emperor Augustus” was wrongly prefixed to this letter, and that it belongs to King Henry V, who, according to the Ursperg Chronicle, undertook another expedition against Robert in Flanders about October 1107, to which Otto might have been invited.

There are two other letters of Henry IV to Otto [Note: [Col. 1275D] In the cited work, p. 813.], in which he implores Otto’s help against his rebellious son Henry and warns him not to join the latter’s party. They were written while the son was besieging the castle of Nuremberg, and therefore in 1105.

XII. During this conflict between the two Henrys, a great assembly of princes was held at Mainz at Christmas 1105, through the agency of the son [Note: [Col. 1275D] Ursperg, under that year.]. At the insistence of apostolic envoys, a solemn embassy to the pope was decreed, so that the Churches throughout Germany, disturbed by long discord, might return to communion with the pope.

Envoys were chosen for this purpose from the chief provinces of the realm, and among them Otto of Bamberg was appointed from Franconia. The Saxon Annalist calls him so on this occasion, since he had not yet been ordained. At the beginning of 1106 all of them set out for Italy. When they reached the valley of Trent, they were captured by Adalbert, count of the province, who had been forewarned by Henry IV. Gebhard of Constance alone reached the pope by hidden paths in the Alps. Otto of Bamberg, of whom Adalbert was the vassal, was also restored to liberty.

I judge that this was done especially through the aid of Duke Welf of Bavaria, who, having learned of the captivity, broke through the barriers of the place, put Adalbert to flight, and restored the captives to liberty [Note: [Col. 1276D] Saxon Annalist, under 1106.]. This is supported by a letter from the clergy of Bamberg addressed to “the illustrious and magnificent Duke N.” [Note: [Col. 1276D] Namely Welf.] concerning the liberation of their bishop [Note: [Col. 1276D] Documentary appendix, no. LIX.]. Among other complaints, they say:

“For he has not merely been treated with cruelty of an ordinary kind. Having laid sacrilegious hands upon a bishop who was travelling in religious habit to the apostolic see, they then plundered the great sums of money which he had prepared for the expenses of so important a journey. Nor, satisfied even with so great a spoil, do they now attempt to extort from him a thousand manses [Note: [Col. 1276D] Perhaps read: *mansos*, ‘manses’ or ‘manors’.], that is, the whole patrimony of the bishopric.”

Otto seems nevertheless to have recovered these things again through Welf. Restored to freedom, he returned to his Church, which had been so anxious on his behalf, waiting for quieter times until a safe access to the pope should be open to him.

XIII. This access was soon opened by the captivity of Henry IV and the coronation of his son Henry V. By this event both tranquillity in the realm and the safety of the roads toward Rome, hitherto disturbed by the elder Henry, were in some measure restored. All this is clear from another letter of Otto to Pope Paschal II requesting his consecration [Note: [Col. 1276D] Documentary appendix, no. LX.]. It begins:

“Because at last, through the Lord’s mercy and his steering of the ship of his Church, the serene light of truth has shone upon the Western Church after the cloudy tempests of errors, before and above all things we desire Your Holiness to know that in all things we have obeyed, as was fitting, your legate, namely Gebhard, bishop of Constance; and that, with the utmost devotion, we have partly performed and are partly, if life be granted us, prepared to perform all that we have learned through him.”

After other matters he adds concerning his ordination:

“With all our heart we desire to rest upon your authority. Stretch out your hand to us; command what you wish us to do. If you command that we come to you, although our resources have been diminished by plunder in the very recent captivity and by fire, nevertheless, out of our desire to see you and to obtain the grace of consecration, we shall present ourselves before the sight of your majesty with the blessing due from our service. May the bowels of your mercy, therefore, deign to make us certain concerning this business by some reply, so that a safer way of coming to you may be pointed out to us beforehand, and it may be signified that we shall receive from you the blessing for which we devoutly entreat.”

He immediately adds why he asks to be consecrated by the pope himself:

“We earnestly seek this from the hand of your Holiness because our metropolitan, although he has received the grace of consecration through you, nevertheless—what we cannot confess without tears—suffers a great lack of fellow-workers in the spiritual gift.”

That is, most German bishops had adhered to the emperor. By “metropolitan” Otto means Ruthard of Mainz, who had remained in Thuringia from 1098 until this year 1106 because of fear of Henry IV.

XIV. There can be no doubt that the pope’s reply was favourable. Upon receiving it, Otto came to Rome on the Ascension of the Lord, which in 1106 fell on 3 May, and proceeded thence to the pope at Anagni. He set before him the whole course of events, laid down his staff, and begged pardon. He was told by the pope to wait until Pentecost and returned to his lodging.

Having spent the night meditating upon the pastoral burden, he decided to live as a private person and return home without consecration. He had already withdrawn with his companions a day’s journey as far as Sutri, when news of this reached the pope. The pope immediately sent envoys and ordered him, under obedience, to return to Anagni.

Otto accordingly returned there; and on the day of Pentecost, at the request of the envoys of his Church, he was consecrated bishop by the pope himself during the solemn celebration of Mass. Ebbo adds that Pentecost then fell on the third Ides of May, or on the feast of St Gingulf or Gangolf, martyr. This feast is entered in the Martyrology on 11 May, but had formerly also been celebrated on 9 or 13 May according to local custom; in the latter case Pentecost fell on that day in this year.

Hence it is most plainly evident that Otto was ordained not already in 1103, as many maintain, but for the first time in this year 1106, three years after his election. From this time also he chiefly reckons the years of his episcopate.

XV. Otto himself reveals several circumstances of this event in his letter to the chapter of Bamberg concerning his consecration [Note: [Col. 1277D] Documentary appendix, no. LXII.]:

“On the holy day of Pentecost, by God’s ordering, in the city of Anagni in Campania, which divides Romagna from Apulia, I received, though unworthy, by the Lord’s bounty, the gift of episcopal blessing. The most blessed Pope Paschal laid on his hand; many other bishops joined in the act; and the clergy of the Roman Church, a great part of whom had assembled in that same city on that day, stood by and consented. And—what has happened in our times to no one consecrated by the Roman pontiff—I was consecrated without the offering of any oath. We earnestly ask you to remember always, with every act of thanksgiving, this place, this day, and this gratuitous mercy of God; especially since several other venerable persons, negotiating weighty matters at the apostolic see, returned with their business unfinished.”

He adds a brief exhortation to implore divine assistance, that he may fulfil his pastoral office properly and beneficially.

XVI. Pope Paschal himself wrote of the same consecration to the clergy and people of Bamberg, exhorting them to render the obedience due [Note: [Col. 1277D] Ibid., no. LXII.]:

“Even if it were unknown to us how greatly the Church of Bamberg has been bound, from the very beginning of its foundation, to the apostolic see by a debt of affection, the communication of your letters makes it plain. It is known that our venerable brother Otto, elect of your Church, has constantly maintained and still maintains this debt of affection, since he hastens through so many and such great dangers to visit the apostolic see. We have therefore received him with the affection of due kindness; and according to the desire of your love, by our hands, as it were by those of Blessed Peter, while preserving the metropolitan’s right, we have by God’s grace ordained for you a bishop.”

In order that this metropolitan right should be preserved, the pope also issued another letter to Archbishop Ruthard of Mainz on 21 May of that year [Note: [Col. 1277D] Ibid., no. LXI.], in which he says:

“We have judged it fitting to receive, with the undiminished and perfect grace of former friendship, our venerable brother Otto, elect of the Church of Bamberg, when he came to us. Moreover, because that Church had now long lacked the care of episcopal office, and because, as a consequence of the past schism, very few in the German lands perform episcopal office, at the request of that Church itself, when this our brother had come to us through many dangers, with the consent and unanimous judgment of all who were present with us, we bestowed upon him, by the Lord’s bounty, the hand [Note: [Col. 1278D] Read: *munus*, ‘gift’ or ‘office’.] of episcopal blessing—while, of course, preserving the reverence due to your metropolitan see.”

That is, as had been established by his predecessors. Ebbo further reports that at this ordination Otto was granted the use of the pallium and the right to carry the cross before him in his own Church. In fact, however, we shall see that this did not occur until 1111.

XVII. Ebbo briefly narrates what was done afterwards at Rome: “Having been honourably advanced by the apostolic lord through solemn consecration, he was kept with him for some time out of kindness.” Perhaps the peace and tranquillity of the German Churches were also discussed there, particularly since Gebhard of Constance, sent to the pope as legate for this purpose, was present at the same time.

These matters were also decreed in the Council of Guastalla on 22 October 1106, in the presence of several bishops of Germany [Note: [Col. 1278D] Labbe, *Councils*.]. I do not, however, find Otto among them; he had therefore already left Italy. Ebbo says of his return:

“Having obtained the wished-for permission to depart at Rome, and after a prosperous journey, he crossed the Alps and came to Carinthia,” perhaps to arrange affairs and possessions of his Church there. “After this Otto, the new bishop, attended the courtly assembly which Emperor Henry had summoned at Regensburg for the leading men of the whole realm.” Ursperg places this at Christmas. Trithemius, under the year 1114, relates that a dream presented to Otto there gave rise to the monastery of Prüfening.

“And so, enriched by royal generosity, after the hardship of an arduous pilgrimage, the pious shepherd entered Bamberg in order to undertake the care of his sheep; and there he was honourably received by clergy and people in the rejoicing proper to the occasion.” This must have occurred at the beginning of 1107.

XVIII. Now established among his sheep as an excellent shepherd, Otto watched over their salvation and welfare with every care. During the ensuing conflict of Henry V, he kept them constant in communion with the pope; only the canons, for the preservation of temporal possessions, favoured the king more than the pope.

“Therefore,” Ebbo says, “solicitous for the charge entrusted to him, he watched over ecclesiastical liberty by day and night, striving to discover how he might either increase the possessions of his Church which he found, or restore those which had been dispersed.” With still greater zeal he undertook to reform the sacred condition of his Church, corrupted by the negligence of his predecessors and the bitterness of long discord. Above all, he strove by the best means he could to bring back a clergy exceedingly corrupted to the canonical rules.

He was especially intent upon restoring monastic discipline, knowing well how greatly this contributed to the reformation both of clergy and people. To this end, at various times, both in his own and in other dioceses—but in places belonging to the temporal jurisdiction of his Church—he built several monasteries from the foundations. “Having,” in the biographer’s words, “furnished them with worthy and elegant buildings, he strove to buy estates, acquire woods, fields, and meadows, or obtain them by other lawful means.”

XIX. The monasteries newly founded by Otto are enumerated by his biographers as follows. In the diocese of Würzburg: Uraugia of St. Lawrence on the Saale, upon hereditary land of the church, in the year 1108; and Uraha of St. Peter, or Herrenaurach, upon acquired land, likewise in 1108; both of which have been treated in the history of that bishopric [Col. 1279C; Note: Part III, p. 419]. In his own diocese of Bamberg he built two monasteries: Langheim, for Cistercians, on acquired land; and Michelfeld, on land belonging to the Church, for black monks. In the diocese of Eichstätt he advanced Heilsbronn to the status of an abbey at great expense. In the diocese of Regensburg he founded six monasteries: five of the Cluniac order; one, Ensdorf, received from Otto, Count Palatine; another, Prüfening, both on acquired land; a third, Münchsmünster, together with the adjacent parish of the same name, purchased from Henry, Duke of Bavaria, and Margrave Diepold, and conferred upon the Church of Bamberg by the royal privilege of Lothair [Col. 1279D]. The fifth and sixth were Biburg and Mallersdorf, both upon acquired land, as likewise was the seventh, Windberg, of the order of Norbertines. In the diocese of Halberstadt he added to the Church of Bamberg the abbey of Wirzenburg, now Reginstorf, together with all its appurtenances, received from Emperor Henry, and doubled the property of that monastery. In the diocese of Passau, Alderbach or Alterspach, and the Cluniac house of Gleink, which he purchased from Margrave Leopold. Finally, in the patriarchate of Aquileia, in Carinthia, he built the fifteenth monastery at the castle of Arnoldstein, in a ruined fortress, in the year 1107 [Col. 1280A].

XX. Besides these fifteen monasteries, he also established five cells, or smaller monastic houses. The first of these was Aspach in the diocese of Regensburg: “its estate and property the Church of Bamberg had lost for a long time; but Otto, having diligently sought it out, made it a cell of monks, and it grew into an abbey, enriched by an abundant grant of estates, first by himself and then by other faithful persons” [Note: See *Monumenta Boica*, vol. V, p. 107]. “The second cell is at Bamberg, situated in the precinct of St. Michael,” concerning which we shall speak below in the history of that monastery. “The third is Rotha in the bishopric of Würzburg, which the bishop received as a gift to the Church of Bamberg from Agnes the Countess Palatine and her sister Adelaide, together with sixty marks [Col. 1280B]; but he bought for the church of the cell the surrounding properties for two hundred and seventy-five marks, together with ministerials—that is, fields, woods and meadows, pastures and mills—and with the usufruct and right which Duke Chuno is known to have possessed in the same estate.”

If I judge correctly, Duke Chuno was none other than Conrad, Duke of Franconia and later emperor. His mother Agnes, who is here called “the Countess Palatine,” was the daughter of Emperor Henry IV and wife of Frederick of Hohenstaufen, just as her sister Adelaide was wife of Bolesław III, King of Poland.

“Count Gotebold [Note: of Henneberg] had begun to build the fourth cell, Veßra; the bishop, receiving it from him as a gift, promoted it at his own expense.” We have already dealt with both of these cells in the bishopric of Würzburg [Col. 1280C; Note: pp. 496 and 486], as also with the other two, Nichardelsehausen or Nitarshausen in the district of Tullefelt, and Tückelhausen [Note: loc. cit., pp. 461 and 493]. Others add still other houses, restored or rather reformed by St. Otto rather than originally founded by him; these will be mentioned here and there, and below in § LXV.

XXI. Moreover, this most discerning bishop could easily foresee that many would criticize this manner of acting and charge him with excessive prodigality in building so many monasteries, with which the world was already burdened from other sources. Yet I prefer to read in his biographer rather than write myself how Otto answered these detractors, and be, like Cicero, assailed for pleading my own cause. In order that all these establishments might endure more securely, he wished them to be strengthened by apostolic authority [Col. 1280D]. Accordingly, he received letters from Pope Calixtus II, dated 3 April 1123 [Note: *Codex probatorius*, no. LXXI], by which the pope received into the protection of the Roman Church the monasteries hitherto built by Otto “at his own expense” and granted to the Church of Bamberg, and decreed that all their possessions should remain secure. He likewise decreed “that they should receive the ordination of their abbots or monks from Catholic diocesan bishops, but established that the care and administration of the affairs of those monasteries should remain in the power of Otto and his successors.”

Among them are listed St. John the Baptist at Reginsdorf, St. John the Evangelist at Michelinvelt, St. James at Entisdorf, St. Lawrence at Urowa, and St. George at Bruviningen [Col. 1281A]; hence the rest seem not yet to have been completed at that time. Moreover, after 1130 he obtained from Innocent II a decree “that in the monasteries which either were built in his parish in ancient times or which he himself established out of devotion, the order of sacred religion should be firmly preserved in them for all future times.” The pope also decreed “that no one should be appointed in those churches through the Simoniac heresy, but that honourable persons, to whom distinction of character and station is assuredly favourable, should there be ordained” [Note: Ludwig, *Script.*, p. 429].

XXII. But now let us pursue Otto’s deeds individually. We have already said that at the beginning of the year 1107 he returned from Rome to his own Church [Col. 1281B]. It is certain that by Easter he was already with the king at Mainz, from the king’s diploma for the monastery of St. Maximin, dated 7 Kalends of May, 1107 [Note: read *Kalends*] [Note: Gudenus, diploma in the same volume, p. 8], in which Otto of Bamberg is noted. What he did in Carinthia before coming to Bamberg is not known. Some hold that he then organized the monastery of Arnoldstein there; I believe this must be understood of its beginning.

The biographer says of it: “He built a monastery in the castle of Arnoldstein after demolishing the fortification. For forty-five years this castle, together with its ninety-five dependent holdings, had been alienated from the Church of Bamberg; but he recovered it with much labour and expense and, adding sixty holdings to it, made it an abbey” [Col. 1281C]. But he did not add the year. In the same year, 1108, the sixth of his pontificate, that is, reckoned from his confirmation, he began to build in another castle, Aurach or Urach, in the diocese of Würzburg, the monastery of St. Lawrence; and in the fifth year thereafter he dedicated it and endowed it with various estates, as he himself declares in his letters on this matter, issued in 1122, which we have elsewhere given in the vernacular from Frisius [Note: *Episcopatus Wirceburgensis, probatoria*, p. 29].

XXIII. In the year 1109, on 25 July, he consecrated the collegiate church of St. James outside the walls of Bamberg, begun in 1071 by Bishop Hermann and completed by himself. The beginnings of the monastery of Prüfening near Regensburg are assigned to this same year. It was formerly a village at the confluence of the Naab and Danube. In 999 Emperor Otto III granted it to Tagino, chaplain of Henry, still Duke of Bavaria; from him it passed to the provostship of the old chapel at Regensburg; later it was bestowed by the same Henry, now king, upon the Church of Bamberg [Col. 1281D].

Otto, therefore, intending to build a monastery there as in a pleasant place, was divinely warned [Note: Trithemius, under the year 1114] and acquired it through exchange for another estate. In the year of the Lord 1109, he founded there, in honour of Almighty God and St. George the Martyr, a monastery of monks living according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict [Note: *Monumenta Boica*, vol. XIII, pp. 2–3], according to the book of traditions. In 1114 he placed over it as first abbot Erminold from Hirsau [Col. 1282A], and assigned it many estates acquired from all quarters; all of these he confirmed in letters issued in 1123 [Note: loc. cit., p. 141].

The other Bavarian monastery, Osterhofen, had formerly been built by St. Pirmin under Duke Uto for Benedictine brethren. After its destruction by the Huns, Henry IV, Duke of Bavaria and brother of St. Cunegunda, restored it for certain secular canons. Emperor Henry II handed it over to the Church of Bamberg. There, in 1110, “the basilica of the Blessed Virgin Mary was built, honourably adorned with surrounding towers, bestowed and dedicated by the venerable lord Otto, Bishop of Bamberg, in honour of God and His Mother Mary.” In it he also instituted the anniversary observance of Duke Hezli—the aforesaid Hezilo or Henry, its restorer [Col. 1282B]—who died there on 1 September 1125 and was buried there with his wife Maria. In 1127 Otto, at the request of Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, established Premonstratensian canons there [Note: *Monumenta Boica*, vol. XII, pp. 323 ff.].

XXIV. Hoffmann assigns to the year 1111, after the emperor had departed for Italy, the restoration of the cathedral church, which had been burned down under Otto’s predecessor Rupert in 1081 [Note: Ludwig, *Scriptores Bambergenses*, p. 97]. The biographer describes it thus: “In the days of Otto himself, the church of the cathedral monastery, which under his predecessor had, by God’s permission, been consumed by fire until only its walls remained, was restored by him at great expense to the nobility of its former splendour.” He then narrates this more fully, as also the properties granted to it.

Yet I can scarcely persuade myself that Otto, so greatly occupied until this point with building other churches, neglected his own cathedral for so long [Col. 1282C]. Equally uncertain appears the bishop’s purported fourth journey to Carinthia, undertaken in the same year according to Hoffmann, during which he finally recovered Arnoldstein Castle and afterwards converted it into a monastery; this has already been discussed above in § XXII. But without controversy, on 15 April 1111 Pope Paschal II granted Bishop Otto “the pallium for celebrating the solemn rites of Mass,” though only on specified days, together with permission to carry the cross before him “within the parish of the Church of Bamberg,” “with due regard, that is, for the reverence owed to the metropolitan see of Mainz” [Note: *Codex probatorius*, no. LXV], whatever others may have written to the contrary.

XXV. Otto is frequently mentioned in many charters in these and the following years [Col. 1282D]. Yet it is of no importance to list them unless some epoch of his life or noteworthy deed is involved. Such, according to Hoffmann, is the year 1112, when Richwin the advocate granted to the Church of Bamberg Albistein or Bothenstein Castle together with its town, and the gift was confirmed by diploma. Otto added to these the towns and castles of Hilpolstein, Geilrut, Hensefeld, and Ebersberg. The biographer says of these:

“He assisted and exalted the temporal estate of the bishopric by buildings and fortifications of castles, as well as by estates and possessions. For in various places and manors of the bishopric he built fourteen basilicas and four halls of elegant construction. Moreover, he added to the lordship of the bishopric six castles which it had not previously possessed: first Abuinestein, second Lupoldenstein, third Geutenreut, fourth Hempfenveld, fifth Ebersperck, sixth Eschenveld. But Albuinenstein Castle, also called Bottenstein, situated almost in the very middle of the bishopric, he purchased for eight hundred pounds of silver and seventeen talents of gold.”

He added many other things besides. To prevent any of his successors from altering them, he sought confirmation from Calixtus II [Col. 1283B]. In letters issued to him on 13 April 1124 [Note: Ludwig, *Script.*, p. 434], the pope confirmed all these things under his ban, decreeing “that no successor, nor any person, may sell those holdings [Note: *mansi*, landed holdings], grant them as lay benefices, or transfer them to other uses; but that, as you have ordained, from each of the aforesaid holdings one denarius shall each year be paid to the Church of Bamberg, for the soul of Emperor Henry, its founder, to maintain the lights. Nor may any person in future alter the abbeys and regular canonries established through your industry in the order of religion, or other things rightly constituted by you.”

In the same year, 1112, according to the same witness, Otto was frightened by a certain prodigy, fell into a serious illness, and asked Wolfram, abbot of St. Michael’s, for the monastic habit [Col. 1283C]. Wolfram accepted his vow; but when he saw him recover, he commanded him under obedience to continue as bishop.

XXVI. Hahn places about the same year, 1112, a letter of Bruno, Archbishop of Trier [Note: *Collectio monumentorum*, vol. I, p. 202], calling our Otto to Speyer to examine the case of that city’s bishop-elect. This Bruno had already become well known to Otto; through him Otto was released from the captivity into which he had fallen with Bruno in the valley of Trento in 1106, while travelling to Rome [Note: *Annales Saxo*, under that year], as has already been partly mentioned above.

At the beginning of 1110, Bruno had been sent with others as an envoy by King Henry V to seek from the pope the imperial crown for him [Col. 1283D; Note: *Annales Hildesheimenses*, under the year 1109]. Perhaps he was also there with him at his coronation in 1111, and remained there afterwards, as may be inferred from the cited letter. Since it is little known, we reproduce it here in full, with occasional explanatory notes:

“Bruno, by the grace of God unworthy overseer of the people of Trier, to O., holy bishop of the Church of Bamberg: the service of sincere charity. I rejoice greatly with Your Blessedness, because I think it has come about not without great merit of your holiness [Note: “I think”], that my lord the pope so sweetly retains remembrance of you [Col. 1284A]. For when I was performing the embassy of my lord the king [Note: A.D. 1110], he spoke with me concerning the obedience of your charity, and through me sent you greeting and apostolic [Note: blessing]. Having taken counsel concerning his dispensation, he charged us to consecrate the bishop-elect of Eichstätt and of Speyer, and to call you as our helper and fellow-worker.”

Thus, while the bishop of Trier was still remaining with the pope, both bishops had meanwhile been elected, or, according to custom, nominated by the king. The certain date of neither is known. If Trithemius is to be believed, Bruno succeeded Gebhard in the see of Speyer as early as 1110, promoted by royal authority. Certainly, Bruno of Speyer is already read in April 1111 at the first agreement concluded at Rome between pope and king [Col. 1284B; Note: see Calles, *Annales ecclesiastici Germaniae*, vol. VI, part I, p. 128].

There is another question regarding Ulrich of Eichstätt. Gretser and Falckenstein, in their catalogue of those bishops, write that he succeeded Eberhard, who died on 6 January 1112; but I should believe that this happened rather in the preceding year, from this very letter. The bishop of Trier continues:

“Yet because certain things had been reported to him”—that is, to the pope—“concerning the bishop of Speyer, he commanded us diligently to examine the matter, and, if he could clear himself of the accusations in due order by the testimony of the brethren present, to ordain him to the honour of God and the necessary provision of the Church. Therefore, on behalf of my lord the pope, I urge you to take care that, because this is God’s cause, it is not delayed through you; and that within fifteen days from the Sunday of the Lord’s Resurrection you come to us at Speyer” [Col. 1284C].

Since, then, Bruno of Speyer, of whom the discussion is concerned, was still at Rome in 1111 on “the Tuesday after Easter,” the day on which the agreement was subscribed, he could not have been examined at Speyer in that year, but either in 1110 or, as I rather believe, in 1112, when the bishop-elect of Eichstätt, likewise mentioned in this letter, was elected. In any event, Bruno’s case was none other than that he had been promoted by royal authority, and therefore by ring and staff while the dispute still continued. Yet he appears to have been found innocent, since he subsequently acted as an excellent pastor of his Church. But these matters arise only on the occasion of our Otto, whose deeds we are pursuing.

XXVII. In 1113 Otto dedicated the church of St. Lawrence at Uraha, and on 21 September 1114 that of the monastery of Banz [Col. 1284D]. Its foundress Alberada had formerly offered it to the Church of Bamberg in 1071; but it had been left desolate “through the negligence of its prelates in spiritual and temporal goods.” Otto himself renewed it and raised it to ecclesiastical status. He appointed Baldwin abbot there with other faithful and religious men, restored the possessions belonging to it from the original foundation, gave it Mount Stekkilze in 1127, and redeemed the right of advocacy from Count Rapoto. All this is clear from Otto’s own letters issued about 1127 [Note: *Episcopatus Wirceburgensis, probatoria*, p. 30], subscribed by Egilbert the dean, Gerunck, dean of Tuirstatt, Count Steriker, and Count Reginboto [Col. 1285A].

XXVIII. Meanwhile Otto incurred the suspicion of Emperor Henry V, lest, during the conflict between himself and the pope, Otto should turn the other bishops away from him. Otto himself abstained from frequenting the court lest he be stained by contagion from another’s fault. The emperor, therefore, intending to test his loyalty, came himself to Bamberg to celebrate Christmas there in 1113. Otto received him magnificently and entertained him during those days, as the Saxon Annalist and the Ursperg Chronicle write under the year 1114:

“The emperor celebrated Christmas at Bamberg with the utmost magnificence and a great multitude of princes. Nor did he do so simply because he held in some suspicion the bishop of the city, Otto, the man of God, who, owing to certain scandals then arising in the kingdom, was reluctant to frequent the court [Col. 1285B]. But Otto himself, sparing no temporal resources for ecclesiastical concord, gloriously overcame the king’s hostility by benefits that never wearied.”

Nor does it appear that Otto abstained from all communion with Emperor Henry, from the conduct of Abbot Erminold of Prüfening, recently appointed by Otto. With a zeal not sufficiently prudent, Erminold refused to receive the emperor when he visited his monastery in Otto’s company; indeed, he in some manner reproved the bishop himself for that communion, as Trithemius relates in his *Annals* under the year 1114.

XXIX. Otto was also reproved by the bishops themselves for what seemed to them excessive favour or connivance towards Emperor Henry [Col. 1285C], thus proving by his own example how difficult it is, even with all prudence employed, to maintain a middle course between two opposing parties. When Henry himself had been struck with anathema at the Council of Beauvais on 6 December of the same year, and again at Reims on 28 March 1115—Otto being always absent—Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, wrote him a rather sharp letter. In it he reproached Otto with negligence and stirred him to defence, or at least to free lamentation over the Church’s gravest misfortune, which Frederick himself bitterly lamented [Note: *Codex probatorius*, no. LXVII]. At length he addressed him thus:

“Do not keep us suspended any longer by prolonged expectation, but certify us in writing of your judgment [Col. 1285D]. My lord Chuno, your great-nephew, bishop and legate of the Roman Church, sends you greeting. With all the bishops of Gaul in the council of Beauvais, he excommunicated the emperor, the bishop of Münster, and Hermann of Winzenburg, and ordered that this be made known to you. He will repeat the same sentence against the aforesaid persons and all their accomplices at the Council of Reims, which will be held on Laetare Jerusalem [Note: that is, 28 March], together with three other bishops recently sent from the Roman See.”

Chuno, Cardinal Bishop of Palestrina, perhaps our Otto’s great-nephew through the maternal line [Col. 1286A], was the son of Egeno, forefather of the counts of Urach in Württemberg [Note: Neugart, *Codex diplomaticus Alemanniae*, vol. II, p. 44, note]. He had a brother, Count Egeno II, and a sister, Matilda, married to Count Manegold of Sumetingen or Sunemotingen [Note: Crusius, *Annales*, part II, book IX, chapter 20; see Schmidlin, *Württembergische Beyträge*, genealogical table, p. 129].

Moved by these letters, Otto came to Cologne before Christmas in the same year, for the synod summoned by the legate. When the legate died, Adalbert of Mainz, who had been awaiting consecration from him, received it from our Otto on the feast of St. Stephen, 26 December [Note: *Annales Saxo*, under the year 1116].

XXX. At the end of 1115 the emperor celebrated Christmas at Speyer and deliberated concerning his journey into Italy, in order to provide for “the Roman See and the commonwealth.” “For this reason we necessarily summon our princes [Col. 1286B], that from them, as is just, we may receive counsel and aid,” as he writes in his letters to Otto [Note: *Codex probatorius*, no. LXIX]. “For this we have the greatest need of the presence of your loyalty and the prudence of your counsel, because we love you from the heart, and we trust you in every matter concerning our honour as undoubtedly as ourselves. Therefore we confidently and earnestly ask your affection to come to us at Speyer on the Friday after the approaching feast of St. Mary [Note: namely the Purification, or 4 February 1116]. There we shall deliberate upon these matters, with your counsel and that of our other princes, for God’s honour and concerning the condition of the realm and Christian peace. Do this gladly, knowing that we shall dismiss you quickly.”

From so familiar a letter one might suppose Otto to have been the emperor’s intimate friend. Yet I do not read that he was present at that assembly [Col. 1286C], nor that he accompanied the Italian expedition undertaken shortly afterwards.

In the same year, in March, Paschal II assembled a council at the Lateran. Investitures were indeed condemned there, but not the emperor himself. This seems to have been the reason why Otto never regarded Henry as excommunicated: he had not yet been declared such by the pope himself. Hence Otto generally abstained from assemblies where this same issue was pressed. Indeed, he did not even appear at the Cologne synod ordered by the pope and summoned by the same legate Chuno during Rogation Days in 1118.

Adalbert of Mainz complained bitterly of this in a letter to Otto [Note: Eccard, *Corpus historicum medii aevi*, vol. II, p. 294]:

“What my lord of Palestrina [Col. 1286D], legate of the Roman Church, recently announced to us by apostolic authority, I, with diligence wholly subject to Roman authority, have carefully fulfilled in every respect, announcing also to you under the same authority and my own that your presence should come to celebrate the council at Cologne. But because this was omitted, I know not through what negligence, the same sentence that was imposed upon the other neglecters of that council would also have been imposed upon you—namely, suspension from the divine office or the dreadful interdict from communion in the body and blood of the Lord [Col. 1287A]—had not the diligence of our petition and the exceptional reverence due to your holiness obtained from the Church that it should not occur. Since these causes came together and cooperated, we at last obtained that your affection should suffer nothing of severity, whose devotion has hitherto prevailed in the Church. For I judged it altogether fitting to spare your honour and reverence in every respect, and according to my power to make provision and take counsel for place and time, since the affection of your holiness has bound itself to us by the great gift of devoted charity.”

Here he means the consecration which he had received from Otto. “For the future, as we have received command, we announce that you are without doubt to come to the council to be held at Fritzlar by the aforesaid legate on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [Col. 1287B], lest, if you become a neglecter of this command also, a decree of a harsher sentence be pronounced against you, my petition no longer being able to prevail.”

But Otto is proved to have abstained from this synod too by another letter of the same Adalbert [Note: Ludwig, loc. cit., p. 822]: “We have long since informed your brotherhood by our letters of the excommunication which, with the common counsel of the brethren and princes [Note: at the Council of Fritzlar in 1119], we pronounced against the invader of the realm.” But because we doubt whether the letters reached you—“for we have heard that your Church wishes to ignore them”—we send these present letters again, admonishing you to do what we have done and command throughout all your churches that the author of this wickedness, together with his supporters, be excluded from Christian communion and from every divine office [Col. 1287C].

That this letter was first written in 1119 is indicated by the title “legate of the Apostolic See,” which Adalbert only then began to give himself in his letters. Unless perhaps it belongs to Adalbert II, who inflicted a similar penalty on Duke Conrad, invader of the kingdom in opposition to Lothair.

XXXI. Callesius wonders with us [Note: *Annales ecclesiastici Germaniae*, vol. VI, part I, p. 169] why Otto of Bamberg was absent from synods of this kind, though otherwise a holy bishop and, if anyone, devoted to the Holy See. He conjectures that Otto avoided councils, as his journeys were beset on every side by the imperial faction and as he was occupied by pastoral cares; he feared that they would bring new and very great disturbances upon Germany, without much benefit to the Church [Col. 1287D].

For Otto cared only for the affairs of his own Church and was little concerned about the other disturbances of the realm. In this he imitated Paschal II, who at the Lateran Council of 1116, when all sought the condemnation of Henry V, was content to condemn the investitures and the other acts wrongly done by him, while still sparing the person of the emperor. He thus adopted sounder counsel than Gregory VII. But Adalbert of Mainz was far removed from this manner of acting: a man of turbulent temper, directed more by private hatred against Henry than by the public good. Thus there could be no agreement between him and Otto, a peaceful man and lover of peace [Col. 1288A].

Adalbert’s hostile disposition toward Otto is also revealed by his rather inflated letter to the clergy, leading men, and subjects of Bamberg, issued on this very occasion [Note: Eccard, *Historia medii aevi*, vol. II, p. 293]:

“We, called to share in the apostolic solicitude and acting in the tenor of the delegated office entrusted to us, because we know that among you there is the anathema of excommunicated communion, prohibit divine offices in every place among you, by the word of the Lord and judgment of the Holy Spirit, until satisfaction is made by your bishop.”

But the bishop, who ought to have the Roman pontiff as his defender, easily turned aside these blind thunderbolts. At least we read nowhere what followed from them.

XXXII. But let us return from these disturbances to Otto’s pious undertakings. In 1117, when an earthquake in Italy as well as Germany overthrew many buildings in various places, the church of the monastery of St. Michael at Bamberg, already cracked through age, was shaken so violently that it threatened the ruin of the whole monastery [Col. 1288B]. Therefore, as the first writer of the *Life* says, Otto “destroyed it from the foundations and, at immense cost and expense, raised a monastery of larger and more elegant construction, to the praise and glory of God and of the heavenly host. He also increased the brethren’s stipends by revenues of more than ninety talents annually. He bestowed many ornaments upon that place as well, and chose it as the dwelling-place of his venerable body until the last trumpet and the voice of the Son of God.” But these matters must be discussed more fully below in the history of that monastery.

XXXIII. Among Otto’s gifts to this monastery, the following especially deserves notice. According to Ebbo, he “gave to the same monastery the church near Albuch, which belonged to him by hereditary right, together with two other churches, namely in memory of himself” [Col. 1288C] and of his parents, whose bodies rested there. Above we saw that the bishop’s parents were Otto and Adelaide, from the province of the Alamanni or Swabia, although their family is not established. At least the passage cited from the biographer casts some light here: Otto is said to have possessed near Albuch a church “belonging to him by hereditary right”; and, since “his parents are buried there,” the whole place and its vicinity appear to have belonged to them.

Geographers place this site in Swabia, on the river Brenz, in the district of Alba [Note: *Chronicon Gottwicense*, p. 534], and consequently on the borders of Württemberg and the territory of Ulm, where the counts of Rechberg held dominion. They maintain that Albuch was a particular tract of the district of Alba; Besold, however, asserts that it ought to be reckoned under the common name of the district of Alba [Note: *Documenta rediviva monasteriorum Würtembergensium*, old edition, p. 329]. Yet in the cited author Albuch is certainly not to be understood as a definite district, but rather as a particular place, as is indicated by mention of the hereditary church and the burial there of Otto’s parents.

Münster mentions a village of this name by the Brenz [Note: *Cosmographia*, book V, chapter 244], but I have thus far been unable to find it on any geographical maps [Col. 1289A]. Nor is it likely that Otto gave to the far-distant monastery of Bamberg a mere village, especially since two other churches are remembered as having existed there as well.

Not without reason, therefore, we conjecture that the Albuch mentioned is none other than Albech or Albeck in Münster, in the same district of Alba; or, according to the Göttweig Chronicle [Note: p. 537], in the adjacent former Alpengau, from which the name Albeck itself seems to have arisen. Albeck is now a partly ruined castle on a hill, with a town of the same name below it, several hours’ distance from Ulm. Knights, and afterwards counts, of Albeck were formerly named from it. Friedrich Lucae adduces the first anonymous one as early as 933, under Henry the Fowler [Note: *Graffensaal*, p. 836]; how reliable this is, he himself may judge.

The first certain branch of this family that I find is “Wittigovus, nobleman of Albecke, who, for the salvation and remedy of his own soul and of all his parents” [Col. 1289B], established in 1183 on the Mount of St. Michael near Ulm a hospice under the care of regular canons. These were later transferred into the city, to the Wengen islands, where they still remain today [Note: Kuon, *Scriptores ecclesiastici*, vol. V, part II, p. 292]. Still noted in the archives of the same canonry are “Count Beringer of Albecke, brother of the founder, and Count Sibotto of Albecke,” their brother, as well as “Wittigovus, son of the said Sibotto,” who is recorded as the last survivor of his family.

From there this county passed to the counts of Werdenberg [Note: see Lazius, book VIII, questions 543, 514, and 558], one of whom, Rudolph, sold the castle to the people of Ulm in 1383. We therefore judge it more probable that the burial-place of Otto’s parents is to be sought in Albeck Castle rather than in the unknown village of Albuch [Col. 1289C], where at least some paternal inheritance had been left to Otto, while his brother “the future knight Frederick possessed what their parents left in possessions and money.”

I find another church at Albuoch in the district of Nahgowe, in Mosellan Lotharingia or New Franconia, in a diploma of Emperor Otto I. By it Otto I granted that church in 962 to the monastery of St. Maximin at Trier [Note: Lünig, *Archiv*, vol. XVI, p. 260]. But it is doubtful whether this is the same place as the village Albecho, situated in the district of Nachowe in the county of Count Emmecho, which in a charter of Archbishop Adalbert I, dated 1135, is said to have been given to the Abbey of St. Alban at Mainz [Note: Joannis, *Rerum Moguntiacarum*, vol. II, p. 746]. It was otherwise called Albacha or Albachermarca, and is today Albich [Col. 1289D], near Alzey in the same district, or in the neighbouring district of Worms [Note: see *Chronicon Gottwicense*, pp. 699 and 869]. But these districts appear far too distant from Alamannia or Swabia, whence Otto’s parents came, were buried at Albuch, and where the place belonged to Otto by right of paternal inheritance.

We do not wish to conjecture further. This one point is certain from the foregoing: Otto had both his inheritance and the burial-place of his parents in Swabia, not in Bavaria. Yet modern writers trace his origin to the illustrious stock of the counts of Andechs [Col. 1290A]. Before Braschius, however, not a single prudent man dreamed of this; or, if some held that opinion, they confused Otto with Bishop Otto II, an undoubted scion of that family. Nor do the matters so far stated concerning his modest means—such that he could not even continue his studies, and eventually became a schoolmaster in Poland—or the fact that he was wholly unknown to the people of Bamberg at his election, reveal lofty or wealthy lineage.

But enough of these genealogical trifles. On this subject one should read the learned dissertation of the distinguished Scholliner on the family of our Otto. Certainly, he had no need of this worldly splendour: by his own deeds and virtues he made his lineage far more illustrious than he received it.

### XXXIV.

In the year 1119, on 6 May, he issued a charter concerning the monastery of St John the Evangelist at Michelvelt, in the Upper Palatinate, built through his support and zeal [Note: [Col. 1290D] Documentary Appendix, no. LXX.]. In it he enumerates the villages which he had bestowed upon it and appointed Count “Berenger of Sulzbach” its advocate. He also granted it “the benefit of confession, communion, baptism, and burial—that is, parochial rights.”

In 1121 Emperor Henry V, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March], indiction XIII [Note: [Col. 1290D] Alternatively XIV.], confirmed to the Church of Bamberg, at Regensburg, the transfer to it of the monastery of Reginstorf in the diocese of Halberstadt. His biographer says of this:

> The abbey of Witzenburch, now called Reginstorf after a change both of site and name, he added to the Church of Bamberg, together with all its appurtenances, having received privileges for it from Emperor Henry.

It is also called Reinsdorf or Reinersdorf, and is situated on the Thuringian river Unstrut, between Scheidungen and Memleben. The author of the foundation of the monastery of Bigung writes thus concerning it [Note: [Col. 1290D] Hofmann, *Rerum Lusaticarum*, vol. I, p. 122.]:

> A certain nobleman, Vizo of Wyzenborch, a kinsman of Wicpert [Note: [Col. 1290D] Margrave of Lusatia.], when dying appointed him his heir. Vizo had established a community of nuns in the same castle. After his death, Wicbert allowed his venerable mother, Lady Sigena, now widowed for the second time, to remain there until the end of her life in holy religious observance. When she had died and been buried there, and all religious life in that place had perished, Wicbert, acting on the advice of Otto, bishop of Bamberg, founded a monastery of monks near the same castle, beside the river Unstrut [Col. 1290D], in a place called Reyndorp. Abbot Wyndoltus [Note: [Col. 1290D] Of Begaugi.] appointed as its abbot Brother Ludiger, recalled from Corvey.

These events are assigned to the year 1110. In 1491 the monks joined the Bursfeld reform; shortly afterwards they were dispersed, and the monastery was converted to secular uses.

In the same year, 1121, Otto consecrated the church of the monastery of St Michael on 1 September, one hundred years after it had first been dedicated.

### XXXV.

[Col. 1291A] At length, wearied by their long discord, the princes of the Empire negotiated peace with the Emperor at a solemn assembly at Würzburg on 29 September of the same year. With his consent, envoys were sent to Rome to submit the decision of his cause to the pope and to a general council.

“Also designated at the present assembly” were “Lord Otto, bishop of Bamberg, Duke Henry, and Count Berenger” [Note: [Col. 1291D] Of Sulzbach.], who were to communicate all these matters to the Bavarian princes. These princes, being perhaps occupied at that time by other public affairs, had been absent from the said assembly; summoned to Regensburg on the Kalends of November [1 November], they were found willing to agree to all these measures [Note: [Col. 1291D] Saxon Annals, under this year.].

But meanwhile a new cause of disagreement arose in 1122. When Erlung, bishop of Würzburg, died, Emperor Henry imposed Gebhard; whereas the clergy and people elected Rugger, who was confirmed by the apostolic legates and consecrated by Adalbert of Mainz in the monastery of Schwarzach.

Because Otto was again absent from this action, Adalbert of Mainz sharply rebuked him in a letter addressed to him [Note: [Col. 1291D] Ludewig, *Script[ores] Bamb[ergenses]*, p. 822.]:

> We previously informed your belovedness that you should meet the legate of the holy apostolic see, our brother bishops your fellow bishops, and the other Catholic princes at the place called Prefeld [Note: [Col. 1291D] Perhaps Pleinfeld, a town in the diocese of Eichstätt.], and attend the ordination of the bishop of Würzburg. You certainly ought to have come with a ready and cheerful spirit, even without being asked: not only because he is your fellow bishop, but also because he is your fellow citizen, and by right of kinship [Col. 1291C] you ought in some measure to love him more familiarly and particularly.

It is uncertain whether this refers to the proximity of Würzburg and Bamberg, or to a blood relationship between Otto and Rugger. If the latter is meant, this would supply a new argument for Bishop Otto’s Swabian origin. For Frisius and others reckon Rugger among the counts of Vaihingen in the duchy of Württemberg [Note: [Col. 1291D] See Sattler, *Historia topographica Wurtembergiae*, p. 244.].

“But because,” the letter continues, “you neglected to come, the lord cardinal, with the consent of the others, wished to suspend you from the divine office until satisfaction had been made. Yet, on account of our particular affection and esteem, we scarcely obtained that no harsher decision should be made against you. [Col. 1291D] Therefore we ask your brotherhood, and by the authority of the lord pope, of the legate of the apostolic see, and of our own authority command you, to present yourself at the general council to be held at Mainz on the Nativity of the Holy Mother of God, setting aside every excuse. There you may learn the legation of the lord pope and take counsel jointly with us concerning the condition of the Church. But if any bishops neglect to attend this holy council, let them know that, by the authority of the lord pope, of the legate of the apostolic [Col. 1292A] see, and of the whole council, they are in every respect subject to the synodal sentence by which such presumptuous persons must be punished.”

### XXXVI.

The plan having changed, however, this synod was subsequently held at Worms on the same day, 8 September 1122. Since the grave question at issue was the restoration of peace between Empire and priesthood, Otto needed no importunate reminder to be present. He therefore attended, and together with the other princes approved the agreement of Emperor Henry V, by which he renounced the investiture of prelates by ring and staff, thereby ending the fatal dispute on 23 September 1122 [Note: [Col. 1292D] Saxon Annals under this year; Harzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. III.].

In the same year Emperor Henry granted Otto and the Church of Bamberg the town of Cronach in perpetual possession; Henry of Marchen had already transferred it to his father Henry IV. The charter was issued at Würzburg in the eleventh year of Henry’s reign, indiction XV [Note: [Col. 1292D] Law V.].

### XXXVII.

Thus far we have reviewed Otto’s deeds in his homeland and bishopric. We must now proceed to recount those which he apostolically performed abroad for the spread of the faith and the conversion of peoples: I mean his apostolate in Pomerania. It was not one mission but two, though writers commonly confuse them or assign them wrongly. If I explain at somewhat greater length this undertaking, so glorious for our Otto, I trust I shall give readers no unwelcome service. Most of these matters are taken from Book II of Otto’s Life; its author, Sefridus, was present at these deeds as a witness, as we noted at the beginning.

### XXXVIII.

[Col. 1292C] The peoples of Pomerania, called by various names, were still enveloped in the blind darkness of paganism. For them one should consult secular writers who treat the history of this people. They obeyed various rulers or dukes. Among these, Suantibor, son of Bogislaus, who died in 1107, divided his land among four sons: Uratislaus, Ratibor, Bogislaus, and Suantopelck. The first two governed the nearer region; the other two, the farther region, later called Lesser Pomerania or Pomerelia [Note: [Col. 1292D] See *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, vol. III, pp. 496 and 505.].

They frequently waged war against their Danish neighbours and especially against the Poles. Boleslaus III, duke of the Poles, inflicted severe defeats upon them in 1117 and 1119, so that, having been subdued by him, they promised to embrace the faith of Christ. This is clear from a letter of Duke Boleslaus himself to our Otto, written about 1123 [Note: [Col. 1292D] Documentary Appendix, no. LXXVIII.]:

> For you know, I think, how the cruel barbarism of the Pomeranians, humbled not by my power but by God’s, sought association with the Church through the washing of baptism and asked to be admitted. But behold, for three years I have laboured because I have been unable to induce any suitable bishops or priests connected with me to undertake this work.

Mindful therefore of his old friendship with Otto, since in the days of his youth he had lived most honourably with Otto’s father, Uladislaus, Duke Boleslaus invited him by letter to this task, promising “all expenses, travelling companions, interpreters of the language, assistant priests, and whatever else might be necessary.” Otto did not long allow himself to be entreated, but requested the customary authorization from Pope Callistus II and easily obtained it.

### XXXIX.

Emperor Henry had summoned a solemn assembly at Bamberg for 17 May 1124; but it was brought forward to April, as is evident from the emperor’s privilege for the monastery of Scheyern [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Monumenta Boica*, vol. X, p. 449.]:

> These things were enacted in the year of the Lord 1124, indiction XIII [Note: [Col. 1293D] Vol. II.], at the court of Bamberg, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April].

Here the Saxon Annalist and the chronicler of Ursberg record of Otto’s generosity the same things which they had already noted under 1113, at the first Bamberg assembly. They then add:

> Once the matters of that assembly had been settled, Otto announced to the august emperor and to all the princes that he had been summoned by very many letters and messengers from Boleslaus, duke of Poland; moreover, that he had been sent, with the permission and blessing of Pope Callistus, to the Pomeranian people, whom the same duke had lately subdued as his neighbours and driven to seek refuge in Christianity. The whole Church there assembled consented; the court also consented, praying success for his pious undertaking. Only the sons of the Church of Bamberg reluctantly left their most beloved father, following him with many tears as though escorting a funeral.

### XL.

[Col. 1293C] Otto’s preparations for this sacred mission might seem contrary to the Gospel, had not the best intention and a happier outcome approved them. Sefridus, his companion on the journey, describes them as follows:

> Otto had heard that the land of the Pomeranians was wealthy; that it had absolutely no poor or beggars, but despised them vehemently; and that, long before, it had scorned certain servants of God who preached but were poor and of slender means, as though they were carrying out the office of preaching not for human salvation but to relieve their own need. On this point Ebbo should be consulted, concerning a certain Bishop Bernard expelled by the Pomeranians because of his mean attire. Otto therefore carefully arranged that he should appear among them not merely free from need, but wealthy: so that they might see that he did not seek their riches for himself, but rather sought to win them for God. Accordingly, having taken suitable clerics and supplied them abundantly for the journey, he had missals and other books, chalices with priestly vestments, and every other implement of the altar carried with him through provident generosity—things which he knew could not suddenly be found among a pagan people—lest the faithful husbandman seem to go out into his lord’s field without tools. The simple and prudent evangelist also brought garments, precious cloths, and other gifts suitable for nobles and rich persons upon the road of the Gospel, lest he seem to preach to the pagans because of poverty [Col. 1294A], but rather to contribute what was his to his new planting than to desire what was theirs.

### XLI.

Therefore, scarcely—or perhaps not even fully—having concluded the aforesaid assembly, “when all things necessary for departure had been prepared, on the day after the feast of St George the Martyr, then observed on 24 April, he bade farewell to his clergy and people. As though he were sanctifying his journey by this work, he consecrated two churches, one at Luchenberge and the other at Voliendrere. Then, after crossing the Bohemian Forest, he came to the Cluniac monastery of Cladrim, where he was honourably received and dedicated the church in honour of St Nicholas.”

This is the monastery of Kladran or Cladrubium in the district of Pilsen, then occupied by monks from Zwiefalten.

“Leaving Cladrim, he came to Prague; thence to the church at Sacischam [Col. 1294B], situated on the bank of the river Elbe”—Sacza is a collegiate church—“and to the castle of the duke of Bohemia, called Mileciam. There he was received by the duke himself and honoured with gifts.”

Ebbo says that this already occurred at Prague and calls the duke of Bohemia Ladislaus. By the castle of Mileciam, Father Gelasius Dobner understands the ancient fortress Miletium in the district of Hradischt [Note: [Col. 1293D] Hager’s *Annals*, Part VI, p. 173.], while he entirely ignores Burda.

“From there, through another castle of his”—that is, of the duke of Bohemia—“named Burda, to the city of the duke of Poland called Nemetia [Note: [Col. 1294D] Nimpsch in Silesia.]; and from there, through three Polish bishoprics, namely Breslau [Note: [Col. 1294D] Bresslau.], Kalisz [Note: [Col. 1294D] Kalisch.], and Poznań, as far as the archbishopric of Gniezno, we were conducted with joy and peace.” Thus writes the companion of the journey.

### XLII.

[Col. 1294C] Sefridus then gives a fuller account of Otto’s and his companions’ journey into Pomerania. At Gniezno they were solemnly received by Duke Boleslaus and the nobles of Poland, hospitably entertained for seven days, and supplied by the duke, besides other provisions for the journey, with interpreters, three chaplains, and the centurion Paulitius. They then began their journey toward Pomerania.

Forewarned of their arrival, Duke Uratislaus—whom the writer calls Worcizlaus—met them at his frontier. Having graciously received them, he gave them guides and attendants from among his own men. They crossed the river, entered Pomerania, and directed their journey to the fortress of Pirissa or Piritsea. After some delay had been imposed upon them there, they instructed the people in the faith of Christ with great fruit. During the said three-day fast, after a stay of twenty days among them [Col. 1294D], they baptized nearly seven thousand persons. The church at Pirissa having thus been established and ordered, they arrived, escorted by envoys, at the duke’s city of Camin on the Nativity of St John the Baptist, 1124.

### XLIII.

With the support of the duchess, Otto and his companions brought a great multitude of people at Camin to the faith through his preaching, and washed them in the sacred font together with the duke and his wife. He also persuaded the duke to dismiss all his concubines; many others followed this example.

> A basilica was also built there; the altar and sanctuary were consecrated; and estates and an endowment for the priest’s support were bestowed upon it by the duke. The most generous father, as he did for all churches in that land, gave it books, priestly vestments, a silver chalice with the other implements, and appointed to that church one of his own priests, able to instruct the people.

### XLIV.

After Otto had remained at Camin for nearly fifty days, he and his companions crossed by ship to Wollin or Julin. The duke added envoys and guides, to bring them safely and without disturbance into that city. Entering the city at night, he spent the night in the duke’s residence. The next day, however, a crowd of citizens assembled, and he was compelled to leave the city again, not without danger to his life.

[Col. 1295B] Yet he encountered graver danger in his flight. A barbarian struck him with a club and threw him from a bridge into the mud; and his companions, while protecting the bishop, were themselves severely beaten with clubs. “As we went away across the lake, having broken down the bridge behind us lest they should again attack us, we rested by lying in a field among threshing-floors and granary sites.” Thus writes Sefridus, the saint’s inseparable companion on this expedition. He also testifies that Otto here complained that his companions had robbed him of the palm of martyrdom.

When they had stayed for fifteen days beside the lake, the people of Julin became somewhat gentler and began to visit the bishop out of respect. He courteously urged them to embrace the faith of Christ, also setting before them the fear of the duke of the Poles. At last they promised that they would follow the example of the people of Stettin:

> For they called that city, the most ancient and noble in Pomerania, the mother of cities; and they said it would be quite unjust if they admitted any observance of the new religion before it had first been confirmed by that city’s authority.

### XLV.

Otto therefore set out by ship with his companions for Stettin. Led into the city at night by Paulitius, he was lodged in the duke’s residence. On the following day the Polish envoys freely explained to the leading men the purpose of the bishop’s coming; but they stubbornly refused to abandon their ancestral laws for the sake of the Gospel. Their hope thus disappointed, they remained there without result for more than two months.

At last they decided to send envoys to the duke of the Poles to ask whether they should remain longer in barren ground [Col. 1295D], or return. The people of Stettin added envoys of their own, promising “that if they could obtain from the duke a firm and perpetual peace, and a reduction of tribute—these terms being confirmed in writing before their own envoys and ours—they would voluntarily submit to Christian laws.” These events took place in 1124.

Meanwhile Otto and his companions at Stettin preached the true faith twice a week in the public square, the cross borne before them and themselves adorned in priestly vesture, while a great crowd of rustic people assembled. Nor was this without fruit:

> For two very handsome youths [Col. 1296A], sons of a certain nobleman of the city, began to visit our house, show themselves friendly toward us, and gradually inquire about our God and our faith.

Delighted by their disposition, Otto baptized them after they had been sufficiently instructed in the faith. When their mother, herself born of Christian parents, learned this, she came running in joy. The bishop gave her a precious cloak of furs, and she also brought her dependants and household servants to the faith of Christ. These boy neophytes, dressed in elegant garments given them by the bishop, drew even their companions to holy Otto and to the faith; they received baptism in bands.

> Thus the grey-haired wisdom of fathers allowed itself to be instructed by boys and youths; and as the flame of faith gradually advanced, the whole city grew warm. No longer did only a few come secretly to the faith: publicly [Col. 1296B], and many together, they came every day.

There remained the father of the two boys, who was then absent from home. He was deeply troubled by this change, but moved by the prayers of his household and by the example of his neighbours, he too changed his mind.

### XLVI.

Meanwhile the envoys returned from Poland with letters from Duke Boleslaus. The writer of the Life quotes them in Henry Canisius [Note: [Col. 1295D] Basnage edition, vol. III, part II, p. 69.] as follows:

> Boleslaus, duke of the Poles by the favouring mercy of almighty God, enemy of all pagans, grants firm peace and lasting friendship to the Pomeranian nation and to the people of Stettin if they keep the promised pledges of faith; but slaughter, fire, and perpetual enmity to those who do not keep them. If I sought occasions against you, my anger could justly arise because I see you, as though transgressors against your pledged faith, turning back, and because you have not received as you ought “my lord and father, Bishop Otto, most worthy of every honour and reverence, eminent in life and reputation among every people and nation, sent by the true God and by our ministry for your salvation”; nor have you hitherto obeyed his teaching in the fear of God.

All these things were grounds for your accusation. But representatives both yours and mine—honourable and prudent men—interceded for you, “and above all the bishop himself who is dwelling among you, your evangelist and apostle.” Judging it fitting to accede to their counsel and petition, I have decided to lighten the burden of servitude and tribute “so that you may take up Christ’s yoke more cheerfully” in this manner. Let the whole land of the Pomeranians pay to the dukes [Col. 1296D] of Poland, whoever they may be, only three hundred marks of silver of public weight each year. If war threatens him, they shall aid him thus: nine householders shall fully provide the tenth man for the expedition with arms and expenses, and shall meanwhile faithfully provide for that same household at home.

If you observe these things and “agree to the Christian faith, you shall obtain our peace through the offering of peace and of the hand, and the joy of eternal life; and in all your needs you shall always experience the protection and assistance of the Poles as allies and friends.”

### XLVII.

When these letters had been read in a public assembly, great joy arose among the people [Col. 1297A], who eagerly offered themselves to be instructed in the faith by the bishop. Thinking this zeal should be used, Otto addressed a public speech to the people of Stettin, calling them to the faith and encouraging them so greatly that, while he and his priests and clerics tore down the city’s temples and idols, the citizens themselves also contributed their labour to demolishing them.

After these things had been done, he instructed them in the faith and baptized a vast number.

> Having ordered there all things believed useful for a newly founded church, having built with diligent care a basilica in the middle of the public square at Stettin, and having supplied everything required for priestly ministry, he ensured, as he did everywhere, that a priest should be installed to preside over the people.

Afterwards he departed for the people of Grätz and Lubin on the frontier. When they too had embraced the faith, he built an altar and appointed priests there; then, with a favourable wind, he returned with his companions by the river Oder to the shores of Julin.

### XLVIII.

In that city, whose inhabitants had learned better things from the example of the people of Stettin, they were received joyfully and in a short time won nearly the whole city and province for God.

> Since this city lies in the middle of Pomerania, and since the citizens of Julin are strong and stiff-necked, Duke Vrotizlaus and the princes of the land judged that it should be the seat of a bishopric: so that the harsh people might be softened by the continuing presence of a teacher and not return to their former errors; and so that chrism and the other things to be received from the bishop could more easily be conveyed from the centre to every boundary of the land. [Col. 1297C] Therefore Otto ordered two basilicas to be built there and consecrated only the altars and sanctuaries, hastening elsewhere.

For, as Sefridus subsequently writes, because of haste the bishop could not then establish the bishopric of Pomerania as he wished; trusting the duke’s judgment, he left its establishment to him when he had leisure. The duke raised one of his own chaplains, named Adalbert—whom he had assigned from his own household to assist the bishop together with two other priests—to the honour of the episcopate among that people.

This is also evident from Innocent’s bull of 1140 [Note: [Col. 1297D] Dreger, *Codex diplomaticus Pomeraniae*, p. 1.] addressed to this same Albert, bishop of the Pomeranians:

> We decree that the episcopal see shall be held in perpetuity in the city of Wollin, in the church of Blessed Albert.

Adelbert himself calls himself the first apostle of the Pomeranians in a charter issued in 1153 [Note: [Col. 1298D] Same work, p. 3.]:

> From the time when the Pomeranian people first received Christ’s faith and baptism through the devout zeal of Lord Boleslaus, glorious duke of the Poles, and the preaching of the venerable Otto, bishop of Bamberg, under their ruler Wartizlaus, the common election of these princes and the consecration of Pope Innocent appointed me, though unworthy, as first bishop over Pomerania, under the attested confirmation of the Apostolic See.

### XLIX.

Leaving Wollin or Julin, the new apostles built at Dordona a notable basilica in honour of the Holy Cross. Having baptized its inhabitants, they came to Colobrega [Col. 1298A], or Colberg, situated on the seacoast. There the work of conversion advanced somewhat more slowly, because most of the citizens of this maritime city were absent on business and trade, while the rest believed that no alteration in religion should be made in their absence. Nevertheless, moved by Otto’s repeated exhortations, they too accepted baptism and were incorporated into the Church; an altar and sanctuary were likewise founded there.

Having gone on a day’s journey from there to the fortress of Belgradia or Belegardia, they set there the limit of their sacred expedition by converting that place also.

So that Otto might return to his Church of Bamberg at Eastertide in 1125, before departing from Pomerania he wished to visit each place again on his return, in order that he might supply or complete by renewed care anything that might have been lacking in the first effort [Col. 1298B]. To his great joy, he found that the churches which he had first left raw and unfinished had already been completed through the work of the priests he had appointed everywhere. He consecrated them and conferred the sacrament of confirmation upon the recently converted faithful. It also gave him great consolation that he could add to the others by the saving water many more persons who had been absent abroad at the time of his first arrival.

### L.

Before bidding farewell to his neophytes, he left them certain written rules concerning discipline and morals. Ursberg testifies to this under 1125, and we insert them here because they provide an excellent understanding of the Church’s discipline and the people’s customs at this time. Sefridus also reports some of them.

[Col. 1298C] Thus, for the Pomeranians “whom he converted and baptized, Otto built and consecrated churches, and taught them to observe the following according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers: namely, that on the sixth day they should abstain from meat and milk, according to the practice of other Christians.” Thus dairy foods as well as meat were then forbidden on days of abstinence; Saturday was not yet counted among them.

“On Sunday let them refrain from every evil work, come to church to hear the divine office, and there diligently devote themselves to prayer.” Here “evil work” may mean both prohibited servile labour and any sinful act, at least any public one.

“Let them observe with every diligence the festivals of the saints, with vigils, or as shall be prescribed to them.” [Col. 1298D] Sefridus enumerates in the Life the feasts they were to observe: the Incarnation, Nativity, Circumcision, Epiphany, Presentation, Baptism, Transfiguration, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, the Coming of the Holy Spirit, and the vigils and feast-days of the apostles, other martyrs, and saints.

“Let them endeavour to observe most diligently the most holy Lent with fasting, vigils, almsgiving, and prayer.” Sefridus adds the Ember Days to these observances.

What follows, omitted by Sefridus, concerns the baptismal rites then customary. Let them bring their children to baptism on the holy Saturday of Easter and Pentecost, with candles, the garment called the white robe, and accompanying godparents; and, clothed in the garment of innocence, let them bring them daily to church until the octave day of that same Saturday, and endeavour to attend the celebration of the divine office.

“He also strictly forbade them to kill their daughters, an abomination that was especially prevalent among them.” Let them not hold their own sons or daughters at baptism, but seek godparents for them; and let them show godparents the faithfulness and friendship owed to natural parents as well. “He also forbade anyone to take his comother as wife, or his own blood-relative within the sixth and seventh degree.” These are degrees of carnal and spiritual kinship. “Let each person be content with one wife.”

[Col. 1299B] The following concerns pagan Pomeranian customs:

> Let them not bury Christian dead among pagans in woods or fields, but in cemeteries, as is the custom of all Christians. Let them not set stakes at their graves. Let them cast off every pagan rite and depravity; let them not build houses for idols; let them not consult female diviners; let them not practise divination.

He adds certain practices taken from the custom of the primitive Church, but at that time impressed upon the Pomeranians temporarily for the same purpose for which they were imposed upon peoples newly converted through the apostles. Indeed, the apostolic decree of the Council of Jerusalem had not yet wholly fallen into disuse even in the twelfth century. For he continues:

> Let them eat nothing unclean: neither carrion, nor what has been strangled, nor food sacrificed to idols, nor the blood of animals. Let them not associate with pagans, nor take food or drink with them or from their vessels, lest in all these matters they resume pagan custom.

[Col. 1299C] “He also enjoined them, while they were healthy, to come to the priests of the Church in order to confess their sins; but in sickness, to summon priests to themselves, confess their sins, and receive the body of the Lord. He further ordained that they should do penance for perjuries, adulteries, murders, and other criminal offences according to the ordinances of the canons, and should be obedient in every Christian religious practice and observance.” These rules testify to the penitential discipline still customary in the Church at that time.

Finally, “let women after childbirth come to church and receive the priest’s blessing, according to custom.” Ursberg then enumerates the names of the cities in which Otto preached, though they are incorrectly rendered in the printed editions: Piriz, Stetin, Vulingumen—that is, Wolin—Camin, Colberch, Belgrado, Lubingresch or Lubin, and Gresch or Gradiz.

### LI.

It is easy to see here that only the principal points of ecclesiastical discipline were written for the Pomeranians, not the dogmatic teaching itself, which they could undoubtedly read in books left to them by Otto, nor the preceding matters. At his farewell he also first commended to them orally, then in a brief written text, the teaching concerning the sacraments. Sefridus reports it, and Harzheim reproduces it from him [Note: [Col. 1299D] *Councils of Germany*, vol. III, p. 302.]; from it we have excerpted the more noteworthy portions.

> As I am about to depart from you, I hand over to you what has been handed down to us by the Lord: the pledge of holy faith between you and God—namely, the seven sacraments of the Church, like seven signifying gifts of the Holy Spirit. By attending to these, your Church may be able not to fail amid the labours and struggle of this life, but to advance and restore its deficiencies. Therefore see to it and hold them fast, so that you may know how diligently to enumerate what we hand over to you as we depart from you.

He then enumerates the sacraments in a somewhat different order: baptism, which he directs should be conferred “at the appropriate time, namely, on the holy Saturday of Easter and Pentecost.” Concerning confirmation, or the anointing with chrism on the forehead, he warns that it should “not [Col. 1300B] be deferred until old age,” “as some suppose,” but received “in the vigour of youth itself, because that age is more subject to temptations.”

Third, he places the anointing of the sick, which every Christian ought to desire and receive in the struggle of death.
