Fourth, he calls the Eucharist a sacrament, and directs that Masses be celebrated frequently for its reception. “Yet,” he adds, “you yourselves ought three or four times a year, if it cannot be done more often, both to make confession and to communicate in the sacrament itself.”

Of the fifth, penance, he gives no other special instruction. “These five sacraments are, as it were, general and necessary for every Christian.” The other two, however, are particular, instituted only for a certain state of life and open to anyone: namely, sixth, marriage; and seventh, holy orders.

Above all, he forbids the plurality of wives customary among this people:

> Therefore, if anyone among you has had several wives before baptism, let him now choose one of them, the one who pleases him most; dismiss the others, and possess this one alone according to Christian rite.

For the sacrament of orders, those “more suitable in morals and learning are to be invited rather than compelled.” He consequently exhorts them to give some of their children to clerical life, “having first carefully instructed them in the liberal studies,” so that they themselves, like other peoples, might have clergy and priests from their own language who know Latin.

He finally concludes his discourse thus:

> Therefore keep and reverence these same sacraments diligently, with every honour and reverence. Teach them to your children, that they may retain them by memory and carefully observe them through all generations. Behold, you have a church; you have a priest who knows how to instruct you more fully in all these matters and in whatever else is necessary for you. Therefore hear him as you hear me, honouring and loving him and doing whatever he tells you. And now I go, soon to return to you again. Farewell in the Lord, beloved ones.

LII. Therefore Otto, torn away only with difficulty and not without tears from his beloved neophytes, returned to Poland while it was still February of the year 1125. He was received with great joy by Duke Boleslaus [Col. 1301A], magnificently endowed, and escorted with a splendid retinue into Bohemia. There he found Duke Vladislaus almost at the point of death, and persuaded him to make peace with his brother Sobieslaus, then an exile and shortly afterward his successor. This one act of Otto alone places his return in the year 1125 beyond all doubt; for Vladislaus died shortly afterward, on 12 April of that year. But Otto, impatient of every delay, hastened to Bamberg, entering his diocese by way of the monastery of Kladruby, where, while passing through in the preceding year, he had dedicated a church.

Ebbo, his second biographer, briefly describes this return: having at last “left the boundaries of his pilgrimage,” he came to the monastery of “Michilvet” on Tuesday of Holy Week, that is, 24 March, where [Col. 1301B], “many of the clergy and people of Bamberg coming to meet him, he celebrated the Lord’s Supper.” On that occasion, it appears, he confirmed for that monastery the donation of Charles of Smalenohe, secured by the obligation of a ban, and fortified it with the impression of his seal, “on the very day on which he personally committed that man’s body to burial there,” as is clear from its archive [Note: [Col. 1301D] Documentary appendix, no. LXXXI.].

Leaving there, “on Holy Saturday of Easter he visited Turstatt,” or Teuerstatt, the church of St James in the suburb of Bamberg, “but deferred entering the city on that day. Thus, on the first morning of the Lord’s Resurrection” [Note: [Col. 1301D] 29 March 1125.], “the Church of Bamberg received him with a twofold joy, made glorious both by the delight of the Paschal feast and by the arrival of pious Otto. The entire city likewise assembled to receive the new apostle of our age.” — “Thus, surrounded by an innumerable [Col. 1301C] throng, he proceeded to the church; to them he poured forth the word of God with his customary sweetness, announcing that Pomerania had been subjected to the laws of Christ and kindling every heart to contemplate the grace of divine mercy.”

Yet amid such great acclamations of joy the pious shepherd did not lack sorrowful compassion for the fire which the city of Bamberg had suffered in his absence, on 28 August 1124, when the feast of St Hermes the Martyr was being celebrated, “a place which had been nobly distinguished at its beginning by its founder, Blessed Henry, with that saint’s precious body.”

LIII. Sefrid briefly recounts what the holy bishop did after his return to his diocese. “He hastened as quickly as possible to complete all the precincts of monasteries and churches which he had previously begun, [Col. 1301D] lest he should later grieve that anything neglected in them had been subtracted from his reward.”

Relevant here is Otto’s charter, “given and confirmed in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, indiction XIV, [Note: [Col. 1301D] Book IV.] on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [21 May], Tuesday, in the synod of Bamberg, in the presence of clergy and people” [Note: [Col. 1301D] Ludwig, *Scriptors of Bamberg*, p. 1122.]. In it Otto declares that he gave “the cell of St Faith,” built by himself on the western side of Mount St Michael, with all its appurtenances, to the monastery of St Michael, on condition that seven brothers [Col. 1302A] and two lay brothers from that same monastery should live there, “keeping daily watch in that cell concerning divine service and attending to their own necessities both outside and within.”

Abbot Hermann also assigned them thirty jugera around the Cell for making gardens and orchards; likewise the bishop assigned various estates together with “the hospital of St Gertrude” on the other side of the river. He entrusted their advocacies to various advocates: “Count Gebehard of Sulzbach, Count Bertolf of Blassenberg, Count Boto of Giech, Count Poppo, Hermann of Bamberg, Count Rapoto,” and others, on this condition: “that they administer them in person, without sub-advocates, and shall in no way hold a court with the tenants except in cases of assault, theft, or violation of a field boundary, or indeed if they are summoned [Note: [Col. 1301D] Perhaps: “are summoned.”] by the provost or prior. Each peasant is to work five days in the year for his advocate.” Among the subscribers are “Eberhard the provost and Egilbert the dean.”

When Emperor Henry V died on 23 May 1125 and was buried at Speyer, Adalbert of Mainz and other bishops and princes sent letters to our Otto inviting him to a court to be held at Mainz on the feast of Blessed Bartholomew for the election of a new king [Note: [Col. 1302D] Documentary appendix, no. LXXXII.]. Yet I do not find that he was present at the election of King Lothair on 30 August. There is also another letter of the same Archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1302D] Harzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. III, p. 298.], inviting Otto to a synod for the appointment of a successor after the death of Roger, bishop of Würzburg. Elsewhere we have shown that this belongs to the year 1125 [Note: [Col. 1302D] *Bishops of Würzburg*, p. 61.]; nevertheless, he does not seem [Col. 1302C] to have appeared there either.

To what year, moreover, the letter of Otto, bishop of Halberstadt, to our Otto belongs [Note: [Col. 1302D] Ludwig, *Writers*, p. 824.], in which he laments his wretched condition and implores his assistance, I should not easily determine. It was sent after a recent campaign in which he had laboured more diligently than the rest for the honour of the kingdom and the Church. I think this should be understood of King Lothair’s disastrous expedition against Sobieslaus, duke of Bohemia, undertaken in February 1126, in which the Saxons participated in great numbers, as the Saxon Annalist and the Hildesheim annals report. This letter therefore seems to be assigned to the same year; its conclusion also persuades one of this:

“Therefore we ask that you direct your letters to the metropolitan and urge him, for your sake, [Col. 1302D] to be diligent in our cause. We also ask that, wherever a council is summoned for examining this matter, you will be willing to be present.”

Thus no synod concerning this matter had yet been held; it was first decided at Mainz in 1129, after Otto had already returned from Pomerania for the second time.

LIV. Until now anxious concern had possessed our Otto for his newly planted community in Pomerania. It was all the more necessary because he had heard that [Col. 1303A] the people of Stettin and Julin, at the urging of their priests, had returned to their ancestral superstitions, worshipping Christ and idols alike, as Ebbo relates at length. He therefore judged a second journey to Pomerania necessary. Sefrid writes of it as follows:

“After this Otto, detained at home for three years, then in the fourth year, although held back by many affairs at home, nevertheless burning with love for his new colony, put everything else aside and undertook to revisit it.”

This has raised doubt among writers as to the year in which this second Pomeranian journey was undertaken, most agreeing on 1128. We judge 1127 to be preferable, led partly by reasons occurring in the narrative itself and partly by those to be given later. Thus we understand Sefrid’s three years only from the beginning—that is, from the return of 29 April 1125 until 31 March 1127. As for the four years, we leave scholars the better way of reconciling the authors by reckoning from the beginning of the first journey, 25 April 1124.

“Therefore the bishop chosen by God,” writes Ebbo, “hearing that the enemy had sown weeds over the good seed, sought the blessing of Pope Honorius II and the most serene King Lothair, and resolved again to enter the lands of the barbarians. Having therefore prepared the necessities for the journey and taken with him many ministers and fellow-workers, on the most holy Thursday of the Lord’s Supper [Note: [Col. 1303D] That year, 31 March.], after the making of chrism and the solemnities of the masses had devoutly been performed, fasting and wearing the sandals in which he had stood at the altar, he set out upon his preaching journey under the uplifted banner of the cross.”

I do not wish here to recount the further events which they mention [Col. 1303C] on this journey. This time, in order not again to trouble the dukes of Bohemia and Poland, he arranged his route through Saxony and the March of Brandenburg. At Halle he loaded vessels with provisions and, travelling down the river Elbe into the Havel, was brought to the shores of Luticia. There he loaded all his effects upon forty wagons and transported them to Timina, now Demmin, a city of Pomerania. There he found Duke Wartislaw returning from a campaign against the Lutici. Received by him in their old friendship, he sent his goods, placed on a vessel, ahead by a three-day journey to Uznoim, now Usedom, while he himself followed the duke there on foot.

LV. Meanwhile, in that place the priests whom Otto had left behind on his first visit had already converted a great part of the people [Col. 1303D]. At the holy bishop’s urging, the duke summoned the leading men of the whole region to a general assembly at Uznoim for the approaching Pentecost, 22 May. Taking the bishop there with him, he persuaded almost all of them in an eloquent speech to receive his preaching and the faith; they therefore listened calmly to the bishop as he concluded his address.

Sefrid thus describes the happy outcome of this assembly:

“Some, already Christians long ago but again defiled by the error of paganism, softened by the present discourse into compunction and deep contrition of heart, he reconciled to the Church through the laying on of hands, to the great profit of those who saw it. Others, eagerly offering themselves, he catechized [Col. 1304A] and baptized after instructing them as time allowed. Throughout that whole week he devoted himself to teaching and sacred works with immense joy, so that the presence of the Holy Spirit was most certainly manifestly there. Accordingly, this council was not dissolved until the princes themselves and all who had come with them had received the sacraments of baptism.”

The bishop remained there with the duke and sent ahead two priests, Udalric and Albinus, to Hologast, or Wolgast, to prepare the way for the Gospel. Otto had wished already in his first preaching mission to penetrate there, as also into the three other cities still remaining, with their villages and islands: Uznoim, Gozgangia, and Timina. When the said priests came to Wolgast, they were indeed kindly received by the prefect’s wife [Col. 1304B], but were soon sought for death by the inhabitants. Nor would they have escaped it, unless the duke, arriving with the bishop, had quieted the disturbance and obtained for him leave to speak publicly.

Then a remarkable change of minds took place. For “he remained in that place disputing and persuading concerning the kingdom of God until the whole people, receiving the sacraments of faith, destroyed their shrines and prepared the sanctuary of a church with an altar. Consecrating it, the bishop ordained John as their priest and instructed him to advance the remaining construction of the basilica after his departure.”

LVI. Leaving Wolgast, Otto came without Duke Wartislaw to Gozgangia, or Gozgavia, then a town with a castle, now a village on the river Peene called Gützkow. The inhabitants, especially through the efforts of Mizlai, lord of the place [Col. 1304C], whom he had recently baptized at Usedom, gave a ready hearing; but they feared for their shrine, which they had recently built on a notable scale at great expense. At length persuaded by the bishop, they themselves demolished the temple and its images with their own hands, and were baptized shortly afterward. To console them for the shrine they had lost, he built a basilica there and, after it had been partly completed, dedicated it with solemn rite.

Meanwhile great alarm arose among the people because Duke Boleslaus of Poland was threatening the borders of Pomerania with a hostile army, intending sternly to punish their perfidy and apostasy. Their sole refuge was the holy bishop. At their request, taking clergy and delegates of the people with him, he went to meet the duke and at length, though with difficulty, persuaded him to return home after the former covenants had been renewed [Col. 1304D] and peace restored. This all the more strengthened them in the faith; and the people of Stettin and Julin were encouraged to embrace once again the faith which they had partly rejected and partly corrupted with pagan superstitions.

Otto therefore went to them and, although not without great danger to his life, immense labour, several miracles, and the energetic efforts among his fellow-citizens of Witsac, a wealthy citizen who had been captured by the Danes and wondrously delivered through Otto, he first brought the people of Stettin, and then those of Julin also, back to the religion they had abjured. He also caused the church of St Adalbert, half demolished by them, to be repaired at his own expense.

[Col. 1305A] The time when these events occurred is clear from Sefrid’s account of a peasant divinely punished while he and his wife were reaping crops in a field on the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary, which fell on a Monday. Warned by a passing priest of Otto to stop and honour the feast, he replied:

“Yesterday we were not permitted to work because of Sunday, and must we again be idle today? What sort of teaching is this, which commands people to refrain from necessary good works? When then shall we see our crops gathered?”

This datum alone fixes the date of this second Pomeranian expedition: namely, the year 1127, when the feast of the Assumption fell on a Monday.

LVII. Having accomplished these things in Pomerania for the faith, he also resolved to go on to the Rutheri, or Rugians. But when he learned that they lay under the jurisdiction of the archbishop of the Danes [Col. 1305B], he did not wish to thrust himself into another’s harvest. He therefore prepared to return home, summoned by threats as well as letters. For, as Ebbo writes, “King Lothair and the other princes, distressed by the long absence of the blessed man, since at that time he was accustomed beyond others to ennoble the kingdom by his counsels and pious arts, command him, both ordering and requesting, to hasten his departure and refresh the Church of Bamberg by his longed-for return.”

Indeed, the king had sworn that he would bring Otto’s affairs under his own control unless he returned immediately [Note: [Col. 1305D] See Goldast, *Imperial Constitutions*, vol. I, p. 260.]. To these threats were added the letters of Abbot Wigand of Tharisi [Note: [Col. 1305D] Documentary appendix, no. LXXXV.], urgently exhorting him to return, as necessary also to prevent losses to his Church [Col. 1305C]. For this reason Wigand had gone as far as Saxony to meet him about the feast of St Maurice.

Thus, unable “to resist these embassies,” the apostle of the Pomeranians, “having visited the faithful around him and confirmed them in the faith, commended them to Christ in whom they had believed and set out with his companions. Having completed the journey and come into Poland, Duke Boleslaus, the faithful guardian of their old friendship, received him with his customary kindness and listened with such eagerness to his honeyed teaching that, after eight days had passed, he scarcely granted the beloved father leave to depart. At last, when the long labour of this pilgrimage had been completed, on the vigil of St Thomas the Apostle, Otto, bishop worthy of God and apostle of the Pomeranians, gladdened his Church by his welcome arrival. All the people of both sexes and orders ran together in one place; with the utmost rejoicing and spiritual joy the father was received by his children.”

This second sacred expedition lasted from 31 March until 20 December 1127, to which year, as we have seen, it should rather be assigned than to the following year, when he was generally at home.

LVIII. From the above-cited letter of Abbot Wigand to Otto it is useful to report further details concerning the condition of Germany and especially of the diocese of Bamberg. “We do not wish you to be ignorant,” he writes, “that from the time you departed [Col. 1306A] a day of distress and tribulation continually threatened us. For the tyrant Conrad, remaining almost the entire year in the castle of Nuremberg, devastated the nearby lands of the bishopric; he took part of the grain from your revenues, ordained that tribute be paid to himself, and twice captured the steward of Rustall, stripping him of all his goods. Moreover, he is said to have attempted by crafty contrivance to seize the city of Bamberg; but, thanks be to God, his wickedness did not prevail. Conrad the custos and I, anxious over the stewardship entrusted to us, appointed garrisons and guards with your other faithful men, paid the soldiers’ wages as necessary, and diligently managed all the rest that you had entrusted to us.”

This Conrad was the brother of Frederick, duke of Swabia of the house of Hohenstaufen [Col. 1306B]. Believing that, through his mother Agnes, sister of Emperor Henry V, he had a nearer right to the kingdom, he rebelled against King Lothair in 1127 and, supported by certain princes favourable to him, assumed the royal title. He was unsuccessfully besieged by the king in Nuremberg Castle after Pentecost and was finally struck with anathema by three archbishops at the assembly of Würzburg on Christmas Day. Adalbert of Mainz notified Otto, who had already returned by then, of this sentence in a letter [Note: [Col. 1306D] Harzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. III, p. 305.].

But I cannot easily say to what the following part of the said letter refers: “There is a great war between Hermann and Frederick; various ambushes are laid on both sides, robberies are repaid with robberies and fires with fires. Amid these events, the village lying beneath Boto’s Stone, together with its church [Col. 1306C], was burned. One night Frederick secretly entered the fortification of Niestein with his soldiers and began to act boldly. But those in the castle, hurling javelins and stones, killed one of his men and wounded several; thus, his enterprise failing, he barely escaped with all his followers. Furthermore, many evils rage throughout the whole province; everything is devastated by robberies and fires.”

LIX. To the year 1128 belong the letters of Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg, to Bishop Otto and the canons of Bamberg concerning their dean, elected patriarch of Aquileia; we shall deal with these below under Egilbert. In the same year King Lothair celebrated the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin at Bamberg, where he confirmed by a most ample privilege the village of Schambach [Col. 1306D], assigned by Emperor St Henry with tithes and possessions to this Church and restored by himself. The document is dated the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September [18 August], indiction VI, the third year of his reign, at Bamberg.

After the death of Pope Honorius II in 1130, a schism arose in the election of his successor. Innocent II therefore sent legates to the king in Germany. The king, on that account, summoned a council at Würzburg in October. The papal legates invited Otto to it in these words:

“Among the princes, we believed that your brotherhood had hastened first, or among the first, to the court for the service of the Church [Col. 1307A], since our mother, the Roman Church, loved you with a certain prerogative among the other bishops of the German kingdom and, treating you as a special son, blessed you with her own hands. We therefore ask your affection, and in the faith and devotion which you owe your mother, the Roman Church, command you to set aside every occasion and excuse and come to us as quickly as possible. In the cause of the Church, assist us as a faithful and catholic man; receive and obey the legation of the lord pope with his letters, together with the other brethren.”

Yet Otto does not seem to have been present at least from the beginning, being hindered by illness, as appears from the letter of King Lothair himself to him [Note: [Col. 1307D] Documentary appendix, no. LXXXVIII.]:

“Because an urgent and most necessary matter of Church and kingdom must be dealt with at Würzburg [Col. 1307B] by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we grieve over your illness, which has delayed your coming to us, because we now especially need the discernment and counsel of your prudence for the work of Church and kingdom. Yet because power is made perfect in weakness, we admonish and most earnestly ask you, in the charity which you owe to the Church—for which, by God’s grace, you have always laboured devoutly—that, if you cannot come by any other conveyance, you hasten to us even by boat and make your welcome appearance at Würzburg, where your venerable fellow-brethren and fellow-bishops await your arrival with us. Farewell.”

A letter of Conrad of Salzburg to him is almost of the same tenor [Note: [Col. 1307D] Hansiz, *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 229.]:

“We wonder and are greatly grieved that you are not present, when in this matter no one could be more necessary to us. Therefore we earnestly admonish and ask your dignity, putting entirely aside every occasion or excuse, still to attempt to come, knowing that all the princes desire and await your presence.”

These matters sufficiently show how great was the authority and esteem enjoyed by this holy bishop, even among Germany’s highest princes, because of his prudence.

LX. In this same year, 1130, on the Nones of April [5 April], indiction VIII, the fifth year of his reign, Lothair, at Bamberg in the round chapel of St Andrew, issued a diploma by which he enclosed the village of Staffelstein in the Radenzgau with towers and walls. Endowing it with a market and specified privileges, he offered it through Count Reginbodo of Giech to the Church of Bamberg [Col. 1307D].

According to Hofmann, Bishop Otto began in the same year to enlarge the monastery of St Michael. He built a paradise [cloister or enclosed court] and a neighbouring lodging for those who came there on business. He added to these a chapel of the Blessed Virgin and oratories of St Bartholomew and St Oswald, richly adorned them all, equipped them with various sacred vestments, and chose the place for his burial.

LXI. An outstanding act of Otto in the year 1131 is recorded by the sole continuator of Cosmas of Prague [Col. 1308A], and is therefore worthy of insertion here among his other deeds. While Meinhard, bishop of Prague, was absent on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, he was accused before Sobieslaus, duke of Bohemia, of a conspiracy formed against him. Returning to Prague, Meinhard heard this and feared that he might be driven from his see by the machinations of his enemies. He therefore sought by letter counsel and help from Otto, whom, from the first Pomeranian journey, he regarded as a most devoted friend.

Otto granted what was asked and, in a letter to him [Note: [Col. 1307D] Eccard, *Corpus of Histories*, vol. II, p. 370.], advised him to endeavour to clear himself in his own Church, before the duke and princes of the land, of the accusations brought against him. Meinhard therefore offered himself to the duke as ready to undergo every judicial examination. By the duke’s command, two ecclesiastical men were sent to submit the decision of the case to Adalbert [Col. 1308B] of Mainz and Otto of Bamberg. After they had examined the case and the bishop’s innocence had been proved, the delegates were sent back to Bohemia, our Otto accompanying them.

“There, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October [28 September] in the year 1131, the bishop of Bamberg and the bishop of Olomouc, together with seven Bohemian abbots, in the presence of Duke Sobieslaus with people and clergy, cleared Meinhard, bishop of the Church of Prague, of every charge previously brought against him by laying down their stoles; namely, they declared that Bishop Meinhard had contemplated nothing hostile against Duke Sobieslaus.”

This laying down of stoles was in that age a solemn rite of ecclesiastical oath, by which the clergy declared themselves unworthy of the office of sacred orders and liable to be deprived of them if they did not speak the truth. I readily believe [Col. 1308C] that this honour was granted to Otto by Duke Sobieslaus chiefly because it was through Otto’s efforts that he had been reconciled to his brother Vladislaus, when Otto had arrived at Prague on his first return from Pomerania in 1125, as we have already shown above from the biographers. Although they do not mention this latter event, it is nevertheless beyond doubt because of the reliability of our writer [Note: [Col. 1307D] See Calles, *Ecclesiastical Annals of Germany*, vol. VI, pt. I, [Col. 1308D] p. 328; and Dobner, *Annals of Hájek*, vol. VI, p. 217 ff.].

LXII. In the following year, 1132, “the place called Lancheim,” as the biographer further relates, “was handed over to him and to his Church by three brothers—Hermann, Wolfram, and Gundeloch, ministerials of St George. He raised it to the rank of an abbey and dedicated it to the most blessed Virgin Mary, granting to that place estates which would serve the needs of the brethren [Col. 1308D] serving God there.” Otto’s successor Egilbert enumerated and confirmed these gifts in 1142 [Note: [Col. 1308D] Documentary appendix, no. XCVIII.].

In the same year, 1132, he founded another Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Eichstätt, called Heilsbronn, or “Fountain of Salvation.” Hocker reproduces the charter of foundation, issued at Bamberg in that year [Note: [Col. 1308D] Documentary appendix, no. LXXXIX.], from which we note the following. He purchased the estate of Heilsbronn from Count Adelbert, his brother Conrad, and their three sisters. Through Adalbero of Tagstetten he offered it to his Church of Bamberg [Col. 1309A]; there he built a monastery and church in honour of the Blessed Virgin and appointed an abbot. Through Wignand of Beerbach he granted to the abbot an estate purchased for a price near Adelsdorf, together with Witramsdorf, Erlehe, Oberendorf, Velsendorf, and Peccemannesdorf. He appointed for it no advocate other than the advocate of the Church of Bamberg. The witnesses were Adelbero of Tagstetten, Adelbert of Dachsbach, Frederick of Hergoldispach, and several others; among the canons was Egilbert the dean.

The year 1133 was distinguished by the dedication of another monastery, namely at Biburg in Bavaria and in the diocese of Regensburg. Hundius writes of it [Note: [Col. 1309D] *Metropolis of Salzburg*, vol. II, p. 138.]:

“In the year 1125 Conrad and Bertha of Biburg, by the counsel and assistance of St Otto, bishop of Bamberg, began to build from [Col. 1309B] their own patrimony a monastery for Benedictine men and women; and they completed it in the eighth year, that is, 1133. In that year also, on the day of Simon and Jude, Lord Otto, bishop of Bamberg, and Henry, bishop of Regensburg, consecrated the church of Biburg.”

Innocent II approved this foundation and confirmed it by diploma. “Given,” that is, on 7 January 1139 [Note: [Col. 1309D] Same work, p. 141.], where he testifies that religious life according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict had been established there “through the zeal and industry of Otto, bishop of Bamberg”; and that “whatever possessions, whatever goods, our same brother Bishop Otto, with the consent of the brethren of Bamberg, bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Mary of Biburg, shall remain inviolate.”

In a bull of Alexander III of 1177 it is decreed that the abbot shall choose an advocate “with the counsel and assistance of the bishop of Bamberg,” and remove one who is useless, with the support of “the bishop of Bamberg by reason of the estate,” and of the bishop of Regensburg by reason of the diocese. The same occurs in the diploma of Emperor Frederick I of 1177; hence it is clear that this monastery was a Bamberg fief.

LXIII. In 1135, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [17 March], Emperor Lothair held a famous assembly at Bamberg, where Frederick, duke of Swabia, was reconciled to him [Note: [Col. 1309D] Saxon Annalist, for this year.]. There the emperor issued a diploma for the monastery of Mallersdorf, also subscribed by Otto of Bamberg. It is read in the *Monumenta Boica* [Note: [Col. 1309D] Vol. XV, p. 266; cf. p. 263.], as is also his confirmation of the said foundation in 1129.

The biographers include the Bavarian monastery of Mallersdorf among those founded or restored by St Otto [Col. 1309D], though I do not find in the charters at least any record of his having contributed to this foundation. The Bavarian academicians themselves conjecture that the first colony of monks was brought there in 1109 from the monastery of St Michael at Bamberg, under its first abbot Burkhard. Yet some connection between this monastery and the Church of Bamberg is disclosed by the bull of Innocent, issued on 7 January 1139 while Otto was still alive, confirming to Abbot Eppo his privileges and possessions, “saving, of course, the right [Col. 1310A] and reverence of the Church of Bamberg, to which it is established that the same monastery, together with its appurtenances, has been assigned and subjected through your zeal and petition” [Note: [Col. 1310D] Same work, p. 271.].

In this same year, 1135, at least according to Hofmann’s assertion, Emperor Lothair granted the Church of Bamberg a privilege by which he remitted the royal tribute in four provinces of the Henetae, or Veneti, and, with the permission of Albert the Bear, margrave of Brandenburg, within whose march these provinces lay, assigned them to Bishop Otto as a benefice. He considered it fitting that one who had first laboured in that neighbourhood to destroy idolatry and convert Slavic barbarism should receive some fruit of his labour in the lands themselves. If only he had produced the documents for this assertion. In the same year Count Godebold of Henneberg gave the monastery of Veßra to the altar of St Peter at Bamberg [Note: [Col. 1310D] *Bishops of Würzburg*, p. 486.].

LXIV. Nor do I find anywhere either the acts or even a mention of the synod which Hofmann alone again reports under the year 1136:

“Otto summoned to Bamberg a numerous assembly of all the clergy and inhabitants of his diocese. Having introduced discussion concerning the ordering of Church and commonwealth, he restrained the declining discipline of the monks. There, abolishing the old rule of the Amorbach monks, he established in the monastery on the Mount of the Archangel Michael the strict and religiously full discipline of Hirsau. To the twenty who had formerly settled there, he added more than fifty monks, conspicuous for learning and piety, and ordered them to live a common life and devote themselves to divine praises [Col. 1310C]. In order to stir the other abbots of his monasteries to imitate this most excellent deed, he exhorted them by letters, invoking the divine majesty.”

These records still lie concealed in archives, or Hofmann erred in dating them, seeming to assign to Otto’s later years matters belonging to earlier ones. For from what has been said thus far and what is to be said in its place, it follows that Otto had established only Hirsau monks in his principal monasteries from their very foundation. In the monastery of St Michael, which he reformed in 1112, he likewise appointed as abbot Wolfram from Hirsau. Thus Hirsau discipline had already then been introduced there, replacing that of Amorbach, which its first abbot Batto had brought in a century earlier [Col. 1310D]. Moreover, for the regular discipline of this otherwise celebrated monastery, which had collapsed and was restored about 1140, again from Hirsau, one should read Father Ignatius Gropp in his history [Note: [Col. 1310D] *History of Amorbach*, p. 150.].

LXV. Hofmann next appeals to St Otto’s letter to the abbots of his monasteries, exhorting them to regular observance. These letters bear no date, which must therefore be derived from other evidence. They are addressed to Wulfram, abbot of St Michael; Wigand of Tharisi; Baldwin of Banz; Eggehard [Col. 1311A] of Uraug; Imbrico of Michelfeld; Walchun of Ensdorf; Eribo of Prüfening; Frederick of Gengenbach; Eberhard of Schuttern; Otto of Stein; Liuger of Regenstorf; Ingram of Arnoldstein; and the provosts of Glunicken and Osterhofen [Note: [Col. 1311D] Documentary appendix, no. LXXVII.].

Thus the abbots named were alive at the same time, and their monasteries had already been handed over to the Church of Bamberg and reformed by Otto. We have already spoken of Mount St Michael, whose abbot Wulfram died on 22 October 1123; consequently the said letter cannot be deferred beyond that year. Indeed, since Imbrico of Michelfeld is recorded as having presided only for two years, from 1119 to 1121, the letters must be assigned within those years, a time at which Wigand, Baldwin, and Eggehard were already abbots.

Eribo, or Erbo, of Prüfening and Walchun of Ensdorf cause difficulty here. The former succeeded St Ermenold, who died on 6 January 1121; but according to domestic records the latter was first sent to Ensdorf from our monastery of St Blasien in 1123. This, however, must have occurred earlier, if he is to be recorded together with Imbrico, who died in 1121. The same must be said of Otto of Stein. We spoke above, under the year 1121, of Ludiger or Luiger of Regensdorf. Ingram was appointed the first abbot of Arnoldstein as early as 1116. Frederick became abbot at Gengenbach in 1118; *Gallia Christiana* writes that he died already on 19 October 1120, which conflicts with the foregoing. Nothing is known concerning the date of Eberhard of Schuttern.

Two provostships remain in the said encyclical: Osterhofen and Glunicken. We have spoken above of the former [Col. 1311C], still a body of secular clergy at that time but a college of Premonstratensian canons from 1127 onward. Thus it may be inferred from this passage that, after Otto had built the basilica there in 1110, a provost had been appointed to it. Glunick, or Gleink, an Order of St Benedict monastery in Upper Austria near Steyr, was founded by Arnhalm of Glunick and his son Pruno. Aquilinus Caesar demonstrates at length that it was handed over to Otto of Bamberg around 1121 [Note: [Col. 1311D] *Styrian Annals*, vol. I, pp. 144, 606, 743, and 841.], although an abbot seems to have been appointed there somewhat later, since this passage names only a provost.

It should further be noted that this letter contains no mention of the other monasteries which he built only after his first or second return from Pomerania [Col. 1311D], and which are likewise not mentioned in the bull of Calixtus II of 1123. Therefore I shall not be far wrong if I assign this encyclical to the year 1121, written still before the said bull of Calixtus, since Otto mentions only his episcopal confirmation, not a papal one.

LXVI. After the death of Lothair, the new king Conrad—previously hostile to the Church of Bamberg—summoned a general assembly of the princes to Bamberg at the following Pentecost in 1138. There the new archbishop [Col. 1312A] of Mainz, Adalbert II, having been ordained to the priesthood on Ember Saturday, 28 May, “was consecrated bishop on the following day, namely the octave of Pentecost, by Otto, bishop of that same Church of Bamberg.” [Note: [Col. 1311D] *Chronicle of St. Pantaleon*, under this year.]

In the same year Otto dedicated, as a Sunday observance, on 16 October, the church which he had built in the monastery of Vessera. On 11 December he issued a most extensive charter for the monastery of Prüfening, by which he again confirmed its foundation, possessions, and subjection to the Church of Bamberg. “Done at Bamberg in the year of the Lord 1138, indiction 1, on the third Ides of December [11 December], in the first year of King Conrad III, and in the thirty-second year, that is, since the consecration, of the ordination of Lord Otto, bishop of Bamberg.” [Note: [Col. 1311D] *Monumenta Boica*, vol. XIII, p. 158.]

[Col. 1312B] LXVII. At last we come to the year 1139, which placed a glorious end upon Otto’s many labours; yet he did not rest from them before he ceased to live. He had indeed completed the monasteries which he had hitherto either built himself or restored to a better condition by other means. Yet, still concerned for their security, he sought from Innocent II confirmation of them all, and obtained a bull issued at the Lateran on 23 January, indiction 2, that is, in 1139. [Note: [Col. 1311D] Documentary appendix, no. XCV.]

Nor, content even with this, he confirmed in 1139, when already near death, the monastery of Aldersbach, which around 1120 he had entrusted, though it was rather poor, to Regular Canons, but which had meanwhile increased: [Note: [Col. 1312D] *Monumenta Boica*, vol. V, pp. 291 and 353.] “Saving the proprietary right and jurisdiction of Bamberg, and likewise the due subjection of the Church of Passau.”

[Col. 1312C] In the same year, on an unspecified day, he issued letters of foundation, endowment, and confirmation for the monastery at Ensdorf, which he had built long before. In them he makes known to all how, “in the bishopric of Regensburg, beside the Vils, upon the estate of Count Palatine Otto of Wittelsbach, at his request, and with his consent, aid, and counsel, we provided for the choice, for the salvation of souls, of a place called Ensdorf, there building in honour of Almighty God and of Saint James the Apostle a monastery of those living according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict.” This monastery the same Count Palatine entrusted to the Church of Bamberg for protection.

He then lists the estates granted both by himself and by the Count Palatine for food and clothing, and confirms and declares them free, [Col. 1312D] “as was established in the beginning by apostolic and royal authority. In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1139, indiction 2. These things were enacted in the second year of King Conrad III, and in the thirty-second year of the episcopate of Lord Otto. Happily at Bamberg. Amen.” [Note: [Col. 1312D] Documentary appendix, no. XCIII, from Anselm Meiller, *History of Ensdorf*, p. 267.]

There too [Note: [Col. 1312D] P. 261.] is found Otto’s charter of an uncertain year, by which he assigned to Ensdorf the tithes from newly cultivated land disputed between Prüfening and Regensburg, lest they should be lost to both.

[Col. 1313A] But here is now the limit of labours which, if any other bishop of his age ever performed them, Otto performed for the conversion of peoples and for the preservation of the purity of ecclesiastical discipline and faith. To this end, everywhere, he either restored houses of sound teaching and piety to better order or founded them with almost boundless generosity. To these must be added the estates and possessions by which he increased his own church, and the alms which he distributed most generously among the poor. He was accustomed to say that “the more he spent upon God’s works, the more he had to spend.”

Besides prudent stewardship, he was supported in his pious undertaking by the assistance and resources of other nobles and wealthy persons. Foremost among them were the dukes Wratislaus of Pomerania, Boleslaus of Poland, and Vladislaus of Bohemia, [Col. 1313B] and also Béla II, king of Hungary, all most closely joined to him in friendship. Assisted by their aid, he was so great in works of mercy that Embrico, bishop of Würzburg, publicly testified in the sermon which he delivered at Otto’s funeral in Bamberg that “the ages of his time had possessed this man alone, this one man, as a man of such great mercy.” Since that sermon embraces his principal praises and virtues, it will appear below among the proofs. [Note: [Col. 1313C] Documentary appendix, no. XCVI.]

LXVIII. Therefore, when he had now passed seventy years of age and had governed the Church for thirty-six years with no less prudence than holiness, worn out by illnesses and by the failure of bodily strength, and when, “pressed more severely by illness, he hoped soon to pass to the Lord, he exercised with so much greater ardour that work of almsgiving which had always been dear and customary to him, because he knew that he would not be granted to practise it much longer. Then,” after humble and pure confession, “anointed with the sacred oil, he received the propitiatory viaticum, the body of the Lord; and, surrounded [Col. 1314A] by that company of religious men always familiar to him, both monks and clerics, who devoutly commended his agony to God with psalms and prayers, he raised to heaven a soul full of good works and alms, full of honour and grace.”

Sefrid does not record the day of his death, which Ebbo specifies: “On the night on which the feast or commemoration of Saint Paul the Apostle is observed, at the first hour of the day, pious Otto rendered his soul to heaven.” He therefore died on the day before the Kalends of July, that is, 30 June, a Friday, in 1139, on which day he is recorded in the necrology of St. Michael’s.

Sefrid continues: “Throughout the three whole days of his repose, the clay of his beloved body was borne through all the churches; by unceasing sacrifice, untiring prayers, and many distributions of alms, his blessed soul was commended to God [Col. 1314B] by all. On the fourth day, when they came to the place of burial, the bishop [Embrico of Würzburg] celebrated the commendation; and, during the solemnities of the Mass, turning to the sorrowing and mourning multitude, he delivered a brief sermon . . . . . Thus, when Mass had ended, his body was buried in the place where it is seen, in the church of Blessed Michael. Counts, margraves, and whatever other nobles were present eagerly bore his bier in turn, lifted the sarcophagus, and most devoutly performed with their own hands, in the manner of workmen, the other tasks necessary there. This was done happily in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, on the third Nones of July [5 July]. Amen.”

Since he was in fact buried only on the sixth, not the fourth, day after his death, Sollerius thinks that here one should read [Col. 1314C] “the third of July” instead of “the third Nones of July.” Otto’s feast is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 2 July; at Bamberg it is celebrated on 30 September, the day on which his sacred body was translated in 1189 at his canonization, as we shall say below under Otto II.

[Col. 1313]

# LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF SAINT OTTO, BISHOP OF BAMBERG. LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO HIM ARE INTERSPERSED.

(*Bishopric of Bamberg*, documentary appendix, p. 55.)

## I. Letter of St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, to Pope Paschal II concerning his election. (1103.)

[Col. 1313D]

To his lord PASCHAL, universal bishop of the holy and apostolic see, OTTO of the Church of Bamberg offers that which he is: prayers and service of devotion no less than of due submission.

“Because the foundation of all ecclesiastical dignity and religion is Christ the rock,” etc. See under Paschal, *Patrology*, vol. CLXIII, col. 464.

### Pope Paschal’s reply

[Col. 1315A]

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to OTTO, beloved brother, bishop-elect of the Church of Bamberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“A wise son makes his mother glad.” Your deeds and your counsel show you to be a prudent man. We have therefore judged it fitting to honour you and to assist your advancement. Accordingly, doubting nothing of our goodwill, present yourself to us as soon as you can. For we are certain that divine wisdom knows how to make good use even of evil men.

## II. Memorable diploma of Emperor Henry IV for the Church of Bamberg. (1103, 15 July.)

[Col. 1315B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, HENRY, by the favouring clemency of God third august emperor of the Romans.

In the judgment of God, who beholds all things, we believe that the merit of him who gives and of him who confirms is equal. We also believe that it belongs to our royal majesty to attend to the concerns of the whole realm, and especially to the welfare of all the holy churches of God, and with all speed to abolish whatever opposes them, lest they either be degraded by grievous injury or, through any occasion arising from our fault, fall away from their former worship and religious observance. Thus, while we faithfully perform this duty alike from love and fear of God, we may share in the merits and glory of those who have bestowed these things upon God with devout affection.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful, future as well as present, that, in this hope and in memory of our grandfather Emperor Conrad, our grandmother the august Empress Gisela, our father Emperor Henry, our mother the Empress Agnes, our late wife the Empress Bertha, and especially in memory of the pious Emperor Henry, our kinsman, founder of the holy Church of Bamberg; moreover, through the intervention of our most beloved son King Henry V, and chiefly by the counsel of our princes who were present—Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; Bruno, archbishop of Trier; Hubert, archbishop of Bremen; Obert, bishop [Col. 1315D] of Liège; John, bishop of Speyer; Burchard, bishop of Münster; Uto, bishop of Hildesheim; Henry, bishop of Heidelberg; Burchard, bishop of Utrecht; Wttilo, bishop of Minden; Mazo, bishop of Verdun; Walcher, bishop of Cambrai; Frederick, duke of Swabia; Henry, duke of Lorraine; Magnus, duke of Saxony; Henry, margrave of Isenburg; Uto, margrave of Stade; and especially the other princes and our other faithful men who were present—and also out of love for our beloved and faithful Otto, the seventh bishop [Note: [Col. 1315D] Not counting Hermann, who had been deposed.] of that Church: we sanction, with the consent of our faithful men, and, all contradiction removed, confirm by the authority of our royal majesty that same place, raised by the divine Emperor Henry II, through the inspiration of divine clemency, in perfect devotion of faith, hope, and charity, into a bishopric in honour of the prince of the Apostles Peter and the martyr Saint George, for the soul of himself and his own.

We likewise confirm all movable and immovable property of that same holy Church of God, which that divine emperor, out of zeal for the heavenly homeland, bestowed there with generous hand, on this condition: that our faithful Otto, seventh bishop of that place, and his successors in perpetuity may possess these things in secure tranquillity and may have free power, with the consent of clergy and people, to regulate, arrange, exchange, and increase the goods and properties of that church.

[Col. 1316B] By our authority we also enact that, in its abbeys, monasteries, counties, markets, market-towns, mints, ferries, tolls, castles, villages, hamlets, building-sites, male and female slaves, tributaries, tithes, forests, woods, hunting rights, fisheries, mills, millworks, waters and watercourses, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, books, gold, silver, jewels, vessels, ornaments, and any utensils bestowed for the worship and service of God there; and throughout all the boundaries and properties of that church, and whatever now belongs to it or may be increased from these—there shall be no harassment by tyrants, no power shall violently invade there, and no count or judge shall presume to make law within the city, apart from [Col. 1316C] the bishop of that place. Every possession of those serving God there shall be held immune.

Let that bishopric be free and secure from every foreign and unjust power, so that those serving God there may be able and willing to celebrate the memory of the first founder, and to commend us, its benefactors and confirmers, to God in their prayers. And that this grant of our authority may remain firm and unshaken, we have ordered this privilege, drawn up for that purpose and confirmed with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The mark of Lord Henry, most invincible third emperor of the Romans.

I, Chancellor Erlongus, [Note: [Col. 1315D] This person, omitted by others, is none other than [Col. 1316D] Erlongus, intruded into the see of Würzburg from the following year onward.] acting in place of Archchancellor Rothard, have authenticated it.

Given on the Ides of July [15 July], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1103, [Col. 1316D] indiction 11; in the fiftieth year of the ordination, the forty-eighth of the reign, and the twentieth of the empire of Lord Henry, third emperor august of the Romans; and in the fourth year of the ordination of his son Henry.

Done happily at Liège, in the name of the Lord. Amen.

## III. Emperor Henry IV congratulates St. Otto of Bamberg upon the beginning of his episcopate. (About 1103.)

HENRY, by God’s grace Emperor of the Romans, to OTTO, bishop of the Church of Bamberg: grace, affection, and every good thing.

Perfect love, since it is assuredly native to the heart, [Col. 1317A] has force not merely before the eye, does not look merely to the eye, and does not depend upon time. The more widely those absent are separated, the more closely are they bound together by mutual concern for one another. We certainly take greater care for you in your absence than when you were present, desiring for you, with the same mind by which we advanced you, every prosperity, and fearing adversities—even should they not occur—because they can occur.

It is therefore a very great joy to us that we have learned welcome news of your affairs: namely, that you have been honourably received by your Church, have pleased all by the gracious manner of your responses and by moderation in your actions, and have commendably shown necessary caution in the conferring of benefices.

For this reason we advise, exhort, and request you to continue what you are doing, lest, if you relax your hand, you lose the first fruits of your good reputation; for a good beginning without an end is like a beautiful body without a head. Let no one turn you away from the choice of ecclesiastical advantage according to justice by fear, bend you by price, or seduce you by the honeyed gall of persuasion. For, if you are tested by all these things and found approved, you will easily repel them all. But if you judge anything too burdensome for your strength, report it to us, assuredly to come to your assistance, under the warrant of our command. [Note: [Col. 1317D] A striking proof of the esteem in which Emperor Henry IV held St. Otto, and one which at the same time declares his own innermost views concerning ecclesiastical government. [Col. 1318D]]

## IV. Emperor Henry IV writes to the bishop of Bamberg concerning an expedition into Flanders. (Year uncertain.)

HENRY, by God’s grace Emperor of the Romans, to the bishop of Bamberg, his dearest faithful man: grace and every good thing.

[Col. 1317C] While we rejoiced that, by God’s providence and the counsel of His great mercy, our kingdom had everywhere been pacified, messengers came to us on behalf of Duke G. of Lotharingia, Count B. Baldwin, and our other faithful men of the march of Flanders. They reported that they could no longer endure the outrages of Count Robert, who has invaded our realm and, to the disgrace of all who belong to it, has usurped for himself our bishopric of Cambrai.

Accordingly, as the matter required, we consulted our assembled princes; and, having prudently considered the situation, we resolved on their advice to undertake an expedition into Flanders against this exceedingly presumptuous enemy, who ought to be our vassal, [Col. 1317D] lest he continue unpunished to exult over the diminution and disgrace of our realm. You ought, if you love your own honour, to weigh in your heart this affront, so manifest and so common to our realm.

Therefore, that you may do this faithfully and prudently, we ask you in hope of a most welcome reward, and admonish you by the fidelity you owe to us and to the realm, that, setting aside every excuse, you come to the expedition, as the honour both of the realm and of yourself requires. Know that at the coming feast of All Saints we shall assemble at Tongeren, near Liège, ready to ride against Flanders. [Col. 1318A] Do not be surprised that our arrival at Regensburg has been altered, as you understood when you were with us, because necessity has intervened. Our expedition against the enemies in Flanders has been firmly and profitably approved by all our men as conducive to the honour of the realm. [Note: [Col. 1318D] Concerning this expedition and letter we have spoken above in the *Life of Otto*, § XI.]

## V. Emperor Henry IV, by letter, implores St. Otto of Bamberg for aid against his son. (About 1104.)

HENRY, by God’s grace Emperor of the Romans, to OTTO, bishop of Bamberg, his beloved and trusted faithful man: grace and every good thing.

Now that necessity is at hand, it ought to become apparent who are faithful to us; the very evidence of the matter must show [Col. 1318B] how much they love us and our honour. Know therefore that we have come as far as Würzburg with many knights, and that we still await more there, desiring, with God’s help, to attack our enemies and to free our castle of Nuremberg, which they are besieging.

Accordingly, as to a most excellent faithful man, we command you by request to hasten to us with all whom you can bring, as we trust you will. We also earnestly ask you in the present crisis to consider our need and to grant A., who is necessary to us, the benefice which he asks of you. Reflect how present danger compels us to entreat many men and, by doing what they wish, to strengthen them in our allegiance. For this reason, compelled by these and many other matters, [Col. 1318C] we must ask you otherwise than we would wish. But, God willing, if prosperity comes, we shall look after you and your church as is fitting. In this matter act according to what N. tells you on our behalf.

## VI. Another letter of the same emperor to the same bishop, of similar subject.

HENRY, by God’s grace Emperor of the Romans, to OTHON, bishop of Bamberg: grace and every good thing.

We know that you are frequently wearied by embassies from our son, as you informed us through your messenger. Yet we trust in the fidelity of your goodness, that you will never yield to the prayers, threats, persuasions, or flatteries of our enemies in opposition to us, but will always remain faithfully with us. Whatever persecutions [Col. 1318D] you suffer from our enemies, nevertheless do not be frightened in any way; rather, be certain that we shall not abandon you, whether in peace or in danger. Place your confidence in the omnipotent Lord that you will soon be delivered with us from the present danger.

Therefore, as we trust concerning you and have instructed you through your messenger, do not hesitate to come on the day and to the place which we designated to you. Accordingly, by the fidelity you owe us, do not allow either prayers or threats in any degree to terrify you into transferring yourself to our son. Cause prayers to be offered without interruption to God for us by the whole Church and by every congregation entrusted to you. [Col. 1319A] Also ensure that your castle is guarded so diligently that none of the guards descends from it. Send your messenger as well to console the people of Nuremberg.

## VII. Letter of the Church of Bamberg to Welf, duke of Bavaria, for the release of its bishop Otto. (1106.)

To the illustrious and magnificent Duke N., the humble and grieving clergy of Bamberg offer devout prayers in Christ.

Since we know that your magnificence is distinguished no less by strength than amenable to clemency, from the fragrance of your good reputation which is widely diffused, [we beseech you] by Christ Himself that the most Christian zeal of your spirit may rise up against the utterly unworthy crime committed against God and our bishop, in proportion to the enormity of the matter. For he has not been treated with ordinary cruelty. When sacrilegious hands had been laid upon him as he was travelling in religious habit, both as a bishop and toward the apostolic see, they then plundered the great sums of money which he had prepared for the expenses of so important a journey; and, not yet content with so great a spoil, they now attempt to extort from him a thousand *manses*, that is, the whole patrimony of the bishopric.

[Col. 1319B] What barbarian, I ask, would treat any captive more cruelly? Certainly this dangerous disturbance of the times, because it bears no title, carries out against us all that we suffer everywhere under the pretext of correcting morals and improving the condition of the Churches. Is it really through sacrileges and robberies that those good morals are to be restored to us? [Col. 1319C] Is it really through the ravaging and plundering of a most flourishing church that we are to hope the losses of churches will be repaired?

We therefore implore your glorious eminence, by every form of supplication, both for the liberation of our shepherd, who is held though wholly innocent, and for the safety of our Church; so that from our patrons, namely blessed Peter and George, you may deserve to obtain a worthy recompense for your merits before that terrible tribunal of Christ.

## VIII. Letter of St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, to Pope Paschal II concerning his ordination. (1106.)

To the apostolic lord PASCHAL, worthily exalted to the summit of the Roman see by the prerogative of his merits [Col. 1319D] and the holiness of his character, OTTO, by God’s grace bishop-elect of Bamberg, offers, with all devotion, most ready prayers and service both voluntary and due.

Since at last, through the Lord’s mercy and His governance of the ship of His Church, after the cloudy storms of errors the serene light of truth has shone upon the Western Church, [Note: [Col. 1319D] That is, after the conflict had been removed by the death of Henry IV.] above all and before all things we desire that your holiness should know that we have obeyed in everything, as was proper, your legate, namely the bishop of Constance [Note: [Col. 1319D] Gebhard.], and have with utmost devotion partly carried out, and partly stand ready, should life be granted us, to carry out all that we have learned through [Col. 1320A] him.

Therefore, casting ourselves at the footsteps of your feet, we earnestly beg that you may patiently hear the servant of your fatherhood. For since the world is now set in evil, and scarcely any man or place can be trusted, [Note: [Col. 1319D] He speaks of his captivity on the earlier journey.] no small anxieties torment us concerning the attainment of our ordination. Therefore, doubtful, anxious, and most like one shipwrecked in waves of cares, I cry to you with the prince of the Apostles, whose office you hold: “Lord, save me.” To state our case briefly: in this hour and power of darkness our eyes look to you alone; we are ready to maintain the obedience due to you; we have resolved either to stand with you or to go to prison for you.

[Col. 1320B] With all our heart, therefore, we desire to rely upon your authority. Extend your hand to us; command what you wish us to do. If you command us to come to you, our resources—though diminished by plunder and fire—we shall nevertheless present before the sight of your majesty, together with the due blessing of our service [Note: [Col. 1320D] The acknowledgement due from the Church of Bamberg.], out of desire to see you and to obtain the grace of consecration.

May the bowels of your compassion therefore deem it worthy to make us certain in this matter by some written reply, so that a safer route for coming to you may be shown to us beforehand and it may be signified that we shall receive the blessing which we devoutly request from you. We so earnestly seek it from the hand of your holiness because our metropolitan [Note: [Col. 1320D] Ruthard of Mainz, an exile in Thuringia.], although through you he possesses the grace of consecration, nevertheless—what we cannot confess without tears—suffers a great injury [perhaps: scarcity] of fellow-workers in the spiritual gift.

## IX. Pope Paschal II commends St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, whom he had ordained, to Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz. (1106, 21 May.)

PASCHAL, bishop, . . . to RUTHARD, archbishop of Mainz, . . .

How closely the Church of Bamberg has been attached to the apostolic see from the beginning of its foundation, we think is known to your prudence. We have therefore judged it fitting, etc. See under Paschal, *Patrology*, vol. CLXIII, col. 191.

## X. Letter of Pope Paschal II to the clergy and people of Bamberg concerning Otto, bishop ordained by him. (1106.)

[Col. 1320D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Bamberg, . . .

Even if it were unknown to us, the communication in your letter makes manifest how closely the Church of Bamberg has been bound in a debt of affection to the apostolic see from the beginning of its own foundation. That debt of affection, etc. See above, col. 192.

## XI. Letter of St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, to his Church concerning the completion of his consecration. (1106.)

[Col. 1321A]

OTTO, by God’s grace bishop of Bamberg, to EGILBERT [Note: [Col. 1321] It was Eberhard; the writer confused him because of the initial letter E.], provost; ADELbert, dean; and the other brethren: every good thing.

From what I have known and experienced of your affection, I know that you have long awaited the outcome of our labour, so that you might rejoice in our success, if indeed it has, through God’s mercy, succeeded well. Therefore, lest you remain longer anxious or uncertain concerning us, and so that, as is just, you may rejoice most sincerely with us, we have resolved to make known to you by this letter how mercifully [Col. 1321B] God, in His accustomed manner, has worked with us after immense labours and very many toils.

On the holy day of Pentecost—the day consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit and rightly solemn to all the faithful—on that day, I say, by God’s ordering, in the city of Anagni in Campania, which divides Romagna from Apulia, unworthy though I was, I received from the Lord the gift of episcopal blessing. Most blessed Pope Paschal laid his hand upon me; many other bishops cooperated; and the clergy of the Roman Church, a great part of whom had gathered in that same city on that day, stood by and gave their consent. And—what has happened in our times to no one consecrated by the Roman pontiff—I was consecrated without making any oath.

We earnestly beg you to remember always this place, this day, and this freely granted mercy of God, with every act of thanksgiving, especially since many other venerable persons who had pursued important business before the apostolic see returned with their affairs unaccomplished.

[Col. 1321C] Therefore magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt His name together—He to whom it is as easy to resist the proud as to give grace to the humble. But because it is hard to be leaders in troubled times, we must take care and strive in every way that hardship may become an occasion of reward. Therefore, while it is time for sowing, let us not cease to sow the seeds of good works, that on the day of harvest we may bring back larger sheaves of joy to our head, who is [Col. 1321D] Christ, clinging to Him through the bond of charity. Let us not, by giving worldly gains more attention than is right, be separated from Him and wither like branches cast out from the vine.

But because in carrying out works of justice we need the assistance of divine grace, implore by constant prayers the mercy of almighty God, that He may grant us both the will and the power to perform these works; and that He may direct us fruitfully in that way which He testified Himself to be, so that, since without Him we can do nothing, through Him we may be able to accomplish all things.

## XII. Pope Paschal II confirms the monastery of Weissenau. (1109, 14 April.)

[Col. 1322A]

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son OTBERTO and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A desire shown to concern religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without delay. The illustrious man Eribo, with his wife Guilla and her niece Hadimuot, founded, in the diocese of Bamberg upon their own estate called Guizna [alternatively, Wizenabe], a church in the name of Blessed Boniface, bishop and martyr. They offered it, with all its endowment and estates, to blessed Peter the Apostle and to his holy Roman Church.

For their devotion, adopting this church from the Roman mother as a daughter, we order all its endowments, both estates and dependent persons, to be carefully entered in this document. These, then, are the estates bestowed upon our daughter by the aforesaid persons on the day of its foundation: Guizna, Nidrendorff, Diedungesdorf, Salewenbergh, Hilteboldesdorf, with the castle situated upon the same estate, Crummenaha, Eppenruit, Suphenruit, Cretsinruit, and Herbendorf.

Moreover, in the district called Mannua [alternatively, Manau]: Churenberch, Bocchesruit, Niwenruit, Paffenruit, Sibenlinten, Liubenstat, Rampogen, Rutenbach, Tittenwiden, Albewinesberch, Utelenhofen, Pulteshofen, Tiuskiendorf, Wolvesbach, Helehenvelt, Nerdesdorf, Moseten, Thetgingen, and Husen. As for dependent persons, to summarize briefly: the founders gave to the church which they founded all male and female persons whom they possessed, except three—Wezelone, Hotescalco, and Potone.

[Col. 1322C] We therefore fortify the foundation of this place by the authority of the apostolic see, so that it may always be preserved in the proper right of our Roman Church under the discipline of monastic order, and that a Byzantine coin shall be paid from it annually to the Lateran palace. Furthermore, we establish—indeed, by the authority of the blessed Apostles we command—that all the aforesaid estates, villages, and dependent persons, and the other goods which the persons named above have bestowed upon the same place, as well as whatever may in future be bestowed from their property, by themselves or by other faithful persons, through the Lord’s generosity, shall always be kept firm and intact for those serving there under the monastic rule.

No person may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, claim for personal use things unjustly bestowed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexation. Rather, let all remain safe and undisturbed, to benefit the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

No abbot is to be appointed there through any intrigue or violence unless the brethren, or the sounder part of their counsel, have chosen him, from their own community or from another if necessary, in common agreement and according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. [Col. 1323A] We freely grant baptism and burial to that place, so that, should any wish to be buried there, no one may hinder their devotion and final wish, unless they are excommunicated.

We likewise permit the abbot, by the common counsel of the brethren, to appoint whichever advocate he judges more advantageous. If this advocate should later prove useless to the monastery and burdensome to the brethren, they may put another in charge, whomever they wish. Nor may any of the abbots whatsoever grant any advocacy to anyone without the election and confirmation of the brethren serving God there, lest a lay person find in the hand of importunity an opportunity and occasion to seize things not his own.

If he does so, by the power of God and our Lord Jesus Christ and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and our own, let him be subject to excommunication and forever deprived of the rank of his office and order. [Col. 1323B] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to violate this document of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he makes fitting amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour. Let him know that he is liable before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance.

But to all who preserve justice for the same place, may there be peace in our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive the fruit of good action and find before the just Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1323C] I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, etc.

I, Rodbert, priest of the title of Saint Eusebius, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April], indiction 2, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1109, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

## XIII. [Note: [Col. 1323D] It appears in Paschal, *Patrology*, vol. CLXIII, col. 285, but less complete. It is published more fully from a copy.] Pope Paschal II grants to St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, and his successors the use of the pallium and the power to bear the cross before them. (15 April 1111.)

Paschal . . . to his venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, and to his successors canonically promoted in perpetuity.

[Col. 1323D] It is characteristic of the good of charity to rejoice together in the progress of others, for charity does not seek its own things. Thus the Apostle says: “Now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 3); and again: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ?” (1 Thessalonians 2). Therefore we are prompted by this debt of charity and compelled by the authority of the apostolic see to render due honour to our brethren and, each according to its proper measure, to impart to other churches the dignity of the holy Roman Church.

Therefore, venerable brother Otto, bishop of the Church of Bamberg, we grant to your love the pallium for the celebration of the sacred solemnities of Mass, which, indeed, your fraternity shall know to use within your own church only on those days specified in the present document: namely, on the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection and Pentecost; likewise on the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ; on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul; on the solemnity of Saint Dionysius the martyr; also on the anniversary day of your consecration and at the dedications of churches.

We desire you in every respect to uphold the character [otherwise, grace] of this pallium; for the honor of this garment is humility and justice. Therefore let your fraternity hasten to show itself humble in prosperity and, in adversity if such should occur, steadfast with justice; friendly toward the good, opposed to the perverse; never accepting anyone’s person against the truth, nor ever suppressing one who speaks for the truth because of his person; applying itself to works of mercy according to the measure of its resources, yet desiring to apply itself beyond that measure also; having compassion on the infirm, rejoicing with those in good health; reckoning others’ losses as its own, exulting in others’ joys as in its own; mercifully severe in correcting vices; soothing the minds of its hearers in fostering virtues; maintaining judgment without anger in anger [otherwise, within judgment], yet in tranquility not abandoning the censure of just severity. This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received. If you carefully preserve it, you shall possess inwardly what you show that you have received outwardly.

[Col. 1324C] Moreover, we grant that the banner of the cross may be borne before you within the parish of the Church of Bamberg, saving, of course, the reverence due to the metropolitan see of Mainz; so that, endowed with a special dignity from the holy Roman Church, you may make a special effort to render it obedience and devoted service. May heavenly graciousness preserve your fraternity unharmed for a long time. Amen, amen.

Written by the hand of John, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at Rome, on the island of Lycaonia, by the hand of John, deacon-cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in place of Lord Frederick, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1324D] Therefore at that time the archbishop of Cologne was still archchancellor of the Holy Roman Church.], on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, [Col. 1324D] in the fourth indiction, in the year 1111 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope, and in the first year of the empire of Emperor Henry IV.

### XIV. Bruno, bishop of Trier, summons Otto of Bamberg to investigate the case of the bishop-elect of Speyer.  
*(About the year 1112.)*

BRUNO, by the grace of God unworthy overseer of the people of Trier, to O., holy bishop of the Church of Bamberg: the service of sincere charity.

I congratulate your blessedness with great joy, since I think it has come about not without great merit on the part of your holiness [Col. 1325A] that my lord the pope retains so sweet a remembrance of you. For when I was carrying out an embassy of my lord the king, he spoke with me concerning the obedience of your charity, and sent you greetings and the apostolic [blessing] through me. Having entered into the counsel of his administration, he charged us to consecrate the elect of Eichstätt and Speyer, [Note: [Col. 1325D] These are dealt with in the Life.] and to call you as our helper and fellow-worker. But because certain things concerning the man of Speyer had been reported to him, he commanded that we should examine him with holy diligence; and, if by his rank and by the testimony of the brethren present he could clear himself of the charges brought against him, that we should ordain him for the honor of God and the necessary governance of the Church.

Therefore, on behalf of the lord pope, I urge you to take care that this matter—because it is God’s cause—is not delayed through you, [Col. 1325B] and to come to us at Speyer within fifteen days from the day of the Lord’s Resurrection.

### XV. Letter of Frederick, bishop of Cologne, to Otto of Bamberg, soliciting him to join his side against Henry V.  
*(1115.)*

To Lord OTTO, venerable bishop of the Church of Bamberg, Frederick, by God’s grace [bishop] of the people of Cologne: that which true and active brotherly love produces in prayers and service.

We already sent certain letters to your holiness. If perhaps you received them, we are not a little astonished at so long a delay in your reply. To recapitulate briefly their lengthy meaning, [Col. 1325C] the chief purpose was to stir your prudence to defend—or at least to lament freely—the exceedingly grave calamity of the holy Church which you see, a calamity which we have long known you inwardly to have cherished with silent longing.

Again, venerable brother, again we say the same thing. If zeal for God’s house—indeed, if true love for the Church, which is God’s house—consumes you to the marrow, do not any longer, through excessive patience, overlook so great a desolation of her, so cruel a plundering and profanation of God’s inheritance. Behold: through God’s mercy a great door has been opened to us, that the truth which long kept silence may come forth into public view, and that our freedom, long suppressed, may lift up its head, because the holy Roman [Col. 1325D] Church has now spoken aloud for us and for herself. France joins herself to us [Note: [Col. 1325D] At the synod of Beauvais in 1114.]; Saxony, as you have heard, professes the truth with a free voice.

And who, dearest brother, would not be moved because every authority of ecclesiastical vigor has been turned to profit for courtiers and palace officials? Synodal assemblies of bishops, annual councils, and, in short, every administration of the ecclesiastical order have been transferred to the royal court, so that they may serve their purses, though they ought to have been examined spiritually. What shall we say of episcopal sees, over which royal stewards preside and which they dispose of, making the house of prayer plainly into a den of robbers? There is no concern whatever for the gain of souls [Col. 1326A] while the insatiable mouth of the royal treasury is filled only with earthly profits.

Here we, who through God’s own grace are pillars of God’s Church, who ought to steer Peter’s ship through the stormy waves of this age—here, I say, we ought to be watchful; here we ought to hold fast the rudder of governance, lest, while we grow sluggish and numb, it drift without the effort of governance, be dashed against these and similar rocks of impious tyranny and broken apart, and—God forbid!—be sunk under the weight of the rushing waves. Let us not be rebuked in the prophet’s words as mute dogs unable to bark (Isa. 56), nor let this be said of us: “Have you not gone up to face [the enemy], to set a wall for the house of Israel?” (Ezek. 13).
