As for ourselves, holy and venerable brother, we confidently promise you this in God’s grace—not from ourselves, but from the power [Col. 1326B] which God works in us—that neither tribulation nor distress, nor death nor life, shall separate us from this free profession of truth which we have begun. For this we know to be our calling; for this we have put on the new man: that we may carry the dying of Jesus in our body, that for his sake we may be delivered over to death, so that the life of Jesus too may at some time be manifested in this mortal flesh of ours.

Therefore we have not failed in this glorious hope; and we hope and earnestly desire the same of your constancy. Since you have suffered unworthily, we urge you to recall this often to mind. Do not keep us any longer in suspense by prolonged expectation, but inform us in writing of your decision. Lord Chuono, [Col. 1326C] your great-nephew, bishop [of Palestrina] and legate of the Roman Church, greets you. Together with all the bishops of Gaul, he excommunicated the emperor [Henry], as well as the bishop of Münster [Burchard] and Hermann of Winzenburg, at the council of Beauvais (6 December 1114), and commanded that this be made known to you. At the council of Reims, to be held on Laetare Jerusalem Sunday (28 March 1115), he will repeat the same sentence against the aforesaid persons and all their accomplices, together with three other bishops newly sent from the Roman See. Farewell. [Note: [Col. 1326D] Consult the Life above concerning these matters.]

### XVI. Emperor Henry V invites Otto to the assembly at Speyer.  
*(About the year 1116.)*

[Col. 1326D]

HENRY, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans Augustus, to OTTO, beloved bishop of the people of Bamberg: abundant favor and every good thing.

Our messengers have returned from Rome and, by God’s grace, have reported to us matters for the most part joyful and favorable. Our faithful men also report that we have an acceptable time in which to provide for the Roman See and the commonwealth. Therefore we necessarily summon our princes, so that, as is right, we may have their counsel and assistance in this matter. For this we greatly need the presence of your fidelity and the prudence of your counsel, [Col. 1327A] because we love you from the heart and place in you an unhesitating confidence, concerning all our honor, as in ourselves.

Therefore with confidence and earnestness we request your affection to come to us at Speyer on the Friday after the next feast of Saint Mary. There, with your counsel and that of our other princes, we shall deliberate upon these matters for the honor of God and the welfare of the realm and of Christian peace. Do this gladly, knowing that we shall dismiss you quickly. And we would gladly spare you this [journey], did not the urgency of so weighty a matter press upon us. Moreover, we command you to send for Count N., whom we entrusted to you, and present him to us. [Note: [Col. 1327D] We remain uncertain whether this letter should be attributed to Henry IV or V, since it suits either. But because no mention is made here of a rebellious son, but of the Roman See, we assign it to the latter and to the year 1116, when concord was again attempted. At least it makes clear [Col. 1328D] the Augustus’s notable estimation of Saint Otto’s prudence.]

Through negligence, the same sentence that was imposed upon the other neglecters of that council would also have been imposed upon you: namely, either suspension from the divine office or the dreadful prohibition from communion in the body and blood of the Lord. Yet the diligence of our petition forestalled this, and the outstanding reverence for your holiness obtained from the Church that it should not be done. With these two grounds concurring and cooperating, we finally obtained that your affection should undergo no severity, since up to now its devotion has availed in the Church. I judged it fitting, indeed, to spare your honor and reverence in every respect, and, as far as possible, to provide and take counsel for place and time, since the affection of your holiness has bound itself to us by a great gift of devoted charity. [Note: [Col. 1328D] For he was consecrated by him.]

Henceforth, as we have received in command, we declare that you are without doubt to come to the council to be held at Fritzlar by the aforesaid legate on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, [Col. 1327C] lest, having become a neglecter of this command also, a decree of harsher sentence be pronounced upon you when my petition can no longer prevail. Moreover, know that Duke Frederick [of Swabia], his brother, G. [Count Palatine Godfrey], and their remaining accomplices have been excommunicated at the aforesaid council. We also request that you send our letters to our brethren, namely the bishops of Prague and Moravia.

### XVII. Letter of Adalbert, bishop of Mainz, to Otto of Bamberg, complaining of his absence from the synod of Cologne.  
*(1118.)*

[Col. 1327D] To the most reverend bishop of the people of Bamberg, A., unworthy minister of the see of Mainz: the inviolable pledge of brotherly affection and prayer.

What the lord bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Roman Church, had recently announced to us by apostolic authority, our diligence, wholly subject to Roman authority, had also carefully carried out in every respect, announcing to you also under that same authority and ours that your presence should come to the council to be held at Cologne (1118). But because I know not by what means this was omitted—

### XVIII. Letters of foundation by Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg, for the monastery of Michelfeld.  
*(6 May 1119.)*

[From the monastery archive; but corrupt in Bruschius.]

[Col. 1328A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. OTTO, by the favoring clemency of God the eighth bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg.

Let the whole body of Christ’s faithful, both of the present age and of the future, know that the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist in the place called Michelvelt was built through our work and our care. Let both present and future persons also recognize with what goods we have endowed that place, from what [Col. 1328B] possessions we have provided the brethren keeping watch there in divine service with the means of temporal life, so that, since this testimony of truth shall have many supporters and many witnesses, the provisions established by our humility may remain continually unshaken.

Let all also know that the very site on which the monastery was built, since it was a holding belonging to forest-right, was restored to the bishopric in exchange for another holding at Risehae [Reisach]. We gave to the monastery itself broad tracts of fields and meadows around the precinct of the monastery, and also a portion of forest as far as the southern road, which stretches transversely through the wood and ends at the western bridge near Seberc; and in this we provided for the monks’ peace. For we foresaw it to be inevitable that they would be burdened by the litigious complaints [Col. 1328C] of their neighbors if their properties were hemmed in by other people’s possessions.

Moreover, from the forest-right belonging to the bishopric, with the consent and at the request of Count Berengar [Note: [Col. 1328D] Of Sulzbach, in the district of Nordgau.] and with the acquiescence of the leading clergy and people of the Church of Bamberg, we transferred the following, as if by the privilege of a benefice, for the use of the monastery and monks: in the flowing river called Begenz, from the village of the same name as far as the rock called Gozenstein, we granted the monastery exclusive fishing rights; pasture for animals below the path which runs from the village of Begenz to meet the road leading toward Velden. From the aforesaid bridge, timber for the use of buildings and the cell may freely be cut by our grant, though scattered timber only, and where the forest wardens direct; for firewood, timber not fit for beam-work may be taken wherever it can be found, except in denser places and the lairs of wild animals. [Col. 1328D] We also granted broad permission to make beehives anywhere in the forest.

The villages which we bestowed upon the monastery itself are these: Michelvelt itself; Heroltesruit; Nuseze; Ruchedorf; Widelwanch; Willeberc; likewise Heroitisrvit; Churbendorf in part; Buchenbach with its parish; Vutenloch; Ruikersberg; Birche in part; [Col. 1329A] Sconenveld; Bucha in part; Benzenrvit, with Risehae; Huwenstein, also called Gernotestein; Sigehartisruit; Urbach; Uveloch; Pileinstein; Luzenbuche; Ebersberg; Friderichesrvit; Perhartsruit; Sumerhawen; Namegast; Hophenahe in part; Franckenahe; Circhendorf in part; likewise Circhendorf in part; Artolfesprunnen; Hagenach; Godesendorf; Steinegewazzer in part; Rachenberc; Cimerberc; Igelsruit; Plez; Toberin; Junruit; Gozemarsberg; Pernhach; Grune; the estate of Henphenvelt and its parish, with its landholding and all its appurtenances; Swaigoltesruit in part; Otenberch; Snelharstesdorf; Welmesgeseze. [Note: [Col. 1329D] These relate to the geographical description of the Upper Palatinate and the old district of Nordgau.]

The most illustrious Count Berengar, whom we had appointed advocate of the same [Col. 1329B] place, transferred them upon the altar of Saint John. Witnesses to all this were Bucco of Culmen; Meinhart of Parchstein; Wignand; Udelscalch; Wirnt of Wolferingen; Wignand of Wolfesbach and his brothers Rapoto and Bruno; Merboto and Eppo of Ebermannesdorf; Rupert of Bibra; Engelmar of Woldelspach and his brother Alibero; Poppo of Sconevelt; Baldewin of Restelbach; Eckenbert of Tennelberc and his brothers Poppo, Reinolt, and Volcholt of Gelhendorf; Hertuinc of Bernrvit; Rupert of Stein; Marquart of Gunzendorf; and Roho, Rupert’s brother. [Note: [Col. 1329D] Here, for the first time in our charters, nobles designated from places occur. [Col. 1330D]]

Therefore, that these things and whatever else has been bestowed upon the monastery either by us or shall afterward be bestowed by Christ’s faithful may stand confirmed by apostolic and royal privilege, [Col. 1329C] granted through our diligence; and that whoever through unjust usurpation takes anything from the Church or alters its privileges may be struck with eternal anathema and held guilty of lèse-majesté: we authenticate this charter, written concerning all these matters, by the impression of our seal, that, with the Lord’s favor, our enactments may be strengthened for all time.

In the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the twelfth indiction, on the second day before the Nones of May. Happily accomplished. Amen.

### XIX. Record concerning the same foundation and the grant of parochial right.

[From the same archive.]

Let the community of our age and the succession [Col. 1329D] of all posterity know how Otto, bishop of Bamberg, founded the monastery of Michelfeld in honor of Saint John the Evangelist and enriched it, to the extent of his ability and knowledge, by various revenues acquired at his own expense. Wishing also to show the place an affection of great devotion, so that it might be more freely frequented by all fellow provincials, he granted it the benefits of confession, communion, baptism, and burial, at the abbot’s discretion, with the assent of Regelo, parish priest of Velden.

Given on the estate of the same Church of Michelfeld, [Col. 1330A] in the presence of the following witnesses, whose ears were drawn [Note: [Col. 1330D] In the Bavarian custom.]: Eberhard, provost; Egilbert, dean of the greater church; Sefrid, chaplain; Regilo, parish priest of Velden; Wernher, chaplain; and many others.

In the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1330D] Read 1119, as above, or the indiction must be changed.], the twelfth indiction, on the second day before the Nones of May. Happily accomplished.

### XX. The same Otto establishes the parish of Michelfeld.

[From the monastery archive.]  
*(6 November 1121.)*

Let it be known to all Christ’s faithful, both present and future, how much benefit is conferred upon all by one who labors in building monasteries. And because it is our will to provide in every way for the peace and prosperity [Col. 1330B] of those who serve God, we ought especially to strive in those places where the diligence of our labor or the necessary support of expenses or estates is established. Among other things, since the site of the monastery of Michelfeld shines as a kind of illustrious monument of our labor, we have specially dedicated that place to him whom the Lord Jesus Christ had made worthy, by the special prerogative of the chastity of his love, of the proclamation of his own affection. And because it is our purpose to raise up and enlarge that place in every respect, so that we may provide for both those now present and those to come far into the future, we have transferred by our authority to the same monastery the church of Saint Leonard, built by a certain chaplain of ours named Herold and adjoining that monastery.

That the place itself may be frequented by all with a more abundant zeal of affection, we decree that the people of all adjacent villages, which are also under the jurisdiction of that monastery, shall receive in the same church all the ordinances of the Christian faith from the person whom the abbot permits. To make all these things more secure, lest any adversary in the future should attempt to violate or invalidate them, we confirm them by ban and mark them with the impression of our seal. Witnesses to all this were Herold, canon of the greater church; Wernher of Erhinbach; Sefrid, chaplain; and the bishop’s ministerials Ezzo of Burgelin, Stercher of Muchindorf, Eberhard of Lapide, Wolfram of Zudinruit, Hadmar of Dornhach, Henry of Churtinruit, [Col. 1330D] Hartwic of Plez, Sigbot of Turndorf, and Erchenbert of Hanbach.

In the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the fourteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of November. Happily accomplished.

### XXI. Stern letter of Adalbert II, bishop of Mainz, to Otto concerning his absence from the synod.  
*(1122.)*

ADELBERT, by God’s grace, though unworthy and humble, minister of the holy Church of Mainz, to OTTO, his beloved and venerable brother, bishop of Bamberg: [Col. 1331A] brotherly love in the Lord and prayers.

That your fraternity has hitherto lived praiseworthily before God and men, and that during this schism you have labored greatly for the Church against heretics, is doubted by scarcely anyone. Therefore, the more ardent we have long known your zeal toward God and the Church to be, the more we now wonder—though we say this without prejudice to brotherly charity—that you appear less devoted to God and the Church and have in some sense grown cold. For a great door has now been opened to us for the recovery of ecclesiastical unity; our good contest, with the Lord’s cooperation, has now reached its end; and now it is especially necessary for us and all orthodox believers to exert ourselves with the utmost diligence, [Col. 1331B] so that what was long ago well begun by us may, in God’s name, obtain the desired result.

We previously informed your affection that you should wish to meet the legate of the holy apostolic see, our brother fellow-bishops, and the other Catholic princes at the place called Plefeld, and to be present with us at the ordination of the bishop of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1331D] Namely Roger, from 1122.]. You ought certainly to have come to it with a ready and cheerful mind even without invitation, not only because he is your fellow bishop, but also because he is your fellow citizen, and by right of kinship you ought in some way to love him more familiarly and specially. But because you neglected to come, the lord cardinal wished, with the consent of the others, to suspend you from the divine office until satisfaction had been made. We, however, for singular love and [Col. 1331C] reverence, fearing lest anything harsher should be determined against you, scarcely obtained that no harsher measure be decided against you.

Now, therefore, we request your fraternity, and by the authority of the lord pope, of the legate of the apostolic see, and of ourselves command you, to present yourself, with every excuse removed, at the general council to be held at Mainz on the Nativity of the holy Mother of God. [Note: [Col. 1331D] It was afterward held at Worms in 1122.] There you may learn the lord pope’s legation and take counsel with us jointly concerning the condition of the Church. If any bishops neglect to attend this holy council, let them know that by the authority of the lord pope, of the legate of the apostolic see, and of the whole council, they are subject to the synodal sentence by which such presumptuous persons ought by every means to be punished.

### XXII. Charter of Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg, for the foundation of the monastery of Aura.  
[Note: [Col. 1331D] There exist, from Frisius in the proofs of the *History of the Bishopric of Würzburg*, no. 29, vernacular versions; we now give them from the Salian book of Thrimberg in the original language.]  
*(1122.)*

[Col. 1331D]

I, OTTO, by the sole grace of almighty God humble bishop of the Holy Church of Bamberg, wish all Christ’s faithful to know how, in contemplation of God, for the propitiation of [Col. 1332A] my sins and in memory of the late gracious Emperor Henry, whose alms I profess myself to have been appointed by God to administer, and also for the remedy and salvation of all my successors, I began to construct at the place called Uraugia a monastery of Saint Lawrence. With divine grace consenting, I completed and consecrated it, dedicated it to the auxiliary patronage of the saints, endowed it with immovable goods, then enlarged it with other revenues, gathered there certain servants of God, provided them and their successors in divine service with necessities for perpetual support, and afterward confirmed it by episcopal authority.

And since, in the year 1108 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the sixth year of our episcopate, with the prior concurrence of the consent and counsel of our clergy and other faithful men, I began that building, brought it to completion five years later, and solemnly dedicated it, as stated above, in honor of the holy martyrs Lawrence and George, I enriched it suitably through the hand of the advocate Starcher. I also transferred to the relics of those same holy martyrs certain chapels, villages, fields, forests, pastures, waters and watercourses, vineyards, persons, and absolutely all other benefits which had hitherto appeared to belong to the aforesaid castle or estate. This estate, once widely renowned, was so built up with structures and fortifications that Duke Ernest of Eastern Francia, dwelling in the strong castle there—as may still plainly be known from its visible traces—[Col. 1332C] [Note: [Col. 1331D] Collector’s note. These traces are still visible today: various arches and pinnacles which enclose on one side the ancient court of the church and what is now the cemetery of Aura. Other monuments also remain: enormous stones, basins, and arches with lilies and eagles, many of which we have accurately drawn. All these are most safely referred by those knowledgeable in antiquities to the tenth century.] made his residence there with his household; and his lineage has not yet died out.

Therefore, lest this grant might ever be deemed injurious by our successors, or through envy—God forbid!—be imputed by any other person as in some way unjust, we restored that estate with its attached properties, whose yearly proceeds at this time were accustomed to yield only seven pounds in annual revenues, by a much better exchange. For we acquired with great labor the castle of Albinstein with all its appurtenances, and the estate immediately adjoining it called Hovestat, and transferred and granted them thenceforth as property to our Church. Thus we caused this exchange to be confirmed by a firm stipulation, indeed by the protection of written apostolic and imperial consent. In addition, we granted to the same monastery, without the objection of any person, certain gifts purchased from our own income, title to them being conferred by the common suffrage of the law of nations, and assigned them to the perpetual service of supporting this monastic congregation.

[Col. 1333A] Wherefore we humbly beseech all successors of our order generally and each of them individually, by the exalted name of the Lord Sabaoth, by the power granted by God to Saint Peter, and by the victory of Saints Lawrence and George, to conform themselves altogether and in every way to this our intention; to protect that place with paternal goodwill; and to extend the helping hand of protection to Christ’s poor dwelling there, so that in all these things they may deserve to share with us the fruit of eternal recompense from this work. May he deign to grant this whose kingdom and majesty endure unceasingly from ages unto ages.

The witnesses are Everhard, provost; Egilward, dean; Thammo [Thaimo], provost; Udalric, custos; Dudo, scholasticus; Ruschelin; Volmar; and Heriman. Laymen: Arnold of Cunstat and his brother Werenzo; Ratlac and his son Migger; Gundelacus of Obirsteineveld; Henry of Weida; Adalbero of Wiselach; and many others.

Done at Bamberg in the year of the Lord 1122, the fifteenth indiction, in the reign of the younger Henry.

### XXIII. Grant by Bishop Otto to the monastery of Saint Michael.  
*(Before 1123.)*

[From the monastery cartulary.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Otto, by God’s grace bishop.

Because matters whose origin is unknown easily pass into oblivion, their sequence ought to be recorded in writing [Col. 1333C] lest their memory escape human minds in the course of succeeding times. Therefore we wish the page of this present charter to make known to all, present and future alike, how the estate at Altenholfeld passed from the hand of Adelold Walpoto into our jurisdiction, and to what uses it was assigned by us, lest, through ignorance of what was done, anyone hereafter be permitted either to suppose something different concerning it or perhaps to dispose of anything from it to less useful effect.

When Udalric Walpoto had deserved to be bound by the chain of anathema on account of his offenses, shortly afterward he ended his present life under that excommunication. While still alive, he had arranged with his brother Adelold that, from his goods, the estate of Damesdorf, [Col. 1333D] where a church stands, and a mill with two other holdings in Dalenvelt should be given to the monastery of Saint Michael on the Mount for the remedy of his soul; so that after his death he himself might receive burial there and the brethren might remember him more devoutly in the fellowship of their prayers and almsgiving.

But when, after his death, he was not permitted burial because of the sentence of excommunication, his brother Adelold approached us and, after taking counsel, transferred to us the estate of Altenholfeld to be possessed by free and absolute right, so that he might obtain for himself a benefice, and for his deceased brother burial through release from the bond of the ban. He therefore obtained what he wished, but he kept back from the monastery [Col. 1334A] of Saint Michael the offering which his brother had arranged. We, however, reduced the estate transferred to us into our possession and lordship by right of ownership, and afterward, upon deliberation, bestowed it without any opposition upon the altar of Saint Michael, so that one perpetual lamp may always be maintained from it there, and that the Lord may deign to grant us eternal light with his saints.

We entrusted the care and defense of that allod to Walter of Streitberg, on the condition that he should be preeminent over the peasants not by the right of an advocate but through a defender’s mercy, oppressing them by no force and injuring them by no unjust exaction. Witnesses of this matter are Eberhard, provost; Egilbert, dean; Udalric, custos; Tuto, scholasticus; Count Reginboto; [Col. 1334B] Count Storker; Arnold of Chunstatt; Ezzo of Willhalmerstorf; Billinc of Memenstorf; and many others.

### XXIV. Letter of Pope Calixtus II to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, confirming monasteries constructed by him.  
[Note: [Col. 1333] From the archive of the monastery of Michelfeld; but incomplete in Ludewig, *Script. Bamb.*, p. 427.]  
*(3 April 1123.)*

Bishop Calixtus … to his venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We ought not only to favor the good undertakings of our brethren, but also to encourage their minds toward them. Therefore, most reverend [otherwise, dearest] and venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, moved by your petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and his Roman Church, to be defended against the wickedness of evil men, the monasteries of Saint John the Baptist at Regnisdorf; Saint John the Evangelist at Michelinvelt; [Col. 1334C] Saint James at Entisdorf; Saint Lawrence the martyr at Vrowa; and Saint George the martyr at Bruviningen. You built these at your own expense and, after granting them to the Church of Bamberg, sought to have them strengthened by the protection of the apostolic see.

For we decree that the possessions, estates, and all goods which your fraternity has bestowed on those monasteries for the love of God, which have been granted by the just offering of other faithful persons, or which may hereafter be justly and lawfully acquired or offered, shall remain secure and inviolate to them by God’s favor. Let them receive the ordinations of their abbots or monks from Catholic diocesan bishops. Yet we decree that the care and administration of the affairs [Col. 1334D] of those monasteries shall remain in the power of you and your successors.

Let no person, therefore, have license rashly to disturb these monasteries, or to take away, retain when taken, diminish, or harass their possessions by reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for those for whose support and governance they were granted, to be beneficial to their uses in every way. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

Written by the hand of Gervasius, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman [Col. 1335A] Church, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus.

### XXV. Encyclical letter of Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg, to the abbots and provosts of monasteries which he either founded or restored, exhorting them to fulfill their office.  
*(About 1123.)*

Otto, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Bamberg, to his venerable brother Wulfram, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael; Wigand of Tharisi; Baldewin of Banz; Eggehard of Aura; Imbrico of Michelfeld; Walchun of Entisdorf; Eribo of Pruveningen; Frederick of Gengenbach; Eberhard of Schuttern; [Col. 1335B] Otto of Stein; Lingerius [or Liuger] of Regenstorf; Ingram of Arnolstein; the provost of Clunicken; the provost of Hosterhoven; and all those who live devoutly under them: greeting and steadfast service in God’s will.

When we first undertook, though unworthy, the governance of pastoral care, we carefully considered the condition in monastic observance of the monasteries subject to our Church; but we found them all far too lax from the strictness of their discipline. Grieved by this, and judging it unsafe for our administration, we laboured long and greatly, pouring out prayers to God that, through divine providence—which does not err in its ordering—this might be changed for the better. At last the God of hosts, from whom comes every good thing [Col. 1335C], regarding the prayers of the humble, bestowed an increase of religious observance in all our monasteries: for He chose you as suitable shepherds for His flock and multiplied the number of your brethren in holy life. This is shown on the nearby Mount of St Michael: whereas we found there no more than twenty brethren, and those under a scant discipline, we now, thanks be to God, see more than seventy there, apart from those living honourably outside.

Therefore, being greatly gladdened, we address all of you, prelates and subjects alike, in holy charity, humbling ourselves at the feet of all in God and for God, and beseeching you to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, and to preserve, as one succeeding another by hereditary right, the rigour of your religious observance and spiritual discipline unto length of days [Col. 1335D].

To preserve the memory of so salutary an exhortation, we add a decree of our episcopal confirmation, to be sent, copied, and read in each monastery. The spiritual warfare of monastic observance—pleasing to God, acceptable to men, renowned among angels, dreadful to enemies—which we have renewed and established throughout all our monasteries under the authority of the Holy Spirit, we sanction and decree henceforth to endure whole and inviolate. We commend it, under the witness of Christ and the Church, to you chosen rulers and beloved brethren, and through [Col. 1336A] you likewise to be commended to all your successors.

Henceforth, in the name of the Lord, we bless you; for God is my witness how I long for all of you in the bowels of Christ. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1335] We discussed this letter and its date in the Life of Otto, § LXV.]

## XXVI. Letter of Bolesław III, Duke of Poland, inviting St Otto of Bamberg to the conversion of Pomerania. (About 1123.)

[Anselm Meiller, *Life of St Otto*, p. 106.]

To his lord and most beloved father Otto, venerable bishop, Bolesław, duke of the Poles, offers the humble devotion of filial obedience.

Because I remember that in the days of your youth you conducted yourself before my father [Col. 1336B] with most becoming honour, and because now too the Lord is with you, strengthening and blessing you in all your ways, I am minded—if it does not displease your dignity—to renew our former friendship and, with the grace of God assisting, to employ your counsel and help alike in advancing the glory of God.

For you know, I think, how the savage barbarism of the Pomeranians, humbled not by my power but by God’s, asked to be joined to the Church through the washing of baptism and to be admitted to it. But behold: for three years I have laboured, because I have been unable to induce any suitable bishops or priests connected with me to undertake this work. Therefore, since your holiness is proclaimed ready and untiring for every good work, we ask, most beloved Father [Col. 1336C], that you not shrink, with our service accompanying you, from undertaking this labour for God’s glory and for the increase of your blessedness. I too, the devoted servant of your fatherhood, will provide all expenses, travelling companions, interpreters of the language, assisting priests, and whatever may be necessary. Only deign to come, most holy Father.

## XXVII. Pope Callixtus II confirms all the institutions of St Otto. (13 April 1124.)

Callixtus . . . to his venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg. . . .

The commands of the holy Fathers and canonical enactments show that the estates and possessions of churches—which are rightly called the offerings of the faithful, the price of sinners, [Col. 1336D] and the patrimony of the poor—ought neither to be sold nor alienated. For things dedicated to the service of the divine majesty and to the use of heavenly mysteries ought not to be brought under another’s right and changed into the form of another service. Indeed, to speak in the words of blessed Symmachus: we do not permit possessions which anyone has given or bequeathed to the Church by his own will to be alienated under any titles or transfers, or under whatever pretext.

Accordingly, assenting to your just petitions, we sanction by the confirmation of this present writing that the holdings assigned to the service of your episcopal table shall remain in future times in the state in which they are known to have been well arranged by you [Col. 1337A]. We decree that none of your successors, nor any person, may sell them, assign them as a benefice to laymen, or convert them to other uses. Rather, as you have ordained, from each of the aforesaid holdings one denarius shall be contributed each year to the Church of Bamberg, for the soul of Emperor Henry, its founder, to provide the lamps. Moreover, no person shall hereafter have the power to alter the abbeys and houses of regular canons which through your diligence have been established in the order of religious observance, or other things rightly instituted by you. But if anyone should presumptuously dare to act against this our confirmation, let him be bound by the bond of excommunication.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April, in the second indiction.

## XXVIII. [Note: [Col. 1337D] Compare the Chronicle of Ursperg, under the year 1125, and above in the Life.] Account of the apostolate of St Otto, bishop of Bamberg, in Pomerania. (1124.)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124, in the second indiction, while Pope Callixtus II presided over the Roman See, Otto, by God’s grace eighth bishop of the Church of Bamberg, inflamed with the fire of divine love and strengthened by the authority and assent of the aforesaid apostolic lord, undertook a mission to the pagan regions of the Pomeranians, together with certain cities of the land of the Lutici, to recall them from the error of paganism and bring them to the way of truth and the knowledge of Christ [Col. 1337C], the Son of God. With the Lord’s help they were converted and baptized; he built and consecrated churches.

Then, according to the institutions of the holy Fathers, he taught them to observe the following: that on the sixth day they should abstain from meat and milk, according to Christian custom; that on the Lord’s Day they should refrain from every evil work and come to church to hear the divine office, there applying themselves diligently to prayer; that they should observe with all care the feasts of the saints together with vigils, as they should be instructed; that they should strive most diligently to observe holy Lent by fasts, vigils, almsgiving, and prayers; and that on the holy Saturdays of Easter and Pentecost they should bring their children to baptism with candles, a white garment called the *vestis candida* [Col. 1337D], and accompanying godparents; and that, clothed in the garment of innocence, they should bring them daily to church until the octave day of that same Saturday and endeavour to attend the celebration of the divine office.

With stern rebuke he also prohibited them from killing their daughters, for this abomination was especially prevalent among them; likewise, from holding their own sons or daughters at baptism, but instead they were to seek godparents for them, and to maintain faith and friendship with godparents as with blood relatives. He also forbade anyone to marry his comother—that is, the mother of his godchild—or his own kinswoman within the sixth and seventh degrees [Col. 1338A]; each man was to be content with one wife. They were not to bury Christian dead among pagans in woods or fields, but in cemeteries, as is the custom of all Christians; nor were they to set stakes at their graves. They were to cast away every rite and corruption of paganism; not build houses for idols; not consult female diviners; not practise divination; nor eat anything unclean: neither carrion, nor what had been strangled, nor food sacrificed to idols, nor the blood of animals. They were not to associate with pagans, nor take food or drink with them or in their vessels, lest in all these things they resume the customs of paganism.

He also enjoined them, while they were healthy, to come to the priests of the Church and confess their sins; but in sickness to call priests to them and, cleansed by pure confession, receive the body of the Lord [Col. 1338B]. He established also that they should perform penance, according to canonical ordinances, for perjuries, adulteries, homicides, and other grave offences; that they should be obedient in every Christian observance and religious duty; and that women after childbirth should come to church and receive the priest’s blessing, as is customary.

## XXIX. St Otto confirms a donation made to Michelfeld Abbey. (March 1125.)

[From the monastery archive.]

Let it be known to all who wish to know how Charles of Smalenahe, upon the altar of St John the Evangelist, gave to the monastery of Michelfeld a holding with a mill in a certain settlement called See. Because he had first endowed this place among laymen and had secured burial there for himself, Otto, bishop of Bamberg, confirmed that freehold to the same monastery under the obligation of the *bannum* and strengthened it by the impression of his seal, on the very day when he himself personally committed Charles’s body there to burial.

[Note: [Col. 1338D] Otto, then returning from Pomerania, stopped at Michelfeld monastery. Consult the Life.]

The witnesses to this matter are Ezzo of Burgeline, Starcher of Mutechendorf, Wolfram of Zudenruit, Hademar of Dornbach, Sigeboto of Turndorf, Erchenbrecht of Hannebach, and Gelphrad of Chungesteine.

## XXX. Letter of certain bishops and princes inviting St Otto to appoint a new king in Henry’s place. (1125.)

[Col. 1338D]

Adalbert of Mainz, Frederick of Cologne, Ulrich of Constance, Bucco of Worms, and Arnold of Speyer, by God’s mercy archbishops and bishops; Ulrich, abbot of Fulda; likewise Duke Henry [of Bavaria], Duke Frederick [of Swabia], Count Palatine Godfrey, Count Berengar of Sulzbach, and the other princes of both estates who attended the emperor’s funeral: to their venerable brother Otto, bishop—on the one hand, brotherly prayers in Christ [Col. 1339A]; on the other, the most faithful service of devoted obedience.

After the lord emperor entered upon the way of all flesh and we completed his funeral rites with due devotion and reverence, the very order of events and the circumstances of the time seemed to demand that we confer somewhat concerning the condition and peace of the realm, if the counsel of your presence and of the other princes—useful and most necessary in so great a business—were not absent. Since it was burdensome and difficult to await this, all of us resolved, provided only that it not displease your agreement, to hold a court at Mainz on the feast of St Bartholomew; and there, with the princes assembled, to settle, as the Holy Spirit should inspire, matters concerning the condition and successor of the kingdom and necessary affairs [Col. 1339B].

[Note: [Col. 1339D] Here I think I have detected something resembling a capitulation.]

Yet we do no injury to your deliberation and will, nor do we claim anything singular or private for ourselves in this matter. Rather, we especially desire that this be made known to your judgment, so that, mindful of the oppression under which the Church together with the whole realm has laboured until now, you may invoke the providence of the divine disposition, that in appointing another person it may so provide for His Church and the kingdom that henceforth they may be free from so great a yoke of servitude, that the Church may be allowed to use her own laws, and that all of us with the people subject to us may enjoy temporal tranquillity. We also earnestly entreat your affection to establish peace for the people entrusted to you from heaven, until the prescribed date of the court and for four weeks thereafter [Col. 1339C], so that the coming together and return of all may be safer; and that you may assemble in courtly fashion, namely according to the custom of the ancient princes, at your own expense and without injuring any poor person.

## XXXI. Letter of Adalbert of Mainz summoning Otto of Bamberg to a synod. (About 1125.)

ADELBERT, humble minister of the holy Church of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop, lord OTTO, beloved in Christ: greeting and the service of brotherly love.

The tribulations and devastations of the Church of Würzburg—what they are, how great they are, and how long they have lasted—have long since become known to your judgment. They have multiplied to such a degree [Col. 1339D] that, unless the almighty and merciful Lord provides for them soon, that Church will in the near future be wholly annihilated. Therefore, if means permitted, we should especially desire the presence and counsel of your brotherhood [Col. 1340A], in order more diligently to deliberate, as far as divine mercy grants, concerning the restoration of its peace and religious order.

Indeed, this is the counsel of the brethren who are with us and whom we have been able to convene in person or by letter. Since our venerable brother and fellow bishop Roger [Note: [Col. 1339D] In the year 1125; see *Bishops of Würzburg*, p. 60.] has entered upon the way of all flesh, let us provide for that Church by promoting Brother Gebehard, so that we may rather gather together in an orderly manner what has been scattered in that Church than, by imposing another upon it, allow what has been grievously scattered to be utterly uprooted.

Therefore we admonish you in brotherly charity to present yourselves at the assembly of our brethren [Col. 1340B], whom we have summoned for this purpose, on the approaching feast of St Luke. Or, if you are altogether unable to do so, do not delay sending letters of your consent to carry out the counsel which the Holy Spirit shall dictate to you. Farewell, and remember us in your prayers.

[Note: [Col. 1339D] There appears to be no mention anywhere of this apparently omitted synod. In the same work, p. 307, another summons of our Otto to a synod at Mainz is read, in the case of Otto, bishop of Halberstadt, who had set out his unhappy situation to our Otto in letters, earnestly seeking his help. He nevertheless could not prevent this man from later being deposed for simony, as is mentioned in the same place.]

## XXXII. Letter of Otto, bishop of Bamberg, on the restoration of Banz Abbey. (1127.)

[From the archives of Banz and Vinar.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Otto, humble eighth bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg. Since the supreme and essentially good Shepherd has deigned to entrust the care of His holy sheepfold [Col. 1340C] to our humility, we ought with wakeful heart to love, foster, and increase the progress of spiritual life, and, to that end, instruct and assist the vows of the faithful by word and example. Accordingly, we have looked with paternal favour upon the church of monastic profession founded and built in the castle of Banz by Countess Alberad, of blessed memory, for the redemption of her soul and of all her people; she assigned it, together with all its estates, to my lord St Peter in this place of Bamberg through the hand of her *mundiburdus*, Margrave Hermann. Neglected by its prelates and desolated in spiritual and temporal goods, we intend by every means to renew it and raise it into an ecclesiastical state.

[Note: [Col. 1340D] Elsewhere (*History of Würzburg*, p. 310) we traced the first origin of this monastery to the year 1058: it was begun by Countess Alberada, then already a widow, and completed in 1069 with her second husband, Margrave Hermann of Vohburg. The reviewer of our history of the bishopric of Würzburg (*Jena Literary Journal*, 1795, vol. III, p. 658) calls Alberada the daughter of Margrave Otto of Schweinfurt, who was also duke of Swabia in 1048; but he assigns to her Henry of Landsberg of Bavaria as her first husband—on what authority, he does not say. See above, no. 40.]

And lest the purpose of our good will should once again run to no effect [Col. 1340D], we appointed there as abbot Baldwin, a man of proven worth and suited to every good work, joining to him faithful and religious men. We solemnly dedicated that church in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, in the seventh indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, in honour of St Peter, prince of the apostles, and the great and precious martyr Dionysius.

On that same day, in accordance with the tenor of her testament and the faith of the ancient grant, with the counsel and testimony of our pious men and ministerials, we enumerated, assigned, and confirmed all her goods to that Church: namely Muggeburg with all its appurtenances, movable and immovable, villages, meadows, woods, pastures, roads and trackless places, revenues and returns; and the whole of Banzgau situated between the Itz and the Main, with its villages, woods, and boundaries—except the estates and benefices of the ministerials, and except Mount Stekkiltze and the estate of Grodeze with its appurtenances [Col. 1341B], and the forest of Banz. Nevertheless, the abbot of that place has free power in the forest to cut wood and pasture animals. Whatever goods of that church, within the bounds of the Muggeburg estate or in any part of its possession, had been usurped and alienated on any pretext or contrivance by our ministerials or other persons through unjust benefices—indeed, through predatory permissions—we caused, by diligent care and frequent expenditure, to be acknowledged and restored to it. We also protected by a divine ban against invasion by others all its property, whether in the places listed, in Volckaba and Cloden, or wherever situated, as the Lord’s portion.

Later, considering that the aforesaid Mount Stekkiltze was a suitable stronghold for importunate and wicked men in support of their madness [Col. 1341C], and providing for future security, we restored it to that church as a perpetual possession under a privilege and suitable witnesses, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1127, in the fifth indiction, while the most glorious Emperor Lothair reigned. The witnesses to this matter are Eberhard, chief provost; Egilbert, dean; Tuto, master of the schools; Eberhard; Uodalric; Count Reginboto; Count Stercker; Babo; Thiemo; Arnolt; Starker; Luipolt; Liupolt; and many others of clergy and people.

We also made this firm agreement with the abbot: that neither through him nor through any of his successors shall it pass to another person by sale, exchange, or benefice [Col. 1341D]. To him likewise and to his successors, by the authority of God and our own, we gave this command and counsel: that from the estates presently held, or to be acquired in future through the offerings of the faithful or any event, no benefice be granted to anyone except for the reason of greater advantage, apart from the hereditary benefices of their faithful men; and that they should strive to redeem and clear even these when the circumstances of person and time make it expedient.

When these matters had been so arranged, and that planting of Christ’s faithful was advancing in divine and human increase through our labour and the diligence of its abbot, the annual services due to the advocates, which were said to have been established for them from paternal inheritance out of the brothers’ cellar, were being paid not without great harm to the household’s resources. Therefore, at the request of the venerable abbot himself, we obtained from Count Rapoto, who was then its advocate [Col. 1342A], that he should relinquish into our hands all right which he asserted was owed him from that abbey. We granted him this as a permanent benefice: that each year two talents should be paid by the abbot of that place to him and his heirs, in satisfaction of the whole service due. We make known and commend all these things as a perpetual memorial to our successors and sons, that they may know and consider that, because of the faith and merit of their founders, and following the example of our humility, they ought to benefit and preside over the Church of Banz with special favour, without prejudice to its privilege of freedom in the canonical election of its prelate.

And that all these things may remain ratified and inviolate, and that no rash person may infringe them [Col. 1342B], we ordered this charter to be written and strengthened with our seal, anathematizing and binding under episcopal ban all who should prove violators of what has here been conveyed or confirmed. The witnesses of our agreement with the advocate are Egilbert, dean; Tuto, master of the schools; Uodalric, custos; Gerunck, dean of Tuirstat; Count Stercker; Count Reginboto; Helmrich; Adelbero; Poppo; Diepolt; Arnolt; Rinmunt; Gotefrit; and many others of the clergy and people of Bamberg.

## XXXIII. Letter of Wigand, abbot of Tharisiensis, urging St Otto to return from Pomerania. (1127.)

[Col. 1342C] To his lord and dearest father, gracious Otto, bishop and apostle of the Pomeranian people, Wigand, unworthy overseer of the monastery of Tharisiensis, offers service worthy in all things and the spiritual duty of prayers.

Blessed is God, Father of mercies, Father of lights, who, forming you from the womb, gave you as His servant for a light to the nations, that through you His salvation might be proclaimed to the ends of the earth and the dark hearts of the gentiles be illumined by the light of faith. Therefore Mother Church rightly rejoices in the new increase of her children, while through your ministry many thousands of the barbarian nation are reborn in holy baptism; the worship of idols is cast aside, their shrines destroyed, churches rebuilt, and the true God is adored and worshipped.

[Col. 1342D] Therefore, after the Gospel has been proclaimed to strangers and the work of so great a ministry completed, as the shepherd returns to his own sheep the whole flock comes joyfully to meet him: clergy with people, and a procession of monks receives its father with singular joy, singing with gladness of heart and voice of exultation: “Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you” (*Song of Songs* 6). But I, the least of them all, though second to none in wholeness of faith and love, came into Saxony about the feast of St Maurice, hoping for my lord’s most desired arrival, so that I might be the first to welcome him whom I had been the last to escort. Yet when your messenger returned, my hope of expectation was disappointed, although I was much rejoiced at the certainty of your return. What I could not do in bodily presence [Col. 1343A], I endeavoured to do first in a spirit of humility, greeting my lord—not merely with the sound of my mouth but also with the most ardent joy of my heart—thus:

> Hail, great Father; speak freely, speak reverently;  
> Speak, I pray, in verse: hail, illustrious bishop.  
> You return, awaited hope of the people, choice of the clergy,  
> Worthy giver of law, sure remedy of the flock.

We do not wish you to be unaware, most holy Father, that since you departed, a day of distress and tribulation has always hung over us. For the tyrant Conrad [Note: [Col. 1343D] Later king and successor of Lothair.] remained almost the whole year in Nuremberg castle and devastated the nearby goods of your bishopric. He took part of the grain from your revenues, ordered a rent to be paid to himself, and twice captured the bailiff of Rustall, stripping him of all his possessions. Moreover, he is said to have attempted by cunning contrivance to seize the city of Bamberg [Col. 1343B], but thanks be to God, his wickedness did not prevail. Conrad the custos and I, being attentive to the administration entrusted to us, assigned garrisons and guards to the city together with your other faithful men, paid the soldiers wages as required, and diligently managed everything else that you committed to us.

A great war is being waged between Hermann and Frederick; various ambushes are laid on either side; robbery is repaid with robbery and fires with fires. Amid these events, the village beneath Botenstein, together with its church, was burned. One night Frederick secretly entered the fortress of Niestein with his soldiers and began to act boldly. But those within the castle sent missiles and hurled stones, killed one of his men [Col. 1343C], wounded several, and thus he barely escaped with all his men, his undertaking unsuccessful. Furthermore, many evils rage throughout the province; everything is laid waste by plundering and fires. Therefore, hoping that your arrival will put an end to so many evils and miseries, each one of us cries out, all of us cry out: “Come, lord, come; hasten, do not delay; come, longed-for one, whom we have awaited amid the darkness of so many tribulations.”

The rest of your affairs in Bavaria and Saxony proceed quite prosperously. But concerning the matter specially entrusted to me, I wish your fatherhood to know that we have purchased copper to the amount of seven hundred centenaria and more, three hundred of which we have brought with the greatest difficulty as far as Smalchalten. Now, our strength exhausted, we await with ardent longing the help of your hand [Col. 1343D], and can scarcely await the return of your holiness, so earnestly desired by the whole realm.

## XXXIV. Letter of Adalbert II, bishop of Mainz, to Otto of Bamberg concerning the excommunication of Conrad, invader of the realm, carried out in 1127. (About 1127.)

Adalbert, by God’s grace archbishop of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg: greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 1344A] We have long since informed your brotherhood by our letters of the excommunication which, with the counsel of our brethren and princes, we pronounced against the invader of the realm. But because we doubt whether the letters reached you—for we have heard that your church wishes to disregard them—we send these present letters again, admonishing you to do what we have done and order throughout all your churches that this author of iniquity, together with his supporters, be excluded from Christian communion and every divine office.

[Note: [Col. 1343D] Those are mistaken who refer this to Emperor Henry V and to 1119. Although he was excluded from communion by the bishops, he was by no means an invader of the realm; that description belongs to Conrad of Hohenstaufen, of whom the preceding letter speaks.]

## XXXV. Letter of Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg, to Otto and the canons of Bamberg concerning their dean, elected patriarch of Aquileia. (1128.)

[Col. 1344B] To his venerable brother O[TTO], bishop of the Church of Bamberg, C[ONRAD], by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Salzburg, offers the affection of devoted prayer and the service of obedience.

When your dean, our brother and most worthy fellow priest, was elected to the Church of Aquileia to the dignity of episcopal eminence, we believed that the foulness of the old corruptions which had long prevailed there had been removed. For, when a person altogether unworthy of ecclesiastical government had been cast aside, we saw clergy and people consider the appointment of another so honourably and canonically and elect with remarkable unanimity such a man as whose person, learning, and life truly presented to us a suitable bishop. In his virtue the Church of Bamberg [Col. 1344C] is adorned and honoured; and, should it be necessary to place hope in him again with greater confidence, we do not doubt that fruits of virtue and discipline will be found in the Church in which we have tasted such sweet first fruits in this man.

Yet, as appears, the sins of the Aquileians are not yet fulfilled. With the same faithlessness which they formerly exercised against that useless offshoot Gerard [otherwise Richard], on account of his wickedness, they now continually rage and make a treacherous tumult against this man canonically elected and therefore rightly to be received, on account of his uprightness, which all ought to embrace. Thus they show that, when evil men chose what was good, it was not their own choice but God’s; and by persecuting an innocent man they make it most evident that their purpose was to choose one like themselves [Col. 1344D]. He endured their malice as patiently as was fitting, rebuked it as gently as circumstances permitted, and then, when obedience was denied him by the clergy, prudently withdrew under an honourable pretext. Thus he gave proof of outstanding virtue and moderation and brought upon the transgressors the reproach of deserved shame.

Now, unable to bear his absence calmly if he should depart, we asked him to remain with us until the insolence of the raging men was corrected and they should acknowledge their elect and seek him again with due reverence. But, fearing that because of the neighbourhood of the places some suspicion might harm his reputation in this matter [Col. 1345A], we could not keep him. Retaining in peace the deposit of his virtues among us, we let him go, beseeching you, both for the sake of ancient friendship and for the glory of honour gained by him and by us, to love him as a brother, honour him as an elected bishop, and protect him as a necessary man. In him we have found nothing but piety and honourableness; and it will be necessary that he be restored anew to the work to which he was called.

### The same letter to the canons of Bamberg

C[ONRAD], by God’s grace, whatever he is, of the Church of Salzburg, to all the brethren of the canonical church of Bamberg: prayer with affection, every good thing with health.

When the tree which was uselessly occupying the ground had been cut down in the Church of Aquileia [Col. 1345B], we were anxious lest the wickedness of the clergy should introduce into the vacant see someone like it, or indeed worse. Then suddenly our lord and brother E[GILBERT], your dean—a man distinguished for uprightness and worthy of every honour—was put forward to receive the priestly mitre. We rejoiced that through his virtue and prudence, exercised in good arts, all our anxiety had been banished. Indeed, to speak truthfully, the honour of your Church is greatly exalted in him, since so useful and outstanding a person is known to have been nurtured there. Since we have experienced in him nothing but what befits an ecclesiastical person, delights the good, and offends the wicked—namely, uprightness in worldly affairs and devotion to God, through which he has also displeased the Aquileians—it is rightly fitting that [Col. 1345C] he be honoured and loved by you and all the children of the Church because of the great testimony to his uprightness: that he has displeased evil men. Blessed Gregory says: “To have displeased only evil men is great commendation from the good.”

## XXXVI. St Otto of Bamberg is invited to the Council of Würzburg for the reception of Pope Innocent. (1130.)

To his brother Otto, venerable bishop of the Church of Bamberg, greatly beloved in Christ, Brother Walter, humble minister of the Church of Ravenna, and Brother Gerard, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, legates of the Apostolic See, offer greeting and every good.

[Col. 1345D] We believe that your brotherhood knows that our lord Pope Innocent sent us with his letters both to the king and to the princes of the realm. The king received us with love and honour, but deferred his response until consultation with the princes. Among them we believed that your brotherhood would hasten first, or among the first, to the court in service of the Church; for among the other bishops of the German realm our mother, the Roman Church, has loved you with a certain prerogative and, creating you as a special son, has blessed you with her own hands. Therefore we ask your affection and command you, in that faith and devotion which you owe to your mother the Roman Church, to put aside every occasion and excuse and come to us as soon as possible. Standing with us in the cause of the Church as [Col. 1346A] a faithful and catholic man, receive and obey the legation of the lord pope together with his letters, in union with the other brethren.

## XXXVII. Invitation of King Lothair

Lothair, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to Otto, his beloved and faithful bishop of Bamberg: his favour and every good.

Because of the pressing and most necessary affair of Church and kingdom to be considered at Würzburg by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we regret your illness, which has delayed your coming to us; for we now especially need the judgment and counsel of your prudence for the work of Church and kingdom. But because strength is made perfect in weakness, we admonish you and most earnestly ask you, in that charity which you owe to the Church, for which by God’s grace you have always laboured devotedly [Col. 1346B], that if you cannot come by another vehicle, you hasten to come at least by boat to us and to the assembly of your venerable fellow brethren and fellow bishops, who await your desired arrival with us at Würzburg. Farewell.

## XXXVIII. Foundation charter of the monastery of Heilsbronn by St Otto of Bamberg. (1132.)

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. OTTO, by God’s grace bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg, to all the faithful of Christ.

Because we remember that we have received from Christ our Redeemer [Col. 1346C] the supports of temporal life, it would be unworthy if we did not also perform such good works as we can to the praise and glory of that same Redeemer. Therefore we wish it to be known to all how we purchased, for a fitting price, an estate at Heilsbronn from Count Adelbert, his brother Chunard, and their three sisters, and gave it to Blessed Peter in the Church of Bamberg, in whose service, by God’s authorship, we are engaged, through the hand of Adelbero of Tagestetten. Moreover, so that, with the Lord’s help, the purpose of our desire might be accomplished in the aforesaid place—namely, that we might establish there the order of monastic religious life—we built there a basilica in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, together with monastic buildings; [Col. 1346D] and, having summoned brothers thither and appointed for them a spiritual father, we raised that place to the status of an abbey. We also gave to that same monastery, through the hand of Wignand of Beerbach, for the use of the brothers, the estate at Adelstorf, which we bought for 195 marks from a certain Dieteric, his sister, and Eberhard, as well as from Irmingard and her children. Likewise, Heilsbronn, Witramdorf, Erlehe, Obpendorf, Velsendorf, and Pecemannesdorf.

We therefore confirm these properties to the aforesaid monastery by the present written instrument, ordaining that whatever possessions or goods that same religious house now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the concession of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, [Col. 1347A] shall remain firm and inviolate for ever to that monastery and to the brothers serving God there.

Certainly, we designate no special advocate for that religious house; rather, we decree that the advocate of the altar of Blessed Peter of the principal church shall be its defender. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact, for the benefit of the brothers there serving the Lord. If anyone, however, should attempt in rash presumption to act contrary to this our constitution, and, when admonished, does not correct his offence, let him know that he is bound by the bond of our ban and is to be dragged with this [Col. 1347B] chain before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be granted the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ and everlasting dwelling with God’s elect in the heavenly kingdom.

The witnesses to this matter are: Adelbert of Tagestetten; Adelberecht of Dahspach; Frederick of Hergoltispach; Heinrich; Eberhart; Megingoz of Otlohesdorf; Otnant of Esenowa; Ezzo of Burgelin; Uro of Willehalmisdorf; Gernot and his son; Rudolf of Putendorf; Macelin and Berhtolt of Husen; Wolfram of Stetebach; Chunrat of Nuisaze; Dietmar of Hohenekke; Egino of Chrigenbrunnen. Among the canons: Egilbert the dean; Chunrad the custos; Dietpert; Udalric the Tall; Volmar; Sefrid [Col. 1347C]; and many others.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1132, in the tenth indiction, in the reign of Emperor Lothair; enacted happily at Bamberg.

### XXXIX. [Note: [Col. 1347D] We restore this charter, corrupted in the printed editions, from the monastery’s cartulary.] St Otto gives to the monastery of St Michael the chapel or cell of St Faith. 25 May 1137.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. OTTO, by the disposing mercy of God, eighth bishop of Bamberg.

Because a matter whose cause is unknown is easily consigned to oblivion, the sequence of deeds done ought to be impressed in writing, lest it slip from the memory of successors. Accordingly, we wish it to be known to all [Col. 1347D] how, prompted by divine love, we built a cell on the western side of the mountain of the blessed archangel Michael, in honour of the Lord and of Blessed Faith the virgin, and gave it, with all its appurtenances, to the monastery of St Michael. In this we wished indeed to provide for both places: so that service might be rendered to one, while the other should not lack assistance in its need. We also obtained from the venerable Abbot Hermann and the other brothers of the aforesaid monastery, and they established it in perpetuity, that they should assign seven brothers and two lay brothers to that cell, who should keep daily watch there in the divine service [Col. 1348A] and attend to their own needs both outside and within.

For their support we bestowed upon that place these estates: Vellendorf, Tragamusil, and Gissital, which, together with the church, serfs, and mill, we bought from Richpert of Saxony for eighty marks, and entrusted to Count Gebehard of Sulzbach for protection. Likewise Silwiz and Grunowa, which we bought from Luitpold of Kirchendorf, together with a ministerial named Bertolf, who holds from that allod two hides as a benefice; these hides, after the death of Bertolf himself, shall belong to St Faith, as shall the rest, because he has children not by a wife of equal rank but by an outsider. We entrusted those goods to Count Bertolf of Blassenberg under his *mundiburdium* [protective guardianship]. [Col. 1348B] Likewise, the estate at Chemtmerice, which we afterwards exchanged for Klucowa, Kumele, Dornowa, Bucha, Revit, Streitruit, and one hide at Goren; these we acquired partly from Count Regniboto of Giech and from our ministerial Eberhard for a fitting price [Note: [Col. 1348D] The parenthesis is absent from the cartulary.], and partly bought from Eckebert of Saxony for forty marks. In addition, we granted to his wife Bertha and his daughter the benefice which that same Eckbert had held from our Church. Count Popo is advocate of those properties. Likewise, the estate and benefice of a certain Thiemo at Alren, Eppental, and Timenreut, which we redeemed from Thiemo himself and his heirs for forty-five marks. Furthermore, we gave to the same cell of St Faith [Col. 1348C] the hospital of St Gertrude, which is on the other side of the river, with its estates, Mirinhule and Potechendorf. We received both from Hermann of Bramberch in exchange for the benefice of his brother Stephen; Hermann himself holds the advocacy of those properties. Likewise, at Schlurispach, sixteen hides together with the church, its endowment, and a mill, which we entrusted to Count Ratpoto for protection. This is the allod which Sigeboto of Wundingesaze gave us in exchange for the advocacy of Holveld and for the benefice which Waldo, husband of his sister, held in addition to Utzingen and Wunckendorf; these too we gave to the same hospital. Of these, we entrusted Utzingen to Arnold of Chunstat and Wunckendorf to Frederick of Luitenbach for protection, ordaining [Col. 1348D] that, from these as well as from the aforementioned estates, six denarii should be given daily to the hospital itself, by which visiting pilgrims may be fed.

Certainly, we granted the advocacies of all the aforesaid properties to the aforementioned persons upon this condition: that they administer them personally, without sub-advocates. They shall not hold a court with the tenants except in cases of assault, theft, breach of a field-boundary, or if they are summoned by the provost or prior. Each peasant shall work five days in the year for his advocate. We gave the same cell to the aforesaid monastery of St Michael with every right belonging to it: that is, male and female serfs, churches, villages, buildings, yards, approaches and revenues, cultivated and uncultivated fields, things acquired and to be acquired, meadows, pastures, roads and trackless places, waters and watercourses, millstones, mills, fisheries, woods, hunting rights, and every benefit whatsoever that may arise from them. We decree that henceforth no person shall have power, on any pretext, to remove that cell with any of its appurtenances from the jurisdiction of that monastery. For the brothers dwelling in that cell, we obtained from the abbot, out of St Michael’s goods, about thirty *jugera* [Col. 1349A] of cultivated and uncultivated land around the cell itself, for making gardens and orchards or other things necessary to their use.

Therefore let no one rashly violate what we have ordained for the honour of the divine [Col. 1349B] name. Let the statutes of our humility remain unshaken through every age. Let none of our successor bishops be permitted to violate them; for their preservation they ought to hope for an eternal reward. We trust in His mercy that He will rather increase than diminish what we have bestowed from love of Him for the use of those serving God. But if anyone attempts to act against these provisions, he shall sin; and, if admonished, he does not correct his offence by fitting amendment, he shall bear the punishment of his wrongdoing at the Lord’s judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that cell, and who provide it assistance from their own gifts, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ and eternal recompense in everlasting life. And so that these things may be known to posterity, we caused the present charter [Col. 1349C] to be drawn up, confirmed it by our ban, and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The witnesses to this matter are Eberhard the provost; Egilbert the dean; Conrad the custos; Tuto the schoolmaster; Pero; Henry; Udalric; Sifrid, canons; Hatho; Bernolt; Hartnit; Gerunch; Megindach; and the other parishioners; Count Ratpoto; Walpoto; Adelber of Steina; Arnold of Cunstat and his brother Wirnt; Heinrich of Hofstete; Pabo of Schonebrunnen; Hermann Otgotz of Lizendorf; Pillunc of Mamesdorff and his brother; Gundeloch; and many others.

Given and confirmed in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1137 [Note: [Col. 1349D] The edition incorrectly reads 1127.], on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, Tuesday, at the synod [Col. 1349D] of Bamberg, in the presence of clergy and people.

### XL. Another donation of the same Otto to the same monastery, made in an uncertain year.

[From its cartulary.]

In the name—Otto, bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg in name only, sends everlasting greeting in the Lord to Christ’s faithful.

Because a matter whose origin is unknown is easily brought into contempt, the sequence of deeds done ought to be impressed in writing, lest it slip from the knowledge of posterity. Therefore we wish it to be known to those both future and present how our venerable Gotefrid, priest of the Church of St Ratisbon, bought for sixteen talents from a certain Nizo and his heirs, Eggehard and Ludewig, an estate at [Col. 1350A] Santae, situated near Wacherode in the county of Count Rapoto, and in our presence gave it with his own hand beneath the altar of St Michael on Bamberg mountain. The condition was that, while he lives this present life, the brothers should be served from its revenues on the anniversary of his mother; but after his death the commemoration shall be transferred to himself. He also offered, with great devotion, to the Blessed Archangel on that day a new chasuble handsomely adorned with gold embroidery, an alb with stole, and a chalice. The venerable Abbot Hermann, together with his brothers, granted the same Gotefrid participation in their full fraternity, so that whatever is bestowed upon any one of the brothers, living or dead, shall be rendered to him in perpetuity [Col. 1350B]. In order that no doubt may arise concerning these things and that they may remain firm and unshaken through succeeding times, at the brothers’ request we caused the present little charter to be written and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

### XLI. Fragment of letters of St Otto, bishop of Bamberg, concerning the foundation of the monastery of Vessera. (1138.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. OTTO, by God’s grace bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg.

Because a matter whose origin is unknown is easily brought into contempt, therefore the sequence of deeds done ought to be impressed in writing, lest its memory slip away to posterity. [Col. 1350C] Accordingly, we wish it to be known to those both future and present how Count Godebald of Honneberg, with his wife Luckhard and by the unanimous consent of his heirs, for love of Christ and for the everlastingness of holy life, released into religious use a place of his own property, which took its name, Vessera, from a certain river, and assigned it to divine service. Establishing there a monastery of regular clerics, he requested that it be dedicated under the patronage of the Blessed Virgin Mary, etc.

### XLII. Letters of St Otto, bishop of Bamberg, concerning the foundation and confirmation of the monastery of Ensdorf. (1139.)

In the name— I, OTTO, eighth bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg [Col. 1350D], to all Christ’s faithful.—

We wish all Christ’s faithful, both future and present, to know how, with the Lord’s cooperation, at the request, consent, aid, and counsel of Count Palatine Otto of Wittelinespahc, we provided for the selection, in the bishopric of Ratisbon beside the Vils, of a place on his estate called Ensdorf, for the salvation of souls. There we built a monastery in honour of almighty God and St James the Apostle, for men living according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, who, by the favour of God’s mercy, are to remain there for ever. In order that this might be firmer and more stable [Col. 1351A], the aforesaid Count Palatine Otto, at our counsel, made that place subject to Blessed Peter, with the intention and agreement that under so great a protection and defence it might be safeguarded and defended from every unjust injury of adversaries. And indeed, by prudent counsel—[lacuna]—a place of refuge may be made manifest.

Accordingly, we notify our own faithful and all the faithful that, through the hand of the advocate, namely the aforesaid Otto, we assigned certain estates to that monastery with every right according to Bavarian custom, and granted them to the servants of Christ dwelling there for food and clothing. These are: Gigant, Gunemars, Gemundi, Lesan, Stresenhoven, Droschenreit, Mulendorf, the mill of Popenreut, Potensteine, Wihesteine, Fridrichesreut, Hasalahe, Schupphe, Chunesbac, Stettebahc, [Col. 1351B] Eschenbahc, Erlebahc, Sugast, Gotesfridesmale, Stadele, Chrandorf, the mill of Steinenla, Erlebahc, Jacobsreut with its mill, the new mill, and meadow with newly cleared land beside Jacobesreut. In Nittenowe wood, twenty-five hides; Rechart; Turne; and on the same estate, four mills; Messenberge with its mill; Eichaha; Hage; Sicenhoven; Drushingen; Hovestetin; Uffheim; Pabenhoven. The aforesaid Count Palatine granted to that monastery these estates: the estate on which the place itself was founded, with the adjacent manor of Wilinbahc; Berengotesrewt with vineyards; Kelwelinc; and Udelscalchesberc.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, second indiction. These acts were performed happily at Bamberg in the second year of King Conrad III and the thirty-second year of the episcopate of Lord Otto. [Col. 1351C] Amen, amen, A.

### XLIII. Ordinance of St Otto, bishop of Bamberg, concerning certain tithes granted to Ensdorf monastery. (Year uncertain.)

OTTO, bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg in name only.

We wish it to be known to present and future generations what was afterwards done with the tithes of newly cleared lands belonging to our church and located in the bishopric of Ratisbon. We had redeemed these from that bishopric by a just exchange and given them to the monastery of St George at Prüfening. Therefore, while the brothers of that monastery possessed these tithes without disturbance and no one brought a claim against them, the venerable Abbot Aribo of that place, with his brothers, considered that they had already many times been troubled by the household of Ratisbon concerning this [Col. 1351D] question. [Col. 1352A] Looking to their future, since they did not wish to endure any longer the annoyances of so many disturbances, they came humbly to us and most earnestly requested that we take those tithes back for our own use. We entirely refused to do this, since we knew that those same tithes had been confirmed to that monastery by the privileges of two apostolic popes, namely Calixtus and Innocent, and also by the authority of three bishops of the Church of Ratisbon—Hartwic, Chuno, and Heinrich.

When, therefore, they could not bend our assent in this matter, they resolved among themselves by common counsel not to touch those tithes at all, and that no one should presume, on any pretext, to bring even the smallest portion of them within the monastery enclosure. When we learned this, [Col. 1352B] we sent to them our venerable brothers Wignand Tharisen and Eberhard of Biburg, to urge them on our behalf with brotherly feeling to retain in peaceful right the tithes which no one was challenging. Yet all of them, from the greatest to the least, opposed this proposal, and unanimously affirmed that they would never comply with such advice or bring anything from those tithes into their monastery.

At length, after taking counsel with our church, in accordance with the tenor of their request, we took those tithes into our own hand, lest they be lost to both us and them, and divided them among other monasteries. In this distribution, before the undersigned witnesses, we gave to the monastery of St James at Ensdorf, for the perpetual [Col. 1352C] benefit of the brothers, these tithes: in the parish of Schlichten—Sweikersrewt, Hemmensigile, Pappenberch, Pernrewt, Sigifridesrewt, Unterloch, Ronahe, Karmanfelden, Schefloe, and three other small villages belonging to it. The witnesses were: Eberhard the provost; Egelwert the dean; Ruzil the provost; Cunrad the custos; Tuto the schoolmaster; Udalric the Tall; Starcker of Muttendechendorf; Ezzo; Gundeloch; Pillunc; Wilhalm; Rudolf; Chunrat the chamberlain; Eberhart; and many others.

### XLIV. Pope Innocent II confirms the religious observance introduced by St Otto into his monasteries. (23 January 1139.)

Innocent, etc.

[Col. 1352D] “Whenever that,” etc. See under Innocent II below, no. 353.
