[Col. 1351] The following letters were published by Eccard, but without a date, in *Corpus Historicorum Medii Aevi*, vol. II, p. 329 and following.

### XLV. To E., the Schoolmaster.

[Col. 1351D]

O[TTO], by God’s grace bishop of the Church of Bamberg; E., provost; A., dean, with the whole congregation of St George, to E., a man devoted to scholastic learning: the affection of paternal and fraternal love.

[Col. 1352D] Because, while you still lived among us, we learned by experience the character of your conduct, your way of life, and the maturity of your liberal studies, we unanimously set our hopes upon you and invite you to become one of us. For while you were with us, we understood your constant and faithful labour [Col. 1353A] in the office entrusted to you, so that it could readily be observed what you desired for us and for our Church; indeed, though set over many things, you then promised to be faithful in few. Since we are deprived of a master for the schools, we send to ask you, by our old friendship, that the proof of your affection may be the performance of the work. We ask that you make yourself readily available in this matter and in no way delay coming to us soon. If anything impedes this haste, we prescribe this definite term for you: without doubt, meet us at Mainz during the September fast.

### XLVI. To *** a cardinal.

To the most worthy cardinal of the Roman see, O[TTO], by God’s grace bishop-elect of Bamberg, offers his most devoted endeavours of both the inner and outer [Col. 1353B] man.

Since, endowed with divine intelligence, you are a hinge and bulwark of holy mother Church, we deem ourselves blessed that in so great a crisis we may consult the authority of your holiness. Let your charity know, therefore, that we have received from the apostolic lord letters of paternal consolation. For this reason we have taken care to append a copy of them for you, so that you may the more confidently accede to our requests. We earnestly entreat you: having more carefully examined the clause by which we are ordered to advise the metropolitan to carry out the duty of his office, give us counsel free and worthy of your authority. For you have not forgotten the command of the apostolic lord imposed through you upon the metropolitan: namely, [Col. 1353C] that he should refrain his hands from the consecration of bishops. Consequently, to seek consecration where we are certain that we cannot obtain it is a frivolous matter, altogether like vanity. Therefore let the authority of your compassion assist us in this difficulty, so that through your intervention an opportunity may be given us to obtain from the archbishop of the see of Mainz the favour which the lord pope deigns to show us. For if, in consideration of our service, you take pains to strive on our behalf, he will not deny you a letter of recommendation for us to carry, on behalf of the Roman see itself, to the pope. May your fatherhood also deign to instruct us concerning this matter, so that we may answer the apostolic lord fittingly concerning the book of acts of the Council of Nicaea. Certainly, we find nothing concerning these matters in our library: neither the twenty chapters decreed [Col. 1353D] in that synod nor the names of the bishops assembled from different parts of the world.

### XLVII. Letter of bishops to Otto, bishop of Bamberg.

To their venerable brother and fellow bishop, Bishop OTTO: C., bishop of Salzburg, and E., bishop of Münster, by God’s grace, such as they are, offer devoted and heartfelt service together with prayers.

Since the princes have gathered at court to destroy the calamity which has overwhelmed the kingdom, we wonder and deeply grieve that you are not present, when in this affair no one could be more necessary to us. Therefore you ought not to withdraw your person on any pretext, since you ought all the more to labour with us for the peace and tranquillity of Church and kingdom. We therefore earnestly, with due affection, admonish and ask your dignity, setting entirely aside every pretext or excuse, still to endeavour to come, knowing that all the princes desire and await your presence.

### XLVIII. Letter of Hermann, bishop of Augsburg, to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, concerning King Lothair.

To OTTO, venerable bishop of the Bambergers and good fragrance of Christ and of the Church, and to his whole Church: HERMANN, humble minister by God’s grace of the Church of Augsburg, with all his clergy and people, offers devout prayers in Christ together with faithful service.

[Col. 1354B] May the Lord look from His holy seat; may every Church of those in heaven and on earth, and especially the Church of Bamberg, consider us—that Church which has always hitherto set itself as a wall for the house of Israel, which has always been consumed by zeal for God’s house. May it incline its ear and hear; may it open its eyes and behold our tribulation. For behold, our city has been laid waste: a holy and ancient city, hitherto called Augusta, but now more fittingly to be called *angusta* [narrow, distressed], or *angustia* [distress]. It sits in sorrow, and there is none to comfort it except our God and those who fear God. For God’s sake, let them compassionately share in love our sufferings, which we endured at the entrance of the lord king. At his coming we awaited peace, and it did not come; we sought good things, [Col. 1354C] and behold, disturbance—our sins indeed demanding it, the sins which we committed not against him but against God. We received him when he came to us with the honour due to him and with joy—we, all our clergy, and people—as king and lord, as him in whose hand are kingdom, power, and dominion, as a just and merciful judge through whom we hoped to recover a peace long lost.

Passing over, therefore, the many and great miseries and injuries of our Church, we complained with tearful voice in the hearing of the lord king and the princes who were present of one sacrilegious outrage which had occurred a few days before the king’s arrival. Certain of our citizens had gone out from us—men not of noble stock, wicked, criminal sons—who, under our escort and almost in our very presence, had despoiled the bishop of Aachen, legate of the apostolic see, as he was passing through our territory to the king’s court. Concerning these matters, I say, we complained before the whole court and humbly demanded the justice owed to kingdom and Church.

While the princes were occupied with this and were taking counsel concerning it, a small quarrel over a trivial cause suddenly arose, through the devil’s contrivance, between sellers and buyers—first among the king’s secretaries in the suburb. Then a great shout arose; the outer-city bells were rung; citizens ran together; the king’s soldiers assembled; all hurried to battle; all were ignorant of the cause of battle; one supposed one thing, another another. The king himself suspected that death was being plotted against him. [Col. 1355A] Seeing the soldiers and ministerials of the Church standing armed before the mother church, he believed that they had gathered by design against him. Yet, as we truly say in the Lord, they had met not through any conspiracy made against the king, but, because of the uproar of the people, had rushed together suddenly and without deliberation, not knowing what they should do; for they too had no doubt that through someone’s machinations they had been betrayed into the king’s hand.

Meanwhile I, unworthy and bishop in name only, forgetful of my years and old age, unmindful of life and death, supported merely between the arms of two of my clerics, the rest having taken flight, cast myself into the crowd between the two battle-lines. I was not protected by shield or helmet, but was clad in sacred [Col. 1355B] vestments and armed with the sign of the cross. For in memory of the Lord’s Passion we carried the crucified one before our breast with our own hands, hoping that we might restrain Christians—as was fitting, mindful of Christ’s cross—from mutual wrong and fraternal slaughter. Immediately, on the Lord’s Day, five days before the Kalends of September, the king and his men rushed upon us and ours. A sacrilegious slaughter of clerics and laypeople took place near the doors of the mother church, within and without, from the sixth hour of the day until evening: very many were killed, very many wounded, very many taken captive, very many put to flight, very many despoiled. Yet I escaped safe through the sign of the cross, crawling on hands and feet amid enemies and dangers, amid swords, arrows, and missiles flying from all directions about my grey head, neck, sides, [Col. 1355C] and back, and about those of my companions. They did not merely carry me, but dragged me by arms and legs, bringing me by another entrance, with the greatest difficulty, over the high wall before the high altar and into the *scunarium* [term uncertain]. There I lay pitiably, pouring out not prayers only but tears, amid the blood of the wounded, awaiting the shedding of my own blood and desiring death.

Meanwhile, outside the city gate, slaughter of people and cattle likewise raged between the men from outside and the king’s soldiers; estates were laid waste and fires spread destruction; sanctuaries were profaned; many churches were burned, many broken open and plundered; communities of clerics, monks, [Col. 1356A] and nuns were stripped and scattered; enclosed women too were miserably expelled; men and women were shamelessly stripped naked; their children were partly killed and partly led away captive. For what we say with sighs from the innermost depths of our hearts is this: the Christian king brought upon Christ’s Church enemies of Christ—inhuman and pagan men, namely Bohemians and Slavs, commonly called Valuwen—who are openly known to all always to have been, and to be, persecutors of Christ and of the Church. Night ended the conflict; but throughout the night the king’s army surrounded the mother church with a siege from every side. That night I myself was driven from my lodging, stripped of all that was mine, and lay abandoned and alone, weeping for a long time in the very street [Col. 1356B] of our city, until, through God’s mercy, I was taken in by Lord N., archbishop of Magdeburg, into his lodging as a guest and pilgrim.

At daybreak, the king dragged away from the besieged church whomever and as many as he wished; and, to say nothing of the rest, he took away with him in chains even those who were wounded and wholly beyond hope. The same day he pitched camp in the field beside the city; and on the third day, returning armed into the city, he demolished and shattered every fortification of the city. When everything had been consumed by plunder and fire, on the fourth day of our destruction and the sixth after his arrival, he departed gladly. The archbishops, bishops, and abbots present had repeatedly warned the royal majesty [the supplied *praemenuerant* is read as *praemonuerant*, “had warned beforehand”] [Col. 1356C] at least to spare the defeated according to royal custom, and, imitating the King of kings, not to destroy the righteous with the impious. But the wrath of royal power was not calmed until our whole city, without judgment and without justice, was utterly destroyed and irretrievably annihilated. Therefore we, with all the clergy and people of our city, entreat through Christ and in Christ the venerable mercy of your fatherhood: compassionately share our griefs, and, tirelessly supporting by counsel and aid the lamentable ruin of our Church, strive, according to your customary manner, to set yourselves as an unconquerable wall for the house of Israel.

[Col. 1355]

### SERMON delivered by St Otto to his first Church, founded in 1124, delivered at Pyrzyce in Pomerania when he was returning to Bamberg from it for the first time.

[Note: Andrew the Biographer, published by Gretser in volume X of the new edition, p. [Col. 1356D] 620, places this sermon of St Otto, delivered to his nascent Church in Pomerania, after the beginning of the first conversion about 1124–1125; but in precisely which year it was delivered is of no consequence. What matters is that Catholics may [Col. 1357D] know what faith Otto, invited into Pomerania by the duke and sent by Pope Calixtus II, preached to the Pomeranian neophytes: namely, a thoroughly Catholic faith, such as Catholics profess in this eighteenth century. Besides these doctrines proclaimed by St Otto, Uspergensis recounts laws of discipline and morals, corresponding to our own, prescribed to the neophytes and derived from the discipline of the German Church. Secondly, I have assigned this teaching, delivered in Pomerania before an assembly of neophytes, whether at Pyrzyce, Demmin, or Usedom, so that the honoured world may see the shamelessness and calumny [Col. 1358D] both of Daniel Cramer in the *grossen Domerschen Kirchen-Chronico*, deservedly rebuked and refuted by Gretser in volume X of the new edition, who dared to write that Christ was not preached to the Pomeranians by St Otto but papist superstitions; and of other non-Catholics, who do not cease, even in this century, to attack with polished buffooneries and calumnies the life and preaching of the most holy apostle, notwithstanding the most illustrious contemporary testimonies collected by Gretser and by the Bollandists for 2 July.]

[Col. 1355D] Brothers, I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy (2 Cor. 11). For all of you who have now gathered to hear me, and who, through my teaching, have believed in Christ [Col. 1356D] and become Christians, have been betrothed in the Lord as one Church to my Lord Jesus Christ through faith. You are all, I say, one Church, [Col. 1357A] the one and only bride of my Lord Jesus Christ, because through faith you have been incorporated into the universal Church. But since, by His grace, I seem to be the agent of this your betrothal—for “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Cor. 7)—therefore I am jealous over you, yet not with just any jealousy, but with God’s jealousy. For there can also be evil jealousy, according to the Apostle: “There are some who are jealous over you, but not rightly” (Gal. 4). To be jealous is to be disposed to indignation, although I find it sometimes used to mean “to emulate,” as in: “Be zealous for the better gifts” (1 Cor. 12). But I wish to be indignant with you, and am prepared to be indignant with you: this is what I said before, “I am jealous over you.” For I cannot and shall not be able to bear it without grief and indignation if, God forbid, to the injury of [Col. 1357B] my Lord Jesus, to whom I betrothed you through faith, you should wish again to defile yourselves with foreign gods. For this is a kind of fornication which most of all separates one from God.

Brothers, attend. Behold: all of you have been baptized into Christ, and all have put on Christ (Gal. 3); you have received from Him forgiveness of original and actual sins; you are clean and holy—not cleansed and sanctified by us, but by Him—because He washed away the sins of the world with His own blood. Therefore do not defile yourselves again by the worship of idols. For this is uncleanness by which God is utterly offended, and which wholly separates one from God. Do not prostitute yourselves to corrupting and unclean spirits. Render divine honour to God alone, your Creator, and to no creature; [Col. 1357C] lest His indignation and wrath come upon you. Rather, advance in faith, hope, and love, so that His blessing may come upon you and your children, and so that, believing in Him and adorning faith with works, you may have life in His name—He who called you from darkness into His marvellous light (John 5; 1 Pet. 2). For you must be certain and in no way doubt that if, by His help, you strive to preserve until the end of life the innocence and sanctification in which you are placed today, you shall not only escape eternal death but shall also possess for ever the joy of the heavenly kingdom.

But because this present life cannot be lived without sins—for “the life of man upon earth is struggle and temptation” (Job 7)—as I depart from you, I hand over to you those things which have been handed down to us by the Lord: the pledge of holy faith between you [Col. 1357D] and God, namely the seven sacraments of the Church, as it were seven sanctifying gifts of the Holy Spirit. By using them amid the labours and struggle of this life, your Church may not fail but advance [Col. 1358A] and repair its deficiencies. Therefore observe and hold them; and, so that you may know, carefully enumerate the things which we delivered to you as we departed from you.

The first sacrament, therefore, with which you have already been imbued, is most holy baptism. This sacrament, my brethren, you must henceforth and always hold fast and venerate; and you must present your little children for it at the appropriate time—namely, on the holy Saturday of Easter and at Pentecost—by the hands of priests, knowing most certainly that whoever departs this life without it will both lack the kingdom of God and, moreover, pay the eternal penalties of the original curse.

The second sacrament is confirmation, that is, the anointing with chrism upon the forehead. This sacrament is necessary for those who are to live: namely, that they may be strengthened by the fortification of the Holy Spirit, if they are to be armed for battle against all the temptations and wickednesses of life. It ought not, however, to be deferred until old age, as some suppose, but received in the ardor of youth itself, because that age is more exposed to temptations.

The third sacrament is the anointing of the sick, which is necessary for those who are dying because, in that anointing, forgiveness of sins is granted through the power of the Holy Spirit; and the person about to die is armed by the same power of the Holy Spirit to fight against spiritual wickednesses—that is, against malignant spirits lying in wait for souls at life’s departure. Every Christian in the agony of death ought to desire this most ardently and receive it most devoutly, as the surest remedy of the soul.

The fourth sacrament is the body and blood of the Lord. This sacrament is necessary both for those who are living and for those who are dying: whether we live or die, this viaticum must always be used. For it is the true food of the soul, possessing eternal life in itself. Therefore Masses ought frequently to be celebrated, and you must gather devoutly for them, so that you may communicate more often in this viaticum. But if, because you are carnal, you cannot personally partake of this most holy thing at every Mass, at least communicate through your mediator, namely the priest, who communicates for you, by hearing Mass faithfully, reverently, and devoutly. Yet you yourselves ought also three or four times a year, if more cannot be done, to make confession and communicate in the sacrament itself.

The fifth sacrament is, through penitence, the reconciliation of the fallen: that is, of those who, after baptism, having been cast out of the Church because of graver offences, are restored to it again by the satisfaction of penance. This sacrament is, as it were, a poultice and recovery for those who fall and are wounded in battle.

The sixth sacrament is marriage, that is, the marital union. The five preceding sacraments are, as it were, general, and necessary to every Christian. This one, however, is particular, because it is not necessary to everyone, but only to those who cannot remain continent. And just as all men must be drawn and invited to the preceding sacraments, so no one should be drawn or invited to this one except those who, as has been said, do not contain themselves but defile and stain themselves by promiscuous and unlawful intercourse. Such persons should be advised to meet their weakness by a more honorable remedy.

But you who until these times have been not Christians but pagans did not possess the sacrament of marriage, because you did not keep faith with one marriage-bed: those of you who wished it had several wives. This will no longer be lawful for you. One man ought to have only one wife, and one woman one husband; what is beyond this is from evil. Therefore, if any among you had several wives before baptism, let him now choose from them the one who pleases him most; having dismissed the others, let him have this one alone according to the Christian rite. And I hear that you are accustomed, O women, to kill female offspring; how great an abomination this is cannot be expressed in words. Consider whether even brute animals do this to their young. Let this parricide no longer occur among you, because it cannot be forgiven without the gravest penitence. Therefore, whether male or female, carefully rear your children. For it belongs to God to beget both male and female.

The seventh sacrament, therefore, is the ordination or consecration of clerics. This too is particular and not general, because it is not necessary for every person. For although all people need clerics, it is not necessary that all people become clerics. Yet those more fit in character and learning ought to be invited, rather than compelled, to this sacrament. Therefore I exhort and invite you—for I ought not compel you—that you commit some of your children to the clerical state, after they have first been diligently instructed in the liberal studies, so that through yourselves, as other peoples do, you may have clerics and priests of your own language who know Latin.

These seven sacraments, then—which I again wish to enumerate for your sake—namely baptism, confirmation, anointing of the sick, the Eucharist, reconciliation of the fallen, marriage, and orders, the heavenly bridegroom has deigned to transmit to you, his Church and bride, through us his humble attendants, as a pledge (*arrha*) of true love. Therefore keep, love, and venerate these sacraments with every honor and reverence. Teach them to your children, that they may hold them in memory and diligently observe them through every generation. Behold, you have a church; you have a priest who knows how to instruct you more fully concerning all these things and whatever is necessary for you. Hear him, therefore, as you have heard me, honoring and loving him and doing whatever he tells you. And now I go, soon to return to you again. Farewell in the Lord.

## Appendix

[Col. 1359]

### I. Assembly or Council in the City of Usedom in Pomerania

Under Duke Wratislaus and St Otto, bishop of Bamberg, apostle of the Pomeranians, sent by the pope, in the year of Christ 1127, the fourth year of Pope Honorius II, and the third year of King Lothair II.—At it the princes of Pomerania and the people, converted to the faith, were baptized by St Otto.

> [Note: The first journey of St Otto, bishop of Bamberg, into Pomerania, with the approval of Pope Calixtus II, occurred in 1124, on 24 April; he returned to Bamberg on 29 March 1125. His second journey from Bamberg into Pomerania occurred in 1127, certainly not later than 1128; under Honorius II he returned to Bamberg. He died on 30 July 1137. This synod was held after the second journey, about 1128. These details are from the *Acts of the Saints*, Antwerp edition, for 2 July.]

(Hartzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. III, p. 301.)

[Col. 1359D]

In this city of Usedom, because the feast of the coming of the Holy Spirit was near, Duke Wratislaus, wholly Christian at heart through Bishop Otto’s prompting, summoned the barons and captains of the entire province to an assembly in the city on the feast of Pentecost. At the same time he announced Christ’s cause: the Gospel and its evangelist, Bishop Otto, had come again.

Accordingly, when all had assembled on the appointed day and the bishop had been brought forward into their midst, the duke said: “Behold why you have come; behold, the messenger of the Most High is before you. He brings peace, not arms; he seeks to gain for himself not your possessions but you yourselves for God. Attend, I pray: four years ago, while teaching in the upper regions of this land, as I myself witnessed—and as you too know—he filled all things with the Gospel. At that time he wished indeed to visit these regions; but, by God’s favor, his affairs kept him occupied there throughout that whole year in holy works. When the year had passed, he was obliged to return to his own concerns, to the affairs of his own see, and could not come to you. But I ask you, together with me, to consider carefully the reasons for both this journey and that one.”

After the duke had delivered a long address to his people, Sefrid continues:

The grace of the Holy Spirit was present and implanted the duke’s speech in the hearts of all more deeply than can be expressed; and all with one wish and one consent answered that whatever the bishop advised should be done. Therefore, taking the occasion of that season, the bishop addressed them in a wonderful discourse concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit, remission of sins, the various gifts of grace, and divine goodness and mercy. He preached Jesus to them; and some, indeed, already Christians long before but again polluted by the error of paganism, softened by the present discourse into compunction and a firm renewal of heart, he reconciled to the Church by the laying on of hands, to the great profit of those looking on. Others, striving to offer themselves, he catechized, instructed as time allowed, and baptized. During that entire week he applied himself to teaching and sacred works with such great joy that it was certainly evident that the presence of the Holy Spirit was truly there. Thus this council was not dissolved until the princes themselves and all who had come with them had received the sacraments of baptism.

> [Note: From the contemporary Sefrid, in the *Life of St Otto*, book III, chapter 1, no. 124; in Canisius, *Antique Readings*, III. The same text, fuller and more accurate, appears under 2 July, p. 407, among the Antwerp hagiographers; again in Gretser, vol. VI of the new edition, p. 645.]

[Col. 1361]

### Sermon at the Funeral of St Otto

Delivered by Embrico, bishop of Würzburg.

(*Bishopric of Bamberg*, documentary appendix, p. 89, from Bollandists, July vol. I, p. 423.)

[Col. 1361C]

“What shall happen? What counsel will there be? Martha is dead. Behold where she lies. Who then will henceforth receive the Lord Jesus when he comes into this castle? Martha is dead—dead indeed—who used to receive him. The hostess of the Lord Jesus is dead, she who offered lodging to him when he came and set a table for him.”

Otto ministered with equal kindness and generosity, except that he not only ministered to Christ but was minister, host, and receiver of Christians. Who will stand in his place? Who will fulfill the office of this ministry? Who, I ask, will do what he used to do? He was greatly useful to every rank, every order, every person of the Church. Behold, there has died, to speak truly, a servant of the servants of God.

What will you do, monks? What will you do, clerics? What will you do, poor and beggars? Who will restore your mother to you? Where henceforth will you seek those maternal breasts, those motherly affections? Yet I tell you where you may seek them: nowhere will you find them. For the ages of his time had, I openly declare, this one man alone, this one man, of such great mercy. For, to pass over his other virtues, which were many and illustrious, he was so great in mercy and works of mercy that I can find no one at all among all those known to me whom I could compare with him.

But what shall I say? I grieve; again I say, I grieve for the condition of those accustomed to flee into this bosom of mercy. I grieve, to confess the truth, for my own condition; and, so to speak, I pity myself and am justly shaken by sorrow. For I have lost much help and much consolation in this friend. He was agreeable, well suited to companionship, and a great support to me. With him I was accustomed confidently and safely to share all my cares, all my affairs, and my deeper counsels. In brief, he was a great helper to me in all my needs.

I speak, certainly, of myself. For the entire order bearing my name—the episcopal order—will deservedly mourn when deprived of such a companion. He was our jewel, our glory, our splendor. At councils he illumined our assemblies as with the golden rays of his virtues. In him, as it were in an ancient book, we saw how we ought to live and what we ought to do; for holy examples and holy deeds teach more than words. But this teaching—alas!—is rare among men. All of us labor more to build up our neighbors by speech than by example; but he both spoke and acted by speech and example. Who can bear with equanimity that such a Martha has been removed from our midst? But I turn to higher matters.

Certainly, O Roman pontiff, head of the most holy Church, you will feel his death; and you, ruler of the world, king of Germany, Roman emperor Augustus, will experience the fall of this bishop. Both of you, most great ones, have been struck by a great loss: for that great ambidextrous Ehud has fallen for you. He has fallen who used either hand as his right hand, that outstanding leader of the people of Israel. He has fallen, I say, who was powerful and energetic, and readily willing to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s.

For you, O imperial Majesty, another pillar will not quickly arise upon which you may lean with such confidence. He supported you not only by riches and worldly prudence, but, what is greater than both, by holiness. By holiness, I say, and by the merits of his virtues he upheld both emperor and empire; for justice and holiness were in his right hand. No small thing has occurred; no small change has taken place in the Church of God. The death of such a man must not, therefore, be lightly borne. Where shall we henceforth find such genius, such prudence, such goodness?

But let us return to the monks; let us return to the spiritual people. Their losses cause us grief. What will become of them? What will become of the monks and poor who were accustomed to look to these hands? You mourn, I see, and weep for our Otto, and certainly not without cause; for he has fallen for you, he has been taken from you. You, O monks, were especially the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand. He was indeed the one who, out of the abundance of the rich of this world, was solicitous to supply your poverty.

He used to boast, with great authority, saying: “By despoiling the Egyptians I enriched the Hebrews.” For in truth, holy and religiously, he extracted much from secular people in order to relieve the want of spiritual persons. By a holy and religious fraud, so to speak, he outwitted the rich so that they made alms which they had sometimes not intended. For he was ingenious in divine gains, and the hand of the Lord was with him. Oh, how many rich men, with all their riches, did he bring over to the spiritual life! Whatever persons, things, or works he could take away from the world, he dedicated to God under the plea of piety and mercy. Why say more? His mercy was over all his works; the mercy of God was always before his eyes.

Pray therefore, most beloved brethren; pray more earnestly, that he too may obtain mercy today. Pray that the most blessed soul may today receive in reality that mercy of God in which he believed, which he hoped for, and which he loved. Certainly he did not receive with deaf ears that Gospel saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy”; and: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.” No one can be merciful who has not also been humble; therefore every merciful person is humble. Hence we may rightly infer that his spirit possessed true humility, proved before God, since he showed such great mercy.

Through the intercession of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, to whom he was always devoted; through the intercession of the blessed archangel Michael, whose church he is seen today to have restored and exalted, whom he chose as patron and protector for both his body and soul; and through the intercession of all blessed spirits, may his spirit obtain divine mercy. By their merits, I say, and by the merits of all God’s saints, if anywhere—as is natural to human frailty—his great works, his great acts of compassion and beneficence, have been tickled or stained by human praise or by an intention of human praise (for nothing is sufficiently pure before the supreme Judge), pray, I beseech you, pray more earnestly. Let us all pray together that he who takes away the sins of the world, the Lamb of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, may deign to abolish and remove this: he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages.

[Col. 1363]

### Babenberg, Ensdorf, and Lesser Augsburg Annals

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. X, p. 1.)

### Note

[Col. 1363]

Heimo, a priest and monk of the monastery of St Michael at Bamberg—[Note: He himself calls Burcard, monk of St Michael, to whom he dedicated the book, his brother and fellow-priest. Andreas Lang, abbot of that monastery, in his *Lives of the Saints of the Order of St Benedict*, among the manuscripts of the Royal Library of Bamberg, no. 57, assigns Heimo to that monastery (Jäck, *Description of the Manuscripts*, etc., vol. I, p. 10; vol. II, p. XIII). Yet in his chronicle of the same monastery, manuscript no. 58 (Jäck, *loc. cit.*, p. 11; II, p. XIII), and in the *Life of Bishop Otto* in Ludewig, p. 463, he writes that Heimo was a canon of St James outside the city walls. This seems to be supported by the catalogue of books brought into the library of St Michael by Abbot Hermann, who held office from 1123 to 1147; for no. 83 lists “The Consideration of the Years of the World and of Christ Jesus, written in 1135 by Heimo, priest in the church of St James outside the walls of Bamberg.” See Jäck and Heller, *Contributions to Literary History*, 1825, pt. I, p. XXIX.]—a man renowned among his contemporaries for his writings and, as they say, dear to Bishop Otto, was instructed by Bishop Bernard, the first apostle of the Pomeranians. In 1135 he issued a chronography intended to correct the computation of times from the beginning of the world down to his own age. For ordering the events of the sixth age, he employed Paschal cycles, to which he appended notices, drawn chiefly from Bernold and the Würzburg annals, down to his own time. He extended the cycles themselves to the year 1595. On this matter he speaks as follows:

> “Finally, from the Passion of the Lord until the year of the Lord 1135, which is the tenth of the reign of Lothair III, there have elapsed fifty-nine lunar cycles and fifteen years; forty solar cycles and sixteen years; two great Paschal cycles and seventy-two years; and seventy-seven cycles of indictions and thirteen years from the birth of Christ. Beyond this year, moreover, I have added 460 years, perhaps yet to come, to complete the third great Paschal cycle. In them I leave it to the posterity which shall follow to discover and determine the condition of future times. I humbly ask all who will read these things to deign to remember before the Lord Jesus Christ the sinner and humble priest Heimo, who have labored upon these modest works not for display of novelty but for the investigation of truth and the encouragement of the younger.”

At the end of the cycle he adds:

> “Thus ends the third great Paschal cycle from the Passion of the Lord. After its completion, should anyone then please, let him add to it as much as he wishes.—And you, most beloved brother Burcard, do not cease to pray for me, that, delivered from the pit of misery and the mire of worldly dregs, I may deserve to become a participant in this kingdom and in the fellowship of the saints.
>
> He has gained every point who has mingled the useful with the sweet.”

The book, after Heimo’s death four years later, was brought into the library of St Michael, and there it was enlarged with historical annotations for about forty years, but today it is lost. Two other manuscripts, however, survive:

1. One, copied from the Bamberg manuscript around 1180, was kept for at least three centuries in the Ensdorf monastery, situated on the river Vils near Amberg and founded by St Otto, bishop of Bamberg—[Note: See Otto’s charter of 1139 in Ussermann, *Documentary Appendix to the Bishopric of Bamberg*, p. 87; Andreas Lang, *Life of Otto*, book I, chapter 29, p. 423.]—and enlarged with historical notices. It was afterward transferred to Marmoutier near Saverne and is now preserved in the University Library of Strasbourg, where I examined it in 1841.

2. The other, a royal Munich manuscript, marked among the Latin folios with the number 2, seems to have been brought several centuries ago from the Augsburg church into the electoral Bavarian library. It contains the Augsburg continuation of Heimo, which we shall publish below, and also the Augsburg annals first brought to light in volume III of the *Scriptores*. I examined it in 1833. I have used these sources in the following way: from Heimo’s chronography, down to the end of the eleventh century, I present only a few notices; then all the remaining notices down to 1135; then the Babenberg and Ensdorf annals; and finally the Augsburg annals, by which a transition is prepared to the remaining annals of Swabia.

### From Heimo’s Chronography

[Col. 1365]

#### I.—From the Ensdorf Manuscript

[Col. 1365A]

**1006.** [Note: I noted, for example, in the tenth century: “915. Pope Lando, the 123rd, sat five months, and after him Leo VI sat two months. Then John X sat fourteen years and two months.”—“920. Henry I reigned seventeen years.”] The bishopric of Bamberg is founded by King Henry II [Note: I supplied “-cond.”], and Eberhard is appointed there as first bishop [cf. Würzburg Annals].

**1012.** The church of St Peter and St George at Bamberg is dedicated.

**1040.** Eberhard, first bishop of Bamberg, died.

**1096.** [Note: Misled by an error, he entered these things under 1092, beside which stands the year of the world 5116.] An expedition [Note: I supplied “Fa-.”] was made [Note: I supplied “cont-.”] against [Note: I supplied “du-.”] the Saracens under Duke Godfrey of Leuven.

**1098.** Jerusalem was taken [Note: I supplied “ca-.”].

**1100.** [This year the Order of St Bernard began; entered by a fourteenth-century hand.]

Paschal II, the 161st pope, sat nineteen years. He consecrated the pious Otto on 12 May, on the holy day of Pentecost, and gave him the pallium along with other privileges.

**1106.** Emperor Henry IV died. His son Henry V succeeded him and reigned after him twenty years.

**1119.** Gelasius II sat one year.

**1120.** Pope Calixtus II sat five years.

**1121.** [Note: The notices for 1121 and 1124, marked with one asterisk, are due to the twelfth-century Ensdorf interpolator.] [Our monastery here at Ensdorf began to be built.]

> [Note: It is useful here to add two historical notices drawn from folio 89 of the same manuscript and written in the twelfth century: “Conrad the subdeacon, a cheerful and lovable man, endowed with a certain wonderful and incomparable talent, weakened for some time in his limbs by the grave illness of paralysis and toward the end reconciled to the Church by Catholic men, completed the course of his present life in a good old age in 1122, on the third day before the Kalends of February. For the remedy of his soul, let all faithful persons, mindful of human frailty, pour forth continual prayers before the Lord.” “Engilger, canon of the church of Augsburg, ordained priest in the Lateran church, being truly Catholic, removed himself to Constance because of the imminent persecution, where the members of the Church, under Bishop Udalric, faithful defender of the Catholic faith, seemed safer. Alas, on 4 July 1121, he ended the pilgrimage of this life in the true confession.”]

**1124.** [Note: Or 1123 (?)] [Here it was dedicated by the venerable Otto, bishop and founder of Bamberg.]—[Watkunus, a monk from the monastery of St Blasius, a man of good life, is set over this place as first abbot; entered by a thirteenth-century hand.]

> [Note: It is useful here to add two historical notices drawn from folio 89 of the same manuscript and written in the twelfth century: “Conrad the subdeacon, a cheerful and lovable man, endowed with a certain wonderful and incomparable talent, weakened for some time in his limbs by the grave illness of paralysis and toward the end reconciled to the Church by Catholic men, completed the course of his present life in a good old age in 1122, on the third day before the Kalends of February. For the remedy of his soul, let all faithful persons, mindful of human frailty, pour forth continual prayers before the Lord.” “Engilger, canon of the church of Augsburg, ordained priest in the Lateran church, being truly Catholic, removed himself to Constance because of the imminent persecution, where the members of the Church, under Bishop Udalric, faithful defender of the Catholic faith, seemed safer. Alas, on 4 July 1121, he ended the pilgrimage of this life in the true confession.”]

**1125.** Honorius II, the 164th pope, sat five years.

Emperor Henry V died on 24 May. Around the Kalends of September he was succeeded by Lothair III, duke of Saxony.

**1130.** Peter, son of Leo, and Gregory, deacon of St Angelo, began to contend for the papacy.

**1133.** An eclipse of the sun occurred on 2 August, the moon being sixteen days old.

**1135.** In this year this collection and arrangement of cycles from the beginning of the world down to this point was made.

#### II.—From the Augsburg Manuscript

**1006.** [Note: From the preceding material our Boehmer, with whom I copied these things at Munich, noted: “955. The Hungarians are slaughtered with immense carnage near Augsburg, city of Germany.”—“1001. Henry II reigned twenty-three years and five months.”] The bishopric of Bamberg is founded by King Henry, and Eberhard is appointed there first bishop.

**1012.** The church of St Peter and St George at Bamberg is dedicated.

**1024.** Emperor Henry II died on 14 July. Conrad succeeded him on 7 September and reigned nearly fifteen years.

**1039.** Empress Cunigunde, wife of Henry II, died on 3 March. In the same year Emperor Conrad died on 4 June; his son Henry III succeeded him and reigned seventeen years.

**1036.** Emperor Henry III died on 5 October, and his son Henry IV reigned fifty years.

**1099.** In this year the first Jerusalem expedition was undertaken by Godfrey, duke of Flanders, and many French and German princes; whence the following:

> In the thousandth year, one hundred lacking one,  
> The Franks take Jerusalem by mighty strength.

**1105.** King Henry, son of Emperor Henry IV, takes arms against his father: mourning and terror everywhere.

**1106.** Emperor Henry IV died. His son Henry V succeeded him and reigned twenty years after him.

**1108.** King Henry, still a boy, entered Italy and thence Rome with a very great army. Because Pope Paschal unjustly resisted his authority, he cast him captive into chains; but, once released, the pope first compelled the same king to surrender the investitures of bishoprics.

**1117.** A great earthquake occurred throughout the world, once by day and once by night.*

**1126.** Emperor Henry V died on 25 May. About the Kalends of September he was succeeded by Lothair III, a Saxon by birth, who reigned eleven years [Note: A second hand: “twelve years and three months”; cf. the entry for 1135.].

**1131.** King Lothair enters Italy on campaign and devastates all of the suburb of Augusta with sword and fire.

**1133.** Hermann, bishop of Augsburg, died. Walther was elected on 19 March. In the same year darkness occurred on 3 August.

**1134.** Walther was ordained bishop at Seligenstadt on 9 September.

**1135.** In this year this collection and arrangement of cycles from the beginning of the world down to this point was made.

### Babenberg Annals

[Col. 1367]

**1137.** Lothair III, emperor, died on 3 December. [Watkunus, abbot, died; Ditwin succeeds him; entered by a thirteenth-century hand.]

**1138.** Conrad III is made king on 24 February.

**1139.** Heimo, author of this work, died on 31 July.

**1140.** [1139.] Otto VIII, pious bishop of the church of Bamberg, full of good works and alms, while heaven rejoiced and earth wept, ascended to the heavenly Jerusalem on 30 June. [Note: Through a certain error, these words were written after “Empress Richenza died.”]

**1142.** Empress Richenza died.

**1144.** Eberhard, of pious memory, provost of the greater church, died.

**1146.** Egilbert, ninth bishop [Note: of Bamberg], a man of mercy and piety, departed to Christ. On the same day Lord Eberhard, provost of St James, conspicuous for every wisdom, integrity, and religious devotion, was appointed in his place by the unanimous election of all clergy and people. In his first year St Henry was canonized by Pope Eugenius.

**1147.** Expedition in 1147. [*Expedition to Jerusalem under King Conrad.]

**1149.** [Note: The notices for 1147, 1149, and 1170, marked with one asterisk, are due to the same Ensdorf interpolator responsible for the notices of 1121 and 1124.] [*King Conrad returned home.]

**1153.** King Conrad III died on 14 February. Frederick succeeded on 4 March of the same year.

**1155.** [Note: The notices for 1155, 1158, 1173, and 1184 were written by the same twelfth-century hand.] **Count Palatine Otto died. [Founder of this monastery, of happy memory; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1158.** [Note: The notices for 1155, 1158, 1173, and 1184 were written by the same twelfth-century hand.] **Victor and Alexander were at variance in the apostolic see.

**1170.** Eberhard, tenth bishop, a man of mercy and piety, departed to Christ. On the same day Hermann, provost, was appointed in his place by the unanimous election of all clergy and people.

*Helmric, fourth abbot of this place, died. Boto succeeds him.

**1173.** [Note: The notices for 1155, 1158, 1173, and 1184 were written by the same twelfth-century hand.] **Heilica, countess palatine, died. [Foundress of this monastery, of pious memory and worthy of every praise; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1177.** Hermann, eleventh bishop, died. Otto, sprung from royal stock and likewise provost of the greater church, succeeds him. A general synod of 514 bishops is held under Pope Alexander. At it the aforesaid Otto obtained the privilege that he and his successors were to be consecrated by the lord pope; he was consecrated on Judica Sunday. [Note: Thus far the hand of the first writer.]

**1180.** [In this year the margraviate of Styria was changed into a duchy. In the same year Otto of Styria became duke of Bavaria; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

### Ensdorf Annals

[Col. 1369]

**1184?** Duke Otto of Bavaria died. [Note: In the twelfth-century hand responsible for 1155, 1158, and 1173. Here and there are different hands of contemporaries.]

**1189.** Expedition under Emperor Frederick.

**1190.** Emperor Frederick was drowned in the waters.

**1196.** [lacuna] In October Frederick, count palatine of pious memory, died. [[lacuna] Babarus died; entered by a fifteenth-century hand. Son of our founder; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1197.** Emperor Henry VI died on 28 September. [Note: The manuscript adds “vux X,” with some letters cut off.]

**1198.** Philip is made king, and Otto of Saxony is set up against him.

**1201.** An earthquake occurred at the ninth hour on 2 May.

**1202.** Boto, the fifth abbot, died; he had presided thirty-three years. Albero succeeds him. [Note: I supplied “-tur.”]

**1203.** Abbot Albero died. Rudiger succeeds him. [Note: I supplied “-tur.”]

**1206.** [In this year the Order of Friars Minor began; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1208.** King Philip was killed at Bamberg by Count Palatine Otto.

**1209.** The same Otto was slain by the marshal of Kalten[?].

**1210.** After Philip’s death Otto of Saxony was crowned by Pope Innocent with the consent of the princes; and after one year he was deposed from the kingdom, and Frederick, son of Emperor Henry, was made king.

**1216.** [In this year the Order of Preachers began; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1218.** [In this year Straubing was built; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1220.** [In this year Abach was founded; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1224.** [In this year Landau [Note: “Landawe.”] was built; entered by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1225.** Henry [Note: word cut off], son of Emperor Frederick, celebrated his marriage at Nuremberg with the daughter of Duke Leopold of Austria.

**1227.** Conrad, bishop of Regensburg, died. Provost Gottfried succeeds him.

**1228.** [Otto, son of Louis duke of Bavaria, is girded with the sword at Straubing; entered by a thirteenth-century hand, end of the fourteenth century.]

**1229.** [Duke Louis is born; entered by a thirteenth-century hand, end of the fourteenth century.]

**1231.** Louis, duke of Bavaria, was killed at Kelheim. Leopold, duke of Austria, died.

**1235.** [Duke Henry is born; entered by a thirteenth-century hand, end of the fourteenth century.]

**1241.** The Tatars attempt to destroy the whole Church.—An eclipse of the sun occurred on 6 October about the ninth hour; the sun was darkened, darkness was made over the whole earth, and the stars appeared plainly.

**1242.** [In this year Count Albert of Bogen died; written by a fifteenth-century hand.]

**1246.** In that year the duke of Austria was killed on the feast day of St Vitus.

In this year the landgrave of Thuringia assumed the Roman kingship and was elevated as king by the apostolic lord and the other spiritual princes. He was marked with the cross against all who sided with the emperor and his supporters [Note: *consentienbant* in the manuscript]. He advanced with a great army on campaign against the king, son of the emperor; when they met, he gained the triumph of victory and ruled powerfully, the apostolic lord supporting him in all things. A very great slaughter and killing of men took place throughout all the kingdoms. At the royal city of Nuremberg, men, mothers, and little children perished miserably from cold, nakedness, and hunger.

**1247.** And that same king, reigning in his omnipotence, died in the first week of Lent of that year.

In this year divine services ceased in the diocese of Regensburg by order of the apostolic lord and the legate, and by order of the bishop of Regensburg, confirmed by the legate.

**1250.** Emperor Frederick died.

**1251.** King Conrad narrowly escaped death at Regensburg.

**1254.** King Conrad, son of Frederick, who had married the daughter of Duke Otto of Bavaria, died.

[Duke Otto of Bavaria died; entered by a thirteenth-century hand, end of text.] Muchs.

**1255.** [Dukes Louis and Henry of Bavaria are girded with the sword; entered by a thirteenth-century hand, end of the fourteenth century.] Abbot Conrad died. Herold succeeds him, on St Michael’s Day.

**1256.** Maria, duchess of Brabant here [Note: wife of Louis, duke of Bavaria], was killed. Two kings were elected at Frankfurt: by the greater party, the king of England; but by three electors, the margrave [Note: *machio* in the manuscript] of Brandenburg. An innumerable multitude of princes had gathered there as well.

[Note: [Col. 1369] all these items added in the year 1261 have now been erased.] Duchess Maria was killed by her husband Duke Louis. These things were written in the hand of Conrad [Note: [Col. 1369] I have supplied *-rad*.] the cantor of Gewangesek [Note: [Col. 1369] word uncertain.]. Frederick.

1267. The king of Bohemia fought the dukes of Bavaria and ravaged Bavaria itself with plundering and fire.

1269. The son of King Conrad was killed in Gaul.

1271. Duchess Anna died. The king of Bohemia entered into conflict with the king of Hungary, and a great slaughter took place [Col. 1370D] in Austria and also in Hungary.

1273. In this year the venerable Count Rudolf was elected king of the Romans on the octave of Michaelmas, worthy of the name and the honour. Herold, our abbot, was appointed to Kastl; Alhard of Prüfening succeeded him on the feast of Mary Magdalene.

[Col. 1371A] 1275. In this year Pope Gregory X held a council at Lyons in Gaul, and decreed under anathema that all Christians should obey King Rudolf.

1276. Lord Alhard resigned the abbacy. Gerung, our monk, entered upon it on Reminiscere Sunday.

1278. Leo, bishop of Regensburg, died; Lord Henry, a canon, was appointed in his place. In this year the illustrious Rudolf, king of the Romans, while remaining in Austria—which, two years earlier, he had subjected to himself with the support of the magnates of that land—by the permission of the most high God, and with the assistance of the king of Hungary and a great army of his Saracens, on the appointed day and at the appointed place laid low with the sword his adversary, the king of Bohemia, and his innumerable army [Col. 1371B]; and the most serene king won victory over his enemy. [Note: [Col. 1371] The scribe had first written “God,” which he erased.]

1280. In this year, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, died the venerable Lord Albert the Great, formerly bishop of the church of Regensburg and master in theology.

1281. At this time we purchased the gift of the church of Wolfspach, with its advocacy, jurisdiction [Note: [Col. 1371] “jurisdiction, advocacy” (thus).], fishing-rights, woodland, and fields, for 85 pounds.

1282. In this year, on the day of Saint Achatius [Note: [Col. 1371] 22 June. [ [Col. 1373D] 1313.] Münchsmünster, diocese of Regensburg, on the Danube below Vohburg.], at noon while the sun shone, a tower split from top to bottom; the chapel was shaken and split [Note: [Col. 1371] *cissa* in the manuscript.] in one part; and, after the altar of Saint Blasius had been moved, it was divided by a stroke of lightning.

On the Tuesday of Pentecost he arrived [Note: [Col. 1371] What is written above appears to concern Abbot Eberhard.].

[Col. 1371C] 1285. Abbot Gerung was deposed. Rüdiger from Saint Emmeram’s succeeded him on the Tuesday after the Ascension of the Lord; he remained ten days. Likewise, in the same year Eberhard was appointed on the feast of Saint Dionysius.

1288. In this year at Cologne a great slaughter took place between the bishop of Cologne and the duke of Brabant; eight thousand men fell in one day, and the bishop himself, his captains, and counts were also killed.

1289. Abbot Eberhard died.

1290. Duke Henry died. Libhard was elected abbot, by unanimous deliberation and consent, ten days after Eberhard’s death, before those ten days had fully elapsed [Col. 1371D], with so fortunate a result that within five successive days he was elected, confirmed at Regensburg, and consecrated joyfully, commendably, auspiciously, and honourably.

1291. In his time the Mass of the Blessed Virgin was authorized by privilege to be celebrated. Meinhard, the custodian, redeemed an estate yielding one talent [Note: [Col. 1371] *m tt.* in the manuscript.]; Lord Libhard [Note: [Col. 1371] *L.* in the manuscript.], [Col. 1372A] the abbot, added half of it [Note: [Col. 1371] *medit.* in the manuscript.] for the brethren’s consolation on every day.

1293. Duke Louis died. He gave us the church of Vilshoven to improve the prebend and to have his anniversary observed solemnly on its day.

1294. Libhard resigned the abbacy; and, on the advice of the lord bishop, Lord Engelmar, prior of the church of Altach, was appointed over our church. He came on Saint Ulrich’s Day. By the unanimous deliberation and consent of the brethren, he established that the prebend of a deceased brother should, throughout the course of that year, be distributed to the poor for the remedy of his soul.

1296. Henry of Rotenegg, bishop, died; Lord Conrad of Lupburg, provost of the high church, succeeded him solemnly on the Thursday. [Note: [Col. 1371] The erased words appear to read: “here made a monk.”]

[Col. 1372B] 1298. Meinhard, custodian and monk of our community, a man of good character and great devotion, who had done much good previously for our church, was elected abbot through the counsel of Lord Conrad, bishop of Regensburg, and Engelmar, formerly our abbot. He was therefore appointed in every respect canonically, properly, commendably, and honourably.

1299. In this year the enemies of Christ, namely the Jews, were burned throughout almost the whole world, so that few escaped; Christians were avenging Christ’s blood. In the same year Albert, duke of Austria, deceitfully attacked the king of the Romans, namely Adolf, near the Rhine with an army of Hungarians; he killed the king himself and usurped the kingdom.

[Col. 1372C] 1300. In this year a very great epidemic among animals, especially cattle, arose throughout the whole world.

1305. After the death of Abbot Meinhard, Abbot Werner succeeded at Münchsmünster. [Note: [Col. 1371] 22 June. [ [Col. 1373D] 1313.] Münchsmünster, diocese of Regensburg, on the Danube below Vohburg.]

1309. After Abbot Werner’s death, Frederick, prior of this church, was appointed.

1310. When Frederick resigned the abbacy, Albert, a monk of Saint Emmeram’s, succeeded him.

1314. In this year, namely on the day of Luke the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 1371] I have supplied *-ste*.], two kings were elected at Frankfurt [Note: [Col. 1371] I have supplied *-ti*.]: Duke Louis of Bavaria by the larger party [Note: [Col. 1371] I have supplied *-arie*.], and Duke Frederick of Austria by the smaller party. [Note: [Col. 1371] I have supplied *-i*.] Both were consecrated kings by their electors, and each styled himself king of the Romans throughout all [Col. 1372D] the years. [Note: [Col. 1371] I have supplied *Roma-*.]

1319. In this year Rudolf, duke of Bavaria, died.

1322. In this year, on the vigil of Saint Michael the Archangel [Note: [Col. 1371] I have supplied *-han*.], the two aforementioned elect, namely King Louis, duke of Bavaria, and Duke Frederick of Austria, met in battle near the town of Mühldorf. Duke Frederick of Austria, with his magnates, was captured by Louis, king of the Romans [Col. 1373A], and many were killed there on both sides.

1328. In this year Louis, king of the Romans, went to Rome with a large army. There, deceived—as is said—by the counsel of the Romans, he set up a pope, or rather an antipope, who crowned him king of the Romans. Yet not long afterward that man hastened to Pope John XXII, who had sat at Avignon for more than eighteen years, resigned the papacy, and surrendered himself to be punished at his pleasure.

1332. In this year Emperor Louis besieged Straubing after Saint Ulrich’s Day.

1334. When Albert resigned the abbacy, Ulrich, provost and monk of this monastery, was appointed; he scarcely survived half a year. In the same year a second Ulrich, prior and monk of this monastery, succeeded him.

1337. In this year Regensburg was secretly undermined by certain treacherous citizens and delivered to Emperor Louis; but by the grace of God and the merits of the blessed bishops Wolfgang and Erhard, they were saved from so great a danger.

1338. In this year a multitude of locusts flew. In the same year Jews were burned at Straubing.

1340. In this year Lord Nicholas, bishop of Regensburg, died on the fifth day before the Ides of October. After he had been buried in the monastery of his diocese called Oberalteich, of the Order of Saint Benedict, Lord Henry of the Stone was raised to possession of the bishopric through the help of Emperor Louis and certain secular lords, who delivered the castles of the bishopric to him without the consent of the whole chapter—above all, without that of Lord Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg, and the lord of Hohenberg, both of whom had the consent of the greater part of the chapter in the episcopal election [Col. 1373C]. In the same year, about the feast of Saint Lucy the Virgin, John, sole and last heir of Lower Bavaria, died; Emperor Louis, duke of Upper Bavaria, took possession of his duchy.

1342. In this year there was such a flood of rain that it devastated all the fruits of the earth on [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied “on.”] the vigil of Praxedes.

In this year the venerable Lord Nicholas, bishop of Regensburg, died on the feast of Gereon.

In this year, around Esto mihi Sunday, Emperor Louis expelled John, duke of Carinthia, son of the king of Bohemia, who had been defamed for sexual incapacity, from the duchy and province of Tyrol; he took away his wife and joined her in marriage to his own son Louis, margrave of Brandenburg. [Col. 1373D]

1347. In this [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied “This.”] year Emperor Louis died on the feast of Saint Maximilian. In the same year [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *ann.*] two kings of the Romans were [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied “were.”] elected: namely Count Günther [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *G-*.] [Col. 1374A] of Schwarzburg [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *-pu-*.] and Charles, king of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *Bo-*.]. The Count of Schwarzburg [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *par-*.] was elected by the larger party [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *-pur-*.], but died after being poisoned [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *-i*.; I have supplied *ob-*.]. Charles reigned; he governed well [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *r-*.] and loved the clergy.

1348. In this year an earthquake occurred on the Conversion of Saint Paul which destroyed Villach.

1349. In this year a great pestilence arose throughout the world. In the same year people appeared, saying that they were repenting of their sins; they went with banners and scourges, striking themselves, and travelled through all [Note: [Col. 1373] *eos* in the manuscript.] regions.

1350. In the year of the Lord 1350, Margrave Louis gathered a great army and entered Brandenburg against the duke of Saxony, who had chosen a certain miller as margrave in the land [Col. 1374B] called the Mark, because the margrave of that land had been missing for more than thirty years, and they said that he had come back to life.

1361. In this year, around the feast of Saint George the Martyr, the empress, wife of Charles, gave birth to a son, namely Wenceslas, in the city of Nuremberg. For his baptism Emperor Charles summoned all the princes of Germany, and they came. There he held an imperial court with honour and displayed the imperial relics. In the same year, on the vigil of Matthew the Apostle, Louis, margrave and duke of Bavaria, died.

1364. In this year, on the day of Boniface, Duke Stephen [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *d-*.] of Bavaria and his sons [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *s-*.], Stephen and Frederick, besieged the town of Mühldorf, wishing to take it by assault. [Col. 1374C] On the day of Blessed Augustine they withdrew from [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *a-*.] the siege with a great army to [Note: [Col. 1373] I have supplied *i-*.] Braunau. With them were Rupert, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, the burgrave of Nuremberg, and very many innumerable others; and they wished to fight Duke Rudolf of Austria, who fled from Ried toward his own territory.

1368. When Ulrich resigned the abbacy, Frederick, infirmarian of our church, succeeded him on the feast of Barbara, Virgin and Martyr.

In the year [Note: [Col. 1373] What follows was written in the fourteenth century in the margin of the final folio of the manuscript.] one thousand three hundred and thirteen [Note: [Col. 1373D] 1313.]

Those whom Austria nourished, Bavaria struck down with the sword,

on the feast of the martyr Theodore; remember this well.

Therefore may Gammelsdorf be the happier village.

[Col. 1374D] There are three M’s, two C’s, two X’s, and two I’s [Note: [Col. 1374D] 1322.].

And beneath the Bavarian yoke Austria falls with Wenceslas.

If you wish to be a monk, you must necessarily regard yourself as

a pig’s snout and an ass’s back,

a dove’s mouth, a sheep’s heart, and an ox’s leg. [Note: [Col. 1373] The final-page inscription, in a fifteenth-century hand, reads: “This book belongs to Saint James of Ensdorf, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Regensburg, situated in the duchy of the count palatine, 1481.”]

# Lesser Annals of Augsburg

[Col. 1375]

[Col. 1375A] 1137. Emperor Lothair III died on the second day before the Nones of December. Conrad, a Swabian by birth, was elected in the year when he was abroad [Note: [Col. 1375D] that is, in the year when he was outside; written before the line, namely 1137.] and reigned fourteen years. Earlier, elected king by certain men in opposition to Lothair, he had been compelled to flee into Italy; afterward he became king.

1146. At this time a certain man, appearing good and clothed in grey, entered Augsburg, called himself a *zodorus* [term uncertain] and a psalmist, and, working many signs through the prince of demons, turned all Germany toward himself.

1147. King Conrad and King Louis of France set out for Jerusalem and against the Saracens with many Christians, but achieved nothing.

1150. The king returned from Jerusalem, many Christians having been captured and killed [Col. 1375B] by the barbarians.

1152. King Conrad died. Frederick, son of his brother, was elected. Bishop Walter, worn out by old age, was deposed. A dispute over the election of a bishop arose between the canons and the ministerials of the church; before King Frederick it was adjudged in favour of the canons. Through his intervention Conrad, a Swabian by nationality, was elected.

1156. King Frederick, proceeding to Rome on campaign, was consecrated emperor by Pope Adrian. Master Arnold was ordered by the pope to be hanged. Spoleto was captured and devastated by the emperor. Milan was declared an enemy of the empire.

Discord arose between the bishop and the canons of Augsburg; both parties appealed to the pope.

1158. Emperor Frederick again marched through [Col. 1375C] Italy on campaign: he besieged and captured Crema and received Milan’s surrender. A schism arose between priesthood and empire.

1162. Emperor Frederick, devastating Italy on a third campaign, utterly destroyed Milan on the Kalends of March because it had broken the agreement, while the schism still continued.

1164. A battle at Tübingen between Duke Frederick, son of King Conrad, and the younger Welf.

1166. Emperor Frederick, advancing as far as Rome on a fourth campaign with a very great army, invaded and destroyed the church of Saint Peter after an immense slaughter of Romans. While he was encamped there in August, a very great disaster, unheard of in our age, fell upon [Col. 1375D] the Germans and killed Welf and Frederick, the dukes, and nearly all the princes. In the same year all Italy rebelled against the emperor and compelled him to flee with very few men over Mont Cenis. [Note: [Col. 1375D] That is, Cenis.]

[Col. 1376A] 1167. Conrad, bishop of Augsburg, died. Hartwig was elected on the Kalends of November, about the second hour of the night, which is the feast of All Saints, while the emperor was still remaining in [Note: [Col. 1375] *l.* in the manuscript.] Italy.

1169. Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, was killed at Mainz in the church of Saint James on the Kalends of July. Rudolf and Christian were elected in discord.

1174. Emperor Frederick, leading a fifth expedition into Italy over Mont Cenis, burned Susa [Note: [Col. 1376D] Susa.], from which he had formerly withdrawn secretly, and received Asti [Note: [Col. 1376D] Asti.] in surrender. He besieged but did not capture Palea, that is, Alexandria; on the vigil of Easter, with a very great loss of his men, he withdrew from it while the schism still continued. [Note: [Col. 1375] I have supplied “continued.”]

1177. The schism that had lasted nineteen years was ended when Pope Alexander and Emperor Frederick met at Venice. The suburb of Augsburg, the church of Saint Maurice, and the church of Saint Peter were consumed by fire. [Col. 1376B]

1179. [Note: [Col. 1375] The sense appears to be that Bishop Hartwig went to Rome for the general Lateran council, at which 290 bishops were present. Hartwig is listed among the approximately 300 bishops present at the council by Martène and Durand, *Collectio amplissima*, VII, p. 85.] . . . . Bishop Hartwig ma. . . of the churches newly super. . . . .ed this very [matter uncertain], at which 290 . . . bishops were present.

1181. Duke Henry of Bavaria and Saxony, since he was said to be guilty of treason against majesty, was deposed by the empire without difficulty. Otto became duke palatine.

1183. The emperor celebrated Pentecost at Regensburg with Duke Otto. The same Duke Otto died a few days later in the castle of Pfullendorf. The Lombards were received into favour at Constance. The church of Saint Ulrich at Augsburg was burned.

[Col. 1376C] 1184. Hartwig, bishop of Augsburg, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of February. Udalschalk was elected the same day. In the same year the emperor’s sons, one of whom was king and the other duke, received the belt of knighthood at Mainz at Pentecost, in the presence of their father and mother. In the same year Christian, archbishop of Mainz, died. Conrad was restored.

1185. At Augsburg, in the bishop’s palace, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, Constance, daughter of the king of Sicily, was confirmed by oath to Henry, the emperor’s son and king. In the following year,

1186. the wedding was celebrated at Milan.

1187. An eclipse of the sun occurred from the sixth hour to the ninth. In the same year the barbarian people under the leadership of Saladin captured Jerusalem and the Lord’s Cross. In the same year the emperor and his son the duke, with many [Col. 1376D] princes, took the cross at Mainz, out of zeal for Christ and in vengeance for him, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April. Philip, archbishop of Cologne, was there restored to favour.

[Col. 1377A] 1188. Henry, formerly duke, not having been granted the duchy, returned to favour. [Note: [Col. 1377] Up to this point, a second hand.]

1208. In this year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, King Philip was killed at Bamberg.

1237. In this year a great earthquake occurred, so that churches and stone structures were shaken, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, on the feast of the holy martyrs Lucian and Gemelliana, after dawn and before the first Mass.

1241. In this year darkness occurred on the Nones of October, a Sunday afternoon, on the feast of the Virgin Faith. [Note: [Col. 1377D] 6 October, which fell on a Sunday in 1241.]

1246. In this year a marriage was contracted between Lord Conrad, king-elect of the Romans, and the daughter of the duke of Bavaria.

In this year, on the Nones of August, namely the feast day of the illustrious King [Col. 1377B] Saint Oswald, Conrad, king-elect of the Romans, with Lord Henry, landgrave of Thuringia, having arrayed and equipped battle-lines on both sides, met in battle near Frankfurt and was put to flight with his men; and in the following year,

1247. the aforementioned landgrave of Thuringia died. After his death Lord William, count of Holland, was elected king. Siboto [Note: [Col. 1377] I have supplied the word.] bishop of Augsburg resigned the bishopric; he was succeeded by the son of the count of Dillingen. [Note: [Col. 1377D] Hartmann, son of Hartmann.]

1256. In this year Louis, duke of Bavaria, killed his wife Maria, daughter of the duke of Brabant, on Saint Anthony’s Day, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Very negligent is the clergy of this church, which allows the deeds of emperors and princes in the present genealogy [Col. 1377C] to remain thus vacant, in no respect imitating the footsteps of its predecessors in proceeding, who hitherto wrote sufficiently elegantly and eloquently.

1271. In this year, while the venerable Lord Hartmann, count of Dillingen, governed the bishopric of Augsburg, and the Roman church, after the death of Pope Clement IV, had then lacked a pontiff for a fourth year, famine grew so severe in Swabia and throughout all the surrounding provinces that in this city a modius of wheat was sold for 4 pounds; a modius of rye for 3 pounds and 4 shillings; a half-modium of barley for 35 shillings; and a modius of oats for 24 Augsburg shillings. Very many poor people, distressed by the misery of hunger and almost lifeless, were found dead in the streets.

[Col. 1377D] 1278. In this year, on Friday, the seventh day before the Kalends of September, a battle was fought near the town of Marchegg between Lord Rudolf of Habsburg, king of the Romans, on the one side, and Lord Ottokar, king of Bohemia, on the other. The king of Bohemia was killed, and with him fell . . . . . thousand men.

1279. In this year, on the Saturday of Pentecost week [Col. 1378A] (27 May), in the morning, a most savage fire broke out from the house of a merchant near Stezenbach Lane. By it very many houses across the clear Lech and all the intervening houses, both within the walls and in the sandy suburb, were burned; and not only wooden buildings, but also eight stone houses were consumed. More than a hundred people of both sexes perished in them: some were found suffocated, others wholly burned. In the same year there was such an abundance of crops that a modius of rye was sold for 4 Augsburg shillings.

1285. In this year the Tatars invaded Hungary around the Purification and, powerfully occupying the land throughout the whole of Lent, killed countless peoples. At last almost their entire army was destroyed by the princes of Hungary. A greater-than-usual livestock epidemic lasted throughout the summer, so that not a tenth part of the cattle remained alive in Augsburg. In the same year the emperor [Note: [Col. 1378D] Frederick the impostor.] was burned at Wetzlar on the Nones of July, a Saturday, the feast of Willibald. Jews also at Munich, in autumn, were burned to the number of 132 for the killing of a certain child of unspecified sex.

1288. In this year Lord Wolfhard, bishop-elect of the church of Augsburg, while the see of Mainz was vacant, was confirmed as bishop with great [Col. 1378C] solemnity in the monastery of Saint Mary at Augsburg, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, by Lord Hugh, son of the Wildgrave, and Lord Werner of Löwenstein, canons sent on behalf of the chapter of the church of Mainz.

1296. In this year, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, the castle called Mergartau [Note: [Col. 1378D] Today Mergenthau on the river Paar, fifteen Roman miles from Augsburg.] was deceitfully besieged by the Bavarians, namely by C. of Haldenberg. In the same year he deceitfully killed his uncle called of Losbach at Lausperch.

1298. In this year Adolf, king of the Romans, was killed in battle, with many others, by Lord Albert, duke of Austria, near Worms, in the field called Haselbühel, on the second day of July. Albert himself was immediately elected king and reigned ten years with great power; at last he died after being killed by a cruel death.

1302. A total eclipse of the moon, on the feast of Saint Felix, in January [Col. 1378D], on Sunday night (14 January), during the brethren’s matins.

1308. In this year Albert, king of the Romans, pierced by three wounds by his nephew John, ended his life in sudden and unexpected death on the feast of the Apostles Philip and James (1 May).

1310. A severe eclipse of the sun at the end of January, which was [Col. 1379A] on the vigil of Bridget [Note: [Col. 1379] Her feast is on the Kalends of February, and in 1310 it was celebrated on Sunday.], around evening, on Saturday.

1311. In the year of the Lord 1311, on the day of Giles (1 September), in the evening, hail came over Augsburg. Round and large stones fell, almost like the yolks of eggs; by their force almost all roofs of houses made from shingles were broken. The glass in the north-facing windows of the churches was completely shattered. Almost all the fruit of the trees was battered and knocked down. Likewise, in gardens grass and vegetables were entirely destroyed, and the heads of cabbages were cut off down to the *magudarium* [uncertain term]. I report marvels: a certain citizen found thirty sparrows struck dead beneath one tree in his orchard. Likewise, a good hundred cranes were found dead in the fields and were carried [Col. 1379B] to the Perlach market to be sold. In the same year there was a great dearth. [Col. 1380A] At harvest-time a modius of rye was sold at Augsburg for 26 shillings. After the harvest, the price of grain began to rise from week to week, so that around Michaelmas a modius of rye was sold for 42 shillings in coin.

1312. A partial eclipse of the sun on the sixth day of July, that is, in the octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul, before the dinner-hour, on Thursday.

1321. A total eclipse of the sun, and darkness over the face of the earth throughout all Germany, in June on the feast of John and Paul, during High Mass, on Friday (26 June).

1457. The most sweet King Ladislaus, king of Hungary and Bohemia, was innocently poisoned at Prague; he had scarcely completed eighteen years.

# In the Year of the Lord 1141: Walter, Monk of Cluny

[Col. 1379]

# On the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary

(Labbe, *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, vol. I, p. 650.)

## Prologue

[Col. 1379C]

Walter, monk of Cluny, to his venerable brother, the monk of Saint-Venant, whom he embraces most affectionately in the bowels of Christ: may you steadfastly bear the burden and heat of the day unto the end.

Mindful both of your request and of my promise, I have committed to writing, for the edification of readers, the miracles of the most holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary which I related before you. I have done so not from presumption, but so that simple people may readily understand what has been composed in a simple style, and through it may be moved to venerate the aforesaid—and ever-to-be-praised—Virgin Mary. And lest anyone should think these things empty and frivolous, and therefore to be rejected, know that I did not see them with my own eyes, but learned them from the report of a venerable man, Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See, speaking in an assembly of noble persons. Now, therefore, what we have heard to the praise of the glorious Mother of God, we shall make known to you and to others like you, little ones in Christ, to whom belongs the kingdom of heaven.

## Chapter I

In Gaul, in a village called Dormientium, there is an image of the Mother of the Lord painted with such loveliness and beauty that nothing surpasses it. Faithful people come from different provinces [Col. 1380C] to see and venerate it, to fulfil vows and implore her aid. The Mother of all mercy demonstrates her presence through frequent miracles, a few of which that have come to us we shall recount.

When, in the year 1133 from the Lord’s Incarnation, divine providence, because our sins deserved it, allowed the bodies of certain persons to be consumed by the holy fire for the correction of many, the aforesaid church so overflowed with the grace of divine bounty that whoever suffering from this affliction came before the countenance of the Blessed Virgin immediately felt, through heavenly grace, relief from the burning.
