Accordingly the church was so filled with sick people that the crowd of arrivals could scarcely stand within it.

It happened that the wife of a certain peasant subject to the church’s jurisdiction, a woman of considerable honour among her own people, was struck in her face by a dreadful and horrifying punishment. She was brought to the common harbour of salvation and led into the aforesaid church by the hands of her children and relatives. Groaning, she prostrated herself before the image of the most holy Virgin; with many tears and sighs she called upon the Mother of mercy and, pitiable and wretched, tearfully begged her to have mercy upon her.

The community of consecrated virgins serving the Queen of Virgins in that church hastened together and interceded for their devoted [Col. 1381A] handmaid, whom they saw afflicted with this wretched kind of sickness. They passed the night in vigil with psalms and prayers, tears and contrition of heart, invoking God’s mercy and the Blessed Virgin’s aid. An unheard-of reversal occurred: mercy hardened. The Virgin’s prayers seemed as though rejected and brought to no effect whatever. The unhappy woman remained and still awaited the Mother of mercy’s compassion.

The illness raged again and occupied the woman’s whole face; a loathsome stench rose from the unhappy woman’s face and filled the entire church. Her husband, overcome by weariness and labour, departed; her sons and daughters were exhausted by vigils, stench, and entreaty. Unveiled, the woman shamelessly raised her disfigured face before the people. Then, herself already despairing after thirteen days’ waiting, she prostrated herself before the Virgin’s image and, bathed in tears, addressed the Mother of God as though present in these words:

> “O Lady,” she said, “I believed you to be the Mother of all mercy, the fountain of compassion, and the harbour of the miserable; but I see that you have become cruel toward me, and that I await your mercy in vain. You restore all strangers who come here and stream together from every direction to their former health; but me, your own handmaid, you disdain, and I find no counsel granted to me by you. Therefore I shall leave your church and no longer cause others either stench or terror by my unheard-of deformity.”

Having said this, the woman left the church; while the entire crowd of onlookers wept with her, she slowly drew out mournful cries and tearful sighs and, as she could, departed from the whole village, all the people going with her and marvelling. She became an object of terror to every person she encountered, for she showed not a human face but the appearance of a shapeless monster. She had lost her entire nose and lower lip, her two cheeks having been joined by the violence of the disease; and with an abundant flow of burned blood now issuing from her eyes, the utterly exhausted unhappy woman at last, as day was already declining, reached the home of a certain peasant and asked him for lodging.

Moved by compassion, he made her a bed of straw in a more private part of his house and put the woman there to rest. He urged her to take a little food, but she refused. As night fell [Col. 1381D], the woman, from weariness and exhaustion, appeared to fall asleep. In that sleep she saw the Blessed Virgin, Mother of God and the Lord, standing beside her in her accustomed brightness. The Virgin threatened and rebuked her, asking why she had departed from the church. But the woman, falling at her feet, begged mercy.

Then the Blessed Mother of God raised the woman with her own hand and commanded her to stand before her. With kindly hand she touched her face and, banishing every pain, in an instant restored her to her former health, so that not even a scar or any trace of any wound remained. Having blessed the woman, the glorious vision vanished.

Returning to herself, uncertain of her health, she recalled the vision; gently touching her face with her hand, she found her face whole and the disease wholly gone. [Col. 1382A] Made certain of the miracle, the woman gave forth cries of praise and thanksgiving; with a loud outcry she disturbed the whole household in which she was lodging. Many lights were kindled, neighbours ran together, and they saw her sitting with a radiant face whom shortly before they had seen reeking with horrible deformity. They asked how it had happened; the woman related the vision she had seen and through which she had been healed.

The woman was brought back to the church, where she prostrated herself before the image of the most holy Mother of God. On bended knees and wailing, she gave thanks to her healer, while the people marvelled and rejoiced with her, shouting praise of the Blessed Virgin. There one might have seen people eagerly running together to kiss the woman’s face, which the Mother of the Lord had shaped with her own hand. The woman gave herself as a perpetual handmaid to that same [Col. 1382B] church, for the praise and glory of the name of Jesus Christ, who with the Father, etc.

## Chapter II
At another time, in the same village there lived a man of the common people who, having abandoned his lawful wife, had deflowered a certain young woman and kept her as a concubine for his own use. His wife, grievously and resentfully bearing such separation, daily prostrated herself before the Blessed Virgin, raising a complaint against that little woman. Every day she said these words: “Holy Mary, Mother of the Lord, do me justice against that harlot who takes my husband from me by enchantments.”

But the sinful woman went daily to church and, before the image of the Mother of the Lord, uttered these words: [Col. 1382C] “Hail, Mary,” etc. The one cried out in complaint; the other offered greeting, until by doing so they passed a year. Then, at dawn on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary appeared to the woman who was making the complaint and said to her: “Woman, seek someone else to do you justice against that woman, for I cannot do it for you in any way.”

She, as it seemed to her, replied: “O Lady, you who possess power over all the hosts of heaven, who always humble worldly pride when it pleases you, and who restrain the cruelty of demons by your power—how can you say, Lady, that you cannot do me justice against this wretched woman, who sins against your Son and against you [Col. 1382D] by taking my husband from me?”

To these words of the woman the Queen of Virgins replied: “You speak truly, woman: power has been given to me over all things in heaven and on earth, and I execute judgment upon demons. But that sinful woman daily recalls to my memory the greatest joy that I ever had in this present world, uttering to me the angelic greeting, which was the joy of the restoration of the human race; and therefore I cannot bear that any misfortune should befall her.”

As she spoke, the vision of her who stood there and conversed vanished. When the woman arose in the morning, recalling the vision she had seen, she indeed went to the church; but she presented herself earnestly before the image of the blessed Mother of the Lord and did not make her customary complaint there. For she believed [Col. 1383A] that she had been deceived by an enchantment, and that, through the malice of the aforesaid concubine, the Mother of God—an unspeakable impiety even to say—had been induced to say these things.

She remained for a long time in the church, astonished and not knowing where to turn or what she ought to do. Afterwards she left the church and at its gate encountered the concubine of whom we speak. Stirred at the sight of her, the woman cried out as if mad: “O unhappy woman, why do you presume to enter this church—you who have taken my lawful husband from me and have so seduced even the Mother of God herself by your enchantments that she told me last night that she delights so much in your greetings that she can take no vengeance upon you?”

But the sinful woman, thus challenged before a crowd of men and women, gave the abusive woman no wicked answer; rather, wishing only [Col. 1383B] to avoid her in the throng, she pressed herself into the midst of the people. The other woman, on the contrary, almost furious and scarcely restraining her hands from her, pursued her with shouting, although the people opposed her.

The disturbed priests and clerics came running and asked the cause of the outcry. The woman recounted everything as we have related it, including the vision which she had seen, as we have recounted it above. The clerics asked the sinful woman what sort of greeting she offered to the Blessed Virgin. She told them; they recognized the angelic greeting which the archangel Gabriel had offered her when he foretold that the Lord would be born from her.

When the sinful woman learned that she had been heard, she bent her knees before the aforesaid image and, in the hearing of the people, vowed perpetual continence and asked to become a nun. Having obtained this, she built herself a cell [Col. 1383C] beside the same church, shut herself within it, and remained faithfully in that purpose until the grave.

## CHAPTER III

It happened that a certain poor woman, alone with her little son whom she carried in her arms, entered the aforesaid church when no one was present in it. When the woman saw this, she knelt before the image of the Mother of God, began to say her own prayer, and humbly prayed that she might deign to be present to her.

By chance, the little boy whom the woman held in her arms was chewing a piece of bread with teeth still weak. Looking at the child whom the Blessed Virgin held in her hands, he broke off part of his bread and offered it to the image of the Virgin’s Son, babbling: “Child, [Col. 1383D] eat.” When he repeated this several times and the likeness of the child, being senseless, made no answer at all, the woman’s child began to weep, because he saw that the other child would not eat the dry bread.

Never-to-be-forgotten mercy of the Savior! The image of that child spoke, through the power of the Holy Spirit, and said to the weeping child: “Until the third day I shall feast with you.” The astonished woman, who held her son in her arms, when she heard the image speaking to her son, cried out in fear.

The nuns immediately came; they asked the reason for the outcry. Trembling, the woman told them how the image of the most holy child had spoken to her son, and what it had said to him. When they heard of so great a miracle, all alike—clerics and laypeople—came running and advised that the child [Col. 1384A] be kept in the church until the third day, so that they might see what would happen to him.

When this pleased everyone, the mother remained with the child in the church until the third day. On the third day the boy’s face shone more brightly than usual, and in that very radiance he breathed out his spirit without distress. The Lord fulfilled what he had promised him, giving him the bread of angels, by which all the orders of heavenly powers are nourished. They buried the little body of the holy boy within the same church, to the praise and glory of the Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

## CHAPTER IV

In a certain monastery there was a quite honorably painted image of the aforesaid Virgin. In that monastery there was a monk who slept in the church [Col. 1384B] and had charge of ringing the sacred hours. Since he served many vices and was given over to lust of the flesh, every night he left the monastery and, while the others slept, abandoned himself in unlawful intercourse with a prostitute whom he kept as his own—abominable to God and men.

While the ancient enemy thus deceived him, and no one knew of his crime, the devout Mother of the Lord manifested the following miracle concerning him. Near the aforesaid church was a pond, across which the unhappy monk, more unhappy still, crossed every night in a little boat to the house of that unhappy woman. When he wished to go there, after the gates had been locked on every side, he would pass before the image of the Blessed Virgin, ask her pardon, place soul and body in her keeping, and thus leave by a small [Col. 1384C] door.

It happened one night, when he was hurrying to his wicked deed, that, after asking pardon before the image, the little boat sank in the pond and the unhappy monk, plunged into the waters, was suffocated. Immediately a crowd of demons came, dragging the unhappy soul toward places of torment. The Mother of God encountered them and snatched the wretched soul from their punishments, saying: “O wretched creatures, unworthy even of pity! Why have you presumed to seize the soul of this monk, who, although he was on his way to sin, nevertheless placed himself under my protection?”

Hearing this, the demons cried out: “Let us be judged before the Lord.” When they had come before God, the Mother of Mercy said: “Dearest Son, demons have seized this soul, placed under my protection; and unless I had come swiftly to its aid, they would have dragged it away with them [Col. 1384D] to their torments. Since they have sought your judgment, behold, standing before you, I pray that it be recalled to its body and henceforth live as a monk, no longer yielding to the illusions and deceits of demons, lest something worse happen to him in the end.”

The most gracious Judge said to his Mother: “Since, venerable Mother, it is not permitted to me to deny you anything, as you have asked, let the monk return to his order and do penance, lest he be judged more severely on the last day.”

Thus the soul, dismissed from heaven, returned to the world. While these things were being done concerning the soul, night had passed; and the monks, unaware that their brother had died, sought him but could not find him. As some of them walked near the pond, [Col. 1385A] they saw him rise from the depths of the water and strive to reach the shore by swimming. When they saw this, they entered the little boat, went to meet him, and drew him out.

He ran swiftly to the church, crying: “Gather here to me, all you who fear the Lord and venerate the Mother of Mercy.” Running on, he came before the image of the Mother of God and, falling on his face with many tears and loud groaning, declared that he had sinned, that he was guilty . . . A crowd of astonished people was present, monks and laypeople alike, entirely ignorant of what these things meant.

After long sighs, the monk at last rose from prayer and, having obtained silence, revealed everything as we have set it forth above: how, through the Mother of Mercy, he had been snatched from the jaws of the devil and restored to salvation. You might have seen the people weeping devoutly with him, striking their breasts in compassion, and praising the glorious one with hearts and voices.

Behold: what we have heard concerning the Blessed Mary, we have committed to writing as best we could. Therefore let penitents come to her, striking their guilty breasts with inward groaning; without doubt, if they truly repent, through the merits of this most holy Virgin they will recover the grace of her most gracious Son and our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives, etc.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1142: GILO, BISHOP OF TUSCULUM

[Col. 1385]

## NOTICE

*(Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. XII, p. 81.)*

Gilon, surnamed “of Paris” because of the long time he spent in that city, was born at Toucy in the county of Auxerre. Moréri, who confuses him with Gilles of Paris, a man a century later, consequently asserts that he taught belles-lettres in the capital. He has better grounds for saying that Gilon entered the clergy of Paris, although he adds without proof that he received the diaconate there. What is certain is that, after distinguishing himself there by his talents, he left in 1119 to withdraw to Cluny.

If in shutting himself up in this monastery he fled renown, he did not find there what he sought. Pope Calixtus II, during a journey to Cluny, had occasion to become acquainted with him, took him shortly afterwards to Rome, and at the same time created him cardinal and bishop of Tusculum. [Note: [Col. 1385A] Duchesne, *Hist. des cardinaux français*, vol. I, p. 98.] Honorius II, Calixtus’s successor, inherited his esteem for Gilon and gave him various proofs of it. In 1127 he invested him with the title of legate, sending him to the Holy Land to settle disturbances that had arisen there among the clergy. We possess this pope’s letters to Bernard, patriarch of Antioch, [Note: [Col. 1385A] William of Tyre, *History*, book LXXIII, ch. 23.] the chief author of the division, by which he commanded him to render to the legate Gilon the honor and obedience due to his office.

This legation having achieved all the success expected of it, Gilon, on his return, found himself entrusted with the same office for Poland. Although neither the object nor the particulars of his activities in that kingdom are known, it may be presumed that there he maintained the high opinion which he had hitherto given of his prudence and ability.

The death of Honorius ended the services which our prelate rendered to the Holy See. Far from being useful to it thereafter, he became its scourge by the side he took in the schism of Innocent and Anacletus, rivals for the papacy. Gilon supported the latter, the less legitimate claimant, with a stubbornness that survived even the death of that antipope. In 1134 he is seen exercising, in that man’s name, the functions of legate in Aquitaine, together with the famous Gérard, bishop of Angoulême. [Note: [Col. 1385A] Helinand, p. 187; *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, vol. VII.]

In vain did Peter the Venerable attempt to bring him back to Innocent’s party by two very urgent letters, the first written during Anacletus’s lifetime and the second after his death: they appear to have made no impression on his mind. Yet if it is true that he lived until 1142, as an able critic believes, [Note: [Col. 1386A] Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. VI, book LXXVII, no. 137.] it is difficult to persuade oneself that he did not come to repentance, especially since at that time no spark of schism remained. Dom Mabillon does not hesitate even to affirm it [Note: [Col. 1386A] Ibid., no. 4.] and, following Ughelli, [Note: [Col. 1386A] *Italia sacra*, vol. I, p. 264.] attributes the credit for this conversion to Saint Bernard. But neither writer gives any positive proof of the fact.

The public possesses, though not in their entirety, two writings of Gilon: one a historical poem on the First Crusade in six books, the other a Life of St Hugh, abbot of Cluny. The first of these works, rescued from obscurity through the efforts of André Duchesne, appears at the end of the fourth volume of his *Collection of Historians of France*. There it forms the last four books of a complete History of that expedition, comprising seven books, the first three of which belong to a certain Fulk.

Since Fulk’s work was represented in that edition only by a manuscript full of lacunae, Dom Martène judged it appropriate to republish it in the third volume of his *Anecdotes*, from a much better copy from the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. This second edition is nevertheless not so complete that it does not still leave several gaps to be filled. Dom Martène himself acknowledges [Col. 1387] that he could have made it more perfect if at that time he had known of another manuscript which he later saw at the abbey of Marchiennes.

This copy bears the title: *History by Cardinal Bishop Gilon concerning the Journey to Jerusalem*; and at the end one reads: “Here ends the little book of Gilon, cleric of Paris, afterwards monk of Cluny, then cardinal and bishop, concerning the journey to Jerusalem, when, after the pagans had been expelled and killed, Nicaea, Antioch, and Jerusalem were conquered by the Christians.” There one sees all the stages through which Gilon passed, and in two words the whole summary of the work.

The same words appear at the end of this poem in a manuscript of the Royal Library, at least as old—it is of the thirteenth century—and even fuller than that of Marchiennes, for it contains a prologue by Gilon in elegiac verse, found neither in the latter nor in the others. Here are its opening couplets, from which it may be seen that this poem was not our author’s first attempt:

> Until now, intent upon trifles, I have spoken childish things,  
> On a light subject suited to a boy.  
>
> I have given no song to Turnus, no song to Achilles;  
> But, a young man to a young man, I have given many poems.  
>
> Our mind wholly shrank from weighty matter;  
> It was wholly devoted to light trifles.  
>
> My age was tender and fit for tender games;  
> It could not bear things that weigh upon the mind.  
>
> I remember that I had dared to write of wars; but, lest  
> The subject weigh me down, my Muse abandoned the work.

To this extract from the prologue we shall add the beginning of the work, which will suffice to enable the reader to judge Gilon’s versification:

> By divine help the ruin of the Turks was brought about.  
> For God’s praise, though unequal to the subject,  
> I sketch it in easy verse and invent no fictions.  
> Christ, be present to my mind, wishing to recount your wars—  
> You whose praise is the theme of this poem—  
> So that it may turn out well, and, with you as guide, the verses be made.

At the end of this historical poem he declares his name, homeland, and residence in these two verses:

> I composed these things—I, Gilo by name,  
> An inhabitant of Paris, an unashamed native of Toucy.

He was therefore not yet a monk of Cluny when he set his hand to this work, but an inhabitant of Paris. Yet Baldwin, second king of Jerusalem, who died in 1118, was already no longer alive, since Gilon speaks of him as a prince whose rule had ended. This proves how well-founded it was to date Gilon’s religious profession only to the year 1119.

Our author had passed from the monastic state to the episcopate when he undertook to write the Life of Saint Hugh, a work of which the Bollandists were content to give extracts, [Note: [Col. 1387] *Bollandists*, vol. III, April 29, p. 655.] as also of Ezelon’s work on the same subject. He himself declares this change of state in his dedicatory epistle to Pons, Saint Hugh’s successor, inserted by Dom Martène in the first volume of his *Anecdotes*. For no other sense can be given to the regrets he expresses there at having returned to the world after leaving it, at having lost in Rome what he had acquired at Cluny. This epistle is well written and full of elevated sentiments.

On the testimony of William of Tyre, [Note: [Col. 1387] William of Tyre, *History*, book LXXIII, ch. 23, p. 847.] one should also presume favorably regarding the letters which he wrote to the clergy of Antioch during his legation in Palestine. Time has deprived us of them [Note: [Col. 1388] See below.], and we know them only from the praise bestowed upon them by that historian. Their purpose was to persuade this clergy and its patriarch to restore to the archbishop of Tyre several churches claimed by that prelate. The letters had their effect: that is the best proof of the legate’s eloquence.

[Col. 1387]

## EPISTLE OF GILON, BISHOP OF TUSCULUM, ON THE LIFE OF THE BLESSED HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY, WRITTEN BY HIMSELF—HE LAMENTS HIS REMOVAL FROM THE CLOISTER  
*(About the year 1110.)*

*(MARTÈNE, Anecdotes, vol. I, p. 321, from a manuscript of the monastery of Igny.)*

[Col. 1387A] To his most beloved Father, Lord PONS, abbot, always to be remembered with joy of heart, Brother [Note: [Col. 1387A] Besides Gilon the cardinal and Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, whose work has been published more than once, the Life of Saint Hugh was written by Hugh, monk of Cluny, and by Raynald, abbot [Col. 1388A] of Vézelay; their manuscript work is preserved in a manuscript codex of Clairmarais (see *Patrology*, vol. CLIX).] GILO, [Col. 1388A] more worthy of a hiding-place than of a name, wishes that your sons, with you and through you, may be satisfied with the honey-sweet delight of paradise.

[Col. 1389A] Since reverence for your exalted rank has urged me too to speak of an ineffable man, I have chosen to appear a rashly presumptuous man rather than one opposed to your will. Indeed, in raising the lamp of so great a light upon a golden candlestick, while bearing it on a reed-like and fragile vehicle, I seem to lower it while wishing to raise it. And as the radiant lights of the sun draw the eyes, so by their excessive splendor the deeds of so great a patron dazzle the dullness of our mind.

But, to use borrowed or jingling words:

> If I had an unbroken voice and a stronger breast,  
> And more mouths with more tongues,  
>
> Not even then would I embrace everything in words,  
> Since the subject exceeds my powers.  
>
> Envious nature confined me within a narrow span;  
> [Col. 1389B] it gave my talent only slight powers.

Yet because good will is often reckoned as the deed itself, if grace cannot be repaid, at least pardon will not be denied. Thus the widow who put two coins into the treasury is preferred to the riches of Croesus, because she is believed to have offered sincere devotion, richer than wealth.

Certainly, one ought not extol in verbal wisdom a saint who shines with the brightness of his merits. Thus, although nectar-like drink is distributed at royal tables in broad bowls, it is sometimes nevertheless offered in narrow cups. It was indeed fitting that his life should be written in portions at Rome, since, while he lived, he is known to have been the greatest devotee of the Roman princes—I mean Peter and [Col. 1390A] Paul.

If by this means I escape blame, the credit will belong to your condescension: you gave me the courage to begin and prescribed an order suited to the subject. Finally, your command is attended by such power that nothing you enjoin is burdensome, even if by nature it is difficult.

I find only one thing difficult: that my sins have made me return to the world, having renounced Pharaoh’s hard slavery. Now for the first time I have known, even on earth, the dwelling-place of the heavenly kingdom. Oh, if it were permitted me to be joined again to the assemblies of the saints! I would fall at your feet, lest, beset by every crime, I be excluded from the fellowship of the blessed.

I, a companion of sins and stripped of virtues, had gone to the physicians of languishing souls; and, again exposed to robbers, with my wounds breaking open anew, [Col. 1390B] I am compelled to cry: “My scars have become putrid and corrupt.” I am a sick sheep wandering far from the folds; unless the merciful shepherd bring me back, I shall quickly fail, and in the very effort to rise my steps will collapse.

I am that prodigal who lost the Father’s substance, because I could not keep in Rome what Cluny taught. I had resolved, lest I perish with the many, to follow Lot as he went out to the mountains; but, looking back, I was turned into a pillar and did not keep to the paths of the righteous. It remains for the mercy of your greatness to command me, who cannot go forward, to return from the city; and may the breath of the Holy Spirit, through the prayer of the brethren, carry me to the desired harbor.

[Col. 1389]

## EPITOME OF THE LIFE OF SAINT HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY

Written soon after the saint’s death by Ezelon and Gilon; excerpted by an anonymous writer.

*(See* Patrology, *vol. CLIX, col. 909.)*

[Col. 1389]

## HISTORY OF THE JOURNEY TO JERUSALEM, BY GILON

*(See* Patrology, *vol. CLIX, col. 909.)*

[Col. 1389]

## THE VERY VEHEMENT DISPUTATION OF GILON, BISHOP OF TUSCULUM AND APOSTOLIC LEGATE, AGAINST THE PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH, BECAUSE HE REFUSES TO CONCEDE PRIMACY TO THE ROMAN POPE, DESPISES THE POPE’S LETTERS, DISGRACES PAPAL LEGATES, AND SAYS THAT HE IS NOT THE POPE’S SON BUT HIS BROTHER, TO THE INJURY OF THE DECALOGUE

In LUDEWIG, *Reliquiae manuscriptarum diplomatum*, p. 452.

[Col. 1389C] AEGIDIUS, bishop of Tusculum and legate of the Apostolic See, to B., patriarch of Antioch. What I have not learned by report or through the deceptive variability of gossip, [Col. 1390C] but rather proclaim in shame under threat of great peril, producing experience and not conjecture—you had already very often despised the holy [Col. 1391A] and Apostolic See, insolently rejecting the letters of the Father of all Christians and rejecting his legates contrary to the sworn obligation of your profession.

Yet I, undertaking the legation of my lord the pope, desired, with those who hate peace, to be peaceful: in hope of correction, not in agreement with malice. The modest degree of familiarity we had shared urged this course, representing me to you as most faithful and more inclined to serve your charity than to accuse you.

Finally, if a powerful person should sometimes send an unsuitable messenger, the humility of the envoy is not despised, because reverence is preserved for the lord who sends him. But you, paying no heed to the command of the supreme pope, drove me, your fellow servant, from your territories, believing that you would stifle me if you imposed silence directly upon the one sent to plead with you. In this deed, indeed, the prophet Zechariah says to you: “Lift up your eyes and see the curse,” like a flying scroll entering the house of one who swears falsely by my name, to consume it.

Henceforth it will certainly be demonstrated to all by written and public arguments how greatly, at your peril, you attempt against all divine and human law to alter the ancient counsel of God, contemptuously scorning Roman authority. After the common promise made in baptism, at your consecration before the Lord’s tomb you promised obedience to the pope, and again received the pledge of the pallium, with the assistance of Lord Mauritius, bishop of Porto.

Long ago, seduced by the phantom of error, you mounted the horse of pride, in order to [Col. 1391C] fall backward in confusion, not upon your face as Saul did. What kind of thing, how lamentable and truly detestable, is that sacrilegious usurpation by which you boast that you are the colleague and brother of the lord pope! Until these times every Christian has shuddered to say it, and the Church has had no one among Christians who said it.

Do you not know that Peter is named from the rock, Christ, upon whose body the whole Church at Rome stands? This Peter fills his sling and strikes the Philistine Goliath upon the forehead, where the profane and impious man has no banner of the cross. For the whole Roman Church sees its adversaries laboring in vain to establish another foundation besides that which has been laid.

Recall at last what sacred history relates: arrogant men departing from the East into the plain of Shinar built [Col. 1391D] the tower of Babel, having bricks for stones and bitumen for mortar. Not without reason Rome is the East of the universal Church; whoever recoils from it makes a stench for all his companions. For Shinar is interpreted as “their stench,” concerning whom the prophet says: “They have rotted in their iniquities.” And Isaiah: “Instead of sweet odor there shall be stench, and instead of a belt,” etc.

Given over to these earthly pleasures, desiring to reach heaven with mud and bricks, while they raise themselves above themselves they build with the Egyptians the Babel of everlasting confusion, suddenly to be cast down into the abyss—those Egyptians who oppressed the children of Israel with similar labor. But if you built the structure of your edifice upon the rock of faith, which is the Roman Church of Peter, and not upon the sand of worldly hope, in which Moses buried the Egyptian, remembering the benefit abundantly bestowed upon you by your devout [Col. 1392A] mother, you would gladly subject yourself to her who subjected to you whatever kings there were.

That you may be able to fulfill this holy course, cry with Isaiah: “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones. The sycamores have been cut down, but we shall replace them with cedars.” Otherwise fear what Proverbs pronounces specifically against you: “The eye that mocks a father and despises a mother—let the ravens of the torrent pluck it out, and the young eagles eat it.”

Without doubt this will truly happen to you, when, justice directing the lord pope, bishops, cardinals, and the whole Church in agreement rise against your presumptions. Then your presumptions will burst, you who, rushing into the wilds, exalt yourself beyond the bounds of your rank, without considering yourself.

Moreover, it is good that the offending eye be plucked out and cast away, so that the gaze of pride and malice may be crushed and the eye of the simplicity of sound faith be opened. Thus the Apostle says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise.” He who is at some time blinded by that proud eye is spiritually enlightened by the Lord.

Are these the returns you make to the Roman Church, which forcibly and powerfully drew wretched Antioch from the very gaping jaws of its enemies when it had already been utterly swallowed up, and daily sends out its children to preserve it, accepting diminution of itself for its liberation? It happened in a wonderful manner, as Amos says: “As a shepherd rescues from the mouth of a lion two legs or the tip of an ear,” so Apostolic mercy rescued you from the incalculable fury of the Persians.

O profound height! Was it too little to neglect the letters of the lord pope, unless you, a bishop, should also refute me, a bishop, through your chaplain and insulting letters, and shamelessly repel the legate of your lord? Perhaps you do not know that wise men call a legation alone the arbiter of peace or war. Would that the Lord opened your eyes as he opened the blind man’s, so that you might see that far more are with us than with you.

But, struck with blindness by shame, unless you are led into Samaria by Elisha, like Ben-hadad, you cannot recover sight: that is, unless through obedience to the lord pope you return to the mother-city of the Israelites, the Roman Church. Otherwise, like Balaam, you will at last have your eyes opened when affliction alone gives understanding.

Certainly it is to be feared—truly feared—that, because of your singular self-exaltation, the Eastern [Col. 1392D] Church may be thrown into confusion, sending internal destruction among itself and losing the aid of the Western Church. This will undoubtedly happen unless you return to yourself and freely release his suffragans to the archbishop of Trier, causing no prejudice to anyone in this matter, if you observe the command of the lord pope.

When these scandals have been removed from the midst, may the Lord, through the Psalmist, speak peace to his people and to his . . .; and “we shall walk in the house of the Lord” in agreement. But in rebellion we have no peace with the obstinate, lest we share in evil works; for the Spirit too did not make such peace, but offered it to people of good will.

Yet we trust in the divine mercy that, warned even by these things, you will desist. Finally, if you maintain that the Church of Antioch proceeded from the school of Peter, recognize that Peter’s ship was built at Jerusalem and, after its anchor was lifted from that harbor, came to your shores through the billows of swelling waves. For, as the Lord testifies, the Gospel had to be preached to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

Therefore [Col. 1394A], since Zion is the beginning of our salvation, for diverse reasons it is fitting that we exalt her, so that we may be exalted. Lastly, acting as legate for Christ, as though God were exhorting through me, I beg you: be reconciled to your Father, that you may live through him who is our peace, who made the two one.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1142: GAUFRIDUS, BISHOP OF CHÂLONS

[Col. 1393]

## NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. IX, p. 879.)*

[Col. 1393B] “When Blessed Bernard,” says Alberic in his *Chronicle*, “had been elected bishop of Châlons, he refused; and through him Gaufridus, abbot of Saint-Médard of Soissons, became bishop of Châlons.” The *Chronicle of Saint-Médard*, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 787, adds the following words: “In the year 1131, Gaufridus, surnamed Stag’s Neck, abbot of the church of Blessed Médard, was made bishop of Châlons.”

Shortly afterwards he was sent, with Matthew, bishop of Albano, by Pope Innocent II to Louis VI, king of the French, to console him over the death of Philip, his eldest son. In the following year, in which he was consecrated, he confirmed to Laurence, abbot of Saint-Vitton, the foundation of the priory of Chaudefontaine and all the other goods of that monastery situated in his diocese; and in [Col. 1393C] 1133 he confirmed certain churches to the church of La Celle.

In 1134 he founded a monastery in Argonne and gave it to regular canons, who later passed to the Cistercian order. In 1137 he subscribed the foundation charter of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu and gave to Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi of Reims, the altar of Loupemont. In 1138, with other arbiters, he settled the dispute between Manasses II, bishop of Meaux, and Risende, abbess of Faremoutiers.

In the same year, at his request, Guarin gave the monastery of Novy the church of Fontaines near Mont-Desir, which was still in lay hands, and gave the monastery of Saint Peter the parsonage of the whole parish of Vitry. In 1140 he attended the Council of Sens against Peter Abelard; he was also present when Count Hugh of Rocey made satisfaction to the church of Saint-Remi of Reims.

In that same year he founded his anniversary observance in the church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs at Paris. At about the same time, together with Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, he settled the dispute that the abbess of Faremoutiers had with the bishop of Meaux.

Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, wrote to him in book II, letter 43, as follows: “You, the first disseminator, founder, and promoter throughout all France of the Cluniac order—indeed, of the divine order; you, I say, the expeller of the ancient dragon from the dens of so many monasteries; you, the awakener from long sleep and prolonged monastic torpor: while I recall, ponder, and retain these and a thousand such things, I am wholly and entirely inflamed with love for your sacred person.

“Therefore I have chosen you as one of two men whom, at the summit of unfeigned charity, I have not only considered worthy to be set before the friends of all Belgian Gaul, but have publicly proclaimed as such. And what of this too: that it is necessary for you to be not only bishop but also prince of so great a city? Let the bishop claim nothing from the monk; let the prince usurp nothing from religion; let the world steal nothing from the ancient order.”

In 1141 he confirmed to the cell of Brienne a third part of the tithe of the church of Saint Mary of Coudray. In 1142 he subscribed the charter of Samson, archbishop of Reims, for the monastery of Saint-Theodoric; and he died on the fifth or sixth day before the Kalends of June, according to the necrologies, in that same year—not the following year, as the *Chronicle of Saint Peter of Châlons* reports (provided, however, that there is no error in the chronology of Saint Bernard’s letters, which we shall cite shortly). He was buried in the choir of the cathedral church between the eagle and the image of Saint Stephen.

[Col. 1393]

## LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF GAUFRIDUS

I. Letter of Gaufridus to Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.

[Col. 1395A]

(It is found among the letters of Peter the Venerable as no. 42. See below under the year 1156.)

II. To Stephen, bishop of Paris.

(See below under Stephen.)

III. Charter of the foundation of the abbey of Monastery in Argonne. (Year 1134.)

*[Gallia Christiana*, X, Documents, 167.]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, I, GAUFRIDUS, humble minister of the Church of Châlons.

If we provide for the interests of Churches, and for the needs of those serving Christ within them, at the request of those entrusted with them, we perform a work of charity and the office of a bishop. Let it therefore be known to all present and future that we have given the place and church called Monasterium to the venerable Eustace, abbot of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and to the brethren serving God there and to their successors, together with the tithe of the same parish, and woodland with meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, free and exempt from every customary due and molestation of bishop, archdeacon, and dean; yet subject and obedient to the Church of Châlons, in such wise that they shall come to consult us and the chapter of the blessed protomartyr whenever the bishop or archdeacon summons them.

We further ordain and confirm that whoever has hitherto held the chapel of Summelle shall forever pay the customary dues which the mother church, namely Monasterium, anciently owed to the bishop, archdeacon, and dean; and shall possess, besides the woodland, whatever lies within the boundaries of Summelle belonging to the parish of Monasterium.

Moreover, Peter of Athis and his nephew Gippuin, with the assent and grant of Lord Galbert of Châlons and Milo of Cernon, granted and gave to the same abbey, for the remedy of their souls and those of their predecessors, the allod which they held from the ford of Ositremont to the land of Noviers near Summelle; and from the land of Noviers through Fornoneium, near Algicourt, as far as Bercholtha; and from Bercholtha to Wambais, near Hattumaisnil, as far as the place where Wambais flows into Gelestre; and from Gelestre as far as Ositremont.

We therefore confirm, under the protection of our seal and with witnesses appointed, that these things, and whatever shall henceforth be piously given to the church of the aforesaid holy Mother of God by the grant of bishops, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, are to be held without contradiction. Should anyone hereafter presumptuously attempt to alter or annul these provisions, we bind him with the bond of anathema.

Sign of Stephen; sign of Odo; sign of Reiner; sign of Guy, archdeacon; sign of Ancher, dean; sign of John; sign of Wibert; sign of Walter, priests; sign of Guarner; sign of Peter, deacons; sign of Bono; sign of Hugh; sign of Segard; sign of Guiard.

Done at Châlons in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1134, epact 12, concurrent 6. Walter, chancellor, wrote it.

## IV. Charter of Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons, confirming the principal gifts made to the monastery of Trois-Fontaines by Peter, abbot of Cluny; Ado, abbot of Saint-Oyend; Benedict, abbot of Saint Peter of Châlons; and the canons of Compiègne. (Year 1136.)

*[Gallia Christiana, ibid., col. 168.]*

**GEOFFREY**, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Châlons.

Let all know that P., abbot of Cluny; A., abbot of Saint-Oyend; P., abbot of Saint Peter of Châlons; and the dean and chapter of the Church of Compiègne—each under the testimony of his own seal and of the witnesses named—at the request of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, made a privilege for the abbot and brethren of Trois-Fontaines concerning the things which they granted and gave them, in the following words:

> “To the venerable Lord Guy, abbot, and the brethren of Trois-Fontaines: Peter, abbot of Cluny, greeting and affection.
>
> At the request of our lord and friend Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, whom we love greatly, we grant to you and your brethren, whom we desire to hold in the same affection of charity, that you may henceforth possess freely that tithe which our brethren of Baudovilliers were accustomed to receive from you. We further make known to you that this gift has been made with the counsel and approval of the community of Cluny.
>
> Sign of Lord Bernard, prior; sign of Bernard of Meilay; sign of Jarenton; sign of Geoffrey, prior of Saint Margaret; sign of Gigo, chamberlain. Farewell, dearest brethren; remember us.”

> “Ado, by God’s grace abbot of the church of Saint-Oyend in the Jura, makes known to all that I established in the chapter of the church of Sarmatia, with the approval of all the brethren and with the consent both of monks and lay brothers, that the same church of Sarmatia should each year, on the Sunday next before mid-Lent Sunday, pay six solidi in the coinage of Châlons, for the church of Saint Mary of Trois-Fontaines, to the canons of Saint Corneille of Compiègne.
>
> Witnesses: Robert, prior of that place; Gerard; Milo. Also present were these men whom Lord Ebles, by God’s grace bishop of Châlons, had sent to hear this matter: Ralph, abbot of Saint Peter, and Master Rainer.”

> “I, Benedict, abbot of Saint Peter, and all the brethren of that church, have received the entreaties of Lord William, bishop of Châlons, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; and we have freely granted in perpetuity to the church of blessed Mary, situated in the wood of Luiz, at the place which the inhabitants called Trois-Fontaines, the allod which we possessed at Lombracum. Lest anyone should presumptuously attempt to invalidate this through the passage of time, we have confirmed it by the protection of our seal and of the witnesses named.
>
> Sign of Duran; sign of Philip; sign of Dudo; sign of Albert. This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1117.”

> “Geoffrey, dean of the holy Church of Compiègne; John, cantor; and we together, the whole community of that place, to all present and future.
>
> We wish all to know that, at the request of Lord King Louis, his consort Queen Adelaide, Count Theobald, and also the venerable men Goslin, bishop of Soissons; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; Guarin, bishop of Amiens; and Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, we granted for habitation to Brother Guy, abbot, and the monks serving there with him, a certain place called Trois-Fontaines in the wood of Luiz, which entirely belongs by right to our church.
>
> Lest this be removed from memory by the long passage of time, we caused it to be recorded in writing. It therefore pleased us that the said monks should possess and cultivate that land and woodland, and whatever more from the lands of our church may in future come to them anywhere in the same wood, preserving the boundaries of others; and that they should freely and peacefully hold in perpetuity whatever right we had therein. For all these things we imposed upon them six solidi of Châlons, to be paid each year, on the Sunday next before mid-Lent, to our officials at Pontigon; and thus they shall remain, throughout the year, in complete peace, so far as lies in our power.
>
> This was therefore confirmed by the present chirograph and strengthened for the knowledge of posterity by the seal and signs of those who were present. Sign of Goslin, bishop of Soissons; sign of Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; sign of Guarin, bishop of Amiens; sign of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; sign of Geoffrey, dean; sign of John, cantor; sign of Odo and Haimo, provosts; sign of Rainald, abbot of Saint Bartholomew; sign of Theodoric, abbot of Saint Eligius of Noyon.
>
> Done at Compiègne in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1130, in public chapter.”

Done at Châlons in the year 1136.

## V. Privilege of Geoffrey, bishop, for the monastery of Saint Peter. (Year 1138.)

*[Ibid., col. 169, from the autograph.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, **GEOFFREY**, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Châlons.

Those who faithfully labour for the interests of the Church and diligently devote themselves to contemplation ought fittingly to be rewarded, so that we may seem worthily to have answered their services, and they may become more useful through the grace of the consolation granted them. Since we sometimes extend a helping hand to those dwelling outside our borders, far more—and far more generously—ought those committed to our care and keeping watch on our behalf to find relief in the bounty of our recompense. Nor is it a great matter if they reap from us temporal things, by whose intercessions we are prepared for eternal ones.

Let it therefore be known to present and future alike that, at the request of our reverend brother and friend Hugh, abbot of Saint Peter of the Mountains, with the assent and will of the chapter of the blessed protomartyr, we have given to the said abbot and his church the *personae* [rights of presentation and parochial revenues] of the whole parish of Vitry, with the same dignity and freedom in which Lord Ancher, dean of Saint Stephen, had held it; provided, however, that on the day of our anniversary the convent of Saint Peter shall receive from it a meal worth twenty solidi, so that our gift may mercifully sustain those whose prayer intercedes with God for us.

And behold the witnesses of this act: sign of Rainer; sign of Odo; sign of Geoffrey; sign of Guy, archdeacon; sign of Garner, cantor; sign of John, chaplain; sign of Garner of Mallei.

Done at Châlons in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, epact 7, concurrent 5.

Walter, chancellor, wrote and subscribed it.

## VI. Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons, establishes his anniversary in the church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, Paris. (Year 1140.)

*[Ibid.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

Since, according to the prophetic and apostolic saying, truth is diminished among the children of men, and since, as the charity of many grows cold, we see iniquity—alas!—abounding, it is expedient that by an abundance of good works we should strive to resist the multiplied iniquity and malice. And although all owe offices of charity to all, the prelates of the Church, by reason of their pastoral charge, ought more earnestly and devoutly to provide for religious faithful persons and to supply their want from their own abundance.

Moved by this reasoning and devotion, I, Geoffrey, by God’s grace bishop of Châlons, for the salvation of my soul and in remembrance of my anniversary, with the grant and assent of Lord Geoffrey our archdeacon, of our other archdeacons, and of our whole chapter, have given to the monks dwelling at Saint-Martin-des-Champs in Paris: the altar of Frévisville; the altar of Noirlieu; the altar of Verrières; the altar of Wallimont; and the altar of Épance, with their chapels, endowments, and all appurtenances belonging to the said altars, while preserving in all things episcopal and archidiaconal right.

That this may remain ratified and firm, we have confirmed it by the impression of our seal and by the witness of our canons. Sign of Master Rainer, archdeacon and dean; sign of Odo of Roset, archdeacon; sign of Geoffrey, archdeacon; sign of Guy, archdeacon; sign of Henry, treasurer; sign of Garner, cantor; sign of Guinibert, sub-cantor; sign of John, chaplain; sign of Walter, priest; sign of Peter; sign of Guarner; sign of Ralph, deacons; sign of Stephen; sign of Renald; sign of Roger, subdeacons; sign of Baldwin; sign of Hugh; sign of Milo, acolytes.

This was done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1140, the tenth of our episcopate.

## VII. Foundation of Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons, in the abbey of Morimond. (Year 1142.)

*[Ibid., col. 172, from the autograph.]*

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I, **JOFFREY**, by God’s grace bishop of the Church of Châlons.

What the Holy Spirit deigns to accomplish through my hands, I have decreed to commit to writing, so that it may remain ratified forever. By the counsel of venerable brethren—namely Anselm, abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon; Nicholas, abbot of Saint Nicasius; and William, abbot of Morimond—we have ordained and established to endure forever that in the monastery of the said Morimond the Mass of blessed Mary ever-virgin shall be celebrated every day without interruption, if there are enough priests there able to fulfill that office.

But if there is only one priest, and he must celebrate any other Mass, even one for the dead, he shall say the office of blessed Mary privately, either by himself or with ministers, as far as the secret prayer. Then, having solemnly said whatever office is necessary, when he comes to the secrets, he shall first celebrate the secret of blessed Mary; and after receiving the Lord’s Body and Blood, likewise privately—as he celebrated the office—so after communion he shall complete it with its collect.

For the celebration of so great a mystery, Guarner, illustrious lord of Aulnay, gave to the church of Morimond the greater part of the tithe that belonged to him from the village called Superturbam, for the remedy of his soul, that of Elizabeth his wife, those of his ancestors, and those of his children; and he confirmed it by free gift. But if anyone—which we do not desire—should dare to treat as nothing this privilege of our ordinance and to despise this commemoration of blessed Mary, let him be anathema on the part of God and of the same Mother of our Lord.

This was done in our presence at Reims, the metropolitan city, on 6 March, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1141, epact 11.

The witnesses of this matter are the aforesaid abbots, and Walter our son, brother of the said Warner; Baldwin, dean [Note: Dean not of the cathedral church, but perhaps of another church in the same city.]; Peter, monk; and many others.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1142: STEPHEN, BISHOP OF PARIS

## NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana, new edition, vol. VII, col. 59.)*

Stephen I—whom some wrongly assert to have been a son of Philip I or Louis the Fat, kings of France, and others, no less falsely, to have sprung from the Garland family and to have been brother of Anseau the seneschal and Stephen of Garland, chancellor of France and archdeacon of Paris—was more truly born of the ancient and illustrious family of Senlis. The error perhaps arose because those who confused their names reported that this man had been honoured with episcopal dignity, whereas the other had been chancellor of France and dean of Orléans.

The family of Senlis had been distinguished by the office of royal butler under the first kings of the third dynasty, as the cartularies of Saint Mary of Corbeil and of the abbeys of Éder, Saint-Victor of Paris, and Notre-Dame de la Charité testify. In the foundation charter of the last-named house he is called brother of William the Wolf of Senlis. He was the son of Guy of Senlis—otherwise “de la Tour,” lord of Chantilly and Ermenonville—and of his wife Bertha.

Cultivated in every kind of learning, he became archdeacon of Paris; then, after the death of Gilbert, he was immediately appointed bishop. Scarcely had he taken possession of the see when, out of his singular affection for the Victorines, he granted them, with the assent of the chapters concerned, the annual revenue of vacant prebends both in the greater church of Saint Mary, in which he held the church of Saint-Jean-le-Rond, and in the churches of Saint-Marcel, Saint-Germain-l’Auxerrois, Saint-Cloud, and Saint-Martin-des-Champs. In compensation he gave one prebend to the church of Saint-Jean-le-Rond in 1124, the first year of his episcopate. [Note: [Col. 1401D] *Hist. Ecclesiae Paris.*, vol. II, p. 23.]

In that same year he granted certain things to the canons of the Church of Paris by an instrument from which one may reasonably infer that the common table of the canons was then begun. To the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés he gave the church of Boissy. He confirmed for the people of Pontoise the gift of Saint-Prix of Tour. He ratified an agreement between Matthew, prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, and Burchard of Montmorency.

He was one of the bishops to whom Pope Calixtus, on 26 August, directed that the interdict pronounced because of the incestuous marriage of William the Norman with the daughter of the Count of Anjou should be observed in their dioceses. [Note: [Col. 1401D] *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 149.] He subscribed Louis the Fat’s diploma confirming the possessions of the Premonstratensians in 1125.

He had a dispute with Theobald Notier, archdeacon, who undertook many things beyond the authority of his office. To settle the case he summoned the abbots and clergy of Paris, who were ready to pronounce judgment, when Theobald appealed to the judgment of the supreme pontiff. [Note: [Col. 1401D] *Hist. Ecclesiae Paris.*, vol. II, p. 29.] The bishop and archdeacon immediately went to Rome, where arbitrators delegated by the pope made peace between them in the third year of Honorius’s pontificate.

A disagreement also arose between the bishop and the canons of the Church of Paris concerning students dwelling in the cloister. [Note: [Col. 1401D] *Ibid.*, p. 31.] Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor, together with Thomas, prior, and Robert, settled it.

In the same year, when Stephen, favourably disposed toward the Victorines, attempted to give them a prebend of his church, King Louis intervened [Note: [Col. 1401D] *Ibid.*, p. 25.], forbidding any diminution of the Church of Paris and forbidding regular canons to hold a prebend there. Stephen, fearing that the liberty of the Church would be impaired by this decree, placed the king and his territory under interdict; the archbishop of Sens and the bishop of Chartres threatened the same. In return, the king spared neither the bishop nor his goods, guests, or tenants, and seized the temporal revenues by royal authority.

Accordingly Stephen called upon both the bishops of his province and the abbots then assembled at Cîteaux to assist him, and asked them, in view of the spiritual brotherhood they had contracted with the king, to entreat him to make peace with Stephen. While these matters were underway, Louis, having received letters from Honorius by which he was absolved from the interdict, became more aggressive and listened to no one. Stephen therefore again sought refuge with the Cistercians. On this matter Hugh, abbot of Pontigny, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, wrote to the supreme pontiff; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, also wrote letters, which are found among Saint Bernard’s correspondence. [Note: [Col. 1402D] Epistles 45, 46, 47, 49.]

In the same year Stephen, together with Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor, witnessed the gift made in December by the canons of Sens of the church of Saint-Sauveur to the regular canons of Saint-Jean dwelling at Sens. The Council of Troyes for the Knights Templar was held on 13 January 1128, and Stephen attended it.

Perhaps made more moderate by the letters of the Cistercian abbots, and at the same time moved by the wrongs which Stephen’s adversaries, supported by royal authority, were plotting against the Church of Paris, Honorius gave letters to the Parisian chapter on 2 March 1129. [Note: [Col. 1402D] *Hist. Ecclesiae Paris.*, vol. II, p. 27.] In these he forbade them to alter anything in the Church of Paris without the bishop’s consent, and annulled whatever they had established to Stephen’s prejudice since he had become bishop.

Stephen attended, on Easter Day of the same year, the coronation of Philip, eldest son of King Louis the Fat. In this year also a council was held at Paris in the monastery of Saint-Germain by Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the apostolic see, formerly prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. There Argenteuil was restored to Saint-Denis at the request of Abbot Suger. Stephen attended and subscribed the letters of Louis VI issued on this matter.

In 1130 a grievous evil afflicted Gaul; the Parisians especially were consumed by the “sacred fire.” To cleanse this plague, Stephen implored the aid of Saint Geneviève and ordered a solemn supplication, in which the sick were healed upon touching her holy relics. In memory of this miracle Innocent II established the feast of the Miracles in the following year; and near the greater basilica, a church of Saint Geneviève of the Burning was built or restored, so called from the sick persons who were termed “burning.”

In October 1131 Innocent held a synod at Reims, where he reconciled King Louis and Stephen. Taking thought both for the king’s dignity and for the liberty of the Church, he requested from the chapter of Paris the prebend which they willingly granted to the canons of Saint-Victor. [Note: [Col. 1402D] *Ibid.*, vol. II, p. 28.] Thus these disputes came to rest.

In the Martyrology of Éder, Stephen is said to have built that abbey in 1132, established there an order of nuns according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, confirmed by the apostolic authority of Pope Innocent, under an anathema forbidding the expulsion of women, and to have done them countless other good works. In the same year Innocent instructed Stephen [Note: [Col. 1402D] *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 154 ff.] to see that Archembald, subdean of Orléans, and his companions recovered the honours and goods taken from them. He also wrote directing him to lift the interdict he had imposed upon the church of Saint Geneviève.

About that time Bishop Stephen had a complaint against Stephen of Garland, archdeacon and kinsman of Henry, archbishop of Sens, who had committed dreadful crimes on the land of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. [Note: [Col. 1403D] *Spicilegium*, pp. 159, 160, 161.] Summoned by the metropolitan to Provins for an examination of the matter, he refused to come, lest he be compelled to obey to the detriment of the honour and dignity of the Church of Paris. It is probable that this affair was settled through the arbitration of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, on the advice of Geoffrey of Chartres. [Note: [Col. 1403D] *Ibid.*, pp. 155, 156, 157, 158.]

At the same period Galo, master of the Parisian school, excommunicated by Stephen for the very grave injury he had inflicted upon Algrin, chancellor of the Church, appealed to Henry, archbishop of Sens, and afterwards to the legate of the Apostolic See. Stephen replied that Henry could not summon the cause of the excommunicated Galo before his tribunal without Stephen’s consent; and that the legate could not absolve Galo and his companions before satisfaction had been made. Stephen declared himself ready to appear before the legate and the pope himself and to defend his authority, since he had acted only with the counsel of the king and bishops and had excommunicated Galo by papal authority and command.

In 1133, the ninth year of his episcopate, he gave to the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs the church of Saint-Denis-de-la-Chartre, with all its appurtenances, and a prebend in the greater basilica. King Louis had transferred this church to him after receiving it from laymen, so that he might give it to the monks; they in turn gave the church they possessed at Montmartre for the instruction of virgins. It is still a priory of Cluniac monks.

In the same year Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor, was killed on 20 August; his murder caused great disturbances. Stephen had gone to Calam to reform and regulate an abbey of nuns, taking Master Thomas with him. But on the return journey, near the castle of Saint Stephen called Gournay, he was suddenly attacked on a Sunday by the nephews of Archdeacon Theobald, who were laying an ambush for the bishop on the road. They fell upon the unarmed Thomas and killed him. [Note: [Col. 1403D] *Ibid.*, vol. III, p. 163.]

Struck by so atrocious a crime, Stephen returned to Paris and at once struck the perpetrators with anathema, ordering the archpriests to promulgate the sentence of excommunication that he had pronounced. [Note: [Col. 1403D] Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 746.] He wrote these matters in almost the same words to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, from the monastery of Clairvaux, to which he had withdrawn in grief after pronouncing the sentence of excommunication against the authors of this crime. [Note: [Col. 1403D] Notes on Saint Bernard, col. LVIII.] At the same time he invited Geoffrey to come and console him, so that they might deliberate what ought to be done in such a matter.

He likewise wrote a letter full of sorrow and mourning to Pope Innocent. [Note: [Col. 1403D] Bernard, Epistle 159.] In it he especially begged Innocent not to allow himself to be deceived by the words of Theobald Notier, should he approach him. Bernard also appended his own letter to Stephen’s letter, [Note: [Col. 1403D] *Ibid.*, Epistle 158.] and the pope, moved by it, decreed that the bishops to whom the case pertained should pass judgment on so great an outrage.

Stirred by Innocent’s letters, [Note: [Col. 1404D] Notes on Saint Bernard, col. LIX.] the bishops of Gaul assembled at Jotrum, not far from the river Marne. What was decreed in the council is not easy to say, for its acts have perished; but Innocent confirmed the bishops’ sentence and imposed further penalties upon the parricides.

Around this time Archembald, subdean of the Church of Orléans, was killed by his adversaries, at roughly the time when Thomas the Victorine was killed. When the authors of the murder had been condemned in an assembly of cardinals and had begged pardon, the supreme pontiff delegated Stephen and Geoffrey to exact expiation for the crime. In letters issued at Pisa on 8 January 1134, he informed them of the sentence which he had pronounced. [Note: [Col. 1404D] *Hist. Ecclesiae Paris.*, vol. II, p. 50.]

After Theobald, abbot, had restored together with Stephen the monastery of Saint Eligius to the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, it having formerly been granted uncanonically by Galo, [Note: [Col. 1404D] *Ibid.*, p. 50.] Stephen gave it again to the Church of Saint-Maur, which had long retained it, in 1134, the eleventh year of his episcopate. In 1136 he made an agreement with King Louis about a certain ditch in the Parisian suburb called Campel: the king was to possess two parts, and the bishop one third. [Note: [Col. 1404D] *Hist. Ecclesiae Paris.*, vol. II, p. 39.]

In the following year, when monks and canons were attempting to withdraw themselves from the jurisdiction and power of bishops, he obtained letters from Innocent on 26 March 1137 directing that churches and monasteries so marked, even if furnished with a privilege of the supreme pontiff, should remain under the authority and jurisdiction of the bishop of Paris. In the same year he subscribed the charter of Louis VI confirming the privileges of the bishops of the province of Bordeaux. [Note: [Col. 1404D] Labbé, *Mélanges curieux*, p. 608.] He attended Louis VI when the king was dying on 26 July and preparing for a better life.

He confirmed Hugh Tirel’s gift of the village of Bofesmont to the monks of Saint-Martin. In 1138 he granted to the nuns of Éder the tithes restored to them and confirmed the gift made to the church of Carolilocus by William, his brother. In 1140 he secured for the priory of Saint Nicholas of Acy the parish churches of Dérencourt and Carrona in his diocese. [Note: [Col. 1404D] *History of Saint-Martin-des-Champs*, p. 296.] He is also mentioned in a charter of King Louis VII, issued in 1141, the fifth year of his reign, preserved in the manuscript history of Saint-Victor.

Several letters, especially nos. 18 and 19, prove Stephen’s high standing with Pope Innocent. In the cartulary of Saint-Florent he is reproved for having installed priests in the church of Dogilo without consulting the monks of Saint-Florent, whose concern it was.

Authors and records disagree concerning the day and year of Stephen’s death. The Victorines maintain that he died on 29 July. John, a writer of that house, writes of his death:

> “At this time Stephen, bishop of Paris, died and was buried in the monastery of Saint-Victor of Paris, in the middle of the choir. Upon his tomb these verses were written:
>
> Here Stephen lies among the sheep: he was  
> The shepherd of the Church of Paris, and of this sheep.  
> This poor, small, and new house the pious father enlarged;  
> He raised it up and adorned it with possessions, honour, and books.  
> He gave much to many; himself to us—and would give more,  
> Had he been able, he who gave his goods and himself.”

The memory of this bishop is likewise celebrated in the Victorine obituary on 29 July in these words:

> “On the fourth day before the Kalends of August: the anniversary of Stephen, bishop of Paris, of pious memory. In his lifetime, embracing our church with a wonderful affection of sincere love and conferring upon it many and great benefits, he left to posterity a worthy and perpetual memorial of his name and love. For in every church in which there are prebends, he gave us one prebend in each: one prebend in the senior church of Blessed Mary of Paris; one in the church of Saint-Marcel; one in Saint-Germain-l’Auxerrois; and one in Saint-Martin-des-Champs. He also gave us the annual revenues of prebends in all the above-mentioned churches; moreover, at his death he left us the very best books that he had acquired.
>
> The anniversary of so great a man and such a special friend must therefore be celebrated specially and solemnly each year, with great devotion, and with the commendation before Mass. It has also been established that for his soul one full prebend shall be given daily in alms; that one poor person shall each year be clothed completely; and that on the day of his anniversary one hundred poor persons shall be fed with bread, wine, and meat. Anniversary of his father and mother. Likewise, anniversary of Bartholomew, bishop of Châlons, his nephew.”

Yet that Stephen did not die in August but in May is clear from the necrology of the Church of Paris itself, where one reads:

> “On 6 May, Stephen, bishop, of the house of Saint Mary, died. He gave us sixty solidi from the revenue of an altar for the provision of four dishes on the feast of Saint Augustine. He also gave us seven modii of grain for the bread of Lent, four cloths, two dalmatics, one tunic, and two silver ewers with a silver censer.”

That this refers to Stephen I is proved by the charter of gifts made by him to his own church in 1124. Stephen therefore died on 6 May; but in what year is the difficult question. Yet letters of Innocent issued in 1141 to Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor, and the charter of Louis VII issued in the fifth year of his reign, in which Stephen is mentioned, make it clear that Stephen was still alive in August 1141. Indeed, according to the cartulary of Éder, he granted to the nuns of Éder in 1142 tithes which knights had unjustly held and restored. And certainly the brief chronicle of the church of Saint-Denis states: [Note: [Col. 1405D] *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 809.] “1142: Stephen, bishop of Paris, died.”

I am not unaware that this inscription is now carved upon his tomb:

> “Here lies the reverend father and lord Stephen, of happy memory, formerly chancellor of France and afterwards bishop of Paris, a special benefactor of this house, who died in the year of the Lord 1140, on the third day before the Kalends of August.”

But first, the epitaph is more recent; and any even moderately learned person will see that an error was made when the tomb was restored and a new inscription written. Second, Stephen was nowhere chancellor: in no charter of King Philip, Louis VI, or Louis the Younger will you find him subscribing under that title. Both Du Chesne, Mabillon, D. du Fourni, and Fathers Angelus and Anselmus number Stephen among the chancellors; [Note: [Col. 1405D] *Hist. dom. Franc.*, vol. VI, p. 250.] but, with due respect to those writers, I would say that they confused Stephen of Senlis with Stephen of Garland. Fathers Angelus and Anselmus themselves acknowledge [Note: [Col. 1406D] *Ibid.*, p. 36.] that Stephen of Garland was already acting as chancellor in 1106, the very year in which, and in following years, they elsewhere make Stephen of Senlis chancellor. Nor was he dean of Orléans, an office belonging only to Stephen of Garland. It is therefore no wonder that the day and year assigned in the epitaph are erroneous. Stephen’s body was found intact in 1515, when the foundations of the new church were laid.

In volume IV of the *Writers of the History of France* edited by Duchesne there is a letter from Hugh of Douci, archbishop of Sens, to the Parisian canons concerning Stephen’s death. In it he laments the loss, in his own childhood and youth, of one who had been his father, guide, and teacher, and urges the canons to concord and unity.

# LITERARY NOTICE

*(Literary History of France, vol. XII, p. 153.)*

The writings of Stephen of Senlis spared by time are less fitted to give us a high idea of his literary attainments than to acquaint us with the principal features of his life and the most notable events of his episcopate. The whole consists only of several fairly short letters and charters. In order not to interrupt the sequence of facts set forth in these two kinds of compositions, we shall present them in chronological order instead of separating them into two classes.

## I.

Resolved to restore order in his diocese, our prelate thought that he should begin with the chapter of his cathedral. The canons had relaxed so greatly in the matter of common life that several had left the cloister to live in private houses. To induce them to rejoin their brethren, Stephen bestowed upon his chapter an annual rent of seven muids of wheat, intended to make bread during Lent solely for canons residing in the cloister.

The instrument of this gift, dated 1124, was followed three years later by another, through which Stephen transferred the public school that had been in the cloister to a place near his audience hall. Hence came the School of the Parvis.

II. In the same year (1124) he showed his generosity toward other canons whose fervour needed no stimulation from such an inducement. We mean the regular canons of Saint-Victor. The benefaction consisted in this. Two priests serving the church of Saint-Jean-le-Rond, believed to have been the ancient baptistery of Paris, possessed the right to receive the *anniversary*—that is, the year’s income during the vacancy of each canonry at Notre-Dame. With his chapter’s consent, Stephen transferred this right to the Victorines by a charter subscribed by Bernier the dean, Adam the precentor, Stephen and Thibaud the archdeacons, eight canons, both priests and deacons, and three boys, *pueri* [Note: [Col. 1407] Du Cange, under *Puer*.], that is, young canons who were not in sacred orders.

III. But, at the same time, in order to compensate the ministers of Saint-Jean-le-Rond, he caused another charter to be issued by which he gave them a prebend of the cathedral; provided, however, as it says, that by reason of this gift they could not call themselves canons of Notre-Dame, and on condition that they should come there in turn to perform the weekly service. Since he likewise had to indemnify his chapter for the prebend detached from it, he granted it, by the same act, the right to institute and to remove the said ministers. At the foot of this document appear the same subscriptions as in the preceding one. Both were published by Fr. Dubois in the second volume of his *Ecclesiastical History of Paris* (p. 94).

After investing the Victorines with the right of annates in his cathedral, Stephen wished them also to possess a canonry there. But in this matter he did not find the same compliance in his chapter. Some canons opposed it, and the consequences became most unfortunate through the intervention of the king. No writings composed by our prelate in this dispute remain.

IV. The bishop of Paris did not have only one disagreeable affair at a time. At the same period, two of his archdeacons, whose excesses he had wished to repress, rose up against him and completed his troubles [Note: [Col. 1407] Dubois, *Hist. eccl. Paris*, vol. II, p. 24.]. The first was Stephen of Garlande. From the beginning of Stephen’s episcopate, the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés had brought formal complaints before the prelate concerning arsons, sacrileges, homicides, and other crimes committed by the followers of this archdeacon on the abbey’s lands. Summoned before the episcopal court, the accused requested time, a safe place, and safe-conduct in order to defend himself. All this was granted; but after obtaining delay upon delay, and seeing that proceedings against him for contumacy were about to begin, he resorted to an expedient very familiar at that time to those who distrusted the merits of their cause: he placed his person and property under the protection of the Apostolic See.

The case nonetheless proceeded. Disregarding this dilatory appeal, Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor and the bishop’s official, pronounced a sentence against the archdeacon placing his land under interdict. Far from yielding, Garlande appealed to the archbishop of Sens, Henry Sanglier, his kinsman. The appeal was accepted. Henry summoned the bishop and Garlande to appear at Provins on the eve of the Ascension to plead their cause. The reply of our prelate, printed in the third volume of the *Spicilegium* (p. 162), was such as might have been expected. After setting out the facts as just related, he declared to his metropolitan that, apart from the ground for recusation arising from the latter’s kinship with the archdeacon, the latter had no right to call such a cause before his tribunal. The outcome of the affair is unknown; but it is certain that it ended in the offender’s submission.

V. Thibaud Notier, the other rebel, was more difficult to subdue and carried matters to the utmost extremity before yielding. His first offence consisted in the flagrant extortions which he practised under colour of his office. The bishop employed interdict to stop them. Thibaud did not fail to appeal to Rome [Note: [Col. 1407] Ibid., pp. 30, 32.]. Matthew of Albano and Peter of León, legates in France, were charged by Pope Honorius II to settle the affair on the spot. These commissioners issued a judgment fixing and limiting the archdeacon’s rights far below his claims. Thibaud appeared to submit; inwardly, however, he could not stomach a setback so fatal to his greed. His nephews, no less avaricious than he but bolder, resolved to take revenge on those who had promoted the judgment.

Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor and the guiding spirit of the bishop’s council, was the first victim of their resentment. As he was returning from Chelles on Sunday, 17 August 1133, with the prelate, they fell upon him and murdered him near Gournay. Upon returning to Paris, Stephen issued a sentence of excommunication against the murderers. It is addressed, in the form of a mandate, to the archpriests of the diocese, to be communicated through them to all the priests of their districts. The prelate includes not only the perpetrators of the murder but also their supporters, those who should give them shelter, or who [Col. 1409] should have any kind of dealings with them. He forbids every priest, canon, abbot, monk, recluse, hermit, and even the abbot of Saint-Victor, to absolve in the tribunal of penance any of the guilty who might present themselves to them, reserving to himself alone the right to absolve them.

This severity on the prelate’s part served only to embitter the assassins and turn all their fury against his person. Warned of the snares laid for him, he sought safety in flight and took refuge in the abbey of Clairvaux. From there he wrote to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, inviting him to come and consult with him on means of making reparation to the Church for so horrible an outrage. His letter is full of episcopal vigour and at the same time shows the keen affliction that filled the prelate’s heart. It is found, together with the sentence, in the extensive notes of Picard and Dom Mabillon on the letters of Saint Bernard, in the tenth volume of Fr. Labbe’s *Councils*, in the sixth of Fr.
