Hardouin’s, and in the second volume of Fr. Dubois’s *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*.

VI. The letter Stephen addressed to Pope Innocent on the same subject is still more moving. Saint Bernard acted as his secretary on that occasion, a circumstance which led the editors of that Father to place it among Bernard’s letters (Ep. 159):

> “Weep, my eyes, and pour out torrents of tears, because my strength has abandoned me and the light that gave me guidance is no longer with me. It is not the venerable person who has just been taken from me: it is myself whom I mourn . . . For in truth, not tears but applause are due to one who lived only for Jesus Christ, and for whom death was gain. But in losing him, I have lost everything. He performed the duties of a bishop, while I had only the name. Despising the honour attached to this dignity, he bore all its burden with all his strength . . . My whole Church mourns with me and awaits consolation only from your fatherly goodness. If Notier should appear before you, let him feel that my Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. His nephews are the authors of the murder; but he is its occasion and perhaps its instigator.”

The persons most eminent for piety joined the prelate in supporting his just complaints. But civil authority does not appear to have taken cognizance of the affair, since causes concerning ecclesiastics were then outside its jurisdiction. The council of Jouarre, held in the same year, 1133, by Pope Innocent’s order, undertook to punish the guilty [Note: [Col. 1409] *Conc.*, vol. X, p. 974; Mabillon, notes on Bernard, Ep. 158.]; but the canonical penalties to which it condemned them seemed too mild to the pontiff, who on that account sharply reproached the fathers of the assembly [Note: [Col. 1409] *Conc.*, ibid., p. 978.].

VII. It was also in this year, but before Thomas’s murder, that the bishop of Paris put the religious of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in possession of the church of Saint-Denis-de-la-Chartre, which had long been in lay hands. The charter issued on this matter states that the gift was made with the consent of King Louis the Fat and Queen Adelaide. It omits to say, however, that it was merely an exchange for the church of Montmartre, acquired from these religious by the king and queen in order to make it into an abbey for women. This act, reported by Fr. Dubois and in the new *Gallia Christiana*, is subscribed by Stephen of Garlande and Thibaut Notier. This proves that the former had returned to favour with his bishop and that the latter had not yet committed the outrage which cost him his benefice.

VIII. The following year, 1134, brought a new misfortune upon this prelate: the insult offered to the chancellor of his church by Galon, master of a school in Paris. The matter was brought before his tribunal, and he had great difficulty obtaining satisfaction [Note: [Col. 1409] Duchesne, *History of the Chancellors of France*, p. 168.]. Having related the outcome of this affair under Galon’s entry (vol. XI, pp. 416–418), we shall content ourselves here with recalling the two letters Stephen wrote on the subject.

The first is to the archbishop of Sens, to prove that Galon’s appeal to him was null by operation of law.

The second, written to the legate of the Apostolic See, seeks to justify the excommunication pronounced against this teacher.

IX. While Stephen was in conflict with Galon, he issued, in favour of the religious of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, a charter whose substance is as follows. Under Bishop Galon, one of his predecessors, the nuns of Saint-Éloi in Paris were expelled because of their misconduct, and their monastery was awarded to the abbey of Saint-Maur. In this instance the prelate’s zeal dispensed with legal formalities: everything was done by force. Abbot Thibaud accepted this gift in 1107 and retained it until the second year of Stephen’s episcopate. Then, troubled by remorse over the irregularity of his acquisition, he chose to resign it into the bishop’s hands. The resignation was accepted, and the abbey of Saint-Éloi remained in Stephen’s hands for nine years.

In turn, Stephen himself experienced a scruple of conscience (*synderesis*) about retaining property which did not belong to him. The pope, the king, his chapter, and other respected persons having supported this scruple, he consented to restore the house to Abbot Ascelin, Thibaud’s successor. This is what he declares in the aforementioned act, by which he united Saint-Éloi to the abbey of Saint-Maur as a priory, on condition that twelve religious should be established there to perform the service. This union was confirmed two years later by Pope Innocent II.

X. The nuns of the abbey of Hières owed their foundation in part to our prelate. They owed him, moreover, their first constitutions, which are no longer extant. Dubreuil, followed by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, published the charter Stephen issued in 1138 for this foundation. Among other things, it says that the abbess’s election was to take place with the bishop’s consent and in the presence of the abbots of Saint-Victor and Sainte-Marie-du-Val. The constitutions drawn up upon the advice of Hugh of Mâcon, bishop of Auxerre and formerly abbot of Pontigny, bore in several places the imprint of Cistercian observances.

XI. Finally, as Stephen of Senlis’s last writing we shall give a letter without date or address, probably written to a legate concerning a dispute between Matthew of Montmorency and his mother-in-law. The lady had complained of a denial of justice because Stephen, before whose tribunal the matter had been brought, was not hurrying to pronounce judgment. The prelate excuses himself by saying that, as the king had requested a delay for Matthew, whom he needed for war against Dreux de Mouchy and Lancelin, he could not refuse it:

> “Nevertheless,” he adds, “in consequence of your orders, we have recently caused him to be notified that he must appear before you at Reims; to this he replied that he would not plead outside his province, though he was otherwise prepared to submit to your judgment within it, provided that a safe place were assigned to him for his defence.”

This letter was published in the third volume of the *Spicilegium* (p. 163).

[Col. 1411]

# LETTERS OF STEPHEN, BISHOP OF PARIS, AND OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO HIM

## I. Henry, Archbishop of Sens, to Stephen.—He urges him to come to Provins to examine the case of Stephen, archdeacon of Paris. (About 1132.)

[Dom Luc d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 158.]

[Col. 1411A]

We are compelled to write to your belovedness by the complaint and outcry of Lord Stephen, your archdeacon. For this same archdeacon of yours complains that, although he offered what was right to the abbot of Saint-Victor, your vicar, and was prepared to carry out justice through him; and although he placed himself with all that was his under the protection of the lord pope, that same abbot imposed a sentence of interdict upon his land, by which, the aforesaid archdeacon says, he is seriously burdened [Col. 1411B].

He adds also that he has been aggrieved in this: that he sought justice from you and could not obtain it concerning property of the Church of Paris and property of his men violently taken away, although, as has been said, this Stephen has placed himself under the protection and guardianship of the lord pope. And because he perceived himself aggrieved in these matters, he has appealed to us and requests that a suitable day and a safe place be given to him and his helpers. Therefore we appoint for you and him the eve of the approaching Ascension of the Lord as the day, and Provins as the place, because it is a safe place; and we command your belovedness to come on the day given and to the place appointed, to make such answer as the matter requires. And we advise you, as one most dear to us, to relax the sentence of interdict. Farewell.

## II. Stephen to Henry, Archbishop of Sens.—He replies that his metropolitan could not summon him outside the metropolitan see for the examination of his archdeacon’s case. (About 1152.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1411C]

Having heard the complaint of your kinsman, namely Lord Stephen, archdeacon of Paris, who has unjustly complained against us before you, you have assigned us a day and a safe place—namely Provins, in hostile territory—and have commanded me, your suffragan, neither first warned in person nor by letter, to come outside the metropolitan see for the administration of justice [Col. 1412A], because your kinsman, as he says, sought justice from us and could not obtain it.

Yet, had it pleased your discretion and metropolitan gravity, even if you could not avoid hearing him, you ought not to have believed him; for, since he is my man, I could not deny him justice without breach of faith. And since we have communicated back and forth by letters, and we still possess almost all of them, when we come together and they are read, they will convict either us or him of falsehood and compel one or the other to blush.

For immediately upon our arrival in Paris we heard the complaint of the abbot concerning sacrilege, arsons, homicides, and other criminal charges committed on the land of Saint-Germain by Lord S., the archdeacon—wrongfully as a cleric, more wrongfully as a deacon, and most wrongfully as an archdeacon and dean [Col. 1412B]. We summoned Lord Stephen, set a day, and, because he seemed very closely related to him, granted him a postponement; we offered him a safe place and a safe-conduct: that of the king and queen, Lord Count Ralph, and ourselves. And is acting with him in this way perhaps denying him justice?

Since, as you have heard, we have in no respect exceeded our authority in this matter, please relax your summons and command requiring us to leave our court; for we neither wish nor ought to obey anything contrary to the honour and dignity of the Church of Paris. Concerning the interdict and the letters of the lord pope, sufficient answer will be given if Lord Stephen does not disdain to have his cause heard where it is proper [Col. 1412C].

## III. Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, to Stephen.—He reports that Stephen the archdeacon chooses Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, as arbiter in his case. (About 1132.)

[Ibid., p. 160.]

Long ago, at your own request, we spoke with you concerning the restoration of peace between you and Stephen of Garlande. But now, since we have heard that, setting aside certain matters which he seemed to have against you, he desires peace with you, we advise the discretion of your holiness—whom we love from the heart and to whom we can offer no counsel except what serves your honour—and we advise and request that you appoint him a suitable day and term in which, in accordance with the consideration of reason, you may restore peace with him. He offers that peace for the consideration and examination of your friends, namely the abbot of Clairvaux.

For it does not become your fatherhood to reject peace when offered, which you ought in every way to seek even when it is not offered. For, following the example of the Lord and Saviour, you ought to seek the wandering sheep and carry it back even upon your shoulders to the fold of peace. If, as the Apostle says, we ought to have peace with all people, how much more with those for whom we must answer to the Lord? Therefore—may it not be so!—if you do not accept the said man’s satisfaction according to the judgment of your friends, it is certain that you incur offence before God and bring shame upon your friends. Farewell.

## IV. Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, to Stephen.—He excuses himself because he cannot attend the conference. (About 1132.)

[Ibid., p. 163.]

We received at Bonneval, on Friday, the letters sent us by your belovedness, in which you requested a conference with us on the following Monday. Neither the multitude of weighty affairs in our hands nor the very shortness of time allowed this to be done in any way. For the monks of Pontlevoy, to whom, God being the author of it, we were endeavouring to provide an abbot, inflicted upon us a grave and unheard-of outrage: with an armed rustic band they threatened death and punishments against our abbots and archdeacons, whom we had sent there for this very purpose. This matter, meanwhile, together with many others, occupies us.

Concerning the question on which you seek our advice, we communicate to your brotherhood what presently occurs to us: in response to the court inviting you to justice, you should, by way of supererogation, if you have safe-conduct, appear in person on a suitable day to answer the charges against you, provided justice has first been done to you and possession has been restored to the dispossessed. Thereafter, if the lord king has anything against you, you should proceed by the judgment of your brethren, in the proper order, insofar as the matter requires, as you will do for the Lord and in every respect.

As we wrote to you, we shall meet you next Thursday at Lagny; and if in the meantime you receive any counsel, send us word that we need not come.

## V. The same to the same.—He asks him to designate for the monastery of Saint-Victor a canon to be appointed abbot of Vertus. (About 1132.)

[Ibid., p. 164.]

Our city, long shaken by a manifold seedbed of discord, is even now in such a state that it cannot endure our absence without great danger [Col. 1414A]. Behold the bond by which I am held; behold the necessity which does not permit us to be present with your holy community. But enough of this.

Our brother and friend, the abbot of Vertus, and the brethren of that place, inflamed, thanks be to God, with a great desire for religious life, have called us and unanimously requested that our care should provide them, for the honour of God and the salvation of their souls, with a pastor profitable to them. The abbot himself resigned care and administration into our hand; the voice of the whole chapter was one, with unanimous consent and election in our presence, that a pastor should be granted them from the monastery of Saint-Victor of Paris.

But because they did not know by name the religious persons of that house [Col. 1414B], they asked for no particular person, but entrusted this care and responsibility to the religious judgment of your holiness. For that place and the religious character of its members are familiar to you. Therefore, with all humility at our command, we beseech the prudence of your holiness to extend a helping hand of counsel and aid to their rightful desire. They will receive with thanksgiving the person whom your election offers them from the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Victor.

## VI. [Note: [Col. 1413D] See Saint Bernard’s Letter 45.] An anonymous writer to Stephen.—He praises the bishop’s constancy and urges him to persevere. (About 1132.)

[Ibid., p. 162.]

Although I have not yet perceived that the constancy of your fatherhood has in any way been changed or weakened [Col. 1414C], nevertheless, anxiously concerned for you as a friend, I admonish and repeatedly admonish you not to depart from your purpose and the rigour of justice, nor permit the liberty of your Church, which flourished in the time of your predecessors, to be destroyed. Keep also faithfully in mind that saying of the Lord: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

Know, moreover, that in all things and through all things I shall persevere with you, nor shall I withdraw from my purpose because of the losses that have come upon me and my guests on your account. For the king and queen gave my guests twelve pounds, and took all this away for the redemption of their property; and my kinsmen and friends gave the king and queen ten pounds when they ordered my vineyards uprooted [Col. 1414D]. All this was done at the instigation of the dean and archdeacons—indeed, through the nocturnal whispering of G., the subchanter.

But, with God assisting you and me, I do not fear that I shall recover all that I have lost; nor do I believe that you will accept peace without my recovery and that of my property. Furthermore, if I did not perceive that you possessed counsel in abundant measure, my lowliness would advise your fatherhood to win over by your prayers and those of your friends the lord archbishop of Sens and your fellow bishops; and, in order to increase the force of your justice, not delay to obtain by every means that, in their dioceses, they cease from divine offices, so that, as participants in that same justice, they may assist you against all persons and, if necessary, come with us to Rome. Farewell.

## VII. Another anonymous writer to Stephen.—He is warned to beware of adversaries who have conspired to kill him. (About 1132.)

[Ibid.]

Because, as God is my witness, I love you not with a feigned heart but in truth, and desire not only your spiritual but also your bodily safety, I grieve from my heart over your tribulations; and if anything that ought to harm you is reported to me, I cannot hear it gladly. Therefore, compelled by this affection for you, I have not delayed to inform you of what I have recently heard concerning you.

For I have heard—and heard it for certain—that certain malicious and treacherous men, not only strangers but even persons most familiar to you, have conspired together and sworn your death, and have determined to kill you either by prosecution or by arms [Note: [Col. 1415] At this time the bishop was attacked by the nephews of Archdeacon Theobald. See Saint Bernard, Ep. 158 and notes.]. Lest you think this frivolous and therefore neglect it, know for certain that one of those who took part in the conspiracy disclosed it to me in confession and earnestly begged me to reveal it to you quickly.

Guard yourselves carefully, therefore, henceforth; and, as it is written, beware of those of your own household. But what am I saying? What, I ask, can human effort achieve if divine protection is absent? O ineffable mercy of God! Behold: almighty God, who has bestowed so many good things upon you in this world and has for so long borne your evils patiently, has not willed now suddenly and unexpectedly to strike you in the present life for your sins. Rather, mercy going before, he has mercifully added mercy to mercy: he has not willed that what the malice of treacherous men secretly planned should remain hidden from you.

What then do you await? Behold, the hidden judge has bent his bow and prepared his arrows; unless you quickly turn to him, he will send forth an arrow and strike the enemy. But may God first guard you by his protection, open the eyes of your heart, pierce your heart unto repentance, and turn you without delay to himself—he who wills not the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live.

## VIII. To the archpriests of the diocese of Paris.—Sentence of excommunication against the killers of Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor, and their supporters. (1133.)

[Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, col. 974.]

[Col. 1415D]

STEPHEN, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to F., R., E., and H., archpriests, greetings.

By the authority of God the Father almighty, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of all the saints, we excommunicate, anathematize, and exclude from the thresholds of holy Mother Church those who killed Lord Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor; those who stood by the killers with force; and those by whose counsel, urging, and assistance he was killed.

We likewise excommunicate all who receive into their lodging the killers and the killers’ present helpers; and those who have any communion or association with them in food and drink, counsel and conversation—unless perhaps for their correction—or buying and selling, sharing what is given and received, reception, or protection. We excommunicate all these until they repent and make satisfaction.

We therefore direct and command you to excommunicate them every Sunday in this manner and with these words, and to cause the other priests to excommunicate them. We command you that each of you, in his archpriesthood, forbid every priest whatsoever—whether secular or religious, abbot, canon, enclosed monk, hermit, or even the abbot of Saint-Victor—to receive for confession anyone guilty of this excommunication who comes to him, or to grant absolution for this offence or impose penance; for I have reserved to myself alone absolution and penance for the entire offence.

We also command that, when the priests pronounce the excommunication, they shall declare this prohibition of ours to everyone. Farewell.

## IX. Stephen to Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres.—Concerning the impious murder of Thomas, the prior. (1133.)

[Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, col. 975.]

[Col. 1416C]

To GEOFFREY, by God’s grace venerable bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See: STEPHEN, by the same grace unworthy minister of the Church of Paris, but now unhappy herald of misery and affliction, greeting in the Lord.

I do not know whether the weight of the new calamity which I am about to lay before your ears—indeed, before your heart—can adequately be expressed in any words: tidings harsh and grievous to hear, especially for all to whom the reproaches cast upon Christ Jesus and holy Mother Church are harsh and grievous, and above all for us who stand beneath the habit and sign of religion. These things will be the more grievous to us than to all others inasmuch as the fall of one man bears especially upon our injury—indeed, upon the assault and ruin of us all.

Know that Master Thomas, prior [Col. 1416D] of the monastery of Saint-Victor, a proven man, beloved and dear to all good people, and a most devoted and resolute helper and defender in the defence of holy Church, has been killed by impious hands: dead indeed in the flesh, but, as we believe without doubt, living with Christ. For he for whom Christ was truly the cause of dying cannot lack a place in glory; since, when he breathed his last spirit in our hands, he declared openly that he died for justice, leaving the surest testimony of his past and present righteousness, by which he had fought in Christ’s Church against the impious, because he was to be brought to completion in that righteousness [Col. 1417A]. For this was both the first and the final cause of his labour.

Indeed, he was then with me for the sake of that justice. At his particular urging—as he always had concern in these matters—and at the request and with the consent of the king, I had gone, having also persuaded him through the king, to reform and order the abbey of nuns at Chelles, taking with me religious men: namely, the abbot of Saint-Victor, the abbot of Saint-Magloire, the subprior of Saint-Martin, and many other monks, canons, and clerics.

When, having accomplished the business to the best of my ability, I was returning near the castle of Lord Stephen called Gournay, I suffered a sudden assault from his men, namely the nephews of Archdeacon Theobald, who had laid an ambush for me on the road [Col. 1417B]. We were unarmed, as was fitting on the Lord’s Day, and proceeding peaceably. Suddenly they rushed upon us with swords drawn and, showing respect neither for God, nor for the holy day, nor for me, nor for the religious men with me, slaughtered the innocent man before our eyes; and they threatened me with death unless I departed quickly from their sight.

But, acting more boldly, we threw ourselves among the swords and pulled him from their hands, already half dead and horribly mangled. Standing round him on every side, we addressed him concerning his confession and the forgiveness of the impiety which he had suffered from his enemies. Then he gladly forgave all who had sinned against him; earnestly sought forgiveness for his own sins; and, at last having received communion of Christ’s body and blood [Col. 1417C], openly declared before all that he was dying for justice, and so gave up his spirit.

Therefore, though the confidence of our hope does not doubt that, so far as his salvation and glory are concerned, we ought wholly to rejoice, and though we know the death of his saints to be precious in the Lord’s sight, nevertheless the heavy sorrow and mourning arising from the loss of our friend and from the common disgrace of us all is not tempered in our mind by any consolation whatsoever. For I see myself slain in him, and myself slain much more than he, because in his death I see myself exposed to dangers, whereas he has been delivered from dangers.

It remains, therefore, that, since you see me now so grievously bereft and distressed, you should not delay to come to comfort and advise me. For, as one unable to endure the hateful aspect of that place itself, I have fled and withdrawn to Clairvaux [Col. 1417D], where I shall await you, that together we may take counsel as to what must be done in response to so intolerable a ruin of holy Church. This assault threatens ruin and will come upon us all unless the Lord prevents it. I therefore direct and most earnestly beseech you to hasten to Clairvaux, putting aside every delay, because dangers surround me on all sides, and counsel concerning them cannot be postponed.

## X. Stephen to Innocent II, Roman pontiff.—On the same subject. (1133.)

[Col. 1418A]

It appears among Saint Bernard’s letters, no. 159, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII, col. 319.

## XI. Stephen to Henry, Archbishop of Sens.—He proves that, without his consent, the metropolitan of Sens cannot summon before his tribunal the case of a certain Galon, master of a Parisian school. (1134.)

[Dom Luc d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 155.]

Your Highness signified to us in your letters what you had decided. We by no means disdain to comply with it, but we fear to transgress the ancient boundaries which our Fathers have set [Col. 1418B]. For the venerable authority of the Fathers has never decreed, nor has antiquity anywhere been accustomed to observe, that it should be lawful for any metropolitan to determine the causes of other Churches, or to judge cases without the consent of the bishop to whom their care has been entrusted.

Hence Pope Callistus, the fifteenth after Peter, writes to his brother Benedict, bishop:

> “Let no metropolitan presume to excommunicate a diocesan’s church or parish, or anyone of that parish, or to undertake anything without his counsel or judgment; rather, let them observe what was established by the apostles, the Fathers, and our predecessors, and confirmed by us.”

Again:

> “If any metropolitan attempts, without the counsel and will of all the bishops of his province [Col. 1418C], to undertake anything beyond that which pertains solely to his own proper parish, he shall be liable to the peril of his rank, and what he has done shall be held void.”

Again:

> “Let no one administer, regulate, or judge another’s parish; for, just as ordination, so also ministration and the administration of other matters are forbidden.”

Pope Nicholas likewise writes to Ralph, Archbishop of Bourges, concerning a similar matter:

> “Our brother Sigebod, Archbishop of Narbonne, has complained to our apostolic office that you compel his clerics, without consulting him, to come before your tribunal, and that, concerning matters belonging to his Church, you make dispositions against his will, as though by right of your patriarchate; whereas neither antiquity—which the Fathers decreed should be held in reverence—admits this, nor do the authorities of the sacred canons [Col. 1418D] admit it at all.”

Strengthened, therefore, by these and other authorities, we neither wish nor ought at present to introduce into our own Churches and those of my brethren an innovation unheard of, and to alter their rights established from ancient times. In saying this, we do not instruct your prudence, which knows well enough how to draw many conclusions from few premises; nor do we deny that metropolitans may summon the bishops of their province and prescribe what ought to be prescribed. But, in our lowliness, we wish to preserve the ancient right.

Therefore we cannot sufficiently wonder that you receive the deceptive words of G. and of R., who are disobedient to us, when you have heard this matter truthfully from ourselves and from religious men, and, if it please you, may more fully learn his manifest fault from him himself. Because of his irrational and uncanonical summons [Col. 1419A]—which we shall show most plainly, when and where appropriate, to be of no weight—we thought it unnecessary at present to appear before you, whom we greatly wish to love and honour. For through us we have offered him and his scholars full justice; and finally we have been summoned into the presence of the lord pope, to whom the conclusion of this cause chiefly belongs.

For we have had a mandate from the Apostolic See, by whose authority he retains and protects both Algrin and all his possessions for him. Moreover, both you and we are commanded that no one judge concerning him, but rather that his whole cause be decided by the judgment of the Apostolic See. Since, therefore, his cause has been summoned to the hearing of the lord pope, and has thus far been reasonably handled by us—as we shall show before his presence [Col. 1419B]—we do not dare, saving your reverence, to relax what we have done justly, because we cannot do so without contempt of the lord pope and without consulting him.

Let your gentleness therefore return to itself; and let it restrain its indignation against us, lest it suddenly rise against a friend. For we are so ready to comply with your friendship that we shall honour your office by satisfying justice. Farewell in the Lord God. Farewell in Christ.

## XII. Stephen to the legate of the Apostolic See.—He maintains that he cannot absolve Gualo and his followers, who have been excommunicated, before satisfaction has been made. (A.D. 1134.)

*[Ibid., p. 157.]*

[Col. 1419C] Having seen your letters, we were greatly grieved and exceedingly disturbed that it could be suggested to you that we were unwilling to heed you. For our court knows, and the Church of Paris knows—as having seen and heard it—that we caused the letters sent us by you to be read in Gualo’s presence, and that we would have done what you commanded, had he wished it. But he, relying not on his cause but on the power of the archbishop and the seneschal, showed contempt and read them in contempt of God and of ourselves.

We, however, took counsel with the king and bishops as to what should be done concerning this; and, because in accordance with their decision we pronounced sentence upon our clerics and parishioners, and because there were no hearers, we compelled Gualo to be silent. Let your charity therefore consider, let your discernment consider, whether we ought to absolve, before inquiry and before satisfaction, those disobedient persons—and therefore persons dead [Col. 1419D] and stinking—whom we have justly bound, especially since it is established that we promulgated the sentence of excommunication by command and authority of the lord pope.

For he receives Lord Algrin into his protection and enjoins us to render him full justice concerning his wrongdoers; and, should any cause concerning him arise, he has reserved it to himself and decreed that it be concluded in the Roman court, as will appear in his letters [Col. 1420A], which we send you, if they are carefully examined. And because we do not wish to remove from the decree and sentence of the lord pope even one apex or one iota, we have resolved to go to Rome, in accordance with Gualo’s summons, on the feast of Saint Andrew, unless meanwhile he has effaced by fitting satisfaction what he has stubbornly committed against us—or rather, against the lord pope.

But if you wish, and if you advise, that this cause be treated in your court and settled by you, we do not refuse. Know beyond doubt that we do not rashly expose ourselves to dangers, but, so far as lies in us, avoid them. Nevertheless, we count as little both the harshness of the Alps and the length of the road, in order that the dignity of the first see and of the Roman pontiff may, so far as concerns us, be preserved, and that Roman authority be in no respect diminished through us.

Therefore we humbly entreat [Col. 1420B] your fatherhood to permit meanwhile to stand what we have justly done by the counsel of the lord pope and the bishops, and not to command it altered until it is discussed at a Roman hearing or at yours—if, as we have said, you so advise, and if Gualo persists in his obstinacy and does not make satisfaction to the Roman Church. We know beyond doubt, and you know certainly, that the Church of Paris and every person therein, with one exception, will uphold that cause if it comes before your hearing. And since we cannot comprehend in the brevity of a letter every circumstance of our affair, we send to your holiness our delegates, namely canons of the Church of Paris, so that with due time and clear diligence you may fully learn our right.

## XIII. To an anonymous recipient. (Date uncertain.)

*[Ibid.]*

[Col. 1420C] We summoned Matthew of Montmorency to trial on account of his stepmother and appointed a day. It happened, however, that before and about the appointed day the lord king was to lead an army at Beauvais against Drogo of Monceaux and Lancelin. Seeing that the knights who had gone with him intended to come to the aforesaid suit—for they were many—the lord king kept them back, and sent and requested us that the case be adjourned. The case was accordingly adjourned by this necessity, and another day appointed.

Meanwhile, by your letters you instructed us to summon Matthew [Col. 1420D] to appear before you at Reims on the Sunday *Gaudete in Domino*, for the execution of justice; and this we did. But he says that he will not come before you outside his province. For he is and has been ready—which we cannot deny—to undergo the case in your presence, and wherever there may be a place safe for him in his own province, and to render his stepmother full justice. Signify to us, therefore, if it please you, what we ought to do. For we are ready to obey.

[Col. 1421]

# Diplomas and Donations of Stephen

## I. Charter for the canons of Saint Mary of Paris. (A.D. 1124.)

*[DUBOIS, History of the Church of Paris, vol. II, p. 53.]*

[Col. 1421A] I, Stephen, humble minister by the grace of God of the Church of Paris, wish it to be known to all the faithful, both future and present, that from the revenues belonging to the priestly benefices of six churches—namely, the churches of Orly, Civry, Châtenay, Sucy, Bagneux, and Choisy—we give and grant in perpetual right to Blessed Mary and to the chapter of the Church of Paris, for the remission of sins and for the increase of God’s service, two *modii* of grain annually from the church of Orly, and one *modius* annually from the church in each of the aforesaid villages.

Yet we establish and command that, during Lent, from the beginning of the fast until the fifth [week], so long as that grain may last and suffice, one loaf shall be given daily from it to every canon having a dwelling in the cloister of Blessed Mary. We ourselves, like the other canons, shall receive one loaf daily from it; but the annual canons shall neither demand nor receive from the priests of the aforesaid churches the annual dues which they had been accustomed annually to demand and receive.

Under pain of anathema we forbid any bishop, archdeacon, ecclesiastical or secular person ever to alter or diminish this institution of our pious intention, or thereafter to harass, on any pretext [Col. 1421C], those who established it with us, etc.

All these things which we have stated above we have done and established with the assent of our archdeacons, namely Theobald and the other Theobald, within whose archdeaconries the aforesaid churches are situated.

Done publicly at Paris in the chapter of Blessed Mary, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1124, in the sixteenth year of King Louis, and the first year of Bishop Stephen.

Sign of Stephen, bishop. Sign of Berner, dean. Sign of Adam, precentor. Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Theobald, archdeacon. [Col. 1421D] Given through the hand of Algrin, chamberlain.

## II. Charter for the regular canons of Saint Victor of Paris. (A.D. 1124.)

*[History of the Church of Paris, ibid., p. 33.]*

I, STEPHEN, by divine grace bishop of Paris, at the petition and prayers of Berner the dean and of the other canons of Blessed Mary, and likewise with the assent of the priests of Saint John, namely William and Hugh, grant to the church of Blessed Victor and to the regular canons serving there that henceforth they shall have the anniversaries of the aforesaid canons, and shall render no service, whether of procession or visitation, on account of those anniversaries, either to the church or to the deceased, as a debt [Col. 1422A]. For we do not wish to disturb them or, against their own will or purpose, compel them to go out in public.

We further add this: if a canon of Blessed Mary surrenders his prebend into the hand of his bishop and intercedes for someone, and if the bishop grants his request concerning the prebend thus surrendered, or if, choosing the life either of hermits, regular canons [Col. 1422B], monks, or any other kind, he relinquishes his prebend, the aforesaid church of Saint Victor shall possess for one year the revenues of his prebend.

And, in order that all matters may be determined clearly and the mouths of those who misunderstand perversely may be shut, we make only this exception: if a canon of Blessed Mary surrenders his prebend into the hand of the bishop and intercedes for someone, and if the bishop grants his request concerning the prebend thus surrendered, the canons of Saint Victor shall have nothing.

Likewise we wish that whatever in the prebends of the canons of Blessed Mary, as determined above, we have granted to the regular canons of Saint Victor, we also grant to the same canons of Saint Victor to hold and possess in perpetual right in the prebends of the canons of Saint Marcellus, Saint Germanus of Auxerre, Saint Cloud, and likewise [Col. 1422C] Saint Martin of the Fields, with the common assent of the deans and canons of those churches. And in order that this may remain ratified and firm forever, we have confirmed the present charter by the authority of our seal and strengthened it with the signs of our canons.

Done publicly at Paris in the chapter of Blessed Mary, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1124, in the sixteenth year of the reign of King Louis and the first year of Bishop Stephen.

Sign of Stephen, bishop; Berner, dean; Adam, precentor; Stephen, archdeacon; Theobald, archdeacon; Landon, priest; Theodoric, priest; [Col. 1422D] Odo, priest; Dombert, deacon; William, deacon; Gimmeran, deacon; Peter, subdeacon; Henry, subdeacon; Theobald, boy; Manasses, boy; Urban, boy.

If anyone should presume to act against this our disposition, let him be anathema.

Given through the hand of Algrin, chancellor.

## III. Charter for the canons of Saint John the Round. (A.D. 1124.)

*[History of the Church, ibid., p. 23.]*

[Col. 1423A] I, STEPHEN, bishop of Paris, wish it to be known both to future and present persons that, by the common assent and petition of Berner the dean and of the whole chapter of Blessed Mary, we have given and, by giving, confirmed one prebend of the church of Saint John for the anniversaries of the canons. But we do not wish to pass over in silence that neither in visitations of the lesser churches do we or the canons of Blessed Mary absolve or release them; rather, we leave them in the same service, the same obligation, and the same condition in which they are, with the anniversaries alone excepted.

Nor do we wish or confirm that they are canons of Blessed Mary, but rather of Saint John. We grant in perpetual right to the dean and chapter of Blessed Mary free power to appoint or remove the priests of that church; and, under anathema, we forbid anything to be given or received in their appointment. We establish also that every member of Saint John shall render a whole week, like a canon, and complete service.

But in order that this may remain ratified and firm forever, we have ordered this present charter to be confirmed by the authority of our seal and have confirmed it beneath with the names of our canons.

Done publicly at Paris, in the chapter of Blessed Mary, in the year 1124, in the sixteenth year of King Louis’s reign, and the first year of Bishop Stephen [Col. 1423C].

## IV. Charter concerning the church of Saint Denis of the Prison. (A.D. 1133.)

*[History of the Church, ibid., p. 45.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, STEPHEN, by the grace of God, though unworthy bishop of the Parisians, not ignorant of what care and what love I owe to the sons of Christ and of the Church, and considering with much fear what a burden I bear in governing the faithful peoples, and how much aid I need for these things, and how much prudence in distributing to them their offerings, have recognized it necessary, in order to support the burden of so great a charge, to seek the aid of the servants [Col. 1423D] of God and to make them participants in our revenues, that they may keep watch and pray with us for the guarding of God’s flock.

Although episcopal dignity requires me, if possible, to be generous and useful to all, I have especially endeavoured to bestow some liberality of my generosity and usefulness upon religious men. Therefore, to the church of Saint Martin of the Fields and to the brethren serving God there, we have given in perpetuity, with all that belongs to it, and with all the rights of the Church of Paris preserved, the church of Saint Denis called “of the Prison,” which the hand of a layman had long unjustly seized and which, in our own time, had come into the king’s hands. We gave it back into our hands with the assent, petition, and will of the lord King Louis himself, with Queen Adelaide approving, and his sons King Louis and Henry, abbot of the same church, consenting [Col. 1424A].

Its appurtenances are: one mill at Mibray; one oven near the same church; the village of Fontaines, with its church and tithe, woodland and harbour; also the village of Simogies with its church and tithe; the village of Furcis with its church and tithe; land and meadows in the place called Rouundel; together with the prebend of Blessed Mary of the greater and episcopal church; and all other appurtenances, but only in the manner in which the clerics of the aforesaid church had held them hitherto.

Providing, however, for the tranquillity of the brethren serving God there, with the assent of Berner the dean, Adam the precentor, and the whole chapter, we have remitted to them only the processions—excepting the cross, chaplain, Gospel-book, and holy water [Col. 1424B]—while retaining for ourselves and our church all the other matters belonging to the right of the Church of Paris.

But in order that this may remain ratified and firm forever, we have confirmed this present charter by the authority of our seal, so that it may carefully set forth our gift and remain forever a safeguard of its stability.

Done at Paris in chapter, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1133, in the twenty-fifth year of King Louis’s reign and the ninth year of our episcopate. We have also decreed that the signs of our brethren be appended, that what has been done may be strengthened by the testimony of truth.

Sign of Berner, dean. Sign of Adam, precentor. Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Theobald, archdeacon. [Col. 1424C] Sign of Theobald, archdeacon. Sign of Gilbert, priest. Sign of Theodoric, priest. Sign of William, deacon. Sign of Ivo, deacon. Sign of Guiveran, deacon. Sign of Anselm, subdeacon. Sign of Peter, subdeacon. Sign of Albert, subdeacon. Sign of Henry, boy. Sign of Manasses, boy. Sign of Henry, boy.

## V. Charter concerning the church of Fossatus. (A.D. 1134.)

*[History of the Church, ibid., p. 48.]*

[Col. 1424D] The examples of the Fathers admonish us, and reason counsels us, to love the order and purity of the house of the Lord in such a way that we strive to correct, by the rigour of judgment, whatever does not accord with holy authorities, and ardently desire to preserve in its proper condition and order, with paternal affection, whatever justice and honour commend; so that we may restrain those who live wickedly from their enormities through fear of judgment, inspire those who live well and honourably, through paternal love, toward a better way of life, and thus provide both for our salvation and theirs.

I therefore, Stephen, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all faithful persons, both future and present, that the monastery of Saint Eligius at Paris [Col. 1425A] was from ancient times assigned to an order of nuns. But because of the excessive frailty of that sex, which, having broken the vow of chastity and cast away the profession of religion, had fallen into an intolerable misery of shamefulness, so that it had made the temple of God a den of fornication, our venerable predecessor of good memory, Galo, bishop of Paris, unable to endure so great a plague, expelled from and completely alienated from the aforesaid monastery persons of evil repute and incapable of correction because of their shameful lives.

Wishing also to adorn the holy place with a higher order, he gave and granted the aforesaid monastery of Saint Eligius, with all that belonged to it, to the church of Saint Peter of Fossatus to hold in perpetual right, though less canonically than was fitting. Since this gift was made irregularly and not as it ought to have been according to God, Theobald, abbot of the Church of Fossatus, a man indeed prudent and honourable, concerned for the reputation and salvation of himself and his subjects, returned and relinquished to us into our hand the aforesaid monastery of Saint Eligius, recognizing that he and the monks of Fossatus had neither acquired the aforesaid monastery according to God nor possessed it rightly.

When we had long held the same monastery in our hand, mercy—which is the friend of all humility—at last presenting itself to our eyes, seemed to require us mercifully to give to the church of Fossatus what the aforesaid abbot had relinquished to us, moved by fear of God and humility. For it was not fitting that any loss [Col. 1425C] or disadvantage should follow for it from what appeared to be the grace of humility. Rather, what the love of humility seemed, so to speak, to have taken away, mercy, which is its friend, ought to restore.

Moved, therefore, by love of mercy, induced by the petition of the lord Pope Innocent and by the prayer of the lord Louis, illustrious and glorious king of the Franks, and persuaded by religious men, with the assent of Berner the dean and of our chapter, we give and grant to Ascelin the abbot and to the church of Saint Peter of Fossatus the aforesaid monastery of Saint Eligius, with all its appurtenances, to hold in perpetuity—while preserving in every respect our own right and that of our successors, and preserving in every respect and entirely the customs of the Church of Paris.

That is to say, the abbot of Fossatus shall possess the aforesaid monastery as his cell and exercise complete and perfect abbatial authority over the monks serving there, so long as he and his successors, the abbots and monks of Fossatus, remain subject to us and to our successors, the bishops of Paris; preserve for the Church of Paris and for us our right, honour, and customs in all things; preserve our customs in all things; and render them in all things [Col. 1425D]. It has nevertheless been established that at least twelve monks, with their prior, be placed there to serve God, who may seem sufficient to maintain the order according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

It must be known that we possess fully, and retain forever, over the abbot of Fossatus the same authority which our predecessors possessed over the monastery of Saint Eligius and the abbess who had been there in ancient times, insofar, that is, as appears to pertain to the monastery of Saint Eligius and its property. But, in order that every occasion of dispute may hereafter be excluded, we have clearly and openly distinguished what authority the bishop, and what right or custom the canons of Saint Mary, formerly possessed and now possess over both the abbess and that monastery.

It must therefore be known that whenever the bishop of Paris summoned her to justice, she undoubtedly appeared before the bishop to render full justice. If, however, any servant, handmaid, or guest of that monastery committed any offence outside it against the person of the bishop or against his property, then, after first hearing the bishop’s command, the abbess was to bring them before the bishop in order that justice might be done; and after the bishop’s justice, the abbess was to receive her own jurisdiction over them, if she wished.

If the abbess wished to grant freedom to servants or handmaids of the monastery, alienate land, or give a warranty, she had no license to do so without the bishop’s assent and without a charter confirmed by his seal and the seal of the chancellor [Col. 1426B]. Our predecessors are known to have possessed this authority over the abbess and monastery of Saint Eligius; and we likewise retain the same authority over the abbot of Fossatus, leaving aside or relaxing none of our right.

The aforesaid monastery also pays the canons of Blessed Mary, as a due, two meals each year: one on the feast of Saint Paul, and the other on the feast of Saint Eligius. Each meal is received in the canons’ refectory. It is also customary that the community of the aforesaid monastery make processions with the canons of Blessed Mary on Rogation Days, on Ascension Day, and at the funerals of canons. Should the canons decide to hold other processions, whether for fair weather, or because of some storm or necessity, the aforesaid community must follow the ordinances of the canons and accompany them in those processions if commanded to do so.

Furthermore, whenever the mother church ceases from the divine office, the monastery of Saint Eligius must of necessity cease as well. Under this distinction, therefore, we grant the monastery of Saint Eligius to the church of Fossatus to possess as a cell [Col. 1426D], on this condition: whenever the abbot of Fossatus makes his required profession in the Church of Paris, in the bishop’s presence, he shall acknowledge that he holds the monastery of Saint Eligius through the gift of the bishop and the benefice of the Church of Paris.

We also will and determine that the men of the aforesaid monastery ought not to go into the king’s army without consulting the bishop; rather, the abbot or prior must send them into the army by the bishop’s command. It is also decreed that on the feast of Saint Eligius the canons of Saint Mary shall occupy the right choir and the monks the left, so that, together with the canon who occupies the choir, either the prior or the monks’ cantor shall occupy the choir; no other person is to be admitted to it. The abbot or prior shall sing the Mass; but if both are absent, someone from our clergy shall celebrate it.

It must also be known that the meal rendered on that day consists of six live pigs of sound flesh, two and a half *modii* of wine according to the measure of our cloister, and three sextaries of well-winnowed grain [Col. 1427A]. The meal rendered on the feast of Saint Paul consists of eight rams, two *modii* of wine and half a sextary, two and a half sextaries of well-winnowed grain, six denarii, and a halfpenny.

In order that this may remain ratified and unshaken, we have commanded this present charter to be made, signed it with our seal, and committed it to be confirmed by the hands of our canons.

Sign of Stephen, bishop. Sign of Berner, dean. Sign, etc.

Done publicly in the chapter of Saint Mary, in the year of the Incarnate Word [Col. 1427B] 1134, in the twenty-seventh year of King Louis’s reign, the third year since Louis the king had been elevated to kingship, and the eleventh year of Stephen’s episcopate.

Given through the hand of Algrin, chancellor.

## VI. Charter of the foundation of the abbey of Éder. (A.D. 1138.)

*[New Gallia Christiana, vol. VII, col. 60.]*

STEPHEN, by the Lord’s appointment bishop of the Parisians, to all Christ’s faithful, both future and present, greeting.

The care of the episcopal office has been entrusted to us by almighty God for this purpose: that we should love religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to the Lord. Let all men therefore know [Col. 1427C] that we have built from the foundations the church of Saint Mary of Éder by our labour and care, God’s grace preceding us in all things; and, having placed religious women in it, we have decreed that the religious order be preserved perpetually in that church.

[Col. 1428A] But because we have recognized the female sex to be frail and so liable to fall, we have therefore taken care to bind the aforesaid nuns to the discipline of a stricter profession, both through ourselves and through religious men. For they have excellent statutes, chiefly drawn up from the order of Cistercian monks and partly collected from the observances of other religious orders. This was done by the counsel of the venerable man Lord Hugh, abbot of Pontigny, through the exertions of our brother William, and by the counsel and will of our dearest daughter Hildiardis, venerable abbess of the same church of Saint Mary, together with the whole convent. We will and command by episcopal authority that the aforesaid nuns shall hold forever the aforesaid statutes as they are set down and written in the books which we call *customaries*, and shall never presume in any respect to diminish or alter them.

Upon the death of the abbess, we decree that her successor shall be elected in this manner: first they shall make known their will and need to the bishop of Paris; then they shall summon to their chapter, in the bishop’s presence, religious men—the abbot of Saint Victor and the abbot of Saint Mary of the Valley. When these have been assembled, they shall deliberate concerning the election of an abbess and, without contradiction, elect whichever woman they wish and judge worthy. But if they cannot have the abbots, the prior together with the three most devout nuns shall appoint a successor in the bishop’s presence.

We also wish it to be known that we grant the same church to be wholly free and undisturbed from every temporal exaction, insofar as pertains to us and to our successors [Col. 1428C], etc.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138.

Given through the hand of Algrin, chancellor.

# Hugh of Sens

[Col. 1427]

## Letter of Hugh of Dociac, Archbishop of Sens, to B., Dean, and the Other Canons of the Church of Paris, consoling them upon the death of the Bishop of Paris

*(DUCHESNE, Writers of French Affairs, vol. IV, p. 446.)*

[Col. 1427D] H., by the grace of God minister of the Church of Sens, to B., dean, and the other canons of the Church of Paris, beloved brothers in Christ: greeting and saving love from the Lord.

As I consider, brothers, the unforeseen fall and setting of your sweetest brother—indeed, if I may say so, of my dearest father, your bishop—I feel more inclined to weep than to write. For he has too stony a breast whom the lamentable departure of so godly a man does not move and soften to grief or groaning. Whatever some may perhaps think, I, for my part, utterly mourn and lament my own great loss and affliction [Col. 1428D]. For I have lost a portion of my soul, the staff of my youth, the comforter and instructor of my life.

For, brothers, as you know, a staff of support is often more necessary to a young man than to an old, because instruction is especially necessary to youth, whereas old age has learned much through experience in the long passage of time. In whom, then, shall there henceforth be for me a like rest, like joy, a like place of repose? Whenever I saw him, I could not fail to rejoice in the presence of my joy.

But what shall I say? “Lord God, why have you withdrawn far away? Why do you look away in times of need, in tribulation?” Now you have removed your untrained and tender child and so swiftly taken from him his guide and teacher. But what am I doing, brothers? While I exaggerate my grief too much, I show myself to you as a burdensome comforter.

Now I commend the soul of that sweetest father to the sweetness and gentleness of our Redeemer. But to you, with whom I suffer, I turn the countenance of my discourse. For I am not moderately anxious concerning you, because in such circumstances envy often creeps in; through envy comes discord, through discord division, and through division the confusion of unity. Then come hostile faces, discordant tongues, diminution of treasures, and the laughter and mockery of the envious and rivalrous [Col. 1430A].

May God avert this from you, brothers. May the fullness of the Holy Spirit descend upon you, unite your spirits, remove divisions, and grant those who are to have one shepherd to taste the same pastures. Having considered these things, dearest brothers, remember continually both our admonition and your salvation. Turn your hearts unceasingly to him who is the salvation of all who hope in him.

# A.D. 1133–1144. History of Milan by Landulf the Younger, or Landulf of Saint Paul (A.D. 1095–1137)

[Col. 1429]

*[MURATORI, Writers of Italian Affairs, vol. V, p. 459, from manuscript codices of the metropolitan library of Milan. Notes by Giuseppe Antonio Sassi, prefect of the Ambrosian Library, are added.]*

## Preface by Ludovico Antonio Muratori

[Col. 1429B] After the histories of Arnulf and Landulf the Elder dealing with Milanese affairs, already published in the preceding volume (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLVII), there now follows a third History of Milan, likewise written by Landulf the Younger, whom we are accustomed to call “of Saint Paul” in order to distinguish him from the other, the Elder.

It extends from the year 1095 to 1137. During these years its author flourished, a Milanese by birth and a priest by rank. We learn from the author himself how much labour and care he devoted to the study of letters, and with what ardour he went as far as Gaul in search of teachers. Thus he writes, in chapter 10, concerning Liprand, his celebrated priestly uncle:

> “All the rest which he possessed in books and other goods he decreed should be preserved for Landulf, his nephew and pupil, and acolyte of the Church, who at that time was studying at Orléans under the distinguished master Alfred and the noble Jacob.”

He relates this at about the year 1103. Then, in chapter 13, he adds:

> “I attached myself to Anselm of Pusterla and Ulric, vicedominus of Milan—both of whom later obtained the archbishopric of Milan. For with Anselm, during a year and a half, I read at Orléans and Paris in the schools of Masters Alfred and William; and by reading, writing, and many other means I rendered Anselm great assistance.”

These words are to be referred to about the year 1106. Having then returned to his homeland, he again began to live at the church of Saint Paul at the Crossroads, which his uncle Liprand had rebuilt and enriched with many ornaments, and which Landulf himself calls “the title of my orders.” From this he acquired the surname Landulf of Saint Paul.

Indeed, in chapter 28 he testifies that while still an infant the name “Bell of Saint Paul” (*Clocha Sancti Pauli*) had been added to him; we would call it *la Campana di San Paolo*. For it was customary in those times to give children some additional name, later used as a personal name or surname, as I have already observed in the *Antiquities of Este*.

But the powerful men of the city allowed our historian very little lasting peace. He was bound to Liprand by very close kinship and friendship, and they utterly hated Liprand; accordingly, their hatred was turned also against his nephew, who was driven from his church [Col. 1431A], although many merits commended him to the Milanese people. For then, as the same author says in chapter 10, he was “a reader, scribe, instructor of boys, participant in public offices and benefices, and composer of the consuls’ letters”—provided that no scribal error has crept into these words. Landulf appears to have gone to Gaul two or three times for the sake of study. For again, in chapter 17, he says that Olric, vice-dominus of Milan, and Anselm of Pusterla were urged to go to the eminent master Anselm of Monte Leoduni—that is, of Laon—and that these two were pleased to take with them me, Landulf, pupil of the priest Liprand. These events occurred about the year 1109.

Then, in 1112, when Jordan was elected and consecrated archbishop of the Church of Milan, our Landulf, still an acolyte, having been admitted to the common benefice of the priests and clerics of Milan, incurred the displeasure of the new archbishop [Col. 1431B], and by his authority was again excluded from the church of Saint Paul, which, as he repeats, “is the title of my ordination.” So he says in chapter 25. Stirred by this injury, Landulf went to Rome in 1116, to the Lateran synod, hoping that he would find there a more equitable judge ready to hear him. There, before Pope Calixtus II, he renewed his complaints at Tortona and Piacenza; but his efforts and words always came to nothing.

Landulf also relates that he was present at the coronation of King Conrad at Monza in 1128—an empty ceremony, however—and that before the pontiff himself, namely Anselm, archbishop of Milan, and the Crowned One himself, namely Conrad, he bore the pontifical staff from the church of Saint Michael, in a splendid procession, as far as the church of Saint John. He had earlier related that the same Anselm had chosen him to preside over his chaplains. Then Lothair III came down into Italy in 1136 to receive the crown of the kingdom and empire; and our Landulf stood before him and implored justice [Col. 1431C].

I have thought it worthwhile to note these few things, which our historian mentions concerning himself in different places of his History, so that the reader may know the man before knowing his book. Let us now add something about the History itself. It is brief, yet it contains great deeds performed in the city of Milan and memorable disturbances; and it vividly portrays what the desire to rule could accomplish—and will always be able to accomplish—in the minds of men of those times [Col. 1432A]. Landulf’s narrative is not confined within the walls of Milan alone: it also includes much that illuminates the history of Italy in that age.

Accordingly, Pagi, in his *Critique of Baronius* under the year 1136, no. 7, after having previously used various published fragments of it to enrich and correct the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, at last breaks out in these words:

> Thus ends the History of Landulf the Younger, extending to the year 1137, in which it was composed. If it should at last see the light, ecclesiastical history may receive great illumination from it.

There is a single very ancient parchment manuscript of this History, which I have examined more than once, in the library of the metropolitan chapter of Milan. It also contains the History of Arnulf printed earlier, and then the Passion of the blessed martyr Ariald, who is buried at Saint Dionysius—that is, the same little work which Puricelli published. The Ambrosian Library [Col. 1432B] also has another copy of Landulf’s History, but one transcribed from the manuscript in the metropolitan library.

Moreover, the first person to establish this writer’s reputation among scholars was the aforementioned Puricelli. In both his *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica* and his *Life of Saints Erlembald and Ariald*, he frequently employed this author’s authority and published numerous excerpts from him, as the purpose of his own undertaking required. Ughelli then inserted the same fragments into volume IV of *Italia Sacra*; afterward scholars, and especially Pagi, turned them to their own use.

Yet it concerned the republic of letters that the complete History of Landulf the Younger should finally be published. It will be dearer to us even than the Milanese Histories of Landulf the Elder and Arnulf, since Landulf the Younger everywhere shows himself Catholic and free from the errors of schismatics, and because he wrote more carefully whatever he undertook to write. So that this offspring may present itself still more agreeably to the eyes [Col. 1432C] of the learned world, it will appear together with the notes of the most distinguished Joseph Antonio Sassi, prefect of the Ambrosian Library. Through his care and study you will find elucidated whatever seemed to require light, or fuller light. If anything nevertheless remains obscure or defective, you should know that this is attributable to the manuscript, which it was not possible to supplement or correct with the help of other manuscripts.

[Col. 1431]

## JOSEPH ANTONIO SASSI, Prefect of the Ambrosian College and Library, to the Benevolent Reader

[Col. 1431D] What scholars had especially desired—that the monuments lying upon the shelves of our native land should be brought to light, not scattered piecemeal here and there, but published complete and arranged before the public in the order of the ages, as Papebroch earnestly urged the Milanese to do in volume VII for May, folio LXXX—we have now undertaken and are pursuing, with the celebrated Ludovico Antonio Muratori voluntarily lending his hand and carrying the torch before us.

For in addition to the materials relating to our city published in the preceding volumes, we now send from the press the long-awaited manuscript of the Histories of Landulf of Saint Paul [Col. 1432D]. It is indeed rough and obscure in its original text, but, as far as possible, we present it polished and drawn out from its native rust by notes, and distributed according to the proper sequence of times into its respective years.

The Palatine Society, itself sparing neither labour nor expense in increasing the store of historical materials and the patrimony of letters, entrusted the labour of this study to me, kindly rather than deservedly—far be envy from the expression. Nevertheless, although I felt myself unequal in strength and ability, I undertook this task in proportion to my obligation of service and added notes, perhaps more fully than some persons of loftier learning [Col. 1433A] require. Yet, because not all have an equal abundance of books or knowledge of ancient matters, I hope that they too will prove useful to some.

A work far more worthy than mine, by the most learned and most dear friend Father Stampa, was contemporary with my labour; but we differed in our judgment when calculating the same events in time. He had undertaken to elucidate with notes the recently printed Anonymous of Como and, following its tracks step by step, as they say, recognized Anselm as archbishop in the year 1123. I, however, relying on the testimony of my Landulf, maintain that he was elected archbishop only in 1126. From this arose between us a chronological disagreement of no small difficulty.

When the aforementioned Muratori learned of it through private letters, he immediately sought, with the facility in historical matters for which he is distinguished, to reconcile it. He composed a preface to the same Anonymous, in which, while candidly affirming that Olric, whom Anselm succeeded, died only in 1126—as I maintained against several eminent writers cited there—he nevertheless says that it is credible that Anselm was elected archbishop while Olric was still living, as we now call a coadjutor, just as Thomassin shows had already been customary in the Church. He further maintains that such a custom existed also in the Church of Milan, relying both on this example of Anselm and on that of Algisius, whom he supposes to have been archbishop already three years before the death of Saint Galdinus. His evidence is the subscriptions to charters, of which the notes will speak, and the authority of the Anonymous himself, who writes under the year 1123: “The archbishop was enthroned, but made a bad bargain.”

But I revere the learning of that most learned man; nevertheless, I cannot be brought around to his opinion, led by arguments of no slight weight, which I defer to note 6 on chapter 37, lest I detain the reader here too long. Nor does that disagreement make even the smallest crack in the union of mind by which the closest bond unites us. Indeed, according to the laws of honourable friendship [Col. 1433C], each person ought to be able freely and sincerely to state his opinion, so that the learned reader may choose the side he judges supported by better foundations.

Moreover, to say something about the excellence of this History, it would suffice to mention this alone: as soon as Puricelli published some of its fragments, learned men received them with such applause that each hurried to transfer them into his own studies. Papebroch enlarged with them his exposition of the bishops of Milan; Ughelli filled gaps concerning several bishops in *Italia Sacra*; Pagi prepared fuller critical notes on Baronius’s History. Not to mention very many individual writers from neighbouring cities and even foreign authors, all greatly valued our author in writing the annals [Col. 1434A] of those times. As a contemporary witness, and for the most part also present at the events he narrates, he commends himself by unquestionable reliability and shines like a beneficent star in that dark age, greatly afflicted by a scarcity of writers.

I can affirm this alone: whenever he goes beyond the boundaries of our own country in recounting the deeds of supreme pontiffs, emperors, and princes, he so consistently adapts his pen to truth that, when I compare him with histories written by foreigners from that age, he seems to agree with them almost completely. Yet the history which receives the greatest illumination from Landulf’s writing is that of Milan. In the chronicles of our Corio, Calco, Morigia, Ripamonti, and others, matters relating to those times are so confused that they can scarcely be disentangled. It is astonishing how much they differ from one another in assigning the tenure of the Milanese bishops: the career of some is at times shortened by a whole decade, while that of others is excessively extended; their succession is also reported in an inverted order [Col. 1434B], some incorrectly placed before others; and finally very many deeds are accumulated in narratives wholly at variance with the truth.

I would establish the point by examples, unless I thought it superfluous here to gather in summary what I have not failed to note throughout almost the entire work. But Landulf is at hand to correct all these things, having as it were given a new face to Milanese history, especially ecclesiastical history. Therefore I also thought it fitting to place at the beginning of this work of Landulf a chronological sequence of the matters pertaining to it, so that with a single glance the reader may conveniently grasp all that is treated there.

To prepare this edition, I had two copies at hand in the Ambrosian Library: one mentioned by the most distinguished Muratori in his preface, and another which I subsequently discovered while turning over the vast mass of manuscripts in order that they might be arranged in their cases and catalogue. On its first page Jo. Antonius Castillioneus, a notary, as he calls himself, publicly authorized by imperial authority [Col. 1434C], attests that he collated this copy with the autograph of Charles of the Basilica of Peter, bishop of Novara, in the college of Saint Mark at Novara.

Along with these I collated the metropolitan manuscript, with the assistance also of the indefatigable Philip Argelati. From it I selected several variant readings which I judged quite suitable for elucidating obscure passages of our author. I marked them with the Arabic numerals 1 and 2, so that the reader might know from which manuscript they were taken: the first number indicates the copy already known to Muratori; the second, the other copy of Charles of the Basilica of Peter, recently discovered by me. These are the things of which I wished to warn you. If you find anything less than satisfactory in this labour of mine, kindly pardon it, and farewell.

[Col. 1433]

## CHRONOLOGICAL SERIES OF EVENTS PERTAINING TO THIS HISTORY, ARRANGED IN THE COMMENTARY

[Col. 1433D] **1093.** Conrad, son of Emperor Henry III or IV, is crowned at Monza and Milan by Archbishop Anselm. Chapter 4, no. 21.—Anselm, archbishop of Milan, dies. *Ibid.*

**1095.** Urban II holds a synod at Piacenza. Chapter 28, no. 6. He comes to Milan. *Ibid.*, no. 7.—Arnulf, successor of Anselm III, is consecrated archbishop of Milan [Col. 1434D]. Chapter 1, no. 1.—Conrad, king of Italy, goes into Tuscany to celebrate his marriage. Chapter 1, no. 31.—Blessed Albert of Cluny founds the monastery of Pontida. Chapter 24, no. 1.

**1096.** Armanus, cardinal, is elected bishop of Brescia. Chapter 1, no. 7.—Urban II, returning from Gaul, comes again to Milan and delivers a sermon to the people from the pulpit in the church of Saint Thecla [Col. 1435A]. Chapter 28, nos. 7 and 8.

**1097.** Arnulf, archbishop of Milan, dies. Chapter 1, no. 8 and chapter 28, no. 13.—Landulf of Badagio, elected archbishop by the Milanese clergy, is rejected by Armanus, cardinal and bishop of Brescia. Chapter 1, nos. 5 and 9.—Anselm of Buis is substituted for him and confirmed by Armanus. *Ibid.*, no. 14. He receives the pallium from Urban II through an apostolic legate. *Ibid.*, no. 18.

**1098.** Anselm IV, archbishop of Milan, grants immunity to those coming to the feast of Saints Protasius and Gervasius. Chapter 2, no. 5.

**1099.** Conrad, son of Henry IV, goes into Tuscany for the second time. Chapter 1, no. 31.—Urban II, supreme pontiff, dies. Chapter 1, no. 32, and chapter 8, no. 1.—Archbishop Anselm IV transfers the body of Saint Ariald from Saint Celsus to the church of Saint Dionysius. Chapter 3, no. 5.

**1100.** Grossulanus is elected and consecrated bishop of Savona [Col. 1435B]. Chapter 3, nos. 4 and 7. He is appointed vicar of Anselm, archbishop of Milan. *Ibid.* He remains in that office for two years. Chapter 4, no. 6.—Anselm, archbishop of Milan, sets out for the Jerusalem war. Chapter 2, no. 5.

**1101.** Conrad, son of Henry IV, dies. Chapter 1, no. 32.—Anselm, archbishop of Milan, dies at Constantinople. Chapter 2, no. 8.

**1102.** Grossulanus is elected archbishop of Milan. Chapter 5, no. 4. He is accused of simony before the supreme pontiff. *Ibid.*, no. 8. He receives the pallium brought by Saint Bernard, cardinal. *Ibid.*, no. 11 and following. He summons a provincial synod to be held at Milan. Chapter 9, no. 2.

**1103.** Grossulanus holds a provincial synod during Lent. Chapter 9, no. 9.—On 25 March the priest Liprand passes unharmed through fire, in order to prove by divine judgment the simony of Archbishop Grossulanus. Chapter 10, nos. 3 and 6.—Grossulanus [Col. 1435C], immediately after the ordeal by fire, goes to Paschal II at Rome. Chapter 11, no. 5. He is loaded with exceptional honours by the same supreme pontiff. *Ibid.*, no. 9.

**1105.** At the Lateran synod celebrated by Paschal II, Grossulanus is restored to the see of Milan. Chapter 11, no. 12. He is expelled by the Milanese. Chapter 12, no. 5.—After the Lateran synod Landulf of Vareglate is elected bishop of Asti. Chapter 11, no. 15.—Henry the Younger rebels against his father. Chapter 13, no. 3.—Notable relics are found in the church of Saint Mary at the Gate in Milan; on that account a most solemn supplication of all the clergy and people is held. Chapter 22, no. 2 and following.

**1106.** A comet drawing a very long tail appears in the west. Chapter 13, no. 5.—Emperor Henry IV dies at Liège. *Ibid.*, no. 4.—The priest Liprand withdraws to Valtellina. Chapter 16, no. 1.—By public decree an annual celebration is established for the discovered sacred relics of Saint Mary at the Gate [Col. 1435D]. Chapter 22, no. 6.

**1107.** The war of Lodi begins. Chapter 16, no. 1.—The priest Liprand returns to Milan from Valtellina. *Ibid.*

**1109.** The Milanese are compelled by the Cremonese immediately to abandon the city of Lodi, which they had unexpectedly captured. Chapter 16, no. 5.

**1110.** Grossulanus makes a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Chapter 17, no. 9.—He appoints Arderic, bishop of Lodi, his vicar at Milan. *Ibid.*—Olric the Vice-Dominus is elected archpriest. *Ibid.*, no. 6.—He receives holy orders at Genoa. *Ibid.*, no. 13.—The Cremonese are defeated by the Milanese in the field of the Brescian people. *Ibid.*, no. 14.—Henry V comes down into Italy. Chapter 18, no. 2.

**1111.** Henry V proceeds to Rome. *Ibid.*, no. 3.—He is crowned by Paschal II on the Ides of April. *Ibid.*, no. 13.—He returns to Germany. *Ibid.*, no. 14.—Otto [Col. 1436A], viscount of Milan, is killed at Rome. *Ibid.*, no. 11.—The city of Lodi is taken and destroyed by the Milanese. *Ibid.*, no. 18.—Jordan of Clivi, later archbishop, is ordained priest at Genoa. Chapter 19, no. 8.—An extraordinary overflowing of rainwaters and rivers fills the peoples with terror in October. Chapter 20, no. 1.

**1112.** Jordan of Clivi is elected archbishop of Milan on the Kalends of January. Chapter 21, no. 3.—Mamardus, bishop of Turin, brings him the pallium from Rome. Chapter 21, no. 9.—Having at first refused it, he receives it six months later, on 6 December. Chapter 25, no. 2.—The priest Liprand goes to the monastery of Pontida on 6 December. Chapter 24, no. 2.

**1113.** The priest Liprand dies piously at the monastery of Pontida on 6 January and is distinguished by miracles. Chapter 24, nos. 1 and 3.—Grossulanus, returning from his Jerusalem pilgrimage, enters Milan in August. Chapter 26, no. 2.—A civil battle is fought between supporters of Grossulanus and Jordan [Col. 1436B]. *Ibid.*, no. 7.—After peace is concluded, Grossulanus withdraws to Piacenza. Chapter 27, no. 1.—Andrew, Primicerius of the Decumani, dies. Chapter 28, no. 3.

**1114.** Nazarius Muricula succeeds the deceased Andrew Dalvultio as Primicerius of the Decumani. Chapter 29, no. 1.

**1115.** Paschal II holds a council at Rome in the Lateran. Chapter 29, no. 4.—A sentence against Grossulanus is pronounced in that same synod. *Ibid.*, no. 15.—Armanus, bishop of Brescia, is deposed and Villanus appointed in his place. Chapter 30, nos. 2 and 3.—Jordan returns to Milan and excommunicates Emperor Henry. Chapter 31, nos. 2 and 3.

**1117.** Grossulanus dies at Rome in the monastery of Saint Sabas, on the eighth day before the Ides of August. Chapter 29, no. 17.—A forty-day earthquake occurs in Lombardy on 3 January. Chapter 31, no. 6.—Jordan holds a provincial council at Milan. *Ibid.*, no. 8.—He deposes Hugh of Noceto, appointed bishop of Cremona by Henry [Col. 1436C], and substitutes Ubert. Chapter 46, no. 7.

**1118.** Paschal II dies on 21 January. Chapter 32, no. 1.—Gelasius II is elected supreme pontiff. Fleeing the plots of Emperor Henry, he withdraws to Gaeta. *Ibid.*, no. 5.—There he is consecrated priest and pontiff. Chapter 33, no. 2.—Having returned to Rome, he departs for Gaul. *Ibid.*, no. 4 and following.—Emperor Henry arranges for Burdinus to be elected at Rome as a pseudo-pontiff.
