Chapter 32, no. 10.—He returns to Germany. *Ibid.*, no. 17.—The war with Como begins. Chapter 34, no. 6.—A council of Lombard bishops and princes is held at Milan. Chapter 34, nos. 11 and 12.

**1119.** Gelasius II dies at Cluny. Chapter 33, no. 7.—Calixtus II succeeds Gelasius. *Ibid.*, no. 8.—He holds a council at Reims on 20 October. *Ibid.*, no. 10.

**1120.** Calixtus II comes from Gaul into Lombardy [Col. 1436D] and stays at Tortona. Chapter 35, no. 1.—Proceeding thence to Piacenza, he celebrates Easter there. *Ibid.*, no. 5.—He is received at Rome on 3 June. *Ibid.*, no. 16.—Jordan, archbishop of Milan, dies. Chapter 36, no. 2.—Olric the Vice-Dominus succeeds Jordan on 17 November. *Ibid.*, no. 3.

**1121.** Burdinus the pseudo-pontiff is captured and disgracefully brought to Rome. Chapter 35, no. 17. He is confined in the monastery of Cava. *Ibid.*, no. 18.

**1122.** Calixtus II removes Burdinus from Cava and transfers him to the fortress of Janula. Chapter 35, no. 18.

**1123.** Calixtus II holds the First General Lateran Council. Chapter 36, no. 4.—Olric, archbishop of Milan, goes to Rome and sits at the right hand of the supreme pontiff in the council, despite the futile opposition of the archbishop of Ravenna. *Ibid.*, no. 8.

**1125.** Emperor Henry V dies on the tenth day before the Kalends of June. Chapter 37, no. 5.

[Col. 1437A] **1126.** Olric, archbishop of Milan, dies on 28 May. Chapter 37, nos. 6 and 7.—Anselm of Pusterla is elected archbishop. *Ibid.*, no. 7.—He goes to Rome to receive the pallium. Chapter 38, no. 2.—Yet he refuses to receive it from the hands of the supreme pontiff. *Ibid.*, no. 3.—Returning to Milan, he is solemnly received on the feast of Saint Michael. *Ibid.*, no. 6.

**1127.** The city of Como is destroyed by the Milanese. Chapter 37, no. 10.

**1128.** Conrad comes into Italy. Chapter 39, no. 2.—He is crowned King of Italy at Monza on 29 June. *Ibid.*, no. 7 and following.—He again receives the crown at Milan, in the church of Saint Ambrose, from Archbishop Anselm. *Ibid.*, no. 11.

**1129.** Conrad returns to Germany. Chapter 39, no. 17.—A provincial council is held at Pavia by Cardinal John of Cremona, and at it Archbishop Anselm is struck with an anathema. Chapter 39, no. 18.—The Cremonese move an army against the fortress of Crema. *Ibid.*, no. 21.

[Col. 1437B] **1130.** Honorius II dies on 14 February. Chapter 40, no. 1.—Innocent II is elected on 15 February. *Ibid.*, no. 2.—Anacletus is made pseudo-pontiff on 16 February. *Ibid.*—Anselm of Pusterla, archbishop, receives through legates the pallium sent by Anacletus, the pseudo-pontiff. Chapter 40, no. 3.

**1133.** A captive Milanese force is led to Cremona. Chapter 41, no. 1.—A council of provincial bishops is held at Milan. *Ibid.*, no. 5.—Archbishop Anselm is driven from the archiepiscopal see by the council and the whole clergy and people. *Ibid.*, no. 9.—Robald, bishop of Alba, is appointed vicar of the Church of Milan. *Ibid.*, no. 10.

**1134.** Innocent II holds a council at Pisa on the third day before the Kalends of June. *Ibid.*, no. 13.—He confirms the deposition of Anselm, archbishop of Milan. *Ibid.*, no. 16.—Thedaldus Landrianus, after the death of Stephen of Guandeca, is named archpriest of the Church of Milan [Col. 1437C]. *Ibid.*, no. 14.—Saint Bernard, legate a latere [Col. 1438A] of Innocent II, comes to Milan. *Ibid.*, no. 18; chapter 42, no. 4.—He is acclaimed archbishop of Milan. Chapter 42, no. 7.—He refuses the Milanese see. *Ibid.*, no. 11.—Conrad renders obedience to Emperor Lothair and is appointed his standard-bearer. Chapter 42, no. 1.

**1135.** Conrad again swears fidelity to Lothair. *Ibid.*—Robald, bishop of Alba, is elected archbishop of Milan on 29 July. Chapter 42, no. 17.—The Milanese declare war on the Cremonese, but with an unsuccessful outcome. Chapter 42, no. 18.—Archbishop Anselm, while going to Rome, is captured by Goyso of Martinengo and sent to Innocent II at Pisa. *Ibid.*, no. 22.

**1136.** The monastery of Clairvaux of the Cistercian Order is founded. Chapter 41, no. 5.—Anselm is sent as a prisoner to Rome by Innocent II and dies there in August. Chapter 42, no. 25.—Archbishop Robald swears fidelity to Innocent at Pisa. Chapter 43, no. 2.—He excommunicates the Cremonese proscribed [Col. 1438B] by Emperor Lothair. *Ibid.*, no. 8.—He receives the pallium sent by the same supreme pontiff. *Ibid.*, no. 3.—Lothair again descends into Italy. *Ibid.*, no. 6.—At Roncaglia he enacts laws. *Ibid.*, no. 12.—He proceeds to Pavia and then to Abbiategrasso, Turin, and Reggio. Chapter 44, no. 11; and chapter 45, nos. 2 and following.—The Pavians are routed in battle by Conrad, commander of Lothair, and are afterward received into the emperor’s favour upon payment of money. Chapter 45, nos. 6 and 8.

**1137.** Innocent II goes in March from Pisa to Viterbo in order to receive Emperor Lothair. Chapter 42, no. 3.—He absolves the Cremonese from the excommunication pronounced against them by Robald. Chapter 46, no. 1.—The Milanese take from the Cremonese the fortress of Juvenalta, and hold their bishop, captured in battle, in custody for several months. *Ibid.*, nos. 4 and 5.—The bishop of Cremona, after poisoning his guard, escapes from prison by flight and returns to Cremona [Col. 1438C]. *Ibid.*

[Col. 1437]

# LANDULF OF SAINT PAUL: BOOK OF HISTORIES OF THE CITY OF MILAN

## CHAPTER ONE. Anselm of Buis is elected archbishop of Milan in the year 1094.

> [Note: [Col. 1437D] CHAPTER I.—I have found precisely this same epoch for the year in all manuscript copies of Landulf. Yet I believe it was falsely prefixed to them through the incompetence of a copyist, who either divided Landulf’s History, written as a single continuous text, into many chapters, or misunderstood the year-number. For it is established that in the ninety-fourth year of the eleventh century Arnulf, who immediately preceded this Anselm, had not yet been consecrated archbishop of Milan; rather, only in the following year was he anointed, at Urban II’s command, by three bishops who had gone to Milan after the Synod of Piacenza, as Berthold, a writer of that age, testifies under the year 1095. And it is certain, as we shall presently say, that Anselm was promoted to the archiepiscopal see only in 1097.]

In the days when Robald, bishop of Alba [Note: Truly of Alba, as it was read in an old manuscript of the metropolitan library, but wrongly altered by a recent hand to “of Albano.” Alba Pompeia, of which he was bishop, is a city of Liguria and Montferrat, still counted among the suffragan bishoprics of the metropolitan see of Milan. I have wished to note this here for all passages in this history in which Robald is mentioned, since this term “Albanensis” is almost always wrongly used.], bore the mitre of the archbishopric of Milan, great grief came upon the Milanese for their soldiers and citizens captured at Cremona and Pavia [Note: What Landulf here alludes to occurred much later than the order of the present history requires. For Robald was elected archbishop of Milan only when the following century was already far advanced, as we shall see in the final chapters of this book. Why our author has introduced here the recollection of events that took place much later, I think he did so in order to set up a comparison between the public disturbance aroused in the time when he wrote and that at the beginning of his history, and thereby seize an occasion to pursue in writing the other events of that troubled age.], I do not forget Arman of Ganardo [Note: This is the name of the town which Aelius Capreolus places, in the geographical map of his Brescian annals, nine miles east of Brescia, on the bank of the Clusio River; the noble family of that city, frequently mentioned by him, likewise drew its surname Gavarda from it. Hence Puricelli’s reading must be corrected: he calls him “de Ganardo,” no. 284.], who, under the appearance of religion, planted a certain root of innovation [Note: I judge that this innovation was none other than that which Landulf relates immediately afterward: namely, that after the election of the archbishop of Milan, established by the clergy and leading men of the city, had been rejected—under a colour of right intention, as one ought to believe, and with some religious pretext introduced—this Arman was responsible for driving the disorderly populace, gathered round like a crown, into sedition. Led by its opinion of his supreme integrity, which it believed him to possess, since he enjoyed such influence with the Roman and Brescian Churches and with Matilda, it elected another archbishop by tumultuous votes, contrary to the ancient custom of this Church. From this poisonous root, as it were, there gradually sprang disputes, dissensions, schisms, and wars, by which not so much our city as the neighbouring peoples were afflicted with prolonged disturbance, until St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, sent to us as an angel of peace, brought help to the whole province of the Lombards, shaken by calamities, and restored its former dignity and peace, as will be related below in chapter 42.]. This gradually disturbed not only the Church of Milan but almost every rank throughout the kingdom of the Lombards, until Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, entered at the command of the Milanese people to cast out demons and to heal and raise up the infirm and crippled.

For that Arman was a monk, as it were a cardinal [Note: The particle *quasi* (“as it were”) is used here and elsewhere throughout the course of this history not to lessen the force of the word before which it is placed, but rather to indicate the thing or dignity itself; with this author it has the same meaning as *nempe* or *videlicet*, “that is.” I wished to warn the reader of this from the outset, lest he hesitate when he encounters in Landulf such rough expressions as *quasi monitus*, *quasi archidiaconus*, and the like. Moreover, that Arman was a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church is proved by the subscription attached to a diploma first published by the distinguished Benedict Bacchini in the *History of the Monastery of Padolirone*, and then inserted in the new edition of *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 541, by my most learned friend Paul Galeard: “I, Armannus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, confirm.” This was nevertheless unknown to Ciaconius and Oldoinus, as well as to the chronologists of the bishops of Brescia, Giovanni Francesco Florentini and Ughelli.

Whether this Arman is the same as Herman, cardinal-priest of the title of the Four Crowned Saints, who is known to have flourished at the same time and who had recently been sent by Urban II to Milan to bring the pallium to our archbishop Arnulf, Ughelli gives some reason for doubt; he writes that this same Arman was also called Arimannus and Hermannus. Yet since Oldoinus reports that that Herman had been made cardinal as early as 1061 by Alexander II and had been raised by Urban II to the dignity of archpriest of the Holy Roman Church; since I have nowhere seen him subscribed or mentioned as a bishop; since I find that this bishop of Brescia survived far beyond the eleventh century—for Landulf teaches in chapter 30 that he was deposed from his bishopric in 1116—and since I have consistently observed that both our author and documents signed in his own hand call him Armannus, not Hermannus, I am led to regard them as altogether different persons.

Since these matters concerning Cardinal Arman had to be brought forward in order to elucidate Landulf’s History, let me incidentally refute Puricelli. In his Nazarene Dissertation, ch. 106, no. 4, seeking to satisfy the learned reader who asks why St Galdinus, after receiving the archbishopric of Milan, never subscribed himself cardinal, although it is beyond doubt that he had been a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church before being called to this mitre, Puricelli says this occurred because—according to Panvinio in his book *On the Episcopal Titles and Cardinal Deacons*—it had anciently been customary down to the time of Alexander III for a cardinal-priest who became bishop to cease being a cardinal. Yet how weak this reason is is clearly proved by the facts we have adduced. For after assuming the government of the bishopric of Brescia, long before the age of Alexander III, Arman is found subscribing himself cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, as may be seen in the works of Bacchini and Ughelli cited above. Add that it is not true that St Galdinus, once entrusted with governing the Church of Milan, always suppressed this title of his dignity. In vol. III of Edmund Martène’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, col. 1235, there survives a brief letter of Alexander III to Garinus, abbot of Pontigny, dated the third day before the Ides of November, in the eighth year of that pontificate—that is, 1166—in which Gualdinus subscribes in the eighth place as follows: “I, Gualdinus, cardinal-priest of St Sabina and archbishop of Milan.”], a Roman, and, through the party of the citizens of Brescia and the favour of Countess Matilda, elected bishop in the Church of Brescia [Note: Bacchini, in the place cited, moved his election—dated by Ughelli to AD 1096—back to 1087, relying on a diploma of Arman published there by himself which he thought had been issued in that year. But because I have carefully examined the diploma itself in Bacchini’s work and it expressly gives the ninety-seventh year, while the day specified in it agrees with this year, not with the other assigned by Bacchini, and only the indiction disagrees, perhaps corrupted through the fault of a copyist, as the learned Galeard observed, Arman’s election must by no means be removed from 1096.], came, after the death of Arnulf [Note: Arnulf died not in 1096, as Ughelli wrongly wrote, but in 1097, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, according to Papebroch’s calculation based on ancient catalogues and also according to Puricelli himself, who in the *Life of St Herlembald*, book IV, ch. 82, no. 1, entirely withdrew his opinion, stated in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 284, which had placed Arnulf’s death in 1096.], archbishop of Milan, to elect another [Note: It may be questioned whether Arman took part in this election as an elected suffragan bishop, as the custom of this Church appears from this very history to have required. For in chapter 37 Landulf relates that Anselm of Pusterla was elected archbishop by the metropolitan clergy and suffragan bishops; and in chapter 42, speaking of the election of Robald—who, as bishop of Alba for many years already, had no need of consecration—he says that three suffragan bishops were summoned to Milan by the ordinary and *decumani* clergy, so that he might be raised by their counsel to the archiepiscopal dignity.

But whether he came here as apostolic legate, as Papebroch shows himself persuaded when in the above-mentioned Exegesis, no. 103, he says that the election of Landulf of Badagio was rendered void by an apostolic legate, who certainly was none other than this Arman, I am more inclined to this latter view. For one can only believe that he was endowed with some higher authority, since he was able both to abolish votes cast by the noble multitude and, as it were at his own nod, to establish another archbishop, as our author relates. Florentini, already cited, states in the chronological index of the bishops of Brescia that Arman was called the pope’s vicar in a diploma issued by him in favour of the monastery of St Peter; but one would wish that he had at least indicated the year of the diploma.].

When he perceived that the noble multitude of Milan was gathering to elect as archbishop Landulf of Badagio, provost of the canonry of St Ambrose, a man well endowed in character and life, he stood firm and did not consent to that election. Therefore the ring of the populace, believing him to be a religious man because of his standing with the Roman and Brescian Churches and the favour of Countess Matilda, as soon as it perceived that this Arman was absent from the election, began to rage against the election itself and to batter the clerics and priests violently with fists and sticks. It even presumed to kill a man of the citizens, named Paganus, in the Porta Orientalis … in the very church called the Winter Church [Note: This church, consecrated to the Virgin Mother of God, was called the Winter Church because the metropolitan clergy performed the divine services there during winter. It stood where the vast building of the greatest church now rises, erected by Giovanni Galeazzo Visconti, lord of Milan and subsequently its first duke. It was called the Winter Church in distinction from the Summer Church, dedicated to the holy martyr Thecla. It stood on the boundary of the portico now called Figini; it was finally demolished and united to the metropolitan chapter by Cardinal Charles Borromeo, archbishop of holy memory. Puricelli provides more information concerning both churches in his Nazarene Dissertation, ch. 100, and elsewhere in his dissertations.].

The noble Landulf escaped this frenzy and, descending into the *secretarium* [Note: Among ecclesiastical writers, *secretarium* means the same as sacristy, as Macrius teaches in the *Hierolexicon*. In our metropolitan Church at this period that place was the repository of the church treasury. Berold, the Milanese writer who flourished at the beginning of the following century and fragments of whose work Puricelli published in the Nazarene Dissertation, ch. 97 and following, describes the order of the metropolitan church. He says that of sixteen custodians, eight called “greater” were assigned to the duty that two of them each week, together with the weekly subdeacon, should sleep in the *secretarium* to guard the church treasury, which was displayed upon the altar on the appointed solemn feasts throughout the year. The other eight, called “lesser,” slept in another place called the church’s tribunal.], of the church, reached his own household church [Note: That is, the church near his paternal home. The fact that the most noble family of Badagio was settled there in a fixed residence is shown by the church of St Hilary, built in those very precincts by Anselm of Badagio, first bishop of Lucca and later supreme pontiff under the name Alexander II, as Puricelli relates in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 284.], which is called St John at the Four Faces.

But that Arman, amid such confusion, said in the church of St Ambrose to the people gathered to him: “It will happen to you as the proverb says: ‘For a foolish people, a deaf bishop’” [Note: A. I reads *lurdus*. In the ancient manuscript of the metropolitan church *surdus* (“deaf”) was read. But a recent hand inserted there the other word *lurdus* (Italian *lordo*, “filthy”), which is likewise read in copies in the Ambrosian Library. Whichever was then used proverbially, either can suit a foolish people.].

Having said this, he immediately chose for himself and for them [Note: He did not choose him himself; rather, perhaps from fear of worse consequences, he allowed the man tumultuously elected by the people and confirmed him by his authority, as is clear from the narrative of this event itself and is even more plainly expressed in chapter 28. There Landulf reports that Nazarius Muricula, with the band of his associates, did almost whatever he wished in the Church of Milan and in the city of Savona: “For in Milan he raised Anselm of Buis, a simple man, to be archbishop of Milan,” etc. The year in which this election occurred is manifestly established, after careful consideration of the ancient catalogues by Papebroch in the Exegesis mentioned and by Puricelli in the *Life of St Herlembald*, ch. 82: it must be dated 3 November 1097.], as archbishop, Anselm of Buis [Note: Galvaneus Flamma, in the *Greater Chronicle* at AD 1094, says that he was from the *valvassors* of Buis, a village ten miles from this city, in the district—or parish—of the town of Desio.], a simple man and provost of the canonry of St Lawrence. When he learned that he had been elected by that Arman of Brescia and acclaimed by the turbulent people, he immediately mounted the archiepiscopal chair and sat down.

And because his suffragan bishops failed him, he received from foreign bishops all ecclesiastical orders up to the priesthood, and likewise episcopal consecration [Note: From this it is clear that the aforesaid Anselm was indeed provost of St Lawrence, but only elected, since he had not yet been initiated into any sacred order.]. He also obtained the pastoral staff through the favour of Abbess Matilda [Note: I think that through the copyist’s error the word *abbatissae*, “abbess,” has fallen from his pen in place of the other word *comitissae*, “countess,” since no account in the histories mentions any abbess’s right or patronage concerning this election. Nor should anyone suppose that an investiture is meant here—one that had at that time repeatedly been condemned by councils and supreme pontiffs under anathema—but only that Anselm ascended the archiepiscopal see with the approval of Countess Matilda, who possessed the highest authority in the Italian kingdom and vigorously defended the cause of the Roman Church.]; and he put on the stole [Note: By this name, used everywhere by our author, the pallium is indicated, as Du Cange also noted in his Glossary.] which had been brought to him by the legate of Pope Urban.

Thereafter this man, having become prudent, disregarded Obert, surnamed Baltricus, who opposed Arman because of the investiture of the bishopric of Brescia which he had received from his king Henry. This man ordained Arman, who had elected him archbishop, bishop of Brescia. This Anselm had avoided doing through the prudence of the archbishops who preceded him, namely Anselm of Rho and Arnulf of Porta Orientalis [Note: From this context of Landulf it is inferred that the preceding archbishops of Milan, Anselm and Arnulf, had tolerated Obert Baltricus in the bishopric of Brescia, presumably by prudent counsel, lest Henry, his supporter, should be more bitterly provoked. Perhaps they also dared not condemn in a suffragan bishop what they had admitted in themselves; for Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book IX, under the years 1084 and 1092, states that both were established as archbishops by Emperor Henry through staff and ring.].

King Cono [Note: That is, Conrad, son of Henry III—also frequently called Henry IV, emperor. In what follows, I too shall follow Pagi in using this numeral when designating this Henry.], while his father Henry was still alive, was crowned at Monza through the negotiation of Countess Matilda and the agency of this Anselm of Rho; and he was crowned in the royal manner in the church of St Ambrose. Yet he paid no regard to the ordination of these pontiffs, namely Anselm of Buis and Arman of Brescia [Note: Conrad was crowned in the year in which he rebelled against his father, who was hostile to the Roman Church, and came down into Italy: namely, 1093. This solemn inauguration was performed by Anselm of Rho, archbishop of Milan—who also died toward the end of that same year. At first in the distinguished town of Monza and then in Milan in the church of St Ambrose, he placed the royal crown of Italy upon Conrad’s head, as appears from contemporary writers, our Landulf and Berthold under the year 1093. Bartholomew Zucchi, otherwise a diligent historian of Monza, did not know of this coronation performed in his native city.].

But while ruling in the place called Borgo San Donnino [Note: Then a distinguished town, now an episcopal city situated between Piacenza and Parma, formerly called Julia Fidentia.], he saw the priest Liprand [Note: The historian Arnulf, already published in vol. IV of this collection, book IV, ch. 9 (Patrologia, vol. CXLVII), calls him Luitprand.], whose nose and ears had been cut off on account of the Pataria [Note: Pagi has offered some observations on the Patarini and the Pataria in his criticism of Baronius under 1058; but a fuller learned discussion may be read in the commentary on the aforesaid Arnulf, published in the same vol. IV under the same year, which need not be repeated here. It may nevertheless be noted that our author clearly shows that at that time the name *Patarini* properly belonged to those who, obedient to pontifical commands, defended chastity against clerics obstinate in marriage.] [Note: The priest Liprand suffered this injury shortly after the martyrdom of St Herlembald, according to Arnulf in the passage cited above: that is, in 1075, as the most learned annotator of Arnulf argues there, no. 23. Indeed, Gregory VII honoured him with the title of martyr for this reason in a letter addressed to him, which we shall see quoted below by our Landulf in chapter 6.], travelling to Urban, pontiff of Rome. The king himself said devoutly to the priest: “Since you are master of the Patarini, what do you think of bishops and priests who possess royal rights and render the king no support?”

And the priest answered him without any rancour, in accordance with the good pleasure of God and of the king himself. Yet on the following day, as he was travelling with the priest Arnald, master of the Milanese schools [Note: That schools existed in this city—the schools which councils had decreed for the instruction of boys and younger clerics and which are known to have flourished of old chiefly in cathedral churches, as Thomassinus teaches in *On Ancient and New Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part II, chs. 92–100—cannot be doubted in light of the already-mentioned Berold. Describing the clergy of our metropolitan church, he repeatedly enumerates four masters of schools, one of whom had always to be present in choir, alternating weekly with the sacred celebrations; all together, on the recurring commemorations of certain saints, performed the divine offices with the rest of that church’s clergy. It is therefore natural to believe that Arnald was one of these masters.

Whether some trace may here be inferred of the Milanese palace school, famous from the time of the most holy archbishop Ambrose, where the great doctor of the Church Augustine publicly taught rhetoric for salary, and which continued to flourish vigorously down to our own age, is a question for which the copy of Landulf used by Puricelli gives occasion for conjecture. In Puricelli’s text, both in the preface to book II of the *Life of St Ariald* and in the *Life of St Herlembald*, ch. 86, the reading is consistently: “master of the schools of Milan.” From that designation one might suppose that no schools are indicated here other than those founded from ancient times by public authority and at the expense of the city of Milan. But this is not the place to discuss these matters. I shall treat more fully of certain matters bearing on this question in the *Literary History of Milan* which I have in hand and, if leisure is at last permitted, intend to commit to print.], and the priest Syrus [Note: Puricelli, in the *Life of St Herlembald*, ch. 86, believes that the Life of St Ariald, now missing, was written by this Syrus; Pagi agrees with him in his criticism under 1061, no. 6, refuting Baronius and Bolland.], of the church of St Mary of Pedone [Note: This church of the Virgin Mother of God is still called Pedone. The manuscript chronicles in the Ambrosian Library, entitled *Flos Florum*, state that it retained the hereditary name of its original founder, Count Pedone, under Angilbert II, archbishop of Milan.], he was captured by the men of the bishop of Parma [Note: It is not clear from the histories who this bishop of Parma was, whose men Landulf says captured Liprand. Eberard, or Evrard, the schismatic bishop of that city and supporter of Antipope Clement, is said by Ughelli, in his account of the bishops of Parma, no. 26, to have thrown into prison in 1079 an abbot who was travelling to Rome for a council; but, according to Berthold, he had died miserably already in 1087, when Urban II had not yet been made supreme pontiff and Conrad had not come into Italy. Ughelli did not know who succeeded him, leaving a gap of almost twenty years in this succession between Eberard and St Bernard, cardinal.

A diploma issued in the name of Henry IV and King Conrad, cited by Francesco Sansovino in *Origins of the Illustrious Families of Italy*, in his treatment of the Martinenga family, names a certain Vado as bishop of that city. A charter of grant from the archive of the canons of the same city, produced by Bonvicini in the additions to the new Venetian edition of *Italia Sacra*, confirms that this Vado was perhaps also called Guido—or else that Guido was another man, distinct from Vado or Vido—and was bishop of Parma. But the beginning and end of his episcopate are wholly unknown; and therefore it remains unknown to which bishop, certainly a schismatic, this outrage of imprisonment and robbery inflicted upon Liprand may safely be attributed.]. He was being led away to undergo punishment at a place called …; there he was held and despoiled for four days, and then returned to Milan.

But the king himself, as I have heard, exacted compensation [Note: *Emenda* is a monetary fine or compensation for loss, as Du Cange states in the Glossary. Pagi, in his criticism under the year 1100, no. 22, notes that it is used here to mean the price which Liprand had offered for his own ransom. I would more rightly believe it was a fine imposed by Conrad upon the abductors for the injury inflicted upon Liprand, as the text shows.] from those abductors, and took possession of the priest’s mule. Soon afterward he attempted to go into Tuscany [Note: Berthold testifies under the year 1095 that Conrad went into Tuscany and Pisa with royal pomp to receive as his bride the daughter of Roger, duke of Sicily. But Landulf clearly shows that he returned from there; for he says that Conrad was ruling in Borgo San Donnino when Anselm was elected archbishop of Milan and Arman consecrated bishop of Brescia, namely in 1097. This, then, is a second journey into Tuscany, hitherto overlooked by historians; Pagi more rightly places it in 1099, against Puricelli, in his criticism under the year 1100, no. 22.]. When he reached Florence, that prudent and wise king, a youth handsome in appearance—alas!—ended his life after taking a potion from Avianus, physician to Countess Matilda [Note: Abbot of Ursperg states that Conrad died in the ninth year after his defection from his father, and therefore in 1101. Under the same year he relates both that king’s outstanding qualities and a certain prodigy observed by an eyewitness at his death and later reported to him. The contemporary writer Donizo, in the *Life of Matilda*, confirms this, declaring that Conrad was taken by fate in the third year after the death of Pope Urban II. In fact, however, this third year can scarcely have begun, since Urban II died in 1099, in the same month of July in which Conrad afterwards died.].

## Chapter II. Anselm crosses the sea against the Saracens and dies at Constantinople.

With the king thus failing in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1445C] CHAPTER II.—These words of Landulf entangled Puricelli in remarkable perplexities. Believing that our author had begun the remainder of his history from Conrad’s death, and observing that all here narrated concerning the eastern expedition organized by Archbishop Anselm with such display and accomplished through such great labours could by no means be reconciled with the king’s death, placed above in the year stated, he anticipated it by three years, assigning Conrad’s death to 1098. Indeed, from Landulf he judged that those authorities of otherwise great reputation mentioned above must be corrected, and in the Life of St Herlembald, ch. 86, he amassed many arguments in order to establish that the authority of this Milanese writer, speaking of an event performed in these regions and concerning his uncle Liprand, ought to be preferred to the others.

Pagius refutes Puricelli; and, as it were striking his sickle at the root [Col. 1445D], he says in his Critique on the year 1100, no. 21, that Puricelli misunderstood Landulf. For Landulf does not write that Anselm’s journey to the East was undertaken after the death of King Conrad, but merely while he was “failing in the kingdom,” that is, when he was already near death, or when he was near to failing in the kingdom. So Pagius says. For my part, I cannot excuse Puricelli from a manifest disturbance of the history; nevertheless, to confess the truth candidly, neither does Pagius’s interpretation please me. It seems far too harsh and foreign to the author’s meaning to suppose that by “failing in the kingdom” he meant a failing of strength and life.

To proceed, then, by a clearer route, I observe that in the preceding chapter Landulf had narrated that Conrad had established the seat of his kingdom among us, when he said: “reigning in the place called Borgo San Donnino.” Therefore, when, having related all that concerned Conrad, he returned to weave the history of our Anselm, by the words “with the king failing in the kingdom” he meant nothing else [Col. 1446A] than that, because of the king’s departure for Tuscany, the seat of the Lombard kingdom—now fixed at Borgo San Donnino and, in the crude expression customary in that barbarous age, called a kingdom—had ceased to be among us. Certainly our Anselm departed for the East [Col. 1446B] while Conrad was still alive. Conrad did not die until the last days of July 1101, only two months before the death of that same Anselm, driven into flight and suffering grievous distress at Constantinople. Accordingly, it must be said not that Conrad’s life, but that his kingdom, failed in the sense explained here, when the archbishop of Milan began to plan his journey toward Jerusalem.]

The aforesaid Anselm of Bovis, Archbishop of Milan, [Col. 1446A] as though prompted by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1446B] It is clear from Baronius, Labbe, and many other writers that Urban II proclaimed the Jerusalem expedition in several councils—Piacenza, Clermont, and the Lateran—and everywhere devoted all his zeal to promoting it. Perhaps, too, after the death of our Archbishop Arnulf, Urban had sent new letters to Anselm exhorting him vigorously to undertake so great a matter; these words of Landulf seem to suggest this.] strove, despite the unwillingness of the priest already mentioned, to gather an army from diverse peoples, with which he might seize the Babylonian kingdom [Note: [Col. 1446B] For the origin and course of this noble design, especially insofar as it concerns our affairs, see Calchus, who has collected it in a concise narrative under the year 1087.]; and in this endeavour he exhorted the chosen youth of Milan to take up the crosses and to sing the chant “Ultreia, Ultreia.” [Note: [Col. 1446C] This word, which occurs nowhere except in Landulf, must have been peculiar to our city and to have arisen only at the time when this expedition was being prepared. Franciscus Bernardinus Ferrari, formerly my predecessor in the prefecture of the Ambrosian Library, attempted to trace its etymology. In book VI, chapter 7, of *On the Acclamations and Applause of the Ancients*, he says that it was formed from the two adverbs *ultra* (“beyond”) and *eia* (“come on!”), by which the people were urged bravely to undertake the journey beyond the sea; when confusedly pronounced, they produced the corrupted word *Ultreia*. Du Cange in his *Glossary* declares this conjecture insufficiently certain; one might wish, however, that he himself had produced a firmer alternative. Meanwhile it must be accepted, unless perhaps one prefers to derive the word from the other expression *ultro eia* (“come on willingly!”), which would signify the voluntary and ready disposition of those taking up the cross. [Col. 1446D]]

At the call of this prudent man, many men of every rank, throughout the cities, villages, and castles of the Lombards, took up crosses and sang the same chant, “Ultreia, Ultreia.” He further ordained that, while he was engaged in this expedition [Note: [Col. 1446D] Puricelli attempted to persuade himself that Anselm went to the East twice, in 1098 and 1100, but without truth, since no trace of this repeated expedition exists and Landulf’s authority opposes it, for he speaks only of a single journey. Indeed, Puricelli is not consistent with himself. He says that about the middle of 1098 Anselm, staying at Milan, by a public decree granted exemption from dues for the feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, and that at the beginning of the following year he subscribed to a judgment rendered in favour of the abbot of St Simplician. But who could believe that an expedition of such importance could have been carried out so swiftly that Anselm departed and returned within the brief interval of a few months?

Add that the abbot of Ursberg, under the year 1101, relates that the bishops of Milan and Pavia persuaded fifty thousand Lombards—whose vows had previously been hindered by fear or distrust, poverty [Col. 1447B] or weakness—to commit themselves to the journey. This is a sign that they had not gone earlier. In what year Anselm went to the East is uncertain. Calchus asserts that Ligurian annals report that Anselm embarked at Genoa in the fleet which sailed thence on the Kalends of August 1100; yet Pagius, on the year 1101, no. 7, observes that the histories of Giustiniani and Foglietta contain nothing on this matter. I would rather believe that Anselm made his way by land to Constantinople late in 1100 or at the beginning of the following year. For the aforementioned writer of Ursberg reports that, after crossing Carinthia, the Lombard army wintered in cities of Bulgaria and finally reached Constantinople in that same year, 1101.], no benefice from the revenues of the archbishopric should be given to priests, Levites, or other clerics, such as we are accustomed to receive at the celebrations of the feasts of holy martyrs, virgins, and confessors. [Note: [Col. 1447C] It was customary in the Ambrosian Church, when the principal feasts of the year recurred, for various gifts and even money to be supplied by the archbishop to those taking part in divine service and offices. Among the works of the aforementioned Beroldus there survives a particular book, *On Order*, in which one also reads: “how the money of all feast days is distributed.” There, in minute detail, are enumerated the things which our bishop was to distribute to ecclesiastical ministers according to their rank and according to the variety of feasts: wine, loaves of rye or wheat bread, wax, and other such things; indeed, even solidi or denarii assigned to each order.

Moreover, the more solemn days are listed on which the greater part of the clergy ought to be invited to dine in the archiepiscopal residence with the archbishop himself. At that time the archbishop ordered this to be announced publicly in choir by the primicerius of the readers, when the canticle *Benedictus* began, in these words: “Refresh yourselves with the Lord.” From this I once concluded in my printed dissertation, *In Defence of the Second Possession of the Bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius*, nos. 19 and 21, that those ancient shared meals called birthday *agapae*, intended to foster mutual charity, had not been entirely abolished in our Church. Their vestiges were these modest tables, granted only to clergy engaged in sacred service after every luxury and the intemperance of an indiscriminate crowd had been removed; they endured in the Ambrosian rite until the fourteenth century. [Col. 1447D]]

Furthermore, a certain brother, most dear to me, named Girismannus, heeding that exhortation, left father and mother, sisters and brothers, and also his wife and only daughter in the cradle; and—returning from Jerusalem, he entered upon the way of all flesh—by God’s grace assisting him, he entered the land of Babylon together with many pilgrims.

But that Archbishop Anselm of Bovis, driven into flight by Turks and Saracens [Note: [Col. 1447D] The battle which went so disastrously for the Catholics that Anselm and others were forced to flee appears to have been none other than that recorded by Orderic Vitalis, a writer of those times. After relating under the year 1101 that the Archbishop of Milan and Albert of Blandrata, a most powerful Italian, had undertaken the Jerusalem journey with bands of Ligurians, he continues that Christians, beset on every side by various misfortunes, passed through trackless forests and perilous rivers [Col. 1448B] and at last reached Gandras, a great city of the barbarians. There an extremely fierce battle was fought, with enormous slaughter on both sides, although victory inclined to neither party. But when the Turks renewed the battle, the Christian army was routed, and Albert of Brandajo, a most valiant hero, was killed in the fighting with many thousands. The remaining chief commanders and their men escaped by flight and returned to Constantinople. From our author it must also be believed that Archbishop Anselm joined them in this flight.

Moreover, I cannot pass over the testimony of Ralph, who was active in the eastern regions, serving under Tancred’s banners in 1107. In no. 147 of *The Deeds of Tancred*, he says: “At that time Anselm, Archbishop of Milan, and William, Count [Col. 1448C] of Poitou, fought against Danismas in Romania; the archbishop was killed, while the count scarcely escaped the hands of the Turks, fleeing away.” If this is accepted, Anselm would have died not at Constantinople but in the battle itself, and then have been carried to that city for burial. Yet, lest our author be charged with error, it may be believed that Anselm, struck down by a grave wound in battle, was treated by his men as they hastened away from danger in flight and was brought to Constantinople, where he died in grievous suffering from that same wound.] died at Constantinople in grievous distress. [Note: [Col. 1448C] Several writers—Sigonius, Puricelli, Ughellus, and others—state that Anselm died in the secular year on the day before the Kalends of October; but the foregoing proves this false. Therefore his death can only be recorded in 1101, as Puricelli himself, aware of his error, was afterwards compelled to acknowledge in the *Life of St Herlembald*, ch. 83, no. 3.]

## CHAPTER III. Anselm consecrates Grossulanus bishop of Savona and makes him his vicar at Milan before his sea-crossing.

[Col. 1447B]

But lest my labour be thought to end here, I say: [Col. 1448A] While this simple man [Note: [Col. 1448C] CHAPTER III.—That is, Anselm.] was still living at Milan and gathering an army, he took counsel to appoint for himself as vicar a man of many skills. Accordingly, certain most shrewd men, priests ordained by him, received orders to go to Savona [Note: [Col. 1448C] A city situated on the Ligurian coast, [Col. 1448D] still a suffragan see of the Archbishop of Milan.] and, in that city, by his command and authority, to bring about and compel the election of a bishop.

While they were on their way, they came to Ferrania [Note: [Col. 1448D] This place called Ferera in geographical maps informs us that Anselm’s envoys went to Savona by land. It lies at the foot of the mountains, about eight miles from Savona, and is encountered by those going there through Alessandria degli Stazi and Acqui—unless one prefers to suppose that the place in which they stopped was Ferrania, situated in the same neighbourhood.], in whose wood they encountered Grossulanus and his counsel. The efforts of those priests prevailed to such an extent that certain men of Savona chose Grossulanus himself as their bishop, though he was distressed in food and shabby in clothing. [Note: [Col. 1448D] Ughellus, in *The Bishops of Savona*, no. 14, asserts that this election occurred in 1098. Yet Landulf implies that it happened later. For he says that Grossulanus was ordained bishop at the same time as he was made vicar of the Archbishop of Milan, and that he remained in this office for two years, namely until he received certain news of Anselm’s death, as the following chapter recounts. It follows clearly that he could not have been elected and ordained bishop as early as 1098; otherwise he would have spent four years administering this Church of Milan, contrary to Landulf’s testimony. This election must therefore be placed in 1100, and indeed before July, as Pagius likewise places it in his *Critique* on that year.]

The electors, together with the man elected, the two priests sent by the archbishop—namely, the priest John Aculeus and the priest Nazarius [Col. 1448B] Muricula—came to Milan. There, by the command of the archbishop, who was already engaged in the expedition [Col. 1449A] [Note: [Col. 1449B] Puricelli believed in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 284, that this was Anselm’s first expedition to the East, undertaken in 1098; but this is false, as we have shown above. Later, in the *Life of St Herlembald*, ch. 86, he postponed it to the following year; but even this cannot be reconciled with Puricelli’s own writings.

For he says that, while Urban II was still alive, Anselm collected an army and at the same time resolved that a vicar should be appointed in his place as he was departing for distant lands. He further relates that, having therefore sent men to Savona, Anselm left Milan so swiftly in the meantime that he was already far away when Grossulanus, elected without any intervening delay, arrived in that city. Thus, by Puricelli’s calculation, our archbishop must have proceeded to the East in July, the month in which Urban finally died, or at least shortly afterwards, if some interval was required to plan and carry out these affairs.

Yet in chapter 83 Puricelli himself shows us Anselm still remaining at Milan much later. He relates that Anselm solemnly transferred the venerable body of St Ariald from St Celsus to the church of St Dionysius. He himself is compelled to admit that this could not have occurred until the end of that year, since the elder Landulf, cited by him and published in volume IV of this Collection (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLVII), ch. 2, no. 6, asserts that it was done after the second anniversary of Anselm’s consecration, namely in November, when two years from his assumption of the Milanese see were completed—unless it occurred even later. For Landulf does not say that the archbishop instituted this new magnificence of sacred worship in honour of St Ariald immediately after those two years had elapsed.

Puricelli’s first journey of Anselm into Syria is therefore empty and fabricated, surrounded on every side by thorns of difficulties. But the formula of Landulf [Col. 1449D], “engaged in the expedition,” deceived that most learned man. He judged it to mean nothing other than Anselm’s departure for the East, whereas, as Pagius rightly observes in his *Critique* on the year 1100, no. 21, it merely indicates that Anselm was absent from Milan in order to stir up the remaining Lombard peoples to take up the cross. This he did accomplish, as Landulf recounts above in chapter 2: “At the call of this prudent man, many men of every rank throughout the cities, villages, and castles of the Lombards took up crosses.”], Grossulanus was ordained bishop and vicar of the archbishop by Armanus of Brescia, Ariald of Genoa [Note: [Col. 1449D] Mention of him will recur in chapter 17.], and Mamardus of Turin. [Note: [Col. 1449D] Ughellus knew nothing of this bishop. He makes Amizo II the successor of Humbert, who died at the end of the eleventh century; yet Mamardus undoubtedly succeeded him immediately. He had already received the episcopal mitre of Turin in 1100, in which year Grossulanus, consecrated by him, appears as a subscribing bishop in the document concerning the dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre performed by Anselm, Archbishop of Milan, in the same year. Whether this Mamardus is the same person whom Landulf mentions as Bishop of Turin in chapter 21 will be examined in its place, namely under chapter 21. [Col. 1450B]]

But because, although ordained, he had not yet taken possession of the see of Savona, he attempted to go to that city and in some fashion arrived there; but whatever rest he had there was very brief. Leaving thence with the greatest speed, he returned to Milan. He exhorted the people of that great city to assemble every Monday at the church of St Ambrose and to make litanies [Note: [Col. 1450B] That is, supplications; Macrius treats of them at length in the *Hierolexicon*.] for Archbishop Anselm and his army.

Grossulanus himself, not only on those weekdays but on almost every feast day, addressed that great people in eloquent sermons; and by his preaching [Col. 1450A] he sought to win them over [Note: [Col. 1450B] Understand: “he conciliated them.”] no less than by the austerity of his clothing and food.

## CHAPTER IV. The priest Liprand reproves Grossulanus for his mean clothing; upon hearing of Anselm’s death, he presses for Grossulanus’s election.

Meanwhile, the priest Liprand said gently to Grossulanus, who was attached to the archbishop’s chair [Note: [Col. 1450B] CHAPTER IV.—That is, exercising the office of vicar.], in the presence of Andrew the primicerius [Note: [Col. 1450B] We learn from the frequently cited Beroldus that at that time there were several ranks of ecclesiastical hierarchy in the Church of Milan, each presided over by its own primicerius. In the Ambrosian Manual, while describing the sacred rites customarily used in the divine offices by this clergy, he lays down a rubric concerning what was to be done on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, in these words:

> “On the Saturday of the Palm Branches, the archbishop gives palms to all the orders of the major church in this manner: to the archpriest, a great palm branch, from which he distributes to the other priests [Col. 1450C] subject to him; likewise one to the archdeacon, from which he gives to his deacons. One to the primicerius of the subdeacons, from which he distributes to the subdeacons; one to the primicerius of the notaries, from which he gives to his own; etc. One to the primicerius of the readers, etc. One branch to the primicerius of the lesser priests, from which he gives to all subject to him,” etc.

Elsewhere he also enumerates a primicerius of the *decumani* priests. Puricelli further reports from ancient writings, in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 652, and in the *Nazarian Dissertation*, ch. 100, no. 16, that the Veglones also had their own primicerius. The Veglones are a part of the metropolitan clergy, called the school of St Ambrose, still surviving today. Although Landulf does not say here which rank the aforesaid Andrew held first, elsewhere he expressly reveals it, calling him primicerius of the *decumani* priests.

How great this dignity then was can be gathered from this very History. For when Grossulanus shortly afterwards dealt with establishing a new archbishop, he is reported first to have approached Andrew, as though this matter of such importance had to be sought from him as its principal author. Indeed, Andrew is said, having summoned clergy and nobles into council, to have determined the election itself. Moreover, in chapter 12, in a phrase expressing the highest dignity, he is called “primicerius of the Church of Milan.” For more on the supreme authority of this primicerius, see the elder Landulf. At present this dignity has been transferred, retaining its ancient legal status and not without splendour, to one of the principal clergy of the metropolitan church, who bears the honourable name of primicerius and occupies the third place among the dignities of the chapter. Some traces of the others still survive in the primicerius of the readers, also called master of the choir, and in the chief members of every order, to whom certain special prerogatives remain in our Church.], and to certain other priests, that he should take off his rough cloak and put on one suitable to so great a vicar. Grossulanus replied to the priest that he did not have the price to buy one.

Then the priest Liprand said to the primicerius: “Primicerius, you are rich and can well furnish this price [Col. 1451A]. Nevertheless, if it pleases you, I shall furnish half so great a price.” The primicerius replied to the priest: “That is enough; I shall accomplish it tomorrow.” But the vicar said that he would not wear it, since he had resolved to lead a life in contempt of the world.

When that priest Liprand heard this, he spoke with a certain show of astonishment, saying: “If you despise the world, why have you come into the world [Note: [Col. 1451B] By “world” here, in the French manner, is apparently meant the crowd of people into which Grossulanus had thrust himself by assuming the archbishop’s vicarial dignity. Yet I would rather believe that his monastic profession is indicated, to which Grossulanus had devoted himself—as I shall show at the end of the following chapter—and by which he had, as it were, placed himself outside the world.]? Look: this city follows its custom of various furs—grey squirrel [*gris*] [Note: [Col. 1451B] Precious furs from the little animal called *gris*. See Laurentius in the onomastic *Amalthea*; Du Cange, under *Griseus*, reports that in French this animal is called *vair*.], marten [Note: [Col. 1451C] Furs from the Scythian weasel, in Italian *armellino*, which is called *martes* and *marterus*. Aldrovandi discusses this Russian animal at length, and most recently Henricus Ruysch in the *Theatre of Animals*.], and other costly adornments—and of fine foods. It will surely be shameful for us if strangers and pilgrims see you shaggy and ragged among us.”

Yet in this his chosen state of hardship, prayer, and preaching, the vicar laboured for two years [Note: [Col. 1451C] It is not easy to determine when these two years began. If what Papebroch states in the *Exegesis of the Archbishops of Milan*, no. 104, were true—namely, that certain news of Anselm’s death did not reach this city until nearly a year had elapsed, in August 1102, the month in which he also infers from our ancient Catalogue that Grossulanus was raised by the votes of the clergy to the Milanese mitre—it could be said that, immediately after the dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre performed on the Ides of July, Anselm set out toward Jerusalem and Grossulanus undertook the laborious office of vicar in August 1100. Thus in the same month of 1102 the two years of preaching and prayers ordained by him for Anselm and his army would be completed.

[Col. 1451D] Certainly, in the subscription to the document concerning the dedication just mentioned, in which Grossulanus calls himself bishop, the title of vicar is absent. Yet since, from Landulf, we have said that he was created bishop and vicar at the same time, it must be admitted that Grossulanus was exercising the archbishop’s functions even before the dedication mentioned. To reconcile all the evidence, I judge that he exercised this office before the Ides of July, at the time when Anselm was absent from Milan, intent on soliciting the Lombard expedition in the neighbouring cities. But when our archbishop truly departed for the East at the end of that year or the beginning of the following year, Grossulanus immediately began to perform the acts Landulf recounts, until in 1102, as we shall say, he received certain news of Anselm’s death—spending two years, though by no means complete years, in this office assumed after Anselm’s final departure.] and, through his labours, received certain news [Col. 1451B] of the death of the aforesaid Anselm of Bovis.

Grossulanus therefore told the primicerius and the canons of the greater Church of Milan that, in his presence, they should choose for themselves and for the people an archbishop suitable to them, before he returned to the bishopric of Savona.

## CHAPTER V. Grossulanus is elected archbishop, and the Roman pontiff sends him the pallium.

Then the primicerius, having taken counsel with the nobles, clergy, and men of Milan, before the people and himself, chose one of the two Landulphs who were ordinarii of the Church of Milan, namely Landulph of Badagio [Note: Ch. V.—That this is the same Landulph whom Armanus, as is related above in ch. I, rejected for a second time when he had already been designated archbishop by common suffrage, seems suggested by the complete identity of the name. Puricelli likewise supports this conjecture in *Mon. bas. Ambr.*, no. 292.], and Landulph of Vareglate [Note: This is a castle only one mile from the city of Asti, commonly called Variglia, from which this family, once lords of the place, took its name, as Ughelli attests in *Epis. Aston.*, no. 29. This Landulph was first provost of the Nazarene basilica at Milan, then bishop of Asti, and finally was enrolled among the saints, being distinguished by a reputation for holiness. His *Life*, composed by Philip Malabayla, may be read in the *Acta Sanctorum* for 7 June.], who were returning from Jerusalem; but Grossulanus forbade an election to be made of an absent person.

Accordingly, a part of the clergy and people, at the prompting of Ariald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis, shouted and acclaimed Grossulanus as their archbishop. As soon as he saw that he had been hailed by a great multitude of commoners and nobles, and applauded by that abbot [Note: Philip Malabayla, in the aforementioned *Life of Blessed Landulph*, reports that, when Grossulanus was acclaimed archbishop amid the favour of the people and nobles, this Abbot Ariald immediately threw an episcopal mantle over his shoulders. If this account deserves any weight, the reading *plaudatum* might perhaps be corrected to *paludatum*, that is, “clothed in a mantle.” Yet I believe that this word, found in all the manuscripts of Landulph, is genuine, having been derived by an author very unskilled in Latin from the verb *plaudo*, and thus means “received with applause” or “commended.”], he mounted the archiepiscopal throne [Col. 1452B] and sat down [Note: There is no single opinion among writers concerning the year when Grossulanus began to occupy the see. Sigonius writes that he succeeded Anselm in 1101, and Puricelli, no. 291, does not disagree. Donatus Bossius, in the *Chronicle of Milan*, places the beginning of this archbishop’s see even earlier, namely in 1100. Conversely, Ughelli, Pagi, and others steadfastly affirm that this pastor was given to the widowed Church of Milan only in the second year after 1100. Papebroch also specifies the month—August, already approaching its last days—and this accords better with historical truth, as is clear from what has been said above.]. While seated, he transferred that Abbot Ariald from one abbey to a greater abbey, namely Clairvaux [Note: Undoubtedly *Clivatensem* is to be read, “the abbey of Clivato,” over which our Landulph later reports, in ch. 14, that Ariald—perhaps this very man—presided. For the monastery of Clairvaux, or rather Caraevallo, was founded only in the thirty-fourth year after Grossulanus’s election, as will be indicated at the end of this history.].

But before this transfer occurred, certain men and clerics of Milan who seemed upright in conduct and life [Note: The word *probi* is absent from all the manuscripts and is written in a recent hand; yet the sense of the context certainly seems to require it.] reported certain shameful matters [Col. 1453A] concerning Grossulanus and his election [Note: Ughelli writes, but wrongly, that the Milanese mitre had been purchased by Grossulanus with money openly conveyed to Emperor Henry. Since Henry IV had long before been renounced by our citizens, as had his son Henry—made king by his father in 1099, but wholly unacceptable to the Milanese, who adhered to his brother Conrad—it is scarcely credible that he involved himself in such an election. Nor does Landulph’s history reveal this anywhere. In this respect Sigonius, Galesini in the *Tabulae synodales*, and other writers who commonly state that this prelate was given to the Insubrian see by Henry must also be corrected. That Grossulanus obtained the archiepiscopal dignity through simoniacal practices is clearly shown by what is narrated in the course of this account.] to the priest Liprandus.

The priest himself advised these men and clerics to send letters and two suitable clerics to Rome, asking the pope [Note: Namely Paschal II.] not to confirm Grossulanus in the archbishopric until he should soon see and hear those who had sent the letters. But Bernard, abbot of Vallombrosa [Note: The fourth superior general of that congregation, afterward included in the catalogue of saints.], and Roman cardinal [Note: Created cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus by Urban II in 1097; at that time he was exercising, in the name of Paschal II, the office of apostolic legate and vicar in the regions of Lombardy.], disregarding these letters and messengers—namely Obizo, called the Black, and Heribert of Bruzzano—and, despising Grossulanus’s case, did not attend to the words before the Apostolic See and its court of his envoys, namely Arderic of Carimate and the priest John of Pioltello. Instead, having received the stole, he entered the court of Countess Matilda.

[Col. 1453B] There, having taken counsel in accordance with the wish of Arderic of Carimate, who had gone to Rome on behalf of Grossulanus and the stole, that Abbot Bernard hastened to Milan. When they saw Milan from afar, the same Arderic carried it on an extended rod [Note: Papebroch, at 27 June, p. 311, no. 5, conjectures that *protensi* may denote a kind of parasol; unless perhaps *protensa*, “extended,” should be read.] as far as the greater church [Note: Namely the winter church mentioned in ch. 1, which was always the metropolitan church and was called the Greater Church. Hence it is clear that the stole, or pallium, was brought to Archbishop Grossulanus after the third Sunday of October, when services began to be celebrated in the Greater, that is, Winter Church, as I shall explain more fully below, ch. 28, no. 8.] of the city, crying: “Here [Col. 1454A] [Note: Read *Eccum* without aspiration; it is a Latin word meaning “behold, here.”] is the stole, here is the stole!” At this cry the whole populace assembled and shouted: “Let whoever opposes it die!”

This shouting was immense and unceasing, until that cardinal-abbot and Grossulanus mounted the pulpit of the Greater Church of Milan. Since both appeared there poorly provided with food and humbly dressed [Note: Puricelli once conjectured, in *Mon. bas. Ambr.*, no. 321, that Grossulanus was a monk of Vallombrosa. Occasion for this conjecture was given by a passage of Landulph, who reports in ch. 27 that, when Grossulanus left Milan—or rather, was driven out by the sword by the followers of Archbishop Jordan—he went to Piacenza and was received there as a guest in the monastery of Saint Mark of the Vallombrosan congregation. I find this expressly stated in the already cited *Life of Blessed Landulph* by Malabayla, where, in no. 4, Grossulanus is called a monk of Vallombrosa. If this is admitted, a certain clearer light seems to arise for this history. For it can more conveniently explain why he long continued in a ragged and rough garment, even when he acted as vicar of the archbishop of Milan; why he answered Liprandus, when urged to wear more noble clothing, that he had resolved to lead a life of contempt for the world; and finally why Cardinal Bernard so ardently favoured him, as a member of the same institute. Perhaps both wore the monastic habit of their order when they were brought before the public and ascended the ambo of the Greater Church of Milan; for these words seem to indicate this: “Both appeared there poorly provided with food and humbly dressed.”], and were distinguished in speech, they heard such applause for themselves as though they were pure angels of God.

There Grossulanus was clothed with the stole; and the abbot, rewarded in his own time, rested and departed. A few days later, through the favour of the aforesaid Countess Matilda, the same abbot received the bishopric of Parma [Note: In 1106, while Paschal II was staying at Parma on his journey to Germany, Bernard was made bishop of that city, as Mabillon relates in the *Annals of the Benedictine Order* for that year. If this is accepted, what is narrated here about the stole or pallium brought to Grossulanus ought to be referred to that same year, since our author asserts that, a few days later, Cardinal Abbot Bernard was adorned with the mitre of Parma. Yet this can by no means be admitted, since otherwise the entire chronological order of this history would be overturned, as will be clear from what follows. I therefore judge that this text has been corrupted, so that a copyist wrote *post paucos dies* (“after a few days”) in place of the phrase *post paucos annos* (“after a few years”), as may be inferred from Landulph’s words shortly before: *in suo tempore remuneratus*, “rewarded in his own time,” which surely suggest a long rather than a few days’ interval. Unless, perhaps, on our author’s authority, those writers who assigned the year 1106 to Bernard’s election as bishop of Parma must be corrected, and it must be moved back to the end of 1102 or the beginning of the following year. The succession of bishops of Parma is confused in this matter: it does not know the bishop immediately preceding Bernard, and no secure foundation is offered on which Bernard’s election should be fixed to the aforesaid year 1106.].

## CHAPTER VI. Grossulanus sought to take from the priest Liprandus his bull of exemption, while admitting that he had favoured his opponents.

[Col. 1454B]

Grossulanus, yielding to human frailty, used delicious foods and costly garments, and requested the girdle [Note: Ch. VI.—A kind of sacred garment, in the form of a small *maniple*, hanging from the left side down to the knees, which the priest wears as though a quiver suspended from him, just as he girds himself with a belt for a bow; so Gemma, book I, ch. 83. Macri, in the *Hierolexicon*, s.v. *Cingulum*, reports that the use of this priestly garment had fallen into disuse in the Latin Church, except that the supreme pontiff alone used it in solemn celebrations; and, s.v. *Epigonation*, he adds that it was still used among leading Greek celebrants in the sixteenth century, as appears from a letter sent from the East.] which the priest Liprandus used in the office of the Mass, according to the custom of a cardinal [Col. 1455A] [Note: Macri, in the place cited, attests that bishops and other ecclesiastical dignitaries used this vestment. Perhaps the name “cardinal” here indicates the ordinarii of the metropolitan Church of Milan, who were formerly honoured with such a title. Indeed, Galvaneus Flamma, in the *Chronicon Maius*, ch. 396, on the authority of Datius, reports that from the time of Saint Ambrose they customarily wore episcopal insignia. This ancient honour, having fallen into disuse through changes of affairs and times, was restored by Clement XI, of blessed memory, on the Ides of July 1716, by briefs granting in perpetuity to all and each of the dignitaries and ordinary canons of Milan the right, in every solemn ecclesiastical function in which sacred vestments are used, to use the mitre and other garments in the manner of abbots entitled to the use of the mitre, both in the city and in the diocese, and to place a mitre upon their family arms, etc.].

But the priest refused to give that girdle to Grossulanus. Then the archbishop tried to terrify with threats those whom he could not win over by flattery [Note: That is, attract by blandishments.], especially the priest Liprandus. When this priest was questioned before all the people of the city of Milan, he said:

> “Very many of those sitting and standing here have spoken at their own pleasure and yours, and have answered you concerning the letters sent to Rome [Note: Namely those which Liprandus himself had advised should be drawn up against Grossulanus and carried to Rome by two suitable clerics, as was narrated in the preceding chapter.], on account of which you are proceeding against me. If you want my answer about this, tell me whether you want me to tell you the truth or a lie; otherwise I shall not give you that answer.”

Grossulanus, having questioned him about this, finally said in the same assembly: “I want you to tell the truth.”

Then the priest [Note: Manuscript A.2: “as though.”], strengthened by the Lord, said [Col. 1455B]:

> “I neither dictated nor wrote the letters about which you question me. But I read other things in Holy Scripture, and in them I did not find a word that confirmed that you could rightfully be archbishop of the Church of Milan. I gave advice and aid to several clerics and men who sent Obizo the Black and Heribert of Bruzzano to Rome, to ask the pope not to send you the stole.”

Whereupon Grossulanus, stirred up, said: “I am now archbishop and possess the stole. Unless you make satisfaction to me for this presumption, I shall do to you what it is my office to do.”

Then the priest presented him with a document sealed with the apostolic seal [Note: Gregory VII had given these letters to Liprandus immediately after Liprandus had suffered the foul mutilation of his ears and nose in defence of priestly chastity, in 1075. That most holy pontiff wrote them not only to congratulate him upon the glory of martyrdom which he had attained, but also to declare by apostolic authority that he was in no way bound by ecclesiastical impediments through which, because of bodily disfigurement, he might have been kept from the altars. The reason Liprandus offered these letters to Grossulanus may have been that the archbishop, angered, appeared by the words, “I shall do to you what it is my office to do,” to threaten that he would prohibit him from sacred ministry.], containing the following:

> **GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to LIPRANDUS [Col. 1455C], priest: greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> If we venerate the memory of the saints whose death and severing of limbs we read of; if we praise the endurance of those whom neither sword nor any punishment separated from faith in Christ: you also, whose nose and ears have been cut off for Christ’s name, are more worthy of praise. You have deserved to attain that grace which all should desire, by which, if you persevere to the end, you do not differ from the saints.
>
> The wholeness of your body has indeed been diminished, but the inward [Col. 1456A] person, who is renewed day by day, has received a great increase in holiness. Your visible form is more unsightly, but the image of God—which is the form of righteousness—has become more pleasing in its diminution, more beautiful in its deformity. Therefore the Church glories in the Song of Songs, saying: “I am black, daughters of Jerusalem.”
>
> But if the inward appearance has suffered no loss, then by those severings your priestly office has not been severed from you. For this belongs properly to holiness and is not considered so much in the integrity of the limbs as in the integrity of virtues. Thus Emperor Constantine often kissed the eye of a certain bishop of Jerusalem which had been torn out for Christ’s name; and by the example of the Fathers and the teaching of our elders we have learned that sacred office is not taken from martyrs because of such mutilation of limbs.
>
> [Col. 1456B] Therefore, martyr of Christ, be strengthened in the Lord. Believe all the more that the office of priesthood is now yours: formerly entrusted to you by the anointing of oil, but now by the dipping of your blood. And the less you possess that can be taken away, the less you should fear to preach what is right and to sow what shall be returned a hundredfold.
>
> We know indeed that you are continually opposed and afflicted by the enemies of Holy Church. But do not fear or be terrified by them, for with great charity we hold both you and all that is yours under our protection and that of the Apostolic See. If it becomes necessary for you in any matter, we grant you leave to appeal to the Apostolic See; and if you come to us and to our See, we are prepared to receive you with joy and great honour.

After these had been read, Grossulanus [Note: Manuscript A.1: “When.”], as though wishing to destroy the seal, grasped it and covered it with his cloak. Then the priest, as though angered, demanded his property; and in demanding it, said to Grossulanus: “Unless he returned the seal and document to him unharmed, he would thereby stir up the entire city.” The sealed document was returned to him unharmed.

Ariald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis [Note: Deeply devoted to Grossulanus, though, as is clear from this passage, he had not yet obtained possession of the more lucrative abbey mentioned above.], drew the priest aside and led him into a chamber. Amid many blandishments [Note: Manuscript A.2: “blandishments.”], he told the priest to give Grossulanus the hand of obedience. But the priest, raising and repeating his voice, said: “The hand of obedience? [Col. 1457A] The hand of obedience? By him who lives forever, I would not give even the smallest finger of my hand for this matter.”

When the assembly of clerics, which was still present in the palace, heard this, it said to itself: “This counsel is not secret [Note: For it had been disclosed by that utterance.].” When the abbot and priest had left the chamber and the archbishop had given the sign for the council to be dissolved, the priest imposed silence upon himself and obtained a hearing, saying: “Do not cause scandal concerning me; know that I shall, in my office [Note: The words lacking in the manuscript seem to have been no other than: “keep it.”] [lacuna] according as he himself keeps me in his.” And in these terms he gave his hand to Grossulanus.

## CHAPTER VII. Liprandus received the sick Heribert into his house, for which, by Grossulanus’s order, he abstained from celebrating Mass.

[Col. 1457B]

Since each regarded the other with suspicion, it happened that Heribert of Bruzzano [Note: One of the messengers who had been sent to Rome against Grossulanus.] came, very severely burdened with fevers, to the aforesaid priest, begging him to give him a remedy against his illness. The priest’s servants provided the sick man with food and a suitable bed, until the Lord of hosts, through the laying on of that priest’s hands, gave a healing remedy to the sick man [Note: That the exceptional holiness of life which shone forth in Liprandus had been confirmed by God through the testimony of miracles is shown both by this illness of Heribert’s being expelled by the laying on of hands alone and by several other miracles which we shall see in the course of the present history. Puricelli gathered these together in *Life of St Herlembald*, ch. 91; see him.].

Grossulanus, provoked by this, said to the priest: “Because you have shared fellowship with Heribert, whom I have excommunicated [Note: This passage informs us that those messengers, whom we have said were sent to Rome against Grossulanus, had been struck by him with a dreadful anathema.], I command you not to celebrate Mass until you have undertaken penance for it and made satisfaction to me.”

The priest replied: “What I did for Heribert was good and came from God; I do not know how to repent of a good and divine work. And although you have no such authority [Col. 1457C] over me [Note: For Liprandus had been exempted both by Gregory VII, who had written him in the apostolic letters quoted above, “We hold both you and all that is yours under our protection and that of the Apostolic See with great charity,” and by Urban II, who fortified the Church of the Most Holy Trinity founded by Liprandus and Liprandus himself with a special privilege, as we shall shortly see.], nevertheless, in order to avoid this scandal [Col. 1458A], I shall accommodate myself to you.”

Therefore the priest Liprandus brought into the house of his own legal possession a scholarly priest [Note: Du Cange in his *Glossary* and Macri in his *Hierolexicon* give the various meanings of this word according to the varying usage of earlier times. I believe that it here denotes a man whose office was teaching, and perhaps Arnald, mentioned in ch. 1.], who celebrated Mass for him in the Church of Saint Paul, called *in Copodo* [Note: Manuscript A.1: *Compedo*; more correctly, *Compito*, for even now this Church of Saint Paul bears the name “in Compito.” Galvaneus Flamma, in the manuscript *Chronicon Extravagans* in the Ambrosian Library, ch. 35, states that it was given this name from the broad street before it, called the *Compitum*, and gives further information concerning the same *Compitum*.]. This church, together with the Church of Saint Germanus located at Niguarda [Note: A village situated about three miles outside the Como gate, now famous for the magnificent houses built there by the most illustrious Lord Marquis George de Clericis, president of the Milanese senate, and for gardens cultivated with every luxury and delight of pleasant enjoyment.], Liprandus himself enriched while rebuilding and embellishing it and, as is now apparent, adorned it. He received for himself and his heirs the right of foundation, as is recorded in charters subscribed and attested by royal judges [Note: That is, envoys of the lord king, whose signatures are seen in a document drawn up in 1123 and reported by Puricelli in *Mon. bas. Ambr.*, no. 336.], laymen, and an ordinary cleric [Note: Namely, a canon of the metropolitan church.]. This is also why he resisted Grossulanus more firmly than the others who were hostile both to him and to his people.

## CHAPTER VIII. Liprandus founded the Church of the Holy Trinity with an exemption from Urban II.

[Col. 1458B]

In order to establish security [Note: Ch. VIII.—The security of which there is discussion here had been secured for himself and his clerics by Liprandus long before these events, under Urban II, who died as July 1099 was ending. The author therefore relates out of chronological order both the merit of the church founded by Liprandus and the honour of the favourable diploma he obtained from that supreme pontiff. It should also be believed that Liprandus shortly afterward presented its copy to Grossulanus, just as he did the letters of Gregory VII described above, in order to invalidate the sentence of interdict imposed upon him and protect himself, as with a saving shield, from the anger of the threatening prelate.] for himself and his clerics, he also began the Church of the Holy Trinity and founded it on his own allodial land at a place called the bridge of Guinizel [Note: If it were known in what part of the city or territory of Milan this bridge stood, we would have some secure indication of the place where Liprandus founded his church, adorned with the privilege of the supreme pontiff. But after carefully examining histories and taking counsel even with men expert in antiquarian matters, nothing has emerged on which I can here set my foot securely; I do not wish to play the prophet.], together [Note: Manuscript A.2: “at the same time.”] with his acolyte and pupil Landulph [Note: This is the same Landulph who wrote this history, as he will reveal more clearly in the following chapter.].
