He offered it also to Blessed Peter; Pope Urban II received it and fortified the priest himself and the church with a privilege, subscribing as follows:

### Copy of the bull

> **URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LIPRANDUS, etc.**
>
> We decree that that church, with the small estate on which it is founded [lacuna], or which may have been bestowed there upon the Lord’s granting it by other faithful persons, shall remain forever free and undisturbed from every secular interference. We grant to the clerics who are to live there the faculty of living according to rule; and we decree that they are to receive both their own ordinations and the consecrations of altars and churches, and the gifts of the other sacraments, from the archbishop of Milan, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the communion and favour of the Apostolic See, and grants these freely and without improper motive. Otherwise, they shall be free to receive these same sacraments from whichever Catholic bishop they choose.
>
> We therefore decree that neither the archbishop of Milan nor any living person may oppress that church or the brothers who serve God there with any yoke of pretext, dissipate their goods and apply them to his own uses, or harass them with rash vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved entire for your benefit and that of your successors in every way [Col. 1459B], while preserving the Catholic reverence due to the same archbishop of Milan.
>
> As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, every four years you shall pay six coins of Milanese currency to the Lateran Palace. If, therefore, in time to come any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, attempts rashly to act against the text of this decree, let him be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of Christ, God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.
>
> But upon all who serve this place rightly, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

## CHAPTER IX. Liprandus declares that Grossulanus is a simoniac and that he will prove it by the judgment of fire.

Grossulanus, however, and his party paid no heed either to this apostolic admonition [Note: [Col. 1459C] CHAP. IX.—That is, the brief letters of Urban II which had been read aloud.] or to the many entreaties made by noble men on behalf of the priest Liprand. [Col. 1460A] Rather, wishing to overthrow him, he exerted himself to stir up the bishops and princes of Lombardy and to hold a synod with them. [Note: [Col. 1459C] The calculation derived from the events narrated immediately afterward compels us to believe that this Milanese synod was convoked toward the end of 1102 or at the beginning of the following year. Meanwhile, note the supreme authority of the archbishop of Milan in that age, at whose command not merely the suffragan bishops but also the princes of Lombardy were stirred.]

As the time of this synod drew near, the agitation of many persons uttered many shameful things against Grossulanus. [Note: [Col. 1459D] That is, it muttered.] And Grossulanus, to suppress that agitation, caused matins to be rung, as though at the first watch [Note: [Col. 1459D] Here is indicated Grossulanus’s exceptional diligence: beyond the customary practice of reciting matins before dawn, he ordered them to be sung at an earlier time, giving the signal with the sacred bell, so that the people, awakened by the novelty, might attend in greater numbers. For among ministers of the Church no practice had become established of distinguishing the first or second watches of the night according to the model of ancient military service.] of each “authentic” night, [Note: [Col. 1459D] It is established that in the Ambrosian Church the last week of Lent, commonly called Major Week, is called “authentic.” Yet that our Landulf is by no means speaking of this week is evident from his own narrative of the event. For in the following chapter he reports that, after various disputes between Liprand and Grossulanus and after a synod had also been held for two days in the major church, Liprand was at last compelled, on the evening of Palm Sunday, to prepare for the ordeal by fire. Thus Grossulanus must have done the things described here much earlier. What, then, were the nights called “authentic” by our author? I would judge that they were none other than the nights preceding the sixth day of each Lenten week. Since, in the Ambrosian rite, these are dedicated to the veneration of the crucified Redeemer with worship so distinctive that on that day priests are commanded to abstain from celebrating the sacred rite, in reverence for the bloody sacrifice performed by Christ the Lord, the first and supreme Priest, they could be called “authentic,” no differently from the days of the final week. Those days, we believe, are called authentic because the remembrance of the Lord’s bloody Passion is solemnly observed by the Church with the utmost devotion of the faithful, as though represented in the very archetype. This is especially likely because I observe that Grossulanus delivered on these very nights a sermon on Christ’s Passion, as Landulf here records.] and, taking the occasion of matins, gathered a large crowd both personally and through his priests and ministers.

When matins had been sung and a great multitude had assembled before him, he delivered a lengthy sermon on Christ’s Passion and Judas the betrayer, adapting the sermon to his own cause. At its conclusion, without anyone questioning him, he publicly swore upon the holy Gospels of God that from the day he came forth from his mother’s womb he had committed no defilement and had not polluted his flesh. [Note: [Col. 1460D] From this may plainly be inferred the substance of the charges directed against Grossulanus, since Landulf had said above that certain shameful things were being muttered by the people against him, as I have already observed in chap. 5, no. 7.] Arialdus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Dionysius, and Guazzo, surnamed “of Orreo,” confirmed the same thing by oath. Grossulanus then immediately added:

“If anyone wishes to say anything against me, let him say it now. But if he is silent now, he shall thereafter receive no hearing against me.”

When this was reported to the priest Liprand, he summoned several leading citizens [Note: [Col. 1460D] A. 1 reads: “principal.”] to the church of Saint Paul one day and said to them:

“You see that for Christ’s name I have had my nose and ears cut off; for this reason a great reward is promised to me, if I persevere to the end. Therefore, for Christ’s love and for your salvation and peace, I ask you to attend to me and to what I shall say to you.” [Col. 1460C]

After saying these things and much else well spoken and persuasive, especially against simony, he set forth his proposition:

“Grossulanus, who is regarded as archbishop, is a simoniac in respect of the archbishopric of Milan: by payment from the hand, by payment from the tongue, and by payment from service.” [Note: [Col. 1460D] These are the three principal heads from which, all theologians teach, simony is contracted; consult them. From this alone gather how ancient is this strict formula of expression familiar among the scholastics.]

As he proceeded with this assertion, he very frequently exhorted all to come to a true knowledge of the matter by divine judgment, [Col. 1461A] demonstrated in his own life or death. [Note: [Col. 1461B] Namely, the judgment by fire, to which it was then permissible to appeal. In the preceding century the same ordeal had been appointed in Florence by Saint John Gualbert, who ordered his Vallumbrosan monk Peter—later cardinal and bishop of Albano—to pass through fire, so that Peter, bishop of Florence, might be publicly proved guilty of simony. This happened as was desired: the monk passed harmlessly through the flames and consequently acquired the name “the Fiery One,” as Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, and Berthold, contemporary writers at the year 1089, relate; so also Baronius at 1063, Puricelli in *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 296, and others. This form of judgment was subsequently abolished, since God seemed to be tested beyond what was proper; severe censures were imposed by the Church, collected by Cardinal Lauraea in the *Epitome of Sacred Canons* and explained by Pallavicino under “Purgation” in the *Polyanthaea*.]

But Grossulanus’s party obstructed this through the authority of the bishops who had come to Milan to hold the synod with Grossulanus. Nevertheless, the priest disputed against the bishops, sustained his position by arguments and examples, and did not yield. Grossulanus, however, disregarding the priest’s words as though they had not been uttered in his presence, conducted his synod in the church of Saint Mary called Winter Saint Mary for two days, [Note: [Col. 1461B] That this synod was held in Lent of the year 1103 can scarcely be doubted. For Landulf said above that, as the time of this synod approached, Grossulanus customarily delivered a sermon on every authentic night; and since Liprand’s ordeal by fire took place in the holier week after the council had been held, it is plainly evident that the synod was conducted within the Lenten days, indeed as they approached their end.] and on the third day, in the meadow called Brorium, [Note: [Col. 1461C] Read *Brolium*. Galvaneus Flamma, in the *Chronicle Major*, chaps. 68 and 73, says that a *brolium* was an orchard planted with trees so thickly that it resembled a wood. It lay in the part of the city between the two distinguished Milanese basilicas of Saint Nazarius and Saint Stephen; its name still survives in “Brolio.” Yet this place could not have been suitable for holding a synod unless, perhaps, the trees had then been cut down and an open area made. The same Flamma describes another Brolium in the manuscript *Manipulus Florum*, fol. 28, as follows: “Outside the city walls was the Great Brolium, [Col. 1461D] where young men gathered in arms and in various combats for the sake of exercise.” Certainly gardens called Brolium existed in the twelfth century, in which Frederick Barbarossa planted military standards when he moved his camp against our city, as Calchus records at the year 1158. From Otho Morena at the same year we learn that the church of Saint Babylas stood at the head of this Brolium. Perhaps this was the very meadow of Brolium of which our Landulf speaks.] before an innumerable multitude, pronounced sentence deposing Andrew the primicerius and other priests whom Anselm of Rode, archbishop of Milan, [Col. 1462A] ordained after they had been invested by King Henry, [Note: [Col. 1461D] Another manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, more in accordance, I think, with the author’s meaning—as is indicated by the particle *et* (“and”)—reads *investitus* (“having been invested”). And indeed Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book IX, at the year 1084, reports that Anselm, while Henry the emperor stubbornly defended ecclesiastical investitures, was elected archbishop of Milan and was therefore rejected by Pope Gregory VII.

Pagius, however, refutes Sigonius on this point of manifest error in his critique at 1085. Since Gregory VII died in that same year, indeed on the very day on which Tedaldus, archbishop of Milan, died, he could not have rejected the election of Anselm as successor. It is beyond doubt, from Berthold, a contemporary writer, that Tedaldus died not in 1084, as Sigonius had believed, but in the following year. Pagius denies that this Anselm was truly the Milanese prelate invested by Henry, relying among other things on Berthold’s authority. After recounting Tedaldus’s death, he says Berthold wrote:

“Once the most powerful invader of the Milanese Church had been removed from the midst, it began to raise its head, and, having shaken from its neck the yoke of the schismatics, it chose for itself as Catholic bishop Anselm, the third of that name.”

Yet that most learned man was mistaken. In Berthold, whom I have examined carefully, nothing is read about this election of Anselm; the quoted words are not Berthold’s but Baronio’s, under this year 1085. Thus Pagius’s principal foundation collapses. The remaining arguments with which Pagius strives to establish his opinion from the same Berthold do not prove the matter at all. For what that author relates concerning the conspiracy of Milan and certain other Lombard cities against Henry, decreed for twenty years, and concerning Anselm’s zealous devotion to Saint Peter’s cause, pertains to 1093, the final year of Anselm’s life, not to the first year, when he was elected archbishop.

Accordingly, we ought not depart from the authority of our Landulf, who expressly says that Anselm was invested by Henry—especially since Papebroch agrees with us in the cited exegesis, no. 101. Although he too wrongly believed that the words quoted above were genuinely found in Berthold, he nevertheless does not depart at all from his opinion that Anselm’s election should be attributed to the authority of Henry, the schismatic emperor: “Granted,” he continues, “that Anselm detested the schism, as soon as Victor III, [Col. 1462D] or Urban II, who succeeded Victor’s brief pontificate and followed Gregory’s course against the schismatics, had been recognized as pope, he took care to be reconciled with the Church.”] had ordained.

This sentence was immediately rejected by the multitude of clergy and people, and not long afterward by Paschal, pope of Rome. [Note: [Col. 1462D] That this sentence of deposition became invalid and void is proved by Andrew’s public exercise of his authority as primicerius, as we shall see in the course of the history. Nothing is reported by the authors concerning a decree of Pope Paschal; nevertheless, it may clearly be inferred from this passage that Andrew and the other deposed priests appealed to the supreme pontiff.]

## CHAPTER X. The priest Liprand passed through fire unharmed.

Nevertheless, while Grossulanus’s party was fighting against the primicerius, it killed with a stone Landulf, clerk of that primicerius. Then, as though by consent of the entire city, the priest was told to gather much wood for conducting the ordeal in the meadow enclosed by a wall beside the monastery of Saint Ambrose.

The priest himself, full of great Spirit, distributed to the poor the food and wine which he had for eating, and pawned his lynx-skin [Note: [Col. 1462D] CHAP. X.—A. 2 reads: *lupitunicam* (“wolf-tunic”).] [Note: [Col. 1462D] The Latin word *lynx*, or rather the Greek word. This foreign animal is so called; its hide, dotted with spots of various colours, is still valuable. Aldrovandus writes that it is popularly called *lupus cervarius* (“deer-wolf”) and treats of it at length.] for wood. He directed that the rest of what he possessed [Col. 1463A] in books and other things should be preserved for Landulf, his nephew [Note: [Col. 1463C] The writer of these things.] and foster-son, and acolyte of the Church, who at that time was studying at Orléans under the distinguished master Alfred and the noble Jacob. [Note: [Col. 1463C] From this Pagius infers the antiquity and renown of studies at Orléans.]

He also ordered that, should he die in that ordeal, whatever remained of his body should be carried to the church of the Holy Trinity, which, as is read above in the privilege, he had founded on his own allodial land and transferred to Blessed Peter. These arrangements and directions having been made, the same . . . went to the church of Ambrose; and when he was about to undertake the ordeal . . . Grossulanus’s force prevailed, scattered the wood arranged in the meadow, and shamefully removed the priest himself from that preparation.

Thereafter the priest remained silent and inactive in his house and in the church of Saint Paul, until shortly afterward boys and girls, men and [Col. 1463B] women cried out: “Out, out, Grossulanus!” Wishing to suppress this outcry, Grossulanus took counsel with his retainers and said to them:

“Go yourselves and publicly choose men from the people to tell Liprand either to come and make satisfaction to me, or to leave this land, or to perform the ordeal which he promised to perform.”

Therefore, on the evening of Palm Sunday, or Olive Sunday, [Note: [Col. 1463D] 22 March, the date on which this Sunday fell in the year 1103.] his councillors came from his side to the public assembly and announced what they had heard from their lord, Archbishop Grossulanus. Consequently, not only did men selected in the assembly come to deliver this message to the priest, but an innumerable multitude came to confirm it.

At their cry, [Col. 1463C] crying, “Let the priest Liprand himself come,” he came out humbly. When he heard and understood the message, he raised his hands to heaven and gave thanks to God. Questioning the messengers, he said: “Does he himself wish and command what you tell me?” All replied: “Indeed he wishes and commands it.” The priest said to them:

“I shall not leave the land; but during these two days I shall fast, and on Wednesday [Note: [Col. 1463D] Namely, in Holy Week. But Puricelli was wholly mistaken as to the year in which it fell. In *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 295, he advanced the opinion that this ordeal by fire must be assigned, by a conclusion certain and evident, as he called it, to 1101. Later, in book IV of the *Life of Saint Arialdus*, chap. 88, having improved his view, he considered it assignable to the following year, 1102. Yet it is clear from what has been said above that it did not occur in that year either. Since we have shown that Grossulanus received the Milanese mitre through the acclamation of people and nobles in August of that year, who does not see that Liprand’s unharmed passage through fire, performed in the final week of Lent, can be assigned only to the third year of the same twelfth century?

The typographical error which slipped into Papebroch’s often-praised exegesis, no. 104, must therefore be corrected: under the same year 1102 it places both Liprand’s ordeal and Grossulanus’s election, although the latter is said to have occurred in the aforementioned month of August. Puricelli could moreover have learned this securely from Galvaneus Flamma’s *Chronicle Major* and from the other manuscript, *Flower of Flowers*, cited by him, in which these words occur: “In the year 1103, according to the chronicle of Gotofredus of Bussero, the ordeal by fire of the priest Aliprand of the church of Saint Paul at the Crossroads took place.” Gotofredus of Bussero, whose manuscript work *Lives of the Saints* exists in the library of the metropolitan chapter, lived near that century. For fuller arguments on this matter see Pagius, *Critique*, at this very year 1103, no. 6.] I shall perform the ordeal, God granting it. But I have nothing with which to buy wood.”

Then the officials of Grossulanus and of the state bought thirty [Col. 1464A] solidi worth of oak wood, highly suitable for flame and heat. They arranged it in the field before the forecourt of the church of Saint Ambrose in two piles facing one another. Each pile was ten cubits long and four cubits in both height and width, exceeding a man’s stature; the path between the two piles was one and a half cubits wide.

When this had been arranged, with certain pieces of wood placed in the path between them, on Wednesday [Note: [Col. 1464D] 25 March.] the priest, dressed in haircloth, a shirt, and a chasuble, carried a cross barefoot, in priestly fashion, from the church of Saint Paul to the church of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius and of the most blessed Ambrose. Upon the altar of those saints, since the other priests failed him, he himself sang Mass for himself. [Note: [Col. 1464D] Edmund Martène, vol. III, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, p. 458 in my edition, reports that it was customary for Mass to be sung before an ordeal by fire.]

After Mass had been sung, Grossulanus also entered the same church carrying a cross, [Col. 1464B] and ascended the pulpit with Arialdus of Meregnano and Berard, judge of Asti. Silence having been made among the people, and the priest standing barefoot upon the marble stone at the entrance of the choir which bears an image of Hercules, [Note: [Col. 1464D] Puricelli discusses this image at greater length in *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 297, and in the *Life of Saint Herlembald*, chap. 88. Yet I have already refuted in the Appendix to the *Defence of the Bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius*, no. 35, what is said there of the counts of Angleria and of the ancient coat of arms of the Visconti.] Grossulanus said to the people:

“Take heed: in three words I shall defeat this man and expose his disgrace.”

Then he said to the priest: “You have alleged that I am a simoniac by payment from the hand. Now say: to whom did I give?” The priest then opened his eyes over the people and extended his finger toward the three men standing in the pulpit, saying:

“See the three greatest devils, who by their cunning and their money think to confound me. And can that devil who persuaded him to become a simoniac through money not persuade him still to give even greater money, conceal the truth, and take from me witnesses and earthly judges? Do you not know that, to avoid the cunning of the devil and of wicked men, I chose God as judge, who can be deceived in judgment neither by money nor in any other way? If you wish to come to his judgment, I am prepared to do what I promised.”

Grossulanus said to him: “Now say what simony you mean.” The priest replied: “You now say which kind is good.” Grossulanus sprang up somewhat and said: “There is a simony which does not depose a simoniac.” [Col. 1465A]

The priest said: “I mean that which deposes an abbot from his abbacy, a bishop from his bishopric, and an archbishop from the archbishopric which he holds.”

When by these words he had satisfied everyone, he heard the people crying: “Go out to the ordeal! Go out to the ordeal!” In this repeated cry the priest, though old, leapt down from the stone bearing Hercules’ image and came with the people into the field where the piles of wood stood.

There, while the wood was being kindled, the priest said to those standing around:

“You see no priest besides me to bless this fire for me, [Note: [Col. 1465D] The aforementioned Martène teaches that this too was customarily observed in such ordeals by fire.] but you see this sheet which I hold, containing holy words and the signs of the holy cross. I, a minister, shall say and make these words and signs below; [Col. 1465B] and God, who is my Lord, shall bless the fire from above.”

Those hearing and understanding well said: “Amen.” When he had said these words and made the signs around the fire, and had sprinkled holy water and incense over the fire, Grossulanus standing there, he hesitated about arranging the oath with Grossulanus and Arialdus of Meregnano, who was, as it were, Grossulanus’s most powerful prince and the manager of the ordeal. Arialdus expected the priest to perish by fire upon the mound, or, through excessive terror, to turn to his lord Grossulanus. For he—[Note: [Col. 1465D] Namely Grossulanus.]—had said to Berard, judge of Asti, that this proceeding should condemn the priest not merely if he died, but also for any burn inflicted upon him.

“Far be it that there should be only an injury; [Note: [Col. 1465D] The meaning seems to be that Judge Berard did not intend merely that Liprand’s skin should be lightly touched by that huge mass of fire which he was planning to kindle, but boldly promised himself that Liprand would be utterly consumed.] rather, I shall make the fire so great [Col. 1465C] that from afar the fire shall tear his eyes out of his head, and burning ashes shall rot in the fire itself!”

Nevertheless, when the priest saw them hesitating about arranging the oath, [Note: [Col. 1465D] That is, the formula of the oath.] he said to them: “Allow me; I shall arrange it properly, and I shall not finish the oath until I have said only as much as will satisfy you.”

Immediately, with their agreement, he seized Grossulanus’s cloak and shook it, saying:

“This Grossulanus, who is under this cloak—and I speak of no other—is a simoniac in respect of the archbishopric of Milan: by payment from the hand, by payment from the tongue, and by payment from service.”

When this appeared sufficient to them, he added:

“And I do not enter this ordeal in reliance upon sorcery, incantation, or charm; so may God and these holy Gospels aid me in this holy [Col. 1465D] judgment.”

Once this oath had been made, Grossulanus at once [Col. 1466A] mounted a horse and went to the church of Saint John called *ad Concam*. [Note: [Col. 1465D] This church, situated in our city on the Roman road, still bears this name, although in antiquity it was called the cemetery of pilgrims.]

The aforementioned Arialdus of Meregnano, searching for and awaiting the full force of the fire, held the priest back; while holding him, he felt his own hand injured far from the heat of the fire. Yet he said to the priest:

“Priest Liprand, behold your death in the fire. Turn to my lord the archbishop, with your life secured; otherwise go and burn yourself under God’s curse.”

The priest said to him: “Satan, get behind me.”

As he withdrew, the priest rose from the ground where he had prostrated himself, made the sign of the cross upon himself, and the vast flame divided itself to south and north. A path appeared, which the priest entered; passing over the very coals of the fire, he felt as though he were treading sand. [Col. 1466B] While he passed through that path, the flame closed together behind him. And, as he himself told me and as I understood clearly, so long as he was upon the path through that fire he offered this prayer to God:

“O God, save me in thy name, and deliver me in thy power; O God, save me in thy name.”

As he uttered for the third time the word “make,” he found himself outside the fire. He felt no injury either upon himself or upon his linen and silk priestly vestments, with which he was clothed, nor upon his haircloth.

## CHAPTER XI. In a synod before Pope Paschal, Liprand accuses Grossulanus, who was present, of simony and makes known the ordeal by fire.

Then the whole people, as if with one voice, rendered praise to God and to this priest, both outside and within the city. Grossulanus, however, undaunted, abandoned the archiepiscopal see [Col. 1466C] and the city, because it had openly been sworn by the common voice of the city [Note: [Col. 1465D] CHAPTER XI.—In another manuscript of the Ambrosian Library one reads: “by the common voice of the city.”] that no harm should be done in consequence of this action to either of them, or to anyone of their party, except what the Lord himself should do to him. But because the presence of the suffragan bishops [Note: [Col. 1465D] For they had not yet departed from Milan after the synod recently held by Grossulanus; this confirms the date of the holding of this synod, established above [Col. 1466D].] did not give its full support to this law and triumph, because the fire injured the priest’s hand when he threw on the water and incense over the fire, and because the horse of John of Rode [Note: [Col. 1466D] Or the district of Rhaude, eight miles distant from Milan.] harshly trod upon the bare foot of the priest as he came out of the fire, the crowd, saddened by Grossulanus’s fall and ruin, within a few days took offence at the priest and at his law [Note: [Col. 1466D] That is, it departed from the right opinion formerly conceived concerning Liprand’s harmless passage through the fire.]; and, taking offence at the urging of certain priests, it committed many battles and murders.

Meanwhile Grossulanus found Pope Paschal favorable to him [Col. 1466D]. [Note: [Col. 1466D] It has been said above that Grossulanus left Milan immediately after the ordeal by fire had been completed. From this we learn that he then went to Rome; but whether this was in the same year, 1103, or the following year is uncertain. Pagius writes, from what follows, that the latter is to be inferred, under the year 1104; yet no argument seems to me to establish this. Indeed, I judge it more probable that Grossulanus made his way to the supreme pontiff Paschal in that very year, 1103, since nine whole months remained to him after the ordeal by fire had been completed. Thus some intervening interval of delay may be allotted to the repeated journeys to Rome and Milan undertaken by Landulph of Vereglate, which are described below [Col. 1467B]. Add that shortly hereafter Grossulanus is related to have already returned from the city of Rome when Landulph, returning there from the expedition to Jerusalem, arrived. But who could persuade himself that that archbishop, increased by so great an honor and entangled in so many affairs at the Roman curia because of all the cases entrusted to him, hastened away from there so quickly that his journey to Rome, his stay, and his return all occurred in the same year before Landulph arrived there, who afterward also set out for Milan [Col. 1467C]? Everything can therefore be reconciled more conveniently if we say that Grossulanus, who is known to have departed Milan immediately after Liprand’s ordeal, went directly to Rome in 1103; that in the following year Landulph of Vareglate, having learned at Rome of the Milanese dissension, returned to his homeland after Grossulanus had already returned from there; and finally that in 1105 both went together to the Roman synod. As we indicated above, no consideration of historical method compels us to crowd all these events into one year.]

Landulph [Col. 1467A] of Vareglate [Note: [Col. 1467C] One of those whom Grossulanus had forbidden, while absent, to be elected archbishop of Milan.], who had been foremost in the flight at Coritiana [Note: [Col. 1467C] Pagius says concerning these words that he does not remember having read anything, either in William of Tyre, who speaks of the city Coritium in book X, chapter 24, or in any other author, concerning this disaster of the Milanese and Lombards. At the end of the first chapter I have already reported [Col. 1467D] what Orderic Vitalis and Ralph, writers of that age, narrated on this matter. I now produce the Abbot of Ursperg, who places under the year 1101 the Christian army’s departure for Nicomedia and its turn from Romania toward the northern region against the land of Coriziana, the homeland of the Turks; there, he says, the Lombard army was so afflicted by four thousand Turks that some were taken captive and others slain, while the pagans armed themselves on every side against them with missiles and flames.], returned from Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1467D] For he had accompanied Anselm IV, archbishop of Milan, there.] and arrived at Rome. There he learned, from Grossulanus, who had already returned from there, not only what had occurred at Milan because of the dispute between the priest and Grossulanus, but also how solemnly the Roman pontiff, after such events, had received Grossulanus. For Pope Paschal himself placed Grossulanus upon his own seat; and for however many days Grossulanus was then at the Lateran, he caused him to sit upon that same seat, yielding to him as he sat and giving him the place [Note: [Col. 1467D] So great a mark of honor granted to this archbishop of Milan can scarcely gain credence; no other example of it will be found in histories.]. He also entrusted to Grossulanus his own court and all ecclesiastical causes to be determined and judged by himself, for Grossulanus to determine and judge.

Yet that Landulph of Vareglate [Col. 1467B], coming to Milan, did not directly despise either the priest or his law. Rather, promising the clergy and people of Milan that he would depose Grossulanus from every ecclesiastical office according to the rule of the canons, he said: “Why do you contend concerning the law of the priest Liprand and Grossulanus, and make battles and murders among yourselves? Behold, I tell you most certainly, and through John of Vicomercate I command Grossulanus, that before Lord Pope Paschal and his court or synod I shall prove, by sure reasons and just and holy canons, that he cannot stand among the number either of bishops or of priests, or indeed in any clerical order.”

The clergy and people, trusting this authoritative man [Note: [Col. 1467D] That is, a man of the highest authority.], and, in consequence of a certain novelty [Note: [Col. 1467D] Mabillon reports in the *Annals of the Benedictines*, under the year 1102, no. 53, that this Landulph of Vareglate, still flourishing in earliest youth, was sent to Pavia to be trained in piety and letters in the monastery of St. Peter in Cielo d’Oro, and was afterward enrolled there in monastic life [Col. 1468B], professing the rule of St. Benedict. The same is asserted by the aforementioned Philip Malabayla in no. 1 of his *Life*; explaining our author’s text, he says that the “novelty” spoken of here consisted in a monk’s being set over the the canonical body of clergy.], strove to arrive with Grossulanus at the Roman synod [Note: [Col. 1468B] Labbe believed that this synod, in which Grossulanus’s case [Col. 1468C] was considered, was held at Rome by Paschal II in 1103. He therefore included it in the Appendix to volume X of the *Councils*, column 1833, relying on Puricelli, who adduces our Landulph, a contemporary writer. Yet, since I have already shown that the entire chronological sequence in this history has been disturbed by him, and since stricter calculation establishes that Grossulanus was elected only in 1102, the ordeal by fire occurred in the following year, and the controversy over Grossulanus was discussed at Rome two years afterward, the entire foundation of the fictitious synod which Puricelli wrongly devised to support his argument collapses. Moreover, Landulph himself clearly indicates the year to which the true synod is to be assigned. For chapter 22 has: “While Grossulanus’s suit was pending, namely in 1105, on the seventh day before the Ides of May the relics were discovered,” etc. Paschal therefore had not pronounced his judgment restoring Grossulanus to the Milanese see before 9 May of that year. It is consequently certain that the synod of which Landulph speaks here was none other than the Second Lateran Council held by Paschal II in that same year, 1105. So too Pagius, in opposition to Labbe and others who place it in the preceding year, holds under this year, Critiques, no. 4, that it was summoned about 26 March [the seventh day before the Kalends of April].].

Therefore Amigo [Note: [Col. 1468D] A. 1 and 2: “Amizo.”] of Landriano, the stern and wise captain of the Milanese, said: “You wish to bind the otter in water” [Note: [Col. 1468D] That is, to drown it. Puricelli judges in his *Life of Herlembald*, chapter 90, that this was then a common proverbial expression, customarily used when someone wished to employ a means contrary to his wishes to attain an end that he otherwise desired above all else. For the *ludria*, or otter, is an amphibious animal, living by turns in water and on dry land with equal preservation of its life.].

But Grossulanus, delaying nothing [Col. 1468B], threw himself at the apostolic’s feet and again sought refuge for himself and his followers. The priest Liprand, now an old man and two years after the law established by him [Note: [Col. 1468D] For, as we showed in the preceding chapter, he had undergone the public ordeal by fire at the end of March 1103.], came to Rome for the synod, having been challenged and, as it were, compelled. At this synod the aforesaid Landulph of Vareglate, who after [Col. 1469A] that synod became bishop of Asti [Note: [Col. 1469C] Malabayla relates in his *Life* that Landulph was elected by the canons of the cathedral of Asti as bishop of his native city in 1103, under the preceding year, 1102. Ughelli, in his work on the bishops of Asti, followed by Mabillon in the *Annals of the Benedictines* under the same year, says the same. The authority of our writer proves that all these have wrongly dated the beginning of his occupancy of that see, since he says that Landulph was promoted to that dignity only after this Roman synod; consequently he could not have been declared bishop of that Church before 1105.], uttered no dishonoring word against Grossulanus before either the pope, his court, or the synod [Note: [Col. 1469C] In the Appendix concerning the Venerable Priest Liprand, under 27 June, Papebroch says that the reason for this silence was perhaps that Landulph had been corrupted in favor of the case by entreaty or payment. Yet I should regard it as far too injurious to suspect this of a man whose memory is enrolled among the saints. Certainly Malabayla, author of the same *Life*, did not interpret the passage so; he expressly asserts that Landulph stood by his promises, but in such a way that he uttered no dishonoring [Col. 1469D] word against Grossulanus.].

But the priest Liprand plainly stated the case which he had against Grossulanus. The apostolic did not praise the law established by the priest and marked by oath and fire; rather, he confirmed in him the grace and office of the priesthood, and said: “If this priest should swear, and twelve priests should, by swearing with him, affirm that Grossulanus compelled this priest to go to the fire, Grossulanus would undergo deposition.” On this point he granted a space of one night for deliberation.

## CHAPTER XII. Grossulanus, swearing before the pope that he had not compelled Liprand to go to the fire, was restored; but he was not received by the citizens.

[Col. 1469B]

When that night had passed, the apostolic received from Grossulanus, before the synod, an oath, in which Grossulanus said: “I, Grossulanus, by the grace of God archbishop, did not compel the said priest Liprand to go to the fire and undergo the ordeal.” Then Arderic, bishop of Lodi [Note: [Col. 1469D] CHAPTER XII.—Our Landulph testifies in chapter 27 that he was Grossulanus’s vicar and afterward a monk at the Vallombrosan monastery in Piacenza.], likewise confirmed this by oath. Azzo, bishop of Acqui [Note: [Col. 1469D] Ughelli reports that he was transferred to the Church of Vercelli in 1135.], when he came forward to swear the same thing on Grossulanus’s behalf, was excused by the apostolic.

Grossulanus therefore came forward to receive the favor of restoration. When he approached to receive restoration, the *gabuta* [Note: [Col. 1469D] The same as *cabuta* or *cambuta*. Macri and Du Cange state that this word signifies the episcopal staff. Landulph explains one and the same thing with two terms: *gabuta* and *virga* mean the same thing, namely the *gabuta*, or pastoral staff; this is shown still more clearly from chapter 29.], or pastoral staff, which Grossulanus himself held in his hand [Col. 1470A] before the synod, fell to the ground. To very many this sign indicated that his oath was an oath of death. Nevertheless, neither pope nor synod then heeded this; but they restored Grossulanus to Azzo of Acqui, Arderic of Lodi, Jordan of Clivi [Note: [Col. 1469D] More will be said in the course of the narrative about this Jordan, who was afterward elected archbishop by the Milanese against Grossulanus in 1112.], and the other Milanese, clergy and laity alike, indeed also to the suffragan bishops of that Church, who wished to have him as archbishop—though only idly [Note: [Col. 1469D] For even after his restoration the stronger party among the Milanese so opposed him that he was unable not only to enjoy tranquil peace in this see, but even to reach it safely, as is read at the end of this chapter.].

For that priest Liprand, although he might have been suspect because of this restoration, nevertheless, after Grossulanus had been restored and after those receiving the restored man, continued as a priest fit for his office at the church of St. Paul and in his own house for seven years after that restoration. Grossulanus, however, through the favor of Abbot William [Col. 1470B] of the monastery of St. Ambrose, Andrew, primicerius of the Church of Milan, Otto the viscount [Note: [Col. 1470C] This man is not mentioned in another manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, nor in the copy used by Puricelli. Moreover, our writers Corio, Merula, and others—followed by Sigonius in book IX of *On the Kingdom of Italy*—relate many things of this Otto down to a miracle of exalted valor. Especially famous among them is the story that, while he was engaged in the siege of Jerusalem as commander of the Milanese army, he overcame in single combat a certain barbarian named Voluce, towering above the rest in bodily stature and terrible to all through his arms and strength; that his spoils included a serpent emblem taken from his helmet; and that this afterward became the banner of the Milanese legions and the hereditary device of his family, an imperishable memorial of so illustrious a deed. Calco, however, was not so credulous. In books III and VII of his *History of His Country*, he accuses the writers who handed down these things of vanity and falsehood, pursuing the favor of a most noble family rather than historical truth [Col. 1470D]. The silence of contemporaries greatly weakens the credibility of this account. Who could believe that so remarkable a proof of courage could have been neglected by everyone, so that even the history of our fellow citizen Landulph, who reports that expedition and in chapter 18 tells with the highest praise of this Otto’s death, should be altogether silent about it? More absurd is what is read in the catalogue of Milanese archbishops entitled *Successors of St. Barnabas*: namely, that this Otto the viscount took the cross and was sent to Jerusalem with seven thousand soldiers by Arnulf III, our bishop. No trace of so hasty an expedition exists in the histories.], and many other prudent clergy and laymen, possessed neither the see nor any stronghold of the archbishopric after the law first [Note: [Col. 1470D] A. 1: “first.”] enacted by the priest, nor after the restoration carried out by the synod.

## CHAPTER XIII. Disturbance arising in the Milanese Church over Grossulanus: Olric the vicedominus and Anselm of Pusterla transfer themselves to Paris for study.

That Church and kingdom also [Note: [Col. 1470D] CHAPTER XIII.—That is, clergy and laity who were acting with opposed zeal in Grossulanus’s case.], which conducted that synod for Grossulanus, maintained dissension within itself [Note: [Col. 1470D] A. 1: “defence.”]; and, maintaining it, who can [Col. 1471A] recount the burnings, desolations, and abominations that burned and devastated Milan and the kingdom, and the priesthood itself, at the time when the law of the priest Liprand came into doubt [Note: [Col. 1471B] Because of the injury to his hand before entering the fire, mentioned above, and to his foot after passing through it.]? For, to pass over the burnings which disturbed and still disturb Milan, I remember the counsel of the princes, which then prompted Henry to call his father Henry king and emperor, his lord [Note: [Col. 1471C] Another reading in the Ambrosian Library manuscript, more consonant with the sense of this text, has “to depose.” This Henry rose in rebellion against his father in the Norican regions in 1105, on the advice of Margrave Theobald and Count Berengar, under the pretext of religion, because his father had been excommunicated by the Roman pontiffs, as Otto of Freising writes, book VII, chapter 8. The chronicler of Hildesheim and the Abbot of Ursperg, whom Baronius follows, narrate at length the events of this war. Landulph laments a manifestation of this tragedy then active in Milan, where the clergy, divided into factions no less than the people, armed itself against itself like opposing fraternal battle-lines.] Henry, his father, king and emperor, his lord. He indeed, abhorring simony in his father, overthrew his father [Note: [Col. 1471C] Henry IV, stripped of the empire by his son, ended his days miserably at Liège in August 1106, as Domnizo in the *Life of Matilda*, Orderic Vitalis, and many others testify.].

During this conflict a splendid star called a comet [Note: [Col. 1471C] Concerning this, Orderic himself, book V, p. 589, says: “In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, at the end of February, a comet sending forth a very long tail appeared in the western regions” [Col. 1471D]. The Saxon annalist in Eckhard, vol. I of the *Writers of the Middle Ages*, fol. 611, reports that it endured from the first week of Lent until the Passion of the Lord.] shone broadly and brilliantly for many days and nights in springtime from the north and, as it were, in the west; it foretold the death of the overthrown Henry. I also, as tribulations increased in this royal and priestly storm [Col. 1471B; Note: [Col. 1471D] Or rather: “as tribulations increased.”], often avoided, with due reverence to him, the company of my often-mentioned uncle the priest because of the reproaches [Note: [Col. 1471D] A. 2 adds: “and are made.”] made against me through fear [Note: [Col. 1471D] The reading of another manuscript of the Ambrosian Library has “hatred,” namely the hatred which the party favoring Grossulanus had conceived against Liprand.]. I attached myself to Anselm of Pusterla [Note: [Col. 1471D] He was afterward elected archbishop of Milan, as was Olric, mentioned immediately here, as we shall see in its place.] and Olric, vicedominus of Milan [Note: [Col. 1471D] A very well-known name of an office and dignity.], to both of whom I was, as is evident, useful and loyal at home and abroad. With Anselm, indeed, I read for a year and a half at Tours and in the Parisian schools under Master Alfred and William [Note: [Col. 1471D] Namely William of Champeaux, so called from the town of Champeaux in Brie, where he was born. He was a man of great renown, archdeacon of the Church of Paris, and publicly taught dialectic there. He afterward entered the order of regular canons and, having returned home, was appointed bishop [Col. 1472B] of Châlons in 1113; he died in 1121. See Mabillon, vol. V of the *Annals of the Benedictines* [Col. 1472C]; Pagius under 1121; *Gallia Christiana*, under the bishops of Châlons; and others.]; by reading, writing, and many other means I rendered Anselm much service.

## CHAPTER XIV. The present historian brings the priest Liprand back to Milan from Valtellina.

[Col. 1472A]

My often-mentioned uncle, within the space of this year and a half, left the people who were disputing about his law and Grossulanus’s restoration not out of love for the divine law and ecclesiastical custom, departed their city, and lived in the valley of Valtellina, more than seventy miles from Milan [Note: [Col. 1472C] CHAPTER XIV.—It is called Valtellina from Tilio, a town that is the chief place of that region. The very learned Peter Angelo Lavizzari, joined to me by the closest affection, has set forth the ancient and modern history of this most celebrated valley in ten books written in Italian and published at Chur, the city of Raetia, in 1716.].

Then I, withdrawn from my studies [Note: [Col. 1472C] The studies at Tours and Paris to which he had applied himself, as was said just above.], found the church of St. Paul and my own house almost deserted of this my patron. Therefore, taking Anselm’s horse [Note: [Col. 1472C] Namely Anselm of Pusterla, his companion in studies in Gaul.] and my own, I hastened with my brother to my patron. When I had traveled twenty-five miles, an angel met me, saying: “The priest [Col. 1472B] Liprand, returning from Valtellina, lies sick at the monastery of Clivate” [Note: [Col. 1472C] We learn from Calco the great antiquity of this monastery. Speaking under the year of Christ 755 of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards, elevated to the Italian throne after Aistulf’s death, he relates this among that ruler’s first deeds: “He founded and richly endowed the monastery at Clivate, in the district of Incinate, in honor of St. Peter the Apostle.” Corio, first part, describes the reason Desiderius undertook this pious work [Col. 1472D]. He says that his son Algisius, while pursuing a boar there with a hunting spear, was struck by sudden blindness, and thereafter was restored to sight by the aid of St. Peter the Apostle, in fulfillment of a vow his father had made to that saint. He also records that distinguished relics of Saints Peter and Marcellinus, sent to him as a gift from Pope Adrian, were placed in that church.].

More quickly than I had hoped, I found him sitting in bed and eating milk. When he saw me [Note: [Col. 1472D] A. 1: “saw.”], he raised both hands and gave thanks to God. Ariald, abbot of that monastery [Note: [Col. 1472D] Landulph narrates in chapter 5 that Ariald, abbot of St. Dionysius, strongly favored Grossulanus and, in reward for the zeal with which he furthered his promotion to the archiepiscopal see, was given a richer abbey. We may therefore easily believe that he is the same Ariald mentioned there.], after hearing that I had arrived and given consolation to the sick man, called my brother and me outside the chamber. In many words he made known to us that he feared for the fidelity which he had sworn to Grossulanus [Note: [Col. 1472D] That is, he made it known.], and, without the monks’ knowledge, warned us to carry the sick man at least two miles away from the monastery.

But when the sick man perceived that my brother and I were anxious about his illness [Col. 1473A] and removal, he said: “Do not be troubled, for through God’s grace I am now much better; and tomorrow, God permitting, we shall travel to the city.” When morning came, he put on certain of his rough garments [Note: [Col. 1473B] The copy used by Puricelli has *ocrudatas*. I believe these words signify nothing other than the rude and harsh clothes that, in the customary manner of holy men, he used for contempt of the world and mortification of the body.], took food, and, as though he had recovered, sat upon a mule. His servant also had his ass loaded with *stambucine* skins [Note: [Col. 1473B] This word is perhaps corrupt, since an animal of that name is wholly unknown. I judge them to have been goatskins. In the Salic Law, title 5, the he-goat is called *buccus*, as Lindenbrog notes in his glossary [Col. 1473C]. Perhaps the skins had also been recently stripped off and were therefore called *stambucinae* because they remained supplied with their fibre or hair.]. Although the servant was normally seized by the falling sickness two or three times a day, yet, while the priest sat on the mule, that same servant came with us in one day as far as St. Damian of Baraza [Note: [Col. 1473C] In the charter of Charles the Fat to be mentioned below are these words: “and likewise as a gift at Baraza, one church called St. Damian with all its appurtenances,” etc. From several documents preserved in the archive of the monastery of St. Ambrose in Milan, to which these things were granted, it is gathered that this village lay not far from Monza.] without any hindrance from that illness [Note: [Col. 1473C] This is a second proof of Liprand’s holiness, which God often attested by miracles, as Puricelli observed in *The Life of St. Ariald*, book IV, chapter 82.].

There, through the grace of God and of most blessed Ambrose, whose cell this place is [Note: [Col. 1473C] Du Cange reports that in later centuries this term designated a community of monks and was also frequently used by authors for small monasteries, formerly called little abbeys or obediences. We can understand from the aforementioned documents of the monastery of St. Ambrose Major at Milan what monastic order occupied this cell [Col. 1473D]: they state that the place was under that monastery’s jurisdiction from the year 881, when Charles the Fat’s diploma was granted, in Puricelli, *Monuments of the Basilica of Ambrose*, no. 131. Therefore any monks then there are to be supposed to have belonged to the same Cluniac observance.], we were received twice [Note: [Col. 1473D] A. 1 and 2: “well.”], spent the night, and passed half the next day. Before sunset we entered the church of St. Paul [Note: [Col. 1473D] Namely at the crossroads of Milan.] and our house [Col. 1473B], and made the household that was there rejoice.

## CHAPTER XV. The historian Landulph separates himself from the priest Liprand.

We perceived very strongly that the Grossulanists and the pretended, deceitful men on the other side murmured about our return. But [Col. 1474A] I, so that I might fear their murmurs less and less and might more fully vindicate and establish my own cause and that of my master, bought a house among my relatives and neighbors, not to remain idle there. For while living in it, I have been a reader, scribe, instructor of boys, participant in public offices [Note: [Col. 1473D] CHAPTER XV.—These were perhaps what were called the common annual distributions, to which not only those of the seventy-two but also the remaining clergy were admitted, each receiving his allotted distributions from the distributor, as is read in Puricelli, *Dissertation on Nazarius*, chapter 112.] and benefices [Note: [Col. 1473D] We have indicated above what is to be understood here by the name “benefice,” chapter 2, no. 6, where it is reported that Anselm the archbishop, departing for Jerusalem, decreed [Col. 1474B] that no benefice should be given from the revenues of the archbishopric to priests, levites, and clerics, such as they were accustomed to receive through the celebration of feast-days.], and composer of the consuls’ letters [Note: [Col. 1474B] Perhaps he supervised scribes who either drafted replies and letters of the consuls relating to the government of the city according to his formulas [Col. 1474C], or entered them in the public records.]. Yet, without prejudice to my claim [Note: [Col. 1474C] For he had not renounced his right, although he had left the companionship of his uncle Liprand and the church to which his title was attached.], I seem to be of little account in the church and in the city of Milan itself [Note: [Col. 1474C] That is, I am held in contempt.]. For the sons of those who killed Herlembald because of the Pataria, and mutilated the priest Liprand’s nose and ears [Note: [Col. 1474C] He recounts in chapter 44 their genealogy, namely those hostile to Herlembald and Liprand.], drive me from the church of St. Paul, which belongs to the titles of my orders; and because I do not despise the freedom and pious way of life found in that priest, I have become as a reproach to them. Although I oppose them, they possess and sell things that are my own legal property [Col. 1474B]. Yet this is not part of the purpose of my little work.

## CHAPTER XVI. While Grossulanus is in exile, the Milanese begin war with the people of Lodi.

Therefore, about the time when the priest Liprand returned from Valtellina [Note: [Col. 1474C] CHAPTER XVI.—From this we can readily infer in what year Liprand went there. Since Landulph says that the Lodi war lasted four years, and since the histories establish that it ended in June 1111, when that city was utterly destroyed by the Milanese, it is clear that his journey into Valtellina must be assigned to 1106 if, after remaining there for a year or even longer, as chapter 14 suggests, he was to return at the beginning of the war declared against the people of Lodi. This war certainly cannot be assigned earlier than 1107, as Sigonius also relates under that year in book X of *On the Kingdom of Italy* [Col. 1474D]. Puricelli therefore erred greatly in thinking, in *Monuments of the Basilica of Ambrose*, no. 295, that Liprand withdrew to that valley after Henry V had received the crown at Milan from Grossulanus—which is also false—and afterward at Rome from Paschal II. This happened in 1111, as we shall see below. The error was caused by the seven years during which Liprand, after the favorable judgment for Grossulanus pronounced in the Roman synod, chapter 12, is said to have held undisturbed possession of his house and the church of St. Paul. Puricelli supposed that he fled the city only after those years had elapsed. But Pagius too, under 1105, no. 7, observed that Puricelli misunderstood our author. Landulph does not say that Liprand remained immovably at Milan, but only that throughout that period no one prevented him from carrying out the duties of his office as a fit priest.], part of the clergy and people of Lodi, fearing perjury in their bishop [Note: [Col. 1474D] Namely Arderic.], who had sworn for Grossulanus at the Roman synod, held that bishop himself suspect. Hence it is also said that Gairard [Note: [Col. 1475B] A. 1: “Gajardus.”], brother of the same bishop of Lodi, and Arderic the bishop himself were supporters and helpers of the Lodi soldiers who delivered their own city over to destruction. While the Milanese were openly striving for the destruction of that city, the two brothers gave counsel and aid both spiritual and temporal [Note: [Col. 1475B] John Mostus, or Cadamostus, writes in the manuscript *Chronicle of Lodi* kept in the Ambrosian Library that the city of Lodi was captured and destroyed through the treachery of its citizens [Col. 1475C]. Yet he names other authors of this crime against their homeland.].

I do not enumerate the countless evils committed during the four years of that war [Note: [Col. 1475C] Tristano Calco, relating under the year 1111 the final calamity of the city of Lodi, razed to the ground by the implacable wrath of the Milanese, admits that he leaves the reader hungry, perhaps desiring a fuller narrative of this overthrow. He says, however, that this was because even after more diligent inquiry fuller materials did not come into his hands. In later centuries the historical memorials of that city were collected by Defendente da Lodi and Giovanni Battista Villanova; in them one finds at length both the occasion of this war and the remaining sequence of events that occurred in these times.], but I mourn the death of Anselm my brother, of many other relatives of mine, and of citizens made manifest through that war; nevertheless, I do not wholly abandon the journey I have begun. For while the city of Lodi still stood and resisted [Col. 1475B] the Milanese who were attempting to destroy it [Note: [Col. 1475C] Antonio Campi, *History of Cremona*, book I, and Sigonius under this year write that in 1109, after the Cremonese and their Lodi allies had been driven from the siege of Brescia, the enraged Brescian people joined the Milanese to avenge the injury, attacked the unprepared city of Lodi, and easily brought it under their power [Col. 1475D]. Yet, they say, this attempt was made unsuccessfully. Warned of Lodi’s loss, the Cremonese immediately flew to the scene with increased forces, recovered the city, and restored it to their allies. Therefore the events that Landulph narrates here and in the following chapter seem to belong to this year.], Grossulanus was exiled from Milan [Note: [Col. 1475D] That is, he was prevented from mounting the archiepiscopal see by the opposing faction of clergy and citizens, whom Grossulanus found constantly resisting him, as Landulph reported at the end of chapter 12.]. That Arderic of Lodi entered his own city only very rarely, but frequented Milan. The priest Liprand, however, devoutly awaited in his house and church of St. Paul the consolation of kingdom and Church.

## CHAPTER XVII. Olric and Anselm, recalled from study, are promoted to orders.

But certain men, who were called friends of the priest who was waiting and of the exiled Grossulanus, while the aforesaid [Col. 1476A] war was being waged between the Milanese and the people of Lodi, with the Pavians and Cremonese also defending the city of Lodi, urged Olricus, vicecomes of Milan, and Anselm surnamed of Pusterla, to go to the eminent master Anselm of the Mount of Laon. [Note: [Col. 1475D] CHAPTER XVII.—The name of this Anselm is famous in histories. For, as dean of Laon, he taught theology publicly at Paris and Laon for more than forty years; distinguished also by his writings and excellent pupils, he died in 1117, according to Pagius, with whom see many further testimonies written in his praise.] It pleased these two to take with them myself, Landulph, foster-child of the priest Liprandus.

And while we were studying with that master and his brother Rodulph [Note: [Col. 1476B] These German brothers, masters at Laon, are mentioned by Otto of Freising, *Deeds of the Emperor Frederick I*, book I, chapter 50.], word was reported there [Note: [Col. 1476C] A. 1 and 2: “to them.”] that Grossulanus held the very strongly fortified castle of Arona, belonging to the archbishopric. [Note: [Col. 1476C] Concerning this fortress, overlooking the shore of Lake Verbano, and many other castles and districts which formerly made up the extensive patrimony of the archbishopric of Milan, I have set forth some observations in the Appendix to the *Vindications of the Bodies of Saints Protasius and Gervasius*, nos. 28 ff.] When he heard this, the vicecomes was greatly enraged, because they said that this second [Note: [Col. 1476C] That is, favourable.] turn of events had befallen Grossulanus because of his absence. Therefore, as is said, they hurried back to Milan [Note: [Col. 1476C] A. 2: “he hurried.”], and the vicecomes found that castle and the other possessions belonging to the archbishopric free from the right and power of Grossulanus.

Those who were called friends on both sides [Note: [Col. 1476C] Understand: on both sides of the dispute.], at whose urging he had gone to Laon, on this return—by I know not what spirit—elected this young man, the vicecomes who was still below the order [Note: [Col. 1476C] For he had not yet been initiated into any order, nor enrolled in the order of canons of the metropolitan church.], as archpriest. After this election, those who were more on Grossulanus’s side advised Grossulanus neither to approve nor condemn the election, but to seek Jerusalem and make Ardericus, bishop of Lodi, his vicar in the Church of Milan.

In this manifest disposition [Note: [Col. 1476C] In the copy used by Puricelli, the reading is *depositione* (“deposition”); hence Pagius, under the year 1110, no. 2, thought that Grossulanus’s pilgrimage was regarded as an abdication—that is, that, through the journey which he undertook to the Holy Land, Grossulanus had in a sense abdicated and relinquished the archiepiscopal mitre. But since *dispositione* is expressly read also in two manuscript codices preserved in the Ambrosian Library, I believe that this reading must be maintained. Nothing else seems to be indicated by this text than that Grossulanus, heeding the advice given him to seek Jerusalem, showed himself openly disposed or prepared for that journey.]—and for other reasons not known to many [Note: [Col. 1476D] One might conjecture here that the reason, not known to many, for Grossulanus’s departure for the East was an embassy to Alexius Comnenus, emperor at Constantinople, which Baronius, under the year 1116, and Ripamontius at the beginning of Decade II of his *Ecclesiastical History of Milan*, report as having been entrusted to him by Paschal II. Certainly it is beyond doubt that he disputed before that same Alexius against Greeks who held erroneous views concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit; for Baronius, already cited, included in his *Annals* Grossulanus’s address before the emperor, translated from Greek into Latin. But whether he was truly sent there by Paschal, or merely took advantage of the occasion of his Jerusalem journey to argue on his own initiative [Col. 1477B] against the Greeks, remains altogether uncertain, since ancient histories provide no secure foundation for such an embassy, while our Landulph expressly affirms only that Grossulanus crossed over to Jerusalem at the persuasion of his friends—as Puricelli likewise observed in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 326. Pagius, under the year 1116, no. 5, calls this embassy plainly fictitious.]—[Col. 1477A] Grossulanus began his journey to Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 1477B] Puricelli, inconsistent with himself, assigned this pilgrimage in the cited *Monuments*, no. 308, to 1109, but in book IV of the *Life of St Arialdus*, chapter 90, moved it to 1111. Pagius shows that neither is true, establishing that it must be assigned to 1110. For immediately after Grossulanus’s departure, in April, Olricus and four canons of the metropolitan church received sacred orders at Milan—or rather, at Genoa—on the Ember Days of Pentecost, which that year fell at the beginning of June, as Landulph says.]

This elected vicecomes, following the counsel of Ardericus of Carimate, who had been especially active in electing him archpriest, began, in the April in which he was elected, to build a canonry. [Note: [Col. 1477B] That is, the canonical residence, perhaps of the metropolitan [Col. 1477C] church, of which he was elected archpriest. Olricus left another notable monument of piety, according to the testimony of Beroldus, which I should consider sacrilegious to pass over in silence. When St Odilo, abbot, in the preceding century, had first introduced into monasteries of the Cluniac observance the praiseworthy custom that the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed should be celebrated on a fixed day, Olricus transferred it to the Ambrosian Church. He fixed it on the Monday after the third Sunday of October and established an annual endowment, by which the whole clergy and the archbishop himself, when present at the divine offices, should receive stipends. This devout custom endured among us even after the Roman Church had adopted the rite and decreed 2 November as the solemn day for the common suffrages offered for souls detained in the fire of purgatory. For in liturgical books of the Ambrosian rite down to 1560 this celebration of funeral prayers is recorded twice: on the day [Col. 1477D] already appointed by Olricus, and on the other day universally received.]

In the following June he went, with certain of his fellow clerics who were *ordinarii*, to Airaldus, bishop of Genoa, to be ordained. Although that bishop was opposed to Grossulanus [Note: [Col. 1477D] From this it is clear that Ughellus is mistaken in stating, in his account of the bishops of Genoa, no. 23, that this Airaldus, or Aycardus, was vicar of the Church of Milan. Our Landulph plainly says that he was opposed to Grossulanus, and it is clear from above that, when Grossulanus departed from Milan, he had appointed Ardericus of Lodi his vicar.], nevertheless, on the recommendation of Ardericus of Carimate—who was held to be the first and greatest deacon [Note: [Col. 1477D] That is, archdeacon.] on Grossulanus’s side—the bishop ordained the vicecomes himself as porter, reader, exorcist, and acolyte. He made Widon Fulcumanus a subdeacon; Anselm of Pusterla and Henry of Birago, levites; and Landulph Caronia, a priest.

These five *ordinarii*, ordained at Genoa in June [Note: [Col. 1477D] Namely on the fourth day of that month, which in 1110 was the Saturday of the fourth Ember Days.], plainly appeared hostile to Grossulanus. At this the Milanese rejoiced, and rejoiced with still greater joy because in that same month they gained a triumph over the defeated Cremonese [Note: [Col. 1477D] Cavitelli, in the *Annals of Cremona*, assigns this defeat inflicted upon the Cremonese by Milanese forces to 1111. But Landulph proves this false, since he says that the Cremonese army was routed before Henry hurried into Italy. [Col. 1478B] Henry arrived here in the preceding year, 1110, as we shall see in the following chapter. Sigonius writes more consistently with historical truth that, before Henry’s arrival, the citizens were defeated in battle, Cremona was taken by the Milanese, and almost destroyed by a shameful fire; nevertheless, he relates this much too early, as though it had occurred in 1109. This much is certain from our author: in the same June in which the five *ordinarii* received sacred orders at Genoa, the Cremonese too were defeated, and Henry’s expedition into Italy immediately followed. From what has been said above and will be said below, all this can only be placed in 1110.] and had overcome them in the field of Brixanorio. [Note: [Col. 1478B] That is, Brixana, in Italian Brezana, a village situated on the bank of the river Ongina near the castle of Busseto, as may be seen in the topographical map of the territory of Cremona made by Antonio Campi.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Emperor Henry captured Pope Paschal and the curia; on the following day, peace having been made, he was solemnly crowned by him.

When this triumph became known throughout the kingdoms, the most valiant King Henry came into Italy with a huge army. [Note: [Col. 1478B] CHAPTER XVIII.—Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 14, reports that Henry had thirty thousand chosen cavalrymen in his camp beside the Po, apart from those who flocked to him from Italy.] [Note: [Col. 1478C] Namely, in 1110, at the beginning of autumn, as Domnizo writes in the *Life of Matilda*. The Hildesheim chronicler, cited by Pagius, testifies that Henry entered Italy about the middle of August and also records that he celebrated Christmas at Florence that year. Puricelli preserves in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 311, a diploma of this Henry issued at Vercelli, 12 October 1110.] At Rome, in the church of St Peter, he stood barefoot before Pope Paschal, awaiting the imperial crown. [Note: [Col. 1478C] He reached the City on 11 February, the Saturday before Quinquagesima, according to Peter the Deacon, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, chapter 38; thus, in 1111.] [Note: [Col. 1478C] Sigonius confidently asserts under this year that Henry had previously received at Milan the royal crown of the Italian kingdom from Archbishop Chrysolaus—more correctly, Grossulanus. Bartholomew Zucchi adds Monza as well; Galvaneus Flamma, *Greater Chronicle*, chapter 251, further reports that this bishop joined Henry’s company on the journey and presented him at Rome to the supreme pontiff to be crowned emperor. Our Landulph convicts them all of manifest error, since he writes that Grossulanus was then far from Milan, having departed shortly before for Jerusalem. Thus he returned to Milan only two years later, as Puricelli rightly observed in the cited passage, no. 310. The author of the manuscript *Garland of Flowers*, chapter 162, and the catalogue entitled *Successors of St Barnabas*, commit a worse anachronism: they state that this coronation took place at Milan under Archbishop Jordan of Clivio, who, as we shall show in chapter 21, was elected archbishop of Milan only in the twelfth year of that century. Puricelli, uncertain whether this royal honour had been bestowed upon Henry, seems finally inclined to the opinion that Henry was girded with the diadem of the Italian kingdom by the abbot of the monastery [Col. 1479A] of the basilica of St Ambrose. Yet I would not hesitate firmly to assert that Henry was not crowned at Milan; [Col. 1479B] it can scarcely be believed that an event attended by the spectacle and ceremony of a sacred pageant would have gone unrecorded by every one of the many writers who described the acts of that time, including our Landulph, who was then living in this city, had it truly happened. I am confirmed all the more strongly in this view because I see that this author relates in detail, as we shall see below, the coronations at Monza and Milan of Henry’s predecessor and his successor Conrad, performed by our archbishops.]

But although this crown had been promised him [Note: [Col. 1479B] This provision had nevertheless been agreed through envoys sent by both sides: that he should leave the churches free and thereafter abstain from every lay investiture of them, while preserving the royal right, as Uspergensis under 1111 and Peter the Deacon, chapter 35, testify.], the pope delayed in giving it to him. [Note: [Col. 1479B] Helmold, chapter 39, gives the reason for this delay in these words: “When they came to the consecration, the lord pope required oaths from him: that he should remain sound in the observance of the Catholic faith, ready in reverence for the apostolic see, and vigilant in the defence of the churches. But the proud king refused to swear, saying that an emperor ought to swear to no one, since the sacramental oaths of all are to be rendered to him. Thus a dispute arose between the lord pope and the king, and the work of consecration was interrupted.” Orderic Vitalis, at the beginning of book X, assigns another reason: the emperor was stirred to anger because Paschal, before celebrating the solemn Mass, ordered four leading men of the emperor’s party, whom he had specifically condemned to the penalty of anathema, to be expelled from the church. Cardinal Aragonius, however, is wholly silent about this in his *Life of Paschal*, published in volume III of this collection.]

The pope himself then experienced the king’s anger and saw himself and his cardinals taken away in a manner neither sought nor desired. [Note: [Col. 1479C] Pandulph, in his published *Life of Paschal II*, volume III of this collection, writes that Henry captured the supreme pontiff, bishops, cardinals, the other orders, and many nobles on 12 February—the very Sunday on which the Gospel was read: “Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled; for he shall be delivered to the Gentiles,” etc. See him.]

Here great slaughter arose. For a crowd of Romans ran armed to free their pope and cardinals. The pope and cardinals having been committed to the custody of the Germans [Note: [Col. 1479D] Otto of Freising, in the passage cited above, says that Paschal was entrusted to the custody of Ulric, patriarch of Aquileia.] [Note: [Col. 1479D] A. 1 and 2: “committing.”], the king came barefoot into the courtyard of St Peter’s church. There he mounted a very spirited horse and, just as he was, barefoot, rode down the marble steps of St Peter’s in the charge; and, as has reached my ears, he killed five Romans with a single lance. [Note: [Col. 1479D] The aforementioned Otto of Freising likewise attests this. Baronius describes the remaining events of this tragic history at length under this year.]

Otto, vicecomes of Milan [Note: [Col. 1479D] This term denotes an office, not a family surname; this is sufficiently shown by the inserted word “of Milan.” Beroldus, repeatedly cited, a writer of those times, explains what this office was in our city. In his work entitled *Order of the Church of Milan*, while describing the order of processions held through the city on more celebrated saints’ days and Sunday solemnities, he says that the vicecomes ought to close the rear [Col. 1480A] of the procession, bearing before him the staff which was the insignia of his office; thereafter, accompanied by a troop of servants with wooden and split whips, he cleared the way for the archbishop who followed. Sigonius also relates, in *The Kingdom of Italy* under 973, that this vicecomes, acting in the archbishop’s place, customarily struck with a drawn sword and transacted all business with the consuls.] fell in that slaughter to a most bitter death, together with many of the king’s warriors, to the grief of men devoted to the city and Church of Milan. [Note: [Col. 1480B] Baronius, under this year, describes the event more fully from the Vatican Acts and Peter the Deacon: “The next day the Romans left the City; joining battle, they slew many of the emperor’s army, captured their spoils, and engaged the Germans more fiercely, so that they nearly drove them back by superior force, even unhorsed the emperor himself and wounded him in the face. When Otto, count—or vicecomes—of Milan saw this, he offered himself to death for the emperor and gave him his own horse so that he might escape. Otto was immediately captured by the Romans, led into the City, cut to pieces limb by limb, and his flesh was left in the street to be devoured by dogs.” By this one may refute Corio, who places the death of this Otto, while travelling into Germany, under 1055.]

But royal resources [Note: [Col. 1480C] A. 1: *facilitas* (“ease” or “readiness”).] and the great prudence of religious princes calmed this disturbance so gently and kindly [Note: [Col. 1480C] Baronius writes that Paschal was held in chains for sixty-one days; Pagius, however, maintains that the number was smaller, as will be said in the following note. Meanwhile Otto of Freising teaches us how the disturbance was settled: “After the supreme pontiff had been held for some time in sacrilegious captivity, an agreement was made; the king was recalled by the citizens and, on the condition that the supreme pontiff be released and that a privilege concerning the investiture of bishops be forcibly extracted from him, he entered the City. Then, as if led by repentance, he reconciled the citizens and pontiff to himself with gifts; crowned by the pontiff, with everyone’s favour he received the name of emperor and augustus.” Read the oath of the cardinals in Pope Paschal’s name [Col. 1480D] and that of Henry issued in this agreement in Cardinal Aragonius, *Life of Paschal*, volume III of our collection.] that on the following day [Note: [Col. 1480D] Baronius judged this to have been 13 April. But since the authors cited by Pagius say that Henry was invested with the imperial crown on the eighth day after Easter, called Low Sunday, this solemn inauguration seems to be moved back to 9 April, the date on which that Sunday fell in 1111. Accordingly, the period of Paschal’s captivity assigned by Baronius must be reduced from sixty-one to fifty-six days, as Pagius endeavours to show more fully under this year. Cardinal Aragonius, however, says: “This was done on the Ides of April, Thursday after the octave of Easter, indiction IV,” and adds from an unquestionably contemporary author: “What we have endured, seen with our own eyes, and heard with our own ears, we have written with unmixed truth.” See volume III cited above.]

In the holy place, namely St Peter’s church, that same Pope Paschal II, with cardinals, bishops, and other men in religious orders, solemnly crowned King Henry, raised him to be emperor, and, after he had been exalted and blessed, communicated to him the body and blood of Christ at the altar of St Peter.

At last the same emperor hurried into Germany, [Note: [Col. 1481B] Sigonius indicates the time of Henry’s return to Germany, saying that he entered [Col. 1481C] Parma, then, after spending three days at Bibianello with Matilda, went to Germany. The Saxon Annalist, cited by Eccard in the passage mentioned, col. 627, testifies that Henry celebrated Pentecost at Verona; it fell that year on 21 May.] where he scarcely had any rest.
