For while the emperor was tortured by very severe fevers in a promontory containing an abbey beside Worms, [Note: [Col. 1481C] Worms, a very ancient city in the Palatinate situated on the Rhine.] [Note: [Col. 1481C] Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, under 838, reports that Louis the Pious founded a convent of Benedictine nuns in the suburbs of Worms. Bucelinus, *Germania Sacra*, part II, folio 58 in my copy, adds that it was begun on Mount Wallemberg near the city, afterwards transferred to the city, and given to the Cistercians. He states that St Mechthild, sister of St Burchard, bishop of Worms, who died in 1025, especially shone among the abbesses of that place and was greatly celebrated for her ability and merits. This is therefore undoubtedly the abbey of which our author speaks.] the people of Worms, hoping more for his death than life in order to claim the regalian rights for themselves, came out armed and, raising cries, approached that hill.

When he sensed this while virtually dying, he ordered the attendants around him, under the obligation of their sworn fidelity, to raise him from his bed, lift and dress him, place him on a horse, and arm him. Once this had been done, sweat flowed from him like water from a spring. Escorted by a few men, he met the people of Worms; in the first encounter he struck down their standard-bearer to death, and destroyed the city itself by the sword and by fire. He ordered only that crowd of the same city which then fled to the church of the saint [Note: [Col. 1481D] Read: *confugit*, “fled for refuge.”] to be spared unharmed.

Moreover, as this emperor hurried from Rome through Verona into Germany, the Milanese utterly destroyed Lodi, another city in Lombardy, by swords, fires, and various engines. [Note: [Col. 1481D] On the destruction of Old Lodi by the Milanese in 1111 and the very harsh laws of servitude imposed upon its people, see Calco under this year and Sigonius. Where the latter has “the Kalends of July,” however, he should be corrected from our author to June, as we shall see in the following chapter.]

## CHAPTER XIX. Jordan of Clivio, recalled from study, was consecrated to the priesthood.

[Col. 1482A]

Therefore, since the city of Milan was now secure from its defeated enemies, Ardericus of Carimate, the vicecomes, and certain other very zealous *ordinarii* resolved to recall Jordan of Clivio [Note: [Col. 1481D] CHAPTER XIX.—A notably important village in Insubria, situated in a valley opening toward Lake Lucano, took its name from being built upon a slope, from which, like a watchtower, the forward and rearward extent of the valley can be widely seen. Consult Bonaventura Castiglioni, book *On the Ancient Settlements of the Insubrian Gauls*, where he describes it at length.] from the province called Saint-Gilles, [Note: [Col. 1481D] This is a part of Narbonensian Gaul, whose metropolis took its name from St Giles dwelling there. Robert of Monte, in his continuation of Sigebert under 1118, reports that it was formerly called Gothic Gaul and, after the expulsion of the Goths, was called the province of Saint-Gilles.] where Jordan was lecturing on writings of non-divine but pagan authors. [Note: [Col. 1482B] Perhaps he was then pursuing the study of dialectic, which flourished especially in Gaul at that time. Puricelli judged, in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 314, that [Col. 1482C] he was a public lecturer there.]

To speak truthfully of him: he spared the psaltery, the timbrel, and the other harmonious instruments in the choir of Milanese church so thoroughly that he neither chanted a psalm nor a canticle suitably for the art of music, whether alone or in company. [Note: [Col. 1482C] I believe that our author speaks allegorically here with words taken from Psalm 150, to show that Jordan was so ignorant of Ambrosian chant—or that his voice was so harsh and wandered so far outside the common measure—that he threw the whole harmony of the choir into confusion. This seems to be indicated by the corrupt word *pepercit* (“spared”), for which I think *pervertit* (“perverted”) should be read.]

Nevertheless, the pleasant appearance of his person pleased Grossulanus so greatly that Grossulanus ordained him subdeacon, when he seemed to hold the archbishopric peacefully. [Note: [Col. 1482C] For he had conferred this order upon him before undertaking his pilgrimage to the East, and perhaps at the time when, having occupied the castle of Arona and with the vicecomes absent, he seemed peacefully to enjoy his rights.]

Thereafter this same Jordan studied so hard in the book of Paul’s Epistles that he was *Paginus* [materially uncertain term]—a reader of that book. [Note: [Col. 1482C] The word is barbarous and unknown to the glossaries. In keeping with what was said above, I think Landulph means here that, although Jordan was unskilled and unteachable in ecclesiastical chant, he laboured with such stubborn diligence to learn properly the epistles [Col. 1482D] of St Paul—which are more frequently read in Masses, and whose reading belongs to the subdeacon when sacred rites are solemnly performed—that he adequately fulfilled his office in publicly reading the sacred pages in church.]

That same Ardericus of Carimate [Note: [Col. 1482D] Namely, archdeacon of the metropolitan church.] presented him, in September [Note: [Col. 1482D] Namely, on the twenty-third day of that month, which in 1111 was the Saturday of the fourth Ember Days.], the fourth month after the June in which the city of Lodi was destroyed, to the already mentioned bishop of Genoa, [Note: [Col. 1482D] Namely Arialdus.] and the bishop ordained Jordan himself and many other Milanese as priests.

It should also be known that this untrained [Note: [Col. 1482D] Namely in matters belonging to ecclesiastical ministry, as Landulph immediately explains; this, I think, confirms what we conjectured above.] priest Jordan, after returning to Milan, sought instruction from the priest Gualdo, of remarkable skill, [Note: [Col. 1482D] Since this author is very ignorant of Latin, I judge that this word should be interpreted more reasonably as derived from *calleo* (“to be skilled”), so that it attributes praise of the highest expertise, rather than the reproach of wickedness, to the priest Gualdo.] [Col. 1483A] in how a priest ought to celebrate the sacrifice; and while he [Note: [Col. 1483D] Read *isto* (“that man”), so that some sense may be made of this mutilated sentence.] was learning these and other things pertaining to a priest’s office.

## CHAPTER XX. Certain priests are chosen to decide whether the absent Grossulanus can worthily remain archbishop.

In the following month of October, the rivers rose so greatly through continual rain that they disturbed not only the villages but the city itself in a remarkable manner. Some even feared an end for themselves and for the world, [Note: [Col. 1483D] CHAPTER XX.—Orderic Vitalis, at the beginning of book X, testifies that the winter was dangerous, with rains and snows exceedingly severe. Sigebert, under 1113—the year in which he also ended his history and his life—relates the calamities that befell Henry after his return to Germany, as though God had armed himself for vengeance.] because the man who had oppressed his own father was ruling. [Note: [Col. 1483D] Namely Henry V.]

Then Guazo Cuminus, together with Amizo of Sala and very many others—both clerics and laymen, induced by Guazo and Amizo—began to go about preaching to others and saying that the dispute over Grossulanus was an evil deserving a second flood. In response to their words, John Manerius and Peter of Carate, who were the first and greatest champions and defenders on Grossulanus’s side, and who knew Guazo’s and Amizo’s plan, answered before the people and said to them: “Tell us what you want us to do on our side.”

They replied: “We want Ardericus of Carimate, who is a levite and an *ordinarius*; the priest John, provost of the church of St Nabor; the priest Nazarius Muricula; the priest Peter of St Carpophorus; the priest Lenterius of St Protasius in Campo; the priest Albericus of St Dalmatius; the priest Anricus of St Victor at the Theatre; the priest Ambrose of St John at the Conca; and also [Col. 1483C] the priest Galdo of St Michael—all of whom you know to be defenders of Grossulanus. And from the other side we want the vicecomes, Anselm of Pusterla, Anselm of Badagio, the priest Richelmus, provost of the church of St Nazarius, the priest Girard, provost of the canonical church of St Ambrose, Rolucus [Note: [Col. 1483D] A. 1: Rubricus.] likewise provost of the church of St Stephen, the priest Arialdus Amerii, the priest Lanfrancus Propheta [lacuna], and we two, namely Guazo and Amizo, to swear with them that until these coming Kalends of January we shall jointly give a just and right judgment according to the canons concerning the dispute over Grossulanus: whether he can be archbishop of Milan or not. If he cannot be, we shall jointly hold a canonical election of another person on that same day.

“We also want Landulph Carogna, who is a priest and an *ordinarius*; Anricus of Birago, who is a levite and an *ordinarius*; the priest John Actilens; the priest Olricus of St Martin; John Manerius; [Col. 1484A] Guazo Tastaguadum; and such other clerics and priests, knights and citizens as we summon, to come and swear to uphold the judgment which we eighteen shall render without discord or schism concerning whether Grossulanus is to be retained or dismissed, or concerning another person whom we shall jointly elect.”

When Guazo and Amizo made these demands, I resisted them to the best of my ability and said to them before the people: “Neither Abraham nor any faithful person of the Old or New Testament gave or accepted such counsel.”

Nevertheless, this preceding [Note: [Col. 1483D] Better: *praecedens*, “preceding.”] oath and the subsequent oath, as set forth and requested by Guazo Cuminus and Amizo of Sala, were sworn by the aforementioned clerics and laymen, by Landulph Carogna and Jordan of Clivio, priests and *ordinarii*, and by other priests and clerics, [Col. 1484B] knights also and citizens, while I humbly stood apart.

It should indeed be known that Ardericus, bishop of Lodi, gave permission for these oaths to be sworn, [Note: [Col. 1483D] For he was Grossulanus’s vicar, as we have seen.] and Ardericus of Carimate first received this permission, swore, and claimed for himself primacy and authority over this business. For after much deliberation about dismissing or retaining Grossulanus and about electing or not electing Jordan, he finally said to all who had sworn this oath with him: “Know without doubt: I shall not dismiss Grossulanus unless I have the power to elect Jordan.” Because of words of this kind from Ardericus, the hearts of those who rejected both Grossulanus and Jordan’s election became like stone and bound to Ardericus’s will.

## CHAPTER XXI. Jordan of Clivio is elected and consecrated archbishop.

[Col. 1484C]

But on the last day of December, when that Arderic and seventeen others were agreed upon electing Jordan, I came to them at the command of Andrew the Primicerius, of the priests, and of the Decumani clergy of Milan [Note: [Col. 1484D] CHAPTER XXI.—They were called Decumani from the hundred-member number which comprised that order. Puricelli composed an excellent dissertation on them, which, God helping, if life and strength suffice, I intend someday to publish together with other matters concerning the Church of Milan, under the title: *Monuments of the Ambrosian Rite*.], and, as the primicerius himself instructed me, I told them that they had taken bad counsel. Yet they did not change their plan; but when morning came, namely on the Kalends of January, the same Arderic, with the vicedominus and the others who had sworn with him either to cast out Grossulanus, or to admit him, or to elect another archbishop, ascended the pulpit publicly [Note: [Col. 1484D] That is, in a public assembly. Pagius explains it under the year 1212, no. 6. I think it preferable to read: “or in electing another archbishop publicly, he ascended the pulpit.” This agrees with what Guazo and Amizo proposed in the preceding chapter, saying: “On that same day we shall unanimously conduct a public election.”]. When silence had been made among the people, he spoke before that mixed multitude [Col. 1484D] and said: “We, saving the reverence due to the pope, declare, according to the authority and justice of the canons, that Grossulanus cannot be archbishop of Milan.” When this had been said and confirmed, he immediately [Col. 1485A] elected the priest Jordan of Clivi as archbishop [Note: [Col. 1485B] There can be no doubt that Jordan was elected on the Kalends of January in the year 1112, as Landulphus, who was present, reports [Col. 1485C]. Calchus, therefore, who asserts that this election took place in 1110, must certainly be corrected.].

When the priest Liprand heard this, he rose sick from his bed, and on the next day offered a fish to the man elected, saying: “Thanks be to God that you now bear testimony to me [Note: [Col. 1485C] Namely, to the judgment carried out by him through passage through the fire.], but those who elected you archbishop acted wrongly [Note: [Col. 1485C] Perhaps because, contrary to Paschal’s decree, they had removed Grossulanus from the Milanese see.], and may God have mercy on them; for you might have been a good priest in a cloister. But now, be a man [Note: [Col. 1485C] That is, conduct yourself as becomes a man.].” Since neither the elect man nor any of the many standing around replied to the priest, the priest himself came nearer, kissed Jordan, and left him as one of the other priests.

Landulph [Note: [Col. 1485C] Namely, Landulph of Vareglate, mentioned above in chapter 5.], bishop of Asti, Ariald of Genoa [Note: [Col. 1485C] He too was said in chapter 3 to have been present at Grossulanus’s consecration.], and Mamard of Turin [Note: [Col. 1485C] Ughelli, in his account of the bishops of Turin, states that this Mamard, whom he calls Mainard, was elected in 1109; but on what basis is unknown. He reports, from a marble monument cited by Baldessano, that Amizo II was bishop of that city in 1104. Yet our author makes it quite clear that Mamard was precisely the same man who, at least in 1100, consecrated Grossulanus bishop of Savona [Col. 1485D], and who in 1112 was present at Jordan’s anointing as archbishop of Milan—unless one wishes to say that there were two bishops of Turin named Mamard, between whom Amizo held that see. This I can scarcely believe; therefore I think Baldessano’s report, which I have not had in hand, ought to be examined more carefully.] came not merely to kiss him, but came to him in the following month of February as though to ordain him bishop [Col. 1485B].

But when the bishop of Asti saw that the bishop of Acqui [Note: [Col. 1485D] Azo.], the bishop of Lodi [Note: [Col. 1485D] Arderic.], and the other suffragan and fellow-provincial bishops were absent from this ordination and novelty, he realized that Jordan’s ordination ought to be postponed. Rising in the night, like a man wishing to flee, he began to depart with his belongings. But Jordan’s watchful hand drew back the bishop of Asti, wounded that bishop’s deacon, and beat and stripped their servants. When day came, after precautions had been taken, Lord Jordan rebuked the same bishop, as though bound and absent, in highly [Col. 1486A] disgraceful language.

Nevertheless, at the urging of the bishop of Genoa, and in his own humility after such disgrace, the bishop of Asti received back the property of himself and of his attendants. On the following day he attended the ordination of Jordan performed by those two bishops [Note: [Col. 1485D] Namely, the bishops of Genoa and Turin. Papebroch must therefore be corrected, for in the cited exegesis, no. 105, he thought that this consecration had been performed by Bernard, bishop of Pavia, together with the aforesaid bishop of Turin.], not clad as a bishop, but as a traveller without speech he watched the ordination itself. While this ordination was being performed in the church called the Winter Church, citizens fought battles over the affair and plundered the canonical house [Note: [Col. 1485D] Or the prebendal residence.] of the priest John Aculeus.

Then very many murmured concerning this matter and ordination; among those murmuring appear to have been the bishops named above, namely Azo of Acqui and Arderic of Lodi [Note: [Col. 1485D] What this murmur was is clearly stated in the letter of Azo himself, bishop of Acqui, to Emperor Henry, published by Eccard from the Udalricus codex of Bamberg in vol. I of *Writers of the Middle Ages*, [Col. 1486B] col. 267. It seems appropriate to extract some passages from it to clarify our subject. He says: “The Milanese [Col. 1486C] elected a certain archbishop (Jordan) and had him consecrated by certain of their diocesan bishops (understand: the suffragans Ariald of Genoa and Mamard of Turin). Seeing this done against the honour of your Empire, I entirely forbade it; and although strongly urged by them to attend such a consecration, I refused both to attend and to give assent. Indeed, I took pains to raise a great wall of people against people, on the pretext of another archbishop (Grossulanus), whom one party of them seeks to depose—a man most perfectly learned, of very shrewd intellect and most eloquent, greatly necessary to your court. For the sake of your honour I enlarged his party so greatly that one half of the people contends against the other half. Now therefore let your piety determine whether you wish me to labour toward this end: that this people remain divided and that the former archbishop receive aid from your majesty; command this by writing.” What Henry replied has not yet come to light. [Col. 1486D] From this, however, we learn who instigated the civil war kindled in our city, which, as our Landulph narrates in chapters 25 and 26, later flared up with great slaughter.].

Accordingly, while this murmur was active [Note: [Col. 1486D] That is, in force.], Mamard of Turin immediately went to Rome [Col. 1486B] and sought the stole; returning from there, he brought the stole and a document containing the oath which the pope demanded from Jordan [Note: [Col. 1486D] There is no doubt that this was an oath of fealty, which we shall see below was sworn at Pisa by Robald, archbishop of Milan, to Innocent II, to the indignation of the clergy, people, and Landulph himself. They believed that such an oath abolished the ancient dignity of the Milanese Church and diminished its liberty. For this reason too, we may readily suppose that Jordan refused the pallium under a condition then regarded as disgraceful.]. Otherwise, as Mamard himself recorded, the pope forbade the stole to be given to Jordan.

Jordan therefore fasted for six months and did not have the stole. Yet within those six months, with the agreement of Bernard, bishop of Pavia, and Jordan of Milan [Note: [Col. 1486D] Ughelli wrongly names Archbishop Grossulanus, instead of Jordan, as assenting to this pact made between the Pavians and Milanese; see his account of the bishops of Pavia, no. 64.], the Pavians and Milanese established and swore mutual treaties. To some these seemed excessively contrary to imperial majesty and apostolic authority. And when these citizens swore to preserve themselves and their property against [Col. 1487A] every mortal man born or to be born [Note: [Col. 1487C] The nature of this kind of oath, which in barbarous terminology is called *ligium*, because the man swearing it is, as it were, firmly and solidly bound, is that the pledged fidelity is understood to apply against every human being, with absolutely none excepted. Hence it is clear why the alliances of which our author speaks are called contrary to papal and imperial authority: the persons of pope and emperor were not excepted, as the laws require and feudal-law writers commonly teach.].

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Feast of Agios, held at Saint Mary at the Vercelline Gate on 9 May

I thought it should not be passed over in silence that, while the dispute concerning Grossulanus continued [Note: [Col. 1487C] CHAPTER XXII.—That is, while Grossulanus’s case had not yet been decided at Rome and the Milanese see awarded to him by Paschal’s papal decree; the stronger party among clergy and people sought to have him expelled in a Roman synod because simony had been proved by the ordeal of fire, [Col. 1487D] as we have said above.], namely in 1105 [Note: [Col. 1487D] Tristan Calchus places the events narrated here in 1107, but incorrectly, as is clear from our author’s stated year.], on the seventh day before the Ides of May [Note: [Col. 1487D] This ninth day of May, made notable by the discovery of so precious a treasure, fell that year on Tuesday of the fifth week after Easter.], precious relics were discovered in the church of Saint Mary at the Gate [Note: [Col. 1487D] So called from its proximity to the gate facing Vercelli, which this ancient church then closely approached. Nevertheless, the church retained this byname even after the city was enlarged—first after the destruction by Ahenobarbus, and later, under Charles V, when the city gates were moved much farther back—and it is still so called today.]. The ordinarii, with the entire clergy, therefore established [Note: [Col. 1487D] That the Church of Milan at that time behaved as though the archiepiscopal see were vacant, although Grossulanus had in fact been declared legitimate bishop of Milan at a Roman synod, is clearly demonstrated by the fact that this feast was proclaimed and celebrated in the name of the entire clergy [Col. 1488C], with no mention whatever of the archbishop. For the city of Milan never consented to recognize Grossulanus as its bishop even after his restoration, as Landulph says at the end of chapter 12.] a solemn feast on that day in the aforesaid church. The following letter exists as testimony to this matter:

> “The ordinarii cardinals [Note: [Col. 1488C] Ancient documents show that the canons of our metropolitan church were commonly called by this name at that time; from this one may infer the dignity of the Church of Milan. Although the distinction of this title was by no means peculiar to our city—as Ursinus, formerly most eminent in learning and piety, has learnedly shown, in addition to Panvinius and Macrius; and as the supreme pontiff Benedict XIII, now rejoicing with the whole assembly of the faithful, has shown in notes on the Second Provincial Council of Benevento, incorporated into his *Synodicon*—we nevertheless read that it was granted only to the chief priests of more distinguished churches. That this noble appellation continued among us for a long age is shown by an oration delivered at the principal sacred ceremonies by Fabricius Castrofranchi, cardinal ordinarius of the greater Church of Milan, published at Milan by Giovanni Ambrogio Bulla in 1557. Such privileges of churches, if any remained, were afterward abolished by Saint Pius V in a diploma issued on 17 February 1568, as Cohellius testifies, chapter 2, § “Et ideo.”], together with the primicerius, the whole priesthood and clergy of the holy Church of Milan, the whole people [Col. 1487B], and every rank of laypeople, to all priests, clergy, and laypeople of whatever rank established in the diocese of the Church of Milan: peace and salvation from the Lord, and participation in full joy.
>
> “Since reason requires, and it is fitting, that when the head rejoices the other members also rejoice with its rejoicing, we do not wish you to be excluded from the immense joy which divine clemency has lately bestowed upon us, unworthy and unsuspecting as we are. We therefore wish it to be known to all of you that, by divine direction and gift, we have lately discovered inestimable treasures and incomparable pearls, brighter than the sun and more fragrant than every spice: namely, a portion of the Lord’s sudarium, and of his burial shroud; of the stone upon which the angels sat when announcing [Col. 1487C] the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ; of authenticated wood of the saving cross of our Saviour; [Col. 1488A] of the garment of Saint Mary; and of the bones of Saints Castus and Polymius, in the church of Saint Mary called ‘at the Gate.’
>
> “Accordingly, not only on that day, but from that day onward, there has been there an unceasing, renowned, and wondrous gathering of people of both sexes, glorifying and magnifying God because in this time he has deigned in his kindness to reveal to us such treasures. Through their patronage we hope, by God’s mercy, for protection and salvation not only for our own church but also for its whole diocese [Note: [Col. 1488D] A. 1 and 2 read: ‘to be.’]. A general procession was also made in honour of God and our Saviour [Note: [Col. 1488D] Doubtless in that year, 1105, although on what day is unknown.], so great, solemn, and wondrous as we have never either seen or remembered to have occurred in earlier times.
>
> “Therefore, every year, all peoples, come devoutly to this solemnity [Col. 1488B], with security of mind as well as bodily observance, never doubting that you will receive a most magnificent reward. For as great as is the power of the saints, so great is the salvation of the people who come to meet them. The title and name of this outstanding feast is that of the Holy Saviour. The date of this celebration is the seventh day before the Ides of May.
>
> “We also request you and, according to the ordinance of our Church, command each and every one of you that, on the day of this feast, in honour of God and our Saviour, you abstain from every servile work, as on the day of the Resurrection and of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. On that same day, for the gathering at this solemnity, an annual fair and [Note: [Col. 1488D] A. 1 lacks this particle, ‘and.’] market have been established; and for all who come to this celebration [Col. 1488C], either for prayer or for trade, and who return from it, a firm and inviolable truce [Col. 1489A] has been established by the whole city for eight days before the feast and eight days after it [Note: [Col. 1489C] An immunity, or peace, granted for the duration of the fair; Du Cange, *Glossary*.]. If anyone violates this truce, he shall not escape God’s indignation and shall unquestionably incur the most severe wrath of the entire city against himself and his property. The *colonen* [Note: [Col. 1489C] A. 1 and 2: *Coloneum*.], commonly called *Turadia*, or *Portenaticum* [Note: [Col. 1489D] On this term and the other synonyms named here, see Puricelli at length, *Dissertation on Nazarius*, chapter 95, no. 7. He maintains that it denotes a kind of toll paid by travellers, especially the archbishop’s customs duty, concerning which Galvaneus Flamma writes in *Greater Chronicle*, chapter 227: “The archbishop of Milan received certain other very great revenues by imperial authority, because on the royal roads at every exit from the district of Milan he had a customs duty; and when any foreigner entered on horseback, by cart, or on foot, he paid the archbishop’s toll collector … a due.”] shall in no way be exacted from anyone on these aforesaid days.
>
> “And, so that what we have decreed by God’s inspiration in honour of God and our Saviour may be more authoritative and never erased by any forgetfulness, let them take care to read and post copies of this letter in every parish church, in the hearing of all who live there; and let them enter this feast in the Martyrology, so that no forgetfulness may erase these days through all years and generations, but that they may be honoured forever [Col. 1489B] and solemnly. Let this letter be carefully preserved among the records of the church and always remain valid.”

The aforesaid treasures—that is, the relics—were discovered: a portion of the Lord’s sudarium, of his burial shroud, of that stone, of the holy wood, and of the saints, in the year of the Lord 1105, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the city of Milan, at the Vercelline Gate, in the church of Saint Mary called “at the Gate.” The aforesaid holy confessors were Castus and Polymius, deacons of Saint Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1489D] We have this on the testimony of Paulinus, who also reports in the *Life of Saint Ambrose* that he lived under the care of one of these men, namely the honourable Castus the deacon.]. Their bodies lie in the church of Saint Victor at the Golden Heaven [Note: [Col. 1489D] Puricelli discusses this church more fully in *The Tomb of Saint Satyrus Explained*, chapter 10 and following, and in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 304, where he also considers whether Saints Castus and Polymius were martyrs, as is read in some places, or only confessors [Col. 1490C].], now called the church of Saint Satyrus, situated beside the church of Saint Ambrose.

At the aforesaid feast, the weekly ordinarii, with the other weekly ministers of the Church of Milan, always proceed in procession from the Summer Church to the aforesaid church of Saint Mary at the Gate [Col. 1489C]. The neighbours and parishioners of that church of Saint Mary go before them, carrying green leaves and branches of trees, with lighted candles tied to them [Note: [Col. 1490C] This annual Ambrosian Church rite of supplication with leaves and tree branches woven around candles is distinctive and worthy of notice; it ought therefore sometime to be included in Nicolaus Serarius’s little book *On the Sacred Processions of the Church*.], and singing *Agios* (“Holy”) [Note: [Col. 1490D] This name, then given to this newly established solemn feast, is a noteworthy trace of the Greek language flourishing in our city at that time.], from which it is called the Feast of *Agios* (“Holy”), which is the name of God. The said ordinarii afterward celebrate Mass in the church of Saint Mary at the Gate. Thanks be to God. Amen, amen.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Liprand admonishes the historian Landulph to abstain from communion with Jordan

[Col. 1490A]

Now I return to my subject. The priest Liprand, being in extreme old age, said to me: “I see that you are somewhat ashamed on my account because of what I said and did against Grossulanus. But so that you may be less ashamed because of it, I tell you truly that I reserve that cause to God Almighty alone. So long as breath remains to me, I greatly desire to end my life in this world in the hands of those through whose protection my body and soul, by the grace of God, may be protected from the hands of those who, by protecting Grossulanus, have wished and still wish to conceal God’s truth.

“As for this Church of Milan, in which you advise [Col. 1490B] me to remain and end my life, I say that for me, who desire to go to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1490D] Understand: the heavenly Jerusalem.], it is like a ship rotting in harbour without pilot or helmsman. If you live to your proper age, you will find it to be such. Meanwhile I too advise you: as quickly as you can, but honourably, relinquish participation at Jordan’s table and his benefices, which you are able to hold because of your election and investiture as deacon of his chapel, which you received from him without my knowledge. Never hope to advance through him. But as long as the vicedominus is favourably and kindly disposed toward you, do not refrain from rendering him your service.”

By these words which my master spoke to me, Jordan himself and his household [Note: [Col. 1490D] A. 1: *familia*, “household.”] became suspect to me, and in part both suspect and welcome, as was the vicedominus [Col. 1490C].

## CHAPTER XXIV. The priest Liprand dies in the monastery of Pontida

Following the counsel of my master, when I wished wholly to abandon Jordan’s administration, that priest was taken, without my knowledge, to the monastery of Pontida [Note: [Col. 1490D] CHAPTER XXIV.—Situated in the district of Bergamo beyond the river Adda. Its first founder and abbot was Blessed Albert of the Cluniac order, who died in 1095 on the Kalends of September, as Mabillon reports in the *Benedictine Annals* under 1087, the year in which that monastery was founded and dedicated to Saint James. Puricelli gives further information in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, nos. 316 and 331.]. There, before the monks and brethren, from the feast of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1490D] That is, from 6 December 1112 until the following 6 January.] until the feast of the Lord’s Epiphany, he lived splendidly [Note: [Col. 1490D] Namely, with great splendour of holiness.]. On the night of that feast, when he gave up his spirit, a great and sweet radiance, to the astonishment of those present, illuminated and made bright the house [Col. 1491A] in which he lay. Thus he had foretold to the brethren: “At the hour when his body was being carried to burial, the brightness of the sun lit up the air, and the cloud with snow ceased.”

While the priest was still alive, when Jordan [Note: [Col. 1491B] Puricelli says that Grossulanus seems to be required here instead of Jordan; but I entirely fail to see why this reading ought to be corrected. Since it has been said above that Jordan pleased Grossulanus and was ordained subdeacon by him, it is not unlikely that he had formerly stood on that archbishop’s side. Indeed, Grossulanus himself seems to imply this when he speaks in Landulph, chapter 26, and complains against Jordan and his supporters: namely, that Jordan had sworn allegiance to him and then broken that oath.] and the other Grossulanists were slandering him and his ordeal, a noble knight of Piacenza was rescued from the jaws of death to Liprand’s glory. For while that knight slept, as it were, he felt the priest touch his throat, and immediately vomited up the fish bone that was choking him [Note: [Col. 1491C] Peter Maria Campi also recounts this miracle in part I of his *History of Piacenza*, under the year 1114.].

At the same time, when the house of one of his kinsmen and adherents was burning, rain suddenly fell and wholly preserved both the straw and the priest’s house. If I were to run through every individual thing that God did to his praise, my spirit would indeed fail. But may God, who lives and reigns through all ages, now and forever bless his soul [Note: [Col. 1491C] Papebroch included a life of this Liprand under the title “Venerable” in the *Acts of the Saints*, appendix to 27 June, after the Life of Saint Herlembald. There he states that no one remembers any cult rendered to him as blessed after his death. Yet, when discussing Saint David the Solitary of Thessalonica on the 26th of the same month, he relates from the Pavia sanctuary of James Gualla that on 25 July 1504, among other sacred remains, bones of Saint Liprand or Luitprand were found in the church of Saint Peter in Golden Heaven at Pavia [Col. 1491D]. He believes that they had been brought there from Pontida and belonged to this Liprand, since it is far from easy to find another person of this name to whom the title “saint” could have been given.]. Amen. And may he grant me the grace to write rightly, for I still sincerely desire to write those things which in Church and kingdom have been sown and carried out by pontiffs and abbots, priests and Levites, by consuls and citizens, and by other ministers of Church and kingdom, not only for the increase but also for the harm of religion and upright custom.

## CHAPTER XXV. Jordan, receiving the papal stole, drives out clergy and removes the historian from the church of Saint Paul

[Col. 1492A]

Therefore, when the priest Liprand had been placed in the monastery of Pontida, the report that Grossulanus was returning from Jerusalem filled the ears of Jordan and his ordinarii. The bishop Mamard of Turin again came to Milan, and the stole, which in the preceding year [Note: [Col. 1491D] CHAPTER XXV.—These words have woven an almost inextricable knot into this history. Since it is certain that Jordan was both elected on the Kalends of January 1112 and received the pallium on 6 December of that year, as Landulph narrates, it cannot be understood how this statement—that the stole had been brought from Rome by Mamard in the preceding year—can be reconciled with historical truth. Puricelli, to free himself from the difficulty, adduces a custom adopted by some of beginning the year on 25 March. He says that Landulph employed it, so that from that day he was already reckoning another year. But this ingenious view can be refuted in several ways. First, it is not established that our author used this era of the Incarnation in narrating this history; indeed chapter 22 rather proves the contrary, since he assigns Grossulanus’s controversy and the discovery of relics in the church of Saint Mary at the Gate to 7 May in the same year 1105. Moreover, even leaving this aside, Landulph’s own narrative contradicts Puricelli’s claim. He states that an interval of six months elapsed from Mamard’s delivery of the pallium until Jordan received it on 6 December. Certainly not merely six but almost nine months had elapsed since 25 March. Pagius, who observed this point very well under the year 1112, no. 8, easily resolves the difficulty by assigning fault to the copyist, from whose pen, he says, “in the preceding year” accidentally fell instead of “in the present year.” Papebroch follows the same route in the Life of Liprand cited above, maintaining that one of these expressions is corrupt, and that “in the preceding year” should read “in the preceding June.” Both explain the matter very well, but at the cost of injuring the author’s text. If I may venture to intrude among men of such distinguished name, I would think all can be reconciled without harming the manuscript’s integrity by saying that Landulph, having already proceeded to narrate Liprand’s death [Col. 1492D] and the miracles following it in 1113, reverted his pen to events which had happened in the preceding year. Thus he used the phrase “in the preceding year” in relation to Liprand’s death already narrated, although the events he then relates had in fact occurred in the immediately preceding year.] Mamard had refused to give without Jordan’s oath and did not give, he now placed upon the altar of Saint Ambrose—namely, on the feast of Saint Nicholas, when the priest Liprand entered Pontida. Jordan kissed it and took it from that altar. This placing and taking were done in the absence of the ordinarii and primicerii [Note: [Col. 1492D] Perhaps Jordan had agreed to the oath required by the supreme pontiff and thus received the pallium secretly and, as it were, in the shadows, with none of the leading clergy present, lest he arouse their indignation against himself.].

Then that archbishop, acting more boldly, injured whom he wished, and at that time he unjustly harassed me. When Andrew the priest and primicerius learned of it, he formally received me into the common benefice [Note: [Col. 1492D] What this benefice was has already been explained above in chapter 2. Perhaps he also admitted him into the body of the Decumani, so that he might assist the priests while they performed the sacred rites.] of the priests and clergy of Milan. Jordan also paid money to my creditor Guido Falcimarius [Note: [Col. 1492D] A. 1 and 2: *creditori*, “creditor.”] on my behalf; yet I did not forgive him [Note: [Col. 1492D] That is, I did not at all forget the injury done to me; he explains below what that injury was.] the injury he did me. But I bore it with equanimity, because, when swords and lances were being sharpened so that, upon Grossulanus’s arrival, Jordan might be expelled from the archiepiscopal see, there was surely [Note: [Col. 1492D] I think one should read *nil mirum*, “no wonder.”] no wonder if he neglected me, a humble acolyte, and took up the priest Ariprand Paliarius [Col. 1493A], a man suited to him and powerful in war.

And, as seemed proper to some, it was not yet absurd [Note: [Col. 1493C] A. 1: “it seems, it ought not to be absurd.” For William the abbot appeared to have acted prudently in withdrawing from this city full of tumults.] that the Venerable Abbot William, at this time smiling and grieving over these misfortunes of clergy, bishops, knights, and citizens, left the monastery of Saint Ambrose and governed—and governs—the abbey of the monastery of Saint Solutor, built in the diocese of Turin [Note: [Col. 1493C] This transfer from the Milanese monastery of Saint Ambrose to Saint Solutor of Turin occurred in 1113, as Mabillon also notes in the *Benedictine Annals* under that year.].

But if I did not seek to be promoted to the rank of subdeacon through the hands of that Jordan, why did my neighbours presume, by his authority, to drive me from the church of Saint Paul, which is the title of my ordination? And by what right can Andrew Sugaliola, who, if he is a priest, is merely a parish priest [Note: [Col. 1493C] Perhaps he was attached to another church in some rural parish. The ancient discipline of the Church seems to be indicated here: decrees of several published councils provided that no one should depart from the title—that is, the church—to which he had been ordained, nor transfer to another, even a greater, title. See letter 173 of Pope John VIII; the Synod of Rheims of 813, chapter 20; the Third Council of Tours, chapter 14; and others in Labbe.], possess my very church? [Col. 1493B] Moreover, why did his hand cast the bones of my parents out of our own tomb—not his—and place his own dead person in it? Further, why does that Andrew Sugaliola seize, sell, and alienate houses, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, and many other things that belong to my own rightful property?

If he, his agents, and his patrons had done these things religiously and reasonably, and had justly tasted [Note: [Col. 1493D] Another manuscript of the Ambrosian Library reads *gustassent*, “had tasted.”] and decided my defenses, I would tear out my own eyes and enter the grave. But lest I die as my adversaries are dying and have died, I have greatly desired and still desire that those who yet seem to live may be enlightened by the sun of righteousness; that, the pride of schismatics and superstitious persons being driven away, they may despise the lies of their patrons and love and [Col. 1493C] uphold the protections of the best king [Note: [Col. 1493D] Henry.] and his bishop [Note: [Col. 1493D] Perhaps Grossulanus, on whose return from Jerusalem swords and lances were being sharpened, as Landulph said shortly before. Landulph had not at all consented to his deposition and, in chapter 21, reported Andrew the primicerius’s statement to Jordan’s electors that they had taken bad counsel.].

## CHAPTER XXVI. A battle is joined between the Grossulanists and the Jordanists, with the bishops themselves addressing their respective parties

[Col. 1494A]

In August [Note: [Col. 1493D] CHAPTER XXVI.—That is, of the year 1113], which was the eighth month after that in which the priest Liprand died. For in this month Grossulanus also returned from Jerusalem, and, for the first time after the law made concerning him by fire, entered Milan [Note: [Col. 1493D] Puricelli, in *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 320, and Pagi, at the year 1113, no. 10, judge that these words indicate that Grossulanus entered Milan twice in this same month of August: first, namely, in the year 1105, after obtaining from Paschal II the restoration of this see; and second, in this very year after his return from Jerusalem. Yet, since at the end of chapter 12 Landulph asserts that Grossulanus possessed neither see nor any stronghold of the archbishopric after the law made by the priest Liprand and the restoration decreed by the Roman synod, I should judge that our author uses the adverb *prius* in the sense of “for the first time,” so that this was the first entry of this prelate into the city of Milan after the ordeal by fire undertaken against him.]. There, at the place where Saint Victor had been imprisoned [Note: [Col. 1494C] We read in the Life of this holy martyr, reported by Boninus Mombritius, that the prison in which St Victor was held stood where the church now dedicated to his name, commonly called St Victorello at the Roman Gate, is located—perhaps because of the narrowness of that sacred building, which was rebuilt more elegantly within the last two years, or to distinguish it from the other church of St Victor, which even now bears the name “the Great.” In antiquity the gate which we call the Roman Gate stood adjacent to it. Only after the destruction wrought by Ahenobarbus, when our city had been enlarged, did its citizens build that gate much farther away from this church. Galvaneus Flamma frequently discusses these matters in his greater Chronicle, and Puricelli likewise relates them in the *Dissertation on Nazarius*, chapter 54, no. 21.], he unfolded to the priests and men whom he thought faithful to himself his labours and his treasures; and in unfolding them he introduced [Note: [Col. 1494D] That is, he introduced into his speech, or recalled, the benefits he had conferred upon Jordan.] the kindness with which he had fed and clothed Jordan, whom he had made a subdeacon [Note: [Col. 1494D] See above, chapter 19.].

He also seemed to press charges against Jordan because, he said, Jordan had sworn to him and then forsworn himself [Note: [Col. 1494D] This shows that Jordan had at one time been counted among Grossulanus’s party, as we said above.]. But Jordan’s strong and powerful crowd did not endure this; [Col. 1494B] taking up arms, it made a very great assault upon Grossulanus. Grossulanus’s own band, rushing together from every side and inflicting and receiving wounds, losses, and many killings of horses and men, bravely and prudently protected Grossulanus himself for fifteen days in the towers of the Roman Gate [Note: [Col. 1494D] Galvaneus Flamma frequently relates that every gate of the city of Milan had its own towers. When our city was razed by Frederick Ahenobarbus, its walls were demolished and its towers thrown down. Yet, as soon as the city could breathe again, its first resolve was to rebuild them, as a stone still set into the side of the arch that overlooks the bridge at the Roman Gate teaches; Puricelli reports its inscription in *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 515.].

Meanwhile Anselm of Pusterla, having heard of the slaughter, came to the church of St John called *ad Concham*. Speaking at the assembly held there on Grossulanus’s side, he offered many counsels so that that destructive plague might cease: they should set a definite place and a definite time, and discover through a lawful and general synod whose cause was just. Since this counsel displeased Jordan and his supporters, the money of both pontiffs reached soldiers and infantry fighting men, and also clerics and women inciting wars. Jordan, with open mouth, sang before [Col. 1495A] his people about Grossulanus as though about Simon Magus; and Grossulanus, among his own people, compared Jordan to an idol, a molten calf, and a faithless and perjured man. Thus each pontiff caused a very great slaughter, in which Roger of Sorexima, a knight and captain; Ariprand of Lampugnano [Note: [Col. 1495C] A. 1: *Lampugnano*.], standard-bearer of the vavassors; and Ariprand of Meda, a most prudent citizen, were killed, together with very many men of the same nobility.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Money having been given to Grossulanus and Anselm of Pusterla, Grossulanus went to Piacenza.

But when Grossulanus’s wallet [Note: [Col. 1495C] CHAPTER XXVII.—That is, a purse.] had been emptied and Jordan’s was still laden, an agreement was made through money promised to Grossulanus, [Col. 1495B] which Grossulanus, as is said, shared with his own party and with the Jordanists. When the sharing had been made, Grossulanus left Milan and went to Piacenza. There, lodging in the monastery of St Mark, which belonged to the congregation of Vallombrosa, he found Arderic of Lodi, whom he had made his deputy and a monk of that congregation in food and clothing.

But the other Arderic, of Carimate, who, while serving as deputy, had received from this man permission to swear, and on the pretext of that oath had pronounced sentence against Grossulanus and elected Jordan archbishop, did not await Grossulanus’s arrival. Rather, while travelling through overseas lands, he was found and slain by the Turks.

It should also be known that, when Grossulanus and Jordan were leaders among the Milanese [Col. 1495C] [Note: [Col. 1495C] Perhaps “prelates”; for one had been restored to the Milanese see by a decree of Paschal II, while the other had been approved by that same Paschal through the sending of the pallium brought by Mamardus, bishop of Turin, as was said above.] of the Milanese church, through the favour of Pope Paschal II, the clergy and people of Milan—noble and religious by nature on both sides—are not without reason called fickle and vain, and ready to presume upon every novelty.

For what religious devotion or nobility of spirit was that which prompted Jordan, his clergy, and his people to reproach and excommunicate [Note: [Col. 1495D] From this it is inferred that, through the persuasion of the clergy and people favouring Jordan, Anselm of Pusterla, who proposed means of peace, was immediately subjected to anathema by him.] Anselm of Pusterla, an ordinary deacon, because he had advised that the cause of Grossulanus and Jordan be decided through a lawful and general [Col. 1496A] synod? Again, on what grounds did it publish that this same man was an *erroneus* [Note: [Col. 1495D] This word seems here to be used for a seducer or impostor, as Du Cange likewise states that it is so signified in a Greco-Latin gloss, and Henri Estienne in his *Thesaurus Graecae Linguae*, under Πλανός.] because, together with Grossulanus’s clergy and people, he conducted the scrutiny [Note: [Col. 1495D] That is, the examination of catechumens held during Lent concerning matters of faith, by which confessors of the faith were tested as to whether they were fit to receive the sacred washing on the coming Holy Saturday, as Macer explains in his *Hierolexicon*.] and baptism? And who could say that Jordan, an archbishop endowed with apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1495D] Or rather, confirmed by the sending of the pallium.], was an idol and a faithless and perjured man? Surely [Note: [Col. 1495D] Here too one seems to have to read *nil mirum*, “no wonder.”], if I inquire: while Grossulanus was in the aforesaid monastery of St Mark, and Anselm was pressing matters in Milan and seeking an undertaking to meet at a general synod, Jordan prevented this from being done [Note: [Col. 1495D] A. 1: *prohiberet*, “was preventing.”]. It is said and believed that money was pledged and given [Col. 1496C] [Note: [Col. 1496C] Namely, by Jordan, as Landulph narrated at the beginning of this chapter.] to Grossulanus and Anselm, so that Jordan’s person might not be impugned by them in any synod.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the character and *imbrata* [Note: [Col. 1496C] CHAPTER XXVIII.—A barbarous word which seems to denote tricks, or foul practices, in the Italian idiom.] of the priest Nazarius Muricula.

[Col. 1496B]

Accordingly, after this precaution [Note: [Col. 1496D] Namely, the disbursement of money to Grossulanus and Anselm, by which Jordan secured the safety of his reputation; its chief instigators were Muricula and Ferrarius, mentioned here.] had been taken by the priest Nazarius Muricula and Lafrancus Ferrarius, as is said, it happened that the priest Andrew, the primicerius of blessed memory, died [Note: [Col. 1496D] From the events narrated above it may be inferred that this Andrew died toward the end of 1113.]. The said priest Nazarius succeeded him. Concerning this Nazarius, there remains something for me to write, as concerning a man who was, as it were, my contemporary and fellow pupil in one neighbourhood and under the instruction of that priest Andrew, who, according to his lineage, was called Dalvultus.

This Nazarius, then, when he was a cleric in minor orders and a young man of very sharp intellect, gave me, while I was a little child, the name Cloca [Note: [Col. 1496D] The same as *campana*, “bell.” Puricelli discusses this name, formerly used in documents, at length in *Monumenta*, no. 391. Another of our manuscripts reads *clerica*.] of St Paul, and not without reason. Moreover, while he himself lived alone in his upper chamber [Note: [Col. 1496D] A raised place where the ancients basked in the sun. Du Cange calls it a larger and upper bedchamber.], he brought me, the Rustic of the Gemmae—or Caccus—and Nazarius Flota up upon that chamber, and gave us a pleasant and sweet repast for his brother’s wedding. From what went before and what followed, which I read from the book of his heart, I foresaw that his mind desired the splendour of the holy Milanese Church no more than it desired that Church’s useful and honourable nobility.

For in the time of our youth and schooling Pope Urban held a synod at Piacenza [Note: [Col. 1496D] This synod was held in 1095, around the middle of Lent, according to Berthold, who describes it fully and asserts that it was so crowded that four thousand clerics and more than thirty thousand laypeople are reported to have gathered for it.], and returned from France [Col. 1497A] to Milan [Note: [Col. 1497B] Calco records, at the year 1095, that Urban II moved directly to this metropolis after the Piacenza synod. This word *redivit*, written by our author, proves this clearly. It is confirmed by a diploma reported by Primo Luigi Tatti in his *Annals of Como*, part II, p. 865, issued “at Milan, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, indiction III, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096”—that is, in the Pisan era, which for us is only the year 1095; Tatti did not observe this and consequently imagined an error in the year of the diploma, which he declares should be corrected to 1095, no. 27—“in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Urban II.” From Berthold, at the year 1096, we learn that he returned from Gaul in 1096 after holding the Council of Tours in the third week of Lent. Indeed, from what that writer adds we may understand that Urban’s return to Milan occurred around the end of September. For he says there: “The lord pope, after putting affairs in Gaul in good order, after the reconciliation of the king of the French, Philip I, and after many councils, at length returned to Lombardy in great triumph and solemnly celebrated the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, on 14 September, at Hortarium near Pavia.” It is credible that he proceeded to Milan from Mortara—there can be no doubt that this is the place meant by Berthold, since no town or castle having a similar name appears on geographical maps—in that same month. Pagi, at the year 1096, no. 15, objects and charges Berthold with error, producing a charter transcribed by Bouche, which reads: “We wish it to be known that the venerable Pope Urban, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, but the eighth of his pontificate, on the third day before the Ides of September, passing through the castle of Tarascon,” etc. From this he endeavours to prove that Urban could not have been at Mortara on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, since three days earlier he was staying at Tarascon, four leagues from Avignon. Yet this charter too uses the Pisan era, as is evident from the eighth year of Urban’s pontificate stated there; Pagi wrongly wishes to amend it to the ninth year. Thus the charter belongs to 1095, when Urban first set out for Gaul, and Berthold must by no means be condemned of error for placing Urban’s arrival at Mortara in the following year, 1096.].

In that city, while the pope himself stood in the pulpit of St Thecla [Note: [Col. 1497D] More correctly, Thecla. This was the church to which the Milanese metropolitan clergy went in summer to celebrate the divine mysteries there. This season began, as Berold teaches, cited also by Puricelli in the *Dissertation on Nazarius*, chapter 100, on Easter Sunday itself, when they carried there in solemn procession an ark fashioned in the likeness of the ark of the Old Testament. Later they brought it back with precisely equal ceremony when, on the third Sunday of October, they returned to their winter church. From this we readily perceive why Pope Urban preached in the church of St Thecla: the summer residence there appointed for the metropolitan clergy to perform the sacred offices was still in force. This also confirms what we asserted above concerning the time of Urban’s arrival in this city; it must undoubtedly have preceded the third Sunday of October.], he preached to an immense multitude of men and women. In preaching, he uttered from his great wisdom this saying: “The lowliest cleric of the Church of God is greater than any mortal king.” He also added that clerics and priests should not be introduced into churches through money, but through the election of persons who were neighbours of those churches.

From these apostolic sayings that cleric [Note: [Col. 1498B] Read *clericus*, “cleric,” as he is called a little earlier, although in orders—that is, initiated only by tonsure.] Nazarius, very sharp in intellect and surnamed Muricula, took wings; and from his upper chamber he flew to the church of St Babylas and St Romanus, which in antiquity is called the Council of Saints [Note: [Col. 1498C] The church of St Babylas continued to be called by this name until the fifteenth century, as is apparent from the Ambrosian calendar of 1402, which reads under 27 September: “The deposition of St Caius, bishop. Station at the Council of Saints.” Otto Morena, describing at the year 1158 Ahenobarbus’s siege of Milan, calls it All Saints, the church of All Saints.], without [Note: [Col. 1498C] A. 1: *sicut*, “as.”] royal or priestly authority. Having gained the favour of the common people of that neighbourhood, he lived there [Col. 1497B] and built a new dwelling, expelling the priests and clerics accustomed to serve those churches.

Following this example [Note: [Col. 1498C] A. 1: *expulsionem*, “expulsion.”], Albinus, a man of Magenta; John Aculeus of Vicomercato; Mayfredus of Limido—men who were literate [Note: [Col. 1498C] Macer testifies in his *Hierolexicon* that this name may also mean “cleric.” I do not think that is its meaning here, since Landulph immediately adds “and without tonsure,” from which we plainly infer that they lacked the tonsure. The word must therefore be defective, and *illitterati*, “illiterate,” should be read in place of *litterati*, as the following words also seem to indicate: “and many townsmen and commoners lacking sufficiency,” namely of learning.] and without tonsure—and many townsmen and commoners who lacked sufficient learning, following the shouts and applause of the popular faction, entered churches, received their benefices, and possessed them unlawfully, until Arnulf of the Eastern Gate [Note: [Col. 1498C] Berthold, at the year 1093, calls him “of the Silver Gate” [Col. 1498D]; for this Eastern Gate was then so called from the silvery rays of the rising sun toward which it faces, as Puricelli explains in *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 280.], then an old man and archbishop of Milan, was buried in the monastery of Clavate [Note: [Col. 1498D] This distinguished monastery was mentioned above at chapter 14. Archbishop Arnulf died in 1097, on 25 or 26 September, as the catalogues of the Milanese archbishops show. Ughelli may accordingly be corrected, where, in his section on the Milanese archbishops, no. 79, he writes that this Arnulf was buried “at St Victor’s, whose church he had enriched with possessions, favours, and privileges.” For it was not this Arnulf but another of the same name, Arnulf II, who had founded and endowed that church—or, more accurately, monastery—as Puricelli reports in *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 213. Landulph’s authority proves that this archbishop was buried in the monastery of Clivate or Clavate, which is the same place.].

Thereafter the aforesaid Nazarius, with the crowd bound to him, did almost whatever he wished in the church of Milan and in the city of Savona. In Milan he raised Anselm of Buis, a simple man, to be archbishop. Once raised, Anselm confirmed by his authority Albinus, John Aculeus, and the others from Nazarius’s crowd of adherents [Col. 1498B] in churches; and he promoted Nazarius himself and Grossulanus through all ecclesiastical orders and made them priests.

Nazarius himself, once made a priest, together with the priest John Aculeus, as is read above, elected Grossulanus bishop in Savona and deputy and successor of Anselm, his own consecrator. Moreover, this priest Nazarius despised the law which the priest Liprand had made against Grossulanus; he also knew that the house of this priest Liprand was being despoiled. Because of this despoiling Peter Pazananus, a man belonging to the school of this priest Nazarius, was killed. The same priest Nazarius rejoiced to see Grossulanus restored in the Roman synod; he received him once restored, and for eleven years was known to obey him as his Catholic archbishop [Note: [Col. 1499C] If these eleven years are reduced to an arithmetical calculation, they cannot fit into the chronology established above: we have said that Grossulanus was elected toward the end of August 1102 and deposed through Jordan’s election on the Kalends of January 1112. I should therefore suppose that our author counted years in the common manner, treating as complete years the second and twelfth years, which Grossulanus touched only in his archiepiscopal rule. We saw Domnizo use this practice near the end of the first chapter, where that writer asserts that three years had elapsed from the death of Urban II to the death of King Conrad, though an exact calculation of the intervening period shows that scarcely two years had passed, as we noted there.].

At length, while Grossulanus was on pilgrimage at Jerusalem, Nazarius deposed him and elected Jordan, from the crowd of his adherents, archbishop [Col. 1499B]. Consequently the priest Nazarius, reproached by his neighbours, abandoned his church; and through the authority of wicked men and of Jordan—whom I then justly accused and still accuse—he usurped my possessions and church. In the course of usurping it, he found the hair-shirt which my master and uncle had carried unharmed through the fire, and ordered that it be taken down from a beam [Note: [Col. 1499C] This passage is defective; a verb such as [Col. 1499D] *jussitque ut*, “and ordered that,” appears to be missing before “from a beam.”] of the church of St Paul and shamefully burned.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Pope Paschal confirms Jordan and deposes Grossulanus, who dies at Rome one year later.

I pass over many things which the priest Nazarius himself did to my loss, injury, and disgrace. Yet I say that, after receiving the dignity [Note: [Col. 1499D] CHAPTER XXIX.—Namely, the primiceriusship of the Decumani. Since Andrew Dalvultus died, as we said, near the end of 1113, we may believe that Nazarius was promoted to it early in the following year.] of the primicerius [Col. 1499C] from Jordan, the prudence of this primicerius [Col. 1500A] had such force that the fury of arms against Grossulanists and Jordanists ceased [Note: [Col. 1499D] Namely, because of the precaution mentioned at the beginning of chapter 28.].

He went to the church of St Thecla, in which the preceding primicerius Andrew had lived and ended his days, and lived in it; and he abandoned it [Note: [Col. 1499D] Without doubt one should read “and abandoned mine,” as immediately follows.]. Yet when he abandoned mine, he and Jordan thrust another man—namely Andrew Sugaliola—into that church of mine. Grieving therefore over this intrusion and the stripping from me of every ecclesiastical benefice and office, I went to the synod which Pope Paschal held at Rome concerning Grossulanus and Jordan [Note: [Col. 1499D] Pope Paschal held this council in the Lateran in 1116, and completed it within a single week. Baronius and others transcribed the acts of this council from Abbot of Ursperg.].

At it the aforesaid Anselm of Pusterla held and occupied an honourable place according to his rank [Note: [Col. 1499D] Namely, as an ordinary cardinal of the church of Milan, in whose hierarchical order he exercised the office of Levite, or deacon, as Landulph testified in chapter 17. It may incidentally be noted how greatly the church of Milan and each of its chief ministers were held in honour.]. But he uttered neither a good nor an ill word at the synod either for Grossulanus or against Jordan. Jordan, however, sat in silence from the beginning of the synod to its end, at the right hand of the apostolic lord, with no intermediary, in the synod itself [Note: [Col. 1500C] The very great dignity of the archbishop of Milan is also apparent from this passage.].

Grossulanus, meanwhile, stood and sat among archbishops and bishops. Like a prudent man, he worked to overthrow Jordan’s imposition [Note: [Col. 1500C] That is, his imposition upon the archiepiscopal see.] and the change of allegiance [Note: [Col. 1500C] The fickle disposition seems here to be noted of those who had first favoured Grossulanus and then turned to Jordan’s party.] of those who had made that imposition. While doing so, he spoke excellently about his appointment and restoration in the church of Milan. No man who contradicted that man in this synod or in the Lateran palace had a secure standing [Note: [Col. 1500C] Since Anselm of Pusterla remained silent, as Landulph has just narrated, perhaps no one dared rise against Grossulanus.].

But Pope Paschal, as though seeking to render him acceptable to God and to himself, praised Grossulanus’s learning and eloquence [Note: [Col. 1500C] How high an opinion Paschal held of Grossulanus’s learning is taught by the matters set out in chapter 11: namely, that the Roman curia and all ecclesiastical causes had been entrusted by that supreme pontiff to this our archbishop, so that he might exercise full jurisdiction in them. Trithemius also, whose words Baronius transcribed at the year 1116, bestowed this notable eulogy upon him [Col. 1500D]: “Chrysolanus”—for this is also the name used by Baronius—“archbishop of the church of Milan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly educated in secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, published certain works of great authority, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity; but none of these has reached our hands.” In later centuries a treatise by him on the Holy Spirit was found and first published by Baronius, although mutilated. Pagi, at the year 1116, no. 5, states that the complete work is preserved in manuscript in the royal library under the title *Peter Grossulanus, Bishop, on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*; from this, together with Ughelli in his section on the bishops of Milan, we may infer that Grossulanus’s given name was Peter.], and before the synod rehearsed the labours which the pope himself, by himself and through his legates at Rome and throughout the province of the Lombards, had borne for [Col. 1500C] Grossulanus [Note: [Col. 1500D] Namely, at the Second Lateran Council, at which, when Milanese clerics and Liprand himself, the advocate of his harmless passage through fire, testified against Grossulanus’s simony, Paschal absolved him; and perhaps he later also worked through legates to reconcile him with the suffragan bishops and our citizens, who were keeping him from the Milanese see [Col. 1501B].].

To soften the hardness and severity of those who had not received, or did not receive, Grossulanus’s appointment or restoration, Paschal mentioned not only the priest Liprand and his law but also adduced the fall of the *gambuta* [Note: [Col. 1501B] Namely, of the pastoral staff, which had fallen from the hand at the aforesaid synod; some had taken its fall as an argument for perjury, as was narrated in chapter [Col. 1501C] 12.]. That fall had appeared when Grossulanus swore and stepped forward to receive restoration. He further alleged that Grossulanus’s translation from the bishopric of Savona to the archbishopric of Milan had brought no benefit. Grossulanus, to some extent, repelled these arguments with the shield of ecclesiastical custom and law [Note: [Col. 1501C] On the custom and law concerning translations of bishops, both in the East and West, consult Louis Thomassin, *De veteri et nova Ecclesiae disciplina*, part II, book LX and following, where he treats this matter, in his usual manner, learnedly and at length.].

Nevertheless, neither the lord pope nor the synod satisfied Grossulanus, who pleaded day by day for himself and his cause in the palace and the synod, on the first, second, third, or fourth day of the synod. But on the fifth day [Note: [Col. 1501C] From the Abbot of Ursperg we learn that the fifth and last day of that synod was Saturday; we also have his testimony that Paschal did not sit in the council on Thursday.], which was the last of that synod, while the apostolic lord pressed him with the aforesaid objections, Grossulanus said in tears: “Lord, Lord, I will come to you, although those to whom you have given authority to judge my cause do not love me.”

Then Peter, bishop of Porto, excused himself and the others who had this authority, honourably and sufficiently, from the charge of ill will toward Grossulanus. When he had made his excuse, by the common agreement [Col. 1502A] of him who made the excuse and of the others possessing this authority, a sentence was pronounced forbidding Grossulanus to disturb the church of Milan and telling him to return to his bishopric [Note: [Col. 1501C] Namely, Savona.].

He did not go to Savona, however, but lived as a bishop for one year and four months in Rome itself, at the monastery called St Sabaoth [Note: [Col. 1501C] Read St Sabba. Greek monks inhabited this monastery, then built on the Aventine Hill; it was very ancient, since John the Deacon mentions it in the Life of St Gregory the Great. Baronius, at the year 1144, testifies that it was later given to the Cluniac monks by Pope Lucius II; this is also clear from Lucius’s letter to Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, in which he writes that he entrusts in perpetuity to him and his successors the monastery of St Sabba, founded at Rome in the time of the most blessed Pope Gregory—namely Gregory the Great—although Pagi shows, in his critical notes at the year 1144, no. 5, that the letter belongs to the following year. Puricelli, in *Life of St Arialdus*, book IV, chapter 90, no. 17, offers this conjecture about why Grossulanus sought refuge there: namely, that because he had disputed vigorously in the East—where, while exiled from Milan, he had gone to Jerusalem—against the Greek schismatics, he later willingly chose, while residing at Rome, to live with the Catholic Greeks in that monastery and to end his final day there. Moreover, Galvaneus Flamma in the *Greater Chronicle*, Galesinius in the synodal table, the catalogue entitled *Successors of St Barnabas*, and others must be corrected here for wrongly giving St Sebastian in place of St Sabba [Col. 1501D].], and was buried there on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August]. [Note: [Col. 1501D] Our author indicates the year of Grossulanus’s death very clearly. Since this Lateran council ended on the eleventh day of March 1116, and since he is said to have survived one year and four months, it is evident that he died in 1117. It is true that, from the calculation of the four months assigned above by Landulph as Grossulanus’s life after the synod, one would infer that he ought to have been buried not on the eighth day before the Ides of August, but on the fifth day before the Ides of July; for precisely four months intervene between March and that day. Yet I think our author should be understood as referring to Grossulanus’s residence among the monks of that monastery for a full year and four months. It may be believed that he did not go there immediately upon the completion of the synod, but after several intervening days—the days which, up to the eighth day before the Ides of August given by Landulph, exceed the calculation of four months. On these grounds our writers who stray far from the truth in assigning the final year of this archbishop’s life must be refuted: Galvaneus Flamma, who places his death in 1120; Tristanus Calchus, who with a graver anachronism boldly asserts that he was already dead in 1110; and, not to mention Donatus Bossius, who says that Grossulanus was taken by fate even earlier, in 1109 [Col. 1502B–C].].

## CHAPTER XXX. Jordan, thanking the pope, consecrates the bishop of Brescia and promises to do justice to the historian.

Jordan, when he had heard and the sentence concerning Grossulanus’s return to his bishopric had been publicly announced before the synod, ascended the Theatre [Note: [Col. 1502C] CHAPTER XXX.—That is, a place rising above the others, in which Paschal II’s throne was fixed; perhaps called a theatre because the supreme pontiff there made a noble spectacle of himself. This word, as used by our Landulph, is absent from the glossaries [Col. 1502D].]. There he prostrated himself at the feet of the apostolic lord [Col. 1502B], gave him thanks, and, raised up by the apostolic lord himself, received favour and the pastoral staff in that Theatre.

On the following day, this Jordan, archbishop, instructed by Landulph, bishop of Asti, and certain other bishops, in a Lateran church consecrated as bishop the bishop-elect of Brescia, named Villanus, in place of Bishop Arman of Brescia, who was still alive and had been deposed [Note: [Col. 1502D] No writer whom I have seen has stated the reason for this deposition. Perhaps one might suspect that he had devoted himself to the party of Emperor Henry, condemned by the Church; but even this is difficult, since another John, bishop of Brescia, intruded by Emperor Henry as early as 1107, is thought to have remained in his favour, as Florentinius teaches from a diploma granted in that John’s favour by the aforesaid Henry in 1123, which the praised Galeardus published in the section on the bishops of Brescia in the new edition of *Italia Sacra*. Since history is silent, we do not wish to divine the matter.].

At this ordination, according to the duty of my order, I read the reading [Col. 1503A] from the book of Exodus, and when the mitre fell by chance from Villanus’s head, I secured it upon his head again. Since this Archbishop Jordan, during the days when Grossulanus was presenting his cause, and when I sought a hearing at the synod in a voice of humility and meekness, with a repeated petition [Note: [Col. 1503C] This passage appears corrupt, and *petitione*, “petition,” should be read. Another reading in a manuscript of the Ambrosian library has *geminatam donationem*, “a repeated gift”; yet no sound sense can be elicited even from this, unless perhaps *geminata devotione*, “with repeated devotion,” should be read.], promised to satisfy me at Milan concerning all the matters of which I wished to complain against Jordan himself in that Roman synod.

At that time I preferred to trust his promise rather than contend in the synod, because if that contest were pursued directly, it would either condemn Grossulanus and the man imposed above him [Note: [Col. 1503C] That is, Jordan, elected archbishop against Grossulanus.], or, saving due reverence for the see, would bury under a wealth [Note: [Col. 1503C] Namely, an abundance of arguments which he himself would have produced.] of argument divine and human law together with the pope—I say this in my judgment [Note: [Col. 1503C] A. 2 omits the words “I say this.”]. Yet the pontiff Jordan himself, after receiving at Rome this victory and ordination [Col. 1503B], wished that no justice should be done to me, and did none; rather, he increased my sorrow.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Jordan excommunicates Emperor Henry at Milan and holds a provincial council, from which he expels the complaining historian.

[Col. 1504A]

Henry the Emperor, in whom I had in some measure hoped, Jordan himself—if it is permissible to say so—together with his clergy and people, excommunicated at Milan from the pulpit of Saint Thecla, at the command of John of Crema, Roman cardinal.

[Note: Col. 1503C. CHAPTER XXXI.—A priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, created by Paschal II, as Oldoinus relates.]

[Note: Col. 1503C. Neither Oldoinus, nor Baronius, nor anyone else has published anything concerning this legation of John of Crema. Yet our author establishes that he was sent here so that an anathema against Emperor Henry might be publicly pronounced; for he could command this only by apostolic authority.]

[Note: Col. 1503C–D. From this it is clear that Jordan returned to this city in the same year, 1116, and that the excommunication pronounced by him against Henry fell within the interval between Easter Sunday and the third Sunday of October, according to what has been said above concerning this metropolitan church of Saint Thecla in the note on chapter 28.]

[Note: Col. 1503D. The cause of this excommunication can have been no other than that set forth by Conon, cardinal-bishop of Palestrina, in the aforesaid Lateran council: namely, the shameful seizure and treatment of the supreme pontiff, the dragging into chains and despoiling of the cardinals and Roman nobles in the year 1111. For these acts Henry had elsewhere repeatedly been struck with anathema, as Conrad, abbot of Ursperg, relates for this year.]

But rather, the earthquake which, while this excommunication was in force, utterly shook and convulsed the kingdom of Lombardy, made me, that is, keep watch.

[Note: Col. 1503D. A phrase familiar to our author, used in the sense “being in force.”]

[Note: Col. 1503D–1504C. Roger of Hoveden, an English writer of the same period, writes that this deadly earthquake among the cities of Italy occurred in 1117. He further reports that it lasted for forty days and so violently shook Lombardy that very many buildings collapsed. He adds an event relating to our own city, and therefore not to be omitted: “While men of patrician rank at Milan were sitting together in one tower to deliberate on public affairs, a voice sounded outside in the ears of all, calling one of them by name and urgently asking him to come out. When he delayed, a certain figure appeared and obtained by entreaty that the man who had been called should leave. As he went out, the tower suddenly fell and crushed, in a pitiable disaster, all who were there.” The chronographer of Hildesheim, cited by Pagius, no. 12, recorded the day on which the earth first began to be shaken by this so mournful a ruin of buildings: namely, the third day of January in the aforesaid year.]

At that time peoples who had seen great destructions in cities and in every kind of place, especially in churches, reported that drops of blood had fallen from heaven like rain; that they had seen monstrous births and many other portents in the air, waters, mountains, plains, and woods; and that they had heard subterranean thunder. In this divine visitation, even those who seemed to be priests did not know where to flee.

[Note: Col. 1504C. These matters are described more fully by Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book X, and by Conrad Lycosthenes in his *Chronicle of Prodigies* for this year.]
