But the cities of Lombardy and their bishops, having heard the summons of Archbishop Jordan and of the consuls of that same city, assembled at Milan in the Pratum Sanctum—what is called the Brolium—where the archbishop and the consuls set up two platforms.

[Note: Col. 1504C–1505C. Puricelli judged that this Milanese council was convened toward the end of February 1117 in his *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 325. He was led by the argument that our Landulf asserts in the following chapter that Paschal II lived no more than ten and a half months after this meeting and the time of the earthquake. But, besides his error in asserting that Paschal died in mid-January—as will be shown in the note on the following chapter—it must also be observed that Landulf fixes the date of Paschal’s death not from the Milanese council but from the meeting at the Arengum, where Jordan granted remission of sins, as the words placed at the beginning of the following chapter show.

I should therefore believe, in accordance with the narrative here, that this synod assembled earlier, about the middle of February. This may be inferred from the words placed a little below: “at that time of the earthquake,” which certainly indicate that these events occurred within the forty-day period of the earthquake noted above from Hoveden. Nor can an earlier date be fixed if some travelling time must be allowed to the suffragan bishops summoned between the proclamation and celebration of this synod in that year.

Yet, if I must candidly confess the truth, it seems very difficult to credit prudently that provincial bishops would have wished to flock to this city during a raging earthquake, and that the synod mentioned could have been celebrated with such solemnity. It would therefore not be unreasonable to suppose that the events narrated below as occurring after the council in fact happened at the time of the earthquake, but that our Landulf assembled them here out of order in order to show that Jordan’s disposition toward him was always hostile; while the council itself was postponed until, once fear of the past disaster had been removed, business could be conducted more safely.

On this supposition the observations made by Puricelli may more readily be admitted: namely, that the council was in fact held ten and a half months before Paschal’s death. The synod would then have fallen on 6 March, when peace could return to minds agitated by fear, since the earth had been still from the Ides of February. But lest I be too indulgent toward this opinion of my own, Landulf himself prevents it. In chapter 33 he relates that at the palace of Tortona bishops and cardinals accompanying Callistus II declared void a certain sentence “which Archbishop Jordan, with his consuls, had proclaimed from his platform at the time of the earthquake.” This undoubtedly appears to refer to this council.]

[Note: Col. 1505C–D. No trace can be found in the ancient records of our city identifying this place called *Pratum Sanctum*, “Holy Meadow.” Perhaps the archetype read only an initial letter S., which the copyist thought should be written out as *Sancto*, “holy,” whereas *scilicet*, “namely,” should have been written, as is expressly read in another manuscript of the Ambrosian Library. Certainly, when Landulf speaks in chapter 9 of another synod held by Grossolanus in this same meadow, he adds no word *Sancti*. See what we have reported there.]

On one platform the archbishop stood and sat with bishops, abbots, and prelates of churches; on the other were the consuls with experts in law, legislation, and custom. Around them was an innumerable multitude of clergy and laity, including women and virgins, awaiting the burial of vices and the raising up of virtues.

Nevertheless, neither the priest Ulric of Saint Martin—who still bore the cross for his lord Grossolanus, then living at Rome—nor I, who sought justice for myself and my master, namely the priest Liprand, now buried at Pontida, and bore the cross, obtained a hearing in that assembly or at that time, Jordan forbidding it and raging against me.

At that time of the earthquake Jordan, and in his place Lord Ulric, descended with a certain crowd of wicked men to the Arengum. There he found many persons in my absence; and, since I was wholly unaware of this gathering or Arengum, Roland, the freedman of Lanfrid, lied before Jordan and all that people, saying that I was a perjurer against Jordan. Jordan, fully aware of this lie, did not correct it, but was silent. The vice-dominus, however, firmly excused me, although he knew beyond doubt that Roland had lied.

[Note: Col. 1505D. Manuscript A.2 reads *paucorum*, “few,” instead of *pravorum*, “wicked.”]

[Note: Col. 1505D. Galvaneus Flamma describes this in his *Greater Chronicle*, chapter 43: “Between the major church and the church of Saint Thecla was a certain building called the Arena, now called the Arengum. It was round and large; its walls were high and faced with black and white marble. It was a place more of severity than consolation, because defendants were punished there,” etc. Tristanus Calchus mentions this Arengum under the year 1162; Puricelli discusses it at greater length in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 441.]

But I, much more troubled, came the next day to the place called the archbishop’s Brolium. There, holding a cross and a pledge in my hands, and seeking a hearing from Jordan himself and from all the people assembled there through fear of the collapse of buildings, in order that he might hear the Mass and my address while justice was preserved for me, Jordan himself shouted abusively at me: “Landulf, man of the devil, be silent!”

[Note: Col. 1505D–1506C. In a manuscript catalogue of the archbishops of Milan in the Ambrosian Library, written by the priest Antonius Confanonerius in 1408, the following is read concerning our Archbishop Alamannus or Adelmannus: “Outside the city was the Brolium, where markets are now held on the sixth day [Friday], called the archiepiscopal Brolium; there, at appointed hours of the day, he heard certain pious causes.” Perhaps the archbishop’s Brolium stood in that area which even now chiefly serves for markets, especially for horses, every Saturday, and which extends in a broad plain before the Ticinese Gate.]

[Note: Col. 1506C. It was an Italian custom for persons with grievances to carry a cross in their hands, as Radevicus testifies in his continuation of Otto of Freising, book II, chapter 5. Felix Osius discusses the matter at length in his notes on the history of Morena, no. 64. To this custom must be referred the many places in this history where Landulf tells of a cross borne by himself or others.]

[Note: Col. 1506C. That is, a *vadium*, a security or surety. The old judicial form required a pledge to be given for pursuing an appeal. An example may be found in the later part of Roger of Hoveden’s *Annals*, p. 693 in my edition. See more in Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Vadium*. For the ancients, *vadari* or *vadimonium sistere* meant to promise, undertake, and obey, as in Brissonius, *On the Meaning of Words*.]

[Note: Col. 1506C–D. From this also it may be recognized that these events occurred while the earthquake was still continuing.]

And when I saw that almost all the people and populace were giving attention to my voice, he sprang from his chair in fury and said: “If you hear him, you will not hear me.” Then the frantic crowd of people, forgetful of the law to which it had sworn, shouted at me: “Get away from here, get away!” I therefore withdrew from them.

[Note: Col. 1506D. That is, the public liberty established by authority, by which everyone was permitted in that place to state his case.]

But those who received peace and remission of sins there and elsewhere, both from this pontiff and from his suffragans and consuls, were not long regarded as merciful or peaceable.

[Note: Col. 1506D. Understand remission as regards temporal punishment, which is the gift of indulgences. It was not plenary, since bishops at that time were extremely sparing in dispensing such indulgences, as Thomassin teaches in *On Ancient and Modern Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 15, no. 3 and following. Certainly, at the solemn dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1100, our Archbishop Anselm granted visitors only remission of a third part of their sins, as is read in a document reported by Puricelli under that year. From Urspergensis it is clear that Paschal II himself, supreme pontiff, granted only an indulgence of forty days in 1116 to those visiting and venerating the thresholds of the apostles.]

## CHAPTER XXXII. After Paschal’s death, the emperor caused Burdinus to be chosen as antipope, and named him Gregory.

Pope Paschal, to whom religion and remission of sins then belonged, lived no more than ten and a half months after this meeting and the time of the earthquake.

[Note: Col. 1507A–B. CHAPTER XXXII.—Paschal died on 21 January 1118, as Peter the Deacon, the chronographer of Malmesbury, and Pandulf of Pisa testify. Although the latter, in his *Life of Paschal*, places the date on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, this is perhaps a copyist’s error: the text should read the twelfth day before the Kalends, as may be inferred from Pandulf himself, who states that, after three days of a vacant see, the election of Paschal’s successor took place on 25 February.]

At the time of his death, the emperor, having received the embassy of the Romans, hastened from the region of the people of Turin to go to Rome.

[Note: Col. 1507B–C. That is, he was informed of the hurried election as supreme pontiff of John of Gaeta, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, under the name Gelasius II. A life of this pontiff, composed by his intimate Pandulf of Pisa with extensive commentaries by Constantine Cajetan, has been published in volume III of the collection.]

[Note: Col. 1507C–D. The abbot of Ursperg writes for 1118 that Henry set out not from the district of Turin but from the Paduan territory to make for Rome; Gobelinus Persona, age VI, chapter 58, and Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, report the same. What if Landulf wrote “from the regions of Treviso,” and a copyist, misunderstanding the word, substituted “of Turin”? If the reading given by the younger Pagius in *Gregory the Antipope*, no. 57, were authentic—where, citing the words of the abbot of Ursperg, he reads “while he remained in the regions of the Po” instead of “in the Paduan regions”—then Landulf’s report of Henry’s departure from the Turin region toward Rome could be reconciled. Yet since in the chronicles of the abbot of Ursperg which I examined the reading is plainly *Paduanis regionibus*, “the Paduan regions,” and I have seen no other manuscript, I leave the matter undecided. It seems to me that it can be clarified only from diplomas, should any emerge.]

[Note: Col. 1507D. Falco recorded the day of Emperor Henry’s entrance into the City: namely, the second of March. For he had entered Rome in the silence of night, with ambushes prepared.]

From that city, together with the Romans, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, he sent envoys to Gaeta, instructing John of Gaeta, elected pope, and the cardinals and bishops who were with him at Gaeta, to return to Rome and, in the church of Blessed Peter, to do jointly with them what ought justly and canonically to be done concerning the appointment of a pope.

[Note: Col. 1507D. That is, Gaeta, the native city of Gelasius II. The aforesaid Falco relates the reason for the departure: “When the apostolic bishop had thus secretly learned of the king’s arrival, remembering how that king had seized his predecessor Lord Pope Paschal and the cardinals by fraud and deceit, he immediately summoned the cardinals and entered the River Tiber. Then, sailing upon the sea with favorable winds, they reached Calenum—or, more correctly, Gaeta, as Pagius also notes.”]

[Note: Col. 1508B. Falco relates this embassy differently. He says that Henry sent messengers to Gelasius II asking him to return to the City, since he desired most willingly to be present at and confirm his consecration. But the supreme pontiff, having perceived the emperor’s wickedness, rebuked the envoys and dismissed them without result.]

But on the seventh day before the Ides of the same March, in the church of Blessed Peter, in the presence of Emperor Henry, the Roman people, and the attending clergy, there was in some manner reported the answer which the emperor’s Roman envoys, or those together with the electors, had heard and received from the aforesaid pope-elect: namely, that in the coming September he would be at Milan or Cremona with the cardinals and bishops of the provinces; and that then the Romans and the emperor should sufficiently learn from the teaching of the cardinals and bishops what was to be done concerning himself, elected pope, or the appointment of another.

[Note: Col. 1508B–C. Gelasius himself relates the same matters in his letter to the Gauls, printed in volume X of Labbe’s *Councils*, p. 817. There, however, Gelasius says that the controversy to be decided was the one between the Church and the kingdom, not the matter here added concerning an election already made or a pope to be appointed. Nor does he say that he would be at Milan or Cremona in the coming September, but on the approaching feast of Saint Luke, celebrated on 18 October.]

But the Romans, judging that this answer would not be sufficient or consonant either with laws and canons or with their demands, were stirred up and cried: “Do those men wish to transfer the honor of Rome to Cremona? Far be it! Rather, so that everywhere we may suppress the schemes of those who have gone out from us and fled to Gaeta, let us choose for ourselves, according to the authority of laws and canons, a wise and good pope”—or words in a similar Roman form.

Master Guarnerius of Bologna and many jurists assembled the Roman people to elect a pope. A certain fluent reader, from the pulpit of Saint Peter, expounded in a lengthy reading the decrees of pontiffs concerning the appointment of a pope. When these had been read and explained, the whole people elected as pope a certain bishop of Spain who was there with the emperor.

[Note: Col. 1508C. Otto Morena mentions him in his *History of the Affairs of Lodi* under 1158, saying that he was teacher of four distinguished doctors of law whom Frederick Barbarossa summoned to the conference begun with the princes of Italy at Roncaglia. He also gives the distich which Guarnerius composed at the end of his life, when his pupils asked which of those four doctors he designated as his successor in the chair.]

[Note: Col. 1508C. That is, “assembled.”]

[Note: Col. 1508C–D. Gelasius himself teaches in the letter mentioned above on what day this impious election took place. He writes that it was forty-four days after his own election: namely, 9 or 10 March. Our author agrees, placing the formation of this deadly schism on the seventh day before the Ides of that month.]

[Note: Col. 1508D. This pseudopontiff had first been bishop of Coimbra; then, after the death of Saint Gerard, archbishop of Braga, he had succeeded to that see in 1110. Gelasius II himself testifies in the letter cited above that he had given him the pallium, when, under Paschal II, he held the office of cardinal-deacon and chancellor.]

The emperor led the man so elected to the pulpit. When asked his name, he said: “My name is Burdinus; but when Pope Urban ordained me bishop, he named me Mauritius.”

[Note: Col. 1508D. Writers debate various matters concerning this name, as Baluzius relates in the life included in volume III of his *Miscellanies*. He follows Rodericus a Chuna in the *Ecclesiastical History of the Archbishops of Braga* in believing that this was his family surname.]

[Note: Col. 1508D–1509B. Whether this name was first bestowed upon him by the supreme pontiff or was his own proper name cannot readily be determined from this. Distinguished writers cited by Baluzius in the place mentioned report that he was called Mauritius Burdinus. Perhaps, since he had previously commonly called himself merely Burdinus, the supreme pontiff called him Mauritius from his baptismal name, according to the custom by which bishops included no mention of their family in their titles.]

Then someone dressed in ecclesiastical garb cried from the pulpit to the people three times: “Do you desire Lord Mauritius as pope?” Three times they replied and cried: “We do.” Then that man, with the other clergy standing by, opened a book over the elect and covered him with a mantle; in a loud voice he cried: “And we praise and confirm Lord Gregory.”

Thus, when the election had been carried out in this manner, the emperor called this pope of his Gregory—Gregory VIII—and led him through the Castle of Saint Angelo to the Lateran palace.

[Note: Col. 1509B. That is, the eighth of this name.]

In that palace this pontiff, if it is permissible to say so, sat in the chair, took a meal, and spent the night. The following day, without delay, the same pope received the same emperor at the palace and returned with him to the church of Saint Peter. Before its altar and upon its altar, he promoted members of the clergy to orders in the presence of the emperor and many Romans on that same day, celebrated Mass, lived there for several days and months, received oaths of fealty, and preached splendidly concerning the law of God and ecclesiastical customs, without any resentment. He proclaimed peace for the kingdom and for himself, and jeered at his pope, John of Gaeta, elected pope.

[Note: Col. 1509B–C. It is certain from Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 64, that Burdinus remained at Rome under the name Gregory VIII until 2 June 1118. On that day, then the feast of Pentecost, the same author testifies that he crowned Emperor Henry again.]

[Note: Col. 1509C. Or, “mocked contemptuously.”]

Until the emperor, returning again to Germany, left his Gregory, his pope, as if secure in the city of Sutri.

[Note: Col. 1509C. Peter the Deacon, in the passage cited, states that Henry returned to Liguria immediately after the coronation. The continuator of Sigebert’s *Chronicle* further adds under 1118: “Emperor Henry returns from Italy to his homeland in Lotharingia; and, according to the saying, ‘He who is feared by many must necessarily fear many,’ he invites the princes of the realm, who had conspired against him, to peace—now by threats, now by blandishments, now by force, now by satisfaction.”]

[Note: Col. 1509C. Another reading in a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library has *securum duxit*, “led him to safety,” but incongruously. For we learn from Pandulf’s *Life of Gelasius* that, when Henry departed, Burdinus did not immediately seek Sutri but remained for a time at Rome. Speaking of Henry, Pandulf says: “He returned to Germany by the route by which he had come, leaving his idol in the City.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Pope Gelasius, consecrated at Gaeta, flees to Genoa and Pisa, and finally to France, where he dies.

At this time, when this Gregory promoted a certain cleric to orders before the altar of Saint Peter, the Gaetan, elected pope and a priest, was solemnly consecrated at Gaeta and called Pope Gelasius II. He also sat for several days and months in the apostolic chair in the Lateran and occupied that palace with cardinals and bishops.

[Note: Col. 1509C–D. CHAPTER XXXIII.—Read *papa*, “pope,” as is correctly written in another manuscript of the Ambrosian Library.]

[Note: Col. 1509D–1510A. The legitimate supreme pontiff Gelasius was consecrated at Gaeta on about the same day on which the pseudopontiff Burdinus was proclaimed at Rome, as we said above. Since he was only a deacon at the time of his promotion to the supreme see, and since, according to Falco of Benevento in the passage cited, sacred orders were conferred only in a fasting season, that is, in the Ember Days, he could not have been ordained priest except on 9 March—the Ember Saturday of spring in that year—and consecrated Roman pontiff on the 10th. Therefore Pagius, under 1118, no. 6, observes that Pandulf’s text was wrongly copied by a scribe where it reads: “Gelasius is consecrated pope before the Kalends of March.”]

[Note: Col. 1509D–1510C. It is clear from what was said above that Gelasius II sat in Rome for only one month and a few days when he first ascended Saint Peter’s chair. Created supreme pontiff on 25 January, he was forced to leave the City on 2 March, fearing Henry, who was secretly hastening by night toward the portico of Saint Peter. After Burdinus and Henry departed Rome following the feast of Pentecost, Gelasius returned to the City, though more in the guise of a pilgrim than of a lord, as Pandulf, companion of that journey, puts it. Yet the excellent pontiff was then able to remain there only a short time also, because Henry’s supporters again rose against him in arms. Thus, scarcely after the Kalends of September had passed, he chose to set sail for Pisa and migrate to Gaul, as the already-mentioned Falco attests.]

Then he went by ship to Pisa, Genoa, and many cities and places situated upon the sea.

[Note: Col. 1510C. Gelasius left everywhere glorious memorials of his piety and pontifical office. It is not the place here to list them, nor the maritime places which he traversed on his journey and which our author indicates, since these may conveniently be read in Pandulf, published in earlier volumes, and in both Pagii.]

His ship put in at Saint-Gilles, and he entered the kingdom of France. Having been kindly received by the princes of that kingdom, he departed this world at Cluny.

[Note: Col. 1510C. Pandulf, cited above, writes that Gelasius reached the port of Saint-Gilles with his ship. Yet since the shrine of Saint Giles, situated in the province of Occitania, lies one league from the River Rhône, Pagius asserts in the place cited above, no. 14, that he came to the Rhône.]

[Note: Col. 1510C. Falco likewise reports this of Gelasius’s arrival in Gaul: “Immediately all the archbishops, bishops, and other nobles received him with inexpressible joy and immense honor.”]

[Note: Col. 1510D. Read *Cluniaci*, “at Cluny.” When he was suffering a very severe illness at Mâcon, he urgently ordered that he be carried there, as Hugh, monk of Cluny, testifies in Pagius under 1119, no. 3. There he ended his life, consumed by pleurisy, on 29 January 1119.]

That bishop of Vienne, born of royal stock, succeeded him and held at Reims the synod which Pope Gelasius himself had convened. But he first intended to hold a conference with the emperor. Concerning this council or conference, I do not strain the finger of my sixty-year-old age to write more.

[Note: Col. 1510D. Guido, archbishop of Vienne, succeeded Gelasius under the name Callistus II after an interpontificate of two days, on the Kalends of February, as Pagius decides against Ordericus and Pape-broch in the place cited, no. 5.]

[Note: Col. 1510D. His father was William, count of Burgundy; he had a sister named Gilla, who, married to Humbert II, count of Maurienne or Savoy, bore Adelaide, whom she gave in marriage in 1115 to Louis VI, king of the Franks, as Pagius attests in the place cited above. Pandulf writes in his *Life* that he traced a line of kinship from the kings of Germany, France, and England.]

[Note: Col. 1511A–C. Eadmer, a contemporary writer cited by Pagius in the same place, no. 2, reports that Gelasius II had summoned a council to be held at Reims in mid-Lent. Callistus II fulfilled Gelasius’s purpose, and the council was held at Reims on 20 October 1119, as reported by Labbe, volume X.]

[Note: Col. 1511C. The sequence of this conference—genuinely arranged but never begun because of Henry’s bad faith—is clearly described in the little commentary of Hesso the scholastic on the Acts of this Council of Reims, included in Labbe’s *Councils*, volume X, col. 872.]

[Note: Col. 1511C. From this the year in which Landulf came into the light may be deduced: he must have been about sixty years old if the calculation of his years is taken from the celebration of this council. Yet because Landulf states in the first chapter of this history that he began writing during the time when Robald was already wearing the mitre of the archbishopric of Milan, his age must be reckoned only from 1135, when Robald was elected archbishop, or from either of the two subsequent years in which this history ends. Therefore it must be said that Landulf was born about 1076.]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. War arises between the Milanese and the people of Como, in which the city of Como is destroyed.

But I return to setting forth in advance the unrest of the Lombards and my own distress. For after the emperor had departed from Rome [Note: [Col. 1511D] That is, after the month of June 1118, as was said above.], and had withdrawn from the aforesaid Pope Gregory, or Burdinus, the hand of Guido, bishop of Como, and of his knights and citizens immediately and violently seized Landulf of Carcano, an ordinary cleric and minister [Col. 1511B] of the Church of Milan [Note: [Col. 1511D] That is, a deacon. The cause of this violent arrest reported by our author was that Landulf had been appointed bishop of that city by Emperor Henry against the same Guido, who adhered to Gelasius II, the legitimate pope; as our Landulf relates in the course of this chapter.], and during the arrest killed Otto, nephew of that Landulf [Note: [Col. 1511D] In this disturbance Tristan Calco, book VII of the *Historia patriae*, and Ughelli, in *Episcopi Comenses*, no. 48, report that not so much Otto as another of his nephews named Bolanus—and indeed even Landulf himself, the pseudo-bishop—was killed when arms were taken up; but falsely. For from our author it is clear that the said Landulf was soon afterward rescued from chains by the Milanese, as is related below.], and a distinguished captain of the city of Milan.

Thereupon Jordan, archbishop of Milan, entered an assembly of knights and citizens crying out against the men of Como [Note: [Col. 1511D] Tristan Calco, in the cited passage, recounts the event which supplied fuel for inflaming Milanese anger against the people of Como; it is also related by Benedetto Giovio, book I of the *Historia Novocomensis* [Col. 1512B]: namely, that the wives and relatives of the slain brought torn garments still stained with blood to Milan and, with tears [Col. 1512C] and piteous wailing, displayed them to Archbishop Jordan and the whole people, begging that such savage and inhuman cruelty should not go unpunished. All were moved to compassion by the tears and the wretched appearance of the mourners, and it was at last decreed that the wrong should be pursued by war. Yet our Landulf gives another motive which Jordan had for arming his people against the men of Como: namely, the harms which they had inflicted upon the property and persons of his archbishopric of Milan.]. There, by recounting and lamenting the many evils which the men of Como had done to the property and persons of the archbishopric of Milan, he inflamed the assembled crowd to exact vengeance.

At the same time, with the doors of the churches shut, Archbishop Jordan denied his people entry [Note: [Col. 1512C] That is, he threatened the penalty of an interdict.], unless they should avenge the malice of the men of Como with the material sword. [Col. 1512A] Finally, at the sound of this bishop’s voice and by his command, the people of Milan began to wage war against the men of Como [Note: [Col. 1512C] Sigonius asserted in *De regno Italiae*, book X, that this war against the people of Como began in 1120; wrongly, however, as is clear from our author, who assigns it to the same year in which Emperor Henry departed Rome—that is, 1118, as we have already noted.]. In their first expedition, when the Milanese pitched camp at Caneto [Note: [Col. 1512C] A district adjoining two notable villages in the territory of Como, namely Grandate and Lucino.], they occupied the city of Como itself and freed from captivity Landulf, who had received investiture of the bishopric of Como from the king [Note: [Col. 1512C] Namely Henry IV, who had installed him as bishop in place of Hartwic, bishop of that city, formerly appointed by Henry himself and dead in 1093 or 1094, as Aloysius Tattus first teaches in the *Annales Comenses*, under 1093, no. 18. For this reason Landulf was excommunicated by Urban II and deprived of episcopal dignity in 1095, as the same Tattus relates for that year.] and ordination from the patriarch of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 1512D] Namely Ulric, whom the additions to Ughelli’s *Italia sacra*, vol. V, Venetian edition, no. 57, prove to have lived beyond 1118.]—his metropolitan.

But the men of Como, immediately restored to power, drove out the Milanese; and those whom they found fallen in flight or burdened with booty they left to death and the edge of the sword [Note: [Col. 1512D] Calco describes this battle expressly; you may read more in the anonymous historian of Como.]. They killed Guilicione Bucardus, Lanterius Sicheri, one of my own nephews, and many distinguished knights and citizens of Milan who resisted those pursuing the fugitives.

[Col. 1512B] In this crisis [Note: [Col. 1512D] That is, in this same year, 1118.] the marquises and counts of Lombardy assembled at Milan, so that there, before the suffragan and provincial bishops, they might set forth the emperor’s innocence and bring the emperor himself into the good favor of the archbishop and bishops. The bishops, therefore, seated in the Milanese palace with the archbishop, attentively heard the marquises and counts faithfully speaking on behalf of their lord. Because of their arguments, many judged the emperor free from the guilt of excommunication [Note: [Col. 1512D] Henry had been excommunicated in several councils, and even in our own church of St. Thecla, as Landulf recounts at the beginning of chapter 31. Finally, Gelasius II had struck him with anathema together with his idol—that is, Burdinus—while he was staying at Capua, according to Abbot of Ursperg under this year.].

But while the archbishop and bishops disputed vigorously against the marquises and counts, [Col. 1513A] dukes and kings [Note: [Col. 1513C] Pagius explains this as the rights claimed by the kings of Lombardy. Certainly it is known from the histories of that age that the kings of Italy intruded very greatly into ecclesiastical rights; against these our archbishop was declaiming.], the knights and citizens of Milan swore in the church courtyard to wage war against the people of Como until they had destroyed the settlement and little colony [Note: [Col. 1513C] Two suburbs of the city of Como, which, like two arms, enclosed the lake flowing between them.] and had likewise razed the city itself. The party of Bishop Guido of Como opposed this oath [Note: [Col. 1513C] Namely, that part of the people which adhered to Guido, bishop of Como.] [Note: [Col. 1513C] Read: “opposed” (*restitit*).]. But Arduin, advocate of that bishopric [Note: [Col. 1513C] Tattus, under the year 1124, was mistaken by supposing from this name that it was the family’s gentilicial name; accordingly, under no. 114 he explicitly maintained that this man sprang from the family of advocates [Col. 1513D]. Yet anyone moderately versed in history will easily discover how far this is from the truth. It was the name of an office, as our author clearly shows and Du Cange explains at length in the *Glossarium*, where he discusses advocates of churches, stating that their duty was to protect the rights and goods of churches; hence they were also commonly called defenders.], agreed and labored much to ensure that the oath was imposed.

Nevertheless, the endeavor of both parties—Guido’s and that advocate’s—is rightly or wrongly called a seedbed of iniquity. For in what seed has anyone living seen so many most grievous works? From this seed many splendid and most pleasant camps and very strong towns, with their inhabitants and villages on both sides, were burned and destroyed, though not equally. Many warships too [Col. 1513B], with their crews and an innumerable multitude of people, lie sunk in the lakes. At last the city itself, emptied of its inhabitants, daily beholds its own ruin with tearful eyes [Note: [Col. 1513D] This war, grievous through the hatreds of a decade, hot with the continual slaughter of both sides, and of deadly memory because of the lamentable ruin of castles and districts, was described in large part by Corio and by Calco, book VII of the *Historia patriae*. Yet it was treated in a complete poem by an anonymous man of Como living at that time, which was recently published here with learned notes by the distinguished P. Joseph Maria Stampa, most dear to me for the charm of his intellect and the excellence of his learning. I therefore judge it superfluous to linger longer here, freely leaving to him the glory of having elucidated this war.].

Or again, many among the clergy and people of the whole world, because of the divergent parties of the Roman pontiff and of the Patrician and advocate of that city and church [Note: [Col. 1514C] Namely, the schism of Burdinus, involving the Catholic Church.], are said, whether piously or impiously, to contend to the destruction of souls and the greatest ruin of bodies. I, however, mindful of these evils, endure diverse disturbances—not because schism dwells in my mind, but because I do not consent to schismatics usurping my property. Concerning them I have sought, and seek, justice from pontiffs, priests, knights, citizens, consuls, and kings.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Before Pope Calixtus at Tortona and Piacenza, the historian complains unsuccessfully against Jordan.

[Col. 1513C]

While the war between the people of Como and Milan was continuing, [Col. 1514A] along with that of their bishops and consuls, I saw Lord Pope Calixtus and Archbishop Jordan sit in the palace at Tortona with many distinguished ecclesiastical and secular men [Note: [Col. 1514C] CHAPTER XXXV.—In 1120 Calixtus II, “having traversed the regions of Provence and crossed the difficult Alps,” in the words of Cardinal Aragon in his published *Life*, vol. III, “arrived with pleasure at St. Ambrose” (a town near Susa); “thence he descended to the populous cities of Lombardy,” and remained at Tortona about the end of Lent.]. In their presence I set forth the ground of my complaint: namely, against Lord Jordan. In making my complaint, I introduced the wrongs and homicide [Note: [Col. 1514C] Landulf says this metaphorically, of his rights as though in some manner cut down; for a dead man could not complain.] which his hand had inflicted upon me, notwithstanding the letter which Lord Pope Gelasius had sent him on my behalf. A copy of it is as follows:

> “G., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JORDAN, archbishop of Milan: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “This brother Landulf complains that he has been driven out of his church. But the demand made of him [Note: [Col. 1514D] Read *queritur*, as in other Ambrosian Library manuscripts.]—that he furnish proof of his title [Note: [Col. 1514D] A. 1: *cohibeat*, ‘restrain.’] according to [Col. 1514B] Blessed Gregory—is shown to be absurd. For what he says must be proved in accordance with the pronouncements of that same blessed Gregory and the enactments of the laws; otherwise, such a charge is not to be brought against him upon grounds of this kind. But unless another cause prevents it, let him be restored to his church. Given at Gaeta, on the Ides of March [Note: [Col. 1514D] Namely, in 1118; for he had arrived there about the sixth day of the same month.].”

Jordan himself, having nothing with which to excuse himself and his party, remained silent there before the pope. When Abraham, priest and master of his chapel, asked him, he said: “What ought I to answer him? He does not regard me as bishop.”

Then Lord Lambert, bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 1514D] Later supreme pontiff under the name Honorius II.], and spokesman for Lord Calixtus [Note: [Col. 1514D] This word is used for an advocate. Du Cange offers many examples in the *Glossarium*, especially this one from the *Life of St. Willibald*: “And in the celebration of the council, as true chancellor and spokesman of the council, he sat immediately to the right of the archbishop.”], almost like the pope [Note: [Col. 1514D] Another reading in an Ambrosian Library manuscript more correctly has *quasi propria*, “as his own”; for the particle *quasi*, frequently employed by our author, diminishes nothing in the word to which it is added, as we have already noted in chapter 1.], took me by the hand as I stood and was saying: “Lord, must I answer these things?” He then said to me publicly:

> “Brother, you have lodged your complaint; but January is not the time for treading grapes in the winepress [Note: [Col. 1514D] A popular proverb by which one is accused of importunity; for the month then current was not January but April.]. For the lord archbishop has come to us on account of those who are plotting against [Col. 1515A] the emperor’s favor [Note: [Col. 1515C] For our Archbishop Jordan had fought vigorously in the Milanese council mentioned above against the marquises and counts who had assembled there to defend Henry’s innocence and bring him into the good favor of Jordan and the suffragans.]. Therefore we now wish to hear of his consolation, not his disturbance, and to discover with him how we may promptly and prosperously go to Rome with this our lord and obtain his see. Meanwhile the archbishop may take counsel with these and his other brethren, and do you good.”

Jordan, therefore, and his company spoke of their wealth in that evening hour; and on the following day he came down from the palace. On the third day, which was Palm Sunday [Note: [Col. 1515C] In this year, 1120, it fell on 11 April.], in the church of St. Martian, he ordained as bishop Peter, elected bishop of Tortona, though now deposed [Note: [Col. 1515C] Ughelli, in *Episcopi Derthonenses*, no. 52, testifies that Innocent II deprived him of the bishopric of Tortona at the council of Pisa because of the most manifest faults of his life.], with his suffragans.

In the same city, likewise on the feast of Palm Sunday, Guazo, a cleric from Orco [Note: [Col. 1515C] A. 1 and 2: *Oreo*.], and reader of the Church of Milan, received a charter subscribed by bishops [Col. 1515B] and cardinals, confirming that Guazo’s marriage was lawful. Archbishop Jordan, together with his advisers, had proclaimed from his platform, at the time of the earthquake [Note: [Col. 1515C] Landulf here refers to the second Milanese council, for the more solemn celebration of which Jordan had ordered a double platform erected in the meadow of Brolo; see chapter 31.], that it was adultery.

On the next day, Monday, the lord pope-elect left Tortona. Ulric, vice-dominus of Milan, went with him as far as Piacenza, while Archbishop Jordan returned to Milan. When this vice-dominus tried to excuse his archbishop, he said to me, as I repeated my complaint in the palace at Piacenza with feeling: “You have a fierce spirit.” A certain brother of mine, named Liprand, answered him: “If he wished to act in accordance with [Col. 1516A] fierceness, he could in one day raise five thousand men to fight for him with weapons of war.” The vice-dominus agreed with this statement.

Then the pope rose and entered his chamber; and the other powerful men present there, bishops and cardinals alike, began to speak of their resources [Note: [Col. 1515C] Perhaps “wealth,” as was related shortly before concerning Jordan.]. But I left them and came to the chamber. The lord pope graciously came out to me and said:

> “Brother, money is a thing by which a man can do much good. You have no money, and this is not now the time for pursuing your cause [Note: [Col. 1515C] That is, examining it.]. But God is able to give; and after this Easter festival has passed [Note: [Col. 1515D] That Calixtus remained at Piacenza even after the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection is inferred from a diploma issued there on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, indiction XIII, in the year 1121 from the Incarnation of the Lord according to the Pisan era, the second year of his pontificate, in favor of the church of St. Evasio of Casale. Benedetto Collio of the town of Lu in Montferrat, a most devoted lover of antiquity, most courteously communicated to me his chronological manuscript history of that church, into which he had inserted this still unpublished document from its archive.], I shall direct the archbishop through the vice-dominus not to trouble you, but to treat you kindly.”

But after that Easter festival the Romans promptly and solemnly received Pope Calixtus himself [Note: [Col. 1515D] Calixtus reached Rome on 3 June, as is clear from the letter of Abbot Aegino in Baronius under this year, 1120.]. [Col. 1516B] He then seized Pope Burdinus at Sutri together with the Romans [Note: [Col. 1515D] What is narrated here of Burdinus, the pseudo-pontiff, belongs not to 1120 but to the following year. From Falco of Benevento we learn that he was defeated by arms, captured, and brought to Rome; there, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, mounted on a camel and stripped of his garments in utmost disgrace [Col. 1516C], he made a most shameful spectacle of himself. Cardinal Aragon relates this procession of public mockery more fully in the previously cited *Life of Calixtus*, which see in vol. III.], and afterward confined him in the place called Cana [Note: [Col. 1516C] The place-name is corrupt; read *Cava*. We read in Cardinal Aragon, cited above, that Burdinus, first confined in the fortress of Fumone and then conveyed to the monastery of Cava, “persisting in his rebellion, ended his life” there. Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. III, describes the matter differently. He says that in the following year, 1122, Burdinus was taken by Calixtus II from Cava and committed for custody to Janula, a fortress on a cliff overhanging the city of San Germano, on the testimony of the Anonymous of Monte Cassino edited by Antonio Caracciolo; finally, that Honorius II removed him from there in 1124 and transferred him to the fortress of Fumone, not far from the Hernican city of Alatri, where he lived to extreme old age and at last died.].

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Jordan’s death, Ulric is elected archbishop and sits at the right hand of Pope Calixtus despite the Ravenna archbishop’s opposition.

Almighty God made Jordan neither gentle nor kindly toward me through Lord Gelasius’s letter nor through Calixtus’s legate [Note: [Col. 1516D] Namely Ulric, the vice-dominus, whom Calixtus, in the preceding chapter, had promised to commission so that, upon returning from Piacenza to Milan, he might convey the papal order to Jordan not to trouble Landulf, but to treat him kindly.], but took him from the world [Note: [Col. 1516D] Jordan died on 4 October 1120, as is gathered from old catalogues of the archbishops of Milan. Calco, who writes that Jordan died before 1118, must therefore be corrected; for how could he have met Calixtus II when the latter came to Tortona in 1120, as Landulf related in the preceding chapter, if he had been removed by fate two years earlier?]. By the favor of the priest Nazarius, primicerius, and of others whom I held, and hold, in suspicion, Ulric the vice-dominus succeeded Jordan [Note: [Col. 1516D] This Ulric, whom others call Henry, Honorius, or Honoricus, was elected archbishop of Milan on 17 November of the same year, 1120—not 1121, as Ughelli wrongly asserted in his account of Ulric. This follows plainly from old catalogues, as may be seen in the cited *Exegesis* of Papebroch, no. 106.]. He oppressed me in almost the same manner as Jordan did—“almost,” because in the common office and benefice he did not prevent me from associating with the ordinary and *decuman* priests [Col. 1517A].

Nevertheless, while that Ulric was archbishop, when Pope Calixtus held a synod at Rome [Note: [Col. 1517B] Baronius assigned this first general Lateran council to 1122; but Pagius, under the year 1123, no. 1, proves from ancient writers that it was held in the following year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.], I, driven out of my church and stripped of my own property and allods, set forth my cause before Lord Pope Calixtus and his court sitting in the Lateran palace; and, in order to explain it in the synod, I entered the synod.

In that synod, out of regard for the ancient dignity of the Church of Milan [Note: [Col. 1517B] The primatial dignity of the Church of Milan above the other churches of Italy after that of Rome had already been established in the years 501, 502, and 503 at three synods held by Pope Symmachus. Archbishop Lawrence of Milan presided over them and subscribed first of all, before the bishop of Ravenna, as may be seen in Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IV, under those years. Consult Puricelli, who in his *Life of Lawrence* fully defends this prerogative of our church against Rubeus, who argued for the Ravennates, chapter 24.] and because I had been Ulric’s fellow student, I grieved deeply at the obstruction which the archbishop of Ravenna was causing him.

For the Ravennate sought the place of sitting immediately at the apostolic’s right in the synod, with no one between [Col. 1517B]. Grossolanus had possessed that place when he was restored [Note: [Col. 1517C] Namely in 1105, when Paschal II held a synod at Rome, as we have already said above against Puricelli, who assigned it to 1103.]. Jordan also, who succeeded Grossolanus, had held the same place when that same Grossolanus sought to depose him [Note: [Col. 1517C] Namely, in another synod held by the same Paschal in 1116; recall chapter 29.]. For this reason, and for many other reasons then not recalled [Note: [Col. 1517C] Especially to be remembered was what Arnulf, published in vol. IV of this collection, recounts: namely, when Conrad was to be girded with the imperial diadem at Rome, in the twenty-seventh year of the preceding century, and the archbishop of Ravenna contended with Heribert of Milan before the supreme pontiff for the honor of the right hand, it was decreed [Col. 1517D] in a full synod “that the bishop of Ravenna should in no wise for ever prefer himself to the bishop of Milan.”], Lord Ulric, archbishop of Milan, did not hesitate to claim that place.

Yet that Ulric of Milan [Col. 1518A], on the Monday when the synod was opened and held [Note: [Col. 1517D] From this passage in our Landulf, Pagius confirms, under the year 1123, no. 1, the practice observed in general synods: that the first session never began on a Sunday.], did not appear, although the place was vacant, either in the palace or in the synod. The synod was not held on Tuesday, and the same man of Milan did not enter the palace. But on Wednesday, when the synod was held, that same Ulric, archbishop of Milan, sat immediately at the right hand of Calixtus, the apostolic.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The historian learns that the emperor to whom he was going has died. Ulric dies. Anselm is elected archbishop.

I, while awaiting another day suitable for my case and complaint, suddenly saw and heard that the lord pope, for the purpose of consecrating an altar, dissolved the synod on that Wednesday itself [Note: [Col. 1517D] **CHAPTER XXXVII.**—Cardinal Aragon, in his *Life of Calixtus II*, published in volume III of this collection, has the following: “He built from the foundations, in the Lateran palace, a chapel of St Nicholas for the continual use of the Roman pontiffs.” It is therefore highly probable that this was the altar for whose consecration he dissolved the synod convened in that same palace.], [Col. 1518B] nor afterwards did I hear or see the synod being held by him.

But, trusting in the Lord, I learned that Lord Olric, archbishop of Milan, as the customary practice of usage and law required [Note: [Col. 1517D] What this law or custom was, by whose ancient observance that duty lay upon the archbishop of Milan—namely, to send palm branches to the emperor—cannot be gathered from our histories. Puricelli, in *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 334, takes it as contributing to the honor and splendor of the Church of Milan [Col. 1518B], and for that reason had this period of Landulf, no less than the other concerning the seat gained at the right hand of the supreme pontiff against the archbishop of Ravenna, printed in larger letters. Perhaps one might suppose that, just as an ancient custom prevailed whereby Roman pontiffs send as a gift to eminent princes a golden rose, solemnly blessed on the fourth Sunday of Lent [Col. 1518C], so among the other distinctions of the Ambrosian Church this too was reckoned: that, after a solemn service of prayers, palm branches sprinkled with lustral water were dispatched to Caesar as a sacred gift. Yet, since Beroldus, a writer of these times frequently cited, describes the entire rite of Palm Sunday and of the other feasts but passes over in silence this custom, so splendid, I would not dare burden our glory with an empty assertion.

Certainly, that palm branches were sent to the emperor in use in earlier centuries is strikingly attested by Letter 32 of Pope John VIII to Emperor Charles the Bald, cited by Labbe, volume IX of the Councils, col. 28. It begins: “Among the other things which, as true religion increases on account of your former ecclesiastical deeds, we have judged should be made known to your piety, behold, we send you the prize of green palms”; and later: “For, desiring you to triumph over all adversaries, we have judged that nothing is more fitting to offer you [Col. 1518D] than branches of palms.” Why, however, our Olric is said to have prayed for Henry only at this time, and to have arranged for the gift of palms to be brought to him, I believe occurred because that emperor had in preceding years been in schism; and therefore Olric also, adhering to Calixtus II, the true vicar of Christ, had by no means acknowledged him as king of Italy. Since, therefore, peace between priesthood and empire was confirmed in the Lateran synod, and Henry was restored to the favor of the Roman Church, no obstacle remained to performing what custom and the usage of law required. Our archbishop at once fulfilled his duty: publicly pouring out prayers for him at the altars and sending him palm branches, by which he testified in him to the royal dignity of the Italian empire and at the same time offered an omen of happy events—just as Hincmar relates that a palm was offered to the kings of France when they first ascended the throne.], prayed for King Henry and sent him palm branches into Germany through Thealdus of Landriano, the distinguished notary of the Church of Milan.

Accordingly, so that I might reach the king himself and make my case known to him as to my father [Col. 1519A] and lord, I set out with a boy [Note: [Col. 1519A] That is, a servant. St Ambrose, *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 9, maintains that even servants of advanced age were called *pueri*, “boys,” by their masters. I would have this noted also for the other places in this history where the same word occurs.]. Avoiding the hands of the men of Como, who at that time were making war upon the Milanese, I went to Verona. There I found Bishop Bernard [Note: [Col. 1519A] Ughelli states, in *The Bishops of Verona*, no. 78, that he was born of an illustrious Brescia family, was promoted to the see of Verona in 1123, and remained in it [Col. 1519B] until 1135.], my former dear fellow student, and through him I fared well almost as far as the entrance to the bishopric of Trent.

And when I hoped there to proceed more successfully, I grieved devoutly and tenderly over the death of King Henry [Note: [Col. 1519B] Henry V, called the Younger, ended his last day in 1125, on 10 Kalends of June [23 May], according to the abbot of Ursberg and others cited by Pagi at this year, no. 7.]. Therefore, deeply weary, I returned sorrowfully to my little house [Col. 1520A]. While sitting there and, according to my customary practice, writing for my livelihood, I heard voices and weeping over the death of Archbishop Olric [Note: [Col. 1519B] There is a serious controversy among historians concerning the precise year in which Olric died. Pagi, under 1120, no. 8, says it is certain that his death fell in 1122—read 1123, since Pagi himself testifies that Olric attended the Lateran council in that year. Calchus, Sigonius, Puricelli, Ughelli, and others agree. But the authority of Landulf, the witness to the present event, stands against them. Having heard of the death of Emperor Henry while he was staying near the borders of the bishopric of Trent, Landulf subsequently returned to his homeland; and, while sitting in his own house, he was informed of Olric’s death by the wailing and weeping of the citizens. Thus Olric must be said to have died no earlier than 1125, when Caesar Henry was taken away.

Add that the synodal table and other more ancient [Col. 1519C] catalogues of the Milanese archbishops agree in assigning Olric five years, six months, and eleven days of rule. It follows that he died on 28 May 1126, as I shall show more precisely in the following note. Those celebrated writers were drawn into their opinion, which antedates Olric’s death, by a document reported by Puricelli in *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 336, subscribed by Anselm, archbishop of Milan. The year 1123 is affixed to it; from this they infer that Olric died in that year and that Anselm was elected his successor.

But I observe that this same document begins in the name of Archbishop Olric, and that one reads in it, among fourteen others named there: “The mark of the hands of Anselm de Pusterla, Arialdus Grassi, etc.” Thus it is reasonable to believe that this charter was first drawn up in the year stated, when Olric was archbishop; and, since it concerned certain disputes between the canons and monks of the Ambrosian basilica, it remained delayed and suspended for so long amid fresh difficulties arising daily [Col. 1519D], until, once all matters had been settled under Anselm, his elevation to the archbishopric was confirmed by his subscription.

An example, taken from Puricelli himself, is ready to hand. In his *Dissertation on Nazarius*, chapter 106, no. 8, he produces two charters drawn up in 1173, at the end of each of which one reads: “I, Algisius, archbishop of Milan, have subscribed”; though it is certain that St Galdinus, whom Algisius succeeded, still survived for three years in the governance of this Church and died only in 1176. Puricelli extricates himself in no other way than by maintaining that “those two subscriptions of Algisius were not made immediately at the time when the documents themselves were drawn up, but some years later; perhaps, indeed, further disputes subsequently arose, for whose removal it was helpful that that subscription of the archbishop should be added.” We give Puricelli this same answer in the controversy over the present document.

For me, certainly, from the very context [Col. 1520A] of the documents, this seems the genuine solution of the knot created by year-dates of this kind appended to writings. For that conjecture, however learned it may be, that Anselm and Algisius were elected archbishops during the lifetimes of Olric and Galdinus respectively, as we commonly say, as coadjutors, seems to me entirely novel in this Ambrosian Church. The silence of all ancient and modern writers, especially of our Landulf, forbids us to believe that such a custom was introduced into it. He describes in detail both Anselm’s election after Olric’s death and every event, even one of lesser consequence; he also records Grossulanus and Arderic as vicars appointed in place of absent archbishops, and Robald, bishop of Alba, as placed in charge of the Church after this same Anselm was expelled by the Milanese. Yet he makes no mention whatsoever of another, earlier election of Anselm before Olric’s death.

But the anonymous poet, likewise a contemporary writer, calls Anselm an enthroned archbishop under the year 1123. I do not deny it; but how obscurely and confusedly he writes, so that it is difficult to attain his true meaning! Further, it is neither novel nor injurious to the poet to say that he spoke figuratively: namely, because in that year, while the Lateran council kept Olric at Rome, Anselm acted in the absent archbishop’s place against the men of Como [Col. 1520C] so proudly that, according to a common expression, he could be called “enthroned.” But it would be highly injurious to our historian to suspect that he negligently omitted a matter of such importance—one for which there had been no other example in the Church of Milan, and of which he could not have been ignorant, since such elections were made in a public assembly of the people.

That conjecture is overthrown still more strongly in the case of Algisius. For the *Life of St Galdinus*, which Henschenius judges in the *Acts of the Saints*, under 18 April, to have been composed shortly after the saint’s death, in describing the last day on which St Galdinus rested, still calls Algisius treasurer, saying: “Because he [Galdinus] suffered from great bodily weakness, he ordered the solemn celebration of the Mass to be performed by the above-mentioned treasurer, who afterwards succeeded him.” Moreover, the older catalogues of the Milanese archbishops state explicitly that ten weeks and four days intervened between St Galdinus’s death and Algisius’s election. Nearly all Milanese historians [Col. 1520D], and indeed Sigonius and Ughelli, assert that in this election the clergy were at first divided, some promoting the archpriest and others the archdeacon; finally, lest the election be drawn out further, all turned to the election of Algisius the treasurer. Given these facts, let the reader judge whether Algisius can be believed to have been appointed coadjutor archbishop while St Galdinus was still alive. So as not to burden him longer, I omit other supports.], and afterwards, compelled by the shared feeling of my kinfolk and neighbors, I rose from that very occupation of mine and came to Lord Anselm de Pusterla, elected archbishop by the priest Nazarius, the primicerius, the other regular clergy, and the suffragan bishops [Note: [Col. 1520D] Before establishing the date of this election of Anselm, since I see everything here thrown into confusion in Papebrochius’s exposition of the Milanese archbishops, as also in Puricelli and Pagi, I consider it necessary to go back more deeply into the matter. By comparing the catalogues produced by Papebrochius and Mabillon with another drawn from the library of the metropolitan chapter—perhaps older even than those—which will be inserted into this Collection, I shall clarify by careful examination the succession of our bishops as far as Obertus.

It is certain that Jordan, mentioned above, was elected in 1112 on the Kalends of January [1 January], as Landulf, then present at this election, testifies. Since all catalogues agree that he sat for eight years, nine months, and three days, and died on 4 Nones of October [4 October], it is established that he died in 1120, on the fourth day of October. Olric follows. The likewise concordant catalogues assign him five years, six months, and eleven days on the see, and assert that he died on 5 Kalends of June [28 May]. Reckoning backwards by this number of years and days, we find that he was elected on 17 November 1120, so that after Jordan’s death the see was vacant for one month and thirteen days; and Olric himself died on 28 May 1126.

Next appears Anselm. The catalogues agree concerning the length of his rule, except that the one published by Papebrochius gives the day of death as 19 Kalends of October, while that of the metropolitan church places it on the nineteenth day—understand, Kalends—of September. Yet the mode of counting itself plainly shows that there was a copyist’s error in the first: there is no nineteenth day before the Kalends of October in September, since that month has only eighteen Kalends. Therefore one must read 19 Kalends of September [14 August]. This agrees with our Landulf, who writes that this Anselm died in August. Ten years, one month, and fourteen days are assigned to Anselm’s archbishopric. If [Col. 1521C] you reckon backwards from 14 August, the day on which he died in 1136, you arrive at 30 June 1126, the day on which he was elected, after the see had been vacant for one month and two days following Olric’s death.

In Papebrochius’s catalogue, before there is any mention of Anselm, one reads: “From the election of Anselm de Pusterla to the election of Robald there are nine years, twenty-nine days.” This is not at all expressed in the metropolitan catalogue or in the other one published in the preceding volume. If, therefore, a calculation is made from this number of years and days, Robald’s election must be said to have fallen on 29 July 1135. Nevertheless, this cannot at all be reconciled with the remaining reading of the catalogues. One of them, Papebrochius’s, assigns Robald eleven years, four months, and twenty-three days of rule; the metropolitan catalogue, like Mabillon’s, assigns only ten years, in addition to four months and twenty-six days. I believe, however, that an error crept into the number eleven printed in Papebrochius’s catalogue [Col. 1521D], since in his elucidation he himself notes only ten years in addition to the months and days stated; likewise in the number twenty-three days, in which Papebrochius says Mabillon’s catalogue should be corrected, although Mabillon’s agrees entirely with the metropolitan one.

All report that Robald died on 3 Kalends of January [30 December]. Therefore, if you reckon backwards from that date, you are brought to 4 August 1135; and thus, according to this calculation, Robald’s election would differ by five days from that number of nine years and twenty-nine days which we saw noted above in Papebrochius’s catalogue. Yet I think the matter can easily be reconciled if we say that one source noted the day of election and another the day on which he entered upon the see, from which he was barred by a decree of the canons forbidding a bishop of one church to be transferred to another without consulting the supreme pontiff. An embassy could have been dispatched at once to him while he was staying at Pisa, as soon as the clergy and suffragans began to consider electing this bishop of Alba. Thus, on the fifth day after [Col. 1522A] his election, once Innocent’s favorable rescript had been obtained, they solemnly proclaimed him archbishop of Milan; from this was derived the beginning date of his archiepiscopal rule.

Certainly St Bernard, in the letter to be mentioned in chapter 42, no. 18, testifies that Innocent II’s approval was involved in this transfer. Therefore Robald [Col. 1522B] must be said to have been elected on 29 July 1135, raised to the see by papal permission on 4 August, and to have died on 30 December 1145.

I would add this one point: there would be no room for the difficulty proposed if we wished to follow the catalogue inserted in the *Acts of the Church of Milan*. In it, beyond the ten years, five complete months are assigned to Robald’s see; with those established, we would reach precisely that 29 July—apart from the day of his death—on which, after nine years and twenty-nine days from Anselm’s election, Papebrochius’s catalogue teaches that Robald was endowed with the Milanese mitre. But since I have seen this recorded in none of the ancient catalogues, I do not wish to call in this one witness to establish such an opinion.

I have chosen to investigate these points in this one place only, lest a discussion of years repeated in the following chapters, wherever the election or death of our bishops is treated, should create weariness for the reader. But, to return from where we digressed, it is clear from what has been said [Col. 1522C] that Anselm de Pusterla was elected on 30 June 1126, not in 1123, as Pagi, Papebrochius, and the others cited above believed, since Olric died only in the former year, as I believe has been more than sufficiently proved from the material so far adduced.

From this Ughelli may also be freed of the scruple under which he allowed himself to be troubled when, in *The Bishops of Lodi*, no. 20, he reported a document subscribed by our Archbishop Olric in 1125. In the Appendix to volume IV of the first edition, he asserted that this year ought to be corrected and 1123 put in its place; as it was likewise corrected in the new Venetian edition, which entirely omitted any year-date where it treats of Arderic, bishop of Lodi. But this was in vain, as we have now plainly shown.]. Over the death of this Anselm I indeed sigh deeply [Col. 1521A] [Note: [Col. 1522C] There will be occasion to discuss Anselm’s death, in addition to what we have noted in the preceding number, in chapter 42.], because, although he was gentle and kind toward those of mine who were under suspicion, my adversaries, and his own betrayers, he was not furious like Jordan, nor forgetful of me like Olric.

For on the very day upon which this Anselm received election to the archbishopric, he chose me to preside over his chaplains [Note: [Col. 1522C] From this too, no little light can be drawn [Col. 1522D] for determining the time of Olric’s death and Anselm’s election. Since Landulf said above that, after hearing of Emperor Henry’s death, he returned to his homeland and, sitting in his little house, earned his livelihood by writing according to custom, it is clear that he was by no means then distinguished with the honor and benefice of this office. Anselm’s election must therefore have occurred only after Henry’s death, if Landulf was appointed on the same day on which it took place to preside over Anselm’s chaplains.]. The counsel of those chaplains, though not of all of them, alienated him from me in almost everything that he did. For in the matter in which he hastened to grant peace to the men of Como, when their city had been captured for destruction [Note: [Col. 1522D] In assigning the year of this destruction of Como also, the ranks of writers are divided into contrary opinions. Weighty authorities—Corio, Calchus, Sigonius, Giovio, Ballarino, Tattus, and others—state that the city of Como was destroyed in the final battle in 1127. Conversely, the author of the *Chronicle, Flower of Flowers*, Puricelli, and Pagi testify that it was accomplished only in the following year. They also disagree among themselves concerning the month of this ruin: some specify March, others [Col. 1523B] July.

From Otto of Freising it certainly appears that Conrad’s arrival in Italy occurred in the same year in which that city was utterly overthrown. For in book VII, chapter 17, he says: “Conrad, made king by his brother and certain others, crossed the Pyrenaean ridge of the seventh mountain, where the rivers Rhine and Inn rise; there he was honorably received by the Milanese, who at that time brought to a successful conclusion the war of Como, most miserably prolonged for ten years to the affliction of the people of both cities, [Col. 1523C] after the city had been captured and destroyed.”

Since the abbot of Ursberg, in his account of Lothair’s years, and writers generally state that Conrad descended into Italy in 1128, it must also be said that the city of Como was plundered and razed to the ground in that year. Moreover, the word “then” would seem less aptly placed if almost a complete year had passed from the destruction of Como to Conrad’s Italian journey. Furthermore, the span of ten years during which Freising says that the war was conducted can easily be fitted only to this year, since we have said that it began in 1118, after Henry had departed Rome in June.

These are the considerations that support this view; I wished to note them lest I seem to fail my own side by passing over things which shine forth from the histories for a closer pursuit of truth. Yet I freely acknowledge that writers about their own country deserve more deference than foreigners. Accordingly [Col. 1523D] I shall more willingly subscribe to the opinion adopted in the commentary upon the poem concerning this war of Como by the aforementioned Father Joseph Maria Stampa. Indeed, to show my modest respect for this most learned friend, I add here, besides the solid arguments he advanced to prove that the date of Como’s destruction should be fixed in the preceding year, the testimony left by Father A. Crispus in his manuscript *Insubrian History*, religiously preserved at Busto, commonly called Arsizio: when, namely, the very ancient church dedicated to St Lawrence, levite and martyr, in the village of Olgiate in our diocese of Olona was being levelled, a marble tablet was found at the entrance of the main door bearing the following inscription:

> + IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD’S INCARNATION, ONE THOUSAND ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SEVEN. WHEN COMO WAS DESTROYED, THIS GATE WAS ERECTED.

], I was indeed pleased.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Anselm, with the agreement of the Milanese, refuses to receive the stole from the Roman pontiff, lest the honor of the archbishopric be diminished.

But when that same archbishop, following the counsel of certain chaplains and of the primicerius, and of Peter, bishop of Tortona [Col. 1523A], went to Rome against the public prohibition [Note: [Col. 1523D] **CHAPTER XXXVIII.**—Understand the outcry of clergy and people resisting his journey to Rome to receive the pallium, which, as we shall see below, they considered injurious to the Church of Milan [Col. 1524B].] of the clergy and people of Milan [Note: [Col. 1524B] The matters narrated below show that our Anselm went to the City as soon as he was elected archbishop, in order to obtain the pallium from the supreme pontiff. Since he is said to have approached Honorius II, who was made supreme pastor on 21 December 1124, it may also be gathered quite clearly that Anselm’s election took place much later than Puricelli and Papebrochius asserted. Puricelli and Pagi certainly place this journey of Anselm to Rome in 1125. But according to the calculation drawn above from the ancient catalogues, it is plainly established that this Anselm could not have departed for Rome until after June 1126.], this did not please me. Nevertheless, being a prudent and wise man, he conferred much with Pope Honorius and his cardinals; and in these discussions he defended, with living and sound arguments, the ecclesiastical customs of the Ambrosian Church and the honors of its archbishopric and city [Note: [Col. 1524C] The custom and honor of his archiepiscopal dignity which Anselm chiefly defended before Honorius and the cardinals was the privilege, which we gather from histories had anciently been granted to the Church of Milan, of receiving the pallium from the supreme pontiff only when it was sent through envoys.

We find this practice as early as 594, when St Gregory the Great, writing in the twelfth indiction to Constantius, bishop of Milan, says in Letter 1, book IV: “Moreover, we send the pallium, according to custom, to be used at the sacred solemnities of Mass.” In about 930, we read in the *History of Liège* that this prerogative of honor was preserved for the archbishop of Milan [Col. 1524D]. There Ratherius, first bishop of Verona and later of Liège, testifies in his letter that he brought to our bishop Hilduin the pallium sent to him by John XII, as I have already noted in volume III of this collection, p. 300.

More recently, Urban II had granted a testimony of this special distinction to Arnulf III and Anselm de Buis, while Paschal II did so to Grossulanus and Jordan, as our Landulf related. How important this distinction was may be understood from Baronius, who records under 1070 that, when Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, requested that Alexander II send him the pallium, it was refused, and Hildebrand the archdeacon, later Gregory VII, replied in these words: “It seems necessary to us that you visit the thresholds of the apostles.”

More striking is what Urban II writes in his letter, printed by Papebrochius in the *Exegesis*, no. 102, to our aforementioned Arnulf: “At the request of your letter, we send the pallium to your brotherhood with the blessing of the apostolic see, contrary to the custom of the Roman Church, which grants this kind of dignity to no one except when present.” [Col. 1525B]].

Therefore the pope said to this prudent man: “Brother, you have come prepared and as a bishop.” [Note: [Col. 1525B] That is, fortified with arguments.] “But if you wish to enjoy the authority of an archbishop in my time, it is necessary that you receive the stole from my hands, or, as I received it, at the altar of St Peter.”

At this, the Milanese lord called upon Robald [Note: [Col. 1525B] Or Robaldus.], bishop of Alba, under oath to advise him. Then that Robald of Alba said [Col. 1523B] that he would first endure having his nose slit up to his eyes before he would give him advice to receive the stole at Rome and prepare for the Church of Milan this new and most grievous burden which Pope Honorius said that he was imposing upon it.

Therefore this Archbishop Anselm returned to Milan without the stole [Note: [Col. 1525C] Puricelli, in *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 338, asserts that this return of Anselm is mentioned in the catalogue both of the metropolitan archpriest and of our city secretary, in the following words: “He entered through the Ticinese gate on the feast of St Michael with a great retinue of Milanese nobles and was installed in his see, as is customary in such cases.” If Anselm made this solemn entry when he returned from the City, it must be admitted that he set out on his Roman journey immediately after he had been elected and consecrated; for before three months had elapsed, he had already returned to Milan on 29 September.], bringing the bishop of Alba back with him. Yet he did not ascend the archiepiscopal seat [Note: [Col. 1525C] Not because he was merely elected and had not yet been consecrated, as Pagi believed Puricelli to mean under 1125, no. 20; for the words, “You have come prepared and as a bishop,” indicate that he had already been ordained. Rather, it was because the clergy and people considered him to have violated the rights of the Church of Milan before the Roman pontiff, as our author [Col. 1525D] explains below.], until Hubert of Merate, his scribe, swore that his lord Anselm had consented to no diminishment of the honor of the Church of Milan, and that Bishop Robald of Alba confirmed this by his authority. [Note: [Col. 1525D] Read: “this same.”]

Then this pontiff Anselm recovered, at the pleasure of clergy and people, the seat and the castles of the archbishopric [Note: [Col. 1525D] I have already shown in the Appendix to the *Vindication of the Bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius*, no. 29, that almost the entire shore of Lake Verbano, with its adjacent towns and fortresses, was subject to our archbishop. More may be read in Corio’s first edition of 1503, p. 85, where Archbishop Cassono Torriani, inveighing with sacred curses against Matteo Visconti, enumerates many castles and places under archiepiscopal jurisdiction, saying: “You, Matthew, hold the entire district of Angera, of Lecco, of Bellano, of Valassina, of Cattaneo, of Travalio, and of Brebbia, which are fortresses and places belonging from ancient times to our ecclesiastical right.”].

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Archbishop Anselm crowns Emperor Conrad, whom Pope Honorius rejects; consequently Anselm is excommunicated at the pope’s command.

Anselm, residing in the castles [Note: [Col. 1525D] That is, those belonging by right to the archbishopric.], learned that the clergy and people of Milan had received the noble prince [Col. 1524B] Conrad with ecclesiastical pomp and a civic triumph appropriate to their natural king [Note: [Col. 1525D] Among the grounds which Conrad advanced for being assumed to the Empire was this also: that, being born of Agnes, daughter of the elder Henry, and therefore nephew of the last deceased Henry, he maintained that the kingdom belonged to him by natural right. For this reason too the Milanese received Conrad as their natural king. We said above that Conrad came into Italy in 1128. Landulf indicates the month in which he was among the Insubrians, when below he states that Conrad was crowned at Monza on 29 June, the feast of St Peter.]. And when clergy and people were discussing the coronation of the king himself, this pontiff Anselm came down from Lecco to Monza, the chief place for the crown of the king of Italy [Note: [Col. 1526C] From this Onofrio Panvinio may be refuted, since in book *On Imperial Assemblies*, chapter 11, he did not at all believe that the Iron Crown, with which the kings of Italy are customarily inaugurated, had been in use at Milan or Monza before the time of Frederick II. Puricelli also solidly refuted him in *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 343.]. There he spent the night and resolved to return to the mountain country.

After an interval of [Col. 1525A] three days he went up to the castle called Plebia [Note: [Col. 1526C] That is, Brebbia, a town not far from Lake Verbano, full of very ancient monuments and formerly famous, but now almost utterly ruined, as Bonaventura Castiglione writes in *On the Ancient Seats of the Insubrian Gauls*, col. 373 in my copy; there he reports the etymology of its name and the remaining traces of its remarkable antiquity.]. There he heard many resounding reports [Note: [Col. 1526C] That is, the widely disseminated report of the Milanese people’s common applause and resolve.] concerning the coronation of King Conrad. And I myself heard, not in anger, from the pontiff that I should go to Milan as quickly as possible and report to him the disposition of all the citizens concerning this royal affair.

Then Unifred Aboriti and his squire gave neither me nor my boy any rest from evening until sunrise. Yet I arrived, about the third hour, at Milan, where the full assembly of clergy and people had been called together; and there clergy and people, as one man, with the greatest and most remarkable approval and acclamation, demanded that the archbishop should come and crown that prince. Moreover Roger Clivellus, [Col. 1525B] a noble and powerful knight, said with the people standing around: “By the body of the Lord, unless it were God’s will that this noble lord be crowned, this blessed people would by no means cry out so unanimously in his praise.”

This cause having therefore been so approved and determined, Anselm of Badaglo, ordinary subdeacon; Guido of Landriano, elected captain; Guerenzus of Puzobonello, a valvassor [Note: [Col. 1526C] Or *vavassor*, a name very well known in that age, denoting greater or lesser feudal vassals, as appears from Du Cange’s *Glossary*.] of distinction; and Rubacastellus, an exceptionally renowned citizen and knight, presented to Pontiff Anselm, on behalf of the entire clergy and [Col. 1526A] people, an embassy concerning the approved and impending coronation of King Conrad.

When he was in the castle of Plebia, he considered their embassy and my report, and hastened to the city.
