Thereafter, as though assenting to the common wish of all ranks, in the church of St Michael [Note: [Col. 1526D] This church is mentioned in a diploma of Pope Clement III given in 1188 to Oberto, archpriest of Monza, and published by Bartholomew Zucchi, chapter 20; among the churches it is listed first after St John.], at Monza, he blessed, anointed, and placed the crown upon the elect Conrad on the feast of St Peter [Note: [Col. 1526D] Namely, 29 June 1128, as we noted above.], while another bishop stood by for the king’s coronation.

In this act I was certainly not idle; rather, before the pontiff himself and the crowned man, I bore the pontifical staff from the church of St Michael, in a splendid procession [Note: [Col. 1526D] Or rather, a multitude of people.] gathered by God’s will in honour of that king, as far as the church of St John. In the church of St John [Note: [Col. 1526D] This church, venerable for its antiquity, since it was built and endowed by Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, is still celebrated today. It enjoys the privilege of pontifical insignia and has lately been brought to a nobler magnificence of sacred worship by ornaments of gold and paintings.] I solemnly heard Mass with this most excellent king. The same pontiff also celebrated that solemnity of coronation in the church of St Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1526D] Namely, at Milan; Sigonius omitted this when he listed only Conrad’s coronation at Monza for this year.], while I was detained elsewhere through no fault of my own [Note: [Col. 1526D] That is, being lawfully prevented.].

Nevertheless, whatever was done directly for that lord, my king, I loved and still love. For, as he proceeded through the counties and marches of Lombardy [Note: [Col. 1526D] Yet not all of them: some cities supported Lothair, as may be gathered from Landulf himself at the end of this chapter. There survives in the Bamberg manuscript, in Eckhard, cited place, col. 361, a letter of Litifred, bishop of Novara, written to Lothair, containing these words: “Let Your Excellency know for certain that Novara, Pavia, Piacenza, Cremona, and Brescia, cities of Italy, steadfastly preserve their loyalty to you and unanimously desire your arrival. But Conrad, the idol of the Milanese, abandoned even by them, has taken flight and has refuge only at Parma, where he lives meanly, so poor and attended by so few that his fame scarcely extends from one place to another.”], the counts and marquises of Tuscany, powerful men of every degree of nobility and humble men alike, joyfully received and [Col. 1527A] loved him. But those who were rebels felt the strength of his exceedingly sharp sword, and suffered death and disgrace, as did Anselm, marquis of the Bosco [Note: [Col. 1527B] Bosco is a place in the district of Alessandria, by the river Orba, on the border between the territories of Genoa and Montferrat. It was formerly celebrated as the dominion and seat of such marquises. Jerome Ghilini, in the final folio of his *Italian Annals of the City of Alessandria*, describes their splendour and very extensive rights, asserting that the site on which the aforesaid city was founded was then subject to their dominion.], and the illustrious . . . count [Note: [Col. 1527C] The name of this count, which has disappeared because it was erased in the time-worn archetype, was supplied from his own imagination by the recent author Alexander Maximilian de Bode. In his *Dissertation on Public Law concerning the Duchy of Etruria*, published at Halle in Magdeburg in 1722, chapter 1, §22, p. 22, he says: “It is likely that the illustrious count whose name could not be read in the manuscript of Landulf the Younger was Albert, or Ingelbert, whom Pope Honorius II had made marquis in the land of Tuscany and his vicar. At least Muratori reports a charter of this Albert, in which he confesses that, through the cooperating grace of blessed Peter and Pope Honorius, and by the office of his vicariate, he had been advanced to the heights of this dignity.” Yet this opinion is unsound. For Landulf says that the illustrious count mentioned in our manuscript was punished with the sword at Conrad’s command, certainly before 1130, when Conrad, repulsed by Honorius II, returned to Germany. Therefore he cannot have been that Marquess Albert, whom the most illustrious Muratori concludes from the documents cited there to have flourished still in 1135, indeed even in 1146, in chapter 30 of the same work, *Este Antiquities*, pp. 293–94. The same must be said of Ingelbert, whom the Saxon Annalist, in Eckhard’s *History of the Middle Ages*, and also Pagius for 1134, no. 1, from the genuine Pisan Chronicles reported by Ughelli, record as still living in 1137—more correctly, 1135—and they offer several clearer details concerning him. But who this count was cannot be inferred from our manuscript, from which a secure judgement may be formed; therefore I do not wish, like blind men, to fight in the air.].

One of these, Anselm, received his life and absolution through the favour of the Milanese, to whom he had been of service as a most valiant soldier in their most difficult field-battles. The other, namely the count, actually suffered death; and Conrad, acting thus graciously and vigorously, approached Rome. But the strong hand of Pope Honorius cast him back [Note: [Col. 1527D] That is, turned him aside from his purpose. Why Pope Honorius was hostile to Conrad is too well known to require repetition. Lothair II had been elected emperor in 1125, on the third day before the Kalends of September, and was anointed king of Germany at Aachen on the Ides of that month, with Honorius’s approval conveyed through his legates Evrard and Romanus. But Conrad, who, after his brother Frederick, had risen against Lothair, was struck with a sentence of excommunication by Honorius, as Otto of Freising, Conrad’s half-brother by the same mother, relates in book VII, chapter 17. This perhaps was the weapon by which our author reports Conrad as repelled from entering Rome, since nowhere have I found that Honorius fought him with arms.], and made him return to Germany, as if to his own proper places [Note: [Col. 1528B] In 1129 Conrad still held Italy against Lothair, as Sigonius testifies for that year; [Col. 1528C] indeed, he had not even departed in September. In Francesco Maria Florentini’s compilation, *History of Matilda*, book II, p. 346 in my copy, there is Conrad’s diploma, issued at Lucca, where he then stayed, on 4 September 1129; in it he grants certain things to the monastery of St Pontianus. Yet within the time remaining from that month to the death of Honorius, who died at the beginning of 1130, it must be said that Conrad returned to Germany if he was compelled by Honorius to go there, as our Landulf relates. Puricelli failed to notice this when, in *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 353, he wrote that Conrad returned to Germany shortly before Innocent II, coming from Gaul, reached Genoa—that is, in 1132.].

Therefore John of Crema, Roman cardinal, summoned to Pavia the suffragan and provincial bishops of the Church of Milan in order to excommunicate the Milanese pontiff [Col. 1527B] [Note: [Col. 1528C] Pagius states, under 1128, no. 14, that this council of provincial bishops was convened at Pavia in 1128. Yet it seems that it should be referred to the following year, since our author reports that this synod was assembled [Col. 1528D] after Conrad’s departure from Italy, which we have shown occurred toward the end of 1129. It is highly credible that Honorius did not proceed to punish Anselm, Conrad’s supporter, until Conrad had been expelled from Italy.].

After they had been summoned, the Milanese pontiff, through several laymen and priests, sent word to the cardinal that they should not presume [Col. 1528A] [Note: [Col. 1528D] That is, they should not act precipitately in pronouncing sentence while he was absent and unheard.], but should await him for the space of one day. But the Pavians, the Cremonese, the Novarese and their bishops, and those of other cities, denouncing this royal undertaking of Anselm as contrary to God and to the great King Lothair [Note: [Col. 1528D] Hence it is evident that the aforesaid cities, as we suggested above, did not receive Conrad at all, since they publicly professed Lothair as king.], did not accept the pontiff’s embassy; rather, under the authority of that Cardinal John, they excommunicated him and resolved to wage war against the Milanese, who were protecting the castle of Crema [Note: [Col. 1528D] Antonio Campo, in his *History of Cremona* under 1129, relates that the people of Crema, who were subject to the Church of Cremona, rashly revolted from it without any just cause pressing them, made an alliance with the Milanese—then enemies of the Cremonese—and consequently the enraged Cremonese declared war upon them in order to avenge the wrong.]. Nevertheless, while Pope Honorius lived, the greater part of the Milanese rendered Catholic reverence [Note: [Col. 1528D] As to their lawful shepherd.] to this pontiff.

## CHAPTER XL. Archbishop Anselm adheres to the antipope Anacletus and receives the stole from him.

[Col. 1528B]

After Honorius died [Note: [Col. 1528D] CHAPTER XL.—Honorius II died on 14 February 1130, as Pagius rightly maintains under that year, nos. 1 and 2.], Anacletus, the second pope of the Romans [Col. 1529A] [Note: [Col. 1529B] On the day after Honorius’s death, that is, 15 February, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St Angelo, was elected Roman pontiff under the name Innocent II—a man conspicuous for such integrity of character “that, as Arnulf of Séez, printed above in vol. III, p. 423, testifies, he seemed already by divine providence uniquely fashioned for the unique dignity.” But the next day after Innocent’s election, that is, 16 February, Peter, son of Peter Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of St Mary across the Tiber, defiled by every vice—as the same Arnulf describes him in chapter 3—was intruded into the chair of St Peter and called Anacletus II. Accordingly, he should be called not pope, as in this manuscript, but beyond doubt pseudo-pope.], sent the stole to this Milanese archbishop through suitable messengers: namely John, bishop of Palestrina [Note: [Col. 1529C] Read: not bishop, but pseudo-bishop, of the Church of Palestrina. For its lawful bishop at that time was William, who in the Life of Innocent II written by Cardinal Aragonio and printed in volume III, p. 434, is listed first among the cardinals present at Innocent’s canonical election. It may therefore be believed that, in hostility to that election, another bishop of Palestrina was created—perhaps that same John whom Oldoinus reports was made, together with others, cardinal-priest of the title of St Pudentiana by the pseudo-pontiff Anacletus on Holy Saturday of 1130.], and Beltram, Roman subdeacon [Note: [Col. 1529C] Sigonius reveals the reason for this hasty gift under 1130. In order to establish himself in the pontifical dignity he had seized, Anacletus pressed the opposing party with ecclesiastical censures and strove “to gather to his cause as many friends as he could.” [Col. 1529D] Oldoinus, in the cited place, also teaches that Anselm was made a cardinal by Anacletus.]. This stole Pontiff Anselm reverently received with clergy and people of Milan gathered around him and applauding Pope Anacletus, his legates, and their embassy.

But the party opposed to Anselm began from this point to disparage him more sharply. Yet the full body of clergy and people flocked to him, and in affection bore fear and reverence also toward King Conrad and Pope Anacletus [Note: [Col. 1529D] Sigonius, in the cited place, makes Archbishop Anselm the author of this most pernicious attachment, saying: “Anselm, archbishop of Milan, surrendered himself to him—that is, to Anacletus—and drew with him the people of Milan and most of the bishops of Lombardy.”]. And while this hope existed [Note: [Col. 1529D] Another manuscript from the Ambrosian Library reads, “while this spirit existed,” a reading that gives Landulf’s words a clearer sense: “while, that is, a spirit of concord—though a most pernicious one—flourished among nearly all the clergy and people, peaceably attached to Anacletus and Conrad.” For our author was one of their adherents: as we have seen, he calls Anacletus pope and believes him to be such.] among the fullness of the Church and city of Milan; and while the payments for alienation [Note: [Col. 1529D] What is paid to the feudal lord for permission to dispose of or sell an estate, as Du Cange explains in his *Glossary*.] and the privileges which the distinguished captains of Besana [Note: [Col. 1530B] Galvano Fiamma, *Greater Chronicle*, chapter 712, says that the captains of the parishes, who later took surnames from them—such as the captains of Incino, Missaglia, and Merate—were instituted by our Archbishop Landulf, elected in 979. Besana is a village in our diocese, in the parish of Agliate.], Porta Orientale [Note: [Col. 1530B] The same Galvano Fiamma, *Greater Chronicle*, chapters 698 and 845, teaches that from ancient times captains were assigned to every gate of the city of Milan; in his *Extravagant Chronicle*, question 18, he offers some rough verses naming the noble families selected for this office in his age: “From the six gates were taken the captains of the city: Nova, Como, Ticino, Orientale, Romana, Vercellina; the Turriani, Badagli, Busti, Oriensi, Carrocci, Crassi.”], and Lomagna [Note: [Col. 1530C] A district of Milanese territory in the parish of Missaglia.], and Pope Gregory VII and Pope Urban II had granted to the priest Liprand [Col. 1529B] [Note: [Col. 1530C] Landulf has already reported these papal diplomas in chapters 6 and 8.] retained their force and escaped the notice of all [Col. 1530A] [Note: [Col. 1530C] The sense is: “They retained their force, although they had neither been produced nor demanded,” as is clearly inferred at the beginning of the next chapter from the word *legere* (“to read”), unless perhaps *laedere* (“to harm”) should be read there, and here *patuerunt* (“were manifest”).], no war dishonoured the Milanese; rather, they Milanese distinguished themselves broadly and splendidly against the Pavians, Cremonese, Novarese, and all their enemies [Note: [Col. 1530C] Read *praestiterunt*, as in other Ambrosian manuscripts. Antonio Campo, in his *History of Cremona* under 1130, and Sigonius under 1131 and 1132, vividly describe the Milanese wars, successfully conducted against the allied cities of Cremona and Pavia. I have nowhere read that the Milanese fought the Novarese in a separate pitched battle; yet it cannot be doubted that their auxiliary troops suffered the same disasters [Col. 1530D] that struck the cities allied with them, our author confirming this.].

## CHAPTER XLI. The clergy of Milan expel Anselm from the archbishopric. Pope Innocent confirms it and sends Blessed Bernard to Milan.

But when Archbishop Anselm wished, and did, to act against those very payments for alienation and privileges, and when the multitude of clergy, people, and consuls wished to read those payments and privileges, it happened that a certain detachment of Milanese soldiers was captured by the Cremonese [Note: [Col. 1530D] CHAPTER XLI. Read “by the Cremonese,” as in the Ambrosian manuscripts. Pagius considers that these events should be referred to 1133, in his critique under 1130, no. 48; and this accords with the history of our author. Since in the preceding year the Milanese were still acting brilliantly against their enemies, spreading terror and slaughter everywhere, as may be read in Sigonius, it must be said that only after that year did they begin to be punished by this disgrace of war. This is especially so because the cited authors relate that in this same year the Cremonese built the castle of Pizzighettone to check Milanese incursions more easily. Secured by that stronghold, they could rush more confidently upon their enemies and perhaps capture a wandering Milanese detachment and lead it in triumph to Cremona.]. And many of the ordinary and decuman priests began, I know not by what spirit, [Col. 1530B] to laugh at the cause of King Conrad and secretly to scorn Anacletus’s cause.

This Archbishop Anselm, [Col. 1531A] enduring many provocations, finally excommunicated the priest Azo, master of the boys who sing at the Masses where priests chiefly celebrate the sacrifices of Christ’s body and blood, and certain others who had acted deceitfully in celebrating the coronation of King Conrad. From the root of this excommunication, the circumcised, who do not know Christ the Son of the Virgin, and the greater part of the Romans and Lombards, who do not love the author of divine and human law, cannot enjoy the peace of heaven or earth without these authors [Note: [Col. 1531B] Does our author mean the Jews then living in Milan? A rescript of King Theodoric given to the Jews of Milan, found in book V of Cassiodorus’s *Variae*, certainly proves that they were established in this city in past centuries. [Col. 1531C] Pagius, under 1133, no. 15, believed that this passage refers to Manichaeans, “who rejected the author of the Law, or the God of the Old Testament, and were multiplying in those regions.” Yet this is unsuitable, since no one has ever asserted that the Romans and Lombards at that time were for the most part infected with this shameful error. The fragments of the *History of the Franks* in Baronius under 1017 and Glaber, book III, chapter 8, testify that it occurred much earlier than this age, namely only at the beginning of the preceding century. I therefore believe that this obscure text of our author can be explained only thus: that minds were so disturbed by these repeated and mutually opposed sentences of anathema that the Jews were confirmed in their error, and the greater part of the Romans and Lombards, not recognizing the lawful pontiff, turned away from Catholic worship of God and so, guilty of violating human and divine law, rightly exposed themselves to misfortunes.].

See, even now much and indeed destructive dissension arose among the people of Milan under the title of excommunication. For if the archbishop excommunicated this priest and others from the pulpit of St Thecla, and the provincial and [Col. 1531B] suffragan bishops, as was said above [Note: [Col. 1531D] Namely, chapter 39.], excommunicated him at Pavia, the ordinary and decuman priests, and the others supporting Pope Innocent II and plotting [Note: [Col. 1531D] Manuscripts A.1 and A.2 read “preparing.”] against this archbishop, spent their money and gave it to men learned in law and morals, and to fighting men.

The archbishop was therefore compelled to enter the public assembly and there contend with those whom he had excommunicated concerning the excommunication. And while he expected arrows concerning whether the excommunication was just or unjust, [Col. 1532A] Nazarius the *primicerius*, a man of remarkable cunning, through a long speech caused weariness in the whole assembly. But Archpriest Stephen [Note: [Col. 1531D] “Of the decumans” is added in the margin, though absent from the other manuscripts.], surnamed Guandeca, seeing that his *primicerius* had spoken tediously, raised his voice and said against the archbishop:

> “What these men do not wish to say to you, I say: you are a heretic, perjurer, sacrilegious man, and guilty of other crimes which are not to be recorded here.”

Hearing this unexpectedly, the archbishop was astonished. But that archpriest, having the book of the Gospels at hand, immediately swore that he would stand by the things he had said were in that Anselm called “of Pusterla,” before the judgement of the bishops of Novara and Alba, who were among the suffragans of the Church of Milan.

[Col. 1532B] The consuls of Milan therefore, in agreement with both parties, decreed that those bishops and other suffragans should come. On the appointed day not only the suffragans came, but also very many persons clothed wholly in rough and unworked wool and shaven with an unusual tonsure [Note: [Col. 1531D] Puricelli, *Monumenta basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 358, judged that those whom Landulf says came with the suffragans, wholly clothed in rough and unworked wool, were Cistercian novices. St Bernard addressed letter 134 to them as persons living at Milan and recently converted. Papebroch, on the contrary, in his *Exegesis*, no. 116, objects; and from the Humiliati codex cited by Puricelli himself he inclines to the opinion “that this passage denotes none other than secular magnates and noble citizens of Milan who, at that same time, intoxicated by the divine Spirit through St Bernard, adopted a manner of life in religious dress while dwelling with their households; they were called the brothers of St Bernard and afterwards became founders of the first and second orders of the Humiliati.” He relies more confidently upon the fact [Col. 1532B] “that the Cistercians had not yet been established in Milan, but were first introduced there after the Council of Pisa, and that the few whom St Bernard had with him in his company could not have constituted the crowd indicated here.” But that most learned man is mistaken. These events did not occur while St Bernard was staying in Milan, but before he departed for the Council of Pisa, at which time he had not yet arrived at Milan. Yet it is clear from the same letter cited above that the Milanese sent an embassy to St Bernard, perhaps to summon him to Milan in order to calm the discord just related. Therefore the passage cannot concern those who were in St Bernard’s company when he later arrived at Milan after the conclusion of the Pisan council. Moreover, it cannot be said that those mentioned here were the magnates and noble citizens of Milan who were later called the brothers of St Bernard and became founders of the first and second orders of the Humiliati. This occurred only after St Bernard’s second arrival in the city, namely in 1134, as Puricelli himself affirms from the Humiliati codex. I therefore think that his opinion should not be abandoned. For although it is true that the monastery of Clairvaux of the Cistercian order was first founded only in 1135 or [Col. 1532D] even 1136, as Puricelli himself maintains in no. 383, the title of the aforesaid letter—which is addressed “to novices converted at Milan”—shows that there was already some residence in the suburbs of Milan where Cistercians had been received. Baronius also expressly affirms this, whatever Ughelli may say in volume IV of *Italia Sacra*, where he judges that the name “novices” in this letter denotes those whom St Bernard, while travelling to the Council of Pisa, had recently converted and who had already sincerely devoted themselves to his instruction.].

When Archbishop Anselm saw them standing together and seeming to the people to be angels from heaven, he said to the people: “All those whom you see here in those white and grey cloaks [Note: [Col. 1532D] From this too a strong support for Puricelli’s opinion is established: namely, that those standing with the people were Cistercians. For in the *Western History* of James of Vitry, who died about the middle of the following century, chapter 19, where he describes the institution and customs of the Cistercians while still flourishing in vigorous observance, one reads among other things: “The first [Col. 1533B] Cistercians, changing their black habit into grey, strove to reform the old and add new things.” The grey habit was no other than one woven from white and black wool.] are heretics.”

[Col. 1533A] Then the simple and the discerning alike [Note: [Col. 1533C] That is, the entire body of clergy and people.] stirred up a conflict to expel and depose [Note: [Col. 1533C] Namely, Anselm.] him. Nevertheless, they could not withstand Anselm’s sword on that day. But during the night, through money freely distributed, the very strong faction of the *primicerius* and the priest [archpriest] Stephen drove Anselm from his see at the first light of dawn. Finding nowhere to turn, he entered his paternal house. The next morning, before his humble people gathered in the church of St Ambrose, Anselm caused his chamberlain to swear in his presence that his lord would not evade the judgement of the suffragans, but would answer before them to the priest Stephen called Guandeca concerning the accusations made against him, setting aside the matter of King Conrad.

But John of Rode, one [Col. 1533B] of the consuls of Milan, returned to the other party which had sent him and reported nothing concerning this oath of Anselm. Instead, he said: “That lord to whom you sent me promises that he will come to us to render no account whatsoever” [Note: [Col. 1533C] This open lie proves the truth of Landulf’s earlier assertion that the proceedings against Archbishop Anselm had been conducted through plots.].

Then those present in that assembly cried: “Let him henceforth be removed from us also.” Thus every suffragan returned to his own see except Robald, bishop of Alba, who assisted the Church of Milan in chrism and its other episcopal rites [Note: [Col. 1533C] Presumably asked by clergy and people, so that, once Archbishop Anselm had been driven from his see, the Church of Milan should not lie deserted.].

That Anselm, as though rejected and expelled by all clergy [Col. 1534A] and people, withdrew to the accustomed castles of the archbishopric [Note: [Col. 1533C] Puricelli, cited place, no. 351, held for certain that Anselm was not rejected and expelled by clergy and people before 1134. Papebroch, conversely, in *Exegesis*, nos. 107 and 114, expressly affirms that it belongs to 1132, but he was deceived by the preconceived opinion—convincingly refuted above, I think—that Anselm had been raised to the archiepiscopal dignity in 1123. He therefore thought the nine years should be counted from Anselm’s election to the election of Robald as acting archbishop, as the catalogues state. Pagius adopts a middle position under 1133, no. 18, assigning this misfortune of Anselm to that year; and I too think this better accords with the ensuing history of Landulf.], where he obtained some sort of rest [Note: [Col. 1533D] Anselm enjoyed this rest not for two years, as Papebroch calculated in no. 117 of his *Exegesis*, but for the interval that elapsed until the celebration of the Council of Pisa. Nor can it have been so slight that our expelled archbishop might not properly be said to have rested. Therefore this also supplies an argument for rejecting Puricelli’s opinion reported in the preceding note.].

Meanwhile Pope Innocent held a synod at Pisa [Note: [Col. 1533D] When Emperor Lothair was at Rome in 1133 and was solemnly crowned with the imperial diadem by Innocent II on the day before the Nones of June—an event which Cavitellus wrongly places in 1137—there was hope that the Church would at last recover peace, with Anacletus forced to better things by the emperor’s presence and the terror of his arms. But the opposing party’s forces prevailed, and the pseudo-pontiff, hardened in schism, frustrated plans for peace. [Col. 1534C] Lothair judged it better to return to Germany and Innocent to withdraw again to Pisa. There, confident of safety, Innocent summoned a council from the whole West, and held it on the third day before the Kalends of June 1134, as Pagius shows under that year, nos. 1 and 2.]. At it Robald, bishop of Alba, acting as representative [Note: [Col. 1534C] Manuscript A.2 reads “being present.”], Tedald of Landriano [Note: [Col. 1534C] He had been sent by Archbishop Olric to the younger Henry in Germany when he was enrolled only in the order of notaries—which still survives in the greater Ambrosian church—as we saw in chapter 37. Since he is here called archpriest of the Church of Milan, it may be believed that he had succeeded Stephen of Guandeca, whom Anselm had found the fiercest author of his expulsion from the city in the preceding year.] archpriest of the Church of Milan, Amizo of La Sala archdeacon, Anselm of Rode ordinary levite, many other ordinary clerics of that Church, and decuman priests together with the *primicerius*, swore fealty to Pope Innocent, contrary to the customary honour of Milan and its Church [Note: [Col. 1534C] Pagius explains, under 1134, no. 6, what was this customary honour of Milan and its Church which our author thought violated: “The Milanese, who had hitherto retained their ancient liberty, persuaded themselves that the oath of fealty decreed by Gregory VII, which is today required from bishops, was contrary to the honour of their Church.”].

But the Cremonese did not release the Milanese soldiers whom they held captive because of this allegiance. Pope Innocent, however, confirmed the deposition [Note: [Col. 1534D] From the archbishopric of Milan, from which he had already been cast down in a public assembly of the clergy and people of that city and in the gathering of its suffragan bishops, as was related shortly before.] and expulsion of the oft-mentioned Anselm of Pusterla.

[Col. 1534B] Yet those who had sworn fealty, fearing these calamities of the city and Church of Milan, delayed returning to Milan unless they had a protector who would confirm before the Milanese people Anselm’s expulsion, reduce Conrad’s coronation to nothing [Note: [Col. 1534D] That is, they were to renounce the ill-advised undertaking of Conrad’s coronation, performed in 1128, now that Conrad himself had been repudiated.], summon the people of so great a city, and strengthen them in devotion to Emperor Lothair and unity with Pope Innocent himself. For accomplishing this, the pope had an angel so fit for the task as Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1534D] The Milanese had sought St Bernard with many supplications, that he might come to our city as reconciler of the schism; and this was long before the Council of Pisa was held, as appears from letters 132 and the two following letters of that holy abbot. Innocent II now sent St Bernard from his own side to reconcile this city, as Ernald testifies in book II, chapter 2, of Bernard’s Life.].

## CHAPTER XLII. St Bernard brings the Milanese to obedience to the Church and to Emperor Lothair. Robald is elected archbishop. Anselm is captured on the Po and dies at Rome.

[Col. 1535A]

Meanwhile Prince Conrad, having adopted a higher counsel, was made standard-bearer of Emperor Lothair. [Note: [Col. 1535B] CH. XLII.—Conrad, the rival for the kingdom and empire, was received by Lothair into submission and favour not in 1133, as perhaps through a printer’s error is stated in Pagi under the year 1135, no. 12, but in the following year, 1134, as Trithemius relates in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*. The Hildesheim chronicler, cited by the same Pagi in the place mentioned, reports that on the feast of St Michael in 1135, at the place called Mülhausen, Conrad was reconciled to the emperor. Thus Conrad must have entered into a friendly alliance with Lothair twice (the original peace of 1134 having been broken off because of some intervening dispute), if these two writers are to be believed. Unless we choose to believe that the obedience first rendered by Conrad to Lothair in 1134 was subsequently confirmed by a repeated oath at a public assembly of princes in 1135. Whatever the reason for this second meeting, it is plainly inferred from what our author immediately adds that he is speaking of Conrad’s first reconciliation.]

And the aforesaid abbot, delaying nothing, entered Milan with the bishop of Chartres [Note: [Col. 1535C] Namely Geoffrey des Lièves, who governed the Church of Chartres from 1116 until 1138, as is recorded in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II.] and Robald of Alba [Note: [Col. 1535C] That is, the man whom the Milanese had chosen, after Anselm’s deposition, as vicar to perform the archiepiscopal duties.]. [Note: [Col. 1535C] All writers relate that, when the Council of Pisa had been dissolved, the abbot of Clairvaux hastened at once to this city in that same year, 1134. Besides Geoffrey of Chartres, the colleagues added to this papal mission were Guy of Pisa and Matthew, bishop of Albano, cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, according to Ernald, *Life of St Bernard*, book II, ch. 2. The joy and applause of the citizens of Milan at the arrival of so great a man can scarcely be explained. The same Ernald testifies that the people came to meet him for as far as seven miles, in such a multitude of every sex and condition that the city seemed almost to have emigrated.]

That city, indeed, he shaped as he wished. At this abbot’s command all the ecclesiastical ornaments, visible in the church of that city in gold, silver, and silken coverings, were, as though scorned by the abbot himself, shut away in chests. Not only men but women also cut their hair; clothed in hair-shirts and the cheapest woollens, they turned to every kind of religious observance. [Col. 1536A] Water was changed into wine, demons were put to flight, the crippled were raised up, [Note: [Col. 1535D] Many remarkable miracles performed by St Bernard in the city of Milan may be read in the aforesaid *Life* and in Puricelli, *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 363 ff.] and the sick were likewise healed of every infirmity. Moreover, whatever sick prisoners the Milanese held in custody from among their enemies, the abbot himself released and set free. By the sacrament of bread, which the abbot himself offered, he confirmed so great a people in love for Emperor Lothair and in obedience to Pope Innocent. [Note: [Col. 1535D] The author of the same *Life* relates the matter thus: “When the business for which both the man of God and the cardinals had come had been publicly discussed, the city, forgetful of its strength and laying aside all fierceness, submitted itself so completely to the abbot that the little verse of the poet could aptly be applied to its obedience:

> To wish to follow commands is for me as necessary as being able to do so.

See letter 137 in the new edition of St Bernard, in which the holy abbot himself writes to Empress Richenza concerning what he did in reconciling the Milanese.]

At last the same people ran to the church of St Lawrence, [Note: [Col. 1536C] That is, the church called Major, one of Milan’s four distinguished basilicas.] where he was lodged, with hymns, praises, and their customary *Kyr.* [Note: [Col. 1536C] Since this is not a sacred supplication but a tumultuous gathering of the people, I wonder whether this was perhaps a particular formula of acclamation then employed by the Milanese people in electing an archbishop. Macrius writes in his *Hierolexicon* that the cry *Kyrie eleison* was sometimes acclaimed in synods. Ferrarius says absolutely nothing of it in his distinguished work *On Ancient Acclamations and Applause*. Whether this custom of our city deserves mention there, let the reader decide.] They wished to have that abbot as archbishop. [Note: [Col. 1535D] In assigning the time of the vacant see when the Milanese mitre was offered to St Bernard, our writers have been remarkably mistaken. Bernardino Corio, under the year 1115—placing the entire history prematurely—writes that St Bernard was called to this dignity immediately after Archbishop Jordan, making no mention whatever of his successor Olric; Merula likewise is not free from this intolerable error. Donato Bossi, contradicting himself, places the holy abbot before Henry, or Olric, in his catalogue, though in his *Chronicles* he had made Bernard later. Sigonius under 1123, Morigia, book II, Bugatti, book III, Galesinius in the synodal table, and nearly all more recent catalogues of the archbishops of Milan place this election before that of Anselm of Pusterla. But that these accounts are false is abundantly proved by our Landulf, an eyewitness, and by the life of the abbot of Clairvaux written by contemporaries. St Bernard was acclaimed archbishop only after Anselm had been deposed and the legation to us had been undertaken after the Council of Pisa: in the same year, 1134, in which he first came to Milan, as this history shows and Pagi and Puricelli attest. [Col. 1536B–C]]

But the abbot did not accept it. [Note: [Col. 1536C] Ernald informs us that St Bernard, with steadfast contempt for honours, rejected not only the Milanese mitre but many other offices offered to him. In book II, ch. 4 of the same *Life*, he writes: “How many churches deprived of pastors chose him as their bishop? His own Church of Langres chose him; Châlons chose him. In Italy the city of Genoa, and Milan, metropolis of Liguria, desired him as shepherd and master. Reims, France’s most noble city and capital of the province of Belgica Secunda, sought his lordship. With all these calls set aside, the honour offered did not stir his soul; his foot did not move to bow toward glory; the tiara and ring pleased him no more than rake and hoe.” [Col. 1536D]] Rather, he said: “Tomorrow I shall mount my palfrey [Note: [Col. 1536D] That is, a pacing horse; see Du Cange, *Glossary*.] and, if it carries me beyond you, [Note: [Col. 1536D] Puricelli’s conjecture is exceedingly uncertain. In *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 368, he thinks that by these words St Bernard wished to allude to what had happened to St Ambrose when he declined the governance of the Church of Milan: fleeing the city and thinking that he had reached Pavia, he found himself in the morning brought to the gate of Milan called the Roman Gate. [Col. 1537B]] I shall not be for you what you seek.” [Col. 1537A] And thus he departed from Milan. [Note: [Col. 1537B] That the Milanese citizens did not acquiesce in the abbot’s answer just mentioned, and that St Bernard was therefore compelled secretly to escape from the city, is suggested by what an anonymous author reports from the mouth of venerable Ramald, St Bernard’s companion and an eyewitness, in Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, under 1134, ch. 2: the Milanese “were so delighted in him that, though they had never seen him before, upon his entry into the city they unanimously seized him to make him archbishop rather than elected him; and when he refused, they were wholly prepared to use force unless he secretly escaped in flight.”]

But some of his disciples who remained went about the city and collected for themselves—and continue to collect—a great contribution of gold, silver, and many other things. [Note: [Col. 1537B] Perhaps for the construction of a monastery of their order, which indeed was founded two years later outside the city through the citizens’ lavish generosity, and was given the name Clairvaux; see Manrique in the same chapter, and [Col. 1537C] following.]

The regular clergy and deans of Milan, who had sworn fidelity to Pope Innocent, encouraged by this conversion of the Milanese [Note: [Col. 1537C] St Bernard’s letter 132, full of congratulation and addressed to the clergy of Milan, survives.], summoned Litifred of Novara, Guy of Ivrea, and other suffragans to Milan. In their council they elevated Robald, bishop of Alba, to be archbishop of Milan, [Note: [Col. 1537C] We have already shown, ch. 37, that Robald was elected our archbishop on 29 July 1135.] having obtained assurance [Note: [Col. 1537C] A. 1: *auctoritate*, “by authority.”] that he might retain, as is said, the bishopric of Alba. [Note: [Col. 1537C] St Bernard, in letter 131, gives us evidence of the translation of this bishop of Alba to the archbishopric of Milan: “If you wished it to be lawful for you to do what the sacred canons judge unlawful except in a great necessity—the translation, that is, of a bishop to an archbishopric—it has been granted.” On this ground I think both Mabillon, in his notes to the same letter, and Pagi under 1134, no. 18, must be refuted. They maintain that these words refer to the restoration of the archiepiscopal dignity which Pope Innocent II had removed from our city on account of the schism. But that St Bernard and Landulf are speaking of Robald, who was bishop of another city and was transferred to ours, will be clear to anyone weighing their words. Whether Robald also retained the bishopric of Alba together with that of Milan, as our author says he had security to retain it, I find in no writer.]

After his elevation, Milan moved its army against the Cremonese. [Note: [Col. 1537D] On leaving Milan, St Bernard went to Pavia and Cremona in order to impose an end, with peace at last confirmed, on the long war which had arisen between them and Milan. But the holy abbot himself declares that he returned to Milan without accomplishing the matter, bearing witness to the obstinacy of the Cremonese before Innocent II in these words: “The Cremonese have hardened themselves, and their prosperity destroys them; the Milanese despise them, and their confidence deceives them. Those who place their hope in chariots and horses frustrated me and made my labour vain.” It may be believed that the war which Milan undertook against the Cremonese after Robald’s elevation to the archiepiscopal see arose from this, though with an unhappy outcome, as will shortly be narrated. [Col. 1538B]] Of that army the Cremonese seized 130 knights [Col. 1538A] wandering by night.

But Anselm of Pusterla, when he heard and clearly understood the capture of these knights, [Note: [Col. 1538B] A. 2: *probi* (“upright men”); *probe* (“clearly”) is better. The other manuscript has no reading.] received no consolation at Robald’s elevation [Note: [Col. 1538B] Which had been carried out by the Milanese after Anselm’s rejection and deposition, and confirmed by Innocent II.], nor did he follow the counsel of Albert of Landriano and his friends. Instead, trusting his Hugh Naso, he wished to discover how he might proceed with Pope Anacletus of the Romans. [Note: [Col. 1538B] Anselm himself, obstinate in that schism and therefore bound by anathema, regarded Anacletus as the true pontiff.] Yet, travelling to Rome with this chaplain of his, he was captured on the River Po near Ferrara by Gorius of Martinengo [Note: [Col. 1538C] In the Ambrosian manuscripts: Goizo. Oldoinus lists among the cardinals created by Innocent II a Goizo, cardinal-priest of the title of St Cecilia; he may be seen subscribing to several diplomas of Innocent II, Celestine II, and Lucius II in Ughelli. Perhaps our Anselm was captured by him and conveyed to Innocent.] and conveyed to Pope Innocent. That pope, in the month of August, sent the captive from Pisa to Rome. [Note: [Col. 1538C] Falco of Benevento, in his *Chronicle*, testifies that Innocent II remained at Pisa until March 1137. He writes that in that month, in the fifteenth indiction, Innocent left Pisa and came to Viterbo to confer with Lothair, whom he had summoned into Italy in the preceding year.]

There, as report has it, that Anselm ended his life in the same month in the hands of Peter Latro, [Note: [Col. 1538C] He seems to be the man whom Emperor Lothair mentions in his letter cited by D’Achery and Pagi under 1133, no. 7, and who is there numbered among the hostages whom the emperor himself testifies were freely delivered into his hands, together with the strongholds, on Innocent II’s side, when in that year he was negotiating at Rome with Anacletus’s supporters for the removal of the schism. [Col. 1538D]] who was Innocent’s procurator. [Note: [Col. 1538D] Nearly all historians and catalogues state that Anselm died on 14 August. There is more serious disagreement among writers concerning the year. Tristano Calco and Morigia, *History of Milan*, book II, ch. 2, say that Anselm died in 1133. Puricelli, Pagi, and the more recent catalogues of the archbishops of Milan assign the following year to his death. Papebroch, *Exegesis*, no. 120, conjectures 1135, because, as he says, it seems impossible that the many and great events narrated by Landulf could have been completed in the very year in which the Council of Pisa was held. But I, both from this very argument of Papebroch and from what I carefully examined in ch. 37, no. 7, believe that Anselm’s death should be placed later still—namely in 1136.

Moreover, nowhere do we learn more clearly than here how important this writing of Landulf is for elucidating Milanese history. So many fabrications about this Anselm occur everywhere in our annals that they must be corrected from this author lest they continue to mislead posterity. [Col. 1539A] Calco, under 1123, reports that Lothair was crowned emperor at Milan by Anselm; and Zucchi confidently asserts the same even of Monza, producing Otto of Freising as his witness, although that writer never narrated anything of the kind, nor did Anselm adhere to Lothair. He was wholly devoted to Conrad and for that reason was excluded both from sacred office and from the see of Milan itself.

More absurd is the account given by Ripamonti, book I of *Ecclesiastical History of Milan*, part II: namely, that Anselm went to Rome to seek absolution from the pontiff and there spent the rest of his life, as though in a second homeland, in high dignity, continually attending Pope Innocent, who treated him generously and as a friend. Innocent was not then at Rome, however, nor did Anselm, committed to prison, survive long in that city; he died in that very August in which he had been sent from Pisa to Rome.

What then of Morigia in the cited place, Galesinius in the synodal table, and the catalogue entitled *Successors of St Barnabas*, who testify that St Bernard was frequently received as a guest by Anselm, and that, in regard for him, the monastery of Clairvaux was built and endowed by Anselm Archinto? [Col. 1539C] All are utterly shameful fictions, since Landulf establishes that this bishop was cast down from his see and an exile before the holy abbot first entered Milan upon his return from the Council of Pisa. Add that Calco affirms that this Anselm died at Milan—than which nothing is more remote from the truth. To omit foreign authors: Angelo Manrique, in *Cistercian Annals* under 1134, ch. 2, no. 7, writes, among other false things narrated of our Anselm throughout that chapter, that, just as he was an accomplice in the schism, so he was a leader of penitence for the Milanese and a persuader of union and due obedience; indeed, that they obtained his restoration to the see. How this can be reconciled with the history of our author, writing of a matter present to him, I do not see at all. And Claudius Robertus writes, in part II of *Gallia Christiana*, that he was buried in the monastery of Clairvaux founded by himself; but older catalogues teach that he was buried at Rome in the church of St John Lateran. [Col. 1539D] From this Pagi concludes, under 1134, no. 12, that Anselm repented of his obstinacy and fell asleep, released from anathema, in the Catholic faith and unity.]

## CHAPTER XLIII. Robald swears fidelity to Pope Innocent, joins Emperor Lothair, and destroys the fortresses of the Cremonese.

[Col. 1539A]

After these things had occurred, up to the capture of Anselm of Pusterla, the standards and battle-lines of the Milanese were captured or put to flight by the Pavians like the gentlest flocks of sheep. [Note: [Col. 1539D] CH. XLIII.—We have seen above that St Bernard went to Pavia immediately after leaving Milan in 1134, in order to establish peace there, as in the other cities of Lombardy. That the holy abbot obtained this in Pavia may be inferred from St Bernard’s letter 314 in the new edition, in which he complains before Innocent II only of the hardness of the Cremonese. Since, then, Landulf tells us that war was renewed against the Pavians after Anselm’s capture—that is, in 1135—we must say that, when new mutual animosities arose, the old hostilities revived and fighting was resumed; but history is wholly silent about these events.]

As these disasters pressed upon Milan, and Anselm had died, as stated above, Robald, archbishop of that city, [Col. 1540A] swore an oath to Pope Innocent at Pisa. [Note: [Col. 1540A] Since our author says that, after Anselm’s death, Robald went to Pisa to make his oath of fidelity before Innocent, it is clear that this occurred only after August 1136.] By swearing, he turned the liberty of the Church of Milan into its opposite. [Note: [Col. 1540B] What this liberty was, which the Milanese believed had been violated, we have already noted from Pagi in ch. 41. Meanwhile, it is worth adding the conjecture which Puricelli set forth on this passage in *Monumenta Basilicae Ambrosianae*, no. 376: Robald did indeed swear fidelity to the supreme pontiff, but did not wish the honour of the Church of Milan to be diminished. By ancient custom, that Church claimed as its particular distinction that our archbishop should receive the archiepiscopal pallium not in person from the pontiff’s hand, but in absence through envoys. Puricelli thinks that Robald remained constant in this respect, mindful of the counsel which, as we saw in ch. 38, he had given at Rome to his predecessor Anselm. St Bernard certainly testifies, in letter 131 to the Milanese, that the pallium was sent to our Archbishop Robald at the request of the Church of Milan. Among the gifts of apostolic kindness which Innocent had granted this illustrious city, he records: “In this final matter, what reasonable petition of a daughter has endured, I do not say refusal, but even delay, with her loving mother? Behold, to complete the matter, the pallium is at hand—the fullness of honour.” [Col. 1540C]]

With this misfortune added—[Note: [Col. 1540C] Namely, the loss of liberty, as the Milanese believed, because of the oath made by Robald.]—Emperor Lothair came into Lombardy with princes of every rank, [Note: [Col. 1540C] That is, both ecclesiastical and lay princes, several of whom are named in Lothair’s diploma for the Church of Monza, mentioned below.] [Note: [Col. 1540C] The Hildesheim chronicler, cited by Pagi under this year, no. 1, teaches that this expedition of the emperor into Italy occurred about the Assumption of St Mary in 1136. But we learn both from this history of Landulf and from a diploma reported by Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, new edition, vol. V, in the epistle concerning Verona, col. 1013, that Lothair came to Lombardy later. It was issued at Procelum near Miriticum—read “near the Mincio,” as Ughelli himself calls it in col. 777—on the seventh day before the Kalends of October. I therefore think Pagi must be corrected, where under this same year, no. 5, he states that Lothair was already in Lombardy in August. He relies on the aforesaid diploma of Lothair to the canons of Monza, issued at the castle of St Bassianus, but that document lacks month and day. [Col. 1540D]]

In the emperor’s camp this man of Milan—that is, Archbishop Robald—[Note: [Col. 1540D] Understand Archbishop Robald.] moved about with his suffragans at the emperor’s command; and, while doing so, he excommunicated the Cremonese because they had not restored to the emperor the Milanese, who were enduring Cremonese chains and captivity. [Note: [Col. 1540D] Sigonius, under 1136, relates: “As soon as Lothair came into Italy, the anxious Italians came to him and immediately referred to his judgment the disputes which they had intended to settle by armed contest.” Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, ch. 19, reports what concerns the Cremonese thus: “Lothair advanced as far as the Po and took Caristallium (Guardastallum). There he encountered the Milanese and Cremonese, who had long been at war with one another; when the case of each city had been examined, the Cremonese were judged enemies by the princes of Italy and departed under proscription.” To this decree of Lothair, Robald added the sentence of his archiepiscopal authority, confirmed by anathema, so that the Cremonese were also barred from the sacred rites.]

Therefore the Milanese army, strengthened by the emperor’s presence and by the bond of excommunication, destroyed Soncino, [Note: [Col. 1541C] This place was made considerably famous when, in 1259, that monster of tyranny and terror of neighbouring cities, Ezzelino—or Azzolino, as Calco calls him—died and was buried there.] St Bassianus, and many other fortresses of the Cremonese. [Note: [Col. 1541C] From the territory of Mantua, where Lothair had issued the diploma mentioned above near the Mincio, he went to the castle of St Bassianus. There he issued another diploma in favour of the clergy of the church of St John the Baptist at Monza, published by Bartholomew Zucchi in his *History of the Iron Crown*: “given in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1136, and enacted at the castle of St Bassianus.” Since Landulf says that the Milanese destroyed this fortress when strengthened by the emperor’s presence, we may believe that this happened in October: both from the diploma mentioned above, issued near the Mincio on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, which shows that Lothair had not yet arrived there at that time; and from the feudal laws issued at Roncaglia on 7 November, which clearly prove that Lothair had already departed thence during that month.]

When these had been destroyed, the multitude of the Milanese returned to the city. But the archbishop and a distinguished portion of the Milanese knighthood encamped with the emperor at Roncaglia, [Note: [Col. 1541D] This place in Cisalpine Gaul, near the city of Piacenza, is well known to all because of the many imperial assemblies held there.] on the Po. There for many days and weeks the emperor held a court in the exercise of authority [Note: [Col. 1541D] A. 1: *potestaturae*, “of authority.”] and issued laws, [Note: [Col. 1541D] Especially the feudal laws issued on 7 November of that same year, 1136, as we have said; they were incorporated into the new body of civil law.] [Col. 1541A–B]

## CHAPTER XLIV. Through the emperor, the historian’s case is vainly entrusted to the consuls of Milan.

Then I too was present there for three days. In the presence of my lord King Conrad, [Note: [Col. 1541D] CH. XLIV.—As we have said, Conrad had long before renounced the Italian kingdom, and Lothair had made him commander of his army. But Landulf, carried away by the greatest affection for him—as shown by the words in ch. 39 of this history, “Whatever was done in that year for my lord king, I love”—continued to call and honour him “king,” from the old designation, even after he had been stripped of royal dignity.] I obtained permission to make lament before the emperor, through his interpreter Sigifred, called his son. [Note: [Col. 1541D] No histories known to me mention a son of Conrad or Lothair named Sigifred; writers assign to the former only Henry and Frederick, and to the latter only Lothair. I therefore suppose that this Sigifred was an honourably placed young man who acted as interpreter of the German language for our author and is described as “son” in that sense. But if anyone insists that he must be considered truly a son of Conrad or of Lothair, that information will be owed to Landulf alone. [Col. 1542B–C]]

As princes of every rank sat around and heard my voice under the emperor’s tent, I made my complaint against Andrew Sugaliola. [Note: [Col. 1542C] In ch. 39 he had already complained that he had been despoiled by Andrew of every ecclesiastical benefice. Andrew had been intruded into the church of St Paul, to which Landulf had a right, after the priest Nazarius Muricula had first occupied it and was subsequently promoted to the dignity of primicerius.] The archbishop of Turin [Note: [Col. 1542C] An error of a copyist which has entered all the manuscripts. The Church of Turin was not honoured with archiepiscopal rank until 1515 by Leo X. Arbert was then bishop; he was elected in 1128 and is carried down to 1147 by Ughelli in the bishops of Turin, no. 31.] understood the complaint with the other archbishops, bishops, and learned men. Like a prudent and wise man, he questioned me; and after my answer, he explained my case to the lord emperor in words barbarous to me [Note: [Col. 1542C] Easily German, which seemed barbarous to Landulf, who did not know that idiom.]. The lord emperor, as the bishops assured me, commanded the consuls of Milan, in accordance with my petition, to deal justly and paternally with my cause in Milan.

But it is no wonder [Note: [Col. 1542C] Read *nil mirum*, “no wonder,” as we have noted elsewhere.] if the body of consuls did not obey this command, because Arnald of Raude, one of those consuls, whispered in their ears that he had received the investiture concerning my benefice. [Note: [Col. 1542C] Namely, Andrew Sugaliola, already mentioned.] My mind knows this in no way, nor could it have been lawful, because Arnald, the grandfather of this Arnald, killed Herlembald, the protector of the priest Liprand. [Note: [Col. 1542C] Herlembald, standard-bearer of the Apostolic See against the Nicolaitans, had fallen under many sword-thrusts in a popular uprising raised against him in 1075, as I noted above. From our Landulf we learn that the chief author of this most wicked murder was the elder Arnald of Raude. Galvano Fiamma likewise reported this in his *Greater Chronicle*, ch. 250, as drawn from the *Calendar Chronicle*, though calling him Ariald rather than Arnald. [Col. 1542D]] He violently brought that very author of my cause to the cutting off of his nose and ears, and to chains and prisons. [Note: [Col. 1542D] Something concerning these outrages and injuries inflicted upon Liprand because he vigorously defended the chastity of priests may be read in the notes to ch. 1, and at length in Puricelli, cited above.]

Arderic also, the uncle of this young Arnald, compelled the same priest to undergo the fire through which he passed. [Note: [Col. 1542D] See ch. 10.] Hugh, another uncle of the same Arnald, protects Andrew, against whom I rightly complain, not reasonably but furiously. And this Arnald, a man of extraordinary cunning, though he has no standing in my case, strives to hinder me and my cause by this allegation of investiture. Therefore I awaited the emperor’s presence. [Note: [Col. 1542D] Puricelli, no. 382, readily admitted that Lothair came to this city and was crowned with the Italian crown first there by Robald and afterwards at Monza, rebuking only Zucchi and others who assert this because they make Anselm the author of that solemn inauguration. Yet, if I have any judgment, I would not even believe that Lothair was received at Milan. Ancient writers are silent about this arrival in our city, and the sequence of the journey described thus far and still to be described forbids belief in it. From Roncaglia he proceeded to Lardiracum near Pavia on 14 November, as we shall say in the next chapter; thence on the 17th of the same month he went to Abbiategrasso, and immediately afterwards to Vercelli and Turin, as we have the testimony of the Saxon annalist and Otto of Freising.

Nevertheless, Lothair must have stayed there briefly, since soon after he visited Piacenza, Parma, and Reggio, where he spent December, as the cited Saxon and Sigonius note. A diploma of his issued at Reggio on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January survives in Ughelli, vol. II, col. 288, new edition. In January of the following year, 1137, he went to Ravenna for winter quarters; from there he travelled through Campania and Apulia, after many journeys through the Flaminian Way, Picenum, Umbria, and other regions, which may be read in Sigonius and others. Returning from there to Germany, he died near Trent in a most wretched hut, leaving, as Otto of Freising says, a miserable reminder of the human condition, on the day before the Nones of December 1137.

Thus there can be no place in this history of Lothair’s expedition for his reception of the Italian crown at Monza or Milan. What Sigonius writes—that Lothair, on his return, came to Milan and, in the war against the Cremonese begun in November, destroyed Soncino, Bassiano, and many other fortresses under their jurisdiction—suffers from an anachronism. These things occurred in the preceding year, 1136, before that emperor set out for Roncaglia and issued laws there, as our Landulf establishes. Correct from him likewise Campo and Cavitelli, who tell similar stories.

Further, it would be very remarkable if Landulf, carrying his history down to 1137 and meeting the emperor everywhere to plead his case, had said not a word of his arrival in this city and left no commemorative word in his writings about his having received the royal crown at Milan and Monza. Elsewhere Landulf did not merely report such royal inaugurations performed in both places, but described them even in detail. [Col. 1543A–D] This silence seemed so significant to Pagi that under 1134, no. 19, he declares the entire coronation fictitious. Yet let this be said without imputing envy to me, as though I wished to deprive our city and the town of Monza of this glory. I pursue the truth, and would most gladly yield if stronger arguments emerge to vindicate this new honour for my native city and for Monza.]

## CHAPTER XLV. Lothair, having routed the Pavians, comes to Milan.

[Note: [Col. 1543D] CH. XLV.—This title was wrongly appended by some copyist, as is shown both by Landulf, who says nothing whatever about Milan, and by the final note to the preceding chapter.]

[Col. 1543A]

Lothair, thereafter emperor, on the fourth day after my complaint, which was the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 1543D] Landulf had gone to Roncaglia at the time when Emperor Lothair was there promulgating the laws related above. Since these were issued on 7 November 1136, as is recorded in the legal collection in the note on them, the following Sabbath fell on the fourteenth of the same month [Col. 1544A]; consequently, Lothair must be believed to have set out toward Pavia on that day [Col. 1544B]], after my complaint, encamped near Pavia at a place called Lardirago [Note: [Col. 1544B] A place in the territory of Pavia, opposite which now stands, a few miles away, the Certosa of Pavia, a marvel of art and magnificence built by Gian Galeazzo, first duke of Milan.], situated on the river Olona [Note: [Col. 1544B] Gaudentius Merula, *On the Antiquities of Cisalpine Gaul*, book I, chapter 7, and Bonaventura Castiglione, *On the Antiquities of Insubrian Gaul*, enumerate several rivers named Orona or Olona. The one mentioned here is described by Bernardo Sacco in his *History of Pavia* as follows: “The Olona, flowing down from the hills and valleys of Milan toward Circiate and Castaneate, first serves the Milanese themselves; having supplied them with drinking water, it winds in great circuits around the territory of Pavia, waters it with its streams, and finally enters the Po between the village of Spessa and San Zeno, ten Roman miles from the city of Pavia.”]. When the emperor had spent the night there and had passed, as it were, half of Sunday [Note: [Col. 1544B] That is, 15 November.], his soldiery rushed against the Pavians, who came out armed [Note: [Col. 1544C] Above, in chapter 43, we saw that the Pavians were hostile to the Milanese in a fierce war. Perhaps, elated by that victory and insulting Lothair, who favored the Milanese, they had refused to submit to imperial authority. Otto of Freising, book VII, chapter 19, certainly testifies that the emperor received them into favor only upon payment of an agreed sum. Yet it exceeds belief that the already cited Saxon annalist writes that it amounted to 20,000 talents, unless perhaps *Tertiolorum* should be read, a coin in use among the Pavians.].

In that battle the very valiant troop of Prince Conrad drove back and captured very many Pavians; nor did it withdraw from battle until it had trampled the Pavians almost to the walls of their city and approached them. Then the Pavians [Col. 1544A], greatly terrified and fearing the hostile army of Milanese gathering for the emperor’s triumph, at the first dawn of the second day of the week [Note: [Col. 1544C] Namely, 16 November.], with the greatest devotion [Note: [Col. 1544C] In the aforementioned Saxon [annalist], col. 673, we read that bodies of clergy and monks, taking crosses and relics of saints, went out from the city and advanced toward the emperor in mournful voice and dress, to implore his clemency.], restored to the emperor all the Milanese whom they held captive [Note: [Col. 1544C] Namely, those whom Landulf said in chapter 43 had been captured by the Pavians like the mildest flocks of sheep.]. Moved by the greatest compassion, the emperor released the Pavians from his custody that same day and let them go free; and on the following day [Note: [Col. 1544D] Namely, 17 November.] he moved his camp and came to the place called Abbiategrasso [Note: [Col. 1544D] A town still well known today, fourteen miles from Milan toward Vigevano, where the great navigable channel drawn from the Ticino flows down toward our city. It was formerly a very strongly fortified castle. Galeazzo Capella, book III of *The Milanese War*, recounts the vigorous deeds performed there by the Milanese against the French for the restoration of Francesco Sforza, their last duke. Felice Osio discusses this town at greater length in his commentary on Otto Morena, no. 275 and following.]; and the entire multitude of Milanese, together with their soldiers freed from Pavia’s captivity, returned to Milan.

Thereafter the emperor crossed the Ticino and the Po [Note: [Col. 1544D] Here Landulf includes the journeys which we described above in chapter 44, no. 11: namely, to the city of Turin and afterwards to Reggio. Calco relates that Lothair stayed in the district of Novara, especially in the village of Momo, in his brief account under the year 1138, where he frees himself from narrating the emperor’s entire Italian expedition.] to his own advantage [Note: [Col. 1544D] That Lothair’s journeys were successfully accomplished, with no enemy raising a hand against him, is testified by the Abbot of Ursperg in his *Life of Lothair*, saying: “Proceeding as far as Turin, he subdued without the sword all of nearer Italy”—not “freer Italy,” as perhaps through a printer’s error entered Struve’s *German History*, dissertation 16, § 26 [Col. 1545B].].

## Chapter XLVI. The Milanese capture the bishop of Cremona, who escapes from chains after his keeper is poisoned

[Col. 1545A]

But Pope Innocent released the Cremonese from the excommunication imposed by Archbishop Robald [Note: [Col. 1545B] Chapter XLVI.—Pagi, under the year 1136, no. 7, maintains that Pope Innocent disapproved the severe punishment inflicted by Robald, archbishop of Milan, upon the Cremonese [Col. 1545C], and, rejecting it, absolved them from the anathema imposed. But I cannot so readily agree with him that this happened in that year, since Landulf relates that the Cremonese were absolved by Innocent after Lothair had crossed the Ticino and the Po to his own advantage toward the end of that same year. These events therefore seem to belong to the following year, when Lothair, himself angered with the Cremonese, had already departed from these regions.]. Nevertheless, the Milanese army spared neither the Cremonese nor their bishop [Note: [Col. 1545C] Oberto, or Uberto, as Landulf calls him below, then held the episcopal see of Cremona and survived until 1169, according to Ughelli, *Bishops of this City*, no. 46.], because, after the absolution [Note: [Col. 1545C] Namely, that of Innocent II.], it seized their castle of Genivolta [Note: [Col. 1545C] This celebrated castle, not far from Romanengo and Soncino, figures prominently in the history of Cremona, where several battles were fought. Under the year 1215, Campo relates that, after a battle had gone badly for the Cremonese, Romanengo and Genivolta were captured, and the Carroccio itself—whose loss in adverse circumstances was then regarded as a particularly grave damage and disgrace—was taken away by the Milanese. He reports another very fierce battle with them at Genivolta in 1239, but with equal slaughter and neither side victorious.], and others, and dragged their bishop from that very castle—armed, exhorting his men to battle, and advancing to commit homicide [Note: [Col. 1545D] A. 2: *perficientem*, “carrying out.”]; he held him in custody for several months [Note: [Col. 1545D] How long the bishop of Cremona remained in the Milanese chains is entirely unknown, since I have found no word in histories concerning this notable exploit or the rich booty brought home by our people from Cremonese territory. Sigonius does indeed relate that the Cremonese, enraged because they had been unable to avenge the injuries of Crema by Lothair’s help, besieged Cremona in 1139 with formidable arms and threats; but when the Milanese swiftly arrived, they were driven from the siege and defeated, many of them captured and sent to prisons in Milan. Yet since he reports that this battle took place at Rivolta, not a little distant from Genivolta, it must be believed that it was a different war from the present one. Meanwhile it may be observed [Col. 1546B] that Landulf’s *History* certainly extends at least to the year 1137. For since he relates that Bishop Uberto was detained for several months and finally escaped by flight and was restored unharmed to Cremona, it is clear, from the matters explained above, that these events cannot at all be compressed into the year 1136.], until Herlembald of Bresorio, the keeper of that prison, having been poisoned, as is said, suddenly fell dead.

And on the very night on which that keeper suddenly died, the bishop escaped from the very house in which he was confined [Col. 1545B], and, set free, arrived at Pavia and then at Cremona. Perhaps this bishop recalls the bitterness [Note: [Col. 1546B] Landulf explains below [Col. 1546C] the cause of this bitterness: namely, the oath of fidelity to the Church of Milan and to Archbishop Jordan, which he was compelled to take at the same time when he was consecrated at Milan. This seemed to hinder the liberty claimed by the cities of Lombardy, as is well known.] with which he was made to drink at Milan on the day of his ordination [Note: [Col. 1546C] Ughelli asserts that Uberto was installed in the see of Cremona by Jordan, archbishop of Milan, in 1117; but I do not see on what basis he assigns this year to his election, since he produces nothing certain concerning the time when Walter, his immediate predecessor, died, or when Hugh of Noceto was intruded by Emperor Henry. Our Landulf makes it certain that this Uberto had been elected and consecrated before October 1120, when Jordan died. In this serious chronological error Ludovico Cavitelli erred in his *Annals of Cremona*: confusing everything, he states that Walter died in 1129, that Hugh was substituted in the following year, and that after Hugh died not long afterward, Uberto succeeded in the same year, 1130. How absurd these statements are is demonstrated by the authority of this history.], though, as some think, not rightly.

For if Archbishop Jordan and his Church removed Hugh of Noceto [Col. 1546A] [Note: [Col. 1546D] Hugh is mentioned nowhere except in our Landulf. What Ughelli, in his work on the bishops of Cremona, and Bordoni, in the *Treasury of the Church of Parma*, have reported was drawn from him.]—a noble man and, as it were, archdeacon of the Church of Parma—from the bishopric of Cremona, in which the Cremonese, by their election, and King Henry, by his investiture, approval, and confirmation, had placed him, and whom they had received reverently and maintained for many years, long both within and without [the city]—what wonder is it if the people of Milan compelled this excellent man Uberto to swear fidelity to the Church of Milan and Archbishop Jordan, when [Note: [Col. 1546D] A. 2: *qui*, “who.”] he consecrated Uberto himself bishop?

But if anyone perhaps says: “The removal of Hugh was just [Note: [Col. 1546D] For very many decrees of supreme pontiffs and councils had inveighed against lay investitures, which Emperors Henry IV and V had claimed for themselves, and the emperors themselves had been struck with anathema.], but the compulsion of Uberto was unjust,” let him not say by the authority of which mortal person Cremona and its Church ought principally to be governed [Note: [Col. 1546D] Landulf here alludes to the rights of a metropolitan see, which the Milanese perhaps claimed, so that the other neighboring cities and churches might be subject to their dominion.]. If he does not [Note: [Col. 1546D] A. 2: *si vero*, “but if.”] say, “Both were evil and unjust,” then let God of hosts arise [Col. 1546B], to correct Milan and Cremona, and to govern and protect by right me, an acolyte oppressed and despoiled, as may be read in this my work containing upright and wicked persons alike.

Thanks be to God. Amen. Amen.

[Col. 1545] Here ends the book of histories by Landulf of San Paolo, *On the Deeds of Milan*, from the year of Christ 1094 to the year of Christ 1133, in the time of Archbishop Robald, who died in the year of Christ 1142, on the second day before the Kalends of January, and lies in the Winter Church. He was succeeded by Ubertus de Pirovano; while he held office, Milan was utterly destroyed by Frederick [Note: [Col. 1546D] What is read here is absent from the other manuscript in the Ambrosian Library. That it was added by some unskilled person is clear from what has been set forth thus far, since Landulf began his history from the year 1097 and carried it at least to the year 1137. On Robald’s death, see what I discussed in chapter 37, no. 7.].

### Landulf the Younger

**History of Milan.** 1429  
Preface by Ludovico Antonio Muratori. 1429  
Another preface by Antonio Sassi. 1431  
Chronological sequence of events relevant to this history. 1433  

Chapter I.—Anselm of Buis is elected archbishop of Milan. 1437  
Chapter II.—Anselm crosses the sea against the Saracens and dies at Constantinople. 1445  
Chapter III.—Before crossing the sea, Anselm consecrates Grossolano bishop of Savona and makes him his vicar in Milan. 1447  
Chapter IV.—Priest Liprand rebukes Grossolano for his mean clothing and, upon hearing of Anselm’s death, presses for Grossolano’s election. 1450  
Chapter V.—Grossolano is elected archbishop, and a pallium is sent to him by the Roman pontiff. 1452  
Chapter VI.—Grossolano wished to take from Priest Liprand his bull of exemption when he confessed that he had favored the opposition. 1454  
Chapter VII.—Liprand received the sick Heribert into his house; consequently, by Grossolano’s order, he abstained from celebrating [Mass]. 1457  
Chapter VIII.—Liprand founded the church of the Holy Trinity, with exemption granted by Urban II. 1458  
Chapter IX.—Liprand preaches that Grossolano is a simoniac and that he will prove it by the ordeal of fire. 1459  
Chapter X.—Priest Liprand passes through fire unharmed. 1462  
Chapter XI.—At a synod before Pope Paschal, Liprand accuses the present Grossolano of simony and demonstrates the ordeal by fire. 1466  
Chapter XII.—When Grossolano swore before the pope that he had not compelled Liprand to undergo the fire, Grossolano was restored, but was not received by the citizens. 1469  
Chapter XIII.—After disturbance arose in the Church of Milan [Col. 1552] over Grossolano, Olric, the *vicedominus*, and Anselm of Pusterla transferred themselves to Paris for study. 1470  
Chapter XIV.—The historian, being present, brings Priest Liprand back to Milan from Valtellina. 1472  
Chapter XV.—The historian Landulf separates himself from Priest Liprand. 1473  
Chapter XVI.—While Grossolano is in exile, the Milanese begin war with the people of Lodi. 1474  
Chapter XVII.—Olric and Anselm are recalled from study and promoted to orders. 1475  
Chapter XVIII.—Emperor Henry captures Pope Paschal together with the curia and, on the following day, after peace is made, is solemnly crowned by him. 1478  
Chapter XIX.—Jordan of Clivio, recalled from study, is consecrated to the priesthood. 1482  
Chapter XX.—Certain priests are chosen to judge whether the absent Grossolano can worthily remain archbishop. 1483  
Chapter XXI.—Jordan of Clivio is elected and consecrated archbishop. 1484  
Chapter XXII.—On the feast of *Agios*, held at Saint Mary’s by the Vercellina Gate on 9 May. 1487  
Chapter XXIII.—Liprand warns the historian Landulf to refrain from communion with Jordan. 1490  
Chapter XXIV.—Priest Liprand dies in the monastery of Pontida. 1490  
Chapter XXV.—On receiving the papal pallium, Jordan drives out clergy and removes the historian from the church of Saint Peter. 1492  
Chapter XXVI.—A battle takes place between the Grossolanists and the Jordanists, their bishops themselves addressing their respective followers. 1494  
Chapter XXVII.—Money having been given to Grossolano and Anselm of Pusterla, Grossolano goes to Piacenza. 1495  
Chapter XXVIII.—On the character and drunkenness of Priest Nazarius Muricula. 1496  
Chapter XXIX.—Pope Paschal confirms Jordan and deposes Grossolano, who dies at Rome a year later. 1499  
Chapter XXX.—Jordan thanks the pope, consecrates the bishop of Brescia, and promises to do justice to the historian. 1502  
Chapter XXXI.—Jordan excommunicates Emperor Henry at Milan and holds a provincial council, from which he expels the complaining historian. 1503  
Chapter XXXII.—After Paschal’s death, the emperor causes Burdinus to be elected antipope, naming him Gregory. 1506  
Chapter XXXIII.—Pope Gelasius, consecrated at Gaeta, flees to Genoa and Pisa and finally to France, where he dies. 1510  
Chapter XXXIV.—War arises between the Milanese and the people of Como, in which the city of Como is destroyed. 1511  
Chapter XXXV.—The historian complains in vain of Jordan before Pope Callixtus at Tortona and Piacenza. 1513  
Chapter XXXVI.—After Jordan’s death, Olric is elected archbishop; he sits at Pope Callixtus’s right hand, despite the Ravennate’s opposition. 1516  
Chapter XXXVII.—The historian learns that the emperor, to whom he was going, has died. Olric dies. Anselm is elected archbishop. 1518  
Chapter XXXVIII.—With the Milanese consenting, Anselm refuses to receive the pallium from the Roman pontiff, lest the dignity of the archbishopric be diminished. 1522  
Chapter XXXIX.—Archbishop Anselm crowns Emperor Conrad, whom Pope Honorius rejects; consequently Anselm is excommunicated by the pope’s order. 1525  
Chapter XL.—Archbishop Anselm adheres to Anacletus, the antipope, and receives the pallium from him. 1528  
Chapter XLI.—The clergy of Milan expel Anselm from the archbishopric. Pope Innocent confirms this and sends Blessed Bernard to Milan. 1530  
Chapter XLII.—Blessed Bernard makes the Milanese obey the Church and Emperor Lothair. Robald is elected archbishop. Anselm, captured on the Po, dies at Rome. 1535  
Chapter XLIII.—Robald swears fidelity to Pope Innocent, joins Emperor Lothair, and destroys the castles of the Cremonese. 1539  
Chapter XLIV.—Through the emperor, the historian’s case is unsuccessfully referred to the consuls of Milan. 1541  
Chapter XLV.—After defeating the Pavians, Lothair comes to Milan. 1543  
Chapter XLVI.—The Milanese capture the bishop of Cremona, who escapes from chains after his keeper is poisoned. 1545  

[Col. 1551] **End of the One Hundred and Seventy-Third Volume.**
